The *Mishnah* then addresses a different type of problem — not a sequencing error but an interruption. If one was in the middle of sprinkling the blood inside the *kodesh kodashim* and the blood spilled — performing *achat*, *achat ve'achat*, *achat ve'shtayim*, and then losing the blood — the remedy is to bring new blood. "Bringing new blood" does not mean drawing from a stored supply; it means slaughtering another ox entirely. The *Mishnah* specifies: *yavi gam acher — v'yachzor bitchila mifnim*. Bring other blood and restart from the beginning of that *avodah*.

This naturally raises a further question: if a new ox must be slaughtered, does that not also require slaughtering a new *se'ir*, since the original sequence of *shechitat hapar* and *shechitat hase'ir* was tied together? The *Mishnah* does not address this directly; its focus is narrowly on where one picks up after an interruption within a single component of the service.

### Three Components

The *Mishnah* then articulates a fundamental conceptual principle: *shekulam kapara bifnei atzman* — each of the three components is an independent *kapara* in its own right. Therefore, if blood spills during the *heichal* service, one goes back to the beginning of the *heichal* service — but not to the *kodesh kodashim*. What was completed there is done; it has been "set aside" and need not be repeated. Similarly, if blood spills during the *mizbeach* service, one repeats only the *mizbeach* component, without returning to the *kodesh kodashim* or the *parochet*. This gives us not only a practical rule but a conceptual framework: the *kodesh kodashim*, the *parochet*, and the *mizbeach* are three structurally independent units of *kapara*.

### Resume Mid-Service View

*Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Shimon* go further: if blood spills mid-service and new blood is obtained, one does not even need to restart the interrupted component from its beginning — one may resume precisely where one stopped. If one had completed *achat ve'shalosh*, one brings new blood and continues from *achat ve'arba*. Their *chiddush* is that the continuity of the *avodah* is not broken by the change of animal; the new blood steps in and continues the same act.

### Ketoret Question

This framework, however, generates a deep difficulty. The *Mishnah* addresses the scenario of spilling blood during the inner service and starting again with a new ox. But if one is starting again with a new ox and going back to the beginning of the *kodesh kodashim* service, one might ask: what about the *ketoret*, which was performed earlier in the sequence? The *ketoret* is part of the ordered service, listed among the steps that precede the inner blood sprinklings. And what if one forgot the *ketoret* entirely — skipping over it and proceeding directly to the blood service?

In that case, everything performed after the missing *ketoret* is by definition *hikdim* — done before the *ketoret* was done. One would have to go back and perform the *ketoret*, and then redo everything that had been rendered out of order. Similarly, if one must now slaughter a new ox and return to step one inside, the question of why one does not also need to re-perform the *ketoret* — which was done earlier in the sequence and is connected to all of this — is not immediately resolved by the *Mishnah* and will be taken up by the *Gemara*.

---

## Order Disputes Debate

### Tanu Rabanan Intro

A *baraita* opens: *kol ma'asei Yom HaKippurim amurim al haseder* — the entirety of the *Yom Kippur* service which has been given an order. The word *amurim* — "stated" — is itself worth noting: it could refer to the order as stated by the Rabbis in the *Mishnah*, or more directly to the order as stated in the *pesukim* themselves, which the *Mishnah* closely follows. In either reading, the point is the same: there is a prescribed sequence, and deviating from it has consequences. *Im hikdim ma'aseh lachaveiro lo asa klum.*

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

*Rabbi Yehuda* asks: when is this true — when does performing something out of order render that act invalid? His answer: *bidvarim hana'asim bevigdei lavan mifnim* — only things done in the white garments inside. Here, *mifnim* does not mean the *heichal* in general; it means specifically the *kodesh kodashim*. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, the binding force of *seder* — such that a deviation renders the act null — applies only to the actions performed in the white garments while inside the *kodesh kodashim*: the *ketoret*, the *dam hapar* sprinklings, and the *dam hase'ir* sprinklings. Outside of that — including the service at the *parochet* and the *mizbeach*, performed in the white garments but in the *heichal* rather than the *kodesh kodashim* — if one performed an act out of order, *ma she'asa asuy*: what was done is done and remains valid *bedi'eved*.

### Rabbi Nechemiah Position

*Rabbi Nechemiah* disagrees. He holds: *bameh devarim amurim — bidvarim hana'asim bevigdei lavan*. The binding *seder* applies to everything done in the white garments, *bein mifnim bein mibachutz* — whether inside the *kodesh kodashim* or in the *heichal*. The *parochet* service and the *mizbeach* service are equally subject to *seder*; going out of order in either location renders the act invalid.

Where does *Rabbi Nechemiah* draw the line? At the golden garments. *Aval devarim hana'asim bevigdei zahav mibachutz* — things performed while wearing the golden garments outside — such as the *tamid*, the *musaf*, and specifically the *ayil* brought by *Aharon* and the *ayil* brought for the people — if performed out of order, the act remains valid *bedi'eved*. The order requirement applies to what is special, and what is special is the white-garment service.

An interesting question arises about *Rabbi Nechemiah*'s position regarding the *se'ir la'azazel* and the *viduy* performed over it. That too is conducted in the white garments, and it takes place in the *azarah* — which, since *Rabbi Nechemiah* frames his rule as *bein mifnim bein mibachutz*, and since *mibachutz* in the context of *bigdei zahav* includes the *azarah*, it would appear that the *se'ir la'azazel* and its *viduy* are also subject to *seder* according to *Rabbi Nechemiah*. Everything performed in the white garments — whether in the *kodesh kodashim*, the *heichal*, or the *azarah* — requires the proper sequence, while the golden-garment service is excluded.

### Pesuk Derivation

Where do *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Nechemiah* derive their respective positions? The *pasuk* in question reads: *vezot lachem lechukat olam — achat bashanah*. "This shall be for you an eternal edict — once a year." The word *chok* (edict, statute) implies that things must be done exactly as prescribed, leaving no room for deviation. The phrase *achat bashanah* — once a year — signals something unique, something that happens only once annually. The question is: which aspects of the *Yom Kippur* service are being described as that uniquely annual *chok*?

### Rabbi Yochanan Analysis

*Rabbi Yochanan* observes that both *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Nechemiah* derive their positions from this single *pasuk* — *sheneihem mikra echad darshu*.

One might think that *Rabbi Yehuda*'s limitation to the *kodesh kodashim* follows from the word *achat* — once a year, the one place entered only once a year is the *kodesh kodashim*, and therefore that is what is uniquely *chok*. But the *Gemara* objects: the *pasuk* does not say "place" (*makom*), it says "once" (*achat*). Why would *achat* specifically indicate the *kodesh kodashim* and not everything done in the white garments, since the entire white-garment service is performed only on this one unique day?

The *Gemara* therefore reconstructs *Rabbi Yehuda*'s derivation differently. The *pasuk* contains two limiting words: the word *zot* ("this") and the word *achat*. *Zot* is a *mi'ut* — it restricts. *Achat* is also a *mi'ut*. Had we only the word *achat*, one might have concluded as *Rabbi Nechemiah* does — that the entire white-garment service is subject to *seder*. But the word *zot* constricts the category further, narrowing it down to an even smaller subset: specifically, things done inside, in the *kodesh kodashim* itself.

*Rabbi Nechemiah* agrees that there are two limiting words — *zot* and *achat* — but reads them differently. One word excludes the golden-garment service from the *chok* of *seder*; the other word excludes not the *heichal* service (which *Rabbi Nechemiah* maintains is subject to *seder*) but rather the *shirayin*, the pouring of the remnant blood at the base of the *mizbeach*. According to *Rabbi Nechemiah*, if the *shirayin* was performed out of order, it does not invalidate what came before or after, because *shirayin* is not an essential component of the *kapara*.

*Rabbi Yehuda* responds to this in a formulation that initially sounds tautological: *im me'akvei me'akvei ve'im lo me'akvei lo me'akvei* — if it is *me'akev* then it is *me'akev*, and if it is not *me'akev* then it is not *me'akev*. What this means is that *Rabbi Yehuda* refuses to treat the *shirayin* as a distinct category unto itself. If, as *Rabbi Nechemiah* maintains, the entire white-garment service is subject to *seder*, then *shirayin*, which is part of that service and is performed in the white garments, should be subject to *seder* as well. And if one wants to argue that *shirayin* is not subject to *seder* because it is not essential, then one should concede *Rabbi Yehuda*'s own position that the binding *seder* applies only to the truly interior, innermost service. There is no principled middle ground, in *Rabbi Yehuda*'s view, between his own position and *Rabbi Nechemiah*'s as *Rabbi Yehuda* understands it.

---

## Shirayin Status Debate

### Vichilah Emphasis

Having established the debate about the scope of *seder*, the *Gemara* turns to the broader question of the *shirayin*'s status in the *Yom Kippur* service. The *pasuk* reads: *vechila mekapper et hakodesh* — "and he completed atoning for the sanctuary." This phrase — the language of completion — becomes the focal point of a dispute about when exactly *kapara* is achieved.

### Akiva vs Yehuda

*Rabbi Akiva* and *Rabbi Yehuda* debate the emphasis of the phrase. *Rabbi Akiva* reads it as: *im kipper — kilah* — if one has performed the atonement, then one is done. The emphasis falls on *kipper*: once the essential acts of atonement are complete, the service is finished. *Rabbi Yehuda* inverts the reading: *im kilah — kipper* — only when one has fully completed everything, only then has the atonement been achieved. The emphasis here falls on *kilah*, completion, as the condition for *kapara*.

The practical formulation of *Rabbi Yehuda*'s view is: *sheim chissar achat min hamattanot lo asa velo klum* — if one omitted even one of the applications of blood, one has accomplished nothing. Nothing in the atonement takes effect until every element is performed.

### Shirayin Integral?

A parallel *sugya* elsewhere in the *Gemara* asks: what is the practical difference between the two readings? *Rabbi Yochanan* and *Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* debate this. One opinion holds that the difference is only hermeneutic — a matter of how one reads the syntax of the *pasuk*, with no practical halakhic consequence; both readings amount to the same thing. The other opinion holds that the practical difference is precisely this: *shirayin me'akvei ika beinayhu* — whether the *shirayin*, the pouring of the remnant blood, is *me'akev* the *kapara* on *Yom Kippur*.

For the rest of the year, the pouring of *shirayin* is generally not *me'akev* — if one omitted it, the *korban* remains valid and the *kapara* is achieved. But on *Yom Kippur*, the *Torah*'s language of *vechila* — "he completed" — may impose a higher standard. If the emphasis is on finishing everything, then even the *shirayin*, normally secondary, becomes integral to the *kapara* of *Yom Kippur*.

### Nechemiah Contradiction

This brings us to the tension in *Rabbi Nechemiah*'s position. *Rabbi Nechemiah* holds, as described above, that the *seder* of the entire white-garment service is *me'akev* — with the one exception that the *shirayin* may be performed out of order without consequence. His reasoning would presumably be that *shirayin* is not essential to the *kapara*, and therefore the *seder* requirement does not apply to it.

But *Rabbi Yochanan* elsewhere states explicitly — *tana Rabbi Nechemiah kedivrei haomer shirayin me'akvei* — that *Rabbi Nechemiah* holds that *shirayin* is indeed *me'akev*. If that is so, how can *Rabbi Nechemiah* simultaneously say that disrupting the order of *shirayin* carries no consequences? If *shirayin* is an essential *me'akev* component of the service, it ought to be fully subject to the *seder* requirement, just as every other essential component is. The *Gemara* is left with *kashya* — an unresolved difficulty.

The context of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s statement about *Rabbi Nechemiah* is itself instructive. It arises not from *Yom Kippur* directly but from a discussion in *Zevachim* about *shchutei chutz* — the prohibition against performing sacrificial acts outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. One who slaughters a *kodesh* animal outside is liable; one who burns *imurim* on an external altar is liable. The question is whether pouring *shirayin* on the base of an external structure also incurs liability. *Rabbi Nechemiah* holds that it does. *Rabbi Yochanan* asks: on what basis? Normally *shirayin* is not *me'akev*, which would seem to mark it as a lesser *avodah* with insufficient weight to trigger the *shchutei chutz* prohibition. *Rabbi Yochanan* concludes that *Rabbi Nechemiah* must hold *shirayin* is *me'akev* — otherwise his position on *shchutei chutz* makes no sense.

### Tosafot Resolution

The difficulty is that this *sugya* in *Zevachim* appears to make *Rabbi Nechemiah*'s position a general one — that *shirayin* is *me'akev* throughout the year — which stands in tension with the position attributed to him in our *sugya*, where he seems to treat *shirayin* as a lesser component excluded from the *seder* requirement.

*Tosfos* resolves this by arguing that *Rabbi Yochanan*'s statement should not be read as attributing to *Rabbi Nechemiah* a general position that *shirayin* is always *me'akev*. Rather, *Rabbi Nechemiah* would never attribute enough weight to the *shirayin* to make it a *shchutei chutz* violation were it not for the fact that on *Yom Kippur*, at least, *shirayin* rises to the level of *me'akev*. That elevated status — the exceptional weight of *shirayin* specifically on *Yom Kippur* — is what justifies treating the act of pouring *shirayin* as a sufficiently significant *avodah* to trigger liability when performed outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. This is comparable to the burning of *imurim*, which is not *me'akev* in general but is nevertheless a recognized *avodah* whose external performance is prohibited. The *Yom Kippur* context, with its uniquely rigorous standards encoded in *vechila*, provides the underlying weight that *Rabbi Nechemiah* requires.

The overall picture that emerges is as follows: *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that the binding *seder* applies only to the *kodesh kodashim* service; *Rabbi Nechemiah* holds that it extends to the entire white-garment service, with the one modification that *shirayin* — whose status as *me'akev* on *Yom Kippur* is itself a matter of debate — is excluded from the *seder* requirement. The tension in *Rabbi Nechemiah*'s position, as identified by the *Gemara*, reflects the deeper ambiguity about whether the unique weight of *Yom Kippur* elevates the *shirayin* to full *me'akev* status (which would make excluding it from *seder* difficult to justify) or whether it remains in a somewhat intermediate category even on *Yom Kippur*.

---

## Chafinat Haketoret Case

### Ketoret Before Par

The *Gemara* now cites a ruling of *Rabbi Yochanan* (transmitted by *Rabbi Chanina*): if one performed the *chafinat haketoret* — the scooping of the incense — before the *shechitat hapar*, the act accomplished nothing: *lo asa velo klum*.

To understand the significance of this ruling, it must be located within the sequence established earlier. The full order of the service assigns the *shechitat hapar* as step one, the *chafinat haketoret* as step 2a (preparing the incense scoop), and the actual *hakravat ketoret* (the burning of the incense inside) as step 2b. If one performed the scooping of the incense before slaughtering the ox, one has gone out of order.

### Not Rabbi Yehuda

The *Gemara* immediately notes: *keman — dela k'Rabbi Yehuda* — this ruling is not in accordance with *Rabbi Yehuda*. Recall that *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that the *seder* requirement is binding only for acts performed in the white garments inside the *kodesh kodashim*. The *chafinat haketoret* and the *shechitat hapar* both take place outside the *kodesh kodashim* — in the *azarah* and the *heichal* respectively. According to *Rabbi Yehuda*, going out of order in that zone carries no *bedi'eved* consequence. Yet *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling says the premature scooping is entirely invalid. This can only be consistent with *Rabbi Nechemiah*'s broader position — or at least with a view that extends the *seder* requirement beyond the *kodesh kodashim* interior.

### Tzorech Pnim

The *Gemara* then proposes a surprising response: *afilu teima Rabbi Yehuda — tzorech pnim k'pnim dami*. One may still attribute this ruling to *Rabbi Yehuda*. Although *Rabbi Yehuda* limits the binding *seder* to what is done inside the *kodesh kodashim*, he would agree that acts which are preparatory to the *kodesh kodashim* service share its *seder* requirements. *Tzorech pnim k'pnim dami* — that which serves the interior is treated as if it were the interior itself.

Under this principle, the scope of the binding *seder* according to *Rabbi Yehuda* is in fact broader than his initial formulation suggests. It covers not only the actions performed inside the *kodesh kodashim* but also all the preparatory steps performed on their behalf: the *shechitat hapar*, the *chafinat haketoret*, the *hakravat haketoret*, the retrieval of the *dam hapar*, and the *shechitat hase'ir* — all of steps one through five and their sub-steps. All of these are done for the sake of what happens inside, and therefore the ordering requirements of the inside apply to them as well. The debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Nechemiah* then narrows: it concerns only those elements of the white-garment service that cannot be characterized as preparatory to the inner service — specifically the blood applications at the *parochet* and the *mizbeach*, and the related question of the *shirayin*. On those, the discussion continues.

---

---

# Yoma 61

## Yehuda vs. Nechemia

### Debate Overview

The sugya begins at the very bottom of 61b with the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia concerning where the order of the *Yom Kippur avodah* is *me'akev* — that is, where performing actions out of sequence invalidates what was done. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the order is *me'akev* only with respect to what is performed in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the realm of *lavan bifnim*. According to Rabbi Nechemia, the order is *me'akev* for everything done *bebigdei Lavan*, whether *bifnim* — inside the Holy of Holies — or *bachutz* — outside, including the blood sprinkled on the *parochet* and on the *mizbeach*. Rabbi Nechemia's position thus encompasses the entire sequence performed in white garments: the *hagrala*, the *shechitas hapar*, the *shechitas hase'ir*, the *chafinas ketoret*, and everything else performed *bebigdei Lavan bachutz*.

### Shirayim Question

One question left open in this debate concerns the *shirayim* — the pouring of the remnants of the blood — which is performed afterward. Ordinarily, the *shirayim* is not *me'akev*, but on *Yom Kippur* there may be a special consideration. The Torah says *vechilah mechaper* — that atonement is achieved only upon completing the entire service — which raises the possibility that the *shirayim* on *Yom Kippur* is *me'akev*. This generates two sub-questions: first, whether failing to perform the *shirayim* renders one *yotzei* at all; and second, if it is indeed *me'akev*, it would naturally be included within the scope of wherever order is mandated. That remains the outstanding question, joined by another external act yet to be discussed — the sending of the *se'ir la'azazel*, which is also performed *bebigdei Lavan bachutz* — but that is deferred for later.

### R. Chanina/Ketoret

The Gemara then cites a statement of Rabbi Chanina: if one performed the *chafinas ketoret* — the scooping of the incense — before the *shechitas hapar*, *lo asah v'lo klum*, it counts for nothing. To review the order: the *shechitas hapar* comes first, followed by the *hagrala*, then the *chafinas ketoret*, then bringing the *ketoret* inside, then taking the blood of the *par* and performing the blood service, then slaughtering the goat, and so on. If one performed the *ketoret* before slaughtering the *par*, that is out of order and the *ketoret* does not count. This appears straightforwardly to follow Rabbi Nechemia's view, since the *chafinas ketoret* is performed outside — *bebigdei Lavan bachutz* — and Rabbi Nechemia is the one who holds that order matters even for external acts.

### Disqualification Logic

A brief clarification is in order: when something is performed out of sequence, what is disqualified is the act done prematurely. So if one performed the *chafina* before the *shechitas hapar*, the *chafina* itself was invalid — *lo asah v'lo klum*. There may be a ripple effect if subsequent actions then follow in an order that presupposes the invalid act, but the fundamental principle is that the premature act itself does not count.

### Tzorech Pnim Question

The Gemara asks: *k'man* — whose view does Rabbi Chanina's statement follow? Apparently not Rabbi Yehuda's, since Rabbi Yehuda holds that order matters only for actions performed inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*, and the *chafinas ketoret* is an external act.

### Tzorech Pnim Resolution

The Gemara responds: *afilu teima Rabbi Yehuda* — one can read the statement as consistent with Rabbi Yehuda as well. The principle invoked is *tzorech pnim kepnim dami* — that which is done outside for the sake of the inside is treated as if it were inside. This significantly narrows the scope of the dispute. Rabbi Yehuda's position is not merely that order matters inside the *Kodesh Kodashim*, but that it also matters for everything performed outside that is necessary for what takes place inside: the *shechitas hapar*, the *chafinas ketoret*, the *shechitas hase'ir* — all of it is *tzorech pnim* and therefore subject to the same order requirement as the inner service itself. The genuine debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemia, then, concerns only the blood on the *parochet*, the blood on the *mizbeach*, and perhaps the *shirayim* — the external acts that are not preparatory to the inner service but constitute an independent outer service.

---

## Blood Spills

### Mishna: Spilled Blood

The Gemara now tests this expanded understanding of Rabbi Yehuda's view against the Mishna. The *seifa* of the Mishna addresses not the question of order per se, but the question of what to do when blood spills mid-process: does one restart from the beginning of the entire unit, or simply from the point of interruption? The Mishna states: *im ad shelo gamar matnos shebifnim nishpach hadam yavi dam acher veyachzor veyachel betchila mibifnim* — if before completing the inner *matanot* in the *Kodesh Kodashim* the blood spilled, one brings fresh blood and restarts from the beginning of the inner service.

### Ketoret Problem

This generates a serious difficulty. If the blood spilled during the inner service of the *par* — say, in the middle of step four — and one must go back to bring new blood, that means *shechting* the animal again. But once one must go back to *shechitas hapar*, if we now hold — as Rabbi Yehuda does, thanks to the principle of *tzorech pnim* — that the order of the external preparatory acts is also *me'akev*, then the sequence following the new *shechita* must observe that entire order as well. That means performing the *chafinas ketoret* again, bringing the *ketoret* inside again, and only then obtaining the new blood and entering the *Kodesh Kodashim*. Yet the Mishna says simply: bring new blood and restart from the beginning of the inner service. It says nothing about repeating the *ketoret*. How can the Mishna remain silent on that?

### Ketoret Solution

The Gemara answers: *beketoret lo kamairi* — the Mishna is simply not discussing the *ketoret*. It does not mean that one skips the *ketoret*; it means the Mishna is focusing exclusively on the blood service. As Rashi makes explicit: *ומיהו ודאי צריך להקטיר קטורת אחרת אחר שחיטת פר זה* — although the Mishna mentions only the blood, it is certainly true that one must also perform another *haktarat ketoret* after the new *shechita* of the *par*. The Mishna's brevity on this point does not imply otherwise; it simply leaves those steps implicit.

---

## Yehuda vs. Nechemia (II)

### Ulla/Se'ir

A parallel statement from Ulla now follows: *se'ir sheshachato kodem matan damo shel par lo asa velo klum* — if one slaughtered the *se'ir* before performing the blood service of the *par*, it counts for nothing. This presumably holds even according to Rabbi Yehuda, for the same reason: the *shechitas hase'ir* is *tzorech pnim*, done for the sake of the inner service, and therefore subject to the same order requirement. This is a statement in the same vein as Rabbi Chanina's: order matters even for these external acts that serve the inner service.

---

## Blood Spills (II)

### Se'ir Problem

Ulla's statement creates a challenge that parallels the one raised against the Mishna above. The Mishna states that if one applied the blood of the *se'ir* before the blood of the *par* — *hikdim damah shel se'ir ledam hapar* — one simply holds the blood of the *se'ir* and, after completing the blood service of the *par*, performs the *se'ir*'s blood service in its proper place. The Mishna says *yachzor veyaze midam hase'ir achar dam hapar* — go back and sprinkle the blood of the *se'ir* after the blood of the *par*. But this is problematic. If one sprinkled the blood of the *se'ir* early, it means one had already *shechted* the *se'ir* before the blood service of the *par* — since to have blood of the *se'ir* available, one must have already slaughtered it. And since the *shechitas hase'ir* is *me'akev* as Ulla states, the Mishna should not say simply "do the blood of the *se'ir* afterward." It should say: complete the blood of the *par*, then slaughter a new *se'ir*, and only then do its blood service. The Mishna implies one simply continues with the existing blood, which seems to violate the very principle Ulla articulated.

### Ulla/Location Fix

The Gemara resolves this by restricting the scope of the Mishna: *targuma Ulla bematanot shebaheichal* — Ulla himself explained that the Mishna is referring to the blood applications performed in the *Heichal*, not those in the *Kodesh Kodashim*. Rav Afis concurs: *vechein amar Rav Afis bematanot shebaheichal*. The distinction is crucial. In the scenario where one performs the blood of the *se'ir* before the blood of the *par* while both are already slaughtered — because everything has already been slaughtered and one is now only at the stage of applying blood in the *Heichal* — no new *shechita* is implicated. Doing step seven before step six, when both animals are already slaughtered, means one simply holds off and performs the *par*'s blood in the *Heichal* first, then performs the *se'ir*'s blood afterward. There is no need to slaughter another *se'ir*. But if one were to *shecht* the *se'ir* out of order — before completing the blood of the *par* — then the entire complex of *tzorech pnim* requirements would have been violated, and a new *se'ir* would need to be slaughtered. The Mishna's case avoids that problem by being situated entirely within the *Heichal* blood applications, where all slaughtering has already occurred.

---

## Separate Units

### Baraita: Units

A *baraita* is now introduced that articulates the foundational principle governing all of these cases: each location — the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the *Heichal*, and the *mizbeach* — constitutes a separate unit of *kapara*, an independent domain of atonement. The source for this will be examined through the *pesukim* momentarily, but the structural point is clear: each location is self-contained.

### Intra-Unit Spill

Within any given unit, if the blood spills in the middle, one must bring new blood and restart from the beginning of that unit. If blood spills during the *Kodesh Kodashim* service, one returns to the beginning of the *Kodesh Kodashim* service. If it spills during the *Heichal* service, one returns to the beginning of the *Heichal* service. If it spills during the *mizbeach* service, one returns to the beginning of the *mizbeach* service. This is the view of the *Tana Kamma*; Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon dispute this and hold instead that one picks up precisely where one left off, a debate to be addressed below.

### Inter-Unit Spill

If the blood spills *between* units — after one unit is fully completed but before the next has begun — there is no question: one brings new blood and simply begins the next unit. One is never required to go back and repeat a unit that has already been completed. The separateness of the units provides clear stopping points.

---

## Pesukim Analysis

### Pesuk Structure

Before examining the debate between the *Tana Kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon in greater depth, the Gemara first turns to the *pesukim* of *Acharei Mot* to ground the theological meaning of the entire *avodah*. The *pesukim* contain multiple statements of *vechipper* — atonement — directed at distinct locations and groups. After the *Kodesh Kodashim* service, the Torah says *vechipper al hakodesh mitumot bnei Yisrael umipisheihem lechol chatotam*. Then, *vechein ya'aseh le'ohel moed hashochen itam betoch tumatam* — referring to the *parochet*. Then *veyatza el hamizbeach vechipper alav*, and *vechilah mechaper et hakodesh ve'et ohel moed ve'et hamizbeach*. After the sending of the *se'ir la'azazel*, at the very end of the *avodah*, the Torah says *vechipper et mikdash hakodesh ve'et ohel moed ve'et hamizbeach yechapper ve'al hakohanim ve'al kol am hakahal yechapper*.

### Gemara Interprets

The Gemara works through this closing *pasuk* systematically. *Vechipper et mikdash hakodesh* — *zeh lifnai velifnim*, this refers to the *Kodesh Kodashim*. *Ohel moed* — *zeh heichal*, this refers to the *Heichal*, since the earlier *pasuk* had already interpreted *vechein ya'aseh le'ohel moed* as referring to the blood applied on the *parochet*, which is for the sake of the *Heichal*. *Mizbeach kemashma'o* — the golden inner altar, taken straightforwardly. *Yechapper* — *elu azarot*, this encompasses the outer courtyard where the outer *mizbeach* stands. *Hakohanim kemashma'o* — the *kohanim*, as the word implies. *Am hakahal* — *elu Yisrael*, the congregation of Israel. And the additional *yechapper* — *elu haLeviyim*, deriving a separate category for the *Leviyim*, who, once the *kohanim* are singled out, would require their own mention rather than being subsumed under *am hakahal*.

### Peshat vs. Chazal

This is a striking Gemara, because the *peshat* of the *pesukim* points in a markedly different direction from the interpretation adopted by *Chazal*. In *peshat*, the entire *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is oriented around the purification — not the personal atonement, but the metaphysical cleansing — of the *mikdash* so that God can continue to dwell therein. The language *vechipper al hakodesh mitumot bnei Yisrael* is about cleansing the sanctuary from the accumulated defilement caused by Israel's sins. Sin pollutes; it adheres, as it were, to the walls of the sacred space. Just as *velo titame'u et ha'aretz* — sin defiles the land — so too sin defiles the *mikdash*, and the ritual of *Yom Kippur* is a national, cosmic cleansing of that defilement so that the *Shechina* can continue to abide there. This is not about you and your relationship with God as an individual; it is about the *mikdash* and the conditions for divine presence.

*Chazal*, however, have shifted this entire frame. They interpret *vechipper et mikdash hakodesh* not as a cleansing of the sanctuary but as atonement for the *sin* of entering the *mikdash* in a state of *tumah*. Every location — the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the *Heichal*, the *mizbeach* — atones not for the defilement of that place but for the personal sin of whoever entered that location in an impure state. And this is quite a narrow category: it applies specifically to the case of *yedi'ah bit'chilah* — awareness at the outset — without *yedi'ah basof* — awareness at the conclusion — such that the person never came to know they had sinned, and therefore never had the opportunity to bring a *korban oleh veyored*. Rashi makes this explicit: this entire elaborate *Yom Kippur* service functions to protect those individuals from punishment *ad sheyivada lo veyavi b'olah veyored* — until they become aware and can bring their own individual atonement-offering.

This reframing is historically and theologically significant. The enormous collective ritual of *Yom Kippur* is, in *Chazal*'s reading, occasioned by one particular sin — *tumat mikdash* — under very specific circumstances. The shift from the *peshat*'s grand national and metaphysical cleansing to this narrowly defined personal transgression reflects a broader movement in *Chazal*'s thinking away from the *mikdash*-centric theology of divine presence and toward an emphasis on personal sin, personal responsibility, and personal atonement.

### Par vs. Se'ir

Within this framework, it is worth attending to the distinct roles of the *par* and the *se'ir la'azazel*. The *par* comes with a *viduy* — *vechipper ba'ado uvead beiso* — and this *viduy* relates to him and his household, understood by *Chazal* to include the *kohanim*. The *shechitas hase'ir* in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, by contrast, does not carry its own *viduy*. The *se'ir la'azazel*, on the other hand, bears the grand confession: *vehitvadah alav et kol avonot bnei Yisrael ve'et kol pisheihem lechol chatotam*. In *peshat*, the most natural reading is that the *par* and the inner *se'ir* are oriented toward the cleansing of the *mikdash* and the *kohanim* who serve in it — the *kohanim* being, in this reading, an extension of the *mikdash* itself, part of its *kelim*, sanctified alongside the sanctuary just as they were at the original *chanukas hamishkan* — while the *se'ir la'azazel* is directed at the sins of the people. The final *pasuk* *ve'al hakohanim ve'al kol am hakahal yechapper* would then refer to the *kohanim* being cleansed through the *par* process and the congregation through the *se'ir la'azazel*'s *viduy*.

### R. Yehuda View

Rabbi Yehuda reads the concluding *pasuk* — *ve'al hakohanim ve'al kol am hakahal yechapper* — as equating *kohanim* and *Yisrael* under a single shared *kapara*. The unifying force of this *yechapper* points, for Rabbi Yehuda, to the *se'ir hamishtaleach* as the single vehicle of atonement for *sha'ar aveirot* — the other transgressions — for both *kohanim* and *Yisrael* alike. The *par* and the inner *se'ir* handle *tumat mikdash vekodashav* specifically. The *se'ir la'azazel* handles everything else — all remaining transgressions for both groups equally.

This reading represents the thoroughgoing *Chazalic* shift: no longer a metaphysical cleansing of the sacred space, but a comprehensive atonement for personal transgression. One sin, *tumat mikdash*, receives special treatment; all other 612 are handled through the *se'ir hamishtaleach*. The strangeness of this reading, however, is notable: a single enormous ritual complex becomes, in effect, dedicated primarily to one out of 613 transgressions under narrow conditions, while the *se'ir hamishtaleach* absorbs everything else.

### R. Shimon View

Rabbi Shimon disagrees. He does not accept the equation implied by the final *yechapper* as mandating a single shared vehicle. Instead, he reads the structure symmetrically: just as the blood of the *se'ir* performed inside atones for *Yisrael* with respect to *tumat mikdash vekodashav*, so too the blood of the *par* atones for the *kohanim* with respect to *tumat mikdash vekodashav* — *keshem shedam hase'ir hana'asah bifnim mechaper al Yisrael betumat mikdash vekodashav, kach dam hapar mechaper al hakohanim betumat mikdash vekodashav*. And just as the *viduy* of the *se'ir hamishtaleach* atones for *Yisrael* with respect to *sha'ar aveirot*, so too the *viduy* of the *par* atones for the *kohanim* with respect to their other transgressions — *kach viduy shel par mechaper lakohanim beshear aveirot*.

Rabbi Shimon's position is fascinating on two counts. First, it establishes that even for personal sin — *sha'ar aveirot* — the *kohanim* have a separate and distinct mechanism of atonement from the rest of *Yisrael*. They do not share in the *se'ir hamishtaleach*'s atonement for other transgressions; their atonement for other transgressions comes through the *viduy* of the *par*. Why the *kohanim* would require a categorically different ritual of personal atonement than the rest of Israel is a question in itself, though it may be connected to their special status as active participants in the *avodah*.

### Blood to Viduy Shift

The second and perhaps more profound point in Rabbi Shimon's view is the radical reallocation of weight within the *avodah*. Notice what is doing the heavy lifting of atonement in Rabbi Shimon's reading: not the blood, not the elaborate ritual of the *matanot* in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, but the *viduy* — the act of confession. The blood of the *par* and the blood of the inner *se'ir* handle *tumat mikdash vekodashav*; everything else — the vast remainder of human transgression — is handled by *viduy*. The *viduy* on the *par* covers the *kohanim* for their other sins. The *viduy* on the *se'ir hamishtaleach* covers *Yisrael* for their other sins. It is not the sending of the *se'ir la'azazel* per se, not the ritual act of dispatching it to the wilderness, but the *viduy* pronounced upon it that achieves the atonement.

This is a complete inversion of emphasis. The *peshat* reading centered the ritual — the blood, the sprinkling, the cleansing of the sacred space. Rabbi Shimon has now placed the *viduy* at the center. The blood is for *tumat mikdash*; the *viduy* is for everything else. And a *viduy*-centered theology of atonement is precisely the theology that can survive the destruction of the *mikdash*, that can function without a *kohen gadol*, without blood, without an inner sanctum. The shift from *dam* to *viduy* is, as Rabbi Shimon articulates it, the conceptual bridge from the *Beit HaMikdash* to *teshuvah*.

---

## Separate Units (II)

### Eliezer/Shimon Debate

Returning to the practical law, a *baraita* now articulates the full structure of the debate between the *Tana Kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon. The *Tana Kamma* holds that if blood spills in the middle of a unit, one returns to the beginning of that unit. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon hold: *eino matchil ela mimakom shepasak* — one picks up exactly where one left off. This applies within the *Kodesh Kodashim*, within the *Heichal*, and within the *mizbeach* service, as the *baraita* makes clear by rehearsing each scenario in turn.

### Shirayim Not Me'akev

The one point on which everyone agrees is that the pouring of the *shirayim* — the remnants — at the base of the outer altar is not *me'akev*. Even on *Yom Kippur*, even given the possibility that *vechilah mechaper* imposes a completeness requirement, the *halakha* as stated here is *divrei hakol lo meakev*: the pouring of the remnants does not invalidate the atonement if it is not performed or if the blood spills before it is done. This directly addresses the question raised at the outset of the sugya about the *shirayim* and its *me'akev* status.

---

## Restart Debate

### Single Pesuk

Rabbi Yochanan now offers a striking observation: both sides of the dispute — those who say one must restart at the beginning of the unit and those who say one picks up where one left off — derive their positions from a single *pasuk*. The verse is *midam chatat hakippurim achat bashana* — "from the blood of the sin-offering of atonement once a year." The word *achat* is the hinge; it can be read in two ways, yielding two incompatible conclusions.

### R. Meir Position

Rabbi Meir understands *achat* as modifying *chatat*: *chatat achat amarti lecha velo shtei chatatot* — I told you one sin-offering, not two. Each unit of the *avodah* may draw only on the blood of a single animal. If blood spills mid-unit and one begins again from the start, one acquires fresh blood from a new *shechita*, and the entire unit is performed with blood from one animal — no mixing of blood from two different animals. This is workable: each unit is a self-contained atonement, and within that unit the blood must come from a single offering. To pick up mid-unit where one left off, however, would mean using blood from one animal for the first portion and blood from another animal for the remainder — that constitutes two sin-offerings, which the *pasuk* prohibits.

### R. Eliezer/Shimon

Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon understand *achat* differently: *chitu echad amarti lecha velo shtei chituyim* — I told you one process of sprinkling, not two. One may not duplicate the process; if one performs, say, four of the seven sprinklings inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* and then restarts and performs all seven again, one has created two overlapping processes of *chitu* — a repetition that the *pasuk* forbids. Therefore one must pick up where one left off: complete the remaining sprinklings from where the interruption occurred, ensuring there is only one continuous process. What does not concern them is whether the blood of the second segment comes from the same animal as the first; the prohibition is against duplicating the *process*, not against using blood of a second animal.

### Log Oil Case

An analogous debate is now introduced by Rabbi, citing what he received from Rabbi Yaakov, concerning the *log shemen* of the *metzora*. The purification process of the *metzora* involves a *log* of oil: the *kohen* sprinkles oil in the *Heichal*, then applies oil to the *metzora*'s ear, thumb, and toe, and finally pours the remaining oil on the *metzora*'s head. If the oil spills mid-process, does one restart at the beginning of the unit or continue from where one left off? Rabbi reports that Rabbi Yaakov taught him a ruling specific to the *log*, though the question arises immediately whether the oil case differs from the blood case.

### Metzora Oil

A *baraita* demonstrates that the same dispute applies to the *log shemen*: the *Tana Kamma* requires restarting from the beginning of the unit in which the oil spilled, while Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon say *mimakom shepasak hu matchil* — one picks up from the point of interruption. Across both units — the sprinkling in the *Heichal* and the application to the *behonot* (ear, thumb, toe) — the debate runs identically to the blood debate. The *baraita* thus demonstrates that what Rabbi Yaakov taught was not a distinction between the *log* case and the blood case — as if the *log* case were undisputed — but rather that Rabbi Yaakov *taught* the dispute itself in the context of the *log*. The Gemara accordingly emends: Rabbi did not mean that Rabbi Yaakov told him the *log* case is categorically different; he meant that Rabbi Yaakov transmitted the same dispute as applied to the *log*.

### Head Not Me'akev

The one point of universal agreement in the *metzora* case is that the pouring of oil on the *metzora*'s head does not *meakev*. The *pasuk* provides two distinct references: when mandating the application to the ear and thumb, it says *umiyeter hashemen asher al kapo* — "from what remains of the oil on his palm." Then, after those applications, it says *vehaNotar bashemen... yiten al rosh hamitaher* — "and what is left over of the oil shall be placed on the head of the one being purified." Rashi formulates this precisely: the applications to the *behonot* are themselves called *shirayim* — leftovers — since the verse describes them as *miyeter hashemen*. The pouring on the head is thus *shirei shirayim* — the leftovers of the leftovers. Just as *shirayim* at the base of the *mizbeach* are not *me'akev*, so too *shirei shirayim* — what is left after the *shirayim* themselves — are certainly not *me'akev*. The parallel to the blood service on *Yom Kippur* is precise: pouring the *shirayim* at the *yesod hamizbeach* is the counterpart to pouring the remaining oil on the *metzora*'s head, and neither is *me'akev*.

---

## Asham Paradox

### Asham Scenario

The Gemara now introduces a case that places the two positions in irreconcilable tension with each other. The *asham* of the *metzora* occupies a unique structural position in the purification ritual: the blood of the *asham* is applied both to the *mizbeach* — as with all *korbanot* — and then directly to the *metzora*'s ear, thumb, and toe, as a separate ritual act. Suppose the blood of the *asham* spills after being applied to the *mizbeach* but before the application to the *behonot*. One is in the middle of a process — analogous to all the cases discussed above — and the blood is gone.

### Meir: New Asham

According to Rabbi Meir's principle — *chatat achat*, focus on one sin-offering, and restart at the beginning of the unit if blood spills — the solution here is to bring another *asham*, *shecht* it, and start the process again from the beginning. Rabbi Meir's framework allows this: the requirement is that within any given process, one works with the blood of one animal; but one may obtain a new animal and begin anew.

### Eliezer/Shimon Stuck

Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon are caught in a paradox. Their principle says *mimakom shepasak hu matchil* — one picks up precisely where one left off — and that one may not duplicate the process. Here, that would mean: bring another *asham*, take its blood, and proceed directly to the *behonot*, skipping the *mizbeach* application since that was already done. But this runs directly into the problem of *oto* — the Torah says *vehikriv oto la'asham*, implying one specific animal, *oto*, the very same one. One cannot use a second animal to complete what was begun with the first. And yet if one cannot use a second animal, and one also cannot go back to the beginning because that would mean two full processes of application, Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon are left with *ein lo takana* — there is no remedy. The *metzora* is stuck in an incomplete state from which there is no halakhic exit under their framework.

### Chisda Challenge

Rav Chisda raises a sharp challenge: if the *pasuk* says *oto* — implying this very *asham* — then even Rabbi Meir should be constrained. How can Rabbi Meir say one brings another *asham* and starts again if the *pasuk* limits the process to *oto*, the specific animal already designated? The Gemara acknowledges the difficulty: *kashya*.

### Becomes Olah

A *baraita* is then cited that provides the resolution. If the *asham metzora* was slaughtered in a manner that disqualifies it for its designated purpose — or, in the *girsa* of Rabbeinu Chananel adopted by *Tosafot*, if the blood spilled before the application to the *behonot* — *harei ze oleh lagabei mizbeach vetatun nesachim*: the animal is brought as an *olah* on the *mizbeach* and requires the accompanying libations. The animal's blood has already been placed on the *mizbeach*, and the animal itself is consumed there as an *olah*. But *vetzarich asham acher lehachshiro* — a separate *asham* is still required to complete the *metzora*'s purification process. The force of *oto* thus applies to one specific aspect of the ritual; but the overall process of *taharah* can still be completed through a subsequent *asham*, resolving the apparent conflict with Rabbi Meir's position — though the precise mechanics carry us into territory that must be deferred to the next session.

---

---

# Yoma 62

## Interruption of Service

### Meir vs. Eliezer/Shimon

The daf opens by returning to a dispute already set in motion: what happens when the *avodah* is interrupted in one of the sections of the *Beit HaMikdash* — whether in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the *Heikhal*, or at the *mizbe'ach* — and the sprinkling of blood is disrupted, requiring the *shechita* of another animal to obtain fresh blood? The debate turns on whether one must begin again from the start of that section or may resume from the point of interruption. Rabbi Meir holds that one starts again from the beginning of that section, ensuring that all of the blood-work within it comes from a single animal. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon hold that one picks up where one left off, so that a single continuous process is not fragmented into two.

### Blood Spill in Asham

Rabbi Yochanan — following the *girsa* of Rabbeinu Chananel as quoted in Tosafot, *shenishpach damo kodem gemar matnotav* — now applies this dispute to the *asham metzora*. When a *metzora* concludes his period of impurity, he brings an *asham* whose blood is sprinkled on the *mizbe'ach* and then applied to his ear, thumb, and toe. If in the middle of that process the blood spills, Rabbi Yochanan says this falls directly into the same dispute. According to Rabbi Meir — who holds that when blood spills mid-section one brings another animal and starts again from the beginning — here too one would bring another *asham*, perform a new *shechita*, and repeat the entire process of sprinkling on the *mizbe'ach* and applying to the ear, thumb, and toe. According to Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon — who hold that one picks up where one left off — the case becomes striking: *hacha ein lo takana*, here there is no remedy. Normally their position forces one to continue from the point of interruption rather than start again; but here the Torah specifies *keves echad*, one ram for the *asham*, which means one cannot use two rams as part of a single process. Unable to start from the beginning and unable to resume mid-process, a person in this situation would be entirely stuck.

### Rav Chisda's Challenge

Rav Chisda presses the analysis further. The verse states *v'hikriv oto le-asham asher hunaf* — the very animal over which the *tenufa* was performed is the one to be brought as the *asham*. The word *oto* is a limiting term: that specific one. Rav Chisda argues that even according to Rabbi Meir, who would otherwise permit bringing another animal and starting again, the word *oto* should prevent this, since the replacement animal is not the one over which the initial *tenufa* was performed. If so, even Rabbi Meir's position leads to an impasse, and the *gemara* registers this as a genuine difficulty: *ve-namshikh kashya*.

### Baraita Evidence

A *baraita* is then cited in support of Rabbi Yochanan's framework. The *baraita* discusses an *asham metzora* that was slaughtered *shelo lishmo*, or — the case relevant to our discussion — where the blood was placed on the *mizbe'ach* but not applied to the ear and thumb of the *metzora*. In such a case, the *baraita* rules *harei zeh oleh legabei mizbe'ach v'te'un nesachim*: the animal is valid as a *korban* and requires the accompanying wine and flour and oil. However, *u-tzarikh asham acher lehakhshiro*: if one now wishes to complete the *metzora*'s purification, a second *asham* is needed. This ruling appears to support Rabbi Meir's position — that the first animal, having had its blood placed on the *mizbe'ach*, achieved partial validity, while a second animal can be brought to complete the purification process. This shows that the framework of bringing another *korban* and resuming the process is at least coherent, and that for Rabbi Meir there is no conceptual barrier to doing so.

### Stuck Position

Rav Chisda, however, reads the *baraita* differently. When the *baraita* says *tzarich asham acher*, it means not that one can bring another *asham* but that one needs to — yet cannot. This is the force of the formulation *tzarich v'ein lo takana*: it is required, and yet there is no remedy. In Rav Chisda's reading, the word *oto* in the verse creates an absolute barrier: you cannot use more than one animal in total for this process, which means that according to everyone — including Rabbi Meir — one is stuck. The *baraita* does not show that a second animal can successfully complete the *metzora*'s purification; it only shows that technically one is needed, while simultaneously making clear that there is no viable path to providing it.

## Tzarich v'Ein Takana

### Tanna's Language

This invites a methodological challenge: would a *tanna* formulate a teaching by saying *tzarich* — you need to do X — when what he really means is that it is required but impossible to fulfill? To say "you need another *asham*" when in fact there is no mechanism by which that *asham* can accomplish anything seems at best misleading and at worst contradictory.

### Nazir Precedent

The *gemara* responds with a parallel case. A *nazir memora* — a *nazir* who is naturally bald — faces an analogous problem. The Torah requires that at the conclusion of his *nezirus* he shave his hair; what happens when he has no hair to shave? Beit Shammai say *tzarich ha'avarat ta'ar* — he must pass a razor over his head. Beit Hillel say *ein tzarich ha'avarat ta'ar* — he does not need to. So when Beit Shammai say *tzarich*, what does that mean in practice?

### Rav Avina's View

Rav Avina explains: when Beit Shammai say *tzarich*, they mean *tzarich v'ein lo takana* — it is required and there is no remedy. The passage of the razor over a bald head accomplishes nothing; it is not a meaningful act. And yet the formulation is simply *tzarich*, without explicit elaboration that the requirement cannot be fulfilled. This vindicates Rav Chisda's reading of the *baraita*: a *tanna* can indeed say *tzarich* to mean "required, yet impossible."

### Rav Padat's View

Rav Padat disagrees with this interpretation of Beit Shammai, arguing instead that *tzarich* means one does what is actually possible. In his reading, Beit Shammai genuinely require the physical act of passing the razor over the head — not as a meaningless gesture, but as the closest available fulfillment of the requirement. This interpretation stands in direct tension with Rav Avina's: Rav Padat reads *tzarich* as "do whatever you can," while Rav Avina reads it as "required but impossible."

### Metzora Missing Limb

Rav Padat draws support from the case of a *metzora* who lacks a thumb or a toe. The *mishna* states *ein lo tahara olamit* — he can never achieve purification. Rabbi Elazar disagrees: *noten al mekomo veyotzei* — one places the blood where the thumb or toe would have been, and the requirement is thereby fulfilled. Rabbi Shimon goes further and says that *bedi'avad* one may even place it on the left thumb if the right is missing.

The significance for Rav Padat is clear: Rabbi Elazar, who holds that one simply places the blood on the stub or the site where the limb would have been, represents the same interpretive move as Beit Shammai. Just as Beit Shammai require the razor to actually pass over the head — not as a legal fiction but as a genuine act, however attenuated — Rabbi Elazar requires placing the blood where the thumb was as the fulfillment of the *mitzvah*, not as a declaration of impossibility. Both positions reflect the principle that *tzarich* means "do whatever is doable," not "it is required but hopeless." This debate has significant implications beyond the immediate cases. The question of whether the Torah demands the specific act or whether it demands the closest achievable approximation touches on how one approaches ritual requirements in the face of physical constraints or disability.

## Two Kohanim Process

### Vessel vs. Hand

The *gemara* shifts to a *baraita* exploring the mechanics of the *asham metzora* ritual. The verse states *v'lakach midam ha'asham*, the *kohen* takes from the blood of the *asham*. One might have thought this blood — like ordinary sacrificial blood — is caught in a vessel and applied from there. The verse's formulation, however, links the *lekicha* (taking) to the *netina* (placing): just as the placing on the ear, thumb, and toe is done *b'atzmo shel kohen*, with the *kohen*'s own body, specifically his finger, so too the taking is *b'atzmo shel kohen*, caught directly in his hand. One might then wonder whether blood destined for the *mizbe'ach* is similarly caught by hand; the Torah answers this by stating *ki kachatat ha'asham hu l'Hashem* — this *asham* is like a *chatat*, and just as a *chatat* requires the blood to be caught in a vessel, so too the blood going on the *mizbe'ach* requires a vessel.

### Two Kohanim Role

The result is a striking structural division within a single *korban*. The *asham metzora* thus has two distinct identities: as a standard *korban* whose blood goes to the *mizbe'ach* via a vessel, and as an instrument of purification whose blood is applied to the *metzora* by hand. The *baraita* draws the logical conclusion: *asham metzora shnei kohanim mikablim et damo*, two *kohanim* are required — *echad b'yad v'echad bikli*, one receiving the blood in his hand and one in a vessel. *Ze shekibel bikli ba lo etzel mizbe'ach* — the one who received in the vessel proceeds to the *mizbe'ach* and performs the standard *korban* rite. *V'ze shekibel b'yad ba lo etzel Metzora* — the one who received in his hand goes to the *metzora* and applies the blood to his ear, thumb, and toe. This is not merely a logistical division. The two processes are functionally segregated: the blood that goes on the *mizbe'ach* and the blood that goes on the *metzora* are not drawn from the same vessel, nor could one process serve the other. They are parallel but independent — two *kohanim*, two modes of reception, two destinations.

## Leftover Animals

### Eliezer: All Equal

Returning to the main thread, the *gemara* takes up the question of what happens to all the animals that were slaughtered in the course of repeated interruptions. When the process of blood-sprinkling is interrupted and a new animal must be slaughtered, multiple carcasses accumulate. The normal rule for the *par* and *se'ir* of Yom Kippur — animals whose blood was brought inside the *Heikhal* — is that they are taken *chutz l'machaneh* and burned outside. Does this apply to all the accumulated animals or only to one of them?

A *Tosefta* is cited: Rabbi Eliezer holds *v'kulam metamin begadim v'nisrafin b'veit hadeshen* — all of them convey impurity to the garments of those who handle them and all of them are burned in the designated place outside the *Mikdash*. Since the blood of each was used in a ritual — even if ideally there should have been only one — each animal has the same *halacha* as if it were the sole animal brought.

### Shimon: Last Only

The *chachamim* disagree: *ein mitam'in begadim ve'ein nisrafin beveit hadeshen ela ha'acharon* — only the last animal has full status, both for conveyance of impurity and for burning outside. The reasoning: *hu ve'gamar bo kapara*, it was with that animal that the *kapara* was completed.

### Completion Principle

This ruling deserves reflection, because one might have expected the opposite conclusion. The blood brought into the *Kodesh Kodashim* seems more significant than blood applied at the *mizbe'ach*; why would the last animal — which may only have contributed to the final stage — be considered the primary one? The answer lies in how the Torah frames completion. The verse states *ve-chilah mikaper et hakodesh ve'et ohel mo'ed ve'et hamizbe'ach* — the atonement for the *kodesh*, the *ohel mo'ed*, and the *mizbe'ach* is described as finished only at the moment of conclusion. Just as one cannot declare a room clean until the last corner has been done, the *kapara* is not *kapara* until it is fully complete. The principle *kilah kiper* — when finished, atonement is achieved — means that real status accrues only to the animal whose blood sealed the process. The earlier animals must still be disposed of properly, but they do not carry the full *halachic* identity of the primary *korban*.

## Which La'Azazel Goat

### Rava's Question

Rava poses a question to Rav Nachman: *kama se'irim meshale'ach* — if the blood of the *se'ir* whose blood was used inside spilled and the entire process had to be repeated multiple times, each time requiring a new pair of goats with a new *hagralah*, how many goats are sent to *azazel*? Each time two goats are brought, a *hagralah* is performed, and one is designated *la'azazel*. Does each of those designated goats get sent?

### One vs. Many

Rav Nachman responds: *vechi eder hu meshale'ach* — would one send an entire flock to *azazel*? Clearly only one can be sent. But Rava pushes back: *vechi eder hu soref* — yet the position just stated holds that all the accumulated animals are burned outside, so why is it not equally absurd to burn more than one?

The *gemara* draws a clear distinction. By the burning, the verse has no limiting word: any animal whose blood was brought inside is burned, and nothing in the text restricts this to one. But by the sending to *azazel*, the verse states *leshale'ach oto la'azazel hamidbarah* — the word *oto*, that one, limits it to a single animal. Moreover, the entire ritual of sending is focused on one act: there is a *viduy*, a confession, a physical journey, a singular dramatic moment of expiation. Multiplying that act undermines its coherence in a way that multiplying a disposal-by-burning does not. So while all animals whose blood was brought inside may be burned, only one can be sent *la'azazel*.

### Last Gets Status

Now the further question: which one? Two opinions are reported in the name of Rava, transmitted through different students.

Rav Shimi, citing Rava, says *acharon meshale'ach* — the last one is sent. This follows directly from the principle of *kilah kiper*: since the animal whose blood completed the process is considered the primary *korban*, its paired *la'azazel* goat bears the primary status. Consistency demands that if the last blood-animal has full status, so too does its mate. The goat sent to *azazel* should be the one paired with the animal whose blood ended the *avodah*.

### First Gets Status

Rav Pappa, also citing Rava, says *rishon meshale'ach* — the first one is sent. His reasoning invokes the principle of Rabbi Yosi: *mitzvah barishon*, in analogous cases priority is given to the first.

### Rabbi Yosi Priority

The *gemara* asks: which Rabbi Yosi holds this? It considers the Rabbi Yosi associated with the *kupot* in the context of *Shekalim*. Three baskets were used to remove money from the *lishkah* for purchasing communal *korbanot*, labeled one, two, three so that the order would be known. A *baraita* records Rabbi Yosi asking why the baskets are labeled at all. His answer: *shemitzvah barishon* — because it is a *mitzvah* to use the first basket's money first, before the second's. By the same logic, the first goat designated *la'azazel* should have priority.

### Rejection of First

The *gemara* rejects this analogy. In the case of the baskets, when the first basket was scooped, the second basket had not yet come into existence. For that moment, however brief, the *mitzvah* focused exclusively on the first basket. There was a period of time during which only the first was fit. Here, however, none of the *la'azazel* goats is ready to be sent at the moment it is designated. A goat becomes fit for *azazel* only after all the blood-work is complete. Until the very end of the entire *avodah*, no designated *la'azazel* goat is yet eligible. Consequently, when the moment of readiness finally arrives, all the designated *la'azazel* goats become simultaneously fit. There is no period during which only the first was ready; they all achieve readiness at the same instant.

The *gemara* then turns to a different case of Rabbi Yosi: *hamaphrish pishcho ve'avad* — one designated a *korban Pesach* and it became lost; one designated a second animal in its place; then the first was found. The *chachamim* say one may bring whichever one he wishes. Rabbi Yosi says *mitzvah barishon* — one should bring the first. Crucially, Rashi points out that this could all have occurred before *chatzos*: both animals were designated earlier in the day, and *chatzos* — the moment they become fit to be brought — arrived while both were present. Rabbi Yosi still gives priority to the one that was sanctified first, even though they became simultaneously fit.

This seems to support Rav Pappa: even when multiple candidates are equally ready at the same moment, Rabbi Yosi awards priority to the one that was first designated. By that logic, the first goat designated *la'azazel* should be the one sent, even though all of them became eligible simultaneously when the *avodah* was completed.

The *gemara*'s conclusion leaves the question unresolved in a straightforward way, though it notes that for the remaining goats one presumably waits until they develop a *mum* and redeems them, since *ein chatas tzibur meisah* — a communal *chatat* is not left to die, unlike an individual's *chatat*.

## Two Goats Matching

### Ideal Requirements

Having completed that extended discussion, the *gemara* turns to the *mishna* that opens the new *perek* and addresses the two goats of Yom Kippur directly. *Shnei se'irei Yom HaKippurim mitzvatan sheyihyu shneihem shavin b'mareh u'v'komah u'v'damim u'vilkichatan k'echad* — the ideal requirement is that the two goats be similar in appearance (*mareh*), similar in height (*komah*), similar in cost (*damim*), and purchased at the same time (*likchiatan k'echad*). Rashi clarifies that *mareh* does not mean they must be identical twins, but that they should be similar — both white or both black, for example. The underlying purpose of these requirements is to reinforce the power of the *hagralah*: when everything about the two animals is equal — their appearance, their stature, their provenance, even the moment of their acquisition — the designation of one *l'Hashem* and one *la'azazel* is entirely a function of the *goral* alone, with nothing external to distinguish one path from the other. That equality is the precondition for the *hagralah* to carry its full significance, whether one understands it in terms of divine providence (*hashgacha*) or the drama of undetermined fate.

### Death Before Lottery

Notwithstanding the ideal requirements, *ve'af al pi she'ein shavin kasher bedi'avad* — even if they are not identical, the *avodah* is valid after the fact. Similarly, if one was purchased today and one tomorrow, it is *kasher bedi'avad*.

If one of the goats dies before the *hagralah* has been performed, the remedy is straightforward: *yikach zug lasheini*, bring a second goat and conduct the lottery with the surviving animal.

### Death After Lottery

If one of the goats dies after the *hagralah* has been conducted — one having been designated *l'Hashem* and one *la'azazel* — the matter is more complex. One cannot simply pair the surviving goat with a new one: the surviving goat's status emerged from a specific *goral*, and a new animal cannot be inserted into that completed lottery retroactively. Therefore *yavi zug acher v'yagril aleihem batchila*: a new pair is brought and a fresh *hagralah* is conducted.

The *mishna* then instructs what to say at the new lottery: if the *l'Hashem* goat died, one declares over whichever of the new pair the lot for *Hashem* falls, *ze she'alah alav hagoral l'Hashem yitkayeim tachtav* — this one that the lot designated for *Hashem* shall stand in its place. The second of the new pair — the one designated *la'azazel* in the new lottery — now creates a surplus: there is one surviving original goat (the *la'azazel* from the first lottery) and one newly designated *la'azazel*. The *mishna* instructs that the second one — which according to its plain reading appears to be the newly acquired one — grazes until it develops a *mum* (*yeireh ad sheyista'eiv*), at which point it is sold and the proceeds go toward a *nedavah* for a communal *korban* such as an *olah*. This is because *ein chatas tzibur meisah* — a communal *chatat* does not die; unlike an individual's *chatat*, which must be left to perish when it cannot be used, a communal one is redeemed.

The *gemara* notes a conceptual awkwardness in this arrangement: if the surviving original *la'azazel* goat and the newly designated *la'azazel* goat were paired with animals that went through different lotteries, there is something peculiar about using them together. The *mishna*'s language, however, strongly implies that it is the newly acquired animal that is set aside, not the surviving original. The *gemara* questions this because it creates the odd situation of a *l'Hashem* goat from one lottery being matched with a *la'azazel* goat from a different lottery — animals that were never designated as a pair through the same *hagralah*. Nevertheless, since the *mishna* says *ze she'alah alav hagoral yitkayeim tachtav* in relation to one animal and then says the second one grazes, the plain reading is that the surviving original remains and the newly acquired one is set aside.

Rabbi Yehuda adds the position that a *chatas tzibur* that cannot be used should in fact die, like an individual's *chatat*, rather than being redeemed as a *nedavah*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Cases

Rabbi Yehuda further extends the analysis to cases where it is not the death of a goat that creates the problem but rather a disruption in the blood-work. If the blood of the *l'Hashem* goat spilled, the *la'azazel* goat must die, and the entire process must begin again with a new lottery. If the *la'azazel* goat died after the *l'Hashem* goat's blood had already been applied, the blood is voided and the process likewise starts again. Once the animal has moved into the stage of becoming *dam* — once it has been slaughtered and its blood collected — the substitution mechanism of the *mishna* no longer applies. At that point, one does not work around the loss by designating a replacement; instead, the entire process begins fresh.

## Paired Animals Rule

### Goats Shnei Teaching

The *gemara* now turns to a systematic derivation of the requirement for matching animals across multiple contexts. A *baraita* begins with the goats of Yom Kippur. The verse says *yikach shnei se'irei izim* — he shall take two he-goats. The word *se'irei* in the plural already implies a minimum of two; why then does the verse add the word *shnei*? The extra word teaches *sheyihyu shneihem shavin* — that they must be similar. How do I know that *bedi'avad*, if they are not similar, the *avodah* is still valid? Because the verse also uses the word *se'ir* individually in multiple places — referring to one and then the other separately — which indicates that each can stand as an independent entity, and *bedi'avad* even unmatched goats are acceptable.

### Se'ir Individual Form

Given that the individual form of *se'ir* teaches *bedi'avad* validity, why would anyone have thought that non-matching would be absolutely invalidating? Because the word *shnei* appears so many times in the relevant passages — *shnei la'azazel*, *shnei asirim*, and so on — one might have concluded that this repetition of the paired form makes matching an absolute requirement, invalid even *bedi'avad*. The individual appearances of *se'ir* therefore come to override that inference and establish that *bedi'avad* it remains *kasher*.

### Multiple Matching Ways

Having established that *bedi'avad* non-matching is acceptable because of the individual *se'ir*, the *gemara* asks: since the individual form frees *bedi'avad* cases from absolute requirement, why does the Torah say *shnei* so many times? The answer: each instance teaches a different dimension of the *lechatchila* matching requirement — one for *mareh* (appearance), one for *komah* (height), and one for *damim* (cost). The multiple uses of the paired form each establish a different way in which the two goats should ideally be alike.

### Metzora Sheep Pattern

The same pattern of derivation applies to the sheep brought in the *korban* of a *metzora*. *Yikach shnei kevasim* — the word *shnei* teaches that they must be similar *lechatchila*. The individual use of *keves* throughout the passages, each referring to one sheep separately, teaches that *bedi'avad* even non-matching sheep are valid. The potential source of *ikuva* — the reason one might have thought non-matching would be absolutely invalidating — is the word *tihyeh* in the verse *zot tihyeh torat hametzora*, which implies an exact and fixed procedure. Without the individual *keves* form, *tihyeh* would suggest that every detail must be performed precisely as stated, with no room for *bedi'avad* leniency. The individual form overrides this, and the *tihyeh* is then reapplied to all the other requirements of the *metzora* for which no comparable dispensation exists.

### Birds Pattern

The same structure governs the birds of the *metzora* ritual. *Tziporim* in the plural implies a minimum of two; the word *shtei* (two) teaches they must be similar *lechatchila*. The individual use of *tzipor* — once for the bird that is slaughtered and once for the bird that is sent free — teaches that *bedi'avad* even non-matching birds are valid. Again, the *tihyeh* of *zot tihyeh torat hametzora* would have imposed an absolute requirement, but the individual form of *tzipor* provides the *bedi'avad* dispensation, and *tihyeh* is redirected to the other requirements of the *metzora*.

### Tamidim No Match

The *gemara* then challenges this pattern by asking whether it should apply equally to the *tamidim*, the daily offerings. The verse says *shnayim layom* — two a day — and one might apply the same reasoning: the word *shnayim* teaches that they should be similar *lechatchila*, and the individual use of *keves* throughout teaches *bedi'avad* validity. If so, the *tamidim* should also require matching in appearance. Yet there is no evidence anywhere in rabbinic literature that the two daily *tamidim* must match, and indeed the tradition never imposes such a requirement.

### Sun Positioning

The *gemara* resolves this by explaining that *shnayim layom* is not available to teach matching, because it is needed for an entirely different purpose — the *baraita* of *keneged hayom*, "opposite the sun." The morning *tamid* was slaughtered on the north-west corner of the *azarah* at the second ring (*taba'at shniya*), and the afternoon *tamid* on the north-east corner at the second ring. This positioning ensured that each *korban* was placed to receive the maximum available sunlight given the architecture of the *Mikdash*: in the morning the sun rises in the east, and the north-west position, furthest from the eastern wall, captures the most light from above; in the afternoon the sun has moved west, and the north-east position similarly optimizes. Why the second ring? Tosafot explains that using the first ring risked the animal soiling the area near the *mizbe'ach*; Rashi explains that the *kohen* used the second row of rings for support while positioning the animal at the first.

Since *shnayim layom* is entirely dedicated to teaching this spatial principle of *keneged hayom*, it cannot simultaneously teach the matching requirement, and therefore the *tamidim* never enter the framework of required similarity at all.

### Shabbat Matching

The *gemara* concludes by noting one exception. The two lambs brought as the *musaf* of Shabbat — the additional offering of the day — do require matching, because the word *shnayim* in that context functions as an *addition* to the standard daily offering rather than as a description of the two *tamidim* themselves. In that capacity it can bear the weight of teaching the matching requirement, just as *shnei* does for the goats and the sheep of the *metzora*. Whether non-matching *bedi'avad* is acceptable for the Shabbat lambs is a question that Rashi and Tosafot address: presumably yes, since no source ever declares them invalid *bedi'avad*, though the *gemara* does not spell out the mechanism for this explicitly.

At the conclusion of this analysis it becomes clear that the matching requirement is not unique to Yom Kippur. It applies to the goats of Yom Kippur, the sheep of the *metzora*, the birds of the *metzora*, and the Shabbat *musaf* lambs. What remains uniquely stringent by the goats of Yom Kippur is not the bare existence of the matching requirement but its scope: only there does the Torah demand similarity in *mareh*, *komah*, *damim*, and *likchiatan k'echad* simultaneously. All those dimensions of equivalence, derived from the multiple instances of *shnei* in the Yom Kippur passages, remain a singular intensification that sets the *shnei se'irei Yom HaKippurim* apart from all other paired offerings.

---

---

# Yoma 63

## Identical Goats

### Daf Overview

We begin today's daf at the very bottom of 62b, picking up from the *tanu rabbanan* approximately five lines down. The preceding discussion has concerned the two goats of Yom Kippur and the drawing of the lots — specifically, the requirement that the two goats appear identical. We concluded with the point that this requirement of looking the same applies not only here but also by the two lambs of Shabbat and in several contexts involving the *metzora*. Nevertheless, the requirement is particularly underscored by the Yom Kippur goats, and in a heightened sense: it is not merely a general resemblance that is demanded, but identical height, identical cost, and purchase at the same time. Even where we find parallels elsewhere, the concern here is of an altogether more rigorous character.

### Same Height, Cost, Time

From this point, the *gemara* transitions to a different topic — one to which the case of the goats serves as an illuminating application — namely, the prohibition of *shechutei chutz*: the *issur* of slaughtering a *korban* outside the *beis hamikdash*.

---

## Shechutei Chutz

### Before/After Lottery

The *tanu rabbanan* addresses the following case: the two *se'irim* of Yom Kippur that were slaughtered outside the *beis hamikdash* — what is the *halacha*? The *baraisa* distinguishes between two stages. Before the *hagralah*, before the lots have been drawn, either goat could theoretically be designated for some purpose. Therefore, *ad shelo higril aleihem chayav al sheneihem* — if one slaughters either goat outside before the drawing of the lots, one is *chayav*. After the lots have been drawn, *chayav al shel Hashem u'patur al shel Azazel* — one is liable only for the goat designated for God but exempt for the one designated *l'azazel*, because the latter is no longer *ra'ui l'pesach ohel mo'ed*: it will not be brought as a *korban* inside the *beis hamikdash*, and therefore slaughtering it outside carries no liability.
