To be precise about the scenario: we are not speaking of a *shechita* performed before the *hagralah* as part of the Yom Kippur service, but rather a case where someone seized one of the designated goats, took it outside the *beis hamikdash*, and slaughtered it there. The question is whether that act incurs *chiyuv* for *shechutei chutz*.

### Mechusar Zman Principle

The *gemara* now asks: before the lots are drawn, for what purpose is each goat considered fit, such that slaughtering it outside generates *chiyuv*? *Le'mai chazi?* Rav Chisda answers: *ho'il v'ra'ui l'se'ir hana'aseh bachutz* — since the goat is fit to be used for the Yom Kippur *musaf* offering, which is brought in the *azarah* (outside the *heichal* but within the *beis hamikdash* complex). True, each goat is not yet fit for the interior *avoda* of the *kodesh kodashim* — the blood-sprinkling service — because the *hagralah* has not yet taken place. But the *musaf* is a separate *korban* that could employ this animal later in the day.

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: just as we say the goat is not yet fit for the *avoda* of the *kodesh kodashim* because it is *mechusar hagralah* — lacking the drawing of lots — so too one should say it is not yet fit for the *musaf*, since it is *mechusar avodot hayom*, lacking all the prior *avodot* of the day that must precede the *musaf*.

### Action vs. Waiting

Rav Chisda's response, as the *gemara* develops it, establishes a fundamental distinction. The reason the goats are not yet fit for the blood-sprinkling inside the *kodesh kodashim* is not merely that time has not yet elapsed — it is because something must be *done to the animal itself*: the lots must be drawn. This is *mechusar ma'aseh*, lacking an action that must be performed directly upon the thing in question. An animal in this condition is considered genuinely unfit.

The *musaf*, by contrast, requires only waiting for external events to transpire. The *ketoret*, the ox-blood service, the goat-blood service — these are not things done to the *musaf* animal itself. They are separate acts that occur elsewhere. Once those external events have taken place, this animal will be fit. The principle Rav Chisda applies is *ein mechusar zman l'vo bayom*: something that will be fit later today is considered fit now, provided that the only obstacle is the passage of time and the completion of external events, rather than an action that must be performed on the animal itself.

*Ravina* draws out the implication of Rav Chisda's position: *hasha d'amar Rav Chisda mechusar hagralah k'mechusar ma'aseh dami* — the lack of the *hagralah* has the same legal character as *mechusar ma'aseh*. The lots must be drawn on the animal itself; without that act, the animal's specific identity for the interior service remains undefined. Its generic *kedusha* exists, but its role as the *se'ir* whose blood enters the *kodesh kodashim* has not yet been established.

### Shelamim/Heichal Doors

Ravina then applies this principle to a ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *shelamim sheshachtan kodem sheniftachu daltot haheichal psulin* — a *shelamim* slaughtered before the doors of the *heichal* have been opened in the morning is invalid, as the *pasuk* states *ushchato pesach ohel mo'ed*, indicating that the doors of the *ohel mo'ed* must be open at the time of *shechita*. If Rav Chisda's framework holds — that lacking an action performed on the animal constitutes genuine unfitness — then by parallel reasoning, if one slaughtered a *shelamim* outside the *beis hamikdash* before the doors of the *heichal* were opened, one would be *patur*, since the animal was not yet fit: *mechusar pticha k'mechusar ma'aseh dami*.

This analogy, however, is somewhat strained. The drawing of lots actively defines the nature and status of the Yom Kippur goat — it determines which animal becomes the *se'ir Lashem* and which becomes the *se'ir l'azazel*. The opening of the doors, by contrast, is an external circumstance that does not redefine the *shelamim* itself; it is more analogous to the *musaf* waiting for prior *avodot* to conclude. Rashi addresses this by pointing to the *pasuk's* specific language — *ushchato pesach ohel mo'ed* — which makes the reality of *pesach ohel mo'ed* definitional to the *shelamim* itself, distinguishing it from a purely external event. The argument is acknowledgeably a stretch, and intuitively one might have classified the doors' opening as the *musaf*-type of waiting rather than the *hagralah*-type of direct action on the animal.

---

## Pesach Shelo Lishmo

### Pesach Liability

The *gemara* now challenges whether Rav Chisda is truly committed to the principle of *ho'il* — the concept that theoretical fitness for an alternative purpose generates *chiyuv*. It does so by citing another ruling in Rav Chisda's own name. A *korban pesach* that one slaughtered outside the *beis hamikdash* during the rest of the year: if one did so *lishmo*, intending it as a *pesach*, one is *patur*, because a *pesach* brought outside of its proper time — not on the fourteenth of Nisan — is invalid inside the *beis hamikdash*, and therefore slaughtering it outside incurs no liability. But if one slaughtered it *shelo lishmo*, intending it as a *shelamim*, one is *chayav* — because with that identity, the animal could have been validly brought inside the *beis hamikdash*.

### Akira Outside

The *gemara* presses: if one is *patur* when slaughtering the *pesach lishmo* outside, why not apply *ho'il* and say one should be *chayav* even *lishmo*, since in theory one could have slaughtered it *shelo lishmo* and thereby rendered it a valid *shelamim*? After all, this is precisely the logic applied to the Yom Kippur goats: even though they are designated for the interior service or for *azazel*, their potential use for the *musaf* creates *chiyuv*.

The *gemara* answers: *hachi hashta? Hasam ba'ei akira, hacha lo ba'ei akira.* The cases are not comparable. By the Yom Kippur goats, before the lots are drawn, the animals have no specifically defined *kedusha* for the interior service — their *kedusha* remains generic. To say they could be used for the *musaf* does not require any change to their basic identity; it simply acknowledges what they already are. By the *korban pesach*, in contrast, its identity is fixed and specific. To make it a *shelamim* requires *akira* — an active change of designation. The *gemara's* position is that we do not hold someone *chayav* for *shechutei chutz* on the basis of a theoretical fitness that would require first changing the animal's established identity.

### Natural Status

This distinction carries a subtle but important point about the nature of *kedusha*. The Yom Kippur goats, prior to the *hagralah*, possess a *kedusha* that has not yet been differentiated into a specific role. There is no identity that needs to be uprooted in order to use them for the *musaf*. The *pesach*, by contrast, carries a defined identity that does need to be uprooted — and that *akira* must take place through a valid *korban* service, not through an act performed outside the *beis hamikdash*.

---

## Pesach Shelo Lishmo (II)

### Rav Dimi/Yochanan

The *gemara* now records a tradition brought by Rav Dimi from *Eretz Yisrael* in the name of Rabbi Yirmiyah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *pesach sheshachto bachutz bish'ar yemot hashanah bein lishmo bein shelo lishmo patur* — a *pesach* slaughtered outside the *beis hamikdash* during the rest of the year is *patur* whether one did so *lishmo* or *shelo lishmo*.

### Challenge to Patur

Rav Dimi recounts that he reported this ruling before Rabbi Yirmiyah himself, who then raised the obvious challenge. The *patur* for *lishmo* is clear: a *pesach* brought as a *pesach* outside its proper time is invalid and therefore carries no *chiyuv* for *shechutei chutz*. But *shelo lishmo* — why should one be *patur* when slaughtering it as a *shelamim*? In that form, the animal could validly have been brought inside the *beis hamikdash*. The animal is fit *shelo lishmo bifnim*, and the act of slaughtering it outside with that intent should create *chiyuv*.

### Akira Rejected

Rabbi Yirmiyah's answer: *akiras chutz lav shemah akira* — an act of identity-change performed outside the *beis hamikdash* does not constitute a valid *akira*. The mechanism by which a *pesach* slaughtered *shelo lishmo* becomes a *shelamim* operates only when the *shechita* is performed as part of a legitimate *korban* service inside the *beis hamikdash*. An act of re-designation performed outside — even if the person declares *shelo lishmo* — leaves the animal's fundamental identity unchanged. It remains a *pesach*. And since it is a *pesach* being slaughtered outside the *beis hamikdash* during the rest of the year, the person is *patur*.

---

## Pesach Chayav

### Both Ways Chayav

The *gemara* then presents the contrasting report of Ravin, who also transmitted a teaching of Rabbi Yirmiyah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan — yet with a diametrically opposite ruling. Ravin reports: *pesach sheshachto bachutz bish'ar yemot hashanah bein lishmo bein shelo lishmo chayav* — one is *chayav* in both cases. The liability for *shelo lishmo* is straightforward: one has designated the animal as a *shelamim*, and with that identity it could have been validly brought inside. But Ravin's version has Rabbi Yochanan ruling *chayav* even *lishmo* — even when one slaughtered the animal explicitly as a *pesach*, despite the fact that in its current state it cannot be brought as such inside the *beis hamikdash*.

### Asham Analogy

The *gemara* supports this position by citing a *baraisa* and a ruling of Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tuvia. The *baraisa* addresses a *zav*, *zava*, *yoledes*, or *metzora* who brought their *chatat* or *asham* outside the *beis hamikdash* before their requisite period had elapsed. Since the *korban* is *mechusar zman* — not yet its proper time — and therefore cannot be validly brought inside, they are *patur*. However, their *olah* and *shelamim*, being generic *korbanot* not tied to a specific remedial purpose, could be brought at any time, and therefore slaughtering those outside incurs *chiyuv*.

Rabbi Chilkiya bar Tuvia then refines the ruling regarding the *asham*: *lo shanu ela lishmo aval shelo lishmo chayav.* It is only when one slaughters the *asham lishmo* — as an *asham*, which is not yet fit because the owner's period has not concluded — that one is *patur*. If one slaughtered it *shelo lishmo*, changing its designation to a different type of *korban* that could validly be brought, one is *chayav*. This maps precisely onto the *pesach* case: *lishmo* the *korban* is unfit; *shelo lishmo* it becomes fit — and therefore *chayav*. This would seem to confirm the position of Rav Chisda and argue against the ruling that one is *chayav* even *lishmo* by the *pesach*.

### Why Lishmo Chayav?

The pressing question then is: why, according to Ravin's version of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling, is one *chayav* even when slaughtering the *pesach lishmo*? The *asham* before its time is *patur lishmo* — why should the *pesach* be different?

One might suggest that even by the *asham lishmo*, one should be *chayav*, since in theory one could have changed its designation to *shelo lishmo* and thereby rendered it fit. But the *gemara* rejects this: *hasam ba'ei akira* — by the *asham*, to make it fit requires actively changing its identity. We do not hold someone *chayav* for *shechutei chutz* on the basis of what they could have done had they changed the animal's identity. The current identity is unfit; one is therefore *patur*. This is the identical logic applied to the *pesach* by Rav Dimi's version: *akiras chutz lav shemah akira*.

### Natural Shelamim

The resolution offered by Ravin's version is a fundamentally different conceptual claim: *hacha pesach bish'ar yemot hashanah shelamim ninhu* — a *pesach* during the rest of the year is, by its very natural status, a *shelamim*. No *akira* is required. Since it cannot be brought as a *pesach* outside of its proper time, it naturally defaults to the category of *shelamim*. Therefore, even when one slaughters it *lishmo* — insisting on treating it as a *pesach* — one is *chayav*, because the animal's actual standing, independent of one's intent, is already that of a *shelamim* fit for the *beis hamikdash*. One cannot escape *chiyuv* by declaring *lishmo* when the animal is naturally a *shelamim* in its present state.

This distinguishes the *pesach* from the *asham*. The *asham* does not naturally become a different type of *korban* when it is not yet the right time; its identity remains that of an *asham*, and one would have to actively change it. The *pesach*, by contrast, naturally inhabits the identity of a *shelamim* during the rest of the year, requiring no *akira* at all. According to this view, the act of declaring *lishmo* is simply an attempt to override a status that already exists — and since the animal is already a *shelamim* in reality, one is *chayav* regardless.

---

## Ashi vs. Yirmiyah

### Ashi Position

The *gemara* records that Rav Ashi teaches: *chayav* — *chayav* in both cases, *lishmo* and *shelo lishmo*. His reasoning follows the line of Ravin's transmission: the *pesach* during the rest of the year is naturally a *shelamim*, and thus always carries *chiyuv* for *shechutei chutz* regardless of the declared intent.

### Yirmiyah Position

Rav Yirmiyah of Difti, by contrast, teaches: *patur* — *patur* in both cases. *Kasavar pesach bish'ar yemot hashanah ba'ei akira*: in his view, the *pesach* does not naturally become a *shelamim*; its identity remains that of a *pesach*, and an active change of designation is required to make it into a *shelamim*. Therefore, when one slaughters it *lishmo*, it is an unfit *pesach* and one is *patur*. When one slaughters it *shelo lishmo*, one has attempted to change its identity, but *akiras chutz lav shemah akira* — identity-change outside the *beis hamikdash* is legally ineffective — and so the animal remains a *pesach*, and again one is *patur*.

### Identity Dispute

The dispute between Rav Ashi and Rav Yirmiyah of Difti therefore turns on a single foundational question: what is the default identity of a *pesach* during the rest of the year? Rav Ashi holds that it naturally is a *shelamim* — no *akira* is required, and *chiyuv* follows in both cases. Rav Yirmiyah of Difti holds that it retains its identity as a *pesach*, that *akira* is necessary to make it a *shelamim*, and that *akira* performed outside the *beis hamikdash* is no *akira* at all — yielding *patur* in both cases. The position that distinguishes *lishmo* from *shelo lishmo*, producing *chiyuv* only in the latter, represents the intermediate view in which the *pesach* does require *akira* but that *akira* is valid even outside — a position rejected by Rav Yirmiyah of Difti via *akiras chutz lav shemah akira*.

---

## Korban/Pesach Definition

### Non-Korban Exclusion

The *gemara* now turns to the scriptural basis of *shechutei chutz*. The *tanu rabbanan* cites the *pasuk* from *ish ish mi-beis Yisrael asher yishchat shor o kesev o ez ba-machane o asher yishchat mi-chutz la-machane v'el pesach ohel mo'ed lo hevi'o l'hakriv korban l'Hashem* — one who slaughters an animal without bringing it to the entrance of the *ohel mo'ed* as a *korban l'Hashem* is *chayav kareis*.

A preliminary question arises: does *korban* in this *pasuk* include *kodshei bedek habayis* — animals consecrated for their monetary value, to fund the upkeep of the *beis hamikdash*? Such animals are called *korban* in another context, as when donations were brought and described with that term. One might therefore think that slaughtering a consecrated animal, even one designated for the *bedek habayis* fund, outside the *beis hamikdash* creates *chiyuv*.

### Pesach Ohel Mo'ed Test

The *gemara* rejects this inclusion on the basis of the continuation of the *pasuk*: *v'el pesach ohel mo'ed lo hevi'o* — the animal must be one that is fit to be brought to the entrance of the *ohel mo'ed* as a *korban*. The interpretive rule established is: *kol hara'uy l'pesach ohel mo'ed chayav alav ba-chutz, kol she'eino ra'uy l'pesach ohel mo'ed ein chayavin alav ba-chutz*. Only an animal that is fit to be brought as a *korban* to the *ohel mo'ed* — that has significance as part of the sacrificial service there — generates *chiyuv* for *shechutei chutz*. Animals consecrated merely for their monetary value have no role as *korbanot* within the *ohel mo'ed* and therefore fall outside the prohibition.

### Sa'ir Excluded?

Having established this standard of *ra'ui l'pesach ohel mo'ed*, the *gemara* raises the question of the *sa'ir hamishtalei'ach*. This goat is brought to the *ohel mo'ed* — the drawing of lots takes place there — and it is an integral part of the Yom Kippur service. One might therefore argue that slaughtering it outside the *beis hamikdash* should incur *chiyuv*, since it is indeed *ra'ui lavo pesach ohel mo'ed*.

### L'Hashem Exclusion

The *gemara* addresses this through the phrase *l'hakriv korban l'Hashem* — to bring a *korban* to God. Only a *korban* that is entirely for God — *mi shemeyuchadim l'Hashem* — creates *chiyuv* when slaughtered outside. The *sa'ir hamishtalei'ach*, being designated *l'azazel* rather than *l'Hashem*, falls outside this category. Once the lot has designated it as *l'azazel*, it is no longer going to be brought as a *korban* inside the *beis hamikdash*, and therefore slaughtering it outside incurs no *chiyuv*. The *se'ir lachatas*, too, is addressed here: its ritual takes place outside the *beis hamikdash*, and it is therefore not a *korban* that generates *chiyuv* for *shechutei chutz* in the conventional sense.

---

## L'Hashem Scope

### Ramba Context

A striking tension now emerges. In the passage just discussed, *l'Hashem* served to *exclude* the *sa'ir l'azazel* from the *chiyuv* of *shechutei chutz*. But elsewhere the same term functions to *include* the *sa'ir l'azazel*. Rava resolves this by stating *hasam me'inyana dikra v'hacha me'inyana dikra*: in each context, the word *l'Hashem* must be read in light of what the surrounding *pasuk* is already speaking about, and its function — inclusive or exclusive — is determined by the default reading in that context.

### Ohel Mo'ed Exclusion

In the context of *shechutei chutz* and the *ohel mo'ed* passage, the *pasuk*'s language already naturally extends to include the *sa'ir* — it is brought to the *ohel mo'ed* and plays a central role in the Yom Kippur service. Since inclusion is the default, *l'Hashem* comes to redirect and *exclude*: it tells us that only what is entirely for God creates *chiyuv*, thereby removing the *sa'ir l'azazel* from the scope of the prohibition.

### Eight-Day Inclusion

In the context of the eight-day requirement — *yeratzeh l'korban isheh l'Hashem miyom hashmini vahal'ah* — the *pasuk* speaks of animals burnt on the altar, which would naturally *exclude* the *sa'ir hamishtalei'ach*, since it is not brought as an *isheh* offering on the altar. Since exclusion is the default there, *l'Hashem* comes to *include*: even the *sa'ir l'azazel* cannot be sanctified or used if it is less than eight days old.

---

## Mechusar Zman

### Lottery Principle

The *gemara* now explores why a separate scriptural derivation is needed to establish that the *sa'ir l'azazel* must be at least eight days old. The principle *ein hagoral kovei'a ela b'ra'uy l'shem* — the lot has legal force only when each goat is theoretically eligible to be designated for God — would seem to demand this automatically. For the lottery to be valid, each goat must be fit to serve as the *se'ir Lashem*; since a goat less than eight days old cannot serve *l'Hashem*, neither could it be eligible for the lot, and therefore it could not be used as a substitute *l'azazel* either.

### Substitute Goat

Rav Yosef answers that the derivation is needed for the position of Chanana ha-Mitzri, who teaches: *afilu dam bekos meivi chaveiro u'mezaveig lo* — even if the blood of the *se'ir Lashem* is already in the cup, ready for the service, and the *se'ir l'azazel* dies, one may bring a replacement goat and pair it with the blood of the first, without performing a new lottery. According to this view, in the scenario of a replacement goat, no lottery takes place — the animal is simply designated directly as the *se'ir l'azazel*. In such a case, there is no requirement that it be theoretically eligible to be the *se'ir Lashem*, and one might have thought an animal less than eight days old could serve. The *pasuk* is therefore necessary to tell us otherwise.

The *gemara* initially questions whether Chanana ha-Mitzri truly dispenses with the lottery, noting that one could read his position as requiring a new lottery with two goats. But Rav Yosef then identifies the ruling more precisely with the position of Rabbi Shimon, who states explicitly: *met echad meihem meivi chaveiro shelo b'hagralah divrei Rabbi Shimon* — if one of the two goats dies, one brings a replacement without a new lottery. Under Rabbi Shimon's view, then, the *sa'ir l'azazel* can be designated independently of the lottery mechanism, and the scriptural derivation for the eight-day requirement is necessary to preclude using an animal less than eight days old in such a case.

### Kedusha Transfer

Ravina offers a further scenario where the *sa'ir l'azazel* can be identified without a new lottery: *k'gon shehumam v'hifrish acher* — if the designated *sa'ir l'azazel* acquired a blemish, rendering it unfit, one brings a replacement and transfers the *kedusha* from the blemished animal to the new one. This is essentially a substitution through *kedusha*-transfer rather than through lottery, and the replacement animal's identity as *l'azazel* is established directly. In this scenario too, one might have thought to use an animal less than eight days old, and the scriptural exclusion is needed.

### Both Needed

The *gemara* then explains why both prohibitions — the eight-day minimum and the exclusion of a *ba'al mum* — require independent scriptural derivation and cannot be inferred from one another. Had the Torah written only the prohibition of *mechusar zman*, one might have thought that a *ba'al mum* poses no problem, since the animal is of proper age and its physical defect alone might not have been considered disqualifying for something designated *l'azazel* rather than *l'Hashem*. Had the Torah written only the exclusion of a *ba'al mum*, one might have thought that *mechusar zman* poses no problem for the *sa'ir l'azazel*, since the animal's immaturity is not a physical deformity and might not have been disqualifying when the destination is not the altar. *Tzricha* — both derivations are independently necessary.

### Sa'ir Status

This concludes with a conceptually rich observation. The *sa'ir l'azazel* is designated not *l'Hashem* but *l'azazel*. One might have thought its ritual function so different from that of a standard *korban* that requirements governing *korbanot* — no blemish, minimum age — simply would not apply. Yet the *gemara* demonstrates from two independent *psukim* that both requirements hold. The *sa'ir l'azazel*, despite its destination, retains a genuine status as a *korban*, and the demands placed upon it by these *psukim* underscore the degree to which it continues to inhabit the conceptual world of *korbanos*. The question of precisely how far that status extends — what it means for the *sa'ir l'azazel* to be, in some sense, *l'Hashem* even as it goes *l'azazel* — opens onto deeper questions about the nature of this remarkable *korban* that the *gemara* here begins, but does not conclude, to explore.

---

---

# Yoma 65

## Rav vs R. Yochanan

### New Lottery Setup

The daf opens in the middle of a debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan that began at the bottom of 64b. The case is as follows: of the two goats brought on Yom Kippur — one designated *l'Hashem* and one *la-Azazel* — one of them dies, necessitating a new lottery with a fresh pair. The question is which goat you ultimately use for the designation that did not die. If, for example, the goat *la-Azazel* died and the goat *l'Hashem* from the original pair is still alive, and you now draw a new lottery, the new goat *la-Azazel* clearly fills the vacancy. But which goat do you use *l'Hashem* — the surviving original, or the one from the new pair?

### Rav's Mitzvah B'Rishon

Rav holds that you use the goat from the original pair. The *Gemara* indicates that the *Mishnah* supports this position. Rav's reasoning rests on the principle of *mitzvah barishon*: as long as the original animal was the first designated for that role, you remain committed to using it. The *Gemara* notes that this position aligns with the teaching of Rabbi Yossi, who derived from an analogous case involving the *Korban Pesach* — where an animal was lost, a replacement was designated, and then the original was found — that the *mitzvah* attaches to the first animal.

### R. Yochanan Nidcheh

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees. He argues that the surviving goat from the original pair has become *nidcheh* — pushed away, rejected — and therefore cannot be used. The reasoning is that during the interval between one animal's death and the drawing of the new lottery, the surviving goat was in a state where it could not be used; that period of disqualification leaves a permanent mark. According to Rabbi Yochanan, the principle of *dichuy* applies, and you must therefore use the goat from the new pair.

### Ba'alei Chayim Nidchim

At the heart of this debate is a broader question: can a living animal be permanently rejected? The principle under discussion is *ba'alei chayim nidchim* — whether a live animal, once rendered temporarily unusable, is permanently stigmatized as though it were dead or otherwise disqualified. Rabbi Yochanan maintains that yes, even a living creature can be pushed away in this irrevocable sense. Rav disagrees: the ongoing vitality of a living animal resists permanent categorization, and it cannot be fully written off as rejected. There is something philosophically striking about this position — the sense that as long as something is alive, it retains a kind of irreducible openness that defies a fixed label of rejection.

### Tosafot Muvchar

Before continuing with the *Gemara*, it is worth pausing on a *Tosafot* at the bottom of 64b that is both incisive and illuminating. Recall that Rabbi Yossi's original teaching about *mitzvah barishon* included a qualification: if the second animal is of superior quality — *muvchar mimenu* — one should use the better one rather than the first. *Tosafot* raises the question of why we do not apply this same principle to the case of the two goats. If the second pair happens to consist of superior animals, should we not favor them over the first pair, even granting Rav's principle of *mitzvah barishon*?

### Tosafot Human Sphere

*Tosafot* answers with a distinction that cuts deep. The first text in *Tosafot* on 64b formulates it this way: the principle of choosing the superior animal — *muvchar mimenu* — applies only in the domain of *gvulin* (outside the Temple), or more precisely, to things that are eaten or that are performed in the *azarah* and thus visible to human beings. But for the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach*, which is sent away from the camp and is not experienced by the onlookers in any direct sense, or for the inner goat that is burned outside the three camps, even if the second animal is superior, one still adheres to the first. *Mitzvah barishon* overrides the quality consideration when the offering is beyond the human sphere of experience.

### Aesthetics Philosophy

Why is this *Tosafot* so striking? Because it addresses one of the fundamental tensions in the study of *Beit HaMikdash*: why does so much of the Temple service emphasize externals — unblemished animals, perfect priests, gleaming gold, flawless aesthetics? The usual answer is that God does not, in some ultimate sense, require these things, but human beings are profoundly shaped by what they see and experience. Beauty and perfection in the sacred space elevate our sense of the holy; a blemished offering would diminish our perception of what the service means.

What *Tosafot* is saying, in effect, is that this entire concern with superior quality is a concession to the human vantage point. It is relevant only when people are actually going to witness and experience the offering — in the *azarah*, or at table. When the offering moves beyond human experience — sent to a remote place, or brought into the innermost sanctum where no congregation follows — the calculus shifts. The priority returns to the intrinsic: which animal was first designated? Appearances and comparative quality, *Tosafot* implies, are accommodations to human psychology, not objective divine demands. This provides a quietly powerful counterweight to any overly literal reading of the Temple's aesthetic standards.

---

## Chatat Tzibur Dies

### Mishnah Chatat Tzibur

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishnah* to attempt to adjudicate the debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan. The *Mishnah* states: *she'ein chatas tzibur meisah* — a communal *chatat* does not die. The implication is that when a replacement is used for a communal *chatat*, the leftover animal is allowed to graze until it develops a blemish, at which point its sanctity is redeemed, rather than being left to die. This rule — that the animal must be left to die — applies specifically to a private *chatat*, not a communal one. Rabbi Yehudah disagrees, holding that even a communal *chatat* must be left to die if it was not used.

### Proving Rav Gemara

The *Gemara* now attempts to use the *Mishnah* to prove Rav's position. The implication of the *Mishnah* — that a communal *chatat* does not die whereas a private one in a similar scenario would — invites us to examine how this works according to both Rav and Rabbi Yochanan.

### Rabbi Abba Lost Offering

The *Gemara* cites a teaching of Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav, found at 60a: *hakol modim she'nitkapar be'she'eina avudah, she'avudah meisah* — all agree that if atonement was made using the animal that was never lost (call it B), then the animal that had been lost (call it A) must be left to die. The scenario: a *chatat* was set aside (A), it got lost, a second animal was sanctified as a replacement (B), and then A was found before B was offered. You now have a choice of which to bring. The *machlokes* concerns what happens to the animal you do not use. But on one point all agree: if you use B — the animal that was never lost — then A, which had been lost and then recovered, must be left to die.

### Niskaper Be'Acher

Why must A die when B is used? Because A had already experienced a period during which it was unusable — it was *avudah*, lost. When you then choose B over it, you compound that rejection: *niskaper beacher*, atonement was achieved through another. The category of *niskaper beacher* is precisely the trigger for a *chatat* to be left to die. A was pushed away once by being lost, pushed away further by having a substitute brought in, and so it has to die.

The debate between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan now comes into focus. According to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that *ba'alei chayim nidchim*, the surviving goat from the original pair is analogous to A in this case: it was unusable for a period, a new pair was brought to replace it, and so it is rejected and must die. That is consistent with the *Mishnah*'s implication that a private *chatat* in a similar scenario dies.

### Replacement vs Backup

But the *Gemara* asks: according to Rav, why would a private *chatat* die in this scenario at all? Rav holds *ba'alei chayim einam nidchim* — a living animal is not permanently pushed away. So the surviving original goat, which was never itself lost and never truly rejected, should remain fully usable. Why, then, should the scenario of the private *chatat* ending in death be the analogy?

The *Gemara* answers by drawing a critical distinction. Rabbi Oshaya teaches: *hamafresh shtei chataot le'achrayus* — if someone separates two sin offerings as mutual backups from the very outset, uses one, and the other is left over, the leftover one grazes; it does not die. The rule that a *chatat* must die in the *niskaper beacher* situation applies specifically when one animal was a replacement for another — when A was there first and B was subsequently designated to substitute for A. In that case, the original A is truly displaced. But when two animals are designated simultaneously as *le'achrayus* — backups for each other, neither subordinate to the other — using one does not condemn the other to death; it simply grazes.

### New Pair as Backup

According to Rav, this is precisely the structure of our case. Since Rav holds *ba'alei chayim einam nidchim*, the surviving original goat was never truly rejected. It remained fully valid throughout. When the new pair was brought, the new goat did not come to substitute for a rejected animal; it came alongside an animal that was still perfectly usable. The two — original and new — are thus in the relation of *le'achrayus*, mutual backups. Rav uses the original because of *mitzvah barishon*, but in principle either could have been used. In such a *le'achrayus* structure, the unused goat grazes rather than dies. This is why Rav holds that the case in the *Mishnah*, where the communal *chatat* grazes, parallels the private *chatat* case — because in his view, the private *chatat* in this scenario would also graze.

### Designated for Loss

The *Gemara* presses further. Rava offers the following resolution: since Rav holds *mitzvah barishon*, he is committed from the outset to using the first animal. That means, from the moment the new goat from the second pair is designated *l'Hashem*, everyone understands it will not actually be used. It was designated not as a genuine alternative, but as a structural necessity to complete the new lottery — *me'ikara ke'mafrish le'ibud dami*, it is as if it were separated to be lost from the start. It was never truly conceived as a viable option. And because it was never genuinely intended to be used, it is not a case of *le'achrayus* — mutual backup — at all. Rather, it is functionally equivalent to an animal that was set aside to be lost, like A in the earlier scenario. And therefore, according to the logic of *niskaper beacher*, this goat — the unused *l'Hashem* from the new pair — would die. And that is precisely why, even for a private *chatat*, the *Mishnah* implies it would die: because the structure here is not true *le'achrayus*, but rather one animal designated in name only, already consigned to irrelevance.

---

## Rabbi Yehudah Chatat

### Rabbi Yehudah Dies

The *Gemara* now turns to Rabbi Yehudah's position. Rabbi Yehudah holds that even a communal *chatat* — not just a private one — must be left to die when it is not used. The Rabbis maintain that a *chatat tzibur* is treated differently from a *chatat yachid*: the unused communal animal grazes. Rabbi Yehudah draws no such distinction: *bein yachid ubein tzibur*, whether private or communal, if the animal was not used, it dies.

### First Goat Dies

One might ask: does this mean Rabbi Yehudah requires the same animal to die twice? No — the *Gemara* clarifies that Rabbi Yehudah is talking about the first goat dying, not the same animal being condemned again. The structure of his position is simply that the rule of *niskaper beacher* applies uniformly, without the exemption the Rabbis carve out for communal sacrifices.

### Reversal of Pairing

Rabbi Yehudah's position involves a second, distinct disagreement — one that concerns not whether the unused animal dies, but *which* animal is left unused. Recall that Rabbi Yochanan holds *ba'alei chayim nidchim*: the surviving original goat is rejected and cannot be used, so you use the goat from the new pair. The Rabbis in the *Mishnah* — following Rav's framework — hold the opposite: use the original goat (*mitzvah barishon*) and let the new goat from the second pair graze. Rabbi Yehudah agrees that *ba'alei chayim nidchim*, and therefore the original surviving goat is the one that is rejected and dies. You use the goat from the new pair. But — and this is where his second disagreement lies — Rabbi Yehudah then says that unused goat from the new pair also dies, rather than grazes. He reverses the pairing in terms of which animal is condemned, precisely because he applies *ba'alei chayim nidchim*, and then demands death rather than grazing even for the communal offering.

### Rav and Rabbi Yehudah

This creates the following architecture of debate. There are effectively two independent disputes. The first is between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehudah over whether a *chatat tzibur* dies or grazes when unused. The second is between the positions that hold *ba'alei chayim nidchim* (Rabbi Yochanan; Rabbi Yehudah) and those that deny it (Rav). According to Rav, both debates are live between Rabbi Yehudah and the Rabbis: Rabbi Yehudah disagrees both on *chatat tzibur* (he says it dies) and on which animal is rejected (he holds *ba'alei chayim nidchim* and thus reverses the pairing). According to Rabbi Yochanan, however, there is really only one clear point of disagreement — the *chatat tzibur* question — because on the matter of *ba'alei chayim nidchim*, Rabbi Yochanan himself agrees with Rabbi Yehudah. The *Gemara* acknowledges this and concedes: *kashya* — it is difficult to identify a clean second dispute according to Rabbi Yochanan.

### Blood Spills Proof

The *Gemara* now turns to the scenario that demonstrates Rabbi Yehudah's position on *ba'alei chayim nidchim*. Rabbi Yehudah states: *nishpach hadam yamut hamishtalei'ach* — if the blood of the inner goat is spilled, the goat designated to be sent away must be left to die. Conversely, *mes hamishtalei'ach yishafech hadam* — if the *mishtalei'ach* dies, the blood must be spilled.

The first half is the clearer of the two. Before the blood is placed on the altar, the *mishtalei'ach* cannot be sent off — *lo avad mitzvato*, the *mitzvah* has not yet been performed. If the blood spills, there is a period during which the *mishtalei'ach* simply cannot be used, and according to Rabbi Yehudah's principle of *ba'alei chayim nidchim*, that temporary disqualification is irrevocable. The *mishtalei'ach* must die.

The second half is the more surprising one: if the *mishtalei'ach* dies, the blood must be spilled. The *Gemara* asks why: *ha avad lei mitzvato* — surely the *mitzvah* of the *mishtalei'ach* has already been accomplished? In what sense? One might think: the lot was drawn, the animal was designated. That is all that was required. But this leads to Rashi's remarkable teaching.

### Rashi Core Lottery

Rashi states something that at first seems shocking. On the question of what obligations are truly *me'akev* — indispensable — with respect to the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach*, he writes: *kol davar me'akev bo eina ela hagrala bilvad* — the only act that is truly indispensable is the *hagralah*, the drawing of the lot, which establishes the animal's identity as the *se'ir* designated *la-Azazel*. We know from an earlier *sugya* that Rabbi Yehudah holds that if the *viduy* — the confession — was not performed, the service is nonetheless *kasher*. Rashi extends this: not only is the *viduy* not *me'akev*, but *kol sheken deshiluach d'lo me'akev* — the sending of the goat off the cliff is also not indispensable *bedi'eved*. If the animal designated *la-Azazel* dropped dead after the *hagralah* and the blood was offered, without any *viduy* and without being pushed off the cliff, the *mitzvah* has been fulfilled.

How does Rashi know this? He derives it from the verse's use of the word *chukah*, which limits the *me'akev* requirements to those things done by the *kohen* in the white garments — the blood service in the inner sanctum — and explicitly excludes the acts performed by the designated individual (*ish iti*) who takes the goat to the wilderness. The central symbol, in this reading, is the *hagralah* — the drawing of the lot that assigns each goat its identity. Everything else, including the dramatic scene of the goat going over the cliff, is important *lechatchilah* but not ultimately *me'akev*.

This is, as Rashi frames it, a powerful and clarifying insight. The *viduy* is what the Sages emphasize as creating the *kaparah* — the confession that transforms the Temple ritual into something that speaks directly to a post-Temple reality of *teshuvah*. But according to Rabbi Yehudah, not even the *viduy* is indispensable. What remains as the absolute core is simply the *hagralah*: the designation, the lottery, the identification of each animal with its role. All the subsequent drama — the confession, the procession, the cliff — is meaningful but not constitutive.

### Scapegoat Stand Alive

The *Gemara* then raises the natural question. If *bedi'eved* all that is required is the *hagralah*, and the *mishtalei'ach* then dropped dead, what obligation remains? Why should the blood need to be spilled? The answer comes from the verse: *ya'amad chai lifnei Hashem l'chaper alav* — the *se'ir* designated *la-Azazel* must stand alive before God to atone. The *Gemara* derives from this that the *mishtalei'ach* must remain alive through the moment of *matan dam* — while the blood of the other goat is being applied in the inner sanctum. The two animals must both be present and functional during the act of atonement: one *l'Hashem*, one *la-Azazel*. After the blood has been offered, it is true that the *mishtalei'ach* could *bedi'eved* drop dead without further consequence — no *viduy*, no sending off the cliff required. But during the blood service, the verse demands that it stand alive.

Therefore, if the *mishtalei'ach* dies before or during the blood offering, a new lottery must be held — not to fulfill some additional *mitzvah* with the live goat, but because the verse requires a living *la-Azazel* goat to be standing while the *kohen* performs the blood service. This also provides a resolution to the theological discomfort some feel with the entire *Azazel* ritual: by establishing that the sending off the cliff is not ultimately *me'akev*, the *Gemara* effectively decenters the dramatic wilderness scene. What matters occurs entirely within the *mikdash*.

---

## Next Year's Offering

### Shekalim Trumah

The *Gemara* transitions to a related question drawn from tractate Shekalim. When a city collects its half-shekel contributions and sends them to the *Beit HaMikdash*, at what point is the city's obligation considered discharged? The answer hinges on the *trumat halishka* — the ritual scooping of funds from the chamber where the collected *shekalim* were stored. Three times a year, the treasurers would formally lift out funds from the chamber to purchase communal *korbanot*. The moment that *terumah* was taken, any money that had already been donated — even if it had not yet physically arrived — was considered registered and paid.

### Lost Money Timeline

If the money sent by the city was lost or stolen after the *terumah* was taken, the city is considered to have paid. The carriers must take an oath before the *gizbarin* (Temple treasurers) that they were not negligent, and the city is absolved. If, however, the loss occurred before the *terumah* was taken, the donation has not yet been officially registered, and the city must contribute again. In that case, the carriers take an oath to the city's residents, and the city itself must collect and send a second round of *shekalim*.

### Duplicate Shekalim

A further question arises: if the lost money is subsequently recovered — or if robbers return it — after the city has already paid a second time, the city now holds two sets of *shekalim*. The first position in the *Mishnah* holds that both sets are applied to the current year's obligation, with no possibility of applying the surplus toward the following year. You cannot prepay next year's tax with this year's designated funds.

### R. Yehudah Obligation

Rabbi Yehudah disagrees. He holds that *chovas hashana hazo kereivah l'shana haba'ah* — an obligation incurred for this year's service, if it was not used, can be carried forward and applied to next year's obligation. This opens the door to the *Gemara*'s next inquiry.

### Abaye Challenge

Abaye challenges this position. If Rabbi Yehudah allows last year's unfulfilled obligation to be redirected toward the following year, why does the *Mishnah* require the leftover *par* and *se'ir* of Yom Kippur — the ox and the goat — to die when not used? And similarly, communal *chataot* brought when the entire community sinned through *avodah zarah* — when a substitute was designated and then the original was found — why not simply hold the unused animal over until next Yom Kippur and use it then?

### This Year's Funds

The initial response invokes a teaching of Rav Tavi in the name of Rav in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya. The verse states: *zos olas hachodesh bechodsho* — this is the burnt offering of each month in its month. From here the Torah teaches: renew and bring a *korban* from new funds. Once an animal has been purchased with this year's *shekalim* — drawn from this year's *trumat halishka* — it is designated as this year's offering. Its identity is bound to the year of its purchase. You cannot carry a 5774 *korban* over to 5775.

This answers the *se'ir* case. But Abaye notes that it does not fully answer the *par* case, because the *Kohen Gadol*'s ox is purchased from his own private funds, not from communal *shekalim*. And even as to the *se'ir*, the principle of buying from new funds is only *lechatchilah*, as Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel: *ve'im hevi min hayashan yatza* — if the communal *korban* was bought with last year's funds, it is valid *bedi'eved*, even if a *mitzvah* was missed. So the obligation to let it die remains unexplained.

---

## Lottery Designation

### Rav Zeira Lottery Year

Rav Zeira offers a more fundamental answer for the *se'ir* case. The lot — the *hagralah* — establishes the animal's identity for that year only. *Ein hagoral kovei'ah mishana lachavertah* — the lottery of one year does not carry forward to bind the next. A goat designated *la-Azazel* in year one cannot carry that designation into year two; in year two, a new lottery must be drawn. So you cannot simply hold the goat over and use it next Yom Kippur under last year's designation.

### Gezerah Old Lot

One might respond: so redraw the lottery! Use the surviving goat this Yom Kippur along with another goat, draw a fresh lot, and if it falls *la-Azazel* again, use it. To this the *Gemara* answers: *gezeirah shema yomru hagoral kovei'ah mishana lachavertah* — we are concerned that people will see the same goat used in the new lottery and assume that last year's *goral* somehow carried over. The appearance of continuity, even when a new lottery is technically performed, creates a misleading impression that must be avoided.

### Kohen Gadol Dies

For the *par* — the ox of the *Kohen Gadol* — the *Gemara* eventually settles on a different reasoning. The ox is purchased from the *Kohen Gadol*'s personal funds. If a new *Kohen Gadol* is appointed by the following Yom Kippur — which, as the *Gemara* notes, was quite common during the Second Temple period — he cannot use his predecessor's ox. The animal belonged to the previous *Kohen Gadol*, and an offering must come from its owner. *Chatas she-meisu be'aleha* — a *chatat* whose owners have died cannot be used. Holding the ox over risks exactly this scenario.

### Gezerah Cycle

The *Gemara* attempts to construct a mutual *gezeirah* between the ox and the goat cases: don't use the ox because people will think the goat is also permitted to carry over, and don't use the goat because people will think the ox is permitted to carry over. The *Gemara* is visibly dissatisfied with this recursive reasoning — *umishum gezeirah yamusu?* — just because of a *gezeirah* should these animals die? The circularity of using each case as a *gezeirah* against the other is recognized as unsatisfying.

### Age Disqualification

The *Gemara* finally arrives at what it acknowledges should have been the straightforward answer all along: *ikara de-chatas she-avrah shenasa hi* — the goat is simply, as a practical matter, too old by next Yom Kippur. A *se'ir* must be within its first year; a goat that sat out one Yom Kippur and is being brought to the next is almost certainly more than a year old. This is not a *gezeirah* — it is the direct application of the animal's *peshut*-level disqualification.

### Solar Year Technicality

The *Gemara* raises one technical qualification: this is not an absolute certainty if one follows the view of Rabbi, who holds that *shenat temimah* — a full year — is measured as three hundred and sixty-five solar days rather than twelve lunar months. Rabbi derives this from the law of *batei arei chomah* (houses in walled cities), where the Torah uses the phrase *shenat temimah*, and Rabbi understands this to mean a full solar year. If one extends this principle generally, then the disqualification of an animal that is "more than a year old" would be measured in solar terms. If the goat was very young when Yom Kippur occurred — eight days old, for example — and the following year is a standard lunar year, it is theoretically possible that by the next Yom Kippur the animal is still within three hundred and sixty-five days of age.

### Final Reasons Deaths

Nevertheless, the practical resolution is clear. The overwhelming majority of cases — one hundred out of one hundred according to the Sages, and ninety-nine out of one hundred even according to Rabbi — the goat will be too old by the following Yom Kippur. That is the real reason the *se'ir* must die rather than be held over. And for the *par*, the most compelling reason is that the *Kohen Gadol* may well have died in the intervening year, in which case the ox of the previous *Kohen Gadol* is unusable for his successor. Both animals thus have sound, non-circular reasons for dying, grounded in the practical realities of what they are and who owns them. The *Gemara* will continue this discussion in the following daf.

---

---

# Yoma 66

## Surplus Animals

### R. Yehuda vs. Chachamim

The Gemara opens with a question that has been under discussion: what happens when one of the paired animals — the goat or the ox — is lost or dies and must be replaced, leaving the original animal unused? A debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the Chachamim governs this situation. The Chachamim hold that a communal *chatas* in this circumstance is sent out to pasture — even if a replacement was ultimately used — while Rabbi Yehuda holds that it must be left to die. The Gemara's question presses on Rabbi Yehuda's position: given that he elsewhere rules that money set aside for the *shekel* and later superseded may be carried forward to the following year, why not simply hold over the unused animal for next year's service? You sanctified the animal for this year; surely it could serve next year instead.

### Goat Age Problem

The Gemara has been working through a series of answers, some applying to the ox, some to the goat, each falling short of a fully satisfying resolution. The most recent and seemingly obvious answer is that by the following year the goat would be more than a year old, and the goat offering must come from within its first year of life. So straightforward is this answer that one wonders why the Gemara did not propose it at the outset.

The Gemara then adds a further wrinkle: it invokes a *gezeira* based on the possibility that the goat will not yet be a year old. The Gemara appeals here to the position of Rebbi, who rules in the context of the sale of a house in a walled city — where the Torah specifies *shana temima*, a full year — that one follows the solar year rather than the lunar year. It is thus theoretically possible, however rarely, that by the following year's *Yom Kippur* the goat would still fall within its first solar year. To cover even that edge case, the Gemara invokes the principle of *lo pelug* — we do not distinguish within the rule. This is admittedly strange on two counts: first, why legislate for such a far-fetched scenario? Second, Rebbi's solar-year calculation was stated specifically in the context of walled-city sales, not animal age. Nevertheless, this line of reasoning explains why the goat cannot simply be held over.

### Ox Gezeira

The Gemara is not yet satisfied. It asks: *hateinach se'ir* — granted, this explains the goat; *par mai ika lemeimar* — but what prevents holding the ox over to next year? The Gemara's answer is *gezeira par atu se'ir*: we decree that the ox may not be held over lest one come to hold the goat over as well, even though the goat would then be too old. The ox, by contrast, has considerably more latitude with respect to age — a range of roughly two to four years depending on the opinion, with Rabbi Meir's position that three years and above is always acceptable — so age is not itself an obstacle for the ox. The concern is one of conflation: permitting the ox to be held over might lead to permitting the goat as well, where the age issue does pose a genuine problem.

But the Gemara remains dissatisfied. Is this *gezeira* — this somewhat remote concern — really sufficient reason to mandate that the animal die? The word *umishum gezeira yamut* captures the Gemara's incredulity.

### Resh Lakish Position

The Gemara now introduces a further complication. Even if one accepts the age argument as a reason not to hold the goat over, why does it follow that the animal must die? Resh Lakish rules that a *chatas* whose year has passed — meaning it can no longer be offered because it is over-age — does not die. Rather, *ro'in osah ke'ilu hi omedes b'veis hakvaros*, we regard it as if it were standing in a cemetery: inaccessible, but not intrinsically invalid. It goes out to pasture. Thus even granting that the goat cannot be used next year due to its age, the proper disposition should be to let it graze — not to let it die. So the Gemara must still explain Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that the animal dies.

---

## Takala Rationale

### Rava's Answer

At this point the Gemara offers the resolution that had in fact been anticipated in prior discussion: *ella amar Rava*, here is Rava's answer. The reason you may not hold these animals over until the following year is *gezeira mishum takala* — a concern of stumbling, meaning a fear that one will come to accidentally derive benefit from or misuse the animal during the intervening period. An animal set aside and awaiting use a year hence sits in your mind as something that will eventually be brought; and precisely because it remains a viable candidate for the altar, you remain engaged with it, and the risk of inadvertent transgression is real.

### Hekdesh Disposal

The Gemara brings a *baraita* to anchor this concern: *ein makdishin ve'ein maarichin ve'ein machrimin bazman hazeh* — nowadays one does not sanctify animals for *hekdesh*, does not undertake *ha'arakhah* (pledging the assessed value of a person or object to the Temple treasury), and does not declare *cherem* (another form of consecration to the treasury). The reason is the very concern of *takala* — that with no functioning Temple to absorb these sanctified items, they will simply sit in one's possession and create opportunities for misuse.

If one has nevertheless done so, the law prescribes specific modes of disposal. An animal — *behema* — is subject to *te'aker*. Fruit, clothing, and ordinary vessels — *peirot, ksut, vekeilim* — are left to rot, *yirakvu*. Money and metal objects — *ma'ot uchlei matachot* — are cast into the Dead Sea, *yolichem leyam hamelach*. The phrase used for money is *yolich hana'ah*, which is slightly unusual — it could suggest transferring the monetary value rather than the object itself, though in context it may simply mean throwing the coins themselves into the sea.

Tosafot raises a pointed question here: why not simply transfer the *kedusha* to a nominal sum of money and dispose of that? There is even a teaching that nowadays, since no actual Temple treasury will benefit, one may transfer *kedusha* at a steep discount — sanctifying something worth a thousand and transferring it to an object worth one. Why not use that mechanism? Tosafot acknowledges that in some cases this is indeed done, but explains that here the law deliberately does not make it so easy. The goal is not merely to solve the technical problem but to introduce a degree of consequence — not so much punitive as preventive — that discourages people from developing the habit of casual sanctification in a world without a Temple.

### Te'aker Definition

The Gemara asks: *ve'eizo hi ikur* — what exactly is *te'aker*? Literally the word suggests something like hamstringing, but the Gemara clarifies: *no'el delet befaneha umeta me'eleha* — you lock the door in front of it, you enclose it in a pen, and you let it die on its own. You do not actively destroy it, because to do so would constitute *bizayon hekdesh* — a degradation of consecrated property. But you do take a definitive step to render it inaccessible and to ensure that it will go to waste. The underlying point is that consecrated property may not simply sit available; it must be placed in a condition where its destruction is assured and its misuse is impossible.

### Takala Analysis

The Gemara now asks a more granular question: *takala demai* — what specific form of stumbling is the concern? Two possibilities are considered. The first is that we fear the person will actually come to offer the animal as a sacrifice, even though it is not currently fit for that purpose — either because its year has not yet come around, or because it was sanctified for a different service. The second possibility is a lesser concern: not that it will be brought to the altar, but that one will come to derive mundane benefit from it, such as shearing its wool or using it for labor.

The Gemara raises an objection to both possibilities: *afillu kol re'uyot nami* — if we are worried about either form of misuse, we should apply the same concern to all animals that are put out to pasture awaiting a blemish so that their value can be redeemed. Why are we comfortable letting those animals graze without worrying about misuse?

The Gemara resolves this by drawing a critical distinction: *le'olam takala de-hakrava* — the concern is indeed that the animal might be accidentally brought as an offering. *Henakh de-lav bar hakrava ninhu lo tarid behu* — those animals that can never be brought to the altar themselves — those that must graze until they develop a blemish and whose value is then redeemed — nobody is thinking of actually bringing the animal itself. Its path to the altar is categorically foreclosed, and so people put it out of their minds. *Ha de-var hakrava hu tarid bah* — but this animal, which one is holding over because it will in fact be eligible to be brought next *Yom Kippur*, remains constantly on one's mind. One is actively anticipating using it, and that mental engagement creates the risk that before the appointed time arrives, one might inadvertently misuse it.

### Animal Categories

The Gemara's answer, it must be admitted, is not entirely satisfying in all directions. Taking stock of where we stand: the case of the ox is now explained — in theory, it could be held over and used next year, but because one's mind remains fixed on it as a future offering, we prohibit holding it over on grounds of *takala* and require that it die. That is somewhat counterintuitive — one might observe that the very seriousness with which someone intends to bring it as a *korban* is being used as the reason to destroy it — but that is the Gemara's logic.

The case of the goat, however, remains partially unresolved. The goat will not be fit for use next year due to its age; it is thus in the same category as an animal that will never be brought to the altar itself. According to the Gemara's own logic, animals in that category are not subject to *takala* concerns — people don't think about them — and accordingly should be left to graze, not die. Furthermore, Resh Lakish's position that an over-age *chatas* goes to pasture and does not die has not been fully addressed. So the answer works cleanly for the ox but leaves something to be desired for the goat — and notably for those who accept Resh Lakish, the question of why the animal must die in either case remains somewhat open.

One might also raise the concern of *tzaar ba'alei chayim* — the prohibition against causing unnecessary animal suffering. It is striking that the Gemara institutes what amounts to a slow death by confinement in order to forestall an admittedly remote risk of human inadvertence. Some Rishonim do cite cases like *te'aker* as evidence that the prohibition of *tzaar ba'alei chayim* can be overridden for legitimate human needs — analogizing, for instance, to the use of animals for medical purposes. But in this context the "human need" is ritual observance and the prevention of transgression, and the suffering imposed on the animal serves no benefit to it whatsoever. The dissonance is real, especially given the Torah's own solicitude for animals — the obligation to assist a struggling donkey, for instance. There is no fully satisfying answer here.

### Takala Debate

The Gemara adds a further observation: *u-v-takala atzma tannai hi* — the underlying question of whether we are concerned about *takala* in cases of animals held over for future use is itself a dispute among Tannaim.

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *pesach she-lo karev be-Rishon yikarev be-Sheni* — if one sanctified an animal for *korban Pesach* and did not bring it on the first *Pesach*, give it to someone who will be bringing on *Pesach Sheni* in Iyar; and if it was not brought then either, hold it over for the following year. A second *baraita* flatly contradicts this: *lo yikarev* — do not bring it the following year.

The Gemara asks: is this not a dispute about *takala* — whether holding a *korban* over for an entire year creates an unacceptable risk of misuse? One *baraita* permits it, unconcerned; the other forbids it, apparently concerned.

The Gemara considers but then partially deflects this reading. The debate over the *Pesach* animal itself may simply turn on whether one follows Rebbi's solar year — the same question about whether the animal can still be within its first year by the time of the next *Pesach*, not a principled dispute about *takala* at all.

However, the Gemara then cites yet another *baraita*: *ve-chen ma'ot* — and similarly with money sanctified for a *korban Pesach*. Here too there is a debate: hold the money over for next year, or do not. And here the age question is entirely irrelevant — money does not become over-age. Therefore, *shma mina*, this dispute must be about *takala* itself: do we fear that holding sanctified money over for a year will lead to misuse?

This is the critical distinction the Gemara has been building toward. At one extreme: an animal put out to pasture to await a blemish, with no expectation of ever being brought itself — no *takala* concern, all opinions agree. At the other extreme: sanctified objects in the present era with no Temple in sight, to be held indefinitely — clearly a *takala* concern, all opinions agree, and the law mandates destruction. The middle case is the one genuinely in dispute: an object sanctified for a *korban* that cannot be used now but will be eligible in a year's time. Is that a *takala* concern or not? That is the debate between the Tannaim, and it is precisely the debate underlying Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about the goat and the ox.

---

## Scapegoat Viduy

### Viduy Procedure

With the questions surrounding surplus animals resolved — at least partially — the Gemara returns to the *Mishnah* and to the actual *avodah* of *Yom Kippur*. By this point in the service, the *Kohen Gadol* has completed the blood rites of the ox and the inner goat: the *ketores* in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the sprinkling of the blood in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, then on the *Parochet*, then on the outer *mizbe'ach*, and finally the pouring of the blood at the base of the altar. Now the Mishnah turns to the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach*, the goat that will be sent away.

*Ba lo eitzel sa'ir hamishtalei'ach* — he comes to the goat that is to be dispatched. *Ve-someich shtei yadav alav* — he places both his hands upon it, and he recites the *viduy*, the confession.

### Viduy Text

The text of the *viduy* is as follows: *Anna Hashem, chatu avu pash'u lifanecha amcha beis Yisrael* — please, God, your people Israel have sinned, transgressed, and rebelled before You. The ordering of these three categories — *chet*, *avon*, and *pesha* — reflecting unintentional sin, deliberate iniquity, and willful rebellion respectively — is a matter that has already been discussed in the Gemara; the *girsa* in the printed *mishnayot* differs from what appears here, and that ordering is significant in its own right.

The *viduy* continues: *Anna Hashem, kaper na lachatayim vela'avonot veli-fsha'im shechatu ve-shavu she-pash'u lifanecha amcha beis Yisrael, kakatuv be-Toras Moshe avdecha leimor: ki vayom hazeh yechaper aleichem letaher eschem mikol chatoseichem lifnei Hashem titharu* — please, God, atone now for the sins, iniquities, and rebellions that Your people Israel have committed before You, as it is written in the Torah of your servant Moshe: for on this day atonement shall be made for you to purify you; from all your sins before God you shall be purified.

### Response Ritual

*Ve-hakohanim ve-ha'am ha'omdim ba'azarah, ke-she-hayu shom'im shem ha-meforash she-hu yotzei mipi Kohen Gadol, hayu kor'im u-mishtachavim ve-noflim al pneihem ve-omrim: baruch shem kevod malchuto le-olam va'ed* — the priests and the people standing in the *azarah*, when they heard the explicit divine name emerging from the mouth of the *Kohen Gadol*, would bow and prostrate themselves and fall upon their faces, saying: blessed is the name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever.

It is worth noting that this formulation differs from the dramatic liturgical climax familiar from our *machzor*. In the prayer service, the sequence builds to a moment where the *Kohen Gadol*, after naming God explicitly, pauses while the people prostrate themselves, and then finishes the verse with *titharu* — "you shall be purified" — in a soaring declaration of communal purity. The *Mishnah* here contains the same basic elements but does not stage them with quite that degree of theatrical buildup, and the word *titharu* does not appear as a climactic final pronouncement in the same way.

---

## Scapegoat Dispatch

### Handoff

Following the *viduy*, the *Mishnah* states: *masru lemi she-hayu molicho* — he handed the goat over to the person who would carry it, running with it through the city and out to the cliff beyond the city limits. The *Mishnah* then establishes: *hakol kesherim leholicho* — anyone is eligible to perform this task.

### Kohein Monopoly

Despite the theoretical eligibility of all, the *Mishnah* records: *ella she-asu hakohanim* — the *Kohanim* established a practice, *teva*, that they would not permit *Yisraelim* to perform this role. Even though the law allowed it, the custodians of the Temple service reserved this function for their own. Rabbi Yose notes an exception: there was a case in which Arselah of Tzippori performed this task, and he was a *Yisrael*. But the general practice remained in *Kohen* hands.

### Ramp Purpose

The *Mishnah* further records that a ramp was constructed for the person carrying out the goat, *mipnei haBavliyim* — on account of the Babylonians, who would pull at his hair and call out to him: *tol vatzei, tol vatzei* — take it and get out, take it and get out — apparently expressing a kind of frenzied urgency to be rid of the communal sins. The ramp provided a protected corridor so that the designated carrier could exit without interference. There is likely also a geographic dimension: the Temple Mount abuts the Kidron Valley, and a ramp spanning from the Temple precincts toward the Mount of Olives — where, notably, the *Parah Adumah* rite was also performed — would enable the carrier to traverse the topography more quickly and directly, just as such a ramp was used to convey the red heifer across the valley without descending all the way to the valley floor.

---

## Scapegoat Viduy (II)

### Viduy Recipients

The *Mishnah* having completed its description of the *viduy* on the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach*, the Gemara now raises a pointed question: *ve-ilu bnei Aharon kedoshecha lo ka'amar* — in this *viduy*, the *Kohen Gadol* made no mention of *Bnei Aharon*, the priests. He spoke only of the people of Israel. *Man tanna* — who is the Tanna that holds this position?

Rabbi Yirmiyah says: this is not according to Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yehuda explicitly holds that the *Kohanim* do receive atonement through the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach* — *yesh lahem kappara be-sa'ir hamishtalei'ach* — and therefore he would expect the *Kohanim* to be named in the *viduy*.

Abaye responds: even according to Rabbi Yehuda, the *Mishnah* can be explained. *Atu Kohanim lav bi-khlal amcha Yisrael ninhu?* — are *Kohanim* not included within "your people Israel"? Perhaps the very reason not to single them out is to emphasize their unity with the entire people. For issues of *tumat Mikdash* — the impurity of entering the Temple in a state of *tumah* — different groups bear distinct legal identities and are addressed separately. But for all other sins, the intent of the *viduy* may be precisely to underscore that *Kohanim* and *Yisraelim* stand together before God, and singling them out would undercut that message.

### Kohein vs. People

To understand the stakes of this debate, it is helpful to map the various atonements of *Yom Kippur*. There is the *par bifnim* — the ox whose blood is brought into the *Kodesh Kodashim* — and the *sa'ir bifnim* — the inner goat. These rites accomplish atonement specifically related to *tumat Mikdash*: the sin of entering or desecrating the Temple while in a state of *tumah*. According to the Gemara, the *par* atones for the *Kohanim* in this regard, and the inner *sa'ir* for the *Yisraelim*. Then there is the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach*, which, on the simpler reading, covers all other sins for all of *Klal Yisrael* — *Kohanim* included in *Yisrael* — the other six hundred and twelve commandments not addressed by the blood rites inside.

A more complex view, however, holds that the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach* with its *viduy* atones for the other sins of the *Yisraelim*, while the *Kohanim*'s atonement for all of their sins — not just *tumat Mikdash* but everything else — flows from a separate track. The *viduy* that the *Kohen Gadol* recited earlier over his own *par*, and the blood brought inside, account for the *Kohanim*'s other sins as well. Under this reading, the *viduy* alone — without any blood rite accompanying it — is what achieves *kappara* for the *Kohanim*'s non-*Mikdash* sins, which is a striking theological point: the power of the confession itself, independent of the sacrificial act, accomplishes atonement.

This connects to the observation we noted earlier: the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach* could, in principle, fall and die immediately after the *viduy* is recited, and the atonement would still be effective. According to one opinion, even without the *viduy*, the mere act of the *goral* — the lottery — suffices. What emerges is that the Yom Kippur service increasingly foregrounds the *viduy* as the locus of atonement, a move that one might read as pointing toward the post-Temple reality in which confession, rather than blood rite, becomes the central act.

The other dimension of the more complex view — that the *Kohanim*'s atonement is entirely separate from and different from that of the people — raises questions of its own. What does it mean that the *Kohanim*, even in their capacity as ordinary human beings rather than Temple functionaries, receive a categorically distinct *kappara*? The simpler reading, which sees the *tumat Mikdash* rites as the only point of differentiation and the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach* as covering everyone equally for all other sins, is in many ways more theologically comfortable. Both readings, however, are present in the Gemara.

---

## Scapegoat Dispatch (II)

### Conditions

The Gemara now takes up a *baraita* that expounds the verse *ve-shillacho be-yad ish itti* — and he shall send it by the hand of a ready man. From this verse the *baraita* derives three separate rules. The word *ish* — man — teaches *lehachshir et ha-zar*, that even a non-*Kohen* is eligible. The word *itti* — timely, designated — teaches that the sending must occur in its proper time, *va-afilu be-Shabbat*, even on *Shabbat*, and *va-afilu be-tumah*, even in a state of *tumah*.

### Non-Kohein

The derivation that a non-*Kohen* may perform this task is, the Gemara notes, not immediately obvious. *Pesita* — it might seem self-evident, since this is not an *avodah* performed within the Temple precincts — but one might have thought that since the verse connects this act to *kappara*, to atonement, perhaps it requires a *Kohen* as performer. The verse therefore specifies *ish* — any man — to preclude that inference.

### Shabbat Issue

The ruling that this may be performed even on *Shabbat* requires explanation: what *Shabbat* violation might arise? The answer given is *techumin de-rabbanan* — the rabbinic restriction on traveling beyond the *Shabbat* boundary — but Rav Sheshet goes further: the verse is needed to permit carrying the goat on one's shoulders if it is sick. Specifically, if the goat became ill and could not walk on its own, may one carry it — an act that would ordinarily be a biblical *melacha* on *Shabbat*?

The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Natan, carrying a live being does not constitute a biblical violation of *Shabbat*, because *chai nosei et atzmo* — a living creature partially supports its own weight. If so, no verse would be needed to permit carrying the sick goat. But the Gemara resolves this: *choleh shani* — a sick animal is different. If the animal is ill, it cannot adequately bear its own weight, and the principle of *chai nosei et atzmo* does not apply. There is therefore a genuine biblical concern of carrying, and the verse is needed to override it. This has broader implications for questions about carrying infants or incapacitated individuals on *Shabbat*, but those discussions belong elsewhere.

### Yom Kippur Carrying

Rafram draws an inference from the fact that the verse had to specify *Shabbat* in particular: *ve-ein eiruv ve-hotza'ah le-Yom HaKippurim* — if *Shabbat* carrying needed explicit biblical permission, it must be because *Yom Kippur* does not carry a biblical prohibition of carrying. Since no verse was needed to permit this act on *Yom Kippur* alone, *Yom Kippur* must be like *Yom Tov* in this regard: no biblical restriction on *hotza'ah*, hence no need for *eiruv* either. The *chiddush* of the verse is therefore only for *Shabbat*.

### Tosafos Rejection

Tosafot flatly rejects this inference, citing the Gemara in Kerisot, which dismisses Rafram's statement as *bedusa* — effectively, a position not worthy of serious consideration. The correct analysis, Tosafot argues, is that the verse does not prove anything about *Yom Kippur* carrying. Rather, there is an obvious reason why no verse is needed for *Yom Kippur*: on *Yom Kippur* itself, one has blanket license to do whatever the *avodah* requires, in the same way one may perform *shechita* and other biblically-prohibited acts on *Yom Kippur* for the purpose of the service. The need for a verse addressing *Shabbat* is thus entirely unremarkable from the standpoint of *Yom Kippur* carrying: one already had permission to carry on *Yom Kippur* for the *avodah* — not because there is no prohibition, but because the *avodah* overrides it. The *chiddush* of the verse is that even on *Shabbat* — where one might have thought that the license extended only to *Yom Kippur* obligations strictly speaking — the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* can override *Shabbat* restrictions as well, including carrying when the animal is sick. Do not be misled: there is a biblical prohibition of *hotza'ah* on *Yom Kippur* just as on *Shabbat*.

### Tumah Override

The *baraita* also teaches that the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach* overrides *tumah*. The Gemara asks: *le-mai hilchata* — in what practical scenario? Rav Sheshet explains: *lomar she-nitma meshallcho* — if the person who had been designated to carry out the goat became *tamei*, he may nevertheless enter the *azarah* in his state of *tumah* and carry out the dispatch. Ordinarily we would simply find a replacement; the *Baraita* teaches that the designated individual, *itti*, has a special status by virtue of having been appointed, and he may perform his role even *be-tumah*, overriding the prohibition of a *tamei* person entering the *azarah*. Whether this follows from the general principle of *tumah hutra be-tzibbur* — that public communal needs override *tumah* concerns — or whether the *itti* designation itself confers elevated status on the specific individual, may be debated.

---

## R. Eliezer Stories

### Sick Goat

The *Mishnah* records a series of questions posed to Rabbi Eliezer, all relating to the dispatch of the *se'ir hamishtalei'ach*, and all met with cryptic non-answers. First: *choleh mahu she-yarkivennu al ketefo* — if the goat became sick, may one carry it on his shoulders? Rabbi Eliezer replied: *yachol le-harkiv ani ve-atem* — it can carry me and you. This response, as Rashi reads it, is simply an evasive deflection, refusing to engage with the question.

The Chachamim, by contrast, answer directly: yes, if the animal is sick, one carries it on his shoulders.

### Sick Messenger

Second question: *choleh meshallcho mahu she-yishlachenu be-yad acher* — if the designated carrier fell ill, may another person be sent in his place? Rabbi Eliezer replied: *yehei be-shalom ani ve-atem* — you and I should all be well. Again, no answer.

The Chachamim say: yes, appoint a substitute.

### Goat Doesn't Die

Third question: *dachfo ve-lo met, mahu she-yered achrav vi-yemitennu* — if the goat was pushed off the cliff but did not die, may one descend after it and kill it? Rabbi Eliezer replied with a verse: *ken yovedu kol oyvecha Hashem* — thus shall all Your enemies perish, O God — as if to say, it will most certainly die; the scenario of surviving the fall is not a real possibility. Once again, no direct answer.

The Chachamim say: yes, go after it and kill it.

Why does the Gemara record these deflections? Apparently, to illustrate how far Rabbi Eliezer would go to avoid answering something he had not received as *mesorah* from his *rebbe* — a principle to which we shall turn directly.

The *Maharsha* offers an alternative reading in which Rabbi Eliezer is actually taking a substantive position in each case, disputing the *Chachamim* rather than simply evading.
