On the first question, *yachol le-harkiv ani ve-atem* means: if the goat is healthy enough to carry both of us, then you may carry it — but if it is genuinely sick and truly cannot support its own weight, then carrying it would be a biblical violation of *Shabbat* and one may not do so. This would represent a disagreement with the Gemara's earlier conclusion that the verse overrides *Shabbat*. On the second question, the *Maharsha* emends the *girsa*: instead of *yehei be-shalom ani ve-ata*, read *yehei be-shilluach ani ve-ata* — you or I can take care of it. On this reading, Rabbi Eliezer holds that neither the sick *shaliach* himself nor anyone he appoints can be his substitute; it is for the *Kohen Gadol* or the Temple authorities to designate a new person entirely. The *Chachamim* hold that the designated *shaliach* himself may appoint his own substitute, which raises interesting questions about whether this role is the *shaliach*'s own to transfer or whether it reverts to the *Kohen Gadol* when he cannot perform it.

### No New Teachings

The Gemara now states the principle underlying Rabbi Eliezer's behavior: *lo amar davar she-lo shama me-rabbo me'olam* — he never in his life said something he had not heard directly from his *rebbe*. Rashi explains that even when Rabbi Eliezer knew the *halacha*, if he had not received it as an explicit teaching from his teacher, he would not transmit it. This commitment to *mesorah* as exclusively transmitted teaching — rather than derived reasoning — explains all three evasive responses. This same trait is also documented in Tractate Sukkah.

### David Stories

The Gemara records a further series of questions posed to Rabbi Eliezer, all of which he deflected in the same manner. Someone asked: *Ploni mahu l'Olam HaBa* — will so-and-so have a portion in the World to Come? Rabbi Eliezer responded: why are you asking me about that one; ask me about the other one instead. When they asked about the second, he said: why ask about that one; ask about the first.

Tosafot cites Rabbeinu Chananel with a brilliant interpretation. The first question was about Avshalom: did he have a portion in the World to Come, given that he had violated his father's *pilegesh*? Does that constitute full adultery or not, given various *halachic* subtleties? Rabbi Eliezer did not want to rule. They then shifted to asking about Shlomo HaMelech, who was entangled in questions about his many wives — and Rabbi Eliezer sent them back to the question about Avshalom.

The second exchange — about whether the shepherd could save the lamb from the lion, and then whether the shepherd could be saved from the lion — is, according to Rabbeinu Chananel, a coded discussion about the story of Bat Sheva, Uriah, and David. *Ha-ari* — the lion — is David. *Ha-kivsa* — the lamb — is Bat Sheva. *Ha-ro'eh* — the shepherd — is Uriah. The question of whether the lion took the lamb is a question about whether David's act with Bat Sheva constituted adultery — a matter *Chazal* tried to mitigate by reading Uriah as having given a conditional *get*. The question of whether the lion killed the shepherd is a question about whether David was culpable for Uriah's death — a matter *Chazal* tried to mitigate by characterizing Uriah as a *mored b'malchut*, one who was flouting the king's authority. Rabbi Eliezer evaded both by sending the questioners from one to the other.

### Mamzer Question

Another series of questions was posed to Rabbi Eliezer: *mamzer mahu l'yarash* — can a *mamzer* inherit his father? This question might seem obvious given that according to *Chazal* a *mamzer* is the halachically recognized child of his father — he can even be bound in a relationship of *yibbum* with his father's widowed *co-wife*, though marriage itself is forbidden — and thus should in principle inherit. Rabbi Eliezer responded: why ask me about inheritance; ask me about plastering the grave. To which Rabbi Eliezer in turn deflected again: why ask about plastering the grave; ask about plastering the house. Rashi understands the house question as asking about the requirement of *zecher le-churban* — the prohibition on fully plastering one's home as a reminder of the Temple's destruction. The *Bach* understands the grave question as relating back to the *mamzer*: does one plaster a *mamzer*'s grave in the usual honorific fashion, or does one leave it unmarked to indicate his status and warn his descendants?

### Woman Question

A *chachama*, a wise woman, asked Rabbi Eliezer: since everyone who worshipped the Golden Calf sinned equally, *mipnei mah ein mitatam shava* — why did they receive different deaths? The Torah describes three modes: those slain by the sword at the hands of the Levites; those who died by divine plague; and those who died from drinking the water into which Moshe had ground the Calf — which *Chazal* read as analogous to the *sotah* trial, with the guilty party's body rupturing.

### Women's Role

Rabbi Eliezer's response was infamous: *ein chochma le-isha ella be-falechah* — a woman has no wisdom except for the spindle. He supports this with the verse *ve-chol isha chachamas lev be-yadeha tavu* — all the wise-hearted women spun with their hands — implying that women's proper domain is weaving, not Torah inquiry. This reflects a position Rabbi Eliezer expresses elsewhere with even greater force — the statement in Tractate Sotah that it is better for words of Torah to be burned than transmitted to women. His relationship with his own wife Imma Shalom provides a richer biographical context to this attitude, but that discussion extends beyond our passage.

---

## Calf Punishments

### Rav/Levi

The Gemara, having declined to answer the wise woman through Rabbi Eliezer, now answers her question through its own discussion. Rav and Levi each offer a classification. One holds: *zivach ve-kitter b'sayif* — one who actually slaughtered animals and offered incense to the Calf, performing genuine acts of *avodah zara*, was executed by sword, the standard capital punishment. *Gibeph ve-nishak* — one who hugged and kissed the Calf, short of a full act of worship — died by divine death, *mita bi-dei shamayim*. *Samach be-libo* — one who merely rejoiced inwardly but took no outward action — died by *hidrokan*, the stomach-exploding affliction associated with drinking the ground-up Calf waters.

### Witnesses View

The other opinion classifies by juridical criteria rather than severity of act. *Edim ve-hatra'ah* — witnesses and warning — yields execution by sword: the case fit for formal court proceedings. *Edim belo hatra'ah* — witnesses but no warning — yields divine death. *Lo edim ve-lo hatra'ah* — no witnesses and no warning — yields *hidrokan*. The analogy here is to the *sotah*, whose violation was committed with no witnesses and who undergoes a quasi-judicial process involving the water ordeal. Those who sinned with the Calf entirely in private, beyond any possibility of formal court action, are dealt with through the same divine mechanism.

### Levi Innocent

The Gemara then records Rav Yehuda's statement: *shivto shel Levi lo avad avodah kochavim* — the tribe of Levi did not worship the Calf at all. This is derived from the verse in which Moshe stands at the gate of the camp and calls out *mi la-Hashem eilai*, and all of Levi gathered to him — implying that the entire tribe had already stood apart from the sin.

### Half-Sibling Logic

This claim is immediately challenged. The Torah in *Ha'azinu* praises Levi by saying that Levi showed no favor to *aviv* — his father — and to *imo* — his mother — and did not recognize *banav*, his children. If all of Levi was innocent, against whom is this praise directed? Who among Levi's tribe was tempted to show such favoritism?

The Gemara resolves this through careful parsing. *Aviv* in the verse does not refer to his father but to *avi imo mi-Yisrael* — his maternal grandfather, who was not a Levite. *Echav* — his brothers — refers to *achav me-imo mi-Yisrael* — his half-brother on his mother's side, born of a non-Levite father. *Banav* — his children — refers to *benei bito mi-Yisrael* — his grandchildren through his daughter, who had married a non-Levite. In each case, the relatives the Levite refused to spare were relatives by maternal lineage whose fathers were *Yisraelim* — members of other tribes who had worshipped the Calf. The Levites themselves, on their father's side, remained entirely innocent. Thus the praise of Levi is preserved without contradiction, and the tribe's complete fidelity to God at the moment of the Golden Calf stands intact.

---

---

# Yoma 67

## Scapegoat Procession

### Rabbi Eliezer Digression

Today's daf is 67. We pick up at the very bottom of 66b, a little before the *mishnah*. We are dealing with the previous *mishnah* concerning sending off the *sa'ir*, the goat. There had been a whole discussion about what happens if the accompanying individual falls ill — that this may be done on *Shabbat*, even carrying him on one's shoulders — and a fascinating digression regarding Rabbi Eliezer's practice of giving only indirect answers and refusing to directly respond to a woman's question. We now pick up four lines down in the wide lines.

### Bavli'im Identity Dispute

The *mishnah* mentions that they made a ramp — *kevesh asu lo* — for the man who would lead out the goat, and it also records that the *Bavli'im* would attack this man, pulling his hair and crying out, "Get out of here — take our sins away!" Rabba Bar Bar Chana comments: *lo Bavli'im hayu* — they were not actually *Bavli'im* — *ella Alexandrim hayu* — they were Alexandrian Jews, who tended toward assimilation, though it is worth noting they may have come to Jerusalem specifically for the solemn *Yom Kippur* service. *Umitoch she-son'im et ha-Bavli'im* — because the *rabbanim*, the authors of the *mishnah*, harbored a certain animosity toward *Bavli'im* — *hayu korin otan al sheman* — they would call any people they viewed as behaving badly by that name.

This is somewhat ironic, of course, since the Alexandrians were among the most acculturated Jews of the ancient world. One wonders what particular associations the *Tannaim* of *Eretz Yisrael* attached to the label *Bavli'im* — ordinarily, when one applies a name pejoratively, it is because the name carries specific connotations, not simply because one dislikes the group. What associations would *Bavli'im* have carried that made it suitable to apply to Alexandrians caught behaving in this manner? Perhaps it was ironic: these Alexandrians prided themselves on their refinement and culture, so to brand them with a term associated with the unlettered or uncultured was particularly cutting. We do find similar formulations elsewhere — the expression *hanei Bavli'ei tipshai*, "stupid Babylonians," appears in a recent context — though one must note that *Bavel* is not identical with the broader category of *Medinat HaYam*, the general Diaspora.

There is also the observation that the exclamation quoted in the text is given in Aramaic: *ma shahita tzapira dein* — why are you tarrying with this goat? — *ve-chovei dara sagi'in* — when the sins of the generation are so great? The fact that the speech is in Aramaic would seem to support the identification as *Bavli'im* rather than Alexandrians, since one would expect Alexandrian Jews to be speaking Greek. This may constitute a *kashya* on the view that they were Alexandrians.

A *baraita* is then cited: *tanu b'raita*, Rabbi Yehuda says *lo Bavli'im hayu ella Alexandrim hayu* — they were not *Bavli'im* but Alexandrians. Rabbi Yosi responds: *tanuach da'atacha she-inachta et da'ati* — your mind should be at ease, for you have set my mind at ease. Rashi explains that Rabbi Yosi himself was descended from *Bavli'im* and was therefore personally relieved by this clarification. Tosafot notes, however, that another *Gemara* records the very same exchange with the names reversed — Rabbi Yosi making the identification and Rabbi Yehuda responding — which raises a textual difficulty. What remains striking in any case is that even while insisting that these particular individuals were *not* Bavli'im, the *mishnah*'s usage of the term as a pejorative still implies something negative about *Bavli'im* in general.

### Jerusalem Procession

The *mishnah* continues: *meyakkirei Yerushalayim* — the honored, distinguished people of Jerusalem — *hayu melavin oto ad sukkah harishonah* — would accompany the man with the goat as far as the first hut. This was not the obligation of anyone in particular; in practice, only *Kohanim* were used for the actual role. Nevertheless, the honored citizens of Jerusalem would accompany the man as far as the first *sukkah* as a mark of dignity, without being the primary escorts themselves.

## Sukkot & Techumin

### 10 Sukkot Layout

There were ten *sukkot* from Jerusalem to the cliff — *eser sukkot miYerushalayim ve'ad tzuk*. The distance was 90 *ris* in total — *tish'im ris* — which, at seven and a half *ris* per *mil*, gives us twelve *mil*. A *mil* corresponds to 2000 *amos* — the distance of *techum Shabbat* — roughly a kilometer, making the total distance approximately twelve kilometers, or about seven miles, from the *Har HaBayit* to the cliff.

If there were ten *sukkot* spread over twelve *mil*, the spacing works as follows: there is one *sukkah* at every *mil* for the first ten *mil*, and then from the final *sukkah* to the cliff is a further two *mil*. Between each *sukkah* — that is, at every kilometer — there was a small hut stationed along the route.

### Techumim Constraints

The arrangement of the *sukkot* is directly tied to the laws of *techum Shabbat*. The people accompanying the man with the goat were limited to walking 2000 *amos* — one *mil* — beyond the boundary of the city. The man from Jerusalem would walk with the *sa'ir* as far as the first *sukkah*, which sat at the edge of Jerusalem's *techum Shabbat*, and then stop. A new escort would then accompany the man from there to the next *sukkah*, and so on down the line, with a fresh person available at each *sukkah* to walk him through the next *mil*.

The man leading the goat himself was granted the necessary dispensation to travel the full distance. The accompanying escorts, however, were each limited to their own *techum Shabbat*. This ensured that the man was not alone for any part of the journey — he had company through every *mil* — yet no escort was required to violate the *techum* restrictions. It should be noted that the honored people of Jerusalem accompanied him only to the first *sukkah* and then returned home; they were not the ones stationed at subsequent *sukkot* throughout *Yom Kippur*. Other individuals took on the role of remaining at each *sukkah* for the entire day, ready to escort the man for their particular segment of the route.

### Pas Be-Salo Principle

At every *sukkah*, the people stationed there would say to the man leading the goat: *harei mazon v'harei mayim* — here is food, here is water — should he need refreshment. A *baraita* records that in fact no one ever needed to avail himself of this offer — *me'olam lo hutzrach adam le-kach* — but the offer was always extended. Why? Because, as the *Gemara* explains with the well-known phrase, *eino domeh mi she-yesh lo pas be-salo le-mi she-ein lo pas be-salo* — it is not the same for someone who has bread in his basket as for someone who does not. When a person knows that food and water are available and within reach, he is far less consumed by hunger or thirst. It is only when one is told that something is unavailable or prohibited that it becomes the sole focus of attention.

This phrase, *pas be-salo*, appears elsewhere in the *Gemara* in a very different context — typically in discussions of permissible sleeping arrangements between a husband and wife when the wife is a *niddah*, or in the account of the *Amoraim* who would travel to a new town and publicly announce their availability for betrothal. In both cases the principle is the same: the awareness of legitimate future availability diminishes present desire.

A practical question arises: would this man have actually been permitted to eat and drink on *Yom Kippur* had he truly needed to? The *Gemara* does not resolve this explicitly. The *Tosafot Yeshanim* at the bottom of 68a addresses the issue. One reading there suggests that just as this *avodah* overrides *Shabbat* and *tumah*, so too it would override the eating prohibitions of *Yom Kippur* — the principle being that once a *mitzvah* overrides certain prohibitions, it may override them in the ideal manner, not merely out of *dechuyah*. A second reading, however, suggests that the food would only have been permitted had the man reached a state of genuine mortal danger — *bulmus*, an overwhelming weakness — in which case it would be permitted not because of the *avodah* itself but because of *pikuach nefesh*. The text of the *Tosafot Yeshanim* at that point is somewhat uncertain, and the two answers may in fact be distinct positions rather than a single coherent view. The word *bulmus*, incidentally, appears to be related etymologically to the word "bulimia," and in other contexts in the *Gemara* refers to a dangerous state of acute starvation or dehydration.

### Final Accompanier

The *mishnah* specifies that every escort accompanied the man from one *sukkah* to the next — *u-melavin oto mi-sukkah le-sukkah* — with one exception: *chutz me-acharon she-bahen*, the last escort. The man at the final *sukkah* would not accompany him all the way to the cliff, because the cliff was two *mil* from the last *sukkah*, and going the full two *mil* would take him beyond his own *techum Shabbat*. Instead, he would walk one *mil* — to the edge of his permitted range — and then stand at a distance and watch: *ela omed me-rachok ve-roeh et ma'asav*.

A question arises regarding how the man managed to keep the goat moving with him for twelve kilometers without a leash. The *mishnah* never mentions any restraint, and the earlier discussions about carrying on *Shabbat* did not raise the issue of a leash. It is possible the goat simply followed alongside, as animals sometimes do. If a leash had been involved, one might have expected the *Gemara* to have addressed the *Shabbat* implications of carrying it.

## Red String Ritual

### String Division

When the man reached the cliff, the *mishnah* describes what he would do: *cholek lashon shel zehorit* — he would divide the red string — *chetzyo kashar ba-sela* — tying half of it to a rock nearby — *ve-chetzyo kashar bein shnei karnav* — and the other half he would tie between the two horns of the goat. The *Gemara* explains the reasoning for this division.

Why not tie the entire string to the rock? Because since there is still a *mitzvah* to be performed — pushing the goat off the cliff — perhaps the string would turn white before the goat was pushed over. *Dilma kadim u-malbin* — perhaps it would turn white prematurely — *u-maitva dateih* — and he would feel settled, thinking the *avodah* was complete, and neglect to push the goat off. If the string is on the goat, he is actively involved with the animal and is less likely to walk away. Rashi adds that while he is in the midst of acting upon the goat, the string might not turn white yet — since the *avodah* is still in process.

Why not tie the entire string to the goat's horns? Because *zimnin de-gamish leih le-reisheih* — sometimes the goat will bend its head downward as it tumbles, tucking it beneath its body — *ve-lav adateih* — and one would not be able to see the string or notice whether it had turned white. The whole purpose of the string is its symbolic and visible efficacy; one needs to be able to observe it.

It is worth noting that the entire institution of the red string — *lashon shel zehorit* — has no explicit source in the *pesukim* of the *Torah*. It is presumably rooted in the verse *im yihyu chataeichem ka-shanim ka-sheleg yalbinu* — "though your sins be as scarlet, they shall become white as snow" — but that verse is of course a metaphor in the *Nevi'im*. Nevertheless, the practice of the red string is taken entirely for granted in the *mishnah* and *Gemara*, and considerable halachic discussion surrounds exactly where and how it should be placed.

The question of whether cutting the string constitutes a *melachah* on *Yom Kippur* is also worth noting. *Kore'a* — tearing — applies to fabrics. A string, however, is not woven fabric, and the relevant category might be *mechatech* — cutting to a precise measure — which would only be prohibited if done to an exact measurement, which this would not be. So it is not entirely clear that cutting the string is halachically problematic. Similarly, tying a knot on the goat's horn could implicate the *melachah* of *kesher*, but a non-permanent or non-expert knot would not constitute a *kesher shel kayama*. There is also the consideration of *mechamer* — using an animal to perform *melachah* — since the goat is carrying something on its body. As one of the earlier comments noted, it is far from obvious where the entire institution of the red string derives its authority or how precisely its performance was reconciled with the *Shabbat* and *Yom Kippur* restrictions.

### Descent & Shattering

The man would then push the goat backwards off the cliff — *ud'chafo le-achorav* — and the goat would tumble down, *v'hu mitgalgel ve-yored*. The cliff was evidently sheer, with outcroppings and rocks, because *ve-lo haya magiya la-chatzi ha-har ad she-na'aseh evarim evarim* — it would not even reach the halfway point of the descent before it shattered into its limbs. This was presumably a domesticated animal from someone's flock, not a mountain goat accustomed to rocky terrain, which would make the handling and the pushing all the more logistically interesting.

### Accompanier Returns

After the goat was pushed off, the *ish iti* — the man who had led the goat — would return and sit in the last *sukkah*: *ba ve-yashav lo tachat sukkah acharonah*. He would walk back two *techumin* — 4000 *amos* — from the cliff to the final *sukkah*. Rashi notes that this is notable: normally, when someone is granted permission to travel beyond the *techum Shabbat* for a *mitzvah* purpose such as *pikuach nefesh* or assisting in childbirth, once the task is complete, the permission ends and they are limited to 2000 *amos* from their current position. This man, however, is permitted to walk back the full two *mil*, because remaining in the *midbar* exposed him to danger — from the elements, and from whatever else might be encountered in an uninhabited wilderness — and he was weak and exhausted from the journey and the fast. There he would remain in the *sukkah* until nightfall — *ad she-techshach*.

### Impurity of Garments

The *mishnah* then raises the question of *tumah*: when during this process does the man who led the goat cause his garments to become *tamei*? The *Torah* states *ve-hameshale'ach et ha-sa'ir la-Azazel yechabes begadav* — the one who sends the goat to *Azazel* shall launder his garments — which indicates he becomes *tamei*. The question is: at what moment?

The *tanna kamma* holds that it is *mi-she-yatza chutz le-chomat Yerushalayim* — from the time he exits the walls of Jerusalem. Rabbi Shimon holds that it is only *mi-sha'at dechiyato la-tzuk* — from the moment of the actual pushing over the cliff.

This question of *tumah* is connected to a broader question about the stages of fulfillment of the *avodah*. As the *Gemara* elsewhere makes clear, there appear to be three distinct stages: first, the drawing of the lot and the *viduy*, after which the *avodah* is considered fulfilled *bedi'avad* — if the goat died at that point, the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* would not have to be repeated. Second, leaving the walls of Jerusalem, at which point *na'asit mitzvato* — the *mitzvah* of the *sa'ir* itself is considered fully accomplished. It is at this second stage that the red string would turn white and the garments would become *tamei*, according to the *tanna kamma*. Third, the actual going over the cliff, which seems to function as a final completion — not the essential threshold but the culmination of the process. We who tend to focus on the dramatic moment of the goat going over the cliff may be surprised to realize that halachically, the *mitzvah* was substantially complete much earlier.

## Sukkot Count Dispute

### Rabbi Meir Position

A *baraita* is cited: *eser sukkot u-shneim asar milim hayu, divrei Rabbi Meir* — ten *sukkot* and twelve *mil*, this being the standard position assumed by our *mishnah*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda says: *tesha sukkot va-asara milim* — only nine *sukkot* and ten *mil*. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the escort from the last *sukkah* could accompany the man all the way to the edge of the cliff, since the distance from the ninth *sukkah* to the end of the tenth *mil* — the cliff — is exactly one *mil*, within the *techum Shabbat* of that escort.

### Rabbi Yosi Position

Rabbi Yosi says: *chamesh sukkot va-asara milim* — five *sukkot* and ten *mil* — *ve-kulam al yedei eruv* — and all of them through the mechanism of *eruv*. Since all the escorts are traveling in one direction — away from Jerusalem toward the cliff — rather than restricting each person to one *mil*, one could make an *eruv* at the far end of the first *mil* and thereby extend one's range to two *mil* in that direction. Each escort stationed at a *sukkah* could place an *eruv* one *mil* further along the route, enabling him to accompany the man for two *mil* rather than one. This halves the number of *sukkot* needed while maintaining full coverage of the ten-*mil* route.

### Elazar Hypothetical

Rabbi Yosi then relates that his son Elazar raised a further point — *sach li Elazar beni* — speaking, Rashi notes, in something of a playful or exploratory tone: if we are going to use *eruvin* to extend coverage, *yachol ani la'asot afilu shtei sukkot va-asara milim* — I could cover the entire ten *mil* with just two *sukkot*, by placing two people at each *sukkah* and having each make an *eruv* in the opposite direction from the other.

The arrangement would work as follows. The people departing Jerusalem place their *eruv* two *mil* out, enabling them to walk two *mil* in that direction. At the first *sukkah*, two people are stationed: one places his *eruv* back toward Jerusalem and can walk two *mil* in that direction to meet the returning man; the other places his *eruv* two *mil* further along the route toward the cliff, enabling him to walk two *mil* forward. At the second *sukkah*, the same arrangement applies. The result is that with two people per *sukkah* making *eruvin* in opposite directions, the entire ten-*mil* route can be covered with only two *sukkot*.

As the *Gemara* makes clear, Elazar is not claiming this is what was actually done — *eruvin* were not used at all in practice — but is simply demonstrating the logical extreme of the principle his father introduced. The *Gemara* then asks: *ke-man azla* — like whom does the *mishnah*'s detail that the final escort does not accompany the man all the way to the cliff go? It goes like Rabbi Meir — because according to Rabbi Yehuda (nine *sukkot*, ten *mil*), the last escort could reach the cliff; and according to Rabbi Yosi (five *sukkot* with *eruv*), again the man could be accompanied to the end. Only according to Rabbi Meir, with ten *sukkot* and twelve *mil*, does the geometry require the last escort to fall short of the cliff by a full *mil*.

## Limbs Permissibility

### Limb Question

The *Gemara* raises a question: *otan evarim mah hen be-hana'ah* — after the goat shatters on its descent, what is the legal status of those limbs with respect to deriving benefit? The goat had been sanctified — it was designated for *Azazel* — and the *Gemara* had noted that *shechitato zo hi shechitato*, the manner of its death constitutes its *shechitah*. The question is whether, once *na'asit mitzvato* — once the *mitzvah* is accomplished — any sanctified status that would prohibit benefit is lifted, or whether it persists.

### Rav/Shmuel Dispute

Rav and Shmuel disagree. *Chad amar mutarin* — one says the limbs are permitted for benefit — *ve-chad amar asurin* — the other says they are forbidden. The one who says they are permitted relies on the word *midbar* — wilderness — which carries a connotation of openness and freedom from restriction, suggesting that whatever is sent there is released from prohibitions. The one who says they are forbidden relies on the word *gezeirah* — the land of cutting or restriction — which implies that the object retains some character of limitation.

Each opinion must then account for the word it does not primarily rely upon. According to the opinion of *mutarin*, what purpose does *gezeirah* serve? It serves to teach, as a *baraita* records, that the cliff must be a sheer drop — *gezeirah ein gezeirah ella chatucha*, *gezeirah* means cut, implying the face of the cliff is cut straight down, a sheer precipice rather than a gradual slope. This is in fact the textual source for the entire requirement to push the goat off a cliff rather than simply releasing it into open wilderness. According to the opinion of *asurin*, what purpose does the repeated use of *midbar* serve? It serves the *derashah* cited elsewhere: *ha-midbarah, ha-midbarah, ba-midbar* — the multiple uses of "wilderness" in the *pesukim* teach that this *avodah* applies not only during the years of the *Mishkan* in the wilderness but also at *Nov*, *Giv'on*, *Shilo*, and the permanent *Beit HaMikdash* — wherever the *Mishkan* was stationed, including the settled land of *Eretz Yisrael*.

## Limbs Permissibility (II)

### Textual Locations

The repeated use of "wilderness" in the relevant *pesukim* — *ve-shillach et ha-sa'ir ha-midbarah*, *ve-shillach oto ha-midbarah* — thus serves to include *Nov*, *Giv'on*, *Shilo*, and the permanent *Beit HaMikdash* as locations where the *avodah* of the *sa'ir* applies. This raises an interesting observation: once the *Mishkan* was in a settled land rather than an actual wilderness, the symbolic resonance of sending something "to the wilderness" shifts. The *pesukim* refer specifically to sending the goat to an uninhabited and wild place; when the *Mishkan* is in a settled territory, the significance of this act may be somewhat different in character.

One participant noted that the *Mishkan* was also stationed at *Gilgal* for several years after the entry into the land, a location in the Jordan Valley that may not have had a suitable sheer cliff nearby. This would be an interesting question: it is not listed among the locations in the *baraita*, which may hint that this period presented its own unique circumstances. In any event, the *baraita*'s inclusion of *Nov*, *Giv'on*, *Shilo*, and the permanent *Beit HaMikdash* also implies a certain foreknowledge of the *Mishkan*'s eventual itinerary — itself a striking observation.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava rules in favor of the opinion that the limbs are permitted: *mistabra ke-man de-amar mutarin*. His reasoning is: *lo amra Torah shillach le-takala* — the *Torah* does not command one to send something into the wilderness only to have it become a stumbling block. If the limbs remain forbidden for benefit, then scattered animal parts lying in a desolate place could lead people who encounter them to inadvertently misuse them — and the *Torah* would not establish a *mitzvah* that creates such a hazard. Rava invokes a similar principle in the context of the *metzora* ritual, where the bird sent away after purification — if it were to later fly into someone's domain — could not possibly remain forbidden for benefit, since no one would know its identity. The *Torah* would not prescribe a practice that routinely generates occasions of stumbling.

## Azazel Etymology

### Azazel Definition

The *Gemara* now turns to the derivation of the word *Azazel* and what the *pesukim* teach about the requirements for the location and manner of the goat's dispatch. *Tanu rabanan*: *Azazel* — *she-yehei az ve-kasheh* — the place must be strong and hard. The word encodes the requirement of a hard, rocky mountain.

### Tzuk Definition

A separate *baraita* teaches: *gezeirah ein gezeirah ella chatucha* — the word *gezeirah* means something cut, from the root *ligzor*, to cut. This is the textual basis for requiring a sheer cliff — something cut straight down — as opposed to merely rough or hard terrain. An alternative reading offered in the *baraita*: *ein gezeirah ella davar ha-mitgazer ve-yored* — something that gets chopped up as it descends — which speaks to the goat's shattering on the way down.

A further alternative reading carries a different significance entirely: *gezeirah shema tomar ma'aseh tohu hu* — lest you say this entire act is foolishness. You look at this ritual — sending a goat over a cliff to *Azazel* — and you wonder: what kind of divine service is this? What meaning can it have? To that, the *Torah* responds: *Ani Hashem gezarti* — I, God, have decreed it — *ve-ein lecha reshut le-harheir bahen* — and you have no license to question it. The word *gezeirah* thus also evokes the concept of a divine edict, a *chok* — something decreed by God that is not subject to rational justification. The verse *chukotai tishmoru* — keep my *chukim* — underscores this: these are the statutes I have set, and your obedience is itself the point.

### Unsettled Land

The *mishnah* teaches: *yachol be-yishuv* — one might think the ritual could be performed in settled territory? *Talmud lomar ba-midbar* — the *Torah* explicitly states "in the wilderness," requiring that it be performed in uninhabited, unsettled land. And how do we know it must specifically involve a cliff — a *tzuk* — and not merely hard terrain? *Talmud lomar gezeirah* — the word *gezeirah*, as derived above, teaches the requirement of a sheer drop.

A separate *baraita* offers an alternative derivation: *Azazel — kasheh she-be-harim* — it must be the hardest of mountains. The word *el* in *Azazel* connotes strength, as in the verse *ve-et eilei ha-aretz lakach* — he took the mighty ones of the land — where *eilei* denotes the strong and powerful.

### Uza/Aza'el Atonement

*Tana d'vei Rabbi Yishmael* offers yet another reading: *Azazel* — *she-mechaper al ma'aseh Uza ve-Aza'el* — it atones for the sin of Uza and Aza'el. Rashi identifies these as *malachei chavala*, angels of destruction, who descended to the earth in the days of Na'amah the sister of Tuval Kayin, and about whom it is said *va-yir'u bnei ha-elohim et bnot ha-adam* — the divine beings saw the daughters of man — a reference to the narrative of the fallen angels who cohabited with human women. Rashi brings this back to the concrete: *klomar al arayot mechaper* — what this means in practice is that the *Azazel* ritual atones for sexual sins. The allusion to these mythic figures thus grounds in a recognizable halachic category, namely, the sin of *gilui arayot*.

## Mishpatim & Chukim

### Rational Laws

The *Gemara* now addresses a broader classification of *mitzvot*, introduced through a *pasuk* from the Torah: *et mishpatai ta'asu ve-et chukotai tishmoru*. The *Gemara* distinguishes *mishpatim* — rational laws — from *chukim* — divine edicts. *Mishpatim* are defined as *devarim she-ilmalei nichetvu din hu she-yichtevu* — things that even had they not been written, reason demands they would have been written. They are the laws that any developed legal or moral system would arrive at independently.

The examples given are: *avodat kochavim* — idolatry, which is a rational prohibition in any monotheistic framework; *gilui arayot* — sexual prohibitions; *shefichut damim* — murder; *gezel* — theft; and *virchat Hashem* — blaspheming God. It is worth noting that every single one of these corresponds precisely to the *mitzvot sichli'yot*, the rationally derivable commandments — and they map almost exactly onto the *sheva mitzvot Bnei Noach*. This has significant implications for the medieval philosophical debate about the nature of those seven laws. Mendelssohn wished to see the *sheva mitzvot Bnei Noach* as natural law — principles derivable without revelation — and this *Gemara* would seem to support that view, explicitly listing them as things reason would have demanded even without divine promulgation. Rambam, however, in his *Mishneh Torah*, emphasizes that a non-Jew acquires the special status associated with observing the *sheva mitzvot* only if he observes them as revealed law — because God commanded them — not merely because reason dictates them. The present *Gemara* therefore appears to sit more comfortably with Mendelssohn's position.

It is also worth noting that the Rambam in *Shemonah Perakim* does not include *gilui arayot* among the *mishpatim*, placing it instead among the *chukim*. This is not necessarily a contradiction: the category of *gilui arayot* is broad, and whether adultery, incest, or *niddah* is the subject may determine whether the prohibition is rationally self-evident or more in the character of a divine edict.

### Divine Edicts

The *chukim*, by contrast, are *devarim she-ha-Satan meishiv aleihem* — things that the *Yetzer HaRa* or the forces of critique would challenge, arguing that they are nonsensical, arbitrary, or irrational. The examples given are: *achilat chazir* — eating pork and other forbidden foods; *levishat shatnez* — wearing *shatnez*, a mixture of wool and linen; *chalitzat yevamah* — the *chalitzah* ceremony for the *yevamah* (notably, the text specifies *chalitzah* rather than *yibbum* itself, since *yibbum* has ancient precedent in the broader ancient world and carries intelligible social rationale, whereas the specific act of *chalitzah* is less obviously purposive); *taharat metzora* — the purification ritual of the *metzora*, with its birds and cedar wood and scarlet thread, which can appear to be almost magical in character; and *sa'ir ha-mishtale'ach* — the scapegoat itself.

*Korbanot* in general can be understood as meaningful religious practice — ancient sacrifice is a near-universal religious form. But sending a goat specifically over a cliff to a place called *Azazel*? This is precisely the kind of practice that invites the critique of *ma'aseh tohu* — sheer foolishness.

### Obedience Theme

To that critique, the *Torah* responds: *Ani Hashem chakaktiv ve-ein lecha reshut le-harheir bahen* — I, God, have inscribed this, and you have no license to second-guess it. This is the meaning of *chukotai tishmoru* together with *Ani Hashem*. The *chukim* are not presented as things requiring rational vindication. They demonstrate, precisely through their resistance to rational justification, the character of pure obedience to divine command. The declaration *Ani Hashem* is what makes them binding — not their intelligibility.

## Mishpatim & Chukim (II)

### Rambam on Values

The Rambam in *Shemonah Perakim* offers a nuanced reconciliation of the rabbinic and philosophical positions on this tension. The *Gemara* elsewhere records the view that it is preferable to say: "I want to sin, but what shall I do — my Father in Heaven has forbidden it," rather than "I have no desire to sin." This formulation would seem to exalt external compliance over internalized virtue, which runs counter to the philosophical ideal — articulated by Aristotle and adopted by many medieval thinkers — that the highest ethical state is one in which a person genuinely does not desire to do wrong, having internalized correct values.

Rambam resolves the apparent conflict by drawing precisely the distinction the *Gemara* has just established: for *mishpatim* — the rational laws — the philosophical ideal holds. One should genuinely not want to murder or steal; one should internalize justice and honesty as values, not merely comply with them under external compulsion. For *chukim*, however — the divine edicts that resist rational justification — the ideal is precisely external obedience. If one wants to eat *chazir* and refrains because God said not to, that is the ideal response, because *chukim* are designed to demonstrate obedience, not to cultivate a particular internal disposition. The two models are thus not in conflict; they apply to different categories of *mitzvot*.

## Garment Impurity Dispute

### Sender Becomes Tamei

The *mishnah*'s discussion of garment impurity is now examined in the *Gemara* in greater detail. *Ha-meshale'ach metamei vegadim* — the one who actually leads the goat becomes *tamei* and must launder his garments — *ve-ein ha-shole'ach et ha-meshale'ach metamei vegadim* — but those who sent him, the dignitaries who accompanied him for portions of the journey, do not become *tamei*. Even though they walked with him, their role was escort, not the act of sending.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

One might have thought that *tumah* sets in as early as when the man leaves the *Azarah* — the Temple courtyard. The *Gemara* rejects this, deriving from the word *ha-meshale'ach* — "the one who sends" — that the act of sending must already be in process, meaning the man must already be in the wilderness. It would then not be *tamei* from departure from the *Azarah*. But one might also think: perhaps *tumah* does not set in until he reaches the *tzuk*, the cliff? The *Gemara* derives from the added *vav* in *ve-ha-meshale'ach* — "and the one who sends" — that once the process of sending toward the wilderness has begun, he becomes *tamei*, which occurs upon leaving the walls of Jerusalem. This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda: *mi-she-yatza chutz le-chomat Yerushalayim* — from the time he exits beyond the walls of Jerusalem.

### Rabbi Yosi Position

Rabbi Yosi takes a different approach. He juxtaposes the word *Azazel* — as he understands it, pointing to the cliff — with the instruction to launder garments: *Azazel ve-chibbes*. Since *Azazel* is associated with the *tzuk*, he holds that *tumah* does not set in until the man reaches the cliff itself — *ad she-yihiyeh la-tzuk*.

### Rabbi Shimon Position

Rabbi Shimon reads the verse most literally: *ve-ha-meshale'ach et ha-sa'ir la-Azazel yechabes begadav* — the one who sends the goat to *Azazel* shall launder his garments. For Rabbi Shimon, the sending is completed only with the actual act of pushing the goat over — *zorko be-vat achat* — in one moment, one act of hurling. Only at that point, when the goat is actually dispatched over the cliff, does the man become *tamei* and his garments require laundering. The mere arrival at the cliff is insufficient; it is the push itself that constitutes the completion of *meshale'ach*, and only then does *tumah* take effect.

---

---

# Yoma 68

## Par V'Sa'ir Nisrafim

### Ba Lo Etzel Par V'Sa'ir

The *mishna* at the bottom of 67b brings us to the next stage of the *Kohen Gadol*'s *avoda* on Yom Kippur. Having completed the blood service — slaughtering the ox, performing the *ketoret*, sprinkling the blood of the ox and the goat in the *Kodesh HaKodashim*, on the *parochet*, in the *Ohel Mo'ed*, on the golden *mizbe'ach*, and at the base of the outer *mizbe'ach* — and having dispatched the *sa'ir la-Azazel* to the wilderness, the *Kohen Gadol* now turns his attention to the carcasses of the ox and the goat whose blood was used in the inner service. The *mishna* states: *ba lo etzel par v'se'ir hanisrafin* — he came to the ox and the goat that are to be burned, for that is what is done with their carcasses.

### Hotzi Es Imureihem

The *mishna* continues: *kera'an v'hotzi es imureihem* — he split them open and removed their inner organs, the fats and the internal parts designated for the *mizbe'ach*. Although the blood of these animals was offered in the inner precincts rather than on the outer *mizbe'ach*, the *imurim* — the fats and inner organs — are treated as in all *korbanot* and are burned on the outer *mizbe'ach*. He then placed them in a vessel, a *magis*, a bowl of some kind, for the purpose of later burning them on the *mizbe'ach*. One might ask why the *Kohen Gadol* himself tears open the carcasses; the subject of the verb is somewhat ambiguous in the *mishna*, and when we reach the phrase *v'hotzi'an l'veis hasreifa* — he took them out to the place of burning — it becomes clear that this was not done personally by the *Kohen Gadol* at all. Whether he himself actually cut them open is therefore a reasonable question, though the text does not resolve it definitively.

### Kela'an B'miklaot

The *mishna* describes a further step: *kela'an b'miklaot* — he twisted them, or as Rashi explains, braided them, onto a type of wooden carrying frame. This allowed the carcasses to be transported securely, interlocked so that nothing would slip free, and then they were taken out to the place where they would be burned. The actual removal is carried out by others, not by the *Kohen Gadol* himself, since the Torah mandates that these carcasses be burned outside the *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Mimasi Mitamim B'gadim

The *mishna* then raises the parallel question to what was asked regarding the *ish iti* who escorted the *sa'ir* to the wilderness: *u'mei'emasi mitam'in bgadim* — from when do the garments become *tamei*? The Torah states *v'hasoref osam yechabes bgadav* — the one who burns them must launder his garments, and he and his garments become *tamei*. The question is when precisely this *tumah* takes effect.

The *tanna kamma* rules: *misheyatze'u chutz l'chomas azara* — as soon as the carcasses leave the wall of the *azara*, the courtyard. This is notably different from the parallel ruling regarding the *sa'ir*, where the *tanna kamma* said the relevant threshold is leaving the walls of Yerushalayim. Here, leaving the *azara* already triggers the *tumah* of the *begadim*, even though the Torah's language refers to the act of burning, which takes place much farther away.

Rabbi Shimon disagrees: *mishetetzat ha'or beruban* — only once the fire has seized the majority of the carcass does the *tumah* begin. This is a consistent position. In the previous *mishna*, Rabbi Shimon held that the person escorting the *sa'ir* becomes *tamei* only when the goat actually goes over the cliff. Here he similarly requires the completion of the act — the fire taking hold of the majority of the carcass — before *tumah* begins. The *tanna kamma*, by contrast, holds that leaving the relevant precincts is sufficient to trigger *tumah*, even before the burning is accomplished.

This discussion also connects to a broader set of three distinct questions that arise regarding the *sa'ir*: when was the *avoda* minimally performed, such that one is considered to have fulfilled the service even *bedi'avad* — perhaps even if the goat died after the *vidui*; when is the *mitzvah* considered fulfilled, *yatza mitzvatah* — perhaps as soon as it leaves Yerushalayim; and when is the full *kappara* achieved, corresponding perhaps to when it goes over the cliff. These questions, and their relationship to when the red string turned white, will be revisited later in the *daf*.

---

## Vehiktiran Salka Da'atach

### Lo Okim Lah

The *Gemara* immediately raises a difficulty with the *mishna*'s phrase *netanam b'magis v'hiktiran al gabei ha'mizbe'ach* — he placed them in a vessel and burned them on the *mizbe'ach*. The *Gemara* asks: *vehiktiran salka da'atach?* — do you really think he burned them at this point? The burning of the inner organs does not occur at this stage in the *seder avoda*. It happens later, after other services, after the *musaf*, after the removal of the *kaf*. The text cannot literally mean that the *Kohen Gadol* offers them immediately at this moment.

The *Gemara* therefore emends the reading: *ella eima lehaktiran* — the *mishna* means he placed them there *for the purpose* of later burning them on the *mizbe'ach*. The act being described is the preparation and holding of the *imurim*, not their immediate offering.

### Magis V'Kli Sherut

This gives rise to a further question addressed by Rashi and a large *Tosafot*, which touches on a parallel *Gemara* elsewhere: why was a bowl, a *magis*, used at all? In the case of the *tamid*, for example, the limbs were carried directly without a vessel. The *imurim* could simply be held by hand and placed on the *mizbe'ach*. The answer is practical: unlike a *mincha*, where placing the *kometz* in a vessel is part of the formal act of sanctification, here no such requirement exists. However, since the *imurim* will not be offered immediately — there will be a wait of some time before they are placed on the fire — they need to be stored somehow. Placing them on the ground is not a reasonable option, particularly given the substantial quantity of material from an ox. The bowl serves as interim storage. When the moment comes to actually place them on the *mizbe'ach*, one does not need to hold the bowl the way one does with the blood; one can simply take them out by hand. The vessel here is a practical necessity, not a halakhic requirement of the offering itself.

### Lo Hayu M'natchin

A *baraita* is introduced: *lo hayu m'natchin nituach basar basar olah* — they would not dismember the carcasses the way one dismembers the meat of an *olah*. The contrast is: *or al gabei basar* — by the *olah*, one flays the skin, and that leather is given to the *kohanim*, who benefit from it significantly. Here, however, the carcasses are burned with the skin still on the flesh. They are dismembered but not flayed.

---

## Or V'basar B'yachad

### Netzar Kan V'Nizchar L'h…

The *Gemara* asks: *minalan de-ha?* — what is the source for this rule? A *baraita* is cited in the name of Rebbe: *ne'emar kan or basar u-feresh* — it says here, in the context of Yom Kippur, that you burn them with their skin, their flesh, and their *peresh*, their excrement or undigested matter. *V'ne'emar l'hallan or u-vasar u-feresh* — and it says elsewhere, by the other cases of animals whose blood is brought inside the *Heichal*, such as the *par kohen gadol* and the *par he'elam davar* described in Vayikra 4, that their skin, flesh, and dung are taken outside and burned.

The connection works as follows. In the *parasha* of the *olah* in Vayikra, the Torah describes the burning of the *olah* and mentions *rosho v'al k'ra'av* — its head and its legs — as well as *v'kirbo u'chra'av*, the inner organs and the legs. Those same terms, *rosho* and *k'ra'av*, appear in our context as well. Because the language parallels that of the *olah*, we derive from the *olah* the law of *nituach* — dismemberment. From the *olah* we learn that the carcass is cut into pieces before burning.

However, from the *olah* we do not derive *hifshit* — flaying. The *olah* is flayed (*v'hifshit es ha'olah*) and dismembered (*v'nitach osah l'nesacheha*), but here we apply only the *nituach* and not the *hifshit*. The reason is grounded in the logic of keeping the carcass as a unified whole.

### Nitach V'Lo Hifshit

The *Gemara* explains why the flaying is excluded even though the dismemberment is learned from the *olah*. The Torah says *v'kirbo u'firsho v'hotzi* — and its innards and its dung, take it outside. The *peresh*, the excrement or undigested contents, remains *inside* the carcass as it is taken out. It is not removed and separated. This teaches us that the carcass goes out as a unit — the contents and the container together. The same logic applies to the skin and the flesh: just as the *peresh* is not separated from the inner cavity, so too the *or* and the *basar* remain together. You flay a carcass when you want to separate skin from flesh; here, since the whole animal goes as a unit, you do not flay it.

Thus, the *gezeirah shavah* from the *olah* teaches *nituach* — that you cut the carcass into pieces — while the internal reasoning of the *parasha* itself, from the principle of keeping the *peresh* inside, teaches us that the skin remains attached to the flesh throughout.

### Kemin Klia V'Or

Rabbi Yochanan had already offered a description of the braiding: *kemin klia* — like a braid. This interlacing on the carrying frame, as noted earlier, allowed the dismembered pieces of both the ox and the goat to be held together securely on the frame for transport. The logic of keeping skin and flesh united is thus further reflected in the physical manner in which the carcasses were transported: wrapped and interlocked, the skin functioning as a container for the flesh, much as it does for the *peresh*, so that the whole goes out and burns as one.

---

## Chutz L'shalosh Machanot

### Michutz Lamachaneh

A *tanna* taught: *v'hotzi el michutz lamachaneh v'sarafu* — you shall take them out of the camp and burn them. This is the verse from the Yom Kippur context. The *baraita* then raises the tension: *l'halan atah nosein lahem shalosh machanot* — in other cases of animals burned outside, you apply three camps; *v'kan atah nosein lahem machaneh achat* — here the Torah says only *michutz lamachaneh*, suggesting a single camp.

To understand this properly, one must recall the structure of the three camps. *Machaneh shechinah* is the *Beis HaMikdash* itself, corresponding in the desert to the area of the *mishkan*. *Machaneh leviyah* corresponds in Temple times to *Har HaBayit*. *Machaneh Yisrael* corresponds to Yerushalayim itself. When the Torah says *el michutz lamachaneh* — take it outside the camp — a single reference would seem to indicate outside only the first camp, meaning you burn the carcasses on *Har HaBayit*, just outside the *azara*. Does that mean you could burn them right there on *Har HaBayit* rather than outside Yerushalayim?

The *baraita* takes for granted that the normal case — such as the *par he'elam davar* in Vayikra 4 — requires burning outside all three camps, outside Yerushalayim. The question is therefore what function the single *michutz lamachaneh* in our Yom Kippur passage serves. The answer: *lomar lach kivan sheyatza chutz lemachaneh achat mitam'in begadim* — to tell you that as soon as it exits the first camp, as soon as it leaves the *Beis HaMikdash*, that is when the garments become *tamei*. The Torah does not intend to limit the burning to one camp; rather, this single reference to leaving the camp establishes the moment at which *tumah* begins.

### Lehalan At Noheg

The *Gemara* then asks: how do we know that in the other cases — the *par kohen gadol* and the *par he'elam davar* — the burning takes place outside all three camps, outside Yerushalayim? A *baraita* teaches the derivation systematically.

By the *par kohen gadol*, the Torah says *el michutz lamachaneh* — take it outside the camp. One might have said this means only outside the first camp, burning it on *Har HaBayit*. But the *par he'elam davar* also says *michutz lamachaneh*, and additionally it says *ka'asher asah et hapar harishon* — just as you did with the first ox. If the Torah already instructs you to treat them identically, why repeat *michutz lamachaneh*? The additional mention teaches a second camp — you must go further out. That gives us two camps.

Then, when the Torah discusses the *trumat hadeshen* — the removal of ashes from the *mizbe'ach* — it says the ashes are to be taken *el michutz lamachaneh*, outside the camp. But we already know from the burning of the *parim* that the ashes go outside the camp; the place of burning, *shefech hadeshen*, already implies outside the camp. Why repeat it? *Tein lo machaneh shlishit* — this gives us a third camp. The burning of all these animals, and similarly the carcasses of the Yom Kippur animals, must be performed outside all three camps — outside Yerushalayim.

### Lifnei Ma Nemar Michutz

Given that we derive from the other cases that the burning is outside Yerushalayim, the single-camp language in the Yom Kippur *parasha* cannot be telling us the location of burning. As established, it comes to teach the moment at which *tumah* takes hold: *kivan sheyatza chutz lemachaneh achat mitam'im begadim* — as soon as it exits the first camp, the *Beis HaMikdash*, the garments become *tamei*. The full burning takes place outside Yerushalayim, but the *tumah* begins the moment the carcasses leave the *azara*.

According to the *chachamim*, the burning takes place to the north of Yerushalayim, since the principle for any *chatat* is that it is associated with the north — the *chatat* is slaughtered on the north side of the *mizbe'ach*, and the north is the directional association for sin offerings generally.

### Rabbi Shimon V'Parah Adu…

Rabbi Shimon, who holds that *tumah* begins only at the moment of actual burning, has no need for the single-camp language to teach the onset of *tumah*. He therefore uses it differently: *ne'emar kan michutz lamachaneh v'ne'emar l'hallan michutz lamachaneh* — it says here *michutz lamachaneh* and it says there, in Bamidbar, *michutz lamachaneh* by the *parah adumah*. This is the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer, which Rabbi Shimon accepts: just as the burning here is outside all three camps, so too the *parah adumah* is performed outside all three camps, outside Yerushalayim — specifically on *Har HaZeitim*, to the east. This is confirmed by the requirement that the blood of the *parah adumah* be sprinkled toward the opening of the *Heichal*, which means the officiant must stand east of *Har HaBayit*, looking westward.

From this linkage Rabbi Shimon derives a reciprocal lesson: *u'mah l'hallan bemizrachah shel Yerushalayim* — just as the *parah adumah* is performed to the east of Yerushalayim, *af kan bemizrachah shel Yerushalayim* — so too the burning of our carcasses is to the east of Yerushalayim. Thus Rabbi Shimon uses the extra *michutz lamachaneh* to forge a *gezeirah shavah* with the *parah adumah*, teaching both that the *parah adumah* is outside Yerushalayim and that the burning of the Yom Kippur animals is specifically to the east.

The *chachamim*, by contrast, do not derive their knowledge of the *parah adumah*'s location from this verse — presumably from another source — and use the single-camp mention to teach the onset of *tumah* rather than to establish direction. They hold the burning is to the north.

---

## Al Beis Hadeshen

### Sheyadim Sham Deshen

The *baraita* records the opinion of Rabbi Yossi: *al beis hadeshen nisrafin* — they are burned at the *beis hadeshen*, the place where the ashes are deposited. This is consistent with the earlier derivation that the Torah says *al shefech hadeshen yisareif* — it shall be burned at the place where the ashes are poured. The *chiddush* in Rabbi Yossi's opinion, as it is understood, is that there must actually be ashes present at the site — not merely that the site is designated as a place for ashes, but that physical ashes must be there at the time of the burning. Since the Torah says *shefech hadeshen*, the word *shefech* implies active presence of ashes, not merely a designated location.

### Makom Meshupach

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov disagrees. He reads *shefech hadeshen* not as requiring the literal presence of ashes but as requiring that the terrain be *meshupach* — sloped, so that ashes poured there would naturally flow downward. The site must have the physical characteristic of a place where things pour and cascade, but it need not have actual ashes present at the time of the burning.

### Dilma Makom Meshupach

Abaye raises a subtle point: perhaps Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov is not actually contradicting Rabbi Yossi on the question of whether ashes must be present. Perhaps he is adding an additional criterion. *Dilma b'makom meshupach hu d'paligi* — perhaps the dispute is specifically about whether the terrain must be sloped. Rabbi Yossi requires ashes but may be silent on the question of slope; Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov requires the sloped terrain and may agree that ashes are also needed. The two positions would then not be mutually exclusive but complementary, with Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov adding a condition that the *tanna kamma* did not specify.

---

## Hasoreif Metamei Begadim

### Velo Hamatzis Es Ha'or

The *Gemara* now turns to the detailed laws of who becomes *tamei* during the burning. A *baraita* teaches: *v'hasoref osam yechabeis begadav* — the one who burns them becomes *tamei*. But *hasoref metamei begadim velo hamatzis es ha'or* — it is only the one who actively burns who becomes *tamei*, not the one who merely lights the fire. Nor does *velo hamasader es hamarachah* — the one who builds up the woodpile and arranges the pyre — become *tamei*. Only the one engaged in the act of burning itself becomes *tamei*.

### Zeh Hamisayeya

Who qualifies as the one who burns? *Zeh hamisayeya b'shas sreifah* — anyone who participates during the time of the burning. This formulation is precise: it is not about preparatory acts, but about involvement during the actual burning. One who is moving the carcass on the woodpile is clearly the *soreif*. What of one who adds a log to the fire while the carcass is burning? That too appears to constitute *misayeya b'shas sreifah* — participation during the burning — and would render that person *tamei*. The criterion is temporal and participatory: are you actively involved at the moment the burning is taking place?

### Yachol Af Mishe'nasu Eif…

One might have thought that if someone continues to tend the fire even after the carcass has become ashes, they too become *tamei*. The *Gemara* rejects this: *talmud lomar osam* — the verse says *osam*, referring to the animals themselves. The *tumah* applies when you burn *them*, when they still have their identity as a carcass. *Osam metamei begadim velo mishe'nasu eifer metamei begadim* — once they have become ashes they no longer exist as carcasses, and continued burning of the ashes does not render one *tamei*.

### Nizach Habasar

Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon takes a stricter position: *nizach habasar* — once the flesh has dissolved, even if it has not yet become ash, the *tumah* no longer applies. The *Gemara* asks: *mai beinaihu?* — what is the practical difference between the *chachamim* and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon? *Ika beinaihu d'shavei charuchah* — the case of charcoal. A piece of meat that is totally charred and blackened but has not yet crumbled into ash: according to Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon, since the flesh has essentially been destroyed, there is no longer *tumah*; according to the *chachamim*, so long as it has not fully become ash, it retains its identity as burnt flesh and renders one *tamei*.

It bears noting that although Rashi reads this entire passage as proceeding according to Rabbi Shimon's view — that *tumah* begins only at the moment of actual burning — this need not be the case. Even the *tanna kamma*, who holds that *tumah* begins when the carcasses leave the *Beis HaMikdash*, would presumably agree that anyone directly involved in the burning also becomes *tamei*, since the Torah explicitly says *v'hasoref osam yechabeis begadav*. The *tanna kamma* does not deny the *tumah* of burning; he simply holds that *tumah* begins earlier as well. The detailed laws of who qualifies as *hasoref* and at what point the *tumah* lapses are therefore relevant to all opinions.

---

## Higia Sa'ir L'midbar

### Amru Lo L'Kohen Gadol

The *mishna* now brings the thread of the *sa'ir la-Azazel* back into view: *amru lo l'Kohen Gadol higia sa'ir la-midbar* — they informed the *Kohen Gadol* that the goat had reached the wilderness.

### Eino Rashai Lehatchil

Rashi explains the significance of this announcement: *she'eino rashai lehatchil b'avodah acheres ad she'yagia sa'ir la-midbar* — the *Kohen Gadol* is not permitted to begin the next stage of service until the goat has reached the wilderness. He can finish handling the carcasses — cutting them open, removing the *imurim*, and sending them out — but he cannot proceed to something fundamentally new from the *sa'ir* and *par* process until the goat's arrival at the wilderness is confirmed. The source is the verse: *v'shilach es ha-sa'ir ha-midbarah ve-achar kach v'es chelev ha-chatat yaktir ha-mizbeicha* — he shall send the goat to the wilderness, and only afterward burn the fats of the sin offering on the *mizbe'ach*. Even though the immediate next act is not the burning of the fats, there is nonetheless a structural dependence: the goat must reach the wilderness before the *Kohen Gadol* moves forward.

### Uminayin Hayu Yodim

How did anyone know when the goat reached the wilderness? *Dirka'ot hayu osim u-menifin bi-sudarin* — appointed individuals were stationed at intervals and would wave cloths or flags. As the goat reached its destination, the person nearest to it would wave, the next person in the chain would see and wave in turn, and so the signal would travel back to the *Beis HaMikdash* like a relay. This was clearly a daytime visual communication system, analogous to the fire-signals once used to announce the *kiddush hachodesh*, though since this occurs on Yom Kippur fire-signals were naturally not an option.

### Siman Gadol Hayah

Rabbi Yehuda observes: *v'halo siman gadol haya lahem* — but they had a simpler sign available. *Miyerushalayim v'ad Beis Chidudo shlosha milin* — from Yerushalayim to the place called *Beis Chidudo*, which marks the edge of the wilderness, is three *mil*. Rashi takes *Beis Chidudo* to refer to the cliff, though its more precise meaning appears to be the beginning of the wilderness boundary. The *Yerushalmi*'s *girsa* reads *Beis Choron*, a known location outside Yerushalayim, which if accurate would also indicate the direction in which the goat was taken.

### Shlosha Milin

Rabbi Yishmael offers a time-based method: the escort party accompanies the goat for one *mil* out of Yerushalayim, then returns — that accounts for two *mil* of travel time. One then waits the equivalent of a third *mil* — the time it takes to travel that distance — and at that point one may conclude that the goat has arrived at the wilderness. No eyewitness relay is needed; a simple calculation of elapsed time suffices. *Ve-yod'im she-higia sa'ir la-midbar* — and in this way they knew the goat had reached the wilderness.

Abaye draws a halakhic inference from this: *shma mina Beis Chidudi bamidbar kayma* — we learn from this that *Beis Chidudi* is considered to be within the wilderness, or at its threshold. Once the goat reaches that boundary, *keivan she-higia la-midbar na'aseit mitzvatah* — the *mitzvah* of *shiluach hase'ir* is considered fulfilled. Although one is ideally supposed to push the goat over the cliff, and although one might be minimally *yotzei* the *avoda* even if the goat died immediately after the *vidui*, the full performance of the *mitzvah* — including the *kappara* — is achieved once the goat reaches the wilderness, before it goes over the cliff. And it is at this moment that the *begadim* of the person who escorted it become *tamei*, and at this moment the *Kohen Gadol* may proceed.

---

## Ba Lo Kohen Gadol Likros

### Ratza Likros B'vagdei Vu…

With the goat having reached the wilderness, the *Kohen Gadol* now proceeds to the next stage. The *mishna* states: *ba lo Kohen Gadol likros* — the *Kohen Gadol* came to read from the Torah. He has a choice regarding his garments: *im ratza likros bivgadei vutz korei* — if he wishes to read in his linen *bigdei kehunah*, the same garments he wore for the *avoda*, he may do so. *Ve-im lav, korei be-itztalit lavan mishelo* — if he prefers not to use those garments, he may wear his own white tunic instead, changing out of the priestly garments and then, when necessary, changing back. The question of *kiddush yadayim v'raglayim* in connection with this change of garments will be addressed in the following *mishna*.

### Chazzan Haknesset Notel

The *Sefer Torah* is passed to the *Kohen Gadol* through an elaborate chain of intermediaries. *Chazzan Haknesset notel Sefer Torah* — the attendant of the synagogue takes the *Sefer Torah*. Rashi explains that there was a *beis haknesset* — a small synagogue — situated on *Har HaBayit*, adjacent to the *azara*. The *Sefer Torah* was kept there. The attendant gives it to the *rosh haknesset* — the head of the congregation, the one responsible for allocating synagogue honors, what Rashi describes as equivalent to the *gabbai*. He in turn gives it to the *segan*, the deputy *Kohen Gadol*, and the *segan* delivers it to the *Kohen Gadol* himself, who stands and receives it. The entire ceremony builds toward this climactic moment of reception.

The existence of a *beis haknesset* on *Har HaBayit* itself is a striking detail, though Rashi is clear that this is where the *chazzan* brings the *Sefer Torah* from — the *Kohen Gadol* himself does not leave the *Beis HaMikdash* for this purpose.

### V'korei Acharei Mot

*Ve-korei Acharei Mot ve-ach be-asor* — he reads the *parasha* of *Acharei Mot*, which describes the Yom Kippur *avoda*, and the *parasha* of *Ach be-asor* from *Emor*, which contains the commandment of fasting and self-affliction and relates to the *musaf* service.

### Yosser Mimah Shekarasi

After reading, the *Kohen Gadol* rolls the *Sefer Torah* closed, holds it against his chest, and announces: *yosser mi-mah she-karasi lifneichem kasuv kan* — more than what I have read to you is written here. This declaration has a specific purpose: he is about to recite a passage from Bamidbar by heart, and he wants the assembled congregation to understand that he is not continuing to read from this scroll.

### Korei Al Peh

*Korei al peh* — he then recites from memory the section *be-asor lachodesh* from the *parasha* of Pinchas in Bamidbar, which contains the *musafim*. It would be an undue burden on the congregation — *tircha de-tzibura* — to roll the *Sefer Torah* all the way from the middle of Vayikra to the end of Bamidbar. Therefore, the *Kohen Gadol* closes the scroll, makes it obvious he is setting it aside, announces that there is more written there, and then reads this additional passage *ba'al peh*, demonstrating clearly that he is not reading from the scroll but from memory. The congregation should not imagine that the two sections are adjacent in the Torah.

### Shemoneh Berachot

After the reading, the *Kohen Gadol* recites eight *berachot*. These are: *al ha-Torah* — over the Torah, a blessing for the gift of Torah; *ve-al ha-avoda* — a blessing resembling *retzeh*, thanking God for the *avoda* he has just completed, closing with words like *ve-otcha levadcha b'yira na'avod*; *ve-al ha-hodaya* — thanksgiving, parallel to *modim*; *ve-al mechilat ha-avon* — for the forgiveness of sin, the central theme of Yom Kippur, closing as Rashi describes: *mocheil avonotenu b'yom hakippurim melech mocheil ve-solei'ach la-avonotenu vela-avonot amo beit Yisrael*; *ve-al ha-mikdash bifnei atzmo* — a blessing for the *Mikdash*, that God should continue to dwell there, closing *baruch she-bachar ba-mikdash*; *ve-al Yisrael bifnei atzman* — a blessing for the people of Israel; *ve-al Yerushalayim bifnei atzmo* — for Yerushalayim; and *ve-al ha-kohanim bifnei atzman* — a blessing specifically for the *kohanim*, which Rashi describes as closing *she-bachar be-zaro shel Aharon*. It is notable that the blessing for the *kohanim* follows the blessing for Yerushalayim rather than immediately following the blessing for Israel — a structural choice that perhaps reflects a view of the *kohanim* as associated primarily with the institution of the *Beis HaMikdash* rather than with the general community. Finally, *ve-al she'ar ha-tefilla* — for the remainder of the prayer, *binichuta*, which will be elaborated in subsequent discussion.

### Derech Rechoka V'melacht…

The *mishna* closes with a striking observation: *haro'eh Kohen Gadol kshehu korei eino ro'eh par v'sa'ir hanisrafim* — one who is present to witness the *Kohen Gadol* reading the Torah cannot simultaneously witness the burning of the *par* and *sa'ir*. And conversely, one who witnesses the burning cannot witness the Torah reading. *V'lo mipnei she'eino rashai* — this is not because one is forbidden to witness both; there is no prohibition. Rather, *ela she-hayeta derech rechoka* — they were simply far apart: one was occurring inside Yerushalayim on *Har HaBayit*, the other outside Yerushalayim entirely. *U-melachtan sheteihen ke'echad* — and both were happening simultaneously. It is simply impossible to be in two places at once.

This simultaneity is itself significant. The *Kohen Gadol*, having completed the central *avoda* and confirmed that the *sa'ir* has reached the wilderness, now engages in the public, communal dimension of the day — reading the Torah and pronouncing eight *berachot* — while, at the same moment, the carcasses are being consumed by fire outside the city. The question of the purpose and nature of this *krias haTorah* will be taken up at the start of the next session.

---

---

# Yoma 69

## Torah Reading Function

### Mishnah Overview

The Mishnah at the opening of this *perek* describes what the *Kohen Gadol* does once the central labors of Yom Kippur have been completed: the *ketoret* has been offered, the blood of the *par* and the *sa'ir* has been sprinkled, the *sa'ir la'azazel* has been sent, and the carcasses of the remaining animals have been dispatched to be burned outside the *Beit Hamikdash*. During the interval while those carcasses are being consumed, the *Kohen Gadol* performs a public reading of the *Torah* and then recites a series of *berakhot* — concerning the *avodah*, the atonement of sin, the people of Israel, and the *kohanim*. He does so either while still wearing his *bigdei lavan*, the linen garments of the *Kohen Gadol*, or in a personal white cloak that he may provide for himself.

### Rashi's Source

Before turning to the *Gemara* itself, it is worth addressing a question that the *Mishnah* naturally occasions: why is the *Kohen Gadol* performing this *Torah* reading? One might say simply that it is to connect the *avodah* being performed to its biblical source, demonstrating that what is being done flows from God's explicit command. But it is instructive to examine the two distinct sources offered by the *rishonim* for this practice.

Rashi, in his comment *ba likro*, directs us to the institution of the *miluim*, the seven-day consecration period that preceded the inauguration of the *Mishkan*. The *Gemara* back on Daf 5, in the first *perek*, derived from the verse *zeh hadavar asher tzivah Hashem* — "this is the word that God commanded" — that Moses was required to recite, or in some sense read aloud, what God had instructed him, and that this act of declaration was itself a necessary component of the *miluim* procedure. Rashi understands that the *Kohen Gadol*'s Torah reading on Yom Kippur is modeled on that paradigm. Just as the *miluim* involved not only the performance of a ritual but also a verbal articulation of the divine command — and indeed, just as the *miluim* were concerned not only with the preparation of the *kohanim* but with the sanctification and purification of the *Mikdash* itself — so too the blood service of Yom Kippur, which cleanses and sanctifies the *Mikdash*, is attended by a similar reading of the *parasha* to establish its divine origin.

### Tosafot Yeshanim View

*Tosfos Yeshanim* offers a strikingly different explanation. At the moment of this reading, the *Kohen Gadol* has reached a natural point of closure. The essential *avodot* of *kapara* have been completed; only peripheral tasks remain. *Tosfos Yeshanim* therefore argues that the reading is not primarily instituted for its own sake — that is, to connect the service to its scriptural foundation — but rather to create an occasion for the *berakhot* that follow. The *berakhot* on the *avodah*, on forgiveness, on the *Mikdash*, on Israel, on the *kohanim*: these are the heart of the matter. The *Torah* reading provides the framework and the formal occasion for those prayers.

This is a significant reframing. Rather than the *berakhot* being secondary to the *Torah* reading, the reading exists in order to give rise to the *berakhot*. What emerges is a remarkable convergence of the *Mikdash* experience with the *beit knesset* reality. The entire apparatus described — the *chazzan haknesset*, the *rosh haknesset*, the public assembly — represents the grafting of synagogue structure onto the *Mikdash* ritual. The closure of the great sacrificial service is framed and articulated through prayer and *Torah* reading, exactly as it would be in a *shul*. One can even say that the *miluim* model, which Rashi invokes, becomes in the hands of *Tosfos Yeshanim* a basis not merely for the reading but for the entire institution of *tefillah* as the interpretive complement to *avodah*.

### Yerushalmi Proof

*Tosfos Yeshanim* also quotes the *Yerushalmi*, which tracks more closely with Rashi's position. Rabbi Idi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives the obligation of the *Torah* reading from the word *vayaas* — "and he did" — in the *miluim* narrative, followed by *kaasher tzivah Hashem*, "as God commanded." From here, says the *Yerushalmi*, we learn *l'kriyat haparsha* — that a formal reading of the *parasha* is required. The derivation thus returns to the *miluim* model, as Rashi argued. Yet *Tosfos Yeshanim*'s underlying point remains striking: even granting that the reading is learned from the *miluim*, the primary function he sees in it is as a vehicle for the closing *berakhot* of the day.

---

## Reading as Avodah?

### Clothing Evidence

The *Gemara* opens its analysis with an inference from the *Mishnah*. Since the *Mishnah* records that the *Kohen Gadol* may wear his own personal white garment (*istali lavan*) rather than the prescribed *bigdei lavan*, this establishes by implication — *michlal d'kriya lav avodah hi* — that the *Torah* reading is not itself an *avodah* in the technical sense. That might have been provable from other considerations as well, but the *Mishnah* makes it explicit: no *bigdei kehuna* are required, therefore this is not formal *avodah*.

Yet the *Mishnah* also notes that if the *Kohen Gadol* wishes, he may perform the reading while still wearing the *bigdei butz*, the official linen priestly garments. This creates an interesting situation: an act that is *not* classified as *avodah* may nonetheless be performed while wearing *bigdei kehuna*. From this the *Gemara* attempts an inference — *shma mina bigdei kehuna nitnu leihanot bahem* — that one may derive benefit from *bigdei kehuna*, meaning that wearing them during an activity unconnected to the formal *avodat hamikdash* is not prohibited.

### Tzorech Avodah

The *Gemara* immediately deflects this inference. Perhaps *kriyat hatorah* is different because it is *tzorech avodah* — it is done for the sake of, and in connection with, the *avodah* of the day. According to Rashi, it is learned from the *psukim* as a necessary component of the day's service; according to *Tosfos Yeshanim*, even if it is not strictly derived from a *pasuk*, it functions as the framing and culmination of the *avodat hayom*. In either case, the reading is organically connected to the *avodah*, and therefore one cannot draw from it any general conclusion about wearing *bigdei kehuna* during activities that have no such connection. The question of *bigdei kehuna nitnu leihanot bahem* thus remains open.

---

## Benefit from Garments

### Fundamental Question
