The *Gemara* now explicitly frames the standing question: *bigdei kehuna nitnu leihanot bahem o lo nitnu leihanot bahem* — may a *kohen* derive benefit from the *bigdei kehuna*, specifically by wearing them at times when he is not engaged in the *avodah*? To derive benefit from wearing clothing — warmth, covering, dignity — is a form of *hana'ah*. The question is whether the sanctified nature of the *bigdei kehuna* restricts that *hana'ah* to the performance of the *avodah* alone.

### Sleeping Prohibition

The *Gemara* brings a first proof: *lo hayu yeshenim b'bigdei kodesh* — the *kohanim* did not sleep in the priestly garments. This suggests that wearing the *bigdei kehuna* outside the immediate context of *avodah* is problematic — otherwise, why not sleep in them? The concern Rashi identifies is that during sleep one might pass gas, which would be disrespectful of the garments. This, incidentally, connects to the parallel concern about *tefillin* at night, where the same worry about *guf naki* motivates the prohibition of wearing them while asleep.

### Other Benefits

The *Gemara* objects that the prohibition against sleeping proves too little. Surely the *kohanim* ate while wearing the *bigdei kehuna* — does eating constitute impermissible *hana'ah*? The *Gemara* responds: no, because eating — specifically eating *korbanot* — is itself *tzorech avodah*. As the *baraita* derives from the verse *ve'achlu otam asher kupar bahem*, the eating of the *kohanim* is part of the *kappara* of the owners. The *kohanim* function as a kind of *klei hamikdash*; their consumption of *korban* meat, particularly *chatat*, is analogous to the consumption of the sacrifice on the *mizbe'ach*. Therefore, eating while wearing *bigdei kehuna* cannot serve as proof that benefit may be derived from them in a general, non-*avodah* context.

The *Gemara* then adds that walking around in the *bigdei kehuna* after the *avodah* is also not necessarily a permitted inference. Perhaps one is truly not allowed to do even that — perhaps one must remove them immediately upon completing the service. The *chiddush* of the teaching that they did not sleep in them is not to imply that all other activities are therefore permitted; rather, the novel teaching is what follows: that they would fold the garments and place them *tachas rasheihem* — under their heads.

---

## Pillow Debate

### Folding Garments

The *Gemara* now turns to the specific case of using the *bigdei kehuna* as a pillow. On first reading, this seems to constitute *hana'ah* — the garments are serving a non-*avodah* function. The *Gemara* therefore suggests, in the name of Rav Pappa, that the phrase *tachas rasheihem* should not be read literally as "under their heads" (i.e., as an actual pillow) but rather as *keneged rasheihem* — "near their heads," with no physical contact. Under this reading, the novel ruling is only that it is permissible to leave the folded garments close by, something one might have thought was itself problematic lest one roll onto them inadvertently or treat them without proper reverence. Rashi explains that the concern about leaving them near the head is precisely that one might forget the *issur hana'ah* and roll over onto them.

Rav Mesharshiya draws a comparison: from the ruling that one may place the *bigdei kehuna* near one's head, we infer that one may similarly wrap up one's *tefillin* and place them near one's head when going to sleep. The parallel is deliberate. Just as the concern with *bigdei kehuna* during sleep relates to the problem of *guf naki* — passing gas while unconscious — so too with *tefillin*, where the same *Chazal*ic concern motivates the prohibition against wearing them at night. This comparison is not incidental: there is a broader theme in *Chazal* that *tefillin* and *tzitzit* function for the layperson in the larger world as a kind of *bigdei kehuna* — garments that frame one's consciousness of God and one's activity as a form of *avodat Hashem*. The *Rosh*'s reason for *netilat yadayim* in the morning — modeled on the *kohanim*'s washing before their *avodah* in the *Mikdash* — reflects the same sensibility.

One might ask why *me'ila* is not a concern here, given that *bigdei kehuna* have been sanctified. Some *rishonim* invoke the principle of *lev beit din masneh aleihem* — the communal sanctity was stipulated with conditions, effectively turning the *kedusha* on and off at designated moments. The more substantive answer, found in *Tosfos Yeshanim*, is rooted in the principle *lo nitna Torah lemalachei hashareis*: if the *kohen* were forbidden to derive any benefit whatsoever from the garments outside the *avodah*, he would be required to strip them off the very instant the service ended — something humanly impossible. Since the *Torah* must grant some practical latitude, the garments cannot be fully within the domain of *kodshei Hashem*, and once they are not 100% exclusively dedicated, the category of *me'ila* does not apply. The residual question is how much latitude is granted: only while remaining in the *Mikdash* environs? Or more broadly? That question will surface shortly.

### Shatnez Issue

At this point the *Gemara* introduces a complication that reframes the entire pillow discussion. The *avnet* — the belt worn by an ordinary *kohen* — is made of *shatnez*, a mixture of wool and linen. Accordingly, even if one were to set aside all *kedusha* concerns, how could it be permissible to sleep on the *bigdei kehuna* as a pillow? Would that not constitute deriving benefit from *kilayim*?

The *Gemara* immediately qualifies: this difficulty only arises according to the opinion that the belt of the *Kohen Gadol* on Yom Kippur — which is entirely linen — is not the same as the belt of a *kohen hedyot*. According to that opinion, the ordinary *kohen*'s belt is indeed *shatnez*. But according to the opinion that the *Kohen Gadol*'s linen belt is the same type as the *kohen hedyot*'s belt, the ordinary priestly garments contain no *shatnez*, and the concern does not arise.

One might respond, however, that the prohibition of *kilayim* is specifically *bilvisha* — in wearing — and not in *hana'ah* generally. The verse says *lo ya'aleh alecha*, don't put it upon you; *lo tilbash*, don't wear it. Using *shatnez* as a pillow, which is neither wearing nor covering oneself with it, should be biblically permitted. The *Gemara* confirms this: the *baraita* explicitly states *aval ata mutar lehatzio tachtecha* — you may lay *shatnez* beneath you. This is not a biblical violation.

### Shatnez Baraita

Nevertheless, the *Gemara* cites a *baraita* establishing a rabbinic prohibition: *aval amru Chachamim assur la'asos kein* — the Sages forbade this, *shema ticharech nima achas al besaro* — lest a single loose strand from the *shatnez* garment come to rest upon one's skin, which would constitute *lo ya'aleh alecha*. Although an unintentional contact with a loose thread might ordinarily be dismissed as *eino miskaven*, *Chazal* were sufficiently concerned about this outcome that they prohibited the practice categorically, even when one has no intention of allowing the *shatnez* to come upon one's body.

### Ten Blankets Rule

Rav Shimon ben Pabi in the name of Rav Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Rabbi, transmitted from the *kahala kadisha* of Jerusalem, extends this rabbinic prohibition absolutely: *afilu eser matzaot zo al gav zo* — even if ten blankets or mattresses are interposed between the person and the *shatnez* garment at the bottom, the rabbinic restriction still applies. Once the Sages prohibited lying upon *shatnez*, they did so categorically and comprehensively, regardless of whether physical contact with a loose strand is actually possible. The prohibition is not conditional on the realistic risk of contact; it is a blanket rabbinic ruling. By the same logic, this rabbinic restriction would apply to the *kohanim*, meaning that using the *bigdei kehuna* — which contain the *shatnez* belt — as an actual pillow is rabbinically forbidden. The *Gemara* therefore concludes *shema mina keneged rasheihem*: the text must mean near the head, not under it. This is taken as a good proof.

### Rav Ashi's View

The *Gemara*, however, does not rest there. Rav Ashi dissents and maintains *le'olam tachat rasheihem* — in truth it does mean literally under the head, and the passage does constitute a proof that *bigdei kehuna nitnu leihanot bahem*. How does he address the *shatnez* concern? Rav Ashi argues: *bigdei kehuna kashim hem* — the material of the priestly garments is stiff and firm. Because of this rigidity, there are no loose strands that might come to rest upon one's body. The rabbinic prohibition was enacted as a precautionary measure for soft garments from which loose threads can escape, not for hard, stiff materials from which this is impossible. He supports this with the teaching of Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, that the hard felt made in the town of Narsh — a thick, compressed material — is similarly permitted, since one need not fear that a strand will come loose from felt.

Thus Rav Ashi's position is nuanced: the rabbinic prohibition on lying over *shatnez* is not categorical across all *shatnez* garments, but is calibrated to the actual risk of contact. Where the material is inherently stiff and no strand can come free, the concern that motivated the rabbinic enactment is absent, and the enactment does not apply. The *bigdei kehuna*, being of such stiff material, fall into this category. Therefore *tachat rasheihem* can be read literally, and the derivation of *nitnu leihanot bahem* stands.

It is worth noting, as *Tosfos Yeshanim* observes, that the *Gemara* raises the *shatnez* concern only in this pillow context, and not in the earlier discussions about wearing the *bigdei kehuna* while walking or during non-*avodah* activities. The implicit logic appears to be that as long as the *Torah* itself has authorized the garment as a worn item — similar to Rabbeinu Tam's ruling that a linen garment with a blue woolen string of *tzitzit* may continue to be worn even at night when the *mitzvah* is not being fulfilled — the *Torah*'s allowance of *shatnez* in that garment extends comprehensively to its use as a worn garment. The *shatnez* concern arises specifically when the garment is stripped off and repurposed as something other than a worn garment, as in the pillow case. This is a fascinating structural point about how the *Torah*'s permission for *shatnez* in *bigdei kehuna* interacts with rabbinic enactments around secondary uses.

---

## Explicit Baraita

### Baraita Rules

The *Gemara* at last adduces a clear proof-text. A *baraita* states explicitly: one who goes out wearing *bigdei kehuna* into the *medina* — anywhere outside the *Mikdash* — is prohibited. But inside the *Mikdash*, whether during the time of the *avodah* or not during the time of the *avodah*, it is permitted — *mipnei shebigdei kehuna nitnu leihanot bahem* — because *bigdei kehuna* were given to derive benefit from them. This is an explicit source establishing that wearing *bigdei kehuna* during non-*avodah* moments within the *Mikdash* is permitted, and the explicit reason given is *hana'ah*. *Shema mina* — this is the proof.

### Rashi's Explanation

This naturally raises the question: why then are they prohibited outside the *Mikdash* entirely? Rashi explains: *shenoheg bahem chol* — wearing the *bigdei kehuna* outside the *Mikdash* treats them in a mundane manner, which is not respectful of their sanctity. One might alternatively frame this in terms of the earlier discussion: the latitude granted by the principle *lo nitna Torah lemalachei hashareis* — the practical necessity of not stripping off immediately upon completing *avodah* — extends only within the *Mikdash* itself, where the garments belong. Once outside, that rationale no longer applies, and the full dignity of the sanctified garments demands that they not be worn in an ordinary context.

At this juncture the *Gemara* introduces an important narrative that bears on whether *bigdei kehuna* may ever be worn outside the *Mikdash*. A *baraita* records, in the mode of the *Megillat Ta'anit*, that the 25th of Tevet is *Yom Har Gerizim* — a day on which one may not eulogize or fast — because on that day the Samaritans (*Kutim*), whose sacred center was Har Gerizim, requested from Alexander of Macedonia permission to destroy the *Beit Hamikdash*, and were ultimately frustrated. The Samaritans had argued to Alexander that the Jews were in rebellion against him, and Alexander acceded, issuing a decree for the temple's destruction. When the news reached Shimon HaTzadik, he donned his *bigdei kehuna* and wrapped himself in them; together with the honored members of the community, carrying torches and walking in solemn procession through the night, they traveled to where Alexander's army was encamped. At dawn they encountered one another. When Alexander saw Shimon HaTzadik, he descended from his chariot and prostrated himself before him. His retinue asked in astonishment: how could a great king bow before a Jew? Alexander replied that the image of this man's face — *demut deyukno* — appeared before him in the heavens and led him to victory in all his wars. The entire civilized world he had conquered was in the merit of this figure. He then turned to the Samaritans and asked who they were. Shimon's companions pointed them out: these standing before you are the ones who sought to destroy the *Mikdash*, the house in which we pray for you and your kingdom. Alexander handed the Samaritans over to the Jews, who pierced their ankles and dragged them behind horses over thorns and thistles until they reached Har Gerizim, which they then plowed over and planted with leeks — precisely what the Samaritans had sought to do to the *Beit Hamikdash*. That day was established as a *Yom Tov*. The story unmistakably echoes the *Purim* narrative in its structure.

The obvious difficulty this story raises is that Shimon HaTzadik wore *bigdei kehuna* entirely outside the *Mikdash*. The *Gemara* offers two responses. First, perhaps what he wore were garments that were *re'uyim l'vigdei kehuna* — appropriate for *bigdei kehuna* in their appearance but not yet formally sanctified, meaning they were not technically *bigdei kehuna* in the halachic sense. Second, *eis la'asos la-Shem heferu Torasecha* — there are extraordinary moments when national exigency overrides ordinary practice.

---

## Passing Torah

### Chazan Role

The *Mishnah* describes the procedure by which the *Sefer Torah* reaches the *Kohen Gadol*: the *chazzan haknesset* takes the *Sefer Torah* and passes it to the head of the *knesset*, who passes it to the *segan*, and so on through a chain until it reaches the *Kohen Gadol*.

### Abaye's Explanation

This procedure raises an apparent difficulty. Does this not constitute giving honor to someone of lesser standing — a student, so to speak — in the presence of his *rav*, namely the *Kohen Gadol*? Abaye resolves this: *kulam mishum kevodo shel Kohen Gadol hen* — the entire procession is for the honor of the *Kohen Gadol* himself. Each person in the chain is not being honored for his own sake; rather, their involvement in the sequential passing of the *Sefer Torah* builds toward and heightens the honor of the *Kohen Gadol* who stands at the end of the chain to receive it.

### Azarah Restriction

The *Mishnah* also states that the *Kohen Gadol* receives the *Sefer Torah* standing and reads from it while standing. The emphasis on *omed* — standing — implies that he had been seated, which raises a difficulty. It is a well-established rule that sitting in the *Azarah* is prohibited for all except the kings of the House of David, as derived from the verse *vayavo hamelech David vayeshev lifnei Hashem* — a special allowance given to Davidic royalty alone. If the reading takes place in the *Azarah*, how can the *Kohen Gadol* have been seated there?

### Ezrat Nashim

Rav Chisda resolves this: *be-ezrat nashim* — the reading does not take place in the *Azarah* proper. After completing his *avodah*, the *Kohen Gadol* moves to the *Ezrat Nashim* to perform the reading. In addition to solving the sitting prohibition, this location also renders the reading significantly more public: the *Ezrat Nashim* was a large, accessible space, welcoming a mixed assembly. The *Torah* reading thus becomes not merely an intimate priestly ceremony but a public occasion for the entire community gathered for Yom Kippur. He had been sitting in the *Ezrat Nashim* while waiting for the reading to begin; upon receiving the *Sefer Torah*, he stood to accept it.

---

## Ezra's Reading

### Location Dispute

The *Gemara* situates Rav Chisda's ruling within a broader debate about where *Torah* readings in the *Mikdash* context took place. The *baraita* presents a dispute: one opinion holds the reading was done *ba-Azara*, in the Temple courtyard proper; Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov says it was on Har HaBayit. Rav Chisda's statement — *be-ezrat nashim* — appears to be clarifying one or both of these positions, specifying that what is meant is neither the inner *Azara* nor some unspecified location on Har HaBayit, but specifically the *Ezrat Nashim*. The three positions may therefore reduce to two real options.

### Rabbi Elazar View

Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov derives his position from the episode in *Nechemia* where Ezra the Scribe conducted a great public reading of the *Torah*. The verse states: *vayikra bo lifnei ha-rechov asher lifnei sha'ar hamayim* — he read from it before the open square that is before the Water Gate. This location — before the Water Gate, on a major thoroughfare outside the *Mikdash* proper — suggests a reading that took place not in the inner courtyard but in a large public setting on Har HaBayit. The echo between that event, with its gathering of *anashim, nashim, v'hataph*, and the Yom Kippur reading is unmistakable, and the verse provides the precedent for a location that is accessible, public, and outside the inner *Azara*.

---

## Blessing After Reading

### Ineffable Name

The *Gemara* now turns to the verse in *Nechemia* that follows the *Torah* reading: *vayevarech Ezra et Hashem haElokim hagadol* — "Ezra blessed the Lord, the great God." What does it mean that he called God *gadol*, great? In what way did Ezra magnify or glorify God? Rav Yosef in the name of Rav answers: *shegidlo b'Shem HaMeforash* — Ezra glorified God by pronouncing the ineffable Name. This draws an implicit parallel to the *Kohen Gadol*'s own enunciation of the *Shem HaMeforash* during the Yom Kippur *avodah*.

### Baruch Hashem

Rav Giddel offers a different interpretation. Rather than the ineffable Name, Ezra glorified God through a formal blessing — *Baruch Hashem Elokei Yisrael min ha'olam ve'ad ha'olam*, the verse from *Divrei HaYamim*. This reading understands the "glorifying" as an act of formal *berakha*, not Name-utterance. Abaye noted the connection between this and the very purpose of the *Torah* reading as articulated by *Tosfos Yeshanim*: the whole design of the reading, on his account, was to allow for precisely these *berakhot*, and here we see *Ezra* himself closing the reading with just such a blessing.

### Name Outside Mikdash

Abaye questions Rav Giddel: why not say Ezra glorified God by saying the ineffable Name, as Rav Yosef suggests? Rav Giddel responds: *ein omrim Shem HaMeforash bigvulin* — one does not pronounce the *Shem HaMeforash* outside the *Mikdash*. If the reading — as established by Rav Chisda and Rabbi Elazar ben Yaakov — takes place in the *Ezrat Nashim* or even on Har HaBayit rather than in the *Azara* proper, then the *Shem HaMeforash* would not have been pronounced there. Therefore Ezra's glorification must have been through *berakha*, not through the ineffable Name. The counter-proof — that Rav Giddel himself elsewhere states that Ezra glorified God with the *Shem HaMeforash* — is resolved by noting that the second event, a later chapter in *Nechemia* where the verse reads *vayitz'aku el Hashem Elokim b'kol gadol*, is a separate occasion entirely, and constituted a *hora'at sha'ah*, a special exception, not the standard practice during the *Torah* reading.

---

## Remove Idolatry Desire

### Avoda Zara Cause

The *Gemara* now turns to the famous *agadata* that the phrase *vayitz'aku el Hashem Elokim b'kol gadol* — "they cried out to God in a great voice" — introduces. What were they crying out about? Rav, and some attribute it to Rabbi Yochanan, explains: *baia baia* — a plea of desperate urgency. They were crying out against the *yetzer d'avoda zara*, the desire for idolatry, which they identified as the very force that had caused the destruction of the *Mikdash*, burned the *heichal*, caused the murder of the righteous, and driven Israel into exile from their land. This is striking, because if one reads the passage in *Nechemia* at face value, there is no explicit mention of *avoda zara* — the text speaks of sin and God's punishments in rather general moral terms, without singling out idolatry. Yet *Chazal* interpret the entire bemoaning of history as directed specifically at the *yetzer* of *avoda zara*, which they regarded as the root cause.

And yet, they said to God, the desire for idolatry was itself given by You only in order that we should receive reward for resisting it. But we do not want the desire, and we do not want the reward it would earn us — *lo ihi ba'inan v'lo agra*. It is too costly a bargain. This echoes the opening of *Berachot*, where one who faces *yisurin* may say *lo hen v'lo s'charan* — neither the suffering nor its reward. The prayer was granted.

### Prayer Granted

A confirmation descended from heaven in the form of a written note — a *pitka merakia* — bearing the single word *emet*, "truth." Rav Chanina derives from this the famous principle: *chotamo shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu emet* — the seal of God is truth. God's affirmation of the people's claim, ratified with the word *emet*, reflects that truth is the fundamental attribute by which God engages with creation. This theme will resonate through the *agadata* that follows tomorrow.

After three days and three nights of fasting, the *yetzer* of *avoda zara* was delivered into their hands.

### Lion of Fire

When it emerged, it came out from the Holy of Holies in the form of a *gorya d'nura* — a lion of fire. A prophet, identified in context as Zechariah, told the people: what you are seeing depart from the Holy of Holies is the *yetzer* of *avoda zara*. The emergence from the Holy of Holies is significant and will be returned to, but for now the story continues with the struggle to contain the force. As the people seized it, a single hair fell from its beard, and its cry carried four hundred *parsangs*. This detail — rooted in the vision of Zechariah where the *yetzer* is depicted as a woman in a pot sealed with lead — also invokes Esau, who is described as hairy and who cried out with a great voice, a convergence of associations that the *Gemara* leaves suggestive.

### Sealing Yetzer Hara

What were the people to do with this force now that they had seized it? They feared that if they held it captive, heavenly mercy might be invoked on its behalf and it would be freed. The prophet directed them to follow the imagery of Zechariah's vision: place it in a lead pot and seal the opening with lead, *d'avra masha'iv kala* — because lead absorbs sound. The very medium that allows the captured *yetzer* to cry out to heaven is neutralized by the properties of lead. The *yetzer* of *avoda zara* was thus sealed and contained — not destroyed, but rendered incapable of acting or appealing to divine compassion.

---

## Sexual Desire Prayer

### World Fails

Emboldened by this success, the people reasoned: *ho'il v'eis ratzon hu* — since it is now a time of divine favor and our prayers are being answered, let us also pray to overcome the *yetzer* of sexual transgression. This prayer too was granted. But almost immediately, the consequences became apparent: the world began to fail. When they searched throughout all of Eretz Yisrael for a fresh egg, none could be found. Even the natural biological processes associated with reproduction — including unfertilized eggs — had ceased. It was not merely that human beings had lost the drive for sexual activity; the entire natural order of procreation was unraveling. The *yetzer* of sexual desire is so fundamental to the continuation of the world that its elimination would bring creation itself to a halt.

### Blinding Eyes

Unable to destroy the *yetzer* outright — *kalya alma*, the world would be destroyed — the people attempted a compromise: asking for the desire to be reduced by half. This too was denied: *palga b'reki'a lo yahavi*, heaven does not grant partial requests of this kind. The solution reached was to blind the *yetzer*'s eyes — *kachlinu l'einei* — placing some obscuring substance on them. This partial dimming achieved one specific benefit: *d'lo migrei beih b'inish b'krivosyei* — the desire no longer drives a person toward his close relatives, diminishing the pull toward incestuous relationships. The connection to vision is apt, echoing the verse in the *parasha* of *tzitzit*: *lo taturu acharei eineichem*, do not go astray after your eyes. The *yetzer* operates through sight, and it is precisely sight that is diminished.

### Holy Holies Question

The *agadata* concludes with a question that will be taken up further: why did the *yetzer* of *avoda zara* emerge specifically from the Holy of Holies? Is that where it resided? This question — about the relationship between the innermost sanctum of the *Mikdash* and the *yetzer hara* of idolatry — will connect as well to the broader theme already established that *God's seal is emet*, and to the *agadata* that follows. That material will be taken up in the next session.

---

---

# Yoma 70

## Yetzer Hara Avodah Zarah

### Yetzer Hara Removal

The daf opens in the middle of a well-known *aggadata* rooted in the *pesukim* in Ezra, where the text describes the people crying out to God in a great cry at the time of the rebuilding of the Second *Beit HaMikdash*. The *Gemara* explains that their cry was directed at the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*, which they identified as the root cause of the First Temple's destruction. They prayed for its elimination, and God delivered it to them — they sealed it in a lead container and destroyed it. Having done so, they sought to do the same with the *yetzer hara* of sexual desire, but quickly recognized that this would be catastrophic: it is the very drive that sustains procreation and the continuity of human civilization. So they left it, albeit constrained.

While most discussion of this *aggadata* focuses on the second part — the *yetzer hara* of sexuality — there is something equally striking in the first part, concerning the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah* itself, and it is worth pausing on two dimensions of it.

### Historical Context

The first dimension is historical. *Chazal* tell us that the First Temple fell due to *avodah zarah*, *gilluy arayos*, and *shefichas damim*, whereas the Second Temple fell due to *sinas chinam*. And indeed, when one reads the *Nevi'im*, the refrain is constant: *od ha'am mezabbechim umekatterim babbamos rak habbamos lo saru* — the people continued sacrificing and burning incense at the *bamot*; *avodah zarah* is a pervasive concern throughout the First Temple period. In the Second Temple period, by contrast, it essentially disappears as a communal sin. This reflects a broader historical reality: the ancient world was undergoing a gradual waning of serious pagan belief, laying the groundwork for the monotheistic faiths that would follow. The *aggadata*, then, is at least partly capturing this genuine historical shift, even though the *pesukim* in Nechemiah that frame the story do not explicitly mention *avodah zarah* — they allude more generally to repeated past sinfulness.

### Keruvim & Physical Conne…

The second dimension is more striking: the *Gemara* describes the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah* as emerging like a lion of fire from the *Kodesh Kodashim*. What is the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah* doing in the *Kodesh Kodashim*?

Different interpretations exist, but the most immediate one follows naturally from what the *Gemara* itself discussed not long before: the *Kodesh Kodashim* as the site of a profound and very physical manifestation of God's connection to Israel. The *Kohen Gadol* enters into the inner chamber — and the *Gemara* had already developed the imagery of that entry in terms of intimate encounter — and central to that encounter are the *keruvim*, those statues intertwined like lovers, which God showed to *Bnei Yisrael* at the *regel* as a demonstration of the relationship between God and Israel.

Now, on one hand, the entire thrust of Judaism is the rejection of physical images of the divine, the awareness of how easily such imagery corrupts the idea of God. And yet: the *Mikdash* contains tremendous physicality, and at its very heart, in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, stand the *keruvim* — not God Godself, perhaps, but statues positioned right there in the holiest space, directly adjacent to the *aron*. These figures are not God, but they represent God's chariot or entourage, and they embody the intense longing for a direct, tangible mode of connection with the divine.

This is precisely the double-edged nature of the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*. Just as the *yetzer hara* of sexuality is not simply evil — it drives procreation and sustains the world, and must be channeled rather than eliminated — so too the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah* is not simply corrupt. It represents the human drive for immediacy and intimacy with God, the desire to connect with something utterly transcendent through means that are familiar and sensory. That is part of what was happening in the *Kodesh Kodashim* — in a constructive way, arguably — but it is also precisely what, when left uncultivated and unchanneled, collapses into paganism and idolatry. When this *yetzer* was destroyed and left the *Kodesh Kodashim*, something profound changed in the Jewish relationship with God. And it is worth noting what else departed from the *Kodesh Kodashim* in the *Bayit Sheni*: the *aron* and the *keruvim* were gone. The Second Temple's *Kodesh Kodashim* contained only the foundation stone. That entire dimension of physical-intimate connection — with all its dangers and all its power — departed together.

### Rav Kook Leibowitz Debate

This tension finds vivid expression in a remarkable juxtaposition between Rav Kook and Yeshayahu Leibowitz. Both are responding to the same *aggadata*, and their disagreement is fundamental.

### Rav Kook's Position

Rav Kook, writing in *Adar HaYakar*, mourns the loss. He writes: *asher me'az shebitel yitzra de'avodah zarah, nistalek koach hachayim hara'anan sheyesod ha'ahava ha'elokit min ha'olam* — from the time the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah* was annulled, the flourishing life-force that is the foundation of divine love departed from the world. He elaborates: *koach ahava elokit kechol koach tiv'i bilti me'ubad shebenefesh ha'adam, tzarich hu lelimud shel pituach vechissun vehadracha* — the power of divine love, like any uncultivated natural force within the human soul, requires cultivation, training, and guidance. Left uncultivated, it runs wild and degenerates into paganism. But the answer is not to eradicate it. If you eradicate it, you lose the passion, the drive, the immediate and emotional connection to God. The religion becomes, in Rav Kook's telling, shriveled, sterile, and morose — a consequence he attributes in part to centuries of exile among the nations.

### Leibowitz Critique

Yeshayahu Leibowitz, in his entry on *avodah zarah* in a lexicon of Jewish ideas, takes the diametrically opposite view — and turns his critique directly on Rav Kook. He writes: *ha'agada mesaperet she'Anshei Knesset HaGedolah hatzlichu lehadbir et yitzra de'avodah zarah beYisrael* — the *aggada* says they succeeded in destroying the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*. *Ach ein ele ela divrei agada* — but that is just a story. *Me'olam lo pasak be'olama shel haYahadut hama'avak hanu'ash shel ha'emuna baHashem Echad neged hamshicha hativ'it shel ha'adam ubechlal ze gam ha'adam miYisrael la'elilut* — never has the disheartening struggle in Judaism against the natural human pull toward idolatry come to an end, including among Jews, even behind the mask of belief in one God.

Leibowitz argues that the failure to sustain a clean distinction between *kodesh* and *chol*, between the genuinely transcendent and the human world, keeps reasserting itself. He indicts, in turn, Christianity, *Kabbalah*, *Chasidut*, the *Kuzari*, the Maharal — and then, pointedly, Rav Kook himself, whose thought, Leibowitz contends, has turned the Jewish people into a kind of physical manifestation of the divine. The *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah*, Leibowitz insists, is alive and well — and Rav Kook and his followers are its latest expression.

The tension these two thinkers articulate is profound: on one side stands the drive for purity of faith, the rejection of imagery and physicality in the approach to God; on the other stands the human impossibility of connecting with something utterly unlike oneself. We are physical beings, and to reach toward something completely *other* requires some form of bridge. Whether losing the *yetzer hara* of *avodah zarah* was a gain or a loss, and whether it was truly lost at all, remains a genuine and unresolved debate.

### Apollo-Dionysian Tension

This tension maps onto a structure the Greeks also recognized: the Apollonian-Dionysian divide. The human being carries within a Dionysian impulse — a pull toward non-rational, passionate, sensory connection — which must be bridled by what Apollo represents: rational structure and discipline. Judaism has always had to negotiate between these poles. The passionate, immediate, embodied dimension of religious experience is not simply a corrupting force; it is a real and powerful human need. The challenge is to channel it without either suppressing it entirely or allowing it to run unconstrained into idolatrous excess.

---

## Men Great Assembly

### Three Attributes

The *Gemara* transitions to a statement from the school of *Eretz Yisrael*: *b'ma'arava matnu hachi* — in the West they taught as follows. Rav Gidel says the word *gadol* refers to the fact that they used God's ineffable name during the reading of the *Torah* at the great gathering with Ezra. Rav Matna says *gadol* refers to the description of God as *ha'Eil hagadol hagibor v'hanora* — great, powerful, and awesome — in the *pasuk* in Nechemia.

The *Gemara* notes that Rav Matna's statement connects to a teaching of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *lama nikra shemam Anshei Knesset HaGedolah?* — Why were they called the Men of the Great Assembly? *She'hechziru atarah l'yoshnah* — because they returned the crown to its former glory.

### Prophets & Their Times

The explanation unfolds as follows. When Moshe spoke, he described God as *ha'Eil hagadol hagibor v'hanora* — great, powerful, and awesome. Then Yirmeyahu came, at the time of the Temple's destruction, with non-Jews dancing and desecrating God's sanctuary, and said: *ayeh nora'otav?* — Where is God's awesome power, that these nations feel free to act this way? And so Yirmeyahu did not say *nora*. (Rashi cites the *pasuk* in Yirmeyahu 32: *ha'Eil hagadol v'hagibor Hashem Tzeva'os shmo* — he said *gadol* and *gibor*, but not *nora*.)

Then Daniel came, during the exile, with non-Jews subjugating God's children: *ayeh gevurosav?* — Where is God's might, if He allows His children to be subjected to foreign domination? And so Daniel did not say *gibor*. The *pasuk* in Daniel reads *ha'Eil hagadol v'hanora* — *gadol* and *nora*, but not *gibor*.

Then the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* came and restored all three terms. But they did not merely restore them mechanically — they reinterpreted them. *Zu hi gevuraso, shekovesh es yitzro* — this is precisely God's might: that He subdues His own desire. He does not lash out immediately at the wicked. *Shemosein erech apayim lareshaim* — He extends patience to evildoers, granting them opportunity for *teshuvah* and allowing human beings the full exercise of free will. And *ve'elu nora'osav* — this is also God's awesomeness: *she'ilmaley mora'osho shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu, heich u'umah achas yachola lehiskayaim bein ha'umos?* — were it not for the awe that God inspires, how could a single small people have survived among the great nations across such a long exile? Even amid catastrophe, some residual awe and fear of God and of the Jewish people has prevented their total annihilation.

It is worth noting that the one term never omitted by either Yirmeyahu or Daniel was *gadol* — so *gadol* required no restoration. But the other two terms were returned, and that restoration is what earned the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* their name. This is borne out by the fact that when Ezra reads the *Torah* publicly, he uses all three: *ha'Eil hagadol hagibor v'hanora*.

### Truth in Liturgy

The *Gemara* then asks: how could Yirmeyahu and Daniel — who are here called *rabanan* — have omitted words that Moshe had established as the way to describe God? After all, this formulation, while not a formal *mitzvah*, was an institution, a way of addressing God that Moshe had set. Where did they get the *chutzpah* to remove a term?

Rabbi Elazar answers: *mitoch sheyodein baHakadosh Baruch Hu she'amiti hu, lefikach lo kizvu bo* — because they knew that God is *amiti*, that God is about truth. (This connects back to the earlier moment in the *aggadata* when the little note of *emes* fell from heaven in response to their prayer.) Since God is fundamentally about truth, they could not speak falsely about God. The Maharsha clarifies: this does not mean, *chas veshalom*, that Moshe was wrong. God truly is great, mighty, and awesome. But in Yirmeyahu's time, God was not *demonstrating* His awesomeness in a visible way, and in Daniel's time, He was not demonstrating His might. To praise God for attributes He was not manifesting in their era would have been a form of falsehood — not an error about God's nature, but a lie about their own experience of God's presence in history.

### Tradition vs. Truth

This *Gemara* carries powerful implications for how one relates to liturgy. The question it raises — how do you say things in prayer that do not feel true to your own religious experience? — is one that many people grapple with. One approach is to avoid *kavanah* altogether; a person who sent a letter to a certain rabbi responded to a sermon about deepening *kavanah* in *davening* by saying, frankly, that the only way he survived *davening* was by not having *kavanah* — that attempting *kavanah* would surface too many points of dissonance. Another approach is to modify the *davening* itself, as various movements have done. The classical *Torah she-ba'al peh* approach is to re-interpret — to find a reading of the words that allows them to remain true to one's religious experience, to *trans-value* rather than abandon the practice. That too is a form of what the *Anshei Knesset HaGedolah* were doing: maintaining the tradition, the continuity, the shared formulation — while insisting that what one says about God must remain anchored in truth.

---

## Torah Reading Rules

### Jumping Rules

The *Gemara* now returns to the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur*. The *Kohen Gadol* reads from the *Torah* before the assembled people — *V'kara acharei mot v'ach be-asor* — the *parsha* of *Acharei Mot*, which describes the *avodah*, and the *pasuk* in *Emor*, *ach be-asor*, which describes the *Mussaf*. These two passages are not adjacent in the *Torah*, which immediately raises a difficulty.

The *Gemara* cites the rule: *m'dalgin b'Navi v'ein m'dalgin b'Torah* — one may skip when reading from the *Navi* (as in the *haftarah*), but one may not skip when reading the *Torah*. How, then, can the *Kohen Gadol* scroll past intervening portions and read from a different section?

The *Gemara* resolves this by introducing the role of the *turgeman*, the translator. The distinction turns on whether the reader is able to reach the new passage before the translator finishes rendering the previous passage. If the skip can be executed without causing an obvious pause — without the congregation having to wait — then it is permitted, even in the *Torah*. This is a striking answer, because one might have expected the prohibition to stem from concern that people would mistakenly believe the two passages are textually adjacent. The *Gemara* locates the concern instead in the interruption itself: the *torach tzibur* of waiting, the disruption to the continuous flow of the reading.

### Single Topic Exception

A further qualification is introduced. The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *medalguim ba-Torah b'inyan echad* — in the *Torah* one may skip if one remains within the same subject matter. *U'vi-Navi bishnei inyanim* — in the *Navi* one may skip even across different subjects. And in both cases, one must do so without causing the translator to pause. Abaye clarifies the rule accordingly: the distinction between single and multiple topics applies to *Torah* readings.

### Absorption & Continuity

Rashi explains the underlying concern in a way that is worth attending to carefully. He writes that *Torah* verses are laden with commandments, consequences, and obligations — *divrei Torah hi atarot v'onashim u'mitzvot* — and *v'tzrichim sheyikansu be-lev hashomim*: they must enter into the hearts of the listeners. They must be absorbed. If a person is jumping between different subjects — *uchshe-ha'adam yotze me-shitta le-shitta acheret eino no'ach lefanav* — it becomes impossible to absorb what one is hearing; the listener is pulled in too many directions at once. This is the *locus* of the concern. It is not, according to Rashi, that people might walk away thinking two passages are adjacent in the text. The concern is the listener's capacity to integrate what is being read to them. As long as both passages address the same theme — as *Acharei Mot* and the relevant section of *Emor* both address the *Yom Kippur avodah* — that concern is resolved, and the skip is permitted.

### Trei Asar Order

The *Gemara* adds an additional ruling: *v'ein medalguim mi-Navi le-Navi* — one may not jump from one prophetic book to another. One does not begin a reading in Yirmeyahu and conclude it with a *pasuk* from Yeshayahu. However, *u'vi-Navi shel Shneim Asar medalguim* — within the *Trei Asar*, the twelve minor prophets, one may jump from one book to another, since halachically they constitute a single *sefer*. This is in fact the basis for the practice on *Shabbat Shuva* of reading the *haftarah* from Hoshea, Yoel, and Micha — different authors, but all part of *Trei Asar* and therefore treated as a single work.

The one constraint is *uvilvad shelo yedaleg mi-sof hasefer l'tchilato* — one may not go backwards within the same *sefer*. The reading must proceed in sequential order. The *Shabbat Shuva* practice indeed reads Hoshea, Yoel, and Micha in their canonical sequence, which satisfies this requirement.

### Avoiding Scroll Delay

Having established that one may read from two separate sections of the *Torah* provided the skip is executed without pause, the *Gemara* addresses the second part of the *Kohen Gadol*'s reading: the portion from *Pinchas*, which contains the *Mussaf* offerings of *Yom Kippur*. Rather than scrolling the *Sefer Torah* to that passage, the *Kohen Gadol* rolls up the scroll, holds it, and recites the portion from *Pinchas* by heart — *b'al peh*. The reason, as Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua explains, is *lefi she'ein golelim Sefer Torah batzibur* — one does not roll a *Sefer Torah* in public in the middle of a reading, because it forces the congregation to wait. The *Gemara* later identifies this concern under the heading of *kvod hatzibur*.

### Torah Integrity

Before he recites the passage by heart, the *Kohen Gadol* makes a declaration: *yatir mima shekarati lifneichem katuv kan* — more than what I have read before you is written here. The purpose of this declaration is *kedei shelo le-hotzi la'az al Sefer Torah* — so that no one should come to suspect that the portion from *Pinchas* was missing or defective in the scroll. He makes clear: the passage exists in the *Sefer Torah*, it is complete, there is nothing wrong with it — I am simply choosing to recite it from memory rather than scroll to it.

### Switching Scrolls

One might ask: why not simply bring a second *Sefer Torah* opened to *Pinchas*, and read from it directly, rather than reciting from memory? The *Gemara* considers this and rejects it for multiple reasons.

Rav Huna bar Yehuda says: *mishum pigmo shel rishon* — because people will assume there was a defect in the first *Sefer Torah*, and that a second had to be brought to replace it. This is a concern of *pegam*, stigma, on the original scroll. The *Gemara* confirms this principle by citing Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha's ruling regarding *Rosh Chodesh Tevet* that falls on *Shabbat* during *Chanukah*: when three separate people each receive an *aliyah* from three different *Sifrei Torah*, there is no *pegam* — each person's reading is complete and self-contained, and nobody has abandoned one scroll in the middle of their own *aliyah*. But if one person were to move from one *Sefer Torah* to another in the middle of his own *kriah*, that is *pegam* — it looks like something went wrong with the first.

Reish Lakish gives a different reason: *mishum bracha she'eina tzricha* — because switching to a new *Sefer Torah* would require making an additional *bracha*, and that *bracha* would be unnecessary. This ruling is itself noteworthy. It raises the question of what exactly the structure of the *brachot* surrounding the *Kohen Gadol*'s *Torah* reading looks like. He clearly recites a *bracha* at the conclusion — *al haTorah*, similar to the closing *bracha* of a standard *aliyah*. But did he also recite an opening *bracha*, such as *asher bachar banu*? The text does not say. What Reish Lakish's concern implies is that the presence of a new *Sefer Torah* would trigger the obligation of another *bracha* — as if the physical *Sefer Torah* being read from is itself an object of the blessing, not merely the reading as an abstract act. Whether this reflects an opening *bracha* that goes unmentioned, or something else about the relationship between the blessing and the physical scroll, is left unresolved. What is clear is that switching scrolls is treated as demanding a new *bracha*, and that unnecessary *bracha* — *she'eina tzricha* — is something to be avoided.

---

## Eight Blessings

### Blessing Structure

Following the *Torah* reading, the *Kohen Gadol* recites eight *brachot*. The *Gemara* enumerates them: *al haTorah* — on the *Torah*, recited in the manner of the closing *bracha* after an *aliyah*; *al ha'avodah* — on the Temple service; *al hahoda'ah* — thanksgiving; *al mechilat ha'avon* — for the forgiveness of sin; *al haMikdash* — for the Temple; *al hakohanim* — for the priests; *al Yisrael* — for Israel; and *al shear tefillah* — a final catch-all prayer.

Several of these correspond to *brachot* familiar from *Shemoneh Esrei*. *Al ha'avodah* corresponds to *Retzei*, which closes with *hamachazir schinato leTzion*; though Rashi suggests that in the Temple context, the closing formulation would reflect the active acceptance of sacrifices, something like *she'otecha levadecha beyirah na'avod* — as said in *birkat kohanim*. *Al hahoda'ah* corresponds to *Modim*, the expression of gratitude that follows God's acceptance of the offerings. *Al mechilat ha'avon* is a *bracha* specific to *Yom Kippur* — *mochel la'avonoteinu vela'avonot amo beit Yisrael ma'avir ashmoteinu bechol shanah veshanah melech mochel vesole'ach* — which the *Kohen Gadol* recites once the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is complete.

The remaining four *brachot* — for the *Mikdash*, the priests, Israel, and the general prayer — are not elaborated upon in the *Gemara* here, though Rashi notes that the Yerushalmi preserves their texts.

It is also worth noting that some versions of the *Mishnah* include a *bracha* for *Yerushalayim*, which would bring the total to nine. In the version before us, and in other witnesses to the *Mishnah*, *Yerushalayim* is absent, yielding eight.

### Shomea Tefillah

The eighth *bracha*, *shear tefillah*, is defined by a *baraita*: *rinah tchinah bakashah milfanecha, al amcha Yisrael shetzrichim lehivashea, vechotem beshome'a tefillah* — a song, a supplication, a request before God for Israel who requires salvation, sealed with the blessing *shome'a tefillah*. This is the blessing we know from the weekday *Shemoneh Esrei*, the one that falls just before *Retzei*.

*Shome'a tefillah* functions as the great catch-all. We have spent the length of *Shemoneh Esrei* making specific, named requests. *Shome'a tefillah* says: please accept all of that — and beyond it. There are things we need that we cannot fully articulate, petitions we have no language for; *shome'a tefillah* invokes God as the one who hears prayer in its fullness, beyond what can be said.

### Sacrifice to Prayer

What is striking about this ordering is the inversion relative to the standard *Shemoneh Esrei* structure. In our daily *tefillah*, *shome'a tefillah* precedes *Retzei*: the generic plea for God to hear our prayers comes before the specific request for God to accept the Temple service. Here, in the *Kohen Gadol*'s eight *brachot*, the order is reversed: it begins with *al ha'avodah* — with *Retzei*, with the *korbanot* — and only after that does it move to *shear tefillah*, the generic prayer. This reflects the direction of the moment: we begin from within the world of *korbanot* and the *Mikdash*, from the sacrificial rite just completed, and from that foundation we move outward toward the broader prayer for Israel's needs. It is the *Mikdash* grafting the *beit knesset* onto itself, rather than the other way around.

There is also a noteworthy structural observation made by the Tosafot Yeshanim (cited in an earlier part of the tractate): the major reason for the public *Torah* reading at this juncture is in order to give *brachot* on the *avodah* — to frame the entire preceding ritual with the language of blessing and *tefillah*. In that reading, the eight *brachot* are the culminating expression of everything that has just taken place in the *Kodesh Kodashim*.

---

## Garment Sequence

### First Linen Set

The *Mishnah* now traces the sequence of garment changes the *Kohen Gadol* undergoes throughout *Yom Kippur*. Each change involves the sanctification of the hands and feet before removing the previous garments, immersion in the *mikvah*, drying off, donning the new garments, and sanctifying the hands and feet again once dressed — five complete cycles in all.

The first set of garments is the *bigdei lavan*, the white linen garments, which the *Kohen Gadol* wears for the *Torah* reading and for the central *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* — the incense offering in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the blood sprinklings, and the associated rites described in *Acharei Mot*.

### First Gold Set

After completing the *avodah* in the white garments, the *Kohen Gadol* immerses and changes into his *bigdei zahav*, the gold garments. He then performs the two rams — his own ram (*eilo*) and the ram of the people (*ayil ha'am*), both of which are *olot* — as well as the *Mussaf* offering.

---

## Mussaf Timing Disput (II)

### Rabbi Eliezer Split

Rabbi Eliezer holds that the *Mussaf* offering is divided: part of it is brought before the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur*, and part of it after. Specifically, according to Rabbi Eliezer's position as it appears in the *Mishnah*, the seven lambs of the *Mussaf* are brought at one point — positioned alongside the *avodah* — while the remaining components of the *Mussaf* (the ox for the *olah* and the goat offered outside on the outer *mizbe'ach*) are brought at another time.

### Rabbi Akiva Morning

Rabbi Akiva disagrees. He holds that the seven lambs — and, in the more developed formulation of his position — all the components of the *Mussaf* that can be brought in the morning are brought together with the morning *tamid*, before the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* even begins. The logic, as we shall see developed below, is that the *Mussaf* is always linked to the morning *tamid*, and the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is a separate ritual with its own internal sequence.

---

## Garment Sequence (II)

### Second Linen Set

Following his first wearing of the gold garments, the *Kohen Gadol* immerses once more and dons the white linen garments a second time. The sole act performed in this second set of white garments is the removal of the fire pan (*kaf*) and the spoon (*machta*) — the vessels used for the incense offering that were left inside the *Kodesh Kodashim* from the earlier *avodah*. With their removal, the interior *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* is fully concluded.

### Third Gold Set

He then immerses a third time and dons the gold garments again. In this third set, he performs the afternoon incense offering (*ketoret shel bein ha'arbayim*) and the lighting of the *nerot* — the *menorah* lamps. The *tamid shel bein ha'arbayim* would also accompany this set, though the *Mishnah*'s language here focuses on the incense and lamps.

### Personal Garments

At the conclusion of all his service, the *Kohen Gadol* performs a final sanctification of the hands — this time without immersing in the *mikvah*, since the *avodah* is complete — removes his *bigdei zahav*, and changes into his own personal clothes, *bigdei atzmo*. A retinue then accompanies him home, and he hosts a celebration for his loved ones: *v'yom tov haya oseh l'ohavav b'shaa sheyatza b'shalom min hakodesh* — a day of rejoicing, upon having emerged safely from the *Kodesh*.

---

## Mussaf Timing Disput (II)

### Mishnah Ambiguity

With the *Mishnah*'s account of the garment sequence now laid out, the *Gemara* returns to examine the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva in detail — and finds that the *Mishnah* itself leaves a great deal unresolved.

First, there is a textual ambiguity in Rabbi Akiva's statement. He says: if the seven lambs were brought with the morning *tamid*, then the ox for the *olah* and the goat offered outside were brought with the afternoon *tamid*. But the *Gemara* asks: does this mean (a) the seven lambs in the morning and the ox and goat together in the afternoon, or (b) the seven lambs and the ox in the morning, with only the goat in the afternoon? While Tosafot argues that the plural form of the verb resolves this ambiguity, the *Gemara* treats it as genuinely open.

More substantially, the *Gemara* identifies what Rabbi Eliezer's position in the *Mishnah* leaves entirely unspecified. Rabbi Eliezer mentioned that the seven lambs (part one of the *Mussaf*) are brought at a particular juncture, but never stated where the ox (*par ha'olah*) and the goat offered outside (*se'ir hana'aseh bachutz*) are brought. Rashi notes that the goat is equally unaddressed.

Furthermore, both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva leave unspecified the question of *imurei chatat* — when the intestinal portions (*eimurim*) of the bull and goat of the *Yom Kippur* service are placed on the outer *mizbe'ach*. Recall that the carcasses of the bull and goat were removed and sent to be burned outside the city, but their *eimurim* — the sacrificial portions — must be offered on the *mizbe'ach*. Neither position in the *Mishnah* specifies when this occurs.

Rava therefore concludes: *lo mashchachat leh metakanta* — you will not find a fully delineated account of the ordering in the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* simply does not provide enough detail to reconstruct the complete sequence with certainty. If one wants a fully specified account, one must turn elsewhere.

### Baraita Clarification

Rava identifies two such sources: a *baraita* from the school of Shmuel presenting a version of Rabbi Eliezer's position, and the *Tosefta* presenting Rabbi Akiva's position. He adds a caveat: the Rabbi Eliezer who appears in the *baraita* from the school of Shmuel does not hold exactly the same position as the Rabbi Eliezer of the *Mishnah*. One should not press the contradiction between them; they represent different traditions.

The *baraita* from the school of Shmuel, attributed to Rabbi Eliezer, states: *yatzah v'asah eilo v'eil ha'am v'imurei chatat* — after the *avodah* proper, he goes out and brings the two rams (*eilo v'ayil ha'am*) and the *imurei chatat*, the intestinal portions of the bull and goat. Then: *aval par ha'olah v'shiva k'vasim v'se'ir hana'aseh bachutz im tamid shel bein ha'arbayim* — the ox for the *olah*, the seven lambs, and the goat offered outside are all brought with the afternoon *tamid*.

This version of Rabbi Eliezer is notable because it shares with Rabbi Akiva the commitment to keeping the *bigdei zahav* section after the *avodah* focused exclusively on *Yom Kippur*-related matters — here, only the *imurei par v'se'ir* and the two rams, which are the organic conclusion of the *Yom Kippur* service. The entire *Mussaf* in this version is deferred to the afternoon.

### Scriptural Linking

The *Tosefta*'s version of Rabbi Akiva's position is: *par ha'olah v'shiva k'vasim im tamid shel shachar hayu k'revim* — the ox for the *olah* and the seven lambs are brought with the morning *tamid*. The scriptural basis is *milvad olas haboker asher le'olas hatamid* — "in addition to the morning burnt offering which is the *tamid*" — which Rabbi Akiva reads as establishing that whenever the *Mussaf* is brought, it must accompany the morning *tamid*. The structural principle at work throughout Rabbi Akiva's position is this: when passages of the *Torah* link two offerings together, they are performed together.

The goat offered outside is then brought after the *avodah*, since the *pasuk* describes it as *milvad chatat hakippurim* — in addition to the *Yom Kippur chatat* — which indicates it comes after the *Yom Kippur chatat* is complete.

### Akiva Ordering

The full ordering according to the *Tosefta*'s version of Rabbi Akiva is as follows. First, the morning *tamid* together with most of the *Mussaf* — the ox (*par ha'olah*) and the seven lambs — since Scripture links the *Mussaf olah* to the morning *tamid*. Then, the *avodah* of *Yom Kippur* — the incense offering in the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the blood sprinklings, and all the attendant rites. Immediately after the *avodah*, the goat offered outside (*se'ir hana'aseh bachutz*) — since it is described as *milvad chatat hakippurim* and must therefore follow the *Yom Kippur chatat*. After that, the two rams: *eilo v'ayil ha'am*, the rams connected to the *Yom Kippur* service. Then the *imurei chatat* — the intestinal portions of the bull and goat placed on the *mizbe'ach*, completing the handling of the *Yom Kippur* offerings. And finally, the afternoon *tamid* — *tamid shel bein ha'arbayim*.

This ordering according to Rabbi Akiva places nearly the entire *Mussaf* at the front, alongside the morning *tamid*, before the *avodah* begins. Only the goat offered outside is held until after the *avodah*, by virtue of its scriptural linkage to the *chatat* of *Yom Kippur*. The *imurei chatat* and the rams close out the *Yom Kippur* rites entirely before the afternoon *tamid* concludes the day.

The precise positions of Rabbi Eliezer in the *baraita* and Rabbi Akiva in the *Tosefta* thus represent two coherent and fully elaborated orderings of the day's sacrificial service — orderings that the *Mishnah* itself, as Rava observed, leaves largely implicit. The *Gemara* will continue to develop the analysis of these positions in the following daf.

---

---

# Yoma 72

## Thread Counts

### Sheish & Six Threads

The *gemara* opens immediately after the final *mishnah* of the *perek*, which catalogued the eight garments worn by the *Kohen Gadol* and the four worn by the ordinary *kohen hedyot*, and concluded with the discussion of the *Urim V'Tumim*. The *tanna'im* now take up the question of thread construction in the priestly garments and Tabernacle vessels.

The *braita* states: *devarim shene'emar bahen sheish* — when the Torah employs the word *sheish* in connection with certain garments, it is to be read literally as six. Specifically, the rule is *chutin kaful sheish*, that each distinct strand of material consisted of six threads twisted together. When the word *meshuzar* appears independently — without the accompanying word *sheish* — it denotes eight threads spun into a single strand.

### Thread Counts

Working from this principle, the *braita* enumerates the thread counts of the major garments and Tabernacle furnishings. The *me'il*, the robe of the *Kohen Gadol*, was woven from strands of twelve threads. The *paroches*, the curtain separating the *kodesh* from the *Kodesh Hakodashim*, required twenty-four. The *choshen* and the *ephod* — the jeweled breastplate and the backwards-worn apron, respectively — each required twenty-eight.

Twenty-eight is, notably, divisible neither by six nor by eight, which immediately raises the question of how garments composed entirely of six- or eight-thread strands can yield a composite of twenty-eight. The resolution, which the *gemara* works through methodically, is that each individual strand woven into the *choshen* and *ephod* was itself a composite of twenty-eight separate threads.

The *gemara* then turns to the first foundational question: *chutin kaful shisha minalan* — where do we derive that the word *sheish*, which literally means linen, should be read as six threads spun together? The proof comes from the verse *vaya'asu es hakotonos sheish* — you shall make the tunics of *sheish* — and the same verse enumerates the turban, the priestly hats, and the breeches, each also described as *sheish* or *sheish meshuzar*. The word *sheish* or its equivalent appears five times in that passage — four as the word *sheish* itself and once as *bad*, a synonym for linen.

The *gemara* accounts for each occurrence. One instance establishes the material itself — *de'kittna nihavei*, it must be linen. A second tells us to read *sheish* as the numeral six, meaning six threads per strand. A third teaches that the threads must be *shizurim*, twisted together — not merely six threads laid parallel but six genuinely spun into a single cord. A fourth extends the rule *leshe'ar begadim*, to garments that do not themselves carry the word *sheish*, so that the default of six applies universally. A fifth establishes *l'akev*, that fewer than six threads invalidates the garment — following the familiar principle, operative in contexts connected to the *korbanos*, that a doubling of the verse signals an invalidating condition.

### Sheish = Linen

The *gemara* now addresses how we know that *sheish* means linen in the first place, beginning with the synonym *bad*. The phrase *davar ha'oleh min hakarka bad b'vad* — something that grows from the ground individually, stalk by stalk — is offered as the etymology: linen grows from a central stalk with small buds branching off it, each unit unto itself, rather than spreading into multiple branches. Hence *bad* connotes linen.

One might ask whether *bad* could refer to wool instead, on the grounds that a single sheep provides a unified, unbranching source of fiber. The *gemara* dismisses this: *imra aftzuchei miftzach* — wool threads naturally separate and splay outward. But then, the *gemara* asks, doesn't flax do the same? The answer is that flax threads spread apart only when beaten; they are naturally more unified than wool. So *bad* means linen.

The *gemara* then pauses over an interesting philological observation. It is remarkable that the *gemara* must resort to etymology at all, rather than simply asserting that the word means linen by tradition. One might note that the word *kitna* (flax) is related to the modern Hebrew *kutna*, and there may be a shared etymological root with words for cotton in other languages — though the Talmudic term for cotton is *tzemer gefen*, wool of the vine, a separate designation entirely.

It is worth noting, by way of broader context, that linen is the primary material of the priestly garments, particularly the *Kohen Gadol*'s white garments on *Yom Kippur*, which are entirely linen. The prohibition of *sha'atnez* — the forbidden mixing of wool and linen — takes on added significance here. One compelling explanation, advanced by scholars of purity systems, is that the Torah organizes the world into distinct categories, and the violation of categorical boundaries is precisely what *sha'atnez* represents. Linen is, uniquely among classical fabrics, entirely from the plant world, while wool is from the animal world; their mixture transgresses an elemental boundary.

### Yechezkel

*Ravina* offers a proof from a different direction. The *gemara* cites the book of *Yechezkel*, which describes the priestly garments using the word *pishtim* — *pe'arei pishtim yihiyu al rosham*, hats of linen shall be on their heads; *umichnesei pishtim yiheyu al matneihem*, and breeches of linen shall be on their loins. Since *Yechezkel* uses *pishtim* to describe the same garments that the Torah calls *bad* and *sheish*, this would seem to confirm that those words mean linen.

*Rav Ashi*, however, objects: *hai mi mikamei d'ati Yechezkel man amrah* — before *Yechezkel* appeared, who would have told us what *bad* meant? One cannot use a later prophetic text to establish the meaning of a Mosaic term.

The *gemara* responds by invoking a parallel principle from *Rav Chisda*. *Rav Chisda* taught that the rule disqualifying a *kohen* who is either an *arel* — uncircumcised — or of uncircumcised heart (an apostate) from serving in the Temple is not derived from the Torah of Moses but from *Yechezkel*: *kol ben nechar arel lev ve'arel basar lo yavo el mikdashi*. And yet, if someone challenged that ruling with the same objection — how did earlier generations know this before *Yechezkel* was written? — the answer would have to be *gemira gemiri lah*: it was an established tradition, and *Yechezkel* came and gave it an anchoring in a verse, *ve'ata Yechezkel ve'asmachah akra*. The same applies here. The meaning of *bad* as linen was known by tradition; *Yechezkel*'s use of *pishtim* for the same garments simply provides an additional scriptural basis.

### Meshuzar = 8

Having established the baseline of six threads per strand, the *gemara* turns to *meshuzar*. *Moshzar shemonah minalan* — how do we know that *meshuzar*, when it stands alone without the word *sheish*, means eight threads?

The answer comes from the verse *vaya'asu al shulei hame'il* — they made on the hem of the robe — *rimonei techeilet ve'argaman vetola'at shani, mashzar*. This is the one instance where *mashzar* appears without the accompanying *sheish*. There are three types of thread in those pomegranates — *techeilet* (blue), *argaman* (purple), and *tola'at shani* (scarlet or crimson) — and the word *mashzar* appears.

The derivation of eight from this verse works by means of a *gezerah shavah*. The *gemara* says *veyalif mashzar mashzar miparoichet* — we learn the meaning of *mashzar* by the pomegranates from the same word by the *paroches*. The *paroches* is woven from four types of material: *techeilet*, *argaman*, *tola'at shani*, and linen — three wools and one linen — each of six threads, totaling twenty-four. By applying *mah lehalan esrim ve'arba*, the same total of twenty-four applies to the pomegranates. But the pomegranates have only three types of thread, not four. Twenty-four divided by three yields eight threads per strand.

### Pomegranates

The *gemara* now asks whether the derivation for the pomegranates should instead come from the *choshen* and the *ephod*, which also use the word *mashzar* and will turn out to require twenty-eight threads. If *mashzar* there yields twenty-eight, perhaps the pomegranates should also be twenty-eight, divided by three, yielding roughly nine or ten per strand.

The *gemara* rejects this on a structural principle: *danim davar shelo ne'emar bo zahav midavar shelo ne'emar bo zahav* — we derive a case where gold is not mentioned from a case where gold is not mentioned, and not from the *choshen* and *ephod* where gold threads are woven in. Gold threads constitute a categorically different element.

The *gemara* then considers the reverse argument. Perhaps it is preferable to learn the pomegranates from the *choshen* and *ephod* because those are garments, like the pomegranates, whereas the *paroches* is part of a structure — *d'ohel hu*. So the *gemara* settles on a third source, the *avneit*, the belt, which is also twenty-four threads, is a garment, and has no gold. *Danim beged mibeged v'davar shelo ne'emar bo zahav* — we derive a garment from a garment and a gold-free item from a gold-free item. Dividing twenty-four by three, each of the three types in the pomegranates carries eight threads.

*Rav Mari* adds a further argument: the verse by the *choshen* says *ta'asenu* — you shall make it — which is taken to mean that this garment's construction is unique to itself and may not serve as a model for others.

*Rav Ashi* adds yet another consideration from the verse by the pomegranates, which also says *ve'asita* — you shall make — implying *she'kol asiyot shavot*, that all the making must be equal. If one were to learn from a model of twenty-eight and apply it to three types, no equal distribution is possible: three times ten yields thirty, and distributing two types at nine and one at ten yields twenty-eight but violates the requirement of equality. Therefore, the model of twenty-four, which divides equally among three, is the only valid one.

### Meíl = 12

How do we arrive at twelve threads for the *me'il*? The robe is *kelil techeilet* — entirely blue, entirely one type of thread. A single type at the standard six threads would yield only six per strand, not twelve.

The *gemara* derives the six as a baseline by means of a *gezeirah shavah*: *veyalif techeilet techeilet miparoichet* — we learn the word *techeilet* by the *me'il* from *techeilet* by the *paroches*, establishing that *techeilet* is six threads. But how do we reach twelve?

*Rashi* explains that the word *kelil* means *gedil*, a braid — and *ein gedil pachot mishnayim*, a braid requires at minimum two. The *me'il* is therefore constructed by braiding two six-thread strands together, producing a twelve-thread composite. Every strand in the *me'il* is itself a six-twisted cord, and two such cords are twisted together, yielding twelve threads per strand.

The *gemara* anticipates an objection: why not learn the thread count for the *me'il* not from the *paroches* but from the pomegranates at its own hem — *rimonei techeilet* — which are eight-thread strands? If the *techeilet* in the pomegranates of the *me'il* itself is eight, should not the *me'il*'s own body also be eight?

The *gemara* gives two replies. First: *danin kli mikli v'ein danin kli mitachshit* — we derive a garment from a whole garment, not from decorative ornamentation. The pomegranates are ornamental, not the garment proper. The rejoinder is: *aderaba danin gufo migufo v'ein danin gufo m'alma* — on the contrary, derive the body of a garment from its own body, not from somewhere else. But the *gemara* ultimately resolves this by invoking the general rule that was derived earlier — *hanei milei d'amrinan ushear begadim shelo ne'emar bahem shesh* — for garments that do not carry the word *sheish*, the baseline of six applies. Since the *me'il*'s body has no explicit thread count, it defaults to six, and then *kelil*, meaning braided double, brings it to twelve.

### Paroches = 24

The *paroches* at twenty-four threads requires almost no derivation at all. The *gemara* states simply: *arba deshisha shisha* — four types of material, each at six threads. *Lo dina velo dayana* — there is nothing worth arguing about. The groundwork has already been fully laid: each type is six threads, there are four distinct types, and four times six is twenty-four, straightforwardly and without complication.

### Choshen/Ephod = 28

For the *choshen* and the *ephod*, the verse specifies: *zahav techeilet ve'argaman vetola'at shani vesheish mashzar* — gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and linen. That is five types. Five times six would yield thirty, not twenty-eight. The resolution: the four fabric threads — *techeilet*, *argaman*, *tola'at shani*, and linen — each carry six threads, totaling twenty-four. The gold contributes only four additional threads, yielding twenty-eight.

Why four strands of gold? *Rav Acha bar Yaakov* derives this from the term *psilim*, which appears when the Torah describes the fabrication of the gold thread — hammering the gold flat and cutting it into strands. The word *psil* suggests two, as twisting requires two strands; the plural *psilim* doubles it, yielding four.

*Rav Ashi* offers an alternative: the verse says *la'asos besoch hatecheilet* — to weave the gold into the *techeilet* — and similarly into the *argaman*, *tola'at shani*, and linen. This means a single gold thread is woven into each of the four fabric types. Each strand is then not six threads but seven — six of its own color plus one of gold — and four times seven equals twenty-eight.

The *gemara* closes this line of reasoning by rejecting the alternative of six gold threads: one cannot simply add six, since six divided equally among four types leaves a remainder, violating the requirement that all constructions be equal. One gold thread per type, distributed evenly among the four fabric strands, is the only arithmetically clean solution.

---

## Prohibitions

### Tearing Garments

*Rachava* said in the name of *Rav Yehuda*: one who tears *bigdei kehunah* — the priestly garments — intentionally receives lashes, as the verse states *lo yikarei*, it shall not be torn. This verse appears specifically by the *me'il*, but the ruling is generalized to all priestly garments.

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* challenges this reading: perhaps the Torah is not issuing a prohibition but rather an instruction for construction. Perhaps the meaning is — make a hem around the collar, *kedei delo nikarei*, so that it should not accidentally tear. The verse would then be describing how to make it durable, not commanding a person.

The *gemara* dismisses the challenge on textual grounds: the verse reads *lo yikarei*, it shall not tear, not *shelo yikarei*, so that it should not tear. The phrasing is read as a categorical prohibition addressed to a person, not as a design specification. The objection retains some force as a matter of interpretive intuition, but the *gemara* holds firm.

### Removing Items

*Elazar* similarly rules: one who removes the *choshen* from the *ephod* while the *Kohen Gadol* is actively engaged in the *avodah*, and one who removes the staves of the *aron* from their rings, each receives lashes. The sources are: *ve-lo yizach ha-choshen me-al ha-ephod* — the breastplate shall not be moved from the *ephod* — and *lo yasuru mimenu* — they shall not be removed from it — referring to the staves of the *aron*.

*Rav Acha bar Yaakov* raises a parallel objection: perhaps the Torah is instructing how the items should be secured — *chadkinuhu*, tighten the breastplate to the *ephod*; do it well, so that it will not slip off — rather than prohibiting any deliberate removal. Again, the *gemara* answers with the same textual observation: the verses do not read *shelo yizach* or *shelo yasuru*, but *lo yizach* and *lo yasuru*, the language of prohibition.

### Ark Staves

*Rabbi Yosi be-Rabbi Chanina* identifies an apparent contradiction within the Torah's own treatment of the staves. One verse states *be-tabba'ot ha-aron yihyu ha-badim lo yasuru mimenu* — the staves shall be in the rings of the *aron* and shall not be removed from it. A second verse states *ve-huva et badav ba-tabba'ot* — the staves shall be brought into the rings — implying that there are times they are placed in and times they are not. If the staves may never be removed, what does the second verse describe?

The resolution: *mishtalfin ve-ein nishmatin* — the staves can be shifted, loosened, and adjusted within the rings, but they can never be fully extracted. *Rashi* explains that the staves were fitted with bulbous heads, allowing them to move back and forth within the rings without ever falling free. The word *ve-huva* in the second verse therefore does not describe an initial installation but rather an adjustment — repositioning the staves within the rings where they permanently reside.

A natural question arises: if the staves were loose in the rings, how would they function when the *aron* was being carried? One answer floats the possibility that the rings were fashioned around the staves after insertion, making removal impossible. Another possibility is that gold, being malleable, might have allowed the staves to be squeezed through initially. The *gemara*'s answer — that they shift but do not slip out — leaves these logistical questions open.

---

## Ark & Service

### Acacia Wood

*Rabbi Chama be-Rabbi Chanina* asks: what is the meaning of *atzei shitim omdim* — standing acacia wood — as the instruction for building the *Mishkan*? The first explanation offered is *she'omdim derech gedilatan* — the wood is to be oriented in the direction of its natural growth. You do not lay the wood horizontally when it grew vertically; you do not invert the grain. *Rashi* adds a further refinement: even the base of each plank should correspond to the root end of the original tree, and the top of the plank to the crown — maintaining the wood's natural orientation in all respects.

A related question: acacia in the wilderness grows as a relatively short bush, yet the planks of the *Mishkan* were ten *amot* — approximately fifteen feet — tall. How was such lumber available? The *gemara* recalls that the wood was brought out of Egypt. The wilderness does support acacia growth, but not at that height. Egyptian acacia, however — a distinct variety — apparently can achieve that stature, which resolves the difficulty.

### Standing Meanings

*Davar acher omdim* — a second interpretation of *omdim*, they stand. This refers to the gold plating that covers the acacia planks: *shema'amidim et tzipuyan* — the planks sustain and hold up their plating. The plating does not peel or corrode. *Rashi* adds the dimension that the wood itself does not rot despite being encased in gold — a remarkable quality, since one would expect the organic material inside to decay over time, regardless of the exterior plating. This is presented as a miraculous property of the *Mishkan*'s construction.

A third meaning of *omdim*: *shema tomar avad sikuyan* — lest you say that all hope for these sacred objects has been lost — *talmud lomar omdim*, the word *standing* teaches that the promise of the *Mishkan* and its vessels endures forever, *she'omdim le-olam u-le-olamim*. Even in the absence of the *Mishkan*, and later the *Beis Hamikdash*, the hope of their restoration remains, and the acacia planks stand symbolically — they have not perished.
