### Garments Serad

*Rabbi Chama bar Chanina* further asks: what is the meaning of *et bigdei ha-serad lesharet ba-kodesh* — the garments of *serad* to serve in the holy? The word *serad* evokes *sarid*, a remnant.

One explanation given: *ilmalei bigdei kehunah lo nishtayer mi-sonaihem shel Yisrael sarid u-falit* — were it not for the *bigdei kehunah*, nothing of the Jewish people would have remained. *Rashi* explains that it was through the priestly garments that the *korbanos* were offered, and those *korbanos* provided atonement; the atonement is what sustained the nation. This is a striking theological claim, situated here in the midst of an extended technical discussion of garment construction — a reminder that all this precision in weaving thread counts and fabric types served the ultimate purpose of the people's spiritual survival.

*Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani* in the name of *Rabbi Shimon* offers a different reading of *serad*: these garments were so perfectly woven that when removed from the loom, they needed almost no finishing work — you would lift them off the frame and the garment would be complete, requiring no subsequent needlework. *U-masardin me-hem klum* — only the smallest amount was left over to stitch. *Resh Lakish* identifies this remnant as *ma'aseh machat*, a small finishing stitch.

The *gemara* raises a challenge: a *baraisa* states explicitly that *bigdei kehunah ein osim osam maaseh machat ela maaseh oreg* — the priestly garments contained no needlework whatsoever, only weaving. *Abaye* resolves this: the sole exception was the sleeves. The cuffs — *veis yad* — were woven separately and then attached to the garment body, reaching to the palm of the hand. That minimal joining stitch is the *serad*, the tiny remnant requiring needlework. Everything else was completed on the loom.

### Survival

The *gemara* then transitions to a discussion of the *aron*, moving between the priestly garments and the vessels of the *Mishkan* in a way that reflects a structural parallel — the *kohen* himself functions as a kind of walking *Mishkan*, carrying the sanctity of the sacred objects within him.

The following passage will be seen as part of a broader thematic current running through the entire section: even while the *gemara* engages in highly technical discussions of thread counts, plating methods, and the dimensions of sacred objects, it consistently introduces a transitional voice gesturing toward the post-*Mikdash* reality. The focus on the *viddui* of the *Kohen Gadol*, the blessings he recited after the *avodah*, and now the assertion that *bigdei kehunah* sustained the people through the atoning power of the *korbanos* — all of these represent the *gemara* building a bridge from the ritual world of the Temple to the spiritual world that must persist without it.

---

## Ark Boxes & Crowns

### Nested Boxes

*Rachava* in the name of *Rav Yehuda* teaches: *Betzalel* made three *aronos* — not three separate *aronos* in the sense of different arks, but three nested boxes that together composed the single *aron*. Rather than taking a wooden box and laminating it with gold directly, *Betzalel* constructed three discrete containers — one of gold for the interior, one of wood in the middle, and one of gold for the exterior — which fit inside one another like nesting vessels.

The dimensions are as follows. The Torah specifies the *aron* as one and a half *amot* in height, equal to nine *tefachim*. The wooden middle box was therefore nine *tefachim* on the outside. The inner gold box was eight *tefachim*, because the thickness of the wooden base consumes one *tefach* from the interior. The outer gold box was ten *tefachim* and a fraction — ten because the outer box extends one *tefach* above the wood to provide a rim on which the *kaporet* rests, and the additional fraction accounts for the thickness of the base of the outer gold box itself.

A *baraisa* records an alternative figure of eleven and a fraction for the outer box. The *gemara* resolves the discrepancy: *ha keman de'amar yesh bo ovi tefach* — the eleven-and-fraction version holds that the base of the outer gold box is itself a full *tefach* thick, which is a great deal of gold; *ha keman de'amar ein bo ovi tefach* — the ten-and-fraction version assumes the outer gold box has only a minimal base. The *mashu*, the fraction beyond ten or eleven, is identified as the *zer*, the small crown-like rim that protrudes above the *kaporet*.

### Three Crowns

*Rabbi Yochanan* teaches: *shelosha zeirim hem* — there are three crowns: the crown on the *mizbeach* (altar), the crown on the *aron*, and the crown on the *shulchan* (table). This immediately calls to mind the famous *mishnah* in *Pirkei Avot*. The crown of the *mizbeach* — representing the sacrificial service — corresponds to the crown of *kehunah*; it was taken by *Aharon* and his descendants. The crown of the *shulchan* — evoking prosperity and dominion — corresponds to the crown of *malchut*; it was taken by the house of *David*. The crown of the *aron* — representing Torah — *adayin munach*, still rests there, *kol ha-rotzeh likach yavo ve-yitol*, and anyone who wishes to take it may come and take it.

### Torah Crown

One might suppose that the *keter Torah*'s accessibility to all implies it is the lesser of the three crowns. The *gemara* counters with the verse from *Mishlei*: *bi melachim yimlochu* — through me, kings reign. The Torah speaks in the first person: it is through Torah that all other crowns are sustained. The crown of Torah is therefore not lesser but greater — the source from which *kehunah* and *malchut* derive their legitimacy.

*Rav Yochanan* further notes a textual curiosity: the word for crown is written *zer* but vocalized as *zeir*. If one merits, *zacha na'asis lo zeir* — it becomes a crown for him. If one does not merit, *zara heimenu* — it becomes foreign to him. The same written form carries two meanings depending on whether the learner is worthy.

It is worth pausing on the cumulative structure of this passage. Throughout the extended technical material on garment threads and the *aron*'s construction, a persistent counterpoint has emerged: even in the midst of all that ritual precision, the *gemara* returns repeatedly to the Torah as the great equalizer — the one sacred object not inherited by lineage, not restricted by tribe or dynasty, but available to whoever will come and take it.

---

## Torah & Sincerity

### Inner/Outer Gold

*Rava* draws a moral teaching from the *aron*'s construction: *kol talmid chacham she'ein tocho k'varo eino talmid chacham* — any Torah scholar whose inside is not like his outside is not truly a Torah scholar. The ark was gold within and gold without; a scholar must be the same. The gold plating is not merely decorative — it expresses that the inner reality must match the outer presentation.

The connection is made explicit by the verse *mibayis umichutz titzapenu* — you shall plate it inside and outside. The physical requirement of the *aron* becomes the ethical standard of the *talmid chacham*.

*Abaye*, citing *Rabba bar Ulla*, intensifies the point: such a scholar is not merely less than a *talmid chacham*, he is actively despised — *nikra nisa'av*, as the verse says, *af ki nisa'av ve'ne'elach ish shoseh chamayim avlah* — even more despised and loathsome is a person who drinks iniquity like water. The image is one who consumes Torah — as water is drunk — yet does so in corruption, without inner truth.

*Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* adds: *lamah zeh mechir b'yad k'sil liknos chochmah v'lev ayin* — what is this purchase in the hand of a fool who seeks to acquire wisdom and has no heart? *Oy lahem l'sonayehem shel talmidei chachamim* — woe to those enemies of scholars, a euphemism meaning woe to those scholars themselves. The charge is *she'oskim baTorah v'ein bahem yiras shamayim* — they engage in Torah and yet have no *yiras shamayim*. The intellect pursues *chochmah* but *v'lev ayin*, the heart is not present.

### Torah Potion

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi* teaches from the verse *vezos haTorah asher sam Moshe* — and this is the Torah that Moshe *placed*. The word *sam* — placed — also means a potion or medicine. *Zacha na'asis lo sam chayim*, if one merits, the Torah becomes a potion of life. *Lo zacha na'asis lo sam misa*, if one does not merit — whether through insincerity, exploitation of Torah's prestige, or study untethered from genuine religious purpose — it becomes a poison.

*Rava* restates this in his own formulation: *d'uman lah sam d'chayei* — one who is expert in it, who engages with it correctly, finds life. *D'lo uman lah suma d'mosa* — one who does not engage with it rightly finds death.

*Rabbi Yonatan* shows a similar contradiction between two verses. One reads *pikudei Hashem yesharim m'samchei lev* — God's statutes are straight and gladden the heart. The other reads *imrat Hashem tzerufa* — the word of God is like a smelting fire, a force that purifies but can also destroy. The resolution parallels what came before: *zacha m'samchato*, if one merits, the Torah gladdens; *lo zacha tzarfato*, if not, it scorches.

*Resh Lakish* observes that the same verse can carry both meanings simultaneously: *zacha tzarfato l'chayim* — if one merits, the refining fire purifies and brings life; *lo zacha tzarfato l'misa* — if not, the same fire consumes.

### Fear & Purity

*Rabbi Chanina* applies the verse *yirat Hashem tehora omedet la'ad* — the fear of God is pure and endures forever — to *Talmud Torah*: *zeh lomeid Torah b'tahara*, this describes one who studies Torah in a state of purity. *Mai hi?* What does purity mean in this context? *Nosei isha v'achar kach lomeid Torah* — one who marries first and then studies Torah, so that the preoccupation of the body is settled and the mind can engage the learning without distraction.

*Rabbi Yannai* makes a proclamation of great force: *chaval al d'leis lei darta v'tara l'darta avid* — woe to the person who has no yard but constructs for himself a gate to the yard. Torah is the gateway — but a gateway to what? To *avodas Hashem*, to *yiras Hashem*, to genuine connection with God. If one focuses entirely on the gateway and builds no yard behind it — if the learning produces no *yirah*, no authentic relationship with the divine — the gate leads nowhere.

*Rava* turns to the assembled scholars with a direct and urgent appeal: *b'matusa minaichu, lo tirsu tarti Gehennom* — please, do not inherit two *gehennoms*. The scholar who dedicates his life to Torah study and denies himself ordinary comforts and pleasures has already accepted hardship in this world. If that sacrifice is not accompanied by sincerity and *yiras shamayim*, it will yield no reward in the next world either. The least he can do is make the sacrifice worth something.

*Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* offers a final thought on the verse *edut Hashem ne'emana* — the testimonies of God are trustworthy: *ne'emana hi l'haid b'lomdeha* — the Torah is trusted to testify about those who study it. One can look at those who have truly absorbed their learning and see it — and one can look at those who have not, and see that too. The Torah bears faithful witness to its students.

The discussion closes with a final phrase — *ma'aseh rokeim ma'aseh choshev* — referring to the distinction between types of woven work in the *Mishkan*, which connects back to the construction of the garments and the *aron* discussed throughout the *daf*. That thread will be picked up in the next session.

---

---

# Yoma 73

## Embroidery vs. Weaving

### Rokeim & Choshev

The daf opens with a final note on textile terminology pertaining to the *bigdei kehunah*. Two modes of craft appear in the relevant *pesukim*: *ma'aseh rokeim*, embroidery, and *ma'aseh choshev*, craftsman weaving. The distinction between these two techniques carries halakhic significance, as different garments of the High Priest were fashioned by one method or the other.

### Rashi: Paint then Embroi…

Rabbi Eliezer's explanation is that *rokmin bemakom she'choshvin* — one embroiders in the place where one has pre-designated. The artisan identifies the area in advance, much as one does needlepoint on a canvas that has already been painted with a pattern, and then fills in the embroidery precisely where the design dictates. Rashi elaborates: *betichila metaken hatzura al habeged al yedei tzeva v'achar kach rokhma bemachat* — first one renders the design on the garment by means of dye or paint, and afterward embroiders it with a needle.

### One Image vs. Two Images

A *tanna* teaching in the name of Rabbi Nechemia draws the distinction differently. *Rokeim* is *ma'aseh machat*, needlework, and therefore produces *partzuf echad* — a single image. *Choshev* is *ma'aseh oreig*, weaving, in which the design is woven into the fabric itself, and therefore produces *shnei partzufot* — two images. Rashi explains that when needlework is done, the same image appears on both the front and back of the fabric, whereas when the design is woven in, a different image appears on each side. This is, admittedly, somewhat counterintuitive: one might have expected that needlework, which can be worked on the surface without penetrating the entire cloth, would yield only one visible face, while a woven pattern, integrated into the structure of the garment, would naturally appear on both sides. Yet that is the distinction as Rashi presents it, and it concludes the discussion of *ma'aseh rokeim* and *ma'aseh choshev* carried over from the previous daf.

---

## Urim V'Tummim Inquir (II)

### Eight Garments Requireme…

The *mishna* introduces the topic of the *Urim v'Tummim*: the oracle housed within the *choshen*, the breastplate of the High Priest. The rule is that one may inquire of the *Urim v'Tummim* only when the *Kohen Gadol* is wearing the *shemonah begadim*, the eight priestly garments. The biblical source for this procedure appears in Bamidbar, in the passage where Moshe is commanded to transfer authority to Yehoshua. There it states that Yehoshua will stand before Elazar the priest, *v'sha'al lo bemishpat haUrim lifnei Hashem* — and he shall inquire of him according to the judgment of the *Urim* before God. It is thus established that the *Urim v'Tummim* is activated through the *Kohen Gadol* while wearing the full complement of eight garments.

### Mashuach Milchama Garmen…

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported a ruling: *begadim sheKohen Gadol meshamesh bahen, Mashuach Milchama meshamesh bahen* — the same garments the *Kohen Gadol* wears in service, the *Mashuach Milchama* wears as well. The *Mashuach Milchama* is the priest anointed to lead the people into battle — the one who rises before the army and addresses those who have built a new house, taken a new wife, and so forth, as the Torah prescribes. If he were to return from the battlefield and serve in the *Beit HaMikdash*, according to Rav Dimi he would do so wearing the eight garments of the *Kohen Gadol*.

### Aharon's Successors

The source for this position is a verse in Vayikra: *uvigdei hakodesh asher l'Aharon yihyu l'vanav acharav* — the holy garments of Aharon shall belong to his descendants after him. The question is raised: why does the verse say *acharav*, "after him"? It would have sufficed to say *yihyu l'vanav*, they shall belong to his sons. The additional word *acharav* is therefore interpreted to mean *lemi sheba bigdula acharav* — whoever succeeds him in a position of authority. On this reading, any figure who follows Aharon in some capacity of elevated status is likewise entitled to wear the *shemonah begadim*. The *Gemara* will proceed to subject this claim to sustained challenge.

---

## Inheritance Debate

### Inheritance Objection

Rav Adda bar Ahava raises a challenge — and some attribute the objection to an anonymous source. The question posed is: *yachol yehei veno shel Mashuach Milchama meshamesh tachtav kederech shebeno shel Kohen Gadol meshamesh tachtav?* Could it be that the son of the *Mashuach Milchama* assumes the role after his father, just as the son of the *Kohen Gadol* is preferentially positioned to succeed his father?

### Asirit Ha'eifah Braita

The question arises in the context of a *braita* that seeks to identify who is obligated to bring the *asirit ha'eifah*, the daily meal-offering of a tenth of an *eifah*, brought half in the morning and half in the afternoon. The *braita* asks whether the *Mashuach Milchama*, who is also anointed with oil, might be included in this obligation. The answer is no, because the relevant verse indicates that this obligation attaches only to a *Kohen* whose status carries an element of inheritance — and the *Mashuach Milchama*'s position does not pass to his son. It is worth noting that even by the *Kohen Gadol*, the inheritance of office is not absolute in the way kingship is: while there is a preference for the son of the outgoing *Kohen Gadol*, if another candidate is manifestly more worthy, that candidate takes precedence. By the *Mashuach Milchama*, however, there is no such preferential inheritance at all — whoever is anointed for leading the people into war carries no transmission of that status to his descendants.

### Seven-Day Initiation Ver…

The *braita* derives this distinction from a verse in Vayikra: *shivat yamim yilbasham hakohen tachtav mibanav asher yavo el ohel moed* — for seven days the *Kohen* who succeeds him from among his sons, who will come to the *Ohel Moed*, shall wear them. This verse connects the seven-day initiation into the garments — recalled from the very opening of the tractate, the seven days of *miluim* — with a particular category of *Kohen*: one who *yavo el ohel moed*, who will enter the *Ohel Moed*. The *Gemara* reads *Ohel Moed* here as referring to the *Kodesh Kodashim*, the Holy of Holies, entered by the *Kohen Gadol* on Yom Kippur. The phrase *hakohen tachtav mibanav* thus signals an inherited aspect of the role, and that inherited dimension belongs exclusively to the *Kohen* who performs the *avodah* on Yom Kippur — the *Kohen Gadol* — rather than the *Mashuach Milchama*.

### Holy of Holies Access

The *Gemara* now connects this to the larger question. If the *Mashuach Milchama* truly wears the eight garments, as Rav Dimi maintains, then — given the *Gemara*'s underlying assumption that wearing the *shemonah begadim* confers the capacity to perform the *avodah* on Yom Kippur — why would the *Mashuach Milchama* be excluded from that service? *Michlal chazi* — by implication, if he is invested with the eight garments, he ought to be fit for the *avodah* of Yom Kippur. That the *braita* takes his exclusion for granted implies that he does not in fact wear the eight garments, and hence cannot perform that service. Rashi notes that the basis for the equation of wearing the *begadim* with fitness for Yom Kippur derives from a verse at the conclusion of the Yom Kippur *avodah*: *v'khiper hakohen asher yimshach oto va'asher yemalei et yado* — the priest who is anointed and whose hands are filled, the latter phrase (*miluy yadayim*) understood elsewhere to refer to initiation through the wearing of the *begadim*.

### Primary Role Distinction

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds: *lo hachi ka'amar* — the *braita* is not making the argument you think it is. Even granting that the *Mashuach Milchama* wears the eight *begadim*, and even granting that in principle he might therefore be capable of performing the *avodah* of Yom Kippur, the verse about inherited status still speaks only of the *Kohen Gadol*. The reason is *kol she'ikar meshichato l'Ohel Moed* — whoever's primary consecration is oriented toward the *Ohel Moed* falls under the verse's purview. *Yatza zeh she'ikar meshichato l'milchama* — but this one, the *Mashuach Milchama*, his essential consecration is for war, not for the *avodah* of Yom Kippur. The verse about *tachtav mibanav* thus continues to speak exclusively of the *Kohen Gadol*, whose primary role is entry into the *Ohel Moed*, without thereby excluding the theoretical possibility that the *Mashuach Milchama* — wearing the same eight *begadim* — might also be capable of that service. The current state of the argument, then, is that Rav Dimi's position still stands: the *Mashuach Milchama* wears the eight *begadim* and, by implication, could perform the *avodah* on Yom Kippur, even though his consecrated status carries no inherited dimension.

---

## Braita Denial & Reinterp…

### No Four, No Eight

The *Gemara* now introduces a more direct challenge. A *braita* states: *Mashuach Milchama eino meshamesh lo b'arba'a k'Kohen Hedyot v'lo b'shmona k'Kohen Gadol* — the *Mashuach Milchama* wears neither four garments like a *Kohen hedyot* nor eight garments like the *Kohen Gadol*. This is a striking statement on its face.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye objects immediately: *ela zar mashvit lei?* — are you making him a non-*Kohen*? He must wear some garments to establish his priestly status and permit him to perform *avoda*. Some minimum must apply.

### Eivah Prevention Doctrine

Abaye therefore proposes a resolution: in principle, the *Mashuach Milchama* should wear the eight garments like the *Kohen Gadol* — this is what Rav Dimi said, and it is what logic demands. However, in practice he does not, because of *eivah* — enmity. The *Kohen Gadol* would perceive it as a threat to his dignity and status were another figure to wear the same eight *begadim*. The rabbinic concern for *eivah* therefore prevents the *Mashuach Milchama* from wearing eight *begadim*, and since he cannot be demoted to four — for one may increase in sanctity but not decrease, *ma'alin bakodesh v'ein moridin* — he ends up wearing neither. Abaye thus reads the *braita* as consistent with Rav Dimi's principle: in theory the *Mashuach Milchama* wears eight *begadim*, but rabbinic ordinance withholds this due to *eivah* concerns.

### Challenge to Eivah Expla…

Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges Abaye's reading directly: I will show you a *tanna* who does not hold of *eivah* concerns at all, yet still denies the *Mashuach Milchama* the eight *begadim*. If the only reason for the denial were *eivah*, any *tanna* unconcerned with such considerations would simply permit the eight *begadim* — but there exists a *tanna* who, even without *eivah* as a factor, maintains that the *Mashuach Milchama* fundamentally does not wear them. The source for this contention is a lengthy *braita*.

---

## Status Distinctions Brai…

### High Priest Privileges

The *braita* — drawn largely from material paralleled in Tractate *Horiyos* — enumerates the distinctions between a *Kohen Gadol* and a *Kohen hedyot*. First, the *par Kohen Gadol*: when the *Kohen Gadol* commits a sin for which a regular person would bring a standard *chatat*, the *Kohen Gadol* brings an ox — a *par* — instead of a lamb, and its blood is brought inside the *heichal*. Second, the *par Yom Kippur*, the bull he brings on Yom Kippur on behalf of himself and the *Kohanim*. Third, the *asirit ha'eifah*, the daily meal-offering of a tenth of an *eifah*, brought half in the morning and half in the afternoon. Fourth, *lo yifra velo yifrom* — he may not let his hair grow wild or rend his garments as signs of mourning when a close relative dies, though he may rend garments below the visible line; a *Kohen hedyot*, by contrast, rends above. Fifth, *v'ein mitamei l'krovav* — he does not become *tamei* even for an immediate relative. Sixth, *u'metzuveh al habetulah* — he is commanded to marry a *betulah*, fulfilling a positive commandment, and is prohibited from marrying a widow: *almanah u'grushah v'chalalah zonah et eileh lo yikach*. Seventh, *u'machazir et harotzeach* — his death releases the inadvertent murderer from the *ir miklat*. Eighth, *u'makriv onen* — even when in the state of *aninut* following the death of a close relative, he continues to offer sacrifices, remaining at his post in the *mikdash* rather than departing.

### Temple Service Privileges

The *braita* continues: *v'eino ochel* — though he brings sacrifices as an *onen*, he does not eat of them. And *v'eino cholek* — since he does not eat that day's portion, he receives no share in the distribution of those offerings, even when his *aninut* has passed. *V'notel chelek berosh* — whenever he arrives at the *Beit HaMikdash*, he takes the first and choicest portion of any distribution of sacrifices. *U'makriv chelek berosh* — he may likewise preempt the regular rotation and perform whichever *avodah* he wishes. *U'meshamesh bishmona keilim* — he wears eight garments rather than four. *U'fatur al tumas mikdash vekodasheha* — if he enters the *Beit HaMikdash* while *tamei*, he is exempt from bringing a *korban* for it, though the act itself is certainly forbidden. *V'chol avodat Yom HaKippurim imeshe bo* — the entire service of Yom Kippur may only be performed by him.

### Non-Anointed & Previous…

All of these privileges apply equally to a *Kohen Gadol* who was not anointed with the *shemen hamishchah* — a *merubeh begadim*, one who was initiated into the position solely through wearing the eight *begadim*, as was the practice after the *shemen hamishchah* was hidden away. The single exception is the *par ha'ba al kol hamitzvot*, the special bull brought for an inadvertent violation of a biblical commandment, which the *Gemara* elsewhere establishes is reserved exclusively for one anointed with the *shemen hamishchah*.

All of these privileges also continue to apply to a *Mashuach she'avar*, a previous *Kohen Gadol* — one who served temporarily, as when a substitute *Kohen Gadol* was appointed in case the acting *Kohen Gadol* became disqualified before Yom Kippur, and who afterward returns to a kind of emeritus status. For such a figure, all the privileges enumerated above continue. Two exceptions apply: the *par Yom Kippur* and the *asirit ha'eifah*. Both of these are singular daily obligations — there is only one *par* on Yom Kippur and only one daily *minchah* — and so they belong exclusively to the currently serving *Kohen Gadol*.

### Mashuach Milchama's Five…

The *braita* then turns to the *Mashuach Milchama*: *v'chulan einan nohagot bemishuach milchama* — none of these privileges apply to the priest anointed for war, *chutz mechamisha devarim ha'amurim baparsha* — except for the five things enumerated explicitly at the beginning of Parashat Emor. These five are: *lo porea v'lo porem* — his hair does not grow wild, and he does not rend his garments in mourning; *v'lo mitamei likrovav* — he does not become *tamei* to his relatives; *u'metzuveh al habetulah* — he is commanded to marry a *betulah*; and *u'muzhar al ha'almana* — he is prohibited from marrying a widow. Rashi notes that the *braita*'s language does not include *makriv onen* among his privileges, and the *Gemara* elsewhere derives that this does not apply to him. According to Rabbi Yehuda, a sixth item applies: *u'machazir et harotzeach* — his death releases the inadvertent murderer from the *ir miklat*; the Sages, however, disagree: *Chachamim omrim eino machazir*.

### Conclusive Proof Against…

The critical conclusion emerges here. The *braita* shows that the *Mashuach she'avar* — the previous *Kohen Gadol* — still wears the eight *begadim* and still serves in the *Beit HaMikdash*. Yet despite the fact that both the *Mashuach she'avar* and the *Mashuach Milchama* are cited in the same context, the *braita* lists wearing the eight *begadim* among the privileges that do *not* apply to the *Mashuach Milchama*. This is taken as conclusive proof that the *Mashuach Milchama* does not wear the eight *begadim* in the *Beit HaMikdash*.

Crucially, the *tanna* of this *braita* is plainly unconcerned with *eivah*: he freely allows the *Mashuach she'avar* — who was literally the *Kohen Gadol* himself — to wear the eight *begadim* and to continue serving. If there were a concern about enmity between two figures both wearing the same prestigious garments, it would be most acute precisely between the current and former *Kohen Gadol*, who had occupied identical roles. Yet no such concern prevents the *Mashuach she'avar* from wearing the eight *begadim*. The same *tanna*, however, excludes the *Mashuach Milchama* entirely. This refutes Abaye's reading: it is not *eivah* that prevents the *Mashuach Milchama* from wearing the eight *begadim*. The exclusion is principled and fundamental.

The *Gemara* attempts to preserve the *eivah* framework by making a distinction: this *tanna* is unconcerned about *eivah* between figures of equivalent status — the current and former *Kohen Gadol* were equals — but *does* consider *eivah* when the competing figure is of lesser standing, *bedizuta mineih*. The *Mashuach Milchama*, being a subordinate figure, would generate *eivah* of a different kind were he to wear the *begadim* of the *Kohen Gadol*: not threatening rivalry, but rather an affront to the dignity of the *shemonah begadim* themselves. The *Gemara* thus maintains that in principle, the *Mashuach Milchama*'s disqualification from wearing the eight *begadim* in the *Beit HaMikdash* remains a rabbinic restriction rooted in *eivah*, not a fundamental incapacity.

---

## Battlefield Inquiry Acco…

### Battle-Context Inquiry

When Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, he offered an entirely different account of the matter. The question, he explained, is not whether the *Mashuach Milchama* wears the eight *begadim* to perform *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash* — he does not. Rather, the *Mashuach Milchama* wears the eight *begadim* specifically for the purpose of being asked via the *Urim v'Tummim* about military decisions. It is in this capacity — at the battlefield, with the *shemonah begadim* upon him — that the inquiry takes place. This accounts for why our *mishna* opens precisely with the topic of who may be asked via the *Urim v'Tummim*: the *Mashuach Milchama*'s wearing of the eight *begadim* is not about service in the *Beit HaMikdash* at all, but about enabling inquiry on behalf of the nation before going out to war. The image is remarkable: the *Mashuach Milchama* stands on or near the battlefield, clothed in the eight garments of the *Kohen Gadol*, as the national leadership turns to him to inquire of God.

### Asked in the Garments

A *braita* supports Ravin's version: *begadim sheKohen Gadol meshamesh bahen, Mashuach Milchama nishal bahen* — the garments in which the *Kohen Gadol* performs his service are the garments in which the *Mashuach Milchama* is asked. The operative word is *nishal* — he is *asked in them*, not that he *serves in them*. The purpose of the *shemonah begadim* for the *Mashuach Milchama* is exclusively for the inquiry of the *Urim v'Tummim*, not for *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash*. This formulation resolves the difficulty posed by the earlier *braita* — which stated that the *Mashuach Milchama* wears neither four nor eight *begadim* — since that *braita* was speaking about temple service, about which the conclusion is clear: he performs no service there at all.

---

## Urim V'Tummim Inquir (II)

### Facing & Response Format

The *Gemara* now addresses the mechanics of consulting the *Urim v'Tummim*. A *braita* describes the procedure: *hashoel panav k'lapei nishal* — the one posing the question faces the one being asked, the *Kohen Gadol* or the *Mashuach Milchama*. *V'hanishal panav k'lapei Shechina* — and the one being asked faces the *Shechina*. Rashi explains that facing the *Shechina* means looking toward the *choshen* itself, which contains God's name written within the *Urim v'Tummim*. The response is then given in God's name, as illustrated by the verse: *koh amar Hashem aleh v'hatzliach* — so says God, go up and succeed. Rabbi Yehuda dissents: *ein tzarich lomar koh amar Hashem* — there is no need to preface the answer with "so says God," since it is self-evident that the response comes in His name. He would simply say *aleh v'hatzliach*, go up and succeed.

### Soft Verbalization Stand…

The *braita* continues: *ein shoalin bekol* — one does not ask in a loud voice. The proof comes from the verse in Bamidbar, *v'sha'al lo* — he shall ask *to him*, meaning privately, audible only to the *Kohen* and not to the surrounding multitude. Conversely, *v'lo meharher belibo* — one does not merely contemplate the question in one's heart without verbalizing it. The proof is the subsequent phrase, *al piv yetzu v'al piv yavo'u* — by his word they shall go out and by his word they shall come back — indicating that the inquiry must be verbally expressed. The manner of speaking is thus precisely that of Chanah's silent prayer: *veChanah hi medaberet al libah, rak sfateiha na'ot v'kolah lo yishama* — Chanah was speaking upon her heart, only her lips moved but her voice could not be heard. The inquiry must be verbalized, not merely thought, but spoken so softly that only the *Kohen* can hear. It is striking that the *braita* frames this mode of address as akin to prayer.

### One Question Rule

One may not ask two questions simultaneously: *ein shoalin shnei dvarim ke'echad*. If two questions are posed at once, only the first is answered: *v'ein machzirin lo ela rishon*. The basis is an episode involving David. The verse records that David asked: *hayasgiruni baalei Keilah beyado hayered Shaul* — will the people of Keilah hand me over into his hand? Will Shaul come down? The response given was *yered* — he will come down — which was the answer to the second question posed. This apparent contradiction with the rule is resolved: *David sha'al shelo keseder* — David asked the questions in the wrong order. The logically prior question was whether Shaul would come down at all, since the question about the people of Keilah was only relevant given Shaul's presence. The *Urim v'Tummim* answered the question that should have been first — whether Shaul would come — and once David recognized that he had asked out of order, *chazar v'sha'al keseder*, he returned and asked in the correct sequence, receiving the answer about the people of Keilah.

### David's Questions Example

The episode is elaborated further. After receiving the answer that Saul would come down, David posed the question again properly: *hayasgiru baalei Keilah oti v'et anashai beyad Shaul* — would the people of Keilah hand over him and his men to Shaul? Now that he knew Shaul was indeed coming, this second question was the relevant and properly ordered one. He received his answer. Additionally, the *braita* notes that if circumstances are pressing and two questions must be answered together, the *Urim v'Tummim* may provide both answers at once. This is demonstrated from another episode with David: *ha'erdof acharei hagdud hazeh ha'asigenu* — shall I pursue this raiding party? Will I overtake them? The response given was: *redof ki haseg tasig v'hatzel tatzil* — pursue them, for you will certainly overtake them and rescue the captives. Both questions — should I pursue? and will I succeed? — were answered together, because the urgency of the situation permitted it.

### Urim V'Tummim Finality

The *braita* then distinguishes the *Urim v'Tummim* from prophecy in one critical respect. Although a prophetic decree can sometimes be reversed — as when the people of Nineveh repented and the decree announced by Yonah was averted — *gezeirat Urim v'Tummim einah chozeret*: a pronouncement of the *Urim v'Tummim* is never reversed. The verse says *bemishpat haUrim* — by the *law* of the *Urim*: its decrees are absolute and cannot be undone. A potential objection arises from the episode of the concubine in Gibeah (*Pilegesh be-Givah*), where the tribes were told to go out against Binyamin and suffered two devastating defeats — suggesting that the *Urim v'Tummim*'s words did not come true. The *Gemara* resolves this: the words did come true. The tribes simply failed to ask the right question. They asked whether they should go to war against Binyamin; they were told to go. They never asked whether they would win. They did not attempt to discern *im lenatze'ach im lehinatze'ach* — whether they would be victorious or defeated. Only at the final inquiry, when Pinchas the son of Elazar stood before God and they explicitly asked whether to continue the campaign, were they told: *alu ki machar etnenu veyadecha* — go up, for tomorrow I will deliver them into your hand. Only then was victory promised, and only then was it achieved. The lesson, as the *Gemara* wryly implies, is that one must know how to ask.

---

## Urim V'Tummim Meanings

### Name Origins

The *Gemara* asks: *lama nikra shemam Urim v'Tummim* — why were they called by this name? *Urim* — *sheme'irin et divreihem* — because they give light to their words; they illuminate God's communication. As will be seen momentarily, this may carry a literal meaning. *Tummim* — *shemashlimin et divreihem* — because they complete their words; what they say is final and will not be reversed, as established above.

### Letter Mechanism Dispute

A dispute follows regarding how precisely the *Urim v'Tummim* communicated. The stones of the *choshen* were engraved with the names of the twelve tribes. Rabbi Yochanan holds that the letters *boltat* — they protruded, becoming raised on the surface, and the reader would combine the raised letters to discern God's message. Reish Lakish holds that the letters *mitztarfot* — they recombined, with the engravings reconfiguring themselves to spell out the word or message.

A problem arises for either view: going through the names of the twelve tribes, one finds no letter *tzadi* — and, as the Vilna Gaon points out, the letters *chet* and *kuf* are also absent. The full alphabet is thus not representable by the tribal names alone. If the communication depended on the existing letters either protruding or recombining, certain messages could never be spelled out.

### Alphabet Completion Solu…

Two resolutions are offered. Rav Acha bar Yaakov proposes that *shivtei Yeshurun katuv sham* — an additional inscription, *shivtei Yeshurun* ("the tribes of Jeshurun"), was also written on the stones, supplementing the names and providing the missing letters. Shmuel bar Yitzchak proposes differently: *Avraham Yitzchak v'Yaakov katuv sham* — the names of the three patriarchs were distributed across the twelve stones alongside the tribal names, completing the full alphabet in that manner.

### Ruach HaKodesh Requireme…

A *braita* introduces a further condition: *kol kohen she'eino medaber b'ruach hakodesh v'shechinah shorah alav ein shoalin bo* — any priest who does not speak with *ruach hakodesh* and upon whom the *Shechina* does not rest is not consulted. The *Urim v'Tummim* is not a mechanical device that operates independently of the spiritual state of the priest. The example cited is Evyatar: when he was asked a question via the *Urim v'Tummim*, no answer came to him, as the verse indicates by the phrase *ya'aseh v'lo alsa lo* — the answer did not ascend to him, in contrast to an inquiry that succeeds.

### Ruach HaKodesh Assists U…

The *Gemara* clarifies the relationship between *ruach hakodesh* and the *Urim v'Tummim*. One might have thought that what the *braita* is saying is that the entire mechanism is simply the priest receiving divine inspiration — that it is *ruach hakodesh* alone, not the letters, that conveys God's message, and that the *Urim v'Tummim* is merely a condition for the priest to attain that inspiration. The *Gemara* rejects this reading. Rather, *siyua havei mesaye b'hadaihu* — the *ruach hakodesh* assists the *Urim v'Tummim*; the two work in conjunction. The *ruach hakodesh* is a necessary precondition — without it the oracle is inoperative, as Evyatar demonstrates — but it does not replace the mechanism of the letters. The communication still occurs through the letters, whether they protrude (Rabbi Yochanan) or recombine (Reish Lakish), and the *ruach hakodesh* enables the priest to correctly read and interpret what the letters convey.

### Eli & Chanah Anecdote

The Vilna Gaon raises a pointed question: Eli the priest famously misread Chanah's silent prayer and concluded she was drunk (*shikorah*). But Eli, as the serving *Kohen Gadol*, presumably had access to the *Urim v'Tummim* — why could he not discern the truth? The Gra's answer is illuminating. The letters that appeared — *kaf, shin, resh, hey* — are in fact ambiguous. They can be read as *keshara*, meaning proper or upright, or they can be rearranged and read as *shikorah*, drunk. Eli arranged them incorrectly and arrived at the wrong conclusion. This little observation reinforces the point just established: the *ruach hakodesh* is required to correctly interpret the letters, and when the spiritual attunement is insufficient, even the priest consulting the *Urim v'Tummim* may misread what appears before him.

---

## Eligible Inquirers

### Eligible Questioners

The *mishna* specifies who may pose questions to the *Urim v'Tummim*: *v'ein shoalin ela l'melech* — only a king may ask, along with the *Beit Din* (or the *Av Beit Din* specifically), and anyone conducting inquiry on behalf of a national need.

### Yehoshua Paradigm

Rabbi Abbahu derives this from the passage in Parashat Pinchas describing Yehoshua's appointment. The verse states: *v'lifnei Elazar haKohen yaamod v'sha'al lo bemishpat haUrim lifnei Hashem, hu v'chol Bnei Yisrael ito v'chol ha'eidah* — before Elazar the priest he shall stand and inquire of him by the judgment of the *Urim* before God, he and all the children of Israel with him and all the congregation. Each phrase identifies a category of inquirer: *hu* — this is the *melech*, the king; *v'chol Bnei Yisrael ito* — this is the *Mashuach Milchama*, representing the people he leads into war; *v'chol ha'eidah* — this is the *Sanhedrin*, the representative body of the entire community.

---

## Masechet Structure

### Seven Plus One Structure

With the words *hadran alach ba lo Kohen*, the *Gemara* concludes the first seven chapters of Masechet *Yoma*. A brief *Tosafot* explains the architecture of the tractate: *techilas nakat shivah yamim kodem Yom Kippur* — it begins with the seven days preceding Yom Kippur; *v'hadar nakat leil Yom Kippur* — then proceeds to the night before, with the preparations of the *Kohen Gadol*; *v'hadar nakat seder avodat hayom* — then the order of the day's *avoda* in the *Beit HaMikdash*; *v'hashta nakat hilchot hayom l'inyan issur v'heter* — and now it turns to the *halachot* of the day that apply outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, to all of Israel.

### Covenant & Structure

There is something structurally elegant here worth noting. Just as there were seven days of preparation before Yom Kippur itself, so too there are seven chapters of foundation before the eighth chapter — which, like Yom Kippur within its preparatory week, represents the culmination. A parallel exists in Masechet *Shabbat*: that tractate opens with material about *erev Shabbat* and *hotza'ah*, and does not arrive at the *lamed-tet melachot* until the seventh chapter. The *Rambam* organized Hilkhot Shabbat identically, with six chapters of foundations before reaching the *melachot* in the seventh. Whether or not the parallel is intentional in every case, there is a recurring structural pattern in which seven preparatory units precede the essential content. And since eight is the number associated with *brit milah* — the sign of the covenant between God and Israel — the eighth chapter, the covenant chapter as it were, takes on added resonance as the unit that speaks to all of Israel beyond the confines of the Temple precincts.

---

## Yom Kippur Prohibitions

### Five Categories

The eighth chapter opens with the *mishna*: *Yom HaKippurim assur be'achilah uveshetiyah* — Yom Kippur is forbidden with respect to eating and drinking. One striking observation: the Torah never formulates these as explicit *lo ta'aseh* prohibitions. The verse says *v'innitem et nafshoteichem* — you shall afflict yourselves — which is descriptive and positive in framing. Yet the *mishna* frames it as *assur*, a prohibition, and as will emerge, violation is subject to *karet*. The full list of prohibited categories is: eating, drinking, bathing (*rechitzah*), anointing (*sichah*), wearing shoes (*ne'ilat hasandal*), and sexual relations (*tashmish hamittah*).

### King & Bride Exceptions

Two exceptions are permitted for washing the face. *Vehamelech v'hakallah yirchatzu et peneihem* — the king and a new bride may wash their faces. The king must maintain a dignified appearance before the people; the new bride must present herself properly before her husband, particularly in a context of arranged marriages where the couple may barely know one another. The latitude is limited strictly to the face.

### Childbirth Shoe Exception

*Vehachaya tin'ol et hasandal* — a woman in childbirth may wear shoes on Yom Kippur. This is the standard reading of *chayah* as a woman who has given birth, the allowance being for warmth and comfort in her vulnerable state. One *acharon*, however, proposes reading *chayah* as a midwife, on the grounds that the midwife must travel to assist with a birth and may therefore wear her shoes. This reading has a certain practical logic to it, though it is not the conventional interpretation. *Divrei Rabbi Eliezer v'Chachamim ossrin* — this is Rabbi Eliezer's view; the Sages prohibit.

### Violation Minimums

*Ha'ochel k'kotevet hagassah, kamoah uchegar'inatah* — one who eats the equivalent of a large pressed date including the volume of its pit is liable. *Vehashoteh meloi lugmav* — one who drinks the fill of one's cheeks is liable. These measures differ from the standard *shiurim* applicable to other prohibitions. The normal minimum for eating is a *kezayit*, and for drinking a *revi'it*. Here, however, the operative principle is different: the prohibition on Yom Kippur does not concern the formal act of eating or drinking as such, but rather the abatement of *innui*, affliction. The measure is therefore whatever amount provides satiation — which for eating corresponds to a large date (including its pit), and for drinking corresponds to the fill of one's cheeks.

### Combination Rules

*Kol ha'ochlin mitztarfin lekhakhotevet* — all foods eaten combine toward the measure of a pressed date. If one eats a variety of foods, their quantities are totaled, and if the sum reaches the *shiur*, one has transgressed. *V'chol hamashkin mitztarfin lemeloi lugmav* — similarly, all drinks combine toward the measure of a cheekful. However, *ha'ochel v'shoteh ein mitztarfin* — eating and drinking do not combine with each other. If one eats slightly less than a *kotevet* and drinks slightly less than a *meloi lugmav*, one has not transgressed, even though the combined intake is substantial.

---

## Assur & Chatzi Shiur

### Assur's Purpose

The *Gemara* focuses on the opening word of the *mishna*: *assur* — forbidden. The *mishna* could simply have enumerated the minimum amounts required for liability and said one is *chayav*; instead it opens with the word *assur*. Rabbi Ila — and some attribute the statement to Rabbi Yirmiyah — explains: *lo nitzrecha ela l'chatzi shiur* — the word *assur* is needed specifically to teach that even eating less than the minimum amount, a *chatzi shiur*, is forbidden. The *mishna* thus signals that the prohibition of Yom Kippur applies not only to a full *shiur* but to any amount at all.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

This opens a broader *sugya* about *chatzi shiur* that is not unique to Yom Kippur. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *assur min haTorah* — eating less than the minimum amount of a forbidden substance is biblically prohibited. Reish Lakish holds: *mutar min haTorah* — it is biblically permitted, though rabbinically forbidden.

### Agreed Prohibition

Both positions agree that *chatzi shiur* is forbidden — the dispute is only whether the source of that prohibition is biblical or rabbinic. The *Gemara* therefore notes: *hani nicha l'Rabbi Yochanan* — the word *assur* is well understood according to Rabbi Yochanan, since even a *chatzi shiur* is biblically prohibited and the *mishna* appropriately designates it as *assur*. According to Reish Lakish, the word *assur* would refer to a rabbinic prohibition. *Modeh Reish Lakish d'assur miderabanan* — Reish Lakish concedes that *chatzi shiur* is rabbinically forbidden, and so the *mishna*'s use of *assur* remains apt, capturing the sub-minimum prohibition that applies though it falls short of biblical *karet* liability.

---

## Oath & Rabbinical Status

### Oath & Non-Kosher Food

The *Gemara* now traces an implication of the *chatzi shiur* debate through the laws of oaths. The scenario drawn from a *mishna* is this: a person takes an oath saying *shvuah shelo ochel* — an oath that he will not eat — and then eats non-kosher food, *neveilot u'treifot, shekhatzim u'remasim*. Is he liable for violating his oath?

The difficulty is the principle of *mushba v'omed meHar Sinai* — one is already foresworn from Mount Sinai against eating forbidden food. The Torah itself prohibits it. A subsequent oath that one will not eat non-kosher food therefore ought not to take effect, since an oath cannot take effect upon something already prohibited. Yet the *mishna* states that one is liable. How?

### Kolel Resolution

Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan all give the same answer: *bekolel devarim hamutarim im devarim ha'asurim* — the case is where the oath encompassed permitted foods together with forbidden ones. When the person said *shvuah shelo ochel*, I will not eat anything, the oath took effect upon all the permissible foods in that category. Once the oath validly attaches to permitted foods, it simultaneously covers the forbidden foods included within the same category — this is the principle of *kolel*. The oath thus takes effect on the non-kosher food as well, carried along by its application to the kosher foods, and eating non-kosher food then constitutes a violation of the oath.

### Reish Lakish's Specifici…

Reish Lakish, however, takes a different approach. He holds that a valid oath can take effect on forbidden food only in two specific scenarios. The first is *bimfareish chatzi shiur* — if one explicitly swears not to eat even a *chatzi shiur* of forbidden food. The oath then takes effect because one is not foresworn from Sinai against a *chatzi shiur* of *chazir*; the Torah only prohibited a full *kezayit*, and the *chatzi shiur* restriction, according to Reish Lakish, is only rabbinic. An oath can take effect upon something that is rabbinically but not biblically prohibited. The second scenario is *b'stam aliba d'Rabbi Akiva* — according to Rabbi Akiva, a general oath (*stam shvuah*) not to eat is understood to prohibit even a tiny amount; since that tiny amount of forbidden food is not itself biblically pre-forsworn, the oath takes hold.

### Rabbinical ≠ Pre-Sworn

The implication of Reish Lakish's position is clear and stated explicitly by the *Gemara*: since Reish Lakish holds that *chatzi shiur* is only rabbinically forbidden, it is *not* considered *mushba v'omed*, not biblically pre-forsworn. One is not foresworn at Sinai against a *chatzi shiur* of non-kosher food. Consequently, an oath can validly take effect upon it. This stands in contrast to a full *kezayit* of *chazir*, regarding which one is entirely *mushba v'omed* — biblically prohibited — and no subsequent oath can add to or operate upon that prohibition.

The *Gemara* is in the process of working through the further implications of this position, noting the question of what transpires when one has *heter min haTorah*, biblical permission or merely rabbinic restriction. This analysis will continue into the next daf.

---

---

# Yoma 74

## Assur vs. Chayav Kares

### Perek Introduction

We begin the final *perek* of Tractate Yoma, moving beyond the *avoda* of the *Kohen Gadol* and turning to Yom Kippur itself from our perspective — focused on its prohibitions. The discussion of *tefillah* will come later; we open at the very top of 74a.

### Mishnah Language

The issue that launches the *gemara* is the language of the *mishnah*, which describes it as *assur* to eat and drink on Yom Kippur. The *gemara* finds this something of an understatement: the prohibition is biblical in force and carries an *issur kares*. Why would the *mishnah* reach for the word *assur*, which typically connotes something lighter — indeed, something closer to a rabbinic prohibition — rather than the weightier *chayav*, or at minimum *chayav kares*?

### Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish…

The *gemara's* answer is that *assur* is the appropriate term when discussing eating less than the minimum *shiur* — *chatzi shiur*. This introduces the famous debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yochanan holds that *chatzi shiur* is *assur min haTorah* — forbidden by the Torah itself. Reish Lakish holds it is only rabbinically prohibited. Either way, the term *assur* fits, because we are speaking of something forbidden but not deserving the full weight of *chayav kares*, since the act involved is less than the minimum *shiur*.

### Shvua and Treifot

Within this broader debate arises a specific question involving *shvuot*. If someone takes an oath not to eat and then eats *treifus*, the *chachamim* (in contrast to Rabbi Shimon) hold that the person has still violated the oath. But one might ask: should the person not already be *mushba ve'omed* — fore-sworn from Sinai — against eating *treifa*? Why does the additional oath take effect at all?

---

## Shvua and Mushba Ve'Omed

### Kulel Explanation

One answer offered is the principle of *kolel*: the oath was a general one not to eat any food. Even though part of what it encompasses — eating *treifa* — is already covered by biblical prohibition, the oath also encompasses many other foods not otherwise forbidden. Since the oath takes effect on the broader category, it takes effect entirely, and eating *treif* food now violates not only the prohibition of *treif* but also the oath itself.

### Reish Lakish Alternative

Reish Lakish offers an alternative resolution: the case involved an oath specifically not to eat *chatzi shiur* — less than a *kezayis*. Since eating half a *kezayis* of forbidden food is not a biblical violation, the person was never biblically fore-sworn against it, and therefore the oath can take effect on that amount.

### Rabbi Akiva View

Rabbi Akiva goes further, holding that one need not even specify *chatzi shiur* explicitly. Any normal oath not to eat implies even the smallest amount. So either by explicit formulation or by implication, the person is not *mushba ve'omed* against *chatzi shiur*, and the oath therefore takes hold.

### Rabbinic Prohibitions Qu…

This raises a pointed question: according to Reish Lakish, who holds that *chatzi shiur* is at least rabbinically forbidden — since rabbinic prohibitions exist under the broader biblical mandate not to violate the words of the Rabbis — shouldn't the person still be *mushba ve'omed* even rabbinically? How can the oath take effect on something that is at minimum rabbinically prohibited?

---

## Biblical vs. Rabbinic

### Keivan D'Is Heter

The *gemara* addresses this with a principle: *keivan de'is lei heter min haTorah* — since biblically it is permissible, the oath can take effect, and therefore a *korban* would result from violating it. Though the Rabbis have forbidden it, the biblical permissibility is sufficient for the oath to operate.

The *gemara* then immediately challenges this principle: if a rabbinic prohibition suffices to block an oath in some contexts, the same should apply here.

### Shvuat Ha'edut

To illustrate this challenge, the *gemara* introduces the case of *shvuat ha'edut* — the oath of testimony. In the absence of formal subpoena, the Torah provides a mechanism by which one may impose an oath upon a person believed to possess relevant testimony. If that person knows the testimony and withholds it, the verse states *im lo yagid venasa avono* — if he does not testify, he bears the burden of his sin. The question becomes: on whom does this oath-obligation operate?

### Mishnah: Eligible Witnes…

The *mishnah* states that *shvuat ha'edut* applies only to those who are *re'uyim lehiahid* — eligible to testify. The *mishnah* had already explicitly excluded women, minors, and *gazlanim*. So the additional phrase "eligible to testify" must be excluding someone beyond those already listed.

---

## Psulei Edut

### Le'ma'utei Mai

The *gemara* asks: *le'ma'utei mai* — what additional category does the phrase "eligible to testify" come to exclude?

### Rav Papa: King

Rav Papa says it excludes a king. A king cannot be brought to court to testify, nor can testimony be given against him — *melech lo dan ve'lo danin*. Though this is not explicitly stated in the *mishnah*, it is implied by the additional qualifying phrase.

### Rav Acha: Gamblers

Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it excludes those who are rabbinically disqualified — specifically, dice players and gamblers — *mesachek b'kivya* — who are disqualified by rabbinic decree, not biblical law.

### Gamblers Disqualified

Two reasons are given for their disqualification. The first is that gamblers are not engaged in *yishuvo shel olam* — productive labor that contributes to the world — making them susceptible to bribery and corruption of testimony. The second reason is more technical: gambling involves a kind of *gezeila*, because the loser of the bet was never truly prepared to part with his money; the bet rests on an *asmachta lo kanya*, a commitment not fully intended. Either way, the disqualification is rabbinic in nature. Nevertheless, when a *shvuat ha'edut* is imposed on such a person, the oath does not take effect — even though biblically he is fully qualified to testify, the rabbinic disqualification suffices to exempt him from any liability.

---

## Rabbinic Prohibition Eff…

### Paradox Raised

This creates a striking difficulty. We see that a rabbinic disqualification from testimony is enough to prevent a *shvuat ha'edut* from taking hold. If so, why doesn't the rabbinic prohibition of eating *chatzi shiur* similarly prevent the oath from taking effect there? In both cases, something is rabbinically off-limits; in both cases, a biblical oath is at play. Why is the result different?

### Practical Ability Requir…

The *gemara* answers by pointing to the precise language of the verse: *im lo yagid* — if he does not testify. The Torah imposes liability only on someone who *has the practical ability* to testify and chooses not to. The gambling dice player, rabbinically barred from court, has no such practical ability — if he were to appear and offer testimony, the court would turn him away. *Ve'hai lav bar hagadah hu klal* — he simply cannot testify in any practical sense. The verse cannot be talking about him.

### Practical vs. Theoretical

The distinction the *gemara* draws is between practical inability and theoretical qualification. Whether the obstacle is a rabbinic disqualification or a physical impossibility — say, the witness is imprisoned — the result is the same: if he cannot actually appear and be accepted in court, the oath does not bind him. It is irrelevant that theoretically, under biblical law, he would be qualified. What matters is whether he has the genuine, operative ability to testify.

### Food Application

In the case of food, the analysis is entirely different. The question of whether one is *mushba ve'omed* — fore-sworn — is about the status of the object: is it something already biblically off-limits? Eating *chatzi shiur* of *chazir* is not biblically forbidden. It may be rabbinically restricted, but one is not biblically fore-sworn against it. Therefore, the oath takes effect on it. The two cases operate on entirely different axes: *shvuat ha'edut* turns on practical ability to act; *mushba ve'omed* turns on biblical prohibition of the object. A rabbinic food restriction is thus not analogous to a rabbinic testimonial disqualification.

As an aside, this analysis opens a broader question regarding witnesses who are *pesulei edut derabbanan* in other halachic contexts — such as witnesses at a wedding or a *get*. There the witnesses are not appearing before a court to testify; their function is to give legal weight and substance to the act of *kiddushin* or *geirushin*. The question of whether a rabbinically disqualified witness renders the act invalid *de'oraisa* is a significant debate among the *rishonim*, and it turns on whether the efficacy of witnesses in those contexts is tied to their practical ability to appear in court or to some other criterion.

---

## Assur and Braisah

### Principle Established

With the foregoing in place, the *gemara* asserts its broader principle: *vechol heicha de'tani enosh kares lo tani assur* — wherever the language of punishment by *kares* applies, the *mishnah* would not employ the word *assur*. This is in line with the Rambam's practice in *Hilchos Shabbos*, where he is more systematic than the *gemara* itself, consistently using *assur* for rabbinic prohibitions and *chayav* for biblical ones. The *gemara* is not always so rigorous, but the basic point stands: *assur* carries an implication of leniency — at most something like *patur aval assur* — and is out of place as a description of a prohibition carrying *kares*.

### Braisah Text

The *gemara* immediately challenges this principle from a *braisah*: *af al pi she'amru assur b'chulan* — even though they said it is forbidden for all of them — referring precisely to our *mishnah* about Yom Kippur, which lists eating, drinking, bathing, anointing, wearing sandals, and marital relations — *lo amru enosh kares ela ochel v'shoseh v'oseh melachah bilvad*. The only activities punishable by *kares* are eating, drinking, and performing *melachah*. So the *braisah* itself acknowledges that the word *assur* appears in the *mishnah* for activities that carry *kares* — and it is the *braisah* that then clarifies the different weight of the items on the list.

### Different Weights

The *braisah* thus confirms that the same word *assur* is used for the entire list, while noting that eating and drinking (and *melachah*) carry *kares* while the others do not. Far from supporting the *gemara's* principle, the *braisah* seems to demonstrate that *assur* can be used even for things punishable by *kares* — it is the *braisah's* clarifying role to explain the differential gravity.

### Chatzi Shiur Interpretat…

The *gemara* responds with what is admittedly a forced rereading of the *braisah*. It maintains its position that *assur* would never properly apply to a prohibition carrying *kares*, and therefore reinterprets the *braisah* as follows: when the *mishnah* says *assur* regarding eating and drinking, it is referring specifically to *chatzi shiur* — less than the minimum amount. For a full *shiur*, one incurs *kares*. The *braisah* comes to point out that of the categories listed, only eating, drinking, and *melachah* can ever reach the level of *kares* — but the use of *assur* in the *mishnah* itself applies only to the *chatzi shiur* case. This is, as noted, quite a strained reading, since the entire point of the *braisah* was precisely to acknowledge that the same term covers activities of differing weight.

---

## Assur for Other Item (II)

### Assur Justification

The *gemara* offers an alternative explanation, which is considerably more compelling and resolves the difficulty with the *braisah* cleanly. It proposes: *ki tani assur asha'ara* — when the *mishnah* uses the word *assur*, it does so because that term is appropriate for the *other* items on the list. The *mishnah* enumerates bathing, anointing, wearing sandals, and marital relations alongside eating and drinking. For all of those other items, *assur* is exactly the right word — they are forbidden but do not carry *kares*. Since the *mishnah* is composing a unified list and needs a term that fits the majority of its items, it employs *assur* even for eating and drinking, which would otherwise warrant the stronger *chayav* or *chayav kares*.

---

## Assur for Other Item (II)

### Braisah Clarifies

The *braisah* then performs its natural function on this reading: it confirms that yes, the same word *assur* applies to everything on the list, but it clarifies that the first two categories — eating, drinking, and *melachah* — are of a categorically different and more severe character than the rest, and it is those that carry *chayav kares*. On this reading, the *mishnah* and *braisah* work harmoniously together, with no need to reread *assur* as a reference to *chatzi shiur*.

---

## Source for Inuyim

### Inuyim Introduction

Having established the terminological framework of the *mishnah*, the *gemara* now turns to the sources for the additional *inuyim* — the prohibitions beyond eating and drinking that apply on Yom Kippur: washing, anointing, wearing sandals, and marital relations.

### Sifrei and Shabbaton

Rabba and Rav Yosef teach, in the name of the other books of the House of Rav — *bishe'ar Sifrei d'vei Rav* — that the source for these additional Yom Kippur prohibitions is the word *Shabbaton*, as written in the verse: *Shabbat Shabbaton hi lachem ve'initem et nafshoteichem*.

### Sifrei D'vei Rav

The phrase *she'ar Sifrei d'vei Rav* warrants brief explanation. Rashi clarifies that it refers to the other *tannaitic midrashim* — those that are not *Torat Kohanim*, i.e., not the *Sifra* on Vayikra. The *Sifrei*, covering Bamidbar and Devarim, is sometimes labeled *Sifrei d'vei Rav* because Rav, as one of the earliest *amoraim*, is regarded as its editor. The very name *Sifrei* — "the books" — is secondary, a contrast to *Sifra*, meaning "the book."

### Sifra and Torat Kohanim

The *Sifra*, also known as *Torat Kohanim*, is the primary *tannaitic* midrash halacha on Vayikra. The fact that it is both called "the book" (*Sifra*) and bears the programmatic title *Torat Kohanim* reflects its centrality among the halachic midrashim. The *Sifrei*, comprising the midrash halacha on Bamidbar and Devarim, thus earns its name as "the other books," in contrast to this preeminent work.

---

## Shabbaton Concept

### Rashi's Parallel

Rashi's comment on the use of *Shabbaton* as the source for the additional *inuyim* is rich and carefully structured. Rashi notes that the verse *Shabbat Shabbaton hi lachem ve'initem* connects *Shabbaton* directly to *inui*. Just as the word *Shabbaton* in the context of Shabbat was used by the Rabbis to extend prohibitions beyond the core *melachot* — to other activities that are, in Rashi's striking phrasing, *she'ar melachot* of a lesser grade (*shelo hayu b'mishkan ve'einam melacha gmura*) — so too here, the word *Shabbaton* in proximity to *inui* comes *lehosif al inui achila ushtiya*: to add to the primary affliction of not eating and drinking these additional forms of self-restraint.

### Biblical or Rabbinic?

Rashi's formulation is deliberately ambiguous on the question of whether the additional *inuyim* are biblical or rabbinic. On the one hand, he uses the language *asmechu bei Rabbanan* — the Rabbis used this as their peg — suggesting an *asmachta*, a rabbinic enactment with a verse serving as a support. On the other hand, he writes that the *pasuk* is coming *lehosif* — to add — which suggests the verse itself is the operative source of the additional prohibitions, not merely a hanger for a rabbinic decree. This tension leaves Rashi's position genuinely ambiguous on the biblical-rabbinic question.

### Rambam and Ramban

The *rishonim* engage this question directly. Both Rambam and Ramban hold that the additional *inuyim* are not simply rabbinic with a verse as a mere *asmachta*. Rather, the process of rabbinic legislation here gives form and definition to a biblical mandate — the concept of *Shabbaton* — that extends beyond the specific prohibitions enumerated. The Rabbis are thus not legislating independently but articulating the content of an underlying biblical imperative.

Interestingly, the same dynamic applies by Shabbat, where both Rambam and Ramban understand the rabbinic restrictions on Shabbat as giving flesh to the biblical concept of *Shabbaton* that exists alongside the *melachot*. The *derabbanans* on Shabbat are not free-standing rabbinic inventions but the concrete expression of this broader biblical category.

### Ramban vs. Rambam

The debate between Ramban and Rambam concerns the nature of *Shabbaton* itself. The Ramban holds that the core concept of *Shabbaton* in the Torah — beyond *melachah* — is about refraining from exertion and labor-like activity, a category related to but conceptually distinct from the specific *melachot*. The Rambam, by contrast, holds that *Shabbaton* instructs us to prohibit not only the *melachot* proper but anything that leads toward *melachah* or resembles it — such as reading by candlelight, or performing an act with a *shinui*. On the Rambam's view, the rabbinic restrictions are defined by proximity and similarity to the *melachot*; on the Ramban's view, they represent a separate biblical category of withdrawal from exertion.

Applied to Yom Kippur, the question becomes whether the concept of *inui* is best understood through the lens of *Shabbaton* — as a form of withdrawal from the physical world — or whether it is a fundamentally different idea rooted in affliction, pain, and the *teshuvah* process. The Rambam, who titles his laws of Yom Kippur *Hilchos Shevisas Asor* — the resting on the tenth — sees the day as a *shabbat*-like stepping back from the physical world: just as one ceases *melachah*, one ceases eating, drinking, and bodily gratification. The *inui* is not about self-inflicted pain but about liberating oneself from anchoring in the physical world. This contrasts with the more intuitive understanding of *inui* as suffering and self-mortification in the service of *teshuvah* and *kapparah*.

---

## Chatzi Shiur Analysis

### Debate Restated

The *gemara* returns *gufa* — on its own terms — to the debate of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding *chatzi shiur*. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *assur min haTorah* — eating less than the minimum *shiur* of a forbidden food is biblically prohibited. Reish Lakish holds: *mutar min haTorah* — it is biblically permitted, though rabbinically forbidden.

### Chazi L'Itztarufei

Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning is: *keivan d'chazi l'itztarufei* — since the *chatzi shiur* is capable in principle of combining with an additional *chatzi shiur* to form a full *shiur*, *issura ka achil* — what one is eating is still the forbidden substance. Notably, Rabbi Yochanan does not say that one has performed an act of eating; rather, he says one has engaged with a forbidden object.

### Act of Eating

Reish Lakish's reasoning is: *achila amar Rachmana* — the Torah prohibits eating, *d'leka* — and here there has been no act of eating. Until one consumes a *kezayis*, the action does not qualify as an act of eating, and the prohibition therefore does not apply.

---

## Two Models of Shiur

### Model One: Transgression

The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish maps onto two fundamentally different ways of understanding why a minimum *shiur* is required for liability in the first place.

The first model holds that the transgression exists regardless of quantity: when the Torah says do not eat *chazir*, even nibbling *chazir* technically violates that command. The *shiur* is a threshold not for the transgression itself but for punishment — one does not receive *malkot* or *kares* below the minimum, but one has still done something wrong. This model sits very naturally with Rabbi Yochanan's position, since on this reading *chatzi shiur assur min haTorah* flows directly from the nature of the prohibition: the act of transgression occurs even below the *shiur*, only the penal threshold has not been met.

### Model Two: Act Itself

The second model holds that the *shiur* is constitutive of the act itself. There is no act of eating until one has consumed a *kezayis*; below that threshold, one has not yet performed the defined act that the Torah prohibits. You might have tasted or nibbled, but you have not *eaten* in the halachically operative sense. This is Reish Lakish's position: *achila amar Rachmana d'leka* — the Torah prohibited eating, and that act simply has not occurred.

### Model Implications

Rabbi Yochanan's position may be understood in a way that transcends both models. He appears not to claim that one has technically performed an act of *achilah* with a *chatzi shiur* — that is Reish Lakish's point, and Rabbi Yochanan does not explicitly contest it. Rather, his argument, captured in the phrase *issura ka achil* — one has ingested a forbidden substance — is that even absent a full act of *achilah*, there is something independently wrong about placing a forbidden object into one's body. It is not simply about whether the act of eating was complete; it is about the inherently problematic character of the object. The *chazi l'itztarufei* formulation supports this: the fact that two *chatzi shiurim* combine demonstrates that each one is already engaging with the forbidden substance, and that engagement is itself what the Torah regards as problematic, even if the act of *achilah* is only consummated at the *kezayis*.

---

## Kol Chelev Derasha

### Challenge Presented

Rabbi Yochanan presses his position against Reish Lakish by citing a *braisah* that derives a *pesuk*-based source for *chatzi shiur*. The verse regarding *chelev* states: *kol chelev lo tochlu* — do not eat any fat — and separately: *ki kol ochel chelev venichretas* — whoever eats fat will be subject to *kares*. From this juxtaposition, the *braisah* derives: I know only that those subject to punishment are subject to the prohibition; what about those not subject to punishment?

### Kol and Non-Punishment

The *braisah* identifies two such categories: one who eats *chelev* of a *koy* (discussed below), and one who eats *chatzi shiur*. In both cases, there is no *kares* — yet might we think there is also no prohibition? The verse therefore states *kol chelev* — any fat — teaching that even these non-punishment categories remain prohibited. Rabbi Yochanan cites this to demonstrate that *chatzi shiur* carries a biblical prohibition.

### Koy and Chatzi Shiur

The *koy* is an animal whose status as *chayah* or *behemah* is indeterminate. Because the prohibition on *chelev* applies to *behemah*, and the *koy* may or may not be a *behemah*, one who eats its *chelev* does not incur *kares* — the uncertainty prevents punishment. Similarly, *chatzi shiur* is below the punishable threshold. The verse *kol chelev* includes both: even these borderline cases remain in the sphere of prohibition.

### Response: Rabbinic

The *gemara* responds: *talmud lomar mi-drabbanan ve-kra asmachata b'alma* — this is actually a rabbinic enactment, and the verse is merely a *peg* upon which the Rabbis hang their decree. The prohibition of *chatzi shiur* is not, in fact, derived biblically from *kol chelev*.

---

## Koy Problem

### Koy Question

The *gemara* now challenges the alternative reading. If the prohibition is indeed biblical and *kol chelev* is the operative source, why would the verse need to include the *koy* at all? The *koy's* status is uncertain to us, not to the Torah. God knows perfectly well whether the *koy* is a *chayah* or *behemah*. The verse's inclusion of the *koy* would be saying: even this thing which you don't know the status of — it is still prohibited. But that seems to say nothing that logic would not already dictate: if it might be *chelev behemah*, of course one should be cautious. Why would divine legislation be needed to state that?

### Koy Its Own Category

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the possibility that the author of this *braisah* holds *koy beria bifnei atzma hi* — the *koy* is its own independent category, neither *chayah* nor *behemah*. If that is so, a genuine question arises: the Torah prohibited *chelev behemah* and permitted *chelev chayah* — but what about something that is categorically neither? On this view, the *koy's* chelev is not simply a case of uncertainty; it is a qualitative borderline case, a quasi-*behemah*, and the verse *kol chelev* genuinely extends the prohibition to it. The verse thus carries its own biblical work, and *chatzi shiur* may similarly be included through the same verse on biblical grounds.

### Dam Parallel

A parallel discussion supports this reading. Rav Idi bar Avin notes that the verse *kol dam lo tocheilu* — do not eat any blood — uses the word *kol*, which the *gemara* says comes to include the blood of a *koy*. Here again the question arises: why would the verse need to include the *koy's* blood, since the Torah prohibits both the blood of *chayah* and *behemah*? The answer, again, is that if the *koy* is its own category, its blood might otherwise not be covered. *Birya shani* — an independent category is treated differently — and the verse therefore extends explicitly to it. The same logic applies in the *chelev* case, and *kol chelev* may therefore carry genuine biblical force in its inclusion of *chatzi shiur*.

---

## Chatzi Shiur Scope

### Foods Only?

Two further questions about *chatzi shiur* emerge from the preceding analysis.

The first is whether the prohibition of *chatzi shiur* applies only to foods or extends to other categories of Torah prohibition as well. If, for instance, one carries on Shabbat half the minimum *shiur*, or melts half the minimum amount of metal, has one biblically violated Shabbat? A number of *poskim* hold that *chatzi shiur* is limited to foods. The reason is that the biblical prohibition derives from the verse *kol chelev lo tochlu* — which, even when extended conceptually, speaks of eating and ingestion. One can broaden that conceptually to all *ma'achalot assurot* and even to all eating, but there is no basis in the verse to extend it to entirely different categories of prohibition such as *melachot* on Shabbat. Accordingly, the biblical prohibition of *chatzi shiur* would not apply there. (We *pasken* like Rabbi Yochanan, and *chatzi shiur* is *de'oraisa*; however, many *poskim* would limit this to food-related prohibitions.)

An additional conceptual justification for limiting *chatzi shiur* to foods is the logic of *issura ka achil* — one has ingested a forbidden substance. When there is a forbidden *cheftza*, a taboo object, the mere ingestion of any part of it is problematic, because the object itself carries a prohibition. When the prohibition is about an *act* rather than an *object* — such as the act of *melachah* — the logic does not transfer: half an act of *melachah* is not an engagement with a forbidden object; it is simply an incomplete act.

### Generic or Subcategory?

The second question is whether *chatzi shiur* constitutes a single generic prohibition — something like a blanket rule derived from *kol chelev* that any *chatzi shiur* of any forbidden food is prohibited — or whether it is a subcategory of each individual prohibition. That is: is *chatzi shiur* of *chelev* a quasi-violation of the *chelev* prohibition, *chatzi shiur* of *chazir* a quasi-violation of the *chazir* prohibition, and so forth — each anchored in its own issur?

### Ramban's Question
