The Ramban already raises a practical consequence of this question. The halacha is that when one must violate a prohibition to save a life, the lesser prohibition is preferred. Suppose both a *chatzi shiur* of *dam* (whose full *shiur* carries *kares*) and a *chatzi shiur* of *chazir* (whose full *shiur* carries a lesser prohibition) are available to sustain a dangerously ill person. Is there a preference for the *chazir*? Or are both instances of *chatzi shiur* simply the same generic prohibition and therefore equivalent? The answer hinges on whether *chatzi shiur* is a subcategory of its underlying *issur* — in which case quasi-*dam* is more severe than quasi-*chazir* — or a uniform generic prohibition.

### Issur Cheftza

This connects to the broader distinction between *issur cheftza* — a prohibition rooted in the forbidden character of the object — and other forms of prohibition. The logic of *chatzi shiur* is most naturally at home in the domain of *issur cheftza*, where any engagement with the taboo substance is itself problematic, because the problem lies in the object rather than exclusively in the act.

---

## Eating Prohibition Nature

### State Not Object

The analysis of *chatzi shiur* connects naturally to the prohibitions of Yom Kippur but also points to an important conceptual difference. The standard categories of *ma'achalot assurot* are paradigm cases of *issur cheftza*: the object — *chazir*, *chelev*, *dam* — is itself the forbidden thing, and any engagement with it is problematic. On Yom Kippur, by contrast, the prohibition of eating is not about the object being forbidden. Any food is permitted at any other time; the problem is not the food but the *state* of the person — whether one is fasting or not, satiated or hungry. The Torah does not declare bread or meat a taboo substance on Yom Kippur; it demands that one remain in a state of *inui*.

### Conceptual Challenge

This distinction makes it conceptually harder to simply transfer the *chatzi shiur* logic from *ma'achalot assurot* to Yom Kippur. The argument *issura ka achil* — you have engaged with a forbidden substance — does not apply in the same way, since the food is not forbidden as an object. Whether and how Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning about *chatzi shiur* extends to Yom Kippur therefore remains a genuine conceptual question.

---

## Eating Prohibition Source

### Te'anu Meaning

Where does the Torah's prohibition of eating and drinking on Yom Kippur come from? The verse says *teanu et nafshoteichem* — afflict yourselves. But *inui* could mean many things. Perhaps it means sitting in the sun, or sitting in the cold, or other forms of bodily discomfort. How do we know it specifically means refraining from food and drink?

### First Braisah

The first *braisah* addresses this by juxtaposing the command of *inui* with the adjacent verse *vechol melachah lo taasu* — do not perform any *melachah*. The *braisah* reasons: just as refraining from *melachah* operates by *shev ve'al taaseh* — by sitting still and not doing — so too *inui nefesh* must operate through *shev ve'al taaseh*: a form of affliction achieved by passively not doing something rather than by actively doing something painful. This rules out sitting in the sun or deliberately exposing oneself to discomfort, which are active forms of self-affliction.

---

## Parallel to Melacha

### Refraining Logic

The logic of the parallel is direct: *melachah* is defined as something one refrains from; *inui* must likewise be defined as refraining. The *gezeira shava* between the two is not a formal lexical one but a structural parallel: they appear together in the verse, and so the character of one illuminates the character of the other.

### No Distinction

One might attempt to preserve a role for active *inui* in certain cases — for instance, if one is already comfortable, perhaps one must actively put oneself in a situation of discomfort. The *gemara* rejects this: just as there is no such distinction by *melachah*, there is no such distinction by *inui*. There is no category of *melachah* that sometimes requires active engagement; *melachah* is always defined by abstention. So too *inui* is always defined by abstention.

### Rashi: Passive Active

Rashi sharpens the point. The distinction the *braisah* draws is between passive and active affliction. By *melachah*, abstention is always passive — one simply does not perform the act. The parallel to *inui* teaches that *inui* must similarly be always achievable through passivity. If the only way to afflict oneself in certain circumstances would be to actively seek out discomfort — sitting in the sun, or staying in the cold — that does not qualify as the Torah's *inui*, because it cannot be framed as *shev ve'al taaseh*.

---

## Second Braisah

### Activity Standard

A second *braisah* takes a different approach to deriving what *inui* means. Again juxtaposing *inui* and *melachah*, it reasons: just as *melachah* on Shabbat is an activity that is punishable *elsewhere* — that is, *melachah* is defined as the kind of act that has halachic consequence and carries punishment in other contexts (as indeed the *melachot* are defined by their roles in other halachic systems) — so too *inui nefesh* must be an activity that is punishable *elsewhere*. The criterion is not merely that it is unpleasant, but that it constitutes the kind of act that in some other context carries liability. This rules out sitting in the sun or cold: there is no halachic context in which one is punished for sitting in the sun.

### Piggul and Notar

What type of eating is punishable elsewhere? The *braisah* answers: eating *piggul* and *notar* — sacred foods rendered invalid through improper intent or left past their allotted time. These carry *kares*, just as performing *melachah* on Shabbat carries *kares*. So the *braisah* establishes its initial category of *inui nefesh* as referring to eating — specifically, a kind of eating that is punishable, analogous to *melachah*.

### Expanding Punishment

But *kares* is not the only form of punishment in the Torah. The *braisah* extends the category through the double language of *te'anu ve'inisem* to include foods punishable by *misa biyedei shamayim* — heavenly death — even where the punishment does not reach *kares*, as with *tevel*. The doubled expression broadens the operative category of prohibited eating.

---

## Narrowing Scope

### Neveilah Inclusion

From foods punishable in some context, the *braisah* moves through a *kal vachomer* to include *neveilah* and other foods carrying a simple *lav* — a biblical prohibition without *kares* or *misa biyedei shamayim*. Even these, the *braisah* establishes, fall under the prohibition of *inui nefesh* through the expansive language of *te'anu ve'inisem*.

### All Foods Included

Once forbidden foods are included, the *braisah* reasons further: all foods must be included. The prohibition of *inui* on Yom Kippur is not merely a prohibition on eating food that is otherwise forbidden; it encompasses ordinary, permitted food. The expansive language of *te'anu* continues to broaden the category.

### Obligatory Foods

The *braisah* continues: having included discretionary eating, one might think that foods one is obligated to eat — such as *terumah*, which carries a *mitzvah* for the *kohen* to consume — might be excluded. The *braisah* includes these as well through the repeated formulation of the verse.

### Kodashim

Finally, the *braisah* addresses *kodashim* — the most obligatory category of eating, where there is not only a *mitzvah* to eat but a positive prohibition of *bal totiru* — leaving the sacred food past its time. One might have thought that where there is an active mandate and a corresponding prohibition against not eating, perhaps eating on Yom Kippur would be permitted or even required. The *braisah* rules otherwise: *ta'anu et nafshoteichem* includes even this case.

What this *braisah* achieves, conceptually, is grounding the prohibition of eating on Yom Kippur in the world of *ma'achalot assurot* — forbidden eating. The idea is: how do we know *te'anu* means don't eat? Because elsewhere in the Torah, eating can be a prohibited, punishable act. The Torah here is prohibiting that same category of activity — eating — but in the broadest possible scope: all eating, even obligatory eating. This is a conceptually striking move: the *inui* of Yom Kippur is understood as a species of forbidden eating, albeit one universalized to encompass all food. Notably, this model — rooting *inui* in the paradigm of *ma'achalot assurot* — connects directly to the model of *melachah* introduced in the first *braisah*, where the parallel was more about *shev ve'al taaseh*. The two *braisos* thus reflect two distinct conceptual frameworks for understanding what *inui* is and where it sits in the halachic system.

---

## V'Avadeti Source

### Verse Quoted

The *gemara* now presents an alternative source for the prohibition of eating and drinking on Yom Kippur: *ve'ha'avadeti et hanefesh hahi* — I will destroy that soul — referring to the one who does not afflict themselves.

### Body Wasting

The *braisah* derives from this verse not a punishment but a definition: *inui she'hu avedat hanefesh* — the type of *inui* being referred to is one that involves the wasting away, the losing, of the body. The word *avadeti* — destruction — signals that the *inui* the Torah has in mind causes a literal diminishment of the body.

### Loss of Calories

What activity causes actual bodily wasting? *Achila ve'shtiya* — eating and drinking. Refraining from food and drink depletes the body of its sustenance, causing a measurable, physical diminishment. This is the third conceptual model for *inui*: not withdrawal (*shev ve'al taaseh*), not a species of *ma'achalot assurot*, but genuine self-affliction in the sense of allowing the body to waste. This model aligns most naturally with the intuitive understanding of Yom Kippur as a day of suffering and *kapparah* — real, bodily discomfort as an instrument of *teshuvah*.

---

## Multiple Sources Why

### Question Raised

The *gemara* asks: why are multiple sources needed? Given the first derivation, why not simply rely on that?

### Arayos Problem

The problem with relying solely on the first derivation — that *inui* must be something punishable elsewhere, leading us to eating — is that there is another activity punishable elsewhere that could plausibly qualify: *arayot*, forbidden sexual relations. Sexual relations with prohibited partners carry severe punishment in many contexts. One might therefore argue that *te'anu* mandates refraining not from food but from marital relations, or that it mandates refraining from both. The first source alone does not clearly exclude this possibility.

### Arayos Excluded

The verse *ve'ha'avadeti et hanefesh* resolves this. The destruction of the body — the wasting signaled by *avadeti* — uniquely identifies eating and drinking as the subject. Sexual relations, while prohibited in many contexts, do not cause bodily wasting of the kind described by *ve'ha'avadeti*. The verse therefore specifically and exclusively points to *achila ve'shtiya* as the operative *inui*, while simultaneously excluding *arayot* from the scope of the prohibition.

---

## Re'avon Parallel

### Gezerah Shava

A final source is presented in the name of the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *ne'emar kan inui ve'ne'emar le-hallan inui* — the word *inui* is stated here, in the Yom Kippur context, and the word *inui* is stated elsewhere in another context. This constitutes a *gezerah shava* — a derivation based on the use of the same word in two separate contexts.

### Inui Re'avon

The parallel context is in Devarim, where God's affliction of Israel in the desert is described: *va-ye'anecha va-yar'ivecha* — He afflicted you and made you go hungry. Here *inui* appears directly alongside *re'avon* — hunger, starvation. The juxtaposition is explicit: affliction is hunger.

### Starving Conclusion

By *gezerah shava*, the *inui* of Yom Kippur is interpreted in light of this parallel: just as the *inui* mentioned in Devarim means going hungry — literal starvation — so too the *inui* of Yom Kippur means the same. *Te'anu et nafshoteichem* is a command to go hungry, to starve, and that means refraining from *achila ve'shtiya*. We will continue from here in the next *shiur*.

---

---

# Yoma 75

## Inuy & Yom Kippur

### Three Sources

We begin at the bottom of 74b, turning from the discussion of *chatzi shiur* to the proper concerns of *Yom Kippur*. The Gemara presents three distinct derivations for why *inuy et nafshoteichem* — the Torah's command to "afflict your souls" — means specifically fasting, given that the expression is quite generic in the *pesukim*.

### Three Approaches

The three derivations proceed as follows: the first learns *inuy* from *melacha*, understanding it as *nefesh* of refraining — a form of disengagement; the second anchors it by comparison to other things the Torah prohibits in different contexts, such as forbidden foods; and the third derives it from *ibud nefesh*, the notion of destroying the self. These three sources correspond to meaningfully different models of what fasting is supposed to accomplish.

### Rambam & Disengagement

The first approach corresponds to the *Rambam*'s emphasis on *shvita* — *shvita* from *melacha*, *shvita* from *achila v'shtiya* — a disengagement from the physical world. On this reading, fasting is not really about hurting or afflicting oneself; it is about withdrawal. The second approach treats fasting as analogous to *ma'achalot asurot* in the Torah: there are times one may eat *chazir*, times one may eat *chametz*, and there are times when all food is forbidden. This doesn't explain the inner logic of the prohibition but anchors it structurally within the body of Torah law. The third approach, by contrast, seems most closely related to the model of self-flagellation — the idea that pain and suffering, *yissurim*, constitute a necessary element of the *teshuva* process.

### Manna Comparison

The Gemara now introduces a *gezeira shava* via the school of *Derei Rabbi Yishmael*: *ne'emar kan inuy* — it says "afflict" here on *Yom Kippur* — *ve'ne'emar la'halan inuy* — and it says "afflict" in another context, namely by the *mahn*. The verse there reads *va'ya'anchecha va'yarivecha*, that God afflicted you and made you go hungry, and then fed you the *mahn*. The parallel is clear: *mah la'halan inuy ra'avon* — there it plainly means going hungry — *af kan inuy ra'avon* — here too it refers to hunger.

### Divine Affliction

The Gemara raises an objection: why not derive from the verse *im te'aneh et benotai*, where Lavan says to Yaakov, "if you afflict my daughters"? This *inuy* could plausibly refer to sexual deprivation or abstention — which would suggest that the primary *inuy* of *Yom Kippur* is sexual abstention rather than fasting. The Gemara responds: *dani inuy d'rabim me'inuy d'rabim, v'ein dani inuy d'rabim me'inuy d'yachid* — we derive a communal *inuy* from a communal *inuy*, and we do not derive a communal *inuy* from an individual one. In the case of Lavan and Yaakov, the concern was about individuals. The *mahn* and *Yom Kippur*, by contrast, both speak about the entire community.

## Communal vs. Private

### Community Focus

The Gemara presses further: there is also an *inuy* recorded in connection with Egypt. As the *Haggadah* expounds the verse *va'yar et onyenu* — "God saw our affliction" — *zu prishut derech eretz*, that the Egyptians forced the Jewish people to abstain from marital relations. This too was a communal *inuy*, applying to the entire people. Why not derive from there?

The Gemara's final answer is: *ela danin inuy bidei shamayim me'inuy bidei shamayim, v'ein danin inuy bidei shamayim me'inuy bidei adam* — we derive an *inuy* decreed from Heaven from another *inuy* decreed from Heaven, and we do not derive a Heaven-decreed *inuy* from a human-imposed one. The affliction in Egypt was imposed by human masters; the *mahn* and *Yom Kippur* are both divinely ordained. That is the more technically grounded criterion for the *gezeira shava*.

### Private vs. Public

Yet the earlier distinction — communal versus individual — is also worth pausing over. Is this purely a technical point about which verse grammatically qualifies for comparison? Or is there something substantively true about the communal nature of fasting that the Gemara is drawing out? One might observe that eating is naturally a public, shared activity — families and communities eat together — whereas sexual activity is inherently private. When an entire community fasts together, there is something meaningfully communal about that experience; everyone is in *shul* together, not eating. But if every household were refraining from marital relations, one would not describe this as a communal abstention from sex in the same organic sense. The experience of the day as a *communal* fast, as opposed to a collection of individual fasts happening simultaneously, may be precisely what is being communicated here. *Rashi* reinforces this by noting that the community in the *mahn* narrative is *Klal Yisrael* as a whole — all of Israel ate the *mahn*, all of Israel went hungry without it on a given day — just as all of Israel does not eat on *Yom Kippur*.

## Eating & Religion (II)

### Manna Discussion

With the *gezeira shava* established, the *mahn* becomes the operative point of comparison. And having mentioned the *mahn*, the Gemara now pivots entirely — spending the better part of a *daf* on an extended discussion of the *mahn*, the *slav*, and related topics. This is, in one sense, a digression: somewhere in *Shas* the Gemara wants to discuss the *mahn*, and this passage furnishes the occasion. But the juxtaposition is striking and deserves attention. We have just been discussing fasting as a religious experience. We are now about to encounter what amounts to a sustained disquisition on eating — on the conditions, textures, visuals, and dependencies that constitute the experience of food. The interplay of these two discussions is not incidental. How do we think religiously about food? How do we think religiously about fasting? Both questions are live as we enter this material.

### No Storage

The Gemara cites the verse *hamachilcha mahn bamidbar lema'an anosecha* — God fed you *mahn* in the desert in order to afflict you. What was the affliction of receiving the *mahn*? *Rav Ami* and *Rav Assi* disagree.

One says: *eino domeh mi sheyesh lo pas besalo lemi she'ein lo pas besalo* — it is not the same for one who has bread in his basket as for one who does not. Even if you receive food every single day, there is a qualitative difference between having provisions stored and facing an empty cupboard each morning. The sense of dependence, the absence of security — that is the *inuy*. And of course it instills something spiritually significant: daily recognition of one's dependence upon God.

### Visual Deprivation

The other opinion says: *eino domeh mi shero'eh ve'ocheil lemi she'eino ro'eh ve'ocheil* — it is not the same for one who sees what he eats as for one who does not. When you ate the *mahn*, it all looked the same. You did not have the aesthetic, visual experience of eating. We know that the way food appears affects how good it tastes and how satisfied you feel from the meal. Presentation matters — you arrange it nicely on the plate, you color it, you create a fully sensory experience. Approximately half of eating, it has been said, is visual. The *Gemara*'s emphasis on why one lights *Shabbos* candles includes precisely the idea of what it means to eat in light versus to eat in the dark.

So the *inuy* of the *mahn* was this: you received the taste, you were filled, but you were deprived of the full sensory experience of eating. The *mahn* may have tasted like anything — as we shall see — but it looked like the same white substance every morning. Whatever taste it produced inwardly, the visual experience matched none of it. If it tasted like an apple, you wanted to see an apple. If it tasted like a hamburger, you wanted to see the meat. The connection between olfactory and visual experience reinforces this point: the two senses are deeply intertwined in the eating experience, and the absence of visual stimulus undermined even the full realization of taste.

### Blind Eating

*Rav Yosef* — who was himself blind — says: *mikan remez l'sumin she'ochlin ve'einam svei'im* — this is an allusion to blind people, who eat and are never fully satisfied, precisely because they lack the visual component of the meal. This ratchets up the earlier point: it is not merely that you lose the pleasure of seeing your food. Without the visual experience, you are not even fully satiated. *Bnei Yisrael* in the desert, eating the *mahn*, may thus have experienced something of what blind people experience at every meal.

### Day Eating

*Abaye* draws a practical lesson: *man d'is lei se'udasa, lo leichlei ela biyemama* — if you have a meal to eat, eat it during the day, so that you can fully experience and enjoy it. The comparison to hospital patients on intravenous drips or to eating arrangements that supply all necessary calories while bypassing the experiential act of eating is apt: you can receive complete nutrition and still feel hungry, because the experience of eating has been bypassed.

### Vision > Appetite

*Rav Zeira* asks: what is the verse that supports this principle? *Tov mareh einayim mehaloch nafesh* — better is the vision of the eyes than the going — or the satisfaction — of the *nafesh*. The word *nafesh* here carries the meaning it sometimes carries in Semitic cognates: appetite, or throat. This also connects back to the phrase *te'anu et nafshoteichem* — some argue that *nafesh* in that context has a particularly grounded meaning tied to fasting, given its association with appetite and hunger. The verse in *Kohelet* thus supports the idea that the visual experience of eating is not merely supplementary; it is in some ways prior to the appetite's satisfaction.

*Reish Lakish* extends this: *tov mareh einayim b'isha yoter migufo shel ma'aseh* — the visual encounter with a woman is, from the male perspective, in some ways more powerful than the act itself. This connects to the earlier Talmudic observation that *hirhurei aveira kasha m'aveira* — the mental experience can be more intense than the deed. The verse — *tov mareh einayim mehaloch nafesh* — thus applies across domains: the visual, anticipatory dimension of an experience frequently exceeds in intensity the satisfying of the appetite that follows.

## Wine & Indulgence

### Wine & Sex

The Gemara moves to another verse — *al tireh yayin ki yisa'dam, ki yitein bekoso eino, yishalech bemeisharim* — do not be drawn after wine because of its redness; you will put your eye upon the cup, and you will go straight away after it. The phrase *yishalech bemeisharim* is now interpreted.

*Rav Ami* and *Rav Assi* debate. One says: *kol hanosein eino bekoso, arayos kulan domos alav k'mishor* — whoever fixes his eye upon his cup, focusing too intensely on his drinking, all the *arayos* will appear to him as flat, as permissible. He will lose his sense of restriction; he will tell himself there are no limits. While there is nothing in the verse itself about *arayos*, the association between drinking and sexual license is the interpretive move being made here.

### Theft Justification

The other opinion says: *kol hanosein eino bekoso, kol ha'olam kula doma alav k'mishor* — not only do the *arayos* appear permissible, but the entire world does. The *Maharsha* distinguishes these two readings precisely: the first is that intoxication gives you license to act on your desires; the second is that over-indulgence in drink creates a need to support the habit, and so one justifies taking other people's money — the world's property becomes flat, ownerless, accessible. These are meaningfully different pathological outcomes of excess.

### Anguish Response

The Gemara then turns to the verse *de'agah belev ish yashchena* — anguish in the heart of a person will subdue it. *Rav Ami* and *Rav Assi* again disagree. One says *yashchena mida'ato* — you should remove the anguish from your mind, distract yourself, engage in something else. The other says *yashchena l'acherim* — you should speak of it to others. If you have anguish, find someone to talk to. Do not try to suppress it through distraction; give voice to it.

### Serpent Curse

The series of disputes between *Rav Ami* and *Rav Assi* continues with a verse from *Yeshayahu*: *v'nachash afar lachmo* — and the serpent's food is dust. One says: *afilu ochel kol ma'adanei olam to'eim bahem ta'am afar* — even if the serpent eats the greatest delicacies in the world, they all taste like dust to him. This is, in a sense, the inverse of the *mahn*: with the *mahn*, one plain-looking substance could produce any taste; for the serpent, any delicacy reduces to the same undifferentiated blandness. The curse is total sensory nullification.

The other opinion says: *afilu ochel kol ma'adanei olam, ein da'ato meyushevet alav ad she'yochal afar* — even if the serpent eats every delicacy, he is never truly satisfied until he eats dust. Only dust provides the serpent with genuine satiation. These are two distinct readings of the same curse: one is about the experience of food being reduced to tastelessness; the other is about an inversion of desire in which only the base and degraded can ever satisfy.

## Mercy in Curses

### God's Mercy

A *baraita* is introduced. *Rabbi Yosei* says: *bo u're'ei shelo kemiddat Hakadosh Baruch Hu middat basar vadam* — come and see how God's ways differ from the ways of flesh and blood. When a human being holds a grievance, he goes straight to his adversary's livelihood — he tries to undermine him, to cause him suffering in the thing that matters most. God does not operate this way. Even when God curses, there is *rachmanus* embedded within the curse.

### Blessings Hidden

Four examples are enumerated. God cursed the serpent — and yet, wherever the serpent goes, its food is there: *oleh lagag mezonosav imo, yored lemata mezonosav imo* — it goes up to a roof, and its food is there; it descends to the ground, and its food is there. The curse is real, but it is livable.

God cursed *Kena'an* — and yet: *ochel mah sherabo ochel, v'shoseh mah sherabo shoseh* — he eats what his master eats and drinks what his master drinks. He is a slave, but he benefits from his master's table. He is not utterly destroyed.

God cursed the woman — the travails of childbirth — and yet *v'el isheich teshukateich*, she is beloved, she is desired: *hakol ratzin achareha* — people pursue her. The curse does not eliminate her desirability or her place.

God cursed the ground — *vekotz vedardar tatzmia'ch lach* — yet: *hakol nizonin heimena* — all creatures are sustained by it. Even the cursed earth remains the source of universal sustenance. In each case, God curses but simultaneously ensures that the curse does not extinguish the life of its recipient.

## Egypt Complaints

### Fish vs. Sex

The Gemara returns to the *mahn* narrative and the complaint of *Bnei Yisrael*: *zacharnu et hadagah asher nochal b'Mitzrayim chinam, et hakishuim ve'et ha'avatichim* — we remember the fish (*dagah*) that we ate in Egypt for free, the cucumbers and the melons. *Rav* and *Shmuel* dispute what *dagah* means. One says: fish, literally. The other says: it is a euphemism for sexual relations — as in *veyidgu larov*, the language of procreation — meaning the people were lamenting a loss of sexual freedom.

The Gemara works through the textual difficulty in each direction. If *dagah* means fish, the word *nochal* — "that we ate" — presents no problem, but what does *chinam*, "for free," mean? If it means sex, the word *nochal* can be defended by analogy: *achlah u'macha piha* (Proverbs 30:20) is a well-known verse using eating as a euphemism for sexual activity, so *nochal* is *lishon ma'alya*, a euphemistic expression. But if it means sex, what then does *chinam* mean? *Rashi* understands it as freedom — they were free of restrictions, they had latitude they no longer have.

### Free Provision

If the simpler reading — literal fish — is adopted, then *chinam* is explained by a tradition: *k'she'hayu Yisrael sho'avim mayim, Hakadosh Baruch Hu mazmin lahem betoch hamayim dagim ketanim bechadeihem* — when the Jewish people would draw water in Egypt for the bricks, small fish would rise up into their buckets. The sustenance was miraculously provided at no cost, from *hefker*, from unowned abundance. So *chinam* means quite literally free of charge.

### Noahide Laws

The Gemara asks: *bishlama le'man d'amar dagim* — if *dagah* means literal fish, good. But if it means sexual relations, does this not imply that the people were sexually unrestrained in Egypt? The verse *gan na'ul achoti kallah* — "a locked garden is my sister, my bride" — is adduced from *Shir HaShirim*, read in the context of the redemption from Egypt, as testimony to *Klal Yisrael*'s sexual propriety. The Gemara resolves this: *mehanach d'asiri lehu lo pritzei behu* — those that were forbidden to them as *Bnei Noach*, they did not transgress. They were not sexually unrestrained before receiving the Torah; they observed the *sheva mitzvot Bnei Noach*.

### New Restrictions

What, then, were they bemoaning? The new restrictions that came with receiving the Torah. As *Bnei Noach*, certain relatives who later become *arayot* under Torah law were permissible. Now they were forbidden. And the laws of *niddah* — which impose separation between husband and wife — were newly binding. The famous teaching that *Moshe* heard *ha'am bocheh lemishpechotav* — the people weeping *al issei mishpechotav*, about matters relating to their families — is invoked: *shenasru lahem lishkav etzlam*, that they could no longer sleep alongside certain relatives, or sleep alongside their wives during *niddah*. They had not acted improperly before. They had simply now been given additional constraints that felt like a loss.

### Multiple Complaints

The Gemara concludes: *ha da v'ha da* — it was both. They were lamenting both the fish and the sexual restrictions. Even those who hold that the primary subject of *zacharnu et hadagah* was not the sexual dimension acknowledge that the people were crying about *mishpechotav* — their family restrictions. And those who understand *dagah* as referring to sexual relations still must account for the fact that the people were also crying about their diet. The complaints were layered: a more restrictive lifestyle across multiple domains, in food, in family life, in freedom.

## Five Missing Flavors

### Taste Only

The Gemara returns to the list in the verse: *et hakishuim ve'et ha'avatichim ve'et hachatzir ve'et habetzalim ve'et hashumim* — the cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. Why specifically these five vegetables? And how do they relate to the *mahn*, which was said to contain all flavors?

*Rav Ami* and *Rav Assi* again disagree. One says: *ta'am kol haminin ta'amu baman* — you could taste any flavor in the *mahn*. These five, however — *ta'am chamisha minin halalu lo ta'amu bo* — the taste of these five specifically could not be experienced in the *mahn*. The absence of their taste is precisely what the people were lamenting.

### Texture Missing

The other opinion says: *ta'am kol haminin ta'amu* — in fact, you could taste anything, including these five. But *ta'aman u'mamashan* — everything else you received both the taste and the *mamash*, the physical substance of the thing — the texture. For these five alone, *ta'aman velo mamashan* — you had the taste but not the textural experience.

### Texture Role

This connects back to the earlier discussion about the dimensions of the eating experience that go beyond mere flavor. Taste alone, it turns out, is insufficient for full satisfaction. When you bite into a pretzel, you want the crunch. You want the resistance, the body, the physical encounter with the food. For all other foods, the *mahn* provided this. For these five, it did not. It is worth noting the slight humor in the list: onions and garlic are not foods for which most people would say texture is the primary value. Yet even here, something was missing. The complaint was not irrational; it was about the totality of sensory experience, and even the loss of texture in an onion could constitute genuine deprivation.

## Manna Description

### Round & White

The Gemara now addresses the physical description of the *mahn*: *vehaman kezera gad hu, lavan* — the *mahn* was like a *zera gad*, a coriander seed, and white. But coriander seeds are not white. *Rav Assi* resolves this: *agol kegida* — it was round like a coriander seed — *velavan kemargalit* — and white like a pearl. The verse is encoding two separate descriptions in the comparison.

### Flax & Story

A *baraita* adds: *gad*, the word for coriander, can be read as suggesting resemblance to *zera pishtan begivolin*, flax seed in its husks, which is very round, very spherical — a different but compatible comparison to the roundness of the *mahn*. *Acherim omrim* — others say — *gad shedomeh lahaggadah*, the *mahn* was like a *haggadah*, like a story: *shemoshechét libo shel adam*, that draws the heart of a person. Just as a story captures everyone's attention — when someone says "I have a story to tell you," everyone wakes up — so too the *mahn* had a magnetic pull, drawing people toward it. Precisely how this manifests is not fully spelled out, but perhaps the smell, appearance, or some ineffable quality made it irresistible. *Shemoshechét libo shel adam kemayim* — it drew people after it like flowing water.

### Secret Telling

Another *baraita*: *gad shemagid lahem leYisrael i ben tisha larishon ve'i ben sheva le'acharon* — the *mahn* would tell the Jewish people whether a child was born after nine months (from the first husband) or seven months (from a second). Because the *mahn* accumulated in each household proportional to the number of members — *omer lagulgoleth* — when collected and measured at home, it would reflect the exact head count of that household. In contested cases of paternity, or in cases where a woman had remarried quickly after divorce, the *mahn* would resolve the question: if the extra *omer* appeared in the first man's house, the child belonged to him; if it appeared in the second man's house, the child belonged there.

### Sin Whitening

The white color — *lavan* — the Gemara says *shemalbin avonoseihem shel Yisrael*, that it whitened, purified, the sins of Israel. *Rashi* connects this most simply to the verse's own framing: *shema lo yereid mahn lemachor* — the daily anxiety that perhaps the *mahn* would not descend the next morning — *hayu meshab'dim libam laMakom* — caused the people to subjugate their hearts to God. Every morning's dependency was a renewal of recognition. And as we are about to see, the *mahn* also forced hidden sins into the open — because when a household's *omer* count did not match its expected membership, the reason would become clear. Transgressions that could otherwise remain concealed were revealed by the mechanism of the *mahn* itself.

## Character Revealed

### Prophet Function

A *baraita* states: *Rabbi Yosei* says — *keshem shehanavi haya magid lahem leYisrael mah shebachorin umah shebasidakim* — just as a prophet would reveal to the Jewish people what was hidden in their nooks and crannies, the skeletons they were trying to hide — *kach haman magid lahem leYisrael mah shebachorin umah shebasidakim* — so too the *mahn* would reveal precisely those things. The *mahn* functioned as a kind of moral prophet, making visible what people most wished to conceal.

### Slave Case

Two cases illustrate this. *Shnayim sheba'u lifnei Moshe ledin* — two people came before *Moshe* for judgment. One says: you stole my slave. The other says: you sold him to me. *Moshe* says: *laboker mishpat* — wait until the morning. If the next day the extra *omer* was found in the first master's house, the slave belonged to him and was stolen; if it was found in the second man's house, the sale was legitimate and the second man was the genuine owner.

### Divorce Case

The second case: a husband and wife come before *Moshe* for judgment. The husband says she committed an offense against him — presumably adultery or some grounds for divorce without *ketubah*. The wife says he committed an offense against her — grounds entitling her to a *ketubah*. Again, *Moshe* says: wait until morning. The *omer*'s location would determine the outcome.

The *girsa* of our text is: if the *omer* was found in the husband's house, she had sinned against him; if found in her father's house, he had sinned against her. This is somewhat difficult: if she sinned against him, why is her *omer* still in his house, as they are presumably headed for divorce regardless? An alternative *girsa* reverses it: if it is his fault, the *omer* remains in his house — because since the divorce is under his control, if he is at fault he will not choose to divorce her, and she remains his. If it is her fault, her *omer* appears at her father's house, because she is being sent away. This alternative reading has a tighter logical coherence.

### Distance Proportional

The Gemara then reconciles three apparently contradictory verses about where the *mahn* was gathered. One verse implies it was in the camp; another says the people went out to gather it; a third says they scattered far. *Ha keitzad?* — how are all three true? *Tzaddikim*: the *mahn* fell at their doorstep — home delivery. *Beinonim*: they had to go out of the camp to gather it. *Reshaim*: they had to scatter far. Every morning, the distance a person had to travel to find his *mahn* was itself a public announcement of his spiritual standing.

### Forms by Merit

A similar structure applies to the form in which the *mahn* arrived. The verse calls it *lechem* in one place, *ugah* (cakes) in another, and yet another verse implies the people had to grind it. *Ha keitzad?* For the *tzaddikim*, it came as finished bread, ready to eat. For the *beinonim*, it came as dough or unbaked cakes — requiring some preparation. For the *reshaim*, it came as wheat grain: *tahanu barechayim, o dachu bamdocha* — they had to grind it in a mill or pound it in a mortar. The eating experience itself — how much effort one had to invest before eating — was calibrated to one's moral standing. The broader point is clear: eating, in the context of the *mahn*, was inextricably a religious experience. Distance, form, and effort all encoded spiritual information.

## Divine Abundance

### Spices & Perfume

The Gemara asks: if the *mahn* came already as bread for the *tzaddikim*, why do the verses speak of grinding and cooking? *Rav Yehuda* said in the name of *Rav*, and some attribute it to *Rabbi Chama bar Chanina*: *melamed sheyarad lahem leYisrael im haman tachshitei nashim davar shenidoch bamdocha* — along with the *mahn* came items used as women's jewelry and cosmetics, aromatic things that required grinding. It was not the *mahn* itself being ground; it was these additional gifts — spices and perfumes — that came down with it.

### Pot Seasonings

Similarly, *Rabbi Chama* teaches: *melamed sheyarad lahem leYisrael im haman tziki kdeira* — with the *mahn* also came pot-seasonings, flavorings for cooking. *Rashi* explains *tziki kdeira* as *tavlin letavshil arev umevusam* — flavorings that make a cooked dish fragrant and delicious. Even if the *mahn* itself had all these tastes, apparently there was also a desire to cook with enhancing flavors. The larger sensory experience of cooking was accommodated. It is notable, given that we earlier said the *mahn* had all these tastes except for five things, that one would still want to cook with seasonings — perhaps because the experiential dimension of cooking, not merely the taste of the result, matters to people.

### Cloud Jewels

The verse records that *hanesi'im hevi'u et avnei hashoham* — the *nesi'im* brought the *shoham* stones. A *baraita* teaches: *nesi'im mamash* — but *nasi* can mean a cloud. The clouds brought the precious stones. Because the *mahn* fell from the clouds, and with the *mahn* came jewels, pearls, and exotic wealth. The verse *nesi'im v'ruach v'geshem ayin* — clouds and wind and no rain — is cited to establish that *nesi'im* indeed denotes clouds. The picture being painted is one of extraordinary abundance: not merely daily food, but perfume, spices, pot-flavorings, and precious gems, all descending daily from Heaven.

## Multiple Tastes

### Breast Milk

The verse says the *mahn* tasted *k'ta'am l'shad hashamen* — like a smear of oil, or *leshad*, which can be read as *shad*, a breast. *Rabbi Abbahu* expounds: *mah shad zeh, tinok to'eim bah kamah ta'amim* — just as a nursing infant tastes many flavors from the breast — influenced, *Rashi* notes, by what the mother eats — *af haman kol zman sheYisrael ochlin oto, motzi'in bo kamah ta'amim* — so too whenever the Jewish people ate the *mahn*, they would draw from it many different flavors. The *mahn* was not static; it was responsive, dynamic, producing different tastes for different people or at different moments.

### Color Change

An alternative reading: *leshed mamash* — the comparison is quite literally to the breast: *mah shed zeh mithapeich l'kamah g'vanei* — just as a breast has varied coloring — the skin, the nipple — *af haman mithapeich l'kamah ta'amim* — so too the *mahn* would shift and change into many tastes. Some identify yet another reading in which the comparison is to a *shed*, a demon, which can shift into many forms and colors. In any case, the underlying point is consistent: the *mahn* was capable of producing a spectrum of flavors, not a single uniform taste.

### Meat & Bread

*Moshe* announces to the people: *b'teit Hashem lachem ba'erev basar le'echol, velachem baboker lisbo'a* — God will give you meat in the evening to eat, and bread in the morning to satisfy. This verse sets the framework for the discussion that follows.

### Improper Meat

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha* teaches: *basar she'sha'alu shelo k'hogen* — the meat they asked for improperly, since meat is a luxury, not a necessity, and they complained and demanded it in a way that was not appropriate. Accordingly, *nitan lahem shelo k'hogen* — it was given to them improperly — towards evening, when there was little time to prepare it, especially without electric light. *Lechem she'sha'alu k'hogen* — bread, which they rightly needed — *nitan lahem k'hogen* — was given to them properly, first thing in the morning.

### Meal Timing

From this, *mikan limdah Torah derech eretz* — the Torah teaches a standard of proper behavior: *shelo yochal adam basar ela balailah* — one should eat meat specifically at night. This is somewhat counterintuitive, since it means eating the heavier food right before sleep. But perhaps the point is that meat ought to remain a delicacy, something consumed sparingly, not a staple of the daytime meal. One might object that this contradicts the earlier *Gemara* which says to eat your meal in the day to enjoy it fully. The *Gemara* resolves this: *ke'ein yimama ka'amina* — what was meant is that you should eat in a well-lit setting; it need not be literally during daylight, provided there is adequate light.

## Derech Eretz

### Chicken Behavior

*Abba bar Yaakov* provides a vivid baseline: *betichila hayu Yisrael domim ketarnagolim shemenakrim ba'ashpah* — originally, the Jewish people were like chickens pecking in a garbage dump, eating at random, constantly grazing with no structure or regularity.

### Regular Times

*Ad sheba Moshe vekava lahem zman se'udah* — until *Moshe* came and established fixed meal times: bread in the morning, meat in the evening. No constant snacking, no nibbling throughout the day. This is the *derech eretz* of eating: a person eats at defined times, not perpetually. The image of the refrigerator in every home, the constant availability of food, the culture of snacking — all of this is, from the *Gemara*'s perspective, sub-optimal. A *mentsch* eats at a morning meal and an evening meal, not continuously. The contrast with the chicken-like pecking is the contrast between structure and appetite run without governance.

## Quail Death

### Teeth Question

The verse states *habasar odenu bein shineihem* — the meat was still between their teeth. Yet another verse says they ate for a full month: *ad chodesh yamim*. Did they eat for a month, or did they die immediately while still eating? *Ha keitzad?* — how can both be true?

*Beinonim le'altar metu* — the *beinonim*, the average sinners, died immediately, even as the meat was still in their teeth. Their death was quick. *Reshaim mitsta'arin veholechin ad chodesh yamim* — the *reshaim* suffered with a stomach ache for the entire month and died at the end of it. The *beinonim* had enough *zechut* that they received a swift death; the *reshaim* suffered the full month before dying.

### Deserving Death

*Reish Lakish* offers a dramatic *al tikrei*: *al tikrei vayishtahu ela vayishchatu* — do not read "they spread out" but "they were slaughtered." *Melamed shenitkayevu soneihem shel Yisrael shechitah* — this teaches that they were deserving of actual *shechita*. The expression *soneihem shel Yisrael* is, as always, a euphemism for *Yisrael* itself — we do not attribute such things directly. The use of their lust for meat as a vehicle of their own punishment carries a grim irony.

### Shechita Source

*Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha* takes the same textual variation and derives a different point: *al tikrei shatuach ela shachut* — do not read "spread out" but "slaughtered": *melamed sheyarad lahem leYisrael im haman davar hata'un shechitah* — the *slav* was something requiring *shechitah*. This is presented as a basis for the requirement to perform *shechitah* on fowl.

*Rabbi* objects: is this really the source for *shechitah* on fowl? There is another verse: *vayamter aleihem ke'afar she'er uchechol yamim of kanaf* — God rained down flesh like dust and birds like the sand of the sea. And the obligation to perform *shechitah* on fowl is derived elsewhere: *detanya, Rabbi omer, vezavachta ka'asher tziviticha* — you shall slaughter as I commanded you — *melamed shenitztavah Moshe al havashet ve'al hakaneh, al rov echad be'of, ve'al rov shenayim bivehemah* — Moshe was commanded on the trachea and esophagus, that for a bird the majority of one suffices, and for a land animal the majority of both is required. That is where the laws of *shechitah* for fowl are derived.

What then is the point of the word *shatuach*? *Melamed sheyarad lahem mashtichain mashtichain* — it teaches that the *slav* fell in layers upon layers. That is the simple *pshat* of the verse: the birds descended in spreading, layered flocks across the ground.

## Age-Based Tastes

### Taste by Age

The Gemara returns to the competing descriptions of the *mahn*'s taste: one verse calls it *lechem*, another *shemen*, another *dvash*. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina* resolves this: *linearim lechem* — for the young people it tasted like bread, which is what young people want; *lazkeinim shemen* — for the elderly it tasted like oil, which is more appropriate to their palate; *latinokot dvash* — for the children it tasted like honey, like candy.

### Tranquility vs. Thorns

The word *slav* is written with a *shin* but read with a *samech* — the two letters being interchangeable in sound. *Rabbi Chanina* plays on the dual reading: read with a *shin*, *slav* suggests *shalvah*, tranquility. *Tzaddikim ochlin oso bishalvah* — the *tzaddikim* ate it in peace and ease. *Reshaim ochlin oso vedomeh lahem kesilon* — for the *reshaim*, eating it was like thorns — *silon*, read with a *samech*. The same food, in the same moment, produced opposite experiences depending on the character of the one consuming it.

### Quail Types

*Rabbi Chanan bar Rava* teaches that there are four varieties of quail: *shichli, kivli, pasyoni*, and *slav*. *Ma'alya dechuhu shichli* — the finest is *shichli*. *Garya dechuhu slav* — the lowest quality is *slav*. And yet even *slav*, the worst of the four, when roasted in an oven — *ve'hava ke'tziporta, umosvinan lah betanura* — would expand from its fat until it filled the oven, and could be spread across thirteen slices of bread, with even the bottom slice so saturated with fat that it could not be eaten plain but only mixed with something else. The abundance and richness of the *slav* was extraordinary, even at its lowest grade.

## Finding Quail

### Yehuda's Barrels

The *Gemara* now transitions to a series of anecdotes about *Amoraim* who miraculously found quail in their everyday surroundings. *Rebbi Yehuda* would find quail among his barrels — they would appear there, available for him to eat, a small daily miracle provided to a Torah scholar.

### Chisda's Chips

*Rav Chisda* would find his quail among the chips of wood. Again, the bird would appear in an unlikely location, a quiet ongoing gift.

### Sharecropper Gift

*Rava* — who was *Rav Chisda*'s son-in-law and student — had a sharecropper who worked his field. Every day, *Rava meiti leh arisei kol yoma*, his sharecropper would bring him *slav* that had fallen into the field. The connection between *Rava*'s merit and the ongoing provision of quail is implicit: it was by virtue of his Torah learning and his relationship to his teacher that this gift continued.

### Death & Blessing

*Yoma chad lo aiti* — one day the sharecropper did not bring any quail. *Rava* wondered what had happened. He went up to the roof and heard a child reciting the verse: *shamati va'tirgaz bitni* — I have heard, and my stomach trembled. *Shma mina nach nafsheih de'Rav Chisda* — from this *Rava* understood that *Rav Chisda*, his father-in-law and *Rebbi*, had died. *Uvidil Rava achal talmida* — the student eats by virtue of his teacher. With the teacher gone, the ongoing flow of blessing that sustained the student was interrupted, and no quail fell that day.

## Eating & Religion (II)

### Fasting & Eating

It is striking to step back and observe the full arc of this *daf*. We began with a discussion of *Yom Kippur* fasting — with the question of what *inuy et nafshoteichem* means and how we derive that it refers specifically to abstaining from food. That discussion led, via a *gezeira shava*, to the *mahn*. And the *mahn* opened into this extended exploration of eating: its sensory dimensions, its social structures, its moral valences, its miraculous forms.

### Complaint Despite

One thread running through the discussion is the extraordinary ease with which people complain even in the midst of abundance. *Bnei Yisrael* received *mahn* daily, received spices and perfumes and jewels from the clouds, received *slav* so delicious that even its lowest grade would expand to fill an oven — and still they wept. They wept about the five vegetables whose texture they missed. They wept about the fish they remembered from Egypt. They wept about the family restrictions that had been placed upon them. The warning implicit in this is not subtle: the capacity for complaint is nearly limitless, and abundance does not automatically generate gratitude.

### Eating Significance

At the same time, something more constructive is being communicated. The *mahn* created a context in which eating was unavoidably a religious act. Dependency on God was built into the structure of daily nourishment: you did not have bread stored for tomorrow; you did not know whether the *mahn* would fall. The distance you walked to gather it announced your spiritual standing. The form in which it arrived reflected your moral condition. The mechanism of the *omer* exposed hidden sins and concealed truths. Eating under these conditions was not merely caloric intake; it was encounter with the divine order.

How that translates into the present — when the refrigerator is full, when the store is always open, when food is neither scarce nor miraculously provided — is a question the *Gemara* does not answer directly. But the juxtaposition with which the *daf* began — fasting as the *inuy* of *Yom Kippur*, eating as the *inuy* of the desert — suggests that the relationship between food and religious experience runs in both directions. The fast and the miraculous meal are, in their different ways, both structured encounters with dependence, with limit, and with the recognition that sustenance, in the end, comes from somewhere beyond ourselves.

---

---

# Yoma 76

## Manna Properties

### Dew Layers

The daf opens in the middle of the Talmudic discussion of the *man*, picking up from the contradiction between two verses. One verse states *v'ta'al shichvat hatal* — the layer of dew rose up in the morning — implying the *man* rested atop the dew. Another verse states *u'veredet hatal alav* — when the dew descended, it descended upon it — implying the *man* was beneath the dew. Rav Yosef bar Hanina resolves the contradiction: *tal milemala v'tal milmata* — there was dew both above and below. The *man* came packaged, as it were, in a protective envelope of dew. The Gemara adds that it was *domeh k'mi shemunach b'kufsa* — like something placed inside a box. It was not merely food; it was food presented beautifully, encased and protected.

### Machaspas Nature

The Torah describes the *man* as *dak mechuspas* — thin, like hoarfrost. The Gemara attempts to unpack the meaning of *mechuspas*. Reish Lakish reads it as a mnemonic: *nimoach* (dissolved) from the *mechas* portion, and *pas* from the hand — meaning it was something that would dissolve in the palm of one's hand. It melted upon contact, which raises the practical question of how one ate it at all, though the Gemara does not resolve this directly.

### 248 Limbs

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different reading of *mechuspas*: it refers to something *shenivla b'matayim arba'im u'shmoneh eivarim* — that was absorbed into the 248 limbs of the body. The *man* was so perfectly digested that it left no waste; it was entirely absorbed. The specific mention of the number 248 signals a *gematria*. The letters of *mechuspas* — two *samechs* (60 each = 120), *peh* (80), *mem* (40), and *chet* (8) — yield 248. The difficulty is that *mechuspas* as written appears to contain an extra *vav*, which would throw off the count. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds: *mechuspas ktiv* — it is written without the *vav*. Whether that is in fact the case in the Torah scroll is a matter for verification.

---

## Manna Spiritual

### Angels' Bread

The *tana'im* debate the meaning of the verse in Tehillim describing the *man* as *lechem abirim* — the bread of the strong ones. Rabbi Akiva interprets *abirim* as referring to the angels: *lechem shemalachei hashareit ochlim oto* — bread that the ministering angels eat. The *man* was thus angelic food, heavenly sustenance brought down to earth.

### Yishmael Critique

When this teaching was reported to Rabbi Yishmael, he sent back a pointed response: *Akiva ta'ita* — Akiva, you have erred. *Vechi malachei hashareit ochlim lechem?* — Do the ministering angels eat bread? The Torah itself testifies that Moshe Rabbeinu did not eat bread during his forty days on Har Sinai, and certainly angels do not eat.

### Limbs & Spirit

Rabbi Yishmael therefore reinterprets *abirim*: *al tikri abirim ela eivarim* — do not read "the strong ones" but "the limbs." *Lechem shenivla b'matayim arba'im u'shmoneh eivarim* — bread absorbed into the 248 limbs. This loops back to Rabbi Yochanan's teaching. It is worth noting that *eivarim* itself is close numerically — 253 — making it not quite a clean *gematria*, though the proximity is suggestive.

One might ask what Rabbi Akiva truly intended. This appears to tie into the broader methodological divide between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Yishmael operates on the principle of *dibra Torah kilshon bnei adam* — the Torah speaks in human language — whereas Rabbi Akiva derives meaning from every detail of the text. Rabbi Akiva may have been trying to bridge heaven and earth: the eating of the *man* was not merely physical nutrition but something that brought one closer to a heavenly mode of existence. There is a spiritual dimension to the *man*, not merely a physical one.

### Malbim View

This reading gains support from the *Malbim*, who addresses the *man* directly and identifies two distinct dimensions within it. There is *lechem min hashamayim* — the physical aspect, which was equal for all — and a spiritual dimension reflected in the verse *vayilketu hamarbeh v'hamam'it*: those who were spiritually elevated received more in that dimension, while the physical portion remained uniform for all. Whether this constitutes the *pshat* of the verse is debatable, but it captures something important about what Rabbi Akiva is pointing toward: the *man* as spiritual sustenance, not merely physical nourishment, and the sense of dependence on God that eating it was meant to cultivate.

---

## Waste Problem

### Shovel Law

If the *man* was so completely absorbed into the body's 248 limbs that it left no waste, the Gemara faces an obvious difficulty: the Torah commands the Israelites *v'yated tihye lecha al azenecha* — you shall have a shovel upon your implements — to go out and dig when relieving oneself outside the camp. Why would such a law be necessary if the *man* left no residue? The Gemara answers: *devarim shetagrei umot ha'olam mochrin lahem* — the waste came not from the *man* itself but from other foods they purchased from merchants of the nations at the oases and encampments along the way. Of course, this invites the further question of why they needed to purchase food at all when they had the *man*. The answer, already established earlier in the tractate, is that despite the *man*'s miraculous capacity to taste like anything desired, they still craved the experience of other foods — real bread, familiar textures and appearances.

### Manna Abates

Rabbi Elazar ben Prata goes further. He says that even the food purchased from the nations — *af devarim shetagrei umot ha'olam mochrin lahem, man mefigan* — the *man* would abate and neutralize even those other foods, correcting their more mundane digestive properties. On this view, the miraculous absorption extended even to non-*man* food, as long as the *man* retained its special status.

### Sin & Loss

This leads to a sharp question: if even that was true, what then is the purpose of the shovel law? The Gemara answers: *leachar shesarchu* — after they sinned. Rashi explains that when the Israelites called the *man* *lechem hakelokel* — the cursed bread, the vile bread — it lost its miraculous properties. Their complaint degraded the food itself. They had something of unparalleled wonder, and their dissatisfaction caused it to fall from its level.

### 3 Parsa Walk

God's response, as the Gemara presents it, is striking. God says: I intended for you to be *kehamalachei hasharet* — like the ministering angels. Note the irony: this is precisely the image that Rabbi Yishmael had objected to when Rabbi Akiva used it. Yet now the Gemara itself employs it, as God's own description of what the Israelites could have been. Because they failed to appreciate this, *achshav ani matriach otam shalosh parsaot* — now I will burden them with a three-*parsah* walk to relieve themselves. Rabbah bar bar Chana testifies that he personally saw the distance between Beit HaYeshimot and Avel HaShittim — the two ends of the encampment — and it was indeed three *parsaot*, twelve *mil*, approximately twelve kilometers.

### Latrine Placement

A *braita* adds that the Israelites could not relieve themselves in front of or to the sides of the camp, because the *anan* — the pillar of cloud — might move in that direction. They were required to go only behind the camp, in the direction from which they had come, since it was known the nation would not retrace its steps. This meant that someone stationed at the far front of the camp might have to walk the full three *parsaot* to reach the designated area behind the camp. This is, to put it plainly, a startling ruling. Every other miracle described here is one thing, but making a person walk such a distance for such a basic need is genuinely difficult to accept at face value.

---

## Manna Complaint

### Soul Dried

The Gemara cites the Israelites' complaint: *v'atah nafshenu yeveishah, ein kol, bilti el haman eineinu* — now our soul is dried up, there is nothing, nothing but the *man* before our eyes. Rashi's comment here is particularly evocative: *man bashacharit, man ba'arvit, man hayom, man emesh, man de'etmol* — *man* in the morning, *man* in the evening, *man* today, *man* yesterday, *man* the day before. The monotony was existentially unbearable for them.

### Bloating Fear

But the Gemara probes deeper into their complaint. *Assi man ze shetifach bimeihem* — they could not accept the miraculous nature of the *man* because they feared it would bloat and expand inside them. *Klum yesh yelud isha shemachnis v'eino motzi* — is there any child of a woman, any human being, who can consume without eventually expelling? Their inability to perceive the miracle as a miracle, their anxiety about what was happening inside their bodies — this was the essence of their complaint, not merely boredom with the taste.

### Joshua Portion

The Gemara revisits Rabbi Yishmael's response to a related matter, and this section introduces a new *davar acher*: *lechem abirim achal ish zeh Yehoshua* — the *ish* who ate the bread of the strong ones was Yehoshua. *Sheyorad lo man kineged kol Yisrael* — his portion of *man* was equivalent in quantity to the entire Jewish people. The derivation uses a *gezerah shavah*: the word *ish* appears here, and *ish* appears in the verse describing Yehoshua bin Nun — *ish asher ruach bo* — a man in whom there is spirit. Rashi reads this quite literally: every Israelite received one *omer*, and before Yehoshua's tent was deposited the equivalent of two million *omers*. The evident symbolism is that the leader is *kineged kol hador* — the weight of the entire generation rests upon him; he represents them all. It is notable, though, that the Gemara singles out Yehoshua, who had not yet formally assumed leadership.

The Gemara asks: why not derive this about Moshe instead, of whom it also says *veha'ish Moshe anav me'od*? The answer is technical: *danin ish me'ish v'ein danin ish mizeh ha'ish* — one derives a *gezerah shavah* using the plain word *ish*, not the expanded form *zeh ha'ish*, which is a different formulation.

---

## Daily Trust

### Why Daily?

The students of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai posed the following question: *mipnei mah lo yarad lahem leYisrael man pa'am achat beshanah?* — why was the *man* not provided once a year? Surely it would have been simpler to deliver a full year's supply at once rather than requiring the Israelites to go out and collect it each morning.

### King Analogy

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai responds with an analogy. A king who provides his son with a full year's food budget will see that son only once a year — when the next year's payment comes due. But a king who provides only a daily allowance will be visited by his son every single day. *Af Yisrael* — so too the Jewish people: a father with four or five children *hayah do'eg v'omer, shema lo yered man lemachar* — would be anxious each evening, fearing the *man* might not descend the next morning, that his whole family would starve. *Nimtzu kulam mechavnim et libam la'avihem shebashamayim* — and so every single day they turned their hearts toward their Father in Heaven.

This is, of course, the *pshat* of the relevant verses. The Torah states *vaya'ancha vayar'ivacha vayachilcha et haman... anotcha ulenasotcha* — He afflicted you, and made you hungry, and then fed you the *man*, in order to afflict you and test you. And the famous conclusion: *ki lo al halechem levado yichyeh ha'adam ki al kol motza pi Hashem yichyeh ha'adam* — man does not live by bread alone but by all that comes forth from the mouth of God. The daily collection — *veyilketu devar yom beyomo lema'an anasenu hayelech betorati im lo* — was itself a test of whether they would follow God's Torah.

### Anxiety vs Faith

Yet the Gemara's framing is worth examining carefully. The *mashal* of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai emphasizes anxiety — the daily uncertainty, the fear that the *man* might not come — as the mechanism producing religious devotion. This is one possible reading of the *pesukei*m: uncertainty and worry drive the Israelites to keep their hearts directed toward God.

But there is a meaningfully different reading. The deeper purpose of the *man*'s daily provision may have been not to induce anxiety but to cultivate genuine *emunah* and *bitachon* — faith and trust. The prohibition on gathering extra, the guarantee that *Erev Shabbat* would yield a double portion, the fact that the *man* did not appear on *Shabbat* — all of these called for active trust, not merely fearful dependence. The person of developed faith does not wake up each morning anxious about whether the *man* will come; rather, he has internalized the truth that God provides, and he goes out confident. These are related dispositions — both involve daily orientation toward God — but they represent significantly different religious personalities. One model aims to keep a person perpetually nervous as an instrument of behavioral compliance; the other aims at genuine, settled faith as the goal of religious life. The *pesukei*m arguably point more toward the latter, even if the Gemara's *mashal* foregrounds the former.

### Fresh & Light

The Gemara offers two additional explanations for daily provision, introduced by *davar acher*. First: *she-hayu ochlim oto k'she-hu cham* — so that they would eat the *man* freshly, like warm bread delivered each morning. The experiential reality of fresh bread matters, even if a miracle could theoretically preserve it. Second: *mipnei masa ha-derech* — so they would not have to carry a full year's supply across the wilderness. These explanations are notably more modest in their spiritual ambition. They speak to the aesthetic and practical dimensions of the experience rather than the theological message of dependency. Compared to the first explanation, they represent a significant shift in register.

---

## 60 Amot Height

### Height Claim

The Gemara introduces a scene: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yishmael, and several elders were sitting together engaged in *Parashat HaMan*. Among them was Rabbi Elazar HaModai. He spoke up and declared: *man sheyarad leYisrael hayah gavo'ah shishim amah* — the *man* that descended for the Jewish people was sixty *amot* high. This is in the genre of wonder-descriptions that the Gemara has been accumulating: pearls came with it, diamonds came with it, and now it stood ninety to a hundred feet tall.

### Tarfon Challenge

Rabbi Tarfon immediately challenged him: *Modai, ad matai atah megavev devarim u'mevi aleinu?* — how long will you pile up words and pile things upon us? Where are you getting this from? The challenge is pointed: Rabbi Elazar HaModai's claim sounds like aggadic embellishment without textual grounding.

### Flood Parallel

Rabbi Elazar HaModai responds: *Rabbi, mikra ani doresh* — I derive it from a verse. His argument begins with the flood narrative. The Torah states that during the flood *chamesh esreh amah milemala gavru hamayim va-yechassu heharim* — the waters rose fifteen *amot* above and covered the mountains. The immediate question is: fifteen *amot* above what? If measured from the valley floor, the water level would differ from place to place and the *tevah* could not navigate a sea of inconsistent depths. *Ve-khi mayim shavin shavin kayamin?* — do waters stand at equal levels from different measurements simultaneously?

The answer is that first, *nivke'u kol ma'aynot tehom rabah* — all the springs of the great deep burst open, filling the world until the waters reached the summit of every mountain on earth, leveling off at the height of the highest peak. Only then did the floodwaters rise an additional fifteen *amot* above that level. Thus, the fifteen *amot* were measured above the mountaintops — which means the total volume of water was vastly greater than fifteen *amot*, encompassing the full height of all the mountains plus fifteen more. This digression is necessary for Rabbi Elazar HaModai's argument, because the fifteen *amot* represents the increment above the highest point, which will become the unit of comparison.

Having established this, the Gemara now invokes the principle: *eizo mida meruba, mida tova o mida puranyut?* — which is greater, God's measure of goodness or His measure of punishment? The answer is well-established: the measure of goodness exceeds punishment. This is demonstrated by comparing *poked avon avot al banim... al shileshim ve'al rive'im* — punishment extending to four generations — with *notzer chesed la'alafim* — lovingkindness extending to two thousand generations.

### Window-Door Ratio

With this principle established, the Gemara compares the language used for the flood with the language used for the *man*. By the flood: *va'arubot hashamayim niftachu* — the windows of heaven were opened. By the *man*: *vayitzav shechakim mima'al, va-daltei shamayim patach* — God commanded the heavens above and opened the doors of heaven, *vayamter aleihem man leechol* — and rained down *man* upon them to eat. The flood opened windows; the *man* opened doors.

How many window-panes fit in a door? The Gemara calculates: four. Two doors thus equal eight window-panes. There were two *arubot* opened for the flood and two doors opened for the *man*, but since each door contains four windows, the two doors equal eight window-equivalents — four times the two windows of the flood. Since the flood waters rose fifteen *amot* above the mountaintops, and the *man* was four times as great, the *man* reached sixty *amot*. *Venimtza man leYisrael gavo'ah shishim amah* — thus the *man* stood sixty *amot* high.

### Visible to Kings

A *baraita* cites Isi ben Yehuda with an alternative formulation: *man sheyarad leYisrael haya mitgaber ve'oleh ad she'ro'u oto kol malchei mizrach uma'arav* — the *man* that descended for Israel rose so high that all the kings of East and West could see it. This is derived from the verse in Tehillim: *ta'aroch lefanai shulchan neged tzorerai* — You have set a table for me before my enemies. The table that God set was the *man*, visible to all the opposing kings of the world. The Gemara's discussion of this verse leads to a brief tangent: *Abaye* notes that *kosi revaya* — my cup overflows — where *revaya* in *gematria* equals *resh* (200) + *vav* (6) + *heh* (5) + *yud* (10) = 221. Thus the cup of David HaMelech in the world to come will hold 221 *log*.

### Rain Objection

The Gemara now raises objections against Rabbi Elazar HaModai's derivation. First: *hatam b'arba'im yomin* — there, by the flood, the rain fell over forty days. *Hacha b'chad sha'ata* — here, the *man* descended in a single moment. Even if it fell at a greater rate than the rain, accumulation takes time; what falls in one moment cannot equal what accumulated over forty days. Second: *hatam lechulei alma* — there, the rain fell over the entire world. *Hacha leYisrael lechodei* — here, the *man* fell for Israel alone. The scale is incomparable. Moreover, the Gemara adds, there was more surplus created by the flood waters, which themselves diminished over time, whereas the *man* was collected and consumed.

Nevertheless, the Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar HaModai's derivation stands on its own terms — *peticha peticha gamar* — he infers from the language of opening in one place to the language of opening in the other, and on that basis derives the sixty *amot*. The objections challenge the magnitude of the comparison but do not dislodge the hermeneutical move.

---

## 5 Afflictions

### 5 vs 6 Count

Having concluded the extended discussion of the *man*, the Gemara turns to the *halacha* of Yom Kippur. The question posed is: *hani chamisha inuyim keneged mi?* — these five afflictions, corresponding to what? Rav Chisda answers: corresponding to five occurrences of the language of *inuy* in the Torah — *be-asor, ach be-asor, Shabbat shabbaton, ve-Shabbat shabbaton, ve-asah lachem* — the various formulations in *Acharei Mot*, *Emor*, and *Pinchas* where Yom Kippur is commanded. Count them and there are five.

But immediately the Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: *hani chamisha hava ve-anan shis tnan* — these are five, yet our *Mishna* teaches six afflictions. The *Mishna* enumerates: eating and drinking (which is effectively two), plus anointing, bathing, wearing leather shoes, and conjugal relations — six in total. Tosafot notes that there is in fact a sixth verse as well — *ki kol hanefesh asher lo te'uneh* — but that verse states the punishment for non-compliance rather than commanding affliction. There are five commandments to afflict, and six *inuyim* listed in the *Mishna*. How does Rav Chisda's count of five reconcile with the *Mishna*'s six?

### Eating-Drinking

The resolution is that eating and drinking are counted as a single category — one form of *inuy* — rather than two. Drinking is subsumed within eating: *shtiyah shehi bichlal achilah*. Rav Chisda thus counts: one (eating-drinking) plus four others = five, matching the five verses.

It should be noted, however, that this is purely for the purpose of counting against the five verses. Halachically, eating and drinking do not combine: if one eats the requisite quantity minus a marginal amount and drinks the requisite quantity minus a marginal amount, he has not transgressed either prohibition, since the two quantities do not aggregate into a combined violation. They are distinct prohibitions with distinct thresholds, even while for purposes of counting the *inuyim* they are treated as one.

Reish Lakish provides the derivation that drinking is included under the rubric of *achilah*: *minayan l'shtiyah shehi bichlal achilah?* — the verse states *ve-achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha ma'asar degancha tiroshcha ve-yitzharecha* — you shall eat before God your *ma'aser* of grain, *tirosh*, and oil. Since *tirosh* is wine — a beverage — and the verse uses the verb *achilah* to describe it, we see that eating can encompass drinking.

### Wine-Mead

The Gemara challenges this: *mi mai?* — how do we know *tirosh* here means wine in its liquid, drinkable form? Perhaps it means *anigron* — a dish of vegetables steeped in wine — in which case it would be an act of eating, not drinking, and the extension to drinking would be unproven. Rabbah bar Shmuel defines terms: *anigron* is the liquid of cooked beets; *achsidron* is the liquid of other cooked vegetables. On this reading, perhaps the verse merely teaches that wine may be consumed as a component of a solid food.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov therefore adduces a different verse: *ve-natata hakesef bechol asher te'aveh nafshecha* — you shall spend the *ma'aser sheni* money on whatever your soul desires — cattle, sheep, wine, and *shichar*. The verse ends *ve-achalta lifnei Hashem Elokecha* — and you shall eat before God. Now *shichar* — beer or mead — is unambiguously a beverage, and the verse applies *achilah* to it. This establishes that the verb *achilah* encompasses drinking.

The Gemara again challenges: perhaps even *shichar* was consumed as an *anigron*-type dish, mixed into food. The response: *shichar ketiv* — the word *shichar* indicates *midi de-meshakker*, something with the capacity to intoxicate. Intoxication results from drinking large quantities, not from eating foods with trace alcoholic content. If the Torah says *shichar*, it means a drink consumed in drinking quantities. The further challenge — *dilma deveilah keilit?* — perhaps it refers to pressed *Keilit* dates, which a *baraita* teaches could also cause intoxication and were included in the prohibition of *yayin ve-shichar al tesht* for a *kohen* entering the *Mikdash* — is met with a *gezerah shavah*: *yalif shichar shichar minazir*. The *nazir* is prohibited from *yayin ve-shichar*, and there the context is clearly liquid; the juxtaposition of *shichar* with *yayin* in the same verse establishes that *shichar* means a drinkable beverage, not a solid food. This clinches the derivation that drinking falls within the category of *achilah*.

### Wine Names

Having established the derivation, the Gemara pauses to examine the names the Torah uses for wine. *Ve-amai kari leh yayin?* — why is wine called *yayin*? *Yayin shemevi yilalah la-olam* — wine brings wailing to the world. Rashi connects *yilalah* to *ta'aniyah*, mourning and lamentation. There is also the tradition identifying the *etz hadaat* of *Gan Eden* as a *gefen*, a vine — which fits with this etymology: from the earliest chapters of human history, wine has been the source of catastrophic moral failure.

*Ve-amai kari leh tirosh?* — why is wine called *tirosh*? *Shechol hamitgareh bo na'aseh rash* — whoever competes with it, whoever gives himself over to it, becomes poor. Indulgence in wine destroys a person financially and morally. The root *rash* — poverty — is embedded in the word.

This leads to a remarkable observation by Rav Kahana: *tirosh* is written in the Torah without the *vav* — *tirash* — but read with the *vav* — *tirosh*. The defective spelling yields *rash*, poverty; the full reading yields *rosh*, a head, a leader. *Zacha na'aseh rosh* — if one merits, if one drinks with discipline and responsibility, wine elevates; *lo zacha na'aseh rash* — if one does not merit, it impoverishes. Wine is not simply negative; it has dual potential depending on the character of the person engaging with it.

This duality is echoed in a further observation attributed to Rava: *yayin yesamach levav enosh* — wine gladdens the heart of man. The word *yesamach* can be pointed as *yesamach* (gladdens) or *yeshameach* (from *shimmamon*, desolation). *Zacha mesamcho* — if one merits, wine gladdens; *lo zacha meshammemo* — if one does not merit, it brings desolation. Rava himself testifies personally: *chamra ve-reichani pikchin* — wine and fragrant spices have sharpened my mind and aided my learning.

The observation that the Gemara uses the language of *zacha* and *lo zacha* — worthy and unworthy — is worth dwelling on. This is not simply about moderation as a behavioral choice. There is an element of predisposition at work: not everyone who overindulges is making a free choice in the same way, and not everyone with a certain temperament succumbs. *Zacha* implies something more like a constitutive quality of character, not merely the outcome of a single decision.

---

## Bathing & Oil

### Daniel Fast

The Gemara turns to locating the biblical sources for the remaining *inuyim* — bathing and anointing. The proof-text is drawn from Daniel. During his period of self-affliction, Daniel declares: *lechem chamudot lo achalti, u-vasar ve-yayin lo va el pi, ve-soch lo sachti* — I did not eat desirable bread, meat and wine did not enter my mouth, and I did not anoint myself.
