Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat explains that *lechem chamudot* — bread of desire — means that Daniel abstained even from fine white wheat bread, not merely from rich or elaborate foods. He was on an austere subsistence regimen.

### Oil Affliction

How do we know that Daniel's abstention from these things constitutes *inuy*? The verse later in Daniel reads: *va-yomer elai al tira Daniel, ki min hayom asher natata et libcha le-havin u-le-hitanot lifnei Elohecha, nishme'u devarecha* — from the day you set your heart to understand and to *lehitanot* — to afflict yourself — before your God, your words have been heard. The angel describes Daniel's conduct as *lehitanot*, affliction. Since Daniel explicitly included *ve-soch lo sachti* among his abstentions, and those abstentions as a whole are called *inuy*, we learn that refraining from anointing is itself a form of *inuy*. This establishes the *d'oraita* basis — or at minimum the *asmachta* — for the prohibition of *sicha* on Yom Kippur.

It is worth noting that for a modern audience the prohibition of anointing requires some contextual grounding. In antiquity, oil was not merely cosmetic; it was the functional equivalent of soap. The Romans used oil as a cleansing agent: hot oil was applied to the body to loosen dirt and then scraped off with an implement called a *strigil*. Archaeological reconstructions of ancient bathhouses include these implements as standard equipment. Anointing was thus an integral part of the bathing and cleansing process, not a luxury supplement to it.

### Bathing Source

Having established anointing from Daniel, the Gemara asks: *rechitza minalan?* — where do we derive bathing? Rav Zutra the son of Rav Tuvia cites the verse: *vatavo chamayim b'kirbo ke-shemen b'atzmotav* — and it came like water within him and like oil into his bones. The comparison between water and oil — water enters from outside, just as oil is rubbed onto the outside of the body — implies that bathing with water is parallel to anointing with oil, and thus both fall under the same category of *inuy*.

### Oil as Drink

The Gemara then presents a *baraita* that uses the same verse in a completely different direction: *minalan le-sicha ke-shtiyah be-Yom HaKippurim?* — where do we derive that anointing is like drinking on Yom Kippur? From the same verse: *vatavo chamayim b'kirbo ke-shemen b'atzmotav* — water inside, oil in the bones — teaching that rubbing oil into one's skin is comparable to drinking, in the sense that both involve the body absorbing a substance. On this reading, the verse does not parallel bathing to anointing; it parallels anointing to drinking.

The consequence is significant: if *sicha* is *ke-shtiyah*, anointing is a form of drinking, which would make the prohibition of *sicha* considerably more serious — it is not merely an additional *inuy* but a quasi-form of consumption, parallel to the most stringent prohibition on Yom Kippur.

At this point Rav Ashi intervenes with an alternative derivation of *rechitza*: *migufa d'kra shamia lei* — bathing can be inferred from Daniel's own verse. Daniel says *ve-soch lo sachti* — the doubled formulation (*soch lo sachti* rather than simply *ve-lo sachti*) encompasses more than simple anointing. Since anointing and bathing are functionally intertwined — oil was used as part of the cleansing process — the expanded language of Daniel's declaration includes bathing within the prohibition of anointing.

### D'oraita Debate

The concept of *sicha ke-shtiyah* requires clarification, because it is not universally applied in *halacha*. Ordinarily, we do not say *sicha ke-shtiyah*: a *nazir* who rubs wine on his skin has not violated the prohibition on drinking wine; one who rubs *chelev* on his skin has not violated the prohibition on consuming *chelev*. The principle is invoked only in specific contexts — primarily where the issue is *inuy* (affliction, as on Yom Kippur) or where the question is one of deriving benefit. In those cases, the definition of the prohibited activity is broad enough to include topical absorption.

This leads directly to the central *machlokes rishonim*: are the *inuyim* of Yom Kippur — beyond eating and drinking — *d'oraita* or *derabbanan*? The Gemara's language, drawn from verses in the Torah and derived through what appear to be genuine *drashot*, sounds like *d'oraita*. And indeed, some *rishonim* hold that all five *inuyim* carry biblical force.

However, Rabbeinu Tam (in the *Tosafot* on the preceding *daf*, 75a, in the middle of the discussion beginning *minayan le-sicha ke-shtiyah*) explicitly states: *u'peirash Rabbeinu Tam d'chol inuyim d'Yom HaKippurim lav ninhu ela miderabbanan, d'kra asmachta be-alma, le-var me-achilah u-shtiyah* — all the *inuyim* of Yom Kippur are merely rabbinic, and the verses are no more than *asmachta*, except for eating and drinking which are clearly biblical. His proof: the Gemara itself permits a person covered in filth to wash it off, and a person with scabs to apply oil. *Mi sheyesh lo chatatim be-rosho, sach ke-darko ve-eino choshesh* — one with scabs on his head may anoint in the normal manner without concern. If the prohibition were biblical, how could such exceptions be permitted?

### Pleasure vs Need

There is, however, a third approach — one that does not require framing the permitted cases as exceptions to a rabbinic prohibition. Rather, the very *definition* of what is prohibited may be the key. What the Torah prohibits may be specifically *rechitza* or *sicha* that constitutes *ta'anug* — pleasure, indulgence — as opposed to *rechitza* or *sicha* undertaken to remove filth or to address a medical condition. Washing off dirt is not pleasurable bathing in the relevant sense; applying oil to a wound or scab is not pleasurable anointing. On this reading, the prohibition is *d'oraita*, but its scope is definitionally limited to acts of luxury and comfort. The permitted cases are not exceptions but simply fall outside the definition from the outset.

This definitional approach carries important implications going forward. As the Gemara continues to address the details of which acts are permitted and which are prohibited on Yom Kippur, two questions will recur: first, whether a given leniency is an *exception* to the prohibition or a case that was never within its *definition*; and second, whether the prohibition in question is of biblical or rabbinic origin. Both questions remain live and contested among the *rishonim*, and the Gemara's treatment sets the stage for that ongoing analysis.

---

---

# Yoma 80

## Kotevet & Shiurim

### Tanya: Shiurim Kezayis

The daf opens with a *baraita* cited in the standard *tanya* formula. The *baraita* records the view of Rebbi: *kol hashiurim bekuleitan kkezayis* — the vast majority of *shiurim* in *halacha* are measured by a *kezayis*. The single exception is *tumat ochalin*, the impurity of foods, regarding which the *baraita* states *sheshina kasuv bemasma'an veshinu chachamim bishiuran* — the Torah employs a slightly different term when speaking of foods becoming *tamei*, and therefore the Sages defined a different minimum amount, not a *kezayis*.

### Yom Kippur Precedent

The *baraita* then invokes *Yom Kippur* as a proof and paradigm for this principle: *vera'aya ledavar Yom Hakippurim*. The Torah does not say "do not eat" on *Yom Kippur*; it says *milo te'uneh* — any soul that does not afflict itself. Because the Torah frames the prohibition in terms of affliction rather than eating, it is conceptually distinct, and consequently the *shiur* is not a *kezayis* but a *kotevet* — the large dried date. The Gemara then asks: what is the purpose of citing *Yom Kippur* as a proof for the principle? Why not simply say that by *tumat ochalin* the Torah also uses a different phrase, and therefore a different size follows, without needing the analogy from *Yom Kippur*?

The answer is illuminating. *De'ee mei'hasam* — had you only the case of *tumat ochalin*, one might have dismissed the variation in language as stylistic rather than substantive: *hava amina dichrahu*, it's just the way the verse speaks, nothing more. *Yom Kippur* provides an incontrovertible demonstration that when the Torah frames a prohibition differently — affliction instead of eating — it genuinely signals a different conceptual reality, and that in turn produces a different *shiur*. Once this is established as an unambiguous precedent, it is all the more compelling to apply the same logic to subtler shifts in language elsewhere.

### Tumat Ochalin

The Gemara now examines the derivation for *tumat ochalin* specifically. The verse states: *mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel asher yavo elav mayim yitma* — from all the food that shall be eaten, that which water comes upon shall become *tamei*. Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Elazar derives: *ochel haba meichamas ochel* — the verse teaches us about food that comes from food. The phrase *asher ye'achel*, food that shall be eaten, signals food that emerges from something that is itself eaten. What fits this description? *Zeh beitzas tarnigoles* — the egg of a chicken. The chicken is food; the egg comes from it; the egg is therefore food from food, and the *shiur* for *tumat ochalin* is *kibeitzah*, an egg-sized amount.

One might immediately ask: there are other foods that come from food — why specifically an egg? The Gemara raises a goat kid: it comes from a goat, which is food. The response is *mechusar shechita* — the kid still requires *shechita* to become permitted for consumption; it is not food the moment it emerges. An egg, by contrast, is ready to eat immediately. The Gemara then raises the *ben pakua* — a fetus found in a slaughtered animal, which halakhically does not require its own *shechita* since the mother's *shechita* takes effect upon it. Even so, the *ben pakua* requires *keria*, being torn open to release its blood; it is not immediately ready as food. Thus the egg stands as the clearest case of food that comes directly and immediately from food.

### Egg Size Debates

Having established that the reference is to an egg, the Gemara asks: *ve'eima beitzat bar yokhni* — perhaps it refers to an ostrich egg, which is enormous? The Gemara's response is the principle *tafasta meruba lo tafasta*: if you try to grasp too much, you grasp nothing. You cannot assume the most extreme case; if both a large and a small interpretation are available, the expansive one cannot simply be asserted. One must settle for the more moderate measure.

Yet this invites a counter-question: *ve'eima beitzat tziporta* — perhaps the verse means the egg of a small bird, something like a sparrow, *dizuta tuvei*, which is very small? This produces a genuine difficulty. The principle of *tafasta meruba lo tafasta* pushes against the largest option, but does not automatically establish the smallest either. The Gemara is effectively left with a question on this derivation — why specifically a hen's egg and not a smaller bird's egg? The derivation of Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Elazar, while establishing the logic of *ochel haba meichamas ochel*, has an unresolved vulnerability at the level of specifying the exact size.

### Abbahu: Beit Hablia

Rabbi Avahu therefore offers his own independent derivation. From the same phrase, *mikol ha'ochel asher ye'achel*, he reads: *ochel she'atah ochlo be'vat achat* — food that you eat in one gulp, food that can be swallowed whole in a single act of swallowing. And the rabbis estimated: *ein beis hablia machzik yoter mi'beitzas tarnigoles* — the esophagus, the gullet, cannot hold more than a hen's egg. This derivation has the advantage of anchoring the *kibeitzah* measure directly to the size of a hen's egg without relying on the chain of reasoning about *ochel haba meichamas ochel* and the difficulties it generated. It also reflects a physiological observation about the capacity of the human *beis hablia*, though the lecture notes that ancient hen's eggs were likely smaller than their modern counterparts and that, in any case, the Gemara never explicitly resolves whether we always operate by reference to a typical, average specimen.

The broader framework is now clear: we have established, first from *Yom Kippur* and then from *tumat ochalin*, that a change in the Torah's terminology signals a change in *shiur*, and that precedent carries over to other contexts where the language similarly departs from the standard formulation.

---

## Record-Keeping & Change

### Cheilev Recording

The Gemara transitions to a new but closely related topic. Rav Elazar states: *ha'ocheil cheilev bazman hazeh* — one who eats *cheilev*, forbidden fat, in the present day, *tzarich sheyichtov lo shiur*, must write down the precise amount consumed. The reason for focusing on *cheilev* is that among the common prohibitions, eating forbidden fat is one of the *issurei kares* for which an unintentional violation (*beshogeg*) obligates a *korban chatat*. By contrast, many other non-*kosher* foods — such as *chazir* or improperly slaughtered meat — carry only a *lav*, a negative prohibition, without *kares*, and therefore do not generate a *korban* obligation. Similarly, *basar bechalav* is only a *lav*. Thus *cheilev* and blood are the paradigmatic everyday prohibitions whose violation generates *korban* liability, along with *chametz bePesach*.

### Future Courts Shift

The requirement to record the amount, continues the Gemara, is *shema yavo beis din acher veyarbe bishiurin* — lest a later *beis din* come and modify the minimum *shiurim*. The intent is practical: when the *Beis Hamikdash* is rebuilt, one will need to know exactly how much *cheilev* was consumed in order to determine whether the appropriate *korban* must be brought. One should not merely record that a *korban* may be owed, but should note the actual quantity — even down to the specific volume — because whether that quantity crosses the threshold for obligation may depend on how a future *beis din* defines the minimum.

There is something deeply striking about this passage. The Gemara takes entirely for granted the practice of maintaining a personal record of *korbanot* one may be liable for — a kind of spiritual ledger. This sits in productive tension with the broader themes of our *masechet*, where *korban* as a vehicle for atonement coexists with *teshuva* as the primary response to sin. And as one participant in the shiur observed, the very act of recording the precise quantity in the notebook simultaneously anticipates the future obligation to bring a *korban* and is itself embedded in a process of *teshuva* and self-accounting — the two realities meeting on the page of the *pinkas*.

### Grandfathering Issue

The Gemara then examines what it means for a future *beis din* to "increase the *shiurim*." One reading is that the *beis din* would make the minimum *smaller* — that is, would require a *korban* even for an amount previously considered sub-threshold, a smaller *kezayis*. The Gemara challenges this immediately from a *baraita*: *asher lo te'asina bishgagah* — the verse on which the *korban chatat* obligation rests describes a sin that the person would have refrained from had they known. *Hashav miyediato meivi korban al shigagato* — one who would have held back brings a *korban* for the inadvertent violation. *Lo shav miyediato* — one who would not have refrained, *ein meivi korban*. If at the time of eating the amount was sub-threshold under the then-prevailing *shiur*, the act was not halakhically defined as an act of *achila* at all. The person is therefore grandfathered in: since the act did not constitute a *chiyuv* at the time it was performed, a later court's retroactive reclassification cannot impose liability. No retroactive shrinkage of the *shiur* can obligate someone for what was, at the time of the act, a permissible or at most sub-threshold quantity.

This point, as noted in the discussion, connects to the foundational question raised at the beginning of *Masechet Horayot*: when *beis din* reinterprets a biblical criterion, is it uncovering an objective truth that was always there, or is it establishing an interpretive truth that takes effect from that point forward? The Gemara here seems to operate on the premise that halakhic obligation is defined by the standard in force at the time of the act — though the framing through *shav miyediato* and psychological culpability is somewhat unusual. As the lecturer suggests, the Gemara may be saying that even if objectively one was liable, the *halacha* of *korban* is anchored in the actor's state of mind and awareness at the moment of the transgression.

### Larger Shiur Relief

Having foreclosed the possibility of retroactive tightening, the Gemara accepts that *yarbe bishiurin* must mean the *beis din* will make the minimum *larger*, thereby relieving someone of an obligation they previously believed they had incurred. This is actually the more intuitive application: one thought a *korban* was owed because the amount eaten met the old threshold; the new *beis din* sets a higher minimum, and that amount now falls short of the new standard. It would be incoherent to bring a *korban* for an act that, according to the authoritative ruling of the *beis din*, does not reach the threshold. Hence the *korban* cannot be brought. This is why the precise amount must be recorded — because depending on how the *shiurim* develop, one may discover that no *korban* is in fact owed at all.

---

## Halacha LeMoshe

### Yochanan Statement

Moving from the practical question of record-keeping, the Gemara takes up a more fundamental issue. Rabbi Yochanan declares: *shiurin v'onshin halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — both the minimum amounts and the punishments for transgressions are *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, transmitted to Moses at Sinai and not derived through textual interpretation. The Gemara immediately presses: punishments are written explicitly in the verses — *kares*, *chayiv misa*, and so forth. What is the novelty in calling them *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*?

One might add: there are aspects of punishment that are not so clearly spelled out. The generalized category of *malkot*, for instance — the very assumption that most negative prohibitions entailing a *maaseh* carry *malkot* as their penalty — is not transparently derived from any single verse. Still, the Gemara resists a broad reading. It concludes: *ela haki ka'amar* — what Rabbi Yochanan means is more precisely *shiurin shel onshin halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* — the minimum amounts that must be reached for punishments to apply are *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*. The *shiurim* themselves, not the existence of the punishments, are the content of the Sinaitic tradition. A *baraita* is then cited in support: *tanya nami hachi* — similarly it was taught, *shiurin shel onshin halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*.

It is worth pausing here. The claim that all *shiurim* are *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* is in one sense axiomatic in rabbinic literature — not just the *shiurim* for punishment but those for *mikveh*, *esrog*, *lulav*, and so on. And yet even within a *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai* there can be uncertainty about the precise parameters. As the lecturer notes, even according to the Rambam, who insists there was never *machloket* about *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, this does not mean there cannot be interpretive questions about its exact scope and application.

### Othniel Tradition

Against this firmly Sinaitic framing, the Gemara introduces a startling dissent: *acherim omrim, Beis Dino shel Yavetz tiknum* — others say that the *beis din* of Yavetz established them. As Rashi identifies, "Yavetz" here refers to Othniel ben Kenaz, the first of the *shoftim*, whose name is connected to this tradition through a *midrashic* identification. The implication is radical: the *shiurim* were not transmitted from Sinai at all, but were established by this early post-Mosaic *beis din*. This would mean that the fixed minimum amounts are not ancient Sinaitic tradition but represent a human, judicial determination — significant, authoritative, but not part of the revelation at Sinai.

### Not New Creation

The Gemara cannot accept this implication as stated. It invokes the verse *elleh hamitzvot* — these are the commandments — from which it derives that no prophet may introduce *chiddush*, a genuinely new law, once the Torah has been given: *she'ein navi rasha'i lechadesh davar mei'attah*. If the *shiurim* were genuinely instituted by Othniel ben Kenaz as a new creation, that would constitute precisely such a *chiddush* by post-Mosaic human authority, which is impermissible. The Gemara therefore resolves: *ella she-shachachum vechazaru veyisadum* — the *shiurim* were always there as part of the Sinaitic tradition, but they had been forgotten in the upheaval of the conquest and settlement of the land, and Othniel ben Kenaz rediscovered and re-established them. He was not creating but recovering.

This resolution is, as the lecturer observes, quite fascinating in its own right — particularly in the context of earlier discussions on this *daf* about the *inuyim* of *Yom Kippur*. There too, the *Rishonim* debate whether the additional afflictions beyond eating and drinking are *d'oraita* or *d'rabbanan*, with some holding that the Torah effectively says *lemosrah hakatuv ela lechakhamim* — the Torah transferred the definition of its own terms to the Sages, granting them unusually broad authority to set the parameters. A parallel question arises by *Chol HaMoed*: the verses hint at the concept but leave the contours of prohibited *melacha* largely to rabbinic determination, which is why exceptions like *hefsed merubah* are possible. The Gemara's resistance to saying that Othniel *instituted* the *shiurim* — as opposed to recovering them — sits in interesting tension with the more expansive model of rabbinic authority invoked in those other contexts.

---

## Melo Lugmav

### One Cheek Full

The *sugya* turns to the *shiur* for drinking on *Yom Kippur*. The minimum amount of liquid whose consumption constitutes a violation is *melo lugmav* — the fill of one's cheeks. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel clarifies: *lo melo lugmav mamash* — not literally the fill of both cheeks, but *kol she'illu yesalkeno letzad echad veyeira'eh k'melo lugmav* — whatever amount, if one were to shift it entirely to one side, would appear to fill that one cheek. The *mishna* itself says simply *melo lugmav*, and the Gemara notes: read it as *k'melo lugmav* — like the fill of the cheeks, not to be taken with absolute literalness.

### Baraita Positions

A *baraita* is then introduced that sets out competing positions. How much must one drink to be liable on *Yom Kippur*? *Beit Shammai omrim revi'it* — Beit Shammai say a *revi'it*, approximately three to three and a half ounces. *Beit Hillel omrim melo lugmav* — Beit Hillel say the fill of one's cheeks. Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *k'melo lugmav* — like the fill of one's cheeks, the formulation we have been discussing. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says: *kedei gmi'ah* — enough for one swallow.

The Gemara asks: is this *baraita* a stronger proof than the *mishna* for the interpretation we have been working with? No — we can read the *baraita*'s *melo lugmav* the same way we read the *mishna*'s, as meaning *k'melo lugmav*, moving the liquid to one side so it appears to fill the cheek. If so, what distinguishes *melo lugmav* from Rabbi Elazar's *k'melo lugmav*? The Gemara answers: *ika beinaihu melo lugmav dachuk* — the difference lies in whether the cheek is firmly packed and fully puffed, or merely noticeably protruding on one side. Both positions refer to one side; they disagree about the degree of fullness required.

### Hoshaia Challenge

Rav Hoshaia then raises a sharp challenge. If *melo lugmav* means one cheek, then Beit Hillel's position should be *stricter* than Beit Shammai's, not more lenient — because one cheek is *less* than a *revi'it*. The standard expectation is that Beit Shammai is more stringent and Beit Hillel more lenient. Yet here, if one cheek is smaller than a *revi'it*, Beit Hillel is setting a lower threshold for liability, making it *easier* to transgress. That is the reverse of the expected pattern.

The response is a memorable line: *pitschil be-Og Melech HaBashan pitschil* — it depends on whom you are talking about. The implicit assumption of *melo lugmav* is that the measure is *personal* — it is the fill of *your* cheeks. For a very large person, Og Melech HaBashan being the paradigm of extraordinary size, the fill of one's cheeks could easily exceed a *revi'it*. When Beit Hillel stated *melo lugmav* and Beit Shammai was understood to be the more stringent position, they were imagining a large individual — for whom the *revi'it* is a smaller amount than the fill of his cheeks. For such a person, Beit Shammai with their *revi'it* is indeed stricter, since his *melo lugmav* is larger.

This point has immediate practical significance. For the *halacha* of *shiurim* on *Yom Kippur* — particularly in cases where one must eat or drink in *shiurim* to avoid transgression — the question of how much constitutes *melo lugmav* matters enormously. The Gemara here implies that the average *melo lugmav* is less than a *revi'it*, since the scenario in which Beit Hillel is more lenient requires a larger-than-average person.

### Zeira Presses

Rav Zeira now presses a deeper conceptual question: *mah yishna achilah dechol chad vechad b'kotevet, u-mah yishna shtiyah dechol chad vechad be-dideih?* — why is eating on *Yom Kippur* governed by a universal standard, the *kotevet*, the same for everyone, while drinking has just been shown to vary by the individual, each person's *melo lugmav* being their own personal measure? This is a striking inconsistency. We are accustomed to *shiurim* being universal — the size of a *mikveh*, the *shiur* for an *esrog*, the size of a *kezayis* — measured against an external, objective standard, not calibrated to each individual's body.

### Abaye: Threshold

Abaye responds: *akimu leih rabanan de-be-kotevet be-hachi mitva dateih* — the rabbis established that a date-sized amount will produce *yishuv hada'at*, an abatement of the sense of affliction, for every person. *Batziar me-hachi lo mitva* — less than that will not achieve this, universally, regardless of the person's size. By contrast, for drinking: *bi-shtiyah be-dideih mitva dateih be-de-chavreih lo* — only the amount proportional to that individual's cheek size produces *yishuv hada'at* for that person; the fill of another person's cheeks would not do so for them. The rabbis *know* this, and they have calibrated the *shiurim* accordingly — universal for food, personal for drink.

### Og Example

Rav Zeira pushes further: very well, but take Og Melech HaBashan himself. You claim a *kotevet*-sized amount achieves *yishuv hada'at* universally — but for a man of Og's dimensions, can a small dried date meaningfully abate the affliction of fasting?

Abaye is unperturbed. *Kim lehu lerabanan de-vehachi mitva dateih, u-vatzir mei-hachi lo mitva dateih* — yes, the rabbis established that that amount achieves some abatement of affliction, and less than that achieves none. The key is a *threshold*: below the threshold, no one — not even a small person — experiences any meaningful relief. Above the threshold, the effect occurs for everyone, but to varying degrees. *Kulei alma tuva* — for most people that minimum amount produces substantial relief. *Og Melech HaBashan purta* — for Og it produces only a little. But even a little is above the threshold; below it, nothing. The structure is thus: the *shiur* marks the point below which there is simply no effect whatsoever, and above which there is some effect, even if the degree varies by individual.

### Food Type Matters

Rav Zeira is still not satisfied. He now shifts from the question of who is eating to what is being eaten: *basar shamen be-kotevet ve-lulavei gefanim be-kotevet?* — rich fatty meat the size of a date and grape leaves the size of a date are supposed to produce the same degree of *yishuv hada'at*? This seems implausible. The question is acute: by the time Abaye has admitted that the effect of the *shiur* varies by person — Og gets less relief than a smaller man — he has already broken the logic of a purely universal standard. And if individual variation is acknowledged, why not variation by food type as well? A satisfying piece of fatty meat surely does more to abate hunger and affliction than a comparable quantity of grape leaves.

### Final Threshold

Abaye's response follows the same structure as before: *kim lehu lerabanan, de-vehachi mitva dateih* — the rabbis established the threshold. Below it, no food, however rich, produces any relief whatsoever. *U-vatzir mei-hachi lo mitva dateih* — less than the threshold amount, neither the fatty meat nor the grape leaves helps at all. *Mihu*, however — once the threshold is crossed: *basar shamen tuva, ve-lulavei gefanim purta* — rich fatty meat produces a great deal of *yishuv hada'at*, and grape leaves produce very little. Above the threshold, the effect varies by food type.

The structure of Abaye's position is thus consistent throughout: the *shiur* is the threshold, not the total measure of the effect. Below it: nothing, universally. Above it: some effect, universally — but the degree varies by person and by food. Rava's subsequent objection moves to a related question that the Gemara takes up in the next *sugya*.

---

## Achilat Pras

### Rava Challenge

Rava raises what is at first a structural puzzle about the combination of eating over time. The halakhic principle is that multiple small amounts consumed within the time it takes to eat half a loaf — *kedei achilat pras* — may combine to reach the minimum *shiur*. This applies to a *kezayis* for ordinary food prohibitions: eat a *kezayis* of *chazir* or *neveilah* within *achilat pras* and the act counts as a single *achila* warranting punishment. The same time window, *kedei achilat pras*, is used on *Yom Kippur* for the *kotevet* — eat a date's worth of food within that window, and the act is complete. But the *kotevet* is approximately twice the size of a *kezayis*. Why should it take the same amount of time to combine? A larger minimum amount should arguably require a proportionally longer window, and the same short window seems incongruous.

### Rabbinic Knowledge

Abaye responds with his characteristic formula: *kim lehu lerabanan, d'hachi mitva dateih ub'hachi lo mitva dateih* — the rabbis know that eating done within the period of *achilat pras* produces *yishuv hada'at* and abates the affliction; eating spread over a longer period does not have the same effect, even if the total quantity consumed is identical. The act of *achila* that matters, whether for incurring punishment or for the *inuy* of *Yom Kippur*, is defined by that same temporal unit — because that is the window within which the consumption registers as a unified physiological and experiential event.

### Tamei Food

Rava then extends the challenge to a different area: eating *tamei* food. Normally, *tamei* food does not render a *person* *tamei* — it can only make *kodshim* *tamei*. However, the rabbis taught that if one eats a *chatzi pras* — half a loaf's worth — of *tamei* food, one's body becomes *tamei* through the act of ingestion: *tumat geviyah*. The time window for that combination is also *kedei achilat pras*. Yet the amount at stake is *chatzi pras* — half the loaf — which is four or five times the *kezayis* and about twice the *kotevet*. Why is the same five-minute window used for all of them: a *kezayis* for standard prohibitions, a *kotevet* for *Yom Kippur*, and a *chatzi pras* for *tumat geviyah*? It seems that the larger the required amount, the longer the combination window should be.

### Rav Pappa Answer

Rav Pappa responds: *hanach l'tumat geviyah d'lav d'Oraita hi* — set aside the case of *tumat geviyah*, making one's body *tamei* through eating, because that is not a biblical requirement. Being rabbinic, the *shiurim* and time windows can be defined as the rabbis see fit, without the constraint of perfect proportionality.

The Gemara immediately objects: does Rav Pappa himself not cite the verse *ve-lo titamu bahem ve-nitmetem bam* — you shall not make yourselves *tamei* through them and you shall become *tamei* through them — as a source for *tumat geviyah d'Oraita*? The answer: *la mi-derabbanan ve-k'ra asmakhta b'alma* — even when Rav Pappa invokes that verse, he means only that it is *mi-derabbanan*, a rabbinic enactment, and the verse serves merely as an *asmakhta*, a scriptural support. Therefore, the time window for *tumat geviyah* can be set as the rabbis determine, and the apparent inconsistency with larger amounts requiring the same temporal window is resolved by the rabbinic nature of the entire *inyan*.

### D'Oraita vs Rabbanan

The Gemara closes on a note that resonates with the major themes running throughout this entire *sugya*. The interplay between *d'Oraita* and *d'rabbanan* has been a consistent thread from the first discussion of *shiurim* all the way through: the Gemara initially resisted the idea that the rabbis defined the *shiurim* through their own authority (as in the *sugya* of Othniel ben Kenaz), yet at the same time repeatedly invoked the rabbis' knowledge and determinations — *kim lehu lerabanan* — to explain how the measures work in practice. The *beis hablia* derivation showed rabbinic input into the measurement of the *kibeitzah*; Abaye's entire series of responses to Rav Zeira rested on rabbinic establishment of thresholds. And now the daf closes with something declared to be *d'Oraita* revealed to be *d'rabbanan* with a verse serving only as *asmakhta*.

Similarly, the question of how the *shiurim* could ever be changed by a future *beis din* — which opened the *sugya* of record-keeping — touches the same fault line: if *shiurim* are *halacha l'Moshe mi-Sinai*, how much interpretive latitude does any later court genuinely have? These interlocking questions — how much is fixed from Sinai, how much is defined by rabbinic wisdom and authority, and where the line between the two lies — form the deep conceptual architecture of the *daf*, and the final *machloket* about *tumat geviyah* brings that architecture fully into view.

---

---

# Yoma 81

## Food Combination

### Kol HaOchlin

The daf begins on 81b, approximately ten lines from the bottom, with the principle of *kol ha'ochlin mistarfin* — all foods combine for the minimum measure of a *kizayit*. The *kizayit*, it should be noted, refers to a measure equivalent in size to an olive, not to the literal consumption of an olive itself; that is what the comparative prefix *kaf* indicates.

### Salt & Meat

Rav Papa teaches: *achal umtza v'melach mistarfin* — if one ate raw meat together with salt, they combine toward the minimum measure. The case raises the question of what qualifies as food and what qualifies as liquid, given the rule, to be encountered shortly, that food and liquid do not combine. Salt on its own might not be considered food in the relevant sense. Nevertheless, the Gemara explains: *v'af al gav d'lav achila hi, kevan d'achli inshi mistarfin* — even though eating salt alone does not constitute eating, since people eat it together with meat as a normal manner of consumption, the salt is subsumed into the food and the two combine.

### Sauce

Reish Lakish teaches: *tzir al gabi yerek mistaref* — the juice or sauce that rests upon a vegetable combines with it for the minimum measure of a *kigrogoret* on Yom Kippur. One might have thought the *tzir* is a liquid and therefore cannot combine with the solid vegetable. Rashi explains the *tzir* here as the cooking juices or sauce that enhances the food — *matka u'mateka d'ochla*, that which sweetens and improves the dish. The Gemara's principle is: *kol shurei ochla ochla hu* — anything whose function is to improve and enhance the food is itself considered food. Accordingly, meat served with sauce does not present a case of food and liquid; all of it is categorized as food and combines toward the minimum. A related question arises concerning Shabbat, where the issue of *bishul achar bishul b'lach* involves dishes that are part solid and part liquid, with determination made on the basis of *ikar v'tafel*. Similarly, the categorization of a dish like vegetable soup — whether its minimum measure is assessed as a solid (*kigrogoret*) or liquid (*melo lugmav*) — presents its own analytical questions, though the Gemara does not resolve them here.

---

## Achila Gassa

### Definition

Reish Lakish further teaches: *achal achila gassa b'Yom HaKippurim patur* — one who eats on Yom Kippur in the manner of *achila gassa*, that is, while already completely satiated and forcing additional food down, is exempt. The case envisions one who filled himself on *Erev Yom Kippur* and then continued to eat upon the arrival of Yom Kippur even though he was entirely full — the Yom Kippur eating constitutes a form of compulsive overindulgence rather than genuine eating.

### Mai Taama

The rationale: *asher lo te'uneh* — the prohibition is derived from the concept of affliction. *Prat l'mazik* — it excludes a form of consumption that does not abate any sense of affliction.

### Prat L'Mazik

Rashi's formulation here is particularly precise. He writes: *l'zeh she'eino mitbatel mimenu shum inuy al yedei achila* — this excludes the person whose eating accomplishes nothing in terms of removing the sense of affliction. And then Rashi adds a striking line: *mazik hu et ha'ochlin v'et atzmo* — this type of eating is damaging to the food and damaging to oneself. It does no good to the eater and it wastes the food. It is not eating; it is destruction.

### Terumah

This principle is applied to a parallel case in the laws of *terumah*. If a non-*kohen* eats *terumah* inadvertently (*bishogeg*), he is required to repay the value along with an additional fifth — though the mathematics should be noted: if the original value is one hundred, he pays twenty-five, and that twenty-five is a fifth of the resulting total of one hundred and twenty-five. However, this enhanced payment applies only when the act constitutes genuine eating. If a *zar* ate *terumah* in the manner of *achila gassa*, *meshalem et ha'keren v'eino meshalem et ha'chomesh* — he pays back only the principal and not the additional fifth. The verse states *ki yochal* — *when he eats* — and *prat l'mazik*: this disqualified form of consumption is categorized as damage, not eating.

The Gemara raises a broader implication: the same logic should presumably apply to other prohibited foods such as *chelev* or *chametz* eaten in the manner of *achila gassa*. With Yom Kippur, the analysis turns on whether the affliction has been abated; with other *ma'achalot assurot*, the severity of the prohibition is rooted in the problematic nature of the substance itself, and one is still placing the forbidden substance into one's body. Nevertheless, the tendency of the halachic literature is to assume that the exemption of *achila gassa* — understood through the lens of *achal prat l'mazik* — applies across these categories as well. Elsewhere in the Gemara there are additional applications of this principle, and the two cases presented here — Yom Kippur and *terumah* — represent classic examples from the domain of *ma'achalot assurot*.

---

## Non-Standard Eating

### Chewing Grain

Rabbi Yirmiya said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *zar she'koses se'orim shel terumah, meshalem et ha'keren v'eino meshalem et ha'chomesh*. If a non-*kohen* chews raw barley of *terumah*, he pays back the principal but not the additional fifth. The term *koses* refers specifically to chewing raw grain in a manner that is not a normal mode of eating. Since the verse says *ki yochal* — *when he eats* — and this is not a normal act of eating, it falls under *prat l'mazik*: it is not eating but a form of damage.

One might ask whether the same conclusion applies on Yom Kippur. The analysis there operates along two separate tracks: one concerns what constitutes a halachic act of eating, and the other concerns whether the act abates the sense of *inuy*. In principle, these could yield different results. Chewing raw grain is not a normal act of eating, yet the process might still fill one's stomach, which could be relevant to the question of affliction. The matter awaits the upcoming *mishnah* which addresses eating substances not normally consumed.

### Prunes

Rav Shizbi said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *zar she'bala shezifin shel terumah, veheki'an, va'achalan acher* — if a non-*kohen* swallowed prunes of *terumah* whole, then regurgitated them, and another person ate the regurgitated prunes. The example is constructed with prunes precisely because they can be swallowed whole and regurgitated while remaining intact, so the second person is eating something that still physically resembles a whole prune, making the case a genuine *chiddush*.

The ruling: *rishon meshalem keren ve'chomesh* — the first person pays both the principal and the fifth. Swallowing something whole, unlike *achila gassa* or chewing raw grain, constitutes a normal act of eating; people sometimes do swallow things whole. Regarding the second person: *eino meshalem ela d'mei etzim le'rishon bilvad* — he owes only the value of firewood, and only to the first person, not to the *kohen*.

### Regurgitated Status

Two independent principles drive the ruling regarding the second person. First, the moment the first person swallowed the prune, he acquired it. The laws of *Bava Kamma* establish that once a thief transforms a stolen object, he takes possession of it and must pay the *kohen* — but from that point on, it is his. Therefore, the second person's obligation runs to the first person, not to the *kohen*. Second, the object is no longer considered food. Even though it remains physically intact as a whole prune, once it has been swallowed and regurgitated, no normal person would eat it; it has lost its status as food and is now valued only as fuel — hence, firewood.

This raises a conceptually interesting question. The Gemara frames the second person's exemption from the enhanced payment in terms of the object no longer being food. But one might ask: is the reason the object is no longer considered food purely a function of the physical reality of its having been swallowed and regurgitated? Or is it because the halachic act performed by the first person constituted a genuine *achila*, and that halachic consumption is what changes the object's status vis-à-vis the second person? The way the Gemara frames the discussion suggests that the halachic classification of the first person's act — whether or not it is deemed an *achila* — may bear on how we assess the object's status for the second person. This remains an open point of analysis.

---

## Food & Drink

### Don't Combine

The *mishnah* states: *ha'ochel veha'shoteh ein mistarfin* — food and drink do not combine for the minimum measure. Rav Chisda raises the question of whose view this represents: *be'machloket shnuya* — it is actually a matter of dispute, and the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Yehoshua.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

The source is a principle stated by Rabbi Yehoshua in a *mishnah* elsewhere: *kol she'tumato ve'shiyuro shaveh mitstareif* — whatever shares identical *tumah* status and identical minimum measure combines. This principle was articulated in the context of *tumah* laws, not Yom Kippur.

To illustrate: if one has half a *kezayit* of *neveilah* and half a *kezayit* from another *neveilah*, they combine because both the type of *tumah* (one day's impurity) and the minimum measure (*kezayit*) are identical. But if the *tumah* differs while the measure is the same — for example, half a *kezayit* of *neveilah* (one day's *tumah*) and half a *kezayit* of a human corpse (seven days' *tumah*) — they do not combine, even toward the more lenient one-day category, because the difference in the *tumah* itself places them in fundamentally distinct categories. Similarly, if the measure differs while the *tumah* is the same — say, a half-*kezayit* of *neveilah* and a half-lentil-sized piece of *sheretz*, where both cause one-day *tumah* but the *neveilah* requires an olive's measure while the *sheretz* requires only a lentil's measure — they likewise do not combine, because the differing minimums reflect a fundamental categorical distinction. And if both the *tumah* and the measure differ, they certainly do not combine.

The implicit view of the *chachamim* is more lenient: even across those lines, combination may be possible for the more lenient category, so that a half-*kezayit* of *neveilah* and a half-lentil piece of *sheretz* might combine for a one-day *tumah*, since both cause that degree of impurity. Only Rabbi Yehoshua insists that any difference along either dimension — *tumah* or measure — prevents combination entirely.

Rav Nachman then argues that even the *rabanan* who disagree with Rabbi Yehoshua in the context of *tumah* would agree that food and drink do not combine on Yom Kippur. Their leniency in the *tumah* context rested on the reasoning that *shem tumah chad hi* — it is all one category of *tumah*, and the distinction between stricter and more lenient subcategories does not prevent combination toward the more lenient outcome. But Yom Kippur is categorically different.

### Psychological Reality

On Yom Kippur, the operative question is not a formalistic one of halachic categories and minimum thresholds. It is a question of *yisuvay da'ata* — whether the affliction has been genuinely abated. *Va'hai lo ka meisyava da'ata* — an amount of food just below the threshold combined with an amount of drink just below the threshold does not achieve that psychological reality. A person who consumes both, each in a sub-threshold quantity, has not genuinely settled his mind and dispelled his discomfort. The threshold of each must be reached independently for the *inuy* to be considered removed.

Rabbi Yochanan takes the further position: *afilu teima rabbanan* — even according to the *rabanan* who disagree with Rabbi Yehoshua in *tumah* laws, here, on Yom Kippur, they would also require that each category reach its minimum independently. The Gemara's reasoning makes clear that this is not merely a technical debate about halachic categories; it reflects a substantive claim about the psychological reality that Yom Kippur law is tracking. This is the consistent theme the Gemara returns to across several discussions: the laws of *inuy* on Yom Kippur are rooted in an actual lived reality, not merely in formal legal classification. The standard, however, remains an objective one — what abates the sense of affliction for a person in normal circumstances — rather than a purely subjective assessment varying from individual to individual, which the Gemara reserves only for the question of *melo lugmav* (the minimum measure of liquid), and even there only for drink, not for food.

---

## Single Korban

### One Aveira

The *mishnah* states: *achal ve'shata be'e'lem echad eino chayav ela chatat achat* — if one ate a minimum measure and drank a minimum measure on Yom Kippur in a single state of forgetfulness, forgetting that it was Yom Kippur, only one *korban* is brought. Although food and drink do not combine to constitute a minimum measure, they do share the same prohibition of *lo te'uneh* — the prohibition against abating one's affliction. When both acts occur within a single uninterrupted state of forgetfulness, they constitute a single commission of that one prohibition and therefore generate only one *korban*. The parallel case of a *nazir* who drank wine throughout an entire day without any intervening awareness of his *nezirut* illustrates the same principle: however many acts are performed, if there is no intervening awareness, they remain one transgression for purposes of the obligation.

It is worth noting that this convergence on a single *korban* does not require that the acts be performed within the time of *bechdei achilat pras* or *bechdei shtiyat revi'it*, which would make them one continuous act. Even acts at distinct moments are not separate enough — under the criterion of a single uninterrupted state of forgetfulness — to generate separate *korbanos*.

### Two Aveiros

However, *achal ve'asah melacha, chayav shtei chatatot* — one who eats and performs *melacha* in a single state of forgetfulness is liable for two *chatatot*. These are two categorically distinct prohibitions: the eating violates *lo te'uneh*, while the *melacha* violates *lo ta'aseh kol melacha*. Even within one continuous forgetting of Yom Kippur, distinct categories of prohibition each require their own *korban*.

---

## Non-Fit Food

### Unfit Food

The *mishnah* continues: *achal ochlin she'einam re'uyim le'achila, ve'shata mashkin she'einam re'uyim lishtiya* — one who consumes foods unfit for eating or liquids unfit for drinking is exempt. This returns to the question raised earlier about whether normal suitability for consumption is a precondition for the prohibition.

### Fish Brine

The *mishnah* gives as examples of non-potable liquid: *tzir* (fish brine) and *moryes* (fish fat). These are liquids that pass through the body without genuinely satisfying thirst or hunger, and their consumption therefore does not constitute the kind of act that falls within the prohibition of *lo te'uneh*.

---

## Azharah

### No Explicit Lav

Reish Lakish poses a fundamental question: *mipnei mah lo ne'emra azhara be'inuy* — why does the Torah never state an explicit negative prohibition (*lav*) concerning fasting? The question has practical halachic force. The general rule is that a *korban chatat* (and *malkot*) require the transgression of an explicit negative prohibition. Many severe prohibitions that carry *karet* — such as the failure to perform *brit milah* or *korban pesach* — do not generate a *korban* because the violation consists of failing to perform a positive *mitzvah* rather than transgressing a *lav*. Yom Kippur eating carries *karet*, but where is the *lav*? The Torah says *ve'initem et nafshoteichem* — a positive command to fast. If one fails to fast, he has not fulfilled a positive *mitzvah*. Where does the Torah say, in negative terms, "do not eat"?

### Grammar Problem

Reish Lakish's answer: *mishum dela efshar* — because it is grammatically impossible for the Torah to articulate such a prohibition. The Gemara walks through the options. Could the Torah have written *lo yochal*, "do not eat"? No — that would have implied the standard *kezayit* measure, whereas we know Yom Kippur operates by the measure of a *kigrogoret* and is organized around the concept of *inuy*. Could the Torah have written *lo te'uneh*, "do not fast"? That is the opposite of the intended meaning — it would be a command to eat. What is needed is something like "do not not fast" — a double negation that neither biblical idiom nor, as the Gemara demonstrates, rabbinic legal grammar can elegantly accommodate.

Rav Hoshaia challenges: could the Torah have written *hishamer pen lo te'aneh* — "guard yourself lest you not fast"? The response is that *hishamer* and *pen* each independently function as signals of a negative prohibition, and using both would generate two *lavin* when only one is desired; and simply writing *hishamer lo te'aneh* is grammatically incoherent. Rav Bibi bar Abaye suggests: *hishamer b'mitzvat inuy* — "guard yourself regarding the commandment of fasting." The response: *hishamer* when appended to a positive *mitzvah* strengthens the positive obligation; it does not transform it into a negative prohibition. Only *hishamer* appended to a prohibitory statement generates a *lav*. Rav Ashi proposes: *al tasur min ha'inuy* — "do not deviate from the fast." The Gemara leaves this with *teiku*.

### Implied Lav

Despite the inability to articulate the prohibition elegantly, the conclusion is that the negative prohibition is nonetheless implied. The Torah's intent to prohibit eating on Yom Kippur is assumed, and this implied *lav* is sufficient to ground the *korban* and the *malkot*. The Gemara will now show that the *baraita* takes a different approach, deriving the negative prohibition through an explicit textual mechanism rather than relying solely on implication.

---

## Gezeirah Shavah

### Linking Punishments

The *baraita* does not rest on the argument that the prohibition is implied despite being inexpressible; it derives the negative prohibition through a formal *derashah*. The verse reads: *ve'inisem et nafshoteichem ve'chol melacha lo ta'asu* — "afflict yourselves and do no *melacha*." From here the *baraita* proceeds through several stages.

First it asks: perhaps one would be punished for performing *melacha* during the period of *tosefet*, the added time at the beginning or end of Yom Kippur. The verse *ve'chol ha'nefesh asher ta'aseh kol melacha b'etzem ha'yom ha'zeh* — "whoever performs *melacha* on the essence of this day" — indicates by the word *b'etzem* ("the essence") that *karet* applies to *melacha* performed on the day itself, *v'eino anush karet al tosefet*, not during the added portion. Then: perhaps even without *karet*, one transgresses a negative prohibition by performing *melacha* during *tosefet*? The verse again says *lo ta'asu b'etzem* — the prohibition applies to the essence of the day. Similarly, by fasting, the verse *ki kol ha'nefesh asher lo te'uneh b'etzem ha'yom ha'zeh* uses the same *b'etzem* language — *karet* for failing to fast applies to the day itself, not to the *tosefet* period. And the exclusion of eating during *tosefet* from negative prohibition is derived through a *kal va'chomer*: *melacha*, which is a universal prohibition applying on Shabbat and *Yom Tov*, does not generate a transgression during *tosefet*; *inuy*, which is particular to Yom Kippur alone and thus a weaker prohibition, certainly does not generate a transgression during *tosefet*.

So through these steps we learn: no *karet* and no negative prohibition apply to either *melacha* or *inuy* during *tosefet*. But then the *baraita* states: *aval azhara l'inuy shel yom atzmo lo lamadnu* — with all of that established, we still have not derived the negative prohibition against eating on Yom Kippur itself. From where is it learned?

### Kal VaChomer

The *baraita* attempts a *kal va'chomer*: since *karet* is prescribed for violating *inuy*, and *inuy* is the less universal prohibition (applying only on Yom Kippur, not on Shabbat or *Yom Tov*), then *melacha* — which is universal — certainly carries *karet*. Therefore, the statement of *karet* by *melacha* is superfluous; one could have derived it from *inuy*. Since it is superfluous, it is *mufneh* — available to serve as the basis of a *gezeirah shavah* — and we link the two: just as *melacha* combines punishment with a negative prohibition, so too does *inuy*.

The Gemara challenges: *ika mifrach* — this inference is rebuttable. *Melacha* has its own stringency — it is universally applicable, applying on Shabbat and *Yom Tov* — which *inuy* lacks. Therefore, one cannot say the *karet* for *melacha* is superfluous; perhaps without the explicit verse one would not have known *melacha* carries *karet*, precisely because *melacha* is sometimes overridden (as in the *Beit HaMikdash* on Shabbat or Yom Kippur). So the *karet* for *melacha* is not superfluous and cannot serve as the basis of the equation.

The *baraita* then reverses direction: let us say instead that the *karet* for *inuy* is superfluous, derivable from *melacha* — since *melacha*, which is sometimes overridden in the *Beit HaMikdash*, nonetheless carries *karet*, how much more so should *inuy*, which is never overridden in that context. Therefore the *karet* for *inuy* is extra and *mufneh*, enabling the equation. The same challenge applies in reverse: *inuy* has its own stringency — it is never permitted in the *Beit HaMikdash* — while *melacha* is universal but sometimes allowed. Each prohibition has dimensions of stringency that the other lacks; neither the *karet* for *melacha* nor the *karet* for *inuy* is demonstrably superfluous given these competing considerations, and neither can be used as the basis of the *gezeirah shavah* on the grounds of being derivable from the other.

### Mufneh

At this point Ravina intervenes: *hai tanna etzem etzem g'mar* — this *tanna* is not trying to identify a superfluous *karet*; he is identifying a superfluous instance of the word *etzem*. The word *b'etzem ha'yom ha'zeh* already appeared to teach us the exclusion of *tosefet*. The *gezeirah shavah* works by finding a word that is *mufneh* — that is, not needed for its plain context, so that it is available to link two topics. The Gemara notes: *d'ilo mufneh, ika mifrach d'varchina* — without a truly superfluous word available, the equation could always be challenged along the lines just discussed. The question is therefore: which instance of *b'etzem* is extra?

### Five Instances

Ravina answers: *chamisha kra'ei k'tivei* — there are five separate verses stating the prohibition against *melacha*. One establishes the negative prohibition for the day; one for the night; one establishes the punishment for the day; one for the night; and the fifth is *l'afnu'ei* — it is extra, available as the basis of the *gezeirah shavah*, to link *inuy* to *melacha* and teach that just as the prohibition of *melacha* is accompanied by a negative prohibition, so too is the prohibition of *inuy*, whether for the day or night. The details of which five verses these are can be verified by examining the relevant passages in the *Chumash*, but the principle is clear: the redundancy in the *melacha* verses creates the textual space for the equation.

A separate tradition then cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *ne'emar kan inuy ve'ne'emar sham inuy* — the word *inuy* appears here (on Yom Kippur) and there (in another context). The referent, per Rashi, is the verse describing the case of rape (*al devar asher ina et eshet re'ehu*), where the act of *inuy* — afflicting another — is backed by a negative prohibition. Just as there the *inuy* is backed by a negative prohibition, so too here. The obvious objection is that there the prohibition is *against* performing the act of *inuy*, while here the *mitzvah* is *to* perform it — the *inuy* of fasting. This asymmetry limits how far the comparison can be pressed, though the *baraita* uses the formal link in terminology to establish the general principle that where *inuy* appears, a negative prohibition accompanies it.

---

## Alternatives

### Shabbat Link

Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers a different derivation: *yalif Shabbat Shabbaton mi-Shabbat Bereishit* — the term *Shabbat Shabbaton* used for Yom Kippur is the same term used for the weekly Shabbat. Just as the weekly Shabbat is accompanied by a negative prohibition against violating it, so too is Yom Kippur. The shared language creates the equation.

### Intrinsic Meaning

Rav Pappa argues differently: *hu gufei Shabbat ikrei* — the very fact that Yom Kippur is itself called *Shabbat* is sufficient. One need not make a formal comparison to Shabbat *Bereishit* through shared language; the application of the word *Shabbat* to Yom Kippur itself carries the intrinsic meaning of a negative prohibition against violating it.

### Word Meaning

The Gemara notes the difference between the two positions. Rav Pappa prefers not to derive the prohibition through an external analogy to Shabbat *Bereishit*; he would rather say that the word *Shabbat* as it appears on Yom Kippur itself carries the negative implication — *dekra dichtiv bei begufei atei*, the word as it stands in its own verse does the work. The challenge to this position is that the word *Shabbat* carries its meaning of prohibition only because of its association with *Shabbat Bereishit* to begin with; intrinsically it does not seem to function as an independent source of a *lav*. The question of why Rav Acha bar Yaakov did not simply adopt Rav Pappa's approach is answered by the Gemara: Rav Acha bar Yaakov needs the verse *tishbetu shabbatchem* for an entirely separate teaching, as the *baraita* cited next demonstrates.

---

## Tosefet

### Ninth Evening

A *baraita* is cited: *ve'inisem et nafshoteichem be'tisha la'chodesh* — "you shall afflict yourselves on the ninth of the month." The verse continues: *ba'erev me'erev ad erev* — "in the evening, from evening until evening." The *baraita* notes an apparent problem: do we actually fast on the ninth? The fast begins on the tenth! Why does the verse say "the ninth"?

### Evening to Evening

One answer is *tosefet*: the verse conveys that the fast already begins before nightfall on the ninth — one adds a portion of the ninth day to the tenth. The words *me'erev ad erev*, "from evening to evening," teach that the addition applies at both ends: just as Yom Kippur begins slightly before sunset on the ninth, so it continues slightly beyond nightfall at the conclusion of the tenth. This is the basis of *mosifin me'chol al ha'kodesh* — the principle of adding from the ordinary day to the sacred one.

### Extension

The verse *tishbetu shabbatchem* then extends this principle beyond Yom Kippur. *Ve'ein li ela Yom Ha'Kippurim; shabbatot minayin? Talmud lomar tishbetu* — I know only Yom Kippur; whence do I know that *tosefet* applies to Shabbat? From the word *tishbetu*. *Ve'ein li ela shabbatot; yamim tovim minayin? Talmud lomar shabbatchem* — and whence for *Yom Tov*? From the word *shabbatchem*. Wherever the language of *shevut* (rest) appears, the principle of adding from the weekday to the sacred day applies.

It should be noted that according to the Rambam, the biblical obligation of *tosefet* applies only to Yom Kippur, derived from the verse *be'tisha la'chodesh ba'erev*. The extension to Shabbat and *Yom Tov* via *tishbetu shabbatchem* is, in his view, only *derabbanan*. The earlier *tanna* in the *baraita* who used the word *etzem* to exclude *tosefet* from punishment implicitly assumed there is a recognized period of *tosefet*, and the question raised is what remains for the verse *be'tisha la'chodesh* to teach once the concept of *tosefet* is already established through the *etzem* derivation. The answer is the teaching of Rav Chiyya bar Rav of Difti, which follows.

---

## Eating Counts

### Ninth Eating

*De'tani Rav Chiyya bar Rav mi'Difti: ve'inisem et nafshoteichem be'tisha* — you shall afflict yourselves on the ninth. The obvious difficulty: *ve'chi be'tisha misa'nin? Ve'halo be'asara misa'nin?* Do we really fast on the ninth? The fast is the tenth! So if *tosefet* is already known, what does "the ninth" add? The answer: *kol ha'ochel ve'shoteh be'tisha, ma'aleh alav ha'katuv ke'illu his'anna tishii va'asiri* — whoever eats and drinks on the ninth, Scripture accounts it as though he fasted both the ninth and the tenth.

### Concept

This teaching opens a significant conceptual question about the nature of Yom Kippur fasting. Earlier in the tractate, the Gemara raised the question of whether *inuy* — affliction — is fundamentally about causing oneself pain and suffering as part of *teshuvah*, a kind of self-chastisement, or whether it is about something else. The Rambam formulates the alternative: fasting on Yom Kippur is about *shevut*, cessation and release from the physical world, freeing oneself from material concerns in order to engage in spiritual matters.

### Enhancement

The teaching of Rav Chiyya bar Rav supports the Rambam's understanding. If fasting were purely about pain and suffering, one would expect that eating heavily on the ninth would undermine the fast by making it easier. The logic would run: the more you eat beforehand, the less it hurts, and the less it hurts, the less effective the *inuy*. But the teaching says the opposite — eating on the ninth is itself credited as a form of fasting. *Ke'illu his'anna* — it is as though one afflicted oneself. The better explanation is that eating appropriately before Yom Kippur enables a person to enter the day without being preoccupied with physical discomfort and hunger, free to focus fully on *teshuvah* and the spiritual work of the day. On this reading, the fast is not about how much one suffers; it is about the state of freedom from the physical world that one achieves. Eating well beforehand, far from undermining that state, actively prepares one for it — and that is why it is itself counted as a form of *inuy*.

---

---

# Yoma 82

## Non-Fit Foods/Drinks

### Intro: Unfit Foods

The daf begins slightly before the midpoint of 81b, approximately ten lines above where the lines widen on the page. The mishna introduces the rule: *akhal okhlin she-aynam re'uyim* — if one ate foods that are not fit for eating, one is *patur*. This continues the broader discussion of the prohibitions of Yom Kippur, which had included, in the preceding material, the derivation of the negative prohibition against feasting on the fast day, and two important *drashot* from the verse *u-ve-tish'ah la-chodesh ba-erev me-erev ad erev*. One of those *drashot* established the principle of *mosifin me-chol al ha-kodesh* — that the fast begins before nightfall and ends somewhat after the close of the day — which is the foundation of *tosefet Yom Kippur*. According to the Rambam, *tosefet* is *d'Oraita* specifically for Yom Kippur, even if it does not carry the same punishment. The other *drasha* taught that one who eats and drinks on the ninth of Tishrei is credited by Scripture as though he fasted on both the ninth and the tenth — emphasizing that the purpose of the day is not self-affliction per se, but freedom from eating, which begins through proper preparation the day before.

With that background established, the mishna turns to foods and drinks that are not *ra'ui* — not fit for consumption — and rules that eating them incurs no liability.

### Rava: Peppers & Ginger

*Amar Rava*: if someone chews peppercorns on Yom Kippur, he is *patur*. Similarly, if someone chews ginger on Yom Kippur, he is likewise *patur*. The reasoning is that these items, in their dried, spice form, are not ordinarily eaten straight. They function as condiments and flavorings but are not consumed as food. The note in the standard edition clarifies that Rava is speaking of pepper berries used as spices rather than peppers that are eaten plain. The fresh, pickled ginger familiar from the table — and the ordinary vegetables one might find in a salad — would present a different question, as will become clear momentarily.

### Baraita: Peppers & Orlah

The Gemara raises an objection from a *baraita*. Rabbi Meir teaches: once the verse already says *ve-araltem orlato et piryo* — that one must render the fruit of a tree subject to *orla* — we already know it is discussing an edible tree. Why, then, does the verse add the words *etz ma'akhal*, specifying a tree meant for eating? To teach that we are dealing even with a case where the taste of the fruit and the taste of the bark are the same: *she-yihyeh ta'am etzo u-firyo shaveh*. The answer typically given in the Gemara for this case is the *etrog*, whose flesh and rind share a similar flavor. However, the *baraita* continues: *hevei omer zeh palpelin* — we are speaking here of the pepper plant. The branches of the pepper plant apparently share a taste profile with the peppercorn itself. The *baraita* then draws the conclusion: *le-lamedekha she-palpelin hayavin be-orla* — peppers are subject to *orla*. And since the laws of *orla* apply only to edible fruit, the fact that peppers carry an *orla* obligation demonstrates that they are considered food. The *baraita* adds the additional point, more aggadic than halachic in character, that Israel lacks nothing — even pepper plants grow there, as the verse says *lo techsar kol bah*.

The objection is clear: if peppers are food, as the *orla* obligation proves, how can Rava say that eating them on Yom Kippur is *patur*?

### Moist vs. Dry Resolution

*Lo kashya*, says the Gemara — there is no difficulty. *Ha bi-retiva ha bi-yavesha*: it depends on whether the pepper is moist or dry. When fresh and moist, pepper can indeed be eaten directly and is considered a normal food. Once dried out and processed into a spice, it is no longer eaten straight by any standard measure of normal consumption, and one who eats it in that form is *patur* on Yom Kippur.

### Himalta Spice Case

Ravina raised a question to Rav Mareima regarding a teaching of Rav Nachman. Rav Nachman had said that *himalta* — a compound of ground spices originating from the house of Handuai (which Rashi identifies as from the land of Cush, i.e., Ethiopia), apparently a preparation of spices with honey — is permitted and does not raise the concern of *bishul nochrim*, because it is edible raw. Furthermore, one recites *borei pri ha-adamah* over it, apparently on account of the spice ingredients it contains. This seems to indicate that spices can be eaten raw and are therefore considered food. But did we not just say that such spices, being dried, are not considered normal food?

The Gemara resolves this in the same way: *lo kashya — ha bi-retiva ha bi-yavesha*. When fresh and moist, yes, these ingredients can be eaten directly and are considered food by any standard. When dried out, they are no longer regarded as fit to be eaten by ordinary people under ordinary circumstances, and eating them in that form does not constitute an act of *achila*.

### Leaves: Reed vs. Grape

The Gemara continues with a *baraita*: *achal alei kanim patur* — if one ate the leaves of reeds, one is exempt, as these are not considered human food, perhaps suitable for animals but not for people. However, *lulvei gefanim* — grape leaves — render one liable. The Gemara then asks: which grape leaves qualify? Rav Yitzchak of Magdala teaches: any that have sprouted from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur — that is, leaves that have been on the vine for no more than ten days, and are still tender and edible. After that point, they harden and are no longer considered suitable food. Rav Kahana disagrees and says: any leaves up to thirty days old are still considered edible. The *baraita* sides with Rav Yitzchak of Magdala: grape leaves are those that have sprouted from Rosh Hashanah until Yom Kippur, and only those count as *lulvei gefanim* for this purpose.

### Brine & Vinegar

A parallel distinction is drawn for liquids. If one drinks fish brine or a certain type of fish fat (*murays*), one is *patur* — these are not considered drinkable in any ordinary sense. The Gemara implies that vinegar, by contrast, would render one liable, since it is more recognizable as a liquid one might actually drink. The question then arises: which tannaitic opinion does the mishna follow?

### Rebbi: Vinegar Effect

The Gemara explains that our mishna follows the view of Rebbi, as taught in a *baraita*: *Rebbi omer — chometz meshivas hanefesh* — vinegar settles the soul. This is the Hebrew equivalent of the Aramaic phrase *yituvei da'ata* that has appeared repeatedly over the preceding two days of the tractate. Since vinegar abates the sense of *inuy* — the affliction of the fast — it constitutes a problem on Yom Kippur. This is the position of Rebbi.

### Rav Gidal Retraction

Rav Gidal bar Menashya from Bei Ridna publicly expounded that we do not rule like Rebbi — that drinking vinegar does not constitute a violation of Yom Kippur. By the following year, word had spread, and people throughout the community mixed vinegar with water and drank it on Yom Kippur. When Rav Gidal heard what had happened, he was furious. He said: what did I actually say? I said it is not a violation *bedi'eved* — after the fact. I never said one may do so *lechatchila* — prospectively, from the outset. And further: when did I say even *bedi'eved* it was not a problem? Only for a small amount — *purta*. For a large amount I said no such thing. And a further precision: I was speaking only about raw vinegar — *chai*. If it is diluted with water — *mazug* — then it is genuinely potable, and I did not permit that even *bedi'eved*.

The episode is instructive quite apart from its halachic content: what a person says in public is heard as people wish to hear it, and a scholar must be extraordinarily precise, because an audience eager for leniency will hear exactly what they want and no more.

### Eating vs. Soul-Settling

This section of the Gemara invites reflection on a conceptual tension that runs through the entire discussion. The Yom Kippur prohibitions are framed around *inuy* — affliction — and the operative notion in these sugyot has consistently been *meshivat hanefesh* or *yituvei da'ata*, the settling or abating of that affliction. Yet the mishna frames the relevant categories in terms of *achila* and *shtia* — normal eating and drinking.

One might ask: is it possible for a substance to abate the *inuy* — to function as *meshivat hanefesh* — without technically constituting an act of *achila* or *shtia*? After all, Rebbi's formulation regarding vinegar was not *chometz shtia hi* — he did not say vinegar is a drink. He said *chometz meshivas hanefesh* — it settles the soul. Could something fall into a halachic grey zone: not an act of eating or drinking by conventional standards, yet effective enough in relieving the fast's discomfort to constitute a violation of the *inuy*? Or, alternatively, is it a *d'Rabbanan* extension of the prohibition — analogous to the concept of *chatzi shiur*, which is a quantitative threshold, but here applied qualitatively: something not ordinarily eaten, yet real enough in its relief-giving effect?

The question does not find a clean resolution in the Gemara, but it is worth holding in mind, particularly when the Gemara elsewhere mentions that smelling pleasant aromas on Yom Kippur is not prohibited. The reason is that *inuy* was derived specifically in the context of eating and drinking; other forms of relief — even those that genuinely settle the soul — fall outside its scope. The case of vinegar, and similar borderline substances, sits in the space between those poles: they enter the mouth, they produce a physiological effect, but they do not qualify as normal food or drink. Whether the prohibition tracks the act of eating or the experience of relief is a question the Gemara leaves, at least partially, open.

The subjective dimension also has limits. The earlier discussion in the tractate established *melo lugmav* — the minimum quantity that satisfies the *inuy* violation — as potentially a more individualized standard than the fixed *k'kosevet* measure. But that subjectivity was found only in the quantitative determination. As regards food types — whether a given substance qualifies as food at all — the Gemara consistently applies an objective, socially normative standard: is this what people ordinarily eat? The question of whether it is a specific person's preferred food does not appear to enter the analysis.

---

## Chinuch of Minors

### Mishna: No Affliction

The Gemara moves to the opening of the following mishna, at the top of 82a: *ha-tinokot ein ma'anin otam be-Yom HaKippurim* — young children are not subjected to *inuy* on Yom Kippur; we do not require them to fast. *Aval mechanchin otam lifnei shana ve-lifnei shnataim* — but we do train them a year or two beforehand, *bishvil she-yihyu regilin be-mitzvot* — so that they should become accustomed to performing *mitzvot*.

This is the general concept of *chinuch*. The institution of *chinuch* applies across many domains: once a child can recite *Shema*, one teaches him *Shema*; once a child can care for *tzitzit*, one provides *tzitzit*; and so on with *tefillin*, *lulav*, *etrog*, and other rituals as the child becomes capable of each. The typical cases of *chinuch* in the literature tend to involve positive ritual performance — *mitzvot aseh*. Here, however, *chinuch* is being applied to what we might more readily classify as a prohibition — the abstention from eating and drinking. Yet the fast of Yom Kippur is itself also a ritual act, a *mitzvah*, not merely a negative restraint. That duality will prove significant when the question of the conceptual scope of *chinuch* is raised later in the discussion.

Unlike some other *mitzvot* where *chinuch* begins at a fixed developmental moment — such as when the child can speak, in the case of *Shema* — fasting *chinuch* is recognized as inappropriate to begin until the child is old enough both to understand what is being asked of them and to bear the physical demand. And as the Gemara will elaborate, even then it is done gradually. The mishna says a year or two before; the precise meaning of that phrase becomes the subject of the Gemara's detailed analysis.

### Rav Chisda: Health/Const…

The opening question is almost self-answering: if one begins training two years before, surely one must begin one year before as well. So what does the mishna add by saying "a year or two"? *Amar Rav Chisda: lo kashya — ha be-chola ha be-vari*. The resolution depends not on the child's religious maturity or level of understanding, but on their physical constitution. For a healthy child (*bari*), training begins two years before; for a child with a weaker or more delicate constitution (*chola*), training begins only one year before.

### Rav Huna: Age Progression

Rav Huna then spells out the progression in more concrete terms. At eight or nine years old — *ben cheit ben tet* — one begins *chinuch* by extending the hours of fasting: the child's regular mealtime is delayed, adding a few hours before eating is permitted, but there is no expectation of completing the full fast. At ten and eleven — *ben yod ben yod-alef* — the child fasts the complete day, but this is on a *d'Rabbanan* level, a rabbinic obligation of *chinuch*. At twelve — *ben yod-bet* — the girl's fasting is biblical. This, as Rav Huna specifies, is the schedule for a girl: *ve-da le-tinoket*.

### Rav Nachman: Later Timel…

Rav Nachman shifts the entire schedule one year later. At nine and ten — *ben tet ben yod* — one adds hours. At eleven and twelve — *ben yod-alef ben yod-bet* — the child fasts the complete day rabbinically. At thirteen — *ben yod-gimel* — the obligation is biblical. And this, as Rav Nachman specifies, is the schedule for a boy: *ve-da le-tinok*.

At first glance, Rav Huna and Rav Nachman appear to disagree. But Rashi suggests, and the logic of the Gemara supports, that they are not actually in conflict. Both opinions are in fact operating with the same *bari/chola* distinction introduced by Rav Chisda. Rav Huna's earlier ages reflect the healthier child; his later ages within the same bracket reflect the child of weaker constitution. Similarly with Rav Nachman. To take the case of a girl: a healthy girl begins adding hours at eight, begins fasting the full day rabbinically at ten. A girl of weaker constitution begins adding hours at nine, begins fasting the full day rabbinically at eleven. Both Rav Huna and Rav Nachman follow this logic; the difference between them is whether they are describing the girl's progression or the boy's, with boys reaching *bar mitzvah* a year later than girls.

### Reconciling Opinions

The Gemara then faces the language of the mishna: *mechanchin otam lifnei shana ve-lifnei shnataim* — one trains them a year or two before.
