According to Rav Huna and Rav Nachman, *chinuch* actually begins three or four years before *bar* or *bat mitzvah* — the phase of adding hours begins well ahead of the full-day rabbinic period. So what does the mishna mean by "a year or two"?

The *Gra*'s reading resolves this. According to his text and interpretation, the mishna is not saying that *chinuch* begins one or two years before *bar mitzvah*. Rather, the hours-based *chinuch* continues until one or two years before — meaning that it runs through those intervening years and gives way to the full-day rabbinic fast in the final period. *Lifnei shana ve-lifnei shnataim* thus describes the horizon at which the preliminary training concludes, not the point at which it begins. For a healthy girl: the hours-based *chinuch* runs until two years before *bat mitzvah*, at which point she begins fasting the full day rabbinically. For a girl of weaker constitution: the hours-based *chinuch* runs until one year before, and then she begins fasting the full day.

### Rabbi Yochanan Dissent

Rabbi Yochanan disagrees with the entire framework of Rav Huna and Rav Nachman. His position is: *hashlama d'rabbanan leka* — there is no rabbinic-level *chinuch* obligation to fast the complete day before the child reaches *bar* or *bat mitzvah*. The full-day fast, in his view, is simply too demanding to impose rabbinically on a child who is not yet obligated. What Rabbi Yochanan does require is the adding of extra hours — but only in the one or two years immediately prior to *bar* or *bat mitzvah*. In practical terms: for a girl, in the years of ten and eleven, one adds hours. At twelve, the biblical obligation begins.

For Rabbi Yochanan, the phrase *lifnei shana ve-lifnei shnataim* is read differently than under the *Gra*'s interpretation. The *samuch le-parkan* — the "close to the time of their obligation" — refers to the biblical age of obligation, not some rabbinic intermediate stage. The hours-based *chinuch* takes place during that final one or two year window immediately preceding *bat* or *bar mitzvah*, and that is the full extent of what is required.

This creates a tension with the mishna's language that is now the mirror image of what was raised against Rav Huna and Rav Nachman. For them, the phrase "a year or two before" seemed too short; for Rabbi Yochanan, the phrase describes exactly the hours-based training period, which falls in those final one or two years.

The Gemara then considers a *baraita*. *Detani Rabba bar Shmuel*: children are not subjected to *inuy* on Yom Kippur, *aval mechanchin otam shana o shtayim lifnei pirkam* — but one trains them one or two years *samuch le-parkan*, close to their coming of age. This reads naturally in support of Rabbi Yochanan: there is no full-day rabbinic fast, only an hours-based *chinuch* in the year or two immediately preceding *bar* or *bat mitzvah*.

This *baraita* now creates a difficulty for Rav Huna and Rav Nachman. If the *baraita* says *chinuch* takes place one or two years before, and the Gemara has been assuming that the word *mechanchin* refers specifically to the hours-based training (as distinct from the full-day fast), then the *baraita* supports a model in which *chinuch* only begins in those final years — contradicting Rav Huna and Rav Nachman, who introduce it much earlier.

Rav Huna and Rav Nachman respond: *mai chinuch nami de-katani — hashlama*. The word *mechanchin* in the *baraita* does not refer to the hours-based *chinuch*; it refers to *hashlama*, the completion, i.e., the full-day fast. The *baraita* is saying that the full-day fasting occurs in the one or two years immediately preceding *bar* or *bat mitzvah* — the hours-based training precedes that and is not what the *baraita* is describing.

But the Gemara presses: would one really use the term *chinuch* to refer to doing the full amount? The term *chinuch* seems to imply something introductory, something less than the complete performance. The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *eizehu chinuch?* — if a child is accustomed to eating at the second hour of the day, one feeds him at the third; if at the third, one feeds him at the fourth. The word *chinuch* is used explicitly for the adding of hours, not for the full performance. So how can Rav Huna and Rav Nachman use it to mean the complete fast?

*Amar Rava bar Ulla: trei chinuchei havei* — there are two types of *chinuch*. The word *chinuch* can refer both to the introductory training — the hours — and to the *chinuch* of doing the full amount just before the age of obligation. Both are legitimately called *chinuch* in different contexts.

### Rabba bar Shmuel Braita

As noted above, the *baraita* of Rabba bar Shmuel — *tinokot ein me'anin otam be-Yom HaKippurim, aval mechanchin otam shana o shtayim lifnei pirkam* — reads naturally with Rabbi Yochanan's position, and creates the interpretive challenge for Rav Huna and Rav Nachman that leads to the analysis in the following subsection.

### Rava bar Ulla: Two Chinu…

Rava bar Ulla's resolution, as explained above, is that *chinuch* is not a monolithic concept. It encompasses two distinct activities: the introductory *chinuch* of adding hours, which may begin several years before *bar* or *bat mitzvah*, and the *chinuch* of completing the full fast, which occurs in the year or two immediately before the age of obligation. The same word is used for both, but they describe different phases of the same pedagogical process.

### Tosafot: Chinuch Concept

The Tosafot Yeshanim — found in the lower left of the page in the standard edition — raises a series of important conceptual questions about *chinuch*. The passage is attributed to Rav Elazar of Metz, who was a student of the Ri and the author of the *Yere'im*.

The first question concerns daughters. There is a *baraita* in tractate Nazir that states: a man can vow his son into *nezirut* as a form of *chinuch*, in keeping with the view of Reish Lakish that this is done *kedei le-chancho be-mitzvot* — in order to train him in *mitzvot*. But the text specifies *beno* — his son, not his daughter, because there is no obligation of *chinuch* regarding one's daughter in the context of *nezirut*. This might suggest that *chinuch* as a concept does not apply to daughters at all. Tosafot Yeshanim rejects this reading: the *baraita* is speaking specifically about *nezirut*, which may have its own reasons for excluding daughters. In general, the obligation of *chinuch* applies to daughters as well as sons, as the present Gemara makes clear by discussing both *tinok* and *tinoket*.

The second question is more conceptually striking. The broader halachic literature states: *katan ochel neveilot — ein beit din metzuvim le-hafrisho* — if a minor is eating non-*kosher* food, the rabbinical court is not obligated to stop him. Yet if parents are obligated to train their children in *mitzvot*, surely all the more so they must prevent their children from committing violations. Why would we say that one need not intervene?

Rav Elazar of Metz provides a fascinating answer: *chinuch lo shayach ela she-ya'aseh mitzvah ve-lo peirushei me-issura* — *chinuch* as a concept applies only to the performance of a *mitzvah*, not to restraining someone from a transgression. *Chinuch* is about habituation to positive activity. It is a process of training through doing, not through refraining.

This idea is admittedly counterintuitive. One might ask: if I am training my child in observance, surely I should also train him not to transgress. And indeed it is easy to think of practices — checking *hechsherim*, avoiding *muktzeh* on *Shabbat*, and the like — that express training in observance through the avoidance of prohibited acts. But the conceptual claim here is that *chinuch* as a formal category is oriented toward *mitzvot aseh* — positive performative acts — and not toward abstention.

But this raises a problem directly relevant to the present context: the obligation of Yom Kippur fasting is framed as a *lav*, a prohibition. How is *chinuch* applicable here? Tosafot Yeshanim answers: *ha-chinuch she-mechanchin oto be-mitzvat ve-anitem et nafshoteichem* — the fast of Yom Kippur can be conceived as a positive *mitzvah*, the fulfillment of *ve-initem et nafshoteichem*. The point of *chinuch* here is not the refraining from food as such, but the active performance of the *mitzvah* of affliction. This is what allows fasting to fall within the scope of *chinuch* despite its prohibitory appearance.

The secondary question raised by Tosafot Yeshanim is: upon whom does the obligation of *chinuch* rest, and does it extend to others beyond the parents? The rule that *beit din* need not stop a minor from eating *treif* is explained, in a second answer, as follows: the obligation of *chinuch* is personal — it falls upon the parent in relation to their own child, not upon bystanders in relation to other people's children. It is not that preventing a child from sinning is categorically outside the scope of *chinuch*; it is that policing other people's children is not one's obligation. A parent, by contrast, would indeed be expected to stop their own child from eating forbidden food.

The further question — whether *chinuch* falls upon the father alone or also upon the mother — is noted as an active debate among the *Rishonim*, but is not developed fully here.

Finally, the status of *chinuch* itself as a formal obligation is worth noting: it is understood to be a *d'Rabbanan* obligation, even if the precise scriptural hook is somewhat loose. The verse *chanoch la-na'ar al pi darko* provides a textual anchor, but the structured legal obligation is rabbinic in character.

### Practical Enforcement

In practice, the gradual approach to fasting *chinuch* — building from extra hours in the early years toward full-day fasting in the year immediately preceding *bar* or *bat mitzvah* — reflects a realistic account of what can reasonably be demanded of children. Rabbi Yochanan's more minimal position, which restricts *chinuch* to hours-based training with no full-day rabbinic obligation, is noted as a dissenting view. The prevailing approach, which builds toward the full day in the final years before *bar* or *bat mitzvah*, is more demanding and requires a gradual ramp-up.

In practice, some parents begin encouraging their children to extend fasting voluntarily a year or more before the formal obligation. The pedagogical logic of permitting the experience to fall short — allowing the child to test their limits in a year when failure carries no consequence — serves the *chinuch* process well, as it prepares the child to succeed when the obligation is real. Whether *chinuch* applies on a *d'Rabbanan* level to the child directly, or falls as an obligation upon the parent, affects how one assesses the limits of enforcement; and whether the obligation rests on the father alone or on both parents equally is an open question in the *Rishonim*.

---

## Pikuach Nefesh & Mar (II)

### Pregnant Woman Case

The Gemara now turns to a new mishna, which opens the topic of *pikuach nefesh* on Yom Kippur. The mishna states: *ubra she-hericha* — a pregnant woman who smelled food and felt an overwhelming need to eat — *machilin otah ad she-tashiv nafshah* — one feeds her until her sense of distress settles. The precise phrase *tashiv nafshah* is strikingly close to the *meshivat hanefesh* language that has appeared throughout the last two days of the sugya. The use of this phrase in the mishna is very likely the source from which Rebbi drew when he described vinegar as *meshivas hanefesh*, and the Aramaic equivalent *yituvei da'ata* carries the same conceptual weight. The mishna thus anchors that language in the concrete scenario of the pregnant woman.

### Sick Person Protocol

The mishna continues: *chola* — a sick person — one feeds based on the assessment of experts (*beki'in*). If no medical experts are available, one follows the sick person's own account of their condition and feeds them accordingly, until the person says they have had enough.

### Gradations of Relief

A *baraita* elaborates on the scenario of the pregnant woman who smelled sacred meat or pig meat and craved it. The procedure is graduated. First, one dips something like a fork or toothpick into the sauce of the dish and touches it to her lips — perhaps that small taste will be enough to settle her. If she calms down, good. If not, one gives her the sauce itself, not the meat. If she calms, good. If not, one gives her the fat itself, and then the meat itself. The underlying principle guiding this progression is that even when a prohibition must be violated for the sake of life, one seeks to commit the lesser transgression first.

### Nothing Before Pikuach

The *baraita* then states the overarching rule: *she-ein lecha davar she-omed bifnei pikuach nefesh* — nothing stands before the preservation of life. However, there is an important exception: *chutz me-avodah zarah ve-gilui arayot u-shfichut damim* — except for the three cardinal sins of idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder. For these three, the rule is reversed: one must give up one's life rather than transgress. The rest of the discussion on this daf concerns the scriptural and logical derivations of this principle.

### Avodah Zarah Basis

*Avodah zarah minalan* — where is it derived that one must die rather than commit idolatry? From a *baraita* in which Rabbi Eliezer teaches: the verse commands loving God *be-chol nafshecha* — with all your soul. That phrase already implies one must love God even at the cost of one's life. Why, then, does the verse also say *be-chol me'odecha* — with all your might, understood as all your wealth?

### Rebbi Eliezer Drasha

Rabbi Eliezer's answer is that not all people are the same. *Yesh lecha adam she-gufo chaviv alav mi-mamono* — some people value their body more than their money. For such a person, commanding them to love God *be-chol me'odecha* ensures that even their wealth must be surrendered for God. Conversely, there are people who value their money more than their bodies — *mamono chaviv alav mi-gufo*. For them, the phrase *be-chol nafshecha* — even your soul — establishes that the obligation extends to life itself. Each formulation is needed to address a different human type.

### Betrayal Principle

The phrasing of the *avodah zarah* obligation in terms of love of God — rather than in terms of the technical prohibition of idolatry — has significant implications. Loving God with all one's soul suggests that what is at stake is not merely the commission of a particular transgression, but the fundamental act of betraying one's relationship with God. This raises the question: what if an act constitutes such a betrayal without technically meeting the halachic parameters of *avodah zarah*?

A relevant historical case is the forced conversion to Islam. Islam is strictly monotheistic, involves no images, and does not worship multiple deities — in the standard halachic taxonomy, it would not be classified as *avodah zarah* in the technical sense. Yet in the time of the Rambam, when communities faced forced conversion (*shmad*), the question arose whether *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* applied to this demand. The Rambam addressed this in his *Iggeres Hashmad*, and the general conclusion that emerged was that the obligation to give up one's life is rooted not in the technical parameters of *avodah zarah* but in *ve-ahavta et Hashem Elokecha be-chol levavecha u-ve-chol nafshecha* — and that accepting another exclusive monotheistic religion constitutes a betrayal of that commitment even when it does not meet the definition of *avodah zarah* per se.

A further nuance is raised by Tosafot in the context of tractate Sanhedrin. The Gemara there discusses *ha-oved me-ahavah u-mi-yira'h* — one who worships *avodah zarah* out of love or fear rather than genuine belief. Rashi explains that worshipping out of fear means doing so because a non-Jew threatens to kill you otherwise. If so, Tosafot asks, how can there ever be a scenario of *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* for *avodah zarah*? Since the person doesn't actually believe in the idol, the act is done entirely under compulsion, and if compulsion voids the transgression, then no genuine act of *avodah zarah* has been committed. If so, there is nothing to die for. The answer, implicit in the discussion, is that while the technical sin of *avodah zarah* may not be committed under such circumstances, the outward act of prostrating oneself before another deity — the public communication of abandoning God — itself constitutes a fundamental betrayal that *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* is designed to prevent. The obligation to die is not contingent on the technical culpability of the specific transgression; it is tied to what the act communicates about one's relationship with God.

### Sex & Murder Derivation

*Gilui arayot u-shfichut damim minalan* — how are forbidden sexual relations and murder derived? From a *baraita* in which Rebbi teaches: the verse *ki ka'asher yakum ish al re'ehu u-retzacho nefesh kein ha-davar hazeh* is stated in the context of a betrothed woman who is raped — the Torah declares that she is like a murder victim, not at fault, just as a person murdered is blameless for their own death. This is the *peshat* of the verse.

### Mutual Derivation

But the Gemara reads the verse as establishing a bilateral teaching. *Vechi mah inyan lamadnu me-rotzeach le-na'arah ha-me'orasah?* What precisely does murder teach about the raped woman, and what does the raped woman teach about murder? The Gemara answers: *harei zeh ba le-lamed ve-nimtza lamed* — it comes to teach and ends up learning.

On one side: from the raped woman, we learn that if someone is being pursued to be raped, a bystander may kill the would-be attacker to save her — this is derived from *ein moshia lah*, from which we infer that if there *is* someone who can save her, he must, even at the cost of the attacker's life. The same principle is then extended to murder: *af rotzeach — nittan le-hatzilo be-nafsho* — one being pursued by a would-be murderer may also be saved by killing the pursuer.

On the other side: from the case of murder, we learn that one must die rather than commit the act. *U-ma rotzeach — yehareg ve-al ya'avor*, just as one gives up one's life rather than commit murder, *af na'arat ha-me'orasah — yehareg ve-al ya'avor*, the same applies to forbidden sexual relations: one must die rather than transgress.

### Rava's Story

*Rotzeach gufa minalan* — but how is the rule for murder itself derived? The Gemara says: *sevara hi* — it is a matter of pure logic. A man came before Rava with the following question: the ruler of his city had told him to kill a specific person, and if he refused, the ruler would kill him. What should he do? Rava told him: *niktlach — ve-lo tiktol* — let him kill you; do not commit murder. *Mai chazit de-dama didach sumak tefei?* — what makes you think your blood is any redder? *Dilma dama de-hu gavra sumak tefei?* — perhaps the blood of that other man is redder? The logic, as Rashi explains, is that the entire basis for overriding a prohibition to save a life is the sanctity of the life being saved. If killing another person is what is required to "save" one's own life, there is nothing to license the transgression: one life is not worth more than another, and so the license does not exist. The prohibition against murder holds.

This same logic is then applied to forbidden sexual relations: just as one may not commit murder even to preserve one's own life, the same applies to *gilui arayot*.

This does not resolve the question of precisely which sexual prohibitions are encompassed by *yehareg ve-al ya'avor*, or whether the principle extends to acts other than intercourse. Those questions require inference from other passages in the Talmud and are not fully articulated here. What is established is the foundational principle: murder, *avodah zarah*, and forbidden sexual relations are the three transgressions that override the otherwise absolute principle of *pikuach nefesh*.

---

## Pikuach Nefesh & Mar (II)

### Rambam: Oness Exception

The Rambam addresses a consequential question raised by the *yehareg ve-al ya'avor* framework: what is the halachic status of one who, rather than accepting martyrdom, yields and commits one of the three cardinal sins under coercion — a gun, as it were, to their head? The Rambam rules that such a person is considered an *oness* — acting under duress — and is therefore not halachically culpable for the specific transgression of *avodah zarah* or murder. He did not commit those sins voluntarily; they were extracted from him by force. The transgression he did commit was the failure to accept martyrdom when required. But the act itself — the killing of another, or the outward act of worshipping an idol — is classified as having been done *be-oness*, and the corresponding *aveirah* of murder or *avodah zarah* is not attributed to him.

### Sex: Erection Test

The Rambam carves out an exception for a man in a case of *gilui arayot*. Even with a weapon held to his head, if he proceeds and engages in a forbidden sexual act, he is not classified as a full *oness*. The reason derives from a Talmudic principle: *ein kishui ela le-da'at* — erection occurs only with the man's actual desire. Physical coercion cannot produce an erection; some degree of the man's own will must be engaged. Therefore, if the act is completed, it demonstrates that the man's will was implicated to some extent, and the full claim of *oness* cannot be sustained. This repositions the agency from the coercing party back to the man himself, at least partially, and accordingly denies him the complete exemption of *oness* that applies in the cases of murder and *avodah zarah*. Tosafot also engages with this question, though in somewhat less direct terms than the Rambam.

---

## Two Pregnant Stories

### First Woman: Calmed

The Gemara now recounts two aggadic narratives involving pregnant women on Yom Kippur. In the first, a pregnant woman smelled food and experienced the urgent craving described in the mishna. The people with her came before Rebbi. He instructed them: *zil u-lechushu lah de-Yoma de-Kippura hu* — go and whisper to her that it is Yom Kippur. They did so, and she was calmed — *ve-alchisha*. She settled without needing to be fed.

### Rebbi: Righteous Fetus

Rebbi then applied a verse to this case: *beterem etzarcha ba-beten yeda'ticha* — before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. The implication is that the fetus itself is responsible for the craving — and yet, when informed that it was Yom Kippur, the craving ceased. The fetus, Rebbi suggests, was already so righteous that even in the womb it deferred to the sanctity of the fast day.

### Rabbi Yochanan Birth

The Gemara identifies the woman in this story as the mother of Rabbi Yochanan. It was Rabbi Yochanan who was the fetus in question — and who, already before birth, demonstrated the spiritual sensitivity that would mark his life as one of the great sages of his generation.

### Second Woman: Not Calmed

A second story follows a parallel structure. Another pregnant woman smelled food on Yom Kippur, and again the people came before a sage — here identified as Rebbi Chanina — seeking guidance. They were again instructed to whisper to her that it was Yom Kippur. They did so, but this time it did not help — *ve-lo alchisha* — and she required feeding.

### Rebbi: Wicked Fetus

Rebbi applied a different verse to this case: *zoru resha'im me-rachem* — the wicked spread out from the womb. The inference is the inverse of the first story: a fetus that demanded to be fed on Yom Kippur even after being informed of the day's sanctity revealed a wicked character already in utero.

### Shabtai Identity

The Gemara identifies the child born from the second woman: *nafak mineh Shabtai otzar peiri* — Shabtai the fruit monopolist emerged from her. This individual held a monopoly on fruit, deliberately withheld supply to drive up prices, and thereby caused ordinary people to go hungry — a form of exploitation that earned him a place in the tradition as an exemplar of wickedness.

### Moral Tension

The juxtaposition of these two stories with the halachic material that precedes them creates a notable tension. The law is unambiguous: *she-ein lecha davar she-omed bifnei pikuach nefesh* — nothing stands before the protection of life, and a pregnant woman in genuine distress must be fed on Yom Kippur without hesitation. Yet immediately following this clear ruling, the Gemara presents stories that attach profound moral significance — and a hint of moral judgment — to which women required feeding and which did not.

The concern is not merely academic. If the moral valence of the fetus is somehow encoded in the woman's craving, a reader might be tempted to hesitate — to wonder whether the woman who cannot be calmed by a whisper is carrying a wicked soul, and whether feeding her is truly urgent. That hesitation, however subtly introduced, could undermine the force of the halachic mandate. The law requires feeding without delay and without moral accounting; the aggadic material seems to introduce precisely the kind of moral accounting that the halacha would exclude. It is a striking and genuinely unsettling editorial juxtaposition, and one does wonder to what degree the moral narrative could, in practice, make those responsible for the woman's care more reluctant to act, or more inclined to probe whether she "really" needs it — precisely the hesitation that the law is designed to prevent.

---

---

# Yoma 83

## Sick Person vs. Doctor

### Choleh vs. Rofeh

The daf opens with the *Gemara*'s discussion of the *Mishnah*'s statement that a sick person may be fed on Yom Kippur *al pi beki'in* — based on the ruling of experts. The *Mishnah* had already addressed the case of a pregnant woman seized by an irresistible craving, but it generalizes from there to the case of any sick person, specifically invoking the testimony of qualified physicians. Rabbi Yannai then introduces a striking ruling: if the *choleh* says he needs to eat and the doctor says he does not, *shomin lacholeh* — you listen to the sick person. Conversely, if the doctor says he needs to eat and the *choleh* says he does not, you listen to the doctor. In either case, the minority voice in favor of feeding prevails.

### Lev Yodea Marat

The reason Rabbi Yannai gives for following the *choleh* against the doctor is the verse *lev yodea marat nafsho* — "the heart knows the bitterness of its own soul." The patient has privileged access to his own subjective experience in a way no outside observer does. This is a remarkable *chidush*. One might have thought that knowing how one feels is distinct from knowing what one medically requires. A person may feel desperately hungry, or feel that he is starving, without that feeling accurately indicating that eating is in fact the correct medical intervention. The doctors, after all, may know that feeding him at this moment would actually worsen his condition. Yet Rabbi Yannai rules that the *choleh*'s self-assessment overrides expert medical opinion — and not merely as testimony to his subjective state, but as a determination of what is medically necessary for him.

### Rav Moshe Feinstein

This principle has been developed extensively by later *poskim*. Rav Moshe Feinstein, in a number of *teshuvot*, consistently weighs a person's psychological state of well-being as a central factor in *pikuach nefesh* determinations. Cases he addresses include whether a family member may violate *Shabbat* to accompany a patient in the hospital who feels he urgently needs that presence, or whether a feeding tube may be forced on a patient who is violently rejecting it. In many such cases, Rav Moshe's position is that the patient's own sense of his needs — including his psychological needs — is dispositive, and that psychological well-being is not peripheral but central to the *pikuach nefesh* calculation. These rulings stand in direct continuity with Rabbi Yannai's foundational principle.

### Assessment vs. Psychology

It is worth distinguishing two separate issues that converge here. The first is epistemic: who is in the best position to assess what the patient requires? Rabbi Yannai's *chidush* is that on this question, the *choleh* himself wins — *lev yodea marat nafsho*. The second issue is not about assessment but about psychological state itself: how does a patient's emotional condition factor into the definition of medical necessity? This second dimension is more prominent in the case of the pregnant woman from the earlier *Mishnah*, where there was no contradicting expert opinion and the driving concern may have been the woman's powerful psychological need. In the case of Rabbi Yannai, the focus is on the first issue — the *choleh*'s ability to assess his own condition — even when a doctor says otherwise. Both dimensions, taken together, articulate a powerful halachic principle: the patient's own voice carries enormous weight, even against the testimony of outside expertise.

### Pshita Response

The *Gemara* then says *pshita* — this seems obvious. The novelty of Rabbi Yannai's ruling, which had just occupied considerable analysis, is brushed aside with the comment: one might have thought *rofe kim lei tefai*, that the doctor simply knows better, so the *Gemara* must teach us otherwise. It is striking that the *Gemara* treats this as needing to be said explicitly, since in contexts where medical and scientific authority carry near-absolute weight, the intuition that the doctor knows better is quite natural. Nevertheless, that is precisely the *chidush*.

---

## Reconciling Sources

### Mishnah's Position

The *Gemara* then raises a contradiction from the *Mishnah* itself. The *Mishnah* says *choleh ma'achilin oto al pi beki'in* — a sick person is fed based on what the experts say — which seems to imply two things that conflict with Rabbi Yannai. First, it is the doctors' opinion that matters, not the patient's own word — *al pi atzmo lo*. Second, the plural *beki'in* suggests that at least two experts are required — *al pi baki echad lo*.

### Chisurei Mechsera

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking *chisurei mechsera* — the *Mishnah* is missing words and must be read as containing an implicit clause. The *Mishnah*, properly understood, is not addressing the case where the *choleh* himself says he needs to eat. It is addressing the case where the *choleh* says he does not need to eat — and in that situation, the doctor's testimony is required to override him.

### Two Doctors Needed

But even granting that, why does the *Mishnah* require two doctors? If the *choleh* says he does not need to eat and one doctor says he does, why is one doctor insufficient? The *Gemara* explains that the *Mishnah* is addressing a case where not only the *choleh* but also one doctor says he does not need to be fed. In that configuration — the *choleh* plus one doctor against feeding — two doctors are needed on the other side to override them.

The *Gemara* initially asks why this is not obvious: surely *safeik nefashos l'hakel*, in any case of doubtful life-threat you are lenient? The *Gemara* answers that the novelty lies in a case where three say not to feed — two doctors and the *choleh* — and only two say to feed. One might have thought that because we are dealing with *umdena*, expert assessment rather than formal testimony, we follow majority opinion, as Rav Safra ruled in monetary contexts where you do follow the weight of numbers among assessors (*batar de'ot azlinan*). Perhaps even in a *pikuach nefesh* context the three-against-two majority would control. The *Gemara* rejects this: *hani mili le'inyan umdana demamona* — that principle applies to monetary assessments, but here it is *safeik nefashos*, and you are always lenient, feeding him based on the two doctors who say to do so.

This raises further questions that the *Gemara* does not fully resolve: what is the relevant threshold of expertise (*beki'in*)? Does the *choleh*'s own statement count as equal to a doctor's? What happens if one hundred doctors say not to feed and only two say to feed? The baseline answer that emerges is that you are always lenient — two opinions in favor of feeding outweigh any number against, once you have the minimum of corroboration. The one limitation that appears is the case of a single opinion in favor against multiple opposing opinions: there, it seems, you would not break Yom Kippur, because one uncorroborated opinion cannot carry the weight.

### Mar bar Rav Ashi

This limitation is itself contested. Mar bar Rav Ashi takes Rabbi Yannai's principle to its logical extreme: *kol heicha de'amar tzarich ani afilu ika me'ah de'amrei lo tzarich, bedidei shami'nan* — wherever the *choleh* himself says he needs to eat, even if a hundred people say he does not, you listen to him, as the verse says *lev yodea marat nafsho*. According to this view, no quantity of outside expert opinion can override the patient's own determination of his need.

### Reinterpreting Mishnah

This creates a difficulty with the *Mishnah*'s statement that when there are no experts (*ein sham beki'im*) you follow the *choleh* — implying that when experts are present, you would follow them against him. Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves this creatively: the *Mishnah*'s phrase *ein sham beki'im* does not mean there are no doctors in the room. It means that when the *choleh* says he needs to eat, expert testimony is as if it does not exist — *al pi atzmo ma'achilin oto*, you feed him based on his own word, and the experts are simply irrelevant to that determination. The only role for experts, on this reading, is when the *choleh* himself says he does not need to eat — then doctors can establish that he does.

The *Gemara*'s conclusion is thus remarkably lenient: if the *choleh* says he needs to eat, you feed him regardless of how many doctors disagree; if the doctor says he needs to eat, you feed him regardless of what the *choleh* says. You are always lenient in the direction of *pikuach nefesh*. The sole possible constraint — one opinion against many, without corroboration — may be a limitation only according to the intermediate position, and is arguably dissolved entirely by Mar bar Rav Ashi.

---

## What Doctors Say

### Rashi's View

Having established the framework of who is listened to, the *Gemara* turns to a question that is equally important in practice: what exactly must the doctor say to trigger the permission to violate Yom Kippur? Rashi's apparent position is that the doctor must state that if the patient is not fed, he may die — a very high threshold.

### Resh's Correction

The *Rosh* sharply disagrees with this reading and quotes the *Tosafot* as well. He argues that requiring the doctor to predict death is an unreasonable stringency, since no doctor speaks that way. Doctors do not say: "If you don't feed him, he might die." Rather, as the *Rosh* puts it in his characteristic formulation, *rofe darko lomar* — the way doctors talk is to say: if you don't feed him, it is possible that his condition will become complicated and that will expose him to risk. The *Rosh* rules that this is sufficient. If the patient is already in a situation of *safeik pikuach nefesh*, then anything that could aggravate that situation and increase the exposure to danger is itself considered *pikuach nefesh* — you do not need the doctor to predict death. Complication and increased risk exposure suffice.

### Practical Implications

This distinction is of enormous practical importance. A doctor consulting on a Yom Kippur case will almost never say categorically that the patient will die if not fed. He will say the situation may worsen, or that fasting creates risk of complications. According to the *Rosh*, that is precisely enough. The threshold is not certain death but meaningful aggravation of a dangerous situation — and that standard, as the *Rosh* emphasizes, is what reflects how medical professionals actually communicate.

---

## Bulmus Case

### Bulmus Definition

The *Mishnah* introduces a new case: *mi she-achazo bulmus* — someone seized by *bulmus*. The term is related etymologically to *bulimia* and in its medical literature refers to a compulsive eating state, but in the *Mishnah* it appears to describe something different: a condition in which a person feels a powerful, urgent need to consume food and does not stabilize until eating to a certain point. The physical sign used by the *Gemara* to measure recovery is *ya'iru einav* — "his eyes light up." Apparently the person's vision becomes clouded or unfocused, and after eating sufficiently, his eyes clear. This has led some to suggest — consistent with the Gemara's own interest in sweetness as the remedy — that the condition reflects a drop in blood sugar, similar to the hypoglycemic episodes one can observe today where a glass of orange juice rapidly revives a person who has become disoriented and vacant.

### Non-Kosher Feeding

The *Mishnah* rules: *ma'achilin oto afilu devarim teme'im* — you feed someone seized by *bulmus* even non-kosher food, until *ya'iru einav*, until his eyes light up. This generalizes the *pikuach nefesh* principle beyond Yom Kippur itself.

### Dietary Law Violation

The *Mishnah* here is no longer exclusively about Yom Kippur. The principle that danger to life overrides prohibitions is extended to the violation of dietary laws in any context where someone's life is at risk. The case of *bulmus* thus serves as a transition: from Yom Kippur, to *treifus*, and eventually to *Shabbat* — each expanded in turn.

---

## Folk Remedies Debate

### Rabid Dog Case

The *Mishnah* then presents the case of *mi she-neshacho kelev shoteh* — someone bitten by a rabid dog. The classic folk remedy was to feed the patient a section of the dog's liver (*chatzer kaved shelo*). The first opinion in the *Mishnah* rules that you do not feed it to him, because it is non-kosher and it is not a medically legitimate treatment — it is merely a folk remedy. The implication is that the rabbis are empowered, and indeed obligated, to assess whether a proposed treatment constitutes real medicine or mere superstition. Only genuine medical necessity justifies violating a prohibition.

### Rabbi Authority

This raises a pointed question about the rabbi's role in *halachic* decision-making: is it the rabbi's place to rule that a given treatment is *narishkeit* and therefore cannot justify a prohibition? The tension is real. On the one hand, the *Gemara* itself contains numerous remedies that from a modern perspective would appear equally fanciful. On the other hand, someone has to make a determination, and if rabbis defer entirely to any claimed medical benefit, the protections of *issur* erode.

### Scorpion Remedy

This question has direct contemporary application. A student who suffered from Bell's palsy — partial facial paralysis — had tried conventional treatments without success and was advised by a holistic practitioner to brew a tea using desiccated scorpion: hot water run through a teabag containing the desiccated insect, producing what amounts to a *ta'am ke'ikar* of scorpion. He asked whether he could drink it. The question involved *treif* status, issues of *bitul*, *nosein ta'am lifgam*, and whether the extreme bitterness of the remedy (requiring large amounts of sugar and honey to make it palatable) affected the ruling. After consulting with colleagues, the conclusion was that the halachic obstacles were surmountable — but the broader question of whether the rabbi should have simply dismissed the remedy as *narishkeit* remained uncomfortable. When Rav Yehuda Herzl Henkin was consulted and asked what kind of remedy this was, the response was skeptical — but the challenge remained: who are we to adjudicate what counts as effective medicine, given the *Gemara*'s own pharmacopoeia?

### Avoiding Narishkeit

The underlying question is whether a rabbi should refuse to engage with a question on the grounds that the underlying premise — this treatment has medical validity — is implausible. The *Gemara* itself seems to treat this as a substantive question on which *tannaim* could disagree, with the first opinion in the *Mishnah* essentially ruling that the liver-of-the-dog remedy does not qualify as medicine and therefore cannot override the prohibition.

### Rabbi Mattia

Rabbi Mattia ben Charash permits feeding the dog's liver to someone who was bitten. His permissive position reflects a broader leniency: where there is any plausible medical rationale, the prohibition can be set aside for *pikuach nefesh*.

### Throat Concern

Rabbi Mattia ben Charash adds a further ruling: *hachoshesh bigrono matilin lo sam betoch piv beShabbat* — if someone has a throat ailment, you may administer medicine into his mouth on *Shabbat*, because *safeik nefashos* overrides *Shabbat*. He generalizes: any concern involving the throat is treated as a potential *pikuach nefesh*. What is notable about this ruling is its placement — it reads almost like a general introductory principle that should have opened the entire discussion, but appears here embedded within Rabbi Mattia's specific legal positions.

---

## Collapsed Building

### Triple Safeik

The *Mishnah* now introduces the well-known case of the collapsed building: *mi she-nafla alav mapoles* — someone upon whom a building has fallen. The *Mishnah* stacks three separate doubts: *safeik hu sham safeik eino sham* — perhaps the person was not even in the building when it collapsed; *safeik chai safeik meit* — perhaps he was there but has already died; *safeik Goy safeik Yisrael* — perhaps the person, even if alive, is not Jewish, which raises the separate question of whether *Shabbat* is overridden to save a non-Jew's life. Each doubt individually could argue against desecrating *Shabbat*; together, they form a *safeik safeik safeika*. Yet the *Mishnah* rules: *mefakchin alav es hagal* — you uncover the rubble.

### Safeik Safeik

The *chidush* is that even a compound series of doubts does not prevent rescue. The principle of *safeik nefashos l'hakel* — when there is any doubt about life, you are lenient — operates even through multiple layers of uncertainty. The *Mishnah* does not permit waiting to resolve each doubt in sequence.

### Alive vs. Dead

If when the rubble is cleared the person is found alive, you continue the work of rescue even though it means continued *Shabbat* violation. If he is found dead, you stop and leave the remaining rubble until after *Shabbat*. This is the straightforward application of the principle.

### Determining Death

The *chidush* that requires most attention is how death is determined. The *Gemara* makes clear that the standard for confirming death is the absence of breath and responsiveness — the cessation of vital function — and this determination must be made carefully before ceasing rescue efforts.

---

## Hierarchy of Violations

### Bulmus Feeding

The *Mishnah* adds that when someone is seized by *bulmus* and must be fed, one does not simply reach for whatever food is available. A new principle operates: *ma'achilim oto hakal hakal* — you feed him with the lesser prohibition first.

### Tevel vs. Nevelah

If the choice is between *tevel* — grain from which *terumot u'ma'asrot* have not been separated — and *nevelah* — an animal that was not slaughtered through proper *shechitah*, you give him the *nevelah*. Although both are forbidden, *nevelah* carries only a *lav*, a negative prohibition, while *tevel* carries the penalty of *chayav mitah bidei shamayim*, death at the hands of Heaven.

### Tevel vs. Shvi'it

If the choice is between *tevel* and *shvi'it* produce — sabbatical-year food that is past the point at which it should have been destroyed — you give him the *shvi'it* produce. The obligation to destroy *shvi'it* produce after its time is a *mitzvat aseh*, a positive commandment, which is less severe than the *lo ta'aseh* of consuming *tevel*.

### Tevel vs. Terumah Debate

The more complex case is *tevel* versus *terumah*. Both carry the penalty of *mitah bidei shamayim*, so neither is obviously lighter than the other. This is the subject of a *tannaitic* dispute. The first opinion says you feed him *tevel* rather than *terumah*. Ben Teima says the opposite — you feed him *terumah* rather than *tevel*.

### Rava's Distinction

Rava clarifies the terms of the debate. If it is possible to separate *terumah* from the grain and feed him the remaining *chulin*, everyone agrees you do that — you take the small portion as *terumah* and give him the bulk as fully permitted food. The dispute applies only where separation is insufficient: where the patient needs the full quantity including what would become *terumah* and *terumat ma'aser*, so that he must eat some portion that is categorically forbidden. In that case, one opinion holds *tevel chamur* — *tevel* is the more severe prohibition — so better to give him *terumah*, which at least is permitted to a *kohen* and thus not absolutely *treif* in all circumstances. The other opinion holds *terumah chamurah* — *terumah* is more severe — because *tevel* can theoretically be rectified: *tevel efshar letakunei*, the status of *tevel* is not permanent, it can be fixed by separation, and therefore it is not treated as fully realized *issur*. On this view, *tevel* is technically the lesser violation.

### Avoiding Slippage

The *Gemara* then raises a question about the case where separation is possible and the prohibition being avoided is only rabbinic. Specifically, what if the *tevel* grew in a sealed flower pot (*atzitz she'eino nakuv*) — disconnected from the ground — making the *tevel* status only rabbinic? Now you have a choice between two *derabanan* violations: feed him rabbinically forbidden *tevel*, or separate *terumah* on *Shabbat* (which is a rabbinic prohibition) and feed him fully permitted food. Which is preferable?

The answer is that it is better to violate the rabbinic *Shabbat* restriction by separating *terumah* than to feed him the rabbinically forbidden food. The reason, as the *Gemara* develops it elsewhere in a related discussion, is not merely about the visceral sense that ingesting forbidden food is particularly serious — though that intuition exists — but about slippage. If one permits eating rabbinic *tevel*, a person may come to permit eating biblical *tevel*; the two categories are easily confused. By contrast, performing the rabbinic act of separating *terumah* on *Shabbat* does not generate the same risk of slippage into violating a biblical *melachah*. The principle therefore is: prefer the *derabanan* violation that does not risk confusion with a *de'oraita*, over the *derabanan* that does.

---

## Snake Bite Remedies

### Multiple Violations

The *Gemara* introduces a *beraita* about someone who has been bitten by a snake: *korin lo rofe mimakom lemakom* — you summon a doctor even from a distant place, involving *Shabbat* travel; *umekarin lo et hatarnegolet* — you tear open a chicken and apply it to the wound, a traditional remedy for snake bites; *uvegozezin lo et hakreishin* — and you harvest cress, apparently another remedy used for snakebites, even though harvesting on *Shabbat* is a *melachah*. All of these are permitted *Shabbat* violations for *pikuach nefesh*.

### Terumot Dispute

The *beraita* then records a dispute about *terumot u'ma'asrot*. The view attributed to *Rabbi* (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) is *ve'ein tzarikh le'aser* — you do not need to take *terumot u'ma'asrot* from the cress before feeding it to the patient. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon says *lo yokhal ad sheye'aser* — he may not eat it until *terumot u'ma'asrot* are separated. This maps onto the broader debate: is it better to feed the patient *tevel* (even rabbinic *tevel*) or to perform the rabbinic act of separation on *Shabbat* and feed him *chulin*?

### Vegetable vs. Grain

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent conflict between these positions and the analysis of Rava. *Rabbi*'s leniency about not separating applies specifically to vegetable cress, for which the obligation of *terumot u'ma'asrot* is only rabbinic (*ma'asar yerek derabanan*). In that case, feeding him without separation is permissible because eating rabbinic *tevel* of a vegetable will not lead anyone to confuse it with the biblical *tevel* of grain. The slippage risk is minimal. But when it comes to grain — even grain that grew in a sealed flower pot and is therefore only rabbinically *tevel* — the categories are more easily confused with biblical *tevel* of grain (*atzitz she'eino nakuv ati lemikhal be'atzitz shehu nakuv*), so in that case even *Rabbi* would agree that it is better to separate on *Shabbat* and avoid feeding the rabbinically prohibited grain altogether.

---

## Sweetness Remedies

### Honey Efficacy

The *Gemara* continues with the physiology of *bulmus* recovery. A *beraita* states: *ma'achilim oto dvash ve'chol minei metika* — you feed someone seized by *bulmus* honey and all sweet things, *she'hadvash ve'chol minei metika me'irin maor einav shel adam* — because honey and sweet things light up a person's eyes. This is strikingly consistent with the blood sugar hypothesis: what restores a hypoglycemic person is precisely a rapid infusion of sugar.

### Honey Timing

Abaye adds an important qualification: *lo shanu ela achar achila* — this is effective only after eating, meaning when there is already food in the stomach. *Aval kodem achila dvash al keiva reika migrar garir* — but honey on an empty stomach does not satisfy; it actually stimulates the appetite further and draws out the craving. This is medically interesting: rapid sugar on a completely empty stomach may cause a spike and subsequent crash, rather than stabilization.

### Egyptian Servant

The *Gemara* offers scriptural support from the story of the Egyptian servant found in the field (*Shmuel I* 30). He had not eaten or drunk for three days. David's men gave him bread and water first, and only afterward gave him *pelach devela* — a portion of pressed figs — and two raisins. The sweet foods came after the bread, demonstrating that sweets restore after food is already in the system, not before. The *Gemara* notes that *Yehonatan*'s famous episode with the honey (*Shmuel I* 14) does not constitute a proof for *bulmus* specifically, since Yehonatan was fasting, not in a state of *bulmus* — the honey revived him from the fast, but one cannot draw from that case to the distinct condition described in the *Mishnah*.

### Various Remedies

Rav Nachman citing Shmuel adds: *mi she-achazo bulmus ma'achilim oto alya bi'dvash* — fatty meat, specifically fat-tail, dipped in honey. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says that fine flour with honey is also effective — not only fat but carbohydrates combined with sweetness. Rav Papa extends it further: even barley flour with honey will do. The range of remedies emphasizes that what matters is the combination of caloric density and sweetness.

### Rabbi Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan recounts a personal experience: *pa'am achas achzani bulmus* — once I was seized by *bulmus*, and he ran to the east side of a fig tree and ate figs from that side. The reason, as elaborated by Rav Yosef, is that figs on the eastern side of the tree, exposed most directly to the sun, are sweetest — the sun draws out the sugars (*mimachar tvu'os shamesh*, "from the sweetness of the sun's yield"). Rabbi Yochanan adds that in doing this he fulfilled for himself the verse *ha'chochmah techayeh ba'aleha* — wisdom gives life to those who possess it — since his knowledge guided him in a moment of potential *pikuach nefesh*.

---

## Rabbinic Stories

### Shepherd Bread

The *Gemara* tells of Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei traveling together. Rav Yehuda was seized by *bulmus* and compelled a shepherd they encountered, taking away all his bread in order to eat and recover. Rabbi Yosei rebuked him: *kapachita es ha'ro'eh* — you forcibly took the shepherd's food.

### Rabbi Yosei

Not long afterward, *ki matu le'masa* — when they arrived at a city — it was Rabbi Yosei who was seized by *bulmus*. The people of the city surrounded him with food and drink until he recovered, pressing all of it upon him. Rav Yehuda then said: *ani kapachti es ha'ro'eh echad* — I forced only one shepherd. *Ve'ata kapachta es ha'ir kulah* — you compelled the entire city.

### Three Tannaim

The *Gemara* then transitions to one of the *daf*'s most memorable stories. Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei were traveling together. Rabbi Meir was in the practice of *diyuk bishma* — attending carefully to people's names as indicators of character — while Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei did not follow this practice.

### Names Character

When the three arrived at an inn and asked the innkeeper his name, he replied: *Kidor*. Rabbi Meir immediately concluded: *shma mina adam rasha hu* — this is obviously a wicked man — for the verse says *ki dor tahapuchot hema*, "they are a generation of perversity," and the name Kidor echoes *ki dor*. Acting on this suspicion, Rabbi Meir refused to leave his wallet with the innkeeper. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, dismissing this as overwrought, entrusted their wallets to him for *Shabbat*.

### Lentil Evidence

Rabbi Meir took his wallet and hid it at the grave of the innkeeper's father. That night, the innkeeper's father appeared to him in a dream telling him to retrieve the wallet resting on his head. The next morning the innkeeper reported the dream to the rabbis, but they told him *chelma d'vei shimshi leit behu mamasha* — dreams on *Shabbat* have no substance — and he was deterred. Rabbi Meir, knowing that the innkeeper now knew the wallet's location, went to the grave and stood watch over it the entire *Shabbat*. After *Shabbat* he retrieved it.

When the rabbis then asked the innkeeper to return their wallets, he claimed no knowledge of them — and they had no recourse. Rabbi Meir asked them: *amai lo dayekitu bishma* — why did you not pay attention to his name? They replied: why did you not warn us? He answered: *eimar d'amri ana chashasha, achzuki mi amina* — I expressed a concern, not a certainty; I could not say he was definitively wicked, only that suspicion was warranted.

### Moral Teaching

Determined to recover the wallets, the rabbis took the innkeeper into a shop and observed *tachlei asfamei* — lentils remaining in his mustache from that morning's meal. They went to his wife and said her husband had sent them to collect the wallets, offering as proof the detail that he had eaten lentils that morning. The wife, convinced by this knowledge that only her husband could have shared, returned the wallets. When the innkeeper came home and discovered what had happened, *katlei l'itetei* — he killed his wife. The *Gemara* links this to the broader teaching: *mayim rishonim he'echilu basar chazir* — inattention to washing *mayim rishonim* caused a man to be served *chazir*; *u'mayim achronim hargu et hanefesh* — and inattention to washing *mayim acharonim* after the meal caused a death, because had the innkeeper washed properly after eating, the lentils would not have been visible, the wife would not have been deceived, and she would not have been killed.

### Final Lesson

In the aftermath, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei adopted Rabbi Meir's practice. When they subsequently came to a house whose owner's name was Bala, *lo ayilu lgabei* — they did not enter. A name evoking *v'amar l'Bala ni'ufim* — associated with promiscuity and wickedness — was sufficient warning. The lesson: pay attention to names; they can, in the right hands, reveal character — and inattention to detail, whether a name, a remnant of lentils, or the washing of one's hands, can have consequences far beyond what one imagines.

---

---

# Yoma 84

## Opening & Daf Setup

### Greeting & Calendar

A brief question opens the session: is there a *mitzvah* of *marbin b'simcha* on *Adar Rishon*, when it is not yet the "true" Adar? The question is left pleasantly unresolved.

### Daf Navigation

Today's *daf* is 84, and we pick up at the very bottom of 83b. The *Mishnah* there reads: *mishe-nashkho kelev shoteh* — someone who was bitten by a rabid dog. The *Mishnah* has moved on from Yom Kippur to the question of when one may eat non-kosher food for a health issue — and certainly when there is a risk to life. Within that framework, a debate arose concerning what constitutes a legitimate *refuah*: specifically, the practice of feeding the lobe of the liver of a rabid dog to a person who was bitten by such a dog. Matya ben Charash permits this; the *Chachamim* do not, holding that it is not a legitimate *refuah*.

## Rabid Dog Symptoms

### Mishnah Transition

The *Mishnah*'s transition from Yom Kippur to the broader category of health emergencies sets the stage for an extended *sugya* touching on medical knowledge, legitimate remedies, and the overarching principle of *pikuach nefesh*.

### Rabies Medical Facts

Rabies, as a modern medical reality, is almost invariably fatal once the disease fully develops. Historically, the number of people who actually contracted rabies and recovered is vanishingly small — essentially one confirmed case in the past several decades, where a treatment was devised in time. The critical point is that when someone is bitten by a rabid dog, what matters halachically and medically is that treatment must begin *before* the rabies develops. In the contemporary context, that means a vaccine — a series of injections administered promptly after exposure — which prevents the virus from taking hold. The shots are not pleasant, and must be given within a specific window of time.

### Five Rabid Dog Signs

The *Gemara* introduces a *Baraita*: *Tanu Rabanan, chamishah devarim ne'emru b'kelev shoteh* — five identifying signs were stated regarding a rabid dog. Its mouth is open (*pee patuach*); its spittle drips (*v'riro notef*); its ears droop (*v'oznav srukhot*); its tail hangs between its thighs (*v'znavo munach al yarkhotav*); and it walks at the sides of roads rather than the middle (*v'mehalech b'tzidei drakhim*). Some add a sixth: it barks, but its bark cannot be heard — a silent bark (*v'yesh omrim af noveach v'ein kolo nishmah*).

### Cause of Rabies

The *Gemara* then asks: *mimai havei* — what causes a dog to become rabid? Rav says: women who practice witchcraft (*nashim kashfaniyot mesakhakot bo*) — they use the dog to demonstrate or experiment with their spells. Shmuel says: an evil spirit (*ruach ra'ah*) seizes the dog.

### Witchcraft vs Spirit

The *Gemara* asks: *mai beiniyu* — what practical difference does it make? The answer, at the top of 84a, is *l'miktelei b'davar hanizrak* — whether one must kill the dog from a distance, by projectile. If the cause is a *ruach ra'ah*, then even coming close to the dog — without being bitten — poses a danger, because the evil spirit may transfer. If the cause is witchcraft, there is apparently no such contagion from proximity alone; one could approach without that additional risk. The *baraita* rules in accordance with Shmuel: *keshe-horgo ein horgo ela b'davar hanizrak* — when killing the dog, one must do so only by means of a thrown projectile.

### Safety Protocols

This ruling brings to mind a reading of the *pasuk* in Parshat Yitro: *skol yisakel o yaroh yiyareh* — Rashi interprets *yaroh yiyareh* as casting a person off a cliff, consistent with the *halachic* procedure of *skilah*. But the plain sense of the verse is a practical instruction: if someone approaches Har Sinai unlawfully, you cannot go close to stop him, so you throw stones or shoot arrows. The parallel to the rabid dog is striking — in both cases, the danger of proximity necessitates acting from a distance.

The *Gemara* then states: *d'chaif bei mistaken* — if you rub up against the rabid dog, you are in danger; *d'nachit lei mayis* — if it bites you, you will die. If contact does occur, the instruction is: *nishlach manei v'nirat* — cast off your clothes and run.

## Rabid Dog Treatment

### Killing Method

The *Gemara* confirms the ruling of Shmuel through a *baraita*: when killing a rabid dog, one does so exclusively by thrown projectile (*b'davar hanizrak*), not by approaching it directly. This may even apply under certain circumstances on Shabbat or Yom Kippur, though that specific question — related to a *sugya* in Shabbat about whether *mazikin* that are not actively pursuing you require concern — is not the focus here.

### Clothes Removal

If one has rubbed up against the rabid dog, the *Gemara* instructs: cast off your clothes immediately and run. The reasoning appears to be that the contagion — or the *ruach ra'ah* — adheres to the clothing, so removing the garments and fleeing cuts off the danger.

### Rav Huna Story

The *Gemara* illustrates this with a story: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua once rubbed up against a rabid dog in the marketplace. He immediately cast off his clothes and ran. He then said: *kiyamti b'atzmi* — I fulfilled in myself the verse, *hachochma techaye v'aleha* — wisdom will keep its owners alive (Kohelet 7:12). Just as we learned earlier that knowing to seek sweet figs could save someone seized by *bulmos*, here too practical wisdom — knowing exactly what to do when a rabid dog makes contact — was what preserved him.

### Hyena Leather Remedy

If the dog actually bites someone, the *Gemara* asks: *mai taknatei* — what is the remedy? Abaye provides an elaborate prescription. One should obtain the leather of a male hyena (*mashka d'apa d'dichra*) and write upon it an incantation: *ana Planya bar Planisa* — I, so-and-so, son of [one's mother's name] — *amashka d'apa dichra ksivna alach* — on the leather of a male hyena I am writing upon you. This is followed by the words *kanti kanti kliros*, or according to some versions, *kandi kandi kloros*, and then: *Ya Ya Hashem Tzeva'ot, Amen Amen Sela*.

After writing this incantation on the hyena leather, one casts off one's clothes, and buries everything (*v'likbrinhu*) in a cemetery — some versions specify at a crossroads. This remains buried for twelve months. At the end of the twelve months, one digs up the clothes, burns them in an oven (*v'naklinhu b'tanura*), and scatters the ashes at a crossroads (*aparsat drachim*). That apparently concludes the *refuah*.

### Twelve-Month Protection

During those twelve months of waiting, the person remains in a state of danger. What precaution must be taken? *Ki shati maya lo lishti ela b'guvta d'nachsha* — when drinking water, one should drink only through a copper tube. The reason: *dilma chazi bavuah d'shida* — lest one see the image of a demon in the water vessel, and come to danger. This protection appears to follow Shmuel's view that the cause of the dog's rabid state is a *ruach ra'ah*, since the concern here is also demonic in nature. There are well-known *aggadot* at the beginning of Berachot that deal similarly with perceiving *mazikin* and *shedim*, and with various types of metal vessels as protection.

### Golden Tube Story

The *Gemara* adds: *ki ha d'Abba bar Marta d'hu Abba bar Minyumi* — just as in the case of Abba bar Marta, who is Abba bar Minyumi: his mother made for him a golden tube through which to drink. Whether this was specifically in response to a rabid dog bite or more generally as protection against *shedim* is unclear, but the *Gemara* cites it as a parallel illustration of the principle.

## Remedy Legitimacy

### Matya's Positions

The *Gemara* now turns to the broader halachic question raised by these discussions. If *pikuach nefesh* permits one to violate Shabbat, Yom Kippur, and *kashrus*, who determines what counts as a legitimate *refuah*? Matya ben Charash articulates positions on three remedies: feeding the lobe of the liver of the rabid dog, a treatment for a throat ailment, and something related to jaundice.

### Sages' Objection

The *Chachamim* object. Their formulation — *b'elu ein bahem mishum refuah* — is that certain of these remedies are not genuine therapeutic interventions. Notably, the debate seems not to be about whether the underlying illnesses are serious, but about whether the proposed treatments are actually efficacious. This raises the sharper question: to what degree does *halacha* get to weigh in on whether a *refuah* is real?

### Medical Authority

This is a striking tension. We learned earlier in the *sugya* that if a *choleh* says he needs to eat and doctors say he does not, the *choleh*'s own assessment takes precedence. Here, however, when the *choleh* says he wants to use a certain *refuah* and the *Chachamim* say it is not a genuine remedy — there appears to be room to overrule the patient. The implication is that a claim of *pikuach nefesh* cannot automatically license any claimed *refuah*; the *refuah* itself must be assessed.

This has obvious contemporary resonance. In an era of holistic medicine and alternative treatments, what is a rabbi's role in saying that a given *refuah* is not legitimate? The question remains genuinely open.

### Rambam vs Geonim

There are two major scholarly frameworks for dealing with the *Gemara*'s medical recommendations more broadly. The Rambam takes the straightforward position: the rabbis were not scientists; they knew the science of their time, and one cannot expect their medical advice — or their astronomical knowledge — to transcend the limits of what was known in their era. If we know better now, we follow current knowledge, and this requires no apology. This is the intellectually honest position, though it raises a concern for some: if we say that *Chazal* could be mistaken about scientific matters, does that open the door to questioning their reliability more broadly?

The *frummer* approach is the one associated with the *Geonim*: rather than saying the rabbis got anything wrong, one says that nature has changed — *nishtanu ha-teva*. The world is different from what it was. This formulation allows one to accept that a given remedy no longer works without conceding rabbinic error. It is a protective move, keeping the honor of *Chazal* intact while acknowledging empirical reality.

Both positions have distinguished adherents. The Rambam's view is arguably more rigorous, while the *Geonim*'s formulation is more sociologically cautious. The observation that scientists today also get things wrong, while true, does not fully resolve the underlying tension — for many people, placing the rabbis within the category of "humans limited by the knowledge of their time" feels theologically fraught.

## Yochanan Scurvy Case

### Illness & Medicine

The *Gemara* now relates: *Rabbi Yochanan chash bitzapidna* — Rabbi Yochanan had *tzapidna*, which appears to be what we call scurvy, a disease associated with vitamin C deficiency and characterized, as the *Gemara* will shortly make clear, by bleeding gums that can progress to involve the throat and inner intestines. Rabbi Yochanan went to a *matronisa* — a non-Jewish woman of standing, apparently a herbalist or physician of sorts — who prepared a medicine for him on Thursday and Friday. Several recipes are later attributed to this treatment: one tradition attributes it to Rav Acha the son of Rav Ami, who says it consisted of *mei se'or* (yeast water), olive oil, and salt; Rav Yeimar says not the water from dough but the actual dough itself combined with olive oil and salt; Rav Ashi says it was the fat from the wing of a goose (*mishcha d'gadpa d'avaza*). Abaye adds that he personally tried all of those remedies and none healed him — until an Arab told him to take incompletely ripened olive pits, burn them on a new shovel, and apply the resulting paste directly to the gums. That, Abaye says, actually worked.

### Oath Dilemma

Rabbi Yochanan, having received two days of treatment, asked the *matronisa*: what should he do on Shabbat, when he cannot travel to her? She replied that he would not need further treatment. He pressed: but what if he does? She was unwilling to divulge her formula — the remedy was her professional secret. She said: *ishtaba li d'lo maglis* — take an oath to me that you will not reveal this. He took an oath: *ishtaba leh l'elaha d'yisrael lo maglina* — by the God of Israel, I will not reveal it.

He then went to the public lecture that Shabbat and, rather than giving his regular *drashah* on the *parashah*, he disclosed the entire remedy to the community.

### Oath Solution

The *Gemara* asks: *v'ha ishtaba lah* — but did he not take an oath? How could he publicly reveal the remedy? The *Gemara* resolves this with a deft reading: *l'elaha d'yisrael lo maglina ha l'ama d'yisrael maglina* — his oath said he would not reveal it *to* the God of Israel; he revealed it *to* the people of Israel. He had constructed the wording of his oath in a way that afforded him this exit.

### Chilul Hashem

But the *Gemara* objects: *v'ika chillul Hashem* — even if technically he did not violate his oath, he is creating a *chillul Hashem*. From the outside, it looks to non-Jews as though he swore by God and then betrayed that oath anyway — both that he deceived the *matronisa* and that he does not respect the sanctity of an oath taken in God's name. This is *chillul Hashem* in the precise sense: God's name was invoked in an oath, and the appearance is that the oath was broken.

The *Gemara* resolves this: *d'magli lah mei-ikara* — after she disclosed the remedy and before he revealed it publicly, he explained to her exactly what his oath had meant. She therefore did not believe he violated the oath. Whether she believed instead that she had been cleverly maneuvered into disclosing a trade secret is another matter — the *Gemara* acknowledges this is a different kind of *chillul Hashem*, one of a lesser or different category. The story is, as noted, fascinating and somewhat unsettling. It raises questions that parallel modern debates about whistleblowing and the disclosure of classified information for the public good — how far one may go, and what costs one may impose on others, for the sake of communal welfare.

According to Artscroll, some *Amoraim* say the *matronisa* was so distressed that her exclusive remedy was now freely available that she took her own life; others say she converted to Judaism, having been so impressed that Rabbi Yochanan shared the cure without charging for it.

## Scurvy Treatments

### Remedy Options

As noted above, the *Gemara* records three competing traditions about what the *matronisa*'s medicine actually consisted of: Rav Acha the son of Rav Ami specifies yeast water, olive oil, and salt; Rav Yeimar specifies the dough itself (rather than the water runoff) combined with olive oil and salt; Rav Ashi specifies the fat of a goose wing. None of these obviously addresses a vitamin C deficiency.

### Olive Pit Cure

Abaye testifies in the first person: he tried all of these remedies without success, until an Arab advised him to take incompletely ripened olive pits — *kashyata d'zeita d'lo malu tilta* — burn them on a new shovel, apply the resulting substance to the gums (*b'kakei d'dari*), and that cured him.

### Scurvy Causes

The *Gemara* also identifies the causes of *tzapidna*: eating overly hot wheaten bread (*mechamimi chamimi d'cheiti*) and consuming leftover fish hash (*mishiyurei kasa d'harsana*). Whether this *tzapidna* corresponds precisely to what we call scurvy remains uncertain — the identification is based on the symptom pattern described.

### Scurvy Symptoms

The symptom the *Gemara* identifies is: *kad rami midi b'kakei v'ata dama* — when you put something between your teeth and blood comes out. Bleeding gums is the presenting sign. As the *Gemara* will now clarify, however, this is only the beginning — the disease progresses from the gums downward.

## Throat & Life Risk

### Scurvy Progression

The *Gemara* establishes that *tzapidna* is not merely a localized oral condition: *ho'il u-maschil b'peh v'gomer bivnei me'ayim* — it begins in the mouth and ends in the inner intestines. This progression through the throat and into the internal organs is what makes it potentially life-threatening.

### Throat Legitimacy

Rav Chiya bar Abba raises a question to Rabbi Yochanan: when Rabbi Yochanan violated Shabbat to treat his *tzapidna*, was he acting in accordance with Rabbi Matya ben Charash — *k'Rabbi Masya ben Charash* — who holds that a throat ailment permits taking medicine on Shabbat? If so, is that not a position disputed by the *Chachamim*? How could Rabbi Yochanan simply rely on it?

### Debate Resolution

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *shani omer d'zu v'lo acheres* — I say that the rabbis argue with Matya ben Charash on only one of his positions, not the other. Matya ben Charash made two claims: one regarding the liver of the rabid dog, and one regarding the throat. The *Chachamim* dispute only the rabid dog case; on the throat, they actually agree. Rabbi Yochanan's conduct on Shabbat was therefore not controversial — the treatment of a throat ailment that progresses internally is something all agree constitutes *pikuach nefesh*.

This also illuminates an important general principle: what kinds of illness does *halacha* recognize as potentially *pikuach nefesh*? While the primary answer is to follow the assessment of doctors, the *Gemara* also provides its own parameters. One of those parameters is that anything from the gums inward — any condition that begins in the mouth and can progress into the body — is treated as potentially life-threatening. This is an important category in *pikuach nefesh* analysis.

There is also the separate question of the rabbinic prohibition on taking medicine on Shabbat for minor ailments. The *Gemara* grounds this prohibition in a concern that one might come to grind medicines. The result is a taxonomy: *pikuach nefesh* overrides all prohibitions, including biblical ones; *choleh kol gufo* — a person whose whole body is ill, or who is severely affected even by a localized condition — permits rabbinic violations including *amira l'akum* and in many views even direct *d'Rabbanan* violations; the category of *mishush b'alma* — a minor, localized irritation — is where the prohibition on taking medicine applies. Many *poskim*, however, interpret *mishush b'alma* extremely narrowly and are prepared to classify most genuine illness within the *choleh kol gufo* category. A famous formulation attributed to Rav Soloveitchik captures this: if you truly need the medicine, you are a *choleh kol gufo* and it is permitted; if you do not truly need it, then it is not really medicine, and it is also permitted.

### Baraita Evidence

The *Gemara* seeks to identify more precisely which remedy the *Chachamim* concede to Matya ben Charash. It introduces a *baraita*: Rav bar Shmuel taught — *ubarah she-hericha ma'achilin otah ad she-tashuv nafshah* — a pregnant woman who smells food and craves it is fed until she is settled; *mi she-nashacho kelev shoteh ma'achilin oto mechatzar keved shelo* — someone bitten by a rabid dog is fed the lobe of the liver; *v'ha-choshesh b'piv matilin lo sam b'Shabbat* — and for a throat ailment, medicine is administered on Shabbat. This is the position of Matya ben Charash. And the *Chachamim* say: *b'zo v'lo b'acheret* — in this one, and not in the other.

The *Gemara* asks: *b'zu a-hei* — which case are they conceding? Surely not the pregnant woman — that one is obvious and requires no special concession. And we know they dispute the rabid dog. Therefore, *ela lav a-sam* — it must be that they are conceding the medicine for the throat ailment. *Shema mina* — this supports the reading that the *Chachamim* agree regarding the throat.

## Throat & Life Risk (II)

### Mishnah Structure

Rav Ashi adds a proof from the structure of our own *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* first records the debate between Matya ben Charash and the *Chachamim* regarding the rabid dog's liver. It then adds: *v'od amar Rav Matya ben Charash* — and furthermore Matya ben Charash says — *ha-choshesh b'piv matilin lo sam b'Shabbat*. Crucially, this second statement is not followed by any dissenting opinion. Had the *Chachamim* disagreed with this as well, the *Mishnah* would have grouped both cases together and recorded a single unified dissent at the end. The fact that the debate appears only at the rabid dog stage, and that the throat statement stands alone with no rebuttal, demonstrates by implication that the *Chachamim* accept the throat ruling.

This also carries an important additional implication: it is Matya ben Charash who formulates the general principle that *safek nefashot docheh et ha-Shabbat* — any doubt of life overrides Shabbat. Since the *Chachamim* concede to his position on the throat, and that concession is bound up with his articulation of the *safek nefashot* principle, that principle now carries the weight of consensus opinion.

## Pikuach Nefesh

### Life Overrides Shabbat

The *Mishnah* states the principle: *mipnei she-safek nefashot hu* — because it involves a risk to life — *v'chol safek nefashot docheh et ha-Shabbat* — and any doubt of life overrides Shabbat. The *Gemara* asks: why is it necessary to state this explicitly? It has been assumed throughout. Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav: the statement is teaching something additional — *lo safek Shabbat zo bilvad amru ella afilu safek Shabbat acheret* — not only is the concern for this Shabbat sufficient to override it, but even concern for a future Shabbat is sufficient.

### Multi-Day Treatment

The practical case: suppose doctors determine that a patient requires treatment over eight consecutive days, and the first day is Shabbat. One might reason: let us wait until Saturday night to begin, thereby avoiding two Shabbat violations instead of one. Since there is no immediate mortal urgency — the patient is not going to die in the next few hours — perhaps delay is reasonable. The *Gemara* teaches: no. *Kamashmalan* — the teaching comes to tell us that if the person is in a *pikuach nefesh* situation, you act immediately. You do not make *cheshbonos* to push off treatment until after Shabbat, even when the urgency is not acute.

### Heated Water

A *baraita* reinforces this: *mechammin chammin l'choleh b'Shabbat* — one heats water for a sick person on Shabbat — *bein l'hashkoto* — whether to drink — *bein l'havroto* — whether to bathe him and restore his strength. And not only for this Shabbat, but for an ongoing course of treatment that extends to the next Shabbat as well.

### All Health Needs

The principle at work here is *osin kol tzorchei choleh b'Shabbat* — one performs all the health needs of the sick person on Shabbat. Once a person is in the status of *pikuach nefesh*, you do not evaluate each individual act by asking: will his life be at risk if I fail to do precisely this? You take care of all of his health needs. The question of whether the person will die if not bathed need not be posed — he is *pikuach nefesh*, and all that pertains to his care follows from that status. This is a critically important principle.

### Immediacy Rule

*V'ein mamtinim lo shema yavri* — one does not wait and say: perhaps he will recover on his own and not need us to heat the water. Rather, *ella mechammin lo miyad* — you heat it immediately. There is no hesitation, no waiting game, no calculation that perhaps the situation will resolve itself.

### No Delegation
