A second *baraita* adds that at nightfall of Yom Kippur one prays seven *brachot* and *viduy*, *ve'choteim bevidui* — and concludes with a *chatima* of *viduy*.

Rabbi Meir holds that the closing *bracha* of *ne'ila* is not the standard *mekadesh Yisrael veyom hakippurim* but rather a *chatima* centered on forgiveness — Rashi suggests the formulation *ha-Eil ha-solechan*, the forgiving God. The term *choteim bevidui* — "concludes with *viduy*" — thus encompasses both confession and the divine response of forgiveness: not a confession in the strict sense, but the affirmation of God as the One who forgives Israel. The identification between these two — the human act of confession and the divine act of forgiveness — is precisely what the entire structure of Yom Kippur prayer has been articulating throughout.

The Sages say: one prays seven *brachot* and may, if one wishes, conclude with a *chatima* of forgiveness; otherwise the standard *chatima* suffices. It is worth noting that the middle *bracha* of the Yom Kippur *Shmoneh Esrei* is unusually long by any standard, precisely because it interweaves the normal *kiddusha hayom* theme of *mekadesh Yisrael veyom hakippurim* with the character of the day as a day of forgiveness — *ki atah solechan l'Yisrael*. Such an extended *chatima* in a *bracha* is exceptional, and it reflects exactly this merger.

The Gemara's conclusion on the Shmuel question: *tiyuvta de-Shmuel tiyuvta* — the *baraita* clearly establishes that *ne'ila* is a *Shmoneh Esrei*, as Rav maintained. Ulla bar Rav led the prayer before Rabba, beginning the middle *bracha* with *Atah Vechartanu* and concluding it with *mah anu mah chayeinu* — the full thematic sweep of the *viduy* sensibility within the *bracha* itself. Rabba praised this. Rav Huna the son of Rav Natan adds that an individual says *mah anu mah chayeinu* after his *Shmoneh Esrei* rather than within it, consistent with the earlier rule about individual *viduy* being recited following the *Shmoneh Esrei*.

---

## Ne'ilah Service (II)

### Ne'ilah and Maariv

Rav rules: *tfillat Ne'ilah poteret shel Arvit* — the *ne'ila* prayer exempts one from *maariv*, since, as Rav holds, *ne'ila* is an additional *Shmoneh Esrei*, and if one has davened a *Shmoneh Esrei* at night, one is exempt from davening *maariv* again.

The Gemara asks: but did Rav not also rule that *halacha ke'divrei ha'omer tfillat arvit reshut* — *maariv* is optional? If *maariv* is optional, what does it mean to be "exempted" from it? The Gemara resolves: Rav's ruling about *ne'ila* exempting *maariv* was directed *le'divrei ha'omer chova* — toward those who hold that *maariv* is obligatory. Even for them, *ne'ila* at night suffices.

A *baraita* then raises a challenge: it lists the five *Shmoneh Esrei* services of Yom Kippur — night, *shacharit*, *mussaf*, *mincha*, and *ne'ila* — and then continues to describe *maariv* as well. So one does daven *maariv* after *ne'ila*. The Gemara concludes: *tanna'ei hi* — this is a dispute among *tannaim*.

For *maariv* after the fast, one *tanna* says to pray seven *brachot* with *Havineinu* — a summary of the eighteen *brachot* compressed into a single middle *bracha* — to spare the exhausted worshipper. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, citing his forebears, says one must daven the full eighteen. The reason: *mipnei she'tzarich lomar havdalah be'Chonein HaDa'at* — one must recite *havdalah* within the fourth *bracha* of *Shmoneh Esrei*, and that requires reciting all the *brachot* individually. The hope of a brief *Shmoneh Esrei* after breaking the fast is thus foreclosed by the need to include *havdalah*. The accepted ruling follows the second opinion: a full *Shmoneh Esrei* with *havdalah*.

### Ne'ilah Timing

The question of whether *ne'ila* is recited during the day or after nightfall is addressed obliquely through the following discussion.

### Ba'al Keri Issues

The *tanna* teaches: *kol chayevei tevilot tovlin ke'darkam be'Yom HaKippurim* — all those obligated to immerse in a *mikvah* may do so on Yom Kippur, since immersion is not a form of *ta'anug* prohibited on the fast. A *nidda* or *yoledet* may immerse on *Kol Nidrei* night. A *ba'al keri* — one who has experienced a seminal emission and was therefore subject to the *takkanah* that he may not pray until immersing — may go to the *mikvah* up until *mincha* time. Once he has davened *mincha* and then became a *ba'al keri*, there is no need to go to the *mikvah* because there is no remaining prayer service of the day.

But what about *ne'ila*? The implicit assumption is that *ne'ila* is at night, and therefore the *ba'al keri* need not go during Yom Kippur itself but can wait until nightfall. Rabbi Yosi, by contrast, says he may go to the *mikvah* the whole day — including after *mincha* — in order to be able to daven *ne'ila*. This implies that *ne'ila* is during the day. The Gemara thus finds within this dispute an implicit *machlokes* over the timing of *ne'ila*.

The Gemara then notes an apparent contradiction from a second *baraita*, in which Rabbi Yosi seems to say the *ba'al keri* may *not* go after *mincha*. The Gemara resolves: in one case he has already davened *ne'ila*, in the other he has not, and Rabbi Yosi remains consistent that *ne'ila* is during the day.

A further question arises: if according to the *rabbanan* the *ba'al keri* goes to the *mikvah* even after *ne'ila*, why — isn't he already done with *ne'ila*? The Gemara answers: *kasavri Rabbanan tevilah bizmanah mitzvah* — the *rabbanan* hold that immersing on the correct day is itself a *mitzvah*, regardless of whether there is any remaining prayer service. Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda, by contrast, holds *tevilah bizmanah* is not a *mitzvah*, and this is demonstrated from his ruling about a woman unsure of her *nidda* timing, where he says one final immersion at the end suffices without concern for the precise day. The two positions about *ba'al keri* on Yom Kippur thus map onto the broader dispute about whether *tevilah bizmanah mitzvah*.

---

## After Yom Kippur

### Maariv After Ne'ilah

As established above, the accepted *halacha* is that one davens a full *Shmoneh Esrei* for *maariv* after *ne'ila*, including *havdalah* in *Chonein HaDa'at*.

### Keri on Yom Kippur

The Gemara closes the tractate with a striking passage. *Haro'eh keri b'Yom HaKippurim* — one who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur. The *baraita* says: *yored v'tovel u'l'erev yeshafshef* — he goes and immerses, and in the evening scrubs himself to remove any *chatzitza*. The Gemara asks: *u'l'erev* — what does scrubbing in the evening accomplish after the immersion has already taken place? *Mai d'hava hava* — what is done is done. The Gemara therefore emends: *me'erev yeshafshef* — he scrubs himself on *erev Yom Kippur*, so as to be able to go properly to the *mikvah* should he become a *ba'al keri* on Yom Kippur itself. Rashi notes that the principle is general — everyone ought to scrub themselves on *erev Yom Kippur* in case they become a *ba'al keri* on Yom Kippur — a characteristically heightened consciousness of potential spiritual contingency.

Finally, the Gemara records a *tanna* teaching before Rav Nachman: *haro'eh keri b'Yom HaKippurim avonotav mechulim lo* — one who experiences a seminal emission on Yom Kippur, his sins are forgiven. This is counterintuitive in the extreme — another *baraita* says *avonotav sedurin*, his sins are laid out; meaning, he will be punished. The Gemara reconciles: *sedurin limachal* — they are laid out to be forgiven. The school of Rabbi Yishmael offers a third reading: he should be anxious the whole year, for it is a bad sign to experience sexual gratification on a day when all others are fasting and restraining. Yet if he survives the year, *muvtach lo shehu ben olam habah* — he is assured a place in the World to Come, for God had evidently wanted to give him that satisfaction on Yom Kippur as a gift. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak frames it simply: *shekol haolam kulo ra'ev v'hu saveia* — the whole world is hungry and he is satisfied. And Rav Dimi adds, citing the verse *yireh zera ya'arich yamim*, that such a person will have abundant life and many children.

It is a characteristically Talmudic ending — inverting expectations, refusing easy moral categorization, and leaving the reader with the strange irony that on the very day of *viduy* and *kappara*, the most seemingly embarrassing spiritual mishap may in fact be a concealed sign of divine favor.

*Hadran alach Yom HaKippurim — selik Masechet Yoma.*

---

---

# Sukkah 2

## Masechet Overview

### Five Chapters Intro

We begin a new *masechta* today: *Sukkah*. *Sukkah* consists of five chapters and is, for the most part, logically organized. One might expect it to open with a discussion of the *mitzvah* of sitting in a *sukkah*, but in fact it begins with the structural requirements of the *sukkah* itself, devoting the first two chapters to that subject. Toward the end of the second chapter it turns to the *mitzvah* of dwelling in a *sukkah*, and then the third chapter is devoted to *lulav* and *esrog*, with the fourth and fifth chapters taking up *Hallel* and related topics. The first three chapters are certainly the primary ones in terms of both the objects of the *mitzvah* and the *mitzvos* themselves that apply on *Sukkos*.

### Rishonim & Sources

In contrast to *Yoma*, where much of the material is no longer practically relevant, *Sukkah* is almost entirely applicable today, and as a result it attracts considerably more *Rishonim*. Beyond *Rashi* and *Tosafot*, there is a *Ritva* on *Sukkah*, as well as extensive discussions by the *Rif*, the *Ramban*, and the *Baal HaMaor*. And that is just on the first two chapters. The third chapter — on *lulav* and *esrog* — inspired entire monographs: the *Ra'avad* composed a *Hilchos Lulav*, and the *Ramban* wrote a *Hilchos Lulav v'Esrog* devoted to the laws of the four species. So there is substantially more *Rishonim* on this *masechta* than on *Yoma*, as one might expect given its ongoing practical relevance.

### Three Criteria

Let us turn now to *daf* 2a. The opening *mishna* reads:

*Sukkah she-hi gevoha lemala me'esrim ama pesula* — A *sukkah* that is higher than twenty *amos* is invalid. *Rebbi Yehuda machshir* — Rabbi Yehuda says it is valid.

*Ve-she'eina gevoha asara tefachim* — If it does not have a minimum height of ten handbreadths; *ve-she'ein la shalosh o shelosha defanos* — if it does not have three walls; *ve-she-chamasa meruba metzilasa* — and if the sunlight inside the *sukkah* is greater than the shade — *pesula*, it is invalid.

So we have three primary criteria. The first concerns height: the *sukkah* must be at least ten handbreadths tall but no more than twenty *amos* high. The second is structural: it requires a minimum of three walls. The third is functional: it must provide shade.

Conspicuously absent from this *mishna* are the horizontal dimensions — there is no mention of minimum area or of minimum length and width. Also absent is any discussion of what materials are valid for walls, or for the *sechach* itself. That absence is itself worth noting.

One point worth thinking about regarding the third criterion: when the *mishna* says that the *sukkah* is invalid if the sun is greater than the shade — is this a statement about the *sechach* itself, about its quality and density? Or is it a statement about the objective reality of being in the *sukkah* at a given moment, regardless of the *sechach*? One can imagine a *sukkah* with perfectly kosher *sechach* where, due to the angle of the sun at a particular time of day, more sunlight enters than shade is produced. Is it the quality of the *sechach* that is being assessed, or the actual state of affairs inside the *sukkah* at any given moment? These are questions the *masechta* will explore.

### Psul vs. Takanta

The *Gemara* now raises a comparative question. It notes: *tenan hasam* — we have taught elsewhere, in the very first *mishna* of *Eruvin*: *mavoi she-hu gavoah me'esrim ama yima'et* — an alleyway whose beam (*korah*) is higher than twenty *amos* must be lowered. *Rebbi Yehuda omer eino tzarich* — Rabbi Yehuda says it need not be lowered.

A brief clarification of what a *mavoi* is: it is a dead-end alleyway into which multiple courtyards open. The courtyards themselves contain houses. The *mavoi* has three walls but is open on one side toward the public domain. In order to permit carrying within the *mavoi*, it requires both a communal sharing arrangement (*shituf mevo'os*) and a structural marker at its open end — either a vertical post (*lechi*) or a horizontal beam (*korah*). This beam must be within twenty *amos* of the ground; if it is higher, it must be lowered.

The *Gemara* observes the striking parallel: both *Sukkah* and *Eruvin* open with essentially the same *mishna* and essentially the same debate — a twenty-*amos* limit that Rabbi Yehuda contests in both cases. The question the *Gemara* then presses is: *mai shna gabei sukkah detani psulah, umai shna gabei mavoi detani takanta* — how is it different by *sukkah* that the *mishna* uses the language of *invalidity* (*pesula*), while by the *mavoi* it uses the language of *repair* (*yima'et*, lower it)? Why not say "invalid" in both cases, or "fix it" in both?

### Rashi: Reality Layer

The *Gemara* answers: *sukkah de'oraisa tani psulah* — *sukkah* is a biblical obligation, so the *mishna* says "invalid." *Mavoi derabbanan tani takanta* — the *mavoi* is rabbinic, so the *mishna* says "fix it." But what is the logic behind that distinction? Why should the biblical or rabbinic character of the law affect which language is used?

*Rashi* offers a profound explanation. He writes: *de'esrim ama hilchesa gmiri lah mide'oraisa ve-kodem she-nishnes ha-mishna ne'emar shiur mi-Sinai* — the twenty-*amos* measure is a tradition received from Sinai as a matter of biblical law. The *mishna*, therefore, is not legislating; it is *reporting an objective fact*. The *sukkah* that exceeds twenty *amos* is, from the perspective of the *Torah*, simply and objectively invalid. The *mishna* uses the language *pesula* because it is describing an objective metaphysical reality: in the *Torah*'s framework, that structure is not a *sukkah*.

The *mavoi*, by contrast, is a rabbinic creation from beginning to end. Biblically, three walls are sufficient for a domain, and no *korah* is required at all. The rabbis decided to require it, and the rabbis decided it must be within twenty *amos*. When the rabbis are themselves the legislators, they cannot say "invalid" in the same categorical way, because there is no pre-existing objective reality they are reporting. They are the ones who instituted the requirement, and what they can say is: "We want it fixed." As *Rashi* puts it, *delo shayach le-misni bei lashon psulah de-man paslah* — who invalidated it before this *mishna* was taught? It was not invalid before the rabbis said so. The *mishna* on the *mavoi* is the very inauguration of that requirement. So it says: lower it. It cannot declare something invalid when it is the first word on the matter.

This is a striking idea. It evokes a kind of *halakhic* realism — a platonic structure in which the *Torah*'s laws correspond to objective *halakhic* realities that exist independently. The *mishna* on *sukkah* is not creating the invalidation; it is discovering and reporting it. The *mishna* on *mavoi*, by contrast, is the creative act itself. It would be odd to call a thing invalid at the very moment one is first calling it into existence.

One might ask whether this distinction carries through consistently — does the *Gemara* always use the language of invalidity for biblical laws and the language of correction for rabbinic ones? The honest answer is no. Neither *Rashi*'s explanation nor *Tosafot*'s is universally applied across the *Talmud*. This is the explanation for this specific context.

### Tosafot: Brevity

*Tosafot* offers two quite different explanations for the same phenomenon.

The first is pragmatic. When a *mishna* says "invalid," there is no ambiguity — it is invalid in all circumstances, even after the fact (*bedi'eved*). One cannot rationalize: "Well, perhaps in practice it is acceptable." But if the *mishna* says "lower it" — *yima'et*, fix it — one might reason: "The *mishna* told me to fix it, but since I did not get around to it, perhaps it is still acceptable after the fact." That potential for misinterpretation is a real risk. When the law is biblical, the *mishna* will not risk that misreading; it uses the unambiguous language of invalidity. When the law is rabbinic, the *mishna* can afford to risk the misinterpretation, because the practical guidance offered by "lower it" — telling the person how to address the situation — is worth something.

The second explanation is stylistic conciseness. The *Gemara* states: *sukkah she-nafishi mileiah tani pasul* — the *sukkah* *mishna* has many parameters to enumerate. It would have to say: if it is too high, lower it; if it is too low, raise it; if the *sechach* is insufficient, add more; if there are too few walls, add more walls. The whole list. Rather than spell out remedies for each problem, the *mishna* simply says *pesula* — invalid — covering everything in one word. *Mavoi de-lo nafishi mileiah tani takanta* — the *mavoi* case in this *mishna* addresses only one scenario (height). There it is possible to say concisely: lower it. This follows the general principle articulated at the opening *sugya* of *Pesachim* that one should always teach in brief.

There is also an interesting structural observation worth making here. Many *masechtos* open with what, based on a letter of Rav Sherira Gaon, scholars identify as *Savoraic* material — that is, text added in the period immediately after the *Gemara*'s final redaction, though the point applies to the opening of a *masechta* more broadly. Such openings characteristically contain no named statements by *Tannaim* or *Amoraim*; they are *stam*, anonymous. They tend to focus on comparative analysis of *mishnayos*, playing with parallels and linguistic distinctions, rather than advancing new *halakhic* rulings. The opening of *Kiddushin*, for example, spends considerable time on why the *mishna* uses the passive form *nikneit* rather than the language of *kiddushin*, and why it speaks from the woman's perspective rather than the man's. Such openings often serve a pedagogical function: easing the student in while also introducing themes that will recur throughout the *masechta*. Here, the parallel between *sukkah* and *mavoi* — both with the same twenty-*amos* limit, both with Rabbi Yehuda disagreeing — is not merely a curiosity. It raises a question that will resonate throughout the *masechta*: is there a single shared source underlying both requirements and both debates?

## 20-Amah Sources

### Rava: Awareness

*Mina hani mili* — where do these laws come from? The *Gemara* now turns to the biblical and conceptual foundations of the twenty-*amos* requirement.

*Amar Rava de'amar kra* — Rava says, the verse states: *lema'an yedu doroseichem ki ba-sukkos hoshavti es bnei Yisrael* — "in order that your generations should know that I caused the children of Israel to dwell in booths." *Ad esrim ama adam yodeia she-hu dar ba-sukkah* — up to twenty *amos*, a person is aware that he is dwelling in a *sukkah*. *Lema'ala me-esrim ama ein adam yodeia she-hu dar ba-sukkah* — higher than twenty *amos*, a person is not aware that he is dwelling in a *sukkah*. Why? *Mishum de-lo shalta bei eina* — because the eye does not take it in.

This requires a brief explanation of a key principle that will govern the entire *masechta*: for *Chazal*, the *ikar* of the *sukkah* is the *sechach*. The walls are necessary, but the defining element of the *sukkah* — the element for which it is named — is the *sechach*. *Rashi* states this explicitly in his comment just before the *Gemara* begins: *ve'al shem ha-sechach keruya sukkah* — the *sukkah* is named for the *sechach*. This means that any verse referring to *sukkah* will be understood as referring primarily to the *sechach*, not the walls.

So when Rava says the eye does not see it — what the eye fails to see is the *sechach*. The walls may be perfectly visible; they dominate the visual field. But if the *sukkah* is more than twenty *amos* tall and the *sechach* is at the top, a person standing inside will see only walls. The *sechach* is too far above to enter naturally into one's awareness. And since the verse commands that future generations should *know* they are dwelling in *sukkos*, Rava reads this as a functional requirement: the *sechach* must be within the range of natural perception. If one must crane one's neck to see it, the awareness the verse demands is absent.

One might note that the plain sense (*pshat*) of the verse is historical: it is an educational imperative to remember what God did for Israel in the wilderness. Rava could be understood as saying that this historical awareness cannot be accessed unless one is presently conscious of sitting under *sechach*. But *Rashi* and the subsequent *Gemara* appear to read Rava as deriving an actual structural requirement directly from the verse — that the *sechach* must be perceptible — not merely as a means to an end.

It is worth noting here as well the connection to a broader theme. The idea that the *sukkah* commemorates the clouds of glory (*ananei kavod*) that accompanied Israel in the wilderness is evocative in this context — one naturally imagines those clouds as being quite high up. We will return to the *ananei kavod* theme later; for now, Rava's derivation focuses squarely on the perceptibility of the *sechach*.

### Rav Zeira: Shade

*Ve-Zeira amar meihacha* — Rav Zeira says, from this verse in *Yeshayahu* (Isaiah 4): *ve-sukkah tihyeh le-tzel yomam meichorev* — "and a *sukkah* shall be for shade in the day from the heat." The full verse in its context is a Messianic vision: in the age of redemption, God will create over all of Mount Zion a cloud by day and a fiery glow by night — evoking the imagery of the exodus — and a protective covering, a *sukkah*, will provide shade from the heat and shelter from the rain.

It is worth pausing over the context, because the verse is not referring to the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* in any direct sense. It is part of an eschatological portrait in *Yeshayahu*, where the prophet foresees that the glory of Mount Zion will be covered: *uvara Hashem al kol machon har Tziyon ve'al mikraeha anan yomam ve'ashan ve-nogah esh lehavah laylah* — "And God will create over all of Mount Zion and over its assemblies a cloud by day and smoke, and the brightness of a flaming fire by night." And then: *ve-sukkah tihyeh le-tzel yomam meichorev ve'al kol kavod chuppah u-lema-chseh u-le-mistor mi-zerem u-mi-matar* — "and a *sukkah* shall be for shade in the day from the heat, and for a canopy, and for shelter and a refuge from storm and rain."

Even setting aside the Messianic context, this verse is already doing something powerful: it connects the *sukkah* of the *mitzvah* to a Messianic vision of divine protection, and it evokes the *anan* — the cloud that accompanied Israel through the wilderness. For those who know their *Tanach* as they should, encountering this verse at the outset of *Sukkah* introduces quietly but significantly the theme of *sukkah ke-neged ananei kavod* — the *sukkah* as representing the clouds of glory. The verse from *Yeshayahu* thus serves double duty in the *Gemara*: it supports a legal derivation, and it sounds a thematic note that will recur.

Now for the legal application. Rav Zeira derives from this verse: *ad esrim ama adam yoshev be-tzel sukkah* — up to twenty *amos*, a person is sitting in the shade of the *sukkah* — meaning, the *sechach* is actually providing shade. *Lema'ala me-esrim ama ein adam yoshev be-tzel sukkah ela be-tzel defanot* — above twenty *amos*, the person is not sitting in the shade of the *sukkah* (the *sechach*), but rather in the shade of the walls. The walls, being so tall, are what shade the space below, while the *sechach* — small and high above — contributes nothing effective. The *sukkah* verse in *Yeshayahu* uses the word *tzel* — shade — and the legal requirement is that the *sechach* must actually function as the source of shade.

### Abaye: Mountains

*Amar lei Abaye* — Abaye challenged Rav Zeira: *ela me'ata, oseh sukkato be-ashrot karnayim, hachi nami de-lo havei sukkah* — if the problem is that the walls rather than the *sechach* are providing the shade, then consider someone who builds his *sukkah* between two very high mountains. Are you going to say that it is not a valid *sukkah* because the mountains are already shading the valley?

### Zeira: Schach Quality

*Amar lei* — Rav Zeira responded: *hatam dal ashrot karnayim ika tzel sukkah* — there, if you remove the mountains, the *sechach* still provides shade. The *sechach* itself, intrinsically, has the quality to shade the space beneath it — the mountains are merely extrinsic additions to what the *sechach* is doing on its own. *Hacha dal defanot leika tzel sukkah* — here, by contrast, if you remove the walls, you have no shade from the *sechach* at all.

This is a crucial distinction. The argument is not simply that the walls happen to be providing more shade than the *sechach* in practice. The argument is that when the *sukkah* exceeds twenty *amos*, the *sechach* is so high that it is incapable of providing shade regardless of the walls — even in the abstract, even if you were to look at the *sechach* in isolation. When sunlight strikes at any angle other than directly overhead (and we can largely discount the moment of absolute zenith), a small patch of *sechach* situated twenty or more *amos* above the ground will cast its shade well outside the interior of the *sukkah*. The shade produced by the *sechach* falls elsewhere. Remove the walls, and you have no shade underneath — the shade is somewhere else entirely. In the mountain case, the *sechach* is perfectly capable of providing shade; it is just being supplemented by the mountains. In the too-tall *sukkah*, the *sechach* is not capable of providing shade in its given position, full stop.

One might ask whether this should depend on the area of the *sechach*: if the *sechach* is very wide, surely it can shade the space beneath it even at a great height? The *Gemara* will address this shortly.

### Rava: Temp Structure

*Ve-Rava amar meha* — Rava (in a second formulation distinct from his verse-based derivation above) offers yet another source: *ba-sukkot teshu shivat yamim* — "you shall dwell in *sukkos* for seven days." *Amra Torah, kol shivat ha-yamim, tze midirat keva ve-shev be-dirat arai* — the *Torah* commands: for all seven days, leave your permanent dwelling and dwell in a temporary structure. The word *sukkah* implicitly contrasts with your house, your permanent residence. The *sukkah* must be, by definition, a *dirat arai* — a temporary dwelling.

*Ve'ad esrim ama adam oseh dirato dirat arai* — up to twenty *amos*, it is possible to construct a dwelling that has the character of a temporary structure. *Lema'ala me-esrim ama, de-adam oseh dirato dirat keva* — above twenty *amos*, the scale and construction required to support such a structure make it inherently a permanent dwelling. *Ein adam oseh dirato dirat arai* — no one builds a temporary dwelling that tall. *Ela dirat keva* — it must be a permanent structure, and it is therefore invalid.

### Abaye: Materials

*Amar lei Abaye* — Abaye challenged this formulation: *asu mechitzot shel barzel ve-sichach gaban, hacha nami dlav sukkah?* — if the requirement is genuinely that the *sukkah* be a *dirat arai*, a temporary structure, then what if someone constructed a *sukkah* of normal dimensions but used metal walls? Is that not a permanent structure? Would you say that building a perfectly standard-sized *sukkah* out of brick and mortar — going out after *Yom Kippur* and constructing four solid walls with cement, then placing *sechach* on top — is invalid because it is a *dirat keva* rather than a *dirat arai*?

### Rava: Dimensions

*Amar lei, hachi ka'amina lach* — Rava clarified: this is what I mean. *Ad esrim ama, de-adam oseh dirato dirat arai* — up to twenty *amos*, the dimensions are such that a structure *can* be a temporary dwelling. *Ki avid dirat keva nami nafik* — so even if you use the materials of a permanent dwelling (metal walls, brick, cement), you are still *yotzei*, because the *dimensions* are within the range of a temporary structure. *Lema'ala me-esrim ama, de-adam oseh dirato dirat keva* — but above twenty *amos*, those dimensions fall exclusively within the range of a permanent structure. *Ki avid dirat arai nami lo nafik* — even if you build your walls out of straw like the first little pig, and it is above twenty *amos*, you are not *yotzei*.

The resolution is elegant: the *halacha* of temporary versus permanent, like most *halacha*, is operationalized through quantifiable criteria — specifically, dimensions — rather than building materials. What distinguishes a *dirat arai* from a *dirat keva* in the law's framework is the scale of the structure, not what it is made of. A structure under twenty *amos* can function as a *dirat arai* in terms of its proportions, whatever material is used. A structure above twenty *amos* takes on the character of a permanent building by its very dimensions alone.

## Tosafot: Permanence

### Tosafot: Nails

This leads to a natural question that *Tosafot* raises. We have said that the wall material is irrelevant — even brick walls are acceptable. But what about the *sechach* itself? Can the *sechach* be made permanent? Specifically, *Tosafot* asks: *ve-halo yachol likvoa ha-nessarim ba-masmerim* — could one not take planks of wood (which are valid *sechach* if the wood is from something that grew from the ground and is no longer attached) and nail them down permanently, *shelo yerdu geshamim ba-sukkah* — so that no rain would enter? Would that be biblically valid?

### Tosafot: Non-Permanent

*Tosafot* answers: *u-veita vadai pasul mi-de'oraita* — using your actual house is clearly invalid, as the *Torah* says *sukkah* and not a house that is established all year round. But what about building a new structure with a permanent wood roof? *Tosafot* writes: *de-nehi de-lo chaishinan bi-defanot i avid lehu keva* — granted, we are not concerned if the *walls* are made permanent, because as we have established, wall material is not what defines the *sukkah*. *Mikol makom ba-sechach she-ikar ha-sukkah al shem ha-sechach* — but the *sechach*, which is the defining element of the *sukkah* (and from which the *sukkah* takes its name), *lo mishtarya ha-sukkah ad de-avid lah arai* — the *sukkah* is not valid unless the *sechach* is made temporary.

*Tosafot* does not spell out a precise quantifiable threshold for what makes *sechach* "permanent" in this sense. The question of when nailed planks cross the line from permissible *sechach* to an invalid permanent roof is one that cannot be fully quantified. But the principle is that at some point, if the roof is constructed in a manner that makes it genuinely permanent, it ceases to be *sechach* and becomes a house. The *sukkah* is no longer a *sukkah*; it is simply a building.

### Rain Sign

One of *Tosafot*'s criteria for identifying *sechach* that has crossed the line into permanent structure is rain impermeability. The verse from *Yeshayahu* that Rav Zeira cited includes, at its end, the phrase *u-le-mistor mi-zerem u-mi-matar* — "and for shelter and refuge from storm and rain." One might have thought that this describes a *virtue* of the *sukkah* — it keeps out the rain. But *Tosafot* argues the opposite: the fact that a Messianic *sukkah* is described as providing shelter from rain is precisely because in the present context, a *sukkah* that is impervious to rain is not a valid *sukkah* at all. If the *sechach* blocks out rain entirely, it is a sign of a permanent roof, a *dirat keva*, not a *dirat arai*. This is why the rain that falls on *Sukkos* is called a *siman kelalah ba-chag* — a sign of a curse on the festival. If it were possible to build a *sukkah* that keeps rain out entirely, there would be no curse in rain on the festival. The very fact that rain is an unwelcome visitor demonstrates that a valid *sukkah* must be open to rain.

This is a structurally interesting point: *Tosafot* uses the theme of the *sukkah*'s vulnerability to rain not merely as a poetic observation about the nature of the *mitzvah*, but as a legal criterion. A *sukkah* that keeps rain out entirely has, by that very quality, identified itself as a permanent structure, and permanent *sechach* is invalid. The emphasis on the *sechach* — *ikar ha-sukkah al shem ha-sechach* — means that the *sechach* cannot be permanent even while the walls can.

## Debate Limits

### Yoshiya: Wall Gap

Having established the three distinct rationales for the twenty-*amos* limit — Rava's awareness/visibility argument, Rav Zeira's shade argument, and Rava's *dirat arai* argument — the *Gemara* now examines how each model generates different qualifications of the debate.

*Ke-man azla ha de-amar Rebbi Yoshiyah?* — According to whom does the following ruling of Rebbi Yoshiyah go? *Amar Rav, machloket be-she'ein defanos megi'os la-sechach* — the whole debate in the *mishna* (between the *Sages* and Rabbi Yehuda) applies only where the walls do not reach all the way up to the *sechach*. There is a gap between the top of the wall and the *sechach*.

*Aval defanos megi'os la-sechach, afilu lema'ala me-esrim ama kesherah* — but if the walls extend all the way up to the *sechach*, even higher than twenty *amos*, everyone would agree it is valid.

### Eye Following

*Ke-man?* — Like whom does this go? *Ke-Rabbah* — it can only make sense according to Rava's first rationale, *de-amar mishum de-lo shalta bei eina* — that the problem is the eye does not naturally see the *sechach*. *Ve-cheivan de-defanos megi'os la-sechach, mishlach shalta bei eina* — if the walls go all the way up to the *sechach*, the eye naturally follows the wall upward, and it will reach the point where wall meets *sechach*, bringing the *sechach* into view. By contrast, if the wall ends and there is a gap of open air before the *sechach*, the eye stops at the top of the wall and does not travel further to find the *sechach*. If the wall meets the *sechach* directly, however high, the gaze is drawn continuously upward until it takes in the *sechach*.

This qualification makes no sense on the other two theories. Whether the walls reach the *sechach* or not is irrelevant to whether the *sechach* provides shade in practice, and irrelevant to whether the dimensions suggest a permanent or temporary structure.

### Huna: Area

*Ke-man azla ha de-amar Rav Huna amar Rav?* — According to whom goes the statement of Rav Huna in the name of Rav? *Machloket be-she'ein bah ela arba amos* — the whole debate applies only when the *sukkah* is no more than four by four *amos* in area. *Aval yesh bah yoter me-arba amos al arba amos, afilu lema'ala me-esrim ama kesherah* — but if the *sukkah* is more than four by four *amos*, even higher than twenty *amos* is valid.

### Shade Proportional

*Ke-man? Ke-Rebbi Zeira* — this can only make sense according to Rav Zeira, *de-amar mishum tzel* — that the problem is whether the *sechach* provides shade in practice. *Ve-cheivan de-rivcha, ika tzel sukkah* — since the *sechach* is wide enough, even at a great height it provides shade. The intuition is clear: a small patch of *sechach* high up will let sunlight come through at most angles; but a large expanse of *sechach* at the same height will block more of the sunlight, and shade will fall beneath it.

### Proportionality

One might ask: should this not be fully proportional? If a *sechach* four by four *amos* wide can be at twenty *amos* height, should a *sechach* twenty by twenty *amos* be permitted at a proportionally greater height? Should there be a sliding scale?

*Tosafot* raises this point and offers two responses. The first is that perhaps it is indeed proportional — as the *sechach* grows wider, greater heights become permissible. *Tosafot* does not rule this out entirely.

But the more characteristic rabbinic answer, which *Tosafot* develops by reference back to *Yoma*, is this: *yesh lomar, de-le'olam tzarikh ha-rochav le-fi ha-govah le-fi cheshbon arba amot le-esrim* — it would always be proportional in principle. But the *Gemara* also says: *i nami, kim lehu le-rabanan de-afilu be-govah elef, de-afilu be-govah elef, i efshar she-lo yikanes tzel sechach purta* — the Rabbis knew that even at a height of a thousand *amos*, once the *sechach* is more than four by four *amos*, it is impossible that no shade at all would enter. And once it is less than four by four, even at twenty *amos* it will fail.

*Tosafot* supports this with a reference to *Yom Kippur*: just as in that context the Rabbis taught that once you have the right minimum quantity — a pressed date — it has an effect even for *Og King of Bashan* who ate it, and a little less than that has no effect for anyone — so too here. Once you cross the threshold of four by four *amos*, there will always be some shade regardless of height. Below that threshold, height above twenty *amos* will always be a problem. The Rabbis knew this and set a fixed number rather than a proportional formula.

### Chana: Minimum

*Ke-man azla ha de-amar Rav Chana bar Rabba amar Rav? Machloket be-she'eina machzeket ela kedei rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano* — According to whom goes the statement of Rav Chana bar Rabba in the name of Rav? He says the debate applies only when the *sukkah* holds no more than the absolute minimum: a person's head, most of his body, and his small table. *Aval machzeket yoter mi-kedei rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano, afilu lema'ala me-esrim ama kesherah* — if it is even slightly larger than that minimum, even above twenty *amos* is valid.

A word of clarification: why would one's "head and most of one's body" not simply mean a person sitting up? The answer lies in the *halacha* that eating in the *sukkah* is ideally done in a reclining position. So the minimum *sukkah* must accommodate one's head and most of one's body while reclining, plus a small tray table. The *Gemara* later establishes this minimum as approximately seven by seven handbreadths (*shiva al shiva tefachim*) — roughly two feet by two feet. This is far smaller than four *amos* by four *amos* (roughly six feet by six feet), which is about sixteen times the area.

*Ke-man azla?* — Like whom does Rav Chana bar Rabba's formulation go? *De-lo ke-chad* — it does not fit any of our three models. If the concern is the *sechach* providing shade, then something just slightly larger than the absolute minimum (*rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano*) — still far less than four by four *amos* — would not be large enough to provide shade at twenty *amos* height. And if the concern is permanent versus temporary structure, it is hard to see how being just above the bare minimum matters.

### Chicken Coop

*Tosafot* proposes an independent logic for this position. *Tosafot* suggests: *lul shel tarnigolim* — a chicken coop. If the *sukkah* is at the absolute minimum size — just barely accommodating one's head, most of one's body, and a table — and it is also extremely tall, the result is an absurd structure that no one would ever recognize as a dwelling of any kind. It is too narrow and too tall. Once it is even slightly larger than the minimum, however, it escapes the category of a structural absurdity and can be recognized as some kind of dwelling, even if a small one. The problem of exceeding twenty *amos* applies only when the structure, combined with its tiny footprint, cannot even pass as a dwelling. Once it is a bit larger, the problem disappears.

### Gemara: Two Models

*Bishlama le-deRebbi Yoshiyah, pligi de-Rav Huna ve-Rav Chana bar Rabba* — it makes sense that Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Rabba's qualifications disagree with each other: Rebbi Yoshiyah's qualification (whether the walls reach the *sechach*) is about a different dimension of the structure entirely — it speaks to the vertical relationship between wall and *sechach* — while Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Rabba both speak to the horizontal dimensions of the *sukkah*. Those two can coexist as independent debates.

But the *Gemara* then asks: perhaps Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Rabba are not debating the *reason* for the twenty-*amos* requirement at all. Perhaps they both agree on the reason, and what they are really debating is simply: *be-hechsher sukkah ka-mifligi* — what is the minimum valid size of a *sukkah*? *Mar savar hechsher sukkah be-arba amot* — one holds the minimum is four by four *amos*. *U-mar savar hechsher sukkah be-machzeket rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano* — the other holds it is only *rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano*. They both agree that the twenty-*amos* debate applies only to a minimum-size *sukkah*, and they are simply disagreeing about what minimum size is.

The *Gemara* rejects this: *de-kulei alma hechsher sukkah be-rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano* — everyone agrees the minimum *sukkah* is *rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano*, *shiva tefachim*. The debate between Rav Huna and Rav Chana bar Rabba is not about the minimum size of a *sukkah*; it is about when height above twenty *amos* becomes a problem.

*De-mar savar machzeket rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano pligi* — according to one, the debate about height applies to *any* size from the bare minimum (*shiva al shiva tefachim*) upward, but *aval yoter me-rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano, divrei ha-kol kesherah* — once it is larger, everyone agrees it is valid. *U-mar savar* — the other holds: yes, I agree that once it is *rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano* it qualifies as a *sukkah*, but the debate does not end there. *Mi-rosho ve-rubo ve-shulchano ad arba amot pligi* — anywhere from the minimum up until four by four *amos*, there is a debate; *aval yoter me-arba amot, divrei ha-kol kesherah* — once it is more than four *amos*, everyone agrees it is valid.

The *Gemara* thus insists on its framing: the various qualifications proposed by Rebbi Yoshiyah, Rav Huna, and Rav Chana bar Rabba each track one of the underlying rationales for the twenty-*amos* limit. Rebbi Yoshiyah's qualification (wall-meets-*sechach*) follows Rava's awareness model. Rav Huna's qualification (four *amos* of area) follows Rav Zeira's shade model, since a larger *sechach* provides shade even at great height. And the *sugya* continues to press toward identifying which of these models best accounts for the full range of qualifications the *Amora'im* propose.

## Hilni Precedent

### Hilni's High Sukkah

The *Gemara* now introduces a *baraita* that presents a historical case, and Rabbi Yehuda uses it as a proof for his position:

*Amar Rebbi Yehuda, ma'aseh be-Hilni ha-malka, be-Lod* — there was an incident with Queen Hilni in Lod, *she-haysa sukkasa gevoha me-esrim ama* — her *sukkah* was higher than twenty *amos*. *Ve-hayu zkeinim nichnasim ve-yotzim le-sham ve-lo amru lah davar* — and elders would enter and exit there and said nothing to her. This is Rabbi Yehuda's proof: the Sages saw the structure and made no objection, which he takes as implicit endorsement that a *sukkah* higher than twenty *amos* is valid.

### Queen Status

*Amru lo, misham ra'aya?* — They challenged him: you want to bring proof from there? *Isha haysa* — she was a woman, *petura min ha-sukkah* — women are exempt from the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*. The elders may simply have kept their silence because it was not their place to correct a queen about an obligation that did not apply to her.

### Seven Sons

*Amar lahen* — Rabbi Yehuda responded: *ve-lo shiva banim havu lah?* — but she had seven sons with her in the *sukkah*! And moreover, *ve-od kol ma'aseh lo asta ela al pi chachamim* — she did everything in accordance with the rulings of the *Sages*.

### Probability Logic

The *Gemara* interjects: *lama li le-misni ve-od kol ma'aseh lo asta ela al pi chachamim* — why does Rabbi Yehuda need to add the second argument about her piety, once he has already mentioned the seven sons? The *Gemara* explains: *hachi ka'amar lehu* — this is what Rabbi Yehuda was anticipating. *Ki teimru banim ketanim hayu, u-ketanim pturim min ha-sukkah* — you might say: all seven boys were young children, and young children are exempt from *sukkah*. To which he answers: *keivan de-shiva havu, i efshar de-lo hava behu chad she-eino tzarich le-imo* — since there were seven of them, it is statistically impossible that not one of them had reached the age of no longer needing his mother in the night. And that — no longer needing his mother — is the *Gemara*'s definition (elaborated later) of when a minor becomes obligated through *chinuch* to sit in a *sukkah*.

Rabbi Yehuda does not actually know this by probability; he knew the story and knew the facts. It is the *Gemara* itself that is reasoning probabilistically, establishing that Rabbi Yehuda's counter-argument was necessarily sound — with seven sons, at least one must have reached the threshold of *chinuch*.

### Piety Argument

But then one might say: even if there was a child obligated through *chinuch*, that is only a rabbinic obligation. *Ve-chi teimru katan she-eino tzarich le-imo mi-derabbanan hu de-michayev, ve-i derabbanan lo mashgecha* — perhaps Queen Hilni was not scrupulous about rabbinic requirements. To this Rabbi Yehuda responds: *ta shema, ve-od kol ma'aseh lo asta ela al pi chachamim* — come and hear: she did everything according to the *Sages*. Her piety encompassed rabbinic law as well.

The *Gemara* is thus using Queen Hilni's case as a test for the various theories about the twenty-*amos* limit. Having established that the case involved obligated parties — children of *chinuch* age, and a queen who scrupulously followed even rabbinic rulings — we cannot dismiss the elders' silence as irrelevant. The case will be used on the following *daf* to probe which of the competing rationales best accounts for the parameters of the debate.

It is worth noting what the *Gemara* is doing here as a piece of Talmudic method. Rabbi Yehuda clearly knew the historical facts of Queen Hilni's household. He would not have needed to count to seven to know whether any of her sons had reached the age of *chinuch*. The *Gemara*'s probabilistic reasoning — *keivan de-shiva havu* — is not Rabbi Yehuda's argument; it is the *Gemara* independently verifying that Rabbi Yehuda's retort was well-grounded. This is a characteristic Talmudic move: reading the logic back into the dispute in order to test its foundations, even when the original disputant was working from specific knowledge rather than inference.

---

---

# Sukkah 3

## Review: Sechach & Height

### Day One Summary

Today's *daf* is *daf* 3 of *Sukkah*. By way of review, the previous session introduced several major themes centered on the discussion of the height limit of twenty *amot*.

### Sechach Definition

The first and most fundamental point established is that the concept of *sukkah* is primarily defined by *sechach*. This was made clear from the way multiple *amoraim* explain the problem of excessive height — the concern is with the *sechach* being too high — and from the focus on *pesukim* that mention the word *sukkah*, which is understood to refer essentially to the *sechach*. The identity of a *sukkah* is thus very much tied up in its roof covering.

### Three Themes

Three major themes emerged from that discussion. The first is the question of permanence versus temporary dwelling: one reason given for the height restriction is that a *sukkah* must constitute a *dirat arai*, a temporary dwelling, and a structure too tall to be recognized as such would be invalid. The second theme is the visibility of the *sechach*: perhaps the requirement is that one be able to perceive the *sechach* overhead, and if it is too high, it will not register meaningfully in one's awareness — an idea loosely connected to the notion of *lema'an yedu doroteichem*, so that generations will know. The third theme is the *sechach*'s practical capacity to provide shade: if the *sechach* is too high, it will not effectively shade the space below.

It is worth noting an important qualification: the *Gemara* states that the question of temporary dwelling is not determined by building material — one may construct a *sukkah* from brick — so the permanence concern pertains to other features of the structure.

### Tosafot: Sechach

*Tosafot* raise a pointed question that goes beyond mere dimensions: can the *sechach* itself be so permanent that it comes to be defined as one's house? Their conclusion is that it can. One criterion *Tosafot* offer for *sechach* being considered permanent — and therefore no longer qualifying as a temporary roof covering — is that it prevents rain from penetrating entirely. There is also a tradition, apparently rooted in the *Yerushalmi*, regarding the ability to see the stars through the *sechach*, though *Tosafot*'s primary focus is on the rain criterion. Additional examples were raised: *sechach* nailed down with planks, nails, and plaster. Whatever the precise standard, the underlying principle is clear — the *sechach* cannot take on the character of a permanent roof.

---

## Queen Hilni Case

### Hilni Proof

The *Gemara* now proceeds to test which of the three explanations for the twenty *amot* height limit is correct by examining the famous case of Queen *Hilni*, who sat in a *sukkah* taller than twenty *amot*. This case was invoked by *Rabbi Yehuda* as a proof that a *sukkah* exceeding twenty *amot* is valid. The Sages responded that her case proves nothing, since she was a woman and exempt from the obligation. *Rabbi Yehuda* replied that her sons were with her, and as the *Gemara* elaborated, her sons were at minimum rabbinically obligated from the standpoint of *chinuch*. The *Gemara* now attempts to determine which theoretical approach to the height limit can actually accommodate this case as a genuine point of debate.

### Walls Not Reaching

The *Gemara* opens: *bishlama leman de'amar beshein defanot megi'ot lasechach* — this works well according to the approach that the entire problem of excessive height arises only when the walls do not reach the *sechach*. According to this view, the concern is whether one will perceive the *sechach*: if the walls reach the *sechach*, one's gaze is naturally drawn upward to where the walls meet the roof, and height poses no problem. The debate applies only when the walls fall short of the *sechach*. This explanation fits the *Hilni* case perfectly, since it is entirely plausible that her *sukkah* — a grand royal structure — was built with walls that did not extend to the *sechach*: *darkah shel malka leishev besukkah she'ein defanot megi'ot lasechach* — it is quite natural for a queen's *sukkah* to have walls not reaching the *sechach*, *mishum avira*, in order to allow for air circulation.

### Small Sukkah Case

The *Gemara* then poses a difficulty against the alternative approach. *Ella leman de'amar besukkah ketana machloket* — but according to the view that the problem is the *sechach*'s inability to provide shade, and that this is a problem only for a small *sukkah* (since a small *sechach* covering a limited area will not provide shade if too high, whereas a larger *sechach* will shade effectively regardless of height), the debate applies only when the *sukkah* is very small, perhaps four by four *amot*. Given that, how could *Hilni*'s *sukkah* have been the subject of this debate? *Vechi darkah shel malka leishev besukkah ketana?* — Would a queen sit in such a tiny *sukkah*? Surely her *sukkah* must have been large, in which case there would be no issue of height at all according to this opinion, and her case would prove nothing.

### Compartments

*Amar Rabba bar Rav Adda*: *lo nitzrecha ela l'sukkah asuyah kitoniyot kitoniyot* — the solution is that the *sukkah* was constructed with small private compartments. The outer structure may indeed have been enormous, like a large building with rooms, but halachically the relevant *sukkah* is not judged by the scale of the outer structure. What matters is the space in which one sits, enclosed by its own four walls. If one sits within an inner chamber, the *sukkah* being evaluated is that chamber — and if the *sechach* directly above that chamber covers only a small area, the question of whether it provides shade at twenty *amot* of height is entirely germane. One might ask whether the walls of such a chamber would also need to reach the *sechach*. The answer is no: that requirement is the concern of the first opinion, which holds that the problem is the visibility of the *sechach*. Under the present opinion — that the problem is the *sechach*'s ability to provide shade — what matters is simply how large an area the *sechach* covers, not whether the walls reach it.

The *Gemara* then challenges this answer as well: *V'chi darkah shel malka leishev besukkah asuyah kitoniyot kitoniyot?* — Would a queen sit in a *sukkah* consisting entirely of tiny little chambers, with no general sitting room at all?

### Outer & Side

*Amar Rav Ashi*: *lo nitzrecha ela l'kitoniyot shebah* — it need only apply to the side chambers within the *sukkah*. The structure in fact contained a large and impressive main hall where guests could be received, but also featured small private side chambers. The queen presumably would greet guests in the large hall, but would retire to a private chamber to eat.

### Rashi & Yehuda

*Rashi* explains the positions of the disputants as follows: *rabbanan savri b'nah b'sukkah ma'alya hava yatvi* — the Sages reasoned that the sons were eating in the large main hall. Since there is no debate about whether a large *sukkah* poses a problem of height under this opinion (height only matters for a small *sukkah*), the sons' presence in a properly sized *sukkah* proves nothing. *Rabbi Yehuda savar b'nah gabah hava yatvi* — but *Rabbi Yehuda* held that the sons were with her in one of the small private chambers. *Ve'afilu hachi lo amru leih davar* — and yet no one said anything to protest, which *Rabbi Yehuda* cites as proof that even in a small *sukkah*, the height above twenty *amot* is not disqualifying.

This raises an obvious difficulty: if all the sons were crowded into a tiny chamber, how could they all fit? Even a chamber of four *amot* by four *amot* would be very cramped, and if the minimum dimension is only seven *tefachim* by seven *tefachim*, it is inconceivable that seven sons could fit inside.

### Tosafot Dimensions

*Tosafot* resolve this difficulty by articulating an important principle: in order for a structure to constitute a *sukkah* of minimum size, it is not sufficient merely that it possess the minimum area — it must satisfy the minimum measurement in both length and width independently. A space that is three and a half *amot* wide but twenty *amot* long is not a minimum-sized *sukkah*, because in one dimension it falls short of the minimum. Accordingly, *Tosafot* suggest that the chamber could have been quite narrow in one direction — say, three and a half *amot* — while extending to twenty *amot* in the other direction, giving ample room for all seven sons to recline side by side, while still counting as a *sukkah* that is too small in the relevant dimension. The same logic would apply regarding the shade concern: for the *sechach* to provide shade, it must achieve the minimum span in both directions; it is not enough for the structure to be very long if it is insufficiently wide.

---

## Minimum Size

### Shmuel: Head/Body

Having examined the various approaches to the twenty *amot* height limit through the lens of the *Hilni* case, the *Gemara* now pivots entirely. The question of height is set aside for the moment, and attention turns to a new issue that arose incidentally — what is the minimum size of a *sukkah*? This applies to an ordinary *sukkah* of normal height, whether six or eight feet tall. *Amar Shmuel bar Yitzchak*: *halacha tsricha kidei machzeket rosho verubo veshulchano* — the *halacha* is that a *sukkah* must be able to contain one's head, the majority of one's body, and one's table. This is significantly smaller than four *amot* by four *amot*, which is the position of *Rebbe* that will be introduced shortly. The requirement of "the majority of one's body" reflects the posture of reclining: since one eats reclining, the relevant measurement runs from the waist to the top of the head, approximately. The table — a small serving tray — measures roughly seven *tefachim* by seven *tefachim*, approximately two feet square.

### Rabbi Abba Query

*Amar lei Rabbi Abba*: *keman?* — Who is this position going like? *Kebet Shammai?* Are you following *Bet Shammai*? *Amar lei, ela keman?* — He replied: yes, and who else would I be following? This brief exchange raises a question: what does *Bet Shammai* have to do with the minimum size of a *sukkah*?

### Mishnah 28a

To understand this, the *Gemara* directs attention to the *mishna* on 28a, which will serve as the reference text for much of what follows on this *daf*.

---

## Table in House

### Mishna: Table Out

The *mishna* on 28a reads: *mi shehaya rosho verubo besukkah veshulchano betoch habayit* — one whose head and the majority of his body was inside the *sukkah* but whose table was inside the house.

### Shammai vs Hillel

*Beit Shammai poslin u'Beit Hillel machshirin* — *Bet Shammai* invalidate and *Bet Hillel* validate.

### Yochanan Story

*Bet Hillel* then presents a proof to *Bet Shammai*: *amru lehei Bet Hillel leBet Shammai* — *Bet Hillel* said to *Bet Shammai*: *lo kach haya maaseh shehalchu ziknei Bet Shammai veziknei Bet Hillel levaker et Yochanan ben haChoranis* — was there not the following incident, that the elders of *Bet Shammai* and the elders of *Bet Hillel* went to visit *Yochanan ben haChoranis*? *Umatsuhu shehaya yoshev rosho verubo besukkah veshulchano betoch habayit* — and they found him sitting with his head and the majority of his body inside the *sukkah* and his table inside the house. *Velo amru lo davar* — and they said nothing to him. This, *Bet Hillel* contends, demonstrates that the arrangement is perfectly acceptable.

### Shammai Rebuttal

*Bet Shammai* responded: *misham raya?* — You want to bring a proof from that incident? *Af hem amru lo* — that was not the whole story. *Bet Shammai* says that their elders did in fact say something to him: *im ken hayita noheg lo kiyamta mitzvat sukkah miyamecha* — if this is how you have been conducting yourself, you have never in your life fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*. So the incident is not a validation of the practice; it was an occasion on which *Bet Shammai*'s elders actually rebuked him.

The scenario being described is worth picturing clearly. The "table" here need not refer to a large dining table; it is more like a serving tray on which the food rests. One sits in the *sukkah*, but the food tray is just inside the house — the *sukkah* is built right up against the house. One reaches over or steps briefly inside to take a piece of food, brings it back, eats it, then goes back for more. The concern *Bet Shammai* articulates is evident: if one allows the food to remain in the house, one will inevitably be drawn back into the house and will end up eating there, not in the *sukkah*. *Bet Hillel* is unconcerned, holding that a person can manage to eat within the *sukkah* even if the food tray is just across the threshold.

Now the *mishna* appears on its face to be debating a scenario — a behavioral question about how one conducts one's eating — not a question about the dimensions of the *sukkah*. Yet the *Gemara* will now show that this same debate is also understood to address the minimum size of the *sukkah*.

### Size Debate?

*Matkif la Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*: *mimmay d'Beit Shammai u'Beit Hillel b'sukkah ketanna pligi?* — What compels us to say that *Bet Shammai* and *Bet Hillel* are debating the minimum size of a *sukkah*? *Dilma b'sukkah gedolah pligi* — perhaps they are debating the case of a perfectly normal large *sukkah*. *U'k'gon d'yatbi a'pumma d'metulta* — specifically the case where one sits right at the entrance of the *sukkah* (note: *metulta* is the Aramaic word for *sukkah*), *veshulchano b'toch ha'bayit* — with the table just inside the house.

### Gezerah Concern

*D'Beit Shammai savri gazrinan shema yimashekh achar shulchano* — *Bet Shammai* holds that this is a *gezeirah*: we are concerned that if we permit this, the person will be drawn after his table and will end up eating inside the house. *U'Beit Hillel savri lo gazrinan* — *Bet Hillel* holds that we do not make this rabbinic edict.

*Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak* then adds a textual argument: *v'dayka nami* — this interpretation can actually be inferred from the precise language of the *mishna* itself. The *mishna* describes the scenario as *mi she'hayah rosho v'rubo b'sukkah v'shulchano b'toch ha'bayit* — it depicts the act of eating with the table in the house, not the capacity of the *sukkah*. *V'i salka da'atach* that they were debating the minimum size, *makhziket v'einah makhziket mibba'ei lei* — the *mishna* should have framed the question as whether the *sukkah* can or cannot contain the table, describing the structure's dimensions rather than the scenario of the table being in the house. Since the *mishna* describes the scenario and not the dimensions, it evidently concerns the rabbinic *gezeirah* about being drawn after one's table, not the question of minimum size.

---

## Rabbi: 4x4 Amot

### Braitot Resolved

The *Gemara* does not rest with this conclusion. *U'b'sukkah ketannah lo pligi?* — But do *Bet Shammai* and *Bet Hillel* not also debate the minimum size? *Ve'hatanya* — we have the following *baraita*: *makhziket rosho v'rubo v'shulchano k'shira* — a *sukkah* that can contain one's head, body, and table is valid. *Rabbi Yehuda omer ad she'yehe bah arba amot al arba amot* — *Rabbi Yehuda* says it must have four *amot* by four *amot*. This is manifestly a debate about dimensions and minimum size. And from a second *baraita*: *Rabbi omer kol sukkah she'ein bah arba amot al arba amot psulah* — *Rebbe* declares any *sukkah* of less than four by four *amot* invalid. *Va'chachamim omrim afillu einah makhziket ella rosho v'rubo k'shira* — but the Sages say it is valid as long as it can contain one's head and body alone. *V'illu shulchano lo katani* — notably, the word "table" does not appear in this second *baraita*. So we have two *braitot*: in both, *Rebbe* requires four by four *amot*, but the opposing position differs — one *baraita* requires head, body, and table; the other requires only head and body. Clearly there are two competing opinions about whether the minimum size must also accommodate the table. *Kashyan adadi* — these two *braitot* contradict one another. *Ela lav shema mina ha Beit Shammai ha Beit Hillel* — it must be that one *baraita* represents *Bet Shammai* (the *sukkah* must contain the table) and the other *Bet Hillel* (it need only contain the body). *Shema mina*.

---

## Table in House…

### Language Evidence

*Amar mar zutra* — *Mar Zutra* now offers further textual support. One might have tried to infer from the *mishna* that the debate concerns a large *sukkah* (from the language describing the scenario of the table in the house), but a close reading of other language in the *mishna* points in the opposite direction. *Midikatani Beit Shammai poslin u-Beit Hillel machshirin* — the *mishna* uses the terms *poslin* (invalidate) and *machshirin* (validate), which are normally applied to an *object* — the *sukkah* itself is declared valid or invalid. This is the language one uses when ruling on the status of a thing, not when ruling on whether a person fulfilled an obligation. *V'im itai* — if the entire debate were only about a rabbinic *gezeirah* regarding one's conduct in a large *sukkah*, *Beit Shammai eima lo yatza u-Beit Hillel eima yatza miba'ei lei* — the *mishna* should have said *Bet Shammai* declares that one has not fulfilled one's obligation (*lo yatza*) and *Bet Hillel* says one has fulfilled it (*yatza*). The use of *poslin* and *machshirin* — language that declares the object valid or invalid — implies that they are ruling on the status of the *sukkah* itself, i.e., its minimum dimensions. So the *mishna*'s language actually points both ways: some of its language (the description of the scenario) suggests a debate about conduct in a large *sukkah*, while other language (*poslin* / *machshirin*) suggests a debate about the *sukkah*'s status.

### Two Debates

*Le-olam bitarti pligi* — both debates are present simultaneously. *Pligi be-sukkah ketana, pligi be-sukkah gedola* — they debate both the minimum size and the scenario of the large *sukkah* with the table in the house. *Ve-hisurei mechsara ve-hachi katani* — the text must be understood as having omitted some words, and here is the full version: *Mi shehaya rosho ve-rubo ba-sukkah ve-shulchano betoch habayit* — one whose head and body was in the *sukkah* and whose table was in the house. *Beit Shammai omrim lo yatza* — *Bet Shammai* says he did not fulfill his obligation. *U-Beit Hillel omrim yatza* — *Bet Hillel* says he did. That is the first debate, concerning a large *sukkah* with the table in the house. Then the second case: *ve-she'eina machzika ela kidei rosho ve-rubo bilvad* — a *sukkah* that can contain only one's head and body. *Beit Shammai poslin* — *Bet Shammai* invalidate it. *U-Beit Hillel machshirin* — *Bet Hillel* validate it. That is the second, separate debate about minimum size.

It is worth acknowledging that when the *Gemara* employs the formula *hisurei mechsara* — that words are missing from the text — one is sometimes left with the feeling that the reading is forced. Some *Acharonim*, including the *Gra* explicitly, maintain that when the *Gemara* says *hisurei mechsara* it is not genuinely claiming there was a different manuscript tradition (*girsa*), but rather consciously reworking a text that does not fit the position being advanced. Here, however, the reading is reasonably persuasive, because there is genuine independent evidence that both debates exist: the *braitot* clearly use dimensional language, and the *mishna*'s language, as shown, points in both directions. The claim that two debates became conflated in a single text is not implausible.

### Linked Debates

Are these two debates logically connected? They appear to be. The question of minimum size is ultimately a question about what constitutes meaningful habitation of a *sukkah*: what does it mean to *dwell* in a *sukkah*? As will emerge later in the *masechta*, dwelling means eating and sleeping. A *sukkah* that can contain one's head and the majority of one's body provides sufficient shelter for sleeping — one's head and most of one's body will be covered and protected. But can such a space also serve as a setting for eating? Eating requires a table. Is a space a genuine dwelling for eating purposes if it cannot accommodate the table?

This connects directly to the *gezeirah* debate. *Bet Shammai*, who does not trust a person to remain rooted in the *sukkah* when the table is in the house, evidently holds that a space without room for the table cannot be considered an eating space at all — there is no permanence of presence there, since one is constantly being pulled outside to retrieve food. If the space cannot contain the table, it is not the kind of space in which a person can genuinely inhabit and eat. *Bet Hillel*, who is unconcerned that the person will be drawn after the table, holds that even without the table present one can be genuinely present and rooted in the *sukkah* — and thus a space of just *rosho v'rubo* is a sufficient minimum for habitation.

This logical linkage raises a further practical question: since we rule — at least in the matter of minimum size — like *Bet Shammai*, do we also rule like *Bet Shammai* regarding the large *sukkah* with the table in the house? This is in fact a *machloket Rishonim*. Several *Rishonim* rule like *Bet Shammai* for minimum size but hold that if the *sukkah* is large and the table is in the house, one still fulfills one's obligation. Others argue that the two positions are logically bound together and must be ruled upon consistently.

*Tosafot* address this question, and also take up the broader issue of when we rule like *Bet Shammai* — itself a rare occurrence. *Tosafot* quote *Rav Amram* among the *Geonim*, who lists six places where the *halacha* follows *Bet Shammai*, and this is one of them: *beseder Rav Amram pasak beshisha mekomot halacha keBeit Shammai chada hai deSukkah tzericha shetehe machzeket rosho verubo veshulchano* — *Rav Amram* ruled in six places according to *Bet Shammai*, one of which is that a *sukkah* must be able to contain one's head, body, and table.

One might also ask whether the ruling of *machshirin* represents a *lechatchila* or *bedieved* position. The term *machshirin* is generally understood as *lechatchila* — it does not merely validate after the fact, but declares the thing kosher categorically. By contrast, *yatza* sometimes carries a *bedieved* implication and sometimes does not, depending on context.

There is a further remarkable dimension to this *sugya* that emerges from *Bet Shammai*'s rebuke of *Yochanan ben haChoranis*: *lo kiyamta mitzvat sukkah miyamecha* — you have never in your life fulfilled the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*. What is the force of this statement? If *Yochanan* was sitting in a large *sukkah* with only his table in the house, at the very least he should have been fulfilling his biblical obligation, even if he was violating a rabbinic *gezeirah*. The implication of *Bet Shammai*'s words is that by violating the rabbinic requirement, he failed to fulfill even the biblical obligation. This is a striking and difficult principle: can the Sages, through a rabbinic edict, deprive a person of credit for a biblical *mitzvah* that he objectively performed?

*Tosafot* confront this directly. Reading the relevant passage: *heicha deBeit Hillel machmirin mid'rabbanan uBeit Shammai mokmi ledi-Oraisa, velo gazrinan* — in a case where *Bet Hillel* is the more stringent position rabbinically and *Bet Shammai* maintains the biblical baseline without the rabbinic stringency, if one acts in accordance with *Bet Shammai*'s position and neglects *Bet Hillel*'s rabbinic addition, *yatza yedei chovaso afilu d'Oraisa* — one has fulfilled one's obligation even on the biblical level. But the reverse case, by contrast — *l'Beis Shammai heicha deyisiv afischa d'matalaltah degazri shema yimashach achar shulchano d'amri lei Beis Shammai lo kiyamtem mitzvas sukkah miyamechem d'afilu m'Oraisa lo kiyam* — where one has a large *sukkah* and the table is in the house and *Bet Shammai* imposed a *gezeirah* out of concern that one will be drawn after the table, *Bet Shammai*'s declaration is that one has not fulfilled the *mitzvah* even on a biblical level.

The precise mechanics of how a rabbinic edict in the domain of *mitzvot asei* can undermine the fulfillment of a biblical obligation is genuinely difficult. Various possibilities are raised — *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*, or the principle of *yesh koach beyad chachamim* — but no definitive explanation is offered. What is clear is that the principle operates differently in the realm of positive commandments than in the more familiar territory of prohibitions. When the Sages legislate in the area of *lo ta'asei*, the consequence of violation is a rabbinic transgression; the question of biblical fulfillment simply does not arise. But when they specify how a *mitzvat asei* must be performed, and someone fails to follow their specification, the question of whether the biblical *mitzvah* was nonetheless performed becomes live and genuinely complex. This does not mean every rabbinic requirement attached to *sukkah* carries this consequence — there are many rabbinic rules regarding valid *sechach*, for instance — but the principle that it can sometimes occur is established here.

---

## Rabbi: 4x4 Amot…

### Size Braitot

*Man tana l'ha d'sanu rabbanan* — who is the *tanna* of the following *baraita*? The *baraita* teaches: *bayis she'ein bo arba amot al arba amot* — a house that does not contain four *amot* by four *amot* — is, as the *baraita* will proceed to list, exempt from a range of *halachos* that require a "house." The thrust of the *baraita* is that four *amot* by four *amot* is the universal minimum dimension for something to be halachically classified as a house, and the *Gemara* raises the question of whether this *baraita* represents the position of *Rebbe* alone or can be attributed to the Sages as well.

---

## 4x4: House

### Mezuzah/Tzaraat

The *baraita* lists the following consequences of a structure being less than four *amot* by four *amot*:

*Patur min hamezuzah* — it is exempt from the obligation of a *mezuzah*, for the verse states *al mezuzot beitecha* — on the doorposts of your *house* — and this does not constitute a house.

*U'min hama'akeh* — it does not require a railing around the roof, for the verse states *ki sivneh bayit chadash* — when you build a new *house* — and this is not a house.

*V'eino mitamei binega'im* — if it develops spots it does not become ritually impure with the impurity of plague-spots on houses, for the relevant verse speaks of *kenega nir'ah li babayit* — an appearance of a plague-spot in a *house*.

### Sale & Draft

*V'eino nechlat bevatei arei chomah* — a sale of such a structure in a walled city does not become irrevocable after a year. The law of houses in walled cities, whereby the buyer acquires the property permanently once the year of redemption has passed, applies only to a *house*. Something smaller than four by four is treated like an open field or courtyard, and can always be redeemed, reverting at the Jubilee.

*V'ein chozrim alav me'orchei hamilchama* — one who built such a structure does not qualify for an exemption from military service. The draft exemption is granted to one who *asher banah bayit chadash* — who built a new *house* — and this is not a house.

### Eruv Exemption

*V'ein me'arvin bo v'ein mishtatfin bo* — it does not have to participate in an *eruv* of a courtyard, and is not required to join the *shituf mevo'ot* of an alleyway. *Mai ta'ama?* — Why? *D'lo chazi l'dira* — because it is not fit for dwelling. The principle here differs slightly from the foregoing: this is not primarily about the conceptual definition of a "house," but about the practical requirement that those who *dwell* in the courtyard join together. Since one does not genuinely dwell in so small a structure, one need not participate.

### Eruv Storage

*V'ein manichin bo eruv* — the collected bread for the *eruv* of the courtyard may not be stored in it, because the rule is that the *eruv* must be placed in one of the houses of the courtyard, and this does not qualify.

The *Gemara* then refines this: *aval shituf manichin bo* — however, the bread for the *shituf mevo'ot* (the joining of the alleyways) may be stored in it. *Mai ta'ama? Delo gara michatzer* — because it is no worse than the courtyard itself.

The basic configuration to keep in mind: houses open onto a *chatzer* (courtyard), and courtyards open onto a *mavoi* (alleyway). When the houses of a courtyard join together in an *eruv chatzeirot*, the bread must be placed in one of the houses. When the courtyards of an alleyway join together in a *shituf mevo'ot*, the bread is placed in one of the courtyards. The *Gemara* then notes that the *mishna* can be misread as saying the *eruv chatzeirot* goes in the courtyard itself, but the correct reading, as a *baraita* clarifies, is: *eiruvi chatzeiros b'bayis shebachatzer* — the *eruv chatzeirot* goes in a house within the courtyard; *v'shitufai mavo'os bachatzer shebamavoi* — and the *shituf mevo'ot* goes in a courtyard within the alleyway. Since the *shituf mevo'ot* can be placed in the yard itself, a small structure that is no worse than a yard is equally acceptable for this purpose, even though it is too small to qualify as a house.

---

## Sukkah vs House

### Inference

The *Gemara* has now established that four by four *amot* is the universal halachic minimum for a "house." The question that naturally arises is: does this imply that *Rebbe*'s ruling — that a *sukkah* must be four by four *amot* — is the only opinion that could endorse this *baraita*, meaning the *baraita* follows *Rebbe* and not the Sages?

### Arai vs Keva

*Afilu teima Rabbanan* — even the Sages can agree to this *baraita*. The Sages said that a *sukkah* can be as small as *rosho v'rubo veshulchano* only because of a specific characteristic of *sukkah*: *d'dirat arai hi* — it is a temporary dwelling. The leniency regarding a *sukkah*'s minimum size is grounded in its nature as something other than a permanent residence. But for a permanent dwelling — *d'dirat keva hu* — everyone agrees that the minimum size is four by four *amot*: *d'ee ika arba amot al arba amot dayri inshi* — four by four is the threshold at which people will genuinely dwell in an ongoing, regular fashion, *v'ee lo lo dayri inshi* — and below that threshold, the space is not one in which people would regularly live.

### Temporary Allows

The introduction of this principle generates an important conceptual point: four by four *amot* is the halachic minimum for a permanent dwelling, and this is apparently uncontested. The smaller size — *rosho v'rubo veshulchano* — is sanctioned specifically because a *sukkah* is a *dirat arai*, a temporary dwelling, and therefore can be smaller. This raises a significant question regarding *Rebbe*'s position: if *Rebbe* requires a *sukkah* to be four by four *amot*, it would appear that *Rebbe* treats a *sukkah* not as a temporary dwelling but as a permanent one. This may indeed be the heart of the dispute: perhaps both *Rebbe* and the Sages agree that four by four characterizes a permanent dwelling and that *rosho v'rubo* characterizes a temporary one, and their dispute is precisely whether a *sukkah* must function as a permanent dwelling or whether its temporary character suffices.

This ties back to the opening theme of the *masechta*. The discussion began with the principle that a *sukkah* must not be so tall as to constitute a permanent structure. Now the inverse is being explored: perhaps a *sukkah* must actually achieve a degree of permanence in order to fulfill the obligation of *basukkot teshvu* — you shall dwell in *sukkot* — since genuine dwelling requires a habitable, somewhat permanent space. The tension between *dirat arai* and *dirat keva* as competing definitions of what a *sukkah* must be is thus a thread running through multiple *sugyot* in this *masechta*.

---

## 4x4: House…

### City Joining

The *baraita* continues with additional laws requiring a four by four structure: *ve'ein osin oto ibur bein shtei ayarot* — it cannot serve to join two cities halachically.

The background: each city has a *techum* — a boundary of two thousand *amot* — extending from its edge in all directions.
