The distinction is real and the *baraita* appears to undercut the *migu* claim, since it demonstrates that *sukkah* walls and *Shabbat* walls operate under different standards.

The *gemara* resolves this by clarifying what the *baraita*'s comparison actually addresses. The statement *yesera Shabbat al ha-Suka* is not comparing *Shabbat Sukkot* to *sukkah* on the rest of *Sukkot*; it is comparing general *Shabbat* standards to the *Shabbat Sukkot* context. The configuration with more open than closed space does not work for *Shabbat* during the rest of the year. On *Sukkot*, the very same configuration counts as a *sukkah* for all days, and on *Shabbat Sukkot* specifically, because it is recognized as a *sukkah* wall, the *migu* principle activates and it also counts as a *reshut ha-yachid* for *Shabbat* purposes. The two categories are not permanently equivalent — they converge only on *Shabbat Sukkot*.

### Shabbat Sukkot Exception

The *migu* discussion also generates a converse scenario: *yeseira Sukkah de-alma a-Sukkah de-Shabbat* — something that works for *sukkah* on the rest of *Sukkot* but not for *Shabbat* in general. Should we not also list the reverse case, where something that works for *Shabbat* should work for *sukkah* on *Shabbat Sukkot*? The case in question involves a *sukkah* built over a *mavoi* fitted with a *lechi* — a post that serves as its fourth-wall marker. For *Shabbat*, this *lechi* constitutes a virtual fourth wall, creating a *reshut ha-yachid*. On *Shabbat Sukkot*, therefore, if one placed *schach* only at the front of the *mavoi*, that post — recognized as a wall for *Shabbat* — works as a third wall for *sukkah* on *Shabbat Sukkot*.

The *gemara* explains why this case need not be enumerated separately alongside the *migu* of *sukkah*-to-*Shabbat*: *hashta mikelita l'khamirta amrinan, me'khamirta l'kelita lo kol sheken* — if we say that from the lenient to the stringent — from *sukkah* to *Shabbat* — the *migu* applies, then all the more obviously from the stringent to the lenient — from *Shabbat* to *sukkah* — it applies. The greater *chiddush* is moving from the lenient category to the strict one; the converse follows automatically.

---

## Mavoi & Bira'ot

### Mavoi with Lechi

Rava states: *schach al gabei mavoi she-yesh lo lechi kesherah* — if one places *schach* over a *mavoi* that has a *lechi*, the *sukkah* is *kasher* on *Shabbat Sukkot*. The *mavoi* has two long parallel walls; the *lechi* is recognized for *Shabbat* purposes as a virtual fourth wall. On *Shabbat Sukkot*, the *migu* principle activates: since these walls are valid *Shabbat* boundaries, they count as *sukkah* walls as well, and the structure is a *kasher sukkah*.

### Psei Bira'ot Case

Rava adds a second case: *schach al gabei pasei bira'ot kesherah* — placing *schach* over the frame of a well structure is also *kasher* on *Shabbat Sukkot*. The framework of *pasei bira'ot* consists of four partial corner-posts, each an *amah* by an *amah*, positioned at the corners of a square enclosure, with large open gaps — up to thirteen *amot* — between them. The Rabbis permitted this configuration as a *reshut ha-yachid* specifically to allow drawing water from wells. Placing *schach* over this framework on *Shabbat Sukkot* produces a *kasher sukkah* by *migu*, since the corner-posts are recognized as walls for *Shabbat*.

### Three Cases Explained

The *gemara* asks why all three cases — the open-space *sukkah* from the *baraita*, the *mavoi* case, and the *pasei bira'ot* case — must each be stated explicitly. Could not one or two suffice?

The answer is that each case makes a distinct point. Had we only been told the *mavoi* case — where one begins with two real full walls — one might think the *migu* works there because there is a foundation of two legitimate walls, but that *pasei bira'ot*, which lacks two full walls and offers only corner-posts, would not qualify. Conversely, had we only been told the *pasei bira'ot* case — where four corners are present, framing a full square — one might think that works because all four walls are at least nominally represented, but the *mavoi*, which lacks that complete frame, would not qualify. And had we only been told the two *migu*-from-*Shabbat*-to-*sukkah* cases, one might think *migu* works only from the stringent to the lenient, but not from the lenient *sukkah* to the stringent *Shabbat*. All three cases together, covering both directions of the *migu* and both structural configurations, are therefore necessary.

---

## Walls & Shade

### Shade Dispute

The *gemara* records a *tannaitic* dispute about whether *sukkah* walls must block sunlight. The view of the Rabbis is that the requirement of shade applies only to the *schach*, not to the walls: *chamata machmat schach ve-lo machmat defanot* — the concern about excessive sunlight penetrating the *sukkah* is a concern about the *schach*, and the walls need provide no shade whatsoever. Rabbi Yoshia disagrees, ruling *af machmat defanot* — even the walls must provide shade.

### Parochet Source

Abaye transmits the reasoning of Rabbi Yoshia in the name of Rabbi Yeimar bar Shmaya. Rabbi Yoshia derives his position from the verse *ve-sakkota al ha-aron et ha-parochet* — "and you shall cover the ark with the *parochet*." The *parochet*, the curtain of the Sanctuary, is described here as a wall, and yet the verb used is from the root of *schach*, *sakkota*. This indicates, in Rabbi Yoshia's view, that walls are also a form of *schach* — they too carry the shading function. A wall worthy of a *sukkah* must therefore function like *schach* in providing shade, just as a normal dwelling's walls block out sunlight.

The Rabbis respond that the verse does not imply that the wall functions as *schach*; rather, it describes folding the top edge of the *parochet* slightly inward over the ark, so that the very tip of the curtain forms a small *schach*-like covering. The wall of the *parochet* itself does not bear the *schach* function — only the bent-over top does. Hence, walls of a *sukkah* are not required to block the sun. One might naturally ask whether Rabbi Yoshia's position would require walls to be constructed from the same materials as kosher *schach* — at least one *Rishon* does indeed draw that conclusion — but the *gemara* does not pursue that implication here.

---

## Permanent Dwelling

### Abaye's Collection

At the close of the *daf*, Abaye introduces a sweeping observation: a significant number of *Tannaim* across widely different discussions of *sukkah* — Rebbi, Rabbi Yoshia, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, Rabban Gamliel, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Eliezer, and others — all share a common underlying premise: *kuhlhu sevira lehu Sukkah dirat keva beinan* — they all hold that a *sukkah* must be a *dirat keva*, a permanent dwelling structure. This is not to say they agree on the specific consequences of that principle; different *tannaim* draw different halachic lines from it. But what Abaye identifies is a shared conceptual foundation: the *sukkah* is not a flimsy temporary shelter but something more enduringly house-like. The various stringencies they espouse are different expressions of this single animating idea.

### Rabbi's Dimension

The case of Rebbi: *kol Sukkah she-ein bah arba amot al arba amot pesulah* — any *sukkah* that does not measure four *amot* by four *amot* is *pasul*. The standard ruling requires only seven *tefachim* by seven *tefachim*, which is considerably smaller. Rebbi's insistence on four by four *amot* reflects his understanding that a *sukkah* must approximate the dimensions of a real permanent dwelling.

### Rabbi Yehuda Height

The case of Rabbi Yehuda: in the first *mishnah* of the tractate, the ruling is that a *sukkah* taller than twenty *amot* is *pasul*, because at that height one does not notice the *schach* and is therefore not dwelling meaningfully beneath it. Rabbi Yehuda declares it *kasher*. A *sukkah* of more than twenty *amot* can only function as a dwelling if one envisions it as a truly permanent structure — the kind of substantial building where great height is a mark of grandeur rather than a halachic defect.

### Rabbi Yoshia Opacity

The case of Rabbi Yoshia has already been discussed: requiring the walls to provide shade reflects the expectation that a *sukkah* resemble an actual house, whose walls protect its occupants from the elements including direct sunlight.

### Rabbi Shimon Walls

Finally, the case of Rabbi Shimon: where the consensus is two walls plus a *tefach*, Rabbi Shimon requires three complete walls plus a *tefach*. As the *gemara* noted earlier with its citation from Yeshayahu, the model of protection Rabbi Shimon has in mind is not merely shade but shelter from wind and rain — the kind of protection a genuine permanent structure provides. This, like the positions of the other *tannaim* in Abaye's collection, is an expression of the fundamental principle that a *sukkah* must aspire to the character of *dirat keva*.

---

---

# Sukkah 8

## Abaye's Tannaim

### Intro: Dirat Keva

Yesterday's discussion introduced a theme that lies at the heart of the laws of *sukkah*: Abaye collected a series of *tannaim* — various positions scattered across different *mishnayot* and *braitot* — all of whom, from his perspective, make greater demands of the *sukkah* that reflect an understanding of it as a *dirat keva*, a more permanent structure. This tension runs through the entire tractate. On one hand, the *sukkah* is by definition temporary — that is precisely what distinguishes it from one's house. On the other hand, the *sukkah* is a substitute for one's house, and so perhaps it must be more house-like. Abaye identified a range of *tannaitic* positions, each with its own unique reasoning, but all of them interpretable as rooted in the concept of the *sukkah* as demanding some greater degree of permanence or structure.

One point is worth flagging at the outset: even among those who hold that a *sukkah* must be more *keva*, the *schach* remains irreducibly temporary. As *Tosafot* noted at the very beginning of the tractate, one may have permanent walls but never a permanent roof. Whatever degree of house-like permanence the *tannaim* require, everyone presumably agrees that the *schach* is what fundamentally distinguishes the *sukkah* from a house. With that in mind, we turn to Abaye's list itself, picking up from the discussion on 7b.

### Rabbi's Requirements

The first *tanna* in Abaye's collection is Rabbi himself. As we learn in a *braita*: *Rabbi omer kol sukkah she-ein ba arba al arba amot pesulah* — any *sukkah* that does not contain four by four *amot* is invalid. Rabbi's requirement is not the standard minimum of seven *tefachim* by seven *tefachim* sufficient to hold one's head, most of one's body (*rosho ve-rubo*), and a small table (*shulchano*). He demands something considerably larger and more substantial. This, in Abaye's reading, reflects a vision of the *sukkah* as requiring a more serious, house-like size.

### Rabbi Yoshiya

Rabbi Yoshiya, as discussed previously, requires that the walls themselves provide shade. A house with transparent walls is not a house. If the *sukkah* is to approximate a more permanent dwelling, its walls must function like real walls — providing actual shade. In this way, Rabbi Yoshiya's demand parallels that of Rabbi Shimon, who requires fuller wall coverage, in that both insist the walls serve a genuinely house-like function, not merely a nominal halachic one.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda presents a slightly different case. As the *Mishnah* records: *sukkah she-hi gevohah lemala me-esrim amah pesulah ve-Rabbi Yehuda machshir* — a *sukkah* higher than twenty *amot* is invalid, but Rabbi Yehuda permits it. This is worth noting: Rabbi Yehuda does not require a *sukkah* to be higher than twenty *amot*, he merely allows it. He is thus the least demanding of the *tannaim* in Abaye's collection, and in a sense his position sits somewhat differently from the others — they impose additional requirements, whereas he removes a restriction. Nevertheless, Abaye includes him because the willingness to validate a grand, imposing structure reflects an openness to the *sukkah* as a more permanent and substantial dwelling.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon's position concerns the number of walls required. In the *braita*: *be-rishona u-shtayim ve-hashlishit afilu tefach* — the standard opinion holds that two full walls plus a third measuring even a *tefach* suffice. *Rabbi Shimon omer: gimel ke-hilchatan ve-dalet afilu tefach* — Rabbi Shimon requires three complete walls plus a fourth measuring even a *tefach*. Like Rabbi Yoshiya's demand that the walls provide shade, this requirement insists that the walls play a more genuinely enclosing, house-like role. Whether the emphasis is on full enclosure or on the walls' shading function, both *tannaim* push the *sukkah* in the direction of a real structure.

### Rabban Gamliel

The *braita* records a dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva: *ha-oseh sukkato be-rosh ha-agalah o be-rosh ha-sefinah* — one who makes his *sukkah* on top of a wagon or on top of a ship. *Rabban Gamliel posel ve-Rabbi Akiva machshir* — Rabban Gamliel invalidates it and Rabbi Akiva validates it. The reason for Rabban Gamliel's position is structural instability. *Tosafot* notes that the case of a ship is particularly problematic because the winds at sea are far stronger than on dry land, and such a structure may not be able to withstand them even if it would stand in port. The wagon too, bouncing along the road, lacks the stability of a fixed structure. Something whose continued integrity is precarious does not satisfy Rabban Gamliel's standard. In Abaye's framework, this is a demand for stability and permanence, even if a different dimension of it than the other *tannaim* emphasize.

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

The *Mishnah*'s dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerns whether a *sukkah* must accommodate one's table as well as one's body: *mi she-haya rosho ve-rubo ba-sukkah ve-shulchano be-toch ha-bayit Beit Shammai poslin ve-Beit Hillel machshirin* — if a person's head and most of his body are in the *sukkah* but his table remains in the house, Beit Shammai invalidates it and Beit Hillel validates it. The gap between these positions may not seem dramatic, but it is real. Even if the *sukkah* only needs to be a *dirat arai*, a temporary dwelling, it still needs to be a *dirah* — a place where one actually lives. If one's table is in the house, one will constantly be running back inside; one is never truly dwelling in the *sukkah*. Abaye places Beit Shammai in this collection, though it should be noted that conceptually Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai are not far apart — they differ only in degree. And since we *pasken* like Beit Hillel, that does not necessarily mean we rule that the *sukkah* is a *dirat keva*, as Beit Shammai represents the most minimal of these demands.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer's position, recorded in the *Mishnah*, concerns the shape of the *sukkah*: *ha-oseh sukkato k'min tzrif* — one who makes his *sukkah* like a teepee — *o she-samcha l'kotel* — or leans it against a wall (a lean-to). *Rashi* adds that the category may also include something like a structure where the roof flows continuously from the walls without any clear demarcation — perhaps like an igloo — where there is no structurally distinguishable line between wall and roof. *Rabbi Eliezer posel lefi she-ein la gag* — Rabbi Eliezer invalidates such a *sukkah* because it has no real roof, even if there may be a *halachic* roof present. *Va-chachamim machshirin* — the *Rabbanan* validate it. In Abaye's reading, the demand for a real, distinguishable roof and walls is another dimension of requiring the *sukkah* to be more house-like.

### Acherim: Corners

The final position in Abaye's collection is that of *acherim*, typically understood as Rabbi Meir: *acherim omrim sukkah asuya k'shuvach pesulah lefi she-ein la zaviyot* — a circular *sukkah* is invalid because it has no corners. Who, after all, lives in a circular house? A *sukkah* without corners lacks the defining architectural feature of a normal human dwelling, and *acherim* therefore disqualify it, even if it has a proper roof and adequate dimensions.

Taken together, all of these positions — requiring greater size, functional walls, structural stability, a distinguishable roof, complete wall coverage, and proper corners — can be read as different articulations of the same underlying orientation: a *sukkah* must be more house-like. The specific *halachic* translation differs from *tanna* to *tanna*, but the common direction is clear.

### Gemara Principle

It is worth noting a general principle that is not uncommon in *halachic* literature: when a *Gemara* has an *amora* collect multiple *tannaim* and declare that they all share a common *shittah*, there is a tendency to understand this as a move to bracket that *shittah* out of normative *halacha*. Assembling them under one heading signals, in some readings, that we do not *pasken* like them. The *Gemara* does not say this explicitly here, but awareness of this pattern is valuable context for evaluating Abaye's collection.

---

## Circular Sukkah Math

### Rabbi Yochanan

Having just discussed the disqualification of a circular *sukkah* by *acherim*, the *Gemara* pivots to explore a different question: what size must a circular *sukkah* be in order to be valid? Rabbi Yochanan states: *sukkah asuya k'kivshan* — a *sukkah* made like a furnace, meaning a circular *sukkah* — *im yesh be-hekeifa k'dei le-sheiv ba esrim ve-arba bnei adam, kesherah* — if its circumference is sufficient to seat twenty-four people, it is valid; if not, it is invalid.

### Four-by-Four Problem

The *Gemara* immediately raises a question. We *pasken* that the minimum *sukkah* size is seven *tefachim* by seven *tefachim*, but Rabbi Yochanan's number — twenty-four people — already implies we are operating under a larger minimum. The *Gemara* therefore assumes: *k'man? k'Rebbi, de-amar kol sukkah she-ein ba arba amot al arba amot pesulah* — we are following Rabbi's opinion that a *sukkah* must be four by four *amot*.

Now the problem becomes quantitative. If a person occupies one *amah* of circumference space, and we need a circle whose internal diameter is four *amot*, then the circumference of that circle should only be twelve — since the *Gemara* estimates *pi* at three, and three times four is twelve. Where, then, does Rabbi Yochanan's twenty-four come from? The *Gemara* considers this step by step.

It begins: *kama meruba yoser al ha-igul? reviya* — how much more is the circumference of the square than the circumference of the circle inscribed in it? A quarter more. This is the *Gemara*'s first calculation: if a circle has a diameter of one unit, its circumference is three (using *pi* = 3); the square that contains it has a circumference of four. So the square's circumference exceeds the circle's by one-quarter. If a four-by-four square has a circumference of sixteen, then the circle inside it has a circumference of twelve — which is exactly the *Gemara*'s opening figure.

### Square in Circle

But here the *Gemara* corrects itself: *hanei milei be-igula de-nafik mi-go ribu'a* — that calculation applies when the circle fits inside the square. What we actually need is the reverse: a square that fits inside the circle. The *sukkah* is circular, and we must ensure that a four-by-four square can fit within it. *Aval ribu'a de-nafik mi-go igul ba-ei tefei* — for a square inscribed in a circle, the circle must be larger still. A circle whose circumference equals the perimeter of the surrounding square is not the same as a circle large enough to contain that square inside it.

### Diagonal Calculation

The key is the diagonal of the square. To inscribe a four-by-four square within a circle, the diameter of that circle must equal the diagonal of the square. By the Pythagorean theorem — *a* squared plus *b* squared equals *c* squared — where *a* and *b* are both four, the diagonal is four times the square root of two. This diagonal becomes the diameter of the required circle, and the circumference of that circle is three (our estimate of *pi*) times this diameter — three times four times the square root of two.

### 1.4 Diagonal

The *Gemara* addresses the square root of two by means of a well-known approximation: *kol amsa be-ribu'a, amsa ve-trei chumshai be-alakhsona* — any unit square has a diagonal of one and two-fifths, that is, 1.4. This is the *Gemara*'s estimate of the square root of two. It is, in fact, a quite good approximation: the actual value is approximately 1.414.

### 16.8 vs 24

With this in hand, we can now calculate. The diagonal of the four-by-four square is four times 1.4, which is 5.6. That is the diameter of the circle. The circumference of that circle is three times 5.6, which is 16.8. The *Gemara* confirms this: *bishivsar naki chumsha sagya* — seventeen minus a fifth, meaning 16.8, should be sufficient. So why did Rabbi Yochanan say twenty-four?

The *Gemara* tries to invoke the principle of *lo dak* — imprecision, rounding — but immediately rejects it in this context. One can accept a minor rounding; going from 16.8 to 24 is not a minor imprecision. Moreover, if we say 24 is sufficient when the true requirement is 16.8, we are being lenient, not stringent. *Eimar de-amrinan lo dak pursa — tuva mi amrinan?* — We can say he rounded a little, but can we say he rounded that much? And *lekula mi amrinan lo dak* — we do not invoke imprecision in the lenient direction.

### People Sitting

At this point Mar Kashisha son of Rav Chisda offers a solution to Rav Ashi: *mi savrat gavra be-amta yasiv? tlata gavri be-trei amata yasvin* — who said one person occupies one *amah*? Three people sit in every two *amot*. On this assumption, a circumference of 16.8 *amot* would accommodate not 16.8 people but rather 16.8 times one and a half, which is 25.2 people — close to 24. Working backwards, the *Gemara* then calculates that 24 people at three per two *amot* corresponds to a circumference of 16 *amot*. We needed 16.8 — so 24 people gets us a circumference of 16. That is still a *kula*, still less than needed. And indeed: *eimar de-amrinan lo dak — lekula mi amrinan lo dak?* Even in this new framework we are still rounding leniently.

The *Gemara* then presents another approach, attributed to Rav Assi: *le-olam gavra be-amah yatvei* — actually, one person does occupy one *amah*, as originally assumed. But *Rabbi Yochanan mekom gavrei lo kachshiv* — Rabbi Yochanan is not counting the space that the people sit in as interior space. The people are sitting on the outside of the circle, surrounding the *sukkah*. When we measure twenty-four people seated around the outside of the *sukkah*, the diameter we calculate is the outer circle — including the bodies of the people. Subtracting one *amah* on each side (since each person occupies one *amah*), the inner diameter of the *sukkah* itself is 5.6 plus 2, that is 7.6 *amot* in diameter. This is being imprecise — rounding the inner diameter up slightly to 6 *amot* — but now the rounding is *lechumra*, in the stringent direction. An inner diameter of 6 *amot* yields a circumference of 18. We needed 16.8. We are demanding slightly more than necessary, and that kind of imprecision is entirely acceptable.

The *Gemara* confirms: *haynu lo dak ve-lechumra lo dak* — this is the acceptable form of imprecision, rounding up for stringency.

### Area Ratio

*Rabbanan de-Kesari*, and some say *Dayanei de-Kesari* (the judges of Caesarea), offer a different statement: *igula de-nafik mi-go ribu'a, riv'a* — a circle inscribed in a square is a quarter less, that is, the ratio of circumference is 3 to 4, as discussed. But *ribu'a de-nafik mi-go igula, palga* — a square inscribed in a circle is related by a half. The *Gemara* rejects this geometrically: *ve-lo hi — de-kachazeina de-la havi kulei hai* — we see that the ratio is not that large.

However, *Tosafot* and the *Ravad* observe that the *Dayanei de-Kesari* may in fact be correct — and indeed have provided the clearest explanation of Rabbi Yochanan's twenty-four — but they are speaking about area, not circumference. If Rabbi Yochanan intended his twenty-four as a measure of area rather than circumference, the problem resolves elegantly. A four-by-four square has an area of sixteen. What is the area of the circle circumscribed around it?

If the square is two by two, its diagonal — and hence the circle's diameter — is two times the square root of two, giving a radius of the square root of two. The area of the circle is *pi* times *r* squared: *pi* times two, which using *pi* = 3 gives an area of six. The area of the square is four. The ratio is 4 to 6, or 2 to 3. Scaling up to a four-by-four square with area sixteen, the enclosing circle has an area of twenty-four. This is precisely the 2-to-3 ratio the *Dayanei de-Kesari* described, and it perfectly explains Rabbi Yochanan's number.

The *Gemara* apparently understood Rabbi Yochanan to be speaking about circumference, and therefore found the *Dayanei de-Kesari*'s ratio too extreme to be geometrically accurate in that context. But if one understands the statement as referring to area, the ratio is exact, and the explanation is strikingly simple: a four-by-four square has an area of sixteen, and the circle that contains it has an area of twenty-four.

### Tosafot Geometry

*Tosafot* appends two remarkable geometric demonstrations to this *sugya*. The first, visible in the illustration at the bottom-left of amud 1, demonstrates that 1.4 is a slightly imprecise estimate for the square root of two. Consider a ten-by-ten square, subdivided into a grid of one hundred units. Connecting the midpoints of each side creates an inner square rotated forty-five degrees; this inner square contains exactly half the area of the outer square, so its area is fifty. Now, each quadrant of the outer square is a five-by-five square. The diagonal of a five-by-five square, at the ratio of 1.4, would be five times 1.4, which is seven. A square with side seven has area forty-nine — not fifty. The one-unit discrepancy demonstrates the slight inaccuracy of the 1.4 estimate. The actual square root of two is approximately 1.414, and the demonstration makes the imprecision vivid.

*Tosafot*'s second illustration anticipates, in a striking way, the integral calculus — centuries before its formal development. To determine the area of a circle, *Tosafot* imagines the circle as composed of an infinite number of concentric rings, or equivalently, infinite radial line segments. Cutting all these segments at their midpoints and laying the two halves out flat produces a triangle. The base of the triangle is the circumference of the circle; the height is the radius. The area of that triangle — one-half times base times height, or one-half times circumference times radius — gives the area of the circle. *Tosafot* realizes this geometrically by folding and rearranging the segments into a rectangle, from which the formula for the area of a circle can be derived.

---

## Smelter's Sukkot

### Inner/Outer Structure

The *Gemara* now turns to a different scenario. Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Meir states: *shtei sukkot shel tzaltarim zu lifnim mi-zu* — if there are two *sukkot* of smelters, one inner and one outer — *ha-penimit eina sukkah* — the inner one cannot serve as a *sukkah* — *de-chayevet be-mezuzah* — because it is obligated in a *mezuzah*. The inner structure is where the smelter actually lives throughout the year; it is his house. Even if it is structurally built like a *sukkah* — perhaps with temporary walls and proper *schach* — it is where he resides, and therefore it cannot be used as his *sukkah* for the festival. *Ve-ha-chitzonah sukkah* — the outer structure, his shop, may serve as a *sukkah* — *u-peturah min ha-mezuzah* — and it is ordinarily exempt from a *mezuzah*, since no one lives there year-round.

This is a striking teaching. Structurally, the inner dwelling may be perfectly constructed. But the *Gemara* makes clear that the validity of a *sukkah* depends not only on structure but on usage: if a space functions as your permanent home throughout the year, you cannot fulfill the *mitzvah* there. The outer room, which is normally a shop and not a dwelling, is precisely the right type of space.

### Gatehouse Rejected

The *Gemara* questions the exemption of the outer structure from *mezuzah*: *de-havei chitzoniyah ke-veit shaar ha-penimit ve-titchayev be-mezuzah* — let the outer room be considered a gatehouse for the inner one, and therefore also obligated in a *mezuzah*. An antechamber that leads into a house requires a *mezuzah* alongside the house it serves; why would the outer shop not function as such an antechamber?

### Temporary Status

The *Gemara* rejects this: *mishum de-lo kvia* — because these structures are not sufficiently fixed. As *Rashi* explains, the concept of a *beit shaar*, a gatehouse obligated in *mezuzah*, applies to substantial, distinguished houses that naturally have entranceways serving them. A structure that is sufficiently temporary in character — even if someone lives in it — does not rise to the level of requiring a proper antechamber. The outer shop, being even less substantial, cannot be considered the antechamber to an inner structure that is itself impermanent. Consequently, it requires no *mezuzah*.

The broader upshot of this *sugya* is significant: even structural conformity to *sukkah* requirements is insufficient if the space is one's year-round residence. The identity of a *sukkah* is shaped by how it is used, not only by how it is built.

---

## Builder Intent

### Ganbakh Cases

The *Gemara* now turns to a question about who may build a *sukkah* and what intentions are required. A *braita* is cited introducing the mnemonic *Ganbakh*: *sukkot goyim* — a *sukkah* built by or for non-Jews; *sukkot nashim* — built for women; *sukkot behemah* — built for animals; *sukkot kutim* — built by or for Samaritans. *Sukkah mikol makom kesherah* — any such *sukkah* is valid — *u-vilvad she-tehei mesukakhat ke-hilkhatah* — as long as it has proper *schach*. The identity of the builder, the intended beneficiary, and the purpose for which it was built are all irrelevant. No intention to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* is required of the builder. No Jewish builder is required. No Jewish beneficiary is required. What matters is whether the structure meets the technical requirements.

### Shade Intent

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *mai ke-hilkhatah* — what does "proper *schach*" mean in this context? Surely the *schach* must always comply with basic requirements — this seems to add nothing. Rav Chisda explains: *vehu she-asah le-tzeil* — it must have been constructed for the purpose of shade. This is a critical and precise point. We do not require that the *schach* be placed with the intent to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*. We do not require that the *schach* be placed for the benefit of Jews, or for any religiously significant purpose. But the *schach* must have been put in place for shade — it must function as a covering intended to provide shade. This is not merely a technical requirement about materials; it is a minimal purposive requirement that the covering be understood as a covering. Something that happens to be overhead but was placed there for an entirely different purpose — not as a roof, not to provide shade — does not have the identity of *schach*. The concept of *schach* is, at its core, a shade-providing covering, and without that purpose present at the time of its installation, the designation does not attach.

### Rakbash Cases

The *braita* continues with a second list, organized around the mnemonic *Rakbash*: *sukkot ro-im* — *sukkot* built by shepherds tending their flocks; *sukkot kayatzim* — built by people watching produce drying in the fields; *sukkot burganin* — built by city watchmen; *sukkot shomrei peirot* — built by fruit-watchers. All of these are structures built by working people who move around and erect temporary shelters in the course of their work. *Sukkah mikol makom kesherah* — any such *sukkah* is valid — *u-vilvad she-tehei mesukakhat ke-hilkhatah* — as long as the *schach* is proper. And again, Rav Chisda: *vehu she-asah le-tzeil* — it was made for shade.

### List Ordering

The *Gemara* observes that each *braita* contains a catchall phrase — *sukkah mikol makom* — and asks what that phrase comes to include. In the *Ganbakh* list, *sukkah mikol makom* comes to include even the *Rakbash* cases. In the *Rakbash* list, *sukkah mikol makom* comes to include even the *Ganbakh* cases. What accounts for each *tanna*'s starting point?

The *tanna* who leads with *Ganbakh* regards those cases as the more prominent or more obvious: *de-kfiei* — they tend to be relatively fixed structures. Non-Jews building *sukkot* for non-Jews, or permanent-looking shelters built for animals or Samaritans, are substantial enough that one might never have doubted their validity — and yet the *tanna* includes them, and then extends even further to include the *Rakbash* cases, which are definitively impermanent and portable.

The *tanna* who leads with *Rakbash* regards those cases differently: *alima leih Rakbash de-vnei chiyyuvah ninhu* — the *Rakbash* builders are themselves liable in *mitzvot*, they are Jewish men building shelters in the course of their labor. That is perhaps the clearer category to start with. The *chiddush* is that even the *Ganbakh* cases — structures built by or for those not obligated in the *mitzvah* — are valid.

### Conclusion

The two lists thus approach the question from opposite default assumptions, but they converge on the same *halachic* conclusion: a *sukkah* need not be built by someone obligated in the *mitzvah*, need not be built for the sake of *sukkot*, and need not even be built for Jewish occupants. The singular non-negotiable requirement is that the *schach* must have been placed there for the purpose of shade. That purpose — shade — is the essential identity of *schach*, and it alone is what determines whether the covering qualifies. Everything else is secondary.

---

---

# Sukkah 9

## Beis Shammai vs. Beis Hi…

### Old Sukkah Definition

The ninth daf of Masechta Sukkah opens as a direct continuation of the preceding discussion, which concluded with the concept of *sukkah ganvach* — an acronym encompassing sukkos made by non-Jews (*goyim*), women (*nashim*), and animals (*behemah*). The ruling established there is that such a *sukkah* is *kosher*: no particular intent is required for the *sukkah* as an object of *mitzvah* to be valid. The sole requirement pertaining to the *sechach* is that it must have been placed there for the purpose of shade (*tzel*).

The *mishnah* on daf 9a continues this theme by presenting a dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel regarding what is called a *sukkah yeshanah* — an old *sukkah*. This refers not merely to a *sukkah* that was built for *Sukkos* and left standing, but more precisely to a structure that was built months earlier for some entirely other purpose. Beis Shammai declares such a *sukkah* invalid (*poslin*), while Beis Hillel declares it valid (*machshirin*), consistent with their general position that a *sukkah* need not be constructed with any thought of the holiday in mind.

The *mishnah* then defines what constitutes an "old" *sukkah*: any structure built more than thirty days before *Sukkos* (*kodem lachag shloshim yom*). Rashi explains that within thirty days of the *chag*, a person naturally begins studying the laws of the upcoming holiday, and therefore even an unstated intent may be presumed. Alternatively, one might argue that the timing itself confers the designation: a Jew who constructs a hut within thirty days of *Sukkos* has, by that very fact, built something that is objectively a *sukkas hachag*, regardless of his explicit thoughts at the time.

The *mishnah* closes with a further qualification: *aval im asah l'shem chag* — but if one built the *sukkah* explicitly for the sake of the holiday, *afilu mi-techilas ha-shanah kesherah* — even if it was built from the very beginning of the year, it is valid. "Beginning of the year" here does not mean a mere fifteen days prior; it means even a full year earlier. The operative factor for Beis Shammai, then, is that the *sukkah* must be identifiable as a *sukkas hachag*, a *sukkah* for the *yom tov*. This identity can be established in one of two ways: either through explicit intent at the time of construction, in which case even a year's advance is acceptable, or through the objective circumstance of having been built within thirty days of the holiday, in which case no conscious intent is needed.

Beis Hillel, as we saw in the previous daf, requires none of this. A *sukkah* built by non-Jews, built to shelter animals, or constructed with no connection whatsoever to the holiday remains fully valid for the *mitzvah*, provided only that it was built to provide shade.

It is worth noting what Tosafos adds here from the Yerushalmi. Tosafos on the words *sukkah yeshanah* cites a Yerushalmi that rules: *tzarich l'chadesh bah davar* — even according to Beis Hillel, if one wishes to use an old *sukkah* not built for the purpose of the *chag*, one must do something new. The *chavrayah* in the Yerushalmi say one must add a *tefach* of new *sechach* for the sake of *Sukkos*; Rabbi Yosi says even a minimal addition suffices (*kol she-hu*), though he qualifies that this minimal strip must extend across the entire length or width of the *sukkah*.

The Yerushalmi is thus pulling back from the full permissiveness of Beis Hillel as recorded in the Bavli. The Bavli's position is that a *sukkah* completely lacking any identity as a *yom tov sukkah* is nonetheless valid according to Beis Hillel, with no requirement to add or designate anything. The Yerushalmi introduces the notion that even according to Beis Hillel some token act of designation is appropriate — or perhaps even strictly required. This raises a genuine practical *halachic* question: how much weight do we give this Yerushalmi *l'halacha*? Consider, for example, a traveler who encounters a gazebo with a thatched roof in a park where no Jews reside. In principle, with appropriate application of *gud asik* or similar constructs regarding the walls, such a structure might technically qualify as a *sukkah*. Yet no Jew will be adding new *sechach* to designate it for the holiday. Whether the Yerushalmi's requirement is strictly mandated or merely a preferable practice — given that the Bavli makes no such demand — remains an open question *l'halacha*.

### Beis Shammai's Intent

The *gemara* proceeds to ask: *mai ta'amayhu d'Beis Shammai* — what is the textual basis for Beis Shammai's position that a *sukkah* must be built with the *chag* in mind? The *gemara* cites the verse: *chag ha-sukkos shivat yamim l'Hashem* — the festival of *Sukkos*, seven days, to God. Just as earlier in the *masechta* the word *sukkos* in a verse was read not merely as the name of the holiday but as a statement about the object itself, so too here. Reading the verse as *sukkah l'Hashem* — a *sukkah* for God — and reading *chag ha-sukkos* as requiring a *sukkas hachag*, Beis Shammai derives that the *sukkah* must be constructed as a *sukkah* for the *yom tov*. It cannot be a neutral hut; it must be identifiable as a *sukkas hachag*. *Sukkah asuyah l'shem chag ba'inan* — we require a *sukkah* that is made for the sake of the *chag*.

### Beis Hillel's Position

Beis Hillel, however, requires this verse for an entirely different derivation. The *gemara* states that Beis Hillel uses the verse for what Rav Sheshet taught in the name of Rabbi Akiva: *minayin l'atzei sukkah she'asurin kol shivah* — from where do we know that the wood of a *sukkah* is forbidden for personal benefit throughout all seven days?

The principle invoked here is ordinarily called *huktzah l'mitzvato* — an object designated for a *mitzvah* may not be diverted to another use. One may not, for instance, take one's *esrog* during *Sukkos* and process it into jam, nor may one remove oil designated for the *menorah* for other purposes. The verse *chag ha-sukkos shivat yamim l'Hashem* establishes that the *sukkah* is consecrated to God and therefore forbidden for personal benefit throughout the seven days.

A *baraisa* elaborates on this with the striking formulation of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira: *k'shem she-chal shem shamayim al ha-chagigah, kach chal shem shamayim al ha-sukkah* — just as God's name descends upon the *korban chagigah* (which is sanctified to God), so too God's name descends upon the *sukkah*. The reading here focuses not on the word *sukkos* but on the word *chag*: since *chag* is often read by *Chazal* as a reference to the *korban chagigah*, the juxtaposition of *chag* and *sukkos* implies that just as the *chagigah* is sanctified, so too the *sukkah* is sanctified. This is the use Beis Hillel makes of the verse — not to require that the *sukkah* be designated as a *sukkas hachag*, but to establish its sanctified status once it is in use.

There is something striking about this position. Beis Hillel maintains on one hand that a *sukkah* requires no designation whatsoever as a *yom tov sukkah* — any hut, built by anyone, for any purpose, suffices — yet on the other hand holds that once it is actually being used as a *sukkah*, the structure becomes almost *kadosh*, sanctified like a *korban*. One might ask: does this mean that every hut in the world becomes forbidden for benefit on *Sukkos* because in theory it could serve as a *sukkah*? Presumably not. The sanctification takes effect when the structure is actually used as a *sukkas hachag* — when one enters it and uses it for the *mitzvah* — not merely because it is theoretically eligible. Still, the irony is apparent: Beis Hillel, the more lenient voice on the question of designation, articulates an almost more potent sanctification of the *sukkah* once it enters use.

### Verse Interpretation

The *gemara* then asks: does Beis Shammai not also need the verse for the *chagigah* derivation — to establish that the *sukkah* is off-limits for personal benefit? The *gemara* answers: *ein hachi nami* — indeed, Beis Shammai does need it for that purpose as well. The word *chag* tells us the *sukkah* is like a *korban chagigah* and is forbidden for benefit. But then the *gemara* asks: if so, from where does Beis Shammai derive the requirement that the *sukkah* be designated for the *chag*? The answer is that Beis Shammai relies on a second verse: *chag ha-sukkos ta'aseh lecha shivat yamim* — the festival of *Sukkos* you shall make for yourself, seven days. Here again the juxtaposition of *chag* and *sukkah* is significant. Rashi reads the verse in a way that intermingles the terms — *sukkos ta'aseh lecha* for the *chag* — deriving that the *sukkah* one makes must be made for the sake of the *chag*. *Sukka asuyah l'shem chag ba'inan.*

### Chol HaMoed Construction

Beis Hillel, however, reads the second verse differently. The emphasis for Beis Hillel falls not on the juxtaposition of *chag* and *sukkah* as a requirement of designation, but on the phrase *shivat yamim* — seven days. This teaches that one may construct a *sukkah* at any point during the seven days, including *chol ha-moed*. *Ha-hu mibayei lei l'oseh sukkah b'chol ha-moed* — Beis Hillel uses the verse to permit building a *sukkah* even during the intermediate days of the festival.

The *gemara* notes that Beis Shammai, by contrast, holds like Rabbi Eliezer, who maintains that one may not build a *sukkah* on *chol ha-moed*. Rabbi Eliezer's broader position — which we will encounter later in the *masechta* — is that a *sukkah* must truly function as one's home for the entire seven days, requiring two full meals per day throughout the week. A derivative of this is that one cannot build the *sukkah* on *chol ha-moed*, since that would mean one has not dwelt in it for all seven days. Saying that Beis Shammai aligns with Rabbi Eliezer is not a surprising *chiddush*, since Rabbi Eliezer is generally understood to be of the school of Beis Shammai.

What emerges from this analysis is a coherent cluster of positions around Beis Shammai: the *sukkah* must be built before the holiday, it must be designated as a *sukkas hachag*, and it must stand for all seven days. Each requirement points in the same direction — toward a *sukkah* that is intentional, serious, and fully identified as a permanent-for-the-week substitute for the home. Beis Hillel is radically liberal by contrast: any hut, built by anyone, for any reason, erected even mid-festival, fulfills the obligation.

### Chal Shem Shamayim

It is worth pausing on the concept of *chal shem shamayim al ha-sukkah* before proceeding. There is an important difference between this formulation and the standard rabbinic concept of *huktzah l'mitzvato*. The ordinary notion of *huktzah l'mitzvato* is generally understood to be rabbinic in origin, and its operative logic is essentially: do not divert the object away from its designated use for the *mitzvah*. Under that framework, what is forbidden is removing the object from its *mitzvah* function — taking the *esrog* to make jam, for instance, since one still needs it for the *mitzvah* of *lulav* and *esrog*.

The language of *chal shem shamayim*, by contrast, is grounded in *pesukim* and sounds far more absolute — an almost biblical-level sanctification. This has led a major strand of *rishonim* to understand that *sukkah* occupies a distinctive category: not merely the standard rabbinic *huktzah l'mitzvato*, but a heightened, biblical concept unique to *sukkah*, which renders the *sechach* (and perhaps the entire structure) more categorically off-limits.

This raises the question posed by a student: if the walls and *sechach* are forbidden for benefit, how can one sit inside the *sukkah* at all? The answer must be that the forbidden benefit is not the natural use of the *sukkah* as a dwelling — the shade, the shelter, the very purpose for which one sits inside. The prohibition must be defined more narrowly: deriving benefit in a manner that redirects the object away from its function, or benefit that is wholly extraneous to the *sukkah*'s role as a *sukkah*. Whether that is the correct limiting principle remains part of the broader discussion, but the point stands that *chal shem shamayim* cannot mean that sitting under *sechach* is itself forbidden.

There is also a fascinating interpretive dimension to why *sukkah* specifically would carry this stronger formulation. The *sechach*, as has been noted in this *masechta*, evokes the *ananei kavod* — the clouds of glory that accompanied Israel in the wilderness. If the *sechach* represents the divine cloud, the manifestation of God's presence that hovered over Israel, then *chal shem shamayim al ha-sukkah* is not merely a legal formula — it captures something deeply real about what the *sechach* symbolizes. The name of Heaven literally descends upon the *sechach* because the *sechach* represents the very medium through which God's presence rested upon the people.

There remains a further debate among the *rishonim* as to whether this concept of *chal shem shamayim* applies only to the *sechach* or extends to the walls of the *sukkah* as well. Given that the primary vehicle of the *sukkah* as a dwelling — and its primary symbolic resonance — is the *sechach*, there is a strong argument to confine the heightened sanctification to the *sechach* alone.

---

## Leshmah Principle

### Tzitzis Leshmah

The discussion now turns to a broader question raised by *Abaye*: does Beis Hillel not hold of the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav? What is that ruling?

Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that if one made *tzitzis* from *kotztzim*, *nimim*, or *gardim* — the natural fringe threads, loose uncut stitching, or hanging weave at the edge of a garment — the *tzitzis* is invalid (*pesulah*). If, however, one used *sisin* — ordinary strings intentionally inserted into the garment for the purpose of serving as *tzitzis* — it is valid (*kesherah*). The critical factor is not the material but the intent: the strings must be placed in the garment specifically to serve as *tzitzis*.

When Rav Yehuda later reported this ruling before Shmuel, Shmuel went further: *af min ha-sisin nami pesulah* — even *sisin* is invalid, because *de-ba'inan teviyah lishmah* — we require that the spinning itself be done for the sake of *tzitzis*. This is the practical significance of the notation on commercially produced *tzitzis* strings: *tavui lishmah* — spun for the sake of the *mitzvah*. One may not simply take a ball of ordinary wool and cut strings from it; the material itself must have been processed for the purpose of *tzitzis*.

This produces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel: Rav holds that as long as the strings are placed in the garment for the sake of *tzitzis*, the underlying material need not have been designated beforehand; Shmuel holds that even the spinning must be done *lishmah*. But critically, both agree that some act of designation — at minimum, the insertion of the strings into the garment — must be performed *lishmah*.

### Sukkah Exception

The *gemara* raises the challenge: given this universal principle that objects of *mitzvah* must be made *lishmah*, why does Beis Hillel permit a *sukkah* that was built with no such intent? Should we not require *sukkah asuyah lishmah*?

The *gemara* answers: *shani hatam de-amar kra — gedilim ta'aseh lach* — it is different there, because the verse says "you shall make twisted threads for yourself." The word *lach* — "for yourself" — is read as *l'shem hovcha*, for the sake of your obligation, meaning the *tzitzis* must be made intentionally for the purpose of fulfilling the *mitzvah*. This is a particular *halachic* demand of *tzitzis*, not a universal requirement.

The *gemara* immediately notes that *sukkos* also contains a comparable expression: *chag ha-sukkos ta'aseh lecha* — the festival of *Sukkos* you shall make for yourself. Does *lecha* not equally imply *lishmah*? The *gemara* responds: *hahu mibayei lei l'miutei gezulah* — that *lecha* is needed to exclude a stolen *sukkah*. One cannot fulfill the obligation with a *sukkah* one does not own. The *lecha* teaches ownership, not intent.

The *gemara* anticipates the rejoinder: by *tzitzis* as well, *lach* could be read as requiring ownership rather than intent. To this the *gemara* answers that *tzitzis* has an additional verse — *ve-asu lahem*, they shall make for themselves — which already establishes the ownership requirement (*mishelahem*). Therefore the *lach* in the *tzitzis* verse is freed up to teach the *lishmah* requirement, whereas no such doubling exists by *sukkah*.

### Mitzvah vs. Kedusha

What emerges from this analysis is an important distinction. The general rule, according to Beis Hillel, is that objects used for a *mitzvah* do not require *lishmah*. The *lulav*, the *esrog*, the *shofar* — there is no requirement that they be fashioned with specific intent for the *mitzvah*. The *lishmah* requirement is a specific *halachic* demand that applies in particular contexts by virtue of a special verse.

It is important, however, to distinguish objects of *mitzvah* from objects of *kedusha*. *Tefillin* and a *Sefer Torah* require *lishmah* for the *klaf* and the writing — but these are not merely functional objects used to perform a *mitzvah*; they are objects that actually bear God's names and possess intrinsic sanctity. The *lishmah* requirement for objects of *kedusha* is of a categorically different character. The debate here concerns only objects of *mitzvah* in the functional sense — and there the basic rule, per Beis Hillel, is that *lishmah* is not required.

Beis Shammai's position remains that *sukkah* does require a form of designation — not *lishmah* in the technical sense, but that it be identifiable as a *sukkas hachag*. Whether Beis Shammai would extend a general *lishmah* requirement to other objects of *mitzvah* such as the *shofar* or the *lulav* is not definitively established by the *gemara* here, but at minimum they hold that a *sukkah* must bear the identity of a *yom tov sukkah*.

### Ownership Issues

The *gemara*'s discussion of the *lecha* and *lahem* verses also clarifies the question of ownership more broadly. By *sukkah*, the ruling is that one may use a borrowed *sukkah* and make a *berachah* in it. One visits a friend's *sukkah* for a meal and fulfills the *mitzvah* without requiring formal transfer of ownership. By *tzitzis*, by contrast, there is a real problem with using a borrowed garment's *tzitzis*, which is why a synagogue that provides a *tallis* for congregants typically arranges some form of notional transfer of ownership to the person using it, in order to allow a *berachah* to be recited. This difference flows from the respective *pesukim* and what they require by way of ownership.

One might ask: why does the Torah need to tell us that a stolen *sukkah* is invalid? Is it not already covered by the general principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* — a *mitzvah* performed by means of a transgression? This question will be addressed in full when the *masechta* reaches the relevant *sugya* in the third *perek*, in the context of *lulav* and *esrog*.

---

## Sukkah Under Tree

### Tree Prohibition

The *mishnah* presents its next case: *ha-oseh sukkato tachas ha-ilan* — one who constructs his *sukkah* under a tree. Such a *sukkah* is invalid — *k'ilu asah b'toch ha-bayis* — it is as if he built it inside the house. A tree constitutes *pasul sechach* because it remains attached to the ground. Were its branches to be severed and placed as *sechach*, they would be entirely valid; but while still attached and living, they are *pasul*. The question that now presents itself is: what is the status of valid *sechach* (*kosher s'chach*) positioned underneath *pasul sechach*?

### Sukkah Tachas Sukkah

The *mishnah* continues with an adjacent case: *sukkah al gabei sukkah* — a double-decker *sukkah*, one *sukkah* constructed directly above another, with both composed of valid *sechach*. The ruling is: *ha-elyonah kesherah ve-ha-tachtonah pesulah* — the upper *sukkah* is valid, the lower one is invalid. This seems counterintuitive: if both use *kosher sechach*, why should the lower one be invalid? The *gemara* derives from a verse the principle of *sukkah tachas sukkah* — one may be under only a single *sukkah*, not beneath two layers of *sukkah*. The upper *sukkah* is under only its own roof; the lower one is beneath two layers of *sukkah*, which renders it invalid.

If the *sukkah tachas sukkah* principle applies even when both layers are *kosher sechach*, it applies all the more so when the upper layer is *pasul sechach*, such as a tree. In the case of a tree, not only is there a double-roof problem, but the upper layer is itself invalid.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Exception

Rabbi Yehuda introduces a qualification: *im ein diyurin ba-elyonah, ha-tachtonah kesherah* — if no one is actually dwelling in the upper *sukkah*, the lower one is valid. Rabbi Yehuda accepts the principle of *sukkah tachas sukkah* in theory, but holds that the upper structure only acquires the functional identity of a *sukkah* when people are actually living in it. If the upper layer of *sechach* is not being used as a *sukkah* — even if it is theoretically usable as one — it does not generate the *sukkah tachas sukkah* problem. It is then simply a double layer of *sechach*, and the lower *sukkah* remains valid.

This is a striking position. A structure of very sturdy, tightly woven *sechach* — thick enough to bear human weight above it — can still be considered *kosher sechach* and not a permanent roof, provided it retains enough porosity for rain to penetrate. Tosafos establishes this criterion: what makes a roof permanent is not that it is immovable or structurally solid, but that it does not allow rain through. A *sechach* that is dense enough to support a person standing on it yet still permits rain to pass through remains valid *sechach* — a remarkable conclusion. The principle of *sukkah tachas sukkah*, then, turns not on the structural properties of the upper layer but on whether it is actually functioning as a *sukkah* in the lived sense.

---

## Rava's Shade Analysis

### Shade-Sunlight Ratio

The *gemara* opens its analysis of the tree case with a ruling from Rava: *lo shanu ela b'ilan she-tzilato meruba mi-chamato* — the *mishnah*'s invalidation of a *sukkah* under a tree applies only when the tree provides more shade than sunlight over the area beneath it. In that case, the tree is functioning as a roof — a second, invalid roof positioned above the valid *sukkah*. Given that *sukkah tachas sukkah* invalidates the lower *sukkah* even when both layers are *kosher*, it certainly applies when the upper layer is *pasul*. But *aval chamato meruba mi-tzilato — kesherah*: if more sunlight comes through than shade, the tree is not functioning as a roof, and the *sukkah* beneath it is valid.

Rava derives this from the *mishnah*'s own language. Rather than simply declaring the *sukkah* under a tree invalid (*pesulah*), the *mishnah* offers the metaphor: *k'ilu asah b'toch ha-bayis* — it is like having built it inside the house. This formulation is not merely rhetorical flourish. The *gemara* reads it as a limiting principle: *ilan dumya de-bayis* — a tree is problematic only when it resembles a house. Just as a house is characterized by its roof providing more shade than sunlight — that is what makes it a genuine covering — a tree functions as an invalidating roof only when it similarly provides more shade than sunlight over the area of the *sukkah*.

### Schach Combination

The *gemara*, however, does not allow Rava's ruling to stand unchallenged. Even if the tree provides only a minority of shade — even if it is not functioning as a full roof — there remains a problem: *ha kamitztaref schach pasul bahadi schach kasher* — the *pasul sechach* of the tree is combining with the *kosher sechach* of the *sukkah*. The problematic branches overhanging the *sukkah*, even if they constitute only a minority of the shade, are still present and interacting with the valid *sechach* below.

This point generates one of the most practically significant debates in the *rishonim* regarding *sukkah* construction. There are two fundamentally different ways to understand what "combining" means here, and they have major implications *l'halacha*.

The first reading — which tends to govern stringent practice — is that any area of *sechach* directly beneath an overhanging branch is itself invalidated. The reasoning would be that the shade in that precise area is being produced, at least in part, by the *pasul sechach* of the tree above. The valid *sechach* below it in that zone is effectively negated. This is why people who build a *sukkah* near a tree must look directly upward: any column of space directly beneath an overhanging branch may lack valid *sechach*, and if enough of the *sukkah*'s area is so affected, the *sukkah* becomes problematic — not only for sitting under those areas, but potentially even for the structural integrity of the *sukkah*'s *sechach* coverage. If the affected area is large enough, it may compromise the wall count of the *sukkah* as well.

The second reading — associated with Rashi and certain other *rishonim* — is considerably more lenient. On this view, the *gemara* does not say that the *pasul sechach* invalidates the *kosher sechach* below it; it says only that the *pasul sechach* is combining with the *kosher sechach*. The only problem, according to this reading, is that one may not use the overhanging branches to supplement the shade of the *sukkah*. If one has sufficient *kosher sechach* on one's own, the overhanging branches are simply irrelevant. Under this reading, as long as one does not need the tree branches to supply additional shade — a non-issue in the era of pre-packaged rolls of *sechach* — a tree with only a minor overhang poses no practical problem for the *sukkah* beneath it.

These are two very different readings of the *gemara*, and the practical consequences are substantial.

### Mixed Schach Solution

The *gemara* proposes a solution to the problem of combining *pasul sechach* with *kosher sechach*: *amar Rav Pappa b'she-chavtan* — Rav Pappa says the case is one where the branches have been beaten down and mixed together with the *kosher sechach*.

The image is of a pliable tree whose overhanging branches have been bent down and intermingled with the valid *sechach* laid on the *sukkah*'s roof. Rather than the *pasul sechach* sitting distinctly above the *kosher sechach*, the two are now genuinely mixed together into a single mass. In such a case, the *halacha* treats the combined unit as a whole and defines its identity by its majority. If the *kosher sechach* constitutes the majority of the mixture, the entire mass is valid.

This is a fascinating *halachic* concept. It is not identical to the classic notion of *bittul* — the nullification of a prohibited substance within a mixture of food. In the food context, if one has identifiable pieces of *treif* mixed with *kosher* food, mere numerical majority does not suffice for *bittul*; the prohibited substance must be truly dissolved into the mixture. Here too, if the *pasul sechach* and the *kosher sechach* were laid side by side in clearly distinct, alternating strips — a metal bar next to a bamboo rod — the *pasul* would not be *batel* even if the *kosher* is the majority. The operative principle is that the mixture must be a genuine, undifferentiated whole. When it is, the entire unit's identity is determined by the character of its majority ingredient.

This concept finds a parallel in other areas of *halacha*: for example, when determining whether a dough is considered bread for purposes of *challah* or *matzah*, when the dough is a true mixture of wheat and another grain, one looks at the overall character of the dough as determined by the majority ingredient.

### Mixed Schach Halacha

The *gemara* asks: if the solution is simply that the branches were mixed together with the *kosher sechach*, what is the *chiddush*? This should be entirely obvious. The *gemara* answers: one might have thought that even when mixed, we should prohibit the *sukkah* as a *gezeirah* — a rabbinic safeguard — lest people assume that mixing is unnecessary and attempt to use *pasul sechach* without mixing it in. The ruling teaches *d'lo gazrinan* — we do not impose such a *gezeirah*. When the mixing has been properly done, the *sukkah* is valid, and we are not concerned that this will lead to laxity.

### Vines and Gourds

The *gemara* then notes that this principle is already taught in another *mishnah*: *hidli aleha et ha-gefen ve-et ha-dala'at ve-et ha-kissom* — if one bent over the *sukkah* a grapevine, a gourd plant, or *kissom* (some other pliable plant), *v'sichech al gaban* — and placed *sechach* on top of them — *pesulah*. The *sukkah* is invalid. However, *im hayah sichuch harbeh mehem* — if the *kosher sechach* was more than the vine and gourd, *o she-katzatztan* — or if one actually severed the plants from their roots — *kesherah*, it is valid. The case of cutting the plants and thereby removing their *pasul* status involves a separate principle that will be addressed later (*ta'aseh v'lo min he-asuy*). The significant *chiddush* here is the first clause: if the *kosher sechach* is the majority and is mixed in with the vine and gourd, the *sukkah* is valid despite the presence of the *pasul sechach*.

This *mishnah* thus already establishes that when *pasul sechach* is genuinely mixed with *kosher sechach* and the *kosher* is the majority, the *sukkah* is valid — and that we do not prohibit the mixture out of concern that one will fail to mix properly.

### Bediavad vs. Lechatila

The *gemara* raises one further refinement. One might have thought that the validity of a mixed *sukkah* applies only *b'diavad* — after the fact, if one has already constructed the *sukkah* in this manner, we will tell him it is valid and he need not dismantle it. But *l'chatchila* — as an initial matter, if one asks what to do — the proper answer should be to cut down the branches or move the *sukkah*. The *gemara* rules *kamashma lan* that even *l'chatchila* one may mix the *pasul sechach* with the *kosher sechach* to resolve the problem. The mixing is a fully acceptable initial solution, not merely a *b'diavad* concession.

### Branch Overhang Impact

The discussion concludes by returning to the fundamental ambiguity in the *gemara*. Rava's ruling that a tree which provides only a minority of shade does not invalidate the *sukkah* is now complicated by the recognition that even minority-shade overhanging branches pose a problem through the combination of *pasul* and *kosher sechach*. The *gemara*'s response — that Rav Pappa's solution of mixing resolves the issue — in turn prompts the question of whether that solution is obvious. And the resolution is that it is a *chiddush* either in terms of avoiding a *gezeirah* or in terms of permitting the practice *l'chatchila*.

What remains genuinely contested — and this is the live *halachic* question — is which of the two interpretations of "combining" governs in practice. Under the reading that overhanging *pasul sechach* invalidates the *kosher sechach* directly below it, a tree with even modest overhang can create zones of invalid *sechach* within one's *sukkah*, with potentially significant consequences for both the obligation to dwell beneath *kosher sechach* and the structural requirements of the *sukkah*'s roof. Under the more lenient reading, as long as one is not relying on the tree branches to supply shade, their presence is simply immaterial. The *gemara* itself is not entirely explicit, and this ambiguity is what drives the divergence in *halachic* practice.

---

---

# Sukkah 10

## Sukkah Tachat Sukkah

### Source & Derivation

The second part of the *mishna* on 9b addresses the case of a *sukkah tachat sukkah* — a sukkah beneath another sukkah. Even if both layers of *skhakh* are individually valid, a special invalidity applies to sitting in the lower one. The *gemara* derives this from the *tanna'im*: the verse states *bassukkot tishvu shivat yamim* — you shall dwell in *sukkot* for seven days. The *baraita* extends the prohibition: not in a *sukkah* beneath another *sukkah*, not beneath a tree, and not beneath a house. The latter two are intuitive, since an invalid roof stands above a valid *skhakh* and undermines its identity as a roof. But the case of *sukkah tachat sukkah* is puzzling — why not simply use the shade of the upper roof?

The *gemara* raises a counterargument: *bassukkot* is written in the plural, and *tartei mashma* — the plural form implies two, suggesting that dwelling beneath two *sukkot* might be specifically endorsed. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this by invoking the principle that *bassukkat ketiv* — the word is written without a *vav*, in the singular form. As the *gemara* earlier discussed in the context of walls, the written form (*ketiv*) can govern even when the vocalized reading (*krei*) differs. The textual basis may be somewhat strained, but it establishes the principle: *sukkah tachat sukkah* is invalid.

### Four Scenarios

Rabbi Yirmiya then presents a systematic analysis. He observes that the relationship between two stacked *skhakh* structures yields four distinct combinations: both may be valid (*kasher*), both may be invalid (*pasul*), the bottom may be valid and the top invalid, or the top may be valid and the bottom invalid. Each of these cases is not only theoretically possible but practically constructible.

### Both Valid

The first case — *pe'amim sheshteihem kesherot*, both are valid — is achieved as follows: the lower *skhakh* has more sunlight than shade (*chamata meruba mitzilata*), meaning it lacks sufficient coverage to constitute valid *skhakh* on its own. The upper *skhakh*, however, has more shade than sunlight (*tzilata meruba mechamata*), and the upper structure stands within twenty *amot* of its own floor. In this case, the lower structure does not truly function as a distinct *sukkah* — it lacks adequate *skhakh*. The actual roofing is provided solely by the upper layer, and since the upper *skhakh* is fully valid and properly sized, both are considered valid. The apparent doubling is not really a doubling at all; there is functionally only one *skhakh*.

### Both Invalid

The second case — *pe'amim sheshteihem pesulot*, both are invalid — is achieved when both layers have more shade than sunlight, but the upper structure stands higher than twenty *amot*. The upper *skhakh* is thus invalid due to excessive height, a disqualification established at the very opening of the *masechet*. The lower *skhakh*, however, is not rescued by the upper one's invalidity. Whether the *skhakh* above is *kasher* or *pasul*, the lower remains invalid by virtue of standing beneath a second layer of *skhakh* — the prohibition of *sukkah tachat sukkah* applies regardless.

### Bottom Valid

The third case — the bottom valid and the top invalid — is the one Rabbi Yirmiya identifies as the true *chiddush*. The bottom has more shade than sunlight and is within twenty *amot*, making it a fully valid *sukkah*. The top has more sunlight than shade, and therefore lacks sufficient *skhakh* to constitute a second roof. Since the upper layer does not qualify as *skhakh*, it cannot impose the invalidity of *sukkah tachat sukkah* on what lies beneath it.

This prompts a concern expressed in the *gemara*: *nigzor dilma mitztaref sechach pasul bahadi sechach kasher* — perhaps we should be worried that invalid *skhakh* might combine with valid *skhakh* below. Rashi explains the concern this way: while in the present case the upper layer is merely insufficient rather than inherently disqualified, if we permit such configurations broadly, we might come to permit a case where the upper *skhakh* is invalid because it exceeds twenty *amot*. *Skhakh* that is invalid due to excessive height carries its own disqualifying force — analogous to the overhang of a tree — and could then corrupt the valid *skhakh* directly beneath it. The *gemara* therefore teaches that this concern does not materialize: a sparse upper layer that lacks sufficient coverage is simply not *skhakh* at all, and creates no problem for what lies below.

An interesting question arises at the margins of this case: if neither the upper nor the lower layer individually has sufficient shade, could the two sparse layers combine to produce adequate coverage? The *gemara* does not address this directly here, but it is a genuine theoretical question.

### Top Valid

The fourth case — *pe'amim sheha'elyona keshera vetachtona pesula*, the top valid and the bottom invalid — is the paradigmatic *sukkah tachat sukkah*. Both layers have more shade than sunlight, and the upper one stands within twenty *amot*. The upper is fully valid; the lower is invalid precisely because it stands beneath a legitimate second *skhakh*. The *gemara* notes that this case is obvious (*peshita*) — it requires no derivation. The genuine novelty lies in the third case, where the bottom remains valid despite the presence of a structure above it, because the upper layer lacks the threshold of coverage required to qualify as *skhakh*.

## Gap Between Skhakhim

### Rav Huna (1 tefach)

Having established the principle of *sukkah tachat sukkah*, the *gemara* asks: *kama yehei bein sukkah lesukkah vetehei tachtona pesula* — what gap between the two layers of *skhakh* is required to render the lower one invalid? The intuitive answer might be ten *tefachim*, since that is the minimum height of a *sukkah*. The earlier opinions, however, do not go that far.

Rav Huna says: *tefach* — a single *tefach* gap suffices. The logic is not that the upper structure must qualify as a *sukkah*; it is enough that it constitute a distinct roof, a *skhakh* in its own right. Once a separate canopy is identifiable, it can impose the prohibition of *sukkah tachat sukkah* on what lies below, even if it would never qualify as an independent *sukkah*.

### Tumah Analogy

The support for the one-*tefach* standard comes from the laws of *ohel tumah*. A corpse imparts *tumah* to anything beneath the same roof, while the roof itself serves as a barrier preventing the *tumah* from spreading upward. But how high must a covering stand above the ground to function as a roof in this sense? The *mishna* in the relevant tractate states: *tefach al tefach be-rum tefach* — a surface of one *tefach* by one *tefach* in area, elevated one *tefach* above the ground, *mevi et ha-tumah* — causes *tumah* to spread beneath it — *ve-chotzetz bifnei ha-tumah* — and blocks the *tumah* from above. If the height is less than one *tefach*, it neither conveys nor blocks.

The operative principle is clear: a *tefach* of clearance is what defines something as a roof in the domain of *tumah* law. By analogy, Rav Huna argues, a *tefach* of clearance is what defines a second layer as a distinct *skhakh* in the domain of *sukkah* law.

### Rav Chisda (4 tefachim)

Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna disagree, requiring a gap of four *tefachim*. Their reasoning: *she-lo matzinu makom chashuv be-makom pachot me-arba'ah* — we do not find a legally significant space in an area smaller than four *tefachim*. The most familiar example is the *reshut ha-yachid* of *Shabbat*, where a minimum area of four *tefachim* by four *tefachim* is required for a space to constitute a private domain. Below that threshold, the space lacks legal significance.

*Tosafot* acknowledges the difficulty with this position: the four-*tefachim* standard normally governs horizontal area, not vertical height. The precedent for four *tefachim* as a significant height measure is rare, making this an unusual application of the principle. Nevertheless, Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna found one *tefach* insufficient while stopping short of the ten-*tefachim* threshold that the next opinion will require.

### Shmuel (10 tefachim)

Shmuel requires ten *tefachim*: *kehachshara kach pesula* — as with its validity, so with its invalidity. Just as a *sukkah* requires a minimum height of ten *tefachim* to be valid, the upper structure must stand ten *tefachim* above the lower *skhakh* to impose the prohibition of *sukkah tachat sukkah*. Shmuel's reasoning reframes the entire question: this is not merely about whether the upper layer constitutes a distinct *skhakh*, but about whether it constitutes a distinct *sukkah*. A *skhakh* under another *skhakh* is only prohibited when the upper one rises to the status of a separate *sukkah*. Anything less than ten *tefachim* remains, in Shmuel's view, categorically beneath that threshold.

## Habitability Requirement

### Rav Dimi Report

The *gemara* now engages the view of Rabbi Yehuda from the *mishna*, who states: *im ein diyur ba'elyona, ha-tachtona keshera* — if nobody dwells in the upper one, the lower one is valid. The *gemara* first considers whether this means actual occupancy — and dismisses the reading immediately: *atu diyur kagarmi* — does the physical fact of whether people happen to be using the space determine its halachic identity? A structure does not lose its status as a *sukkah* simply because it is unoccupied at the moment. The *gemara* therefore reinterprets Rabbi Yehuda: *kol she'aino reuia ledira* — the upper structure must be unfit for habitation. And the primary case of uninhabitability is that it stands less than ten *tefachim* high. This brings Rabbi Yehuda into alignment with Shmuel's position: the upper structure must have the dimensions of a real *sukkah* to impose invalidity on the one below.

When Rav Dimi returned from Eretz Yisrael, he reported a further clarification of Rabbi Yehuda's view: *im ein ha-tachtona yekholah lekabbel karim ukesatot shel elyona, ha-tachtona keshera* — if the lower structure cannot support the pillows and blankets of the upper one, the lower one is valid. This introduces an additional consideration beyond dimensional thresholds. Even if the upper structure technically has the correct parameters for a *sukkah*, if its floor cannot structurally bear weight — if anyone who tried to walk in would cause the floor to collapse — it lacks the practical habitability that makes it a real *sukkah*.

### Floor Collapse

The underlying image is vivid: a *sukkah* built upon the *skhakh* of another *sukkah* has no proper floor. The surface beneath your feet is simply *skhakh* material — branches and reeds that could give way under any significant weight. Rabbi Yehuda holds that such structural inadequacy means the upper structure never truly qualifies as a *sukkah*, and therefore cannot impose the prohibition of *sukkah tachat sukkah*. The *gemara* notes that the condition is framed in terms of pillows and blankets rather than a person — Rashi adds that the full phrase, drawn from his commentary, includes sleeping on those pillows and blankets, so the weight of a reclining person is implicitly part of the test. The formulation nonetheless sounds understated compared to the actual structural question of whether a person can stand in the space.

### Emergency Habitability

The *gemara* resolves the apparent dispute between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda through a fine distinction: *ikha beinaihu deyekhola lekabbel al yedei ha-dechak* — the point of disagreement is a case where the floor can support weight, but only precariously, only under emergency conditions. According to Shmuel's reading of the *tanna kamma*, even precarious habitability suffices — if it can bear weight at a stretch, the upper structure qualifies as a *sukkah* and invalidates the lower one. Rabbi Yehuda, as interpreted by Rav Dimi, requires stable, genuine habitability. The disagreement is thus remarkably narrow: both opinions agree that ten *tefachim* of height is necessary, and both agree that the structure must be capable of bearing a person's weight. They differ only on whether barely adequate support — the structural equivalent of an emergency measure — is enough to confer full *sukkah* status on the upper level.

## Sheets & Decorations

### Mishna Cases

The *mishna* presents three cases of a sheet invalidating a *sukkah*: spreading a sheet over the *skhakh* because of the heat (*mipnei hachama*), spreading one beneath the *skhakh* to catch falling debris (*mipnei ha-nesher* — the pine needles or other small material falling from above), and spreading a sheet over the poles of a four-poster bed (*al gabei ha-kinof*) inside the *sukkah*. All three are declared *pesulah*.

The underlying logic unifies the cases. A *sukkah* under a tree is invalid because the tree branches serve as a distinct roof above the *skhakh*. A *sukkah* under a house is clearly invalid for the same reason. When a sheet is placed above the *skhakh*, the sheet becomes the functional roof, displacing the *skhakh*. When placed below, it introduces an interposing layer beneath the valid *skhakh*, so that the person sitting inside is effectively under the sheet rather than the *skhakh*.
