Since it is a question of function rather than identity, perhaps *machshava* can freely toggle it back and forth — *machshava mashvia lei umachshava mafkia lei*.

The *Gemara* rejects this distinction, however, citing the *mishna* in *Uktzin* dealing with the stems of food, which provides an illuminating parallel case.

---

## Uktzin Stems

### Stems of Food

The *Gemara* introduces the relevant passage from *Uktzin*: *kol yadot ha'ochlim shebissasan bagoren, tehoros* — all the stems of food that were *bissasan* in the threshing floor are *tahor*, meaning the stems are no longer classified as *yadot* of the food. Rabbi Yossi, however, says they remain *tamei*, indicating that he regards the stems as still part of the food even after *bissasan* in the threshing floor.

### Bissasan Meanings

The key dispute within this *mishna* turns on what *bissasan* means. Two *Amora'im* disagree. Rabbi Elazar says *bissasan* means *hitar agdan* — one undid the bundle. Rabbi Yochanan says *bissasan mamash* — one literally threshed the grain.

To understand why this matters, one must consider the role the stem plays for wheat. The stem — the straw — serves the wheat by allowing it to be bundled into a sheaf, which makes carrying possible. Once the bundle is brought to the threshing floor and the owner undoes it, intending to thresh the grain, the straw no longer serves this carrying function. According to Rabbi Elazar, this undoing of the bundle suffices to change the stem's status: even without physically altering the grain or the straw, the act of unbundling in the threshing floor makes clear that the stem is no longer needed, and it loses its classification as a *yad*.

The parallel to the *schach* case is striking: just as placing the branch on top of the *sukkah* is an act done *with* the object rather than *to* it, so too undoing the bundle is an act done in context of a new purpose without physically changing the object itself. According to Rabbi Elazar, such contextual action is sufficient to dissolve the *yad* status.

### Rabbi Yossi View

According to Rabbi Yochanan, however, *bissasan* means literal threshing — a physical act performed on the grain itself. On this reading, only a direct physical change to the object can reclassify the stem's status. The parallel for *schach* would be that one must physically alter the branch — beating it down, flattening it — before the stem can change its classification.

But if that is so, why does Rabbi Yossi maintain that even after literal threshing, the stem remains a *yad*? The *Gemara* cites Resh Lakish's explanation: *hoil ve'raui le'hofchan be'atara* — since the straw remains fit to be turned over with a pitchfork. Even after one begins threshing the wheat, the straw still serves a functional purpose: it can be used to maneuver the grain with a pitchfork when flipping it to thresh from the other side. Because the straw retains this use, Rabbi Yossi holds that it continues to be a *yad*.

At this point, the *Gemara* quotes a beautiful *derasha* from Rabbi Elazar: why does the Torah use the word *vaye'etar* — etymologically connected to *attar*, pitchfork — to describe Yitzchak's prayer on behalf of his wife? Just as a pitchfork turns the grain from one side to another in the threshing floor, so does the prayer of the righteous turn God's attribute of — the text uses striking language — *middat achzariyut* to *middat rachamanut*, from cruelty to compassion. The imagery of prayer as an implement of reversal, turning over the divine disposition, is powerful.

### Stem Function

Returning to the *schach* case: the *Gemara* now presses on the analogy. If on Rabbi Yochanan's reading one must physically alter the object to change the *yad* status, and the *Gemara* posits that this was done — that one actually did something physical to make the branch into *schach* — why would anyone still consider the stem part of the fruit? If even in the threshing case Rabbi Yossi only maintains the *yad* status because the straw retains a useful function (turning the grain with a pitchfork), what useful function does the stem serve here, after the branch has been physically worked into *schach*?

The *Gemara* answers: *chazya lechisasa lemi'intelei bigila'ei* — it remains fit for use after *Sukkot* ends. The Yom Tov will not last forever. When one dismantles the *sukkah* after *Sukkot*, the branch will still have fruit attached, and the owner — who originally cut the branch with eating in mind — will want to handle the fruit using the stem. Therefore, even in the midst of using it as *schach*, the stem retains its functional connection to the fruit, and its *yad* status is not fully dissolved.

This conclusion provides the key to the entire debate. The question of whether the stem is counted as invalid *schach* or as valid *schach* depends on whether, under the circumstances, the stem still serves the fruit. The underlying point of disagreement — what physical act is required to sever that connection, and whether any act suffices given the stem's anticipated future use — is what the *tanna'im* dispute.

The *Gemara* then returns to the *mishna* of *Uktzin* proper, introducing the discussion with the word *gufa* — signaling that what had been quoted piecemeal in the course of the earlier argument will now be examined as a whole. Rashi notes, in what appears to be a student's gloss, that *gufa* is ordinarily used to reexamine a *baraita* or an amoraic statement, not a *mishna*. The explanation offered is that this *mishna* is from the order of *Taharot*, for which there is no *Gemara* in the world — the *Babylonian Talmud* contains no tractate *Gemara* on *Taharot*. Therefore, the only opportunity to examine and explicate this *mishna* is in the course of a discussion elsewhere, which justifies the unusual use of *gufa* here.

The *mishna* in *Uktzin* is then quoted in full: *kol yadot ha'ochlim shebissasan bagoren, tehoros, v'Rabbi Yossi metamei*. The *Gemara* presents the debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar over what *bissasan* means, as described above, and concludes with Resh Lakish's rationale for Rabbi Yossi's position: the straw remains useful as a *yad* even after threshing, because it can be moved with a pitchfork.

---

## Planks of Wood

### Planks Debate

The *mishna* now moves to a new topic: *mesachin b'nisarin divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — one may use planks of wood as *schach*, according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Meir, however, forbids it. The most obvious reason for Rabbi Meir's position is the *gezeirat tikra* — the rabbinic concern that planks of wood laid across the top of a structure look like a standard roof, and using them as *schach* might blur the distinction between a *sukkah* and an ordinary roofed structure. The *mishna* then adds: if one placed a plank that is four *tefachim* wide upon the *sukkah*, it remains *keshera* — provided one does not sleep beneath it. Rashi explains this is referring to a plank placed adjacent to the wall, where it can be treated as a bent extension of the wall (*dofen akuma*), but since it is invalid *schach* it may not be slept under.

### Rav's View

Rav explains the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir as follows: *machlokes b'nisarin sheyesh bahen arba'ah* — they argue specifically about planks that are four *tefachim* wide. Rabbi Meir holds the *gezeirat tikra*, and therefore invalidates such planks. Rabbi Yehuda does not hold the *gezeirat tikra* at all, and therefore permits even four-*tefach* planks. But below four *tefachim*, *divrei hakol keshera* — all agree the *sukkah* is valid, because no one would mistake such a narrow piece of wood for a roofing plank.

### Shmuel's View

Shmuel disagrees. In his reading, the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir concerns planks *less* than four *tefachim*. Once a plank reaches four *tefachim* in width, *divrei hakol psula* — everyone agrees it is invalid. Every *tanna* concedes the *gezeirat tikra* at that size. The argument is only about smaller planks: Rabbi Meir says even they are problematic; Rabbi Yehuda says they are not.

### Size Significance

Rav Pappa refines the position of Rav. He clarifies that below three *tefachim*, all agree the *sukkah* is valid — the *Gemara* dismisses such a thin piece of wood as *kani b'alma*, nothing more than a stick. Above four *tefachim*, all agree it is problematic. The debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir, on Rav's view, is confined to the range of three to four *tefachim*.

The conceptual stakes are sharpened here. Both positions agree that the *gezeirat tikra* is a real concern at some size threshold; the argument is about which size qualifies. Rabbi Meir holds that three *tefachim* or more is significant, because once something exceeds the range of *lavud* — the halachic principle that gaps of less than three *tefachim* are treated as closed — it constitutes a recognizable width. Rabbi Yehuda holds that below four *tefachim* one does not yet have *shiur makom*, a significant spatial unit unto itself, and therefore the *gezeirat tikra* does not yet apply. It is a striking feature of this analysis that what begins as a pragmatic concern — does this look like a roof? — is resolved not by asking what roofs actually look like, but by applying formal halachic categories: *lavud* and *shiur makom*.

---

## Combining Planks

### Sheets vs. Planks

The *mishna* teaches that *shnei sadinim mitztarfin* — two sheets combine to create a problematic measure of invalid *schach*. The *Gemara* now asks whether the same combination rule applies to planks. The *mishna* continues: *shnei nesarim ein mitztarfin* — two planks do not combine. Rabbi Meir, however, says they do: *af nesarim k'sadinim*, planks are like sheets.

### Two Planks Case

To understand the combination question, one must clarify what measure the combining is meant to create. Two sheets of invalid *schach*, each less than four *tefachim* wide, placed side by side, combine to produce four *tefachim* of invalid *schach*. Could two planks do the same? This question fits naturally with Shmuel's reading of the debate. If Rabbi Meir holds that planks less than four *tefachim* are already problematic — say, a plank of three *tefachim* — then a second such plank placed alongside the first would combine with it, and the total invalid *schach* would exceed four *tefachim*. Rabbi Yehuda, on this reading, says no such plank is problematic on its own and therefore there is nothing to combine.

On Rav's reading, however, this case is difficult to construct. If Rabbi Meir says planks are only problematic at four *tefachim*, then a single plank already constitutes four *tefachim* of invalid *schach* — there is nothing left to combine toward. And if the plank is less than four *tefachim*, Rabbi Meir himself says it is fine.

### Side Combination

The *Gemara* resolves this difficulty for Rav's position. The combining is not toward a measure of four *tefachim* of invalid *schach* in the center of the *sukkah*, but rather toward *arba amot min hatzad* — four *amot* worth of planks placed along the side. The significance of four *amot* along the side is its relationship to *dofen akuma*: the principle that invalid *schach* adjacent to a wall can be treated as a bent extension of that wall, thereby preserving the *sukkah*'s validity. This leniency applies only when the invalid *schach* extends no more than four *amot* from the wall. If plank after plank is placed along the side and the total exceeds four *amot*, the *dofen akuma* principle can no longer save the *sukkah*. According to Rav, Rabbi Meir's concern about planks combining is precisely this: accumulation along the side until the four-*amot* limit of *dofen akuma* is exceeded.

On this reading, Rabbi Yehuda, who maintains that planks are valid *schach*, would say they simply do not combine — because they are not invalid to begin with. The *Gemara* notes that Rabbi Yehuda could equally have said these planks are all perfectly valid *schach*; his statement that they do not combine is essentially a reactive formulation, stated in counterpoint to Rabbi Meir's claim that they do.

### Baraita Evidence

The *Gemara* then notes that there is a *baraita* that supports Rav and a *baraita* that supports Shmuel. The *baraita* supporting Rav explicitly states: if one used cedar planks less than four *tefachim* wide, *divrei hakol kesheira* — all agree it is valid. Once the plank is four *tefachim* wide, Rabbi Meir invalidates and Rabbi Yehuda validates. This maps precisely onto Rav's position that the debate concerns four *tefachim* and larger, with no debate below that threshold.

---

## Historical Anecdote

### Persecution Account

Within the *baraita* supporting Rav, Rabbi Yehuda himself offers an account from personal experience to demonstrate that four-*tefach* planks are permitted. He relates: *ma'aseh bi'she'at hassakana* — there was an incident during a time of persecution, when it was dangerous to build a *sukkah* openly. He speaks in the first-person plural, and given that Rabbi Yehuda was a student of Rabbi Akiva, this *she'at hassakana* appears to be something he actually lived through. He describes how they brought planks that were four *tefachim* wide, placed them atop a porch, and dwelt beneath them — to all appearances sitting under an ordinary covered portico, while in fact fulfilling the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*.

### Sakana Caveat

The *Gemara* immediately deflects the proof: *ein she'at hassakana re'ayah* — conduct during a time of persecution cannot serve as a normative halachic proof. What the rabbis permitted under conditions of mortal danger does not establish what is permissible in ordinary circumstances. The historical note is poignant, but it carries no probative weight.

### Shmuel Baraita

The *baraita* supporting Shmuel presents the opposite ruling: once a plank reaches four *tefachim*, *divrei hakol pesula* — all agree it is invalid. Below four *tefachim*, that is where the debate lies: Rabbi Meir invalidates and Rabbi Yehuda validates.

### Meir's Concession

The *baraita* continues with a significant concession: *u'modeh Rabbi Meir* — even Rabbi Meir agrees that if there is a gap between one plank and the next equal in width to a plank itself, and one fills that gap with valid *schach* — *pesoles goren veyekev*, the term used for valid *schach* — the *sukkah* is valid. The *Gemara* explains the mechanics of this ruling, but the essential point is that interspersing valid *schach* between the planks can rescue the *sukkah* through a combination of halachic principles, including *dofen akuma* applied on both sides. Correspondingly, *u'modeh Rabbi Yehuda* — Rabbi Yehuda, who is generally lenient, admits that if a plank four *tefachim* wide is placed on the *sukkah*, even if the *sukkah* remains valid by virtue of *dofen akuma*, one may not sleep beneath that plank — and if one does, one has not fulfilled the obligation.

---

## Rotating Planks

### Side Rotation

The *Gemara* now raises a new question: *hafkhan al tzideihen* — what if one takes these four-*tefach* planks, which are invalid, and rotates them ninety degrees before placing them on the *sukkah*? Oriented on their side, they are no longer four *tefachim* wide in the way that triggered the *gezeirat tikra*. Does this rotation render them valid *schach*? Three *Amora'im* address this question. Rav Huna says the *sukkah* remains *pesula*. Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna — the latter being Rav Huna's own son — say it is *keshera*.

### Rav Nachman Rules

When Rav Nachman happened to visit Sura, Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna came to him and posed the question. Rav Nachman ruled: *pesula* — it remains invalid. His reasoning: *na'asu k'shfudim shel matechet* — once the rabbis declared these planks invalid, they confer upon them the full status of invalid *schach*, comparable to metal bars. Metal bars are invalid *schach* regardless of how they are oriented, because the invalidation is categorical. The same applies here: the *gezeirat tikra* did not merely forbid a particular configuration; it rendered the planks themselves invalid *schach* in a wholesale manner, such that reorienting them effects no change.

### Huna Vindicated

Rav Huna, upon hearing this, turned to Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna with a pointed remark: had he not told them to rule as he did? They replied that he had never given them his reasoning, and that Rav Nachman had now supplied the rationale they needed to accept the ruling. Rav Huna countered: had they ever asked him for a reason and he had failed to give one? If they wanted a reason, they should have asked.

### Doorway Proof

The *Gemara* then attempts to bring a proof for the position that reorientation does not help. The *baraita* cited enumerates three ways a *sukkah* can be invalidated, one of which is: *shenatan aleha neser sherachav arba'ah tefachim* — if a plank four *tefachim* wide was placed on it. The *baraita* adds: *af al pi shelo hichnis letocha ella shlosha tefachim, pesula* — even if only three of the four *tefachim* extend over the interior of the *sukkah*, it is invalid. The *Gemara* initially reads this as a case where the plank has been rotated: four *tefachim* in one orientation becomes three *tefachim* covering the *sukkah* in the rotated orientation — and still it is invalid.

The *Gemara* rejects this reading, however. The case is not one of rotation. Rather, it describes a plank laid flat in its normal orientation, but positioned so that three *tefachim* extend over the interior of the *sukkah* and one *tefach* extends beyond the wall to the outside. The reason this is nonetheless treated as a four-*tefach* plank is the principle of *psal hayotzei min hasukkah*: any *schach* extending beyond the *sukkah*'s boundary is halachically treated as though it is inside the *sukkah*. If this principle makes a small overhang count toward valid *sukkah* coverage when the *schach* is valid, the same principle causes the overhanging portion of an invalid plank to count toward its full four-*tefach* measurement, even though only three *tefachim* actually lie over the interior.

The net result is that this *baraita* does not prove the case about rotation directly. Nevertheless, the ruling is clear from the earlier amoraic discussion: once *Chazal* invalidated the planks, they are treated as categorically invalid *schach*, and rotation does not help.

---

## Practical Ruling

### 3-1 Scenario

The *Gemara's* final discussion examines the case of the plank positioned with three *tefachim* inside the *sukkah* and one *tefach* outside. As noted, the principle of *psal hayotzei min hasukkah* treats the overhanging portion as though it, too, is inside, making the full four-*tefach* width operative. This principle — that *schach* extending outside the *sukkah* is treated as if it were inside for purposes of the relevant halachic rules — thus applies symmetrically: if it makes valid *schach* outside count for valid coverage inside, it equally makes invalid *schach* outside count toward the full measure of invalidity inside.

### Extension Rule

The *Gemara* establishes that the extension of *psal* outside the *sukkah* is counted as *sukkah* for halachic purposes in both directions. This resolves the question about the three-in, one-out scenario: the *baraita*'s ruling that such a plank invalidates the *sukkah* as a full four-*tefach* plank follows directly from this principle.

### Tosafot Psak

A practical question remains: the *Gemara* presents two competing *baraitot*, one supporting Rav and one supporting Shmuel. Which interpretation governs the *halacha*? Tosafot conclude that from the plain reading of this *Gemara*, the ruling follows Shmuel's interpretation. Although as a general rule we follow Rav over Shmuel in halachic disputes, Tosafot infer from the *Gemara*'s treatment of the material that here we rule like Shmuel. The practical consequence is that even planks between three and four *tefachim* in width remain within the scope of the debate — and Rabbi Meir's position that they are invalid would need to be taken into account.

---

---

# Sukkah 15

## Planks & Gezeirat Tikrah

### Planks Overview

Yesterday's discussion centered on the use of wooden planks as *schach* and whether doing so raises a concern that the *sukkah* would come to resemble an ordinary house. *Rabbi Meir* clearly holds that such a concern exists. The question left open was whether *Rabbi Yehuda* disagrees categorically — rejecting any notion of a rabbinic prohibition on planks — or whether the two *Tannaim* in fact agree in principle but dispute only the threshold: *Rabbi Meir* considering planks of three *tefachim* problematic, while *Rabbi Yehuda* would only raise an objection once they reach four *tefachim* in width. We also established the important principle that even if a plank reaches the problematic width of four *tefachim*, it does not invalidate the *sukkah* as a whole; it merely means one may not sit or sleep beneath that particular plank. This distinction — between what renders a *sukkah* invalid entirely and what merely creates a restricted zone within an otherwise valid *sukkah* — will recur throughout our study.

### Mishnah: Three Views

The *mishnah* before us appears to be a continuation of that earlier discussion. It addresses the case of a *tikrah she-ein aleha ma'aziva* — a roof made of wooden planks that lacks plaster, and which therefore consists of material that is technically valid *schach* but raises the rabbinic concern discussed previously. *Rabbi Yehuda* frames this as a dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, and then *Rabbi Meir* offers his own independent ruling.

### Beit Shammai: Both Acts

*Beit Shammai* holds that two acts are required: *mefakpek* — one must lift up and set back down each individual board — and *notel achat mibeintayim* — one must also remove every alternate board and replace it with valid *schach*. The rationale for requiring both actions simultaneously is not immediately obvious, and the *Gemara* will address this.

### Beit Hillel: One Act

*Beit Hillel* holds that either action alone is sufficient: either *mefakpek* — lifting up and setting back down — or *notel achat mibeintayim* — replacing every alternate board with valid *schach*. One of the two remedies will suffice.

### Rabbi Meir: Replace Only

*Rabbi Meir* rules that the only effective remedy is *notel achat mibeintayim* — replacing alternate boards. Lifting up and setting back down, he holds, accomplishes nothing.

### Two Problem Types

The *mishnah* thus presents two possible underlying problems. The first is *gezeirat tikrah* — the rabbinic concern that wide planks of wood resemble a permanent rooftop and are therefore intrinsically invalid as *schach*. The second is *taasah v'lo min ha'asuy* — the requirement that *schach* be placed actively for the purpose of the *sukkah*, which is violated when material was originally installed as an ordinary roof. Even if there is no intrinsic problem with the planks themselves, the fact that they were installed to serve as a year-round roof may mean they cannot automatically become *schach* without some new deliberate act.

The *taasah v'lo min ha'asuy* explanation seems especially apt for *Beit Hillel* as read by *Rabbi Yehuda*. Since *Rabbi Yehuda* includes *mefakpek* — lifting up and setting back down — as a valid remedy, and since that act does nothing to change the physical character of a plank, the obvious implication is that the plank itself is not problematic. The only issue is one of intent and designation: the roof was installed for the house; one must now perform a new act to dedicate it as *schach* for the *sukkah*.

---

## Gemara: Problem Type

### Beit Hillel via Intent

The *Gemara* opens its analysis by observing that *Beit Hillel*'s position is straightforwardly understood through *taasah v'lo min ha'asuy*. The planks are intrinsically valid *schach*; the only deficiency is that they were placed to serve as a house roof rather than as a *sukkah*. If one performs *mefakpek* — lifting up and setting back down — one has performed a new act, and the planks are now designated for the *sukkah*. Equally, if one replaces every alternate board, one has likewise performed an act with the majority of the material, which may suffice to redefine the entire covering as having been newly placed for the *sukkah*. Either way, the problem is remedied by a demonstrative act of rededication.

### Beit Shammai via Gezeira

The difficulty lies with *Beit Shammai*. If the only problem is *taasah v'lo min ha'asuy*, then a single act — either *mefakpek* or alternating — should be sufficient. Why does *Beit Shammai* require both? Conversely, if the problem is *gezeirat tikrah* — if the planks are intrinsically rabbinically invalid — then *mefakpek* accomplishes nothing at all. Lifting an invalid plank and setting it back down does not transform it into valid *schach*. In that case, the only operative remedy would be replacing alternate boards and relying on some form of majority. If so, why does *Beit Shammai* include *mefakpek* as a required component?

### Gemara: Shammai Reread

The *Gemara* resolves this by re-reading *Beit Shammai*'s formulation. The correct understanding, the *Gemara* explains, is not that *Beit Shammai* requires both acts as joint conditions; rather, *Beit Shammai* is making the following statement: even if one performs *mefakpek*, it is of no avail — it does nothing — because the planks are intrinsically invalid due to *gezeirat tikrah*. The only thing that is effective is *notel achat mibeintayim*, replacing the alternate boards. *Mefakpek* is mentioned only to be dismissed. *Beit Hillel*, by contrast, holds that the planks are fundamentally valid *schach*, and therefore lifting up and setting back down is sufficient to address the intent problem.

The crux of the debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* is thus whether the planks are intrinsically invalid *schach* or intrinsically valid *schach*: *Beit Shammai* holds they are rabbinically invalid, and the only remedy is alternating; *Beit Hillel* holds they are valid, and a new act of dedication suffices.

### Rabbi Meir: No Dispute

The *Gemara* then turns to *Rabbi Meir*'s ruling — that the only effective remedy is replacing the alternate boards and that *mefakpek* does not help — and observes that this sounds precisely like *Beit Shammai* as now understood. How could *Rabbi Meir* be adopting a *Beit Shammai* position?

The *Gemara* explains that *Rabbi Meir* is responding to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s framing. *Rabbi Yehuda* had presented the question as a debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, implying that *Rabbi Meir*'s insistence on the invalidity of planks aligns him with *Beit Shammai* against the ruling of *Beit Hillel*. *Rabbi Meir* pushes back: *lo necheleku Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel ba-davar zeh* — *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* did not dispute this matter. What he is presenting is not the opinion of *Beit Shammai* against *Beit Hillel*, but rather the consensus of all — *divrei hakol*. There is no *Tannaic* authority who validates planks. The apparent debate attributed by *Rabbi Yehuda* to *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* simply did not occur, in *Rabbi Meir*'s view. The positions of *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir* thus come into sharp relief: *Rabbi Yehuda* holds that planks are valid *schach* and the only concern is the intent under which they were placed, while *Rabbi Meir* holds that planks are intrinsically rabbinically invalid and must be interspersed with valid *schach*.

---

## Repetition Question

### Repetition Problem

The *Gemara* then raises a pointed question: if the underlying issue of this *mishnah* is simply whether *gezeirat tikrah* applies to planks, that is precisely the debate already recorded in yesterday's *mishnah* — where *Rabbi Yehuda* permits the use of planks as *schach* and *Rabbi Meir* prohibits it. What novel teaching does the present *mishnah* add? Why repeat the same dispute?

### Chiya: Different Issues

*Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* in the name of *Rabbi Yochanan* offers a radical re-reading: the earlier *mishnah* did not concern wide planks and *gezeirat tikrah* at all. Rather, the earlier debate involved thin, finely smoothed planks — planks that are not wide enough to suggest a permanent rooftop but are so well-crafted and polished that they begin to resemble finished wooden objects. The concern in the earlier *mishnah*, on this reading, was not that the planks look like a roof but that they approach the appearance of a *kli* — a vessel. If thin boards are sanded and refined to the point where they look like manufactured items, perhaps there is a concern that they carry a vessel-like quality that disqualifies them from serving as *schach*, since *schach* must be material that does not *mekabel tumah*. The present *mishnah*, by contrast, deals with genuinely wide planks and the concern that they look like a permanent rooftop — *gezeirat tikrah* in the classic sense. Under this reading, the two *mishnayot* address entirely different problems, and the repetition is fully justified.

### Gemara Rejects

The *Gemara* rejects this alternative reading. It invokes a ruling cited earlier: *Rav Yehuda* in the name of *Rav* stated that if one used male wooden pegs (*chitzin zachar*) as *schach*, the *sukkah* is valid, but if one used female wooden pegs (*chitzin nekeiva*) — which have a receptacle — the *sukkah* is invalid. What is significant here is that the male pegs are entirely usable, smooth, and functional as objects; they simply lack a *beit kibul*, a cavity that would constitute them as a vessel in the halachic sense. And yet their use as *schach* is permitted without any concern that they too closely resemble a vessel or that allowing them will lead people to use the female pegs. The *Gemara* draws the explicit conclusion: *lo gazar zachar atu nekeiva* — we do not extend the prohibition of vessel-like objects to non-vessels merely because they look similar to vessels. If so, there is no basis for the proposed reading that the earlier *mishnah* was concerned with smoothed planks resembling vessels. That simply is not how the *halacha* works. A plank that is not a *kli* is not a *kli*, regardless of how polished it appears.

### Both Are Tikrah

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *al korchacha*, inescapably, both the earlier *mishnah* and the present one concern the same category of wide planks and the same question of *gezeirat tikrah*. Both debates are about whether planks wide enough to evoke a permanent rooftop are rabbinically disqualified as *schach*. If so, the repetition requires explanation on different grounds.

The *Gemara* resolves this by explaining that the current *mishnah* is not simply a restatement but a substantive rhetorical move by *Rabbi Yehuda* addressed directly to *Rabbi Meir*. *Rabbi Yehuda* is saying: you, *Rabbi Meir*, object to planks because of *gezeirat tikrah* — because they look like a permanent roof. But know that this concern belongs to *Beit Shammai* alone. There exists a *machloket* between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* in which *Beit Hillel* does not hold of *gezeirat tikrah* at all: in *Beit Hillel*'s view, the planks are perfectly valid, and all that is required is a new act of dedication. So by insisting on the invalidity of planks, *Rabbi Meir* is adopting a *Beit Shammai* position against *Beit Hillel*. *Rabbi Meir* responds that there was no such dispute — *lo necheleku Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel* — and that his ruling reflects universal consensus.

The *chiddush* of the present *mishnah* thus lies not in introducing a new category of law but in the context it provides: the application of the plank dispute to a case where boards were actually functioning as a house rooftop throughout the year. This raises the additional dimension of *taasah v'lo min ha'asuy* — material designated and used for a permanent dwelling must be actively rededicated for *schach*. *Beit Hillel*'s allowance of *mefakpek* captures this: since the planks are valid in themselves, lifting up and setting back down constitutes the necessary act of rededication. According to *Rabbi Meir*, who holds the planks rabbinically invalid regardless, no such act of rededication can rehabilitate them; only alternating with valid *schach* helps.

One might ask why alternating should suffice at all, given that one is left with fifty percent invalid and fifty percent valid *schach* that are not physically intermingled but arranged side by side. This question — about how *rov* operates in non-intermingled arrangements — will be taken up more fully in the subsequent *mishnah*, but even at this stage it is in many ways the more structurally interesting question that the *Gemara* does not fully draw out in this context. The simple reading of this *mishnah* appears to be that four *tefachim* of invalid *schach* does not invalidate the *sukkah* as a whole; rather, the *sukkah* remains valid and one is simply obligated to position oneself beneath the valid *schach*. Alternating thus ensures that a fully valid *sukkah* exists with accessible valid *schach* sections, even if other sections remain problematic. This reading — though we do not rule in accordance with it ultimately — is the *pshat* of the *mishnah* as it stands.

---

## Rav vs. Shmuel

### Rav: Categorical

With the structure of the *mishnah* established, the *Gemara* turns to the interpretive dispute between *Rav* and *Shmuel* regarding the earlier *mishnah* about planks, and shows how each reading plays out in relation to the present *mishnah*. *Rav* reads the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir* as categorical: *Rabbi Yehuda* holds no position of *gezeirat tikrah* whatsoever, while *Rabbi Meir* accepts it fully. On *Rav*'s reading, the current *mishnah* works elegantly: a rooftop functioning during the year would by assumption be constructed of planks that are four *tefachim* wide, and regarding such planks *Rabbi Yehuda* categorically rejects the problem while *Rabbi Meir* affirms it. The present *mishnah* is thus a clean application of the earlier categorical debate to a practically important case: the plank-roofed structure that was used as an ordinary dwelling.

### Shmuel: Threshold

*Shmuel* reads the earlier dispute differently: *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir* debate only in cases where the planks are less than four *tefachim* wide. Once planks reach four *tefachim*, all authorities — *divrei hakol* — agree they are invalid. On *Shmuel*'s reading, a functional rooftop would obviously be constructed of four-*tefach* planks, meaning that on the present *mishnah*'s facts, both *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Meir* should agree the planks are rabbinically invalid.

### Shmuel's Problem

This creates a significant difficulty for *Shmuel*: if four-*tefach* planks are universally invalid, how does *Rabbi Yehuda* permit the remedy of *mefakpek* — lifting up and setting back down? If the planks are categorically invalid *schach*, *mefakpek* should accomplish nothing, just as *Rabbi Meir* insists.

### Bitul Tikrah

The *Gemara*'s answer on behalf of *Shmuel* is *bitul tikrah* — the negation of the roof's status. The thrust of the explanation is as follows: the reason wide planks are rabbinically invalid as *schach* is the concern that they resemble a permanent rooftop. When the very same planks that have been functioning as one's actual roof throughout the year are now lifted up and placed back down intentionally for the purpose of *schach*, the act constitutes a dramatic public declaration that these are no longer understood as a permanent roof but are now being consciously repurposed as *schach*. This act of *mefakpek* thus has the effect of negating the *tikrah* status — *batla* — and therefore the rabbinic invalidity that stemmed from the roof-like appearance is dissolved.

This is a striking explanation, and the *Gemara* itself seems to sense its difficulty. Throughout the earlier analysis, the principle had been stated that the rabbinic invalidity of planks is unconditional — so unconditional that even turning a plank ninety degrees does not help, because once the rabbis declared it invalid they treated it as categorically disqualified, like a metal pipe. It would seem inconsistent to then say that *mefakpek* — which is nothing more than lifting and setting down — can dissolve that same rabbinic disqualification. Moreover, the general principle of *lo plug* resists this kind of individualized remedy: when the rabbis issued a broad prohibition, we do not allow individuals to perform workarounds that demonstrate their personal awareness of the concern. The *gemara* is acknowledging, in effect, that *Shmuel*'s reading requires an explanation that is difficult to sustain on first principles, and that *Rav*'s reading — under which *Rabbi Yehuda* simply rejects *gezeirat tikrah* entirely — provides a far cleaner account of the entire *sugyah*.

Indeed, the *sugyot* consistently work more smoothly according to *Rav*, and the categorical nature of the debate is the reading that fits the *mishnaiot* most naturally. This will be true elsewhere as well. Nonetheless, as is often the case in areas of *issur*, where we would ordinarily rule like *Rav*, we ultimately rule like *Shmuel* in most of these *sugyot* — even though the explanatory burden falls more heavily on *Shmuel*'s reading.

---

## Alternating Schach

### Mishnah Text

The next *mishnah* returns to the theme of alternating valid and invalid *schach*, this time in a more sharply defined form. *Ha-mekareh sukato bi-shfudin o be-aruchot ha-mittah* — if one roofs one's *sukkah* with metal bars or with bed legs. Metal bars are clearly invalid *schach*, as metal objects are *mekabel tumah* regardless of whether they possess a *beit kibul*; for metal, the absence of a receptacle is irrelevant. Bed legs are wood, and wooden objects without a *beit kibul* are not ordinarily *mekabel tumah*; however, a bed is *tamei*, and when the legs are attached to the bed they participate in the bed's *tum'ah* status. Why the legs remain problematic when detached is a question the *Gemara* will take up — but the *mishnah* proceeds by assuming they are invalid.

*Im yesh revach beneihem ke-motem, kesherah* — if there is a gap between the invalid elements that is equivalent in width to the invalid elements themselves, and if one fills that gap with valid *schach*, the *sukkah* is valid.

### 50% Threshold

This immediately raises the question of why fifty percent suffices. The principle of *rov* — majority — ordinarily requires more than half, something closer to fifty-one percent. And even when *rov* is invoked, it applies where the elements are intermingled to form a single undifferentiated mass; here, the valid and invalid *schach* are arranged in alternating strips, each clearly distinct from the other. Why should such an arrangement render the whole *sukkah* valid?

One possible reading, suggested by the earlier discussion, is that the *mishnah* does not in fact assert that the entire *sukkah* is uniformly valid. Rather, the *sukkah* as a unit is not invalidated, but one must position oneself beneath the valid sections. This is the *pshat* reading — aligned with the position that four *tefachim* of invalid *schach* does not invalidate a *sukkah* entirely. However, this is not the *halacha* as we rule.

### Wall Debate

The *Gemara* observes that the question of whether fifty percent is sufficient parallels a debate regarding walls. For *Shabbat* purposes, a valid enclosure must have walls sufficient to constitute a *reshut ha-yachid*. If the wall consists of alternating solid sections and open gaps — *parutz ke-omeid*, where the gap equals the standing portion — is it a valid partition or not?

*Rav Papa* holds it is permitted, since the majority is not broken through. *Rav Huna bei de-Rav Yehoshua* holds it is forbidden. The *Gemara* notes that this debate turns on how one frames the question. If one defines the requirement of a wall as "the majority must be sealed," then fifty percent sealed is not a majority and fails. If one instead frames the requirement as "the wall is invalid only if the majority is breached," then fifty percent breached is not a majority breach, and the wall is valid. The *Gemara* suggests that the *sukkah* case may be analogous, and applies the same structural question to the roofing scenario.

### Solutions

To explain how the *mishnah* could rule the *sukkah* valid even on the stricter view that majority is required, the *Gemara* offers two solutions.

The first, attributed to *Rav Ami*, is *bema'atif* — that the valid *schach* is added in slightly greater quantity than the invalid material, so the strict threshold of majority is met even on *Rav Huna bei de-Rav Yehoshua*'s position. When the *mishnah* says the gap equals the invalid material, it means the gap is large enough to allow the insertion of material of that size with room to spare — so the valid *schach* that is inserted is actually slightly more than the invalid material beside it.

The second solution, attributed to *Rava*, is more structurally elegant and more broadly significant. Even if the gap and the invalid sections are exactly equal in dimension, the arrangement the *mishnah* envisions involves *sheti* and *erev* — the valid *schach* runs perpendicular to the invalid material. In other words, the invalid material are like beams running in one direction, and the valid *schach* is laid across them in the other direction. Given this crossing configuration, the valid *schach* must extend beyond the beams on either side in order to be supported, so it naturally covers somewhat more than its nominal width. There is therefore inherently more valid *schach* than the measurement would suggest, entirely apart from intentional additions.

*Tosafot* reads the *Gemara* as also addressing a second underlying question: even granted sufficient quantity, how can the valid *schach* and the invalid material be treated as a single unified covering when they are not genuinely intermingled? *Tosafot* understands that for the purposes of *rov* in *schach*, genuine physical intermingling is not required. It is sufficient that the valid *schach* overlaps or rests upon the invalid material at the point of support. That minimal physical contact — where the valid *schach* lies across the invalid beam — constitutes sufficient intermingling to treat the covering as a single unit and apply the principle of *rov* to it as a whole. This is a significant *chiddush*: *Tosafot*'s threshold for what constitutes intermingling is notably low, requiring only that the materials make contact at a crossing point rather than being truly mixed together. Crucially, once this intermingling standard is met and *rov* applies, the entire covering is judged as valid *schach* — meaning one may sit anywhere beneath it and need not restrict oneself to the valid sections alone.

---

## Bed Legs Issue

### Leg Problem

The *Gemara* now takes up the question it had bracketed earlier: why are bed legs invalid *schach*? *Rabbi Ami bar Tuvyumi* states that if one used *blaei kelim* — worn-out garments or worn-out vessels — as *schach*, it is invalid. This ruling addresses a practically important question: if an object was once a *kli* and hence *mekabel tumah*, but has since worn out or broken and no longer technically qualifies as a vessel, does its former status as a *kli* leave a residual disqualification? The answer *Rabbi Ami bar Tuvyumi* offers is yes — *sikacha bi-vla'ei kelim pesula*. Even if the object no longer presently constitutes a vessel, its prior history as one renders it invalid as *schach*. Applied to bed legs: when attached to a bed, they partook of the bed's *tum'ah*; once detached, they may no longer be independently *mekabel tumah*, but the prior vessel status leaves them disqualified as *schach*.

### Segmented Bed

The *Gemara*, however, does not accept this as the explanation for the *mishnah*'s case. It invokes a ruling by *Rav Chanan* in the name of *Rebbi* from *Mishnah Kelim* 18, *mishnah* 4. That *mishnah* states that a bed becomes *tamei* and becomes *tahor* as a complete unit — the position of *Rabbi Eliezer*. The *Chachamim* disagree, holding that individual segments of a bed can become *tamei* and can be immersed in a *mikveh* as segments. The *Gemara* uses this *mishnah* as a springboard: *Rav Chanan* in the name of *Rebbi* specifies which segments of a bed retain *kli* status even in their segmented form — namely, the long half of the bed with two legs, or the short half of the bed with two legs.

### Half-Bed Status

The ruling of *Rav Chanan* in the name of *Rebbi* thus identifies the specific configuration of bed segments that retain independent *kli* status: *arucha u-shnei krayim* — the long section with two legs — or *ktzara u-shnei krayim* — the short section with two legs. In the current *mishnah*, the *Gemara* suggests, we are dealing not with bare detached legs but with precisely such a segment — a portion of the bed including two legs that retains its *kli* identity because it remains functional in its current form.

### Function Test

What function does such a segment serve? *Rav Chanan* explains: *le-mismichinhu aguda* — one can lean it against a wall; *u-le-meitav alaihu* — and sit upon it; *u-mashdi ashlei* — and secure it with ropes as needed. In other words, a half-bed standing against a wall serves as a functional seat or resting surface. Because it can still be used in this way, it retains the status of a *kli* and remains *mekabel tumah* — not merely by virtue of its history but because it is presently functional. *Tosafot* notes that this functional use alone might not be entirely sufficient for *kli* status, and that the fact that one intends to reassemble the bed contributes as well: the combination of present usability and anticipated reassembly together sustain the *kli* identity for the *Chachamim*.

The practical significance for our *mishnah* is thus: bed legs are invalid *schach* not because they once participated in a *kli* and carry residual historical disqualification — the position of *Rabbi Ami bar Tuvyumi* — but because they presently constitute part of a *kli* in their segmented form. The question of whether historical *kli* status alone suffices to disqualify material from serving as *schach* remains unresolved and will continue to be addressed as the *sugyah* develops.

---

---

# Sukkah 16

## Former Vessels

### Bed Legs & Tumah

The *gemara* picks up with *gufa* — returning to the original statement under analysis — six lines from the top of the *daf*. The background to this discussion is the *mishna*'s reference to using the legs of a bed as *schach*, which the *mishna* appeared to assume were susceptible to *tumah*. The *gemara* had raised the difficulty: how can detached bed legs be *mekabel tumah*? They are no longer part of a vessel; they are merely wood, and wood requires a receptacle-form to be susceptible. The *gemara* connected this to a debate found in a *mishna* in *Kelim* concerning a disassembled or partially broken bed. One opinion there holds that even a partially disassembled bed can still become *tamei*, because it is destined to be reassembled — and as *Tosafot* notes, because it retains some functional use in its current state. This would apply to the case of half a bed with two legs still attached.

That explanation, however, is set aside. The *gemara* proposes a fundamentally different approach: the bed legs no longer can become *tamei*, having been detached and rendered non-functional as a vessel. But perhaps, precisely because they *once were* a vessel, they remain invalid as *schach* — permanently labeled by their history. The *gemara* now pursues this question directly.

### Worn-Out Vessels

*Gufa* — returning to the original statement: Rav Ami bar Tavyumi teaches that if one used *bivlei kelim* — worn-out vessels or worn-out clothing — as *schach*, the *sukkah* is invalid. Even though these items are no longer *halachically* considered vessels or garments, having deteriorated past any measure of usability and therefore no longer susceptible to *tumah*, they were once vessels, once clothing — and that history disqualifies them from serving as *schach*.

### Cloth Size Measures

Abaye clarifies what is meant by *bivlei kelim*: pieces of cloth (*matlaniyot*) that are less than three finger-widths by three finger-widths, and which are not fit for use either by wealthy people or by the poor. This requires understanding the *gemara*'s three-tier framework for cloth size.

The largest threshold is *shlosha al shlosha tefachim* — three *tefachim* by three *tefachim*, roughly nine inches by nine inches. A wealthy person discards anything smaller than this; for that person, such a fragment has ceased to function as clothing. A poor person, however, will still use smaller pieces for patching garments. The lower threshold is *shalosh al shalosh* — three finger-widths by three finger-widths, roughly an inch and a half by an inch and a half. Anything smaller than this, nobody uses — not the wealthy, not the poor. Such a piece is beneath any standard of utility.

The *gemara* exploits the gendered grammar of Hebrew to mark this distinction precisely: *tefach* is masculine, so "three *tefachim*" is *shlosha* — the number taking its feminine form in agreement with the masculine noun, per the grammatical inversion. *Shalosh al shalosh*, with the feminine numeral, refers to fingers, a different unit entirely. The notation is not incidental; it encodes the distinction between the two thresholds.

The *halacha* for *schach* follows from this: even once a piece of cloth has fallen below the smallest threshold — below *shalosh al shalosh* finger-widths — so that literally no one would use it and it is not *mekabel tumah* under any measure, it remains *pasul* for *schach* because it originated as a *keli*, as usable clothing. This has immediate practical application: if one were to gather wood from a discarded broken table left out on the street before *Sukkot*, that wood would in fact be problematic as *schach* under this teaching.

### Sedge Mat Rules

The *gemara* now brings a *baraita* that runs parallel to the ruling of Rav Ami bar Tavyumi. If one has a *machatzelet* — a mat woven from *shaifa*, a type of sedge or rush, papyrus or reed grass — and what remains is a remnant smaller than the standard *shiur*, that remnant is invalid as *schach*. The relevant *shiur* here is not a *shiur* for *schach* itself, but the *shiur* for *tumah*: a mat must be at least six *tefachim* by six *tefachim* — roughly a foot and a half by a foot and a half — to be considered a functional vessel susceptible to *tumah*. Once the mat has broken down to a piece smaller than this, it is no longer *mekabel tumah* and is no longer classified as a vessel. Nevertheless, *ein mesachachin bahem* — one may not use it as *schach*, because it originated from something that once had the status of a vessel. The same principle that applies to worn-out clothing applies equally to worn-out mats.

### Reed Mat Sizes

The *gemara* turns to a related but structurally different case. A mat made from reeds or sticks: *gedolah mesachachin bah* — a large one may be used as *schach*; *ketanah ein mesachachin bah* — a small one may not. This is, at first glance, counterintuitive. Everything discussed until now has followed the logic that the larger the item, the more it functions as a vessel, the more it is *mekabel tumah*, and therefore the more it is disqualified as *schach*. Here the relationship is inverted.

The resolution lies in a distinction about functional identity. A small reed mat — large enough for one person to sit on — is classified as a sitting mat, a *keli* designed for human use, and is therefore *mekabel tumah*. A very large reed mat is not used for sitting; people use it as a wall covering, a roofing material, or a partition. It ceases to be a *keli* in the relevant sense and becomes a structural material — not *mekabel tumah*, and therefore *kosher* as *schach*. The greater its size, the more clearly it is identified as something other than a vessel. This point is directly relevant to contemporary practice: the bamboo *schach* mats now sold commercially, or the type sold in home improvement stores, raise precisely this question — are they sitting mats (*mekabel tumah*) or structural coverings? The *gemara* resolves the question by size.

Rabbi Eliezer dissents. Even a large reed mat, he says, remains *mekabel tumah* — people do in fact use them for sitting, and therefore even the large ones cannot be used as *schach*. This debate will be developed further in the *gemara* in subsequent days.

The bottom line established by this section for the *hilkhot schach*: once something has been a vessel, it retains its disqualification from serving as *schach* even after it no longer meets the threshold for *tumah* susceptibility.

---

## Haystack Sukkah

### Rav Huna's Solution

The *gemara* now moves to the second part of the *mishna*: the case of one who hollows out a cavity inside a haystack in order to create a *sukkah*. The structure yields walls and a roof made of hay, which in principle should be valid *schach*. The problem, however, is *taaseh v'lo min ha'asuy*: the *sukkah* — meaning specifically the *schach* — must be made through a direct act. Here the roof was created not by any positive act of placing *schach* but indirectly, as a consequence of removing the interior of the haystack. It was, in a sense, pre-made by the removal rather than made directly.

Rav Huna resolves the problem: *lo shanu* — this was only taught to be invalid in the standard case, *ela she'ein sham challal tefach bemeshech shivah* — where there was no pre-existing cavity of one *tefach* in height extending over an area of seven by seven *tefachim*, the minimum dimensions of a *sukkah*. But *aval yesh sham challal tefach bemeshech shivah* — if there was already such a cavity, *harei zu sukkah* — it is valid.

What does this mean in practice? The ordinary case is a solid haystack that one hollows out entirely, creating the *schach* only through the act of removal. But suppose the haystack was initially piled on top of some kind of platform, so that there was already a cavity of seven by seven *tefachim* in area and one *tefach* in height at the outset, before any digging. In that case, when the hay was first placed over the cavity, an act of making *schach* was performed: one placed hay over a space of *sukkah* dimensions. The deficiency at that point was only in wall height — the cavity was only one *tefach* high, not ten *tefachim*. But that is a wall problem, not a *schach* problem. Kosher *schach* was established at the moment the hay was placed over the one-*tefach*-high space, because a *tefach* of height already constitutes an *ohel* — a tent — for purposes of *tumah* law and, by extension, for establishing *schach* identity. The subsequent digging to create the full ten *tefachim* of height merely completes the walls; it does not create the *schach* anew.

### Mishna/Baraita Conflict

The *gemara* notes that this resolution is confirmed independently. *Tanya nami hachi* — a *baraita* teaches the very same thing, stating that one who hollows out a haystack (*ha-chotet begadish la'asot lo sukkah*) has a valid *sukkah*. But this seems to contradict the *mishna*, which rules it invalid. Rather than treating this as a *machloket*, the *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *ela lav shema mina keRav Huna* — the *baraita* that validates it is discussing the case with a pre-existing cavity of one *tefach* over seven by seven *tefachim*, while the *mishna* that invalidates it is discussing the ordinary case without any such pre-existing cavity.

Some transmit this slightly differently: the statement of Rav Huna began not as a commentary on the *mishna* but as a direct resolution of the contradiction between the *mishna* and the *baraita*. The substance, however, is identical. *Lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. *Kan sheyesh sham challal tefach bemeshech shivah* — the *baraita* speaks where there was such a cavity, *kan she'ein sham challal bemeshech shivah* — the *mishna* speaks where there was none. *Shema mina* — this is a solid proof.

### Tosafot Analysis

*Tosafot* observes a beautiful instance of *leshitateh* — a *amora* holding a consistent position across different contexts. Four lines down in the wide text of *Tosafot*, he notes: *mashkachat lemeimar Rav Huna leta'ameih* — one can say that Rav Huna here follows the same reasoning he articulated earlier in the *gemara*, approximately six days earlier in the *daf yomi* cycle, in the context of *bein sukkah lesukkah tefach* — the question of one *sukkah* placed beneath another. That discussion concerned the minimum height by which the upper *schach* must be separated from the lower *schach* in order to be identified as an independent *sukkah* in its own right. Rav Huna ruled there that once the upper *schach* is one *tefach* higher, it already acquires the independent identity of *schach*. The same principle operates here: a one-*tefach* space already has the identity of *schach* — it is not yet a *kosher sukkah* due to insufficient wall height, but it has established the requisite identity of *schach*. Once Rav Huna makes the walls ten *tefachim* the *sukkah* is complete.

*Tosafot* further notes: *veshama man de'amar hatam arba hacha modeh* — it is possible that an opinion that requires four *tefachim* of separation in the *sukkah-under-sukkah* case might still agree with Rav Huna here, because the considerations differ. As for Shmuel, who requires ten *tefachim* of separation in the *sukkah-under-sukkah* case — *Tosafot* reasons that Shmuel's stringency there derives from his view that one needs a full *sukkah* beneath a *sukkah*, not merely *schach* beneath *schach*. In the present case, the question is only about *schach* identity, and so Shmuel might well agree. The connecting thread is the same Rav Huna who said that one *tefach* of separation yields *schach* identity also says here that one *tefach* of height over a *sukkah*-sized area constitutes the making of *schach*.

### Schach Before Walls

This ruling raises a directly practical question that is debated among the *acharonim*: if one places *kosher schach* on the frame of a *sukkah* before erecting the walls, does *taaseh v'lo min ha'asuy* apply? Was the *schach* "made" before the *sukkah* was a *sukkah*?

The present *gemara* strongly suggests that this is permissible. The case here is nearly identical: *kosher schach* was established when the walls were only one *tefach* high, and the walls were then completed to ten *tefachim* afterward. The *schach* was not re-laid; it was considered valid as it was, and the subsequent wall construction completed the *sukkah*. As *Rashi* analogizes, this parallels the earlier *gemara* concerning a nine-*tefach*-high *sukkah* where one digs a hole in the floor to achieve the required ten *tefachim* — there too, the *schach* was kosher and the walls were completed afterward. The implication is that *schach* placed before fully kosher walls are in place does not require the ritual of lifting and re-laying; it was placed *kosher* at the time of placing, and the subsequent wall construction does not retroactively impair it.

One might distinguish: here there was at least a one-*tefach* wall at the time the *schach* was placed, whereas if one places *schach* on a bare frame there are no walls at all yet. But the straightforward reading of this *gemara* suggests the principle is sound regardless — *schach* may precede fully completed walls.

A separate question was raised concerning whether the haystack's hay would qualify as *schach* at all, given that very dense *schach* that does not allow rain through is considered a roof rather than *schach*. *Tosafot* addressed this in an earlier passage, ruling that the relevant criterion is not whether sunlight penetrates but whether rain penetrates. A haystack, it would seem, does allow rain through, and therefore the hay can qualify as *schach*.

---

## Wall Heights

### Top-Down Walls

The *gemara* turns to the next *mishna*, which addresses the height requirements for *sukkah* walls constructed in different ways. *Hamshalshel dfanot* — one who lowers walls downward, meaning one who hangs a curtain or partition starting from near the top of the *schach* and letting it drop toward the ground: *im gavoha min ha'aretz shlosha tefachim pesulah* — if the bottom edge of the wall is three or more *tefachim* above the ground, the *sukkah* is invalid. The reason is the principle of *lavud*: within less than three *tefachim*, a gap is considered legally closed — the two surfaces are treated as if joined. Three *tefachim* or more cannot be bridged by *lavud*, and the wall is no longer considered attached to the ground. There is also a related *mechitza* rationale: a gap of three *tefachim* or more allows goats to pass beneath, and something that cannot stop even animals from passing under it cannot be called a wall. But most simply, it is the application of *lavud*.

### Bottom-Up Walls

Building a wall from the ground up: *im gavoah asarah tefachim kosher* — once the wall reaches ten *tefachim*, it is valid even if it does not reach the *schach*. This might seem to require explanation, since in principle a *sukkah* wall should be adjacent to the *schach*. The answer involves the principle of *gud asik* — but first, one might have proposed a simpler reason: the wall is physically below the *schach*, not outside it, and perhaps mere presence beneath the *schach* suffices. The more precise answer, however, is *gud asik mechitzta* — once a wall achieves the status of a valid *mechitza*, we envision it as extending upward indefinitely, closing the gap between its top and the *schach*. The wall does not have to physically touch; its legal extension reaches the *schach*.

### Magic Wall Extension

The *gemara* introduces the two complementary principles of *gud achis* and *gud asik* — what the lecturer characterizes as the "magic extending walls" of *sukkah* law, analogous to the "magic bending wall" of *dofen akuma*. *Gud achis mechitzta* means we pull the wall downward; *gud asik* means we extend it upward. The word *gud* is glossed by *Rashi* as meaning to stretch, though it also carries a connotation of wall.

The logic of the *mishna* now becomes clear: once a wall is a valid *mechitza* — which requires it to be attached to the ground and ten *tefachim* high — *gud asik* extends it up to the *schach*, and there is no deficiency. The wall functions completely. One who grasps this will immediately ask: if we can use *gud asik* to extend a bottom-up wall to the *schach*, why can we not use *gud achis* to extend a top-down wall down to the ground, even when it is more than three *tefachim* away? The *mishna* already tells us the answer — the rabbis say no — and the next opinion challenges that.

### Rabbi Yose Two Ways

Rabbi Yose says: *kesheim she'mimata lema'ala asarah tefachim kosher, kach mimaala lemata asarah tefachim kosher* — just as ten *tefachim* of wall from the ground upward is sufficient without reaching the *schach*, so too ten *tefachim* of wall from above downward is sufficient without reaching the ground. Rabbi Yose holds that any ten-*tefach* span in a vertical plane constitutes a *mechitza*, and therefore even a wall suspended in mid-air can be extended downward by *gud achis* to reach the ground.

The rabbis disagree. Their view is that the fundamental concept of a *mechitza* is a wall at ground level. A suspended wall in mid-air, unconnected to the ground, never acquires the identity of a *mechitza* in the first place. *Gud asik* can operate upward once a wall is grounded, because it is extending an established *mechitza*. But there is no base identity to extend downward from a hanging curtain. One might further note that this implies an interesting question according to Rabbi Yose: if ten *tefachim* of wall anywhere in the vertical plane is a *mechitza*, could one extend it both up and down simultaneously? That will be addressed when the *gemara* returns to the question.

---

## Suspended Walls

### Well Boundary Case

The *gemara* now asks: *bimai kamipligi* — what exactly is the conceptual dispute between the rabbis and Rabbi Yose? The *gemara* frames it in terms borrowed from *hilkhot Shabbat*: *mar savar mechitza teluyah materet* — one holds that a suspended *mechitza* makes the space it encloses permissible, and *umar savar mechitza teluyah einah materet* — the other holds it does not. The word *materet* — permissible — is the language of *Shabbat* law, where a *mechitza* of ten *tefachim* creates a *reshut hayachid*, a private domain, permitting carrying within it. The *gemara* is thus assuming that the debate about suspended walls is the same debate whether it arises in the context of *sukkah* or *Shabbat*.

To explore this, the *gemara* cites a *mishna* in *Eruvin*: if there is a well situated between two adjacent courtyards, each of which has made its own *eruv* separately, one may not draw water from the well on *Shabbat* — *ein memale'in mimenu beShabbat*. The situation is as follows: two courtyards share a common area, each is a *reshut hayachid* in its own right, and the well sits on the boundary between them. Drawing water from the shared well means taking from the domain of one courtyard into the other, which is prohibited since they have not combined their *eruvin*. Both courtyards are *reshut hayachid*; carrying between two separate *reshuyot hayachid* that have not made a joint *eruv* is a *de-rabbanan* prohibition.

*Ela im kein* — unless one constructed a *mechitza* of ten *tefachim* within the well itself, whether positioned near the top of the well or near the bottom, or right beneath the lip — then access to the water is permitted.

### Water Leniency

The *mishna*'s ruling raises an obvious question: why does a wall positioned inside the well permit drawing water, while the ordinary wall already running between the two courtyards above the well does not? In either case — whether the wall is inside the well near the top or near the bottom — the wall is not physically at the water level; in both cases we would be saying we envision the wall as extending all the way down to the water. What, then, is the practical difference?

The answer lies in a principle specific to water access. The *gemara* articulates this as *kalu hu shehetiru chachamim bamayim* — a leniency that the Sages instituted specifically to preserve access to water. Water was not a convenience in the world of *Chazal*; access to water was a critical necessity. Accordingly, the Sages permitted certain applications of the principle of envisioning walls as extending downward — specifically in contexts where a *mechitza* was constructed expressly to enable access to water. A wall built inside the well, within the well itself, is built specifically for that purpose, and therefore the water leniency applies: we envision it as extending to the water. The wall running above the well between the courtyards was not constructed for that purpose, and so the special leniency does not apply to it.

In practical terms, there is an analogous case: a person on a balcony or ship adjacent to a body of water may construct a small enclosure on the balcony and lower a bucket through it to draw water, because the enclosure is built specifically to enable water access, and we envision the walls as extending down to the water, making the water-drawing a transfer within a single *reshut hayachid*.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel frames the question differently, presenting it as a dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*: *Beit Shammai omrim milma'ala* — the wall may be near the top of the well, *uBeit Hillel omrim milmata* — it must be near the water. *Tosafot* notes that in the manuscripts of *Eruvin*, the *girsaot* read the positions in reverse — *Beit Shammai* as the *machmir* requiring the wall near the water, and *Beit Hillel* as the *meikil* allowing it near the top — which would be the more expected alignment with their usual tendencies. The reading in *Sukkah* chapter 109 of *Shabbat* presents it differently, and *Tosafot* observes the discrepancy across the texts.

### Rav Yehuda Position

Now comes the statement that is directly relevant to the debate in our *mishna*. Rav Yehuda says: *lo tehei mechitza gedolah min hakosel shebeinehem* — should this wall inside the well have more legal force than the great wall that runs between the courtyards above? If we permit access to the well on the basis of the interior wall, ought we not be able to permit it on the basis of the already-existing exterior wall above?

Rav Yehuda is thus asserting that the exterior wall can serve to extend downward and create a *reshut hayachid* in the water — not as a water leniency, but as a general principle. A suspended wall can, as a matter of general *halacha*, be extended downward. This positions Rav Yehuda as holding that *mechitza teluyah materet* as a general rule, not merely as a water-specific dispensation.

### Cross-Context Debate

Rav Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan notes: *Rav Yehuda beshitat Rabbi Yose amra* — Rav Yehuda's position in *Eruvin* corresponds precisely to Rabbi Yose's position in our *mishna* in *Sukkah*. Both hold that a suspended *mechitza* is legally effective — Rav Yehuda in the context of *Shabbat* and carrying, Rabbi Yose in the context of *sukkah* walls. Since the underlying conceptual position is the same — *mechitza teluyah materet* — the two rulings should reflect the same view.

### Rava's Answer

The *gemara* says *velo hi* — this is not necessarily so. The *gemara* resists the equivalence and holds that one might accept the principle for *Shabbat* and not for *sukkah*, or for *sukkah* and not for *Shabbat*.

The reasoning: *lo Rav Yehuda savar lah keRabbi Yose* — Rav Yehuda would not necessarily hold with Rabbi Yose in *sukkah*. *Ad kan lo ka'amar Rav Yehuda hatam ela be'eruvei chatzeirot de-rabbanan* — Rav Yehuda there in *Eruvin* is speaking only in the context of the joint *eruv* of courtyards, which is a rabbinic prohibition. Both courtyards are *reshuyot hayachid* already; the issue of drawing from one to the other is only a *de-rabbanan* concern. For a rabbinic prohibition, Rav Yehuda is willing to allow the suspended wall. *Aval hacha sukkah de-oraita* — but here, where *sukkah* is a biblical obligation, he would not extend the leniency of the suspended wall to a biblical-level question.

Conversely, *velo Rabbi Yose savar keRav Yehuda* — Rabbi Yose would not necessarily agree with Rav Yehuda in *Shabbat*. *Ad kan lo ka'amar Rabbi Yose hacha ela be-sukkah de-mitzvas aseh* — Rabbi Yose's leniency by *sukkah* reflects the fact that the worst consequence of a flawed *sukkah* is failing to fulfill a positive commandment, a *mitzvas aseh*. *Aval Shabbat de-skila lo* — but *Shabbat*, where violations can carry the penalty of death and the entire system of *Shabbat* law is enormously consequential, he would be more stringent even in a case that is technically only *de-rabbanan*.

This is a striking resolution. Rather than a conceptual distinction — one might have argued, for instance, that *sukkah* requires a wall that makes the space *habitable*, which demands ground-to-*schach* closure in a way that *Shabbat mechitzot* do not — the *gemara* here grounds the divergence simply in degrees of stringency and leniency. The *Shabbat* case is more lenient because it is only *de-rabbanan*; the *sukkah* case is more lenient because the worst outcome is only a failed *mitzvas aseh*. Each authority applies his principle selectively based on the severity of the legal domain involved.

### Tzipori Story

The *gemara* anticipates an objection: there is a famous story that took place in *Tzipori* — the city of Rabbi Yose — in which a suspended *mechitza* was used to permit carrying on *Shabbat*. Does this not prove that Rabbi Yose applied his principle equally to *Shabbat*?

*Al pi mi na'asah* — on whose authority was this done? *Lo al pi Rabbi Yose* — not Rabbi Yose's. *Ela al pi Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yose* — it was done on the authority of his son, Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yose. Rabbi Yose himself had already passed away when this ruling was given in *Tzipori*. One therefore cannot derive Rabbi Yose's own view on the *Shabbat* application from the story; the ruling was his son's. Perhaps his son extended the principle to *Shabbat*, but Rabbi Yose himself — from what we know — applied it only to *sukkah*.

The story itself is as follows: on one occasion, the community forgot to bring the *Sefer Torah* from its storage location before *Shabbat* to the place where it was needed for reading. The *Sefer Torah* was in one location, the *beit knesset* was across the *mavoi*, and without a *shituf mevo'ot* having been arranged beforehand, carrying through the shared space was prohibited (*de-rabbanan*). The solution: *matzu sadinim perusim al gabei amudim* — they found sheets already spread across posts, which created the necessary enclosure, and they were then able to bring the *Sefer Torah* and read from it.

The *gemara* questions the original formulation — how could they have *spread* the sheets on *Shabbat* at all? Carrying implies an already-existing *reshut hayachid*, which requires the walls to be in place first; making the walls is what one is trying to do. The answer given is that the sheets were already spread — found in place rather than actively arranged on *Shabbat* itself. Perhaps someone had hung out laundry, and the community realized it could serve as the necessary *mechitza*. Laundry spread between posts over a sufficient span is a natural example of a *mechitza teluyah*.

The question of whether one may make a *mechitza* on *Shabbat* is addressed at this point. *Rashi* rules that making a *mechitza* — hanging a partition — is not categorized as making an *ohel* on *Shabbat* and is therefore permitted; he crossed out the alternative *girsah* in the *gemara* that seemed to raise an *ohel* concern. *Tosafot* disagrees. *Tosafot* acknowledges that other *gemarot* seem to permit wall-making on *Shabbat*, and introduces a crucial distinction: one may erect a partition on *Shabbat* for purely functional purposes — privacy, screening, aesthetic purposes. What one may not do is create a *mechitza hamattir*, a partition that serves a *halachic* function of changing the legal status of a space. Rabbeinu Tam formulates this explicitly: *venireh leRabbeinu Tam di-mina tzad nami shayach asiyat ohel vekhe-hai gavna de-mechitza zo mo'elet lehattir* — a wall that is built specifically to render a space permissible in a *halachic* sense is itself categorized as a form of making an *ohel* and is prohibited. A wall built for privacy is not.

This is in fact the accepted *halacha*. The application to contemporary synagogue *mechitzot* is instructive: a *mechitza* erected in a synagogue for the purpose of allowing prayer — creating a separate space for women — is permitted on *Shabbat* because its function is understood as providing privacy rather than effecting a *halachic* status change. However, if the *mechitza* functions *halachically* as a formal *mechitza* in the *Shabbat* sense — for instance, a *mechitza* of only ten *tefachim* used to create a *reshut hayachid* — one would be prohibited from erecting it on *Shabbat* itself, because it is precisely a *mechitza hamattir*. Indeed, there is a tradition that the Rav Soloveitchik held that ten *tefachim* is the sufficient height for a *mechitza*, and Rav Yehuda Herzl Henkin publicly articulated the same position, though he added that it may not be a suspended fabric partition — precisely because of the *mechitza teluyah* issues developed throughout this *gemara*.

---

## Mechitza Function

### Permitting Walls

*Tosafot*'s principle — that a *mechitza* intended to create a *halachic* permission (*mechitza hamattir*) may not be erected on *Shabbat* — emerges directly from the *Tzipori* story and the surrounding *gemara*. The act of hanging sheets, when done to create a domain that permits carrying, constitutes *asiyat ohel* in the relevant halachic sense, even though in physical terms one is only suspending a fabric curtain. What triggers the prohibition is the *function* the wall is meant to perform, not its material form.

### Privacy vs. Status

The operative distinction is between a wall that serves a *halachic* status-changing function and one that serves a practical or social function. Hanging a curtain to change in privacy, to separate a space visually, or to prevent passersby from seeing within — these do not create a *mechitza hamattir* and are permitted on *Shabbat*. Hanging a curtain specifically to constitute the third or fourth wall of a *reshut hayachid*, or to permit an act that was otherwise prohibited, is the type of wall the prohibition targets.

### Shul Mechitza Rules

This distinction plays out directly in the *halacha* of synagogue *mechitzot*. A *mechitza* installed to create the environment for prayer functions more like a privacy partition — it enables prayer to take place in an appropriate setting — rather than as a wall that *halachically* transforms the nature of the space in the *Shabbat* sense. That is why it may be erected on *Shabbat*. Where the *mechitza* is sized and positioned to serve its formal *halachic* function — specifically the minimum of ten *tefachim* required by the law of *mechitzot* — the equation changes. A ten-*tefach mechitza* that is treated as formally operative under *Shabbat* law cannot be put up on *Shabbat* itself. The higher *mechitzot* common in most synagogues, understood as privacy or decorum structures rather than *halachic* status-changers, do not raise this concern.

---

## Lavud Solutions

### Mid-Height Mat

Rav Chisda, citing Avimi, states: *machatzelet arba'ah umashehu materet besukkah mishum dofen* — a mat of four *tefachim* and a bit (*umashehu*) renders a *sukkah* valid as a wall. The context is a *sukkah* of exactly ten *tefachim* in height. One takes such a mat and hangs it precisely in the middle of the wall space — *tolehu be'emtza*. Positioned at the center, its lower edge is less than three *tefachim* from the ground, and its upper edge is less than three *tefachim* from the *schach*. *Lavud* applies in both directions: *pachot mishlosha lemata, pachot mishlosha lema'ala* — less than three below and less than three above. Since any gap of less than three *tefachim* is treated as closed by *lavud*, the mat effectively spans the entire ten *tefachim*, constituting a complete wall.

### Double Lavud

The *gemara* anticipates an objection: is this not obvious? The *gemara* responds: *mahu deteima chad lavud amrinan, trei lavud lo amrinan* — one might have thought that *lavud* can be invoked once but not twice — that applying the principle simultaneously at both ends of the same surface is a step too far. The ruling of Rav Chisda therefore teaches *kamashma lan* — that double *lavud* at opposite ends is in fact permitted.

### Seven-Tefach Mat

A *baraita* is then cited that seems to contradict this: *machatzelet shivah umashehu materet basukkah mishum dofen* — a mat of seven *tefachim* and a bit is needed to render the *sukkah* valid.
