This implies that double *lavud* cannot be used and only a single *lavud* at one end is permitted, requiring the mat itself to cover seven of the ten *tefachim*, with *lavud* closing the remaining less-than-three.

### Gud Achis Application

The *gemara* resolves: *lo kashya* — there is no contradiction. *Ki tanya hahi besukkah gedolah* — that *baraita* speaks about a large *sukkah*, not a standard ten-*tefach sukkah*. In a large *sukkah*, the mat must be seven and a bit. Why? Because in a large *sukkah*, one cannot position the mat in the middle and apply *lavud* to both ends — there are constraints on how this works when the sukkah height is greater than ten *tefachim*. Instead, the mat is positioned near the top of the wall space, with *lavud* closing the gap upward to the *schach*. That gives the mat *schach*-adjacent validity and yields ten *tefachim* of wall counting from the top down. But then, to close the remaining space between the bottom of the mat and the ground, one must invoke *gud achis* — extending the wall downward — and that only follows according to Rabbi Yose. Hence the *baraita* implicitly follows Rabbi Yose's position, which permits suspended walls to extend downward. There is also another *girsah* noted by *Rashi* in which the mat is placed near the ground with *lavud* at the bottom, yielding ten *tefachim* from the ground up, and then *gud asik* extends the wall upward to the *schach*. That case is less controversial, since *gud asik* extends an already-grounded wall, which the rabbis permit. The more surprising *chiddush* in the standard *girsah* is the top-down case requiring *gud achis* — which follows only Rabbi Yose.

### Vertical Plank Wall

Rav Yosef adds: *pas arba'ah arba'ah* — a vertical plank (*pas*) of four and a bit *tefachim* likewise renders the *sukkah* valid as a wall. While the *machatzelet* — the mat discussed above — runs horizontally between the *schach* and the ground, a *pas* here refers to a plank positioned vertically along the wall in the plane of the *sukkah*'s width or length. A *sukkah*'s minimum dimension is seven *tefachim* in each direction. If one wall is complete and the second wall needs to be formed, a vertical plank of four *tefachim* and a bit placed within less than three *tefachim* of the existing wall creates a total of more than seven *tefachim* through *lavud* — the plank's four-plus *tefachim* combined with the closing of the sub-three-*tefach* gap on the side. *Umokmi lah bepachot mishlosha tefachim samuch ladofen* — it is positioned within three *tefachim* of the wall, and *vechol pachot mishlosha tefachim kelavud dami* — any gap of less than three *tefachim* is considered closed.

### Seven-Tefach Minimum

*Mai kamashma lan* — what does Rav Yosef's ruling teach us that we did not already know? *Ha kamashma lan* — it teaches us *shiur meshech sukkah ketanah shivah* — that the minimum dimension of a *sukkah* is seven *tefachim*. This fundamental measurement of *sukkah* law is, perhaps unexpectedly, embedded in and derivable from this precise *halacha* about vertical planks and *lavud*. An unusual vehicle for transmitting the basic minimum of *sukkah* dimensions — but that, concludes the *daf*, is the *chiddush* contained within it.

---

---

# Sukkah 17

## Schach Distance & Gud As…

### Three Tefachim Air Gap

The present *daf* opens with a *mishna* that serves as a natural companion to the preceding one, which treated the principle of *gud asik* — the conceptual extension of a valid wall upward through empty space. That earlier *mishna* addressed gaps on the *vertical* plane: a wall standing ten *tefachim* from the ground may be imagined as rising all the way to the *schach*, even if there is air between the top of the wall and the roof. The principle of *lavud* — which treats a gap of less than three *tefachim* as legally closed — was central there as well.

This *mishna* now turns to a different problem: a gap on the *horizontal* plane. The case is one in which the wall rises to the full height of the *sukkah*, but at the level of the roof there is a gap of three *tefachim* or more between the edge of the wall and where the *schach* begins. In such a case, the *mishna* rules *pesulah* — the *sukkah* is invalid. The wall, although it rises to the proper height, is not connected to the *schach*, and since the horizontal gap exceeds three *tefachim*, *lavud* cannot close it. Without that connection, the *sukkah* lacks a proper wall.

### Gud Asik Extension

It is worth distinguishing this scenario from the previous *mishna*'s case. When the wall does not reach the full height but stands a valid ten *tefachim* from the ground, *gud asik* — "extend the wall upward" — applies, and the wall is treated as though it rises to meet the *schach*. But *gud asik* operates on the vertical axis; it imagines the existing wall continuing upward into space above it. Here, by contrast, the gap is lateral — a horizontal space at the level of the *schach* between the wall's edge and the *schach* itself. *Gud asik* cannot close that gap.

### Vertical vs Horizontal

This raises an immediate question: why does *dofen akuma* — the principle of the "bent wall" — not apply here to bridge the gap? *Dofen akuma* permits treating up to four *amot* of invalid *schach* adjacent to a wall as though it were a bent extension of that wall. If so, could one not invoke *dofen akuma* even for an air gap, imagining the wall as bending sideways through the open space?

The answer is that *dofen akuma* is operative only when something physical occupies that lateral space — specifically, *pasul schach*, invalid *schach*. An invalid material such as metal bars can be reconceived as a portion of the wall that has bent over horizontally. Empty air, by contrast, has no physical substance that could be re-categorized as part of the wall. Air is simply absence, and one cannot bend a wall through nothing.

### Rashi on Dofen Akuma

*Rashi* on this *daf* explicitly reflects on why he adopts one conceptual model of *dofen akuma* over another — a remarkably self-aware methodological comment. Two lines from the top of the *amud*, *Rashi* writes: *de-avir poseil beshelosha afilu min hatzad* — air invalidates at three *tefachim* even from the side, on the horizontal plane. He then adds: *umikan ani omer umefaresh* — and it is from this *mishna* that I derive and explain the following point about *dofen akuma*.

*Rashi* proceeds to articulate two possible models of *dofen akuma* and then explains which one he rejects and why. The model he accepts: *dechashvinan leschach ke'ilu min hadofen* — we treat the invalid *schach* as though it is actually part of the wall, *venekaf venichpaf lemala* — and the wall has simply bent upward and over. On this reading, the metal bars or wooden planks of the *pasul schach* are reconceived as a physical extension of the wall that has folded across the top. Since *pasul schach* is perfectly valid material for a wall, this reconceptualization is coherent.

The model *Rashi* rejects is the one that would make *dofen akuma* analogous to *gud asik*: *roein et hadofen ke'ilu hu okem veholech tachat haschach hapasul umagia laschach hakesher umotzi et hapasul min hasukkah* — we imagine the wall as bending and traveling beneath the invalid *schach* until it reaches the valid *schach*, thereby pulling the invalid section outside the *sukkah*. On this reading, *dofen akuma* would be an invisible extension of the wall through space, much as *gud asik* is an invisible extension of the wall upward. But if that were the model, then even air could function the same way — one would simply imagine the wall extending horizontally through the empty space. Since the *mishna* demonstrates that air does *not* permit such an extension, *Rashi* concludes that the invisible-extension model is wrong. *Dofen akuma* does not extend the existing wall through empty space; rather, it reclassifies whatever *physical material* is present — the *pasul schach* — as part of the wall itself. Since air cannot be reclassified as a wall, air does not trigger *dofen akuma*.

This is a striking piece of *Rashi*: he is not merely offering a definition but explaining the interpretive reasoning that led him to choose one model over the other, with the *mishna* itself serving as the decisive proof.

---

## Three Dofen Akuma Cases

### Collapsed Roof Case

The *mishna* now presents three distinct applications of the *dofen akuma* principle. The first is the case of *bayit shenifchat* — a house whose roof partially collapsed. The house retains its walls and portions of its original roof, but there is now an opening in the middle through which the owner wishes to place valid *schach* and observe *Sukkot*. The remaining portions of the original roof are invalid *schach*: although the material may be wood or other fundamentally kosher material, the roof was constructed as a permanent fixture and was not built *leshem tzel* — for the purpose of shade in the manner of a *sukkah* — and therefore does not qualify. It is the collapsed center that becomes the *sukkah*, with the original rooftop surrounding it as *pasul schach*.

The rule: *im yesh min hakosel lesichuch arba amot pesulah* — if there are four *amot* or more of the original roof between the wall and the valid *schach* in the center, the *sukkah* is invalid. If the distance is less than four *amot*, *dofen akuma* applies — the wall is imagined as bending over and encompassing that strip of invalid *schach* — and the *sukkah* is valid.

### Portico Case

The second case is *chatzer mukkefet achsadra* — a courtyard surrounded by a portico. Imagine a central open courtyard enclosed on all sides by a colonnade: columns supporting a covered walkway or arcade running around the perimeter, with the buildings' walls forming the outer boundary. The owner wishes to place valid *schach* over the central courtyard and use it as a *sukkah*. The covered portico roof, being a permanent structure, constitutes *pasul schach* separating the valid *schach* of the center from the walls of the surrounding buildings.

*Rashi*, in a passage about eight lines before the wider-margined lines begin, describes this structure and then offers a contemporary analogy: *dugma ledavar*, comparable to this concept, is a *cloister* — *lashon Ashkenaz* — the kind of courtyard with grass in the center and a covered walkway surrounding it found in ecclesiastical institutions. He writes: *ken hagallakhim* — just as the priests have such a structure — *sheyesh lahem la-avir sheyesh bah asavim vehekef akhsadra saviv lo* — with an open interior containing greenery and an arcade surrounding it.

As in the first case, if the portico is less than four *amot* wide, *dofen akuma* permits treating the covered walkway as a bent extension of the wall, and the central courtyard may serve as a valid *sukkah*.

### Invalid Edge Case

The third case is straightforward: *sukkah gedolah shehikifuha bedavar she'ein mesakh'khin bo* — a large *sukkah* whose perimeter of *schach* adjacent to the walls consists entirely of material that is intrinsically *pasul* — such as metal bars. Here the invalidity is not a matter of intent or permanence but of the material itself, which is categorically unfit for *schach*. Again the rule is the same: *im yesh tachtav arba amot pesulah* — four *amot* of such *pasul schach* at the edge renders the *sukkah* invalid; less than four *amot* allows *dofen akuma* to apply.

### Why Three Cases?

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *kol hani lamma li* — why do we need all three cases? They all seem to be identical applications of the same rule.

The answer is *tzricha* — each case is independently necessary. Had the *mishna* taught only the *bayit shenifchat*, one might have thought *dofen akuma* applies exclusively because the walls there are genuine interior walls — walls built for and serving the house itself — and their strong halakhic status makes it easier to extend them conceptually. But in the portico case, the walls used for the *sukkah* are the outer walls of the surrounding buildings, which were not built to enclose the courtyard at all; one might have thought such walls are too weak to trigger *dofen akuma*. Hence the second case is needed.

Had the *mishna* taught only those two cases, one might have thought that *dofen akuma* works because the invalid material in both cases is at least made of fundamentally kosher material — wood or similar substances that would be valid *schach* if placed correctly. Perhaps it is specifically that quasi-kosher quality that allows the material to be reconceived as a bent wall. But in the third case the *pasul schach* is intrinsically invalid material — metal bars or the like — and one might have thought that so severe an invalidity cannot be overcome by *dofen akuma*. The third case therefore teaches that even material that is categorically unfit for *schach* can function as a bent wall up to four *amot*.

The *mishna* thus conveys: whatever purpose the walls serve, however severe the invalidity of the *schach*, *dofen akuma* operates up to four *amot* without exception.

---

## Air vs Pasul Schach

### Yeshiva Positions

Following this analysis of the *mishna*, the *Gemara* turns to a closely related question not addressed in any *mishna*: how much *pasul schach* in the *middle* of the *sukkah* — not at the edge — is sufficient to invalidate it? The *mishna* establishes the rule for the edge; the center requires its own discussion.

*Rabba* reports that he came upon the students of Rav's *yeshiva* — *rabbanan d'vei Rav* — seated and teaching the following: *avir posel bishelosha* — air invalidates at three *tefachim*; *sechach pasul posel be'arba'ah* — invalid *schach* invalidates at four *tefachim*. These measures apply wherever the gap or the *pasul schach* occurs — at the edge or in the middle.

### Separation Mechanism

It is worth pausing to understand the mechanism by which air or *pasul schach* invalidates. The invalidity is not a matter of one section of *schach* "contaminating" the whole; rather, air or *pasul schach* creates a *separation* between two portions of the *sukkah*, preventing them from being halakhically combined.

Consider a *sukkah* with three walls and valid *schach* throughout, save for a strip of air or *pasul schach*. If that strip runs in one direction, it may sever only one half of the *sukkah* from a wall, leaving the other half with three walls and still viable. If it runs in the perpendicular direction, it divides the *sukkah* into two halves, each of which possesses only two walls — and neither half is a valid *sukkah*. The rule is therefore about structural continuity: once the gap or *pasul schach* is sufficient to constitute a meaningful separation, the two sides cannot be combined, and each side must independently qualify as a *sukkah*.

*Tosafot* has a careful discussion of this mechanism, including the edge case in which a patch of *pasul schach* or air does not run from wall to wall but sits as an isolated square in the center. In such a case, if the surrounding portion of the *sukkah* independently meets the minimum size of seven by seven *tefachim*, the *sukkah* remains valid — the isolated patch is treated as an extension of the larger valid space, and one should simply not sit directly beneath that patch.

What of a patch smaller than the invalidating measure? Less than four *tefachim* of *pasul schach*, or less than three *tefachim* of air, does not break the structural continuity of the *sukkah* at all. The *schach* is treated as continuous, and one may even sit directly beneath such a small segment of *pasul schach* — a somewhat surprising conclusion, but that is the *halakha*.

### Four Tefachim Cases

*Rabba* challenges the students' position. He says: *avir depasel bishelosha mena lachu* — where do you derive that air invalidates at three *tefachim*? From the *mishna* itself: *hirchik et hasichuch min hadafnos shelosha tefachim pesulah* — if you distance the *schach* from the walls three *tefachim* on the horizontal plane, it is invalid. But if the *mishna* is your source, *Rabba* argues, then the *mishna*'s other case should also be your guide: *sechach pasul nami lo lifsol ela bearba amot* — invalid *schach* should not invalidate until four *amot*, even in the middle. After all, the *mishna* teaches four *amot* regarding *pasul schach* at the edge (*bayit shenifchat*), and *Rabba* sees no principled distinction between the edge and the middle — the same measure should apply throughout.

The students respond: *bar minah dehi* — that case cannot serve as proof, because Rav and Shmuel both explain that case as involving *dofen akuma* — the special rule of the bent wall, which is inherently a principle about the *edge*, not the middle.

This response reveals that *Rabba* fundamentally disagrees with the *dofen akuma* framework as an independent principle. In his view, there is no special bent-wall rule. Rather, the single governing principle is that *pasul schach* up to four *amot* does not break the continuity of the *sukkah* — whether at the edge or in the middle. Under 3.9 *amot*, one should not sit beneath the *pasul schach*, but the *sukkah* as a whole remains intact. Once four *amot* are reached, the continuity breaks. The asymmetry between edge and middle that Rav and Shmuel posit — four *amot* at the edge due to *dofen akuma*, only four *tefachim* in the middle — does not exist for *Rabba*.

### Rava's Thought Exp

*Rabba* then poses a striking logical thought experiment against the students' position. He says: *mah ilu ika sechach pasul pachot me'arba'ah veavir pachot mishloshah* — suppose you had three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* together with two *tefachim* of air. Each element individually is below its threshold — three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* is less than four, and two *tefachim* of air is less than three — and so the students would say the *sukkah* is *kasher*. Now, *milao beshpudim* — fill those two *tefachim* of air with metal bars. Now you have five *tefachim* of *pasul schach*, which exceeds four, and the *sukkah* is *pasul*. *Rabba* asks: *velo yehei avir haposel bishelosha kesechach pasul haposel bearba'ah* — is this not internally inconsistent? Air is the *stronger* invalidator — it creates a break at only three *tefachim*, while *pasul schach* requires four *tefachim* to create the same break. How can it be that the combination is *kasher* when the stronger element (air) is present in its full two *tefachim*, but becomes *pasul* when those same two *tefachim* are replaced by the *weaker* invalidator (*pasul schach*)?

---

## Rava vs Rav/Shmuel

### Rava's Shiur View

The students, unfazed, turn the question back on *Rabba*: *le'didech nami* — the same challenge applies to you. According to *Rabba*, *pasul schach* invalidates at four *amot* whether at the edge or in the middle. Construct the parallel case: 3.9 *amot* of *pasul schach* together with two *tefachim* of air — valid by *Rabba*'s standard. Fill the air with metal bars: five *amot* minus a fraction of *pasul schach* — invalid. The same paradox obtains: why should introducing the *weaker* element (more *pasul schach*) cause what the *stronger* element (air) did not?

*Rabba* accepts the symmetry of the challenge but argues that his position resolves it cleanly: *bishlama ledidi de'amina arba amot mishum shiura d'lav shiura hu* — for me, the four *amot* figure is simply an arbitrary quantitative *shiur*, nothing more. Just as on *Yom Kippur* one does not combine slightly less than a *k'kotevet* of food with slightly less than a *melo lugmav* of liquid on the grounds that one is a stronger prohibition than the other — because these are simply different categories with different independent measures — so too here. Air has its measure: three *tefachim*. *Pasul schach* has its measure: four *amot*. Since they are different categories with different measures, *keivan d'lo shavu shiureihu lahadei* — since their measures are not equal to each other — *lo mitztarfi* — they do not combine. This is not a logical paradox; it is simply the nature of distinct categories with distinct *shiurim*.

### Rav/Shmuel Haflaga

The challenge to Rav and Shmuel's position, however, is of a fundamentally different character. *Rabba*'s question is not merely that the numbers seem inconsistent. It is that Rav and Shmuel did not derive the four-*tefachim* figure from any *mishna* or *braita*. They arrived at it through their own reasoning. What logic could have produced it?

The only available logic — and *Rabba* argues this is precisely what Rav and Shmuel must have been thinking — is that four *tefachim* defines a minimal independent *reshut*, a space unto itself. Once *pasul schach* occupies four *tefachim*, that strip constitutes its own separate space, and the two halves of the *sukkah* are thereby *separated*. The invalidating concept is not an arbitrary quantity of a particular substance; it is the reality of *haflaga* — separation, division — between the two sections of *schach*.

But if the concept is separation, then *Rabba*'s question returns with full force: *mah li hiflig besechach pasul mah li hiflig besechach pasul ve-avir* — why should I care whether the separating material is entirely *pasul schach* or a mix of *pasul schach* and air? In either case, the two halves of the *schach* are separated by four *tefachim* of space. The reality of the gap is the same. On Rav and Shmuel's own logic, combining *pasul schach* and air should produce the same result as four *tefachim* of *pasul schach* alone.

The underlying *machloket* is thus a fundamental difference in how one conceptualizes invalidation. For *Rabba*, the question is quantitative: how much of a given substance is present, and does it reach the specified *shiur* for that substance? For Rav and Shmuel, the question is qualitative and structural: is there a sufficient break in continuity, regardless of what fills the gap?

### Abaye's Objection

*Abaye* raises an objection to *Rabba*'s position from within its own framework. He says: *u-le-mar nami hai de-lo shavu shi'ureihu be-sukkah gedolah* — according to you it is true that in a large *sukkah*, air and *pasul schach* have different measures (three *tefachim* and four *amot* respectively) and therefore do not combine. But *be-sukkah ketanah mi lo shavu shi'ureihu* — in a minimum-size *sukkah* of seven by seven *tefachim*, don't their measures effectively become the same?

*Abaye*'s argument is as follows: in a minimum *sukkah*, four *amot* is simply not available — the entire *sukkah* is only seven *tefachim* across. What, then, is the operative measure for *pasul schach* in such a *sukkah*? *Rashi* explains in the relevant passage: *she-shi'urah metzumtzam mi lo shavu shi'ureihu* — since the *sukkah*'s measure is contracted, one must admit that three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* becomes problematic in a small *sukkah*. The reasoning: *keivan de-nafik mi-torat lavud, chashiv levatzurei le-shi'urei de-sukkah* — once the *pasul schach* exceeds the *lavud* threshold of three *tefachim*, it is significant enough to diminish the effective size of the *sukkah* below the minimum, since the entire *sukkah* is barely above minimum size to begin with. Therefore, in a small *sukkah*, both air and *pasul schach* become problematic at three *tefachim* — their measures coincide. And if there is a context in which they share a common measure, argues *Abaye*, this should provide a basis for combining them even in the large-*sukkah* case.

### Rava's Response

*Rabba* rejects the premise. *Amar lei hatam lav mishum de-shavu shi'ureihu le-hadadi hu — ella mishum de-leiteih* — the convergence at three *tefachim* in the small *sukkah* is not because three *tefachim* is the formal, principled *shiur* for *pasul schach* in that context. The formal *shiur* for *pasul schach* remains four *amot* even in a small *sukkah*. What happens in a small *sukkah* is simply a practical consequence: once you have three *tefachim* of *pasul schach*, that strip cannot be counted toward the *sukkah*'s required minimum area, and so the *sukkah* falls below *shi'ur* — but that is a side effect of size constraints, not an independent *din* of *pasul schach* being problematic at three *tefachim*. The measures of the two categories are therefore *never* formally equivalent; air is always three *tefachim* and *pasul schach* is always four *amot*, and they do not combine.

---

## Tumaot Analogy

### Material Minimums

Having established *Rabba*'s principle that different categories with different *shiurim* do not combine, the *Gemara* tests this principle against the laws of *tumah*. It cites a *mishna*: *ha-beged sheloshah al sheloshah* — a cloth garment becomes susceptible to *tumah* at a minimum size of three *tefachim* by three *tefachim*. *Ha-sak* — sackcloth — requires four *tefachim* by four *tefachim*. *Ha-or* — leather — requires five by five *tefachim*. *Mapatz* — a reed mat — requires six by six *tefachim*. These different materials, because of their varying quality and practical utility, each have their own minimum size below which they are considered insignificant and do not contract *tumah*.

### Stronger Fills Weaker

A *braita* then teaches: if one combines contiguous materials from adjacent categories on this list — cloth with sackcloth, sackcloth with leather, or leather with a mat — *mitztarfin zeh im zeh* — they combine with each other. The combination is governed by the measure of the weaker (larger-*shiur*) material, but the stronger (smaller-*shiur*) material fills out whatever portion is needed. For example: three *tefachim* of sackcloth (just below its four-*tefachim* threshold) together with one *tefach* of cloth (cloth has a three-*tefachim* threshold, making it the "stronger" material in the sense that a smaller amount matters) — the combination meets the four-*tefachim* requirement for sackcloth *tumah*.

The parallel to the *sukkah* question is immediate. Air is the "stronger" invalidator, analogous to cloth (problematic at a smaller measure). *Pasul schach* is the "weaker" invalidator, analogous to sackcloth. Why, then, cannot air combine with *pasul schach* to meet the four-*amot* threshold — with the stronger air doing the work of the weaker *pasul schach*, just as the stronger cloth does the work of the weaker sackcloth?

### Common Application

The *Gemara* answers by citing the reason given by *Rabbi Shimon*: *hoil ve-raui le-tamei moshav* — these materials combine because they share a common application in one area of *tumah* law, namely the laws of a seat used by a *zav*. Specifically, a *Tanna* teaches: *ha-mekatzea mikullan tefach al tefach tamei* — if one cuts out a piece of any of these materials measuring one *tefach* by one *tefach*, it is *tamei*. As *Reish Lakish* explains in the name of *Rabbi Yannai*, this is because a one-*tefach* square from any of these materials is fit to serve as a patch on a saddle seat — *hoil ve-raui le-tala'i agav chamor*. In that specific application, all four materials share the same minimum size: one *tefach* by one *tefach*. This common measure in at least one halakhic context is what legitimizes treating them as sufficiently related to allow combination in other *tumah* contexts as well. The stronger material can fill out the measure of the weaker precisely because they share a common minimum somewhere in the legal landscape.

### No Combination

Air and *pasul schach*, by contrast, share no common halakhic context in which they have the same measure. There is no application — not in the laws of *sukkah*, not elsewhere — where three *tefachim* of air and three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* are treated identically and both become significant at the same threshold. Without any common category or shared minimum, they remain fundamentally distinct, and the stronger one cannot fill out the measure of the weaker. Combination requires not just that both elements be capable of producing the same effect in principle, but that there exist some recognized halakhic context in which they share equivalent status.

*Abaye*'s attempt to create such a context — pointing to the small *sukkah* where both measures effectively converge at three *tefachim* — was rejected precisely on these grounds: that convergence is a practical side effect, not a formal equivalence in *din*. Since there is no context in which air and *pasul schach* share a formal common measure, they cannot combine to invalidate a *sukkah*.

---

## Version Differences

### Sura Version

*Rav Chisda* notes that the entire foregoing discussion — *Rabba* finding the students of Rav's *yeshiva*, the back-and-forth about four *tefachim* and four *amot*, the challenge and counter-challenge — represents the version of this teaching as it circulated in *Sura*, the *yeshiva* of Rav himself. In this version, Rav and Shmuel together held the combined position: four *amot* from the edge by virtue of *dofen akuma*, four *tefachim* in the middle. That was the shared, unified position attributed to both Sages in Sura.

### Naharda'a Version

In *Naharda'a* — the *yeshiva* of Shmuel — the tradition was different. There, the teaching was transmitted as *amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: Shmuel holds that *sechach pasul be-emtza posel be-arba'ah* — *pasul schach* in the middle invalidates at four *tefachim* — while *min hatzad posel be-arba amot* — from the side it invalidates at four *amot* (the *dofen akuma* rule). And in this version, *Rav* takes a different position: *bein min hatzad bein be-emtza be-arba amot* — whether at the edge or in the middle, the threshold is four *amot*. This is precisely the position that in the Sura version was *Rabba*'s challenge to the yeshiva students. In the Naharda'a version, it is Rav's own stated position, and the *machloket* is between Rav and Shmuel directly.

### Chananel's Girsa

*Rabbeinu Chananel* preserves a *girsa* — a manuscript tradition — that differs from the standard text in one significant detail. His version reads: *be-Sura matnu hachi amrin* — in Sura they taught as we have above, followed by the joint formulation and the ruling *ve-chen hilchata*. But where our printed text says the alternative version was taught in *Naharda'a*, *Rabbeinu Chananel* writes *u-ve-Pumbedita matnu* — it was in *Pumbedita* that they taught the version attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel.

This alternative reading is illuminating. *Pumbedita* was the *yeshiva* of *Rav Yehuda* — himself a student of both Rav and Shmuel. The teaching *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* would thus have been taught in Rav Yehuda's own *yeshiva* in Pumbedita, linking the transmission to Shmuel through Rav Yehuda. In our standard text, the same teaching is located in Naharda'a — Shmuel's city — which also makes sense, given that the ruling is transmitted in Shmuel's name. The tradition in *Rabbeinu Chananel*'s text bridges the two *yeshivot*: the teaching *Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* connects Pumbedita (Rav Yehuda) with Naharda'a (Shmuel), and either location could serve as its point of transmission.

In either version of the *girsa*, the substantive conclusion is the same. In Rav's *yeshiva* (Sura), the single combined position of Rav and Shmuel was: four *amot* on the side, four *tefachim* in the middle. In the Shmuel/Rav Yehuda tradition (Naharda'a or Pumbedita), this is a debate: Shmuel holds four *amot* on the side and four *tefachim* in the middle, while Rav holds four *amot* in both cases.

---

---

# Sukkah 18

## Neharde'a vs. Sura

### Two versions intro

The daf opens in the middle of 17b, where the Gemara presents two distinct traditions regarding the Rav-Shmuel debate on *pasul schach*. The two academies — Sura, the yeshiva of Rav, and Neharde'a, the yeshiva of Shmuel — transmitted the debate in fundamentally different terms, and the practical ruling depends on which version one accepts.

### Sura version

According to the Sura version, both Rav and Shmuel agree on the underlying distinction: the threshold for *pasul schach* to be problematic depends on where it is located. If the *pasul schach* is on the side of the *sukkah*, the relevant measure is *arba amot*, because anything less than that can be incorporated into the wall via *dofen akumah*. If the *pasul schach* is in the middle of the *sukkah*, the relevant measure is *arba tefachim*, because even that amount creates its own distinct zone, effectively dividing the *schach* in half. As discussed in connection with Tosafot, this division does not invalidate the entire *sukkah* at once; rather, it cuts the *schach* into two sections, sometimes leaving one *kasher* half and one *pasul* half, and sometimes leaving two *pasul* halves.

One might ask whether it is possible to be left with two *kasher* halves. The Gemara assumes a three-walled *sukkah*. In a four-walled *sukkah*, if the *pasul schach* runs down the middle between two stretches of *kasher schach*, the result would indeed be two separate *kasher sukkot*, each with three walls — and one would simply be unable to sit in the middle. But the Gemara's analysis proceeds on the basis of the three-walled case.

### Neharde'a version

According to the Neharde'a version, this distinction between side and middle was not a shared position of Rav and Shmuel but rather the very point of their disagreement. In Neharde'a, the tradition was transmitted as follows: *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel* — *schach be'emtza pasul be'arba'ah; min hatzad pasul be'arba amot*. Shmuel is the one who distinguishes between the two locations, holding that *arba tefachim* suffices to divide the *schach* in the middle, while *arba amot* are required on the side. Rav, by contrast — *bein min hatzad uvein be'emtza be'arba amot* — holds that the measure of *arba amot* applies uniformly, whether the *pasul schach* is on the side or in the middle.

### Practical ruling

This generates a striking ruling. In almost all disputes between Rav and Shmuel, the *halacha* follows Rav. Yet here, as in one or two other places in this *masechet*, we rule like Shmuel. Practically speaking, this means that *arba tefachim* of *pasul schach* in the middle of one's *sukkah* is already a problem — a conclusion few would have assumed on their own. According to the Sura version, this is the consensus of both Rav and Shmuel; according to the Neharde'a version, we are departing from our usual practice of following Rav in favor of Shmuel's more stringent position in the middle.

---

## Textual proofs

### Plank mishna

Having established the two versions of the debate through logical argument, the Gemara now turns to textual proofs — examining *mishnayot* and *baraitot* to see which position they support. The first source is the *mishnah* that teaches: *natan aleha neser sherochav arba'ah tefachim* — if one placed on the *sukkah* a plank four *tefachim* wide, the *sukkah* remains *kesherah*. This *mishnah* operates on the assumption, held by Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yehuda, that such planks constitute *pasul schach*. Yet the *mishnah* rules that the *sukkah* is valid — though one may not eat or sleep beneath the plank.

This fits effortlessly with Rav's position. Rav holds that *pasul schach*, whether on the side or in the middle, requires *arba amot* to invalidate the *sukkah*. A plank of four *tefachim* falls well short of that threshold and therefore does not compromise the *sukkah's* validity, even though it is significant enough to prohibit sitting beneath it.

### Shmuel's reinterpretation

The difficulty is with Shmuel's position. If four *tefachim* of *pasul schach* in the middle suffices to divide the *sukkah*, why does the *mishnah* say the *sukkah* remains *kesherah*? The Gemara answers: *hacha b'mai askinan — min hatzad*. The *mishnah* is not discussing a plank placed in the middle of the *sukkah* but rather one placed on the side. There, since we can invoke *dofen akumah*, anything less than *arba amot* does not invalidate — and the *mishnah* is simply describing such a case. This reading is forced on Shmuel; the *mishnah* reads far more naturally according to Rav.

### Sheets vs. planks

The Gemara presses further with a *baraita*: *shnei sadinim mitztarfin* — two sheets combine to produce enough *pasul schach*. If one sheet is three *tefachim* wide and another is one *tefach* wide, together they constitute four *tefachim* (or, if needed, they combine toward *arba amot*). By contrast, *shnei nesarin ein mitztarfin* — two planks do not combine. The reason, according to this view, is that planks do not constitute genuine *pasul schach* and therefore there is no problem to aggregate. Rabbi Meir dissents: *nesarin k'sadinim* — planks are like sheets and do combine.

To understand this *baraita*, one must first clarify what size planks are under debate. Recall the earlier discussion of whether Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda dispute planks in the range of three to four *tefachim*, or planks of four *tefachim* and above. The Gemara will now test both versions of Rav against this *baraita*.

### Rav's approach tested

According to the Neharde'a version of Rav — that *pasul schach* requires *arba amot* everywhere, middle and side alike — the debate of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns planks of four *tefachim* and above. These planks are individually large enough to be *pasul* even according to Rabbi Yehuda. If so, why does Rabbi Meir say they must combine? The answer is that *mitztarfin l'arba amot*: they must combine until one has *arba amot*, because that is the threshold Rav sets even in the middle. A single four-*tefach* plank does not invalidate; only a collection adding up to *arba amot* does. This works elegantly with Rav's position as transmitted in Neharde'a.

### Sura Rav tested

But the Sura version of Rav creates a problem. There, Rav holds that even in the middle, *pasul schach* invalidates at *arba tefachim*. And Rav there also maintains that the debate of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda concerns planks of four *tefachim* and above. If so — *ei d'is behu arba*, if the plank is four *tefachim*, it already invalidates on its own; *lama lehu l'tzerufei* — why would you need to combine? And *ei d'les behu arba* — if the plank is less than four *tefachim*, then *kanya b'alma ninhu* — it is merely a stick, not even considered a plank, and there is nothing to combine.

The Gemara resolves this: *le'olam de'is behu arba* — indeed the planks are four *tefachim* wide, and the need to combine (*mitztarfin*) applies not to produce four *tefachim* but to produce *arba amot* — because we are discussing planks placed on the *side* of the *sukkah*. There, the threshold is *arba amot*, and the planks must accumulate to that measure. In other words, once again, anything that seems to indicate that four *tefachim* is insufficient, the Gemara redirects to the case of *min hatzad*, where the *amot*-measure applies.

The pattern that has now emerged is significant: every time a *mishnah* or *baraita* seems to imply that four *tefachim* is insufficient to invalidate, the Gemara answers that the source is speaking *min hatzad*. This allows Shmuel's position — and the Sura version of Rav's position, which is effectively identical regarding the middle — to survive the textual challenges, since any scenario appearing to require more than four *tefachim* can be attributed to the side case.

A related question was raised regarding *gud assik* and *dofen akumah* — whether one can combine the two principles, extending a wall upward via *gud assik* and then bending it horizontally through *dofen akumah*. This may be possible, as there is apparently a *Ran* addressing that question, but one cannot use *dofen akumah* at the very top of the *schach* layer itself.

### Cedar planks baraita

A further *baraita* is adduced: *sikcha bensarim shel erez* — if one covered a *sukkah* with cedar planks. *Sheyesh bahen arba* — if they are four *tefachim* wide, *divrei hakol pesulah* — universally invalid. This indicates that below four *tefachim*, the debate of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is live, but once a plank is four *tefachim* wide, even Rabbi Yehuda concedes invalidity. And conversely, *ein bahen arba* — if the planks are between three and four *tefachim*, Rabbi Meir rules invalid and Rabbi Yehuda permits.

### Rabbi Meir concedes

At the top of 18a comes a particularly instructive ruling: *u'modeh Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Meir himself concedes — *she'im yesh bein neser leneser kemlo neser* — that if between one plank and the next there is a gap equal in width to a plank, *she'maniach pesal beineihem u'kesherah* — and one fills that gap with valid *schach* (*pesal*, in the unusual usage of the Gemara for *kasher schach*), the *sukkah* is *kosher*.

This requires explanation. If four *tefachim* of *pasul schach* invalidates in the middle, how can alternating planks with *kasher schach* render the *sukkah* valid? One plank is already four *tefachim* of *pasul schach* — it should divide the *sukkah*. The Gemara presents this as a *gotcha*: in all previous cases, the Gemara escaped by saying we are speaking *min hatzad*, but here, the planks alternate across the entire roof. One cannot claim it is a side case — the *pasul schach* runs through the middle as well.

### Rav Huna's solution

The resolution comes from Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: *hacha be'sukkah de'la havya ela shemoneh metzumtzamot askinan* — we are dealing with a *sukkah* that is precisely eight *amot* wide. The planks and *kasher schach* alternate in the following manner: starting from one side, one lays a plank, then valid *schach*, then a plank, and so on — proceeding inward from each side simultaneously, meeting in the middle. The result is that from each wall, the stretch of *pasul* material never reaches *arba amot*. Each side, taken as a unit, is less than *arba amot* of *pasul schach* from the wall, which means *dofen akumah* can incorporate it. The middle zone of *kasher schach*, where the two sides converge, is thereby protected.

What Rav Huna has done is demonstrate that even this seemingly devastating case reduces to a *min hatzad* scenario: the *pasul schach* from each side never exceeds the *dofen akumah* limit, so it is treated as part of the wall's bend, and the valid *schach* in the middle is kosher. It is worth noting that *dofen akumah* can incorporate *kasher schach* — not only *pasul schach* — within four *amot* of the wall. These principles — *gud assik*, *levud*, and *dofen akumah* — were explicitly included in the *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* listed by the Gemara at the top of 5b, by the *Tosafot* there, in the context of partitions.

---

## Abaye's small sukkah

### Three tefachim rule

Having concluded the extended analysis of textual proofs, the Gemara states that the ruling follows Shmuel — four *tefachim* in the middle invalidates — without dwelling on a formal declaration. The Gemara then transitions to a new ruling: *Amar Abaye: oviya shlosha besukkah gedolah umiato, bein bekanim bein bishpudin havei miyut* — if one has a *sukkah* that was diminished by three *tefachim* of some material, both valid *schach* (reeds) and *pasul schach* (metal skewers) constitute a reduction in a large *sukkah*. *Besukkah ketana* — but in a minimum-size *sukkah* of exactly seven by seven *tefachim* — *bekanim havei miyut* — valid *schach* that fills the gap solves the problem (and one can even invoke *levud* if not all is filled), *bishpudin lo havei miyut* — but *pasul schach* placed there does not solve the problem.

### Space definition

Abaye's reasoning introduces a genuinely new principle. It is not that three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* divides the *sukkah* in the way that four *tefachim* does in a larger *sukkah* — that threshold has already been established. Rather, Abaye holds that once a *sukkah* is at its minimum size, every *tefach* matters in a way it does not for a larger structure. Three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* in this context establishes its own zone — one that cannot simply be folded into the dimensions of the *sukkah*. Even if it does not formally divide the *schach*, it cannot be incorporated into the count of the *sukkah's* usable space.

A loose analogy: in a spacious apartment, one might count even auxiliary spaces when measuring floor area, but in a tiny studio where every square foot is precious, one cannot treat a non-living zone as part of the living space. The point is that in a minimum-size *sukkah*, even three *tefachim* of *pasul schach* is enough to render that zone dimensionally excluded — leaving the *sukkah* below the minimum size. This was implicit in Abaye's assumption from the previous day's discussion; here he makes it explicit.

---

## Levud in middle

### Levud question

The Gemara pivots from discussing the threshold for *pasul schach* to a related question: does *levud* — the principle that a gap of less than three *tefachim* is treated as closed — apply only at the edge of a roof, or equally in the middle? The previous discussion has shown that the laws of *pasul schach* can differ depending on whether the material is at the side or in the center of the *sukkah*. Now the Gemara asks whether *levud*, applied to gaps of air, follows the same logic.

The phrase *ve'hani mili min hatzad* — "this applies only on the side" — serves as the transition, signaling, as Rashi explains, that we are reverting to the more general question about *levud* and not continuing Abaye's ruling about minimum-size *sukkot*. The Gemara notes that *levud* has always been applied without apparent geographic restriction; it is a foundational principle by which objects less than three *tefachim* apart are considered connected. Yet perhaps, at least for roofs, the middle presents different considerations.

### Rav Acha position

Rav Acha holds *yesh levud be'emtza* — *levud* applies even in the middle of a roof. This is the more intuitive position: *levud* is a general principle, and there is no obvious reason to restrict it to the edges of any structure.

### Ravina position

Ravina holds *ein levud be'emtza* — *levud* does not apply in the middle of a roof. This is a striking claim. Tosafot is sensitive to the apparent novelty: we apply *levud* all the time, including in contexts where gaps occur far from any edge — for instance, constructing a virtual wall from posts spaced less than three *tefachim* apart throughout their entire length, not just at the sides. Tosafot therefore restricts Ravina's view specifically to roofs: something about the geometry or legal function of a roof surface may make *levud* inapplicable in its center.

### Beam proof

The Gemara seeks textual support for each position. In favor of *yesh levud be'emtza*, a *baraita* is cited concerning the laws of *Shabbat* and carrying in a *chatzer*: *kora ha'yotze mi'kotel ze ve'eina noga'at be'kotel acher* — a beam (*kora*) that projects from one wall but does not reach the opposite wall; or alternatively, two beams, *achat yotze mi'kotel ze ve'achat yotze mi'kotel acher ve'einan nogot zu be'zo* — one from each wall, meeting in the middle without touching. The rule: *pachot mi'shlosha eino tzarich le'havi kora acheret* — if the gap is less than three *tefachim*, no additional beam is needed to validate the *eruv* arrangement; *shlosha — tzarich le'havi kora acheret* — at three *tefachim*, a supplementary beam is required. This shows *levud* being invoked where two beams nearly meet in the middle — a case that is emphatically not about the edges. It thus supports the position that *levud* applies in the middle.

There is an interesting nuance here: one opinion holds *kora mishum mechitza* — the functional rationale for a *kora* is that it creates a virtual wall beneath it. Even so, the *baraita* applies *levud* to it, suggesting no restriction to edges.

### Skylight proof

Against *levud be'emtza*, the Gemara cites a *mishnah* in the laws of *tumah ve'tahara*: *aruba she'be'bayit* — a skylight in a house. If the skylight is a *tefach* wide and there is *tumah* in the house, the entire house is *tamei* but what is directly beneath the skylight remains *tahor*, since there is no roof over that column of space. Conversely, if the *tumah* is beneath the skylight, the rest of the house is *tahor*. Now, if we applied *levud* in the middle of a roof — and the skylight is less than three *tefachim* — we should close the gap and treat the roof as whole. But the *mishnah* clearly treats the skylight as creating a distinct, unroofed zone, even when it is small. This suggests that in the middle of a roof, *levud* does not apply.

### Exception response

The Gemara dismisses this proof: *shani hilchos tumah, ve'hachi gmiri lah* — the laws of *tumah* constitute their own independent category, transmitted as a specific tradition, and one cannot generalize from them to other legal domains. The *tumah* rules regarding roofs and skylights reflect a particular received tradition, not the general operative principle of *levud*. Thus the general rule remains that *levud* applies everywhere, and the *tumah* case is treated as exceptional. As one formulation puts it: for physical structures, the gap is closed; for the metaphysical operation of *tumah*, the opening remains open.

---

## Public teachings

### Roof hole teaching

The Gemara now records a series of public rulings delivered by Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Ilai. The use of the term *darash* — he expounded publicly — signals that these were teachings given in an open forum, apparently before *Sukkot*, not private transmissions. The first: *bayis shenifchat vesichach al gabav kesheira* — a house whose roof partially collapsed, and one covered the gap with valid *schach*, is a *kosher sukkah*. This is a restatement of the *dofen akumah* principle in its simplest form: if the gap in the middle of the existing roof is filled with *kasher schach*, the existing walls of the house serve as the *sukkah's* walls.

### Four amot qualification

Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosi was present and challenged the ruling: *Rabbi, parish* — Rabbi, you must qualify what you are saying. He then transmits his father Rabbi Yosi's formulation: *arba amot pesulah, pachot mi'arba amot keshera* — if the *kasher schach* in the middle of the roof is *arba amot* or more removed from the wall, the *sukkah* is invalid, since *dofen akumah* cannot extend that far; if it is less than *arba amot* from the wall, the *sukkah* is valid. A public ruling offered without this qualification is incomplete, even if technically correct in many cases.

### Avruma fish

In the same public setting, Rabbi Yehuda the son of Rabbi Ilai delivered a second ruling: *avruma sharya* — the *avruma* fish is permissible. As Rashi explains two lines down, *avruma* is a species of small fish in which tiny parasites may become embedded in the skin in a manner not immediately visible: *min dagim ktanim ve'ein shratzim nikarim bahem*. The question was whether one must be concerned about these nearly imperceptible organisms.

### Location dependency

Once again, Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yosi intervened: *Rabbi, parish* — you must be more precise. His father's teaching was location-dependent: *she'makom ploni asura, she'makom ploni mutara* — fish of a specific place are forbidden, while those of another are permitted.

### Modern prohibition

Abaye had previously explained this distinction by reference to a river called Bav: fish from the river Bav (*sakanta de'Bav nahara*) were permitted because the conditions of that river did not support the proliferation of the relevant parasites. The question of whether rushing water, salty water, or the absence of particular mud accounts for this was debated, with the Gemara noting — in a striking appeal to empirical evidence — that some proposed explanations were contradicted by direct observation. The conclusion was that the mud of that particular river simply did not sustain the reproduction of the relevant organisms, analogous to how a particular municipal water source may or may not contain certain microorganisms. Ravina adds a practical epilogue: *ve'idna, de'shafchi Nahar Eitan ve'Nahar Gamda le'hasam* — nowadays, the rivers Eitan and Gamda have diverted and empty into what was once the Bav river, and therefore *assira* — all such fish are currently forbidden, as the ecological conditions that once made them safe no longer pertain.

---

## Portico sukkah

### Portico case

The Gemara introduces a new case: *sikcha al gabei achsadra she'yesh la patzimin* — one placed *schach* over a portico (*achsadra*) that has posts (*patzimin*). The visual setting is a yard with a covered walkway running along one side, supported by columns. If the columns are spaced close enough together — within three *tefachim* of one another — they can function as a valid wall through the principle of *levud*, and the *sukkah* is valid. The harder case, taken up next, is when the posts cannot serve as walls.

---

## Portico sukkah (II)

### Abaye allows it

When the posts cannot be utilized as walls — whether because they are too far apart or otherwise inadequate — Abaye rules *kesheira*: the *sukkah* is still valid. His basis: *amrinan pi tikra yored ve'sotem* — we invoke the principle that the edge of a roof descends and closes off the space below.

### Rava forbids

Rava rules *pesula*: the *sukkah* is invalid. *Lo amrinan pi tikra yored ve'sotem* — we do not apply this principle here.

### Roof edge as wall

The principle of *pi tikra yored ve'sotem* is a genuinely new concept, distinct from everything previously discussed. *Dofen akumah* bends the wall upward and then inward across the *schach*. *Gud assik* projects a physical wall upward to a full height. *Levud* closes a gap between nearby objects. *Pi tikra yored ve'sotem* does something different: it treats the squared-off edge of a roof as the beginning of a virtual wall descending downward from that edge. If the portico has solid, square-edged beams, the outer face of those beams can be treated as the top of a wall that descends and encloses the space beneath.

This principle is not limited to *sukkah*; it appears in the context of *eruv* as well. On the question of whether the roof edge must be a *tefach* wide to qualify, this would need to be verified, but three *tefachim* is certainly not required.

A further clarification follows from Rashi and Tosafot's extensive discussion in the *tosafot* here. Rashi reads Abaye as permitting *pi tikra yored ve'sotem* to supply all three walls of the *sukkah*. Tosafot finds this difficult and argues that no one is suggesting the concept can substitute for more than one wall; the scenario discussed by Abaye already involves two genuine perpendicular walls, and *pi tikra* is invoked only to supply the third.

Reading the Gemara according to Tosafot: Abaye's case involves a *sukkah* with two legitimate walls already in place, and he uses *pi tikra* to close the third. Rava denies that *pi tikra* can accomplish even this.

---

## Abaye-Rava in Shabbat

### Parallel debate?

The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Abaye and Rava here reflects and maps onto the earlier dispute between Rav and Shmuel concerning *Shabbat*. This is not merely an academic observation; if the mapping holds, the analysis of the *Shabbat* case sheds light on the limits and rationale of each position.

### Shabbat parallel

The *Shabbat* case involves an *achsadra b'bik'a* — a portico in an open valley. Carrying in a valley is normally prohibited (*karmelit*), but an enclosed space within it would permit carrying. The question is whether a portico — again, Tosafot reads this as already possessing two walls — can be considered sufficiently enclosed to permit carrying throughout.

### Rav on Shabbat

Rav holds *mutar letaltel b'kulo* — one may carry throughout the entire portico. His rationale: *d'amrinan pi tikra yored ve'sotem* — we apply the principle that the roof edge descends and encloses.

### Shmuel on Shabbat

Shmuel holds *ein metaltelin bah ela b'arba amot* — one may carry only within four *amot*, as in any open *karmelit*. His rationale: *delo amrinan pi tikra yored ve'sotem* — we do not apply the principle.

### Shmuel consistent

The Gemara notes that according to Shmuel, who rejects *pi tikra yored ve'sotem* entirely, there is no debate: he would apply the same position to *sukkah*. He consistently rejects the concept, and his position aligns with Rava's ruling that the *sukkah* without usable posts is *pesulah*. The interesting question is whether Rava's position in *sukkah* necessarily mirrors Rav's position in *Shabbat*, and whether Abaye necessarily mirrors Rav.

### Two-wall concession

The Gemara reports Abaye's concession in response to a challenge from Rava. Rava asked: if you accept *pi tikra yored ve'sotem*, would you apply it even to supply the middle (back) wall of a *sukkah* — that is, where you have only two parallel side walls and no perpendicular back wall at all? Abaye concedes: *modina lach b'hahi — d'hava lah k'mavoy hamefulash* — in that case, I agree it does not work. Two parallel walls without a connecting back wall resemble a *mavoy hamefulash*, a thoroughfare open at both ends, which is not perceived as an enclosed space at all. *Pi tikra* can complete a third wall only when one already begins with a configuration that reads as an enclosed space — a corner, a designated area. Without that, the concept has nothing to work with.

This concession by Abaye is what drives Tosafot to read all the cases in this *sugya* as involving two pre-existing perpendicular walls: since Abaye himself concedes the *mavoy hamefulash* scenario, the simple reading of the Gemara that Abaye permits *pi tikra* to supply all walls must be wrong. He must be speaking only of cases where two proper walls already define a space.

### Roofed portico

Rava then refines the comparison to the *Shabbat* case. He says: even I — who reject *pi tikra yored ve'sotem* for *sukkah* — would concede the *Shabbat* ruling of Rav. Why the asymmetry? Because in the *Shabbat* case, the *achsadra* in question is a *covered* portico. It has an actual roof above it. *Ed kan lo amar Rava hatam ela demchitzot le'achsadra hu de'avidi* — the walls and roof of that portico were built to serve the enclosed space beneath them. When the walls are constructed for the sake of the space below, using the roof edge to seal a third wall is coherent: the roof is organically connected to the space it encloses.

### Roof serves space

The critical distinction Rava articulates is this: *hatam demchitzot le'achsadra hu de'avidi, aval hacha delav le'hachi avidi lo* — there, the partitions serve the *achsadra*; here, they do not. In the *sukkah* case, the edge one wishes to use as a virtual wall is the edge of a roof external to the *sukkah* itself — the overhanging roof of the adjacent building, for instance. The edge of a roof that exists to serve a different space cannot function as the defining border of a new space. For *pi tikra yored ve'sotem* to apply, the roof from which the virtual wall descends must be one that was constructed to serve the enclosed area in question.

The Gemara does not make explicit in its running text the assumption that two walls are already in place; this emerges only from Abaye's concession regarding the *mavoy hamefulash* case. But Tosafot, integrating this concession with other *Gemarot*, concludes that the *pi tikra* concept throughout this entire *sugya* operates against the background of two legitimate existing walls — serving, at most, to supply the third.

---

---

# Sukkah 20

## Mats & Tumah Intro

### Daf Overview

Daf 20 completes the perek, and the Mishnah that occupies us through the end of the chapter is devoted entirely to the laws of *tumah* and *taharah* as they bear on the materials used for *s'chach*. The transition into this territory is not incidental: the question of what may be used to roof a *sukkah* is inextricably bound up with the question of what kinds of objects are susceptible to *tumah*, and the Mishnah works through a series of cases to untangle the two.

### Mat Susceptibility

The basic issue concerns mats. The rule governing *s'chach* is well known: it must be made of something that is not susceptible to *tumah*. And mats present a genuine question, because a mat's susceptibility turns entirely on its designated purpose. If a mat is made for sitting — for reclining or lying upon — then it is subject to *tumat midras*. When a *zav* or *zavah* sits on an object that has been designated as a seat, that object becomes an *av ha-tumah*, a primary source of *tumah*. The mat in that case is functioning as a vessel — specifically, as a seat — and is therefore *mekabel tumah*.

### Purpose Definition

If, however, the mat is not made for sitting, the analysis changes. An object made of reeds, hemp, or wood that is flat and lacks a receptacle (*beit kibul*) would ordinarily be *tahor*, since *peshutei klei etz* — flat wooden or wood-like vessels without a receptacle — cannot receive *tumah*. And beyond that structural consideration, a mat made for roofing is treated as part of a structure rather than as a vessel, and objects that are part of a structure cannot become *tamei*. The practical upshot is that we must determine, when examining any given mat, what its basic purpose is — and how that purpose is established when it has not been explicitly stated.

This was a live question before dedicated *sukkah* mats with *hechsherim* became commercially available. If one went to a hardware store and purchased a thin bamboo mat, what was it for? Was it a wall hanging? Was it for roofing? Was it for sitting? What if the manufacturer simply produced it to meet demand, without specifying any use? Does one follow the majority of actual usage? Does the purchaser's intent matter? Does the season of purchase? These are the questions the Mishnah sets out to address.

---

## Mishnah: Express Cases

### Large Reed Mats

The Mishnah opens: *machatzelet kanim gedolah* — a large reed mat. The Mishnah states two express cases and then, through Rabbi Eliezer's addendum, hints at the problem of the unstated case.

### Reclining vs. Roofing

If one made the large mat *l'shchivah* — explicitly for the purpose of reclining, sitting, or lying on it — then it is *mekabelet tumah* and may not be used for *s'chach*. If one made it *l'sichuch* — for roofing purposes, not necessarily for a *sukkah* specifically, but for any roofing use — then one may use it for *s'chach* and it does not receive *tumah*. These two cases represent the obvious poles: express designation in one direction or the other is unambiguous. The crucial question — what happens when the mat was made without any express purpose — is precisely what the Gemara will interrogate.

### Rabbi Eliezer

Rabbi Eliezer says: *achas ktanah v'achas gedolah* — whether small or large, if made for reclining it is *mekabelet tumah* and may not be used for *s'chach*; if made for *s'chach* it may be used and is not susceptible. The reason Rabbi Eliezer adds this is intelligible against the background assumption that the larger something is, the more naturally it is associated with construction and roofing purposes, while the smaller it is, the more naturally it is assumed to have been made for personal use and reclining. Rabbi Eliezer is therefore coming to include the small mat in the same framework: the express purpose, not the size, is what determines the status. But since both Rabbi Eliezer and the *tanna kamma* address only express cases, it remains entirely unclear what either holds about the *stama* — the case where no purpose was stated.

---

## Contradiction Issue

### Internal Contradiction

The Gemara observes: *hagufa kashya* — the Mishnah is internally contradictory. The opening line states that if made for reclining, the mat is *mekabelet tumah*. The implication is that the decisive factor is the express designation *l'shchivah*. If you made it for reclining — yes, it is a vessel. But that phrasing implies: if you did *not* make it explicitly for reclining, then by default it is considered made for *s'chach* and there is no problem.

### Stama Case Problem

Then the Mishnah states the second case: if made for *s'chach*, one may use it for *s'chach* and it is not *mekabelet tumah*. But this phrasing implies the opposite: only if you expressly made it for *s'chach* is it permitted; absent that explicit designation, one would assume it is made for reclining and it would be problematic. The two halves of the Mishnah thus pull in opposite directions on the *stama* case. The first half implies that *stama* is good; the second half implies that *stama* is not good. The same difficulty arises with even greater force in Rabbi Eliezer's formulation, since he explicitly states the rule applies whether small or large — yet his two statements are equally contradictory about what the *stama* case looks like.

### Lo Kashya Resolution

The Gemara's first answer is *lo kashya* — it is not difficult — *kan b'gedolah kan b'ktanah*: the two halves of the Mishnah are not talking about the same size mat. The opening speaks of a large mat (*gedolah*), whose *stama* is assumed to be made for roofing. For a large mat, then, explicit designation *l'shchivah* is the thing that creates a problem; absent that, one may use it for *s'chach*. The second half of the Mishnah shifts, without flagging the transition, to a small mat (*ktanah*), whose *stama* is assumed to be made for reclining. For a small mat, explicit designation *l'sichuch* is what permits it; absent that, it is assumed to be a seat and may not be used.

This resolution handles the *tanna kamma* adequately — the word *gedolah* in the opening clause signals which case is being discussed, and the small mat case is implicit in the second clause. But Rabbi Eliezer's formulation is harder to resolve this way, since he explicitly says *achas ktanah v'achas gedolah* — he covers both sizes — yet his two halves remain contradictory about the *stama*.

---

## Rava's Solution

### Rava Framework

The Gemara therefore introduces Rava's explanation. Rava proposes: *b'gedolah kulei alma lo pligi d'stama l'sichuch* — concerning a large mat, nobody disagrees that the *stama* is considered made for roofing. A large mat, by its nature, is not made for personal reclining and is universally assumed to be intended for construction or roofing purposes. The debate between the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer, Rava says, concerns only the *ktanah*, the small mat.

### Tanna Kamma View

The *tanna kamma* holds *ktanah l'shchivah*: a small mat, when its purpose is unstated, is assumed to be made for reclining. Therefore, a small mat is *mekabelet tumah* in its default state and requires explicit designation *l'sichuch* to be usable for *s'chach*.

### Rabbi Eliezer View

Rabbi Eliezer holds *stam ktanah nami l'sichuch*: even a small mat, when its purpose is unstated, is assumed to be made for roofing. Rabbi Eliezer therefore comes to teach that whether small or large, the default is permissible; only explicit designation *l'shchivah* creates a problem.

### L'sichuch Reinterpretati…

This reading requires a subtle but important reinterpretation of the word *l'sichuch* as it appears in the Mishnah. On Rava's reading, when the Mishnah says "if made *l'sichuch*, one may use it for *s'chach*," the phrase *l'sichuch* does not mean literally that it must have been expressly designated for roofing. Rather, it means everything other than *l'shchivah* — any purpose other than explicit reclining counts. The *tanna kamma* is saying: for a *gedolah*, the only thing that creates a problem is explicit *l'shchivah*; everything else is treated as though it were made for roofing, and the mat is permitted. The *stama* of a *gedolah* is thus good, and the *stama* of a *ktanah* is implicitly not good under the *tanna kamma*'s position. Rabbi Eliezer then comes and says: whether *gedolah* or *ktanah*, the rule is the same — only explicit *l'shchivah* disqualifies.

Rava's reading is an elegant solution to the contradiction within Rabbi Eliezer's statement. The phrase *l'sichuch* effectively means "in any case other than *l'shchivah*," and the debate is simply whether this default-permissive rule applies only to large mats or to small mats as well.

The Gemara then raises a grammatical objection from Abaye: if Rabbi Eliezer's point is that even a *ktanah* is permissible, he should have said "whether large or even small" — placing the *gedolah* first as the obvious case and adding the *ktanah* as the novel point — rather than placing the *ktanah* first. There is in fact a textual variant debated between Rashi and Tosafot regarding the precise reading, and this grammatical issue turns on which version one accepts. Rather than parsing the full textual debate, the Gemara moves on to a more decisive challenge.

The Gemara cites a *baraita* that appears to contradict Rava's framing entirely. In the *baraita*, the *tanna kamma* says: a *gedolah* of reed mats, one may use for *s'chach* — that is, the *stama* of a *gedolah* is permitted. Rabbi Eliezer responds: only if it is not *mekabelet tumah* may one use it for *s'chach* — meaning Rabbi Eliezer is saying one may not assume it is not *mekabelet tumah* without explicit evidence. The *tanna kamma* in the *baraita* assumes the *stama* of a *gedolah* is fine; Rabbi Eliezer requires something more. This reverses the roles completely: Rabbi Eliezer here appears not as the lenient voice extending the *gedolah*'s default-permissive rule to the *ktanah*, but as the stringent voice who will not accept even the *gedolah*'s *stama* without explicit designation.

The Gemara therefore rejects Rava's solution and instead adopts Rav Pappa's formulation. Rav Pappa says: *b'ktanah kulei alma lo pligi d'stama l'shchivah* — concerning a small mat, nobody disagrees that the *stama* is for reclining. The debate is about the large mat. The *tanna kamma* holds that a *stama gedolah* is for *s'chach* — the default assumption for a large mat is that it was made for roofing and it is permissible. Rabbi Eliezer holds that even a *stama gedolah* is treated like it is for reclining; unless one expressly makes it for *s'chach*, one may not use it.

On this reading, what does Rabbi Eliezer mean when he says "whether small or large, if made for reclining it is *mekabelet tumah*"? The Gemara explains: the phrase "if made for reclining" in Rabbi Eliezer's statement is not referring to an explicit act of designation. Rather, since Rabbi Eliezer holds that even a *gedolah* is *stama* treated as though made for reclining, the phrase *asuyah l'shchivah* means: even the ordinary, unstated construction of a mat is treated as being for reclining — unless you go out of your way to make it *l'sichuch* explicitly. So when Rabbi Eliezer says "made for reclining," he means: every case that has not been explicitly designated for *s'chach* is treated as made for reclining. This is a very hard read of the Mishnah, but the Gemara commits to it in order to reconcile the Mishnah with the *baraita*. The phrase that now carries precise weight in Rabbi Eliezer's statement is the second phrase, *l'sichuch* — because only that explicit designation will save the mat from being treated as *l'shchivah*.

To summarize the positions as ultimately resolved: the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Eliezer agree that a *stama ktanah* is for reclining and is not usable for *s'chach*. They dispute the *stama gedolah*. The *tanna kamma* says a *stama gedolah* is permitted. Rabbi Eliezer says even a *stama gedolah* is treated as though made for reclining and may only be used if explicitly designated for *s'chach*. This is the mirror image of what Rava had proposed.

---

## Baraita: Mat Materials

### Soft Materials

The Gemara now cites a *baraita* that addresses the same underlying questions from a different angle, focusing on the material of the mat rather than its size alone. The *baraita* discusses mats of *shaifa* and *gemi* — papyrus and bullrush, soft water plants — which are softer materials and therefore more naturally associated with reclining and personal use.

### Soft Mats Size

For a large mat of these soft materials, one may use it for *s'chach*. This is consistent with what we have seen: even soft materials, when made large, carry the presumption of roofing use. A small mat of *shaifa* and *gemi*, however, may not be used for *s'chach* — the small size combined with the soft material makes it clearly a reclining mat.

### Hard Materials

The *baraita* then turns to mats of *kanim* and *chilat* — reeds and another harder material — which are less likely to be made for reclining and more likely to be made for construction purposes. For a large mat of these harder materials, one may obviously use it for *s'chach*.

### Hard Mats Weave

For a small mat of the harder material, the analysis becomes more nuanced and turns on how the mat is woven. If it is woven in a basket-weave style (*gedilim*) — a coarser weave using thicker strands — even a small mat may be used for *s'chach*, since such a weave is not associated with soft reclining surfaces. If, however, it is tightly woven (*arugah*) — using finer, thinner strands in a tight pattern — even a small hard-material mat may not be used for *s'chach*, since the tighter weave creates a softer surface more appropriate for sitting.

### Lenient Views

Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosi says in the name of his father: in either case of the harder material — whether basket-woven or tightly woven — one may use it for *s'chach*. Rabbi Dosa holds similarly, that when it comes to the harder material, even the small mat is permissible for *s'chach* in all cases of weave. The Gemara does not attempt to map these positions onto the earlier dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the *tanna kamma*.

---

## Eduyot Mishnah

### Chutzlot Tumah

The Gemara now introduces a Mishnah from tractate Eduyot. The Mishnah discusses *chutzlot* — a term that sounds similar to *machatzlot* (mats), though the precise identity of *chutzlot* will itself become a question. The Mishnah in Eduyot states: *kol ha-chutzlot metam'in tumei meit* — all *chutzlot* can receive the *tumah* of a dead body. This is the opinion of Rabbi Dosa, whom we just encountered in the *baraita* on hard-material mats.

### Rabbi Dosa Debate

The *chachamim* disagree and say the *chutzlot* can become *tamei midras* — the *tumah* of seats. So according to Rabbi Dosa, these objects can receive *tumat meit* but are not subject to *tumat midras*; according to the *chachamim*, they are susceptible to the more stringent *tumah* of *midras*.

### Midras-Mei Meis Link

The Gemara immediately questions the *chachamim*'s position. *Midras* — does that mean *midras* yes but *tumei meit* no? But we have a rule: *kol ha-metamei midras metamei tumei meit* — anything that can become *tamei midras* can also become *tamei meit*. Anything that functions as a seat and is therefore subject to the *tumah* of a *zav* or *zavah* sitting on it is *ipso facto* also susceptible to *tumat meit*. The categories are not parallel: anything that is *mekabel midras* is *mekabel tumei meit*, but not vice versa. A wooden spoon with a receptacle can become *tamei meit* without being subject to *midras*; but anything subject to *midras* is also susceptible to *tumat meit*. So when the *chachamim* say *midras*, they are implying *tumei meit* as well. The Gemara therefore amends its reading: the *chachamim* mean the *chutzlot* can receive *af midras* — even *midras*, and by extension *tumei meit* as well.

This also clarifies the structure of the dispute. Rabbi Dosa acknowledges that these objects are vessels of some kind — he says they can become *tamei meit* — but denies that they are designated as seats. The *chachamim* say they are made for sitting and are therefore subject to *tumat midras*. In the context of our earlier discussion, this is striking: until now we had assumed that if a mat is not designated for sitting, its only alternative is roofing, making it *tahor* altogether. Here Rabbi Dosa says something is not made for sitting and yet can still become *tamei*. This anomaly will require explanation.

---

## Reish Lakish Digression

### Chutzlot Identity

Before resolving the substance of the dispute, the Gemara pauses to ask: *mai chutzlot* — what are *chutzlot*? Rav Avdimi bar Hamduri says they are *marzuvli*. The Gemara asks what *marzuvli* means. Rava answers: *mazvli* — which Rashi explains refers to objects used for a pillow-like function, perhaps something like a pillowcase or a sack, an object that might be used to contain things. This interpretation suggests the *chutzlot* might not be mats in the ordinary sense at all but rather some type of enclosed or semi-enclosed textile object.

Reish Lakish, however, says: *machatzlot mamash* — they are simply mats, like the *machatzlot* we have been discussing throughout the chapter.

### Torah History Excursus

The Gemara then notes that Reish Lakish follows his own reasoning, for Reish Lakish made the following declaration: *hareini kapparat Rebbi Chiyya u-vanav* — I am the atonement for Rabbi Chiyya and his sons. This phrase, as Rashi explains, is the traditional expression one uses when mentioning a deceased *rav* or parent: one says *hareini kapparat mishkavo*, meaning that any suffering that comes upon me should serve as atonement for any shortcomings of the deceased. The Talmud in Kiddushin teaches that this is specifically appropriate during the first twelve months after death, when the *neshamah* is in a particular period of judgment; thereafter, one says *zichrono livracha l'chayei ha-olam ha-ba*.

Reish Lakish then proceeds with a remarkable account of Torah history. He says: *she-b'tchilla kshe-nishtachacha torah mi-Yisrael* — when Torah was forgotten from Israel, *ala Ezra mi-Bavel v'yisdah* — Ezra came up from Babylonia and laid its foundation anew. After the *churban ha-bayit*, when the *talmidei chachamim* were removed from Eretz Yisrael, Ezra had to come from Bavel to reinstitute Torah learning in the land. Then it went into decline again, and *ala Hillel HaBavli v'yisdah* — Hillel the Babylonian came and reinstituted it. The irony noted here is that Hillel, whom we think of as a foundational figure of rabbinic learning in Eretz Yisrael, was himself originally from Bavel — the famous story of the people of Eretz Yisrael who did not know whether a *korban pesach* could be brought on *erev shabbat* and had to be answered by "somebody from Bavel named Hillel." The further irony is that Hillel himself knew the answer from *Shemaya and Avtalyon*, who were themselves in Eretz Yisrael.

### Rabbi Chiyya Legacy

Then Torah declined again, and *v'alu Rebbi Chiyya u-vanav v'yisduha* — Rabbi Chiyya and his sons came and reinstituted it once more. This places Rabbi Chiyya and his sons in a line of succession with Ezra and Hillel as those who restored Torah to Eretz Yisrael from outside. This is why Reish Lakish prefaces his citation of Rabbi Chiyya's teaching with this declaration of atonement — he is about to quote a *halacha* in Rabbi Chiyya's name, which is precisely the context in which the *gemara* in Kiddushin situates the formula *hareini kapparat mishkavo*.

---

## Chutzlot Resolution

### Usha vs. Tiberias

Rabbi Chiyya and his sons say: *lo nechelku Rebbi Dosa v'chachamim ela al machatzlot shel Usha* — Rabbi Dosa and the *chachamim* were not debating the mats of Usha or the mats of Tiberias.
