Abaye initially proposes a clean resolution: the *mishna* permitting her to eat *terumah* reflects Rabbi Meir's position — Rabbi Meir does not worry about death. The case of the conditional *get* that forbids her reflects Rabbi Yehuda's position — Rabbi Yehuda is concerned about death. There is no contradiction; the two cases simply represent the two sides of a *machlokes* between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.

### Wine Flask

The evidence for this attribution of positions comes from a *baraita* concerning wine purchased from Samaritans. Since Samaritans are suspected of not separating *terumot u-ma'asrot*, the buyer is obligated to separate. If *Shabbat* is about to begin and there is no time to perform the separation properly, a leniency is offered — attributed to Rabbi Meir — allowing one to declare: "The two *log* that I will eventually separate shall be *terumah*; ten units shall be *maaser rishon*; nine shall be *maaser sheni*" — and one may then begin drinking immediately. The designated portions are not identified now but will be retroactively determined by what one separates after *Shabbat*.

This leniency depends on the principle of *breira* — that a present designation whose referent is unspecified can be validated retroactively by future action. Rabbi Meir holds *yesh breira*: such retroactive determination is valid. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Shimon forbid this practice.

### Ipcha Reversal

The *gemara* identifies a problem, however. The same Abaye who assigned the "not concerned about death" position to Rabbi Meir must now confront the *sukkah* case: it is Rabbi Meir who invalidates the use of an animal as a *dofen*, and Abaye's own explanation was that Rabbi Meir is concerned the animal will die. That would make Rabbi Meir the one *who is* concerned about death — the opposite of what Abaye just said.

The *gemara* therefore inverts the attribution: *ipcha* — reverse it. Rabbi Meir is concerned about death (*chayish le-mita*), and Rabbi Yehuda is not concerned about death. This is consistent with the *sukkah* case.

### Meir Defense

But now a new contradiction arises regarding Rabbi Meir. In the wine case, Rabbi Meir permits drinking without worrying about whether the wine flasks will break before *Shabbat* is out — suggesting he is unconcerned about unlikely negative events. Yet in the *sukkah* case, Rabbi Meir prohibits using the animal because he is concerned it will die — treating an unlikely event as a serious worry. Is Rabbi Meir contradicting himself?

The *gemara* answers in Rabbi Meir's voice: *mita shechicha, pkiyat nod lo shechicha* — death is common; a wine flask breaking is not common. Moreover, a flask breaking is something that can be guarded against (*efshar de-masrei lei le-shomer* — one can hand it to a watchman), whereas death cannot be prevented. Rabbi Meir's position is thus internally consistent: he is concerned about death precisely because it is a real and unavoidable occurrence, while he is unbothered by the prospect of a flask breaking because that is both rare and preventable.

### Yehuda Breira

The *gemara* then raises a parallel challenge regarding Rabbi Yehuda. If Rabbi Yehuda is not concerned about the animal dying, how does he forbid the wine scheme? The *gemara*'s answer: Rabbi Yehuda's objection to the wine leniency has nothing to do with the flask breaking. His real objection is that he does not hold of *breira* at all (*leis lei breira*). The retroactive designation mechanism is fundamentally invalid in his view. The flask-breaking argument was actually Rabbi Yehuda's way of challenging Rabbi Meir *on Rabbi Meir's own terms* — even granting *breira*, shouldn't you worry about the flask? To which Rabbi Meir responds: when it breaks, I'll worry about it.

### Debate Separation

The *gemara* thus separates two distinct debates that had initially appeared conflated. The dispute over the wine and the retroactive designation is fundamentally a *machlokes* about *breira*, not about whether unlikely events — death or breakage — are halachically cognizable concerns. The dispute over the animal *sukkah*, by contrast, is genuinely about whether death is a concern sufficient to disqualify the structure. These are independent questions.

What remains to be resolved is the case of the *kohen*'s wife. Abaye had originally assigned the permissive *terumah* position to Rabbi Meir (not concerned about death) and the restrictive conditional-*get* position to Rabbi Yehuda (concerned about death). Now that the positions have been inverted — Rabbi Meir is the one concerned about death, Rabbi Yehuda the one who is not — the earlier harmonization must be revisited in reverse. The *gemara* has bracketed that question for the moment, having resolved the wine-flask issue as a *breira* dispute rather than a death-concern dispute, and the resolution of the *kohen* case will need to follow the newly established framework: Rabbi Meir concerned about death, Rabbi Yehuda not.

---

---

# Sukkah 24

## Animal Wall Debate

### Recap & Framework

Today's daf is 24, and we pick up already halfway into 24a. To recall the discussion from the previous session: there was a debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about whether one may use an animal as a wall of a *sukkah*. The *gemara* framed that debate in two ways. According to Abaye, the concern underlying Rabbi Meir's disqualification is that the animal might die. According to Rav Zeira, the concern is that the animal might run away — a form of *gezeirah*. In either case, the worry is that the *sukkah* wall would then shrink to less than *asarah tefachim*.

The *gemara* then challenged Abaye's framing: how could Abaye characterize the debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda as turning on the concern for an animal's death, when a separate *mishnah* appears to assign them reversed positions on exactly that question? The case in question involved the wife of a *kohen*: if the *kohen* traveled abroad, his wife may continue eating *terumah* on the assumption that he is still alive — suggesting no concern for his death. But if the *kohen* gave her a *get* with the stipulation "this shall take effect one minute before I die," she may not eat *terumah*, because every moment could be the moment before his death. Abaye sought to link this case to a *machlokes* between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda — but the positions turned out to be the reverse of what he needed for his reading of the animal wall debate.

### Grain & Breira

The *mishnah* Abaye cited to establish the debate involved taking *terumos u-ma'asros* from grain purchased from *Kutim* (Samaritans). Two points deserve clarification. First, the grain in question is treated as *vadai tevel* — not *safek*, not *demai*, but definitively untithed grain. Second, the scenario involves *bein hashmashos*, the twilight period which is a *safek Shabbos*. One is ordinarily forbidden to designate *terumos u-ma'asros* from *vadai tevel* during *bein hashmashos* — not because of a separate *gezeirah*, but because doing so constitutes *tikkun*, fixing the grain, which is impermissible on *Shabbos* or even during the *safek* period. However, the *mishnah* permits a roundabout approach: rather than directly designating which portion is *terumah* now, one takes the grain and declares that the *terumos u-ma'asros* will be designated after *Shabbos* — and that later designation retroactively applies to what was done now. This is the concept of *breira*: what one designates *Motzaei Shabbos* retroactively determines the identity of what was separated *bein hashmashos*.

Rabbi Meir permits this approach; Rabbi Yehuda does not. In Abaye's reading, this dispute reflects a concern about whether the wine flasks containing the wine will break before *Motzaei Shabbos* — if they break, there will be nothing to designate after *Shabbos*, and the earlier act will retroactively have been invalid. Thus Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids the practice, would seem to be the one concerned that the flask will break, while Rabbi Meir, who permits it, is unconcerned.

### Reconciling Views

This creates the apparent contradiction. In the animal wall case (as Abaye framed it), Rabbi Meir is concerned the animal will die and Rabbi Yehuda is not. But in the wine flask case, Rabbi Meir seems unconcerned about breakage while Rabbi Yehuda is concerned. The positions appear reversed.

The *gemara*'s resolution is to say *eippoch* — reverse the attribution. The concern about the *kohen*'s wife eating *terumah* is not mapped onto the wine flask debate, but rather onto the animal wall debate itself. The general principle animating the animal wall case — *Rabbi Meir chish l'miyuta*, Rabbi Meir is concerned about minority possibilities, and *Rabbi Yehuda lo chish l'miyuta*, Rabbi Yehuda is not — is the same principle at stake in the *kohen*'s wife scenario: are we concerned the *kohen* might die? As the *gemara* cites explicitly: *asa'o livehema dofen lesukkah, Rabbi Meir posel, Rabbi Yehuda machshir* — one who made an animal a wall of a *sukkah*: Rabbi Meir disqualifies, Rabbi Yehuda validates.

### Wine Flask Problem

Having established that mapping, the *gemara* must now account for the wine flask case. If Rabbi Meir is concerned about death — the animal dying, the *kohen* dying — why is he not concerned about the flask breaking? And if Rabbi Yehuda is unconcerned about death, why does he appear concerned about the flask?

On the first question, the *gemara* answers: *misa sh'chicha, bkiyat hanod lo sh'chicha* — death is common, a flask breaking is not. Moreover, *v'efshar d'matzei lei lishomer* — one can arrange for a guard to watch over the flask; no one can protect against death. So Rabbi Meir's concern about death is consistent with his lack of concern about flask breakage: they are simply not equivalent risks.

On the second question, the *gemara* resolves it more fundamentally. Rabbi Yehuda's objection to the wine flask scheme has nothing to do with flask breakage at all. *Ta'ama d'Rabbi Yehuda lav mishum d'chaish l'vkiyat hanod* — Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is not that he fears the flask will break. *Ella mishum d'leis lei breira* — he simply does not accept the concept of *breira*. He rejects the entire mechanism by which a later designation can retroactively define a prior act. Death, broken flasks — none of that is his concern. His concern is purely conceptual: one cannot use *breira* to retroactively identify which wine was separated as *terumah*.

But then the *gemara* notes a difficulty. The *mishnah* itself records that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Shimon challenged Rabbi Meir: *"Iy atta modeh shema yibaka hanod v'nimtza zeh shoteh tevalim l'mafrea?"* — do you not concede that if the flask breaks, this person will retroactively have drunk *tevel*? And Rabbi Meir responded: *l'chsheyibaka* — I'll worry about it when it happens. This exchange seems to show that Rabbi Yehuda himself raises the concern of flask breakage, contradicting the *gemara*'s claim that he is indifferent to it.

The *gemara* resolves this: *Rabbi Yehuda hu d'ka'amar l'Rabbi Meir* — Rabbi Yehuda is arguing to Rabbi Meir on Rabbi Meir's own terms. *L'didi* — as far as I myself am concerned, *leis lei breira*, I reject *breira* entirely and this scheme is impermissible on that basis alone. But since *you*, Rabbi Meir, accept *breira* — at least concede that even on your own view you should be concerned the flask might break. Rabbi Meir replies that he is not worried about it. This is not Rabbi Yehuda expressing his own concern about flask breakage; it is a rhetorical argument directed at Rabbi Meir from within Rabbi Meir's own framework.

### Status Quo Analysis

With the wine flask issue resolved, the *gemara* turns to a further question about consistency: if Rabbi Yehuda is not concerned about death generally, how does one explain the well-known *mishnah* at the opening of *Yoma*, where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a replacement wife must be prepared for the *Kohen Gadol* — *shema tamus ishto*, lest his wife die? That would seem to show Rabbi Yehuda very much concerned about death.

The *gemara* answers: *mah lo asu b'chapara* — extraordinary precautions are taken for the *Yom Kippur* service. The *Kohen Gadol*'s situation is uniquely sensitive and the measures taken there are not representative of general halachic reasoning.

It is worth noting, however, that a different *gemara* elsewhere presents a more conceptually refined distinction between the two cases involving the *kohen*'s wife. The two scenarios differ not in how much we worry about death, but in the nature of the uncertainty involved. When the *kohen* travels abroad and the wife continues eating *terumah*, the question is: *shema met*, is he currently dead? For this we invoke the principle of status quo — he was alive when he left, we assume he remains alive. But when the *kohen* gives a *get* and stipulates that it takes effect one minute before his death, the question is not whether he is dead *now* — he is clearly alive now. The question is: *shema yamut*, might he die a minute from now? The fact that he is currently alive does not tell us what will happen in the next minute. Status quo establishes present facts; it cannot predict the future. This is a fundamentally different logical structure, and that *gemara* explains the two cases through this distinction rather than through a dispute about how worried we are about the probability of death. This distinction is not developed here in our *gemara*, which instead frames the question as a debate between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.

### Tnai vs. Breira

The discussion of *breira* naturally raises the question of how it differs from *tnai* — a conditional act. The distinction is conceptually important, though the boundary between them is a subject of extensive treatment by the *Tosafot*.

A *tnai* is a condition on whether an act takes effect. All the constituent elements of the act are defined: this is the *get*, this is the woman to whom it is given, this is the *kesef kiddushin*. What is held in abeyance is only whether the act will become operative, depending on whether a specified condition is met. If the condition is met, the act takes effect — potentially retroactively, from the moment it was performed.

*Breira*, by contrast, is a situation in which the very objects constituting the act are not defined at the time of performance. The question of which wine is the *terumah* and which is *chulin* — the constituent subject-matter of the act of *hafrashat terumah* itself — is not yet determined. That is what *breira* resolves retroactively: not whether the act takes effect, but what the act was actually performed *on*. The later designation fills in the undefined object of the earlier act.

There are, it should be noted, one or two *gemaras* that appear to conflate the two categories, and significant discussion among the *Rishonim* about whether these categories are always cleanly separable.

---

## Ruach Analysis

### Shift in Framework

All of the foregoing — the extended analysis of who is concerned about death, who about running away, how the wine flask case fits in, how it maps onto the *kohen*'s wife — operated under Abaye's explanatory framework: Rabbi Meir disqualifies the animal wall because he is concerned it might die or run away. The *gemara* framed this explicitly as a rabbinic concern: *mide'oraisa mechitza ma'alya hi, verabbanan hu d'gazru bah* — biblically it is a perfectly valid *mechitza*, and the rabbinic disqualification is a protective decree.

The problem with this entire framework is that it can only ever produce *stringency*. If the concern is merely that the animal might die or run away — leaving you unwittingly without a valid wall — that concern justifies prohibiting the use of animals. It cannot justify treating the animal as having a *lesser* status than an ordinary inanimate object. Yet the *gemara* cites a *mishnah* that does exactly that, and in a direction that is more lenient than the norm: *Rabbi Yehuda metamei mishum golel* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that an animal used as such has the *tumah* of a *golel*, a gravestone slab; *veRabbi Meir metaher* — while Rabbi Meir holds it is *tahor*.

A *gezeirah* — a protective decree — cannot explain a leniency. If Rabbi Meir's concern were purely precautionary, he would simply prohibit using the animal; he would not go further and declare that in the *tumah* context it lacks the status an object in its position would ordinarily carry. There must be something more fundamental at stake in Rabbi Meir's position. The entire death-and-running-away framework is therefore set aside.

### Mechitza by Spirit

*Ella amar Rav Acha bar Yaakov* — Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers an entirely different explanation of Rabbi Meir's reasoning. *Kasavar Rabbi Meir: kol mechitza she'omedes beruach einah mechitza* — Rabbi Meir holds that any *mechitza* that stands only by virtue of *ruach*, the animating life-spirit, is not a valid *mechitza*.

This formulation is striking because the standard criterion for a *mechitza* has been the opposite: *kol mechitza she'einah yechola la'amod beruach metzuya einah mechitza* — any *mechitza* that cannot withstand an ordinary wind is not a valid *mechitza*. The same word *ruach* now appears in a very different role. Previously, *ruach* was the external force a wall must be able to resist. Here, *ruach* is the internal animating force that sustains the wall — and according to Rabbi Meir, a wall sustained in this way lacks halachic substance.

### Two Interpretations

The *gemara* records a second version of Rav Acha bar Yaakov's statement. *Ika d'amri*: some say his formulation was: *kol mechitza she'eina asuya biydei adam einah mechitza* — any *mechitza* not made by human hands is not a valid *mechitza*.

*Mai beinaihu* — what is the practical difference between these two formulations? *Ika beinaihu d'ukma b'nod tapuach* — the case of an inflated vessel, a large balloon, used as a wall. According to the first version — a *mechitza* standing by *ruach* is invalid — the balloon fails: it stands only because of the air inside it, which is *ruach*. According to the second version — the problem is that it is not made by human hands — the balloon is perfectly valid: it was made and inflated by human beings.

### Physical Substance

The concept underlying the first version is that the halachic status of a *mechitza* requires material substance — *mamash*. Air, and the animating life-spirit of a living creature, are both classified as *ruach*: something real in a physical sense, as air does have weight, yet experienced as non-material, invisible, intangible. For Rabbi Meir, a structure sustained by something of this non-physical character cannot constitute a *mechitza*, because what gives it its standing is not a genuinely material substance.

An analogy might be drawn to the concept of *mamash* in other areas of *halacha* — where, for instance, a substance that is imperceptible but lends form to an object may or may not be accorded halachic significance depending on context. Here, the claim is the inverse: what sustains this wall and gives it its shape is not a tangible physical substance, and therefore the wall does not have the halachic character of a *mechitza*.

### Golel & Tumah

The second formulation — requiring that a *mechitza* be *made by human hands* — is harder to sustain, precisely because Rabbi Meir does not appear to disqualify trees used as walls of a *sukkah*. Trees are not made by human hands, and yet Rabbi Meir does not rule against them. Moreover, extending the principle to all naturally occurring formations would eliminate the use of rock faces, earthen banks, and other geological features as walls for any halachic purpose — an implication the sources do not seem to support. The first formulation, focusing on the animating *ruach* of a living creature as the specific deficiency, fits more precisely with the scope of Rabbi Meir's position.

This analysis also resolves the *tumah* question that prompted the shift in frameworks. When Rabbi Meir rules that the animal used as a wall does not have the *tumah* of a *golel*, it is not because of a precautionary decree that happens to result in leniency. Rather, since for Rabbi Meir the halachic significance of this object in its role — as something standing in the position of a grave marker — depends entirely on the animating life force sustaining it, and since that life force is *ruach* and therefore halachically non-substantial, the animal cannot be granted the status of a *golel*. The ruling is not a *gezeirah*; it follows directly from the same underlying principle. A halachic status cannot be anchored in something that is, from Rabbi Meir's perspective, not genuinely physical.

---

## Get on Animal

### Not Alive, Not Food

Having established Rabbi Meir's position through Rav Acha bar Yaakov's framework, the *gemara* turns to Rabbi Yose HaGlili, who adds a further restriction: one may not write a *get* on an animal. The *gemara* cites a *braisa* that derives this from the verse: *ve-kasav lah sefer krisus* — and he shall write her a *sefer krisus*, a bill of divorce.

The *braisa* reasons as follows. The word *sefer* — book — would seem to limit the permissible writing surface to something parchment-like. Yet the verse also says *ve-kasav* — he shall write — without qualification, implying that any surface is acceptable. If *ve-kasav* broadens the permissible surfaces beyond *sefer*, what is the function of the word *sefer*? It comes to teach: just as a book (*sefer*) is something that has no life-spirit (*ruach chayim*) and is not food, so too anything on which a *get* may be written must be something that has no *ruach chayim* and is not food. An animal, being alive, fails the first criterion. This is Rabbi Yose HaGlili's source.

### Tosafot Analysis

A natural question arises: why specifically these two characteristics? A piece of *klaf* has many properties — it is thin, it is smooth, it comes from an animal, it is classically used for writing. Why select "not alive" and "not food" as the operative criteria to the exclusion of others?

*Tosafot* addresses this directly. The closing line of a key *Tosafot* states: *be-chol echad kefi mah she-domeh la-chachamim inyan ha-ra'uy lo* — in each instance, [the relevant characteristics are identified] according to what the *chachamim* deem the appropriate matter for that context. There is no algorithmic method for determining, in a *klal u-ferat u-klal* or similar derivation, which attributes of the *prat* (the specific item used as the interpretive paradigm) are the ones that define the scope of the rule. That determination is itself an act of halachic reasoning, a matter of discretion exercised by the *chachamim* based on their understanding of what is most contextually appropriate.

This is a significant methodological statement about the nature of *Torah she-be'al peh*. It does not mean that the *chachamim* are free to choose arbitrarily; it means that the exercise of halachic interpretation is not mechanical, and that identifying the salient characteristics of a paradigm case requires judgment that cannot be fully reduced to formal rules.

One might add — though *Tosafot* does not say this explicitly — that there is a broader question among the *Rishonim* about how many of the *gemara*'s *drashos* represent a genuine derivation of halachic content from the text, versus cases where the content was known through tradition and the *drashah* serves as an *asmachta* or as a hermeneutically-articulated confirmation. This distinction matters: an *asmachta* in the strict sense implies only rabbinic authority, while a genuine derivation carries biblical weight. The *gemara* typically presents its derivations as substantive, but some *Rishonim* understand at least certain cases as the retroactive articulation of an antecedently known rule.

### Sefer Krisus Debate

The Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yose HaGlili's reading. According to the Rabbis, *sefer* in the verse does not mean "book" in the sense that would limit permissible materials. Rather, *le-sfiras devarim be'alma hu de-ata* — the word *sefer krisus* comes to say: write a narrative of severance, a document that narrates the fact of the divorce. It does not restrict the material on which the *get* is written. Since the Rabbis never used *sefer* to limit permissible materials, they have no need to invoke *ve-kasav* to broaden them.

The *gemara* then asks: if that is so, what do the Rabbis learn from *ve-kasav*? The answer is: *bi-chsiva misgareshes ve-eina misgareshes be-chesef* — a woman is divorced only through an act of writing, not through the giving of money. One might have thought, from the *gezeirah shavah* linking *yetzia* (departure from marriage) and *havayah* (entry into marriage), that just as marriage can be effected with money, so too divorce might be effected with money. *Ve-kasav* therefore establishes: only through writing.

### Severance Rules

Rabbi Yose HaGlili, having used *ve-kasav* together with *sefer* to establish what materials are permissible, must find a different source to exclude monetary divorce. He derives it from the juxtaposition of *sefer krisus* itself: *sefer karas ve-ein davar acher karas* — only through a *sefer* does the severance take effect, and not through anything else.

The Rabbis, in turn, derive something else from *sefer krisus*: the requirement that the *get* effect complete and unconditional severance. This emerges from a *braisa*: if a husband gives his wife a *get* on the condition that she never drink wine for the rest of her life, or never visit her father's house again — *ein zeh krisus*, this is not a valid *get*. The condition binds her to her husband indefinitely, since one can never be certain the condition will not be violated. A *get* given under such a condition never fully severs the relationship. If, however, the condition is limited in time — *al menas she-loshim yom*, for thirty days — *harei zeh krisus*, it is valid, because after thirty days she will be fully and completely free.

Rabbi Yose HaGlili learns the same requirement — complete severance — from the doubling of *kares krisus*: the two forms of the same root appearing together indicate two teachings, one about permissible materials and one about complete severance. The Rabbis respond: *kares krisus lo darshi* — they do not read significance into this doubling.

---

## Tree Walls

### Tree Walls Mishnah

The *gemara* moves to a new *mishnah*: *ha-oseh sukato bein ha-ilanot veha-ilanot defanot lah, kesheirah* — one who makes his *sukkah* between trees, with the trees serving as its walls, the *sukkah* is valid. This does not initially appear to be a dramatic ruling.

### Swaying Problem

Rav Acha bar Yaakov's principle, cited earlier in the context of the animal wall, is now invoked: *kol mechitza she'einah yechola la'amod beruach metzuya einah mechitza* — any *mechitza* that cannot withstand an ordinary wind is not a valid *mechitza*. This applies universally — to *sukkah*, to *Shabbos* domains, to any halachic context requiring a wall. The problem the *gemara* raises is then obvious: *veha ka'azil ve'atei* — the trees sway in the wind. How can they serve as valid walls?

### Binding Solution

The *gemara* resolves this by specifying the conditions under which the *mishnah*'s ruling applies. *Hacha be-mai askinan* — what are we dealing with? *B'kishim* — old, solid trees whose trunks do not sway. But what about the foliage? Even on an old tree, the canopy sways. The *gemara* answers: *ve'avzayei behotza vedafna* — the foliage is tied down with ropes and cords. With the foliage secured, the walls as a whole can withstand a normal wind.

### Non-Usage Concern

This leads the *gemara* to ask: *ai hachi mai lemimra* — if everything is tied down and the *sukkah* is entirely valid for structural reasons, what is the *chiddush* of the *mishnah*? Why does the *mishnah* need to tell us that trees may serve as walls?

The answer is: *mahu d'teima nigzor dilma atei l'ishtamushi b'ilan* — one might have thought we should issue a *gezeirah* prohibiting the use of trees as walls, lest one come to make use of the tree itself on *Yom Tov*. Using a tree on *Yom Tov* — placing objects on it, breaking off branches — is forbidden. If one's *sukkah* is built around trees, one might inadvertently interact with the tree in a prohibited way. *Ka mashma lan* — the *mishnah* teaches that we do not issue such a decree. The *chiddush* is not structural but halachic policy: we do not extend the prohibition to the use of trees as *sukkah* walls out of concern that one might come to use the tree improperly.

---

## Extended Cases

### Well Corners

The *gemara* continues to probe the principle of a *mechitza* that sways in the wind through a series of cases. The first involves the well-known construct of corners (*diyomadin*) placed around a public well to create a *reshut hayachid*, permitting drawing water from it on *Shabbos*. The question is what materials may serve as those corners. The *gemara* cites: *hayah sham ilan o geder o mechitzat hakanim, nidon mishum diyomed* — if there was a tree, or a stone fence, or a wall of reeds at one of the required corners, it may serve as a corner for this purpose. The *gemara* addresses the swaying objection as before: *hacha nami mishum de'avdye behotza vedafna* — here too, it is tied down with ropes.

### Willow Branches

The *gemara* adduces another case: *ilan hamaysech al ha'aretz* — a tree whose branches hang downward and form a canopy over the ground, like a willow. *Im ein nofo gavoha min ha'aretz sheloshah tefachim, metaltelin tachtav* — if the lowest point of the hanging branches is within three *tefachim* of the ground, one may carry beneath it on *Shabbos*. The picture is of branches descending from the tree and approaching the ground on all sides, such that if the gap between the branch-tips and the ground is less than three *tefachim*, the principle of *lavud* renders them as if touching the ground, forming continuous walls. The enclosed space beneath the canopy then constitutes a *reshut hayachid*.

### Tying vs. Natural

The same challenge is raised: *ha ka'azil ve'atei* — the branches sway in the wind and will move above three *tefachim* from the ground. The answer is again: *hacha nami de'avdye behotza vedafna* — tied down.

But this creates a new problem. If the branches are tied down by human effort, then this is a human-made *mechitza*. A human-made *mechitza* that is created for the purpose of habitation should, in principle, create a full *reshut hayachid* of unlimited size. *Metaltel bekulah* — one should be able to carry in the entire enclosed space regardless of its dimensions. Yet Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua rules: *ein metaltelin bo ela beit satayim* — one may only carry within a *beit satayim*, an area of 5000 square *amot* (fifty by one hundred *amot*). Why should this limitation apply if human hands have secured the *mechitza*?

### Beit Satayim Limit

The *beit satayim* limitation ordinarily applies to enclosures that were not *hukaf ledira* — not surrounded for the purpose of habitation. The paradigmatic case is an area enclosed for some purpose other than dwelling — for instance, a fence erected around a forest to keep out intruders. Such an enclosure, even if structurally sound, lacks the character of a dwelling-space and therefore does not qualify as a full *reshut hayachid* beyond the *beit satayim* limit.

If the willow's branches were entirely natural and no human intervention occurred, this would explain the limitation straightforwardly: no human surrounded the area for habitation; it is simply a natural formation. But once a human tied down the branches, the *mechitza* was made by human hands. The question is whether it was made for the purpose of habitation — *hukaf ledira* — which would remove the limitation.

### For the Air

The *gemara* answers: *mishum dehavi dira detashmisheih la'avir* — because this is a *dira* whose use is oriented toward the air, toward the outside. *Vechol dira detashmisheih la'avir ein metaltelin bo ela beit satayim* — and any such space, even if enclosed by human hands, is subject to the *beit satayim* limit.

Rashi explains: the person who takes shelter beneath the overhanging tree does so not for the sake of being enclosed in a private space, but in order to look out and attend to what is happening outside — watching crops or flocks from a shaded position. The enclosed space is thus instrumentally oriented toward its exterior, not toward creating an interior dwelling. That is the sense of *dira detashmisheih la'avir*: the enclosure exists for the sake of the open air beyond it. Such an enclosure, even when formed by deliberate human action, does not achieve the status of *hukaf ledira* that would grant it the full dimensions of a *reshut hayachid*.

### Mound & Crevice

The *gemara* adduces further cases. One who begins *Shabbos* atop a mound — *gavo'ah asarah*, ten *tefachim* high, and between four *amot* and *beit satayim* in area — may treat the edges of the mound as virtual walls and measure his *techum* of two thousand *amot* from the outer edges rather than from his own position. The mound is a *reshut hayachid*, but only up to *beit satayim*, because it is entirely natural. Similarly, *benika* — a crevice ten *tefachim* deep and between four *amot* and *beit satayim* in area — functions the same way.

A third case: if one began *Shabbos* in the midst of cut wheat, *shibbolim makkifot oto* — with sheaves of grain surrounding him — *mehallich et kullah vechutz lah alpaim amah* — the entire enclosed area is treated as his base and he measures two thousand *amot* from its outer boundary. The *gemara* again raises the swaying objection — *afgav de'azal ve'atei* — and resolves it: *dekatarnehu bemichta vehadiv bemichta* — the sheaves were tied down.

The practical concern underlying much of this discussion bears on the contemporary question of canvas *sukkah* walls that billow in the wind. The question is not merely whether the wall sways, but whether, after the wind acts on it, the wall retains its halachic status as a wall. If the canvas, even when billowing, remains within three *tefachim* of its original position and remains anchored at the bottom, it may still satisfy the requirements of *lavud* and not lose its wall-status. What *einah yechola la'amod beruach metzuya* must mean, on this analysis, is that the wind moves the wall so dramatically that it can no longer function as a wall at all — not merely that it shifts somewhat. This is why contemporary *sukkot* with canvas walls commonly use straps to ensure the walls remain secured even when the canvas itself billows outward.

---

---

# Sukkah 25

## Intro: Dwelling & Exempt…

### Overview & Transition

Daf 25 marks a significant transition in the second *perek* of *Masechet Sukkah*. Having spent the preceding folios working through exactly what a *sukkah* is supposed to look like and how it is supposed to be constructed, the *gemara* now turns to the parameters of the *mitzvah* of dwelling within it. The *mishnah* that opens this daf moves from form to function, from the laws of construction to the laws of sitting.

### Why Start w/ Exemptions

There is something structurally notable about how this *mishnah* approaches its subject. Just as the tractate's opening *mishnah* led with what *invalidates* a *sukkah* rather than what constitutes one, so too here the *mishnah* does not begin by laying out the positive parameters of the *mitzvah*. It begins instead with the exemptions. One might have expected the *masechet*, having worked through all the construction details, to now arrive at a clear articulation of the obligation itself — and only thereafter proceed to its exceptions. Instead it does the reverse. This inversion is worth dwelling on, and the reason for it turns out to be conceptually significant.

### Enumeration of Exemptions

The *mishnah* enumerates three categories of exemption. *Shluchei mitzvah peturim min ha-sukkah* — those who are traveling or otherwise engaged in the performance of a *mitzvah* are exempt from sitting in the *sukkah*. *Cholim umeshamsheihem peturim min ha-sukkah* — sick people and their attendants are likewise exempt. And *ochlin veshotin arai chutz la-sukkah* — one may eat and drink temporarily, meaning a casual snack rather than a fixed meal, outside the *sukkah*. These are the activities that need not be performed inside the *sukkah*.

### Basukot Teshvu

The reason the *mishnah* leads with exemptions rather than with the basic obligation actually reflects a profound conceptual point about the nature of the *mitzvah* itself. The verse states *basukot teshvu shivat yamim* — dwell in *sukkot* seven days. At the most fundamental level, the *mitzvah* is conceived as *living* in the *sukkah*. Everything is to be done inside it. That does not mean the *sukkah* is a prison — one's house is not a prison either — but the starting assumption is total residency. You eat in the *sukkah*, you sleep in the *sukkah*, you do everything in the *sukkah*. Given that, the *mishnah* quite naturally begins by telling us what does *not* have to be done there, because the baseline presumes that everything does. This orientation — *teshvu*, you shall dwell — frames the entire discussion that follows, and it is an important lens through which to understand why the *mishnah* structures itself as it does.

---

## Osek B'Mitzvah Principle

### Source: Shema & Berakhot

The *gemara* opens with the question *mana hanei milei* — from where do we know that a person engaged in a *mitzvah* is exempt from the *sukkah*? The answer comes from a *beraita* discussed in *Berakhot* concerning a *chatan* and the recitation of *Shema*. The verse in *Shema* states *beshivtecha b'veitecha uvlechtecha vaderech* — when you sit in your house and when you go on your way. From *beshivtecha b'veitecha* we learn *prat le-osek b'mitzvah*, excluding one who is engaged in a *mitzvah* from the obligation to recite *Shema*. From *uvlechtecha vaderech* we learn *prat le-chatan*, excluding a groom.

The context here is important. The *pesukim* of *veshinnantam levanecha vedibarta bam* are understood by *Chazal* to speak both to *talmud Torah* generally and to the *mitzvah* of *keri'at Shema* specifically — that obligation also appears in the *pasuk* of *v'hayah im shamoa*, where one is commanded to speak of these matters. The obligation of *keri'at Shema* is therefore tied to the conditions of *beshivtecha b'veitecha u'velechtecha vaderech*, and these conditions are what generate the two exemptions.

From this *beraita* the *mishnah* in *Berakhot* derives that a man who marries a *betulah* — a virgin — is exempt from reciting *Shema* on his wedding night, whereas one who marries a widow is obligated. That distinction will require explanation. But first the *gemara* asks: *mai mashma* — what precisely in the verse suggests the exemption for one who is *osek b'mitzvah*?

### Derech/Discretionary Act…

Rav Huna explains: *k'derech* — the word *vaderech*, "on the way," indicates something like going on a journey, which is a discretionary, volitional activity. *Mah derech reshut* — just as going on a journey is something one chooses to do, *af kol reshut* — so too the obligation to recite *Shema* applies whenever one is engaged in discretionary activities. *Le-apukei hai d'v'mitzvah asik* — this excludes a person who is engaged in a *mitzvah*, whose activity is obligatory rather than volitional, and who is therefore exempt from *Shema*.

The *gemara* pushes back: who says that *derech* means only a discretionary journey? Perhaps the verse means to obligate *Shema* in all situations, even when traveling for a *mitzvah*, and *v'ka'amar Rachmana likrei* — the Torah is simply telling you to recite *Shema*. The *gemara* responds: if that were so, the verse should have said *b'sheves u'veleches* — in sitting and going — using simple unmodified forms. What does the possessive *beshivtecha uvlechtecha* — *your* sitting and *your* going — add? It tells you that it is specifically *your* going, your discretionary activity, that creates the obligation. *Beleches d'mitzvah patires* — when you are going because of a *mitzvah*, you are exempt.

There is a parallel in the laws of *Shabbat*. The principle of *chafatzecha asurim v'cheftzei shamayim mutarin* captures the same possessive dynamic: it is *your* affairs that are restricted on *Shabbat*, while matters of heaven remain permitted. The possessive language does halachic work in both contexts.

### Two Rishonic Approaches

Before proceeding further, it is important to introduce a fundamental *machlokes rishonim* about the nature of the principle *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah*. The *rishonim* are divided on what this principle actually means.

According to *Rashi* and *Tosafot*, the rule operates as follows: if one is performing *mitzvah* A and *mitzvah* B comes along, one does not stop A to do B — *but only in a scenario where performing B would compromise or take one away from A*. If fulfilling B would not detract from A at all, there is no exemption. For example, if one is reciting *Shema* and would have to stop in order to give *tzedakah* to a poor person, that interruption would compromise the *Shema*, and so one is exempt from doing so. But if one is walking to perform a *mitzvah* and a poor person is walking alongside and it would cost nothing in terms of the first *mitzvah* to reach into one's pocket, the principle would not apply.

The *rishonim* who hold this position are themselves challenged by a pointed question: if that is all the rule means, why does one need a *pasuk* to tell it? If stopping A to do B means abandoning A, one could object to the interruption on independent grounds. One might answer that there are situations where B could appear more pressing — perhaps B is a *mitzvah kiyum* with a passing window, or perhaps B is by some measure more weighty — and in such cases one might think the right move is to abandon A for B. The principle therefore comes to tell us: do not abandon A for B.

Other *rishonim*, however, read the principle in a more expansive way that they argue fits the *pasuk* more naturally. The verse *beshivtecha b'veitecha uvlechtecha vaderech* means: the obligation of any given *mitzvah* applies to you during your discretionary time. When you are already engaged in a *mitzvah*, you are not in your discretionary time, and the Torah therefore does not impose the obligation of any further *mitzvah* upon you — even one whose performance would not compromise the first. The *Torah* addresses its obligations to a person who is free; a person already committed to a *mitzvah* is not free, and so the obligation does not land on him.

The obvious objection to this second approach is that it proves too much: one who is wearing *tzitzit* is fulfilling a *mitzvah*, so by this logic he would be exempt from everything? The response is that the principle is *osek b'mitzvah* — actively engaged — not merely *mekayem mitzvah*, merely receiving the credit of a *mitzvah* one happens to be doing. Wearing *tzitzit* passively does not constitute being *osek*; actively traveling to perform a *mitzvah* does. The distinction matters, but the boundary between them requires attention. This debate will have direct implications for the *sukkah* case, and it also shapes how one understands the case of the *chatan*.

---

## Chatan Exemption

### Chatan & Distraction

Why is a *chatan* exempt from saying *Shema*? The most natural and intuitive answer — the one that appears to animate the presentation in *Berakhot* itself — is that he is distracted. He cannot achieve the requisite *kavanah*. One recalls the famous *mishnah* in which *Rabban Gamliel* recited *Shema* on his wedding night and his students challenged him: did he not himself teach that a *chatan* is exempt? He replied, *ani lo k'she'ar kol adam* — I am not like ordinary people, I cannot bear to go even a moment without accepting the yoke of heaven. The clear implication of that exchange is that the reason other *chatanot* are exempt is precisely because they cannot have *kavanah* — they will be too distracted.

The *gemara* here, however, is framing the *chatan*'s exemption not as a matter of distraction but as an instance of *osek b'mitzvah*. That reframing requires explanation.

### Rashi: Preoccupation Imp…

*Rashi* addresses this directly. He writes that the *chatan* is *tarud* — preoccupied — *libo tarud b'machshavat bi'ah*. He is mentally occupied with the fact that he will be having marital relations that night. And *Rashi* adds — crucially — *u-mistaber ki patrei kra mishum tirda patrei v'eino yachol la'asok bishnayim k'echad*: the Torah exempts him because of this preoccupation, and he cannot be engaged in two things simultaneously. The logic is that stopping to recite *Shema* would take him away from thinking about the *mitzvah* he is about to perform.

A few lines later *Rashi* elaborates: *choson tarud tirda d'mitzvah, v'ashmi'inan kra d'lo mechayev l'hasir da'ato mimachshavat mitzvah rishona* — the *chatan* is preoccupied with a *tirda d'mitzvah*, and the verse teaches us not to require him to remove his mind from that first *mitzvah*. He should continue mentally engaging with the first *mitzvah*, and ensure he performs it well.

This is a demanding construction. According to *Rashi*, who holds that *osek b'mitzvah* exempts only when performing the second *mitzvah* would compromise the first, one must argue that stopping to recite *Shema* would actually compromise the *chatan*'s performance of the *mitzvah* of *bi'at mitzvah* on his wedding night. The exemption is not simply that he is distracted; the distraction must be understood as constituting a form of *osek b'mitzvah* in which interrupting it would harm the *mitzvah* he is engaged with.

The second approach — that of those *rishonim* who hold that *osek b'mitzvah* exempts even absent any compromise — handles the case more smoothly. On that view, one need not argue that stopping for *Shema* would harm the *bi'at mitzvah*. It is sufficient that the *chatan* is mentally engaged with a *mitzvah*. That mental engagement itself constitutes *osek b'mitzvah* and exempts him from other obligations, regardless of whether performing those obligations would have any practical impact on the *mitzvah* he is engaged in. The *chiddush* of the *chatan*'s case is precisely that even *mental* preoccupation — not physical activity — qualifies as being *osek b'mitzvah*.

This also raises the question of why the *bi'at mitzvah* on the wedding night is described as a *mitzvah* at all. If it is because of *peru u'revu*, then every act of marital relations would be a *mitzvah*, not only the first. Some *rishonim* say precisely that — *ein hachi nami*, every such act qualifies — and what is special about this first act is only that even it qualifies, since one might otherwise have argued that conception is unlikely from the very first act and therefore even this initial act is not technically *peru u'revu*. Others propose that the first act of *bi'ah* with a *betulah* is uniquely significant because of the profound physiological and relational bond it creates, as reflected in the principle *ein ishah koretet berit ela lemi she'asah keli* — a woman forms her deepest covenant of loyalty with the man who first made her into, as it were, a completed vessel. Whether or not that constitutes one of the *taryag mitzvot* is itself a question worth considering.

### Virgin vs. Widow

The distinction between marrying a *betulah* and marrying an *almanah* is now addressed. One might assume that since marrying a widow also involves a *bi'at mitzvah* — presumably because of *peru u'revu* — the *chatan* in that case should also be considered *osek b'mitzvah*. The *gemara* therefore asks: *kones almanah nami?* Should the one marrying a widow also be exempt? The answer is: *kones betulah tarid, kones almanah lo tarid* — one who marries a virgin is preoccupied; one who marries a widow is not. In both cases there may be a *mitzvah*, but in one case the preoccupation that defines *osek b'mitzvah* is present and in the other it is not. The difference is not whether a *mitzvah* will be performed, but whether the person is mentally *osek* with it.

### Avel Counterexample

The word *tarid* — preoccupied — appearing in this answer prompts the *gemara* to consider whether the exemption might have nothing to do with *mitzvah* at all, and everything to do simply with being distracted. *Vechol heicha de-tarid hachi nami de-patur?* — whenever someone is preoccupied, are they exempt from *Shema*? What about someone whose ship sank at sea, who just lost a fortune — is he exempt because he is preoccupied?

The *gemara* might have been inclined to entertain this, but it is immediately refuted by the ruling of Rav Abba bar Zavda in the name of Rav: *avel chayav bechol hamitzvot ha'amoros ba-Torah chutz min ha-tefillin* — a mourner is obligated in all *mitzvot* in the *Torah* except for *tefillin*, which are described in *Yechezkel* as *pe'er*, glory, and whose wearing would therefore be inappropriate during the acute phase of mourning. But for *Shema* — the mourner is obligated. A person in the most profound state of grief, surely the most genuinely preoccupied individual one can imagine, is still required to recite *Shema*. Preoccupation alone cannot be the basis for exemption.

### Tirda Categories

The *gemara* therefore reanchors the exemption: *hacha tarid tirda d'mitzvah, hatam tarid tirda d'reshut* — here, in the case of the *chatan*, the preoccupation is *tirda d'mitzvah*, preoccupation arising from a *mitzvah*; whereas in the case of the person who lost his fortune at sea or the *avel* dwelling on the loss of a loved one, the preoccupation is *tirda d'reshut* — a discretionary or at least non-*mitzvah* preoccupation.

This distinction, *tirda d'mitzvah* versus *tirda d'reshut*, is the *gemara*'s resolution, but it is a striking one. Labeling an *avel*'s grief as *tirda d'reshut* is remarkable. One might have thought that the entire framework of *aveilut* is constructed around the idea that thinking about the *met*, dwelling in one's loss, is not only emotionally natural but religiously appropriate — perhaps even obligatory. *Rashi* engages with this tension directly. He writes that the *avel* is obligated to engage in all the *practices* of *aveilut* — the prohibitions of washing, anointing, and wearing shoes — as expressions of *kavod ha-met*, honor to the deceased. But there is no obligation to *suffer*; the acts of *aveilut* are demonstrations of respect, not necessarily of self-affliction. One could argue that the period of *aveilut*, following as it does upon the period of *aninut*, is already a period of *tanchumim* — of consolation and working through the loss — and that it is unhealthy and inappropriate to remain in a state of acute, unprocessed anguish. The *gemara* is calling upon the *avel* to settle his mind.

Yet the *gemara*'s language — *ihu d'ka mitzta'er nafshei* — goes further than that. It says the *avel* brings the suffering upon himself, implying a degree of volitional choice in remaining in that state. And even on the first day of mourning, the day the *gemara* elsewhere calls *k'yom mar* — a bitter day — and uses as the reason to exempt the *avel* from *tefillin*, the same *gemara* still classifies his preoccupation as *tirda d'reshut* when it comes to *Shema*. The tension between using the *avel*'s mental state to inform his *tefillin* obligation while simultaneously dismissing it as *tirda d'reshut* for *Shema* purposes is, to say the least, a challenging and fascinating corner of these *sugyot*.

What the *gemara* does ultimately affirm is this: the exemption of the *chatan* from *Shema* is an instance of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah*. The *chiddush* is that mental preoccupation with a *mitzvah* is sufficient to constitute being *osek* — one does not need to be physically executing the *mitzvah* at that moment. The distinction between *betulah* and *almanah* is not about whether there is a *mitzvah* to be performed, but about the degree of mental *osek*: when marrying a *betulah* the *chatan* is genuinely preoccupied; when marrying a widow he is not.

---

## Korban Pesach Source

### Joseph's Coffin Braita

The *gemara* then raises a challenge: *me-hacha nafka* — are you deriving *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* from the *Shema* case? It was already derived from the case of *Korban Pesach*. The *gemara* cites a *beraita* about the verse *vayehi anashim asher hayu teme'im le-nefesh adam* — there were men who were *tamei* on account of a human corpse and could not bring the *Korban Pesach*, who then came before Moshe. Their coming to Moshe is the event that generated the institution of *Pesach Sheni*. The *beraita* asks: who were those men?

### Identity Debates

Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says: they were the carriers of Yosef's coffin. When it says *vayikach Moshe et atzmot Yosef immo*, Moshe took the bones of Yosef with him — those who had been carrying that coffin became *tamei* and could not bring the *Korban Pesach*. Rabbi Akiva says: they were Mishael and Eltzafan, the nephews of Aharon who removed the bodies of Nadav and Avihu from the Mishkan after the fire consumed them — *she-hayu oskim be-Nadav ve-Avihu* — and thereby became *tamei*.

Rabbi Yitzchak then challenges both identifications with the same argument. If they were the carriers of Yosef's coffin: the *Bnei Yisrael* made this *Pesach* while encamped at Har Sinai, approximately ten months after the Exodus. Those who carried the coffin had set it down long before and would have had ample time to become *tahor*. Moreover, the laws of *Parah Adumah*, which enable purification from corpse *tumah*, were taught at *Rosh Chodesh Nisan* — giving anyone who was *tamei* at that point fifteen full days to purify themselves before *Pesach*. The same objection applies to Mishael and Eltzafan: the death of Nadav and Avihu also occurred on *Rosh Chodesh Nisan*, leaving fifteen days for purification. Therefore Rabbi Yitzchak concludes: *ela oskim be-met mitzvah hayu* — they were simply people who happened to be engaged in burying a relative, *she-chal shevi'i shelahem lihyot be-erev ha-pesach* — and their seventh day of *tumah* fell out on *Erev Pesach*, leaving them unable to purify in time.

### Tamei on Erev Pesach

The proof that it was specifically the seventh day is derived from the verse itself: *ve-lo yachlu la'asot ha-pesach ba-yom ha-hu* — they could not do the *Pesach* on that day, implying that *bayom ha-hu* — on that particular day — they could not, but *le-machar yecholim la'asot* — one day later they could have. This indicates they were at the last stage of their *tumah* — had their seventh day fallen one day earlier, they would have been *tahor* in time. And had it fallen even one day later, they would have been able to bring the *Korban Pesach*.

This *sugya* also illustrates *Chazal*'s characteristic impulse to make the anonymous concrete, to tie unidentified figures in a *pasuk* to known people and events. Rabbi Yitzchak ultimately resists this and acknowledges that these were simply unnamed individuals in an unremarkable situation, which is also an important kind of intellectual honesty within the *midrashic* enterprise.

---

## Korban Pesach Source (II)

### Pesach vs. Shema

The *gemara*'s question was whether the principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* is derived from the *Korban Pesach* case, rendering the derivation from *Shema* unnecessary. The answer is that both sources are needed, because each one teaches something the other cannot.

The *Korban Pesach* case illustrates a situation where the person engaged in *mitzvah* A — the burial — knew well in advance that doing so would prevent them from performing *mitzvah* B — the *Korban Pesach* — a week later. At the time of the burial, *mitzvah* B was not yet present; it lay in the future. The argument there is: go ahead and do A because B is not yet on the scene. *Mishum d'lo mata zman chiyuva d'Pesach* — the time of the obligation of *Pesach* had not yet arrived. In such a case it is comparatively obvious that one performs the *mitzvah* in front of one right now. *Aval hacha d'mata zman kri'at Shema* — but here by *kri'at Shema*, one is in the middle of performing *mitzvah* A when *mitzvah* B presents itself right now, in real time. Perhaps in that situation one should stop A and do B? *Eima lo* — one might say no, you must now switch. *Tzricha* — you need this case to teach you that even when B comes along and presents itself while you are doing A, you still do not abandon A.

### Both Sources Needed

Conversely, had one only had the *Shema* case, one might have reasoned that the reason to continue with A rather than switch to B is that B is merely *keri'at Shema* — a *mitzvah* that does not carry *karet*. The *Korban Pesach*, however, does carry *karet*. *D'ika karet* — B there is of far greater halachic weight. *Aima lo* — in that case perhaps one should abandon A and ensure B is fulfilled. *Tzricha* — both cases are therefore necessary. From the *Korban Pesach* case one learns not to abandon A even when B is weightier. From the *kri'at Shema* case one learns not to abandon A even when B is present and pressing right now. Neither case alone would have established the full principle.

*Tosafot* notes that this analysis still leaves one open case: what happens when B presents itself *in the moment* — as in the *Shema* case — *and* B is of greater weight, carrying *karet* as in the *Pesach* case? Neither source addresses the combination of the two. *Tosafot* raises this as an unresolved question about the outer limits of the principle.

---

## Application to Sukkah

### Translation to Sukkah

Now that the principle of *osek b'mitzvah patur min hamitzvah* has been established and its sources examined, the *gemara* turns to how it applies to the case of *shluchei mitzvah* and the *sukkah*. The *mishnah*'s exemption of those traveling to perform a *mitzvah* from the obligation of *sukkah* is derived directly from this principle. As *Rashi*'s example has it, if one is traveling to perform *pidyon shevuyim* — the redemption of captives — one is *osek b'mitzvah* and therefore exempt from *sukkah*.

But a nuance must be addressed. It is one thing to say that the traveler need not stop his journey and search for a *sukkah* in which to eat — stopping would obviously delay him and compromise his mission. But what about nighttime? When he stops to sleep, why is he exempt from sleeping in a *sukkah*? He is no longer in transit. Perhaps he could simply find a friend with a *sukkah* nearby.

### Tosafot Compromise Model

*Tosafot* addresses this tension directly, stating that the *gemara*'s own formulation — *holchei li-dvar mitzvah peturim min ha-sukkah bein ba-yom bein ba-laylah* — explicitly includes both day and night. The reason for this, *Tosafot* explains, is that travelers move during the day but not at night, so one might have thought the nighttime exemption requires independent justification. *Tosafot* then provides that justification: *de-hacha nami ayiri be-hai gavna di-matrid be-kiyum mitzvat sukkah havei mevatlei mi-mitzvot* — the exemption applies when the act of sitting or sleeping in a *sukkah* would itself compromise the performance of the *mitzvah*. One has to construct the scenario such that searching for a *sukkah*, sleeping less comfortably, or losing time will have some actual impact on the execution of their mission. According to *Tosafot*, this is required because they follow the *rishonim* who hold that *osek b'mitzvah* exempts only when performing *mitzvah* B would compromise *mitzvah* A.

### Non-compromise Approach

The alternative approach, as outlined earlier, does not require this construction. On that view, once someone is in the process of performing a *mitzvah* — traveling to perform it, sleeping to maintain their capacity to perform it — they are *osek b'mitzvah* throughout. Everything that is part of this process of being engaged in the *mitzvah* falls under the umbrella of *osek*. There is no requirement to argue that sleeping in a *sukkah* would specifically compromise the mission. Being *osek b'mitzvah* is its own complete exemption from other *mitzvot*, regardless of whether fulfilling them would cause any practical interference.

### Trivial Activity Limits

The broader implications of the non-compromise approach raise a practical concern, as is evident from the *rishonim* who hold it. If one is *osek b'mitzvah* and therefore entirely exempt from all other *mitzvot*, the principle risks becoming extreme. As one might ask: if these *shluchei mitzvah* are on a boat traveling to their destination, and they have nothing to do but sit — does *osek b'mitzvah* exempt them from everything during those idle hours? The *rishonim* who take the broader view acknowledge this implication and pull back from its most extreme application: when the performance of another *mitzvah* is entirely trivial — when it costs nothing in terms of time, energy, or focus — the exemption arguably does not apply, or at minimum one should fulfill the other *mitzvah* in that case. The outer limits remain somewhat open-ended, but even those who hold the broader view resist the conclusion that *osek b'mitzvah* functions as an unlimited blanket exemption from all religious obligation.

---

## Avel in Sukkah

### Avel & Tefillin Exemption

The *gemara* now turns to a separate ruling of Rav Abba bar Zavda in the name of Rav — the same tradent who earlier established that an *avel* is obligated in *keri'at Shema* even on the first day. The ruling is: *avel chayav bechol mitzvot ha'amoros ba-Torah chutz min ha-tefillin* — a mourner is obligated in all *mitzvot* in the *Torah* with the exception of *tefillin*. The source for the *tefillin* exemption is *Yechezkel*, where God commands the prophet *pe'ercha chavosh alecha* — bind your glory upon you — meaning *tefillin*, in the context of telling him to behave differently than a normal *avel*. From this, *Chazal* derive that for an ordinary *avel*, wearing *tefillin* — described as *pe'er*, glory — is inappropriate and therefore prohibited. It would be disrespectful to the deceased for the *avel* to adorn himself with an object of glory while in mourning.

This exemption is limited to the first day of mourning. The verse in *Yechezkel* also alludes to *acharitah k'yom mar* — its aftermath is like a bitter day — and it is that acute bitterness of the first day that justifies the exemption. Many *rishonim* connect this to the position that the obligation of *aveilut* is *de-oraita* only on the first day, and the suspension of *tefillin* is correspondingly limited.

There is a genuine tension worth noting here. The *gemara* uses the *avel*'s mental state on the first day — the bitterness, the devastation — as the basis for his *tefillin* exemption. Yet the same *gemara* has already classified the *avel*'s grief as *tirda d'reshut* when it comes to *keri'at Shema*. Even on this first bitter day, even when that bitterness is invoked to exempt him from *tefillin*, the *gemara* does not allow that same state to exempt him from *Shema*. The intersection of these two rulings is genuinely challenging.

### Avel Obligated in Sukkah

The *gemara* then records a second ruling from the same tradition: *avel chayav ba-sukkah* — a mourner is obligated in the *sukkah*. The *gemara* immediately asks *peshita* — is this not obvious? We have already established that the *avel*'s preoccupation is *tirda d'reshut*, not *tirda d'mitzvah*, and therefore he is not considered *osek b'mitzvah* and has no ground for exemption on that basis. Of course he is obligated. So why is this ruling stated?

### Self-Inflicted Tzaar

The *gemara* explains: *mahu d'teima* — one might have thought otherwise, because of the ruling that *mitzta'er patur min ha-sukkah* — one who is suffering is exempt from the *sukkah*. And *hai nami mitzta'er hu* — this *avel* is also suffering. Perhaps he should be exempt on those grounds?

The *gemara* therefore needs to state: *ka-mashma lan — hanei milei tza'ara de-mimeila* — the exemption of *mitzta'er* applies to suffering that comes on its own accord, from without. *Aval hacha ihu deka mitzta'er nafshei* — here, the *avel* is bringing this suffering upon himself. *Iba'ei lei le-yisuvei da'atei* — he should settle his mind and compose himself. It is a striking statement, and not for the first time in this *sugya*: the *gemara* is distinctly unsympathetic to the *avel*'s *tza'ar*, treating it as something he has the capacity to manage and is choosing not to.

### Rashi: Source of Tzaar

There is an important ambiguity in how to understand the exemption of *mitzta'er* from *sukkah* in the first place, and how the *avel* case bears on it. *Rashi* explains *tza'ara de-mimeila* as follows: *she-ha-sukkah mitzta'arto* — the *sukkah* itself is the source of the suffering. The paradigmatic case is heat, cold, or a foul smell from the *sechach*. The Torah says *teshvu k'ein taduru* — dwell in the *sukkah* as you dwell in your home — and one does not live in a house that causes discomfort. Therefore when the *sukkah* causes the suffering, one is exempt. When the *sukkah* is not the source of the suffering — as in the case of the *avel*, whose grief follows him wherever he goes — the exemption does not apply.

On *Rashi*'s reading, the *gemara* should have simply said: the reason the *avel* is obligated is that his suffering does not come from the *sukkah*. The *avel*'s *tza'ar* is entirely independent of the *sukkah* environment. Therefore he falls outside the parameters of *mitzta'er patur min ha-sukkah* from the outset.

### Denying Credence to Tzaar

The difficulty is that the *gemara* does not say that. It does not say the *avel* is obligated because the *sukkah* is not the source of his *tza'ar*. It says the *avel* is bringing it upon himself and should settle his mind. This formulation opens up a different reading: perhaps *mitzta'er patur min ha-sukkah* applies even when the *sukkah* is not the source of the suffering — whenever a person is genuinely in a state of *tza'ar*, regardless of its origin, they are exempt. The reason the *avel* is obligated, on this reading, is not that the *sukkah* isn't causing his distress, but rather that the *gemara* simply refuses to credit his *tza'ar* as legitimate grounds for exemption. He is capable of setting it aside and he should do so.

### Mitzta'er Ambiguity

This ambiguity has practical consequences. Consider a person who has a severe rash or mosquito bites all over his body — genuinely and highly uncomfortable regardless of where he is. The *sukkah* is not the source of his discomfort; he would be in the same state in his house. Is he exempt from *sukkah* or not? *Rashi*'s reading would say he is not exempt, because the exemption of *mitzta'er* requires that the *sukkah* itself be the cause. The alternative reading — that *mitzta'er patur min ha-sukkah* is a general principle covering any state of genuine suffering regardless of its source — would exempt him, since his suffering is real and not something he is bringing upon himself through volitional choices the way the *avel* is characterized as doing.

The *gemara* thus leaves the scope of *mitzta'er patur min ha-sukkah* in a genuine state of ambiguity: is it a narrow exemption triggered only when the *sukkah* causes the *tza'ar*, or a broader one covering any state of *tza'ar*, with the *avel* case being a special exception because the *gemara* denies credence to his particular form of grief? Both readings are anchored in the text, and both raise their own questions about the relationship between suffering, *mitzvah* obligation, and the *sukkah*'s requirement of genuine, livable dwelling.

---

---

# Sukkah 27

## Achilat Arai

### Broader Context

The daf we take up today is 27a, though we begin slightly earlier, near the bottom of 26b, with the mishnah's ruling that *ochlin achilat arai chutz lasukkah* — one may eat a temporary eating outside the *sukkah*. We spent considerable time previously examining the broad range of exemptions granted to the sick, to those in discomfort (*mitzta'er*), and to travelers, and we looked there at the larger conceptual issue: the *mitzvah* in its core is not a narrow technical matter of eating a precise quantity inside a *sukkah*, but a broader concept of fundamentally living there. Because it is that broader, more abstract obligation, there is correspondingly greater latitude in determining what kinds of circumstances genuinely constitute "living" in a place and what do not. This stands in sharp contrast to the way we have come to experience the obligation today — translated into a very limited, narrowly defined technical sense, focused on eating a particular quantity, with sleeping effectively set aside entirely. In that contemporary framing, the wide range of exemptions can seem surprising. But the more all-encompassing the obligation is, the more those exemptions make intuitive sense.

### Shiur Achilat Arai

With that context in place, the *gemara* turns to quantifying exactly how much food constitutes *achilat arai*. The text reads: *vekamah achilat arai* — how much is considered only a temporary eating, up to what amount?

*Amar Rav Yosef*: *tarti u'tlat bei* — two or three eggs' worth. Rashi, it should be noted, did not have the word *bei* in his version of the text; his reading is *tarti u'tlat*, meaning two or three morsels, though the amount one can swallow in a single go is generally assumed to be an egg's worth, making his reading consistent with two to three eggs.

*Amar leih Abaye*: Abaye objects, pointing out that for some people, two or three eggs' worth is already enough to constitute a full meal — *ve'havia leih seudat keva*. That would be a *keva* meal, a fixed, permanent eating, not a temporary one. *Ella amar Abaye*: rather, the measure is *kedei te'imat bar bei rav de'azeil l'bei kallah* — like the taste a *yeshiva bachur* takes before going in to his learning for the day. The precise quantity is not fully specified, but it is understood to be what one can swallow in a single go — approximately one egg's worth. Up to that amount is considered temporary.

### Food Type Categories

Interestingly, the *gemara* here does not address what *type* of food is in question, only the quantity. There is a *gemara* elsewhere in Yoma that takes up the question of *peiri* — whether fruit requires a *sukkah* at all — and the conclusion there is that fruit does not. The question then becomes which foods fall into the category of fruit and which do not. The general assumption is that bread and *mezonot* are the paradigmatic cases requiring a *sukkah*, while fruit clearly does not. Where meat and potatoes or similar foods fall is a matter of debate among the *rishonim*. The practical tendency is to adopt a narrow definition of what is technically obligated in a *sukkah*, focusing on bread, *mezonot*, and to some extent wine. But the fact remains: in our *gemara* here, the nature of the food is not discussed at all — only the quantity.

### Sleeping in Sukkah

The *gemara* then introduces a *braitah*: *ochlin achilat arai chutz lasukkah* — one may eat a temporary eating outside the *sukkah* — *v'ein yeshenin shenat arai chutz lasukkah* — but one may not take even a temporary nap outside of it. *Mai ta'ama* — why is a nap treated differently from a temporary snack? The question is a genuine one: if the logic of *achilat arai* is that a small amount does not constitute the kind of fixed presence the *mitzvah* demands, why doesn't the same reasoning apply to a brief nap?

## Shenat Arai Debate

### Gezeirah Shema Yiradem

*Amar Rav Ashi*: the answer is *gezeirah shema yiradem* — a rabbinic decree based on the concern that one might fall into a deep sleep. Technically, a nap itself is not the problem; rather, we are afraid of where it might lead.

### Tefillin Challenge

Abaye immediately challenges this reasoning: if every permitted nap carries the risk of becoming a deep sleep, how can the *halacha* ever draw a meaningful distinction between the two? For there is a *braitah* that explicitly rules *yeshan adam shenat arai bitfillin aval lo shenat keva* — a person may take a temporary nap while wearing *tefillin*, but not a permanent sleep. According to Rav Ashi's logic, that nap too should be prohibited by the same *gezeirah* — since a nap can always slide into deep sleep, how can any *halachic* framework permit it?

### Moser Shinato

*Amar Rav Yosef brei deRav Ilai*: the case of the permitted nap in *tefillin* is a special one — *b'moser shinato l'acherim* — where one has designated others to wake him up. That special circumstance accounts for why a nap is permitted in that context: the concern of the *gezeirah* is neutralized when someone else is serving as a guarantor.

### Co-Guarantor Problem

*Matkif lah Rav Mesharsheya*: your co-signer himself needs a co-signer. How can you trust that the person you've asked to wake you won't himself fall asleep? This difficulty — that delegating vigilance to another person does not eliminate the underlying risk — is a real one. It arises in other contexts as well, such as whether one can rely on another person to remind him before a deadline. The conclusion here seems to be that this answer cannot stand: if the *gezeirah* applies, a human guarantor does not suffice to remove it.

### Rosho Bein Birkav

*Ella amar Rabbah bar bar Chanah amar Rabbi Yochanan*: the resolution lies elsewhere entirely. The permitted nap in *tefillin* is a case of *bimeniach rosho bein birkav* — where one puts his head between his knees. This is not a matter of lying down on a couch for a real nap; one is simply putting one's head down on a desk, like trying to sleep on an airplane. In that position, there is no serious concern that the brief rest will turn into a full sleep. So fundamentally there is nothing wrong with a nap, but the concern is always that a nap might become a deep sleep. With *tefillin*, the case is only permitted because of this special circumstance in which that escalation is not realistically feared.

## Rava's Distinction

### Ein Keva LeSheinah

Rava rejects this entire approach. *Amar Rava*: *ein keva lesheinah* — there is no fixed category for sleep when it comes to *tefillin*. Rava is drawing a fundamental distinction between the two *mitzvot* and argues that the reasoning for prohibiting a nap outside the *sukkah* has nothing to do with the fear that it might turn into a deeper sleep.

### Keva as Dwelling

Rava's core argument is that by *sukkah*, the issue is not what a nap might become, but what a nap already is. Sleep — even a brief nap — is categorically different from eating as an expression of where one lives. When one is somewhere other than home, one might snack: on the street, in the office, wherever. Snacking is something that does not inherently speak to where one resides. But sleeping — even briefly — is strongly tied to where one sets down roots. It would be quite rare to sleep somewhere that is not one's home. And therefore, even a nap is considered an act that is central to and constitutive of the concept of living in a place. That is what *ein keva lesheinah* means in this context: even a brief sleep is already *keva* in the sense of defining where one dwells.

### Tefillin vs. Sukkah

By *tefillin*, the concern is not about sleep as an expression of residence but about something physiologically distinct: the concern is passing gas in the presence of *tefillin*, which would be a disrespect to the *mitzvah*. A brief nap does not present a serious risk of that — only a deep sleep does. And Rava maintains there is no meaningful concern that a nap will turn into a deep sleep; a nap is a nap. Therefore, by *tefillin*, where the sole issue is passing gas, a nap is permissible because it does not present that risk. By *sukkah*, however, the very act of napping — regardless of how long it lasts — is already defined as *keva*, because it is the kind of act that expresses where one is living. That is the conceptual difference: not what the nap might become, but what it already means.

## Three Braitot

### Contradictory Braitot

Having established the theoretical framework for the distinction between napping and sleeping in the context of *tefillin*, the *gemara* now introduces three *braitot* that appear to contradict one another. The first says *yeshan adam bitfillin shenat arai velo shenat keva* — one may sleep temporarily but not permanently. The second says *bein keva bein arai* — both are permitted. The third says *lo keva velo arai* — neither is permitted. Rather than treating these as an unresolved three-way dispute, the *gemara* reconciles them: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty.

### Nekitum Bidei

*Ha denakit lehu bideih*: the strictest case — where even a nap is forbidden — is where one is holding the *tefillin* in one's hands. If one's hands relax during sleep, the *tefillin* will fall. Even though the issue of passing gas does not apply when the *tefillin* is not being worn, the physical risk of dropping what one is holding means that even a brief nap is too risky, and the prohibition applies *afilu arai*.

### Manach BeReisheih

*Ha dmanach beireisheih*: the middle case — napping permitted but deep sleep prohibited — is where one is actually wearing the *tefillin* on one's head. It is notable that the *gemara* throughout tends to emphasize the *tefillin shel rosh* in these discussions, as with the famous phrase *karkafta dlo manach tefillin* — a skull that never had *tefillin* placed upon it. When one is wearing the *tefillin*, a nap is permitted because we are not afraid of passing gas during a brief rest, but a deep sleep is forbidden because it will eventually lead there.

### Faris Sudra

*Ha defaris sudra ilaviyei*: the most lenient case — both napping and sleeping permitted — is where the *tefillin* is wrapped in a handkerchief and one is simply sleeping nearby it, not wearing it. Since it is wrapped and not being worn, the concern about disrespect through passing gas does not apply in the same way, and sleep near the protected *tefillin* is permitted.

## Shiur Shenat Arai

### Kedei Hiluch Me'ah Amah

Now that the *gemara* has distinguished — at least for *tefillin* purposes — between a nap and a deep sleep, it turns to the question of quantity: how much time constitutes a temporary sleep? *Tani Rami bar Yechezkel*: *kedei hiluch me'ah amah* — the time it takes to walk one hundred *amot*. To work out that duration: the *halachic* standard is that walking a *mil* — two thousand *amot* — takes eighteen minutes, or roughly twenty minutes for round figures. If two thousand *amot* takes twenty minutes, then one hundred *amot* takes approximately one minute. So a *shenat arai* is, by this measure, about one minute — a genuine power nap in the most extreme sense.

The *gemara* continues with a supporting *braitah*: *ha-menamnem ha-yashen bitfillin vera'ah keri* — if one is napping with *tefillin* and has a seminal emission, *ocheiz baretzu'ah v'eino ocheiz baketzitzah* — one grasps the *tefillin* by the strap to remove it but not by the housing itself.
