That is the ruling of Rabbi Yaakov. The *chachamim* then add their familiar formulation: one may sleep temporarily but not permanently. Tosafot notes the ambiguity in Rabbi Yaakov's position — it is not entirely clear whether he is engaging with the *arai/keva* distinction or debating a separate question about when the concern of leading to a deeper sleep applies, perhaps specifically at night.

### Shinat HaSus

The *gemara* next introduces a separate teaching of Rav regarding daytime sleep more generally — not specifically in the context of *tefillin*, but as a broader statement about one's conduct. *Asur le'adam lishan bayom yoter mishnat hasus* — it is forbidden to sleep during the day for longer than a horse sleeps. Rashi explains the prohibition in terms of *bittul Torah*. And how long does a horse sleep? *Shitin nishmei* — sixty breaths.

The precise duration of sixty horse breaths generates considerable uncertainty. The respiratory rate of a resting horse is approximately eight to sixteen breaths per minute, which would place sixty breaths somewhere in the range of four to seven and a half minutes. The authorities who have attempted to quantify this — including the *Sha'arei Teshuvah* and Rabbeinu Yonah — arrive at figures in the range of three to three and a half minutes for humans; the empirical basis for these calculations is, to say the least, not entirely transparent. The practical upshot is that a permitted daytime nap is a very short one.

### Abaye's Nap

*Amar Abaye*: the sleeping of his master — Rabbah — was *ke-deRav*, following the standard of Rav. And Rav learned how much to nap from his own *Rebbi*, and that *Rebbi* in turn learned from the practice going all the way back to David, who slept *ke-susya* — like a horse — meaning sixty breaths.

*Abaye hava noyam kedei me'al miPumbedita leVei Kuvi* — Abaye, however, would nap for the duration of the journey from Pumbedita to Bei Kuvi. Rashi, in another context, records that this distance is six *parsaot*. Since a *parsa* is four *mil* and a *mil* is eighteen minutes, six *parsaot* works out to roughly six hours — a rather dramatic figure, far removed from the one-minute *shenat arai* or the horse's sixty breaths. *Kari alei Rav Yosef* — Rav Yosef, who was Abaye's teacher, said about him: *ad masai atzel tishkav masai takum mishinasecha* — "How long, O sluggard, will you lie down? When will you rise from your slumber?" — quoting the verse of rebuke. The irony is notable: on one extreme we have a one-minute power nap as the *halachic* standard, and at the other extreme, Rashi's reading of Abaye's practice suggests a six-hour rest.

## Tefillin Sleep Rules

### Day vs. Night

The *gemara* turns to a new *braitah* on the rules governing *tefillin* during sleep and under various conditions. *Ha-nichnas lishon bayom* — if one goes to sleep during the day, *ratza choletz ratza meniach* — if he wishes he may remove the *tefillin* and if he wishes he may leave them on. Since daytime sleep is presumably only a nap and not a deep sleep, there is latitude. *Ba-layla* — at night, however, *choletz ve'eino meniach* — one must remove them and may not leave them on, since nighttime sleep carries a greater concern of leading to a deep sleep, or perhaps even a nap at night more readily escalates than one during the day. Tosafot discusses this distinction between day and night.

### Young Men Rule

*Divrei Rabbi Nosson* — that is Rabbi Nosson's position. *Rabbi Yossi omer*: *ha-yeladim* — the young men — *le'olam chaltzim ve'einam menichim* — must always remove their *tefillin* and may never leave them on, even during the day. The reason given is *mipnei she-ragilim betumah* — because they are more accustomed to *tumah*, meaning they will more regularly experience seminal emission during sleep. The *gemara* considers whether this implies that Rabbi Yossi holds that a *baal keri* is forbidden from wearing *tefillin* altogether. That would be a far-reaching position — but the *gemara* notices an oddity in the very framing of the question. The concern here is not about someone who has already become a *baal keri* before putting on *tefillin*; it is about someone who might become a *baal keri* while wearing them. Yet the *gemara* treats these as presenting the same underlying question, which is itself striking, since the latter concern — desecrating the *tefillin* in the moment — would seem categorically more severe than the former.

### Wives Context

*Amar Abaye*: the resolution is that we are not discussing young unmarried men who may have seminal emissions in their sleep, but rather *be-yeladim u-neshoseihem imahen* — young men who are with their wives. The concern is that even if one is only going to bed briefly, the proximity of his wife may lead to marital relations. What is also notable here — and the *gemara* does not explicitly flag it but the implication is clear — is that apparently men of more advanced age who lie in bed next to their wives while wearing *tefillin* do not raise the same concern. The *gemara* seems to assume that younger men are at particular risk of this escalation in a way that others are not.

### Shachach Veshmish

*Shachach v'shimish mitato bitfillin* — if one forgot and had marital relations while wearing *tefillin*. All of this — and it is worth pausing here — reflects a world in which *tefillin* were worn throughout the entire day. The regulations governing what happens when one lies in bed, when one is with a spouse, when one forgets — all of this presupposes that *tefillin* are a constant presence, not a brief morning ritual. This is a powerful parallel to the situation with *sukkah*. Just as *sukkah* used to be a genuinely all-encompassing obligation of living for the entire week — with all the corresponding leniencies and exemptions flowing from that all-embracing character — so too *tefillin* used to be worn all day. And just as we have now narrowed the *sukkah* obligation into a series of very precise technical requirements, so too we have narrowed *tefillin* to a brief morning wearing, with the result that the situations described in these *braitot* seem almost inconceivably remote from our experience.

Returning to the *halacha*: *eino ocheiz lo biktzitzah velo birtzuo* — in the case of one who forgot and had relations while wearing *tefillin*, he may not take them off even by holding the straps. *Ad sheyitol yadav veyitlam* — he must first wash his hands. The reason is that while in the earlier case (seminal emission without relations), the concern was the person's own state but his hands were not implicated, here his hands have been in direct contact with places that are not clean — *mipnei sheyadav askaniyot hen* — because hands are constantly busy. Only after washing his hands may he come into contact even with the straps of the *tefillin*.

## Tefillin-Sukkah Parallel

### All-Day Tefillin

This digression into *tefillin* law, which might seem to be a departure from the *sukkah* discussion, in fact illuminates something deeper about the relationship between how these two *mitzvot* once functioned and how they function now. The scenarios the *gemara* addresses — lying in bed with one's wife while wearing *tefillin*, forgetting and having relations while wearing them, napping with them on — all presuppose a world in which *tefillin* were part of one's daily garb from morning until night. There are *gemarot* that speak at length about the constant consciousness required in connection with *tefillin*, particularly the *tefillin shel rosh*, comparing that awareness to the consciousness required of the *Kohen Gadol* wearing the *tzitz*. Whether anyone truly lived up to that level of sustained mindfulness is a separate question, but the baseline assumption of constant wearing is clear.

### Evolving Observance

There is a striking conceptual parallel. The *sukkah*, at its fullest expression, was understood as one's actual home for seven days — an all-encompassing form of dwelling, with all the latitude and all the depth that implies. Today we have translated that into a narrow technical obligation focused on precise quantities of specific foods, with sleeping removed from the picture almost entirely. The *tefillin* underwent an analogous evolution: from a full-day *mitzvah* with all the attendant regulations about sleeping, marital relations, and bodily functions, to the circumscribed morning practice most people observe today. Both *mitzvot* moved from being all-encompassing to being narrowly technical, and that shift profoundly changes the texture of the questions one asks — and the answers one gives — about each.

## Maase Stories

### Taste vs. Dates

The *gemara* now presents several *maase* stories — accounts of how the *tanna'im* actually conducted themselves — and it is notable how many such stories appear throughout *Masechet Sukkah* relative to other *masechtot*. The *mishna* records: *maase ve-heviu lo le-Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai lit'om et hatavshil* — they brought Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai a taste of the stew — *u-l'Rabban Gamliel shenei kotevot u-dli shel mayim* — and to Rabban Gamliel two pressed dates and a bucket of water — *ve-omru ha'alum lasukkah* — and they said: bring it up to the *sukkah*. These amounts — a taste of stew, two dates — would seem to qualify as *achilat arai*, which we have just established may be eaten outside the *sukkah*. Why then were they brought inside?

### Baa Lehachmir

*Maase listor*? — is this a story that comes to contradict the preceding ruling? No: *chissurei mechsera* — the *mishna* is missing some words, and what it means to say is this: *im ba lehachmir al atzmo machmir, veleit bei mishum yuhara* — if one wishes to be strict upon oneself, one may be strict, and this does not constitute *yuhara* — religious arrogance. So the *mishna* is not establishing a contradiction; it is adding a clarification. The minimum thresholds are minima: one is not obligated to bring a small snack into the *sukkah*. But if one wishes to do so as a *chumrah*, that is entirely appropriate and does not cross the line into unseemly religious display.

The point is a nuanced one. Some acts of stringency might indeed constitute *yuhara* — particularly if the act being performed is not typically associated with a fixed domestic context, such as snacking on the street, so that insisting on doing even that in the *sukkah* might look like a performance of religiosity. But the *gemara* rules that even this does not cross that line. In fact, one might even argue that things like sitting and reading, watching and *schmoozing* — the kinds of leisure activities one naturally does at home — represent not even a *chumrah* but the *lechatchila* fulfillment of *sukkah* in its fuller sense.

### Rabbi Tzadok

The *mishna* then records: *u-keshenatnu lo le-Rabbi Tzadok ochel pachat mi-kebeitzah* — when they gave Rabbi Tzadok bread less than an egg's worth, *netalo bemappah* — he would take it in a handkerchief — *ve-achalo chutz lasukkah* — and eat it outside the *sukkah* — *ve-lo berach acharayiv* — and he did not bench.

### Shiur Netilah

The *gemara* asks: *ha kibeitzah basukkah*? — does it mean that once one has a full egg's worth one must eat in the *sukkah*? This would appear to be a direct challenge to Rav Yosef and Abaye, both of whom set the threshold for *achilat keva* at one egg's worth or more. But the *gemara* clarifies: the point of the Rabbi Tzadok story is not primarily about *sukkah* at all. What it is teaching is that *pachos mikibeitzah* — less than an egg's worth — exempts one from *netilat yadayim* and *Birkat HaMazon* as well. *Ha kibeitzah ba'ei netilah uvracha* — once one reaches an egg's worth, one is obligated in handwashing and *Birkat HaMazon* — though not necessarily yet in eating in a *sukkah*, which by Rav Yosef's standard only kicks in at two or three eggs.

Several practical points are worth noting here. Our current practice is to rule that *Birkat HaMazon* is required even for a *kezayit*, following the large Tosafot on that point. For handwashing, there is a debate among the *rishonim* about whether the threshold is a *kezayit* or a *kibeitzah*, and the practical ruling *halacha l'maaseh* requires careful review. As for the question of why Rabbi Tzadok wrapped the food in a handkerchief rather than washing his hands: Rashi understands this as simply a cleanliness measure. Tosafot, however, explains that Rabbi Tzadok was a *Kohen* who would eat his food as though it were *terumah*, and therefore even where general handwashing was not technically required, he would not touch the food directly, treating it with the level of care appropriate to *terumah* food.

The question of the bucket of water in the case of Rabban Gamliel — which clearly exceeds any egg-based threshold — is answered by returning to the food type question. Presumably, water is never considered a *keva* food regardless of quantity, in the same way that fruit requires no *sukkah* however much one consumes.

## Rabbi Eliezer Fourteen

### Arba Esrei Seudot

The *mishna* now presents Rabbi Eliezer's ruling: *arba esrei seudot chayav adam le'echol basukkah achat bayom v'achat balailah* — a person is obligated to eat fourteen meals in the *sukkah*, one during the day and one at night, for all seven days.

### Chachamim View

*Ve-Chachamim omrim*: the Sages disagree. *Ein ladavar kitzvah* — there is no fixed minimum. Importantly, this does not mean that one may eat outside the *sukkah* freely — the prohibition on *keva* eating outside the *sukkah* remains in force. Rather, it means there is no positive obligation to ensure that one eats a *keva* meal. One may eat fruit, eat tiny amounts, fast, or otherwise arrange one's eating so that no formal *seudah* is ever triggered — except on the first night.

### Tashlumin

*Ve'od amar Rabbi Eliezer*: Rabbi Eliezer adds a further ruling — *mi shelo achal leil yom tov harishon yashlim bleil yom tov ha'acharon* — if one did not eat the first night of *Sukkot*, one may make up that meal on the final night of the festival, meaning the night of *Shemini Atzeret*. This raises an internal difficulty: Rabbi Eliezer just said one is obligated in fourteen meals, giving equal weight to all of them. Why single out the first night as something specially compensable? And conversely, if it is specifically about the first night's meal, how does one discharge that makeup obligation on *Shemini Atzeret* when presumably one is no longer eating in a *sukkah*?

### Ein Tashlumin

*Ve-Chachamim omrim*: the Sages reject the possibility of any *tashlumin* for a missed *sukkah* meal. *Ve'al zeh ne'emar me'uvas lo yuchal liskon ve-cheisaron lo yuchal lehimanos* — "that which is crooked cannot be made straight, and that which is lacking cannot be counted" (Kohelet). Something missed cannot be retroactively repaired in this domain. The parallel to *Masechet Chagigah* — where one may bring a missed *chagigah* offering on any day of the *chag* up to and including the last day — was presumably in Rabbi Eliezer's mind, but the Sages reject its applicability here.

## Tashvu Ke'ein Taduru

### Dwelling Analogy

*Mai ta'ama deRabbi Eliezer*? — what is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning for the fourteen-meal obligation? The verse says *tashvu* — you shall dwell — *ke'ein taduru* — as you dwell in a house. *Mah dirah achas bayom ve'achas balaila* — just as in a house one typically eats two meals a day, one during the day and one at night — *af sukkah achas bayom ve'achas balaila* — so too in the *sukkah*, one must eat one meal by day and one by night.

Tosafot notes that in the *Yerushalmi*, Rabbi Eliezer's position is grounded in a *gezeirah shavah*: the word *tashvu* appears both in the context of *Sukkot* and in the context of the *Mishkan*, where Aharon and his sons dwelt in the *Ohel Moed* for seven days — *yomam valaila shivas yamim* — and just as that dwelling made nights equivalent to days, so too in the *sukkah* the nighttime meals are as obligatory as the daytime ones. This is a rich parallel: not only is it about what it means to fully inhabit a place, but it also evokes the imagery of dwelling in the divine presence, in the sphere of the *Kodesh HaKodashim* with the *kapores* and the *keruvim*.

### Free Choice

*Ve-rabanan* respond: the verse says *ke-dirah* — like dwelling. And just as when one lives in a house one chooses whether to eat — no one compels a person to eat twice a day — *af sukkah ei ba'ei achil ei ba'ei lo achil* — so too in the *sukkah*, one may choose whether to eat. The *sukkah* is not supposed to be a prison. It is supposed to be treated as one would treat one's home — which means being granted the latitude and freedom of choice that one has at home.

## First Night Obligation

### First Night Chiyuv

If it is entirely volitional whether one has a meal — and one may construct one's eating over the entire *chag* such that no obligatory *seudah* is ever triggered — then how can there be any fixed obligation even on the first night?

### Gezeirah Shavah

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak*: the answer lies in a *gezeirah shavah*. The fifteenth of Tishrei is linked by shared language to the fifteenth of Nisan, the first night of *Chag HaMatzot*.

### Matzah Comparison

By *Pesach*, the first night of *matzah* is a firm obligation — *laila harishon chovah* — while from the second night onward it is *reshut*, optional. The verse *ba'erev tochlu matzot* is read as fixing the first night as obligatory, even though the broader context speaks of seven days. The word *ba'erev* isolates that first evening as uniquely obligatory. By the same *gezeirah shavah*, the same structure applies to *Sukkot*: *af kan laila harishon chovah, mikan va'eilach reshut* — here too the first night is obligatory, and from the second day onward it is volitional.

### No Obligation Days

The distinction between *sukkah* and *matzah* on the non-obligatory nights is worth spelling out precisely. After the first night of *Pesach*, one may entirely refrain from eating *matzah* on the remaining days — there is no circumstance in which eating will trigger a *matzah* obligation. By *Sukkot*, however, even after the first night, if one chooses to eat bread or *mezonot* in the requisite quantity, one becomes obligated to do so in the *sukkah* and makes a *bracha* — *leishev basukkah*. So it is not that the *sukkah* is irrelevant after the first night; it is that there is no positive obligation to bring oneself into a situation that requires it.

Tosafot raises an important implication: if there is no *chiyuv* of *se'udah* on the other days of *Yom Tov*, does that mean one has no obligation of a *Yom Tov seudah* on the other days of *Sukkot*? And if so, would forgetting *Ya'aleh VeYavo* in *bentching* carry no requirement to repeat, since the repetition obligation is tied to the existence of a mandatory *seudah*? Tosafot is inclined to accept this as a genuine consequence of the *gemara*'s logic. One might distinguish between a *kezayit* — which may still be technically required — and a *kibeitzah*, which is what triggers the full *sukkah* obligation, but Tosafot's analysis points in a striking direction.

## Rishonim Debates

### Shiur Comparison

A first question among the *rishonim* concerns the *shiur* — the minimum quantity of eating — required on the first night. If the first night is modeled directly on *matzah*, then perhaps one is *yotzei* with a *kezayit*. But if the first night is understood as an expression of *dirat sukkah* — the broader obligation of dwelling in the *sukkah* — that must be performed on the first night through the act of eating, then perhaps a *kibeitzah* or more is required, as that is the threshold for *achilat keva* that the *sukkah* obligation normally tracks.

### Food Type

A second question concerns the type of food. If we derive the first night's obligation from *matzah*, and *matzah* must be made from grain — *dagan* — then perhaps the first night's meal must specifically consist of bread, not merely *mezonot* and certainly not meat or other foods. *Rav Zeira* in the *Yerushalmi* raises exactly this question: *ima lehalan ad sheyochal kezayit dagan matzah af kan ad sheyochal kezayit dagan basukkah* — just as the *matzah* obligation requires grain, so too perhaps the first night of *sukkah* requires grain. This would rule out satisfying the first night's obligation through meat, potatoes, or fruit — only bread would do.

### Pesak on Rain

A third question is circumstantial: do the normal exemptions — rain, *mitzta'er*, illness — apply on the first night? This becomes the practical question that preoccupies *poskim* on the first night of *Sukkot* when it rains: until what hour does one wait for the rain to stop? After *chatzot*? Before? When can one give up and simply eat inside? If the first night's obligation is a form of *dirat sukkah* and the *mitzta'er* exemption applies to *dirat sukkah*, then perhaps rain exempts one from the first night as well. But if the first night is modeled strictly on *matzah* — a focused eating obligation that does not depend on whether the conditions for dwelling are met — then the normal *sukkah* exemptions would not apply. This remains a major *machlokes rishonim*.

### Tosafot Ta'avah

Tosafot cites a fascinating position from the *Yerushalmi* on a further implication of the *matzah* analogy. Just as one is cautioned not to eat heavily before the first night of *Pesach* so that one comes to the *matzah* eating with an appetite — *ta'avah* — perhaps the same applies to the first night of *sukkah*: *af kan ad sheyikanes lesukkah beta'avah* — one should enter the *sukkah* meal with an appetite. If the first night is truly modeled on *matzah*, then not only the quantity and food type but even the psychological state of genuine appetite may be part of the obligation.

## Tashlumin Details

### Mashlimin Bamah

The *gemara* now returns to the question of Rabbi Eliezer's *tashlumin*: with what does one make up a missed meal? *I-leima be-rifta* — if it is bread, that is simply the regular meal one would be having anyway, with nothing to distinguish it as a makeup. If one were eating a second meal on *Shemini Atzeret*, what marks it as the compensation for the missed first-night meal rather than merely one's regular meal? *Ella mai*: *yashlim beminei targima* — one makes it up with various delicacies, cooked dishes of distinction.

### Rashi Position

Rashi explains *minei targima* as cooked delicacies — various foods like fruit, legumes, roasted items, and cooked dishes — brought after the main meal has been cleared. The point is that the *minei targima* make the makeup visible and apparent: this additional course marks the occasion as a deliberate fulfillment of a missed obligation, not merely a regular meal.

### Tosafot Requirement

Tosafot adds a further layer: since what one is making up is an *achilah basukkah* — an eating that was required to take place in the *sukkah* — the *minei targima* used for the makeup must themselves be the type of foods that require a *sukkah*. Fruit, which by Tosafot's understanding does not require a *sukkah*, cannot serve as the *tashlumin* food. The *minei targima* must therefore be things like meat and cooked dishes — precisely those foods that Tosafot holds are categorically obligated in a *sukkah*. This again reflects Tosafot's position that there is a broader category of foods beyond bread and *mezonot* that require a *sukkah*.

### Braita Confirmation

*Tanya nami hachi*: a supporting *braitah* confirms that *im hishlim beminei targima yatza* — if one made up the missed meal with *minei targima*, one has fulfilled the obligation. Rashi's reading of this *braitah* is that *minei targima* clearly works, and *a fortiori* a full bread meal — *se'uda belebechem uvasar* — would certainly also work. This introduces some tension with the earlier discussion, where bread alone seemed insufficient to constitute a distinctive makeup. The *gemara* before had implied that the makeup must be distinct from a regular meal; the *braitah*'s language of *im hishlim* — "if one fulfilled it with" — sounds more like a standard that bread a *fortiori* exceeds rather than something that bread alone cannot satisfy.

## Agrippas Manager

### Single Meal

*Sha'al apotropas shel Agrippas ha-melech et Rabbi Eliezer* — the manager of King Agrippas asked Rabbi Eliezer: a person such as himself, who is accustomed to eating only one meal a day, is being told by Rabbi Eliezer that he must eat two meals daily in the *sukkah* throughout *Sukkot*. *Mahu she-ochal se'uda achat ve-ipater* — may he fulfill the obligation with a single meal per day?

### Parpara Argument

*Amar lo*: Rabbi Eliezer replies: every day you provide yourself with numerous delicacies — *parpara'ot* — for your own honor and pleasure. And now you cannot offer even one small delicacy — *parparet achat* — in honor of your Creator? The response is notable for two reasons. First, it confirms — consistent with Tosafot's reading — that Rabbi Eliezer did not retract his position about fourteen meals. Second, the concept of *parpara'ot* connects directly to the *minei targima* discussed earlier: the implication is that even without a full bread meal, one can count certain delicacies toward the fourteen, making the obligation somewhat more flexible in practice.

## Two Sukkot

### Splitting Meals

The same manager poses a second question: he has two wives, one in Tiberias and one in Sepphoris, and correspondingly two *sukkot*, one in each city. *Mahu she-etzei mi-sukkah le-sukkah ve-ipater* — may he alternate between them, spending some nights in one *sukkah* and some in the other, and thereby fulfill his obligation?

### Yotzei Misukah

*Amar lo*: Rabbi Eliezer says no. *She-ani omer kol ha-yotzei mi-sukkah le-sukkah biteil mitzvata shel rishona* — whoever leaves one *sukkah* for another has cancelled the *mitzvah* of the first one.

### One Bayit

The conceptual foundation of this ruling is essential to understanding Rabbi Eliezer's entire position. The *mitzvah* of *sukkah* is not merely a personal obligation to eat a certain number of meals in a *sukkah*-like structure. What makes the *sukkah* a legitimate fulfillment of the *mitzvah* is that it functions as one's *bayit* — one's actual house — for all seven days. A house is not a house if one uses it intermittently alongside another dwelling. If one splits one's presence between two *sukkot*, neither becomes one's *bayit*, and neither fulfills the *mitzvah*. The continuity of dwelling in a single structure for the entire duration of the festival is intrinsic to what the *sukkah* is supposed to be.

## Building Sukkah

### Chol Hamoed Building

A *braitah* reinforces this principle. *Rabbi Eliezer omer*: *ein yotzin mi-sukkah le-sukkah* — one may not go from one *sukkah* to another — and *ein osin sukkah becholo shel mo'ed* — one may not construct a *sukkah* during *Chol HaMoed*. The reasoning follows directly: if the *sukkah* must be one's *bayit* for all seven days, beginning to build one's *sukkah* partway through the *chag* is self-defeating — it cannot be one's house for the full week and therefore cannot satisfy the *mitzvah*.

### Sages Allow

*Ve-Chachamim omrim*: the Sages permit both. One may go from *sukkah* to *sukkah*, and one may build a new *sukkah* during *Chol HaMoed*. Since the Sages reject the fourteen-meal framework and the requirement of continuous single-*sukkah* dwelling, neither restriction applies.

However — *ve-shavin* — both agree that *shenofla shechozer uvoneh bechol hamoed* — if a *sukkah* collapsed during *Chol HaMoed*, one may rebuild it. That rebuilding is considered a continuation of the original *sukkah* and not the construction of a new one.

### Ship Problem

This last point raises a fascinating conceptual question, one that echoes the ancient philosophical puzzle about the ship of Theseus — whether an object that has been entirely rebuilt from new components remains the same object. Tosafot holds that in order for the rebuilt *sukkah* to be considered the same *sukkah* in Rabbi Eliezer's terms, one must use the same wood that was used originally. If the original materials are replaced, the rebuilt structure is a new *sukkah*, not a continuation of the old one — and by Rabbi Eliezer's logic, it would fail the continuity requirement. Rashi, by contrast, seems to take the view that since the *sukkah* genuinely fell down, anything rebuilt on that conceptual foundation serves as a legitimate substitute, even if the wood differs or the location shifts slightly. The *sukkah*'s identity, on Rashi's reading, is tied more to the person's ongoing relationship with it than to the physical materials of which it happens to be composed.

---

---

# Sukkah 28

## Reb Eliezer Sukkah Rules

### 14 Meals in Sukkah

We pick up at the very top of 27b with the position of Rabbi Eliezer, who maintains that one must eat fourteen meals in a *sukkah* — two each day across all seven days of *Sukkos*. Related to this, Rabbi Eliezer holds that one does not fulfill the obligation with a *sukkah* built on *Chol HaMoed*, nor by visiting a friend's *sukkah*. The same *sukkah* must be used for all seven days, establishing it as a genuine substitute for one's home. This is an exceptionally demanding position, rooted in the idea that the *sukkah* must function as a true replacement dwelling.

### Collapsed Sukkah Rebuilt

There is, however, one concession. The *Gemara* cites the ruling: *umodim she'im nafla shechozer uvona bechol hamoed* — all agree that if one's *sukkah* collapsed, he may rebuild it on *Chol HaMoed* and it is treated as a continuation of the original *sukkah*. The *Gemara* notes that this might seem obvious, but the *chiddush* is that one might have thought the newly rebuilt structure constitutes a separate *sukkah*, disqualified because it was not standing for all seven days. The ruling teaches us that this is not so.

### Verse-Based Reasoning

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai ta'ama d'Rabbi Eliezer* — what is the reason behind Rabbi Eliezer's position? The answer is that the verse states *chag hasukkos ta'ase lecha shivas yamim* — you shall make it for yourself, seven days. This implies the *sukkah* must be a seven-day structure. The Rabbis respond that the verse simply means: make a *sukkah* for the *yom tov*, without requiring that it stand for the entire seven days.

A *baraisa* then spells out Rabbi Eliezer's position further: just as one does not fulfill the obligation of *lulav* on the first day with a borrowed *lulav* — since the verse says *ulakachtem lachem*, you shall take for yourselves, meaning from what is yours — so too, one does not fulfill the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* in another person's *sukkah*, since the verse says *ta'ase lecha*, it must be yours. The underlying principle seems unified: to qualify as a substitute house, the *sukkah* must be personally yours and continuously so throughout all seven days.

### Tosafos Ownership

*Tosafos* raises a pointed question against Rabbi Eliezer's position: if the *sukkah* must belong to the individual — *mishelcha* — does this mean that every member of a household requires his own separate *sukkah*? Would two people ever be able to fulfill the obligation together in a single *sukkah*? *Tosafos* suggests that perhaps the concept of *teshvu k'ein taduru* — dwelling in a *sukkah* as one dwells in a home — permits household members to share one *sukkah*, since that reflects the natural structure of a household. But beyond family members, partnership with a neighbor would be disqualified. This means, according to Rabbi Eliezer, that one could not *sukkah*-hop: all fourteen meals must be in one's own household *sukkah*.

### Rabbis' Counter-Verse

The Rabbis disagree: *af al pi she'omru ein adam yotzei yedei chovato b'yom tov harishon b'lulavo shel chaveiro, aval yotzei yedei chovato b'sukkato shel chaveiro* — although one cannot fulfill the *lulav* obligation on the first day with a borrowed *lulav*, one may nonetheless fulfill the *sukkah* obligation in another's *sukkah*. Their proof: *kol ha'ezrach b'Yisrael yeshvu basukkos* — all citizens of Israel shall dwell in *sukkos*. From this the *Gemara* derives that all of Israel could potentially dwell in a single *sukkah*, which implies that private ownership is not required; partnership or borrowing suffices.

*Rashi* proposes that perhaps all Israel owns it jointly — but *Tosafos* presses that this only strengthens the contrast with Rabbi Eliezer, who requires genuine individual ownership. The Rabbis hold that once the verse makes clear that partnership is acceptable, borrowing another's *sukkah* is likewise permitted.

The *Gemara* then asks what the Rabbis do with the word *lecha* — "yours" — in the verse. Their answer: it excludes a stolen *sukkah*. A borrowed *sukkah* is permitted by inference from *kol ha'ezrach*. And what does Rabbi Eliezer do with *kol ha'ezrach*, given that he does not permit sharing? He applies it to a novel case: a convert who converted *bein hashmashos* during *Sukkos*, or a minor who came of age *bein hashmashos*. Since Rabbi Eliezer generally requires all seven days, one might have thought these individuals could never fulfill the obligation. The verse teaches that since no other option was available to them, they fulfill the *mitzvah* with whatever portion of the *chag* remains.

The Rabbis respond that since they already hold a *sukkah* built on *Chol HaMoed* is valid, they have no need for a special verse to address this case — it is already subsumed within their general position.

---

## Learning Dedication (II)

### No Holiday Visits

The *Gemara* relates a story: Rabbi Ilai once traveled to greet his teacher Rabbi Eliezer in Lod on the *regel*. Rabbi Eliezer said to him: *Ilai eincha mishovsei ha'regel* — Ilai, you are not among those who stay home on the festival. The remark implies disapproval. The *Gemara* notes that even if this was not *Sukkos*, and even setting aside the problem of Rabbi Eliezer's own view that one must be in his own *sukkah* all seven days, Rabbi Eliezer objected to the very act of traveling to visit one's teacher during the *regel*.

### Praise for Staying Home

Why? Because *she'hayah Rabbi Eliezer omer: meshabeach ani et ha'atzlanim she'ein yotzin mibateihem baragel* — Rabbi Eliezer used to say: I praise the lazy people who do not leave their homes on the *regel*. He does not actually admire laziness, of course; the point is more like a stopped clock being right twice a day. Even if one stays home for the wrong reasons, the result — remaining at home during *yom tov* — is the right outcome.

### Household Rejoicing

The basis for this is the verse *v'samachta b'chagecha* — you shall rejoice on your festival — together with the formulation *v'samachta atah u'veisecha*, you and your household. The *mitzvah* of *simchas ha'regel* obligates a man to celebrate the festival together with his wife. This was already a live tension in earlier generations, as men would travel to visit their rebbes or undertake other pilgrimages on *yom tov*, much as people today travel on *Rosh Hashana* to Uman or elsewhere. Rabbi Eliezer's position was that the *mitzvah* begins at home, with one's family.

The *Gemara* raises a counterpoint: Rabbi Yitzchak cites a proof that one is actually *obligated* to greet one's teacher on the *regel*, derived from the story of the *Isha HaShunamis*, whose husband asks: *madua at holechet elav hayom lo chodesh velo Shabbos* — why are you going today? It is neither *Rosh Chodesh* nor *Shabbos*. The implication is that on *Rosh Chodesh* and *Shabbos* one does go to greet a holy man. Rabbi Yitzchak derives from this that on the *regel* as well there is an obligation of *hakbalas penei rabbo*. The *Gemara* resolves the tension: there is no contradiction. If one goes and returns the same day, that is compatible with fulfilling *simchas ha'regel* with one's household. If one leaves and does not return the same day — abandoning one's family for the entire festival — that violates the obligation of *v'samachta atah u'veisecha*.

This discussion opens a broader reflection. The very language *makbil penei rabbo baragel* echoes the *aliya la'regel* — the pilgrimage to the Temple. Post-*churban*, the pilgrimage to encounter the divine is replaced, in some sense, by the act of going to be in the presence of the holy man, the *penei rabbo*. And that stands in tension with the domestic reality of the *regel*, the obligation to experience it within one's household. Rabbi Eliezer weighed in favor of the domestic dimension; the *Gemara* accommodates both, provided the visit is completed within the same day.

---

## Sheet on Sukkah Story

### Heard from Rebbe Only

The *Gemara* then relates a second *ma'aseh*: Rabbi Eliezer spent a *Shabbos* in the Upper Galilee, in the *sukkah* of Yochanan bar Rabbi Ilai in Caesarea — or, according to some versions, Caesareon. The sun began beating down on the *sukkah*, and his host, concerned for Rabbi Eliezer's comfort, asked: *mahu she'efros aleha sadin* — what is the ruling regarding spreading a sheet over the *sukkah* to provide shade?

Rabbi Eliezer did not answer. Instead, he deflected the question entirely, remarking that there was not one tribe of Israel that had not produced a *shofet* during the period of the *Shoftim*. The sun continued advancing. When it reached the midpoint of the *sukkah*, the question was raised again, and again Rabbi Eliezer deflected — this time noting that every tribe had produced *neviim*. When the sun finally reached Rabbi Eliezer's feet, Yochanan bar Rabbi Ilai had enough; he took the sheet and spread it over the *sukkah* himself. At that point, Rabbi Eliezer *hifshil talito lachorav veyatza* — put on his cloak and walked out of the *sukkah*.

The *Gemara* explains: *lo mipnei she'hifligo bidvarim* — he was not evading the question out of disrespect or unwillingness to teach. Rather, *mipnei shelo amar davar shelo shama mipi rabbo le'olam* — because he had never in his life said anything he had not heard from his teacher. Since his teacher had never ruled on the question of spreading a sheet over a *sukkah* on *Shabbos*, he refused to issue a ruling. He would not say yes, he would not say no, and so he deflected until the situation resolved itself by his walking out.

The irony is not lost: the man who objected to visiting one's teacher on *yom tov* is the very same man who never uttered a ruling he had not received from his teacher.

### Tent-Making Analysis

The *Gemara* then tries to resolve the underlying *halacha* from Rabbi Eliezer's other rulings. Is spreading a sheet over a *sukkah* on *Shabbos* a problem of *oseh ohel arai* — creating a temporary canopy? The sheet was clearly temporary and was being spread over an existing covered structure, so the question is whether even this modest addition constitutes a prohibited *ohel*. The *Gemara* attempts to derive a position from Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in a related case.

### Window Stopper Case

The *Gemara* cites a *mishna*: *pkak hachalon* — the case of a window stopper. If a block is used to fill and seal a window, is inserting it on *Shabbos* problematic because it effectively adds to the wall? Rabbi Eliezer rules: *bizman she'kashur vetalui, pokekin bo* — if the stopper is tied to a string and suspended off the ground, one may stop up the window, since it is already effectively attached, like a hinged element of the wall. But if it is not suspended — even if it is on a string but dragging on the ground — *ein pokekin bo*, one may not use it, because placing it constitutes creating something new. The *chachamim* rule leniently in both cases.

From this it would seem that Rabbi Eliezer should have answered the sheet question directly, presumably prohibiting it as he prohibited the unsuspended window stopper. The *Gemara* explains why he nonetheless refrained: *hatam hu de'mevatel, hacha lo mevatel*. In the window-stopper case, the stopper is being left in place and becomes integrated into the wall. The sheet over the *sukkah* is removed almost immediately once the sun moves; it is far more transitory. Rabbi Eliezer may have reasoned that this case was distinguishable and therefore sufficiently uncertain that he could not rule without a direct tradition from his teacher.

---

## Learning Dedication (II)

### 30 Sukkah Laws

The *Gemara* transitions to another *ma'aseh* involving Rabbi Eliezer. He spent a *Shabbos* — perhaps the same *Shabbos*, perhaps a different one — in the Upper Galilee, and the people there posed thirty *halachos* to him regarding the laws of *sukkah*. The *Gemara* is at the top of 28a. Of the thirty, Rabbi Eliezer said *shamati* — I have a received tradition — for twelve. For the remaining eighteen, he said *lo shamati* — I have no tradition. Rabbi Yosi son of Rabbi Yehuda records the inverse: eighteen he had heard and twelve he had not.

When the people challenged him — *kol devarecha einam ela mipi hashemua*, your entire learning amounts to nothing but transmitted traditions, where are your own views? — Rabbi Eliezer responded: *hizkaktuni lomar davar shelo shamati mipi rabosai?* Are you forcing me to say something I never heard from my teachers?

### Always in Beis Midrash

He then offered a defense that was not a justification of limitation but of completeness. *Miyami lo kidmani adam b'veis hamidrash* — in all my days, no one ever preceded me to the *beis midrash*. I was always first. *Velo yashanti b'veis hamidrash lo shinat keva velo shinat arai* — I never slept in the *beis midrash*, not a deep sleep and not even a light nap. *Velo hinachti adam b'veis hamidrash veyatzasi* — I never left the *beis midrash* while anyone else was still there; I was the last to leave. *Velo shachti sichas chulin* — I never engaged in idle conversation. *Velo amarti davar shelo shamati mipi rabbi me'olam* — and I never said anything I had not heard from my teacher.

The *Maharsha*, echoing *Rashi*, explains why Rabbi Eliezer begins with those first points before arriving at the last. The point is not merely that he transmitted faithfully, but that he had ensured total, exhaustive absorption of his teacher's teaching. He was there before anyone else, he stayed later than anyone else, he never wasted a moment. If something is missing from his repertoire, it is because his teacher never taught it — not because Rabbi Eliezer failed to be present for it.

This formulation reflects a distinctive and coherent vision of *Torah she'be'al peh*. Rabbi Eliezer's approach was *masorah* — tradition as the supreme mode of Torah transmission. He would not speculate. He would not derive on his own. He was a faithful, complete conduit. This stands in pointed contrast to the approach of Rabbi Akiva, who was the great embodiment of the creative interpretive tradition, using human reasoning and textual analysis to derive new *halachos* and new understandings. In the famous *aggados* involving the two — especially the deathbed encounter — that contrast emerges with particular sharpness.

There is also a striking internal parallel in Rabbi Eliezer's own character. His insistence that the *sukkah* must be the same *sukkah* all seven days, that one must remain planted in it with total consistency, that one does not travel around even to visit his teacher on *yom tov* — this mirrors his approach to the *beis midrash*: plant yourself, stay, do not move, do not wander. The constancy he demanded of the *sukkah* is the constancy he embodied in his own life of learning.

### Yochanan Ben Zakkai

The *Gemara* then records the *middos* of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who was Rabbi Eliezer's teacher. *Miyamav lo sach sichas chulin* — he never spoke idle words. *Velo halach arba amos b'lo Torah u'vlo tefillin* — he did not walk four *amos* without Torah and without *tefillin*. The *Maharsha* notes that *tefillin* itself is an embodiment of Torah. *Velo kidmo adam b'veis hamidrash* — no one preceded him to the *beis midrash*. *Velo yashan b'veis hamidrash lo shinat keva velo shinat arai* — he never slept there, not deeply and not lightly. *Velo hirher b'mevo'os hametunofos* — even though his mind was constantly engaged in Torah, when walking through filthy alleyways, he was able to restrain his thoughts and not think Torah there. *Velo hiniach adam b'veis hamidrash veyatza* — he never left the *beis midrash* while others remained. *Velo matza'o adam yoshev vedomeh* — no one ever caught him sitting in silence, doing nothing. *Ela yoshev veshoneh* — he was always sitting and learning.

Then a detail that seems out of place in this list: *velo pasach adam deles letalmidav ela hu b'atzmo* — he himself opened the door for his students, not relying on anyone else to do so. The *Gemara* suggests the resonance: just as the Torah says God is *Elohei ha'elohim* and then immediately describes his care for the orphan and the widow, so here too, alongside his towering greatness, he performed this small act of service for his students. The *Maharsha* adds that there may have been competition among students jostling at the door; Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai wanted to ensure that every student could enter without obstruction — recalling the contrast with the story of Hillel, who was once barred at the door by a guard.

*Velo amar higia et la'amod mi'beis hamidrash* — he never told others it was time to leave the *beis midrash*, except on *Erev Pesach* and *Erev Yom Kippur*, where *mitzvos* demanded it: on *Erev Pesach*, because of the *Korban Pesach* and the obligation to eat the *Seder* while children are awake; on *Erev Yom Kippur*, because of the *mitzvah* to eat. The *Gemara* then notes: *v'chein hayah Rabbi Eliezer talmido noheig acharyav* — Rabbi Eliezer, his student, followed the same practice. The *middos* listed about Rabbi Eliezer earlier were a subset of those practiced by his teacher.

### Yonatan ben Uziel

The *Gemara* now introduces a broader context. *Shemonim talmidim hayu lo l'Hillel haZaken* — Hillel had eighty students. Thirty of them were at such a level that the *Shechinah* could have rested upon them as it did upon Moshe. Thirty were worthy of having the sun stand still for them as it did for Yehoshua. Twenty were *beinonim*. *Gadol shebakulam Yonasan ben Uziel* — the greatest of all was Yonasan ben Uziel, to whom the *Targum* on *Nevi'im* is ascribed. *Katan shebakulam Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai* — and the smallest of all of them was Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.

This is a striking *Gemara*. All of the remarkable qualities we have just catalogued in Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, and he was the *least* of Hillel's eighty disciples. The *Gemara* naturally notes the implication: *gadol shebakulam al achas kamah v'chamah* — how incomparably greater must Yonasan ben Uziel have been.

Of Yonasan ben Uziel: *shebesha'ah she'yosheiv v'oseik baTorah, kol of she'poreiach alav miyad nisraf* — when he would sit and learn Torah, any bird that flew overhead was burned. *Tosafos* explains that his learning had the character of the original *matan Torah*, in which fire accompanied the giving of the Torah at Sinai; the fiery angels hovering above him to participate in his learning consumed any bird that passed over.

The contrast between Yonasan ben Uziel and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai invites reflection on what is listed as the totality of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's mastery: *Mikra, Mishnah, Gemara, halachos, aggados, dikdukei Torah, dikdukei Soferim, kal v'chomer, gezeirah shavah, tekufos, gematrios, sichas malachei hashareis, sichas sheidim, sichas dekalim, meshalos kovsim, meshalos shualim, davar gadol v'davar katan*. What is the *davar gadol*? *Ma'aseh Merkavah*. What is the *davar katan*? *Havayos d'Abaye v'Rava* — the analytical discussions of the Talmud. The verse it fulfills: *lehancheil ohavai yesh, v'otzroseihem amalei* — to bequeath to those who love me substance, and fill their storehouses.

This passage bears directly on the earlier question about the two paradigms of *Torah she'be'al peh*. One might have assumed that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai — who, like his student Rabbi Eliezer, said he never uttered something not heard from his teachers — was purely a *masorah* figure. But the list of what he mastered does not support that reading. *Gemara, kal v'chomer, gezeirah shavah, havayos d'Abaye v'Rava* — these are not passive transmissions. They are analytical enterprises, requiring the exercise of human reasoning. One cannot derive a *kal v'chomer* or analyze a *gezeirah shavah* purely by receiving and repeating a tradition.

The resolution appears to lie in the complexity of the *rebbe* himself. Different students of a great figure absorb different dimensions of his teaching. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was not simply a conduit; his *takkanos*, his decision to negotiate with the Romans, his reorientation of Jewish life after the *churban* toward *Torah* and *Yavneh* — none of this is the work of a pure *masorah* figure. He embodied both the fidelity of tradition and the creativity of human interpretation. Rabbi Eliezer, his student, absorbed one dimension of that — the *masorah* — and made it the totality of his approach.

This is illuminated by the earlier story of Hillel. When Hillel proved from thirty different derivations that the *Korban Pesach* overrides *Shabbos*, the *Bnei Batera* would not accept it. Only when he said he had a *masorah* from Shemaya and Avtalyon did they capitulate. Hillel's entire career represented the argument that creative interpretation is a legitimate mode of Torah transmission — but he met with resistance. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, his student, carried both modes. Rabbi Eliezer, student of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, appears to have inherited only one.

The *Rambam*'s approach is also relevant here. He uses this very *Gemara* — that *ma'aseh Merkavah* is *davar gadol* and *havayos d'Abaye v'Rava* is *davar katan* — to argue that the proper trajectory of learning is to master *halacha* through *Gemara* study and then devote one's higher energies to philosophy and theology. The *davar katan* is not demeaned; it is the path that gives access to the *davar gadol*. For the *Rambam*, the ultimate goal is the theological and philosophical endeavor, which is accessible to all — even if *ma'aseh Merkavah* in its deepest form is not.

---

## Exemptions Categories

### Exempt Groups

The *Gemara* turns to a new *Mishnah*: *nashim va'avadim u'ktanim peturim min hasukkah* — women, slaves, and minors are exempt from *sukkah*. This is the standard application of the principle that women are exempt from positive time-bound *mitzvos*. The *Mishnah* then adds: *katan she'eino tzarich le'imo, chayav basukkah* — a minor who no longer needs his mother is obligated in *sukkah*.

### Shammai Stringency

The *Mishnah* records a story: *veyalda kalato shel Shammai haZaken* — Shammai's daughter-in-law gave birth, and Shammai was so stringent that he knocked a hole in the plaster of the ceiling and placed *sechach* directly over the cradle, so that the newborn infant would be in a *sukkah*. He used the principle of *dofen akuma* — the bending wall — to extend the *sukkah* coverage to the area of the crib. This is acknowledged as beyond what the *halacha* requires; even by Shammai's own logic, this was *lechumra* beyond the threshold of the *chinuch* obligation, since the infant was one day old.

### Verse Exclusions

The *Gemara* asks: *mena hani mili* — from where are these exemptions derived? The *baraisa* teaches: the verse states *kol ha'ezrach b'Yisrael yeshvu basukkos* — all *ezrach* among Israel shall dwell in *sukkos*. The word *ezrach* alone would include both men and women. The added letter *hei* — *ha'ezrach* — comes, the *baraisa* says, to exclude women: *lehotzi et hanashim*. Yet the word *kol* — "all" — comes to include minors: *lerabos et haktanim*.

This immediately raises a difficulty. A different *baraisa* states the opposite: in the context of *Yom Kippur*, the verse says *ha'ezrach veha'ger* — and from *ha'ezrach* we include women in the obligation to fast. This implies that *ezrach* alone means men, and *ha'ezrach* is expansive and inclusive. So which is it: does *ha'ezrach* include or exclude women?

Rava responds: *hilchasa ninhu* — both rulings are actually *halachos*, traditional teachings, and the verses are merely *asmachtos*, rabbinic supports. The *Gemara* then presses further: if they are both traditions, and both are linked to verses, why were the verses needed at all? In the case of *sukkah*, the exemption of women follows automatically from the general rule of *mitzvas asei shehazman gerama nashim peturos* — women are exempt from positive time-bound commandments. And in the case of *Yom Kippur*, the obligation of women follows automatically from Rav Yehuda's teaching in the name of Rav: *hishva hakasuv isha le'ish lechol onashin shebatorah* — the Torah equates men and women with respect to all punishments, and since *Yom Kippur* fasting carries the punishment of *kares*, women are equally bound.

### Yom Kippur Comparison

The *Gemara* thus asks why we need either the *masorah* or the verse in each case. Abaye answers: in truth, the exemption of women from *sukkah* is the *halacha*, and the verse is its *asmachta*. But why was a special *halachah* needed to exempt women, given the general principle? Because there was reason to think otherwise.

First: the verse says *teshvu* — you shall dwell — interpreted as *ke'ein taduru*, like your normal dwelling. One's normal dwelling involves both husband and wife. One might therefore have concluded that a *sukkah*, to function as a genuine domestic substitute, must obligate women as well. Hence the special *halachah* is needed to teach that despite this logic, the general rule of positive time-bound exemption applies.

Rava adds a second reason. The *Gemara* derives the obligation to dwell in the *sukkah* on the first night by a *gezeirah shavah* linking the fifteenth of *Tishrei* to the fifteenth of *Nisan*. Since women are obligated in *matzah* on the first night of *Pesach* — because the obligation is tied to the prohibition of *chametz*, which binds everyone — one might have argued that for the first night of *sukkah* as well, women should be obligated. The *halachah* is needed to exclude this inference and confirm that women remain exempt even on the first night.

Turning to *Yom Kippur*: the verse is needed not for the primary obligation to fast, which follows from the general rule. It is needed for the *tosefet inuy* — the additional period of fasting beyond the day itself. Since this extra period carries no punishment and is not independently a negative prohibition, one might have thought women are exempt from it. The verse teaches that since women are obligated in the primary fast, they are equally obligated in the added portion.

The *Rashash* raises an interesting question: why does the *Gemara* not similarly derive that women are obligated in *tosefet* regarding *melacha* — the requirement to cease work slightly before *Yom Kippur* begins? He suggests this may be a basis for the *Rambam*'s position that the biblical obligation of *tosefet* applies to *Yom Kippur* only, and there only regarding the *inuy*, not the prohibition of *melacha*. A further debate among the *acharonim* is whether women are obligated in the *mitzvah* of eating on *Erev Yom Kippur*, given that the obligation to eat on *Erev Yom Kippur* is linked to the obligation to fast — much as they are obligated in both the primary fast and the *tosefet*.

As for the verse *ha'ezrach* in the context of *sukkah*: since women are excluded by *halachah*, and minors are included only rabbinically, what biblical function does *ha'ezrach* serve? The *Gemara* answers: *lerabos et hagerim* — to include converts. One might have thought that *ha'ezrach b'Yisrael* refers only to native-born Jews. The verse teaches that converts are equally obligated.

### Minors Chinuch Age

Returning to the exemption of minors: the verse *kol* is interpreted as including them, but the *Gemara* clarifies that a minor's obligation in *sukkah* is rabbinic, not biblical — it is the *mitzvah* of *chinuch*, training children in the performance of *mitzvos*. The verse serves as a mere *asmachta*.

The *Mishnah* establishes the threshold as *katan she'eino tzarich le'imo* — a minor who no longer needs his mother. The *Gemara* asks: what precisely does this mean? The school of Rabbi Yannai answers: *kol she'nifneh ve'ein imo mekancheto* — any minor who uses the bathroom without requiring his mother to clean him up afterward. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish defines it differently: *kol she'ne'or misheinaso ve'eino kore Ima* — any minor who wakes in the night without calling for his mother. The *Gemara* gently objects: even grown people sometimes call out that way. The formulation is refined: one who wakes and does not cry *Ima Ima Ima Ima* — repeatedly, until the mother comes.

This definition is worth pausing over. The age of *chinuch* is not fixed across all *mitzvos*; as *Tosafos* explains, it depends on the specific *mitzvah*. Can the child shake a *lulav*? Then *chinuch* for *lulav* begins. Can he wear *tzitzis* without ruining them? Then that obligation of *chinuch* begins. Can he walk on his own? Then *chinuch* for *aliyah la'regel* is relevant. The definition here — independence from the mother — is not arbitrary. The obligation of *sukkah* is to dwell in the *sukkah* as one dwells in a house. A child who is entirely dependent on his mother for basic bodily functions is not truly the one *dwelling* in a place; he is being tended to there. Only when a minor achieves a meaningful degree of independence — the capacity to be truly present as a self-sufficient person — does it become meaningful to say that he is dwelling in the *sukkah*. This mirrors the broader principle that a sick person or a *mitzta'er* may be physically present in a *sukkah* and yet not be considered as truly dwelling in it.

The *Mishnah*'s story about Shammai is then reconciled: the *Gemara* explains that the *Mishnah* is incomplete in its present form. The full reading is: Shammai applied his stringency even beyond the age of *chinuch*, all the way to a newborn. Hence the story of breaking open the ceiling to place *sechach* over the infant's crib. That was Shammai's exceptional stringency — *lechumra* even beyond what the *halacha* requires — and it provides no contradiction to the rule that the *chinuch* obligation begins only when the minor achieves independence from his mother.

---

---

# Sukkah 29

## Fixed Abode & Ideal

### Fixed Sukkah Principle

The *gemara* on 28b opens by establishing the foundational principle of how one dwells in the *sukkah* for the seven days of the festival. The *braita* derives this principle from the verse *teshvu* — "you shall dwell seven days in *sukkot*" — which is read through the lens of *ke'ein taduru*: dwell in the *sukkah* as you dwell in your house. From this the Rabbis formulated the rule: *kol shiv'at yamim oseh adam sukkato keva uveito arai* — for all seven days a person makes his *sukkah* fixed and his house temporary. This *braita* parallels an earlier one but adds something important: it anchors the principle in a verse, grounding the halakhic ideal in scriptural obligation rather than mere custom.

### Vessels & Furnishings

The practical translation of *sukkato keva* is spelled out concretely. If one has nice vessels — *kelim na'im* — one brings them up to the *sukkah*. If one has fine bedding — *matzo'ot na'im* — those too belong in the *sukkah*. The image is of relocating the full quality of one's domestic life into the *sukkah* for the duration of the festival. The *sukkah* is not to be furnished like a camping tent but like a proper home.

### Activities in Sukkah

The *braita* continues: *ochel veshotteh umtiyel basukkah* — one eats, drinks, and spends time in the *sukkah*. And then it adds something not present in the earlier formulation: *umeshaneh basukkah* — one even does one's learning in the *sukkah*. The ideal of *ke'ein taduru* extends not only to the physical furnishing of the space but to the full range of human activity that would normally take place in one's home.

---

## Learning in Sukkah

### Migras vs Iyunei

The *gemara* immediately raises a difficulty with the requirement to learn in the *sukkah*. The word *umeshaneh* suggests analytical, *talmudic*-style learning — the kind of intensive intellectual engagement one associates with *gemara* study. But doesn't Rava say explicitly: *mikra umishna bimtalulta* — *mikra*, *psukim*, *tanakh*, and *mishna*, the received traditions one recites and memorizes, those belong in the *sukkah* — *vetanuyei bar mimtalulta* — but analytical learning, *iyunei*, one does outside the *sukkah*, in a better environment, perhaps outdoors with fresh air, or in the *beit midrash* where conditions are more conducive to intense concentration? How does Rava's statement square with the *braita*'s injunction to learn in the *sukkah*?

The *gemara* resolves this: *lo kashya — ha bemigras ha bei'yunei*. Even within *gemara* study itself there are two distinct modes. *Migras* refers to memorization and recitation — running through material that has already been analyzed and received. *Iyunei* refers to the analytical work itself, the independent reasoning and probing of the text. The *sukkah* is suitable for the former but not necessarily for the latter.

### Rava & Rami Example

The *gemara* illustrates this distinction with a concrete example: *ki ha deRava veRami bar Chama ki hava kamei deRav Chisda meratzi beGemara bahadi hadadei* — when Rava and Rami bar Chama sat before their teacher Rav Chisda, they would first run through the material together, reviewing and memorizing what had been taught. That was stage one. *VeHadar ma'aynei bisevara* — only after they had the tradition firmly in hand would they then turn to independent analysis, asking what the teacher meant, what objections arose, what implications followed. The memorization phase — even of *gemara* material — is analogous to *mikra* and *mishna* in that it does not demand the same level of environmental focus. The analytical phase does.

### Sukkah as Home

This distinction also need not be framed as a competition between *talmud Torah* and *sukkah* in which *talmud Torah* wins. The more natural framing follows the logic that has governed all the *sukkah* discussions until this point: the *sukkah* is not a prison. Just as one is not required to perform in the *sukkah* activities that one would not normally perform in one's home, so too with learning. If the conditions in the *sukkah* are not conducive to a particular type of study — the kind one would typically pursue in the *beit midrash* or in a quieter setting — then the same reality applies in the *sukkah*. This coheres with the broader principle of *ke'ein taduru*, which defines the *sukkah* by analogy to genuine domestic living, not by an artificial standard of maximal enclosure.

It is worth pausing here to note what is being said. We are not merely discussing the bare minimum *d'oraita* obligation — sleeping and eating a *achilas keva* in the *sukkah*, with its various exemptions for *shomer iro* and *mahalchei drachim*. We are discussing the ideal. And even that ideal is not to be understood in narrow, quantitative terms. The fullest expression of *yoshev basukkah* is to live in the *sukkah* as one lives in one's house — and that means bringing in not only the obligations but the natural rhythms of domestic life, including one's learning, while recognizing that even in one's home there are activities one does elsewhere.

---

## Vessels & Environment

### Glasses vs Dishes

Rava now turns from activities to the physical setup of the *sukkah* environment. *Manei d'mishtaya* — drinking vessels — *bimatalalta* — may be left in the *sukkah* even after one has finished drinking. They do not become objectionable or disrespectful to the space. *Manei d'michla* — eating vessels, the dishes — *bar mimatalalta* — must be removed from the *sukkah* after the meal. Dirty plates, greasy bowls, and leftover food debris are disrespectful to the sanctity of the *mitzvah*, and beyond that, if the goal is to create an environment one actually wants to inhabit — a genuine domestic space — then clearing the table is simply what one would do in any home after a meal.

### Pitchers & Buckets

Similarly, *chatzba veshichaya* — a pottery pitcher or a wooden bucket — once one has poured from them what one needs, these too should be removed from the *sukkah*. The governing principle in all of these cases is the same: keep the *sukkah* a welcoming and pleasant space. Objects that serve their immediate purpose and then become clutter or eyesores have no place lingering in the *sukkah*.

### Candles Placement

Regarding *sharaga* — the candle — the first opinion holds it should remain *bimatalalta*, inside the *sukkah*. Light encourages one to stay in the *sukkah*. A second opinion says *bar mimatalalta* — the candle should be kept outside. The *gemara* resolves: *lo pligi — ha besukkah gedolah ha besukkah ketanah*. They do not actually disagree. In a large *sukkah*, there is no concern and the candle remains inside. In a small *sukkah*, a lit candle poses a fire risk — one will fear the *sukkah* burning down and will not want to remain inside — and therefore the candle is placed outside. This discussion concerns a lit candle, distinct from the earlier discussions about objects left over after use.

### Welcoming Environment

The cumulative picture painted by these *halakhot* is striking. What would it mean to take this seriously in practice? One would set up the *sukkah* so that it is genuinely comfortable and conducive — proper lighting, furnishings that make it inviting, cleared dishes after meals, and an atmosphere that makes one want to remain. If one would read a novel at home, one reads it in the *sukkah*. If one would set up a fan or a portable air conditioner to manage the heat, that belongs in the *sukkah* too. The *mitzvah* does not demand austerity; it demands authenticity — that the *sukkah* actually function as one's home.

One powerful dimension of this is the interplay between the *sukkah* as home and the *sukkah* as a place of divine presence — the *ananei hakavod*. The model in the background is the *mishkan* and the seven days of *miluim*, when the divine presence hovered over the space in which Aaron and his sons dwelt. The insight, developed at length by Rabbi Yaakov Nagen in his work on the religious themes of Masechet Sukkah, is that the *sukkah* represents the merging of two realities that are ordinarily separate: one's home and the place of the divine presence. The *beit hamikdash* is where one goes to encounter God; home is where one lives. The *sukkah* collapses that distinction. And therefore bringing the full texture of domestic life — including the comfortable, the quotidian, even the intimate — into the *sukkah* is not a compromise of its sacred character but its fullest realization.

---

## Rain & Discomfort

### Spoiled Porridge

The *gemara* turns to the question of when rain compels one to leave the *sukkah*. A *tana* teaches: *mishetyisrach hamikpah* — once the porridge, made of *grisin* (split beans or similar pounded grain, a dish that spoils quickly), is spoiled by the rain falling into it, one may go inside. This is the threshold: not the first drops, but a degree of rain that meaningfully disrupts the meal.

One might assume this flows naturally from the principle that a *mitzta'er* — someone experiencing genuine discomfort — is exempt from the *sukkah*, a principle attributed to Rava. But there is a subtlety worth noting. The *mishnah* does not use the language of *tza'ar* at all. The reason may be different: it is not merely that the person is personally distressed, but that a house with rain pouring through its roof is no longer a domicile in any meaningful sense. A leaky roof may be closer to a condemned building than to a home, and the *sukkah* then loses its identity as the kind of dwelling that *ke'ein taduru* requires. Rava's principle of *mitzta'er patur min hasukkah* may therefore be a distinct *chiddush*, addressing personal subjective distress rather than the objective habitability of the *sukkah* itself.

### Rav Yosef Fastidious

The *gemara* relates: *Abaye hava yatav kamei deRav Yosef bimtalalta* — Abaye was sitting before his teacher Rav Yosef in the *sukkah*. A wind blew — *nashav zika* — and material from the *schach* began falling into the food and onto the people below. Rav Yosef said: *pinu li manei meihacha* — remove my belongings; we are going inside. Abaye questioned him: but we learned that only once the porridge has spoiled may one leave — surely small debris from the *schach* falling has not reached that threshold? Rav Yosef replied: *lididi kivan d'aninai da'ati — k'mishetitroach hamikpah dami* — for me, since I am so fastidious, so sensitive, it is equivalent to the porridge having spoiled.

This is an important statement. The criterion for *mitzta'er* is not purely objective, applied uniformly to all people. A person who is genuinely *aninei da'at* — particularly sensitive to disturbances in their environment — may reach the threshold of intolerable discomfort at a point that others would not. Rashi connects *aninei da'at* to a passage in Pesachim identifying three types of people whose lives are not truly lives: those who are overly empathetic, those who are easily angered, and those who are so fastidious that the slightest change in their environment distresses them. Rav Yosef identifies himself as having all three of those qualities.

This also shifts the discussion. The *mishnah*'s rain case may have been about the *sukkah*'s objective status as a domicile. Rav Yosef and Abaye, however, interpret the *halakha* more in terms of personal *mitzta'er* — and once it is personal, it becomes inherently more subjective. The disruption here is not even rain but debris from the *schach*, and yet it qualifies because for Rav Yosef it is genuinely intolerable.

This raises a broader question *l'halacha*: if a *sukkah* is regularly invaded by mosquitoes, or is located in a climate so cold that sleeping in it is never truly feasible, does the recurring *mitzta'er* affect not only the obligation in those moments but the identity of the *sukkah* itself? Could one argue that a space regularly unfit for habitation cannot truly be called a domicile? The tendency in *halakhic* practice has been to resist that conclusion — to evaluate each moment independently, granting exemption when *mitzta'er* is present and obligating when it is not, rather than allowing situational unfitness to undermine the *sukkah*'s status altogether.

The observation that the Talmud's climate is the Mediterranean context of *Eretz Yisrael* — where *Sukkot* falls at the transition from the dry season to the rainy season, and where rain carries deep theological weight — is relevant here. When communities moved northward to Germany, France, and eventually Poland, where the nights of *Sukkot* could be genuinely freezing, questions arose. The Rama records that the *minhag* is not to sleep in the *sukkah*, and the Mishnah Berurah addresses how much accumulation of snow inside the *sukkah* would be needed before one may leave. The question of whether the climate renders such a *sukkah* permanently unfit as a domicile remains a live theoretical concern.

### Continuity Rule

The *gemara* provides further *halakhot* regarding continuity once one has lawfully left the *sukkah*. *Haya ochel basukkah veyardu geshamim veyarad* — one is eating in the *sukkah*, it begins to rain, and one goes inside. Then the rain stops. *Ein matrikhin oto la'alot ad sheyigmor seudato* — one need not return to the *sukkah* to complete the meal. Once the exemption permitted departure, one may finish eating where one is.

Note that the *sukkah* is described as being on the rooftop — hence the language of going "down" — echoing the earlier passage about *he'alum lasukkah*, bringing things "up" to the *sukkah*. The basis of this leniency may be the concept of *mitzta'er* — interrupting a meal midway would itself be a *tza'ar* — or it may follow from *ke'ein taduru*: one does not ordinarily change locations in the middle of a meal, and so since one was legitimately where one is, one may remain there.

The same principle applies to sleep. *Haya yashen tachat hasukkah veyardu geshamim veyarad* — one is sleeping in the *sukkah* and rain comes and one goes inside. *Ein matrikhin oto la'alot* — and then it stops. Must one return? The *gemara* raises a textual question: is the limit *ad sheyei'or* — with an *ayin* — until one wakes up, or *ad sheyei'or* — with an *aleph* — until it becomes light? The distinction matters: does the exemption expire only when the person themselves wakes, or does it expire at daybreak regardless? A *braita* provides both markers together: *ad sheyei'or veya'aleh amud hashachar* — until one wakes and the morning star rises. The *gemara* reads these conjunctively: the exemption holds until both conditions are met — the person has woken and dawn has arrived. Waking in the middle of the night does not obligate returning; and if it is already morning but one remains asleep, no one need rouse them. Only once one has woken of one's own accord and it is genuinely morning must one return to the *sukkah*. The analogy to ordinary life is apt: if one moved to a neighbor's home during construction and was told at two in the morning that the work was done, one would not pack up immediately — one would return in the morning.

---

## Rain Theology

### Master Parable

The *gemara* now addresses the theological significance of rain falling in the *sukkah*. *Mashal l'mah hadavar domeh* — a parable: a servant comes to pour for the master, and the pitcher of water is spilled on the master's face.

### Two Interpretations

The question the *gemara* poses is *mi shafach l'mi* — who is spilling the water on whom? Two readings present themselves. In the first, the servant is coming to perform the *mitzvah* — to pour for the master — and trips, causing the water to spill on the master's face. The theological message would be that one has come to perform the *mitzvah* but has somehow made a mess of it, and God is displeased. In the second reading, and the one that more naturally fits the imagery of water being thrown at a face, the master himself takes the pitcher and throws the water at the servant: *shafach lo rabbo kiton al panav v'amar lo ee efshi beshimushecha* — the master spills the water on the servant's face and says, "I have no interest in your service." This is a powerful image of rejection. One comes to perform the *mitzvah*, and God turns one away. The first interpretation attributes the problem to some failure on the servant's part; the second frames it as God's expression of anger for unrelated reasons.

### God's Presence

Why, one might ask, would rain be interpreted with such theological weight, in a way we would not apply to, say, difficulty finding a *lulav*? Two factors converge. First, as noted, rain during *Sukkot* arrives precisely at the transition to the rainy season in *Eretz Yisrael*, a time already laden with theological meaning — the time of *mashiv haruach umorid hagashem*, when rain carries the weight of divine favor or its withdrawal. Second, the nature of the *mitzvah* itself: activities like *tefillah*, blowing *shofar*, and dwelling under the *ananei hakavod* are modes of direct encounter with the divine. When something goes wrong in those moments — when the *ba'al tokeiah* cannot produce a sound, when rain drives one from the *sukkah* — we are already primed to read these events theologically. The image of the *sukkah* as standing under God's presence, under the *ananei hakavod*, means that being expelled from the *sukkah* by rain is being expelled from the master's presence. "Get out of my place." That reading lends the *mashal* its force.

---

## Eclipses & Signs

### Solar Eclipse

The *gemara* expands its theological reading of natural phenomena beyond rain to the far rarer and more dramatic events of celestial affliction. *Bizman shehachamah lokah* — when the sun is smitten, meaning an eclipse, partial or total — *siman ra l'chol ha'olam* — it is a bad sign for the entire world. The sun is universal; it belongs to everyone. The parable offered: a human king makes a feast for his servants, places a lantern before them, and then in anger commands his servant to remove the lantern and leave them sitting in darkness. The Maharsha connects this to the *midrash* on creation: God laid out the feast of creation for humanity, the sun and moon and stars set in place with the declaration *vehayu leotot* — they shall be for signs. When God removes the light, it is a statement about the entire created order.

### Lunar Eclipse

A *braita* presents Rabbi Meir's teaching: *kol zeman shehamaorot lokim* — whenever the *maorot* are afflicted — here referring not to the sun but to the lesser luminaries, primarily the moon — *siman ra leson'eihem shel Yisrael* — it is a bad sign for the Jewish people, expressed euphemistically. Why specifically the Jewish people? *Mipnei shemelumadim bemakoteihem* — because they are accustomed to being smitten; they know that when trouble comes to the world, they are often the ones it falls upon. The parable: a schoolteacher enters the classroom with a strap in hand. Which student begins to worry? The one who gets whipped every day. It is a somber metaphor.

The Maharsha softens this reading by pointing out that a teacher only disciplines children from whom discipline can produce some good. The child who is a lost cause is ignored. The implication is that Israel's suffering carries the possibility of *teshuvah* and growth — it is not mere punishment but purposeful correction directed at those who have the capacity to respond. The connection between lunar eclipses and Israel also has an astronomical dimension worth noting: since the major festivals — Pesach, Sukkot — fall on the fifteenth of the month, lunar eclipses at full moon naturally tend to cluster around these dates.

### Eclipse Position

The *gemara* continues with further specifications. *Laka bamizrach* — if the eclipse occurs when the luminary is in the east — *siman ra leyoshvei mizrach* — it is a bad sign specifically for those who dwell in the east. *Bamaarav* — if in the west — it is a bad sign for those in the west. *Beemtza harakia* — if it occurs when the luminary is in the middle of the sky — *siman ra lechol haolam kulo* — it is bad for the entire world.

### Color & Timing

Color matters as well. *Panav domim ledam* — if the face of the afflicted luminary appears blood-red — *cherev ba laolam* — it signals war, the redness of blood. *Lesak* — if it takes on the ashen gray of sackcloth — *chizei raav ba'in laolam* — famine is coming. Rashi's reading: the gray-black color suggests the darkened face of fasting. The Maharsha reads the sackcloth as referencing what is contained in such a sack — grain — and thus the absence of grain. A reddish-and-sacklike appearance together signals both war and famine.

Timing within the day also carries meaning. *Laka bechnisato* — if the eclipse strikes when the luminary is setting — *puranut shoah lavo* — the affliction is slow to arrive. *Beyetziato* — if it strikes when the luminary is rising — *memaheret lavo* — it is imminent.
