Some reverse this: Rashi explains the alternate view that an eclipse at setting, leaving no time remaining in the day, signals something coming swiftly with no time to spare.

### Lesser Deities

Finally, a sweeping principle: *ve'ein lecha kol uma vauma sheloka sheein eloheiha loka ima* — there is no nation that is struck without its presiding deity being struck as well. The proof text: *uvchol elohei mitzrayim eeseh shefatim* — "with all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments." The idea is that the forces governing the nations below — understood as angels or lesser celestial powers — are themselves afflicted when their nations suffer. The celestial events thus reflect disturbances in both the earthly and the heavenly order simultaneously.

---

## Righteous Protected

### God's Will Protection

Having described the threatening significance of celestial afflictions, the *gemara* introduces its crucial qualification. *Uvizman sheyisrael osim retzono shel Makom* — when the Jewish people do the will of God — *ein mityar'im mikol elu* — they need not fear any of these signs. The signs operate within the domain of natural-metaphysical forces, but those who are connected to God transcend that domain. The *gemara* invokes the famous tradition about Avraham: when Avraham complained that he saw in the stars that he would have no children, God "took him outside" — *vayotze oto hachutzah* — lifting him beyond the influence of the constellations. Those who are not doing God's will remain subject to these forces; those who do God's will are lifted above them.

### Separation Principle

The *gemara* cites a verse to anchor this: *koh amar Hashem el derech hagoyim al tilmadu — umeotot hashamayim al tichatu* — "Thus says God: do not learn from the ways of the nations, and do not be broken by the signs of heaven." *Ki yeichatu hagoyim mehemah* — let the nations be broken by them; those who separate themselves from the ways of the nations need not fear the signs. *Ovdei kochavim yeichatu ve'ein Yisrael yeichatu* — it is something for idolaters to worry about, not for Israel, when Israel is doing God's will.

---

## Sins & Afflictions

### Four Solar Reasons

The *gemara* now enumerates the specific sins that bring about these celestial afflictions. *Bishvil arba'ah devarim chamah lokah* — for four things the sun is smitten. Rashi acknowledges that he does not see a clear reason why these particular sins are matched to solar affliction specifically, but proceeds with the list. First: *al av beit din shemet ve'eino nispad kahalacha* — the head of the *beit din* dies and is not mourned as is fitting, reflecting a failure to value the institution of a functioning legal system. Second: *al naara me'orasa shetzakah la'ir ve'ein moshia lah* — a betrothed maiden who cries out in the city and no one comes to her aid, an evocation of the verse in the Torah describing rape in the city and the failure of those nearby to intervene, a breakdown of public accountability for justice. Third: *al mishkav zachor* — on male homosexuality. Fourth: *al shenei achim shenishpach damam ke'echad* — two brothers whose blood is shed simultaneously. The first two cases connect readily to themes of judicial failure and communal responsibility; the latter two are harder to integrate into a single coherent framework.

### Four Lunar Reasons

*Uvishvil arba devarim hame'orot lokin* — for four things the luminaries, primarily the moon, are afflicted, relating to Israel's failures. First: *al kotvei plastar* — people who write falsehood, which Rashi glosses as either false documents or libelous writings. Second: *al me'idei edut sheker* — people who give false testimony, continuing the theme of dishonesty in civic life. Third: *al megadlei behemah dakah be'Eretz Yisrael* — those who raise small livestock in *Eretz Yisrael*, because grazing animals destroy the vegetation of the land, causing harm to the communal environment. Fourth: *al kotzei ilanot tovot* — those who cut down good trees, which Rashi says applies even to trees one owns, because it destroys the beauty of the world God has given. The connection among these four is not immediately obvious; there may be a loose theme of falsehood and betrayal in the first two and wanton destruction in the latter two.

### Four Seizure Reasons

*Bishvil arba devarim nichsei ba'alei batim nimsarin la'malchut* — for four reasons the property of wealthy homeowners is seized by the government. First: *al mash'ei shetarot pru'im* — holding promissory notes that have already been repaid, perhaps to collect twice or to use as leverage in litigation — even if one does not intend outright theft, the Maharsha notes, the retention of such documents is a form of extortion. Second: *al malvei b'ribit* — lending with *ribit*, charging interest in violation of Torah law. Third: *al she'haya sfeika b'yadam limchot v'lo michu* — when they had the standing and influence to protest wrongdoing and failed to use it; a person of wealth and authority who remains silent when they could speak is culpable. Fourth: *al she'poskim tzedakah b'rabim v'einam notnim* — those who make public pledges of charity and do not fulfill them, a betrayal of the public trust they cultivated.

A parallel teaching from Rav: *bishvil arba devarim nichsei ba'alei batim yotzin l'timyon* — for four reasons the property of wealthy people is not merely seized by the government but simply disappears, swallowed up entirely: *al kovshei sachar sachir* — withholding wages from hired workers; *al oshkei sachar sachir* — an even greater degree, outright denial of their funds; *al she'porkin ol me'al tzavareihem v'notnim al chavreihem* — whenever obligations arise, they shed them and place them on others; and *al gasut haruach* — arrogance.

### Arrogance Root

*V'gasut haruach k'neged kulam* — and arrogance outweighs all of them together. The Maharsha explains this not as a simple ranking but as a causal claim: arrogance is probably the underlying root from which all the other transgressions listed flow. The wealthy man who thinks himself above accountability — who says "I am wealthy, I can do what I want" — is the one who withholds wages, charges interest, sheds responsibility, and ignores the suffering of others. All of these behaviors are expressions of the same foundational *gasut haruach*.

The *gemara* concludes this section with a counterpoint: *aval ba'anavim ktiv — v'anavim yirshu aretz v'hit'angu al rov shalom* — but regarding the humble it is written: "The meek shall inherit the earth, and they shall delight in abundant peace." This verse from Tehillim — which is indeed the source of the famous phrase — carries a reassurance about the ultimate order of things: those who amass wealth through transgression and arrogance will lose it, while those who act with integrity will in the end receive their portion.

---

## Lulav & Etrog

### Stolen & Dried

With *Hadran alach haya yashen*, the *gemara* concludes the second *perek* and opens the third, which is devoted in its entirety to the *lulav* and *etrog* and the *arba minim*. The structure mirrors the opening of the tractate: just as the first *perek* began not with the *mitzvah* of dwelling in the *sukkah* but with the physical qualities that render the *sukkah* fit or unfit, so this *perek* begins not with the *mitzvah* of taking the *lulav* and *etrog* but with the physical properties that make them *kosher* or *pasul*.

The *mishnah* opens: *lulav hagazul vehayavesh pasul* — a stolen *lulav* or a dried-up *lulav* is invalid.

### Avodah Zarah Trees

*Shel asherah v'shel ir hanidachat* — if the *lulav* comes from an *asherah*, a tree that was the object of idol worship, or from the trees of a condemned city — *ir hanidachat*, a city whose inhabitants worshipped *avodah zarah* collectively and whose property is therefore condemned to destruction — it is *pasul*. The underlying principle is that an object that is under a verdict of destruction has, in a sense, no standing — it is as though it no longer legally exists — and therefore cannot serve as the vehicle for a *mitzvah*.

### Cut/Spread Leaves

*Niktam rosho* — if the *lulav*'s head, the central spine, is cut off — *pasul*. *Nifretzu alav* — if the leaves are spread, meaning, according to Rashi, that they have been removed from the spine and reattached, or according to Tosafos, that the double leaves have all been split open along their middle crease — *pasul*. *Nifredu alav* — if the leaves fan outward from the center without being split or removed, this is actually *kasher*; Rabbi Yehudah says one should nevertheless flatten them and bind them toward the spine so it looks more whole and beautiful, but it remains valid as is. The *lulav* from the iron mountain — *tzinai har habarzel* — which has naturally short leaves, is *kasherah*.

### Height Requirement

Finally: *lulav sheyesh bo shloshah tefachim kedei lena'anea bo kasher* — a *lulav* that has three *tefachim*, sufficient to shake, is *kosher*. The *gemara* will interpret this to require three *tefachim* plus an additional *tefach* to enable shaking, yielding an effective minimum of four *tefachim*.

---

## Hadar Principle

### Rashi on Hadar

What is the underlying basis for these invalidities? Why does a dried *lulav* fail, or a *lulav* whose spine is cut? Rashi's formulation is: *deba'inan mitzvah mehuderet* — we require the *mitzvah* to be performed beautifully — *dikesiv ve'anveihu* — as it is written "this is my God and I will glorify him," the principle of *zeh keili ve'anveihu* that one should make the performance of *mitzvot* beautiful. Notice that Rashi himself uses the word *mehuderet*, borrowed from the root *hadar*, signaling that he is drawing on the very concept the verse in the *arba minim* passage encodes.

### Tosafos on Hadar

Tosafos raises an objection: ordinarily, the principle of *noy mitzvah* — beautifying a *mitzvah* — does not invalidate the *mitzvah* if not observed. One who performs a *mitzvah* without aesthetic enhancement has still fulfilled the obligation. Why should lack of beauty *pasul* the *lulav*? Tosafos therefore grounds the invalidity not in the general principle of *ve'anveihu* but in the specific verse *peri etz hadar* — "the fruit of a beautiful tree" — where the word *hadar* is part of the Torah's own definition of what the object must be. The requirement of aesthetic integrity is not an add-on enhancement but a constitutive element of the *mitzvah* itself.

Rashi likely does not disagree with this; his language of *mitzvah mehuderet* is itself a usage of *hadar*. The practical difference is that Rashi applies *hadar* to all four of the *arba minim* through the general language of *ve'anveihu*, while Tosafos prefers to anchor it directly in the verse *peri etz hadar*. In either case, the governing principle is the same: *hadar* — beauty and aesthetic integrity — is a substantive halakhic requirement that can render the *arba minim* invalid, not merely a recommendation for enhancement.

---

## First vs Other Days

### Chol HaMoed Question

The *gemara* observes that the *mishnah* presents these invalidities categorically — *kapaska vetani* — without distinguishing between the first day of *Yom Tov* and subsequent days. *Lo shna beyom tov rishon velo shna beyom tov sheni* — it makes no distinction. The *rishonim* understand "second day" here to refer primarily to *Chol HaMoed* rather than the second day *Yom Tov* of the diaspora. Does the same standard of invalidity apply on *Chol HaMoed* as on the first day? The question has force because the first day obligation is *d'oraita* — *u'lekachtem lachem bayom harishon* — while the taking of the *arba minim* on *Chol HaMoed* is only rabbinic, a *zecher lemikdash*, a commemoration of the Temple practice. Should the rabbinic enactment carry the same stringencies as the biblical one?

### Hadar All Days

The *gemara* proceeds to distinguish between the different grounds for invalidity. *Bishlama yavesh* — I understand why a dried *lulav* is invalid even on *Chol HaMoed*: *hadar beinan veleka* — the requirement of *hadar* plainly applies. A dried-up *lulav* is not *hadar*, and that requirement applies across all the days of the festival regardless of whether the obligation is biblical or rabbinic.

### Stolen Lulav Problem

*Ela gazul* — but a stolen *lulav*: why is it invalid on *Chol HaMoed*? *Bishlama Yom Tov Rishon ksiv lachem — mishelachem* — I understand the first day: the verse says *lachem*, you shall take "for yourselves," which is read as *mishelachem* — from what is yours — imposing a requirement of ownership. But on *Chol HaMoed*, when we know that one may even borrow a *lulav* without owning it, why should a stolen *lulav* be any worse? If ownership is not required on *Chol HaMoed*, what precisely disqualifies a stolen one? The *gemara* leaves this question open at this point, to be taken up in the continuation.

---

---

# Sukkah 30

## Stolen & Dried Lulav

### Hadar & Aesthetics

The third *perek* opens with a subject already touched upon briefly: the invalidity of a stolen or dried *lulav*. A foundational principle underlies much of what follows. Many of the invalidities governing the *lulav*, the *etrog*, and the other *minim* derive from the use of the word *hadar* in the verse *peri etz hadar* — the fruit of a beautiful tree. The Gemara understands *hadar* to characterize all of the components of the *lulav* bundle. Rashi on the Mishnah situates this within the broader ideal of *zeh keli v'anvehu* — beautifying one's performance of *mitzvot*. While ordinarily that aspiration does not rise to the level of an absolute requirement whose absence invalidates the act, Rashi understands that the explicit use of *hadar* in the verse makes it central here, so that without it the object is disqualified entirely.

### Mishnah: No Distinction

The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah states its rule categorically — *ka pasik v'tani*, it simply states and states — without any qualification. A stolen or dried *lulav* is invalid. The Gemara observes: *lo shna b'yom tov rishon v'lo shna b'yom tov sheni* — no distinction is drawn between the first day of *Yom Tov* and the second day. It is clear from context and from the *Rishonim* that "the second day" here does not refer to the second day of *Yom Tov* in the *galus* sense, but rather to *Chol HaMoed*. The verse states *u'lekachtem lachem bayom harishon* — take on the first day — and concludes *u'smachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem shivat yamim*, rejoice before God seven days. The Rabbis understand those seven days to refer specifically to performance *lifnei Hashem* — in the Temple. Outside the *Beit HaMikdash*, only the first day carries a biblical obligation. The remaining days of *Chol HaMoed* are observed only as a *zecher l'mikdash*, a rabbinic enactment commemorating the Temple. The Mishnah's undifferentiated language, then, implies that both invalidity of *yavesh* and invalidity of *gazul* apply throughout the seven days, whether on the biblical first day or on the rabbinic *Chol HaMoed*.

### Hadar vs. Ownership

The Gemara then poses a pointed question. *Bishlama yavesh* — I understand why a dried-out *lulav* is invalid throughout: *hadar ba'inan ve'leika*, the requirement of aesthetic quality is simply absent. That logic applies uniformly across all seven days. But *gazul*? On the first day I understand: *u'lekachtem lachem* requires that the *lulav* be yours, and a stolen *lulav* is not yours. But why should it be invalid on *Chol HaMoed*, when the requirement of *lachem* — of personal ownership — is not in force? After all, we know as an accepted *halacha* that a borrowed *lulav* and *etrog* may be used on *Chol HaMoed*. So why should stolen be problematic?

This question pushes the *Rishonim* to articulate what principle distinguishes the aesthetic requirements from the ownership requirement, and why the former persist rabbinicaly on *Chol HaMoed* while the latter does not. Rashi and Tosafos offer the following framework: the remaining days are rabbinic in character, and we do not demand at the rabbinic level everything demanded at the biblical level. The key distinction is that *hadar* — and the related idea of *zeh keli v'anvehu* — touches a deeper theme, the notion of performing the *mitzvah* beautifully, which is important enough that the Rabbis insist upon it even on the other days. A question of ownership, by contrast, is a more technical and external requirement and is not demanded rabinically on *Chol HaMoed*.

### Central vs. Tangential

There is a further way to articulate this distinction. The aesthetic quality of *hadar* describes something about the very nature of the object being taken. A shriveled, dried-out *etrog* is a different physical object from a beautiful one; the nature of what you are doing is itself different. Ownership, by contrast, is not visible and is not part of the physical reality of the act. Whether the *lulav* belongs to you or is borrowed is an attribute entirely external to the object itself. This asymmetry explains why aesthetic requirements — being properties of the object — remain in force even on the rabbinic days, while the ownership requirement — being a more tangential, non-physical condition — is assumed not to apply. Rashi and Tosafos essentially embrace this approach, with some also noting a possible textual basis: in the verse, the word *lachem* precedes *bayom harishon*, suggesting it is limited to that day, while *hadar* appears after *yom rishon* and might apply to all seven.

### Sefarad vs. Ashkenaz

A significant *machloket Rishonim* surfaces here, rooted in a very practical historical reality: in many communities, particularly in *Ashkenaz*, a single valid *lulav* and *etrog* might serve an entire town, and often whatever *lulav* and *etrog* was available had long since dried out from prior years' use. The *Rishonim* of *Ashkenaz* largely held that all the *pesulim* remain in force on *Chol HaMoed* as well, and that if the *lulav* fails to satisfy them one cannot be fully *yotzei*. At most, one might take it and recite a *bracha* as a *zecher* — a commemoration — but not as a full discharge of the obligation. The *Rishonei Sefarad* took a starkly different view: even if a *lulav* is *yavesh*, even if it is dried out and fails the requirement of *hadar*, one is still *yotzei* with it on *Chol HaMoed*. This appears to run directly against the plain reading of our Gemara, which states that *yavesh* is a problem precisely because *hadar ba'inan ve'leika* — and this applies across all seven days.

### Ramban's Resolution

The Ramban offers a brilliant resolution — whether or not it is the *pshat* of the Gemara. He argues that when the Gemara speaks of "the second day of *Yom Tov*" as a day on which the aesthetic requirement of *hadar* applies, it is not referring to the rabbinic *mitzvah* of *Chol HaMoed* as we observe it today. Rather, it is speaking of the biblical *mitzvah* as performed in the *Beit HaMikdash* all seven days. In that context, one might say that the verse limits *lachem* to the first day — since *lachem* precedes *bayom harishon* — while *hadar* extends across all seven because it appears after *yom rishon*. But this entire discussion concerns the *mitzvah* as it exists in the *Mikdash*, not the rabbinic enactment of *zecher l'mikdash* that applies today. Therefore, when it comes to our rabbinic obligation, even a *yavesh lulav* would suffice on *Chol HaMoed*, consistent with the view of the *Rishonei Sefarad*. The Ramban's approach thus preserves the Gemara's logic for the biblical context while permitting the Sephardic leniency for the rabbinic context of *Chol HaMoed* in our times.

The essential takeaway from this opening section is twofold. First, *hadar* is understood as a deeper requirement than *lachem* — it touches the nature of the act itself and therefore persists even on the rabbinic days, while ownership is a more peripheral condition that does not. Second, the *Rishonei Sefarad* and *Ramban* effectively argue that our entire Gemara may be addressing the biblical *mitzvah* in the *Mikdash*, leaving the rabbinic obligation of *Chol HaMoed* considerably more lenient.

---

## Mitzvah B'Aveirah

### Lame Animal Analogy

The Gemara now supplies the source for why a stolen *lulav* is invalid even on *Chol HaMoed*, when there is no requirement of *lachem*. Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the reason is *mishum de-havei leih mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* — because it constitutes a *mitzvah* that comes through sin. One may not fulfill a *mitzvah* by means of an act of transgression.

The source is a verse: *v'heveisem gazul es hapisayach v'es hacholeh* — if you bring a stolen animal or a lame or sick animal to sacrifice, *hayertzeh lifnei Hashem* — will this be acceptable before God? The verse groups *gazul* and *pisayach* together. The Gemara draws a comparison: *gazul dumya d'pisayach* — stolen is placed in the same category as lame. Just as a lame animal has no remedy — it is permanently disqualified and can never be rectified for use as a *korban* — so too a stolen animal (and by extension, a stolen *lulav*) admits of no remedy: *leis lei takanta*, it cannot be fixed. And this applies regardless of whether we are speaking before the owner's despair or after: *lo shena lifnei ye'ush lo shena achar ye'ush*.

### Ye'ush & Ownership

This raises a significant question. *Bishlama lifnei ye'ush* — before the owner gives up hope — I understand why a stolen animal cannot be used as a *korban*: *adam ki yakriv mikem amar rachmana* — the verse at the opening of this week's *parasha* requires that the offering come *mikem*, from among you. A stolen animal is not the offerer's own. But *achar ye'ush* — after the original owner has despaired of recovering it? The principle of *ye'ush* holds that once an owner gives up hope of recovering a lost or stolen object, the thief may acquire ownership of it. If so, after *ye'ush* the stolen animal belongs to the one who took it — why then can it not be brought as a *korban*?

The Gemara's answer: *ela lav mishum de-havei leih mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* — it can only be because of the principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*. Once stolen, the object is stigmatized. Even if the thief subsequently owns it, it remains categorically disqualified. The same logic applies to the *lulav*.

A closer look at the mechanics of *ye'ush* is warranted here, because the large Tosafos on this amud engages it directly. The standard rule is that *ye'ush* alone does not transfer ownership to a *ganav* or *gazlan*. If I steal an object and the owner subsequently despairs, that despair does not, by itself, cause me to own the object; I encountered it and took it with an obligation to return it, and his subsequent *ye'ush* cannot alter that. What transfers ownership is the combination of *ye'ush* followed by *shinui reshus* — a change of possession — specifically when a third party acquires the object after the owner has already despaired. So if I steal a sheep and sell it to a third party after *ye'ush*, that third party owns it because he encountered it when the owner had already given up hope. But I myself, having stolen it, never acquire it through *ye'ush* alone.

Yet the plain sense of this Gemara appears to assume that *ye'ush* does transfer ownership even to the *gazlan* himself. One approach is to accept that there is an opinion in the Gemara that *ye'ush kidei kani* — *ye'ush* alone does confer ownership in such a case. Another approach is that the act of sanctification — dedicating the animal to *hekdesh* — itself constitutes a kind of *shinui* that completes the acquisition in conjunction with *ye'ush*. The Gemara proceeds on the simpler assumption: the *gazlan* owns the animal after *ye'ush*, and yet it remains invalid because of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*.

### King's Parable

Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai a second time on this theme. The verse says: *ki ani Hashem ohev mishpat, sonei gezel b'olah* — I, God, love justice; I hate theft in a burnt-offering. What does this mean? The Gemara offers a parable: a human king was passing the tax house, the customs station. He instructed his servants: *tnu mekhes lamokhes* — pay the customs duty to the tax collector. His servants were astonished: *halo kol hamekhes kuloh shelkha hu* — all the tax revenue ultimately flows to you! Why are you paying taxes on your own property? He replied: *mimeni yilmedu kol ovrei derakhim, v'lo yavrikhu atzman min hamekhes* — let all those who travel this road learn from me, and they will not seek to evade their customs obligations. I wish to set the proper example.

It is worth pausing on the historical context. There are *mishnayot* in Nedarim that discuss whether one may make a technically misleading statement to a tax collector in order to avoid payment, and that discussion reflects a real and fraught reality in Roman Palestine, where taxation was often associated with oppression or illegitimate seizure. The parable here, by contrast, calls for scrupulous compliance — and for God to model that compliance. The parallel to our case is that someone might reason: all animals ultimately belong to God, so why should it matter to God whether the *korban* I bring was mine or stolen from someone else? I am returning it to its ultimate Owner. The parable answers: God refuses to condone the underlying sin, refuses to allow the act of coming before Him to serve as a retrospective justification for wrongdoing. Even when the act is ostensibly dedicated to Him, God does not wish to lend divine sanction to theft.

The *Yerushalmi* frames this principle in two distinct formulations, and both are illuminating. One formulation is *ein aveira mitzvah* — a sin cannot become a *mitzvah*, cannot be transformed into something meritorious through the mere fact that it enables a holy act. The other formulation is *ein mitzvah b'aveira* — a *mitzvah* cannot be performed through transgression. These two framings are not identical, and the tension between them is instructive. We do sometimes invoke the principle of *asei docheh lo ta'asei* — a positive commandment overrides a negative prohibition. The blue thread of *tzitzit* must be wool even when attached to a linen garment; the *mitzvah* of *tzitzit* overrides the concern of *shaatnez*. So there is a logic by which performing a *mitzvah* could override the transgression involved. *Mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* says no — at least in defined circumstances, doing a *mitzvah* does not condone the *aveirah* that enabled or accompanies it, and God does not wish to be party to that rationalization.

### Object vs. Action Focus

A fundamental conceptual question about *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* deserves attention. Does it operate by stigmatizing the *object*, or by invalidating the *act*? The first source — the comparison to a lame animal — clearly focuses on the object. A lame animal is permanently disqualified; the *object* itself carries the disability. By analogy, a stolen *lulav* is disqualified as an object. The second source — the king's parable — seems to focus on the *action*: what you are doing is intertwined with sin, and God refuses to accept it.

This distinction has practical consequences. Consider a stolen *shofar*: are you *yotzei* if you blow it? The Rambam, citing a *Yerushalmi*, rules that you are, reasoning that the *mitzvah* of *shofar* is technically fulfilled through the sound, not through the instrument itself, and the sound is not stolen — only the *shofar* is. This is a creative argument, but the underlying logic is clear: if *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* stigmatizes the *object*, we must identify what exactly is the operative object of the *mitzvah*; if the *mitzvah* is associated with something other than the stolen item itself, the principle may not apply. This reading also aligns with the language of the Mishnah, which says *lulav hagazul... pasul* — the *lulav* is *pasul* — not "one does not fulfill the obligation." The invalidity attaches to the object. The Rambam, similarly, categorizes *gezul* alongside physical blemishes of the *lulav*, which is entirely consistent with an object-focused understanding of the principle.

The action-focused interpretation, meanwhile, raises a different question: what does it mean for the sin to be sufficiently *intertwined* with the *mitzvah* to invalidate it? Carrying one's *lulav* on *Shabbat* and then shaking it in shul — one committed a sin that arguably facilitated the *mitzvah*, yet the *lulav* itself is not stigmatized, because the carrying does not alter the object's identity. With theft, however, the entanglement is direct and constitutive: one would not have the *lulav* at all were it not for the act of stealing. That connection is what makes it a genuine *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*.

### Scope & Application

This raises a further question about scope. Both sources for *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* are drawn from the context of *korban*. Yet the Gemara assumes without hesitation that the principle extends to the *lulav*. Some *Rishonim* accept this as a general principle operative across all *mitzvot*. Others note a difficulty: several other *Gemarot* seem unaware of the concept. A *Gemara* discussing a stolen *sukkah* raises ownership concerns but never invokes *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*. A *Gemara* about eating *matzah* that is *tevel* — where eating it constitutes an *aveirah* — never raises the concept either. If the principle were truly global, one would expect it to surface in those discussions as well.

One response is that *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* outside the context of *korban* is only a rabbinic disqualification, and the other *Gemarot* are addressing the issue at the biblical level where the rabbinic principle does not apply. The Ramban takes a different and instructive approach. He argues that the principle is biblically operative specifically where the *mitzvah* has the character of *lehirtzot* — of seeking divine favor and acceptance — as the very language of the verse implies: *hayertzeh lifnei Hashem*. A *korban* is an act of direct supplication and connection with God. A *lulav*, shaken during *Hallel* and during *tefillah*, particularly in the context of praying for rain, similarly functions as a vehicle of *tefillah*, a form of direct appeal to God. Therefore, when you approach God in that mode and your means of doing so is tainted by transgression, the contradiction is biblically intolerable. By contrast, eating *matzah* or sitting in a *sukkah*, while profound *mitzvot*, do not carry that same immediate quality of direct divine appeal. The Ramban thus limits the biblical application of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* to acts that are functionally analogous to *korban* in their orientation toward divine acceptance.

---

## Yochanan vs. Shmuel

### Rabbi Ami's Statement

The Gemara records a parallel statement: *itmar nami amar Rabbi Ami* — Rabbi Ami stated as well that *yavesh pasul mipnei she'ein hadar*, a dried *lulav* is invalid because it lacks *hadar*, and *gazul pasul mishum de-havei leih mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*, a stolen *lulav* is invalid because of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*. This formulation explicitly attributes the two invalidities to two distinct principles — one grounded in aesthetics, the other in the prohibition against sin — and, as stated, the implication is that the principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* renders the stolen *lulav* invalid across all seven days.

### Shmuel's Limitation

Against this, the Gemara cites a competing position: *de'amar Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani amar Shmuel* — Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani quoted Shmuel as saying *lo shanu ela b'yom tov rishon* — the invalidity of *gazul* applies only on the first day of *Yom Tov*. But *mitoch she-yotzei b'shaul, yotzei nami b'gazul* — since on *Chol HaMoed* a borrowed *lulav* suffices and ownership is not required, a stolen *lulav* is equally permissible. On Shmuel's view, the invalidity of a stolen *lulav* derives entirely from the absence of ownership, and there is no independent operative principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* that would extend the disqualification to *Chol HaMoed*.

### Rav Nachman's Objection

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenged Shmuel's position from the Mishnah. The Mishnah says *lulav hagazul vehayavesh pasul* — stolen and dried is invalid. If the Mishnah lists *gazul* as invalid but never mentions *shaul* — a borrowed *lulav* — as invalid, the implication is that *shaul* is valid and *gazul* is not. When would this contrast be meaningful? If the Mishnah's ruling about *gazul* applies only to the first day, then the point of comparison with *shaul* would have to be made on the first day as well — but on the first day, *shaul* is itself invalid because of *lachem*. So if both *gazul* and *shaul* are invalid on the first day, there is nothing distinctive about listing *gazul* as invalid. The Mishnah's implied contrast between *gazul* (invalid) and *shaul* (valid) must therefore refer to *Chol HaMoed*. But this means the Mishnah is saying that on *Chol HaMoed*, when *shaul* is permissible, *gazul* is nonetheless invalid — directly contradicting Shmuel.

### Rava's Defense

Rava defended Shmuel's position. The Mishnah is in fact speaking only about the first day, he argued, and the contrast between *gazul* and *shaul* is entirely explicable: the Mishnah employs the rhetorical form of *lo mibaiya* — it goes without saying. Borrowed is invalid on the first day — it goes without saying that it is invalid, since you clearly have no ownership over a borrowed object. The Mishnah therefore mentions only *gazul*, which is the less obvious case. One might have thought that a stolen object, once the owner has despaired, belongs to the thief — and therefore that a stolen *lulav* could be used on the first day. The Mishnah teaches that this is wrong: *gazul* is invalid even on the first day. The Mishnah's omission of *shaul* reflects not that *shaul* is valid on *Chol HaMoed* while *gazul* is not, but rather that *shaul* is so obviously invalid on the first day that it needs no mention.

### Ye'ush in Robbery

Rava's reasoning carries an important implication. On the first day, the sole basis for the invalidity of *gazul* is the absence of *lachem* — the object is not truly yours. But one might think that with *gezeilah* — robbery — *ye'ush* comes almost automatically, since in the case of open robbery the owner witnesses the taking and is immediately aware of the loss. Perhaps then one should reason that *stam gezeilah ye'ush be'alim hu* — typically a robbery brings with it the owner's immediate despair — and therefore the robber immediately acquires ownership and can use it on the first day. Rava teaches that the Mishnah's ruling comes to exclude this reasoning: the stolen *lulav* is still invalid on the first day despite *ye'ush*. Whether this is because *ye'ush* alone is insufficient to confer ownership, or whether *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* independently invalidates it even on the first day, remains the crux of the deeper debate. What is clear is that on Rava's reading, Shmuel's position — that *gazul* is valid on *Chol HaMoed* because ownership is irrelevant there — stands unchallenged, and there is no need to invoke *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* as an independent ground of disqualification operating throughout the seven days.

---

## Hadasim from Non-Jews

### The Problem

The Gemara now moves to a striking practical application. Rav Huna addressed a group of *avankri* — merchants (or, according to the Aruch, something closer to royal officers) — with the following instruction concerning the purchase of *hadasim* for the community's *lulav* bundles.

### Rav Huna's Solution

*Ki zavnitu asa me-akum* — when you buy *hadasim* from non-Jews — *lo tagzu atun ela ligzoza inehu* — do not be the ones to cut the *hadasim* from the tree; let them cut the *hadasim* and then hand the branches to you. Why? *Stam ovdei kochavim gazlanei arata ninhu* — the non-Jews are generally assumed to be occupying land that is not rightfully theirs. This statement clearly reflects the particular historical and geographic reality of its time — Rav Huna was in *Bavel* — where land had been seized, whether through governmental confiscation or other means, in ways that *halacha* did not recognize as legitimate acquisition. The land was therefore considered *gazul*, and by extension the *hadas* trees growing on it were connected to stolen land. If a Jewish merchant cut the *hadasim* himself, he would be taking possession of an object directly connected to that status, and using such *hadasim* for the *mitzvah* would involve using a stolen object.

### Karka Eina Nigzelet

The resolution turns on the principle of *karka eina nigzelet* — land cannot be stolen. While one certainly transgresses by seizing another's property, the legal status of land does not change in the manner that movable property does. One cannot carry land away, place it in one's possession, or transfer it as chattel. Therefore, *halachically*, the land's identity never acquires the label of being stolen: you have sinned, but the land remains the original owner's land in terms of its legal status. As a consequence, the *hadas* trees that grow from the ground — while connected to that land — likewise do not yet bear the identity of stolen movable property. As long as they remain attached to the ground, the *karka eina nigzelet* principle shields them.

### Ye'ush & Shinui

When the *hadasim* are cut, the situation changes. They are now detached from the ground and have become movable property — *mitaltelim*. At the moment of cutting, they become capable of bearing the identity of stolen chattel. But crucially, the original owners of the land have long since despaired — *ye'ush* took effect long ago — and so these *hadasim*, the instant they are cut, simultaneously carry the status of stolen movable property *and* the owner's *ye'ush*. The *ye'ush* that had been legally inoperative while they were attached to the ground now becomes operative the moment they detach. If the non-Jew cuts them, then he is the first one holding them as movable property after *ye'ush* has taken effect. The Gemara frames this as *ye'ush* taking effect *b'yadaihu* — in their hands. When the Jewish merchant then purchases from the non-Jew, this constitutes *shinui reshus* — a change of possession — occurring after *ye'ush*. The combination of *ye'ush* plus *shinui reshus* is sufficient to confer clean ownership on the merchant. At the moment the merchant acquires the *hadasim*, their history as stolen objects is ancient and irrelevant; he is purchasing an object that, by the time it reaches him, is owned by the seller.

### Merchants' Interest

The Gemara raises an objection: why does all this require the *non-Jews* to be the ones cutting? Surely the merchants could cut the *hadasim* themselves, take possession of them as the first holders of a movable object after *ye'ush*, and then *shinui reshus* would take effect in their own hands — which would then be perfectly adequate for selling to others. The answer is: *tzricha b'oshana d'avanteri gufaihu* — the concern arises specifically for the merchants' own *hoshana*, their own use of the *hadasim* for the *mitzvah*. If a merchant cuts the *hadasim* himself, he is the first one to take hold of them as movable, stolen property. Even with *ye'ush* in effect, he himself is the one who encountered the object in its status as a *gezeilah* — and for him, even if *ye'ush* plus *shinui reshus* would eventually confer ownership, he cannot use it for a *mitzvah* because he originally handled it as a stolen object. But if the non-Jew cuts it first and then transfers it to the merchant, by the time the merchant encounters it, *ye'ush* has already taken effect in someone else's hands, *shinui reshus* takes place at the moment of purchase, and the merchant acquires an object whose problematic history has already been resolved. For purposes of his own *mitzvah*, his slate is clean.

This requires a careful look at the mechanics of *ye'ush ve'shinui reshus*. The standard *halacha* is that *ye'ush* alone does not transfer ownership to the *gazlan*. The *gazlan* who steals and then the owner despairs — the *gazlan* still does not own it; he still has an obligation to return it. What does work is *ye'ush* followed by a transfer to a third party who receives it after *ye'ush* has taken effect. It is that combination — *ye'ush* in one's hands, *shinui reshus* when transferring to another — that creates clean ownership for the recipient. This is exactly what the Gemara describes with the language *ye'ush be'alim b'yadaihu* and *shinui reshus b'yadaichem*. The *ye'ush* takes effect when they — the non-Jews — hold it; the *shinui reshus* happens when it passes into the merchants' hands. At that point the merchants acquire it fully. Notably, this *Gemara* does not invoke the language of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*, which is consistent with the possibility raised earlier that the invalidity of *gazul* in the context of the *lulav* may be entirely a function of ownership rather than of an independent principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*. If ownership is the only concern, then once the merchant genuinely owns the *hadasim* at the moment he takes them, they may be used for the *mitzvah* without any further concern — regardless of what their history was before *ye'ush*.

A question arises in this context about the permissibility of purchasing goods that are reasonably assumed to be stolen at all — quite apart from the *mitzvah* application. The Gemara in Bava Kamma addresses this explicitly: purchasing objects one has reason to believe are stolen is itself prohibited, because doing so creates a market for the *ganav* and *gazlan* and renders the buyer complicit in the ongoing cycle of theft. That concern is a separate layer from the question of whether one acquires valid title after the fact. The scenario here involves a particular type of land seizure — governmental or large-scale — that does not fit neatly into the paradigm of someone stealing in order to sell *hadasim* to the Jewish community, and that distinction may be relevant. Nevertheless, the issue is real and should not be dismissed.

---

## Shinui Ma'aseh Debate

### Binding as Shinui

The Gemara now raises a further avenue by which the merchant might acquire ownership of the *hadasim*, independent of *ye'ush ve'shinui reshus*. The principle of *shinui ma'aseh* — a physical change to a stolen object — is another recognized mechanism by which a *gazlan* can acquire ownership. When the *gazlan* so substantially transforms the object that it is no longer recognizable as the original, that transformation severs the original owner's claim and the new identity of the object belongs to the one who created it. Could the merchant acquire the *hadasim* through *shinui ma'aseh* — specifically by binding them together into a *lulav* bundle?

### Change Reverts

The Gemara dismisses this on two grounds. First, *kasavar lulav ein tzarich eged* — the *lulav* does not actually require binding; the binding is not a *halachic* necessity. If so, the act of tying the *hadasim* into the *lulav* bundle does not create a new *halachic* identity for the object and cannot serve as a meaningful *shinui*. Second, even granting that the *lulav* does require *eged* for its validity, and that there is therefore some formal transformation occurring — *shinui hachozer livriyaso hu*: it is a change that reverts to its original form. After *Sukkot*, the *lulav* bundle is undone and the *hadas* branches return to being simple *hadasim*, indistinguishable from what they were before. A change that reverts is, by definition, not a permanent transformation of identity.

### Shinui Hachozer

The Gemara states the general principle explicitly: *shinui hachozer livriyaso lo shemei shinui* — a change that reverts to its original form is not considered a true *shinui*. The rationale is clear: the legal mechanism of *shinui* as a mode of acquisition depends on a genuine and lasting transformation of the object's identity. When the object will eventually revert — when the *hadas* branch will once again just be a *hadas* branch after the holiday — no lasting change has been effected and no new identity has been created. The temporary function the object serves during *Sukkot* does not alter what it fundamentally is.

### Shinui HaShem

The Gemara then considers a different type of change altogether: *shinui hashem*, a change of name or identity. Even without any physical transformation, could the object acquire a new identity — and thereby new ownership — simply by virtue of being called by a different name? The specific question is: before *Sukkot*, the branch was an *asa* — a myrtle branch, identified by its botanical name. Once *Sukkot* arrives and the branch is designated for the *mitzvah*, it is no longer called an *asa* — it is now a *hoshana*. It acquires a new name by virtue of its ritual function. Does this renaming constitute a *shinui hashem* sufficient to effect a change of ownership and allow the merchant to use it for the *mitzvah*?

### Name Existed Before

The Gemara rejects this as well. *Me'ikara nami le'asa hoshana kari lei* — in fact, people were calling the myrtle branch a *hoshana* even before it was cut, even before *Sukkot* arrived. As the month of Tishrei approaches, what was known a month earlier simply as a willow is now being called an *arava*, and what was simply a myrtle is already being called a *hadas* or *hoshana*. The renaming precedes the cutting. Since the name *hoshana* was already in use before the relevant moment — before the branch became detached from the ground and capable of being treated as stolen movable property — there is no point in time at which the name change could constitute a new *shinui hashem* that would effect acquisition. The name was not created by the act of taking; it already existed.

The conclusion, therefore, is that neither *shinui ma'aseh* (physical change) nor *shinui hashem* (change of name) provides a viable mechanism here. The only effective path to clean ownership of the *hadasim* is *ye'ush ve'shinui reshus* — ensuring that the owner's despair takes effect before the merchant takes possession, achieved practically by having the non-Jews cut the *hadasim* first and then selling them to the merchants.

---

---

# Sukkah 31

## Stolen Sukkah

### Lulav to Sukkah

The *gemara* on 31a opens with a *tanna de-vei rabanan* that shifts our focus from the *lulav* to the *sukkah*. In the preceding discussion, we had examined the problems presented by a stolen *lulav*: first, the concern of *mitzvah haba'ah be'aveirah*, a *mitzvah* performed through the agency of sin, and second, the requirement of *lachem* — that the *arba minim* must belong to the one performing the *mitzvah*. The latter concern explains why even a borrowed *lulav* is problematic on the first day, and it led us into a further discussion about purchasing *hadassim* growing on stolen land — at what point the buyer is considered the owner, and at what point the taint of *gezeilah* is sufficiently in the past that it no longer clouds the *mitzvah*. With that background in place, the *gemara* now turns to the parallel issues in the context of *sukkah*.

### Eliezer vs. Rabbis

The *baraita* states: *sukkah gezulah* — a stolen *sukkah* — and one who constructs a *sukkah* in *reshut ha-rabim*, public space, are cases in which Rabbi Eliezer *posel*, invalidates the *sukkah*, while the *chachamim* hold it to be *machshir*, valid. The case of *reshut ha-rabim* is instructive: by building in public space, one is not stealing portable objects but rather seizing land one does not own — land belonging to the public. The *gemara* uses the word *mesachech* deliberately, indicating one who actually builds and covers a *sukkah* in that space, effectively stealing the public's land by occupying it.

### Two Problems

Rav Nachman steps in to clarify the precise parameters of the debate. *Machlokes shetokaf chavero ve-hotzio mi-sukkato* — the dispute pertains specifically to the case where one physically seized one's fellow's *sukkah* by ejecting him from it. The thief did not carry the *sukkah* away; he stole the land, or more precisely, he seized control of it. This brings us immediately to the fundamental question underlying the entire discussion: *karka einah nigzelet* — can land be considered legally stolen? The general principle in *halacha* is that land does not acquire the status of stolen property, because the land itself has not been physically removed or transformed. Even so, there is a position in *Bava Kamma* — notably attributed to Rabbi Eliezer himself — that *karka nigzelet*, that land can indeed take on the status of stolen property.

### Land Status

Rav Nachman explains Rabbi Eliezer's position as follows: *Rabbi Eliezer le-taimei de-amar ein adam yotzei chovaso be-sukkato shel chaveiro* — Rabbi Eliezer famously holds, as we saw at the end of the previous chapter, that one can only fulfill the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* in one's own *sukkah*, not in a borrowed one. Given that principle, Rabbi Eliezer invalidates this *sukkah* under either of two possible characterizations of the seized land. *I karka nigzeles* — if land can be legally stolen, then the *sukkah* is a *sukkah gezulah* and one is not *yotzei* with a stolen *sukkah*. *Ve-inami karka einah nigzeles* — and if land cannot be considered stolen, then the person's relationship to the *sukkah* is akin to that of a borrower; it is a *sukkah she'ulah*, and according to Rabbi Eliezer, borrowing likewise does not suffice. Either way, the *sukkah* is not his, and since Rabbi Eliezer demands ownership, one does not fulfill the *mitzvah*.

### Rabbis' Position

The *rabanan*, by contrast, hold *adam yotzei yedei chovato be-sukkato shel chaveiro* — one can fulfill the obligation in another's *sukkah*. For the *rabanan*, the only remaining concern would be if the *karka* were actually labeled as stolen, which would introduce a distinct problem of *gezeilah*. But since *karka einah nigzelet* — since land does not acquire the legal identity of stolen property — the *sukkah* is simply one that the person does not own. And since the *rabanan* do not require ownership of the *sukkah*, there is no problem at all. This neatly maps onto the two problems we identified by *lulav*: the ownership concern and the *gezeilah* label. For Rabbi Eliezer, both are in play. For the *rabanan*, neither is.

### Stolen Schach

Having established the parameters of the debate over land, the *gemara* turns to a categorically different case: *aval gazal eitzim ve-sichach bahen* — if one actually stole the wood and used it as *schach*. Here one might have expected a unanimous ruling of invalidity, since the *schach* itself now carries the full legal identity of stolen property. Yet the *gemara* says *divrei ha-kol ein lo ela dmei eitzim* — by universal agreement, the thief owes only the monetary value of the wood, and the *sukkah* is valid. The reason is a combination of two related principles. First, placing the wood as *schach* may constitute a *shinuy* or at least a *shinuy ha-shem* — a transformation of the object's name and character, as what was "wood" is now called "*schach*." Second, and more decisively, there is the concept of *takkanat marish*, a rabbinic enactment discussed in *Bava Kamma*: if one steals a beam and builds it into one's house, even if the construction could technically be undone, the *rabanan* enacted that the thief need not dismantle the structure — payment suffices. The rationale is *takkanat ha-shavim*, a *takkana* designed to facilitate *teshuva*. Rather than demand that the wrongdoer undo every physical consequence of his sin — an obstacle that might deter repentance altogether — the Rabbis preferred a regime that demands restitution but not demolition. The analogy to modern amnesty programs is apt: the goal is reintegration and compensation, not perpetual liability. Once the *rabanan* enacted that the thief becomes the legal owner of the stolen *schach* upon building it into his *sukkah*, the object is no longer *gezulah* — it sheds both the problem of lacking ownership and the label of *gezeilah* — and the *sukkah* is fully valid.

---

## Schach vs. Land

### Gemara's Question

The *gemara* now asks: *mi-mai* — how do we know that the *machlokes* between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* pertains only to the case of *karka* and not to stolen *schach*?

### Dumya Argument

The answer is *mi-dekatani dumya de-reshut ha-rabim* — because the *baraita* presents the stolen *sukkah* as comparable to a *sukkah* built in *reshut ha-rabim*. *Mah reshut ha-rabim karka lav didei hu* — in the case of *reshut ha-rabim*, the problem is not the wood but the land, which does not belong to the builder. *Sukkah nami karka lav didei hu* — so too in the disputed case of the stolen *sukkah*, the problem is the land, not the *schach*. The debate between Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* is therefore confined to the scenario where only the *karka* is problematic.

### Schach Consensus

When the *schach* itself is stolen, the picture is different in both directions. Biblically, one should universally agree that such a *sukkah* is invalid, since the *schach* genuinely carries the *gezeilah* label. Rabbinically, however, the *takkanat marish* takes effect, and one becomes the owner of the stolen *schach* once it is placed — and both Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* therefore agree the *sukkah* is valid post facto. This explains the otherwise puzzling formulation: *divrei ha-kol ein lo ela dmei eitzim*. It is not that the theft is unproblematic; it is that the rabbinic enactment transforms the property status and thereby resolves the *mitzvah* concern, even as it leaves intact the obligation to compensate the original owner.

It is worth noting that by *sukkah*, unlike by *lulav*, the *gemara* never invokes *mitzvah haba'ah be'aveirah* as an independent concern. The problem of *gezeilah* is addressed on its own terms, and once the *takkana* renders the thief the legal owner, the issue is simply closed — the *aveira* recedes into the past without further consequence for the *mitzvah*.

---

## Woman's Complaint

### Servants' Theft

The *gemara* now presents a striking narrative. Rav Nachman was closely associated with the *Reish Galuta* — the political head of Babylonian Jewry — serving as his rabbinic authority in residence. The *Reish Galuta*'s household was not always a model of restraint, and the servants who went to procure *schach* for the *Reish Galuta*'s *sukkah* on the eve of *Sukkot* apparently helped themselves to wood from the property of others.

### Woman Complains

An elderly woman appeared before Rav Nachman with a complaint: *Reish Galuta ve-chulhu rabbanan de-vei Reish Galuta be-sukkah gezulah atitu* — the *Reish Galuta* and all the rabbis gathered in his house were sitting in a stolen *sukkah*, because the servants had cut down trees from her property without permission to use as *schach*. *Tzavcha ve-lo ashgechu bah* — she cried out, and no one paid her any attention. Remarkably, even Rav Nachman himself did not respond.

### Abraham Reference

Stung by the dismissal, the woman addressed Rav Nachman directly: *itata de-hava leh le-avuh tlas me'a ve-samni sarei avdei tzavcha kammaichu ve-lo ashgechisun bah* — a woman whose father had three hundred and eighteen servants is crying out before you and you ignore her? The reference is unmistakable: the number three hundred and eighteen is the count of Avraham's servants who accompanied him in the pursuit to rescue Lot. She was invoking her lineage from Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, and insisting on her dignity as a Jew and a person: how could she be so casually dismissed?

### Payment Suffices

Rav Nachman responded to those present in the *sukkah*: *pita hi da* — this woman is a chatterbox — *ve-ein lah ela dmei eitzim bilvad*. Yes, the servants stole the *schach*, but the *Reish Galuta* owns it by virtue of the *takkanat marish*, and the woman is owed only monetary compensation. The *mitzvah* obligation is discharged.

What makes this narrative genuinely disquieting is the mismatch between the woman's complaint and Rav Nachman's response. She was not primarily raising a *halakhic* objection about the validity of the *sukkah*; she was raising a moral complaint about theft and being ignored. The technically correct answer — that you fulfill the *mitzvah* regardless, and she need only be compensated — is not actually an answer to her grievance. Rav Nachman could at minimum have said: you are right that it was wrong, you will be paid. The *gemara* does not editorialize clearly, leaving the reader to observe this gap between legal sufficiency and moral responsiveness.

---

## Takkanat Marish

### Ravina's Statement

Ravina now formally restates the underlying principle: *hai kishura de-matalalta de-gezulah avdu leh rabbanan takanta mishum takkanat marish* — for a beam of a *sukkah* that has been stolen, the Rabbis applied the same *takkana* as that of the *takkanat marish* from *Bava Kamma*, whereby monetary restitution suffices and the stolen material need not be physically returned.

### Common vs. Uncommon

The *gemara* objects: *pshita* — is this not obvious? We already established this principle for ordinary *schach* material. Why would a beam be any different? The answer is that *eitzim shechichi* — ordinary branches and sticks are common and readily available. If I owe you money instead of returning your sticks, you can easily go purchase replacements. But a beam — *lo shchicha* — is not so common. A custom-cut beam may be difficult to replace, and the original owner may rightly prefer the return of the actual object rather than a cash substitute. One might therefore have thought the *takkana* would not extend to items that are hard to replace, since money is a less adequate substitute. The *gemara* teaches that even so, *kol mashma lan* — the *takkana* applies universally: we still require only monetary restitution, because the broader social and religious benefit of facilitating *teshuva* outweighs the relative inconvenience to the owner.

### Seven-Day Rule

The *gemara* adds an important qualification: *hanei milei be-go shiva* — this *takkana* applies only during the seven days of *Sukkot*. If the thief performs *teshuva* and wishes to make restitution while *Sukkot* is ongoing, money suffices. *Aval le-vatar shiva* — but if *Sukkot* has passed and the beam is still in place, *hadar be-einei* — the thief must return the actual beam. The reasoning is that the *sukkah* was only meant to endure for the week; once the week is over, the construction has no ongoing purpose analogous to a house, and the force of the *takkana* dissolves.

### Permanence Factor

There is one exception: *ve-i chibro be-tina* — if the beam was secured with plaster, rendering the construction more permanent, then even after *Sukkot* the thief acquires the beam and owes only money. The underlying principle is that a *shinuy ha-chozer li-vriyato* — a reversible change — is insufficient to effect a *kinyan* under normal rules of property. Only because of the special rabbinic *takkana* does the thief acquire ownership during the week. Once the week ends and the temporary structure is no longer serving its purpose, the *takkana*'s force lapses — unless the permanence of the construction through plaster brings the situation back within the spirit of the original *takkanat marish* as applied to permanent buildings.

---

## Gezeilah Conclusion

### Summary

With this, the *gemara* concludes its extended treatment of *gezeilah* in the context of the *arba minim* and *sukkah*. By *lulav*, the analysis turned on whether the problem is one of ownership — relevant only on the first day, when *lachem* applies — or one of *mitzvah haba'ah be'aveirah*, which would persist all seven days. By *sukkah*, the concept of *mitzvah haba'ah be'aveirah* does not arise; instead, the analysis focuses entirely on the *gezeilah* label and the ownership question. Because *karka einah nigzelet*, land does not acquire the status of stolen property, and because the *rabanan* do not require ownership of the *sukkah*, most scenarios are resolved without invalidating the *mitzvah*. And in the case of stolen *schach*, the *takkanat marish* effectively eliminates the problem by transferring ownership to the thief, leaving only the monetary obligation to the original owner.

### Yaavesh Intro

Having set aside the *gezeilah* discussion, the *gemara* returns to the opening phrase of the *mishna*: *lulav ha-gazul ve-ha-yavesh* — a stolen *lulav* and a dried-out *lulav*. The *gezeilah* side has been extensively analyzed; now comes the turn of *yavesh*, the dried-out *lulav*, and the question of what role aesthetic quality plays in the *mitzvah* of the *arba minim*.

---

## Hadar Debate

### Rava's Claim

The *gemara* cites a *baraita*: *t'na yavesh pasul* — a dried-out *lulav* is invalid; *Rabbi Yehuda machshir* — Rabbi Yehuda permits it. Rava then offers an analysis of the underlying dispute. The word *hadar* appears in the *pasuk*: *pri eitz hadar* — the fruit of a beautiful tree. Everyone agrees that this word *hadar* is rooted in the *esrog*, describing the character of the fruit and its tree. The question is whether this aesthetic criterion extends to the other *minim* as well.

### Rabbis Connect

Rava states: *machlokes be-lulav* — the dispute concerns only a dried-out *lulav*. The *rabanan* hold *makshinan lulav le-esrog*: we draw an analogy between the *lulav* and the *esrog*, and just as *hadar* is a requirement for the *esrog*, so too it applies to the *lulav*, the *hadas*, and the *arava*. A dried-out *lulav* therefore fails the *hadar* standard.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, holds *lo makshinan lulav le-esrog* — the analogy is not drawn. For him, *hadar* is an *esrog* concern only, not applicable to the other three *minim*. Those *minim* may be dried out and still be valid. And *aval be-esrog*, says Rava, *divrei ha-kol hadar ba'inan* — regarding the *esrog*, everyone agrees that *hadar* is required. Rava is thus making two claims simultaneously: that Rabbi Yehuda in principle rejects any aesthetic demand for the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *arava*, and that even Rabbi Yehuda concedes the *hadar* requirement for the *esrog*. Both claims, as we will see, will be challenged.

---

## Challenge Rava

### Bound Leaves

The *gemara* challenges the first of Rava's claims. *Ve-lo ba'i Rabbi Yehuda hadar?* — do you really mean that Rabbi Yehuda has no *hadar* demands for the *lulav*? But our *mishna* states: Rabbi Yehuda says that if the leaves of the *lulav* are fanned out, one must bind them together against the spine from above. Surely this is an aesthetic demand — the *lulav* must look a certain way. Is this not because *ba'i hadar*?

The *gemara* rejects this inference. *Ki-dekatani ta'ama* — a *baraita* supplies the reason explicitly: Rabbi Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that the word *kapot temarim* means *kafut* — bound. If the *pasuk* describes the *lulav* as bound, and in practice it is spread out, *yachftenu* — one must bind it. The demand that the leaves be aligned and gathered is not an aesthetic preference but a formal definitional requirement derived from the word *kapot*: the *lulav* must be bound. Rabbi Yehuda has a specific structural requirement, not a general aesthetic one.

### Palm Binding

The *gemara* presses further. Our *mishna* also states: *ein ogdin et ha-lulav ela be-mino divrei Rabbi Yehuda* — when one binds together the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *arava*, Rabbi Yehuda requires that the binding itself be from the same species, specifically from the palm. One cannot use a string or a rubber band. Is this not an aesthetic concern — that it looks more pleasing when everything is from the same species?

### Rava's Response

Again the *gemara* rejects this. Rava explains: *afilu be-siva ve-afilu be-ikra de-dikla* — Rabbi Yehuda permits even ugly parts of the palm, even fibrous bark or material from the base of the trunk. If his concern were aesthetic, he would not permit ugly palm material. Clearly, aesthetics are not his motivation.

### Bal Tosif

*Ela mai ta'ama de-Rabbi Yehuda* — what then is the reason? Because Rabbi Yehuda holds *lulav tzarich egged* — the *lulav* requires binding as a formal Torah requirement. Binding the four *minim* together is not merely a nice custom; it is what constitutes the *mitzvah* object. If that is so, *ve-im meivi min achrin* — if one introduces a foreign material as the binding, *havei lehu chamisha minim* — one has effectively added a fifth component to the *mitzvah* object. This is a *bal tosif* concern, and it redefines what one is holding. For the *rabanan*, binding is only a practical convenience or aesthetic enhancement, and one may use any material. But for Rabbi Yehuda, the binding is constitutive of the *mitzvah* object, and its composition matters.

This distinction — between an aesthetic criterion and a formal definitional one — is the heart of Rava's defense. Rabbi Yehuda demands things of the *lulav*, but his demands arise from the legal definition of the object, not from any preference for beauty. He has no *hadar* requirement.

---

## Etrog Challenge

### City Dwellers

The *gemara* now turns to challenge the second limb of Rava's claim: that even Rabbi Yehuda requires *hadar* for the *esrog*. A *baraita* is cited that discusses all four *minim* together. Among its rulings: *kemushin kesheirim* — wilting *minim* are valid; *yeveshim pesulim* — dried-out ones are invalid; *Rabbi Yehuda omer af yeveshim* — Rabbi Yehuda permits even dried-out ones. Rabbi Yehuda then offers a proof: *ma'aseh bi-vnei krakhin* — there was a practice among city dwellers who, lacking easy access to fresh *arba minim*, *she-hayu morishim et lulaveihem li-vnei veneihem* — would bequeath their *lulavim* and *etrogim* to their children and grandchildren. By that point, the objects would long have dried out — and they used them anyway. Clearly, says Rabbi Yehuda, dried-out is acceptable.

### Urgency Objection

The *chachamim* respond: *misham re'aya? Ein she'at ha-dechak re'aya* — is that a proof? A situation of pressing necessity does not serve as a legal precedent. Under normal circumstances, when alternatives are available, a dried-out *lulav* remains invalid. The behavior of the city dwellers proves only that one may make concessions in extremis, not that the *mitzvah* is regularly fulfilled with dried-out *minim*.

### Rava Defended

But the *gemara* notes that Rabbi Yehuda says *af yeveshim* — even dried-out ones are valid — in a *baraita* that appears to encompass all four *minim*. *Mai lav esrog* — does this not include the *esrog*? In defense of Rava, the *gemara* answers *lo, alulav* — no, the statement refers only to the *lulav* (and presumably the *hadas* and *arava*). When Rabbi Yehuda invokes the practice of bequeathing dried-out *arba minim*, he means the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *arava*, not the *esrog*. Rava's position is thus preserved at this stage: Rabbi Yehuda still concedes that the *esrog* requires *hadar* and cannot be dried out.

### She'at Implications

The exchange about *she'at ha-dechak* carries significant *halakhic* weight. If the *chachamim* concede that under pressing circumstances one uses a dried-out *lulav* — and, as the *rishonim* point out, those city dwellers were presumably reciting a *beracha* — this implies that even a *pasul* object may be used with a *beracha* under *she'at ha-dechak*. The *Tosafot* on 31a draws this inference: *im lo matza kasher, mevarekh be-pasul* — if one cannot find a *kasher lulav* or *esrog*, one may use a *pasul* one and recite the *beracha*.

### Ashkenazi-Sefardi

This question was not merely theoretical. There were historical periods in which access to *kasher arba minim* was genuinely difficult, and different communities responded differently. The *chakhmei Sefarad* held that the *psulim* of *hadar* and *yavesh* apply only to the first day, and on *chol ha-moed* these concerns are absent — so at minimum, one fulfills the *mitzvah* on *chol ha-moed* even with such objects. The *chakhmei Ashkenaz* took a stricter view: these *psulim* apply all seven days — but, they held, *be-she'at ha-dechak* one may use *pasulim* and make a *beracha* even on the first day. A notable point of difference emerges: the Ashkenazi position enables use of *pasulim* with a *beracha* on the first day — which the Sefardi position, rooted in the first-day *lachem* requirement, would not permit. Some *rishonim* raise an additional consideration: the category of *yavesh* may be partially relative. If fresh *lulavim* are unknown in a community and only dried ones exist, perhaps a dried *lulav* is *hadar* by the standards of that environment. But other *rishonim* resist this, noting that the relativity argument cannot be extended to other types of *psulim* that are more absolute in character.

---

## Rava Rejected

### Old Etrog Proof

The *gemara* now adduces a definitive proof against Rava's position regarding the *esrog*. *Ta shma: esrog ha-yashan pasul* — an old *esrog* is invalid. *Rav Yehuda machshir* — Rav Yehuda permits it. This is explicit: the *baraita* is discussing an *esrog*, and Rav Yehuda validates it even when old. Rava claimed that on this point all agree — that an *esrog* requires *hadar* — and Rabbi Yehuda differs only regarding the *lulav*. This *baraita* directly contradicts that claim.

### Tyufta

*Tyufta de-Rava tyufta* — Rava's position is refuted. The *gemara* accepts the refutation. Rava was correct that Rabbi Yehuda rejects *hadar* as a principle, but he was wrong to limit that rejection to the *lulav*. Rabbi Yehuda rejects aesthetic demands for all four *minim*, including the *esrog*. A dried-out or old *esrog* is as valid as a dried-out *lulav*, according to Rabbi Yehuda.

---

## Non-Aesthetic Criteria

### Green Etrog

Having established that Rabbi Yehuda has no *hadar* requirement, the *gemara* works through several apparent counterexamples — cases where Rabbi Yehuda does impose demands on the *esrog* — and demonstrates that each arises from non-aesthetic considerations. First: our *mishna* states that an *esrog* that is green like a leek — *yarok ke-karti* — is invalid according to Rav Yehuda, while Rabbi Meir permits it. Is this not because Rav Yehuda demands *hadar* — that the *esrog* must look a certain way? The *gemara* answers: *mishum de-lo gamar peira* — because it has not yet ripened. An *esrog* that is still green has not completed its growth and is therefore not yet a fruit in the full sense. *Pri eitz hadar* requires a *pri*, and a fully ripened fruit is definitional. This is not an aesthetic judgment but a factual one about the fruit's developmental stage.

### Minimum Size

A second apparent counterexample: the *mishna* records a dispute about the minimum size of a valid *esrog*. Rabbi Meir holds *ke-egoz* — the size of a walnut. Rav Yehuda holds *ke-veitzia* — the size of an egg, a stricter and larger minimum. Does Rav Yehuda's higher minimum not reflect a *hadar* concern, a sense that an aesthetically appropriate *esrog* must meet a certain scale? The *gemara* again rejects this. The minimum size derives not from aesthetics but from the definition of what constitutes the fruit. Even if a particular *esrog* specimen will never grow larger, the legal standard looks at what a recognizable, fully formed *esrog* is — and something smaller than an egg does not meet that definition. As the *Tosafot* observe, even a small-variety fruit that typically grows to this size would still be subject to this standard, because the criterion is the definition of an *esrog* as a legal category, not its individual growth.

### Maximum Size

A third challenge involves the upper size limit. Rav Yehuda holds that an *esrog* is valid only if two can be held in one hand simultaneously — implying a maximum size beyond which the *esrog* is invalid. Rav Yosi disagrees and permits even an *esrog* so large that a single one requires both hands. Is Rav Yehuda's upper limit not an aesthetic one — that an excessively large *esrog* departs from the normative image of beauty?

### Teimani Etrogim

This question is practically significant given the existence of the large *Teimani esrogim*, which can be quite massive. According to Rav Yosi, even these are valid; there is no upper limit.

### Hand-Switching

Rava explains Rav Yehuda's concern with larger sizes on purely practical grounds: *lulav be-yamin ve-esrog be-smol* — the *lulav* is held in the right hand and the *esrog* in the left, because the *lulav* contains three *minim* and one generally favors the right hand for the primary object. *Zimnin de-michalflei* — sometimes one will accidentally reverse the arrangement, and then one must switch hands. At the moment of switching, one hand briefly holds both objects simultaneously. If the *esrog* is too large, it cannot fit alongside the *lulav* in the same hand even momentarily, and it will drop. Therefore Rav Yehuda requires that the *esrog* be small enough so that two of them could fit in one hand — meaning one *esrog* plus a *lulav* can fit together during the switch. This is an entirely practical concern, not an aesthetic one.

---

## Hadar Linguistics

### Tree Identifier

The *gemara* now reaches a resolution. Having established that Rabbi Yehuda has no *hadar* requirement by any of the four *minim* — not by *lulav*, not by *esrog* — it asks: *ve-ela le-Rav Yehuda, hai ketiv hadar* — what does Rabbi Yehuda do with the word *hadar* in the *pasuk*? If it does not create an aesthetic criterion, what does it mean?

### Perennial Meaning

The *gemara* answers: *hahu hadar be-ilano mi-shana le-shana* — the word *hadar* identifies the character of the tree, not an aesthetic demand on the fruit. Specifically, *hadar* is related to the root meaning "to dwell" — the fruit of an *esrog* tree dwells on its branches from year to year. The *esrog* tree is a perennial fruit-bearing tree, on which the fruit remains across growing seasons. The word *hadar* in *pri eitz hadar* tells us what type of tree to look for — one whose fruit persists year-round — not that the fruit must meet a standard of beauty. The *Ramban* on the *Torah* advances a parallel reading, suggesting that *esrog* itself derives from an Aramaic root meaning attractive or appealing, and that *hadar* may function as a proper descriptive name for the fruit rather than an operative *halakhic* criterion. In either reading, the word *hadar* serves an identifying or classifying function, not a prescriptive aesthetic one — and this is the foundation of Rabbi Yehuda's position throughout.

---

---

# Sukkah 32

## Gazul, Yavesh, Hadar

### Previous: Gazul, Yavesh

Today's *daf* is 32, and we pick up near the bottom of 31b, three lines in, moving on from the various invalidities of the *lulav*. We have already covered *gazul* and *yavesh* — two of the principal disqualifications. *Gazul* raised all the issues of ownership and the principle of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*. *Yavesh* opened into a central discussion of the requirement of *hadar* — beauty or splendor — a concept derived from the *esrog* but applied across the *arba minim*.

### Hadar Requirement

Rabbi Yehuda, at the conclusion of that sugya, rejects the requirement of *hadar* as applied both to *lulav* and to *esrog*. Even the *esrog*, where the word appears in its original context, is governed by other criteria not rooted in *hadar* per se — criteria related to the fullness of the fruit and its being a fully developed specimen — rather than beauty in the strict aesthetic sense.

### Baked Lulavim

The other important issue that emerged was the *gemara* discussing *b'kafiffin* — dried-up *lulavim* — and whether one may recite a *bracha* over them. The Rabbis concluded with the principle *ein sha'as ha'dechak ra'aya* — the fact that something is permitted in a time of emergency is not proof that it is valid under normal conditions. This raised questions among the *rishonim*: can one use otherwise invalid *arba minim* and recite a *bracha* over them, in a situation analogous to the *sha'as ha'dechak* described in the *gemara*?

---

## Asheira & Ir Nidachas

### Asheira, Ir Nidachas

We now move on from *gazul* and *yavesh* to the next category of invalidities: *shel asheira veshel ir nidachas*. The *gemara* states that a *lulav* taken from an *asheira* — a tree that is worshiped as an idol — or from an *ir nidachas* — a city whose inhabitants worshiped *avodah zarah* and which must therefore be destroyed and burned in its entirety — is *pasul*, invalid.

### Rava: Lo Yitol

But this immediately raises a difficulty. The *gemara* cites Rava: *lulav shel avodah zarah lo yitol, ve'im natal kasher* — a *lulav* of idolatry, one should not take it, but if one did take and use it, one has fulfilled the *mitzvah*. Why, then, does the *mishna* categorically invalidate a *lulav* of *asheira*? Should it not follow the same rule — do not take it, but if you did, you are *yotzei*?

### Avodah Zarah Definition

Before addressing the resolution, an important clarification is in order. *Avodah zarah* in this context does not mean an idolatrous religion. It means a specific physical object — an idol — that has been worshiped. The legal framework here concerns not the religion of *avodah zarah* or what constitutes forbidden worship, but rather: when worship is directed toward an object, that object becomes an idol and becomes *assur b'hana'ah* — forbidden to derive benefit from. The further question is what else, connected to that object, also becomes *assur b'hana'ah* by extension.

To illustrate: if someone picks up a hymnbook from a Hindu religious service, that alone does not make it *tashmishei avodah zarah*. The operative question for *issur hana'ah* is whether the object was used in direct connection with the idol itself, because the idol is *assur b'hana'ah* and objects connected to it become *assur b'hana'ah* by extension.

### Tashmishei AZ

Rashi gives two scenarios in which a *lulav* can become *shel avodah zarah*. The first: *sheshimeshu bo l'avodah zarah l'chabed lefaneha karka* — it was used as a broom to sweep the ground in front of the idol. This is the category of *tashmishei avodah zarah* — an appurtenance used in the service of the idol. The second scenario Rashi raises: *she'avodatah b'lulav l'ha'avir lefaneha ul'zorkah bah* — the *lulav* itself was used in an act of worship before the idol, such as waving it in front of the idol. This also falls under *tashmishei avodah zarah*, as distinct from *tikroves avodah zarah*, which would apply if the *lulav* were actually offered up as a sacrifice to the idol.

It is worth noting that *tikroves avodah zarah* does not even require a physical idol to be present: if someone slaughters an animal and offers it to Zeus, even without any idol in the room, it becomes forbidden as an offering to a pagan deity. But in our case, what matters is the *lulav*'s use as an appurtenance of the idol's service, which renders it *assur b'hana'ah*.

Given all of this, the *gemara* asks: if this *lulav* is *assur b'hana'ah* and you use it on *Sukkos*, it seems you should not take it. But *ve'im natal kasher* — if you did, you fulfilled the *mitzvah*. How so, if it is forbidden in benefit?
