### Mitzvot Lav Lehenot

This is the classic principle of *mitzvot lav lehenot nitnu* — *mitzvot* are not given for physical benefit. Rashi explains here: *ve'af al gav de'isura de'hana'ah hu* — even though it is forbidden in benefit — *demitzvot lav lehenot nitnu* — for *mitzvot* are not given for benefit. He elaborates: *ein kiyum mitzvot hana'at ha'guf* — fulfilling a *mitzvah* is not a physical benefit to the body — *ela avodat eved l'rabo* — it is the service of a servant to his master. In other contexts Rashi expresses this even more sharply, saying that *mitzvot* were given *le'ol tzavareihem nitnu* — as a yoke upon one's neck — a formulation noticeably harsher than the familiar *ratzah Hakadosh Baruch Hu lezakot et Yisrael*.

### Halacha This-Worldly

The simpler and more fundamental point, however, has nothing to do with whether we experience *mitzvot* as spiritually fulfilling. It is a precise *halachic* point: *halacha* deals with physical, this-worldly realities. If something is *assur b'hana'ah*, benefit is measured strictly by concrete, this-worldly benefit. Otherworldly benefit — reward in *olam ha'ba*, divine favor, spiritual fulfillment — is not relevant within the framework of *halacha*. This is, in a sense, one of the surprising and philosophically rich features of *halacha*: though it is religious law, it is profoundly grounded in the measurable, this-worldly dimension of human experience.

One might ask: even setting aside *olam ha'ba*, surely a person derives personal satisfaction and enjoyment from performing a *mitzvah* — does that not constitute *hana'ah*? This question connects to the broader principle stated in the *gemara*: *kol kol u'mareh v'reiach ein bahem mishum me'ilah* — aesthetic pleasures of sound, sight, and smell are not technically classified as forbidden benefit in the biblical sense. Visual or aesthetic pleasure is not considered a physical benefit; smell is treated somewhat differently because it engages the body more directly. So too the internal satisfaction of performing a *mitzvah* does not rise to the level of concrete, physical *hana'ah* that *halacha* recognizes. Hence, if one took the *lulav* of *avodah zarah* and used it, one did not technically derive forbidden benefit, and one has fulfilled the *mitzvah*. The reason not to take it in the first place, as Rashi states in two words, is *dema'is ligvoah* — it is disgusting before God. One should not bring something associated with idolatry into the service of God. But as a matter of strict law, if one did, one is *yotzei*.

### Stolen vs. AZ Lulav

This raises a pointed question: why is a *stolen* *lulav* invalid — and not merely ill-advised — while a *lulav* used for *avodah zarah* is only disgraceful, not technically invalid? Surely something used in idolatrous worship carries a more severe stigma than something merely stolen. Shouldn't *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* disqualify it?

Tosafot addresses this earlier in the sugya of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* and offers two important points. First, he argues that the *aveirah* of worshiping *avodah zarah* was entirely unrelated to the *mitzvah* of *lulav*. He draws an analogy: if someone used a *lulav* to dig a hole on *Shabbat*, or carried it through *reshut ha'rabim* on *Shabbat*, would the *lulav* thereby become invalid for a *mitzvah*? Clearly not. The *aveirah* of *Shabbat* desecration is not intertwined with the *mitzvah* of *lulav*. Similarly, even though worshiping the *lulav* as *avodah zarah* is a severe *aveirah*, it did not cause the *mitzvah* to come about — the *mitzvah* is entirely independent. When one *steals* a *lulav*, by contrast, the very act of stealing is what enabled one to perform the *mitzvah*; the *aveirah* and the *mitzvah* are intertwined.

That said, one must acknowledge the force of the difficulty here. If the problem of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* lies not only in the intertwining of actions but also in the stigmatization of the *object* — if using something for *aveirah* taints it as a *mitzvah* vehicle — then surely worshiping something as *avodah zarah* would seem to place it far beyond the pale of any *mitzvah* use. It is genuinely striking that the *gemara* does not invoke *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah* here. Tosafot's answer focuses on the action, not the object — the *aveirah* did not enable the *mitzvah* — but the intuitive difficulty remains.

### Chitutei Mechatat

So the *gemara* resolves the original question differently. The *lulav* of *asheira* is invalid — not because it is *assur b'hana'ah*, but for an entirely different reason. The *gemara* states: *hacha b'asherah d'Moshe askinan* — we are speaking of a *Moshe-type asheira* — *d'chitutei mechatat shiurei* — because its *shiur*, its legal size and standing, is ground up and destroyed.

The principle of *chitutei mechatat shiurei* holds that an object which is obligated to be destroyed is treated as though it were already burnt and annihilated, and therefore cannot serve as a *mitzvah* object. The logic is this: the entire concept of a *shiur* — a minimum size or quantity — is a measure of significance. An object that is commanded to be destroyed has no significance; its obligatory destruction undermines any weight it could have as a *mitzvah* object. Hence a *lulav* from an *ir nidachas* — where the *lulav* itself was not used for any forbidden purpose, but is merely located in a city that must be destroyed — is invalid precisely because it is subject to destruction. The same applies to the *asheira*: not because of *issur hana'ah*, but because the obligation to destroy it means it is treated *halachically* as though already destroyed.

### Moshe's Asheira

But this raises a further question: which *asheiros* fall under the obligation of destruction? The *gemara* seems to distinguish between different categories of idols, identifying the relevant case as *asherah d'Moshe* — Moshe's *asheira*. What does this mean?

Rashi explains: *otam she'hayu bi-sha'at kibbush Eretz Yisrael* — those *asheiros* that existed at the time of the conquest of the land, *she-hitzrichan ha-katuv sereifah* — which the Torah required to be burned, as it is written *va-ashereihem tisrefun ba-esh*. This is a striking Rashi. He appears to limit the *mitzvah* to destroy *avodah zarah* to the idols present during the conquest of Eretz Yisrael under Moshe and Yehoshua. After that period, according to this reading of Rashi, there is no *mitzvah* to destroy *avodah zarah*.

This is remarkable, because the received understanding in most *poskim* and *rishonim* is that the obligation to destroy *avodah zarah* is not limited to the conquest period. And yet, if one surveys the *mishnayot* and *gemarot* of *Masechet Avodah Zarah* — which discusses *yayin nesech*, objects *assur b'hana'ah*, forbidden forms of worship, and much else — one will search in vain for a sustained discussion of the *mitzvah* to destroy *avodah zarah*. Scholars have noted the likely explanation: the *Mishnah* was edited in Eretz Yisrael under Roman rule, which was saturated with pagan idols. Under those conditions, any discussion of a practical obligation to destroy the idols of the surrounding culture would have been not only impractical but potentially dangerous. The topic was therefore set aside. This has resonance for contemporary discussions as well, where questions about *avodah zarah* in the land of Israel are sometimes raised; it is instructive to note which topics were, for purely practical reasons, effectively bracketed by the Tannaim and Amoraim.

Rashi's formulation actually renders this bracketing *halachically* operative — limiting the *mitzvah* to destroy to the conquest period — which is indeed a remarkable position.

Tosafot does not accept Rashi's approach. Tosafot explains the distinction differently: *Moshe* refers not to a time period but to a type of ownership — Jewish-owned *avodah zarah*. A non-Jew who owns and worships an idol can annul it — be *mevatel* it — declare it no longer sacred, and it reverts to being a permissible object. But once an idol is owned or worshiped by a Jew, its status becomes permanently fixed and cannot be reversed. Therefore Tosafot says: the distinction is between *avodah zarah* that can still potentially be nullified — in which case it need not be destroyed and *chitutei mechatat shiurei* does not apply — and *avodah zarah* owned by a Jew that can never have its status changed and must be destroyed. Only the latter falls under the principle of *chitutei mechatat shiurei* and is therefore invalid as a *mitzvah* object.

The conclusion of this section, then, is striking: mere prohibition of *hana'ah* — even if the object was used for *avodah zarah* — is not sufficient to disqualify the *lulav* as a *mitzvah* object, because *mitzvot lav lehenot nitnu*. What does disqualify it is the obligation of destruction, which strips the object of all *halachic* standing. A stolen *lulav* fails because of *mitzvah haba'ah b'aveirah*, the intertwining of the *aveirah* with the *mitzvah* act. An *avodah zarah lulav* that lacks the destruction obligation fails only in the moral-aesthetic sense — *dema'is ligvoah* — but technically one would be *yotzei*. Only when the destruction obligation attaches does it become categorically invalid.

---

## Lulav Defects

### Niktam vs. Nisdak

We turn now from these questions of origin and ownership to physical defects of the *lulav* itself. The *mishnah* states that *niktam rosho* — if the head of the *lulav* is cut off — it is invalid. Rav Huna qualifies: *lo shanu ela niktam* — this applies only if it is cut off — *aval nisdak kasher* — but if it is split, it remains *kasher*. The case of *nisdak*, as Rashi explains, refers to the splitting of the leaf-tips themselves. Without getting into the full practical *halacha*, the basic point is a valuable leniency: split leaves do not, in and of themselves, constitute a defect.

### Braita: Bent, Thorny

The *gemara* then poses a challenge from a *braita*, which lists multiple forms of invalid *lulavim*: *lulav kafuf* — bent; *kavatz* — thorny; *saduk* — split; *akum domeh lemagal* — bent like a scythe, meaning severely curved; *charut* — hardened like a stick, where the leaves have fused; all of these are *pasul*. However, *domeh lecharut* — resembling hardened but where the leaves are still separable — is *kasher*. Rav Papa resolves the apparent contradiction between the *braita* which lists *saduk* as *pasul* and Rav Huna's ruling that *nisdak* is *kasher* by specifying that the *braita* refers to a severe split — one that effectively produces two separate spines, analogous to a scribal tool with two separate tips used to make simultaneous copies. A *lulav* whose spine bifurcates into two distinct heads is invalid. Ordinary splitting of the leaves is not a problem.

### Bent Lulav

Regarding *akum domeh lemagal* — bent like a scythe — Rava offers a nuanced distinction: *lo amran ela lifanav* — the problem applies only if the *lulav* bends forward, meaning toward the side of the leaves rather than toward the spine. *Aval le'achorav briya hi* — if it bends backward toward the spine, that is the natural growth pattern of the *lulav* and does not constitute a defect. The precise application of this distinction in practice — since *lulavim* typically tend to curve in one direction when they bend — is a genuine question, and the further teaching of Rav Nachman adds complexity: if the *lulav* bends to the side, one opinion equates that with bending forward (invalid), and another opinion equates it with bending backward (valid). The question of how much curvature is tolerable, and in which direction, is directly relevant to the examination of *lulavim* before *Sukkos*.

### Symmetry Requirement

Rava adds a further ruling: *hai lulava desalik bechad hutza* — a *lulav* whose leaves all emerge from only one side of the spine — *ba'al mum hu pasul* — is like a blemished specimen and is invalid. This is not stated explicitly in the *mishnah*, but reflects a broader aesthetic principle: symmetry. The concept of symmetry is, in fact, central to aesthetics going back to classical philosophy, and its application here — to the requirement that leaves be present on both sides of the spine — gives concrete *halachic* expression to the general requirement that the *lulav* be a proper specimen.

### Nifretzu vs. Nifraду

The *mishnah* lists two further conditions: *nifretzu alav* — invalid — and *nifredu* — valid. *Nifredu* is not difficult to understand: the leaves are fanned out, separated from the spine but still attached to it; they have simply spread open rather than lying flat. Rabbi Yehuda rules that such a *lulav* is *kasher* but one must bind the leaves flat against the spine. The case of *nifretzu* — which is invalid — requires clarification.

### Nifretzu as Broom

Rav Papa explains: *nifretzu de'avid ke'hufya* — *nifretzu* means it has come to look like a broom. Rashi understands this as referring to a case where the leaves actually fell off and were tied back onto the spine, producing a broom-like appearance. Tosafot disagrees, arguing that this is too obvious to require stating; Tosafot understands *nifretzu* as referring to leaves that have been split fully open, their two halves completely separated — which produces the broom-like appearance. The practical and theoretical disagreement about what exactly constitutes *nifretzu* remains unresolved between Rashi and Tosafot.

### Split Tip Issue

Rav Papa then poses the most practically significant question of the entire section: *nechleka hatayomes mahu* — what is the law if the tip of the *lulav* is split? This is the question most people have in mind when carefully examining their *lulav* before purchase. One might think that since ordinary split leaves are permissible, a split tip would be similarly treated. But the tip is uniquely significant because it is the crown of the *lulav*.

The *gemara* brings the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan (or in another version, Rav Matna citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi): *nitlah hatayomes pasul* — if the tip is removed, it is invalid. The first approach in the *gemara* argues that a split tip (*nechleka*) is not equivalent to a removed tip (*nitlah*): removal is worse because the tip is actually missing (*de'chasar lei*), and a split alone would be permissible. A second version of the tradition states the opposite: *nechleka hatayomes na'aseh kemi shenitlah hatayomes u'pasul* — a split tip is treated as equivalent to a removed tip and is therefore invalid.

### Rashi: Full Separation

This second version is what generates the intense scrutiny of *lulav* tips that every consumer of *lulavim* before *Sukkos* knows well. However, Rashi's definition of what constitutes a problematic split offers significant relief. Rashi states: the *nechleka* refers to the case where the two uppermost central leaves — at the point where the spine terminates — split apart from one another, *venisdekah hashidrah ad ha'alim shelematta mehem* — and the spine itself splits all the way down until it reaches the leaves below. In other words, according to Rashi, a truly problematic split is one that runs the full length of the terminal section, all the way down to where the next leaves emerge. A small split at the very tip alone does not constitute *nechleka hatayomes* under Rashi's definition. According to this view, the stringent behavior many people adopt when examining *lulav* tips goes beyond what Rashi requires. Other authorities, however, take the position that even a minimal separation at the top is a disqualifying *nechleka*, which explains why this issue generates such careful attention.

---

## Kapot Tmarim, Hadas ID

### Binding Fanned Leaves

The *gemara* now records the ruling of Rabbi Yehuda: if the leaves of the *lulav* are spread out (*nifraду*), one must bind them so that they are flat against the spine. A *braita* attributes this teaching to Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon, connecting it to the term *kapot tmarim* in the Torah: *kapot* — implying bound — means that if the leaves are spread apart, one must bind them together against the spine.

### Kapot Tmarim Debate

Ravina poses a foundational question to Rav Ashi: *mimai de'hai kapot tmarim de'lulav hu* — how do we know that the phrase *kapot tmarim* refers specifically to the *lulav* as we know it? The word *tmarim* does derive from the palm tree, but the palm tree has many distinct components. Perhaps *kapot tmarim* refers to a different part of the palm tree entirely.

### Charuta Problem

Ravina's first suggestion: *eima cheruta* — perhaps it means the *cheruta*, the stage at which young palm branches have hardened and the leaves have fused into stick-like extensions. Could the Torah mean to take a larger palm branch bearing multiple such hardened offshoots? The *gemara* rejects this: *be'inan kaput ve'leika* — we need something that is actually *bindable* — *kapot* implies there are separate elements that can be drawn together. A hardened stick has no separate elements to bind; it is simply a stick.

### Uptzala Problem

The second suggestion: *ve'eima uptzala* — what about the fiber of the trunk itself, a single unified structure? The *gemara* rejects this as well: *kaput miklal de'ika parud* — *kaput* implies that there is a plurality of elements that, although separate, are situated together. Something that is entirely a single, undifferentiated unit cannot be described as *kaput* — bound together — because there is nothing to bind. The *lulav* must have both features: separate elements (the individual leaves) and a unity that encompasses them (the spine along which they are arranged).

### Kufra Case

A third suggestion: *ve'eima kufra* — what about the stage just before full hardening, when branches are still young enough that one could physically force them together with binding? Rashi describes this as branches roughly one or two years old whose wood has not yet fully thickened, such that one could still fold the offshoots together by tying. Could this be *kapot tmarim*?

### Pleasant Ways

Abaye dismisses this on a different ground: *deracheha darchei noam vechol nesivoseha shalom* — the Torah's ways are pleasant and all its paths are peace. At this stage of development, the branches bear thorns that would scratch and injure the hand. It is inconceivable that the Torah would mandate taking something in hand that would cause injury. This is a principled *halachic* inference from the general character of the Torah, not merely an aesthetic preference.

### Kapot Singular

Rava Tosfa'ah raises another possibility before Ravina: *ve'eima tarti kapei de'timarei* — perhaps *kapot tmarim* means two palm-clusters, i.e., a cluster of dates. A cluster of dates is, after all, a unified whole (*kapot*) composed of separate elements. The *gemara* responds: *kapat kesiv* — the word is written without a *vav*, in a form that indicates singular rather than plural. Thus it cannot mean multiple clusters. But then perhaps one cluster of dates — *ve'eima chada*? The *gemara* answers: *la'hu kaf kari lei* — a single cluster would simply be called a *kaf*, not *kapot*. The specific form *kapot* implies one thing that is inherently multiple — a single unit composed of many separate elements — and the only candidate from the palm tree that fits this description is the *lulav* itself: its individual leaves are distinct, yet they all emerge from and are unified along a single spine.

### Lulav Identified

This is the conclusion: *kapot tmarim* refers to the *lulav*, precisely because it uniquely combines separate elements (the leaves) within a single unified structure (the spine). The other parts of the palm tree each fail on one or the other dimension — either they lack separate elements or they lack the essential unity.

At this point it is worth noting the observation of the Rambam in his *Perush Hamishnayot*. These derivations — similarly to those we will encounter shortly regarding *anaf etz avot* and *pri etz hadar* — can appear somewhat forced. Did the Sages truly not know which plant was meant, and only figure it out by parsing the grammar of *kapot*? The Rambam argues that in reality, the identities of the *arba minim* were always known by tradition — by an oral culture that transmitted the meaning of these terms from generation to generation. The *gemara*'s etymological and botanical derivations are, in his view, not the actual source of knowledge but rather retroactive demonstrations of how the verse can be seen to support what was already known. The Rambam classifies this traditional knowledge as a form of *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* — not derived from the verse, but received as transmitted tradition.

---

## Shiur: Tefachim

### Halacha Tradition

The Rambam's point connects to the broader question of *shiurim* — minimum measurements — which the *gemara* now begins to address. The measurement requirements for *lulav*, *hadas*, and *aravah* are not, in his view, derived analytically from the verses, but represent received knowledge about what the Torah always meant. Just as the identification of the species was a matter of transmitted knowledge, so too the specific minimum dimensions required for each of the *minim* belong to a category of *halacha le'Moshe mi'Sinai* — tradition rather than derivation.

---

## Tzinei Har Habarzel

### Leaf Overlap Rule

Before proceeding to the main discussion of *shiurim*, the *gemara* addresses the ruling of the *mishnah* that *tzinei har habarzel* — *lulavim* from the iron mountain — are *kasher*. These are *lulavim* whose leaves are unusually short. Abaye establishes the operative distinction: *lo shanu ella she'rosho shel zeh magi'a le'tzad ikaro shel zeh* — the ruling of *kasher* applies only when the tip of one leaf reaches at least to the base of the next leaf. *Aval ein rosho shel zeh magi'a le'tzad ikaro shel zeh pasul* — if the leaves are so short that the tip of one does not even reach the base of the next, the *lulav* is invalid.

### Mishna-Braita Harmony

This distinction resolves an apparent contradiction. The *mishnah* states that *tzinei har habarzel* is *kasher*, while a *braita* states it is *pasul*. Abaye's ruling harmonizes the two: the *mishnah* speaks of the case where each leaf reaches the base of the next — *kasher*; the *braita* speaks of the case where leaves are so stunted they do not even reach the base of the next — *pasul*. *Ela shema mina ke'Abaye* — this confirms Abaye's resolution.

### Gei Ben Hinnom

The *gemara* then appends an intriguing aggadic tradition. Rabbi Miryon citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and in a parallel tradition Rabba bar Mari citing Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, teach: *shtei tmarot yesh b'gei ben Hinnom* — there are two palm trees in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, which lies outside Jerusalem. *Ve'ole ashan mi'beineihem* — smoke rises from between them. This is the valley whose name gives us the word *Gehennom*. The *gemara* identifies these palm trees as the *tzinei har habarzel* referred to in the *mishnah*, explaining that the *mishnah* speaks of the distinctive *lulavim* that grow from these particular trees in this valley. And the *gemara* adds: *v'zo hi pitcha shel Gehennom* — the space between those two smoke-emitting palm trees is the gateway to *Gehennom*. The image is striking — the two palm trees stand like pillars framing an archway, and from between them smoke rises from below. That the *lulav* from such trees is nonetheless *kasher* is itself a remarkable detail.

---

## Shiur: Tefachim (II)

### Three and Four

The *gemara* now turns to the primary discussion of minimum sizes. Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states: *shiur hadas va'aravah shlosha* — the minimum size of the *hadas* and *aravah* is three *tefachim* — *ha'lulav arba'ah* — and the *lulav* is four *tefachim*, *kedai she'yehei lulav yotzei min ha'hadas tefach* — so that the *lulav* protrudes one *tefach* above the *hadas*. It is worth recalling the broader context: the reason the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *aravah* are bound together as a single unit derives from the way the *pasuk* is written — *pri etz hadar*, then *kapot tmarim* without a connecting *vav*, then *ve'anaf etz avot ve'arvei nachal* — the three non-*esrog* species are thus bound together. This also explains why we recite the *bracha* as *al netilat lulav* rather than *al netilat arba minim* or *al netilat esrog*: the *lulav* is the tallest and most dominant member of the bundle, and the *pasuk* centers on *kapot tmarim* with the other two appended to it.

### Spine Protrusion

Rav Parnach citing Rabbi Yochanan adds a further specification: *shidra shel lulav tzarich she'yeitzei min ha'hadas tefach* — not merely the top of the *lulav*'s leaves, but the *spine* of the *lulav* must protrude a full *tefach* above the *hadas*. This is a more demanding requirement: it is not enough that the leaves of the *lulav* extend above the *hadas*; the spine itself must reach a full *tefach* higher. Practically, this is something to attend to when assembling the *lulav*: one should verify not merely that the general tip of the *lulav* is higher, but specifically that the spine protrudes.

### Three vs. Four

The *mishnah* says that a *lulav* of three *tefachim* — *kedai lenane'ah bo kasher* — sufficient to shake it — is valid. But Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel just stated that the *lulav* must be four *tefachim*. The resolution: read the *mishnah* as *u'khedai lenane'ah bo kasher* — meaning three *tefachim plus* enough to shake it, i.e., three *tefachim* plus one more. *Mar ki'islei u'Mar ki'islei* — each Amora read the *mishnah* in accordance with his own position. According to Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, the extra *tefach* brings the overall *lulav* to four *tefachim* measured including the leaves. According to Rav Parnach citing Rabbi Yochanan, who demands that the spine itself protrude a *tefach*, the four *tefachim* are measured along the spine alone, yielding a still more demanding standard.

### Five-Tefach Amah

Rabbi Tarfon's position, as taught in the *braita*: *be'amah bat chamisha tefachim* — measured with a five-*tefach amah*. One reading of this would be that Rabbi Tarfon demands five *tefachim* for the *hadas* and *aravah* and a proportionally greater amount for the *lulav*. Rava reacts sharply: *shara lei marei l'Rabbi Tarfon* — may his Master forgive Rabbi Tarfon for such a requirement! *Hashta avud shlosha lo meshkachinan* — we struggle to find even three *tefachim* of properly braided leaves; *bat chamisha miba'aya* — could we possibly find five?

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael he offered a different reading. Rabbi Tarfon does not disagree with the quantities of three and four; he agrees that it is three for *hadas* and *aravah* and four for *lulav*. His innovation concerns the *size of the tefach* used to measure. He says: take a normal six-*tefach amah* and divide it into five parts instead of six. Each resulting unit is therefore one *tefach* plus one-fifth — that is, 1.2 normal *tefachim*. Use those enlarged *tefachim* as your measuring units: three of them for *hadas* and *aravah* (equaling 3.6 normal *tefachim*), four for *lulav* (equaling 4.8). *Tsei meihem shlosha la'hadas ve'hashar la'lulav* — three units for the *hadas* and the remainder for the *lulav*.

This raises a further difficulty: *kashya de'Shmuel a'd'Shmuel* — Shmuel contradicts himself. Rav Yehuda cited Shmuel as saying the *shiur* of *hadas* and *aravah* is three *tefachim*; yet Rav Huna cited Shmuel as ruling *halacha k'Rabbi Tarfon* — we follow Rabbi Tarfon. If Rabbi Tarfon means three units of 1.2, requiring 3.6 normal *tefachim*, how can Shmuel also say simply "three"? The *gemara* answers: *lo dak* — Shmuel was not being precise when he said three; he was approximating. But the *gemara* objects: surely we would only accept imprecision in the direction of stringency (*l'chumra*), not leniency (*l'kula*). Rounding down from 3.6 to 3 would be a leniency, which is not how we apply the principle of *lo dak*.

### 5/6 Tefach Standard

This leads to the alternative interpretation brought by Ravin when he arrived from Eretz Yisrael. Ravin reverses the direction of the calculation. Rather than taking a six-*tefach amah* and dividing by five (yielding a 1.2 unit), Ravin says: take a *short amah* of only five *tefachim* and divide it into six parts. Each resulting unit is therefore 5/6 of a normal *tefach*. Use those smaller *tefachim* to measure the requirements: three units of 5/6 for *hadas* and *aravah* yields 2.5 normal *tefachim*; the remainder for *lulav*.

This is a significant leniency, particularly for the *hadas*: the minimum requirement for the braided-leaf portion of the *hadas* reduces to two and a half normal *tefachim*, rather than three. Given how difficult it is to find *hadasim* with properly braided leaves running for an extended length, this becomes an important practical *halacha*.

Now *Shmuel*'s statement that the *shiur* is three makes sense: *lo dak l'chumra* — he was approximating upward, rounding 2.5 to 3. That is acceptable imprecision since it is in the direction of stringency. And the ruling *halacha k'Rabbi Tarfon* means: we use the 5/6 *tefach* standard, so the effective minimums are 2.5 *tefachim* for *hadas* and *aravah* and a proportionally adjusted amount for the *lulav*.

The practical takeaways from this entire section are substantial: the standard regarding split leaves, the question of bending (forward versus backward, and how much), the critical issue of the *nechleka hatayomes* and Rashi's relatively lenient definition of it, the question of whether the *lulav* spine must protrude above the bundle, and finally the issue of minimum sizes and the use of the 5/6 *tefach* standard to make the *hadas* requirement more achievable.

---

## Hadas Specifics

### Hadas Invalid Cases

We turn now to the next *mishnah*, which addresses the *hadas*. The structure of the *mishnah* mirrors that of the *lulav mishna* with adaptations for the particular characteristics of each species. *Hadas ha'gazul ve'ha'yavesh pasul* — if it is stolen or dried, it is invalid. *Shel asherah v'shel ir ha'nidachat pasul* — if it comes from an *asheira* or from an *ir nidachas*, it is invalid. *Niktam rosho, nifretzu alav* — if its head was cut off or its leaves fell off, it is invalid. These applications require no additional discussion, as they follow directly from what was established regarding the *lulav*.

### Berries Problem

The *mishnah* then introduces a disqualification unique to the *hadas*: *o she'hayu anavav merubot me'alav pasul* — if there were more berries than leaves on the *hadas*, it is invalid. The *hadas* can grow berries, and if the berries come to outnumber the leaves, the character of the branch changes — it is no longer predominantly a leafy branch of the type required. *Ve'im mi'atan kasher* — if one removes enough berries to restore the predominance of leaves, it is valid. However, *ve'ein mematin b'Yom Tov* — one may not pluck the berries on *Yom Tov* itself. The reason for this restriction will require further discussion.

### Anaf Etz Avot

The *gemara* then moves to the identification of the *hadas* from the verse *anaf etz avot* — a branch of braided wood. The *gemara* derives that the *anaf* must be one whose leaves cover the branch — *she'anavav chofin et etzo* — and from this concludes: *hevei omer zeh hadas* — this must be the *hadas*. But how do we know that? Why not another tree?

### Eliminating Trees

The *gemara* runs through several candidates and eliminates them. *Teima zeita* — perhaps an olive branch? No: *be'inan avot ve'leika* — we require braided leaves, and the olive does not produce them. *Ve'teima dulba* — what about the *dulba*, which Rashi identifies as the chestnut (*etz armon*)? Here the problem is the opposite: *be'inan anafav chofin et etzo ve'leika* — the chestnut may produce braided leaves but they do not cover the branch. *Ve'teima hirduf* — what about the *hirduf*, which does have braided leaves that cover the branch, but whose leaves are spiky and sharp and will cut the hand? Abaye responds: *deracheha darchei noam ve'leika* — the Torah's ways are pleasant, and such a branch would injure those who hold it; the Torah could not demand this. Rava adds a further scriptural grounding: *ha'emet ve'hashalom ehavu* — love truth and peace — and Rashi connects this to the requirement that what one holds in hand be something one can hold in peace, without injury. Whether the Sages truly reasoned to the identification of the *hadas* through these eliminations, or whether — as the Rambam maintains — they already knew it from transmitted tradition and were simply showing how it can be derived from the verses, is the underlying question that runs through this entire series of discussions.

---

# Sukkah 34

## Dichuy & Berries

### Dichuy Intro

The daf begins slightly before the formal start of 34, on 33b, with the words *ve'ein mematin beyom tov* — one may not reduce the berries of the *hadas* on *Yom Tov*. The surrounding sugya has been wrestling with the question of *dichuy bi-mitzvot*: whether a *mitzvah* object that was initially unfit at the moment it became designated for the *mitzvah* retains a permanent status of rejection, even after it subsequently becomes fit. Up to this point, the *Gemara* has deliberately avoided reaching any definitive conclusion on this question. Now the final clause of the *mishnah* — the prohibition against removing berries on *Yom Tov* — opens a new avenue of inquiry.

### Black Before Yom Tov

The *Gemara* poses the case of *ha'avar ve-liktan*: suppose one transgressed and actually did pick the berries on *Yom Tov* — what is the status of the *hadas*? The implication of the *mishnah* is *kasher*: one is not permitted to do so, but if it was done, the *hadas* is rendered valid. The *Gemara* then asks: when precisely did the berries turn black? If the answer is *de-ashchar me'etmol* — they were already black before *Yom Tov* began — then from the very moment this *hadas* entered the category of the *mitzvah* on *Yom Tov*, it was already unfit. This is *dichuy mei'ikara*: the object was pushed away from the outset. And yet by picking the berries one can render it *kasher*. The *Gemara* therefore says: *tifshot mineh dichuy mei'ikara delo havei dichuy* — one should be able to infer from this that initial rejection does not necessarily constitute an irreversible disqualification.

### Black During Yom Tov

As an alternative reading, the *Gemara* proposes: perhaps the berries were fine when *Yom Tov* began and only turned black during *Yom Tov* itself. If so, the *hadas* was fit at the outset and then became unfit — this is the category of *nireh ve-nidcheh*, something that was seen and then rejected. In that case, one could infer *shema mina nireh ve-nidcheh chozer ve-nireh* — something that was fit, became disqualified, can return to fitness.

The *Gemara* notes that of the two categories, *dichuy mei'ikara* is actually the less troubling case. If an object was never fit even when the *mitzvah* framework began, it is more as though it was simply not yet ready, and its subsequent fitness is less fraught. The case of *nireh ve-nidcheh* — where the object was fully within the category, was actively rejected, and then became fit again — is the stronger and more problematic form of *dichuy*. Since one of the two cases must be operative whenever berries are picked on *Yom Tov*, at minimum something must be valid.

### Conclusion on Dichuy

The *Gemara* concludes by conceding the less contested inference: *dichuy mei'ikara* — initial unfitness — is not a disqualifying problem. If the berries were black when *Yom Tov* began, the *hadas* was unfit from the start, yet removing the berries renders it valid. This much one can prove from the *mishnah*. However, the *Gemara* declines to extend this inference to *nireh ve-nidcheh*: one cannot necessarily prove from this case that something which was fit and then became disqualified can recover its fitness. The case may well have been one of *dichuy mei'ikara* all along.

It is worth noting that the *Gemara's* argument could be pushed even further: one might contend that there is simply no concept of *dichuy bi-mitzvot* at all. What the *Gemara* is saying is: even granting that such a concept exists, at minimum we see that *dichuy mei'ikara* presents no obstacle. The broader question of whether *dichuy* applies at all remains in suspension. A related but distinct question — whether the relevant concept for *kodshim* is *dichuy* or *hutra*, i.e., whether a prohibition is merely pushed aside or fully released — is a different inquiry entirely; the *dichuy* discussed here is not about overriding a prohibition but about the stigma that attaches to a *mitzvah* object that was rejected.

## Picking Berries Issue

### Prohibition Stated

The *Gemara* now turns to the reason underlying the prohibition itself. A *baraita* states: *ein mematin be-Yom Tov* — one may not reduce the berries on *Yom Tov*. Yet *mishum Rabbi Elazar berabi Shimon amru mematin* — in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, it is taught that one may remove them. The *Gemara* challenges: is one not thereby performing *tikkun mana* on *Yom Tov*, actively fixing an object into a state of ritual fitness? Rav Ashi answers: the case in question is one where one picks the berries in order to eat them — *kegon she-liktan le-achilah*. The intent is culinary, not to repair the *hadas*.

### Psik Reisha Concept

The *Gemara* then explains the underlying rationale for Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's leniency: he follows his father Rabbi Shimon's ruling that *davar she-eino mitkaven mutar* — an act performed without intent to produce a prohibited consequence is permitted. One is eating the berries; one is not intending to render the *hadas* fit for the *lulav*.

The *Gemara* immediately raises the objection articulated by Abaye and Rava: *modeh Rabbi Shimon bi-psik reisha ve-lo yamut* — even Rabbi Shimon concedes that the principle of *ein mitkaven* does not apply in a case of *psik reisha*, the proverbial "cut off its head and will it not die?" When a prohibited consequence is absolutely certain — not merely possible — one cannot disclaim intent. The classic illustration is dragging a bench across soft ground: if one genuinely cannot predict whether a furrow will be formed, one may invoke *ein mitkaven*. But if the ground is so soft and the bench so heavy that a furrow is inevitable, the consequence cannot be treated as unintended. Applied here: once the berries are removed, the *hadas* is necessarily rendered fit — assuming nothing else is wrong with it. That being the case, the fixing is a *psik reisha* and cannot be waved away as unintended.

### Rashi Explanation

The *Gemara* resolves this by saying: *de-it leih hoshanah achriti* — the person already has another *hadas*. Rashi and Tosafot disagree sharply on what this fact changes.

According to Rashi, the answer is straightforward. The question of whether one has "fixed" the *hadas* is not purely a matter of objective physical reality but of contextual significance. When one already has a complete and ready *lulav* bundle — with *hadas* and *aravah* already assembled — and is picking berries from a different *hadas*, that other *hadas* is simply not being perceived or experienced as a *mitzvah* object requiring repair. It is like plucking grapes from a cluster. In a context where no one is treating this *hadas* as something to be fixed, the act of removing its berries does not constitute the "fixing" of a ritual object. The transformation from "disqualified *hadas*" to "qualified *hadas*" only registers as a meaningful act of *tikkun* when there is a need for it to serve in that capacity. According to several *rishonim*, including the Rambam, even intentional removal of the berries does not constitute a biblical *melacha*, since the concept of qualifying a *hadas* for *lulav* is too amorphous to constitute *maka b'patish* or *boneh*. Given that the act is at most of rabbinic concern, and given that in this context the person did not need or perceive it as a repair, it is as though nothing of substance was done.

### Tosafot Explanation

Tosafot offers a different and far-reaching explanation. Tosafot invokes the principle of *psik reisha delo nicha lei*: yes, it was a necessary consequence — we do not dispute that the *hadas* became fit — but it was a consequence the person had no interest in whatsoever, since he already had another *hadas*. Since the outcome was both undesired and irrelevant to him, it cannot be attributed to him as an intentional act. Tosafot goes further and compares this to *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*: the act was performed, but not for the inherent purpose of that prohibited act, and therefore it cannot be fully tagged as his doing.

The distinction between Rashi and Tosafot here is significant. For Rashi, the case is local: in this particular context, with another *hadas* already available, the act objectively did not constitute a meaningful *tikkun*. For Tosafot, the case illustrates a general halachic category — *psik reisha delo nicha lei* — applicable wherever a *psik reisha* produces a result the actor genuinely has no interest in. Tosafot's principle became a dominant and widely accepted category in the laws of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, though it should be noted that the *Gemara* itself never states it explicitly; it is derived by Tosafot and other *rishonim* from cases such as this one.

One might ask: what about the analogous case of dragging the bench — if one is completely indifferent to whether a furrow forms, is that *psik reisha delo nicha lei*? According to Tosafot's position, the answer is yes. The *rishonim* do not distinguish between *lo nicha lei* — actively not wanting the result — and *lo ichpat lei* — simple indifference. Either way, if the consequence is genuinely of no concern to the actor, it falls within this more lenient category.

## Lulav Knot on Yom Tov

### Vegetable Bundle Tying

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* addressing a practical problem: *hutar agdo be-Yom Tov ogdo ke-agudah shel yerek* — if the knot of the *lulav* bundle comes undone on *Yom Tov*, one reties it in the manner of a vegetable bundle, meaning one simply wraps the binding around and tucks it in, without making a formal knot. This is because making a proper knot on *Yom Tov* is prohibited.

### Rabbi Yehuda Knot Req.

The *Gemara* asks: *Ha mani* — whose view does this represent? Why should one be limited to the wrap-and-tuck approach? Why not make a proper *aniva*, a bow knot? The *Gemara* answers: *Rabbi Yehuda hi de'amar aniva keshira ma'alya hi* — the *baraita* follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds in another context that a bow knot constitutes a fully prohibited knot for purposes of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. Accordingly, even a bow knot would be forbidden.

But there is a further layer to Rabbi Yehuda's position. Rabbi Yehuda holds *lulav tzarich eged* — the *lulav* requires a formal binding. For him, the *mitzvah* demands a real, halachically recognized knot. Since such a knot cannot be made on *Yom Tov*, a *lulav* whose binding has come undone on *Yom Tov* simply cannot be corrected according to Rabbi Yehuda. The *Gemara* concludes that the *baraita* reflects a *tanna* who agrees with Rabbi Yehuda in one respect — that a bow knot on *Yom Tov* is prohibited — but disagrees in another: this *tanna* holds that one is *yotzei* with a *lulav* even without a formal binding. Therefore, while the *lulav* is technically valid even without the knot, if one wants to retie it on *Yom Tov*, the most one may do is the vegetable-bundle style wrap.

### Rashi on Real Knot

Rashi offers an important comment here. On the word *alei*, Rashi states: *be-lulav de-ein tzarich eged* — a *lulav* does not require binding, which is why a mere tucking-in suffices, since *bedi'avad* one is *yotzei* even without any knot. Rashi then draws a further inference: *shema mina de-be'inan be-lulav kesher gamur she-yikshor shenei rashei ha-eged* — we learn from here that the knot demanded for the *lulav* must be a complete, formal knot, meaning one ties both ends of the binding. *Ve-ogdan ke-agudah shel yerek, lav eged hu* — merely wrapping it in the vegetable-bundle fashion does not constitute a proper *eged* according to Rabbi Yehuda.

Rashi then adds a crucial clarification: *afilu Rabbanan de-paligi alei de-Rabbi Yehuda ve-amrei lulav she-eino agud kasher, modu de-mitzvah le-ogdo* — even the Rabbis who rule that an unbound *lulav* is valid *bedi'avad*, would agree that it is a *mitzvah* to bind it properly, as derived from *zeh eli ve-anvehu*. *Ve-kayma lan ke-Rabbanan.* The halacha follows the Rabbis.

This is a critical point. When the *Gemara* says the Rabbis concede that binding is a *mitzvah* on account of *zeh eli ve-anvehu*, is this merely an aesthetic preference, or does it mean that the *lechatchila* standard of the Rabbis demands the same quality of knot that Rabbi Yehuda requires as a matter of strict law? Rashi indicates clearly: the *lechatchila* requirement for the Rabbis is a full, halachically recognized knot — a double knot — not a mere bow knot or tuck.

### Modern Practices

This leads to a practical question about the accordion-style holders commonly used today. The question is whether such a holder constitutes a proper *eged* according to this analysis. Either one does not require a double knot for the Rabbis' *lechatchila*, or one holds that any form of permanent securing — even without a classic double knot — would satisfy the requirement, potentially even according to Rabbi Yehuda. A preferable approach, consistent with Rashi's position, is to use actual strips — for instance, a *lulav* leaf split into thin strips, which have excellent tensile strength — and tie genuine double knots at multiple points along the bundle. Such an approach satisfies the *lechatchila* requirement of the Rabbis as Rashi understands it and likely Rabbi Yehuda's requirement as well, while also producing a result that is aesthetically unified and natural-looking. It also happens to be the practice of *Minhag Chabad*.

A related question concerns the slipknot rings often placed on the *lulav* itself. Those are used to bundle the *lulav* leaves prior to combining with the other *minim*. The halacha of *eged* applies specifically to binding the *lulav* together with the other *minim*; there is no *eged* requirement for the *lulav* itself considered in isolation. Accordingly, those rings are halachically unproblematic for that purpose, though one may prefer the consistency of the strip-binding method throughout.

## Aravah vs Tzaftzafah

### Aravah Disqualifications

The *mishnah* now turns to the *aravah*: *aravah gezulah ve-yaveshah pesulah* — a stolen or dried-out *aravah* is invalid. *Shel ashera ve-shel ir ha-nidachas pesulah* — one from a tree worshiped as an idol or from a condemned city is invalid. *Niktam rosho, nifretzu alav* — if its top is cut off or its leaves have fallen off, it is invalid. *Tzaftzafah* — a certain species of willow-like plant — is similarly invalid. On the other hand, *kemusheh* — a wilted *aravah* — or one from which some leaves have fallen, or one that grows in an unirrigated field (*shel ba'al*), is *kesheirah*.

Rashi, commenting on the phrase *aravah gezulah ve-yaveshah pesulah*, notes: *lulav d'lachem akula hu kai* — the requirement of *lachem*, derived from the verse *u-lekachtem lachem*, applies not only to the *lulav* and *esrog* but to the *hadas* and *aravah* as well. This observation is somewhat surprising given that the same comment could have been made earlier in the chapter by the *hadas*. More significantly, Rashi's formulation here frames the disqualification of a stolen *aravah* entirely in terms of ownership, setting aside the separate concept of *mitzvah haba'ah ba'aveirah*.

### Arvei Nachal Defined

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita*: *arvei nachal ha-gedelim al ha-nachal* — the willows of the river are those that grow by the river, and *davar acher: arvei nachal she-aleh shelahen mashuch k'nachal* — another characterization: their leaves are elongated like a river. This second description will prove important in distinguishing the valid *aravah* from the invalid *tzaftzafah*, which has rounded rather than elongated leaves.

### Arvei Nachal Anywhere

A second *baraita* addresses the geographic requirement: *arvei nachal — ein li ela arvei nachal* — one might think only those that literally grow by the river qualify. But what of those that grow in a field, surviving on rainfall, or on the mountains? *Talmud lomar arvei nachal mikol makom* — the plural form *arvei* serves to include all specimens of the species wherever they grow. The Rashash adds a lovely observation: the word *nachal* carries two meanings — wadi and river — and accordingly the *baraita* contrasts two distinct cases: growing in a field (not by a river) and growing in the mountains (not in a wadi). Neither geographic restriction applies. What matters is the species, not the location of growth.

This raises a question: given that the Torah says *arvei nachal*, is there a *lechatchila* preference for willows that actually grow by the river? Rashi, in his first comment on the *Gemara*, states *mitzvah be-zo* — there is indeed a *lechatchila* consideration to obtain willows that grow by the river, though the absence of this quality does not invalidate.

The *baraita* continues. At the top of 34a, Abba Shaul derives from the plural *arvei* a different teaching: *achas le-lulav ve-achas le-mikdash* — one *aravah* for the *lulav* and one for the Temple. This is his basis for the existence of two distinct *mitzvot* of *aravah*: the *aravah* that is part of the *lulav* bundle, and the separate Temple *aravah* performed by circling the altar, which we will encounter later in the tractate. The Rabbis, who would derive the number two from the plural *arvei* differently, ask regarding the Temple *aravah*: *l'mikdash minalan* — from where do they derive it? The answer: *hilkheta gemiri lah* — it is a received tradition, a *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*.

This is articulated by Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *asara netiyot, aravah, ve-nisukh ha-mayim — halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — three practices are *halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*: the law of the ten saplings in a *shemitta* field, the Temple *aravah*, and the water libation. Rashi suggests that these three were simply taught together in the *beit midrash* at the same time. But there is likely a deeper connection: all three relate to water. The *aravah* grows by water, the water libation involves water directly, and the law of the ten saplings concerns irrigation and the working of the land in relation to the *shemitta* year.

Tosafot raises a pointed question. Tosafot asks: according to Abba Shaul, who uses the double form *arvei* to derive two *mitzvot* of *aravah* — one for the *lulav* and one for the Temple — how does he know that a *shel harim*, a mountain-grown *aravah*, is still valid for the *lulav*? He lacks the plural derivation to include it. Tosafot suggests that perhaps for Abba Shaul, only willows that literally grow by the river are valid. Tosafot then considers whether this might apply to us as well, since later the *Gemara* will derive the requirement of *two aravos* from the plural *arvei*. If we use that plural to teach the number two, perhaps we cannot simultaneously use it to include non-riverbank willows. Tosafot concludes that it would then be required *lechatchila* to use only willows that grow by the river. This is not the accepted practice — it would constitute an unusual *chumra* — but the derivational problem Tosafot identifies is real.

### Tzaftzafah Verse

Returning to the *baraita*: *arvei nachal ha-gedelot al ha-nachal — prat le-tzaftzafah ha-gedeilah bein he-harim* — this excludes the *tzaftzafah* species, which fundamentally grows in the mountains. The point is not about where a particular specimen happens to grow, but about the identity of the species itself. The *tzaftzafah* is a different kind of plant whose natural habitat is the mountains rather than the riverbank, and it does not qualify as *arvei nachal* regardless of where it actually grows.

Rabbi Zeira asks: *mai kra* — is there a verse that establishes the *tzaftzafah*'s inferior status? He cites: *kach al mayim rabbim tzaftzafah samo* — it had been taken upon many waters, yet it was made into a *tzaftzafah*. This verse, which appears in a context of rebuke directed at Israel, describes something that used to stand by great waters and has now become a *tzaftzafah*, implying that the *tzaftzafah* is a lesser plant — specifically, one that does not grow by the waters.

Abaye challenges: *ve-dilma perushei kamfaresh* — perhaps the verse is simply identifying the term, meaning: that which grows on many waters, what is it called? A *tzaftzafah*. Maybe it is not a diminished plant at all. Rabbi Zeira responds: *im kein mai samo* — if so, what does *samo* mean? The word implies transformation into something lesser: it *was* a noble riverbank plant and *became* a *tzaftzafah*. This establishes that the *tzaftzafah* is categorically distinct from and inferior to the *aravah*, and is not the species designated for the *mitzvah*.

Rabbi Abbahu expounds the verse homiletically: *ani amarti she-yihyu Yisrael lefanai ke-kach al mayim rabbim* — God said the Jewish people should stand before Him like the species taken for the *mitzvah*, flourishing upon many waters. *Ve-hein samu atzman ke-tzaftzafah she-be-harim* — but they made themselves like the *tzaftzafah* of the mountains, pushing themselves outside the holy framework. A variant tradition embeds this verse directly in the *baraita* rather than having Rabbi Zeira cite it, with Rabbi Zeira then raising the objection against it and receiving the same resolution.

### Physical Characteristics

Having established that the *tzaftzafah* is an invalid species, the *Gemara* now provides the physical criteria by which valid and invalid specimens are distinguished. A *baraita* asks: *eizu aravah ve-eizu tzaftzafah* — which is the *aravah* and which the *tzaftzafah*?

The *aravah* has three identifying features: *kanah shelah adom* — its twig is red; *aleh shelah mashoch* — its leaf is elongated; *u-piha chalak* — its leaf edge is smooth. The *tzaftzafah* is the opposite in all three respects: *kanah shelah lavan* — its twig is white; *aleh shelah agol* — its leaf is round; *u-piha domeh le-magal* — its leaf edge resembles a scythe, i.e., it is serrated.

This raises an obvious question: what is the status of a specimen that has some but not all of the *aravah*'s characteristics? Tosafot addresses this directly. Tosafot argues that since the *baraita* already stated the three positive signs of the *aravah*, it could have stopped there — anything lacking these three qualities would be invalid. The fact that the *baraita* then spells out the three negative signs of the *tzaftzafah* must be to teach a leniency: only if a specimen possesses all three negative characteristics is it disqualified. A specimen that has some of the negative features but not all may still be valid. This is a strikingly lenient reading, driven by the structural redundancy of the *baraita*.

In practice, this is relevant because valid *aravos* are not always textbook specimens. The twig is not always red — some may have turned color — and the leaves vary considerably in shape across specimens.

### Chilfah Gila Species

The *Gemara* now presents a complication. A second *baraita* states: *domeh le-magal kasher* — a leaf resembling a scythe is valid; *domeh le-masar pasul* — a leaf resembling a saw is invalid. This appears to contradict the previous *baraita*, which listed scythe-like serration as one of the disqualifying characteristics of the *tzaftzafah*. 

The distinction is between two types of serration. A saw (*masar*) has teeth that project symmetrically on both sides, cutting in both directions. A scythe (*magal*) has serrations that all angle in one direction, cutting only on one stroke. These are two different physical profiles and apparently two different halachic categories.

Abaye resolves the apparent contradiction: *ki tanya hi be-chilfah gila* — the leniency in the second *baraita* refers specifically to a species called *chilfah gila*. Rashi explains: *chilfah gila min aravah kesheira hi, u-piha domeh le-magal, aval she'ar aravah piha chalak* — the *chilfah gila* is a species of valid *aravah* whose leaf edge happens to be scythe-like serrated; for all other *aravah* species, the edge must be smooth. This shows that the physical characteristics are not fully universal rules but species-specific markers, and there exist subspecies of valid *aravah* that display features which in other contexts would be disqualifying.

Tosafot draws on this to reinforce the lenient ruling articulated above: the *chilfah gila* is presumably valid because, although it has serrated edges, its other two characteristics — twig color and leaf shape — are those of a valid *aravah*. It does not possess all three negative signs, and therefore it remains within the category of *arvei nachal*. This supports Tosafot's general reading that only the full combination of all three disqualifying features renders a specimen invalid.

Abaye adds: *shema mina hai chilfah gila kashra le-hoshana* — we may infer from the fact that the *Gemara* had to identify this species by name that it is indeed a valid *aravah* for the *lulav* bundle. One might have thought that since it carries a descriptive qualifying name — *chilfah gila* rather than simply *aravah* — the *shem livai*, the attached designation, disqualifies it. The *Gemara* responds: *arvei nachal amar Rachmana mi-kol makom* — the Torah's plural *arvei nachal* serves to include all subspecies of the *aravah* family, provided they are genuinely within that family. The *tzaftzafah* is excluded not because of a *shem livai* but because it is fundamentally a different species that does not belong to the category that grows by the *nachal*. The *chilfah gila*, as a subspecies of genuine *aravah*, is fully included.

One clarification regarding the *ba'al* reference in the *mishnah*: the term *shel ba'al* does not distinguish between irrigated and non-irrigated fields, but rather contrasts with growth specifically by the river. Whether a field is irrigated artificially or depends on rainfall is irrelevant; what matters is whether the plant is of the *aravah* species, not how it is watered.

### Names Changed Post-Destr…

Rav Chisda teaches: *hani telat milei ishtanu shemayehu mi-de-charav Beis HaMikdash* — the following three things had their names reversed from the time the Temple was destroyed. *Chilfasa aravsa, aravsa chilfasa* — what used to be called *aravsa* (the valid willow species) is now called *chilfasa*, and what used to be called *chilfasa* (the invalid species, comparable to *tzaftzafah*) is now called *aravsa*. The practical implication — *le-lulav* — is that if one wants to identify the kosher *aravah* species today, one should ask for what people call *chilfasa*, since the names have inverted.

*Shipura chatzotzarta, chatzotzarta shipura* — what used to be called a *shofar* is now called a *chatzotzeret* (trumpet), and vice versa. The practical implication — *le-shofar shel Rosh HaShanah* — is that if one goes to purchase a *shofar* for Rosh HaShanah and uses the word *shofar*, one may be handed a trumpet. One must ask for a *chatzotzeret* to receive the proper instrument. Rashi clarifies that this is not about a metal instrument versus an animal horn; rather, the distinction is between a straight instrument and a bent one, and the *halakha* requires a bent *shofar* for Rosh HaShanah. This name reversal explains the formulation in the *She'iltos* — the Geonic work — which states that Jews are obligated to sound the *chatzotzarta* on Rosh HaShanah, reflecting the linguistic shift in which the word *chatzotzeret* had come to denote the *shofar*.

*Patorta patora, patora patorta* — two different words for tables of different sizes had their names exchanged. The practical implication — *le-mekach u-memkar* — is for commercial transactions: one must know which word refers to which size in order to specify correctly what one is buying or selling.

Abaye adds to this list: *beis kasei hovleila, hovleila beis kasei* — the names of two internal organs of an animal were reversed. The practical implication — *le-machat ha-nimtzeis be-ovi beis ha-kosos* — concerns the halachic status of a needle found within the walls of one of these organs, a question that will receive full treatment in tractate Chullin.

Rava bar Yosef further adds: *Bavel Borsif, Borsif Bavel* — what used to be called Bavel is now called Borsif, and vice versa. The practical implication — *le-gitei nashim* — concerns the *Gemara* in Gittin that exempts a *shaliach* bringing a *get* from Bavel from the requirement to declare *bifnai nichtav u-bifnai nechtam*. This exemption applies to the area that used to be called Bavel, which is now referred to as Borsif. As both Rashi and Tosafot note, the *nafka mina* cannot be about what one writes in the *get*, since countries are not specified in a *get*, only cities. The relevance is strictly to which geographic area benefits from the Bavel exemption in Gittin.

## Species Quantities

### R. Yishmael Quantities

The *mishnah* now turns to the number of each species required for the *lulav* bundle. Rabbi Yishmael says: three *hadassim*, two *aravos*, one *lulav*, and one *esrog* — precisely the practice observed today. He adds, however, that even two of the three *hadassim* may be *ketumim*, i.e., with their tops cut off, provided one is intact.

### R. Tarfon Position

Rabbi Tarfon says: *afilu sheloshtam ketumim* — all three *hadassim* may have their tops cut off. This is a notable leniency, and it raises an immediate question: why is the issue of *katum* apparently exclusive to *hadas*? Why is there a separate halachic treatment of whether the head may be cut for *hadas* but not for *aravah*? Rashi explains: *delo ba'ei hadar be-hadas* — Rabbi Tarfon holds that *hadar* is not required for the *hadas*. Yet this is puzzling. If *hadar* applies to *lulav* and *aravah*, why should *hadas* be uniquely exempt? One might argue that a *hadas katum* does not aesthetically undermine the *hadar* quality to the same degree as a *lulav* or *aravah* with its head cut off. But Rashi's formulation — that *hadar* is not required in principle for *hadas* — remains difficult to fully account for.

### R. Akiva One Each

Rabbi Akiva says: *keshem she-lulav echad ve-esrog echad kach hadas echad ve-aravah achas* — just as there is one *lulav* and one *esrog*, so too one *hadas* and one *aravah*. This position stands in striking contrast to Rabbi Yishmael's, who derives three *hadassim* from the three words in *anaf etz avos* and two *aravos* from the plural *arvei*. It is worth noting in this context a remarkable *midrash* associated with Rabbi Akiva, in which he describes each of the *arba'ah minim* as corresponding to the Holy One Blessed be He — *lulav zeh HaKadosh Baruch Hu, esrog zeh HaKadosh Baruch Hu, hadas zeh HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — evoking a profound kabbalistic sensibility in which the four species represent different aspects of the divine being united in the act of *lulav*. The simplicity of Rabbi Akiva's numerical position — one of each, corresponding to the oneness of the divine — may not be coincidental.

### Etrog Binding

The *mishnah* in the *baraita* also records the view of Rabbi Eliezer, who asks: *yehi esrog imahem ba-agudah achas* — should the *esrog* perhaps be bound together with the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *aravah* in a single bundle? The response is: the verse does not connect *peri etz hadar* to *kapos temarim* with a *vav*. The conjunction *vav* appears between *kapos temarim ve-anaf etz avos ve-arvei nachal* — linking *lulav*, *hadas*, and *aravah* into one grouped unit — but *peri etz hadar* stands apart, without a connecting *vav*. This teaches that the *esrog* is held separately, not bound into the same bundle as the other three.

### Taking All Together

The *baraita* then asks: *u-minayin she-me'akvin zeh et zeh* — how do we know that all four species are mutually indispensable, such that lacking any one of them renders one not *yotzei*? The answer is derived from the word *u-lekachtem*: *she-tehei lekichah tamah* — the taking must be complete. One must take all four species; one cannot be *yotzei* with fewer. It is worth noting that while the taking may be sequential — picking up the *lulav*, then the *hadas*, then the *aravah*, then the *esrog* — the requirement of *u-lekachtem* means all four must ultimately be held. None can be omitted.

## Hadassim Quantity Halacha

### R. Yishmael Questioned

The *Gemara* poses the challenge against Rabbi Yishmael's position. His ruling — that three *hadassim* are required, yet two may be *ketumim* — is internally inconsistent. *Ei shelemim ba'ei, benei nami kuleihu* — if whole *hadassim* are required, all three should be required to be whole. *Ei lo ba'ei shelemim, afilu chad nami lo* — if whole ones are not required, then even one intact *hadas* should be unnecessary. Rabbi Yishmael's position that two may be cut but one must be whole seems to lack a coherent rationale.

### R. Yishmael Reversal

The *Gemara* resolves this: *chazar bo Rabbi Yishmael* — Rabbi Yishmael reversed his position. Rashi explains: he reversed himself from the requirement of three, ultimately conceding that *bedi'avad* one *hadas* suffices. It is this underlying position — that really only one *hadas* is strictly necessary — that explains why two may be *ketumim* even while one must be intact. Still, one must admit the resolution feels somewhat awkward; Rabbi Yishmael's original formulation does not obviously convey that one *hadas* is the core requirement and the other two are supplementary.

### Halacha Like Tarfon

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *halacha ke-Rabbi Tarfon* — the *halakha* follows Rabbi Tarfon, who permits all three *hadassim* to be *ketumim*. This is a striking ruling, and it amplifies the difficulty noted above: if all three may have their tops cut off, what does this mean for the requirement of *hadar* vis-à-vis the *hadas*? The question of why the *hadas* alone is treated differently in this regard — whether because *hadar* does not apply, or because *katum* does not undermine *hadar* in this context — remains significant.

### Shmuel Market Threat

The *Gemara* adds: *va-azda Shmuel le-ta'amei* — Shmuel acted consistently with this ruling in practice. He issued a warning to the *hadas* merchants: *azlu ve-zabinu* — go and sell at reasonable prices, *ve-i lo, darshina lechem ke-Rabbi Tarfon* — and if you do not, I will publicly expound the position of Rabbi Tarfon, ruling that *hadassim* with cut tops are valid. Once people know they can fulfill the *mitzvah* with *ketumim*, the merchants would lose the premium they charged for intact specimens.

### Why Tarfon Threatens

The *Gemara* notes that this threat is more effective than it might first appear. One might ask: why threaten with Rabbi Tarfon and not with Rabbi Akiva, whose position is even more lenient — requiring only a single *hadas*? The answer: *telata ketumei shechichi, chad ve-lo katum lo shechich* — three *ketumim* are commonly available and easy to find, whereas a single perfectly intact specimen is actually harder to come by. Paradoxically, requiring three while permitting all to be *ketumim* makes the *mitzvah* far easier to fulfill than requiring only one but demanding it be intact. By invoking Rabbi Tarfon, Shmuel's threat would flood the market with easily obtainable *ketumim* and collapse demand for premium specimens — a more potent economic lever than citing Rabbi Akiva.

Rashi clarifies: this also serves as evidence for why Shmuel genuinely ruled like Rabbi Tarfon and was not merely issuing an empty threat. Since Rabbi Tarfon's position turns out to be the more threatening one, the fact that Shmuel invoked it rather than Rabbi Akiva suggests he was working from his actual *psak*. Still, the deeper halachic puzzle remains: if we rule like Rabbi Tarfon that all three may be *ketumim*, what is the principled basis for treating *hadar* differently for *hadas* than for the other species? This question will bear further examination.

# Sukkah 35

## Multiple Hadasim/Aravot

### Excess Hadasim/Aravot

The daf picks up at the *mishnah* at the bottom of 33b. Before moving to the *mishnah* itself, two prefatory observations are worth noting. The first concerns a widespread practice — attested already among the *rishonim* and continuing to this day — of taking many more than the minimum number of *hadasim*, and sometimes also *aravot*. The obvious question this raises is how such a practice is permitted, given the general principle of *bal tosif*: adding to a *mitzvah* beyond its prescribed form.

### Tosafot: Not Bal Tosif

*Tosafot*, in the discussion beginning *arba nachal shtayim*, addresses this directly. *Tosafot* writes that *afilu noten kama hadasim ve-kama aravot be-lulav ein zeh bal tosif* — even if one takes many, many *hadasim* and *aravot*, this does not constitute *bal tosif*. The qualification is *afilu man d'tzarich eged*, that even according to the opinion that requires a binding, the problem only arises *ella im ken mosif min acher* — if one adds an extraneous species. The statement clearly reflects and seeks to justify a widespread practice.

### Min vs. Max/Yishmael

One way to understand why adding more *hadasim* and *aravot* is not a violation is to read the prescribed numbers as a minimum rather than a maximum. This reading gains support from the structure of the *arba minim* itself: the *lulav* and *etrog* are singular by nature, while the *hadasim* and *aravot* are inherently grouped as bunches, with the numbers three and two representing merely the minimum size of each bunch. This conceptual framing also helps explain the position of Rabbi Yishmael, who permits two of the *hadasim* to be trimmed at the top while one remains intact. If the *hadasim* are conceived less as discrete individual units and more as a collective bunch, this allowance becomes considerably more intuitive.

---

## Etrog Invalidity Cases

### Gazul/Yavesh/Ashera

The *mishnah* opens its treatment of the *etrog* with several cases of invalidity that parallel the structure seen in earlier *mishnayot* for the other *minim*. An *etrog ha-gazul*, a stolen *etrog*, is *pasul*. An *etrog ha-yavesh*, a dried-up *etrog*, is likewise *pasul*. An *etrog shel ashera* — from a tree used for idolatrous worship — or *shel ir ha-nidachat* — from a condemned city — is also *pasul*.

### Orlah Requirement

The *mishnah* then introduces a category unique to the *etrog*: *shel orlah pasul* — an *etrog* from a tree within its first three years of growth is invalid. As will be developed in the *Gemara*, the *etrog* carries a distinct requirement that it be edible, or at least potentially edible, in order to be *kosher*. The *orlah* prohibition, which bars consumption of the fruit during those years, thus strikes at this foundational requirement.

### Terumah Cases

The *mishnah* continues: *shel trumah tmei'ah pasul* — a *tamei* *terumah* *etrog*, which cannot be eaten, is invalid. By contrast, *shel trumah tehorah* — a *tahor* *terumah* *etrog*, which may be eaten by *kohanim* — presents a different picture: *lo yitol*, one should not take it *lechatchila*, *ve-im natal kasher*, but if one did take it, it is valid. The reasons for the *lechatchila* prohibition will be examined in the *Gemara*.

### Demai Dispute

*Shel demai* — an *etrog* from an *am ha-aretz* whose tithing status is uncertain — is the subject of a dispute. Biblically, one may assume such produce is permissible, but the Rabbis required the separation of *trumot u-ma'asrot* nonetheless. The one thing one could assume had already been separated is *terumah gedolah*, so the produce occupies a kind of intermediate status. *Beit Shammai poslin* — *Beit Shammai* declares it invalid — *u-Beit Hillel machshirin* — and *Beit Hillel* declares it *kosher*. It is presumably self-evident that ordinary *tevel*, untithed produce, would be invalid since it cannot be eaten.

### Ma'aser Sheni

*Shel ma'aser sheni bi-Yerushalayim* raises a case where the *etrog* is indeed edible — in fact there is a *mitzvah* to eat it — but one's relationship to it as owner may be constrained. The *mishnah* rules *lo yitol* — do not take it *lechatchila* — *ve-im natal kasher* — but if one did take it, it is valid. The rationale for both the prohibition and the *bediavad* validity will be examined in the *Gemara*, but the recurring structure is already apparent: edibility, or the potential for it, is the central criterion.

### Aesthetic Defects

The *mishnah* then turns to aesthetic defects. *Alta chazazit al rubo* — if a wart-like growth covers the majority of the *etrog* — it is invalid. *Natal pitamto* — if the *pitam*, the small mushroom-shaped protrusion at the top, has been removed — it is invalid. *Niklaf* — if peeled — *nisdak* — if cracked — *nikav ve-chasar kol shehu* — if it has a hole and something is missing as a result — these are all invalid. Conversely, if the *chazazit* is on a minority of the *etrog*, if the *oketz* (the stem) was removed rather than the *pitam*, or if there is a hole but nothing is actually missing, then *kasher* — the *etrog* remains valid.

### Color/Size Debates

The *mishnah* closes with questions of color and size. *Etrog ha-kushi pasul* — a black *etrog* is invalid. If it is as green as a leek (*yarok ke-karti*), *Rabbi Meir machshir* — Rabbi Meir declares it valid — *Rabbi Yehuda posel* — Rabbi Yehuda declares it invalid. On size: *Rabbi Meir omer ke'egoz* — the minimum is the size of a walnut — while *Rabbi Yehuda omer ke-beitzah* — the minimum is the size of an egg. As for the maximum, Rabbi Yehuda requires that one be able to hold two in one hand; Rabbi Yose permits one so large it requires both hands to hold. As was noted in an earlier *Gemara*, these debates need not be read purely as disputes about *hadar* — beauty — but may reflect questions about *gmar peira*, whether the fruit is considered fully ripened and complete, or concerns about dropping it in the case of excessive size.

---

## Etrog Species ID

### Hadar Definition

The *Gemara* opens at the top of 35b. *Tanu rabbanan*: *pri etz hadar* — the fruit of a beautiful tree — is interpreted as *shetaam etzo u-piryo shaveh*, a tree whose wood and fruit share the same flavor. The reading draws on the juxtaposition of *pri* and *etz*: just as there is a *midrash* on *maaseh bereishit* where God commands *etz pri oseh pri* — that the wood of the tree itself should taste like its fruit — so here the *Torah* alludes to a tree whose bark carries something of the taste of its fruit. *Hevei omer zeh etrog* — this must refer to the *etrog*. While one need not assume the bark is digestible, it does carry that characteristic taste.

### Pepper Vine Example

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *ve-eima pilpelin* — perhaps this refers to pepper? Pepper, it turns out, is a perennial woody vine whose vine itself apparently carries a peppery flavor. The *Gemara* supports this identification from a *baraita*: *hayah Rabbi Meir omer*, since the verse dealing with *orlah* says *u-netaatem kol etz* — you shall plant any tree — and then speaks of the fruit, why must it specify *etz maachal*, a food tree? *Mah talmud lomar etz maachal* — to tell us that even the tree itself is a food, that its wood carries the taste of the fruit. *Hevei omer zeh pilpelin* — this refers to the pepper vine. The *baraita* derives two lessons from this hint: first, that peppercorns are obligated in *orlah*, lest one think that since they grow on a vine they are not considered fruit; and second, *ve-ein eretz Yisrael chasera klum* — the land of Israel lacks nothing, even peppercorns, as the verse says *lo techsar kol bo*. So one might conclude that the pepper vine, whose bark tastes like its fruit, is the *pri etz hadar*.

### Pepper Impracticality

The *Gemara* rejects this possibility: *mishum d'lo efshar* — it is simply not feasible. *Heichi na'avid* — what would one do? *Ninkot chada* — take one peppercorn? *Lo mitchazei lekichato* — that would not constitute a visible, evident act of taking, as the verse *u-lekachtem lachem* implies. *Ninkot tray o tlat* — take two or three? But *amar rachmana pri etz hadar* — the *Torah* says one fruit — *velo shenayim ve-shlosha peirot* — not two or three fruits. *Hilkach lo efshar* — therefore, pepper is impossible. This continues the pattern seen throughout the *arba minim*: the *Gemara* attempts to derive the identity of each species from descriptive language in the verse. As the *Rambam* notes, it is difficult to imagine that the identity of these species was genuinely unknown and discovered only through *drashot*, since the language is vague enough to admit other possibilities. The *Rambam*'s position is that the identifications were always known through tradition and the *Gemara* is retroactively anchoring them in the text.

### Dir as Pen

*Rebbi omer*: *al tikrei hadar* — do not read it as "beautiful" — *ela ha-dir* — read it as a pen, an enclosure for animals. *Ma dir zeh*, just as a pen contains *gedolim u-ktanim*, older and younger animals, and *temimim u-va'alei mumim*, unblemished and blemished ones — *hacha nami*, so too an *etrog* comes in large and small, perfect and imperfect, and one encounters *etrogim* of widely varied shapes. The *Gemara* pushes back: *atu shear peirot leis bo gedolim u-ktanim temimim u-va'alei mumim* — don't other fruits also come in varying sizes and degrees of perfection? The *Gemara* answers: *ela hachi kama* — the real point of the *derasha* is *ad she-ba'im ktanim adayin gedolim kayamim* — while new fruits are already blossoming, the older fruits from the previous year are still present on the tree. The *dir* image, then, is not merely about variety within a single year, but about the *etrog* tree bearing fruit simultaneously from multiple growing seasons.

It is worth pausing to note the suggestive associations embedded in *Rebbi*'s formulation. This is the second time the *sugya* has forged a connection between the *lulav* and *korbanot*. The opening of the *sugya* derived the concept of *mitzvah ha-ba'ah ba-aveirah* from verses about *korbanot*, and now *Rebbi* invokes the imagery of a livestock pen — explicitly using the language *temimim u-va'alei mumim*, which is the precise vocabulary of blemish inspection applied to sacrificial animals. The *etrog* is, in a sense, the one object in contemporary religious life that receives something approaching the rigorous inspection once applied to *korbanot* in the *Beit Hamikdash*. The association with *Sukkot* more broadly is worth considering: to the extent that *Sukkot* connects to the *Mishkan* — given the approximate timing of its construction — and stands in the immediate aftermath of *Yom Kippur*, the holiday carries a pronounced *mikdash* dimension. Additionally, the seventy bulls of the *Musaf* offerings throughout *Sukkot* reinforce this linkage to the sacrificial system.

### Dir as Dwelling
