*Rabbi Abbahu amar*: *al tikrei hadar* — do not read "beautiful" — *ela hadar* — read it as "dwells." *Davar she-dar be-ilano mishana le-shana* — something that dwells on its tree from year to year. This conveys the same essential point as *Rebbi*'s teaching — that the *etrog*'s fruit persists on the tree across multiple years — but through a different reading of the root *dalet-vav-resh*, as *dar*, to dwell, rather than *dir*, a pen. Both *Rebbi* and *Rabbi Abbahu* arrive at the same conclusion by different routes, each working within the awareness that the identification of the *etrog* is the given answer.

### Idur/Water Etymology

*Ben Azzai omer*: *al tikrei hadar* — do not read it as "beautiful" — *ela hadur* or *idur* — *she-ken bi-leshon Yavani korin le-mayim idur* — for in Greek, the word for water is *idur*. The *etrog* is thus described as a water tree: *ve-eizeh zeh she-gadel al kol mayim* — what is a tree that grows on all types of water, whether irrigated or rain-fed? *Hevei omer zeh etrog* — it is the *etrog*. The Greek word *idur* appears to correspond to the classical Greek *hydor*, as in *hydro-*, which helps make sense of a term that sounds nothing like modern Greek *nero*. Whether the intent is that the *etrog* requires abundant water or that it can thrive under varied water conditions is not entirely clear.

### Ramban Etymology

The *Ramban al ha-Torah* offers a complementary observation: the Aramaic word for beautiful is *mirageg*, and he speculates that the word *etrog* itself may be an Aramaic term essentially meaning "beautiful." If so, *hadar* in the verse and *etrog* as the name of the fruit may be near-synonymous — both denoting beauty — making *hadar* not merely a descriptor but, in effect, the very name of the fruit. Just as we have fruits named for their qualities (the Ramban's point evokes the way fruit names can encode descriptions), *etrog* and *hadar* may represent the same semantic content in two languages.

---

## Heter Achila/Din Mammon

### Ashera/Ir Hanidachat

Having identified the *etrog*, the *Gemara* returns to the cases in the *mishnah*. The invalidity of *ashera* and *ir ha-nidachat* — both mentioned at the *mishnah*'s opening alongside *gazul* — follows the same logic applied to the other *minim*: *keivan de-lisreifa ka'i*, since such objects are condemned to burning, *kitutei mechtat shiu'rei*, it is as though they are already reduced to nothing, their legal substance dissolved, and they can no longer function for a *mitzvah*. (The analysis of *gazul* and the question of whether invalidity flows from ownership on the first day or from *mitzvah ha-ba'ah ba-aveirah* on subsequent days was addressed in the earlier treatment of the *lulav*.)

### Orlah Reasons

The *Gemara* now turns to the novel requirements specific to the *etrog* — the various conditions requiring that it be fit for consumption. *Orlah pasul* — an *etrog* from *orlah* is invalid. *Mai ta'ama* — what is the reason? *Pligi ba Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba ve-Rabbi Ami* — it is the subject of a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Ami. *Chad amar lefi she-ein ba heter achila* — one holds it is invalid because the *etrog* has no *heter achila*, no halachic permission to be eaten. *Ve-chad amar lefi she-ein ba din mamon* — the other holds it is because there is no monetary value to it: *orlah* is *asur be-hana'ah*, forbidden to derive any benefit from, and anything from which one may not benefit is considered halachically worthless.

A brief note on the *orlah* case: even though there may technically be some unusual, indirect benefit one could theoretically derive, the halachic consensus is that this does not matter. Since ordinary benefit is forbidden, the object is treated as valueless. The classic illustration is a man who attempts to betroth a woman with an object of *orlah* — the betrothal does not take effect because the object lacks even a *shaveh prutah*, a penny's worth of legal value.

The two positions differ in what they emphasize about the word *lachem* — "yours" — in the verse *u-lekachtem lachem*. According to *Rashi*, followed by *Tosafot*, both reasons are variations on the same *lachem* requirement: one emphasizes the practical inability to eat it, the other the accounting sense that it has no value and thus cannot be truly "yours." According to *Rashi*, then, these are two formulations of a single ownership deficiency, which would suggest that the problem would apply only on the first day, when *lachem* is operative. The *Rambam* in *Peirush Hamishnayot* takes a markedly different approach: *heter achila* is not about ownership at all, but about the definition of *fruit*. The verse says *pri etz hadar* — how can something be called a fruit if it cannot be eaten? Even if what prevents its consumption is halachic rather than physical, that prohibition undermines its very identity as fruit. According to the *Rambam*, therefore, the inability to eat would invalidate the *etrog* on all seven days, not only the first.

### Heter/Mammon Debate

The *Gemara* proceeds on the assumption that these two positions are mutually exclusive: *man d'ba'ei heter achila lo ba'ei din mamon* — whoever requires edibility would not require monetary value — *u-man d'ba'ei din mamon lo ba'ei heter achila* — and whoever requires monetary value would not require edibility. What scenarios illustrate the difference? *Rashi* points to *ma'aser sheni* in *Yerushalayim*: one is not only permitted to eat it but obligated to do so, yet Rabbi Meir holds that *ma'aser sheni* is *mamon gavoha* — God's property — not the individual's, analogous to *kohanim* eating *korbanot* where the *mitzvah* to eat belongs to them but the *korban* does not. So *ma'aser sheni* in *Yerushalayim* represents something with *heter achila* but potentially without *din mamon*. Conversely, *Rashi* gives *tevel* as an example of something with monetary value — since once *terumos u-ma'asrot* are separated it will be fully edible, it retains real market worth — that nonetheless cannot be eaten.

### Consensus Heter Achila

The *Gemara* now tests whether the two positions are truly independent. The *mishnah* rules that *terumah tmei'ah* is invalid. *Bishlama l'man d'amar lefi she-ein bo heter achila* — if the requirement is edibility, this is straightforwardly explained: *terumah tmei'ah* cannot be eaten. But *l'man d'amar lefi she-ein bo din mamon* — what of the position that only monetary value matters? *Terumah tmei'ah* may be used as fuel to heat a pot, *masika tachat tavshilo* — surely that gives it monetary value and makes the holder an owner? The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *b'heter achila kuli alma lo pligi d'ba'ina* — everyone agrees that *heter achila* is required. All the cases in the *mishnah* are disqualified precisely because they lack *heter achila*. This is also consistent with the *Rambam*'s position that edibility is necessary to define something as fruit, and with *Rashi*'s position that edibility defines ownership in the context of *lachem*.

### Din Mammon Extra

The remaining debate, then, is narrower: *ki pligi* — where they actually disagree — is on *din mamon*. *Mar savar heter achila ba'inan din mamon lo ba'inan* — one holds that edibility is sufficient and no additional monetary requirement is needed — *u-mar savar din mamon nami ba'inan* — the other holds that even given *heter achila*, one must also establish full technical monetary ownership. This is an additional layer beyond the agreed-upon baseline.

### Ma'aser Sheni Test

*Mai beinayhu* — what case would distinguish these two positions? *Ika beinayhu ma'aser sheni she-bi-Yerushalayim* — the difference is *ma'aser sheni* in *Yerushalayim*, and specifically *va-aliba de-Rabbi Meir*, according to Rabbi Meir who holds it is *mamon gavoha*. *Heter achila* is certainly present — there is an obligation to eat it. But according to Rabbi Meir, the ownership is God's, not the individual's. If *heter achila* alone is sufficient, one would fulfill the *mitzvah*; if *din mamon* is also required, one would not — since, per Rabbi Meir, one is not the technical monetary owner. The *Gemara* identifies this as the position of Rabbi Assi: *tistayem*, it is proven that Rabbi Assi is the one who requires *din mamon* as an additional criterion, for Rabbi Assi states explicitly that an *etrog shel ma'aser sheni*, according to Rabbi Meir, would not fulfill one's obligation on *Yom Tov*, whereas according to the *chachamim* — who hold that *ma'aser sheni* is the individual's property — it would.

---

## Terumah/Demai Analysis

### Terumah Tehoah

The *Gemara* now proceeds through the individual cases of the *mishnah*. *Terumah tmei'ah* is straightforward: *leit bei heter achila* — it cannot be eaten. But *terumah tehorah* presents the more interesting question. *Bediavad* one is *yotze* because *terumah tehorah* is edible — a *kohen* can eat it — but *lo yitol lechatchila*, one should not take it initially. Why not?

### Machshira/Mafsida

*Pligi bar Ami ve-Rav Assi* — it is a dispute. *Chad amar mishum de-machshira* — one holds the concern is that taking the *etrog* together with the *lulav* — which is kept in water to stay fresh — causes the *etrog* to come into contact with water, thereby rendering it *mekabel tum'ah*, susceptible to *tum'ah*. Once a detached fruit comes into contact with water, it becomes susceptible. The best protection for the *terumah* is to prevent that susceptibility in the first place. *Ve-chad amar mishum de-mafsida* — the other holds the concern is that daily handling causes the rind to wear away, damaging the *terumah* through repeated use.

### Rind Exclusion Test

*Mai beinayhu* — what would distinguish these two positions? The *Gemara* constructs the following test case: *kegon de-kara lei shem chutz mi-klipata ha-chitzonis* — suppose one designated this *etrog* as *terumah* but specifically excluded the outer rind, making only the inner flesh *terumah* while the rind retains ordinary status. Is it possible to make such a designation? Yes: one may define which portion of one's produce constitutes the *terumah* separation. Practically, when the time comes to give the *etrog* to the *kohen*, one would say: here is your *terumah* — but return the rind, which I never made *terumah*.

In this scenario: *l'man d'amar mishum de-machshira* — if the concern is susceptibility to *tum'ah* — *ika*, the problem remains. When water contacts the outer rind and renders it *mekabel tum'ah*, the *tum'ah* does not stop at the rind; the entire fruit becomes *tamei*. *Man d'amar mishum de-mafsida* — if the concern is wasting *terumah* — *leika*, no problem, since the rind is not *terumah* and wearing it away causes no loss of consecrated material.

If one did take such a *terumah* *etrog*, *lechatchila* or *bediavad*: *lem'an d'amar mipnei she-ein bah heter achila* — if the criterion is edibility — *harei yesh bah heter achila* — it is clearly edible, whether by the *kohen* directly, or because one can give it to a *kohen* to eat. *Tosafot* addresses the implicit question here: even if the non-*kohen* owner cannot personally eat it, the fact that he controls who eats it — he can give it to a *kohen* son-in-law or the like — is sufficient to constitute the ownership relationship that *lachem* requires. *Lem'an d'amar mipnei she-ein bah din mamon* — if the criterion is also full monetary ownership — *harei yesh bah din mamon* — the owner of *terumah tehorah* is certainly its full monetary owner. The interesting edge case left unexplored is where *terumah* has been separated but not yet given to a *kohen*: there the original owner controls its disposition but is arguably no longer its true owner, raising a genuine question about whether the *lachem* requirement would be met.

### Demai Lechatchila

*Shel demai* — the *mishnah* records a dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*. *Beit Hillel* permits the use of a *demai* *etrog* and considers one *yotze bediavad*, while *Beit Shammai* invalidates it. *Mah ta'ama de-Beit Hillel* — why does *Beit Hillel* permit it? *Kivan de-i ba'ei mafkir le-nichsei ve-havei ani ve-chazi lei* — because one could renounce all one's possessions, become legally poor, and then eat the *demai* oneself, since the Rabbis waived the tithing requirement for the poor. Therefore *lachem karena bei* — it retains the quality of "yours."

*Tosafot* points out that this reasoning is actually stronger than necessary: even without the theoretical *hefker* pathway, as long as there exists someone who can eat the *demai* — such as a poor person to whom one could give it — that should suffice for *heter achila*, just as with *terumah tehorah*. And one certainly owns it outright. The *Gemara*'s reasoning is therefore something of an overstatement.

### Ani Eats Demai

*De-tnan* — we learned in the *mishnah*: *machilin et ha-aniyim demai ve-et ha-achsenia demai* — one may feed *demai* to the poor and to quartered soldiers. This is the source that a poor person is permitted to eat *demai*. *U-Beit Shammai* — and *Beit Shammai*'s position — *ani lo achil demai* — a poor person is not permitted to eat *demai* according to *Beit Shammai*, as a *baraita* cited by Rav Huna confirms: *Beit Shammai omrim ein machilin et ha-aniyim ve-et ha-achsenia demai*, *Beit Hillel omrim machilin*. This is *Beit Shammai*'s grounds for disqualification: since *demai* cannot be eaten in its current state even by a poor person per *Beit Shammai*, there is no *heter achila*, and the *etrog* is invalid.

A clarification on the nature of the *demai* leniency for the poor: *demai* is not treated as *ma'achalot asurot* in the ordinary sense. The Rabbis imposed the obligation to tithe it, but did not transform the *cheftza* of the produce into a prohibited substance. It is a Rabbinic obligation with built-in weakness — an acknowledgment that the produce is quite likely already tithed — and so the Rabbis waived the requirement for the poor entirely. This is different from other Rabbinic prohibitions, where poverty would not be grounds for a general waiver.

### Ma'aser Sheni Rules

*Uma'aser sheni bi-Yerushalayim* — the *mishnah* rules one is *yotze*, and the *Gemara* has already analyzed this case at length. *Leman de-amar mamon gavoha hu lo ka machshir* — the question, per Rabbi Meir's position that it is God's property, is whether *din mamon* is required in addition to *heter achila*. The *lechatchila* prohibition parallels that of *terumah tehorah*: if the concern is susceptibility to *tum'ah*, that applies equally here since one may not render *ma'aser sheni tamei*; if the concern is causing material loss through handling, that likewise applies. *Ve-im natal keshera* — and if one took it, it is valid — with the same analysis as above applying: according to all who require only *heter achila*, one is *yotze* even according to Rabbi Meir, since the ability to eat is present; and for those who also require *din mamon*, the *chachamim* who hold that *ma'aser sheni* is the individual's property would render one *yotze*, and indeed the *mishnah*'s ruling reflects their view.

---

## Aesthetic Defects

### Chazazit Majority

The *Gemara* now turns to the aesthetic defects enumerated in the *mishnah*, beginning with *chazazit* — a wart-like growth. Rav Chisda transmits a teaching in the name of *rabbeinu ha-gadol*, identified by *Rashi* as Rav — noting, *Hamakom yihiye b'ezro* — that Rav said: *lo shanu ela b'makom echad* — when is a *chazazit* covering the majority of the *etrog* invalid? Only when it is concentrated in one location.

### Chazazit Minority

However, Rava challenges this: *aderaba* — quite the contrary — *b'shenayim u-shlosha mekomot havlei ke-manumar pasul* — if the growth is spread over two or three places, it looks spotted and mottled, which is worse, not better, and should therefore be invalid. *Ela i itmar a-seifa itmar* — Rava therefore argues that Rav's teaching was not said on the opening case of a majority, which is invalid regardless of location, but on the closing case: when *chazazit* is on a minority, the *mishnah* says it is *kosher*. On that Rav adds: *lo shanu ela be-makom echad* — this *kashrut* applies only when the warts are gathered in one place. *Aval bi-shnayim u-shlosha mekomot havlei ke-manumar u-fasul* — but if spread over two or three places, it appears spotty and mottled, and is therefore invalid even though each individual wart affects only a minority. What began as a seeming leniency — the minority case being valid — thus generates a significant stringency: even two warts in different locations invalidates.

### Chotam Strictness

*De-amar Rava* — Rava further adds: *ve-al chotmo* — if a *chazazit* appears on the *chotam*, the upper slope of the *etrog* where the body begins to narrow upward toward the top — *va-afilu be-mashehu nami pasul* — even the smallest blemish there invalidates. *Rashi* identifies the *chotam* as the portion where the *etrog* begins its upward taper, literally its "nose." This strictness regarding the upper portion of the *etrog*, particularly the slope leading to the *pitam*, underlies the careful examination many are accustomed to perform. While the *Gemara* is technically discussing *chazazit*, a wart-like growth, the heightened sensitivity at the *chotam* has informed the contemporary practice of scrutinizing even very small discolorations on the upper third of the *etrog*.

### Pitam/Oketz

*Nital pitamto* — if the *pitam* has been removed, the *etrog* is invalid. *Tani Rav Yitzchak ben Elazar*: *nital bochanto* — he clarifies the *pitam* by identifying it as the *bochna*, a pestle. The shape of a pestle — held at one end with a bulbous rounded knob at the other used for pounding — describes exactly the appearance of the *pitam*: a stem with a rounded protrusion at its top. This identification also makes clear which end is meant, resolving any ambiguity in the term.

### Pitam Location

Some *rishonim* actually identify the *pitom* as the opposite end — the stem end of the *etrog* rather than the apical protrusion. According to this view, the *pitom* is the portion embedded inside the fruit at the base, and its removal invalidates the *etrog*. This would then require distinguishing it from the *oketz*, the stem, whose removal the *mishnah* explicitly states does not invalidate. Those *rishonim* would say that the *oketz* is the external protrusion and the *pitom* is the internal structure, so that removing the outer stem is acceptable whereas disrupting the inner connection invalidates. The accepted *pesak*, however, follows the pestle identification: the *pitam* is the apical protrusion at the top, and this is obviously the more intuitive reading given *Rav Yitzchak ben Elazar*'s comparison to the knob end of a pestle.

One further observation regarding *Rashi* deserves mention in connection with the *terumah tehorah* case discussed earlier. *Rashi* there writes *harei yesh bah heter achila* and then adds *aval pidyon ein lah* — but it cannot be redeemed — apparently responding to an interpretation he had encountered that claimed the reason *terumah tehorah* has a *heter achila* is because one could redeem the *terumah* and then eat it freely. *Rashi* dismisses this as completely false — *terumah* cannot be redeemed — and then adds: *ve-ha-omer ken rasha hu* — and one who says so is wicked. The concern is not merely a mistaken interpretation but a dangerous one that would mislead people into thinking they could redeem *terumah* and render it permissible to non-*kohanim*. The force of *Rashi*'s language here — going beyond "incorrect" to "wicked" — reflects the severity of a ruling that would cause others to transgress.

---

---

# Sukkah 36

## Niklaf - Peeling

### Total vs. Partial Peeling

The daf opens at the very bottom of 35b, continuing the Gemara's analysis of the mishna's aesthetic requirements for the *etrog*. Having addressed the issues of protrusions and the *pitam* in previous sessions, the Gemara now turns to the question of *niklaf* — peeling.

Rava rules: an *etrog* that has been peeled like a red date is *kosher*. Yet the mishna explicitly states that a peeled *etrog* is *pasul*. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction with the formula *lo kashya*: the two sources address different scenarios. Where the *etrog* is entirely peeled, it is *kosher*; where it is only partially peeled, it is *pasul*. That is the reading of the Gemara as stated.

### Rashi v. Tosafot

Rashi explains the logic perhaps somewhat ironically: when the *etrog* is entirely peeled, it presents a uniform appearance; when it is only partially peeled, it looks blotchy and *menumar* — spotted — which the Gemara elsewhere treated as a disqualifying defect. It is that mottled, uneven appearance that renders it *pasul*.

Tosafot, however, approaches the question differently, anticipating the Gemara's imminent comparison between the defects of the *etrog* and the signs of *treifa* in animals. In the laws of *treifos*, an animal whose skin has been entirely stripped — a condition called *gluda* — is a *treifa*, while an animal that retains some of its skin can potentially regenerate and heal, and is therefore not disqualified. Extrapolating from this parallel, Tosafot argues that the same logic applies here in reverse: if some skin remains on the *etrog*, it is *kosher*; if the *etrog* is entirely peeled, it is *pasul*.

A natural question arises: if any portion of the outer layer is missing, does that not create a problem of *chaser* — the invalidity of a physically incomplete *etrog*? This distinction between *niklaf* and *chaser* is not entirely resolved, and it may be that *niklaf* refers only to the outermost thin layer of the rind rather than to the rind as a whole — something closer to flaking than to peeling the fruit bare.

---

## Nikav - Holes

### Through-holes & Chaser

The Gemara proceeds to *nistak* — cracking — and *nikav* — holes. A hole that causes missing flesh is a problem; a hole without *chaser* is not. On this latter category, Ulla bar Chanina offers a more precise formulation: a hole that passes completely through the *etrog* — *nekev mefulash* — is *pasul* even if it is the smallest possible size, even if nothing physically fell away from the fruit. If the hole does not go through and through, then it must be at least the size of an *issar*, a coin of modest but not negligible size, to be disqualifying.

### Limiting the Mishna

Both Rashi and Tosafot understand Ulla bar Chanina's ruling as a qualification of the mishna's statement that a hole without any missing flesh is valid. They read him as saying: not all such holes are valid. If the hole passes from one side of the *etrog* to the other — even without any physical material falling away, though one imagines that some juice would escape — that degree of penetration is sufficient to render it *pasul*. Similarly, even a hole that does not go all the way through is *pasul* if it is as wide as an *issar*, even without any portion of the *etrog* being physically absent.

---

## Treifa Signs & Etrog

### Three Treifa Parallels

The Gemara records Rava's query: *nolda be-etrog simanei treifa mahu* — what is the law if an *etrog* displays the signs that would render an animal a *treifa*? The Gemara immediately asks what the question is, since the mishna already covers each of the relevant defects. If the skin is peeled (*niklaf*), that corresponds to the *treifa* category of *gluda*, and the mishna addresses it. If it is cracked (*nistak*), that corresponds to a cracked trachea in *hilkhot treifos*, and the mishna addresses that too. And if it has a hole (*nikav*), the vast majority of *treifa* cases involve holes — in the lung, the heart, the intestines — and again the mishna deals with this. So what exactly is Rava asking?

The Gemara responds: Rava's question was framed *kide-Ulla* — along the lines of the ruling of Ulla, specifically as qualified by Rabbi Yochanan. Rabbi Yochanan stated that a lung that has liquefied on the inside, spilling out like liquid from a ladle, is nonetheless *kosher* — *ve-hu de-kaimi simponaha* — provided that the bronchial tubes, the inner structural channels of the lung, remain intact. If those structures are gone, then the animal is a *treifa*.

### Tosafot's Strict Reading

Before examining the substance of Rava's question, it is worth noting the remarkable interpretive stance of Tosafot across all three defect categories. Tosafot does not treat the analogy to *treifa* as a loose rhetorical parallel. He reads it with full legal precision. On *niklaf*, as noted, Tosafot holds that the *etrog* must be entirely peeled to be *pasul*, mirroring the rule for *gluda*. On *nistak*, Tosafot holds that the crack must run the entire length of the *etrog*, just as a disqualifying crack in the trachea must extend the full length from the lower to the upper cartilage. The parallel is being imported not merely in concept but in its specific parameters. Tosafot is assuming that the details of the *psulim* by *etrog* are to be learned directly from the corresponding *psulim* by *treifa*.

### Liquefied Insides

Rava's actual question, then, concerns the *etrog* whose interior has liquefied — where the flesh and juice of the fruit have turned to liquid. The baseline assumption of the Gemara seems to be that total liquefaction would render the *etrog pasul*, by analogy to the *treifa* lung. The question is whether the qualification that applied to the lung — that if the inner structural chambers (*simponaha*) remain, the animal is *kosher* — would likewise apply to the *etrog*. In the *etrog*, the flesh exists within a chamber structure, much like any citrus fruit. If the flesh has liquefied but the chamber walls remain intact, would the *etrog* remain valid, paralleling the lung?

The Gemara considers an argument for distinguishing the two cases. *Dilma hatam hu delo shalit bei avira* — perhaps the reason the lung can recover is that air does not have direct access to the interior, and therefore the remaining structure can heal. This is admittedly a striking observation given that the lung is the very organ through which air passes, and the Gemara acknowledges the irony. The point seems to be that while air cycles through the lung, the interior tissue is not directly exposed in the same way the inside of an *etrog* would be if it began to liquefy. The *etrog*, being exposed to air — *shalit bei avira* — would only continue to rot: *srochi masracha*. On the other hand, perhaps the rule is the same regardless, and as long as the inner chamber structure is present, the *etrog* remains valid.

### Tapuach Saruach Proof

The Gemara attempts to resolve this from the mishna's list. The mishna mentions *tapuach saruach* — an *etrog* that is bloated or spoiled — as *pasul*. The Gemara suggests: perhaps *tapuach* refers to external bloating and *saruach* refers to internal rot or liquefaction, and since both render the *etrog pasul*, we have our answer regarding internal liquefaction.

The Gemara rejects this reading: *idi ve-idi min ha-chutz* — both terms describe external conditions, not internal ones. The proof therefore fails. What is striking, as the Gemara itself makes clear, is the underlying assumption driving the entire discussion: if the insides were totally liquefied, the Gemara takes for granted that it would be *pasul*, despite the fact that this is purely internal and would present no external aesthetic problem at all. There is no obvious *hadar* violation if the inside has liquefied and the outside remains intact. And yet the Gemara treats the parallel to *treifa* as compelling enough to assume the *etrog* would be disqualified even in such a case — not because of aesthetics, but because the *treifa* analogy demands it. This is the third occasion in these sugyas where the laws of *korbanos* and temple-related aesthetics seem to be doing genuine legal work in defining the *etrog's* validity.

Tosafot raises an additional point here regarding *nikav*. In *hilkhot treifos*, a hole in the lung does not need to go from one wall of the lung through to the opposite wall; it need only penetrate the wall of the lung into the interior chamber. Tosafot therefore suggests that the ruling requiring a *nekev mefulash* — a hole that goes all the way through — applies specifically to those parts of the *etrog* where there is only a single wall and no inner chamber: namely, the top and bottom of the fruit. But in the middle of the *etrog*, where there is a rind and then an inner chamber beyond, a hole that penetrates as far as the inner chamber would already be *pasul*, just like a hole in the wall of a lung. The through-and-through requirement applies only where the structure is entirely wall, with no inner space. Again, Tosafot insists on applying the *treifa* parameters with remarkable precision.

---

## Invalid Etrog Types

### Mishna's Full List

The Gemara proceeds to a lengthy mishna cataloguing additional categories of invalid *etrogim*. The list includes: *tapuach saruach* — bloated or rotting; *kavush* — pickled; *shaluk* — boiled; *kushi* — Ethiopian or black; *lavan* — white; *menumar* — spotted; *ke-kadur* — perfectly spherical like a ball; *teyom* — a twin *etrog*, two fruits that grew joined together; *ha-boser* — unripe; and *gidlu b'dfus* — one that was grown in a mold and consequently looks like a completely different species of fruit.

This is a rich and varied list, encompassing defects of color, texture, shape, ripeness, and artificial manipulation. The remainder of this shiur works through these categories one by one.

One observation about the list as a whole: an attentive reader will notice that most of these defects are externally visible and relate directly to the *etrog*'s aesthetic presentation — its *hadar*. The internal liquefaction discussed in the previous segment stands apart as the only defect that would not necessarily be apparent from the outside, which underscores the observation that the *treifa* comparison is doing independent legal work beyond mere aesthetic judgment.

---

## Kushi - Black Etrog

### Ethiopian v. Black Defin…

The Gemara addresses *kushi*. The mishna states that a *kushi etrog* is *pasul*. But a *baraisa* seems to contradict this, ruling that a *kushi etrog* is *kosher*, while one that merely resembles a *kushi* is *pasul*. The *baraisa* thus appears to draw a sharp distinction: an *etrog* that is genuinely Ethiopian is valid, whereas one that has merely turned black while growing locally is not.

Abaye's initial response is that when our mishna calls a *kushi etrog pasul*, it means one that resembles an Ethiopian *etrog* — i.e., one that is black — rather than one that actually originated in Ethiopia. On this reading, both sources condemn the same thing: a locally grown *etrog* that has turned black, not a genuinely Ethiopian one.

### Regional Familiarity

Rava offers a different resolution: *ha lan ve-ha lehu* — one ruling is for us and the other is for them. According to Rashi, the mishna's disqualification of the *kushi etrog* reflects the standard for *Eretz Yisrael*, where Ethiopian *etrogim* are unfamiliar and would appear strange. The *baraisa*'s validation reflects the standard for *Bavel*, where the Jewish community lived in geographic proximity to Ethiopia — or at least had more regular commercial contact with it — and Ethiopian *etrogim* were not an unusual sight.

Rashi adds an important clarification: regardless of geography, everyone would agree that a locally grown *etrog* that turns black is *pasul*. This case is described with the term *bilas* — counterfeit — because such an *etrog* appears to be pretending to be something it is not: a Babylonian *etrog* impersonating an Ethiopian one. The authentic Ethiopian *etrog*, by contrast, is black because that is its natural character. In *Bavel*, where people encounter such fruits regularly, the natural black color of a genuine Ethiopian *etrog* does not strike observers as foreign or defective.

The note in Steinsaltz regarding geography is worth acknowledging: the *Rashash* observes that Ethiopia is actually closer to *Eretz Yisrael* than to Babylonia when measured overland. The response offered is that the land route from Ethiopia to *Eretz Yisrael* crosses the Sinai Desert and is exceedingly difficult, while the route to Babylonia, proceeding by sea across the Red Sea and up through the Persian Gulf region or along the Tigris and Euphrates, was more navigable. Rashi's geography thus implies that trade and familiarity with Ethiopian produce was more characteristic of the Babylonian Jewish community than of those in *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Subjectivity of Hadar

What makes this discussion particularly striking from a *halachic* standpoint is the implication that *hadar* — the beauty requirement for the *etrog* — is not a fixed, universal standard but contains a genuinely subjective, culturally relative element. The same *etrog* that is *kosher* in *Bavel* becomes *pasul* if transported to *Eretz Yisrael*, not because anything changed about the fruit itself, but because its appearance is unfamiliar and striking to a different population. Beauty, or at least the negative judgment that something is not beautiful, is partly a function of what one is accustomed to seeing. The same principle appears in other *halachic* contexts — most notably in the case of a *Kohen* with an unusual physical appearance who is exempt from *duchan* in his own city (*d'dash b'iro*), since his neighbors are accustomed to him and he will not cause distraction, but who may not lead services in a place where he is unknown.

### Bilas - Counterfeit

The distinction between the genuinely Ethiopian *etrog* and the locally grown black *etrog* turns on authenticity. The locally grown *etrog* that has turned black is *bilas* — counterfeit — because it is something presenting itself as what it is not. A Babylonian *etrog* that grows black carries an air of wrongness, a sense of inauthenticity, that is distinct from the natural character of a fruit that simply grows black because that is what its species does. The genuine Ethiopian *etrog* may look unusual to an *Eretz Yisrael* audience, but it is not pretending to be anything other than what it is.

---

## Boser - Unripe

### Akiva v. Sages

The mishna records a dispute regarding the *boser* — the unripe *etrog*. Rabbi Akiva declares it *pasul*; the Sages declare it *kosher*. The Gemara notes that Rabba identifies a parallel between Rabbi Akiva's position here and that of Rabbi Shimon in *Ma'asros*, where Rabbi Shimon rules that small, unripe *etrogim* are exempt from *ma'aser*. Rabba suggests that both sages share a common underlying position: an unripe *etrog* does not yet have the status of a fruit, and therefore Rabbi Akiva disqualifies it for *lulav* and Rabbi Shimon exempts it from *ma'aser*.

### Hadar v. Ripeness

Abaye challenges this linkage. The concern Rabbi Akiva addresses with the *boser* for *lulav* is aesthetic — the *etrog* must have *hadar*, and an unripe *etrog* lacks that beauty. This has nothing to do with whether the fruit has achieved full botanical status. Rabbi Akiva could simultaneously hold that it is indeed a *pri* — a fruit — and is *chayav* in *ma'aser*, while still ruling it *pasul* for *lulav* on purely aesthetic grounds.

Conversely, Rabbi Shimon's exemption of small *etrogim* from *ma'aser* does not necessarily mean he considers them non-fruits. The verse in *Ma'asros* requires *ma'aser* to be taken from produce *ke-derech she-b'nei adam motzi'im l'zri'ah* — in the manner that people use it for replanting — meaning the produce must have reached a stage of ripeness sufficient for its seeds to be viable for planting. An unripe *etrog*, even if it fully qualifies as a fruit, may not yet have reached the stage of *motzi l'zera*, and therefore Rabbi Shimon would exempt it from *ma'aser* without denying its status as a fruit. The two positions operate on entirely different axes and there is no necessary connection between them. Abaye's response is emphatic: *batlu midi* — enough, these are clearly unrelated concerns.

---

## Invalid Etrog Types (II)

### Molded Etrog (Dfus)

The mishna disqualifies an *etrog gidlu b'dfus* — one grown in a mold — if the mold caused it to look like a completely different species. Rava clarifies: this disqualification applies only when the resulting shape makes the *etrog* look like an entirely different creature. If the mold kept the *etrog* looking like an *etrog*, it is obviously *kosher*. The Gemara asks: is that not self-evident? The *baraisa* itself specifies *k'min birya acheret* — something that looks like a different species. What does Rava add?

Rava's *chiddush* addresses an intermediate case. What if the mold produced an *etrog* with a surface pattern of overlapping plates or ridges — *dapei dapei* — somewhat like the paddles of a water wheel, as Rashi describes? One might have thought that such a dramatically altered surface texture would render it a different kind of creature. Rava teaches that even this remains within *k'vriyaso* — it still looks like an *etrog* — and is therefore *kosher*. The threshold for being disqualified as a different species is quite high. Rashi reads this *le-kula*: even a markedly unusual texture remains within the acceptable range. The *etrog* can look quite strange and still be *kosher*, so long as it has not crossed into looking like an entirely different fruit altogether.

---

## Chanina's Bite - Holidays

### Rat Bites & Hadar

The Gemara introduces a dramatic case. An *etrog* in which rats have chewed — *esrog she-nikvu achbarim*. Rav rules: *ein zeh hadar* — such an *etrog* lacks *hadar* and is *pasul*. The Gemara immediately challenges this from the story of Rabbi Chanina: Rabbi Chanina was in the practice of dipping his *etrog* in salt — as was common, given the practice of dipping foods in condiments — and would take a bite from it, and then fulfill the *mitzvah* with that same bitten *etrog*. The question of *huktza l'mitzvah* — the prohibition against using a *mitzvah* object for personal use — is acknowledged but set aside for the moment.

If Rabbi Chanina took a bite from the *etrog* and used it, and the mishna states that a hole accompanied by missing flesh is *pasul*, how did Rabbi Chanina act as he did?

### Rashi: Two Problems

The Gemara resolves: the mishna's disqualification for *chaser* and Rabbi Chanina's practice are not in conflict because they address different days. The mishna's *psul* of *chaser* applies to *Yom Tov rishon*; Rabbi Chanina used his bitten *etrog* on *chol ha-moed*.

But this raises the question: why can the same logic not reconcile Rav's ruling with Rabbi Chanina? If the hole-*chaser* disqualification is limited to the first day, perhaps Rav's ruling that a rat-bitten *etrog* lacks *hadar* is similarly limited to the first day, and Rabbi Chanina used his *etrog* on the other days?

According to Rashi's reading — and this is the dominant *girsa* — this solution is unavailable. The reason is that Rav specifically invoked the language of *hadar*. And *hadar* is a seven-day requirement. If Rav's disqualification is grounded in the absence of *hadar*, then it is a disqualification that extends across all seven days of *Sukkos*, not merely the first. Rabbi Chanina's case, therefore, must be distinguished on a different basis.

Rav's response is that rats are *meisin* — particularly repulsive — in a way that human bite marks are not. The implication is that a human bite does not destroy the *etrog*'s *hadar*, while a rat bite does. Therefore, Rabbi Chanina's bitten *etrog* was still considered *hadar* and valid for all seven days, while a rat-bitten *etrog* lacks *hadar* throughout.

Rashi further explains that the mishna's disqualification for a hole with missing flesh is not a *hadar* problem at all — it is a separate *psul* derived from the word *u'lekachtem* and its implication of *lekichah tamah*, the requirement that the taking be complete, meaning the *etrog* itself must be whole. This is a *Yom Tov rishon* problem only, rooted in the specific wording of *u'lekachtem lachem ba-yom ha-rishon*. The two categories are thus: defects of *hadar*, which are disqualifying for all seven days; and defects of wholeness (*chaser*), which are disqualifying only on the first day.

### Alternative Girsa

Some *rishonim* possessed a different *girsa* of this Gemara, in which Rav's ruling — *ein zeh hadar* — is actually rejected by the Gemara. In this reading, the proof from Rabbi Chanina is not about reconciling rat bites with human bites; rather, the Gemara's conclusion is that even a *hadar* deficiency is only a first-day disqualification, not a seven-day one. Rabbi Chanina's use of the bitten *etrog* on *chol ha-moed* demonstrates not that the bite mark was still aesthetically acceptable, but that aesthetic deficiencies do not matter at all beyond the first day. Rav's principle — that *hadar* is a seven-day requirement — is simply rejected.

### Ashkenazi v. Sephardi

This dispute over *girsa* maps directly onto a major *halachic* disagreement between *Ashkenazim* and *Sephardim* that descends into the *Shulchan Aruch* and the *Rama*. The *Shulchan Aruch* rules that the *psulim* of *etrog* are largely confined to *Yom Tov rishon*, and on *chol ha-moed* one may use an *etrog* that would otherwise be disqualified. The *Rama*, reflecting the Ashkenazi tradition, rules that the *psulim* continue to apply through *chol ha-moed*. The distinction in *girsa* is thus not merely a textual curiosity but the foundation for a practical *halachic* difference observed to this day.

The term *Yom Tov sheini* as it appears in this sugya refers to *chol ha-moed*, not to *Yom Tov sheini shel galuyos*. The *rishonim* so understand it, and while there is some discussion about the matter, it appears that *Yom Tov rishon* and *Yom Tov sheini* here contrast the first day of the *chag* with its intermediate days, not the first day of *Yom Tov* with the second *Yom Tov* day outside *Eretz Yisrael*.

---

## Size Requirements

### Egoz v. Beitzah

The mishna addresses *esrog katan* — a small *etrog* — and the question of the minimum size. The Gemara, through Ravin bar Papa, notes a parallel: the same debate that governs the size of the *etrog* mirrors the debate over *avanim mekurzalos* — the stones used for personal hygiene in place of toilet paper. On *Shabbos*, the Sages permitted one to carry such stones into a *beis hakissei*, waiving the *muktzah* prohibition out of consideration for *kevod ha-beriyot*. The question of how large these stones should be is debated: Rabbi Meir says the size of a walnut (*egoz*); Rabbi Yehuda says the size of an egg (*beitzah*). In the context of the stones, this represents a *maximum* size — larger stones would be impractical. For the *etrog*, the same measures represent a *minimum* size.

Remarkably, it is the same Rabbi Meir who sets the minimum *etrog* size at an *egoz* who also sets the maximum stone size at an *egoz*, and the same Rabbi Yehuda who requires a *beitzah*-sized *etrog* who sets the maximum stone size at a *beitzah*. The Gemara does not suggest any logical connection between the two disputes; it is simply an observation of a consistent parallel. The context is unmistakably reminiscent of the discussion in *Berachos*, as the lecturer wryly observes.

Tosafot in *Shabbos* raises the question of whether the leniency regarding carrying these stones applies in later times, when people have fixed indoor bathrooms and could have prepared their toilet paper before *Shabbos*. Tosafot entertains the view that since preparation is now easy, one cannot claim the necessity that justified the leniency in Talmudic times when the outhouses were far out in the fields. However, Tosafot then considers the counterargument: in a household with many people, the supply of pre-cut paper may be exhausted, and in such circumstances — *lo efshar* — the leniency might still apply. The practical *halakha* in cases of genuine need on *Shabbos*, where *kevod ha-beriyot* is at stake, remains governed by the principle that *kevod ha-beriyot* overrides rabbinic restrictions, particularly when the underlying prohibition is itself of rabbinic character.

### Huge Etrog Story

Rabbi Yosi cites a story to establish that a very large *etrog* can also be *pasul*. Rabbi Akiva once came to the *beis ha-knesses* carrying his *etrog* on his shoulder — so enormous was the fruit. Rabbi Yehuda challenged him: is that really a proof? The very people around Rabbi Akiva said to him, *ein zeh hadar* — this is not beautiful. Sheer size, beyond a certain threshold, does not enhance the *etrog*; it detracts from it.

Rashi notes that the Gemara had earlier framed the maximum-size concern in practical terms: the *etrog* must be small enough to hold together with the *lulav* in one hand without dropping. Rabbi Yehuda, Rashi explains, does not abandon that practical concern, but adds that even apart from practicality, an *etrog* of extreme size fails the *hadar* standard on aesthetic grounds alone.

---

## Binding the Lulav

### Yehuda v. Meir

The mishna introduces a new topic: the binding of the *lulav*. The rule *ein ogdin es ha-lulav ela b'mino* — one may bind the *lulav* only with one of the *arba minim* — reflects the position of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Meir disagrees, permitting even a string or a band of any material.

### Jerusalem Practice

Rabbi Meir invokes a precedent: the people of Jerusalem would bind their *lulavim* with golden chains — *gimoniyos shel zahav*. The respondents to Rabbi Meir clarify: the golden chains were added decoratively, but the underlying binding at the base of the *lulav* was done with one of the *minim* themselves. The golden chain was an embellishment on top of a valid binding, not a substitute for it.

### Rava's Reasoning

Rava explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning. According to Rabbi Yehuda, *lulav tzarich egged* — the *lulav* requires formal binding to be valid; simply holding the three species together is insufficient. Given that the binding is a necessary component of the *mitzvah* object, Rava reasons that any material used for that binding becomes incorporated into the *mitzvah* object itself. Introducing material from outside the *arba minim* — a string, a cloth strip — would be adding a fifth species to what should be a four-species *mitzvah* object, contaminating it with something extraneous.

### Palm-tree Components

Rava continues: even within the requirement to use materials from the *minim*, the standard is generous. *Afilu b'siva afilu b'ikra d'dikla* — one may even use a vine-like strip from around a palm tree, or even a strip fashioned from the trunk of the palm tree itself. These materials need not be beautiful or aesthetically refined; the point is simply that they derive from the *lulav* tree. Rava's source for the principle that a vine or trunk strip from the palm counts as part of the same species comes from a *baraisa* to be discussed imminently.

---

## Sukkah Materials Debate

### Meir v. Yehuda

The *baraisa* Rava cites moves the discussion into the laws of *sukkah*. Rabbi Meir rules *sukkah shel kol davar* — one may construct the *s'chach* of the *sukkah* from any material. Rabbi Yehuda rules that the *sukkah* may only be constructed using the *arba minim*.

### Kal V'Chomer Rejected

Rabbi Yehuda offers a *kal v'chomer*: if the *lulav*, which is obligatory only during the day and not at night, must consist of the *arba minim*, then surely the *sukkah*, which is obligatory both day and night, should also require the *arba minim*. The *kal v'chomer* is bracing in its scope. The respondents reject it with a counter-principle: *kol din she-atah dan techilato le-hachmir ve-sofo le-hakel eino din* — any legal argument that begins as a stringency and ends as a leniency is invalid. What is the resultant leniency here? If a person cannot find *arba minim* to construct a *sukkah*, he will simply not sit in a *sukkah*. By setting an impossibly demanding standard, Rabbi Yehuda's stringency effectively permits people to exempt themselves from the *mitzvah* entirely. A *chumra* that prevents observance is, paradoxically, a *kula*. Such a *kal v'chomer* cannot stand.

### Torah's Purpose

The *baraisa* concludes by affirming Rabbi Meir's position in the most direct terms: *ba-sukkot teshvu shivat yamim sukkah shel kol davar* — the Torah commands dwelling in *sukkos* for seven days, and that *sukkah* may be made of any material. The Torah's purpose is to enable observance, not to erect barriers to it. The shiur closes with the note that this discussion will continue tomorrow, where the Gemara will develop further how Rava's broad definition of what qualifies from the palm tree informs the scope of what Rabbi Yehuda himself permits when binding the *lulav*.

---

---

# Sukkah 37

## Arba Minim for Agud

### Lulav Knot Debate

The daf opens at the very top of 37a, picking up from the *mishna*'s debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* regarding the material from which the knot of the *lulav* must be fashioned. According to Rabbi Yehuda, the binding must be made exclusively from the *arba'ah minim* themselves — from *min mino*, of the same species. An interesting question arises in passing: could one use a part of the *etrog* tree for this purpose? After all, the *eged* consists of three *minim*, not four, which would make a binding from the *etrog* tree somewhat anomalous. This is worth pausing over, though the *gemara* does not resolve it explicitly here.

### Rava's Logic

Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda's requirement is not an aesthetic point. Rather, it flows from the conceptual principle that the *lulav* requires a knot, and therefore to use anything extraneous to the *arba'ah minim* would be to add something foreign to the *mitzvah* object itself. Once we understand that this is the underlying rationale — and not aesthetics — it follows that even parts of the *lulav* tree that are not themselves beautiful, such as a strip of bark, may be used to tie the *lulav*. The bark of the palm tree is still part of that species and therefore not extraneous.

### Tree Parts & Minim

Rava goes further to demonstrate that even non-standard parts of the relevant trees — trunk, bark, and imperfect specimens — are halachically classified as part of the *arba'ah minim*. His proof comes from a fascinating debate about the *sukkah* itself, a debate that did not surface during the earlier chapters of the tractate. It is to this debate that we now turn.

---

## Sukkah & Arba Minim

### Baraita: Schach Rules

Near the bottom of 36b, Rava introduces a *baraita* that bears directly on his point. The verse *basukkot teshvu* — you shall dwell in *sukkot* — is interpreted by Rabbi Meir as permitting *sechach* made of any material, provided it meets the standard criteria of not being susceptible to *tumah* and growing from the ground. Rabbi Yehuda, however, takes a far more restrictive position: *ein sukkah noheget ela b'arba minim she'balulav* — the *sukkah* may only be made from the same *arba'ah minim* used for the *lulav*. That is, the *sechach* itself must consist of the four species.

### Kal VaChomer Issue

Rabbi Yehuda supports this position with a *kal vachomer*: if the *lulav*, which is not observed at night as it is during the day, nonetheless requires the *arba'ah minim*, then a *sukkah*, which is observed equally by night and by day, should certainly require the *arba'ah minim*. This is, admittedly, a peculiar *kal vachomer*. One can construct almost any stringency through such reasoning. Still, the argument has some intuitive pull, and we will shortly see *p'sukim* in Ezra that seem to link the two *mitzvot* and push in this direction.

### Rabbinic Pushback

The *chachamim* respond with a pointed methodological objection: *kol davar she'attah datcha techillato le'hachmir vesofo le'hakel eino din* — any *kal vachomer* that begins with a stringency but ends in a leniency is not a valid argument. The stringency here is obvious, but where is the leniency? The *gemara* transitions to 37a to answer this.

### Torah Overrides

*Lo matzah arba minim, yaishiv u'batel?* — If one cannot find sufficient *arba'ah minim* to cover a *sukkah* with *sechach*, should one simply not fulfill the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* at all? But the Torah says *basukkot teshvu shivat yamim* — you shall dwell in *sukkot* for seven days — and a *sukkah* made of any valid material satisfies that obligation. Rabbi Yehuda's stringency, taken to its logical conclusion, would cause people to forfeit the *mitzvah* entirely when they cannot source the required species. This is the *kula* embedded within the *chumra*.

This exchange carries an important broader lesson: nearly every *chumra* has an associated *kula*. One cannot simply assume that being *machmir* is automatically the safer course. Stringencies can exclude people, waste their time and money, and — most critically — push them away from performing the *mitzvah* altogether. A notable *teshuva* from Rabbi Yehuda Herzl Henkin in *Bnei Banim* makes precisely this point: one cannot reflexively play it safe by adopting a *chumra* without accounting for the *kulos* it necessarily produces.

---

## Ezra Pasuk Analysis

### Ezra's Plant List

The *gemara* adduces a verse from Ezra in support of both positions. When the returned exiles built their *sukkot*, the text instructs them: *tzu ha-har* — go out to the mountain — *ve-heviu alei zayit* — bring olive leaves — *ve-alei etz shemen* — and oil-tree leaves, presumably also a type of olive — *ve-alei hadas* — myrtle leaves — *ve-alei tmarim* — date leaves — *ve-alei etz avot* — which is also a variety of *hadas* — *la'asot sukkot ka-katuv* — to make *sukkot* as it is written. The verse is describing the construction of *sukkot* and it identifies specific plant materials, materials strikingly associated with the *lulav*. This lends real texture to Rabbi Yehuda's position.

### Olive Leaves Problem

And yet the very same verse undermines him. Among the materials listed is the olive branch — *alei zayit* — which is plainly not one of the *arba'ah minim* as Rabbi Yehuda understands them. If Rabbi Yehuda holds that *peri etz hadar* refers to the *etrog* and not the olive, then olive branches should not be appearing in this list as *sukkah* material. The *chachamim* seize on this: you see, they argue, the verse in Ezra proves that you may use materials *outside* the *arba'ah minim* for the *sukkah*.

### Tzadukim & Pasuk

It is worth noting at this point that certain Second Temple-era groups — most likely the *Tzedukim*, though possibly also the Karaites — read the verse *u-lekachtem lachem ba-yom ha-rishon peri etz hadar kapot tmarim* not as establishing a separate *mitzvah* of taking the *lulav* and *etrog*, but as instructing the people to gather these species and use them to construct the *sukkah*. On their reading, *u-lekachtem lachem* means: take these things and build your *sukkah* with them. There is no independent *mitzvah* of *netilat lulav* in their framework.

Some scholars suggest this may actually reflect the plain sense of that verse, and that the passage in Ezra-Nehemiah — originally one book — may have been written with precisely that reading in mind. On this interpretation, *peri etz hadar* would refer to the olive, with its beautiful, fruit-bearing tree producing oil. This would explain why olive branches appear in Ezra's list alongside the other species: they are all there as *sukkah*-building materials. That reading is itself a fascinating possibility for understanding the *peshat* of the Ezra passage.

### Yehuda's Solution

How does Rabbi Yehuda respond to the mention of *alei zayit*? He resolves the problem by partitioning the list: *savar hani le-dfanot* — he maintains that the olive wood mentioned in Ezra was used for the *walls* of the *sukkah*, not the *sechach*. Everything else — *alei hadas*, *alei tmarim*, *ve-alei etz avot* — was used for the *sechach* itself. With this move, Rabbi Yehuda insulates his position: the *sechach* in Ezra is still composed entirely of species associated with the *lulav*, while the olive is accounted for by its use in the walls, which have no *arba'ah minim* requirement.

---

## Yehuda & Planks

### Contradiction Setup

Now that Rabbi Yehuda's position has been articulated — *sechach* must come from the *arba'ah minim* — the *gemara* identifies an apparent internal contradiction. In another *mishna*, we find the ruling *mesachchin be-nesarim* — one may make *sechach* with planks — and this is attributed to Rabbi Yehuda. But planks are not *hadas* twigs or *arava* branches. How can Rabbi Yehuda permit *sechach* from planks while simultaneously insisting that *sechach* must be made from the *arba'ah minim*?

### Trunk Solution

The resolution is precisely the point Rava sought to establish from the outset: planks can be cut from the trunks of *hadas* trees or palm trees. If Rabbi Yehuda permits such planks as *sechach*, it is because he regards the trunk of these trees as halachically part of their respective *min*. The trunk of a palm tree is classified as part of the *lulav* species; the trunk of a *hadas* tree is part of the *hadas* species. This is *the* proof Rava was building toward.

### Eikra Definition

The *gemara* states: *amar siv ve-ikra de-dikla mina de-lulav hu shma mina* — the *siv* (a vine or fibrous material attached to the palm) and the *ikra de-dikla* (the trunk of the palm tree) are considered part of the species of *lulav*. Rashi explains that *ikar* here means the essence or core of the tree — i.e., the trunk. Although *akarin* ordinarily refers to roots, the context and Rashi's explanation together support reading *ikra* as the trunk. The same Rabbi Yehuda who demands that the *lulav* be bound *be-mino* — with material from its own species — and that the *sechach* be from the *arba'ah minim*, does not restrict this requirement to the decorative, leafy portions of those species. The woody core of the tree qualifies as well.

### Cedar & Hadass

A further challenge arises from the *braita* about planks: *sechachah binesarim shel erez* — if one covered a *sukkah* with planks of *erez* (cedar) — *sheyesh bahen arba'ah tefachim*, planks four *tefachim* wide, *divrei hakol pesulah* — all opinions agree it is invalid. *Ein bahen arba'ah tefachim* — if the planks are less than four *tefachim* — that is the dispute: Rabbi Meir invalidates and Rabbi Yehuda validates. The *braita* continues: Rabbi Meir concedes that if there is a gap between the planks equal to the width of one plank, and one fills that gap with valid *sechach*, the *sukkah* is *kasher*. The key question for us is: how can Rabbi Yehuda validate cedar planks if cedar is not one of the *arba'ah minim*?

The *gemara* answers: *mai erez hadas* — when the *braita* says *erez*, it actually refers to a species of myrtle tree. This is not a claim that cedar and myrtle are botanically identical, but rather that there exists a variety of *hadas* tree called *erez*. The proof comes from the teaching of Rabbah bar Rav Huna: *amri bei Rav asarah minei arazim hem* — there are ten species of *erez* — and the verse cited (*eten bamidbar erez shitah vehadas*) lists *erez* and *hadas* in the same breath, implying they share a botanical classification. Whether the *gemara* means that cedar *is* a type of *hadas* or that there is a *hadas*-type tree called *erez* remains somewhat ambiguous, but the former is a bold claim that invites scrutiny. Rashi's view and the overall thrust of the *sugya* support the latter reading.

Taken together, Rabbi Yehuda's position is a remarkable and internally consistent system: the *lulav* requires a binding *be-mino*; the *sechach* must be drawn from the *arba'ah minim*; and the *arba'ah minim* encompass not only the canonical leafy components but the trunks of the relevant trees as well — all of which finds a kind of quasi-support in the *pasuk* in Ezra, save for the complicating presence of the olive, which Rabbi Yehuda deftly reroutes to the walls.

---

## Lulav Binding Rules

### Rava to Builders

The *gemara* transitions to practical instructions about the construction and wrapping of the *lulav* bundle. Rava addressed the craftsmen who would assemble the *hoshana* — the bundled combination of *hadas*, *lulav*, and *arava* — for the house of the *Reish Galusa*. The practice was apparently to wrap some decorative material, perhaps silk, around the bundle to hold it together. Rava instructed them: *shari bei beis yad* — leave an unwrapped space at the bottom — *ki heichi d'lo tehavi chatzitza* — so that it will not constitute an obstruction between the hand and the *lulav* itself.

The concern is straightforward: if the entire lower portion of the bundle is covered in wrapping, the person holding it is not actually gripping the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *arava* directly — he is gripping the silk. That interposition would constitute a *chatzitza*, an obstruction, potentially invalidating the *lekicha*. By leaving some unwrapped space at the bottom, the holder can make direct physical contact with the *arba'ah minim* themselves.

This is analogous to the modern practice, where the accordion-like holder used today is itself made from the *arba'ah minim* — which raises a distinct point addressed momentarily. But for now, the operative concern is the wrapping material acting as an obstruction.

### Kol L'Naoso

Rava then articulates a general principle: *kol l'naoso eino chotzetz* — anything that is present in order to beautify the *lulav* does not constitute an obstruction. If a material is there to enhance the appearance of the *mitzvah* object, it is not treated as foreign matter interposed between the hand and the *lulav*. It is, in some sense, part of the *lulav* as a beautified *mitzvah* object.

### Rabba's Objection

Rabba raises a separate objection. He rules: *lo lincub inish hoshana besudara* — one should not hold the *hoshana* with a cloth — *d'beina lekicha tamah v'leika* — because the Torah requires a complete act of taking, and you do not have it. The *lekicha* must be direct; holding the bundle via an interposed cloth means you are not truly taking the *lulav* but rather taking the cloth that happens to be holding the *lulav*. This is not merely a *chatzitza* concern — it is a concern about whether the act of taking has been performed at all.

### Rava: Indirect OK

Rava disagrees: *lekicha al yedei davar acher sh'ma lekicha* — taking something indirectly through another object still constitutes a valid act of taking. These are two distinct principles — the *chatzitza* concern and the *lekicha al yedei davar acher* concern — and Rava accepts both as non-disqualifying, while Rabba rejects both. The proof Rava adduces for indirect taking comes from an altogether different domain, to which the *gemara* now turns.

---

## Hyssop Precedent

### Hyssop Extension

Rava sources his principle of *lekicha al yedei davar acher* from the laws of *Para Aduma*. The *eizov* — hyssop — would be placed into a thin applicator tube containing the mixture of ashes and water from the *parah adumah*. This was the standard method for transporting and deploying the purifying mixture: the tube protected the ashes, and one would insert the *eizov*, allow it to absorb the mixture, withdraw it, and sprinkle it on the person requiring purification.

The *baraita* presents a case where the stem of the *eizov* has broken and is now too short to reach the water at the bottom of the tube. The solution: *metapko bechut uv'kush* — one extends it with a string or with a spindle, some additional piece affixed to the short stem — *ve'tovel v'ma'aleh* — dips the extended bundle into the tube and withdraws it — *v'ochez be'eizov u'mazeh* — grasps the *eizov* itself and sprinkles. Rashi notes that the instruction to grasp the *eizov* directly at the point of sprinkling is for practical control and accuracy; you want to sprinkle it directly on the person, and holding a string gives you poor aim. But the act of dipping — the *tevilah* — was never performed by direct contact; the *eizov* was lowered into the tube through the medium of the string.

### Indirect Taking

The Torah requires *v'lakach v'taval* — he shall take and dip. Yet the hyssop was dipped not through a direct taking but through the medium of the string. Why is this valid? *Ela lav shma mina l'kichah al yedei davar acher sh'ma l'kichah* — learn from this that taking something indirectly is considered a valid act of taking.

### Ashes Proof

The *gemara* initially deflects this proof: *dilma shani hatam* — perhaps it is different there — *kivan d'chavreih k'gufeih dami* — since the string was *attached* to the *eizov*, the string becomes like the *eizov* itself. An attached extension becomes part of the object; an unattached tool does not. So perhaps the ruling permitting the dipped *eizov* rests not on a general principle of indirect taking but on the specific fact of attachment.

The *gemara* therefore turns to a second proof from *Para Aduma*: *nafla mishfoperet l'shoket* — if ashes fell from their container into the vessel of water by accident, the mixture is *pasul*, because the Torah requires intentional human agency — *v'lakchu v'natnu*, he shall take and place. Accidental spillage does not constitute taking and placing. But: *hepilo hu*, if one *intentionally* tilted the container and poured the ashes in, *kasher* — it is valid — even though one never touched the ashes directly. One took them by holding the container and pouring. *Ela lav shma mina l'kichah al yedei davar acher sh'ma l'kichah* — here too, indirect taking counts as taking.

### Attached vs. Unattached

The *gemara* draws the distinction: the first hyssop proof could be deflected on the grounds that attachment makes the string part of the *eizov*. The ashes proof cannot be so deflected — the container is not attached to the ashes in any integral way — and it therefore stands as a clean demonstration that *lekicha al yedei davar acher sh'ma lekicha*.

---

## Two Principles

### Redundancy Question

Having established both that *chatzitza* is a concern and that *lekicha al yedei davar acher* is a concern, a natural question presents itself: why are these two separate discussions necessary? If Rabba's first objection — that there must be no *chatzitza* — already requires direct contact between hand and *lulav*, then his second objection — that indirect taking is invalid — adds nothing. The *chatzitza* rule already mandates the directness that the *lekicha* rule is also demanding. And conversely, if Rava's response to the *chatzitza* concern (*kol l'naoso eino chotzetz*) already dispenses with the requirement for unobstructed contact, why does he need a second response about *lekicha al yedei davar acher* being valid?

### Tosafot Resolution

Tosafot addresses this at length and arrives at a nuanced resolution. The two principles operate in distinct conceptual registers. The *chatzitza* concern arises when one intends to take the *lulav* directly — that is, one's act is defined as direct gripping — but something stands between the hand and the object. In that case, the intervening material is an obstruction to the act one is trying to perform. Rava's response: if that intervening material is there to beautify the *lulav*, it is not classified as foreign matter and therefore does not obstruct.

The *lekicha al yedei davar acher* concern is categorically different. Here, one is not even attempting to take the *lulav* directly — one is using some tool or holder to lift it. The question is whether this type of act — indirect taking — counts as *lekicha* at all. Rabba says it does not; Rava says it does.

To illustrate the distinction: imagine wrapping the *lulav* in silk and gripping it. One's intent is to hold the *lulav* directly through one's hand, but the silk is in the way. That is a *chatzitza* question. Now imagine instead fashioning some kind of holder, placing the *lulav* in it, and lifting the entire holder. Here one is not trying to grip the *lulav* directly — one is using the holder as an instrument of taking. That is a *lekicha al yedei davar acher* question.

One can further distinguish: in the *chatzitza* scenario, one might argue that the interposing material, by being attached in some sense to the *lulav* or being *l'naoso*, becomes like part of the *lulav* — akin to the string attached to the *eizov*, which became like the *eizov* itself. But in the *lekicha al yedei davar acher* scenario, where one uses tongs or a holder that is not attached to the *lulav*, perhaps the tool is an extension of one's hand rather than part of the *lulav*. Rabba rejects even this, and Rava permits it.

A practical example helps crystallize the issue: carrying the *lulav* inside its bag. Taking the *lulav* out of its bag while reciting the *bracha* is an excellent instance of *lekicha al yedei davar acher* — the bag is certainly not there to beautify the *lulav*, but one is lifting it through the bag. Whether one thereby fulfills the *mitzvah* at that moment depends on one's *kavanah*, but the structural question is real, and it is worth noting that if one *does* already discharge the *mitzvah* in this fashion, one can still recite the *bracha* afterward according to certain *rishonim* if one has not yet performed the *nanuim*.

### Min B'Mino

Tosafot raises yet a third principle: *min b'mino eino chotzetz* — an object of the same type does not constitute an obstruction. If *hadas* leaves or *lulav* leaves are interposed between the hand and the *lulav* bundle, they do not count as foreign matter.

### Context Matters

These three principles — *kol l'naoso*, *lekicha al yedei davar acher*, and *min b'mino eino chotzetz* — do not operate identically in every context. In the laws of *mikvah*, for instance, the baseline requirement is *v'rachatz besaro bamayim* — the body must contact the water — and consequently the stakes for *chatzitza* are higher. An argument that something is there to beautify, or that it is the same type of material, may carry far less weight when the Torah explicitly demands bodily contact with the purifying water. Similarly, in the *Beit HaMikdash*, the *kohanim*'s feet must be in contact with the ground, since that physical connection is part of the sanctity of service. The *chatzitza* standards there are correspondingly more demanding.

In the context of *lulav*, however, the Torah never says the *lulav* must touch one's flesh. The requirement is *u-lekachtem lachem* — you shall take for yourselves. The question is whether the act constitutes a *lekicha*. Here, arguments about what does and does not count as an obstruction to that act can afford to be more accommodating, because the underlying norm is about the *action* of taking, not about the *physical contact* between body and object. The final words of the relevant Tosafot capture this exactly: *v'ein l'damot kol had'varim* — one cannot simply transpose these principles from one context to another; each domain has its own governing logic.

---

## Assembly Warnings

### No Cramping

The *gemara* records a series of practical warnings from Rabba regarding the physical assembly of the *lulav* bundle. Rabba warns: *lo raduz inish lulava be-Hoshana* — one should not cram the *lulav* into the *hoshana* (the bound *hadas*-and-*arava* bundle). The concern is *d'dilma natri tarfei ve-havei chatzitza* — that in the process of forcing the *lulav* in, leaves of the *hadas* or *arava* will be torn off and become loose, lying between the hand and the still-attached portions of the bundle, thereby creating a *chatzitza*.

### Rava Counters

Rava counters: *min be-mino eino chotzetz* — leaves of *hadas*, *arava*, or *lulav* that have come loose are not foreign matter; they are the same species as the species one is holding. Therefore, they cannot function as an obstruction. It is also worth noting in passing that Rabba's warning assumes a certain number of leaves can fall without rendering the *lulav* itself *pasul* — which implicitly acknowledges that some leaf loss does not disqualify the *hadas* or *arava*, though the *gemara* does not spell out exactly how many leaves may fall.

### No Cutting

Rabba issues a second warning: *lo ligoz inish lulava be-Hoshana* — one should not cut the *lulav* shorter while it is already assembled within the *hoshana* bundle. Trimming the bottom of the *lulav* to reduce its length severs the lowest junction points, where leaves are attached. Once those junctions are cut, leaves that were previously attached at the very bottom are now free and floating — *de-mishtari hutza ve-havei chatzitza* — and they will constitute a *chatzitza* between the hand and the intact *lulav* above.

### Rava Again

Again Rava responds with the same principle: *min be-mino eino chotzetz*. Severed *lulav* leaves lying at the base of the bundle are not classified as obstructing matter, since they are of the same species as the *lulav* one is holding. The *chatzitza* category, in this context, is reserved for genuinely foreign and heterogeneous material.

---

## Smelling Rules

### Huktza Principle

The *gemara* now moves beyond *chatzitza* to a distinct but related topic: the status of *mitzvah* objects with respect to other uses during the period of the *mitzvah*. Rava rules: *hadas shel mitzvah assur le-hariach bo* — it is forbidden to smell the *hadas* designated for the *mitzvah*. The operative concept is *huktza le-mitzvato* — an object set aside for a *mitzvah* is considered fully given over to that sacred purpose and may not be used for other purposes, even incidental ones that do not detract from the *mitzvah* at all.

### Etrog Analysis

The same principle applies to the *etrog*, but with an inverse result: *etrog shel mitzvah mutar le-hariach bo* — one may smell the *etrog* of the *mitzvah*. Why? *Etrog le-achila kai* — the *etrog's* primary use is eating. Therefore, *ki aktzyei me-achila aktzyei* — when it is designated for *mitzvah* use, it is the eating that is made off-limits, not the smelling. Smelling is an incidental benefit, not the central function of an *etrog*, and so smelling it remains permitted.

### Hadass Analysis

By contrast, *hadas le-reicha kai* — the primary use of *hadas* is for its fragrance. People smell *hadas*; that is what one does with myrtle. Therefore, *me-reicha aktzyei* — when the *hadas* is set aside for the *mitzvah*, it is the smelling that is made off-limits. The *mitzvah* object's central identity determines which use is foreclosed.

### Rashi's Source

Rashi's comment here is significant. Rather than invoking a general principle of *huktza le-mitzvato* applicable across all *mitzvot*, Rashi derives this ruling specifically from the *sukkah*: *de-gamrinan mi-sukkah de-yalfinan be-perek kama de-chal shem shamayim al atzei sukkah ve-asiri be-hana'ah kol shiva ve-havei huktza le-mitzvah* — we learn from the *sukkah*, where we established in the first chapter that the name of God rests upon the wood of the *sukkah* and it is therefore forbidden for personal benefit for all seven days — that same principle of *huktza le-mitzvah* extends to the *lulav* as well. This is a notably specific derivation. It is not merely a general legal category but one rooted in the elevated, *Mikdash*-infused sanctity of the *sukkah* and, by extension, its associated *mitzvot*. This reinforces a broader thematic pattern in *masechet Sukkah*: the *sukkah* and its *mitzvot* are understood through a vocabulary of divine presence and sanctity that approaches the language of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

---

## Shabbat Smelling

### Hadass Permitted

The *gemara* now pivots to a related but distinct scenario: not the *hadas* or *etrog* of the *mitzvah*, but *hadas* or *etrog* growing on a tree during *Shabbat* — any *Shabbat* of the year, entirely apart from *Sukkot*. Rava rules: *hadas bimchubar mutar le-hariach bo* — one may smell *hadas* growing on a tree on *Shabbat*. There is no concern that smelling it will lead to detaching it.

### Etrog Banned

The ruling is reversed for *etrog*: *etrog bimchubar assur le-hariach bo* — one may not smell an *etrog* growing on a tree on *Shabbat*.

### Prevention Logic

The rationale follows directly from the identities established above. *Hadas dile-ariach ka'ei* — the entire point of *hadas* is to smell it. *Sharei lei lo ati lemigzyei* — if you let someone smell it right there on the branch, they have obtained the benefit they sought and have no reason to pluck it. But *etrog de-achila ka'ei* — the *etrog's* purpose is eating. *Ei shreit lei* — if you permit smelling it, the person smells its fragrance, desires to taste it, and *ati lemigzyei* — will come to pluck it or, as Rashi notes, bite into it directly from the tree, which is itself a *Shabbat* violation of detachment. *Ein lecha talush gadol mizeh* — there is no more complete form of detachment than biting. The primary use determines the risk: give someone access to the incidental use and they will pursue the primary use, which on *Shabbat* requires severing a growing thing.

---

## Hand Placement

### Placement Rule

Rava rules: *lulav biyamin ve'etrog bismoal* — the *lulav* is held in the right hand and the *etrog* in the left. For a left-handed person, the halacha reverses: the stronger hand takes the *lulav*. The principle is that the dominant hand should hold the *lulav*.

### 3 vs 1 Logic

The reasoning: *hanei telat mitzvot ve-hai chada mitzvah* — the *lulav* bundle represents three of the four species (the *lulav* itself, *hadas*, and *arava*), while the *etrog* represents only one. Three species outweigh one, and the stronger hand is given the larger share of the *mitzvah*.

### Practical Custom

It is worth noting that even though we do not rule like Rabbi Yehuda that the *lulav tzarich oged* — that the *lulav* strictly requires an *eged* — all of the preceding discussions about assembly, *chatzitza*, cutting, and holding clearly assume that one *does* assemble the *lulav*, *hadas*, and *arava* together into a bound bundle. Even according to the *chachamim*, this is the universal custom, and the combined bundle of three species, held in the right hand, constitutes the *lulav* side of the four-species taking. The *etrog* is held separately in the left hand and brought together with the bundle for the *lekicha*.

---

## Bracha Formulation

### RY Question

Rabbi Yirmiya poses a question to Rabbi Zerika: *mai ta'ama lo mevarchinan ela al netilat lulav?* — why does the *bracha* mention only *netilat lulav* and not reference all four species? Why not say *al netilat arba minim* or spell out all four — *peri etz hadar, kapot tmarim, anaf etz avot, ve-arvei nachal*?

### RZ Answer

Rabbi Zerika answers: *hu degavo'a mikulam* — the *lulav* is naturally the tallest of the four species. It visually dominates the bundle. When people look at the assembled *mitzvah* object, their eye is drawn to the *lulav*, and thus the *bracha* is named after what stands out.

### Height Insufficient

Rabbi Yirmiya then pushes back: *veligbeihye le'etrog ulevarech* — one could simply raise the *etrog* high above the rest and then make the *bracha* in its name. Rabbi Zerika responds: *hu bemino gavo'a mikulam* — it is naturally taller than all the others. The *lulav's* dominance is intrinsic and organic, not a function of how one happens to be holding things at a given moment.
