Artificially elevating the *etrog* does not override the natural prominence of the *lulav*.

### Rambam Option

This discussion about the *bracha* and the *lulav's* dominance touches on a striking *halakha* noted by the Rambam in connection with the principle that *arba'ah minim she'balulav me'akvim zeh et zeh* — all four species are required to discharge the *mitzvah*. The *Geonim*, whose position the Rambam accepts, hold that one need not take all four species simultaneously. If, after the fact, one took each species separately at different times during the day, one has been *yotze*. Tosafot disagrees, arguing that the Torah's formulation implies a single act of taking encompassing all four.

Within the Rambam's position, however, the *brachot* would be differentiated accordingly: upon taking the *lulav*, one would say *al netilat* (or *lekichat*) *kapot tmarim*; upon taking the *etrog*, *al lekichat peri etz hadar*; upon taking the *hadas*, *al lekichat anaf etz avot*; and so on. The Rambam presumably draws on Geonic tradition for these formulations, given that most *brachot* were crystallized during the Geonic period and the principle of not introducing new *brachot* extends through that era. It is a striking contrast to our practice of a single *bracha* of *al netilat lulav* covering all four species in one act.

---

## Shaking Location

### Mishna Q

The *gemara* introduces a new *mishna*: *heichan hayu m'na'anim?* — where did one shake the *lulav*? The question arises somewhat abruptly, since the *mishna* has not yet formally introduced the topic of *nanuim* at all. The *gemara* notes that the *nanuim* were already implied earlier, where it was established that a *lulav* must be three *tefachim* in length in order to be shakeable — *k'dei l'na'anea bo kasher* — which presupposed that shaking is an inherent part of the *mitzvah*. The current *mishna* now addresses the question of when and where during *Hallel* this shaking takes place.

### BH Position

Beit Hillel rules: *be'Hodu laShem techila v'sof* — at *Hodu laShem* at the beginning and at the end of the relevant *perek* of *Tehillim*.

### Psalm Structure

Rashi draws attention to something that is easy to overlook: what we experience as separate chapters in *Tehillim* — 117 and 118 — are, according to the *masora*, actually a single *perek*. *Tehillim* 117 opens *Hallelu et Hashem kol goyim*, and *Tehillim* 118 begins *Hodu laShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo*, continues through *yomar na Yisrael*, *yomar na veit Aharon*, *yomar na yirei Hashem*, *min hametzar karati Yah*, and concludes with *Hodu laShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo*. It is all one *perek*. The *Hodu* at the start of what we call chapter 118 and the *Hodu* at the very end of that chapter — which is also the end of *Hallel* — are the *techila v'sof* referred to by Beit Hillel. The centrality of *Hodu laShem* to *Hallel* is so self-evident to those who recite it that the *gemara* can refer to it simply as the beginning and the end and be immediately understood.

### BS Addition

Beit Shammai adds: *af be'anna Hashem hatzlicha na* — one should also shake at *Anna Hashem hatzlicha na*, the verse that follows *Anna Hashem hoshi'ah na*. The precise rationale for Beit Shammai's addition is not entirely transparent from the *sugyat* itself.

---

## R. Akiva Observation

### Eyewitness

Rabbi Akiva reports: *tzofeh hayiti b'Rabban Gamliel v'Rabbi Yehoshua* — I was observing Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua during *Hallel* on *Sukkot*. Such first-person eyewitness accounts of how great *tannaim* conducted themselves in practice are a recurring and distinctive feature of *masechet Sukkah* — more so, it seems, than in many other *masechetot*. Rabbi Akiva says that he watched carefully how these two figures held and shook their *lulavim*.

### Practice Contrast

What he observed was a striking divergence between popular practice and expert practice: *she'kol ha'am hayu m'na'anim et lulaveihem* — the entire crowd was shaking their *lulavim* at various points throughout *Hallel* — *v'hem lo na'anu ela b'Ana Hashem Hoshi'ana v'Ana Hashem Hatzlicha Na* — but Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua shook only at *Ana Hashem Hoshi'ah Na* and *Ana Hashem Hatzlicha Na*, and not at additional points. The masses shook broadly; the *gedolim* were precise and limited.

---

## Tosafot Custom

### Rite Differences

The *gemara's* discussion of where to shake prompts an examination of current practice, which Tosafot addresses. The Sephardic custom is for the entire congregation to recite *Hodu laShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo* together simultaneously, performing the *nanuim* once at *Hodu laShem ki tov* — no responsive recitation, simply a unified communal declaration with shaking. The Ashkenazic custom involves a responsive format: the *shaliach tzibbur* leads, the *kahal* responds, and the shaking accompanies the congregational responses. These represent genuinely different practices, both of which Tosafot engages with.

### Trees Burst Forth

Tosafot explains the underlying scriptural logic of Beit Hillel's positions — specifically, why one shakes both at *Hodu laShem ki tov* and at *Ana Hashem Hoshi'ah Na*. A verse in *Divrei HaYamim* reads: *az yerannenu atzei haya'ar milifnei Hashem ki va lishpot et ha'aretz* — then the trees of the forest will burst forth in song before God, for He comes to judge the earth. The immediately following verse says *Hodu laShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo*, and the verse after that reads *v'imru hoshi'enu elohei yishenu*. The shaking of the *lulav* — the trees, as it were, expressing themselves — accompanies precisely these two moments of praise: *Hodu laShem* and *Ana Hashem Hoshi'ah Na*. The trees bursting into song are the *arba'ah minim* being waved; the words they accompany are these two key verses. This is, in Tosafot's own assessment, a beautiful explanation of Beit Hillel's ruling.

### Responsive Format

Returning to the Ashkenazic practice: the *shaliach tzibbur* recites *yomar na Yisrael* and the *tzibbur* responds *Hodu laShem ki tov ki l'olam chasdo*, shaking at each *Hodu* response. This responsive format gives a congregational, antiphonal quality to the *Hallel* at this juncture, and the shaking accompanies each of the *kahal's* *Hodu* responses throughout the sequence.

### Chazan Timing

As for the *shaliach tzibbur* himself: when does he perform the *nanuim*? Tosafot presents two views. The primary view is that the *shaliach tzibbur* does not shake during his own portions — the *yomar na Yisrael*, *yomar na veit Aharon*, and *yomar na yirei Hashem* — since those are his leading parts, not the congregational responses. However, Tosafot also records a second view: *yesh mefarshim* — some explain — that since the *tzibbur* responds with *Hodu* and shakes at each repetition, the *shaliach tzibbur* also shakes during his *yomar na* verses in concert with the congregation's ongoing participation. On this latter view, the *shaliach tzibbur* shakes throughout the responsive sequence — his verses and the congregational responses together form a continuous unit of praise and waving.

The discussion of the end of Tosafot on the relationship between shaking the *lulav* at the time of the *bracha* versus shaking it during *Hallel*, and the interaction between *lekicha* and *nanuim*, is left for the following day's shiur.

---

---

# Sukkah 38

## Waving (Tenufah)

### Intro & Menachot

Today's daf is 38, and we pick up at the bottom of 37b, approximately ten lines from the bottom — three lines after the *gemara* begins following the *mishnah*. The *gemara* opens with *tnan hatam*, "we taught over there in Menachot," because the *mishnah* had mentioned the waving of the *lulav* and discussed waving it at different points during *hallel*: at *hodu lashem* at the beginning and end, and at *ana Hashem hoshia na* — and according to Beit Shammai, at *ana Hashem hatzlicha na* as well.

Tosafot had already brought a beautiful explanation linking this to *psukim* in Divrei Hayamim, which speaks of the trees of the forest bursting into song and then quotes the actual *psukim* of *hodu lashem ki tov* and *hoshienu Elohei yishenu*. The shaking of the *lulav*, then, is connected to the image of trees bursting into song, and to the responsiveness of *hodu lashem* and *ana Hashem hoshia na*. There was also the question of our precise practice — not merely the initial *hodu lashem*, but the *shliach tzibur* reciting *yomar na Yisrael*, *yomar na beit Aharon*, with the *tzibbur* responding *hodu lashem* — and Tosafot discussed how that becomes our current practice of waving the *lulav* during *hallel*.

### Shtei Halechem

Now the *gemara* connects this idea of waving to another context entirely. The *mishnah* in Menachot teaches: *shtei halechem ushnei kivsei atzeret* — on *shavuot*, one brings the two loaves of bread from the newly cut wheat together with the two lambs. What is the procedure for waving them? *Maniach shtei halechem al gabei shenei hakvasim* — you place the loaves on top of the lambs — *umaniach yadav tachtehen* — and place your hands beneath them — *umanif umolich umavi ma'aleh umorid* — and you wave, bringing forward and back, up and down.

The verse cited is *asher hunaf va'asher huram* — "that which was waved and that which was lifted up." That specific verse belongs to the *miluim*, the inauguration of the *kohanim* in the *beit hamikdash*, but it is taken as a model for the type of *tnufah* performed throughout the *beit hamikdash*, and therefore assumed to apply here as well.

### Four Winds

What does this waving signify? *Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *molich umavi lemi she'arba ruchot shelo* — the bringing forward and back is directed toward the One to whom the four winds belong, that is, toward God. The *mishnah* in Menachot had said *umanif umolich umavi* — wave, bring forward and back — suggesting that *manif* might refer to side-to-side motion while *molich umavi* refers to front and back, together encompassing all four directions. And then *ma'aleh umorid* — up and down — *lemi sheshamayim va'aretz shelo*, to the One to whom heaven and earth belong.

### Ward Off Bad

In *eretz Yisrael* they taught this differently. *Amar Rabbi Chama bar Ukva amar Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina*: *molich umavi kedei la'atzor ruchot ra'ot* — you bring forward and back in order to hold back the bad winds — *ma'aleh umorid kedei la'atzor tlalim ra'im* — and up and down in order to hold back bad rains. It is notable that the purpose is framed negatively: not to draw down good, but to ward off the bad.

### Shirei Mitzvah

*Amar Rabbi Yose bar Avin ve'itayma Rabbi Yose bar Zavda*: *zot omeret* — this teaches us — *shiyarei mitzvah me'akvin et hapuranut*, that even the remnants of a *mitzvah* hold back calamity. Why characterize the *tnufah* as a *shirei mitzvah*, a remnant? Because if one failed to perform the waving, the *korban* remains valid — the waving is important but not indispensable. And yet: *sheharei tnufah shirei mitzvah hi ve'otzeret ruchot utlalim ra'im* — the waving, though not strictly necessary, still holds back bad winds and bad rains.

### Satan's Eyes

*Ve'amar Rava*: *vechein balulav* — and the same applies to the *lulav*. According to Rashi, the direct application is practical: *molich umavi ma'aleh umorid* — this is how the waving is to be performed, to all four directions and then up and down. *Rav Acha bar Yaakov manfi lei umaytei lei* — Rav Acha bar Yaakov would bring it out and bring it in, implementing *molich umavi* in a quite forceful way. Indeed, those who performed it that way would say *dein gira be'einei desitna* — this is like a spear in the eyes of the *satan*. But the *gemara* pushes back: *velav nichuta hi, mishum de'ati le'agruyei beih* — that is not ideal conduct, because you risk provoking the *satan* and drawing his attention rather than warding him off.

### Model Source

This raises an important structural question. Where does the very idea of *nanu'im* — waving — with the *lulav* come from at all? The *Torah* says *ulekachtem lachem* — "you shall take for yourselves" — which might suggest a vigorous taking, but does not obviously mandate waving in a liturgical context. What the *gemara* is doing here is introducing a model: we have an established practice of waving in a religious context — the *tnufah* of the *shtei halechem* — and that serves as the paradigm for what we do with the *lulav*. This is significant because it once again connects the *arba minim* and the *lulav* and *etrog* to the world of *korbanot*, a point that has come up multiple times — the *lulav* is being fashioned into something analogous to a *korban*.

### Agricultural Parallel

But Tosafot goes further and observes that the connection is not merely technical. When you wave the *shtei halechem*, what are you waving? The new grain — the distinctive agricultural product of *shavuot*. And what is the new agricultural product at *sukkot*? The *arba minim*, representing the full harvest gathered in from the fields. So the parallel is not arbitrary: just as we wave the produce of the season on *shavuot*, we wave the produce of the season on *sukkot*. This is a powerful structural correspondence.

### Tosafot Application

Tosafot raises a further question: in *perek kol hamenachot ba'ot matzah* there is a list of all the offerings that require *tnufah*, and perhaps not all of them are performed in precisely these multiple directions. *Ela davka bitnufat shtei halechem de'atzeret, vechein lulav* — perhaps it is only by the *shtei halechem* of *shavuot* that the full directional waving is performed, and we apply that same waving to the *lulav* as well.

### Prayer for Rain

The reason is then drawn from a teaching in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah: *gezar din nechtam bePesach al hatvu'ah uve'atzeret al peirot ha'ilan uvachag al hamayim* — the judgment is sealed at Pesach regarding grain, at *shavuot* regarding fruit of the trees, and on *sukkot* regarding water, that is, rain. Tosafot therefore says: *ulachen anu menan'im balulav sheyesh bo holachah vahava'ah* — we wave the *lulav* as a type of *tefillah* for rain. The specific application of the *shtei halechem* waving to *sukkot* is thus rooted in the parallel *gezar din*: just as the waving at *shavuot* is oriented toward that season's agricultural judgment, so too the waving at *sukkot* is a prayer for the water upon which the coming year depends.

### Divine vs. Petition

Two distinct symbolic orientations for the *lulav* thus emerge from this discussion. The first, expressed by Rabbi Yochanan, frames the waving as directed toward God — an act of religious expression. The second approach, reflected in the *eretz Yisrael* teaching and Tosafot's application, frames it as a petition: the *lulav* becomes a vehicle for prayer for beneficial agricultural conditions.

There is also a *midrash* — not in our *gemara* and likely later, so its antiquity is uncertain — in which Rabbi Akiva reads each of the *arba minim* as representing *hakadosh baruch hu* directly: *ha-lulav zu ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu, etrog zu ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu*. On that reading, the waving represents our direct connection to God; the *lulav* is not primarily a prayer vehicle but an expression of divine relationship, and the singularity of each species may itself be part of that symbolism.

### Three Symbolisms

Three distinct symbolic orientations therefore present themselves in this sugya. The first situates the waving as pure divine service — directed toward God, as Rabbi Yochanan describes. The second situates it as prophylactic petition — warding off bad winds and rains, and more broadly as a *tefillah* for rain at *sukkot's* *gezar din*. The third connects it to the culmination of the *yamim nora'im* and the *yom hadin* dimension of *sukkot*, which the *gemara* elsewhere associates with *l'arbev et ha-satan* — confusing the *satan* — at the shofar blowing. The heightened mention of the *satan* in *gemara* is concentrated around the *yamim nora'im*, and so the image of poking the *satan*'s eyes may be situating the *lulav* waving as a continuation of that dynamic.

Tosafot also raises a practical question about how exactly to count the wavings, since the Yerushalmi mentions performing the waving three times. Does one count "out" as one and "in" as two, or is "out and in" together counted as one? And does one complete three cycles at a single direction before moving on, or perform the full directional sequence three times over? Our *gemara* does not specify three repetitions, but once the Yerushalmi introduces that number, the counting questions multiply.

---

## Outside Proper Time

### Journey Scenario

We now turn to the next *mishnah*, which raises a fascinating issue implicit in everything discussed thus far — namely, what happens when a person takes the *lulav* outside the primary context of *hallel* in the *beit knesset*. The *mishnah* states: *mi sheba baderech velo hayah beyado lulav* — someone who has returned from a journey without a *lulav* in hand. *L'kshe'yikanes leveito yitol al shulchano* — when he enters his house, he takes it at the table.

There is already a *chiddush* here before one even arrives at the question of interrupting a meal: he takes it at home, not in the *beit knesset* during *hallel*, which was clearly the assumed primary context. The *mishnah* then continues: *lo natla Shacharis yitol bein ha'arbayim, shekol hayom kasher l'lulav* — if he did not take it in the morning, he may take it in the afternoon, for the entire day is valid for *lulav*. The point of the *mishnah* appears to be that even if the proper time and context were missed — morning, *hallel*, *shul* — the *mitzvah* may still be performed at any point during the day.

### Interrupt Meal

The phrase "at the table" suggests that one interrupts a meal in order to take the *lulav*. This invites comparison to the *mishnah* elsewhere concerning activities one must not begin before *davening Mincha* — but if one already began, *im hitchilu ein mafsikin*, one does not interrupt. Why, then, should one interrupt a meal for *lulav* but not interrupt a meal for *Mincha*?

### Internal Kashya

The internal tension within the *mishnah* itself also demands attention. The first clause — "take it at the table" — implies one interrupts the meal. The second clause — "if he did not take it in the morning, take it in the afternoon" — implies one does not interrupt, for apparently he ate his morning meal without interrupting.

### Rav Safra

*Amar Rav Safra lo kashya*: there is no difficulty. *Ha d'ika sha'os bayom ha d'leika sha'os bayom* — the cases differ depending on whether time remains in the day. When the *mishnah* says to interrupt, it refers to a case where one is eating in the afternoon and night will arrive before he finishes. When it says to take it later in the afternoon, it refers to a case where the morning meal could be completed with time still remaining.

### Rava's View

*Amar Rava*: I do not understand what bothered you at all. *D'omar ha d'Oraisa ha d'Rabbanan* — the *Mincha* case poses no difficulty because *davening Mincha* is *derabbanan*. While there may be a *d'Oraisa* obligation to pray once a day, the specific institution of *Shacharis*, *Mincha*, and *Maariv* is rabbinic. One does not interrupt an ongoing activity to perform a rabbinic *mitzvah*. Taking the *lulav*, by contrast, is a biblical *mitzvah*, so the question never arose. *Ella amar Rava, i kushya ha kushya* — if there is a genuine internal tension in the *mishnah*, Rava reformulates it precisely: the first clause implies one interrupts, and the second clause — the one about taking it in the afternoon because one did not take it in the morning — implies one does not interrupt. That is the actual internal contradiction Rav Safra was resolving.

### Rebbe Zeira

*Amar Rebbe Zeira*: even that formulation is not a problem. *D'omar mitzvah l'afsoukay* — the plain reading of the *mishnah* is simply that you should interrupt your meal. *V'ilo pasak, yitol bein ha'arbayim* — but if you did not interrupt, you can still take it in the afternoon. The *mishnah* states the ideal but does not specify consequences for failure; the fact that someone might not have interrupted their morning meal does not mean the *mishnah* permitted that. And the *Mincha* case remains distinguished by the *d'Oraisa/d'Rabbanan* distinction — no additional resolution is required.

### Chol Hamoed

The *gemara* then notes: *ella amar Rebbe Zeira l'olam k'dikamina me'ikara* — there actually was a problem with the comparison to *Mincha*, and the answer is: *hacha b'Yom Tov Sheni d'Rabbanan askinan* — we are dealing here with *Yom Tov Sheni*, which in this context means *Chol Hamoed*, not the second day of *Yom Tov* observed outside *Eretz Yisrael*. How do we know? The *mishnah* itself says *mi sheba baderech* — he came back from a journey. One does not travel on *Yom Tov*. Therefore the *mishnah* must be discussing *Chol Hamoed*, when travel is permitted. And since taking the *lulav* on *Chol Hamoed* is rabbinic — it applies only *d'Rabbanan* — there is now a genuine problem: why does one interrupt a meal for a rabbinic *mitzvah* here, when one does not interrupt a meal for *Mincha*, also a rabbinic obligation?

### Time Principle

The resolution is now operative at the level of principle. For rabbinic *mitzvot*, whether one must interrupt depends on whether time remains to perform the *mitzvah* afterward. If time remains, one does not interrupt; if time will run out, one does interrupt. For biblical *mitzvot* — the *lulav* on the first day, reciting *Shema* — one interrupts regardless of whether time remains, since having already delayed and then begun another activity while the obligation is pending, one must prioritize the biblical command immediately.

There is a qualification worth noting: if one has a fixed and predictable time to perform the *mitzvah* later — say, attending a *minyan* where *Shema* will be recited — the obligation to interrupt may not be triggered in the same way. But where the obligation was already pending and one began another activity, the biblical *mitzvah* takes precedence unconditionally.

The larger point of the *mishnah* in context remains significant. The *gemara*'s hyper-focus on the interruption question should not obscure the broader implication: the ideal is morning, *hallel*, *shul*. Everything else — taking it at home, taking it in the afternoon — is accommodation to deviation from that ideal.

---

## Shaking Centrality

### During Hallel

The *mishnah* returns to *hallel*, and this transition itself is revealing. The natural structure of the *daf* has been: an elaborate discussion of waving during *hallel*, then a brief digression about taking the *lulav* outside its proper time and context, and now a return to *hallel*. The implication is that the primary context of the *mitzvah* of *lulav* is precisely the shaking during *hallel* in *shul*. This is not presented as a supplemental enhancement — "first you make the *beracha*, take the *lulav*, and by the way also shake it during *hallel*." Rather, the shaking in the context of *hallel* is the *mitzvah*.

### Tosafot Minor's Obligati…

Tosafot raises a pointed question: when one makes the *beracha* at the moment of taking the *lulav*, must one shake it then, or does merely holding it suffice? *Lo matzinu dechayav lina'anea bitchilat netilah* — we do not find any explicit source requiring shaking at the moment of taking. But then Tosafot invokes the principle underlying the *mishnah*'s formulation of a minor's obligation: *katan hayodeia lina'anea chayav belulav* — a minor who knows how to shake is obligated in *lulav*. Notice: not "a minor who is able to take it," but "a minor who knows how to shake it." This is how the threshold of educational obligation is defined. Since the capacity to shake defines when the *mitzvah* begins to be taught, shaking is evidently central to what the act of the *mitzvah* is.

Tosafot therefore concludes that one does shake the *lulav* when making the *beracha* — even, he adds, *af al pi she'eino yode'a likros es ha'hallel*, even if one does not know how to recite *hallel*. While one would technically be *yotzei* without shaking, shaking is central to the act. This also advances an important independent claim: shaking can be meaningfully performed outside the context of *hallel*.

### Three Possibilities

Three conceptual positions thus emerge. The first is that the *mitzvah* consists purely in *netilah* — the taking — and shaking is entirely secondary. This position is *bedi'eved* true in the sense that one is *yotzei* without shaking, but it cannot represent the *lechatchilah* ideal, given how consistently shaking is foregrounded throughout the *sugya*. The second is that shaking is central to the *mitzvah* and is specifically associated with the *hallel* context. The third — Tosafot's position — is that shaking is central and can exist independently of *hallel*, as evidenced by the minor who shakes without reciting *hallel*.

### Early Departure

Tosafot adduces a further proof from a *baraita* in Berachos: *hikdim latzeis laderech* — if one had to depart early on a journey before *Shacharis* — *mevi'im lo shofar vetoke'a lulav umenane'a megillah vekorei bah* — they bring him a shofar and he blows, a *lulav* and he shakes, a *megillah* and he reads. He makes the *beracha*, shakes the *lulav*, and goes — without *hallel*. *Mashma de'menane'a belo hallel* — this implies one can shake without *hallel*.

One might argue that this case is purely *bedi'eved*, however — he had no choice. It no more proves that shaking is *lechatchilah* independent of *hallel* than it proves that early-morning *lulav* is the ideal.

### Lechatchildlah Ideal

The stronger evidence, one can argue, runs in the opposite direction: the entire opening discussion of the *daf* places shaking squarely in the context of *hallel*. Even the minor's case does not require shaking *without* *hallel* — the minor could perfectly well be in *shul* while others are reciting *hallel*, and the principle of *shomea k'oneh*, which the *gemara* will discuss shortly, means that listening to *hallel* is like reciting it. The fact that he cannot recite it himself does not remove him from the *hallel* context.

This understanding aligns with the actual practice observed: most people wait to make the *beracha* in *shul* and take the *lulav* in the context of *hallel*. Some invoke *zrizin makdimin lemitzvot* — the principle of zealously performing *mitzvot* at the earliest opportunity — to take the *lulav* at home first thing in the morning. But the stronger *lechatchilah* is clearly the shaking in the context of *hallel*, not simply as something done afterward but as the very manner in which the *mitzvah* is performed.

### No Torah Source

This question carries significant weight when one considers that shaking is not mentioned anywhere in the *Torah* at all. *Ulekachtem lachem* — "you shall take for yourselves" — is the relevant verse, and it says nothing about waving. The entire architecture of shaking has been constructed from the connection to *hallel*, from the image of *az yerannenu atzei haya'ar* ("the trees of the forest will burst into song") that Tosafot invokes, and from the model of *tnufah* in the world of *korbanot*. Without the *hallel* context, the very concept of shaking loses its primary grounding.

### Simcha Connection

This connects to the end of the *pasuk* itself: *ulekachtem lachem bayom harishon... usmachtem lifnei Hashem Elokeichem shivas yamim* — you shall take on the first day... and you shall rejoice before God seven days. The *simcha* of the *lulav* — expressed in *simchat beit hasho'evah* and in the festival's character as a gathering of the harvest — finds its natural liturgical expression in *hallel*. Tosafot's citation of *az yerannenu atzei haya'ar* is precisely about trees bursting into song, and that image of joyful expression before God is what *hallel* embodies. The context of *hallel* is not incidental; it is where *simcha* and religious expression converge.

---

## Hallel Responsive

### Unobligated Reader

The next *mishnah* reads: *mi shehayah eved o isha o katan makrin oto* — if a slave, woman, or minor was reciting *hallel* for you — *oneh achareihem mah shehem omrim* — you repeat after them what they say. This describes a word-for-word responsive recitation.

### Word-for-Word

The scenario assumes the person does not know *hallel* and must be fed the words phrase by phrase, repeating each phrase after the unobligated leader says it.

### Curse & Ignorance

*Vetavo lo me'eira* — a curse should fall upon that person. Why?

### Rashi vs Tosafot

Rashi understands the curse as arising from the display of ignorance: why must you rely on someone else to feed you the words? The very fact of not knowing *hallel* is deeply problematic. Tosafot, however, objects: even if an adult male leads and you repeat after him, you are equally ignorant. Rashi's explanation does not account for why the leader's identity — slave, woman, or minor — matters. Tosafot argues that the problem lies specifically in relying on someone who is themselves not obligated in *hallel*. A woman and minor are exempt from time-bound *mitzvot* and therefore not obligated; a slave similarly. When an unobligated person serves as your conduit, the word-for-word repetition more explicitly displays your ignorance, since there is no official obligated-and-responding structure behind which your lack of knowledge can be concealed. Yet the issue may also be that being led by the unobligated simply looks bad — it reveals reliance on people who are not themselves bound by the obligation.

### Adult Leader

If an adult male leads, the dynamic changes. *Im haya gadol mikra oto oneh acharav Hallelujah* — if an adult was reciting for you, you respond with *Hallelujah* after each phrase. The *chazzan* says *Hallelujah*, the congregation responds *Hallelujah*; he says *hallelu avdei Hashem*, they respond *Hallelujah*; he says *yehi shem Hashem mevorach*, they respond *Hallelujah*. And so on through the chapters. Depending on how the *mishnah* is read, this may have been the standard communal practice even for those who knew *hallel* — the *shliach tzibbur* recites and the *tzibbur* responds *Hallelujah* at each phrase — or it may describe only what those who do not know *hallel* should do when led by an obligated adult.

### Custom Variations

*Makom shenahagu lichpol yichpol* — where the custom was to double certain *psukim* (as we do with *odecha Hashem ki anitani*), one doubles them. *Lifshot* — where the custom was to recite straight, one does so. *Levarech* — where the custom was to add a blessing, one blesses. *Hakol keminhag hamedina* — all follows local practice. This is a notable embrace of diversity in practice across communities.

### Women Leadership

This discussion opens a broader question about women leading *hallel* in a contemporary setting. Our current practice is entirely different from the one assumed by the *mishnah*: everyone recites from the *siddur* independently, there is no responsive structure, and no one is feeding another person the words. The concerns about displaying ignorance and relying on an unobligated leader do not apply in the same way, since everyone fulfills the obligation independently. The limited responsive moment that does exist in our *hallel* raises an interesting question about how to map these *halachot* onto our current realities.

The deeper issue of *tavo me'eira* — the curse — is also important in a different way. In the social reality of the *gemara*, male ignorance contrasted with female knowledge carried particular weight and shame; the *gemara* elsewhere notes that a woman could theoretically receive an *aliyah* but should not out of *kevod hatzibbur*, which may reflect related sensitivities about this kind of inversion. How much of the *tavo me'eira* is rooted in halachic categories — specifically, the asymmetry of obligation levels — and how much is a sociological judgment about what is appropriate or fitting in those societies, is a genuine question that affects how one applies these sources today.

### Women Birchat

Tosafot's final lines are relevant here too. Tosafot mentions: *mishum derabim zila behu milsa* — even if a woman is obligated, having her lead *birkat hamazon* in a setting with many people is considered disrespectful or inappropriate. He supports this with the position of the *Halachot Gedolos* (*Bahag*), which rules that women cannot be *motzi* men in *megillah* reading. Various later Tosafot try to ground that ruling in a technical argument — perhaps men are obligated to *read* the *megillah* while women are obligated only to *hear* it, creating an asymmetry — but this Tosafot appears to frame it as a purely sociological or propriety issue independent of technical obligation levels. This distinction is significant for contemporary discussions of women's liturgical roles.

---

## Obligation & Blessing

### Son & Slave

A *baraita* teaches: *ben mevarech l'aviv ve'eved mevarech l'rabo* — a son may lead *birkat hamazon* for his father, and a slave for his master. This is despite the fact that a minor son and a slave are at most rabbinically obligated, while the adult father may be biblically obligated.

### Woman Blessing

*Ve'ishah mevareches l'ba'alah* — a woman may lead *birkat hamazon* for her husband as well. Whether women are biblically obligated in *birkat hamazon* is itself a debate in Berachos. *Aval amru chachamim, tavo me'eira l'adam she'ishah u'vanim mevarchin lo* — nevertheless, the Sages said: a curse should come upon a man whose wife and children recite the blessing for him.

### Curse Reason

Why the curse? One explanation focuses on the levels of obligation: a minor is only rabbinically obligated, while an adult man may be biblically obligated, and having the less-obligated party *motzi* the more-obligated party is halachically problematic. A subtle scenario could make the minor rabbinic and the adult rabbinic in the same particular instance — for example, if the man ate only a *kezayit* and his biblical obligation is not triggered, while the minor ate his fill — but even then, the man remains fundamentally in the *d'Oraisa* category and the child does not, and the *baraita* evidently views this as inappropriate.

### Sociological Issue

Tosafot adds the alternative framing that even matching levels of obligation would not fully resolve the issue. There is a deeper propriety concern — the inappropriateness of relying on those who are not generally counted in the same obligatory framework. Whether that is a halachic constraint or a social-contextual one is precisely the question left open by the *sugya*.

---

## Rava's Approach

### Contemporary Practice

*Amar Rava: hilchata gevirta ika lemishma mei-ha minhaga de-halleila* — Rava says that many important *halachot* can be inferred from the contemporary practice of *hallel* in his time. By Rava's era the original responsive structure had largely fallen away, and most people recited *hallel* in full themselves. But certain vestiges of the older practice had been preserved, and Rava reads those preserved moments as deliberate signals of the underlying *halachot*.

### Opening Hallel

*Hu omer Hallelujah vehem omrim Hallelujah* — the *chazzan* opens with *Hallelujah* and the congregation responds *Hallelujah*. Then he says *hallelu avdei Hashem* and they again say *Hallelujah*. *Mikan she-mitzvah la'anot Hallelujah* — from this we infer that there is a *mitzvah* to respond *Hallelujah* at the opening of *hallel*, even for those who know the full text and are reciting it themselves. This vestige was preserved specifically to signal that responding *Hallelujah* is an obligatory element of *hallel* participation, not merely optional.

### Hodu Lashem

*Hu omer Hodu Lashem vehem omrim Hodu Lashem* — later, when the *chazzan* reaches *hodu lashem*, the congregation again responds *hodu lashem* rather than continuing in unison. *Mikan she-mitzvah la'anot rashei prakim* — from this we infer that there is a *mitzvah* to respond at the opening of each new chapter.

### Chapter Heads

What exactly does *rashei prakim* — responding at chapter beginnings — mean? The answer depends on how one understands the structure of *hallel*. Rashi and Tosafot diverge here.

According to Rashi, each new *perek* of Tehillim within *hallel* would have prompted a shift in the responsive formula. Under the word-for-word practice, the opening phrase of each *perek* would be said by the congregation together (rather than in the usual call-and-response), signaling the transition. So *mitzvas la'anot rashei prakim* means that at each chapter break, the response changes to mark the new section.

Tosafot suggests a different structure. In Rava's time — and perhaps in the original practice as well — the congregation understood all the *psukim* from the initial *Hallelujah* through the *hodu lashem* section to form a single large unit. The opening of that second unit, *hodu lashem ki tov*, was the moment for a new responsive phrase. Accordingly, Tosafot reads the full *hallel* as divided into two great sections: in the first, the response is *Hallelujah*; in the second, the response is *hodu lashem ki tov* — *ki le'olam chasdo* after each phrase. That would have been a genuinely stirring communal experience: half the assembly calling *hodu lashem ki tov* and the other half responding *ki le'olam chasdo* through the entire second half.

### Ana Hashem

*Hu omer Ana Hashem hoshia na vehem omrim Ana Hashem hoshia na. Hu omer Ana Hashem hatzlicha na vehem omrim Ana Hashem hatzlicha na.* Here there are two distinct inferences. The repetition of *ana Hashem hoshia na* — with the congregation echoing exactly — teaches *mikan she'im haya katan makri oto onin acharav mah shehu omer*: if a minor were feeding you the lines, you would need to repeat word for word precisely what he says, not a standard responsive formula. This is word-for-word repetition preserved as a vestige to remind us of that rule.

And what about the second repetition, *ana Hashem hatzlicha na*? *Mikan she'im ba lichfol kofel* — this teaches that doubling certain *psukim* is permitted. We maintain one repeated *pasuk* precisely to signal that the practice of doubling was legitimate and in use.

### Shomeia K'Oneh

*Hu omer Baruch Haba vehem omrim B'Shem Hashem.* Here, uniquely, the congregation does not repeat what the *chazzan* said, nor respond with a fixed formula. Instead the *chazzan* says the first half of a *pasuk* and the congregation completes it with the second half. *Mikan l'shomea k'oneh* — from this we derive the principle that hearing is like saying.

---

## Shomeia K'Oneh

### Technical Meaning

Why does this particular exchange — the *chazzan* beginning and the congregation completing — teach *shomea k'oneh*? The answer lies in the precise technical meaning of the term. *Shomea k'oneh* is usually translated as "hearing is like saying," but that is imprecise. The word *oneh* does not simply mean "to say" — *vayaanu haleviyim ve'amru kol ha'am* — it means "to answer," to respond. In a responsive context, what is the proper response when the *chazzan* says something? *Hallelujah*, or *hodu lashem*, or *amen*. If one hears and responds with the expected reply, one has clearly fulfilled the obligation. But the *baruch haba / b'shem Hashem* exchange is structurally different: you are not affirming what was said with a responsive *amen* or *Hallelujah* — you are completing the speaker's sentence. Yet even here, the principle holds that having heard is sufficient. This is why the exchange teaches *shomea k'oneh* in a deeper sense than the earlier responses: it establishes that even when there is no verbal response at all, merely hearing the words fulfills the obligation.

### Rambam Hierarchy

The Rambam formulates a hierarchy on this basis. *Ha'oneh amen kemotzi beracha mipiv dami* — one who responds *amen* is treated as if he personally voiced the blessing, because *amen* functions as endorsement and identification: "ditto, I affirm those words as my own." But *vehasho'meia harei zeh ke'oneh* — one who only hears, without saying *amen*, is treated as if he responded with *amen*, though this is one step down from actually saying *amen*. The optimal fulfillment is responding; the acceptable fulfillment is hearing; and the principle that hearing functions as responding is what *shomea k'oneh* denotes.

### Rashi Davening

Rashi applies the principle immediately to the *davening* context: if one is in the middle of *Shmoneh Esrei* and *Kaddish* or *Kedushah* is being recited, one should stand silently and listen — and that listening functions as having made the proper response. One is not required to interrupt *Shmoneh Esrei*.

### Tosafot Interruption

Tosafot objects. If *shomea k'oneh* truly means that hearing is equivalent to responding, then listening to *Kaddish* during *Shmoneh Esrei* constitutes an act of response, which is itself an interruption of *Shmoneh Esrei*. We rule in practice like Rashi — that listening counts as *yotzei* without constituting a formal interruption — but the underlying tension Tosafot identifies is real, and it reflects the precision with which the principle of *shomea k'oneh* needs to be applied.

### Tannaitic View

The *gemara* records *amar Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* that when asked whether hearing without responding counts: *chachamaya vesafraya, rashei ama, vedarshaya* — the wise men, the teachers, the communal leaders, and the expounders have all said *shama velo ana yatza* — hearing without responding, one has fulfilled the obligation.

### Yoshiyahu Source

A formal textual source is then provided: *amar Rebbi Shimon Pazi amar Rebbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: *minayin l'shomea k'oneh?* — from where do we derive the principle? *Dechsiv, es kol divrei hasefer asher kara melech Yehuda* — "all the words of the book that the king of Judah had read." This verse, from the story of the discovery of the *Sefer Torah* in the *Beit Hamikdash* during the reign of Yoshiyahu, describes the king as having "read" the words.

### Hearing = Reading

*Vecha'i Yoshiyahu kara? Velo Shafan keraan?* — but did Yoshiyahu actually read them? Shafan read them, as the verse explicitly says: *vayikraehu Shafan* — Shafan read it before the king. Yet the verse describes the king as the one who read. *Ela mikan l'shomea k'oneh* — this teaches that hearing is like reading. And for the *megillah* context this is particularly important: not merely that hearing is like saying the words, but that hearing is like *reading* the words — which means one who listens to the *megillah* is treated as if one read it.

### Humiliation Proof

*Amar Rav Acha bar Yaakov*: one might object that after Shafan read it, Yoshiyahu himself then read it, and the verse reflects that subsequent personal reading. But *lo salka datchach* — that reading is untenable. The verse says *yaan rach levavcha vatichna lefanai beshamacha* — "because your heart was softened and you humbled yourself before me *when you heard* these things." *Beshamacha velo b'karacha* — when you heard, not when you read. The verse's own language confirms that Yoshiyahu heard rather than read — and yet he is described as having "read." This is the Scriptural grounding for *shomea k'oneh*.

### Our Minhag

Tosafot notes that our current *minhag* of *hallel* does not even follow Rava's practice: we do not respond *Hallelujah* to the opening *Hallelujah* at the beginning of *hallel*. Since the *gemara* itself has already framed the entire discussion in terms of *minhagim* — with the *mishnah* saying *hakol keminhag hamedina* — Tosafot accepts that Rava had a different *minhag* from the *mishnah*, and we have a different *minhag* from Rava, and all of this is consistent with legitimate halachic diversity.

### Practical Use

The practical importance of *shomea k'oneh* is most evident in *megillah* reading. The *mitzvah* is specifically *kria*, reading — yet the universal practice is to listen to one person read rather than for each individual to read independently. This only works because of the principle that hearing is equivalent to reading.

### Self-Performance

One question the *gemara* does not fully address is whether saying something oneself is categorically preferable to hearing it, even when hearing suffices. For communal *mitzvot* — *megillah* reading, where participation in the *tzibbur* is itself part of the *mitzvah* — being part of the communal reading clearly outweighs going off to recite privately. For more private *mitzvot* — *Kiddush*, for example — one occasionally encounters people who prefer to recite *Kiddush* themselves rather than rely on the host, precisely because they feel that active performance is superior to *shomea k'oneh*. The *gemara* leaves open whether *shomea k'oneh* is fully equivalent to *oneh* or merely adequate in the absence of the preferred mode.

Returning in closing to the experience of *hallel* itself: Rava's careful reading of what his contemporaries preserved as vestiges of the older responsive practice reminds us of what that *hallel* was. It was not many individuals reciting in parallel from their prayer books, converging only briefly at *hodu lashem*. It was a communal call-and-response — *Hallelujah* after every phrase, *hodu lashem ki tov* through the second half — a genuinely unified *tzibbur* experience of joy and praise. The *halachot* of *shomea k'oneh* and of responsive recitation are not merely technical accommodations for the ignorant; they are the structure of a liturgical act meant to be experienced together.

---

---

# Sukkah 39

## Shomea Koneh

### Hallel & Response

The daf opens by wrapping up the principle of *shomea koneh* as it emerged in the context of *Hallel*. The earlier discussion traced how the recitation of *Hallel* originally operated through a responsive format: one person would recite a phrase and the congregation would respond with *halleluyah*. From this context arose the principle that even if one did not actively produce the response, the act of listening counted as though one had. The *Rambam* extends this to the context of *brachot*: if one hears a *bracha* and responds *Amen*, that *Amen* constitutes an affirmation tantamount to having recited the *bracha* itself, while the act of listening alone is equivalent to having given the response.

### Technical Definition

Technically, therefore, *shomea koneh* does not mean "listening is like saying" — it means "listening is like responding," since its origin lies in the responsive *Hallel* format where the congregant's role was to give the *halleluyah* reply. This distinction matters for precision, but the principle is understood more broadly in practice.

### Torah & Megillah

The principle extends well beyond *Hallel*. The *Gemara* earlier cited verses about hearing the *Torah* being read, treating that listening as equivalent to having read it oneself — a context in which no notion of "responding" is present at all. Similarly, listening to the *Megillah* read aloud is treated as equivalent to having read it oneself. These applications demonstrate that *shomea koneh* takes on the broader formulation of "listening is like saying," which carries significant practical *halachic* weight, particularly as *Purim* approaches.

---

## Breaking God's Name

### Baruch Haba Rule

The *Gemara* at the bottom of 38b turns to a related but distinct concern. Rava rules that one should not say *baruch haba* — pause — and then *b'shem Hashem* as two separate utterances. Rather, *baruch haba b'shem Hashem* must be said as a single, continuous phrase. The reason is that if one breaks the phrase at *baruch haba*, that fragment stands as a complete statement on its own, leaving *b'shem Hashem* floating without context — an invocation of the divine name unmoored from meaning.

The same logic applies to *Kaddish*. Rava rules that one should not say *yehei shmei rabba* — pause — and then *mevorach* separately. Rather, the phrase *yehei shmei rabba mevorach* — "may His great name be blessed" — must be recited as a unit, ensuring that the meaning is clear and the divine name is embedded within a proper context.

### Context & Completion

Rav Safra pushes back, addressing Rava with the honorific *Moshe* — meaning "great one" — and asking whether the concern is really warranted. His response: *hasam vehacha asuki miltha hu velais ban bah* — here and in that case, we are simply completing what we have begun to say, and listeners will understand the meaning from context. An unusual pause in the middle of a phrase does not fundamentally alter its meaning if the speaker is going to finish the thought a moment later; the full statement will be understood based on context. The connection to the preceding discussion of *shomea koneh* is apparent: just as the first half of a *pasuk* and the second half form a coherent whole, so too a brief pause within a phrase does not sever its unity, provided the completion follows immediately.

---

## Doubling in Hallel

### Local Customs

The *Gemara* now turns to the practice of *kefilah* — doubling or repeating sections within *Hallel*. The rule is: *makom shenahagu lichfol*, where the local custom is to repeat lines in *Hallel*, one repeats them.

### Rebbi's Practice

A *baraisa* is cited: Rebbi would practice *kefilah* — he would repeat certain sections of *Hallel*. The *baraisa* does not specify exactly which sections, but Rashi explains that Rebbi repeated from *Ana Hashem Hoshia Na* onward to the conclusion — which corresponds to current practice. Rabbi Elazar ben Perata, however, would add to what Rebbi did: as Abaye clarifies, he would begin the repetition earlier, starting from *Odecha Hashem ki anitani*.

### Odecha Hashem

This is precisely the practice observed today. Looking at the *Hallel* in the *siddur*, it is easy to miss that the repetitions begin at *Odecha Hashem ki anitani* and continue to the end — that entire section is doubled in the recitation, not just the *Ana Hashem Hoshia Na* passage.

### Poetic Structure

Rashi on the *Mishnah* explains the structural rationale for where the doubling begins. Throughout the earlier portions of *Hallel*, the *pesukim* are composed in a natural doubling or parallelism. Lines echo one another with the same or closely related language — *yemin Hashem osa chayil, yemin Hashem romema, yemin Hashem osa chayil*; *savuni gam sevavuni... savuni kidvorim* — couplets and near-repetitions run through the text organically. At the point of *Odecha Hashem*, this structural doubling ceases in the original text, and so the custom of vocal repetition was introduced to maintain the same thematic texture through to the end.

### Ana Hashem

It is worth noting that *Ana Hashem Hoshia Na* is not actually doubled in the text of *Tehillim*. The passage in *Tehillim* reads: *ze hayom asa Hashem nagila venismecha bo, Ana Hashem Hoshia Na, Ana Hashem hatzlicha na, baruch haba beshem Hashem* — *Ana Hashem Hoshia Na* appears once and *Ana Hashem hatzlicha na* appears once; there is no doubling in the written text. Because the *siddur* prints the doubled version as it is recited in practice, one might mistakenly assume the repetition is original to *Tehillim*, but from *Odecha Hashem* through the conclusion, everything is a liturgical doubling added to the original text. This practice likely also reflects the needs of the responsive recitation format, in which repetition served the musical or participatory structure of communal *Hallel*.

---

## Blessing Hallel

### Levarech Yevarech

The *Mishnah* states: *levarech yevarech* — where there is a custom to make a *bracha* over *Hallel*, one makes it.

### Blessing at End

Abaye immediately clarifies: this teaching refers only to the *bracha* at the end of *Hallel*. At the beginning, there is no need for a *Mishnah* to establish the obligation — that is already obvious.

### Shmuel's Principle

The *Gemara* explains: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel — *kol hamitzvos kulan mevarech aleihen over le'asiyasan* — for all *mitzvot*, one recites the *bracha* before their performance. Since *Hallel* is a *mitzvah*, the *bracha* at the outset is self-evidently required. The *Mishnah*'s ruling about making a *bracha* addresses only the *bracha* at the conclusion, which is the novel point requiring instruction.

### Over L'Asiyasan

The *Gemara* then asks: what is the linguistic basis for the word *over* in Shmuel's formulation of *over le'asiyasan*, indicating "before" the act? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives it from a verse: *vayarotz Achima'atz derech hakikar vaya'avor es ha-Kushi* — Achima'atz ran by the way of the valley and *passed in front of* the Ethiopian. To be *over le'asiyasan* means to pass in front, to come before.

Abaye adds another source: *vehu avar lifneihem* — he passed in front of them. A third source is also proposed: *vaya'avor malkam lifneihem v'Hashem berosham* — the king passed in front of them and God was at their head.

### Going Before

It is striking that Shmuel chose the word *over* rather than the simpler *kodem asiyasan*. The *pesukim* cited to explain this word do more than establish a technical meaning — they evoke a particular image. To pass in front, to run ahead, to go before the king: these are not merely sequential acts but acts of announcement and framing. The one who goes before prepares and presents what is about to come. There is in this image a sense that the *bracha* is not merely a prelude to the *mitzvah* but frames and announces it, setting its significance before the act begins.

### Mitzvah vs Liturgy

At this point it is worth pausing to appreciate why the *Gemara* cites Shmuel's principle here at all. The primary *chiddush* of Shmuel's statement in other contexts is to establish that the *bracha* must come *before* rather than *after* the *mitzvah*. Here, the *Gemara* is citing it not to emphasize the timing but to establish the obligation itself — that since *Hallel* is a *mitzvah*, there is an obligation to make a *bracha*. The *Mishnah* might have been read as treating all *brachot* around *Hallel* as merely customary. The *Gemara* insists: no, the *bracha* at the beginning is obligatory by virtue of *mitzvah*, and Shmuel's principle establishes this.

### Pesukei D'Zimra

This raises a broader question worth exploring: is *Hallel* treated as a *mitzvah* act or as liturgy? One might ask whether a *bracha* is made at other points in *davening* to introduce a liturgical section. In fact there are parallels — *Pesukei D'Zimra* and *Krias Shema* both have *brachot* framing them — but the character of those *brachot* differs significantly from a standard *birchas hamitzvah*.

The *brachot* before *Krias Shema* — *Yotzer Or* and *Ahavat Olam* (or *Ahavah Rabbah*) — do not say "Who has commanded us to read the *Shema*." Rather, they expand on the themes of the *Shema* itself. *Ahavat Olam* / *Ahavah Rabbah*, with its emphasis on God's love for Israel and the giving of the *Torah*, leads naturally into the *Shema*'s declaration of accepting God's sovereignty — *Asher bachar banu*, God has chosen us, and we in turn acknowledge God. Even *Yotzer Or* can be connected to *Hashem Echad*, the universal dimension of the *Shema*'s proclamation. The *brachot* are not marking a *mitzvah* act in the way *al netilat yadayim* or *al akilas matzah* do; they are amplifying and elaborating the liturgical theme.

*Pesukei D'Zimra* is even clearer. There is no *mitzvah d'Oraisa* or *d'Rabbanan* to recite *Pesukei D'Zimra* — indeed, *Pesukei D'Zimra* only developed after the *Gemara*'s period. The framing *brachot* of *Pesukei D'Zimra* are similarly liturgical in character rather than marking a *mitzvah* act. The closing *bracha* of *Pesukei D'Zimra* says *Melech Meshubach u'Mefoar Adei Ad Shemo HaGadol, Melech Mehulal BaTishbachot* — the very act of blessing God is an extension of the praise being offered, not an announcement of an obligation. Similarly, *HaBochar BeShirei Zimra, Melech Kel Chai HaOlamim* and *Melech Gadol BaTishbachot* — these *brachot* are themselves praises of God, woven into the fabric of the liturgy.

### Hallel as Mitzvah

*Hallel* is categorically different. It is not a routine part of *davening*. According to some *Rishonim*, saying *Hallel* at the time of the *chagim* is actually a *mitzvah d'Oraisa* — according to the *Rambam*, it is part of the *mitzvah* of *simchat hachag*. The specific *pesukim* of *Hallel* may have been composed later, but the obligation to praise and give thanks to God at the festivals is embedded in the *mitzvat aseh* of *simcha*. When the *Gemara* introduces Shmuel's principle of *over le'asiyasan* and frames the *bracha* before *Hallel* as a *birchas hamitzvah*, this is a genuine *chiddush*: we are treating *Hallel* as a *mitzvah* act, and the introductory *bracha* — *asher kidshanu bemitzvotav vetzivanu likro es ha-Hallel* (or *ligmor* in the *Sefardi* formulation) — is a *birchas hamitzvah* in the full sense.

### Melech Mehulal

The *bracha* at the end of *Hallel* — *Melech Mehulal BaTishbachot* — is an entirely different matter. This is not a *birchas hamitzvah*; one does not ordinarily recite a *bracha* after completing a *mitzvah*. Rather, this concluding *bracha* is of a liturgical character, parallel to the closing *bracha* of *Pesukei D'Zimra*. It integrates *Hallel* into the fabric of the davening, framing it as an act of praise rather than marking an obligation. The *Mishnah*'s statement — *levarech yevarech*, where the custom is to make a *bracha* — refers to this concluding *bracha*, which is a matter of *minhag* and liturgical framing rather than strict *mitzvah* obligation. The opening *bracha*, by contrast, is obligatory by virtue of Shmuel's principle, because *Hallel* is a *mitzvah*.

What emerges from the *Gemara*'s analysis is a nuanced distinction: the *Mishnah* could have been read as treating all *brachot* around *Hallel* as purely customary liturgy. The *Gemara* corrects this: the *bracha* at the beginning is a genuine *birchas hamitzvah* and is obligatory; the *bracha* at the end is the one that is a matter of custom, because it is a liturgical *bracha* of the kind that frames and expands the act of praise rather than announcing a *mitzvah*.

---

## Tosafot: Timing & Nanuim

### Taking Lulav

Tosafot raises a closely related practical question under the heading of *over le'asiyasan*: since one must make the *bracha* before performing the *mitzvah*, at what precise moment must the *bracha* over the *lulav* be recited? At first glance, the *bracha* should be said before picking up the *lulav* at all. Yet Tosafot finds this unsatisfying, and notes: *midai d'agbeih nafik beih* — the moment one lifts the *lulav*, one has already fulfilled the *mitzvah*, as is stated at the end of the chapter. If the *bracha* must precede the *mitzvah* act and the act is completed by lifting, the *bracha* cannot be said while the *lulav* is still sitting in its holder.

### Esrog Position

Tosafot also notes the parallel from *Tefillin*: one makes the *bracha* on *tefillin* after placing the *shel yad* on the arm but before tightening the knot, because until that moment the *mitzvah* is not yet complete. The principle is that the *bracha* must be recited at a moment when the *mitzvah* is *mezumenes b'yado la'asos* — immediately at hand and ready to be performed. This is the concept of *over l'over*: the *bracha* must come immediately before, not long before.

Applying this to the *lulav*, Tosafot proposes two solutions. The first: one might pick up the *lulav* before taking the *esrog*, making the *bracha* at that point, since without the *esrog* one is not yet *yotzei* — the *mitzvah* is not yet complete, and the *bracha* thus precedes the completion. The second: one takes both the *lulav* and the *esrog* but holds the *esrog* upside down. Holding it inverted means one is not yet *yotzei*, and so the *bracha* can be made in that interval. Tosafot also mentions the possibility of having explicit *kavanah* not to be *yotzei* when lifting, but notes that people do not rely on this since such mental intent is easily forgotten. The practical custom therefore is to pick up the *esrog* in the inverted position.

### Nanuim Complete

Tosafot adds a further principle that resolves a scenario where one has already picked up the *lulav* and *esrog* properly before making the *bracha*. He writes: *mishum delo gmar mitzvato ad achar nianua* — one has not yet completed the *mitzvah* until after the *nanuim*, the shaking. Therefore, even after taking the *lulav* and *esrog*, the *bracha* may still be made between the taking and the shaking, since the full *mitzvah* is not yet complete.

### Netilat Yadayim

Tosafot draws a parallel to *netilat yadayim*: one makes the *bracha al netilat yadayim* after the washing and before drying, because *delo gmar mitzvato ad achar niguv* — the *mitzvah* is not complete until the hands are dried, as stated in the relevant *perek* that eating without drying is forbidden. The *bracha* is thus situated within the performance of the *mitzvah*, not before it begins.

### Nanuim Status

However, Tosafot himself notes that the parallel is not perfect. *Denianua eino ela machshirei mitzvah* — the shaking is part of the fuller fulfillment of the *mitzvah*, an enhancement and completion of it, but it does not prevent one from being *yotzei b'alam* without it. As the end of the chapter states, the moment one lifts the *lulav* one is already *yotzei*. The shaking does not strictly *me'akev* — it is not indispensable to basic fulfillment. Nevertheless, Tosafot concludes: *emet hu delavatar denafik bei mevarech* — in practice, even after one has already picked it up and is technically *yotzei*, one may still make the *bracha* before shaking, because the shaking constitutes the fuller expression of the *mitzvah*.

This has direct practical implications. If one forgets to hold the *esrog* upside down and picks it up in the correct position before making the *bracha*, one should not be flustered — simply go ahead and recite the *bracha*, because the *nanuim* remain ahead and the *mitzvah* is not yet fully performed in its ideal form. The *pshat* of the *mishnayot* is that the primary expression of the *mitzvah* is taking the *lulav* with the shaking in *shul*, which is why most people wait to make the *bracha* until just before that moment.

---

## Shemitah & Commerce

### Mishnah Setup

The *Gemara* now turns to a new *Mishnah* of immediate practical relevance, given the approaching *shemitah* year. The *Mishnah* states: *halokeach lulav mechaveiro bashvi'it* — one who purchases a *lulav* from his fellow during the *shemitah* year. In such a case, *noten lo esrog bematanah* — the seller should give the *esrog* as a gift — *lefi shein rashai lelokcho bashvi'it*, because one is not permitted to purchase it during *shemitah*.

### Esrog vs Lulav

Two questions arise immediately. First, why is the *esrog* different from the *lulav*? The obvious answer is that an *esrog* is a fruit and carries *kedushat shevi'it*, while a *lulav* is merely a stalk — a stick — and would seem not to bear *kedushat shevi'it* at all. We will discover in the *Gemara* that this assumption is incorrect, and that even a *lulav* has *kedushat shevi'it* — but the reason they are treated differently in this *Mishnah* turns out to be a matter of timing, which year's produce each belongs to based on when it grew and when it was picked. Second, why can one not simply purchase the *esrog*?

### No Gift Given

The *Gemara* asks: what if the seller simply refuses to give the *esrog* as a gift? What then?

---

## Bundling Price

### Free Gift Strategy

Rav Huna offers a practical solution: *mavliya lei dmei esrog belulav* — one buries the price of the *esrog* within the price of the *lulav*. The *lulav* is sold at a price that incorporates the value of the *esrog*, while the *esrog* itself is presented as a gift that accompanies the *lulav* purchase. The price of the *lulav* is set higher to absorb the *esrog*'s value, and the *esrog* is formally given as a bonus — free with the *lulav*.

---

## Money Misuse

### Three Meals Limit

But the *Gemara* presses further: why not simply pay for the *esrog* directly? *Veliteiv lei behedya* — why not give him the money straightforwardly? The answer: *lefi she'ein mosrin dmei peirot shevi'it le'am ha'aretz* — one may not hand over money paid for *shemitah* produce to an *am ha'aretz*. A *baraisa* establishes the rule: *ein mosrin dmei peirot shevi'it le'am ha'aretz yoter mimazon shalosh se'udot* — one may not give an *am ha'aretz* money for *shemitah* produce in an amount exceeding three meals' worth. The assumption is that if the amount is limited to three meals' worth, the *am ha'aretz* will likely use it immediately to buy food for his next few meals, which is the proper use of *shemitah* money. An ordinary person with only a few coins in hand will convert them to food without delay. Beyond three meals' worth, however, one cannot be confident the money will be used appropriately.

### Money Kedusha

The underlying *halacha* is as follows. When one purchases *shemitah* produce, the fruit retains its *kedushat shevi'it* — buying it does not alter the status of the fruit. But the money used to purchase *shemitah* produce also acquires *kedushat shevi'it*. That money must now be used to purchase food, which must then be eaten *bekedushat shevi'it*. This is the proper channeling of *shemitah* sanctity through the monetary medium.

### Kedusha Transfer

The *baraisa* continues: *ve'im masar* — if one did give more money than permitted — *yomar harei ma'ot halalu yehu mekhulalim al peirot she'yesh li betokh beiti* — one declares that the *kedushat shevi'it* of that money is transferred onto fruit already in one's possession at home (non-*shemitah* fruit from a prior year), *uva ve'okhalan bekedushat shevi'it* — and one then eats that fruit with the sanctity of *shevi'it*. So one who gave excessive *shemitah* money to an *am ha'aretz* must transfer the *kedushah* from that money onto other fruit in one's home and treat that fruit accordingly. One wonders, as the *Gemara* itself notes, whether such a transfer is even effective when the money is no longer in one's control — according to one opinion, the transfer does not work, and the restriction functions as a *knas*, a penalty: what was done wrong was done wrong, and the goal is simply not to habituate oneself to misusing *shemitah* funds.

### Esrog Cost

Tosafot (39a, the second-to-last entry, *mazon shalosh se'udot*) makes a sharp observation: the very fact that there is a problem with paying for the *esrog* implies that an *esrog* costs more than three meals' worth — otherwise, why would there be any issue? Tosafot then asks from a *Mishnah* in *Meilah* (chapter 6) where it says one can send an agent to buy an *esrog* for a single *perutah*. Tosafot resolves the contradiction: that *Mishnah* refers to a *pasul* esrog, one not needed for the *mitzvah* — bought only for eating. Here, by contrast, we are speaking of a *kasher esrog*, one that is *hadar*, beautiful and fit for the *bracha* — and the price of such an *esrog* has always been considerable, far exceeding three meals' worth.

### Am Ha'aretz Risk

In a preceding passage, Tosafot enumerates the ways an *am ha'aretz* might misuse *shemitah* money: buying non-kosher animals, purchasing land or slaves, spending it on clothing, paying debts, giving it to a launderer or barber or sailor. The permitted uses are only food, drink, and anointing — *l'achilah ulish'tiyah ulisichah*. Tosafot concludes with a sweeping observation: there is no end to the *dinim* and *isurim* involved in *peirot shevi'it* that must be treated with *kedushat shevi'it*. This is an apt summary of the complexity one encounters when engaging with *hilchos shevi'it* in practice.

---

## Business vs Sales

### Intent to Sell

Tosafot raises the question: given that there is a prohibition on doing *business* with *peirot shevi'it*, why does the *Gemara* explain the problem in the *Mishnah* as arising from the transfer of money rather than from the prohibition on commerce itself? Tosafot answers that the prohibition on commerce — *sechorah* — refers specifically to picking produce with the *intent* to sell it commercially. During *shemitah* as properly observed, fields are left open and anyone may enter and take produce for personal use. If one enters a field, picks apples for one's family, and then has surplus that one sells informally, that is not commerce — that is merely selling what one happens to have. The *issur* of doing business with *shemitah* produce is violated only when one goes out to pick *with the purpose of selling*, treating the produce as inventory in a commercial enterprise.

### Family Workarounds

Tosafot notes that a workaround exists: one may go and pick the produce oneself without intending to sell it, and then give it to a family member — a son or a brother — who proceeds to sell it. Since the one who picked it did not pick it for commerce, and the one who sells it did not pick it, the direct chain of commercial intent is broken. This is characterized as a *ha'aramah*, a legal stratagem, but one that Tosafot indicates is permissible.

### Fixed Stand

A bright-line indicator of commerce, according to Tosafot, is maintaining a fixed stand in the marketplace — a regular stall set up to sell *shemitah* produce. Regardless of the circumstances of picking, operating a fixed marketplace stand constitutes doing business with *peirot shevi'it* and is forbidden.

### Reselling Profit

Tosafot identifies a further category of prohibited commerce: purchasing *shemitah* produce from one person and reselling it to another for profit. Even if one did none of the picking and had no role in the original harvest, buying produce with the intent to resell at a higher price — arbitrage — constitutes *sechorah* with *peirot shevi'it* and is forbidden. The distinction Tosafot draws is between *selling* (which is sometimes permitted) and *doing business* (which is not): one who has produce and sells it occasionally is not engaged in commerce; one who buys and sells for the spread is.

---

## Lulav Question

### Lulav Parallel

The *Gemara* now turns to the structural difficulty in the *Mishnah*. The *Mishnah* presented the purchase of a *lulav* as unproblematic and the purchase of an *esrog* as prohibited. But if the concern about paying for *shemitah* produce stems from the *kedushah* of that produce — which triggers the *kedushah* of the money used to buy it, which then risks being misused — then the *lulav* should present the same problem. The *lulav* also has *kedushat shevi'it*, as the *Gemara* will now establish. Why then can the *lulav* be purchased straightforwardly?

---

## Year Determination

### Lulav by Blossoming

The *Gemara* answers: *lulav bar shishis hanichnas lishvi'is hi* — the *lulav* being sold *erev Sukkot* at the onset of *shemitah* is actually sixth-year produce, not *shemitah* produce. The *shemitah* year began just two weeks before *Sukkot*. The rule for trees is that the year of produce is determined by *chanata* — blossoming, the beginning of growth. A *lulav* stalk of the size suitable for the *mitzvah* did not grow in the final two weeks of the sixth year or the first two weeks of *shemitah*; its growth began well before *shemitah*, placing it in the sixth year. Therefore, the *lulav* is sixth-year produce, carries no *kedushat shevi'it*, and may be purchased normally.

### Esrog Question

This immediately raises the parallel question: the *esrog* also began growing before *shemitah* — it too was on the tree during the sixth year. Why does the *esrog* not follow the same rule and also be considered sixth-year produce?

### Esrog Irrigation

The *Gemara* answers: *esrog batar lekita azlinan* — for the *esrog*, we follow the time of picking, not the time of blossoming. The reason is that the *esrog*, unlike ordinary trees, requires regular irrigation — it cannot survive on rainwater alone. Because it needs constant watering, it is in this respect similar to a vegetable. And the *halacha* for vegetables is that their year is determined not by when growth begins but by when they are harvested.

### Vegetable Analogy

For vegetables, *shemitah* status and *maaser* year are both determined by *lekita* — picking time — because vegetables depend continuously on human intervention for their water supply and cannot be classified by a single moment of blossoming as trees can. Since the *esrog* shares this characteristic, its year follows picking time. An *esrog* sold *erev Sukkot* was picked within the two weeks of *shemitah*, and therefore it is a *shemitah* esrog — even though it began growing the prior year.

---

## Tree vs Vegetable

### Rabban Gamliel Debate

The *Gemara* anticipates a difficulty. There is a well-known dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer regarding the *esrog*. The *Gemara* notes that according to both opinions, for the purposes of *shemitah* the *esrog* goes by *chanata* — blossoming — not by *lekita*. If that is so, why does the *Gemara* claim the *esrog* follows picking time for *shemitah*?

### Bikkurim Sources

The *Gemara* cites the *Mishnah* in *Bikkurim*: *esrog shaveh l'ilan b'gimmel drachim u'lyerek b'derech echad* — the *esrog* is comparable to a tree in three respects and to a vegetable in one respect.

### Tree Traits

Its three tree-like characteristics are: it is subject to *orlah* (the prohibition on fruit of the first three years), to *neta revai* (the fourth-year sanctity), and to *shemitah* — going by the year of blossoming. These three *halachot* apply to the *esrog* as they do to any fruit tree.

### Vegetable Trait

Its one vegetable-like characteristic: *she'bish'as lekitato isuro* — its *maaser* obligation is determined at the time of picking. So *maaser* follows *lekita*, while *shemitah* follows *chanata*. This is the position associated with Rabban Gamliel — the *de'vei Rabban Gamliel* reading. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, holds that the *esrog* is like a tree in all respects, and *maaser* too follows *chanata*.

### Abutulmos Testimony

The *Gemara* introduces a *baraisa*: Rabbi Yosei reports that Avtulmos testified in the name of five elders — *esrog achar lekita lemaaser* — that the *esrog* follows picking time for *maaser*. The sages then convened at Usha and ruled: *bein lemaaser bein lishvi'it* — both for *maaser* and for *shemitah*, the *esrog* goes by picking time. The *Gemara* notes that the *baraisa* as originally stated only mentioned *maaser*, and *shemitah* was not explicitly included. The *Gemara* therefore reads the *baraisa* as telescoped — *chisorei mechasra vehachi katani* — and reconstructs its full meaning: the earlier opinion was that *esrog* follows picking for *maaser* but blossoming for *shemitah*, and the ruling at Usha was that it follows picking for *both*.

### Final Ruling

The ruling of the sages at Usha — *esrog basar lekita bein lemaaser bein lishvi'it* — represents the operative conclusion: the *esrog* follows picking time for both *maaser* and *shemitah*. This is the position that explains the *Mishnah*: an *esrog* picked during *shemitah* is a *shemitah esrog*, regardless of when its growth began.

---

## Practical Timing

### Lulav Status

The practical upshot is now clear. The *lulav* sold *erev Sukkot* at the beginning of *shemitah* blossomed and began growing last year — it is therefore sixth-year produce and carries no *kedushat shevi'it*.

### Esrog Status

The *esrog* also began growing last year, but was picked this year — within the *shemitah* year. Because the *esrog* follows picking time for *shemitah*, it is a *shemitah* esrog despite having grown during the sixth year. The result is an asymmetry: the *lulav* is sixth-year produce and the *esrog* is *shemitah* produce, both taken from trees that blossomed in the same prior year — their difference in status owing entirely to the different legal frameworks governing when their respective years are determined.

### Lulav Kedusha Q

This, however, raises an additional question that remains to be addressed. If the *lulav* follows blossoming time and is therefore sixth-year produce this year, one might still ask: shouldn't the *lulav* carry *kedushat shevi'it* altogether on some other basis? Is a *lulav* stalk even subject to *kedushat shevi'it* at all, given that it is not fruit but merely a stalk — and *kedushat shevi'it* is conventionally associated with food? This question is left open and will be taken up in the next *shiur*.

---

---

# Sukkah 41

## Lulav Obligation History

### Original Law

The *mishnah* opens a new subject: *barishona hayah lulav nital bamikdash shiva u-vamedina yom echad* — originally, the *lulav* was taken in the *beit hamikdash* for all seven days, and in the *medina* for only one day. Having spent the entirety of the preceding *perek* discussing the four species, the act of *hallel*, and the special case of *shemitta*, the *mishnah* finally arrives at the fundamental question of the nature and scope of the *lulav* obligation itself.

### Medina Definition

What exactly is the *medina*? The term stands in contrast to *mikdash*, and the most natural reading is that it refers to anywhere outside the *beit hamikdash*. However, the Rambam, in his *Perush Hamishnayot* here and in several analogous *mishnayot*, interprets *mikdash* to encompass not merely the Temple precinct itself but all of *Yerushalayim*. A parallel case involves blowing the *shofar* on *rosh hashana* that falls on *shabbos*: this was permitted in the *mikdash* but not in the *medina*, and for the Rambam that privilege extended throughout *Yerushalayim*. The majority of authorities, however, understand *mikdash* in the strict sense — the Temple compound alone — and *medina* as everywhere outside it.

### Biblical Source

The biblical source for the seven-day obligation in the *mikdash* is the verse *v'likachtem lachem bayom harishon* — take for yourselves on the first day — followed at the end of the passage by *v'semachtem lifnei Hashem elokeichem shivat yamim*, rejoice before Hashem your God for seven days. The phrase *lifnei Hashem*, before God, is understood to mean in the *beit hamikdash* — or, according to the Rambam, in the *mikdash* and *Yerushalayim* — and that presence before God carries a seven-day *mitzvah*. Outside the *mikdash*, only the first day applied.

### Post-Destruction Enactme…

Once the *beit hamikdash* was destroyed, Raban Yochanan ben Zakai enacted that the *lulav* should be taken all seven days everywhere — *sheyehei lulav nital bamedina shiva* — as a *zecher lamikdash*, a remembrance of the Temple. Since the seven-day *mitzvah* could no longer be performed in the *mikdash*, it would henceforth be observed universally. The *mishnah* then adds a second element: *v'yehei yom hanaf kulo asur*, the day of the waving of the *omer* should be entirely forbidden. The juxtaposition of these two rulings — the *lulav* and the *omer* prohibition — may seem surprising, but Tosafot suggests that both were enacted by Raban Yochanan ben Zakai as *takanot* of *zecher lamikdash*, and these happen to be the two recorded in our *mishnah*.

---

## Zecher Lamikdash Theology

### Source Question
