The *gemara* does something striking: it completely bypasses the fascinating question of the one-day versus seven-day *lulav* obligation — a topic that will be taken up at the beginning of the next *perek* — and leaps directly to the concept of *zecher lamikdash*. The *gemara* asks: *minalan d'avdinan zecher lamikdash* — what is the source for the idea that one should institute practices to remember the *beit hamikdash*?

### Jeremiah Source

Rabbi Yochanan answers with a verse: *ki nidchah kar'u lach, Tziyon hee doreish ein lah* — they have called you a castaway, Zion that no one seeks after. The verse is a lament over the fate of *Yerushalayim* after the *churban*, bemoaning that no one is seeking it out. The *gemara* reads this negatively — *doreish ein lah*, no one seeks after it — as implying a positive obligation: *miklal d'ba'i doreish*, we are in fact required to seek after it, to maintain practices that keep the memory of the *churban* and of *Yerushalayim* alive.

### Ben Zakkai's Vision

The concept of *zecher lamikdash* invites a broader reflection on what Raban Yochanan ben Zakai was actually doing. He is typically understood as being deeply preoccupied with ensuring that the *churban habayit* remain at the forefront of Jewish consciousness. Yet the same Raban Yochanan ben Zakai was precisely the figure who helped the Jewish people navigate the transition away from a *mikdash*-centered Judaism toward a *Torah*-centered Judaism. The famous story in *Gittin* recounts how he negotiated with Vespasian and requested: *tenu li Yavne v'chachameha* — give me Yavneh and its scholars. Rabbi Akiva later criticized this as a missed opportunity to save *Yerushalayim*, but the *gemara* explains that Raban Yochanan ben Zakai regarded saving *Yerushalayim* as a lost cause and sought to preserve what could actually be preserved.

This tension is illustrated by two parallel stories about walking past the ruins of the *har habayit*. In the story involving Rabbi Akiva, the sages weep upon seeing foxes emerging from the site of the *beit hamikdash*, while Rabbi Akiva laughs, explaining that the fulfillment of the prophecy of destruction assures him the prophecy of rebuilding will also be fulfilled. It is a deeply optimistic vision, but one that remains centered on the *mikdash* — the *mikdash* was destroyed, and the *mikdash* will be rebuilt. In the parallel account in *Avos de-Rabbi Noson*, Raban Yochanan ben Zakai walks past the ruins and laughs. When his students ask why, he does not speak of the future rebuilding. Instead he invokes the verse *chesed chafatzti v'lo zavach* — I desire loving-kindness, not sacrifice — arguing that prayer, *Torah*, and *maasim tovim* are not mere substitutes for the *mikdash* but are independently what God desires. The center of religious life has genuinely shifted, not simply relocated.

### Paradox & Effect

Against this backdrop, the *takanot* of *zecher lamikdash* take on a paradoxical quality. They ostensibly exist to remind us of the *beit hamikdash* and to keep its loss present to consciousness. Yet if one were to ask today why we take the *lulav* for seven days, the natural answer would be: because it is a seven-day *mitzvah*. The practice does not typically evoke the sense of loss or yearning for the *mikdash*; if anything, it creates a full and expansive seven-day religious experience that stands entirely on its own. Rather than heightening the sense of absence, the enactment actually generates a vibrant religious practice that operates independently of the *mikdash*. Indeed, by extending the seven-day *mitzvah* to all of Israel rather than confining it to the Temple compound and a handful of participants, the *takana* arguably produced something richer than what had existed before.

This is the deeper signature of Raban Yochanan ben Zakai's project. The *takanot* framed as *zecher lamikdash* do not in practice cultivate ongoing yearning for the *mikdash* — they supplant that yearning with a flourishing Judaism that needs no *mikdash* to sustain it. The ostensible purpose and the actual effect run in opposite directions.

---

## Yom Hanaf Prohibition

### Problem Setup

The *mishnah* also includes Raban Yochanan ben Zakai's ruling that *yom hanaf* — the sixteenth of *Nissan*, the day the *omer* was waved — should be *kulo asur*, entirely forbidden for consumption of the new grain. The underlying law is *ad yom havi'achem et korban Elokeichem* — the new grain is prohibited until the *korban* of the *omer* is brought on the second day of *Pesach*. In the absence of a *beit hamikdash*, there is no *korban* to bring, and a separate verse — *v'lechem vekali v'karmel lo tochlu ad etzem hayom hazeh* — is understood to mean that when there is no *omer*, the grain becomes permissible as soon as the day itself begins, i.e., at nightfall entering the sixteenth. Paradoxically, the absence of the *mikdash* makes the grain permissible earlier than when the *mikdash* stands, since it is the bringing of the *omer* that creates the permission.

### Rebuilding Scenario

Why then did Raban Yochanan ben Zakai forbid the new grain for the entire day? The *gemara* explains with a remarkably concrete scenario: *meheira yibaneh beit hamikdash* — when the *beit hamikdash* is quickly rebuilt — people will say that last year they were eating new grain from daybreak of the sixteenth, *he'ir mizrach hitir*. When the *mikdash* is rebuilt and they must now wait for the *omer* to be brought, they will not understand the distinction and will continue eating from daybreak, not realizing that last year there was no *mikdash* and so daybreak sufficed, whereas now the *omer* must be brought. The *gemara* then asks with characteristic precision: when exactly does this concern arise? If the *beit hamikdash* were rebuilt on the sixteenth itself, then since it had not yet been built at daybreak, the grain was already permissible at that moment — so there is nothing problematic about having eaten at daybreak. Rather, the concern is that the *beit hamikdash* will be rebuilt on the fifteenth, on *yom tov* itself.

### Noon Question

This raises a further difficulty. A *mishnah* teaches that those who lived far from *Yerushalayim* were permitted to eat new grain from noon onward — *mechatzot hayom u'lehallan* — because *beit din* was never delinquent in ensuring the *omer* was brought by noon at the very latest. If the *beit hamikdash* is rebuilt on the fifteenth and the *omer* will invariably be brought by noon, why not simply establish the practice of refraining until noon? Whatever happens when the *mikdash* is rebuilt, people will know not to eat until noon — which will be after the *omer* is brought in any case. Why must the prohibition extend through the entire day?

### Night-Before Solution

The *gemara* resolves this with a specific scenario: *d'ivni b'leilya* — the *beit hamikdash* is built on the night entering the sixteenth. More precisely, it is completed right before sunset at the end of the fifteenth. In that case, when dawn breaks on the sixteenth, the *mikdash* already stands and the new grain requires the *omer* before it may be eaten. However, bringing the *omer* was not a simple act — it required going out to the fields, identifying and cutting the wheat, grinding it, and performing thirteen separate siftings. This preparatory process demanded substantial lead time. If the *mikdash* was completed only the previous night, there would be insufficient time to complete all preparations by noon. The *omer* could not be brought by noon, and the new grain would remain forbidden past midday. Had the practice been to permit eating from noon — since the *omer* is always brought by then — people in this scenario would eat at noon and in fact violate the prohibition, not realizing the situation was different. Therefore the practice had to be to forbid the new grain the entire day.

### Rashi on Future Temple

Rashi and Tosafot both address an obvious question: building the *beit hamikdash* is prohibited on *yom tov*, and also at night — so how can the *gemara* contemplate a scenario in which the *mikdash* is built at night or on *yom tov*? Rashi explains: *hani mili binyan habanui bidei adam* — those restrictions apply to a *mikdash* built by human hands. But the future *mikdash* that we await — *mikdash ha'asid she'anu mitzapin* — is already built and perfected, and it will be *yigale veyavo mishamayim*, revealed and descend from heaven, as the verse says *Mikdash Hashem konenu yadecha*, the Temple that God's own hands established. This understanding — that the future *mikdash* is already complete and awaits only its revelation — carries significant theological weight regarding the respective roles of human initiative and divine action in redemption.

### Rabbi Yehuda View

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes an entirely different reading of the *mishnah*. Rather than understanding Raban Yochanan ben Zakai's ruling as a *gezeira* — a rabbinic fence against confusion — he argues that Raban Yochanan ben Zakai was following the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the all-day prohibition is in fact *min haTorah*, a biblical law. The basis is the verse *ad etzem hayom hazeh* — until the very essence of this day — which Rabbi Yehuda reads as *ad itzumo shel yom*, until the day itself has completely passed. The word *ad* is understood as inclusive: the new grain is forbidden through the entirety of the day, unless the *omer* is brought, in which case it becomes permissible earlier. Under this reading, when the *omer* is brought it does not delay permission — it accelerates it. There is a certain logical elegance to this: rather than the presence of the *korban* imposing a stricter regime, the *korban* actively creates an earlier *heter*.

The *gemara* challenges this by noting that Rabbi Yehuda explicitly objects to Raban Yochanan ben Zakai's ruling elsewhere, suggesting he disagrees with it. The *gemara* resolves this by saying Rabbi Yehuda misunderstood Raban Yochanan ben Zakai: he thought Raban Yochanan ben Zakai was issuing a new *d'rabbanan* prohibition, and he responded that no new enactment is needed since the all-day prohibition already exists biblically. But Raban Yochanan ben Zakai was in fact doing something different — *darash v'hitkin* — he was expounding and publicizing what the biblical law actually is. Since there had always been a *mikdash*, no one had ever needed to know what the *halacha* was in its absence. Once the *mikdash* was destroyed, Raban Yochanan ben Zakai taught the masses the existing biblical rule. The word *hitkin* here means he expounded and established the practice, not that he created new rabbinic legislation.

---

## First Day on Shabbat

### Pre-positioning Practice

The *mishnah* turns to the case of *yom tov rishon shel chag she-chal lihyot be-Shabbos* — the first day of *sukkos* that falls on *shabbos*. We noted earlier that the first day of *lulav* is biblically mandated everywhere, and in the era when this *mishnah* was operative, people would in fact take the *lulav* even on *shabbos* if the first day fell then. The challenge was how to get the *lulav* to *shul* without carrying on *shabbos*. The solution was to prepare in advance: on *erev shabbos*, everyone would bring their *lulavim* to the synagogue. The next morning, people would rise early — *mashkimin u-va'in* — and each person would identify and take his own *lulav*, *kol echad ve-echad makir shelo ve-notel lo*, since the sages ruled that one cannot fulfill the obligation on the first day with someone else's *lulav*.

### Ownership Requirement

The *mishnah* states explicitly: *ein adam yotzei yedei chovaso be-yom tov rishon be-lulavo shel chaveiro* — a person does not fulfill his obligation on the first day of *yom tov* with his friend's *lulav*. This is why early arrival mattered: with many *lulavim* gathered together, each person had to identify and retrieve his own. For the remaining days of *chol hamoed*, however, a person may use his friend's *lulav*; the ownership requirement is specific to the first day.

### Accidental Carrying

Rabbi Yosi addresses a case of someone who did not bring his *lulav* to *shul* before *shabbos* and then, on the morning of *yom tov shabbos*, absentmindedly picked it up and walked out of his house. He realizes only after stepping outside that he has just carried in a public domain on *shabbos*. Rabbi Yosi rules *patur* — exempt from a *korban chatas* — because the carrying occurred in the context of performing a *mitzvah*. This reflects the general principle of *toeh bidvar mitzvah*: one who commits an unintentional transgression while engaged in a *mitzvah* is exempt from the *korban*. This same debate appears in the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua. A classic parallel is a *mohel* who on the eighth day inadvertently performs *milah* on the wrong infant; he is engaged in a *mitzvah* and acted without intent — the accidental *aveira* in the course of the *mitzvah* exempts him from the *korban*.

### Plural vs Singular

The *gemara* asks: what is the source for the requirement of individual ownership specifically on the first day? The *gemara* derives it from careful attention to grammatical number in the verse. *Ulekachtem lachem* is in the plural, and the counterintuitive principle that emerges is that plural language in the *Torah* means each individual is separately obligated, while singular language addresses the community as a corporate whole. This can be seen in the two *mitzvot* of counting: *usefartem lachem* — the plural form — is the *mitzvah* of counting the *omer*, which falls on each individual. *Vesafarta lecha* — the singular form — is the counting for the *yovel*, which is an obligation of *beit din* on behalf of the entire community. The plural addresses each member of the group individually; the singular addresses the collective as one entity. Applied here: had the verse said *ulekachta lecha*, one person could have taken the *lulav* on behalf of all. *Ulekachtem lachem* means every individual must take it personally.

### Biblical Ownership Source

The second element derived from *ulekachtem lachem* is the word *lachem* — for yourselves — which is read as *mishelachem*, from what belongs to you. This excludes a borrowed or stolen *lulav* and *esrog*. *Mikan amru chachamim* — from this the sages derived — that one does not fulfill the obligation on the first day of the holiday with a *lulav* belonging to someone else, unless it has been given as an outright gift: *ela im ken nesano lo be-matana*.

---

## Four Rabbis Story

### Story Narrative

The *mishnah* then records a story that illustrates and sharpens this principle. Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and Rabbi Akiva were traveling together on a ship — there is interesting speculation that this journey may have been connected to one of the delegations to the Roman government in that period. Rabban Gamliel was the only one who had brought a *lulav* and *esrog*, and he had purchased it for a thousand *zuz* — an extraordinary sum, reflecting how precious the *mitzvah* was to him. Who else on a ship was selling *lulavim ve-esrogim*? Apparently the one person who had one charged accordingly.

Rabban Gamliel took the *lulav* and *esrog* and fulfilled his obligation. He then gave it to Rabbi Yehoshua *be-matana* — as a gift, not a loan, since a loan would not allow him to fulfill the obligation. Rabbi Yehoshua was *yotzei*, and then gave it as a gift to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, who in turn gave it as a gift to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Akiva was *yotzei* and then returned it to Rabban Gamliel. It is, in the spirit of the season, an early documented instance of regifting.

### Conditional Gift

The *gemara* asks why the *mishnah* bothers telling us it was returned to Rabban Gamliel — this seems like an incidental detail. The *gemara* answers: *agav orcha kamashma lan* — it is teaching us something in passing. The return was not simply Rabbi Akiva's courtesy; it reflects the implicit understanding that the gift was given *al menat le-hachzir* — on the condition that it would ultimately be returned to Rabban Gamliel. And the *chiddush* is: *matana al menat le-hachzir shema matana* — even a conditional gift of this kind constitutes a genuine *matana*. One might have argued that if you give something only on the condition it comes back, it is really a loan, not a gift, and the recipient is therefore not *yotzei*. Rava states explicitly: if one says *helach lecha esrog ze al menat she-tachzirehu li* — here is this *esrog* on condition you return it to me — and the recipient takes it and fulfills the *mitzvah*, he is indeed *yotzei*. If he returns it, the condition is satisfied and the *yetzia* stands. If he does not return it, *lo yatza* — he was not *yotzei* — because the condition's failure retroactively negates the gift, meaning he was in effect taking an object that was not his.

An interesting nuance from the story: Rabban Gamliel's condition was not that the first recipient return it immediately, but that it eventually find its way back. Each subsequent recipient was receiving a genuine gift for the duration of his use of it.

### Communal Ownership

Tosafot draws out two important practical applications. First, Tosafot notes that a partnership *esrog* — one owned jointly by multiple people — also does not satisfy the *mitzvah* on the first day; sole ownership is required. Tosafot then addresses the historical reality in European communities, where individuals could not afford a *lulav* and *esrog* and communities would purchase a set with communal funds. How could this work if shared ownership disqualifies? The answer is that the implicit arrangement — and the practice was to make it explicit — was that when each person's turn came to take the *esrog*, every other member of the partnership was simultaneously giving his share to that person as a *matana al menat le-hachzir*. At the moment of taking, the individual is the sole owner of all the shares, satisfying the requirement of *lachem*. This is the implicit, if not always explicit, understanding operative in such communal purchases: *stama d'milsa k'ilu peirshu dami* — by default, the situation is treated as though all the terms were spelled out.

An analogous question arises with communal *tallitot* in a synagogue. Taking a *shul's tallis* and reciting a *bracha* depends on whether one has acquired it sufficiently — some treat the arrangement as a *matana al menat le-hachzir* or a similar form of temporary acquisition. The same logic applied historically to communal wedding rings, large decorative rings found in Jewish museums, which communities owned jointly but transferred temporarily to the groom as sole owner at the moment of *kiddushin*.

### Practical Lending

The practical *halacha* for someone who needs to borrow a *lulav* and *esrog* on the first day of *yom tov* follows directly from these principles. One cannot simply lend it — that would leave the borrower without ownership. The owner should give it as a genuine *matana al menat le-hachzir*, on the condition that it be returned. Ideally, the condition can be stated explicitly. Tosafot in the next passage raises a separate concern: whether giving something *al menat le-hachzir* requires satisfying the technical requirements of stipulations derived from the *tnai b'nei Gad u'v'nei Re'uven* — that the condition must precede the action, must be stated in a double form with both the positive and negative clause, and so on. That Tosafot suggests these conditions must be satisfied, while elsewhere the same Tosafot indicates that where the intent is clear, the conditions may be assumed. In the communal purchase scenario, Tosafot had already concluded that an implicit understanding suffices; the question of technical *tnai* requirements is more acute when one is making an explicit conditional gift on the spot.

---

## Holding During Prayer

### Ameimar Story

Mar bar Ameimar reports to Rav Ashi that his father, Ameimar, would hold his *lulav* and *esrog* while he was *davening* — that is, he held onto the four species throughout his prayer. The *gemara* immediately raises an objection from a *baraita*: a person should not hold *tefillin* in his hand or a *sefer Torah* in his chest while *davening*, because he will be distracted — divided between focusing on his prayer and ensuring he does not drop these sacred objects. Shmuel extends the concern to non-sacred objects as well: a knife, a plate, bread, or money — all of these are things one fears dropping during prayer, and therefore they too constitute a distraction.

### No Distraction

How then could Ameimar hold a *lulav* and *esrog* while *davening*? The *gemara* resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between the nature of the objects. In the cases of *tefillin*, a *sefer Torah*, and the objects listed by Shmuel, there is no *mitzvah* in the holding itself — *lav mitzvah ninhu l'ochzan* — and as a result the holding is experienced as a burden and a distraction. Rashi explains: *v'havu lehu l'masa* — psychologically, holding them is a weight; one is anxious about maintaining hold of them, and that anxiety pulls focus away from *davening*. But with the *lulav* and *esrog*, the holding itself is the *mitzvah*: *netilata u'lekichata mitzvah hi*. And because the *mitzvah* is beloved — *mitech shechaviva mitzvah alav* — it does not feel like a burden. The holding is not an additional concern layered on top of prayer; it is itself a cherished act, and therefore psychologically it does not distract. This is admittedly counterintuitive — one still needs to avoid dropping it — but Rashi's explanation is that when an act is experienced as *chaviv*, the anxiety of maintaining it does not register as a drain on attention.

### Jerusalem Practice

A *baraita* records that this was in fact the established practice of the people of *Yerushalayim*. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok testifies: *adam yotzei mibeito v'lulavo beyado* — a person would leave his home with his *lulav* in hand; he would walk to the synagogue holding his *lulav*; he would recite *krias shema* and *daven* holding his *lulav*. This is consistent with the assumption that dominates the preceding discussion throughout this *perek*: the primary and natural context for taking the *lulav* is in *shul* during *hallel* and prayer. The people of *Yerushalayim* took this further by holding the *lulav* not just during the designated moments but throughout the day. After *davening*, they would visit the sick and comfort mourners — *v'lulavo beyado* — holding the *lulav* the entire time.

### Placing Down

Two activities required setting the *lulav* down. When called up for a *Torah* reading, one needs both hands free to open and roll the *Torah*. And when a *kohen* performed *duchening* — the *priestly blessing* — his hands obviously needed to be free and raised. In those moments, the *lulav* was placed on the ground. Upon entering the *beit midrash* for learning, a person would send the *lulav* home with a son, a servant, or a messenger rather than leave it on the floor, since abandoning it there would be disrespectful. The *gemara* notes that the entire *baraita* serves *l'hodiacha kama hayu zerizin bemitzvot* — to show how zealous the people of *Yerushalayim* were in the performance of *mitzvot*. The practice also reflects the understanding that holding the *lulav* is not exhausted in the single moment of *netila* — *ulekachtem lachem*, the act of taking, continues as a *mitzvah* throughout the duration of holding it.

---

## Exemption Conditions

### Abaye Position

The *gemara* returns to the case of Rabbi Yosi: one who accidentally carries the *lulav* out into the public domain on the *shabbos* of the first day of *sukkos* is *patur* because he was *toeh bidvar mitzvah*. Abaye qualifies this: *lo shanu ela shelo yatza bo* — the exemption applies only if at the moment of carrying he had not yet been *yotzei*. If he was *already yotzei* and then stepped outside with the *lulav* in hand, *chayav* — he is liable for the sin offering, since the act of carrying was no longer part of the *mitzvah* itself.

### Upside Down

This raises an immediate difficulty: as soon as one picks up the *lulav* and *esrog*, one is *yotzei*, so when would it ever be the case that one carries it outside and has not yet been *yotzei*? Abaye answers: *keshehafacho* — when one picked it up upside down. As discussed earlier, one turns the *lulav* upside down before the *bracha* in order not to be *yotzei* prematurely; the *mitzvah* of *lekicha* requires the *lulav* to be in its proper orientation. So if a person grabbed his *lulav* upside down, intending to flip it right before the *bracha* in *shul*, and in that state walked out of his house, he had not yet been *yotzei* and the exemption of *toeh bidvar mitzvah* would apply.

### Vessel Carrying

Rava offers an alternative: *afilu teima shelo hafacho* — even if the *lulav* was held right-side up, the exemption can still apply. *Kegon shehotzio bikli* — if the person was carrying it out inside a vessel or container, and he is not *yotzei* because he was not holding it directly. The *gemara* presses back: but Rava himself had said *lekicha al yedei davar acher shema lekicha* — taking through an intermediary object still counts as taking. Rava responds: that is only true *derech kavod* — if the manner of taking is respectful. If it is *derech bizayon*, a disrespectful manner, it does not count. Rashi clarifies that holding the *lulav* in a fine silk handkerchief as a handle, for example, is *derech kavod* and constitutes valid *lekicha*, whereas placing it inside an ordinary vessel is not *derech bizayon* per se but also lacks the quality of *kavod* required. For indirect *lekicha* to be valid, it must be conducted in a manner that reflects respect for the *mitzvah*. In most ordinary circumstances — walking out of one's house with the *esrog* in its box and the *lulav* in its holder — the act likely does not meet the threshold of *lekicha derech kavod*, which is why one does not automatically become *yotzei* through such casual handling.

---

## Toeh Bidvar Mitzvah

### Olah-Chatat Example

Rav Huna extends the application of Rabbi Yosi's principle of *toeh bidvar mitzvah*. He cites the following case: if a *kohen* finds a bird *olah* among the bird *chatat* offerings near the base of the *mizbeach* — they are normally in separate corners, but due to overflow one has ended up in the wrong place — and he reasonably assumes it is a *chatat* and eats it, *patur*. He is exempt from the *korban*, since a *kohen* eating a *chatat* bird is a *mitzvah*, and his error occurred in the course of intending to perform that *mitzvah*.

### Exemption Extension

The *gemara* asks: what is novel here? We already know from Rabbi Yosi's case that *toeh bidvar mitzvah* exempts. The *gemara* answers: one might have thought the exemption applies only when the error leads to the actual performance of a *mitzvah* — the person was trying to take a *lulav* and in the process committed an unintentional *aveira*, but he did end up performing the *mitzvah* of *lulav*. In Rav Huna's case, the person intended to eat a *chatat* bird as a *mitzvah*, but what he actually ate was an *olah* — he committed only an *aveira* and never performed any *mitzvah* at all. The *chiddush* is that even in this case, the intention to perform a *mitzvah* is sufficient; the exemption of *toeh bidvar mitzvah* does not require the error to culminate in the actual fulfillment of a *mitzvah*.

### Tamid Objection

The *gemara* raises an objection from a *mishnah*: Rabbi Yosi himself rules that one who slaughters a *tamid she'eino mevukar* on *shabbos* — a daily offering animal that had not been inspected for blemishes four days in advance as required — is *chayav chatas*, liable for the sin offering, and must bring an additional *tamid* since the offering was invalid. But this is the same Rabbi Yosi who exempts *toeh bidvar mitzvah*. Here too, the person was performing what he believed to be the *mitzvah* of the *tamid* and yet wound up not performing a valid *mitzvah* — just as in the *olah-chatat* case. Why is he liable?

### Negligence Resolve

The *gemara* resolves the contradiction through a tradition transmitted in a chain of authorities: Rav Shmuel bar Shilas in the name of Rav Hamnuna Saba, in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan, in the name of Rav Huna, in the name of Rav — the case of the *tamid* involved an animal *shehevi'o milishkah she'eino mevukarim*, brought from a pen of animals that had not been pre-inspected. This was not an innocent error; it constituted genuine negligence. The *tamid* offering process was sufficiently structured that bringing an animal from an un-inspected pen reflects a failure of care that cannot be excused under the rubric of *toeh bidvar mitzvah*. The exemption covers genuine inadvertent error in the course of a *mitzvah*, but not errors that arise from one's own negligence in carrying out the requirements of the *mitzvah* properly. Whether the disqualifying factor is the negligence alone, or the combination of negligence and the failure to culminate in an actual *mitzvah*, the *halacha* is clear: in a case of *toeh bidvar mitzvah* that stems from the person's own carelessness, the exemption does not apply.

*Chazak.*

---

---

# Sukkah 42

## Review & Context

### Daf Overview

Today's *daf* is 42. We pick up at the last line of 41b and emerge from what was a difficult and challenging section on *shemittah*. We are now back to the basic *mitzvah* structure of *lulav* and the *sukkah*.

### Prior Topics

The previous discussions established that the *mitzvah* of *lulav* is a seven-day obligation in the *Beis HaMikdash* and a one-day obligation outside it — a question the *Gemara* chose not to pursue here, reserving it for later. The discussion also touched on the scenario where the first day of *Yom Tov* coincides with *Shabbos* and people brought their *lulavim* to the *beis haknesses* in advance; the requirement of owning one's *lulav*, and the concept of *matana al menas lehachazir*; and the position of Rabbi Yose that one who inadvertently violates *Shabbos* in the course of performing a *mitzvah* is exempt from a *korban* — even in a case where the *mitzvah* itself was not ultimately fulfilled. With those discussions concluded, the *Gemara* turns to the *Mishnah* at the opening of 42a, which touches on *Shabbos* themes in a different key.

---

## Women & Water

### Woman Taking Lulav

The *Mishnah* states: *mekabeles isha miyad b'nah umiyad ba'alah* — a woman may take the *lulav* from her husband's or son's hand. The context makes clear that in the normative practice depicted by the *Mishnah*, it would be the males who took the *lulav* and *esrog*; the men would pass their *lulavim* along to their wives afterward. Although we know that women are not obligated, it is common enough in *Ashkenazi* circles for women to perform this *mitzvah*, but the *Mishnah* reflects a world where that was not the standard practice.

The *Mishnah* further states: *u'machaziraso l'mayim b'Shabbos* — she may return it to water on *Shabbos*, because one keeps the *lulav* in water to preserve its freshness. This is not analogous to watering a plant still growing from the ground, where there would be a genuine prohibition; rather, one places it in a container of water, and this is permitted on *Shabbos*.

### Yehuda Water Rules

Rabbi Yehuda elaborates with a three-part distinction: *b'Shabbos machazirin* — on *Shabbos* one may only return the *lulav* to water it was already in; *b'Yom Tov mosifin* — on *Yom Tov* one may add fresh water; and *uvemoed machalifin* — on *Chol HaMoed* one may even exchange the water entirely. Rashi goes so far as to say that on *Chol HaMoed* it is actually a *mitzvah* to exchange the water, presumably in order to keep the *lulav* as fresh as possible. The precise nature of the problem — what exactly constitutes the forbidden *tircha* on *Shabbos* — is not spelled out in the *Mishnah*, and Rashi simply characterizes it in general terms as *tircha*. The degree of the concern remains somewhat unclear from the text alone.

### Minor's Obligation

Notably, the *Gemara* skips entirely over the *Shabbos* water laws and instead homes in on the final line of the *Mishnah*: *katan hayodeia l'na'aneia chayav belulav* — once a minor knows how to shake the *lulav*, he becomes obligated in it. This is a rabbinic obligation of *chinuch*. As we will see in the *Gemara*, the general principle of *chinuch* is that it begins when the child is capable of performing the physical act of the *mitzvah*. The *Mishnah's* framing in terms of the ability to shake — rather than merely hold — the *lulav* underscores the centrality of *na'anu'a* to the act of the *mitzvah*. While *b'dieved* one is *yotzei* even without shaking, the shaking is the defining gesture. Tosafos pointed out that the *Mishnah* does not say the child must be able to recite *Hallel*, and from this wished to infer that the shaking of the *lulav* during *Hallel* is not so central — though one might respond that the child can be *yotzei* through *shomei'a k'oneh* while others recite. In any case, the centrality of the shaking is unmistakable.

---

## Muktzah & Objects

### Woman Can Take

The *Gemara* opens with *pshita* — isn't it obvious that the woman can take the *lulav* from her husband? The question, says the *Gemara*, is that one might have thought: since a woman is not obligated in *lulav*, perhaps she should not be permitted to take it — *eima lo tikabel* — because from her perspective, it might be no different from *muktzah*, a mere stick. The *Gemara* therefore teaches that she may take it.

### Muktzah Analysis

Rashi explains the reasoning: the *lulav* is not *muktzah* because it is a *mitzvah* object for her husband. For him, it has the full status of a sacred ritual implement, and that status protects it from *muktzah* classification even when the woman handles it. This analysis naturally raises interesting questions. For *Ashkenazim*, who follow the practice that women may take the *lulav* and recite a *beracha*, the *lulav* would presumably not be *muktzah* vis-à-vis women either, since it functions as a *mitzvah* object for them as well. But where the practice is that women do not take it and it would not be considered a *mitzvah* for them, the only reason it is not *muktzah* in a woman's hands is because of its status vis-à-vis the husband.

### Shofar Parallel

This raises a parallel question regarding the *shofar* on *Yom Tov*. The *Mishnah* elsewhere discusses children who blow the *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah* — *misaskin bahem*, they may engage in blowing — but what is the conceptual framework? Ordinarily one may not play musical instruments on *Yom Tov*. So when someone blows the *shofar* outside the context of a *mitzvah* on *Rosh Hashanah*, are they violating the prohibition against playing musical instruments? Or is the *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah* categorically outside that concern — does it receive a blanket exemption from the musical-instrument prohibition simply by virtue of being the *mitzvah* object of the day? Is this fundamentally a *muktzah* question, or a separate question about the categorization of the object? The parallel with the *lulav* and the woman's ability to take it sits within the same family of questions, and the *Gemara* here does not resolve it fully — but it is worth noting the structural similarity.

---

## Chinuch Braita

### Tanu Rabanan Intro

The *Gemara* continues: *tanu rabanan* — a *braita* now presents a comprehensive list of the various *mitzvos* in which a minor, upon becoming capable of performing the defining physical act, becomes rabbinically obligated — or more precisely, his father becomes obligated to train him. The list is significant not only for the *chinuch* framework it establishes, but because each entry implicitly identifies what the central act of that *mitzvah* is.

### Lulav Waving

*Katan hayodeia l'na'aneia chayav belulav* — once a minor knows how to wave, he is obligated in *lulav*. This echoes the *Mishnah* exactly and confirms that the wave is the defining act of the *mitzvah*.

### Tzitzit Wrapping

*Hitateif* — once he is able to wrap himself in a garment, he is obligated in *tzitzis*. This is striking. One might have thought the *mitzvah* of *tzitzis* consists simply in having fringes attached to a four-cornered garment. Yet the *beracha* we recite is *lehitateif batzitzis* — to wrap oneself — and in fact a number of *Geonim* and *Rishonim* hold that the biblical obligation of *mitzvas tzitzis* applies only to a garment that is genuinely a *bar ituf*, something one wraps around oneself and over one's head. The centrality of *ituf* is thus reflected already in the *braita's* criterion for *chinuch*.

### Tefillin Body Guard

*Lishmor tefillin* — once he is able to guard his *tefillin*, meaning, as Rashi explains, that he is capable of not entering a bathroom while wearing them and — the more demanding concern noted by the *Gemara* — of not passing gas while wearing them, then *aviv lokeach lo tefillin*, his father purchases *tefillin* for him. One notices a linguistic difference: by *lulav* and *tzitzis* the *braita* uses the word *chayav*, whereas by *tefillin* it says *aviv lokeach lo tefillin* — his father acquires them for him. The marginal note flags this discrepancy. The likely explanation is practical: with *lulav* and *tzitzis*, a garment or an extra *lulav* may already be available in the home, but *tefillin* must be purchased fresh, hence the language of acquisition.

### Tefillin Delay

The *tefillin* entry is qualitatively different from the others. For *lulav* and *tzitzis*, the onset of *chinuch* corresponds to the child's ability to perform the central act. Here, however, the issue is not the inability to perform the act at a young age — a young child could physically put on *tefillin* — but rather the concern that he cannot yet maintain the required bodily state, *shomer gufo*, while wearing them. This is precisely why in practice we begin training children in *tzitzis* from the age of three, and in *lulav* from a similarly young age, but we wait until just before *bar mitzvah* to begin training in *tefillin* — because the *shomer gufo* requirement is so demanding.

### Torah Learning

*Yodea ledaber aviv lomdo Torah* — once he knows how to speak, his father must begin teaching him *Torah*. It is worth noting that this entry appears in a somewhat curious position in the list, since one assumes that knowing how to speak comes chronologically before all the other entries. The obligation of teaching him *Torah* may also be categorically different from the other items: it may not be *mitzvas chinuch* per se but rather the father's own personal obligation of *v'shinantam l'vanecha*. The *braita* then adds *u'krias shema*, training him in the *mitzvah* of *krias shema* — this clearly is the son's own *mitzvah*. The *Gemara* asks: what is the *Torah* that the father begins with? Rav Hamnuna answers: *Torah tziva lanu Moshe morasha kehilas Yaakov*. There is something deeply beautiful about this. The first line of *Torah* a child learns is not a verse about God's power or the creation of the world, but a verse about the nature of *Torah* itself as a *morasha*, an inheritance, a handed-down tradition. The father, in teaching the child, enacts the very idea the verse describes — one generation transmitting to the next. And notably, even the mention of God is absent from this verse; it is *Moshe* and *Klal Yisrael* who stand at the center.

### Rambam's Method

The approach of the Rambam here is characteristically distinctive and worth examining. When the Rambam codifies the obligation of teaching one's child, he writes: *me'eimatai aviv chayav lelamdo Torah? mishe'yachal ledaber melamdo Torah tziva lanu Moshe u'shma Yisrael. V'achar kach melamdo me'at me'at pesukim pesukim ad sheyehei ben shesh ben sheva hakol kefi buryo u'molicho eitzel melamed tinokos.* The Rambam folds *shema Yisrael* into the *mitzvas talmud Torah* rather than treating it as a separate instance of *mitzvas chinuch* for *krias shema*. He is not simply quoting the *Gemara*; he appears to be making a deliberate move consistent with his broader approach. Throughout the Mishneh Torah, the Rambam consistently foregrounds *emunah* and theological first principles in places where the *Gemara* discusses only *mitzvos*. The clearest parallel is in the laws of conversion: the *Gemara* says you teach the prospective convert the lighter and weightier *mitzvos*; the Rambam says you teach him about belief in God and the prohibition of idolatry, spending substantial time there before turning to *mitzvos*. Here too, the Rambam seems to be saying that you cannot begin teaching *Torah* without immediately bringing *Shma Yisrael* — the declaration of *emunah* — into the equation. The *Shma* is not merely another *mitzvah* to train him in; it is inseparable from the first act of Torah transmission itself.

### Tumah Guards

Returning to the *braita*: *hayodea lishmor gufo* — once a minor knows how to guard his body from encountering *tumah* and from touching *tamei* things — *ochlin al gufo taharos*. Foods in a state of *taharah* that his body has come into contact with may still be eaten; one can trust him. This is a remarkable standard. It is one thing to say we begin training a child in *tefillin* once he can be trusted not to pass gas while wearing them. It is another to say: once he reaches this level of bodily awareness, even if he touches your *tahor terumah*, you may eat it. He need not be an adult; his demonstrated capacity for *shmirat ha-guf* is sufficient.

*Lishmor es yadav* represents a further, more demanding level: one's hands are constantly moving and touching things without conscious awareness. Once a minor can also guard what his hands are touching, *ochlin al yadav taharos* — even food he has handled with his hands may be eaten in its *tahor* state.

### Safek Tamei Principle

*Hayodea lishol b'reshus hayachid sefeko tamei b'reshus harabim sefeko tahor.* If a child has reached the developmental level where one can meaningfully question him — "was there anything *tamei* near this *terumah* on the street?" — and he can give a coherent and reliable answer, then the general rule applies: a doubtful *tumah* in *reshus hayachid* is judged *tamei*, and a doubtful *tumah* in *reshus harabim* is judged *tahor*. One might ask: what difference does it make how old he is or what he can answer? Once he says "I don't know," you simply apply the standard rule — *safek* in *reshus hayachid* is *tamei*, *safek* in *reshus harabim* is *tahor*. The *halacha*, however, is that this rule applies only when the knowledge was theoretically accessible to someone who was there. If the only witness was someone too young to give a coherent account, even a *safek* in *reshus hayachid* is *tahor*.

The source of the principle that *safek tumah* in *reshus hayachid* is *tamei* is derived from a completely different domain: the laws of *sotah*. A woman who enters private seclusion with a man against her husband's explicit warning acquires a doubtful status — if the seclusion was in *reshus hayachid*, she is forbidden to her husband pending the *sotah* ritual; if in *reshus harabim*, she is not. From there we abstract the general principle about doubtful *tumah* in *reshus hayachid* versus *reshus harabim*, even though the underlying subject matter is entirely different. The logic of why *reshus hayachid* produces a *tamei* ruling is that the information is in principle accessible: someone was there who could know. The ruling of *tamei* creates a kind of normative pressure to produce that information. The logic therefore applies only when there actually is someone present who could in theory have known. If the only person present was a child too young to give a reliable answer, the very premise collapses — the knowledge was not knowable — and we revert to the default that a *safek* is *tahor*. Hence it matters greatly that the child has reached the developmental level where he could in principle have given an accurate answer; only then does a *safek* in *reshus hayachid* yield a ruling of *tamei*.

### Kohen Duchenan

*Hayodea lifros kapav* — once he knows how to spread his hands for *duchening*, *cholkin lo terumah b'veis hagranot* — one may give him *terumah* grain publicly at the threshing floor. If, however, he does not yet *duchen* in public, even if he is a *kohen* and is trusted to eat the *terumah* in a *tahor* state, one may send it to his home but not give it to him publicly. The distinction is meaningful: once he regularly *duchens* in public — and recall that the *Gemara* describes *duchening* as a daily practice, as is the *Sefardic* custom today — everyone in the community knows he is a *kohen*, and there is no confusion or misrepresentation in giving him grain at the threshing floor. But if his status as a *kohen* is not yet publicly established, a public distribution of *terumah* to him would be confusing or potentially misleading to onlookers. Only once he is publicly identified as a *kohen* through the act of *duchening* can one give him *terumah* in public.

One should note that much of the latter part of this *braita* has moved beyond the domain of *chinuch* strictly speaking. The earlier entries concerned training a child in *mitzvos* he will perform as an adult. The later entries — guarding *tahor* food, *duchening*, the rules of *safek tumah* — concern questions of trustworthiness and halachic status in various ritual contexts. The *tefillin* entry was already a transitional case: not that he cannot physically perform the act, but that we cannot yet trust him to maintain the required bodily state. From there the *braita* widens its scope to encompass the broader question of when a minor's conduct and testimony can be relied upon.

### Shechita Skill

The *Gemara* at the top of 42b states: *hayodea lishchot, ochlin mishchitato* — once a minor knows how to slaughter, one may eat his *shechita*. Rav Huna adds: *vehu shegadol omed al gabav* — this is only when an adult is standing over him observing.

### Shechita Knowledge

Rashi explains *hayodea lishchot* as meaning he has the physical skill of *shechting* — *le'amen yadav lishchita* — even if he does not have expert knowledge of the laws of *shechita*. In other words, the physical capability is the threshold, and one then supplements it through adult observation to verify that the laws were followed. Tosafos develops this point explicitly. He first quotes Rashi's formulation — *shelo shahah velo daras*, that the observer confirms there was no *shehiya* or *derasa* — and then notes what is implicit: that even complete observation from beginning to end is not sufficient if the child lacks the physical skill to perform *shechita* properly. You cannot compensate for physical incapacity through observation alone. One might have argued the opposite: perhaps you need knowledge of the laws, because certain violations cannot be observed, while the physical act is entirely visible. But Rashi and Tosafos hold that the physical skill is what the child must possess, and observation supplies verification of legal compliance.

One student raised an observation worth noting: common to all the entries in the *braita* is an emphasis on behavioral and physical developmental capacity rather than on theoretical or conceptual knowledge. The criteria are consistently about what the child can *do*. Even *lishmor gufo* and *lishmor es yadav*, which involve a kind of awareness, are about vigilant behavioral practice rather than intellectual mastery. The one apparent exception — *yodea ledaber*, the ability to speak, as the threshold for *talmud Torah* — may itself point in this direction: *Torah* learning is not merely internal cognition but an act of articulation, of *vedibarta bam*.

### Grain Odor

*Yachol leechol kezayis dagan* — once a minor can eat a *kezayis* of grain, *merchikin mitzoaso umimei raglav* — one must distance oneself from his excrement and urine before reciting *davening* or *Shema*. This has immediate practical application: when an infant is still nursing, his excrement does not yet carry the halachically relevant odor that creates a problem. Only once he has begun eating grain products does the excrement become malodorous and halachically problematic. The requirement applies to the urine as well, not only to the excrement. Rav Chisda refines this: *vehu sheyachol leechol bichdei achilas pras* — the criterion is not just that he can eat grain, but that he can eat a *kezayis* within the time span of *achilas pras*, the halachically defined act of eating. Rav Chiya the son of Rav Yeiva then adds an ironic coda: by an adult, even if he cannot manage a *kezayis* within *achilas pras* due to age or infirmity, his excrement still poses the problem — as the verse says, *yosif da'as yosif makhov*, one who adds knowledge adds pain. Apparently, it seems, with age comes a different kind of potency.

### Pesach Meat

*Yachol leechol kezayis tzali* — once he can eat a *kezayis* of roasted meat, *shochtin alav es ha'Pesach* — he can be counted in the group for a *korban Pesach*. The verse says *ish lefi ochlo*, each person according to their eating capacity; one must be able to eat at least a minimum amount. Roasted meat requires more developed teeth than soft or cooked meat, and this serves as the developmental marker for being counted in the *Pesach* group.

### Food Discernment

Rabbi Yehuda adds a further criterion: *ad she'yachol l'varer achila* — until he can identify and distinguish food from non-food. How so? *Nosnim lo tzror v'zorka, egoz v'notla* — if you give him a stone he throws it away; if you give him a walnut he takes it. He recognizes the walnut as something to eat. The implied reasoning seems to concern the nature of eating itself: if a child merely chews and swallows whatever is placed in his mouth, that is being fed, not eating. The act of *eating* in the relevant sense requires the subject to make a volitional identification — *this is food, this is not* — and to act accordingly. That capacity for discernment is what Rabbi Yehuda considers the threshold for being meaningfully counted among those who eat the *korban Pesach*.

---

## Perek 4 Overview

### Perek Structure

With the *Hadran* on *Lulav V'Arava*, the *Gemara* concludes the third *perek*. To step back: the first two *perakim* were devoted largely to the physical structure of the *sukkah* — a full *perek* and a half on the actual construction — and the latter half of the second *perek* to the *mitzvah* of dwelling in it. The third *perek* was devoted to *lulav*, *hadas*, *arava*, and *esrog*, primarily their physical specifications, with the final sections addressing the act of taking them — notably emphasizing the shaking of the *lulav* and its performance during *Hallel* — before moving into discussions of *shemittah*, ownership, and the *Shabbos* complications. The fourth *perek* now takes a different structural approach. Rather than focusing on one *mitzvah* at a time, it surveys all the *mitzvos* of *Sukkos* together and examines how many days each one applies, creating a kind of master map of the festival's obligations.

---

## Days & Rituals

### Lulav & Arava

The *Mishnah* begins: *lulav v'arava shisha v'shiva* — the *mitzvah* of *lulav* and the *mitzvah* of *arava* each apply for either six or seven days. The *mitzvah* of *arava* here refers to what we call *Hoshanos* — the procession with the *lulav* in which the *arava* is the central element. The variability between six and seven days for both *lulav* and *arava* is a function of where *Shabbos* falls during *Sukkos*, as we will see below.

### Hallel & Simcha

*HaHallel v'hasimcha* — reciting *Hallel* and the obligation of *simcha*, which in the context of the *Beis Hamikdash* refers specifically to *shalmei simcha*, the peace-offerings brought on the *Yom Tov* — these apply for *shmonah*, all eight days. That is, both throughout the seven days of *Sukkos* and including *Shmini Atzeres*. One brings *shalmei simcha* and recites *Hallel* on all eight days — even if, as will be clarified, one might bring the offerings on the seventh day and eat them extending into the eighth.

### Sukkah & Water

*Sukkah v'nisuch hamayim* — dwelling in the *sukkah* and the *nisuch hamayim*, the water-pouring ceremony performed in the *Beis Hamikdash* during the morning sacrifices, apply for *shiva*, only the seven days of *Sukkos* proper and not *Shmini Atzeres*.

### Chalil Days

*Hachalil chamisha v'shisha* — the *chalil*, a wind instrument, was played to accompany the *Simchas Beis Hashoeva* for either five or six days. The logic: across the seven days of *Sukkos*, you immediately lose the first day of *Yom Tov*, on which musical instruments are not played. That leaves at most six days. If *Shabbos* additionally falls during the week of *Chol HaMoed*, you lose another day, bringing the total to five.

---

## Lulav Days Detail

### Lulav 7 Days

*Lulav shiva keitzad?* The *Mishnah* explains: *Yom Tov harishon shel chag shechal lihyos b'Shabbos* — if the first day of *Yom Tov* falls on *Shabbos*, one takes the *lulav* on all seven days, including *Shabbos*, as we saw in the previous *perek* — that is when the procedure of bringing it to the *beis haknesses* in advance was employed.

### Lulav 6 Days

*Ushar kol hayamim shisha* — if *Shabbos* falls on any other day of the week, i.e., during *Chol HaMoed*, one does not take *lulav* on that *Shabbos*, and the total is six days.

---

## Arava Days

### Arava 7 Days

*Arava shiva keitzad? Yom shevii shel arava shechal lihyos b'Shabbos* — if the seventh day of *arava*, which is *Hoshana Rabbah*, falls on *Shabbos*, one performs the *arava* ritual even on *Shabbos*, yielding seven days. *Hoshana Rabbah* stands in relation to *arava* the way the first day of *Sukkos* stands in relation to *lulav*: it is the primary day of the *mitzvah*. Just as taking *lulav* on the first day overrides *Shabbos*, so too the *arava* on *Hoshana Rabbah* would be performed even on *Shabbos*.

### Arava 6 Days

*Ushar kol hayamim shisha* — if *Shabbos* falls on any day other than *Hoshana Rabbah*, one does not perform *arava* on that *Shabbos*, and the *mitzvah* is performed for six days only.

---

## Temple Procedure

### Bringing to Temple

The *Mishnah* now returns to describe the procedure when the first day of *Yom Tov* coincides with *Shabbos* — specifically in the context of the *Beis Hamikdash*, which is distinct from the *beis haknesses* procedure described in the previous *perek*. *Molichim es lulaveihem l'Har HaBayis* — people would bring their *lulavim* to the Temple Mount before *Shabbos*. The *chazzanim* — the functionaries, the sextons — would receive them.

### Portico Storage

*V'sodrin osan al gabei itztava* — they would arrange them on the *itztava*, the portico. Rashi explains that this was not the roof in the open sun, which would dry out the *lulavim*, but rather the benches under a roofed colonnade in the courtyard of *Har HaBayis*, where they would be shaded. *V'hazekeinim manichim es shelahem b'lishka* — the elders were accorded the privilege of placing their *lulavim* and *esrogim* in private chambers, which, as will become clear, spared them from the chaos of the masses.

### Gift Declaration

*Umelamdim osam lomar: kol mi shemagia lulavi l'yado, harei hu lo b'matana* — people were taught to declare: whoever picks up my *lulav* receives it as a gift. This was necessitated by the requirement established earlier that one must own one's *lulav*. In a small *shul* of fifty or a hundred people, it was realistic to find one's own *lulav* after *Shabbos*. But in the *Beis HaMikdash*, with enormous crowds, that was simply impossible. The declaration of gift solved the ownership problem pre-emptively.

### Shabbat Chaos

*Lemachor, mashkimim u'va'in* — on *Shabbos* morning, people would rise early to be ahead of the crowds. *V'hachazzanim zorkim osam lifneihem* — the *chazzanim* would throw the *lulavim* down in front of the assembled multitudes. *V'hein machatfin u'makin ish es chaveiro* — and people would grab and strike one another trying to secure a *lulav*, presumably either their own or the best available. The scene was a complete *balagan*. One cannot help but note the jarring contrast: the *Mishnah* describes this elaborate, careful procedure — receiving the *lulavim*, arranging them on the benches, teaching the declaration — and then arrives at: and they threw them in front of the crowd. One wonders why a more orderly system was not devised from the outset, in the way that the *Gemara* in Yoma describes a different crisis — people falling off the *mizbeiach* in the rush to perform *terumas hadeshen* — being resolved not by canceling the practice but by instituting a lottery.

### Takkanah Decision

*Uchesherau beis din sheba'u lidei sakana, hitkinu sheyehei kol echad v'echad notel b'veiso* — when the *beis din* saw that people were coming to real physical danger, they enacted that everyone should take the *lulav* at home. This is one of those striking *takanos* in which the response to a dangerous situation is not to fix the procedure but to relocate the practice entirely. How exactly this affected what was already being done in the *shuls* outside the Temple precinct — where, as we saw, people brought their *lulavim* ahead of time but the practice did not descend into violence — is a question the *Mishnah* does not fully address here.

---

## Shabbat Question

### Tiltul Question

The *Gemara* now presses on the fundamental question underlying the entire discussion: *amai? Tiltul b'alma hu v'lidchei Shabbos?* Why isn't the *lulav* taken on *Shabbos* of *Chol HaMoed*? It is only a question of moving an object — let the *mitzvah* override whatever *Shabbos* concern there might be. If it is a *muktzah* concern, should not the *mitzvah* simply exempt it from *muktzah* status altogether?

### Tosafos Muktzah

Tosafos addresses this directly. He notes that the *Gemara's* phrase *tiltul b'alma hu* raises the very question of whether *muktzah* applies here: *af al gav d'chazi l'mitzvah* — even though it is a *mitzvah* object. And Tosafos then answers that *muktzah* does indeed apply, because the *lulav* is not a *kli* — it is not a formally designated implement — *v'ein assui kli*, and he then points to a parallel case involving the poles of the *lechem hapanim*. So the *Gemara* proceeds on the understanding that *muktzah* does apply to the *lulav* on *Shabbos*, even on *Yom Tov*. This generates the fascinating question: is the *lulav* intrinsically *muktzah*, with permission to handle it on *Yom Tov* derived solely from the *mitzvah* obligation? Or is it that on *Yom Tov* of *Sukkos*, the *lulav* is simply not *muktzah* at all? The *Gemara's* framing — letting the *mitzvah* override the *muktzah* concern — seems to suggest the former: fundamentally, it is *muktzah*, and the *mitzvah* creates an override. This is a nuanced and unresolved question.

### Rabbah Gezeirah

Rabbah provides the answer: *gezeirah shema yitlenu b'yado v'yeilech etzel baki lilmod* — it is a *gezeirah* lest he take it in his hand and go to an expert to learn how to perform the *mitzvah* — perhaps how to shake it properly, or how to recite the *beracha* — *v'ya'avirenu daled amos b'reshus harabim* (continuing at the top of 43a), and in the process carry it four *amos* in *reshus harabim*, violating *Shabbos*. The concern is not *muktzah* at all; it is accidental *Shabbos* carrying. This makes excellent sense in light of all the preceding *mishnayos*, which devoted great attention to precisely this concern — bringing the *lulav* to the *beis haknesses* or *Har HaBayis* before *Shabbos*, all the elaborate procedures designed to prevent carrying on *Shabbos*. Rabbah is saying: those procedures reflect the underlying rationale for not permitting *lulav* on *Shabbos Chol HaMoed* at all.

The *Gemara* then extends this reasoning: *v'hainu ta'ama d'shofar v'hainu ta'ama d'megillah* — and this is likewise the reason for not blowing *shofar* on *Shabbos*, and not reading *megillah* on *Shabbos*. This is worth pausing over. The prohibition on blowing *shofar* on *Shabbos* is assumed by the *Mishnayos* but not explained there. The *Mishnayos* simply present it as given, and one could have understood it on intrinsic grounds — blowing *shofar* is playing a musical instrument, and there is something inherently conflicting with the character of *Shabbos* in that; similarly, handling a *lulav* might be conceived as fundamentally inconsistent with *Shabbos* rather than merely instrumentally risky. It is Rabbah, as an *amora*, who for the first time articulates the rationale as a *gezeirah* against carrying — and moreover, it is the *Gemara* that extends Rabbah's stated logic to *shofar* and *megillah*, going beyond Rabbah's own formulation. The historical development of these explanations is worth appreciating in its own right.

---

## First Day Exception

### First Day Home Rule

The *Gemara* now raises an immediate challenge: *ei hachi, yom rishon nami?* If that is the reason — fear of carrying — then we should not permit *lulav* even on the first day of *Yom Tov* when it coincides with *Shabbos*. The *Gemara* responds: *rishon hitkinu lei rabanan b'veiso* — for the first day, the *Rabbanan* enacted that one takes the *lulav* at home. After the *takkanah*, one is instructed to take it at home, so the concern that one will go to an expert and carry in *reshus harabim* is nullified.

### Biblical vs Rabbinic

But the *Gemara* presses further: *kodem takkanah mai ika lemeimar?* — before the *takkanah* was enacted, when people were bringing their *lulavim* to the *shul* and later to the *Beis HaMikdash*, they were clearly not taking it at home. How was the first day permitted then? The *Gemara* answers: *ela rishon d'isay mineh hatorah bigvulin, lo gazru bah rabanan* — the first day, which carries biblical force everywhere, not only in the *Beis HaMikdash*, was not subject to the rabbinic *gezeirah*. *Hanach delisnehu mineh hatorah bigvulin, gazru bah rabanan* — the remaining days, which are biblically obligatory only within the *Beis HaMikdash* but not outside it, were subject to the *gezeirah*, and therefore *lulav* on those days is not permitted on *Shabbos* — even in the *Beis HaMikdash* itself, where technically the *mitzvah* on those days is biblical. The criterion for applying or not applying the *gezeirah* is not whether the *mitzvah* is biblical in that specific location, but whether it is biblical everywhere. The first day, being universally biblical, was left untouched by the *gezeirah*; all other days, having at most a biblical dimension limited to the *Beis HaMikdash*, were subject to the *gezeirah*.

### Shofar Puzzle

This leads to the natural and pressing question with which the *Gemara* closes — and which we leave as a *cliffhanger* for the next *daf*: if the first day is exempt from the *gezeirah* because its *mitzvah* is biblical everywhere, then why do we not blow *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah* when it falls on *Shabbos*? The *mitzvah* of *shofar* on *Rosh Hashanah* is equally biblical everywhere and on the first day. Why is *lulav* on the first day exempt from the *gezeirah* while *shofar* is not? That question awaits tomorrow's *shiur*.

---

---

# Sukkah 43

## Carrying Concern

### Intro: Lulav on Shabbat

The daf opens at the very top of 43a, picking up a discussion that had begun at the close of 42b. The *mishna* describes how the *lulav* was taken both in the *Beis Hamikdash* and outside of it on *Shabbos* when the first day *Yom Tov* fell on *Shabbos*. The more pressing question the *gemara* must first resolve, however, is a different one: why is the *lulav* not taken on *Shabbos* when *Shabbos* falls during *Chol Hamoed*?

The *gemara* on 42b puts the question directly: *amai* — why should it be a problem even during the week when *Shabbos* falls on *Chol Hamoed*? Taking the *lulav* is *tiltul b'alma* — merely a question of *muktzah* — so let *Shabbos* override the *muktzah* concern and allow it.

### Rabba's Gezeirah

Rabba answers: *gezeirah shema yitlenu beyado veyeileich eitzel baki lilmod* — we are concerned that a person will pick up his *lulav* and walk out of his house to find an expert who can teach him the *brachos* and the *na'anuim*, and in doing so will inadvertently carry it *daled amos b'reshus harabim*. That is why the *lulav* is not taken on *Shabbos* during *Chol Hamoed* — because it might lead to a biblical violation of carrying.

It is worth noting that this is Rabba's explanation; it is not stated in the *mishna* itself. The *Yerushalmi* may not share this reasoning, and other possibilities exist. Nevertheless, Rabba's explanation is taken as the operative rationale. The *mishna* does hint at this concern: it describes how the *lulav* was brought to the *Beis Hamikdash* in advance, and it acknowledges that one who accidentally carried it on *Shabbos* for the purpose of the *mitzvah* is exempt from a *chatas* — which itself implicitly acknowledges the very real danger of carrying.

### Shofar & Megillah

The *gemara* immediately extends Rabba's reasoning: *v'hainu ta'ama d'shofar v'hainu ta'ama d'megillah* — this same concern explains why the *shofar* is not blown on *Shabbos* when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on *Shabbos*, and why the *megillah* is not read on *Shabbos* when the fourteenth of Adar falls on *Shabbos* in walled cities. In each case, the fear is that a person will carry the instrument or scroll through a *reshus harabim*. The *mishnayos* themselves state these prohibitions plainly; what Rabba supplies — and what the *gemara* now extends — is the unifying rationale.

### Reshus Harabim

This *gemara* opens a significant side discussion about the nature of *reshus harabim*. There is a well-known debate among the *rishonim* about what constitutes a biblical *reshus harabim*. The *geonim* add the requirement that 600,000 people must regularly traverse it — a criterion that does not appear anywhere in the *gemara* itself. The practical consequence of that criterion is significant: it renders a genuine biblical *reshus harabim* exceedingly rare, which in turn allows for an *eiruv* in most circumstances.

One pointed critique of this position, raised by some *rishonim*, is drawn precisely from our context. The *gemara* here makes *gezeiros* that entirely suspend biblical *mitzvos* — not taking the *lulav*, not blowing *shofar*, not reading the *megillah* — specifically out of concern for the biblical prohibition of carrying in a *reshus harabim*. Such a sweeping *gezeirah* would only make sense if *reshus harabim* were a common, everyday reality. If a *reshus harabim* were as rare as the 600,000 criterion would suggest, it is difficult to understand why the rabbis would have suspended biblical *mitzvos* to guard against so remote a concern. This remains a genuine challenge to the *geonic* position.

There is also a question, discussed by both Rashi and *Tosafos*, about why the concern is framed as carrying *daled amos b'reshus harabim* rather than the more immediate act of stepping out of one's house — which would itself constitute the primary violation. *Tosafos* explains that crossing the threshold of one's house is more noticeable and surrounded by more signals that remind one it is *Shabbos*, whereas once a person is already in the street with the *lulav* in hand, the transition is less perceptible.

---

## First Day vs. Chol HaMoed

### Question on First Day

With Rabba's concern established, the *gemara* raises a sharp question: *ei hachi* — if this is the rationale, then even the first day of *Yom Tov* when it falls on *Shabbos* should be prohibited. Yet the *mishna* makes clear that in the *Beis Hamikdash*, and even outside of it, the *lulav* was taken on *Shabbos* when *Yom Tov* fell on *Shabbos*. Why does the concern of carrying not apply equally on the first day?

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

The *gemara* resolves this with a fundamental distinction. The first day of *Yom Tov* — *yom rishon d'isah minei haTorah bigvulin* — carries a biblical *mitzvah* even outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, for everyone everywhere. Given the weight of a biblical obligation, the rabbis ruled: *lo gazru behu rabanan* — they did not extend the *gezeirah* to this day. The *mitzvah* is important enough that we trust people to take the necessary precautions; we are not going to suppress the biblical *mitzvah* out of anxiety that someone might forget.

The other days of *Chol Hamoed*, by contrast — *d'leisnhu minei haTorah bigvulin* — carry no biblical *mitzvah* outside the *Beis Hamikdash*. There, *gazru behu rabanan* — the rabbis applied the *gezeirah* and the *lulav* is not taken on *Shabbos*.

This distinction also explains a subtlety in the *gemara*'s language. The *gemara* specifies "biblical outside the *Beis Hamikdash*" rather than simply "biblical" because the *mishna* is describing practice *inside* the *Beis Hamikdash*. Within the *Beis Hamikdash*, taking the *lulav* is biblical even on *Chol Hamoed* — yet even there, on *Shabbos*, it is not done. The reason: since it is not biblical outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, the *mitzvah* does not carry sufficient weight in the broader world to override the rabbinic concern. The concern of carrying therefore prevails on *Chol Hamoed*, even in the *Beis Hamikdash* itself.

An important clarification must be stated: allowing the *lulav* on the first day does not mean that carrying it is *mutar*. Carrying on *Shabbos* remains absolutely prohibited. The question is only whether the rabbis will trust people to take the necessary precautions — bringing the *lulav* to the *Beis Hamikdash* or to *shul* the day before — rather than suppressing the biblical *mitzvah* entirely. Just as a *bris milah* on *Shabbos* requires all preparations to be made beforehand, so too with *lulav*: prepare in advance, do not carry, but do perform the *mitzvah*.

### Takanah of Bringing Home

The *gemara* pushes further. Once the *takanah* was instituted — following the violent episode in the *Beis Hamikdash* — requiring people to bring the *lulav* home rather than leave it, there is no longer any concern that someone will walk out carrying it. That explains why after the *takanah* the first day could be done on *Shabbos* without concern. But the *gemara* asks: *kodem ha-takkana mai* — what about before the *takanah*? The *mishna* is clear that even before the *takanah* they would take the *lulav* on *Shabbos* on the first day; that is why they brought it to *shul* on *erev Shabbos* in advance. So even without that particular institutional safeguard, the first-day biblical *mitzvah* was sufficient reason to allow it.

The *gemara* ultimately answers: *mai ika l'meimar* — the answer is the straightforward distinction. *Rishon d'isah minei haTorah bigvulin, lo gazru behu rabanan*. On the first day, which is biblical everywhere, the rabbis did not apply the *gezeirah*. On *Chol Hamoed*, which is not biblical outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, they did. That is the operative principle.

### Modern Practice Outside…

The *gemara* then turns to contemporary practice. If the first day is biblical and the rabbis allow it, why do we not take the *lulav* nowadays when *Yom Tov* falls on *Shabbos*? The *gemara* answers: *anan lo yedinan bekivu'a deyarcha* — we do not know when *Rosh Chodesh* was established. This does not mean literal ignorance — we have a fixed calendar — but it reflects the institutional reality of *galus*: outside *Eretz Yisrael*, we live as though we were in the era of the *Beis Hamikdash* when those outside Israel could never be certain which day *Rosh Chodesh* had been declared. We therefore observe two days of *Yom Tov* and inhabit, as it were, a state of virtual uncertainty. Because we cannot definitively say that today is certainly the first day — the biblical day — the earlier allowance does not apply to us.

### Practice in Israel

The *gemara* then asks: what about those in *Eretz Yisrael* who do know when *Rosh Chodesh* is and who observe only one day of *Yom Tov*? For them the uncertainty does not exist — *inhu d'yeidi bekivu'a deyarcha*, they live in the reality of knowing. Should they not take the *lulav* on *Shabbos* on the first day? The *gemara* answers: *ein hachi nami* — indeed they do, or should.

### Mishna Proof

The *gemara* supports this from two *mishnayos*. One *mishna* states that when *Yom Tov* fell on *Shabbos* they would bring their *lulavim* to the *Beis Hamikdash* on *erev Shabbos*. A second *mishna*, at the end of the previous chapter, states that they would bring them to *shul* on *erev Shabbos*. The apparent contradiction — *Beis Hamikdash* or *shul*? — is resolved by the *gemara*: *kan b'zman she'Beis Hamikdash kayam, kan b'zman she'ein Beis Hamikdash kayam*. One *mishna* describes the period of the *Beis Hamikdash*, when people brought their *lulavim* there on Friday; the other describes the period after the *Beis Hamikdash*, when people brought them to their local *shuls* on Friday. The *gemara*'s implication is clear: even after the *Beis Hamikdash* was destroyed, those in *Eretz Yisrael* would still take the *lulav* on *Shabbos* on the first day, bringing it to *shul* the day before as preparation.

This is, at this point in the *gemara*, the working conclusion — though it will ultimately be revisited and rejected later in the *daf*. We do not in fact take the *lulav* in *Eretz Yisrael* today even when the first day falls on *Shabbos*, and the *gemara* will explain why. But for now, the *gemara* reads the *mishna* as evidence that the practice existed and was expected to continue.

---

## Carrying Concern (II)

### Tosafos: Shofar vs. Lulav

At this point it is worth stepping back and asking why the *mishna* treats *lulav* as more readily permitted on *Shabbos* than *shofar*. After all, if *Rosh Hashanah* and *Sukkos* fall in the same year — and the same calendar — why is it that when *Rosh Hashanah* falls on *Shabbos*, the *shofar* was never blown locally outside the *Beis Hamikdash*, while by *Sukkos* the *mishna* assumes the *lulav* would be taken on *Shabbos* outside the *Beis Hamikdash* as well?

*Tosafos* offers two answers. The first is calendrical. By *Rosh Hashanah*, only those in the immediate vicinity of the *Beis Hamikdash* knew which day had been declared *Rosh Hashanah* — the news had not spread. By *Sukkos*, two weeks had passed since *Rosh Hashanah* was established, giving communities time to learn the date. Since the allowance to take the *lulav* on *Shabbos* rests on the certainty that today is the biblical first day, greater certainty about the date translates into greater latitude. With *shofar*, that certainty was largely absent, which tipped the balance toward caution.

*Tosafos*'s second answer addresses the intrinsic nature of the act. Shaking a *lulav* is essentially a matter of *muktzah* at the rabbinic level — moving an object. In the scale of *Shabbos* concerns, it is not a deeply disruptive act. Blowing a *shofar*, however, is a skilled musical act. While it is not technically a *melacha*, it has the character of craft and skilled labor, which is inherently more at odds with the atmosphere of *Shabbos*. It was therefore obvious from the outset that *shofar* would not be blown locally on *Shabbos*, whereas *lulav* — being a lesser intrusion on *Shabbos* and involving a clearer calendar date — was permitted on the first day.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer's Position

### Source: Ulekachtem

Having established the practical *halacha*, the *gemara* now asks where the biblical source is for the *mitzvah* of *lulav* applying outside the *Beis Hamikdash* on the first day. This might seem obvious, but it is worth noting that the greater innovation is actually the *Beis Hamikdash*'s practice for the full seven days — that is learned from *lifnei Hashem*, which is understood as referring to the *Beis Hamikdash*. The first-day obligation for everyone, by contrast, is the plain reading of the verse.

The *gemara* cites a *braisa*: *ulekachtem* — you shall take. The plural form teaches *she-tei lekicha biyad kol echad v'echad*, that each individual must take it himself, not through the collective act of one person. *Lachem* — for yourselves — teaches *mishelachem*, that it must belong to you: hence the rules against a borrowed or stolen *lulav* on the first day. Then *bayom harishon* — on the first day — and even on *Shabbos*: *va'afillu b'Shabbos*. The *harishon*, the definite article *heh*, then teaches that it is only the first day that can override the Shabbat concerns, not the other days.

The *gemara* initially reads this as a *prisumat d'pasuq*, a derivation from the language of the verse. But it immediately raises a challenge: *michdi tiltul b'alma hu, itztarich kra l'mishrei tiltul?* If taking the *lulav* is only a matter of *muktzah* — a rabbinic concern — why would a biblical verse need to permit it? A verse teaches us about biblical matters; it would be strange for a biblical derivation to address a rabbinic *gezeirah*. This is the classic problem of an *asmachta*: the *gemara* suspects that the verse is merely being used as a hook for a rabbinic rule.

### Bayom Derivation

Rabba — the *amora* — reframes the derivation. He says the verse is not being used to permit *muktzah* at all; rather, *nitzrecha ela l'machshirei lulav* — the verse is necessary to permit the preparations for *lulav* even when those preparations would involve a genuine biblical violation of *Shabbos*. The verse is a real *drasha*, not an *asmachta* — but it is a *drasha* that follows the position of a particular *tanna*, as the *gemara* now makes clear.

### Eliezer's Chiddush

The *braisa* states: *lulav v'chol machshirav dochin es ha-Shabbos, divrei Rabbi Eliezer* — the *lulav* and all its preparatory acts override *Shabbos*, in the words of Rabbi Eliezer. This is a striking and far-reaching position with two dimensions. First, there is the general principle, familiar from *bris milah*, that once an act itself overrides *Shabbos*, its preparations may override *Shabbos* as well. Rabbi Eliezer applies this even to *machshirei milah* — he famously holds that if one did not prepare the knife before *Shabbos*, one may even chop down a tree to make a fire to heat the knife, because the preparations for *milah* override *Shabbos* just as *milah* itself does.

But *lulav* presents an even greater *chiddush*. With *bris milah*, the act itself is already known to override *Shabbos* — the extension to preparations follows logically. With *lulav*, however, there is no prior basis in the *Torah* for it to override *Shabbos* at all. Rabbi Eliezer is saying two things simultaneously: first, that the act of *lulav* itself overrides *Shabbos*; and second, that all the preparations for *lulav* override *Shabbos*. This is a radical double *chiddush*. The reasoning parallels the principle of *be-mo'ado* by *pesach* — just as *be-mo'ado* means even on *Shabbos* with respect to the *korban Pesach*, so *bayom harishon* by *lulav* means even on *Shabbos*, whatever one needs to do.

We do not *pasken* like Rabbi Eliezer.

### Majority View
