### Lulav vs Aravah

Rav Huna asks: what is the reasoning of Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka, who emphasized the *chariyot shel dekel* — palm branches — rather than (or in addition to) the *aravos*? The verse says *kapot* in the context of the four species — *kefes*, dual form — and the *chariyot* custom was built around the palm. What is the *derash*?

The verse in *Vayikra* says *kapot temarim*, and the plural form of *kapot* suggested to some that there are two distinct *lulav*-related acts in the *Mikdash*: *achas lulav ve'achas mizbe'ach* — one the general *mitzvah* of taking the *lulav*, and one a special ritual around the *mizbe'ach*. It is this second act that Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka is describing, built around the palm. The *Rabbanan*, however, read *kapat* as written deficiently — without the *vav* — meaning only one act, not two.

### One Heart Teaching

Levi offers a completely different approach, bypassing the *derash* of the verse altogether. *Kitamar*, he says — like the palm tree. *Mah tamar zeh ein lo ela lev echad* — just as the palm tree has only one heart. Rashi explains that the marrow and internal structure of the palm tree is centralized, like a human heart, rather than distributed across branches as in other trees. *Af Yisrael ein lahem ela lev echad la'avihem shebashamayim* — so too Israel has only one heart directed toward their Father in Heaven.

The palm tree grows with a singular, straight, undivided thrust — no branching, no spreading, just one continuous upward column. That visual unity symbolizes a unified, undivided devotion to God. This evokes the statement of Rabbi Akiva in an earlier part of the tractate: one *lulav*, one *esrog*, one *hadas*, one *aravah* — all expressing the singular fidelity of Israel to God. When the *chariyot shel dekel* are brought to the *mizbe'ach*, they embody this message: we have one heart, and it is turned entirely toward You.

*Af Yisrael ein lahem ela lev echad la'avihem shebashamayim.* Israel has only one heart to their Father in Heaven. That is the final word of this section of the *daf* — a fitting culmination to a passage that has moved from the mechanics of willow branches and altar dimensions to the deepest expressions of Israel's relationship with God.

---

---

# Sukkah 46

## Lulav vs. Sukkah Blessin…

### Rav Yehuda's Position

The daf opens with a statement of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *lulav shiva ve-sukkah yom echad* — the *lulav* is blessed all seven days, while the *sukkah* receives a *bracha* on only one day. This is not a statement about when one is obligated to sit in the *sukkah*, but about when one recites the *bracha*. The counter-intuitive element is this: one blesses the *lulav* every day of the seven, including days that are presumably not biblical, yet one blesses the *sukkah* only once, despite the *sukkah* being a biblical *mitzvah* every day of the week. What is the underlying logic?

### Discrete vs. Continuous

The conceptual distinction that animates Rav Yehuda's position concerns whether a *mitzvah* consists of discrete acts or a single continuous process. We tend to think of sitting in a *sukkah* as a series of individual acts — this meal, that nap — each requiring its own *bracha*. But in truth, the nature of the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* is expressed in the verse *basukkot teshvu shivat yamim*: dwelling in the *sukkah* for the entire week. When one initially enters the *sukkah* and begins that dwelling, the *bracha* is recited; for the remainder of the week, each return is simply a continuation of the same uninterrupted act of residence.

The *Gemara* articulates this precisely. The reason *lulav* receives a *bracha* every day is that *lulav de-mafsik leilot mi-yamim* — the nights divide the days; the *mitzvah* of *lulav* does not apply at night, and therefore each day constitutes a distinct, separate act. *Kol yoma mitzvah bifnei atzmah hu* — every day stands on its own. By contrast, *sukkah de-lo mafsik leilot mi-yamim* — for *sukkah*, the nights do not interrupt the days. *Kulu shiva ke-chad yoma arichta damu* — all seven days are like one long day, one unbroken process of dwelling. The logic is elegant and reflects the genuine phenomenology of what it means to live in a *sukkah* for a week.

### Rabba bar Bar Chana

Rabba bar Bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states the precise opposite: *sukkah shiva ve-lulav yom echad* — seven days for *sukkah*, one day for *lulav*. His reasoning operates on an entirely different axis. *Sukkah de-oraita shiva* — every day of *sukkah* is a biblical *mitzvah*, and therefore warrants its own *bracha* each day. *Lulav de-rabbanan sagi lei be-chad yoma* — *lulav* is rabbinic after the first day, and one day suffices. More precisely: the first day is the only biblically mandated day, and the *bracha* of *asher kidishanu be-mitzvotav* belongs only to the biblical obligation. If one missed the first day of *lulav*, one would presumably not recite the *bracha* on the second day at all. The phrase *sagi lei be-chad yoma* thus means not that one day is sufficient as a matter of convenience, but that only one day is truly entitled to the *bracha*.

For this position, the argument about continuous process is unpersuasive — every day one continues to perform the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*, every day one ought to acknowledge it afresh with a *bracha*.

### Ravin's View

When Ravin arrived from Eretz Yisrael, he brought a different version of Rabbi Yochanan's position: *echad zeh ve-echad zeh sheva* — both *lulav* and *sukkah* receive *brachot* all seven days. For *lulav*, the rabbinic character of the subsequent days does not preclude a *bracha* — each day remains distinct. For *sukkah*, the biblical obligation every day demands daily acknowledgment regardless of the theoretical continuity of the process.

For the sake of completeness, there exists a logical fourth possibility — one *bracha* once for the entire week for both *sukkah* (because it is a continuous process) and *lulav* (because only the first day is biblical). This position, however, does not appear in the *Gemara*.

### Rav Yosef's Ruling

Rav Yosef concludes: *nechot hadin de-Rabba bar Bar Chana be-yadecha* — take hold firmly of the position of Rabba bar Bar Chana. *De-kulei Amoraim kaymi ke-vateih* — all the *Amoraim* agree with it, at least with respect to *sukkah*. The consensus, he claims, is seven days for *sukkah* and one day for *lulav*.

It bears noting that this is not our actual *psak*. Our practice treats *sukkah* not as a single continuous act with a *bracha* once daily, but as a series of discrete acts — each *shiur* of eating in the *sukkah* generates its own *bracha*. This effectively transforms the *sukkah* from something conceptually resembling an uninterrupted process into something more like the *lulav* model of distinct acts. Where does this come from? That will emerge as the *sugya* develops.

---

## Shehecheyanu on Sukkot

### Tosefta on Lulav

The *Gemara* cites a *Tosefta*: one who constructs a *lulav* for personal use — binding the *hadasim* and *aravot* together in preparation for the *mitzvah* — recites *baruch Shehecheyanu ve-kiyimanu ve-higianu lazman hazeh*. This is an important *halacha* that many are unaware of in practice.

### Two Aspects

There are two distinct aspects of *Shehecheyanu* on *Yamim Tovim*. The first is the *Shehecheyanu* of the sanctity of the day itself — *kedushat hayom* — recited at *Kiddush* as the *Yom Tov* begins. The second is the *Shehecheyanu* recited upon encountering a new periodic *mitzvah*, such as taking the *lulav* for the first time in the season. These are conceptually independent. The *Shehecheyanu* in *Kiddush* responds to the arrival of the *Yom Tov*; the *Shehecheyanu* on the *mitzvah* responds to one's initial engagement with that *mitzvah*.

### When Shehecheyanu Applies

This distinction explains a curious asymmetry. On the second night of *Sukkot* one does recite *Shehecheyanu* in *Kiddush*, but one does not recite *Shehecheyanu* when taking the *lulav* on the second day. Why the difference?

The *Shehecheyanu* of *kedushat hayom* must be recited at the actual moment of the day's sanctity — when the day begins. On the second night of *Yom Tov*, operating under *sfeika d'yoma*, one reasons: if yesterday was not truly *Yom Tov*, then yesterday's *Shehecheyanu* was meaningless, and today is the first real day of *Yom Tov*, demanding its own *Shehecheyanu*. Hence the second-night *Shehecheyanu* is recited again.

The *Shehecheyanu* upon a *mitzvah*, however, operates differently. It marks the encounter with a new periodic *mitzvah*, and that encounter can begin at various stages of engagement — not necessarily at the moment of performance. One may recite *Shehecheyanu* on a new garment when purchasing it, or when wearing it for the first time; the blessing responds to any meaningful stage of initial contact. Therefore, even if yesterday were not truly *Yom Tov*, the act of taking the *lulav* yesterday — or even the act of constructing and preparing it — already constituted an encounter with the *mitzvah*, and that *Shehecheyanu* holds. Today, even if it were the first actual performance of the *mitzvah*, the *Shehecheyanu* was already covered. One does not recite it again.

This is why the *Tosefta* says the ideal time to recite *Shehecheyanu* on the *lulav* is when constructing it — upon first genuine engagement. Similarly, *ha'oseh sukkah le'atzmo omer Shehecheyanu* — one who builds the *sukkah* for personal use recites *Shehecheyanu* at that moment. This is the principle underlying the *Tosefta*.

The *Shehecheyanu* recited over *Kiddush* on *Sukkot* night thus does double duty — it covers both the arrival of the *Yom Tov* and the initial engagement with the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*. This double function has practical implications for the ordering of *brachot* on the first and second nights, though a full treatment of that topic is a discussion unto itself.

---

## Baraita Contradiction

### Baraita vs. Amoraim

The *Gemara* now cites a *baraita* that creates a sharp tension. The *baraita* states: one who constructs a *lulav* recites *Shehecheyanu*; when taking it to fulfill the *mitzvah*, one recites *al netilat lulav*. And further: *af al pi shebeirach alav yom rishon, chozer umevarech kol shivah* — even though one blessed the *lulav* on the first day, one returns and blesses it all seven days. For *sukkah*: one who builds it recites *Shehecheyanu*, and when first entering recites *asher kidishanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu leishev basukkah*. But then: *keivan shebeirach yom rishon, shuv eino mevarech* — once one has blessed it on the first day, one never blesses it again.

This is the exact inversion of the earlier *Amoraic* statement endorsed by Rav Yosef: seven days for *lulav* and one day for *sukkah*, rather than one for *lulav* and seven for *sukkah*. The *Gemara* therefore declares: *kashya lulav a'lulav, kashya sukkah a'sukkah* — there is a contradiction on both *lulav* and *sukkah*.

### Beit HaMikdash Context

The contradiction regarding *lulav* is readily resolved. *Bishlama lulav a'lulav lo kashya* — for *lulav*, there is no real difficulty: *kan bizman she-Beit HaMikdash kayam, kan bizman she-ein Beit HaMikdash kayam*. The *baraita* that requires a *bracha* all seven days may reflect the context of the *Beit HaMikdash*, when *lulav* was a biblical obligation every day. Rashi adds that this specifically addresses one who went up to the *Beit HaMikdash* and performed the *mitzvah* there each day. In that context, every day is biblical and warrants its own *bracha*. The earlier *Amoraic* position that only one day receives a *bracha* assumes the post-Temple situation, in which only the first day is biblical. These are simply two different historical contexts.

### Tannaitic Debate

The contradiction regarding *sukkah* is more fundamental and cannot be resolved by appeal to historical context. *Ella sukkah a'sukkah kashya* — the *baraita* says one *bracha* at the beginning; the *Amoraic* consensus says seven days. The *Gemara* responds: *tannai hi* — this is in fact a *Tannaitic* dispute. What the *Amoraim* debated reflects an underlying disagreement between *Tannaim*, the traces of which appear in the *baraita* on *tefillin* to which the *Gemara* now turns.

---

## Tefillin Analogy

### Rabbi's View

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* on *tefillin*: *kol zman she-menichan mevarech aleihem, divrei Rabbi* — whenever one puts on *tefillin*, one recites a *bracha*, even if one puts them on multiple times in a single day. Rabbi's position is that each act of donning *tefillin* is a discrete act requiring its own *bracha*, even within the same continuous day.

### Chachamim's View

The *Chachamim* disagree: *eino mevarech ella shacharit bilvad* — one recites the *bracha* only once in the morning. Their reasoning is that wearing *tefillin* is a continuous process throughout the day; it is not a series of distinct acts but a single extended act of fulfilling the *mitzvah*. Taking them off briefly and putting them back on does not generate a new *bracha* because the process has not ended — it has merely been interrupted.

This dispute maps directly onto the question of *sukkah*. The *Chachamim*'s position — once for the whole process — is the basis for the view that *sukkah* receives a single *bracha* at the start of the seven days. The entire week is one uninterrupted process, and the initial *bracha* covers it. Rabbi's position — that even within a continuous process there are multiple moments that generate a new *bracha* — supports the view that *sukkah* too receives multiple *brachot* across the week.

What precisely constitutes those multiple opportunities? Rashi, reading the earlier *Gemara* discussion simply, understands it to mean once per day — each day is somehow a distinct enough unit even within the ongoing process. Tosafot, drawing the comparison to *tefillin* more tightly, understands it as every discrete act of re-entering the *sukkah* for a purposeful act — eating or sleeping — just as each distinct act of donning *tefillin* generates a new *bracha*. This reading of Tosafot is in fact our practice.

### Abaye vs. Rava

*Itmar* — it was stated. Abaye rules *hilcheta ke-Rabbi* — the *halacha* follows Rabbi, and therefore for *tefillin* one blesses each time it is donned anew, and for *sukkah* one blesses multiple times throughout the week. Rava rules *hilcheta ke-Rabbanan* — the *halacha* follows the *Chachamim*: once for the process of *tefillin* per day, and perhaps once for the entire week of *sukkah*.

### Rava's Inconsistency

Rav Mari, son of Shmuel's daughter, reports: *chazina lei le-Rava de-lo avid kishmatei* — I observed that Rava did not act in accordance with his own stated position. Rava's practice was to rise early, go to the bathroom, come out, wash his hands, put on *tefillin*, and recite a *bracha*. Later in the day, when he needed to use the bathroom again, he would remove his *tefillin*, enter the bathroom, come out, wash his hands, re-don his *tefillin*, and recite a *bracha* again. Thus Rava himself recited multiple *brachot* on *tefillin* in a single day.

One might argue this is a special case. When *tefillin* are removed to enter the bathroom — a space where one is prohibited from wearing them — that prohibition constitutes an absolute break in the process. It is not merely an interruption; it is a mandated discontinuity. The same logic would not apply to simply removing *tefillin* temporarily and replacing them without entering a prohibited space, nor would it necessarily apply to *sukkah*, where there is never a moment one is forbidden from being inside. However, since Rava had categorically said *hilcheta ke-Rabbanan* — once and no more — and yet in practice recited a second *bracha*, the observation stands: even Rava conceded that "once per day" does not always hold. The upshot is *ve-anan nami ke-Rabbi avidna* — we too follow Rabbi's position, not the *Rabbanan*. By *tefillin*, one recites a *bracha* each time it is newly donned, and *umi-varchim kol shiva* — similarly for *sukkah*, one recites a *bracha* throughout all seven days.

The *Gemara* also cites the practice of the students of Rav Ashi, who would make a *bracha* every time they touched their *tefillin*, even while wearing them continuously. This is the most striking parallel to *sukkah*: even without removing and replacing the *tefillin*, a conscious re-engagement with the *mitzvah* prompted a new *bracha*. One can see how the *sukkah*, in which the process is never actually interrupted, might similarly admit of multiple *brachot* whenever one returns to the *sukkah* with renewed purposeful intent.

---

## Final Sukkah Ruling

### Anu Nami k'Rabbi

The *Gemara*'s conclusion is that we follow Rabbi's position with respect to *tefillin*, and by the parallel logic, we recite a *bracha* on *sukkah* throughout the seven days — *umi-varchim kol shiva*. The phrase *kol shiva* — all seven — is understood differently by Rashi and Tosafot.

### Rashi's Interpretation

Rashi reads *kol shiva* simply: once per day, every day. Each day is treated as a renewed encounter with the *mitzvah*, and each morning one recites the *bracha* afresh. This is an acknowledgment that even a continuous process benefits from daily re-labeling — a way of ensuring that the *mitzvah* remains present in one's conscious experience each day rather than fading into the background of routine.

### Tosafot's Interpretation

Tosafot's reading maps the comparison to *tefillin* more precisely. *Lulav eino mevarech ella pa'am achat ba-yom* — for *lulav*, one blesses only once per day, since shaking the *lulav* is a single act completed at one moment. *Aval sukkah kol eimat de-nichnas lah* — but for *sukkah*, every time one enters it for a purposeful act — eating, sitting, sleeping — *ve-afilu eser pe'amim ba-yom mevarech al kol achat ve-achat* — one blesses each such act, even ten times in a day.

This precisely mirrors the *tefillin* framework: just as each discrete act of donning *tefillin* generates a *bracha*, each discrete act of entering the *sukkah* for fulfillment of the *mitzvah* generates a *bracha*. And this is our practice. In this way, what is conceptually a continuous seven-day process has been transformed — via the *tefillin* analogy — into a series of discrete acts, each with its own *bracha*.

One additional point deserves mention. The *sukkah* is, in a genuine sense, more continuous than *tefillin*. With *tefillin*, there are real moments of non-wearing: one is forbidden from wearing *tefillin* into a bathroom, and one is not permitted to sleep in them. With *sukkah*, there is no such interruption. Even when one is not physically inside the *sukkah*, one can still be said to be "living" in the *sukkah* — just as a person lives in their home without being physically present in it at every moment. The idea that the entire week constitutes one uninterrupted act of dwelling has real conceptual power. Nevertheless, following the *tefillin* model, the *Gemara* concludes that multiple *brachot* are appropriate, and that is what we do.

---

## Blessings on Rabbinic Mi…

### All Seven Days

The *Gemara* returns to the *lulav* question with a new set of statements. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says: *Mitzvat Lulav kol shiva* — the *mitzvah* of *lulav* is all seven days. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: *yom rishon Mitzvat Lulav, mi-kan va-eilah Mitzvat zekenim* — the first day is the Torah's *mitzvah* of *lulav*; thereafter it is a rabbinic institution. The question is not whether one is obligated to take the *lulav* on those subsequent days — that is agreed — but whether one recites the *bracha* of *asher kidishanu be-mitzvotav* on days that are rabbinic in character.

### Biblical vs. Rabbinic

Rav Yehuda's statement that *Mitzvat Lulav kol shiva* should be understood in this context to mean: one recites the *bracha* all seven days. The association of making a *bracha* with "fully owning" the identity of an act as a *mitzvah* is striking and recurring. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that only the first day, which is biblical, warrants the *bracha*; the remaining days are rabbinic and receive no *bracha*.

Rabbi Yitzchak appears to say *kol yoma Mitzvat zekenim* — every day is rabbinic, and no *bracha* is made. The *Gemara* immediately challenges: does he mean even the first day is only rabbinic? That is a remarkable position, seemingly denying a biblical obligation in *lulav* outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *Gemara* reinterprets: *bar mi-yom rishon* — he means all the days after the first are rabbinic. But then this is indistinguishable from the position of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and the *Gemara* accepts this reconciliation. What the simple reading of Rabbi Yitzchak's statement may suggest — that he considered *lulav* outside the *Beit HaMikdash* to be entirely rabbinic — is a striking position that the *Gemara* is compelled to reinterpret.

### Chanukah Example

Rav is then cited as also holding that the *mitzvah* of *lulav* is all seven days — meaning he recites the *bracha* all seven days. The *Gemara* demonstrates this from a statement of Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav: *ha-madlik ner shel Chanukah tzarich levarech* — one who lights the *Chanukah* candle must recite a *bracha*. This demonstrates that Rav has no objection to reciting *asher kidishanu be-mitzvotav* on a rabbinic *mitzvah*.

The *Gemara* adds the ruling of Rabbi Yirmiyah: *ha-ro'eh ner shel Chanukah tzarich levarech* — even one who merely sees *Chanukah* candles and did not light them recites a *bracha*. What *bracha*? *She'asah nissim*. For *Chanukah* and *Purim*, the *bracha* of *she'asah nissim* is appropriate because these *mitzvot* are centered on publicizing the miracle — *pirsumei nisa*. The person who sees the lit candles is the recipient of that publicized miracle and therefore recites the *bracha* as a participant in that act of *pirsumei nisa*.

The *Gemara* then records the precise text and structure of the *Chanukah brachot*. On the first night, the lighter recites three *brachot*: *l'hadlik ner shel Chanukah*, *she'asah nissim*, and *Shehecheyanu*. The one who merely sees recites two: *she'asah nissim* and *Shehecheyanu* — for *Shehecheyanu* marks one's encounter with the *mitzvah*, and this encounter occurs even without performing the act of lighting. From the second night onward, the lighter recites two: *l'hadlik* and *she'asah nissim*, dropping *Shehecheyanu*; the observer recites one: *she'asah nissim* alone.

### Rabbinic Authority

Now that the *Gemara* has established that a *bracha* is recited on *Chanukah* candles, the obvious question arises: *ve-heichan tzivanu* — where exactly were we commanded to light? This is the foundational question for any *bracha* recited on a rabbinic *mitzvah*.

Two sources are offered. *Mi-lo tasur* — from the verse prohibiting deviation from the rulings of the *Beit Din ha-Gadol*, the *kohanim* and *shofet* at the place God will choose. We are biblically mandated to follow rabbinic authority, and therefore we may say *ve-tzivanu* even regarding rabbinic enactments. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative: *sha'al avicha ve-yageidcha* — ask your father and he will tell you; follow the traditions and rulings of prior generations.

Why seek a second *pasuk* beyond *lo tasur*? Because *lo tasur* addresses the rabbis' interpretive function — their role in determining how biblical *mitzvot* are to be understood and applied. That is the classic domain of *lo tasur*: go to the sages when there is a question about how to observe the Torah's laws, and do not deviate from their ruling. When it comes to the rabbis establishing entirely new practices — like *Chanukah* — that is arguably outside *lo tasur*'s stated scope. *Sha'al avicha ve-yageidcha* speaks to a broader mandate: simply follow what your elders have established, even in their creative and legislative capacity, not only in their interpretive one.

The *Gemara* does not raise this question for *Purim*, because *Purim* followed a different path: the effort to include *Megillat Esther* within *Tanach* — as expressed in the *midrash* of Esther's request *kitvuni le-dorot* — meant that once the *Megillah* was canonized, reading it could be said to be commanded by God directly through *Tanach*, not merely through rabbinic enactment. The question of *ve-heichan tzivanu* thus resolved itself for *Purim* through canonization. For *Chanukah*, where no such claim was available, the *Gemara* had to address the authority question directly through *lo tasur* and *sha'al avicha*.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explicitly teaches this ruling regarding *lulav* as well — not merely as an inference from the *Chanukah* precedent, but directly: Rav stated that *Mitzvat Lulav kol shiva*, meaning one recites the *bracha* all seven days, including the rabbinic days of *Chol HaMoed*.

---

## Practical Application

### Pre-Built Sukkah

The *Gemara* returns to the practical *halacha* of *brachot* on *sukkah*. The *baraita* states: one who builds a *sukkah* recites *Shehecheyanu*; when entering for the first time to fulfill the *mitzvah*, one recites *asher kidishanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu leishev basukkah*. But what of a person whose *sukkah* was already standing — *hayetah asuyah ve-omedet* — pre-built from before the holiday? There was no act of construction to serve as the occasion for *Shehecheyanu*.

The ruling is: *im yachol lechadesh bah davar* — if one can add something new to the *sukkah* — new decorations, additional *sechach* — do so, and use that new engagement as the occasion for *Shehecheyanu*. If not, *ve-im lav*, then when one enters the *sukkah* to perform the *mitzvah* for the first time, one recites both *brachot* — the *bracha* of *leishev ba-sukkah* and the *Shehecheyanu* — together.

### Integration Into Kiddush

Rav Assi reports: *chazina lei le-Rav Kahana de-kamar lehu le-kulhu akasa de-kiddush*a — I saw Rav Kahana recite all the *brachot* over the *Kiddush* cup. This is our practice.

It is instructive to observe the stages through which the *Gemara* moves. Ideally: recite *Shehecheyanu* when constructing the *sukkah*. Did not do so? Add something new to the *sukkah* and recite it then. Did not do so? Recite it upon first entering the *sukkah*. Did not do so? Recite it over *Kiddush*, where it does double duty — for the *Yom Tov* and for the *sukkah* simultaneously. That last stage is where we have settled in practice, and Rav Kahana's usage suggests this is not merely *bedi'eved* but a considered and complete fulfillment. Reciting *Shehecheyanu* in *Kiddush* before one has actually performed the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* is permissible because, as established earlier, *Shehecheyanu* on a *mitzvah* can be recited at the stage of first engagement, not only at the moment of performance.

---

## Multiple Mitzvot

### Multiple Mitzvot Options

The *Gemara* broadens the discussion of *brachot* to the case of multiple *mitzvot* performed simultaneously. A *baraita* addresses the scenario in which several *mitzvot* are before a person at once — Rashi offers the example of taking the *lulav*, sitting in the *sukkah*, putting on *tefillin*, and putting on *tzitzit*. One option is to recite a single comprehensive *bracha*: *baruch asher kidishanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu al ha-mitzvot* — a single blessing covering all the obligations at once.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *mevarech al kol achat ve-achat bifnei atzmah* — one must recite a separate *bracha* for each *mitzvah* individually.

### Halacha Ruling

Rabbi Zeira — and some attribute this to Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa — rules that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda: each *mitzvah* receives its own individual *bracha*.

### Theological Basis

What is the reasoning behind Rabbi Yehuda's position? The *Gemara* cites the verse *baruch Hashem yom yom* — blessed is God day by day. One might ask: does this mean one blesses God during the day but not at night? The *Gemara* responds: *bechol yom va-yom ten lo me'ein birchotav* — each day, acknowledge God in a manner that reflects the distinct character and gifts of that day. On *Rosh Chodesh* one mentions *Rosh Chodesh*; on *Chanukah* one mentions *Chanukah*. Each day carries its own unique quality, and one's acknowledgment of God should reflect that particularity.

The same principle applies to multiple *mitzvot*: *bechol davar va-davar ten lo me'ein birchotav* — for each distinct *mitzvah*, acknowledge God in a manner befitting that specific blessing. The *mitzvah* of *sukkah* represents a distinct and particular way God has sanctified us, different from the *mitzvah* of *lulav*, different from the *mitzvah* of *tallit*, different from the *mitzvah* of *tefillin*. To lump them into a single *bracha* diminishes the distinctive character of each one, both theologically — in terms of how we acknowledge God's unique blessings — and experientially — in terms of how we relate to each *mitzvah* as its own special bond.

---

## Fullness and Emptiness

### The Parable

The same sage — Rabbi Zeira, or some say Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa — offers a striking teaching on the difference between human ways and divine ways. *Bo re'eh shelo ke-middat ha-kadosh baruch hu middat basar va-dam* — come and see that God's ways are not the ways of human beings. In the realm of human experience, *kli reikan machazik* — an empty vessel can hold new content; *malei eino machazik* — a full vessel cannot. This is the normal logic of physical containment. But with God, the reverse obtains: *malei machazik* — a full vessel holds more; *reikan eino machazik* — an empty vessel cannot hold.

### Im Shamoa Tishma

The proof-text: *ve-hayah im shamoa tishma* — if you have truly listened. The conditional structure is read as: *im shamoa* — if you have already listened before, *tishma* — then you will be able to hear more.

### Disposition and Attention

Rashi explains: one who has trained oneself in the disposition of paying attention and listening has developed a capacity that enables continued and deeper learning. The more one has listened before, the more one is capable of listening going forward. Conversely, *ve-im lav* — if one has not cultivated this disposition, future listening will be fruitless: *lo tishma* — you will not succeed in hearing again.

### Learning in Context

One may also understand this principle in terms of the association of ideas. When a learner encounters a new concept and already possesses an existing network of related knowledge, the new idea finds connections and anchors itself within that network. It is held more securely, understood more deeply, because it does not arrive in an empty space but into a context of meaning. If the mind is empty of prior learning, there are no connections to be made, and the new material passes through without taking hold. This is not merely an ancient insight; it reflects what contemporary educational theory recognizes as constructivist learning — that understanding is built by connecting new knowledge to prior knowledge.

### Review and Continuity

The *Gemara* adds a *davar acher* — another reading of the same verse — drawing on the following phrase: *ve-im yifneh levavecha ve-lo tishma* — and if your heart turns away and you do not hear. Reading this alongside the first clause: *im shamoa ba-yashan tishma ba-chadash* — if you have reviewed the old material, you will be able to hear the new. The act of *chazarah* — review — keeps prior learning active and available, creating the cognitive and dispositional conditions under which new learning can be absorbed. But *ve-im yifneh levavecha ve-lo tishma* — if you abandon review, if your heart turns away, *shuv lo tishma* — you will not be able to learn anew.

The deeper point of the parable is that God, in making the human mind, fashioned a vessel whose capacity increases with use and filling. The human being is a container unlike any made by human hands — the more that is placed within it, the more it can receive. It is God's handiwork, and this is how He has made us: *malei machazik, reikan eino machazik*.

---

---

# Sukkah 48

## Shemini Atzeret Status

### Shehecheyanu Review

The present daf opens by returning to the very last line of 47b, where the preceding discussion concluded. That discussion had explored at length whether one recites *shehecheyanu* on *Shemini Atzeret* — whether *Shemini Atzeret* stands as a sufficiently independent *chag* to warrant its own blessing of time. The Gemara there resolved the matter: *v'hilchasa omin zman b'Shemini haChag* — the *halacha* is that one does recite *shehecheyanu* on *Shemini Atzeret*. The Gemara then adds that this ruling follows the position of Rav Nachman, citing a *tanna'itic* source in its support: *tani k'vasei d'Rav Nachman*. That source is, in fact, a Tosefta, which enumerates the ways in which *Shemini Atzeret* is treated as a *regel bifnei atzmo* — a holiday unto itself.

### Pezer Keshev

The Tosefta formulates its list through a mnemonic: *pezer keshev* — פז"ר קש"ב — six letters standing for six dimensions of *Shemini Atzeret*'s distinct status. Each letter is the initial of a phrase: *pais bifnei atzmo*, *zman bifnei atzmo*, *regel bifnei atzmo*, *korban bifnei atzmo*, *shira bifnei atzma*, *bracha bifnei atzma*. Each represents a specific domain in which *Shemini Atzeret* operates independently of *Sukkot*, and we now turn to each in sequence.

### Pais Bifnei Atzmo

The פ of *pezer keshev* stands for *pais bifnei atzmo* — an independent lottery. In the *Beis HaMikdash*, the *kohanim* were organized into twenty-four *mishmarot*, each of which served for a designated week of the year, such that every group served approximately two weeks annually. On the *regalim*, however, all twenty-four groups served simultaneously. To distribute the *korbanot* of *Musaf* fairly among them, a lottery was held. The *mussaf* offerings of *Sukkot* involved a famously large number of animals — beginning with thirteen bulls on the first day and decreasing by one each day, producing a total of seventy bulls across the seven days of *Sukkot*. Dividing seventy by twenty-four yields slightly less than three: twenty-two groups received three bulls each, while two groups received only two.

When *Shemini Atzeret* arrived, there was only a single bull to distribute. One might suppose that simple equity dictated giving it to one of those last two groups who had received only two — completing the equalization across the holiday. But *pais bifnei atzmo* teaches otherwise: a completely fresh lottery was conducted, entirely independent of what had preceded. Whatever group won that lottery received the bull — irrespective of how many they had received during *Sukkot*. This independence is itself significant beyond the question of *korbanot*: even considerations of institutional fairness that might seem to link *Shemini Atzeret* to *Sukkot* are set aside. It is a new beginning.

### Zman Bifnei Atzmo

The ז stands for *zman bifnei atzmo*: *Shemini Atzeret* has its own *zman*, its own moment — and accordingly its own *shehecheyanu*. This is what the preceding passage on 47b established as *halacha*, and it requires no further elaboration here.

### Regel Bifnei Atzmo

The ר stands for *regel bifnei atzmo* — *Shemini Atzeret* is itself a *regel*. At first glance this appears circular: one of the six ways it is its own *regel* is that it is its own *regel*. But the substance is clear. Rashi explains that the ר signifies that on *Shemini Atzeret* one does not sit in a *sukkah* and does not take a *lulav* — the defining *mitzvot* of *Sukkot* are entirely absent. This is admittedly more of a negative characterization than a positive one, defining *Shemini Atzeret* by what it lacks rather than by what it is. Nevertheless, it establishes unambiguously that *Shemini Atzeret* is not an extension of *Sukkot*.

Tosafot offers an additional interpretation. In the laws of *aveilus*, if a family member passes away shortly before *Sukkot*, the onset of *Yom Tov* interrupts the *shiva*. The *shloshim* then continues to count, with the days of *Chol HaMoed Sukkot* contributing to its depletion. The question then arises: how is *Shemini Atzeret* reckoned in this context? The answer given by Tosafot is striking — *Shemini Atzeret* itself counts as the equivalent of a full seven-day *chag* for purposes of *shloshim* calculation. This demonstrates that *Shemini Atzeret* possesses an independent status as its own *Yom Tov*, one that bears its own weight even in halachic domains quite removed from the Temple service.

### Korban Bifnei Atzmo

The כ stands for *korban bifnei atzmo* — distinct offerings. This is perhaps the most straightforward of the six. The *musaf* of *Shemini Atzeret* is entirely its own: one bull rather than a decreasing series, seven sheep rather than fourteen, one ram rather than two. These are not a continuation of the pattern of *Sukkot* but constitute an independent *musaf* for an independent day.

Tosafot adds a possible identification for the שׁ of *shira bifnei atzma* — the distinct song: it may refer to *Lamnatzeach Al HaSheminis* (Psalm 12), the psalm whose heading makes explicit reference to the eighth. The songs that accompanied the *musaf* offerings of *Sukkot* were associated with the agricultural distribution to the poor from the harvest; *Shemini Atzeret* had its own song.

### Shira & Bracha

The ב stands for *bracha bifnei atzma* — a distinct blessing. Rashi connects this to what the Gemara had established earlier: in the liturgy, one does not refer to the day as *Chag HaSukkot* but rather as *Yom Shemini Chag HaAtzeret Hazeh* — a distinct name that reflects its distinct identity. Other interpretations exist, including a special blessing given to the king, but Rashi's primary reading ties it to the liturgical name.

A brief note before moving to the next *mishnah*: the discussion of all six items in *pezer keshev* grew out of the enumeration of multi-day practices — beginning with *lulav* and *aravah* at six and seven days respectively, together with the *mishnah* specifically addressing *Hoshana Rabba*, and then the status of the *lulav* and *esrog* on *Shemini Atzeret*. Now the text turns to a different multi-day item: *hallel* and *simcha* for eight days.

---

## Hallel & Simcha

### Eight Days

The Gemara now takes up the teaching that *hallel* and *simcha* both extend for all eight days of the *chag* — including *Shemini Atzeret*.

### Mishnah Cited

The *mishnah* states: *heHallel vehaSimcha shemonah* — *hallel* and *simcha* for eight days. This is noteworthy because *Sukkot* stands in contrast to *Pesach* in precisely this regard. On *Pesach*, the rule is that full *hallel* is recited only on the first day; the prevalent practice of reciting a half-*hallel* on the remaining days of *Pesach* reflects a later custom acknowledged by the Gemara, but the full *hallel* is reserved for the first day alone. On *Sukkot*, by contrast, full *hallel* is recited every single day. The Gemara elsewhere explains this distinction: since each day of *Sukkot* has a different complement of *korbanot* in its *musaf*, each day carries a distinct identity, and therefore each warrants its own full *hallel*.

The *mishnah* then focuses more closely on *simcha*, and this is where the real *chiddush* lies — especially once we appreciate that *Shemini Atzeret* is a separate *regel* altogether. That the obligation of *shalmei simcha* continues through *Shemini Atzeret* is not self-evident, and the *mishnah* teaches: *melamed shechayav adam b'hallel uv'simcha uv'chavod Yom Tov Acharon shel chag k'sha'ar kol yemot haChag* — a person is obligated in *hallel*, *simcha*, and honoring the last day of *Yom Tov* just as on all the other days of the holiday. Honoring *Yom Tov Acharon* is not itself surprising — *Yom Tov Acharon* of *Pesach* is also honored — but the *chiddush* of *hallel* every single day and, especially, of *shalmei simcha* extending into *Shemini Atzeret* is the heart of the teaching.

### Vehayisa Ach

The Gemara asks: *mina hanei milei* — from where is this derived? The *baraisa* cites the verse in Devarim 16. The passage there describes *Chag HaSukkot* as a seven-day celebration: *chag haSukkot ta'aseh lecha shivat yamim* — seven days. It commands joy: *v'samachta b'chagecha atah u'vincha u'vitecha...* It then repeats the count: *shivat yamim tachog la'Hashem Elokecha*. Notably, *Shemini Atzeret* is not mentioned anywhere in this passage, nor in the surrounding verses that enumerate the *shalosh regalim*. The holiday called *Chag HaSukkot* is emphatically seven days.

So how does one derive that *simcha* applies to *Shemini Atzeret* as well? The answer lies in the closing words of that passage: *v'hayita ach sameach* — and you shall be exceedingly, or entirely, happy. The *baraisa* reads this as an extension: *lerabbos leil Yom Tov haAchron* — to include the night of the last *Yom Tov*, meaning the night of *Shemini Atzeret*. The word *ach* would serve as the limiting term, and *v'hayita sameach* the expanding one.

### Last vs First

But the *baraisa* does not leave this without challenge. Perhaps *v'hayita ach sameach* comes to include not the last night but the *first* night — the night that opens *Sukkot*? After all, one might think that *simcha* in the sense of *shalmei simcha* requires the prior offering of a *korban*, which cannot be done at night; perhaps the verse is extending *simcha* to cover that first night, even though no *korban* was brought on it.

The *baraisa* resolves this by invoking the limiting force of *ach*: one must choose between extending to the first night and extending to the last night, not both. And the choice is clear: *marbeh ani leil Yom Tov haAchron sheyesh simcha lefanav* — I extend to the last night, which is preceded by *simcha*, because a *korban* was in fact brought during the preceding day of *Sukkot*, and its continued consumption now extends the *simcha* into that night. *U'motzi ani leil Yom Tov haRishon she'ein simcha lefanav* — I exclude the first night, which has no *simcha* preceding it, because no *korban* was brought that day from which the eating could flow.

### Night Extension

This resolution illuminates something important about the nature of *simcha* itself. It is not merely our subjective experience of happiness, nor simply the act of eating. Rather, it is the eating as the *culmination* of having brought the *korban* before God. The Gemara states explicitly: *ein simcha ela b'vasar shelamim* — true *simcha* is realized through the meat of *shelamim*. The connection to God through the act of offering, followed by consuming the sacred meat in God's presence, is what constitutes *simchat Yom Tov* in its fullest sense. This is why the first night of *Sukkot* is excluded from this particular form of *simcha*: no *korban* was brought that day, and thus nothing precedes the eating that would give it its character of *simcha*. The last night, by contrast, emerges directly from the *korban* brought on *Sukkot*, whose eating extends lawfully into *Shemini Atzeret*.

### Shalmei Simcha

This understanding raises a further question: does the obligation of *simcha* require bringing a new *korban* on each individual day of the *chag*? A *shelamim* may be eaten on the day it is brought and the following day — so does one need to bring a fresh offering every day, or every other day at minimum? The Gemara's language — *lerabbos leil Yom Tov haAchron* — does not speak in terms of *chiyuv* per se; it speaks of inclusion within the category of *simcha*. The precise extent of the daily obligation remains genuinely ambiguous from this passage, including the question of what exactly "including the last night" entails in practical terms.

What is clear is that the meat of *shelamim* — the act of offering before God and eating in that context — is the heart of *simchat Yom Tov* in the time of the *Mikdash*. It is not that the meat tastes different from non-sacred meat; it is that the *simcha* generated by standing before God and completing the act of offering is qualitatively distinct. That is the *simcha* the Torah commands.

### Rambam Simcha

The Rambam in *Hilchos Yom Tov* (end of perek 6) makes two important points that grow naturally from this discussion. First, he underscores what the *gemara* states: *ein simcha ela b'vasar shelamim* — in the time of the *Mikdash*, true *simcha* was the *shelamim*. In our own time, he applies the principle differently, describing what each member of the household should receive to experience joy: men with meat and wine, women with fine clothing, and so forth.

But the Rambam's second point is even more striking, and it draws directly from the *psukim* themselves. The *pasuk* that commands *simcha* — *v'samachta b'chagecha atah u'vincha u'vitecha v'avdecha va'amatecha v'halevi v'hager v'hayatom v'ha'almanah asher bisharecha* — lists not only one's own household but the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. This is no accident. *Sukkot* is the season of ingathering: the agricultural year has concluded, crops are stored, success is palpable. The natural response is great joy. The Torah's demand is that this joy be directed toward God — expressed through the *lulav* and *esrog*, through sitting in the *sukkah*, through *shelamim*. But alongside this, the *psukim* insist that those who have no land, no harvest, no share in the year's bounty must also be included in the *simcha*.

The Rambam is uncompromising: *u'kh'she-hu ochel v'shote chayav l'hachil la-ger la-yatom v'la-almanah v'sha'ar ha-aniyim ha-umlalim* — when one eats and drinks, one is obligated to provide food to the stranger, orphan, widow, and the unfortunate. One who locks the doors of his courtyard and feasts with his family alone, giving nothing to the poor and the distressed: *ein zo simchat mitzvah ela simchat kerso* — this is not the *simcha* of a *mitzvah* but the *simcha* of one's stomach. And on such a person, the Rambam invokes the verse: *v'zeriti feresh al p'neichem peresh chagichem* — I will spread the refuse of your festival offerings on your faces. *V'simcha kazu kelon hi lahem* — such joy is a disgrace.

This explains why *simcha* is so heavily underscored specifically in the context of *Sukkot*: it is the *chag* of abundance, of completed harvest, and therefore the *chag* that most powerfully demands that abundance be shared.

---

## Leaving Sukkah

### Removing Vessels

The Gemara now takes up the *mishnah* that addresses the practical transition out of the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret*. The *mishnah* states: *gamar mil'echol* — once one has finished eating on *Hoshana Rabba*, at the close of *Sukkot*, one does not immediately dismantle the *sukkah* — *lo yatir sukkato* — because one might need to eat again before nightfall. But from *mincha* time onward, one begins bringing one's vessels and furnishings down from the *sukkah* into the house: *aval morid et hakelim min hamincha u'lemala*, and this is done *mipnei kavod Yom Tov haAcharon shel Chag* — out of honor for the last day of *Yom Tov*.

### Kavod Yom Tov

The practical reason is straightforward: one needs one's bedding, dishes, and furnishings for the *Yom Tov* meal of *Shemini Atzeret* in the house. But the *mishnah*'s language carries a deeper subtext. It is not merely that one needs the items; rather, the very act of removing them from the *sukkah* is itself an expression of *kavod* for *Shemini Atzeret*. The implication is that one should ideally be taking the *sukkah* apart altogether — demonstrating departure — but since the *sukkah* may still be needed and cannot be dismantled, one does the next best thing: one removes everything from it, signaling that it is being abandoned.

### No Vessels?

The Gemara presses on this: *ein lo kelim lehorid mahu* — if one has no vessels to bring down, what is one to do? The Gemara itself immediately asks: if you have no vessels, what have you been using all week? What have you been sleeping on, eating from? The question is somewhat facetious, but it exposes an important assumption built into the original ruling. The anxiety expressed — what if there is nothing to bring down? — only makes sense if the act of bringing items down is itself a required demonstration of departure from the *sukkah*, not merely a practical convenience. One must *do something* to show one is leaving.

The Gemara reformulates: *ela ein lo makom lehorid kelim mahu* — perhaps one simply has no space in the house to receive the items. Perhaps one's house is unavailable — one cannot return the furnishings there. And again, what is the problem? If there is no room, one stays in the *sukkah* and eats *Shemini Atzeret* there. The answer the Gemara gives reveals how seriously this obligation is taken.

### Invalidation

Rabbi Chiya bar Rav (or bar Ashi) says: *pocheis ba'arba* — one invalidates the *sukkah* by making a breach of four *tefachim* in it. Tosafot asks why specifically four rather than three, but the principle is clear: even if one must remain in the *sukkah* physically, one must render it halachically invalid. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi offers a different solution: *madlik bah ner* — one lights a candle inside the *sukkah*. We learned earlier that in a small *sukkah*, lighting a candle causes discomfort and anxiety about fire hazard, and this is precisely the point.

The Gemara resolves that these are not competing opinions: *ha lan veha lehu* — one applies in Eretz Yisrael and the other in Babylonia. Those in Eretz Yisrael, following the practice that *Shemini Atzeret* does not require eating in the *sukkah*, can simply invalidate the *sukkah* structurally. Those outside Eretz Yisrael, who must continue to eat in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret*, cannot invalidate it — yet they must still do something to convey that they do not genuinely belong there. The solution: light a candle that makes the *sukkah* uncomfortable, and continue eating without a *beracha* over the *sukkah*.

### EY vs Bavel

This is a striking passage. Until this point the discussion had centered on whether to recite a *beracha* in the *sukkah* on *Shemini Atzeret*. Now the Gemara goes further: not reciting a *beracha* is insufficient. One must actively undermine the *sukkah*'s character, even while sitting in it — even while eating in it in fulfillment of *Shemini Atzeret*'s requirements for those in the *diaspora*.

### Dirty Dishes

The Gemara continues: *hateniach Sukkah ketanah* — the lighting solution works for a small *sukkah*, where a candle genuinely causes anxiety. But for a large *sukkah*, where a candle poses no concern and creates no discomfort, what can one do? *Meiayeil bei mane demichla* — one brings dirty dishes into it. Rava had taught elsewhere: *mane demichla bar mimtaltesa* — one clears dirty dishes immediately out of the *sukkah*, while *mane deshtaya bimetaltasa* — drinking vessels may remain inside. The reason is obvious: dirty dishes are unpleasant and one naturally removes them without delay. Bringing dirty dishes into the *sukkah* is therefore an act that would *never* be done during *Sukkot* proper, precisely because it is so contrary to the *sukkah*'s dignity. On *Shemini Atzeret*, for one who must eat there but must simultaneously signal non-belonging, this act serves the purpose.

### Targum Onkelos

This series of *sugyot* points toward a deeper understanding of what *Shemini Atzeret* actually represents. Targum Onkelos translates the *pasuk* *bayom hashemini atzeret tihyeh lachem* in a revealing way: *bayoma timinaia atzarta min mitalalaya leveitaya* — on the eighth day shall be a gathering in from your *sukkah* into your house. Onkelos understands *atzeret* — the very name of the day — as a gathering inward, a transition from the *sukkah* back into the home.

### Transition Theme

This reading illuminates the entire structure of the *yamim tovim*. The *Yamim Noraim* — *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur* — were about bringing God into one's inner life, culminating in entry into the *Kodesh Kodashim*. *Sukkot* then took that experience and externalized it: we moved out of the home into the *sukkah*, dwelling in a structure that evokes the *Ananei HaKavod* and the presence of God, symbolizing through the *sukkah* walls the very *Kodesh Kodashim* itself. The *gemara* elsewhere makes those connections explicit.

But the challenge has always been the follow-through. The *sukkah* makes God's presence accessible — the structure itself frames and sustains the consciousness. The real difficulty is re-entering ordinary life without losing what one has built. *Shemini Atzeret*, understood through Targum Onkelos and through the Gemara's insistence on the physical act of *leaving* the *sukkah*, is precisely the *Yom Tov* of that transition. It is the day on which one pauses at the threshold, before the ordinary rhythms of the year resume, and carries the *kedushah* of the season consciously into the house. *Kavod Yom Tov Acharon* — the honor of the final day — consists in making that departure deliberate and sacred.

This, then, is one important answer to the question of what *Shemini Atzeret* is about positively, beyond the list of what it is not. Its identity is precisely the threshold: the moment of return, the conscious crossing back from *sukkah* to house, from the sheltered presence of God to the dailiness of the year — and the aspiration that one should carry that presence with one into what comes next.

---

## Nisuch HaMayim

### Golden Vessel

The *mishnah* now turns to *nisuch hamayim* — the water-pouring ritual performed each morning during *Sukkot*. It begins: *tzelochit shel zahav mahazeket shlosha lugin* — a golden pitcher containing three *log* of water. To give a sense of measure: a *revi'it* — the minimum size of a *kiddush* cup, roughly three and a half ounces — is one quarter of a *log*. So a *log* is approximately fourteen ounces, and three *log* is roughly forty-two ounces.

### Process

This pitcher was filled from the *Shiloach* — a flowing spring outside the *Beis HaMikdash*. The water-drawer then proceeded to *Sha'ar HaMayim*, the Gate of Water on the southern side of the *Beis HaMikdash* near the ramp leading to the *mizbei'ach*. Upon reaching the gate: *teka'u veheru uteka'u* — they sounded *tekiah*, *teruah*, *tekiah*. This corresponds to the trumpet-blowing we encountered earlier in connection with the *aravah* ceremony; many of *Sukkot*'s rituals were accompanied by these blasts. The *kohen* then ascended the ramp — *alu b'kevesh ufana lismolo* — and turned left, contrary to the standard practice of turning right, which we will address shortly.

### Two Funnels

At the southwest corner of the *mizbei'ach* were two silver funnels: *shnei sfalim shel kesef hayu sham*. Rabbi Yehudah disputes this, claiming they were actually made of plaster — *shel sid hayu* — but that they appeared black and silver-toned because of the wine poured through them repeatedly: *ella she-hayu mushcharim pneihem mipnei hayayin*.

The funnels had openings of different sizes: *menukavim k'min shnei chotamim dakim* — like two thin nostrils, but *echad mevo'e v'echad dak* — one thicker and one thinner, meaning one had a larger opening and one a smaller. The reason: *kedei she-yiyu shneihem kalim b'vas achas* — so that both would empty simultaneously.

The logic of this requires explanation. Wine was poured at the *mizbei'ach* every single day of the year as part of the libations accompanying the daily *korbanot*. Water was poured only during the seven days of *Sukkot* — *nisuch hamayim* was an annual ritual unique to this season. Each morning, the wine and water were to be poured simultaneously into their respective funnels. Since wine is more viscous than water, it flows more slowly. To ensure both completed their flow at the same moment, the wine funnel required a wider opening even when equal quantities were involved.

### Placement

*Ma'aravo shel mayim mizracho shel yayin* — the western funnel was for water, the eastern for wine. They were positioned at the southwest corner of the *mizbei'ach*. The *kohen* arriving from the south, having turned left at the top of the ramp, was therefore immediately at this corner. If one accidentally poured the water into the wine funnel or the wine into the water funnel: *yatza* — the obligation was discharged after the fact.

### R. Yehudah

Rabbi Yehudah disagrees in two respects: first, the quantity of water was not three *log* but only one *log*; and second, *nisuch hamayim* was performed not for seven days but for all eight — including *Shemini Atzeret*.

### Sadducee

The *mishnah* records a notorious incident: the assembly would instruct the *kohen* performing the pouring to raise his hand — *hagbeh yadcha* — so that everyone could see that he was pouring into the funnel and not elsewhere. This instruction arose because on one occasion a *kohen* who was a *Tzadoki* — a Sadducee, who rejected the *nisuch hamayim* ritual as having no Scriptural basis — poured the water on his own feet rather than into the funnel. He apparently did so covertly, hoping not to be noticed. When the crowd perceived what had happened, *regemuhu kol ha'am b'etrogeihem* — the entire assembly pelted him with their *etrogim*.

### Shabbat Prep

When the seventh day of *nisuch hamayim* fell on *Shabbat*, a modification was required. Normally the water was drawn from the *Shiloach* on the morning of the ritual. But carrying on *Shabbat* was prohibited. Therefore, on *Erev Shabbat* the water was filled into a golden barrel — *chavit shel zahav she-einah mekudeshet* — that was deliberately *not* sanctified. The reason: if the vessel were sanctified, the water inside it would undergo sanctification and thereby become invalid through *linah* — passing the night in an unsanctified state outside the Temple vessels. By keeping the barrel unsanctified, the water remained unaffected by *linah*, and could be used on *Shabbat* itself. This barrel was stored in one of the *lishkos* — the chambers of the *Beis HaMikdash* — overnight, and drawn from the following morning.

### Laver Backup

Two contingencies could disrupt this arrangement: *nishpachah* — the barrel spilled — or *nitgaltah* — the water was left uncovered. The Gemara has a concern about *gilui*, uncovered water, as it was considered a potential health hazard on account of snakes drinking from it and leaving venom behind. In either case, the *kohen* would fill the pitcher *min hakiyor* — from the *kiyor*, the laver used for the *kohanim*'s hand-washing. The laver was connected to an underground well, and water drawn from it did not suffer from *pasul belinah* because when lowered back, it reconnected to the underground water source, effectively "rejoining" flowing water. The downside was that it was not drawn directly from the *Shiloach*, and thus lacked the symbolism of flowing springwater. This source was therefore a backup only.

There is an interesting dispute between Rashi and Tosafot regarding what happened after the water passed through the funnel. Rashi maintains that the water flowed from the *sefel* — the funnel — down across the top of the *mizbei'ach* and into a cavity below, passing through or near the fire. Tosafot finds no source for this and maintains the water simply flowed directly down into the cavity below without traversing the top of the *mizbei'ach* at all.

---

## Sources & Heretics

### Ushavtem Mayim

The Gemara asks: *mina hanei milei* — from where is the ritual of *nisuch hamayim* derived? Rashi understands the question as asking specifically about the accompanying *simcha* — the *tekiah teruah tekiah* and the rejoicing. Tosafot understands it as asking how we know the water must come specifically from a flowing spring (*ma'ayan*) rather than from a well.

Rav Eina cites the verse: *ushavtem mayim besasson mima'ainei hayeshuah* — "and you shall draw water with joy from the springs of salvation" (Yeshayahu 12:3). Rashi derives from *besasson* — with joy — the obligation to accompany the ritual with *tekiah* and celebration. Tosafot derives from *mima'ainei* — from springs — the requirement to draw from a flowing source. The verse serves both purposes, though how *besasson* specifically mandates *tekiah* is not entirely transparent.

### Sasson Simcha

The Gemara now introduces a playful interlude involving two *minim* — heretics. In Talmudic usage, *minim* very often refers to Jewish Christians. One heretic was named *Sasson* (Joy) and the other *Simcha* (Joy in Hebrew). Sasson said to Simcha: *ana adifa minach* — I am greater than you — for the verse says *sasson v'simcha yasigu* (Yeshayahu 35:10), listing *sasson* first. Simcha replied: *ana adifa minach* — I am greater — for the verse says *simcha v'sasson laYehudim* (Esther 8:17), listing *simcha* first.

Then Sasson turned the tables: *chad yoma shavkuich v'shavyuich parvanka* — one day they will abandon you and make you a mere attendant who runs before the procession — *ki b'simcha tetzeu* (Yeshayahu 55:12), you shall go out *with* simcha, meaning *simcha* becomes the one who goes, while others simply accompany. Simcha retorted: *chad yoma shavkuich u'malo bach maya* — one day they will turn you into a flask and fill you with water — *ushavtem mayim besasson*, you shall draw water *with* sasson, meaning *sasson* is the vessel. The wordplay on the verse establishing *nisuch hamayim* — *ushavtem mayim besasson* — is of course the structural link to the surrounding discussion.

### Rabbi Abbahu

The same verse then features in a more pointed exchange. A *min* whose name was *Sasson* said to Rabbi Abbahu: *atiditu d'timlu li maya l'alma d'atei* — in the World to Come, you Jews will draw water for me, for the verse says *ushavtem mayim besasson* — you will draw water *for Sasson*, for me. Rabbi Abbahu replied: *ei hava ktiv l'Sasson*, had it been written *for Sasson* — with a *lamed* of purpose — your reading would have some basis. *Hashta d'chtiv b'sasson* — now that it says *with Sasson* — with a *beis* of accompaniment — *mashka d'hahu gavra mashvinan leih guda u'malina beih maya* — we will make a flask out of the skin of that man and fill it with water. The mockery turns on a simple grammatical distinction: *besasson* with a *beis* means *with joy*, not *for Sasson*. Rabbi Abbahu, who was based in the heavily pagan and religiously mixed city of Caesarea, is repeatedly found in these sharp exchanges with *minim*. The Gemara's broader point may be a general deflation of the heretics' enterprise of reading Scriptural support for their positions — they simply cannot read the text with precision.

---

## Right Turn Rule

### Standard

The *mishnah* had stated that the *kohen* performing *nisuch hamayim* ascended the ramp and turned left. The Gemara now contextualizes this within the general rule. *Tanu rabanan*: *kol ha'olim l'mizbeach olin derech yamin* — all who ascend the *mizbei'ach* ramp do so on the right side — *u'makifin v'yordin derech smol* — they circle and descend on the left. This ensures continuous right-ward traffic flow on the ramp and altar, reflecting the general halachic preference for the right.

### Three Exceptions

Three rituals are exceptions: *nisuch hamayim*, *nisuch hayayin*, and bird *olot* when they are in excess on the eastern side of the *mizbei'ach*. Normally, bird *olot* were performed on the eastern side and bird *chataot* on a different location. But *olah* offerings were among the cheapest to bring — a bird cost very little — and therefore were extremely common. When there were too many bird *olot* to accommodate on the east, the overflow was handled elsewhere. In all three cases, rather than circling the ramp to arrive at the relevant location, the *kohen* made an immediate left turn upon reaching the top of the ramp and went directly to the appropriate corner.

### Smoke Hazard

Rashi explains the reason for these exceptions. It is not merely a matter of efficiency. The standard rule of circling rightward is a religious preference, not a mere traffic protocol. Yet it is overridden here because the southwest corner — where *nisuch hamayim* and *nisuch hayayin* were performed — was particularly smoke-laden, being near the main fire of the *mizbei'ach*. A bird brought all the way around through that smoke would die from inhalation before it could be offered. Similarly, wine or water carried that route would become smoky and unfit for use. Therefore the immediate left turn was permitted as a departure from the general rule.

---

## Black Funnels

### Wine Staining

The *mishnah* stated, according to Rabbi Yehudah's position, that the funnels appeared black, stained by wine. The Gemara now raises a difficulty: *bishlama deyayin mashcher* — I understand why the wine funnel was black, it was used for wine all year long. *Ella demaya amai mashcher* — but why was the water funnel black? It only had water poured through it. Water does not stain.

### Post-Facto

The answer: *afilu de'amar mar irah shel mayim letoch shel yayin v'shel yayin letoch shel mayim yatza* — since the ruling is that if one accidentally poured the water into the wine funnel or the wine into the water funnel *bidi'avad* it is still valid, the wine funnel was not the only vessel through which wine ever passed. Wine was sometimes poured down the water funnel by mistake, and since the error was *bidi'avad* acceptable, it presumably happened with some regularity — enough to stain the water funnel as well.

### Psychology

What is striking about this answer is not merely the legal point but the psychological one the Gemara implicitly makes. Rather than simply noting that people occasionally made mistakes, the Gemara introduces the *bidi'avad* ruling as the *explanation* for the frequency of the mistake. Once the officiant knew that pouring wine into the wrong funnel was not catastrophic — that *bidi'avad* he was *yotze* — he became less careful. The awareness of leniency generated the error. The halachic ruling that mistakes are tolerable after the fact actually made mistakes more likely to occur. This is a remarkable observation about the relationship between leniency and human behavior, embedded quietly within an otherwise technical discussion.

---

## Funnel Viscosity

### R. Yehudah View

The Gemara now raises a further question about the different-sized funnel openings. The *mishnah* records that one funnel had a wider opening and one a narrower opening — *echad mevo'e v'echad dak*. The Gemara suggests: perhaps the *mishnah* follows the position of Rabbi Yehudah specifically. Rabbi Yehudah held that the water quantity was only one *log*, whereas the wine quantity was three *log* — the standard libation amount. Given that disparity in volume, it would make excellent sense to have different-sized openings: the wine needed a wider funnel to drain three *log* at the same rate as one *log* of water.

### Viscosity

But the Gemara immediately pushes back: even according to the Rabbis — who held that both wine and water were three *log* — different openings would still be needed. *Chamra samich maya kalish* — wine is viscous, water is thin. Even with equal volumes, the wine would drain more slowly than the water through an identical opening. To achieve simultaneous completion — *kedei sheyehu shneihem kalin b'vas achas* — one must widen the wine funnel even when quantities are identical.

### Braita Proof

The Gemara adds that there is actually good textual evidence that the *mishnah* does not follow Rabbi Yehudah's position. Rabbi Yehudah, in a *braita*, describes the funnels using different terminology: *rachav v'katzar* — wide and narrow. The *mishnah*, by contrast, uses *mevo'e vedak* — thick and thin. These are distinct formulations, which suggests the *mishnah* reflects the *Rabbis*' position and not Rabbi Yehudah's.

### Conclusion

The conclusion is therefore that even the Rabbis — who held equal volumes of wine and water — required differently sized funnel openings, because viscosity alone is sufficient grounds to need a wider opening for wine. The purpose in both accounts is the same: *kedei sheyehu shneihem kalin b'vas achas* — wine and water must complete their flow simultaneously, and physics requires adjusting for the difference in fluidity. With this, the Gemara's treatment of *nisuch hamayim* on this daf comes to a close, with further discussion to continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Sukkah 49

## Sadducee & Broken Horn

### Sadducee Water Incident

The gemara opens by returning to the context of the *nisuach hamayim*, the water libation performed on Sukkot. As discussed previously, the *kohen* would ascend the ramp, make a left turn and then a right turn, arriving at the two funnels atop the altar — the eastern funnel for the wine libation and the western funnel for the water. The people would demand that the *kohen* raise his hand so they could verify he was performing the libation correctly into the funnel, because on a prior occasion a *kohen* who was a *tzaduki* — a Sadducee who did not believe in the obligation of *nisuach hamayim* — had deliberately poured the water on his feet rather than into the funnel, whereupon the entire assembly pelted him with their *esrogim*.

The *tanna'im* now revisit this incident explicitly: *maaseh b'tzaduki echad shenisach al gabei raglav* — there was an incident with a certain Sadducee who poured the water libation on his feet, *veragmuhu kol ha'am b'esrogim* — and the entire people stoned him with their *esrogim*. Although this episode was already visible in the *mishnah*, the *baraita* here adds the explicit identification of the officiant as a *tzaduki*.

### Horn Damage & Salt Fix

The *baraita* continues: *oso hayom nifgemah keren hamizbeach* — that very day, the horn of the altar was chipped. To appreciate what this means, one must recall the physical structure of the altar. At each of the four upper corners of the *mizbeach* stood a projecting cube, one *amah* by one *amah* by one *amah*, known as the *keren*, the horn. The Sadducee had been pouring near this corner, and when the crowd hurled their *esrogim* at him, some struck the horn, chipping it.

In response, *hiviu gush shel melach l'sasmuhu* — they brought a clump of salt to fill in the chip. The precise mechanics of this repair are admittedly puzzling, given that these altar components were constructed of plaster rather than raw stone. Whatever the method, the text is unambiguous that the repair was not halachically effective: *lo mipnei shehuchshar l'avoda* — not because this rendered the altar fit for *avodah*; the salt patch did not constitute a genuine structural restoration. Rather, *ella mipnei shelo yiraeh mizbeach pagum* — it was done solely so that the altar would not appear damaged or lacking. There is a value in ensuring that the altar presents itself with dignity even while awaiting proper repair, without resorting to the visual equivalent of scaffolding bearing an apologetic notice. But one could not actually continue performing the *avodah* on an altar in this condition.

### Altar Requirements

The gemara explains why the damaged horn renders the altar unfit. At the top of 49a: *shekol mizbeach she'ein lo lo kevesh v'lo keren v'lo yesod v'lo ribua pasul l'avoda* — any altar lacking a ramp (*kevesh*), a horn (*keren*), a foundation (*yesod*) — that lowest projecting base — or proper squareness (*ribua*) is invalid for the *avodah*. Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda adds that even the *sovev* — the encircling ledge that runs around the altar — is indispensable.

It is worth noting in passing that the concern for *ribua* — the precise square shape — and the disqualifying effect of chipping appear in another halachic context as well: *tefillin*, where the cube-with-base structure and the requirement of perfect squareness are strikingly analogous.

### Rashi's Torah Links

The natural question is why these specific components carry disqualifying force. Rashi explains the underlying principle: *kol makom shene'emar hamizbeach le'akev* — wherever the Torah uses the definite article *hamizbeach*, "the altar," it implies that the altar must conform precisely to its prescribed form. *De'hachi mashma hamizbeach ze hu hamizbeach ha'asuy kach* — the phrasing "the altar" indicates it must be exactly as specified. Rashi then traces each component to its biblical source: the horns are derived from the phrase *el karnot hamizbeach*; the ramp from *el penei hamizbeach*, since the ramp is, as Rashi explains, *panav shel mizbeach* — the face of the altar, its entrance and ascent; the foundation from *el yesod hamizbeach*; and the squareness from the explicit formulation *ravu'a yihiyeh hamizbeach*. Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda's inclusion of the *sovev* rests on his identification of *karkov hamizbeach* with the *sovev*, and the appearance of the definite article in connection with it.

### Tosafot Materials

The question remains: what exactly renders a chip on the horn disqualifying? If one still has a horn, merely chipped, why is that not sufficient? This becomes a question about the threshold at which a component ceases to exist in the halachically required sense.

There is an additional complexity. If the altar were constructed of stone, a separate principle would apply: *avanim shleimot* — the stones must be whole — and *lo tanif aleihem barzel* — iron may not be used upon them. This creates an apparent paradox: you cannot shape the stones with iron tools, yet the stones must fit together precisely. One interpretation of *shleimot* therefore shifts from "complete" in the sense of unbroken to "smooth and unchipped" in the sense of unblemished. This is the background for the tradition of the *shamir*, the creature whose secretions could cut stone without iron, or alternatively, as Tosafot suggests, one might break stones without metal — though such breakage would itself compromise *shleimut*.

In practice, however, as Tosafot clarifies, the *mizbeach* in the Temple was not built from hewn field stones in this manner. The sheer practical impossibility of achieving precise dimensions with the constraints described makes plain that the altar was constructed using plaster — essentially a form of early concrete, with small pebbles and filler material poured into molds, which allowed for precision of shape far more tractably. Given this construction method, a chip in itself is not automatically problematic in the way that a damaged stone would be. The disqualifying question is rather one of degree: at what point does damage to the horn render it no longer a horn in the halachically cognizable sense? Or how much loss of right-angle shape compromises *ribua*? The gemara does not spell this out precisely, but it was evidently the case that the damage inflicted by the *esrogim* on that day crossed that threshold, such that the *avodah* could not be resumed until a proper repair was effected.

---

## Shitin Cavities

### Yochanan's View

The gemara now transitions to a famous passage concerning the *shitin* — the cavities into which the wine libation descended after being poured into the funnel atop the altar. There are two fundamental positions about what the *shitin* actually were and where the wine ultimately went.

One opinion holds that the wine descended through the interior of the altar via a kind of internal pipe or channel and collected in a cavity within the altar's base. The other holds that it passed through the altar entirely, broke through the tiled floor of the Temple court, and descended into natural underground caverns reaching to the very depths of the earth. Both positions agree on the name *shitin* for the destination; they differ on whether that destination was inside the altar or beneath it.

Rabbi Yochanan expresses himself on this matter: *Shitin misheshet yemei bereishit nivreu* — the *shitin* are natural underground caverns beneath the Temple Mount, and they were fashioned during the six days of Creation. His support comes from a verse in Shir HaShirim: *chamukei yereichayich kemo chala'im maaseh yedei omman* — "the hidden roundness of your thighs is like *chala'im*, the handiwork of a craftsman." The gemara reads *chamukei* as deriving from a root meaning hidden or concealed, and *yereichayich* as referring to the sides (*yerech*) of the altar — a usage well-attested in the Torah itself, which describes the northern side of the altar as *al yerech hamizbeach tzafona*. Thus *chamukei yereichayich elu hashitin* — the hidden parts of the altar's sides are the *shitin*. And *kemo chala'im shemechulalin veyoredim ad hatehom* — they are like hollow cavities that descend all the way to the depths. *Maaseh yedei omman zeh maaseh yedei umnuto shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu* — the "handiwork of a craftsman" in the verse refers to the handiwork of the Holy One Himself; these were created by God as natural formations.

### Chamukei Yereichayich

The gemara continues with a *derashah* from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *al tikrei Bereishit ella bara shit* — do not read the first word of the Torah as merely "In the beginning," but rather as "He created the *shit*" — that is, God created the *shitin* in the very act of creation. This reading reinforces Rabbi Yochanan's naturalistic account: the underground caverns were not constructed by human hands but were part of the primordial structure of the world, placed there in anticipation of their eventual role in the Temple service.

A *baraita* corroborates this view: *Rabbi Yoshiya omer shitin mechulalin veyoredim ad hatehom* — Rabbi Yoshiya teaches that the *shitin* are hollowed out and descend to the depths of the earth.

### Isaiah Vineyard

Rabbi Yoshiya then cites a striking midrashic reading of the opening verses of Isaiah 5 — the parable of the beloved's vineyard — as support. The passage reads: *ashira na lididi shirat dodi lecharmo* — let me sing to my beloved a song of his vineyard. *Kerem hayah lididi bekeren ben shamen* — a vineyard belonged to my beloved on a richly fertile hill. *Vayazkehu vayeskalehu* — he dug it out and cleared it of stones. *Vayitaehu sorek* — he planted it with choice vines. *Vayiven migdal betocho* — he built a tower in its midst. *Vegam yekev chatzav bo* — and he even dug a wine vat within it. The verse then laments how the vineyard, despite all this care, yielded only sour grapes — the prophetic metaphor for Israel's betrayal of God. But the opening description of investment and cultivation yields a layered midrashic reading.

The gemara — according to Rashi's version — reads the verse as follows: *vayitaehu sorek ze Beit HaMikdash* — "he planted the choice vine" refers to the Temple itself; *vayiven migdal betocho ze Mizbeach* — "he built a tower in its midst" refers to the altar, a tall, imposing structure; *vegam yekev chatzav bo elu hashitin* — "he dug a wine vat within it" refers to the *shitin*, since a vat is precisely the receptacle into which wine flows.

### Cavern vs. Cavity

Tosafot's version of the text reads somewhat differently: *vayiven migdal betocho ze Heichal* — "he built a tower" refers to the *Heichal*, the great hall of the Temple, which was indeed the towering structure; *vegam yekev chatzav bo ze Mizbeach* — "he dug a wine vat" refers to the altar itself, since the altar is where the wine is first poured before descending, making it the vat. And the *shitin* are derived not from *yekev* directly but from the seemingly superfluous word *vegam* — "and also" — indicating an extension beyond the altar proper into what lies beneath it.
