This version is consistent with what Tosafot says is the reading of the *Tosefta*.

This textual divergence between Rashi and Tosafot reflects and maps onto the underlying dispute about the nature of the *shitin*. According to Rashi, the straightforward reading identifies the wine vat with the *shitin* — the underground cavern is where the wine ends up. According to the Tosafot version, the vat is the altar itself, and the *shitin* are a further extension beneath it, derived from the word *vegam*. Crucially, those who read the Isaiah passage in the Tosafot fashion understand the construction of the *Heichal* and *Mizbeach* as referring to human building activity — and therefore, even though they agree that there are underground caverns, they do not hold that these caverns were naturally created from the six days of Creation. Rather, they were excavated as part of the construction of the *Beit HaMikdash*. This stands in tension with Rabbi Yochanan's position, which attributes the *shitin* to divine creation at the dawn of time.

---

## Cleaning Shitin

### Trapdoor Location

The gemara introduces a *baraita* from Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok: *lul katan haya bein kevesh leMizbeach bamaaravo shel kevesh* — there was a small trapdoor between the ramp and the altar, on the western side of the ramp. The location of this trapdoor on the western side makes sense given the geography of the libations: the wine was poured at the northwestern corner of the altar, and whatever collected in the cavity would be accessible from the west.

### 70-Year Cleaning

*Ve'achat leshiv'im shana pirchei kehuna yordin lesham* — once every seventy years, the young *kohanim* — *pirchei kehuna*, literally those whose facial hair was just beginning to appear, small enough to fit through the trapdoor — would descend through this opening to clean out the accumulated wine. *Umelaketin misham yayin karush shedomeh leigulei deveila* — they would collect from within the cavity congealed wine that had solidified into forms resembling pressed fig cakes. *Uba'in vesorfin oto bikdusha* — and they would bring this material out and burn it in holiness, as befitting a sacred substance. The gemara derives this requirement to burn it in holiness through a *gezeirah shavah* connecting the word *kodesh* in the verse *bakodesh hasech nesech sheichar* — "in the holy place perform the libation, a libation of intoxicating drink to God" — with the burning of *nosar*, leftovers of offerings, where the Torah says *lo yei'acheil ki kodesh hu* — "it shall not be eaten for it is holy." Just as *nosar* must be burned in its sanctity, so must this congealed wine be disposed of in a manner consistent with its holy status.

### Ramp-Altar Gap

This picture of the trapdoor located between the ramp and the altar prompts reflection on the spatial relationship between those two structures. The ramp did not actually touch the top of the altar; there was an intentional gap between them. This gap existed because of the halachic requirement for *zrikah* — throwing. As Rashi notes by citing the verse *veasita olotecha habasar vehadam*, and drawing the inference *mah dam b'zrikah af basar b'zrikah* — just as the blood is cast upon the altar with a throwing motion from below, so too the placement of the limbs (*evarim*) upon the altar must involve a throwing action. A *kohen* standing at the top of the ramp would therefore throw the limbs across the gap onto the altar surface. This gap, while halachically necessary, would have made the top of the ramp a place requiring considerable care.

---

## Me'ilah Status

### Mishnah Me'ilah

The gemara now addresses the question of *me'ilah* — the prohibition against deriving unauthorized benefit from consecrated objects — in relation to the libation wine. The *mishnah* teaches: *nisachim b'tchilah moalin bahem* — with wines designated for libation, *me'ilah* applies initially; *yardu l'shittin ayn moalin bahem* — once they have descended into the *shitin*, *me'ilah* no longer applies.

### Sage Positions

This raises the question of which rabbinic opinion this *mishnah* aligns with. The gemara first suggests: *laima Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Tzadok* — perhaps this *mishnah* follows the position of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, who holds that the wine collected in an internal cavity of the altar rather than descending to underground depths. For according to the rabbis, who hold that the wine descended all the way to the abyss, how would there ever be a practical circumstance in which someone could misuse the wine once it entered the *shitin*? If it has gone to the depths of the earth, it is entirely inaccessible, and the *mishnah*'s statement that *me'ilah* no longer applies would be obvious and unremarkable.

The gemara responds: even according to the rabbis, the *mishnah* can be understood — *bediklava* — in the case where someone caught the wine as it was passing through the altar's interior cavity on its way down to the underground cavern. Such a person might have a reason to think *me'ilah* still applies since the mitzvah has not yet fully been discharged by the wine's arrival at its final destination.

The gemara then proposes the inverse: *ve'ika de'amri* — others say the reasoning should be reversed. Perhaps it is specifically according to the rabbis — who hold the wine goes underground — that this *mishnah* makes sense, while it does not easily fit with Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok. For according to Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, once the wine has collected in the internal cavity, its holiness remains intact — *kedushah bikdushatei kai* — and one might think *me'ilah* still applies, since after all the wine must still be burned in holiness.

### Pappa Resolution

The gemara resolves this: *afilu teima Rabbi Elazar* — even according to Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, *ein lecha davar shena'aseit mitzvatah umoalin bah* — there is no object in all of halacha that, once its designated mitzvah has been performed with it, remains subject to *me'ilah*. The fact that the wine retains some residual sanctity — enough to require burning — does not mean it remains subject to *me'ilah*. These are distinct categories. Once the mitzvah of *nisuach* has been accomplished by pouring the wine into the funnel, the wine has fulfilled its halachic role, and *me'ilah* no longer applies to it, regardless of what happens subsequently.

---

## Stopping Drains

### Reish Lakish

The gemara introduces a further teaching about the mechanics of the libation: *amar Reish Lakish* — Reish Lakish taught that *bizman shemenaschin yayin al gabei hamizbeach, pokekin et hashitin* — when they would pour the wine libation atop the altar, they would first stop up the *shitin*. According to Rashi, they would plug the openings near the top of the cavity. The wine would then not immediately run down into the depths. This practice is grounded in the verse: *bakodesh hasech nesech sheichar LaHashem* — "in the holy place pour a libation, a libation of *sheichar* to God."

### Pappa Sheichar

The connection between stopping the drains and this verse requires explanation. Rav Pappa provides it: *sheichar lashon shetiah* — the word *sheichar* connotes drinking; *lashon seviah* — it denotes a drinking that satisfies; *lashon shichrut* — it suggests the kind of drinking that actually produces intoxication. What does this have to do with plugging a drain?

The gemara proceeds to draw a physiological analogy: *ki sava inish chamra migronei sava* — when a person truly feels satisfied and full from wine, that satisfaction comes from the throat, not merely from the stomach. Wine that rushes straight down without pausing in the mouth and throat does not produce the sensation of *seviah*, of true satiation. Holding wine in the mouth before swallowing — allowing it to fill the mouth and linger in the throat — produces the experience of genuinely satisfied drinking, the kind that has intoxicating effect.

Applied to the libation: if the wine were poured in and immediately ran straight down through the *shitin* without any pause, it would be like swallowing a drink without savoring it. By stopping up the *shitin*, one allows the wine to fill the cavity at the top — the "mouth" of the altar, as it were — before releasing. This constitutes a *sheichar* — a truly satisfied drinking, a libation that is complete in the sense that the wine has fully occupied its designated space before descending.

### Rava's Teaching

Rava applies this physiological insight to a practical teaching: *tzurba miRabanan dela nafish lei chamra* — a Torah student who cannot afford much wine — perhaps he has access to some on *Shabbos* but it is limited — *ligma gimei* — he should take large swallows and hold them before swallowing. This is more effective at producing satisfaction than sipping small amounts repeatedly. Taking big gulps and holding the wine in the throat before swallowing will derive the full benefit from a small quantity of wine.

### Blessing Cup

In connection with this, the gemara notes that Rava himself, with the *kassa de'birchasa* — the cup over which he recited *Kiddush* or *Birkat HaMazon* — would similarly *agmah gimuaye*, take a substantial gulp and hold it before swallowing. For Rava, this was an expression of the honor due the *kos shel berachah*: just as the altar paused to receive the wine fully, Rava paused to honor the cup of blessing.

---

## Mah Yafu Footsteps

### Rava Ascent

The gemara records a *derashah* of Rava on the verse *mah yafu pe'amayich bane'alim bat nadiv* — "how beautiful are your footsteps in sandals, O daughter of the generous one." Rava interprets: *mah yafu pe'amoteihem shel Yisrael besha'ah she'olim laregel* — how beautiful are the footsteps of the Jewish people when they go up to Jerusalem for the *regel*, the pilgrimage festival. The word *pe'amayich*, footsteps, evokes the *aliyah laregel*, the ascending pilgrimage; and *ne'alim*, sandals, carries also the connotation of *oleh*, ascending.

### Abraham Convert

*Bat nadiv* — daughter of the generous one — is interpreted as *bito shel Avraham Avinu* — the daughter of our father Abraham, *shenikra nadiv* — who was called the generous one. The proof text is *nedivei amim ne'esafu am Elohei Avraham* — "the generous ones of the nations have gathered, the people of Abraham's God." This verse speaks of the people as belonging to the God of Abraham specifically — *velo Elohei Yitzchak veYaakov?* Why Abraham and not also Isaac and Jacob? The gemara answers: *ella Elohei Avraham shehayah techilah lagerim* — because Abraham was the first of the converts, the first to come near to God of his own volition.

Rashi notes that this is the point of the word *nadiv* applied to Abraham. *Nadiv* suggests not merely generosity with wealth but an internal motivating force — the kind of heart-driven desire to give and to act, *kol nediv lev*. Abraham's heart drove him toward God, toward knowledge of God, and this is why he is the archetypal *ger*, the father of all future converts whose hearts similarly move them to draw near. When Israel goes up to Jerusalem on *aliyah laregel*, they are enacting this same impulse — leaving the familiar, moving toward God — and in that sense they are *bat nadiv*, children of Abraham's quality of heart-driven approach. The *lech lecha* — the command to leave one's land and birthplace — resonates each time a person makes that personal journey toward *kedushah*.

---

## Torah Modesty

### Torah Hidden

The gemara returns to the phrase *chamukei yereichayich* — which it had earlier interpreted in relation to the *shitin* of the altar — and now applies it in a completely different direction: as a metaphor for Torah study. *Tanna devei Rav Anani* asks: *lamah nimshalu divrei Torah k'yerech?* — Why is Torah compared to a thigh? *Lomar lecha mah yerech beseter, af divrei Torah beseter* — to teach you that just as the thigh is kept covered and private, so too words of Torah belong in a private, modest setting. Torah study is not meant to be ostentatious. You do not perform it at a mountaintop to be seen; it has an intimacy to it — a *rebbe* and students, earnest engagement rather than display.

Rashi explains that the connection between Torah and *chala'im* — the other word in the verse, which in its plain sense means jewelry or precious stones — reflects the tradition that the Tablets of the Law were fashioned from precious stone.

### Humility Teaching

*Vehaynu de'amar Rabbi Elazar* — and this is what Rabbi Elazar teaches when he asks: *mai d'ichtiv higid lecha adam mah tov, umah Hashem doresh mimcha* — "He has told you, O man, what is good; what does the Lord require of you?" *Ki im asot mishpat ve'ahavat chesed vehatzne'a lechet im Elohecha* — "but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God."

The gemara unpacks each phrase: *asot mishpat zeh hadin* — doing justice means building a society based on law. *Ve'ahavat chesed zu gemilut chasadim* — loving kindness means performing acts of loving-kindness for one another. *Vehatzne'a lechet im Elohecha* — walking humbly with your God: *zu hotza'at hamet vehachnasat kallah lachuppah* — this refers to accompanying the dead to burial and bringing a bride to the *chuppah*.

### Hidden Mitzvot

Why are these two particular *mitzvot* associated with *hatzne'a lechet*, walking humbly? Rashi points to the verse *tov lalechet lebeit ha'avel milalechet el beit mishteh* — "it is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting" — where the word *lechet*, going, appears. The *beit mishteh* evokes the setting of a wedding celebration. These two acts — accompanying the dead and rejoicing with a bride — are paradigmatically public occasions; the proper honor of the deceased calls for a public *levayah*, and the joy of *chatan vakallah* is heightened by communal participation.

Yet the Torah says: *hatzne'a lechet* — do them with modesty. This is striking. The *kal vachomer* the gemara draws is: *kal vachomer* — if the Torah requires modesty in acts that are by their nature public, how much more so must modesty govern acts that are by nature private? And this naturally connects back to Torah study, which is inherently more intimate, making modesty in that domain all the more expected.

### Modest Display

What does modesty mean in the context of a wedding or a funeral, which are inherently public? Rashi offers two explanations, both of powerful practical relevance.

The first: do not allow the externals to overshadow the essence. A wedding must not become an exercise in conspicuous consumption where the sheer expense and spectacle distract from the genuine *simchah* of *chatan vakallah*. The *hatzne'a lechet* is a call to keep one's focus on what is actually meaningful — the couple, the celebration, the sacred moment — rather than on the apparatus of display. And this applies not only to the organizers but to every guest: how does one comport oneself at a wedding? Does one participate in the *simchah* or primarily attend to the food and social spectacle?

The second explanation Rashi gives is equally demanding. When one contributes financially to make a wedding or a funeral happen — and *hachnasat kallah* includes the communal collection of *tzedakah* for those who cannot afford their own weddings — the fact that many people will inevitably know how much things cost, who paid what, how the bills were settled, does not license one to broadcast one's generosity. *Hatzne'a lechet* requires that even when the act of giving is visible by necessity, one refrain from calling attention to it, from saying, "You know how much that wedding cost? I was the one who made it happen." That restraint in speech, that refusal to capitalize on the visibility of one's contribution, is itself the *tzniut* demanded by this verse.

---

## Tzedakah Hierarchy

### Elazar Hierarchy

The gemara presents a hierarchy of virtues articulated by Rabbi Elazar. First: *gadol ha'oseh tzedakah yoter mikol hakorbanot* — one who performs *tzedakah* is greater than one who offers all the sacrifices. This is a striking statement given how central the *korbanot* are to Torah life and how keenly their absence is felt. The source is the verse *asoh tzedakah umishpat nivchar laHashem mizevach* — "doing charity and justice is more desired by God than sacrifice."

Rabbi Elazar then adds: *gedolah gemilut chasadim yoter min hatzedakah* — *gemilut chasadim* is greater even than *tzedakah*. The proof text is *ziru lachem litzedakah vekitzru lefi chesed* — "plant for yourselves in *tzedakah* and harvest according to *chesed*." Planting involves uncertainty: *im adam zorea safek ochel safek eino ochel* — when you plant, you are not yet guaranteed a yield. But *adam kotzer vaday ochel* — when you harvest, you eat with certainty. *Chesed* is the harvest — the more assured and complete form of the good.

### Reciprocal Kindness

It is important not to reduce *gemilut chasadim* to charity performed toward the unfortunate. The word *gomel* itself, as in *gomel chesed*, ordinarily means to repay or reciprocate. There is an inherent reciprocity in *gemilut chasadim* that distinguishes it from top-down giving. Going to a friend's wedding is *gemilut chasadim*. Going to a funeral is *gemilut chasadim*. Being there for someone in a moment of need is *gemilut chasadim*. These are acts that flow between equals, between community members who are there for one another across all of life's occasions — not merely from those who have to those who lack.

This reciprocal quality is captured by the image of the community *gemach* — a loan society in which members share resources: a ladder, a lawn mower, any item one household has and another temporarily needs. The insight is that *gemilut chasadim* is not the province of the wealthy helping the poor; it is the fabric of mutual care that holds any community together, and in which anyone, regardless of means, can be a full participant as both giver and recipient.

### Tzedakah Reward

Rabbi Elazar adds a third teaching: *ein tzedakah mishtalemet ela lefi chesed she-bah* — *tzedakah* is rewarded only in proportion to the *chesed* that is within it. The same verse is cited: *ziru lachem litzedakah vekitzru lefi chesed* — you plant in *tzedakah*, but you harvest according to *chesed*. This is not merely a ranking of two separate virtues; it is an interweaving of them. Even when you are giving *tzedakah*, how you give it determines its ultimate value.

### Rashi Effort

Rashi's comment here is particularly illuminating. He explains: *gemilut chasadim she-bah, ha-netinah hi ha-tzedakah, veha-torach hu ha-chesed* — the monetary giving is the *tzedakah*; the effort you invest is the *chesed*. What kind of effort? *Kigun molicho le-beito* — walking the recipient to his home, accompanying him. Or *o torach she-taaleh lo le-harbeh* — working to ensure the money actually increases for him, helping him invest or use it wisely. Or *kigun noten lo pat afuyah o beged lilvosh o maot be-et tzarah metzuyah* — giving him bread already baked, or a garment to wear, or money at the moment when it can be obtained cheaply. *Shelo yotzi ma'ot le'ibud shenoten libo vedaato letovato shel ani* — ensuring the money is not wasted, because you genuinely think through what will serve this person's actual good. That attentiveness — that investment of thought and effort — is the *chesed* within the *tzedakah*.

### Three Distinctions

The *baraita* then formalizes the superiority of *gemilut chasadim* over *tzedakah* along three axes. *Tzedakah bimmono* — *tzedakah* is performed with one's money alone. *Gemilut chasadim bein begufo bein bimmono* — *gemilut chasadim* is performed with one's person as well as one's money; one can give of one's time, one's physical presence, one's personal assistance — or one can provide a loan rather than a gift. *Tzedakah la'aniyim* — *tzedakah* is directed only toward the poor. *Gemilut chasadim bein la'aniyim bein la'ashirim* — *gemilut chasadim* extends to the wealthy as well, for everyone stands in need of someone else at some point. And *tzedakah lachayim* — *tzedakah* is for the living. *Gemilut chasadim bein lachayim bein lametim* — *gemilut chasadim* extends even to the dead, as when one participates in a *levayah* and honors the deceased. This is the *chesed shel emet*, the truest act of kindness, for there is no possibility of the recipient repaying it. And yet, understood within the framework of a community, it is precisely this act that embodies the deepest reciprocity — honoring what this person meant, being present for a family in grief, participating in the continuity of human solidarity.

---

## Justice & Kindness

### Tzedakah Mishpat

Rabbi Elazar expands the teaching further: *kol ha'oseh tzedakah umishpat ke'ilu milei kol ha'olam kulo chesed* — anyone who performs *tzedakah* and *mishpat* is as though he has filled the entire world with *chesed*. The verse is *ohev tzedakah umishpat chesed Hashem mala'ah ha'aretz* — "He who loves *tzedakah* and *mishpat*, the *chesed* of God fills the earth." This formulation links individual human conduct to cosmic *chesed*.

The insight here is that a society genuinely built on justice — where law is applied equally, where systemic conditions allow for the flourishing of all members, and where those who fall through the cracks are caught by *tzedakah* — constitutes a form of *chesed* for the world. It does not achieve the full quality of personal *chesed*, but *ke'ilu* — as if — one has filled the world with *chesed*. The *chesed* of God, which pervades creation, finds its human analog in the construction of a just and caring society.

### Rare Kindness

The gemara immediately adds a qualification. *Shema tomar kol haba likpotz kofetz* — lest you say that anyone who wishes can simply commit to acts of *tzedakah* and *chesed* and succeed: *talmud lomar mah yakar chasdecha Elokim* — "how rare, how precious is Your kindness, O God." Rashi interprets this as a caution: good intentions do not automatically produce effective results. To genuinely do *tzedakah* and *mishpat* and *chesed* in ways that actually help, rather than harm or miss the mark, requires forethought, discernment, and genuine engagement. The verse acknowledges that even truly valuable *chesed* is precious partly because it is not easy to achieve.

### God's Grace

Yet the difficulty is not insurmountable for those who approach it with the right orientation: *yachol af yere shamayim ken* — perhaps even a God-fearing person faces this difficulty? *Talmud lomar vechesed Hashem meolam vead olam al yerayav* — "and the *chesed* of God is from eternity to eternity upon those who fear Him." The opportunities for true *chesed*, and the *siyata dishmaya* to perform it well, are more accessible to the genuinely *yere shamayim*, perhaps because a hidden agenda — even one of which the person is themselves unaware — can quietly distort even well-meaning acts of generosity. The *yere shamayim* is more likely to be free of such distortions.

Rabbi Chama bar Pappa adds: *kol adam sheyesh lo chen beyadu'a shehu yere shamayim* — anyone who possesses *chen* — that quality of grace and favor in others' eyes — one can know that person is God-fearing. The source is again the verse connecting *chesed* with those who fear God. The inference is that *chesed* generates *chen*, and therefore *chen* is a marker of genuine *yirat shamayim*.

---

## Torah Lishmah

### Woman Wisdom

The gemara concludes with a verse from Proverbs: *piha patcha be'chochma vetorat chesed al leshona* — "she opens her mouth with wisdom, and the Torah of kindness is on her tongue." Rabbi Elazar asks: *veki yesh Torah shel chesed veyesh Torah she'eina shel chesed?* — is there then a Torah of kindness and a Torah that is not of kindness? The question is serious: all Torah is presumably one — what distinguishes these two?

### Lishmah View

The first answer: *ella Torah lishmah zu hi Torah shel chesed* — Torah studied for its own sake is Torah of *chesed*. When a person learns Torah purely because it is the word of God, because Torah itself is the beloved object and the relationship with the Divine is the purpose, there is no intervening agenda. This is *chesed* toward God, as it were — a relationship of pure devotion. *Veshelo lishmah, zu hi Torah she'eina shel chesed* — Torah studied with other agendas — prestige, livelihood, status — lacks this quality of *chesed*.

### Teaching View

The second opinion says: *Torah lelamda zu hi Torah shel chesed* — Torah studied with the intent to teach it to others is Torah of *chesed*, because the learning opens outward, it is given over to others, it multiplies. *Shelo lelamda* — Torah studied purely for oneself, to accumulate knowledge and standing as a *talmid chacham* without any orientation toward transmitting it, *zu hi Torah she'eina shel chesed* — this is Torah that is not of *chesed*, because it remains entirely self-directed and does not flow outward to others.

---

---

# Sukkah 50

## Nisuch Hamayim

### Perek Overview

We conclude the discussion of the *nisuch hamayim* at the end of the fourth *perek* of Sukkah, which has been devoted to the collection of *mitzvot* that apply on *Sukkot*. The *perek* began with *lulav*, elaborated on *aravah* — which has both an aspect outside the *Mikdash* and a specific *Mikdash* ritual — and has been dominated by the laws of *nisuch hamayim*, the water libation. This water libation theme will carry forward into the fifth *perek*, which opens with the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah*, the celebration that took place the preceding night. The *avodah* itself — the pouring of the water — was performed during the day, accompanying the *tamid shel shachar*, together with the wine libations. The *Simchat Beit HaShoevah* was the all-night celebration that led into that morning ritual.

### Weekday vs Shabbat

The final *Mishna* of the fourth *perek* states that what they did on a weekday, they also did on *Shabbat* — with one logistical adjustment. On a weekday, they would draw water from the spring. On *erev Shabbat*, they would draw the water in advance, fill it into a barrel, and leave it there so that on *Shabbat* morning they could draw from the barrel rather than carry it from outside. The barrel was kept within the *Mikdash*, already positioned for use the next morning.

### Non-Sanctified Barrel

The *Mishna* specifies that the barrel used was a gold barrel that was *ainah mekudeshes* — non-sanctified. The *Gemara* asks the obvious question: *v'na'avid b'mekudeshes* — why not simply use a sanctified gold barrel? Why insist on a non-sanctified vessel?

Ze'iri explains that this *Tanna* holds two principles. First, *ain shiur l'mayim* — there is no exact prescribed amount of water; while we use three *log*, it need not be precisely three *log*. Second, *klei shares mekadshin shelo m'da'as* — sanctified vessels sanctify their contents even without intent.

To understand why both principles are necessary, consider the underlying concern. For inanimate objects such as a *mincha*, *kedushah* at the level of *kedushat haguf* — intrinsic sanctity, the sanctity of a *korban* proper — is conferred when the item is placed into a *kli shares*. Once something reaches *kedushat haguf*, the full consequences of *korban* status apply: if it remains overnight (*linah*), it becomes invalid; if it is removed from the *Beit HaMikdash*, it becomes invalid. Therefore, if the barrel were sanctified and one filled it with water the day before, the water would acquire *kedushat haguf* and become invalid by the following morning — precisely when it was needed.

Now, why must Ze'iri state *shelo m'da'as*? Because one might argue that *klei shares* only sanctify when the officiant intends them to do so. If the *Kohen* specifically intended that the water should not yet be sanctified — since it would not be used until morning — perhaps that intent could prevent the sanctification from taking effect. *Shelo m'da'as* answers this: the mere act of placing something in a *kli shares* imparts sanctity, regardless of intent, even contrary intent.

And why is *ain shiur l'mayim* also required? Because one might concede that intent is irrelevant, yet argue that the objective reality of the situation prevents sanctification. A *kli shares* and *kedushat haguf* represent an object that is, so to speak, *ready to be offered* — in the full state of being about to be used for the service. If the barrel contains five *log* and the libation requires three, the objective reality suggests the water is not yet ready: it is not in the precise state of an offering prepared for use. The *Gemara* therefore adds *ain shiur l'mayim*: technically, any amount suffices, so the objective reality cannot provide this escape. Once the water is in the vessel, it is automatically sanctified regardless of quantity.

It is worth noting that *Tosafot* raises an important question here. Why is the concern specifically about *linah* — invalidation by remaining overnight? The moment one walks outside the *Mikdash* to draw the water, the vessel is outside the Temple precinct, and if it were sanctified it would immediately become invalid through *yotzei* — being removed from the sacred space. The answer is that something cannot become sanctified outside the *Mikdash* in the first place. Sanctification requires the vessel to be inside the *Beit HaMikdash*. Only once the water is brought in does the sanctification take effect — and at that point, the problem of *linah* applies.

### Sanctification Without I…

Chizkiyya offers a counterargument: *kli shares ein mekadshin ela midaas* — sanctified vessels do not sanctify their contents unless one intends them to do so. According to Chizkiyya, the officiant could stipulate that the water should not be sanctified when it is placed in the barrel on *erev Shabbat*, and this would be effective. If so, there should be no problem using a sanctified barrel — simply stipulate that the sanctification not take effect until morning.

### Gezeira Concern

The *Gemara* responds that even granting Chizkiyya's position, there is a rabbinic concern: *gezeira shema yomru l'daas niskadshu* — a decree against using a sanctified barrel lest people observe that a sanctified vessel was used and the water was kept overnight, and draw the mistaken conclusion that sanctified objects may routinely be left overnight. Since no one else can see the officiant's internal stipulation, onlookers will think the water was sanctified in the normal way and will derive an incorrect *halacha* from the practice.

### Rav Zeira's Position

Rav Zeira, in the name of Rav Yannai, extends the concern even further. Even if one accepts both of the following propositions — that there is a fixed exact measurement of three *log* for the *nisuch hamayim*, and that *klei shares* do not sanctify without intent — there is still a reason not to use a sanctified barrel. In this scenario one might think: since the barrel obviously contains much more than three *log*, any observer will objectively recognize that the water cannot yet be in the state of a prepared offering, and no one will draw any mistaken conclusions. Rav Zeira answers that even so, there is a concern: *gezeira shema yomru l'kiddush yadayim v'raglayim mela'un* — people will not know why the barrel was filled. They will assume it was filled for the *Kohen Gadol*'s hand-washing the next morning, a practice that had no fixed minimum amount of water, and they will then conclude that sanctified water could be left overnight and used the following day. Thus across all the variants — whether or not there is an exact measurement, whether or not intent matters — there is always grounds for concern about using a sanctified vessel.

### Uncovered Water Problem

The *Mishna* further states that if the water drawn on *erev Shabbat* was spilled or left uncovered (*nitgalta*), it could not be used. The *Gemara* focuses on the problem of uncovered water. As is well known from other *Mishnayot*, *mayim megulim* — uncovered liquids — are forbidden out of concern that a snake may have drunk from them and introduced venom.

The *Gemara* asks: why not pass the uncovered water through a *mesannenet* — a strainer or filter — to remove the poison? Perhaps our *Mishna* does not follow the opinion of Rabbi Nechemia, since there is a *tannaitic* debate on this point. A *Baraita* teaches that if a strainer is placed over water, the water is still considered to have the status of *gilui* — exposure — and may not be used. Rabbi Nechemia qualifies this: when is the water still considered exposed? Only when the lower vessel — the one actually containing the liquid — is itself uncovered, so that a snake could access it from below. However, if the lower vessel is covered, even if the upper vessel is uncovered, there is no problem. The reasoning is that *eires nachash* — snake venom — *domeh lisvog, tzaf ve'omeid bimkomo* — is like a sponge, floating at the surface, and will be filtered out as the liquid passes through.

### Filter & Sanctity

The *Gemara* answers that even according to Rabbi Nechemia, such water cannot be used for the *nisuch hamayim*. Rabbi Nechemia only permits filtered water for a *hedyot* — an ordinary person. For *gavoah* — for God — would he ever sanction such a thing? The *Gemara* invokes the *pasuk*: *hakrivehu na lefachatecha hayirtzecha o hayissa panecha* — would you bring such a thing before your governor and expect it to find favor? Even if technically the water is safe to drink after filtration, the fact that it had to undergo such a process makes it categorically unacceptable as an offering on the *mizbei'ach*.

There is a deeper point here worth noting. What makes water that has been filtered through a *mesannenet* unacceptable is not necessarily any residual fear of poison. Rather, it is the inherent degraded character of the water itself — that it was in such a state in the first place. Even if one were fully confident the filter worked perfectly, there is something unsavory about using water that passed through such a process, something analogous to drinking water one knows was reclaimed from waste, however thoroughly treated. The concern for the *Mikdash* is not merely technical safety but the dignity of what is brought before God.

---

## Thematic Integration

### Malachi Theme

Before closing the fourth *perek*, it is worth pausing to note a striking structural connection. The third *perek* opened with the *lulav* framed in the language of a *korban*: the *Gemara* there derived the invalidity of a stolen *lulav* from the concept of *mitzvah haba'ah ba'aveirah*, and it did so through a *pasuk*: *ve'heveitem gazul v'et hapiseach v'et hacholeh* — is this the type of thing you want to bring before God? Something stolen, something lame, something sick? Now, the fourth *perek* closes with the same question, invoked against using filtered water for the *nisuch hamayim*: *hakrivehu na lefachatecha hayirtzecha o hayissa panecha*. Not only are these two *pesukim* making the same theological point, they are both drawn from the very same *parasha* — **Malachi, Chapter 1**.

### Opening & Closing

This is not coincidental. The entire first chapter of Malachi is a *parasha* of God's grievance against the people for the degradation of His service. The opening of the relevant passage reads:

> *V'im adonim ani aye morai amar Hashem tzevaot lachem hakohanim bozei shemi v'amartem bameh bazinu et shemecha. Magishim al mizbechi lechem m'go'al v'amartem bameh ge'al nucha. B'omrachem shulchan Hashem nivzeh hu. V'chi tagishun iver lizboach ein ra v'chi tagishu piseach v'choleh ein ra. Hakrivehu na l'pachatecha hayirtzecha o hayissa panecha amar Hashem tzevaot.*

You bring the blind, the lame, the sick, and you say there is nothing wrong with it. Would you bring that to your governor? And then the *parasha* continues:

> *Mimizrach shemesh v'ad mevo'o gadol shemi bagoyim uv'chol makom muktar mugash lishmi mincha tehorah ki gadol shemi bagoyim amar Hashem tzevaot.*

My name is great among the nations — yet look at how you treat Me. And then:

> *V'havetem gazul v'et hapiseach v'et hacholeh v'havetem et hamincha ha'ertzeh otah miyedchem amar Hashem.*

This context carries a tone of *klalah* — prophetic rebuke — which somewhat complicates the celebratory associations one might initially expect. Yet if *Sukkot* is, at its core, about drawing close to God and continuing the spiritual work initiated on *Yom Kippur*, and if the *lulav*, the *aravah*, the *nisuch hamayim*, and all the *Mikdash* rituals of these *perakim* represent the ideal of offering our very best to God — then the way the third and fourth *perek* are bookended by two *pesukim* from this same *parasha* in Malachi is remarkably powerful. The theme of *Sukkot* — agricultural success, gratitude, joy before God — is inseparable from the question of what is truly worthy to be brought before Him.

---

## Simchat Beit HaShoeva

### Fifth Perek Intro

We now open the fifth *perek* of Maseches Sukkah, which concerns the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah* — the all-night celebration that began the evening before the drawing of the water and continued through the night, building toward the morning *nisuch hamayim*.

### Chalil Schedule

The *Mishna* states: *hechalil chamishah v'shishah* — the *chalil* (a flute or recorder-like instrument) was played five or six days. This refers to the musical instruments played for the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah*. The *Mishna* continues: *she'einah dochah lo et haShabbat v'lo et Yom Tov* — this music did not override *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. Since the *nisuch hamayim* was performed each of the seven days of *Sukkot*, and the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah* celebration began the night before each drawing, one would expect seven nights of celebration. However, since *Yom Tov* itself fell on the first night and the music could not be played then, that eliminated at least one night. If *Shabbat* also fell during *Sukkot*, it too would be excluded — both the musical celebration the night before and the water-drawing itself, since carrying from outside the *Mikdash* on *Shabbat* was not done. Hence the formula: five or six days.

### Textual Variants

The *Gemara* at the top of 51b records that there were two variant readings of the name of the celebration. One *tanna* read *Shoeva* — the drawing — which is the familiar and intuitive reading, evoking *u'shavtem mayim b'sasson*, the drawing of water with joy. The other *tanna* read *Chashuva* — the important — yielding *Simchat Beit HaChashuva*. This variant is striking evidence of an oral culture: in written form such a confusion would be nearly impossible, but in oral transmission the similarity of *Shoeva* and *Chashuva* could plausibly yield two traditions.

Mar Zutra rules that neither version is corrupt. The reading of *Shoeva* is not corrupt, as it is grounded in the *pasuk u'shavtem mayim b'sasson* — the drawing of water with joy. The reading of *Chashuva* is also not corrupt, as Rav Nachman explains: *mitzvah chashuva hi u'va'ah misheshet yimei bereishit* — this is a *mitzvah* of great importance and it derives from the six days of Creation.

### Divine Spirit Symbolism

*Tosafot* cites the *Yerushalmi* in connection with the reading of *Shoeva*: *shemisham shoavim Ruach HaKodesh, she'haShechina shorah mitoch Simcha* — from the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah* they drew the divine spirit, for the *Shechina* rests only amidst joy. The *Yerushalmi* derives this from the verse *vayehi kenagen hamenagen vatehi alav ruach Hashem* — and it was when the musician played that the spirit of God rested upon him — and from the story of Yona.

This symbolic reading is particularly valuable because the literal significance of water — as the essential ingredient of agricultural success — can be difficult for those outside *Eretz Yisrael* to feel viscerally. But the deeper symbolism connects powerfully to the spiritual arc of the season. Beginning from *Rosh Hashanah*, through *Yom Kippur*, into the *Sukkah* with its *ananei kavod*, the theme throughout has been the drawing of God's presence into our lives. The *Simchat Beit HaShoevah*, understood this way, is not merely joy in anticipation of rain — it is the joy of closeness to God, and that joy itself enables the *Shechina* to rest. The drawing of water becomes the drawing of divine spirit, and the *Simcha* is not only the response to blessing received but the very vehicle through which further blessing flows.

### Creation Motif

The connection to *sheishet yimei bereishit* deserves elaboration. *Rashi* explains that Rav Nachman refers to what was discussed the previous *daf* — that the underground caverns of the *Mikdash* (*shittin*) were created from the six days of Creation in order to receive the libations. This is somewhat curious, since those caverns primarily received the wine libations offered year-round, and the water libation was performed only during the one week of *Sukkot*. One might also note that the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah* would be held at most six nights — corresponding to *sheishet yimei bereishit*.

A broader reading presents itself as well. Way back at the beginning of the *masechet*, one of the derivations connecting the *s'chach* of the *Sukkah* to *ananei kavod* drew on the verse *v'eid ya'aleh min ha'aretz v'hishka et kol pnei ha'adamah* — the original mist that rose from the earth to water all of the ground in the story of *beriah*. The *Sukkah* and its associations with God's presence evoke not only the *midbar* experience but the primordial creative moment when God first brought water to the world. Water runs through creation from its very opening — *tohu vavohu*, earth and water, the mists of the beginning. The *Simchat Beit HaShoevah*, with its water motif, its joy at the renewal of the natural cycle, and its resonance with *beri'at ha'olam*, pulls all of this together: the beginning of a new year, the drawing of God's presence, and the celebration of the world as God created it.

---

## Musical Instruments

### Chalil on Shabbat

The *Gemara* now cites a *tannaitic* dispute: *hachalil docheh et haShabbat* — the *chalil* overrides *Shabbat* — *divrei Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda*. The *Chachamim* go further and say: *af Yom Tov eino docheh* — not only does it not override *Shabbat*, it does not override *Yom Tov* either. This appears to be the ruling of our *Mishna*.

### Rav Yosef Distinction

Rav Yosef clarifies what this dispute is actually about. It would be a mistake to think that anyone is suggesting the musical instruments of the *Simchat Beit HaShoevah* celebration — the all-night party — could override *Shabbat*. That was never on the table; it is simply *Simcha*, joy, and not an *avodah*, and no one disputes that it cannot override *Shabbat*. The debate, Rav Yosef says, concerns the *shir shel korban* — the song of the Levites that accompanied the wine libations of the communal obligatory sacrifices, namely the *tamid shel shachar*, the *tamid shel bein ha'arba'ayim*, and the *mussafin*. With every such sacrifice, at the moment of the pouring of the *nesachim*, the Levites would sing — this is the principle of *ein shira ela al ha'yayin*, that song is performed over wine, which is also the basis for performing *kiddush* and *havdalah* over wine. That song was accompanied by musical instruments. The question is whether those instruments, played at the time of the *korban*, constitute an *avodah* that overrides *Shabbat*.

### Ikar Shira Debate

Rav Yosef formulates the underlying issue: *ikar shira b'kli* — is the essence of the *shira* the musical instruments — or *ikar shira b'peh* — is the essence the vocal song, with instruments serving merely as accompaniment?

If *ikar shira b'kli*, then the musical instrument is the central *avodah* of the Levites, the *avodah* being the instrumental performance itself, and since it is an *avodah* it would override *Shabbat*. This is the position of Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda.

If *ikar shira b'peh*, then the primary *avodah* is the vocal song, and the instruments are ancillary. They are not the essential *avodah*, and therefore they do not override *Shabbat*. This is the position of the *Rabbanan*.

An important *halachic* note attaches here. The *Rambam* rules *ikar shira b'peh*, and this has a practical consequence: since the instrumental music is not the core *avodah*, it need not be performed exclusively by Levites. Even *Yisraelim* could participate in the instrumental music. By contrast, the *chatzotzrot* — the silver trumpets — which are explicitly commanded in the *Torah* (*u'v'yom simchatchem u'v'moadichem u'v'roshei chodsheichem u'tkatem bachatzotzrot*), are a full *Torah*-ordained *avodah* and are performed exclusively by *Kohanim*. The Levites' *avodah* in the *Mikdash*, after the era of the *Mishkan* (when they carried the *Mishkan*), consisted of two things: guarding the gates of the *Mikdash* and performing the *shir*. It is the nature of that *shir* — whether instrumental or vocal — that is in dispute.

*Tosafot* raises a difficulty here. The playing of musical instruments on *Shabbat* is ordinarily only a *rabbinic* prohibition — the concern being, for example, that one might come to fix the instrument. And we have the general principle of *ein shvut b'Mikdash* — rabbinic *Shabbat* concerns are set aside in the *Mikdash* for the sake of the *avodah*. If so, why would this be a serious debate at all? Even if the instruments are not strictly *ikar*, and even if playing them is only rabbinically prohibited, surely *ein shvut b'Mikdash* would resolve the question. *Tosafot* notes that other *Gemaras* seem to treat the playing of instruments in the *Mikdash* on *Shabbat* as a non-issue for precisely this reason, yet our *Gemara* treats it as a genuine *machloket*. This tension remains noteworthy.

### Wooden Vessels Link

Rav Yosef now explains the source for his interpretation of the *machloket* — namely, that it concerns the *shir shel korban* and the question of *ikar shira b'kli* or *b'peh*. He cites a *Baraita*: if one fashioned *klei shares* — service vessels of the *Mikdash* — from wood, Rabbi invalidates them and Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda declares them valid.

The connection Rav Yosef draws is as follows. The *chalil* used in the *Mikdash* — like all flutes — was made of wood or reed. It could not be coated with metal; other *Gemaras* state explicitly that the *Mikdash* flute was wooden. If the instrumental music is *ikar shira b'kli*, then those wooden instruments are *klei shares* — holy service vessels — and they demonstrate that wooden *klei shares* are valid. This is Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda's position: *man de'machshir savar ikar shira b'kli*, the one who validates wooden vessels holds that the instrumental music is the primary *avodah*, and the wooden musical instruments are themselves *klei shares*, thereby establishing that wooden *klei shares* are acceptable. *V'yalfinan me'avuva de'Moshe* — and we derive this from the flute that dates to the days of Moshe. *Rashi* explains: there was a flute in the *Mikdash* from the days of Moshe, a reed instrument, and they even sought at one point to plate it in gold — the very antiquity and sanctity of this wooden instrument grounds the principle.

Conversely, *man de'pasel savar ikar shira b'peh* — the one who invalidates wooden vessels holds that the *ikar avodah* of the Levites is the vocal song, not the instrumental music. Therefore the wooden instruments were never *klei shares* to begin with, and they provide no precedent. *Delo yalfinan me'avuva de'Moshe* — we do not derive from Moshe's flute.

### Impossible Cases Rule

The *Gemara* now offers a counterproposal: perhaps the two positions in the *machloket* need not map onto the question of *ikar shira b'kli* versus *b'peh* at all. Perhaps *everyone* agrees that *ikar shira b'kli* — the musical instruments are primary — and therefore everyone agrees that the wooden instruments of the Levites were *klei shares*. So what is the debate about wooden *klei shares*?

*D'hacha b'danin efshar mish'ee efshar kamiflagi* — here the dispute concerns the hermeneutic principle of whether one may learn from a case of *ee efshar* (no available alternative) to a case of *efshar* (where alternatives exist). The wooden musical instruments were made of wood *out of necessity* — the sonic properties required for the service could not be achieved with metal. This was a case of *ee efshar*: there was no alternative. One might argue that this necessity justified wooden *klei shares* in that specific context, but that this does not establish a general principle permitting wooden *klei shares* where metal could have been used instead.

*Man de'machshir* holds *danin efshar mish'ee efshar* — one may draw a legal principle from a case of no alternative and apply it to cases where alternatives exist. The wooden instruments teach that wooden *klei shares* are valid as a general rule. *Man de'pasel* holds *lo danin efshar mish'ee efshar* — a case that arose from necessity cannot set a precedent for cases where necessity is absent.

The *Gemara* then offers a further alternative: *v'ee ba'it eima d'kulei alma d'ikar shira b'peh v'ein danin efshar mish'ee efshar* — everyone could hold both that *ikar shira b'peh* and that one cannot derive from *ee efshar* to *efshar*. In this reading, the wooden musical instruments are not *klei shares* and the impossibility argument is irrelevant — yet there is still a debate about whether wooden *klei shares* can be derived. The source of *that* debate, the *Gemara* now says, is an entirely different question: how to apply hermeneutic principles to derive from the *Menorah* what materials are permissible for *klei shares*.

---

## Hermeneutics & Menorah

### Hermeneutic Methods

The *Gemara* now introduces the underlying dispute about hermeneutics as applied to the *Menorah*. The *Menorah* functions as the paradigm case for the permissible materials of *klei shares*. The question is: given the *Torah*'s description of the *Menorah*, what can be derived about other *klei shares*? And the answer depends entirely on which hermeneutic system one employs — *klal u'prat* or *ribuy u'miyut*.

### Klal U'Prat Structure

The *klal u'prat* system works as follows. When the *Torah* presents a general statement (*klal*) followed by a specific example (*prat*), the principle of *ein baklal ella mah shebaprat* applies: you limit the general to precisely what the specific contains. An illuminating example from *Parshat Ma'aser Sheni*: the *Torah* says *v'natata hakesef b'chol asher te'aveh nafshecha* — you may spend the money on whatever you desire — and then enumerates *bakar u'tzon v'yayin v'shachar* — cattle, sheep, wine, and strong drink — followed by *u'v'chol asher tishalecha nafshecha* — and whatever else you desire. At the *klal-prat* stage (general, then specific), the rule is: I said "anything," but what I really mean is the specific examples that follow. The opening "anything" does not mean literally anything; it is delimited by the *prat*.

When a second *klal* follows, yielding the structure of *klal u'prat u'klal*, the rule shifts: you may include anything *similar* to the *prat*. The first *klal* says "anything," the *prat* gives examples, and the second *klal* says "really anything" — but the combination means: anything that resembles the specific examples. You can serve hamburgers or chicken; you cannot serve tofu salad, which is completely different in kind. The result is *ke'ein haprat* — like the *prat*, similar in character to what was specified.

### Ribuy U'Miyut Approach

*Ribuy u'miyut* operates by a different logic. Here the terms are not *klal* (general/specifying) and *prat* (specific), but *ribuy* (inclusive/expanding) and *miyut* (limiting). The crucial difference is that whereas *prat* is specific, *miyut* is merely limiting without being fully specific. This means that at the *ribuy-miyut* stage (the equivalent of the two-step *klal-prat*), one already arrives at the conclusion that the *ribuy u'miyut* system only reaches at the three-step level. That is, a single *miyut* already implies "anything like the example given," not "only exactly the example." When a second *ribuy* follows (*ribuy u'miyut u'ribuy*), the result is all-inclusive except for something completely different in kind. Where *klal u'prat u'klal* produced "anything similar to the *prat*," *ribuy u'miyut u'ribuy* produces "anything except what is entirely unlike."

### Menorah Application

How does this play out with the *Menorah*? The relevant verses present: *ve'asita menorat* (and you shall make a *menorah*) — *klal* / *ribuy* — followed by *zahav tahor* (pure gold) — *prat* / *miyut* — followed by *mikshah tei'aseh hamenorah* (it shall be hammered work, the *menorah* shall be made) — which reopens the general.

Rabbi uses *klal u'prat*. *Ve'asita menorat* is *klal*, *zahav tahor* is *prat*, *mikshah tei'aseh hamenorah* is a second *klal* — giving *klal u'prat u'klal*. The rule: anything similar to the *prat*. The *prat* is gold — *mah haprat meforash shel matechet, af kol shel matechet* — since gold is a metal, anything similar must also be a metal. The *Menorah* could be made of any metal, and by extension, *klei shares* must be metallic. Wood is excluded.

Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda uses *ribuy u'miyut*. *Ve'asita menorat* is *ribuy*, *zahav tahor* is *miyut*, *mikshah tei'aseh hamenorah* is a second *ribuy* — giving *ribuy u'miyut u'ribuy*. The rule: anything except what is completely unlike. The *miyut* of gold means gold is the example, but the *ribuy u'miyut* structure already implies "anything like gold" at stage one — meaning metal in general. The final *ribuy* then expands further to include anything at all, with the only exclusion being something entirely different in kind. *Mai mi'et? Mi'et shel cheres* — the only thing excluded is pottery. Wood, however, is not so completely unlike metal as to be excluded, and therefore wooden *klei shares* are valid.

This hermeneutic dispute, then, is entirely independent of the question of *ikar shira b'kli* or *b'peh*, and independent of the question of *danin efshar mish'ee efshar*. It provides a third possible basis on which the debate about wooden *klei shares* could rest — one grounded purely in the methodology of *Torah* interpretation.

---

---

# Sukkah 51

## Ikar Shira: Song or Music

### Opening Debate

The daf begins at the very bottom of 50b, picking up a discussion about whether one may play musical instruments — specifically the *chalil*, the flute — on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*. There is a three-way dispute among *Tannaim*: Rabbi Yose, Rabbi Yehuda, and the *Chachamim*. The initial framing attributed to Rabbi Yose is that the debate concerns the musical instruments played in accompaniment to the *korban* — the daily sacrificial service — and whether this music may be performed even on *Shabbos*. The crux of that question is how central the instrumental music is to the *avodah* of the *Levi'im* relative to their vocal singing. By contrast, when it comes to the musical instruments played during the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* — the nocturnal water-drawing celebration of *Sukkot* — everyone agrees that this constitutes mere *simcha* and may not be performed on *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*. The use of the phrase *docheh es haShabbos* is itself somewhat striking, since what is at stake is a rabbinic prohibition against playing musical instruments; the language of overriding *Shabbos* in such a context is notable and worth bearing in mind.

### Rav Papa's Theory

Rav Papa, whose statement spans the last three words of 50b and continues to the top of 51a, reframes the question. He says *k'tannai* — this dispute between *Amora'im* about whether *ikar shirah b'peh* or *ikar shirah b'kli*, whether the primary *shira* accompanying the *korban* is the vocal singing or the instrumental music, is itself mirrored in a prior *Tannaitic* debate. His reading invites us to look at a *Mishnah* that asks not who sang but who actually played the instruments.

### Who Played Music

The *Mishnah* records three opinions. Rabbi Meir says the instrument players were *avdei Kohanim* — slaves of *Kohanim*. Rabbi Yose says they were from two named families, *mishpachat Beit Hapgaram* and *mishpachat Beit Tzipparya*, from a place called Ammaum — families of distinguished *Yisraelim* who, though not *Kohanim* themselves, were of such good *yichus* that *Kohanim* would seek to marry their widowed women. Rashi notes that these were *mishpachot meyuchasot* of *Yisrael*. Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says they were *Levi'im*. This last position is the one most people naturally assume when they picture the Temple service — yet it is only one of three opinions.

Rav Papa suggests these opinions map onto the halakhic dispute: the one who says they were slaves (*avdim*) presumably holds that *ikar shirah b'peh* — since if instrumental music were the primary *avodah*, one could hardly permit slaves to perform it, and so the music was secondary enough to allow for that. The one who says they were *Levi'im* holds *ikar shirah b'kli* — instrumental music is itself the core Levitical service and therefore could only be performed by *Levi'im*.

### Consensus on Vocal Prima…

The *Gemara* challenges this neat alignment. It asks what Rabbi Yose's position — that they were distinguished families of *Yisraelim* — actually implies about *ikar shirah*. If he holds *ikar shirah b'peh*, then he should have no reason to object to slaves performing the music; if he holds *ikar shirah b'kli*, then he should require *Levi'im*, not merely distinguished *Yisraelim*. Neither option explains his middle position. The *Gemara* concludes that the three opinions cannot be a debate about halakhic principle at all: *tisbra* — does that really make sense?

Rather, says the *Gemara* — *ela* — the debate is one of historical fact. And if that is so, the very possibility of the debate reveals something important: for it to be factually possible that the instrument players were slaves or *Yisraelim*, everyone must agree that *ikar shirah b'peh* — the primary Levitical *avodah* was the singing, not the instruments. Only under that assumption could someone credibly report that non-*Levi'im* played the instruments. Hence: *de-kulei alma ikar shira b'peh* — all *Tannaim* concede that the primary service of the *Levi'im* was vocal. What they dispute is purely factual — *de-mar savar hachi havei ma'aseh u-mar savar hachi havei ma'aseh* — one says it happened this way, another says it happened that way.

This leads naturally to a wry observation. Talmudic *Tannaim* were not historians. Why do we care about a factual dispute? The answer is that facts carry halakhic weight.

One might further note how quickly historical memory can erode. Rabbi Meir was a student of Rabbi Akiva, meaning these discussions took place roughly a hundred years after the destruction. The instrument players' identities were already a matter of competing oral traditions. Whatever one's grandfather reported, another's grandfather may have reported something different.

### Nafka Mina: Status

The *Gemara* asks: *le-mai nafka mina* — what practical difference does this factual dispute make? The answer is: *le-ma'alin mi-duchan le-yuchasin u-le-ma'aser* — the implications concern whether one may draw conclusions from the fact that someone stood on the *duchan*. The *duchan* was the platform where the *Levi'im* performed; here the question is not about singing but about playing instruments. If one witnessed someone playing a musical instrument on the *duchan*, can one conclude anything about his status — either in terms of *yuchasin* (eligibility to marry into his family) or *ma'aser* (whether one may give him tithes on the assumption that he is a *Levi*)?

The three positions yield three different answers. The one who says they were slaves (*avdim*) holds *ein ma'alin mi-duchan le-yuchasin ve-lo le-ma'aser* — you cannot infer anything from having seen someone play the instrument; he may well have been a slave. The one who says they were distinguished *Yisraelim* holds *ma'alin mi-duchan le-yuchasin aval lo le-ma'aser* — you may infer that he is of good lineage and suitable for marriage, but you may not give him *ma'aser*, as he is not necessarily a *Levi*. The one who says they were *Levi'im* holds *ma'alin mi-duchan bein le-yuchasin bein le-ma'aser* — you may infer both *yuchasin* and *Levi* status from his having played on the *duchan*.

This is a useful reminder that knowing facts matters even when the underlying *halakhah* is clear. The *halakhah* — that anyone could play the instruments, since *ikar shirah b'peh* — is agreed upon. But who actually stood there historically determines what status we attribute to a person seen performing. The *Rambam* rules accordingly: *ikar shirah b'peh*, and non-*Levi'im* could indeed have played the instruments.

---

## Shir Sho'eva vs. Shir Ko…

### Yirmiya's Distinction

The *Gemara* now presents a different approach attributed to Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba. Rather than framing the debate about playing instruments on *Shabbos* as a question about the *korban*'s music, Rabbi Yirmiya bar Abba says: *machloket b'shir shel sho'eva* — the entire dispute is about the music accompanying the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva*, not about the music that accompanies the *korban* itself.

### Simcha Yeterah Debate

On this reading, Rabbi Yosef bar Yehuda holds *simcha yeteira nami docha et haShabbos* — even the "extra rejoicing" of the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva*, rooted in the verse *ushavtem mayim b'sasson*, is of sufficient religious weight that it may be practiced on *Shabbos* within the *Beit Hamikdash*. The *Rabbanan* disagree: *simcha yeteira eino docha et haShabbos* — additional joy of this kind does not permit the playing of musical instruments on *Shabbos*.

### Korban Override

On one point, however, all agree: *aval b'shir shel korban divrei hakol avoda hi v'docha et haShabbos* — when it comes to the music that accompanies the actual *korbanot*, everyone agrees that this constitutes *avodah* and therefore overrides *Shabbos*. The musical instruments may be played together with the *korbanot* even on *Shabbos*, according to all opinions.

### Reconciling Premises

A careful reader will immediately notice a tension. Just moments ago the *Gemara* seemed to firmly conclude that *ikar shirah b'peh* — the primary service was vocal, and instrumental music was secondary enough that even slaves or *Yisraelim* could perform it. Now the *Gemara* asserts that everyone agrees the instrumental music accompanying the *korban* constitutes *avodah* and overrides *Shabbos*. If the instruments were so peripheral that their performance was entrusted to slaves, how can they simultaneously be an *avodah* that overrides *Shabbos*?

### Three Explanations

Three approaches address this tension.

The first explanation is that the language *avoda hi* should not be taken too literally. Since playing musical instruments on *Shabbos* is in any case only a rabbinic prohibition, there is no great jurisprudential obstacle to permitting it when it accompanies a *korban*. It is not so much that the instruments constitute a formal *avodah* of the highest order; rather, their connection to the *korban* service is close enough that the rabbinic restriction yields.

The second explanation, a variation on the first, draws a distinction between incorporation and primacy. Even if the instruments are not the *ikar* of the service, when they are actually performed at the time of the *korban* they become absorbed into the *avodah* in a meaningful way — unlike the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* music, which, however joyful, is preparatory or collateral to the *avodah*. The temporal and functional proximity to the *korban* lends the instrumental music enough *avodah* character to override the rabbinic restriction.

The third explanation is the most intriguing and is implicit in the *Rambam*. The *Rambam* distinguishes between two categories of Temple music. The ordinary orchestral instruments accompanying the daily *korbanot* are not themselves an *avodah* and need not be performed by *Levi'im* — this is precisely what flows from *ikar shirah b'peh*. However, on *Yamim Tovim* and *Rosh Chodesh* there is a biblical *mitzvah* to sound the *chatzotzrot*, the trumpets, and that *mitzvah* can only be performed by *Kohanim*. The *Rambam* draws on this to explain a further category: specifically on *Yom Tov* — not on *Rosh Chodesh* — the *chalil* was added to the Temple orchestra. This *chalil* was not part of the ordinary daily music; it was a special instrument used only on *Yom Tov*, and the *Rambam* rules that it constituted an *avodah* proper to the *Levi'im* alone, modeled on the logic of the *chatzotzrot*.

This reading of the *Rambam* raises a fascinating corollary. The name of the entire *perek* is *Hechalil*, and the *chalil* surfaces throughout as an instrument of special significance. If the *Rambam*'s position is followed strictly, it may mean not merely that the *chalil* was added to an existing orchestra on *Yom Tov*, but that on *Yom Tov* only the *chalil* — with its special *avodah* status — was played, while the ordinary orchestral instruments that required no particular *avodah* status were not used on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* at all. That would be a rather different image of the Temple service on sacred days. Thus when the *Gemara* says that the instrumental music accompanying the *korban* overrides *Shabbos*, it may specifically mean this *Yom Tov chalil* with its full *avodah* status, not the general orchestra of the daily service.

The *Gemara* then records a *baraita* stating explicitly: *shir shel sho'eva docha et haShabbos divrei Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda — ve-Chachamim omrim af Yom Tov eino doche* — confirming that the *Tannaitic* debate was indeed about the music of the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva*. This directly contradicts Rav Yosef's earlier framing that the debate was about the music of the *korban*. The *Gemara* declares *tiyuvta de-Rav Yosef tiyuvta* — a decisive refutation of Rav Yosef on both counts. The *Mishnah*'s language *zehu chalil shel beit hashoeva she'eino doche lo et haShabbos ve-lo et haYom Tov* — "this is the flute of the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* that overrides neither *Shabbos* nor *Yom Tov*" — implies a contrast: *aval de-korban doche* — the flute of the *korban* does override *Shabbos*. And the attribution of this *Mishnah* to the *Rabbanan* — who hold that the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* music does not override *Shabbos* — shows that even the *Rabbanan* agree the *korban* music overrides *Shabbos*, contradicting Rav Yosef's claim that they debated that question too.

Rav Yosef's response would have been that the *Tannaim* debate both: they focused their *machloket* on the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* in order to show the strength of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position — *lehodia kocho* — that he permits instrument playing even for the *sho'eva*, not only for the *korban*. But the *Gemara* reads the *Mishnah* as not supporting this reconciliation, and the *tiyuvta* stands.

In summary: the three explanations for how *ikar shirah b'peh* coexists with the permissibility of playing instruments with the *korban* on *Shabbos* remain on the table — the *d'rabanan* leniency argument, the incorporation argument, and the *Rambam*'s unique status for the *Yom Tov chalil*.

---

## Simchat Beit Hasho'eva

### Unsurpassable Joy

The *Mishnah* opens with a sweeping declaration: *mi shelo ra'ah simchat beit hasho'eva lo ra'ah simcha miyamav* — one who never witnessed the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* has never in his life truly seen joy. What follows is a vivid account of a nightlong celebration of extraordinary sensory and spiritual intensity.

One detail in the opening merits passing attention. The *Mishnah* states that the celebration took place *b'motzei Yom Tov ha-rishon shel chag* — following the conclusion of the first day of *Yom Tov*. This is consistent with the earlier discussion: since playing musical instruments on *Yom Tov* was contested, and since even carrying the water on *Shabbos* would be impermissible, the celebration as a full event — with music and procession — could not begin until the first *Yom Tov* had ended. The *Mishnah* makes clear that without the music, there was no party. The celebration began only once the instruments could be brought out.

### Golden Candelabras

The celebration was set in the *Ezrat Nashim* — the Women's Courtyard — which functioned as something of a great hall, the gathering space before entry into the inner *azara*. The *Mishnah* describes a *tikkun gadol* — a major installation — prepared there for the occasion.

*Menorot shel zahav hayu sham* — there were great golden candelabras set up in the courtyard. These were not the *Menorah* of the *Heichal*, but large candelabras clearly evocative of it. At the top of each were four golden bowls — *arba'ah sefalim shel zahav b'rosheihem* — and leading up to each bowl were four ladders — *arba'ah sulamot l'chol echad ve-echad*. Young *Kohanim* — described as *yeladim mipirchei kehunah*, whether boys or young men — would ascend with pitchers of oil. The *Mishnah* states each pitcher held 120 *log*. A *log* is approximately 12 to 14 ounces, which puts each pitcher at somewhere around 13 to 15 gallons — a figure that strains credulity as a literal description of what a young person could carry up a ladder. It is best understood as a stylized or aggregate figure for the total oil consumed per bowl over the course of the night.

The wicks for these lamps were made *mi-blaei michnesei Kohanim u-mehemeihem* — from the worn-out trousers and belts of the *Kohanim*, from which strips were torn and fashioned into wicks. From these they would kindle the great bowls of oil.

### City Lit Up

The result of this illumination was dramatic: *v'lo hayah chatzer bi-Yerushalayim she-eina me'ira me-or beit hasho'eva* — there was not a single courtyard in all of Jerusalem that was not lit up by the light emanating from the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva*. The scale of the light, emanating from the Temple Mount outward across the entire city, must have been breathtaking.

### Dance and Music

The *Mishnah* then describes the celebration itself. *Chasidim va-anshei ma'aseh hayu merakdim bifneihem* — pious men and men of great deeds would dance before the assembled crowds, *va-avukot shel or she-b'yadeihem* — with torches of fire in their hands, *ve-omrim lifneihem divrei tishbachot* — singing praises and songs as they performed.

Rashi offers a charming aside on the phrase *avukot shel or*, describing in detail what juggling with torches looks like: you throw them up into the air and catch them, and those skilled in the art could do so with four or eight torches simultaneously, throwing one while catching another. The *chasidim* and *anshei ma'aseh* who led this performance were thus engaged in a physically impressive display of fire-juggling while simultaneously singing praises.

The *Levi'im* accompanied them with every manner of instrument: *b'chinorot u-vinvalim u-v'metziltayim u-v'chatzotzrot u-v'chelei shir v'lo mispar* — with harps, lyres, cymbals, trumpets, and instruments beyond counting. They stood *al chamisha asar ma'alot ha-yordot me-Ezrat Yisrael l'Ezrat Nashim* — on the fifteen steps descending from the *Ezrat Yisrael* to the *Ezrat Nashim*, steps corresponding to the fifteen *Shirei Hama'alot*, the Songs of Ascent in *Tehillim*.

A clarification is in order about the spatial arrangement. The *Levi'im* standing on these fifteen steps for the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* were not standing on the *duchan* — the platform from which they would sing and play during the *korban* service. Rashi is explicit on this point: the place where the *Levi'im* stood for the *korban* was a different location. One should not conflate the festive nocturnal celebration in the *Ezrat Nashim* with the formal *avodah* of the *korban* that took place in the inner courtyard.

### Trumpet Proclamation

At daybreak — when the rooster crowed — two *Kohanim* stationed at the upper gate leading from the *Ezrat Yisrael* down to the *Ezrat Nashim* held trumpets in their hands. *Kara ha-gever* — the cock crowed — and they sounded *teki'ah teru'ah teki'ah*. The sequence of *teki'ah teru'ah teki'ah* had already appeared earlier in the tractate in multiple contexts: accompanying the pouring of the water libation, and accompanying the *aravah* ceremony on *Hoshana Rabba*. Here it marked the transition from the nightlong celebration to the morning procession — the moment when the assembled crowd began to move from the *Ezrat Nashim* toward the Shiloach spring to draw the water that would be poured on the *mizbe'ach*.

### Procession Declaration

The procession moved downward, with the trumpeters sounding *teki'ah teru'ah teki'ah* again at the tenth step, and again upon reaching the floor of the *Ezrat Nashim*. They then continued — still sounding the trumpet sequence — until they reached *sha'ar ha-yotzei mi-mizrach*, the easternmost gate of the *Ezrat Nashim*, from which they would descend off the Temple Mount and make their way to the Shiloach.

At that eastern gate, they turned. *Hafchu pneihem mi-mizrach le-ma'arav* — they turned their faces from east back toward the west, facing the *Beit Hamikdash*.

### Avoteinu Statement

Standing at the eastern gate and facing the Temple, they made the following declaration: *avoteinu she-hayu ba-makom ha-zeh achoreihem el ha-Heichal u-fneihem kedma ve-hem mishtachavim kedma la-shemesh* — our ancestors who stood in this very place during the era of the First Temple had their backs to the *Heichal* and their faces to the east, bowing down to the sun. This is an allusion to the sin of the *ovdei avodah zarah* described in *Tanach*, who would worship the sun by turning away from the Temple. *Va-anu l'Yah eineinu* — but we, our eyes are to God.

Rabbi Yehuda adds that they would repeat this declaration: *anu l'Yah u-l'Yah eineinu* — we are to God, and to God are our eyes.

This moment is striking. Why, in the middle of a joyous water-drawing procession, would the participants evoke the sin of their ancestors? It is not a simple declaration of faith; it is a pointed narrative contrast — we are not what our ancestors once were. The structure has a parallel to the *Haggadah*, which similarly brings the shame of ancestors into a moment of celebration: *mitchilah ovdei avodah zarah hayu avoteinu*. Here too, a narrative of contrast is embedded in the ritual itself, making the joy all the more conscious of what it is rejecting.

---

## Comparative Splendor

### Marble Like Waves

Having described the glory of the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva*, the *Gemara* transitions into a broader meditation on things of unsurpassable beauty. A *Baraita* extends the earlier declaration of the *Mishnah*: just as one who never saw the *Simchat Beit Hasho'eva* has never seen real joy, so too one who never saw Jerusalem in its glory — *lo ra'ah krach nechmad me'olam* — has never seen a truly magnificent city. And one who never saw the *Beit Hamikdash be-vinyano* — in its built state — has never seen a truly magnificent building.

The *Gemara* then asks: *mai hi* — what specifically was so beautiful? The answer, attributed to Abaye or alternatively Rav Chisda, is that the reference is to the Second Temple as renovated by Herod: *zeh binyan Hordus*. And what materials did Herod use? *Be-avnei shaisha u-marmara* — with marble, alternating in and out, jutting and recessed in such a way that the surface could accept plaster where needed. Herod apparently considered then gilding the façade with gold. The rabbis who were consulted — an interesting detail in itself, that the rabbis were advising Herod directly — told him: *shabkieh*, leave it. *De-hachi shapir tfei* — it is more beautiful this way. *De-michzei ke-advata de-yama* — it looks like the waves of the sea. The alternating white and darker marble, jutting in and out, produced a visual effect of undulating waves, at once beautiful and serene. According to the tradition, that was apparently the one time Herod followed rabbinic advice.

### Alexandria Synagogue

Rabbi Yehuda in the *Baraita* adds a comparable institution to the list: *mi shelo ra'ah dyoplostin shel Alexandriya shel Mitzrayim lo ra'ah be-chivodan shel Yisrael* — one who never saw the great *dyoplostin* of Alexandria in Egypt has never seen the glory of Israel. The word *dyoplostin* is a Greek term indicating a double colonnade — Rashi explains it as some form of vast coliseum or double-porticoed structure. What is notable about Rabbi Yehuda's formulation is that he does not say "you have never seen a magnificent building" but "you have never seen the *kivod* of Israel" — the grandeur, the collective honor, of the Jewish people. The building was impressive, but the statement is about what it represented as a gathering of Jews.

The *Gemara* describes it: *ke-min basilki gedola hayta* — it was like a great Basilica, *stav lifnim mi-stav* — a double colonnade or stoa. The population figures given are hyperbolic in the extreme — the *girsa* of *shishim ribo al shishim ribo* yields an impossibly vast number, and the more plausible reading is *kiflayim ke-yotzei Mitzrayim*, double the number of those who left Egypt — that is, approximately 1.2 million Jews in the synagogue. Even this figure is remarkable, and one should read it as expressing the sense of an incomprehensibly vast gathering rather than a precise census.

Within this structure were seventy-one golden thrones — *ayin-alef katedra'ot shel zahav* — corresponding to the seventy-one members of the *Sanhedrin*, each throne reportedly not less than twenty-one *kikarim* (talents) of gold, a figure that the *Gemara* likewise reads as hyperbolic. The architecture of the institution thus mirrored the architecture of Jewish governance: the community of Israel, represented by its scholars, seated in golden dignity.

### Flag Signaling

At the center of this enormous structure stood a wooden *bimah* — *bimah shel etz be-emtzayita* — and the *chazzan ha-knesset*, the sexton or attendant of the synagogue, stood upon it. Here *chazzan* does not mean the prayer leader but the functionary responsible for the logistics of the service. He held flags — *sudarim* — in his hands. The problem he was solving was straightforward: in a building so vast that one could not hear the *chazan* leading the prayers, how would the congregation know when to respond *amen*? His solution was to wave the flags at the appropriate moment — *hala menif be-sudar* — and upon seeing the signal, *ve-chol ha-am onim amen*, the entire assembly would respond in unison. The architecture demanded innovation; the innovation allowed the community to function as one despite the distances involved.

### Occupational Seating

The seating arrangement in this enormous synagogue was not random. *Ve-lo hayu yoshvim me'uravim* — they did not sit mixed together. Rather, each trade sat in its own section: *zehavim bifnei atzman* — goldsmiths together, *kesafim bifnei atzman* — silversmiths together, *nafachim bifnei atzman* — ironsmiths together, *tarsiyim bifnei atzman* — coppersmiths together, *gardiyim bifnei atzman* — weavers together.

The practical purpose was economic networking.
