A craftsman newly arrived in Alexandria — or a craftsman's son seeking an apprenticeship or a business connection — could enter the synagogue, identify the section of his trade, and find the people he needed. *Ve-chol ha-am onim amen* gave way to a social function: *misham parnasato u-farnasat anshei beito* — from there came his livelihood and the livelihood of his household. The synagogue was simultaneously a house of prayer, a gathering of the community, and a center of commerce and *parnasah*. This is not a modern innovation; it is described here as an ancient and celebrated feature of one of the greatest Jewish communities in the ancient world. The *beit knesset* — the gathering place — was conceived as a place of gathering in every dimension.

---

## Alexandria's Destruction

### Community Wiped Out

Abaye then delivers the devastating coda: *ve-kulhu katlinu* — they were all wiped out. The text as it stands names Alexander of Macedonia (*Alexandros Mokdon*), but this is clearly a scribal difficulty: Alexander the Great had no role in massacring Egyptian Jews, and chronologically the dates do not align by several centuries. Marginal notes in manuscripts cross out *Mokdon*, and various authorities, including Steinsaltz, identify the Roman general responsible as Trajan. The *Gra*'s *girsa* reads Trajan as well. Others suggest Severus. What is not in dispute is that the community — however vast and glorious — was destroyed by Roman imperial violence.

### Returning to Egypt

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama i'enshu* — why were they punished? One might expect the answer to invoke the community's well-documented Hellenization or religious laxity. What the *Gemara* actually says is more pointed: *mishum de-avru a-hai kra* — they transgressed the verse: *lo tosifun lashuv baderech hazeh od* — you shall not return this way again. By settling in Egypt following the Exodus, they violated the Torah's explicit prohibition. *Ve-innu hadur* — and yet they returned. The punishment, on this reading, was a direct consequence of ignoring the Torah's warning against Egyptian settlement — a warning addressed to Israel at the moment of its founding as a people.

### Verse Omen

The account closes with a striking anecdote. When the Roman general arrived — ahead of schedule, his ten-day sea journey having taken only five days due to favorable winds — he encountered a child in the community reading aloud from a *sefer*. The verse the child happened to be reading was: *yisa Hashem alecha goy merachok* — God will bring upon you a nation from afar. The general reflected: *hahu gavra* — this man, meaning himself, *ba'ei l'meiti sefinta b'asara yomei, ve-dalyei zika ve-ati sefinta b'chamsha yomei* — was supposed to arrive in ten days, and yet favorable wind brought him in five. He understood this as a *siman min ha-shamayim* — a heavenly sign — that God was directing him to this place to fulfill the verse's warning. *Nafal alaive ve-katleinu* — he fell upon them and slaughtered them.

The juxtaposition is deeply unsettling: a child's voice reading scripture serves as the omen that seals the community's fate. The same Torah that had warned them not to return to Egypt now, in the mouth of one of their own children, announces the arrival of the instrument of their destruction.

---

---

# Sukkah 52

## Ezrat Nashim & Mechitzah

### Overview

Daf 52 covers two major topics. The first is a *gemara* that has been used classically — and in more recent periods with particular intensity — as the primary basis for the requirement of a *mechitzah* in a *shul*. The remainder of the *daf* constitutes an extended *agadata* centered on the concept of *yetzer hara*, touching on its nature, its names, its strategies, and ultimately its messianic defeat.

### Tikun Gadol

The *gemara* begins seven lines from the bottom of 51b. The *mishnah* states that on the night following *Yom Tov*, they would enter the *Ezrat Nashim* and perform a *tikun gadol* — a great fixing-up — in preparation for the *Simchat Beit Hashoeva* celebrations, which would take place at night and continue into the following morning when the water was drawn from the well.

The *gemara* asks: *mai tikun gadol* — what exactly was this great arrangement? Rabbi Eleazar answers by citing a *mishnah* in *Middot*: originally, the *azara* — the *Ezrat Nashim* — was flat and smooth. Then they surrounded it with a *gazustra* and instituted that women should sit above and men below. This, it turns out, was the first balcony arrangement in Jewish communal life.

### Gazustra Interpretation

There is an interesting debate, based on the *Rambam* in *Peirush Hamishnayot* and others, about precisely what the *gazustra* was and what *milmala umilmata* — above and below — means in practice. One might ask: if the arrangement involved women sitting above, that clearly suggests a balcony. But the *mishnah* is contrasting this with the fact that the floor had previously been smooth and flat. Building a balcony does not make the floor unflat — you could support it with poles — so the description seems to be pointing at something else.

*Rashi* explains that the walls had previously been smooth, and they then fashioned protrusions from the walls to support a balcony — the *gazustra* being these wall-projections. Steinsaltz notes that the word derives from a Greek term for a projection from the side of a building upon which boards are laid, which aligns with *Rashi*'s reading. Others, however — and the *Rambam* in *Peirush Hamishnayot* seems to lean in this direction — suggest that it was less a suspended balcony and more a raised platform on the floor, behind which women would stand. Why a raised platform rather than a balcony? Perhaps so that women standing behind a barrier could still see what was happening. In any case, the plain meaning of *milmala umilmata* most naturally points to a balcony arrangement.

### Separation Progression

The *gemara* then cites a *Tana* teaching that describes the progression of separation arrangements. Originally, *barishona hayu nashim mibifnim veanashim mibachutz* — women were on the inside and men on the outside. *Rashi* suggests that "outside" might mean outside the *Ezrat Nashim* entirely, on the *Har Habayit* itself. But *vehayu baim lidei kalut rosh* — this arrangement led to levity, to inappropriate mixing and heightened sexual tension. So they reversed it: women outside, men inside. Yet *ve'adayin hayu baim lidei kalut rosh* — even that still led to frivolity. Finally, they instituted that women sit entirely above and men below, which completely prevented interaction.

### Authority Question

This raises a striking question: *heichi avid hachi* — how could they do this? Does not the verse say *hakol bichsav miyad Hashem alai hiskil* — that everything about the construction of the *Beit Hamikdash* was revealed from God's hand, as King David declared when transmitting the plans for the *Beit Hamikdash*? Admittedly, this question carries several complications: that verse refers to the *Beit Rishon*, whereas this is the *Beit Sheni*; the *Beit Sheni* already differed substantially from the *Beit Rishon* in many respects; and the *Ezrat Nashim* is not technically part of the *Beit Hamikdash* proper. But whatever the precise contours of the question, the *gemara* proceeds to provide an answer.

### Kal Vachomer Argument

Rav answers: *kra ashkechu v'darash* — they found a *pasuk* and explicated it to justify the modification. The verse is from *Zechariah*, in a prophecy about the war of Armageddon: *veSafda ha'aretz mishpachot mishpachot levad* — the land will eulogize, family by family, separately. And specifically: *mishpachat beit David levad u'nesheihem levad* — the family of the house of David separately, and their wives separately. Within each family, men and women mourn apart.

From this, the Sages constructed a *kal v'chomer*: *u'mah le'atid lavo she'oskim b'hesped* — in the future time, when everyone is occupied with mourning, *v'ein yetzer hara sholet bahem* — and the *yetzer hara* does not have dominion over them. This could mean simply that at a time of tragedy and grief, sexual desire naturally subsides. But *Rashi* adds a second dimension: since this is a messianic vision, it is a time in history when the *yetzer hara* will have been eliminated entirely. And yet, *amra Torah anashim levad v'nashim levad* — even then, the Torah requires men and women to be separate.

*Al achat kama v'kama* — how much more so in the present, when *she'oskim b'simcha* — people are engaged in joy and festivity, which heightens desire and leads to frivolity, and when *yetzer hara sholet bahem* — the *yetzer hara* is very much operative. This was their justification for implementing the separation.

### Modern Mechitzah Practice

This *gemara* has become, in halachic literature of recent centuries, one of the primary textual bases for the requirement of a *mechitzah* between men and women during *davening*. It is worth noting something striking: there is no explicit statement anywhere in the *gemara* that a *mechitzah* is required during *davening*, nor any explicit statement that men and women were mixed during *davening*, nor any explicit statement that they were separated. The historical evidence for the practice dates from the time of the *Geonim* onward, where separate seating appears simply to have been taken for granted and required no justification. The need to articulate and defend the requirement arose later.

The issue first became contested in the period of the *Chatam Sofer*, even before the Reform movement had introduced mixed seating. Mixed seating appears, in fact, to have originated in America — the Albany congregation being a commonly cited early example, rather than in early European Reform communities. When the *Chatam Sofer* addressed the topic — initially in the context of a question about a mixed choir to be presented before the Czar in Saint Petersburg, which led into a broader discussion of *kol b'isha erva* and the separation of the sexes — this *gemara* became a central source.

There are, however, real difficulties in using this *gemara* as the proof-text for a *mechitzah* during *davening*. The argument cuts in two opposing directions simultaneously. On one hand, it seems too narrow: the concern here is with an atmosphere of festivity and frivolity — *Simchat Beit Hashoeva* — which might suggest the requirement applies only in such contexts, not during the solemnity of prayer. But then the *gemara* itself counters this by constructing the *kal v'chomer* from the scene of mourning, when there is no such frivolity and when the *yetzer hara* is absent — and still men and women are separate. That makes the argument too broad: it would require separation at all times and in all contexts. How one derives specifically the middle position — that separation is required during *davening* but not universally — is genuinely unclear from this *gemara* alone.

The question of *what kind* of separation is also illuminated by this source. The *gemara* presents two models: the balcony and the side-by-side separation. If a balcony ultimately suffices — and that is indeed what was instituted in the end — then the concern is with intermingling and physical contact, not with visual separation, since from a balcony one can see perfectly well. If, on the other hand, the relevant model is the side-by-side division with a wall, then perhaps sight itself is the concern. The plain sense of this *gemara* strongly underscores the intermingling concern, and this has significant implications for how one understands the nature and purpose of *mechitzah* requirements derived from this source.

### Yetzer Hara Development

Before proceeding further into the *sugya*, it is worth pausing on the association already present in the *gemara* between *kalut rosh* — levity — and *yetzer hara* in the context of the mixing of men and women. This raises a broader question about what exactly *yetzer hara* means and how it has been understood across rabbinic periods. A careful reading of the literature suggests that our instinctive contemporary understanding — that *yetzer hara* is an internalized psychological drive, often primarily associated with sexual desire, to be contrasted with the *yetzer hatov* — may not reflect the earlier, Tannaitic conception.

The phrase *yetzer hara sholet bahem* — the *yetzer hara* has dominion over them — is itself ambiguous. Is *sholet* describing an internal dominion, or something more like a demonic external force that exercises power over us from outside? The earlier understanding may have been closer to the latter: an external enticement toward evil, not specifically associated with appetitive desire, akin to a demonic power that tempts human beings to sin. The shift toward the internalized, psychological model — the *yetzer hara* as one's own drives and inclinations, powerful energies that can be channeled for good or ill — appears to develop over time.

As this image from the prophecy of *Kayin* illustrates — *lappetach chatat roveitz, ve-atah timshol bo* — the *yetzer hara* is depicted crouching at the entrance, an external, almost animal force, yet one that the human being is capable of mastering. As we read through the rest of the *daf*, this interplay between the external and internal models will be visible throughout.

---

## Mashiach ben Yosef vs Ye…

### Eulogy Identity Debate

The *gemara* now identifies the subject of the mourning described in *Zechariah*. *Peligei bah Rabbi Dosa veRabbanan* — Rabbi Dosa and the Rabbis debate whose eulogy this is. One view says: *mashiach ben Yosef sheneharg* — it is the mourning over *Mashiach ben Yosef* who was killed. The concept of *Mashiach ben Yosef* does not appear explicitly in any single canonical source, but it is a well-developed Rabbinic understanding. Based on the verse *vehayah beit Yosef eish uveit Yaakov lehavah vehayah Eisav lekash* — the house of *Yosef* compared to a fire — the Rabbis understand that the leader who will go to war against the enemies of Israel in the eschatological battle will be from the house of *Yosef*, a figure known as *Mashiach ben Yosef*. He will die in that war, after which *Mashiach ben David*, the ultimate *Mashiach*, will arrive. It is *Mashiach ben Yosef*'s death that triggers the mourning.

The alternative view: *ve-chad amar al yetzer hara sheneharg* — the mourning is over the *yetzer hara*, which will be killed in the messianic era.

### Logical Problem

This second view immediately encounters a devastating logical objection. *Bishlama le-man d'amar Mashiach ben Yosef sheneharg* — the view that it refers to *Mashiach ben Yosef* works well: *hayinu dechtiv vehibitu elai et asher dakaru* — and they will look toward me, the one who was pierced, *ve-safdu alav ke-misped al ha-yachid* — and they will mourn over him like the mourning over an only child. That makes sense: a heroic leader falls in battle, and the people mourn him deeply.

But *ella le-man d'amar al yetzer hara sheneharg* — if it refers to the *yetzer hara* being destroyed — *hai speda ba'ei le-me'ebad?* Why would you hold a eulogy? *Simcha ba'ei le-me'ebad!* You should be having a celebration! And beyond the question of the eulogy: *amai bachu?* Why were they crying?

### Mourning Perspectives

The answer comes from the teaching of Rabbi Yehuda. *Le-atid lavo*, in the future time, *mevi ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu le-yetzer hara* — God will bring the *yetzer hara* and *ve-shochato bifnei ha-tzaddikim uvifnei ha-resha'im* — slaughter it before the righteous and before the wicked. *Tzaddikim nidmeh lahem ke-har gavoha* — to the righteous it appears like an enormous mountain; *ve-resha'im nidmeh lahem ke-chut hase'ara* — to the wicked it appears like a single thread of hair. *Halalu bochim ve-halalu bochim* — these cry and those cry.

The righteous cry and say: *heich yacholnu lichbosh har gavoha kaze* — how did we ever manage to conquer something as immense as this mountain? The wicked cry and say: *heich lo yacholnu lichbosh et chut hase'ara haze* — how could we not have overcome something as trivial as this thread?

### Mountain & Hair

The *Maharsha* makes a brilliant observation about the imagery of the mountain and the hair. *Har Seir* — Mount Seir — is the paradigmatic home of *Eisav*, who represents both the human enemies of Israel and, allegorically, the *yetzer hara* itself. *Har* is the mountain; *se'ar* is hair. The same root thus encapsulates both images simultaneously, making the choice of metaphors anything but arbitrary.

### Righteous Tears

Why exactly the righteous are weeping is not immediately obvious. *Rashi* explains: they are crying as they recall how difficult the struggle with the *yetzer hara* was throughout their lives. It is a weeping over past suffering and difficulty — the enormity of what they had to overcome.

### Lost Opportunity

The *Maharsha* offers a different reading. He notes that the plain sense of the text seems to suggest the righteous are crying from joy — and indeed that would make sense. But if it is joy, it is not a *hesped*, a eulogy. So perhaps, he suggests, the righteous are crying because they are now losing the opportunity for religious struggle — the struggle through which they earned their reward. Now that the *yetzer hara* is gone, the arena of striving and merit has closed. That loss is genuinely mourned.

There remains a further puzzle: why does the *yetzer hara* appear to the righteous as a mountain and to the wicked as a thread? Intuitively, one would expect the reverse. The image seems to suggest that in some sense, the truth is revealed: for the wicked, who always complained that resisting temptation was impossibly hard, it becomes clear that it was never more than a thread — it only needed a small act of will to begin redirecting the course of one's life. Once a person begins making incremental improvements, each step is manageable, and looking back one realizes the path was not as impossible as it seemed. Like someone who has never run before who trains steadily and eventually completes a marathon — while in the training, no single step feels like climbing a mountain; only in retrospect does the enormity become apparent.

For the righteous, the reverse is true: they did not experience the *yetzer hara* as an overwhelming obstacle because they were constantly exercising the right spiritual muscles, making incremental progress. But when the scales finally fall from their eyes, they see that what they conquered was, in fact, a mountain of immense proportions.

### God's Astonishment

*Ve-af ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu tameh imahem* — and even God is astonished with them. As the verse says: *ki yipaleh be-einei she'erit ha-am haze ba-yamim ha-heim, gam be-einai yipaleh* — if it will be wondrous in the eyes of this people in those days, even in My eyes it will be wondrous. Whether God's astonishment is directed at the *resha'im* — how could you not have managed this? — or at the *tzaddikim* — how did you manage to accomplish that much? — is left open.

---

## Spider Web to Wagon Cord

### Rav Assi Teaching

*Amar Rav Assi*: *yetzer hara batchila domeh le-chut shel buchya* — the *yetzer hara* originally resembles a spider web. This resonates directly with the imagery of the *chut hase'ara* discussed above: the initial temptation is barely perceptible, almost nothing.

### Accumulation Metaphor

But *u-vasof domeh ka-avotot ha-agala* — by the end, it resembles the thick cords used to drag a wagon. The dynamic is familiar: small temptations, if yielded to, build upon one another. Each capitulation makes the next easier, each sin strengthens the habit, until what began as a barely-visible thread has become an almost unbreakable cord. The pattern of addiction — the incremental strengthening of destructive habits until they feel impossible to escape — is precisely what is being described here with remarkable psychological acuity.

### Yeshayahu Source

*She-ne'emar: hoy moshchei he-avon be-chavlei ha-shava* — woe to those who drag sin upon themselves with ropes of nothingness: *u-cha-avotot ha-agala chata'ah* — and like the cords of a wagon, they bring sin upon themselves. It begins from nothing, *chavlei ha-shava*, ropes of emptiness, and ends with the thickness of wagon cords.

---

## Mashiach ben David

### God's Offer

*Tanu rabanan*: *Mashiach ben David she-atid lehitgalot bimheira be-yameinu* — *Mashiach ben David*, who will be revealed speedily in our days. The *gemara* invokes this title — rather than simply *Mashiach* — because the discussion has been distinguishing between *Mashiach ben Yosef* and *Mashiach ben David*. At the moment of revelation, *omer lo ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu: she-al mimeni davar ve-eten lach* — God says to him: ask me for anything and I will give it to you. The source is the opening of *Tehillim Perek 2*, which in context is understood as a messianic psalm: *asapra el chok, ani ha-yom yeladeticha* — I will tell of the decree, I have today given birth to you — and then: *she-al mimeni ve-etnah goyim nachalatecha* — ask of me and I will give the nations as your inheritance.

### Mashiach's Request

But then — *ve-keivan she-ra'ah Mashiach ben Yosef she-neherag* — when *Mashiach ben David* sees that *Mashiach ben Yosef* has been killed in battle, his response is striking. *Amar lefanav: Ribono shel Olam, eini mevakesh mimcha ela chayim* — Master of the Universe, I ask nothing of you but life. He does not ask to conquer nations, to inherit the earth, to be given worldly dominion. In the face of death and war and the killing of *Mashiach ben Yosef*, he asks only for *chayim*. Whether he is asking for his own life — not to die as *Mashiach ben Yosef* did — or for life in a more universal sense, a world without death, perhaps anticipating *techiyat hameitim*, is not entirely clear. But the choice is deliberate: he turns away from conquest and toward life.

### God's Reply

*Omer lo*: *chayim? Ad she-lo amarta kvar hitnabei alecha David avicha* — life? Before you even asked, your father David already prophesied that this would be given to you. *She-ne'emar: chayim sha-al mimcha natata lo* — he asked of You life, and You gave it to him. The *mizmor* referenced is one that speaks of God's gifts to the king, here read as referring to *Mashiach*. The request was already granted before it was made.

---

## Seven Names of Yetzer Ha…

### Seven Names Intro

*Darash Rav Avira ve-iteima Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: the *yetzer hara* has seven names. Each name was given by a different figure — God, Moses, David, Solomon, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Joel — and each reflects a different aspect of what the *yetzer hara* is and how it operates.

### God's Name: Evil

God called it *ra* — evil. *She-ne'emar: ki yetzer lev ha-adam ra mine-urav* — for the inclination of the human heart is evil from its youth.

### Moses: Uncircumcised

Moses called it *arel* — uncircumcised. *She-ne'emar: u-maltem et orlat levavchem* — you shall circumcise the foreskin of your hearts. The *yetzer hara* is the spiritual foreskin that covers and constricts the heart.

### David: Impure

David called it *tamei* — impure. *She-ne'emar: lev tahor bera li Elohim* — create for me a pure heart, O God. *Miklal de-ika tamei* — the implication being that there is also an impure heart.

### Solomon: Enemy

Solomon called it *sonei* — hater, enemy. *She-ne'emar: im ra-ev sonecha he-achilehu lechem ve-im tzamei hashkehu mayim* — if your enemy is hungry, feed him bread; if he is thirsty, give him water; *ki gechalim ata choteh al rosho* — for in doing so you are heaping coals on his head. *Al tikrei yeshalem lach ela yashlimenu lach* — do not read it as God repaying you, but as God making peace between you and it. *Rashi* explains: this is being read not as literally about human enemies, but about the *yetzer hara* as your enemy. And what does it mean to feed it bread and water? It means feeding it *Torah*. If the *yetzer hara* is hungry and demands to be fed with sin, feed it instead with *Torah* — and you will be able to redirect and ultimately make peace with it.

### Isaiah: Stumbling Block

Isaiah called it *michshol* — a stumbling block. *She-ne'emar: solu solu panu derech, harimu michshol miderech ami* — clear, clear the way, remove the stumbling block from the path of my people.

### Ezekiel: Stone Heart

Ezekiel called it *even* — stone. *She-ne'emar: va-hasiroti et lev ha-even mi-vsarchem ve-natati lachem lev basar* — I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.

### Joel: Hidden One

Joel called it *tzefoni* — the northern one, or the hidden one. *She-ne'emar: ve-et ha-tzefoni archik me-aleichem* — I will distance the hidden one from you.

It is worth noting, in light of the earlier discussion about the internal versus external conception of *yetzer hara*, that the seven names are not uniform in their orientation. The uncircumcised heart, the stone heart, the pure and impure heart — these are deeply internal images. The stumbling block and the enemy are external. The "evil" and the "hidden one" occupy an ambiguous middle ground. The tension between externalized and internalized understandings of the *yetzer hara* is built into the very language the tradition uses to name it.

---

## Assault on Beit Hamikdash

### Joel Reinterpretation

*Tanu rabanan* — a Rabbinic teaching expands on Joel's verse. *Ve-et ha-tzefoni archik me-aleichem* — this is the *yetzer hara*, *she-tzafun ve-omed be-libo shel adam* — that is hidden and stands in the heart of a person. Here the image is explicitly internal: the *yetzer hara* is concealed within.

### Dispersal Metaphor

But then the verse continues: *ve-hidachtiv el eretz tziya u-shemama* — I will thrust it away to a barren and desolate land, *li-mkom she-ein bnei adam metzuyim le-hitgarot bahen* — to a place without people, so that it cannot entice or provoke anyone. This shifts back to an external image: the *yetzer hara* is taken out from inside the person and cast away to a desolate place where it has no one to tempt. The passage thus moves fluidly between the internal and external models, without resolving the tension between them.

### Beit Hamikdash Assault

The *gemara* then reads further into the verse. *Et panav el ha-yam ha-kadmoni* — his face toward the eastern sea. The word *yam* — sea — is interpreted as referring to the *Beit Hamikdash*, since just as God gathers all the waters, all people gather to the *Beit Hamikdash*. And *kadmon* — first, or eastern — refers to the *Beit Hamikdash Rishon*, the first Temple. *She-natan einav be-Mikdash rishon ve-hecherivo* — the *yetzer hara* turned its gaze toward the first *Beit Hamikdash* and destroyed it, *ve-harag talmidei chachamim she-bo* — and killed the Torah scholars within it.

*Ve-sofo el ha-yam ha-acharon* — and its end toward the western sea: *she-natan einav be-Mikdash sheni ve-hecherivo* — it also trained its gaze on the second *Beit Hamikdash* and destroyed it, *ve-harag talmidei chachamim she-bo* — and killed the Torah scholars within it. The pairing of the destruction of the *batei hamikdash* with the killing of *talmidei chachamim* is notably consistent and pointed.

### Enmity to Scholars

*Ve-ala va-asho ve-ta-al tzachanato* — and its stench rises. *She-maniach umot ha-olam u-mitgare be-son-eihem shel Yisrael* — it abandons the other nations and focuses its attacks on the Jewish people. *Ki higdil la-asot* — for it has acted greatly, hugely.

*Amar Abaye*: and specifically, *be-talmidei chachamim yoter mi-kulam* — the *yetzer hara* targets Torah scholars more than anyone else. The mention of *talmidei chachamim* has appeared twice already in the description of the *Beit Hamikdash*'s destruction; Abaye now makes this into an explicit principle.

### Abaye's Story

The *gemara* illustrates this with a famous story. Abaye once overheard a man saying to a woman: *nakdim ve-nizil be-orcha* — let us get up early and travel the road together. Abaye, suspecting an assignation in the making, decided to follow them discreetly to prevent anything improper from happening. He followed them for three *parsaot* — a considerable distance, perhaps eight miles or more — through a marshy field. When they reached a crossroads and parted ways, he heard them say to one another: *orcha rachika ve-tzavta basuma* — the road was long but the company was so pleasant. They had simply been walking companions, and nothing improper had occurred.

At this, Abaye said: if that had been himself — he speaks euphemistically, referring to himself as "the one who hates me" — *lo havay matzi le-okmei nafshay* — he would not have been able to withstand the temptation. He had assumed himself to be at a high level of religious and moral attainment, and now he realized that in those same circumstances, he would have been overcome. One might also note that the very act of following them — that sustained attention, traveling eight miles behind a couple — suggests something about where his own thoughts had already gone.

### Elder's Consolation

Abaye went and leaned against a doorpost in anguish, *u-mitztayer* — utterly despondent. *Ata hahu saba* — a certain elder came to him and taught him: *kol ha-gadol me-chavero yitzro gadol himenu* — the greater a person is than his fellow, the greater his *yetzer* is.

This principle invites the same internal/external tension noted throughout the *daf*. Read in the internalized, psychological register — and recalling the *midrash* that *Rashi* cites on *ve-hineh tov me'od zu yetzer hara* — the *yetzer hara* is understood as a powerful drive that, when properly channeled, propels great achievement. If it had not been for the *yetzer hara*, no one would build a house, no one would marry, no one would accomplish anything of consequence. The same ambition and desire that can lead a person astray can, when redirected, lead to monumental good. The *Ramban* reads *tov me'od* as meaning that creation is mostly good, and the *yetzer hara* represents the small part that is not — but the *midrash* seems to intend something more: that even the *yetzer hara* is part of what is *tov me'od*. From this perspective, *kol ha-gadol me-chavero yitzro gadol himenu* is straightforwardly true: the greatest people often have the most powerful drives, and what makes them great is precisely the way they have harnessed those energies.

There is, however, a real danger in this reading: it can serve as a license. "I have such a great *yetzer hara*, therefore I may be excused for giving in to it" is an obvious corruption of the principle.

Read through the externalized lens — where the *yetzer hara* abandoned the *umot ha-olam* to focus on Israel, where it destroyed the *batei hamikdash*, where it is an almost demonic force in the world — *kol ha-gadol me-chavero yitzro gadol himenu* means something quite different: the metaphysical force of evil is specifically deployed against those who are doing the most good, and the greater the person, the more targeted they become. These are two genuinely distinct theological and psychological frameworks, and the *gemara* moves between them without announcing the transition.

---

## Daily Struggle

### Daily Growth

*Amar Rav Yitzchak*: *yitzro shel adam*, the *yetzer* of a person — note the shift in language, from the *yetzer hara* as a distinct entity to *yitzro shel adam*, "his *yetzer*," possessive and personal — *mitgaber alav be-chol yom* — grows stronger over him every day. *She-ne'emar: rak ra kol ha-yom* — it is only evil the whole day. The *yetzer* does not plateau; it gains strength daily, losing no momentum.

### Seeking Death

*Amar Reish Lakish*: *yitzro shel adam mitgaber alav be-chol yom u-mevakesh lahamito* — not only does it grow stronger each day, it seeks to kill him — to bring him into spiritual death, destruction of the soul. *She-ne'emar: tzofeh rasha la-tzaddik u-mevakesh lahamito* — the wicked one watches for the righteous and seeks to kill him. *Ve-ilmalei ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu she-ozer lo, eino yachol lo* — were it not for God helping him, a person would not have the strength to withstand it on his own. *She-ne'emar: Hashem lo ya-azvennu ve-yado ve-lo yarshi-ennu be-hishafeto* — God will not abandon him into its hands and will not let him be condemned through its judgment.

### Beit Midrash Refuge

*Tana devei Rabbi Yishmael*: *im paga becha menuval zeh* — if this disgusting one accosts you, *mashcheihu le-veit ha-midrash* — drag it into the *beit midrash*. When the *yetzer hara* has seized hold of you, bring it with you into the *beit midrash*, make it your study partner — meaning: learn *Torah*. That is the remedy.

*She-im even hu nimoach* — if it is as hard as stone, *Torah* will dissolve it like water, as the verse says: *hoy kol tzamei lechu la-mayim* — come, all who are thirsty, to the water — and elsewhere: *avanim shachaku mayim* — stones are worn away by water. *Ve-im barzel hu mitpotzetz* — and if it is like iron, *Torah* will shatter it. *She-ne'emar: halo koh devarai ka-esh ne-um Hashem u-che-fatish yefotzetz sela* — are not My words like fire, says God, and like a hammer shattering rock?

### Torah as Antidote

A subtle difficulty arises here that both *Rashi* and *Tosafot* address. The verse as cited introduces an apparent tension: if iron shatters, the natural image would be of something breaking the iron. But in the verse, it is the rock that is shattered by the hammer, not the iron. *Rashi* resolves this by focusing on the first half of the verse: God's word is like fire — and fire melts iron, causes it to spark and dissolve. The image for the iron, then, is not the hammer and rock but the fire. *Tosafot* suggests reading the verse differently — that the hammer itself is what *yefotzetz sela*, shatters the rock — but this is admittedly a strained reading. In any case, the *gemara*'s point stands: bring the *yetzer hara* into the *beit midrash* and engage it with *Torah*, whether as melting water against stone or as divine fire against iron.

---

## Seduction & Testimony

### Dual Role

*Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani amar Rabbi Yonatan*: *yetzer hara mesito la-adam ba-olam ha-zeh* — the *yetzer hara* seduces a person in this world, *u-me-id alav le-olam ha-ba* — and will testify against him in the world to come. What seems in this world like your companion, your indulgent friend who encourages you to give in to desire, will in the end turn against you entirely and stand as a witness for the prosecution.

### Servant Parable

*She-ne'emar: me-faneik mi-no-ar avdo, ve-acharito yihyeh manon* — one who indulges his servant from youth, in the end he will be a *manon*. The *yetzer hara* is here called your servant — *Rashi* explains that it is ultimately subject to your control — but it has been indulging you and encouraging indulgence since you were young. And in the end, *manon*: which, the *gemara* explains, equals *sahada*, witness, through the letter-substitution cipher known as *atbach* of Rabbi Chiya. In *atbach*, letters are substituted according to a systematic pairing of the alphabet folded over itself and incorporating the *sofit* forms. Through this cipher, the letters of *manon* yield *sahad-a* — witness. The *yetzer hara* was always taking notes.

---

## Passerby to Master

### External vs Internal

*Rav Huna rami ksiv* — Rav Huna raises a contradiction between two verses. One verse says *ki ruach znunim hit-ah* — a licentious spirit led them astray, suggesting an external force. Another says *be-kirbam* — in their midst, suggesting something internal. How are these reconciled?

### Three Stages

*Bitchila hit-am* — initially it merely led them astray; it was an external force that occasionally deflected them from the right path. *Aval be-sof be-kirbam* — but in the end it became *within* them, embedded inside, a regular and internalized presence.

*Amar Rava*: this mirrors the progression described elsewhere about the spiderweb and the thick cords. *Bitchila kara-o holech* — at first it was called a passerby, merely passing through and occasionally creating temptation. *U-ve-sof kara-o oreach* — then it became a guest, a more regular visitor who stays awhile. *U-ve-sof kara-o ish* — and in the end it became the *ba-al ha-bayit*, the master of the house.

### Natan's Parable

This is illustrated by the *mashal* that *Natan* told David to rebuke him for the sin involving *Bat Sheva*. *Vayavo helech le-ish he-ashir* — a passerby came to the wealthy man — the man who had enormous flocks and yet, when a visitor needed to be fed, he took instead the one beloved lamb of his poor neighbor. The wealthy man's sheep are David's wives; the one lamb is *Bat Sheva*, wife of *Uriah*. The passerby who needs feeding — the one whose need David chose to satisfy at another's expense — is David's own *yetzer hara*. What began as a passing desire became a guest, and then became the master of the house.

---

## Sexual Desire

### Appetite Paradox

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *eiver katan*, a small limb, the *gemara* now turning explicitly to sexual desire. *Yesh lo le-adam* — a person has this limb. *Mar-ivo savea* — if he starves it, he is satisfied; *u-mashi-vo ra-ev* — if he satiates it, he is always hungry. Feeding the desire whets it further; the more one gives in, the more insistent the appetite becomes. *She-ne'emar: ke-mar-isam va-yisba-u* — as they grazed, so they were satisfied (here read against its grain to make the point). A degree of abstinence, counter-intuitively, is what actually brings satisfaction; indulgence only deepens the hunger.

---

## Four Regretted Creations

### Four Entities

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan bar Abba amrei bei Rav*: *arba-ah mischarat aleihem ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu she-bera-am* — four entities God, as it were, regrets having created. Not in the literal sense of divine error, but in the sense that they produce enormous evil in the world. *Ve-eilu hein*: exile, the Chaldeans, the Ishmaelites, and the *yetzer hara*.

### Three Nations

Regarding exile: *v-atah mah li foh ne-um Hashem, ki lukach ami chinam* — what am I doing here, says God? My people were taken for nothing. The exile was purposeless devastation. Regarding the Chaldeans: *hein eretz Kasdim zeh ha-am lo hayah* — this is a nation that should not have been. Regarding the Ishmaelites: *yishlayu ohalim le-shodedim, u-vtuchos le-margizei El* — tranquil tents for highway robbers, security for those who provoke God — *la-asher heivi Eloah be-yado*, that God brought into existence through His own hand. The regret is that God created them, and yet they have become a source of violence and evil in the world.

### Yetzer Creation

And finally: *yetzer hara dichsiv, va-asher hareiti* — and that which I have made evil. This is read as God expressing something like regret over creating the *yetzer hara*, acknowledging that it has led human beings into destruction.

### Three Verses Defense

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *ilmalei shalosh mikra-ot halalu, nismotetu ragleihem shel son-eihem shel Yisrael* — were it not for the following three verses, the legs of the Jewish people (spoken of euphemistically as "their enemies") would have given way entirely under the weight of their sins.

The first verse: *va-asher hareiti* — God acknowledges responsibility for creating the *yetzer hara*, and thus bears part of the burden for the sins it causes. The second: *hine kachomer be-yad ha-yotzer kein atem be-yadi ne-um Hashem* — as clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand — meaning that God has the power to strengthen us and reshape us; the fact that we have sometimes failed is not entirely on our own account. The third: *va-hasiroti et lev ha-even mi-vsarchem ve-natati lachem lev basar* — God has placed this stone heart within us, and God alone can replace it with a heart of flesh. Together, these verses provide a kind of theological scaffolding: we are not absolved of responsibility, but we are also not entirely abandoned to it. We were created this way, and God could have made it otherwise. *Rav Pappa* adds a fourth verse: *ve-et ruchi eten be-kirbechem* — I will place my spirit within you — which again promises divine assistance in the struggle against the *yetzer hara*.

---

## Craftsmen & Horns

### Four Craftsmen

The *gemara* now turns to a vision in *Zechariah*: *vayar-eni Hashem arba-ah charashim* — God showed me four craftsmen. *Amar Rav Chana bar Bizna amar Rabbi Shimon Chasida*: the four craftsmen are *Mashiach ben David, Mashiach ben Yosef, Eliyahu*, and *Kohen Tzedek*. *Rashi* explains: *Mashiach ben David* and *Mashiach ben Yosef* will build the *Beit Hamikdash*, hence they are craftsmen. *Eliyahu* built the altar on *Har Carmel* for his confrontation with the *neviei ha-Ba-al*. And *Kohen Tzedek* is read as *Malki-Tzedek*, son of *Noach*, who helped build the *tevah*.

### Rav Sheshet's Challenge

*Masiv Rav Sheshet*: if these are good figures, what is meant by the next verse — *vayomer elai eleh ha-kranot asher zeru et Yehudah* — these are the horns that scattered Judah? How can these same four craftsmen be identified as the ones who scattered Judah?

### Resolution

*Shafil le-seifa di-kra* — look at the end of the verse: *vayavo-u eleh le-hacharid otam lidot et karnot ha-goyim ha-nosim keren el eretz Yehudah le-zarosah* — these came to terrify them and to cast down the horns of the nations who lifted their horn against the land of Judah to scatter it. The verse contains two different "these": the first refers to the horns that scattered Judah, and the second refers to the four craftsmen who have come to destroy those horns. The craftsmen are not the scatterers; they are the destroyers of the scatterers.

### Rav Chana's Modesty

*Be-ha Chana be-agadeta la matzisai* — I should have known better than to try to compete with Chana in *agadeta*, says one of the Sages. The comment is somewhat humorous, since the resolution was actually a matter of careful reading of the *pesukim* — closer to *peshat* than to *agadeta* — but the point about intellectual humility in the face of a colleague's superior mastery stands.

---

## Shepherds & Leaders

### Seven Shepherds

*Ve-hayah zeh shalom Ashur ki yavo be-artzeinu* — this will be peace when Ashur comes against our land — *va-hakimonu alav shiv-ah ro-im u-shmonah nesichei adam* — we will raise up against them seven shepherds and eight leaders of people, who will ultimately take over the land of Ashur. *Mani nihu shiv-ah ro-im?* — who are the seven shepherds? *David ba-emtza* — David in the center. *Adam, Shet, u-Mesushalach mi-yimino* — Adam, Seth, and Methuselah on his right. *Avraham, Yaakov, u-Moshe bi-smolo* — Abraham, Jacob, and Moses on his left. The *Maharsha* notes that most of these figures were, in fact, literally shepherds as well as spiritual leaders, which gives the choice of imagery an additional layer of resonance. The absence of Isaac from the list is not addressed.

### Eight Leaders

*U-mani nihu shmonah nesichei adam?* — who are the eight leaders? *Yishai ve-Shaul u-Shmuel, Amos ve-Tzefaniah, Tzidkiyahu, u-Mashiach ve-Eliyahu*. What precisely connects these eight figures to one another is left for further study.

### Anti-Christian Notes

It is noted that the aggadic material at the end of this *daf*, concerning the messianic figures and their roles, reflects a polemical anti-Christian dimension, as is often found in *agadeta* of this period. The full explication of those dimensions would require engagement with the relevant patristic parallels, but the pattern is characteristic of much late Amoraic aggadic literature on messianic themes.

---

---

# Sukkah 53

## Menora & Priests

### Candelabra Height

The daf opens in the middle of the discussion of *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah*, picking up from the bottom of 52b. A *tanna* teaches: *gova shel menora chamishim ama* — the height of the candelabra used for the illumination of the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* was fifty *amot*, comparable in stature to the tree from which Haman was hanged. Four young *kohanim* — *arba yeladim shepirchei kehunah* — would ascend on four separate ladders, each carrying pitchers of oil: *uveyadeihem kadei shemen shel me'ah v'esrim log*, a combined total of a hundred and twenty *log*.

### Oil Distribution

The *gemara* raises a question: *me'ah v'esrim log kulhu o dilma l'chol chad v'chad* — was the hundred and twenty *log* the total carried collectively, or did each priest carry a hundred and twenty *log* individually? The latter figure, roughly thirteen or fourteen gallons per person, would have been extraordinary. A *braita* resolves the matter: *uveyadeihem kadei shemen shel shloshim shloshim log* — each carried thirty *log*, and *she'kulam me'ah v'esrim log*, together they amounted to a hundred and twenty *log*. This is a more manageable figure, approximately three to five gallons per person.

### Martha's Son

The *braita* continues with a striking comparison: *v'hem meshubachim hayu yoseir mibnasha d'Mirta bas Paitos* — these priests were considered more praiseworthy, in the specific sense of stronger, than the son of Marta bat Boethus. The tradition relates that this man would take *shtei yerechot shel shor hagadol*, the two thighs of a large ox purchased for a thousand *zuz*, and walk up the ramp to offer them, placing heel immediately beside the big toe of the next foot — tiny, deliberate steps — while bearing this enormous weight. His brother priests, however, would not permit him to do so, invoking the principle of *b'rov am hadrat melech*: the greater the number of participants, the greater the glory to God. The task was to be divided appropriately rather than performed as a feat of individual strength.

### Ramp vs Ladder

This raises the question: *mai meshubachim* — in what way were the oil-carrying priests actually superior? If the argument rests on weight, it fails, for *hani yakiri tfei* — the two thighs of a large ox are considerably heavier than thirty *log* of oil. The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing the physical challenge: *hasham kevesh u'meruba v'lo zakif* — there, in the case of Martha's son, the ascent was via a ramp, angled and not perpendicular; *hacha sulamot v'zakif tuva* — here, the priests climbed ladders that were nearly vertical. Even if the load was lighter, ascending almost straight up with oil is a far greater physical challenge than walking up a gradual incline.

One question raised in passing is worth noting: it is well known that Marta bat Boethus married Yehoshua ben Gamla, who became *kohen gadol*. Why then does the tradition identify the son by his mother's name rather than his father's? The answer remains uncertain — perhaps the son was from a prior marriage — and the *gemara* does not resolve it.

---

## Simchat Choreography

### Light & Illumination

The *mishnah* had stated that there was no courtyard in Jerusalem that was not illuminated by the light of the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah*. Situated on *Har HaBayit* at an elevated position, the light from the fifty-*amah* candelabra radiated throughout the city. A *braita* illustrates the intensity of this illumination: *isha hayta boreret chitim le'or Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* — a woman could sort and sift wheat, separating even the finest chaff, by the light of the celebration alone.

### Torch Juggling

The *mishnah* describes how *chasidim ve'anshei ma'aseh* — the righteous and those of good deeds — would take center stage in the rejoicing, dancing and juggling torches while singing words of praise. The *levi'im* would accompany on their musical instruments.

### Songs of Praise

A *braita* records two distinct categories of song sung during the celebration. Some would say: *ashrei yaldutenu shelo biysha et ziknutenu* — praised is our youth, which brought no shame upon our old age. These are identified as *chasidim ve'anshei ma'aseh*, those who had been righteous throughout their lives. Others would say: *ashrei ziknutenu she'kapra al yaldutenu* — praised is our old age, which atoned for our youth. These are *ba'alei teshuva*, those who had lived more recklessly in their younger years and had since returned.

### Repentance Teaching

Both groups together would say: *ashrei mi shelo chata* — praised is the one who has never sinned — *u'mi shechata yashuv ve'yimchol lo* — and one who has sinned should repent, and it will be forgiven. This formulation coexists in some tension with the well-known teaching that *ba'alei teshuva* occupy a place that even the perfectly righteous cannot attain. Nevertheless, the *gemara* here affirms that it is still preferable never to have sinned in the first place.

---

## Hillel's Teaching

### Hillel's Statement

A *braita* records that about Hillel the Elder it was said: *keshehaya same'ach be'Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* — when he would rejoice at the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* — *amar ken: im ani kan hakol kan, ve'im eini kan mi kan* — he would say: "If I am here, everyone is here; and if I am not here, who is here?" Taken at face value, this sounds strikingly arrogant. After all, Hillel's other celebrated statement — *im ein ani li mi li, u'cheshe'ani le'atzmi mah ani* — "If I am not for myself, who will be for me? But if I am only for myself, what am I?" — is a carefully balanced formulation. The present statement, by contrast, seems to simply repeat the same self-centered point twice. The resolution, as *Rashi* explains, is that Hillel is not speaking in his own voice.

### God's Presence

*Rashi* explains: *doresh haya lerabbim shelo yechete'u bishmo shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu* — Hillel was teaching the masses in the name of God, speaking as it were in the divine voice. The full meaning is: *kol zman she'ani chafetz babayit hazeh u'shchinati sruya bo* — as long as I, God, desire this house and My presence dwells within it — *yihiye kevodo kayam ve'yavo hakol kan* — its glory will endure and all will come here. *Ve'im techete'u ve'asallek shchinati, mi yavo kan* — but if you sin and My *shekhinah* departs, who will come here?

This is a pointed message delivered in the very midst of celebration. The *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* is a time of tremendous joy and communal gathering, a moment when it would be easy to lose sight of the deeper reality: this place matters not because it is a magnificent venue for celebration, but because of the divine presence that inhabits it. If that presence departs, the gathering means nothing. The parallel to the role a *beit knesset* has always played — simultaneously a gathering place and a *mikdash me'at*, a site of worship and divine presence — is instructive.

### Reciprocal Homes

Hillel would also say: *lemakom she'ani ohev, sham raglai molichot oti* — the place that I love, there my legs will bring me. *Im tavo el beiti, ani avo el beitecha; im atah lo tavo el beiti, ani lo avo el beitecha* — if you come to my house, I will come to your house; if you do not come to my house, I will not come to your house. Again Hillel speaks in God's voice: if the Jewish people come to the *Beit HaMikdash*, God in turn will bring His presence into their homes. The verse cited in support is *bechol hamakom asher azkir et shemi avo elecha uverachticha* — wherever I cause My name to be invoked, I will come to you and bless you.

This teaching resonates beautifully with the broader themes of *Sukkot* — the *sukkah* as simultaneously a human dwelling and an evocation of the *ananei kavod*, the divine clouds of glory and the imagery of the *Mikdash*. The *sukkah* represents precisely this intersection: coming to God's house and, in turn, receiving God's presence within one's own.

---

## Skull & Angel

### Floating Skull

At this point the *gemara* introduces the passage familiar from Pirkei Avot: *af hu ra'ah gulgoret achat shetzafah al pnei hamayim* — Hillel also once saw a skull floating on the water, and said to it: *al de'atpacht atpuch, ve'sof mativeych yetufun* — because you drowned others, you were drowned; and those who drowned you will themselves be drowned. The message is one of cosmic justice: suffering does not arrive without cause, and those who inflict it will ultimately face it themselves.

---

## Hillel's Teaching (II)

### Legs Guarantors

Rabbi Yochanan offers a related reflection on the phrase *sham raglai molichot oti* — there my legs bring me: *ragloi d'var enash inun arvin bei* — a person's legs are his guarantors — *l'atar d'mitbe'i taman movilin yatei* — to the place where he is needed, they bring him. This is not merely a romantic statement about going where one loves; it carries a darker undertone. A person is brought by his legs to the place he must go — ultimately, to the place of his death.

---

## Skull & Angel (II)

### Shlomo & Luz

The *gemara* now provides the narrative that gives this teaching its full force. There were two Kushim — *Rashi* notes the term is used here, notwithstanding its generally negative connotation in rabbinic literature, to indicate that they were remarkably distinguished individuals — who served as scribes before King Shlomo, named Elihoreph and Achiyah, sons of Shisha, as recorded in Melachim. One day Shlomo perceived that the Angel of Death was deeply sorrowful. When he asked why, the Angel replied: *de-ka ba'u minei hani tartei Kushei* — I have been tasked with taking these two Kushim, *ve-yasvi hakha* — and they are sitting right here. Shlomo, moved to protect them, entrusted them to the *shedim* and sent them to the city of Luz — *shadruhu le-mahoza de-Luz*. As the *gemara* in Sotah records, Luz was a place over which the Angel of Death had no dominion; no one died there.

### Angel Laughs

When the two men arrived at Luz, however — *ki matu le-mahoza de-Luz* — they died at its very gates, just before crossing into the city's protection. The next day Shlomo saw the Angel of Death, this time laughing. When he asked why, the Angel replied: *be-asra de-ba'u minei taman shadartinu* — the very place where I needed to take them, that is where you sent them. Shlomo had unwittingly delivered them to the precise location the Angel of Death had been assigned. Immediately, Shlomo declared: *raglohi de-var inish inun arvin bei, le-asra de-misba'ei taman movilin yatei* — the legs of a person are his guarantors; to the place where he is needed, there they bring him. The point is sobering: a person cannot outrun the destination decreed for him. His own legs will carry him there.

---

## Juggling Acts

### Torches & Kida

The *gemara* returns to the theme of the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* and the acts performed during the celebration. It is related that Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, *keshehaya same'ach simchat Beit HaShoeivah* — when he would rejoice at the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* — *haya notel shemonah avukot shel ur* — would take eight torches of flame — *ve-zorek achat ve-notel achat ve-ein nog'ot zu be-zu* — throw one and catch the next, the torches moving in a perfect circle without ever touching one another. He would then perform the *kida* prostration: *ve-no'etz shenei gudlav ba-aretz* — he would plant his two thumbs in the ground (not the flat of his palms), *ve-shocheh ve-noshek et ha-ritzpah* — bow down to kiss the floor in the manner of a prostration done entirely on the thumbs — *ve-zokef* — and then push himself back upright. *Ve-ein kol beryah yecholah la'asot kein* — no other creature could do this.

The *gemara* notes that Levi once demonstrated *kida* before Rabbi, after the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, to show what this act entailed — and *ve-itla*, he was injured, becoming lame as a result. The *gemara* raises the question whether the lameness was caused by the demonstration itself. It cites Rabbi Elazar's teaching: *le-olam al yati'ach adam devarim klapei ma'alah* — a person should never cast complaints heavenward — *she-harei adam gadol hitich devarim klapei ma'alah ve-itla, u-manu Levi* — for a great person once did so and became lame, and that was Levi. *Rashi* references the passage in Ta'anit where Levi said before God: *alita ve-yashavta lach ba-marom ve-eincha mashgi'ach al banecha* — You have ascended and sat in the heights and are not paying attention to what is happening to Your children. The *gemara* concludes: *ha ve-ha garmu lei* — both factors contributed, the complaint against God and the physical strain of the *kida* demonstration.

### Levi's Knives

Continuing with Levi: *Levi hava metayel kamei d'Rebbi b'tamnei skinei* — Levi would perform before Rabbi, juggling eight knives. *Rashi* clarifies that this was not at the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* itself but at some form of celebration in Rabbi's home. *Rashi* adds a poignant detail: Rabbi was the one who bore perpetual anxiety for the welfare of *Klal Yisrael*, and Levi was attempting to cheer him up — *yoma de-michaich bei Rebbi asi puranus le-olam*, a day on which Rabbi would laugh, disaster would befall the world. One assumes this juggling took place before Levi sustained his injury, though the *gemara* does not say so explicitly.

### Wine Juggling

Shmuel, *kamei de-Shvor Malka b'tamnei mazgei chamra* — would juggle eight cups of wine before King Shapur. How one juggles a filled cup of wine without spilling it strains the imagination, yet the *gemara* presents it matter-of-factly.

### Egg Juggling

Abaye, *kamei de-Rava b'tamneya beyei* — before Rava with eight eggs — *ve-amri lah b'arba beyei* — and some say four eggs. There is a clear progression in the tradition: from torches to knives to wine cups to eggs, from eight to four. The *gemara* is essentially presenting a descending ladder of danger and difficulty, and the point is implicit: if one wishes to practice juggling, one is better advised to start with eggs.

---

## Sleepless Rejoicing

### No Sleep

A *braita* records the testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya: *kshehayinu smeichim Simchat Beit HaShoeivah, lo ra'inu sheina b'eineinu* — when we would rejoice at the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah*, our eyes would not see sleep.

### Daily Schedule

He explains the schedule that made this possible. The first hour of the day was the morning *tamid shel Shachar*; then *tefillah*; then witnessing the *korban musaf*; then *tefillat hamusafin*; then study in the *beit midrash*; then eating and drinking. Notably, no mention is made of the *sukkah*, despite the fact that it is *Sukkot* and eating presumably took place in one. Then *tefillat mincha*; then the *tamid shel bein ha'arbayim*; and then, once the day's sacrificial service was concluded, *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* — which would last through the night until the cycle began again.

### Dozing Reality

The *gemara* challenges this: *ve-eini*? Is this truly possible? For Rabbi Yochanan taught that if someone takes an oath not to sleep for three days, he is given lashes immediately and may sleep at once, because the oath is impossible to fulfill — three days without sleep is beyond human capacity. How then could these celebrations last five or six days without sleep? The *gemara* resolves: *ela hachi ka'amar: lo ta'amnu ta'am sheina* — what Rabbi Yehoshua meant was not that they slept not at all, but that they never truly tasted deep, satisfying sleep. *Dahavu minamnamai akatfei d'hadadi* — they would doze off on one another's shoulders, but a proper restful sleep was never had during the entire festival.

---

## Fifteen Steps

### Steps Setup

The *mishnah* introduces the fifteen steps — *chamesh esrei ma'alot* — that led from the *Ezrat Nashim* up to the *Ezrat Yisrael*. These steps corresponded to the fifteen *Shirei HaMa'alot*, the Songs of Ascent in Tehillim, and it was on these steps that the *levi'im* would stand during the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah*. *Rashi* notes that these steps were on the western side of the *Ezrat Nashim* as it opened into the *Ezrat Yisrael*, and that the *levi'im* standing there were not in the position for the regular *korban* service — that was the eastern end — but specifically for this celebration.

### Songs Origin

Rav Chisda posed a question to a scholar who specialized in *agaddata* and was presenting traditional homiletic material before him: *shemia lach hani chamisar ma'alot keneged mi amaran David* — have you heard what the fifteen *Shirei HaMa'alot* correspond to? The scholar replied in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *beshah shekarah David shitin* — when David dug the *shitin*, those underground caverns beneath the *mizbei'ach*. The *gemara* had previously recorded three opinions about the *shitin* — that they were a natural formation, that they were dug, or that they were simply a hollow in the *mizbei'ach* where the wine would drain — but this tradition proceeds on the assumption that they were dug by David himself.

What happened was this: *kafa tehoma* — David dug too deep and broke through into the underground depths, the *tehom*, and the waters threatened to burst forth and flood the world. David recited fifteen songs of ascent and the waters receded. Rav Chisda immediately objected: if the songs brought the waters back down, they should be called songs of *descent*, not songs of ascent — *achutei mibai leh*! The scholar who had conveyed the tradition replied: *ah, ve'izkartan* — you've helped me remember something. Let me correct the account.

Here is the corrected version: when David dug the *shitin* and the *tehom* burst forth threatening to flood the world, David asked: *mi ika de-yada ee sharei lemichtav shem achaspa ve-nishdi bitehoma u-manach* — is there anyone who knows whether it is permissible to write the divine name on a piece of pottery and cast it into the depths to stop them up? No one answered. David then declared: *kol ha-yodeia lomar ve-eino omer yichanek bi-gerono* — anyone who knows the answer and is not saying it, let him be strangled in his throat.

At this, Achitofel constructed a *kal va-chomer*: if the Torah permitted the divine name — written in sanctity — to be dissolved in water in order to make peace between a husband and his wife in the case of a *sotah*, then all the more so should writing the name on pottery and casting it into the depths be permitted in order to restore peace to the entire world. *Amar lei: shari* — David was told: it is permissible.

The name was written on a shard of pottery — *Rashi* explains that pottery sinks rather than floats, making it suitable for this purpose — and cast into the *tehom*. The *gemara* also preserves an additional dimension cited by *Rashi*: the shard David discovered upon digging was not an ordinary piece of pottery but bore an inscription indicating it had been in place since the six days of creation. By disturbing this primordial seal, David allowed the waters to surge, and it was now necessary to return something to that place.

### Water Correction

The *tehom* receded — but it receded too far. It went down *shiteisar alfei garmidi* — sixteen thousand *amot*. When it was observed that the waters had descended so dramatically, concern arose in the other direction: *kama de-midlei tefei mirtav alma* — the closer the depths are to the surface, the more moisture reaches the earth above, which is beneficial for the world. David then recited the fifteen *Shirei HaMa'alot*, which raised the water back up *chamesh esreh alfei garmidi* — fifteen thousand *amot* — *ve-ukmeih be-alfei garmidi* — leaving it a thousand *amot* below the earth's surface. Close enough to benefit the world through moisture, but far enough to pose no danger of flooding.

### Earth Depth

Ulla derived a ruling from this episode: *shema mina ovyah de-ara alfei garmidi* — we learn that the depth of the earth's crust, from the surface down to the *tehom*, is a thousand *amot*, since that is where the *tehom* now rests. The *gemara* raises an obvious objection: we dig far less than a thousand *amot* and reach water — wells are not nearly that deep. Rav Mesharshiya responds: *hahu misuma de-Prat* — those are waters that come through the underground channels of the Prat, the Euphrates. *Rashi* explains that the Prat originates from a great height, and as recorded in Bechorot, *kol ha-neharot le-mata mi-Prat* — all rivers lie lower than the Prat in elevation. Waters from a high source can travel through subterranean veins and emerge at considerable distances, even reaching a similar elevation to their source. What one finds in wells dug in the lowlands of Bavel are these tributary channels of the Prat — not the waters of the *tehom* itself, which lies a full thousand *amot* below the surface.

---

## Water Procession

### Step Counting

The *mishnah* describes how the *kohanim* stood at the upper gate and descended in procession, blowing *tekiah teruah tekiah* at the various stages of the water-drawing ceremony. Rabbi Yirmiya raises a precise question about the choreography: when the *kohanim* performed their blast at what is described as the relevant step — was that the tenth step counting from the bottom, meaning they had descended five from the top? Or was it the tenth step counting from the top, meaning they had gone down ten and were five from the bottom? *Teiku* — this question is left unresolved.

### Eastward Turn

A *baraita* now addresses the gesture of turning eastward at the conclusion of the procession. The verse in Yechezkel states: *upneihem keimah* — their faces were to the east — describing the sin of those at the time of the First *Beit HaMikdash*. One might think this means simply that their backs were turned to the *Heichal*. The *baraita* points out that this is self-evident — if faces are east, backs face the *Heichal* to the west — so why specify it? *Melamed she'hayu por'in atzman u-matrizin klapei ma'alah* — it teaches that they would expose their rear ends and perform acts of deliberate degradation toward the *Heichal*, combining idolatrous worship with an act of contempt toward God's house.

### God Dialogue

Against this backdrop of the forefathers' disgrace, those at the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* would turn and declare: *anu leYah uleYah eineinu* — we are for God and our eyes are toward God. The *gemara* raises a concern: Rabbi Zeira taught that one who says *Shema Yisrael* twice in succession is as if saying *modim modim* — an expression that suggests dualism. Does not the formula *anu leYah uleYah eineinu* repeat God's name consecutively in a way that raises the same concern? The *gemara* resolves: *anu heyma mishtachavim keimah ve-anu leYah* — they would say that our forefathers bowed toward the east, but we bow to God — *ve-eineinu leYah meyachalot* — and our eyes long for God. By inserting the phrase *eineinu* between the two divine references, the formula avoids the problematic juxtaposition.

There is something deeply striking about the overall choreography here. At the *Simchat Beit HaShoeivah* one finds an extended dialogue taking shape: when the *aravah* is circled, the people declare *yofi lach mizbei'ach, yofi lach mizbei'ach*. Here, before departing, they contrast themselves with their forefathers and declare their fidelity to God. And Hillel, as discussed earlier, embodied God's own voice responding — welcoming those who come to His house and promising to come to theirs. Something about *Sukkot* and the intersection of God's presence and our dwelling evokes this uniquely intimate, reciprocal dialogue between Israel and the divine.

---

## Tekiot Count

### Tekiot Range

Having mentioned the *tekiot* that accompanied the water-drawing procession, the *mishnah* turns to the general institution of trumpet blasts in the *Beit HaMikdash*. The rule is: *ein pochtin m'esrim v'achat tekiot bamikdash* — there are no fewer than twenty-one *tekiot* in the *Mikdash* — *ve-ein mosifin al arbaim u-shmonah* — and no more than forty-eight. Each set of *tekiot* follows the pattern of *tekiah teruah tekiah*, a unit of three blasts. Twenty-one therefore represents seven such units, and forty-eight represents sixteen.

### Daily Blasts

How does the daily total of twenty-one come about? *Shalosh bif'tichat she'arim* — three *tekiot*, one unit, upon opening the gates in the morning. *Tesha l'tamid shel shachar* — nine more, three units, for the morning *tamid*. *Rashi* clarifies when these nine were blown: at the wine libation accompanying the *tamid*, during which the *levi'im* would sing. *Ha-levi'im omrim shir*, and the song was structured with three pauses — *u-shlosha prakim hayu ba-shir she-hayu mafsikin bo* — at each pause the *kohanim* would sound the *chatzotzrot* and the people would bow down. This choreography transformed the service from a spectacle into a participatory act of worship — the music would pause, the trumpets would sound, and the entire assembly would prostrate themselves. The same nine *tekiot* were then repeated for *tesha l'tamid shel bein ha'arbayim*, the afternoon *tamid*. That yields a total of seven units — twenty-one *tekiot* — as the daily baseline.

### Shabbat Blasts

If *musafin* were brought, *uv'musafin hayu mosifin od tesha* — an additional nine *tekiot* were added, three more units, for the same reason: the *musaf* offering also involved wine libations with the *levi'im*' song and its three breaks. This brings the total on a *yom tov* to thirty. On *Erev Shabbat*, *uv'erev shabbat hayu mosifin sheish* — six additional *tekiot* were added, two more units. *Shalosh l'havtil et ha'am mi'melacha* — three to announce that labor must cease, communicated presumably by relay through torches visible across the city. *Ve-shalosh l'havdil bein kodesh l'chol* — and three more to mark the onset of *Shabbat* itself. The use of *l'havdil* here in the direction of entering *kedushah* rather than departing from it is an interesting nuance.

### Full Schedule

When *Erev Shabbat* fell in the middle of *Sukkot*, both sets of additional *tekiot* applied simultaneously, yielding the maximum of forty-eight — sixteen units. The full accounting: one unit for the opening of the gates; one unit for the procession from the upper gate; one unit at the lower gate as the procession exits the *Beit HaMikdash*; one unit at the filling of the water; one unit at the pouring of the water on the *mizbei'ach*; three units for the *tamid shel shachar*, *musaf*, and *tamid shel bein ha'arbayim* respectively — totaling nine units thus far, which is fourteen. Then two more units for the *Erev Shabbat* warnings brings the total to sixteen. Sixteen times three is forty-eight.

One might note that the *tekiot* accompanying the *aravah* ceremony — *taku v'heriu v'taku* — do not appear in this count. Whether *Hoshanah Rabbah* fell on *Erev Shabbat* would presumably have added further *tekiot* beyond the forty-eight, though the *gemara* does not address this directly.

---

## Tekiot Dispute

### Rabbi Yehuda

*Matenin d'lo k'Rabbi Yehuda* — the *mishnah* does not follow the position of Rabbi Yehuda. A *baraita* records: *Rabbi Yehuda omer ha-pochet lo yifchos mi-sheva ve-ha-mosif lo yosif al sheish esreh* — Rabbi Yehuda holds the minimum is seven and the maximum is sixteen. He counts precisely as the units were enumerated above — seven rather than twenty-one, sixteen rather than forty-eight.

### One or Three

The *gemara* asks: *bimai kamifligi* — what is the substance of the dispute? *Rabbi Yehuda savar tekiah-teruah-tekiah achas hi* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* constitutes one unit. *Ve-Rabbanan savari tekiah lachud u-teruah lachud* — the Sages hold they are distinct sounds. This is not merely a dispute about how to label or count; there is a real halakhic difference regarding whether one takes a breath between the sounds or whether the entire sequence is blown as one continuous unit.

### Verb Analysis

What is Rabbi Yehuda's source? *Amar kra utkatem teruah* — the Torah uses the verb *u-tekia* in relation to *teruah*, which Rabbi Yehuda reads as indicating that the two are halakhically one. The Sages counter: *hahu l'pishuta lifneyha u-le'achareyha hu d'ata* — that verse is merely informing us that a *tekiah* precedes and follows the *teruah*, not that they constitute one sound.

### Torah Allowance

Where do the Sages derive that *tekiah* and *teruah* are distinct? *D'chtiv u-v'hakheil et ha-kahal titke'u ve-lo tari'u* — the Torah permits *tekiah* to be performed without *teruah* in certain contexts, demonstrating that *tekiah* can exist as an independent sound. *Ve-ei salka daitach tekiah-teruah achas hi* — if one held that *tekiah-teruah* were truly one unit — *amar Rachmana palga d'mitzvah avid u-palga lo avid* — the Torah would be instructing one to perform half a *mitzvah* and not the other half. That is impossible. The sounds must therefore be distinct. Rabbi Yehuda responds: *hahu l'simana b'alma hu d'ata* — that verse is simply establishing a *tekiah* as an independent signal for gathering, a function the Torah elevates into a *mitzvah*, but this does not disprove that when performed together they constitute one halakhic unit.

### Yochanan Extreme

The *gemara* then asks whose position is served by the statement of Rav Kahana: *ein bein tekiah li-teruah ve-lo klum* — there is absolutely no pause whatsoever between *tekiah* and *teruah*. One might think this statement is so basic that it would be agreed upon by all. But the *gemara* clarifies that it is specifically coming to exclude the extreme position of Rabbi Yochanan: *d'amar shama tesha tekiot b'tesha sha'ot ha-yom yatza* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that on Rosh Hashanah, if one heard the nine *tekiot* spread across nine different hours of the day, one has fulfilled the obligation. This is a dramatic position — not only are the sounds conceptually distinct, they need not even be grouped together; they can be heard individually over the course of an entire day.

### Resolution

The *gemara* initially suggests that Rav Kahana's statement need not go as far as Rabbi Yehuda; perhaps it is simply rejecting Rabbi Yochanan's extreme position, saying that while the sounds are distinct, one cannot space them hours apart — without claiming they must be blown with literally zero pause. The *gemara* rejects this: *im ken mai ve-lo klum* — if that were the intent, the statement would simply say do not interrupt; the emphatic phrase *ve-lo klum*, not even the slightest pause, indicates that this is indeed the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the entire unit is blown without any break at all.

The result is three logically distinct positions. Rabbi Yehuda holds that *tekiah-teruah-tekiah* is one halakhic unit, blown without any pause. The Sages hold that the sounds are distinct, with a pause between them, though they must presumably be grouped in reasonably close succession. And Rabbi Yochanan takes the most expansive view: the sounds are fully independent and can even be heard across nine separate hours of the day. The dispute ranges from one continuous sound to a unit of three tightly grouped sounds to three entirely independent sonic events spread over the course of a day.

---

---

# Sukkah 54

## Opening & Dedication

### Rivka Haut Memorial

Our learning today is dedicated *le'ilui nishmata* — to the elevation of the soul of Rivka Haut, whose funeral was held this morning. She was a truly important member of our community — of the *daf* community, and of the broader Orthodox Jewish world. Particularly as we witness the ongoing and worsening situation of *agunot*, her tremendous work on their behalf, and on behalf of so many people, deserves to be remembered and honored. May her memory always be for a blessing.

### Daf Navigation

We begin at the top of 56a, the last *daf* of *Masechet Sukkah*, picking up six lines from the top.

---

## Shavuot Offerings

### Shavuot Division

*Be'atzeret omer lo heilach* — "On *Shavuot* he says to him, here take" — and so on. This passage discusses how, on the *Regalim*, all the *Kohanim* would gather at the *Beit Hamikdash* and divide both the service and the eating of the offerings equally. Normally, the *Lechem Hapanim* — the showbread — was not a *regel*-specific matter; as we will see shortly, its standard division was between the outgoing and incoming priestly shifts. Nevertheless, based on a *pasuk*, on *Shavuot* the *Lechem Hapanim* was divided equally among all the *Kohanim* who had gathered for the *regel*.

In addition to the *Lechem Hapanim*, on *Shavuot* they would also divide the *Shtei Halechem* — the two loaves — which were *chametz*, the distinctive offering of that *chag*. Every *kohen* thus received a small portion of *chametz* and a small portion of *matzah*.

### Mishnah Order

The *Mishnah* states: *heilach matzah heilach chametz* — "here is your *matzah*, here is your *chametz*." It is worth noting that the *Mishnah* mentions *matzah* first. This reflects a preference for the more common item — the *Lechem Hapanim*, which is *matzah* — over the *chametz* of the *Shtei Halechem*, which is distinctive to the particular *chag* of *Shavuot*. This ordering will become central to the discussion that follows.

---

## Blessing Order Debate

### Rava's Position

The *Gemara* now launches into a fascinating discussion that, while perhaps better suited to an earlier point in *Masechet Sukkah*, is introduced here as the *masechet* nears its end and tied into this *Mishnah*. *Itmar* — it was stated: *Rava amar sukkah ve'achar kach zman* — Rava holds that on the first night of *Sukkot*, when reciting the blessings, one first says *leishev basukkah* and only then says *Shehecheyanu*.

### Rabbah's Position

*Rabbah bar Bar Chana amar zman ve'achar kach sukkah* — Rabbah bar Bar Chana holds the opposite: one recites *Shehecheyanu* first, and then says *leishev basukkah*.

As background, it is worth recalling that according to an earlier *baraita* cited in the *Gemara*, one is supposed to recite *Shehecheyanu* when building the *sukkah*, not only when one enters it on *Sukkot*. In practice, however, even by the time of the *Gemara*, this was not universally observed — at least one *amora* would bundle both blessings together over the *cos* when reciting *Kiddush* on the first night, rather than saying *Shehecheyanu* at the earlier moment of construction. *Rashi* explains that the scenario under discussion applies when one forgot to say *Shehecheyanu* earlier, or when one is in someone else's *sukkah* and therefore did not build one.

It is also important to recall that the *Shehecheyanu* recited on the first night serves a double function: one dimension connects it to the commencement of the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* — which is why it could in principle have been recited when the *sukkah* was built — and the other is the *Shehecheyanu* said at the outset of every *Yom Tov*, which marks the arrival of a new festival. This second function is entirely independent of any particular *mitzvah*, just as one recites *Shehecheyanu* on *Shavuot* night without it being linked to any specific *mitzvah* — it is simply a *Shehecheyanu* on the *yom*.

### Distinctive vs. Common

The underlying question, then, is: when ordering two *brachot*, do we prioritize the one that is more distinctive to the occasion, or the one that is more commonly recited?

### Chiyuva D'Yoma

Rava's reasoning is: *chiyuva de'yoma adif* — the obligation of the day takes priority. One begins with the *mitzvah* that is unique to this moment — *leishev basukkah*. The *Shehecheyanu*, while connected to the *mitzvah*, is in some sense secondary to it; moreover, *leishev basukkah* is the *bracha* that most distinctively identifies the character of the day, whereas *Shehecheyanu* is a far more generic blessing applicable across many circumstances.

### Tadir Principle
