Rabbah bar Bar Chana's reasoning is: *tadir ve-she'eino tadir, tadir kodem* — when one item is more common and another less so, the more common one comes first. He acknowledges that *Shehecheyanu* is broad and abstract, applying in a wide range of situations. That breadth, he argues, is precisely the reason it should be said first.

The *Gemara* has thus framed the core dispute: is priority given to the more *distinctive* blessing, or to the more *common* one?

---

## Beit Shammai vs. Hillel

### Beit Shammai View

The *Gemara* now asks: *leima Rav ve-Rabbah bar bar Chana bi-plugta de-Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel ka-mifligi* — perhaps these two *Amoraim* are simply reprising the famous dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. *De-tanu Rabbanan* — for the Rabbis taught: *devarim she-bein Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel bi-se'udah* — the matters of dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerning a meal. We focus on the first item in that list. *Beit Shammai omrim: mevarech al ha-yom ve'achar kach mevarech al ha-yayin* — Beit Shammai holds that for *Kiddush*, one first recites the blessing over the day — *Mekadesh HaShabbat* — and only afterward *Borei Peri HaGafen*. This is, of course, the reverse of our practice.

### Beit Hillel View

*U-Veit Hillel omrim: mevarech al ha-yayin ve'achar kach mevarech al ha-yom* — Beit Hillel holds that one begins with *Borei Peri HaGafen* and then recites *Mekadesh HaShabbat*, which is indeed the practice we follow.

### Shammai's Reasoning

What is Beit Shammai's reason? *Beit Shammai omrim: mevarech al ha-yom ve'achar kach mevarech al ha-yayin* — first *Mekadesh HaShabbat*, then *Borei Peri HaGafen*. The first reason: *she-ha-yom goreim la-yayin she-yavo* — the day is the cause of the wine's arrival. Were it not *Shabbat*, there would be no particular reason to be making *Kiddush*, and while one might say *Borei Peri HaGafen* simply because one wishes to drink wine, the structured ritual of *Kiddush* is entirely a product of *Shabbat*. You therefore begin with the anchor of the whole enterprise — the sanctity of the day.

The second reason: *u-khevar kidesh ha-yom ve-adayin yayin lo ba* — chronologically, *Shabbat* has already arrived before *Kiddush* is recited. Even if one may formally accept *Shabbat* early, in the normal order of things *Shabbat* precedes the act of *Kiddush* — both conceptually and chronologically. It is therefore logically fitting to begin with *Mekadesh HaShabbat*.

### Hillel's Reasoning

*U-Veit Hillel omrim: mevarech al ha-yayin ve'achar kach mevarech al ha-yom* — Beit Hillel says you begin with *Borei Peri HaGafen*. First reason: *she-ha-yayin goreim le-Kiddush she-te'amer* — it is the wine that enables *Kiddush* to be recited. It is true that *Kiddush* is said because it is *Shabbat*; but what transforms this moment into a proper act of *Kiddush* is the presence of wine (or bread, in which case one would recite *Hamotzi Lechem Min HaAretz* first). The medium of *Kiddush* therefore comes first.

Second reason, *davar acher*: *birchat ha-yayin tedira, u-virchat ha-yom einah tedira* — the blessing *Borei Peri HaGafen* is a more frequently recited blessing, while the blessing *Mekadesh HaShabbat* is said less often. *Tadir ve-she'eino tadir, tadir kodem* — when one blessing is more common and another less so, the more common one precedes.

Focusing on the reasons most relevant to our discussion: Beit Hillel holds that one says the more common blessing first, i.e., *Borei Peri HaGafen*; and Beit Shammai holds that one says the more distinctive blessing first — the one that defines and occasions the entire ritual, *Mekadesh HaShabbat*. The parallel to the debate about *sukkah* and *Shehecheyanu* seems clear: should one begin with the more common *Shehecheyanu*, or with the more distinctive *leishev basukkah*?

### Amoraim Alignment

The *Gemara* asks: *leima Rav d'amar ke-Veit Shammai, ve-Rabbah bar bar Chana d'amar ke-Veit Hillel* — does it follow that Rav, who says *sukkah* first, is aligned with Beit Shammai, who say the blessing over the day first; and Rabbah bar Bar Chana, who says *Shehecheyanu* first, is aligned with Beit Hillel, who say *Borei Peri HaGafen* first?

### Rav's Distinction

The *Gemara* rejects this mapping. *Amar lach Rav: ana d'amri afilu ke-Veit Hillel* — Rav would say: I hold my position even according to Beit Hillel. Why? *Ad kan lo ka'amri Veit Hillel hatam ela she-ha-yayin goreim le-Kiddush she-te'amer* — Beit Hillel's primary reason for saying *Borei Peri HaGafen* first is not the principle of *tadir* at all. Their *ikkar* reason is that wine is what constitutes *Kiddush* — the wine is not merely accompanying the blessing; it is what makes the act into *Kiddush* in the first place. The reason of *tadir* is secondary.

*Aval hacha* — but here, *ilav zman mi lo amrinan sukkah* — if you were not saying *Shehecheyanu*, would you not still say *leishev basukkah* and sit in the *sukkah*? Of course you would. The *Shehecheyanu* is not what enables or constitutes the *mitzvah* of sitting in a *sukkah*. It does not play the role that wine plays in *Kiddush*. And since their primary reason does not apply here, Rav maintains that the *sukkah* blessing comes first, even according to Beit Hillel.

### Rabbah's Counter

*Rabbah bar bar Chana amar lach: ana damya afilu ke-Veit Shammai* — Rabbah bar Bar Chana would counter: I hold my position even according to Beit Shammai. Why? *Ad kan lo amri Veit Shammai hatam ela she-ha-yom goreim la-yayin she-yavo* — Beit Shammai's reason for putting the blessing over the day first is that *Shabbat* is the cause of the wine's being brought for *Kiddush*. You begin with the thing that occasions the whole ritual, and the wine follows from it.

*Aval hacha, ilav sukkah mi lo amrinan zman* — but here, even without *sukkah*, would we not say *Shehecheyanu*? Yes, we would — because *Shehecheyanu* has independent significance. As *Rashi* notes, even someone traveling on the road with no access to a *sukkah* would still recite *Shehecheyanu* because it is *Yom Tov*. The *Shehecheyanu* here is not the *Shehecheyanu* of the *mitzvah* of *sukkah*; it is the *Shehecheyanu* of the *chag* itself, and that would be said regardless.

Rabbah bar Bar Chana thus makes a powerful argument on two levels. First, *Shehecheyanu* is *tadir* — more commonly recited than *leishev basukkah*. Second, and more decisively, the *Shehecheyanu* here is not merely an appendage to the *sukkah* blessing; it possesses independent standing, connected to the sanctity of the *chag* rather than to the act of sitting in a *sukkah*. Since the two blessings are thus not linked to each other the way wine and *Kiddush* are, the *tadir* principle applies in full: the more common blessing, *Shehecheyanu*, comes first.

The observation is made that the *Amoraim* are doing something we see elsewhere as well: when a *tanna* or *amora* gives two reasons for a position, a later authority may argue that one of those two reasons is the *ikkar* — the primary one — while the other is secondary. By showing which reason is genuinely operative, each *amora* can maintain his own ruling even while nominally accepting the other school's framework.

---

## Mishnah Evidence

### Matzah Before Chametz

*Tenan* — we have learned in our *Mishnah*: *Atzeret omer lo heilach matzah heilach chametz* — on *Shavuot* they say, here is your *matzah* from the *Lechem Hapanim*, and here is your *chametz* from the *Shtei Halechem*. Now, *v'hacha de-chametz ikkar matzah tafel* — here the *chametz* is the more distinctive item (it is what is unique to *Shavuot*) and the *matzah* is the more generic item — yet the *Mishnah* lists *matzah* first. This demonstrates that we prefer the more common item, following the *tadir* principle, over what is distinctive to the day. The *Gemara* concludes that this is precisely what the dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar Bar Chana hinges on — *tadir* versus what is distinctive to the occasion — and that both sides have agreed this is not directly parallel to the Beit Shammai / Beit Hillel debate.

*Tiyuvta de-Rav* — this constitutes a refutation of Rav's position, since the *Mishnah* appears to rule in favor of the *tadir* principle, supporting Rabbah bar Bar Chana.

### Abba Shaul Dissent

The *Gemara* responds: *amar lach Rav tanna'ei hi* — Rav will say it is a dispute among *Tannaim*. For a *baraita* reports: the main text records *heilach matzah ve-heilach chametz*, mentioning *matzah* first, but *Abba Shaul omer: heilach chametz ve-heilach matzah* — Abba Shaul dissents and holds that *chametz* is mentioned first, because it is distinctive to *Shavuot*, and *matzah* follows as the more generic item.

### Rav Minority

Thus, Rav's position aligns with the minority view of Abba Shaul, while the mainstream ruling follows the principle of *tadir* — listing the more common item first.

---

## Final Ruling

### Rav Nachman Ruling

*Darash Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda: lo ke-divrei Rav de-amar sukkah ve'achar kach zman, ella zman ve'achar kach sukkah* — Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda ruled publicly that we do not follow Rav's position. Rather, we say *Shehecheyanu* first and then *leishev basukkah*.

### Rav Sheshet Support

*Rav Sheshet brei de-Rav Idi amar: sukkah ve'achar kach zman* — Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi, however, counters that one says *sukkah* first and then *Shehecheyanu*, in accordance with Rav.

### Halacha: Sukkah First

*Ve-hilchta sukkah ve'achar kach zman* — the final ruling is that one says *leishev basukkah* first and *Shehecheyanu* second.

### Parallel Mitzvot

This follows the natural pattern established across other *mitzvot*: just as one says *al netilat lulav* and then *Shehecheyanu*, and just as one says *le-hadlik ner shel Chanukah* and then *Shehecheyanu*, so too with *sukkah* — the *birchat ha-mitzvah* precedes *Shehecheyanu*. In those parallel cases, the *Shehecheyanu* is unambiguously linked to the *mitzvah* itself and is not doing double duty as a festival blessing. It is worth noting a certain irony: according to the *baraita* cited earlier in the tractate and the *ikkar halacha*, *Shehecheyanu* should ideally be said when one begins to construct the *lulav* or build the *sukkah*. But if one did not do so at that point and waited until the performance of the *mitzvah*, then one says the *birchat ha-mitzvah* first and *Shehecheyanu* second.

### Second Day Exception

There remains the question of *Shehecheyanu*'s independent role as a festival blessing. Some *siddurim* note that on the second night of *Yom Tov*, the order is reversed: *Shehecheyanu* is said before *leishev basukkah*. This is not merely an attempt to satisfy all opinions; the reversal is principled.

On the first night, the *Shehecheyanu* serves double duty — it functions both as the *Shehecheyanu* for the *mitzvah* of *sukkah* and as the *Shehecheyanu* of *Kiddush* for the new *Yom Tov*. When it functions as the *Shehecheyanu* of the *mitzvah*, it naturally follows *leishev basukkah*, just as it follows *al netilat lulav* and *le-hadlik ner shel Chanukah*. But by the second night, the *Shehecheyanu* connected to *leishev basukkah* is no longer at issue — the *mitzvah* has already been introduced. Even in the *sefika de-yoma* framework of the second day of *Yom Tov*, the *Shehecheyanu* tied to the *sukkah* itself was already discharged on the first night (or, in principle, when building the *sukkah*).

What remains on the second night is exclusively the *Shehecheyanu* of *Kiddush* — the *zman* recited at the start of a *Yom Tov*, as on the second night of *Shavuot* or *Pesach*, where no *mitzvah* is involved. Since this *Shehecheyanu* belongs to the *Kiddush*, and since *Kiddush* concludes with *Mekadesh Yisrael ve-ha-zmanim*, the *Shehecheyanu* follows as an organic conclusion to that blessing. Only afterward does one recite *leishev basukkah*. The dynamic has thus fundamentally changed: on the first night, the *Shehecheyanu* of the *sukkah* takes center stage, and since the *birchat ha-mitzvah* precedes its *Shehecheyanu*, *leishev basukkah* comes first. On the second night, only the *Shehecheyanu* of *Kiddush* remains, and it follows *Mekadesh Yisrael ve-ha-zmanim* before *leishev basukkah*.

---

## Communal Sacrifices

### Mishmar Division

The *Mishnah* now concludes by specifying what was *not* subject to equal division: *mishmar she-zmano kavu'a v'she'ar korbanot tzibbur* — things that were not unique to the *chag* would not be divided equally. The regular communal offerings — the *tamid* and *musaf* — were not distinctive to the *regel*, and would therefore go to the *mishmar* whose turn it actually was. Private *vows and freewill offerings* likewise belonged to the relevant *mishmar*.

### Other Communal

*V'she'ar korbanot tzibbur la'atuyei mai* — what do the other communal offerings mentioned in the *Mishnah* come to include? *La'atuyei par he-alem davar shel tzibbur u-se'irei avodat kochavim* — they include the bull brought when the *Beit Din* issues an erroneous ruling that the entire community follows, and the goats brought when the community collectively commits an act of idolatry. These communal sin offerings are not linked to the festival calendar, yet they would be brought if the occasion arose, and all *Kohanim* present would participate.

### Kayitz Ha-Mizbeiach

*La'atuyei kayitz ha-mizbe'ach* — the phrase *ve-hu makriv et ha-kol* also comes to include the *kayitz ha-mizbe'ach*, which *Rashi* describes as the "dessert" or surplus fund of the altar. When animals were redeemed or other funds accumulated, the money was directed to this dedicated pool. If there were times when no offerings were being brought, it would be unseemly for the altar to stand idle, so these communal funds were used to purchase burnt offerings that would keep the altar active. This too was included in the category of offerings brought during the festival.

---

## Yom Tov & Shabbat

### Yom Tov-Shabbat Adjacency

The *Mishnah* turns to a special calendrical scenario: *Yom Tov ha-samuch le-Shabbat bein milfaneha bein me-achareha* — when *Yom Tov* falls immediately adjacent to *Shabbat*, whether immediately before or immediately after. This cannot occur under the fixed calendar in use today, but in the era of the *Beit Hamikdash* it was a real possibility. If, for example, *Sukkot* began on Sunday, *Kohanim* would have had to arrive a day early — on Friday — since they could not travel on *Shabbat*. Alternatively, if the last day of *Yom Tov* fell on Friday, *Kohanim* could not depart immediately afterward and would be stuck for an extra *Shabbat*. In either case, *Kohanim* were obligated to be present for an additional day that was not technically the *regel* itself.

---

## Communal Sacrifices…

### Tamid/Musaf Exclusion

*Mashmash she-zmano kavu'a* — the *mishmar* with the fixed assignment on *Shabbat* would not equally divide the *tamid* and *musaf* of that *Shabbat* with the others. The reasoning is that even on the *regel* itself, when *Kohanim* were present and required to be there, the *tamid* and *musaf* were not distinctive to the *regel* and were therefore not shared equally. By the same logic, the *Shabbat* which merely flanked the *regel* certainly confers no entitlement to those offerings.

---

## Yom Tov & Shabbat…

### All Mishmarot Equal

*Yom Tov ha-samuch le-Shabbat bein milfaneha bein me-achareha hayu kol ha-mishmarot shavot be-chiluk Lechem Hapanim* — when *Yom Tov* was directly adjacent to *Shabbat*, all the priestly divisions shared equally in the distribution of the *Lechem Hapanim*. The *Lechem Hapanim* is divided on *Shabbat*, precisely when the change of guard takes place. Since all *Kohanim* had been compelled to remain or to arrive early because of the juxtaposition of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* — they had no choice — all groups share equally in the *Lechem Hapanim* of that *Shabbat*.

### One-Day Gap Division

*Chal yom echad le-hafsik bein-tayim* — if there was a single intervening day between *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* — for example, *Shabbat*, then Sunday, then the first day of *Yom Tov* on Monday, or the last day of *Yom Tov* on Thursday followed by Friday *Shabbat* — the situation changes. In those circumstances, while many *Kohanim* would in practice arrive early or stay late (since traveling home and back within a single day was very difficult), they were not technically required to do so. These *Kohanim* therefore receive only a reduced share: *mishmar she-zmano kavu'a hayah notel eser chalos* — the two *mishmarot* that were the fixed shifts for that *Shabbat* (the one departing and the one arriving) received ten of the twelve loaves between them, while *ve-ha-mitakev* — the extra *Kohanim* who stayed late or came early — received only two loaves to divide among themselves.

---

## Regular Lechem Division

### Six-Six Division

Returning to the standard weekly arrangement: *u-vi-she'ar yemot ha-shanah, ha-nichnas notel shesh ve-ha-yotze notel shesh* — in the normal course of the year, the incoming *mishmar* and the outgoing *mishmar* each receive six loaves of *Lechem Hapanim*, dividing the twelve equally.

### Seven-Five Division

*Rabbi Yehuda omer: ha-nichnas notel sheva ve-ha-yotze notel chamesh* — Rabbi Yehuda disagrees. He holds that the incoming *mishmar* receives seven loaves and the outgoing *mishmar* receives five. As the *Gemara* will explain, this differential reflects an additional task that falls upon the incoming group.

### North-South Placement

*Ha-nichnasin cholkin ba-tzafon ve-ha-yotzin ba-darom* — the incoming *mishmar* divides its loaves in the northern part of the *Azara*, and the outgoing *mishmar* divides in the south. The north is the holier and more prestigious area of the *Azara*: it is there that *kodshei kodashim* — the most sacred category of offerings — must be slaughtered, as the Torah requires *al yerech ha-mizbe'ach tzafonah* — on the northern side of the altar. Accordingly, the north carries greater status, and that higher-status position is assigned to those arriving, who are about to take up their week of service, while those departing are situated in the south. There is also a practical function: distinguishing the two groups spatially makes it obvious who is coming in and who is going out, serving as a visible reminder to the incoming *mishmar* of where their primary obligations lie.

The *Mishnah* then introduces the exception of the *mishmar* of *Bilgah*, which will be addressed in detail shortly: *Bilgah le-olam choleket ba-darom* — the division of *Bilgah* always takes place in the south, even when it is the incoming group. Furthermore, *ve-taba'atah kavu'ah* — its ring, used to secure the neck of an animal before *shechitah*, was permanently fixed shut, and *ve-chalonoteha setumah* — its cubbyhole where its knives were stored was sealed. Clearly *Bilgah* had been subjected to a lasting penalty, the reasons for which the *Gemara* will now explore.

---

## Yom Tov & Shabbat…

### Communal Eating

*Mai ta'ama? Keivan de-hani makdemi ve-hani maachari* — what is the reason all groups divide equally when *Yom Tov* is directly adjacent to *Shabbat*? Since in those cases some groups had to arrive early and others had to depart late, with no choice in the matter, *tikkenu rabbanan milta ke-hei de-neichu be-hadei hadadi* — the Rabbis established an arrangement so that everyone should eat together. The phrasing is telling: not merely that it was fair for those present to receive a share, but that the Rabbis specifically wanted the *Kohanim* to eat together as a community. Everyone is there, and the desire was for communal eating, not just equitable distribution.

---

## Regular Lechem Divisio…

### Door Closing Reward

The *Gemara* asks regarding Rabbi Yehuda's position: *ve-hanei tartei mai avidteihu* — why do the incoming *mishmar* receive two extra loaves according to Rabbi Yehuda? *Amar Rav Yitzchak: bi-s'char hagafat delatot* — because of the reward for closing the doors that were opened by the outgoing group. The departing *mishmar* opened the doors, and now the incoming group must close them behind them. There is something quite striking about this reasoning: it is another group's task being completed — "you started it, and now I have to finish your job" — and yet this minor extra responsibility apparently warranted a meaningful material reward relative to the week of service ahead.

### Dal B'Dal Logic

The *Gemara* asks: *ve-neima lei dal be-dal* — why not simply say it all evens out? *Rashi* explains that *dal* means "to remove" — what is taken from you equals what is taken from me. *Rabbeinu Chananel* offers a somewhat different reading: *di li ve-di lei* — belonging to me and belonging to you — so that *dal be-dal* means that whatever one gains, the other loses, and over time it all balances out. The logic would be: the incoming group gets seven this week, but next week when they are the outgoing group they will get only five. So why not simply keep it at six throughout?

### Bird in Hand

*Amar Abaye: butzina tava mi-kara* — Abaye responds with a folk idiom that captures the principle of a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush. *Butzina* is a small gourd that ripens quickly; *kara* is a large gourd that takes much longer to mature. If offered the choice between the small gourd now or waiting weeks for the large one, one takes the small gourd immediately. So too, the incoming group would say: yes, when we depart in a week we will receive only five — but we will worry about that then. Right now, give us seven.

The deeper point seems to be about the deliberate elevation of those arriving. Giving the incoming *mishmar* the north side, an extra loaf, and framing their arrival as a moment of distinction — all this seems designed, in Rabbi Yehuda's view, to build a sense of honor and significance for those beginning their week of service. The one who has been there all week is on the way out; the one arriving is being welcomed and honored.

---

## Musaf Distribution

### Rav Yehuda View

*Amar Rav Yehuda: u-ve-musafim cholkin* — Rav Yehuda holds that both the incoming and outgoing *mishmarot* divide the skins of the *musaf* offerings between them. The context here is that on *Shabbat*, the *musaf* consists of two lambs brought as burnt offerings, so there is no meat to be eaten — but the skins of the animals would still be divided among the *Kohanim*.

### Baraita Contradiction

*Meisivei* — an objection is raised from a *baraita*: *mishmarah ha-yotzeis osah Tamid shel Shachar u-musafim. Mishmarah ha-nichneises osah Tamid shel bein ha-arbayim u-vazichin* — the outgoing *mishmar* performed the morning *tamid* and the *musafim*, while the incoming *mishmar* performed the afternoon *tamid* and the incense cup service (*vazichin*) — the offering of the two small cups of frankincense that accompanied the *Lechem Hapanim* and enabled it to be eaten. *Ve-ilu musafim cholkin lo katani* — and yet the *baraita* does not state that the *musaf* was divided between both groups. This appears to contradict Rav Yehuda's position.

### Leather Division

*Amar Rav Yehuda: be-mai? Be-oros* — Rav Yehuda clarifies: when I said they divide the *musaf*, I was speaking not about who performs the *avodah* but about who receives the skins. The *baraita* addresses the question of which group performs the service; I am addressing the question of how the benefit — the skins — is distributed. I acknowledge that the *avodah* of the *musaf* is performed by the outgoing *mishmar*; I claim only that its leather is divided between both groups.

### Joint Lechem Removal

*Amar Rava* — Rava then cites a *tanna* from the school of *Shmuel* who directly addresses the question of division of benefits. *De-tanna devei Shmuel*: *mishmarah ha-yotzeis osah Tamid shel Shachar u-musafim. Mishmarah ha-nichneises osah Tamid shel bein ha-arbayim u-vazichin. Arba'ah Kohanim hayu nichnasin sham, shnayim mi-mishmar zu u-shnayim mi-mishmar zu, ve-cholkin Lechem Hapanim* — four *Kohanim* would enter together for the removal of the *Lechem Hapanim*: two from the outgoing *mishmar* and two from the incoming *mishmar*, and together they would divide the *Lechem Hapanim*.

This detail reflects a beautifully coordinated transition. The *shulchan* — the table — had shelves open at both ends. As the incoming *Kohanim* slid the new loaves in from one side, the outgoing *Kohanim* drew the old ones out from the other side. The two groups worked in tandem, and that joint participation in the removal of the bread was naturally mirrored in the equal division of the loaves between them.

Crucially, this source from the school of *Shmuel* is discussing not merely who performs the *avodah* but who benefits from it — it explicitly addresses the division of the *Lechem Hapanim*. And since it discusses the division of benefits in detail:

### Final Contradiction

*Ve-ilu musafim cholkin lo katani* — it does not state that the *musaf* skins were divided between the two groups. This is a source that directly concerns benefit distribution, not merely service assignment, and it does not support Rav Yehuda's claim that the *musaf* skins were shared. *Tiyuvta de-Rav Yehuda tiyuvta* — this stands as a full refutation of Rav Yehuda's position. The *musaf* skins were not divided equally; the *Lechem Hapanim* was a joint undertaking with joint benefits, but the *musaf* belonged entirely to the group that performed its service.

*Rashi* raises the question of what the *hava amina* even was for sharing the *musaf* skins, given that the morning *mishmar* clearly brought them. He answers that the incoming *mishmar* did have some residual involvement — they would tend to the meat still burning on the altar, rotating or pushing back pieces that had not yet been fully consumed, completing the work of those who came before them. Nevertheless, the *musaf* was fundamentally the outgoing group's *avodah*, and they retained its skin entirely. The *Lechem Hapanim*, by contrast, was a genuinely joint service, and was divided jointly.

---

## Bilgah Penalty

### Bilgah South Always

*Bilgah le-olam choleket ba-darom* — the *mishmar* of *Bilgah* always divides its bread in the south, even when it is the incoming group taking up its week of service. Moreover, its ring used for *shechitah* was permanently fastened, and its cubbyhole for knives was sealed.

### Miriam Apostasy

*Tanu Rabbanan. Maaseh be-Miriam bat Bilgah* — the Rabbis taught: there was an incident involving Miriam the daughter of *Bilgah*. To be precise, she was not literally the daughter of the division's founder — the twenty-four *mishmarot* were established far back in the *Bayit Rishon* period — but she was from the family that belonged to the *mishmar* of *Bilgah*. *She-himira datah* — she became an apostate, rejecting Judaism entirely. This occurred during the period of the *Yevanim* — the Greek-Seleucid dominion — and she identified fully with Hellenism. *Ve-halcha ve-nisset le-sardyot echad mi-malchei Yevanim* — she went and married an officer in the Greek army.

It is worth pausing to note the broader context. We tend to think of the *Chanukah* story as a conflict between Jews and Greeks, but in reality much of the struggle was internal — between observant Jews and Hellenizing Jews. Large numbers of Jews enthusiastically embraced Greek culture and sought to dismantle the distinctives of Jewish religious life. Miriam bat Bilgah was squarely in this camp.

### Altar Desecration

*Keshe-nichnesu Yevanim le-heichal* — when the Greeks entered the *Heichal*, Miriam was with them. *Hayatah meva'etet be-sandalah al gabei ha-mizbe'ach* — she was kicking the altar with her sandal. *Ve-amerat lo: Lukus Lukus* — and she said to it, *wolf, wolf* — *ad matai atah mechaleh mamonam shel Yisrael ve-i atah omeid lahem be-sha'at hadechak* — how long will you consume the wealth of the Jewish people, and yet you are not there to defend them in their hour of need?

She was thus doing two things simultaneously: performing a public act of desecration and offering a rationalization for her apostasy. The altar had taken the people's resources and had not protected them when they needed it most.

### Punishment Imposed

*Keshe-shamu chachamim ba-davar* — when the Sages heard of this, they imposed a lasting penalty on the entire *mishmar* of *Bilgah*: *kave'u et taba'atah* — they permanently fixed its ring; *ve-satmu et chalonah* — and they sealed its cubbyhole.

### Negligence Theory

*Ve-yeish omrim* — an alternative explanation for the penalty: *mishmarto she-hi-lo lavo ve-nichnas Yeshevav achiv immo ve-shimeish tachtav* — on a given *Shabbat*, the *mishmar* of *Bilgah* simply failed to show up for their assigned week of service. *Yeshevav*, the *mishmar* that had preceded them, had to stay on and cover for them, performing the service in their place. This ongoing negligence — an apparently systemic failure to fulfill their responsibilities — was what occasioned the permanent penalty.

---

## Collective Punishment

### Punishment Question

The *Gemara* raises a pointed question. *Bishlama le-man de-amar mishmarto she-hayah lo lavo* — if you adopt the second explanation, that the entire *mishmar* was habitually negligent, then the collective punishment is understandable — *hainu de-kansinan le-chulah mishmar*, that is why we penalize the entire group. But *ella le-man de-amar Miriam bat Bilgah she-hemira datah* — according to the first explanation, which attributes everything to one woman's apostasy — *mishum barta kansinan le-dideih* — because of his daughter, we fine the entire *mishmar* of *Bilgah*? Is that fair? One individual's act of rebellion becomes the basis for collective punishment of an entire priestly division?

### Neighbor Fate

*Amar Abaye: in* — yes, says Abaye, that is the principle. And here is why.

### Home Influence

*Hainami inshi: shuta de-yanuka be-shuka, o de-avuha o de-imeih* — as people say: the casual talk of a child in the marketplace — where did he pick it up? From his father or his mother. The premise is that a child's attitudes, speech, and instilled values are a product of the home environment. When Miriam bat Bilgah performed this public act of desecration — kicking the altar, mocking its function, rationalizing her abandonment of Judaism in terms of the altar's failure to protect the Jewish people — this was not merely a personal deviation. An attitude of contempt for the *avodah* and cynicism about what the *Beit Hamikdash* represents does not arise in a vacuum; it is cultivated. *Rashi* notes that this does not mean every act of apostasy should be attributed to parental failure, but that Miriam's specific public act — its boldness, its articulate theological contempt — reflects attitudes that must have permeated her environment. That environment was the *mishmar* of *Bilgah*, and therefore the community bears some measure of responsibility for what she became.

The *Gemara* then extends the challenge: *u-mishum avuha ve-imeih kansinan le-chulah mishmar* — granted, her immediate family bears responsibility, but on that basis we punish the entire *mishmar* — hundreds or thousands of families? *Amar Abaye: oi le-rasha oi li-shcheno* — says Abaye: woe to the wicked person and woe to his neighbor.

### Woe/Blessing Principle

There are two dimensions to this principle. Sometimes the community genuinely shares in the responsibility for what one of its members does — the communal environment, attitudes, and failures of intervention contribute to the individual's conduct. In those cases, the collective punishment is in some sense deserved.

But Abaye acknowledges a second dimension as well: sometimes the collective punishment is not fully deserved, yet the community is caught in the crossfire. *Oi le-rasha oi li-shcheno* — when disaster comes to the wicked, those nearby suffer with them, not necessarily because they earned it but simply because that is how proximity works. And there is, in this painful dynamic, a constructive purpose: from this point forward, communities will exert pressure on their members to ensure that such things do not recur.

The principle cuts both ways: *tov la-tzaddik tov li-shcheno* — good for the righteous person and good for his neighbor. *She-ne'emar: imru tzaddik ki tov ki pri ma'alaleihem yocheilu* — as it is said, *declare the righteous one to be good, for the fruit of their deeds they will eat* — note the shift from the singular *tzaddik* to the plural *ma'alaleihem*: not only will the *tzaddik* eat of the fruits of righteousness, but multiple people will benefit. The neighbors, the community, those in proximity to the *tzaddik* — all share in the blessing that flows from associating with goodness. This is the positive counterpart to the tragedy of *Bilgah*: surround yourself with good company and a good community, and you benefit from them as well.

---

## Conclusion

### Thematic Reflection

*Hadran alach ha-chalil u-selika lach Masechet Sukkah* — we have completed *Masechet Sukkah*.

It is admittedly difficult to know what to make of this as an ending to the tractate. *Masechet Sukkah* is so richly about the *sukkah* — about dwelling in God's presence, about the intimacy of inhabiting a sacred space — and yet it closes with an extended discussion of the *Lechem Hapanim* and the extraordinary story of *Bilgah* and Miriam.

One thread that seems to connect these final passages is a theme of *dialogue* — of speaking to and within a sacred space. Throughout *Masechet Sukkah*, we encountered moments of direct address to the *Beit Hamikdash* and its vessels: when the *Kohanim* would exit the *aravah* service, they would say *yofi lach mizbe'ach, yofi lach mizbe'ach* — beautiful are you, altar, beautiful are you, altar. When they would turn to depart from the *nisuch ha-mayim*, they would declare *anu la-Ya ve-eineinu la-Ya* — we are God's and our eyes are toward God. *Hillel* himself, we learned, gave voice to what was almost a divine response in dialogue: *im ani kan ha-kol kan* — if I am here, everything is here. And here, at the very end, we have Miriam bat Bilgah speaking to the altar — albeit in a mode of desecration and contempt.

Perhaps this is part of what *Sukkot* is ultimately about: the intimacy of being in God's house creates the conditions for dialogue. The *sukkah* is about bringing God into our dwelling and ourselves into God's space — and that proximity generates conversation, both the holy and, tragically, the profane. The very capacity for intimate address can be turned either toward devotion or toward contempt.

One might also say — in the spirit of *drush* — that the *masechet* ends with a reminder that even within the *Beit Hamikdash*, the complications of family and community are never absent. The move from the elevated world of *Sukkot* back into ordinary life, back into the house, involves a reckoning with the reality that even the most sacred settings are inhabited by real human beings and real communities — and communities bear responsibility for one another.

### Next Masechet

Tomorrow we begin *Masechet Beitzah*.

---

---

# Sukkah 55

## One Shir, One Tekia

### Rosh Chodesh Unity

We pick up with three lines from the top of 55a, continuing the discussion of what would be done for each separate *musaf* on a day when multiple *musafim* coincide. The question has two intertwined dimensions: would they perform separate blasts of the trumpets (*chatzotzrot*) for each *musaf*, and would they recite a separate *shir shel yom* for each? The claim under scrutiny is that yes, separate sets would be performed — but the *Gemara* now moves toward decisively closing that off.

*Meitvei* — the *Gemara* raises a challenge: *d'tani Rabba Bar Shmuel* — as Rabba bar Shmuel taught in a *baraita*: *Yachol k'shem she-tokin al Shabbat bifnei atzmah v'al Rosh Chodesh bifnei atzmo* — perhaps just as you have a separate set of blasts for the *Shabbat musaf* by itself and for *Rosh Chodesh* by itself, when they coincide you would likewise have separate blasts for each? *Talmud lomar u'vroshei chodsheichem* — the verse teaches otherwise: *Ani Rosh Chodesh* — I am [the single] *Rosh Chodesh*. While the precise derivation from this verse will be explored momentarily, the intent of the *baraita* is unmistakable: you do not perform separate trumpet blasts for each separate *musaf*. *Tiyuvta d'Rabbi Akha tiyuvta* — this stands as a complete refutation of Rabbi Acha's position.

### Abaye: All Unified

The *Gemara* now examines how the verse actually proves this. *Amar Abaye amar Kra* — *Abaye* explained: the verse says *u'vroshei chodsheichem* — *hukshu kol hachodashim kulam zeh lazeh* — all instances of *Rosh Chodesh* are placed in one unified category. Whether it is an ordinary *Rosh Chodesh*, a *Rosh Chodesh* that falls on *Shabbat*, or a *Rosh Chodesh* that is also *Rosh Hashanah* — they are all treated as a single category, and you perform only one set of blasts.

This derives from the verse in Numbers that discusses the trumpet blasts: *u'v'yom simchatchem u'v'moadeichem u'v'roshei chodsheichem u'tekatem bachatzotzrot al oloteichem v'al zivchei shalmeichem* — on your days of rejoicing, your appointed festivals, and your *Rosh Chodesh* occasions, you shall sound the trumpets over your offerings. The phrase *u'vroshei chodsheichem* groups all *Rosh Chodesh* occasions together as a single category — and therefore even a *Shabbat Rosh Chodesh* or a *Rosh Hashanah Rosh Chodesh* receives only one set of blasts.

### Rav Ashi: Ktiv/Kri

*Rav Ashi* offered a different reading, playing on a *kri u'ksiv* discrepancy in the same verse. *Rav Ashi amar: ksiv chodsh'chem* — the word is written without a *yud*, rendering it singular, *v'ksiv u'vroshei* — yet it is read in a plural form. *Eizu chodesh she-yesh lo shenei rashim* — which month has two heads? *Hevei omer zeh Rosh Hashanah* — it must be *Rosh Chodesh* that is simultaneously *Rosh Hashanah*. *Amar Rachmana chodsh'chem* — yet the Torah calls it singular, *chada hi* — treat it as one. The written form insists on singularity even when the day carries a double identity.

### One Set Determined

The *pshat* is thus clear: even when multiple *musafim* coincide, you perform only a single set of blasts. There is some variation in how the verse yields this conclusion — whether by reading *u'vroshei chodsheichem* as a unified category (*Abaye*) or by the *kri u'ksiv* pointing to the doubled day being treated as singular (*Rav Ashi*) — but the ruling itself is not in doubt.

---

## Six Psalms of Chol HaMoed

*V'od tanya* — a further *baraita* is introduced. *Bechol hamoed ba-rishon mah hayu omrim* — what would they recite on the various days of *chol hamoed Sukkot* as the *shir shel yom*? It is worth noting, by way of background, that the *minhag haGra* — and apparently the *minhag Sefardim* as well — is that on *Yom Tov* and *chol hamoed* one recites the special psalm associated with that day rather than the psalm for that day of the week. Some communities may recite both, but the *minhag haGra* is to recite only the special one.

There is also a broader point at stake in this *baraita*: if one held that each *musaf* generates its own separate *shir shel yom*, then on a day with multiple *musafim* one would recite both and no selection would be necessary. The fact that the *baraita* requires choosing confirms that even when multiple *musafim* coincide, only one *shir shel yom* is recited — because the *shir* and the trumpet blasts are intertwined.

### Day 1: Havu L'Hashem

The psalm recited on the first day of *chol hamoed* is Psalm 29 — *Havu L'Hashem Bnei Eilim*. Its connection to *Sukkot* is transparent: *Kol Hashem Al Hamayim Keil Hakavod Hir'im Hashem Al Mayim Rabim* — the voice of God over the waters, God thundering over the mighty waters. The theme of water is a central motif of *Sukkot*, the time when the world is judged concerning rainfall.

### Day 2: V'Larasha

On the second day they would recite *V'larasha Amar Elokim* — the opening of Psalm 50. The full psalm is worth examining. It opens with a divine summons: *Keil Elokim Hashem diber vayikra aretz mimizrach shemesh ad mevo'o* — God, the Lord, spoke and called the earth from the rising to the setting of the sun. It proceeds to declare that God does not need Israel's sacrifices on their own account — *Lo al zvachecha ochichecha ve'olotecha lenegdi tamid* — yet it simultaneously demands that one fulfill vows: *Zvach L'Elokim todah veshalem L'Elyon nedarecha* — offer thanksgiving to God and pay your vows to the Most High.

*Rashi* focuses on the verse about paying vows. The time of the *Regalim* was the deadline by which one was obligated to fulfill vows made during the year; allowing multiple *Regalim* to pass without fulfillment transgresses the prohibition of *bal te'acher* — delaying the discharge of one's vows. So *Rashi* explains that this psalm emphasizes the obligation of presenting one's outstanding vows upon arriving at the Temple. One could alternatively read the emphasis as falling on the broader ethical and spiritual dimension of the psalm — that God cares more about genuine religious conduct than about the mechanical offering of sacrifices. In either reading, the connection to *Sukkot* specifically is indirect; it is more generally about arriving at the Temple and fulfilling one's obligations.

### Day 3: Mi Yakum

On the third day: *Mi Yakum Li Im Mere'im* — Psalm 94. This psalm opens with a call for divine vengeance — *Keil Nekamot Hashem Keil Nekamot Hofia, Hinasei Shofet Haaretz Hashev Gmul Al Ge'im* — God of retribution, appear; rise up, O Judge of the earth, render recompense to the arrogant. It then addresses the suffering of Israel under foreign oppression: *Amcha Hashem Yedake'u Venachalatcha Ye'anu, Almana Veger Yaharogu Vitomim Yeratzachu* — Your people, O Lord, they crush; Your heritage they oppress; they slay the widow and the stranger and murder the orphans. It asserts divine awareness: *Hashoteil Ozen Halo Yishma Im Yotzer Ayin Halo Yabit* — does the One who implanted the ear not hear? Does the One who formed the eye not see? And it culminates with the blessing of the one whom God corrects: *Ashrei Hagever Asher Teyasrenu Kah Umitoratcha Telamdenu* — happy is the man whom You discipline, O Lord, and whom You instruct from Your Torah.

*Rashi* connects this psalm to *Sukkot* in two ways. First, it alludes to the oppression of Israel under foreign powers — the Greeks and Romans — during the era of the Temple and between the two Temples; the *Sukkot* period is one in which Israel nevertheless persisted and was sustained. Second, the declaration that God knows what lies in one's heart — *Binu Boarim Ba'am Uchsilim Matay Tashkilu* — addresses those who might think they can evade their agricultural obligations at this season: the giving of tithes, the gifts to the poor, *leket*, *shichcha*, and *pe'ah*, all of which reach their culmination at harvest time. The message is that God sees and knows, and one cannot escape the consequences of failing to fulfill these duties. Admittedly, as *Rashi* concedes, the direct connection to *Sukkot* in these middle psalms is fairly general.

### Day 4: Binu Bo'arim

On the fourth day: *Binu Boarim Ba'am* — this is the second half of Psalm 94, returning to the theme that God is aware of what is in one's heart. *Rashi* applies this again to the concern about performing the agricultural obligations at harvest time, when people might presume that their compliance or non-compliance goes unobserved. Those who think they can neglect the gifts to the poor — God knows, and they should understand this.

### Day 5: Hasiroti

On the fifth day: *Hasiroti missevel shikmo* — Psalm 81. This psalm is far more transparently connected to the themes of *Sukkot*. It opens: *Harninu L'Elohim uzeinu hari'u L'Elohei Yaakov* — sing joyfully to God our strength, shout to the God of Jacob. It then continues: *Se'u zimrah utnu tof kinnor na'im im navel tiku vachodesh shofar bakesseh l'yom hagenu* — raise a song, beat the drum, the sweet harp with the lute, sound the *shofar* at the new moon, at the full moon on our festival day. This verse encompasses all the musical instruments of the *Simchat Beit HaShoeva*, and the phrase *bakesseh l'yom hagenu* alludes famously to *Rosh Hashanah*. The psalm also recalls the exodus: *hama'alcha me'eretz Mitzrayim* — I brought you up from the land of Egypt — an explicit reference to *Yetziat Mitzrayim*. And it declares: *Harchav picha va'amaleihu* — open your mouth wide and I will fill it — a promise of sustenance and future blessing. *Rashi* states explicitly that this verse is about water and rain: you open your mouth and God will give you blessing. The connection to *Sukkot* and the prayer for rain is direct and manifest.

### Day 6: Yamutu

On the sixth day: *Yamutu kol mosdei aretz* — Psalm 82. The psalm opens with divine judgment in the heavenly court: *Bekerev Elohim yishpot* — God stands in the divine assembly. It then turns to a call for justice: *Shiftu dal veyatom ani varash hatzdiku, Paletu dal ve'evyon miyad resha'im hatzilu* — render justice to the poor and orphan, vindicate the afflicted and impoverished, rescue the poor and needy from the hands of the wicked. It concludes with the unsettling observation that despite their grandeur, even those who have been called *Elohim* will die like humans: *achen ke'adam temutun uke'achad hasarim tipolu* — yet you shall die like men and fall like any prince. The concern for the poor and vulnerable — *ani varash hatzdiku* — connects directly to the obligations of giving *terumot* and *ma'asrot*, *leket*, *shichcha*, and *pe'ah* that characterize this season of ingathering.

### Shabbat Pushes Off

*Ve'im chal Shabbat be'echad mehem* — if *Shabbat* falls on one of the days of *chol hamoed*, the *Shabbat* psalm takes precedence over the *chol hamoed* psalm for that day. This should be distinguished from the earlier ruling regarding *Rosh Chodesh*: there, *Rosh Chodesh* takes precedence over *Shabbat* in the choice of *shir shel yom*, because it is important to announce the *Rosh Chodesh*. Between *Shabbat* and *chol hamoed Sukkot*, however, *Shabbat* takes precedence.

When *Shabbat* displaces one of the six *chol hamoed* psalms, the result is a domino effect: *yamutu yidcheh* — the last psalm, *yamutu*, is the one that gets pushed off entirely. So if *Shabbat* falls on day three, the psalm that would have been said on day three is said on day four, day four's psalm is said on day five, and so on — and the psalm of the sixth day, *yamutu*, is never recited that year. The name *yamutu* — "they will be moved" — lends itself to the slight wordplay of being the one that gets "moved away."

The significance of this ruling for the larger argument should not be missed: the fact that one must choose which psalm to displace confirms that on any given day — even one with multiple *musafim*, such as *Shabbat chol hamoed* — there is only one *shir shel yom* and only one set of trumpet blasts. If there were a separate set for each *musaf*, you would recite both psalms and no displacement would be necessary.

---

## Tiyuvta d'Rav Acha

### Rav Acha's Position

*Tiyuvta de-Rav Acha bar Chanina tiyuvta* — this *baraita* constitutes another refutation of *Rav Acha bar Chanina*'s position. If multiple *musafim* each generated their own independent *shir shel yom* and set of blasts, then on *Shabbat chol hamoed* one would simply recite all of them; the domino effect and the displacement of *yamutu* would never arise. The very fact that the *baraita* describes displacement proves that even a day with multiple *musafim* receives only one *shir shel yom* and one set of trumpet blasts.

The *Gemara* asks: *Ve-Rav Acha bar Chanina kra masnisa kama*? — but *Rav Acha bar Chanina* had a verse and a *baraita* of his own. The verse states *B'nei Aharon ha-Kohanim yitke'u ba-chatzotzrot*, and there was a *baraita* indicating that the trumpet blasts correspond to the *musafim* — which sounds as though a multiplication of *musafim* generates a multiplication of blasts. If we conclude that only one set of blasts and one *shir* is performed, how do we account for that *baraita*?

---

## Six Psalms of Chol HaM…

### Mnemonics: Humbahi

*Rav Safra manach be-simani* — *Rav Safra* provided a mnemonic to remember the order of the six psalms recited during *chol hamoed Sukkot*: *Humbahi*. Each letter stands for the opening word of one of the six psalms in order: *Havu l'Hashem* (Psalm 29), *U'lerasha amar* (Psalm 50), *Mi yakum li* (Psalm 94), *Binu bo'arim* (the second half of Psalm 94), *Hasiroti* (Psalm 81), *Yamutu* (Psalm 82). This is the *Humbahi* sequence of *Rav Safra*, where *beis* precedes *heh* — that is, *Binu* comes before *Hasiroti*.

*Rav Pappa manach be-simana* — *Rav Pappa* had a slightly different mnemonic: *Humbabi*. In *Rav Pappa*'s ordering, the *heh* and the second *beis* are reversed — *Hasiroti* comes before *Binu bo'arim*. The sequence sounds like Hammurabi: *Humbabi*.

*Ve-simanch* — how do you remember which mnemonic belongs to which *Amora*? *Ambuha de-sifrei* — the crowds that gather at the schoolteachers at drop-off and pick-up time. *Sifrei* resonates with *Safra*, and *Safra* said *Humbahi* — with the *heh* (*Hasiroti*) at the end — as opposed to *Rav Pappa*'s *Humbabi*. The crowd (*ambuha*) of the schoolteachers (*sifrei*) reminds you that it is *Rav Safra* who has the *Humbahi* order.

---

## Tiyuvta d'Rav Acha…

### Ravina: Length Not Quant…

*Amar Ravina* — *Ravina* resolved the difficulty: *lomar she-ma'arichim bi-tkiyot* — what the *baraita* means when it says the trumpet blasts correspond to the *musafim* is not that you perform an additional set of blasts for each *musaf*, but that when you perform the single set of blasts you play the notes longer to signal that it is a doubled day. The quantity of sets remains one; only the duration increases.

### More Blowers, One Set

*Rabbanan de-Keisari mishmei de-Rav Acha amri* — the rabbis of *Keisari* said in the name of *Rav Acha*: *lomar she-marbin be-tokim* — you add more players, more people sounding the trumpet. Rather than performing another complete set of blasts, you increase the number of those who blow, while still performing only a single unified set. The identity of the day remains singular; what multiplies is the grandeur of execution, not the number of performances.

---

## Safek Yom: Which Musaf

### Two-Day Yom Tov Problem

Having settled that multiple *musafim* on the same day yield only one *shir shel yom* and one set of blasts, the *Gemara* raises an analogous problem by analogy: *Va-anan de-it lan trei yomei heichi avidnan* — we who observe two days of *Yom Tov*, what do we do?

The question is not quite identical to the *Shabbat*-plus-*chol hamoed* case. Here the doubling is of a different kind. The specific question concerns the *musaf* prayer of *Shemoneh Esreh* on *chol hamoed Sukkot* in a diaspora community that observes two days of *Yom Tov*. When we arrive at the first day of *chol hamoed*, it is simultaneously day two of *Sukkot* by the true reckoning — and yet by virtue of *sfeika de-yoma* it is also treated as a potential day one of *Sukkot* (since the second day of *Yom Tov* was observed as a doubtful day). The *musaf* prayer on *chol hamoed* contains verses from the Torah enumerating the special offerings for each day of the festival, and each day's verses are different. Which day's verses do we recite in the *musaf Shemoneh Esreh*?

### Abaye: Sheni Yidachei

*Abaye amar sheni yidachei* — *Abaye* says: push off the second day of *Yom Tov*. That is to say, since we know that the second day of *Yom Tov* was observed only because of *sfeika de-yoma*, we return now to the true reckoning. Accordingly, the first day of *chol hamoed* is treated as day three of *Sukkot*, and we recite the verses of day three. From that point the days proceed as three, four, five, six, seven — the normal true count. Day two is simply set aside.

### Rava: Shvi'i Yidachei

*Rava amar shevi'i yidachei* — *Rava* disagrees. *Rava* maintains that we continue from where we are: having treated the second day of *Yom Tov* as a genuine day, we now act as though we are at the beginning of *chol hamoed*, and the first day of *chol hamoed* is treated as day two of *Sukkot*. From there the days proceed two, three, four, five, six — and day seven is never reached in the *musaf* recitation. It simply falls off.

*Abaye*'s position has a certain intuitive logic: it restores alignment with the true count. *Rava*'s position, by contrast, maintains continuity from where we have been and accepts the consequence that the seventh day's verses are never said. The *Gemara* notes that undermining the status of the second day of *Yom Tov* — as *Abaye* might seem to do — is itself a concern.

### Baraita Backs Rava

*Tanya k'vatiei d'Rava* — a *baraita* is adduced in support of *Rava*: *im chal Shabbat be'echad meihen, yamotei yidacheh* — if *Shabbat* falls on one of the intermediate days of *chol hamoed*, the last psalm, *yamutu*, is pushed off. The *Gemara* understands this as analogous to *Rava*'s ruling: just as *Shabbat* entering on a day of *chol hamoed* pushes everything down the line until the last psalm falls off, so too the second day of *Yom Tov* pushes the count forward and the seventh day falls off the edge. One might argue the two cases operate on different logic, but the *Gemara* sees them as analogous.

### Ameimar: Both Days

*Atkin Ameimar b'Nehardea d'medalgei dilugei* — *Ameimar* of *Nehardea* instituted a practice of jumping back and forth. Rather than choosing one day's identity and forfeiting the other, on the first day of *chol hamoed* one recites both the verses of day two and the verses of day three — and similarly throughout. This is in fact what we do in practice today.

### Rashi: Torah Reading

*Rashi* addresses a parallel question regarding the Torah reading on *chol hamoed* under two-day *Yom Tov* conditions. *Rashi* rules that on the fourth portion (*revii*) of the Torah reading on the first day of *chol hamoed*, one reads from both the second and third day's sections. For the first three portions, *Rashi* says one reads from the second, third, and fourth day's sections in sequence, then returns to read the second and third. The result for the full reading is: second, third, fourth, and then second and third again.

### Tosafot: Consistency

*Tosafot* takes issue with *Rashi*'s approach on grounds of inconsistency. According to *Rashi*, the reading would be two, three, four, two, three. *Tosafot* prefers a consistent pattern: two, three, two, three throughout. One might ask what we actually do on *Hoshana Rabbah*: there, the reading goes through the very end of the festival — five, six, seven, and then back to six and seven — and cannot go to eight since that would encroach on *Shemini Atzeret*. *Tosafot*'s concern is that *Rashi*'s approach lacks consistency, since the *musaf* recitation and the Torah reading are not identical in their treatment.

---

## First Day Korbanot

### 13 Bulls, 2 Rams, 1 Goat

The *masechta* now turns to a new *Mishnah* at the top of 55b. *Yom Tov Harishon Shel Chag hayu sham yud-gimmel parim eilim shnayim v'sa'ir echad* — on the first *Yom Tov* of the festival there were thirteen bulls, two rams, and one goat. The goat was the *chatat* offering; the remainder were *olot*. This is drawn directly from the Torah's enumeration in Numbers.

### Sheep Distribution

*Nishtayru sham yud-dalet kvasim l'shmonah mishmarot* — in addition, there were fourteen sheep remaining to be distributed among eight of the twenty-four divisions (*mishmarot*) of priests.

The twenty-four *mishmarot* normally rotated on a weekly schedule, each division serving two weeks out of the year. On the *Regalim*, however, since all Israel was obligated to make the pilgrimage, all twenty-four divisions came together and served simultaneously in the Temple — a very crowded arrangement. The *musaf* animals for each day were distributed one per priestly division, so that each division had the privilege — and the practical benefit — of performing the service of at least one animal. (Beyond the service itself, the performing division would receive at minimum the hide of the animal they brought, since the flesh of an *olah* goes entirely on the altar.)

There were thirty animals on the first day: thirteen bulls, two rams, one goat, and fourteen sheep — totaling thirty. With twenty-four divisions, every division receives one animal and six animals remain. Therefore, six divisions would receive a second animal — two portions instead of one. *Byom rishon shishah makrivim shnayim shnayim v'hashar echad echad* — on the first day, six divisions bring two animals each, and the remainder each bring one.

### Daily Countdown

As the days of *Sukkot* proceed, the number of bulls decreases by one each day: twelve, eleven, ten, and so on. Because there is one fewer animal to distribute each day, the number of divisions receiving a double portion likewise decreases by one each day. *Bashaini, hamishah makrivim shnayim shnayim v'hashar echad echad* — on the second day, five divisions receive double. *Bashlishi, arba'ah makrivim shnayim shnayim v'hashar echad echad* — on the third day, four divisions. *Barvi'i, shloshah makrivim shnayim shnayim v'hashar echad echad* — on the fourth day, three. *Bachamishi, shnayim makrivim shnayim shnayim v'hashar echad echad* — on the fifth day, two. *Bashishi, echad makriv shnayim shnayim v'hashar echad echad* — on the sixth day, only one division receives double.

The distribution is managed so that a division that received double on one day does not receive double the following day, and similarly a division that received a bull one day does not receive a bull the next day, since the bulls are the most coveted animals and there are not enough to go around for everyone to receive one repeatedly. One way to visualize this is as two concentric rotating wheels: one wheel tracking which divisions receive the bulls, advancing by the number of bulls distributed each day, and a separate inner wheel tracking which divisions receive the double sheep portion, advancing by the number of doubles each day. The two wheels rotate at different speeds, so the tracking of who receives a bull and who receives a double are independent of each other.

### Day 7: Perfect Split

*Bashvi'i, kulam shavim* — on the seventh day of *Sukkot*, the count works out perfectly. There are seven bulls, two rams, one goat, and fourteen sheep — totaling twenty-four — exactly one animal per division, with no doubles required whatsoever.

Over the seven days of *Sukkot*, the total number of bulls is 70 (13 + 12 + 11 + 10 + 9 + 8 + 7). Since 3 × 24 = 72, distributing bulls three per division over the seven days leaves two divisions that received only two bulls rather than three.

---

## Shemini Atzeret Lottery

### Rabbi: Fresh Start

*Bashmini* — on *Shemini Atzeret*, one bull is brought. The question is how to determine which division has the privilege of bringing it. *Neima matnisin Rabbi hi velo Rabbanan* — the *Gemara* asks: does our *Mishnah* reflect only the view of *Rabbi* and not that of the *Rabbanan*?

*De'tanya: Par ha-ba b'shemini techilah mafisin alav, Divrei Rabbi* — as taught in a *baraita*: for the bull brought on *Shemini Atzeret*, you begin anew with a completely fresh lottery, taking no account of anything that occurred during the seven days of *Sukkot*. This is the view of *Rabbi*.

### Chachamim: Remaining Two

*V'Chachamim omrim: achas mi-shtei mishmarot she-lo shilshu b'parim osa otah* — the *Chachamim* say: we give the privilege to one of the two divisions that did not manage to bring three bulls over the course of *Sukkot*. Those two divisions were shorted, and *Shemini Atzeret* provides the opportunity to remedy that imbalance.

### Compromise: Lottery

*Afilu teima Rabbanan* — the *Gemara* resolves that even according to the *Rabbanan*, our *Mishnah* can be consistent with their view. When the *Mishnah* says to start a fresh lottery on *Shemini Atzeret*, that does not necessarily mean a lottery among all twenty-four divisions. *Atu shtei mishmarot lav afusei ba'ei* — the two remaining divisions still need a lottery between themselves to determine which one gets the privilege. So the *Mishnah*'s language of conducting a lottery is not incompatible with the *Rabbanan*'s view that the lottery is limited to the two remaining divisions.

### Math: Two Left Out

*K'man azla ha de'tanya: kol hamishmarot shonot u-meshaleshot, chutz mi-shtei mishmarot she-shonot ve-ein meshaleshot* — who does this *baraita* accord with? The *baraita* teaches: all the divisions received double and triple (in the distribution of bulls over *Sukkot*), except for two of them which received double but not triple. Does this *baraita* accord only with *Rabbi*?

*Afilu teima Rabbanan* — again the *Gemara* resolves: it could accord even with the *Rabbanan*. *Mai lo shilshu b'parei ha-chag* — when the *baraita* says they did not receive triple, it means among the bulls brought specifically on *Sukkot* — not counting the bull of *Shemini Atzeret*. On *Shemini Atzeret*, one of the two remaining divisions will receive a bull, bringing one of them to triple after all; but two divisions do not achieve triple from the *Sukkot* bulls alone. *U-mai kamashma lan? Ha kamashma lan: mi she-hikriv parei ha-yom lo yakriv le-machar ela chozer chalilah* — what is this *baraita* teaching us? It teaches that a division which brought a bull today does not bring a bull again tomorrow; the rotation continuously advances.

---

## 70 Bulls, 70 Nations

### Elazar: 70 Nations

*Amar Rabbi Elazar: haneh shiv'im parim k'neged mi?* — Rabbi Elazar asked: these seventy bulls, whom do they represent? *K'neged shiv'im umot* — they correspond to the seventy nations of the world. *Par yechidi lamah li? K'neged uma yechidah* — and what is the single bull of *Shemini Atzeret* for? It corresponds to the singular nation among the seventy — Israel.

### King's Parable

*Mashal le-melech basar va-dam she-amar la'avadav asu li se'udah gedolah, u-le-yom acharon amar le-o'havo asu li se'udah ktanah k'dei she-aneh mimcha* — it can be compared to a king of flesh and blood who said to his servants: make for me a great feast. Then, on the last day, he said to his beloved: make for me a small, private meal, so that I can have special, intimate time with you.

This *mashal* is famous well beyond its immediate context. It gives *Shemini Atzeret* its essential identity. After the vast, universalist festival of *Sukkot* — with its seventy bulls for seventy nations, its water libations, its *Simchat Beit HaShoeva* — there comes one quiet, private day for Israel alone with God. The transition out of the entire *Yamim Noraim* period is marked not by fanfare but by intimacy.

### Rashi: Universal Rain

*Rashi* makes the universalist dimension of *Sukkot* explicit. Commenting on the seventy bulls, he writes: *Pareh He-chag shivim hem chutz mi-shel shmini k'neged shivim umot l'chaper aleihem she-yeirdu g'shamim be-chol ha-olam le-fi she-nidonu be-chag al ha-mayim* — the bulls of the festival are seventy, excluding the one of *Shemini Atzeret*, and they correspond to the seventy nations, to atone for them so that rain should fall throughout the entire world, since the world is judged on *Sukkot* concerning water.

This is a striking and profound point. The *haftarot* of *Sukkot* speak of all the nations coming to celebrate *Chag HaSukkot*, and of rain being withheld from those that do not come. *Pesach* is fundamentally particularistic — about *Yetziat Mitzrayim*, about the birth of one people. *Sukkot*, even while it commemorates the clouds of glory that sheltered Israel in the wilderness — *Ki va-sukkot hoshavti* — is not primarily a historical celebration. It is about vulnerability, about dependence on God for sustenance and protection, and that reality is universal. Every nation needs rain. Every human being lives under the same sky. The universalist dimension of *Sukkot* is not incidental; it is inscribed into the very architecture of the *musaf* sacrifices.

### Yochanan: What Was Lost

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan: Oy lahem le-ovdei kochavim she-avdu ve-ein yod'im mah avdu. Bizman she-Beit Ha-mikdash kayam mizbe'ach mechaper aleihem. Ve-achshav mi mechaper aleihem?* — Rabbi Yochanan said: woe to the nations of the world, for they have lost something without knowing what they have lost. When the Temple stood, the altar atoned for them. Now, who atones for them?

This is a striking *Gemara*. Israel knows what it has lost with the destruction of the Temple; we work to address that loss through Torah study and good deeds. But the nations benefited from the Temple's atonement without awareness, and without awareness there can be no response to its loss. The posture here is not hostility toward the nations — quite the opposite. It is an expression of genuine concern for the larger world, an extension of the universalist ethos that defines *Sukkot*.

---

## Three Yearly Equalities

### Shared Portions

The *masechta* now transitions to a new *Mishnah*: *Be-shloshah prakim ba-shanah hayu kol ha-mishmarot shavot be-imurei ha-regalim u-ve-chiluk lechem ha-panim* — at three times during the year, all twenty-four divisions of priests were equal in the special service of the pilgrimage festivals and in the division of the *lechem ha-panim*. The three times are the three *Regalim* — *Pesach*, *Shavuot*, and *Sukkot*.

The *Gemara* immediately notes a linguistic curiosity: *imurei ha-regalim* — "the inner fats of the festivals." But *emurim* — the inner fats — go entirely onto the altar and are not divided among the priests! *Amar Rav Chisda: mashe'amur biRegalim* — it means not the *emurim* themselves, but "the things said" or designated for the *Regalim*, i.e., the special festival offerings. It is an unusual way of expressing this, but the intent is clear: all divisions share equally in bringing the *musaf* offerings of the *Regalim* and in dividing the *lechem ha-panim*.

On *Shavuot* — which in Tannaitic usage is called *Atzeret* — one says to each priest: *Heilech matzah heilech chametz* — here is your *matzah* (a small portion from the *lechem ha-panim*, which is unleavened) and here is your *chametz* (a small portion from the *shtei ha-lechem*, the two loaves brought on *Shavuot*, which are leavened).

### Regular Mishmar Rights

*Mishmar she-zmano kavua hu makriv temidim nedarim u-nedavot* — the division whose regular week it is — the one that would have served that week in the normal rotation even aside from the *regel* — retains its exclusive claim to the regular daily offerings: the *temidim* (morning and evening), the free-will and vow offerings that private individuals bring (*nedarim* and *nedavot*), and other public offerings not unique to the *regel* itself. These are not shared with the other twenty-three divisions.

This exclusivity made the coincidence of one's regular week with a *regel* extraordinarily valuable. If all of Israel is making pilgrimage and presenting the vowed offerings and free-will gifts they have been accumulating throughout the year, the division whose week it happens to be stands to perform an enormous amount of service. Even if the special *regel korbanot* are shared, the tide of personal *korbanot* flowing in from all over *Klal Yisrael* — fulfilling *nedarim* before the *bal te'acher* deadline, offering *nedavot*, performing the *olat re'iya* — falls exclusively to the regular division. And while the flesh of an *olah* goes entirely to the altar, the hide belongs to the officiating priests. The practical windfall of having one's regular week coincide with a *regel* was substantial.

*Ve-sha'ar korbanot tzibbur u-makriv et ha-kol* — the *Mishnah* adds that the regular division also brings all other public *korbanot* not unique to the *regel*, with the *Gemara* to clarify what this includes.

### Devarim 18 Source

*Tanu Rabbanan: minayin shekol hamishmarot shavot be'emurei haRegalim?* — how do we know that all divisions are equal in the service of the *Regalim*? The source is *Devarim* 18: *ubah bekhol avat nafsho vesheret* — and he may come according to his heart's desire and serve. The verse addresses a Levite (understood by the Sages to refer to a priest in the context of Temple service) who arrives at the Temple outside of his assigned week. The simple reading of the verse would permit such service at any time. The Sages read *meAchad she'arekha* — "from one of your gates" — as limiting this permission to the moment when all Israel enters through a single gate, i.e., the *regel*, when everyone makes pilgrimage together.

### Gate Limitation

*Yachol af bish'ar yemot hashanah ken? Talmud lomar me'achad she'arekha* — one might think a priest could come and serve at any time of year, but the verse specifies one of your gates — *lo amarti ela besha'ah shekol Yisrael nikhnasin besha'ar echad* — this applies only when all Israel is entering through one gate together. So the entitlement to serve for all divisions equally is limited to the three *Regalim*.

### Lechem HaPanim Exception

The *Mishnah* also includes the *lechem ha-panim* in the equal division, and this requires its own derivation, since the *lechem ha-panim* is not unique to the *regel*. It is placed on the *shulchan* each week and divided among the serving division at the end of the week. The *regel* week's division has already performed the service of placing the *lechem ha-panim*, so there is no question of their entitlement to eat it. The question is: why do all twenty-four divisions share equally in the *lechem ha-panim* specifically during the *regel*?

*Tanu Rabbanan: minayin shekol hamishmarot shavot bikhiluk Lechem HaPanim?* — the source is the continuation of the verse in *Devarim* 18: *chelek kechelek yokhelu* — they shall eat portion as portion.

### Service Equals Eating

*Talmud lomar chelek kechelek yokhelu: kechelek avodah, kakh chelek akhilah* — just as there is an equal portion in the service, so too there is an equal portion in the eating. Once we establish that all divisions share equally in the *regel* service, it follows that they share equally in the eating as well. But this alone would only entitle them to eat the things they brought as *regel korbanot*. How do we derive that they eat the *lechem ha-panim*, for which they performed no service?

*U-mai akhilah? Ileima korbanot — meihasam nafka. Lakohen hamakriv oto lo tihyeh* — if the "eating" refers to the normal *korban* eating, that is already known from a different verse: the priest who brings a *korban* is entitled to its portions. So the additional eating derived from *chelek kechelek yokhelu* must refer to something for which no service was performed — namely, the *lechem ha-panim*. *Ella Lechem HaPanim* — it is specifically the *lechem ha-panim* that is the subject of this additional derivation.

### Regal-Related Only

*Yachol af bekhol baz shebo machamat haregel baregel?* — one might think that the equal entitlement in eating extends to absolutely everything that comes in by virtue of the *regel*, even things not specifically designated for the *regel* itself? *Talmud lomar levad mimkarav al ha'avot* — except for that which was sold to the fathers. This phrase refers to the ancestral rotation of divisions: *ani beshabbati v'atah beshabbatekha* — I serve in my week and you serve in yours. The things that belong to a division by virtue of their assigned week in the normal rotation — the *temidim*, the personal *nedarim* and *nedavot* — are not shared with the other divisions. Only what is unique to the *regel* itself is divided equally, with the one additional exception of the *lechem ha-panim*.

It is worth noting that the use of a verse in *Devarim* to establish the mechanics of priestly rotations is somewhat striking, since the system of twenty-four rotating *mishmarot* as formalized by David was not yet in place at the time of *Devarim*. The *Gemara* does not explore this point further here.

---

---

# Beitzah 2

## Masechet Overview

### Names & Context

We begin a new *masechet*. According to some *rishonim*, although books in the ancient world were named after their first word — hence the names of *parshiyot* and the books of the *Chumash* — this tractate is called *Beitzah* simply because that is its opening word. Nevertheless, the *rishonim* sometimes refer to it as *Masechet Yom Tov*, which is in many ways the more descriptive title, since the entire *masechet*, short as it is, deals with aspects of *yom tov*.

### Content Structure

The first *perek* deals heavily with *muktzah*, a topic scattered throughout the *Gemara* but with a particularly high concentration here. The second *perek* opens with a discussion of *eruv tavshilin* before moving into various *d'rabanans* that apply on *yom tov*. The third *perek* turns to the *melachot* themselves — what is permitted on *yom tov* under the category of *melacha ochel nefesh* — and as the tractate continues through the fourth and fifth *perakim*, a wide range of rabbinic enactments surrounding *yom tov* are addressed. This is not *Masechet Moed Katan*, which deals with *Chol HaMoed*; *Beitzah* is specifically about *yom tov* and, in particular, *muktzah* in its opening sections.

### B.H. vs B.S. Debates

The other truly distinctive feature of this *masechet* worth noting at the outset is the remarkable prevalence of *machloket Beit Hillel u'Beit Shammai*. *Mishna* after *mishna* is structured as a string of debates: here is what *Beit Hillel* says, here is what *Beit Shammai* says. In most *masechtot*, the primary speakers in the *mishna* are *talmidei Rabbi Akiva* — *Rabbi Yehuda*, *Rabbi Meir*, *Rabbi Shimon* — who represent the generation immediately preceding *Rebbi*, the editor of the *Mishna*. But *Hillel* and *Shammai* lived roughly a hundred years before the *Churban HaBayit*, when the *Beit HaMikdash* still stood. What one encounters in *Beitzah* is therefore a collection of very early *mishnayot*, ones that seem to bear almost no editorial hand of *Rebbi* — they are simply the raw, direct *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* debates as they were preserved. Why so much *Beit Hillel u'Beit Shammai* specifically in the domain of *yom tov* is a fascinating question without an obvious full answer, but it is one of the most distinctive features of the *masechet*.

---

## Opening Mishna

### Case Statement

*Beitzah shenol'da b'yom tov* — what is the *halacha* regarding an egg born on *yom tov*? *Beit Shammai omrim te'achel* — *Beit Shammai* says it may be eaten. *U'Beit Hillel omrim lo te'achel* — *Beit Hillel* says it may not be eaten. This is the opening case of the *masechet*, and the *Gemara* will devote its initial analysis to understanding precisely why *Beit Hillel* forbids it.

### Muktzah Question

At first glance, this appears to be a question of *nolad* — *she'nolad*, something newly created — which is a category related to *muktzah*: an object that was not and could not have been set aside prior to *yom tov*. On that reading, *Beit Shammai* is unbothered by this concern and permits the egg, while *Beit Hillel* forbids it.

One might ask, however: if this is truly a *muktzah* issue, why does the *mishna* frame it only in terms of eating? *Muktzah* would normally also prohibit *tiltul* — moving the object — and there are cases where something may be forbidden to eat but still permitted to move. The simplest answer is that if it is indeed a *muktzah* debate, *Beit Shammai*, who rejects *muktzah* entirely, permits both moving and eating, while *Beit Hillel*, who holds of *muktzah*, would forbid both. Their discussion focuses on eating because that is, after all, the primary reason one would want the egg. Whether the issue is specifically about eating or encompasses handling as well is a question the *Gemara* will explore further.

Notably, this opening *mishna* belongs to what is clearly a deliberate collection of three *Beit Hillel*–*Beit Shammai* debates — joined together not only because they all concern *yom tov*, but because in all three cases *Beit Shammai* is the lenient party and *Beit Hillel* the strict one, which inverts the expected pattern.

### Two More Cases

The second case in the *mishna* concerns *chametz*: *Beit Shammai omrim se'or b'kezayit v'chametz b'kikhotevet* — *Beit Shammai* holds that the prohibited quantity of *se'or* (sourdough/leaven) is an *kezayit*, and of ordinary *chametz* is a *kikhotevet* (the size of a large date). *Beit Hillel* takes the stricter position, treating even smaller amounts as actionable — since a *kezayit* is smaller than a *kikhotevet*, *Beit Hillel* is more stringent on both.

The third case concerns *kisuy hadam*. If one slaughtered a *chaya* or a bird on *yom tov* — a permissible act, as one may *shecht* fresh meat for a *yom tov* meal — one incurs the obligation of *kisuy hadam*, covering the blood. This *mitzvah*, however, is tangential to the act of eating; it does not facilitate the meal and is not part of the cooking process. The question is whether one may perform it on *yom tov*. *Beit Shammai* says *yachpor b'deker v'yechaseh* — one may take a hoe or shovel and dig up dirt to cover the blood. *Beit Hillel* says *lo yishchot ela im kein haya lo afar muchan m'be'od yom* — one should not *shecht* in the first place unless one already has dirt that was set aside the day before, so that there is no need to dig and no *muktzah* problem with the soil.

*Beit Hillel* notably leaves open the question of what one does if one went ahead and *shechted* without pre-prepared dirt. The *mishna* then supplies the answer: *u'modim she'im shachat she'yachpor b'deker v'yechaseh* — they agree that after the fact, one may dig and cover. The debate, then, is only *l'chatchilah*: may one rely on the option of digging? *Beit Hillel* says no; one should not create this situation. But if one already has, everyone permits the digging.

The *mishna* closes with the statement *she'afar kiro muchan hu* — the ashes of one's oven are *muchan*, already prepared and not *muktzah*, and therefore constitute a valid covering material. This raises an interesting question about the status of ashes that came into existence on *yom tov* itself, given that one may have a fire burning on *yom tov*. The grammar of this clause is somewhat elliptical, but the plain reading is that it offers an additional option: if one has ashes from the oven, those may be used without any concern; it is only if one lacks both pre-prepared dirt and ashes that the question of digging arises.

Two of the three cases clearly implicate *muktzah* or *nolad* type concerns, though the case of digging raises additional considerations. The *Gemara* will now turn to the first case and probe its conceptual foundations.

---

## Gemara Opening

### Hen Setup

*B'mai askinan?* — what are the precise circumstances of the case? The *Gemara* opens by asking what type of hen we are dealing with.

*Ileim a b'tarnigoles omedes l'achilah* — suppose the hen is designated for eating, meaning one intends eventually to slaughter and consume it. If so, *mai ta'ama d'Beit Hillel* — what is *Beit Hillel*'s reason to forbid the egg? The egg, in that case, is simply *uchla d'afrush hu* — food that has separated from food. The hen itself is, on *yom tov*, accessible unprepared food — since one may *shecht* it on *yom tov*, it is not *muktzah*.
