The egg that emerges from it is conceptually no different from any other portion of the hen that might become detached. It is food from food. One might picture the hen the way a butcher views a carcass: here is the breast, the thigh, the wing — it is all food. A piece of that food emerging in the form of an egg is not something new; it is just food in a slightly different configuration. There is nothing about which one should say, "this is a novelty."

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ella b'tarnigoles omedes l'gadel beitzim* — the case must be a hen that is designated for laying eggs, not for eating. Such a hen is *muktzah* on *yom tov*; one has no intention of slaughtering it and no reason to handle it. The egg it produces comes from something that was *muktzah*, and it is itself something entirely new. That explains *Beit Hillel*'s position.

But then the *Gemara* asks: *mai ta'ama d'Beit Shammai*? If the hen is *muktzah* and the egg is *nolad*, why does *Beit Shammai* permit it? The answer the *Gemara* initially suggests is *dilma Beit Shammai leit lehu muktzah* — perhaps *Beit Shammai* simply does not hold of the category of *muktzah* at all.

### Key Concepts

At this point, the *Gemara* introduces a crucial distinction between three related concepts. *Muchan* means that an object is set aside and ready for use — it is in one's mental and physical domain, prepared for *Shabbat* or *yom tov*. *Muktzah* is its opposite: an object that has been designated as off-limits, pushed away from use, either because one has no purpose for it on *Shabbat* (like a hen kept for eggs) or because the object itself cannot be used (like money or matches). Between these two poles lies everything else in the world — the vast category of objects that one has neither explicitly prepared nor explicitly designated as off-limits.

The *halachic* question is whether one needs something to be actively *muchan*, or whether the only problem is when something is actively *muktzah*. This will be explored further as the *masechet* continues.

*Nolad* is a third and distinct category. *Nolad* is something brand new — it did not exist before *Shabbat* began. The *Gemara* raises the question: even granting that some *tanna'im* reject the category of *muktzah* entirely, surely they would still acknowledge that *nolad* is a problem? The reasoning is that *muktzah* objects were at least theoretically within one's domain when *Shabbat* began — even if one designated them as off-limits, they existed and could in principle have been used. Something *nolad*, by contrast, did not exist at all when *Shabbat* began; there is no sense in which it was ever within the realm of what one could have prepared or planned to use. The *Gemara* therefore assumes: *afilu man d'shari b'muktzah b'nolad assar* — even one who permits *muktzah* would still prohibit *nolad*.

This is why the case of the hen designated for eggs is problematic: the egg it produces is *nolad*, something newly brought into existence, and even *Beit Shammai* — if they agree in principle that things must be ready when *Shabbat* begins — ought to forbid it.

There is an important and somewhat surprising conceptual point here: one might have thought that when the hen is designated for eating, the egg's appearance is more of a *nolad* — something unexpected and new — whereas when the hen is designated for laying eggs, the egg is anticipated and therefore not *nolad*. The *Gemara* assumes the reverse. If the hen is designated for eating, the egg is not considered something conceptually new; it is just food that has emerged from food, like a piece of the chicken that took on a slightly different form. But if the hen is an egg-laying machine, the egg it produces is conceptually distinct from the machine itself — the machine is there to produce eggs, and the egg is what gets produced. That egg is genuinely new and different from the entity that generated it. Counterintuitive as this is, it is the framework the *Gemara* operates with.

### Rashi on Nolad

*Rashi* articulates the distinction between *muktzah* and *nolad* with characteristic precision. By *muktzah*, he explains: *de'ilu bemuktzeh sevira lei lo masach inish dateih midei dechazi lei* — even when something has been designated as off-limits, a person never truly, at a deep level, pushes it entirely out of his domain. One never fully severs one's connection to something one owns. But *nolad* is categorically different: *aval nolad lo hava yada dehavai dateih ilaveih* — since the *nolad* item did not yet exist, there was no possibility of having any mental relationship to it whatsoever. It was simply not there. This makes *nolad* a more fundamental and serious problem than *muktzah*, which is why the *Gemara* assumed that everyone, even those who reject *muktzah*, should acknowledge *nolad* as a real concern.

It is worth noting, as *Tosafot* points out, that there are degrees of *nolad*. Some forms of *nolad* involve physical matter that already existed but was transformed into something new — ink and paper combined into a newspaper, for instance, or a state change like water to ice. The case of the egg is a more extreme form: as far as one is concerned, the egg simply did not exist before, and now it does. *Tosafot* also addresses the question of whether one could circumvent the *nolad* problem by declaring in advance, before *Shabbat*, "I am setting aside the egg that is currently inside this hen." The answer is that this does not help: since the egg does not yet exist in an accessible, visible form, it cannot be set aside. One's intention has no operative force over something that is not yet in one's domain.

---

## Rav Nachman

### R.N. Framework

Having established that the case involves a hen set aside for laying eggs, and having clarified the conceptual distinction between *muktzah* and *nolad*, the *Gemara* now turns to *Rav Nachman*'s proposed explanation of the *mishna*.

*Amar Rav Nachman* — *Rav Nachman* says: *le'olam b'tarnigoles ha'omedes l'gadel beitzim* — it is indeed a hen set aside for laying eggs. And the debate between *Beit Hillel* and *Beit Shammai* maps precisely onto the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and *Rabbi Shimon* among the later *tanna'im*. *Ude'is lei muktzah is lei nolad, udelais lei muktzah lais lei nolad* — the one who holds of *muktzah* necessarily holds of *nolad* as a problem; the one who rejects *muktzah* likewise rejects *nolad*. These are not two independent positions; they are expressions of a single, unified stance on whether there is any concept of an object needing to be in a usable state when *Shabbat* begins.

The *Gemara* had previously assumed that everyone agreed in principle that things must be ready when *Shabbat* begins, and that the debate concerned only the particulars of application — you might say that what I call *muktzah* objects were never truly unavailable, but surely something that didn't exist at all (*nolad*) was not ready. *Rav Nachman* rejects this framing entirely. *Beit Shammai* does not merely disagree about the application; they reject the concept wholesale. There is no category of preparation that must precede *Shabbat*, and therefore neither *muktzah* nor *nolad* poses any problem. *Beit Hillel*, by contrast, holds the entire framework: things must be available and ready when *Shabbat* or *yom tov* begins, and this gives rise to both *muktzah* and *nolad* as operative prohibitions.

On this reading, *Beit Shammai k'Rabbi Shimon* — *Beit Shammai* holds like *Rabbi Shimon*, who is known as not holding of *muktzah* — and *Beit Hillel k'Rabbi Yehuda*, who does. This is a clean and attractive explanation of the *mishna*. *Tosafot* does note several places where *Beit Shammai* appears to have its own concerns about *muktzah*-like issues, but the *Gemara* accepts *Rav Nachman*'s framing as the operative explanation at this stage, treating those as exceptions that do not undermine the general principle.

### Bones Mishna

The *Gemara* then challenges *Rav Nachman* from a different *mishna*. *Ve'hasnnan* — there is a *mishna* in *Shabbat* that reads: *Beit Shammai omrim m'taltelin al hashulchan atzamot u'kelipin* — *Beit Shammai* says one may pick up the bones and shells left on the table after a meal and move them. *Beit Hillel*, by contrast, says *mesalek et hatavla kulo um'narah* — one takes the entire tray and shakes it out, but one may not directly handle the bones and shells.

Here, *Beit Hillel*'s position reflects the principle of *tiltul min hatzad* — indirect handling — which gives one considerably more latitude with *muktzah* items than direct handling would. *Beit Hillel* holds that the bones are *muktzah* and therefore may not be directly moved; they may only be handled indirectly. *Beit Shammai*, on the other hand, permits direct handling — consistent with his position that *muktzah* is not a concern.

This *mishna*, then, perfectly corroborates *Rav Nachman*'s framework. So far, so good. The problem arises because *Rav Nachman* himself, in a different context, stated the reverse: *anu ein lanu ella Beit Shammai k'Rabbi Yehuda u'Beit Hillel k'Rabbi Shimon* — we hold only that *Beit Shammai* goes like *Rabbi Yehuda* (who holds of *muktzah*) and *Beit Hillel* goes like *Rabbi Shimon* (who does not). In that statement, *Rav Nachman* reverses the very assignment he made here: *Beit Hillel* would permit picking up the bones directly, and *Beit Shammai* would require only indirect handling. *Rav Nachman* thus appears to have contradicted himself.

### Shabbat vs. Yom Tov

The resolution *Rav Nachman* offers is striking. He says there is a principled distinction between *Shabbat* and *yom tov* that explains why the positions must be assigned differently in the two contexts.

By *Shabbat*, *Rav Nachman* argues, the *stam mishna* — the anonymous, authoritative *mishna* — follows *Rabbi Shimon*, who does not hold of *muktzah*. The proof is from a *mishna* in *Shabbat*: *m'chatchen et hadelu'in lifnei habehema* — one may chop up raw gourd for animals, and *et haneveilah lifnei haklavim* — one may take an animal that died on *Shabbat* and chop it up as dog food. In this latter case, the carcass was not set aside before *Shabbat* — when *Shabbat* began, the animal was alive and there was no plan to use it as animal feed. Yet the *mishna* permits it without any *muktzah* concern. This *stam mishna* thus embodies the position of *Rabbi Shimon* that there is no *muktzah* on *Shabbat*.

By *yom tov*, however, the *stam mishna* follows *Rabbi Yehuda*, who holds that *muktzah* is a real prohibition. The proof is from a *mishna* in *Beitzah* itself: *ein mevak'in eitzim min hakorot* — one may not chop firewood from construction beams that were designated for building, *velo min hakorah shenafela b'yom tov* — nor from a beam that collapsed on *yom tov* itself. The collapsed beam is the parallel case to the animal that died on *Shabbat*, and yet on *yom tov* it is forbidden. This *stam mishna* reflects the position that *muktzah* applies on *yom tov*.

*Rav Nachman*'s conclusion is that *Rebbi*, the editor of the *Mishna*, made a deliberate and conscious choice to *pasken* differently in the two domains: like *Rabbi Shimon* (no *muktzah*) for *Shabbat*, and like *Rabbi Yehuda* (yes *muktzah*) for *yom tov*. In order to keep *Beit Hillel* — whose position is always normative *halacha* — consistent with this split ruling, one must reverse the attribution of positions in the *mishna* about the bones. On *Shabbat*, *Beit Hillel* must be the one who permits picking up the bones directly (consistent with the ruling that there is no *muktzah* on *Shabbat*), and *Beit Shammai* must be the one who requires indirect handling. The *mishna* in our *masechet*, by contrast, where *Beit Hillel* forbids the egg laid on *yom tov*, is entirely consistent: on *yom tov*, there is *muktzah*, and *Beit Hillel* holds accordingly.

### Rashi Rationale

This leads to a pointed question: why did *Rebbi* adopt opposing positions for *Shabbat* and *yom tov*? The *Gemara* explains: *Shabbat de-chamira lo atu le-zilzulei bah* — *Shabbat* is intrinsically more stringent and treated with greater gravity, so one need not fear that people will come to treat it lightly. Therefore, *Rebbi* ruled like *Rabbi Shimon* and did not impose *muktzah* on *Shabbat*. *Yom tov de-kil ve-atu le-zilzulei beih* — *yom tov*, however, is more lenient in a range of ways: one may cook, *shecht*, carry, and engage in many forms of labor permitted by *melacha ochel nefesh*. Given this latitude, people might come to be insufficiently mindful of *yom tov*'s sanctity. Therefore *Rebbi* ruled like *Rabbi Yehuda* and imposed *muktzah* on *yom tov*.

*Rashi*'s treatment of this passage adds a layer that is worth examining carefully. The *Gemara* notes that it was *Rebbi* who decided which *mishnayot* to render as *stam* — anonymous and therefore authoritative. *Rashi* explains: *u'man stam lan le-masnisin? Rebbe she-sider ha-mishna* — it was *Rebbi* who arranged the *mishna*. *Ve-chaza divrei chacham ve-yashru be-einav, shanam stam* — when an opinion appeared correct to him, he taught it anonymously. *Ve-lo hizkir shem omro aleihem, kedei she-lo yishnu mipi yachid* — he did not attribute it to a single authority, so that it would not be seen as one individual's view. *Ve-yeira'u ke-illu nishnu mipi ha-merubim ve-ya'asu kemosam* — to give the appearance of a consensus opinion, so that people would follow it. This is a striking *Rashi*: *Rebbi* was not merely expressing his own *psak* by choosing which *mishna* to make anonymous; according to *Rashi*, he was deliberately creating the impression of a consensus that did not exist, in order to ensure that people would follow it. One may re-read *Rashi* more charitably — that *Rebbi* was giving authoritative voice to a position rather than literally deceiving anyone — but the plain language is quite arresting.

The upshot is that the difference between *Shabbat* and *yom tov* in the area of *muktzah* is not a product of some earlier *tannaitic* dispute in which one *tanna* held these two positions simultaneously. It was *Rebbi*'s considered editorial decision to apply different *halachic* frameworks to the two domains, based on the practical concern that *yom tov*'s greater permissiveness creates a risk of diminished sensitivity to its sanctity. Imposing *muktzah* on *yom tov* keeps one conscious of which objects are within the *yom tov* framework and which are not — and that consciousness itself serves to preserve awareness of *kedushat ha-yom*.

---

## Critique & Alternatives

### Why Just Egg?

The *Gemara* now presses a pointed objection against *Rav Nachman*'s framework. *B'mai okimta* — you have placed our *mishna* as discussing a hen set aside for laying eggs, and the debate is about *muktzah*. *Ei hachi* — if so, *ad d'miflegi b'beitzah, liflegu b'tarnegolet* — why does the *mishna* debate only the egg? Let them debate the hen itself! If the issue is *muktzah*, then handling or eating the hen on *yom tov* is at least as problematic, and *Beit Shammai* permitting that and *Beit Hillel* forbidding it would be the more direct formulation of the debate.

### Koach Heteira

The *Gemara* responds: *lehodi'acha kochan d'Beit Shammai, de'benolad sharei* — the point of choosing the egg as the case is to demonstrate the full strength of *Beit Shammai*'s lenient position. Not only does *Beit Shammai* permit the hen itself, which is merely *muktzah*, he permits even the egg, which is *nolad* — a more severe category. Choosing the egg as the illustrative case showcases how far-reaching *Beit Shammai*'s leniency goes.

The counterpoint — why not instead mention the hen to showcase *Beit Hillel*'s stringency? — is answered by the principle of *koach deheteira adif*: the power of permitting is greater than the power of forbidding. Anyone can forbid something; it is easy to say "I am not sure, better not to do it." It takes real conviction and clarity of position to permit. Therefore it is more significant and more telling to demonstrate how far *Beit Shammai*'s permissive position extends than to demonstrate how far *Beit Hillel*'s stringent position reaches.

### Rejection

The *Gemara* is not satisfied. *V'niflegu betarveihu* — why not simply mention both? It would require only a small modification to the *mishna*: state that the hen designated for eggs and its egg — *hi u'veitzatah* — are what *Beit Shammai* permits and *Beit Hillel* forbids. The additional words are not a significant burden, and the formulation would make the debate over the hen itself fully explicit. The *Gemara* concludes that if *muktzah* of the hen were truly the *ikar* of the dispute, the *mishna* would have said so directly. The fact that only the egg is mentioned suggests the issue at stake is something intrinsic to the egg, not merely a derivative of the hen's *muktzah* status.

This is, admittedly, not an overwhelmingly powerful rejection of *Rav Nachman*'s reading. *Rav Nachman*'s explanation is quite straightforward and is supported by other *mishnayot*. The *Gemara* appears to use this objection primarily as a formal reason to transition to an alternative explanation — signaling that there are other, richer ways to read the *mishna*, particularly at the opening of a *masechet* where the *stam* has an interest in introducing broader conceptual frameworks.

---

## Rava Hachana

### Egg Readiness

*Amar Rava* — *Rava* offers an entirely different explanation. *Le'olam b'tarnigoles ha'omedes l'achilah* — let us return to the original assumption: the hen is set aside for eating. The egg is therefore not *nolad* in the sense discussed until now; it is conceptually just food that separated from food. So why does *Beit Hillel* forbid it?

*U'b'yom tov she'chal lihyos achar ha'Shabbat askinan* — we are discussing the specific case where *yom tov* falls immediately after *Shabbat*. And the issue is *mishum hachana* — preparation. *Kol beitzah d'misvalda haidana nigmrah lah me'esmol* — any egg laid today was fully formed and completed yesterday. In the scenario where *yom tov* follows *Shabbat*, "yesterday" — when the egg reached completion — was *Shabbat* itself. The egg was therefore "prepared" on *Shabbat* for use on *yom tov*, and that is a problem.

### Preparation Principle

*Rava litaimei* — *Rava* grounds this in a biblical verse: *vehayah bayom hashishi v'hechinu et asher yavi'u* — "And it shall be on the sixth day, and they shall prepare what they bring." This verse appeared to be redundant, since the Torah had already said *et asher tofu efu v'et asher tevashlu bashelu* — do all your baking and cooking. *Rava* derives from the extra language of "prepare" that the principle of *hachana* — preparation — is embedded in the Torah itself: *chol mechin l'Shabbat* — a weekday must prepare for *Shabbat*; *v'chol mechin l'yom tov* — a weekday must prepare for *yom tov*. And crucially: *v'ein yom tov mechin l'Shabbat v'ein Shabbat mechina l'yom tov* — *yom tov* cannot prepare for *Shabbat*, and *Shabbat* cannot prepare for *yom tov*.

The *chiddush* here is significant. This is not about a person actively violating *Shabbat* in order to cook for *yom tov* — that prohibition needs no special verse. The *chiddush* is that even when the preparation happens entirely on its own, without any human act of violation — like an egg naturally completing its development inside a hen — if that completion occurs on *Shabbat* or *yom tov*, and the result is intended to be used on the other sacred day, it is considered as if *Shabbat* or *yom tov* "prepared" for that other day, which is prohibited.

### Sanctity of Meals

*Rashi* frames the conceptual basis of *hachana* in terms of the *seudah*: the Torah gives special *chashivut* — weight and importance — to the meal of *Shabbat* and the meal of *yom tov*. For something to have a rightful place at that meal, it must have been ready — objectively, even if not through one's own active preparation — on a preceding weekday. The ideal expressed in *Rav Soloveitchik*'s observation, that we have many *shomrei Shabbat* but not enough *shomrei erev Shabbat*, captures the spirit of this idea: the sacred character of *Shabbat* and *yom tov* meals demands that their preparation be rooted in the weekday that precedes them, not in another sacred day.

There is a question, noted explicitly in the *Gemara*, that is somewhat counterintuitive about *Rava*'s framework: if the problem is *yom tov* preparing for *Shabbat*, it would seem that the even greater problem should be *Shabbat* preparing for Sunday. But *Rashi* makes clear that the issue is not a sense of violation of *Shabbat* or *yom tov*'s sanctity — it is not that *Shabbat* is somehow compromised by the egg's development. The problem is rather that for an item to be eligible for the *seudah* of *Shabbat* or *yom tov*, it must have been ready on a weekday. Something prepared on another sacred day lacks that qualification.

### Scope Question

Whether *Rava*'s principle of *hachana* applies broadly to all objects or specifically to food and the *seudah* remains an open question. The *mishna* itself, after all, frames the debate in terms of eating the egg — *te'achel* or *lo te'achel* — not in terms of moving it. This may reflect the possibility that *Rava*'s framework is specifically about the meal: items intended for the *seudah* of *Shabbat* or *yom tov* must be prepared from weekday; but *hachana* may not operate as a general prohibition on handling all objects. The egg, as food, falls squarely within the domain where the principle applies.

*Tosafot* addresses a closely related question. The *pesukim* speak explicitly about baking and cooking before *Shabbat* — *et asher tofu efu v'et asher tevashlu bashelu*. If the problem is *yom tov* preparing for *Shabbat*, how is it that one may cook on *yom tov* for use on the same *yom tov*? Does *eruv tavshilin*, which permits cooking on *yom tov* for *Shabbat*, not itself constitute *yom tov* preparing for *Shabbat*? *Tosafot* responds by distinguishing between degrees of readiness — just as there are degrees of *nolad*, there are degrees of *muchan*. If all the raw materials exist and are physically present before *Shabbat* or *yom tov* begins, and what remains is merely their preparation — cooking, baking — that is categorically different from something like an egg, which did not even exist in accessible form beforehand. The egg, *Tosafot* writes, *she'eino mechusar rak tikkun be'alma vemeikara havah chazi lei* — when something lacks only its finishing preparation but existed beforehand, it is in a meaningfully different position from the egg, which came into being entirely anew.

### Abaye Challenge

*Amar lei Abaye* — *Abaye* challenges *Rava*. If the paradigm case is *yom tov* following *Shabbat*, then a regular *yom tov* that does not follow *Shabbat* should be entirely permitted, since the egg was completed the day before on a weekday. Similarly, *Shabbat* on its own — not preceded by *yom tov* — should be permitted as well (setting aside the separate *muktzah* concern about the hen). *Rava* responds: *gezeirah mishum yom tov achar Shabbat* — the *rabbanan* issued a *gezeirah* applying the prohibition to all cases of *yom tov* because of the paradigm scenario of *yom tov* after *Shabbat*. And similarly, *gezeirah mishum Shabbat achar yom tov* — all cases of *Shabbat* are covered because of the scenario in which *Shabbat* follows *yom tov*. The practical result is that the prohibition extends universally: on any *yom tov* and any *Shabbat*, an egg laid on that day may not be eaten, derived by rabbinic *gezeirah* from the specific problematic cases of adjacent sacred days.

### Internal Eggs

One further question remains: *ve'hatanya, hashocheit et ha'tarnegolet u'matza bah beitzim gemurot, mutarot le'ochlam b'yom tov* — it was taught that if one *shechted* a hen on *yom tov* and found completed, unlaid eggs inside her, they are permitted to eat on *yom tov*. This appears to conflict with *Rava*'s framework. Even granting that eggs found inside a slaughtered hen are considered part of the hen's food status and not independently *nolad*, if one extends *Rava*'s prohibition through *gezeirah*, should one not also forbid these internal eggs lest they be confused with laid eggs?

*Rava* responds: *beitzim gemurot b'mei imman milsa de'lo shechicha hi* — finding complete unlaid eggs in the hen's body when it is slaughtered is an uncommon occurrence. *Milsa de'lo shechicha lo gazru bah rabbanan* — for something uncommon, the *rabbanan* did not issue a *gezeirah*. One does not extend rabbinic protective decrees to rare and unusual cases.

This is, as the *Gemara* acknowledges, a difficult explanation. *Rava*'s framework requires accepting that automatic, passive preparation — an egg completing its development without any human act — is prohibited when it occurs on one sacred day for use on another. It requires further accepting that *Abaye*'s challenge is resolved by *gezeirah* extending the prohibition to all cases. And it involves the somewhat puzzling premise, as *Tosafot* probes at length, that although the *pesukim* speak about cooking and baking as the paradigm acts of preparation, what *Rava* ultimately derives from the verse is a principle about the objective readiness of food before a sacred day, not about the acts of preparation themselves. The *Gemara* will continue tomorrow with yet another explanation.

# Beitzah 3

## Four Beitzah Explana (II)

### Rav Nachman: Muktzah

The daf begins at the very bottom of 2b, where we have already encountered two explanations for the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel in the *mishnah*. The first and simplest explanation was Rav Nachman's: Beit Shammai does not hold of *muktzah* or *nolad*, while Beit Hillel does. The *gemara* rejected this explanation for what seems a fairly minor textual reason — though perhaps a questionable one — which nonetheless allowed the discussion to advance to the next explanation.

### Rabbah: Hachana

The second explanation is Rabbah's, which introduces the concept of *hachana* — preparation — derived from a biblical verse. This is not a rabbinic *muktzah* concern but a verse-based principle. As Rashi points out, *hachana* is specifically bound up with preparing for the *seudah* of Shabbat and Yom Tov. Accordingly, something completed not on a weekday, but intended for the Shabbat or Yom Tov meal, poses a problem even when its completion occurs naturally. The egg, which finishes developing inside the chicken on a Shabbat that precedes Yom Tov, is problematic because it was not already prepared and ready on a weekday for the Yom Tov meal. Whether this principle is limited specifically to food-related items is perhaps not fully clear, but that is Rabbah's framework.

### Rav Yosef: Peiros Hanosh…

The third explanation appears two lines from the bottom of 2b, where Rav Yosef states: *gezeirah mishum peiros hanoshrin* — it is a rabbinic concern modeled on the case of fruit that drops from a tree. On Shabbat and Yom Tov, one may not eat fruit that has fallen from a tree, even if *muktzah* is not technically a problem, because permitting it might lead one to go and pluck fruit directly from the tree. Rav Yosef argues that an egg dropping from a chicken belongs to the same category: it is like food that has fallen from its originating source. Accordingly, even when the chicken was designated for eating — meaning there is no *muktzah* or *nolad* concern — the egg remains forbidden by analogy to *peiros hanoshrin*.

Before continuing, one might ask: if the chicken was designated for eating, why is there a *muktzah* problem to begin with? Tosafot raises this point, noting that if the fruit on the tree were about to drop naturally — say, because ravens in the area would normally eat it — perhaps the fruit would not be considered out of reach and therefore not *muktzah*. Yet it would still be forbidden due to this rabbinic concern. The question of why *muktzah* does not itself suffice to prohibit it is therefore a real one, and Tosafot suggests constructing a scenario where the imminent and natural detachment of the item removes the *muktzah* problem while the rabbinic decree still applies.

## Abaye: Gezeirah L'Gezeir…

### Abaye's Question

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef with a pointed question. He asks: *peiros hanoshrin* — fruit that falls from a tree — why is that forbidden? Because of a *gezeirah shema yaaleh veyitlosh*: we are concerned one will climb the tree and pluck the fruit directly. But that prohibition is itself already a rabbinic *gezeirah*. So Rav Yosef is proposing that the egg be forbidden lest it lead to the fruit-from-the-tree scenario — which is itself only a fence around a Torah prohibition. This amounts to a *gezeirah legezeirah* — a fence around a fence. The general principle is that one rabbinic safeguard is sufficient to protect a Torah prohibition; constructing a second layer of protection around the first exceeds the rabbinic mandate.

### Kula Chada Gezeirah

The *gemara* responds: *kula chada gezeirah hi* — it is all one single *gezeirah*. This answer requires careful unpacking. The claim is not simply that the rabbis chose to make an extra fence for additional protection — though Tosafot does note in other contexts, such as the rules of meat and milk, that rabbis sometimes deliberately construct multiple layers of protection. The poultry-meat prohibition, the prohibition against eating chicken and milk even cold, the six-hour waiting period — Tosafot acknowledges that in certain areas, a *gezeirah legezeirah* is indeed erected. But that is not what *kula chada gezeirah* means here.

### Rashi: Abstract Category

Rashi explains the principle differently and more precisely. The rabbis did not say: "Fruit fallen from a tree is forbidden — and therefore, by extension, let us also forbid the egg lest it lead to that case." Rather, when the rabbis formulated the decree about *peiros hanoshrin*, they framed it in an abstract and expansive category: any food that separates from its originating source on Shabbat is forbidden. The egg was therefore included within that original *gezeirah* from the outset — not as a derivative safeguard, but as part of the same conceptual decree. The egg is not prohibited because it might lead someone to pick fallen fruit; rather, the egg is itself a species of "food that fell from its originating source," and that is the very category the rabbis meant to address. Beit Hillel endorses this concern; Beit Shammai does not.

## Four Beitzah Explana (II)

### Rav Yitzchak: Mashkin Sh…

Rav Yitzchak, in the third line from the top of the new daf, offers a fourth explanation: *gezeirah mishum mashkin shezavu* — a rabbinic concern modeled on the case of liquids that flow from fruit. One is forbidden to squeeze fruit on Shabbat and Yom Tov, and by extension, even liquid that drains spontaneously from fruit is forbidden — lest permitting the naturally-expressed juice lead one to actively squeeze the fruit. Rav Yitzchak argues that the egg, which flows out of the chicken on its own, belongs to this same category of something that emerged from its source without active intervention. The egg, in his view, is analogous to grape juice that seeps out on its own.

## Abaye: Mashkin Gezeirah

### Abaye vs. Rav Yitzchak

Abaye raises the same structural challenge against Rav Yitzchak that he raised against Rav Yosef. *Mashkin shezavu* — liquids that flow from fruit — why are they forbidden? Because of *gezeirah shema yisochot*: we fear one will come to actively squeeze the fruit. That is itself a rabbinic safeguard. Is Rav Yitzchak then proposing that the egg be forbidden because it resembles a case that is itself already a *gezeirah*? That would again constitute a *gezeirah legezeirah*.

### Kula Chada (Liquids)

The *gemara* gives the same answer: *kula chada gezeirah hi*. Just as with Rav Yosef's explanation, the decree concerning *mashkin shezavu* was formulated at an abstract level that already encompassed the egg. When the rabbis said that things which flow out of their originating source are forbidden, they were speaking broadly enough to include the egg within that category. The egg is thus not a fence built around the fence of flowing liquids — it is part of the same original fence.

## Fruit vs. Liquids Debate

### Assessment of Positions

The *gemara* now pauses to take stock of where matters stand. It notes that all the remaining *Amoraim* — those offering the third and fourth explanations — declined to adopt Rav Nachman's position. The objection to Rav Nachman, recall, was a textual one: if the debate were simply about *muktzah* and the chicken were designated for laying eggs, we would expect the *mishnah* to address the chicken as well, not only the egg. Rav Nachman's explanation is therefore set aside. Similarly, the remaining *Amoraim* did not adopt Rabbah's position — they do not hold of this biblical concept of *hachana*. *Muktzah* as a rabbinic category they accept; the independent biblical principle of *hachana*, tied to preparation for Shabbat and Yom Tov meals, is Rabbah's alone.

### Rav Yosef's Choice

The *gemara* then asks: Rav Yosef, who frames the egg as analogous to *peiros hanoshrin* — why does he not instead adopt Rav Yitzchak's reasoning and analogize it to flowing liquids? The answer: *beitzah ochla* — an egg is food, a solid foodstuff. *Peiros ochla* — fruit is likewise food. The egg and the fallen fruit share the same category of solid edibles, and the analogy is therefore more natural. Liquids, *mashkin*, are a different type of entity entirely, and the egg is less similar to juice than it is to fruit. The closer analogy is therefore to *peiros hanoshrin*.

### Rav Yitzchak's Choice

Conversely, the *gemara* asks: Rav Yitzchak, who uses the flowing-liquids framework — why does he not adopt Rav Yosef's fruit-from-a-tree analogy? He acknowledges the difference in physical form, but argues that a more fundamental distinction governs the comparison. *Beitzah blu'ah* — an egg is absorbed, contained, held within the chicken. What emerges is something that was enclosed inside its source and then came out. That dynamic is precisely what characterizes juice inside a grape: it is held within the fruit and then flows out. Fruit hanging on a tree, by contrast, is *miglo v'kaimu* — exposed and present in front of you, visible and exterior. The egg's enclosed origin makes it more like the contained-and-released liquid than like the externally hanging fruit.

This comparison points once more to the fact that neither of these explanations involves a *gezeirah legezeirah* in the strict sense. The prohibition is not: "Avoid the egg lest it lead you to the other case." Rather, the egg is conceptually similar enough to one of these categories that when the rabbis originally formulated the decree in abstract terms, the egg was already included. The debate between Rav Yosef and Rav Yitzchak is simply about which abstract category the egg more closely resembles.

## Fruit Picking on Yom Tov

### Tosafot's Challenge

An important question now emerges. Both of these final explanations presuppose that picking fruit from a tree or squeezing fruit is forbidden even on Yom Tov. But this requires examination, because on Yom Tov, acts performed for the purpose of food preparation are generally permitted. One can perform *shechitah*, one can cook — why, then, can one not pick fruit from a tree? Is that not equally a food-related act?

Tosafot raises this question in the passage beginning with the word *yivla'enu*, approximately in the middle of the relevant discussion. He writes: *ach teima* — it is a wonder. Why must we worry, *shema ya'aleh veyitlosh*, that one will climb and pluck fruit from a tree? *Ha afilu l'chatchila mutar litlosh* — should it not be permitted outright on Yom Tov? After all, *ochel nefesh mutar* — acts for the purpose of food are permitted, and the fact that one could have prepared in advance is no disqualification: cooking on Yom Tov is permitted even though one could have cooked beforehand. So why is plucking fruit from a tree forbidden?

### Yerushalmi: Milishah V'E…

Tosafot cites an explanation from Rabbeinu Nesanel in the name of the Yerushalmi. The verse states: *ach asher ye'achel l'chol nefesh* — whatever is needed for eating — and this is immediately juxtaposed with *ushmartem et hamatzos* — you shall guard the *matzos*. The Yerushalmi learns from this juxtaposition that the *melachot* permitted for food preparation on Yom Tov are those that correspond to the stage of production at which one must begin guarding *matzah* from becoming *chametz*. When does one begin guarding? From the moment water meets flour — that is, from the stage of kneading. The Yerushalmi therefore derives: *mishimur va'eilach, hem mutarot d'haynu milisha va'eilach* — from kneading onwards, these *melachot* are permitted. *Aval she'ar melachot d'mikodem lachen asurin* — but all earlier stages of production are forbidden.

### Home vs. Field Preparati…

This becomes a foundational conceptual principle about what *ochel nefesh* permits on Yom Tov. It does not extend to going out into the field with a scythe and cutting down wheat. The Yerushalmi establishes a limit — understood by the Yerushalmi as biblical — and ties it to the analogy of *matzah*: only from kneading onward is preparation permitted.

What underlies this distinction conceptually? Some *Acharonim* suggest the key is the locus of the preparation: acts of food preparation that are performed within the domestic sphere — in the home — are permitted, while harvesting, grinding, and sifting, which take place in the field or at industrial scale, are not. Interestingly, *shechitah* in our context might seem to belong in the field, but in the ancient household one would slaughter in one's own courtyard, so it still fell within the domestic domain.

It should be noted that this principle is not universally accepted in precisely this form. Not all authorities hold that the Yerushalmi's formulation is the basis, nor that the cutoff is *de'oraita*. And there are complicating cases later in the tractate: certain spices, for example, may be ground on Yom Tov — a stage of production that precedes *lishahby far — because freshly ground spices are superior in a way that cannot be replicated in advance. Grinding is much earlier in the sequence than kneading, yet the *halachah* may permit it under certain conditions. So *milisha va'eilach* is not necessarily an absolute cutoff in every case, but what it establishes unambiguously is that not every food-related act is permitted on Yom Tov — there are limits, and the paradigmatic phrase is *milisha va'eilach*.

## Rabbi Yochanan's Problem

### R. Yochanan: Mashkin

The *gemara* now states that Rabbi Yochanan likewise holds that the reason behind the *mishnah*'s prohibition of the egg is *gezeirah mishum mashkin shezavu* — it is in the category of liquids that flow from their source. This is demonstrated by a question Rabbi Yochanan raises: he notes what appears to be a contradiction between two positions attributed to Rabbi Yehuda and proceeds to resolve it — but the very fact that he perceives a tension between these two positions reveals his underlying assumption about the egg.

The first statement of Rabbi Yehuda comes from a *mishnah* in Shabbat: *ein sochtin et hapeiros lehotzi mehen mashkin* — one may not squeeze fruit to extract liquid from it, and even if liquids flow out on their own, *v'im yatzu me'atzman asurin* — they are forbidden. But Rabbi Yehuda qualifies this: *im l'ochlin, hayotzei mehen mutar* — if the fruit was designated for eating, the liquid that comes out naturally is permitted. *V'im l'mashkin, hayotzei mehen assur* — but if the fruit was designated to be turned into liquid, what flows out is forbidden.

The logic is straightforward: the rabbinic concern is that permitting naturally-expressed juice will lead one to actively squeeze the fruit. But that concern only applies when the fruit's purpose is to yield juice — as with grapes designated for wine. If the fruit is meant to be eaten — like a grapefruit set aside for consumption — there is no reason to fear that allowing a bit of runoff juice will lead to active squeezing. The rabbinic decree therefore does not apply in that case.

### R. Yochanan's Contradict…

Rabbi Yochanan now identifies what appears to be a contradiction. The principle stated above is that any food that comes from food set aside for eating is permissible — *ochla de'afreshei* — like the juice from a grapefruit. But Rabbi Yehuda, in another context, speaks of an egg laid on Yom Tov as problematic. Rabbi Yochanan asks: the egg comes from a chicken that is set aside for eating. Should that not make it analogous to the grapefruit case, where the derived food is permitted? Why does Rabbi Yehuda treat the egg as a problem?

The very fact that Rabbi Yochanan finds this contradiction significant — that he is troubled by the apparent inconsistency between the egg case and the grapefruit case — reveals his assumption. He assumes that the egg's prohibition is grounded in the same principle as the *mashkin shezavu* concern. If he held that the egg was forbidden for a different reason — *muktzah*, or *hachana*, or fruit from a tree — the grapefruit case would be wholly irrelevant, and no contradiction would arise. The *gemara* notes this explicitly: from the fact that Rabbi Yochanan connects these two positions and is troubled by their apparent inconsistency, *shema mina chad ta'ama hu* — we infer that he holds they share a common basis. Rabbi Yochanan therefore sides with the view that the egg falls into the category of *mashkin shezavu*.

### Rosh Hashanah Two-Day Is…

The second statement of Rabbi Yehuda, which Rabbi Yochanan finds in tension with the first, comes from a debate in Eiruvin concerning the status of the two days of Rosh Hashanah. The question there is whether the two days of Rosh Hashanah function as a single continuous *kedushah* — one indivisible unit — or whether each day is independently uncertain, like a standard two-day Yom Tov of *sefeka deyoma*: each day is treated as though one does not know whether it is Yom Tov or a weekday.

The practical difference is significant. In a standard two-day Yom Tov, one can stipulate regarding a basket of *tevel* fruit as follows: on the first day, one declares that if today is Yom Tov, this designation has no effect, but if today is a weekday, one is hereby separating *trumos u'ma'asros*. On the second day, one repeats the process. Since one of the two days must actually be a weekday, the *ma'asros* will have been validly separated on whichever day was the weekday, and the fruit becomes permissible on the second day. Rabbi Yehuda holds that the two days of Rosh Hashanah may be treated this way — each day is independently uncertain, and this mechanism functions there just as it does on a normal two-day Yom Tov.

Rabbi Yehuda further states: *beitzah shenolda berishon, tochel besheini* — an egg laid on the first day of Rosh Hashanah may be eaten on the second day. The reasoning: if the second day is Yom Tov, then the first day was a weekday, and the egg was laid on a weekday and is perfectly permissible. If the second day is a weekday, then even if the egg was laid on Yom Tov, today is *chol* and the *muktzah* or other concern no longer applies. The Rabbis disagree, holding that Rosh Hashanah is a single continuous *kedushah* — *kedushah achat hi* — and the egg therefore remains forbidden on the second day as well.

The point for our purposes is that Rabbi Yehuda's discussion of the egg in the context of Rosh Hashanah confirms that he accepts, at least at some level, that there is an issue with an egg laid on Yom Tov. This is what triggers Rabbi Yochanan's question: Rabbi Yehuda allows the juice from a grapefruit yet acknowledges a problem with the egg — how are these consistent?

## Solutions to Contradicti…

### Ravina: Reverse Position

Rabbi Yochanan's own resolution is *muchlefet hashita* — reverse the positions. Originally, the understanding was that it is Rabbi Yehuda who permits the juice from the grapefruit while the Rabbis forbid all flowing liquids indiscriminately. Rabbi Yochanan proposes switching this: it is the Rabbis who make the distinction between fruit designated for eating versus fruit designated for squeezing, while Rabbi Yehuda forbids all naturally-expressed liquids without distinction. If Rabbi Yehuda's position is that all flowing liquids are forbidden regardless of the fruit's designation, then the egg — which is like a liquid that emerged from its source — would be forbidden consistently with his other rulings. This resolves the contradiction, even if it is not the most elegant of solutions.

The *gemara* adds that the very act of Rabbi Yochanan connecting these two statements and resolving them together confirms, *shema mina*, that he views both as resting on the same underlying principle — the *mashkin shezavu* framework.

### Ravina: Chicken for Eggs

Two alternative answers are then offered that avoid the need to reverse Rabbi Yehuda's position entirely.

The first is from Ravina: *le'olam lo teipoch* — there is no need to reverse anything. Rabbi Yehuda can consistently hold both that the juice of a grapefruit is permitted and that the egg is a problem — because in his statement about Rosh Hashanah, Rabbi Yehuda is not actually asserting that he himself believes the egg is forbidden. Rather, *Rabbi Yehuda lidvreihem deRabbanan ka'amar* — Rabbi Yehuda is speaking in terms of the Rabbis' position, not his own. His own view is that the egg presents no problem, just as the grapefruit juice presents no problem: *de'uchla de'aparsei hu* — it is simply food that derived from food. But he addresses the case of the egg on Rosh Hashanah as a vehicle for making a different point: to the Rabbis, who hold that the egg is forbidden, he says at minimum you must concede that on the second day of Rosh Hashanah it should be permitted, since on a standard two-day Yom Tov the second day's egg would be allowed. The Rabbis respond that Rosh Hashanah is different — *kedushah achat hi* — and the egg remains forbidden. So the egg case in the Rosh Hashanah debate is really a proxy argument about the nature of the two days, not a concession by Rabbi Yehuda that the egg is inherently problematic.

The second answer comes from Ravina son of Rav Ulla, who sidesteps the entire difficulty by reframing the case in the Rosh Hashanah discussion altogether: *hacha betarnegolet hamedet legadel beitzim* — there, the discussion concerns a chicken that was designated for laying eggs, not for eating. In such a case, Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that the egg is problematic poses no difficulty whatsoever, because a chicken set aside for egg-laying presents a straightforward *muktzah* issue that everyone agrees on — even Beit Shammai. *Rabbi Yehuda litaimei d'it lei muktzah* — and Rabbi Yehuda, who holds strongly of *muktzah* against Rabbi Shimon's more lenient position, would naturally rule that such an egg is forbidden.

This answer also clarifies the overall landscape of the four explanations. The three later explanations — Rabbah's *hachana*, Rav Yosef's *peiros hanoshrin*, and Rav Yitzchak's *mashkin shezavu* — all presuppose that the debate in the *mishnah* involves a chicken designated for eating, where a *muktzah* problem does not straightforwardly apply. In that case one needs a separate reason to prohibit the egg — hence the three alternative frameworks. But if the chicken is there for laying eggs, there is no need for any of these additional reasons: *muktzah* is sufficient, and there is no debate. The debate in the *mishnah* must therefore be about the more difficult case, where the chicken is designated for eating.

## Baraita on Eggs

### Baraita: Egg Prohibition

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* to test how the various explanations hold up under scrutiny. The *baraita* states: whether an egg was laid on Shabbat or on Yom Tov, *ein metaletlin otah* — one may not move it; it is effectively *muktzah*. One may not use it to cover a vessel — as one might plug up the top of a bottle with an egg — nor may one use it to support the legs of a bed. However, one may invert a vessel over the egg to prevent it from being broken. This raises an interesting sub-question: may one move a vessel for the sake of a *muktzah* object, to protect it? The *baraita* seems to permit this, in contrast to the position that *ein kli nital ela litzorech davar hanital* — a vessel may only be moved for the sake of something that is itself permitted to be moved.

The *baraita* then adds two further rulings: *usfeika asura* — a doubtful egg is likewise forbidden; and *v'im nitarva be'elef kullan assurot* — if the egg became mixed into a thousand other eggs, all of them are forbidden. The *gemara* now examines how each of these rulings fares under the different explanations of the egg's prohibition.

### Rabbah & Safek D'Oraita

The ruling about *sfeika* — doubt — fits naturally with Rabbah's position. Rabbah grounds the egg's prohibition in the biblical concept of *hachana*, and therefore any doubt about whether the egg was laid today or yesterday is a doubt in a *de'oraita* matter. *Vekol sfeika d'oraita lechumra* — all biblical doubts are resolved stringently. It should be noted that Rabbah's concern with *hachana* applies primarily when Yom Tov and Shabbat are juxtaposed, whereas the *baraita* is discussing a regular Yom Tov. Nevertheless, the *gemara*'s point is that Rabbah's framework involves a genuine biblical dimension, and it is therefore coherent that a case of doubt would be treated strictly.

### Rav Yosef/Yitzchak: Safe…

The difficulty arises for Rav Yosef and Rav Yitzchak, whose explanations are purely rabbinic in origin. For them, the egg's prohibition is a rabbinic decree — either by analogy to *peiros hanoshrin* or to *mashkin shezavu* — with no biblical basis. A doubt in a purely rabbinic matter is *sfeika d'rabbanan*, and *vekol sfeika d'rabbanan lekula* — all rabbinic doubts are resolved leniently. Why, then, does the *baraita* rule that a doubtful egg is forbidden?

## Shift to Treifah Cas (II)

### Gemara's Reinterpretation

To resolve this difficulty, the *gemara* proposes a forced but necessary reinterpretation: *seifa atan lesafek treifah*. The ruling about doubt in the *baraita* does not continue to discuss an egg whose status is uncertain with respect to Yom Tov. Rather, the *baraita* shifts mid-passage — without announcing the transition — to a different type of doubtful egg: one where the uncertainty concerns whether the chicken that laid it was a *treifah*. If the chicken itself was *treifah*, the egg it lays is likewise *treifah* and forbidden. A doubt about whether the chicken was a *treifah* is a doubt in a *de'oraita* matter, and such doubts are resolved stringently. Hence the ruling that the doubtful egg is forbidden.

This reading is admittedly strained. Shifting from the case of an egg laid on Yom Tov to the case of an egg from a possibly *treifah* chicken without any textual marker is not a natural reading of the *baraita*. But the *gemara* accepts this reinterpretation as the price of reconciling the *baraita*'s stringent ruling on doubt with the positions of Rav Yosef and Rav Yitzchak.

## Shift to Treifah Cas (II)

### Davar Sheyesh Lo Matirin

With the *sfeika* ruling accounted for, the *gemara* now turns to the final clause: the egg mixed into a thousand. Here the analysis branches depending on which case the *baraita* is addressing.

If the *baraita* is discussing an egg that is forbidden because of Yom Tov — a purely rabbinic prohibition — then the reason it is not *batel* even in a thousand is the principle of *davar sheyesh lo matirin*: something that will become permissible at a later time. The egg forbidden on Yom Tov will be perfectly permissible tomorrow, when Yom Tov ends. Since the egg has a natural path to becoming permitted — simply by waiting — we do not allow *bittul* to serve as a workaround. *Vekol davar sheyesh lo matirin, afilu be'elef lo batel* — anything that has a permitting factor does not become *batel* even in a thousand. Rashi explains the logic: rather than eating something that is presently forbidden — even if *bittul* would technically permit it — it is better to simply wait and eat it when it is fully permitted without any workaround. *Ad she'tochlenu be'issur, tochlenu beheter* — rather than eating it under a dispensation, wait to eat it when it is entirely permitted.

This principle has notable relevance to *Pesach*: the stringency by which even the tiniest amount of *chametz* is forbidden is understood by some as an application of *davar sheyesh lo matirin* — since *chametz* will become permissible after *Pesach*, *bittul* cannot work to permit it during *Pesach*, no matter the ratio.

## Bittul and Eggs

### No Bittul via Matirin

So if the final clause of the *baraita* — the egg mixed into a thousand — is addressing the Yom Tov case, the explanation is clean: *davar sheyesh lo matirin* accounts for the absence of *bittul*, and the stringency follows naturally.

### Egg as Davar Shebeminyan

But the *gemara* has just proposed that the *sfeika* clause refers to a *treifah* egg. It now asks whether the final clause — the mixing into a thousand — also refers to the *treifah* case. If so, the *davar sheyesh lo matirin* rationale does not apply: a *treifah* egg has no path to becoming permissible, so that principle is irrelevant. Why, then, would the egg not become *batel*?

The *gemara* answers: *vechi teima beitzah chashuva velo batla* — one might say that an egg is a significant, discrete item and therefore does not become *batel* through mixture. The underlying principle is *davar shebeminyan*: something that is always counted individually, that is always treated as a distinct unit rather than as part of an undifferentiated mass, does not lose its identity in a mixture and therefore cannot undergo *bittul*.

The conceptual point is that *bittul* operates by causing an item to lose its individual identity — to be subsumed into the larger mass around it, like a single drop of non-kosher liquid dissolved into a vast quantity of kosher liquid. But items that are always perceived as discrete, counted units never acquire this quality of being subsumed. Each one is always its own entity, always treated individually, and therefore *bittul* cannot conceptually apply.

One might wonder: does this not apply to any physically discrete object, such as a potato? The answer is that physical discreteness is necessary but not sufficient. What matters is whether the item is *socially* treated as always individually counted and significant — whether, in other words, people always relate to it as an independent unit, never as part of a conglomerate.

### Mishna: Six/Seven Items

This raises the question of what the rule is. The *gemara* cites a *mishnah*: someone had bundles of *tiltan* — fenugreek — that were *kilei hakerem*, grown together with grapevines and therefore forbidden, requiring burning. If these became mixed with other bundles of fenugreek, and something from that mixture fell into yet another mixture, Rabbi Meir says *kulan yidlaku* — everything must be burned; *bittul* does not apply. The Rabbis say *ya'alu b'echad u'matayim* — 200-to-1 suffices to create *bittul*, as is the normal rule for *kilayim*.

Rabbi Meir grounds his ruling in the principle that *et she'darko limnot mekadesh* — items that are counted by number sanctify their mixture, meaning they do not undergo *bittul*. The Rabbis, rejecting the abstract rule, hold instead that only specific enumerated items are immune to *bittul*: *eino mekadesh ela shisha devarim bilvad* — only six things sanctify their mixture — or seven, according to Rabbi Akiva. These are: nuts from Phrach, pomegranates from Badan, sealed barrels of wine, bundles of spinach, bundles of cabbage, a Greek gourd, and — according to Rabbi Akiva — home-baked bread. These items are *chashuvim*, significant discrete units, and *bittul* does not apply to them. Rambam understands this list not as fixed for all time, but as contextually dependent: each era and locale must identify which items carry that quality of individual significance. But the underlying framework remains: not all counted items are equal — only those that are always treated as individual units of particular significance are immune from *bittul*.

### Et vs. Kol She'Darko

Within Rabbi Meir's position, there is a crucial textual debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish. Rabbi Yochanan reads Rabbi Meir as saying *et she'darko limnot shaninu* — we are speaking only of items that are *exclusively* counted, never sold by weight or volume. Reish Lakish reads Rabbi Meir as saying *kol she'darko limnot shaninu* — anything that is *ever* counted, even if it is sometimes sold in bulk, is immune from *bittul*.

This debate directly bears on the egg. Eggs are sometimes sold by number — by the dozen — and sometimes bundled together in baskets without individual counting. Under Reish Lakish's reading of Rabbi Meir, the fact that eggs are sometimes counted suffices to render them immune from *bittul*, and the *baraita*'s ruling that the egg mixed into a thousand remains forbidden is explained. Under Rabbi Yochanan's reading, however, the egg is not exclusively counted, and therefore Rabbi Meir's rule would not apply to it — leaving open the question of why *bittul* does not work when the egg's prohibition is one of *treifah* rather than Yom Tov.

The *gemara* thus concludes this daf with an unresolved tension: according to Reish Lakish's reading of Rabbi Meir, the egg as *davar shebeminyan* explains the *baraita*'s stringency even in the *treifah* scenario. But according to Rabbi Yochanan's own reading of Rabbi Meir, the egg does not qualify as exclusively counted, and the explanation fails. The *gemara* will continue with this question on the following daf.

---

---

# Beitzah 4

## Egg in Mixtures

### Egg Bitel Challenge

The daf begins by picking up at the bottom of 3b, continuing the discussion of a *brayta* concerning the status of an egg laid on *Yom Tov*. One of the rulings in that *brayta* was that in a case of doubt, the egg is forbidden. The *Gemara* challenges this on several grounds. If the underlying prohibition is rabbinic in nature — such as the concern about fruit falling from a tree or flowing liquids, which constitutes *muktzah* — then a doubt in a rabbinic matter should ordinarily be treated leniently. The *Gemara* therefore suggests that perhaps the *brayta* is addressing a case involving *trefah*, a biblical concern, rather than a purely rabbinic *Yom Tov* issue.

But this creates a further difficulty. The *brayta* also states that if such an egg becomes mixed up with a thousand others, all of them are forbidden. If the issue is *Yom Tov*-related, this is well understood: the principle of *dabar she'yesh lo matirin* — that something which will become permitted on its own need not and should not be permitted through other means — explains why the egg cannot be nullified through a mixture. You simply wait until tomorrow. But if the underlying issue is *trefah*, why would the egg not become *batel* when mixed with so many others?

The *Gemara* suggests that the egg might be considered a *dabar she'be'minyan* — a counted item — and as such retains its individual identity and cannot be subsumed into a mixture. However, this only holds if one applies the opinion that anything with a tendency to be sold by count (*kol she'darko limnot*) is never *batel*. If the narrower position is correct — that only items *exclusively* sold by count (*et she'darko limnot*) are exempt from *bitul* — then an egg, which is sometimes sold by volume or weight rather than individually, ought to become *batel*. The question therefore remains: why, on the *trefah* reading, is the egg not *batel*?

### Rav Pappa: Counted Items

*Rav Pappa* resolves this by identifying the author of the *brayta* in question. He says: *hai tanna tanna de'litra ketzi'ot hu* — the author of this *brayta* is the same *tanna* who authored the *brayta* of the *litra ketzi'ot*, the barrel of pressed figs. That source establishes the principle: *kol dabar she'be'minyan afilu de'rabbanan lo battel* — anything that is sometimes sold by count is never *batel*, even if the prohibition involved is only rabbinic. And *kal va'homer*, how much more so in a case of a biblical concern like *trefah*.

This resolves the difficulty. The reason the egg is not *batel* even in the *trefah* reading is not that eggs are exclusively sold by count — they are not — but because this particular *tanna* holds that even things *sometimes* sold by count are never *batel*, and this applies even to rabbinic-level prohibitions.

### Pressed Figs Brayta

The *brayta* of the *litra ketzi'ot* describes the following scenario. In ancient times, figs were pressed into large rounds or cakes and stacked within barrels (*chaviot*). Merchants would sell sections of these pressed-fig rounds by weight or volume. Now suppose one *litra* — a measured quantity — of such figs that are *terumah* was pressed into the top of one of many barrels, but you no longer know which barrel. The normal rule for *terumah* falling into *chulin* is that one requires a hundred times the amount of *terumah* to achieve *bitul*. But the question here is: what counts as "a hundred times"? Should you tally the total volume of figs across all barrels, or must you count specifically the tops of the barrels — since you know the *terumah* was pressed at the top, and the only genuine uncertainty is which barrel's top contains it?

A further nuance: *terumah* of fruit, as opposed to *terumah* of grain, wine, or oil (*dagan tirosh veyitzhar*), is only a rabbinic obligation. This bears on how stringently the requirement is applied. One might argue that, particularly for rabbinic *terumah*, leniency in calculating the required ratio is appropriate. The Rabbis in some contexts did go easy in precisely this way — not by waiving the requirement, but by permitting a creative interpretation of what satisfies it.

The *brayta* sets out this scenario in three parallel formulations: pressing figs into a barrel (*chavit*) without knowing which barrel; pressing them into a round container (*igul*) without knowing which one; and pressing them into a cylindrical vessel (*kiveret*) without knowing which. In all three cases, the essential question is the same: what quantity of permissible figs is required to render the *terumah batel*?

### Barrels Debate

*Rabbi Meir* in the *brayta* presents a debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* on this question, though *Rabbi Yehuda* presents the same debate in a different formulation — and the two versions assign the positions in reverse.

According to *Rabbi Meir*'s version: *Rabbi Eliezer* takes a lenient approach, ruling *ro'in et ha'elyonot ke'ilu hen perudot* — we treat the tops of the barrels as if they are distinct, while *hatachtonot ma'alot et ha'elyonot* — the bottoms of the barrels can be counted together with the tops to create *bitul*. In other words, you need not find a hundred other barrel-tops; you may include the total volume of all the figs across the barrels, tops and bottoms alike, to achieve the hundredfold ratio. *Rabbi Yehoshua*, in this version, is more stringent: *im yesh me'ah pumim ya'alu* — only if there are a hundred other barrel-tops does *bitul* take effect. If not, the tops of all the barrels are forbidden but the bottoms are permitted.

According to *Rabbi Yehuda*'s version, the positions are shifted one degree of stringency. *Rabbi Eliezer* already holds the stricter view: you must have a hundred other tops. *Rabbi Yehoshua* goes even further, ruling: *afilu yesh sham shelosh me'ot pumim lo ya'alu* — even if there are three hundred other barrel-tops, *bitul* still does not apply.

The *Gemara* then notes a third case: if the *terumah* figs were pressed into a barrel but you do not know *where within* the barrel they are — north, south, top, bottom — then *divrei hakol ya'alu*, all agree that *bitul* works. This makes sense because in that scenario the uncertainty is not just which barrel-top, but where among all the figs in all the barrels the *terumah* may be, and it is genuinely distributed throughout. *Rav Pappa* clarifies that this is the correct reading of the final line of the *brayta*: "pressed into an *igul* without knowing where" means not knowing the position *within* the barrel, and in that case everyone agrees.

The significance of this entire discussion for our original question is now clear. *Rabbi Yehoshua* in *Rabbi Yehuda*'s version holds that even three hundred tops do not create *bitul*. Why? Because these pressed-fig rounds are sometimes sold by count — you might say "sell me one round of pressed figs." Since they are sometimes sold as individual units, this *tanna* holds that they never become *batel*, and this applies even to rabbinic-level *terumah*. This is precisely the opinion *Rav Pappa* identifies as the one underpinning our *brayta* about the egg. An egg, too, is sometimes sold by count. Therefore, according to this *tanna*, even a rabbinic concern — and certainly a biblical one like *trefah* — is never rendered *batel* when the item in question is sometimes counted.

The concept of *dabar she'be'minyan* can be understood intuitively: *bitul* operates by dissolving an item's individual identity into a larger whole. But an item that is sold and treated as a discrete, countable unit resists this dissolution. Each egg, like each person, has its own identity and refuses to become merely part of an aggregate. Because of this irreducible individuality, *bitul* simply cannot take hold.

This resolution, though logically coherent, is admittedly a somewhat strained reading of the *brayta*. It requires introducing the category of *trefah* into a *brayta* that appears on its face to be discussing a *Yom Tov* concern, and then invoking an expansive opinion about *dabar she'be'minyan* to explain why even that *trefah*-based concern would not be subject to *bitul*. Both steps carry some difficulty.

### Rav Ashi: Yom Tov Issue

*Rav Ashi* offers an alternative that is textually cleaner. He says: *le'olam safek Yom Tov safek chol* — the *brayta* is indeed discussing only the straightforward *Yom Tov* concern, exactly as it appears. There is no need to introduce *trefah* at all. The egg is *muktzah* due to the rabbinic concern about items that came into being on *Yom Tov* — fruit that drops from a tree, liquids that flow — and the underlying prohibition is rabbinic throughout.

The question then returns: why should a *safek* — a mere doubt as to whether the egg was laid on *Yom Tov* or on a weekday — be treated stringently? The ordinary rule is *safek de'rabbanan l'kula* — we are lenient in cases of doubt when the underlying prohibition is only rabbinic.

*Rav Ashi*'s answer: *havei davar she'yesh lo matirin afilu be'rabbanan lo batil*. The same principle that explains why the egg mixed into a thousand others is not *batel* — namely, that something which will become permitted on its own (*davar she'yesh lo matirin*) cannot be dissolved through *bitul* — applies equally to explain why a doubt about such an item does not invoke the leniency of *safek de'rabbanan*. Why invoke that principle of leniency when you can simply wait until tomorrow? The egg will be permitted then; use it then.

This is a striking extension of *davar she'yesh lo matirin*. Until now the principle was understood as applying specifically within the laws of *ta'aroves* — mixtures. *Rav Ashi* applies it to the entirely separate domain of how we adjudicate doubt in rabbinic matters. The practical implications are considerable. One prominent example: the question of *chadash* — consuming grain of uncertain vintage, possibly grown before the *omer* offering of the previous *Pesach*. Many medieval authorities permitted this by constructing a *safek sefeka*, a double doubt: perhaps the grain was from the prior year's harvest; and even if it was this year's, perhaps it took root before the *omer*. But *chadash* is precisely a *davar she'yesh lo matirin* — it becomes permitted after the second day of *Pesach* the following year. If *Rav Ashi*'s principle is applied beyond *ta'aroves* to the general logic of permitting something in the face of doubt, then the entire *safek sefeka* argument for *chadash* would be undermined: why rely on a constructed double doubt when you can simply wait until next year?

One might distinguish between a *safek sefeka* and a simple *safek de'rabbanan*, but the principle as articulated here has far-reaching potential. *Rav Ashi*'s read of the *brayta* is the cleaner one — everything remains within the framework of the *Yom Tov* egg, no detour through *trefah* is required — but the implications of extending *davar she'yesh lo matirin* into the logic of halakhic doubt are profound.

---

## Egg & Mother

### Rabbi Eliezer Brayta

The *Gemara* now introduces a *Tosefta*: *Acherim omrim mishum Rabbi Eliezer* — others say in the name of *Rabbi Eliezer*: *beitzah techal hi ve-imma* — the egg may be eaten, and so may its mother. The *Gemara* asks what the case must be. If the hen was designated for eating (*tarnegolet ha-omedet la-achilah*), then it should obviously be permitted — as *Rashi* notes, nobody debates the permissibility of the mother in such a case. Why would it need to be stated? The *Gemara* therefore considers the alternative: perhaps the *brayta* is discussing a hen designated for laying eggs. But in that case the hen would be *muktzah*, and stating that both may be eaten becomes puzzling in the opposite direction.

### Hen Sans Purpose

*Rav Zeira* explains: *tochal agav imah* — you may eat the egg on the basis of its mother. *Abaye* then specifies the case: *kegon she-lekachah stam* — a hen that was purchased without specifying its purpose. The buyer has not yet decided whether this hen will be slaughtered for food or kept for laying eggs.

This is precisely the case that resolves the difficulty. If the hen was set aside for eating, there is no *muktzah* issue — neither for the hen nor for the egg. If it was set aside for laying, both would be *muktzah*. But when no determination has been made, the *halacha* depends on what ultimately happens. If you slaughter it on *Yom Tov* — *huverar d'la-achilah omedet* — it is thereby retroactively clarified that this was a hen intended for food, and both the hen and the egg are permitted. If you do not slaughter it through *Yom Tov* — *lo nishcheta huverar d'l'beitzim omedet* — that itself indicates that the hen was being kept for eggs, rendering both hen and egg *muktzah*.

This seemingly incidental phrase — "and its mother" — thus leads the *Gemara* to address the case of *stam*, the undesignated hen, and the use of *breira*, retroactive clarification, to determine the egg's status. It is worth noting that one need not even invoke *breira* as a formal principle here; there is a reasonable argument that an item of uncertain *muktzah* status — *safek muktzah* — may itself be permitted, since *muktzah* requires a definitive designation. The *Gemara*, however, resolves it through the mechanism of retroactive determination via the fate of the mother.

### Guzma Interpretation

*Rav Mari* offers a simpler and more elegant explanation of the *brayta*: *guzma katani* — the *brayta* employs *guzma*, embellishment for emphasis. The *chiddush* of the teaching is exclusively about the egg. But to convey just how permitted the egg is, the *brayta* states in expansive terms: eat the egg, eat the mother, eat the chick, eat the shell. The mention of the mother, the chick, and the shell adds nothing legally; it is rhetorical amplification.

A second *brayta* is cited in support: *Acherim omrim mishum Rabbi Eliezer* — the same tradition of *Rabbi Eliezer* — states: *beitzatah te'achel, hi, ve-imah, ve-efrochah, ve-klipatah* — eat the egg, eat the mother, eat the chick, and eat the shell. *Gezuntaheit* — eat everything. Taken literally, this cannot be the intent, since no one eats an eggshell. The *Gemara* therefore considers whether *klipatah* might mean the chick *within* its shell — that is, an egg containing a live chick. But this too is untenable: there is a debate between *Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov* and the *rabbanan* about a chick that has emerged from the egg but not yet opened its eyes. That debate, the *Gemara* says, only applies once the chick has entered the world (*yatza l'avir ha-olam*). While the chick is still within the shell, all agree it is forbidden — it has the status of *eiver min ha-chai*, a limb from a living animal, since it remains part of the mother. Eating the chick-in-the-shell is therefore *assur* regardless of *Yom Tov*. The phrase cannot be taken as a *halakhic* ruling; it must be *guzma*. And the same applies to the earlier version: eat the egg, eat the mother — *guzma*, pure embellishment to underscore the permissibility of the egg.

What this *brayta* also reveals is that *Rabbi Eliezer* — who was, notably, of *Beis Shammai* — held the *Beis Shammai* position that the egg laid on *Yom Tov* is permitted, at least when the hen is designated for eating. The tradition is not an independent one; it is the *Beis Shammai* position transmitted in the name of one of its prominent adherents.

---

## Shabbat/Yom Tov Egg

### Shabbat-Yom Tov Egg

The *Gemara* now turns to a new *itmar*: the case of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* falling back to back. *Rav* says: *nolda be-zeh asurah be-zeh* — if an egg is born on one of the two days, it remains forbidden on the other. *Rabbi Yochanan* says the opposite: *nolda be-zeh muteret be-zeh* — if born on one day, it is permitted on the following day.

### Kedusha Unity

One might suppose the debate turns on whether *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* are regarded as a single continuous *kedusha* or as two distinct *kedushos*. If they are one *kedusha*, then an egg born on either day is still within that single prohibited period when the other day arrives, and remains forbidden. If they are two *kedushos*, then on the second day the egg is treated as something that already existed beforehand, and there is no reason to prohibit it.

However, the *Gemara* immediately rejects this framing. *Rav* himself explicitly rules, in a different context, *halakha k'arba'a zekenim ve-aliba de-Rabbi Eliezer d'amar shtei kedushot hen* — the *halacha* follows the four elders according to *Rabbi Eliezer* who says *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* constitute two *kedushos*. *Rav* cannot, therefore, be forbidding the egg because he views them as one *kedusha*.

### Hachana Debate

The *Gemara* resolves: *hacha be-hachana de-Rabbah kamiflegi* — the dispute concerns *hachana de-Rabbah*, the principle introduced by *Rabbah* requiring that an item be "prepared" during a weekday to be usable on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. Both sides agree it is *shtei kedushot*. The question is whether the fact that the egg's formation was completed on one sacred day — rather than on a weekday — renders it unavailable for the next sacred day. *Rav* holds that *hachana de-Rabbah* applies, and therefore an egg finished on *Yom Tov* or *Shabbat* is not considered "prepared" and cannot be used on the subsequent sacred day. *Rabbi Yochanan* does not accept *hachana de-Rabbah* as a binding concern, and therefore since the egg was in existence on the prior day, it may be used on the day that follows.

The *Gemara* anchors this debate in the *Tannaim*: one view holds that if the egg was born on *Shabbat*, it may be eaten on the following *Yom Tov*, and vice versa. *Rabbi Yehuda* in the name of *Rabbi Eliezer* says the debate of *Beis Shammai* and *Beis Hillel* remains active even in this case — *Beis Shammai* permitting and *Beis Hillel* forbidding. This *Tannaitic* debate is the precursor to the *Amoraic* dispute of *Rav* and *Rabbi Yochanan*, and the root of the disagreement, the *Gemara* confirms, is precisely *hachana de-Rabbah*.

### Rav Adda Story

The *Gemara* illustrates the practical stakes with a story. The proprietor of *Rav Adda bar Ahava*'s lodgings had eggs that were born on *Yom Tov* and wanted to know whether he could use them on the following *Shabbat*. More specifically, could he cook them on *Yom Tov* for consumption on *Shabbat*? The question of cooking on *Yom Tov* for the sake of the following *Shabbat* is itself a significant issue involving *Eruv Tavshilin*. But *Rav Adda bar Ahava* pointed out a prior difficulty: even according to *Rabbi Yochanan*, who permits using the egg on the following day, that permission is only to swallow it raw — *le-gomao le-machar*. Today on *Yom Tov*, when it was laid, it is *muktzah*, and you cannot handle it. The question of cooking for tomorrow therefore does not even arise: you cannot touch the egg today. Tomorrow — on *Shabbat* — it may be eaten, but only raw, since you cannot cook on *Shabbat*. The proprietor's assumption that he could cook it today in preparation for tomorrow rested on a misapplication of *Rabbi Yochanan*'s leniency.

The *Gemara* then cites an explicit *brayta* that supports this: *ein metaltelin osa* — neither an egg born on *Shabbat* nor one born on *Yom Tov* may be moved, neither to cover a vessel nor to prop up a bed-leg. This confirms that on the day it is laid, the egg is *muktzah* per *Beis Hillel*, even according to those who permit it the following day.

### Rav Pappa Story

A parallel story is told about *Rav Pappa*'s establishment. A man came to him with the inverse case: eggs born on *Shabbat*, and a question whether they could be eaten on the following *Yom Tov*. *Rav Pappa* declined to answer immediately, telling the man to return the next day. The reason, the *Gemara* explains, is that *Rav* would not appoint an *amora* to relay his rulings on the night of *Yom Tov* — *mishum shichrus*, because he had been drinking. This is not incidental: just as the *Torah*'s prohibition on priestly service while intoxicated connects the state of mind required for teaching *halacha* to the prohibition of *shikrus*, *Rav Pappa* knew that in the course of giving a *shiur* while drunk he might blurt out an unreliable *psak*. He therefore deferred.

When the man returned the next day, *Rav Pappa* said: it is fortunate I did not answer yesterday. Had I done so, he said, *isru hashta istalai* — I would have erred. He would have reflexively said *Rav u-Rabbi Yochanan halacha ke-Rabbi Yochanan* — we rule like *Rabbi Yochanan*, and therefore the egg born on *Shabbat* is permitted on the following *Yom Tov*. But upon sober reflection, he withdrew that answer.

### Rava's Ruling

*Rava* then establishes the binding rule: *hilchata kevusei de-Rav behani telasa* — the *halacha* follows *Rav* in these three matters, *bein lekula bein lechumra*, whether the ruling of *Rav* is the lenient or the stringent one. One of these three is the case of the egg and the juxtaposed days of *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. The final *halacha* is therefore like *Rav*: an egg born on one of the two days remains forbidden on the other, due to *hachana de-Rabbah*.

---

## Fallen Wood

### Fallen Wood Rule

*Rabbi Yochanan* now introduces a case that is related but distinct.
