If branches fell from a tree on *Shabbat*, they may not be used as firewood on the following *Yom Tov* — *assur le-hatzikam be-Yom Tov*. He anticipates the obvious objection — "but by an egg you said it *is* permitted on the following day" — and preempts it: *al tachshiveini beitza*, do not compare this case to the egg.

### Egg vs. Wood

The distinction is fundamental and deserves careful attention. The egg was forbidden on *Shabbat* for one reason only: *muktzah*. On *Shabbat* itself the egg could theoretically have been swallowed raw; the only impediment was the *muktzah* prohibition. When we then say the egg is permitted on *Yom Tov*, we are conveying a clear and coherent message: *muktzah* is a day-specific prohibition, and *shtei kedushot* means the second day stands on its own. Anyone who hears that the egg — which could have been eaten yesterday — is permitted today will understand that *muktzah* ended with *Shabbat* and does not carry over. The two-day structure is internally transparent.

The wood, however, is different. A branch that has fallen from a tree on *Shabbat* has no permissible use on *Shabbat* whatsoever — you cannot burn wood on *Shabbat*. If we were then to say that this same branch may be used on the following *Yom Tov*, an observer would draw the wrong conclusion. He would reason: the branch was not used yesterday — but that was because there was nothing to do with a branch on *Shabbat*, not because of *muktzah*. If we allow it on *Yom Tov*, he will infer that fallen branches are not *muktzah* at all, and from there he will conclude that branches fallen on *Yom Tov* itself were already permissible. The experiential logic collapses the two days into one, precisely the inference we want to avoid. Permitting the wood on *Yom Tov* would thus create the false impression that *muktzah* never applied, undermining the entire framework.

This is a subtle but important distinction. It is not that the two cases involve different principles. Both involve *shtei kedushot* and *muktzah*. The difference is phenomenological: by the egg, the reason for non-use on *Shabbat* is transparent and understood; by the wood, it is not, and the inference drawn from permitting it on the following day would be structurally misleading. Notably, the same logic suggests — as one might observe — that if a branch falls on the first day of *Yom Tov*, it *could* be permissible on the second day of *Yom Tov*, since burning wood is something one can do on *Yom Tov*, and the parallel to the egg would then hold.

### Extra Wood Solution

*Rav Masna* addresses a practical scenario: what if wood falls from an overhanging tree directly into a lit oven on *Yom Tov*? In this case, *marbe lahem etzim muchanim umasiken* — one should add additional, pre-prepared permitted wood into the oven, creating a majority of permitted wood, and then use the fire. The *muktzah* wood is rendered *batel* within the larger quantity through *rov*, majority.

### Bitel Muktzah Query

The *Gemara* challenges this on two grounds. First: when you stir the fire, are you not inevitably stirring the *muktzah* wood as well, which constitutes moving *muktzah*? Second, and more fundamentally: is this not a case of *mevattel issur l'chatchila* — proactively causing the nullification of a forbidden item? We have a *mishnah* that states explicitly: *ein mevatlin issur l'chatchila* — one does not create *bitul* of a forbidden substance at the outset. *Bitul* is a *post facto* relief, not a deliberate strategy.

On the first question, the *Gemara* resolves that once a majority of the wood is permitted — *keivan de-ruba heteira ninhu* — when one stirs the fire one is considered to be stirring the permitted majority. The *muktzah* minority loses its legal significance within the whole.

### Bitel Resolution

On the second question — the prohibition against proactive *bitul* — the *Gemara* answers: *hani mili de'Oraisa*, that rule applies to biblical prohibitions. *Aval be'rabbanan mevatlinan* — but for a rabbinic prohibition, one may actively create *bitul*. Since *muktzah* is rabbinic, throwing in extra wood to achieve *bitul* is permissible.

A critical caveat must be noted here. This statement, taken at face value, would have sweeping implications: a large proportion of *kashrut* problems are rabbinic in nature, and if proactive *bitul* were universally permitted in rabbinic matters, *kashrut* practice would be transformed. Other *Gemaras* make clear that this is not the correct universal rule, and *poskim* throughout the generations have understood this passage as referring specifically to the weak form of rabbinic prohibition represented by *muktzah*, especially in this context where the wood is in the process of being actively consumed by fire. The *Gemara* itself shortly supplies a further reason: *mikla kali issura* — the prohibited item is in the process of being burned up and is losing its identity as it burns, such that treating it as something possessing ongoing status requiring standard *bitul* rules is itself inappropriate. The statement *aval be'rabbanan mevatlinan* should therefore not be generalized beyond the context that supports it.

The *Gemara* then raises a final complication. *Rav Ashi* had argued earlier in the daf that *davar she'yesh lo matirin* prevents *bitul* even in rabbinic matters. The *muktzah* wood is precisely a *davar she'yesh lo matirin* — it will become permitted tonight when *Yom Tov* ends. If that principle blocks *bitul* even for rabbinic concerns, how can we permit *bitul* of the wood? The *Gemara* answers: *hani mili heicha de-ise l'issura be'einah* — that rule applies when the prohibited object still exists in its full form. *Hacha mikla kali issura* — here, the wood is being actively burned and is in the process of losing its identity entirely. A branch that is being consumed by fire cannot meaningfully be described as something that "will become permitted tomorrow," because by tomorrow it will no longer exist. The principle of *davar she'yesh lo matirin* therefore does not apply to an object in the act of destruction, and *bitul* can take effect.

---

---

# Beitzah 5

## Two Days Yom Tov

### Egg Permissibility

The daf opens mid-discussion at the bottom of 4b, three lines before the text widens, beginning with the word *itmar*. The subject is *shnei yamim tovim shel galuyos* — the two-day *yom tov* of the Diaspora — examined through the lens of the egg question that has occupied the preceding sugyot.

*Itmar*: Rav and Rav Ashi dispute the status of an egg laid on the first day of *yom tov*. Rav holds — *nolda b'zeh muteres b'zeh* — that an egg born on one day of *yom tov* is permitted on the second. Rav Ashi holds the opposite: *nolda b'zeh asura b'zeh* — born on the first day, it is forbidden on the second.

### One Kedusha

The *Gemara* immediately asks: what is the underlying reasoning of Rav Ashi? *Kasavar Rav Ashi kedusha achas hi* — Rav Ashi appears to hold that the two days of *yom tov* constitute one continuous *kedusha*. The logic is as follows: the standard conceptual framework for two-day *yom tov* is that we do not know which of the two days is the actual *yom tov*, owing to uncertainty about which day was *Rosh Chodesh*. If the days are genuinely independent of one another — one *yom tov* and one *chol*, even if we are uncertain which is which — then by the time day two begins, the *muktzah* considerations of day two ask only whether the egg existed before day two commenced. Since it did, it should be permitted. The only basis to forbid it is to treat both days as a single, unified unit of *kedusha*, making an egg born on day one analogous to an egg born mid-*yom tov* — forbidden for the duration.

### Havdalah Contradiction

But the *Gemara* immediately raises a difficulty: *v'ha Rav Ashi mavdil miyoma tava lachavrei* — Rav Ashi himself makes *havdalah* from the first day of *yom tov* to the second. Rashi adds the striking detail that Rav Ashi would recite *hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol*, treating the second day as *chol* for purposes of the *havdalah* formula. Whatever the precise text of his *havdalah*, the act itself clearly reflects a view that the two days are distinct — not a single continuous unit. If so, why would the egg born on day one be forbidden on day two?

### Safek Resolution

The *Gemara* resolves this apparent contradiction by explaining that Rav Ashi did not in fact hold a definitive position on the nature of the two days. Rather, *safoka mesafeka lei* — he was genuinely uncertain. And so he adopted *chumra* on both fronts: *hacha l'chumra v'hacha l'chumra*. On the one hand, perhaps the two days are one continuous *kedusha* — and therefore he forbids the egg born on day one on day two. On the other hand, perhaps they are two distinct *kedushos*, or even a *kedusha* and a *chol* — and therefore he makes *havdalah* between them. Both positions reflect a stringent response to doubt. (One might naturally ask how he could recite a *bracha* in a state of uncertainty; presumably he made *havdalah* without the associated *brachot*, saying only the formula of *hamavdil bein kodesh l'chol* or *bein kodesh l'kodesh*.)

The upshot of this opening section is that the underlying question — one *kedusha* or two *kedushos* — is now the explicit subject of the *Gemara's* attention. Rav holds *shtei kedushos*; Rav Ashi's ruling reflects uncertainty but leads practically to treating them as *kedusha achas*.

---

## Minhag vs. Takana

### Modern Calendar Logic

Rav Zeira enters the discussion: *k'vasei de'Rav Ashi mistabra* — the position of *kedusha achas* makes good logical sense. His reasoning: *de'hashta yedinan b'keviya d'yarcha* — today we know when *Rosh Chodesh* is. The calendar has been fixed in advance and there is no genuine uncertainty. Yet *v'ka avdinan trei yomei* — we nevertheless keep two days. If there were genuine doubt about which day is *yom tov*, each day would carry its own independent weight. But since we keep two days not out of doubt but because the Rabbis told us to do so, the two days form a single legislated unit — one *kedusha* with both days carrying equal weight.

### Historical Minhag

Abaye disagrees: *k'vatei d'Rav mistabra* — Rav's position of two independent *kedushos* is the more logical one. And he cites a *Mishnah* in support.

### Beacon System

*Tnan: barishona hayu masin masa'ot* — originally there was a remarkably efficient system for communicating the establishment of *Rosh Chodesh* to communities in the Diaspora. Bonfires would be lit on mountaintops in a chain, each peak visible to the next, transmitting the information across great distances almost instantaneously. The entire Jewish world could know when *Rosh Chodesh* had been declared in time for *yom tov*.

But *mishe'kilkalu ha'Kutim* (or, according to some versions, *ha'minim*) — when sectarians began to sabotage the system by lighting false fires on the wrong days — the chain could no longer be trusted. The sabotage was not merely mischievous; it was ideologically motivated. The Sadducees, for instance, disputed the interpretation of the verse counting fifty days *mimacharat haShabbat* — whether *Shabbat* meant the literal Sabbath or the first day of *Pesach* — and had reason to manipulate when the fires were lit so that *Shavuot* would always fall on the day after a literal Shabbat. The response was to shift to a system of *shluchim* — official messengers dispatched by the *beit din*, who could carry verifiable credentials. But messengers travel slowly, and so communities in the Diaspora would often find that *yom tov* arrived before the messengers did — hence the genuine uncertainty that gave rise to two-day *yom tov*.

### Regional Flexibility

Abaye now draws the critical inference. *V'ilu bitlu Kutim* — had the sabotage of the beacon system never occurred and the fires continued, *adinan chad yoma* — communities in the Diaspora would have kept only one day. Moreover, even within the period of the messenger system, *v'heicha d'matu shluchim* — areas close enough to Israel that the messengers could arrive in time for *Sukkot* and *Pesach* — those areas kept only one day. The practice of two days is therefore not a flat, uniform rabbinic legislation. It is flexible: it depends on geography, on circumstances, on what would have been necessary at the time.

### Minhag Continuity

This is the point Rashi crystallizes. The debate here is whether two-day *yom tov* is a *takana* — an active rabbinic ordinance — or a *minhag* — the continuation of a historical practice. If it is a *takana*, the Rabbis have told us: keep two days of *yom tov*. That makes it a unified, two-day unit — *kedusha achas*. If it is a *minhag*, then we are preserving the way things were actually practiced during the period of uncertainty. And during that period, each day was independent: one was *yom tov* and one was *chol*, nobody knew which was which, and each stood on its own. If our practice is the continuation of that reality, then each day retains its independent status — *shtei kedushos*.

The flexibility Abaye points to — areas close to Israel keeping one day, areas far away keeping two, the theoretical possibility that improved communication could reduce the practice — all of this is inconsistent with the character of a *takana*. A rabbinic *takana* does not draw those kinds of geographic distinctions, nor would it dissolve if circumstances changed. The flexibility reflects the organic nature of *minhag*: we continue to practice what would have been done had we been living through those original circumstances.

### Chacham Tzvi

This distinction has direct contemporary relevance. The question of what a resident of *Chutz La'aretz* visiting *Eretz Yisrael* for *yom tov* should do — one day or two — was for many decades answered instinctively with two days. The Chacham Tzvi, however, argues for a fundamentally different framework. If one thinks of two-day *yom tov* as a *takana* — a rule binding on those from *Chutz La'aretz* — then a person from *Chutz La'aretz* takes that obligation wherever he goes. But the Chacham Tzvi says the correct framework is to ask: what would you have done at the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*? At that time, a resident of *Chutz La'aretz* visiting *Eretz Yisrael* for *yom tov* would have known the calendar — the *beit din* had declared *Rosh Chodesh* and the information was available — and would have kept one day. That is therefore what such a visitor should do today. This is precisely Abaye's position brought to its practical conclusion: two-day *yom tov* reflects how things would have been done in the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*, not a flat halachic obligation attached to one's status as a *ben Chutz La'aretz*.

### Future Persecution

The *Gemara* then poses the obvious question: given that we now have a fixed calendar and know exactly when *Rosh Chodesh* is, why do we still keep two days? The answer, transmitted from *Eretz Yisrael*, is *hizaharu beminhag avoteichem b'yadeichem* — be scrupulous about the practice of your forefathers. But then the *Gemara* — as indicated by the shift from Hebrew to Aramaic — adds an additional layer: *zimnin degazra hamalchut gezeira v'atei leakalkulei* — there may come a time when government persecution will disrupt access to the traditions of the calendar, and communities will genuinely not know which day is *yom tov*. Rashi explains that this refers to the possibility that under persecution the chain of transmission of the calendar could be lost, creating a real *safek* once again. This explains why the *minhag* is treated with the full gravity of a *yom tov* obligation and not merely as a quaint historical preservation. The two-day practice is rooted in the concept of *safek* — the uncertainty of which day is the real one — and may again become a genuine *safek*. That is Abaye's position, and it is in service of Rav's ruling that the two days constitute *shtei kedushos*, each independent.

---

## Rosh Hashanah

### RH One Kedusha

The *Gemara* now turns to two days of *Rosh Hashanah*, which occupy a fundamentally different category. Rabba and Shmuel bar Ami both agree — *modu bazei asuru bazei* — that even Rav, who ruled *shtei kedushos* for normal two-day *yom tov*, concedes that two days of *Rosh Hashanah* are *kedusha achas*. An egg born on day one of *Rosh Hashanah* is forbidden on day two. The question is why.

### Witness Rules

The *Mishnah* provides the historical background. *Barishona hayu mekabelin edut hachodesh kol hayom* — originally, *beit din* would accept testimony about the new moon throughout the entire day of the thirtieth of *Elul*, the potential first day of *Rosh Hashanah*. This created an inherent uncertainty: witnesses might appear at any point during the day to testify that they had seen the new moon the previous night. Until they appeared, no one knew with certainty whether that day would be declared *Rosh Chodesh Tishrei* — and hence *Rosh Hashanah* — or whether *Rosh Hashanah* would fall the following day.

### Levim Mistake

One year, *nishtahu eidim lavo* — the witnesses came very late. Assuming no witnesses would arrive, those at the *Beis HaMikdash* proceeded with the afternoon service on the assumption that it was an ordinary weekday. *V'nitkalkelu haLevi'im bashir* — the *Levi'im* sang the wrong *shir*. The *shir shel yom* recited during the *tamid shebein ha'arbayim* — the afternoon daily offering — was supposed to be the *yom tov* one, since witnesses were still within the window of acceptance. Instead, the *Levi'im* sang the weekday *shir*, believing the day would remain *chol*.

This error had layered consequences. Rashi notes that at *Shacharit*, it was always too early to know whether the day would be declared *Rosh Hashanah* — the witnesses had not yet arrived — so the weekday *shir* was always sung in the morning by design. By *Musaf* and *Mincha* time, however, the determination should have been possible, and the appropriate *yom tov* *shir* should have been sung. Tosafot raises an additional complication: if the *Musaf* offerings had not yet been brought — because everyone assumed it was a weekday — then when the witnesses did arrive late and *Rosh Hashanah* was declared, the *Musaf* korbanot would have had to be brought after the afternoon *tamid*, which is normally prohibited. This too is alluded to in the tractate of *Rosh Hashanah*. In short, the late arrival of witnesses created a cascade of halachic disruption.

### Mincha Cutoff

The response was a *takana*: *hitkinu shelo yehu mekabelin et ha'eidim ela ad haMincha* — witnesses would no longer be accepted after *Mincha* time, meaning after the time of the afternoon *tamid*. Once the *tamid* was to be brought, the *beit din* closed its doors. If witnesses had not appeared by then, the *Levi'im* would sing the weekday *shir*, the *Musaf* would not be brought (since it was being treated as a weekday), and if witnesses subsequently arrived, they would be turned away.

### Post-Mincha Kedusha

This *takana* had a striking consequence. Once *Mincha* time arrived and witnesses could no longer be accepted, everyone knew with certainty that the following day — not the current one — would be the calendar's *Rosh Hashanah*. And yet the ruling was: *nogin oso hayom kodesh u'l'machar kodesh* — they would continue treating that day with the sanctity of *Rosh Hashanah*, not resuming *melacha* until the end of the day, and the following day would be kept as *Rosh Hashanah* as well. If people were permitted to begin performing *melacha* partway through a day they had begun keeping as *Rosh Hashanah*, the concern was that in future years they would begin doing *melacha* from the morning itself. The integrity of the day required that once it was begun as *Rosh Hashanah*, it be completed as such.

The halachic implication is critical. In cases where witnesses arrived after *Mincha*, there would be two days of *Rosh Hashanah* — and the second portion of day one was kept not out of *safek* but out of *takana*. There was certainty that the official *Rosh Hashanah* was tomorrow, yet the day continued to be treated as sacred. That is not the character of *shtei kedushos* — independent days, each kept because it might be the real one. That is the character of *kedusha achas* — a single extended unit of sanctity that the Rabbis have mandated regardless of what is actually known. This is why two days of *Rosh Hashanah* are categorically different from normal two-day *yom tov*, and why they are called *yoma arichta* — one long day. This also has implications beyond the egg question: it bears on the recitation of *Shehecheyanu* on the second night of *Rosh Hashanah*. For ordinary two-day *yom tov*, one says *Shehecheyanu* on the second night because perhaps yesterday was *chol* and today is the real *yom tov*. For *Rosh Hashanah*, the logic is different — the two days are one extended unit, and the *Shehecheyanu* on the second night is accommodated through legal fictions such as a new fruit.

---

## Post-Churban Reform

### Rava's View

Rava now introduces a new position: *mitakanas Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai va'eilach, beitzah muteres* — from the time of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's reform onward, the egg should be *permitted*, meaning the two days of *Rosh Hashanah* revert to *shtei kedushos*. The reasoning draws on a *Mishnah* in tractate *Rosh Hashanah*: *mishecharav Beis HaMikdash, hiskin Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai she'mekablin eidus hachodesh kol hayom* — after the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai ordained that witnesses could be accepted throughout the entire day once again. With the *Beis HaMikdash* gone, there were no more sacrificial consequences — no danger of singing the wrong *shir*, no problem of bringing *Musaf* after the *tamid*. The old *takana* restricting witnesses to before *Mincha* had no remaining rationale, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai lifted it.

Rava's logic follows directly: if witnesses can now be accepted all day, then the element of non-*safek* that had characterized part of the first day of *Rosh Hashanah* — the portion after *Mincha* when one kept the day as sacred even though one knew it was not *Rosh Hashanah* — disappears. The situation reverts to one of pure *safek*, just like ordinary two-day *yom tov*. And pure *safek* means *shtei kedushos*, not *kedusha achas*. Therefore, born on day one, permitted on day two.

### Abaye Objects

Abaye challenges Rava: *v'ha Rav u'Shmuel de'amri tarvaihu beitzah asurah* — but Rav and Shmuel both hold that the egg remains forbidden, meaning they hold *kedusha achas* even after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's reform. How can Rava simply assert that the reform of accepting witnesses changes everything about the nature of the two days?

Rava's response is striking: *amina lach ana Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai v'at amrat li Rav u'Shmuel?* — I bring you Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai himself, an explicit *Mishnah* showing that the witness reality changed, which logically entails a shift to *shtei kedushos*, and you counter with Rav and Shmuel? The weight of the *Mishnah* overrides the Amoraic opinion.

### EY vs. CL

The *Gemara* acknowledges the force of Rava's argument: *lo kashya, ha lan ha lehu* — it is not difficult; the ruling differs by location. The *Gemara* now draws a distinction between *Eretz Yisrael* and *Chutz La'aretz*.

### Practice Divergence

In *Eretz Yisrael*, once Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's *takana* took effect and witnesses could be accepted all day, the practice of two-day *Rosh Hashanah* became variable. When witnesses came early on the first day, it would be a one-day *Rosh Hashanah*. When they came late and the first day had been kept out of doubt — uncertainty as to whether witnesses would arrive — and then witnesses came on day two, there would be two days, but those two days would now be characterized by *safek*, not by the old *takana*-based *kedusha achas*. In *Eretz Yisrael*, then, the reform genuinely changed the halachic character of two-day *Rosh Hashanah* into *shtei kedushos*, consistent with Rava's position. This is what *ha lan* — "this is for them [in *Eretz Yisrael*]" — refers to.

In *Chutz La'aretz*, however, Rashi explains that the situation is different. Two-day *yom tov* always remained a universal practice; there was never any year in which a community in *Chutz La'aretz* kept only one day of *Rosh Hashanah*. Because the two-day practice continued without interruption, and because it had begun under the character of *kedusha achas* — shaped by the old *takana* of not accepting witnesses — that character was never dislodged. The practice continued with the same halachic character it always had. Even though the underlying logic shifted, the unbroken continuity of practice preserved the original status. That is *ha lehu* — "this is for us [in *Chutz La'aretz*]." In *Chutz La'aretz*, two days of *Rosh Hashanah* remain *kedusha achas*, and an egg born on day one is forbidden on day two.

Tosafot in *Sukkah* offers a somewhat different explanation for why the distinction between *Eretz Yisrael* and *Chutz La'aretz* holds, but the essential point is the same: in *Chutz La'aretz*, because the practice of two days was never interrupted and never shifted to a variable reality, the *kedusha achas* framework persists.

---

## Davar She'beminyan

### Legislation Permanence

Rav Yosef now enters with a different explanation for why the egg remains forbidden — and in doing so advances one of the most consequential halachic principles in this entire chapter. *Af mishtakanat Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai va'eilach beitzah asurah* — even after the reform, the egg is forbidden. Why? *Havei davar she'be'minyan, v'chol davar she'be'minyan tzarich minyan acher l'hatiro* — it is a *davar she'be'minyan*: a matter that was established by legislative vote, and any such matter requires another act of legislation to retract it.

The principle is this: when the Rabbis officially enact a *takana*, a change in the underlying circumstances does not automatically void the legislation. The old law remains on the books until it is actively repealed by a new legislative act. In our case, the *takana* that established the two days of *Rosh Hashanah* as *kedusha achas* — with all its consequences, including the prohibition of an egg born on day one — was never explicitly retracted. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai changed the *takana* about accepting witnesses. He did not issue a new *takana* about the nature of the two days. Therefore, the halachic character of *kedusha achas* remains in force.

One might ask: is this not already obvious from the earlier *Mishnah* in *Eduyot*, which states that no *beit din* can overturn the ruling of a previous *beit din* unless it surpasses it in wisdom and in number? Rav Yosef appears to be making a sharper point: not merely that you need a greater *beit din* to overturn a ruling, but that even when the circumstances that gave rise to the ruling have entirely disappeared, the ruling does not lapse by itself. The circumstances changing is not equivalent to legislation reversing. This has broad practical implications — as, for example, in the debate over *cholov stam*: if the *takana* requiring Jewish supervision of milk was enacted because of concern about *treif* milk being mixed in, does the *takana* lapse automatically in an environment where that concern is demonstrably absent? Rav Yosef's principle says no: the *takana* remains until it is actively repealed, unless the circumstances were explicitly built into the *takana* itself.

### Biblical Proofs

Rav Yosef proceeds to demonstrate this principle from biblical sources. *Dichtiv: heyu nechonim lishloshes yamim, al tigshu el isha* — God commanded the Jewish people at Sinai to abstain from marital relations for three days in preparation for *Ma'amad Har Sinai*. Once *Ma'amad Har Sinai* was concluded, one might think the command automatically lapsed — the reason had been fulfilled. Yet the verse tells us that God subsequently commanded: *lechu imru lahem shuvu lachem l'ohaleichem* — go tell them to return to their tents, meaning to resume marital relations. *Shema mina*: even though the reason for the original command had clearly passed, it required an active divine act to retract it.

The *Gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps *shuvu lachem l'ohaleichem* was not a retraction but a new *mitzva* of *onah* — the obligation to resume marital relations after a period of separation. If so, it proves nothing about the need to retract the original prohibition. The *Gemara* therefore adduces a second biblical proof: *bimshoch hayovel heimah ya'alu vahar* — when the great blast of the *shofar* sounds, they may ascend the mountain. The mountain had been forbidden to approach during the *Sinai* experience: *gam hatzon vehabakar al yiru el mul hahar hahu*. Rashi cites a *Midrash* understanding *hahar hahu* as the mountain suffused with divine presence — and clearly, once the divine presence had departed, the prohibition on approaching should have lapsed automatically. Yet the Torah still had to say explicitly: when the *shofar* sounds, they may ascend. *Shema mina: kol davar she'be'minyan tzarich minyan acher l'hatiro* — even when the logical basis for a prohibition has been removed, an active retraction is required.

### Kerem Revai

The *Gemara* continues to shore up the principle. *V'chi teima hani milei de'oraisa* — perhaps one might say this applies only to biblical commands. By contrast, *d'rabbanan* legislation might not require active retraction when circumstances change. The *Gemara* therefore cites a case from rabbinic law.

The *Mishnah* teaches: *kerem revai haya oleh l'Yerushalayim mahalakh yom echad l'chol tzad* — produce of a fourth-year vineyard (*kerem revai*) had to be brought up to Jerusalem to be eaten there. The ordinary practice of redeeming the produce and bringing up its monetary equivalent was not permitted for those living within a day's journey of Jerusalem in any direction — they had to bring the actual fruit. The boundaries: Lod to the west, the Jordan to the east, and two northern/southern markers according to the *girsa*. The stated reason for this requirement was *kedei le'ater shukei Yerushalayim b'peirot* — to adorn the marketplaces of Jerusalem with fruit, to create an atmosphere of vibrant Jewish life in the holy city.

The *Gemara* then relates: Rabbi Eliezer had a *kerem revai* east of Lod, within a day's journey of Jerusalem, near the village of Tebi. He wished to declare it *hefker* — ownerless — so that the poor could take it to Jerusalem themselves and eat it there, sparing him the obligation to bring it personally. His students told him: *nimnu alecha chaveirecha v'hitiru* — your colleagues have already taken a vote and retracted the *takana*. This occurred after the *churban habayit*, when Jerusalem was no longer a vibrant Jewish center and the whole rationale for insisting on bringing the actual fruit no longer applied. And yet the *takana* did not lapse automatically when the *Beis HaMikdash* was destroyed. *Ta'ama deninmnu* — the reason Rabbi Eliezer was now exempt was that a new vote had been taken to retract it. *Halo nimnu lo, lo* — had they not taken a new vote, the *takana* would have remained in force despite the changed circumstances. This is the *d'rabbanan* proof for the principle of *davar she'be'minyan*.

### Tosafot Refinement

At this point Tosafot raises a subtle but important refinement, which has significant practical implications. One might ask: if a community enacts a *cherem* — a ban backed by excommunication — for a defined period (say, "until *Pesach*" or "for thirty days"), does that *cherem* require a formal vote to dissolve when the period expires? By analogy to the *Sinai* case — where abstention was commanded for three days and God still needed to actively permit its cessation — one might argue yes.

Tosafot answers no. The *Sinai* command was not formulated as "do not have relations for three days." It said: *al tigshu el isha* — abstain from relations. The *reason* one could infer a time limit of three days, but it was never explicitly built into the command. Therefore, an explicit act was needed to retract it. But if the time limit is itself written into the *takana* — "this prohibition lasts until *Pesach*" — then the expiration is part of the legislation itself, and the *takana* self-expires without need of a new vote.

This distinction is enormously consequential for many *d'rabbanan* questions. The classic case is *cholov Yisroel*. The *takana* prohibiting milk without Jewish supervision was enacted because of concern that *treif* milk might have been mixed in. If the *takana* was formulated flatly — milk without Jewish supervision is forbidden — then it remains in force regardless of changed circumstances, and one needs an active new legislation to permit *cholov stam* in an environment where the concern is absent. If, however, the *takana* was formulated conditionally — when there is concern about *treif* milk being mixed in, milk without Jewish supervision is forbidden — then the circumstances are built into the *takana*, and it would self-expire when those circumstances change. This is precisely the question that underlies the debates about *cholov stam* in modern *halacha*. Rav Yosef's principle, refined by Tosafot, is thus one of the central tools for analyzing a vast range of rabbinic legislation.

### Takana Application

Returning now to the case at hand: the *Gemara* establishes that the *takana* forbidding acceptance of witnesses after *Mincha* was retracted by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. But a separate question is whether the halachic status of two days of *Rosh Hashanah* as *kedusha achas* was itself ever the subject of a legislative enactment. Rav Yosef's claim is that *kedusha achas* was itself a *davar she'be'minyan*, independently established, and not merely a consequence of the witness *takana*. Therefore, even when the witness *takana* was retracted, *kedusha achas* remained — it would require its own separate retraction. *Ki nimnu a'eidus* — when Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai and his *beit din* voted, they voted about accepting witnesses. *A'beitza lo nimnu* — they never voted to change the status of the egg. That separate question was never revisited, and so it remains.

---

## Emergent Reality

### Dependent Reality

Abaye offers a sharp retort to Rav Yosef's entire framework. *Atu beitzah be'minyan mi havay?* — when exactly was there ever a formal legislative vote about the egg? No *beit din* ever sat down and enacted a *takana* saying: an egg born on day one of *Rosh Hashanah* is forbidden on day two. That was never a standalone piece of legislation that now needs to be separately retracted.

### Automatic Shift

Rather, says Abaye, *beitzah be'eidus talya milsa* — the egg question is entirely dependent on the witness question. The prohibition of the egg — or more precisely, the status of *kedusha achas* that generates that prohibition — was not an independent enactment. It was an emergent consequence of the fact that witnesses were not accepted after *Mincha*, creating moments of non-*safek* sanctity that unified the two days into a single extended *kedusha*. *Issur eidus, itsa issura d'beitzah* — the witness *takana* brought about the egg prohibition. *Istari eidus, istari beitzah* — once the witness *takana* was lifted, the egg prohibition dissolves automatically, because there is no longer any independent basis for it. It was always a derivative reality, not a legislated one, and a *davar she'be'minyan* principle does not apply to something that was never itself the subject of a *minyan*. Therefore, says Abaye, the logic of *davar she'be'minyan* is not a sufficient explanation for why *kedusha achas* persists after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's reform.

---

## Maintaining Kedusha

### Rebuilding Concern

The *Gemara* now presents two further explanations for why *kedusha achas* is maintained even after the reform. Rav Adda bar Ahava — and both he and his colleague from the house of Kluchei — say: *af midirshat Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai va'eilach beitzah asurah*. Even after the reform, the egg remains forbidden. Why? *Mehera yibaneh Beis HaMikdash* — may the *Beis HaMikdash* be rebuilt speedily. *V'yomru: ishtakad milo achlanu beitzah b'Yom Tov Sheini?* — and people will say: last year, when an egg was born on day one, we ate it on day two. *Hashta nami neichol* — let us do the same now. *V'lo yad'u* — and they will not know *de'ishtakad shtei kedushos hein v'hashta kedusha achas hi* — that last year, without a *Beis HaMikdash*, there was genuine *safek* and *shtei kedushos*, whereas now, with the *Beis HaMikdash* restored and witnesses not accepted after *Mincha*, it is *kedusha achas*.

To prevent that confusion, we proactively maintain *kedusha achas* even in the post-*churban* period. This is not that we are stuck with a *takana* that was never retracted; it is that we are making a new, forward-looking decision to preserve the old practice in anticipation of the rebuilt *Beis HaMikdash*.

### Authority Distinction

The *Gemara* then raises an objection: if we are so worried about post-*churban* practice being confused with post-*churban* times once the *Beis HaMikdash* is rebuilt, why did Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai allow witnesses to be accepted all day at all? Should we not have maintained the restriction on witnesses as well, lest people after the rebuilding assume they can accept witnesses all day?

*Hachi hashta?* — the comparison is misplaced. *Eidus mesura l'veit din* — the acceptance of witnesses is entrusted to the *beit din*. The *beit din* knows the *halacha*. When the *Beis HaMikdash* is rebuilt, the *beit din* will know that witnesses are no longer accepted after *Mincha* time, and they will not make the mistake of assuming otherwise based on what was done in the post-*churban* period. *Beitzah l'chol mesura* — but the egg question is something every farmer faces. A farmer who saw eggs eaten on day two last year will eat them on day two this year, without knowing that the halachic regime has changed. Therefore the concern about popular confusion applies to the egg but not to the witness practice.

### Deliberate Preservation

Rava offers a third and somewhat different formulation: *af midirshat Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai va'eilach beitzah asurah*. Even Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai himself — *mi lo modeh Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai she'im ba'u eidim min haMincha u'l'ma'ala she'nohagim oto yom kodesh u'l'machar kodesh* — would acknowledge that when witnesses arrive after *Mincha* time, we continue treating that day with *kedusha* and the next day as well. This principle was not abrogated.

Rava's point, as Rashi and Tosafot both work to articulate, is that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's intervention was targeted and surgical. He used a scalpel, not a cleaver. He changed the specific *takana* about accepting witnesses. But the broader halachic reality of *kedusha achas* — the idea that once a day of *Rosh Hashanah* is begun, it must be completed as sacred, and that two days form a single extended unit — that he deliberately left intact. One cannot infer from his reform of the witness rules that he intended to alter the fundamental character of the two days.

### Final Ruling

The *Gemara* concludes with Rava's ruling: *v'amar Rava: hilchata k'vatei de'Rav be'hani telat, bein l'kula bein l'chumra* — the *halacha* follows Rav in all three cases, whether toward leniency or toward stringency.

The three cases are as follows. First, the case of *Shabbat* and *yom tov* back-to-back: there, *halacha* follows Rav strictly — an egg born on *Shabbat* is forbidden on *yom tov*, and vice versa, because they are treated as a continuous unit (or alternatively because of *hachana d'rabbah*). Second, normal two-day *yom tov* of *Chutz La'aretz*: there, *halacha* follows Rav leniently — the two days are *shtei kedushos*, each independent, and an egg born on day one is permitted on day two. Third, the case of two days of *Rosh Hashanah*: even after Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's reform, *kedusha achas* is maintained, and an egg born on day one remains forbidden on day two — this too follows Rav.

---

## Rishonim Dispute

### Rif Always Two

Having established that the *halacha* treats two days of *Rosh Hashanah* as *kedusha achas* — a single extended sanctity — the Rif draws a further conclusion. Quoting the entire *Gemara* and its rulings, he states that we therefore always keep two days of *Rosh Hashanah*, even in *Eretz Yisrael*. The maintenance of *kedusha achas* implies, in his reading, the perpetual observance of two days. This is how *Rosh Hashanah* is observed in *Eretz Yisrael* today: two days, treated as *kedusha achas* — the only *yom tov* on which *Eretz Yisrael* and *Chutz La'aretz* observe the same number of days.

### Rishonim One Day

It is striking, however, that this conclusion is not explicit in the *Gemara* itself. The Baal HaMaor and other *Rishonim* dispute the Rif's ruling. In their view, the *Gemara's* analysis of *kedusha achas* addresses only the halachic character of those years when two days of *Rosh Hashanah* are kept — not whether two days must always be kept in *Eretz Yisrael*. According to these *Rishonim*, when witnesses would have arrived on the first day — or, equivalently, when the fixed calendar places *Rosh Hashanah* on the thirtieth day of *Elul* (which, since *Elul* is never given thirty days, is effectively always) — only one day would be kept in *Eretz Yisrael*. Two days would apply only in years when witnesses arrived late, which created the two-day reality of keeping the first day out of doubt and the second day as the actual *Rosh Hashanah*.

### Modern Practice

In practice, the universal observance of two days of *Rosh Hashanah* — including in *Eretz Yisrael* — reflects the Rif's position. But it is important to appreciate that this universality is not self-evident from the *Gemara* and that a significant body of *Rishonim* held otherwise. The question of whether *Eretz Yisrael* should keep one or two days of *Rosh Hashanah* is a genuine dispute among the *Rishonim*, even though the *Gemara* is the source from which all parties argue.

---

---

# Beitzah 7

## Egg Completion & Mekach…

### Rav's Statement

The *daf* opens at the very bottom of 8b, continuing the interpretation of Rav's statement that an egg is only complete when it comes out — that is, only after a fertilized egg has been laid does it possess the potential to hatch a chick. An egg removed from inside a *shechted* hen, even if fertilized, cannot hatch. The *Gemara* asks *l'mai nafka mina* — what practical *halachic* difference does this make? The answer: it matters for *mekach ta'ut*, transactions in which a sale may be voided due to error.

### Pachya Eggs & Intent

The *Gemara* presents a case: someone went to the marketplace asking *d'pachya l'man* — who has *pachya* eggs, that is, laid eggs? *Rashi* explains that *pachya* refers to eggs from a hen that cooed while laying. The merchant sold him eggs taken from inside a *shechted* hen without disclosing this. The buyer later came before *Rabi Ami*, who ruled that this was a *mekach ta'us* — a sale in error — and reversed the transaction.

The *Gemara* objects: this seems obvious — if he explicitly asked for laid eggs and received something else, of course it is a *mekach ta'us*. The *Gemara* responds: one might have thought the buyer merely wanted the eggs for eating, and his request for laid eggs was simply because *mishum d'shafra* — a laid egg represents a further degree of completion. If so, this would not be a fundamental error voiding the entire sale, but only an overcharge — entitling the buyer to the *beini beinei*, the price differential between the two types of eggs. The ruling teaches us that we assume a buyer asking for laid eggs intends to hatch chicks, since only a laid egg can produce a chick (per Rav's statement). This constitutes a fundamental mismatch between what was sought and what was sold, rendering the entire transaction void.

This raises a broader conceptual point: not every error in a sale automatically voids the whole transaction. The distinction turns on whether the mistake goes to the heart of the buyer's purpose. Consider a case where someone buys a car and requests a specific accessories package, but receives a different one — that may entitle him to a price adjustment or a replacement, but it does not necessarily void the entire sale. The reason is that his core *da'as* — his underlying intent — was still to buy the car. Here, by contrast, if the buyer's fundamental purpose was to raise chicks, and the eggs he received cannot possibly hatch, the entire transaction was misconceived from the outset. One might ask how much of this depends on what a reasonable person in the marketplace would have understood the request to mean, as opposed to the buyer's actual private intent. The answer is that we generally require the intent to be reasonably self-evident from context; otherwise, we are dealing with *devarim she-belev*, and monetary matters are not resolved by unexpressed intentions alone.

### Dichrei Eggs Case

A parallel case follows. Someone went around the marketplace asking *bei dichrei l'man* — who has eggs from a male, meaning eggs fertilized by a rooster? The merchant sold him *bei d'safna me-ara* — eggs produced by friction from the ground, meaning unfertilized eggs laid without a male. He came before *Rabi Ami*, who ruled: *mekach ta'us ve-hadar* — it is a sale in error and is reversed.

Again the *Gemara* objects: *pshita* — this is obvious. He asked for fertilized eggs and received unfertilized ones. The *Gemara* responds: one might have thought he wanted fertilized eggs for eating — perhaps because *mishum d'shaminan tvei*, they are fattier and of higher quality. If so, this is merely a quality difference warranting the *beini beinei* price adjustment, not a full reversal. The ruling teaches that if someone asks specifically for fertilized eggs, we assume he wants them for the purpose of hatching chicks — which is the fundamental and exclusive reason to insist on fertilization — and therefore the entire transaction is voided.

The *Gemara* then introduces a second answer (*ve-i ba'it eima*), transitioning away from the *mekach ta'us* discussion entirely.

---

## Completion Defined

### Rubah vs. Kulah

The second interpretation of Rav's phrase *im yetziata nigmera* — "when it comes out, it is complete" — concerns the precise moment of birth for the *halachot* of an egg born on *Yom Tov*. According to one view, *im yetziat ruban nigmera*: the egg is considered complete — i.e., born — once the majority of it has emerged, even if it has not fully exited.

The opposing view holds *im yetziat kulan nigmera*: only when the egg has fully emerged is it considered born. Each formulation has direct implications for whether an egg is treated as *muktzeh* on *Yom Tov*.

### Yochanan's Ruling

The relevance of the *rubah* interpretation is established through the ruling of *Rabi Yochanan*: an egg whose majority emerged before *Yom Tov* and then retreated is considered already born from *erev Yom Tov* and is permitted for consumption on *Yom Tov*. According to the *rubah* interpretation, Rav's statement supports *Rabi Yochanan* — the egg is complete once its majority has emerged. The opposing *kulah* view is presented *u-le-afkuei me-de-Rabbi Yochanan* — specifically to reject *Rabi Yochanan*'s position, holding that full emergence is required before the egg is considered born.

Of the two interpretations of Rav's statement, this second one — concerning the moment of birth — is probably more likely to represent what Rav was addressing, since it speaks directly to the central *sugya* of when an egg is forbidden on *Yom Tov*, rather than to the ancillary question of *mekach ta'us*.

---

## Eggs in Slaughtered Hen

### Complete Eggs Status

The *Gemara* now transitions back to a matter raised earlier in the discussion: when eggs found inside a *shechted* hen are considered part of the hen's meat, and when they are regarded as separate — which determines their status regarding *basar be-chalav*. The *Gemara* states: *ha-shocheit et ha-tarnegolet u-matza bah beitzim gemurot* — one who slaughters a hen and finds complete eggs inside her. *Tosafot* notes that the correct *girsa* likely refers to near-complete rather than fully complete eggs, as the subsequent discussion implies. *Rashi* explains that these eggs lack a hardened shell. In such a case, *mutarot le-echolan be-chalav* — they may be eaten with milk, as they are not considered the flesh of the hen.

*Rabi Yaakov* disagrees: if the eggs were still *me'urot be-gidim* — intertwined with the sinews — they are forbidden. At that stage, he holds, they remain essentially part of the hen's body and therefore carry the status of meat for the prohibition of *basar be-chalav*.

### Braita on Neveilah

The *Gemara* asks who is the author of a *braita* concerning the *tum'ah* generated by eating from a *neveilah* of a kosher bird. The *halacha* is that one becomes *tamei* by swallowing a *kebeitzah* of the bird's flesh. The *braita* enumerates what counts as flesh for this purpose and what does not. On the permissive side: *ha-shalal shel beitzim* — the cluster of developing eggs — as well as bones, sinews, and flesh torn from the bird while it was still alive. On the stringent side: *ha-eshkol shel beitzim* — the ovary sac — along with the crop, the intestines, and liquefied fat, all of which render one *tamei*.

The distinction between *shalal* and *eshkol* is as follows: the *eshkol* is the ovary sac itself, while the *shalal* refers to the cluster of eggs that have separated from the sac and are developing, though still within the body. Since the *braita* rules that eating from the egg cluster does not generate *tum'ah*, the *Gemara* identifies this position as incompatible with *Rabi Yaakov*, who holds those same eggs are considered meat when intertwined with sinews.

### Authorship Question

*Rav Yosef* states: *delo k'Rabbi Yaakov* — the *braita* is not in accordance with *Rabi Yaakov*, since *Rabi Yaakov* holds that eggs intertwined with sinews are forbidden, implying he treats them as meat. The *braita*, which categorically excludes the egg cluster from the *tum'ah*-generating flesh of the bird, cannot reflect his view.

### Abaye's Resolution

*Abaye* challenges *Rav Yosef*: *minai* — how do you know this? Perhaps *Rabi Yaakov*'s stringency applies exclusively *le-inyan issura* — to the prohibition of *basar be-chalav* — and not to the laws of *tum'ah*. On a fundamental level, *Rabi Yaakov* may agree that these eggs are not technically meat; his ruling may be an additional stringency specific to *basar be-chalav*, where there are well-known extensions of the prohibition beyond the strictly technical.

The *Gemara* then raises an obvious follow-up: if we are willing to be stringent for *basar be-chalav*, why not apply the same stringency to *tum'ah*? The answer is *apushi tum'ah hu* — that would expand the scope of ritual impurity. *Apushi tum'ah mi-de-rabanan lo mapshinan* — we do not rabbinically extend *tum'ah* beyond its established parameters when there is no compelling reason to do so. *Rashi* acknowledges that this principle does not prevent all rabbinic extensions of *tum'ah* — there are many such *gezeirot* — but the point is that here there is no sufficient justification to do so, and at some point one must say enough.

The upshot of *Abaye*'s position is that the *braita* could in theory be consistent with *Rabi Yaakov*: he may be strict for *basar be-chalav* rabbinically, while agreeing that for *tum'ah* the egg cluster does not qualify as meat.

A second version of the exchange (*ve-ika de-amri*) reverses the framing: rather than asking who authored the permissive ruling about *shalal*, it asks who authored the stringent ruling about *eshkol*. *Rav Yosef* suggests it is *Rabi Yaakov*, since the *eshkol* in the *braita* refers to eggs that have emerged from the sac but remain suspended within it — the very scenario *Rabi Yaakov* calls forbidden. *Abaye* again challenges: perhaps *eshkol* refers simply to the ovary sac itself, not to the eggs growing outside of it. And the *braita*'s novelty in mentioning the ovary sac is comparable to its novelty in mentioning the crop and intestines — these are all inner organs that some people do not eat and one might think are not considered *ochel* sufficient to generate *tum'ah*. The *braita* teaches that despite being unusual foods, they are considered part of the bird's flesh. This reading of the *braita* would place it in opposition to *Rabi Yaakov*, not in support of him.

---

## Birth Timing & Mating

### General Principle

A *braita* is introduced establishing a general biological principle: *kol she-tashmisho ba-yom, nolad ba-yom* — any species that mates during the day gives birth during the day; *kol she-tashmisho ba-lailah, nolad ba-lailah* — any species that mates at night gives birth at night; and *kol she-tashmisho bein ba-yom u-vein ba-lailah, nolad bein ba-yom u-vein ba-lailah* — any species that mates both by day and by night gives birth in both.

### Hens & Daytime Birth

The *Gemara* identifies examples: the hen is a diurnal species — *kol she-tashmisho ba-yom nolad ba-yom, zu tarnigolas* — and therefore only lays eggs during the day. The bat is nocturnal — *kol she-tashmisho ba-lailah nolad ba-lailah, zu atalef*. Humans and all species similar to them mate and give birth both by day and by night.

---

## Coop Egg Case

### Rav Mari Case

The *halachic* relevance of hens laying only during the day emerges from a ruling of *Rav Mari the son of Rav Kahana*. He teaches: *badak be-kana shel tarnigolas me-erev Yom Tov ve-lo matza bah beitza* — if one checked the hen's roost right before *Yom Tov* and found no egg, and the next morning woke up early and found an egg, *mutteres* — it is permitted. The reasoning: since we found the egg before daybreak, one would normally assume it was laid at night — which would mean it was born on *Yom Tov* and would be problematic. But since hens cannot lay eggs at night, one of two explanations must apply: either one did not check well enough (*lo badak shapir*) and there was already an egg present, or — even if one checked carefully — one must say *eimur yatza rubah ve-chazra hava*: the majority of the egg had already emerged before *Yom Tov* and then retreated, so by *Rabi Yochanan*'s ruling it was already considered born before *Yom Tov* began.

This is a striking instance of the pre-empirical orientation of Talmudic reasoning: rather than accepting the apparent evidence that the egg was laid at night, the *Gemara* prefers to invoke the authoritative principle that hens do not lay at night and constructs an alternative explanation — however unusual — to preserve consistency with that principle.

### Rooster Presence

The *Gemara* raises an apparent contradiction from a statement of *Rav Yosef bar Shaul amar Rav*: if one checked the roost right before *Yom Tov* and found no egg, and then found one the next morning before daybreak, *asura* — it is forbidden, because it was evidently laid overnight. The *Gemara* resolves the contradiction: *hatam be-dasfna me-ara* — that case involves an unfertilized egg. The principle that hens do not lay at night applies only to fertilized eggs, since the underlying rule links birth timing to mating. An unfertilized egg, having no connection to daytime mating, may be laid at any time, including at night. It is therefore possible for an egg found before daybreak to have been laid overnight if it is unfertilized.

The *Gemara* now objects to *Rav Mari*'s leniency: if we are worried about the possibility of an unfertilized egg, then even in his case one should assume the egg might have been laid at night. The response: *de-ika zachar ba-hada* — there is a rooster in the vicinity, which means we presume the egg is fertilized and therefore could not have been laid at night.

The *Gemara* pushes back: even with a rooster present, perhaps the hen laid an unfertilized egg. This leads to a new principle.

### Ravina's Tradition

*Ravina* provides a tradition — *gemiri* — that wherever a rooster is present, a hen will not lay unfertilized eggs: *kol heicha de-ika zachar lo safna me-ara*. Whether this means the rooster will mate with every available hen, or that the hen's biology responds to the rooster's presence such that it will not lay without fertilization, the tradition establishes the principle categorically.

### Rooster Voice Range

How close must the rooster be for this principle to apply? *Rav Gamda in the name of Rav* teaches: as far as the rooster's voice can be heard *bi-ymama* — during the daytime. The qualifier "daytime" is significant: since hens mate and lay during the day, and sounds carry less far in the day than at night, the relevant question is whether the hen can hear the rooster's crowing during daytime hours. If it can, it will not lay unfertilized eggs; if it cannot, it might.

### Sixty Houses Rule

*Rav Mari* issued a practical ruling in a case where the rooster was sixty houses away, determining that this was still within hearing range and therefore the hen would not lay an unfertilized egg. Consequently, any egg found in such a coop could be presumed fertilized and therefore could not have been laid at night — lending support to the conclusion that it was laid before *Yom Tov*.

### Rooster Obstacles

The *Gemara* then addresses physical obstacles that might prevent a rooster from crossing to reach a hen. If there is a river between them, *lo avra* — the rooster will not cross. If there is a bridge, *avra* — it will cross. If there is a thin plank — *metzra*, which *Rashi* describes as a narrow board one would traverse while holding a thin rope — then *lo avra*, it will not cross. Yet the *Gemara* reports an actual incident in which a rooster did cross a *metzra*. The discussion here evokes the *Gemara*'s observation elsewhere that *ein apotropos le-arayos* — no barrier can be fully trusted to prevent mating — so that even significant obstacles may not deter a rooster.

### Safek Resolution

The *Gemara* then circles back to resolve a conceptual difficulty. Returning to the scenario where one checked before *Yom Tov* and found no egg but then found one the next morning: the entire discussion had assumed the egg's unfertilized status as the problematic case. But the *Gemara* now asks: *mai irya badak* — why is it significant that one checked right before *Yom Tov*? Even if one had not checked, one could simply assume the egg might have been laid from *erev Yom Tov*. The ruling: *ki lo badak, eima mei'etmol havei* — if one did not check before *Yom Tov*, and found an egg the next morning, one may be lenient and assume it was laid before *Yom Tov*. Since the prohibition on a *Yom Tov*-born egg is rabbinic, *safek de-rabbanan l'kula* — in cases of doubt regarding rabbinic prohibitions, we rule leniently.

The *Gemara* asks: if that is so, even when one did check and found nothing, one should still be lenient — perhaps the egg had been laid with its majority emerged and then retreated, as per *Rabi Yochanan*. The *Gemara* answers: *d'Rabbi Yochanan lo shchiach* — that scenario is uncommon. So if one checked carefully and found nothing, the possibility of *Rabi Yochanan*'s scenario is too remote to rely upon. But if one did not check at all, and there is a genuine possibility the egg was already laid from before *Yom Tov*, the doubt is real and one may rule leniently.

This yields a practically important ruling: if one finds an egg in a coop on *Yom Tov* morning and there is no certainty that it was laid overnight, it is *muttar* — unless one checked right before *Yom Tov* and confirmed the coop was empty.

### Tosafot's Caveat

*Tosafot* raises a significant question on this leniency. The egg in question is a *davar she-yeish lo matirin* — something that will become permissible on its own after *Yom Tov*. The general principle of *davar she-yeish lo matirin* holds that we do not apply certain leniencies — such as *bittul* in a mixture — to objects that will become permitted later; why not wait? If so, should *safek de-rabbanan l'kula* not apply here either, and one should instead wait until after *Yom Tov* to eat the egg?

*Tosafot* answers: *shani hacha* — this case is different, because in any event it is more common for a hen to lay during the day than at night, so even without the specific analysis about fertilization and roosters, the statistical likelihood favors the egg having been laid before *Yom Tov*. The simple sense of the *Gemara*, however, is that the leniency of *safek de-rabbanan l'kula* applies straightforwardly here: the prohibition is rabbinic and the doubt is genuine. *Tosafot*'s caveat reminds us of the earlier discussion of *davar she-yeish lo matirin* — the question of whether that principle extends to block other forms of leniency beyond *bittul* — but the *Gemara* itself appears to permit the egg in the straightforward doubt scenario without invoking that concern.

---

## Chametz & Se'or

### Shammai's Amounts

The *Gemara* now proceeds to the second of the three *Mishnah* disputes between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* recorded in this *masechta*: the minimum quantities of *chametz* and *se'or* on *Pesach*. *Se'or* is sourdough — not itself edible in normal circumstances, but used as a fermenting agent to leaven dough. The Torah prohibits both *chametz* and *se'or*. *Beit Shammai* holds that *se'or* carries its prohibition at the size of a *kezayit*, while *chametz* carries its prohibition only at the larger size of a *kakosevet* — approximately the volume of a pressed date.

### Shammai's Reasoning

The *Gemara* asks for *Beit Shammai*'s reasoning. Their position rests on the logic that since *se'or* has more powerful leavening ability — *chimutzo kasheh* — one might assume it would be more stringently forbidden. If so, why did the Torah need to prohibit *se'or* at all? Had it only said *chametz*, one could have derived *se'or* a fortiori: if ordinary bread, whose leavening power is weak, is forbidden, certainly sourdough, whose leavening power is strong, is forbidden. The very fact that the Torah explicitly mentions *se'or* separately must be *l'malfatcha* — to teach something new: namely, that their *shiurim* are not identical. Since the baseline measure for eating-related prohibitions is a *kezayit*, that minimum applies to the more powerful *se'or*. For *chametz*, which is less potent as a leavening agent, *Rashi* explains that the next logical size — the *kakosevet*, which is the measure that provides some minimal satiation (as established in the context of *Yom Kippur*) — applies.

### Hillel's Amounts

*Beit Hillel* holds that both *chametz* and *se'or* are governed by the same measure: a *kezayit*.

### Hillel's Reasoning

*Beit Hillel* reasons that both *chametz* and *se'or* needed to be stated explicitly because each has a stringent dimension not possessed by the other: *se'or* is stringent because of its powerful leavening capacity, while *chametz* is stringent because it is *ra'ui le-achila* — fit for ordinary human consumption. Neither can be derived from the other. *Se'or* cannot be derived from *chametz* alone, since one might have thought that since *se'or* is not normally eaten, it would not be prohibited. *Chametz* cannot be derived from *se'or* alone, since one might have thought the prohibition stems specifically from the capacity to leaven, which *chametz* lacks to the same degree. Since each has its own independent basis for stringency, both must be stated, and both are governed by the same *shiur* of a *kezayit*.

### Eating vs. Ownership

The *Gemara* introduces the position of *Rabi Zeira*: one verse opens with *se'or* and closes with *chametz* — *shivat yamim se'or lo yimatzei be-vateichem ki kol ochel machmetzet* — equating them *le-halacha*. The *Gemara* then clarifies the scope of the dispute: *l'inyan achila, kulei alma lo pligi* — regarding eating, nobody disagrees. All agree that one transgresses upon eating a *kezayit* of either. *Ki pligi l'inyan biyur* — the dispute concerns *biyur*, the prohibition of owning or possessing *chametz* on *Pesach*. *Beit Shammai savri lo yalpinan biyur me-achila* — *Beit Shammai* holds that we do not derive the *shiur* for the prohibition of ownership from the *shiur* of eating. Consequently, although eating a *kezayit* of either would be a transgression, owning *chametz* only becomes prohibited when the amount reaches a *kakosevet*. *Beit Hillel* holds *yalpinan biyur me-achila*: we learn the *shiur* for ownership from the *shiur* for eating, and both are a *kezayit*. This reading is confirmed by *Rabi Yose bar Hanina* and by a *braita* that cites the verse *ve-lo yera-eh lecha chametz ve-lo yera-eh lecha se'or* — the doubling of the prohibition teaches that this is precisely the point of the dispute.

### Ownership Concept

*Beit Shammai*'s position opens an interesting conceptual window onto the nature of the prohibition of owning *chametz*. There are two possible understandings of why the Torah prohibits possessing *chametz* in one's home. The first is that it serves as a safeguard against eating: since we eat *chametz* throughout the year and it is not inherently associated in our minds with *issur*, we might forget ourselves and eat it. Owning it therefore risks violation, and the Torah preemptively prohibits possession. Under this understanding, the prohibition of ownership is functionally derivative of the prohibition of eating — it is the Torah's own *seyag*. The second understanding is that ownership of *chametz* is itself antithetical to the identity of the day as *Chag ha-Matzot*: the entire theme of the festival is *matzah* and the departure from Egypt, which was so rapid that the dough did not have time to leaven. On this view, the presence of *chametz* in one's domain contradicts the essence of the day, quite apart from any risk of eating.

*Beit Shammai*'s position — that the *shiur* for *biyur* is larger than the *shiur* for eating — seems more compatible with the second understanding. If the entire basis of the ownership prohibition were simply "lest you come to eat it," then a *kezayit* of *chametz* — the exact amount whose consumption would be a transgression — should trigger the ownership prohibition as well, since one could pop it in one's mouth at any moment. The fact that *Beit Shammai* requires a *kakosevet* for the ownership violation, despite agreeing that eating a *kezayit* is forbidden, suggests that the prohibition of ownership is not simply a derivative of the eating concern but reflects something independent — perhaps the thematic incompatibility of *chametz* with the day — and therefore requires a more substantial presence to be triggered.

---

## Blood Coverage on Yom Tov

### Lechatchila vs. Di-eved

The *Gemara* now addresses the third and final dispute in the *Mishnah*: the question of covering the blood of a *chayah* or *of* — a wild animal or bird — when *shechita* is performed on *Yom Tov*. The *mitzvah* of *kisuy ha-dam* requires the blood to be covered with earth above and below. The *Mishnah* frames the question using the phrase *ha-shochet*, which could be read either as referring to someone who has already slaughtered (*di-eved*) or to someone who is asking prospectively whether he may slaughter (*lechatchila*).

The *Gemara* identifies a textual problem. On one hand, the opening of the *Mishnah* sounds like a *di-eved* scenario — what does one do after the fact? On the other hand, *Beit Hillel*'s response — *lo yishchot* — is a prohibition against slaughtering, which can only make sense as a *lechatchila* ruling. Furthermore, at the end of the *Mishnah*, both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree that *im shachat, she-yachpor be-deker ve-yichaseh* — if one already slaughtered, one may dig and cover — making clear that *di-eved* is agreed upon by both. Therefore the dispute must be *lechatchila*.

### Rava's Reading

*Rava* explains the *Mishnah* as follows: *ha-shochet she-ba l'himalekh keitzad* — the *Mishnah* addresses a slaughterer who comes to ask for practical instruction: what is he to do? *Beit Shammai* tells him: *shechot, chapor ve-chaseh* — slaughter, then dig, then cover. *Beit Hillel* tells him: *lo yishchot ela im kein haya lo afar muchan mi-be'od yom* — do not slaughter unless you already had dirt prepared before *Yom Tov*. The question throughout is therefore *lechatchila*. *Beit Shammai* permits proceeding with the slaughter and covering even without pre-prepared dirt; *Beit Hillel* prohibits the slaughter entirely unless dirt was prepared beforehand.

### Rav Yosef's Version

*Rav Yosef* presents the same basic ruling but with a subtle difference: according to *Beit Shammai*, he formulates the instruction as *lech chapor, shechot ve-chaseh* — go dig first, then slaughter, then cover — rather than *Rava*'s formulation of slaughter first and dig afterward.

### Rav Zeira's Requirement

*Abaye* identifies what he believes to be the underlying disagreement between *Rava* and *Rav Yosef*. He suggests they are arguing *bid-Rabbi Zeira amar Rav*: *Rav Zeira* rules in the name of *Rav* that when performing *shechita* on a *chayah* or *of*, one must place earth both below the blood and above it, not just on top. The source is the verse *ve-shaphach et damo ve-chisahu be-afar* — the blood is to be covered *be-afar*, "with earth," implying that the blood must be *within* the earth, surrounded above and below. This is a somewhat unexpected reading of the verse, yet it is the established *halacha* of *Rav Zeira*.

*Abaye* suggests that *Rav Yosef* — who instructs *dig first, then slaughter* — holds of *Rav Zeira*: one must lay a bed of loose earth before slaughtering so that blood falls onto it, and then cover from above afterward. *Rava*, who instructs *slaughter first, then dig*, apparently does not require pre-existing loose earth below, meaning he does not hold of *Rav Zeira*.

### Pre-existing Dirt

*Rav Yosef* rejects *Abaye*'s diagnosis: *bein l'didi bein l'Rava it lan d'Rabbi Zeira* — both he and *Rava* hold of *Rav Zeira* and require earth below the blood as well as above. The difference between their formulations of *Beit Shammai*'s instruction reflects a different dispute entirely.

### Rava's Caution

*Rava* holds *ika afar le-mata in, i lo lo*: even according to *Beit Shammai*, who permits the slaughter *lechatchila* on *Yom Tov*, this is only permitted if loose earth already exists below — that is, if the physical precondition of *Rav Zeira*'s requirement is already in place before the question arises. If there is no pre-existing loose earth and one would need to dig in order to create the lower layer, *Rava* rules that *Beit Shammai* would not permit the slaughter at all. The concern is *dilma mimrekh ve-lo shakhat* — that the person might dig the lower layer, then change his mind and decide not to slaughter, and the digging on *Yom Tov* will have been performed for nothing. Rather than risk a purposeless violation, *Rava* requires that the earth already be present.

### Yosef's Leniency

*Rav Yosef* disagrees: he would instruct the person to go ahead, dig the lower layer, then slaughter, then cover — accepting the risk that the slaughter might ultimately not take place. His reasoning is *adraba ha-adifa*: this is actually preferable, because insisting on pre-existing loose earth makes it harder for people to perform *shechita* on *Yom Tov* when they wish to, thereby depriving them of *simchat Yom Tov*. Better to allow the digging and accept the theoretical risk of abandonment than to impose a practical barrier to the joyous consumption of fresh meat on the festival.

It should be noted that this entire dispute between *Rava* and *Rav Yosef* is framed within *Beit Shammai*'s position, which permits the slaughter *lechatchila*. The practical *halacha* follows *Beit Hillel*, who requires that earth be prepared before *Yom Tov* as a precondition for slaughtering at all. The question of what happens if one slaughtered without preparation — the *di-eved* scenario where all agree one may dig and cover — will be addressed in the continuation of the *sugya*.

---

---

# Beitzah 8

## Digging & Blood Cover

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

The sugya opens two lines from the bottom of 7b, where Rav Zreika cites a tradition concerning the debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* regarding *kisuy hadam* — the obligation to cover the blood of a *chayah* or *of* (a deer or chicken) slaughtered on *Yom Tov*. The earlier discussion had established that the debate is framed *lechatchila*: *Beit Shammai* permits one to slaughter *lechatchila* and then dig and cover the blood, while *Beit Hillel* holds that one should not do so *lechatchila*, though both agree that *bedi'avad* — if one went ahead and slaughtered — one may dig and cover.

The question that now arises is how digging and covering could be permitted at all. Covering blood after *shechita* is not *tzorech ochel nefesh*; the animal is already *kosher* to eat without it. It fulfills a *mitzvat aseh*, but it is not necessary to render the food edible. So how is this permitted on *Yom Tov*?

### Muktzeh & Shovel

Two distinct problems immediately present themselves. The first concerns *muktzeh*. Rav Yehuda teaches: *vehu she'yesh lo dikar na'utz miba'od yom* — this is only permitted when one has a shovel already stuck into the dirt from before *Yom Tov*. The dirt in question was not loose but packed into the ground, and dirt under normal circumstances has no designated use and would be *muktzeh*. Having the shovel pre-positioned from *erev Yom Tov* addresses this: it signals that the dirt was already contemplated for use before *Yom Tov* began.

### Melacha Problem

The second problem runs deeper. Even with the *muktzeh* issue resolved, digging on *Yom Tov* raises an independent concern: *ve'ha ka'avid tichsha* — you are grinding. Taking clumps of compacted earth and pulverizing them into loose granular material is a form of *tochen*, the *melacha* of grinding. That is a biblical prohibition. The Gemara answers: *be'afar tichuach* — we are speaking of loose dirt, where one is simply scooping out material that is already granular, not transforming a hard clod into powder.

But then a further problem surfaces: *ve'ha ka'avid gumma* — even if the dirt is already loose, you are making a hole. Making a hole can constitute one of two *melachot*: *boneh*, constructing something usable, or *choreish*, plowing, if done in soil suited for cultivation. The Gemara resolves this by invoking the principle of Rabbi Abba: *hachofer gumma be'Shabbat ve'ein tzarich ela la'afarah* — one who digs a hole on *Shabbat* but is interested only in the extracted dirt, not in the hole itself, is *patur*, because the hole is merely a byproduct of the act. The purpose of the *melacha* of digging a hole is the hole itself; here, the hole is incidental. This is the principle of *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa* — a *melacha* performed for a purpose other than the intrinsic function of that *melacha*. While such an act is minimally forbidden *d'rabbanan*, it is exempt from the biblical prohibition.

### Rashi & Tosafot

Rashi adds a further consideration: beyond *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa*, there is an element of *kilkul* — the act is in a sense destructive to the ground — which provides additional grounds for leniency. Tosafot takes a different approach. Tosafot acknowledges that the issue is at minimum a *d'rabbanan* violation, one that is *patur aval assur lechatchila*, and argues that it is permitted here *mishum simchas Yom Tov* — for the sake of the joy of *Yom Tov*, the Rabbis granted latitude even *lechatchila*. This framing is, as should be noted, somewhat curious, since according to *Beit Hillel* one should not have slaughtered the animal in the first place; framing the allowance of covering blood *bedi'avad* in terms of *simchas Yom Tov* is a somewhat strained rationale.

Tosafot himself anticipates a difficulty: if *simchas Yom Tov* provides the basis for the allowance, why does the Gemara require that the shovel be pre-positioned from before *Yom Tov*? His answer is that notwithstanding the broader latitude for *Yom Tov* joy, the *muktzeh*/*muchan* problem must still be independently addressed. We will override a *d'rabbanan* concern of digging a hole that one does not need, but we will not override the requirement that items be properly *muchan* before *Yom Tov*. This is, on its face, somewhat counterintuitive: one might expect the law to be stricter about what more closely resembles a *melacha* than about a purely rabbinic concern of *muktzeh*. Nevertheless, the principle holds: one must address the *muchan* issue through the pre-positioned shovel, and once that is done, the residual issue of digging a hole — reduced to a *melacha she'eina tzricha legufa* — can be permitted.

This also surfaces a terminological distinction worth noting. The discussion moves between the language of *muktzeh* and *muchan*/*eino min hamuchan*. These are related but not identical concepts. The terminology of *muchan* and *eino min hamuchan* appears to be earlier, rooted in the period of *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, while *muktzeh* as a term seems to emerge from the generation of Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda. Conceptually they point in opposite directions: *muchan* requires affirmatively designating what is usable, while *muktzeh* requires identifying what is excluded. In the present *sugya* the operative language is that of *muchan*, which is a somewhat stricter framing.

### Muchan Status

The Gemara then shifts to the matter of covering material and introduces the case of *eifer kera* — ashes of an oven. A student asking why this is suddenly mentioned prompts the clarification that Rabbah explains the earlier statement as teaching two things: first, that one may dig with a pre-positioned shovel, and second, that if one has ashes from an oven already present, those ashes are considered *muchan* and may be used to cover the blood. The ashes of a *kirah* are not an item one would simply discard; they have enough potential household uses that they do not fall into the category of *eino min hamuchan*.

---

## Ashes & Dirt

### Oven Ashes

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches: *lo shanu ela shehusak me'erev Yom Tov* — this applies only where the fire was lit and the wood reduced to ashes before *Yom Tov* began. Ashes that existed at the onset of *Yom Tov* are considered *muchan* because ashes are the sort of item one might foreseeably use. They are not garbage; they are something one might use around the house for any number of purposes. But if the fire was kindled and the ashes created on *Yom Tov* itself, those ashes are *assur* — forbidden for use.

### New Ashes Exception

The reason newly created ashes are forbidden follows the same logic as the *beitzah* of the tractate's name: even though one anticipated using the wood and knew it would become ashes, the ashes did not yet exist when *Yom Tov* began and cannot be considered *muchan*. However, there is an exception: *ve'im ra'uy litzlot bo beitzah* — if the ashes are still hot enough and substantial enough that one could bake an egg in them, they are *mutar*.
