The question at stake is how much latitude we have to carry on Yom Tov. Most people assume that carrying on Yom Tov is essentially unrestricted — that there is simply no prohibition. This Mishnah reveals that according to Beis Shammai that assumption is incorrect.

### Beis Shammai Rule

Even carrying a child, a *lulav*, or a *sefer torah* — all of which involve *mitzvah* purposes — is forbidden according to Beis Shammai. Rabbeinu Chananel explains the case of the minor as referring to a *bris milah*, making the *mitzvah* context explicit. Yet despite these weighty purposes, Beis Shammai prohibits the carrying. The reason is that none of these acts serves the one explicitly sanctioned purpose: *ochel nefesh*, food preparation. Beis Shammai holds that carrying is no different from any other *melacha* — permitted only when directed toward food, forbidden otherwise. As the Gemara will make clear, this is not merely a rabbinic restriction: performing such carrying would constitute a biblical violation of Yom Tov, subject to lashes.

### Beis Hillel Permits

Beis Hillel permits carrying in these cases. But the Mishnah leaves open a broader question: Beis Hillel permits carrying for *mitzvah* purposes — what about carrying for other purposes entirely? In practice, we carry freely on Yom Tov without pausing to ask whether our carrying serves a *mitzvah* or food-related purpose. Whether that reflects the full scope of Beis Hillel's position is precisely what the Gemara will explore. Two questions thus frame the coming discussion: how broad is Beis Hillel's allowance, and to which *melachos* does it extend?

---

## Shechitah Olah

### Baraita on Olah

A *tana* — one of the memorizers of the oral tradition — taught a *baraita* before Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abdimi: one who *shechts* a free-will *olah* on Yom Tov receives lashes. The choice of a *nedavah olah* is deliberate and instructive. An *olah* is entirely consumed on the altar; the one who offers it eats nothing from it. The case therefore is not one of *mekalkel* — purposeless destruction — but of a constructive, meaningful act that simply lacks the specific purpose of eating. The question it poses is: what is the *halacha* if one performs *shechitah* on Yom Tov for a purpose other than eating? The *baraita* answers: lashes. It makes no difference that the act is *shechitah*; if it is not performed for the purpose of eating, it constitutes a violation of Yom Tov.

### Beis Shammai Source

Rabbi Yitzchak bar Abdimi responded to the *tana*: who is the source of this teaching? This is a Beis Shammai ruling. The reason is that our Mishnah explicitly demonstrates that Beis Shammai does not apply the principle of *mitoch* — the idea that once a *melacha* is permitted for one purpose, it is permitted more broadly. The Mishnah shows that even though carrying may be permitted for food purposes, it remains forbidden for non-food purposes. The implication carries over to *shechitah*: permitted for eating, forbidden for other purposes, and not merely rabbinically — one receives lashes for the violation.

### Mitoch Principle

What then is Beis Hillel's position? The Gemara infers it from the Mishnah: *mitoch she-huttra hotza'ah le-tzorech huttra nami she-lo le-tzorech* — since carrying was permitted for a purpose (food), it is permitted even without that purpose. And since Beis Hillel says *mitoch* by carrying, the same logic would apply to *shechitah*: once permitted for the purpose of eating, it is permitted even when the purpose is a *korban* that will not be eaten.

This suggests that the Beis Shammai–Beis Hillel debate is not confined to carrying. Formulated in the context of carrying, it now appears to be a broader dispute running through the *melachos* of Yom Tov generally — with Beis Shammai holding the allowance is always limited to *ochel nefesh*, and Beis Hillel holding that once a *melacha* was permitted for food it carries a broader license. Two critical questions remain about Beis Hillel's position: first, how much of a *tzorech* is required, if any at all — is a *mitzvah* purpose required, or something less? And second, to which *melachos* does the principle apply? Both questions will occupy much of the Gemara's analysis.

---

## Rabbah Questions

### Scope of Debate

Rabbah challenges the inference just drawn. The Gemara has treated the Beis Shammai–Beis Hillel dispute as a general debate about whether *mitoch* applies across the *melachos* of Yom Tov. Rabbah asks: who says that is what they are debating? Perhaps their dispute is narrow — concerned specifically with carrying, not with a general principle applicable to all *melachos*.

### Eruv & Hotza'ah

The phrase Rabbah uses is *eruv ve-hotza'ah*, which Rashi explains as referring to whether carrying as a category is subject to prohibition at all. There is unquestionably a prohibition of carrying on Shabbos — from which the Rabbanan derived the entire framework of *eruv chatzeiros* and its related laws. But perhaps, Rabbah suggests, there is no prohibition of carrying on Yom Tov, and consequently none of the *derabbanan* structures of *eruv* apply either.

### Carrying Status

On this reading, the Beis Shammai–Beis Hillel debate would be solely about whether carrying is forbidden on Yom Tov at all. Beis Shammai holds that there is indeed such a prohibition on Yom Tov, just as on Shabbos, and therefore the only permissible carrying is for *ochel nefesh*. Beis Hillel holds there is no prohibition of carrying on Yom Tov — and therefore carrying requires no justification whatsoever. If that is so, the debate is entirely about carrying and cannot be generalized to other *melachos*, which would remain governed by the requirement of *ochel nefesh*.

### Jeremiah Source

The biblical basis for Beis Hillel's view, on this reading, is the verse in Yirmiyahu: *ve-lo totzi'u masa mibateichem be-yom ha-Shabbat* — do not carry a load from your house on the Shabbos day. From *be-yom ha-Shabbat* the Gemara derives: on Shabbos yes, on Yom Tov no. Carrying is a Shabbos prohibition, not a Yom Tov one. If Beis Hillel holds this, the implication is a blanket allowance for carrying — no justification required — but also a clear limit: this reasoning is specific to carrying and cannot extend to *shechitah*, fire, or cooking, which remain governed by the requirement of *ochel nefesh* as standard *melachos* of Yom Tov.

---

## Carrying Unique

### Rashi: Not Core

Rashi's explanation sheds light on why carrying stands apart. In the narrow commentary, Rashi notes: even granting that there is a prohibition of *hotza'ah*, we learn it not from the core verse *lo ta'aseh kol melacha* but from the verse *vaya'aviru kol bamachaneh* — the announcement in the wilderness calling for an end to donations for the *Beis Hamikdash*, from which we derive the prohibition of carrying. And the *pasuk* in Yirmiyahu limits that prohibition to Shabbos. Rashi thus suggests that carrying is not fundamentally included in the prohibition of *lo ta'aseh kol melacha*. To know that carrying is forbidden at all we needed a separate verse. *Shechitah*, by contrast, is an *av melacha*, squarely within *lo ta'aseh kol melacha* as applied on Yom Tov — and therefore even Beis Hillel would not extend a blanket allowance to *shechitah* on the basis of this reasoning alone.

### Melacha Gru'ah

This leads to an idea developed by Tosafot as well, and discussed by the *Rishonim* generally: carrying is a *melacha gru'ah* — a deficient or degraded *melacha*. The conceptual reason is that carrying is the one *melacha* that is non-creative. Every other *melacha* produces something new — it transforms raw material into a finished state. Carrying merely moves an object from point A to point B. Nothing is made; nothing is changed. This is why, when the Gemara in Shabbos discusses the parameters of carrying, it requires extensive *pesukim* to define its particulars — what distance, what domain, what direction — because the act itself has no intrinsic productive character. For all other *melachos*, what matters is the end result: it makes no difference whether food was cooked by frying or roasting; what defines the prohibition is the transformed object. Carrying is categorically different.

### Commerce Role

There is also a distinct sociological dimension to carrying. The verses in Yirmiyahu describing violations of Shabbos in Yerushalayim depict people streaming into the city carrying wheat and goods to the marketplace. The image is not of craftsmen creating objects but of merchants transporting wares for sale. Transportation and conveyance are central to commerce — the shipping and transport industries are the lifeblood of trade — but commerce is not the same as *melacha*. *Melacha* is fundamentally about creating; commerce is about moving and exchanging. Carrying thus belongs as much to the commercial world as to the creative one, and its inclusion within the thirty-nine *melachos* reflects a deliberate extension on Shabbos, not an organic fit.

### Shopping Purpose

This point becomes even sharper in the context of Yom Tov. We have already learned that on Yom Tov one may engage in quasi-commercial activity — going to a shopkeeper and "borrowing" goods to be paid for afterward — in order to procure what is needed for cooking. If someone were told that Yom Tov permits acts related to food, the first things that come to mind are fire and cooking, not carrying. Yet when one reflects on the full process of food production, the first step is going shopping — acquiring the ingredients, conveying them home. Carrying is the act of procurement; it is essential to food preparation at its earliest stage. This is precisely why, conceptually, carrying has a natural connection to the Yom Tov allowance, and why Beis Hillel's broad permission for it — whether grounded in the *mitoch* principle or in a categorical exclusion — makes sense.

---

## Rambam Framework

### Two Verses

To understand the *mitoch* principle at a deeper structural level, one must attend to a significant point that Ramban raises about the nature of the *melachos* of Yom Tov. There are, in fact, two distinct formulations in the Torah. In one place, the Torah speaks of *ach asher ye'achel le-chol nefesh hu levado ye'aseh lachem* — only what is eaten for any person may you prepare. Elsewhere, wherever the Torah prohibits work on Yom Tov, it uses a qualifier: *kol meleches avodah lo ta'asu* — all laborious work you shall not do — rather than the unqualified *lo ta'aseh kol melacha* of Shabbos.

### Case-by-Case

The *ochel nefesh* formulation implies a case-by-case analysis. Every act must be evaluated: is this being done for the sake of *ochel nefesh*? The baseline is prohibition; the *hetter* is the justification of food preparation. Under this framework, every time one decides whether to perform a *melacha* on Yom Tov, the question is whether the specific act is directed toward eating.

### Categorical Exclusion

The *meleches avodah* formulation implies something structurally different. Rather than requiring justification act by act, it categorically excludes certain types of *melacha* from the prohibition. What counts as *meleches avodah*? Laborious work — the kind done in the field, in industry, in commerce — as opposed to the kind done in the home to produce a meal, which is qualitatively different in character. Under this framework, certain *melachos* are simply not in the prohibited category. Ramban notes that these two formulations are in fact parallel: one place says *kol melacha* and supplies the *hetter* of *asher ye'achel le-chol nefesh*; elsewhere it simply says *meleches avodah*, using the very *ochel nefesh* criterion to define which *melachos* are prohibited in the first place. They point to the same result, but they conceptualize the allowance differently — one as a narrow exception, the other as a categorical exclusion.

---

## Mitoch Scope

### Building Excluded

This question of categorical breadth has immediate practical implications. Tosafot in Shabbos notes that the Gemara there holds that making cheese is a violation of *boneh* — constructing — because milk coagulates and solidifies into a formed object. One might therefore reason: since *boneh* can be performed for food purposes (making cheese), *mitoch she-huttra le-tzorech huttra nami she-lo le-tzorech* — once permitted for a purpose, it is permitted even without that purpose — and therefore one could build a building on Yom Tov for any reason at all. Tosafot raises this inference and acknowledges that biblically it might in fact follow, while suggesting it remains rabbinically forbidden. This is a striking position — and it highlights why the scope of *mitoch* is not self-evident. Does the principle apply to every *melacha* for which a food-related use can be found? Or is it limited to specific *melachos*?

The Gemara, when it applies *mitoch*, does so only in connection with carrying, *shechitah*, fire, and cooking — precisely the *melachos* that are directly and essentially involved in food production. The Gemara never suggests extending *mitoch* to *boneh* on account of cheese-making. This strongly implies that *mitoch* is anchored to the *melachos* that are functionally constitutive of food preparation, not extended mechanically to any *melacha* that happens to admit a food-related application.

---

## Tosafot View

### Requires Tzorech

Up to this point the question has been whether the *mitoch* debate is a general principle or limited to carrying. Now the question shifts to the interior of Beis Hillel's position: even granting *mitoch*, how broad is the allowance?

Rav Yosef presses the Gemara with a challenge: if Beis Hillel held that carrying was categorically not forbidden on Yom Tov — that there was simply no prohibition of *hotza'ah* — then they should have permitted carrying stones. Instead they enumerated specific cases of permissible carrying: a minor, a *lulav*, a *sefer torah*. The fact that Beis Hillel's Mishnah lists these cases, rather than simply declaring carrying universally permitted, implies that even according to Beis Hillel there is a prohibition of carrying on Yom Tov — and it becomes permitted through *mitoch*. But *mitoch* is not infinite. Carrying stones for no purpose at all falls outside its scope. Tosafot reads this as the natural and correct reading of the Gemara: you still need some *tzorech*, some justification, even according to Beis Hillel.

Rashi, it should be noted, reads this differently: *mitoch*, once invoked, is infinite. Once the allowance is established, everything is permitted and no justification is needed. But the Gemara's own question — why not debate stones? — argues more naturally for Tosafot's reading.

### Chananel Strict

Rabbeinu Chananel adopts the most stringent reading of this requirement: the *tzorech* must be a *mitzvah* purpose. Only an act serving a *mitzvah* constitutes a sufficient *tzorech yom tov* to bring it within the *mitoch* allowance. On this view, the Mishnah's examples are not illustrative of a broader class; they define the class.

### Simcha Standard

Tosafot explicitly rejects this strict reading. He notes: *lav davka katan le-molo* — it is not specifically a case of *bris milah* that qualifies the *katan*. Even if one simply wants to take a child on a walk on Yom Tov, carrying the child falls within *mitoch*. The standard is not *mitzvah* but *tzorech yom tov* — any purpose fitting the spirit of Yom Tov enjoyment and *simcha*.

### Ball Game

Tosafot invokes an evocative proof: people on Yom Tov play ball — in Tosafot's idiom, *pelota* — in the public domain. They carry for the sake of fun, not for any *mitzvah* purpose. This is not merely a theoretical allowance; it reflects observed practice. Any act that genuinely serves the Yom Tov spirit of *simcha* and joy satisfies the *tzorech* threshold. The limit is at the other extreme: carrying a bookcase to a friend's house — *schlepping* something that has nothing to do with Yom Tov — would not qualify. But that threshold is extremely easy to clear in practice, which is why we carry freely without thinking about justification. The theoretical requirement exists; practically, almost everything qualifies.

---

## Yochanan & Cooking

### Mitoch Extended

The Gemara now introduces Rabbi Yochanan's view: he holds that the *mitoch* principle operates not merely for carrying but as a general principle applying to other *melachos* as well — specifically, fire and cooking. This is the issue raised earlier in passing: just as we tend to carry on Yom Tov without asking whether justification is needed, we also light fire and cook without a moment's hesitation.

### Gid Baraita

A *tana* taught before Rabbi Yochanan the following *baraita*: one who cooks *gid ha-nasheh* with milk on Yom Tov and eats it receives five sets of lashes. The enumeration is instructive. First: lashes for cooking the *gid* on Yom Tov without legitimate purpose — since one may not eat *gid ha-nasheh*, the cooking serves no permissible food purpose. Second: lashes for eating *gid ha-nasheh*, which is prohibited regardless of milk. Third: lashes for cooking meat with milk, the cooking prohibition of *basar be-chalav* — and Rashi here pointedly notes that one must prove this prohibition even exists, citing the principle that *lo tevashel gdi be-chalav imo* is stated three times: once for eating, once for *hana'ah*, and once for cooking. It is striking that Rashi must argue for the prohibition of cooking meat and milk at all, so thoroughly have we internalized the focus on eating. Fourth: lashes for eating *basar be-chalav*. Fifth: lashes for *havarah* — for the fire kindled on Yom Tov without legitimate purpose.

The *baraita* thus contemplates receiving lashes both for cooking without a proper *tzorech* and for making a fire without a proper *tzorech*. This implies that cooking and fire, like *shechitah*, require justification on Yom Tov, and that absent justification, one has violated a biblical prohibition.

### Rejection & Reason

Rabbi Yochanan rejected the *baraita* outright: *puk tani le-vara* — take this teaching outside. It has no place. Specifically, the components concerning *havarah* and *bishul* — fire and cooking — do not belong. If the *baraita* is accepted at all, it represents the position of Beis Shammai, who holds that *mitoch* does not apply, and therefore fire and cooking remain biblically restricted to food purposes. But according to Beis Hillel — and Rabbi Yochanan holds that the *halacha* follows Beis Hillel — *mitoch she-huttra le-tzorech huttra nami she-lo le-tzorech* applies equally to fire and cooking. Just as carrying became broadly permitted once the food-related allowance was established, so too fire and cooking carry a broader license. Therefore, one would not receive lashes for making a fire or cooking on Yom Tov even without a specific food purpose.

---

## Mitoch Scope (II)

### Food Melachos

The Gemara's application of *mitoch* is thus confirmed across four *melachos*: carrying, *shechitah*, fire, and cooking. These are the *melachos* that are directly constitutive of food preparation — from procurement through processing. The Gemara does not extend *mitoch* beyond this cluster, reinforcing the understanding that the principle is anchored to what is functionally essential to Yom Tov food production.

### Open Questions

Two questions remain open. The first concerns the threshold of justification: must every individual act of cooking or carrying be purposeful, or is *mitoch* an infinite license once the category is established? Rashi holds the latter — *mitoch* is total, and no justification is needed. Tosafot holds that justification is always required, though the threshold is low and almost universally reachable. The second question concerns which *melachos* fall within *mitoch*: the Gemara confirms the four food-related *melachos*, but the principle of *meleches avodah* — categorical exclusion of non-laborious work — might operate differently.

### Candle Case

A practical instance of these open questions emerges from a case discussed in the Yerushalmi: *ner shel batalah* — lighting a candle on Yom Tov for no purpose. Is this permitted? The question arises in a contemporary context as well: since we have electric lights, the practical necessity of a *ner* on Yom Tov is often absent. When it comes to *havdalah* between Shabbos and Yom Tov, the question arises whether one may light two flames for the *ner* if the second flame serves only a *minhag* and not a strict *halachic* requirement. The *Poskim* resolve this by treating the *minhag* itself as sufficient *tzorech*. But the underlying question — must some degree of justification be present, or is making a fire on Yom Tov categorically unrestricted — remains a live issue. The psychological reality is that we treat fire and carrying on Yom Tov as though no restriction exists; the theoretical framework revealed by the Gemara is more nuanced.

Notably, just as carrying is identified as *melacha gru'ah* — on the edges of the thirty-nine *melachos* — fire has a parallel status in one Talmudic opinion: *havarah le-lav yatzas*, that making a fire is not one of the thirty-nine *melachos* for which one is liable to death, but only a negative prohibition. It is perhaps not coincidental that the two *melachos* for which we most naturally assume a near-categorical Yom Tov allowance are precisely those which occupy the margins of the *lamed tes melachos*.

---

## Challah & Gifts

### Mishnah Rule

With this the Gemara shifts from biblical analysis to a *derabbanan* realm, and the contrast in register is notable. The next Mishnah states: Beis Shammai say one may not deliver *challah* or the priestly gifts (*matanos*) to the *kohen* on Yom Tov; Beis Hillel permit it.

### Separation Allowed

The context is as follows. We have established that one may bake bread on Yom Tov and may *shecht* an animal. Once bread is baked, one must separate *challah* before eating. Once an animal is *shechted*, one must set aside the *matanos* — the *zero'a*, *lechayayim*, and *keivah*, the foreleg, cheeks, and maw — for the *kohen*. While the food does not become *treif* if the *matanos* are not separated, practically one sets them aside immediately lest they become mixed in and one inadvertently deprive the *kohen* of his portion. So the separation of *challah* and *matanos* is permitted and expected on Yom Tov as a necessary adjunct to permitted activities.

### Gezeira Fear

The question is whether, having separated them, one may deliver them to the *kohen* on Yom Tov. The concern is that permitting delivery of *challah* and *matanos* may lead to delivering *terumah* to the *kohen* — and if one delivers *terumah*, one may come to separate *terumah*, which is forbidden on Yom Tov. This is admittedly a *gezeira le-gezeira* — a rabbinic precaution built on another rabbinic precaution — but that is the basis of Beis Shammai's restriction.

### Hillel Argument

Beis Hillel responds: *challah* and *matanos* are permitted to be separated on Yom Tov; *terumah* is not. Therefore these cases are categorically different and cannot be assimilated to one another. Beis Shammai's comparison — both are gifts to the *kohen*, so if you cannot give *terumah* you cannot give these either — fails because the underlying act of separation has a different status. Where separation is permitted, delivery should follow. Where it is not, the prohibition on delivery stands.

---

## Three Versions

### Yehuda Version

The Gemara asks which of three *tanna'im* our Mishnah follows, and quotes a *baraita* presenting three distinct versions of the Beis Shammai–Beis Hillel debate. The first version, that of Rabbi Yehuda, holds that Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel do not dispute the case where the animal was *shechted* today or the bread was baked today — in such cases, since there was no opportunity to do anything before Yom Tov, everyone agrees the *matanos* may be delivered. Moreover, Beis Shammai even permits bundling yesterday's gifts together with today's when making the delivery. The dispute in this version is narrow: only gifts that were separated as stand-alone items from the previous day, delivered by themselves, are contested.

### Yosi Version

Rabbi Yosi's version is broader in its area of agreement. He holds that Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel do not dispute *matanos* at all — both agree they may be delivered on Yom Tov in all cases. The sole dispute is whether *terumah* may be delivered. Beis Shammai says it may not; Beis Hillel says it may. In this version it is Beis Hillel making the comparison: just as everyone agrees *matanos* may be delivered, so too *terumah* — both are gifts to the *kohen*, and the prior allowance to separate *matanos* supports the allowance to deliver. Beis Shammai counters that the cases differ: *matanos* you are entitled to separate on Yom Tov; *terumah* you are not.

### Acherim Version

The third version, attributed to *Acherim*, holds the strictest position for Beis Shammai: Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree only that *terumah* may not be delivered. On *matanos*, they dispute: Beis Shammai forbids delivery in all cases; Beis Hillel permits it. This version, unlike the first two, gives Beis Shammai no concession on gifts at all. Since our Mishnah presents Beis Shammai as forbidding delivery whether the items were separated yesterday or today, it sounds — at first — like the *Acherim* position.

---

## Rava Resolution

### Separation Today

Rava clarifies: the Mishnah's language is *shehurmu* — they were separated. The operative variable is when the separation occurred, not when the *shechitah* or baking took place. The Mishnah is discussing a case where separation happened on Yom Tov, but the underlying *shechitah* or baking occurred the previous day. In this framing, Beis Shammai's blanket refusal is consistent with the possibility that even *Acherim* would concede when the *shechitah* itself took place today.

### Concession

Rava argues that even *Acherim* — the strictest version — would agree that Beis Shammai permits delivery when the animal was *shechted* on Yom Tov itself. The dispute in *Acherim*'s formulation concerns only items connected to a *shechitah* done yesterday. Accordingly, our Mishnah's case, which stipulates separation today but leaves *shechitah* from yesterday, is fully compatible with *Acherim*.

### Bundling

The remaining difference between the positions is then identified: *tfeila* — the bundling together of yesterday's items with today's. Rabbi Yehuda's version holds that Beis Shammai, conceding about today's items, permits bundling yesterday's gifts along with them into a single delivery. *Acherim*'s version does not include this concession. Where Rabbi Yehuda adds the bundling allowance, *Acherim* grants nothing beyond the case of today's *shechitah*.

---

## Ruling

### Halacha Decision

The *halacha* is stated by Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: the ruling follows Rabbi Yosi. This is the broadest position in terms of Beis Shammai's concessions — indeed, on Rabbi Yosi's reading, Beis Shammai concedes *matanos* entirely and disputes only *terumah*. And on that debate, the ruling follows Beis Hillel, who permits delivering even *terumah* to the *kohen* on Yom Tov.

### Case Study

The ruling is illustrated by a practical case. Tuvi, son of Rav Nechemiah, had a flask of wine that was *terumah* — it had been separated prior to Yom Tov and was sitting in his possession. He came before Rabbi Yosi with a question: may he deliver this wine to a *kohen* on Yom Tov? The wine had been set aside before Yom Tov, not freshly separated that day.

### Yosi Permits

Rabbi Yosi responded by transmitting the ruling: thus said Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel — the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yosi. Go ahead and deliver it to the *kohen* today. According to this ruling, both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree that *matanos* may be delivered; the debate is only about *terumah*; and we rule like Beis Hillel that *terumah* too may be delivered on Yom Tov. The only restriction that remains undisputed is the separation of *terumah* on Yom Tov — that one may not do. But *terumah* that was already separated and is sitting in one's possession may be brought to the *kohen* on Yom Tov itself.

---

---

# Beitzah 14

## Melila Methods

### Melila Overview

The daf begins five lines from the bottom of 13b, in the midst of a discussion that arose in connection with the question of separating *terumah* on *Yom Tov*. That inquiry led to an extended treatment of removing husks from kernels of grain and legumes on *Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* had already established that such removal — *melila* — is permitted in principle, with one concern relating to quantity or the use of specialized vessels. Rashi explains: *keitzad molel b'Yom Tov* — how does one perform *melila* on *Yom Tov*? Before examining the *Gemara*'s answer, Rashi makes a foundational point: *v'havaday shinuy ba-ei* — it is assumed that even when using one's bare hands, the *melila* must be performed with some degree of *shinuy*, some departure from the ordinary weekday manner. The reason, Rashi explains, is *shinuy bo mi-uvda d'chol* — the act must be distinguished from what would constitute a weekday appearance. Not every permitted *melacha* on *Yom Tov* requires a *shinuy*; cooking certainly does not. But certain food-preparation activities, particularly those that are sometimes performed not in the immediate kitchen context but as part of a prior, large-scale pre-processing stage, carry with them a concern of *uvda d'chol*. For those, the *Chachamim* required some modification even on *Yom Tov*.

It is worth noting parenthetically that Tosafot confirms this discussion concerns *Yom Tov*: *u'veShabbat assur limlol* — on *Shabbat*, *melila* is simply forbidden. The Rif, somewhat remarkably, holds that *melila* may be performed even on *Shabbat* with a *shinuy*, and most *Rishonim* reject this outright. It is difficult to understand how a *melacha* could be permitted on *Shabbat* merely through a *shinuy*. And yet there are isolated food-preparation *melachot* that *Chazal* permitted on *Shabbat* with a *shinuy* performed in small quantities — *lisha* being the classic example. Anyone who has attempted to make oatmeal on *Shabbat* will appreciate the complexity: mixing water with a granular substance to produce a dough-like consistency is precisely the concern, yet some permit it with a *shinuy*, such as reversing the order of mixing or using the back of a spoon. The Rif apparently extends this framework to *melila*, though the consensus is that we are dealing exclusively with *Yom Tov*.

### Finger Techniques

The *Gemara* asks: *keitzad molel?* — what is the proper technique? Abaye in the name of Rav Yosef says: *chada achada* — one finger against one finger, rubbing the husk off between two fingers. Rav Avya in the name of Rav Yosef says: *chada atartei* — one finger against two fingers, a slightly easier method. Rava says: *keivan d'meshani* — since in any case you are doing it differently from the most convenient manner, even using the thumb against all the fingers at once is acceptable. All of these presumably constitute a departure from whatever the standard large-scale method would be — perhaps using the palms, or a vessel altogether.

### Winnowing Technique

Having removed the husk, one must now separate the loosened chaff from the kernel. This is a form of *borer*. Rav Adda bar Abba said in the name of Rav: *minapeiach mikishrei etzba'otav u-l'ma'ala* — one blows or waves the mixture while holding it at the tips of the fingers, not cupped in the palms. In Eretz Yisrael they laughed at this restriction: *keivan d'meshani* — once you are doing it differently in some respect, even waving with the whole hand is fine. The final ruling comes from Rav Abba bar Alazar: *minapeiach b'yado achat u-v'chol kocho* — one holds it in one hand and fans with full force, as opposed to placing it in a sifter, which would constitute the kind of specialized vessel associated with large-scale, pre-kitchen processing.

This establishes the principle that will animate the discussions to follow: certain food-preparation acts on *Yom Tov* require some degree of *shinuy* because of the concern of *uvda d'chol*, and Rashi explicitly attributes this concern to the appearance of large-scale production. What exactly falls into this category — and why — will continue to be worked out as the *Gemara* progresses.

## Grinding Spices

### Beit Shammai Rules

The *Mishnah* transitions directly into the question of grinding spices on *Yom Tov*, a natural continuation of the discussion about *shinuy* and *uvda d'chol*. Beit Shammai rules: *tavlin* — ordinary spices — must be ground with a wooden pestle rather than the normal stone one, a modest *shinuy*. Salt requires an even greater departure: it must be ground either in a pottery vessel or with the back of a wooden spoon — *etz haparur* — a substantially more modified technique.

### Beit Hillel Position

Beit Hillel disagrees with the first ruling. *Tavlin nidochin kedarkan b'madoch shel even* — ordinary spices may be ground in the normal stone mortar and pestle without any *shinuy* at all. Since these are *tzorech ochel nefesh* — freshly ground spices needed for food preparation on *Yom Tov* — no modification is required. Salt, however, even Beit Hillel agrees requires some departure: *b'madoch shel etz* — a wooden rather than stone mortar. So while Beit Hillel reduces Beit Shammai's two-level stringency for salt to one level, the basic structure — that salt requires a *shinuy* while other spices do not — is preserved.

### Salt vs. Spices

The *Gemara* asks: *d'kulei alma miha melach ba'ya shinuy* — everyone agrees salt requires *some* form of *shinuy*. But why? It is *Yom Tov*, it is *melachat ochel nefesh* — food preparation — so what is the basis for any special restriction? Rav Huna and Rav Chisda debate this question, each offering a different rationale.

One of them says: *kol hakedeirot kulan tzrichin melach v'ein kol hakedeirot tzrichin tavlin* — all dishes require salt, while not all dishes require other spices. Salt is universally needed in the kitchen, and therefore one should have anticipated this need before *Yom Tov*. Having failed to prepare it in advance, one is penalized with the requirement of a *shinuy* on *Yom Tov* itself. Other spices, by contrast, are not so universally anticipated, and one cannot be faulted for not grinding them ahead of time.

The other opinion holds: *kol hatavlin mifihei ta'ama* — all other spices, if ground in advance, lose some of their pungency and sharpness. Freshly ground pepper or garlic has a quality that diminishes over time. Salt, however, *eina mifiha ta'ama* — does not lose its character if ground beforehand. There is therefore no justification for waiting until *Yom Tov* to grind it, and having done so, one must perform it with a *shinuy*.

The *Gemara* proceeds to identify the practical differences between these two explanations. If the reasoning is one of anticipation — you should have known you would need it — then any spice for a meal one had already planned in advance would likewise require a *shinuy*: *d'yada mai kdeira ba'ei l'mishlei* — if you knew in advance what dish you intended to cook, you had ample opportunity to prepare its spices beforehand. Under the pungency rationale, however, this would be irrelevant; the justification for grinding on *Yom Tov* is precisely the freshness advantage, regardless of whether the meal was anticipated.

A second difference involves saffron — *demorika*. Rashi notes that saffron apparently does not lose its pungency when ground in advance. Under the pungency rationale, one should therefore have ground saffron ahead of time and, having failed to do so, would require a *shinuy* on *Yom Tov*. Under the anticipation rationale, the question would simply be whether one knew one would need it. These differences matter significantly for practical *halacha*, because which rationale we adopt will determine which spices require a *shinuy* and which can always be ground normally.

### Shmuel's Position

Before the *Gemara* settles this question, Rav Yehuda cites a sweeping ruling in the name of Shmuel: *kol hanidochin nidochin kedarkon va'afilu melach* — all spices may be ground in the normal manner on *Yom Tov*, and this includes even salt. The *Gemara* challenges this immediately: but the *Mishnah* itself states that salt requires a *shinuy*! Shmuel, the *Gemara* explains, holds in accordance with a particular *tanna*: Rabbi Meir, in a *braita*, states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not dispute the principle that all spices — salt included — may be ground normally when they are ground together as part of a single session. The phrase *u'melach imahen* — "and salt with them" — does not necessarily mean grinding them simultaneously in the same vessel; it means that when one sits down to grind the spices needed for the meal and salt is among them, the salt is carried along with the general permission and requires no special modification.

The dispute, Rabbi Meir clarifies, concerns only the case where one sits down exclusively to grind salt — *al hadocha bifnei atzma*. In that specific case, Beit Shammai requires a pottery vessel and the back of a spoon, and limits the quantity to that needed for roasting (*litzli*) rather than for salting meat in a pot (*l'kdeira*). Beit Hillel, in the *braita*, extends the permission broadly — *bechol davar* — for any purpose and in any amount. The *Gemara* notes that the literal reading, "with any thing," would be puzzling — could one use a *muktzah* object? — and therefore emends it to *l'chol davar*, meaning for any culinary purpose.

The upshot of Shmuel's position is therefore a significant simplification: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel debate only the standalone grinding of salt, and Beit Hillel permits even that without restriction. The multi-tiered distinctions that emerged from the earlier explanations of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda — spices that one anticipated needing, spices that do not lose pungency, and so forth — would under Shmuel's view be irrelevant, since the *Mishnah*'s basic rule is simply that normal spices need no *shinuy* and even salt is at most a minor issue.

### Practical Method

Rav Acha Bardala gave his son a practical instruction: *ki daichat atzli atzluyei* — when you grind salt on *Yom Tov*, lean the vessel at an angle. This minimal modification — tilting the mortar rather than using it perfectly upright — constitutes a sufficient *shinuy*. There is no need to switch vessels or use an entirely different implement; the slight change in orientation satisfies the concern.

### Rav Sheshet Test

The *Gemara* relates that on *Yom Tov*, Rav Sheshet heard the sound of a mortar and pestle and declared: *hai lav migabai d'veitai hu* — that sound is certainly not coming from my house. He had established in his household that no grinding is permitted on *Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* challenges: perhaps it was coming from his house, and they were grinding salt at an angle as Rav Acha Bardala had instructed, which is permitted? No — *deshomei dehavei tzalil kalei* — the sound was too pure, too clear, the resonance of a pestle striking straight down, not angled. Perhaps it was other spices, which require no restriction at all? No — *tavlin ivuchei minavach kalei* — spices produce a different quality of sound when pounded, something more like a popping or cracking, whereas salt produces a crushing sound. Rav Sheshet, from the acoustics alone, could identify that it was salt being ground in the ordinary, perpendicular manner, and he knew his household would never do so.

The narrative illustrates the direction the *Gemara* has been moving: following the thrust of Shmuel's position, normal spices present no issue whatsoever, consistent with the *Mishnah*. For salt, the maximum requirement is the modest *shinuy* of tilting the vessel — otherwise even the choice of vessel can remain unchanged.

### Tosafot Rules

Tosafot addresses the practical question of how we rule. The two explanations of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda — anticipation versus pungency — each generate their own leniencies and stringencies. Under the first rationale (*lishna kama*), spices one could not have anticipated require no *shinuy*, while those one could have anticipated do. Under the second rationale (*lishna batra*), spices that lose their pungency may be ground normally, while those that do not — because there would have been no downside to grinding them beforehand — require a *shinuy*.

The Ri rules stringently on both counts: *she'yesh le'esor bechol inyan* — one must be strict in every case. One might think that since these are rabbinic matters, one should follow the lenient position. But the Ri argues that since each opinion has its own leniencies and stringencies, there is no single lenient position to follow. Adopting leniency across the board would mean rejecting both opinions entirely. Since one cannot simply discard all the *poskim*, one must be *machmir* in both directions. He invokes a parallel from the laws of the *Seder*, where the *Gemara* is uncertain whether to lean during the first or last two cups of wine, and concludes that since leniency would eliminate leaning altogether, one must lean for all four — the *Ra'ah* makes this explicit.

Tosafot then partially retreats. For garlic — *shum* — he permits grinding on *Yom Tov* without a *shinuy*, because garlic loses its pungency dramatically and would certainly fall under the lenient category even according to the stringent position.

But then Tosafot draws a further conclusion that governs the practical *halacha*: *de'ha kaima lan ke'Shmuel* — in the end, we rule like Shmuel, that all spices may be ground normally — *kol hanidochin nidochin kedarkon* — and the only possible residual restriction is for salt alone, which requires a minor *shinuy* of tilting the vessel. The Rif rules this way, as does Rav Yehuda Hai Gaon, and Tosafot confirms that this is the established practice: *vechen yesh minhag halacha l'ma'aseh d'hach milta taluy b'ashlei ravrevei* — this is the custom in practice and it rests on major authorities.

### Halacha L'Maaseh

At this point one might conclude that freshly ground pepper on *Yom Tov* is entirely unproblematic. Tosafot introduces a caveat: *assur l'itchon pilpilin b'reichayim shelahem* — it is forbidden to grind pepper in *their* grinder, the kind referred to as a *molinta* — because this constitutes *uvda d'chol*. However, *aval b'madoch shel even mutar l'duchan b'lo shinuy* — grinding in a normal stone mortar and pestle is fully permitted without any *shinuy*. The *melacha* itself — *tochen* — is not the concern, since it is permitted on *Yom Tov* for food preparation. The concern is the specific type of vessel.

This distinction is important and requires clarification. One contemporary approach, reflected throughout *Shemiras Shabbos Kehilchasa*, effectively translates *uvda d'chol* as "modern labor-saving appliances," so that virtually any kitchen device is categorically prohibited. Rav Moshe completely rejects this definition. His position is that what makes something *uvda d'chol* is not that it saves labor, but that it evokes the kind of processing that takes place not in the home kitchen but at a larger, pre-kitchen, industrial stage. The *systra* that Rashi cited earlier — the large sieve — is forbidden precisely because it is the type of vessel used in large-scale grain processing, not household cooking. A home mortar and pestle, by contrast, is the domestic instrument for preparing spices in the kitchen, and its use is entirely consonant with the spirit of *Yom Tov* food preparation.

Notably, using a mortar and pestle requires considerably more effort than a hand grinder. The concern with *uvda d'chol* is therefore not about how much work is involved. If anything, it runs in the opposite direction from a "labor-saving devices" definition. The question is whether the vessel belongs to the world of domestic food preparation or to the world of commercial, large-scale processing. A small home pepper grinder — the handheld kind one finds on dining tables — would therefore seem to be fully permitted, as it is the household analog to the mortar and pestle, not an industrial device. The practical conclusion is that grinding spices on *Yom Tov* is permitted, and one may use a home grinder. The sole residual question is salt, for which a slight *shinuy* — tilting the vessel — is the standard practice.

## Wheat Dishes

### Tisni Prohibition

The *Gemara* cites a *Tanu Rabbanan*: *ein osin Tisni b'Yom Tov* — one may not prepare *Tisni* on *Yom Tov*. *Tisni* is a grain-based dish made from wheat kernels that are split into quarters — something resembling grits — and its preparation involves considerable effort. Even though *ochel nefesh* preparation is permitted on *Yom Tov*, the *Chachamim* sought to limit excessive *tircha*, and *Tisni*, with its laborious process, crosses that line.

### Grinding Wheat

The *Gemara* continues: *ve'ein kotzin b'machteshes* — and one may not use a grinder for the wheat. This might seem to imply a categorical prohibition on grinding wheat at all on *Yom Tov* — not merely a restriction on the specific dish. One might wonder: grinding spices involves *tochen* and is permitted on *Yom Tov*; why should grinding wheat be treated differently? The *Gemara* observes that the *braita* seems internally inconsistent, prohibiting both the dish and the grinding, as though they are independent concerns. The *Gemara* resolves: *hachi ka'amar* — the two clauses are not parallel prohibitions but rather explanatory. The reason one cannot make *Tisni* is because fundamentally one cannot grind with this *machteshes* on *Yom Tov* — the dish is unavailable because its prerequisite is unavailable.

Why cannot one use a wheat grinder? Presumably, as with the earlier discussions, large-scale wheat grinding evokes *uvda d'chol*. Wheat flour production is not home-based in the immediate kitchen sense; it belongs to the world of mills, not kitchens.

The *Gemara* then presses: if the rule is simply *ein kotzin b'machteshes*, why mention the specific dish at all? Because without the concrete example of *Tisni*, one might think the prohibition applies only to a large grinder — the *machteshes gedola* — while a small, home-based grinder would be permitted. By coupling the prohibition with the specific dish, the *braita* signals that even a small wheat grinder is covered, leaving no opening to permit *Tisni* production even with modest equipment.

### Small Grinders

A *braita*, however, contradicts this: *ein kotzin b'machteshes gedola* — one may not use a large grinder — *aval kotzin b'machteshes ktana* — but one may use a small wheat grinder. Rashi explains the small grinder's leniency: *de'havei ke'lochar yad de'eina ela l'tavlin* — a small grinder is ordinarily used for spices, so using it for wheat constitutes a *shinuy* of sorts. In any case, the large grinder is the *uvda d'chol* concern; the small one does not carry that association.

Abaye resolves the contradiction: *ki tanya matnisin machteshes gedola tanya* — when the *braita* prohibited *Tisni* and all grinding, it was speaking of a large grinder. The reconciled position is: do not make *Tisni* at all — even with a small grinder, because of the *tircha* involved — and do not use a large grinder for anything. But a small wheat grinder for other purposes is permitted.

Rava offers an alternative resolution: *lo kashya ha lan v'ha lehu* — this is not a contradiction but a geographic difference between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael. In Eretz Yisrael, where household servants were less scrupulous about *halacha*, if one permitted small grinders, people would claim to have used the small one while actually using the large one. Therefore the stringent position that prohibits even small grinders was established there. In Bavel, where such concerns were less acute, the small grinder is permitted.

### Oatmeal Story

A narrative illustrates the application of these rules. Rav Papi came to the house of Mar Shmuel on *Yom Tov*, and they served him freshly ground oatmeal. He refused to eat it. The *Gemara* probes: perhaps it was prepared with a small grinder, which is permitted even by the stricter view in Bavel? No — *de-chaza de-hava dayek tfei* — Rav Papi observed that the grain had been ground to a fineness achievable only with a large grinder. Perhaps it was prepared the day before? No — *de-chaza de-hava klif tzaharei* — the flakes were visibly bright and fresh, unmistakably ground that very day.

An alternative explanation is also offered: *shani bei Mar Shmuel de-ika pritzuta de-avdei* — the house of Mar Shmuel is exceptional because the servants there were known to be not scrupulous, making it analogous to the situation in Eretz Yisrael. In such a household, even a small grinder should not be permitted, because one cannot trust that the line between small and large will be observed. But the basic *halacha* for ordinary households in Bavel remains: a small grinder is permitted, a large one is not — and the underlying concern with the large grinder is, once again, *uvda d'chol*.

The conceptual organizing principle for this entire series of discussions deserves emphasis. The *Gemara* elsewhere, in a *Yerushalmi* cited by Tosafot, raises the principle of *lisha va'eilach* — that only *melachot* from kneading onwards are permitted on *Yom Tov*, meaning that threshing, grinding, sifting and winnowing are excluded. Yet the *Gemara* here clearly permits these activities in various forms. The most coherent resolution is not a categorical list of *melachot* but a distinction based on *locus*: acts that belong to the domestic, immediate food-preparation context of the home kitchen are permitted; those that evoke the pre-kitchen, field-or-mill stage of processing are not. This explains both the permission for spice grinding and the restrictions on wheat grinding, and it likewise explains the *uvda d'chol* concern — the prohibited vessel is prohibited precisely because it evokes that pre-domestic, large-scale world.

## Borer Rules

### Shammai Strict

The *Mishnah* turns to *borer* — sorting and selection — completing the sequence of *melachot* associated with grain: *dasha*, *tochen*, and now *borer*. The question is what *borer* looks like on *Yom Tov*, where food preparation is in principle permitted. Beit Shammai rules: *borer ochel ve-ochel* — one sorts food and eats it. The formulation mirrors the rules of *borer* on *Shabbat*: one performs *ochel mitoch psolet*, focusing on the food itself, and consumes it immediately. For Beit Shammai, it is unclear that *Yom Tov* confers any additional latitude beyond what *Shabbat* allows in this domain; the model remains *derech achila*, taking the food directly.

### Hillel Lenient

Beit Hillel is more permissive: *borer kederko* — one may sort in the normal manner. This apparently includes removing the *psolet* rather than the food — the inverse of the *Shabbat* rule. In terms of technique, one may do it *b'cheiko* — in one's lap — *b'kanon uvetamcho* — using a vessel or funnel. What remains prohibited, however, is *tavla*, *nafah*, and *kivara* — the large sieve, strainer, and colander. As has been the pattern throughout this *daf*, the prohibited implements are precisely those associated with large-scale, professionalized processing rather than home-based food preparation. Beit Hillel's ruling thus reflects the same underlying framework: *borer* itself presents no fundamental *halachic* problem on *Yom Tov*; the concerns are *tircha* and the use of *uvda d'chol* vessels.

### Minority Rule

A *braita* cites Rabban Gamliel's clarification: *bamei devarim amurim* — when does Beit Hillel's rule permitting removal of the *psolet* apply? When *ochel merubeh al hapsolet* — the food outnumbers the waste. In that case, removing the *psolet* — the minority — is the efficient method, and that is what Beit Hillel permits. But when *psolet merubeh al ha-ochel* — the waste exceeds the food — *divrei hakol notel et ha-ochel* — all agree that one removes the food. One might think this is because the mixture, being predominantly waste, is *muktzah* as a unit. But the *Gemara* rejects this: *lo tzricha* — the ruling is needed for a different case entirely.

The case is: *de-nafis betircha vezutar beshiva* — the *psolet* is numerically a minority, but the effort required to remove it is greater than the effort to remove the food. In this situation, one removes whichever is less effort, regardless of which is smaller in quantity. This is the key principle: *denafish betircha* — on *Yom Tov*, *borer* is fundamentally permitted, and the governing concern is not the definition of *borer* as it would be on *Shabbat*, but *tircha* — excessive effort. One must always choose the method that minimizes labor. This also means that on *Yom Tov*, cutting vegetables and dealing with seeds and scraps in the kitchen does not trigger the *borer* concerns that operate on *Shabbat*; what matters is simply doing it in a home-based, effort-minimizing manner without professionalized sifting equipment.

The distinction between *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* in this context is fundamental. On *Shabbat*, the question of *borer* is entirely about halachic definition — whether the act constitutes *ochel mitoch psolet* and *derech achila*. On *Yom Tov*, since the *melacha* is permitted for food purposes, the question is purely one of *tircha* and *uvda d'chol* vessels. These are the two recurrent concerns throughout the *daf*.

### Water Method

Rabban Gamliel adds his own method: *af madiach veshola* — one may even submerge the legumes in water and scoop from the surface, exploiting the difference in buoyancy between the food and the chaff. A *braita* relates that this was the actual practice in the house of Rabban Gamliel: they would bring buckets of lentils, pour water over them, and the chaff would separate. A second *braita* appears to contradict the first regarding which component rises and which sinks, but the *Gemara* resolves the apparent discrepancy: *ha b'afra ha b'gilei* — the two *baraitot* describe different types of impurity. Dirt and heavier debris sink; light chaff floats. The two statements simply describe different situations.

## Gift Sending

### Food Gifts

With the discussion of food-preparation *melachot* concluded, the *Mishnah* shifts to the laws of sending gifts on *Yom Tov*. Beit Shammai rules: *ein meshallchin b'Yom Tov ela manos* — one may send on *Yom Tov* only portions that are ready to eat. Something that requires further preparation — even preparation technically permitted on *Yom Tov* — may not be sent. The apparent concern is that sending a recipient something raw or unready, which they had not planned to cook, is either a *tircha* or *muktzah* problem for the recipient, or more broadly, it fails to constitute a genuine *Yom Tov* gift of ready-to-enjoy food.

Beit Hillel takes a substantially broader view: *meshallchin beheima chaya v'of* — one may send livestock, whether alive or slaughtered. *Meshallchin yeinos shmanim u'soltos* — one may send wine, oil, and flour, the last of which still requires kneading and baking. *U'kitniyos* — legumes are also permitted. The principle is that anything which could in theory be used on *Yom Tov* — even if it requires effort — may be sent. *Aval lo tevuah* — but unground grain may not be sent, since under normal circumstances there is no practical way to use whole grain on *Yom Tov*.

### Livestock Gifts

Beit Hillel's inclusion of livestock is expansive: since one can perform *shechita* on *Yom Tov* for the purpose of eating, a live animal is in principle usable on *Yom Tov* and may therefore be sent.

### Rabbi Shimon

Rabbi Shimon goes further and permits sending even unground grain: *Rabbi Shimon matir bitvuah*. Rashi explains this by reference to the discussion above — since one may use a small grinder on *Yom Tov* in certain circumstances, grain is at least theoretically usable, and Rabbi Shimon regards this theoretical usability as sufficient.

### Procession Rule

Even Beit Hillel's broad permission is limited by Rav Chiya's teaching: *u'vilvad shelo ya'asenu b'shurah* — one may not arrange the gifts in a procession, a *shurah*. Sending a long line of bearers carrying successive gifts is forbidden. Rashi explains that this resembles going to sell goods in the marketplace — *kemolichin lemakor hashuk* — and is therefore inappropriate on *Yom Tov*. The concern likely reflects the Roman culture of gift-giving and patronage, in which a formal procession of gift-bearers was a recognizable commercial or social spectacle.

A *shurah* requires a minimum of three people, as the *Gemara* specifies. Rav Ashi raises a further question: what if three people are each sent with a different type of gift — does the diversity of items break up what would otherwise constitute a *shurah*, since each bearer is carrying something distinct? *Teiku* — this remains unresolved.

## Non-Food Gifts

### General Rule

The *Mishnah* extends the discussion to non-consumable items: *meshallchin keilim* — vessels and clothing may be sent on *Yom Tov*, whether sewn or unsewn — this being according to Beit Hillel's broader framework — provided they can be used on *Yom Tov*.

### Shatnez Garments

Remarkably, the *Mishnah* includes: *ve'af al pi she'yesh bahen kilayim* — even garments containing *shatnez* may be sent. This seems counterintuitive — what possible use could one have for *shatnez* on *Yom Tov*, given that wearing it is forbidden? The *Mishnah* states: *ve'hein letzorech hamoed* — they must be for use on *Yom Tov*. An alternate textual reading has *she'ein letzorech hamoed* — even if they are not for *Yom Tov* — meaning that even if the practical intention is for after the holiday, the mere theoretical possibility of *Yom Tov* use suffices. The challenge, of course, is identifying what that theoretical use could be.

### Excluded Items

The *Mishnah* lists items that may not be sent: *aval lo sandal hamesumar* — a nailed sandal, which the Rabbis forbade wearing on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* entirely due to a historical incident. *Velo min'al she'eino tafur* — an unsewn shoe, which has no use whatsoever until the leather is properly sewn together, and therefore lacks even hypothetical *Yom Tov* utility. Rabbi Yehuda adds: *af lo min'al lavan* — even a white shoe, meaning an untanned or unblackened leather shoe, which requires a craftsman to finish and which no one would wear publicly as-is. Since it has no practical or even theoretical use in its current state, it may not be sent.

The operative principle is stated explicitly: *zeh haklal kol she'nehenin bo beyom tov meshallchin oto* — the rule is that anything one could theoretically benefit from on *Yom Tov* may be sent, even if that is not the primary intention in sending it.

### Shatnez Cushion

The *Gemara* traces through the logic for each permitted category. Sewn garments may clearly be worn — *chazu lemalbush*. Unsewn garments may be used as blankets or coverings — *chazu lechisuyei*. But *shatnez* — what possible use is there? Perhaps, the *Gemara* suggests, one could use it as a mat to sit upon — *chazu lemitmachtei* — without wearing it. But a *braita* is cited: *lo ya'aleh alecha* — the prohibition on *shatnez* extends beyond wearing; the *Rabbis* forbade even reclining on it, lest a strand come into contact with one's body — *shema tichroch nima al besaro*. 

What if one places a pillow between oneself and the *shatnez* mat, creating an interposition? Perhaps that should be sufficient to allay the concern about bodily contact.

### Jerusalem Stringency

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, citing Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul, citing Rebbi in the name of the holy community of Jerusalem — *kehila kadisha de-Yerushalayim* — rules: *afilu eser matzot zo al gav zo vekilayim tachtehem assur lishon aleihem* — even ten mats stacked one atop the other with the *shatnez* at the very bottom, like the princess and the pea, it is forbidden to sleep upon them. Once the Rabbis prohibited reclining on *shatnez*, the prohibition was absolute, regardless of how many intervening layers separated the person from the forbidden garment.

This leaves the *Gemara* — and us — in suspense: if one cannot wear *shatnez*, cannot sit on it, and cannot use it even as the bottommost layer under ten cushions, what theoretical use could there possibly be for *shatnez* on *Yom Tov* that would permit sending it as a gift? This question will be taken up on the following daf.

---

---

# Beitzah 15

## Shatnez & Nolad

### Overview & Intro

Today's daf is 15. We will conclude the first *perek* and begin the second *perek*, starting at the very bottom of 14b. The *mishna* states that one may send all various types of items on *Yom Tov* according to *Beis Hillel*, provided the item has at least some theoretical use on *Yom Tov*. One of the items listed is *kilayim shatnez* — a mixture of linen and wool. The *gemara* therefore seeks to determine what legitimate use can be made of *shatnez* on *Yom Tov*.

### Shatnez as Curtain

One cannot claim it may be used for sitting, because although that is technically permitted on a biblical level, the Rabbis prohibited sitting on *shatnez* even when it is beneath ten cushions, out of concern that a thread might come to rest directly against one's skin in a manner that would constitute wearing. The *gemara* therefore concludes — with the word *ella* at the very last line of 14b — *ella b'vilo*: we are discussing using the *shatnez* as a curtain, a *vilon*. Since it functions as a hanging curtain rather than a garment worn against the skin, there is no prohibition.

At this point the *gemara* cites a teaching of Ulla: *mipnei mah amru vilon tamei* — why did the Rabbis rule that a *vilon* is susceptible to *tumah*? Why is a curtain not considered a structural part of the house, exempt from the laws of *tumah* applicable to vessels? Ulla answers: *mipnei she'hashamash mischamem kenegdo* — because an attendant will warm himself by the curtain, wrapping himself in it, thereby qualifying it as a vessel with a functional use. If this is so, however, the same concern ought to apply to *shatnez*: one might come to wrap oneself in the curtain for warmth, which would constitute wearing. The *gemara* therefore recognizes a difficulty.

### Hard Shatnez

The *gemara* resolves this on 15a by saying *ella b'kashan* — we must be speaking of a very stiff, hard type of cloth, one with no loose threads, which produces no warmth and therefore raises no concern, even rabbinically, that one will come to wear it. The rabbinic restriction on sitting on *shatnez* would similarly not apply: the cloth is hard and stiff, sitting on it is in any case biblically permitted, and since a loose thread cannot migrate onto one's body and produce warmth, the concern is absent.

This principle — that warmth is a defining characteristic of wearing — is articulated by Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua: *hai namta gamda d'Narash sharei* — that hard garment from the town of Narash is permitted. According to Rashi, this means it is permitted not to wear, but to sit on: it is *shatnez*, but because it is hard and one is sitting on it rather than wearing it, it is permitted.

Rav Pappa then adds: *ardelin ein bahem mishum kilayim* — the *ardelin*, which Rashi explains on the basis of Geonic literature as a type of material placed at the heel of the foot, perhaps an insole or a heel-pad, does not constitute *kilayim*. Though it is part of one's footwear, it sits beneath the foot rather than on the body, and being hard, it raises no concern of warmth.

Rava adds a further case: *hanei tzrari d'pshiti* — those small coin-pouches made of *shatnez* fabric that one keeps pressed against the chest contain no *kilayim* violation, because although the pouch rests against the body, it provides no warmth and therefore does not meet the definition of wearing.

One might ask whether this warmth-based leniency extends to something genuinely worn, such as a belt. Rashi is clear, and *Tosafot* discusses this at length: the relevance of warmth as a limiting criterion applies only within the rabbinic domain, in cases where the item is not functioning as ordinary clothing. Where something is genuinely being worn — worn in the full biblical sense — the question of warmth does not operate as a leniency. If something is real clothing, it is prohibited regardless.

The *gemara* adds a nuance with respect to the coin-pouches: if one keeps coins in the pouch, it remains stiff and provides no warmth — *ein bahem mishum kilayim*. But if one keeps seeds (*bazreini*) in it, the pouch becomes malleable and effectively supple against the body — *yesh bahem mishum kilayim*, this is a problem. Rav Ashi, however, rules that in either case there is no violation, reasoning that since this is not the normal manner of warming oneself, even if it happens to provide warmth, it does not constitute *derech chimum* and therefore does not meet the legal definition of wearing. The centrality of this concept of purposive warmth as the defining criterion of *levisha* is thus the thread running through this entire sugya.

### Nails & Unsewn

The *mishna* then states: *aval lo sandal hamesumar* — but one may not send a nailed sandal as a gift on *Yom Tov*. This is followed by additional cases: one may also not send a shoe that is not yet sewn (*min'al she'eino tafur*), and Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may not send an unsewn white leather shoe.

### Sandal Story

The *gemara* asks: *sandal hamesumar mai ta'ama lo* — why not send a nailed sandal? The answer is *mishum ma'aseh shehayah* — because of the famous incident. This refers to an episode discussed in Masechet Shabbat: Jews hiding from the Romans in a cave heard a noise, feared it was the enemy, and in their panic rushed out of the cave. In the resulting crush, people were trampled to death, and the nailed sandals — whose nails apparently protruded from the sole like metal cleats — contributed to the carnage. The Rabbis thereafter decreed that one may never wear a *sandal hamesumar*.

One might ask: why does this prohibition apply specifically on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*? The *gemara* implies that the incident occurred in that context, but logically there is no reason to limit the prohibition to those days. One practical answer is that on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, when there is already a long list of restrictions, people are more likely to heed an additional prohibition. As Rav Moshe was once asked about recorded music during *Sefirah*: he responded that he believes recorded music is problematic throughout the year, but since nobody listens, at least one can enforce the restriction during *Sefirah* when people are already accustomed to restrictions.

### Abaye on Sandals

Abaye clarifies the precise contours of the *sandal hamesumar* prohibition: *sandal hamesumar assur lina'alo umutar letaltelo* — one may not wear it, but it is not *muktzeh* and may be moved. The proof that it is not *muktzeh* comes from the language of the *mishna* itself: *ein meshalchin* — one does not send it as a gift. If the sandal were truly *muktzeh*, the *mishna* would not need to specify that one cannot send it; the *muktzeh* prohibition would already cover that. The fact that sending it is singled out as the prohibition implies that moving it is otherwise permitted — that it has some use, just not wearing.

If so, one might ask: since it does have some use — one might scratch one's back with it or find another incidental purpose — why can it not be sent as a gift on *Yom Tov*, just as *shatnez* can be sent because it has some use? The answer, which will become clearer presently, is that the concern here is not merely one of usability but of appearance: if one sends a nailed sandal as a gift, the recipient will assume the sender intended it to be worn, and will come to wear it. It is this specific concern that led the Rabbis to prohibit sending it.

### Unsewn Shoes

The *mishna* also addresses *min'al she'eino tafur* — a shoe whose leather has not yet been sewn to the sole. The *gemara* notes: *pshita* — this is obvious, there is no use for it on *Yom Tov*. The *gemara* counters: *lo tzericha*, the ruling is necessary even in a case where the shoe is held together by small pegs (*pasiche*), so that it is nominally attached but not fully sewn. One might have thought that since it can temporarily be worn in that state, it is permissible to send — the *mishna* teaches it is not.

Rabbi Yehuda adds: *af lo min'al lavan* — not even a white shoe may be sent. *Tanya*: a *baraisa* records that Rabbi Yehuda permits a shoe once the leather has been blackened (*bashachor matir*) but forbids it while it remains white (*ossur belavan*), because it still requires the blackening compound to be worked into it. Rabbi Yosi goes further: even a blackened shoe is forbidden because it still requires polishing — *mipnei shetzarich letzachtzacho* — it is not yet complete.

### Shoe Regions

The *gemara* resolves the apparent dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi by observing that each ruled in accordance with local practice in his region: *mar ki atreih u-mar ki atreih*. In one sage's locale, the leather was placed flesh-side down against the foot — that is, the inner surface of the hide, which was softer, faced the wearer. In such a case the outer surface, which had more cracks and crevices, was on the outside and required more preparation before it was presentable. In the other sage's locale, the flesh side faced outward, and therefore it was that surface which was rough and required shining. Each sage's ruling thus reflects the particular construction methods and finishing standards of his region, and there is no actual disagreement in principle.

### Principle: Usage

The *mishna* concludes with a general rule: *zeh ha-klal kol she-na'asim bo b'Yom Tov meshalechin oto* — the principle is that anything that can be used on *Yom Tov* may be sent as a gift.

---

## Tefillin & Yom Tov

### Rav Sheshet

The *gemara* states: *Rav Sheshet shara lehu l'rabanan l'shidurei tfillin b'yoma tava* — Rav Sheshet permitted the rabbinic students to send *tefillin* as gifts on *Yom Tov*. This is immediately striking, because the obvious question is: what use can one make of *tefillin* on *Yom Tov*? *Tefillin* are not worn on *Yom Tov* — *Yom Tov* is itself referred to as an *os*, a sign, as is *Shabbat*, and where the sign of *Yom Tov* or *Shabbat* is present, the sign of *tefillin* is not required.

The *gemara* therefore reinterprets the *mishna*'s principle. The language of the *mishna* is: *zeh ha-klal kol she-na'asim bo b'Yom Tov meshalechin oto*. The word *b'Yom Tov* may modify either the use (*she-na'asim*) — anything usable on *Yom Tov* itself may be sent — or the sending (*meshalechin*) — anything usable at all may be sent on *Yom Tov*. Rav Yosef reads it the latter way: *kol she-na'asim bo b'chol meshalechin oto b'Yom Tov* — anything that one can use on a weekday may be sent on *Yom Tov* as a gift, even if it cannot be used on *Yom Tov* itself. This is an admittedly broad reading, but it resolves the *tefillin* question.

### Rashi/Tosafot

This solution, however, raises the problem of the *sandal hamesumar*: by the same logic, one could use a nailed sandal on a weekday, so why not send it on *Yom Tov*? Rashi and *Tosafot* address this directly, though interestingly the *gemara* itself does not. Their answer is that the concern with the *sandal hamesumar* is not merely about usability but about the risk that the recipient will assume the item is permitted for wearing and will come to wear it on *Yom Tov*. With *tefillin*, this concern does not apply: everyone knows that *tefillin* are not worn on *Yom Tov*, so no one will be misled.

Rashi and *Tosafot* also make a fascinating comparative observation. Even if someone were to err and put on *tefillin* on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov* — when it is *lav zman tefillin*, not the time for *tefillin* — the violation involved is arguably less severe than transgressing the rabbinic prohibition of wearing a *sandal hamesumar*. Wearing *tefillin* when it is not their time is a matter of debate but does not clearly constitute a violation of a specific prohibition. By contrast, wearing a *sandal hamesumar* violates an explicit rabbinic enactment rooted in a tragic historical incident.

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye challenges Rav Sheshet's ruling directly: *v'anan tnan kol she-na'asim bo b'Yom Tov meshalechin oto* — the *mishna* says anything usable on *Yom Tov* may be sent. Since *tefillin* cannot be used on *Yom Tov*, how can one send them? The *gemara* responds with the reinterpretation described above — that *b'Yom Tov* modifies the sending rather than the use.

### Road Scenario

Abaye, perhaps dissatisfied with that exchange, pivots: *tfillin ho'il v'atu l'idan neima behu milta* — since we have arrived at the topic of *tefillin*, let us say something further about them. The *gemara* presents the case of one who was traveling on the road wearing *tefillin* and the sun set — either nightfall on a weekday, when one should not wear *tefillin*, or, as Rashi explains, Friday afternoon when *Shabbat* arrives and *tefillin* must not be worn on *Shabbat*. The ruling is: *mani'ach yado aleihem ad shemagi'a l'veito* — one places one's hand over the *tefillin* and walks home without removing them. On a weekday, removing them risks dropping them; on *Shabbat*, removing them would constitute carrying. Covering them prevents the misleading appearance of wearing *tefillin* at night or on *Shabbat*, and one waits until reaching home.

### Study Hall

The *gemara* then presents a parallel case: one was sitting in the *beis medrash* with *tefillin* on one's head — and *ukiddesh alav hayom* — *Shabbat* commenced. Note the distinction in formulation: *shak'ah alav chamah* (the sun set) in the road case, versus *ukiddesh alav hayom* (the day became sanctified) here, indicating that the second scenario explicitly involves *Shabbat*. Now one faces a compound problem: wearing *tefillin* at night, the prohibition on *Shabbat* itself, and the issue of carrying them home — for the *beis medrash* is out in the fields, unguarded and unlocked, and leaving *tefillin* there unprotected is unacceptable. The ruling is again: *mani'ach yado aleihem ad shemagi'a l'veito* — cover them and walk home.

One might wonder: does wearing something on one's body on *Shabbat* not constitute carrying? The answer is that carrying in the manner of wearing (*derech levisha*) is treated differently from ordinary carrying. However, for *tefillin* — which are not normally worn on *Shabbat* or at night — this is not genuinely *derech levisha*, and at minimum it places the act in the rabbinic domain. The Rabbis permitted this rabbinic form of carrying in order to bring the *tefillin* to safety, even though under ordinary circumstances one would not be permitted to do so.

### Three Cases

The *gemara* now introduces a challenge from a *baraisa* that presents the same scenarios but with different rulings. In the road case: *mani'ach yado aleihem ad shemagi'a l'vais hasamuch lechomah* — one covers the *tefillin* and may bring them only to the first house near the city wall, not all the way home. In the *beis medrash* case: *mani'ach yado aleihem ad shemagi'a l'vais hasamuch l'veis hamedrash* — one may bring them only to the nearest private house that will safeguard them.

The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya — ha demintara, ha delo mintara* — there is no difficulty. If the *tefillin* will be adequately protected in the first available house, one must leave them there. If they will not be protected even in the first house, one is permitted to carry them all the way home.

The *gemara* then presses further: if the concern is that they are entirely unprotected, why limit the leniency to cases where one is already wearing the *tefillin*? Even if they were lying on the ground, one should be permitted to put them on and carry them home by wearing them. And indeed, from the *mishna* in Masechet Shabbat: *hamotzei tefillin — machenesam zug zug* — one who finds *tefillin* may bring them in one pair at a time, putting them on and wearing them as the means of carrying them into the city. So why does the *baraisa* only permit this when one was already wearing the *tefillin*?

### Jewish Robbers

The *gemara* resolves this by distinguishing three distinct cases. The first: the *tefillin* are exposed to all manner of danger — dogs, theft, any threat. In this case, even if the *tefillin* were lying on the ground, one may pick them up, put them on, and wear them all the way home. The second: *demintara mechamas kalbei v'lo demintara mechamas ganvei* — the *tefillin* are protected from dogs (they are inside the *beis medrash*) but not from thieves, since the building is unlocked. Here is where the *gemara* makes its striking observation: *mahu deseima rov listim Yisrael ninhu v'lo mezalzelu behu* — one might have thought that since most thieves in the area are Jewish, and a Jewish thief would not treat *tefillin* disrespectfully, perhaps there is no real danger to the sanctity of the *tefillin* even if they are stolen. Therefore, one might think, there is no grounds to permit putting on the *tefillin* on *Shabbat* to bring them home. The *gemara* rules — *ka mashma lan* — that this reasoning is rejected, and the leniency does apply: since thieves might still steal them, even if they would not mistreat them, the leniency of wearing them home is granted. However, this applies only if one is already wearing them; if the *tefillin* are merely lying there, one may not pick them up and put them on in this intermediate scenario. The third case: the *tefillin* are safe from all significant danger — in that situation, the latitude given is minimal, and one may bring them only to the first available house, not all the way home.

Thus there are three graduated scenarios: fully unprotected, permitting one to put on the *tefillin* and carry them home; partially unprotected from thieves who would respect them, permitting continuation of wearing but not initiating it; and sufficiently safe, in which case only minimal transport to the nearest house is allowed.

With that, *hadran alach pirka* — we conclude the first *perek*.

---

## Eruv Tavshilin

### Prohibition/Permission

The second *perek* opens with the case of *Yom Tov she'chal l'hiyos erev Shabbos* — a one-day *Yom Tov* that falls on Friday (as in *Eretz Yisrael*). The *mishna* states: *lo yevashel betchila miyom tov l'Shabbos* — one may not, at the outset, cook on *Yom Tov* simply in order to prepare for *Shabbat*. However: *aval mevashel hu l'Yom Tov v'im hosir hosir l'Shabbos* — one may cook for *Yom Tov*, and whatever is left over from the *Yom Tov* meal may be used for *Shabbat*.

One might initially think this creates a wink-and-nod solution: cook abundantly for *Yom Tov* and enjoy the leftovers on *Shabbat*. The *gemara*, however, will make clear that this cannot be done *derech haarama* — as a contrived strategy. Only if one genuinely cooked for *Yom Tov* may one benefit from the leftovers; one cannot pretend to require a large quantity in order to manufacture surplus for *Shabbat*.

### Eruv Remedy
