The proper mechanism for cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat* is the *eruv tavshilin*. The *mishna* states: *v'oseh tavshil me'erev Yom Tov v'somech alav l'Shabbos* — one prepares a cooked dish on *erev Yom Tov* and relies upon it for *Shabbat*, thereby permitting one to continue cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat's* sake. The rationale is that by cooking something on *erev Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*, one has already begun the *Shabbat* preparations before *Yom Tov* began. The cooking on *Yom Tov* is thus a continuation of what was initiated on Thursday, and not a fresh act of cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat* from scratch — *betchila*.

### Shammai/Hillel

How much must one cook for the *eruv tavshilin*? *Beis Shammai* says *sheni tavshilin* — two separate cooked dishes. *Beis Hillel* says *tavshil echad* — one cooked dish suffices. Despite this dispute, they agree that if one has a fish and the egg used to prepare it, *she'hein sheni tavshilin* — this counts as two dishes for *Beis Shammai*, who is thus somewhat flexible in how the second item may be constituted.

### Loss of Eruv

If the *eruv tavshilin* was eaten or lost — *achlo o she'avad* — then even though it was properly prepared on *erev Yom Tov*, one may not continue cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*, because the *eruv* no longer exists. However: *v'im shayar mimeno kol shehu somech alav l'Shabbos* — if even a minimal amount of the *eruv* remains, one may continue cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*.

### Zachor Verse

The *gemara* asks: *mena hanei milei* — what is the source for this institution? Shmuel cites the verse: *Zachor et yom haShabbos l'kadsho* — Remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it. The *gemara* derives from this: *zochreihu me'acher sheba l'hashkicho* — remember it because something is coming that will cause you to forget it. The whole institution of *eruv tavshilin* is rooted in the fear that *Shabbat* will be forgotten.

### Rashi View

What does it mean that one will forget *Shabbat*? Rashi explains: one becomes so absorbed in the festivity of *Yom Tov* — in the permitted cooking, in the *simchas Yom Tov* — that one simply neglects to prepare adequately for *Shabbat*. The *eruv tavshilin* prepared on *erev Yom Tov* serves as a reminder: when *Yom Tov* arrives and one sees what was set aside, one remembers that *Shabbat* is still coming and that preparations must be made. It is, on this reading, essentially a mnemonic device, a string around one's finger.

### Ran View

The Ran offers a different explanation. The forgetting is not psychological but legal: because of the prohibition on cooking from *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*, one will come to have nothing prepared for *Shabbat* — not because one forgot it exists, but because one was legally constrained from preparing for it. The *eruv tavshilin* therefore serves not merely as a reminder but as the mechanism that unlocks the legal permission to cook for *Shabbat*. On this reading, cooking from *Yom Tov* to *Shabbat* is fundamentally prohibited, and the *eruv tavshilin* is the Rabbinic remedy — the tool that converts the otherwise forbidden act into a permitted continuation of prior preparations.

The Ran presses his own position further: if the purpose of requiring an *eruv tavshilin* is to ensure one prepares for *Shabbat*, one might expect that forgetting to make the *eruv* would be remedied leniently, since after all the entire institution is meant to help. But in fact the opposite is true: if one forgot to make an *eruv tavshilin*, one cannot cook for *Shabbat* at all. This, the Ran explains, is intentional — the penalty for negligence on this *Yom Tov* is that one is unable to prepare for *Shabbat*, so that one will be more careful on the next *Yom Tov*.

### Rava Logic

How does the *eruv tavshilin* actually function as a legal mechanism? The *gemara* records the explanation of Rava: *kedei sheyivru maneh yafeh l'Shabbos u'maneh yafeh l'Yom Tov* — so that one will designate a fine dish for *Shabbat* and a fine dish for *Yom Tov*. The act of setting aside a dish on *erev Yom Tov* for *Shabbat* trains one to think, when *Yom Tov* arrives, that *Shabbat* still requires its own fine preparation. This is the functional analog of Rashi's explanation: the *eruv* is a reminder mechanism, and the consequence of not making it is the penalty of being unable to cook for *Shabbat* on *Yom Tov*, which provides the incentive to remember in the future.

One might ask: but what is the actual legal logic? The reminder reminds one to cook — but what permits the cooking? The Ran articulates the difficulty precisely: on Rava's reading, the entire point is to ensure that one has food for *Shabbat*. If one forgot to make an *eruv tavshilin*, the punishment is to have no food for *Shabbat* — which makes the situation worse, not better. The Ran's resolution, already noted above, is that this outcome is intentional: the short-term penalty produces long-term compliance. But this does mean, on Rava's reading, that fundamentally the cooking from *Yom Tov* to *Shabbat* is permitted, and the *eruv* requirement is a rabbinic imposition designed to ensure appropriate mindfulness — not a gateway through which an otherwise forbidden act becomes permitted.

### Rav Ashi Logic

Rav Ashi offers a substantially different and more internally coherent explanation: *kedei she'yomru ein ofin miYom Tov l'Shabbos kal v'chomer miYom Tov l'chol* — the purpose is so that people will say: one may not bake on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat*, and certainly not from *Yom Tov* for a weekday. Without this requirement, people would come to assume that *Yom Tov* is of sufficiently lower sanctity that one may freely cook on it for the next day, including even for a weekday. To underscore the sacred character of *Yom Tov* and prevent this erosion, cooking from *Yom Tov* to *Shabbat* is only permitted when structured as a continuation of what was begun before *Yom Tov*.

On Rav Ashi's reading, then, there is a fundamental legal problem with cooking on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat* — or even more so for a weekday — and the *eruv tavshilin* is the mechanism by which what would otherwise be an independent, prohibited act is reframed as a legitimate continuation. This reading is characterized as *l'k'vod Yom Tov* — the whole institution is designed to honor the sanctity of *Yom Tov* — whereas Rava's reading is *l'k'vod Shabbos* — it is designed to ensure proper honor for *Shabbat*.

The question of *hachanah d'Rabbah* is relevant here: Rabbah elsewhere derived from the verse *et asher tofu efu* that there is a *d'oraisa* prohibition of preparing on *Yom Tov* for the next day. *Tosafot*, in a discussion on 2b, asks how a rabbinic institution like *eruv tavshilin* can uproot a biblical prohibition of *hachanah*. *Tosafot* addresses this, suggesting that the biblical *hachanah* concern applies to things that are complete in themselves and only lack preparation — and that there are other resolutions as well, including Rava's principle of *ho'il u'miklei orchin*. The question is acknowledged as a penetrating one, and it is satisfying to see that *Tosafot* explicitly raises it.

### Why Erev?

The *gemara* now asks: the *mishna* states that the *eruv tavshilin* must be made on *erev Yom Tov*. On Rav Ashi's reading this is self-evident — the entire point is that one must begin the cooking before *Yom Tov* commences, so that the *Yom Tov* cooking is a continuation rather than an independent act. But on Rava's reading — where the *eruv* is simply a reminder — why must it specifically be made on *erev Yom Tov*? One could make such a reminder even on *Yom Tov* itself. The *gemara* responds: *in hachi nami* — in principle that would suffice, since making the *eruv* at any point reminds one to prepare for *Shabbat*. However, *gezeirah shema yifsha* — we decree otherwise out of concern for negligence. If one is permitted to wait until *Yom Tov* begins, one will be caught up in *Yom Tov* and forget to make it at all. Therefore the Rabbis required it to be made before *Yom Tov*, so that it becomes part of one's pre-*Yom Tov* checklist.

### Bake/Cook Verse

The *gemara* then cites a *baraisa* that grounds the *eruv tavshilin* in a different verse: *et asher tofu efu v'et asher tevashelu bashelu* — bake what you are going to bake and cook what you are going to cook. Rabbi Eliezer derives from this: *ein ofin ela al ha'afui v'ein mevashelin ela al hamevushal* — one may only continue baking on something that has already been baked, and only continue cooking on something already cooked. This is the direct textual support, serving as an *asmachta*, for the principle that one may cook on *Yom Tov* for *Shabbat* only by extending what one began previously — and this verse's dual mention of baking and cooking separately will later give rise to the requirement for an *eruv* containing both a baked item (*matzah*) and a cooked one (typically an egg).

---

## Rabbi Eliezer Story

### Six Groups

The *gemara* has just mentioned Rabbi Eliezer in connection with the *eruv tavshilin*, and now introduces a narrative about him. *Maaseh b'Rabbi Eliezer shehaya yoshev v'doresh kol hayom kulo* — there is a story that Rabbi Eliezer was teaching *halachos* of *Yom Tov* on *Yom Tov* itself, and the *shiur* went on for the entire day. As groups of students successively rose and departed, Rabbi Eliezer commented on each departure. When the first group left — *yatzta kas rishonah* — he said: *halalu baalei pitasos* — these are people with great barrels of wine; they are so abundantly supplied that they cannot wait. As the second group departed he called them *baalei chaviyos* — people with standard barrels. The third group departing earned the appellation *baalei kadim* — people with pitchers. The fourth, *baalei luginim* — people with smaller vessels. The fifth, *baalei kosos* — people who have cups of wine waiting.

### Criticism Escalates

When the sixth group began to leave — *hischilu kas shishis latzes* — Rabbi Eliezer said: *halalu baalei me'eira* — these are people of curse. Rashi explains this harsh judgment: by this point, virtually no one remained in the *beis medrash* from the general congregation, and Rabbi Eliezer feared he would be left with only his students. The *Aruch* offers an alternative reading: they are cursed because they have sacrificed the best of the *shiur* by staying so long without gaining its full benefit, and yet they are returning so late that they will not enjoy a proper meal either — they have lost in both directions.

### Reassurance

At this point, Rabbi Eliezer turned his gaze upon his students: *nosnu einov b'talmidim* — he fixed his eyes on them. Their faces began to change color — *hayesa p'neihem mishtannim* — for now only the students remained, and they feared his displeasure was directed at them. Rabbi Eliezer immediately reassured them: *banai, lo lachem ani omer* — my sons, what I said was not about you. *Ella l'hallalu sheyatzu* — it was about those who left. *Shemanichim chayei olam v'oskim b'chayei sha'ah* — they abandoned eternal life, the Torah, and busied themselves with the life of the moment, choosing food over the opportunity to learn on the *regel*.

### Permission to Eat

When the *shiur* finally concluded, Rabbi Eliezer said to his remaining students: *lechu ochlu mashmannim ush'su mamtakim v'shilchu manos l'ein nachon lo* — go, eat fine foods and drink sweet drinks, and send portions to one who has nothing prepared. *Ki kadosh hayom l'Adoneinu* — today is consecrated to our Lord. This verse is from the time of Ezra. *V'al te'atzeivu ki chedvas Hashem hi mauzchem* — do not be saddened, for the joy of God is your strength. Rabbi Eliezer reassured the students: do not be distressed that you have not yet eaten, for you have been sustained by the joy of Torah. Now the time has come to go home and enjoy the *Yom Tov* meal.

### All-or-Nothing

The *gemara* asks: *v'ha simchas Yom Tov mitzvah hi* — but *simchas Yom Tov* is a *mitzvah*! Why did Rabbi Eliezer give people a hard time for going home to eat? The *gemara* answers: *Rabbi Eliezer l'taimei* — Rabbi Eliezer acts consistently with his own position. *D'amar simchas Yom Tov reshus* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that the physical dimension of *simcha* on *Yom Tov* — eating and drinking — is optional, not obligatory. This is stated explicitly in a *baraisa*: *Rabbi Eliezer omer, ein lo l'adam b'Yom Tov ella, o ochel v'shoseh, o yoshev v'shoneh* — a person on *Yom Tov* must choose: either spend the entire day eating and drinking, or sit and learn. It is an all-or-nothing proposition. There are two forms of *simcha*, physical and spiritual, and Rabbi Eliezer demands full commitment to one or the other. His critique of the departing groups was therefore not that they left to fulfill a *mitzvah*, but that they attended the *shiur* and then abandoned it midway. If one intended to devote the day to food, one should have stayed home; if one came to learn, one should have remained until the end.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua

### Verse Reconciliation

Rabbi Yehoshua takes the more moderate and familiar position. The *gemara* records: Rabbi Yochanan observed that both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua derive their positions from a single verse — or rather, from a tension between two formulations.

### Two Interpretations

One verse states: *atzeres l'Hashem Elokecha* — it is a holy convocation for God. Another states: *atzeres tihyeh lachem* — it shall be for you. Is the day dedicated entirely to God, or entirely to you? Rabbi Eliezer resolves the tension by ruling: *o kulo l'Hashem o kulo lachem* — either all of it for God, spent entirely in Torah study, or all of it for you, spent entirely in eating and drinking. Rabbi Yehoshua resolves it with his characteristic principle of *chelkeihu*: divide it. *Chetzyo l'Hashem v'chetzyo lachem* — half of the day is devoted to God through Torah and prayer, and the other half to one's own physical enjoyment of *Yom Tov*. This is the normative halachic position.

It is worth noting a certain tension in Rabbi Eliezer's overall corpus: in a different context involving *Sukkos*, Rabbi Eliezer praised those who remain at home on the *regel* and celebrated *v'samachta atah u'veisecha* — you and your household — emphasizing the physical, domestic dimension of *simcha*. Here, by contrast, he emphasizes total dedication to Torah. The two positions are not easily harmonized, and the difficulty is worth noting.

---

## Divine Support

### No Eruv Gift

The *gemara* now returns to the verse cited in the story of Rabbi Eliezer: *v'shilchu manos l'ein nachon lo* — send portions to one who has nothing prepared. What does *l'ein nachon lo* mean? Rav Chisda interprets: *l'mi shelo hinniach eruv tavshilin* — it refers to someone who did not make an *eruv tavshilin* and therefore has nothing to cook for *Shabbat*. One who has properly prepared should send food to this person on *Yom Tov*.

---

## Divine Support (II)

### Compassion View

A second interpretation is recorded: *ika d'amri* — some say — *l'ein nachon lo* refers to someone who did not have an opportunity to make an *eruv tavshilin* because he was too busy in the time immediately before *Shabbat*. On this reading, one should have compassion (*rachmanus*) on such a person and send him food. However, someone who had ample opportunity to make an *eruv tavshilin* and simply neglected to do so — *poshea hu* — is considered negligent, and perhaps one need not send him anything at all. This is a striking position; the full implications regarding relying on a communal *eruv* established by the *rav* of the city will be addressed in subsequent discussion.

### God Pays Debts

The *gemara* concludes the daf with a teaching of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon: *amar lahem hakadosh baruch hu l'Yisrael, banai, lovu alai u'kadshu kedushas hayom* — God says to the Jewish people: my children, borrow against My account and sanctify the day; spend money on food and on the honor of *Yom Tov* even if you must go into debt. *Eminu bi* — trust in Me. *Va'ani poreia* — I will repay your debts. The message with which the daf concludes is one of trust in divine support: one who spends generously on *simchas Yom Tov* need not fear the financial burden, for God promises to stand behind those expenses.

---

## Rabbi Yehoshua (II)

### Eruv Connection

The discussion of *simchas Yom Tov* and the *eruv tavshilin* are thus bound together in a common concern: ensuring that both dimensions of *Yom Tov* — the spiritual and the physical — are honored properly, that *Shabbat* is not forgotten in the midst of celebration, and that no one is left without food on the holy day. We will continue with this material tomorrow.

---

---

# Beitzah 18

## Intro & Context Review

### Hillel vs. Shammai

Today's daf is 18, and we pick up from the very top, with two lines of context drawn from the bottom of 17b. The *mishnah* there records the dispute between Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai regarding what may be brought to the *mikvah* on *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*. Crucially, both schools agree on one point: *kelim* — vessels — may not be immersed. The dispute concerns only whether a person may immerse.

### Rava: Gezeira Carrying

The *gemara* opens with Rava's explanation of why vessel immersion is universally forbidden. The prohibition is a *gezeirah shema yitlenu be-yado ve-yavirenu arba amot bi-reshut ha-rabbim* — a rabbinic decree lest one take the vessel in hand and carry it four *amot* in the public domain. This is precisely the same language Rava employs to explain why one may not take a *lulav* to the public domain on *Shabbos*, and one might ask whether he formulated this reasoning independently for both cases or whether the *gemara* applied a statement made in one context to the other.

### Abaye Challenges

Abaye presses: what of someone who has a well in his *chatzer*? A private courtyard well is effectively a *mikvah*, and the surrounding courtyard walls — the very infrastructure that made *eruv chatzerot* necessary — would prevent any carrying into a public domain. Since people routinely drew their water from such wells, this was hardly an unusual configuration.

### Rava Responds

Rava answers: *gezeirah bor be-chatzeiro atu bor bi-reshut ha-rabbim* — even when the well is in one's courtyard, we decree against immersion lest it lead to cases where the only available well is in the public domain, which would entail carrying. The *gemara* then presses further: granted, this reasoning holds for *Shabbos*, where carrying is forbidden. But on *Yom Tov*, when carrying is generally permitted, why maintain the prohibition? The *gemara* answers: *gazru Yom Tov atu Shabbos* — the Rabbis extended the prohibition to *Yom Tov* as a protective measure against its violation on *Shabbos*.

### Merchatza'ot Tangent

This logic — extending a *Shabbos* prohibition to *Yom Tov* — is admittedly counterintuitive given how many leniencies are unique to *Yom Tov*, including *ochel nefesh* and activities that are entirely permitted precisely because the relevant *melachot* are not forbidden on *Yom Tov*. A notable parallel is the *gezeirat merchatza'ot*, the prohibition against bathing in heated water even when the water was heated before *Shabbos*, lest one come to heat water on *Shabbos* itself. There is no compelling reason this concern should apply on *Yom Tov*, yet it was nonetheless extended there. In fact, a number of *poskim* — including the present lecturer's own practice — hold that one may take a hot shower on *Yom Tov*, provided one takes care not to squeeze out one's hair and uses liquid rather than bar soap. However, soaking in a hot bath remains forbidden on account of the *gezeirat merchatza'ot*, even though the underlying concern is not truly operative on *Yom Tov*. Occasionally, then, a *gezeirah* that originated in the context of *Shabbos* is extended to *Yom Tov*, even where the core concern is inapplicable.

---

## Gezeira L'Gezeira

### Hashakah Water Q

The *gemara* now raises a pointed methodological objection. The prohibition as Rava has framed it involves considerable layering: we forbid immersing a vessel in one's courtyard because it might lead to carrying, and we further extend this to *Yom Tov* lest it lead to *Shabbos* violation. This amounts to *gezeirah l'gezeirah* — a safeguard built upon a safeguard. The *gemara* therefore challenges: if we are indeed comfortable making such layered decrees, why does the *mishnah* permit *hashakah* of water? *Hashakah* refers to lowering a vessel containing water into a *mikvah* so that the waters connect and are thereby purified, even though the vessel itself may not be immersed for its own purification. If we are so vigilant about *gezeirah l'gezeirah*, we ought to forbid *hashakah* as well, since it could too easily lead to the case of immersing the vessel itself.

### Lo Shchiach

The *gemara* responds with a question of its own: *ve-tisbra?* Does that concern really make sense? If one has perfectly good, pure water available, why would one bother with the involved process of *hashakah*? The only reason anyone performs *hashakah* is that they have no other water. And if they have no other water — *miz-dazar behu* — they will be careful. As Rashi explains, this is an application of the principle *milsa d'lo sh'chiach lo gazru rabbanan*: the Rabbis do not issue decrees against uncommon circumstances. The initial scenario requiring *hashakah* is itself rare. While *gezeirah l'gezeirah* typically addresses common circumstances where A might lead to B, the Rabbis decline to extend their protective decrees to cases where the very starting point is an unusual situation.

### Tosafot Water Q

Tosafot raises a sharper question. The *gemara* framed the concern as: why don't we worry that permitting *hashakah* of water will lead to immersing the *keli* itself? But there is a more straightforward concern: why not worry that permitting the bringing of water to the *mikvah* will lead to carrying the water? Setting aside entirely the question of the vessel, the act of transporting water to the *mikvah* itself could constitute a carrying violation if one exits the *chatzer*. Tosafot observes that one is far more pressed and urgent when needing to immerse a vessel — *shaholv* — and so the concern that haste might lead to a violation is more acute there. With water, where alternatives exist, the urgency is lower. While this explanation is not entirely airtight — particularly given that water must be carried in some vessel anyway — it reflects the *gemara*'s underlying assumption that the concern for violation tracks the urgency of the need.

### Drawing vs. Immersing

The *gemara* then introduces a new challenge: *madlin bi-dli tamei ve-hu tahor* — one may draw water using an impure bucket, and in the process the bucket becomes pure. This seems to be another case where we allow an act closely resembling vessel immersion without concern that it will lead to the prohibited act itself.

### Rashi Category

Rashi explains the critical distinction. When one draws water from a well using a bucket, the fundamental category of the act is *she'ivat mayim* — drawing water. One is not formally performing *tevilat keli*; the purification of the vessel is entirely incidental to the purpose of the act. Because the act falls formally outside the category of *tevilah*, it is not governed by the decree against vessel immersion.

### Why Not Vessels

The *gemara* presses further: granted that this is formally an act of drawing water rather than *tevilah*, why are we not concerned that it will lead to carrying the bucket — not because it formally resembles *tevilah*, but simply because someone is going to a well with a *keli*?

### Category Boundaries

The *gemara* answers: *shani hatam, mitoch she-lo hutar lo ela al yedei dalyo, dalyo zachur hu* — because one is only permitted to perform this act through the bucket, and the entire permission is framed as an act of drawing water, one will remember and not come to perform a full act of *tevilah*. The fundamental logic here, as the lecturer notes, is internally consistent: *gezeirah l'gezeirah* is not a claim that we genuinely believe A will always lead to B will always lead to C. Rather, it is a formalistic principle. When we forbid a category, we forbid everything within the formal definition of that category. What falls outside the formal definition — drawing water, *hashakah*, wearing clothes into the *mikvah* — is also formally outside the prohibition and does not require its own protective layer. This is not an evasion; it is precisely what makes *gezeirah l'gezeirah* coherent. We forbid a category broadly, but that breadth is delimited by the formal contours of the category itself.

### Mikvah as Well

A brief but illuminating digression: it is worth noting that in the ancient world, and well into the medieval period, the *mikvah* and the well were often one and the same structure. One dug down to the water table, and that subterranean water — not collected rainwater — constitutes *mayim chayim*. This explains how the stringent position of certain *Geonim*, that a *zavah* requires *mayim chayim* just as a *zav* does, could ever have been practically maintained. If the community's *mikvah* was already a natural spring or well, the requirement for *mayim chayim* imposed no additional burden. Thankfully, this position was rejected by the *rishonim*, without which contemporary *mikvaot* would be entirely unusable.

### Tamei Timing Q

The *gemara* now raises a challenge from a different direction. A ruling is cited: if a vessel became *tamei* before *Yom Tov* — on *erev Yom Tov* — one may not immerse it on *Yom Tov* itself, because one should have attended to it beforehand. But if it became *tamei* on *Yom Tov* itself, one may immerse it then. This introduces a fine distinction that sits awkwardly with the sweeping categorical approach Rava has been advocating. If we are categorically forbidding all vessel immersion as a broad decree, why do we carve out an exception for vessels that became *tamei* on *Yom Tov* itself?

### Tumah Lo Shchiach

The *gemara* answers: *tumah be-Yom Tov milsa d'lo sh'chicha* — it is uncommon for a vessel to become *tamei* on *Yom Tov* itself. Why? Because everyone endeavors to be in a state of *taharah* for the *regel*, for the *aliyah la-regel*, and therefore vessels becoming *tamei* on *Yom Tov* is a rare occurrence. Since it is a rare circumstance, the Rabbis did not apply their decree to it — in keeping with the principle that *milsa d'lo sh'chicha lo gazru rabbanan*.

### Tumah Levels

Yet another distinction is introduced: *keli she-nitma be-av ha-tumah ein matbilin oto be-Yom Tov, be-vlad ha-tumah matbilin oto be-Yom Tov* — a vessel that became *tamei* through a primary source of impurity (*av ha-tumah*, making the vessel a *rishon*) may not be immersed on *Yom Tov*, but a vessel that became *tamei* through a secondary source (*vlad ha-tumah*, making the vessel a *sheni*) may be immersed. Rashi clarifies that this latter leniency applies even if the vessel became *tamei* on *erev Yom Tov* — an additional layer of permission beyond the rule regarding vessels that became *tamei* on *Yom Tov* itself. The logic is that *sheni* status for a vessel is only rabbinically significant, and only relevant in the context of *terumah*, since vessels technically cannot become *sheniyim* from the Torah. It is not considered a true *tumah* in the full sense, and therefore it was not subsumed within the categorical decree.

### Kohanim Careful

The *gemara* asks why we do not extend the decree to this case as well, given that a *sheni* vessel can render *terumah* into a *shlishi* — which is a real consequence in the context of *kohanim* eating *terumah*. The *gemara* answers: *kohanim zerizin heim* — *kohanim* are careful. The very people who would be affected by this concern are those who are most scrupulous in their conduct, and so the Rabbis did not feel the need to impose a protective decree in that case.

The *gemara* then introduces the case of *niddah she-ein lah begadim* — a woman who is a *niddah* and has no *tahor* clothing to wear after immersion, only the *tamei* garments she has been wearing throughout. She may enter the *mikvah* while wearing her clothes, provided they are sufficiently loose-fitting not to constitute a *chatzitzah*. The *gemara* asks: if we are making so many layers of *gezeirah*, why do we not decree against this lest it lead to immersing garments independently of the body? The *gemara* answers: *shani hatam mitoch she-hutrah lah al yedei malbush zchurah hi* — because her permission is so specifically framed as immersing herself while clothed, the memory of that specific context will prevent any confusion with the forbidden act of immersing a garment on its own.

Tosafot raises a further difficulty: immersing clothing in water is itself an act of *shiriya*, and *amrinan shiriyato zu hi kibuso* — soaking is considered the beginning of laundering and would be forbidden on *Shabbos* as *mechabes u-melaben*. Tosafot answers that since the *mikvah* waters are not clean, and the woman's body is not clean, the soaking is *derech tinuf* rather than *derech libun*, and the act of immersing something in a manner that makes it dirty rather than clean does not constitute laundering. Tosafot extends this logic to the question of wiping hands on a towel on *Shabbos*, noting that even slight dampness might constitute *shiriya*, but the soiling quality of the act exempts it.

The *gemara*'s ultimate point here is clarified by the lecturer: the various answers to the challenge of *gezeirah l'gezeirah* fall into two broad categories. The first is the principle of *lo sh'chiach* — where the initial circumstances are sufficiently uncommon that the Rabbis simply did not extend their decrees there. The second is a formalistic argument — even within the framework of categorical *gezeirot*, what falls outside the formal definition of the category is not subject to the prohibition. These are not inconsistent answers; together they map the actual contours of how the Rabbis applied protective decrees.

---

## Alternative Reasons

### Rav Yosef Squeeze

With the foregoing analysis of Rava's first explanation complete, the *gemara* turns to alternative bases for the prohibition. Rav Yosef explains: *gezeirah mishum sechitah* — the decree is a protection against squeezing. If one immerses a vessel such as a garment in a *mikvah*, one may come to wring it out, which violates the prohibition of *sechitah* on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*.

### Abaye Non-Squeeze

Abaye challenges immediately: this reasoning is compelling for garments and similar *kelim* that are susceptible to squeezing, but what of vessels that cannot be wrung out — wooden bowls, metal utensils, and the like? Rav Yosef answers: *gezeirah hani atu hani* — we prohibit the latter category as a safeguard against the former. This, of course, introduces yet another layer of *gezeirah l'gezeirah*, and the *gemara* notes that once one invokes that principle, all the previously discussed challenges resurface. Rav Yosef would need to give the same answers we already provided to Rava's first explanation — whether based on *lo sh'chiach* or on formalistic category distinctions — and the *gemara* records that he does so.

### Rav Bibi Delay

Rav Bibi offers a third explanation: *gezeirah shema yisheheh* — the decree is a protection against deliberate delay. If one is permitted to immerse vessels on *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*, people will intentionally defer their *taharah* obligations to those days, when they have leisure time available. This concern is particularly acute on *Yom Tov*, when one wishes to be *tahor* for the occasion and may deliberately leave immersion to that day rather than attending to it earlier.

### Braita Tanaic

Rav Bibi's explanation is explicitly supported by a *tanaic* source. The *baraita* states: *keli she-nitma me-erev Yom Tov ein matbilin oto be-Yom Tov, gezeirah shema yisheheh* — a vessel that became *tamei* before *Yom Tov* may not be immersed on *Yom Tov* itself, and the *baraita* gives the explicit reason: lest one intentionally leave it over. This explanation also has the advantage of addressing both *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* within a single unified concern, and it more directly accounts for the distinction between vessels that became *tamei* before versus on *Yom Tov* — a distinction that the earlier *gezeirah*-based explanations handled less elegantly.

### Rava Nireh

Rava now offers his final and preferred explanation: *mipnei she-nireh k'metaken keli* — because immersing a vessel appears to be an act of fixing or improving it. By transitioning the vessel from *tamei* to *tahor* status, one is in effect rendering it serviceable in a new domain, and this looks like the rabbinic prohibition of *makeh ba-patish* — the finishing blow, the act of completing an object. This reasoning applies equally to *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov* without requiring any secondary *gezeirah*. It also explains the exceptions more naturally: the act of drawing water with a bucket, or performing *hashakah* on the water, does not appear as an act of *tikun* because the focus of the act is on the water or the drawing, not on the vessel. Similarly, the difference between a *vlad ha-tumah* and an *av ha-tumah* can be understood experientially — a vessel with only minor *tumah* does not look as dramatically improved by the immersion. Rava's explanation does not, however, satisfyingly distinguish between vessels that became *tamei* on *erev Yom Tov* versus on *Yom Tov* itself — for that distinction, we are left with a degree of leniency that is better explained by the *milsa d'lo sh'chicha* principle than by *nireh k'metaken*.

---

## Person vs Vessel

### Adam Nireh Q

With Rava's explanation now established as primary, the *gemara* raises the natural question: if the problem is *nireh k'metaken* — that the act of immersion appears to be fixing — then why is a person permitted to immerse at all on *Shabbos* or *Yom Tov*? Surely a person transitioning from *tamei* to *tahor* also appears to be fixing themselves.

### Cooling Not Fixing

The *gemara* answers: *adam nireh ke-meiker* — a person going to the *mikvah* looks like they are simply cooling themselves off. The act is indistinguishable from ordinary bathing, and therefore it does not carry the appearance of a formal act of improvement or fixing.

### Winter Dirty Q

The *gemara* immediately challenges: this reasoning works for warm weather and clean water, but what about in winter, or when the *mikvah* water is dirty? In such cases, it is obviously not a cooling or pleasurable bath. One would not willingly immerse in cold, muddy water for comfort. The act then seems clearly to be performed for the purpose of *taharah* — and that looks like *metaken*.

### Rav Nachman Heat

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak responds with two answers. First: *pe'amim she-adam ba be-sharav ve-rocheitz afilu be-mei mishrah* — sometimes a person arrives from outdoors in intense heat and will bathe even in water used for soaking flax, water that is foul and dirty. In the summer, even unpleasant water offers relief, and so immersion in a dirty *mikvah* can still look like bathing. Second, regarding winter: *pe'amim she-adam ba min ha-sadeh u-muluchlach be-tit u-ve-tzoah ve-rocheitz afilu bi-ymot ha-geshamim* — sometimes a person comes from the field covered in mud and excrement, and in that case they will immerse even in cold water in winter, because the *mikvah* water, however cold and impure, is still cleaner than what they are covered with.

### Yom Kippur Q

The *gemara* then asks: granted, this reasoning accounts for *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, since one can always construct a scenario where the immersion looks like bathing or cleaning. But what about *Yom Kippur*? On *Yom Kippur*, bathing is explicitly prohibited. One cannot claim that going to the *mikvah* on *Yom Kippur* resembles a normal bath; everyone knows that bathing on *Yom Kippur* is forbidden. So if a person immerses on *Yom Kippur*, it is obviously not for the purpose of cooling down or cleaning — it can only be for the sake of *taharah*. Should it not then be forbidden as *nireh k'metaken*?

### Ho'il Shabbat

Rava responds with the principle of *ho'il*: *mi ika midi de-be-Shabbos shari u-ve-Yom ha-Kippurim assur?* — Is there any matter that is permitted on *Shabbos* and yet forbidden on *Yom Kippur*? Rashi qualifies: in matters related to *melachot*, no such asymmetry exists. Eating, drinking, and bathing are forbidden on *Yom Kippur* but not because of *melachah*; they are a separate category of prohibition. But for anything that is permitted on *Shabbos* because it is not considered a forbidden labor, it should likewise be permitted on *Yom Kippur*. Therefore, since we permit person-immersion on *Shabbos* — because it does not rise to the level of *nireh k'metaken* when a person is the subject — that same logic carries over to *Yom Kippur*: *ho'il u-ve-Shabbos shari, be-Yom ha-Kippurim nami shari*.

### Vinegar Test

The *gemara* now tests whether Rava consistently holds this *ho'il* principle. The *mishnah* rules: if one has a toothache on *Shabbos*, one may not swallow vinegar directly over the gums for relief — doing so would constitute a transparent act of *refuah*, which is rabbinically forbidden on *Shabbos*. However, one may dip bread in vinegar in the normal manner and eat it; if the vinegar incidentally helps the toothache, *ve-im nitrapei nitrapei* — so be it.

### Vinegar Contradiction

A *baraita* appears to contradict the *mishnah*: *lo yigma u-falat* — one may not take vinegar and spit it out (clearly a medical application), *aval megama u-vole'a* — but one may take vinegar and swallow it. Here the *baraita* seems to permit swallowing vinegar directly, which the *mishnah* appears to forbid.

### Abaye Timing

Abaye resolves the contradiction: when the *mishnah* forbids taking vinegar, it refers specifically to *megama u-falat* — taking it in and spitting it out, which is an obvious medical procedure. Taking vinegar and swallowing it is permitted, and the *mishnah* was not addressing that case. Rava then offers his own resolution, one that accepts that swallowing itself is the subject of dispute. The two sources are reconciled on the basis of *timing*: *kan kodem tibul, kan le'achar tibul* — the distinction depends on where one is in the course of the meal. Before or during the phase of dipping — when sauces, vinegar, and condiments are present at the table — drinking vinegar directly is not so unusual. But after the dipping course is concluded, taking straight vinegar would be bizarre except as medicine. It is worth noting that the practice of reclining and multiple dippings at a formal meal was standard in the era when the *mishnah* was written, not the peculiar custom it became in later periods when the *rishonim* composed their works during *Pesach*.

### Rava Reverses

But now the *gemara* turns Rava's *ho'il* principle against this very distinction. If we hold, as Rava does, that anything permitted on *Shabbos* must also be permitted on *Yom Kippur* — and by extension, anything permitted during one phase of *Shabbos* must be permitted throughout — then how can Rava draw a line between before and after the dipping? If swallowing vinegar is permitted before the dipping, *ho'il* would demand it be permitted after as well. The *gemara* therefore concludes: *hadar bei Rava me-hai* — Rava reversed himself from his distinction between before and after the dipping. In the end he accepts Abaye's explanation: the *mishnah* forbids only *megama u-falat*, while swallowing is always permitted.

### Braita Override

The *gemara* then raises the question of which position Rava ultimately retracted: was it the vinegar explanation or his broader *ho'il* principle applied to *Yom Kippur*? The *gemara* answers decisively: *lo salka da'atach* — it is inconceivable that Rava retracted from his *Yom Kippur* position, because a *baraita* explicitly supports it. *Ve-tanya: kol chayavei tevilos tovilin ke-darkan bein be-Tisha be-Av bein be-Yom ha-Kippurim* — anyone who is obligated in immersion immerses normally, even on *Tisha be-Av* and on *Yom Kippur*. This *baraita* confirms that person-immersion is permitted on *Yom Kippur*, which means Rava must maintain his *ho'il* position there, and must therefore have retracted his before-and-after-dipping distinction in the vinegar case so as to be consistent.

---

## Ho'il Yom Kippur

### Tanaic Tisha Yom

The *baraita* just cited — that all those obligated in immersion may do so even on *Tisha be-Av* and *Yom Kippur* — deserves careful attention. The principle that immersion is permitted even on these days reflects the understanding that *tevilah* performed for the purpose of becoming *tahor*, rather than for the pleasure of bathing, does not fall within the prohibition of washing that applies on those days. Even on *Yom Kippur*, where bathing is explicitly prohibited, immersion *l'shem taharah* is categorically different. The prohibition of washing on *Yom Kippur* is directed at bathing *derech ta'anug* — in a manner of pleasure and comfort — and immersion in a *mikvah* for the purpose of *taharah* is not that. It may sit close to the line, but it is formally outside the category of the forbidden act. Hence the *baraita*'s ruling: one who is obligated immerses even on those days.

### Aveilus Principle

Tosafot addresses *Tisha be-Av* separately. Technically, the *baraita* permits immersion on that day as well, and Tosafot notes that in principle there is no prohibition that would bar it. Rather, the restraint on *Tisha be-Av* is not a formal *isur* but an expression of *aveilus* — mourning. Rebbi Chananya ben Antignos articulates the principle: *kedai hu beit Eloheinu le-abeid tevilah achas ba-shanah* — the mourning for the Temple is sufficient cause to forgo one immersion in the year. The Yerushalmi records that Rebbi Levi ruled in accordance with this view. So while one is technically permitted, the spirit of the day calls for foregoing the immersion as an expression of mourning.

### Yom Kippur Modern

Tosafot then addresses *Yom Kippur*. In the present era, Tosafot rules, the common practice is that women do not immerse on either *Yom Kippur* or *Tisha be-Av*. The reason, he explains, is tied to the conditions under which immersion would be practically necessary.

### Practical Need

Tosafot distinguishes between two very different motivations for immersion. In the era when *taharot* — the laws of ritual purity — were actively practiced, there were immediate and weighty consequences to remaining *tamei*, and immersion was therefore urgently required. Even without the principle of *tevilah bi-zmanah mitzvah* — that immersing at the proper time is itself a *mitzvah* — there was a pressing practical need that justified immersion even on those days. Today, however, the sole operative consequence of a woman remaining *tamei* is that she is forbidden to her husband. And since marital relations are forbidden on both *Tisha be-Av* and *Yom Kippur*, there is no immediate benefit to immersing on those days. The permission to immerse granted by the *baraita* was conditioned on there being an immediate and practical need; where that need is absent, the immersion is simply deferred. Tosafot further notes that a woman can arrange to wash her hair on *erev Yom Kippur* and then immerse on *motzai Yom Kippur* — which requires *chafifah* close to the immersion — thus satisfying her obligation without any need to immerse on the day itself. This practical arrangement confirms that no *halakhic* loss results from deferring. Tosafot applies the same reasoning to *Tisha be-Av*. The question of whether immersion would be permitted in a case of immediate need — for example, to permit non-sexual touch for a husband who is ill — is left open.

---

## Water Vessel

### Mishna Hashakah

The *gemara* returns to examine the *mishnah*'s ruling directly. The *mishnah* permits *hashakah* — connecting the impure water to the *mikvah* via a stone vessel — but prohibits using an impure vessel as a means of immersing the vessel itself alongside the water. More precisely: one lowers a stone vessel containing impure water into the *mikvah*, and the waters connect and are purified; but one may not use a *tamei keli* for this purpose with the intent to purify the vessel in the same act.

### Attribution Q

The *gemara* asks: *mani matnisin* — whose view does our *mishnah* reflect? It does not appear to match either Rebbi or the *Chachamim*, based on the positions recorded in a *baraita*.

### Braita Positions

The *baraita* reads as follows: Rebbi holds *ein matbilin et ha-keli al gabbei meimav le-taharo ve-ein mashikin et ha-mayim bi-khli even le-taharan* — one may neither immerse the vessel to purify it, nor may one perform *hashakah* on the water. Rebbi forbids both. The *Chachamim* say the opposite: *matbilin keli even al gabbei meimav le-taharo u-mashikin et ha-mayim bi-khli even le-taharan* — one may do both, both the immersion of the vessel and the *hashakah* of the water. Our *mishnah*, which permits *hashakah* but forbids immersing the vessel, matches neither position.

### Temporal Reading

The *gemara* resolves the problem through a creative reading: *reisha de-Braitah be-Yom Tov, ve-seifa be-Shabbos* — the two clauses of the *baraita* are addressing different time contexts. The first clause, prohibiting vessel immersion, speaks of *Yom Tov*. The second clause, prohibiting *hashakah* of the water, speaks of *Shabbos*.

### Dispute Division

With this reading, both Rebbi and the *Chachamim* can be harmonized with the *mishnah*. According to Rebbi: on *Yom Tov*, one may not immerse the vessel — but the first clause's silence on water implies that *hashakah* of water is permitted on *Yom Tov*. On *Shabbos*, Rebbi goes further and prohibits even the *hashakah* of water. Thus Rebbi distinguishes between *Yom Tov* and *Shabbos* regarding the water, and our *mishnah*, which permits *hashakah* while forbidding vessel immersion, reflects Rebbi's position on *Yom Tov*. According to the *Chachamim*: on *Yom Tov*, they permit both vessel immersion and *hashakah* of water; but on *Shabbos*, they draw the distinction our *mishnah* reflects — permitting *hashakah* but not vessel immersion. Thus our *mishnah*, read as governing *Shabbos*, reflects the position of the *Chachamim*. Both readings are available: *ibba'it eima Rebbi ibba'it eima Rabbanan* — the *mishnah*'s water-vessel distinction can be attributed to either authority, depending on whether one reads the *mishnah* as speaking of *Yom Tov* or *Shabbos* respectively.

---

---

# Beitzah 19

## Tevilat Keilim Erev YT

### Bein Hashmashot Issue

The daf begins on the second line of 19b. A *baraita* is introduced: *keli she-nitma b'erev Yom Tov ein matbilin oso bein hashmashos* — a vessel that became *tamei* on *erev Yom Tov* may not be immersed during *bein hashmashos*. The preceding discussion had established that *tevilat keilim* is prohibited on *Shabbos* and *Yom Tov*, and had explored various technical distinctions: whether the vessel became *tamei* on *Yom Tov* or before it, and whether the immersion is being performed for the sake of the water (which is permitted) or for the sake of the vessel itself (which is not). The present *baraita* addresses a case of *safek*: since the vessel became *tamei* on *erev Yom Tov*, one cannot immerse it during *bein hashmashos*, because it may already be *Yom Tov*, making the immersion an *issur d'Rabbanan*.

### R. Shimon Shezuri

*Rabbi Shimon Shezuri omer: af be-chol ein matbilin oso mipnei she-tzarich ha'erev shemesh* — Rabbi Shimon Shezuri goes further and says that even on a weekday one may not immerse a vessel during *bein hashmashos*, because the vessel requires *ha'erev shemesh* — the onset of nightfall — to attain full *taharah*. Just as a person who immerses in a *mikvah* achieves complete *taharah* only at nightfall (a distinction relevant for eating *terumah* and *kodshim*, though not practically for a woman who is a *niddah*), so too a vessel requires *ha'erev shemesh*.

The concern, as Rashi explains, is that someone immersing a vessel at *bein hashmashos* is evidently planning to use it that very night. Since he dunked the vessel precisely at *bein hashmashos*, it is possible that nightfall had already arrived, meaning he may never actually have had *ha'erev shemesh*. One might ask: the same concern should apply to someone immersing at night, who also clearly wants to use the vessel that evening. But *bein hashmashos* is particularly dangerous, because the person can convince himself that he got the immersion in before nightfall and that *ha'erev shemesh* therefore applies, when in fact it may not. Those who require *ha'erev shemesh* are admittedly a limited population — people eating *terumah* or *kodshim* — and one might think such people know the law. But the concern is not ignorance so much as self-persuasion: convincing oneself that the timing worked out when it may not have.

### Tanna Kamma Query

The *Gemara* presses: *u'ma Tanna Kamma lo ba'ei ha'erev shemesh*? Does the first *tanna* not require *ha'erev shemesh*? That is, how does the *Tanna Kamma* address the concern Rabbi Shimon Shezuri raises about weekday immersions at *bein hashmashos*?

### Machshavto Nikares

Rava answers: *ashkachinhu l'Rabbanan d'bei Rav d'yasvi v'ka'amri* — he found the rabbinic students sitting and saying that the debate turns on the principle of *machshavto nikares mitoch ma'asav* — one's intention is visible through one's actions. The question is how much one can infer, from the way a person is behaving, that he is fully aware of the applicable *halacha*. The case: *kegon d'nakit mana b'yadeih ve-rahit ve-azil bein hashmashos l'atbolei* — he is holding a vessel and running to reach the *mikvah* at *bein hashmashos*. The act of running demonstrates some urgency. One view: *mada yada d'ba'ei ha'erev shemesh* — the fact that he is running shows he understands he must arrive before nightfall if he wants nightfall to count as *ha'erev shemesh*. Rashi notes that even if he arrives and realizes he has missed the ideal timing, he is already there with his vessel and will proceed to immerse; but the running itself shows he understands the law, and thus no *gezeirah* is needed.

### Intent & Knowledge

The opposing view holds: *machmas melacha hu d'karahit* — people run because they have work to do, not because they understand the significance of nightfall. The running proves nothing about his *halachic* awareness. The dispute is therefore whether one can reliably read a person's intent and knowledge from the manner in which he acts.

The *Gemara* clarifies that the parties do not disagree when the intent is unambiguous. Rather, *ki peligi* — where they disagree — is in a case where the person's level of knowledge is genuinely uncertain from his behavior alone.

### Pachot Mik'adasha

The specific case of uncertain knowledge: someone whose vessel became *tamei* through contact with less than a *k'adasha* — less than a lentil-size portion of a dead rodent — came to the rabbis to ask whether his vessel in fact contracted *tumah* from an amount smaller than the minimum. The answer is no, but he had another vessel that required immersion.

One view holds: *mi d'hai lo gamir* — someone who does not know the basic *halacha* of the minimum size for *tumah* clearly lacks knowledge of the laws of *tumah ve-taharah* generally, and therefore we may assume he also does not know the requirement of *ha'erev shemesh*. Accordingly, we do not permit such a person to immerse at *bein hashmashos*, lest he come to use the vessel before full *taharah* is achieved.

The opposing view holds: *ha hu d'lo gamir* — that particular law, the minimum size, he does not know, but that is because, as Rashi says, it is not written explicitly in the *Torah*. The requirement of *ha'erev shemesh*, by contrast, is written explicitly and is more commonly known. We do not impute ignorance of one law from ignorance of another.

This whole passage strikes one as curious. The *Gemara* appears to be discussing a policy of whether to permit immersion at *bein hashmashos*, yet it frames the question as an assessment of a specific individual's knowledge. If the person is standing right in front of the rabbis asking about *pachot mik'adasha*, why not simply inform him of the *halacha* of *ha'erev shemesh* directly? What does it mean to condition the policy on an assessment of whether his ignorance of one *halacha* implies ignorance of another? And even if the policy is to deny him access to the *mikvah* based on his apparent ignorance, how would he ever come to learn the rule at all? The phrase *machshavto nikares mitoch ma'asav* is worth noting independently, as it appears in other *halachic* contexts as well — for instance, in discussions of whether a minor can be presumed to possess *da'at* based on the evident thoughtfulness of his behavior.

---

## Mi-Gav L'Gav & Michiburah

### Mi-Gav L'Gav

The *Mishnah* had stated briefly that one may immerse vessels *mi-gav l'gav* and *mi-chaburah l'chaburah*. A *Tosefta* explains: *keitzad mi-gav l'gav* — what does "from back to back" mean? If someone had purified his vessels for use in his *gat* (olive press) and then decided to use them instead in his *bet ha-bad* (wine press), and wishes to re-immerse them before doing so — *gezunterheit*, let him. This is true even though there is no *halachic* requirement to do so: both contexts involve the same level of *taharah*, and the vessels are already *tahor*. The person has simply adopted a personal practice of immersing all vessels before any new use. Since the *tevilah* is entirely unnecessary, he may go ahead and perform it on *Yom Tov*.

### Michiburah L'Chiburah

*Keitzad mi-chaburah l'chaburah* — what does "from group to group" mean? Rashi specifies this refers to *Pesach* groups: *hayah ochel ba-chaburah zo ve-rotzeh le'echol ba-chaburah acheret* — someone was intending to eat with one group and then wished to change to another group. Since once one has actually begun eating with a group one may not transfer the *Pesach* to another *chaburah*, the *Mishnah* must be speaking of a case where he had merely intended to eat with one group and changed his mind before the *shechitah*. He now wishes to immerse his vessels anew before joining the second group — perhaps out of a practice of immersing vessels before joining a *Pesach* group. *Ha-reshut be-yado* — he may do so.

### Non-Halachic Tevilah

This leads to a striking observation. Every concern the *Gemara* raised earlier about *tevilah* on *Yom Tov* — that one might come to carry in a public domain, or that it looks like one is performing a *tikkun* — applies equally in these cases. The person is carrying his vessel to the *mikvah* for a purpose that serves no *halachic* function. Yet because this is not a *halachically* required *tevilah*, it is permitted. The same internal logic governs other distinctions in the preceding discussion: whether the vessel became *tamei* on *erev Yom Tov* or on *Yom Tov* itself, whether the source of *tumah* was an *av ha-tumah* or a *sheni le-tumah* — distinctions that map onto which immersions are permitted and which are not, even though the underlying concerns seem equally present in every case. The *Gemara* is operating with a formalistic principle: where the *tevilah* is technically not required, the concerns are set aside.

---

## Shelamim & Olot YT

### Beit S. vs. Beit H.

The *Gemara* now returns to a central *Yom Tov* debate of the *masechta*. *Beit Shammai omrim: mevi'im shelamim ve-ein somchin aleihem, aval lo olot* — Beit Shammai holds that *shelamim* (peace offerings) may be brought on *Yom Tov*, since their meat will be eaten and thus constitute a *tzorech Yom Tov*, but *semicha* — the act of pressing one's full weight on the animal — may not be performed, as it constitutes a form of using an animal on *Yom Tov*, which is rabbinically prohibited. Moreover, *olot* (burnt offerings) may not be brought at all, since no food benefit accrues to the offerer.

*U-Veit Hillel omrim: mevi'im shelamim ve-olot ve-somchin aleihem* — Beit Hillel holds that both *shelamim* and *olot* may be brought, and that *semicha* may be performed as well. The debate thus involves two questions: whether an *olah* — from which one derives no food — may be brought as a legitimate use of *melachah* on *Yom Tov*, and whether *semicha* is a prohibited use of an animal on *Yom Tov*.

This is worth placing in a broader context. This dispute is one of the earliest recorded debates in rabbinic history. The tractate *Chagigah* lists a chain of the *Nasi* and *Av Beit Din* going back centuries, all of whom debated the question of whether one performs *semicha* on *shelamim* brought on *Yom Tov*. It is somewhat puzzling that this particular question — which is, after all, a rabbinic concern — became the defining controversy across so many generations. It is also worth observing how much of *Masechet Beitzah* as a whole consists of Beit Shammai–Beit Hillel disputes, from *d'oraita* questions about carrying and bringing *korbanot*, to *d'Rabbanan* questions like the egg and *eruv tavshilin*. That a single *masechta* should be so thoroughly organized around this one set of disputants is itself remarkable and, as yet, not readily explained.

One further technical note: since *semicha* is not *me'akev* — it does not invalidate the offering if omitted — Beit Shammai's position that one may bring *shelamim* without *semicha* is coherent. The act can simply be performed on *erev Yom Tov* instead.

### Ulla's View

Ulla refines the scope of the dispute: *machloket be-shalmei chagigah lismoch ve-olat re'iyah le-hakriv* — the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel concerns specifically *shalmei chagigah* (the festival peace offerings incumbent upon every pilgrim, based on the verse *va-chagosem oto chag la-Shem*, which obligates bringing *shelamim* as part of the festival celebration) and *olat re'iyah* (the burnt offering that fulfills the commandment *lo yeira'u fanai reikam*, that one shall not appear before God empty-handed).

According to Ulla, both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that *shalmei chagigah* may be brought on *Yom Tov* — it is a festival obligation and its meat is eaten, making the rationale for *Yom Tov* permission straightforward. Their dispute about *shelamim* is limited to the question of *semicha*. On *olot*, the dispute is whether *olat re'iyah* — a genuine *Yom Tov* obligation — may be brought on *Yom Tov* itself. Beit Hillel says yes; Beit Shammai says no, let it be deferred to the days following *Yom Tov*.

This also illuminates the position of Beit Shammai with respect to *Shavuot*, where there is no *Chol ha-Mo'ed*. According to Beit Shammai, one could never actually fulfill the obligation of *olat re'iyah* on *Shavuot* itself; it would always have to be made up in the days following, by an extension learned from the extra days of *Pesach* and *Sukkot*.

The underlying disagreement: Beit Shammai reads *va-chagosem oto chag la-Shem* as limiting permissible activity to the *chagigah* itself — *chagigah in, olat re'iyah lo*. Beit Hillel reads the phrase *la-Shem* expansively — *kol de-la-Shem*, any *korban* that is brought for God's honor as part of the *chag* may be brought. But with respect to *nedarim u-nedavot* — freewill offerings unrelated to the festival — *divrei ha-kol ein krevin be-Yom Tov*, all agree they may not be brought.

This conclusion about *nedarim u-nedavot* also connects to the earlier discussion in the *masechta* about the principle of *mitoch she-hutrah le-tzorech hutrah nami she-lo le-tzorech* — the rule that what is permitted for one purpose on *Yom Tov* may be permitted even for other purposes. The *Gemara* there concluded that one who brings an *olat nedavah* on *Yom Tov* would be liable to *malkut* according to Beit Shammai but not according to Beit Hillel. The present discussion, which says even Beit Hillel agrees *lechatchila* that unrelated offerings cannot be brought, is consistent: Beit Hillel's greater leniency, rooted in *mitoch*, means that *bedi'avad* one might not be penalized, but certainly *lechatchila* such offerings are not to be brought.

One might also ask why Beit Shammai, even without *mitoch*, should object to a *shelamim* that is not a *shalmei chagigah*, given that the offerer will eat its meat — seemingly no different from slaughtering an animal at home. The answer must be that the eating of a *shelamim* is understood as eating in the context of a *korban*: it is not primarily about satisfying hunger but about bringing an offering to God, with the eating as a secondary dimension. It is even somewhat ironic that Beit Shammai, who does not hold of *mitoch*, ends up not allowing *shelamim* that are not *shalmei chagigah*, when one might have thought that the *shelamim*'s eating component would make it the paradigmatic case of *tzorech Yom Tov*. But *shalmei simchah* — the peace offerings of rejoicing — which we will encounter shortly, bring the two elements together: the *shelamim* dimension and the *simchat ha-chag* dimension. Without that combination, even *shelamim* in isolation do not suffice.

### Braita Alternative

A *braita* is cited in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: *lo necheleku Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel al olah she-einah shel Yom Tov she-einah kreivah be-Yom Tov* — there was no dispute that an *olah* unrelated to *Yom Tov* may not be brought. And: *al shelamim she-hein shel Yom Tov she-kreivim be-Yom Tov* — there was also no dispute that *shelamim* that are festival obligations may be brought. The debate, says this *baraita*, was twofold: *al olah she-hi shel Yom Tov* — an *olah* that is a *Yom Tov* obligation (*olat re'iyah*), and *shelamim she-einam shel Yom Tov* — *shelamim* not connected to the festival at all. Beit Shammai says neither may be brought; Beit Hillel says both may.

This version diverges from Ulla's reading. On the *olah*, the two agree. But this *baraita* has Beit Hillel permitting even *shelamim* that are unrelated to the festival, because in the end the offerer will eat the meat — and it has Beit Shammai prohibiting even such *shelamim*. This is a direct contradiction to Ulla's claim that even Beit Hillel would concede that unrelated *shelamim* cannot be brought.

### Tannai Dispute

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve the contradiction by proposing an emendation of the *baraita*: *targima ve-eima hachi* — reinterpret the text. Under the revised reading, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is made to say that there was no dispute that *olah* and *shelamim* unrelated to *Yom Tov* cannot be brought, and no dispute that *shelamim* related to *Yom Tov* can be brought. The sole subject of debate is *olat re'iyah*, precisely as Ulla had said. This resolution effectively cuts and pastes the *baraita* to align it with Ulla. The straightforward reading of the *baraita*, however, is that Beit Hillel would permit even unrelated *shelamim* — for the reason already stated, that one will eat the meat.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef's response to the contradiction is blunter: *Tannai shakalat me'alma* — do not think there are no tannaim who disagree with Ulla. There are other tannaitic opinions in the world; finding one that contradicts Ulla merely establishes that it is a *tannaic* dispute. The *baraita* of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar represents one view; Ulla's reading reflects another. The matter is *tannai*.

### Shelamim YT

A further *baraita* is cited: *shlamim ha-ba'im machmat Yom Tov be-Yom Tov* — *shelamim* brought specifically for the sake of *Yom Tov*, that is, *shalmei chagigah* or *shalmei simchah* as we will see. *Beit Shammai omrim: somech aleihem me-erev Yom Tov ve-shochtan be-Yom Tov* — Beit Shammai holds that *semicha* must be performed on *erev Yom Tov*, since it cannot be done on *Yom Tov* itself, but the actual slaughter occurs on *Yom Tov*. *U-Veit Hillel omrim: somech aleihem be-Yom Tov ve-shochtan be-Yom Tov* — Beit Hillel holds that *semicha* may be performed on *Yom Tov* as well. So what is debated is an *Yom Tov*-related *shelamim*; the question is only whether *semicha* is permitted.

### Nedarim V'Nedavot

The *baraita* continues: *aval nedarim u-nedavot divrei ha-kol ein krevin be-Yom Tov* — but freewill sacrifices unrelated to *Yom Tov*, all agree may not be brought. This supports Ulla's position. Both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that *shelamim* that carry no connection to the *chag* — even though their meat will be eaten — may not be brought on *Yom Tov lechatchila*. As noted, even if Beit Hillel's *mitoch* principle might provide a *bedi'avad* defense, it does not license *lechatchila* conduct.

The *baraita* then moves to a seemingly unrelated case: *ein mevi'in toda be-Chag ha-Matzot mipnei chametz she-bah* — a *toda* (thanksgiving offering), which is a type of *shelamim* requiring both *matzah* and *chametz* loaves, may not be brought on *Pesach* because its *chametz* component cannot be presented. And *ve-lo be-Atzeret mipnei she-hu Yom Tov* — nor may it be brought on *Shavuot*, because it is *Yom Tov*. This establishes that a *toda*, which is a *shelamim* not connected to the festival, may not be brought on *Yom Tov*. *Aval mevi adam todato be-Chag ha-Sukkot* — but it may be brought during *Sukkot*.

When it says *ein mevi'in toda be-Chag ha-Matzot*, one might think this is obvious since the *chametz* loaves cannot be presented on *Pesach*. In fact, the *Gemara* clarifies that the ruling extends even to the fourteenth of Nisan — *erev Pesach* — based on the principle *ein mevi'im kodashim l'veit ha-pasul*: one does not bring sacrifices into a situation where they are likely to become invalid. If one brings a *toda* in the morning of the fourteenth, there is barely enough time to eat all the *chametz* loaves before midday, risking that they will become *notar* and require burning. This is also the reason we do not recite *Mizmor le-Todah* on *erev Pesach*.

---

## Toda & Bal Te'acher

### Toda Fulfillment

Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon introduces a further distinction: *mevi adam todato be-Chag ha-Sukkot ve-yotzei bo yedei chovato mishum simchah ve-ein yotzei bo mishum chagigah* — a person may bring his *toda* on *Sukkot* and thereby fulfill his obligation of *simchah*, but he does not thereby fulfill his obligation of *chagigah*. This requires some unpacking.

There are two distinct categories of festival *shelamim* incumbent on a pilgrim. One is *shalmei chagigah*, grounded in the verse *va-chagosem oto chag* — the obligation to bring *shelamim* as an expression of the *chag* itself. The other is *shalmei simchah*, grounded in *ve-samachta atah u-veitecha* — the obligation of *simchat Yom Tov*, rejoicing on the festival. While *shalmei chagigah* focuses on the act of bringing the *korban*, *shalmei simchah* is primarily about eating meat that was brought as a *korban* in the context of God's presence. The distinction is significant: it is specifically eating the meat of a *korban* that constitutes the fulfillment, not merely eating meat. This is why *Chazal* teach that in the absence of the *Beit ha-Mikdash*, *simchah* for men is expressed through wine — the eating of *korban* meat being no longer available. (The *Rambam*'s *girsa* adds meat alongside wine, but our *girsa* in the *Gemara* mentions only wine.)

Now, if someone had already accepted an obligation to bring a *toda* — perhaps due to a dangerous journey from which he was saved — and he brings it on the *regel*, may he count that as his *shalmei simchah* as well? Yes: since *shalmei simchah* is fundamentally about eating meat that has been brought as a *shelamim* in a *kodesh* context, there is no reason one cannot eat the *toda* meat and simultaneously fulfill *simchah*. But can he use his *toda* to fulfill *shalmei chagigah*? No. *Shalmei chagigah* is a *davar she-be-chovah* — an independent obligation — and *ve-chol davar she-be-chovah eino ba ela min ha-chulin*: an obligatory offering can only be fulfilled by something not already dedicated to satisfying a prior obligation. One cannot discharge one obligation through another preexisting one.

When the *Gemara* asks whether this ruling about *chagigah* is so obvious as to require no statement, it answers: *lo tzericha* — yes it does, because it comes to tell us that even if one *explicitly stipulated* at the time of accepting the *toda* that he intends it also to satisfy his *chagigah* obligation, it still cannot. And this is what leads into the discussion of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan.

### Abaye's Frame

At this point, Rav Zeira raises an objection to Rabbi Shimon's position — in Tosafot's reading of the text, where Rabbi Shimon says that if you cannot bring the *toda* on *Pesach* and *Shavuot*, you cannot bring it on *Sukkot* either. *Ha-shta shulusei mesaltinan* — we allow gathering wood from forests on *Chol ha-Mo'ed*, a form of labor with considerable latitude. *Ve-nedarim u-nedavot mibaya* — and you mean to tell me one cannot bring a *toda* on *Chol ha-Mo'ed Sukkot*?

Abaye resolves this: *be-hakravah kulei alma lo pligi de-sharei* — regarding the actual bringing of the *toda* on *Chol ha-Mo'ed Sukkot*, nobody disputes that it is permitted. The *baraita* was never discussing that. *Ki pligi le-makam aleih be-val te'acher* — the entire dispute in this *baraita* concerns the prohibition of *bal te'acher*, the *Torah* prohibition against delaying the fulfillment of one's vows: *ki tidor neder la-Shem Elokecha lo te'acher le-shallemo*.

Abaye's framing is not merely an *ukimta* for this one line; Rashi emphasizes that Abaye is explaining the fundamental subject matter of the entire *baraita*. Ask yourself: what was this *baraita* really about? The answer, says Abaye, is *bal te'acher*. *Chazal* understood the prohibition as linked to the *regalim* — the pilgrimages — because the three *regalim* represent one's greatest opportunities to present himself at the *Beit ha-Mikdash* and discharge his obligations. The question is: what constitutes the cycle? How many *regalim* must pass before one transgresses *bal te'acher*?

### Tanna Kamma

The *Tanna Kamma* holds: *shalosh regalim amar Rachmana afilu shelo kesidran* — the *Torah* requires three *regalim*, and the order does not matter. Once three *regalim* have passed — regardless of which *regel* one started from — without one having brought his *korban*, he is in violation. In the case of a *toda*, which cannot be brought on *Pesach* (due to *chametz*) or on *Shavuot* (because it is *Yom Tov*), only *Sukkot* provides an actual opportunity. Therefore: *Sukkot* is the one *regel* where one must bring it, and if *Sukkot* passes without the offering being brought, *bal te'acher* has been violated.

### R. Shimon

Rabbi Shimon holds: *kesidran in, shelo kesidran lo* — only the sequence matters. One is not in violation unless the three *regalim* have passed *ke-sidran*, in order, beginning with *Pesach*. Using Tosafot's *girsa* of the *baraita*: *kol she-ba be-Chag ha-Matzot u-ve-Chag ha-Shavuot ba be-Chag ha-Sukkot* — any offering that can be brought on *Pesach* and *Shavuot* must then be brought on *Sukkot* or one is in violation. But if the obligation did not yet exist on *Pesach* and *Shavuot* — if one's vow was taken after those occasions — then *Sukkot* is not yet the deadline; another full cycle remains. Rashi reads the language this way: if you were already obligated on *Pesach* and had the opportunity on *Shavuot*, then *Sukkot* is your last chance. But if you were not yet obligated at those earlier times, you will have another opportunity.

The language is admittedly awkward to map cleanly onto the *baraita*'s words, but the principle is clear: *kesidran* is required, and *shelo kesidran* does not trigger *bal te'acher*.

### R. Elazar b. Shimon

Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon offers yet a third position, and a separate *baraita* is cited in his name to clarify it: *lomar she-zeh acharon* — the reason the *Torah* mentioned *Sukkot* again at the end of its list is to say that *Sukkot* is the final one, the concluding deadline. This aligns with Rabbi Shimon's view that order matters and *Sukkot* closes the cycle. But Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon goes further: *lomar she-zeh gorem* — *Sukkot* alone is the cause, the decisive point. *Sukkot* is the universal deadline for all outstanding obligations, regardless of when the vow was made. If one made a *neder* the day before *Sukkot*, he must bring it on *Sukkot* or be in violation. If he made it the day after *Sukkot*, he has until the following *Sukkot*. The deadline is *Sukkot*, period, independent of the cycle of the other *regalim*.

This position may evoke the dual calendrical framework in the *Torah*: alongside the calendar that begins with *ha-chodesh ha-zeh lachem* — where *Pesach* is the starting point of the *regalim* — there is also the calendar in which *Sukkot* is *tekufat ha-shanah* or *be-tzet ha-shanah*, the close of the year, associated with *Rosh Hashanah* and the end of the annual cycle. Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon draws on this notion: *Sukkot* is always the year's terminus for *korbanot*.

The *Gemara* then connects this back to our question of *shelamim* on *Yom Tov*. Since Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon says one must bring one's *toda* on *Sukkot*, and since *Chol ha-Mo'ed Sukkot* would be no different from the *Tanna Kamma*'s position (about which there is no dispute), his statement must mean something more — namely, that one can bring it even on *Yom Tov* of *Sukkot* itself. This would make him the tannaitic source for the view that *nedarim u-nedavot* — unrelated *shelamim* — may be brought even on *Yom Tov*, in contrast to the position that all agree they may not. The *Gemara* acknowledges that this reading is somewhat forced: Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon was primarily discussing *bal te'acher*, not *Yom Tov* policy. But because the *Gemara* has been reading the entire *baraita* through the lens of Abaye's *bal te'acher* framework, it draws Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon into the earlier dispute as well.

To summarize the landscape: the *olah* unrelated to *Yom Tov* cannot be brought, and even Beit Hillel agrees *lechatchila*. The *olat re'iyah* is debated between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. *Shalmei chagigah* and *shalmei simchah* everyone agrees can be brought; the debate is only about *semicha*. The key question is whether *shelamim* not related to *Yom Tov* — represented paradigmatically by the *toda* — can be brought on *Yom Tov*. According to Ulla (and the *baraita* that supports him), everyone agrees they may not. According to the straightforward reading of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's *baraita*, Beit Hillel would permit them. And according to the *Gemara*'s reading of Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon's position, he is the *tanna* who holds they can be brought even on *Yom Tov* itself.

---

## Tenai & Ma'aseh Order

### Toda L'Chagigah

The *Gemara* returns to the question raised by Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish to Rabbi Yochanan: *ha-omer harei alai toda ve-etzei bah yedei chagigah* — someone declares, "I accept the obligation of a *toda*, and I intend to use it to fulfill my *chagigah* obligation." Or: *hareini nazir ve-agaleach demi ma'aser sheni* — I am a *nazir*, and when I bring the *korbanot* of *nezirut*, I will use my *ma'aser sheni* funds for them. In both cases, the person stipulates at the moment of accepting his vow that he will simultaneously discharge another obligation. What is the *halacha*?

Rabbi Yochanan responded: *neder ve-eino yotzei* — the vow takes effect, but the *toda* cannot be used to fulfill the *chagigah*; *nazir ve-eino megaleach* — he is a *nazir*, but he cannot use *ma'aser sheni* money for his *korbanot*. The *Gemara* notes that this ruling is not merely about *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah* — stipulating against a *Torah* rule — though that is one way to frame the problem. Rashi's explanation goes to the order of declaration: the moment one says *harei alai toda* or *hareini nazir*, that declaration takes immediate effect. The *al menat* that follows comes too late; the obligation is already binding. If so, the logic of the ruling is not about substance but sequence.

### Neder & Tenai

If the problem is the order of the statements — the obligating declaration preceded the condition — then reversing the order might produce a different result. This is the key principle of *tenai kodem le-ma'aseh*: the condition must precede the act to be operative. A condition stated after the binding act cannot retroactively limit or redirect that act.

### Schiv Mera

This principle is illustrated through the story of a *shechiv mera* — a person on his deathbed — whose declarations carry the special legal status of *matnat shechiv mera*, a deathbed gift that takes effect immediately (so as not to agitate the dying person). The case: *hahu gavra de-amar lehu* — a certain man said to those gathered around him, *havu lei arba me'ah zuzie le-ploni ve-linsov barti* — give 400 *zuz* to a certain person, and let him marry my daughter.

Rav Pappa ruled: *arba me'ah shakil* — he takes the 400 *zuz*; *u-varti ei ba'ei nasiv ve-ei ba'ei lo nasiv* — but with respect to the daughter, he may marry her if he wishes and need not if he does not. The two statements are independent: the 400 *zuz* was stated first and became binding as soon as it was uttered; the subsequent mention of the marriage cannot retroactively make the money conditional upon it.

But if the man had said instead, *linsav u-havu lei* — let him marry my daughter and then give him 400 *zuz* — then *ei nasiv shakil ve-ei lo nasiv lo shakil*: if he marries her he gets the money; if he does not, he does not. There the condition of marriage was stated first, before the grant of money, and so the money was understood from the outset as conditional upon the marriage.

### Mareimar & Ravina

Mareimar was teaching this ruling in his own name — *mi-shamei de-nafshei* — describing the principle about the *toda* and the *chagigah* obligation. Ravina said to Mareimar: *atun hachi matnitu lah* — you teach it as an anonymous ruling. *Anan ke-di ba'ei minei Reish Lakish me-Rabbi Yochanan matninan lah* — we have this teaching with attribution, as a question that Reish Lakish posed to Rabbi Yochanan.

### Tosafot Synthesis

Tosafot draws the natural conclusion: if the order of declaration determines the outcome, then reversing it should be effective. Specifically, someone who says *al menat she-etzei bo yedei chagigah, harei alai toda* — stipulating the condition *before* accepting the *toda* obligation — should indeed be able to use the *toda* to fulfill his *chagigah*. The condition preceded the act, so the act was accepted from its inception in the context of the condition.

Tosafot acknowledges that this case is not quite the same as a typical *matneh al mah she-katuv ba-Torah*, where the problem is that the stipulation contradicts the substance of a *Torah* rule. Here, the question is purely about sequencing. The broader principle is the *halachic* framework of *tenai kodem le-ma'aseh* — the condition must precede the deed — which applies throughout *hilchot tena'im*.
