Where the sequence is respected, the condition can shape the legal effect of the act; where it is not, the act takes hold unconditionally and the subsequent condition is inoperative.

---

---

# Beitzah 25

## Review: Melacha YT

### New Perek Intro

The present *daf* is 25. We back up slightly and pick up from the bottom of 24b in order to review two important points that arose over the preceding days at the opening of the new *perek*.

### Catching Fish/Animals

The new *perek* introduces the principle that one may not catch fish or wild animals on *Yom Tov*. This immediately generates an important discussion among the *Rishonim*: if one is permitted to *shecht* animals on *Yom Tov*, why is catching forbidden? And this leads to the broader question of whether it is truly the case that any *melacha* associated with the preparation of food is permitted on *Yom Tov*.

### Rashi's Approach

*Rashi*'s basic answer is that the problem with catching is that one could have done it beforehand — one could have taken care of it from *erev Yom Tov*. This implies that only *melachos* that could not have been attended to before *Yom Tov* are permitted, or at least that performing a *melacha* which was deferrable raises a question of biblical prohibition.

### Rishonim Challenge

The *Rishonim* challenge this position. They argue that if something is directly related to food preparation — not in an indirect or merely preparatory sense, but genuinely direct — then even if one could have attended to it beforehand, it remains permitted on *Yom Tov*. There is also a broader difficulty with *Rashi*'s framework: it is not clear that deferrability alone would render a *melacha* biblically forbidden. After all, grinding spices is permitted on *Yom Tov* even though one could presumably have ground them the day before, because freshly ground spices are of superior quality — but that is a difference in degree, not kind. In any case, *Rashi*'s approach is effectively rejected by the *Rishonim* on the weight of evidence against it.

### Tosafot/Yerushalmi

*Tosafos* quotes the famous *Yerushalmi* that connects the laws of *melacha* on *Yom Tov* to the verse *ushmartem es hamatzos*, juxtaposing *melacha* with the duty to guard the *matzos* from becoming *chametz*. The point at which one must guard the dough is when the flour is added to the water — the kneading. The implication, as the *Yerushalmi* develops it, is that only *melachos* from the kneading (*lisha*) onward are permitted on *Yom Tov*. Trapping, which occurs far earlier in the food-production process, falls outside this range. The difficulty, however, is that we find in the *Gemara* that *borer* under certain immediate circumstances and grinding of spices are permitted — and these *melachos* occur in the flour-processing stage, before any analog to kneading. This creates a tension with the *Yerushalmi*'s framework and requires a reconceptualization of what *milisha va'eilach* actually means.

### Ramban Framework

The *Ramban* provides what is probably the most compelling resolution. His formulation appears to be stated at the level of *de'oraisa*. He notes that two distinct *pesukim* permit food-related activity on *Yom Tov*: one speaks of *ach asher ye'aseh lechol nefesh* — things done for the sake of food — and the other, in contexts where that explicit permission is absent, uses the phrase *meleches avodah* rather than the categorical *melacha* of *Shabbos*. The *Ramban* focuses precisely on this term *meleches avodah*.

His distinction is not a categorical list of prohibited *melachos* but a contextual one. *Meleches avodah* refers to work performed out in the field, on a large scale, over extended periods — *leyamim harbeh* — as a major processing operation. By contrast, work done in the home or kitchen in immediate preparation for eating is not *meleches avodah* and is therefore permitted. Thus grinding wheat into flour is *meleches avodah*, but grinding spices for freshly seasoned food tonight is a home-based, kitchen-based activity and is not. Catching wild animals belongs to that prior, large-scale category of field work — it is not the kind of thing one does in the immediate context of preparing a meal. Indeed, the *Ramban* adds that anyone living a domesticated life would plan to have meat caught days in advance rather than depend on a successful hunt the same day.

### Ran's View

The *Ran* finds himself sympathetic to the *Ramban*'s type of distinction but ultimately cannot accept it as a framework operating at the biblical level. His difficulty is that if the distinction were biblical, it ought to track clear categories of *melacha* rather than the context in which a given *melacha* is performed. He therefore concludes that all these distinctions are rabbinic — that biblically one would be permitted to go out and catch animals, harvest wheat, and grind it on *Yom Tov*, and that it is only rabbinic legislation that drew the line. The majority of *Rishonim*, however, hold that these distinctions do operate at the biblical level, and the *Ramban*'s conceptualization remains the most coherent account of where the line falls.

---

## Non-Jew Bringing Items

### Rav Pappa Ruling

Turning now to the other important topic under discussion: the case of a non-Jew who brings items on *Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* records the ruling of Rav Pappa: *hilcheta*, *nochri sheheivi doron leyisrael beyom tov* — if a non-Jew brings a gift for a Jew on *Yom Tov* — *im yesh me'oto hamin bimechubar assur* — if that type of produce is currently in a state where it could have been harvested that day, it is forbidden.

### Muktzeh Concerns

The reason in this first case is *muktzeh*. Since we have already established that *safek muchan* is *assur*, one must assume the produce was attached to the ground and harvested on *Yom Tov* itself, rendering it *muktzeh*.

### Post-YT Restriction

The *Gemara* continues: *le'erev nami assurin* — even in the evening after *Yom Tov*, when *muktzeh* is no longer a concern, the produce remains forbidden. The reason is *bichdei sheye'aseh* — one must wait after *Yom Tov* the amount of time it would have taken to complete the work had it been done at that point.

### Bikhdei Sheya'asu

An interesting question arises as to how one measures *bikhdei sheya'asu* in practice. If the non-Jew brings a hundred bushels of apples, does one measure by how long it would take a crew to harvest them, or by the time for the actual *melacha* of picking a single apple, or by the time it would take to transport the goods to the recipient's location? This question of quantification is left open, but the operative principle is clear: one cannot benefit from these items until one has waited, after *Yom Tov*, the amount of time that would have been required to produce them.

### Techumim Concern

The second case: *ve'im ein me'oto hamin bimechubar* — if it is past the harvest season for that species, so there is no concern that the items were picked today. Here there is no *muktzeh* issue. On *Yom Tov*, the only remaining concern is *techumim* — the possibility that the non-Jew brought the items from beyond the *techum*. If he brought them from within the *techum*, they are permitted (*toch hatchum mutar*). If he brought them from beyond the *techum* (*chutz latchum*) — this appears at the top of 25a — they are forbidden, again with the same rule of *bichdei sheye'aseh*. So even when *muktzeh* is not at issue, there remains a principle that one cannot immediately benefit from what a non-Jew did in violation of *Yom Tov* restrictions.

### Jew-to-Jew Exception

There is, however, an exception: *ve'haba bishvil Yisrael zeh mutar leyisrael acher* — if the non-Jew brought the items for one particular Jew, another Jew is permitted to benefit from them. The significance of this exception will be clarified in the discussion of the underlying rationale below.

---

## Rashi: Neheneh

### Neheneh Concept

Two major approaches are offered to explain why a Jew cannot benefit from what a non-Jew brought for him. *Rashi* ties the case to the concept found in the laws of *Shabbos* of being *neheneh* from *melachet nochri* — deriving benefit from *melacha* performed by a non-Jew on *Shabbos* for a Jew. If a non-Jew cooks food for a Jew on *Shabbos* — even entirely of his own initiative, without being asked — the Jew is forbidden to benefit from it. This principle, says *Rashi*, applies equally when the non-Jew performs a *melacha* for a Jew on *Yom Tov*.

### Rashi Logic

This explains the extension of the prohibition into *motzaei Yom Tov* as well. Normally, once *Shabbos* ends, one may derive benefit from what a non-Jew did. *Rashi* explains that the waiting period of *bikhdei sheya'asu* is required because during that window one is still effectively deriving benefit from the *Shabbos* violation: had the *melacha* not been performed on *Shabbos*, one would have had to wait at least that long after *Shabbos* for it to be completed. By benefiting within that time, one is benefiting from the fact that it was done on *Shabbos*. Only once *bikhdei sheya'asu* has elapsed can one be said to derive no benefit from the violation itself.

By this logic, *Rashi* also explains the *Jew-to-Jew* exception: since in the *techum* case the violation is only rabbinic, the Sages were lenient and permitted another Jew to benefit.

### Ramban Refinement

The *Ramban* sharpens the conceptual analysis further. The principle of being *neheneh* from *melacha* on *Shabbos* applies, he argues, only where the *melacha* produced something new — a new reality that did not previously exist. Cooked food is a new reality; the *Shabbos* violation created something that was not there before.

### Carrying Exception

Carrying, by contrast, does not create a new reality. The object is exactly what it was; it has merely changed location. Accordingly, there is a genuine debate among the *poskim* as to whether the concept of *neheneh mimelachet Shabbat* applies to carrying at all. The item is now accessible to the beneficiary, which is something new for him — but the object itself is unchanged.

### Techumim Weakest

*Techumim* is an even weaker case than carrying, because the issue with *techumim* is not even the physical relocation of an object so much as a question of one's position relative to where the object was. Other Jews theoretically had access to the same items; it is merely a matter of the recipient's location versus the item's location. This, says the *Ramban*, is why the *Gemara* goes more lenient in the *techum* case and permits another Jew to derive benefit — particularly since hypothetically any Jew within range of the items could have had access to them.

---

## Tosafot Reject Rashi

### Non-Jew More Problem

*Tosafos*, the *Ramban*, and the other *Rishonim* reject *Rashi*'s approach entirely, and this rejection is the position accepted *le-halacha*. Their argument is that the concept of *neheneh mimelachet Shabbat* cannot be what is driving the ruling here. The reason is that this concept — benefiting from a *Shabbos* violation — applies equally when a Jew performs the *melacha* and when a non-Jew does, yet we find that *bikhdei sheya'asu* applies uniquely to the case of a non-Jew.

### Risk of Request

Specifically, when a Jew violates *Shabbos* and, say, picks an apple for another Jew, that apple is forbidden to the violator but *immediately* permitted to others after *Shabbos*. There is no requirement to wait *bikhdei sheya'asu*. *Bikhdei sheya'asu* applies only when a non-Jew performed the *melacha*. Why the difference? Because the concern in the case of the non-Jew is not merely conceptual — the worry that one has derived benefit from a violation — but entirely practical: if one is permitted to benefit immediately after *Yom Tov* from what the non-Jew did, one will arrange in advance for the non-Jew to perform *melacha* on *Yom Tov* so that the benefit is available immediately at *motzaei Yom Tov*. It is this proactive arrangement that the Rabbis sought to prevent.

### Modern Application

This concern has a practical dimension in later *halachic* discussion as well. Some *poskim* note, in connection with hospital Shabbos scheduling, that one should not specifically assign a non-observant Jewish doctor to a *Shabbos* shift on the reasoning that "he doesn't keep *Shabbos* anyway." On the contrary — an observant Jewish doctor taking the shift will be careful to perform only what *halacha* permits, while the other arrangement risks producing precisely the casual attitude toward *Shabbos melacha* that the Rabbis were concerned about.

### Non-Jew Only Rule

To summarize: the prohibition of *bikhdei sheya'asu* does not apply to *melacha* done by a Jew. It applies specifically to *melacha* done by a non-Jew, because only in that case is there a risk of proactively arranging for forbidden work to be done for one's benefit.

### Two-Day YT Debate

This analysis generates an important practical *nafka mina* regarding two-day *Yom Tov*. If the non-Jew performs *melacha* for a Jew on the first day of *Yom Tov*, may the Jew benefit from it on the second day within *bikhdei sheya'asu*?

### Rashi vs Tosafot

*Rashi* would say yes. His reasoning flows from *sefeika deyoma*: if yesterday were *chol*, the non-Jew was permitted to pick the apples; if yesterday were *Yom Tov*, then today is *chol* and one could hypothetically have had the apples picked during the hours since the second day began. Either way, one is not benefiting from a *Yom Tov* violation, because whichever day was truly *Yom Tov*, there exists a hypothetical scenario in which the work could have been done on the other day. Therefore, by *Rashi*'s logic, two hours into the second day one may already benefit.

*Tosafos* rejects this. For *Tosafos*, the concern has nothing to do with the conceptual question of whether one is benefiting from a violation. The concern is purely practical: will this arrangement lead you to ask the non-Jew to work for you? And the answer is clearly yes. If you are permitted to benefit on day two from what the non-Jew did on day one, you will arrange for exactly that next year. The *shakla ve'tarya* of *sefeika deyoma* is intellectually elegant but practically irrelevant to the concern at hand. One must therefore wait until after *Yom Tov* entirely before benefiting. The *halacha* follows the interpretation of *Tosafos*.

---

## Fish Channel Case

### Sluice Gate Case

The *Gemara* now presents the ruling of Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav: *hasocher amat hamayim me'erev Yom Tov* — if one closed off an irrigation channel or waterway with sluice gates on *erev Yom Tov*, creating a closed system, and the next morning on *Yom Tov* one found fish in it — they are permitted.

### Fish Already Caught

The reasoning is that since the system was closed from before *Yom Tov*, anything inside is considered already caught. The fish were effectively secured from *erev Yom Tov* and are therefore *muchan* — prepared and designated from before *Yom Tov* — and may be used.

---

## Wild Animal Nesting

### Rav Chisda Inference

Rav Chisda draws an inference from this ruling: *chaya shekinina bepardes* — a wild animal, say a deer, that has made its nest in a garden — *eina tzericha zimmun* — does not require prior verbal designation (*zimmun*). The reasoning by analogy is that just as the fish caught in a closed channel are considered *muchan* without requiring special designation, so too a young wild animal that has settled in one's garden is considered effectively caught and *muchan* without any act of *zimmun*.

### Rav Nachman Objection

Rav Nachman objects that Rav Chisda — or, according to the alternative version, Rabbah bar Rav Huna himself, in which case it is Rav Nachman who notes that the son of their colleague got himself into a debate of *gedolim* — has made an inference that does not hold. One cannot simply move from the fish case to the wild animal case.

### Active vs Passive

The distinction is clear: *hatam lo ka avid ma'aseh* — in the wild animal case, the owner did nothing. The animal simply wandered into the garden and nested on its own. Even if the animal is practically inaccessible and one is already thinking of using it, what has the owner actually done to establish that he intends to use it? There is no act that reflects any planning. *Hacha ka avid ma'aseh* — in the fish case, by contrast, the owner actively closed the sluice gates, performing a deliberate act that caught the fish. That active step both secures the fish and reflects the owner's intention to use them.

### Shmaya V'Abtalyon

The *Gemara* brings a *braita* as evidence that in the wild animal case, *zimmun* is indeed required: *chaya shekinina bepardes tzericha lezamen* — a wild animal that has taken up lodging in a garden must be verbally designated before *Yom Tov*. The *braita* also notes that a *tzippor dror* — a particular species of bird — must have its wings bound so as not to be confused with its mother, since the young of this species resemble the parent closely in size. This testimony is traced back to the authority of *Shmaya ve'Abtalyon*, the teachers of Hillel and Shammai. The *Gemara* declares this a *tiyufta* — a refutation of the inference that no *zimmun* is needed.

### Bird Wing Binding

The wing-binding requirement for the *tzippor dror* is not an act of *zimmun* in itself but rather a practical measure: *kedei shelo titchalef be'imah* — so that the designated bird not be confused with its mother. Even after one has performed *zimmun* on the young bird, without binding its wings one cannot reliably identify which bird was designated.

### Counter-Braita

The *Gemara* immediately complicates this picture. A second *braita* records Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that if one designated birds inside a nest and then found birds outside the nest, those outside birds are forbidden — because one cannot be certain they are the same ones that were designated. This rule applies to *yonei shovach* and *yonei aliyah* (birds of the coop and the loft) and birds that have nested in crevices in walls. These are species one would not automatically assume one plans to eat, and so they require *zimmun*.

However, the *braita* then distinguishes: *avazin ve'tarnigolin* — ducks and chickens — and *yonei hordisiyot* (Herodian pigeons kept regularly for eating), and *chayah shekinena bepardes* — a wild animal that has taken up lodging in one's garden — *muttarin*, they are permitted without any *zimmun*. Here, then, we have a direct contradiction: one *braita* in the name of *Shmaya ve'Abtalyon* requires *zimmun* for the nesting wild animal, while this second *braita* explicitly exempts it.

The *braita* also reiterates that the *tzippor dror* must have its wings bound even after *zimmun*, so as not to be confused with its mother. It further notes that birds found bound or obviously handled (*keshurim u'vimnu'im*) — and birds found in wells, cisterns (*shichin*), or caves — are permitted, while those found in trees are forbidden even if previously designated, because accessing them would require climbing and potentially breaking branches, which constitutes *uvda d'chol*. And birds that have been tagged by others are forbidden everywhere on account of *gezel*.

### Mother vs Baby

Rav Nachman initially suggests resolving the contradiction by distinguishing between the mother deer and the baby: it is the mother that requires *zimmun*, and the baby that does not. The *Gemara* presses him: how can *zimmun* alone suffice for the mother? It is not simply a *muktzeh* question — *tzeida me'alya ba'ya* — the mother is a fully mobile wild animal; one would need to actually trap her. A mere verbal designation does not address the fact that catching her requires a genuine act of *tzida*. Indeed, up to this point in the discussion one might have thought that the *kinyan chatzer* of the garden treats even the mother as effectively caught, but the *Gemara* now reveals that this assumption is untenable: the mother deer will not wait around to be caught simply because she has nested in a domesticated space. Only the young animal, which cannot easily escape, can be considered effectively caught by virtue of its presence in the owner's domain.

### Garden Location

The *Gemara* therefore accepts the resolution of Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: *idi ve'idi bedida* — in both contradicting *braisos* we are discussing the young animal, not the mother. The question of *zimmun* is solely a *muktzeh* issue, not a trapping issue. The difference between the two *braisos* is one of location: *ha begina smucha le'ir ha begina she'eina smucha* — one *braita* addresses a garden close to the city (effectively the owner's backyard), and the other addresses a garden at some distance. If the young deer is in one's backyard, one may presume one was aware of it and planned to use it; no verbal *zimmun* is required. If it is in a more distant orchard or garden, *zimmun* is required.

---

## Mesukenet Animal

### Mesukenet Shechita

The *Mishnah* now takes up the case of a *behema mesukenet* — an animal in danger of imminent death, whether from old age or illness. Such an animal is not a *treifa* (which would render *shechita* ineffective), but if it dies before *shechita*, it becomes a *neveilah*. One therefore wishes to *shecht* it on *Yom Tov* not so much because one needs an extra portion of meat that day but in order to preserve the animal's *kashrus* status. The *Mishnah* rules: *lo yishchot ella im ken yesh shahut bayom le'echol mimena kezayit tzli* — one may not *shecht* the *mesukenet* unless there is sufficient time remaining in the day to eat at least one roasted *kezayit* from it on *Yom Tov*. Only then can the *shechita* be said to have been performed, at least in part, for the sake of *Yom Tov* itself.

Notably, the *Mishnah* does not require that one actually go ahead and eat that *kezayit*, but only that there be time to do so in theory. How much of a *lecha'tchila* requirement this imposes — and to what extent eating the *kezayit* is merely a formal pretext versus a genuine expression of *Yom Tov* need — remains a question.

### Rabi Akiva Raw

Rabbi Akiva offers a more lenient position: *afilu kezayit chai mibeis tevichaso* — even a raw *kezayit* of meat from the site of the *shechita* suffices. Since one could in principle eat raw meat, and one can immediately access meat from the neck of the animal right where the *shechita* was performed, this minimal possibility of consumption is enough to validate the *shechita* for *Yom Tov* purposes.

### Field Shechita

The *Mishnah* addresses a further case: *shachata basadeh* — if one *shecht* the animal out in a field. One may not bring it back using carrying beams or poles, in the manner of people transporting a whole slaughtered animal from the market — that would constitute *uvda d'chol*, weekday-like activity. Instead, one must bring it back section by section by hand (*evarim evarim*). This is more laborious (*tircha*) but avoids the appearance of a commercial weekday transaction.

---

## Flaying Dismember

### Torah Flaying

Rami bar Abba observes that the *Torah* mentions flaying (*hefsheit*) and dismemberment (*nituach*) in the context of the *korban olah* — *hiphshit es ha'olah ve'nitach osah linetacheha* — and states that the same principle applies to butchers: one should not eat meat before the animal has been flayed and dismembered. The teaching is introduced as: *mikan limdah Torah derech eretz shelo yochal adam basar kodem hefsheit venituach* — from here the *Torah* teaches proper conduct, that one should not eat meat before it has been flayed and cut up. The *Gemara* will consider whether this is purely a matter of *derech eretz* or whether it carries *halachic* implications.

### Derech Eretz Not Law

The *Gemara* asks: *mai ka mashma lan* — what is this teaching us? Could it be that Rami bar Abba is coming to reject the position of Rav Huna? The answer, as the *Gemara* establishes, is that his teaching is not *halachic* in nature. Rather, as Rami bar Abba himself indicates, he is teaching *derech eretz* — proper conduct — not a *halacha*.

### Rav Huna Issur

Rav Huna's position is as follows: *behemah bechayeha bechezkas issur omedes ad sheyivada lecha bemah shechitah* — a living animal stands in a presumptive status of prohibition (*chezkas issur*) until one definitively knows that it was *shecht* properly. The significance of this goes beyond the obvious requirement to *shecht*: it means that in a case of *safek* — for instance, if there is uncertainty whether a nick in the knife occurred before or after the *shechita* — one cannot remove the *chezkas issur* without definitive knowledge that the *shechita* was valid. (*Tosafos* formulates a distinct prohibition called *eino zavuach* — the state of not having been *shecht*, derived from the positive commandment *ve'zavachta ve'achalta* — which applies whether the animal is alive or dead, further grounding the *chezkas issur* framework.)

### After Shechita Heter

Once one knows definitively that the *shechita* was performed correctly — the knife examined, the act observed and confirmed — the animal shifts to a *chezkas heter*: *ad sheyivada lecha bemah nitreifah* — it is presumptively permitted until one knows for certain that it is a *treifa*. This means one is not required to examine every organ for potential *treifos*; any doubt is resolved in favor of *heter* unless one has positive knowledge of a *treifa*.

### Meiyut Threshold

This is not, however, the full picture as the *halacha* ultimately stands. A distinction is drawn between *mi'ut she'eino matzui* — an uncommon defect occurring in fewer than approximately 5% of cases — and *mi'ut hamatzui* — a defect occurring at that threshold or above. For defects in the former category, the *chezkas heter* operates fully and no checking is required even when checking is possible. But once a defect occurs with sufficient regularity, if it is possible to check, one must check. This is why the lungs are examined: problems in the lungs occur often enough to qualify as *mi'ut hamatzui*, and since the lungs are accessible, they must be inspected. If the lungs are lost after *shechita*, however — for instance, if an animal made off with them — the animal remains permitted, because the *chezkas heter* holds in the absence of positive knowledge of *treifus*.

### Flaying Question

Given this framework, the *Gemara* considers whether Rami bar Abba's teaching about flaying and dismemberment might carry *halachic* content: perhaps requiring flaying and dismemberment before eating is meant to mandate checking for *treifos* before consuming the meat.

### No Checking Required

The *Gemara* rejects this interpretation. The *Mishnah* itself supports Rav Huna's position that there is no *halachic* requirement to check before eating: *de-tenan*, Rabbi Akiva says one may eat even a raw *kezayit* from the site of the *shechita* — before any flaying, dismemberment, or inspection. (The *Gemara* briefly considers whether *mibeis tevichaso* means literally from the neck area, or — as one reading suggests — from the stomach meat, something easier to eat raw; Rabbi Chiya's *braita* confirms the literal reading: it means the actual place of *shechita*, the neck meat.) Thus there is no *halachic* objection to eating before checking.

### Ravenousness Point

Accordingly, the conclusion is that Rami bar Abba's teaching is precisely what it appeared to be at the outset: *orchis de-aretz kamashma lan* — he is imparting proper conduct. The point is not *halacha*; it is the admonition against ravenousness. One should not tear at the meat before it has been properly flayed and cut up, simply because one cannot restrain oneself.

---

## Derech Eretz

### Garlic Onion

The *Gemara* continues with a series of teachings on restraint in eating and drinking. A *braita* rules: *lo yochal adam shum u'vatzal me'rosho ella me'alav* — one should not eat a garlic or an onion from the root end but rather from where the leaves emerge (what we would call the top). Eating from the root end is a sign of ravenousness — apparently because it suggests one cannot even be bothered to hold the vegetable in the normal way. *Ve'im achal harei ze ra'avtan* — if one does eat that way, one has shown oneself to be ravenous. The point in bringing this *braita* is to demonstrate that Rabbinic literature regularly addresses not *halachic* questions but matters of how not to conduct oneself in a gluttonous manner.

### Drinking Gulps

Similarly: *lo yishkeh adam koso be'vat achat* — one should not drink an entire cup of wine in a single gulp. *Ve'im shasah harei ze gargran* — if one does, one is a glutton. A further *braita* elaborates: drinking in one gulp is gluttonous; drinking in two gulps is *derech eretz* — the normal, proper manner; drinking in three or more very small sips, however, is *migasay haruach* — a mark of haughtiness. Proper comportment lies in the middle.

### Orlah Lesson

The same Rami bar Abba teaches: *neti'ah mekate'a ragleihen de-kasvaya ud'baalei niddot* — the principle of planting and waiting is what undercuts the legs of two groups who lack patience. The reference is to *orlah*: one invests years of care in a tree but must wait three full years before eating any of its fruit. This demands sustained patience and self-restraint, and the *Torah* holds it up as a lesson.

### Butchers Restraint

The lesson of *orlah* is directed at butchers and at *baalei niddot*. For butchers: even though *halachically* one may eat from meat before checking it for *treifos*, acting with some patience and restraint — not tearing at the meat the moment it is *shecht* — is the proper conduct. Who wants to discover a week later that by rushing one consumed *treifa* meat? The *orlah* model teaches that certain pleasures require patience. Similarly, *baalei niddot* — men who cannot restrain themselves from approaching their wives before *tehara* and immersion in the *mikvah* — should internalize the lesson of *orlah*: some of the deepest pleasures in life require waiting before they may be enjoyed.

### Turmus Bean

*Tormusa mekate'a ragleihen de-soneihen de-Yisrael* — the *turmus* bean undercuts the legs of the enemies of the Jews, which idiomatically refers to the Jews themselves. The *turmus* is a type of bean that must be cooked seven times before it is edible, yet even after all that labor it is eaten only as a light dessert course, not as a main dish. The significance of this image is developed in the next section.

---

## Torah to Israel

### Seven Gods

The seven cookings of the *turmus* are placed in correspondence with a verse in *Shoftim*: *Vayosifu Bnei Yisrael la'asot ha-ra be'einei Hashem vaya'avdu et ha-Ba'alim* — and they continued to do evil and worship foreign gods. Counting the deities mentioned in the verse: *Ba'alim* (1), *Ashtarot* (2), *elohei Aram* (3), *elohei Tzidon* (4), *elohei Moav* (5), *elohei Bnei Amon* (6), *elohei Plishtim* (7). Seven foreign gods — corresponding to seven cookings.

### Turmus Metaphor

The verse concludes: *ve'et Hashem azvu ve'lo avaduhu* — they abandoned God and did not worship Him. Once the verse states they abandoned God, it is obvious they did not worship Him; what then is the additional import of the phrase *ve'lo avaduhu*? The *Gemara* answers: *amar Elazar amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu afilu k'tormusa hazeh shesholkin oto sheva pe'amim ve'ochlin oto be'kinuach seuda lo asuni banai* — even like this bean that is cooked seven times and eaten only as a dessert, My children did not make Me even that. *Rashi* offers two readings: either the Jewish people are the bean — subjected to seven punishments for their seven apostasies, yet still they strayed, making them harder to "cook" than the bean — or God Himself is the bean, and the point is that Israel did not even keep God around as a dessert, something one has alongside seven other dishes. They abandoned Him entirely, not even maintaining Him as an afterthought alongside their seven foreign gods. The *Maharsha* favors the second reading.

### Tough Nature

The sugya transitions to a *tana* who teaches in the name of Rabbi Meir: *mipnei mah nitna Torah le-Yisrael mipnei shehen azim* — why was the *Torah* given to Israel? Because they are hard and stubborn. The tradition from the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives this from the verse *mimino esh dat lamo* — from God's right hand, a fiery law for His people.

### Torah Fire

One reading of this verse is: *re'uyin elu she-tinaten lahem dat esh* — these people are worthy of receiving a law of fire, they are tough enough to handle it. An alternative reading: *datehem shel elu esh* — their very nature is fire. *She-ilmalei nitna Torah le-Yisrael ein kol uma ve-lashon yecholim la'amod bifneihem* — had the *Torah* not been given to Israel, no nation on earth could withstand them. The *Torah* is what tames and channels that fierce, unyielding quality; without it, Israel's intensity would be entirely destructive. The sugya thus attempts to present the attribute of *keshiyut* — stubbornness — in a dual light: it is what has led Israel to sin repeatedly, but it is also what enables Israel to hold fast to God and *Torah* when properly directed.

### Three Tough Groups

Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish concludes with a list of three that are exceptionally tough: *Yisrael be-umot* — Israel among the nations; *kelev be-chayot* — the dog among animals (not the fiercest, but the most tenacious and persistent); *tarnegol be-ofot* — the rooster among birds. Some add: *ez bi-vehemah daka* — the goat among small domesticated animals; and some further add *tzalaf be-ilanot* — the *tzalaf* among trees, though *Rashi* is uncertain of the precise significance of this last addition.

---

---

# Beitzah 28

## Neveila & Muktzeh

### Dead Animal Prohibition

The *mishna* on Beitzah 28a opens with a case that might appear straightforward but quickly reveals layers of complexity: *behema shemessa lo yezizena mimekomah* — if an animal dies on *yom tov*, one may not move it from its place, because it is *muktzeh* and has no permitted use. The question of whether it might serve as dog food will be addressed in due course.

### Tarfon's Question

Immediately following this ruling, the *mishna* records a historical episode: *u'maaseh she'shalu es Rebbe Tarfon aleha* — they brought the question before Rebbe Tarfon. Two cases were posed together: the dead animal and the case of *challah* — dough separated as *terumah* — that had become *tamei*. *Terumah* that becomes *tamei* can only be burned; there is no other permitted use. Rebbe Tarfon entered the *beis medrash* and solicited the opinion of the assembled scholars, and they replied: *lo yezizam mimekomam* — neither may be moved from its place. It is striking that Rebbe Tarfon, normally counted among the great authorities, goes to consult the anonymous *beis medrash*, but that was the conclusion: both *tamei challah* and a dead animal are *muktzeh* on *yom tov*.

### Rebbe Shimon Debate

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge: *lema t'nan stama d'lo k'Rebbe Shimon*? Is the anonymous *mishna* departing from the position of Rebbe Shimon? A *beraisa* records that Rebbe Shimon permits one to chop up a gourd for an animal and, more relevantly, to chop up a *neveila* — an animal carcass — to feed to dogs on *Shabbos*. Rebbe Yehuda in that *beraisa* disagrees, holding that if the animal had not already died by *erev Shabbos*, it is *assur*, because when *Shabbos* began, the animal's use as dog food had not yet been contemplated.

The underlying logic of Rebbe Shimon's leniency is clear: since the animal might have been used for food had it been slaughtered before death, its potential utility was at least thinkable, and thus *muktzeh* is not so severe. A *kal v'chomer* would suggest this is even more lenient on *yom tov*, when *shechita* is permitted and the animal could plausibly have been slaughtered for food before it died.

### Healthy vs. Sickly

The *gemara* responds: *afilu tema Rebbe Shimon* — even if the *mishna* represents Rebbe Shimon's view, there is a basis to distinguish. According to the tradition cited in the name of Rava by Mar bar Ameimar, Rebbe Shimon concedes that a healthy animal that dropped dead is *assur* — *modeh haya Rebbe Shimon bebaalei chayim shemesu she'asurim*. Based on this, Rashi explains that the *beraisa* in which Rebbe Shimon permits chopping the carcass for dogs concerns an animal that was visibly near death — sickly and expected to die. The distinction is embedded in the language: our *mishna* says *behema shemessa*, which evokes a sudden, unexpected death, whereas the *beraisa* speaks of *haneveila*, already framing the animal as a carcass, suggesting it was anticipated.

However, a second tradition — Mar brei d'Rav Yosef, also in the name of Rava — holds that Rebbe Shimon's leniency would apply even to a healthy animal that died unexpectedly: *chaluk haya Rebbe Shimon afilu bebaalei chayim shemesu shemutarim*. According to this view, Rebbe Shimon sees no *muktzeh* problem in any case of a dead animal that can be used as dog food, and if so, the question arises again: how can our *mishna* forbid it while still representing Rebbe Shimon's position?

### Kodshim Exception

The *gemara* offers a resolution: *targmuha Ze'iri bevehemas kodshim* — the *mishna* is speaking of a sanctified animal, one that had been consecrated as a *korban*. Even Rebbe Shimon would agree that a sanctified animal which dies is *muktzeh*, because once it is dead it cannot simply be fed to dogs.

Rashi explains the double prohibition in this case. First, a dead animal cannot be redeemed — redemption of *kodshim* requires a living animal. Second, and even if we were to entertain the possibility of redeeming a dead animal, there is an independent principle: *ain podin es hakodshim lehachilam le'klavim* — one may not redeem *kodshim* for the purpose of feeding the carcass to dogs. Such an act would be a *bizayon* to *kodshim*, a degradation of sanctified property. Therefore, what must be done with such an animal is to bury it. It is *muktzeh* in the fullest sense: there is simply no permitted use for it on *yom tov*.

The *gemara* then notes that this interpretation is supported by the parallel structure of the *mishna* itself: *deika nami* — it can be inferred from the fact that the *mishna* links the dead animal to *challah* that became *tamei*. *Mai challa dikdusha* — what characterizes the *challah* case? It is sanctified. *Af behema dikdusha* — so too, the animal in question is sanctified. The two cases are thus paired as instances of *kodshim*-related *muktzeh*, and the *mishna* may indeed represent Rebbe Shimon's position.

The *gemara* then tests this resolution. According to Mar brei d'Rav Yosef, who holds that Rebbe Shimon would permit even a healthy *chulin* animal that dropped dead, the distinction works cleanly: only *kodshim* remains *assur*, while *chulin* would be *mutar* — *shapir*. But according to Mar bar Ameimar, who holds that Rebbe Shimon concedes the prohibition even in a healthy *chulin* animal, there is a difficulty: if even a healthy *chulin* animal is *assur* according to Rebbe Shimon, why does the *mishna* need to be limited to the exceptional case of *kodshim*? The *gemara* answers: *hacha bemai askinan bimesuchenes vedivrei hakol* — the *mishna* may be describing a sickly animal on the verge of death, a case in which Rebbe Shimon would normally permit, and the only reason it is *assur* here is the additional factor of *kodshim*.

In summary, the *gemara* offers two approaches to reconcile the *mishna* with Rebbe Shimon: the first is a distinction between healthy and sickly animals, the second is the special stringency of *kodshim*. Each approach works differently depending on which tradition in Rava's name one accepts regarding Rebbe Shimon's position.

### Impure Challah Problem

While the *gemara*'s analysis focuses on the dead animal, Tosafot observes that the more interesting question is actually the case of *tamei challah*. If *tamei challah* must be burned, and the *halacha* is that one is permitted to derive benefit from it in the course of burning it — meaning one may cook over its flames — why should it be *muktzeh*? Why not burn it on *yom tov* and use the heat for cooking?

Tosafot's answer draws an analogy to the prohibition against bringing *shelamim* on *yom tov* when the obligation does not arise on that day. The *gemara* earlier explained that *shelamim* is fundamentally a *korban*, and the eating from it is only secondary; therefore, the act of slaughtering it is an act of bringing a *korban*, not an act of *ochel nefesh*. Tosafot applies the same logic here: burning *tamei challah* is fundamentally the fulfillment of the *mitzvah* of destroying *terumah* that became *tamei* — the incidental benefit derived from the fire is secondary and does not transform the act into one done *letzorech ochel nefesh*. It is this reasoning that accounts for the *muktzeh* status of *tamei challah* on *yom tov*, even though benefit from it is technically permitted. Tosafot regards this as a more substantive question than the one the *gemara* itself chose to address.

---

## Commerce & Divisions

### No Money Talk

The following *mishna* addresses another dimension of *yom tov* practice: the prohibition against organizing the purchase or division of an animal on *yom tov* itself. *Ein nimnin al habehema lechatchila beYom Tov* — one may not appoint oneself upon an animal, that is, join a group for it, at the outset on *yom tov*. However, one may join together before *yom tov*, and then slaughter and divide on *yom tov* itself.

The *gemara* asks what this prohibition means precisely, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains: *ein poskin damim lechatchila al habehema beYom Tov* — one may not set prices for an animal on *yom tov*. The concern is explicitly financial: going through the calculation of who pays how much and who therefore receives what proportion is a form of *mekach u'mimkar*, commercial transaction, even if no money physically changes hands on *yom tov* itself.

### Equal Division Method

One might ask how, then, one is to acquire meat on *yom tov* at all. Rav provides an answer: *mevi shtei behemot u'maamidam zu etzel zu ve'omer zu kazu* — bring two animals and stand them side by side, and say "this one is like that one." After *yom tov*, one assesses the value of the remaining living animal, and since both were agreed to be equivalent, the value of the acquired animal follows. This method works equally for cut portions: two steaks that appear roughly equal in size can be treated the same way. Crucially, no money is discussed on *yom tov* — only an equivalence is established.

### Proportion Division

A *beraisa* then spells this out explicitly: *lo yomar adam lachaveiro hareini imcha be'sela hareini imcha be'shtayim* — one may not say "I'll chip in a *sela*" or "I'll chip in two." But one may say: *hareini imcha l'mechtza l'shlish l'revia* — "I'll take half," "I'll take a third," "I'll take a quarter." One speaks in proportions, not in prices. After *yom tov*, the monetary value of the proportion is worked out. The money itself is deferred; what is transacted on *yom tov* is only the allocation of shares.

This is a striking degree of latitude, and one that many people may be unaware of. The logic, however, is coherent: the *Torah* permits *melechet ochel nefesh* — labor related to food preparation — and obtaining possession of the food itself is an integral part of that process. The latitude given here for acquisition and division is part of the same logic that permits carrying on *yom tov*: conveyance and transfer are themselves part of what it means to prepare food. The concern about this resembling *uvda d'chol* is real — and the *gemara* itself raises it — but it is considered sufficiently addressed by the fact that explicit monetary discussion is avoided and the context is clearly food for *simchat Yom Tov*.

### Scale Usage Debate

The next *mishna* continues this theme. Rabbi Yehuda says: *shokel adam basar k'neged hakli o k'neged hakopitz* — one may weigh meat against a vessel or against the cleaver. Rather than using calibrated weights on a balance scale, one places a hammer or some other utensil on one side and meat on the other, establishing a rough equivalence. After *yom tov* one weighs the utensil and determines the monetary value accordingly. The *Chachamim* disagree: *ein mashgichin b'chaf moznayim kol ikar* — one may not consult the scale at all, in any form.

### Scale Prohibition

The *gemara* probes the phrase *kol ikar* — "at all." Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains: even using the scale to protect meat from mice is forbidden. One might have imagined that placing meat on a high-hanging scale purely to keep it away from animals, with no intention of weighing it, would be permissible — but no. The scale is a *keli omanut*, a professional instrument, and it is categorically off-limits on *yom tov*. It is entirely associated with commerce and transaction.

Rav Adda bar Avin adds a qualification: the prohibition applies specifically when the scale is hanging from its standard ring — that is, when it is positioned as it would be in its functional mode. If it is taken off its standard peg and used for some unrelated purpose, that restriction may not apply.

### Expert Butcher Rules

Further restrictions follow in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel. An expert butcher may not weigh meat by hand on *yom tov* — even though this involves no scale, a practiced professional holding two items and pronouncing them equivalent is itself a weighing act, and is forbidden. Similarly, such a butcher may not weigh meat by water displacement, using the volume of displaced water to assess the quantity. Both of these methods, while not using the scale directly, constitute real acts of measurement and are therefore forbidden. All of this follows the *Chachamim* against Rabbi Yehuda: a *shinui* is not sufficient to permit what is fundamentally a commercial act of measurement.

### Handle & Mark Rules

Rav Chiya bar Ashi adds that one may not make a *beis yad* — a handle — in a side of meat on *yom tov*. One might carve a hole through a large cut to enable easier carrying, but this act of preparation makes the purchase conspicuous — it presents the appearance of having come directly from a commercial establishment. However, Ravina clarifies: *u'veyado shari* — making an informal opening with one's hand alone, without using a tool and without professional appearance, is permitted, as it does not project the same commercial character.

Rav Huna adds that one is permitted to mark a portion of meat with a distinguishing cut to prevent confusion about whose it is — as in the practice of Rabbah bar Huna, who would cut his meat with a triangular pattern on three corners and then send it home, where it would be recognized as his.

### Mana K'Neged Mana

Against this background, the *gemara* introduces an episode: *Rabbi Chiya v'Rabbi Shimon b'rebi shoklin mana k'neged mana b'Yom Tov* — Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shimon the son of Rebbe would weigh *mana* against *mana* on *yom tov*. That is, when dividing a jointly owned side of beef, they would place equal portions on opposite sides of a balance scale and divide accordingly, each taking half. Neither knew the objective weight; they simply ensured the halves were equal.

This is plainly at odds with the *Chachamim*'s position of *ein mashgichin b'chaf moznayim kol ikar*. Nor does it fit Rabbi Yehuda's more lenient ruling, which the *gemara* reads as permitting only an asymmetric weighing — meat against some unrelated vessel — not meat against meat on opposing sides of the scale. As Rashi explains, *lo shinui* — weighing equal portions against each other is precisely the standard weekday method of dividing a jointly owned object, and Rabbi Yehuda would presumably disallow it for that reason.

The *gemara* therefore concludes that Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe were following the view of Rabbi Yehoshua, as taught in a *beraisa*: *shoklin maneh k'neged maneh b'Yom Tov* — one may weigh equal amounts against each other on *yom tov*. Rav Yosef adds: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehoshua* — we rule like Rabbi Yehoshua, *ho'il v'snan b'Bechoros k'vaseih* — since the *mishna* in Bechoros follows his position.

The citation from Bechoros requires some background. The *bechor*, the firstborn animal, acquires its *kedusha* automatically at birth, not through a verbal act of consecration. Because the *kedusha* was not instilled by the owner, it cannot be removed by the owner either; there is no mechanism of redemption. When a *bechor* develops a *mum* (a blemish) and can no longer be brought as a *korban*, it is eaten by the *kohen* even without being redeemed — the *kedusha* remains in place. Precisely because it retains full *kedusha* and cannot be redeemed, there are additional restrictions on how it may be sold. Unlike a standard *korban* that has been redeemed — which may be sold in the marketplace and weighed in the normal fashion, because the greater the retail value, the more the owner can claim when redeeming the *kedusha* onto its monetary equivalent, thereby benefiting *hekdesh* — a *bechor* that has developed a *mum* may not be sold openly in the *shuk* or weighed in the standard commercial manner. Yet the *mishna* in Bechoros does permit *shoklin maneh k'neged maneh b'bechor* — weighing equal portions against each other in the division of a *bechor*. This is the ruling associated with Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rav Yosef argues: just as *mana k'neged mana* is not treated as degrading *kodshim* in the context of *bechor*, so too it should not be treated as *uvda d'chol* on *yom tov*.

### Bizayon vs Uvda

Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's comparison on two distinct grounds. First, he suggests that the direction of analogy might run the opposite way for *bechor*: perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua permits *mana k'neged mana* by *bechor* precisely because the only concern there is *bizayon kodshim*, and equal-weight division is not regarded as disrespectful. But when it comes to *yom tov*, there is an entirely different concern — *uvda d'chol*, the appearance of weekday commercial activity. A ruling that resolves a *bizayon kodshim* question does not necessarily govern a *uvda d'chol* question.

Alternatively, Abaye raises the inverse possibility: perhaps the Rabbis in Bechoros allow *mana k'neged mana* because their concern there is whether the division shows disrespect to the *kodshim*, and they determine it does not — but they are not ruling on whether it resembles weekday activity. On *yom tov*, where *uvda d'chol* is the operative concern, the Rabbis might be more stringent. The two domains — *bizayon kodshim* and *uvda d'chol* — address different questions, and a lenient ruling in one context does not automatically carry over to the other.

The *gemara* then notes an apparent tension within the story about Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe themselves: if they were so punctilious with each other as to divide their meat in equal portions on a scale, they seem to have been quite *makpid* about each other's shares — yet we know from another account that Rabbi Chiya helped himself to five of seven fish that came to Rebbe's house, and Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe did not object, evidently because their relationship was one of complete mutual generosity. Rav Pappa resolves this by suggesting that the story about *mana k'neged mana* did not involve both of them as a pair — either the second party was not Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe but Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yossi, or if it was Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbe, the other party was Bar Kappara — people with whom a more precise division would have been expected.

The episode ultimately leaves the practical ruling on *mana k'neged mana* unresolved, but it crystallizes the analytical distinction between the two relevant concerns: *bizayon kodshim* governs how sacred objects are treated and pertains to the standing of the object, while *uvda d'chol* governs the general character of one's activities on *yom tov* and pertains to the tone of the day. These are genuinely different considerations, and the *gemara*'s conclusion — implicit in Abaye's challenge — is that they cannot be simply equated.

---

## Sharpening Knives

### Knife Sharpening Ban

A new *mishna* opens with the rule: *ein mashchizin es hasakin b'Yom Tov* — one may not sharpen knives on *yom tov*. However, *aval mesiach al gabi chavertah* — one may rub one knife against another. The familiar method used by chefs of drawing two blades against each other is thus permitted. That is the *shinui*, the indirect method.

Rav Huna further refines the prohibition: *lo shanu ela bemashchezet shel even* — the prohibition of the *mishna* applies specifically to a stone whetstone; a wooden sharpening board (*bemashchezet shel etz*) would be permitted. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel adds another dimension: even the stone whetstone is forbidden only when the purpose is to sharpen — *lo ameru ela lechadada* — but if one's purpose is merely to remove the *shamnunita*, the oil and residue left on the blade, that is permitted even on the whetstone.

The *gemara* then presents two different versions of this discussion. In one reading, the statement about *shamnunita* appears in connection with the stone whetstone, implying that with wood, sharpening itself is permitted. In a stricter reading, the same statement is applied to the knife-against-knife method: even rubbing one blade against another is permitted only to remove *shamnunita*, not to sharpen intentionally. Under this version, intentional sharpening is forbidden regardless of the method — against a stone, against wood, or against another blade — while the only permissible act in any of these contexts is incidental removal of residue. The various permutations of stone or wood, and sharpening or *shamnunita* removal, generate a matrix of opinions, and the *gemara* traces each carefully.

### Sharpening Intent

One might note that Rashi's comment on the *mishna* frames the prohibition in terms of *uvda d'chol* — sharpening a knife on a whetstone is too much of a weekday activity. But the *gemara*'s discussion suggests this may not be the complete picture. If the concern were purely *uvda d'chol*, the details about stone versus wood or intentional sharpening versus *shamnunita* removal would be harder to explain in those terms alone. A different conceptual category seems to be operating as well: the concern that sharpening a sufficiently dull knife might constitute *tikkun mana* — the making or repairing of a utensil. Rashi himself in another place invokes this framing, noting that sharpening resembles *metaken keli*, and if the concern is a real *melacha*, the permissibility of *ochel nefesh* becomes relevant.

### Rebbe Yehuda Position

The *gemara* brings this into focus by asking: *man tanna demashchezet assur?* — who is the *tanna* behind the *mishna's* prohibition of the whetstone? Rav Chisda answers: *d'lo k'Rabbi Yehuda* — not like Rabbi Yehuda. A *beraisa* establishes the principle: *ein bein Yom Tov l'Shabbat ela ochel nefesh bilvad* — the sole difference between *yom tov* and *Shabbos* is that acts of food preparation are permitted. Rabbi Yehuda adds: *Rabbi Yehuda mattir af machshirei ochel nefesh* — Rabbi Yehuda permits even *machshirei ochel nefesh*, acts preparatory to food preparation. Sharpening a knife before slaughter falls squarely into this category. The *mishna*'s prohibition therefore reflects the *Chachamim*, not Rabbi Yehuda.

This reframes the entire issue. If the problem were purely *uvda d'chol*, it would be strange for this to be a *machlokes* between Rabbi Yehuda and the *Chachamim* at all. The *gemara* is now treating it as a substantive question about the scope of permitted labor on *yom tov*: does the *Torah*'s authorization of *melacha* for food purposes extend to acts preparatory to food preparation, or only to the immediate acts of food preparation themselves?

### Halacha V'Ein Morin

Rava, upon hearing Rav Chisda's statement that the *mishna* is not like Rabbi Yehuda, infers that Rav Chisda himself rules like Rabbi Yehuda, and asks him directly: *d'shaminan mishmach halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda?* — should we announce in your name that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda? Rav Chisda responds enthusiastically: *yehei Rava d'kol ki hani millei ma'alyata tidrashun mishmai* — may it be Rava who publicizes all such excellent rulings in my name. He embraces the position warmly.

The implications are significant: if the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda, then preparing the tools needed for cooking — sharpening a knife, or repairing a spit — is permitted on *yom tov*. This represents a substantial expansion of what one may do in the service of *yom tov* food preparation.

Yet the *gemara* immediately qualifies this with a striking episode. Rav Nechemya the son of Rav Yosef reports: *hava ka'imna kamei d'Rava* — I was standing before Rava, and Rava was sharpening his knife against the lip of a wicker basket. Rav Nechemya asked him: are you doing it to sharpen it, or to remove the *shamnunita*? Rava answered: to remove the *shamnunita*. But Rav Nechemya could infer from what Rava was actually doing that he was genuinely sharpening the knife. The conclusion: *v'kasvar halacha v'ein morin ken* — Rava held that the *halacha* is like Rabbi Yehuda, but one does not rule that way publicly.

### Publicity Concerns

Why does Rava not publicize this ruling? Rashi explains: Rabbi Yehuda's leniency for *machshirei ochel nefesh* applies only when one could not have done the preparatory act before *yom tov* — *ee efshar la'asos me'erev Yom Tov*. This is a crucial qualification: when we permit even *melacha* for direct food preparation, we permit it regardless of whether it could have been done earlier, because that is the explicit gift of *yom tov*. But *machshirei ochel nefesh* — preparatory acts — are only permitted when there was no genuine opportunity to do them before *yom tov*. Telling people that *machshirei ochel nefesh* are permitted would inevitably lead people to assume broad latitude, taking it upon themselves to sharpen knives on *yom tov* even when they could easily have done so the day before. The concern is that leniency, once publicized, will be abused.

This is a remarkable application of the principle of *halacha v'ein morin ken* — the *halacha* is one thing, but what one declares publicly is another. It reflects a paternalistic dimension of *psak*: the posek bears responsibility not only for the accuracy of the ruling but for the foreseeable consequences of publicizing it. The pattern appears elsewhere in the *gemara* as well. The question earlier about extinguishing fire for the sake of marital privacy on *yom tov* — where the *gemara* declined to give a straight answer, suggesting instead various workarounds — has been explained by a number of *Rishonim* as another case of *halacha v'ein morin ken*: technically permissible as a *machshir*, but not something the *posek* would openly declare. Once pressed into a corner, the response was an outright *issur*, but the underlying *halacha* was more complex.

A parallel episode is then recorded in Abaye's name: Abaye similarly reports standing before his master (presumably Rabbah), who was sharpening his knife against a millstone. The same question was asked, the same answer was given — *l'ha'avori shamnunita* — and Abaye similarly observed that the real intent was sharpening. The same conclusion follows: *halacha v'ein morin ken*.

### Knife Inspection

A related question is then raised: *mahu l'haros sakin l'chacham b'Yom Tov?* — may one show a knife to a *chacham* on *yom tov* for inspection? Rashi frames the concern as *uvda d'chol*: butchers showing their knives to the local *rav* for approval is a professional weekday activity, and performing it on *yom tov* evokes the commercial routine. Rav Mari the son of Rav Bisna rules leniently; the other Rabbis rule stringently. Rav Yosef offers a middle position: a *talmid chacham* who is himself capable of inspecting a knife may check his own knife in private — without the public character of a butcher presenting himself before a *rav* — and may then lend it to others who wish to slaughter.

### Dull vs. Broken

Rav Yosef then distinguishes two degrees of impairment in a blade: *sakin she'amda muttar l'chadeda b'Yom Tov* — a knife that has become dull is permitted to be sharpened on *yom tov*. The qualifier: *ha d'paskah agav duchka* — this refers to a blade that still cuts under pressure, meaning it is merely dull. In that case, the act of sharpening is closer to routine maintenance — perhaps an *uvda d'chol* concern — and since we follow Rabbi Yehuda's leniency (*halacha v'ein morin ken* notwithstanding), it is technically permitted.

But if the blade cannot cut at all, sharpening it would constitute an act of *tikkun mana* — actually making the utensil functional from a state of non-functionality. That would be a genuine *melacha*, distinct from mere maintenance, and the question of whether even Rabbi Yehuda's leniency of *machshirei ochel nefesh* extends to creating a utensil anew — rather than maintaining one — is a more serious question. This distinction thus separates the *uvda d'chol* analysis from the *tikkun mana* analysis: a dull knife implicates the former; a broken or useless one implicates the latter.

### Preparatory Acts Debate

The *gemara* concludes with the *beraisa* that grounds the entire discussion. *Ein bein Yom Tov l'Shabbat ela ochel nefesh bilvad* — the sole permissible difference is food preparation. *Rabbi Yehuda mattir af machshirei ochel nefesh* — Rabbi Yehuda permits preparatory acts as well. The *gemara* then identifies the scriptural basis for each position. The *Tanna Kamma* derives from the verse *hu levaddo ye'aseh lakhem* — *hu*, "it alone," limiting permissibility to direct food acts, *velo machshirav* — and not their preparatory stages. Rabbi Yehuda counters with the word *lakhem* — "for you" — reading it expansively as *lekhol tzorkheikhem*, for all your needs, which would include the preparatory steps needed to enable food preparation.

The *Tanna Kamma* resolves the tension between *hu* and *lakhem* by reading *lakhem* as excluding non-Jews — a familiar teaching. Rabbi Yehuda, for his part, reconciles the limiting *hu* with the inclusive *lakhem* by introducing a further distinction: *kan b'machshirin she-efshar la'asotan me'erev Yom Tov, kan b'machshirin she-i efshar la'asotan me'erev Yom Tov* — where it was possible to perform the preparatory act before *yom tov*, it is biblically forbidden even according to Rabbi Yehuda; where it was not possible, it is permitted. This is not merely a rabbinic restriction for those who had the option — it is the line that *hu* draws. Acts one could have done before *yom tov* fall on the restrictive side of *hu*; acts that could not have been done earlier are encompassed by *lakhem*.

Rashi notes that "could not have done it earlier" need not mean the obstacle was absolute — even someone who was simply too busy on *erev Yom Tov* may fall into this category. This is a surprising reading: personal circumstance, not objective impossibility, can suffice to bring a preparatory act within the scope of what *lakhem* permits. It is precisely this looseness in the criterion that makes *halacha v'ein morin ken* so necessary — were this leniency publicized, the determination of "I couldn't do it earlier" would become dangerously self-serving.

The *gemara* closes with the case of the bent spit: *shappud she-nirtzaf assur letakno b'Yom Tov* — a spit that has bent may not be straightened on *yom tov*. This seems obvious — surely it remains usable, if inconveniently. The *gemara* clarifies: *lo tzrikha de-af al gav de-mifshat b'yadei* — it is necessary to teach even where it can be straightened by hand, which might seem too minor to constitute a real repair. Even so, it is a *tikkun* and remains forbidden.

This leaves us with a question to carry forward: given that we have stated the *halacha* is like Rabbi Yehuda regarding *machshirei ochel nefesh* — at least where one could not have done it before *yom tov* — why does the *gemara* continue to present rulings that seem to forbid such acts? Is this all subsumed under the doctrine of *halacha v'ein morin ken*, or is it possible that even Rabbi Yehuda, who permits *machshirei ochel nefesh*, would draw the line at genuinely creating a new functional vessel — what would amount to a full *tikkun kli* — as opposed to merely maintaining one that is already functional? That question will be taken up in the continuation.
