# Beitzah 29

## Machshirei Ochel Nefesh

### Rabbi Yehuda's Position

The daf begins by revisiting the discussion that concluded on 28b regarding the fundamental question of *machshirei ochel nefesh* — preparatory work performed in advance of food preparation on *Yom Tov*. Rabbi Yehuda's position, as distinct from Rav Yehuda the Amora, is that one may perform not only acts directly involved in food preparation — such as lighting a fire or cooking — but even acts that are one stage removed from that process, such as sharpening knives or repairing an oven. Rabbi Yehuda permits these preparatory acts provided they satisfy the criterion of *ee efshar la'asoso me'od yom*: it was not possible to perform them the day before. This is a striking principle, as one normally expects such a limiting condition to apply on a rabbinic level, yet here it appears to operate on a biblical one. If time or circumstances genuinely prevented the act from being done on *erev Yom Tov*, the Torah itself permits it on *Yom Tov*; if it could have been done beforehand, it is biblically forbidden.

The upshot of the *Gemara* is that the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda: *machshirei ochel nefesh* that could not have been attended to the day before are permitted. The *Gemara* does hedge with the principle of *halacha ve'ein morin ken* — the ruling exists but one may prefer not to publicize it broadly, lest people come to permit such acts even when they could have been performed beforehand.

### Ee Efshar Principle

The *ee efshar la'asoso me'od yom* criterion thus serves as the biblical threshold for permitting preparatory work on *Yom Tov*. What could not have been addressed on *erev Yom Tov* is permitted; what could have been addressed is forbidden at the Torah level. This makes Rabbi Yehuda's position both expansive and carefully bounded, and it is precisely that boundary which the subsequent analysis explores.

### Ran's Distinction

There is, however, an important qualification that emerges from the *Rishonim*. While Rashi explains that fixing a knife that has become so dull as to be non-functional — as opposed to merely sharpening a blade that has lost some of its edge — is problematic because of excessive *tircha* or *uvda de'chol*, the Ran and other *Rishonim* frame the limitation differently and more precisely. Even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who permits *machshirei ochel nefesh*, one may not engage in *asiyas kli* — creating a vessel entirely from scratch. One cannot say, for instance, that lacking any knives, one will melt metal and pour it into a mold to produce a knife on *Yom Tov*. One may repair something that has become dulled, but one may not manufacture something that has crossed the threshold into the category of being made anew.

The Ran grounds this limitation in the same principle that explains why one may not go out to the field, harvest wheat, grind it, and make flour on *Yom Tov* — or why hunting and catching fish are problematic. Acts that are not situated within the immediate context of kitchen-based cooking, that belong instead to large-scale, long-term, factory-style production, fall outside the scope of *ochel nefesh* as the Torah envisions it. One may grind pepper — a kitchen act — but not grind wheat into flour, which is an industrial process. Similarly, one may sharpen a dulled knife, but taking something that has ceased to function as a knife and reconstituting it from that state is akin to factory production and is therefore not permitted, even according to Rabbi Yehuda.

The cases in the *Gemara* where *shinuyim* are required — using something other than a whetstone — and the cases where the knife is completely non-functional, are precisely the cases that approach the category of *asiyas kli* rather than mere repair.

### Bottle Caps Example

A practical application of this distinction concerns the question of opening bottle caps on *Yom Tov*. There is an opinion that when one first opens a bottle and breaks off the plastic ring at the base of the cap, one has transformed the cap into a *kli* — it was previously only capable of keeping the bottle sealed, but after the ring is broken it can function as a removable closure used on any bottle. On *Shabbos*, there are those who are *machmir* on this basis.

On *Yom Tov*, however, the question takes a different form. Even if one accepts that opening a bottle technically constitutes *asiyas kli*, it is an *asiyas kli* that occurs entirely within the immediate context of accessing food or drink — it is not remotely analogous to the Ran's example of going out to harvest wheat or working in a factory. The Ran's concern is with acts that are structurally and contextually removed from the kitchen and the act of eating; opening a bottle cap is squarely within that immediate context. Furthermore, the *ee efshar* consideration applies: opening a carbonated bottle on *erev Yom Tov* causes the contents to lose their fizz, making it genuinely impossible to prepare it beforehand in the same condition. Thus, even one who is *machmir* on bottle caps on *Shabbos* has good grounds to open them on *Yom Tov*.

## Spit as Muktzeh

### Disgusting Spit

The *Gemara* now returns to a *muktzeh* discussion, which is the natural conclusion of the foregoing section. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: a spit upon which meat was roasted on *Yom Tov* — once the meat has been removed — becomes disgusting and may no longer be handled on *Yom Tov*, since it has taken on the status of *muktzeh machmas miyus*.

Rav Adda bar Abba said in the name of Rav Malkio: what one may do is *shomto* — push or drag it off to a corner. Rashi explains that *shomto* implies not picking it up directly with one's hands but rather kicking or nudging it to the side, although that detail is not entirely explicit in the *Gemara* itself.

### Ravina's Allowance

Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi said in the name of Rav Huna: even this much — pushing it to a corner — applies only if there remains a *kezayis* worth of meat still on the spit, so that it has not yet become entirely *muktzeh* on account of the food still adhering to it.

Ravina offers a different view: even if no meat remains on the spit at all, one is permitted to move it. The reason is derived from the analogy of a dangerous object lying in a *reshus ha'rabim* — a sharp or rusty object posing a hazard to passersby may be removed despite its *muktzeh* status. Here too, a sharp metal spit may be moved even in a fully disgusting state because of the potential hazard it poses. One could alternatively have invoked the category of *graf shel re'ei* — objects so repulsive that requiring one to leave them in place would be an unreasonable imposition on the sanctity of the day — though perhaps the spit, however visually unpleasant, does not rise to that level of active offense.

### Malkio vs Malkia

The *Gemara* takes the opportunity to clarify a persistent source of confusion: the distinction between Rav Malkio and Rav Malkia, two Amoraim with nearly identical names, each of whom made three statements that are easily attributed to the wrong one.

Rav Chinana, son of Rav Ika, provides the organizational framework. The ruling concerning the spit — that it may be pushed to a corner — was stated in the name of Rav Malkio. The case of *shifchos* — maidservants — concerns a *Mishnah* in which Rabbi Eliezer rules that even a woman attended by many maidservants should not be entirely exempt from household labor, because complete idleness is harmful; Rav Malkio rules that we follow Rabbi Eliezer in this matter. The case of *gumot* concerns the appearance of the indentations from which pubic hairs grow: even if the hairs themselves are not yet visible, the presence of the indentations suffices to establish adulthood for legal purposes. These three — the spit, the maidservants, and the indentations — belong to Rav Malkio.

The three statements of Rav Malkia concern *blorit* — a form of hair cutting associated with pagan practice, regarding which Rav Malkia rules that one must stop cutting within three fingerbreadths of the affected area; *efer mikleh* — burnt ashes that may not be applied to a wound lest the skin appear tattooed; and *gevinah* — the prohibition on eating cheese produced by non-Jews. These three belong to Rav Malkia.

Rav Papa offers a further mnemonic principle: any statement that involves interpreting or ruling in accordance with a *Mishnah* or *Braisa* (a Tannaitic source) belongs to Rav Malkio, while any purely Amoraic statement belongs to Rav Malkia. The mnemonic is *matnisin malchusa* — the Tannaitic material is the "royalty," the more authoritative stratum. The practical difference between Rav Chinana's and Rav Papa's organizational frameworks concerns the case of *shifchos*, which shifts attribution depending on whether one categorizes it as a Tannaitic ruling or otherwise — but the details of that realignment need not be worked through fully here.

## Purchasing Food

### Price Prohibition

With the *muktzeh* discussion concluded, the *Gemara* transitions to a new *Mishnah* that will occupy the remainder of the third *perek*: the question of how to acquire food on *Yom Tov* when one has not made arrangements beforehand, in a manner that avoids the appearance of commerce and *uvdin de'chol*. The *Mishnah* states: a person may not say to a butcher, "Give me a *dinar*'s worth of meat" — that is, one may not describe the desired quantity in monetary terms. Even without actually exchanging money, framing the transaction in the language of price is too reminiscent of a weekday commercial exchange.

### Slaughter & Divide

What is permitted instead is for the butcher to slaughter the animal and divide the meat among his customers. The *Gemara* asks how this works in practice — how does one determine what portion a customer is owed? The answer is that different communities used established, recognized cuts of meat by name, so that a customer could simply request a standard portion without any explicit negotiation of weight or price. In Sura they would speak of a *tarmasa* or half a *tarmasa*; in Narsh, a *chalka* or half a *chalka*; in Pumbedita, an *uzia* or half an *uzia*; in Nehardea and Mata Mechasya, a *riva* or half a *riva*. Rashi explains these as names for standard cuts of meat — akin to what we might call a flank or rib — though one might also read them as standard sizes or weights, and the Steinsaltz commentary does not clearly resolve the question. In any case, the point is that a recognized, named portion — whether cut or measure — allows the transaction to proceed without explicit monetary framing.

### Meat Cuts

The regional variation in terminology is itself illuminating. The *Gemara*'s catalogue of four different terms across four major Babylonian communities reflects a world in which communal convention, not standardized commerce, governed how food changed hands on *Yom Tov*. The recognized cut was both a social and halakhic solution: it allowed people to obtain what they needed without either weighing it or pricing it.

## Borrowing Flour

### Vessel Types

The next *Mishnah* shifts from the butcher to the neighbor. When one person borrows food from a friend on *Yom Tov* — with an implicit understanding that it will be repaid afterward — how does one determine the quantity without engaging in prohibited *medidah*? The *Mishnah* permits a person to say to a friend: fill up this vessel for me — *malei li kli zeh* — bringing over a container to be filled with flour, oil, or similar. This is permitted. What is not permitted, according to the *tanna kamma*, is specifying a quantity by measure: do not say "a cup of flour" or "three ounces."

### Rabbi Yehuda Strict

Rabbi Yehuda adds a further stringency: even if you do not name a measure, if the vessel you bring over is itself designated as a measuring vessel — a *kli ha-meyuchad le-midda* — you may not fill it up either. The *Gemara* works to identify the precise disagreement between these two positions.

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: the *tanna kamma*'s prohibition on measurement means specifically that one may not use a vessel that has already been designated and used for measuring — a measuring cup, as it were. But a vessel that *could* serve as a measuring vessel but has not yet been put to that use — *kli ha-omed le-midda* — may still be filled up, since it has not yet been identified with the function of measuring. Rabbi Yehuda goes further: even a vessel that could eventually serve as a measuring vessel — even without having been formally used for that purpose — may not be filled up on *Yom Tov*, because doing so too clearly defines the exact quantity being borrowed and crosses into the territory of *uvda de'chol* or commercial transaction.

The *Gemara* then observes that this alignment — Rabbi Yehuda strict, the Rabbis lenient — appears to be the reverse of another *Mishnah*, in which Rabbi Yehuda permits weighing meat on a balance scale so long as what is placed on the other side is not a standard weight but some other object such as a hatchet, while the *Chachamim* prohibit using the balance scale at all. There, Rabbi Yehuda is the more lenient and the Rabbis are the stricter.

The *Gemara* resolves this apparent contradiction for both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis: neither party is simply globally lenient or globally strict. Each takes positions based on the specifics of the case. For Rabbi Yehuda: when someone uses a hatchet on a scale, the act is visually bizarre and clearly not a normal commercial transaction — the use of an obviously non-standard counterweight reframes the entire act so that it does not resemble weekday commerce. But a vessel that could serve as a measuring vessel, even if it has not formally been designated as such, looks sufficiently like a normal transaction that Rabbi Yehuda refuses to permit it. For the Rabbis: the use of a balance scale — regardless of what is placed on the other side — is inherently a business instrument and therefore *uvda de'chol*. But a vessel that has not been formally used for measuring does not carry that same visual association, and therefore the Rabbis permit filling it up.

### Simchas Yom Tov

The *Gemara* frames all these leniencies in allowing food-related transactions on *Yom Tov* under the rubric of *simchas Yom Tov*. This is worth pausing over. The Ramban argues that the Torah's specific allowance for cooking on *Yom Tov* — which is absent on *Shabbos* — is not incidental but rooted in the centrality of *simcha* to *Yom Tov*. *Ve-hayisa ach sameach*: the obligation to rejoice is a distinctively *Yom Tov* obligation, and the Torah therefore permits the preparation of food on *Yom Tov* itself in order to maximize that joy. This stands in contrast to *Shabbos*, where *oneg* — sensory pleasure — is the operative concept, derived from the *Nevi'im* rather than the Torah, and carries less structural weight in this context. One might argue that fresh food, cooked on the day rather than reheated from before, speaks more directly to *oneg* — physical pleasure — than to *simcha* in the elevated sense the Ramban intends. But the Ramban's point may be that the very freedom to cook, the ability to engage actively in preparing for the day's enjoyment, is itself a dimension of *simcha* beyond mere sensory gratification. In any case, the *Gemara* explicitly ties the rabbinic allowances for food-related borrowing and quasi-commercial exchanges to this framework of *simchas Yom Tov*.

## Contradiction Resolution

### Scales Lenience

The contradiction identified above — between Rabbi Yehuda's leniency regarding the balance scale and his strictness regarding measuring vessels — is worth examining further in its own right. In the earlier *Mishnah*, Rabbi Yehuda rules that one may weigh meat on a balance scale, provided the counterweight is not a formal standard weight but an unconventional object such as a hatchet or another vessel. This represents a meaningful leniency in the context of acquiring food on *Yom Tov*, since it gives the customer a mechanism to obtain a roughly precise portion. The Rabbis, by contrast, prohibit use of the scale entirely, on the grounds that the very act of weighing on a scale is quintessentially a commercial act — *uvda de'chol* — regardless of what one uses as a counterweight.

### Vessel Strictness

Yet in the *Mishnah* before us, Rabbi Yehuda is the stricter voice: he prohibits filling even a vessel that has only potential use as a measuring vessel, while the Rabbis permit it so long as the vessel has not been formally designated for measuring. The resolution, as noted, turns not on global dispositions toward leniency or stringency but on case-specific reasoning. For Rabbi Yehuda, the decisive factor in the scales case is that the use of a hatchet on the other side of the scale visually and functionally marks the transaction as something other than ordinary commerce. For him, the appearance of normalcy determines permissibility. In the vessel case, even a vessel not yet formally used for measuring looks sufficiently like a normal measuring vessel that it fails to create the same visual departure from commerce.

### Case-Specific Approach

This brings into focus an important methodological point about how we read *psakim*. It is tempting to characterize a given authority as categorically lenient or categorically strict — and this temptation is especially strong with figures like the *Chazon Ish*, who is often portrayed as a systematic *machmir*. But the reality is that any careful *posek* evaluates each case on its own terms. A given *sugya* may yield a more lenient conclusion from someone commonly regarded as strict, because the specifics of that case, in that *posek*'s reading, simply do not support a prohibition. Rabbi Yehuda's reversals here illustrate precisely this dynamic: the same concern — avoiding commercial-looking transactions on *Yom Tov* — leads him to leniency in one case and stringency in another, depending entirely on whether the specific act in question resembles weekday commerce.

## Rava's Reading

### Mention vs. Vessel

Rava offers an alternative reading of the *Mishnah* that is arguably the more straightforward one. According to Rava, the *tanna kamma*'s prohibition — *aval lo be-midda* — is not about what vessel is used at all. Rather, it is a prohibition on explicitly mentioning a measurement. One may not go to one's neighbor and say, "May I please have half a cup of flour?" or "Could you give me three ounces?" Naming a specific measure is what is forbidden, because it too explicitly labels the exchange as a transaction. However, one *may* bring over one's own measuring cup and ask the neighbor to fill it up — even a vessel clearly designated for measuring — because the act of filling a vessel, without naming the quantity verbally, does not carry the same transactional character.

Rabbi Yehuda, on this reading, is stricter: he prohibits filling even a formally designated measuring vessel, regardless of whether any measurement is mentioned verbally. The mere use of such a vessel is enough to make the exchange appear like a formal commercial transaction.

The *Gemara* then runs through the same contradiction — Rabbi Yehuda lenient by the scale, strict by the vessel — and resolves it in a parallel fashion. For Rabbi Yehuda: the hatchet on the scale removes the commercial character of the weighing entirely, while the use of a designated measuring vessel, even without verbal labeling, preserves it. For the Rabbis: the scale itself, regardless of its counterweight, is a business instrument and thus *uvda de'chol*; the use of a measuring cup to convey flour to a neighbor, on the other hand, is not inherently transactional.

### Wine Example

The Rabbis' reasoning is made explicit in the *Gemara*: *de-avidi inshi de-mekarvei chamra be-mana de-kila ve-shatu* — people routinely bring wine to a friend's house in a measuring vessel and drink it together. The measuring cup, in other words, is not exclusively a commercial instrument; it also serves as an ordinary conveyance. Since people use such vessels in non-commercial social contexts all the time, filling a neighbor's measuring cup with flour on *Yom Tov* does not necessarily signal a formal transaction. But if one says, "I need exactly a cup of flour," one has verbally labeled the quantity and the exchange, making it look unmistakably like a purchase.

## Abba Shaul Story

### Pre-Measuring

The *Mishnah* records the practice of Abba Shaul ben Botnit: he would fill his measuring vessels with wine, oil, and similar goods before *Yom Tov*, so that on *Yom Tov* itself all measuring had already been completed. When customers came to his store, he would hand them pre-measured containers without performing any act of *medidah* on the holiday itself, and without needing to name any quantity. The pre-measurement was a complete solution to the *Yom Tov* concerns about both explicit labeling and prohibited measuring.

The *tanna* then extends this: Abba Shaul would do the same even on *Chol HaMoed*, and the *Gemara* explains — not primarily for reasons of commercial precision but in order to avoid *bittul Beis HaMedrash*. On *Chol HaMoed*, Abba Shaul had more time available for Torah study, as did the people who came to learn with him and pose questions. By pre-filling all the vessels at night, he ensured that during the day he would be free to sit and learn without interruption, just as the stories told of the *Chofetz Chaim* describe a similar discipline of managing a store around the priority of *Torah* study.

### Leftover Accumulation

The *Gemara* now reveals a remarkable consequence of Abba Shaul ben Botnit's practice — one that goes beyond the *Yom Tov* question entirely. When wine is poured into a vessel it initially appears full, but as bubbles settle the level drops slightly and the measure is actually somewhat less than it seemed. If one waits for the wine to settle fully, the measure is more precise, but in a commercial setting one cannot simply leave a customer's vessel sitting while waiting for the liquid to settle. The result is that the measurement appears complete but a small surplus accumulates. Similarly, oil poured into a vessel will slowly continue to drip for an extended period — sometimes for hours — so that if one pours an exact measure and hands it over, a small residue remains in the original vessel. This residue, over time, also accumulates into surplus.

Over the course of a year or more, Abba Shaul ben Botnit and his colleagues found that they had each accumulated hundreds of flasks' worth of leftover wine and oil respectively — he from the air pockets in wine, his colleagues from the slow dripping of oil. The numbers are likely an exaggeration in service of the point, but the phenomenon itself is real. The analogy to the rounding error in banking is apt: each individual instance is trivial, but aggregated across all the transactions it becomes substantial.

### Distribution to Poor

Feeling that this accumulated surplus was not rightfully theirs to keep, they brought it to the officers of the Temple treasury in Jerusalem. The treasurers responded: you are not obligated to do this; people generally forgo (*mochel*) these small discrepancies and you bear no real liability. Abba Shaul and his colleagues replied: that may well be true, but we ourselves are not comfortable keeping it.

The treasurers then said — and the phrase is striking — *ho'il ve-hichmartem al atzmechem*: since you are being stringent upon yourselves, the money should nevertheless not go to the Temple treasury. It should go back to the people. The model invoked is the *halacha* regarding stolen property when the victim cannot be identified: one does not simply donate to *tzedakah* — that does not restore anything to the original owner. Rather, *ya'asem be-tzorchei rabbim* — use it for communal needs, so that the public as a whole benefits, including those from whom the small surpluses were inadvertently withheld. Rav Chisda specifies: the appropriate use is *borot, shichin u'mearot* — digging public wells and cisterns. The lesson is that when one assumes personal stringency about money that may not be fully one's own, the remedy is not personal piety through donation to sacred purposes but communal restitution through public works.

## Animals & Professionals

### Animal Feed

The *Gemara* now addresses the question of measuring on *Yom Tov* in contexts beyond food for people. Rav Chisda, through the medium of Rabana Ukva who delivered the exposition publicly, ruled: one may not measure out barley and place it before one's animal on *Yom Tov*. The prohibition of *medidah* applies even when the measurement is for animal feed, not for human consumption, and even when no transactional context is involved — the prohibition is on the act of measuring itself, which carries an inherent association with commercial activity. However, what is permitted is *koder* — scooping: one may scoop out a *kav* or two *kavayim* and place it before the animal. The distinction Rashi draws is between scooping with the vessel that will also convey the grain to the animal — using the same vessel as both measure and delivery — versus measuring into one vessel and then transferring to a separate container. The former is permitted; it resembles the earlier case of asking a friend to "fill this up for me," where the vessel is used directly rather than as an intermediate measure.

### Professional Cooks

A *nachtom* — a professional cook or baker — is granted a special allowance to measure out spices on *Yom Tov*, *kdei shelo yakdiach tavshilo*: in order not to ruin the dish by over-spicing it. Professional cooking, far more than home cooking, depends on precise measurement of seasonings, and allowing that precision is justified by the *Yom Tov* need for proper food. Rashi notes that *nachtom* should be read broadly enough to include anyone cooking a pot, not exclusively a professional baker, but the language still implies a more formal or competent culinary context. The practical question of whether an ordinary home cook may use tablespoons and teaspoons on *Yom Tov* is not entirely resolved by this passage; the allowance appears to be most clearly established in a professional context.

### Flour & Challah

Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba said in the name of Rav: a woman may measure flour on *Yom Tov* and add it to her dough in order to ensure that when she separates *challah* she does so generously — *be-ayin yafa*. Knowing the precise quantity of flour enables her to separate the correct amount of *challah* with confidence rather than being overly stingy out of uncertainty. Shmuel disagrees: this is not measuring for the direct purpose of food but for the purpose of *challah* separation, and he would not permit it.

The *Gemara* then raises an objection: a *braisa* from the school of Shmuel apparently permits this very act. Abaye resolves the tension: Shmuel's ruling represents the *halacha le-ma'aseh* — the practical, applied ruling — rather than the theoretical *halacha*, and this is another instance of *halacha ve'ein morin ken*. The theoretical position allows measuring flour for *challah* purposes; in practice Shmuel prefers that people refrain. Whether we rule like Rav or like Shmuel on this question remains a live issue.

Tosafot addresses a further dimension of the problem relevant to contemporary practice. Since we no longer give *challah* to the *Kohen* but separate only symbolically and burn it, the size of the separated portion is not practically at stake. However, Tosafot notes that one still needs to know how much flour is in the dough in order to determine: first, whether *challah* must be separated at all; and second, whether a *beracha* is required over the separation. Could one measure the flour on *Yom Tov* to clarify the *beracha* question? Tosafot's conclusion is no — one should simply use either a generous quantity, ensuring clear obligation, or a smaller quantity, ensuring clear exemption. But the question itself reveals how the underlying concern about *medidah* intersects with the requirements of *challah* separation even today.

## Re-Sifting Flour

### Sifting Dispute

The *Gemara* presents a dispute among Tannaim regarding re-sifting flour on *Yom Tov*. The *tanna kamma* prohibits it: sifting belongs to the pre-processing stage of flour production, and doing it again on *Yom Tov* is not a kitchen act in the immediate sense but rather a continuation of the milling and refining process that should have been completed beforehand. Against this, Rabbi Papi and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira both hold that re-sifting is permitted. All opinions agree on one point: if a foreign object — a stone or a wood chip — has fallen into the flour, one may re-sift to remove it.

### Nachman's Rebuttal

A *tanna* taught a *braisa* before Ravina: one may not re-sift flour on *Yom Tov*, but if a stone or wood chip has fallen in, one should pick it out by hand rather than re-sift. Ravina responded: *kol sheken d'assur* — picking it out by hand is actually more problematic than re-sifting it, because picking it out by hand constitutes a more obvious act of *borer* — sorting the unwanted from the wanted. Rashi explains the distinction: when one re-sifts flour that has already been sifted, the visual impression is ambiguous — it is not obvious that anything is being removed, since the flour is already refined. But going in with one's hand and deliberately extracting a foreign object is visually and functionally a clear act of *borer*.

This raises the underlying question of why sifting is not itself *borer* — after all, the whole purpose of sifting is separation. Rashi's answer is that once flour has already been sifted, re-sifting it does not look like a sorting operation in any evident way. The act of *borer* as a prohibited *melacha* on *Yom Tov* involves either a biblical or an *uvda de'chol* concern depending on the context, and the case of re-sifted flour may fall into a more ambiguous zone.

Rava bar Rav Huna Zuta then delivered a public ruling at the gates of Nahardea that re-sifting flour on *Yom Tov* is entirely permitted. Rav Nachman's response was dismissive: go tell this person to take his magnanimity and throw it on the thorns — *shekilo tivotaich ve-shadi achaziri*. Go look around Nahardea and see how many sifters are circulating on *Yom Tov*: everyone knows re-sifting is permitted, and this announcement adds nothing.

### Shinuyim Practice

Despite this general permissibility, the *Gemara* records that certain Amoraic wives performed the re-sifting with a *shinuy* — a modification of the normal method. Rav Yosef's wife re-sifted using the back of the sifter rather than the normal sifting face. Rav Yosef told her plainly: I would like good bread — do it the proper way, without the modification. Rav Ashi's wife re-sifted onto the back of the table rather than into a normal vessel. Rav Ashi noted that his wife, the daughter of Rami bar Chama — who was known as a man of exceptional piety — would not have adopted this practice unless she had seen it done this way in her mother's house. The tradition of mimetic practice, transmitted from mother to daughter, lent legitimacy to the *shinuy*, even as Rav Yosef's comment made clear that such modifications are not obligatory and may even compromise the result.

## Storekeeper Purchase

### Final Mishnah

The final *Mishnah* of the third *perek* addresses one more category of food acquisition on *Yom Tov*: going to a familiar storekeeper. One may say to such a storekeeper: give me a dozen eggs, give me fifty nuts — specifying items by number. Why is this permitted? *She'ken derech ba'al ha-bayit li'heyot moneh be-toch beito* — because people routinely count items in the context of household use, not only in the context of commercial transactions. Saying "I need three eggs for this cake" or "give me ten walnuts" is not inherently commercial language. It is categorically different from naming a weight or a price, which are unambiguously transactional.

### Gemara Expansion

The *Gemara* expands this framework with a *braita* that extends the same principle across a variety of suppliers. One may go to a familiar shepherd and say: give me one kid or one lamb. One may go to a familiar butcher and say: give me a thigh or a shoulder — naming the cut but not the weight. One may go to a familiar fattener of birds and say: give me one pigeon or one dove. One may go to a familiar baker and say: give me one loaf or one cake. And one may go to a familiar storekeeper and say: give me twenty eggs, five nuts, ten quinces or peaches, five pomegranates, one *etrog*. The specificity of the list is itself revealing — particularly the single *etrog*, which suggests that *etrogim* were available from stores during the *Yom Tov* season.

### Numbers Principle

The closing principle is: *u'vilvad she-lo yazkir lo skum midah* — as long as one does not mention a specific measurement or sum. Numbers of discrete objects do not constitute a commercial designation in the way that weights and prices do. Rashi reads this to prohibit explicit mention of weight; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reads it to prohibit explicit mention of cost. In either reading, the principle is the same: what makes an exchange look like a formal weekday transaction is the invocation of standardized commercial metrics — weight, volume, money. Counting discrete objects by number does not cross that line. With this principle, the third *perek* concludes.

*Hadran alach Ein Tzadin.*

# Beitzah 30

## Measuring Spices

### Measuring Spices

The daf we study today is 30, which opens the next *perek*. Before turning to that new chapter, a loose end from the previous daf deserves attention. The *gemara* there discussed measuring on *yom tov* — measuring out flour and similar ingredients — and noted that a *nachtom*, a professional cook, may measure spices in order to ensure a dish comes out properly. The question left open was whether the same latitude extends to an ordinary person.

The *halacha* is that even a regular *ba'al habayis* or *ba'alas habayis* who is cooking on *yom tov* may use measuring spoons — a teaspoon of this, a half-teaspoon of that — because this is the kind of normal kitchen measuring that is necessary to ensure the dish comes out right. The one qualification the *poskim* add is that if a person habitually does not measure but simply adds a dash or a pinch of salt, that person should not begin measuring on *yom tov*. But for those who ordinarily measure, this is entirely permitted.

### New Perek: uvda d'chol

The new *perek* opens with a cluster of issues that sit just before the activity of cooking itself — matters of transporting items to the house — and the central concerns are *uvda d'chol*, the appearance of weekday activity, and the related concern of *tircha*, undue effort.

## Wine/Straw Transport

### Mishnah: Wine & Straw

The *mishnah* at the bottom of 29b begins: *hamayvee kadey yayin mimakom lemakom* — one who brings jugs of wine from one place to another, say from a storage shed to the house. The *mishnah* rules: *lo yavi besal uv'kuppa* — do not bring them in a large basket or box, carrying twenty jugs at once. Rather, *aval mayvee hu al ketayfo o lefanav* — bring them on your shoulder or holding them in front of you, but do not haul a large quantity all at once.

Similarly, *vechein hamolich es hateven* — one who brings straw to his animals: *lo yafshil es hakuppa lachora* — should not take a huge container of straw and carry it on his back; rather, *aval mayveehu beyado* — carry it in your hand, in front of you.

The *mishnah* continues: *umatchilin ba'arimat hateven* — one may break into a pile of straw that had not yet been opened before *yom tov*, and the assumption is that the straw will be used as fuel. However, *aval lo b'etzim shebemuktza* — not from wood stored in the *muktza*, which Rashi explains refers to the alleyway behind the house used as a storage area. This is the same root as *muktza* in the sense of items set aside and off-limits: things stored away and not designated for use. So one may break into a haystack of straw to begin using it as firewood, but not into a storage shed of wood not yet opened for that purpose.

### Rashi: uvda d'chol

What exactly is the concern behind the first part of the *mishnah*? Rashi explains — in a comment several lines into the *perek* — *d'nireh k'masa dechol laseis masa'os*: it looks like a thoroughly weekday activity to be carrying large burdens the way one does during the week. On the other hand, Rashi continues, *aval mayvee al ketayfo achas o shtayim d'mucha d'letzorech yom tov*: if you carry only a small amount, it is obvious why — you need wine for the *yom tov* meal, you need some straw for your animals. Large quantities, by contrast, suggest commercial transport or farm management of the sort associated with weekday life. Rashi's concern is thus squarely one of *uvda d'chol*, and he does not emphasize the *tircha* dimension.

### Tosafot: Shabbat/YomTov

Tosafot raises a challenge. A *mishnah* in *Shabbos* in the chapter *mafnin* appears to be more lenient: *mafnin arba kupot o chameish* — you may move out four or five boxes of straw. If on *Shabbos* one may haul several boxes at once, why does our *mishnah* restrict even a single basket on *yom tov*?

Tosafot's resolution is illuminating. He argues that on *Shabbos*, in the absence of an *eiruv* encompassing the city, most carrying takes place *mizavit l'zavit b'oto bayis* — from one corner to another within the house, or within a courtyard sharing an *eiruv*. In that confined context, there is no concern of *uvdin d'chol*: nobody watching you shuffle items within your courtyard thinks you are engaged in weekday commerce. The concern on *Shabbos* is therefore primarily *tircha*, undue effort, and since fewer trips means less effort, the *gemara* there prefers you carry more at once even if it is a heavier load.

*Yom tov* is different. Since carrying in the street is permitted on *yom tov*, transport genuinely takes place over longer distances where it is visible to others. The dominant concern therefore shifts to *uvdin d'chol*, and the principle becomes: *adif tfei l'afushei b'hilucha v'ya'aseh derech shinui ki heichi d'lo litchazei k'uvdin d'chol* — better to make more trips and carry less at a time, even at the cost of greater effort, so long as it does not look like weekday commercial transport.

These are genuinely competing values. By *Shabbos*, minimizing effort takes priority and we prefer fewer trips. By *yom tov*, once carrying is permitted at all, the visual reality of that carrying creates a stronger *uvdin d'chol* concern, and so we insist on small quantities per trip even if that multiplies the number of journeys.

### Exception: No Other Way

A *baraita* qualifies the rule: *im ee efshar l'shanot muttar* — if there is no feasible way to carry the items differently — say the item is bulky and can only be transported in the normal manner — it is permitted to do so as-is.

### Rava's Takanah

Rava established a set of guidelines in Mechuza, his city, for situations where some form of *shinui* is required. Items normally carried on the shoulder (*d'daru b'katfa*) should be carried with a pitchfork-like implement (*d'daru b'rigla*) — Rashi understands *rigla* not as "leg" literally but as such a tool. Items normally carried that way should instead be carried on a beam shared between two people (*d'daru b'igra* — *b'mote bishnayim*, a rod borne on shoulders together). And for items where no other mode is available, *nifra sudra iluya* — drape a cloth over the items, so they are covered and the transport is less conspicuous.

Here the logic is clearly visual: covering items does not reduce the weight, but it reduces the *uvda d'chol* appearance. This is precisely where Rashi and Tosafot diverge. Rashi holds that a *shinui* should ideally also lighten the burden and certainly not increase it. Tosafot holds that since the concern is *uvda d'chol* and not effort per se, even a *shinui* that does nothing to reduce the burden is valid. Finally, *ve'im lo efshar shari* — if no alternative whatsoever is feasible, one may carry in the normal way, as the *baraita* stated at the outset.

## Water Drawing Issue

### Women Drawing Water

Rav Chanan bar Rava said to Rav Ashi: the rabbis have said that to the extent possible we require a *shinui* on *yom tov*. Yet *de-kamalyan khatzivayhu maya beyoma tova* — the women go and fill their buckets with water on *yom tov* from the river or well, *velo kamashanyian* — and they do not draw the water any differently than on a weekday. *Velo amrinan lehu velo midi* — and we say nothing to them. How can we tolerate this without comment?

The response is: this falls into the category of things one cannot reasonably change. What practical *shinui* would you demand? *Heichi liyavid* — what are they supposed to do? If those who normally use a large bucket (*d'daru b'khatzba raba*) are told to use a small bucket (*d'malyi b'chatzva zuta*), the result is *kamaphish behiluha* — they will have to make multiple extra trips. That alone would make it more burdensome.

Now, Tosafot had just argued in connection with the *mishnah* that multiple trips are exactly what we prefer when it reduces *uvda d'chol* — and Tosafot is aware of the tension. His resolution is that in the *mishnah*, hauling small quantities is itself unusual enough to signal that this is for an immediate *yom tov* need. With water, the situation is different: some people always carry large buckets, others always carry small ones. Whichever way a particular woman switches, it will not look different from the weekday practice of someone else in the community. The *shinui* accomplishes nothing cosmetically, while imposing real cost.

Conversely, if those who normally use small buckets (*d'malyi b'chatzva zuta*) are told to switch to large buckets (*t'malyi b'chatzva rabba*), *ka mafish b'masoi* — you are increasing the weight they must carry. Every option carries a cost without producing a meaningful *uvda d'chol* benefit.

What about covering the bucket with a wooden plank? *Zimin d'nafel v'ati l'asuyei* — sometimes the cover will fall and there will be an impulse to carry it; and *tikatrei* — they will want to tie the cover down, but *zimin d'mafsik* — the knot will sometimes break, and they will end up tying a new knot on *yom tov*, which is forbidden. Covering with a cloth scarf instead? *Zimin d'mitatmei b'maya v'ati l'dey s'chita* — the cloth will become soaked with water and one will come to wring it out, which is forbidden. The concern about *s'chita* here is specifically because the liquid absorbed is water: wringing water from a cloth implicates the prohibition of laundering, whereas wringing out a cloth that absorbed wine or juice — where the liquid would go to waste — presents less of a problem. Because it is water, and because the bucket has a wide open mouth making saturation likely, this is a genuine concern.

*Hilkach lo efshar* — therefore, there is no feasible alternative, and the women draw water in the normal manner.

This discussion also points to something worth pausing over: the language of the *mishnah* itself is instructive. It does not say *assur l'havi* — it is forbidden to bring. It says *lo yavi'eim b'sal u'v'kupah* — in the style of guidance about how one should go about it. The entire domain of *uvda d'chol* is in many ways amorphous and contextual. It resists quantification precisely because it is about the experiential texture of the day — what does it feel like? What does it look like? On the one hand, this makes it one of the most important concerns in the spirit of *shabbos* and *yom tov*. On the other hand, it rarely generates a hard and formally articulated *issur d'rabbanan* in the way other areas of *halacha* do. The *gemara* here reads more like principled guidance than strict prohibition, and that tension plays out in practice whenever a *shailah* involves *uvda d'chol* as the primary concern.

### Rav Chanan's Challenge

Rava bar Rav Hanin said to Abaye: we have learned in a *mishnah* (to be studied in about a week) *ein metapchin bein masapkin u-vein merakdin* — one does not clap, slap the thigh, or dance on *yom tov*. The reason, as the *gemara* understands it, is a *gezerah* lest one come to fix a musical instrument. Interestingly, the parallel source in the *Tosefta* frames this quite differently, presenting these as activities — clapping, jumping — performed out in the field to scare birds away from crops, and framing the prohibition as *al yaaseh ke-derech she-hu oseh be-chol*, do not do it the way you do on a weekday. That parallel is directly about *uvda d'chol*. The *Bavli*, however, reframes it around the concern of repairing musical instruments.

Whatever the underlying concern, *ve-ha-idna de-chazinan de-avdi hachi* — we observe that people go ahead and do these things, *velo amrinan lehu velo midi* — and we say nothing. How do we permit ourselves this silence?

A parallel is cited: Rava ruled that a person should not sit at the mouth of a courtyard right beside the *lechi*, the post that demarcates the boundary. The reason is *dilma migandar lei chefetz v'asi l'asuyei* — perhaps an object will roll away and the person, sitting right at the threshold with his back to the marker, will chase after it and carry it out without noticing. Here too the concern is what the act might lead to. And yet: *ve'ha hani nashi deshaklan chatzuvaihu v'azlan v'yavlan apuma d'mavoi* — women take their buckets and sit right at the mouth of the *mavoi*. This is itself a violation of Rava's rule. *Velo amrinan lehu velo midi* — and we say nothing.

### Shogeg vs. Mezid

Abaye's response is the principle: *ela hanoch lahem l'Yisrael mutav sheyihyu shoggin v'al yihyu mezidin* — leave the Jewish people alone; better they sin unintentionally than sin deliberately. This principle has two dimensions. At the individual level, if one tells them and they ignore the rebuke, they have moved from *shogeg* to *mezid*. At the communal level, if a rabbinic instruction is openly flouted, it undermines rabbinic authority itself. One must therefore judge whether speaking will do any good, and if it clearly will not, silence is sometimes the more responsible choice. This logic applies, the *gemara* continues, to the case of the dancing and clapping as well: *hacha nami hanoch lahem l'Yisrael mutav sheyihyu shoggin v'al yihyu mezidin*.

### Tochacha Discussion

A natural question follows: how far does this principle extend? Is there ever a case where we must speak even when it will do no good?

The *gemara* initially suggests a distinction: *v'hani mili b'drabbanan* — this tolerance of silence applies to rabbinic violations. And indeed, both cases discussed — the concern about fixing a musical instrument and the concern about carrying past the *lechi* — are themselves *gezerot*, rabbinic safeguards against potential violations. *Aval b'doraisa lo* — but for a biblical violation, perhaps we are required to speak up regardless.

### D'Oraisa Distinctions

The *gemara* then rejects this distinction: *lo shena d'oraisa velo shena d'rabbanan* — it makes no difference; even for a biblical violation, if the rebuke will not be heeded, we say nothing. The proof: *tosefes Yom HaKippurim* — adding to *Yom Kippur* is a biblical concept derived from *me'erev ad erev*, the idea of beginning the fast before sunset. Yet *ve'achlu veshassu ad shechashecha* — people eat right up to sunset, and *velo amrinan lehu velo midi* — we say nothing. This real-world rabbinic practice demonstrates that silence is sometimes appropriate even regarding a *d'oraisa*.

Tosafot notes that this cannot literally mean eating until the very last instant before sunset, since no one can time it so precisely and people would then surely eat on *Yom Kippur* itself. There must be some interval before sunset. That observation leads the *rishonim* to discuss what minimum duration constitutes *tosefes Yom HaKippurim* — opinions range from a half-hour down to considerably less.

The *gemara*'s conclusion, as developed *lehalacha*, is that the case where one must speak even if confident the rebuke will not be heeded is where the prohibition is both biblical and *meforash bakra* — explicitly stated in the Torah. The reasoning operates on several levels. First, one is never truly a prophet: perhaps repeated remonstration will eventually reach the person. Second, when a prohibition is explicit, the status of *shogeg* is weaker — it is harder to claim genuine ignorance of something plainly written. The *shogeg* argument therefore carries less exculpatory weight, making silence less justified.

A further dimension of *tochacha* is worth noting: sometimes the obligation to speak has less to do with the individual violator and more to do with the communal witness. If violations occur and no one speaks, the implicit message is that the conduct is tolerated. Even when the particular transgressor will not listen, articulating that something is wrong ensures that everyone else present understands there is a problem. This public dimension of *tochacha* may itself be an independent consideration, particularly regarding explicit biblical prohibitions.

## Straw vs. Wood

### Storage Shed Issue

The *gemara* now returns to the *mishnah*'s distinction between opening a pile of straw (*matchilin ba'areimas hateven*) and opening the storage shed of wood (*aval lo b'etzim shebemuktza*).

### Rav Kahana: Muktzah

Rav Kahana reads the *risha*, the opening clause, as teaching: *zos omeres matchilin b'otzar techilah* — one is permitted to break into a storage supply, a closed cache of goods, and begin using it on *yom tov*, without this constituting a *muktza* problem. *Mani?* — whose view does this follow? *Rabbi Shimon d'leis lei muktza* — it follows Rabbi Shimon, who has a significantly lower threshold for *muktza*. For Rabbi Shimon, the mere fact that something is stored away does not render it off-limits if it is fundamentally usable.

*Eima seifa* — but look at the end of the *mishnah*: *aval lo b'etzim shebemuktza* — one may not use the wood in the storage shed. *Atan l'Rabbi Yehuda d'is lei muktza* — this shifts to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that setting items aside in storage is itself sufficient to create *muktza* status. The *mishnah* thus appears to contain the positions of both *tanna'im*, and the question is what distinguishes the straw from the wood.

### Straw/Cedar Diff

The *gemara* resolves the tension: *hacha b'arzei d'ashuchei askinan* — the wood prohibited in the storage shed is not ordinary firewood but valuable cedar beams. This is a case of *muktza machmas chisaron kis* — *muktza* by reason of financial loss, meaning the item is so valuable that one would never consider using it as fuel under normal circumstances. Even Rabbi Shimon agrees that this category of *muktza* is genuine.

An alternative reading (*ika d'masni lah asseifa*) starts from the prohibition of the wood and asks about the permission for the straw. Under this reading, the prohibition follows Rabbi Yehuda: *zos omeres ein matchilin b'otzar techilah* — one may not initially break into stored goods on *yom tov*, because in Rabbi Yehuda's view, setting items aside in storage renders them *muktza*. The permission for the straw then follows Rabbi Shimon. But how, under this reading, does Rabbi Yehuda's position accommodate the straw? The *gemara* answers: *hasham b'tivna sarya* — the straw there is somewhat spoiled. Once straw is no longer usable for animals, one would naturally be thinking about burning it, and it therefore no longer has the psychological character of something fully stored away and reserved.

One might object: perhaps the spoiled straw can still be used for making plaster (*hachazi l'tina*). The *gemara* responds: *d'ika kotzim* — the straw is mixed with thorns and therefore not even suitable for plaster. At that point, one would obviously be mentally prepared to begin using it as fuel, so it does not carry the *muktza* character of something genuinely reserved in storage.

The core debate between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon thus concerns: when something is usable but has been set aside and stored, does that storage alone create *muktza*? Rabbi Yehuda says yes; Rabbi Shimon says no — only when the item is inherently off-limits does *muktza* apply. The cedar beams represent a case that even Rabbi Shimon agrees is *muktza*, not by virtue of storage but by virtue of the item's value.

Tosafot notes an interesting wrinkle: the straw being used for firewood rather than for animals — its designated storage purpose — seems like an additional factor. One would think it is actually more permissible to use something for the purpose you stored it for, and stranger to divert it to a different use. Tosafot raises this as a genuine difficulty: using the straw for firewood is in one sense further from the storage designation, yet in another sense the straw was "in your mind" insofar as you always knew you might burn it. This does not receive a clean resolution, but Tosafot acknowledges the tension.

## Sukkah Sticks

### Mishnah: Sukkah

The *mishnah* states: *ein notlin eitzim min hasukkah ela min hasamukh lah* — one may not take sticks from the *sukkah*, but only from what is near the *sukkah*. In context, this appears to be another *muktza* question — parallel to the wood-in-the-shed issue — though as we will see, further considerations are involved.

The *gemara* immediately presses: what is the distinction? *Mai shna min hasukkah de-lo* — why can you not take from the *sukkah* itself? Is it because of *muktza*, or is it *soter* — the prohibition of dismantling a structure? Taking a beam from a roof, even without demolishing the entire building, constitutes *soter*, the *melacha* of demolition, which is prohibited on *yom tov*. And yet, *min hasamukh lah nami de-ka-assar aleh* — Rashi's initial reading is that "near the *sukkah*" means sticks lying on top of the *sechach*, and those too would become incorporated into the *sechach* and be subject to the same *soter* prohibition. The distinction therefore collapses.

### Rav Yehuda: Wall Sticks

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: *mai samukh? samukh ledofanos* — "near the *sukkah*" does not mean on top of the *sechach*, but sticks leaning against the wall of the *sukkah* from outside. Sticks lying on the *sechach* become incorporated into it and removing them is *soter*. Sticks leaning against the outside wall, by contrast, are clearly external to the structure — they are not part of the wall — and therefore neither are they *muktza* nor does their removal constitute *soter*.

The sticks that form the walls themselves, *min hadofanos*, cannot be removed either — that would be dismantling the structure. But something merely resting against the outside of the wall is a separate matter entirely.

### Bundle Distinct

Rav Menashya offers a different resolution: *afilu teima b'she-ein samukh ledofanos* — one may say we are even speaking of something on the *sechach* itself, not just leaning against the wall. *Ki tanya hi ba-asurayta* — when the *baraita* permits taking from "near the *sukkah*," it refers specifically to a distinct bundle of wood resting on top of the *sechach*. A bundle is self-evidently separate — it never merges into the *sechach*, which consists of scattered branches and thatch. The bundle retains its identity as a discrete object on top of the roof and therefore does not become part of the structure. Removing it raises neither a *soter* problem nor a *muktza* problem.

## Huktzah L'Mitzvah

### Fallen Sukkah

The *mishnah* continues: *ein notlin eitzim min hasukkah* — and then introduces Rabbi Shimon's position and the agreement about a *sukkat he-chag*. A *baraita* is cited: *ain notlin eitzim min hasukkah ela min hasamukh lah. Rabbi Shimon matir* — Rabbi Shimon permits taking wood from the *sukkah* itself. But this seems impossible: even if *muktza* is not the concern for Rabbi Shimon, how can he permit *soter* — dismantling a structure?

The *mishnah* and *baraita* then note a further point: *veshavin be-sukkas he-chag be-chag she-asurah* — both Rabbi Shimon and the *tanna kamma* agree that a *sukkah* used for the *mitzvah* of *sukkot* on *sukkot* is absolutely forbidden, for a reason beyond *muktza* and beyond *soter*. And: *ve-hisnah aleiha ha-kol lefi tina'o* — if one stipulated beforehand, the stipulation is effective. We will need to unpack both of these points.

### Shaky Sukkah

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers the question about Rabbi Shimon: *hacha be-sukkah nufeles askinan* — we are dealing with a *sukkah* that has fallen down. Once the *sukkah* has collapsed, there is no longer a *soter* concern — there is nothing left to demolish. The question that remains is only *muktza*: the wood was off-limits when *yom tov* began, since at that moment removing it would have constituted *soter*. Rabbi Shimon, however, does not recognize *muktza* of this kind — since the wood is fundamentally usable, now that the structure has fallen it may be used.

This parallels the case of leftover oil in a lamp: *mosar shemen she-ba-ner she-be-ke'arah asur* — oil remaining in the dish after the flame goes out is *muktza* because it was off-limits when *shabbos* began (removing it would have diminished the flame — *kibbu'i*). *Ve-Rabbi Shimon matir* — Rabbi Shimon permits using it once the flame has naturally gone out. Similarly, once the *sukkah* collapses, Rabbi Shimon permits using the wood.

The *gemara* objects: *mi dami?* Are these cases truly comparable? *Hasam adam yoshev u-metzapeh eimasai tichbeh neiro* — in the oil case, a person anticipates that the candle will burn down and leave oil; the prospect of leftover oil was always in mind. *Aval hacha adam yoshev u-metzapeh eimasai tipol sukkaso?* — does a person actually expect his *sukkah* to collapse? If not, even Rabbi Shimon should not permit it, since nothing about the outcome was anticipated when *yom tov* began.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves this: *hacha be-sukkah re'u'ah askinan, dem-e'asmol da'ato alaveih* — we speak of a rickety, fragile *sukkah*. Since the person was already expecting it might fall, the eventuality was in mind from before *yom tov*. Under those conditions, Rabbi Shimon permits using the wood when it does fall.

### Pesukim Source

Now the *gemara* turns to the second part of the *mishnah*: the agreement that a *sukkat he-chag* on *sukkot* is forbidden. The *gemara* cites Rav Sheshes in the name of Rabbi Akiva: *minayin l'atzei sukkah she'asurin kol shiva?* — from where do we know that the wood of the *sukkah* (according to some opinions, including the walls; according to others, only the *sechach*) is forbidden for the entire week of *sukkot*? This is not ordinary *muktza*, which does not normally apply on *chol ha-moed*. It is a separate category.

The source: *shene'emar Chag haSukkos shivat yamim l'Hashem* — "a celebration of *sukkot* seven days to God." A *baraita* teaches: just as God's name, so to speak, descends upon the *korban chagiga* — sanctifying it — so too does it descend upon the *sukkah* itself. *Talmud lomar: Chag haSukkos shivat yamim l'Hashem* — the *sukkah* is "to God." *Ma chag l'Hashem af sukkah l'Hashem* — just as the *chagiga* is dedicated to God, so is the *sukkah*. This sanctity does not prohibit sitting in the *sukkah* — obviously one must sit in it — but it does prohibit using the *sukkah*'s materials for any other purpose throughout the seven days. Some hold this to be a genuine *d'oraisa* concept.

Given this level of sanctity, what good can a *tnai* — a prior stipulation — do? A stipulation affects one's mental state and designation, but it cannot undo an objective *kedushah* that takes effect by Torah law.

### Stipulation & Noy

Rav Menashya resolves the contradiction: *seifa aslan l'sukkah d'alma* — the clause permitting stipulation does not refer to a *sukkat he-chag* on *sukkot* at all. It refers back to the hut used on *pesach* — the fallen *sukkah* case. Even according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that *muktza* applies, if one explicitly declared before *yom tov* "should this *sukkah* fall, I intend to use it for firewood," the stipulation removes the *muktza* status. *Aval sukkah d'mitzvah lo mahani bah tnai* — but for the *mitzvah*-*sukkah* of *sukkot*, no stipulation will help. Even if the *sukkah* falls, the wood remains forbidden, because the prohibition is not about mental designation but about inherent sanctity.

But the *gemara* immediately confronts an apparent contradiction: a *baraita* teaches that if one decorated the *sukkah* — *sichcha k'hilchasa, v'itrah b'kramim u'v'sadinim hametzuyarim* — covered it properly with *sechach* and adorned it with illustrated sheets and cloths, hung from it nuts, almonds, peaches, pomegranates, clusters of grapes, wine, oil, flour, and decorated wheat sheaves — then *asur l'histapeik meihen ad motzaei yom tov acharon shel chag*: all these are forbidden for use until after the final day of *sukkot*. However, *v'im hitna aleihem hakol l'fi tna'o* — if one stipulated beforehand, the stipulation is effective. So here, stipulation does work for the *sukkah* of the *mitzvah*.

The resolution is that the *baraita* is speaking not of the *sukkah*'s structural materials but of its *noi* — the decorations. Abaye and Rava both rule: *b'omer eini boded meihem kol bein hashmashos* — if one declares at the onset of *sukkot*, "I am not fully separating myself from these decorations throughout *bein hashmashos*," meaning he does not wholly surrender his rights to the fruit and adornments as *sukkot* begins — then *lo chala kedushah alaihu*: the sanctity of the *sukkah* never takes full hold of the *noi*, and one's stipulation retains effectiveness. *Aval atzei sukkah, de-chala kedushah alaihu, itkatsai le-shiva* — but the wood of the *sukkah* itself, upon which the sanctity does fully descend, remains off-limits for the entire seven days. No stipulation can undo that.

This introduces the broader principle of *huktza le-mitzvah*, designation for a *mitzvah*: an item committed to the performance of a *mitzvah* — like the oil of a *chanukah* menorah — is off-limits for other uses, independent of the sanctity of the day and independent of ordinary *muktza*. For the *sukkah*'s structural wood, this principle applies in its fullest form. The *noi*, by contrast, can be kept outside that designation through a prior stipulation, so long as the stipulation is made before the *kedushah* takes hold.

### Esrog Comparison

The *gemara* presses further: if the *sukkah* can be designated for only one day at a time — perhaps one could stipulate "I am designating this *sukkah* for day one, and that *sukkah* for day two," similar to a case involving *esrogim*. The case: if one sets aside seven *esrogim* for the seven days of *sukkot*, Rav rules *kol achas ve-achas yotzei bah ve-ocheil le-alter* — each *esrog*, once the *mitzvah* has been performed with it, may be eaten immediately. Rav Assi rules *kol achas ve-achas yotzei bah ve-ocheil le-machar* — one must wait until the following day to eat it, since the *esrog* remains designated for the entire day on which it is used. Yet both agree the *esrog* is not designated beyond its own day. If so, why couldn't one cycle through *sukkot* the same way, with each day's *sukkah* becoming permissible the following day?

### Seven Days Continuous

The *gemara* distinguishes: *hasam de-mafski leilos mi-yamim* — with the *lulav* and *esrog*, night interrupts day. Since the *mitzvah* of *lulav* is not performed at night, each day is a discrete and self-contained *mitzvah* period. *Kol chad ve-chad yoma mitzvah be-anpei nafsheih hu* — each day stands as its own independent *mitzvah*. The *esrog* designated for Monday is not designated for Tuesday; they are seven separate *mitzvos*.

*Hacha de-lo mafski leilos mi-yamim* — with *sukkah*, by contrast, night does not interrupt. One sleeps in the *sukkah*; the *mitzvah* continues through the night. *Kulei yoma ke-chad yoma arichta dami* — the entire seven-day period is like one single extended day. Once the *sukkah* is designated for the beginning of this long unified period, it remains designated — and therefore off-limits for other use — for the entire week.

# Beitzah 31

## Wood from Field/Karpef

### Muktzah & Wood Theme

Daf 31 returns to one of the dominant themes of this *perek*: gaining access to food and materials that have been set aside, with the ever-present specter of *muktzah* hovering over nearly every discussion. The *mishnah* opens with a relatively accessible case: *mevi'im etzim min hasadeh min hamikhunas* — one may bring wood from the field if it has been gathered into a pile. Since the wood has been collected and stacked, it is evident that the owner intends to use it for firewood or a similar purpose, and it therefore does not carry *muktzah* status. The *mishnah* adds: *umin hakarfaf* — one may also bring wood from a *karfaf*, which, as we shall see, is a fenced enclosure closer in character to a courtyard than to a distant open field.

### Karpef Definition

A *karfaf* is not simply any outdoor space. It occupies an intermediate category — neither one's home nor a remote agricultural field. It is a fenced enclosure that bears enough of a relationship to the domestic sphere to render its contents more readily "on one's radar screen." This concept will be immediately familiar to anyone who learned the relevant *sugya* in Shabbat, where *karfaf* featured prominently in the laws of *hukaf ledira*. The *mishnah* further specifies that if the wood is brought from a *karfaf*, it is permitted *afilu min hamifuzarin* — even if the sticks are scattered and not gathered into a pile — since the nature of the *karfaf* itself suffices to establish that these items are intended for human use.

### R. Yehuda vs. R. Yosi

The *mishnah* then raises the definitional question: *eizu karfaf*? Rabbi Yehuda says: *kol shesamuch la'ir* — any enclosure that is near the city qualifies as a *karfaf*. Rabbi Yosi, by contrast, introduces an additional or alternative criterion: *kol shenichnasin lo bepotachat* — any enclosure that one enters with a key, meaning it is fenced and locked. Rabbi Yosi adds that this definition applies *afilu betoch techum Shabbat* — even if the enclosure is situated at the far edge of the *techum Shabbat*, which on *Yom Tov* extends two thousand *amot* from the city. The force of Rabbi Yosi's position is that even an enclosure located as far away as one may travel on *Yom Tov* retains the status of a *karfaf* if it is properly fenced and locked, because that physical security signals human intention and control over the contents within.

### Tosafot on Imur

Before proceeding to the *gemara*'s analysis, *Tosafot* raises a striking question that deserves careful attention. The *mishnah* speaks of taking wood from the *karfaf* even when the sticks are scattered, and of gathering sticks from the field when they are piled. But if one is gathering scattered sticks, is that not the *melachah* of *me'amer* — the agricultural labor of bundling, which figures in the Torah's account of the *mekoshish etzim*? Indeed, *me'amer* is an *av melachah de'oraita*, and the concern is entirely real.

*Tosafot* resolves this by limiting the prohibition of *me'amer* to its natural agricultural context: *imur* applies specifically where the produce is gathered in the place where it grew — the wheat lying in the field after the harvest, the apples that have fallen from the tree. The act of bundling produce *in situ* as part of the harvest process constitutes *me'amer*. By contrast, sticks that lie scattered in a *karfaf* — which functions more like a lot or a park than a cultivated agricultural field — are not being gathered as part of a harvesting process, and therefore do not implicate *me'amer*. *Tosafot* acknowledges, however, that in certain field scenarios, gathering scattered sticks that fell from trees could theoretically raise a *de'oraita* concern. The point is important: the discussion in the *mishnah* is not so simple that it can be read without awareness of this potential biblical dimension.

### Rav Yehuda's Position

The *gemara* now introduces a ruling from Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *ein mevi'im etzim ela min hamikhunasin she-be-karfaf* — one may bring wood only from sticks that are both gathered *and* located within a *karfaf*. This immediately stands in tension with our *mishnah*, which appears to require only one of the two criteria: either gathered (in the field) or in the *karfaf* (even if scattered). The *gemara* responds that our *mishnah* represents a *da'at yachid* — a minority position — and that there exists an opposing view requiring both criteria simultaneously.

### Beit Shammai/Hillel

To support this claim, the *gemara* cites a *baraita* in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: *lo necheleku Beit Shammai ve-Beit Hillel al hamefuzarin sheba-sadot she-ein mevi'im* — both schools agree that scattered wood in an open field is forbidden; it is *muktzah*, and as *Tosafot* noted, gathering it might even pose a *de'oraita* problem. Similarly, both agree that gathered wood within a *karfaf* — the case with both criteria — is permitted. *Al mah necheleku?* What was the actual dispute? It was the intermediate cases: either scattered wood in a *karfaf*, or gathered wood out in the field. *Beit Shammai* says one criterion is insufficient; *Beit Hillel* says one criterion suffices.

### R. Shimon Interpretation

The *gemara* draws its conclusion: according to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, *Beit Hillel*'s position is that one criterion suffices, and this is consistent with our *mishnah*. But the attribution to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is itself significant. It implies that others disagree with his reading of the dispute — they hold that *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* never debated the intermediate cases at all, and that everyone agrees both criteria are necessary. This is precisely the position of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: the *mishnah* follows only Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's lenient reading, which is itself a minority position, while the authoritative ruling requires both that the wood be gathered *and* that it be located in a *karfaf*.

### Rava on Easy-Scatter Items

Rava introduces a further refinement. Even where gathered wood is found in the appropriate location, not every physical pile qualifies as *mukhunas*. *Alei kanei ve-alei gefanim* — leaves of reeds or grapevine leaves — *af al gav de-mekhansei ve-motvi*, even if they are piled up, *keivan de-im madli zika mevader lehu, ke-mefuzarin damu* — since a wind could easily scatter them, they are treated as if they were scattered to begin with. A pile of leaves is, in Rava's view, not a genuine pile, because the owner had no reasonable expectation that the pile would remain intact. Without that expectation, there is no *da'at* — no cognitive presence — that would classify the material as set aside for use. The principle is that *muktzah* is fundamentally about what is "on one's radar screen," and something whose stability cannot be assumed does not make it onto that screen.

### Rava's Tarp Solution

Rava then offers the remedy: *ve-ee itnach mana me-etmol la-layeh* — if, on the day before *Yom Tov*, one placed a vessel or some covering over the pile to protect it from the wind, *shapir dami* — that is entirely acceptable. By taking a concrete action before *Yom Tov* to ensure the pile's stability, one demonstrates genuine intention to use the material and overcomes the wind-scattering problem. The practical upshot is that someone who intends to use a pile of lightweight material — leaves, reed leaves, and the like — should place a covering over it before *Yom Tov* commences.

### Karpef Criteria Debate

The *gemara* now returns to the definitional dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi regarding what constitutes a *karfaf*, and raises a pointed question about how to read their exchange: *heichi ka'amar* — precisely what is each one claiming?

One reading: Rabbi Yehuda assumes that a *karfaf* by definition has a fence and lock, and adds that it must *also* be near the city. Rabbi Yosi then comes to say: *keivan de'it lei potachat afilu betoch techum Shabbat* — once it has the fence and lock, proximity to the city is irrelevant. On this reading, Rabbi Yosi is being lenient relative to Rabbi Yehuda, who requires both proximity and a lock.

An alternative reading: Rabbi Yehuda is not requiring two criteria but rather insisting that proximity to the city is the *only* relevant criterion — *kol shesamuch la'ir, bein de'it lei potachat bein deleit lei potachat*. Whether or not it is locked, if it is near the city it is a *karfaf*. Rabbi Yosi, in response, says the only determinative criterion is the fence and lock — *davka de'it lei potachat* — and proximity to the city is neither necessary nor sufficient. On this reading, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosi are not arguing about how many criteria are required but about *which* criterion is the operative one.

The *gemara* attempts to resolve this question from the language of the *mishnah* itself — specifically from Rabbi Yosi's formulation, which includes the phrase *afilu betoch techum Shabbat*. The *gemara* concludes: *shema mina, tartei lekula ka'amar* — from the fact that Rabbi Yosi says "even within the *techum Shabbat*," one can infer that Rabbi Yosi is being lenient in two directions simultaneously: either criterion is sufficient on its own. If it has a lock, distance from the city does not matter; if it is near the city, the absence of a lock does not disqualify it. Rabbi Yehuda, by contrast, requires both. The resolution hinges on the logical force of the word *afilu* in Rabbi Yosi's formulation, though the precise reasoning is itself the subject of a lengthy discussion in *Rashi* and *Tosafot*, who grapple with exactly how the *gemara* derives this conclusion from the *mishnah*'s language.

### Resolution: One vs. Two

The *gemara* concludes, based on the above analysis, that Rabbi Yehuda demands both criteria to define something as a *karfaf*, while Rabbi Yosi holds that either criterion independently suffices. Our *mishnah*, which required only one criterion (either gathered or in a *karfaf*), aligns with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's reading of *Beit Hillel*'s position; and the more stringent position of Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel aligns with those who read the debate as one in which both criteria are universally required.

### Practical Halacha

Rav Sala in the name of Rabbi Yirmeyah rules: *halacha ke-Rabbi Yosi lehakel* — the law follows Rabbi Yosi's lenient position in *defining* what constitutes a *karfaf*, such that either proximity to the city or a fence-and-lock arrangement suffices for that definitional question. However, when it comes to the separate question of what is required to *permit use* of the sticks themselves, one follows Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel's stricter standard, which demands both that the wood be gathered *and* that it be located in a *karfaf*.

It is worth pausing to note what makes this class of *muktzah* conceptually distinctive from others encountered earlier in the *masechta*. Most prior examples of *muktzah* involved items that are naturally within the human sphere — food, vessels — that were somehow pushed out of that sphere by being set aside, stored away, or designated for another purpose. Here the situation is the reverse: scattered sticks and stones are naturally *outside* the human sphere, and the question is what brings them *into* it. Gathering them and placing them in a controlled enclosure are the mechanisms by which these objects of the natural world become integrated into the domain of human intention and anticipated use.

---

## Chopping Wood Issue

### Chopping Prohibition

The next *mishnah* states: *ein mevak'in etzim lo min hakorot velo min hakorah shenishberah beYom Tov* — one may not chop wood from beams, nor from a beam that fell on *Yom Tov* itself. The case of the beam that fell on *Yom Tov* is straightforwardly a *muktzah* problem: when *Yom Tov* began, the beam was part of the building's rafters and entirely outside one's contemplated use. Once it crashes down on *Yom Tov*, it does not automatically become available firewood, since it was not designated as such at the onset of *Yom Tov*.

### Muktzah Beam Status

But what of simple beams — logs of wood that were already present before *Yom Tov*? The *mishnah*'s prohibition on chopping from *korot* (beams) seems at first puzzling: if they were there before *Yom Tov*, why are they *muktzah*? The *gemara* will address this directly, and the resolution involves reconsidering exactly what the *mishnah* means by *korot*.

### Tools Permitted/Forbidden

The *mishnah* then addresses the act of chopping itself. When chopping is permitted, it may not be done *lo bekardom velo bemgirah velo bemagal ela bekupitz* — not with an axe, not with a crosscut saw, not with a scythe, but only with a *kupitz*, which *Rashi* identifies as *sakin shel katzavim* — a butcher's cleaver.

### Avoda Dechol Concept

*Rashi*'s explanation for why the axe and the saw are forbidden illuminates an important principle: *avoda dechol* — the appearance of weekday labor. Chopping wood with an axe, going out to the yard with a full-sized crosscut saw — these evoke the image of someone at work, out in the field, engaged in the kind of labor associated with professional woodcutting. The prohibition on *Yom Tov* against activities that appear as *avoda dechol* is not about the specific *melachah* being performed, but about the overall experiential reality being created. Using a meat cleaver to reduce a log into usable pieces for the fire is a different experience altogether — it places the activity squarely within the domestic context, the preparation of one's home for the needs of the day. The concern, in other words, is not merely technical compliance but the *character* of the act.

### Gemara Reframe

The *gemara* initially reads the first part of the *mishnah* — the prohibition on chopping from *korot* — as also relating to the *avoda dechol* issue, i.e., as a general prohibition on the act of chopping. But this creates a contradiction with the *mishnah*'s own conclusion, which permits chopping with a *kupitz*. The *gemara* therefore says: *ha'amarta reisha ein mevak'in klal* — how can you permit chopping at the end if the beginning seems to prohibit chopping altogether?

### Savar Definition

The resolution comes from Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *chisuri mechasra vehachi katani* — the *mishnah* is elliptical and must be read with an implied context. The prohibition in the first clause is not about the act of chopping per se but about *muktzah*: *ein mevak'in min hasavar shel korot* — one may not chop from a *savar* of beams, meaning a pile of beams that has been set aside specifically for construction purposes. Neatly stacked construction lumber — what we might picture as pre-cut 2×4s arranged on a building site — is designated for construction, not for fuel. Using it for firewood on *Yom Tov* therefore constitutes a violation of *muktzah*, because such materials were mentally assigned to a different purpose entirely.
