A *baraita* confirms this reading explicitly, using the word *savar* rather than the ambiguous *korot*, making clear that the context is a pile of construction materials. The *baraita* states the reason: *l'fi she'eino min hamukhan* — because these items are not set aside for *Yom Tov* use. Alongside this, it confirms the prohibition against chopping with an axe for the separate reason of *avoda dechol*. The two prohibitions — *muktzah* applying to construction lumber, and *avoda dechol* applying to the use of professional woodcutting tools — are thus properly distinguished.

### Axe Gender Parts

The *gemara* cites Rav Chinena bar Shamaya in the name of Rav: *lo shanu ela be-nekeivot shelo aval be-zachrot shelo mutar* — when the axe is prohibited, the prohibition applies only to the *feminine* part of the axe; the *masculine* part remains permitted. The terminology here maps onto the distinction between the broader, more robust chopping surface of the axe — associated with the heavy, professional woodcutting work that constitutes *avoda dechol* — and the narrower, more refined edge that functions similarly to a cleaver. The *masculine* part, being narrower and more precise in its cutting action, resembles the *kupitz* in its domestic character and is therefore permitted.

The *gemara* initially objects: *pshita* — this seems obvious. If the *mishnah* permits using a *kupitz*, and this part of the axe functions like a *kupitz*, what is the novel teaching? The answer is that one might have thought: *migu de-hai gisa asur* — since one part of the implement is forbidden, the presence of the forbidden component contaminates the entire implement, making even the permissible part forbidden by association. The ruling comes to teach that this is not so: one may use the cleaver-like portion of the implement even if the axe-like portion of the same tool would be forbidden.

### Cleaver Use Debate

A parallel discussion is then introduced regarding the *kupitz* itself. The *mishnah* permits using a *kupitz*, but the *kupitz* too has component parts that differ in character. The ruling is stated again by Rav Chinena bar Shamaya: when the *kupitz* is permitted, that refers specifically to its *masculine* — narrower — portion, which is the genuine cleaver-like edge. The *feminine* — broader — portion of the *kupitz* more closely resembles an axe and is therefore forbidden for the same *avoda dechol* reason.

Again the *gemara* says *pshita* — the *mishnah* forbids axes, so of course the axe-like portion of the *kupitz* should be forbidden. And again the novelty requires articulation: one might have thought that since the *kupitz* is generically permitted, the permissibility extends to all its functions — *migu de-hai gisa shari, hai gisa nami shari* — since one part of the *kupitz* is permitted, perhaps the other part is permitted as well. The ruling comes to teach that only the genuinely cleaver-like function of the *kupitz* is permitted; the axe-like function remains forbidden.

One might note that the more internally consistent position would be to forbid even the cleaver-like part of the *kupitz* when the *kupitz* itself also has an axe-like component, since the totality of the implement evokes professional woodcutting. The *gemara* acknowledges this intuition and presents it as the view of an alternative version of the tradition — *ve-ika de-matni la asayfa* — which applies the principle in the stricter direction: even some cleavers will be forbidden depending on their dual-function character and the overall experiential reality they create.

---

## Locked House Fruit

### Storage House Scenario

The next *mishnah* presents a scenario that at first glance might seem straightforward but opens onto a rich discussion of *muktzah*, *soter*, and the special latitude granted on *Yom Tov* for food access. The case: *bayis she-malei peiros* — a house filled with fruit, understood here not as a living room stocked with apples but as a storage facility — a shed, a granary — packed with produce. Before *Yom Tov*, the house was locked and there was no access to the fruit. The owner intended to use the fruit but found no way in. Then *nifchas* — the wall was breached, an opening appeared — and access became possible.

The word *nifchas* itself, as distinct from *niftach* (simply opened), suggests a structural collapse or a section of wall falling away, rather than a door swinging open. One might read it as the wall having been diminished — something fell away and created an opening. The connection to the earlier discussion of *matchilin be-otzar techilah* is real: this scenario also involves gaining access to stored produce, and one might have thought the fruit itself was *muktzah* as undisturbed stored goods.

### Standard Permission

The *mishnah* rules that *notel mimakom hapachas* — one may take fruit from the place of the breach. The fruit itself is accessible, and the opening that has appeared may be used.

### R. Meir Leniency

The significant *chiddush* of the *mishnah* is Rabbi Meir's position: *af poches lechatchilah venotel* — one may actively break open the wall and then take the fruit. Rabbi Meir thus permits the deliberate demolition of a section of the storage structure in order to gain access to the food within.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

Why, before reaching Rabbi Meir's ruling, is the fruit not *muktzah*? If the house was locked and the fruit inaccessible, why is the fruit available at all once the wall is breached? *Rashi* answers that the only obstacle to accessing the fruit was the need to break the wall, and since — as the *gemara* will demonstrate — breaking an unplastered brick wall may constitute only a rabbinic prohibition, that alone is insufficient to render the fruit *muktzah*. A rabbinic barrier to access does not place the fruit outside one's anticipated reach in the way that a biblical prohibition would.

*Tosafot* finds this unsatisfying. Why should the biblical or rabbinic character of the obstacle matter to the question of *muktzah*? If the fruit is out of reach, it is out of reach, and the *muktzah* status should follow. *Tosafot* therefore argues that the *mishnah* must be understood as following the position of Rabbi Shimon, who holds a significantly narrower conception of *muktzah* — one that would not extend to fruit that is physically present and intended for use, even if access to it happened to be blocked by a structural obstruction.

### Soter Problem

The *gemara* focuses its analysis on Rabbi Meir's ruling. *Amai? Veha kasater ahala* — why does Rabbi Meir permit this? Is one not demolishing a structure — engaging in *soter*, which is a *melachah*?

### Avira Delivnei

The answer comes from Rav Nechumi bar Ada in the name of Shmuel: *be'avira delivnei* — the case involves bricks stacked without mortar. Since there is no mortar binding the bricks together, dismantling the wall does not constitute genuine *soter*, as there is no truly permanent structure being deconstructed. *Nifchas* — the wall's having collapsed — is also consistent with this explanation, since an unplastered wall of stacked bricks is inherently unstable and prone to collapse. One might object that even unmortered walls can be extraordinarily stable — as the ancient stone fences of England and Ireland demonstrate, skilled construction without mortar can last centuries. Still, a wall of regularly-shaped bricks without mortar lacks the structural permanence of a plastered wall, and the *gemara*'s position is that this falls below the threshold of biblical *soter*.

### Rav Nachman Bricks

But even granting that *soter* is not a biblical issue here, the *gemara* raises an independent problem: *muktzah*. Does Rav Nachman not teach that *hani livni deyasmi mibinyana* — leftover bricks from a construction site — are not *muktzah*, since they can be used as seating (*hо'il vechazi lemizga aleihu*)? So far so good: leftover bricks, no longer designated for construction, are available. However, *shargineihu* — if one then stacks those bricks neatly, *aktsineihu* — one has re-designated them for construction use and rendered them *muktzah* once more. A neatly stacked pile of bricks signals that they are being reserved for a building project.

Apply this to our case: the bricks of the storage house were arranged and stacked to form a wall before *Yom Tov*. That arrangement constitutes a designation for structural use. Even if the wall has no mortar, the bricks, by virtue of being stacked to form a structure, are *muktzah*. How, then, can Rabbi Meir permit one to dismantle the wall and use the bricks — or at least, to move and handle them in the course of breaching the wall — if those bricks are themselves *muktzah*?

### Yom Tov Limited

Rabbi Zeira resolves this: *be-Yom Tov amru aval lo be-Shabbat* — the *mishnah*'s permission is stated specifically for *Yom Tov*, not for *Shabbat*. The question then becomes: what does *Yom Tov* change? If the bricks are *muktzah* and the act of dismantling is *soter*, how does the *Yom Tov* context alter the analysis?

### Okhel Nefesh Waiver

*Tosafot* makes explicit what the *gemara* implies: *she-hitiru muktzah mishum okhel nefesh* — the concern of *muktzah* is waived on *Yom Tov* when the *muktzah* item constitutes an obstacle to food access, because the Torah's permission for *okhel nefesh* on *Yom Tov* extends to removing impediments to food preparation and access. *Rashi* appears to take the same position, though it is *Tosafot* that formulates it as a principle, citing it in the name of the *Ritzba* who had stated it earlier.

This is a striking conceptual claim. *Muktzah* has throughout the *masechta* been treated as a robust rabbinic framework that applies across many contexts. To say that *Yom Tov*'s *okhel nefesh* license can waive *muktzah* concerns is to significantly expand the reach of that leniency. The question of how to integrate this principle with the earlier discussions — *matchilin be-otzar*, the egg of the first *mishnah*, and all the other *muktzah* scenarios explored throughout the *perek* — remains genuinely complex, and the *gemara* does not fully resolve it here. One observation that helps: if the food itself is *muktzah*, the *okhel nefesh* rationale cannot rescue it, because the food's *muktzah* status effectively disqualifies it from being food-for-*Yom Tov* in the relevant sense. The *okhel nefesh* waiver applies when the food is legitimate but the *muktzah* concern is an external obstacle preventing access. That said, threading this through all the earlier cases is not without difficulty.

---

## Wells & Seals Issue

### Shmuel Seals

The *gemara* now pivots to a broader discussion of *boneh* and *soter* as they apply to ground-connected structures and to vessels, a discussion triggered by Shmuel's teaching but extending into a wide-ranging analysis of the distinctions between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, between structures and vessels, and between different modes of undoing a fastening.

Shmuel's teaching: *khotamot she-ba-karka, matir* — one may undo the knots on ground-connected seals on *Shabbat*. The image to have in mind is a well covered by something analogous to a manhole cover, which is roped or chained to the well to prevent it from being lost or stolen. The rope or chain is tied with a knot designed to be undone and retied — it is not a *kesher shel kayama*, a permanent knot — and so untying it raises no concern of *matir kesher*. Nor does simply undoing the knot constitute *soter*, the deconstruction of a structure. Why not? Because this is simply how the well is used: the cover is opened by undoing the knot, and the expectation is that the cover will be replaced afterward. The act of opening the well is part of the well's normal functioning; it does not structurally alter anything in a lasting way. Just as opening a door is not *soter* even though one momentarily breaks the connection between the door and the doorpost, so too undoing the well cover's rope is not *soter*.

### Matir/Mafki'a/Chotech

However, *aval lo mafki'a velo chotech* — one may not *unravel* the rope (*mafki'a*: to unbraid or unwind the braiding of the rope itself) nor cut it. The distinction here is fundamental. In all three actions — undoing the knot, unraveling the rope, and cutting — the physical result is the same: the cover is detached from the well. But the character of the acts differs entirely. Undoing the knot is the intended mode of operation; it is reversible and does not structurally change the connection. Unraveling the rope destroys the rope's integrity and makes it very difficult or impossible to restore to its previous state. Cutting severs the connection permanently. Both unraveling and cutting, therefore, constitute genuine structural deconstruction — *soter* of the well-as-structure — and are prohibited on *Shabbat*.

### Soter vs. Vessels

A critical principle is now stated: *ein boneh vesoter bekeilim* — the prohibitions of *boneh* (building) and *soter* (demolishing) do not apply to vessels. This parallels the intuitive distinction between knocking down a house to access food and tearing open a bag of potato chips to access food. *Soter* is a concern for structures connected to the ground; it is not a concern for moveable vessels.

### Vessel Exception

Consequently, if the same scenario — a rope holding a cover in place — involves not a ground-connected well but a vessel (imagine a covered box in one's home, secured by a rope), then on *Shabbat* one may undo the knot, unravel the rope, and even cut the rope. Since the prohibition of *soter* does not apply to vessels, all modes of detaching the cover are permitted. The analogy to tearing open a bag of potato chips captures the principle well.

### Braitah on Ground

The *gemara* then cites a *braitah*: *khotamot she-ba-karka, be-Shabbat matir aval lo mafki'a velo chotech* — confirming the ruling for ground-connected seals on *Shabbat*. Significantly, the *braitah* then states: *be-Yom Tov matir mafki'a ve-chotech* — on *Yom Tov*, one may even cut the rope securing the well cover. This introduces an apparent inconsistency with Shmuel's ruling, which gave no distinction between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* for ground-connected seals.

### R. Meir Attribution

The *gemara* resolves this by attributing the permissive *braitah* to Rabbi Meir: *ha mani Rabbi Meir hi* — this is Rabbi Meir, who, as established in the previous *mishnah*, permits *soter* of a structure to gain access to food. Just as Rabbi Meir permits breaking down the wall of the storage house, he permits cutting the rope securing the well cover in order to access the water.

### Rabbis Agree

The *gemara* then notes a *braitah* stating that the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Meir regarding ground-connected seals on *Shabbat* — that one may undo the knot (*matir*) but may not cut. Shmuel's position aligns with the Rabbis, not Rabbi Meir: one may undo the knot on *Shabbat*, but the Rabbis dispute Rabbi Meir's permission to cut on *Yom Tov* in the case of a ground-connected structure.

### Braitah Vessels

For vessels, a separate *braitah* rules: *be-Shabbat matir aval lo mafki'a velo chotech; be-Yom Tov matir u-mafki'a ve-chotech* — on *Shabbat*, one may undo the knot on a vessel's rope but may not unravel or cut it; on *Yom Tov*, one may do all three. This is more stringent than what Shmuel stated for vessels, since Shmuel appeared to permit even cutting the rope of a vessel on *Shabbat*.

### R. Nechemya Position

The *gemara* attributes this stricter *braitah* on vessels to Rabbi Nechemya: *ha mani Rabbi Nechemya hi*. Rabbi Nechemya's concern is unrelated to *soter*; he operates from a completely different principle: *kol ha-kelim ein nitalin ela derech tashmishan* — all vessels may only be used in their designated manner. Rabbi Nechemya holds that even an ordinary kitchen knife, which carries no *muktzah* status, may not be used for purposes other than its normal function. One may not use a kitchen knife to cut a rope, scratch an itch, or pick one's teeth — it is a knife for cutting food, and that is the extent of its permitted use on *Shabbat*.

### R. Nechemya Strictness

Consequently, according to Rabbi Nechemya, the prohibition on cutting the rope securing a vessel on *Shabbat* has nothing to do with *soter*. The act of dismantling the vessel's closure is perfectly acceptable in principle (since *ein boneh vesoter bekeilim*); the problem is that cutting a rope is not what knives are for, and no available vessel is designated for rope-cutting. The restriction, in other words, targets the *instrument* of the action, not the act itself.

### R. Nechemya Yom Tov

The *gemara* raises the obvious question: if Rabbi Nechemya's principle — that vessels may only be used in their designated manner — is a general rule about how vessels may be employed, why is it limited to *Shabbat*? The *braitah* permits cutting on *Yom Tov*, implying that Rabbi Nechemya's restriction does not apply on *Yom Tov*. Does Rabbi Nechemya truly distinguish between the *shevut* of *Shabbat* and the *shevut* of *Yom Tov*?

### Firewood Vessels

To test whether Rabbi Nechemya makes such a distinction, the *gemara* turns to a set of *braitot* concerning which items may be used as firewood on *Yom Tov* — a context that is unambiguously *Yom Tov*. The first *braitah*: *masikin be-kelim ve-ein masikin be-shivrei kelim* — one may use whole vessels as firewood but not broken vessels. The reasoning is that a vessel which broke on *Yom Tov* is *muktzah* — it was not designated as firewood when *Yom Tov* began, and its breakage on *Yom Tov* created a *nolad* (a newly-created status) that renders it *muktzah*. The whole vessel, by contrast, was available before *Yom Tov* and has not undergone a status change. This is the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds of *muktzah*.

The second *braitah*: *masikin bein be-kelim bein be-shivrei kelim* — one may use both whole and broken vessels as firewood. This is the position of Rabbi Shimon, who does not hold of *muktzah* in its broad form and therefore does not treat a vessel that breaks on *Yom Tov* as newly *muktzah*.

The third *braitah*: *ein masikin lo be-kelim velo be-shivrei kelim* — neither whole vessels nor broken vessels may be used as firewood. This is Rabbi Nechemya's position. Whole vessels may not be burned as firewood because vessels are not designated for burning — *ein nitalin ela derech tashmishan* — and this principle applies on *Yom Tov* as well as on *Shabbat*. Since this third *braitah* is unambiguously about *Yom Tov* and yet Rabbi Nechemya's restriction applies within it, the *gemara* has established that Rabbi Nechemya does indeed apply his principle on *Yom Tov*. The *gemara* therefore resolves: *trei tanna'ei aliba de-Rabbi Nechemya* — there is a debate among *tannaim* about Rabbi Nechemya's position: one *tanna* holds that he extends his restriction to *Yom Tov*, while another holds that he distinguishes *Shabbat*'s *shevut* from *Yom Tov*'s *shevut* and is lenient on *Yom Tov*.

### Unresolved Soter Q

It is worth noting in closing that the *gemara* never fully resolves the foundational *soter* question with which this entire discussion began. When the *gemara* first asked how Rabbi Meir could permit breaking into the storage house, it reframed the case as involving unmortered bricks (*avira delivnei*) — thereby reducing or eliminating the *soter* concern. But when the discussion later moved to the well covers and the permission to cut the rope on *Yom Tov* even on a ground-connected structure, the *gemara* seemed to attribute this to Rabbi Meir's general willingness to permit *soter* for food access — without again invoking the *avira delivnei* limitation. One could offer a principled resolution: perhaps the authentic *de'oraita* prohibition of *soter* applies only to *soter al menat livnot* — demolition undertaken as part of a construction project — and destructive acts undertaken purely to gain access to food, with no reconstructive purpose, constitute *mekalkel* (a purely destructive act) rather than *soter*, and thus remain at most rabbinically forbidden. On *Yom Tov*, Rabbi Meir would then be willing to waive the rabbinic concern in the interest of food access. But the *gemara* leaves this reasoning implicit, and the question of precisely how *soter* and *mekalkel* interact in these cases — and how Rabbi Meir's principle is properly delimited — remains, as the *gemara* concludes, without explicit clarification.

---

---

# Beitzah 32

## Lamp Obstructions

### Pochet Haneir

The Gemara continues on 32a, approximately ten lines from the bottom. The *mishna* rules that one may not perform *pochet haneir* — removing the stuffing from a lamp that has undergone only its first firing and has not yet finished hardening — because doing so constitutes an act of completing a vessel. Tosafot understands the *mishna* in precisely these terms: the removal of the obstruction before the second firing transforms the lamp into a functional vessel, and that act of completion is prohibited on *Yom Tov*.

### Vessel Completion

The Gemara seeks to identify which *tanna* holds that removing something from a partially completed vessel — even before the hardening process is finished — renders it a vessel. It first compares the lamp case to a general tannaitic statement about pottery, which Tosafot understood as addressing exactly this scenario. The Gemara then turns to a parallel dispute involving frying pans. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that even while the cover remains sealed on, the frying pan already possesses vessel status — it is considered a vessel at an earlier stage. Rabbi Eliezer berabbi Tzadok disagrees, arguing *lefi shelo nigmar melachtan* — their work is not yet complete — which is understood to mean that the cover has not yet been removed. Once the cover is removed, however, even before the firing and hardening process is complete, the frying pan attains vessel status. According to Rabbi Eliezer berabbi Tzadok, then, it is precisely the removal of the obstruction that makes it a vessel, even prior to the completion of the manufacturing process.

### Village Frying Pans

Abaye challenges this analogy. He suggests that perhaps Rabbi Eliezer berabbi Tzadok's ruling applies only there — to the frying pan — because once the cover is removed, even if the pan has not yet hardened fully, it is still *chazi lekippulei bei midi*, fit to receive and store objects. But this small lamp, he asks, *lemai chazi* — what use could it possibly serve? The Gemara responds: *lekippulei bei peshiti* — one can place small coins or objects inside it. Therefore, even the partially processed lamp has a functional use sufficient to confer vessel status, and the *mishna*'s prohibition on removing its obstruction is justified on those grounds.

In sum, the Gemara understands the *mishna* as prohibiting the removal of an obstruction that is part of the vessel-making process, on the grounds that the act of removal itself — even before full hardening — completes the vessel. Two tannaitic disputes in the domain of *tumah ve'taharah* are invoked to support this understanding, since both address the question of at what stage a partially manufactured vessel becomes susceptible to impurity.

### Function vs. Form

The Gemara briefly revisits the *charniyes* frying pans. The *baraita* quoted earlier defines these as *iraniot* — village frying pans — and Abaye explains that the term refers to *tzachei chaklaita*, field platters. Frying pans with the cover still sealed could still serve as platters, and in villages where people are less fastidious about such things, they might be willing to use them at that stage. There is a deeper conceptual tension underlying this entire discussion: one mode of thought holds that functionality determines vessel status — if it can be used, it is a vessel; another holds that formal completion of the manufacturing process is what matters, regardless of interim functional utility. Both considerations are at work in the tannaitic debate, intertwined rather than neatly separated.

---

## Charcoal & Bathhouses

### Charniyes Vessels

The Gemara cites a *baraita*: *ein pochtin et haneir ve'ein osin ilpas ilpasin charaniot beYom Tov* — one may not remove the stuffing from a lamp, and one may not make *ilpasin charaniot*, village frying pans, on *Yom Tov*. Interestingly, this *baraita* combines the lamp discussion from the *mishna* with the *Yom Tov* context, applying to both the same principle that had been debated in *tumah ve'taharah*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits the village frying pans, apparently taking a different position on when vessel status is attained.

### Charcoal Prohibition

The Gemara states: *ve'ein osin pechamin* — one may not make charcoal on *Yom Tov*. The Gemara immediately asks: *p'shita* — is this not obvious? And then: *lemai chazi* — what would one use it for? This is a striking formulation. One might have thought the sole question is whether the act is prohibited, not whether the charcoal has a use. The implicit reasoning is as follows: making a fire on *Yom Tov* is permitted. If charcoal were used for cooking, one might argue — by analogy to permitted fire-making — that producing it should also be allowed. But charcoal, as Rashi explains, is used primarily for metalwork and smelting, not for cooking. Hence the prohibition is obvious and requires no further analysis.

### Charcoal Definition

But what then is the *hava amina*, the initial assumption that the *mishna* needs to dispel? The Gemara answers through a *baraita* of Rabbi Chiyya: *lo nitzrecha ela lemosran le'ulyarin bo bayom* — the ruling is needed for a case where one intended to deliver the charcoal to *ulyarin*, the bathhouse workers who heat the water. One might have thought: heating water for bathing is *ochel nefesh*, or at least *tzorech kol gufo*, a whole-body need — so producing charcoal for that purpose should be permitted. It is to exclude this possibility that the *baraita* speaks.

### Bathhouse Ban

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *bo bayom nishtero* — since when is it permitted to use a heated bathhouse on *Yom Tov* at all? This leads to an important *halacha*. The Sages decreed — *gzeirat merchatzaot* — that one may not enter a heated bathhouse on *Shabbos*, even if the water was heated before *Shabbos*, out of concern that one might come to heat water on *Shabbos* itself. The question is whether this decree extended to *Yom Tov* as well. On *Yom Tov*, heating water for one's face, hands, and feet would in any case be a legitimate act; and one might suppose that heating water for the whole body, as a *tzorech kol gufo*, would also be permitted, making bathhouse use permissible. Nevertheless, the Gemara makes clear that the *gzeirat merchatzaot* applied to *Yom Tov* as well — bathhouses were entirely off-limits — even if under certain circumstances heating the water itself might have been technically permissible. Since bathhouse use is prohibited on *Yom Tov*, the argument that charcoal may be produced for the *ulyarin* collapses.

### Steam Before Decree

The Gemara then cites Rava: *lehazia* — one could, however, have used the charcoal for the steam room, the sauna portion of the bathhouse. Rava teaches that when the *gzeira* was first enacted against bathhouses, the steam room was not yet included in the prohibition. At that earlier stage, using a steam room would have been a *tzorech kol gufo* and rabbinically unobjectionable. The *mishna* therefore needs to teach that even under those circumstances — when steam use was legitimate and constituted a valid bodily need — one still may not produce charcoal on *Yom Tov* to fuel it.

### Vessel Ban Hierarchy

This point carries significant halakhic weight. Even if the purpose is genuinely *tzorech kol haguf*, and even if Rabbi Yehuda — who appears in the *mishna* and who permits *machshirei ochel nefesh* — does not contest this prohibition, the production of charcoal remains forbidden. The reason is that charcoal, whatever its use, is being fashioned into something — it was a piece of wood and is now a processed, functional material with a degree of permanence. Making it involves a quality of *tikkun kli*, of making a vessel, that places it in a different category from mere fire-related acts. The Gemara's treatment implies that Rabbi Yehuda himself would concede this point: even he, who permits preparatory acts for *ochel nefesh*, would not permit the making of something that has this character of vessel-production, even if the ultimate use is legitimate. The question of whether charcoal truly fits our intuitive category of *kli* is itself interesting — charcoal is used by being destroyed, unlike most vessels — but the Gemara treats it as sufficiently vessel-like to trigger the prohibition.

### Yom Tov Bathing

This discussion of *gzeirat merchatzaot* has direct contemporary relevance for the question of bathing on *Yom Tov*. The Gemara elsewhere records a dispute between Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel: Beis Hillel permits heating water on *Yom Tov* for *panav yadav ve'raglav* — one's face, hands, and feet — but not for *kol gufo*, one's whole body. Tosafot explains that heating water for one's whole body was not considered a universal need — not everyone, in that era, required a full hot bath. Many *poskim* reason, however, that in our times a hot shower or bath is entirely universal, and therefore constitutes a genuine *tzorech kol haguf*, making it permissible to heat water for bathing on *Yom Tov*.

Yet even if one accepts that a hot shower is permitted on *Yom Tov* — and many *poskim* do permit it — a hot bath remains forbidden. The *gzeirat merchatzaot* specifically targeted immersion in a bathhouse, and that prohibition remains in force rabbinically even today. The practical upshot is that a hot shower may be taken on *Yom Tov*, as a *tzorech kol haguf* falling within the *ochel nefesh* framework of permitted *Yom Tov* acts, while a hot bath remains off-limits by virtue of the original *gzeira*. The two acts, though closely related, are subject to distinct halakhic analyses.

---

## Wick Modification

### Cutting Wicks

The Gemara teaches: *ve'ein chotzin et haptilah lishnayim* — one may not cut a wick into two pieces on *Yom Tov*. This too falls under the prohibition of making a vessel. One might initially think: where is the act of creation here? Before cutting, the wick was usable; after cutting, it is still usable, merely more appropriately sized. Yet the Gemara treats the cutting as an act of *tikkun* — fashioning the wick into its more functional, properly sized form. This connects to the broader question raised by the cutting of paper towels, tin foil, and similar materials on *Yom Tov*: even if the item was usable before, cutting it to its optimal size constitutes an act that is at minimum rabbinically problematic, and potentially involves the biblical prohibition of *mechatech*, cutting to a precise measurement. The Gemara here establishes that creating the wick in its more appropriate form is indeed a concern.

Rabbi Yehuda, however, permits dividing the wick by means of fire. The Gemara asks: *mai shena besakin delo* — why is a knife forbidden? Because *kematakin mana* — one is fixing a vessel. Whether this phrase denotes a biblical violation of *makeh bepatish*, the final blow in vessel-making, or only a rabbinic prohibition resembling vessel-completion, is debated among the *Rishonim*. Either way, it is forbidden. But if so, the Gemara asks, *or nami kematakin mana* — using fire also makes it a vessel; why does Rabbi Yehuda permit it?

### Fire Cutting Rationale

Rabbi Chiyya's *baraita* resolves this: *chotcho ba'or befi shtei nerot* — one divides it by fire at the mouth of two lamps. The image is of two lamps positioned side by side, with a single wick running between them. Rather than cutting the wick and then lighting it, one lights the wick in the middle, between the two lamps, so that the flame naturally divides it into two functional wicks, each serving one lamp. The act is primarily one of lighting the lamp; the division of the wick is incidental to it.

As Rashi explains: *delo mochiacha deletikunei mana mechatech* — it is not apparent that one's purpose is to fashion a vessel. At first glance, one appears simply to be lighting a lamp. This reasoning works most cleanly if the underlying prohibition is rabbinic in nature — if the problem is not a genuine biblical act of vessel-making but a rabbinic enactment against acts that resemble vessel-making. Where the experiential character of the act is primarily that of lamp-lighting, and the division is a byproduct, the rabbinic concern does not apply. This is not a matter of deceiving anyone; it is that the nature of the act, as experienced and performed, does not fall within the category the Sages prohibited.

### Wick Needling

Rav Natan bar Abba said in the name of Rav: *mochtin et haptilah beyom tov* — one may needle a wick on *Yom Tov*. Rav Chanina bar Shemaya explains: *le'aduyei chashocha* — to remove the blackness, meaning one takes a sharp instrument and scrapes the charred residue from a previously used wick, straightening the threads and preparing it for reuse. This raises the question: is this not also a form of *tikkun kli*, repairing a vessel? The answer is analogous to the permitted sharpening of a dull knife, which was discussed earlier in the *masechta*, particularly according to Rabbi Yehuda's more lenient approach. One is not creating something new; one is restoring what had already been functional. That is permitted.

### Six Wick Rules

Bar Kappara taught a *baraita* summarizing six rulings regarding wicks — *sheisha devarim ne'emru b'ptila* — three stringent and three lenient.

The three stringent rulings are: one may not braid a wick (*ein gozdin oto l'chat-chila b'yom tov*) — taking strands and twisting them into a wick from scratch is a genuine act of making something; one may not char the tip of a wick in fire (*ve'ein mehavvin oto ba'ur*) — pre-charring, which appears in the language of *Bameh Madlikin*, facilitates lighting and constitutes fashioning the wick; and one may not cut a wick into two (*ve'ein chotchin oto lishnayim*) — as discussed above.

The three lenient rulings are: *memacha b'yad* — one may roll or flatten the wick in one's hand to help it absorb oil better. Rashi notes that this is a *tikkun kal al yad* — a light adjustment made by hand, without precision or craftsmanship, and thus not within the scope of vessel-making. The absence of any artisanal character, and the fact that the wick was already functional beforehand, distinguish this from the prohibited acts. *Ve'shora bashemen* — one may soak the wick in oil, pre-saturating it; this too is closer to beginning to use the wick than to making it. And *ve'chotcha ba'ur* — one may divide the wick by fire between two lamps, ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda's position and the method described in Rabbi Chiyya's *baraita*.

---

## Compassion & Identity

### Shabsai Incident

Rav Natan bar Abba — the same *amora* who discussed the needling of wicks — said in the name of Rav: *atirei Bavel yordei Gehennam hen* — the wealthy people of Babylonia are destined for Gehinnom. The reason is illustrated by the case of Shabsai bar Marinos, who arrived in Babylonia. He was not himself wealthy; rather, the story exposes a culture of indifference among the Babylonian rich. Shabsai sought to engage in some business dealings with the local community — not a handout, but the opportunity to participate in commerce. They refused him. When reduced to asking for food, they refused that as well. Shabsai declared: *hanei me'eirev rav ka'asu* — these people must be descended from the *Eirev Rav*, the mixed multitude that left Egypt with the Israelites but were not truly of them. They are not real Jews.

### Rachamim Lineage

The basis for this declaration is a *pasuk*: *ve'nasan lecha rachamim ve'richamcha... ka'asher nishba la'avosecha* — God will give you compassion and have compassion on you, as He swore to your forefathers. The conventional reading of this verse — which appears after the commandment to destroy an *Ir Hanidachas* — is that God will restore His mercy to you after you have had to perform this harsh act. But the Gemara reads it differently, and several *mefarshim* on the verse share this reading: *ve'nasan lecha rachamim* means that God will have implanted within you the capacity for compassion — and the question of whether He has done so, whether you truly carry the compassion of your forefathers, is demonstrated by your behavior toward others.

From this the Gemara derives: *kol hamerachem al habriyot, beyadua shehu mizar'o shel Avraham Avinu* — anyone who has compassion upon God's creatures is known to be of the descendants of Abraham our father. *Ve'chol she'eino merachem al habriyot, beyadua she'eino mizar'o shel Avraham Avinu* — and one who lacks compassion is known not to be of his descendants. The wealth of Babylonia, then, is not the problem in itself; it is the culture it apparently produced — indifference to those in need, unwillingness to extend even basic sustenance to a fellow Jew in distress — that constitutes a severance from the Abrahamic inheritance.

### Three Miserable Lives

From this *aggadic* passage, the Gemara transitions to a related statement of Rav Natan bar Abba in the name of Rav: *kol hametzapeh al shulchan acherim olam chashoch ba'ado* — whoever is always looking toward another's table, the whole world grows dark before him. Rashi connects this to the verse: *noded hu lalechem aye, yada ki nachon beyado yom choshech* — he wanders seeking bread, though he should know that a day of darkness is ready at hand. The person who is never content, always measuring his portion against someone else's, cannot experience the life he actually has. Rav Chisda adds: *af chayav einam chayim* — such a person's life is not truly a life.

This leads to a *baraita*: *gimel chayav einam chayim* — three people whose lives are not real lives. The first is one who constantly gazes at another's table, as just described. The second is *mi she'ishto moshelet alav* — a man over whom his wife rules. The third is one *she'yisurin moshlin begufo* — whose body is racked by suffering; overwhelmed by physical pain, such a person cannot feel truly alive. A fourth opinion adds: *af mi she'ein lo ela chaluk echad* — even one who has only a single shirt, because that garment will accumulate filth and lice, making his existence miserable. The *Tanna Kamma*, who omits this last case, responds that one can de-louse a shirt while wearing it — an anti-climactic but characteristically Talmudic precision.

---

## Pottery & Paper

### Breaking Vessels

The *mishna* continues with related prohibitions. *Ein shovrin et hacheres* — one may not break pottery on *Yom Tov*, even to use the shard as a scoop, a scraper, or a surface on which to cook a fish over fire. *Ve'ein chotchin haniyar litzlot bo maliach* — one may not cut papyrus to roast a salted fish upon it. These acts — breaking pottery or cutting papyrus to create a usable cooking surface — constitute the making of a vessel even in the direct context of food preparation.

### Oven Sweeping

*Ve'ein gorfin et hatannur vehakiyrayim* — one may not sweep out an oven or stove. The seemingly simple act of removing ashes is, according to Rashi, actually a form of repair: he understands the case to involve a partially damaged oven, where some plaster or structural material has fallen in, and the sweeping constitutes a meaningful act of restoration. However, one is permitted to *mechabshin* — pat down the ashes against the walls and floor of the oven — thereby making the oven usable without crossing into the prohibited act of repair.

Rashi adds a practical dimension: if the ashes or debris are excessive, they will adhere to the bread or food being cooked, ruining it. Patting the ashes down prevents this without constituting a forbidden repair.

### Barrel Ovens

*Ve'ein makkivin shtei chaviyos lispot aleihen kdeira* — one may not position two large barrels side by side to create an impromptu oven, with a fire burning between them and a pot resting across their tops. This is striking: no physical change is made to the barrels themselves. They are simply moved into proximity with one another. Yet the act is prohibited, and the Gemara will address the reason.

### Wood Support Restrictions

*Ve'ein somchin es hakdeira bevika'at* — one may not prop up a cooking pot with a piece of wood or a beam. *Ve'chein badeles* — nor with a door, which apparently refers to a detached door being used as a support. Rashi explains that the underlying assumption of this *mishna* is that wood is categorically treated as fuel for fire; it is not considered a *kli* even if one wishes to use it for another purpose. Hence using a beam or a detached door to support a pot is prohibited.

### Stick & Animals

*Ve'ein manhigin es habeheima bemakel* — one may not lead an animal with a stick on *Yom Tov*. Whether this prohibition stems from *muktzeh*, from *uvdin dechol* (weekday activities), or from some other concern remains to be resolved in the Gemara. Rabbi Eliezer bar Shimon permits it. Rashi connects the final several cases of this *mishna* — the wood support and the stick used with animals — under the rubric of the assumption that wood has the status of fuel and nothing more.

---

## Oven Sweeping Analysis

### Vessel-Making Rationale

The Gemara explains the prohibition on breaking pottery and cutting papyrus for cooking: *mishum dekamatakin mana* — because one is fashioning a vessel, and this is forbidden even in the direct context of *ochel nefesh*. This is a significant ruling. Most of the earlier debate in the *masechta* concerned whether *machshirei ochel nefesh* — preparatory acts for food — are permitted or forbidden. But here, even acts that directly serve food preparation are prohibited when they involve *tikkun kli*, making or completing a vessel.

The same reasoning is applied to sweeping the oven: *ve'ein gorfin tanur vekirayim* — one may not sweep out the oven, again on the grounds of vessel repair. However, Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef taught before Rav Nachman: *ve'im iy efshar le'ofos ela im kein gorfo, mutar* — if it is impossible to bake without sweeping the oven, it is permitted. This exception is telling. It implies that the prohibition on sweeping, of all the items in this *mishna*, is not at the level of a biblical act of *tikkun kli*. Indeed, sweeping ashes from an oven is the least convincing candidate for a full prohibit of vessel-making — far less so than breaking pottery or cutting papyrus. Some *Rishonim* maintain that all these prohibitions are biblical; others hold they are rabbinic in nature, their status being one of resembling vessel-completion rather than genuinely constituting it. The halakhic ambiguity is reflected in the Gemara's willingness to grant an exception for necessity in this particular case, while not extending the same exception to the other categories. The category of *efshar la'asos mibod yom* — the principle that acts which could have been performed before *Yom Tov* are forbidden even if they relate to *machshirei ochel nefesh* — is relevant here as well, though the Gemara grounds the prohibition primarily in *tikkun kli* rather than in that consideration.

### Brick Incident

The source of Rashi's understanding — that the oven sweeping case involves structural damage, not merely natural ash accumulation — is an incident involving Rabbi Chiyya's wife. A brick fell into the oven, leaving it in a damaged state. Rabbi Chiyya said to her: *chazi d'ana rifta me'alyesta ba'ina* — see to it, I need good bread. This statement indicates that the situation met the standard of *iy efshar*, impossibility of baking without repair, and therefore the sweeping or repair was permitted. Crucially, this incident occurred on *Yom Tov* itself — the damage was not foreseeable and could not have been addressed beforehand, which addresses the concern of *efshar la'asos mibod yom*.

### Roasting Goose

Rava said to his attendant: *tavi li bar avza* — roast a goose for me — *ve'izdaharei me'charucha* — and be careful that it does not come into contact with the charcoal, which would blacken and ruin it. This statement illustrates precisely the practical concern that underlies the oven-related rulings: contact with charcoal and ash ruins food. The patting-down of ashes, and in cases of necessity the sweeping of the oven, address this concern. Whether Rava's instruction yields a specific new *halacha* or merely contextualizes the practical stakes is not made explicit.

### Sealing Ovens

Ravina said to Rav Ashi: Rav Acha from Hutzal told us that you seal your oven on *Yom Tov* — *de'mar sharik leh tanura be'yoma tava*. The practice of sealing an oven door with a plaster-like substance creates an airtight heat environment optimal for roasting. But is this not a form of *lisha*, kneading, when one prepares the sealing material? Is it permissible?

Rav Ashi replied: *anan arkata de'Frat samchinan* — we rely on the banks of the Euphrates. That is, he does not prepare plaster; he uses mud taken directly from the banks of the Euphrates, which is already in a workable state without any kneading or preparation. However, he adds: *ve'hani mili hu de'tzayirei me'etmol* — this is only permitted if one designated the mud before *Yom Tov*. One must have marked off a portion of the mud — creating a small indentation or boundary around it — on *Erev Yom Tov*, so that it is not *muktzeh* and is considered designated for use. Under those conditions, applying pre-formed riverside mud to seal the oven door involves no prohibited act.

Ravina adds: *u've'kitma shari* — using ashes would also be acceptable. Tosafot disagrees with Rashi's reading on this point: Rashi understands this as ashes mixed with water, which Tosafot would consider *lisha*. Tosafot instead explains that one simply packs dry ashes into the crevices around the oven door to seal it, which involves no kneading and is straightforwardly permitted.

---

---

# Beitzah 33

## Bathroom Stones vs. Pot…

### Rav Nachman: Bathroom St…

The daf begins toward the bottom of 34b, at the words *ve-ein makifin*. The *mishnah* has been discussing activities forbidden on *yom tov* even in the context of food preparation — particularly activities that involve creating vessels. Even Rabbi Yehuda, who generally permits *machshirei ochel nefesh*, would seemingly not allow such things. The analogy raised earlier holds: just as one does not go out to harvest wheat in the field — even though harvesting serves *ochel nefesh* — because it is something done for the long term and not within the immediate domestic context of food preparation, so too even in a home setting, breaking a piece of pottery to use for frying a fish partakes of vessel-making, and is at minimum a *de'rabanan* prohibition.

The *mishnah* now continues into territory where the underlying concern is less obvious: it prohibits positioning two barrels adjacent to one another, building a fire between them, and suspending a pot atop them to serve as an improvised stove. Before turning to this case, Rav Nachman offers a ruling on a related matter. He states that stones set aside for use in the bathroom — not for wiping, but for constructing a kind of seat — may be arranged on *yom tov* even if they had been in disarray. Since these stones are not *muktzah*, having been designated for bathroom use, one is permitted to stack them to reconstitute the toilet structure.

### Rava's Challenge: Pot Su…

Rava challenges Rav Nachman from the *mishnah* itself: *ve-ein makifin shtei chaviyot lispot aleihen et hakedirah* — one may not flank two barrels to suspend a pot above them. The parallel is evident: in one case you are arranging an ad hoc structure for a pot, in the other for the human body. What distinguishes them?

Rav Nachman responds: *shani hatam mishum deka avid ohala* — there it is different because one is creating an *ohel*. The two barrels constitute walls, and the pot suspended above them functions as a kind of roof. Even though the pot is not a permanent structural element — indeed it is there for cooking — if one cooks over an extended period, the pot will remain in place for hours, lending the configuration something of a permanent, roof-like character. This stands in contrast to the bathroom arrangement, where the temporary nature of use is manifest.

### Ohel vs. Temporary Struc…

The matter is, on reflection, quite striking. One might argue that even in the barrel-and-pot case, the pot is not really functioning as a roof in any structural sense — it is not there to protect the space below it, but simply to be heated. An *ohel* in the halachic sense requires not merely a horizontal surface above an enclosed space, but a covering that serves the space beneath it. If the pot serves the space above — the cooking surface — and not the space below, the *ohel* characterization seems strained. Nevertheless, the *gemara* treats it as problematic, and we will return to the practical implications.

### Binyan Keva Principle

Rav Zutra raises a sharp objection from the opposite direction to Rav Ashi: if the only issue is the creation of an *ohel*, then building a platform — an ottoman, say — on *yom tov* should be entirely permitted, since a platform has no roof. Would we really say that? Surely even a structure without a roof should present a problem.

Rav Ashi replies: *hatam binyan keva assur* — there, the problem is that one is erecting a permanent structure, and permanent construction is forbidden regardless of whether there is a roof. *Binyan arai lo assur* — a temporary arrangement, by contrast, does not carry a biblical prohibition. However, since the rabbinic sages did extend the prohibition to *binyan arai* as well — lest it lead to *binyan keva* — one might have expected the bathroom-stone arrangement to be forbidden rabbinically. Yet the *gemara* concludes: *mishum kvodo lo gazru beih Rabbanan* — out of concern for human dignity, the rabbis did not issue that decree here. Notably, this formulation shifts the reasoning away from the *ohel* distinction and frames the bathroom case instead as a special dispensation on grounds of *kvod habriyot* — the same principle that allows one to handle otherwise *muktzah* stones for bathroom purposes, since *kvod habriyot* overrides rabbinic prohibitions.

One may still maintain both rationales simultaneously: permanent construction is forbidden even without a roof; temporary construction is only problematic when it involves both walls and a roof; and in the bathroom case, the special dispensation of *kvod habriyot* removes even any lingering rabbinic concern. That is broadly the approach taken *lehalacha*.

---

## Fire Building & Assembly…

### Bonfire Assembly Directi…

The *gemara* continues with a ruling of Rav Yehuda regarding the construction of a bonfire on *yom tov*. He rules that assembling a bonfire from below to above is permissible, while assembling it from above to below is forbidden. The reason is that building a bonfire in the normal fashion — stacking logs in a crisscross structure, creating what amounts to walls — resembles the prohibited labor of building. Even without a roof and even in an entirely temporary context, the creation of walls is problematic. What is permitted is a departure from the normal manner of construction: somehow holding the upper level of wood in place while sliding wood beneath it, so that the assembly proceeds in an inverted, atypical fashion, which removes it from the rubric of normal construction.

### Eggs, Beds, Barrels

The *gemara* extends this principle to a series of analogous cases. *V'chen* — similarly with an egg: Rashi understands this as placing a pot upon an impromptu tripod, but this seems odd since the concern appears to be about the walls and not the resting surface. Tosafot therefore understands the case as stacking eggs — piling eggs atop one another in a way that constitutes, however oddly, something like a wall structure.

The case of the *purya* — a folding bed — is more intuitive. One takes out the frame and then lays a surface across it. The prohibited manner is to set out the legs first and then lay the frame across them (bottom to top); the permitted manner is to hold the crossbeams above while another person slides the legs into place below. And *v'chen chavita* — similarly with a barrel: Rashi here understands it as Tosafot understood the egg, namely a stacking of barrels that somehow constitutes the construction of a wall.

### Tosafot: Wall & Roof Cri…

If taken at face value, these cases raise a troubling question. Must one really refrain from stacking books on *shabbat* or *yom tov*? There is no roof, the arrangement is entirely ephemeral, and the height is nowhere near ten *tefachim*. Tosafot, on 32b, attempts to clarify the scope of the prohibition. At the beginning of his comment (*mimalah lemata assur mishum dehavi derech binyan*), Tosafot establishes that the underlying concern is that this constitutes the manner of building. He then asks: how do we account for the common practice of arranging a table — placing cylindrical supports on the ground and then laying a tabletop across them — which is precisely a bottom-to-top construction with walls and a covering surface?

Tosafot answers: *dehoil veein lahem mchitzot shari* — those supports are not *mchitzot*; they are individual legs, not planar walls. A prohibited construction requires walls in the full sense — surfaces that extend continuously and reach down to the ground. He concludes: *vechol hani mairi deit lehu mchitzot letzdadim hamagiot la'aretz* — all the cases in the *gemara* involve walls that form actual planes reaching to the ground.

Even granting this, the concern about stacking books remains. The *halacha* therefore develops a further set of criteria: the prohibition applies only when one constructs both walls and a roof simultaneously; only when there is a genuine cavity beneath the roof structure; only when the covering surface is itself a plane and not merely a line; and, most significantly, only when there are four walls. Thus, placing two books and a single book across them — with only two sides enclosed — would not constitute the prohibited pattern. Only if four walls are formed and a surface laid across them, leaving a space beneath, does the full concern arise.

### Stacking Books Limitation

Even with all these limiting criteria in hand, the *gemara*'s position remains somewhat difficult to apply in a satisfying way. An important additional consideration — one that is often determinative in practice — is whether the covering surface is designed to serve the space beneath it. A tabletop, while it creates an *ohel*-like space underneath, is plainly intended to serve the space above: things are placed on it, not beneath it. If the surface does not function as a covering for the enclosed space below, it may not constitute an *ohel* in the operative sense. The difficulty is that many of the cases in the *gemara* itself fit precisely this description — a pot or a barrel top is not there to shelter the space below — yet the *gemara* still regards them as problematic under certain conditions.

The cumulative picture is therefore: the prohibition on temporary construction (*binyan arai*) does exist as a rabbinic enactment; it is limited to cases where one builds walls of a planar character on all four sides, installs a roof, creates a cavity beneath that roof of at least a *tefach*, and does so in the standard bottom-to-top manner. When all these criteria converge, the concern remains real even if the overall permanence is negligible. When they do not all converge, as is true in most everyday situations, there is no prohibition. This is a genuinely challenging area of *halacha lema'aseh*, and the attempt to derive principled limits from these cases continues to occupy the *poskim*.

---

## Wood Usage Restrictions

### Lo Nitnu Etzim Principle

The *mishnah* states: *ve-ein somchin es hakedira bevika* — one may not support a pot with a stick — *ve'ein somchin es hadeles* — and similarly one may not use a stick to prop up a door. This leads the *gemara* into a discussion of a principle that underlies both rulings: *lo nitnu eitzim ela lehassaka* — wood on *yom tov* has been given only for burning. It may not be used for any other purpose.

The reason for this restriction is not immediately obvious. If a bundle of firewood is not *muktzah* — having been set aside for use on *yom tov* — one would ordinarily expect it to be available for any legitimate use, as is the case with any non-*muktzah* object. Why should wood be uniquely restricted to a single function?

Rashi addresses this later in the sugya and suggests it is not precisely a *muktzah* issue but rather a new rabbinic restriction. His reasoning is that wood is a ready raw material easily applied to forbidden activities — principally the fashioning of vessels (*ma'aseh keilim*) — and the rabbis therefore restricted its permitted uses on *yom tov* exclusively to fuel. This would make it analogous to a *kli shemelachto le'issur*, extended to a new domain by rabbinic decree. The alternative reading, suggested by how the *gemara* itself frames the debate that follows, treats it as a form of *muktzah*: wood is so thoroughly identified with its role as fuel that it is halachically "set aside" for that purpose and unavailable for others.

### Rabbi Shimon vs. Sages:…

A *baraita* is quoted that sharpens the issue. It states: *shelo nitnu eitzim ela l'hasaka* — wood is only for burning — and then notes that *Rabbi Shimon matir*, Rabbi Shimon permits using wood for other purposes. Since Rabbi Shimon is consistently the opinion in our tractate that does not accept *muktzah* in most forms — *leis lei muktzah* — his permitting the use of wood for other purposes suggests strongly that the underlying prohibition is indeed a form of *muktzah* and not a freestanding rabbinic decree. If it were only a decree about what wood may be used for, Rabbi Shimon's position on *muktzah* would be irrelevant. His permitting it indicates that for him the issue does not arise precisely because he does not accept that category of limitation.

The *gemara* also notes a further matter: Rabbi Elazar the son of Rabbi Shimon permits leading an animal with a stick on *yom tov*. One might assume this is simply because he follows his father's view on *muktzah*, making the stick available for any use. The *gemara* initially suggests this, but then pulls back: *afilu Rebbi Shimon modei* — even Rabbi Shimon might agree that leading animals with a stick is forbidden in this context.

### Leading Animals with Sti…

The reason leading animals with a stick is forbidden is not the specific issue of wood at all; it is *uvdin d'chol* — weekday appearances. Someone walking with a stick driving animals before him looks exactly as though he is heading to the marketplace. Rashi glosses *chinga* as a fairground or market gathering, the kind of circuit one makes through a market. The concern here is not *maris ayin* in the narrow sense of giving others the impression that one is violating the law. Rather, it is the broader principle that on *shabbat* and *yom tov* the texture of experience matters: certain activities, even when technically permissible, carry an unmistakably weekday character that is inappropriate for the day. Driving animals to market is paradigmatically such an activity. This concern stands independently of any *muktzah* question.

### Bamboo Spit: Dry vs. Moi…

The *gemara* then turns to the case of *chazra* — bamboo — which has a naturally sharp tip and could serve as a spit for roasting. Rav Nachman forbids using it as a spit; Rav Sheshes permits it. The *gemara* qualifies the disagreement according to the state of the bamboo.

If it is moist (*retiva*), all agree it is forbidden, since moist wood cannot realistically serve as firewood, and therefore it begins *yom tov* without any clear permissible use — it is effectively *muktzah* with no accessible function.

If it is dry (*yavishta*), one version of the *gemara* says the dispute applies: Rav Nachman invokes *lo nitnu eitzim ela lehassaka* and says it may only serve as fuel; Rav Sheshes says *ma li litzlot bo ma li litzlot be-gechalato* — what difference does it make whether one roasts on the stick itself or on its embers? Using dry wood as a spit is effectively a form of its *hasaka* function, making it permissible.

An alternative version reverses the framing: if it is dry, all agree it is permitted, since the wood's status as fuel makes it fully available; if it is moist, the dispute is whether the theoretical possibility of burning even moist wood in a strong fire is sufficient to bring it within the *hasaka* category and thus permit its use as a spit.

The *gemara* concludes: *yavishta shari, rativuta assur* — the dry ones are permissible for use as a spit, the moist ones are forbidden.

---

## Muktzah & Fire Items

### Broken Pokers & Dry Wood

Rava expounds: a woman may not enter the woodshed to take a stick to use as a poker. And, conversely, a poker that breaks on *yom tov* may not thereafter be used as firewood. The second ruling reflects a principle encountered earlier: an object that began *yom tov* as a functional vessel — in this case a poker — and then broke during *yom tov* may not be converted to use as fuel. It started the day designated as a vessel; its new role as raw firewood is a form of *nolad*, a new status that came into being on *yom tov* itself. *Le-fi she-masikin be-kelim ve-ein masikin be-shivrei kelim* — one may use whole vessels as fuel, but not broken vessels.

### Goose Entrails Disposal

The *gemara* then asks whether Rava's rulings place him in the camp of Rabbi Yehuda, who accepts a broader category of *muktzah*. The question is sharpened by a counter-example: Rava once told his attendant to roast a duck — or goose — and throw the entrails to the cat. If Rava held like Rabbi Yehuda, the entrails, which are not normally set aside for human consumption and would spoil, should have been considered *muktzah*. The *gemara* resolves the tension: *d'mistarchi meatzma daitei alavih* — since the entrails naturally spoil, Rava was already mentally preparing for their spoilage from the outset of *yom tov*. He anticipated feeding them to the cat, and that anticipated use removes the *muktzah* concern even according to Rabbi Yehuda.

### Rashi: Muktzah Disagreem…

The *gemara* then issues a *hilchata* — a ruling — in support of the positions articulated in this entire section. But Rashi, in a striking move, effectively dismisses the entire *hilchata* as inapplicable. He writes: *ha hilchata aliba d'man d'it lei muktzah itmara* — this ruling was stated according to the view that accepts *muktzah*. *Aval anan k'Rabbi Shimon sevira lan* — but we hold like Rabbi Shimon — in matters of *muktzah* and in matters of *davar she'eino mitkavein*, and we hold like Rabbi Yehuda only in matters of *machshirei ochel nefesh*. Therefore, Rashi concludes, *v'chulo shari* — it is all permitted.

Even more remarkably, Rashi extends this ruling backward to the earlier discussions in the *sugya*. He writes that whether we are speaking of the bamboo spit (*chazra*), the supporting of a pot with a stick (*smichat kdera*), the barrel-and-pot arrangement (*akvot chaviyot*), or all the matters raised in connection with constructing a fire — all of these rulings were stated by *amora'im* who were students of Rav, and Rav held like Rabbi Yehuda on *muktzah*. Since we hold like Rabbi Shimon, none of those restrictions apply. Furthermore, since we hold like Rabbi Yehuda on *machshirei ochel nefesh*, the barrel-and-pot arrangement — being food-related — is permitted on those grounds as well.

This is not the accepted *halacha*. Tosafot and most *rishonim* disagree with Rashi's approach. They maintain that even Rabbi Yehuda does not permit *machshirei ochel nefesh* when the activity involves the construction of a structure or the fashioning of a vessel — categories in which the prohibition is not rooted in *muktzah* at all. Tosafot also maintains that *uvdin d'chol* is a concern that operates across all opinions. The breadth of Rashi's ruling — sweeping away a *hilchata* and multiple *amora'ic* rulings in a single stroke — is notable, and it is a point where the school of Tosafot in France explicitly parted ways with him.

---

## Yard Wood & Toothpicks

### Rabbi Eliezer: Twigs & Y…

The *mishnah* now introduces a new question: which wood is free of *muktzah* concerns to begin with? Rabbi Eliezer says: *notel adam kisam mishlifanav lachatzot bo shinav* — one may take a twig from what is in front of him to use as a toothpick. *Umagavev min he-chatzer umadlik* — and one may gather loose wood from the yard and use it as firewood, for *kol mah she-ba-chatzer muchan hu* — anything lying in one's yard is implicitly designated for use and is therefore not *muktzah*. One need not have explicitly designated the sticks before *yom tov*; their natural presence in the yard makes their use for fuel self-evident.

### Sages: House Wood Only

The Sages disagree. *Megavev mishel le-fanav u-madlik* — one may gather and burn wood from what is immediately before him, meaning wood that has been brought into the house. Wood lying in the yard has not been sufficiently designated and therefore retains its *muktzah* status. The underlying dispute concerns what level of implicit designation removes wood from the category of *muktzah*: Rabbi Eliezer requires only proximity and obvious utility; the Sages require more explicit preparation, manifested by having the wood inside the house. The question of using a twig as a toothpick — permitted by Rabbi Eliezer — may relate separately to the principle of *lo nitnu eitzim ela lehassaka*, or alternatively, as Tosafot notes, the Sages may have been concerned that one will come to fashion and carve the twig into a proper toothpick, which would constitute making a vessel. That issue is developed further in the *gemara* that follows.

---

## Fire Creation Ban

### Fire Sources Prohibited

The *mishnah* then states: *ein motzi-in et ha-or lo min ha-etzim ve-lo min ha-avanim ve-lo min he-afar ve-lo min ha-re-afim ve-lo min ha-mayim* — one may not bring forth fire from wood, nor from stones, nor from dirt, nor from tiles (*re-afim*), nor from water. The prohibition encompasses every known method of producing new fire. Rubbing sticks together, striking flint, digging into superheated ground, using a tile that has absorbed heat to ignite straw, and using a curved vessel of water as a magnifying glass — all are forbidden. One may only use fire that is transferred from an existing flame.

The *mishnah* adds a further prohibition: *ve-ein melabnin et ha-re-afim litzlot bahen* — one may not heat a tile to a white-hot state in order to use it for roasting. The reason for this prohibition is less immediately clear, since using heat to cook would seem to be part of the ordinary *yom tov* cooking process; this matter is addressed in the *gemara* below.

Tosafot notes the relevance of the *lo nitnu eitzim ela lehassaka* principle to the broader context of this *mishnah* as well, linking the wood restrictions and the fire restrictions within a unified framework of what is and is not permitted in the sphere of fire-related activity on *yom tov*.

---

## Breaking Objects: Vessel…

### Animal Food Straw Permis…

Rav Yehuda rules: *ochlei behemah ein bahem mishum tikkun keli* — materials used as animal fodder are not subject to the prohibition of fashioning a vessel. If one takes a piece of straw — the sort one might picture held loosely between the teeth in the manner of Tom Sawyer — and breaks it off to use as a toothpick, one has not thereby committed an act of vessel-making. The reason lies not merely in the impermanence of the item, since even a twig is temporary and yet, as we will see, breaking a twig to use as a toothpick can rise to the level of a biblical violation. Rather, the decisive factor is that animal fodder is defined within an entirely different category of objects. Something so thoroughly characterized as consumable feed — to be eaten by animals immediately — cannot be viewed as the raw material for a vessel, however briefly it might serve a vessel-like function.

### Cedar Wood: Smell vs. To…

Rav Kahana challenges Rav Yehuda from a *baraita*: one may handle (*metaltelin*) fragrant wood to smell it — cedar, for instance, is highly fragrant — and to wave it before a sick person as an air freshener. One may rub it between the fingers to release more scent. However, *ve-lo yiktemenu le-hariach bo* — one may not snap it to expose a fresh surface for smelling. And *asur lachatzotz bo shinav* — one may not use it as a toothpick. Moreover, *ve-im kitmo chayav chatat* — if one snapped it, one is liable to bring a sin offering.

On the surface this seems to directly contradict Rav Yehuda, who said these things are entirely permitted. Rav Yehuda responds: the *baraita* itself presents a problem to him already when it forbids snapping the wood to smell — since he holds it should be entirely permitted. But the part about *chayav chatat*, a biblical violation, is so extreme a ruling against his position that the *baraita* must be discussing something else entirely.

His resolution: *ki tanya hahi bekashin* — that *baraita* is speaking of hard wood, not soft pliable plant matter used as animal food. Hard wood, when fashioned into a toothpick, becomes a real, durable, reusable vessel.

### Soft vs. Hard Wood Break…

The *gemara* presses back: *bekashin benei melila ninhu* — hard sticks are not the kind of thing you rub between the fingers to release scent; that is a characteristic of soft, pliable material. If the first part of the *baraita* describes rubbing to smell, it must be speaking of soft material — yet the later part of the *baraita* prohibits snapping it. The *gemara* resolves this by invoking the principle of *chisurei mechsera* — the *baraita* is incomplete and must be read with an implied gap. The complete reading is: one may rub soft wood and smell it; one may even snap soft wood and smell it. When is snapping forbidden? Only with hard wood. And if one snapped hard wood, one is not biblically liable — merely rabbinically forbidden — for snapping it to smell. But if one snapped it to make a toothpick, then one has biblically violated.

Two *beraitot* that appeared to contradict each other — one permitting snapping to smell, one forbidding it — are thus reconciled by Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Chisda: *ha berakkim ha bekashin*, soft wood versus hard wood. When soft, snapping to smell is entirely permitted. When hard, it is rabbinically forbidden.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects to the rabbinic restriction on hard wood. If the concern is that snapping it for a different purpose would be a forbidden act, why does the *mishnah* permit breaking open a barrel to get to pressed figs, as long as one does not intend to fashion a nice opening? There, an intent to make a vessel would be wrong, yet without that intent the act of breaking is permitted. Why should breaking a hard stick to smell differ? He further cites the sons of Rav Adda, who report that when they were in the household of Rav Yehuda he would hand them pieces of — apparently cedar-like — sticks which they would snap and smell, even though the broken piece could have served as a handle for a hatchet or a spade. Rav Yehuda permitted them to snap hard wood, provided it was done to smell and not to fashion a vessel.

### Breaking Stick: Biblical…

The *gemara* resolves the apparent inconsistency by anchoring it in the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages recorded in our *mishnah*. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *notel adam kisam meshlifanav lachatzetz bo shinav* — one may take a twig and use it as a toothpick. *Veshavin shelo yiktamenu* — yet everyone agrees one may not snap it. And if one does snap it intentionally to make a toothpick or a lock pick: on *shabbat*, performed inadvertently, one brings a sin offering; on *yom tov*, performed deliberately, one incurs forty lashes. The snapping itself, when done with the intent of making a vessel, is a biblical violation according to Rabbi Eliezer.

The Sages disagree: *echad ze ve'echad ze eino ela mishum shevus* — neither the breaking of a barrel nor the snapping of a stick constitutes a biblical violation of vessel-making; at most it is rabbinic.

The two positions now map neatly onto the earlier tension. Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that intentional snapping for a vessel is biblically forbidden, would correspondingly hold that snapping for a non-vessel purpose — like smelling — is rabbinically forbidden, as a protective measure. This explains the *baraita* that forbids snapping hard wood to smell: it reflects Rabbi Eliezer's position. The Sages, who hold that even intentional fashioning of a vessel in this informal manner is only rabbinic, would allow snapping for a non-vessel purpose *lechatchila* — which explains both the barrel-breaking *mishnah* and Rav Yehuda's practice of handing out sticks to be snapped for smelling.

### Mostaki & Disposable Pac…

A further question arises: does Rabbi Eliezer himself agree with the *mishnah* that permits breaking open a barrel? If he holds that informal fashioning of a vessel is biblically prohibited, would he not forbid breaking into the barrel entirely? Rav Ashi answers: *ki tanya hi bemostaki* — the *mishnah* is speaking of a *mostaki*, a barrel assembled from scraps of wood, patched together, and thoroughly temporary in character. For such an object, even Rabbi Eliezer would agree that making an opening in it does not constitute biblical vessel-making, since the vessel itself is too impermanent and informal to be treated as a genuine *kli*. Accordingly, breaking into it is permitted even according to the stricter view.

This ruling has significant contemporary application. Rav Moshe Feinstein observes that virtually all modern packaging falls into the *mostaki* category. Disposable containers, cardboard boxes, plastic bags, foil trays — none of these rise to the level of a genuine vessel in the biblical sense. Therefore, even according to the position of Rabbi Eliezer, opening such packaging would at most be a rabbinic concern, not a biblical one. And since the prohibition is only rabbinic, opening it in a manner that does not intentionally create a new vessel is permitted. The operative question in modern *shabbat* and *yom tov* practice is therefore not whether breaking open packaging involves a biblical violation — it does not, given the disposable nature of virtually all contemporary containers — but rather whether the specific manner of opening constitutes the fashioning of a useful vessel, which remains a rabbinic concern worth attention.

---

## Wood Piles & Long-Term U…

### Wood Piles Debate

A *tosefta* addresses the question of gathering wood from the yard. It rules: *megavev min hachatzar umadlik she-kol mah she-ba-chatzer muchan hu* — one may gather wood from the yard and burn it, since everything in the yard is considered implicitly designated. However, *uvilvad she-lo ya'aseh tziburim tziburim* — one should not form the wood into large piles. Rabbi Shimon, however, permits making large piles.

### Tomorrow vs. Present Need

The underlying dispute, the *gemara* explains, concerns appearances. One view holds that assembling large piles of wood carries the look of preparing for the future — *mechazi de-kamachnis le-machar u-le-yoma achrina* — as if one were stocking up for tomorrow or another day, which creates the *uvdin d'chol* problem of weekday-like long-term planning. Rabbi Shimon holds that the burning pot on the fire speaks for itself: *kederato mochachas alav* — the pot demonstrates that the wood is being gathered for immediate present use, and there is therefore no reason to restrict the formation of larger piles.

---

## Fire Creation Ban (II)

### Molid Principle

The *mishnah*'s prohibition on creating new fire is explained by the *gemara* with the principle of *molid*: *mishum de-ka molid be-Yom Tov* — because one is creating something new on *yom tov*. Fire that did not exist is brought into existence through human effort, and this creation of a genuinely new entity is forbidden.

Some *rishonim*, including the Ritva, suggest that the concern of *molid* is not only about the ontological newness of the fire but also about the extraordinary degree of effort required to produce it. Making fire from scratch — rubbing wood, striking stones, coaxing a spark into flame — approaches the character of *yesh me-ayin*, creation from nothing, and represents a form of labor incompatible with *yom tov*. This dimension of the prohibition is worth noting in light of contemporary reality, where producing fire requires virtually no effort: a match is struck in a second. The fire remains a genuine *yesh me-ayin* in some sense, so the prohibition clearly applies. Yet the *rishonic* emphasis on the effort involved raises interesting questions about the outer boundaries of the category — for instance, whether activating an electric burner that glows red-hot constitutes *eish* in the halachic sense, and whether if it does, doing so would fall under *molid* as the *gemara* understands it here. These questions about the intersection of the *molid* principle with modern appliances are among the most consequential practical applications of this *sugya*.

---

---

# Beitzah 35

## Shabbat Koveia?

### Intro: Shabbat Koveia

The central question animating the opening of daf 35a concerns whether *shabbat* functions as *koveia* — that is, whether the onset of *shabbat* imposes a permanent, meal-like status upon fruit that has not yet undergone *gemar melacha*, the completion of its processing. The background *halacha* is as follows: produce whose *gemar melacha* has not been completed, or which has been completed but not yet brought indoors (*re'iyat pnei habayit*), may be eaten in a temporary, incidental manner (*derech arai*) without first separating *terumot u'ma'asrot*. One may snack, but not make a fixed meal (*derech keva*). The further principle under discussion is that *shabbat*, on account of the sanctity and importance of eating on that day, functions as *koveia* — rendering even incidental eating into something permanent and obligatory for *terumot u'ma'asrot*. The Gemara's question is whether this principle applies only where *gemar melacha* has already been completed and only *re'iyat pnei habayit* remains, or whether *shabbat* is *koveia* even when the fruit's processing is altogether unfinished — *lo nigmar melachto*.

### Mishna: Erev Shabbat

This question bears on the *mishna*, which addresses a case of standing over fruit on *erev shabbat* and on *erev shvi'it* during the *shemitah* year. The implication of that *mishna* is that when *shabbat* arrives, if the fruit were truly obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*, one would find oneself in a bind. That implication sounds like *shabbat* is indeed *koveia*. However, the Gemara works to escape this inference. We now resume with that very question at the top of 35a.

The Gemara asks: *ve'halo* — is it not the case that in the *mishna*'s scenario of designating fruit, one would indeed be unable to snack from it?
