And either that is because *shabbat* is *koveia*, or, the Gemara had previously suggested, perhaps it is because the verbal designation itself — the declaration *mikan ani ochel*, "I will eat from this" — transforms the eating into something permanent (*keva*), even without invoking the principle of *shabbat koveia*.

### Challenge: Dibbur Koveya

The Gemara now challenges whether a verbal declaration alone can accomplish this transformation. *Ve'halo*, it asks, does not *motaro chozer* — the leftover returns? If one declares "I will eat from this section," one eats what one eats and simply leaves the rest in place. There is not even a need to return it; it remains undisturbed. If the physical act of removing a handful and then returning the remainder does not constitute *keva*, how much less so a mere verbal designation, where nothing has even been disturbed and everything that will not be eaten remains precisely where it was?

### R. Eliezer: Motaro Chozer

The Gemara invokes the known position of Rabbi Eliezer — the *tanna* at the center of the *mishna* — who holds that *kol heicha de'motaro chozer, lo kava*: wherever the remainder of what one takes will return to its original place, the eating is not considered permanent and one may eat in a temporary fashion. The Gemara then cites the relevant *mishna* to illustrate this principle.

### Olives Mishna

*De'tnan*: if one takes olives from the *ma'atan* — a vessel in which olives are placed prior to pressing, where gravity gradually causes their juices to begin flowing out — one may dip them one by one in salt and eat them. These olives are not *nigmar melachto*; they are in the process of becoming olive oil, and eating one or two is snacking. Indeed, the *torat* obligation of *gemar melacha* for olives is only completed when the oil is finished, as the Torah speaks of *dagan tirosh v'yitzhar* — and *yitzhar* is oil, not the olive itself. Hence one may snack without separating *terumot u'ma'asrot*.

However, if one dipped a whole group and placed them before oneself — sitting down with a full plate — that is *achilat keva* and one is *chayav*. Then the *mishna* introduces a dispute: *Rabbi Eliezer omer*, if one took from a *tahor* vessel, one is obligated in *terumot u'ma'asrot*; if from a *tamei* vessel, one is exempt — *mipnei shehu machzir es ha'mutar*, because one returns what is left over.

The Gemara asks: *mai shna reisha u'mai shna seifa* — what difference does it make whether the vessel was *tahor* or *tamei*? Rabbi Abbahu explains: the first case (*reisha*) involves a *tahor* vessel and a *tamei* person. When one reaches in to take olives, the ones one touches become *tamei*, and one cannot return them without contaminating the rest. Hence *de'lo matzi mahadar leh* — one cannot return what is left over — and the taking is therefore *keva*. The second case (*seifa*) involves a *tamei* vessel and a *tamei* person; one can eat what one eats and return the rest without consequence, since everything was already *tamei*. There, *dematzi mahadar leh*, and so the eating remains *arai*.

The basic *halacha* at stake, then, is: if one removes a group of olives and sits down with them before *gemar melacha*, is that *keva* or *arai*? The *tanna kamma* says it is *keva*. Rabbi Eliezer says that if one intends to return what remains, that remains *arai*, and one may eat even before separating *terumot u'ma'asrot*.

### Keva Context Matters

This is the crux of the Gemara's challenge. We wished to say that in the *mishna* on *erev shabbat* and *shvi'it*, the verbal declaration *mikan ani ochel* is what makes the eating *keva*. But the Gemara objects: if physically removing a pile of olives and sitting down to eat them does not constitute *keva* when one intends to return the remainder — because the remainder is going back into the context of ongoing processing — then how could a verbal designation, where nothing has even been disturbed and everything remains where it was, possibly constitute *keva*? The leftover is not merely going back; it never left. It is already, in the most complete sense, back. The eating is purely incidental — one is merely snacking from within a process that is still ongoing.

The Gemara therefore presses: rather than saying the verbal declaration is *koveia*, we must say it is *shabbat* itself that is *koveia*. That must be what the *mishna* implies — that the reason one cannot snack on *shabbat* from unfinished produce is the principle of *shabbat koveia*.

This leads to the suggestion of Rav Shimi bar Ashi: one must be careful not to read too much into the *mishna*, because the *mishna* reflects the position of Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Eliezer *letamei* — he follows his own reasoning. Rabbi Eliezer in general is more inclined to see various halachic events as transforming food into a state of *achilat keva*. Specifically, *de'amar teruma kav'a* — Rabbi Eliezer holds that the act of taking *teruma* from produce renders the remainder absolutely obligated as *tevel*, and *ve'chol sheken shabbat*, certainly *shabbat* would do so as well.

The relevant *mishna* from *Ma'asrot* is cited: *perot she'traman ad shelo nigmar melachtan* — fruit from which one separated *teruma* before their processing was complete. Rabbi Eliezer holds one may no longer eat from such fruit even *b'arai*, because having taken *teruma* — even voluntarily before the obligatory stage — locks the remainder into full *tevel* status. The *chachamim*, however, permit continued snacking. The point is that Rabbi Eliezer's view that *teruma* changes the status of unfinished produce is a more expansive conception of what constitutes halachic transformation. One who accepts that principle can readily accept that *shabbat* equally transforms the eating. But that is Rabbi Eliezer's singular view, and it has not been demonstrated that the *chachamim* agree.

The Gemara then turns to the *seifa* of the *mishna* — the position of the *chachamim* — where it says: *ve'ha'chachamim omrim ad sheyomar mikan ve'ad kan*, that one must verbally declare "from here to here" in order to address the *muktza* concern. The Gemara notes that both Rabbi Eliezer and the *chachamim* implicitly agree that were this not *shemitah*, one would be forbidden to eat the fruit on *shabbat*. Their only dispute is how to resolve the *muktza* problem; neither doubts that without *shemitah*, the fruit would be inaccessible. The question, then, remains: why could one not simply snack?

The Gemara responds for the *chachamim*: *shani hasam*, the situation is different, *keivan de'amar mikan ve'ad kan ani ochel lemachar* — since the *chachamim* require one to declare "from here to here I will eat tomorrow," that verbal designation is itself what renders the eating *keva*. It is not *shabbat* that is *koveia*; it is the act of specific designation. One is caught, as it were, in a halachic bind: the designation is necessary to escape *muktza*, but the very act of designating transforms the food into *achilat keva*.

This resolution works for the *chachamim* in a way it did not for Rabbi Eliezer, because the *motaro chozer* objection applied only to Rabbi Eliezer. It was Rabbi Eliezer who held that returning the remainder preserves *arai* status. The *chachamim*, by contrast, do not recognize that principle — for them, even returning the remainder does not necessarily preserve *arai* status. Hence the verbal designation can indeed function as *koveia* according to the *chachamim* without being undercut by the *motaro chozer* reasoning.

The Gemara then asks: *ei hachi, mai irya shabbat, afilu bechol nami* — if the *chiddush* is merely that verbal designation constitutes *keva*, why is this being taught in the context of *shabbat* and *muktza*? Why not simply teach it in a weekday context regarding *terumot u'ma'asrot*? The Gemara responds: *ha kamashma lan de'tevel muchan hu eitzel shabbat* — the *mishna* is teaching an additional ruling, namely that even *tevel* — produce rabbinically forbidden to eat because *terumot u'ma'asrot* have not been separated — does not acquire *muktza* status on *shabbat*, provided that *de'im avar v'tikno metukan*, if someone *b'dieved* went ahead and separated *terumot u'ma'asrot* on *shabbat*, the produce is rendered permissible and is not treated as *muktza*. This is a genuinely striking *halacha*: ordinarily we might assume that anything forbidden when *shabbat* commenced, whether by biblical or rabbinic prohibition, ought to be treated as *muktza*. Yet because food occupies such a central and expected place in *shabbat* life, even rabbinically forbidden produce does not become *muktza* in the full sense — it retains, as it were, a latent fitness. The *muktza* problem in the *mishna* arises not from the *tevel* status itself but from the physical state of the fruit, which is still in the process of drying out on the rooftop, and it is that condition — not *tevel* — that creates the *muktza* concern.

This is the *mishna*'s actual *chiddush* being conveyed through the *shabbat* context: *lechatchila* one cannot designate *tevel* for eating on *shabbat*, but *b'dieved*, the fixing does not retroactively render it *muktza*.

### Grapes Mishna

The Gemara now raises a *ramei* — a contradiction — from another *mishna* in *Terumos*. The case: *haya ochel be'eshkol venichnas migina l'chatzer* — one was eating from a cluster of grapes (not *nigmar melachto*, since grapes are intended to become wine), and then walked from the garden into the courtyard. Entering the *chatzer* would normally be significant if the produce were *nigmar melachto*, but here it is not. Nevertheless, a dispute arises: Rabbi Yehoshua says one may not finish the snacking; Rabbi Eliezer says go ahead and finish.

Then comes the directly relevant case: *chashcha beleilei shabbat* — one was snacking on these grapes on Friday, and *shabbat* arrived. Rabbi Eliezer says one may finish eating; Rabbi Yehoshua says one may not. This appears to be a direct and explicit dispute about whether *shabbat* is *koveia* — exactly the question the Gemara has been circling around. Rabbi Yehoshua holds *shabbat* is *koveia*, Rabbi Eliezer holds it is not. Yet this contradicts what we established earlier — that according to Rabbi Eliezer, *shabbat* should be *koveia* (since he is even more expansive about such things, holding that *teruma* itself is *koveia*).

### Both Agree Shabbat

The Gemara resolves this through a teaching of Rabbi Natan: when Rabbi Eliezer said "finish eating" in the *chatzer* case, he did not mean to continue eating while inside the *chatzer* — he meant take the grapes *out* of the *chatzer* and finish them there. The *chatzer* does not permanently change the status of the grapes, but it does mean one may not eat from them while inside it; remove them, and the snacking is permissible again.

Similarly, when Rabbi Eliezer said "finish eating" in the *shabbat* case, he did not mean to continue eating on *shabbat* itself. He meant *mamtin lemotzaei shabbat veyigmor* — wait until after *shabbat* and finish the grapes then. The onset of *shabbat* does not permanently alter the status of the grapes such that they become forbidden even on Sunday; it only means that eating them on *shabbat* itself cannot be considered mere snacking.

This clarifies what *shabbat koveia* actually means. It does not mean that the grapes' halachic status is transformed permanently once *shabbat* passes over them. The rationale for *shabbat koveia* — *ve'karata la'shabbat oneg* — is that eating on *shabbat* is inherently weighty and significant. Hence eating on *shabbat* itself cannot be characterized as *arai*. But that applies to the act of eating on *shabbat*, not to the ontological status of the grapes. Once it is after *shabbat*, the grapes remain exactly as they were before, and the earlier, unfinished *gemar melacha* means one may still snack from them. (Rashi notes, however, that if one had specifically designated the grapes for *shabbat* — setting them aside and declaring their purpose — then even after *shabbat* the status may be different, but that is a separate question from where the grapes simply happen to be present when *shabbat* arrives.)

With this understanding, the contradiction within Rabbi Eliezer's position dissolves. In the *mishna* regarding *erev shabbat*, Rabbi Eliezer's implication that one could not snack reflects his view that *shabbat* is indeed *koveia* in the sense that eating on *shabbat* cannot be *arai*. In the grapes case, his ruling to "finish eating" means waiting until *motzaei shabbat* — he is not contradicting himself; he is consistent. Eating on *shabbat* is forbidden, but the grapes' status is not permanently changed.

What emerges is striking: both Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua agree that one cannot eat the grapes on *shabbat* itself. Their dispute is only about whether after *shabbat* the grapes retain the restriction. Rabbi Eliezer says after *shabbat* one may resume; Rabbi Yehoshua says the restriction persists even afterward. Both, however, accept that *shabbat* is *koveia* in the sense that eating on *shabbat* from unfinished produce constitutes *achilat keva*. This makes the Gemara's earlier contortions to avoid that conclusion seem, in retrospect, puzzling — but such is the nature of this particular *sugya*.

### R. Yochanan: Gemar Melac…

Despite all of the foregoing evidence pushing toward the conclusion that *shabbat* is *koveia*, a definitive ruling arrives from Eretz Yisrael. *Ki asa Ravin amar Rabbi Yochanan*: whether it is *shabbat*, whether it is *teruma*, whether it is a *chatzer*, whether it is a *mekach* — a sale or purchase — none of these makes unfinished produce *keva*. *Kulam ein kovin ela bedavar shenigmerah melachtan*: all of them operate only where the produce has already reached *gemar melacha*. Before that point, no halachic event — not the arrival of *shabbat*, not the separation of *teruma*, not bringing the produce into a *chatzer*, not a commercial transaction — changes the produce's fundamental status. One may still snack from it. All of the readings of the *mishna* and the positions attributed to various *tannaim* that pointed toward *shabbat* or *teruma* being *koveia* are thereby set aside, at least as normative *halacha*.

## Rejecting Positions

### Shabbat Not Koveia

Having stated Rabbi Yochanan's overarching ruling, the Gemara proceeds to work through each of the positions being rejected, one by one.

Regarding *shabbat*: it is not *koveia* for produce that has not yet reached *gemar melacha*. This is stated as a positive ruling, and immediately the Gemara specifies against whom it is directed.

### Hillel Alone

*Ve'apukei mide'Hillel*: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling excludes the position of Hillel. A *baraisa* is cited: *hama'avir peiros mimakom lemakom lekatzetz* — one who is transporting fruit to be dried out (hence *lo nigmerah melachtan*), and *shabbat* arrives (*vekidesh aleihem hayom*). Amar Rabbi Yehuda: *Hillel le'atzmo oser* — Hillel alone held that this was now forbidden, that *shabbat* made the eating problematic. This is a peculiar state of affairs. The Gemara has just spent a sustained discussion showing that various *tannaim* — Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua — seemed to accept that *shabbat* is *koveia*, at least for eating on *shabbat* itself. Yet now the Gemara identifies Hillel as the lone voice for that position and uses his isolation to marginalize it. The effect is to narrow the camp of *shabbat koveia* proponents to a single, minority *tanna*, and on that basis to rule that we do not *pasken* accordingly.

### Chatzer Not Koveia

Similarly, bringing unfinished produce into a *chatzer* does not make eating from it *keva*. This rejects the position of Rabbi Yaakov. *De'tnan*: the *mishna* in *Ma'asrot* teaches that one who transports figs (*hama'avir te'einim bechatzeiro lekatzetz*) — and members of his household may eat from them *b'arai* and are exempt from *ma'aser*. The *mishna* is explicit that the *chatzer* does not change the status of produce not yet at *gemar melacha*. *Ve'tanya alah*: a *baraisa* on that *mishna* teaches that Rabbi Yaakov holds them *chayav* — once the produce enters the *chatzer*, he regards it as *koveia*. Rabbi Yose be'Rabbi Yehuda exempts. Rabbi Yochanan's ruling sides with the exempting position, against Rabbi Yaakov.

### Teruma Not Koveia

Nor does the act of taking *teruma* from unprocessed produce lock the remainder into permanent *tevel* status that would preclude snacking. The relevant *mishna* states it plainly: *perot she'traman ad shelo nigmar melachtan* — fruit from which *teruma* was separated before completion of processing. *Rabbi Eliezer oser le'echol mehem arai, ve'chachamim matirin*. Rabbi Yochanan follows the *chachamim*. The taking of *teruma*, however significant a halachic act, does not alter the physical-halachic reality that the produce remains in an incomplete state and may still be eaten incidentally.

### Mekach Not Koveia

Nor does purchase. One might have thought that a commercial transaction transforms the identity of the produce and removes it from the category of "still in process." A *baraisa* disproves this.

### Figs Purchase Baraita

*Halokeach te'einim me'am ha'aretz* — one who purchases figs from an *am ha'aretz* in a locale where *rov bnei adam dorsim*, where the majority of people trample the figs into pressed rounds and do not eat them fresh, meaning the figs are not yet at *gemar melacha* for most purchasers: *ochel mehen arai, u'me'asran demai*. One may snack from them, and one treats them as *demai* — subject only to rabbinic doubt-obligation for *ma'asrot* — rather than as *vaday tevel*, which would be a biblical prohibition.

The Gemara notes that *shma mina tlas* — three teachings emerge. First and most directly relevant: *mekach eina kova'at* — the act of purchase does not make the unfinished produce *keva*; one may still eat from it *b'arai*. Second: *rov amei ha'aretz me'asrin hen* — the majority of *amei ha'aretz* do tithe, which explains why even when purchasing from an *am ha'aretz* the obligation is only *demai* and not *vaday*. Third, and most striking: *me'asrin demai me'am ha'aretz afilu bedavar shelo nigmar melacha* — one takes *demai* from an *am ha'aretz* even when the processing is not yet complete. This is a genuinely bold ruling. One might have thought that at this earlier stage — where there is both the general doubt attendant on *am ha'aretz* produce and the added consideration that most people have not yet tithed at this stage — the result should be a *vaday* obligation, not merely *demai*. Nevertheless, the Gemara teaches that we still assume the majority probably did tithe even at this earlier stage, and the obligation remains at the level of *demai*.

This *baraisa* stands in tension with another *mishna* (*ha'machlif peiros im chaveiro*) that implies *mekach* does render unfinished produce obligated. In that *mishna*, one exchanges one's fruit for another's — whether both are drying out, or one is fresh and one is drying — and in all cases one is *chayav*. The exchange constitutes a kind of sale, and the *mishna* appears to say that even where the produce is not yet at *gemar melacha*, the sale is *koveia*. Rabbi Yehuda, however, disputes the blanket ruling and holds *le'echol chayav u'le'katzos patur* — if the produce is designated for eating, the purchaser is *chayav*, but if it is designated for drying (not yet at *gemar melacha*), the sale is not *koveia* and one may still eat *b'arai*. Rabbi Yochanan rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda's narrower position.

### Only Gemar Melacha

The conclusion is unambiguous. We began the *sugya* with the question of whether *shabbat* is *koveia* for produce not yet at *gemar melacha*. Through an extended and at times convoluted discussion, the Gemara examined the *mishna* from multiple angles, explored the positions of Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, Hillel, Rabbi Yaakov, and others, and progressively dismantled each position that attributed *koveia* status to anything other than *gemar melacha* itself. The statement of Rabbi Yochanan is the definitive resolution: none of these factors — not *shabbat*, not *chatzer*, not *teruma*, not *mekach* — changes the fundamental status of produce that has not yet completed its processing. Only *gemar melacha* does that. Before that threshold is crossed, all of these events are halachically inert with respect to the obligation in *terumot u'ma'asrot*, and the produce may still be eaten in a temporary fashion.

## Yom Tov Food Handling

### Skylight Lowering

With *Hadran Alach Hamavi*, the Gemara transitions to the final *perek* of the tractate. Much of the preceding *perek* addressed questions around fire, cooking, and the prohibition against fashioning vessels even in the course of food preparation. This final *perek* will focus significantly on questions of *techum* — the *shabbat* boundary — and how *techum* restrictions intersect with food on *Yom Tov*. But the *mishna* opens with a different issue: the general question of physical effort (*tircha*) and its limits on *Yom Tov*.

*Mashilin peiros derech arubbah b'Yom Tov* — one may lower fruit through a skylight on *Yom Tov*. The scenario is that fruit has been drying on the rooftop; whether the *muktza* concern has been resolved through prior designation or because *gemar melacha* has been completed, the fruit is accessible. One wishes to bring it inside. The *mishna* permits lowering it through the skylight. *Aval lo beShabbat* — but not on *shabbat*. The difference is the principle being invoked. The *chiddush* of the *mishna* is permitting this act on *Yom Tov* despite the concern of *tircha yeteira* — excessive effort. There is room to argue whether this is better characterized as a *tircha* problem or as *uvda de'chol* — carrying on weekday-like labor — since hauling baskets of fruit down from a rooftop evokes the mundane work of ordinary weekdays. The skylight method, however, involves a *shinui* (deviation from the weekday manner) and does not convey the same sense of weekday labor, which is why it is permitted. On *shabbat*, however, even this is forbidden.

### Covering from Rain

*U'mechassin peirot bikeilim mipnei ha'delef* — one may cover fruit with vessels to protect them from rain. Similarly, pitchers of wine or oil may be covered if rain threatens to fall in and ruin their contents. These acts are permitted on *Yom Tov*. By contrast, the *Yerushalmi* adds — and the parallel is preserved in the *mishna*'s structure — that such covering is not done on *shabbat*.

### Vessel Under Drip

*Notnin kli tachat ha'delef beShabbat* — one may, however, place a vessel underneath a dripping hole in the roof even on *shabbat*. This is taught in *Masechet Shabbat* as well and is permitted despite the various restrictions that attach to *shabbat*.

### Rashi: Hefsed Mammon

Rashi's analysis of this *mishna* is instructive. He characterizes the problem in all these cases as *tircha* — excessive effort — rather than primarily *uvda de'chol*. More importantly, he explains why the *mishna* permits covering the fruit and pitchers on *Yom Tov* even though these acts involve some effort and are not being done for immediate benefit today: *mishum hefsed mamon*, because of financial loss. The produce or wine will be ruined if not protected, and the concern for *hefsed mamon* provides sufficient grounds for leniency.

This raises a conceptual question. The phrase Rashi uses — *shelo letzorech Yom Tov* — suggests that the problem is not merely the quantity of effort but whether the act is being performed for the benefit of *Yom Tov* itself. The general license of *ochel nefesh* on *Yom Tov* permits effort expended for the purpose of eating and benefiting on the day itself. Covering produce from rain, however, does not benefit one today — the benefit is preventing future loss. This is analogous to a common question about returning milk to a refrigerator toward the end of *shabbat*: if one is doing so to prevent spoilage rather than to prepare for a weekday use, this should not constitute *hachana*; one is protecting one's property, not preparing for afterwards. Similarly here, no one claims that covering the fruit is *hachana* for a weekday. But neither is it *ochel nefesh*. The question is how much latitude is given to protect property on *Yom Tov*, and Rashi's answer is that *hefsed mamon* provides that latitude.

## Textual Variants

### Four Verb Options

The Gemara records a dispute between Rav Yehuda and Rav Natan concerning the precise verb used in the *mishna*. One *tanna* read the *mishna* as *mashilin*, another as *mashchilin*. Both versions are transmitted. Mar Zutra states that neither reading is necessarily a corruption — *man de'tani mashilin lo mishtabash, u'man de'tani mashchilin lo mishtabash*. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds further that a third version, *mashirin*, is equally defensible, and — though Rashi notes that no one actually claimed this as their text — a fourth form, *menashirin*, could also be legitimate. All four verbs share a rough semantic range having to do with dropping, falling off, or lowering, and each can be traced to a biblical or *mishnaic* precedent.

### Mashilin: Drop

*Man de'tani mashilin lo mishtabash* — the form *mashilin* is supported by the verse *ki yashal zeitecha*, "your olive tree will drop its fruit" (Devarim 28:40). The verb *yashal* means for fruit to fall from a tree, and *mashilin* would accordingly mean to cause fruit to drop — entirely appropriate for the act of sending fruit down through the skylight.

### Mashchilin: Dislocate

*U'man de'tani mashchilin lo mishtabash* — the form *mashchilin* is supported by the *mishnaic* terms *ha'shchul ve'ha'kasul*, two types of *mumim* (blemishes) that disqualify an animal. *Shchul shenishmeta yarecho* — the animal's thigh has been dislocated; *kasul she-echad mi'yarchotav gavoah me'chaverta* — one thigh is positioned higher than the other. In both cases, the root *shin-chet-lamed* conveys some form of dislocation or displacement from a normal position, and *mashchilin* could therefore similarly mean to move or shift fruit downward through the skylight.

### Mashirin: Fall

*Man de'tani mashirin lo mishtabash* — the form *mashirin* is supported by a *mishnaic* teaching regarding *nazir*: Rabbi Yishmael says a *nazir* may not wash his hair with earth, *mipnei she'meshir et ha'se'ar* — because doing so causes the hair to fall out, and a *nazir* is forbidden to cut his hair. The verb *meshir* thus means to cause to fall off, and *mashirin* would mean to cause the fruit to fall — an apt description of lowering them through the opening.

### Menashirin: Drop Off

*U'man de'tani menashirin lo mishtabash* — the form *menashirin* is supported by the *mishna* regarding *nazir*, through a different formulation: *mi she'nashru kelav ba'mayim*, one whose garments fell into the water, may walk in them and need not be concerned (people will not suspect he did laundry on *shabbat*; it is obvious the clothes accidentally fell in). The root *nun-shin-reish* carries the meaning of falling or dropping off. More directly, the Gemara adds: *eizu leket — ha'nosher bi'sh'at ketzirah* — *leket* is defined as grain that falls during the act of harvesting. The word *nosher* and its cognate *menashirin* thus share the meaning of grain or produce dropping off, which is relevant both to the agricultural imagery of the *mishna* and to the earlier discussion in the tractate of *gezeirat peirot ha'noshrin* — the rabbinic concern about fruit that falls from trees. All four forms, then, converge on the same basic meaning, and the Gemara is content to note that none of them represents a corrupt text. The substantive *halachic* discussion arising from the *mishna* will continue in the following session.

---

---

# Beitzah 36

## Mashilin & Hefsed

### Intro to Mashilin

We begin the fifth and final *perek* of *Beitzah*, with one week remaining in the *masechta*. Daf 36 picks up from the bottom of 35b, seven lines from the end, at the word *tnan*. The context is the *mishnah* that discusses the permissibility of various protective actions on *Yom Tov*: specifically, the allowance to lower fruit from a rooftop through a skylight, and to cover produce that is about to be rained upon — even though this is not done for the sake of *ochel nefesh*, since one will not be eating the fruit that day. Nevertheless, the action is permitted in order to prevent *hefsed*. The counterbalancing concern, as Rashi notes, is one of *tircha* — excessive effort — and, always lurking in the background, the concern of *uvda d'chol*, conducting oneself in a manner indistinguishable from ordinary weekday activity.

### Mishnah: Fruit & Rain

The *mishnah* teaches: *mashilin peiros derech arubba b'Yom Tov* — one may lower fruit through the skylight on *Yom Tov* from the rooftop. Similarly, fruit may be covered to protect it from rain, even though the motivation is not immediate consumption but rather the prevention of spoilage.

### Ad Kama: Limits

The Gemara immediately asks: *ad kama* — how much is one permitted to do before the activity crosses the threshold into problematic *tircha* or *uvda d'chol*? The answer given is attributed in two versions: *amar Rav Zeira Rav Assi*, and in another formulation, *amar Rav Assi amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *k'mot sheshaninu* — like what we taught in *Shabbat*. A parallel discussion about moving fruit and grain appears in tractate *Shabbat*, and the parameters established there should guide us here as well.

---

## Shabbat Parallel

### 4-5 Baskets

The *mishnah* in *Shabbat* teaches: *mafnin arba v'chamesha kuppot shel teven v'shel tvuah* — one may clear away the equivalent of four or five baskets of straw or grain. Two justifications are offered: *mipnei orchim*, in order to make space for guests, and *u'mipnei bittul beit HaMidrash*, to prevent the cancellation of Torah study — that is, to open up space where people can gather to learn. The Gemara understands this not as an open-ended allowance but as establishing a quantitative limit.

### Chamira vs. Kala

The Gemara immediately notes that the two cases differ in important ways and raises arguments in both directions. On one hand: *shani hatam d'ika bittul beit HaMidrash* — perhaps the *Shabbat* case is more lenient because the justification there (guests and Torah study) is weightier, whereas here on *Yom Tov* — *d'leika bittul beit HaMidrash* — where no such consideration applies, we would not permit as much. On the other hand, one can argue the exact opposite: *hatam hai ta'ama arba v'chamesha kuppot shari mishum Shabbat d'chamira v'lo ati lezilzulei bei* — perhaps it is precisely because *Shabbat* is weightier that even a generous allowance of four or five baskets does not lead to disregard for its laws. *Aval Yom Tov d'kila ati lezilzulei bei* — but *Yom Tov*, which is experientially lighter, and during which one already engages in considerably more activity by virtue of permitted cooking and food preparation, may lead people to treat it too casually. Therefore, on *Yom Tov* one might say *clal clal lo* — we would not permit it at all. This, of course, cannot mean a total prohibition since the *mishnah* explicitly permits the action; it means we would not permit it to the same degree.

Both arguments are coherent. One can argue that *Shabbat* should be more lenient because of the pull of *bittul beit HaMidrash* and because its own gravity ensures it is not taken lightly. Or one can argue that *Yom Tov* should be more lenient because the concern of *hefsed mamon* — financial loss — is a more pressing justification than guests or Torah study. Beyond the simple concern about waste, *hefsed mamon* also carries a practical dimension: if no leniency is granted, people may simply act on their own and incur even greater violations.

### Uvda D'chol Worry

The Gemara continues to press the comparison across several parameters. The first concerns whether one may clear out an entire storage space (*otzar*). The *mishnah* in *Shabbat* teaches *aval lo es ha'otzar* — one may not clear out the entire shed. Shmuel explains: *aval lo yigmor es ha'otzar kulo* — do not empty the entire space. Even if the shed contains only four or five baskets, one may not clear the whole floor. The reason: *dilma asi l'ashvuyei gumos* — if the entire floor is exposed, one may come to fill in furrows and indentations, which would constitute a prohibited act akin to *boneh* on a dirt floor.

The Gemara then asks whether the same restriction applies to clearing a roof on *Yom Tov*. One argument runs: *hatam hu b'Shabbos d'assir mishum d'chamir* — on *Shabbat*, which is weightier, the concern that one will come to violate justifies even distant protective enactments. *Aval Yom Tov d'kal* — but since *Yom Tov*'s violation is less severe, we would not extend the *gezeira* to prohibit clearing the whole space; *shappir dami*, it would be permitted. Conversely: *hatam d'ikka bittul beit HaMidrash amarta lo* — if even when there exists the strong justification of preventing the loss of Torah study we still do not permit clearing the entire space, then *hacha d'leika bittul beit HaMidrash lo kol she-ken* — here on *Yom Tov*, where that justification is absent, surely we should be equally or more restrictive.

It is worth noting that the concern about sweeping the floor seems more naturally connected to the *Shabbat* case, where people intend to use the cleared space and would want to tidy it up. The roof scenario, by contrast, involves lowering fruit — one does not plan to sit on the roof, and dirt floors are not an obvious feature of rooftops. So even the conceptual underpinning of the restriction maps imperfectly onto the *Yom Tov* case. No resolution is reached.

---

## Full Space Clearing

### Lo et HaOtzar

As noted above, Shmuel clarifies that the *mishnah*'s prohibition against clearing the *otzar* refers to the prohibition against clearing it entirely: *aval lo yigmor es ha'otzar kulo*. Even when the total contents fall within the permitted range of four or five baskets, one may not leave the whole floor exposed.

### Furrows Concern

The rationale is that a completely cleared floor invites sweeping and leveling: *dilma asi l'ashvuyei gumos* — one will come to smooth over the furrows and depressions in the dirt floor, which constitutes a form of forbidden labor on *Shabbat* analogous to *boneh*.

### Roof vs. Shed

When applying this restriction to the roof on *Yom Tov*, the Gemara proceeds as outlined above — arguing in both directions without resolution. What is clear is that the Gemara takes seriously both the possibility of stringency (since *Yom Tov*'s lighter character may require more protective fencing) and the possibility of leniency (since the specific concern about sweeping a dirt floor does not transfer cleanly to a rooftop context, and the violation of *Yom Tov* is less weighty than that of *Shabbat*).

---

## Migag Legag Limit

### Skylight Only

The Gemara introduces a ruling by Rav Nachman that introduces a new dimension of the *Yom Tov* case, and then asks whether the same applies to *Shabbat*. Rav Nachman rules: *lo shanu ela b'oso gag* — the permission to lower fruit was only taught with respect to the same roof; *aval migag legag lo* — but one may not transport fruit from one rooftop to another rooftop and then lower it through the other skylight. This constitutes excessive *tircha* or *uvda d'chol*, or both.

### Tania: Migag Legag

A *braita* confirms this: *ein metaltelin migag legag* — one may not move produce from one rooftop to another, *afilu kshe-gagoseihen shavin* — even when the two roofs are level with one another and no climbing or descending is required. The mere act of crossing from one rooftop to another, even with minimal effort, already exceeds the permitted scope.

### Shabbat Scenario

The Gemara asks: *hatam mai* — what would be the ruling in the analogous *Shabbat* scenario, where instead of lowering fruit from a roof, one would need to transport grain some distance from one shed to another? The Gemara then presents competing arguments in the now-familiar structure. One argument: *hacha hu d'asar mishum Yom Tov d'kal v'asi l'zalzulei beih* — it is specifically here on *Yom Tov* that we impose extra restrictions, since *Yom Tov*'s lighter character means people may come to treat it disrespectfully; *aval Shabbos d'chamira leih* — but *Shabbat*, which is weightier, does not require as many protective fences, and such extra effort might well be permitted. The counter-argument: *mah hacha d'ika hefsed peiros amarta lo* — since there is a concern for loss of produce here and even so the restriction applies, then *hatam d'leika hefsed peiros lo kol she-ken* — where there is no such loss involved, the restriction should apply all the more. *Teiku* — the question remains unresolved.

The broader pattern becomes clear: in every case, there are arguments to say *Shabbat* should be more lenient (it's weightier, so people are more careful) and arguments to say *Yom Tov* should be more lenient (the loss of produce justifies latitude). Neither consistently prevails.

---

## No Ropes or Ladders

### Braita: Rope Ban

A *braita* further specifies the limitations on how fruit may be lowered: *lo yeshalshelem b'chevel b'chalonos v'lo yoridem derech sulamos* — one may not lower fruit by means of a rope through a window, nor may one bring it down by way of a ladder.

### Direct Drop Only

The only permitted method is, in effect, dropping it directly through the skylight. If the roof is enclosed by a wall with a window, and one must lift the produce and lower it through the window — that is prohibited. Similarly, bringing it down via a ladder is forbidden. The reason, as with the roof-to-roof restriction, is either excessive *tircha* in Rashi's reading, or the broader concern of *uvda d'chol* — the entire operation begins to resemble ordinary weekday labor. The *mishnah*'s permission is thus narrowly confined.

The Gemara again poses the question *hatam mai* — what would the *Shabbat* equivalent be? — and again works through the competing arguments. On *Yom Tov*, one might restrict the method because *d'leika bittul beit HaMidrash* — there is no pressing reason such as Torah study — while on *Shabbat*, where *bittul beit HaMidrash* does apply, the more cumbersome method might be permitted. Or one might argue the reverse: *hacha ika hefsed peiros* — here, the concern of produce loss is present, and even so the restriction holds; *hatam d'leika hefsed peiros lo kol she-ken* — where there is no such concern, the restriction should apply with even greater force. Again: *teiku*.

---

## Covering Fruit

### Fruit Protection

The *mishnah* also permits covering fruit when rain threatens. The justification is *hefsed* — the fruit, typically grain or other produce, will begin to rot if left exposed. This is permitted even though it is not an act of *ochel nefesh* and even though it involves a degree of effort.

### Ulla: Bricks Too

Ulla extends this ruling: *v'afilu avira d'livnei* — one may even cover bricks stacked for construction purposes. Rashi explains this refers to bricks that are set aside for building and are therefore *muktzah*. The *chiddush* is that despite their status as *muktzah*, one may cover them to protect them from rain, since rain will damage them and create delay and wasted effort when they need to dry.

### Reb Yitzchak: No Muktzah

Rabbi Yitzchak disagrees: *peiros haru'uyin* — one may only cover items that are themselves fit and permitted to be handled. One may not expend effort — by moving a vessel or a tarp — for the sake of something that is itself *muktzah* and cannot be handled. The Gemara notes that this ruling is consistent with Rabbi Yitzchak's general principle: *amar Rabbi Yitzchak ein kli nital ela l'davar hanital b'Shabbos* — a vessel may only be moved for the sake of something that is itself permitted to be moved on *Shabbat*. The *muktzah* status of the object in question thus extends, in Rabbi Yitzchak's view, to prohibit even indirect acts taken for its benefit.

---

## Muktzah Movement

### Food Examples

The Gemara attempts to resolve this dispute by scrutinizing the *mishnah*'s language. The *mishnah* says *mechassin es ha'peiros b'keilim* — one covers the fruit with vessels. The inference is attempted: since the *mishnah* specifically mentions *peiros* — fruit — perhaps this is intentional, indicating that only non-*muktzah* items may be protected, but *muktzah* objects like bricks (*arraiya d'livnei*) may not. The Gemara deflects this: *hu hadin afilu arraiya d'livnei* — the same rule applies even for covering bricks. The *mishnah* mentioned fruit only because the earlier clause dealt with fruit — *mashilin peiros* — and so the later clause followed suit. The example of fruit is not restrictive; it is simply contextually parallel.

### Tevel Wine & Oil

The *mishnah* continues: *v'chein kadi yayin v'kadi shemen* — and similarly one may cover jugs of wine and oil. The Gemara asks: why give a second example of food when we already have fruit? The Gemara answers: *hacha b'mai askinan b'tevel* — the wine and oil here are *tevel*, produce from which *terumos u'ma'asros* have not yet been separated, and which is therefore *muktzah*. As Tosafot notes, while separating *terumos u'ma'asros* retroactively removes the *muktzah* status, the wine and oil remain *muktzah* for the time being.

### Small Loss OK

The Gemara then entertains a different reading: perhaps the second example of wine and oil is not about *tevel* and *muktzah* at all, but rather comes to teach that even a minor loss — *hefsed mu'at* — justifies covering. One might have thought: *l'hefsed merubeh chasshinan* — we are concerned about significant spoilage (like grain rotting in the rain), but *l'hefsed mu'at lo chasshinan* — for a minor loss, such as some water seeping into a barrel of wine, we are not concerned. The *mishnah* therefore teaches that even a modest loss suffices to permit the protective action. The Gemara leaves both readings on the table — the *tevel* reading and the *hefsed mu'at* reading — with neither fully dispositive.

The underlying question of whether one may move objects on behalf of *muktzah* items — whether the *mishnah*'s food-based examples reflect a principled limitation or are merely contextually determined — thus remains open as the Gemara turns to examine a series of Tannaitic parallels.

---

## Shabbat Parallels

### Pot Under Drip

The Gemara brings a *mishnah* in *Shabbat*: *nosnim kli tachat ha'delef b'Shabbat* — one may place a vessel under a roof drip on *Shabbat*. A roof drip is presumably dirty water that would be *muktzah*, yet we are placing a pot there for its sake. One might counter that the motive is protecting the floor, not collecting the water — but the Gemara treats this as equivalent to moving something for the sake of *muktzah*. The Gemara therefore limits this case: *b'delef ha'rauy* — we are speaking of a drip that is fit for use, such as clean water coming off the roof, which is not *muktzah*.

### Mat Over Bricks

A *braita* states: *porsin machatzel al gabei l'veinim b'Shabbat* — one may spread a mat over bricks on *Shabbat*. Prima facie this is a clear case of protecting *muktzah* bricks. The Gemara limits this as well: *d'yitmi mibinyana d'chazi l'mizgalaya* — these are leftover bricks from a construction project that is complete, and they are fit to be sat upon. Bricks that are no longer designated for active construction use, and which by their context are understood as objects people would casually use for sitting, are not *muktzah*. A further *braita* mentions spreading a mat over stones (*avanim*) on *Shabbat*, and again the Gemara limits this: *b'avanim mkurzalot d'chazyun l'beit ha'kisei* — these are smoothed stones suitable for use in place of toilet paper, and therefore not *muktzah*.

### Hive Protection

A *braita* teaches: *porsin machatzel al gabei kiveret devorim b'Shabbat* — one may spread a mat over a beehive on *Shabbat*, both to shield it from sun and from rain. The Gemara observes that at this point the cumulative weight of the evidence is suggestive: the *braita* offers a beehive, bricks, and stones — all of which, on their face, are *muktzah*. In each case the Gemara finds a way to reclassify them as not truly *muktzah*, but the sheer breadth of these cases seems to indicate that one may indeed move things to protect *muktzah* objects. The Gemara nevertheless continues to press the "special case" approach.

---

## Beehive Intent

### Honey Designation

The *braita* adds the qualification *u'vilvad shelo yitkaven latzud* — provided one does not intend to trap the bees. The Gemara addresses the beehive's *muktzah* status: *hatam nami d'ika devash* — there is honey inside, and one is effectively moving the mat to protect the honey, which is not *muktzah*. This prompts the challenge from Mar Ukva of Meishan to Rav Ashi: *hateneich biyemot ha'chama d'ika devash* — this works in summer when there is honey; *biyemot ha'geshamim mai ikka l'meimar* — but the *braita* also speaks of protection from rain, which is a wintertime concern, and in winter there is no honey. The Gemara responds: *lo nitzrecha ela l'otan shetei chalot* — even in winter, two combs of honey are left in the hive to feed the bees through the cold months, and it is those combs one is protecting.

Mar Ukva presses further: *otan shetei chalot muktzot hen* — those two combs are themselves *muktzah*, since the beekeeper deliberately leaves them so the bees will survive and the business will continue. The Gemara answers: *hacha b'mai askinan she'chishev aleihem* — this is speaking of a case where the beekeeper designated the combs before *Shabbat*, indicating he would make use of them if necessary, thereby removing their *muktzah* status.

### Trapping Worry

The Gemara then asks: *v'i lo chishev aleihem mai* — and what if he had not designated them? *Assur* — it would be forbidden, since they would be *muktzah*. This being so, the *braita* should have made its limiting case the *lack of prior designation* rather than the issue of intent to trap. *Lifrosh v'litni bedidi* — it should have simply said: when applies, and when does it not?

The Gemara responds: *hachi ka'amar* — what the *braita* means to say is that even when designation has been made and the honey is not *muktzah*, there remains a further condition that can invalidate the act: *af al pi she'chishev aleihem*, even when he designated them, *u'vilvad she'lo yitkaven latzud* — he must not cover the hive in a way that traps the bees.

### Not Intent-Based

The Gemara now scrutinizes this last clause carefully. The phrase *shelo yitkaven* — that he not *intend* to trap — suggests that intent is the operative factor. But this presents a difficulty: Abaye and Rava both rule *modeh Rabbi Shimon b'psik reisha v'lo yamut* — even Rabbi Shimon, who permits unintended acts (*davar she'eino miskavein*), agrees that when a prohibited consequence is inevitable, intent is irrelevant. If spreading the mat will definitely trap the bees, why should lack of intent make any difference?

The Gemara therefore reframes the clause. *L'olam kullah Rabbi Yehuda hi* — the entire *braita* follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds of *muktzah*, and the "intent" language is not about mental state but about physical action. *D'hacha b'mai askinan d'is bei kavei* — the case involves a hive that has small openings through which bees can escape. Therefore it is not a true case of *tzeida* — trapping — at all. *Ella eima u'vilvad shelo ya'asenah metzudah* — the clause should be understood as: do not cover it in a way that actually seals them in. The prohibition is not on intending to trap, but on covering in a manner that results in genuine entrapment. Leave them an escape route.

The Gemara anticipates a further objection: *peshita* — this is obvious. If you actually trap them, you have clearly violated the prohibition regardless of intent. The answer is that the *braita* comes to rule on a borderline case: bees are not ordinarily the subject of trapping (*shelo b'mino nitzod*) — the prohibition of *tzeida* applies most clearly to animals like deer. Since the prohibition as applied to bees is only *d'rabbanan*, one might have thought that since one does not intend to trap and the bees are not a primary target of trapping, there is room for leniency. The *braita* teaches that even in this case, if the mat is spread in a way that definitively traps them, it is forbidden.

Tosafot adds a nuance: even if the *braita* is read as being about Rabbi Yehuda, there may still be a residual difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon in how to define entrapment in borderline cases. Rabbi Yehuda, who does not consider intent relevant, might count as "trapped" a situation where escape is theoretically possible but highly unlikely. Rabbi Shimon, who is more permissive regarding unintended consequences, might hold that unless escape is truly impossible (*psik reisha*), the bees are not considered trapped. The Gemara's resolution, however, focuses on the physical configuration: the instruction is to ensure the hive has openings, making this a question of what one *does*, not what one *intends*.

Rav Ashi revisits the earlier problem about summer versus winter. He notes that the *braita* does not say "in summer" and "in winter" — it says *bachama mipnei ha'chama u'vageshamim mipnei ha'geshamim*: cover it because of the sun's heat, cover it because of rain. Rain can fall in summer; sun can be a problem in winter. *Tani bimei Nisan u'vimei Tishrei* — we may be speaking of spring or fall, when both sunshine and rain are present and when honey is available in the hive. The dilemma about the honey-free winter is therefore resolved by recognizing that the two weather conditions need not correspond to the two seasons.

The Gemara's bottom line regarding the core *muktzah* question is this: our *mishnah*'s exclusive use of food examples seems to restrict the allowance to non-*muktzah* objects. Yet every Tannaitic source in *Shabbat* — the roof drip, the bricks, the stones, the beehive — appears on its face to permit covering or protecting *muktzah* objects. In each case the Gemara successfully reclassifies the object as non-*muktzah* through a special interpretive move. One could have deflected all of these sources at once by attributing them all to Rabbi Shimon, who does not accept *muktzah* in the same scope as Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara's refusal to do so — its insistence on reading them all as consistent with Rabbi Yehuda — implicitly strengthens the principle that moving something for the sake of *muktzah* is indeed forbidden, even as the *peshat* of those same sources continues to pull in the opposite direction.

---

## Geraf Shel Rei

### Bed Strategy

The Gemara now takes a brief turn to a narrative involving Abaye's mill. During a rain, the millstones were getting wet, and Abaye came before Rava to ask what could be done. Rava's advice: *zil ayeilei lepurayich lehasam* — go bring your bed into the mill room. *D'leihavei k'geraf shel re'i* — this will render the millstone's situation equivalent to a *geraf shel re'i*, a chamber pot: the rain dripping onto the millstone, in a room where you are now sleeping, becomes intolerable and disgusting to be around, giving you grounds to remove the millstone even though it is effectively *muktzah*.

### Abaye Hesitant

Abaye did not act on this *heter*. The reason: *v'chi osin geraf shel re'i lechatchila* — may one deliberately construct a *geraf shel re'i* situation in order to create the pretext for removing *muktzah*? To Abaye, this felt like too clever a maneuver — engineering the circumstances specifically so as to manufacture an excuse for a leniency. While he sat deliberating, the mill collapsed. He then lamented: *teifach lei d'avri admar* — I deserve this, for I did not follow my teacher's ruling.

Tosafot notes that while Abaye's scruple is understandable, Rava's position may have been that the case was already borderline legitimate: the situation was already unpleasant and damaging, and Abaye was not creating a *geraf shel re'i* from nothing — he was merely placing himself within proximity of an already-developing problem. This contextual proximity, rather than artificial construction, is what lends the leniency its basis.

### Disgusting Items

The principle of *geraf shel rei* — that one may move a disgusting item even though it is *muktzah* — is a recognized exception within the laws of *muktzah*. Its application is not limited to literal excrement; as the cases below illustrate, it extends to anything that is sufficiently revolting and whose presence in one's living space is intolerable.

### Dead Rat Case

Shmuel formalizes the principle: *geraf shel re'i v'avit shel mei raglayim mutar l'hotzi'an l'ashpah* — a chamber pot for excrement and a vessel for urine may be taken out to the refuse heap. The Gemara then asks about replacing the chamber pot after it has been emptied: *nosein bo mayim u'machziro* — one puts water into it, and may then return it with the water inside, making the act of carrying it back more defensible.

The Gemara initially considers whether the principle of *geraf shel re'i* only permits moving the disgusting item in conjunction with a vessel — *agav mana*, by way of the containing vessel — but not by directly handling the repulsive contents themselves. The doubt is then resolved. A story is cited: there was a dead rat or weasel found in the perfume room of Rav Ashi on *Shabbat*. Rav Ashi instructed those present: *naktuha b'danveteih v'afkuha* — take it by the tail and remove it. Here one is directly handling the carcass, not by way of a container. This establishes that the *geraf shel rei* allowance extends even to direct handling, provided the object is sufficiently revolting and its presence intolerable in one's space. The juxtaposition of a putrefying carcass in a perfume room captures the principle well: the intolerable degradation of one's environment is what triggers the exception.

---

## Shvut Mishna

### Equal on Both

The Gemara now arrives at a *mishnah* that introduces several important conceptual categories. *Kol she'chayavin alav mishum shevus, mishum reshus, o mishum mitzvah — b'Shabbos chayavin alav b'Yom Tov*. Anything that is rabbinically prohibited under the heading of *shevus*, and equally anything that falls under *reshus* or *mitzvah* (as explained below), is equally forbidden on both *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. Two principles are embedded here: first, this entire category of rabbinic enactments applies identically across both holy days; second, the presence of some justification — whether *reshus* (discretionary benefit) or *mitzvah* (commandment) — does not override the prohibition. The *mishnah* thus stands in interesting tension with the preceding discussion, which found considerable ambiguity about whether *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* track each other, and which recognized that *hefsed* and *bittul beit HaMidrash* could generate latitude for specific acts.

### Climbing & Riding

The *mishnah* enumerates the *shevus* category — pure rabbinic prohibitions with no countervailing justification: *lo olin b'ilan* — one does not climb a tree; *v'lo rochvin al gabei beheimah* — one does not ride an animal; *v'lo shatin al pnei hamayim* — one does not float or travel on water.

### Clapping & Dancing

The list continues: *v'lo metapchin, v'lo mesapkin, v'lo merakdin* — one does not clap hands, does not slap one's thigh, and does not dance. Rashi distinguishes the first two as two forms of clapping. All of these are included in the *shevus* category.

### Din & Kiddushin

The *mishnah* then lists the *reshus* category — activities one might have thought had sufficient justification, yet which are nonetheless forbidden: *lo danin* — one does not convene a court; *v'lo mekadeshin* — one does not perform *kiddushin*; *v'lo choltzin* — one does not perform *chalitza*; *v'lo meyabmin* — one does not perform *yibum*. The Gemara will note a certain strangeness here: *kiddushin*, *chalitza*, and *yibum* would normally be categorized as *mitzvah* rather than *reshus*, and the Gemara will address this classification.

### Mitzvot Examples

Finally, the *mitzvah* category: *lo makdishin* — one does not sanctify objects to the Temple; *v'lo maarichin* — one does not undertake an *erech* obligation; *v'lo machrimin* — one does not declare objects *cherem*; these represent three distinct forms of Temple-related dedications. *V'lo magbihin terumos u'ma'asros* — and one does not separate *terumos* and *ma'asros*.

The *mishnah* then concludes with a striking formulation: *kol eilu b'Yom Tov amru, kal v'chomer b'Shabbos* — all of these were taught with reference to *Yom Tov*, and how much more so do they apply on *Shabbat*. This is surprising, since the opening clause stated the converse: what is forbidden on *Shabbat* is also forbidden on *Yom Tov*. Here the original context appears to have been *Yom Tov*, and the application to *Shabbat* follows by *kal v'chomer*. The *masechta* is *Beitzah*, not *Shabbat*. The *mishnah* then closes with *ein bein Yom Tov l'Shabbos ela ochel nefesh bilvad* — the only difference between *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* is acts directly related to eating. This final line is characteristic of the *ein bein* formulations found in the *mishnayot* of *Megillah* and is generally regarded as early. Whether this casts the entire *mishnah* as early, or whether these are two distinct components joined together, is a fascinating question in its own right.

It is also worth noting that the *reshus* and *mitzvah* categories function differently from the *shevus* category in a structural sense. The *shevus* items were identified as activities to avoid, and the prohibition was framed directly around those acts. The *reshut* and *mitzvah* items represent cases where a pre-existing rabbinic prohibition encounters a potentially overriding consideration — yet the *mishnah* rules that the override does not apply. This is distinct from the *geraf shel re'i* framework we encountered earlier, where an exceptional circumstance does succeed in overriding a rabbinic restriction.

---

## Bavli Reframe

### Tree & Animal

The Gemara provides reasons for each *shevus* prohibition in the form of a *gezeira*: *lo olin b'ilan, gezeira shema yitlosh* — the prohibition on climbing a tree is a safeguard lest one pull off a branch. *V'lo rochvin al gabei beheimah, gezeira shema yachtotz zmora* — riding an animal is prohibited lest one break off a branch to use as a switch to prod the animal.

A brief digression arises: one might infer from the formulation *gezeira shema yeitzei chutz l'tchum* — lest one ride beyond the *techum* — that *tchumin* are biblical, since one constructs a *gezeira* to protect a biblical violation. The Gemara deflects this by substituting the alternative *gezeira* about cutting a branch, thereby avoiding any inference about the biblical status of *tchumin*.

### Swimming & Music

*V'lo shatin al pnei hamayim, gezeira shema ya'aseh chavis shel shayitin* — one may not float on water lest one construct a flotation device. Tosafot suggests this could refer to something like an inflatable barrel or raft. *V'lo metapchin v'lo mesapkin v'lo merakdin, gezeira shema yitaken kli shir* — one may not clap or dance lest one come to repair a musical instrument.

### Gezeira Framework

This is a striking move by the *Bavli*, and it deserves careful attention. The Gemara has taken the category of *shevus* and reframed each of its constituent prohibitions as a *gezeira* — a protective fence around some other violation. In doing so, the *Bavli* departs from what is likely the original meaning of *shevus*. Riding an animal on *Shabbat*, floating on a river, clapping and jumping in a field — these do not feel like acts that require the explanation that one might eventually come to cut a branch or repair an instrument. The sense is rather that these activities are intrinsically problematic on *Shabbat*: they are, in the language developed throughout this tractate, *uvda d'chol* — they belong to the weekday world of commerce, transport, and work. Climbing trees was the activity of agricultural laborers. Traveling by animal or by raft was a primary means of transporting goods. Clapping and jumping in a field, as the *Tosefta* makes clear, was a method for scaring birds away from crops. These are paradigmatic work-related activities.

The concept of *shevus* is not, etymologically or conceptually, about *gezeirot*. *Shevus* points toward *Shabbat* — *shavat*, rest. It is about preserving the quality and experience of the day, about demarcating the sacred from the ordinary. Many scholars believe that in the *mishnah*, the *Tosefta*, and likely in the *Yerushalmi* as well, these prohibitions remain grounded in the intrinsic concern of *uvda d'chol*: they are things that are fundamentally out of place on *Shabbat*, and specific acts were identified and prohibited accordingly. Looking at the *reshus* and *mitzvah* categories in this *mishnah*, the same logic applies: convening a court, performing *kiddushin*, sanctifying objects to the Temple — these are not prohibited because one might thereby come to violate some other act. They are themselves activities of a certain character that belong to the weekday sphere.

### Gezeira Implications

The *Bavli*'s reframing of *shevus* as *gezeira* carries significant halakhic implications. On one hand, framing these prohibitions as *gezeirot* arguably devalues the independent weight of *uvda d'chol* as a concern. If climbing a tree is only prohibited because you might pull off a branch, it becomes harder to articulate why *uvda d'chol* in general should constrain activity on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* — the concern seems to dissolve into a collection of specific technical safeguards rather than a general principle about the nature of the day.

On the other hand, the *gezeira* framework opens the door to contextual exceptions. Tosafot famously uses this logic to permit clapping and dancing in synagogue on *Shabbat*: since nowadays people are not capable of repairing musical instruments quickly or easily, the concern that animated the *gezeira* no longer applies, and therefore the *gezeira* itself does not operate. One can only reason this way if the prohibition is grounded in a *gezeira* — a safeguard against some external violation — rather than being an intrinsic expression of *shevus*. If the prohibition on clapping were understood as a direct statement that clapping is *uvda d'chol* — inherently incompatible with the sanctity of *Shabbat* — no contextual exception would be possible.

The same logic applies across the most familiar rabbinic restrictions governing *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*. The *Bavli* frames the prohibition on blowing *shofar* on *Shabbat*, on reading the *megillah* on *Shabbat*, on taking the *lulav* on *Shabbat*, all as *gezeirot shema yavi* — lest one come to carry in the public domain. This is not necessarily what those prohibitions were originally about. Blowing the *shofar*, for instance, could more naturally be understood as involving the creation of sound through a musical instrument — the sort of activity that disturbs the stillness and quiet that is central to the *Shabbat* experience. The *gezeira* framing, while providing important halakhic flexibility, displaces the more fundamental concern about what kind of day *Shabbat* is meant to be. Recognizing this tension — between the *Bavli*'s systematic *gezeira* framework and the earlier, more experientially-grounded understanding of *shevus* — is essential to understanding how the halakhic tradition developed, and why some of the categories we have spent this entire *daf* examining feel both precise and, in certain respects, elusive.

---

---

# Beitzah 37

## Shvut & Gezeirah

### Shvut Definition

The *mishnah* before us presents a category of rabbinic prohibitions described as *asur mishum shvut* — forbidden on account of *shvut*. This category applies broadly to *issurei d'rabbanan* on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov*, though the *mishnah* enumerates only a select collection of cases, which invites the question of what makes these particular instances distinctive.

As discussed in the previous session, the *Bavli* frames several of these prohibitions — climbing a tree, riding an animal, swimming, clapping, and dancing — as *gezeirot*: safeguards against performing a prohibited *melachah*. One must not ride an animal lest one break off a branch; one must not clap or dance lest one come to repair a musical instrument. Yet there is no indication in the *mishnah* itself that this is the conceptual basis of the prohibition, and neither the *Tosefta* nor the *Yerushalmi* frames these restrictions in terms of *gezeirah* at all.

What appears to be the original conception underlying the *mishnah* — and this bears repeating — is that these activities fall under the category of *uvda d'chol*, weekday-type conduct, and *shvut* in its most basic sense: the preservation of the character of *Shabbat*. Riding one's animal, tending to crops by chasing away birds, climbing trees to harvest fruit — these were quintessentially weekday activities, and prohibiting them reflects the imperative to distinguish the sacred day from ordinary life. The *Bavli*, however, characteristically reframes everything in terms of *gezeirah*, as a safeguard against some further prohibition.

### Tosafot Dancing

This *Bavli* framing is precisely what *Tosafot* engages when confronting the widespread practice of clapping and dancing — not in the agricultural context of scaring away birds, but in the context of the synagogue or a *simchah*. *Tosafot* argues that since the entire prohibition was formulated as a *gezeirah* lest one come to repair a musical instrument, and since in their time people did not routinely repair musical instruments themselves, the *gezeirah* no longer applies and the activity is therefore permitted.

This reasoning, however, stands in tension with the general principle established already at the opening of *Beitzah*: *af al pi shebatla hata'am lo batla hagezeirah* — even when the reason disappears, the *gezeirah* does not disappear — *d'kol davar she'b'minyan tzarich minyan acher l'hati'ro*, for anything enacted by a rabbinic assembly requires another assembly to annul it. Normally, one would need substantial evidence to demonstrate that a prohibition was intended to be conditional on the continuing relevance of its rationale.

It should be noted that *Tosafot* did not invoke this principle casually as a general license. *Tosafot* characteristically employed such reasoning when confronted with a divergence between established practice in the community and what the *Gemara* appeared to prohibit. Rather than declare the community in violation, *Tosafot* sought to interpret the *Gemara* in a way that harmonizes with observed practice. The possibility that a *gezeirah* lapses when its reason no longer applies was one such interpretive tool, deployed specifically when the facts on the ground demanded an explanation.

### Medicine Gezeirah

A striking parallel arises in a related area not found on our *daf* but directly relevant to this discussion: the prohibition against taking medicine on *Shabbat*. Here again, the *Bavli* formulates the restriction as a *gezeirah* — lest one come to grind the medicine. Yet earlier sources show no evidence that grinding was the underlying concern. It may well be that the prohibition was originally understood as intrinsic: going to a healer, involving oneself in a professional therapeutic process, engaging with remedies — all of this was simply the kind of weekday activity one does not conduct on *Shabbat*. The Gospel accounts of healing on *Shabbat*, incidentally, reflect precisely this sensibility: the Pharisees' objection appears to be to the intrinsic inappropriateness of the activity on *Shabbat*, not to any fear of grinding.

But by framing it as a *gezeirah*, the *Bavli* opens a door. On *Yom Tov*, for instance, grinding spices is explicitly permitted, and one might therefore argue that the *gezeirah* against medicine never applied to *Yom Tov* categorically. Similarly, some have argued that in contemporary circumstances — where patients do not grind their own medications — the *gezeirah* does not apply with the same force. It is rare to find a *posek* who will state outright that the prohibition has lapsed entirely, since the basic assumption remains *af al pi shebatla hata'am*. But the framing of the prohibition as a *gezeirah* has led *poskim* to interpret its parameters more creatively. The category of *choleh kol haguf*, for example — one whose entire body is affected — was excluded from the restriction from the outset, and many contemporary authorities define that category broadly in order to permit medication in a wide range of circumstances. This is the practical consequence of the tension between the stated rationale and the ongoing prohibition: even when the principle holds that the *gezeirah* survives its reason, the gap between reason and rule can lead to expansive readings of the exceptions.

### Af Al Pi Shebatla

This brings us to the broader methodological point. The *Bavli* consistently frames these *shvut* prohibitions as *gezeirot* rather than as intrinsic restrictions. With perhaps one exception — the separation of *terumot u'ma'asrot*, to which we will return — every prohibition in the *mishnah*'s catalogue is assigned a *gezeirah* rationale. This is a recurring and deliberate feature of *Bavli* legal reasoning. The framing is consequential: it invites the question of whether the prohibition survives a change in circumstances, even as the classical answer is that it does. *Tosafot* applies this possibility selectively, and only when practice has already diverged. *Poskim* apply it creatively, shaping the contours of the exceptions. But the underlying principle — *af al pi shebatla hata'am lo batla hagezeirah* — remains the default, and departing from it demands strong justification.

---

## Rashut Category

### Beit Din Debate

The *mishnah* then turns to a second category, introduced with the phrase *v'eilu hein mishum reshut* — and the following things are prohibited on account of *reshut*. The term *reshut* here does not mean something entirely discretionary or neutral. Rather, it designates activities that carry some *mitzvah* component, yet fall short of being obligatory *mitzvot* — and are nonetheless forbidden as *shvut*.

The first item is sitting in *beit din*: one may not convene a court on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. The obvious question is: *v'ha mitzvah ka avid* — is this not a *mitzvah*? There are numerous verses commanding judges to adjudicate. The *Gemara* answers: *lo tzricha d'ika d'adif minei* — there is always someone more qualified to sit in judgment. This is a significant observation. While there is certainly a *mitzvah* dimension to serving as a *dayan*, in any given case one can almost always point to someone more competent. This diminishes the obligatory character of the act without eliminating its *mitzvah* quality entirely.

### Kiddushin & Pru Urvu

The second item is *kiddushin* — one may not betroth a woman on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. Again the *Gemara* asks: is this not a *mitzvah*? And again the *Gemara* qualifies: *lo tzricha d'it lei isha u'vanim* — we are speaking of a case where the man already has a wife and children and has fulfilled the obligation of *pru u'rvu*.

This ruling raises a fascinating question that is the subject of a genuine *machloket rishonim*. The *Gemara*'s formulation seems to suggest that the entire *mitzvah* dimension of marriage lies in enabling the fulfillment of *pru u'rvu*. The *Rambam*, *Meiri*, and others among the *Rishonim* understand marriage as a *mitzvah* in the sense that it is a *hechsher mitzvah* — an enabling act for *pru u'rvu*. The *Rosh*, by contrast, argues that marriage is not even a *mitzvah* in its own right, since in principle *pru u'rvu* could be fulfilled outside of wedlock — and if the *mitzvah* is *pru u'rvu* alone, then the marriage itself carries no independent obligatory status.

This has practical implications. Once a man has fulfilled *pru u'rvu*, does he remain obligated to remarry if his wife dies or they divorce? The *Gemara* implies not — at that point the *kiddushin* falls into the *reshut* category. And yet it must be noted, as one present in the study rightly observed, that *reshut* does not mean the complete absence of a *mitzvah*. *Rashi* himself notes *k'tzat mitzvah ika* — there is still some *mitzvah* dimension, which he identifies with the verse *be-voker zera et zar'acha vela-erev al tanach yadecha*, the value of having more than the minimal number of children. The *reshut* category therefore denotes not the absence of *mitzvah* but its relative diminishment. Elsewhere the *Gemara* speaks of the intrinsic value of marriage quite apart from children — *lo tov heyot ha'adam levado*, *kol adam she-sharui belo ishah sharui belo simchah* — but for the specific purposes of this categorization, the *Gemara* focuses on the obligatory dimension, which is primarily tied to *pru u'rvu*.

### Tosafot Kiddushin

*Tosafot* raises an alternative and striking reading of the *Gemara*'s question. The *Gemara* asks why *kiddushin* is categorized as *reshut* rather than *mitzvah*. *Tosafot* suggests that this question carries a more radical implication: if *kiddushin* were truly a *mitzvah*, it ought to be permitted on *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* outright. That is, *Tosafot* reads the *Gemara* as raising the possibility that a full-fledged *mitzvah* might override the *shvut* prohibition entirely — and therefore, when the man has not yet fulfilled *pru u'rvu*, the *kiddushin* should actually be permitted.

This is admittedly a difficult reading of the *Gemara*, because the final category of the *mishnah* — the *mitzvah* category — explicitly lists genuine *mitzvot* that are nonetheless prohibited. Still, *Tosafot*'s position is worth noting. In the spirit of this line of thinking, *Tosafot* elsewhere — citing *Rabbeinu Tam* — finds grounds to be lenient about *kiddushin* in pressing circumstances, such as when one party is in *avelut*. The argument runs that the urgency of fulfilling *pru u'rvu* or the social realities of ensuring timely marriage can generate leniency even where a prohibition would otherwise apply. This likely reflects the reality of medieval life, in which death and violence created frequent and pressing need to remarry quickly.

### Chalitzah Yibum

The third item is *chalitzah* and *yibum* — the levirate obligations — which are likewise forbidden. Again the question: *be-mitzvah ka avid*! And again the answer: *lo tzricha de-ika gadol* — there is an older brother, and *mitzvah be-gadol leyabem*, the obligation of *yibum* falls first on the eldest brother. So while there is certainly a *mitzvah* to perform *yibum* or *chalitzah*, if there is an older brother who bears the primary obligation, the younger brother's performance of it is not as full a *mitzvah*. The parallel to the *beit din* case is precise. In neither instance does the *reshut* designation imply that the *mitzvah* dimension is entirely absent; it means only that the obligation is attenuated by circumstances.

---

## Sanctification Gezeirah

### Mekach Umemkar

The *mishnah* continues with the category introduced by the phrase *v'eilu hein mishum mitzvah* — and the following are prohibited despite being genuine *mitzvot*. These include: *lo makdishin v'lo maarichin v'lo machrimin* — one does not consecrate objects, assess their value for redemption purposes, or declare them banned. The *Gemara* states: *gezeirah mishum mekach u'memkar* — this is a safeguard against business dealings.

Why is *mekach u'memkar* itself problematic? Here *Rashi* presents two distinct explanations that map precisely onto the conceptual tension discussed throughout this session. His first explanation is that consecrating an object — transferring it from one's domain to that of *hekdesh* — resembles a transaction. And *mekach u'memkar* is prohibited from the *Torah* itself on the basis of *mimtzo cheftzecha v'daber davar*: one may not pursue one's own affairs on *Shabbat*, and commercial activity is intrinsically a "worldly pursuit." On this reading, *mekach u'memkar* is an *issur* in its own right, and the prohibition against consecration is a *gezeirah* against something already intrinsically forbidden.

*Rashi*'s second explanation is that *mekach u'memkar* is itself a *gezeirah* — lest one come to write things down. On this reading, consecration leads to business, which leads to writing. The *Gemara* addresses the objection that this would constitute a *gezeirah l'gezeirah*: a safeguard against a safeguard. The response is that *kula chad gezeirah hi* — it is all part of a single integrated prohibition. Even so, the underlying question — is *mekach u'memkar* intrinsically forbidden, or only as a *gezeirah* against writing? — mirrors the same structural ambiguity we have traced throughout.

The verse *mimtzo cheftzecha v'daber davar* does ordinarily admit an exemption for *cheftzei shamayim* — the affairs of Heaven. One might therefore argue that *kiddushin* or *yibum*, which are *cheftzei shamayim*, should be free of the *mekach u'memkar* concern. But the *Gemara* identifies a further concern even in those cases — the concern of *shema yichtov*, that one will come to write — which applies regardless of whether the underlying activity is religious or commercial in character.

### Terumot Ma'asrot

The *mishnah* also prohibits *lo magbihin trumos u'maasros* — one may not separate *terumot* and *ma'asrot* on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*, even though this is a *mitzvah*. The *Gemara* responds: *pshita* — this is obvious. And presumably the reason it is obvious is that this prohibition is not cast as a *gezeirah* at all but is intrinsically problematic: separating *terumah* changes the status of the produce and "fixes" it, an act analogous to making or completing an object on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*. This stands as a notable exception to the *Bavli*'s general tendency to frame everything in terms of *gezeirah*.

### Terumah to Kohen

*Rav Yosef* adds a qualification: *lo nitzrecha ela litnah l'kohen bo bayom* — the *chiddush* is that one may not even separate the *terumah* and give it directly to the *kohen* on the same day. One might have thought that reframing the act as giving a gift of food to the *kohen* — rather than fixing the produce — would render it permissible. After all, giving gifts of food is generally permitted on *Yom Tov*. Nevertheless, the prohibition stands.

### Challah Separation

There is, however, an important exception. The *Gemara* distinguishes between *pira d'tavil me'etmol* — produce that was *tevel* from before *Yom Tov*, for which the prohibition applies in full — and *pira d'tavil ha'idna* — produce that becomes *tevel* on *Yom Tov* itself. The only produce that can become *tevel* on *Yom Tov* is dough: on *Yom Tov* one may bake bread, and dough that is freshly made on *Yom Tov* becomes obligated in *challah* on that day. The *Gemara* rules that one may separate *challah* from such dough and give it to the *kohen*: *mafrishin u'mavilin l'kohein*.

Two points emerge.
