First, this falls under the *ochel nefesh* dispensation — since the baking of bread is permitted on *Yom Tov* for the sake of eating, separating *challah* from that dough is an integral part of the permitted food-preparation process. Second, the *Gemara* emphasizes that one should give the *challah* to the *kohen*, not merely separate it and set it aside. This presentation — transferring it as a gift to the *kohen* — helps reframe the act away from the impression of "fixing" the dough and toward the impression of gift-giving. That said, the *poskim* do not require giving the *challah* to the *kohen* as a strict condition for permissibility; in our time, *challat chutz la'aretz* is not given to the *kohen* at all, and one may still separate *challah* on *Yom Tov* from dough made on *Yom Tov*.

---

## Category Framework

### Shvut Levels

At this point the *Gemara* addresses an apparent difficulty in the *mishnah*'s structure. If the categories are labeled *reshut* and *mitzvah*, one might think the label implies these activities are not subject to *shvut* at all. Conversely, calling something *mishum mitzvah* seems to say the opposite of why it is forbidden. *Rabbi Yitzchak* clarifies: *lav mibaya ka'amar* — the *mishnah* is employing a *lav mibaya* formulation. It goes without saying that activities which are pure *shvut* with no redeeming quality — *shvus gerideta* — are forbidden. The *mishnah*'s contribution is to teach that even *shvut d'reshut* — activities that carry a quasi-*mitzvah* component — are likewise forbidden; and even further, *afilu shvus d'mitzvah nami assur* — even activities that are genuine *mitzvot* but whose performance entails a *shvut* violation remain prohibited. The categories do not denote the presence or absence of *shvut*; they denote ascending degrees of *mitzvah* quality, all of which nonetheless fall before the *shvut* prohibition.

### Shabbat Yom Tov

The final line of this section states that all of these prohibitions apply on *Yom Tov* — and *kal va'chomer* on *Shabbat*. The sole distinction between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* in this entire domain is *ochel nefesh* — food preparation. *Kol elu b'Yom Tov amru*: all these were declared with reference to *Yom Tov*, and they apply with equal force on *Shabbat*.

---

## Shabbat Yom Tov Diff

### Lowering Fruit

The *Gemara* immediately raises a contradiction. If the *mishnah* claims there is no difference between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* except for *ochel nefesh*, what of the ruling in a previous *mishnah* that *mashilin derech arubah b'Yom Tov aval lo b'Shabbat* — one may lower fruit through a skylight on *Yom Tov* but not on *Shabbat*? This is a *d'rabbanan* difference that has nothing directly to do with food preparation. *Rashi* had noted in the preceding *daf* that the concern driving that *mishnah* was *hefsed* — preventing loss — not eating, since the fruit was not going to be eaten that day. Yet the *mishnah* explicitly permits lowering it on *Yom Tov* and not on *Shabbat*. We have before us, then, a demonstrable rabbinic distinction between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* that does not fall under the *ochel nefesh* rubric.

### Abuye Resolution

*Rav Yosef* proposes resolving the contradiction by attributing the two *mishnayot* to different *Tannaim*: the ruling about the skylight follows *Rabbi Yehoshua*, while the ruling that there are no distinctions except *ochel nefesh* follows *Rabbi Eliezer*. A *beraita* records their dispute in the context of a mother animal and its calf that fell into a pit on *Yom Tov* — one cannot slaughter both on the same day due to the prohibition of *oto v'et beno*. *Rabbi Eliezer* rules that one may raise the first animal in order to slaughter it, and must leave the second in the pit with food provided below. *Rabbi Yehoshua* rules that one may raise the first, declare intent to slaughter it, and then change one's mind — raising the second and choosing which to slaughter. *Rabbi Yehoshua* thus permits a kind of creative flexibility to prevent loss, while *Rabbi Eliezer* allows only the minimum.

*Abaye* challenges this identification. Perhaps *Rabbi Eliezer* was strict in the animal case only because there was an alternative — one could lower food to the animal in the pit. But in the skylight case, where there is no alternative means of protection, *Rabbi Eliezer* might permit lowering the fruit. Conversely, *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s leniency in the animal case rested on the trick of declaring intent and retracting it — *de'efshar la'arumey*, one could make it appear as though each act was for the purpose of eating. In the skylight case, no such trick is available — it is evident that one is not going to eat a large quantity of drying fruit. So *Rabbi Yehoshua* might well be strict there. *Abaye*'s conclusion is that neither *mishnah* can be straightforwardly attributed to either *Tanna*, and the contradiction remains unresolved on this approach.

### Beit Shammai Hillel

*Rav Papa* offers a different resolution: the two *mishnayot* reflect the dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*. A *mishnah* records that *Beit Shammai* prohibits carrying a minor, a *lulav*, or a *Sefer Torah* into the public domain on *Yom Tov*, while *Beit Hillel* permits it. *Beit Shammai* maintained extensive restrictions on carrying on *Yom Tov*; *Beit Hillel* did not. On this reading, the *mishnah* permitting lowering fruit through the skylight follows *Beit Hillel*, who is lenient with respect to such movement, while the *mishnah* asserting no differences aside from *ochel nefesh* follows *Beit Shammai*, who restricts all non-food movement to mirror *Shabbat*.

At this point *Tosafot* raises a difficulty: the *mishnah*'s claim of no difference is explicitly about *d'rabbanan* distinctions. At the biblical level, obviously *Yom Tov* and *Shabbat* differ — carrying and kindling fire are permitted on *Yom Tov* — but these permissions derive from or connect to *ochel nefesh*. The question, then, is whether there are any purely *d'rabbanan* differences, and our previous *mishnah* appeared to show that there are.

### Muktza Carrying

The *Gemara* then addresses how the *Beit Shammai* / *Beit Hillel* dispute on carrying connects to the question of lowering fruit. One might say *Beit Shammai* was strict about carrying but not about other forms of movement — after all, lowering fruit through a skylight might all occur within a *reshut hayachid*, without any carrying issue. The *Gemara* responds: *atu tiltul lav tsorech hotza'ah hu* — movement is the first step toward carrying. Because *Beit Shammai* was strict about *hotza'ah*, they were also strict about *tiltul* — general movement — lest it lead to carrying.

Many *rishonim* understand *tiltul* here as a reference to *muktza*: one of the functions of the *muktza* prohibition is to instill a general caution around the handling of objects, thereby reducing the risk of inadvertent *hotza'ah*. *Beit Shammai*'s greater stringency regarding carrying on *Yom Tov* generated corresponding stringency regarding *muktza*, while *Beit Hillel*'s greater permissiveness regarding carrying generated less restrictive *muktza* rules.

It should be noted, however, that the previous *mishnah* about the skylight was assumed not to involve *muktza* at all. *Rashi*'s entire discussion there centered on *tircha* — exertion — not on *muktza*. If the issue is *muktza*, the conceptual framework shifts. What must be said is that even in a case where *muktza* is not the concern, *Beit Shammai* would be stricter about *schlepping* in general — *tiltul* meaning simply the moving of objects — as a precautionary measure against *hotza'ah*.

### Unresolved Gaps

This resolution, while coherent on its own terms, leaves substantial gaps. As noted, yesterday's *daf* included an extended analysis that openly acknowledged multiple *d'rabbanan* differences between *Shabbat* and *Yom Tov* entirely unrelated to *ochel nefesh* — for instance, the question of whether *Yom Tov* is treated more stringently than *Shabbat* because of *asi lezulzulei beh*, or whether it is treated more leniently. That passage assumed a whole system of differentiated rabbinic restrictions without limiting the differences to a single skylight case. The *Gemara* here addresses only one *mishnah* and declares it a *Beit Shammai* / *Beit Hillel* dispute — but many further differences remain unaddressed. The solution is incomplete, and a fully satisfying resolution of the tension between these two *mishnayot* is not reached.

One final observation: the *Gemara*'s insistence on framing *tiltul* as the first step toward *hotza'ah* is itself another instance of the *Bavli*'s preference for causal, *gezeirah*-style reasoning. It would have been equally natural to say that extensive *schlepping* is simply *mechazei uvdin d'chol* — it looks like weekday activity — without tethering it to the prohibition of *hotza'ah*. The *Gemara* declines that framing.

---

## Techumim Intro

### Behemah Keilim

A new *mishnah* introduces a concept that will dominate the remainder of the tractate: *ha-behemah ve-ha-keilim k'raglei ha-baalim* — animals and vessels follow the feet of their owner. This concerns the laws of *techumim*: the prohibition against traveling more than 2,000 *amot* from the edge of one's city on *Shabbat* or *Yom Tov*, unless one has placed an *eiruv techumim* to extend one's range in a particular direction.

The *mishnah* teaches that this restriction applies not only to one's own movement but to one's possessions. If another person wishes to use your vessels on *Yom Tov*, he may not take them to a location that falls within his *techum* but outside of yours. They are bound by your *techum*, not his. This raises a fascinating question — not addressed explicitly in the *Gemara* here, though it relates to the broader discussion of *shvitat keilim* — concerning objects located far from their owner. If one is abroad for *Yom Tov* and grants permission to someone at home to use one's property, it is not clear how the laws of *techum* apply, since the objects are already located entirely outside of the owner's *techum*. The answer to that case would require further investigation.

### Shepherd Animal

The *mishnah* continues: *ha-moser behemah livno o l'ro'eh* — if one hands over an animal to one's son or to a shepherd, and that shepherd's *eiruv* extends in a direction opposite to the owner's — the animal remains bound by the owner's *techum*. Even in the care of the shepherd, the animal follows the original owner's feet.

### Shared Estate

The *mishnah* then addresses the case of brothers who share an undivided estate. Where particular vessels have been designated for one brother's use — *keilim ha-myuchadim l'echad min ha-achim she-ba-bayit* — even though legal ownership remains undivided, those vessels follow the *techum* of the brother who uses them. Vessels that are not specifically designated for any one brother — *she-ein meyuchadim* — are bound to the place accessible to all, meaning they may be taken only within the intersection of all the brothers' *techumim*.

This can be visualized as follows. Suppose two brothers have made their *eiruvei techumim* in opposite directions. Each can travel up to 4,000 *amot* in one direction but may not step even a single *amah* in the opposite direction. Shared vessels may be taken only within the area accessible to both — the overlap between their respective ranges. If those ranges do not overlap at all, the shared vessels cannot be moved.

### Borrowing Timing

The *mishnah* addresses a further nuance: *hashoel kli mechavero me'erev Yom Tov* — if one borrows a vessel before *Yom Tov*, the vessel follows the borrower's *techum*, since when *Yom Tov* began the item was under the borrower's control. *BeYom Tov* — if the borrowing occurred on *Yom Tov* itself — the vessel follows the lender's *techum*, since at the onset of *Yom Tov* the item was still in the lender's domain. The *Gemara* therefore raises the interesting question of when the borrower's control is established: at the moment of physical possession, or at the moment permission is granted? The flexibility seen throughout this *mishnah* in defining "ownership" for purposes of *techum* suggests that the answer may not require formal physical *kinyan* — perhaps a grant of permission before *Yom Tov* suffices.

### Dough Techum

The *mishnah* extends the same principle to a woman who borrows spices, water, or salt from her neighbor to incorporate into her dough: *harei elu keraglei sheteihen* — the dough follows the *techum* of both women, since it contains components that, when *Yom Tov* began, were under the neighbor's ownership and therefore subject to the neighbor's *techum*. Even though the neighbor no longer has a claim to those specific particles in the finished dough — she will be repaid with equivalent spices after *Yom Tov* — the *techum* designation follows the status at the onset of *Yom Tov*. The dough therefore may be taken only to places accessible to both women simultaneously.

### Water Exemption

*Rabbi Yehudah* exempts water from this rule: *poter bamayim mipnei she-ein bahem mamash* — water is excluded because it is insubstantial. This requires some unpacking. Water is hardly trivial — it is essential for life, and so much of *Bereishit* revolves around wells and water sources. But the point is not that water lacks importance; it is that water loses its perceptible identity when incorporated into dough. Spices and salt can be tasted or, in some forms, seen. Water cannot be sensed in the finished product — its presence becomes invisible. Once a substance loses its perceptible identity within a mixture, *Rabbi Yehudah* rules that it no longer carries its *techum* restriction into the composite product.

---

## Rabbi Dosa

### Purchase Possession

The *Gemara* opens by noting that our *mishnah* does not accord with *Rabbi Dosa*. A *beraita* teaches: *Rabbi Dosa* (and some say *Abba Shaul*) holds that *halokeach behemah mechavero me'erev Yom Tov* — one who purchases an animal before *Yom Tov*, even though the animal was not actually transferred until *Yom Tov* itself, the animal follows the purchaser's *techum*. Formal legal possession — which in *halacha* typically requires a physical act of *kinyan* — has not yet been accomplished, yet the animal is treated as though it already belongs to the purchaser, because the transaction was concluded on *erev Yom Tov*.

This teaches something significant about the governing concept here. *Techum* restrictions are not triggered by strict legal ownership but by a more functional notion of under whose control or domain an object falls. One who has paid and agreed to a transaction but not yet physically acquired the object is already, for *techum* purposes, treated as the owner.

### Shepherd Transfer

The *beraita* continues: *vehamoseir behema lero'eh* — one who gives an animal to a shepherd *on Yom Tov* itself — the animal nonetheless follows the shepherd's *techum*. This directly contradicts our *mishnah*, which states that an animal given to a shepherd follows the owner's *techum*. The *mishnah* is therefore *dela keRabbi Dosa* — it does not accord with this view.

### Shepherd Choice

The *Gemara* reconciles the apparent contradiction: *kan bero'eh echad kan beshnei ro'im* — the difference is whether there is one shepherd in town or two. If there is only one shepherd, then even before the owner formally hands over the animal on *Yom Tov*, it was already understood — indeed, self-evident — that this animal would be entrusted to that shepherd. The assignment was pre-determined, and therefore when *Yom Tov* began, the animal was already effectively under the shepherd's domain. No formal act of transfer was needed, because there was no choice to be made.

If there are two shepherds, however, the recipient is not self-evident. A choice must be made, and that choice cannot retroactively define the status as of *Yom Tov*'s onset. In that case, the animal must have been formally transferred before *Yom Tov* in order for the shepherd's *techum* to govern it.

The *Gemara* notes that this reading is supported by the *mishnah* itself: *detani livno o lero'eh* — the *mishnah* presents a case of two potential recipients, one's son or the shepherd. Where there is a choice between two people, the transfer must be deliberate and explicit. This is consistent with the *Gemara*'s reading: the *mishnah* addresses the two-recipient scenario, while *Rabbi Dosa*'s ruling addresses the single-shepherd scenario. The *diyyuk* from the *mishnah* reinforces the reconciliation.

### Rav Yochanan Psak

*Rabbah bar bar Chana* cites *Rabbi Yochanan*: the *halacha* follows *Rabbi Dosa* — that in a case with a single predetermined shepherd, the animal follows the shepherd's *techum* even when formally transferred on *Yom Tov*. The *Gemara* then asks: but *Rabbi Yochanan* himself holds that the *halacha* follows the *stam mishnah* — the anonymously stated *mishnah* — and our *mishnah* appears to contradict *Rabbi Dosa*. The *Gemara* responds: the reconciliation already established — one shepherd versus two — resolves the tension. Our *mishnah* deals with two options; *Rabbi Dosa* deals with one. *Rabbi Yochanan*'s ruling follows *Rabbi Dosa* for the single-shepherd case, and this is fully consistent with the *stam mishnah*, which addresses a different scenario.

---

## Two Borrowers

### Opposing Eiruv

The *Gemara* cites a *baraita* concerning two people who borrowed a single shirt together as partners: one wished to wear it in the morning on *Yom Tov* to go to the *beit midrash*, the other wished to wear it in the evening of *Yom Tov* to go to a festive gathering. Crucially, the two borrowers placed their *eiruvei techumim* in exactly opposite directions. One placed his *eiruv* in the north, giving him access 4,000 *amot* to the north but no access whatsoever to the south. The other placed his *eiruv* in the south, giving him access to the south and none to the north. Their respective *techumim* do not overlap at all.

### Intersection Rule

The rule established by the *mishnah* and operative here is that jointly owned or borrowed objects may be taken only within the intersection of all relevant owners' *techumim*. Each co-owner's restriction applies to the object, and the object is bound by whichever restriction is more limiting in any given direction.

### Day Night

One might think that since the two borrowers intended to use the shirt at different times of day — one in the morning, one in the evening — the shirt could be treated as effectively belonging to each one during his respective period. This reasoning is rejected. *Yom Tov* is a single halakhic unit; the *techum* status of an object is fixed at the onset of *Yom Tov* and cannot be subdivided by time of day. There is no mechanism for dividing *Yom Tov* into morning and evening for the purpose of *techum* assignment.

### Zero Overlap

Since the two owners' *techumim* are in opposite directions with zero overlap, the intersection of their domains is zero. The conclusion is stark: *lo yezizenu mi-mkomo* — the shirt cannot be moved at all. It is fixed in its place for the entirety of *Yom Tov*. One cannot hand it off at the boundary either, since the moment it crosses from one *techum* into territory accessible only to the other, it has been moved beyond the first owner's permitted range.

---

## Partnership Property

### Rav Barrel

The *Gemara* presents a dispute: two people purchased a barrel of wine and an animal together as partners, with their *techumim* pointing in opposite directions. *Rav* rules that the barrel is permitted — *chavit muteret*. Each partner may take his half of the wine within his own *techum*, without being constrained by the other's direction. The animal, however, is forbidden — *behema asura* — and remains bound by the overlap of both owners' *techumim*.

### Shmuel Both

*Shmuel* disagrees: *chavit nami asura* — even the barrel is forbidden and must remain within the overlapping zone. On *Shmuel*'s view, when *Yom Tov* began the entire barrel was jointly owned, and the fact that it was subsequently divided does not alter the status fixed at the onset of *Yom Tov*.

### Bereira Theory

The *Gemara* analyzes *Rav*'s position. If *Rav* holds *yesh bereira* — that retroactive clarification is halakhically operative — then when the barrel is divided and each partner takes his half, we say retroactively that each partner always owned precisely that half. At the onset of *Yom Tov*, there was no joint ownership in the relevant sense — each half belonged to its eventual recipient from the beginning, definitionally. On this view, each partner may take his half wherever his *techum* allows, unconstrained by the other.

But if *Rav* holds *yesh bereira*, why is the animal different? And if *Rav* holds *ein bereira*, why is the barrel permitted? The apparent inconsistency demands explanation.

### Animal Nutrients

The *Gemara* resolves this by stating: *le-olam kasavar yesh bereira* — *Rav* does indeed hold *yesh bereira*, and this is why the barrel is permitted. The animal is different for a distinct biological reason: *dekaymi tchumei mehadadi* — the two halves of the living animal are mutually sustaining. *Tosafot* explains: even if we say retroactively that the front half always belonged to one partner and the back half always belonged to the other, the front half was, while the animal was alive at the onset of *Yom Tov*, drawing sustenance from the back half — blood, nutrients, oxygen — and vice versa. Each half contained within itself something belonging to the other owner. The situation therefore resembles the woman's dough that contained borrowed spices: even though the dough belongs fully to her, it contains components whose *techum* points in a different direction. Similarly, even if *bereira* establishes that each half of the animal "always" belonged to its eventual owner, each half physically contained something of the other's domain at the onset of *Yom Tov*. The barrel of wine presents no such difficulty: individual droplets do not organically sustain one another, and if *bereira* identifies which droplets belonged to whom, those droplets never derived anything from the other's share.

### Muktza Challenge

*Rav Kahana* and *Rav Assi* challenge *Rav* with an analogy: *le'issur muktza lo chasht ve'le'issur tchumin chasht*? If *Rav* is not concerned about a *muktza* problem with the animal, why is he concerned about a *techum* problem? The analogy runs as follows: if one is worried that the animal's halves are intermingled and that each half derives from the other, then by the same logic, any microscopic amount of meat or weight gained by the animal between the onset of *Yom Tov* and its slaughter ought to be *nolad* and *muktza* — newly created matter that was not in existence at the onset of *Yom Tov*. Yet clearly no one applies *muktza* to the imperceptible biological changes occurring within a living animal. Why then should the same microscopic biological interdependence generate a *techum* restriction? *Tosafot* acknowledges that the analogy is not entirely persuasive, but it is what the *Gemara* presents. *Rav* fell silent — *shtik Rav* — without offering a response.

### Rav Ushaya

The *Gemara* then reports the ultimate practical ruling: *Rav Oshaya amar yesh bereira* — there is *bereira*, and therefore both the barrel and the animal are permitted. Each partner may take his portion wherever his *techum* allows, since *bereira* retroactively establishes that each portion was always his. *Rabbi Yochanan amar ein bereira* — there is no *bereira*, and therefore both the barrel and the animal are forbidden and limited to the intersection of the two *techumim*.

---

## Corpse Tumah

### Multiple Exits

The *Gemara* now raises a challenge to *Rav Oshaya*'s position from an apparently contradictory ruling. A *mishnah* discusses the case of a corpse in a house with multiple exits. The concern is which exits become *tamei*: ordinarily, all exits through which the corpse might be removed are presumed to convey *tum'at ohel*. If one exit is opened and thereby identified as the definitive exit through which the corpse will be removed, that exit is *tamei* and the others are spared.

### Before Death

*Beit Shammai* rules: *vehu she'chishev alav ad she'lo yamus ha-meis* — the thought that identifies an exit as the intended removal point is effective only if it occurred before the person died. Once the person has died, all exits are simultaneously potential conduits for the corpse, and a subsequent thought cannot retroactively redefine one exit as the designated one.

### After Death

*Beit Hillel* is more lenient: *af mishe'yamus ha-meis* — even after the person has died, a mental designation of one exit can define it as *tamei* and spare the others. The identification need not be made before death; it can occur subsequently.

### Forward Only

*Rav Oshaya* comments on this *mishnah*: *le'taher ha-p'tachim mikan u'leha'ba* — the entire debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel*, and the mechanism of definition generally, operates only going forward from the moment of identification, *mikan u'leha'va*. *Lema'frea lo* — it does not work retroactively. That is, once one designates an exit, the other doorways are *tahor* going forward from that point. But the designation does not reach back in time to declare that those other exits were always *tahor*, retroactively protecting vessels that had been sitting in their thresholds before the designation was made.

### Contradiction

Here lies the apparent contradiction. *Rav Oshaya* has just been quoted as holding *yesh bereira* in the case of the barrel and the animal — meaning that dividing partnership property on *Yom Tov* retroactively establishes that each half was always the respective owner's. Yet in the *tumah* case, *Rav Oshaya* explicitly rules that the identification mechanism works only going forward and not retroactively — which is the essence of *ein bereira*. How can *Rav Oshaya* hold *yesh bereira* in one domain and *ein bereira* in another?

We leave this question open. The *daf* ends with this unresolved tension: *Rav Oshaya* in the context of *tumah* and doorways appears to hold *ein bereira* — no retroactive definition — while in the context of *techum* and partnership property he appears to hold *yesh bereira* — full retroactive clarification. Reconciling these positions will carry us into the next session.

*Chazak chazak.*

---

---

# Beitzah 39

## Intro & Tchumim Overview

### 39 Melachos Context

We arrive at the penultimate daf of *Beitzah* — daf 39 — as the masechta draws to a close. It is worth noting that while there are 39 *melachos*, the tractate runs from daf 2 through daf 40, yielding precisely 39 *dapim* of content. Not all 39 *melachos* apply with equal force on *yom tov*, and the discussions of this daf continue to explore the intersection of *yom tov* law with the principles of *tchumim* — the boundaries within which people and objects may travel on *Shabbat* and *yom tov*.

### Tchumim on Yom Tov

Although *tchumim* applies equally on *Shabbat* and *yom tov*, the practical concern about transporting objects — and especially food — is distinctively a *yom tov* issue. On *Shabbat*, carrying outdoors is prohibited categorically, so the question of how far one may transport an object rarely arises in the same way. On *yom tov*, however, where carrying food is permitted and one need not rely on walls or an *eiruv* in the conventional sense, the concern about moving food across *tchum* boundaries becomes acute. It is in this context that the present daf continues its inquiry.

---

## Coal & Flame

### Coal vs. Flame

The *Mishnah* opens with a fundamental distinction: a *gachelet* — a coal or ember — is subject to the *tchum* of its owner, just like any other object in one's possession. The *shalevet* — the flame — however, may be taken *bechol makom*, anywhere at all, without restriction. The practical scenario is straightforward: if one forgot to light a *yahrtzeit* candle before *yom tov* and needs to kindle a light, one may transfer a flame from someone else's candle or fire. One may not, however, take that person's physical candle beyond its owner's *tchum*. The flame, by contrast, carries no such limitation.

### Flame Nature

This raises an immediate question: why is the flame exempt? One possible explanation is that the transferred flame is considered a new entity — it is now yours, not the original owner's. But the *Mishnah*'s language of *bechol makom*, "in every place," without qualification, suggests something deeper: the flame is not considered a *davar mamash* — a real, substantial object — at all. It belongs to no one because it is not the kind of thing that can be owned. That is why there is no *tchum* limitation tied to any particular person; it is not that the flame belongs to the new recipient, but rather that flame as such is not a possessable thing.

### Hekdesh Coal & Flame

This same distinction carries through to the domain of *hekdesh*. A *gachelet shel hekdesh* — an ember belonging to the *Beit HaMikdash* — is subject to *me'ilah*: misappropriating it constitutes a biblical violation. The *shalevet* of *hekdesh*, however, occupies a different category: *lo nehenin velo mo'alin* — one may not derive benefit from it rabbinically, yet one does not incur the biblical prohibition of *me'ilah*.

This raises a genuine conceptual difficulty. One can understand why a transferred flame might not be subject to *me'ilah* if it is regarded as a new entity no longer connected to the original coal. But what if one is simply standing near a fire of *hekdesh* and benefiting from the light or heat emanating from it? The flame is still directly rooted in the coal of *hekdesh*. Is that not equivalent to deriving benefit from the coal itself?

The difficulty is real and connects to a broader *gemara* discussion about whether one who burns wood is considered to be deriving benefit from the wood as it burns, or only from what has already been consumed — that is, whether the energy being released is still "the wood" in any meaningful sense. In contemporary terms, this is something like the relationship between matter and energy: the flame is the conversion of mass into energy, and perhaps at that point of conversion the substance of the coal is no longer the operative reality. What one derives benefit from is the flame — the energy — not the coal that gave rise to it. Though the *Gemara* does not frame the discussion in these terms, the underlying intuition tracks closely with the scientific understanding of combustion.

If one were to take a piece of straw and press it directly against a smoldering ember of *hekdesh*, that would appear to be a straightforward case of *me'ilah* — one is deriving benefit from the coal itself, before the conversion. But if one touches one's straw to the *flame* rising from that coal, the question becomes whether that flame is still the coal or whether it has become something categorically distinct.

### Carrying Fire

The *Mishnah* then addresses the *Shabbat* context. One who carries a *gachelet* — a coal — into a *reshut harabbim* is *chayav*, liable, because the coal is a physical object of sufficient significance. One who carries out a *shalevet* is *patur* — exempt — because the flame lacks the substantiality required to incur *Shabbat* liability for carrying.

### Five Coal Rules

A *Tosefta* compiles five rules stated about the *gachelet*, presenting them in parallel: for *tchumim*, the coal follows the owner while the flame is unrestricted; for *hekdesh*, there is *me'ilah* on the coal but not on the flame; for *avodah zarah*, the coal is forbidden while the flame is permitted; for carrying on *Shabbat*, one is liable for the coal but exempt for the flame; and for *mudar hana'ah*, one who has forsworn benefit from another's possessions is forbidden from using that person's coal but may transfer and benefit from the flame.

The *Tosefta* also adds, found in the margin, that one recites *borei meorei ha'esh* only on a flame, not on a coal. The logic is consistent: a *berachah* does not require a physical object — one recites a blessing on thunder — but ownership and *halachic* substantiality do require physicality, and the flame lacks that quality.

### Avodah Zarah Fire

Among these five rules, the *avodah zarah* case is the most striking. A coal used in idol worship is *asur* — forbidden by biblical prohibition — while the flame is not only exempt from *me'ilah* (which of course does not apply here at all) but is entirely *mutar*, permitted without even a *derabbanan* restriction. The *Gemara* finds this worthy of explanation, particularly given the asymmetry with *hekdesh*, where the flame is at least rabbinically forbidden.

### Hekdesh vs. AZ

The *Gemara* resolves the asymmetry as follows: *avodah zarah demi'isa badilei inshi minah* — *avodah zarah* is intrinsically repulsive, and people naturally distance themselves from it. Because of this innate taboo, the Rabbis did not need to enact a *gezeirah* against benefiting from its flame; people will avoid it on their own. *Hekdesh*, by contrast, *delo ma'is velo badilei inshi mineih* — it is not disgusting and people do not instinctively keep away from it. People regularly enter the *Beit HaMikdash* and interact with *hekdesh*. Therefore the Rabbis enacted a protective measure, making even the flame of *hekdesh* rabbinically forbidden.

The precise contours of the scenario — whether the prohibition applies only to a transferred flame or also to direct benefit from a flame still rooted in the coal — are left unresolved by the *Gemara*. But the possibility that the ruling may depend on whether the flame remains physically anchored will become relevant in the next section.

---

## Flame & Shabbat

### Flame Transport

The *Gemara* now probes the *Shabbat* liability question more carefully. The *Mishnah* states that one who carries a *shalevet* is *patur*, yet a *baraita* states that one who carries even the smallest flame is *chayav*. These appear to be a direct contradiction. *Rav Sheshet* resolves it: the *baraita* refers to a case where the flame is being carried out on a *kisam* — a small twig or toothpick. The *Mishnah*'s exemption applies only to a flame carried without any physical substrate.

The *Gemara* immediately asks: if one is carrying the twig, why does the flame matter at all — is one not liable simply for carrying the twig? The answer is that the twig is below the *shiur* for wood: to be liable for carrying wood, one needs enough to cook a light egg, as the *Mishnah* in the relevant context teaches. A match-sized sliver of wood does not meet that threshold. However, because the flame is now *rooted in a physical object*, the flame itself acquires *halachic* significance and one becomes liable on account of the flame.

### Oil & Vessel

*Abaye* introduces a further case: one who smears oil on a vessel and lights it on fire. Here there is no obvious wick being consumed; what burns is a thin film of oil on what is, let us say, a shard of pottery. The *Gemara* again asks: why mention the flame — is one not liable for carrying the pottery? Again, the pottery shard is below the *shiur*: to be liable for carrying broken pottery, the piece must be large enough to wedge between beams in a house, as the *Mishnah* rules. The shard does not reach that *shiur*. But here too, because the flame is anchored in a physical object — even an oil-smeared potsherd — it gains substantiality, and one is liable.

### Flame Exemption

The *Gemara* now asks: given all this, what scenario would produce the exemption in the *Mishnah* — a case where one carries a flame and is genuinely *patur*? The answer: *kegon de'adei aduyei lirshut harabbim* — one blew or pushed the flame across the boundary.

### Blown Flame

*Rashi* explains: one has a fire on one side of the boundary between private and public domain, and blows or waves it such that something on the other side catches fire. The object that was burning in the private domain never moved, and the object now burning in the public domain was already there. There was no act of carrying — no transfer of a flame-bearing object from one domain to another. Only in this fashion does one "carry" a flame in the technical sense without it being anchored in a physical object that itself crossed the boundary.

This conclusion now circles back to the earlier discussions. If *Shabbat* liability for carrying a flame depends on whether it is rooted in a physical object, perhaps the same principle governs the *hekdesh* and *avodah zarah* cases as well. Perhaps the flame of *hekdesh* is only rabbinically forbidden — and the flame of *avodah zarah* entirely permitted — in a case where the flame has been detached from its original coal and transferred. But if one is benefiting directly from a flame still rising from its original fuel, perhaps the coal's status reasserts itself, and one would be treated as deriving benefit from the coal itself. The *Gemara* does not revisit the earlier cases in light of this conclusion, leaving the question open.

---

## Wells & Ownership

### Three Well Types

The next *Mishnah* turns from fire to water, introducing a parallel set of rules about wells and the *tchum* of their water. Three categories are distinguished, each governed by a different principle of ownership.

### Private vs. City

A *bor shel yachid* — a privately owned well — has its water go by the owner's *tchum*, like any other object in private ownership. A well belonging to the residents of a city goes by the *tchum* of the city collectively: even if individual residents have personally extended their *tchum* through an *eiruv tchumin*, that does not affect the city's water, which is defined by the two-thousand *amah* radius of the city as a whole.

### Olei Bavel Wells

A third category is wells designated for *olei Bavel* — travelers who came up for the *regel*. These wells were established along roads for the use of pilgrims and wayfarers, not for a defined community. They are not owned by any collective. Accordingly, the water goes *keraglei hamemallei* — by the *tchum* of whoever fills the water on *yom tov*. It is worth noting the *Mishnah*'s choice of language: even writing after the *Churban*, it speaks of *olei Bavel* as a living reality, evoking the sense that the pilgrimage remains a live institution.

### Breira & Filling

*Rashi* notes an implicit assumption in this ruling that deserves attention. At the onset of *yom tov*, this water is ownerless — *hefker*. Given that, one might have expected it either to acquire its *shvisah* in place (as *Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri* held for ownerless objects), giving it a two-thousand *amah* radius from the well itself, or alternatively to have no *tchum* at all, free of any restriction. Instead, the *Mishnah* rules that it goes by the filler. *Rashi* explains that this reflects the principle of *breira*: since the person ultimately acquires the water on *yom tov*, we say retroactively that from the beginning of *yom tov* this water was already under that person's effective ownership, and so it is properly governed by that person's *tchum*.

---

## Water Flow Debate

### Rava's Question

*Rava* raises a contradiction against *Rav Nachman*. The *Mishnah* states that a private well goes by its owner's *tchum*. Yet a *baraita* teaches: *haneharos hamoshchin veha-ma'ayanos hanov'in harei hen keraglei kol adam* — rivers that flow and springs that surge go by every person, meaning they are not limited by anyone's *tchum* at all.

### Flowing Water

The resolution lies in the nature of the water. The *baraita* speaks of *moshchin* — flowing — and *nov'in* — surging. Such water begins *yom tov* not at rest in a fixed location. Since *kinyan shvisah* requires the object to be stationary, water that is continuously moving cannot acquire a *shvisah* at all. Even if it is privately owned, it never becomes *koneh shvisah*, and therefore no *tchum* applies.

### Collected Water

The *Mishnah*, by contrast, discusses a *bor* — a cistern of collected rain water. This water is stationary at the onset of *yom tov* and can acquire a *shvisah*. *Rava* states, and *Chiya bar Abba* in the name of *Shmuel* confirms: *bi'mekhunasim* — the *Mishnah* is dealing with collected water. The contrast with the *baraita* is thus resolved: the *baraita* addresses flowing water, the *Mishnah* addresses collected water.

---

## Hefker Dispute

### Who Owns Water

The *Mishnah*'s ruling — *keraglei hamemallei* — assumes that the *olei Bavel* well is in some sense *hefker*, or at least not collectively owned in the way a city's well is. The question that now arises concerns a specific scenario: what if one fills the water from such a well not for oneself but for someone else?

### Rav Nachman

*Rav Nachman* rules: the water goes by *mi she-nitmilu lo* — the person for whom it was filled.

### Rav Sheshet

*Rav Sheshet* rules: the water goes by *keraglei hamemallei* — the filler, not the recipient.

### Hefker Principle

*Rashi* clarifies the scope of the dispute immediately: this is not a case where one first filled the water for oneself and then gave it to a friend. That case is covered by the *Mishnah* itself — once I have acquired the water, it is mine, limited by my *tchum*, and my subsequent gift to someone else does not change the *tchum* that was already fixed. The dispute concerns rather the case — analogous to *Rivkah* and *Eliezer* — where from the outset I fill the water *in order to* give it to someone else. My act of drawing is entirely in service of providing water for the other person. Whose water is it?

*Rashi* connects this to the principle of *magbia metzia l'chavero*: if I pick up an ownerless object in order to acquire it on behalf of someone else, does that other person become the owner? The general rule in *Bava Metzia* is that *magbia metzia l'chavero lo kanah chavero* — the recipient does not acquire, because by picking it up for him I am depriving others of the opportunity to take it themselves. Thus, if the well is *hefker*, I — the filler — acquire the water, and it goes by my *tchum*, not the recipient's.

### Hefker vs. Shutafut

*Rav Nachman* and *Rav Sheshet* thus disagree about the underlying nature of the *olei Bavel* well. *Mar savar bira de'hefkera hu* — one holds the well is *hefker*, ownerless. *U'mar savar bira de'shutfei hu* — the other holds the well is effectively a partnership, belonging collectively to all of *Klal Yisrael*.

If the well is *hefker*, then filling it for another person does not transfer ownership to that person, since the principle of *magbia metzia l'chavero* blocks the acquisition — and therefore it goes by the filler. If the well is a form of *shutafut* — collective partnership — then the picture changes. Every Jew is already a *shutaf*, a co-owner, in the water. When I draw it for Charlie, I am not taking something from the commons at others' expense; I am merely facilitating Charlie's access to his own portion. In that case, Charlie can acquire it, and the water goes by him.

---

## Noder Hana'ah

### Vow Scenario

*Rabbah* challenges *Rav Nachman* — who holds the water goes by the recipient, implying the well is *shutafut* — from a *baraita* concerning *mudar hana'ah*. The case: one person says *hareini alecha cherem* — my possessions are forbidden to you — and the other reciprocates: *harei atah alai cherem* — your possessions are forbidden to me. Both vows take effect simultaneously: *shneihem asurim zeh bazeh*, each is forbidden from deriving benefit from the other.

### City Property

The *baraita* then specifies what is and is not included in this mutual prohibition. *V'asurin beshel ota ha'ir* — they are forbidden from the property belonging to their city collectively: the streets (*harechov*), the bathhouse (*beit hamerchatz*), and the synagogue (*beit haknesset*). The rationale is that each person holds a partial ownership in these communal institutions, and deriving benefit from them thus constitutes deriving benefit from the other. This has far-reaching practical implications: as soon as a mutual *issur hana'ah* takes effect, one cannot walk on city streets, enter the communal synagogue, or use the bathhouse.

### Olei Bavel Permitted

By contrast, *umutarin beshel olei Bavel* — they are permitted to benefit from things belonging to *olei Bavel*. These are not subject to the mutual prohibition, even though the water in such wells and the pilgrimage infrastructure generally belongs in some sense to all of *Klal Yisrael*.

### Olei Bavel Examples

The *baraita* enumerates: *Har HaBayit*, the Temple Mount; the chambers (*lishkot*); the *azarot*; and the wells along the roads. Though *Har HaBayit* belongs to all of *Klal Yisrael*, and not only to *olei Bavel* in the narrow sense, its inclusion here illustrates the category: public property of a national rather than a local character, accessible to all without the quality of partial individual ownership.

### City Examples

The city examples — streets, bathhouse, synagogue — represent a different kind of communal ownership: one where the individual members of the local community hold genuine, partial stakes, such that benefiting from them counts as benefiting from one another. The *Gemara* here touches on questions that later jurisprudence would address through the concept of corporate personality. The *halacha* has a developed sense that city property is not the same as partnership property and not the same as *hefker*, yet it still treats it as sufficiently connected to the individual members that an *issur hana'ah* between individuals extends to it.

---

## Partnership Analysis

### Partnership Logic

The *baraita* has established that one may derive benefit from *olei Bavel* property even under *mudar hana'ah*. This becomes the basis for a logical inference: if the *olei Bavel* well were a *shutafut* — a genuine partnership among co-owners — it would be no different from any other jointly owned property. *Tosafot* makes this point directly: if the well were a partnership like city property, the *baraita* would have forbidden it just as it forbids city property. The fact that it is permitted implies the well is not a partnership.

### Breira Logic

But the *Gemara* refines this argument. The prohibition on city property does not rest simply on partnership ownership in the abstract; it rests on the way in which one *uses* the shared resource. The *Mishnah* in *Nedarim* teaches: *hashutafin shenidru hana'ah ze mizeh asurin l'hikanes l'chatzer* — partners who are mutually subject to *issur hana'ah* may not enter a jointly owned courtyard, and may not *lirchotz b'vor* — bathe in a shared well. The reason is that when one bathes in the well, one uses the entire shared space as a single unit; one is not taking one's discrete portion, but rather immersing oneself in the whole. One cannot apply *breira* to say "this part of the water is mine" when one is using all of it simultaneously.

### Water Apportionment

Drawing water from a well, however, is different. When one takes water from the well, one removes a discrete, bounded quantity. That quantity was always, retroactively, the portion destined for this person. This is the operation of *breira*: the act of drawing apportions the water, and retroactively that water was always one's own portion. Therefore, even in a *shutafut* framework, drawing water does not involve deriving benefit from the other person's share — it involves taking only one's own share, which is determined at the moment of drawing. One is not forbidden from drawing water from a jointly owned well under *mudar hana'ah*, because *breira* ensures that the water drawn was always yours.

### Rav Nachman Position

On this basis, *Rav Nachman*'s position can be maintained with the well as *shutafut*: the *mudar hana'ah* problem is avoided not because the well is *hefker* but because *breira* governs the taking of water in a *shutafut* framework. And on *yom tov*, when one draws water on behalf of another, that other person acquires their portion through the same *breira* mechanism — the water drawn was always their intended portion. Hence, according to *Rav Nachman*, the water goes by the recipient.

---

## Estate Division

### Brothers' Estate

The *Gemara* now questions whether *Rav Nachman* truly holds *yesh breira*. A *Mishnah* is cited concerning *achim hashutafim* — brothers who inherited an estate and then became partners in it. The question is whether their reconstitution as a partnership changes the legal status of the estate. Before division, the estate functions as a single corporate-like entity — *tfisat habayit* — rather than as a partnership of individual owners. After division, if they pool their holdings again, the estate functions as a *shutafut*, a genuine partnership. The difference between these two statuses carries significant practical consequences in two areas: *ma'aser behemah* and the *kalbon*.

### Obligations Differ

*Ma'aser behemah* — the animal tithe — requires that one drive all newborn animals through a narrow opening and consecrate every tenth one. This obligation does not apply to animals owned in partnership; it applies only to privately owned animals. As long as the estate remains undivided, its animals are owned by a single corporate entity — the estate — and the brothers are obligated in *ma'aser behemah* as one collective owner. Once they divide and reconstitute as a partnership, however, the animals are owned by multiple individuals in partnership, and the obligation of *ma'aser behemah* does not apply.

The *kalbon* — the moneychanger's surcharge — works in the opposite direction. When two partners contribute a single *shekel* between them, they are still two individuals and must pay two *pundions* (the surcharge). But if the estate remains undivided and functions as a single entity, only one *kalbon* is required, even though two brothers are involved.

Thus: when they are obligated in the *kalbon* — meaning they divided and reconstituted as a partnership — they are exempt from *ma'aser behemah*; when they are obligated in *ma'aser behemah* — meaning the estate remains as one entity — they are exempt from the *kalbon*.

### Rav Anan View

*Rav Anan* introduces a nuance: the ruling that division followed by reconstitution creates a *shutafut* applies only when the division was uneven, specifically when brothers exchanged unlike categories — *g'dayim k'neged tla'im* — goats for sheep, or sheep for goats. In such a case, the division was effectively a commercial exchange: I took all the goats and gave you my share in them in exchange for your share in the sheep. Since there was a genuine transaction at the moment of division, the estate was dissolved and what was reconstituted is a new partnership.

### Even Division

But if the division was even — *g'dayim k'neged g'dayim, tla'im k'neged tla'im* — each brother took exactly half of every category — then *Rav Anan* holds that *breira* applies. This half was always what you were destined to receive; this is the portion that was always coming to you from the inheritance. There was no purchase, no exchange, no transaction; just a clarification of what was always yours. Since the division was merely the actualization of what was always each person's portion by inheritance, it did not break the corporate unity of the estate. Reconstituting it is therefore not creating a new partnership; it is reverting to the natural state that was only temporarily obscured.

### Rav Nachman View

*Rav Nachman* disagrees: *afilu chilku g'dayim k'neged g'dayim utla'im k'neged tla'im — ein omer ze chelko hamagia mishaa rishona lakach*. Even an even division does not admit of *breira*. Any division of an estate involves an element of purchase and exchange: by taking these specific goats rather than those specific goats, I am effectively buying out your portion in these goats and surrendering my portion in those. There is always a transactional element, and therefore no division can be said to have been predetermined by the original inheritance. Once divided, the estate cannot be reconstituted; what is formed is always a new partnership.

### No Reconstitution

The consequence of *Rav Nachman*'s position is that *ein breira* governs the estate scenario. Brothers who divide and reconstitute are always partners, never a reconstituted estate. And this reveals that *Rav Nachman* holds *ein breira* — at least at the biblical level.

---

## Well Resolution

### Well is Hefker

The *Gemara* now draws the threads together. Given that *Rav Nachman* holds *ein breira*, his earlier position in the *mudar hana'ah* case — that deriving benefit from a *shutafut* well is permitted because *breira* apportions one's share — is no longer available to him. One cannot explain the permissibility of the well under *issur hana'ah* through *breira* if one holds *ein breira*. Therefore, the *Gemara* concludes: *d'kulei alma bira d'hefkira hu* — it is universally agreed that the *olei Bavel* well is *hefker*. That is what distinguishes it from city property and explains why there is no *mudar hana'ah* problem: the well does not belong to anyone, and therefore deriving benefit from it does not constitute deriving benefit from one's counterpart.

### Filled for Other

This resolution, however, creates a new problem for *Rav Nachman*'s position in the earlier dispute with *Rav Sheshet*. If the well is *hefker*, and one fills the water for someone else, then the principle of *magbia metzia l'chavero lo kanah chavero* should apply: the recipient does not acquire, and the water goes by the filler. Yet *Rav Nachman* ruled that the water goes by the recipient. How can that be reconciled?

### Magbia Dispute

The *Gemara* therefore explains: *Rav Nachman* and *Rav Sheshet* are in fact disagreeing about the application of *magbia metzia l'chavero*. Specifically, they dispute whether one who draws water from this well on behalf of another person has in fact made that other person the owner. *Rav Nachman* holds that the recipient acquires; *Rav Sheshet* holds that the recipient does not acquire, and the filler retains ownership.

### Tosafot Resolution

*Tosafot* offers an elegant explanation for *Rav Nachman*'s position. The rule that *magbia metzia l'chavero lo kanah chavero* — the recipient does not acquire — is premised on the fact that by picking up the object for one person, one deprives others of the opportunity. But is that concern relevant at a well with ample water, sufficient for all who need it? If there is enough water for every traveler, no one loses out when I draw for Charlie. In such a case, *Rav Nachman* holds, the standard objection to *magbia metzia l'chavero* does not apply, and Charlie does acquire. The water therefore goes by the recipient.

---

## Fruit in Another City

### Two-City Setup

The final *Mishnah* of the daf introduces a scenario that encapsulates the broader themes of *tchum* and food transport on *yom tov*. The case: my fruit is in City B. I am in City A. City A and City B are within reach of one another — perhaps within two thousand *amot* — but the fruit begins *yom tov* outside my *tchum*. Residents of City B wish to come to City A on *yom tov* and offer to bring me my fruit on their way.

### Fruit Transport Ban

The *Mishnah* rules: *lo yavi'u lo* — they may not bring the fruit to him. The fruit began *yom tov* outside the owner's *tchum*. Once an object begins *yom tov chutz latchum*, it may not be moved in a manner that extends its reach beyond where it could have gone from its starting point. It is not merely that the fruit cannot travel all the way to the owner; the fruit cannot be moved at all in a direction that exceeds its own two-thousand *amah* radius from its location at the onset of *yom tov*.

### Eruv Solution

However, if the owner had made an *eiruv tchumin* before *yom tov* — extending his personal *tchum* toward City B — then the fruit is considered to begin *yom tov* within his *tchum*. In that case, the fruit is treated as his object that was always within his domain, and it may be transported.

### Guest Gift Rules

The *Mishnah* addresses a related scenario: one who invited guests from another city, and when those guests are departing on *yom tov*, wishes to send food back with them as a gift. This too is forbidden: the food is limited by the host's *tchum*, and once the guests leave the host's two-thousand *amah* boundary they may not take the host's food with them. The exception: if before *yom tov* the host formally transferred ownership of the food to the guests — *zachah lahem manoteihem me'erev yom tov* — then the food begins *yom tov* already belonging to the guests, governed by their *tchum*, and they may carry it back when they depart.

---

---

# Beitzah 40

## Fruit Outside Techum

### Intro & Mishnah Setup

We conclude *masechet* Beitzah with Daf 40, opening with the *mishnah* at the bottom of 39b. The case: a person's fruit are located in another city — that is, outside his *techum*. He is in city A; his fruit are in city B, some three thousand *amot* away.

### No Eruv Case

Because he did not make an *eruv techumim*, his *techum* ends before city B. His fruit began *Yom Tov* outside his *techum* and therefore cannot be moved toward him. Even if the residents of city B made an *eruv* allowing them to travel to city A, they still cannot bring him his fruit — because the fruit's *techum* is determined by him, and his *techum* does not reach city B. The *mishnah* states accordingly: *lo yavi'u lo* — they may not bring it to him.

### Owner's Eruv Case

However, *ve-im eirev hu, peirotav kamohu* — if he was the one who made the *eruv*, extending his *techum* into city B, then his fruit follow him. Just as he may travel to city B, so too his fruit may be transported back with him.

### Guests Scenario

The *mishnah* then presents a related case: *mi she-zimen etzlo orchim* — one who invites guests from city B to his home in city A for *Yom Tov*. Those guests made an *eruv* enabling them to walk to city A; however, the host did not make an *eruv*, since he had no need to travel. After the meal, the host cannot give the guests a package of food to take home with them to city B. His food is governed by his *techum*, which does not extend to city B. The guests may bring food *to* him — food that began *Yom Tov* in their possession may travel with them — but he cannot send his food out of his *techum* with them.

### Zikuya on Erev YT

There is, however, a solution: *ela im ken zika lahem manoteihem me-erev Yom Tov* — unless the host had already transferred ownership of the food to his guests before *Yom Tov* began. If, on *erev Yom Tov*, he designated specific food for them — a package of bottles and sandwiches, for instance — and effected a *zikuya*, a legal transfer of ownership through a third party acting on the guests' behalf, then when *Yom Tov* commenced, that food was already theirs. It therefore began *Yom Tov* governed by *their* *techum*, and they may carry it home with them.

### Techum Application

This prompts a clarifying observation: the rule that fruit or objects cannot be moved beyond a certain *techum* is not simply a function of legal title. The object's *techum* is defined by whose domain it is practically associated with when *Yom Tov* begins — and determining that relationship is precisely what drives the *gemara*'s ensuing debate.

---

## Rav vs Shmuel

### Entrusted Fruit

The *gemara* introduces a new case: *ha-mafkid peirot etzel chaveiro* — one who deposits fruit with a friend before *Yom Tov* for safekeeping. When *Yom Tov* begins, whose *techum* governs those fruit? The fruit are physically in city B with the guardian, while the owner is in city A. Two great *amora'im* disagree.

### Rav's View

*Rav amar keraglei mi she-hupkidu lo* — Rav holds that the fruit follow the *techum* of the one with whom they were deposited, the guardian (*nifkad*). Since the guardian has taken physical possession of the fruit, it is his domain, not the owner's, that governs their movement on *Yom Tov*.

### Shmuel's View

*u-Shmuel amar keraglei ha-mafkid* — Shmuel holds that the fruit follow the owner, the one who entrusted them. The guardian is merely an extension of the owner; it is the owner who truly retains control.

### Lending Contrast

A useful contrast is the case of lending. When one lends an object to a borrower before *Yom Tov* — and the *gemara* elsewhere indicated that even a verbal commitment to lend suffices — the object follows the borrower's *techum*. The borrower takes it for his own use; he is the one who has control and practical dominion over it. That case is therefore clear. The depositum case is more nuanced, because there is a split between who physically holds the object and who retains authority over it. The guardian holds it, but the owner remains the one with ultimate say.

### Guardian Status

The deeper issue here is not merely the technical question of *hilkhot shomrim* — at what legal moment does one become a *shomer* and assume liability — but a different, more conceptual question: to what degree has the guardian assumed a quasi-ownership relationship with the object, the kind of practical control that governs *hilkhot techumin*? Consider the shepherd: even though he is working for the owner, the *gemara* elsewhere holds that when an owner gives his flock to a shepherd before *Yom Tov*, the flock follows the shepherd's *techum*. The shepherd walks the animals, decides where they graze, and exercises genuine control over them. But if an item is merely stored in someone's house — locked away, with the guardian having no real say over it — then despite his legal liability as a *shomer*, it may well remain, for purposes of *techumin*, under the owner's domain. That is precisely where Rav and Shmuel diverge.

---

## Tannaim Connection

### Ox in Yard

The *gemara* proposes that this dispute between Rav and Shmuel mirrors an earlier *tannaitic* controversy. The *mishnah* discussed in this connection involves a person who brings his cow into someone else's yard. The general rule is that if he entered without permission — in effect trespassing — he bears all risk himself, and any damage done to his cow by the yard owner's animals or property creates no liability for the host. But the *mishnah* states: *im hikhnis bi-reshut ba'al ha-chatzer, chayav* — if he entered with the permission of the yard owner, then the yard owner is liable should something happen to the cow.

The logic is that by welcoming the visitor and his animal onto his property, the yard owner implicitly assumes responsibility for them. This is analogous, in some respects, to the concept of liability in hosting: once you invite someone into your domain, you undertake a degree of responsibility for what befalls them there.

*Rebbi*, however, disagrees: *l'olam eino chayav ad she-yikabel alav ba'al ha-bayit lishmor* — the yard owner is never liable merely by virtue of having extended an invitation. A formal, explicit assumption of guardianship is required.

### Halakhic Mapping

Rav Huna then transmits a ruling: *amar Rav Huna amar Rav, halakha ki-divrei chakhamim* — Rav holds like the *chakhamim*, the majority, who say that the implicit welcome suffices to impose liability. *u-Shmuel amar halakha ke-Rebbi* — Shmuel holds like Rebbi, requiring an explicit acceptance of responsibility. The *gemara* proposes that these rulings map precisely onto the depositum dispute: Rav holds that implicit circumstances create legal and relational consequences, while Shmuel insists on explicitness.

### Rav's Logic

But Rav immediately deflects: *ana de-amri afilu le-Rabbi* — I could say my ruling even according to Rebbi. Rebbi required an explicit assumption of *shemira* only in the case of welcoming someone into one's yard, because the act of invitation carries no inherent implication of assuming guardianship. Someone saying "come visit me" is not saying "I will take responsibility for your animals." The contexts are entirely different, and without more, liability does not follow. *Aval hacha, ha kibel alei netiruta* — but in the depositum case, the context *is* one of safeguarding. When someone says "here, watch my fruit," the very act of handing over the object in that context is itself an implicit assumption of *shemira*. Rav therefore argues that there is no need to say anything explicit: the nature of the interaction is self-evidently one of entrusting.

### Shmuel's Logic

Shmuel responds in kind: *ana de-amri afilu le-Rabbanan* — I could say my ruling even according to the *chakhamim* who hold that an invitation implicitly creates liability in the yard case. Why do the *chakhamim* rule that way? Because, says Shmuel, *nicha lei le-inish de-ne-kamte netirei bi-reshutei de-ba'al ha-chatzer* — it is to the *benefit* of the animal owner that the yard owner should assume responsibility. When I bring my cow into your yard and you welcome me in, I want you to be responsible for my cow. I want to be free of worry; I want the liability to shift. That desire, even when unexpressed, is obvious and reasonable, and that is why the *chakhamim* read the implicit welcome as creating liability. *Aval hacha* — but in the depositum case, says Shmuel, *mi nicha lei le-inish de-leikei peirei bi-reshutei de-chavreih?* Why should we assume the owner wants his fruit to become associated with, to fall under the domain of, his friend? That seems counterintuitive. He wants them stored, not taken over.

This is a genuinely striking argument, because superficially the *mafkid* is asking his friend to watch his fruit — yet Shmuel is saying the owner does not want those fruit to be considered under the friend's domain, even though he has literally placed them in the friend's house. What is happening here is not a dispute about technical *halakhot* of *shomrim* — about at what legal moment the duty of *shemira* attaches — but about a more conceptual question: to what degree does the *shomer*'s relationship to the object constitute a meaningful form of control, a quasi-ownership, of the kind that governs *techumin*? A *shomer* in the ordinary sense is merely an extension of the *ba'al ha-bayit*. For the object to follow the *shomer*'s *techum*, there must be something more — a degree of practical dominance over the object that rises above mere custodianship. Rav maintains this is present in any depositum; Shmuel maintains the owner retains that underlying control even while temporarily placing the object with another.

---

## Mishnah Proof

### Mishnah Evidence

The *gemara* attempts to bring a proof from our very *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states: *ve-im eirev hu, peirotav kamohu* — if the owner made an *eruv*, his fruit follow him. By implication, if he did not make an *eruv*, his fruit do not follow him — they are stranded. But those fruit are presumably being watched by someone in city B. If the object followed the watcher's *techum*, as Rav holds, then why does the owner's *eruv* make any difference? The fruit would go by the watcher in city B regardless. The *mishnah* seems to indicate that the fruit follow the owner — apparently vindicating Shmuel.

### Keren Zavit

Rav Huna responds on Rav's behalf: *ke-gon she-yichad lo keren zavit* — the *mishnah* speaks of a case where the owner designated a specific space for the fruit, a locked corner or closet. In that case, everyone agrees the fruit follow the owner, because the person watching them has no real control: their entire role is to stand guard over something that has been sealed away, with explicit instructions not to touch it. The practical domain remains entirely the owner's. The dispute between Rav and Shmuel, therefore, concerns only cases where no specific space was designated — where the guardian has genuine discretion over the fruit's handling and placement.

### Control Degrees

This distinction illuminates the underlying principle. When the guardian has discretion — can move the fruit, decide where to keep them, respond to changing circumstances — he exercises a form of control that approaches quasi-ownership, and Rav holds that in such cases the fruit follow his *techum*. When the guardian is merely standing watch over a sealed space, he has no such control, and even Rav concedes the fruit follow the owner. The debate thus hinges on degrees of practical control.

---

## Guests & Zikuya

### Transfer Problem

Returning to the *mishnah*'s case of guests and the *zikuya* effected on *erev Yom Tov*: a question arises. The host transferred ownership of the food to his guests before *Yom Tov* — but between the moment of transfer and the arrival of the guests, who is watching the food? The host is. He is effectively the guardian of the guests' food when *Yom Tov* begins. According to Rav, who holds that deposited objects follow the guardian's *techum*, why should the *zikuya* accomplish anything? The food is under the host's control when *Yom Tov* commences, so it should still follow *his* *techum* — and the guests would still be unable to take it home.

### Keren Zavit Answer

The *gemara* offers one answer: *keivan she-zika lahem al yedei acher, ke-mi she-yichad lo keren zavit dami* — since the host transferred ownership formally through another party, it is as if he designated a specific corner for the food. He has, in effect, locked it away for the guests' use and relinquished any practical control over it. It therefore follows the guests' *techum* even according to Rav.

### Zikuya Special

The *gemara* then offers a second, more fundamental answer: *zika shani* — a *zikuya* is categorically different. Rashi explains that when the host performs a *zikuya*, his entire intent is to enable the guests to take the food home. That intent itself constitutes a relinquishment of control. He is not watching the food in any meaningful sense of "control" — he is holding it temporarily for someone else, with the express purpose of handing it over. In such a case, there is no ambiguity about whose domain the food belongs to: it is clearly the guests'. The second answer thus distinguishes *zikuya* not merely as analogous to *keren zavit* but as a categorically distinct act in which the transferor explicitly steps out of the picture.

---

## Meat Hanging Case

### Setup

The *gemara* now presents a vivid practical case involving Rav Chana bar Chanilai. Meat was suspended — hung out to dry — at *ivra de-dasha*, the other side of the door or door-bar, on *erev Yom Tov*. Rav Chana bar Chanilai had traveled from city B to city A; some people in city A hung out meat for him to dry, and now he wishes to take it back with him to city B on *Yom Tov*. Whose *techum* governs the meat?

### Rav Huna Rules

Rav Huna ruled: *ei at talit, tishkol* — if you were the one who hung the meat out to dry, then take it. *Ve-ei inhu talu lach, lo tishkol* — but if they were the ones who hung it and managed it, then do not take it. The ruling implies that whoever had practical control over the meat when *Yom Tov* began — whoever was the active party in handling it — determines whose *techum* governs it.

### Gemara Challenge

The *gemara* presses: even if Rav Chana bar Chanilai was the one who hung the meat, why should he be able to take it? He went back to city B before *Yom Tov* began, and the meat was left in city A, presumably under the watch of those in city A. Even granting Rav Huna's fidelity to Rav's position, the meat should follow the *techum* of those watching it in city A — not of Rav Chana bar Chanilai who is now in city B.

### Keren Zavit Applied

The *gemara* resolves this by invoking *keren zavit*: *shani ivra de-dasha de-kimei she-yikhdu keren zavit dami* — hanging meat out to dry is like designating a locked corner. The meat is suspended specifically to dry; it is not to be touched or moved. Whoever is present in city A has no control over it. Their role is entirely passive — do not disturb the drying meat. It is therefore like a sealed space, and everyone agrees the meat follows the owner, not the passive watchers.

### Ravina Challenges

Ravina then poses a three-part challenge to Rav Ashi: if the others were the ones who hung the meat and controlled it, how can you say Rav Chana bar Chanilai cannot take it?

### Fattened Ox

Ravina's first point invokes the *shor shel pitam* — the fattened ox. Shmuel ruled that an ox being fattened for sale follows *ke-raglei kol adam*, the *techum* of all people — because the entire point of fattening it is to give it to whoever comes to purchase it on *Yom Tov*. The object is not really "belonging" to the owner in the usual sense; its whole purpose is to be transferred to a buyer. Similarly here: those who hung the meat for Rav Chana bar Chanilai did so entirely for his benefit and with the expectation that he would come to collect it on *Yom Tov*. If the meat was prepared with the intent that he would pick it up, it should follow his *techum* regardless of who physically prepared it. Ravina's second point appeals to the *baraita* of Rabbi Dosa: Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the *halakha* follows Rabbi Dosa, who holds that even if one did not entrust his flock to the shepherd before *Yom Tov*, but the sheep normally go to a shepherd, the sheep follow the shepherd's *techum*. If the normal expectation is that Rav Chana bar Chanilai will come pick up the meat — just as sheep normally go to the shepherd — then the meat should follow him. Ravina's third point is a reading of our *mishnah*'s principle *ha-behemah ve-ha-kelim ke-raglei ha-be'alim* — that it goes by the owners — which he reads through the lens of his previous arguments to suggest that the effective owner, the one for whom the item is destined, determines the *techum*.

### Rav Ashi Response

Rav Ashi responds: *ela shani Rav Chanana bar Chanilai* — you have misread this case entirely. Rav Huna's ruling to Rav Chana bar Chanilai had nothing to do with *techumin* at all. *Gavra raba hu ve-tarid bi-shma'ateta* — he was a great Torah scholar, always absorbed in learning, and characteristically inattentive to practical matters.

### Kashrus Issue

What Rav Huna was actually addressing was a *kashrut* concern: *ei at talit, is lach simana be-gaveih* — if you were the one who hung the meat, you have a *siman*, a distinguishing mark or recognition, and you know it is the same meat you originally handled. You would not have taken your attention off it. But *ve-ei inhu talu lach, maschas da'atach mineih* — if others hung the meat for you and you were not present, your attention was diverted from it; it is a case of *basar she-nis'alem min ha-ayin*, meat that has been out of sight and unattended. In that case, *lo tishkol* — you may not take it, not because of *techumin*, but because of the *kashrut* concern about unattended meat. The entire exchange with Rav Chana bar Chanilai was about whether the meat could be identified as the same meat originally set out — a question of *kashrut*, not *techumin* at all.

---

## Control Theme

### Ownership to Control

The long discussion across this *daf* reflects a fundamental conceptual shift in how *techumin* operate: the governing criterion is not formal legal ownership but practical control.

### Examples

This emerges from multiple cases. When one promises to lend an object to another — even before physically handing it over — the object follows the borrower's *techum*, because the relationship of control and anticipated use has already taken effect. When one prepares a *shor shel pitam* to be given to a buyer on *Yom Tov*, it follows *ke-raglei kol adam*, not the owner's *techum*, because the owner has effectively relinquished meaningful control in anticipation of the transfer. When food is transferred to guests via *zikuya* on *erev Yom Tov*, it follows the guests' *techum* because the transferor has explicitly stepped aside.

### Core Principle

The core principle that emerges is: *techumin* go by who controls, not merely who owns. Formal ownership is relevant insofar as it tracks real-world control, but where ownership and control diverge — where someone else has meaningful practical dominion over an object — it is that dominion which determines the object's *techum*. The debate between Rav and Shmuel in the depositum case is therefore a debate about when guardianship rises to the level of meaningful control for the purposes of this principle.

---

## Domestic vs Wild

### Mishnah Rule

The final *mishnah* of *masechet* Beitzah returns us to *muktzah*, the theme that opened the entire tractate. *Ein mashkin ve-shochtin et ha-midbariyot* — one may not water or slaughter wilderness animals on *Yom Tov*. *Aval mashkin ve-shochtin et ha-bayashot* — but one may water and slaughter domestic animals.

### Watering Advice

One might ask what watering has to do with the prohibition: surely the primary question is *shechita*, not watering. The *gemara* explains that the *mishnah*'s mention of watering is incidental practical advice: *mishum sircha de-mishcha* — because of the adhesions of the hide. Giving an animal a great deal of water to drink immediately before *shechita* makes it significantly easier to flay the hide afterward. The *mishnah* is therefore not legislating about watering as a separate category but offering a *milta agav urchiah*, a practical recommendation embedded in the ruling: if you are going to slaughter a domestic animal on *Yom Tov*, water it well first.

### Domestic Def

What counts as a *beheimah bayit*, a domestic animal? The *baraita* defines it as *kol she-yotzot ve-ro'ot chutz la-techum u-va'ot ve-lanot be-tokh ha-techum* — animals that graze outside the city limits during the day but return every night to sleep within the *techum*, within the inhabited area of the town.

### Wilderness Def

*Behemot midbariyot* are defined as *kol she-yotzot be-Pesach ve-ro'ot ba-afar ve-nikhnasot bi-revi'ah rishonah* — animals that leave the home territory at *Pesach* time, graze out in the wilderness for the entire summer, and do not return until the first rains of *Marcheshvan*, the beginning of the winter rainy season. They spend approximately six months of the year entirely away from their owners. These animals, because they are so remote from their owner's domain when *Yom Tov* arrives, are considered *muktzah* and may not be slaughtered on *Yom Tov*.

---

## Muktzah Debate

### Rebbi & Muktzah

The *gemara* then raises a striking question: *u-mi it lei le-Rebbi muktzah?* — does Rebbi actually hold of the concept of *muktzah*? Rebbi is associated with the position that *muktzah* is an extremely narrow category. Why is he participating in a debate that seems to presuppose *muktzah* as a relevant concern?

### Unripe Dates

To understand Rebbi's position, the *gemara* cites a related exchange. Rabbi Shimon bar Rebbi — Rebbi's own son — once asked Rebbi about the case of *ptzilei tamrah*, unripe dates, as it pertained to the view of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: do the unripe dates constitute *muktzah* according to Rabbi Shimon?

### Rashi vs Tosafot

The precise nature of these *ptzilei tamrah* is itself a matter of dispute between Rashi and Tosafot. Rashi holds they are dates picked before ripening and placed in a wicker basket to ripen; the process requires waiting.
