Tosafot holds they are dates placed on a rooftop to dry out and become edible — a process of desiccation rather than ripening. Both agree, however, that the dates are not yet edible and are being processed toward edibility.

### R Shimon View

Rebbi's answer to his son was: *ein muktzah le-Rabbi Shimon ela grogrot ve-tzimukim bilvad* — Rabbi Shimon recognizes *muktzah* only in the single case of drying figs and raisins. In that case, one takes fruit that was edible — grapes, figs — and deliberately places it in a state of temporary inedibility in order to transform it into something else. One consciously *pushes the fruit away* from its current edible state. That is the paradigm of *muktzah* for Rabbi Shimon. But the *ptzilei tamrah* are different: they were never edible, and the entire process is oriented toward making them edible as soon as possible. There is no "pushing away" — quite the opposite. Therefore, Rabbi Shimon would not consider them *muktzah* at all. The distinction Tosafot draws is particularly elegant: in the *grogrot* case, one has actively chosen *not* to eat the fruit as fruit, converting it into something else; in the *ptzilei tamrah* case, one is actively working to bring the item into edibility.

### Rebbi Resolution

Given this framework, the *gemara* offers three possible resolutions of the question whether Rebbi holds *muktzah*. First: *hanei nami ki-grogrot u-tzimukin dami* — these wilderness animals are indeed analogous to drying figs and raisins. The owner sends them out at *Pesach* time and they do not return until the rainy season; they are completely removed from his practical domain for half the year. Until they are actually slaughtered and brought to market, they are in a state of being wholly "pushed away" — more so, one might argue, than figs being converted to raisins. In that case, even Rebbi, following Rabbi Shimon's own logic, would consider them *muktzah*. Second: *li-dvarav de-Rabbi Shimon ka-amar ve-lo sevira lei* — Rebbi was not stating his own position but answering the question as put to him: "according to Rabbi Shimon, would the dates be *muktzah*?" Rebbi answered, no, according to Rabbi Shimon they would not be. His own view may differ entirely. Third: *li-dvreihem de-Rabbanan ka-amar* — Rebbi was addressing the *rabbinic* position, not his own. His own view, *le-didi ein muktzah* — in the sense that he holds of an extremely minimal category of *muktzah* — remains fully intact. He was simply telling the *rabbanan*: even granted your broader approach to *muktzah*, you should at least concede that animals which return in the rainy season are domestic, not wilderness animals, and not *muktzah*. The *rabbanan* respond: *lo mi-havei havu* — no, we hold of *muktzah*, and we hold of a broad category, and those animals that spend six months away are wilderness animals, and they are *muktzah*.

### Masechet End

With this exchange — *Rabbanan* insisting on the broad scope of *muktzah*, Rebbi pressing for a more limited application — *masechet* Beitzah comes to its close. *Hadran alakh mashilin peirot u-selikah masekhta.*

---

---

# Ta'anit 2

## Intro: Taanit Theme

### Masechet Overview

With *Masechet Taanit* we begin a sequence of smaller tractates — *Taanit*, *Megillah*, *Moed Katan*, and *Chagigah* — bundled together in this single volume of *Seder Moed*. As its title indicates, the tractate focuses on fasting. When we first think of fasting, our minds go naturally to what might be called the historical fasts: the fixed days commemorating tragedies of the past, already reflected in the *nevi'im* when the returning exiles ask whether they should continue to observe *Tsom Ha-chamishi*, *Tsom Ha-shivi'i*, and *Tsom Ha-asiri*. The *navi* responds that with the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash*, those fast days will be transformed into days of rejoicing. We touched on some of this in *Masechet Rosh Hashanah* during the discussion of *Megillat Taanit*. But the historical fasts are very much a secondary concern in this tractate. The primary subject is fasting — and, more broadly, religious response — to tragedy or impending tragedy, specifically centered on the absence of rain.

### Rain & Tragedy

This focus becomes clearer when one recalls the *tefilla* of *Shlomo* at the dedication of the *Beit HaMikdash* (*Melachim Aleph*, Perek 8). There *Shlomo* describes the central reasons people will turn to God in prayer: *beheatzer hashamayim velo yihye matar* — when the heavens are shut and there is no rain; *raav ki yihye baaretz*, *dever*, *shidafon*, *yerakon*, *arbe*, *chasil* — famine, pestilence, blight, locust, infestation. The consistent refrain is *veata tishma hashamayim vsalachta*: You will hear from the heavens and forgive. In an agricultural society, the most recurring source of existential precariousness — the thing that makes your life feel uncertain and drives you toward God — is what is happening with the crops, and above all whether it will rain.

In this light, *Masechet Taanit* can be seen in some ways as a counterpart to *Masechet Berachot*. *Masechet Berachot* concerns fixed liturgy: the *Shema*, the *Shemoneh Esrei*, the regular rhythms of prayer that respond to the natural cadences of day and night. To the extent that *Berachot* addresses more immediate religious responses — to sudden events, to changes in circumstance — it does so at the very end, in the *birchot hashevach*: seeing lightning, seeing trees blossom, hearing good news and saying *she-he-che-yanu*, hearing bad news and saying *Baruch Dayan HaEmet*. *Masechet Taanit*, by contrast, is fundamentally about religious engagement with the world — seeing God's presence, or feeling God's absence, in the circumstances of one's life, and knowing how to respond.

### Religious Engagement

This tractate is therefore less about ritual structure and more about that thoroughgoing religious responsiveness: calling out to God when things go wrong, praying for greater divine presence in the world, seeking rain as a expression of one's entire relationship with the Creator. More than almost any other tractate, *Taanit* deals with what it means to inhabit a religious mindset attuned to circumstances — to see the world through the lens of God's involvement, whether manifest or withheld.

### Q: Why Fasting?

This raises a pointed question: if the tractate is ultimately about religious response to tragedy and the absence of rain, why is *taanit* — fasting — the dominant theme? After all, one might imagine several religious responses to calamity: prayer, *teshuva*, acts of charity. Yet the tractate is named for the fast. And that framing shapes our entire perception of what the religious response to difficulty looks like. This is a question worth carrying throughout the tractate rather than answering prematurely.

### Sin & Forgiveness

A crucial observation emerges from the refrain in *Shlomo*'s prayer: *vsalachta* — and You shall forgive. Tragedy, in the biblical framework, is conceptualized as punishment for human failing. The response to calamity therefore involves not merely petition but the acknowledgment of sin and the need for forgiveness. This connects the fast to *teshuva* and, by extension, to *Yom Kippur*: fasting as a form of self-affliction that signals repentance, perhaps even a kind of self-imposed suffering that stands in place of the punishment deserved. The connection between agricultural productivity and *mitzvot* observance — already anticipated by the *Shema* itself — undergirds this entire framework, as will become clear on the very first *daf*.

---

## Mishna: Gevurot Geshamim

### Meamatai Opening

The first *mishna* opens with *me'ematai mazkirim gevurot geshamim* — from when do we begin mentioning the *gevurot geshamim*, the power of the rain? The specific insertion in question is *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem*, the phrase we add to the second *bracha* of *Shemoneh Esrei*. Notably, no tragedy has yet entered the picture. This first *mishna* describes a normal year, a year where everything is expected to proceed in its proper course. No anxiety, no drought, no impending calamity — simply the question of when, in the course of the liturgical calendar, one begins acknowledging God as the one who brings rain.

### R. Eliezer v. R. Yehoshua

*Rabbi Eliezer* says one begins on *yom tov harishon shel chag* — the first day of the *chag*, meaning *Sukkot*, since *chag* without qualification refers to *Sukkot*. *Rabbi Yehoshua* says only from *yom tov ha'acharon shel chag* — the last day of the *chag*. This likely means after *Sukkot* has concluded, beginning on *Shemini Atzeret*, though the precise moment will be clarified later.

### Rain as Curse

*Rabbi Yehoshua* objects to *Rabbi Eliezer*'s position: *ho'il ve'ein hageshamim ela siman kelala bachag* — rain on *Sukkot* is nothing but a sign of curse. The source for this is the well-known *mishna* in *Sukkah* comparing rain on *Sukkot* to a master's servant who comes to pour water, only to have the master throw the jug back at him. We are trying to dwell in the *sukkah* and perform the *mitzvah*, and rain drives us out — it is therefore a sign of divine displeasure. Given this, why would one begin reciting *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* during *Sukkot*, when rain itself is unwanted?

### Hazkarah v. Sheolah

*Rabbi Eliezer* responds: *af ani lo amarti lish'ol ela lehazkir* — I never said to begin *asking* for rain; I said only to begin *mentioning* it. The distinction is between *hazkarah* — acknowledging God's power to bring rain — and *she'ela* — the actual petition that it rain now. *Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* is a form of praise, not a request. One is not petitioning God for rain during *Sukkot*; one is simply acknowledging, within the *bracha* of *gevurot*, that God is the master of wind and rain.

### Ein Shoalin

The *mishna* briefly introduces a further distinction: *ein sho'alin et hageshamim ela samuch lagashamim* — one does not actually request rain (*veten tal umatar*) until close to the time when rain is genuinely expected. This insertion appears somewhat out of place in the flow of the *mishna*, but its purpose is clarificatory: since the debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* turned on whether *hazkarah* implies *she'ela*, the *mishna* makes clear that the petition itself — *veten tal umatar* — is an entirely separate matter that occurs even later. The *mishna* will expand on this in a subsequent passage; it is mentioned here only to sharpen the terms of the current debate.

### R. Yehuda Ruling

*Rabbi Yehuda* then articulates a precise structural ruling: *ha'over lifnei hateiva beyom tov ha'acharon shel chag* — the *shliach tzibbur* on the last day of *chag* (i.e., *Shemini Atzeret*) — *ha'acharon mazkir, harishon eino mazkir*: the *ba'al musaf* recites *mashiv haruach*, while the *ba'al shacharit* does not. Conversely, on *yom tov harishon shel Pesach*, *harishon mazkir, ha'acharon eino mazkir*: the *ba'al shacharit* still recites it, but the *ba'al musaf* stops. This is precisely our practice today: *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* is said from *musaf* of *Shemini Atzeret* through *shacharit* of the first day of *Pesach*.

*Rabbi Yehuda*'s position is subtly different from *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s. *Rabbi Yehoshua* had said one begins after the last day of *Sukkot*, which might mean the night of *Shemini Atzeret* or *shacharit* of *Shemini Atzeret*. *Rabbi Yehuda* imposes a much cleaner symmetry: the period runs precisely from *musaf* of *Shemini Atzeret* to — but not including — *musaf* of *Pesach*. Why *musaf* specifically will be addressed in the *Gemara*.

---

## Gevurot Geshamim Sources

### Textual Grounding

The *Gemara* opens with a structural question mirroring the famous opening of *Masechet Berachot*: *Tanna heicha kai diktani me'eimatai?* — from what frame of reference is the *Tanna* asking *when* we begin the *hazkarah*? The question presupposes that we already know we are obligated to recite it in the first place. Where is that obligation established?

The *Gemara* answers that the *Tanna* is departing from the *mishna* in *Berachot* which lists various insertions made in *Shemoneh Esrei* — among them, *mazkirin gevurot geshamim bitchiyat hameitim* (the mention of rain is in the second *bracha*, that of *techiyat hameitim*) and *shoalin bevirkat hashanim* (the request for rain is in the ninth *bracha*, that of the years). But the *Gemara* immediately challenges this: if so, why not address the timing there, in *Berachot*, rather than waiting until now? The *Gemara* responds: *Tanna me'Rosh Hashanah salik* — the *Tanna* is departing from *Masechet Rosh Hashanah*, which immediately preceded this tractate. There we taught *uvechag nidonim al hamayim* — on *Sukkot* we are judged regarding water. Having just taught that *Sukkot* is the time of divine judgment over water, it is natural to proceed directly to: from when do we begin mentioning rain in prayer?

This leads to a further question: if the frame of reference is *Rosh Hashanah* and the *mishna* of *nidonim al hamayim*, why not simply say *me'ematai mazkirin al hageshamim* — from when do we mention the rain? What is the significance of the word *gevurot*? *Mai gevurot?* What do the "powers" of rain mean?

It is worth noting an interesting bibliographic aside here. *Rashi* and *Tosafot* explain the reference to *Rosh Hashanah* by saying it is in the same *seder* — *Seder Moed* — as opposed to *Berachot*, which is in *Seder Zeraim*. They do not emphasize the more obvious point, which is that *Rosh Hashanah* immediately preceded *Taanit* in the *Daf Yomi* cycle. This raises a genuine historical question about whether the ordering of *Rosh Hashanah, Yoma, Sukkah* — reorganized to follow the chronological sequence of the holidays — was already in place during the time of the *rishonim*, or whether the original order of the *mishna* was different. It is a bibliographic curiosity worth noting, though not one that can be resolved here.

### Pessukim Chain

*Rabbi Yochanan* answers: *mipnei she'yordin bigvurah* — rain descends through God's *gevurah*, God's might. He derives this through a chain of *pessukim*. The verse in *Iyov* describes God as *oseh gedolot ve'ein cheker* — doing great things beyond comprehension — and immediately follows with *hanoten matar al pnei aretz*, giving rain upon the face of the earth. The connection between rain and *ein cheker* (beyond comprehension) is thereby established. Then *Rabba bar Shila* links this via a *gezerah shavah* on the word *cheker* to *Yeshayahu*, which in the context of creation describes God as *lo yi'af velo yiga ein cheker litvunato* — unfathomable in wisdom. That same context then connects to a verse in *Tehillim* that, speaking of *briat ha'olam*, says *machin harim bekocho ne'ezar bigvura* — God establishes the mountains with His strength, girded in *gevurah*. The chain thus runs: rain is linked through *ein cheker* to creation, and creation is linked through its context to *gevurah*.

### Gevurot & Creation

It is admittedly a convoluted derivation. But the underlying point is theologically significant. By linking *geshamim* to *gevurah* through the context of *maaseh bereishit*, the *Gemara* frames the mention of rain not primarily as a prelude to petition but as an acknowledgment of God's creative power. When we say *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem*, we are not merely warming up to ask for rain — we are recognizing that the rain belongs to the same order as the creation of the world itself. Rain, like creation, is beyond human comprehension; it is an act of divine *gevurah* directly manifest in the world.

### Tosafot: Why Gevurot

*Tosafot* presses the point further: there are other terms in these very *pessukim* — *koach*, *ne'ezar* — so why specifically *gevurah*? Why is it called *gevurot geshamim* rather than, say, *koach geshamim*? *Tosafot* acknowledges the convoluted chain of derivations but then, in the final two lines of the *dibbur*, offers what is clearly the more compelling answer: *mishum dehabracha matchala bigvurah* — because the *bracha* itself begins with *atah gibor*. The phrase *gevurot geshamim* is appropriate because the mention of rain occurs within the *bracha* of *gevurot*, the second *bracha* of *Shemoneh Esrei*, which begins *Atah gibor le'olam Hashem*. While *Tosafot* introduces this as *ee nami* — an alternative — it is universally understood to be the more substantive explanation, and the *Gemara*'s elaborate *pessukim*-chain serves to demonstrate that applying the term *gevurah* to rain is conceptually apt, even if the proximate reason for the name is the placement within that *bracha*.

The debate over the *Gemara*'s frame of reference — is it responding to the *mishna* in *Berachot* or the *mishna* in *Rosh Hashanah*? — is itself connected to the underlying dispute between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua*. If *mashiv haruach* is anchored in *Berachot*, where *Havdala* in *chonen hadaat* is simply the appropriate insertion for the occasion, then the mention of rain is similarly a contextually appropriate insertion — a piece of *shevach* suited to the season — with no inherent connection to petitioning for rain. This is *Rabbi Eliezer*'s orientation. If, however, the frame of reference is *Rosh Hashanah* and *nidonim al hamayim*, then the mention of *mashiv haruach* is the beginning of a movement toward *ten tal umatar*, a lead-in to the petition — which is *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s orientation.

### Avodah Shebalev

A *beraita* is now cited to establish why rain belongs in prayer at all. The verse in *Devarim* reads: *le'ahava et Hashem Elokeichem ule'avdo bechol levavchem* — to love God and to serve Him with all your heart. The *beraita* asks: *eizehu avodah shebalev?* — what is the service of the heart? *Hevei omer zo tefilla* — it is prayer. This is a foundational statement: prayer is defined as *avodah shebalev*, the service of the heart. Immediately following that verse, the Torah states: *venatati matar artzechem be'ito yoreh umalkosh* — I will give rain in its time, the early rain and the late rain. The juxtaposition establishes the connection: serving God with the heart through prayer is directly tied to God's granting of rain.

### Mitzvot & Agriculture

The significance of this connection runs deeper than a textual hint. Rain in *Eretz Yisrael* is explicitly conditioned on *mitzvot* observance throughout the *Torah*, and the *Shema* itself makes precisely this point. If you truly believe that the rain — and therefore your entire livelihood and sustenance — depends on your faithfulness to God's commandments, then prayer is not merely reciting words at appointed times. It is the ongoing expression of that consciousness of dependency, of the recognition that God is directly involved in the provision of life's most basic necessities.

The contrast with *Mitzrayim* is illuminating. Egypt is watered by the Nile, a predictable, naturalistic process. *Eretz Yisrael* depends on rain from the sky — rain that comes from above, that is unpredictable, that is explicitly described in the *Torah* as *einei Hashem Elokecha bah mereshit hashanah v'ad acharit shanah* — God's eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year to the end. This creates a fundamentally different religious consciousness. When your sustenance literally descends from the heavens and depends on your relationship with God, the acknowledgment of that dependency becomes woven into the very texture of daily life. The mention of rain in prayer is therefore not a minor liturgical detail but the expression of a pervasive and thoroughgoing religious mindset.

---

## Maftechot: Divine Keys

### R. Yochanan: 3 Keys

*Rabbi Yochanan* states: *gimmel maftechot beyado shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu shelo nimsru beyad shaliach* — there are three keys held directly in God's hands that were not entrusted to any intermediary. These are: *mafteach shel geshamim* (the key of rain), *mafteach shel chaya* (the key of childbirth), and *mafteach shel techiyat hameitim* (the key of resurrection). It is worth noting, as a general observation, that the first *perek* of *Taanit* features a disproportionate number of *Amora'im* from *Eretz Yisrael*, *Rabbi Yochanan* prominent among them — a reflection, perhaps, of the acuteness with which the reality of rain dependence was felt there.

### Key of Rain

For the key of rain: *yiftach Hashem lecha et otzaro hatov et hashamayim latet matar artzecha be'ito* — God will open for you His good storehouse, the heavens, to give rain to your land in its time.

### Key of Childbirth

For the key of childbirth: *vayizkor Elokim et Rachel vayishma eleiha Elokim vayiftach et rachmah* — God remembered Rachel, God heard her, and opened her womb.

### Key of Resurrection

For the key of resurrection: *viyadatem ki ani Hashem b'fitchi et kivroteichem* — you shall know that I am God when I open your graves.

### Direct Control

Two features of these prooftexts are worth highlighting. First, in all three cases the operative verb is a form of *pticha* — opening — which is precisely the root of *mafteach*, key. Second, and more significantly, in each verse God's name is immediately juxtaposed with the act of opening, with no intermediary. This is why, for example, the verse about *Leah* whose womb was opened is not used despite occurring earlier in the narrative: in that verse, God's name and the act of opening are not immediately adjacent. The insistence on direct juxtaposition makes the theological point emphatically: these three things are under God's exclusive, unmediated control. There is no *shaliach*, no natural mechanism standing between God and the act. God holds the key directly.

The message for our religious life is profound. It would be easy — and is perhaps a common inclination today — to think of rain in meteorological terms, as the product of atmospheric conditions, with God perhaps involved at some remove. The *Gemara* resists this entirely. *Einei Hashem Elokecha bah* — God's eyes are directly upon it. When rain comes, it is God opening the heavens. When it does not, the absence is equally direct. Your prayer and your relationship with God have a direct and unmediated impact on this outcome. The key is in God's hands, but — as one reading puts it — the key to the key is in human hands: *Rachel* cries out and God opens; you observe the *mitzvot* and God brings rain. It is ultimately our direct relationship with God that determines the outcome.

### Parnassah & Geshamim

A tradition from *Maarava* (the *Amora'im* of *Eretz Yisrael*) adds a fourth key: *mafteach shel parnassah* — the key of livelihood more generally — citing the verse *pose'ach et yadecha umasbia l'chol chai ratzon*. The *Gemara* asks why *Rabbi Yochanan* did not include this. The answer: *geshamim hainu parnassah* — rain simply is *parnassah* in an agricultural society. For *Rabbi Yochanan*, the concrete image of rain is more powerful precisely because it is more specific. To abstract it to *parnassah* in general loses something. The verse about *parnassah* also does not have God's name immediately juxtaposed with the act of opening, which weakens the proof for direct, unmediated divine control.

### Life & Resurrection

The grouping of rain, childbirth, and resurrection carries its own theological weight. All three concern the giving and sustaining of life. Rain gives life to the crops; childbirth brings new life into the world; resurrection restores life to those who have died. By placing rain alongside these two other forms of direct divine life-giving, the *Gemara* frames *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* not merely as a weather petition but as a recognition of God's ongoing role as *mechayeh meitim* — the One who gives life in all its forms. The rain that falls from heaven, the womb that opens, and the grave that releases are all expressions of the same divine power.

### Kimelman: Rain Metaphor

This connection between rain and *techiyat hameitim* also appears in the *bracha* of *Atah gibor* itself, where *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* is embedded within the *bracha* most associated with resurrection: *mechayeh meitim Atah rav l'hoshia*, *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem*, *mechalkel chayyim bechesed mechayeh meitim berachamim rabbim*. Reuven Kimelman has suggested a striking interpretation of this juxtaposition. Rather than seeing rain as a secondary element appended to a *bracha* about resurrection, he argues that the insertion of *geshamim* functions to make *techiyat hameitim* itself more credible and more concrete. Consider: the world appears dead in drought. Seeds are buried in the ground, invisible and inert. Rain descends, and what was buried in the earth rises to life. In the observed, daily reality of agricultural existence, one witnesses something very much like resurrection. By anchoring *techiyat hameitim* to this experiential reality, the *bracha* renders the abstract doctrine tangible. Rain is not merely placed alongside resurrection; it is what makes resurrection believable.

---

## Timing of Hazkarah

### Source of Timing

Having established the textual and theological basis for *gevurot geshamim*, the *Gemara* now inquires into *Rabbi Eliezer*'s specific position regarding the timing of *hazkarah*. The question is: what is his source for beginning on the first day of *Sukkot*? The *Gemara* considers two possibilities: did he derive it from *lulav*, or from *nisuch hamayim* — the water libation performed on *Sukkot*? The practical difference matters, because if derived from *lulav*, *hazkarah* begins in the daytime on the first day of *Sukkot*; if derived from *nisuch hamayim*, it might begin the night before.

### Beraita Sources

The *Gemara* cites a *beraita* that resolves the question. *Rabbi Eliezer omer mishaat netilat lulav* — from the time one takes the *lulav*. *Rabbi Yehoshua omer mishaat hanachato* — from the time one puts it down, i.e., only after *Sukkot* concludes, beginning with *Shemini Atzeret*. The *beraita* thus confirms that *Rabbi Eliezer*'s source is indeed *lulav*, not *nisuch hamayim*.

### Lulav Symbolism

*Rabbi Eliezer* explains his reasoning: *hu ve'arba'ah minim hallalu einam ba'im ella lirtzot al hamayim* — the *lulav* and the four species come specifically as an act of supplication regarding water. The four species are plants that depend on water; by taking them, we are implicitly acknowledging the world's dependence on water and praying for God's provision of it. *Keshem she'arba'ah minim hallalu i efshar bahem belo mayim, kach i efshar la'olam belo mayim* — just as these species cannot exist without water, so the world cannot exist without water. If the very act of taking *lulav* is a prayer for rain, then one should begin saying *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* from that moment.

### Yehoshua Counter

*Rabbi Yehoshua* counters: *vehalo geshamim bachag einan ella siman klalah* — rain on *Sukkot* is nothing but a sign of curse. One cannot begin mentioning the coming of rain when rain at that moment would itself be a misfortune.

### Eliezer Response

*Rabbi Eliezer* responds, as in the *mishna*: *af ani lo amarti lish'ol ella lehazkir* — I am speaking of *hazkarah*, not *she'ela*. The analogy he invokes is striking: *ukeshem shetechiyat hameitim mazkir kol hashanah kullah ve'einah ella bizmanah, kach mazkir gevurot geshamim kol hashanah ve'einan ella bizmanan* — just as we mention *techiyat hameitim* throughout the entire year even though it will only occur at the appointed time, so too we may mention the *gevurot geshamim* throughout the year even though the rain itself comes only in its season. The mention of something is not the same as requesting it.

### Rainy Season Obligation

From this reasoning, *Rabbi Eliezer* draws a further consequence: if one wishes to recite *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* throughout the entire year, one may. The *hazkarah* is a form of *shevach* that is not inherently limited to any season. However, one is obligated to recite it once the rainy season begins — that is, from the first day of *Sukkot*. *Tosafot* makes this point explicit: *Rabbi Eliezer* distinguishes between the theoretical permissibility of year-round *hazkarah* and the seasonal obligation. The obligation arises when it is now the appropriate time for rain; the permission to mention it at other times demonstrates that *hazkarah* is of a fundamentally different character than *she'ela*.

### Rabbi Yehuda Link

*Rabbi* (i.e., *Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi*) then offers a position in implicit support of *Rabbi Yehoshua*: *mishat she-poskin she'ila, kach mafsik lehazkira* — at the moment one ceases asking for rain (after the first day of *Pesach*), one must also cease the *hazkarah*. This means that if you stop *mashiv haruach* when you stop *ten tal umatar*, then the two are inextricably linked — the *hazkarah* is not an independent *shevach* that can be recited at will, but is bound to the *she'ela*. Similarly, if the *hazkarah* can only continue as long as the *she'ela* is relevant, it also cannot begin before the *she'ela* is appropriate.

*Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira* offers a variation within *Rabbi Eliezer*'s general framework: he places the beginning of *hazkarah* on the second day of *Sukkot*, because he holds that *nisuch hamayim* — which he views as the source — began on the second day. *Rabbi Akiva* similarly ties *hazkarah* to *nisuch hamayim* but places its beginning on the sixth day of *Sukkot*.

### Shevach v. Bakasha

The debate between *Rabbi Eliezer* and *Rabbi Yehoshua* (as elaborated by *Rabbi*) thus resolves into a fundamental philosophical question about the nature of *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem*. Is it a general *shevach* — a praise of God's power that, like the mention of *techiyat hameitim*, is conceptually unconstrained by the calendar? Or is it a *bakasha* in liturgical form, inseparably tied to the request of *ten tal umatar* and therefore governed entirely by the same seasonal constraints? *Rabbi Eliezer* holds the former; *Rabbi Yehoshua* and *Rabbi* hold the latter.

---

## Validating Eliezer

### Techiyat Analogy

The *Gemara* pauses to assess *Rabbi Eliezer*'s analogy: *shafir ka'amar lei Rabbi Eliezer le-Rabbi Yehoshua* — *Rabbi Eliezer* made a good argument to *Rabbi Yehoshua*. If we mention *techiyat hameitim* the whole year even though it will only come in its proper time, why should *mashiv haruach* be different? The analogy appears sound.

### Rain Timing Problem

Nevertheless, the *Gemara* reconstructs *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s response: *bishlama techiyat hameitim mazkir de-chol yoma zmanei hu* — it is understandable that we mention *techiyat hameitim* every day, because every day would be an appropriate day for it to occur; we would welcome it at any time. Rain, however, is categorically different: *kol eimat de-ati zmanaihu?* — is there truly no bad time for rain to come? The premise of the analogy fails.

### Yatzah Nisan

The *Gemara* marshals a *mishna* from elsewhere in the tractate: *yatza Nisan ve-yardu geshamim siman klala hein* — if *Nisan* has passed and rain falls, it is a sign of curse. The supporting verse — *halo katzir chitim hayom* — underscores that rain at the time of wheat harvest is categorically inappropriate. Unlike *techiyat hameitim*, which would be welcome on any day, rain outside its season is not merely untimely but harmful. The analogy therefore cannot hold, and *Rabbi Yehoshua*'s position is vindicated: *hazkarah* of rain, unlike that of *techiyat hameitim*, is season-dependent, and one should not mention it during *Sukkot* if rain at that time would itself be a curse.

---

## Religious Rhythms

### Non-Holiday Period

A final observation bears directly on the meaning of *mashiv haruach* within the larger structure of the liturgical year. Rabbi Dov Berkowitz notes a striking pattern: *mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* is said only during what might be called the "dead time" of the year — the months when there are no *yomim tovim*. It appears at the very conclusion of *Shemini Atzeret* and runs through the beginning of *Pesach*, occupying precisely the stretch of the calendar with no major holidays.

### Human Activity Period

The period from *Nisan* through *Sukkot* is the period of active human endeavor in the agricultural cycle. You are out in the fields — plowing, planting, tending, harvesting. This is the time of human initiative and physical labor.

### Chagim Structure

The *chagim* of this period serve to take that human activity and direct it toward God. *Pesach* arrives at the time of the barley harvest; *Shavuot* at the wheat harvest, the time of *bikkurim*; *Sukkot* at the ingathering of all the harvest. The *mitzvot* of these holidays — *bikkurim*, *lulav*, *simcha lefanei Hashem Elokecha* — are structures for taking the products of human labor and acknowledging them as gifts of God. You share the harvest with the *ani*, the *ger*, and the *yatom*; you take the *lulav* and *etrog* and rejoice before God. Human endeavor is transposed into religious expression.

### Waiting & Dependency

From *Sukkot* through *Pesach*, the human role is fundamentally different. The planting has been done; now one waits. The outcome is entirely beyond human control. Whether the crops will grow depends on whether it rains, and rain is, as the *Gemara* has established, held directly in God's hands.

### Passive Reliance

*Mashiv haruach umorid hageshem* is the liturgical expression of this waiting, this passive reliance. It is recited precisely during the months when there is nothing the farmer can do but pray. The religious posture of this period is one of dependency, of acknowledging that the result lies entirely with God. Prayer — *avodah shebalev* — is the appropriate act when human activity cannot determine the outcome.

### Seasonal Religiosity

What emerges is a picture of two distinct religious modes corresponding to two distinct phases of the agricultural year. During the *chagim*, the religious task is to take active human endeavor and consecrate it — to prevent the labors of the field from being understood as purely human achievements, and to channel them toward acknowledgment of and gratitude to God. During the months of *mashiv haruach*, the religious task is different: to inhabit a posture of conscious dependency, of waiting and prayer, of recognizing that the outcome of all that labor now rests with God alone. The *hazkarah* of *geshamim* is therefore not merely a seasonal liturgical insertion. It is the marker of an entire religious orientation — one that the structure of the year itself is designed to cultivate.

---

---

# Ta'anit 4

## Rava's Statements

### Tzurba Merabbanan

The daf opens with a continuation of Rava's meteorological statements from the previous day, now broadening into observations about the character of Torah scholars. Rava begins with an agricultural metaphor: *hai tzurba merabbanan dami le-partzida de-tusei kala, de-keivan de-navat navat* — a young rabbinic student is like a tiny seed or sprout buried beneath a clump of earth. Once it begins to shoot upward, it continues to grow. The image captures something essential about the early career of a *talmid chacham*: the beginnings may be hidden and halting, but once growth commences, the momentum sustains itself.

Rava then turns from the agricultural to the temperamental. If a young *talmid chacham* is *de-ratach* — that is, given to flashes of anger or passion — one should be understanding, because *oraita hu de-kamratach lei*: it is the Torah within him that burns and may cause him to overreact. The verse is adduced in support: *halo ko devarai ka-esh neum Hashem* — "Are not My words like fire, says God?" The passion of Torah learning, in other words, can produce a kind of holy fire that occasionally manifests as excessive zeal.

### Hard as Iron

Rav Ashi moves in a more demanding direction. Whereas Rava's statement could be read as contextualizing — even excusing — passionate behavior, Rav Ashi appears to actively endorse a certain hardness of character: *kol talmid chacham she-eino kasheh ke-varzel, eino talmid chacham* — any *talmid chacham* who is not as hard as iron is not truly a *talmid chacham*. The proof text is *u-kefatish yifotzetz sela* — "like a hammer that shatters rock." The implication is that the pursuit of Torah requires an iron-willed single-mindedness, a refusal to be a pushover in one's convictions and focus.

### Builders/Boneha

Rav Abba responds to Rav Ashi: *atun me-hatam matnitu lah, anan me-hacha matninan lah* — you derive it from that verse; we derive it from a different one. The verse is *eretz asher avaneha varzel* — "a land whose rocks are iron" — with the interpretive reading: *al tikrei avaneha ela boneha*, do not read "its rocks" but "its builders." This is the well-known *derashah* applied elsewhere as well: *rav shalom bonayikh al tikrei vanayikh ela vonayikh*. The *boneha* formulation shifts the emphasis subtly — these are not merely hard individuals but builders, those who construct the world. The iron, then, is not mere stubbornness but the structural integrity of one who bears the weight of *Torah* and *avodah*. It is worth noting that a student raised the additional layer present in this *derashah*, connecting *boneha* to the *shoresh* of *binah* and understanding — a point acknowledged as a meaningful additional dimension of the classical reading.

### Pleasant Interaction

Ravina supplies the necessary counterweight. *Afilu hakhi, miba'ei lei le-inish lemeilef nafshiah be-nichusa* — even granted all of the above, a person must train himself to conduct his interpersonal affairs pleasantly. The verse cited is *ve-haser ka'as mi-libecha* — "remove anger from your heart." This juxtaposition with Rav Ashi's statement is deliberate. It is well and good to have passion and conviction and a strength of character that does not bend; but there is simultaneously a *derekh eretz* that must govern one's dealings with other people. The *talmid chacham* who is as hard as iron in his learning and convictions must also know how to *meilef nafshiah be-nichusa* — to school himself in pleasant interaction. The two qualities are not in tension but in balance, and the *sugya* here presents them as a unified portrait of the ideal scholar.

---

## Three Petitioners

### Eliezer & Rivka

The *Gemara* now shifts into an extended *aggadic* mode, introduced by Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *shlosha sha'alu shelo ke-hogen* — three people made requests inappropriately. Of these three, *u-lishnayim heshivuhu ke-hogen* — two received fitting responses despite the problematic framing of their requests, while *u-le-echad heshivuhu shelo ke-hogen* — one received a response that matched the carelessness of his petition.

The three are: Eliezer the servant of Avraham, Shaul ben Kish, and Yiftach the Gileadite.

Eliezer — called here *eved Avraham* because the Torah never names him in the episode with Rivka, though *Chazal* identify him as Eliezer — set up the following test: the young woman who responds to his request for water by also offering to water his camels will be the chosen bride for Yitzchak. The problem: *yakhol afilu chigeret afilu suma* — what if the woman who passes the test happens to be lame or blind, someone who would be entirely unsuitable for Yitzchak for other reasons? His criterion was too narrowly drawn, and a different woman might theoretically have fit it. Rashi and Tosafot grapple with why he could not have checked other matters first, with the suggestion that not every disability is immediately apparent. In any event, *heshivuhu ke-hogen* — he received the right result. *Ve-nizdamna lo Rivka* — Rivka herself appeared, the perfectly appropriate match.

### Saul & David

Shaul ben Kish made the proclamation that whoever slays Goliath will receive great wealth from the king and the hand of his daughter in marriage: *ha-ish asher yakenu ya'asrenu ha-melech osher gadol ve-et bito yiten lo*. The flaw in his framing: *yakhol afilu eved afilu mamzer* — what if the victor were a slave or a *mamzer*? The offer as stated makes no exception, and marrying one's daughter to such a person would be deeply problematic. Yet *heshivuhu ke-hogen* — the outcome was fitting. *Ve-nizdamen lo David* — it was David who stepped forward. Whatever the later complications in the relationship between Shaul and David, at the moment of the challenge, David was plainly the right answer.

### Yiftach's Daughter

Yiftach's case is the most striking. He vowed: *ve-haya ha-yotze asher yetzei mi-daltei beiti* — whatever emerges first from the doors of my house when I return from battle, I will offer as a sacrifice to God. The *Gemara* points out that he was insufficiently careful — *yakhol afilu davar tamei* — what if something non-kosher had emerged first? He had not thought through even that basic scenario. Of course, the graver problem — which the *Gemara* pointedly does not spell out at this stage — is that it could be, and was, a person. *Heshivuhu shelo ke-hogen* — he received an inappropriate response corresponding to his careless request. *Ve-nizdamna lo bito* — his own daughter was the first to come out.

The *Gemara* then connects this to the prophet's lament in Yirmeyahu: *hatzori ein b'Gil'ad im rofeh ein sham* — is there no balm in Gilead, is there no healer there? *Gil'ad* is Yiftach the Gileadite, and the *navi* is expressing distress that the situation was not remedied. This connects to the tradition cited by Rav Yosef that Pinchas was alive at the time and could have served as the authority to annul the vow — *matir ha-neder* — but both parties stood on their dignity: Yiftach said let Pinchas come to me, Pinchas said let Yiftach come to me. Neither moved, and the tragedy unfolded.

This raises a genuinely uncomfortable question about the narrative in *Sefer Shoftim*. If one reads the story of Yiftach without external commentary, there is nothing in the text that condemns what he did as religiously abhorrent. The daughter mourns that she will die a virgin; the tone is that of tragedy, not denunciation. And yet the *Gemara* here is working to establish that God did not want this and never sanctioned it — even while the narrative structure of the *Gemara* itself emphasizes that God could have arranged for something other than his daughter to emerge and chose not to. The tension is present and deliberate.

### Child Sacrifice

The *Gemara* now introduces a verse from Yirmeyahu bearing on the practice of child sacrifice more broadly: *asher lo tziviti ve-lo dibarti ve-lo altah al libi* — I did not command it, I did not speak of it, and it never even entered My mind. This verse is applied with striking precision to three cases.

*Asher lo tziviti* — that which I never commanded: this refers to the son of Mesha, king of Moav, who, with defeat imminent in battle against Israel, took his firstborn son and offered him as a sacrifice upon the wall. The disquieting detail in the biblical account is that after this sacrifice the Israelite siege broke off and Moav was not vanquished. The *Gemara* here does not ignore the implication. It does not claim the narrative is entirely comfortable. It simply asserts: God never wanted that. *Ve-lo dibarti* — that which I never spoke: this is Yiftach. God never instructed Yiftach to do what he did; it was Yiftach's own reckless vow. *Ve-lo altah al libi* — that which never entered My mind: this is Yitzchak son of Avraham. God said *ha'alehu l'olah*, bring him up as a sacrifice, but it never truly entered the divine mind that it would be carried out in that manner. Rashi, quoting the *Midrash*, notes that God's intention was not literal.

This is a remarkable passage. The *Gemara* is working through cases in *Tanakh* where child sacrifice — or something perilously close to it — appears without explicit divine condemnation in the immediate narrative. The verse in Yirmeyahu is deployed as a sweeping theological rejection: none of these episodes should be read as divine endorsement of child sacrifice in any form.

The *Midrash Bereishit Rabbah*'s account of the *Akeidah* is relevant here. When Avraham brought the ram as a substitute for Yitzchak, the *Midrash* has him say: let this be as though I am slaughtering Yitzchak; as he sprinkles the blood, let this be as Yitzchak's blood. The imagery is graphic, but the point is that the impulse does not simply disappear upon being redirected. The *Gemara* here, drawing on Yirmeyahu's categorical statement, insists that however these stories have been read, the divine word is unambiguous: *lo tziviti, ve-lo dibarti, ve-lo altah al libi*.

The section of the three petitioners, then, performs double work. It makes a point about the dangers of careless *she'eilah* — imprecise or poorly considered requests that leave open disastrous possibilities — and simultaneously uses the case of Yiftach to confront, through the lens of Yirmeyahu, the question of how certain morally troubling episodes in *Tanakh* are to be understood theologically.

---

## Israel's Request

### Dew Response

The *Gemara* transitions to a final *aggadic* passage that ties back directly to the themes of the *masechet*. Rav Brachia introduces an additional instance of an inappropriate request: *af Knesset Yisrael sha'alah shelo ke-hogen, ve-ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu heshivah ke-hogen* — even the *Knesset Yisrael* asked inappropriately, yet God responded appropriately.

The request: *ve-nei'dah nird'fah lada'at et Hashem, k'shachar nakhon motzao, ve-yavo ke-gashem lanu* — let us know God, let us pursue knowing Him; His rising is as certain as the morning, and He shall come to us like rain. The people are expressing their longing for divine closeness with the image of rain: reliable, sustaining, life-giving. And yet God's response is gently corrective: *biti, at sho'elet davar she-pe'amim mitbakeit ve-pe'amim eino mitbakeit* — My daughter, you are asking for something that is sometimes desirable and sometimes is not. Rain in the wrong season is a *klalah*, a curse, as the *masechet* has already established. *Aval ani eheyeh lakh davar ha-mitbakeit le-olam* — I will be for you something that is always desirable. *Shene'emar: ehyeh ke-tal le-Yisrael* — I will be like the dew to Israel. The dew, as was learned on the previous daf, never ceases, is never untimely, is always a blessing.

This exchange carries the major thematic statement of the *masechet* in miniature. Rain is not merely an agricultural phenomenon; it is an expression of *yedidut*, of closeness and favor between God and *Bnei Yisrael*. The people's longing for divine presence is expressed in meteorological terms, and God responds in kind — but with the superior image of dew, which is unconditional and constant where rain is contingent and seasonal.

### Seal on Heart

The *Gemara* records one further exchange. *Knesset Yisrael* requests: *simeini kha-chotam al libecha kha-chotam al zero'echa* — place me like a seal upon Your heart, like a seal upon Your arm. Again God responds that this is *she-pe'amim nireh ve-pe'amim eino nireh* — sometimes visible, sometimes not visible. A seal on the arm can be covered by a sleeve; closeness that depends on visibility is closeness that can be obscured.

God's counter-offer: *hen al kapayim chakotikh* — behold, I have engraved you upon My very palms. The palms are never covered; what is written there is always seen. The promise is not merely closeness but perpetual, unconcealed visibility. God's relationship to Israel is carved into His hands, not sealed upon a covered arm.

The pairing of these two exchanges — rain replaced by dew, a seal on the heart replaced by an engraving on the palms — reinforces the same theological movement: Israel reaches toward something genuine and beautiful, but God redirects each request toward something more permanent and more unconditional. This is the larger frame in which the entire discussion of *geshem*, *tal*, and their proper seasons operates: behind the *halachic* discussion of when to mention rain and when to request it lies the understanding that rain itself is a modality of divine relationship, and the texture of that relationship — conditional or unconditional, seasonal or constant — matters profoundly.

It should be noted *le-halakhah* that *Tosafot* cites a *Yerushalmi* supporting the practice of saying *morid ha-tal* throughout the year, including the summer months. This is not the practice of the *Rema* and most *Ashkenazim*, but it is the practice of *Sefardim* and certain strands of *Ashkenazi nusach*. The practical benefit is significant: if one says *morid ha-tal* habitually throughout the year, then forgetting to say *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-geshem* in the autumn immediately after *Sukkot* does not require *chazarah*, since *morid ha-tal* serves as an acceptable substitute and one has not omitted a *shevach* of *HaKadosh Baruch Hu* entirely. The logic depends on whether *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-geshem* is understood as a precursor to *she'eilah* or as an independent *shevach* of divine power over rain and meteorological sustenance. If the latter, then *morid ha-tal* belongs to the same category — acknowledging God's mastery over the water cycle — and can function as a *be-di'eved* substitute. This question — whether *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-geshem* is primarily a *ritztui she'eilah*, a lead-in to request, or an independent *shevach* — is precisely the conceptual axis around which the *sugya* that follows will turn.

---

## Mention vs. Ask

### Same Act?

The *Gemara* now turns to the *Mishnah*'s statement *ein sho'alin et ha-geshamim ela samuch la-geshamim* — one does not request rain except close to the rainy season. The *Gemara* initially assumes — *savruha* — that *she'eilah* and *hazkarah* are the same act and occur simultaneously: *she'eilah ve-hazkarah chad milta hi*. This assumption is plausible at least in the view of Rabbi Yehoshua, who does not maintain any gap between mentioning and asking. Rabbi Yehoshua's entire position is that one does not say *mashiv ha-ruach* until rain is genuinely wanted and seasonally appropriate — so one might reasonably infer that for him, mentioning and asking begin and end together.

*Man tanna?* — whose *Tanna* is this? Rava answers: it is Rabbi Yehoshua, *de-amar mish'at hanachato* — who holds that one begins at the time of putting down the *lulav*, which corresponds to *Shemini Atzeret*, meaning one would presumably start saying *ve-ten tal u-matar* as well from that point.

The *Gemara* then reads the *Mishnah* differently: *afilu teima Rabbi Eliezer* — it could even be Rabbi Eliezer. Even Rabbi Eliezer, who does say *mashiv ha-ruach* earlier during *Sukkot*, would agree that one asks for rain later. The mentioning comes early; the asking comes when the season is right: *she'eilah le-chud ve-hazkarah le-chud*. This is in fact what Rabbi Eliezer says explicitly in the *Mishnah*, but the *Gemara* is asking whether the same gap could exist, in a different configuration, for Rabbi Yehoshua as well.

The *Gemara* proceeds to the opposite formulation: *leima Rabbi Yehoshua hi* — maybe the *Mishnah* about asking only near the rainy season represents only Rabbi Yehoshua? If so, asking later would imply mentioning later — which is Rabbi Yehoshua's position. Rava responds: *afilu teima Rabbi Eliezer — she'eilah le-chud ve-hazkarah le-chud*. Even Rabbi Eliezer can hold that the asking is delayed relative to the mentioning. This seems obvious from the *Mishnah* itself, yet the *Gemara* is pressing on whether Rabbi Yehoshua accepts any gap at all between the two.

### Abiyi's Objection

The *Gemara* next sets two *Mishnayot* against each other. The upcoming *Mishnah* on 10a — *ad mosai sho'alin et ha-geshamim* — asks until when rain is requested. Rabbi Yehuda answers: until *Pesach* has passed. But the current *Mishnah* governs the transition of the *sheliach tzibur* at *musaf* of the first day of *Pesach*, stopping *mashiv ha-ruach* there. Rav Chisda attempts to resolve this: *kan lish'ol kan le-hazkir* — one *Mishnah* speaks of the cessation of asking, the other of the cessation of mentioning. Thus one could continue to ask for rain throughout *Pesach* while having already stopped saying *mashiv ha-ruach* from the first day.

Ulla objects strenuously. The suggestion that one would continue asking for rain while no longer mentioning *mashiv ha-ruach* is *kashya khe-chometz la-shinayim ukhe-ashan la-einayim* — as vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, a citation from *Mishlei*. The objection is logical: *uma be-makom she-eino sho'el mazkir* — in the period before asking is appropriate, one mentions; certainly then, *be-makom she-sho'el*, in the period of active asking, one should also be mentioning. How could asking continue without mentioning?

### Ulla's Solution

Ulla resolves the tension differently: *trei tanna'ei aliba de-Rabbi Yehuda* — there are simply two *Tanna'im* reporting Rabbi Yehuda's position, each representing a different version. The *Mishnah* that has the transition at *musaf* of the first day of *Pesach* holds that both *she'eilah* and *hazkarah* end there simultaneously. The other *Mishnah* holds that both continue through all of *Pesach*. There is no need to posit a gap between the two; it is simply a dispute about what Rabbi Yehuda said.

Rav Yosef attempts a more creative resolution. *Mai ad she-ya'avor ha-Pesach?* — what does "until *Pesach* has passed" mean? He proposes: *ad she-ya'avor sheliach tzibur rishon ha-yored be-yom tov rishon shel Pesach* — until the first *sheliach tzibur* who descends before the congregation on the first day of *Pesach* has finished. The word *she-ya'avor* is read not as "until *Pesach* has passed over" but as "until the prayer leader passes." This would mean both *Mishnayot* speak of the same moment — the *musaf* transition on the first day — and there is no gap.

### Raba's Pesach

Rava offers yet another reconciliation. *Mai ad she-ya'avor ha-Pesach* — until the time of the *shechitat ha-Pesach* has passed: *Pesach* in its more biblical sense refers not to the holiday of *Chag HaMatzot* but to the *korban Pesach* itself, offered on the afternoon of the fourteenth of Nisan. The *shechita* occurs in the afternoon; by extension, the morning before is when asking ceases.

The logic Rava builds upon this: *ma techilato mazkir af al pi she-eino sho'el, af sofo* — just as at the beginning of the season one begins mentioning before one begins asking, so too at the end, one continues mentioning even after one has ceased asking. The parallel is structurally elegant: mentioning brackets the asking on both sides, preceding it and following it.

Abaye challenges this. *Bishlama techilato mazkir* — I understand why mentioning precedes asking at the outset. *Hazkara nami ritztui she'eilah hi* — the mention of *mashiv ha-ruach* is a *ritztui she'eilah*, a preparatory appeasement, laying the groundwork for the petition. First one praises God for this capacity, then one asks God to exercise it. But *sofo* — at the end — *mai ritztui she'eilah ika?* — once one is done asking, what function does the mention serve? If *mashiv ha-ruach* is conceived entirely as a lead-in to *she'eilah*, then once the asking ends, the mentioning has no further purpose.

The *Gemara* again concludes: *ela mivarta ke-de-Ulla* — the clearest resolution remains Ulla's, that it is a dispute about the position of Rabbi Yehuda. Nevertheless, this extended back-and-forth has sharpened the central conceptual question considerably: is *mashiv ha-ruach* an independent *shevach* with its own standing in *Shemoneh Esrei*, or is it a *ritztui she'eilah*, meaningful only as a prelude to asking? The answer has practical consequences in both directions — for when it can precede asking and whether it can follow asking — and the *Gemara* has not resolved this cleanly but has laid out the terms.

A parallel use of *ritztui* is worth noting here. The same term appears in Rabbi Eliezer's language in the *baraita* on 2b: *elu arba'ah minim hallalu einam ba'im ela le-ratzot al ha-mayim* — the four species come only to appease regarding the water. The *lulav* and its companions are understood as a *ritztui* for water, an act that makes God, as it were, favorably disposed toward granting rain — before the explicit asking has even begun. This is the liturgical and sacrificial logic that underlies the whole structure: *ritztui* can precede *bakasha*, and indeed should. What the *Gemara* here is asking is whether *ritztui* can also trail behind *bakasha* once the asking is done, and Abaye's answer is that it cannot — at least not if we understand *hazkarah* purely in this *ritztui* capacity.

---

## Halachic Timeline

### Yochanan's Position

The *Gemara* now moves to the *psak halakhah*. Rav Assi cites Rabbi Yochanan: *halakhah ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — we rule like Rabbi Yehuda. We are accustomed to this ruling: the transition to *mashiv ha-ruach u-morid ha-geshem* occurs at *musaf* of *Shemini Atzeret* and the cessation occurs at *musaf* of the first day of *Pesach*.

But what does Rabbi Yochanan actually hold about the relationship between *hazkarah* and *she'eilah*? Remarkably, the *Gemara* surfaces an explicit statement: *hitchil le-hazkir matchil lish'ol, posek milisho'el posek mile-hazkir* — as soon as one begins mentioning, one begins asking; when one stops asking, one stops mentioning. For Rabbi Yochanan, *mashiv ha-ruach* and *ve-ten tal u-matar* are completely co-extensive. They begin at exactly the same moment and end at exactly the same moment. This is the position that the *Gemara* had earlier been trying to avoid, the one that seemed too extreme — and it turns out to be Rabbi Yochanan's explicit view.

### Rav Assi Challenge

This generates an immediate problem. Rav Zeira raises it to Rav Assi: *u-mi amar Rabbi Yochanan hakhi?* — did Rabbi Yochanan really say that? *Ve-hatnan — be-shlosha be-Marcheshvan sho'alin et ha-geshamim* — the *Mishnah* (on 10a) states that one begins asking for rain on the third of *Marcheshvan*, with Rabban Gamliel saying the seventh, and *Rabbi Elazar* rules the *halakhah* follows Rabban Gamliel, meaning we start saying *ve-ten tal u-matar* on the seventh of *Marcheshvan* in *Eretz Yisrael*.

If Rabbi Yochanan holds that *mashiv ha-ruach* and *ve-ten tal u-matar* are perfectly co-extensive, how can he rule like Rabbi Yehuda — meaning the transition at *Shemini Atzeret* — and simultaneously be consistent with the ruling that *ve-ten tal u-matar* is delayed until the seventh of *Marcheshvan*? If they occur together, they should both transition at *Shemini Atzeret* or both begin at *Zayin Marcheshvan*. The apparent inconsistency is glaring.

Rav Assi's first deflection: *gabra a-gabra ka ramit* — you are citing one authority against another, Rabbi Yochanan against Rabbi Elazar; that is not an internal contradiction. But the *Gemara* presses further. *Ve-iba'it eima lo kashya — kan lish'ol kan le-hazkir* — perhaps even for Rabbi Yochanan one could distinguish: *she'eilah* begins at *Zayin Marcheshvan* and *hazkarah* begins at *Shemini Atzeret*. But the *Gemara* rejects this immediately by citing Rabbi Yochanan's own explicit statement — *hitchil le-hazkir matchil lish'ol* — which rules out any such gap. Rabbi Yochanan himself says they are simultaneous.

### Land Distinction

The resolution: *ela lo kashya — ha lan ve-ha lehu* — this is not difficult; one ruling is for us and one is for them. The *Mishnah* about *Zayin Marcheshvan* — which might seem to describe *Eretz Yisrael* practice — is actually describing *Bavel*. In Babylon the crops remain in the field and premature rain would damage them; hence one delays both *hazkarah* and *she'eilah* until *Zayin Marcheshvan*. Rabbi Yehuda's position, which is what Rabbi Yochanan rules as *halakhah*, applies to *Eretz Yisrael*, where rain is needed and wanted right after *Sukkot*.

The *Gemara* then refines further. *Mai shna le-didan? De-it lan pirei be-dabra* — what distinguishes us in Babylon? We have produce still in the fields. But then the obvious response: *le-didehu nami it lehu olei regalim* — in *Eretz Yisrael* they also had a reason to delay, namely the *olei regalim*, the pilgrims who came up for *Sukkot* and needed time to return home before rain would fall upon the roads. The *Mishnah* itself gives this as the reason for the delay.

The answer: *ki ka'amar Rabbi Yehuda bi-zman she-ein Beit HaMikdash kayam* — Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that we switch over immediately after *Sukkot* applies specifically to the time when there is no *Beit HaMikdash*, because without a *Beit HaMikdash* there are no *olei regalim* and no reason to delay in *Eretz Yisrael*. The *Mishnah* about *Zayin Marcheshvan*, on the other hand, reflects the period when the *Beit HaMikdash* stood and the pilgrim traffic made the delay necessary. *Ve-lo kashya — kan bi-zman she-Beit HaMikdash kayam, kan bi-zman she-ein Beit HaMikdash kayam.* With this distinction, the two *Mishnayot* are reconciled within *Eretz Yisrael* itself across two historical periods, without needing to invoke *Bavel* at all.

### Two Days Practice

Finally, the *Gemara* addresses a practical question for diaspora communities that observe two days of *Shemini Atzeret* — the first day (*Shemini Atzeret*) and the second day (*Simchat Torah*). *Heichi avdinan?* — how do we handle the transition? Since the identity of the "true" *Shemini Atzeret* is uncertain across the two days, the question is which *musaf* triggers the permanent switch to *mashiv ha-ruach*.

Rav's position: one begins saying *mashiv ha-ruach* at *musaf* of the first day, then stops at *mincha*, then stops again through *maariv* and *shacharit* of the second day, and resumes again only at *musaf* of the second day — essentially replaying the transition on both days. Shmuel objects: *achar she-asito kodesh* — once you have said *mashiv ha-ruach* at *musaf* of *Shemini Atzeret*, you have declared the day to be *Shemini Atzeret*; going back and not saying it would be to implicitly declare it still *Sukkot*, which is internally inconsistent. Therefore Shmuel rules: one begins at *musaf* and continues through *mincha* to close out the day fully as *Shemini Atzeret*, then stops through *maariv* and *shacharit* of the second day — effectively treating *Simchat Torah* as if it might be *Shemini Atzeret* — and resumes at *musaf* of the second day.

Rava's ruling is the one we follow: *keivan she-hitchil shuv ein posek* — once one has begun, one does not stop. From *musaf* of *Shemini Atzeret* onward, one says *mashiv ha-ruach* continuously without interruption. This is the accepted *psak*.

What the *Gemara* has accomplished in this final stretch is to surface and then resolve the apparent paradox embedded in Rabbi Yochanan's position. He rules that *hazkarah* and *she'eilah* are perfectly co-extensive — and simultaneously rules like Rabbi Yehuda, which in context means the immediate post-*Sukkot* transition. The resolution through *Bavel* versus *Eretz Yisrael*, and then further through the *Beit HaMikdash* versus post-*Beit HaMikdash* distinction, elegantly untangles what appeared to be an internal contradiction. And throughout, the *Gemara* has been probing a question it has not fully resolved: whether *mashiv ha-ruach* is best understood as a *ritztui she'eilah* — a preparatory praise that exists in service of the petition — or as an independent *shevach* with its own standing. Rabbi Yochanan's position, requiring perfect co-extensiveness in both directions, implicitly favors the former reading, while the practice of saying *mashiv ha-ruach* from *Shemini Atzeret* without yet saying *ve-ten tal u-matar* — which is in fact how we rule — points in a more complex direction.

---

---

# Ta'anit 5

## Mashiv HaRuach & Shmini…

### Three Solutions Debate

The daf opens at the very top of 5a, picking up directly where the previous session left off. The debate concerned the recitation of *mashiv ha'ruach u'morid ha'gashem* on *Shmini Atzeret* for those living in *chutz la'aretz*, where *Simchat Torah* carries the status of *safek Shmini Atzeret*. The Gemara had entertained several proposed solutions. The first was to recite *mashiv ha'ruach* at *Musaf* of *Shmini Atzeret*, then stop, and resume at *Musaf* of *Simchat Torah*. The Gemara rejected this on the grounds that once one begins reciting *mashiv ha'ruach* at *Musaf* of *Shmini Atzeret*, one has signaled the day's sanctity as *Shmini Atzeret*, and one cannot then reverse that signal for the remainder of the day by ceasing. A second proposal was therefore advanced: recite it at *Musaf* and *Mincha*, then cease at *Ma'ariv* of *Simchat Torah*, so that the entire day of *Shmini Atzeret* is treated consistently, after which one performs a kind of reset and begins *Simchat Torah* as if the recitation had not yet commenced.

### Rava's Position

Rava rejects all of these proposals. The ruling at the top of 5a reads: *Rava amar, kivan she'hitchil shuv ein posek* — once one has begun reciting *mashiv ha'ruach* on *Shmini Atzeret*, there is no basis for stopping and restarting on *Simchat Torah*. It is not merely impractical — it is self-contradictory. Having already signaled that the season of rain has commenced, one continues without interruption.

### Rav & Rav Sheshet Agree

The Gemara records that Rav Sheshet concurred: *ve'chein amar Rav Sheshet, kivan she'hitchil shuv ein posek* — once begun, one does not stop. And even Rav, who had previously maintained the peculiar position that one recites *mashiv ha'ruach* at *Musaf* of *Shmini Atzeret* and then suspends it until *Musaf* of *Simchat Torah*, retracted that view.

### Twenty-One Days Count

The Gemara conveys this retraction in the name of Rav Chananel: *de'amar Rav Chananel amar Rav, moneh esrim ve'chad yom ke'derech she'moneh asarah yamim me'Rosh Hashanah ve'ad Yom Kippurim* — one counts twenty-one days, analogously to the way one counts the ten days from *Rosh Hashanah* to *Yom Kippur*. Counting twenty-one days from *Rosh Hashanah* brings one to *Shevi'i shel Sukkot*, *Hoshana Rabbah*, and on day twenty-two — *Shmini Atzeret* — one begins reciting *mashiv ha'ruach*. And once begun, *kivan she'hitchil shuv ein posek*, the *halacha* follows: one does not stop. This is stated as the operative ruling.

### Rashi's Explanation

The comparison to the ten days from *Rosh Hashanah* to *Yom Kippur* invites scrutiny. On the surface it seems inapt, because the ten days of *teshuvah* are counted inclusively of both endpoints, whereas here one counts twenty-one days and only begins on day twenty-two — the endpoints are not included in the same way. Rashi resolves this by situating the discussion in the era of *kiddush ha'chodesh*, when the precise date of *Rosh Hashanah* might have been uncertain — since *Rosh Hashanah* itself is a two-day holiday, it was possible not to know with certainty which of the two days was the true first day. What Rav is therefore saying, according to Rashi, is: use the same starting point you would use to count ten days to *Yom Kippur* — because by *Yom Kippur* the true date of *Rosh Hashanah* was presumably known — and from that same starting point count twenty-one days forward to arrive at *Shmini Atzeret*. The counting back from *Yom Kippur* to establish *Rosh Hashanah* provides the anchor from which to count forward.

### Yom Tov vs. Season

There is something conceptually striking about the entire thrust of this discussion, and it is worth pausing on it. The reason one recites *mashiv ha'ruach* is, presumably, because the rainy season has arrived and there is no longer any concern of rain interrupting one's dwelling in the *sukkah* — the concern of *siman klalah*. Once *Sukkot* has passed, the rainy season is unproblematic, and one begins invoking it in prayer. If that is the rationale, then the question of whether *Simchat Torah* is a *safek Shmini Atzeret* becomes essentially irrelevant: the rainy season has arrived regardless, and once one is no longer sitting in the *sukkah*, one should simply begin reciting *mashiv ha'ruach* and continue. Why would anyone think to restart the formula on *Simchat Torah*?

The very fact that the Gemara seriously entertained the possibility of stopping and restarting on *Simchat Torah* reflects a different conceptual framework — one in which the recitation of *mashiv ha'ruach* is linked not merely to the season but to the identity of the *yom tov* itself. This connection is reminiscent of Rabbi Eliezer's argument about the *lulav* and the *aravah*, and of the Gemara in *Rosh Hashanah* that teaches *bechag nidonim al ha'mayim* — we are judged concerning water on *Sukkot* — just as *Pesach* is the season of judgment concerning grain. The liturgical shift appears to be tied directly to the identity of the *yom tov*, not merely to the calendar date of the season. Indeed, the Gemara elsewhere notes that *mashiv ha'ruach* is introduced specifically at *Musaf*, arguably because *Musaf* is the *tefillah* that most fully embodies the distinctive identity of the *yom tov*.

Against that backdrop, the concern that *Simchat Torah*, as a *safek Shmini Atzeret*, demands its own fresh commencement of *mashiv ha'ruach* becomes intelligible — one wanted to ensure that the recitation was properly anchored to the *yom tov* rather than carried forward by inertia. When Rav ultimately rules *kivan she'hitchil shuv ein posek*, he need not be entirely abandoning the *yom tov* framework. He may simply be saying: yes, there is an intrinsic link between the recitation and *yom tov* — but once one has begun, one cannot reverse course. The act of commencing has already established the connection.

Rav Chananel's formulation is illuminating in a different way. By framing the matter as a count of twenty-one days from *Rosh Hashanah*, he conspicuously avoids anchoring the recitation to *Shmini Atzeret* as a *yom tov*. He does not say "begin on *Yom Tov ha'acharon shel chag*"; he says count twenty-one days after *Rosh Hashanah*, and it happens to land on *Shmini Atzeret*. This reframes the entire question: the link is not to the *yom tov* per se, but perhaps to the *din* of *Rosh Hashanah* and the principle of *bechag nidonim al ha'mayim*. In this reading, it is the period of divine judgment regarding water, anchored in *Rosh Hashanah*, that determines when we begin invoking rain — and the *yom tov* of *Shmini Atzeret* is incidental to that count. This is a meaningfully different way of understanding when and why we begin saying *mashiv ha'ruach*, and the contrast between the two framings runs quietly through the entire sugyah.

---

## When to Stop Rain Prayers

### Until When Ask Rain

The Mishnah now asks: *ad matay sho'alin et ha'geshamim* — until when does one recite *veten tal u'matar*? One might expect the Mishnah to have addressed when one *begins* asking for rain before addressing when one stops. The reversal of order is deliberate: the following Mishnah takes up the question of when one begins asking for rain in *Marcheshvan*, and that discussion opens naturally into the arc of what happens when rain does not come — the progression toward public fasting. In order to flow into that narrative of escalating response to drought, the tractate first dispatches the question of when the rain prayers cease, and only then returns to when they begin.

### Rabbi Yehuda: Until Pesa…

Rabbi Yehuda holds: *ad she'ya'avor ha'Pesach* — until *Pesach* has passed. This can be reconciled with another formulation attributed to Rabbi Yehuda specifying the first day of *Pesach*; the two may represent variant traditions of his view.

### Rabbi Meir: Until Nisan…

Rabbi Meir goes further: *ad she'yeitzei Nisan* — one continues reciting *veten tal u'matar* through the entire month of *Nisan*.

### Yoel's Verse Cited

Rabbi Meir derives this from the verse in *Yoel*: *ve'yored lachem geshem moreh u'malkosh ba'rishon* — God will bring down for you rain, *moreh* being the early rain and *malkosh* the late rain, *ba'rishon*, in the first month — that is, in *Nisan*. The verse describes an event during the days of *Yoel* in which both the early rain and the late rain fell during *Nisan*, demonstrating that rain remains appropriate, and therefore petitionable, through the end of *Nisan*.

---

## Yoreh in Nisan Probl (II)

### Early Rain in Nisan?

Rav Nachman challenges the verse cited by Rabbi Meir. He poses his difficulty to Rav Yitzchak: *yoreh b'Nisan* — fine, the *malkosh*, the late rain, falls in *Nisan*, that much is understandable. But *yoreh* is the *early* rain. Since when does the early rain fall in *Nisan*?

### Braita on Seasons

The challenge is grounded in a *Braita*: *yoreh b'Marcheshvan u'malkosh b'Nisan* — the *yoreh* comes in *Marcheshvan* and the *malkosh* in *Nisan*. This is indeed the normal annual pattern reflected in *Kri'at Shema* itself, *yoreh u'malkosh*. If that is the fixed seasonal reality, how can the verse in *Yoel* speak of *yoreh* occurring in *Nisan*?

### Rabbi Yochanan's Answer

Rav Yitzchak responds in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *b'imei Yoel ben Petu'el nitkayem mikra zeh* — this verse was fulfilled uniquely in the days of Yoel ben Petu'el. It describes not a normative seasonal pattern but an exceptional miracle.

---

## Yoel's Miracle Story

### Drought Context

The background to the miracle is established from the verse in *Yoel* itself: *yeter ha'gazam achal ha'arbeh* — what one plague of locusts left, the next consumed. It was a period of devastating destruction. The Gemara then reports: *oso shanah yatza Adar ve'lo yardu geshamim* — that year, *Adar* had already passed and no rain had fallen. The entire rainy season had come and gone without rain. Then: *yardah lahem revi'ah rishonah be'echad b'Nisan* — the first rainfall, the *revi'ah rishonah*, came down on the first of *Nisan*.

A word on terminology: the word *yoreh* connotes shooting, like *yoreh cheitz*, shooting an arrow. The word *revi'ah* carries connotations of *hav'a'ah*, a term used for sexual union, particularly in the context of animals — as does the word *yoreh* in a certain register. The imagery is deliberate: rain descends and penetrates the earth, from which grows forth life. These are the words the Gemara will use throughout.

### Eat or Plant Choice

When Yoel instructed the people to go out and plant, they confronted an agonizing dilemma. They said to him: *mi she'yesh lo kav chitin o kabayim se'orim, yochlenu ve'yichyeh o yizra'enu ve'yamut* — whoever has a measure of wheat or two measures of barley: should he eat it and live, or plant it and risk death from starvation while waiting for the harvest? The people were in the grip of famine; planting seemed to prioritize distant hope over immediate survival.

### Yoel's Command

Yoel's response was unequivocal: *amar lahem af al pi chen, tze'u ve'zar'u* — nevertheless, go out and plant. Plant in trust.

### Grain Discovery

A miracle then occurred: *ve'nitgaleh lahem mah she'biketalim u'mah she'be'chorim nemalim* — grain was discovered stored within the walls of houses and in the burrows of ants, in ant-hills. There is a dispute between Rabbeinu Chananel and Rashi regarding the sequence. Rashi holds that the people first planted what they had stored for their own sustenance — an act of extraordinary faith — and *then* the hidden grain was revealed to sustain them while they waited for the harvest. Rabbeinu Chananel reverses the order: the miracle of the discovered grain occurred first, and they used that surplus for planting while retaining their original stores for eating. Rashi's reading makes the act of planting the more dramatic gesture of *emunah*.

### Eleven-Day Growth

The sequence of events: they went out and planted on the second, third, and fourth of *Nisan*. On the fifth of *Nisan*, the second rainfall, the *revi'ah shniyah*, came down. The *Omer* was brought on the sixteenth of *Nisan*, meaning the grain had reached full maturity. *Nimtza tevuah gedolah be'shishah chodashim gedelah be'echad asar yom* — grain that normally takes six months to grow reached full maturity in eleven days. The *Omer* offering, ordinarily brought from grain that requires six months, was brought from grain that had grown in eleven days. An additional detail: *kaneh zeret, shibolet zartayim* — normally a stalk of grain is overwhelmingly straw with a small proportion of actual grain; in this miracle, one unit of stalk yielded two units of grain, reversing the ordinary proportions.

### Sowing in Tears

The Gemara links this to the verse: *ha'zor'im be'dimah be'rinah yiktzoru* — those who sow in tears will reap in joy. They sowed in tears, not only from the remembered anguish of the famine, but because they were surrendering the very grain they had stored to keep themselves alive. Yet they reaped in joy — within eleven days. The verse continues: *haloch yelech u'vacho nosei meshech ha'zara* — one goes forth and weeps, carrying the pouch of seed. Rav Yehuda interprets this as referring even to the ox: as it plows, it weeps from exertion and hunger, yet as it returns along the furrow it can already eat *chaziz min ha'telem* — the first shoots already sprouting from the ground so rapidly had growth commenced. Even the ox did not complete a single pass before the miracle of growth was visible.

---

## Aggadic Dialogue Ser (II)

### Famine Food Sources

Rav Nachman said to Rav Yitzchak: *mai de'chtiv, ki kara Hashem la'ra'av ve'gam ba el ha'aretz sheva shanim* — what is meant by the verse, "God has called forth the famine and it came upon the land for seven years"? *Be'hanei sheva shanim mai achlu* — what did people eat during those seven years when there was no rain and no harvest?

---

## Yoreh in Nisan Probl (II)

### Seven-Year Famine

This question concerns the miraculous seven-year famine — a period of total agricultural collapse, in which no rain fell and no natural food source was available.

---

## Aggadic Dialogue Ser (II)

### Consumption Progression

Rav Yitzchak replied in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, tracing a grim progression across the seven years. *Shanah rishonah achlu mah she'be'vatim* — in the first year they consumed what was stored in the house. *Sheniyah achlu mah she'be'sadot* — in the second year they ate whatever continued to grow on its own in the fields; trees and residual vegetation perhaps, whatever nature yielded without cultivation. *Shelishit besar behemah tehorah* — in the third year they slaughtered and ate *kosher* animals. *Revi'it besar behemah teme'ah* — in the fourth year, *non-kosher* animals. *Chamishit besar shekatzim u'remasim* — in the fifth year, rodents and creeping things. *Shishit besar beneihem u'venoseihem* — in the sixth year, evoking the terrible verses in *Yirmiyahu* and *Eichah* regarding the siege of *Yerushalayim*, the flesh of their own sons and daughters. *Sheviit besar zero'oseihem* — in the seventh year, even the flesh of their own arms. *Le'kayem mah she'ne'emar: ish besar zero'o yoChelu* — fulfilling the verse, "A man shall eat the flesh of his own arm."

### Jerusalem Above & Below

Rav Nachman then posed a second question to Rav Yitzchak: *mai de'chtiv, be'kirbecha kadosh ve'lo avo be'ir* — what is meant by the verse, "In your midst is the Holy One, and I will not enter the city"? The apparent difficulty is stark: *because* the Holy is in your midst, God will *not* enter the city?
