Rav Yitzchak replied in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu, lo avo bi'Yerushalayim shel ma'alah ad she'avo li'Yerushalayim shel matah* — God says: I will not enter the heavenly Jerusalem until I enter the Jerusalem below. The verse is to be read: because the Holy is in your midst — that is, because My presence must first dwell among you below — I will not yet enter the city above.

### Twin Jerusalems

The Gemara then asks: is there truly such a concept as a *Yerushalayim shel ma'alah*, a heavenly Jerusalem? The answer is yes, derived from the verse: *Yerushalayim ha'bnuyah ke'ir she'chubrah lah yachdav* — the built Jerusalem, like the city that is twinned with it in perfect correspondence. Rashi explains: the Jerusalem below shall be built as a city twinned with its counterpart, which is its heavenly reflection — *she'hu ke'yotzei bah chavertah*, one corresponds exactly to the other.

This is a powerful idea that resonates across Jewish thought, with roots reaching back to the *Sulam shel Ya'akov* and *Sha'ar ha'Shamayim* — the notion that the earthly *Har ha'Bayit* has a celestial counterpart, that what transpires below is bound to and reflects what exists above. It is a concept that was also developed extensively in early Christian theological literature, notably by Augustine in *City of God*, who built an elaborate theology around the image of an earthly city reflecting the divine city of God. Whether the Christian tradition drew from the same earlier sources or developed the concept independently, its centrality in that literature is striking.

### One Sin, Two Evils

Rav Nachman posed a third question to Rav Yitzchak: *mai de'chtiv, u've'achat yiva'aru ve'yichsalu musar havalim eitz hu* — what is meant by this verse? The JPS translation itself acknowledges the meaning of the Hebrew as uncertain; the verse is genuinely obscure. Rav Yitzchak answered in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *achat hi she'meva'eret resha'im ba'Gehinnom* — there is one sin that destroys the wicked in *Gehinnom*, one sin above all others. What is it? *Avodah zarah* — idolatry. The word *ba'achat yiva'aru* is linked to texts that speak of hewn images and worthless idols, and the term *musar havalim* — the chastisement of emptiness — clearly refers to the folly of idol worship.

### Shtayim Raot Asah Ami

Rav Nachman posed a fourth question: *mai de'chtiv, ki shtayim ra'ot asah ami* — what is meant by "My nation did two evils to Me"? The response Rav Yitzchak gives in the name of Rabbi Yochanan is at first glance more puzzling than clarifying. Is it only two evils? *Esrin ve'arba shviku lehu* — they abandoned twenty-four things. Some have the reading of twenty-two. In any case, Israel committed far more than two sins — whether one counts the twenty-four books of *Tanakh* against whose teachings they transgressed, or the twenty-four sins enumerated in *Yechezkel*. So what does the verse mean when it says "two evils"?

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *achat she'hi ke'shtayim* — there was one sin that counts as two. And that sin is, again, *avodah zarah*. The verse in *Yirmiyahu* continues: *oti azavu mekor mayim chayim, ve'lachtzov lahem borot borot nishbarim* — they abandoned Me, the source of living water, to dig for themselves broken cisterns that hold no water. The first evil is the abandonment of God; the second is that the replacement they chose was utterly worthless.

### Loyalty vs. Truth

To underscore the double offense, the Gemara cites the surrounding verses from *Yirmiyahu*: *ki avru Iyei Kittiyim u're'u, u'Kedar shalchu ve'hitbonenu me'od* — they looked across to the islands of *Kittiyim* and to *Kedar* and observed with astonishment: *ha'heimir goy elohim ve'hemah lo elohim* — has any nation ever exchanged its gods? And these nations have not done so — *even though their gods are not real gods*. Yet my nation exchanged My *kavod* for something worthless.

The Gemara adds a striking detail by way of *Baraita*: the *Kutim* worshiped fire, and the *Kadriyim* worshiped water. The fire-worshipers understood perfectly well that water extinguishes fire — meaning, they had rational grounds for concluding that the god of water was more powerful and should be adopted in place of their god. Yet they did not exchange their god. The double indictment against Israel thus comes into sharp focus. The first evil is relational: abandonment of the covenant. The second evil compounds it: if at least there had been some intelligible reason for the exchange — some superior competing attraction — the sin might have been comprehensible, however terrible. But there was no such reason. The gods they chose had no power, no reality, no advantage. The pagan nations who worshiped false gods of fire and water at least maintained *loyalty* to what they had. Israel abandoned the true God in exchange for nothing.

It is also notable that the questions in this dialogue seem to come in thematic pairs. The first two questions concerned famine — first the verse in *Yoel* about *yoreh u'malkosh ba'rishon*, which arises from the famine in *Yoel*'s time, and then the seven-year famine and its stages of consumption. The next two questions both concern *avodah zarah*: the verse *ba'achat yiva'aru* and the verse *shtayim ra'ot asah ami*.

---

## Conduct & Blessings

### No Talk at Meals

The Gemara now shifts from these extended textual dialogues to a scene: *Rav Nachman ve'Rav Yitzchak havu yasvei bi'sudasa* — Rav Nachman and Rav Yitzchak were sitting together at a meal. Rav Nachman invited Rav Yitzchak to share a *dvar Torah*. Rav Yitzchak's response was itself a ruling: *hachi amar Rabbi Yochanan, ein mesichin bi'sudah* — one does not converse during a meal, *shema yakdim kaneh le'veshet* — lest the trachea precede the esophagus, meaning lest food enter the windpipe rather than the food pipe, which could lead to danger.

Rashi's clarification here has practical relevance beyond the immediate context. In tractate *Pesachim*, the requirement of *haseivah* — reclining during the *Seder* — is explained in part by the concern that reclining on the wrong side will cause *yakdim kaneh le'veshet*. Many *Rishonim* interpret this as implying that the trachea and esophagus are positioned side by side, left and right, such that reclining on the right side literally causes food to enter the trachea first. If that anatomical picture is accurate, then even a left-handed person should recline on the left side just as a right-handed person does, since the geographical relationship between *kaneh* and *veshet* is fixed regardless of handedness. However, Rashi's formulation here suggests a different reading: *yakdim kaneh le'veshet* simply means food will go down the wrong pipe — it describes the general hazard of speaking while eating, not a left-right anatomical sequence. If one adopts this understanding, the logic of *haseivah* changes: the concern is that reclining on the side of one's dominant hand makes eating awkward, and awkward eating increases the risk of food going down the wrong way. Under this interpretation, a left-handed person reclines on the right. This is a consequential distinction for the *halacha* of a left-handed person at the *Seder*, and the operative *psak* in most authorities — that even a left-handed person reclines to the left — follows the anatomical reading rather than Rashi's functional one.

After they finished eating, Rav Yitzchak said: now we may speak Torah.

### Yaakov Never Died

Rabbi Yochanan's teaching, as conveyed by Rav Yitzchak, is this: *Yaakov Avinu lo meis* — Yaakov our father never died.

### Linked to Descendants

Rav Nachman's immediate objection is pointed: *ve'chi be'chidi safdu safdanaya ve'chantu chantanaya ve'kavru kavraya* — was it for nothing that the eulogizers eulogized him, the embalmers embalmed him, and the buriers buried him? Rav Yitzchak replies: *mikra ani doresh* — I derive this from a verse. The verse in *Yirmiyahu* reads: *ve'atah al tira avdi Yaakov ne'um Hashem ve'al tichat Yisrael, ki hineni moshi'acha me'rachok ve'et zar'acha me'eretz shivyam* — do not fear, My servant Yaakov, says God, and do not be dismayed, Yisrael, for I will save you from afar and your children from the land of their captivity. The Gemara reads this verse as drawing an analogy between Yaakov and his descendants: *makish hu le'zar'o — mah zar'o ba'chayim af hu ba'chayim* — just as his descendants are alive, so too he is alive.

Tosafot adds a textual observation: by every other *tzaddik* whose death the Torah records, the verses use both *vayigva* (he expired) and *vayamot* (he died). By Yaakov, the word *vayamot* is conspicuously absent. This anomaly points to what Rabbi Yochanan is drawing out.

Rashi seems to treat the statement quite literally — Yaakov was not truly dead even during the embalming and burial. The *Maharsha* interprets it as referring to the soul's continued life, but then asks: why is this unique to Yaakov? The Gemara in various places teaches that *tzaddikim afilu be'mitatam keruyim chayim* — the righteous are called alive even in death. The *Maharsha* suggests the concern may specifically relate to the fact that Yaakov was buried in *chutz la'aretz*, unlike Avraham and Yitzchak who were buried in *Eretz Yisrael*; the Gemara elsewhere implies a connection between burial in *Eretz Yisrael* and resurrection, and so the verse must underscore Yaakov's continuing vitality.

There is, however, a deeper dimension. Avraham had descendants outside the covenant — Yishmael; Yitzchak had Esav. But Yaakov's descendants are entirely identified with *Bnei Yisrael*; the nation itself carries his name, *Yisrael*. The equation *zaro ba'chayim af hu ba'chayim* — his descendants are alive, therefore he is alive — carries particular force by Yaakov because his identity is fully continuous with theirs. The people *are* Yaakov. *Mah zar'o ba'chayim af hu ba'chayim* is thus not merely a claim about personal immortality but about the way a person lives on through what they have created and transmitted. The teaching is well-suited for a *hesped* — a eulogy — precisely because it articulates how the living presence of one's children and descendants constitutes a form of the parent's own continued life.

### Rachav's Name Danger

Rav Yitzchak then offered an independent teaching: *kol ha'omer Rachav Rachav miyad nikri* — anyone who says the name "Rachav" — the woman from the story of *Yehoshua*, who was a prostitute — twice in succession immediately experiences a seminal emission. Rav Nachman responded: *ana amina ve'lo ichpat li* — I tried saying it, and nothing happened. Rav Yitzchak clarified: *beyoda u'makira* — this applies only to one who knew her and recognized her. Tosafot goes further, suggesting that *yoda* implies actual intimate knowledge. It is the evocation of a real memory that produces the effect, not the mere utterance of a name.

### Tree Parable

As they prepared to part, Rav Nachman asked Rav Yitzchak for a *berachah*. Rav Yitzchak responded with a *mashal*, a parable that has become among the most celebrated in the Gemara. *Le'adam she'hayah holech ba'midbar ve'hayah ra'ev ve'ayef ve'tzameh u'matza ilan she'perotav metukim ve'tzilo na'eh ve'amat ha'mayim overet tachtav* — a man was traveling through the wilderness, hungry, weary, and thirsty. He found a tree whose fruit was sweet, whose shade was pleasant, and beneath which ran a brook of water. He ate of the fruit, drank of the water, and rested in the shade. When the time came to leave, he addressed the tree: *ilan ilan, ba'meh avarechecha?* — Tree, tree, what blessing can I give you? If I bless you that your fruit should be sweet — your fruit is already sweet. That your shade should be pleasant — your shade is already pleasant. That a brook should pass beneath you — the brook already flows. So he said: *yehi ratzon she'kol neti'ot she'not'im mimcha yihyu kamotcha* — may it be God's will that all the saplings planted from you be just like you.

### Blessing Future Generati…

Rav Yitzchak then turned this *mashal* on Rav Nachman: *af atah* — so too you. How shall I bless you? *Im ba'Torah harei Torah, im be'osher harei osher, im be'vanim harei vanim* — in Torah, you already have Torah; in wealth, you already have wealth; in children, you already have children. Therefore: *yehi ratzon mi'pi ha'Gadol she'yihyu tze'etza'ei me'echa kamotcha* — may it be the will of the Great One that the descendants who emerge from you be just like you.

---

---

# Ta'anit 7

## Rain's Greatness

### Rain vs Resurrection

The *gemara* on daf 7 opens a broader discussion of rain's power and religious significance — if not the central theme of *Masechet Taanit*, then certainly one of its defining concerns. Rabbi Abahu declares: *gadol yom geshamim mi-techiyat ha-metim* — the day of rain is greater than the resurrection of the dead. The reasoning is that *techiyat ha-metim* will benefit only the righteous, whereas rain benefits both the righteous and the wicked alike. One might object that this universality is actually a weakness — why should the wicked benefit? But the *gemara* treats it as a strength: rain brings life to all. This stands in tension with Rav Yosef, who had said that rain was placed in the *beracha* of *techiyat ha-metim* because the two are of equivalent weight — *shkulah k'techiyat ha-metim*. Rabbi Abahu goes further still, asserting rain's superiority over resurrection.

Rav Yehuda then says that the day of rain is as great as the day the *Torah* was given, citing the verse *ya'arof kamatar likhi* — "let my giving flow like rain" — and identifying *lekach* with *Torah* via the verse *ki lekach tov natati lakhem, Torati al ta'azovu*. Rava pushes further: rain is even greater than the giving of the *Torah*. The proof text is the same — *ya'arof kamatar likhi* — but the interpretive move is different.

### Rain & Torah

Rav Yehuda reads the verse as an equivalence: the giving of *Torah* is *like* rain. Rava reads it as an elevation of rain itself.

### Mi Natleh B'Mi

This brings us to a fascinating question of hermeneutic logic: *mi natleh b'mi* — which entity depends on which in a comparison? The principle is *katan nitleh b'gadol*: when you say "A is like B," it is A whose stature you are trying to communicate, and B is the more powerful, emotionally resonant image. If *Torah* is compared to rain — "let it flow like rain" — then rain is the *gadol*, the primary reference point. The comparison is being made to help the audience appreciate something they don't already viscerally grasp by invoking something they do.

This is a striking observation about the *gemara*'s own frame of reference. In the *pesukim*, rain is used to make *Torah* vivid — "you understand rain, so understand that *Torah* is like that." The *gemara* reverses the direction entirely: "you understand *Torah*, so understand that rain is *like that*." The image that serves as the ground of comparison has shifted. For the authors of the biblical verses, rain was the common, deeply felt reality; *Torah*'s greatness needed to be communicated by invoking rain. For the *gemara*, or at least for the audience the *gemara* is addressing, the experience of *Torah* is the more immediate felt reality, and it is now rain whose significance needs to be conveyed.

This is not merely a rhetorical curiosity. It reflects something deep about shifts in collective experience and framing. Most of us are not farmers. We do not feel in our bones what it means to wait for rain, to need it, to have it arrive or fail to arrive. The *gemara* therefore has to work harder to communicate rain's weight, and it does so by reaching for the things its audience does understand and hold sacred.

Rava then raises a contradiction. One verse says *ya'arof kamatar likhi* — "let it break forth like powerful rain" — and another says *tizal k'tal imrati* — "let it flow gently like dew." These are two very different images: *ya'arof* shares its root with *arifat* of the *egla arufa*, connoting a forceful breaking; *tizal* is soft, flowing, gentle. Which is it? The answer depends on the student. *Im talmid chacham hagun hu* — if the *talmid chacham* is an appropriate student — then *ketal*, let the *Torah* drop on him gently like dew, with nurturing care. *Ve-im lav* — but if he has character failings — then *ya'arof kamatar*, the *Torah* must be taught with force, because something stronger is needed to do its corrective work. The manner of teaching *Torah* is not one-size-fits-all; it is shaped by who is receiving it.

---

## Torah Lishma

### Sam Chayim/Sam Mavet

The *gemara* introduces a *beraita* in the name of Rabbi Bana'ah: *kol ha-osek ba-Torah lishma, Torato na'aset lo sam chayim* — whoever engages in *Torah* for its own sake, his *Torah* becomes an elixir of life. Three verses are brought in support: *etz chayim hi la-machazikm bah* (it is a tree of life for those who hold fast to it); *rif'ut tehi le-sharekha* (it will be a healing to your flesh); and *ki motz'ai matza chayim* (one who finds me finds life). Conversely, *kol ha-osek ba-Torah shelo lishma na'aset lo sam ha-mavet* — one who engages in *Torah* not for its own sake, his *Torah* becomes a poison. The proof text is again *ya'arof kamatar likhi*, and the word *arifa* is now taken to mean literal death, as in *ve-arafu sham et ha-egla ba-nachal*.

### Tosafot's Answer

This is obviously a difficult *gemara*, because the Rabbis elsewhere operate on the principle of *mitoch shelo lishma ba lishma* — that beginning from impure motivations can lead to pure ones. Tosafot raises the question explicitly: we say *le-olam ya'asok adam ba-Torah af al gav de-eina lishma, she-mitoch shelo lishma ba lishma* — a person should always engage in *Torah* even if not *lishma*, because from *shelo lishma* one arrives at *lishma*. How can the same text call *shelo lishma* a poison?

Tosafot resolves this by distinguishing two entirely different types of *shelo lishma*. The case where we say *mitoch shelo lishma ba lishma* — where we are lenient and even encourage *Torah* study despite impure motives — refers to someone learning *kedei she-yikarei rabbi o kedei she-yekabduhu*, for honor, for social recognition, for selfish personal interest. That is a human failing, but it is not a perversion of *Torah* itself. The case where *Torah* becomes *sam ha-mavet* is where *lomed le-kanteir* — learning in order to attack, to disprove, to subvert, to lead others astray. That is not merely impure motivation; it is weaponization.

### Literal vs Spiritual

One might also ask what *sam ha-mavet* means here — is this a literal punishment, a divine smiting, or something understood at a more spiritual register? The same question applies to the image of *Torah* as light and life — does that refer to physical life, to *techiyat ha-metim*, or to spiritual vitality? One reading would understand *sam ha-mavet* to mean a spiritual death: you may believe you are engaged in a religious enterprise, but the very activity is hollowing you out from within, leading to spiritual ruin. One student offers a comparison to the *Rambam*'s understanding of *hashgacha pratit* — that the world's consequences are built in rather than externally imposed, and that just as misuse of the body brings physical harm, misuse of *Torah* brings its own natural spiritual consequence. That framing does not require a supernatural punishment and captures the sense that *Torah* taken the wrong way genuinely destroys.

Rashi's comment is also worth noting. When he explains *lishma*, he writes *ka'asher tzivani Hashem Elokai velo kedei le-hikarei rabbi* — as God commanded me, and not in order to be called *rabbi*. Rashi thus defines *lishma* in straightforward positive terms: the fulfillment of a divine command for its own sake.

This entire passage initiates a larger *sugya* about *Torah* and its multiple valences, which the *gemara* expresses not through a single image but through an expanding series of metaphors. The transition is natural: we started with rain, rain was compared to *Torah* and *Torah* to rain, and now, with *Torah* as the central concern, the *gemara* feels it cannot be contained by a single image. The richness and complexity of *Torah* demands a range of metaphors, and that is precisely what follows.

---

## Torah Metaphors

### Tree Metaphor

Rabbi Ami asks Rabbi Zeira to teach some *Torah*, and when Rabbi Zeira says he is too weak for a formal *shiur*, Rabbi Ami invites him to share *aggadta* instead. Rabbi Zeira then transmits in the name of Rabbi Yochanan a reading of the verse *ki ha-adam etz ha-sadeh* — "for a person is a tree of the field" (Devarim 20:19). Taken at face value, the verse is rhetorical — is a person a tree that you should besiege the tree? But Rabbi Yochanan reads it non-rhetorically. Yes, a person is like a tree. How?

The verse continues: *ki mimenu tochal ve-oto lo tichrot* — from it you shall eat, and you shall not cut it down (if it bears fruit). But if it is not fruit-bearing: *oto tashchit ve-charat* — you shall destroy and cut it down. Translated into human terms: *im talmid chacham hagun hu* — if he is a fitting *talmid chacham*, one whose learning bears fruit and nourishes others — *mimenu tochal*, you can eat from him, you should learn from him. *Ve-oto lo tichrot* — do not cut off your connection to him. Tosafot adds: even if you are not actively learning from him at the moment, do not sever the relationship. But *ve-im lav* — if he is not fitting, if his *middot* are flawed — *oto tashchit ve-charat*, cut off your relationship with him entirely.

This raises a point of tension with the earlier teaching, which suggested that if a student has poor character you should teach *Torah* more forcefully, presumably to correct him. Here, the advice runs in the opposite direction: if the *talmid chacham* himself is of poor character, you should not benefit from his Torah. The throughline in both cases is that *Torah* and character are deeply intertwined, and the quality of what is transmitted is inseparable from the character of the one transmitting or receiving it.

### Iron Sharpening

Rabbi Chama berebi Chanina asks about the verse *barzel be-varzel yachad* — "iron sharpens iron together" (Mishlei 27:17). Just as two blades sharpen one another when rubbed together, so too *shenei talmidei chachamim mechadedim zeh et zeh be-halachah* — two students of the sages sharpen one another in the study of *halachah*. The shift from *Torah* to *halachah* here is worth noting, though no explicit explanation is given. It may reflect the particular quality of precision and sharpness that halachic reasoning demands — the give and take of *chavruta* in *halachah* as distinct from the more expansive mode of *aggadta*. This is the first explicit turn toward *chavruta* learning as a theme.

### Fire Metaphor

Rabbah bar bar Chanah asks: *lama nimshalu divrei Torah ka-esh?* — why is *Torah* compared to fire? The verse says *halo koh devarei ka-esh ne'um Hashem* — are not My words like fire, says God. Just as fire cannot sustain itself from a single log of wood — *ma esh eino dolek yechidi*, fire does not burn alone — so *Torah* cannot sustain itself through one person alone. *Torah* requires a community; it is not a solitary enterprise.

### Chavruta Imperative

Rabbi Yose berebi Chanina sharpens this further with an interpretation of *cherev el ha-badim ve-no'alu* — "a sword against the *badim*, and they shall be foolish." The *gemara* reads *badim* as those who learn *bad be-vad* — singly, alone, without a *chavruta*. *Cherev al soneihem shel talmidei chachamim* — a sword against those sages who study in isolation. And not only is this a failure of method; such scholars do not merely fail to grow sharper — *ela she-mitapshin* — they become stupider. *Shene'emar ve-no'alu* — and they will be foolish. And not only foolish — it is a *chet*, a sin, because *no'alu* is connected to the verse *asher no'alnu va'asher chatanu* — "we acted foolishly and we sinned." Foolishness in *Torah*, particularly in *halachah*, leads to going astray oneself, to misleading others, and ultimately to sin.

### Small Sharpens Large

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks: *lama nimshalu divrei Torah ke-etz?* — why is *Torah* compared to a tree? The verse says *etz chayim hi la-machazikm bah*. Just as kindling a great fire requires small twigs to ignite the large logs, *af talmidei chachamim ktanim mechadedim et ha-gedolim* — the younger, smaller students sharpen the greater ones. This is a nuance beyond the earlier teaching about *chavruta* between peers; here it is the junior students who provide the spark that gets the larger fire burning.

### Three Sources

This connects naturally to the famous statement of Rabbi Chanina: *harbeh lamadti me-rabotai, u-me-chaverai yoter me-rabotai, u-mi-talmidai yoter mi-kulam* — I have learned much from my masters, more from my colleagues than my masters, and more from my students than from all of them. Why is it that students outstrip even colleagues? Rashi, at the bottom of *amud bet*, explains: *she-sho'alim kol sha'ah* — they ask constantly, relentlessly, with the insistence and perhaps the naivety of those not yet bound by the conventions of the discipline. Sometimes a student asks what the more senior scholar would not dare ask, and those turn out to be the most important questions. The enthusiasm of the student, the freshness of the question, forces the teacher to think more carefully, more fundamentally.

Looking back at this entire collection of images, what is most striking is their multiplicity and their dynamism. Rain is nurturing, but it is somewhat static in its imagery — water falls, things grow. Fire sharpening, iron against iron, small twigs igniting large logs — these images carry urgency, friction, energy. For those of us removed from agricultural reality, they may communicate something about *Torah*'s vitality that rain alone cannot.

---

## Water Metaphor

### Water Seeking

The *gemara* now returns to water as a metaphor for *Torah*, and Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa surfaces a contradiction between two verses. One says *likrat tzameh hatayu mayim* — "go out to meet the thirsty and bring them water." Another says *hoy kol tzameh lechu la-mayim* — "come, all who are thirsty, go to the water." One verse says bring the water to the thirsty person; the other says let the thirsty person come. The resolution follows the now-familiar pattern: *im talmid hagun hu* — if the student is fitting — go out and bring him the water, go out of your way to teach him. *Ve-im lav* — and if not — let him come to the water himself; let him demonstrate his motivation, prove his perseverance.

One should note, however, that even the student who must come to the water is still described as *tzameh* — thirsty. He still desires *Torah*. The question of *eino hagun* is not about a student who is indifferent or hostile, but perhaps about one who has not yet proven his readiness, or whose character needs some tempering before he is given full access. The withholding of the teacher's outreach may itself be a form of pedagogy.

### Wellsprings

Rabbi Hanina bar Hama raises a similar tension between two verses. One says *yafutzu ma'aynotecha chutza* — "let your wellsprings burst forth to the outside" — the famous verse later invoked in the letter of the *Ba'al Shem Tov*, where it is said that *mashiach* will not come until *yafutzu ma'aynotecha chutza*, until the teachings spread outward to the world. The other says *yihyu lecha levadecha* — keep it for yourself alone. Again the same resolution: *im talmid hagun hu*, share your *Torah* freely, let the wellsprings burst forth. *Ve-im lav*, keep it to yourself. Rashi specifies that what must be withheld from the unworthy student is the esoteric — *ma'aseh merkavah*, *ma'aseh bereshit*. But Tosafot suggests a broader concern: some students hear only what they want to hear, and discernment in what one shares and how one says it is always called for.

### Humility Vessel

Rabbi Hanina bar Idi asks explicitly: *lama nimshalu divrei Torah la-mayim?* — why is *Torah* compared to water? *De-ketiv: hoy kol tzameh lechu la-mayim.* The answer is structural: *ma mayim manichim makom gavo'ah ve-holchim le-makom namuch* — water flows away from high places and seeks out low places. *Af divrei Torah ein mitkaymim ela be-mi she-da'ato shfela* — *Torah* is only sustained in one whose mind is *shfela*, humble, lowly. The humble person is the low place into which *Torah* naturally flows and in which it finds its home.

### Three Liquids

Rabbi Oshaya extends the metaphor further. Why is *Torah* compared not just to water but to three liquids — water, wine, and milk? The verse for water is *hoy kol tzameh lechu la-mayim*; for wine and milk: *lechu shivru ve-acholu, lechu shivru belo chesef u-velo mechir, yayin va-chalav*. The answer: *mah shlosha mashkin halalu ein mitkaymim ela ba-pachot she-ba-keilim* — these three liquids are best preserved not in elegant vessels of gold and silver, but in the simplest pottery vessels. *Af divrei Torah ein mitkaymim ela be-mi she-da'ato shfela* — similarly, *Torah* is only truly preserved in the humble person. The lowliness of the vessel is what keeps the contents fresh and alive.

### Caesar's Daughter

This teaching leads directly into one of the more memorable anecdotes in the *sugya*. The daughter of Caesar said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanania: *ai chochma me'uara bi-chli mechoar* — what beautiful wisdom is kept in such an ugly vessel! Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanania, apparently, was not a handsome man. He replied: does your father keep his wine in pottery vessels? She was taken aback — what else would one use? He said: you are the Caesar's household, people of great importance — why not keep your wine in vessels of gold and silver?

She went and told her father, who duly transferred the wine into gold and silver vessels — and it turned sour. The Caesar summoned Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chanania and demanded to know who had given this advice. When Rabbi Yehoshua explained, the Caesar pointed out that Rabbi Yehoshua had not explicitly told her to change the vessels. Rashi's comment is important here: Rabbi Yehoshua had not actually recommended the change — that would have been imprudent in the Caesar's household. He had spoken rhetorically, responding in kind to her rhetorical provocation, and she had taken it as a literal suggestion.

The *gemara* then raises an empirical objection: *ve-ika shapiri de-gmiri* — but there are handsome, beautiful people who are accomplished Torah scholars! The response: *ei havu sanu tfei havu gmiri* — if they were uglier, they would know even more. Tosafot softens this: it is not that ugliness as such is the desired state, but rather that being excessively drawn to one's own beauty, or living in a society that prizes beauty excessively, diverts attention and self-investment away from the self-abnegation that full *Torah* commitment requires. Our sense of our own importance, our self-regard, prevents us from becoming the genuinely lowly vessel that can hold everything.

### Hesech Hadaat

The *gemara* adds a second interpretation of the three-liquids teaching. *Mah shlosha mashkin halalu ein nifsalim ela be-hesech ha-da'at* — these three liquids spoil only through *hesech ha-da'at*, through inattention, through failing to cover them and put them away properly. *Af divrei Torah ein mishtakchim ela be-hesech ha-da'at* — *Torah* is forgotten only through *hesech ha-da'at*. This is subtly different from the vessel teaching. There the emphasis was on the character of the person who holds the *Torah* — the humble vessel preserves it. Here the emphasis is on continuity of attention: as long as one does not remove one's focus, the *Torah* will not be lost.

There is something quietly reassuring in the phrasing. Rather than saying *Torah* must be constantly repeated or it will certainly be forgotten, the formulation is its reverse: it will only be forgotten if you stop paying attention. The onus shifts slightly; the assumption is that *Torah* tends to stay with you as long as you do not actively disengage.

---

## Rain's Greatness (II)

### Rain & Creation

After the extended digression into metaphors for *Torah*, the *gemara* circles back to where it began — the greatness of rain. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina now adds a third point of comparison: *gadol yom ha-geshamim ki-yom she-nivreu shamayim va-aretz* — the day of rain is as great as the day of the creation of heaven and earth. The proof is from the verse: *har'ifu shamayim mi-ma'al u-shchakim yizlu tzedek, tiftach eretz ve-yifru yesha u-tzedakah tatzmia yachad, Ani Hashem berativ* — the heavens shall drip from above, and the clouds shall flow with righteousness; the earth shall open, and salvation and righteousness shall blossom together — I, God, have created *it*. The *gemara* notes that the text says *berativ* — He created *it* (singular) — not *beratim* (plural). The singular referent is the rain, and the verb *bara* connects the rain to the act of creation.

This is a fitting moment to articulate what may be the *sugya*'s underlying theological current. There are two ways one might understand why rain occupies such an exalted place in *Masechet Taanit*. The first is the straightforward physical argument: rain sustains life, therefore it is important, therefore we pray for it. But the *gemara* consistently reaches for comparisons — *techiyat ha-metim*, the giving of *Torah*, the creation of the world — that go well beyond practical necessity. These comparisons all share a common character: they are moments of divine self-disclosure, of God's direct and manifest engagement with the world. *Techiyat ha-metim* is the ultimate eschatological intervention; *matan Torah* is the paradigmatic revelation; creation is the founding act. Rain, in this reading, is not merely a physical phenomenon that sustains agriculture. It is a medium through which God's presence, closeness, and active care are made palpable in the world.

This is not simply our reading back onto the text. It is the texture of the *sugya* itself. The authors of the *gemara* lived in a world without scientific distance from nature; rain was not explained by meteorological models but was experienced as a direct expression of divine relationship. *Geshamim* arriving meant God was close; their absence meant something in that relationship had gone wrong. And that is precisely the frame within which the remainder of the *masechet* operates.

---

## Rain = Forgiveness

### Salvation

Rabbi Oshaya says: *gadol yom geshamim she-afilu yeshua para ve-raba bo* — great is the day of rain, for even salvation is fruitful and multiplies on a day of rain. The verse: *tiftach eretz ve-yifru yesha* — the earth will open, and salvation will flourish. Rain is not merely the precondition for agricultural growth; it is the moment when *yeshua*, divine salvation, is most abundantly present.

### Sins Forgiven

Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai takes this a striking step further: *ein geshamim yordim ela im ken nimchalu avonoteihem shel Yisrael* — rain descends only when the sins of Israel have been forgiven. The proof verse is *ratzita Hashem artzecha, shavta shevut Yaakov, nasata avon amecha, kisita kol chatatam sela* — You have desired Your land, You have returned the captivity of Jacob, You have lifted off the sin of Your nation, You have covered all their sins.

This is worth pausing over. The structure of *Masechet Taanit* most naturally invites the reading of sin as the cause of drought — we sinned, rain was withheld, we do *teshuva*, rain returns. But Rabbi Tanchum's formulation is not about a drought-and-response cycle. It begins with rain falling and reads from that falling the conclusion that sins have been forgiven. Nobody first acknowledged having sinned. The rain itself is the announcement of divine forgiveness, an expression of unconditional grace and divine desire.

*Ze'iri mi-Dehavat* (as Rashi notes, a different *Ze'iri* from the earlier *amora* of the same name) says to *Ravina*: you derive this from that verse; we derive it from here — *ve-atah tishma ha-shamayim ve-salachta le-chatat amecha* — and You shall hear from the heavens and shall forgive the sins of Your people. That verse, familiar from the *tefilla* of Shlomo at the opening of *Masechet Taanit*, does follow the classic sequence: drought, cry, forgiveness, rain. But Rabbi Tanchum's formulation reads in the opposite direction: the mere presence of rain is itself already the sign of forgiveness and divine closeness.

---

## Rain Withheld

### Withheld Rain

Rabbi Tanchum bereih de-Rabbi Chiya ish Kefar Akko turns to the obverse: *ein geshamim ne'etzarim ela im ken nitchayvu soneihem shel Yisrael kelaya* — rains are withheld only when the enemies of Israel (a circumlocution for Israel itself) deserve destruction. The verse: *tziya gam chom yigzelu meimei sheleg, sheol chatu* — the thirst and the heat have stolen the waters of the snow, they have sinned to the very depth of *sheol*. Rains withheld, no snow waters — they deserve to descend to *sheol* because of their sins.

*Ze'iri mi-Dehavat* again addresses *Ravina*: you derive it from that verse; we derive it from *ve-atzarta ha-shamayim ve-lo yihyeh matar va-avadtem meheira* — I will hold back the heavens, there will be no rain, and you shall be quickly driven from the land. This second verse is plainer and more direct — indeed, it comes from the *Torah* itself. Why the first derivation favored the less obvious verse remains somewhat unexplained; the first verse points toward utter destruction and *sheol*, while the second is about exile. Perhaps they are understood as pointing to different dimensions of consequence.

### Terumot Maasrot

Rav Chisda says: *ein geshamim ne'atzarim ela bishvil bitul trumos u-ma'asros* — rains are withheld because of the neglect of *terumot* and *ma'asrot*. The verse is the same as before — *tziya gam chom yigzelu meimei sheleg* — and the derivation comes from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: *bishvil devarim she-tzivisi eschem bi-ymot ha-chama*, because of things I commanded you in the warm months — the harvest season, when *terumot u-ma'asros* are separated — *ve-lo asisem*, and you did not do them, *yigzlu mi-kem meimei sheleg bi-ymot ha-geshamim*, the rains of the winter season will be stolen from you.

The inner logic here is transparent and even elegant. *Terumot u-ma'asros* are the obligatory gifts given from the grain harvest, acknowledging that God's hand produced the abundance. To take the agricultural bounty and fail to acknowledge its divine source is a kind of ingratitude and a denial of the relationship that the rain itself represents. The punishment therefore corresponds: those who refuse to acknowledge God's generosity in the summer will not receive it in the winter. It is a *middah ke-neged middah* of the most coherent kind.

### Lashon Hara

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi says: *ein geshamim ne'atzarim ela bishvil mesaperei lashon hara* — rains are withheld because of those who speak *lashon hara*. The verse: *ruach tzafon techolel geshem u-fanim niz'amim lashon sater* — the north wind drives away rain, and an angry face is like a secret speech. The *lashon sater* — speech spoken in hiding, in private — is *lashon hara*, and like the north wind it drives the rain away.

The correspondence here is less immediately obvious than with *terumot u-ma'asros*, but the connection can be drawn. *Lashon hara* is often described as a kind of destructive power that, like the wind, operates invisibly. The *ruach* of *lashon hara* mirrors the *ruach* that disperses the rain clouds. More directly: just as rain gives life, the tongue can take it away; the one who speaks *lashon hara* deploys a life-destroying wind and therefore forfeits the life-giving rain.

### Brazenness

Rav Sala in the name of Rav Hamnuna: *ein geshamim ne'atzarim ela bishvil azei fanim* — rains are withheld on account of brazenness, *azut panim*. The verse: *va-yimane'u revivim u-malkosh lo haya u-metzach isha zona haya lach* — the early rains were withheld, and there was no *malkosh* late rain, and the forehead of a brazen woman, of a *zona*, you had. The *metzach*, the brazen forehead, appears in the same verse as the withholding of rain.

The same *amora* then adds a further teaching: *kol adam she-yesh lo azus panim, sof nichshal ba-aveirah* — any person who possesses brazenness will ultimately stumble into sin, specifically sexual sin as indicated by the *zona* of that verse. A further nuance from the *pasuk*: the text uses *haya lach* — you *had* — rather than *yihyeh lach* — you *will have*. Brazenness is therefore read not as a predictor of future sin but as an indicator of existing sin; the shameless bearing is the outward expression of a hidden transgression already committed, a kind of cover.

Rabbah bar Avuna then adds: any person who possesses *azut panim* may be called a *rasha* — as the verse says *he'ez ish rasha be-fanav*, the wicked man hardens his face. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak goes further: *mutar lisno'o* — one is permitted to hate him — citing *ve-oz panav yishuneh*, reading *yishuneh* not as "will be changed" but through *al tikri* as *yisaneh*, "shall be hated." Whether this carries practical behavioral implications or remains primarily an internal permission, in the manner of the verse *lo sisna et achicha bi-lvavecha*, is not elaborated here, though *Gemaras* elsewhere do draw practical consequences from such permissions.

### Bitul Torah

Rav Katina brings the *sugya* full circle: *ein geshamim ne'etzarin ella bishvil bitul Torah* — rains are withheld because of the neglect of *Torah* study. This is a fitting conclusion to a *daf* that began by comparing rain to the giving of *Torah*. Having identified rain with *Torah*, *Torah* with life, and the relationship between Israel and God as mediated through both, it follows that the abandonment of *Torah* disrupts the very channel through which that relationship flows.

The verse: *ba-atzaltayim yimach ha-mikreh* — through laziness the *mikreh* will become weak. *Bishvil atzlus she-haya be-Yisrael shelo asuku ba-Torah* — because of the laziness of Israel in not engaging with *Torah* — *na'asah sono'o shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu*, it is as if God's enemy — which is a circumlocution meaning God Himself — became weak, *mach*. The *gemara* derives that *mikreh* refers to God from *ha-mikreh ba-mayim aliyosav* — He who spreads His upper chambers with water. And so the circle closes: rain (*mayim*) and *Torah* (compared to *mayim*) and God — the failure of our *Torah* weakens, as it were, God's presence in the world, and the result is the absence of rain.

The connection here runs deeper than a simple correspondence between sin and punishment. Our learning of *Torah* is our way of receiving *devar Hashem* — the word that comes down from heaven as the rain comes down. *Yizal ka-matar likchi*: God's giving descends like rain. When we weaken our side of that relationship, we weaken the channel itself, and the rain — the manifest expression of God's closeness — is withheld.

### Torah as Light

Rav Yosef adds a final image, drawing from the verse *ve-atah lo ra'u or bahir hu ba-shchakim, ve-ruach avra va-tihaarem* — and they did not see the clear light in the heavens, and a wind passed through and cleared them. *Ve-ein or ella Torah* — the light is nothing other than *Torah* — as the verse says *ki ner mitzvah ve-Torah or*. *Bahir hu ba-shchakim* — it is clear in the heavens. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds: even at the moment when the sky is becoming overcast, cloud upon cloud, and it appears rain is imminent — if Israel has not seen the light of *Torah* — *ruach avra va-tihaarem*, a wind passes through and sweeps the clouds away, and no rain falls.

The image is vivid and, in this context, theologically precise: *Torah* is the light in the heavens that causes the clouds to hold, the rain to descend. When that light is absent, the clouds cannot sustain themselves; the wind scatters them before a drop falls.

---

---

# Ta'anit 8

## Rain's Power & Sins

### Gadol Yom HaGeshamim

Today's *daf* is 8. We pick up at the very bottom of 7b, working through a list of statements about how powerful a day of rain is — *gadol yom hageshamim* — along with related digressions.

### Ruach Avrah VaTetaharem

The *Tanna de-bei Rabbi Ishmael* teaches: even at a time when the heavens appear to be covered in dark splotches, as if they are ready to pour down rain — *afilu besha'ah sherakia na'aseh bahurin bahurin lehorid tal u-matar* — nevertheless, *veruach avrah vatetaharem*, a wind will pass and cleanse the clouds away. This statement is based on the verse "וְעַתָּה לֹא רָאוּ אוֹר בָּהִיר הוּא בַּשְּׁחָקִים וְרוּחַ עָבְרָה וַתְּטַהֲרֵם" — the clouds are ready, yet a wind disperses them. The reason given is the sin of *bitul Torah*.

### Bitul Torah

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: the opening of this discussion likely should have begun here, approximately ten lines from the bottom of the page. This passage is part of a broader catalog — on one side, a catalog of the ways in which a day of rain is praised and the things it resembles; on the other, a catalog of the sins that cause rain to be withheld.

It is worth exploring whether these correspondences represent causal explanations for the absence of rain, or whether they reflect a deeper logical and religious-symbolic relationship. The sin of *bitul Torah* makes a great deal of sense in this framework: rain is not merely about sustenance; it is seen as a manifestation of God's closeness and connection to the people. *Torah* and *tefillah* are the means through which the people express that relationship from their side. The correspondence between *bitul Torah* and the withholding of rain therefore carries a profound internal logic.

### Gezel & Theft

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *ein geshamim ne'etzarin ella ba'avon gezel* — rain is withheld only because of the sin of *gezel*, of theft and coveting. The verse states: "עַל כַּפַּיִם כִּסָּה אוֹר" — on the palms, light is hidden. *Ve-ein kapayim ella chamas* — and *kapayim* refers to *chamas*, to theft and coveting, as the verse continues: "וּמִן הַחָמָס אֲשֶׁר בְּכַפֵּיהֶם." *Ve-ein or ella matar* — and *or*, light, refers to rain, as the verse says: "יָפִיץ עָנָן אוֹרוֹ," the cloud spreads forth its light.

### Gezel & Tefillah

*Mai takantei?* What is the remedy? *Yarbeh bitfillah* — one should increase in prayer, as the verse states: "וַיְצַו עָלֶיהָ בַּמַּפְגִּיעַ" — and *ein pegi'ah ella tfillah*, and *pegi'ah*, encountering, refers only to *tefillah*, as the verse says: "וְאַתָּה אַל תִּתְפַּלֵּל בְּעַד הָעָם הַזֶּה וְאַל תִּשָּׂא בַעֲדָם רִנָּה וּתְפִלָּה וְאַל תִּפְגַּע בִּי."

One might ask why the remedy for *gezel* is not *teshuvah* and return of the stolen property, which is the normative correction for theft. One could also note the distinction elsewhere in the *Gemara* between *gezeilah* and *geneivah* — by *gezeilah* one fears neither man nor God — and from that perspective, the remedy of *tefillah* functions to re-establish that very relationship with God that *gezeilah* represents a rejection of. But the major theme of this *masechet* is that rain is God's favor and presence, and the response to its absence is fasting and prayer — the act of reaching out to re-establish that connection.

The connection between *gezel* and the withholding of rain also parallels the earlier discussion of *terumot u-ma'asrot*: God provides; one's acknowledgment of that provision is expressed through giving what is designated. To steal from another is, in its way, to fail to acknowledge that God gives to all — and so what God gives is withheld.

### Rakia Kehah Kabarzel

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *mai de-chtiv im kehah habarzel vehu lo fanim kilkel?* If you see the heavens as dull as iron — *im raita rakia shekehah kabarzel milehorid tal u-matar* — it is because of the corruption of the entire generation: *bishvil maaseh hador shehein mekulkallin*, as the verse states, *vehu lo fanim kilkel*. The word *lo* can be read as the possessive *lo* — their faces, the way they present themselves, are corrupted — meaning the entire nation has sinned.

This statement is not connected to any particular sin. It echoes the *pesukim* of the *Shema* — you observe the *mitzvot* and rain follows; you transgress and it does not. The absence of rain is a sign of a generation that has gone astray.

### Yitgabru BeRachamim

*Mah takanatam?* Again, strikingly, the remedy is not *teshuvah* but prayer: *yitgabru berachamim*, they should strengthen themselves with compassion — that is, call out to God in prayer — as the verse states: "וְחַיָּלִים יִגְבַּר וְיִתְרוֹן הַכְשֵׁר חָכְמָה."

*Veyitron hachsher chochmah kol shekein im hichshiru maaseihem mei'ikara* — it would have been better had they been wise from the outset and corrected their deeds before sinning. But now that they have sinned and rain is not coming, they should call out to God. Not *teshuvah* — call out to God. The emphasis throughout this passage, and indeed throughout this *masechet*, is on prayer as the primary mode of reconnecting with the Divine.

---

## Talmud Torah & Rain

### Talmid & Kasheh

*Reish Lakish* now shifts the discussion — as happens repeatedly in this *daf* — from rain to *Talmud Torah*. *Im raita talmid shelimudo kasheh alav kabarzel* — if you see a student whose learning is as hard as iron, who is hitting his head against the wall and cannot make progress — the reason is *bishvil mishnato she'einah sdura alav*: because his information is not well organized. In an oral culture, one must first internalize and memorize all the material; only then can one analyze and think through issues clearly. If a student struggles to think through halachic problems with clarity, it is because his foundational knowledge is not in order.

The verse says: *vehu lo fanim kilkel* — he has, as it were, corrupted the face of things, disordered the basic organization of his knowledge. *Mah takanto?* The remedy is *yirbeh bishivah* — *Rashi* explains this not merely as sitting, but as spending time in the *yeshiva* environment, as the verse says: *vechayalim yigaber*. *Rashi* reads this as: the students are like troops — *chayalot b'machanot* — and through interaction with fellow *yeshiva* students one's knowledge becomes strengthened. *Veyitron hichshir chachmah kol shekein im mishnato sedurah alav mei'ikara* — it would have been better had his material been organized and clear from the outset.

The same verse that was applied to rain is now applied to *talmud Torah*, and the fit here with the word *chachmah* is even more natural than it was in the rain context.

### Seider Matnitei

The *Gemara* goes on to stress the importance of organizing one's material before moving to analysis.

### Forty vs. Twenty-Four

*Ki ha d'Reish Lakish hava mesader matnitei arba'in zimnin* — *Reish Lakish* would organize his material forty times, *k'neged mem yom shenitnah Torah*, corresponding to the forty days on which the *Torah* was given. The point is that one must fully own the *Torah* received — in an oral culture, all previous teachings and *mishnayot* had to be held entirely in the mind. Having invested that effort in mastery, *v'ayeil l'kamei d'Rabbi Yochanan*, he would then go before *Rabbi Yochanan* to apply his intellect and analysis.

This evokes the broader *Gemara*ic discussion of *Sinai v'oker harim* — whether greater importance lies in erudition and breadth of knowledge, or in the power of analysis. The *Gemara* there concludes that analysis cannot precede the facts. The same principle operates here, with the added emphasis that the material must not merely be learned but thoroughly organized and clarified before one begins to think it through. First own the material; then develop the *chiddushim*.

*Rav Adda bar Abba mesader matnitei esrin v'arba zimnin* — Rav Adda bar Abba would organize his material twenty-four times, *k'neged Torah Nevi'im u-Khtuvim*, corresponding to the twenty-four books of *Tanakh*, and *v'ayeil l'kamei d'Rava*, he would then go before *Rava*. Since the twenty-four books of *Tanakh* are written, one works to internalize them to the point that they are as if written before one's eyes — and only then does one turn to analysis.

In both cases the correspondence is elegant: whether it is the forty days of *matan Torah* or the twenty-four books of *Tanakh*, what is received must be fully owned before one's own analytic contribution begins. The relationship between the received material and one's own analysis mirrors, in a certain sense, the relationship between *Torah she-bichtav* and *Torah she-be'al peh*, though here it applies equally to the received dimension of *Torah she-be'al peh* itself.

### Master's Responsibility

*Rava* returns to the verse about iron: *ei chazit talmid shelimudo kasheh alav k'varzel* — if you see a student whose learning is as hard as iron and he cannot grasp what is being taught — *bishvil rabo*, this is not the student's failure to do sufficient *chazarah*, but the master's failure: *she'eino masbir lo panim*, that he does not show the student a friendly, welcoming face. The word *masbir* here carries a double meaning — *sever panim yafot*, a welcoming countenance, but also the plain sense of not explaining things well. Both may be intended.

*Shene'emar vehu lo panim kilkel* — here *lo* may be read as written with a *vav*, meaning the master shows him an unfavorable face. *Vehu keha* — he is not nourishing the student. The *masbirah* is the remedy in both senses.

### Yarbeh Alav Rei'im

*Mah takantei?* Interestingly, the *Gemara* addresses not the master but the student. *Yarbeh alav rei'im* — the student should cultivate friends and social connections around the master, sending people who will speak well of him and cultivate a more positive relationship. *Uvichayalim yigaber* — amass people around him and try to influence the dynamic.

*Veyitron hachshir chochmah kol sheken im huchshru ma'asav lifnei rabbo mei'ikara* — this does not remove the student's own responsibility. The master is presumably not being cold without reason; it would have been better had the student not demonstrated whatever initially caused the rift. But once the dynamic is set, sometimes an initial offense has a disproportionately long impact. Rather than merely complaining about it, the student should think constructively about how to cultivate a more positive relationship.

The movement throughout this section — between rain and *Torah* — is itself significant. Rain is understood as the *shefa*, the divine abundance, that comes from God to the world; what human beings do in return to create and sustain that relationship is *Torah* and *tefillah*. But beyond that: the same *pesukim* that speak about rain keep being read back through the lens of *talmud Torah*, because *Torah* is also spiritual sustenance that comes from God. The parallel runs deep. If the *rebbe* is in some sense a figure for God withholding the rain, then the student's effort to cultivate the relationship through friends echoes the community's turn to prayer to restore the connection with the Divine.

---

## Lachash & Prayer

### Nachash Belo Lachash

*V'amar Rabbi Ami*: *im yishoch hanachash belo lachash v'ein yitron l'va'al halashon* — if the snake bites without hissing, there is no benefit to the person of the tongue. *Im raita dor she-hashamayim mishtachshin k'nechoshet milehorid tal u-matar* — if you see a generation in which the heavens are reddened and rusted over like bronze and no rain is coming — *bishvil lochshei lechishot*, it is because of the absence of those who should be doing the whisperings of prayer. *She'ein bador* — they are not found in that generation.

Whereas in prior passages, sin was the cause and prayer was the remedy, here the very absence of prayer itself is what causes the heavens to be closed. The very absence of *tefillah* — the speech that sustains the relationship with God — is what produces the drought.

### Yeilech Eitzel Mi Sheyod…

*Mai takantei?* — *yeilech eitzel mi sheyodei'a lelachash* — go find someone who knows how to pray. *Dechtiv yagid alav re'o* — let his neighbor speak about him, let his neighbor pray on his behalf.

This evokes the structure of the *Mishnayot* of this *masechet*: when rain fails, the *yechidim* begin to fast; if that does not suffice, the *tzibur* takes on the fasts; ultimately the *tzibur* ceases its efforts while the *yechidim* continue. The special role of the *yachid* in prayer — exemplified most dramatically by the story of *Choni HaMa'agel* — is a sustained theme of this *masechet*. Here it finds expression: if your own prayers are not working, seek out the *yachid* who can pray on your behalf.

*Ve-ein yitron l'va'al halashon* — and the one who has the power of speech and does not use it to pray when he could make a difference — *mah hanayah lo?* What benefit is he?

### Chasid Shebador

*Ve-im lachash velo ne'enah* — and if you prayed and were not answered — *mai takantei?* — *yeilech eitzel chasid shebador veyeitar alav bitfillah* — go to the most pious person in the generation and have him entreat God on your behalf. *Shenemar vayitzav alav bamafgia*, and *ein pegiah ella tefillah*, as the verse says: "וְאַתָּה אַל תִּתְפַּלֵּל בְּעַד הָעָם הַזֶּה וְאַל תִּשָּׂא בַעֲדָם רִנָּה וּתְפִלָּה וְאַל תִּפְגַּע בִּי."

There are two stages: first, find someone who simply knows how to *daven* — in an oral culture, perhaps not everyone even knows the text of the *tefillah*. If that is not sufficient, proceed to a genuine *chasid*, someone of elevated spiritual stature who can serve as a *mafgia*, one who can encounter and entreat God. The entire passage functions as a distillation of themes encountered throughout the *daf*: whereas before prayer was the *takanah* for a range of other sins, here the presence or absence of rain is itself a function of whether prayer is being offered at all, and of how effectively.

### Magis Da'ato Alav

*Ve-im lachash ve-altah beyado* — but if the prayer was successful and rain fell — *umagis da'ato alav*, if the one who prayed becomes haughty as a result, swelling with pride over the efficacy of his prayers — *meivi af la'olam*, this brings anger to the world. *Shenemar mikneh af* — one who acquires anger because of *oleh da'ato alav*, because his sense of himself has risen up.

One wonders whether this is an allusion to *Choni HaMa'agel*, who famously ordered God around with great specificity regarding the manner of the rain. The power of speech in shaping the relationship with God is immense; but that very power demands profound humility. Haughtiness in the wake of answered prayer is itself a trigger for divine anger.

---

## Talmidei Chachamim D (II)

### Mitkana'im B'Af

*Rava* says: *shenei talmidei chachamim sheyoshvim b'ir achat v'ein noachin zeh l'zeh b'halacha* — if two Torah scholars live in the same city and are not pleasant to one another in *halacha*, if there is no good collaboration, no genuine shared discourse — *mitkana'im b'af*, it leads to jealousy with anger, *umalin oto*, and it rises up. *Shenemar makne af al olah.*

It is worth noting that the word here is *halacha* rather than *Torah* — perhaps because *halacha* with its practical application carries a particular weight that makes disputes especially charged. As soon as there is this: I rule this way, you rule the other way — things can deteriorate quickly. The reference is to the second half of the verse *yagid alav re'o makne af al olah* — *Rashi* explains that one should be *yagid alav re'o*, speaking and collaborating with one's neighbor; failing that, the result is an escalation of jealousy and anger.

---

## Talmidei Chachamim D (II)

### Yigid Alav Re'o

The transition here is immediate — from the discussion of rain to *Torah* and back again, without any formal break. *Amar Reish Lakish*: *mai dichtig im yishoch hanachash belo lachash v'ein yitron l'va'al halashon* — returning to the verse about the serpent that bites without hissing. The passage now takes a fresh direction.

---

## Lashon HaRa & Speech

### Chayot & Nachash

*Le-atid lavo*, in the future, all the animals will gather around the serpent and confront it. We understand, they say, why other predators do what they do: *ari dores v'ochel* — the lion tramples and eats; *ze'ev toref v'ochel* — the wolf tears its prey and eats. They commit violence in the service of sustenance. But you — *atah mah hana'ah yesh lach?* — what benefit do you derive? For occasionally a snake kills a creature — a large animal, a human being — that it does not then consume.

### Ein Yitron LeBaal HaLash…

The snake replies: *ve-ein yitron l'va'al halashon* — you can ask the same question of one who speaks *lashon hara*. With words alone, such a person can destroy reputations and ruin lives — and what do they gain? No material benefit, no sustenance. Yet the response is somewhat rhetorical: there *is* a kind of *hana'ah* that people derive from using speech to harm others — not a legitimate *hana'ah*, but a felt one. And so the snake, in turn, derives its own form of *hana'ah* from what it does. The parable is a striking indictment of *lashon hara* as, like the snake's bite, a form of harm that profits the one who inflicts it nothing.

---

## Sincerity & Prayer

### Nisa Levavenu El Kapayim

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *ein tfilato shel adam nishma'at ela im kein masim nafsho b'kapo* — a person's prayer is heard only if he truly places his soul in his hands, exposing his genuine self and bringing it before God. *Shenemar nisa levavenu el kapayim el El bashamayim* — let us lift our hearts on our hands to God in heaven. Only if you come with your heart truly in hand will your prayer be answered.

### Veyefatuhu BeFilhem

The *Gemara* challenges this: *eini?* Is that really true? *V'hukim Shmuel amora alei v'darash*: Shmuel set up an *amora* to proclaim the following teaching: "וַיְפַתּוּהוּ בְּפִיהֶם וּבִלְשׁוֹנָם יְכַזְּבוּ לוֹ וְלִבָּם לֹא נָכוֹן עִמּוֹ וְלֹא נֶאֶמְנוּ בִּבְרִיתוֹ" — they seduced God with their mouths and lied with their tongues, their hearts were not faithful to Him, they were not true to the covenant. And yet the very next verse says: "וְהוּא רַחוּם יְכַפֵּר עָוֹן" — God, in His mercy, will forgive. Even insincere prayer, it seems, is answered.

### Yachid vs. Tzibur

*Lo kashya* — *kan b'yachid kan b'tzibur*. The resolution is that for an individual, sincerity is required; one must truly bring one's heart. For the community, even prayer that is not fully sincere is answered.

This is a striking and genuinely bold claim. It is one thing to say that communal prayer is *more powerful* than individual prayer — we encounter that in other *Gemarot*, such as *ein tfilat shel tzibur chozeret reikam*. But this is a qualitatively different claim: that prayer which is, as stated explicitly in the verse, insincere — where the heart is not true, where the lips lie — is nonetheless answered when offered by the community.

*Rashi* reads the verse as suggesting that not all the members of the community are insincere — *she'ein lev kulam shalem* — and so the community as a whole can absorb individual insincerity. The *Gemara*, however, uses plural language throughout — *vayefatuhu befihem, uvilshonam yekhazvu lo* — suggesting the entire community is insincere. One might understand the *Gemara* to be making a point about the nature of communication itself: the very act of speech, even when not fully sincere, sustains the relationship. Better to be in communication than not. At the communal level, there is a power in the collective act of reaching out to God even when individual sincerity is lacking — it preserves the structure and reality of the relationship itself, expressed through the medium of *avodah she-balev*.

---

## Baalei Amana

### Emet Me-Eretz Tizmakh

*Amar Rabbi Ami*: *ein geshamim yordim ella bishvil baalei amana* — rain falls only because of those who deal faithfully with one another in business. Not those who profess a creed, but those who conduct their commercial affairs with trustworthiness. *Shenemar emet me-eretz tizmakh ve-tzedek mishamayim nishkaf* — truth sprouts from the ground, and justice — here understood as the rain — looks down from heaven. The rain from above is the divine response to the faithful dealing that emerges from below.

### Chulda U-Vor

*De-amar Rabbi Ami bo u-re'eh kama gedolim baalei amana* — come and see how great are those who deal in good faith. *Minayin?* — *me-chulda u-vor*, from the weasel and the pit. *U-ma hamaamin be-chulda u-vor kach hamaamin ba-Kadosh Baruch Hu al achat kama ve-khama* — if one who holds a weasel and a well as witnesses to an oath is held to account by those very witnesses, how much more so one who holds God as witness.

*Rashi* and *Tosafot* cite the *midrash*: a young man and woman fell in love and swore not to marry anyone else until they were of age. When asked who would hold him to his oath, the young man named the weasel and the pit as witnesses. Years passed; he broke his promise, married another, and had two children. One child fell into a well and died; the other was killed by a weasel. His wife asked what had happened, he told her the story, and she urged him to keep his oath. He divorced her and married the woman to whom he had originally sworn.

Whether the story teaches the power of dealing faithfully or the consequences of bad faith, the *Gemara*'s point is that faithful dealing implicitly or explicitly invokes God — bringing God into the transaction as a presence and a witness. To deal faithfully with another is therefore to sustain God as a partner in one's daily life. And therefore the natural divine response, the rain, follows. It is not merely an ethical correspondence; it flows from the same logic of relationship that animates the entire *masechet*.

---

## Matztik Atzmo

### Din Min Shamayim

*Amar Rabbi Yochanan*: *kol hamatztik et atzmo milmata maztikin alav et hadin milmala* — whoever acts with scrupulous righteousness below, the judgment will be exacting upon him from above. *Tzidduk hadin* is not necessarily a term of comfort: it means that things happen, bad things even, but they are all ultimately just. *Rashi* explains that if someone acts with great scrupulousness, Heaven will be very exacting in judging his own small missteps, and he will be held to a higher standard. *Shenemar emet me-eretz tizmakh ve-tzedek mishamayim nishkaf* — again the same verse: if you are truthful on the ground, a precise accounting comes from above.

### Veki'Yiratekha Evratekha

*Rabbi Chiya bar Avin amar Rav Huna* cites: *u-kheyiratekha evratekha* — as great as your fear of God is, so too is Your anger. The more one fears God and acts accordingly, the more exacting the Divine judgment becomes.

### Oseh Tzedek BiDrachekha

*Reish Lakish* adds a verse: "פָּגַעְתָּ אֶת שָׂשׂ וְעֹשֵׂה צֶדֶק בִּדְרָכֶיךָ יִזְכְּרוּךָ הֵן אָתָּה קָצַפְתָּ וַנֶּחֱטָא בָהֶם עוֹלָם וְנִוָּשֵׁע" — You have smitten and become angry at the very ones who rejoice in doing righteousness in Your ways; yet through this, the world will be saved.

### Sameach BeYissurin

*Amar Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi*: *kol hasameach beyissurin sheba'in alav meivi yeshua la'olam* — whoever rejoices in the afflictions that befall him brings salvation to the world. *Shenemar bahem olam venivashea* — through the very anger and smiting, salvation comes.

This teaching functions on two levels. On one level, it addresses those who might be deterred from righteousness by the prospect of exacting divine judgment — the answer is that there is a larger salvific meaning. On another level, it addresses the problem of *tzadik ve-ra lo* — the righteous who suffer. The suffering of a *tzadik* is not arbitrary; God holds that person to a standard of perfect accounting, and in the end it all works out in the divine reckoning.

It is worth noting here that this *masechet* is not principally about *teshuvah*. While *teshuvah* appears, the dominant concern is prayer and fasting. The question of why it does not rain is, in this *masechet*, less a question of exactly how righteous or sinful people are and more a question of the *relationship* — whether the people are reaching out to God or not. That framing alleviates some of the tension raised by the *tzadik vera lo* problem: if the issue of rain is primarily relational rather than strictly retributive, then the contradictions introduced by righteous suffering are somewhat less severe.

---

## Holida & Pekida

### Atzrat HaShamayim

*Amar Reish Lakish*: *mai de-chtiv ve-atzart hashamayim* — what is meant by the verse in which God will close up the heavens? *Besha'ah shehashamayim ne'etzarin milehorid tal u-matar* — when the heavens are closed from bringing rain — *domeh le'isha shemechabelet ve'eina yoledet* — it is like a woman undergoing the pains of labor and unable to give birth.

*Rashi* connects this image to sin — it is difficult for the world because of *cheit*. But that connection is not self-evident from the imagery. If the heavens are straining and unable to deliver, the more natural reading is not divine punishment but divine longing: God wants to bring the rain, is in pain, and is unable to deliver. The image speaks powerfully to the idea of God's desire to connect with Israel, the suffering that results when that connection is blocked, and the relationship itself as the central concern.

### Atzira & Leida

*Vehainu de-amar Reish Lakish mishum Bar Kappara*: the same word *atzira* — closing, being held back — is used both in the context of rain and in the context of women; and the same word *leida* — birth — is used in both contexts as well. *Ne-emra atzira be-isha*: "כִּי עָצֹר עָצַר ה' בְּעַד כָּל רָחֶם" — God had closed every womb in the household of Avimelech. *Ve-ne-emra atzira bigshamim*: "וְעָצַר אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם" — the heavens will be stopped up. *Ne-emra leida be-isha*: "וַתַּהַר וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן." *Ve-ne-emra leida bigshamim*: "וְהוֹלִידָה וְהִצְמִיחָה."

It should be noted that *veholidah* is in *hif'il* — the rain causes the earth to give birth. So in the *pesukim* themselves, the rain is masculine and the earth is feminine; it is the earth, the mother, that *holidedt*. The *Gemara* somewhat elides these distinctions as it draws the parallel between woman and rain.

### Pekida

*Ne-emra pekida be-isha vene-emra pekida bigshamim* — the word *pekida*, divine remembrance and visitation, is used both for a woman and for rain. *Ne-emra pekida be-isha*: "וַה' פָּקַד אֶת שָׂרָה" — God remembered Sarah. *Ve-ne-emra pekida bigshamim*: "פָּקַדְתָּ הָאָרֶץ וַתְּשֹׁקְקֶהָ רַבַּת תַּעְשְׁרֶנָּה פֶּלֶג אֱלֹהִים מָלֵא מָיִם" — You have remembered the earth and watered it, greatly enriched it; the *peleg Elokim* is full of water.

What is being remembered here is not the clouds or the heavens — it is *ha-aretz*, the earth. The earth is the feminine presence that receives the rain and brings forth life. In two of the three parallel pairs, it is the earth — mother earth — that is the feminine counterpart to the divine: she is *atzura*, she gives birth, she is *nifkedet*. The *Gemara* draws all of this together even though in the underlying *pesukim* the feminine role belongs to the earth rather than to the rain.

### Peleg Elokim

*Mai peleg Elokim malei mayim?* — *tana kemin kubba yesh barakia she-mimmenah geshamim yotzim* — there is, as it were, a chamber or hut in the heavens from which the rain issues forth. The imagery throughout this entire passage — of birth, of divine remembrance, of feminine longing and release — speaks to a vision of rain as the expression of an intimate, nurturing, generative relationship between heaven and earth, between God and the world.

---

## Rain Calibration

### Im Leshevet Letzedaka

*Amar Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani*: *mai de-chtiv im leshevet im le-artzo im le-chesed yamtzi-ehu?* Rain is not uniform; it is calibrated according to what has been decreed.

*Im leshevet* — if the rain was decreed to be for smiting, harsh and destructive, but then the people did *teshuvah* or God relented, *beharim uvigva'ot* — God will bring it down on the mountains and valleys where it will do no harm. *Im le-artzo* — if it was decreed as beneficial rain for the land, *bisadot uvekramim*, it goes to the fields and vineyards. *Im le-chesed* — if for kindness, *yamtzi-ehu berosh sichin ume'arot*, it goes to fill the wells and cisterns.

*Rashi* refines this: harsh rains (*leshevet*) are directed toward the trees, where they are beneficial; rain for the land (*le-artzo*) goes to the seeds and growing crops; and rain for kindness (*le-chesed*) fills the wells. Each type of rain is precisely targeted according to both the decree and the need. Rain is not merely a natural phenomenon but a calibrated divine communication, directed with specificity to serve the precise purpose intended.

---

## Famine & Plague

### Kafna U'Motna

*Bimei Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani hava kafna umotna* — in the time of *Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani* there was simultaneously a famine and a plague. The people deliberated: *amri heichi na'avid? niba'ei rachmei a'tarti?* Should we pray for relief from both? *Lo efshar* — that is not possible. The impulse was to prioritize the plague: *ella niba'ei rachmei a'motna v'kafna nisbal* — pray for the plague to cease, and we will somehow endure the famine; at least we will be alive.

### Yod Chodesh Mamtir

*Amar lahem Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani*: No — *niba'ei rachmei a'kafna* — we should pray for the famine, for rain. The reasoning: *de-chi yahav rachmana sova l'chayei hu d'yahiv* — when God gives plenty, He gives it in order to sustain life. God will not end a season of famine except for the purpose of preserving life, and therefore if our prayer for rain is answered, the plague will cease as well, for God gives sustenance to the living. *Dechtiv potei'ach et yadecha u-masbia l'chol chai ratzon* — when You open Your hand, You satisfy all living things with their desire.

### Nitzuma Vinvakshah

*U-minalan d'lo matzlinan a'tarti?* Where does the principle derive that one cannot pray for two things simultaneously? *Dechtiv v'natzuma v'nivakshah m'elokeinu al zot* — let us fast and ask from our God *on this*, on this one thing. *Michlal d'ika achriti* — the implication is that there is another matter as well, but we direct our petition to only one at a time. The verse from the west (*u-mimarav amri mishemei d'Rabbi Chagai me'ha*) similarly reads: "לְרַחֲמִין לְמִבְעֵי מִן קֳדָם אֱלָהּ שְׁמַיָּא עַל רָזָא דְנָה" — to seek mercy from the God of heaven *on this matter*, implying there is another matter, but only one is being addressed.

It is worth noting that the verse *v'natzuma v'nivakshah* links fasting and prayer in a single formulation — the pairing is central to the concerns of this *masechet*.

---

## Gezera & Fasting

### Lo Lemitav B'Ta'anita

*Be-mei Rabbi Zeira gezar gzeira* — in the time of *Rabbi Zeira* the government issued an edict: *d'gazar d'lo l'mitav b'ta'anita* — one may not sit in public religious fast. This is distinct from other persecutory decrees such as bans on *Shabbat* observance or *brit milah*; here the edict specifically targeted communal fasting, at a time when presumably there was a drought and a fasting was urgently needed.

### Nikblu Aleivan

*Amar lahem Rabbi Zeira*: *nikblun aleivan* — let us formally accept upon ourselves the obligation to fast, *u-l'chi batla hagezeira leisvei* — and when the edict passes, we will fulfill it. The community will make a formal commitment to fast now, to be discharged as soon as circumstances permit.

### Natata Libcha L'Hitanot

The *Gemara* asks: *minalan lach ha?* — what is the source for the idea that the very acceptance of an obligation to fast, even before the fast is fulfilled, carries religious efficacy? *Dechtiv*: "אַל תִּירָא דָנִיֵּאל כִּי מִן הַיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן אֲשֶׁר נָתַתָּ אֶת לִבְּךָ לְהָבִין וּלְהִתְעַנּוֹת לִפְנֵי אֱלֹהֶיךָ נִשְׁמְעוּ דְבָרֶיךָ" — from the very first day that you placed your heart to understand and to fast before your God, your words were heard. *Natata libcha* — not from the day you actually fasted, but from the day you intended to fast, your prayer was already heard.

### Ta'anit & Anah

The connection between *hit'anot* and *nishma'u devarecha* — between fasting and the hearing of prayer — is deeply embedded in the language. *Ta'anit* and *anah*, fasting and being answered, share a root; and the earliest prayer we will encounter in the *Mishnayot* is the *Anenu* prayer, the prayer to be answered, *k'anenu kmo she-anita*. The equation of *ta'anit* with being heard runs throughout this *masechet*.

The nature of fasting here must be understood correctly. Throughout this *masechet*, fasting has not been presented primarily as a form of *teshuvah*. Rather, fasting is a mode of non-verbal prayer — an intensification of the act of reaching out to God. One throws one's entire self — body and soul — into the outreach. The very desire to fast, that essence of self-sacrifice and dedication to the act of petition, itself carries the power to be heard. The commitment to fast is already a prayer.

---

## Rain on Fridays

### Siman Klala

*Amar Rav Yitzchak*: *afilu shanim k'shnei Eliyahu* — even if the years were like the years of *Eliyahu*, years of drought and famine lasting many years — *yardu geshamim b'arvei shabatot* — if the rain comes on Friday afternoons, *einam ela siman klala* — it is nonetheless a sign of curse, because it disrupts the *Shabbat* preparations and makes it difficult to go to the marketplace.

### Yoma D'Mitra

*Hainu de-amar Rabba bar Shila*: *kashya yoma d'mitra k'yoma d'dina* — a day of rain can be as burdensome as a day of *din*, a day of judgment. *Rashi* explains this in terms of Mondays and Thursdays — court days and market days — when things are busy and tumultuous, and heavy rain makes the practical demands of the day that much harder.

### Divine Communication

This conclusion can seem jarring after all the foregoing praise of rain as *gadol yom hageshamim*. The crops need the rain; why should it matter that it arrives on a Friday? But the key distinction is between *klala* and *siman klala*. The rain itself may be a *bracha*, necessary and beneficial, yet the fact that God brings it at an inconvenient time — when it disrupts the preparations for *Shabbat* and makes people's lives difficult — is itself a divine message of disfavor.

Rain is throughout this *masechet* a medium of divine communication. It communicates closeness or distance, blessing or withholding, favor or displeasure. Here, even when the substance of what is given is genuinely needed and beneficial, the *timing* communicates something. Not that rain on Friday is objectively evil — but that God is sending a message. Why at this moment of difficulty rather than at a more propitious time? The theological question is not whether rain is good or bad, but what is being communicated through the manner and moment of its arrival.

---

---

# Ta'anit 9

## Siman Klala & Omens

### Friday Rain Curse

The Gemara opens this section by shifting from the importance of rain — what brings it, what causes it to cease — to a series of observations about rain as a *siman klala*, a sign of a curse. The emphasis here is not that rain itself constitutes a *klala*, but rather that the timing or circumstances of its arrival can carry negative religious symbolism.
