Rain is seen as a vehicle through which God communicates with us, and even a beneficial rain can, under the wrong conditions, carry an ominous message.

Rabbi Yitzchak teaches: *afilu shanim kishnei Eliyahu* — even if the years have been like the years of Eliyahu, meaning years of terrible drought, and then the rains finally arrive — if they fall on *erev Shabbat*, that is still nothing but a *siman klala*. Rashi explains the difficulty: preparations for Shabbat require going outdoors, and rain on a Friday creates genuine inconvenience. The Gemara reinforces this with a statement attributed to Rava bar Shila: a day of rain can be as difficult and disruptive as a day when the courts are in session — the crowds, the commotion, the general inconvenience. It is quite striking that after years of drought, one would have grounds to complain that rain finally came — but on a Friday. The point, again, is not that the rain is bad, but that God chose to send it precisely on a Friday, and that timing is the *siman klala*.

### Rain Complaint

The Gemara then records a more sweeping, discordant voice on the matter. It quotes a statement that if rain were not so necessary for the survival of the world — if it were not indispensable to *briyata*, to creation itself — one would simply pray that rain never come at all. This is someone whose primary experience of rain is the inconvenience it causes. This is a fascinating outlier within the sustained discussion of rain's importance and religious grandeur — a dissenting voice complaining about the very thing the Gemara has been celebrating.

### Shabbat Sun Blessing

Rabbi Yitzchak adds another dimension to this picture: *shemesh b'Shabbat tzedaka le'aniyim* — sunshine on Shabbat is an act of charity and righteousness to the poor. The verse cited is: *vezarcha lachem yirei shemi shemesh tzedaka u'marpe* — and the sun of righteousness will shine for those who fear My name, with healing in its wings. The precise connection to the poor is not entirely spelled out, but Rashi seems to suggest that the poor, who have no field and no outdoor obligations on Shabbat, can simply enjoy a pleasant day. Unlike the landowner who dreads the inconvenience of Friday rain, the poor person can relax in the sun, walk somewhere pleasant, and perhaps even be the beneficiary of others' generosity — as one might put it, a sunny Shabbat puts people in a good mood and they are more inclined to share.

---

## Bracha Samui

### Hidden Blessing

Rabbi Yitzchak continues with one of his most famous teachings: *ein habracha metzuya ela bedavar hasamui min ha'ayin* — blessing is only found in something hidden from the eye. The verse cited is *yetzav Hashem itcha et habracha be'asamecha* — God should command the blessing upon you in your storehouse. The word *be'asamecha*, "in your storehouse," is read as playing on the word *samui*, hidden, concealed from view. The implication is that *bracha* operates beneath the surface; once something is identified, quantified, and publicly visible, it becomes harder for blessing to take hold. This is the same logic underlying the custom of saying *keina hora* — there is a concern that publicizing and pointing out one's good fortune invites the *ayin hara* and removes it from the domain of hidden, growing blessing.

The idea runs deeper than superstition. If God's blessing is to operate, it is more naturally accommodated in a space of ambiguity — where a miraculous augmentation of what one has would not require an obvious violation of the laws of nature. If you count your money and have exactly a thousand dollars, and tomorrow you have two thousand, that is a manifest miracle. But if you never measured, the blessing can work invisibly. The *Tana devei Rabbi Yishmael* states this slightly differently: *ein habracha metzuya ela bedavar she'ein ha'ayin sholetet bo* — blessing is found only where the eye has no dominion. Again, the same verse supports the point.

One might note an interesting counterreading of Rabbi Yitzchak's collected statements. Rather than asserting that God operates through supernatural hidden channels, one could read him as arguing precisely the opposite — that God works through the broad, natural strokes of history and meteorology, and that those who claim to see God's hand being specially revealed in particular events are mistaken. On this reading, the blessing in the granary and the blessing that comes with rain are both thoroughly naturalistic: when rain falls, the entire economy is stimulated, agricultural productivity improves, consumer demand rises, and the macroeconomy benefits — hence even the money in your pocket is blessed. God's blessing works through nature, not in spite of it, and the admonition against measuring is an admonition against claiming that you can isolate and quantify divine intervention.

### Day of Rain

Rabbi Yitzchak further states: *gadol yom geshamim*, great is a day of rain — not merely in the metaphorical comparisons we have seen elsewhere, but in terms of the concrete blessing it brings — *she'afilu peruta shebakis mitbarechet bo*, that even the coin in one's pocket is blessed on a day of rain. The verse cited is *latet matar artzecha be'ito u'levarech et kol ma'aseh yadecha* — to give rain to your land in its season and to bless all the work of your hands. The rain is not merely an agricultural event; it is accompanied by a general divine favor that extends to all endeavors. Whether one understands this literally or economically, the point is the same: rain signifies God's connection to the land and His favor to the people, and that favor radiates outward to all of one's activities.

### Measuring Grain

A *Tanu Rabbanan* passage spells out the practical implications of the *bracha samui* principle with great clarity. One who enters to measure his granary should say beforehand: *Yehi ratzon milfanecha Hashem Elokeinu shetishlach bracha bema'aseh yadeinu* — may it be Your will, God, to send blessing upon the work of our hands. Once he begins measuring, he may say *Baruch hasholeach bracha bakari hazeh* — blessed is the One who sends His blessing into this mound of grain. But if one has already finished measuring and only then recites a blessing that there should be increase — that is a *tefillat shav*, a futile prayer, *lefi she'ein habracha metzuya lo bedavar hashakul velo bedavar hamadud velo bedavar hamanoi ela bedavar hasamui min ha'ayin* — because blessing is not found in something weighed, measured, or counted, only in something hidden from the eye.

The logic here is precise: before the measurement, God could in principle effect an increase that would not register as a blatant supernatural intervention. Once the granary is measured and the quantity is known, any further increase would be an obvious miracle — a violation of the natural order that God, while capable of performing, does not do. The parallel to the Vilna Gaon's discussion of *tefillat shav* in Berakhot is apt: one who hears of a disaster and prays it did not happen in his house is not praying for the impossible — the Gra holds God *could* change the past — but for something God simply will not do once the event is fixed and known. The principle extends, incidentally, to the prohibition against counting people directly, which connects to the phrase *veyidgu larov* — like fish hidden from the eye, and the general principle that quantifying blessing tends to diminish it.

---

## Rain Metaphors

### Kibbutz Galuyot

The Gemara introduces here a *siman* — a mnemonic device — for the series of statements that follows: *kibbutz, geshamim, tzedaka, parnasa*. The first: Rav Yochanan teaches that *gadol yom hageshamim k'yom kibbutz galuyot* — great is a day of rain like the day of the ingathering of the exiles. The verse cited is *shuva Hashem et sheviteinu k'afikim baNegev* — return our captivity, God, like the *afikim* of the Negev. The *afikim* are identified as rain, supported by the verse *vayera'u afikei yam* — the streams of the ocean were seen. Rashi understands *afikei yam* as *motzai yam*, the outflows of the sea. More simply, when rain falls in the Negev and rushes into the dry *wadis*, it creates sudden, powerful flash floods — the *nachal* which is bone dry becomes a roaring torrent in moments. The comparison is apt: the return of the exiles, like water pouring into a desert *wadi*, is sudden, overwhelming, and transformative.

### Armies Rest

Rav Yochanan adds: *gadol yom hageshamim she'afilu gaysot paskot bo* — great is a day of rain in that even armies cease their activities on that day. Whether this means they stop marching, stop fighting, or simply rest, the verse supports the reading: *tlameha ravvei nachat gdudeha* — you have saturated its furrows, and its troops have rested. The *gdudim* here, the "troops," may also be read as referring to the riverbanks — when the rain saturates the furrows, even the armies are stilled.

### Poskei Tzedaka

Rav Yochanan further teaches that *ein hageshamim ne'etzarim ela bishvil poskei tzedakah barabbim v'ein notnim* — rain is withheld only on account of those who publicly pledge charity and then fail to fulfill their pledge. The verse cited is *nesi'im veruach vegeshem ayin, ish mithallel bematat shaker* — clouds and wind but no rain: a man boasting of gifts he will never give. The parallel is precise and direct: the *poskei tzedakah*, those who make public promises of charity, are like clouds that promise rain. There is wind, there are clouds, there are all the signs of a great downpour — but the rain never comes. The lack of rain is thus a *middah keneged middah* reflection of the lack of follow-through in human generosity.

---

## Aser Te'aser

### Tithes Wealth

Rav Yochanan expounds the verse *aser te'aser* — you shall surely tithe — as a play on words: *aser bishvil shetit'asher*, give tithes in order that you shall become wealthy. The doubling of the root *ayin-shin-reish* encodes both the obligation and the reward: tithe and you will become rich. This sits within the broader framework the Gemara has been developing — the correspondence between human action, particularly in giving to God and to others, and God's response in the form of material blessing. Whereas the earlier discussions made this correspondence through the metaphor of rain, here the equation is stated directly and without meteorological mediation.

It is worth noting what is implied by removing rain from the equation. Rather than focusing on the symbolic and religious resonance of rain, the discussion pivots to the bottom line: give your ten percent and you will get more back. This framing makes the principle immediately practical and also more easily generalizable beyond agriculture.

### Test God

The Gemara here presents a charming and instructive exchange. Rav Yochanan encounters the young son of Reish Lakish — who was also Rav Yochanan's nephew, since Reish Lakish had married Rav Yochanan's sister. Reish Lakish had already died by this point. Rav Yochanan asks the child: tell me the verse you are learning. The child responds: *aser te'aser* — I am learning the verse about tithes. Rav Yochanan explains the play on words: *aser bishvil shetit'asher* — give tithes in order to become wealthy. The child pushes back: how do you know? That is a nice *drash*, but what is the proof it actually works? Rav Yochanan answers simply: go ahead, try it — *zil nasei*.

The child's response is sharp: is it permissible to test God? Does not the verse say *lo tenasu et Hashem* — do not test God? Rav Yochanan replies in the name of Rabbi Oshaya: this is the one exception — *chutz mizo*. The verse in Malachi states explicitly: *havi'u et kol hama'aser el beit ha'otzar... uvchanuni na bazot amar Hashem Tzeva'ot im lo eftach lachem et arubot hashamayim vaharicoti lachem bracha ad bli dai* — bring all the tithes to the storehouse, test Me in this, says the Lord of Hosts, and I will open the windows of heaven and pour out blessing without limit. God Himself invites the test in this single instance.

What does *ad bli dai* — blessing without limit — mean? Ami bar Chama says in the name of Rav: *ad sheyivlu siftoteichem milomar dai* — until your lips grow weary from saying "enough." There will be so much blessing that you will exhaust yourself declaring it sufficient.

The child then delivers a pointed response: had I already reached that passage in Malachi in my learning, I would not have needed you or your teacher Rabbi Oshaya to derive it. The *peshat* of the verse says it outright. One person might read this as intellectual enthusiasm — here is a child so engaged in *Torah* that he confidently engages his uncle's scholarship. Another might read it as somewhat sharp, even *chutzpadik*. As will become clear shortly, this child may carry some emotional baggage toward his uncle that colors the exchange.

The passage about *aser te'aser* leads naturally into a broader discussion of the medieval institution of *maaser kesafim* — tithing one's income — which Tosafot cites in the name of the *Sifrei*, though this passage does not appear in the *Sifrei* we have. The *Sifrei* as quoted by Tosafot derives from the words *et kol* — "all of your tithe" — an obligation that extends beyond grain to include *ribbit u'prakmatya vechol davar shemarviach bo* — interest, commerce, and all other income-generating activities. A clear sign that this is a medieval formulation rather than a tannaic one is the very first item in the list: *ribbit*, charging interest. The practice of Jews making money through *ribbit* was essentially a medieval phenomenon. This passage does not appear in any *Sifrei* we possess, and while some *Rishonei Ashkenaz* argued that *maaser kesafim* has biblical or rabbinic force, the overwhelming consensus is that it is a *minhag*. Nevertheless, it represents a remarkable act of halakhic creativity — the transference of a central agricultural and theological obligation into a context where the original framework no longer applies: neither residence in *Eretz Yisrael* nor an agrarian economy. Aggadic statements about the consequences of giving and withholding *maaser* — that it enriches and impoverishes — serve as a powerful motivational framework for observing a practice that, technically speaking, carries no formal *halachic* obligation.

### Mishlei Pasuk

On another occasion, Rav Yochanan encounters Reish Lakish's son sitting and reciting the verse: *ivelet adam tesalef darko, ve'al Hashem yiza'af libo* — the foolishness of a man perverts his own path, yet he directs his anger at God. Rav Yochanan is struck by this and sits wondering: is there anything written in the *Kesuvim* that is not already hinted to in the *Torah*? Before Rav Yochanan can answer, the child responds for him: of course this is hinted to in the *Torah* — the verse says *vayeitzei libam vayechredu ish el achiv leimor mah zot asah Elokim lanu* — the brothers' hearts sank and they trembled, saying to one another: what has God done to us? Here are the brothers, suffering the consequences of their own act of selling Yosef, and yet directing their distress at God — precisely the dynamic described in Mishlei.

---

## Rebi Student

### Reish Lakish Death

Rav Yochanan lifts his eyes and looks at the boy. His mother — Rav Yochanan's sister and Reish Lakish's widow — comes and takes the child away, saying to him: *ta mikamei delo le'avid lach k'da'avad le'avuch* — go away from him, lest he do to you what he did to your father. There is a well-known narrative in which Rav Yochanan directed a look at Reish Lakish that caused Reish Lakish's death. Rav Yochanan, evidently displeased by the child's sharp responses, gave the boy such a look — and the mother, recognizing what this could mean, intervened to remove her son from danger.

This episode illuminates the earlier exchange about *aser te'aser* in a new light. The boy's confident, even confrontational tone toward his uncle — *I wouldn't have needed you or your teacher to figure that out* — may reflect not merely intellectual enthusiasm but genuine emotional charge. A child whose mother believes his uncle killed his father can hardly be expected to be uniformly deferential. And yet the mother herself evidently felt her son had crossed a line, since she rushed to remove him before the consequences became fatal.

The Gemara here places this story in a broader thematic context that has been developing throughout the daf: the relationship between a *rebbi* and a student, and what happens when that relationship is strained. What is striking is the contrast with how God relates to human beings through rain. On the one hand, God — as we have seen — will bring rain even for the sake of a single individual, is infinitely precise in His provision, and responds with abundant blessing to even minimal human gestures like giving *maaser*. On the other hand, human teachers — Rav Yochanan looking at Reish Lakish, and now at Reish Lakish's son — respond to perceived disrespect with devastating and fatal consequence. If there is an implicit theological argument being made here, it may be that God's relationship to human beings is characterized by a compassion and patience that human relationships, even among the greatest sages, cannot always approximate.

---

## Yachid vs. Rabbim

### Individual Rain

Rav Yochanan teaches: *matar bishvil yachid, parnasa bishvil rabbim* — God will bring rain even for the sake of a single individual, but general *parnasa* — broad sustenance and economic wellbeing — only comes when the masses deserve it. Rain for an individual: the verse says *yiftach Hashem lecha et otzaro hatov latet matar artzecha* — God shall open for you, in the singular, His good storehouse, to give the rain of your land. *Parnasa* for the masses: the verse says *hineni mamtir lachem lechem min hashamayim* — I will rain down for you, in the plural, bread from the heavens.

This distinction is notable in the context of the larger tractate. Taanit is fundamentally about communal fasting in response to the withholding of rain — rain as a communal concern, its absence as a communal affliction. Yet here we see that the positive dimension of rain — rain actually falling — can be for the merit of a single individual. A recurrent theme in the tractate, one that will be developed further, is the role of *yechidim*, exceptional individuals like Choni HaMa'agel, who pray for rain and are answered even before the community's formal prayers take effect.

### Three Providers

A *Beraita* is cited as a challenge to this principle. Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda teaches that three great leaders — *parnasim* — stood up for the Jewish people: Moshe, Aharon, and Miriam. Three great gifts were given through them: the *be'er*, the well, in the merit of Miriam; the *amud anan*, the pillar of cloud, in the merit of Aharon; and the *man*, the manna, in the merit of Moshe.

When Miriam died, the well disappeared — as inferred from the juxtaposition: *vatamot sham Miriam* followed immediately by the verse stating there was no water for the congregation. The connection of Miriam to water runs deep throughout the *Torah*, and her association with the nurturing, life-giving aspects of water is fitting. The well returned in the merit of the two remaining leaders — Moshe and Aharon — as evidenced by God's command to both of them to speak to the rock and bring forth water.

When Aharon died, the *ananei hakavod*, the clouds of glory, departed. This is derived from the verse *vayishma HaKena'ani Melech Arad* — the Canaanite king of Arad heard something and came to attack. What did he hear? That Aharon had died and the clouds had departed, leaving Israel exposed and apparently unprotected. Rabbi Abbahu adds: do not read *vayiru* — they saw that Aharon had died — but *vayyere'u* — they became visible, they were exposed, *because Aharon had died*, employing the principle that *ki* can carry the meaning of "because" (*deha*), one of its four usages as enumerated by Reish Lakish.

When Moshe died, all three gifts ceased simultaneously. The verse *va'achchid shloshet haro'im beyerach echad* — I will destroy the three shepherds in one month — is cited to confirm this. The apparent difficulty is that Miriam died in Nisan, Aharon in Av, and Moshe in Adar — hardly one month. The resolution: all three *gifts* ceased in a single month. This implies that Moshe had restored all three gifts — the well, the clouds, and the manna — during his lifetime, so when he died, all three disappeared at once.

### Moshe Exception

The relevance of this *Beraita* to Rav Yochanan's teaching becomes clear. If *parnasa* only comes for the *rabbim*, how can we account for the fact that the *man* came in the merit of Moshe — a single individual? The Gemara resolves: *shani Moshe, kivan delarabim hu ba'ei kerabim dami* — Moshe is different, because he is needed for the masses, he is considered equivalent to the masses. A leader of Moshe's stature is, in a legal and theological sense, coextensive with the community he leads. Rain or *parnasa* granted in his merit is therefore effectively granted for the *rabbim*. The principle of *yachid* applying to rain thus holds: for an individual of non-extraordinary standing, God will still bring rain, but general *parnasa* requires communal merit.

---

## Rebi Student (II)

### Three Shepherds

The Gemara now revisits the verse *va'achchid shloshet haro'im beyerach echad* in a strikingly different context — not to discuss the three leaders of Israel in the desert, but to frame an episode involving Rav Papa and three of his students. Rav Huna bar Manoach, Rav Shmuel bar Idi, and Rav Chiyya miVastanya had studied regularly before Rava. After Rava died, they came to learn from Rav Papa. Every time Rav Papa would teach a *sugya*, and it was not coming across clearly or sharply to them, they would signal one another — a look exchanged that communicated wordlessly: this is not what it was like with Rava. The unspoken comparison was devastating.

Rav Papa became deeply despondent — *chalash datei* — weighed down by the repeated experience of not measuring up in the eyes of these students. Then, in a dream, the verse was read to him: *va'achchid shloshet haro'im* — I will destroy the three shepherds. The heavenly message, whatever its exact theological valence, was that these three students would be removed. The next morning, when they took their leave, Rav Papa said: *leizil rabanan beshalma* — the rabbis should go in peace. Whether this constitutes a blessing or simply a farewell is debated. A marginal note suggests Rav Papa blessed them to protect them from the consequences implied by his dream; others find this reading overly apologetic, and the plain sense is a certain resignation to the outcome.

The episode reinforces a pattern visible throughout the daf: the rabbi-student relationship, when the student's behavior tilts toward disrespect or condescension, leads to severe and fatal results. Human relationships among the greatest sages operate with a kind of hair-trigger sensitivity that God's relationship to human beings — expressed through the patient, individual-level provision of rain — does not.

### Shimi Silence

A related episode involving Rav Shimi bar Ashi provides a cautionary counterpoint. Rav Shimi bar Ashi regularly studied before Rav Papa and regularly posed sharp *kashyot* against him — question after strong question. One day, Rav Shimi saw Rav Papa fall on his face — visibly overwhelmed — and overheard him say: *Rachmana litzlan mikisufa deShimi* — God save us from the embarrassment of Shimi. Rav Shimi now understood precisely what it could mean for God to save Rav Papa from such embarrassment. He immediately took upon himself a vow of silence — *kibeil alei shitikusa* — and asked no more questions. He chose to suppress his intellectual engagement entirely rather than risk what his questions might bring upon him.

The juxtaposition of these two stories makes the stakes vivid. Students who signal their contempt for their teacher — even without words — face elimination. A student who recognizes what his sharp questions are doing to his teacher chooses silence as the only safe path. In both cases, the relationship between *rebbi* and *talmid* is portrayed as one of extraordinary power imbalance, where the teacher's dignity must be guarded at enormous personal cost.

---

## Precise Rain

### One Blade Grass

The Gemara returns to the theme of divine precision in rainfall. Reish Lakish derives from the verse *sha'alu meHashem matar b'eis malkosh, Hashem oseh chazizim u'matar geshem yitein lahem l'ish eisev basadeh* — ask God for rain in the season of the late rains; God makes *chazizim* and gives rain; He gives to each man *eisev* in the field — that rain can come even for a single individual. The word *l'ish* — to a man, in the singular — establishes this.

A *Beraita* then refines the point further. Perhaps *l'ish* means all of his fields — all of one individual's land will receive rain even if the community does not deserve it? No: *talmud lomar sadeh* — a single field. Perhaps the whole field? *Talmud lomar eisev* — even a single blade of grass. The rain can be precise to the level of a single blade of grass. This is not simply fanciful aggadah; it reflects the experiential reality that rain can be highly localized, that one area receives rainfall while an adjacent area does not, that a cloud can drop its water on a very specific patch of ground. Theologically interpreted, this means God's providence in rain is not broad and indiscriminate but exquisitely calibrated to need.

### Garden Precision

A vivid illustration is provided by the story of Rav Daniel bar Katina. He had a garden, and every day he would walk through it and inspect each furrow: *hai mishra ba'ei maya* — this bed needs water; *veha mishra lo ba'ei maya* — this bed does not. Then the rain would come and water exactly those places that needed water and none of those that did not. What is remarkable about this account is the confidence embedded in it: Rav Daniel would make his assessment, and the rain would follow accordingly, as though responding to his survey. The image suggests something beyond mere meteorological coincidence — a man so attuned to his land and to divine providence that his judgment and God's provision move in alignment.

### Chazizim

The Gemara now asks: what are the *chazizim* mentioned in the verse? Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Chanina explains: the verse teaches that for every individual *tzaddik*, God makes a distinct, individual *chaziz* — a particular flash, a particular sign. Rain is not simply God's general gift to the world at large; within the rain, each righteous individual has something addressed specifically to him. This is the fullest expression of *hashgacha pratis* in the context of rainfall: not only can rain come for a single individual, but within any rain event, each *tzaddik* receives something tailored to him alone.

---

## Rain Signs

### Porchot Drizzle

Rav Yehuda teaches that the *chazizim* in the verse are *porchos* — thin clouds. Rav Papa explains: *eiva klisha tusei eiva smikta* — a thin, wispy cloud beneath a thick, heavy cloud. This formation is a sign of significant rainfall to come.

Rav Yehuda adds a related observation about *nehila* — a drizzle, a thin rain. A drizzle before the main rain comes — *mikmi matra ati matra* — is a sign that the rain will be good and substantial, like a sieve where the fine material passes through first before the heavier substance follows. A drizzle after the rain — *basar matra pasik matra* — means the rain is about to stop, like the diminishing output at the end of a goat's excretion (the Gemara's rather earthy comparison). In each case, the *porchot* or *nehila* serve as interpretive signals about what the rain will do.

### Ulla Bavel

Ulla once came to Bavel and observed these *porchos* — either the thin clouds or the drizzle. He told the people around him: *pnu manei de'hashta ati matra* — clear out your vessels, bring everything indoors, a heavy rain is about to fall. But the rain did not come. Ulla's response was pointed: *ke'eichi de'meshakrei Bavla'ei hachi meshakrei matra'ei* — just as the Babylonians are liars, so too their rain is a liar. The signs that portend rain in one place apparently do not operate reliably in another. But one might also note, as the Gemara tacitly invites us to, that it is rather more convenient to blame the rain — or the people — than to simply acknowledge a misprediction.

The Gemara then draws an explicit parallel: just as the *poskei tzedakah* who publicly promise charity and never deliver are like clouds that promise rain and produce nothing, so too Ulla's experience in Bavel — all the signs of rain and none of the substance — mirrors the character he perceives in its inhabitants.

### Dates Honey

A second episode involving Ulla in Bavel: he saw a basket full of dates for sale for only a *zuz* — a remarkably low price. He was astonished at the abundance and cheapness of food: *mala tana d'duvsha b'zuza* — a basket full of something as sweet as honey for a *zuz*! And with such easy living available to them, how is it that the Babylonians do not immerse themselves more fully in *Torah* study? That night, however, the dates caused him considerable digestive distress. His view shifted: *mala tana d'sachina b'zuza* — it is as though a basket of knives were available for a *zuz*, such danger lurks in this plenty. And he revised his earlier complaint: given what this food does to you, the fact that the Babylonians manage to learn *Torah* at all is actually remarkable.

The self-revision is charming, but the underlying tension is real. Ulla's initial assumption — easy material conditions should produce more *Torah* learning — and his revised conclusion — privation might actually sharpen dedication — reflect a genuine debate about the relationship between material ease and spiritual productivity. Life in Bavel was materially more comfortable than in *Eretz Yisrael*, and whether that comfort helped or hindered *Torah* study was a live question. The observation also captures an overarching structural feature of this entire daf: the constant interleaving of rain and *Torah* study as paired themes, each illuminating the other. Rain can be a blessing or an obstacle; *Torah* can flourish in privation or be undermined by plenty. Both are nuanced, contextual, and dependent on the person, the place, and the inner posture — the *kavana* — of those involved.

---

## Water Cycle

### Ocean Source

A *Beraita* now turns to the cosmological question of where rain actually comes from. Rabbi Eliezer holds: *kol olam kulo m'mei Okeinos hu shoteh* — the entire world drinks from the waters of the ocean. The water cycle as he understands it is essentially correct: evaporation from the ocean leads to cloud formation, which leads to rainfall, which eventually finds its way back to the ocean. The verse cited is *v'eid ya'aleh min ha'aretz v'hishka kol p'nei ha'adama* — a cloud rises from the ground and waters the entire earth. The ocean's waters rise, form clouds, and fall as rain.

### Heavenly Waters

Rabbi Yehoshua challenges: *m'mei Okeinos meluchin hein* — ocean water is salty; how can it become the fresh rainwater we drink? Rabbi Eliezer responds: *mematkin b'avim* — they are sweetened in the clouds. This is, in essence, a correct description of evaporation: the water evaporates and leaves the salt behind, emerging as fresh water in the clouds.

Rabbi Yehoshua, however, holds an entirely different cosmology: *kol olam kulo m'mayim elyonim hu shoteh* — the entire world drinks from the waters above the *rakia*, the firmament, which separated the upper and lower waters at the time of creation. Rain does not originate in the ocean at all, but descends from the waters stored above the heavens. The verse supporting this is *l'matar hashamayim tishteh mayim* — from the rain of the heavens you shall drink water.

How then does Rabbi Yehoshua understand the verse about the cloud rising from the ground? *Melamed she'ananim mitgavrin v'olin l'rakia* — the clouds strengthen and ascend to the *rakia*, *u'potechin pihem k'nod* — they open their mouths like a waterskin or canteen, *u'mekablin m'mei matar* — and they receive the rainwater. On this view, the clouds are not carriers of evaporated ocean water but rather empty vessels that ascend to the heavens, are filled with water from above the *rakia*, and then descend to deliver it.

### Sieve Clouds

The verse *yazoku matar l'eido* is cited: God will pour out rain to His cloud. And: *u'menuvavos hein k'kivara* — the clouds are perforated like a sieve. The water does not fall in a single rush but in individual drops, as through the many small holes of a sieve. *V'ein bein tipa l'tipa ela kemlo nima* — between one drop and the next there is only a hairbreadth of separation. The clouds thus function as a kind of celestial delivery system: filled above and dispensing below through their many small perforations.

Rabbi Yehoshua's view — that rain comes from the waters above the *rakia* — connects naturally to the theme of *maaseh bereishit*, the cosmology of creation, in which God separated the waters above from the waters below. On his reading, rain is not part of a natural water cycle rooted in the earth, but a continuous act of divine provision drawing on the primordial waters stored in heaven. It is accordingly Rabbi Yehoshua who concludes with the declaration that *gadol yom hageshamim k'yom she-nivreu bo shamayim va'aretz* — great is a day of rain like the day on which the heavens and earth were created — supported by the verse *ose gadolot v'ein cheker*, God does wonders without limit, and by the verses connecting rain and divine incomprehensibility. For Rabbi Yehoshua, to interpret rain as miraculous is inherent to his cosmology: the clouds ascend, receive the waters of creation from above the firmament, and deliver them to the earth. The discussion will continue on the following daf.

---

---

# Ta'anit 11

## Yachid v'Tzibur Intro

### Opening & Dedication

We dedicate the learning of this *daf* for the well-being of the kidnapped teenagers and pray that they return safely to their families.

### Yachid/Tzibur Theme

Before turning to the material of 11a, it is worth drawing out one or two important themes from the previous day's learning, as they resurface with considerable force throughout the pages ahead. A major organizing theme of this *masechet* is the dynamic between *yachid* and *tzibbur* — the individual and the community. This tension appears already in the earlier *Mishnah*, where Rabban Gamliel holds that one does not begin praying for rain until the seventh of *Marheshvan* — not because the third of *Marheshvan* is necessarily too early, but rather *kedei sheyagia acharon shebeyisrael lenahar parat*, so that even the last stragglers among Israel can make it back to the Euphrates. Here the *tzibbur* waits on behalf of even a few *yachidim* — an inversion of the dynamic we might expect, where the needs of the many override those of the few. This sense of communal responsibility toward the individual is a defining motif.

### Who are the Yachidim

The *Gemara* then raises the question of who precisely constitutes the *yachidim* who begin fasting before the community reaches a state of crisis. The *Gemara*'s initial answer — that they are *rabbanan*, the Torah sages — is, on reflection, a little surprising. After all, the figure who most captures the imagination throughout this *masechet* is *Choni HaMa'agel*, who draws his circle and enjoys an almost uniquely intimate relationship with the Almighty. He is a charismatic *chasid*, not a Torah scholar — he is not "Rabbi Choni"; he is *Choni HaMa'agel*. The *Gemara* elsewhere contrasts the *yachidim* with the *talmidim* — Torah students who know Torah and may aspire to the role of *yachid*, and about whom the previous day's discussion considered whether doing so would constitute *yohara*, a kind of religious arrogance, particularly since fasting is genuinely demanding.

### Leadership Models

But the *Gemara*'s more definitive identification of the *yachidim* is striking: *kol hara'uyim limnot parnas al hatzibbur* — those who are fit to be appointed as *parnas*, a lay leader of the community. The word *parnas* derives from *leparnes*, to provide sustenance, and that etymology is meaningful. It is about a sense of responsibility for the well-being of the community. This is a very different model from Torah leadership. The *ra'uy limnot parnas al tzibbur* is not necessarily a great *talmid chacham*; rather, even before occupying any formal position, such a person is someone who assumes responsibility, has the capacity for it, and is constitutively oriented toward the welfare of the *tzibbur*. These, then, are the *yachidim* — people who see it as their duty to act for the community even before things have reached a crisis level.

It is worth pausing on the significance of this. The *Gemara* acknowledges that Torah scholars can aspire to this role, but the definition itself reflects an awareness that there are two parallel tracks of leadership — Torah leadership and lay leadership — and that the role of the *yachid* in this context is tied not to scholarship but to communal responsibility. The *parnas* model is about commitment to *tzibbur*, not primarily about learning. One might ask whether the category includes major donors or financial patrons of the community. The language of the *Gemara* — *ra'uy limnot parnas* — does not appear to carry that connotation; it is about the disposition and capacity to lead, not about wealth. This ongoing question of *yachid ve-tzibbur*, who bears responsibility to whom and in what direction, is a theme we will encounter repeatedly.

---

## V'ten Tal U'Matar Calend…

### Tekufot & Sixty Days

The *Gemara* states that in *Bavel* one begins reciting *v'ten tal u'matar* sixty days after the *tekufah*. The *tekufot* are the astronomical turning points of the year: the two equinoxes and the two solstices. *Tekufat Tishrei* corresponds to the autumnal equinox, *tekufat Tevet* to the winter solstice, *tekufat Nissan* to the vernal equinox, and *tekufat Tammuz* to the summer solstice — all falling approximately on the 21st of their respective secular months. Sixty days after September 21st brings us to approximately November 20th or 21st — and indeed, if one consults an older *siddur*, one will find that date recorded.

### Julian-Gregorian Shift

And yet in practice today, the insertion of *v'ten tal u'matar* in *Shemoneh Esrei* begins on the night of December 4th or 5th. The gap between November 20th and December 5th requires explanation.

The answer lies in the difference between the Julian and the Gregorian calendars. *Chazal* reckoned the *tekufot* according to the Julian calendar, which accounted for the roughly quarter-day surplus beyond 365 days by inserting a leap year every four years. The difficulty is that the solar year is actually slightly less than 365 and a quarter days. The Gregorian calendar corrected for this by eliminating three leap years every four hundred years — specifically, century years not divisible by four hundred do not receive a leap year under the Gregorian system, though they would under the Julian. This produces a drift of three days every four hundred years. Over enough centuries, the divergence between the two calendars becomes significant. By the time Pope Gregory introduced the reformed calendar, the accumulated discrepancy required adding eleven days, which means that November 20th on the Julian calendar falls on December 5th on the Gregorian.

What this means in practice is that we are not observing a Gregorian calendar date at all — we are observing the Julian date of November 20th, which happens to correspond in our era to December 5th Gregorian. Because the divergence continues to grow (except in years divisible by four hundred, which do not diverge — hence the start date remained December 5th across the year 2000), by the year 2100 the accumulated drift will shift the observance to December 6th.

This raises a genuine question that does not have a fully satisfying answer: why have we enshrined the secular date rather than the astronomical reality? The *tekufot* are phenomena of sun and season, not artifacts of any secular calendar system. The natural approach would be to calculate sixty days from the actual autumnal equinox and begin saying *v'ten tal u'matar* on approximately November 20th by the Gregorian reckoning — which is where the astronomical *tekufah* actually falls. The fact that we instead track the Julian date means we have, in effect, enshrined a historical calendar convention rather than the underlying astronomical fact.

### Rosh's Spain Case

This brings us to a famous *teshuvah* of the *Rosh*. When the *Rosh* arrived in Toledo, Spain, he encountered a striking scene: the community was engaged in special *tefillot* for rain and *ta'aniot* for rain — every practice described in this *masechet* — because it had not rained and rain was desperately needed. And yet they were not saying *v'ten tal u'matar*, because sixty days after the *tekufah* had not yet arrived. The *Rosh* expressed astonishment. This, he insisted, is not a dispute between the *Bavli* and the *Yerushalmi* in which we follow the *Bavli* as the more authoritative text. The very reason the *Gemara* fixes the date at sixty days after the *tekufah* is because that is when *Bavel* begins to need rain. In Spain, rain is needed at a much earlier point — closer to the schedule of *Eretz Yisrael* than of *Bavel* — and this is not an anomalous year but the regular pattern of the climate. The *Rosh* therefore ruled that in Spain, *v'ten tal u'matar* should be inserted whenever the season in that land typically requires rain, not sixty days after the *tekufah*.

His summary of the community's response is memorable: *tzovei'ach k'kruchiya velo ashgechu bi* — "I screeched like a crane and no one paid attention to me." This is, one might note, a certain comfort to any rabbi who has ever struggled to persuade a community of a straightforward halachic position in its own best interest. The *Rosh* — of his stature, on a matter of pure logic and clear halachic reasoning — was simply ignored. The community was not going to change what they had always done. *L'halacha*, regrettably or ironically, the community prevailed: we do not rule like the *Rosh*. The one echo of his position that does survive in *halacha* is the following: if one is living in a country that needs rain earlier than sixty days after the *tekufah* and one forgot and accidentally inserted *v'ten tal u'matar* earlier, one need not repeat *Shemoneh Esrei*. That is the degree to which we rule like the *Rosh*.

### Prayer to Liturgy Shift

This discussion points toward something deeper about how the character of *tefillah* has shifted over time. The *masechet* is built on a vision of rain as the expression of God's living relationship to the land and to the people — a relationship that is responsive and dynamic. The sequence of the *Mishnah* is almost urgent: begin praying on *zayin Marheshvan*; if rain has not come by *yud-zayin*, it is time to escalate. There is an implicit confidence in the efficaciousness of prayer, an assumption of divine responsiveness.

What the story of the *Rosh* in Toledo illustrates is that this vision has given way to something quite different: a fixed liturgy, a calendar date in the *siddur*, a practice defined by the *Mishnah Berurah*. The community that desperately needed rain and was fasting for it was nonetheless treating *v'ten tal u'matar* as a liturgical formula to be recited on its appointed date, disconnected from whether rain was actually needed. The shift from prayer as responsive communication with God toward fixed liturgy is one that this *masechet* makes us feel acutely. Part of what drives this shift, it should be noted, is geography and agriculture. *Bavel* was irrigated by rivers and was not rain-dependent in the same way as *Eretz Yisrael* or the Mediterranean lands of Spain and the Levant. In an irrigation-based agricultural system, rain is less existentially urgent, and that may be precisely where the practice of *v'ten tal u'matar* begins to feel more like liturgy and less like a genuine cry of need.

---

## Perishah Min Tzibur

### Mar'iv Atzmo Famine

We now return to the *yachid* and *tzibbur* theme directly, picking up at the top of 11a. The *Gemara* cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *kol hamar'iv atzmo bishnei ra'avon, nitzal mimitah meshunah* — anyone who causes himself to go hungry in a time of famine is saved from an unnatural death. This does not mean one literally starves; it means that even if one has food and resources, one eats sparingly, identifying with the community's suffering rather than insulating oneself from it. The *Gemara* derives this from the verse *birav padekha mimavet* — in famine He has redeemed you from death. The *Gemara* reads the unusual formulation *birav* not as "from famine" but as containing the root *mar'iv*, hungering: in the merit of causing oneself to go hungry during the years of famine, one is saved from an unnatural death.

The theme is unmistakable: here is the *yachid* who could insulate himself from the community's suffering but who chooses instead to place himself within it — not merely emotionally but in concrete behavior.

### Tashmish Hamitah Ban

*Reish Lakish* extends this principle beyond food: *assur l'adam leshamesh mitato bishnei ra'avon* — it is forbidden to engage in *tashmish hamitah* during years of famine. The verse adduced is the one describing Yosef's two sons: they were born before the period of famine arrived, but once the famine came, no more. There is a parallel here to the earlier material — just as there is *ta'anit* in the sense of *mar'iv atzmo*, so too there is the prohibition of *tashmish hamitah*, a further way of denying oneself pleasures in solidarity with communal suffering, and perhaps also an acknowledgment that bringing more mouths into the world at such a time reflects an indifference to what is happening around one.

However, a *braisa* qualifies this: *chasochei banim* — those who have not yet fulfilled the obligation of having children — are permitted *tashmish hamitah* even during famine years. This exception reflects the ongoing tension between individual need and communal obligation. The profound personal need of *peru u'revu* is not simply overridden by the imperative of identifying with the community's suffering. The balance between *yachid* and *tzibbur* here is not absolute; particular individual circumstances can and must be weighed.

### Heavenly Angels Declare

The *Gemara* continues with a *braisa*: *bizman she'Yisrael sheruyim be'tza'ar u'peirash echad mehen* — when Israel is dwelling in suffering and one individual separates himself from them, the two heavenly angels that accompany every person come and place their hands upon his head, and declare: *ploni zeh she'peirash min ha'tzibbur, al yeira'eh be'nechamas ha'tzibbur* — this person who has separated himself from the community shall not see the community's consolation.

### Must Participate Tzaar

A second *braisa* shifts from pronouncement to imperative: *bizman she'hatzibbur sharui be'tza'ar, al yomar adam: eilech le'veisi ve'ochal ve'eshteh ve'shalom alayich nafshi* — when the community is in suffering, a person may not say "I will go home and eat and drink and be at peace." The verse invoked against one who does this — *ve'hineh sason ve'simcha, harog bakar ve'shachot tzon, achol basar u'shasos yayin, achol u'shaseh ki machar namus*, "and behold, joy and gladness, slaughtering cattle and killing sheep, eating meat and drinking wine: let us eat and drink for tomorrow we die" — is followed immediately by *ve'niglah be'oznei Hashem Tze-vaos, im yechupar he'avon hazeh lachem ad temusun*: this sin will not be atoned until you die. The severity is notable: *perishah min ha'tzibbur* through self-indulgence is placed among those sins for which one has no portion in *olam ha'ba*, the whole notion of *ein lo chelek le'olam ha'ba* rooted in the act of cutting oneself off from the community — which is, the *Gemara* notes, precisely what *kareis* means: *nichras me'amecha*, cut off from your people. The ultimate punishment is this very severance from the community.

The *Gemara* then sharpens the distinction. What was just described — going home to eat and drink while others suffer — represents *middas beinonim*, the level of average sinners. The truly wicked, *middas resha'im*, are characterized differently: *esu ve'ekcha yayin venisbe'a shechar vehaya kaze yom machar* — "come, let us take wine and drink deeply of strong drink, and tomorrow will be like today." Rashi distinguishes the two: in the first case, the verse says *machar namus*, "tomorrow we die" — the person indulges out of genuine fear of death, a kind of desperate hedonism born of anxiety. In the second case, there is no such fear; the person simply wants to revel without any sense of mortality or urgency. That unqualified self-indulgence is what marks the *rasha*. The verse that follows — *hatzadik avad ve'ein ish sam al lev ki mipnei hara ne'esaf hatzadik* — tells us that the sins of such a person cause even the *tzadikim* in the community to die. Rashi reads this as meaning that the *tzadikim* who could have prayed on behalf of the community are taken away. And here again the *yachid* dimension reasserts itself: it is the *tzadik*, the *yachid*, who could come to the defense of the *tzibbur* — and the self-serving individual's sin undermines even that resource.

### Moshe's Example

Rather than separation, says the *Gemara*: *yetzayer adam atzmo im ha'tzibbur* — a person must afflict himself together with the community, *shekein matzinu be'Moshe Rabbeinu*, as we find with Moshe. During the war against Amalek, they brought Moshe a stone to sit on. Did Moshe not have a cushion or a blanket? The *Gemara* explains: Moshe said, *ho'il ve'Yisrael shruyim be'tza'ar, af ani eheyeh imahem be'tza'ar* — since Israel is in pain, I too will be with them in their pain. One does not sit at home watching on television in comfortable detachment; one finds ways to genuinely participate in communal suffering.

### See Consolation

*Vechol hametzayer atzmo im ha'tzibbur, zocha vero'eh be'nechamas ha'tzibbur* — whoever afflicts himself together with the community will merit to see the community's consolation.

One might then ask: what if a person simply performs the public gestures of participation — fasting and praying with the community — while privately withdrawing? Who will testify to the inner reality?

### House Stones Testify

The *Gemara* answers: *avnei beiso shel adam vekoros beiso shel adam me'idim bo* — the stones of a person's house and the beams of his house will testify against him. The verse cited is *ki even mikir tiz'ak, vechafis mei'etz ya'anena* — the stone will cry out from the wall, and the beam (*chafis*, which Rashi explains as the stones inserted between wood to provide stability) will answer it. Whatever one imagines is concealed within the privacy of the home will somehow be brought into the public sphere. The very structure of the house that enables the privacy of one's separation becomes the instrument of its exposure.

### Witnesses of Separation

The *Gemara* adds further witnesses. The school of Rabbi Shila teaches that the two heavenly angels who accompany a person throughout his life testify against him, as the verse says: *ki malachav yetzaveh lach* — God commands His angel concerning you. Rabbi Chalafta says it is a person's own soul that testifies against him: *mishocheves cheikecha shmor pischei ficha* — from what lies in your bosom, guard the openings of your mouth. And still another opinion holds that a person's own limbs testify against him: *atem eidai neum Hashem* — you are My witnesses, declares God.

The accumulation of witnesses is striking: the heavenly angels, the soul, the very limbs — all testify against private separation from communal suffering. There may be something deeper being said here. The point is not only that one's private behavior will eventually be made public by miraculous means, though the image of the house stones crying out gestures in that direction. Perhaps the stronger claim is that such separation creates a fracture within the person himself — a gap between the self one presents and the self one inhabits, between *neshamah* and action, between *evarim* and integrity. One cannot truly separate oneself from the community without it fracturing something within.

### El Emunah Theodicy

The *Gemara* now touches on the theodicy theme that runs throughout *Masechet Taanit*. From *Ha'azinu*: *el emunah ve'ein avel* — a God of faithfulness, there is no perversion. The *Gemara* explains: just as the wicked are punished in *olam ha'ba* even for small sins, so too the righteous are punished in this world even for small sins. And just as the righteous receive reward in *olam ha'ba* even for small *mitzvot*, so too the wicked receive reward in this world even for small *mitzvot*. God is *tzadik veyashar* — righteous and upright.

This is *Chazal*'s approach to theodicy, and it is worth noting how it intersects with the themes of *Taanit*. The *masechet* is not primarily organized around the question of sin and *teshuvah*; its primary concern is the relationship between Israel and God, expressed through rain and prayer, through crying out and being heard. And yet theodicy cannot be avoided here, because the empirical world does not straightforwardly confirm the biblical promise that observance brings rain and sin brings drought. *Chazal*'s resolution is to push the full accounting to *olam ha'ba*. The *resha'im* prosper in this world because they are receiving their reward for small *mitzvot* — the ledger is being cleared so they can be fully accountable for their *aveirot* in *olam ha'ba*. The *tzadikim* suffer in this world because their minor *aveirot* are being paid off here so they can receive their full reward in *olam ha'ba*. That is *el emunah*: the account is always perfectly balanced, even if the settlement happens across two worlds rather than one.

### Deeds Enumerated Death

The passage concludes with a striking image: *besha'at ptirato shel adam le'beit olamo, kol ma'asav mifratim lefanav* — at the time of a person's death, all his deeds are enumerated before him. The angels say to him: *kach vekach asita, bimkom ploni, beyom ploni* — here is what you did, in this place, at this time. And he must say *hein* — yes. He must sign, as the verse says: *beyad kol adam yachtom* — in every person's hand it is sealed. And not only does he admit to everything, but *matzdik alav et hadin* — he accepts the justice of the judgment against him: *yafe dantuni*, you have judged me correctly, *lema'an tizdak bidvarecha* — that God may be found righteous in His word.

It is a sobering image. At the moment of death, every deed performed in private, every act of separation from the community, will be played back — and one will have to acknowledge it all and affirm the justice of what follows. In this way the image of death's accounting serves as the ultimate rejoinder to the person who asks *mi me'id bi* — who will testify against me? The answer is: you yourself, your soul, your limbs, the angels, the stones of your house — and ultimately, your own voice.

---

## Fasting as Sin

### Hayoshev B'Ta'anit

With the preceding discussion behind us — the dangers of separation from communal suffering, the imperative to identify with the community — the *Gemara* pivots to Shmuel's remarkable statement: *kol hayoshev be'ta'anit nikra choteh* — anyone who sits in a fast is called a sinner.

This is a striking formulation in a *masechet* devoted in large measure to the practice of fasting. The qualifier embedded in the word *hayoshev* — one who sits in a fast, habitually, regularly — is important. This is not a statement about the single communal fast undertaken in times of drought; it is a statement about the individual who makes fasting a regular personal practice.

### Asceticism Holy

Shmuel's view follows the opinion of Rabbi Elazar haKappar, who asks: what does the Torah mean when it says, with respect to the *nazir*, *vechiper alav me'asher chata al hanefesh* — he shall atone for him, for he sinned upon the soul? With which soul did the *nazir* sin? Rabbi Elazar haKappar answers: *shetzi'er atzmo min hayayin* — he sinned against his own soul by depriving himself of wine. And if this person who deprived himself only of wine is called a sinner, a *kal vachomer* follows: one who denies himself all things is all the more so a sinner.

A parenthetical observation is in order here. The *nazir*'s abstention from wine is often read through the lens of asceticism, and the *Gemara* uses this *kal vachomer* in precisely that spirit. But one might question whether the *nazir*'s relationship to wine is really about pleasure-denial at all. Wine intoxicates; it clouds the mind and undermines clarity of thought. The *nazir* denies himself wine, but he does not deny himself all physical pleasure — wine and meat (*basar ve'yayin*) are not the same, and the *nazir* abstains only from *yayin*. There is a question whether the *Gemara*'s reframing of the *nazir* as an ascetic properly represents the nature of the practice. Nevertheless, within the *Gemara*'s reading, the *nazir* is the paradigm case for self-denial, and it is on that basis that both Shmuel and the opposing view build their arguments.

In direct contrast, Rabbi Elazar holds that the *nazir* is called *kadosh* — holy — as the verse says: *kadosh yihyeh gadel pera se'ar rosho*, holy shall he be in the growth of the wild hair of his head. And if one who denied himself only one thing is called holy, *kal vachomer* one who afflicts himself from all things is all the more holy.

### Hair vs. Person Holy

How does Shmuel handle the verse that calls the *nazir* holy? The *Gemara* explains: *hahu agidul perah kai* — "holy" there refers to the hair, meaning the *nazir*'s hair is what is designated as holy; it does not imply that the *nazir* himself achieves holiness through his practice of abstention. And Rabbi Elazar, confronted with the verse that calls the *nazir* a sinner? *Hahu desaiyeb nafshieh* — that verse simply refers to the *nazir* who became *tamei* by contact with a corpse, the plain sense of the *pasuk*, not a condemnation of the *nazir*'s practice as such.

It is worth noting that this dispute has deep roots. The *Ramban*, reading the plain meaning of the *psukim*, argues that the *nazir* ideally should have remained a *nazir* his whole life, and the sin offering brought at the conclusion of the *nezirut* period atones for the sin of ending it. For the *Rambam*, by contrast — writing in *Shemonah Perakim* and drawing on the *Yerushalmi*'s even sharper formulation, *vekhi lo dayekha mah she-asrah Torah*, is it not enough for you what the Torah has forbidden that you go and add more prohibitions upon yourself? — asceticism as a religious practice represents a fundamental distortion, one he traces to Christian influence and one that is foreign to the Torah's vision of the *golden mean*, moderation rather than denial.

### Kadosh B'Kirbecha

The *Gemara* challenges Rabbi Elazar's position from within his own corpus. Did Rabbi Elazar not himself say: *le'olam yamod adam le'atzmo ke'ilu kadosh sharuy betoch me'av* — a person should always regard himself as if the Holy One dwells within his very innards? The verse cited is *be'kirbecha kadosh velo avo be'ir* — in your very midst is the Holy. If the Holy dwells within you, denying yourself food is not an act of holiness toward God; it is a failure of responsibility toward the divine presence within you. To feed oneself, to care for one's body, is itself a religious obligation — even more, it is caring for the vessel of the *Shechina*. The theology here is integrative rather than dualistic: the physical and spiritual are not competing; the body is not an obstacle to holiness but its container.

### Capacity Determines

The *Gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction within Rabbi Elazar's views with a practical distinction: *ha de'matzi letzaro'ei nafshieh, ha de'la matzi letzaro'ei nafshieh* — the one who is physically capable of enduring the affliction without damaging his body, for him it is holy; the one whose body cannot sustain it and who would be harmed by the practice, for him it is not. This resolution leans toward vindicating asceticism in cases where the body can manage it — though one may feel that this sits somewhat uneasily with the deeper theological point of *ke'ilu kadosh sharuy betoch me'av*, which seems to argue against self-denial on principle, not merely in cases where one's constitution cannot bear it.

### Gomel Nafsho

*Reish Lakish* offers a further position, though the textual tradition here bifurcates. The standard text of the *Gemara* appears to cite *Reish Lakish* as saying the habitual faster is called a *chasid* — pious — from the verse *gomel nafsho ish chesed ve'ocher she'ero achzari*, one who is good to his soul is a man of kindness and one who afflicts his flesh is cruel. But *Rabbeinu Chananel* and *Tosafot* preserve an alternative *girsa* that reverses the reading entirely: *kol hamoneia atzmo min ha'ta'anit nikra chasid* — one who refrains from fasting is called pious. On this reading, the verse is understood straightforwardly: *gomel nafsho*, caring for one's soul and body, is the definition of *chesed* — of piety toward oneself — while self-denial is called cruelty. This *girsa* aligns directly with Shmuel's original position and represents the stronger anti-ascetic strand.

### Let Dog Eat

*Rav Sheshet* formulates this most bluntly: *amar Rav Sheshet, hai bar bei rav de'yatib be'ta'anita, leichol kalba sheiruteih* — a Torah student who sits in a fast: let a dog eat his meal. The force of the image is not merely rhetorical. The *Gemara* will make explicit what is implicit here: the *talmid chacham* who fasts is squandering something, wasting potential that belongs to a higher purpose.

### No Fast in Bavel

At this point the *Gemara* inserts a statement of *Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba* that sits somewhat incongruously in this context: *ein ta'anit tzibbur be'Bavel ela Tisha B'Av bilvad* — there is no public fast in *Bavel* except for *Tisha B'Av* alone. The reason is that *Bavel* is not rain-dependent; it is irrigated by rivers. The entire structure of communal fasting described throughout this *masechet* — the escalating regimen in response to drought — simply does not apply in *Bavel*. The only practice that rises to the level of a full *ta'anit tzibbur* in *Bavel*, with all its attendant restrictions beginning from the night before, is *Tisha B'Av*. All of which is to say that the fasting discourse of this *masechet* has its natural home in the rain-dependent agricultural world of *Eretz Yisrael*; in *Bavel* it is largely theoretical.

### Talmid Chacham Can't Fast

The *Gemara* closes this sugya with *Reish Lakish*'s definitive statement: *ein talmid chacham rashai leishev be'ta'anit, mipnei shemema'et be'mlechet shamayim* — a *talmid chacham* is not permitted to sit in a fast because it diminishes *mlechet shamayim*, the work of Heaven. This is the explicit justification for Rav Sheshet's imagery about the dog. The *talmid chacham* who fasts is not simply failing himself physically; he is diminishing his capacity for Torah study, which is itself the *avodah* — the divine service — that defines his role. The fast is not intrinsically lacking in religious value; the problem is what it costs. And what it costs here is something more important.

This brings the discussion full circle. The *ta'anit yachid* undertaken as a private religious practice — not as part of a *ta'anit tzibbur*, not as part of the communal cry to God in times of drought, but as a self-standing act of self-denial — is viewed here with considerable skepticism, and in the case of a *talmid chacham*, with outright prohibition. The *yachidim* of this *masechet* who fast before the community reaches a crisis are fasting for the *tzibbur*, not for themselves. The fast that turns inward, that becomes a project of personal spiritual achievement separate from communal need, is the one that Shmuel calls sinful — the mirror image, in its way, of the earlier critique of the person who insulates himself from the community's suffering in order to indulge.

---

---

# Ta'anit 12

## Personal Fast & Aneinu

### Eating Before Fast

The daf opens with the continuation of a discussion about the nature of a personal fast, picking up at the two dots on 11b where the *mishnah* states *ochlin u'shotin mishechashecha* — one may eat and drink from nightfall. This follows from the broader conversation about the relationship of the *yachid* to the *tzibur* in the context of fasting: whereas the concern on a *ta'anit tzibur* is that one should not indulge in pleasure while the community is in distress, here the *yachid* accepts *tza'ar* upon himself while the community goes about its normal affairs. The nature of this personal *ta'anit* is fundamentally different from the communal *ta'anit* that forms the primary subject of the *masechet*, which concerns fasting in the context of rain.

The *mishnah* establishes that when the process of fasting begins — first with the *yechidim* and then, if it reaches Rosh Chodesh Kislev without rain, as a communal fast — the initial stages are of a lighter character. One may eat and drink the previous night, and other restrictions such as anointing, bathing, and marital relations are not forbidden. This applies to the first three individual fasts and the first three communal ones.

On this basis, the *gemara* states: *amar Rav Zeira amar Rav Huna yachid shekibel alav ta'anit afilu achal v'shata kol halailah l'machar hu mispallel tefillas ta'anit* — an individual who has accepted a *ta'anit* upon himself, even if he ate and drank the entire preceding night, the next day recites the prayer of a *ta'anit*. He is still considered to be observing a *ta'anit* and says *tefillas ta'anit* — that is, *Aneinu* — in the *shemoneh esrei* the following morning, even though the fast only begins with the day itself and does not include the preceding night. Tosafot already noted that this seems to have little by way of *chiddush*, since the *mishnah* itself establishes that this is the standard form of the first three individual and communal fasts — of course one recites *tefillas ta'anit*. The *gemara* therefore has likely framed it this way in order to set up the contrast that follows.

### No Kabbalah, No Prayer

The *gemara* then presents the contrast: *lan b'ta'aniso* — one who "slept in his fast," meaning that after the fast day concluded, he did not eat that night either. To use a concrete example: one ate the entire night leading into the 17th of Tammuz, fasted throughout the day of the 17th, and then when the night of the 17th arrived, did not eat dinner. He wakes up the following morning — the 18th of Tammuz — having now not eaten for a full twenty-four hours. Yet *eino mispallel shel ta'anit* — he does not recite *Aneinu* at *Shacharis* of the 18th.

This is striking. In the first case, a person may have eaten ten minutes before *amud hashachar* and still recites *Aneinu*. In the contrast case, a person has not eaten for twenty-four hours and does not recite *Aneinu*. The reason, as the *gemara* will develop, is that he has not accepted this continuation as a *ta'anit*. It is true that he has not eaten, but because he has not formally accepted the fast from the prior day, it lacks the status of a *ta'anit* entirely. The first statement of Rav Huna was therefore offered precisely to create this contrast — even eating moments before does not undermine the *ta'anit* when there is proper *kabbalah*; even twenty-four hours of fasting counts for nothing without it.

Rav Yosef then asks: what exactly is Rav Huna's position? Is it *ein mit'anin lasha'os* — that there is no such thing as a part-day fast, and therefore the nighttime extension in the contrast case has no status at all, and one could freely eat whenever one wished, as there is no binding fast in effect? Or does he hold *mit'anin lasha'os* — that a part-day fast does carry some weight — but *mit'aneh lasha'os eino mispallel tefillat Aneinu*, meaning that while a partial fast has some binding quality, it is not sufficient to generate the recitation of *Aneinu*, which requires a full-day fast? The practical difference between these two positions is whether one who is in the middle of such a part-day fast is at all bound by it — may one simply begin eating? — and whether such a fast might count toward some total number of fasts one has vowed to observe.

### Kabbalah from Before

Abaye resolves the question: *le'olam kasavar Rav Huna mit'anin lasha'os u'mit'aneh lasha'os mitpalel tefillat Aneinu* — Rav Huna actually holds that a part-day fast carries full weight, and one who fasts for a part of the day recites *Aneinu*. If someone accepts a fast until midday, that acceptance is binding and he recites *Aneinu* at *Shacharis*. Why then does the contrast case fail? *V'shani hacha d'ika shavata d'me'alya v'lo kibla alei mei'ikara* — the problem in the contrast case is not that it is only a part-day fast, but that there was no *kabbalah me'ikara*, no formal acceptance from the prior day.

This clarification identifies two distinct components that the *gemara* will continue to examine. The first is *kabbalah* — the formal acceptance of the fast, which must precede the day itself. The second is duration — how long the fast must last to carry its weight. For a *ta'anit tzibur*, the matter of *kabbalah* is moot, since the fast is *gozrin*, decreed communally without depending on individual acceptance. But for a personal *ta'anit*, these two factors — the prior *kabbalah* and the duration — are what give the fast its status.

Rav Chisda elaborates on the duration question: *ha d'amart mit'anin lasha'os vehu shelo ta'am klum ad ha'erev* — when we said one can have a part-day fast, that is only if one does not eat anything until nightfall. Abaye immediately objects: *ha tanita ma'alya'ta hi* — but then that is a full *ta'anit*! The *gemara* responds: *lo tzericha d'imlecha imluchi* — the novelty is the case where one changed one's mind midstream. Rashi explains: one had no intention of fasting at all, but the day became hectic and one simply did not eat until midday, at which point one decided to continue and complete the fast. The problem here is that even this account leaves the tension with the requirement of *kabbalah me'ikara* unresolved. Tosafot in *Avodah Zarah* offers a more elaborate explanation, but even so, it is difficult to reconcile the two passages. The easier reading may be that these two *sugyot* reflect different conceptions of *ta'anit sha'os*: the earlier passage envisions a genuinely partial fast — one accepted to fast only until noon — while this passage envisions a full day of not eating, but one whose fast-character only crystallized in the middle of the day, not from the outset. Whether what is missing for a *ta'anit sha'os* is the completion or the prior *kabbalah* may itself be the underlying dispute between these two sources.

### When to Say Aneinu

One of the participants observed that in our practice, individuals do not recite *Aneinu* during *Shacharis*. The *gemara* itself does not explicitly address the timing of *Aneinu*, but Tosafot raises it directly. At the end of the Tosafot entry *lama b'ta'aniso*, approximately ten lines in, beginning with the word *achal*, Tosafot writes: *umefareish b'Hilchos Gedolos* — the Bahag explains *de'eino omer Aneinu bitfillat Shacharis shema nimtza shakran bitfillato de'shema lo yashlim hata'anit* — one does not say *Aneinu* at *Shacharis* lest one be found a liar in one's prayer, since one might not complete the fast. Tosafot himself pushes back: *v'li neereh d'lo nikra shakran keivan shehaya b'da'ato l'hisanos afilu ira'o ones achar kach v'lo matsi l'hashlim nafshai* — if at the time of *Shacharis* one sincerely intended to fast the whole day, why should one be called a liar even if circumstances later prevented completion?

Five lines from the bottom, Tosafot records the actual practice: *v'nohagim she'shliach tzibur omero b'Shacharis k'dei l'hodia l'olam u'l'hazkir hata'anit* — the *shliach tzibur* says *Aneinu* at *Shacharis* in order to inform everyone that there is a fast day today. *Aval yachid eino omer ad ha'mincha* — the individual, however, does not recite it until *Mincha*, following the position of the Bahag. Tosafot also quotes the Tur *Orach Chaim* in this passage, which is of course a later insertion into the Tosafot. The Sephardic practice, it should be noted, is that all individuals recite *Aneinu* at *Shacharis* as well.

On the broader question of whether *kabbalah* must be verbal, and the question of whether *Maariv* of the night before a fast that begins only in the morning is a relevant opportunity for *kabbalah* — these points will be taken up further as the *gemara* continues. Much of the detail, as Tosafot acknowledges, remains imprecise even in the *rishonim*.

---

## Fasting Until Sunset

### Sunset Requirement

The *gemara* states: *amar Rav Chisda kol ta'anit she'lo shak'ah alav chama lo shemei ta'anit* — any fast upon which the sun did not set does not count as a *ta'anit*. This is a formulation that, on one hand, imposes a stringency — the fast must be completed through sunset — but implicitly also contains a *kula*, that one need not continue beyond *shki'ah*. It is interesting that this leniency is not the ruling we actually follow in practice. Some *rishonim* do hold that for minor fast days one may begin eating at *shki'at hachamah*, and the formulation of *shak'ah alav chama* would seem to support that view. However, Tosafot and the developed *psak* either interpret *shki'at hachamah* in accordance with Tosafot's conception of two *shki'ot* — the second of which corresponds closely to *tzeis* — or otherwise understand the phrase not literally.

The question of when exactly to end minor fasts is something that various *poskim* approach differently. The underlying principle from the *gemara*, however, is clear: the fast must extend through the completion of the day; ending before *shki'ah* categorically disqualifies it.

### Mishmar Exception

The *gemara* raises a challenge from a well-known practice: *anshei mishmar mit'anin v'lo mashlimin* — the *kohanim* and *levi'im* of the rotating priestly watch would fast on the day of their service in the *beit hamikdash* but would not complete the fast through the end of the day. This apparently contradicts Rav Chisda's ruling that an incomplete fast has no validity.

The *gemara* resolves this: *hasam l'tza'arei nafshei b'alma hu* — there, the *mishmar* was not observing a formal *ta'anit* at all. Their practice of not eating was a form of self-affliction, an expression of *tza'ar*, but not a formal *ta'anit* with the halakhic status that Rav Chisda was describing. The *gemara* will return to this distinction — the difference between afflicting oneself and a formally constituted *ta'anit* — in subsequent passages as well.

### Holiday Override

A second challenge is brought from the statement of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok: he traces his lineage to the family of Sanav ben Binyamin, one of the families that, in the time of Ezra, donated wood to the *mizbeach* of the *beit hamikdash* and as a result established the tenth of Av as a family holiday. When Tisha B'Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed to the tenth of Av — coinciding exactly with this family's *yom tov* — Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok reports: *v'hisaneinu bo v'lo hishlamnuho mipnei she'yom tov shelanu hu* — we fasted but did not complete the fast, because it was our *yom tov*.

This seems to present a case of an incomplete but presumably valid *ta'anit*. After all, the *gemara* assumes that he observed some form of Tisha B'Av — otherwise why fast at all? — and if an incomplete fast were entirely without value, what was the point?

The *gemara* again responds: *hasam nami l'tza'arei nafshei b'alma hu* — here too, the family's *yom tov* could theoretically have overridden Tisha B'Av entirely; they could have eaten all day. What they observed was not a formal *ta'anit* but an act of self-affliction, participating in the suffering of the community even while their own holiday technically exempted them from the full fast. This is reminiscent of the earlier discussion in the *gemara* on 11b about *matsi l'tza'arei nafshei delo matsi l'tza'arei nafshei* — whether it is appropriate to afflict oneself — and the principle that one should not indulge when the community is in *tza'ar*. Here, he did not want to set himself apart from the *tzibur* even though his family's *yom tov* technically permitted it. One participant raised a further nuance: because Tisha B'Av was itself a *nidche* — postponed — it may not have had the same force as Tisha B'Av *bizmano*, which would make the family's *yom tov* all the more capable of overriding it.

The key conceptual distinction throughout these cases is that *tza'ar* without the formal frame of *ta'anit* is simply self-inflicted suffering. That can have its own value — particularly when the *tzibur* is *sharui b'tza'ar* and one does not wish to be seen indulging — but it is not a *ta'anit* in the halakhic sense and therefore does not carry its formal status or complete its formal requirements.

### Partial Day Fast

A third challenge comes from Rabbi Yochanan himself, who would say from time to time: *ehei b'ta'anit ad she'avo l'veisi* — I will be in a *ta'anit* until I get to my house. This appears to be a *ta'anit* that explicitly does not extend through the end of the day.

The *gemara* resolves this as well: *hacha mishum bi'utei nafshei mibei nesi'a hu d'avid* — Rabbi Yochanan said this out of concern that the *bei nesi'a*, the household of the *Nasi*, would invite him for a meal, so he would declare himself in a *ta'anit* as a way of declining. It was not an actual formal *ta'anit* at all, but a social stratagem. With that, the *gemara* has disposed of all three challenges, and Rav Chisda's ruling stands: a *ta'anit* must be completed through *shki'ah* to count.

---

## Kabbalah Requirements

### Mibe'od Yom Rule

Alongside Rav Chisda's ruling about *shki'ah*, Shmuel now states: *kol ta'anit shelo kibel alav mibe'od yom lo shemei ta'anit* — any *ta'anit* for which one did not formally accept upon oneself *mibe'od yom* — from while it is still day, meaning from the afternoon before — does not count as a *ta'anit*. Taken together, Rav Chisda and Shmuel establish the two boundary conditions: the fast must be accepted before the day begins and must be completed when the day ends. Once these two requirements are combined, it becomes exceedingly difficult to construct a coherent space for a *ta'anit sha'os* — which likely reflects the underlying tension between the different *sugyot*, as discussed earlier.

### Bellows Analogy

Rav Yosef raises a practical question: if someone went ahead and fasted the entire day without any prior *kabbalah*, what is the status of that fast?
