Rabbah bar Shila answers with a vivid image: *dami lemapucha demalya zika* — it is like a bellows filled with air. The body was filled with air, as it were — there was no eating, but there was also nothing of substance. The fast is entirely without value; it does not count, *Aneinu* is not recited, and it registers as nothing. This is a remarkably uncompromising formulation.

### Mincha Acceptance

When should one accept a *ta'anit*? Rava says: *b'Mincha* — at *Mincha* time, meaning by the time of the afternoon, though not necessarily during the prayer itself. Shmuel, the same authority who ruled that *mibe'od yom* acceptance is required, goes further: *bitfillas haMincha* — during the *Mincha* prayer itself, in the *shmoneh esrei*.

This second formulation is striking. If *kabbalah* of a *ta'anit* is essentially a personal vow — a *neder* of some kind — why should it be incorporated into the formal *davening* at all? One could simply say it. The fact that Shmuel situates it specifically within the *tefillah* already points toward a deep connection between *ta'anit* and *tefillah* that is not merely incidental.

### Davening Integration

Tosafot makes this connection explicit. In the Tosafot on *kol ta'anit shelo shaka*, Tosafot states: *kol ta'anit tzarich lekablo mibe'od yom bitfillat hamincha b'shomea tefillah v'im hu Shabbat b'Elokai netzor* — every *ta'anit* must be accepted during the *Mincha* prayer in the blessing of *Shomea Tefillah*, and on *Shabbat*, when *Shomea Tefillah* is not recited, one inserts it in *Elokai netzor*. The choice of *Shomea Tefillah* is particularly telling: why does the acceptance of a *ta'anit* — which is a personal *kabbalah* one is making upon oneself — belong in a blessing whose content is about God hearing prayer?

### Ta'anit & Tefillah Link

The answer must lie in the fundamental character of *ta'anit* as it is conceived in this *masechet* and in the personal fast as well. A *ta'anit* is not merely an act of behavioral abstinence, an exercise in not eating. It is, at its core, an intensifier of prayer — a means by which one's supplications are placed before God in a heightened mode. The formulation *lihyot b'ta'anit lefanecha*, which the *gemara* will cite shortly — to be in a *ta'anit* before You — evokes the idea of *da lifnei mi atah omed*, standing in awareness of the divine presence. Accepting the *ta'anit* in *Shomea Tefillah* is therefore not incidental; it is a declaration that the fast is an act directed toward God as a form of deepened prayer, not simply a personal dietary practice.

This connection between *ta'anit* and *tefillah* is clearer in the context of a communal *ta'anit* for rain, where the fast is explicitly an amplifier of the community's prayers. For a personal *ta'anit* — whether for a bad dream, *ta'anit chalom*, or for one's own religious development — the connection is less obvious but still present. The fact that Shmuel requires the *kabbalah* to occur within the *tefillah* itself, and specifically in *Shomea Tefillah*, suggests that the formal constitution of a *ta'anit* is inherently a prayerful act and not simply a personal resolution. The *kabbalah* also needs to precede nightfall — even though the fasting itself only begins in the morning — because the *ta'anit* is not merely a practice one undertakes during certain hours; it confers a status on the day itself. The entire day is a *yom ta'anit*. To give status to the day, the *kabbalah* must occur while it is still the previous day.

---

## Megillat Ta'anit

### Holidays & Vows

Rav Yosef now adduces support for Shmuel's position from *Megillat Ta'anit*, employing the language *dechativ b'Megillat Ta'anit* — "as it is written in *Megillat Ta'anit*" — the same locution one uses for a biblical verse, which is appropriate since *Megillat Ta'anit*, unlike the oral tradition, was a written text. This short scroll, dating from the *bayit sheni* period, lists the days on which fasting was prohibited — minor holidays of various kinds — and was later elaborated by a *scholion*. The *megillah* itself comprises only thirty-eight short lines, listing dates with a few words of explanation for each. The full text has recently been published in a careful critical edition by Vered Noam.

The last line of the *megillah* reads: *beasrin vetamnya bei atat besurta tava lihudai dela yadun min oraita vela lemispad* — on the 28th of Adar, good tidings came to the Jews that they would not be removed from the Torah, and it is not a day of mourning. And then the very final line states: *lahen inish deiti alohi yeaser betzalu* — "any person who brings this upon himself is forbidden in prayer." The word *betzalu*, "in prayer," appears in the text of the *megillah* itself.

### Textual Variants

The *gemara* quotes the relevant line from *Megillat Ta'anit* as: *lahen kol inish deyaasi alohi mikadmat dena yeaser* — "any person who accepted this upon himself from prior to this is forbidden." The question is how to understand *yeaser*. The *gemara* asks: *mai lav yeaser atzmo betzalo* — does "forbid himself" mean he does so through prayer? The *gemara* initially demurs, suggesting *yeaser* simply means a personal acceptance without prayer. However, as Rav Yosef notes, a number of manuscripts of the *gemara* actually included the word *betzalu* in the quotation itself — *lahen kol inish dyeaser alohi mikamatna yeaser betzalu* — meaning the debate was not about interpreting the word *yeaser* at all, but about which *girsa* of *Megillat Ta'anit* one held: did one's text include the word *betzalu* or not?

Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon berebbi dispute this: *chad amar yeaser v'chad amar yeaser* — one holds the text includes *betzalu* (in prayer) and one does not. The one who reads *yeaser* without the word for prayer understands it simply as *kedamran* — as we explained, a personal acceptance. The one who reads the text with *betzalu* takes that phrase to mean the acceptance occurs within *tefillah*.

### Monday Thursday Fasts

The *gemara* now turns to the *scholion* of *Megillat Ta'anit* — introduced with *detanya b'Megillat Ta'anit* rather than *dechativ*, since the *scholion* is regarded as a taught oral tradition elaborating on the written *megillah*, not as the written text itself. The *scholion* elaborates on the practical implications of the rule that one who accepted a fast "from prior" retains that acceptance even when it conflicts with a declared holiday.

The case the *scholion* presents is striking in its particularity: *yachid shekibel alav sheni v'chamishi shel kol hashana kula* — an individual who accepted upon himself to fast every Monday and Thursday of the entire year. This practice of regular Monday and Thursday fasting was evidently not uncommon. The question is: *v'iru bahem yamim tovim haktuvim b'Megillat Ta'anit* — what happens when one of these recurring fasts falls on a *yom tov* listed in *Megillat Ta'anit*?

The *scholion* answers: *im nidro kodem ligzeiratenu yevatel nidro et gezeiratenu* — if his *neder* preceded the communal *gezeira* declaring those days as *yamim tovim*, his *neder* overrides the *gezeira* and he fasts even on those days. Conversely, *v'im gezeiratenu kodemet lenidro tevatel gezeiratenu et nidro* — if the communal decree preceded his vow, the *gezeira* wins out. Both Rashi and Tosafot understand "preceded" not temporally within a single year but rather that the person made his *neder* before those days were ever declared as *yamim tovim*. Once those days are on the calendar, they are there permanently; the rule effectively means that only someone who made his vow in the year the decree was first promulgated could be "grandfathered in." For any subsequent year, the days were already established and would take precedence. This, then, is a narrow window — and really the ruling was only practically relevant in that first year of the decree.

### Making Up Fasts

If the *gezeira* overrides the individual's *neder*, what happens to the fast he was supposed to observe on that day? There is a discussion about whether he must *mashlim* — make it up on a different day. Rashi holds that the *neder* is simply set aside entirely: *yidache nidro mikol v'chol v'lo yashlim oto ta'anit* — the *neder* is deferred entirely and he does not make up that fast. Tosafot expresses uncertainty and suggests one should be *machmir*.

The very concept of "making up" a fast is worth pausing over. Where else do we encounter this idea of compensation for a missed religious obligation? In *tefillah* — one who missed a *tefillah* may say *tashlumin*. The parallel is not coincidental; it reinforces the deep structural affinity between *ta'anit* and *tefillah* noted earlier.

### Reification

But there is a further dimension to the *mashlim* concept. One only "makes up" something if there is a discrete unit to be made up. If the *neder* were simply a commitment to a behavioral practice — I will not eat on Thursdays — then a missed Thursday is simply a missed Thursday; there is nothing to carry forward. One does not "make up" a practice. But if the *ta'anit* is conceived as a thing — a unit, an object with status, like a *nazir*'s period of *nezirut* — then it makes sense to say that the unit was not fulfilled and can be discharged on another occasion. This is what is meant by the reification of the fast: the *ta'anit* is treated not merely as a behavioral practice but as a formal status, an object in the halakhic sense, that can be deferred, counted, and transferred. This connects to the earlier discussion about *neder* and *kabbalah*: a *neder* typically creates a status on a thing, not merely a commitment to a behavior. What the individual is doing when he accepts a *ta'anit* is creating the status of *yom ta'anit* on a day, in much the same way a *nazir* creates a status upon himself. That status, once created, can be fulfilled on an alternate day if circumstances prevent it on the designated one.

---

## Eating & Day Status

### Eating Until When

The *gemara* now addresses a different dimension of the personal fast: until what point in the night may one eat before the fast day begins? *Tanu Rabbanan*: *eimatai ochel v'shoteh* — until when may one eat and drink? *Ad she'ya'aleh amud hashachar* — until the *amud hashachar*, the break of dawn, approximately seventy-two minutes before sunrise, which is the halakhic onset of the day. This is the view of Rabbi. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon says: *ad krias hagever* — until the crowing of the cock, which is generally understood to be a somewhat later point than *amud hashachar*.

### Finishing the Meal

Abaye introduces a crucial qualification: *lo shanu ela shelo gamar seudaso* — the ruling that one may eat until *amud hashachar* applies only when one has not yet concluded one's meal. *Aval gamar seudaso eino ochel* — but once one has finished the meal, one may not return to eating. The logic is that finishing the meal implicitly signifies the beginning of the fast; the person has, in effect, concluded his pre-fast eating and begun his *ta'anit*, even if the formal halakhic start of the day has not yet arrived.

### Rising & Sleep

The *gemara* immediately challenges this. *Gamar v'amad harei zeh ochel* — if one finished and got up from the table, one may still eat. This seems to contradict Abaye's position. The resolution: *hasam k'shelo silek* — that case refers to when one has not yet cleared the table; the food is still present. Rising from the table while the food remains does not constitute the conclusion of the meal. But once one removes the food from the table, that seals the fast.

A second version of the dispute is then presented. Some say it was Rava who ruled: *lo shanu ela k'shelo yashan* — the rule that one may continue eating applies only when one has not yet slept. *Aval yashan eino ochel* — but once one has slept, one may no longer eat, as sleep signifies the transition into the new day. Abaye challenges this as well: *yashan v'amad harei zeh ochel* — if one slept and got up, one may still eat. The resolution: *hasam b'misnamnem* — that refers to the case of dozing, not full sleep.

### Dozing State

What constitutes *misnamnem* — dozing? Rav Ashi defines it: *nim v'lo nim teir v'lo teir* — asleep but not asleep, awake but not awake. The practical test: *d'kru leh v'anei* — if called, one responds, *v'lo yada ahadorei svara* — but one cannot formulate a coherent answer or reason. *V'chi madkru leh madkar* — if reminded of something, one recalls it. This is the liminal state that does not constitute true sleep and therefore does not seal the onset of the fast.

### Intent & Preparation

The practical *halakha* that emerges from this discussion is nuanced in terms of intent. If one woke before *amud hashachar* without having planned to do so — simply an unintended awakening — and one had not set an alarm or formed any prior intention to wake and eat, then one may not eat. But if one deliberately set an alarm, or had in mind when going to sleep that one might wake up and eat, then an unplanned awakening before *amud hashachar* would also permit eating. What governs is not merely the physical state of sleep or wakefulness but the prior intent and preparation.

This is itself illuminating about the nature of *ta'anit*. The fast formally begins only in the morning — it is a day fast — yet the determination of whether one may eat in the hours before dawn depends on one's earlier intentions and on whether one has concluded the pre-fast eating phase. This reinforces the concept discussed earlier: the entire day is a *yom ta'anit*, and even though eating is permitted the prior evening, the status of the day as a *yom ta'anit* means that once one's eating concludes, one enters the fast's orbit. The *seudah mafseket* — the final meal — is so called precisely because it "cuts off" the eating, not merely because it happens to be the last one eaten.

---

## Personal vs Communal

### Shoe Precaution

Rav Chana rules: *yachid shekibel alav ta'anit asur binedilat hasandal* — an individual who has accepted a personal fast is forbidden to wear shoes. This is surprising. A personal *ta'anit*, as the *gemara* has established, is a lighter form of fasting: other *inuyim* such as anointing, bathing, and marital relations are not prohibited. Why then should shoes be different?

The reason given is: *chashinan shema ta'anit tzibur kibel alav* — we are concerned that perhaps when he accepted the *ta'anit*, he was not specific and may have intended a *ta'anit tzibur*, not merely a personal *ta'anit yachid*. The uncertainty about which type of fast he accepted means that we must apply the stringencies of *ta'anit tzibur* in the area most publicly observable.

### Fast Types as Objects

This ruling contains within it a remarkable conceptual assumption: that it is possible for an individual to accept upon himself a *ta'anit tzibur*. How can a *yachid* accept a *ta'anit tzibur*? By definition, a *ta'anit tzibur* is something decreed by the community. Yet the *gemara* treats this as a coherent possibility. The reason is the reification of fast types discussed earlier: *ta'anit tzibur* is not merely a sociological description of who is fasting — it is a formal object, a type of fast with its own properties, that can be "selected" by a *yachid* in his *kabbalah*. One might say in one's *davening*: *hareini b'ta'anit tzibur l'machar* — specifying the more stringent variety, just as one might select among different halakhic categories of something. This is the full implication of treating the fast as a thing rather than merely a practice.

The specific properties of a full-blown *ta'anit tzibur* — as distinguished from the initial lighter communal fasts — include beginning from the night before, prohibiting shoes, bathing, anointing, and marital relations. It is this full-blown version that Shmuel had in mind when he said there is no *ta'anit tzibur* in Babylon except Tisha B'Av.

### Rav Sheshet Challenge

The *gemara* then recounts a sharp exchange. Rabbinic students came to *bei ta'anita* — the place where the community was observing a fast — while wearing shoes. Rav Sheshet noticed this and challenged them: *dilema meichol nami achol* — perhaps you are also eating? In other words, if you are wearing shoes during a fast, you might as well be eating — the shoes betray a failure to observe even the most publicly visible *inuy*.

### Compromise Measures

The *gemara* records a range of practices among the Amoraim for this situation. Abaye and Rava would come in wearing a *hapantza* — some form of slipper or partial footwear, not a full shoe — as a compromise. Mar Zutra would exchange his shoes from foot to foot, wearing the right shoe on the left foot and vice versa, as a *shinuy* — a modification that signals that this is not ordinary shoe-wearing.

### Babylonian Practice

The rabbinic students of Rav Ashi's academy went out *ki'orchayhu* — in their normal manner, with shoes on their proper feet. Their reasoning: *savri ki'ha d'amar Shmuel ein ta'anit tzibur b'Bavel ela Tisha B'Av bilvad* — they ruled in accordance with Shmuel's position that there is no *ta'anit tzibur* in Babylon except for Tisha B'Av. This does not mean there were never communal fasts in Babylon; clearly the *gemara* is describing a communal fast in progress. What it means is that no communal fast in Babylon ever reaches the halakhic weight and stringency of what is technically called a *ta'anit tzibur* — a fast that begins the night before and carries all the *inuyim*. Babylon simply does not need rain desperately enough for fasts to escalate to that level, and therefore the shoe prohibition, which belongs to that heavier category of fast, never applies.

### Community Perception

Yet this ruling creates a public perception problem. The individual who knows the *halakha* — that in Babylon a communal fast never acquires the full stringencies of *ta'anit tzibur* and shoes are therefore permitted — acts on that knowledge and goes about normally. But the community at large is observing the fast with a degree of stringency, refraining from shoes. When a rabbinic student walks into the *shul* with shoes on a fast day, it creates the appearance that he is not participating in the community's observance. This is the perennial tension between the *yachid* and the *tzibur*: the individual who knows a leniency and acts upon it individually risks a form of public separation from the community's practice — a concern that the *gemara* takes seriously throughout this discussion.

---

---

# Ta'anit 13

## Private Fasting Rules

### Components of Ta'anit Ya…

The *Gemara* on this *daf* continues a sustained discussion of the private fast, *ta'anit yachid*, returning to it briefly before the next *mishna*. Three distinct components have already emerged in the preceding sugya: the requirement of *kabbalah mibe'od yom* — accepting the fast while it is still day — the obligation to maintain the fast through the end of the day, and now a third element introduced here by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *loveh adam ta'anito upore'a* — a person may borrow against his fast and pay it back. The language is striking. It frames the private fast not as a fixed obligation tied to a particular calendar day, but as a kind of personal debt that can be discharged on a different occasion. If circumstances arise that make fasting on the designated day difficult or impossible, one may eat, and fulfill the fast on another day.

### Shmuel's Non-Binding View

When Rav Yehuda reported this teaching to *Shmuel*, the response was astonishing: *vechi neder kibal alei d'lo sagi d'lo m'tzarei nafshia?* — Is this some kind of vow, that it would not be sufficient unless he fulfilled it? *Letzarei nafshia kibal alei* — he merely accepted upon himself to undergo some self-denial. If he is able to do it, well and good. If not, he simply does not. On this reading, Shmuel holds that the private fast carries no binding legal force whatsoever. It is nothing more than a good intention, a voluntary expression of self-denial, without the weight of obligation. If it is not fulfilled, nothing has been violated.

This position is, however, quite difficult to reconcile with what we learned previously, where it was Shmuel himself who insisted that a *ta'anit* requires *kabbalah mibe'od yom* — accepting it while still daytime on the preceding day. That requirement strongly implies a transformation of the act into something with legal weight, something akin to a vow and an obligation. Why else would the timing of the *kabbalah* matter so much if the entire undertaking were nothing more than a pious wish? The two versions of Shmuel appear to be in tension with each other.

### Shmuel's Vow Analogy

The *Gemara* therefore offers an alternative version of the same exchange: *ika d'amri*, some say. In this version, when Rav Yehuda reported the teaching of Rav — that one may borrow and repay a fast — Shmuel responded not with a dismissal but with astonishment: *peshita*, of course! *Lo yehei ela neder* — it should be no different from a *neder*. If someone takes a vow, can he not pay it the following day or another day altogether? This version is far more consistent with what we know of Shmuel's position, since it takes for granted both that the private fast is legally binding in the manner of a vow, and that the specific day of fulfillment is not absolutely fixed, such that it may be discharged on a different occasion. The question, however, remains: how can a vow simply be deferred to another day?

### Types of Vows

To understand this, one must distinguish between two fundamentally different conceptions of a *neder*. The biblical *neder* is essentially a personal commitment — an acceptance of obligation — as illustrated by the vow of *Yaakov Avinu*: *vayidor Yaakov neder lemor im yiheye Elokim imadi ushmarani baderech hazeh*, and if God watches over me, I will give a tenth of all that I receive, and this stone I have set as a *matzeva* will be the House of God. This is a promise to perform a religious act. The specific date of performance is not necessarily what defines whether the vow has been fulfilled; what matters is the act itself. Indeed, God later appeared to Yaakov at *Beit El* and reminded him that it was time to discharge his *neder*, implying that some latitude exists regarding when the act is finally carried out.

The rabbis also speak of *nidrei mitzvah* — vows relating to the performance of a religious act — as a recognized category. For example, one who vows to learn a hundred *daf* for someone's *shloshim*, or to complete certain *mishnayos* by a particular date: if the deadline passes without fulfillment, is there still an obligation to follow through? The principle of *bal te'acher*, the prohibition against unreasonably delaying vow fulfillment, applies, yet missing a single appointed day does not necessarily sever the obligation entirely. The vow remains, even if imperfectly timed.

This stands in sharp contrast to the rabbinic conception of a *neder*, which is not about personal obligation at all but about transforming the halakhic status of an object. When one says "all fruit is forbidden to me," one has not sworn to refrain from eating; one has rendered the fruit itself into a *davar assur* through the power of speech — in the same way one may sanctify an object by designating it as consecrated, or render something forbidden through declaration. A *shvuah*, by contrast, is an oath that invokes God as witness to one's own conduct; its violation is a desecration of God's name, as in *lo yenakeh Hashem es asher yisa es shemo lashav*.

Some authorities have attempted to apply the rabbinic model of *neder* to a private fast, arguing that through the *kabbalah* one transforms the day itself — the way one might sanctify an object, one makes that specific day a *yom ta'anit*, a forbidden day from which one may not derive benefit. But this model does not accommodate the idea of deferral and repayment, since one has changed the status of a specific day, not incurred a personal debt. The framework of borrowing and paying back is far more coherent within the biblical model of *neder*, understood as *nidrei mitzvah* — a personal religious obligation, the act itself being the primary thing, with the date being secondary. On this reading, *Shmuel* takes it for granted that the fast operates in precisely this mode: it is a personal commitment to give something — one's fasting — to God, and like other such commitments, it can be discharged on a different day without invalidating the essential act.

### Steak Story

This principle is illustrated through a vivid episode. Rav Yehoshua the son of Rav Idi came to the house of Rav Ashi. The household prepared for him an *egla tilta* — a choice veal, considered the finest dish in the *Gemara* — and placed it before him. He did not eat. They said to him: *lita'om mar midi*, taste a little of it. He replied: *beta'anisa yasivna*, I am fasting. At this point the people at the table said to him: *lozif mar uleifrei* — borrow and pay it back! Based on the ruling of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, you can eat today and make up your fast on another day.

What is particularly striking here is that this offer of deferral was extended apparently without any special circumstance. It was not said because the man was ill, or because refusing would cause great social awkwardness, or because some urgent matter required him to eat. It seems simply that a superb steak appeared before him and the view of those present was: eat, you can fast tomorrow. This implies that the right to borrow and repay operates with considerable ease, not requiring any exceptional justification.

Another noteworthy point is that Rav Yehoshua was already in the midst of his fast. The *Gemara* does not suggest that only a fast not yet begun can be deferred; the implication is that even a fast already underway may be transferred to another day. This assumption, though embedded casually in the story, raises significant questions.

### Dream Fasting Exception

Rav Yehoshua's reply identifies the single exception to the borrowing principle: *tanis chalom hu* — this is a fast for a dream. He had dreamt a bad dream, and fasting is the prescribed remedy for such a dream. As the *Gemara* cites in the name of Rabba bar Machasya citing Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav: *yaffa tanis l'chalom k'esh l'neoros* — a fast is as effective for a dream as fire is for flax. The image is one of instantaneous consumption: just as fire burns through flax in a moment, the fast burns away the negative portent of the dream.

Critically, Rav Chisda adds: *uvo bayom* — the fast must take place on the same day, meaning the day following the dream. And Rav Yosef goes so far as to say that a *tanis chalom* may even be observed on *Shabbat*, despite the general obligation to derive pleasure from the Shabbat day, *oneg Shabbat* — so urgent is the need to act immediately. It follows that a *tanis chalom* cannot be borrowed and deferred, since its entire efficacy depends on the immediacy of the response. Delay defeats the purpose.

The *Gemara* adds a further complication: if one did fast on *Shabbat* for a bad dream, one has simultaneously violated the positive obligation of *oneg Shabbat*. The remedy — *leisiv tanita l'tanita* — is to observe an additional fast to account for the one conducted improperly on *Shabbat*. This curious solution echoes the broader logic of fasting as a transferable act: one fast to make up for another. One might also observe, drawing on the earlier discussion, that just as eating on *Shabbat* confers a special sanctity on the day, transforming an ordinary day into a fast day endows it with a kind of religious significance — a parallel way of elevating a day through a designated act.

It is worth noting here the broader theological context: even as earlier in the *Gemara* there were serious questions raised about the religious value of *ta'anit yachid* when practiced outside the framework of communal crisis, the entire discussion here takes for granted that the private fast is a religiously meaningful and legitimate act. The fact that it is placed in the category of *nidrei mitzvah*, that it requires genuine fulfillment, that there is a recognized remedy when a fast fails — all of this presupposes that the individual act of fasting carries authentic religious weight.

### Tosafos Limitations

*Tosafos* is not entirely comfortable with the apparent ease with which borrowing and deferral is permitted, and seeks to qualify the ruling. Reading the earlier formulation of *Shmuel* — that if one is able to fast, do so, if not, one need not — *Tosafos* construes that passage as providing the limiting principle for the borrowing framework. The rule of *loveh adam ta'anito upore'a* applies, according to *Tosafos*, only where the person genuinely cannot fast: *davka heicha d'lo mati mitzarei nafshia* — specifically where one is unable to impose the self-denial. Where one is capable of fasting on the designated day, one may not simply elect to defer.

This reading is difficult to reconcile with the steak story, which involved no indication of incapacity. Unless one argues that encountering a truly exceptional dish constitutes a form of inability — a stretch, even if one has sympathies in that direction — the story appears to contemplate deferral even in circumstances of full ability.

*Tosafos* further raises a question about whether an already-begun fast may be deferred. If one has already passed the morning, or has reached the midday meal without eating, perhaps the day itself has already been established as a *ta'anit*, such that borrowing against it is no longer available. The fast may have crystallized into an irrevocable observance once a significant portion of it has elapsed. This too sits uneasily with the steak story, which appears to assume that borrowing remains available even mid-fast. *Tosafos* leaves this as an open question — a responsible and reasonable reservation, even if the *maskana* of the *Gemara* seems to push the other way.

One additional subtlety deserves mention: the *ta'anit chalom* also lacks the *kabbalah mibe'od yom* that is ordinarily required to establish the legal status of a private fast. This raises the question of how precisely a *tanis chalom* works halakhically — whether its efficacy in counteracting the dream requires that it bear full legal status as a *ta'anit*, or whether some independent power inheres in the act of self-denial regardless of formal legal status. The *Gemara* does not resolve this, but it is a genuine and penetrating question.

---

## Communal Fasting

### Three-Plus-Three Fast Cy…

The *Gemara* now turns to the next *mishna*, which continues the account of the communal response to drought. The sequence established previously had *yechidim* — private, especially pious individuals — beginning to fast when the seventeenth of *Marcheshvan* arrived without rain. When *Rosh Chodesh Kislev* arrived and still no rain had fallen, the community began its three fasts. Those first three communal fasts, it is important to note, were daytime fasts only, without the additional restrictions characteristic of a full *ta'anit tzibur*. They were fasts of the community without the full panoply of self-denial.

### Full-Blown Restrictions

The *mishna* now proceeds to describe what occurs if those three communal fasts pass without result: *avru elu v'lo na'anu* — these passed and they were not answered. At this point, *Beit Din* decrees three additional fasts upon the community. The language shifts decisively. *Ochlin v'shosim mibe'od yom* — one may eat and drink only while it is still daylight before the fast begins. This is a full-blown fast beginning from the night before, in the classic mode of *ta'anit tzibur*. To the prohibition of eating is added the prohibition of *melacha* — labor — as well as the four additional forms of self-denial familiar from *Yom Kippur*: bathing (*rechitza*), anointing (*sicha*), wearing shoes (*neilat hasandal*), and marital relations (*tashmish hamitah*). The bathhouses are closed: *ve'no'alin et hamerchatzaot*.

### Seven More Fasts

If these three full fasts also pass without result, *Beit Din* decrees seven additional fasts, bringing the total to thirteen: the initial three individual fasts, then three communal, then seven. The seven final fasts are described as exceeding the earlier ones in severity: *she'be'elu matri'in* — in these, the *shofar* is sounded. The situation has become grave enough to warrant the most dramatic public expression of communal distress. Additionally, the stores are locked: *ve'no'alin et hachanuyot*. Certain leniencies are built in around commercial necessity: on Mondays, as darkness approaches, stores may open briefly so that people can purchase food for the following morning. On Thursdays, stores may open in honor of *Shabbat* preparation — *mutarin mipnei kvod haShabbat*.

### Crisis Escalation

At this point it is important to pause and observe a significant shift in the language of the *mishna*. The first set of fasts was triggered by the formula: *higia v'lo yardu geshamim* — the time arrived and rain did not fall. That is a response to a physical absence, a natural failure. The second set of three, and subsequently the seven, are triggered by: *avru elu v'lo na'anu* — these passed and they were not answered. The difference is profound. The first phase responds to the absence of rain as a material crisis: we need water, we are fasting to bring rain. The second phase responds to the silence of God: we are fasting, and God is not responding. This is no longer a material or economic crisis; it is a spiritual and relational one.

The *na'anu* — being answered — points to the hoped-for divine response to the communal fast and prayer. To not be answered is to discover that the fast has not moved God, that the relationship between the community and the divine is in some deeper state of rupture. To press the point with an analogy: if one needs something from a parent and the parent does not pick up the phone for two weeks, one first worries about not getting what one needs. After a certain point, the worry shifts to the relationship itself. The community has crossed that threshold. The stakes are no longer merely agricultural; they are theological.

This distinction carries halakhic implications as well. The full-blown *ta'anit tzibur*, with its nighttime commencement, its prohibition of labor, its closure of bathhouses and stores, and eventually the sounding of the *shofar* — all of these are responses not merely to the absence of rain but to the silence of God. The community must come together not just to petition but to grapple with its own standing before the Almighty.

The public closure of the stores and bathhouses deserves particular attention. Even in the earlier three-fast period, where *melacha* was already prohibited, the *mishna* still specifies that the stores are locked. This suggests something beyond the logical consequence of individual prohibition. It is a communal, regulatory expression of the severity of the moment: the entire street is transformed, the public character of the day is visible to anyone who walks through it. In the same way one feels the day in a city that observes *Shabbat*, the closed storefronts and shuttered bathhouses make the reality of the fast palpable in the public sphere, not just in the interior behavior of individuals.

### Shift to Mourning

If all thirteen fasts pass without result, the community enters a new mode entirely: *mema'atin bemasa umatan* — decreasing commercial activity; *bebinyan uvineti'ah* — in building and planting; *be'erusin uvenisu'in* — in betrothals and marriages; and *uvishe'ilat shalom bein adam lachaveiro* — in greeting one another and inquiring after each other's welfare. The *mishna* names this posture: *kivnei adam hanizufim lamakom* — like people who are being rejected by God.

The shift from *ta'anit* to *avelut* is arresting. Fasting has ceased to be the primary response. After thirteen communal fasts have failed to elicit rain or divine acknowledgment, the community is no longer trying to change God's mind. That effort has run its course. The appropriate response now is to accept the reality — God's displeasure or distance — and to demonstrate, through practices of mourning, that this reality is understood and felt as the tragedy it is. Just as when God told the people *lo e'eleh bekirbecha*, I will not go up among you, the people mourned — demonstrating that they grasped the weight of what it meant to be distanced from God — so too here. Not fasting, but mourning, becomes the expression of the community's recognition that it is, in some sense, *nozuf* — rejected, or at least distanced.

### Yechidim Persistence

The *mishna* adds one final and striking element: *vehayechidim chozrim umit'anim* — the private, especially pious individuals resume fasting, and they continue: *ad sheyeitzei Nissan* — until Nissan has concluded. The *yechidim* are distinguished here as those who neither began fasting when the community did, having started earlier at the seventeenth of *Marcheshvan*, nor stop when the community stops. They persist even through the period when communal fasting has given way to mourning practices, maintaining their vigil of petition and hope. They are the ones who feel the earliest tremors of crisis and the last to abandon the effort of changing the divine decree.

If rain finally falls after Nissan has ended: *siman kelalah* — it is a sign of curse. This should not be misread as a purely agricultural statement, though there may be an element of that — late rain damages rather than helps crops. More fundamentally, it is a *siman*, a signal. God is communicating something about the relationship. The verse cited, *Halo katzir chitim hayom* — is it not the wheat harvest today? — will be explored further in the *Gemara*, but the thrust is clear: rain at this point does not signal divine bounty but divine displeasure. The timing itself carries a message.

This *siman kelalah* echoes the first *mishna* of the tractate, which taught that rain during *Sukkot* is also a *siman kelalah* — rain too early, a sign of rejection. Here, rain too late carries the same negative valence. The *siman* in both cases is not primarily about the rain itself but about what the timing reveals of the divine posture. One might also notice the particular role of the *yechidim* here: they start earlier and end later, and their persistence may reflect not only heightened sensitivity to communal crisis but something akin to what we will later see in the story of *Choni Hame'agel* — the idea that certain individuals possess a special relationship with God that gives their prayers singular power, and that perhaps where the community's prayers have failed, theirs may yet succeed.

---

## Fast Structure & Meaning

### Labor Prohibition

Returning now to the *Gemara's* analysis of the *mishna*, the first question raised is one that might strike a reader as counterintuitive. The *mishna* lists the prohibition of labor on a communal fast alongside restrictions like bathing and anointing. But while bathing and anointing are straightforwardly forms of *ta'anug* — indulgence — not working is generally experienced as a *tzaar*, a burden or imposition, at least from the perspective of someone who must earn a living. Why should the cessation of labor be categorized alongside pleasures that are being withheld?

### Scriptural Source

Rav Chisda citing Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba answers by deriving the prohibition from the verse in *Yeshayahu*: *Kadshu tzom kiru atzarah, ispu zekenim* — sanctify a fast, call an assembly of gathering, gather the elders. The verse uses the word *atzarah*, which is the same term applied to *Shemini Atzeret* and *Shavuot* — days on which *melacha* is prohibited. The *Gemara* draws the analogy: just as an *atzeret* carries a prohibition of labor, so too the communal fast carries a prohibition of labor — *mah Atzeret assur be'asiyat melacha af ta'anit assur be'asiyat melacha*.

The deeper logic goes beyond the formal analogy. The word *kadshu* — sanctify — is notable. The fast day, at this level of communal severity, is being invested with a kind of sanctity, a special character that sets it apart from an ordinary day. Prohibiting labor, like the *Yom Tov* prohibition, gives expression to that special character. But more than sanctity, the prohibition achieves something practical: it compels everyone to stop their ordinary activities, to cease being distracted by their work and commerce, and to come together in shared attention to what is happening. The community cannot be scattered across its workplaces while it is supposed to be gathered in response to divine silence.

A subsequent question in the *Gemara* probes whether, by analogy to *Yom Tov*, the prohibition of *melacha* should also begin the night before the fast. After all, these fasts begin from the night before — the community does not eat from the previous evening onward. Rashi explains that the *Gemara* will later establish that the *issur melacha* begins only with the day itself, not the night. The reason is drawn from the same verse: *ispu zekenim* — gather the elders. As Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba explained, the public gathering of elders takes place in the daytime; gathering at night is not the normative mode of communal assembly. Therefore, the aspect of the fast that is modeled on the communal gathering — the prohibition of labor — also applies only during the day, even though the fast itself and other restrictions begin the night before.

The *Gemara* further asks whether the prohibition should begin only from noon, since noon is also a reasonable hour for communal gathering. The response — cited in the name of Rav Huna — is that *mitzaphra kinufya*: the gathering takes place in the morning. Morning is the right time to bring people together, and that is when the public dimension of the day, including the labor prohibition, takes effect.

### Community Inspection

The *Gemara* then asks: *heichi avdi* — how is the fast day actually structured? Abaye describes the shape of the day in three stages. From morning until midday: *me'aynin bemilei demata* — one examines the matters of the city. This is a crucial element that might otherwise seem puzzling. What do civic or municipal matters have to do with a fast for rain?

Rashi's gloss is illuminating: *drisha vachakira livdok bemaaseihen shel benei ha'ir im gezel vechamas bideyhen umefaysin otan* — inquiry and investigation to examine the conduct of the townspeople, to determine whether theft or robbery is in their hands, and to appease the wronged parties. The morning of the fast day is devoted to a communal audit: have wrongs been done? Are there debts unpaid, injuries uncompensated, people who have been cheated or robbed and never made whole? If so, these must be identified and corrected.

### Justice vs. Repentance

This emphasis on *milei demata* — civic rectification — rather than *teshuva* deserves careful attention, because it represents a particular and perhaps surprising framing of how a community responds to divine silence. The instinctive modern religious response might be to say: God is not answering because we sinned; therefore we must do *teshuva* — feel regret, commit to change, undergo interior transformation. The *Gemara* here points in a different direction. The first order of business is not interior repentance but the repair of concrete wrongs.

*Teshuva* as a concept focuses on the inner process: recognition of sin, remorse, confession, and genuine commitment not to repeat the failing. What is described here is something more pragmatic and more immediately correctable: someone was robbed and has not been compensated; a debt was never paid; a wrong was done and never righted. These are not problems that await interior transformation — they await action. Fix the wrong. Return the money. Make the person whole.

This distinction applies even within the domain of *bein adam lachaveiro*. If one damaged another's property and now pays for the damage, the practical wrong has been corrected, but that alone does not constitute *teshuva* in the full sense. Yet the *Gemara's* emphasis here is on the correction, not on the spiritual process. The world has been put out of balance; the task is to restore the balance. This is not a rejection of *teshuva* as a value, but the *Gemara* is pointing to a more immediate and perhaps more tractable first step.

### Liturgical Structure

After the morning devoted to examining and rectifying civic wrongs, the second quarter of the day — from noon onward — is given over to reading from the *Sefer Torah* and the *Haftarah*: *riv'ah deyoma karinan besifra va'aftarta*. The readings chosen for fast days are those that prompt deep religious reflection and confrontation with the gravity of the community's situation. And then, in the final portion of the day: prayer. *Mikan ve'eilach* — from that point onward — the community prays.

### Action Before Prayer

This sequencing is remarkable and worth dwelling on. In a discussion that has been centrally concerned with *ta'anit* and *tefillah* — fasting and prayer — the *Gemara* here makes clear that prayer comes last. First the community gathers. First it examines what is wrong. First it makes things right. Then it reads. Then it prays. The sequence is not: pray, and if God does not answer, fast more. The sequence is: fix what is broken, and then approach God.

### Ezra Model

The *Gemara* provides scriptural support for this ordering from the book of *Ezra*: *ve'elai ye'asefu kol chareid bedivrei Elohei Yisrael al ma'al hagolah* — they gathered to Ezra regarding the trespass of the exile, the sin of intermarriage and breach of covenant. The communal problem — a failing that had compromised the relationship between the people and God — was addressed first, examined and confronted. Only then does the verse record: *uvminchat ha'erev kamti mita'anita uvfarsi chapai el Hashem* — and at the time of the afternoon offering I arose from my fasting and spread my hands to God. Rashi clarifies that this does not mean Ezra ended his fast and ate; rather, in the midst of his suffering and with his garments rent, he turned to prayer. The prayer emerges from within the state of distress and self-confrontation, not as a replacement for it.

The verse from *Yeshayahu* read on *Yom Kippur* is recalled here in spirit: *Halo zeh tsom evcharehu* — is this the fast I desire? — followed by a catalogue of justice and compassion that God actually demands. A fast disconnected from the repair of social wrongs is not the fast God seeks. The *Gemara* enshrines this principle in the structure of the fast day itself: first you fix things, then you pray.

The example of the people of *Nineveh* (*Anshei Ninveh*) is also invoked in this context. God saw not their sackcloth and their fasting — *vayar et sakkam veta'anitam* — but rather *vayar ki shavu midarkam hara'ah* — He saw that they turned from their evil way. The outward act of fasting matters far less than the inward and practical transformation it is meant to accompany. Again, whether this reaches the full interior process of *teshuva* or represents something more structural — a community taking responsibility for fixing what has gone wrong — remains an open question, but the direction the *Gemara* points is consistent throughout.

---

## Mourning vs. Fasting

### Two Categories

Having established through the *mishna* and its discussion the broad framework of communal fast practice, the *Gemara* now turns to a more precise analytical question: what is the halakhic structure of the various self-denials associated with fast days, and how do they differ depending on whether the context is *avelut* or *ta'anit*? Rav Chisda articulates the governing principle by establishing two distinct categories.

### Avelut Severity

The first category is *kol shehu mishum avel* — any observance whose purpose is mourning. The paradigmatic cases are *Tisha B'Av* and the state of an *avel* during *shiva*. In this category, the person is forbidden from using both hot and cold water. Even cold water, which provides minimal comfort and could hardly be called an indulgence, is prohibited.

### Ta'anit Leniency

The second category is *kol shehu mishum ta'anug* — any observance whose purpose is the denial of pleasure or the embrace of suffering. The paradigmatic case here is *ta'anit tzibur*, the communal fast, where along with the prohibition of eating one also refrains from bathing, anointing, and so forth. In this category, only hot water is prohibited; cold water is permitted. *B'chamin assur b'tzonen mutar*.

### Reasoning

The distinction reflects a genuine difference in what each category of observance is meant to achieve. The *ta'anit* framework focuses on *letzarei nafshei* — imposing suffering or denying indulgences. The restrictions are about withholding pleasure, withdrawing from comfort. Hot water for bathing is a pleasure; cold water is not — or at least not obviously so. Cold water meets a basic need without rising to the level of indulgence. Therefore, within the *ta'anit* framework, cold water is not the target of the prohibition.

*Avelut*, by contrast, carries a heightened severity. As Rashi phrases it: *d'it lei tzara tuva* — there is an especially great personal anguish. The mourner is overwhelmed by grief; the community on *Tisha B'Av* is overwhelmed by the weight of historical catastrophe. In this state, even cold water is forbidden — not because cold water is a luxury, but because the totality of self-withdrawal from ordinary life is the expression of the mourning state. The person in acute mourning does not even have the presence of mind for the basic acts of self-care; they are entirely consumed by their grief.

One might have expected the logic to run in the opposite direction — that *ta'anit*, with its explicit focus on suffering, would be more stringent, while *avelut*, which permits eating, would be more lenient on other fronts. The *Gemara* inverts this expectation. The answer may lie in precisely the fact that *ta'anit* is specifically about withholding pleasure, *ta'anug*, and therefore its restrictions track the category of pleasure precisely. *Avelut* is about something different — total immersion in the reality of loss — and that totalizing immersion extends even to things that are not pleasures in any meaningful sense.

### Bathhouse Closure

The closure of bathhouses during *ta'anit tzibur*, mentioned in the *mishna*, is now understood through this lens. Bathhouses in the ancient world were primarily steam facilities, establishments of hot water and heated rooms. The closure of the bathhouse underscores and gives public expression to the prohibition of hot water specifically — it is the *chamim*, the hot water, that is the focus of the restriction on a fast day. Cold water, by contrast, falls outside the prohibition.

### Mikvah Braita

A *braita* is cited to probe the cold-water question on the *avelut* side: *kol chayavei tvilot tovlin kedarkan bein b'Tisha B'Av bein b'Yom HaKippurim* — all who are obligated to immerse in the *mikvah* may do so in the normal fashion on both *Tisha B'Av* and *Yom Kippur*. Though this is not the ruling we follow in practice, it is the position of this *braita*, and it illuminates the halakhic landscape. The fact that the *braita* feels compelled to state that these individuals *may* immerse on *Tisha B'Av* implies that bathing on *Tisha B'Av* is otherwise categorically forbidden — and since *mikvah* water is cold, it follows that even cold water is prohibited on *Tisha B'Av*. There would be no need for a special dispensation if cold water were in any case permitted.

Rabbi Chanina *sgan hakohanim* adds the evocative statement: *kedai hu beit elokeinu l'abeid alav tvilah b'paam achat b'shanah* — the destruction of the Temple is sufficient reason to forego immersion in the *mikvah* one time a year. Even for those who are obligated, it is appropriate to miss immersion on *Tisha B'Av* in recognition of what the day represents. If cold water were permitted on *Tisha B'Av*, his statement would be puzzling — why make the sacrifice of missing *mikvah* when one could simply immerse in cold water without violating anything? The implication is clear: cold water is forbidden, and therefore even those with an obligation to immerse are foregoing something real by abstaining.

### Hot/Cold Status

The *Gemara* anticipates a possible rebuttal: perhaps the *braita* is discussing a case where only hot water is available — specifically the hot springs of Tiberias, *chamei Tverya*, which are naturally heated and therefore constitute genuine hot water without the drawbacks of drawn water (*she'uvim*). If so, the question of whether cold water is forbidden on *Tisha B'Av* would remain unanswered by the *braita*. But the *Gemara* pushes back: if that were the scenario, then Rabbi Chanina *sgan hakohanim's* statement — that it is appropriate to forgo *mikvah* one day a year for the sake of the Temple's memory — loses its force. If cold water were available and permitted, one could simply go to a cold *mikvah*; there would be nothing to forgo. The force of his statement depends precisely on the assumption that cold water itself is also forbidden on *Tisha B'Av*. This strongly supports the position that *avelut*, including *Tisha B'Av*, prohibits even cold water.

One further complication is noted but left for the continuing discussion: *Yom Kippur* presents its own case. Unlike *ta'anit tzibur*, which prohibits only hot water, and unlike *Tisha B'Av*, which is classified under *avelut* — *Yom Kippur* also prohibits cold water, yet it does not fit neatly into either of the two categories established by Rav Chisda. *Yom Kippur* is not simply *avelut*, nor is it simply *ta'anit*; it may constitute a third category of its own. This question, and the ongoing question of whether the hot-water-only principle for *ta'anit tzibur* has been established with full certainty or only partially proven, will carry forward into the continuation of the *sugya* on the following *daf*.

---

---

# Ta'anit 13b

## Bathing Rules: Aveil

### Intro: Taanit vs Aveil

The sugya at the bottom of 13b continues a discussion already well underway: the distinction between the bathing restrictions that apply on *Tisha B'Av* and those that apply during *avelut*. The operative question is whether cold water is forbidden only for an *aveil* or also for someone observing a *ta'anit*, and conversely whether the prohibition for a *ta'anit* reaches no further than hot water. Both possibilities remain theoretically on the table as the *Gemara* proceeds.

### Taanit Exceptions

The *Gemara* opens with a *braita* that establishes two permitted exceptions to the general *ta'anit* restrictions. First, regarding the prohibition of *melacha*: when the rabbis said that work is forbidden on the more serious communal fast days, they said so only for the daytime — at night, before the fast, it remains permitted. Second, regarding *ne'ilat hasandal*, the prohibition against wearing shoes: when they said one may not wear shoes, they meant only within the city. On the road — *baderech* — it is permitted. The straightforward explanation for the travel exemption is the practical impossibility of demanding that someone journey barefoot. There is also, however, a distinctly public dimension to many of these practices. Closing bathhouses, closing shops, going unshod in public — all of these carry a communal, visible character. The shoe prohibition, even as it applies to the private *aveil*, expresses a kind of withdrawal from normal civic life; within the city that public dimension is operative, while travel removes the person from that context. The *braita* then adds the practical application: as one leaves the city, one puts on the shoe; the moment one enters the city, one removes it.

### Hands, Face, Feet

The *braita* continues: when the rabbis said that bathing is forbidden, they meant only bathing the entire body. But washing the face, hands, and feet — *panav yadav v'raglav* — remains permitted. This represents the minimal level of hygiene needed for basic well-being and dignity, and so it is carved out as an exception even on a full fast day.

### Menudeh and Aveil

The *braita* then states: *vechen atah motzei bimnudeh uve'avel* — the same rules and the same allowances found in the *ta'anit* context apply equally to a person in *niduy* (*menudeh*) and to an *aveil*. It is worth pausing on the pairing of *menudeh* and *aveil* here, because it echoes a formulation from the *Mishnah* studied earlier. The *Mishnah*, describing the posture of the community once all the fasts have passed without rain, says the people conduct themselves *kevnei adam hanezofim lamakom* — like people who have been rejected by God. The *menudeh* is precisely the worldly, social counterpart of that theological status. Just as God has rejected the community, the community formally excludes the *menudeh*. What the *Mishnah* calls *nezufim lamakom* finds its halakhic parallel in the institution of *niduy*. Many of the individual practices associated with *niduy* — not merely the communal dimension — parallel the practices of *avelut*. This is instructive on a deeper level. *Avelut* simultaneously expresses the grief of personal loss, the profound sense of being cut off from ordinary life, and the inability to re-integrate into the communal fabric. The *menudeh* occupies a structurally similar place: excluded, unable to engage normally with community and with God. The pairing in the *braita* thus resonates meaningfully with the *mishna*'s *nezufim lamakom*.

### Braita Proof

This identification becomes directly relevant to the cold-water question. The *Gemara* asks: *mai lav akuleihu* — when the *braita* equates the rules for *menudeh* and *aveil* with those of the *ta'anit*, does it not mean to equate all of them, including the bathing? And specifically, when discussing bathing with the allowance for face, hands, and feet — what type of water are we talking about? If we are talking about hot water, then permitting face, hands, and feet would be impossible to maintain, given Rav Sheshet's ruling that an *aveil* may not even dip a finger into hot water. For the allowance to be coherent, it must refer to cold water. This in turn implies that cold water is what is generally forbidden — not only for an *aveil* but, since the *braita* equates the two, for a *ta'anit* as well.

### Rav Sheshet

Rav Sheshet's position is stated starkly: *aveil assur lehoshit etzba'o bechamim* — an *aveil* may not insert even a single finger into hot water. This is an extreme stringency and the *Gemara* treats it as unassailable, unwilling to carve out any exceptions within the category of hot water for an *aveil*. The implication is that whatever allowance does exist for an *aveil* in the domain of bathing must be operating exclusively in the domain of cold water.

### Gemara's Resolution

The *Gemara* pushes back on what appeared to be an airtight proof. It rejects the inference that the *braita* equates *ta'anit* and *avelut* with respect to bathing. Rather — *ashe'ara ka'ei* — the equation only concerns the rest of the listed practices, not the bathing. The problem with this resolution is apparent. Of the three cases listed in the *braita* — *melacha*, shoes, and bathing — the *melacha* exception (permitted at night) does not actually apply to an *aveil*, whose prohibition of *melacha* is not confined to daytime. So the equation is not even accurate for all of "the rest." *Rashi* and *Tosafot* attempt to invoke *sichah* (anointing) as a fourth item that could be equated, but anointing was not mentioned in the *braita* at all. The resolution is, as the *Gemara* itself seems to sense, strained. The simple reading of the *braita* is that *avelut* and *ta'anit* are being compared on the question of bathing. The cumulative force of the evidence — the *braita* here, and the earlier discussion about the problem of going to the *mikveh* on *Tisha B'Av*, which strongly suggests that cold water is forbidden — pushes toward the conclusion that cold water is *assur* whether for a *ta'anit* or for an *aveil*. The *Gemara*, however, continues to maneuver, keeping alive the possibility that a *ta'anit* forbids only hot water while *avelut* extends the prohibition to cold water.

---

## Cold Water Evidence

### Rabi Yosi Story

The *Gemara* introduces a story: Rabi Abba HaKohen citing Rabi Yosi HaKohen reported that there was an incident in which the children of Rabi Yosi ben Rabi Chanina all died — a terrible tragedy, likely from some disease or plague — and Rabi Yosi ben Rabi Chanina bathed in cold water throughout the entire *shiva*. This appears to be direct evidence that cold water is permitted for an *aveil*, apparently contradicting the position being developed.

### Multiple Mournings

The *Gemara* deflects the proof immediately: *hatam keshetakfuhu avalav havay* — that was a special case where multiple mourning periods had piled up one after another. A *braita* is cited in support: if a person's *aveluyot* come in rapid succession — *takfuhu avalav zeh achar zeh*, Heaven forbid — certain leniencies are granted. If his hair has grown heavy from weeks of not cutting, he may lighten it with a razor. If his clothes are filthy, he may launder them in water. Rav Chisda specifies the limits precisely: a razor, not scissors; water without soap or cleansing agents such as sand (*neter* or *chol*). By analogy, someone in such exceptional circumstances might be permitted to bathe in cold water, but this in no way represents the general rule. Indeed, the very framing of the story — emphasizing the exceptional nature of overlapping mournings — underscores that an *aveil* ordinarily may not bathe in cold water.

### Hair & Clothes Care

The *braita* and Rav Chisda's gloss articulate a carefully calibrated set of allowances. The razor but not scissors distinction reflects a principle of minimal intervention: enough relief to prevent the person from being incapacitated by physical discomfort, but not so much as to constitute normal grooming. Similarly, water without detergents permits basic laundering without the comfort of clean, fresh-smelling clothes that full laundering would produce. These calibrations reveal the underlying logic: *avelut* restrictions are designed to impose a real degree of withdrawal from normal bodily care, with targeted relief only where the situation has become literally unmanageable.

### Rava's Position

At this point, Rava stakes out a strikingly different position: *avel mutar lirchotz betzonen kol shiva* — an *aveil* is permitted to bathe in cold water for all seven days of mourning. This directly contradicts the trajectory of the discussion as it had been developing, and the *Gemara* notes the challenge this poses against the evidence considered thus far.

### Meat & Wine Analogy

Rava grounds his position in a pointed analogy: *midi dehavay abisra vechamra* — the same principle that governs meat and wine. The argument is that *avelut* is not fundamentally about physical suffering, *tzaar*. If it were, meat and wine would be forbidden for an *aveil* — and yet they are not. An *aveil* is permitted to eat meat and drink wine throughout the *shiva*. Therefore, the logic of denying cold water on grounds of imposing *tzaar* collapses: the practices of *avelut* must be serving some other purpose. Rather than expressing physical self-affliction, *avelut* might be understood as a total withdrawal from normal engagement with society — a focus so complete that ordinary distraction falls away — without necessarily requiring the positive infliction of pain. If that is the framework, then the relevant prohibition is hot water, which is a genuine indulgence, not cold water, which is not. This is a genuinely fascinating position, and the *Gemara* will now test it against the available evidence.

---

## Bogeret Proof

### Bogeret Concern

The *Gemara* challenges Rava's position with a *meitivei* from a *braita*: *ein habogeret resha'ah lenabbel atzmah bimei avel aviha* — a *bogeret*, a young woman of mature age who has not yet married, may not make herself repulsive during the *shiva* for her father. The term *bogeret* designates a girl who has passed the age of twelve and a half; she is at marriageable age and still unmarried. The *braita* then adds that the *na'ara* — the younger girl, not yet twelve and a half but already obligated in *avelut* — is permitted or in fact required to conduct herself in the standard manner of *avelut*, which would include all the normal forms of self-neglect. The implication is that a special dispensation is being extended to the *bogeret*: because she needs to present herself as marriageable, and *shiva* visits bring many potential matches through the house, she cannot afford to make herself look disheveled or repulsive in the ways that *avelut* ordinarily demands. It is also worth noting, as was pointed out, that the heightened concern for the *bogeret*'s marriage prospects at this specific moment is likely sharpened by the fact that her father has just died — he was presumably the one who would have been arranging and facilitating her match.

### Hot Water Analysis

The *Gemara* now investigates what exactly this dispensation for the *bogeret* involves. If it concerns bathing in hot water — meaning the *braita* is saying the *bogeret* may not deprive herself of hot water bathing as other *aveilim* do — this is immediately untenable. Rav Chisda's ruling stands: an *aveil* may not insert even a finger into hot water. Given the extreme nature of that prohibition, the *Gemara* is unwilling to entertain the possibility that any leniency would be extended to the *bogeret* with respect to hot water. Surely the *braita* cannot be saying that.

### Cold Water Exception

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *ela lav betzonen* — the *braita* must be discussing cold water. The general rule is that cold water is forbidden for an *aveil*; the *bogeret* is granted a special exception to this rule precisely because of her marriage-related circumstances. Hot water remains entirely off the table for all *aveilim* without exception. Cold water is what is normally forbidden, and it is only cold water in which the *bogeret* is exceptionally permitted to bathe. This appears to be a strong proof against Rava's position that cold water is generally permitted.

### Makeup Alternative

The *Gemara* deflects the proof once more, proposing that the *braita* may not be discussing water bathing at all. Rather, it may be discussing *kichul u'firchus* — eye shadow, rouge, and the various cosmetic preparations used to enhance appearance. On this reading, the *braita* says the *bogeret* may not deprive herself of makeup during *shiva*, while the *na'ara* is either obligated or has no such exception. Makeup, it should be noted, is not obviously *assur* during *avelut* in the first place; the *braita* may simply be addressing the question of whether an *aveil* has leeway to practice makeup *bifnei ish* in the context of receiving visitors. In any case, under this interpretation, the proof against Rava dissolves, since the *braita* says nothing about cold water at all.

---

## Tzaar vs Indulgence

### Logical Parallel

The *Gemara* now turns to examine the underlying logical structure of the debate with greater precision. If one accepts, as the second version of Rava's position holds, that cold water is forbidden for an *aveil*, then a question arises from the meat-and-wine argument used by the first version of Rava: if the basis for forbidding cold water is *tzaar*, why should meat and wine be permitted? The logic cuts both ways. If *avelut* is grounded in physical *tzaar*, then cold water should be *assur*, but so should meat and wine. If meat and wine are permitted, then apparently *avelut* is not about *tzaar*, in which case cold water should also be permitted.

### Anxiety Exception

The *Gemara* resolves this tension with a sophisticated move. It accepts the premise that *avelut* is, in principle, grounded in *tzaar* — meaning the prohibition of cold water makes sense within that framework. But it then explains why meat and wine are nonetheless permitted despite this underlying principle: *hasam letachuchei pachtei hu de'avid* — there, the person eats and drinks in order to abate his fear, to relieve his anxiety. In other words, meat and wine serve a functional purpose that overrides the general principle of *tzaar*: they provide the *aveil* with a measure of relief from the overwhelming emotional burden of mourning. Without that relief, the person may not be able to cope at all.

This is a genuinely important idea in its own right. It parallels other exceptions we have already seen in the laws of *avelut* — the allowance to wear shoes when traveling outside the city, the leniencies granted when multiple *aveluyot* pile up in succession. In each case, there is an acknowledgment that the principle must yield where it would become literally unreasonable to maintain. The *Gemara* is saying that within the framework of *avelut*, which does rest on an idea of *tzaar*, the *aveil*'s emotional and psychological needs create a carve-out for meat and wine, even though the underlying principle would logically forbid them. The parallel to *aninuth* is worth noting: an *onein* is forbidden in *basar veyayin*, and there is a view among the *Rishonim* that *aninuth* and *avelut* are not entirely distinct categories but rather the same underlying framework with different exceptions applicable at different stages. By *avelut*, we make the exception for meat and wine; by *aninuth*, we do not, because the *onein* must remain focused entirely on the burial arrangements.

### Tzaar Assumption

The *Gemara*'s acceptance of the logical parallel between cold water and meat and wine has an important structural implication: it confirms that the *Gemara* is treating *tzaar* as the operative framework for *avelut* restrictions. Both cold water and meat and wine are being measured on the same axis — one of physical deprivation and indulgence. Hot water is an indulgence and is thus forbidden; cold water, though less of an indulgence, still represents a form of bodily comfort that falls on the prohibited side of the line when *tzaar* is the standard. Meat and wine should also be prohibited on this logic, but a targeted exception is created for them because the *aveil* needs them to function.

One might have argued an entirely different framework: that *avelut* restrictions have nothing to do with *tzaar* as such, but rather with the idea of withdrawal from society and from normal, engaged life. Under that reading, cold water would not necessarily be *assur* — it is not an expression of worldly engagement in the way that elaborate grooming or festive eating might be. But the *Gemara*, by framing the debate the way it does and accepting the premise linking cold water to meat and wine, seems to be settling on the *tzaar* framework as the operative one, even while acknowledging that the picture is complicated by necessary exceptions.

---

## Final Bathing Rules

### Aveil Bathing

The *Gemara* now draws its formal conclusions. The *halacha* is as the thrust of the entire discussion had been trending: an *aveil* is forbidden in cold water throughout the seven days of *shiva*. However, the allowance for face, hands, and feet — *panav yadav v'raglav* — does apply, but only with cold water. Given that even dipping a finger in hot water is forbidden for an *aveil* (following Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet), the allowance for face, hands, and feet is exclusively in the domain of cold water.

### Sichah Anointing

Regarding *sichah* — anointing the body with oil — the conclusion is that an *aveil* is forbidden even in the smallest amount, *afilu kol shehu assur*. The analogy is roughly to hot water: anointing with oil was understood as a genuine bodily indulgence, even more so in ancient times when it served significant hygienic and aesthetic functions. Because it falls into the category of indulgence rather than basic necessity, no minimum threshold is permitted. There is, however, a critical exception: if the anointing is done *l'haavir es hazuhama* — to remove stench — it is permitted. Since people regularly used oil for deodorant purposes in the absence of other means, this exception was both practically important and logically coherent within the *tzaar* framework: the goal of *avelut* is *tzaar* and withdrawal, not the imposition of social offense.

### Tisha B'Av Parallel

A parallel set of allowances exists for *Tisha B'Av*. As one would expect from the comparison that has been running throughout the sugya, *Tisha B'Av* bathing restrictions track the *ta'anit* side of the distinction: hot water is what is fundamentally forbidden, but exceptions exist where water is needed not for the pleasure of bathing but for the direct removal of dirt or grime. Where the intent is genuine cleanliness rather than bodily indulgence, certain allowances apply. This concludes a *sugya* that has illuminated the comparative structure of *ta'anit* and *avelut* restrictions, the question of whether *avelut* practices are grounded in *tzaar* or in some other conceptual framework, and the relationship between the *menudeh*, the *aveil*, and the *nezufim lamakom* of the *Mishnah*.

---

## Aneinu Placement

### Individual Aneinu

The *Gemara* shifts — without any transitional signal — to an entirely new topic: the placement of the *Aneinu* prayer within the *Shemoneh Esrei* on fast days. The question is posed directly: *tzlusa d'taanisa heichi madkrinan* — where do we mention the prayer of the fast in the *Shemoneh Esrei*?

Rav Yehuda told his son Rav Yitzchak, and expounded: an individual (*yachid*) who has accepted a personal fast upon himself must still recite the special fast-day *tefillah* — the *Aneinu* — even though this is not a communal fast. The question is where: *bein Goel l'Rofei* — between the blessing of *Goel Yisrael* and the blessing of *Rofei cholei amo Yisrael*.

This is, of course, the familiar practice of the *shliach tzibur* on communal fast days: a standalone *bracha* of *Aneinu* inserted between *Goel* and *Rofei* in the *chazarat hashatz*. It is worth asking why this particular location was chosen. The *Shemoneh Esrei* has a notable structural shift midway through its middle blessings: the earlier ones — *Da'as*, *Slichah*, *Geulah*, *Refuah*, *Birkat Hashanim* — address primarily personal needs, while the later ones — gathering the exiles, loving justice, against informers — shift toward national concerns. The blessing of *Goel Yisrael* belongs in the more personal register: *re'eh b'onyeinu* — see our affliction, and redeem us from it. It is not *Geulah* in the grand national-historical sense, but rather a plea for God to perceive and respond to individual distress. *Aneinu* — whose very name means "answer us" — belongs thematically with this category of appeal. The dominant themes of the *Aneinu* prayer confirm this: *ki b'tzarah gedolah anachnu*, *al tefen el risheinu*, *al tasteir panecha mimenu*, *heyeh na karov leshav'atenu*, *she'atah ha'oneh b'eit tzarah podeh umatzil* — the overwhelming focus is on God's responsiveness and closeness in a moment of distress, not on formal *kapparah* or *slichah*. The prayer would not fit naturally after *Selach* lanu, since the theme of divine forgiveness is not its primary emphasis; it fits after *Goel* precisely because *Geulah* at this level is about God seeing our *tzarah* and answering.

It is also worth observing that the *Aneinu* prayer is formulated in the plural: *aneinu Hashem aneinu*, *ki b'tzarah gedolah anachnu*. This raises a natural question when it is being said by a private individual. The *Gemara* will address this implicitly in the resolution to follow, but the plural formulation is worth noting as an indication that the prayer was originally conceived for a communal context — which is precisely why the question of how a *yachid* uses it deserves examination.

The question of who the *yachid* is in this context is not entirely simple. It might refer to the pious individual who voluntarily takes on a fast as a personal religious act. Or it might refer to the *yechidim* of our *Mishnah* — the more spiritually sensitive individuals who begin fasting ahead of the community in response to a drought. Whether or not this *yachid* is still situationally connected to the communal rain-crisis context, or whether the discussion applies equally to any individual voluntary fast, the *Gemara* does not here resolve.

### Individual Challenge

Rav Yitzchak challenges the proposed placement directly: *vachi yachid koveia brachah le'atzmo*? — can an individual simply institute a new independent blessing for himself? The liturgy is fixed. An individual may insert language into an existing blessing at a designated point, but one does not simply add a new standalone *bracha* to the *Shemoneh Esrei* as a private person. Only a *tzibur* — or more precisely, the rabbinic institution acting on behalf of the community — has the authority to establish a new *bracha* in the liturgy.

### Resolution: Shomea Tefil…

Rav Yitzchak therefore offers a revised ruling: the *yachid* inserts *Aneinu* within *Shomea Tefillah*, the sixteenth blessing of the *Shemoneh Esrei* that serves as a general receptacle for personal petitions. Rav Sheshet concurs: *vekhen amar Rav Sheshet — b'Shomea Tefillah*. This is indeed our practice: in one's private *Shemoneh Esrei* on a fast day, even on *Tisha B'Av*, *Aneinu* is not said as a standalone *bracha* but is inserted within *Shomea Tefillah* without its closing formula (*chatimah*).

The *Gemara* then raises a challenge from a *braita*: *ein bein yachid litzibur ella shezeh mitpallel shmoneh esrei vezeh mitpallel tisha esrei* — the only difference between a *yachid* and a *tzibur* on a fast day is that this one prays 18 and that one prays 19. If the 19 refers to the *shliach tzibur* adding a standalone *Aneinu bracha*, then the text makes sense. But the *Gemara* notes that this cannot quite be right, because on the later, more serious fast days the *shliach tzibur* recites 24 blessings — not 19. If the *braita* is contrasting 18 with 19, it cannot be talking about the *shliach tzibur* on those later fasts.

The *Gemara* therefore reinterprets the *braita*: the contrast is not between a literally private individual and the *shliach tzibur*, but between two types of individual fasting — a *yachid* who has accepted a lighter *ta'anit yachid* (daytime only, no extra *inuyim*) versus a *yachid* who has accepted a heavier *ta'anit tzibur*-style fast (beginning the night before, with the full range of *inuyim*). The "19" refers to the latter: a private individual keeping the heavy-style fast does say *Aneinu* as an additional blessing — making his *Shemoneh Esrei* 19 rather than 18. This would appear to support the original position of Rav Yehuda, proving that a *yachid* can indeed add a standalone *bracha*.

The *Gemara* rejects this inference, however: *le'olam eima lach shliach tzibur* — it is the *shliach tzibur* after all.
