As for why 19 rather than 24: on the first three lighter communal fasts, the *shliach tzibur* says *Aneinu* as a standalone *bracha*, bringing the total to 19. The 24-*bracha* liturgy applies only to the final seven, more severe fasts. A *yachid*, under this reading, never makes a standalone *bracha* of *Aneinu* in his private *Shemoneh Esrei* regardless of which type of fast he is keeping.

The *Gemara* then addresses the question of the middle three fasts — do they warrant the 24-*bracha* liturgy of the later fasts, or are they treated like the earlier ones with only 19? A *braita* states there is no difference between the middle three and the last seven except for the *matri'in* (sounding blasts, presumably *shofar*) and the closing of the stores. This implies that the 24 *brachot* apply equally to the middle. The *Gemara* pushes back: the *braita* is an incomplete list, since it also omits the bringing of the *aron* into the street — which is clearly reserved for the last seven. One resolution proposed is that things done publicly (*beferahesya*) were omitted while things done indoors (*betzin'a*) were included — though this is admittedly a somewhat strained distinction, since *shofar* blasts and communal prayer are not exactly private. The stronger resolution offered later is that the *aron* is described in detail in a later *perek* (chapter) specifically as a feature of the final seven fasts, and the same is true of the 24-*bracha* liturgy — both are mentioned in that later *perek* as distinctive to the final seven. Therefore neither should be inferred from the equation made here between the middle three and the last seven.

The *Gemara*'s conclusion is that the 24-*bracha* liturgy belongs exclusively to the final seven fasts, where it appears together with the *matri'in* and the bringing out of the *aron* — all of which represent a qualitative escalation in the communal response. The final ruling on the placement of *Aneinu* is stated by Rav Shmuel bar Sasartai and confirmed by Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav: *bein Goel l'Rofei* — for the *shliach tzibur*. And Rav Ashi in the name of Rav Yannai the son of Rav Yishmael rules: *b'Shomea Tefillah*. The *halacha* follows: *v'hilchata b'Shomea Tefillah*. In one's private *Shemoneh Esrei*, whether on a *ta'anit yachid* or a *ta'anit tzibur*, one inserts *Aneinu* in *Shomea Tefillah*. In the *chazarat hashatz* of the *shliach tzibur*, for the lighter communal fasts, it appears as a standalone *bracha* between *Goel* and *Rofei*, bringing the total to 19. For the final seven, it becomes part of the full 24-*bracha* liturgy.

---

## Pregnant Women Fasting

### Braita 1

The *Gemara* pivots once more, now to the question of pregnant and nursing women (*ubarot umeinikos*) and their obligation to fast on the communal fast days for rain. The first *braita* states: pregnant and nursing women fast during the early fasts (*rishonot*) but not during the later fasts (*acharonot*). The reasoning seems to be that by the time the later and more extended fasts arrive, the burden would be too great for women in those conditions to bear.

### Braita 2

A second *braita* contradicts this entirely: pregnant and nursing women fast during the later fasts (*acharonot*) but not during the early fasts (*rishonot*). By this view, the early fasts are too light to impose on these women — they are not yet serious enough to demand their participation — while the gravity of the later fasts brings them within its scope.

### Braita 3

A third *braita* contradicts both: pregnant and nursing women do not fast during the early fasts or the later fasts — *lo b'rishonot velo b'acharonot*. All three *beraitot* thus appear to be in direct contradiction: one says A and not B; one says B and not A; one says neither A nor B.

### Rav Ashi's Solution

Rav Ashi resolves all three with a single elegant observation: *nekut amtzeita biyadech d'metartzan kulhu* — take hold of the middle fasts and everything fits. His insight is that the terms *rishonot* (early/first) and *acharonot* (later/last) are relative, not absolute. Using the three-stage structure of the fast calendar — early, middle, and late — all three *beraitot* can be reconciled without changing any text.

The middle fasts are the ones where pregnant and nursing women do fast: heavy enough to be meaningful and obligating, but not so protracted as to become unbearable. With this as the reference point, the *braita* that says they fast during the *rishonot* and not the *acharonot* is using *rishonot* to mean the earlier of two groups — here, the middle fasts in relation to the final seven. The *braita* that says they fast during the *acharonot* and not the *rishonot* is using *acharonot* to mean the later of two groups — again the middle fasts, this time in relation to the initial three. And the *braita* that says they do not fast in either *rishonot* or *acharonot* means literally the first three and the last seven — leaving the middle as the window during which they do fast. The apparent contradictions dissolve entirely once one recognizes that first and last are relative terms pointing toward the same middle ground.

It should be noted that there is a tradition associated with the *Rambam* that pregnant and nursing women fast only during the final seven fasts — a position that appears to run against the *Gemara*'s conclusion here. One possible resolution is that the *Rambam*'s position takes *amtzeita* to mean not the middle set of fasts, but rather the middle of the sequence in some other sense — though this remains a matter requiring further analysis.

---

---

# Ta'anit 14

## Final Seven Fasts

### Shift to Late Fasts

The Gemara on 14a opens with the question *ma elu yeterot al harishonot* — in what ways are the final seven fasts weightier than the earlier ones? The preceding discussion has already established a gradation of seriousness across the three sets of fasts. In the first three, one fasts only during the day. In the middle set, the fast begins the night before and additional *inuyim* are observed. By the time we reach the final seven, the stores are closed, the fast begins from the previous night, and most significantly, the nature of the *tefillot* themselves is transformed. The *mishnah* states: *ela shebe'elu matri'in veno'alin et hachanutot* — the distinguishing features are *matri'in* and the closing of the stores. The community shuts down entirely, with everyone focusing on prayer. It is these two features — and particularly the term *matri'in* — that the Gemara now proceeds to examine.

### Matri'in Debate

The Gemara asks: *bema matri'in* — what exactly is the nature of this *matri'in*? Rav Yehuda says *beshofarot* — it refers to shofar blasts. This reading is intuitive, since the word *matri'in* derives from *teruah*, which we naturally associate with the shofar. Rav Yehuda the son of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat, however, citing Rav, says *be'anenu* — the *matri'in* refers to the special prayer of *anenu*, the crying out to God, rather than to any instrumental blast. On this reading, *teruah* is being understood not as a shofar sound but as a form of wailing or calling out through prayer.

### Rashi on Shofar

Rashi's commentary illuminates both positions. On the opinion of *be'anenu*, Rashi explains that the community would cry out *bekol ram* — loudly — saying *anenu avinu anenu*, *anenu elohei Avraham anenu*, *anenu elohei Yitzchak anenu*, and so forth. This is, as Rashi notes, the very text one recognizes from the end of *selichot* — *hakol kefi she'omerim besof haselichot*. It is worth pausing here: this *anenu* liturgy is among the earliest organized prayers we have outside of the *shemoneh esrei* itself, and its structure centers on invoking God's past responsiveness to the patriarchs. Rashi also clarifies that this is not the standard *anenu* blessing said on fast days as a separate *berachah* within the *amidah*, which is said even on the first three fasts and even by an individual. Rather, this refers to the elaborated *anenu* structure tied to the additional six *berachot* of the final seven fasts. It may be, as Rashi suggests, that they also said it outside the *shemoneh esrei* entirely.

On the shofar position, Rashi notes that the word *hatra'ah* is the language of *teruah*, a blast preceded and followed by a *tekiah*, as we know from tractate Rosh Hashanah. The scriptural basis is the verse *utkatem bachatzotzrot al hatzar hatzorer etchem* — you shall sound the trumpets when an enemy oppresses you. Rashi draws two ideas together: the shofar is a mode of calling out to God and of being remembered before Him, and it is simultaneously a means of awakening the community to *teshuvah*, causing hearts to be subdued by its sound and stirring people away from their sins. These are recognizably the same two functions developed in the context of Rosh Hashanah — one directed heavenward, one directed inward.

### Shofar + Anenu

The Gemara initially assumes the two opinions are mutually exclusive — that whoever says *matri'in* means *anenu* does not require shofar blasts, and vice versa. A *baraita* quickly challenges this: *ein pochtim misheva taniyot al hatzibbur shebahen yud chet hatra'ot* — one may not have fewer than seven communal fasts, and within them no fewer than eighteen *hatra'ot*. The *siman* for remembering this is *Yericho*. Why eighteen? To understand this, one must look ahead to the *mishnah* later in the tractate, where the additional six *berachot* of the final seven fasts are enumerated. Each *berachah* is structured around a *mi she'anah* formula — *mi she'anah Avraham avinu behar hamoriyah hu ya'aneh etchem* — and ends with its own *chatimah*. If there are six such *berachot*, and each is accompanied by a *tekiah teruah tekiah* — three blasts per *berachah* — the total comes to eighteen *hatra'ot*. This *baraita* clearly presupposes shofar blasts as integral to the seven fasts, constituting a refutation of any view that would exclude them entirely.

The Gemara therefore revises its understanding of the dispute: *beshofar kulei alma lo* — everyone agrees that shofar blasts are performed and that the term *hatra'ah* refers to them. The disagreement is only about *anenu*: does the word *matri'in* in the *mishnah* encompass *anenu* as well, or does the *mishnah*'s emphasis on *matri'in* as the distinguishing feature of the final seven refer exclusively to the shofar blasts?

### Matri'in Scope

With this reframing, the positions are clarified. According to the view that *matri'in* means *be'anenu*, the *mishnah* is highlighting *anenu* as the distinctive feature — but of course shofar blasts are performed as well, since everyone agrees on that. According to the view that *matri'in* means *beshofarot*, the *mishnah* highlights the shofar as the distinctive feature, and whether *anenu* is also added remains unaddressed by the word *matri'in* itself.

There is a deeper question worth raising here: is this dispute purely terminological — what the word *matri'in* technically denotes — or does it reflect a genuine disagreement about what the community actually does? Given that the subsequent *mishnah* clearly describes both the shofar blasts and the *anenu* structure in the context of the final seven fasts, it is more plausible that both were always practiced. The real debate is which practice the *mishnah* is calling attention to as the defining difference from the earlier fasts. Is it the instrumental blast that signals a new level of urgency, or is it the transformed mode of prayer? This is ultimately a question about what is considered the more powerful and fundamental way of calling out to God — the ritual object of the shofar or the emotional register of the *anenu* cry.

### Tzoa'kin vs Matri'in

A *baraita* is cited that sharpens the distinction further: *u'vesh'ar kol minei pur'aniyot hamitragshot* — for other types of anticipated calamities, such as infestations of locusts, flies, wasps, mosquitoes, or the sending of snakes and scorpions, *lo hayu matri'in* — they would not perform *matri'in*. Instead, *ela tzo'akin* — they would only cry out verbally. The Gemara draws the logical conclusion: since *tzo'akin* here unambiguously means verbal crying out, the term *matri'in* is being set in explicit contrast to it. *Hatra'ah beshofar* — the *hatra'ah* referred to by *matri'in* can only mean shofar blasts, not verbal outcry. This seems to resolve the matter decisively in favor of the shofar interpretation.

### Matri'in Shabbat

The Gemara responds, however, that this is a dispute among *tanna'im*. A second *baraita* records: *al elu matri'in beshabbat* — for the following situations one may perform *matri'in* even on Shabbat: a city surrounded by troops, a river threatening to overflow its banks, or a ship endangered at sea. Rabbi Yossi qualifies: *l'ezra* — one may sound the alarm to summon help, *aval lo l'tze'akah* — but not as an act of prayer addressed to God. This statement is striking in its this-worldly practicality: when a city is besieged, the more urgent priority is mobilizing human assistance, not divine petition. One may sound whatever signal summons people to help.

The Gemara presses: when Rabbi Yossi speaks of *matri'in* for help, what is being sounded? *Ilema beshofaro* — if it is a shofar, *shofaro beshabbat mi sharei* — is a shofar even permitted on Shabbat? The Gemara is not suggesting that pikuach nefesh would fail to override the prohibition; rather, the earlier position contemplated sounding the alarm as a form of *tefillah*, and we do not blow the shofar on Shabbat even for prayer — which is precisely why we do not blow on Rosh Hashanah when it falls on Shabbat. The conclusion is therefore: *ela lav be'anenu* — clearly what is being referred to here is *anenu*, verbal calling out, and the *baraita* uses the term *matri'in* to describe it. *Ve'kari lei hatra'ah* — and it uses the language of *hatra'ah*. This proves that for some *tanna'im*, *matri'in* does include verbal calling out, not only shofar blasts.

### Matri'in Resolution

The upshot is that *matri'in* as a technical term definitively refers to shofar blasts — this is what the *baraita* about *hatra'ot* and the numerical calculation of eighteen establish beyond dispute. The debate between *tanna'im* is only about whether the word can *also* encompass the *anenu* cry. In practice, both are performed during the final seven fasts: shofar blasts accompany the six additional *berachot*, each *berachah* structured around the *mi she'anah* formula, and the *anenu* prayer gives expressive content to each segment. The *mishnah*'s use of the word *matri'in* emphasizes the shofar dimension, though the *anenu* dimension is simultaneously present. The question that lingers is fundamentally one of emphasis and theology: is the essential mode of urgent supplication an instrumental one, calling upon the power of the shofar to reach God and stir the heart, or is it a personal one, the raw crying out of the human voice?

---

## Post-13 Cessation

### Rabbi Yehuda Nesia

In the years of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia — grandson of Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi, and thus an Amora — there was some form of communal distress. He decreed the full complement of thirteen fasts, *velo i'anu* — and they were not answered. The *mishnah* itself describes what happens in this situation: the community enters a posture of *aveilut*. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, however, *savar lemigzar tefei* — contemplated decreeing additional fasts beyond the thirteen. Rabbi Ami objected: *harei amru ein matrihin al hatzibbur yoter midai* — the stated principle is that one does not burden the community beyond what is reasonable, and thirteen fasts is the prescribed limit.

This exchange opens a deeper question about the rationale for stopping at thirteen. Is the limit one of communal burden — at a certain point, enough is enough and life must go on — or is it specific to rain, because after a certain point in the season even answered prayer would come too late? The answer matters considerably: if the limit is about communal burden, it is universal and applies to all types of distress. If it is about the futility of late rain, it applies only to drought-related fasts and other calamities would require fasting indefinitely until relief arrives.

### Rain-Specific Limit

Rav Abba the son of Rav Hiyya bar Abba responds that Rabbi Ami's ruling about communal burden, while not incorrect, reflects only his own view — *Rabbi Ami de'avad legarmeh hu de'avad*. The real teaching, as stated by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, is: *lo shanu ela ligshamim* — the limit of thirteen fasts was said only with respect to rain. *Aval lish'ar minei pur'aniyot*, for all other forms of calamity, *mit'anim v'holchim ad she'ya'anu min hashamayim* — one fasts and continues until Heaven responds. There is no ceiling. One never despairs of eventually being answered.

There is something deeply important in this formulation. The end of the *mishnah* describing the post-thirteen state — the community sitting as those rejected by God, wrapped in mourning — conveys an atmosphere of near-despair, a severed relationship. Rabbi Yochanan's teaching restores that relationship. The reason one stops praying for rain after thirteen is not theological resignation; it is simply that rain after a certain point in the season is no longer beneficial. It is analogous to praying for a person's recovery after he has already died — one stops not because God cannot act, but because the specific request is no longer applicable. For every other calamity, however, the distress is ongoing, the request remains relevant, and hope is never abandoned. One continues indefinitely until relief comes.

### Tannaitic Debate

A *baraita* confirms that this very dispute has *tanna'itic* roots. Rabbi holds: *ein gozrim yoter mishlosh esrei ta'aniyot al hatzibbur lefi she'ein matrihin et hatzibbur yoter midai* — the reason for stopping at thirteen is the principle of not overburdening the community, and this principle applies universally. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees: *lo min hashem hu zeh* — that is not the reason at all. Rather, *mipnei sheyatzah zemana shel revi'ah* — it is because the season for beneficial rainfall has passed. The dispute of Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan among the Amoraim thus maps precisely onto the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel among the *tanna'im*. Even Rabbi's reasoning — that we stop to avoid burdening the community — is considerably more humane and relationally intact than the stark language of *benei adam hanizufim lamakom*. To say "reality must eventually reassert itself" is a far cry from "God has rejected you."

---

## Regional Rain Requests

### Nineveh Question

The Gemara now addresses a question related to the timing of prayer for rain in unusual geographic circumstances. The people of Nineveh — a striking choice of locale, given Nineveh's forthcoming role elsewhere in the tractate as a paradigm of *teshuvah* — sent a question to Rabbi: *kegon anan d'afilu b'tekufat Tammuz ba'inan mitra* — we are a community that needs rain even in the summer months. Normally the communal request for rain ceases at Pesach time. But our region regularly requires rainfall well beyond that point. *Heichi na'avid* — what should we do? *K'yechidim daminan o k'rabbim daminan* — should we be treated as individuals or as the community?

### Shomeah Tefillah

The Gemara's interpretation of this question is revealing. It does not read the question as being about whether to fast — whether to treat this as a *ta'anit yachid* or a *ta'anit tzibbur*. The question is not framed in crisis terms at all: the people of Nineveh are simply asking about the regular structure of their prayer throughout the year. *Kegon anan d'afilu b'tekufat Tammuz* — as a matter of regular course, we need rain even then. The question is therefore one of liturgical placement: should we say *v'sein tal umatar l'vracha* as individuals would — in *shomeah tefillah*, the catch-all blessing that hears individual petitions — or should we treat ourselves as the community does with the rain prayer incorporated directly into *birkat hashanim*, the ninth blessing?

Rabbi responds: *ki'yechidim damitu* — you are to be treated as individuals, *uv'shomeah tefillah* — and you say it in *shomeah tefillah*. The underlying principle is that the calendar of communal liturgy — including when *v'sein tal umatar* is inserted into and removed from *birkat hashanim* — is fixed for all of *Klal Yisrael*. Regional variations exist, as is well known: *Eretz Yisrael* and *Bavel* do not share the same starting date for *v'sein tal umatar*. But once the standard cessation date arrives at Pesach, that applies universally. A community whose rainfall needs extend beyond that date has a legitimate need, but addresses it through the individual's recourse of *shomeah tefillah*, not by altering the communal liturgical calendar.

### Standard Calendar

The Gemara raises a challenge from a *baraita*: Rabbi Yehuda is quoted as saying that the standard schedule applies *bizman shehashanim ketiknan v'Yisrael sheruyim al admatam* — when the years are normal and Israel dwells on its own land. But *bizman hazeh* — in the present era — the rule shifts: *hakol lefi hashanim hakol lefi hamkomos v'hakol lefi hazman* — everything follows the specific conditions of that year, that place, and that time. This would seem to say that the liturgical calendar for *v'sein tal umatar* is not fixed at all, but fluctuates community by community and year by year based on actual rainfall needs — a remarkable position. The Gemara deflects this challenge: *Rabbi Tanna hu u'falig* — Rabbi is himself a *Tanna* and may simply disagree with this *baraita*.

### Amoraic Consensus

Among the Amoraim, the matter is debated: Rav Nachman holds *b'birkat hashanim* — a community with unusual rain needs may continue saying *v'sein tal umatar* within *birkat hashanim*, while Rav Sheshet holds *b'shomeah tefillah* — it must be said in *shomeah tefillah*. The Gemara rules: *v'hilcheta b'shomeah tefillah*. Even if a community's need for rain persists past Pesach, the universal cessation of *v'sein tal umatar* in *birkat hashanim* at Pesach time holds for everyone. Late rainfall needs are addressed through *shomeah tefillah*.

The Rosh encountered precisely this issue when he relocated to Toledo and became its rabbinic authority. The communities there not only needed rain regularly after Pesach — they were actually holding communal fasts for lack of rain — yet were not saying *v'sein tal umatar l'vracha*. The Rosh argued vigorously that the case of Nineveh involves a single city, while an entire country the size of Spain represents a different category entirely. Just as the calendar differs between *Eretz Yisrael* and *Bavel*, so too Spain should have its own calendar for *v'sein tal umatar*. He writes that *tzaveach k'kruchiya v'lo ishtakach bi* — he cried out like a crane and was not heeded. The halachic consensus rejected his position. Even an entire country with consistently late rainfall needs does not shift the placement of *v'sein tal umatar* from *shomeah tefillah* back into *birkat hashanim* — though if one accidentally said it in *birkat hashanim* in such circumstances, one need not repeat the *shemoneh esrei*.

---

## Final Seven Fasts (II)

### Store Closures

The *mishnah* states: *b'sheni matin min hachasheicha u'vachamishi kol hayom mipnei kvod Shabbat* — on Mondays the stores are partially opened toward evening, and on Thursdays they are open all day out of honor for Shabbat. The Gemara raises an *ibaya*: does the verb *matin* — meaning to incline or make available — apply to both Monday and Thursday, with the only difference being the duration? Or does Thursday represent a fundamentally different status, where the stores are *potchin* — fully open for normal business — while only Monday maintains the partial-availability posture?

A *baraita* resolves this: *b'sheni matim ad ha'erev* — on Mondays they operate in that limited, inclined manner until evening, *u'vachamishi potchin kol hayom kulo* — and on Thursdays they are fully open all day, *mipnei kvod Shabbat*. Thursdays are therefore qualitatively different: the store closure does not apply at all on Thursdays. Two refinements follow. If a storekeeper has two entrances, he opens one and locks the other — even if fully open for business, some visible expression of the fast's atmosphere is maintained. If, however, there is a booth or stall in front of the entrance, *poteach k'darko v'eino choshesh* — he may open in his normal manner without concern. Rashi reads this extension broadly: *afilu b'sheni* — even on Monday, if a booth stands before the entrance and the open doors are not fully exposed to the street, the store may be fully opened. This functions as a significant practical accommodation. The principle underlying the store closures is that the entire community must visibly and collectively shut down during the final seven fasts; the accommodations are calibrated to allow life to continue where the communal signal is already sufficiently attenuated.

---

## Avelut Practices

### Avelut Restrictions

After the thirteen fasts have passed without response, the community enters a period characterized not by continued fasting but by behaviors expressive of *aveilut*. The *mishnah* states: *mema'atim b'masa umatan u've'vinyan u've'neti'ah* — one curtails commerce, construction, and planting. A *tanna* clarifies that these limitations are not absolute. *Vinyan shel simcha* — only a construction of joyous character is prohibited. Specifically: *zeh haboneh beit chatnut livno* — one who builds a wedding house for his son, whether that means a home for the newlywed couple or a special wedding canopy structure. Ordinary construction for practical needs — repairing a leaking roof, for example — is not included. Similarly, *neti'ah shel simcha* — joyful planting is what is forbidden. *Zeh hanotea avzarnaki shel melachim* — this refers to the kind of decorative royal orchard or pleasure garden planted for aesthetic enjoyment rather than sustenance. Essential agricultural work is not prohibited. The limitation is thus defined quite narrowly: what is curtailed is the category of activity undertaken for pleasure, celebration, and expansive living — precisely the activities incompatible with a community in mourning.

### She'ilat Shalom

The practices of *aveilut* extend to social interaction as well. The period restricts *she'ilat shalom* — the formal inquiry after another's welfare, a greeting more substantial than a simple hello, implying *ma shlomcha*, wishing another peace and asking after their condition. On Tisha B'Av, for instance, even simple greetings are suspended. The *gemara* emphasizes that *she'ilat shalom* carries the word *shalom* within it and conveys a quality of engagement and warmth that is incompatible with communal mourning.

A distinction is drawn between two groups. *Chaverim ein she'ilat shalom beineihem* — those of the knowledgeable and scrupulous rabbinic class do not engage in any inquiry after welfare at all. *Amei ha'aretz she'sho'alim* — the common people, unaware of the restriction, may still greet you. What should you do when they approach you with a cheerful greeting? *Machzirim lahem b'safah rafah u'vechoved rosh* — you answer them in a soft voice and with a heaviness of head. Brevity and solemnity without rudeness.

### Mourning Garb

Beyond the curtailment of activity and greeting, the community adopts visible expressions of mourning. *V'hem mit'atefim v'yoshvim ke'aveilim u'che'menudim* — they wrap themselves in their *tallit* and sit as mourners and as those in a state of *niduy*, *kivnei adam hanizufim lamakom* — like people who have been rejected by God — *ad sheyerachamu aleihem min hashamayim* — until Heaven shows compassion. Two distinct purposes are served by this practice. On one level, it is the honest owning of the religious significance of what is happening — not carrying on as though nothing is amiss, but allowing the external expression to match the internal reality of communal distress. On another level, there is an implicit theology here: making oneself so visibly and thoroughly miserable may itself move God to compassion. *Ad sheyerachamu* — until He takes pity. The possibility that the *ta'anit* itself functions partly in this way — that self-imposed suffering invites divine mercy — is not far beneath the surface.

---

## Ostentatious Behavior

### Falling on Face

Rabbi Eleazar offers a series of rulings that together form a critique of ostentatious religious behavior during this period — a topic implicitly connected to the earlier theme of *yechidim* who continue to fast and to set themselves apart from the community. He says: *ein adam chashuv rashai lipol al panav ela im ken ne'ena kiyehoshua bin nun* — an important person is not permitted to fall on his face in prayer unless he is confident of being answered as Yehoshua bin Nun was. The proof text: *vayomer Hashem el Yehoshua kum lach lama zeh ata nofel al panecha* — God said to Yehoshua, rise, why are you fallen on your face? The verse confirms that Yehoshua did fall on his face and was addressed by God — meaning he was answered. Unless a person has that level of assurance about his standing before God, the demonstrative act of falling on one's face amounts to *yuhara* — ostentatious religiosity.

This connects to the earlier portrait of the *yachid* who continues to fast. Being a *yachid* means setting oneself apart from the community in a way that carries spiritual weight. But there is a difference between private persistence in fasting and theatrical expressions of piety. The comparison to Choni Hame'agel — who drew a circle and demanded rain from God — captures the dangerous edge of that kind of self-presentation: it can tip from genuine *avodah* into a kind of religious *chutzpah*. Rabbi Eleazar is setting a firm limit on the demonstrative behaviors appropriate even for *gedolim*.

### Sackcloth Warning

Rabbi Eleazar adds: *ein adam chashuv rashai lachgor sak ela im ken ne'ena kiyoram ben Achav* — an important person is not permitted to gird himself in sackcloth unless he expects to be answered as Yoram ben Achav was. This is a striking choice of exemplar, since Yoram was a wicked king. Yet the point is precisely that: even Yoram, when he tore his garments and wore sackcloth in response to dire news, was answered. The proof text: *vayehi kishmoa hamelech et divrei ha'isha vayikra et bgadav vehu over al hachoma vayar ha'am vehineh hasak al bsaro* — the king tore his garments as he walked the wall, and the people saw the sackcloth on his flesh. Unless you have reason to believe you will be answered — even as Yoram was — putting on sackcloth publicly is not appropriate for a person of standing.

### Varied Expressions

Rabbi Eleazar extends his observation beyond the specific behaviors to a general principle: *lo hakol bikriyah velo hakol binefilah* — not everyone in the biblical record used both rending of garments and falling on one's face. Different biblical figures employed different modes of expressing grief and supplication. *Moshe ve'Aharon binefilah* — Moshe and Aharon fell on their faces; *Yehoshua veCalev bikriyah* — Yehoshua and Calev rent their garments. The proof texts are familiar from the story of the *meraglim*: *vayipol Moshe ve'Aharon al pneihem*, and *vYehoshua bin nun veCalev ben Yefuneh kare'u bigdeihem*. It is worth noting that in context, Yehoshua and Calev were not tearing their garments as an act of prayer addressed to God; they were expressing grief at the people's behavior. This is entirely consistent with where the community now finds itself in the post-thirteen-fast stage: the focus is not on achieving an answered prayer but on owning the tragedy. The acts of Yehoshua, Calev, Moshe, and Aharon in response to the catastrophe of the *meraglim* are the appropriate models for this phase of *aveilut*, not for the earlier phase of urgent supplication.

### Challenge & Resolution

Rabbi Zeira — or some say Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani — challenges Rabbi Eleazar's distinction. If the verse had simply written *Yehoshua* without the prefix *vav*, you could argue that Yehoshua and Calev did one thing while Moshe and Aharon did another. But since the verse writes *vYehoshua* — with the connective *vav* — it implies that Yehoshua and Calev did both: they fell on their faces as Moshe and Aharon did, *and* they rent their garments. *Ha veha avdi.* The *vav* connects their action to that of Moshe and Aharon rather than contrasting it, suggesting they performed both expressions. Doing more than one demonstrative act is therefore not so problematic after all — though the pushback does not entirely undo Rabbi Eleazar's larger concern about ostentatious behavior.

### Rising & Bowing

Rabbi Eleazar makes one further observation, moving beyond the context of grief and prayer to forms of honor and respect: *lo hakol bekima velo hakol behishtachavaya* — not everyone rises, and not everyone bows down. Different forms of expressing honor are appropriate for different people. *Melachim bekima* — kings rise: *melachim yiru vekamu* — kings will see and rise up before you, as the verse in Isaiah promises. *V'sarim behishtachavaya* — princes bow down: *sarim veyishtachavu* — and princes will prostrate themselves. Rabbi Zeira challenges this as well: the verse writes *sarim veyishtachavu* — with a *vav* before the verb — which implies they will also rise first and then bow down, performing both acts. *Ha veha avdi* — they do both. The point is parallel to the earlier challenge: the *vav* in these formulations connects rather than contrasts, suggesting that combining expressions is natural rather than excessive.

### Righteous & Upright

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak appends a final observation: *af ani omer, lo hakol le'orah velo hakol lesimcha* — let me add, not everyone will see the same end. *Tzadikim le'orah* — the righteous will have light; *lisharim lesimcha* — the upright will have joy. *De'tzadikim le'orah dichsiv or zarua latzadik* — for the righteous, light is sown; *u'le'yesharim simcha dichsiv u'le'yishrei lev simcha* — and for the upright of heart, joy. The observation ends the section on an unexpectedly positive note, though it also raises a question worth sitting with: does a *tzadik* not receive joy? Does a *yashar* not receive light? What exactly distinguishes these two categories?

Whatever the precise answer, this ending coheres with the larger thrust of the section. The entire discussion — Rabbi Eleazar's warnings against falling on one's face, wearing sackcloth, rending garments, and the various challenges about whether combining expressions is acceptable — reflects a sustained concern with authentic versus performative religiosity. The *yachid* who privately persists in fasting occupies a legitimate and honored role. What Rabbi Eleazar resists is the public theater of piety: the layering of demonstrative acts that signal one's special standing before God, when in truth only someone of Yehoshua's or even Yoram's stature has grounds for such confidence. The *perek* opens with the gradations of fasting that escalate with communal urgency and closes with a caution that even in the most intense stages, inward sincerity must govern outward expression.

---

---

# Ta'anit 15

## Perek Seder Ta'aniyot

### Ch. Overview

With the opening of the new *perek*, the focus of the tractate shifts markedly. Whereas the previous chapter concerned itself primarily with the mechanics of fasting — the structure of the three, three, and seven *ta'aniyot tzibbur* — this chapter turns to what might be called the liturgical and communal architecture of the fast day. The operative verse, *kar'u tzom kidshu atzara*, calls not only for a fast but for a day of gathering, *tefillot*, and communal self-assessment. That is the animating concern of *Seder Ta'aniyot*: not merely that one fasts, but how the entire order of the day is organized as a communal experience.

### Mishna Structure

The printers of the Talmud made the unusual decision to gather all the *mishnayot* of this *perek* into a single extended first *mishna*. What follows, then, is less a single discrete teaching than a compendium — essentially all six or seven *mishnayot* of the chapter stitched together. The *mishna* opens with the question *Seder Ta'aniyot keitzad* — "What is the order of the fast days?" — a formulation that recalls the *Pesach Seder*: not what we do, but in what sequence, according to what agenda, do we do it.

---

## Ark & Ashes

### Teiva & Eifer

The first element of the order is *motzi'in et hateiva* — they bring out the ark to *rechovah shel ir*, the public square of the city. The *rechov* here is not a side street but the central public gathering place. The *Gemara* will later clarify, through a *beraita*, that this ritual belongs to the final seven fasts rather than the earlier ones, but the *mishna* itself does not specify; it describes the order of the day without identifying to which tier of fasts it applies.

Once the ark is brought out, the community places *eifer mikleh* — ashes of something burnt — upon it. One might ask why the *mishna* specifies *eifer mikleh* rather than simply *eifer*. *Rashi* addresses this directly: *eifer mamash velo afar* — we mean actual ashes, not dust. The reason precision is required is that the word *eifer* on its own can equally denote dust, as the verse *me'afar sereifat hachatat* demonstrates, where *afar* clearly refers to ashes. Conversely, *afar* can be called *eifer*, as in *Avraham*'s declaration *v'anochi afar va'eifer*. Because the two terms bleed into one another, the modifier *mikleh* — of something burnt — is necessary to establish unambiguously that actual fire-produced ashes are intended.

### Leadership Mourning

The ashes are placed not only upon the ark but *u'verosh hanasi u'verosh av beit din* — upon the head of the *nasi* and the head of the *av beit din*. In the context of *Eretz Yisrael* this would mean figures like *Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi* as the political head, alongside the *av beit din* as the rabbinic head — the model of dual leadership represented by the *zugot* who preceded *Hillel* and *Shammai*, in which one served as *nasi* and the other as *av beit din*.

A natural question arises: does this happen only in the city where these offices are actually located, or does it occur everywhere? The *mishna* does not resolve this explicitly. It seems most reasonable to understand it as describing whoever occupies the analogous roles of political and religious leadership in each locale — the *nasi* and *av beit din* functioning as designations of role-type rather than of specific individuals. The placement of ashes on these figures carries a clear message: communal crisis is ultimately a matter of leadership responsibility. If things are going wrong in the community, the process of *me'aynin b'milei d'mata* — assessing what the community has done wrong — places the burden squarely on those at the top.

Why ashes on the *aron* itself? One reading is purely functional and psychological: having the symbol prominently in front of the assembled community, facing the ark, drives home the weight of the moment. But there may be a deeper resonance. *Chazal*'s principle of *imo anochi b'tzara* — God too suffers when Israel suffers — suggests that the ashes on the ark may symbolize God's participation in the mourning. If the relationship between the community and God has been weakened, the distancing is felt on both sides. The ashes on the *aron* may be a way of expressing precisely this: we are all in mourning, God included.

### Individual Ashes

*V'chol echad v'echad noten b'rosho* — every individual also places ashes on his own head. The practice of placing ashes on the head as a sign of mourning has parallels elsewhere: some communities maintain the *minhag* of a *chatan* placing ashes on his forehead at a wedding, evoking *na'aleh Yerushalayim al rosh simchatenu*. The symbolic resonance here is the mourning of the community as a whole — not just the leadership, not just the ark, but every person present. We are all experiencing this moment of rupture and distance. The burnt quality of the ashes — *Rashi*'s insistence on *eifer mamash* — reinforces the sense of destruction and tragedy, evoking what has been lost and what is at stake.

The communal mourning is oriented toward a specific grief: not an abstract misfortune, but the weakening of the relationship with God. If the process ultimately reaches the stage of *k'vnei adam hanizufim laMakom*, the community is in full mourning over that distance. Even at this earlier stage, that horizon is present and felt. The fasting, the ashes, the gathering — all are means of translating that interior grief into a communal posture that can become the basis for *teshuvah* and renewed connection.

### Outdoor Ritual

The decision to bring the *teiva* outdoors — rather than remaining in the *shul* — carries its own significance. Practically, the public square may simply be large enough to hold the entire community in a way that an interior space cannot. The outdoor setting also has the quality of *parhesia*, a public declaration that heightens the seriousness of what is being done.

But there is yet another dimension worth considering. There is a tradition that the *Torah* should not remain secluded in the *beit knesset* or *beit midrash* — that it ought to be brought into the wider life of the community. Read in that light, one element of what may have gone wrong, prompting the fast in the first place, is that the *Torah* has not been integrated into public life as deeply as it should be. Bringing the *teiva* out into the square may thus be not merely a logistical or dramatic choice, but a symbolic statement: the *Torah* belongs here, in the midst of the people, and its displacement into a purely private or institutional domain is itself part of what we are mourning.

---

## Hazaken's Drasha

### Words of Kibushan

*Hazakein shebahem* — the elder among them, who need not be the *nasi* or the *av beit din* but may simply be the appropriate figure for this role, perhaps a skilled *darshan* — stands before the assembled community and delivers *divrei kivushin*. *Rashi* traces the word to the pressing of olives: words that press, that humble, that stir people toward honest self-reflection.

The substance of the *drasha* turns on a pointed reading of the *Yonah* narrative. *Lo ne'emar beanshei Ninveh vayar elohim et sakam ve'et ta'anitam* — it does not say that God saw the sackcloth and fasting of the Ninevites. *Ella vayar elohim et ma'aseihem ki shavu midarkam hara'ah* — it says God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil way. The lesson is explicit: the external practices are not the point. God responds to what people actually do, to the change in behavior, not to the performance of ritual acts.

### Rend Your Heart

The *drasha* continues with a verse from the prophets: *vekiru levavchem ve'al bigdeichem* — rend your hearts, not your garments. Whatever is being done outwardly must ultimately express a real interior rupture, a genuine *teshuvah*.

One might ask why the *mishna* introduces the second quotation with the phrase *uvakabala hu omer* when both *Yonah* and *Yoel* belong to the *Trei Asar* and are therefore from the same prophetic corpus. The likely explanation is structural: the first quotation is embedded in a rhetorical contrast (*lo ne'emar...ella*) that flows naturally into the *pasuk* itself. To insert *uvakabala hu omer* there would disrupt the rhetorical rhythm. The second quotation, by contrast, needs a transitional phrase — "and it further says" — and that is precisely what *uvakabala* provides.

There is also a view that *kabala* is used specifically when *pesukim* from *Nach* function as direct *mussar* — explicit moral instruction — rather than as narrative from which a lesson is drawn. The *Yonah* passage is narrative; the verse *vekiru levavchem* is directly admonitory. Whether or not that distinction accounts for the terminology here, it is worth noting.

One further observation deserves attention. The *hazakein* speaks of sackcloth, fasting, and rending of garments — yet the community has, at this point in the order, only been fasting. Sackcloth never becomes an obligatory *halachic* practice, despite its pervasive presence throughout *Tanakh*. Rending of garments is similarly not part of the formal ritual. The exhortation not to rend garments but to rend the heart is addressed, in a sense, to a community that was not actually rending garments to begin with — which makes the contrast all the more pointed.

### Teshuva Focus

It is worth pausing to note that this *drasha* of the *hazakein* represents essentially the only place in the entire *masechet* where *teshuvah* is explicitly raised as a central theme. That is striking. One might be tempted to conclude that *teshuvah* is therefore the whole point of *ta'anit tzibbur*, but the weight of that conclusion should be measured carefully. *Teshuvah* is certainly one element, and here it is foregrounded, but the larger context of the *mishna* — the *tefillot*, the communal gathering, the reaching out to God — suggests a broader range of concerns. This *drasha* is the one moment where the internal dimension is explicitly named.

---

## Prayer Leader

### Zakein Veragil

With the *drasha* concluded, the community rises for *tefillah* — *amdu bitfilah*. Whether this is *shacharit* or *mincha* is not entirely clear from the *mishna*. It is worth recalling that the earlier *Gemara* described the first half of the fast day as devoted to *milei demata* — communal assessment — with the latter half devoted to *tefillah*, which might suggest *mincha*. On the other hand, in the *Gemara*'s conception of *shacharit*, the service consisted essentially of *birchos krias shema* and *shemoneh esrei*, without *pesukei dezimrah* or *birchos hashachar* as part of the synagogue liturgy. It is therefore not impossible that the *drasha* immediately preceded *shemoneh esrei* of *shacharit*. The question remains open.

For this *tefillah*, the community appoints a *shliach tzibbur* who is *moridim lifnei hateivah zakein veragil* — elderly and accustomed to leading prayer, someone who knows how to *daven* without error and who can bring genuine feeling to the role. The elderly prayer leader carries natural authority and the perspective that comes with years and experience.

### Qualifications

The *mishna* specifies two additional qualities. First, *vayeish lo banim* — he should have children. The significance here is the development of a capacity for genuine compassion: someone who knows what it means to care deeply for others and to feel responsibility for their wellbeing is better positioned to represent the *tzibbur* in its moment of need and to intercede on their behalf.

Second, *uveiso reikam* — his house should be empty. *Rashi*'s understanding is that this refers to a lack of material possessions, so that the *shliach tzibbur* approaches God from a place of genuine humility rather than self-sufficiency. The *Gemara* will offer an alternative explanation. The overarching purpose of these qualities is captured in the *mishna*'s concluding phrase: *kedei sheyehei libo shaleim bitfilah* — so that his heart should be whole and fully present in the prayer.

### Rent vs. Whole

This formulation creates a striking contrast with the *drasha* that immediately preceded it. The *hazakein* quoted *vekiru levavchem* — rend your hearts. The *shliach tzibbur* is chosen so that *libo shaleim* — his heart is whole. Is the heart rent or whole?

The tension may be productive rather than contradictory. One reads the rent heart as the work of *teshuvah* and self-examination — cutting through the armor of habit and self-justification to arrive at genuine feeling. The whole heart then describes the mode of one who, having done that work, turns fully toward God in prayer. The two states correspond to two distinct moments in the spiritual process: first the rupture of honest self-reckoning, then the wholeness of complete devotion. Both the *hazakein* and the *shliach tzibbur* are *zekeinim*, but their roles call forth different qualities of heart.

---

## 24 Brachot

### Six Additions

The *shliach tzibbur* leads the *chazarat hashatz* — the repetition of *shemoneh esrei* — not in the usual form of eighteen (or nineteen) *brachot* but with six additional ones: *u'mosif aleihem od sheish*. The eighteen standard *brachot* serve as the base; these six are added in the repetition only. They are inserted in the same place that *Anenu* is inserted on ordinary fast days — between *goel* and *rofei*. If *Anenu* represents the brief fast-day supplement, these six *brachot* represent the full elaboration for when the situation has reached its most serious stage.

### Zichronot/Shofrot

The first two of the six additions are *zichronot* and *shofrot* — immediately evoking *Rosh Hashanah* and the *musaf* liturgy of that day. The connection is not coincidental. The *Gemara* earlier in the tractate had already noted that *ta'aniyot* and *Rosh Hashanah* share structural parallels in their *brachot*, and the *mishna* in *Rosh Hashanah* had discussed the *shofar* and *chatzotzrot* in juxtaposition with these very themes.

*Zichronot*, with the *chatima* of *zocher habrit* — God, remember the covenant — speaks directly to the anxiety of distance. We are asking God to recall the bond that ties us together, the relationship that must not be abandoned even now. *Shofrot*, in our familiar *nusach* of *shomei'a kol teruat amo Yisrael b'rachamim*, frames the *shofar* blast as Israel's attempt to reach God and asks God to listen. Since the *mishna* will describe actual *shofar* blowing as part of this service, the liturgical content and the ritual act reinforce each other: the *tefillah* speaks of the *shofar* and the *shofar* sounds during the *tefillah*. *Rashi* notes that these *brachot* would include the full complement of *pesukim* drawn from *zichronot* and *shofrot*, giving them the full textual weight of their *Rosh Hashanah* counterparts.

The remaining four *brachot* are constituted from *prakim b'Tehillim*. The third addition opens with *el Hashem batzarata li karati vaya'aneini* — I called to God in my distress and He answered me. The fourth is *essa einai el heharim* — I lift my eyes to the mountains; whence comes my help? The fifth is *mima'amakim keraticha Hashem* — from the depths I have called to You. The sixth is *tefillah l'ani ki ya'atof* — a prayer of the afflicted man when he grows faint, as he pours out his speech before God.

The thematic unity of these four *prakim* is unmistakable: in each, a person in distress turns entirely toward God and calls out for help. Notably, none of these *pesukim* speaks to the theme of *teshuvah* or the acknowledgment of sin. They speak of *tefillah*, of calling out, of God's capacity to hear and answer. This observation will prove relevant to the dispute that follows.

### Rabbi Yehuda

*Rabbi Yehuda omer lo haya tzarich lomar zichronot v'shofrot* — Rabbi Yehuda holds that *zichronot* and *shofrot* should not be recited. He may have felt that these *brachot* were too evocative of *Rosh Hashanah* and inappropriate in this different liturgical context. In their place, Rabbi Yehuda substitutes different texts.

### Psalmic Texts

The substitutions Rabbi Yehuda proposes are: *ra'av ki yihyeh ba'aretz* from *Melachim* — the passage in *Shlomo*'s dedication prayer for the *Beit HaMikdash* — and the passage beginning *asher hayah devar Hashem el Yirmiyahu al divrei habatzarot*, the word of God to *Yirmiyahu* concerning the drought.

To understand why Rabbi Yehuda prefers these texts, it is worth examining their content. The *Melachim* passage recounts *Shlomo*'s prayer at the dedication of the *Beit HaMikdash*, in which he anticipates every form of national crisis — enemy defeat, drought, famine, pestilence — and asks God to hear the prayers that will be directed toward this house. The verses immediately before the explicit mention of *ra'av* describe people who sin, turn to God, acknowledge their wrongdoing, and ask for forgiveness. The dominant language throughout is: because of *cheit*, the people will do *teshuvah*, and therefore God will respond. The final lines affirm that God will hear, forgive, and act — but only because the people have turned from their wrong path.

The *Yirmiyahu* passage similarly opens with the desolation caused by drought (*avlah Yehudah*, *lo hayah geshem ba'aretz*) and then arrives, in *pasuk zayin*, at *im avoneinu anu vanu* — if our sins have testified against us. It follows with *ki rabu meshuvoteinu lecha chatanu* — we have multiplied our turnings-away, we have sinned against You. The cry to God — *mikveh Yisrael Hashem moshio be'et tzarah*, why are you like a stranger to us, why are you like one who cannot save? — is embedded in a context saturated with the acknowledgment of sin.

This stands in sharp contrast to the four *prakim b'Tehillim* endorsed by the *tanna kamma*, which speak exclusively of calling out and being answered, without any element of sin or *teshuvah*. The difference illuminates what is at stake in the dispute. Rabbi Yehuda's position seems to be that what must be foregrounded in this liturgical moment is precisely the acknowledgment of sin and the call to *teshuvah*. The *Rosh Hashanah* theme may not be the wrong mode — it is not entirely inappropriate — but it may not be the most urgent priority. What needs to open and drive these *brachot* is the theme of turning away from sin and returning to God.

### Dispute Analysis

There may be a second dimension to Rabbi Yehuda's position. Recall the earlier discussion in the tractate about whether *matri'in* refers to blowing the *shofar* or to reciting *Anenu*. The possibility arises that Rabbi Yehuda's objection is also, in part, to the emphasis on ritual — particularly the *shofar* — at the expense of the more demanding interior work of *tefillah* and *teshuvah*. Ritual acts like *shofar* blowing have genuine power: they focus attention, stir feeling, and motivate. But they also carry the risk of creating a sense of having discharged one's obligation through external performance. If there is no *shofar* ritual to point to, the community must ask harder questions — have we actually prayed enough, have we actually turned?

It seems likely, then, that two distinct concerns animate Rabbi Yehuda's position: first, that the *Rosh Hashanah* framing be replaced with a framework more directly centered on sin and *teshuvah*; and second, that the emphasis on ritual observance not be permitted to substitute for the deeper interior reckoning that constitutes genuine return.

---

## Mi She'ana Formulas

### Abraham Formula

After the six *brachot* are recited, each concludes with a *chatima* — a closing formula of the blessing. *V'omer chotmeihen*: and he says their closing lines. The first does not belong to the six new additions but to the standard *goel Yisrael* that precedes them. *Al harishona hu omer: mi she'ana et Avraham Avinu behar haMoriah hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem goel Yisrael.*

This formula — "He who answered Abraham our father at *Har haMoriah* should answer you and hear the sound of your cry today" — is inserted immediately before the standard *chatima* of *goel Yisrael*, functioning precisely as an interpolation that frames and enriches the *chatima* without replacing it. The principle that the last line before a *chatima* shapes the meaning of the *chatima* itself is operative here: by saying the *mi she'ana l'Avraham* formula right before the seal, the *bracha* of *goel Yisrael* now resonates with the plea for direct divine response in a moment of acute need.

This is not only the earliest structural instance of this form of prayer but also the liturgical ancestor of the *selichot* service as we know it today. The *mi she'ana* formulas of *selichot* derive from precisely this *mishna*.

The *chatima* of *goel Yisrael* here is the standard one. Both the *tanna kamma* and Rabbi Yehuda agree on the *chatimot*; the dispute was only about which *pesukim* frame the body of the *brachot*. From the *chatimot* onward, there is no *machloket*.

### Sea Formula

*Al hashniyah hu omer: mi she'ana l'avoteinu al yam suf hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma kol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem zocher hanishkachot.* The one who answered the ancestors at the *Yam Suf* should answer you. The *chatima* is *zocher hanishkachot* — who remembers what has been forgotten.

*Rashi* explains the thematic connection: Israel was in Egypt for many years, seemingly forgotten for generations, to the point that they despaired of redemption — *nitya'ashu min hage'ulah*. Then God remembered them. The *bracha* of *zichronot* and its *chatima* of *zocher hanishkachot* tie precisely into the moment of the *Yam Suf*: what seemed like total abandonment became the moment of the most dramatic remembrance. This is a particularly tight and elegant thematic connection.

### Gilgal Formula

*Al hashlishit hu omer: mi she'ana l'Yehoshua b'Gilgal hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem shome'a teruah.* The one who answered *Yehoshua* at *Gilgal* — which *Rashi* confirms refers to the battle of *Yericho* — should answer you. The *chatima* is *shome'a teruah*.

Here everything aligns cleanly. *Yehoshua* was answered at *Yericho* through the *shofarot* — the walls fell to the blast of the *shofar*. The *bracha* is *shofrot*, the theme is *shofar*, the *mi she'ana* is the paradigmatic instance of *shofar*-led military deliverance, and the *chatima* of *shome'a teruah* seals it all together. This is the most internally consistent of all the formulas.

### Samuel Formula

*Al harevi'it hu omer: mi she'ana li'Shmuel baMitzpah hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem shome'a tze'akah.* The one who answered *Shmuel* at *Mitzpah* should answer you. The *chatima* is *shome'a tze'akah*.

The corresponding *perek* is *el Hashem batzarata li karati vaya'aneini*. The connection between *Shmuel* and *tze'akah* is supported by *Rashi*, who notes that the text by *Shmuel* uses the language of *vayitz'ak el Hashem* — and he cried out to God. The *chatima* of *shome'a tze'akah* thus reflects the specific scriptural language associated with *Shmuel*'s intercession.

### Elijah Formula

*Al hachamishit hu omer: mi she'ana l'Eliyahu b'Har Karmel hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem shome'a tefillah.* The one who answered *Eliyahu* at *Har Karmel* should answer you. The *chatima* is *shome'a tefillah*.

The corresponding *perek* is *essa einai el heharim* — I lift my eyes to the mountains. *Rashi* connects *Eliyahu* to this by observing *keneged asiri harrim* — it corresponds to the theme of mountains, and *Eliyahu ne'eneh b'Har HaCarmel me'ein asiri harrim*. The *har* of *Har Karmel* ties into the *harim* of the *perek*. As for the *chatima* of *shome'a tefillah*, *Rashi* connects it to the text by *Eliyahu* that uses the language of *aneni* — answer me — which he glosses as *zo tefillah*, this is *tefillah*. The connection is present but less tightly woven than in some of the other cases.

### Jonah Formula

*Al hashishit hu omer: mi she'ana et Yonah mib'ei hadagah hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem ha'oneh b'eit tzarah.* The one who answered *Yonah* from the belly of the fish should answer you. The *chatima* is *ha'oneh b'eit tzarah*.

The corresponding *perek* is *mima'amakim keraticha Hashem* — from the depths I have called to You. The tie between *mib'ei hadagah* and *mima'amakim* is vivid and direct: the belly of the fish is the paradigmatic depth. *Rashi* links the *chatima* of *ha'oneh b'eit tzarah* to the language in *Yonah* of *karasi mitzara li* — I called from my distress — confirming the thematic resonance. *Yonah* was preeminently in an *eit tzarah*, and the *chatima* makes that explicit.

### David/Solomon

*Al hashvi'it hu omer: mi she'ana et David u'Shlomo b'no b'Yerushalayim hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh. Baruch atah Hashem hamerachem al ha'aretz.* The one who answered *David* and his son *Shlomo* in *Yerushalayim* should answer you. The *chatima* is *hamerachem al ha'aretz*.

The corresponding *perek* is *tefillah l'ani ki ya'atof* — a prayer of the poor man when he grows faint. The *chatima* of *merachem al ha'aretz* requires explanation. When were *David* and *Shlomo* answered in *Yerushalayim*? The *Gemara* explains: *David* in connection with a famine — *vayehi ra'av bimei David shalosh shanim shana achar shana* — a famine that lasted three consecutive years. *Shlomo* in connection with his bringing the *aron* into the *kodesh hakodashim* at the dedication of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The former is directly relevant to the crisis at hand; the latter evokes the ultimate moment of closeness between God and Israel in *Yerushalayim*.

### Rashi Analysis

*Rashi* explains the *chatima* of *merachem al ha'aretz* as follows: *she'hein hitpalelu al Eretz Yisrael u'tefillah l'ani ki ya'atof lahania dochak geshamim* — because *David* and *Shlomo* prayed for the land of Israel, and the *perek* of *tefillah l'ani* speaks of *be'atzar geshamim*, the withholding of rain. This makes the final *bracha* the most explicitly connected to the actual crisis motivating the fast: the fear of famine, the lack of rain, the land under threat. *Rashi*'s broader comment — *v'chen kulam l'fi inyan hamizmorim* — indicates that the thematic connections between each *mi she'ana* figure, the *perek* assigned to that *bracha*, and the *chatima* are generally intended to cohere, even if some instances are more tightly woven than others.

Stepping back, a pattern emerges across all seven formulas. The *chatimot* move from the generic to the specific. The earlier ones — *goel Yisrael*, *zocher hanishkachot*, *shome'a teruah* — are broad invocations. The later ones become more particular, and the final *chatima* of *merachem al ha'aretz* arrives at the precise, concrete concern: the land, the rain, the famine. This structure reinforces the observation made throughout this *perek*: the dominant theme of these prayers is God's responsiveness to those who call out to Him in distress. The concern about sin and *teshuvah*, however theologically important, is proportionally a smaller thread. The overwhelming weight of the liturgy here is: we call, God answers.

---

## Maaseh Account

### Shofar Blowing

The *mishna* now records a historical incident. *Maaseh bi'yemei Rebbi Chalafta ve'Rebbi Chananya ben Teradyon she'avar echad lifnei hateivah* — it happened in the days of *Rebbi Chalafta* and *Rebbi Chananya ben Teradyon* that someone came before the ark to lead the service. After he concluded the full text of the first *bracha* — *ve'gamar et haberachah kula* — the community did not respond *amen*. Instead, an announcer called out *tik'u kohanim*, and the *kohanim* blew. Then the *mi she'ana* formula was recited — *mi she'ana et Avraham Avinu behar haMoriah, hu ya'aneh etchem veyishma bekol tza'akatchem hayom hazeh* — and then, separately, came the call *hari'u bnei Aharon hari'u*, and they sounded a *teruah*.

What was deviant about this practice? Several elements: the community did not say *amen* after the *chatima*; the *mi she'ana* formula was separated from the *bracha* and placed after the *chatima* rather than integrated before it; and the blowing was structured so as to give the *mi she'ana* the weight of a separate announcement accompanied by *teki'ot* and *teru'ot*, rather than being embedded within the *bracha*. The effect was something like twelve distinct acts — *brachot*, separate *mi she'ana* formulas, and interleaved *teki'ot* and *teru'ot* — rather than the unified structure the *mishna* prescribes.

### Rabbinic Limit

*Uksheba hadavar eitzel chachamim amru: lo hayu nohagim ken ela besha'ar mizrach uvehar habayit* — when the matter came before the sages, they ruled that this practice was done only at the eastern gate or on the Temple Mount, not outside the precincts of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

What precisely was being censured? The *Gemara* will clarify that the *teki'ot* and *teru'ot* themselves were not the problem — blowing the *shofar* together with the twenty-four *brachot* was standard practice even outside the *Beit HaMikdash*. What the sages objected to was the failure to answer *amen* and, possibly, the structural displacement of the *mi she'ana* formula outside the *bracha* itself. It is, however, quite possible to read the *mishna* differently: a straightforward reading of the text suggests that the blowing itself — the prominent role of the *kohanim* with the *chatzotzrot* or *shofar* — was the practice restricted to the Temple precinct. That reading cannot be dismissed. The *Gemara*'s resolution will address this, but the *mishna* as written leaves the question genuinely open.

---

## Fasting Levels

### First 3 Fasts

The *mishna* now turns to how the priests in the *Beit HaMikdash* would participate in the communal fasts. The connection to what precedes is not accidental: the *mishna* has just concluded with a reference to *beit hamikdash*, and the previous *bracha* centered on *Shlomo b'Yerushalayim*. The entire *perek* has maintained a thread of connection to the *mikdash*, and now that connection is made explicit in terms of who fasts and to what degree.

According to *Rabbi Yehoshua*: during the first three fasts, *anshei mishmar* — the division of priests on call for that week — would fast but not complete the fast. *Anshei beit av* — those assigned to the service on that specific day — would not fast at all. The logic is clear: their *avodah* took priority, and those actively engaged in the Temple service could not be expected to weaken themselves unnecessarily.

### Middle 3 Fasts

During the middle three fasts, the obligations escalate by one degree. *Anshei mishmar* would now fast and complete the fast — a full-day fast. *Anshei beit av* would fast but not complete it, breaking their fast at some point in the afternoon to sustain themselves for the *avodah*.

### Last 7 Fasts

During the last seven fasts, *elu v'elu mit'anim umashlimim* — both groups would fast completely through the day. This represents the maximal level of communal participation, in which even those performing active Temple service are included in the full fast. This corresponds to the moment when the *teiva* is brought out, the ashes are placed, and the full twenty-four *brachot* are recited. Everything escalates together. Even inside the *mikdash*, where the *kohanim* are engaged in the service that is itself an expression of closeness to God, the community-wide fast is total.

### Rabbi Yehoshua

The scheme above reflects the position of *Rabbi Yehoshua*. *Vachachamim omrim* — the sages hold a somewhat less severe position, in which each tier is reduced by one level of stringency. According to the sages: during the first three fasts, *elu v'elu lo hayu mit'anim klal* — neither group would fast at all in the *Beit HaMikdash*. During the middle three fasts, *anshei mishmar* would fast but not complete it, while *anshei beit av* would not fast at all. During the last seven fasts, *anshei mishmar* would fast and complete the fast, but *anshei beit av mit'anim v'lo mashlimim* — those actively working in the *mikdash* would fast but not complete it, even at the most severe stage.

The underlying question in the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and the sages is how to weigh the demands of the communal fast against the priority of the Temple service. Rabbi Yehoshua is more willing to impose fasting on those actively engaged in the *avodah*; the sages are more protective of the *avodah*'s integrity and maintain a distinction even at the highest level of communal urgency.

---

*Mi shebeirach avoteinu Avraham Yitzchak v'Ya'akov asher hotzi et Yosef mibor tachtiyot v'anah l'Daniel b'gov ha'arayot el shomei'a l'tza'akat avot v'imahot hapotei'ach b'chol eit sha'arei dema'ot hu yishmor v'yashgiach al hane'arim hachatufim Ya'akov Naftali ben Rachel Devorah, Gilad Michael ben Bat Galim, Eyal ben Iris Teshurah b'toch shear nidchei ameinu v'tzivoteinu. El rachum v'chanun shomeir Yisrael asher lo yanum v'lo yishan totzi'eim mitzara l'revacha mei'afela l'ora umeshibud l'geulah v'tachzirem l'cheik avoteihem v'imoteihem bivriut uv'shalom. Bizchut avoteinu toshia baneinu viyikayeim bahem mah shekatuv: hotzia mimasger nafshi l'hodot et shemecha. Hashta ba'agala uvizman kariv v'nomar amen.*
