But let us see what he did with it. *Ve-sayer leh le-chulah mata* — he would inspect the entire city. *Ve-chol ashista de-hava rei'ata* — every wall that was shaky — and here again we return to the recurring theme of shaky walls — *hava satar lah* — he would demolish it. *Ei efshar le-mar benei lah* — if the owners had the means, they were required to rebuild it themselves, since a hazardous wall was their responsibility. *Ve-i lo efshar, benei lah ihu mi-dideih* — and if they lacked the means, he would rebuild it from his own funds.

One commentator suggests that Rav Huna deliberately went out in the gold chair because he would pass through non-Jewish neighborhoods, and the display of wealth gave him credibility — a man of such means who concerned himself with the community's welfare would be taken seriously and followed. There is also the reading that it was a display of authority, a kind of official inspection. In any case, the picture is striking: here is someone who takes considerable *kavod* for himself, traveling in a golden seat, and yet is entirely and proactively engaged with the material welfare of the community, using his own funds to ensure public safety.

### Price Support Markets

*U-ve-chol panya de-ma'alei shabbata* — every *erev Shabbat*, *hava meshader shlucha le-shuka* — he would send a messenger to the marketplace. *Ve-chol yarka de-hava payish lehu le-ginai* — any produce or food that was left over late Friday afternoon, which clearly could not be kept without refrigeration and would be discarded, *zavin leh* — he would buy it up. *Ve-shadi leh le-nahara* — and throw it into the river. He had no use for the food; the purpose was to encourage merchants to bring their full stock to market, so that the community would have ample food available for *Shabbat* and sellers would not fear that their wares would go unsold.

### Why Not Give Poor

The *gemara* raises an obvious question: *ve-liteiv le-aniyim* — why not give the leftover food to the poor rather than throw it into the river? The *gemara* answers: *zimnin de-samcha da'atayhu ve-lo atu le-mizban* — because then people would assume that Rav Huna would buy everything up and distribute it, and so they would not bother to purchase food for *Shabbat* themselves. But why would that be a problem — let him just do that? Rashi explains: *de-nisamchu ahanei u-ve-li lo atu le-mizban* — if people relied on the end-of-day giveaway, and Rav Huna only bought what was left over at the last moment, perhaps there would be nothing left and they would have nothing to eat for *Shabbat*. He did not want them to become overly dependent on that.

The *gemara* continues: *ve-lishdyeih le-behemah* — well, at least give it to animals? The answer: *kasavar ma'achal adam ein ma'achilin livheima* — he held that one does not feed human food to animals. This is somewhat paradoxical, since the food is going to waste regardless. Apparently, feeding human food to animals is considered more disrespectful to the food — or perhaps more dehumanizing in some sense — than simply discarding it. One might raise the *pasuk* of *l'ger asher b'isharecha titnena o machor l'nochri*, which speaks of giving *treif* meat to non-Jews, but *treif* meat is outside the boundary of what one's community would eat, which makes that a different case.

*V'lo yizbeney klal* — so why bother buying it at all? Because *nimtzas machshilan l'atid lavo* — not buying it would harm the economy and discourage merchants from bringing their goods to market, which would ultimately hurt the community.

The story presents an interesting tension: on the one hand, Rav Huna goes out in a gold chair, which represents a certain ostentatiousness of wealth; on the other hand, he is deeply concerned with communal well-being and acts entirely from his own funds. And the whole logic of the market intervention — why not give it to the poor, why not feed it to animals — reflects a careful, practical engagement with economic reality. These *chachamim* are not miracle workers. They operate entirely in a real-world mode, which reads, in some sense, as a sustained counterpoint to the *Choni* model.

### Public Health Care

*Ki hava leh milsa d'asuta* — when Rav Huna had some type of remedy or medicine, *hava malei kuza* — he would fill a container, *v'taley lei b'sifa d'dasha* — and hang it outside his house, *v'amar kol d'tzarich l'eisei v'lishkol* — so that anyone who needed the medicine could come and take it. This served two purposes: it made medicine available to the community, and it allowed people to take it privately, without having to announce that they were sick or come to him directly.

*V'ika d'amrei* — some say the version is slightly different: he knew the matters relating to *shivsa* — a harmful spirit said by the *gemara* to afflict one who fails to wash hands — *hava manach kuza d'maya*, and he would fill a vessel of water, *v'amar kol d'tzarich l'eisei v'liel, d'lo l'istakein* — so that anyone who needed water to wash their hands should come and do so, that they should not be endangered. In either version, Rav Huna is attending to public health concerns, making provisions available to all without requiring them to seek him out personally.

### Hospitality Meals

*Ki hava karich rifta* — when he would eat bread, when he would break bread for a meal, *hava patach l'vaveih* — he would open his doors, *v'amar kol man d'tzarich l'eisei v'lechol* — and announce: anyone who needs to eat should come and eat. It evokes the *Seder* night declaration: *kol dichfin yeitei veyeichol* — whoever is hungry, let him come and eat.

### Rava Response Limits

Rava responded: *kuleihu matzinan mekaymi* — I could fulfill all of these practices — though one wonders whether Rava had the financial means, yet presumably he felt he could. *Livar meiha* — except for that last one, *d'lo matzina l'me'avad* — which I cannot do. *Mishum d'nafishei benei Mechuza* — because the population of Mechuza is simply too large. He could not open his doors to everyone without being completely overwhelmed. The word in the text appears to be *l'vaveih* — his doors — rather than his heart, that is, he opened his gates and called anyone who wished to enter. Rava acknowledges that even the most admirable model has its practical limits.

## Ilfa & Yochanan

### Leave for Business

At the top of 25a appears what is now a well-known story. *Ilfa v'Rav Yochanan havah garsi b'Oraisa* — Ilfa and Rav Yochanan were learning *Torah*, *dachika lehu milta tuva* — but they were suffering greatly from financial hardship. *Amru: neikum v'neizil v'na'avid iska* — they said: perhaps we should set aside the learning and go into business, we have to start earning money. *U'nekayeim b'nafshein: efes ki lo yihyeh becha evyon* — and we should fulfill in ourselves the verse "there shall be no poor among you." That is, *lo yihyeh becha* — you yourself should not be poor. You have a responsibility not to remain impoverished, and going out to support yourself is a legitimate obligation.

*Azlu, osevi tusei guda* — they went and, on their journey away from the *Beis Medrash*, were sitting beneath a bridge — and again notice the recurring theme: shaky walls, shaky bridges. We have already encountered the motif of the shaky wall whose collapse was held in abeyance by the merit of a great man. The background is very much present here: sitting under a shaky bridge, without sufficient merit, is not a safe place to be.

### Angel Debate

*Havah ka karchi rifta* — they were eating. *Asu terei malachei hashareis* — two heavenly angels came. *Shama Rav Yochanan* — Rav Yochanan overheard the angels speaking to each other. One said to the other: *nishdi aleihu hai guda v'niktlineihu* — let us cast this bridge upon them and kill them. Why? *Shemanichim chayei olam v'oskim b'chayei sha'ah* — because they have abandoned eternal life, the learning of *Torah*, and are occupying themselves with the temporal life of making money. Such a grave abandonment warrants death. *Amar lei idach: shavkeinu* — the second angel replied: leave them be. *D'ika behu chad, d'kaima lei sha'ata* — because there is one among them for whom the time is standing, meaning he is destined to rise to great heights and must not be harmed.

### Yochanan Returns

*Rav Yochanan shama, Ilfa lo shama* — Rav Yochanan heard this conversation; Ilfa did not. *Amar lei Rav Yochanan l'Ilfa: shama mar midi?* — Did you hear anything? *Amar lei: lo* — No. *Mi'desham'ei ana v'Ilfa lo shama, shma mina l'didi kaima li sha'ata* — since I heard it and Ilfa did not, it must be that they were speaking about me; my time has come in terms of *Torah* greatness. *Amar lei Rav Yochanan: ahadar* — I am going back to the *Beis Medrash*. *V'okei b'nafshai: ki lo yechdal evyon mikerev ha'aretz* — and I will fulfill in myself not the first verse but the second: "the poor shall never cease from the land." There will always be poor people; let it be me. I will be one of the poor, and I will go back and learn *Torah*.

### Ilfa Success

*Rav Yochanan hadar* — Rav Yochanan returned to the *Beis Medrash*. *Ilfa lo hadar* — Ilfa did not return. *Ad d'ata Ilfa* — by the time Ilfa came back, after what may have been many years out in the world earning his fortune, *amlikh Rabbi Yochanan* — Rabbi Yochanan had become king, meaning he had been appointed *Rosh Yeshiva*. As Rashi notes on the third narrow line of his commentary — *minuhu Rosh Yeshiva* — and it was the custom that whoever was appointed *Rosh Yeshiva*, *hayu migadlin oto mi-she-lahen u-ma'ashirin oto* — they would elevate him and make him wealthy from their own resources. Rashi cites a parallel with the *Kohen Gadol*, where the verse *veha-Kohen ha-Gadol mei-echav gadleihu mi-shel echav* is interpreted to mean that his brothers would help make him the greatest among them. So Rabbi Yochanan's poverty was no longer a concern — his position brought with it the material support he needed. He was given a desk, an office, and the community's backing.

### Ilfa Regrets

*Amru lo* — they said to Ilfa: *ei otiv Mar ve-garis, lo havei malikh Mar* — if you, the master, had remained in the *Beis Medrash* and continued learning, it would have been you who was appointed *Rosh Yeshiva*, not Rabbi Yochanan. You were sharper, you knew more — had you only stayed, it would have been you. One can imagine how that made him feel.

### Mast Challenge

*Azal tali nafshia be-askarya de-sefunta* — so he went and suspended himself from the mast of the ship, the great central pole. *Amar: ei ika de-sha'il li be-matnita de-Rabbi Hiyya ve-Rabbi Oshaya* — if anyone can ask me anything from the *braitot* of Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Oshaya — who are the ones who edited the *braitot* and the *Tosefta* — *de-lo pashitna lei mi-matnitin* — and I cannot demonstrate that it is already rooted and anchored in a *Mishnah*, *nafilna mi-askarya de-sefunta ve-tavana* — then I will cast myself from the mast and drown. It is a little dramatic, admittedly, but the point is clear: I will prove that my mastery is complete — not only do I know *Mishnah* and *braita*, I can show you how they are all organically connected.

### Deathbed Wishes

Someone took him up on his challenge. *Tana lei ha-omer tenu shekel le-vanai be-shabbat* — he was taught the following *braita*: if someone is dying and leaves a trust for his children, instructing the trustees to provide each child with one *shekel* per week. *Ve-hem re'uyim latet lahem sela* — but the children's reasonable needs require a *sela*, which is worth more than a *shekel*. What does one do? *Notnim lahem sela* — one gives them the *sela*. The principle invoked is *yesh bi-khlal matayim maneh*: if he said "give them a hundred," he did not say "give them only a hundred" — two hundred is still a hundred, it is already contained within it. Therefore one may give more.

*Ve-im amar al titnu lahem ela shekel* — but if he explicitly said "give them no more than a *shekel*," *ein notnim lahem ela shekel* — then one may give them only a *shekel*, no more.

Now, if he said give them a certain amount weekly, but added: *metu yirshu acherim tachteihem* — if they die, others should take their place as beneficiaries of the trust — then *bein she-amar tenu bein she-amar al titnu, ein notnim lahem ela shekel*: whether he said "give them" or "don't give them more," you give them only the stated amount. Why? Because the money is not ultimately all going to these children — there are other intended recipients — and therefore one cannot apply the same interpretive latitude. The implied intent was that the stated amount was precise, not that the children should eventually receive the full fund.

### Knowledge Mastery

*Amar lei: ha mani Rabbi Meir hi* — this *braita*, Ilfa declared, follows the position of Rabbi Meir. For Rabbi Meir holds that *mitzvah lekayem divrei hamet* — it is a *mitzvah* to fulfill the instructions of the deceased. The entire *braita* is working out the parameters of how to interpret what the dying person actually meant — does saying "give them a hundred" mean exactly one hundred, or at least one hundred, and does the answer depend on other conditions he stipulated? But all of that elaboration rests on the foundational premise that one must honor the deceased's instructions, a principle established in the *Mishnah* under Rabbi Meir's ruling.

This is not exactly the same point as the *Mishnah*, of course — there is considerably more elaboration in the *braita* than in the *Mishnah* itself. But Ilfa's claim is that he has all the material organized: he knows not only the *braitot* but can locate them, situate them within the *Mishnayot*, and demonstrate which *Mishnah* each *braita* is working out. What he is demonstrating is less a display of sharp analytic ability and more a command of the *corpus* in its entirety — organized, linked, categorized, and coherent. This is distinct from the person the *gemara* sometimes describes dismissively as a *chamor nosei sefarim*, a donkey laden with books — someone who knows a great deal of information but has not integrated it. What Ilfa demonstrates is mastery in the sense of having it all meaningfully organized and interconnected.

One student in the shiur noted astutely that the *gemara* does not use the terms *braita* or *Tosefta* here — it says "their *Mishnah*" (*matnitin de-Rabbi Hiyya*) as opposed to "our *Mishnah*" (*matnitin*). This is correct. The use of *matnitin* — our *Mishnah* — carries the implication of canonicity and authority. Linking everything back to *our Mishnah* arguably strengthens rather than levels the hierarchy: all the other compilations are in some sense derivative of or secondary to the canonical *Mishnah*. Nowhere in the *gemara* do we sense that *braita* and *Mishnah* stand on an equal playing field.

The broader point of the Ilfa and Rav Yochanan story seems clearly to be a critique of Ilfa's choice. We have just been reading about the importance of using one's funds and resources for the community — and there is much to be said for taking care of the material world. But that should not be read as a license to abandon *Torah* entirely in favor of business. Rav Yochanan, who returned to the *Beis Medrash* and accepted poverty, ultimately became *Rosh Yeshiva* and had his poverty resolved through his position. Ilfa, who went out to seek his fortune and succeeded, came back to find himself displaced — and rather than reflecting quietly on what he had lost, he climbed a ship's mast to make a spectacle of his learning. The critique falls clearly on him.

One student offered a beautiful additional reading: the *braita* about deathbed wishes and the trust fund may itself be a kind of mirror for the story. The deceased leaves a limited fund, and the question is whether one stretches the interpretation to give the heirs more, or adheres to the stated terms. Rav Yochanan, in effect, said: I will accept the *divrei hamet*, I will live within the constraints, I will be poor — *ki lo yechdal evyon* — and not try to stretch beyond what is given. Ilfa tried to stretch, to find more, and ultimately came back to find that the canonical appointment had been filled by another.

## Nachum Ish Gamzu

### Physical Afflictions

The *gemara* now brings the stories of Nachum Ish Gamzu. *Amru alav al Nachum Ish Gamzu shehaya suma mishtei einav* — they said about him that he was blind in both eyes. *Gidem mishtei yadav* — he had lost both arms. *Kiteia mishtei raglav* — both his legs were cut off. *Vechol gufo malei shechin* — and his entire body was covered with boils and sores. *Vehaya mutal beveit ra'ua* — and — another link to the recurring theme — he was in a shaky house. *Veraglei mitato munachim besefalim shel mayim* — the legs of his bed were placed in buckets of water, *kdei shelo ya'alu alav nemalim* — so that ants could not climb up onto him, since he had no limbs with which to push them away.

### House Protection

*Pa'am achat hayta mitato munachat beveit ra'ua* — once, his bed was in a shaky house. *Bikshu talmidav lifnot mitato* — his students wanted to move his bed out first so the house would not collapse on him — paralleling the earlier story where there was concern about rescuing vessels from a shaky structure. *Ve'achar kach lifnot et hakelim* — and only then remove the other vessels.

*Amar lahem: banai, panu et hakelim ve'achar kach panu et mitati* — he said to them: my children, take out the vessels first and then take me out. *Shemuvtach lachem shekol zman she'ani babayit ein habayit nofel* — for I assure you, as long as I am in the house it will not fall down. Here, in contrast to the earlier Rav Adda bar Abba story where his *Torah* protected him without his awareness, Nachum Ish Gamzu is fully conscious of the protection surrounding him. The painful irony, of course, is that the house is not falling — and yet look at what has already befallen his body.

*Pinu et hakelim ve'achar kach pinu et mitato venafal habayit* — they followed his instructions: took out the vessels, took him out, and the house collapsed. A direct parallel to the earlier story.

### Question Afflictions

*Amru lo talmidav* — his students then said to him: *Rebbi, vechi me'achar shetzadik gamur ata, lama alta lecha kach* — Rabbi, since you are so righteous that your merit protected the house from falling, how could such terrible things have happened to your body?

### Poor Man Neglect

*Amar lahem banai, ani garamti le'atzmi* — he said: my children, I brought it upon myself. *Shepa'am achat hayiti mehalekh baderekh leveit chami* — once I was traveling on the way to my father-in-law's house. *Vehaya imi masui gimel chamorim: echad shel ma'achal, echad shel mishteh, ve'echad shel minei megadim* — and with me I carried the load of three donkeys: one of food, one of drink, and one of delicacies. The evocation of *Eved Avraham* traveling laden to his future father-in-law's house is difficult to miss.

*Ba ani echad ve-amad li ba-derech ve-amar li: Rabbi, parneseni* — a poor person came and stood before him on the road and said: my master, support me, feed me. *Amarti lo: hamten ad she-efrok min ha-chamor* — I said to him: wait a moment while I unload it from the donkey. I have bundles of food; let me untie them and I will give you something. *Ve-lo hispakti lifrok min ha-chamor ad she-yatzata nishmato* — but I did not manage to unload from the donkey before the man died of hunger.

One student suggested that Nachum may not have meant "wait while I untie the bundle right here on the road" but rather "wait until I reach my destination and unpack" — a reading that would make the sin considerably more serious. Rather than meeting the man's immediate need, he was in effect saying: come see me later, in the office. If that reading is correct, the guilt is far more understandable.

### Self-Imposed Curses

*Halachti ve-nafalti al panav ve-amarti* — I went and fell upon his face and said: *einai she-lo chasu al einecha, yasumu* — my eyes that had no compassion on your eyes, may they go blind. *Yadai she-lo chasu al yadecha, yitgadmu* — my hands that had no compassion on your hands, may they be cut off. *Raglai she-lo chasu al raglecha, yitkate'u* — my legs that had no compassion on your legs, may they be cut off. *Ve-lo nitkarrera da'ati ad she-amarti: kol gufi yihiye malei shechin* — and I was still not calmed until I said: let my entire body be filled with boils.

*Amru lo: oy lanu she-re'inucha be-kach* — they said to him: woe to us that we have seen you in such a state. *Amar lahem: oy li im lo re'ituni be-kach* — he said: woe to me had you not seen me like this, for then I would not have been properly punished for my wrongdoing.

This is a striking passage, and a genuinely difficult one. The question of what exactly he did wrong is not simple. His food was packed in bundles on the donkeys — what was he supposed to do? One might argue he should have anticipated encountering poor people and kept food more readily accessible. One might also note, as was suggested in discussion, that the word *hamten* — "wait" — already signals a distancing. A different person might have said yes immediately, might have been thinking ahead about how to help rather than how to manage his luggage. The contrast with Rav Huna, who went out daily, proactively and in his gold chair, inspecting the city for how he could be useful, is perhaps the deeper point: here is someone absorbed in his personal journey, traveling to his father-in-law laden with goods, not thinking of himself as someone who might have a communal obligation along the way.

And yet his reaction — self-imposing the most extreme physical afflictions imaginable — seems difficult to justify, let alone to hold up as a model. To an extent, the *gemara* studying *Masechet Ta'anit* has not been especially focused on *teshuvah* through bodily self-punishment; that theme is largely absent from the *masechet*'s dominant framework. And to impose upon oneself blindness, the loss of limbs, and a body covered in sores over what might have been, at worst, a momentary hesitation, seems far beyond any proportionate response. It is difficult to read this straightforwardly as an instructive model. That said, the *gemara* does not seem to be presenting it as a counter-example either — the tone is not critical of Nachum Ish Gamzu, even if his response strikes us as extreme.

## Gam Zu Letovah

### Name Etymology

*Amai karu lei Nachum Ish Gamzu?* — Why was he called Nachum Ish Gamzu? *De-chol milta de-hava salka lei amar gam zu letovah* — because whatever happened to him he would say: *gam zu letovah*, this too is for the best. Holding that alongside everything we just read about his afflictions, this is an impressive statement.

### Caesar Gift

*Zimna chada bau leshadurei Yisrael doron levei keisar* — once, the Jewish people wanted to send a gift to the house of Caesar. *Amru man yeizil yezil Nachum Ish Gamzu, demelumad benissin* — they said: let Nachum Ish Gamzu go, for he is accustomed to having miracles occur to him. One of the miracles, of course, that had occurred to him was that his prayers for self-affliction were fulfilled — he did not cut off his own arms, so presumably the power of his prayer brought about what happened to his body. Whether this episode took place before or after his terrible physical state is not entirely clear. In any case, they knew that miracles attended him.

*Shadru bideih malei sifta de'avnin tavan umargaliyot* — they sent in his hands a full crate of precious jewels and gems. *Azal bat behahu dira* — he traveled and lodged for the night at a certain inn. *Beleilya kamu hanach daryei veshaklinhu lesifta* — in the night the other lodgers got up and took everything from his crate. *Umalunhu afra* — and filled it with dirt.

*Ki mata hatam, sareinhu lesifta, chazyu demalu afra* — when he arrived at Caesar's house, they opened the crate and saw it was full of dirt. *Ba'ah malka lemaktalinhu lekulhu* — the king wanted to kill Nachum and his entire retinue. *Amar kamachaychi bi Yehuda'ei* — the Jews are mocking me. *Amar gam zu letovah* — this too will be for the best.

### Magic Dust

*Ata Eliyahu* — Elijah the prophet appeared. Perhaps he was waiting to see how Nachum would respond, and now that Nachum had maintained his faith, *Eliyahu* came. *Idmi lei kechad mineihu* — he appeared as one of the Caesar's own retinue. *Ve-amar lei: dilma hai afra me'afra de-Avraham avuhon* — perhaps this is the dust of Avraham their forefather. *Dechi havah shadi afra havah sayyifei* — for when Avraham would throw dust it would turn to swords, *vegila havah girei* — and when he would throw straw it would turn to arrows. The *pasuk* in Yeshayahu — *mi he'ir mimizrach*, who was stirred from the east — is understood to refer to Avraham, that his dust was like his swords and his straw was like his bow.

### Subdue Country

*Havah chada medinta dela matzu lemichbasha* — there was a certain country the Caesars had not yet been able to conquer. *Badku mineih vechavshuha* — they tested this dirt against that country and were able to subdue it, for when thrown it turned to swords and destroyed the enemy. *Ayiluhu levei ganzeih* — they brought Nachum Ish Gamzu and his retinue into the treasure house. *Umaluhu lesifteih avnin tavan umargaliyot* — and filled his crate with precious jewels — the very thing he had come to bring them, they now gave him. *Veshadruhu beyikra raba* — and sent him out with great honor. It is hard not to notice the parallel with Avraham going down to Egypt and being sent out with great wealth.

### Innkeepers Killed

*Ki atu batu behahu dira* — when he returned, he lodged again at the same inn. *Amru leh: mai ayis behadach de'avdi lach yikra kulei hai?* — they said to him: what did you bring to Caesar that he gave you such honor? *Amar lehu: mai de-shakli mehacha amti lahatam* — whatever I took from here when I left, that is what I brought there. Understanding this to mean the dirt of their inn was somehow magical, *setaru ledireihu* — they knocked down their entire inn, *ve-amtinu levei malka* — and brought it to Caesar. *Amru leh: hai afra dayti hacha min didan hu* — the dirt that Nachum brought you was our dirt. *Badkuhu vela ashkachuh* — they tested it and it was not magical. *Vkatlinhu lehanhu darya* — and they were all killed.

### Faith Critique

Everything, then, came out for the best — at least for Nachum and the Jewish people, if not for the innkeepers. But it is worth pausing to consider what the *gam zu letovah* approach carries with it. It is a beautiful and deeply faithful stance — in the face of catastrophe, to hold firm to the conviction that God's hand is guiding events and it will all turn out well. And for Nachum himself, that faith was vindicated. But the approach can also mask a detachment from responsibility. If everything is already going to be for the best, one might not feel sufficient urgency to guard one's jewels, to take practical precautions, or — and here we return to the earlier story — to respond immediately and decisively when a hungry man appears on the road. The *Yosef* model, one might say, is *gam zu letovah*: God's plan will unfold. The *Yehuda* model is to step forward, take responsibility, and act. Taken as an all-encompassing life philosophy, *gam zu letovah* risks, at its edges, a kind of withdrawal from the urgent demands of the world around us.

## Dever Definition

### Dever Parameters

The *gemara* now returns to its legal discussion: *eizu dever* — what constitutes pestilence (*dever*) severe enough to warrant fasting? The *Mishnah* established a baseline: a city that sends out 500 foot soldiers and loses three people to disease over three days. *Tanu rabanan* — the *gemara* now expands this with a *braita*: a city like Akko with 1,500 able-bodied men — interestingly called a *kfar* (village) despite its size — from which nine people die over three days, one after another, *harei zeh dever* — that is pestilence. *Beyom echad o bearbaa yamim ein zeh dever* — if all the deaths occur in a single day, or conversely if spread over four days, it is not considered *dever*.

The reasoning on the time dimension deserves attention. The *gemara* correctly calculates: if 500 people means three deaths in three days, then 1,500 people still means three deaths per day — it is the same rate, which is still nine deaths over three days, not nine deaths over nine days. The point being that the severity threshold is a *daily rate*, not a cumulative number spread across more days. On the other side, if all nine die in one day, even though that seems more severe, it may represent a freak occurrence rather than a persistent epidemic — and if spread over four days, perhaps the situation is not severe enough to qualify.

A city with 500 men, like a smaller village, requires three deaths over three consecutive days to qualify. The same time conditions apply: a single day or four-day spread does not constitute *dever*.

### Drokrat Case

*Drokrat* was a city with 500 able-bodied men. *V'yatzeu mimenu shalosh meisim b'yom echad* — and three people died all in one day. *Gazar Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda tanisa* — Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda ruled that this constituted *dever* and declared a fast.

### Nachman Dispute

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: k'man k'Rabbi Meir?* — Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenged him: whose opinion are you following in ruling that three deaths in one day equals three deaths over three days? That is the position of Rabbi Meir, who argues with respect to a goring ox that if the ox gored three people in a single day it is a *muad* — a habitual gorer. The general rule is that an ox becomes *muad* by goring once a day over three consecutive days. But Rabbi Meir reasons: *rikhak negichosov chayav* — if spreading out the gorings makes it *muad*, then *kirev negichosov lo kol sheken* — if they are compressed into a shorter time, how much more so is the ox more dangerous? Nevertheless, the counter-position holds that intensity in a single day does not establish the persistent habit required for the designation. So too here: three deaths in one day may indicate something intense but not an ongoing epidemic.

## Anonymous Merit

### Move Invitation

*Amar lei Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda l'Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: leisay mar l'gaban* — Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda invited Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak to move to his city. The implicit suggestion was that Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's city was a more significant place of *Torah*, and why remain in a smaller, less distinguished place?

### Person Honors Place

*Amar lei: tanina* — he replied: I will teach you a *braisa*. *Rabbi Yosi omer lo mekomo shel adam mechabdo ela adam mechabed es mekomo* — a person's place does not give him honor; it is the person who gives honor to his place.

*Sheken matzinu b'Har Sinai* — we find this demonstrated by Har Sinai. *Shekol zman shehashchina shruya alav* — as long as the Divine Presence dwelled upon it — *amra Torah: gam hatzon v'habakar al yiru el mul hahar hahu* — the *Torah* forbade even the animals from grazing near the mountain. *Nistalka shchina heimenu* — but when the *Shechina* departed from it, *amra Torah: bimshoch hayovel heimah yaalu v'har* — then people could ascend the mountain freely. It was never the mountain that was significant in itself; it was God's presence that mattered. Once that presence lifted, the mountain was just a mountain.

*V'chen matzinu b'Ohel Moed shebamidbar* — similarly with the *Ohel Moed* in the wilderness. *Shekol zman shehu natuy* — as long as it was erected and spread, *amra Torah: v'yishalchu min hamachaneh kol tzarua* — the *Torah* required all *tamei* people to be expelled from the camp, the *Ohel Moed* conferring holiness on the surrounding space. *Hukplu hayerios* — once the curtains were folded and the *Ohel Moed* dismantled, *hutru zavin u'metzorain l'ikanes sham* — all those who were *tamei* could freely enter that space. The space itself had no inherent sanctity; it was the *Ohel Moed*'s presence that created the significance.

Thank you very much — I am content where I am. My presence gives honor to my place; I do not need a place to confer honor on me. *Amar lei: i hachi neisay mar l'gavei mar* — so Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda then said: well, if that is the principle, perhaps I should move to you. It is somewhat humorous: the very principle you just cited argues that you honor your place, so why should I be the one to move? *Amar lei: mutav yavo maneh ben pras eitzel maneh ben maneh* — no, it is more fitting for a hundred the son of fifty to come to a hundred the son of a hundred. *V'al yavo maneh ben maneh eitzel maneh ben pras* — the son of a hundred should not go to the son of fifty. That is, Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's father was himself a *Rav*, whereas Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's father was not. So the one with more distinguished lineage should not be moving toward the one of lesser lineage — rather, the lesser should come toward the greater. Whether Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak genuinely considered Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda the more distinguished person, or whether he was gracefully deflecting the earlier invitation by turning it on its head, is a matter of how one reads the exchange.

### Sura Shovel Lender

*Besura hava de-varta be-shivuvoteih de-Rav lo hava* — in Sura there was pestilence, but in Rav's own neighborhood there was none. *Savru minah mishum zechuteih de-Rav de-nafish* — the people assumed it was owing to Rav's great merit that his neighborhood was spared — again evoking the earlier stories of great men whose merit protected against physical harm. But now observe how the *gemara* pushes back. *Itchazi lehu be-chalma* — it was shown to them in a dream: *rav nafisha zechuteih tuva, ha milta zutra lei le-Rav* — Rav's merit is indeed great; this matter is too minor to require Rav's *zechus* to address it. *Ela mishum hahu gavra de-shayel mara ve-zavila likvura* — rather, this was on the merit of a certain unnamed person who would lend out a *mara* and *zavila* — a shovel and a digging tool — to help with burials. Because he performed this act of anonymous *chesed* at the moment of death, his merit was sufficient to protect the neighborhood from the plague.

### Drokrat Oven Woman

*Be-Drokert hava delikta u-ve-shivuvoteih de-Rav Huna lo hava delikta* — in Drokrat there was a fire, but in Rav Huna's neighborhood there was none. *Savru minah bizchuta de-Rav Huna de-nafish* — the people attributed this to Rav Huna's great merit. *Itchazi lehu be-chalma: hai zutra lei le-Rav Huna* — it was shown to them in a dream: this is too minor a matter for Rav Huna's merit. *Ela mishum hahi iteta de-mechamema tanura u-meshayela le-shivuvoteih* — rather, it was on the merit of a certain woman, unnamed, who, when she heated her oven and got it burning, would let her neighbors use the already-heated oven. The fuel was spent, the oven was already hot — come and use it, do not waste your own wood. That small, anonymous, daily act of generosity was enough to save the neighborhood from fire.

These two closing stories are a beautiful counterpoint to everything that came before. We are not denying that great rabbis possess great *zechus* and that *zechus* can protect from significant harm. The *gemara* does not say otherwise — it says these particular events were too minor for such great *zechus* to be needed. But the implication resonates: the small, quiet, anonymous deeds of ordinary people carry a power of their own. The woman who lets her neighbor use her heated oven. The man who lends out a shovel for burials. Neither of them climbed a ship's mast or was carried through town in a gold chair. No one knows their names. And yet the protection they generated — from pestilence, from fire — was real, tangible, and sufficient.

---

---

# Ta'anit 22

## Great to Anonymous

### Theme Shift

The daf opens in the middle of 21b, and it is worth pausing to appreciate the thematic shift that has been building. The preceding material dealt with figures of towering individual stature — Choni HaMa'agel looms large in the background, even before the Gemara has formally introduced his story, and alongside him we have encountered figures such as Rav Adda bar Ahava, in whose merit walls refrained from falling, and Nachum Ish Gamzu, whose presence likewise protected buildings from collapse. These are figures one might describe as *echad bedoro* — singular individuals of their generation, possessing extraordinary personal merit.

The Gemara now pivots deliberately away from this model. What follows is a sustained meditation on anonymous people performing small deeds of kindness, and the remarkable power such deeds carry. The shift is profound: we move from the great and the famous to the unrecognized and the modest, from dramatic miraculous protection to the quiet infusion of *yashrus* into the fabric of daily life.

### Midah KeNeged Midah

Two brief examples anchor this new theme. An entire neighborhood was spared from pestilence because of a person who had lent shovels to others to dig graves — since pestilence causes death, there is an evident *midah keneged midah* at work. Another neighborhood was saved from fire because a woman had shared her heated oven. Here too the *midah keneged midah* is transparent. These are not grand gestures; they are the ordinary generosities of ordinary people, and yet they carry the weight of divine protection for entire communities.

---

## Rav Yehuda

### Locusts

With this thematic backdrop established, the Gemara turns to a series of stories about sages who were acutely sensitive to the potential spread of calamity. They said to Rav Yehuda: *atu kimtzei* — locusts are arriving. He immediately declared a fast. The people around him said *lo ka mafsidan* — don't worry, it won't really affect us. Presumably they felt the locusts were still far away. Rav Yehuda responded: *zavda aisu bahadehayehu?* — did they perhaps bring their lunch with them? His point was sharp: do not trivialize the threat. The locusts will consume the crops; the only way they could spare you is if they arrived with their own provisions. This connects to the theme of the Mishnah regarding distant places joining the fast, though the Gemara does not make this explicit here.

### Plague Species

The Gemara then relates a second incident involving Rav Yehuda. He was told *ika motana bechazirei* — there is a pestilence among the pigs — and he declared a fast. The concern is that such a disease could cross the species barrier and affect human beings. The Gemara raises the question: perhaps Rav Yehuda holds that a plague spreading among one species will spread to all species — *makat meshulachat miMin echad meshulachat mikol haminim*? The Gemara deflects this generalization: *shani chazirei dedamyan ma'ayeihu livnei inshi* — pigs are a special case because their intestines are similar to human intestines, making cross-species transmission particularly plausible in this instance. The observation is empirical rather than theoretical, and the Gemara resists extending it into a universal principle. Indeed, some of the most devastating diseases in history have been precisely those that crossed species lines.

---

## Distant Plagues

### Shmuel

The Gemara now presents a parallel series involving Shmuel, Rav Yehuda's teacher. They told Shmuel: *ika mosana beChuzai* — there is a plague in Chuzai, a distant place. He declared a fast. They objected: is it not far away? He replied: *leka ma'abra hacha depasik lei?* — is there no crossing-point, no ford or pass, that would stop it from reaching us? There is nothing to prevent it from spreading here. The concern about disease spreading over distance thus connects back to the Mishnah's discussion of surrounding areas that join the fast, though the Gemara will revisit the precise scope of this principle.

It is worth noting that among the categories listed in the Mishnah, *dever* — plague — was notably not included among those for which one is *matri'in bechol makom*, proclaiming everywhere. The Mishnah indicated: *vechen ir she-yesh bah dever umapoles, oso ha-ir misanis umasri'a, vechol sevivoseha misanios velo masrios* — the immediate surroundings fast, but not distant places. Yet here Shmuel is fasting for *dever* in a place not considered its immediate surroundings.

### Rav Nachman

The series continues with Rav Nachman. He was told: *ika mosana be-Eretz Yisrael* — there is a plague in Eretz Yisrael. He, sitting in Bavel, declared a fast. This is a considerably larger leap: from Eretz Yisrael to Bavel, and moreover for *dever*, which the Mishnah treats as only a local concern. His reasoning was expressed in a striking phrase: *im gvira loka shefacha lo kol sheken?* — if the mistress of the house is being smitten, will the maidservant not certainly be affected as well? His framing is not naturalistic but metaphysical or theological: if Eretz Yisrael is being punished, Bavel will not be spared either.

### Caravan Spread

The Gemara now analyzes these two cases together. If Rav Nachman's reasoning rests on the *gvira-shefacha* principle — Eretz Yisrael to Bavel — what follows is that this logic would *not* apply to two places both in *Chutz La'aretz*, *shifcha ve-shifcha*, maidservant to maidservant, so to speak. Yet Shmuel fasted for a plague in Chuzai, also in Bavel, also *Chutz La'aretz*. How so?

The Gemara resolves: *shani hasam keivan de-ika shayrusa de-levai ve-asya bahadya bahadya* — that case is different, since there are caravans that travel between those places, accompanying the disease and bringing it along. People traveling between those cities carry the disease with them. This is the practical reason Shmuel said there is no crossing that would stop it: the regular traffic between these places is itself the vector of transmission. The Mishnah's limited scope for *dever* thus gives way to a more dynamic assessment — what matters is not raw geographic distance but the degree of human travel and contact between places.

In sum: Rav Nachman's fast for Eretz Yisrael is explained theologically, while Shmuel's fast for Chuzai is explained epidemiologically. Both represent an expansion beyond the Mishnah's literal parameters, each justified on its own terms.

---

## Abba Umna

### Heavenly Greetings

The Gemara now resumes the central theme of anonymous individuals possessing remarkable merit. *Abba Umna* — Abba the bloodletter — would receive a daily greeting from the heavenly *yeshiva*. Abaye received such a greeting every *erev Shabbos*, and Rava only once a year, on *erev Yom Kippur*. Here, set against the names of two of the greatest Amoraim, stands a bloodletter whom no one had previously heard of — and he outranks them both in this daily heavenly recognition. The contrast is striking and deliberate, continuing the Gemara's sustained meditation on the hidden greatness of unassuming individuals.

### Deeds Explained

Abaye felt despondent upon learning this — *chalusha da'atei de-Abaye mishum de-Abba Umna* — and the heavenly voice replied: *lo matzis leme'evad ke-ovdei* — you cannot replicate his deeds. What, then, were the deeds of Abba Umna?

When he performed *milta* — bloodletting — he would seat men separately and women separately, since the procedure required exposing parts of the body and mixing the sexes would not be *tzeni'us*. Beyond this, he had fashioned a special garment with a pre-made slit positioned precisely at the shoulder, through which the bloodletting horn was already inserted. When a woman came to him, he would dress her in this robe so that the procedure could be performed without his seeing her uncovered body. The care taken here — both the separation of the sexes as a general matter and the specially designed garment for female patients — reflects an extraordinary commitment to *tzni'us* in the context of his professional practice.

He also maintained a private box where patients could leave payment discreetly as they departed. Those who had money would deposit it; those who could not afford to pay would simply leave without embarrassment — *deleis leh lo michsif*. There was no collection moment, no direct exchange of money, no opportunity for a patient to be shamed by an inability to pay.

### Torah Students

When a *tzurva me-rabbanan* — a Torah student — came for treatment, Rav Abba Umna would not charge any fee — *agra minei lo shakil* — even if the student could have afforded to pay. This was professional courtesy of the most generous sort. Moreover, after the student rose from the procedure, Abba Umna would press money into his hands and say: *zil barei nafshach* — go and nourish yourself, recognizing that after bloodletting a person might feel weakened and hungry. He gave them money for a proper meal. Not only did he forgo his fee — he actively subsidized their recovery.

One participant in the shiur raised an important observation: when the heavenly voice tells Abaye *you cannot do like his deeds*, this should not be read as a comment on Abaye's level of righteousness. Rather, Abaye sat in the *beit medrash*; he did not have the daily opportunity to do these kinds of things. The person in the world, in the marketplace, in a profession that brings him into contact with suffering people every single day, has a kind of access to *gemilus chasadim* that the scholar sequestered in learning simply does not. These are deeds born of circumstance and opportunity, and that, it seems, is precisely the Gemara's point.

### Bedding Test

One day, Abaye sent two of his students to test Abba Umna — *shadar Abaye zuga de-rabbanan le-mivdakeih*. Abba Umna welcomed them warmly, fed them, gave them drink, and prepared fine bedding for them to sleep on. In the morning, the students rolled up the expensive bedding, took it with them, and went out to the marketplace — they had effectively stolen it.

When they encountered Abba Umna in the market, they said to him: *le-shimei mar heichi shavu* — tell us, what do you think these are worth? They asked him to appraise the very items they had taken from him. He gave them a figure. They pressed: perhaps it is worth more? He replied: *be-hachi shaklinu* — that is what I paid for them. He knew the items, understood what had happened, and said nothing about the theft.

### Pidyon Shvuyim

They then told him: *didach ninhu ve-shaklinu minach* — they are yours, and we took them from you. They asked: *be-mai chashatin* — what did you suspect us of? He answered: *amina pidyon shvuyim iklu lehu le-rabbanan* — I assumed that the Torah scholars must have had a pressing need for funds, perhaps to redeem captives, and they were embarrassed to ask me directly. He did not entertain the thought that they had simply stolen.

When they urged him to take back the items, he declined: *me-hahu sha'ata asachtinhu mi-da'tai le-tzedakah* — from the moment I assumed you would use them for *pidyon shvuyim*, I had already mentally dedicated them to charity in my heart. He would not reclaim them.

This story evokes a well-known account told of the Chofetz Chaim: that when guests he had taken in overnight made off with his silver *menorahs*, he ran after them calling *ani mochel, ani mochel* — I forgive, I forgive — so that they would not be guilty of the prohibition of theft. A lawyer recounting this story to a judge was asked: do you really believe that? He replied: I don't know, but I can tell you they don't tell stories like that about you and me.

The larger significance of Abba Umna's story is profound. It is not that his individual acts are unheard of in kind; it is that they represent the total and quiet infusion of *yashrus* and sensitivity into every dimension of his professional life — in his treatment of patients, in his protection of their dignity, in his generosity toward Torah students, in his response to what looked like outright theft.

---

## Abaye vs. Rava

### City Protection

The Gemara turns now to Rava's despondence at receiving his heavenly greeting only once a year, compared to Abaye's weekly greeting. The heavenly response was: *mistayecha de-mageni zachutach akula karchach* — it is sufficient for you that your merit protects the entire city. This is a remarkable consolation: even if Rava stands below Abaye on this particular hierarchy of *Olam Haba* greetings, his merit functions as a shield for an entire city. One might point out that Abaye's merit presumably protected his city as well, which means the distinction between the two remains somewhat unexplained — but the Gemara does not resolve this fully. What it does underscore is the recurring theme: the hierarchy of *zechut* is not transparent to human perception, and even those we consider the greatest must look upward and recognize those who surpass them.

---

## Rav Beroka

### Olam Haba Query

The Gemara introduces Rav Beroka Choza'ah, who would frequent the marketplace of Bei Lapat. Eliyahu the prophet would regularly appear to him there — a mark of his own considerable righteousness. Rav Beroka once asked Eliyahu: *ika behai shuka bar alma de-ati* — is there anyone in this marketplace who is deserving of *Olam Haba*? The question presumably referred to others, not himself. Eliyahu answered: no.

### Unlikely Candidate

As they stood there, a man appeared who was wearing black shoes — not the Jewish practice — and whose garment bore no *tzitzit*, or more precisely, no string of *techelet*. Eliyahu pointed to him: *hai bar alma de-ati hu* — this man is a *ben olam haba*. Rav Beroka ran after him and asked: *mai ovdach* — what are your deeds? The man replied: *zil idna ve-ta lemachar* — go now and come back tomorrow.

---

## Prison Guard

### Prisoner Separation

The next day, Rav Beroka returned and asked again. The man identified himself: *zandukna ana* — I am a prison guard. *Ve-asarna gavra lachod ve-nashi lachod* — I lock up male prisoners separately from female prisoners to prevent immoral behavior and the possibility of assault. He went further: *ve-ramina puraya bein hanei le-hanei ki heicha de-lo leitu lidei issura* — he would place his own bed between the two sections so that no transgression could occur. The commitment to *tzni'us* as a central organizing value — seen already in Abba Umna's practice — recurs here with striking force.

### Woman Protection

He continued: *ki chazina bat Yisrael de-yahvei nuchrim ala einaihu, masrana nafshai u-matzilna lah* — when I see a Jewish woman upon whom the non-Jewish prisoners have cast their eye with evil intent, I am willing to risk myself to save her. Once, there was a betrothed young woman in the prison upon whom the non-Jews had set their sights. He took the dregs of wine — *durdaya de-chamra* — and smeared them on the hem of her cloak, so that they would think she was in a state of *niddah* and recoil from her. Their revulsion at the thought of approaching a menstruating woman protected her, and he accomplished this without placing himself in direct physical confrontation.

### Decree Warning

As for his non-Jewish appearance — the black shoes, the absence of *tzitzit* — the man explained: *ayeilna ve-nafkina beini nuchrim ki heicha de-lo leidu de-yuhada'ei ana* — I move in and out among non-Jews so that they will not know I am Jewish. When an anti-Jewish decree is issued — *ki hava gezeirata* — *modena lehu le-rabbanan de-libau rachamei u-vatli le-gezeirataihu* — I inform the Rabbis so that they can pray and the decree will be annulled.

When Rav Beroka asked why he had not answered the first day, the man explained: at that moment he had just learned of a new decree and needed to go immediately to warn the Rabbis. He could not afford to be delayed answering questions.

The Gemara then notes — and Rav Beroka's earlier question prompted this comparison — that Eliyahu had initially said there was *no one* in that marketplace deserving of *Olam Haba*. This requires a moment's reflection. The principle of *kol Yisrael yesh lahem chelek le-olam haba* — that all of Israel has a share in the world to come — is actually not standard rabbinic theology. Standard rabbinic theology holds that *tzaddikim* earn *olam haba* and *resha'im* face *gehinnom*, with the *beinonim* in uncertain status. The reassuring declaration that begins tractate Sanhedrin — *kol Yisrael yesh lahem chelek* — was added later as an introductory statement so that the tractate would not begin with a harsh enumeration of those who have *no* share, but it represents an outlier in the broader sweep of rabbinic theological thought.

The deeper significance of this figure is perhaps the most powerful expression of the Gemara's recurring theme. Here is not merely an anonymous person, but a person who *looks like a sinner* — no *kippa*, no *tzitzit*, dressed like a non-Jew. The person you would most readily dismiss, or worse, condemn, is in fact among those with the greatest merit. And notably, unlike the earlier stories where righteous individuals protected people through their metaphysical *zechut* — as Rav Adda bar Ahava's merit held up walls — this man saves people through direct, worldly, practical action: separating prisoners, outwitting would-be assailants, warning Rabbis of decrees. His *hashpa'a* on the world is entirely this-worldly.

---

## Jesters

### Joy & Peace

As Rav Beroka and Eliyahu stood speaking, two men approached. Eliyahu said: *hani nami bnei alma de-ati* — these two also have a share in *Olam Haba*. Rav Beroka asked them what they did. They replied: *inash beduchei anan* — we are jesters. *Mevadchinan atzvei* — we make sad people laugh. And when they see two people who are quarreling with one another — *de-it lehu tigra* — *tarchinnan ve-avdinan lehu shelama* — they work to lighten the atmosphere and bring them to make peace with one another.

This passage was widely cited in early Chassidic literature as testimony to the power of joy and laughter. But what strikes here, in the context of all that has preceded, is the consistent pattern: people whom society would consider the most marginal and lowly — a bloodletter, a prison guard, a pair of clowns — are the ones the Gemara holds up as exemplars of *Olam Haba*. And in each case their deeds are deeply practical, utterly this-worldly: protecting dignity, preventing assault, bringing laughter to a grieving person, reconciling enemies.

One might add, as a participant observed: these are all people who are *in the world*, working, and it is precisely their working lives that give them the opportunity for these acts. The scholar in the *beit medrash* cannot do what Abba Umna did, not because he is less righteous, but because he does not have that particular field of action. There is something here that validates the entire rabbinic enterprise in a deeper sense — the claim that *kedushah* is not the province of those who withdraw from the world, but of those who inhabit it with full integrity.

---

## Mishnah Matri'in

### Four Categories

The Gemara returns to the Mishnah's halachic material. *Al elu matri'in bechol makom* — for the following one calls out in every place. The term *matri'in* minimally refers to special prayers; it may also incorporate fasting, and the Mishnah leaves some ambiguity. The Rabbis taught: *al ha-shidafon ve-al ha-yerakon* — blight and jaundice, diseases of grain; *ve-al ha-arbeh ve-al ha-chasil* — locusts in their various forms; *ve-al chaya ra'ah* — dangerous wild animals appearing in inhabited areas.

### Rabbi Akiva

Rabbi Akiva held: for *shidafon* and *yerakon*, even the slightest amount — *bechol shehu* — is sufficient to trigger the universal proclamation. There is no minimum threshold; the slightest sign of grain disease requires everyone to pray everywhere. Similarly, regarding locusts: *afilu lo nira be-Eretz Yisrael ela kanaf echad, matri'in aleihem* — even if only a single wing is sighted in Eretz Yisrael, the response must be universal, because locusts travel in swarms and a single sighting is ominous for all. Whether Rabbi Akiva is disagreeing with the *Tanna Kamma* or merely explicating it is not entirely resolved.

---

## Wild Animals

### Location Time

The Gemara elaborates on the case of *chaya ra'ah*. When is a dangerous wild animal considered *meshulachat* — a spreading, rampage-type problem that triggers the public response — and when is it an isolated occurrence? *Nir'asa ba-ir* — seen in a city — that is *meshulachat*. *Ba-sadeh* — in the field — is *eina meshulachat*. *Ba-yom* — in the daytime — is *meshulachat*; *ba-layla* — at night — is *eina meshulachat*.

### Behavior Indicators

Further criteria: if the animal sees two people and runs after them both, *meshulachat* — an animal that pursues multiple people has become dangerously untamed. If it hides from two people, *eina meshulachat*. If it attacked two people and ate one of them, *meshulachat*. Somewhat counterintuitively, if it ate both of them, *eina meshulachat* — perhaps it was merely hungry, and a hungry animal acting out of hunger is different from an animal on an unprovoked rampage.

### Contextual Analysis

The Gemara identifies an internal contradiction in these criteria. It was said: seen in the city — *meshulachat*, regardless of day or night. But separately it was said: daytime is *meshulachat*, nighttime is not. Which standard governs?

The Gemara resolves: the two conditions are conjunctive, not disjunctive. An animal is *meshulachat* only if it appears *in the city* and *in the daytime*. If it comes to the city only at night, the concern is lesser. And if it is in the field, even by day, it is not yet *meshulachat* — unless it additionally takes action.

There is then a further contradiction: it was said that chasing two people is *meshulachat*, while hiding from them is *eina meshulachat* — implying that merely standing without running away is an intermediate case that is *meshulachat*. But separately it was suggested that even standing in a field is not a problem. The Gemara resolves: *kan be-sadeh ha-smucha le-agam kan be-sadeh she-eina smucha le-agam* — two types of field: a field adjacent to a forest or swamp, and a field that is not.

The result is a graduated analysis. In the city, daytime: *meshulachat* by appearance alone. In a field near a forest: only if the animal actively chases people, since near its natural habitat a bolder presence is less alarming. In a field not near a forest: even if it merely stands without fleeing from people, *meshulachat*, since that itself is anomalous behavior. And in the forest itself, the animal's home terrain, even a killing is not automatically *meshulachat* — unless it killed people and did not eat them, demonstrating aggression unconnected to hunger.

### Infant Case

The Gemara also addressed the case of *alta la-gag ve-natla tinok me-arisa* — an animal that went up to a rooftop and took an infant from its cradle — which is *meshulachat*. Rav Pappa explains this involves the hide of hunters — a concealed location where, it seems, the infant was being kept, making the act of theft by a wild animal even more remarkable. The point is that this remains *meshulachat* even in such unusual circumstances.

---

## Sword

### Peaceful Sword

The Gemara next addresses *cherev* — troop movements — as a category requiring proclamation *bechol makom*. The Rabbis taught: *cherev she-amru eino tzarich lomar cherev she-eino shel shalom* — it goes without saying that hostile troops constitute a crisis. *Ela afilu cherev shel shalom* — even troops on a peaceful passage, not directed against the local population but merely crossing through on their way to fight elsewhere, require the public fast. Once armies are on the march, no one knows where things will end.

### Paroh Necho

The paradigmatic case of a *cherev shel shalom* is that of Paroh Necho, passing through Eretz Yisrael in the time of King Yoshiyahu. Paroh Necho was marching eastward to wage war against other nations; his quarrel was not with Yoshiyahu or with Yehuda. Yet Yoshiyahu went out to block his passage, and the result was Yoshiyahu's death.

The Gemara cites the verse: Paroh Necho sent messengers to Yoshiyahu saying: *ma li valach melech Yehuda* — what business do I have with you, king of Yehuda? *Lo alecha ata ha-yom* — I am not coming against you today. *Ki el beit milchamti* — I am going to the place of my war. *Ve-elohim amar le-vahalani* — and God has commanded me to hurry. *Chadal lecha me-elohim asher imi ve-al yashchitecha* — desist from opposing God who is with me, lest He destroy you.

The end of the story is Yoshiyahu's mortal wounding by archers, his being carried back to die. It is a story that resonates in many of the *kinot* recited on Tisha B'Av.

### Yoshiyahu Punishment

The Gemara asks: *mah elohim asher imi* — what is this "God who is with me" that Paroh Necho invokes? Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *zu avoda zara* — he meant his idol, his god in the lowercase sense. This gave Yoshiyahu a reason to discount the warning: *ho'il ve-ka batach be-avoda zara, nachilina lei* — since he relies on idolatry, I can prevail against him.

The verse then says *vayoru ha-morim la-melech Yoshiyahu* — the archers shot at King Yoshiyahu — and he cried out *ha'avirouni ki hechaleti me'od*. The Gemara asks what *hechaleti* means. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: *mela'med she-asu kol gufo ki-kivra* — they made his entire body like a sieve, pierced through with innumerable arrows.

The Gemara then asks: *mipnei ma ne'enash Yoshiyahu* — why was Yoshiyahu punished? He was among the most righteous kings. Rav Shmuel bar Nachmeni said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: *mipnei she-haya lo le-malech be-Yirmiyahu ve-lo nimlach* — because he should have consulted the prophet Yirmiyahu and did not.

### Yoshiyahu Reasoning

What was Yoshiyahu's own reasoning? He derived it from the verse in the *berachot*: *ve-cherev lo ta'avor be-artzechem* — no sword shall pass through your land. He reasoned: *ilima cherev she-eino shel shalom* — if this means hostile troops will not attack us, that is already implied by *ve-nasati shalom ba-aretz*; peace in the land means no one attacks us. The verse adding *no sword shall pass through* must therefore mean something beyond that — *afilu shel shalom*, even a peaceful sword, even troops merely transiting, shall not pass through when the nation is worthy. He concluded that the generation was worthy, that he was a righteous king, and therefore he was obligated to uphold this blessing.

### Generation Unworthiness

The Gemara counters: *ve-hu eino yodeia she-ein doro domeh yafeh* — he did not know that his generation was not worthy. He may have been righteous, but the sins of his generation undermined the very blessing he sought to invoke on their behalf.

As he lay dying, Yirmiyahu saw his lips moving. Concerned — *shema chas ve-shalom milsa de-lo hagna amar* — perhaps in his pain he was saying something improper, perhaps complaining against God — Yirmiyahu leaned close and heard that Yoshiyahu was in fact *matzdik ha-din*, affirming the justice of God's judgment. He was whispering: *tzadik hu Hashem ki fihu marisi* — God is righteous, for I have defied His word.

The Gemara ties this to Megillat Eichah, authored by Yirmiyahu: this verse from Eichah is understood as Yirmiyahu recording the final words of Yoshiyahu. And Yirmiyahu then opened his lament: *ruach apeinu mashiach Hashem* — the breath of our nostrils, God's anointed — he who had been the great hope of the generation, who might have been the *mashiach* who could have prevented the destruction, was caught, stumbled, because the generation had gone so far astray that even a righteous king could not fully escape the consequences. This is indeed the subject of the *kina* beginning *vayekonen Yirmiyahu al Yoshiyahu*.

As for the precise relevance to *cherev shel shalom*: Yoshiyahu's own *derashah* demonstrates the principle — the *beracha* guarantees that even a peaceful sword shall not pass through, which means even a peaceful sword is by nature a cause for concern and action. The fact that he was punished for acting on that reasoning does not invalidate the underlying principle; it was his generation's unworthiness, not the principle itself, that brought about his downfall.

---

## Diseased Grain

### Grain Amount

The Gemara relates that elders descended from Yerushalayim to their cities and declared a fast because of an oven-full — *malei pi kivshan* — of *yerakon* observed in Ashkelon. A question arises: when the text says *kemalei pi tannur*, does it mean the quantity of grain that literally fills an oven, or the quantity of grain that, when baked into bread, would fill an oven? Since bread expands in baking, the latter represents considerably less grain. The Gemara suggests the answer is bread filling the mouth of the oven.

### Teiku

But a further ambiguity remains: *kekisuyah de-tannura* — is it just enough bread to cover the opening of the oven? Or *kidara de-rifta de-hadra lei le-fuma de-tannura* — bread stacked from the floor of the oven all the way up to and filling the opening? The Gemara leaves this unresolved: *teiku*. The story itself implies there is some minimum amount below which one would not declare a fast — which stands in some tension with Rabbi Akiva's view that even the slightest amount requires universal proclamation.

---

## Wolves Story

### Tumah Analysis

The Gemara then cites Ulla in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak: *ma'aseh ba'u ze'evim shnei tinokot ve-kiyium derech beit ha-re'i* — a story in which wolves devoured two children and excreted them. The case came before the *chachamim*, who ruled: *teharu et ha-basar ve-tim'u et ha-atzamot* — the flesh, having passed through the animal's digestive tract and been transformed into excrement, is no longer halachically considered meat and is therefore *tahor*; the bones, remaining structurally bones, retain their status and are *tamei*.

### Discourse Shift

One cannot help but notice the sharp shift in register. Within the very material dealing with the halachos of *ta'anit*, we had been engaged with questions that carried a sense of religious urgency and lived experience — what does it mean when a plague spreads, what does it mean when troops march, how do we respond as a community? The discussion of the diseased grain and now the *tumah* and *taharah* status of what wolves excreted is clinical, detached, almost coldly analytical. It is the mode of standard halachic discourse, and that is not a criticism — it is how *halacha* operates. But the contrast with the more experientially engaged halachic discussions earlier in the tractate is notable and worth marking.

---

## Shabbat Proclamation

### Four Situations

The Mishnah states: *al elu matri'in be-Shabbat* — for the following one cries out even on Shabbat. The Rabbis taught: *ir she-heikifuha acherim o nahar, ve-achas sefina ha-mitarefet ba-yam, ve-achas yachid she-nirdaf mipnei acherim u-mipnei listim u-mipnei ruach ra'ah* — a city under siege or threatened by a flooding river, a ship caught in a storm at sea, or an individual being pursued by hostile forces, by bandits, or by an evil spirit.

### Individual Fast

To this the Rabbis add: *al kulan yachid rashai lehageif et atzmo be-ta'anis* — in all these situations, an individual may afflict himself with a fast. This is noteworthy: the general rule is that *ta'anis tzibbur* is decreed by the community. The *chiddush* here is that in these urgent situations — particularly given that this may be referring specifically to Shabbat, when a public fast would not be declared — an individual may nevertheless fast on his own.

### Rabbi Yosi

Rabbi Yosi disagrees: *ein ha-yachid rashai lehageif et atzmo be-ta'anis*. An individual may not afflict himself with a fast in these circumstances. His reason: *shema yitzarech la-briyot ve-ein ha-briyot merachamim alav* — lest he subsequently need others to care for him and others will not have compassion on him, either because they feel he brought his weakness upon himself or simply out of indifference. One may not put oneself in a position of need through voluntary deprivation.

### Soul Alive

Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name: what is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosi? The verse *vayehi ha-adam le-nefesh chaya* — the person became a living soul — is interpreted as a divine command: *neshama she-natati becha, hachaye* — the soul I have given you, keep it alive.

But Rabbi Yosi's position may be operating on an additional level, consistent with his position elsewhere in the Mishnah. Rabbi Yosi had said earlier in the tractate that one may cry out on Shabbat to summon people to *action*, but not to add special *tefillos*. His reasoning there was that the correct response to an emergency is to act, not to pray. Here, similarly, Rabbi Yosi may be saying: when the ship is sinking, when the river is flooding, when the city is under siege — this is not the moment to fast and weaken yourself. This is the moment to act, to lift sandbags, to fight, to save lives. Fasting on Shabbat in these circumstances does not help the cause; it undermines it. Keep yourself strong and act. This reading would make Rabbi Yosi's position here entirely consistent with his position in the Mishnah and would ground the principle of *hachaye* — keep the soul alive — not merely as a prohibition on self-harm but as an affirmative command: when there is work to be done, keep yourself capable of doing it.

---

---

# Ta'anit 23

## Rov Tovah & Shimon

### Pestilence Debate

The *gemara* picks up in the middle of 27b, resuming its treatment of the *mishnah*'s list of calamities that warrant sounding the alarm — *matrian* — and the recitation of special *tefillot*, even on *Shabbat*. We had previously encountered the interesting position of Rabbi Yosi, who urged attention to practical remedies over *tefillot*, a position that may also have intersected with the question of whether an individual may fast on *Shabbat*.

The *mishnah* then introduces the view of Shimon HaTeimani: *af al hadever* — even pestilence warrants the alarm on *Shabbat* — *velo hodu lo chachamim*, and the Sages did not agree with him. The *gemara* raises the question: does their disagreement pertain specifically to *Shabbat*, while on a weekday everyone would concede that *dever* warrants a *taanit* and special *tefillot*? After all, we saw earlier how *dever* in one locale would prompt response even in distant communities because of the danger of its spread through caravans. Or perhaps the Sages reject the view *kol ikkar* — entirely, even on a weekday?

*Ta shma* — come and hear — from a *baraita*: *matrian al hadever b'Shabbat*, you do sound the alarm for *dever* on *Shabbat*, *v'ein tzarich lomar b'chol*, and it goes without saying on a weekday. Yet Chanan ben Pitom, a student of Rabbi Akiva, says in his teacher's name: *ein matrian al hadever kol ikkar* — you never recite the special *teruah* for *dever* at all. This is a striking position, offered without explanation, and the *gemara* treats it as the view of the Sages who dispute Shimon HaTeimani. It sits in notable tension with the earlier *gemara* that treated *dever* as precisely the kind of traveling danger that warranted communal response.

### No Rov Tovah

The *mishnah* continues: *al kol tzara shelo tavo al hatzibbor matrian aleha* — on any calamity, God forbid it should not come, one sounds the alarm — *chutz mirov geshamim*, except for too much rain. This exception serves as the transition into the extended treatment of Choni HaMa'agel, whose entire story revolves around precisely this issue.

A *baraita* reiterates: on any calamity you sound the alarm, except for too much rain. *Mai ta'ama?* What is the reason? Rabbi Yochanan answers: *lefi she'ein mitpalelin al rov hatova* — because one does not pray against an excess of good. Rabbi Yochanan frames this as a general principle, not limited to rain. Yet the formulation is somewhat tautological: you do not pray about it because it is an excess of good. The deeper logic requires unpacking.

One might ask why, if too much rain is practically harmful — flooding fields, ruining crops — it should be categorically off-limits as a subject of prayer. The principle seems to gesture at something beyond pragmatics. If rain carries symbolic weight as the manifest expression of divine favor and connection — the presence of rain meaning God is blessing the people, its absence meaning estrangement — then to cry out against rain, even when it causes damage, is to reject that expression of divine goodness. It is a form of *kafui tovah*, ingratitude, that undermines the entire symbolic framework.

Rabbi Yochanan then cites the verse in support: *vaharikofi lachem et aruvot hashamayim ad bli dai* — I will open the storehouses of heaven until there is *bli dai*. Rami bar Rav Yud interprets *ad bli dai* to mean until your lips grow weary of saying *dai* — enough, enough, enough. The proof is that there will be so much blessing that you will keep saying stop, but the *gemara* acknowledges the difficulty: if one is saying *dai*, one is in effect asking God to stop. Perhaps the distinction lies between the informal exclamation of *dai* and a formal act of prayer to halt the blessing, but the *gemara* does not resolve this cleanly.

The *gemara* then qualifies the rule: *uva-golah*, in exile — that is, in Bavel — where conditions differ fundamentally, one does in fact sound the alarm for excessive rain. A *baraita* specifies that in a very rainy year, the *anshei mishmar* — the priestly rotation on Temple duty — would send word to the *anshei ma'amad*, the Israelite representatives, urging them to pray for their brethren in the *golah*, *shelo yihiyu bateihem kivreihem*, that their houses should not become their graves. The phrase, familiar from the *kohen gadol*'s *Yom Kippur* prayer, here conveys the genuine mortal danger of flooding.

The permission to pray against excessive rain in Bavel highlights, by contrast, why the prohibition applies in the Land of Israel. In Bavel, rain is never in dire scarcity; the wetlands mean the pendulum can swing either way and prayer in either direction carries no particular symbolic freight. In the Land of Israel, however, rain is perpetually and urgently needed. To ever voice the sentiment that there is too much would subtly corrode the sense of absolute dependence and dire necessity that characterizes Israel's relationship with rain throughout the year. The community's willingness to declare *enough* would undermine the very seriousness of its perennial cry for rain.

They then asked Rabbi Eliezer: up to what point should rain descend before one would pray for it to stop? He answered: until a person could stand on the rock called *Keren Afel* — an enormously elevated outcropping — and dip his toes in the water, meaning the water would need to rise to an extraordinary height. A *baraita* variant mentions hands rather than feet, but the *gemara* harmonizes these as equivalent. Rabbah bar bar Chana vouches for the height of *Keren Afel*: he himself saw a nomad riding a camel and holding up a spear, and the figure appeared to him as an ant. The practical upshot is that one would never in fact reach the threshold for praying to stop rain in the Land of Israel.

### Gashmim B'Itam

A *baraita* expounds the verse *v'natati gishmeichem b'itam* — I will give your rains in their proper time. What does *b'itam* mean? The first interpretation: not drunken — that is, not excessive — and not thirsty, not too sparse. Rather, a medium amount. For when rain is excessive, *metashteshin et ha'aretz*, it churns up the earth into mud, and the land cannot bring forth fruit. This *baraita* states explicitly what the earlier discussion implied: the divine promise of rain in its proper time envisions precisely the right quantity.

*Davar acher* — a second interpretation addresses the *timing* rather than the quantity. *B'leilei revi'iyot u'v'leilei shabbatot* — on Tuesday nights, the night going into Wednesday, and on Friday nights. The reasoning is that on those nights people are already at home: on *Shabbat* one returns before dark, and on Tuesday nights there was a traditional concern about going out that likewise kept people indoors. Thus the rain comes when no one is traveling and no one is inconvenienced. The point is not merely convenience, however; it is the *siman bracha*, the sign of blessing, that such rainfall represents. Rain at precisely the right time, accommodating the rhythms of human life, is not only practically beneficial but symbolically laden — a manifestation of God's attentive care for the people.

### Shimon's Era

The *baraita* continues: *sheken matzinu bimei Shimon ben Shatach* — we find that in the days of Shimon ben Shatach this is precisely what occurred. Rain fell on Tuesday nights and Friday nights, *ad she-na'asu chittin kichlayot* — until the wheat grains were as large as kidneys, the barley grains as large as olive pits, and the lentils as large as gold *dinarei*. The crops reached extraordinary proportions as an expression of divine blessing.

These specimens were preserved: *vetzarerum mehem dugma ledorot*, they bound them up as a model for future generations, *lehodia kama hachet gorem* — to demonstrate that in other years, when crops do not grow so abundantly, it is sin that causes the diminishment. The verses from Yirmiyahu are cited: *avonoteichem hitu eleh* — your iniquities have caused these things to turn away — *vechatoteichem mane'u hatov mikem*, and your sins have withheld the good from you.

The *gemara* notes that this emphasis on *siman bracha* runs throughout. The extraordinary produce of Shimon ben Shatach's era is not presented as mere agricultural luck; it is held up as evidence of what divine favor, expressed through perfectly timed and correctly apportioned rain, can produce.

### Herod's Rains

*Vechen matzinu bimei Hordos* — similarly in the days of Herod, who was no great *tzaddik* but who was engaged in rebuilding the *Beit HaMikdash*. The people were occupied with *binyan Beit HaMikdash*, and the rain would fall at night. In the morning, the wind would come, the clouds would scatter, the sun would shine, and everyone would go out to their work. The construction could proceed unimpeded, the days were bright and clear, and the nights brought the necessary rain.

*Veyad'u shemelachet shamayim biyadeihem* — and they knew that the work of heaven was in their hands, that their labor was godly work. The environment itself testified to the divine sanction of their enterprise. Here again the emphasis falls not merely on the convenience of nocturnal rain but on its character as *siman bracha* — and, correspondingly, on the terrifying alternative, *siman kelala*, when rain comes at the wrong time and in the wrong measure.

---

## Choni Circle Story

### Drought & Prayer

With the *halacha* of *rov tovah* established, the *gemara* transitions to the figure who has been hovering at the edge of the discussion: Choni HaMa'agel. It is significant that the very era whose perfect rainfall the *gemara* just praised — the time of Shimon ben Shatach — is also the setting for the Choni story. The two are intertwined.

*Pa'am achat yatza rov Adar velo yardu geshamim* — once, most of Adar had already passed and rain had still not fallen. By this point the situation was dire: *Cheshvan*, *Kislev*, *Teves* had all gone by, and the prospect of rain providing any agricultural benefit was dwindling. They sent to Choni HaMa'agel: pray that the rains should come. He prayed — *hitpalel velo yardu geshamim* — and it did not rain.

### Circle & Torrents
