# Megillah 4

## Hierarchy: Megilla

### Rava: Megilla > Avodah

Today's daf is 4. We pick up in the middle of 3b, still in the midst of discussions about the hierarchy of which activities carry greater weight: the *avodah* in the *Beis HaMikdash*, *Talmud Torah* of the individual, *Talmud Torah* of the *rabbim*, and *mikra megilla*. This fits into the larger theme about the tremendous weight given to the *megilla* — a weight that has been explored almost as one would treat a biblical text, with the innovation of the holiday and the *mitzvah* of *mikra megilla* treated not as a novelty but as something of absolute standing.

Rava opens: *pshita li avodah umikra megilla mikra megilla adif* — it is clear to me that if it comes to a choice between the *avodah* in the *Beis HaMikdash* and reading the *megilla*, reading the *megilla* takes precedence. This is derived from the principle established by Rav Yosef bar Chanina, which we examined on the previous daf, learned from the phrase *mishpacha mishpacha* — even the priestly and levitical families suspend their service. What makes this striking is that we are speaking about a *galus* holiday: even after returning to *Eretz Yisrael* with the *Beis HaMikdash* rebuilt, one might have supposed the whole enterprise of *mikra megilla* would appear trivial. Nevertheless, even the *avodah* — the central religious act of Temple service — is set aside for the sake of *mikra megilla*.

### Megilla > Talmud Torah

Rava continues: *Talmud Torah umikra megilla mikra megilla adif* — and if it comes to a choice between Torah study and *mikra megilla*, *megilla* again takes precedence. *Talmud Torah* is, of course, what takes the place of *korbanot* in the absence of the Temple, and yet *megilla* comes first. This is derived from the principle established by *Beis Rabbi*, that one is *mevatel Talmud Torah* for this purpose. While the *Gemara* earlier appeared to limit the *kal vachomer* specifically to *Talmud Torah d'yachid*, in the end the *Gemara* does not draw a sharp distinction, and it remains at least ambiguous whether *Talmud Torah d'rabbim* is likewise set aside for *mikra megilla*. In any case, *mikra megilla* takes precedence over everything considered so far.

Rava then adds a further point that is clear to him: *Talmud Torah umes mitzvah mes mitzvah adif* — between Torah study and attending to a *mes mitzvah*, a corpse with no one else to bury it, the *mes mitzvah* takes precedence. The source is a *Beraita*: *mevatlin Talmud Torah lehotza'as hameis ulehachnasas kallah* — one sets aside Torah study to escort a body to burial and to escort a bride, because these are acts whose honor increases with greater participation, whether in mourning or in rejoicing.

Tosafot notes, however, that the *hachnasat kallah* mentioned here is not the same as *mes mitzvah*. The statement does not say one acts specifically for *mes mitzvah*; rather, as Tosafot explains, *lav davka mes mitzvah* — the rule applies to all the dead of the world, not only to a *mes mitzvah*. The practical qualification is that this does not mean everyone leaves the *yeshiva* for every funeral. The question of whether it is *lefi kevodo* — appropriate to the honor of the deceased — matters. But where more people are needed for a burial to be conducted properly, and no one else is available, that overrides *Talmud Torah* even without reaching the specific category of *mes mitzvah*.

Turning to *mes mitzvah* proper: *Avodah umes mitzvah mes mitzvah adif* — if it comes to a choice between the *avodah* and a *mes mitzvah*, the *mes mitzvah* takes precedence. A *kohen* would leave the *avodah* in the *Beis HaMikdash* to attend to it. The source is the verse *velachoto* in the context of the *nazir*, who may not contract corpse-impurity even for an immediate relative. A *kohen gadol* is similarly prohibited, as is a *nazir*. Yet the *Torah*'s repetition — specifying father, mother, brother, sister — even after having already stated the general prohibition for any relative, teaches through each additional word that one would still become *tamei* for a *mes mitzvah*. And the final word, *velachoto*, yields the most extreme case.

A *Beraita* elaborates: *velachoto mah talmud lomar* — why does the verse say "to his sister"? To tell you: not to your sister, but yes to a *mes mitzvah*. The extreme example given is a person on his way to slaughter his *korban pesach* and to perform *bris milah* for his son — two urgent *mitzvos*, one of which cannot be made up later — who then learns that an immediate relative has died. One might think he should involve himself in the burial. No: the verse says he may not become *tamei* to a relative. But perhaps he likewise may not become *tamei* even for a *mes mitzvah*? The verse therefore teaches: *le'achoto hu de'eino metame aval metame lemes mitzvah* — to his sister he does not become *tamei*, but he does become *tamei* for a *mes mitzvah*, even at the cost of the *korban pesach* and the *bris milah*, and even if the person in question is a *nazir* who is also a *kohen gadol*. The *Gemara* is making an extremely powerful statement: all these accumulated levels of *kedusha* and all these other *mitzvos* yield to the imperative of *mes mitzvah*.

## Met Mitzvah Debate

### Nazir Textual Proof

The textual derivation itself warrants attention. The *Torah* states the general rule that the *nazir* may not come into contact with any dead, and then elaborates: father, mother, brother, sister. Since the general prohibition was already stated, the *Torah*'s enumeration of specific relatives serves to teach that these are the ones for whom he does not become *tamei* — but only because they are relatives. For a *mes mitzvah*, however, he would. And with each successive relative mentioned, the case becomes more extreme: even to one's sister he will not become *tamei*, and yet he will become *tamei* to a *mes mitzvah* regardless of what other *mitzvos* must thereby be forfeited.

### Rava's Question

Rava has now established that *megilla* surpasses *avodah* and *Talmud Torah*, and that *mes mitzvah* similarly surpasses *avodah* and *Talmud Torah*. The one relationship left unresolved is that between *mikra megilla* and *mes mitzvah*. So *baei Rava* — Rava poses the question: *mikra megilla umes mitzvah hai minaihu adif* — which of these two takes precedence? Given the extraordinary weight assigned to *mes mitzvah* throughout the preceding discussion, it would seem difficult to argue that *megilla* could outweigh it. Yet the answer is not foregone.

## Hierarchy: Megilla (II)

### Pirsumei Nisa

The *Gemara* now articulates for the first time the principle underlying *megilla*'s remarkable weight: *mikra megilla adif mishum pirsumei nisa* — reading the *megilla* takes precedence because of the publicizing of the miracle. This is an important point that extends beyond the *megilla* itself. The concern is not merely that a *mitzvah* be performed, but that everyone actively participates together — for the sake of *pirsumei nisa*, the public proclamation of the miracle. And this may well explain what we observed on the previous daf: why the *kohanim* leave the *Beis HaMikdash*, why the *yeshiva* students leave the *beis medrash*. The demand is not just to read the *megilla* privately at a convenient time. It is that everyone comes together, because the essence of the *mitzvah* is the communal act of publicizing the miracle. Perhaps, then, this same logic would cause *megilla* to override even *mes mitzvah*.

## Met Mitzvah Debate (II)

### Kevod Habriyot

Yet the *Gemara* entertains the counter-argument: *o dilma mes mitzvah adif mishum kevod habriyos* — perhaps *mes mitzvah* takes precedence on account of the honor due to God's creatures. The theme of *kevod habriyos* here names what is at stake: a body lying unattended, treated with disregard, is a profound affront to human dignity. After deliberating, *sofo debayei ahadar pashiteih* — after raising the question, Rava came to a conclusion: *mes mitzvah adif*. The reason: *gadol kevod habriyos shedocheh lo sa'aseh shebaTorah* — the principle of *kevod habriyos* is so weighty that it overrides a negative prohibition in the *Torah*.

This ruling rests on a *Gemara* in *Berachos*. The primary context there is that a person of great dignity — a scholar or elder — for whom it would be beneath their station to personally retrieve a lost object would not do so even for their own property. Such a person may therefore set aside not only the positive *mitzvah* of *hashevas aveida* but also the negative prohibition of *lo suchal lehitalem* — one may not avert one's eyes from an *aveida*. The *Gemara* there limits this significantly, and the application to *de'oraisa* prohibitions is quite narrow. But the significance of the principle remains. The common assumption — that ritual activities directed toward God are of greater religious weight than those directed toward human beings — is here turned on its head. Here, a *mitzvah* whose foundation is *kevod habriyos*, the honor owed to a human being even in death, overrides all of the others.

One might ask: but didn't we just establish that *Talmud Torah keneged kulam* — Torah study outweighs everything? The response is that the teaching of *Talmud Torah keneged kulam* speaks to the *sechar* of the *mitzvah*, not to the question of momentary precedence. For this particular moment, one must address the immediate situation. The more striking case is *avodah*, since one might ask whether the *avodah* is truly lost or merely delayed — and indeed, *Talmud Torah* often yields to other *mitzvos* precisely because it can be performed at another time, as part of the broader principle that *oseik bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah*.

## Walled City Status

### Kerach & Neighbors

With these hierarchies established, the *Gemara* turns to a series of statements by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi addressing specific *halachos* of *mikra megilla*. The first: *kerach vechol hasamuch lo vechol hanireh imo nidon kekerach* — a walled city (*kerach*), and any place near it and any place visible together with it, is judged like the walled city and reads on the fifteenth of Adar.

A *Braisa* refines this: *samuch af al pi she'eino nireh, nireh af al pi she'eino samuch* — either condition suffices. Being close even without being visible, or being visible even without being close. The *Gemara* asks: how can something be visible without being close? The answer: *deyavsa berosh hahar* — if the city sits atop a mountain, a village far below may have a clear line of sight to it, and the distance is no obstacle.

The reverse case — nearby but not visible — is explained by Rabbi Yirmiya: *sheyeshevet benachal* — the city sits in a wadi, and what lies at ground level above cannot be seen from within it, even though it is not far. The precise meaning of *nira imo* — "visible with it" — admits of some discussion. It may mean both places are visible from a third vantage point rather than each from the other, but the *Gemara*'s answer concerning the mountain suggests the perspective is that of the city itself.

### Wall-Then-Settle Rule

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi further states: *krach veyashevu ulebasof hukaf nidon kekfar* — a *kerach* that was first settled and only afterward walled is treated like a village. The wall must precede the settlement; if settlement came first, the later wall does not confer *kerach* status.

The source is the verse concerning houses in walled cities in the laws of *Yovel*: *ve'ish ki yimkor beis moshav ir chomah* — if a person sells a house of settlement in a walled city. The verse specifies *beis moshav* within an *ir chomah*, implying the *ir chomah* existed prior to it being a *beis moshav*. Rashi reads this statement as applying only to the laws of houses in walled cities and not to *hilchos megilla*, where, he maintains, the order of settlement and walling would be irrelevant. But Tosafot disagrees with Rashi, and indeed the flow of the *Gemara* suggests otherwise.

What the *Gemara* appears to be doing is borrowing a pre-existing category from *batei arei chomah* — the laws of houses in walled cities — and applying it to the definition of what constitutes a walled city for *megilla*. This is a recognizable rabbinic technique: rather than constructing a new definition from scratch, one borrows and repurposes a prior category. A parallel example appears at the beginning of *Gittin*, where the parameters of *Eretz Yisrael* for the obligation of saying *bifnai nichtav uvifnai nechtam* are derived from the laws of *trumos umaasros*, even though the considerations are quite different. The convenience of reusing a definition outweighs the imperfect fit.

This also helps explain the otherwise puzzling requirement of *mukaf choma mi'yimos Yehoshua bin Nun* — walled from the time of Joshua son of Nun. This criterion is not arbitrary. It is a *halacha* that exists in other contexts. The *Mishnayos* at the beginning of *Keilim* list levels of *kedusha* in *Eretz Yisrael*, and between *Yerushalayim* and the remainder of the land stands an intermediate category: walled cities from the time of Joshua son of Nun. Such cities carry the status of *machaneh Yisrael*: just as the *metzora* must be sent outside the *machaneh*, so too must the *metzora* be sent outside these walled cities. This pre-existing *halacha* — which already attached significance to walled cities specifically from the time of Joshua's conquest — is what the *Gemara* borrows and applies here. The criterion of *yimos Yehoshua bin Nun* is not invented for *megilla*; it is imported from an already operative legal category.

### Asara Batlanim

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds a further requirement: *krach she'ein bo asara batlanim nidon kekfar* — a *kerach* that does not have ten *batlanim*, ten people who sit available for communal needs at all times, is treated as a village. The *Gemara* asks what novelty this adds, since the later *Mishnah* already states: *eizu hi ir gedola kol sheyesh bah asara batlanim* — what is a large city? Any that has ten *batlanim*; fewer than that, it is a village.

The answer is: *krach itztricha lei* — the novelty is specifically regarding a *kerach*, a walled city or major metropolitan center. One might have thought that a *kerach*, which draws enormous foot traffic from outside its walls, never lacks for people and therefore need not have *asara batlanim* as a resident requirement. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that even so, *asara batlanim* is required.

The question is what status the *asara batlanim* requirement governs. The later *Mishnah* uses it to determine whether a place is an *ir gedola* reading on the proper date or a *kfar* that reads on a market day. The question here is whether the *Gemara* means that without *asara batlanim*, even a city walled from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun* cannot read on the fifteenth. Tosafot resists this reading. Tosafot holds that a city genuinely walled from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun* requires no further conditions — the *Gemara* would have stated explicitly that even such a city loses its status without *asara batlanim*. Tosafot therefore reads the case as involving a city with a wall, but not one from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun*, and the question is whether such a city has at least the status of an *ir* for reading on the fourteenth, as opposed to being demoted to a *kfar* that reads on a market day. The plain reading of the *Gemara* likely goes the other way — that even the question of reading on the fifteenth requires *asara batlanim* — but Tosafot explicitly rejects this.

### Destroyed City

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi continues: *krach she-charav u-le-sof yashav nidon ke-krach* — if a *kerach* was destroyed and subsequently resettled, it retains the status of a *kerach*.

The *Gemara* asks: what precisely does "destroyed" mean? If it means the walls were knocked down while people continued to live there, and the walls were later rebuilt, one might read the statement as saying: only when people are present does it retain its status. But a *Beraita* cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yose interpreting the phrase *asher lo chomah* — "which has a wall" — by reading it both ways: *lo* with a *vav*, meaning it has a wall, and *lo* with an *alef*, meaning it does not. The implication is that even if the city currently has no wall, as long as it once had one, it retains the status of a house in a walled city. The same principle, borrowed once again from *batei arei chomah*, applies here: a city need not have its wall standing right now to retain its status. This has significant practical implications. One cannot assume that a city with a wall today reads on the fifteenth — it must be determined whether the wall dates to the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun*. But equally, one cannot assume that a city without a wall today fails to qualify — it may once have had such a wall.

If the destruction of walls is irrelevant to status, what kind of destruction matters? The *Gemara* concludes: *she-charav me-asara batlanim* — it lost its ten *batlanim*. A city that once had *asara batlanim* and lost them loses its status, and when it regains them it regains the status.

The *Gemara* has thus introduced two principles borrowed from *batei arei chomah* and applied to *megilla*: first, the wall must precede the settlement; second, the absence of a wall today does not strip a city of its prior status. These, together with the underlying criterion of *yimos Yehoshua bin Nun*, form a coherent system largely constructed by transplanting pre-existing legal categories.

### City Examples

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites a specific tradition: *Lod ve-Ono ve-Gai ha-Charashim* — these three cities, mentioned in *Tanach* in connection with the tribe of Binyamin, were *mukafot chomah mi-yemos Yehoshua bin Nun*. He had a reliable tradition to this effect.

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: were these walls built by Joshua? A verse in *Divrei HaYamim* states that the sons of Elpaal — Eber, Misham, and Shemer — built *Ono* and *Lod* and its daughters. Since Elpaal lived at the time of *pilegesh be-Giv'ah*, long after Joshua, these walls would appear to postdate Joshua's conquest. The *Gemara* counters: but perhaps it was Asa who built them, as derived from a verse indicating that Asa built fortified cities in Yehudah and Binyamin.

Rabbi Elazar resolves the apparent contradiction: all three accounts are accurate. These cities were indeed walled from the time of *Yehoshua bin Nun*. The walls were destroyed in the time of *pilegesh be-Giv'ah*, when Binyamin was devastated and its cities ruined. Elpaal then came and rebuilt those walls. Over time they deteriorated further, and Asa came and reinforced them. The verse supporting Asa's role — *va-yomer li-Yehudah nivneh et he-arim ha-eleh* — indicates that "these cities" already existed; he was improving, not building from nothing. All three figures acted upon walls that originally dated to Joshua.

This leaves open a number of important practical *halacha* questions. What does one do in the absence of a tradition? If a city has a wall but one does not know whether it dates to *Yehoshua bin Nun*, does one assume everything defaults to the fourteenth, or does doubt require reading on both the fourteenth and fifteenth? And what of cases like *Yerushalayim* today, where there is continuous urban development far beyond the ancient walls — is the expanded city *samuch ve-nireh* to the walled portion throughout? These questions are left for further analysis.

## Women & Megilla

### Af Hen Hayu

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states: *nashim chayavot be-mikra megilla she-af hen hayu be-oto ha-nes* — women are obligated in the reading of the *megilla*, because they too were included in that miracle. Although *mikra megilla* is a *mitzvas aseh she-hazman gerama* from which women would ordinarily be exempt, their obligation derives from the fact that they were equally subject to the decree and equally part of the salvation.

This same formulation — *af hen hayu be-oto ha-nes* — appears in two other contexts: the obligation of women in lighting *Chanukah* candles, and their obligation in the *arba kosos* on Pesach night. Three questions arise. First, what exactly does the phrase mean? The straightforward reading is that women were among those saved by the miracle, which would seem to apply to virtually every *mitzvah* commemorating a national deliverance. Why is the principle invoked only in these three cases?

A second, more expansive reading is offered by the Rashbam, cited in Tosafot: *she-ikar hanes haya al yadan* — the miracle was primarily effected through women. For *Purim*, this refers to Esther; for *Chanukah*, to Yehudit; for Pesach, to the famous *Gemara* that Israel was redeemed in the merit of the righteous women of that generation. Tosafot raises a difficulty with this reading: the language *af hen* — "even they" — implies a secondary role rather than a primary one. Though one could read *af* as "also instrumental" rather than "primarily responsible," the Rashbam's interpretation faces this linguistic challenge.

One answer to why specifically these three, offered by Tosafot, is that the principle of *af hen hayu be-oto ha-nes* operates on the rabbinic level. It is a *rabbanan* mechanism for including women in *mitzvos* that are themselves rabbinic in origin. Women's biblical obligation in *matzah*, for example, is derived separately. This principle is reserved for *rabbanan mitzvos*, which is why *Sukkah* and *lulav* are not subject to it.

The Rav Soloveitchik offers what is arguably the more satisfying answer. The three *mitzvos* in question share a specific and distinctive character: they are *mitzvos shel pirsum hanes*. How do we know that *mikra megilla* and lighting *Chanukah* candles carry this specific identity? Because they are the only two *mitzvos* for which one recites the *bracha* of *she'asa nissim*. No other *mitzvah* carries this *bracha*. The entire character of these *mitzvos* — the lighting of *neiros Chanukah* for all to see, the public reading of the *megilla* — is oriented toward *pirsumei nisa*. If the goal is to publicize the miracle, one wants maximum participation. And if women were part of the *nes*, then excluding them would undermine the very purpose of the *mitzvah*. The *arba kosos* similarly carries this character: drinking wine and reclining are the acts that demonstrate *bnei chorin*, that make freedom publicly manifest, rather than the eating of *matzah* and *maror*, which, while commemorative, are not in the same way acts of *pirsum*. Both the *nes* dimension and the *pirsumei* dimension work together to explain the inclusion of women in these specific *mitzvos*.

### Women Motzi Men?

The practical *halacha* that flows from this is debated. Tosafot notes: *mikan mashma she-nashim motzi'os et ha-acherim yedei chovatan* — the language of the *Gemara* implies that women can discharge the obligation of others, including men. The *Gemara* does not say women are obligated *to hear* the *megilla* — a formulation that would suggest a lesser level of obligation — but rather that they are obligated to read it, implying equal standing. A *Beraita* in *Arachin* states *hakol kesheirim likros et ha-megilla* — everyone is eligible to read the *megilla* — and the *Gemara* there clarifies that *hakol* comes to include women. This implies they may discharge the obligation even for men.

However, Tosafot raises a difficulty from a *Tosefta*: a *tumtum*, a person of indeterminate sex, cannot discharge the obligation of another *tumtum*, because the first may be female and the second male. This appears to presuppose that a woman cannot discharge a man's obligation. On this basis, *Hilchos Gedolos* rules: *isha motzi'a mina aval lo anashim* — a woman may discharge the obligation of another woman, but not of a man. Under this view, women's obligation is different in kind from men's — they are obligated to hear but not to read, which is a different level of obligation.

This ruling of *Hilchos Gedolos* runs against the simple reading of the *Gemara* and against many *Rishonim* who rule that women are fully and equally obligated. Yet many *Rishonei Ashkenaz* follow Tosafot in following *Hilchos Gedolos*, and this is the source of the ongoing discussion about women reading the *megilla* for men.

## Night & Day Reading

### Shabbat Purim

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states: *Purim she-chal lihyot be-Shabbos sho'alin ve-dorshin be-inyano shel yom* — if *Purim* falls on *Shabbos*, even though the *megilla* is not read, one is obligated to teach and expound on the matters of the day. Rashi specifies that this means not merely discussing *hilchos Purim* in the abstract, but delivering a *shiur* on the *megilla* itself, as a substitute for the act of reading it.

The *Gemara* asks: what is the novelty here? Even on *Yom Tov* the same principle applies, as a *Beraita* states that Moshe ordained that Israel should inquire and expound the matters of each day: *hilchos Pesach be-Pesach, hilchos Atzeres be-Atzeres, hilchos chag be-chag*. Tosafot explains the actual *chiddush*: for *Yom Tov*, one begins discussing the *halachos* thirty days before the festival, and one continues teaching on the day itself. For *Purim*, there is no such thirty-day advance preparation; the entire obligation is concentrated on the day. It would thus be obvious that one must discuss *Purim* matters on *Purim* itself. The true novelty is different: one might have thought that expounding on the *megilla* on *Shabbos* is prohibited, on the grounds that studying it intensely might lead one to take out the *megilla* scroll, which cannot be carried on *Shabbos* — the same concern that, according to Rabbah, underlies the prohibition of reading the *megilla* itself on *Shabbos*. The *Gemara* therefore teaches that this concern does not apply to a *derasha*: delivering a *shiur* on the *megilla* does not engender the fear of carrying, since one does not bring a *megilla* to a lecture the way one brings it to a reader.

This teaching also connects to the principle of *pirsumei nisa*. The reading of the *megilla* is the primary act of publicizing the miracle. When that act cannot take place on the correct day, the obligation to engage the community with the content of the day — through *derasha* — reflects the same underlying imperative.

### Leil v'Yom

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also states: *chayav adam likros es ha-megilla ba-layla u-lishnosah va-yom* — a person must read the *megilla* at night and repeat it in the day. The source is a verse from the *mizmor* beginning *Lamenatze'ach al Ayelet HaShachar* — understood to have been said in the context of Esther — which reads: *Elokai ekra yomam ve-lo ta'aneh ve-layla ve-lo dumiyah li*: God I call out to You by day and You do not answer, and by night I will not be silent. Rashi explains: the reading of the *megilla* at night and day is a *zeicher la-nes* — a commemoration of the miracle — recalling that in those days they cried out to God day and night. The *pesuk* thus frames *mikra megilla* in terms of the cry that preceded the miracle: one cannot fully appreciate the *nes* without appreciating the *tzara* that came before it.

### Shanota Meaning

When people heard the statement *u-lishnosah va-yom*, they interpreted *lishnosah* in its familiar rabbinic sense: *nikrevah ba-layla ve-nimni masnisa de-yomah* — we will read it at night and learn the *mishnaios* of *megilla* in the day. *Lishnosah* was understood as a form of *mishna* — a technical term for the rabbinic oral tradition — rather than simply "to repeat it."

Rabbi Yirmiyah corrected this: *lidi di mefarsha li minei de-Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* — it was explained to me by Rabbi Chiya bar Abba that the word simply means *kegone de-amri inshi, kol parsha da ve-asnayyah* — "let me go over this passage and repeat it." *Lishnosah* derives from *sheni* — doing something a second time — not from *leshanen* in the sense of rabbinic study. The intent is simply to read the *megilla* twice: once at night and once during the day.

The *hava amina* here is itself instructive. That it was even momentarily conceivable to substitute *Mishnah* learning for the day reading of the *megilla* reflects the broader context: the *megilla* arrives at the juncture between the era of *nevuah* and the era of rabbinic transmission, between *Ezra HaSofer* and the beginnings of *Torah she-ba'al peh*. The idea that *mishna* learning could stand in for *mikra megilla* captures something of the ambiguity of this transitional period.

### Constant Praise

A parallel statement is cited: Rabbi Chelbo said in the name of Ulla Bira — *chayav adam likros es ha-megilla ba-layla u-leshonosa ba-yom* — one must read the *megilla* at night and repeat it in the day, based on a different verse: *lema'an yezamercha chavod ve-lo yidom, Hashem Elokai le'olam odeka* — so that my soul may sing to You and not be silent; Lord my God, I will thank You forever. Here the emphasis is on continuous praise throughout the day, framing the two readings as an act of unceasing thanksgiving for the miracle. Together with the previous source, which stressed the cry of distress, the two *pesukim* jointly frame the *mitzvah*: the *tzara* that preceded the *nes* and the praise that follows it.

One point of practical consequence must be noted. The phrasing throughout — read at night and "repeat" in the day — implies that the night reading is primary and the day reading secondary. Yet all the *mishnaios* that follow treat the *mitzvah* of *megilla* as a daytime *mitzvah*; the question of when the *mitzvah* begins is addressed entirely in terms of the day. The correct understanding, as some *Acharonim* frame it, is that the daytime reading is the primary *mitzvah*, grounded in the *psukim*, while the nighttime reading is a pure *rabbanan* addition. Tosafot presses the language of the *Gemara* to arrive at the same conclusion. The practical implication is significant: if one can attend only one reading, one should attend the day reading rather than the night reading. In practice, many are insufficiently careful about attending the day reading after having attended the night before — but it is the day reading that is *halachically* primary.

## Village Market Days

### Early Reading Reason

The *Gemara* now introduces Rabbi Chanina's explanation of the institution allowing villages to read the *megilla* early, on market days: *Chachamim he-kilu al ha-kefarim lihyos makdimin le-yom ha-knisa* — the Sages were lenient with the villages to allow them to advance the reading to the market day. The stated reason is *kedei she-yispeku mayim u-mazon la-acheihem she-ba-krachim* — so that they could provide water and food to their brethren in the large cities.

This framing is striking. It positions the villages in an entirely secondary role: their early reading is arranged not for their own convenience but so that on *Purim* itself they will be free to staff their stores and supply provisions to the large cities. They are, in effect, told to complete their religious obligation in advance so as to be available to serve others on the proper day. It is worth noting that while Rashi on the first daf of the tractate states that the market day was chosen because the *batei dinim* were convened then and villagers came to town, Rabbeinu Chananel frames it differently: people came to the large towns on Mondays and Thursdays in order to pray with a *tzibbur* and hear the *Sefer Torah* read. In either case, these were days when villagers were already traveling to town.

### Corrected Reading

The *Gemara* challenges this framing. If the early reading is intended to benefit the large cities, then on weeks when *Purim* falls on a Monday or Thursday, the villages should be pushed even further back — to a prior Thursday or Monday — so as to be fully available on *Purim* itself. The *Gemara* tests this against several cases. When *Purim* falls on a Monday, both villages and large towns read on that same Monday; the villages are not pushed back to the previous Thursday. When *Purim* falls on a Thursday, similarly everyone reads on Thursday. In neither case are the villagers reading early for the stated purpose.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *lo teima kedei she-yispeku* — do not read it as "so that they should provide." Rather: *aval ela eima mipnei she-mesapkim* — because they regularly provide. The inversion is significant. The early reading is not instituted *in order that* the villagers should serve the large cities; rather, *because* villagers characteristically come in on market days and provide for the larger communities, the Sages were kind to them and extended them the leniency of reading early on those same days. The institution is a favor to the villages, not to the cities.

### Conditional Application

Rabbi Yehudah's statement clinches this reinterpretation: *ematai bimkom she-nichnasim be-sheni uve-chamishi* — the leniency of early reading applies only in places where villagers regularly come in on Mondays and Thursdays. *Aval makom she-ein nichnasim be-sheni uve-chamishi ein korin ela bizmana* — but if villagers in a given locale do not regularly come in on those days, they have no dispensation to read early and must read on the proper day.

If the entire purpose were to benefit the large cities, this limitation would make no sense. The *Gemara* asks as much: if we are doing all this for the betterment of the large cities, what difference does it make whether the villagers normally come in on those days? Make them come in anyway and be available to serve. The fact that the leniency is conditional on the villages' regular practice of coming in demonstrates conclusively that the institution is for the villages' own benefit. As Rabbeinu Chananel explains, the underlying logic is that on a market day the villagers are already in town — in effect, if this provision were not made, they would simply not come in on Thursday, reasoning that they had to come anyway the next day for *Purim*. Allowing them to read on the market day keeps the markets functioning and rewards the villages for the service they already provide.

# Megillah 5

## Reading Dates & Tannaic…

### Month vs. Day-of-Week Or…

The Gemara on this daf opens by picking up in the middle of 4b, roughly ten lines down from the top, with the doubled word *keitzad keitzad* — "how so, how so?" — as the Mishnah begins working through the variations in reading dates. The Mishnah establishes that when *Purim* falls on a Monday, both the *kfarim* (villages) and the *ayarot gedolot* (large cities) simply read on that day. There is no complexity when the fourteenth of Adar falls on a Monday or Thursday, since those are already the designated market days on which the villages come in to town. The scheduling problem only arises when the fourteenth does not fall on one of those days.

The Gemara then raises a subtle structural question. The beginning of the Mishnah organized its discussion by the order of the days of the month — the 12th, 13th, and 14th — yet when the Mishnah proceeds to give its specific examples, it shifts to the day of the week: does *Purim* fall on a Monday? On a Tuesday? On a Wednesday? Why abandon the day-of-month ordering? The Gemara answers: *aidi demitpachei lei nakat sidura deyoma* — because if you were to organize the examples by day of the month, you would be forced to work backwards through the week, producing a counterintuitive and non-logical sequence. It is far cleaner to name the day of the week on which the fourteenth falls and let the reader do the arithmetic forward, rather than presenting the arithmetic in reverse.

### Friday Scenario Dispute

The Gemara focuses on the Friday scenario: *chal lihyot b'erev Shabbat* — when the fourteenth falls on a Friday. In this case the Mishnah states that the *ayarot gedolot* and the *mukafot choma* (walled cities) both read on Friday — the 14th — and the villages read on Thursday, since the walled cities cannot read on *Shabbat* and the villages move to the market day. The Gemara then asks: *matnitin mani* — whose position is reflected in this Mishnah? It answers: *ei Rabbi ei Rabbi Yosi* — it could be either Rabbi (Judah ha-Nasi) or Rabbi Yosi, since both of their positions turn out to be consistent with the Mishnah's ruling, but a *braita* reveals that the matter is in fact disputed among *Tannaim*.

The *braita* presents the position of the *Tanna Kamma*: when the fourteenth falls on a Friday, both the *kfarim* and the *ayarot gedolot* advance their reading to Thursday, and the *mukafot choma* read on Friday itself. The underlying logic is that the Torah states *achen haprazim b'arei haprazot*, contrasting open cities with walled cities — the two categories must always read on different days, their times must remain distinct. Since the walled cities cannot read on *Shabbat*, they are pushed to Friday, and once Friday is occupied by the walled cities, the large cities can no longer remain on Friday and must retreat to Thursday.

### Three Positions

Rabbi then disagrees: *lo yidachu ha-ayarot mimkomam* — the large cities do not get pushed from their fixed place. His view is that the walled and unwalled cities may both read on Friday, the 14th. That is indeed the position of our Mishnah.

Rabbi Yosi introduces a third possibility. In his *braita*, when the fourteenth falls on a Friday, it is the *mukafin* and the *kfarim* together who advance to Thursday — the walled cities and the villages both go back — while the *ayarot gedolot* read on Friday. His reasoning is that while he agrees the walled cities and unwalled cities must remain distinct, the walled cities cannot precede the unwalled ones. To have the walled cities read on the 14th before the unwalled read on the 15th would be perverse, since the entire logic of the walled cities celebrating later is that their miracle continued an extra day. To place them earlier would undermine the very content the calendar is meant to commemorate.

The Gemara then carefully articulates the competing principles at stake for each position.

### Competing Principles

For the *Tanna Kamma*, the Gemara cites the verse *b'chol shana v'shana* — "every year" — and draws the inference that just as in every normal year the unwalled cities precede the walled cities, so too here the unwalled cities must read before the walled. If the walled are pushed to Friday, the unwalled must go to Thursday. The Gemara raises the counterargument: perhaps *b'chol shana v'shana* means instead that just as in every normal year the unwalled cities are not moved from their fixed date, so here too we should not move the 14th? The Gemara responds: *shani hacha d'lo efshar* — this case is different because it is not possible to maintain all principles simultaneously; the priority of keeping the 14th and 15th distinct overrides the preference for keeping the 14th in place.

For Rabbi, the Gemara likewise cites *b'chol shana v'shana* to mean: just as normally we do not displace the unwalled cities from their date, here too — *lo yidachu mimkoman* — they remain on the 14th. And if that results in the walled and the unwalled reading on the same day, let it be. The Gemara raises the competing inference — perhaps we should insist they read on different days — and again answers *shani hacha d'lo efshar*: one cannot satisfy every principle, and Rabbi's priority is the integrity of the 14th.

The Gemara then works through Rabbi Yosi's position in parallel: his *b'chol shana v'shana* principle insists that the walled cities never precede the unwalled, even if they wind up on the same day, so the walled cities go all the way back to Thursday. The Gemara again probes whether perhaps we should insist on distinct days, and again receives the same answer — *shani hacha d'lo efshar* — something must give.

The Gemara then establishes, parenthetically, that Rabbi himself is not categorically opposed to the villagers reading on a Thursday in the *Shabbat* scenario. A *braita* records that when the fourteenth falls on *Shabbat*, Rabbi says: *ho'il v'nidchu ayaros mimkoman, yidchu leyom ha-kenisah* — since the unwalled cities are already being displaced from *Shabbat*, push them all the way back to Thursday so that everyone among the unwalled reads on the same day. The Gemara thus clarifies that Rabbi's reluctance to push the large cities back to Thursday in the Friday case was precisely because there the 14th is a perfectly valid reading day and he would not move them unnecessarily. But when the 14th itself falls on *Shabbat* and movement is unavoidable, Rabbi is willing and even prefers consolidating the displaced groups onto Thursday. The Gemara notes that a teaching of Rav Huna — that when *Purim* falls on *Shabbat*, *hakol nidchin leyom ha-kenisah*, everyone who is being displaced is displaced to Thursday — goes according to Rabbi, since it is consistent with his principle of consolidation once displacement becomes unavoidable.

### Multiple Purim Days

One of the most conceptually striking features of this Masechet is how *Chazal* have institutionalized the idea of different groups celebrating *Purim* on different days. The Megilla itself only records in passing that *Shushan* had an additional day and designates the 14th for the *perazim*; it never explicitly mandates separate days for the *mukafim*. Yet the Mishnah and these *braitot* not only preserve the distinction between 14th and 15th but expand it, creating a range of possible reading dates spanning the 11th through the 15th.

This raises a genuine question: is the fragmentation of the communal celebration not troubling? The unity of a shared liturgical calendar is one of the features that binds a people. The difference between Eastern Orthodox and Western Christian practice is precisely its divergent calendar of holidays. Two opinions among these *Tannaim* actually insist on preserving the distinctness of the 14th and 15th even at the cost of displacing one group, suggesting they regard the integrity of the two-day distinction as paramount.

And yet our Mishnah — the ruling of Rabbi — is willing to have the walled and unwalled read on the same day in certain circumstances, and indeed when *Purim* falls on *Shabbat*, Rabbi prefers to collapse the multiple displaced populations onto a single Thursday. It seems that for Rabbi the proliferation of separate days is not a value in itself. One might observe that a full range of possible reading dates from the 11th through the 15th actually softens the symbolic division: it is not that there are simply two peoples with two festivals, but rather a complex calendrical system in which any given community may find itself on one of many possible days. Whether the multiplication of dates reinforces or ameliorates the division is a question the sugya leaves genuinely open.

## No Reading on Shabbat

### Rava's Carrying Concern

With the ground cleared, the Gemara makes explicit what all the foregoing discussions assume: *megilla b'Shabbos lo karinan* — we do not read the Megilla on *Shabbat*. The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama* — what is the reason? The reason is never stated in the Tannaitic sources and must be supplied by the Amoraim.

Rava provides the famous explanation: *hakol chayavin b'krias Megilla* — everyone is obligated to read the Megilla — *v'ein hakol baki'in b'mikra Megilla* — but not everyone knows how to read it themselves. Therefore, *gezira shema yitlena b'yado v'yeilech etzel baki lilmod v'ya'avirenu arba amos b'reshus ha-rabbim* — the Rabbis decreed a safeguard lest someone take his Megilla in hand, walk over to a neighbor who knows how to read it, and in the process carry it four *amot* in the public domain.

### Shofar, Lulav, & Carrying

It is important to recognize that the next line — *v'hainu ta'ama d'shofar v'hainu ta'ama d'lulav* — is introduced not by Rava but by the *stam* of the Gemara. The anonymous editorial voice extends Rava's carrying rationale to *shofar* and *lulav*, two other observances that are similarly not performed on *Shabbat*. But when we studied Masechet Sukkah and Masechet Rosh Hashanah, we encountered other possible reasons for those prohibitions. By *shofar*, for instance, the Gemara elsewhere cites the distinction between *zichron teruah* and *yom teruah*, suggesting a more intrinsic connection to *Shabbat* observance rather than merely a carrying concern. The *Yerushalmi* does not necessarily accept that the carrying rationale is the exclusive or even the primary reason for those prohibitions. All we have from Tannaitic sources is the prohibition itself; the attribution of the carrying rationale to all three — Megilla, shofar, and lulav — stems entirely from Rava's statement about the Megilla, which the *stam* then extrapolates.

### Rav Yosef's Reason

Rav Yosef offers a substantially different rationale, one with no reference to carrying at all: *mipnei she-eineihem shel aniyim nesuot b'mikra Megilla* — because the eyes of the poor are directed toward the reading of the Megilla. When the Megilla is read publicly, the passage *matanot l'evyonim* is recited, and the poor gather in the synagogue in anticipation of receiving gifts. Were the reading to take place on *Shabbat*, when giving and receiving money is prohibited, the poor would come with hope and leave with nothing — a state of acute despair at the very moment the Megilla is being read. Rav Yosef's reason thus focuses on the social reality of *matanot l'evyonim* and the experience of the impoverished members of the community.

This is a structurally different type of reason. It implies nothing about *shofar* and *lulav* — those observances have no corresponding collection for the poor — and so one might say that according to Rav Yosef, the Megilla has its own reason distinct from those other cases.

Tosafot, troubled by the apparent conflict between Rava's and Rav Yosef's explanations, argues that Rav Yosef does not actually dispute Rava's carrying rationale but merely adds an additional reason. His argument is that since there is no parallel reason available for *shofar* and *lulav* beyond carrying, carrying must remain in play; for the Megilla Rav Yosef simply identifies a second independent rationale. But this reading is not obviously correct. The plain sense of the Gemara is that Rav Yosef offers an alternative, and it is the *stam* alone that extended Rava to *shofar* and *lulav*; Rav Yosef may well hold that those cases have their own reasons entirely.

### Gifts & Early Reading

A *braita* is then cited that confirms and elaborates on Rav Yosef's position: even though the Rabbis said the *kfarim* advance their reading to the market day, they also collect and distribute *matanot l'evyonim* on that same day — *govin bo bayom u'machalkin bo bayom* — because the eyes of the poor are directed toward the reading of the Megilla. The coupling is deliberate: *matanot l'evyonim* follows the Megilla reading wherever it goes. The poor gather on account of the reading, and so the distribution must happen on the day of the reading, not on the actual fourteenth.

Not only that — the *braita* insists on same-day distribution, not merely same-day collection. One might have thought: collect early while the communal gathering is happening, but hold the funds and distribute them on the real *Purim* date. No. The *braita* requires distribution *bo bayom* as well, precisely because the poor are expecting it at the moment of the reading.

### Seudah & Mishloach Manot

The *braita* then adds: *simcha einah noheges ela bizmanah* — rejoicing, meaning the *Seudas Purim*, is only observed at its proper time. The festive meal does not follow the Megilla reading to an early date; it remains fixed on the actual 14th or 15th.

This creates a clear division of the four *mitzvot* of *Purim*. The *mikra megillah* moves early; *matanot l'evyonim* travels with the Megilla. The *seudah* stays on the real date. That leaves *mishloach manot*. The *mishloach manot* is understood to be food sent in connection with the *seudah* — it is a way of sharing in the festive meal — and so *mishloach manot* goes with the *seudah*, not with the Megilla, and both remain on the real date.

However, the case of *Purim meshulash* in *Yerushalayim*, where the fifteenth falls on *Shabbat*, introduces a further wrinkle. There the Megilla is read on Friday, the *seudah* is on *Shabbat*, and *mishloach manot* — given the concern about carrying on *Shabbat* — is done on Sunday. So while in the village scenario *mishloach manot* and the *seudah* remain together on the actual *Purim* date, in the *Shabbat* case the two can be separated by the practical constraints of *Shabbat* observance.

## Private vs. Public Readi…

### Rav's Position

The Gemara now turns to a question that emerges naturally from the centrality of *pirsumei nisa* to *mikra megillah*: if publicizing the miracle is so essential — sufficient to include even those normally exempt from time-bound commandments, as we saw earlier in the Masechet — does one need to read the Megilla specifically before a *tzibur*, or can an individual fulfill the obligation alone?

Rav states: *megilla bizmanah korin otah afilu beyachid, shelo bizmanah ba-asarah* — if reading on the right time, even an individual may read it; if reading off the right time — meaning on the early dates, such as the village's Monday or Thursday reading — you need ten people.

The distinction draws on the idea that when the reading is *bizmanah*, meaning on the actual designated day, the entire population is involved in the observance, so even an individual reading participates in a broader communal act. Rashi explains this explicitly: *mitokh she-chovah bo bayom al kol yachid v'yachid korin otah afilu beyachid, de-hakol korin bo v'ika pirsum hanes* — since the obligation is universal on that day and everyone is reading, even a private reading partakes of the overall *pirsum ha-nes*. When it is *shelo bizmanah*, by contrast, the population is split: some are reading early, others will read on the actual date. There is no universal participation, and so the *pirsumei nisa* must be secured explicitly through a quorum.

One should also note that the question of whether "ten" here means specifically ten men — the standard *minyan* — or whether it invokes a broader concept of *rabbim* (many people) is not entirely settled. The *mitzvah* of *pirsumei nisa* is not a *davar sheb'kedushah* requiring a formal *minyan*; the Maharam MiRothenburg, for instance, rules that *b'rabbim* for the purposes of *kiddush Hashem* is not defined by ten men. The same ambiguity may apply here.

### Rav Assi Stricter

Rav Assi takes a stricter position: *bein bizmanah bein shelo bizmanah ba-asarah* — whether on the right time or not, you always need ten. For Rav Assi, the essential character of *mikra megillah* is *pirsumei nisa*, and *pirsumei nisa* always requires a communal setting. There is no scenario in which a private reading fully instantiates the *mitzvah*; the publicization of the miracle is, by definition, a public act.

This is somewhat analogous to the question of *pirsumei nisa* by *Chanukah* candles — whether one can fulfill the obligation with a purely internal household publicization, or whether the miracle must be broadcast outward to others. Rav Assi takes the maximalist position: the miracle always requires publicization to *rabbim*.

### Rav & Rav Assi Reconciled

The Gemara then reports a practical episode: there was a case in which the Megilla was read *bizmanah*, and although Rav himself had stated that *bizmanah* allows individual reading, he was nonetheless concerned for the position of Rav Assi and insisted on reading *b'rabbim*. In practice, then, Rav leaned toward the stricter standard.

The Gemara then challenges this: would Rav really say that even *bizmanah* requires ten people? It cites a teaching in Rav's name — *Purim she-chal lihyos b'Shabbat, erev Shabbat zmanam* — that when *Purim* falls on *Shabbat*, Friday becomes their time. The Gemara initially reads this as implying a halachic distinction: Friday has the status of *zmanah*, and therefore it can be read *bizmanah* even as an individual. But this reading would only make sense if Rav held that *bizmanah* and *shelo bizmanah* carry different requirements — exactly his original position.

### Purim on Shabbat Case

The case of *Purim* falling on *Shabbat* introduces an important conceptual refinement. When the entire date shifts — not just the villagers reading early while the town reads on the real date, but the entire population displaced from *Shabbat* to Friday — the Friday reading takes on the character of *zmanah*. In the village scenario, the population is genuinely split: some read on Monday or Thursday, others on the actual date. That is a real *shelo bizmanah* for those who read early. But when *Purim* falls on *Shabbat* and everyone, everywhere is reading on Friday, Friday has functionally become the day, and its character is more like *zmanah* than *shelo bizmanah*.

### Rav Consistent with Rav…

The Gemara ultimately resolves the apparent contradiction differently. It concludes that *le-inyan mikra megillah ba-asarah* — when it comes to reading the Megilla with ten people — Rav may in fact hold like Rav Assi and always require ten. The statement *erev Shabbat zmanam* is not intended to convey a halachic distinction for the purpose of whether ten are required; rather, it is a statement directed against the position of Rabbi. Rabbi, as we saw, holds that since the reading is being displaced from *Shabbat* regardless, it might as well be pushed all the way back to Thursday. *Erev Shabbat zmanam* rejects that: Friday — not Thursday — is the appropriate day, and the statement underscores that Friday is the proper substitute, not to teach anything about the *bizmanah/shelo bizmanah* distinction for the purposes of requiring ten people.

In the end, the Gemara reads Rav as consistent with Rav Assi: even *bizmanah*, one should read with ten. Rashi and Tosafot both note, however, that from another Gemara it is clear that one can technically fulfill the obligation *biyachid*, and the practical *halacha* does not require ten. What Rav Assi's position establishes is not that a private reading is entirely invalid, but that it represents a significantly diminished — almost *bedi'eved* — fulfillment. Tosafot even raises a view that when reading alone one might not be entitled to recite the *bracha* of *she-asa nissim*, since the *pirsum ha-nes* component, which arguably gives rise to that blessing, is so attenuated. Even if one fulfills the minimum obligation, the reading without a *tzibur* may lack the core character of the *mitzvah*.

This has practical implications. If someone must choose between a rushed private reading in the morning and a full reading with a *minyan* at a less convenient time, the consideration is not merely the usual calculation of *b'rov am hadrat melech* — performing commandments with a larger community for the sake of divine honor. Here the very substance of the *mitzvah*, its *pirsumei nisa* dimension, is at stake when reading alone.

## Big Cities & Villages

### Ten Batlanim Definition

The Mishnah defines *ir gedolah* — a big city — as any settlement that has *asarah batlanim* — ten men who are available to be present in the synagogue at all times and are supported by the community for that purpose. Rashi explains: *beteilim mi-milachtam v'nizonim mishel tzibur kedei lihyot metzuyim b'tefillah b'veit ha-knesset* — they are free from their regular work and are sustained from communal funds so that they can always be present for prayer in the synagogue. Anything below this threshold is classified as a *kfar*, a village, and its inhabitants would need to advance their reading to the market day.

### Early Not Late

The Mishnah then states the general rule for the Megilla: *b'eilu amru makdimin v'lo ma'acharin* — regarding these cases, the Rabbis said you advance the reading and never delay it. The reading of the Megilla on the 14th or 15th may be moved to an earlier date under the relevant circumstances; it never gets pushed to a later date. The Gemara cites Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel who grounds this in the verse *v'lo ya'avor* — it shall not pass. The deadline is fixed; the reading cannot be performed after the designated time. Moving it earlier, under the appropriate conditions, is permitted; moving it later is never permitted.

The same passage of the Gemara also records two additional statements from Rabbi Abba bar Shmuel. One establishes that years are counted by months, not days — derived from *l'chodshei ha-shana*, "according to the months of the year" — meaning that if someone takes a vow for a year, we measure the year by the calendar date one year later, not by counting 354 or 365 individual days. The other establishes that months are counted by days, not hours — derived from *ad chodesh yamim*, "until the month of days" — meaning a month expires on the same date the following month, not after precisely 29 days and 12 hours. Rashi illustrates with the example of one who vows not to eat something for a year beginning on the third of *Sivan*: the year concludes on the second of *Sivan* the following year, not by counting out the precise number of days.

### Rabbi Yehuda's Caveat

Rabbi Yehuda adds a crucial qualification to the village's early reading: *eimatai* — when is it true that the villagers read early? *Makom she-nichnasim b'sheini u'v'chamishi* — only in a place where the villagers actually come into town on Mondays and Thursdays. If this particular set of villages does not in practice come to the town on those days — *lo b'sheini v'lo b'chamishi* — then we do not allow them to read early. *Ein korin otah ela bizmanah* — they read it only at its proper time.

The entire institution of the early village reading was predicated on a practical reality: the villagers gathered in the town on market days to hear the Torah read, and the Rabbis arranged for the Megilla to be read at that same gathering so as not to burden the villages with a separate trip. If the villages in question do not actually gather in town on those days, the rationale dissolves and the concession does not apply.

### Other Times Not Moveable

The Mishnah then contrasts the Megilla with several other observances: *zman atzei kohanim v'ha-am* — the day designated for bringing wood to the *Beit ha-Mikdash* — *Tisha B'Av*, *Chagiga*, and *Hakhel*. For all of these, the rule is the reverse: *ma'acharin v'lo makdimin* — they may be postponed but never advanced. If these observances fall on *Shabbat*, or cannot be performed on their designated day for another reason, they move to a later date, never to an earlier one.

## Postponement vs. Advance…

### Tisha B'Av Recoil

The Gemara explains the rationale for each case. Why does *Tisha B'Av* get postponed rather than advanced? *Akdumei puranuta lo makdemi* — one does not rush to bring bad things forward. *Tisha B'Av* marks catastrophe and mourning. We naturally recoil from it; we would never choose to fast and mourn a day early. The very character of the day as an occasion of communal suffering means that the human instinct is to push it away, not to draw it closer.

### Obligation & Timing

For *Chagiga* and *Hakhel*, the reason is different: *mishum di-kdem lehu zman chiyuva* — because the obligation has not yet come into force before the designated time. The *Chagiga* offering may only be brought during the *chag*; one cannot bring it before the *chag* begins because the obligation does not yet exist. Similarly, *Hakhel* takes place at the outset of the *Shmita* cycle, on the first day of *Chol ha-Moed Sukkot* of the *Shmita* year; if that day falls on *Shabbat*, the assembly is postponed to the following day. The obligation cannot precede its own inception point. One cannot discharge an obligation that has not yet arisen, and therefore advancement is structurally impossible, while postponement — doing it after the time has already arrived — remains valid.

Rashi extends this logic to *atzei kohanim* as well, though the reasoning is somewhat circular: we assume that if something cannot be done on its fixed day, it can be done later but not earlier, because the obligation is tied to the arrival of its time rather than preceding it.

### Rava on Chagiga

A *tanna* teaches: *chagiga v'chol zman chagiga ma'acharin* — the *Chagiga* and the entire period of *Chagiga* can be postponed. The Gemara asks: what does "the entire period of *Chagiga*" mean? The Gemara first explores a more complex reading proposed by Rav Oshaya: perhaps it refers to two distinct scenarios — the case where the *Chagiga* itself falls on *Shabbat* and must be postponed, and the case of the *olat re'iyah*, which even on a normal *Yom Tov* cannot be brought on the first day of *Yom Tov* (since it is not an *ochel nefesh* activity as would be required to permit *melacha* on *Yom Tov*) and must always be postponed. The Gemara notes that this second reading follows the position of *Beit Shammai*, who hold that *olot* may not be brought on *Yom Tov* at all, while *Beit Hillel* permit it.

Rava then offers a simpler and more elegant reading: *chagiga v'chol zman chagiga ma'acharin* — the *Chagiga* can be postponed for the entire duration of the *zman chagiga*, meaning the full length of the *regel*, but no later. If the first day of *Yom Tov* falls on *Shabbat* and the *Chagiga* cannot be brought, it may be brought on any subsequent day of the *chag*. The Mishnah confirms: *mi shelo chag b'yom tov rishon shel chag, chogeg v'holech kol ha-regel kulo u'v'yom tov ha-acharon shel chag* — one who did not bring the *Chagiga* on the first day may bring it throughout the entire *regel* including the last day of *Yom Tov*. But *avar ha-regel v'lo chag, eino chayav b'achrayuso* — if the entire *regel* passed without bringing it, the obligation lapses and cannot be discharged afterward.

Rava adds one further point: even for *Shavuot*, which is a single day, the same principle of postponement applies. If *Shavuot* falls on *Shabbat*, the *Chagiga* can be brought on Sunday. The Mishnah confirms: *modin Beit Shammai u-Veit Hillel d'im chal Atzeret lihyot b'Shabbat she-yom tivoach achar Shabbat* — both *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* agree that if *Shavuot* falls on *Shabbat*, the day of slaughter (i.e., bringing the *Chagiga*) is the following Sunday. The six days following *Shavuot* retain a connection to the *chag* analogous to the *Chol ha-Moed* days of the other *Chagim*, preserving the window for bringing the *Chagiga*.

## Rabbi & Tisha B'Av

### Rabbi's Actions

The Gemara records a remarkable tradition in the name of Rabbi Elazar, who said it in the name of Rabbi Chanina: Rabbi planted a sapling on *Purim* and bathed publicly in *Kronah shel Tzipori* — in the wagon-district of *Tzipori* — on the 17th of *Tammuz*. The planting on *Purim* speaks to the question of whether *Purim* carries a prohibition against *melacha*, a topic the Gemara will address in the following daf. The public bathing on the 17th of *Tammuz* was a deliberate demonstration: although that date is a fast day, it carries none of the additional *inuyim* — afflictions such as prohibitions on bathing, anointing, and wearing leather shoes — that apply on *Tisha B'Av* and *Yom Kippur*.

### Uproot Tisha B'Av

The *braita* then adds the explosive detail: *vi-bikeish la'akor Tisha B'Av v'lo hodu lo* — Rabbi sought to uproot *Tisha B'Av* entirely, and the Rabbis did not agree. The statement is stunning. How could any authority seek to abolish *Tisha B'Av*, and on what grounds?

### Correction: Shabbat Case

Rabbi Abba bar Zavda corrects the record before Rabbi Elazar: *lo kach hayah ma'aseh*, Rabbi, that is not what happened. *Ela Tisha B'Av she-chal lihyot b'Shabbat havah* — it was a specific year in which *Tisha B'Av* fell on *Shabbat*, so the fast was postponed to the tenth of *Av*. In that year, Rabbi argued: *ho'il v'nidcha yidcha* — since we are already not observing *Tisha B'Av* on its correct day, we might as well waive it entirely for that year. His reasoning was not an attempt to permanently abolish the fast, but a one-time application of the principle that once a day is displaced from its proper time, its observance loses the specific grounding that makes it obligatory. The Rabbis did not accept this reasoning and insisted on observing the fast on the tenth.

### Two Witnesses Better

Rabbi Elazar then applies a verse to the exchange: *tovim ha-shnayim min ha-echad* — two are better than one. Without Rabbi Abba bar Zavda's correction, the original report would have portrayed Rabbi as having attempted a wholesale abolition of *Tisha B'Av*. With his clarification, the picture is far more limited and legally coherent. The statement is thus both a compliment to Rabbi Abba bar Zavda and a reflection on the importance of accurate transmission: a single tradition, even when preserved by a reliable authority, benefits from being checked against additional witnesses.

---

---

# Megillah 5b

## Purim on Shabbat

### Megillah & Shabbat Q&A

Before resuming the *sugia*, two questions from the previous session warrant brief attention. The first concerned why the concern that one might carry the *megillah* through a public domain — the rationale behind not reading the *megillah* on *Shabbat* — applies even in walled cities. Despite considerable research, no source could be found that directly addresses this question. The *gemara* does acknowledge the existence of a *reshut ha-rabim* even within walled cities, and the silence of the *rishonim* and *acharonim* on this specific point is itself striking.

### Mishloach Manot Timing

The second question concerned the timing of *mishloach manot* and the *seudah* when the *megillah* is read early not merely because of a Monday-Thursday calendar adjustment, but because the fifteenth falls on *Shabbat*. Here the initial position holds: *mishloach manot* travels together with the *seudah*. The underlying principle is that *mishloach manot* is organically connected to the *seudah*, and the two are not separated.

### Jerusalem Practice

When the fifteenth of Adar falls on *Shabbat*, the current practice in Jerusalem is as follows: *mikra megillah* is performed on the fourteenth (Friday), the *seudah* and *mishloach manot* are both observed on Sunday, and the only observance that takes place on the fifteenth itself — on *Shabbat* — is *al ha-nissim*. The day is called *meshulash* precisely because its observances are distributed across three days, though in practice only *al ha-nissim* falls on the fifteenth proper. The reason given for moving the *seudah* to Sunday is not the concern about carrying *mishloach manot* on *Shabbat*, but rather that a *seudah* of *simchat Purim* ought to be distinct from *oneg Shabbat* and should not compete with it.

### Achronim Debate

There is, however, a genuine debate among the *acharonim* on this matter. Some argue strongly, on the basis of the Bavli, that *simcha* is *bo ba-yom* — that the *seudah* belongs on the fifteenth itself — and therefore that both the *seudah* and *mishloach manot* should be observed on *Shabbat*. This position openly acknowledges the difficulty raised earlier: if we are concerned about carrying when reading the *megillah*, why are we not equally concerned about carrying *mishloach manot*? Yet this view holds nonetheless. The two positions are thus: either the *seudah* and *mishloach manot* fall on *Shabbat* itself, or they fall on Sunday with only *al ha-nissim* remaining on *Shabbat*. Jerusalem practice follows the latter.

---

## Rabbi Plants on Purim

### Gemara's Question

The *gemara* now resumes from the story involving Rabbi, one element of which is that Rabbi planted something on Purim. This leads directly into the question of whether, in addition to *mikra megillah*, *matanot la-evyonim*, the *seudah*, and *mishloach manot*, there is an obligation to refrain from *melacha* on Purim — not in the manner of *Shabbat*, but perhaps analogous to *Chol Ha-Moed*, where *melacha* is restricted but not entirely prohibited. The *gemara* frames the question simply: *v'Rabbi heichi nata b'Purim?* — how did Rabbi plant something on Purim?

### Baraita on Purim

Rav Yosef cites a *baraita* in response. The *baraita* derives its principles from the verse *la'asot otam yemei mishteh ve-simcha ve-yom tov u-mishloach manot ish l're'eihu* — to make these days of feasting and rejoicing, of *yom tov*, and of sending gifts to one another. The *baraita* reads each element as prohibiting something that would undermine it: *simcha* teaches that *hesped* is forbidden on Purim; *mishteh* teaches that fasting is forbidden; and *yom tov* teaches that *melacha* is forbidden. It is worth noting the pattern: each element is translated not into an affirmative obligation but into something one may *not* do. According to this *baraita*, performing *melacha* on Purim is prohibited.

### Melacha Prohibition

The *gemara* thus accepts the premise that *melacha* is forbidden on Purim, and proceeds to explain Rabbi's planting on that basis.

### Unwalled City Explanation

The first explanation offered is that Rabbi was from an unwalled city, where Purim is observed on the fourteenth. When he planted, he planted on the fifteenth — which was not *his* Purim — and there was therefore no prohibition in force.

### Tiberia Walled

The *gemara* challenges this: Rabbi was from Tiberias, *ve-Tverya mukefes chomah mi-yemot Yehoshua bin Nun hi* — and Tiberias is a walled city from the time of Joshua ben Nun. Consequently, Tiberias observes the fifteenth. The explanation is then revised: Rabbi planted on the fourteenth, which was not his day of observance. This too the *gemara* considers satisfactory.

### Chizkiya's Doubt

But the *gemara* pushes further. The revised explanation assumes that it was obvious to Rabbi that Tiberias had the status of a walled city from Joshua's time. Yet this very assumption is called into question: Chizkiya read the *megillah* in Tiberias on both the fourteenth and the fifteenth because he was uncertain — *misafka lei* — whether Tiberias had been surrounded by a wall from the time of Joshua. When such a doubt arises, the practice is to read on both days; the *bracha*, however, is recited on the fourteenth, since the fourteenth is the norm, and the *megillah* itself, in the phrase *al kein ha-perazim ha-yoshvim*, speaks explicitly of the reading of the fourteenth without even explicitly prescribing what the non-*perazim* do.

The *gemara* resolves the tension simply: Chizkiya had a genuine doubt; Rabbi did not. Rabbi was certain that Tiberias was a walled city and therefore observed the fifteenth as his Purim, planting on the fourteenth without any prohibition.

---

## Melacha Status

### Non-Purim Day

Having established that Rabbi planted on what was not his Purim day, the *gemara* raises a broader question: even granting that Rabbi's day of obligation was the fifteenth, does the fourteenth carry no status at all for residents of walled cities? Is there truly no restriction on *melacha* on the non-Purim day for such a person?

### Megillas Taanis

The *gemara* invokes *Megillas Taanis*, which lists the minor holidays on which *hesped* and *ta'anit* are forbidden. *Megillas Taanis* states *es yom arba-asar ve-es yom chamisha-asar* — both the fourteenth and the fifteenth — calling them *yemei Purim inun*, the days of Purim: *de-lo le-misped be-hon*, that one does not eulogize on those days and does not fast. As we learned extensively in *Masechet Ta'anit*, while most of *Megillas Taanis* no longer applies — *batla Megillas Taanis* — Purim and Chanukah remain in force with respect to the prohibitions of *hesped* and *ta'anit*.

### Rava's Ruling

Rava asks: why does *Megillas Taanis* need to mention the days of Purim at all, since they are already mentioned in the *megillah* itself? He answers: *lo nitzrecha ella le-asur de-zeh be-zeh ve-de-zeh be-zeh* — the only reason *Megillas Taanis* repeats both dates is to establish that the fourteenth and fifteenth form a package. Regardless of which city a person is from, both days are days on which *hesped* and *ta'anit* are forbidden. Just as we do not say *tachanun* on *Shushan Purim*, both days carry this minimal status.

### Own Day Only

The *gemara* might then assume that if both days carry the prohibition of *hesped* and *ta'anit*, perhaps both should also carry a prohibition of *melacha*. The *gemara* rejects this: *hani mili be-hesped u-ve-ta'anit* — the package deal applies only to *hesped* and *ta'anit*. When it comes to *melacha*, *yom echad u-tu lo* — only on one's own day of observance does any restriction on *melacha* apply; the other day carries none.

### Rav Curses Planter

The *gemara* then cites a striking story. Rav saw a man planting flax on Purim, cursed him, and the flax never sprouted. This seems to demonstrate that *melacha* is seriously forbidden on Purim. The *gemara* answers: that was the man's own Purim day — *bar yomei hava* — not the other day. And with that, the *gemara* appears to maintain a firm prohibition of *melacha* on one's own day.

Before moving to the next stage of the discussion, the *tosafot* here raise a remarkable challenge worth pausing over. *Tosafot* quotes a *teshuvah* of Rashi in which Rashi asks: *ve-khi mintan koach li-yemei Megillat Esther lidchos aveilus?* — since when does the *megillah* have the authority to override *aveilus* by prohibiting *hesped*? This is a penetrating question. *Megillas Taanis* is full of such prohibitions even for far more minor occasions, and we have emphasized throughout the enormous authority that *Chazal* ascribed to the *megillah*. Yet Rashi, motivated by the evident practice of his time — *ve-hachazina de-choi amma nahagu bo heter*, people were in fact delivering *hespedim* on Purim — problematizes the *gemara*'s ruling entirely. Rashi concludes in that *teshuvah* that the prohibition of *hesped* on Purim amounts to nothing more than not falling on one's face — that is, not reciting *tachanun* — because Purim is *yom simcha* rather than *yom tzara*. It does not actually prohibit a formal *hesped*. This is a striking position, essentially dismantling the very ruling we have just studied. And if it applies to Purim, it presumably applies to Chanukah as well.

---

## Melacha Not Obligatory

### Rabba's Position

The entire foregoing discussion proceeded on the premise that *melacha* is genuinely forbidden on Purim. Rabba the son of Rav now overturns that premise entirely. He states: *hesped ve-ta'anit kibilu aleihu* — the Jews ultimately accepted upon themselves the prohibition of *hesped* and *ta'anit*; *melacha lo kibilu aleihu* — but they never accepted the prohibition of *melacha*. The restriction on *melacha* was simply never taken on as a binding obligation.

### Verses Analysis

The *gemara* provides the textual basis for this claim. Initially, when Mordechai and Esther sent word, the formulation included *yom tov*: *la'asot otam yemei mishte ve-simcha ve-yom tov u-mishloach manot ish le-re'eihu*. The Jewish people were asked to make these days into a *yom tov*.

### Acceptance Limited

But when the Jews confirmed their acceptance, the formulation changed. The verse reads: *kiyemu ve-kiblu ha-Yehudim aleihem ve-al zaram lihyot osim et yemei ha-Purim ha-eleh la'asot otam yemei mishte ve-simcha* — and the words *ve-yom tov* do not appear. The Jews accepted *mishte ve-simcha* — feasting and rejoicing — but they did not accept the *yom tov* status that entails the prohibition of *melacha*. Purim, in the end, is not *assur be-melacha*.

This point runs far deeper than a technical question about *melacha*. The entire *sugia* of *megillah* is shadowed by questions about the authority to create new holidays. The *megillah* itself was a late addition to *Sifrei Tanach*, and the authority of its verses to obligate various practices has been a recurring theme. In that light, it is significant that both Purim and Chanukah — the two rabbinic holidays — do not carry the full weight of *yom tov*. One says *al ha-nissim*, one lights candles, one reads the *megillah*; but the day does not become a *yom tov* in the full sense. That reflects something essential about the character of these days, not merely a technicality. To create a full *yom tov* would have required a different level of authority entirely.

### Minhag vs. Halacha

This raises the practical question: if *melacha* is permitted on Purim, why did Rav curse the man who planted? And if people generally did not do *melacha* on Purim, what was the status of that practice? The *gemara* answers: *devarim ha-mutarim va-acherim nahagu bahen issur* — these are things that are technically permitted but which others have taken on as a custom of stringency. In Rav's locale, there was an established *minhag* not to perform *melacha* on Purim, and the man was violating that *minhag*. As for Rabbi, in his locale no such *minhag* existed — or alternatively, Rabbi was demonstrating by his action that the restriction is only a *minhag* and not a binding *halacha*.

### Simcha Planting

A further possibility is also offered: *le-olam nahug* — perhaps Rabbi's locale did observe the *minhag*. In that case, why did Rabbi plant? Because *Rabbi netiya shel simcha nata* — what Rabbi planted was a *netiya shel simcha*, a planting associated with joy. The *minhag* of not performing *melacha* on Purim is not modeled on the *yom tov* prohibition of *melacha*. It is rooted, rather, in the idea that one should not distract oneself from the *simcha* of the day. A *melacha* that is itself an expression of *simcha* — that contributes to rather than detracts from joy — falls outside the scope of this *minhag* entirely. Rabbi could therefore plant without violating anything, because his planting was itself an act of *simcha*.

This distinction is important for understanding the character of the *minhag*. Even within the framework of the *minhag*, we are not treating Purim as a quasi-*yom tov*. The *minhag* is not "avoid *melacha* because this day is like a *yom tov*"; it is "avoid *melacha* because it distracts from *simcha*." That is a fundamentally different rationale, and it produces a fundamentally different boundary.

### Simcha Work Types

The *gemara* brings a parallel from the opposite direction — from the realm of *aveilus* — to substantiate the concept of *netiya shel simcha*. The *mishna* in *Ta'anit* teaches that if the public fast days passed without the community being answered, one curtails *massa u-mattan* (commercial activity), *binyan*, *netiya*, *erusin*, and *nisu'in*. A *baraita* then specifies that the *binyan* referred to is *binyan shel simcha* — joyous construction — and the *netiya* is *netiya shel simcha* — joyous planting. *Eizo hi binyan shel simcha?* — what is joyous construction? Building a *beit chatnut* for one's son, that is, a wedding house, a deeply celebratory undertaking. *Eizo hi netiya shel simcha?* — what is joyous planting? A royal garden, an *avroneki shel melachim*, something planted for pleasure and majesty rather than for commerce.

The halachic category of *netiya shel simcha* thus has independent standing in *halacha*: it is singled out for prohibition when one enters an *aveilus*-like mode because it is the paradigmatic act of joy.
