By the same logic, it is precisely the type of *melacha* that remains permitted under the Purim *minhag* — because the *minhag* is about not abandoning *simcha*, and a *netiya shel simcha* is *simcha* itself. Even within the *minhag*, we do not treat Purim as a *yom tov*; we treat the *minhag* as an expression of the day's *simcha*, and work that embodies *simcha* is therefore not only permitted but fitting.

---

## Walled Cities ID

### Tiberia Walls

The *gemara* now returns to the earlier statement about Chizkiya reading the *megillah* in Tiberias on both the fourteenth and the fifteenth due to his uncertainty about its status. The *gemara* asks: how could there be any genuine doubt about whether Tiberias was a walled city from the time of Joshua? The verse in *Yehoshua* lists among the fortified cities of Naftali: *Tzidim, Tzer, Chamat, Rakas, ve-Chinneres*. And as we will establish momentarily, *Rakas* is Tiberias. The verse identifies it explicitly as a walled city. How then was Chizkiya uncertain?

The *gemara* answers: *mishum de-chad gisa shura de-yama hava* — on one side, Tiberias is bounded not by a wall but by the water. It is not fully enclosed by walls; one side is open to the Sea of Galilee. That is the source of the doubt.

### Walled Definition

But if one side is unenclosed, why is there even a doubt? The *gemara* pursues this: if one side has no wall, surely it simply does not qualify — *vadai lav chomah hi*. And indeed a *baraita* addressing the laws of houses in walled cities for *yovel* — *asher lo chomah saviv* — specifies that Tiberias does not qualify for that category, because *yamma chomatah*, the sea serves as its wall. The *baraita* requires *saviv*, full encirclement. So for *battei arei chomah* there would be no doubt: Tiberias does not qualify.

Yet for *mikra megillah*, the *gemara* says, there *is* a doubt: *ki ka mesafka lei le-inyan mikra Megillah*. This introduces a critical point: the criteria for *ir chomah* in *megillah* law may not be identical to those borrowed from *battei arei chomah*. Much is certainly borrowed from that pre-existing category, as *Tosafot* discusses, but the borrowing may not be total.

### Megillah Definition

Why might *megillah* law define the category differently? Rashi's approach here is illuminating. The *pesukim* in the *megillah* do not define walled cities directly; they define *perazim* — unwalled villages. The negative is defined, not the positive. This asymmetry matters: the opposite of a defined category is not simply another defined category but rather everything that is *not* that category. A city that is partially walled, like Tiberias, is not a *peruza* — an open, unwalled settlement — but may also not satisfy a strict definition of *ir chomah*. Depending on which end one defines, these intermediate cases fall differently.

### Exposed vs. Protected

This leads the *gemara* to articulate two possible understandings of what distinguishes *perazim* from *mukkafin*. The first: *mishum de-hani miglu ve-hani lo miglu* — the distinction is between being exposed and being concealed from view. On this reading, *perazim* are settlements that lie open and visible. If so, Tiberias, which is exposed on its water-side, might fall into the *perazim* category — *ve-hani nami mighalya*, it too is exposed. The second possibility: *mishum de-hani mignu ve-hani lo mignu* — the distinction is about security and protection, whether a city is defended or not. On this reading, Tiberias, which has walls on three sides and the sea on the fourth, is genuinely defended — *ve-ha nami mignu* — and therefore might qualify as a walled city.

Because neither criterion produces a clear answer for Tiberias, Chizkiya had a genuine doubt. The *gemara* adds a broader consideration offered by Ramban, who raises the question of why two separate holidays were created at all — the fourteenth for unwalled cities and the fifteenth for walled ones. Ramban argues, based on a close reading of the final chapters of the *megillah*, that those in walled cities initially felt the miracle less directly, since they were better defended and less exposed to the threat. This would explain why *mukkafin* status was tied to defensibility — *mignu* — and why residents of walled cities may have initially resisted accepting Purim altogether. This thesis has significant difficulties, but it anchors itself precisely in this *gemara*'s question about whether the relevant criterion is exposure or protection.

---

## Biblical City ID

### Rav Ashi Case

The *gemara* now turns to a related case. Rav Ashi read the *megillah* in Hutzo on both the fourteenth and the fifteenth — *maspka lei im mukefet chomah mi-yemot Yehoshua bin Nun hi o lo* — uncertain whether it was walled from Joshua's time. Alternatively, some report that Rav Ashi had no such uncertainty and stated definitively that this Hutzo of Binyamin was indeed walled from Joshua's time, in which case the account of him reading on both days may refer to a different Hutzo altogether.

### RY Identifications

Rabbi Yochanan introduces an identification that he had made in his youth and later confirmed was correct. He reports: *ki havina talya*, when I was just a boy, *amina milta dishailna le-savaya*, I said something and asked the elders, *ve-hishtakach kevasi*, and it was found that I was right. His identifications concern the cities listed in *Yehoshua* as walled: *Chamat zu Tverya* — Chamat is Tiberias; *Rakas zu Tzipori* — Rakas is Tzipori; *Kinneret zu Ginnosar* — Kinneret is Ginosar.

### City Identities

The etymologies are explained. *Chamat* is Tiberias because of the *chamei Tverya*, the hot springs of Tiberias — the name reflects the city's most famous natural feature. *Rakas* is Tzipori because *midalya ke-rikta de-nahara* — Tzipori sits atop a mountain, elevated like the bank of a river above the river's bed. *Kinneret* is Ginosar because *dematiki peiraheha ke-kala de-kinri* — its fruits are as sweet as the sound of a harp; some also note the harp-like shape of the lake itself as a possible basis for the name.

### Eulogy Evidence

Rava now asks: how can anyone claim that *Rakas* is not Tiberias? The eulogies delivered in Tiberias make this identification unmistakably clear. When a great sage died, the *hesped* delivered there was: *gadol hu be-Sheshach ve-shem lo be-Rakas* — he was great in *Sheshach* (a name in *Tanach* for Bavel) and he made a name for himself in *Rakas*. When the *aron* arrived in Tiberias for burial, the eulogy proclaimed: *ohavei seridim, yoshvei Rakas, tze'u ve-kiblu harugei omek* — lovers of the remnant, dwellers of Rakas, go out and receive those slain in the depths, *omek* referring to Bavel's low-lying terrain. And when Rabbi Zeira died — born in Bavel, raised to greatness in *Eretz Yisrael*, and residing in Tiberias — the *hesped* opened: *eretz Shinar hara ve-yalda, eretz tzvi gidla sha'ashu'eha, oy na la amra Rakas ki avda kli chemdatah* — woe says Rakas, for it has lost its precious vessel. Rakas is unambiguously Tiberias.

### Rabba Disputes

Rava therefore disputes Rabbi Yochanan's identification. He accepts that *Rakas* is Tiberias, but rejects the claim that *Chamat* is Tiberias. Instead, *Chamat zu chamei Gader* — Chamat is the hot springs of Gader. And since *Rakas* is Tiberias, not Tzipori, the identification of *Rakas* with Tzipori must be abandoned.

For the etymology of *Rakas* and Tiberias, Rava offers two explanations. Rabbi Yirmi holds that *Rakas* is simply the city's proper name, carrying no symbolic meaning, and that *Tiberias* is the additional name given to it. Why was it called *Tverya*? *She-yoshevet be-tibura shel Eretz Yisrael* — because it sits at the navel, the center, of the Land of Israel. Rava himself holds similarly that *Rakas* is the original name, while *Tverya* was given because *she-tova re'iyata* — its appearance is good, it has a fine and distinguished reputation.

### Kitron & Tzipori

With *Rakas* now identified as Tiberias rather than Tzipori, the *gemara* must locate Tzipori elsewhere. Ze'iri provides the identification: *Kitron zu Tzipori* — Kitron is Tzipori. The etymology of the name Tzipori is that *she-yoshevet be-rosho shel tzippor* — the city sits atop a mountain like a bird perched on high.

### Zebulun Complaint

But the *gemara* immediately challenges this. Kitron appears in *Shoftim*: *Zvulun lo horish et yoshvei Kitron ve-et yoshvei Nahalol* — Zebulun did not dispossess the inhabitants of Kitron. Kitron was thus in the portion of Zebulun. If Kitron were Tzipori, Zebulun would have had Tzipori in its *chelek* from the outset. Yet Zebulun is known to have complained bitterly about its inheritance.

The *gemara* recalls the relevant passage. The verse in *Shirat Devorah* — *Zvulun am charaf nafsho lamut* — is read here not as simple praise of Zebulun's courage but as evidence of Zebulun's complaint, since the verse continues *ve-Naftali al meromei sadeh*, pointing to Naftali's fields. Zebulun said before the Holy One: *Ribono shel Olam*, to my brother Naftali You gave fields and vineyards; to me You gave mountains and hills. To him You gave productive land; to me, You gave seas and rivers. God responded: *kulam tzrichin lach* — everyone will need you. Through the *chalazon* — the sea-creature that produces the blue dye for *techelet* — and through the hidden treasures of the sand (*shefunei temunei chol*), Zebulun would thrive. Rav Yosef explains: *sefunei* is the *chalazon*; *temunei* is *tarit* (tuna); *chol* is the fine sand from which precious white *levanah* glass is produced. Zebulun's concern about protection from theft is addressed with the assurance that *sham yizbechu zivchei tzedek* — any who take from Zebulun without payment will find their commerce fail.

If Zebulun had possessed Tzipori — *ve-ha Tzipori milta de-adifa tuva* — it would have had no basis for complaint. Reish Lakish testifies: *le-didi chazi li zavat chalav u-devash de-Tzipori* — I myself saw the flowing of milk and honey of Tzipori, extending sixteen *mil* by sixteen *mil*. Rabbah bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan reports that the milk-and-honey region of all of *Eretz Yisrael* stretched twenty-two *parsa* in length and six *parsa* in width, a vast area, and Zebulun's share exceeded what any single tribe should have in terms of *zavat chalav u-devash*. How then could they complain?

The *gemara* resolves this: *afilu hakhi sadot u-chramim adifa lei* — despite everything Zebulun possessed, what it fixed its gaze on was the one thing it lacked: fields and vineyards. This is precisely what *ve-Naftali al meromei sadeh* captures — it was Naftali's fields that Zebulun could not stop comparing its portion to. *Shema mina* — and this allows us to accept the identification of Kitron with Tzipori, since Zebulun's complaint is vindicated by the realization that Tzipori, for all its splendor, did not offer what Zebulun actually wanted.

---

## Rome & Jerusalem

### Ekron=Caesarea

Rabbi Abbahu opens a new set of identifications anchored in a verse from *Tzephaniah*: *ve-Ekron te-aker* — Ekron will be uprooted. *Zu Keisari bat Edom* — this is Caesarea, daughter of Edom, the Roman outpost situated *bein ha-cholot*, among the coastal sands. *She-hi hayeta yated teku'a le-Yisrael bi-yemei Yevanim* — it was a thorn, or rather a peg, driven into Israel's side in the days of the Greeks, that is, before the rise of Rome proper, in the era of the Hellenistic kingdoms. When the Hasmoneans prevailed and presumably seized Caesarea, *hayu korim otah achidat migdal shir* — they renamed it the conquered tower of *Shir*.

### Destruction Promise

Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina turns to another verse: *ve-hasiroti damav mi-piv ve-shikutzav mi-bein shinav ve-nishar gam hu l'Eloheinu* — I will remove the blood from their mouth and the abomination from their teeth, and they will remain for our God. *Ve-hasiroti damav mi-piv* — this refers to *beit bamya shelahen*, their altars of sacrifice. *Ve-shikutzav mi-bein shinav* — this refers to *beit galya shelahen*; some understand this as another idolatrous installation, others as their oracular sites, from *legalot*, to reveal. And *ve-nishar gam hu l'Eloheinu* — what will remain, what will endure? *Elu batei knesiyot u-vatei midrashot she-be-Edom* — the synagogues and houses of study in the Roman Empire. Everything else will be uprooted; these will survive. The promise of reversal is clear: what is good in the empire will remain and be reclaimed; what is corrupt will be destroyed.

### Theaters to Study

Rabbi Yitzchak adds to this theme, identifying *Leshem* as Pamyas (Banias), and Rabbi Abbahu returns to *Ekron te-aker*: *zu Keisari bat Edom*, Caesarea, daughter of Edom, *she-hayita metropolis shel melachim* — it was a metropolis of kings. Some understand this to mean that kings were raised there; others, that kings were appointed from its population.

The verse continues: *ve-haya ke-aluf bi-Yehuda ve-Ekron ke-Yevusi*. This is read as: *elu teratiyot ve-kirkasiyot she-be-Edom* — these are the theaters and circuses of Rome. *She-atidim sarei Yehuda le-lamed ba-hem Torah ba-rabbim* — the great auditoriums of Rome are destined to become places where the princes of Judah teach Torah in public. *Yevusi*, Rashi explains, is Jerusalem, since Jerusalem was originally the city of the Yevusites. So Ekron — Caesarea — will become like the Yevusi city, like Jerusalem: its theaters and circuses will be transformed into *batei midrash*.

### Caesarea & Jerusalem

The *gemara* distills the essential dynamic into a stark formulation: *im yomar lecha adam charvu shteihem* — if someone tells you both Caesarea and Jerusalem are destroyed, *al ta'amen* — do not believe it. *Yashvu shteihem* — both are flourishing, *al ta'amen* — do not believe that either. But if someone says *charva Keisari ve-yashva Yerushalayim*, Caesarea is destroyed and Jerusalem is settled — or *charva Yerushalayim ve-yashva Keisari*, Jerusalem is destroyed and Caesarea is settled — *ta'amen*, believe it. *She-ne'emar imalei ha-charava* — as the verse says, I will fill the desolate one. If one is filled, the other is desolate; if that one is filled, the first becomes desolate. These two cities cannot both thrive simultaneously; their fates are locked in an inverse relationship.

### Jacob & Esau

This relationship is, at its deepest level, the relationship of Jacob and Esau — *Yaakov ve-Esav* — whose eternal conflict is encoded in the verse *u-leom mi-leom ye'ematz*, one nation will be stronger than the other. Rome and Israel, Caesarea and Jerusalem, are the historical instantiation of that primal conflict. One is always ascendant; the other, not. They cannot both flourish together.

The significance of this *aggadata* at this point in the *masechta* is worth pausing over. Purim is, in a certain sense, the holiday of persistent subjugation. The *gemara* elsewhere observes that we do not say *Hallel* on Purim because *akati avdei Achashveirosh anan* — we remain servants of Achashveirosh. Unlike Chanukah, which marked a genuine historical transformation — the restoration of Jewish self-governance — Purim marked only the removal of an immediate threat, while the underlying historical condition of exile and subjugation remained unchanged. These closing *drashot* about Rome, Caesarea, and Jerusalem thus speak precisely to that condition. They acknowledge that the Jews remain under the yoke of Rome, and they look forward — through biblical verses and rabbinic reading — to the reversal that is promised. In doing so, they give voice to the poignant dimension of Purim: a holiday of survival, not yet of redemption; a day of *simcha*, but not yet of *geula*.

---

---

# Megillah 6b

## Rabbi Yitzchak: Providen…

### Isaac Pleads for Esau

The *gemara* picks up with yet another statement of Rabbi Yitzchak. The verse he addresses is: *yuchan rasha bal lamad tzedek* — "when it is good for the wicked person, he does not learn righteousness." Rabbi Yitzchak reads this not as a general moral observation but as a record of an actual exchange between the patriarch Yitzchak and the Holy One, blessed be He. Yitzchak pleaded before God: *yuchan Esav* — let it go well for Esav, he is my son too. God responded: *rasha hu* — he is wicked. Yitzchak pushed back: *bal lamad tzedek* — he simply has not had the opportunity to learn righteousness; he is not essentially evil, his circumstances have not allowed him to develop properly.

There is something striking about this exchange being attributed to Yitzchak rather than to Avraham, but the reason is contextual: the *gemara* is dealing with the relationship between Yaakov and Esav, and it is Yitzchak who stands in tension between them. Yitzchak's plea reflects a more sympathetic posture — an argument from nurture over nature, an appeal to context and circumstance as mitigating factors in Esav's wickedness.

### God's Response to Isaac

God's reply to Yitzchak's intercession is sharp. *B'eretz nechochos ye'avel* — in the land of uprightness he will deal treacherously. That is, Esav — understood here as the forefather of Rome — will attack *Bnei Yisrael*, destroy the *Beit HaMikdash*, and exercise dominion over the Land of Israel. Upon hearing this, Yitzchak immediately reverses course: *u'val yireh ge'us Hashem* — then let him not behold the greatness of God. If Esav is going to do that to my other son, to Yaakov, then he deserves what is coming to him.

The subtextual message here is significant. There is a tradition elsewhere in the *gemara* — notably at the opening of *Avodah Zarah* — that presents conflicted views of Rome: Rome builds bridges, bathhouses, and roads; Rome has a civilizational dimension. One can always rationalize the deeds of the wicked: it was their upbringing, their environment, the pressures upon them. But at a certain point, none of that matters. The evil that is being done overwhelms every sympathetic framework, and that is precisely the point being made here. The *gemara* is pushing back on an overly sympathetic reading of Rome.

### Jacob's Prayer vs Esau

The next statement of Rabbi Yitzchak addresses the verse: *al titten Hashem ma'avei rasha zmamo al tapek, yarumu sela* — God, do not give the wicked person the desires of his heart; do not remove the bit from his mouth, lest they be lifted up forever. Rabbi Yitzchak reads this as the prayer of Yaakov before God. Whereas Yitzchak had asked for some measure of compassion toward Esav, Yaakov — whose direct adversary Esav is — prays in precisely the opposite direction: *al titten l'Esav harasha ta'avas libo* — do not give Esav the wicked one what his heart desires. *Zmamo al tapek* — do not remove the bit from his mouth.

What does Esav desire, and what would happen if that restraint were removed? *Zu Germamya shel Edom* — this is Germamya of Edom, of Rome. *She'imale hem yotzim machrivim kol ha'olam kulo* — for if they were released, if the bit were removed, they would destroy the entire world. The word *Germamya* is obviously close to Germania, and given the events of modern history it is impossible not to notice; there are certainly those who see in this a resonance with later catastrophe. But whatever the *gemara* intends geographically, the point is theological: even all the destruction that Rome has already wrought is not the full measure of its potential for evil. Given full freedom, it would annihilate the world entirely.

### Germamia's Crown Princes

Rav Chama bar Chanina adds a further dimension to this picture. He teaches: *tlas me'ah katiri taga ika b'Germamya* — there are three hundred crown princes in Germamya. And *shin-samech-hei marzavnei ika b'Romi* — there are 365 officers of high rank in Rome itself, equal to the days of the solar year. Every single day these groups go out and engage one another in battle — *umaktei chad mineihu umitredi l'okmei malka* — and each day one of them is killed, which creates such upheaval that they are unable to appoint a king. 

The picture being drawn is of a place — Germamya — that is teeming with potential leaders, men of ambition and power, who are constantly being suppressed by the current Roman government. It is only because they are perpetually engaged in internal conflict with Rome's own ruling class that they are held in check. Were that check removed, the implications would be catastrophic.

One student raised the question of whether *zmamo* — the "bit" — is related to *edim zomemim*, scheming witnesses. The connection is suggestive: *zamam* means to plan or scheme, so *zmamo* could indeed carry the sense of "his scheme" or "his desire" alongside the image of a bit restraining a horse's mouth. Both readings are present in the *gemara*'s usage here.

### Toil and Success

The *gemara* then records another statement of Rabbi Yitzchak, one of the most famous formulations in the tractate: *im yomar lecha adam yagati v'lo matzati, al ta'amin* — if a person tells you that he toiled and did not find, do not believe him. Conversely, *lo yagati u'matzati, al ta'amin* — if he says he succeeded without having toiled, do not believe that either. Only *yagati u'matzati ta'amin* — if he says he worked hard and achieved what he sought, that you may believe.

The *gemara* immediately qualifies: *hanei milei b'divrei Torah* — this applies specifically to Torah study. In Torah, effort and achievement are directly correlated. But *aval b'masa u'matan* — when it comes to commerce and making a living — *siyata hu min shamaya* — that is a matter of divine assistance. One person can work extremely hard and fail entirely; another can stumble into a fortunate investment through pure luck. The world of business does not operate according to the principle that effort guarantees reward. Torah study does.

### Sharpness vs Memory

Even the principle as it applies to Torah is further refined. *Divrei Torah lo amran ela l'chadudei* — when we speak of effort producing results in Torah, we are referring specifically to *chadudei*, to analytical sharpness, to the capacity for incisive reasoning. If you put in the effort, you will achieve clarity of analysis. *Aval l'okmei girsa* — but when it comes to retaining what one has learned, to establishing it in memory — *siyata hi min shamaya* — that too requires divine assistance. Rashi explains *l'okmei girsa* as meaning *shelo tishtakeach mimenu* — that it should not be forgotten. Some people have strong memories, others do not, and that is not simply a function of effort.

It is worth noting that one could read *l'okmei girsa* differently — in the spirit of the phrase *l'okmei shma'ta aliba d'hilchta*, arriving at the correct halachic conclusion — and that reading would connect to a well-known account of Rav Chaim Soloveitchik, the founder of the *Brisker derech*. When people came to Rav Chaim with halachic questions, he would send them instead to Rav Yitzchak Elchanan, explaining that Rav Yitzchak Elchanan possessed *siyata dishmaya* in arriving at the correct *halacha*. Sharp analysis is not always sufficient to reach the right *psak*. But that is not precisely how Rashi reads this passage — Rashi's focus is on memory, not on correct legal conclusion.

### Don't Compete Wicked

Rabbi Yitzchak then offers a teaching that stands in a certain tension with the optimistic framework of *yagati u'matzati*. He addresses the verse: *al titchar bamre'im* — do not compete against the wicked. *Im ra'ita rasha she'sha'ah m'sacheket lo* — if you see a wicked person for whom things are going well, *al titchare bo* — do not try to take him on. *V'lo od* — and not only that — *ella she'drachav matzlichim* — his ways will be successful. Do not assume that because you are righteous and he is wicked, the outcome will naturally favor you. *V'lo od* — and further — *ella she'zoche badin* — he may even prevail if you press the matter in judgment. 

It is instructive to hold this alongside the earlier statement of *yagati u'matzati*: there, effort guarantees result; here, righteousness does not guarantee victory over wickedness. The parallel with *Kohelet* is apt — *ki lo lakalim hamerotz ve'lo lagiborim hamilchama* — success does not always go to the swift or the strong. The world does not always function the way we would prefer. The verse continues: *marom mishpatecha minegdo* — his judgment towers above you. *V'lo od ella she'ro'eh b'sonav* — he will even witness the downfall of his enemies; *kol tzorrav yafiach bahem* — all his oppressors he will blow down.

## Dispute: Compete Wicked

### Yochanan: May Compete

The *gemara* challenges this position. *Ve'ha'amar Rabbi Yochanan mishum Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai* — but Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: *muttar le'hisgar ba'resha'im ba'olam hazeh* — it is permitted to compete against the wicked in this world. The verse cited is: *ozvei Torah yehalelu rasha, v'shomrei Torah yitgaru bam* — those who abandon the Torah will praise the wicked, but those who observe the Torah will contend against them. This seems to directly contradict Rabbi Yitzchak's warning to keep one's distance.

### Dostai: Realm Distinction

A *baraita* is then cited. Rabbi Dostai bar Matton teaches: *muttar le'hisgar ba'resha'im ba'olam hazeh* — it is permissible to contend against the wicked in this world. If someone whispers to you the verse *al titchar bamre'im* as a reason to hold back, *mi she'libo noke'fo omer ken* — it is someone whose own heart pounds with uncertainty, who is not fully confident in his own righteousness, who says that. What, then, do those cautionary verses actually mean? *Al titchar bamre'im — lihyot k'mre'im* — do not compete against the wicked by trying to become like them. Do not be envious of their success to the point where you adopt their methods. Do not cheat in business because you see a wicked person cheating in business and succeeding. That is what those verses prohibit — not taking the wicked on, but imitating them.

### Resolution Two Ways

The *gemara* concludes: *lo kashya — ha bemilei didey ha bemilei deshmaya*. The two positions are not in conflict; they apply to different domains. When it comes to matters in the wicked person's own realm — say, a legal dispute, a business contest — there, if things are going well for him, give him a wide berth. But *bemilei deshmaya* — when it comes to matters of heaven — if someone is actively working to undermine religious life, to draw people away from Torah, you do not step back because he appears to be succeeding. That is precisely when you step forward.

A second resolution is also offered: *iba'is eima — ha veha bemilei didey, velo kashya — ha betzadik gamur ha betzadik she'eino gamur*. Even in the secular realm, a truly righteous person may take on the wicked. It is only someone who is not fully righteous — as was hinted by the phrase *libo noke'fo* — who must give the wicked a wide berth.

One student asked whether dishonesty in business does not itself constitute a *chilul Hashem* and therefore a matter of heaven. The distinction being drawn is more specific: publicly exposing someone's fraudulent business practices as a *chilul Hashem* — that would be *milei deshmaya*. Taking that same dishonest person to court and expecting to prevail because you are righteous — that is *milei didey*, and there the caution applies.

### Huna: Righteous Safe

Rav Huna offers a further gloss. He addresses the verse: *lama tabit bogdim tacharish bevala rasha tzadik mimenu* — why do you look on while the wicked swallows up someone more righteous than he? The operative phrase is *tzadik mimenu* — more righteous than he, but only relatively so. Such a person the wicked can indeed swallow up. But *tzadik gamur* — a fully, objectively righteous person — *eino bolea* — the wicked cannot overcome.

And even this principle has a caveat: *iba'is eima, sha'ah meshachekes lo shani* — even for a *tzadik gamur*, when the wicked person is in a period of exceptional fortune, when things are going particularly well for him, then everyone must give him distance. The *gemara* here reflects a sober and clear-eyed recognition of how the world actually functions — not always in alignment with the moral order we would expect.

## Rome's Grandeur

### Rome's Size

The *gemara* transitions with a statement of Ulla. This passage connects to the earlier theme of Yaakov versus Esav, of Yerushalayim versus Rome — what the rabbis called the fundamental competition of civilizations. Ulla states: *Italya shel Yavan* — Italy of Greece, meaning Hellenist Italy — *zu krach gadol shel Romi* — this is the great city of Rome. Rashi, citing what appears to be a Jewish foundational myth parallel to the Roman story of Romulus and Remus, notes that this great city grew as a consequence of Jewish sin, specifically the introduction of an idol into the *heichal* — that the angel Gavriel drove a rod into the sea, and from it grew a great sandbar upon which Italya shel Yavan was built.

Whatever the precise geographic identification, the *gemara* presents the city's dimensions as *tlas me'ah parsa al tlas me'ah parsa* — 300 parasangs by 300 parasangs. A colossal expanse.

### 365 Marketplaces

Within that city, *yesh bah shin-samech-hei shevakei* — there were 365 marketplaces, corresponding to the number of days in the solar year. These numbers are clearly formulaic rather than documentary — 300 and 365 are the *gemara*'s way of saying an incomprehensibly large quantity. Even the smallest of these marketplaces, the one that sold only birds, was *sheis-asar mil al sheis-asar mil* — 16 miles by 16 miles. Each day, a king could feast from just one of these marketplaces alone.

### Roman Citizenship

*U'melech so'ed bechol yom be-achad meihen* — a king would feast daily from just one of them. The *gemara* then describes two categories of people who received support from the royal house: *af al pi she'eino nolad bah* — even one who was not born in the city but lived there received a *pras*, a stipend from the king. And *ha-nolad bah af al pi she'eino dar bah* — one who was born there, even if he did not currently reside there, likewise received a royal stipend. This likely reflects the historical Roman practice of state subsidies to citizens — a distinction between residency-based and birth-based citizenship, both of which conferred material benefits.

### Rome's Defenses

Rome's physical invincibility was ensured from every direction. *Tzido echad yam* — one side was the ocean. *Tzido echad harim u-geva'ot* — another side was mountains and hills. *Tzido echad mechitza shel barzel* — one side was a wall of iron. *Tzido echad chulusit u-metzola* — another side was marshland and pebbles. It was, in effect, an impregnable fortress. 

This extended description of Rome's grandeur and power is not merely antiquarian. Part of what the *gemara* is doing, in the context of Megillah, is reminding us that the *nes Purim* did not fundamentally transform Jewish political reality. It was not like the Exodus or the entry into the Land. The Jews were still living under the successors of Persia — now Rome — and the world remained very much as it was.

## Megillah Leap Year

### Mishnah: Adar II

The *gemara* turns to the next *mishnah*. The *mishnah* states: *kara et ha-megillah be-Adar ha-rishon, ve-nit'abra ha-shanah* — if one read the *megillah* in the first Adar, and then the year was subsequently declared a leap year so that a second Adar followed — *korin otah be-Adar sheni* — he must read it again in Adar Sheni. The reasoning is clear enough: had he known in advance that there would be two months of Adar, he obviously would have waited for Adar Sheni. The question is whether the prior reading in what was then simply "Adar" can be grandfathered in. The *mishnah* answers definitively: no. The second Adar is the real Adar; the reading must be done again.

The *mishnah* further states: *ein bein Adar rishon le-Adar sheni ella keri'at ha-megillah u-matanot la-evyonim* — the only difference between Adar Rishon and Adar Sheni is the reading of the *megillah* and *matanot la-evyonim*. This raises an immediate question: what about the *se'udah* and *mishlo'ach manot*? Does one have to do them on both? Is one *yotzei* if done in the first?

It is worth noting, before proceeding, that the *se'udah* and *mishlo'ach manot* are strikingly under-discussed in Tannaitic literature. The *mishnayot* focus on *keri'at ha-megillah* and *matanot la-evyonim* but largely leave the *se'udah* and *mishlo'ach manot* to the *Amoraim*. This silence is significant, and the *gemara*'s own analysis reflects it: when searching for what else might need to be repeated in Adar Sheni, the *gemara* goes to *seder parshiyot* — the special Torah readings of Adar, such as *Shekalim*, *Zachor*, *Parah*, and *Chodesh* — rather than to *mishlo'ach manot*.

### Tannaitic Dispute

The *gemara* presents a *baraita* in which three *tanna'im* debate the matter. The *Tanna Kamma* holds: if one read the *megillah* in Adar Rishon and the year then became a leap year, one reads it again in Adar Sheni. Everything that applies in Adar Sheni applies equally in Adar Rishon — with the sole exception of *mikra Megilla*. That must be repeated in Adar Sheni.

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose takes the opposite extreme: *ein koreh otah be-Adar Sheni* — one need not read it again in Adar Sheni. *She'kol mitzvot ha-noahgot be-sheni noahgot be-rishon* — anything that applies in the second applies equally in the first. If you have already performed the *mitzvot* of Adar in Adar Rishon, you are *yotzei*, including *mikra Megilla*. You may even *lechatchila* read the *megillah* in Adar Rishon.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, citing Rabbi Yossi, takes the other extreme: *af koreh otah be-Adar Sheni* — one must indeed read in Adar Sheni, because *she'kol mitzvot ha-noahgot be-sheni einan noahgot be-rishon* — anything that applies in the second does not apply at all in the first. Adar Rishon counts for nothing; everything must be done in Adar Sheni. The one point of universal agreement — *ve-shavin be-hesped u-ve-ta'anit* — is that both Adars share the prohibition of *hesped* and *ta'anit*, which is forbidden in both equally.

The *gemara* then notes: *Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hainu Tanna Kamma* — on the face of it, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the *Tanna Kamma* appear to say the same thing: you must read the *megillah* in Adar Sheni. What distinguishes them?

### Rav Papa Resolution

Rav Papa resolves the question: *seder parshiyot ika beinaihu* — the point of disagreement between the *Tanna Kamma* and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is the *seder parshiyot*, the special Torah readings. Both agree that the *megillah* must be read in Adar Sheni. The *Tanna Kamma* holds that *lechatchila* everything should be done in Adar Sheni, but *de'avad be-rishon avad* — if one performed the other *mitzvot* in Adar Rishon *bede'avad*, one is *yotzei* — except for *mikra Megilla*, which must always be re-read in Adar Sheni. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that if one read the *parshiyot* in Adar Rishon, one must read them again in Adar Sheni; nothing performed in Adar Rishon is *yotzei* for Adar Sheni purposes.

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose, the other extreme, says that even *mikra Megilla* may be fulfilled *lechatchila* in Adar Rishon.

So the positions align as follows: Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose — Adar Rishon is fully equivalent, even for *mikra Megilla lechatchila*. The *Tanna Kamma* — Adar Rishon counts *bede'avad* for everything except *mikra Megilla*. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — Adar Rishon counts for nothing; everything must be done in Adar Sheni.

### Which Opinion

The *gemara* then asks: whose opinion does our *mishnah* follow? Our *mishnah* states that you must repeat *mikra Megilla* and *matanot la-evyonim* in Adar Sheni. This does not match any of the three *tanna'im* cleanly. *Ei Tanna Kamma — kashya matanot*: the *Tanna Kamma* says only *mikra Megilla* must be repeated, but our *mishnah* adds *matanot la-evyonim*. *Ei Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose — kashya nami mikra Megilla*: he allows even *megillah* in Adar Rishon. *Ei Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — kashya seder parshiyot*: he requires everything to be repeated, and our *mishnah* does not address the *parshiyot* at all.

The *gemara* offers two resolutions. The first: *le-olam Tanna Kamma* — our *mishnah* follows the *Tanna Kamma*, who says only *mikra Megilla* must be repeated. As for *matanot la-evyonim*, the *mishnah* adds it because *de-ha be-ha talya* — they are a package deal: wherever *mikra Megilla* applies, *matanot la-evyonim* follows automatically, as we have learned previously. So the *mishnah* is entirely consistent with the *Tanna Kamma*.

The second resolution: *ve-ei ba'it eima le-olam Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — our *mishnah* follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the *mishnah* is to be read as *chasorei mechasra* — as incomplete, requiring supplementation. The *mishnah* is actually addressing the fourteenth of Adar specifically, and its point is that the fourteenth of Adar Rishon and the fourteenth of Adar Sheni are the same with respect to *issur hesped ve-ta'anit* — both are equally prohibited for mourning and fasting — but *mikra Megilla* must be performed in Adar Sheni. The *mishnah* is not addressing *seder parshiyot* at all because *seder parshiyot* concerns the month as a whole, not the fourteenth specifically.

This second reading raises a further question, however. If we are following Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who says nothing from Adar Rishon carries over, then on the fourteenth of Adar Sheni one must repeat not only *mikra Megilla* and *matanot la-evyonim* but also the *se'udah* and *mishlo'ach manot*. Some *rishonim* suggest that the prohibition of *ta'anit* implies its positive counterpart — the obligation of *se'udah* — so that the *se'udah* is subsumed under the statement about *hesped ve-ta'anit*. But even this reading is strained, and the silence of the *mishnah* on the *se'udah* and *mishlo'ach manot* remains striking. The *gemara* itself is comfortable proceeding without resolving it.

A student raised an important historical question: when would the rabbinical court actually decide to add a leap year? The *gemara* indicates this could be done as late as the final day of Adar Rishon — which would effectively retroactively annul the observance of Purim just completed. The *Rosh* addresses this directly: even according to Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose, who says you receive credit for observances performed in Adar Rishon, that is only because at the time of performance it was still the sole Adar. Had Adar Sheni already been declared, no credit would accrue.

## Biblical Basis Adar II

### Yitzchak Rules

Rabbi Chiya bar Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *hilchata k'Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel she'amru mishum Rabbi Yose* — the *halacha* follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as stated in the name of Rabbi Yossi: nothing performed in Adar Rishon counts; all *mitzvot* of Purim must be observed in Adar Sheni.

### Same Verse Both

Rabbi Yochanan adds a remarkable observation: *u'shneihem mikra echad darshu* — both extreme positions, that of Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose and that of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, are derived from the same verse. The verse is: *bechol shanah v'shanah laka'im et yemei haPurim ha-eleh* — every single year, consistently, to establish these days of Purim.

### Close to Shevat

Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose reads *bechol shanah v'shanah* as teaching consistency: just as in every regular year, Adar is the month immediately following Shevat, so too in a leap year the Adar that counts is the one adjacent to Shevat — that is, Adar Rishon. The principle of *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot* — one does not pass over a *mitzvah* — further supports this: when the opportunity to perform the *mitzvah* first presents itself, one should not bypass it.

### Close to Nisan

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reads the same phrase differently: *ma kol shanah v'shanah Adar hasamuch l'Nisan* — just as in every regular year, Adar is the month immediately preceding Nissan, so too in a leap year the Adar that counts is the one adjacent to Nissan — that is, Adar Sheni. The *gemara* acknowledges that Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose's position has an intuitive appeal based on *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot*, but asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rationale is for requiring the second month. Rav Tabi answers: *taama d'Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel mishum mismach geulah l'geulah adif* — it is better to juxtapose the redemption of Purim to the redemption of Pesach. The two festivals of redemption should be adjacent to one another.

This is a genuinely interesting *machloket*. One position stays close to the text — the natural Adar that first arises — while the other brings a broader theological perspective: the meaning of *geulah* and the relationship between Purim and Pesach as companion celebrations of divine rescue.

### Textual Support

The *gemara* then examines the textual basis for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling. Rabbi Elazar cites the verse: *lekayem et iggeret haPurim hazot hashenis* — to establish this *second* letter of Purim. The word *hashenis* — "the second" — teaches that Purim is to be observed in the second Adar. 

But could one not have derived this from *bechol shanah v'shanah* alone? The *gemara* explains that both terms are necessary. Had the Torah said only *bechol shanah v'shanah*, one might have thought: be consistent — observe it in the Adar that follows Shevat, Adar Rishon. *Hashenis* comes to teach: no, observe it in the second of the two Adars. And had the Torah said only *hashenis*, one might have thought: observe it in both Adar Rishon and Adar Sheni. *Bechol shanah v'shanah* comes to teach: be consistent, observe it in only one month — the second one.

As for Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Yose, who holds that Adar Rishon suffices — what does he do with the word *hashenis*? He reads it *l'chiderav Shmuel bar Yehuda*: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda taught that the initial observance of Purim was established in Shushan, and only subsequently, through a second letter, was it extended to all Jews everywhere. The word *hashenis* refers to that second letter of proclamation, not to the second month of Adar.

## Esther's Request

### Establish Me

The *gemara* now arrives at a famous *aggadah* that goes to the heart of the religious significance of Purim: the authority of Megillat Esther, the innovation of a new festival, and the question of canonization. These themes have been lurking beneath the surface throughout the tractate.

Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda teaches: *shalcha lahem Esther lachachamim* — Esther sent a message to the Sages. *Kavuni l'doros* — establish me for future generations. She was asking them to formally institute Purim as a permanent fixture on the Jewish calendar. This echoes the earlier phrase *lekayem et yemei haPurim ha-eleh, me-iggeret hazot hashenis* — it took time and deliberate effort to establish the holiday. As one student noted, they waited a year, as is reflected in the principle that the holiday was formally established *l'shana acheret*, the following year — parallel to the story of Chanukah in Shabbat 21, where they similarly waited to see whether the event carried lasting significance rather than being merely a momentary victory.

### Jealousy Concern

The Sages replied: *kinah me'oreret aleinu l'vein ha'umot* — you are going to arouse jealousy among the nations. If Jews publicly celebrate a victory in which their enemies were slain throughout the provinces of Achashverosh, this will generate resentment and danger for the Jewish communities still living in exile. The tension here is profound: establishing a holiday that celebrates victory within the ongoing reality of exile, with no fundamental change in the political situation. This was not like the Exodus; the Jews were still subjects of foreign powers. How does one celebrate such a victory — and should one?

### Already Written

Esther replied: *kvar ketuva hi al divrei hayamim l'malchei Madai u'Faras* — it is already written in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. The events are already part of the official historical record of the empire; there is nothing to hide by establishing the holiday. The *gemara* acknowledges the distinction between something being part of imperial archives and Jews publicly celebrating it — these are not the same thing — but Esther's counterargument establishes the premise that the story is already public knowledge and the concern about arousing jealousy is therefore moot.

## Canonization Debate

### Write Me

The *gemara* records a further exchange involving a different group of Sages — Rav, Rav Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva, with a note that throughout Seder Moed wherever Rabbi Yochanan appears in this grouping, it should in fact be Rabbi Yonatan. Esther sent them a different request: *katvuni l'doros* — not merely *kavuni* (establish the holiday), but *katvuni* — write me into the books for future generations. She was asking for canonization of the *megillah* as part of *Tanakh*. This is a separate and more ambitious claim: not just that Purim be observed, but that Megillat Esther be included among the sacred writings.

### Three Times Already

The Sages responded: *halo katavti lach shalishim* — I have already written you out three times. The story of Amalek — the overarching narrative of which the Purim story is the culmination — already appears three times in the Torah and prophets: in Shemot, in Devarim, and in Sefer Shmuel. *Shalishim v'lo revi'im* — three times, not four times. There is no room for a fourth iteration.

This rejection is more nuanced than it appears. In framing its resistance in these terms, the Sages are simultaneously making a theological argument for inclusion: they are identifying Megillat Esther as part of the continuous biblical narrative about Amalek. The story of Esther is not a new story; it is the final chapter of a saga that began in Shemot. The resistance and the justification for acceptance are therefore rooted in the same logic.

### Four Times Amalek

The *gemara* then traces how the Sages came to accept the *megillah*. They found the textual warrant in Shemot 17:14: *kesov zot zikaron basefer* — write this remembrance in the book. The verse contains three distinct elements. *Kesov zot* — write this — refers to what is written in that passage and in *Mishneh Torah*, i.e., Shemot and Devarim. *Zikaron* — a remembrance — refers to what is written in the prophets, i.e., Sefer Shmuel. *Basefer* — in the book — refers to what is written in the *megillah*. In this reading, the authorization to write Megillat Esther was already embedded in the original command given to Moshe at the battle with Amalek. The *megillah* was not a novelty; it was always anticipated by the text of the Torah.

### Tannaim Positions

The *gemara* records a Tannaitic dispute about how to parse the same verse. Rabbi Yehoshua reads *kesov zot* as referring only to Shemot and Devarim, *zikaron* as referring to the prophets, and *basefer* as referring to Sefer Shmuel — leaving no textual hook for Megillat Esther. Rabbi Elazar HaModai reads *kesov zot* as encompassing both Shemot and Devarim together, *zikaron* as the prophets, and *basefer* as Megillat Esther — which is the reading we have been following. The practical consequence is that Rabbi Yehoshua's position leaves Megillat Esther without scriptural authorization for canonization, while Rabbi Elazar HaModai's position embeds it directly into the original Mosaic command.

## Divine Inspiration

### Not Canonical

The *gemara* records the position of Shmuel as transmitted by Rav Yehuda: *Esther eina metameh et hayadayim* — Megillat Esther does not render the hands impure. This is the technical *halachic* criterion for canonization. The Sages instituted that contact with any of the books of *Tanakh* renders the hands ritually impure — a rule instituted, according to one explanation, because people were storing *Tanakh* together with *terumah*, and the rats that came for the *terumah* were damaging the books. The rule of *metamei et hayadayim* expressed the sanctity of the canonical text and discouraged casual storage alongside consecrated produce. Whatever the precise rationale, this became the operative measure of whether a given work belonged to *Tanakh*. When Shmuel says Esther does not render the hands impure, he is saying it is not one of the canonical books.

### Question Paradox

This generates an immediate difficulty. If Shmuel holds that Esther is not canonical, does he believe it was not written with *ruach hakodesh* — divine inspiration? For presumably, if it were written with divine inspiration, it ought to be canonized.

### Read Not Written

The *gemara* resolves the tension with a precise distinction: *ne'emrah likrot v'lo ne'emrah likhtov* — it was given with divine inspiration to be *read*, not to be included among the *written* canonical books. Rashi suggests this might mean one could theoretically be *yotzei* by reciting the *megillah* orally without reading from a written scroll — though this is difficult to sustain practically, and Rashi notes it may apply only *miderabbanan*.

### Ritva Distinction

The better resolution is offered by the Ritva, and it is conceptually important. The Ritva draws a distinction between two entirely different categories: membership in the canon of *Tanakh*, and status as a *mitzvah* object. A *lulav* is not one of the books of *Tanakh*. Yet one cannot be *yotzei* the *mitzvah* of *lulav* without a physical *lulav* to shake. Similarly, says the Ritva, the scroll of Esther functions as a *mitzvah* object — one must have a written scroll from which to read in order to fulfill the *mitzvah* of *megillah*. The obligation to write a scroll of Esther flows from the nature of the *mitzvah*, not from its status as scripture. The fact that it must be written, and that it was written with *ruach hakodesh*, does not by itself establish that it belongs to *Tanakh*. Divine inspiration is a necessary but not sufficient condition for canonization. Esther was written with *ruach hakodesh* and is used to fulfill a *mitzvah*, but in Shmuel's view it remains outside the formal canon.

## Canonicity Disputes

### Kohelet Status

The *gemara* then challenges Shmuel's position by introducing a *baraita* on the canonicity of other books. Rabbi Meir states: *Kohelet eino metamei et hayadayim* — Kohelet does not render the hands impure and is therefore not canonical. His reasoning: it is the philosophical wisdom of Shlomo, not a divinely inspired composition. There is also a *machloket* regarding Shir HaShirim. Rabbi Yossi holds that Shir HaShirim does render the hands impure and is unquestionably canonical; the debate, he clarifies, is only about Kohelet. Rabbi Shimon adds that Kohelet was one of the *kulei Beit Shammai u'chumrei Beit Hillel* — a leniency of Beit Shammai and a stringency of Beit Hillel. That is, Beit Shammai held it was not canonical (the lenient position, avoiding the obligation to handle it with special care), while Beit Hillel held it was canonical. This is a striking inversion, as the worldview of Kohelet seems temperamentally more aligned with Beit Shammai than Beit Hillel.

The *baraita* then states that Ruth, Shir HaShirim, and Esther all render the hands impure — all three are canonical. The *gemara* notes that this poses a difficulty for Shmuel, since this Tannaitic source lists Esther among the canonical books.

### Kohelet Proof

A further *baraita* is cited. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya argues that Kohelet does not render the hands impure because it is solely the wisdom of Shlomo, not a divine composition. The Sages respond: but did Shlomo say only this? The verse states that Shlomo spoke *shloshes alafim mashal* — three thousand proverbs. Clearly he wrote far more than Kohelet. Why then was Kohelet preserved with special status if not because it was distinctively written with *ruach hakodesh*? And the verse in Kohelet itself states *al tosef al devarav* — do not add to his words — treating the text as inviolable divine utterance, not merely human philosophy.

### Selective Canon

The *gemara* articulates a broader principle underlying these debates: many books were written, but only some were included in the canon. The fact that a figure like Shlomo composed vastly more than what appears in *Tanakh* demonstrates that inclusion in the canon requires more than simply having been written; it requires a judgment that the work was composed with *ruach hakodesh* and carries the weight of sacred scripture.

## Esther Divine Proof

### Hidden Thoughts

Having established that divine inspiration is necessary for canonization, the *gemara* now marshals proof that Megillat Esther specifically was written with *ruach hakodesh*. Rabbi Eliezer: *asher b'ruach hakodesh ne'emra, shene'emar vayomer Haman belibo* — Haman said in his heart. How could the author of the *megillah* know what Haman was thinking internally? Only an author writing with divine, prophetically inspired knowledge could report the private thoughts of a character. This is what literary analysis would call the use of an omniscient narrator — one who has access to the inner lives of characters — and Rabbi Eliezer takes that narratorial posture as proof of *ruach hakodesh*.

### Universal Favor

Rabbi Akiva's proof: *vatehi Esther noses chen be'einei chol ro'eha* — Esther found favor in the eyes of all who saw her. How could the narrator know that she found favor with every single person who beheld her? Only divine inspiration would grant such universal knowledge.

### Kingdom Knowledge

Rabbi Meir's proof: *vayivada hadavar leMordechai* — the matter became known to Mordechai. Specifically, the plot of Bigsan and Seresh against the king. How did the author know that Mordechai came to know of this? Rabbi Meir connects this to the teaching of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba that Bigsan and Seresh were both from Tarsus, though the precise logical link remains somewhat elusive in the *gemara*'s brief formulation.

### Spoils Omniscience

Rabbi Yose bar Dumaskit's proof: *u'vaviza lo shalchu et yadam* — and in the spoils they did not lay their hand. How could the narrator know that across the entire empire of Achashverosh, the Jews took none of the plunder? Only an omnipresent, divinely inspired narrator could report this universal fact.

### Shmuel Best Proof

Shmuel demurs from all of these and claims he would have offered a superior proof had he been present in that discussion: *kiyemu ve-kiblu* — they established and accepted. Shmuel reads this phrase as: *kiyemu lema'ala mah shekiblu lemata* — they accepted in heaven above what they established below. The Jews below instituted Purim as a festival; God above ratified that decision. How could the author of the *megillah* know that God had approved the festival in the heavenly realm? Only through *ruach hakodesh* could one report such a thing.

This proof is elegant not only as evidence for *ruach hakodesh* but also for the broader question of the *megillah*'s authority. If God ratified the institution of Purim in heaven, that divine approval is itself embedded in the text of the *megillah* — giving the *chag* and the book alike a theological grounding that transcends the merely human process by which they were established.

### Sharp Answer

Ravina comments on the superiority of Shmuel's proof: *hainu d'amrei inshi — tava chada pilpela charifta mimali sani kari* — this is what people say: one good sharp peppercorn is worth more than a basketful of bland gourds. One piercing, well-constructed answer surpasses many mediocre ones. The proofs of Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Meir, and Rabbi Yose bar Dumaskit are each individually subject to challenge — as the *gemara* demonstrates, showing how each could be explained by natural means. Shmuel's proof is not subject to the same challenge, precisely because it depends on reading the verse to record something knowable only through divine access.

### Never Cease

The *gemara* closes with two final proofs for *ruach hakodesh* in the *megillah*. Rav Yosef cites the verse: *vimei haPurim ha-eleh lo ya'avru mi-toch haYehudim* — these days of Purim will never cease from among the Jews. How could the author assert with certainty that the celebration would endure forever? Only prophetic, divinely inspired knowledge could make such a claim. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak adds the parallel phrase: *vezichram lo yasuf mizaram* — and their memory will not cease from their descendants. The confident assertion of eternal perpetuity is itself evidence that the *megillah* was composed under divine inspiration.

The *gemara*'s final position thus preserves a distinction that is genuinely subtle: Megillat Esther was written with *ruach hakodesh* — this is established by multiple proofs, with Shmuel's being the strongest. Yet divine inspiration, while necessary, is not sufficient for canonization. In Shmuel's view, the *megillah* functions as a *mitzvah* object — it must be written, it must be read — without belonging to the formal canon of *Tanakh*. Whether this ultimately reflects the *halacha* is another matter, as the Tannaitic tradition cited earlier does include Esther among the books that render the hands impure. The fascinating historical footnote is that among all the books of *Tanakh*, only Megillat Esther is absent from the Dead Sea Scrolls — a detail that invites reflection on the complexity of the canonization question across different Jewish communities in the Second Temple period.

---

---

# Megillah 11

## Psichas & Midrashic Mode

### Psicha Genre

The *daf* opens in the middle of a series of *psichas* — the homiletic openings that introduce midrashic exposition of *Megillat Esther*. Anyone who has learned *Midrash Rabbah* will recognize the genre immediately: when the *Midrash Rabbah* opens a *parasha*, it typically begins not with the *pasuk* at hand but with a seemingly unrelated verse from elsewhere in *Tanakh* — often an obscure verse from *Nach* — and then finds a way to weave it into the story being expounded. That is precisely the mode at work here. The *Gemara* has been proceeding essentially as a *Midrash Rabbah* on *Megillat Esther*, moving through the *pesukim* of the *Megillah* one by one, and interspersing *Amoraic midrashim* throughout. The *psichas* belong to this same tradition: before the actual expository treatment of the opening verse begins, various Sages open from a different *pasuk* and find a way to tie it into the *Megillah*.

### Tanakh Unity

One of the primary effects achieved by this mode is a sense of the unity and interconnectedness of all of *Tanakh*. When a later verse in *Nevi'im* is shown to relate back to a story in the *Torah*, one can say that it is not surprising — the later text came after and could allude back. But what gets communicated in either direction is that it is all one great interconnected text.

### Esther & Earlier Texts

There is, however, a particular power in starting from *pesukim* in *Esther*, which stands at the very end of *Tanakh*, and relating them back to earlier *pesukim* — especially since so many of the *psichas* draw on verses from the *Torah* itself. The effect is to demonstrate that even this very late book was already foreshadowed, its ideas already present in earlier portions of scripture. The *Megillah* is thus anchored within the larger religious-historical arc of *Tanakh* as an integral part of that whole.

---

## Rava's Psicha

### Birbot Tzadikim

*Rava pasach lapitcha l'ha parshata* — Rava opened the beginning of the *parasha* of the *Megillah* from the following verse (*Mishlei* 29:2): *birbot tzadikim yismach ha'am, uvimshol rasha ye'aneich am* — "with the increase of the righteous the nation will rejoice; with the dominion of the wicked the people will moan."

### Mordechai vs Haman

The application is immediate. *Birbot tzadikim yismach ha'am* — this refers to Mordechai and Esther, as it is written: *v'ha'ir Shushan tzahala v'sameicha* — the city of Shushan was joyous and rejoicing. *Uvimshol rasha ye'aneich am* — this refers to Haman, as it is written: *v'ha'ir Shushan navocha* — the city of Shushan was bewildered and distraught. The contrast between the joy of the city under righteous leadership and its distress under wicked oppression maps precisely onto the trajectory of the Purim story.

---

## Rav Masna's Psicha

### God's Closeness

*Rav Masna amar meihacha* — Rav Masna would open from the verse in *Devarim* (4:7): *ki mi goy gadol asher lo elohim kerovim eilav k'Hashem elokeinu bechol koreinu eilav* — "for what great nation has a God as close to it as Hashem our God is whenever we call out to Him?" This is a striking choice: the verse expresses confidence in God's closeness, yet the story of Purim is defined by the sensation of God's absence — His name does not appear, and the people face imminent annihilation. Yet viewed in retrospect, even the story of Purim demonstrates that *bechol koreinu eilav* — at the time when God felt absent, when they called out, God was there for them.

---

## Rav Ashi's Psicha

### Nes Galui vs Hester

*Rav Ashi amar meihacha* — Rav Ashi opens from *Devarim* (4:34): *o hanissah elohim lavo lakachat lo goy mikerev goy bemasos uv'otot uv'moftim uv'milchama... kechol asher asah Hashem elokeichem lachem bemitzrayim l'einecha* — "Has God ever attempted to take for Himself a nation from the midst of another nation, with trials, signs, wonders, and war... like all that Hashem your God did for you in Egypt before your eyes?" This is quite fascinating: the verse is drawn from the context of *Yetziat Mitzrayim*, where the miracle was a *nes galui* — openly revealed, God's presence unmistakable to all. Yet Rav Ashi applies it to Purim, a period defined by *hester panim* — divine concealment. The point is that even in a time when it seemed as though it was not going to happen, it happened nonetheless: the same type of thing occurred.

### Jewish Distinctiveness

One also wonders whether there is a further hint embedded in the phrase *lavo lakachat lo goy mikerev goy* — taking a nation from the midst of another nation. The whole *Megillah* is deeply concerned with the degree of assimilation that had occurred; the people had become so thoroughly integrated into Persian society that they risked losing their distinctiveness entirely. It was only the pressure of Achashverosh's oppression — and ultimately the events of Purim — that caused them to crystallize their identity once again. There are *midrashim* that describe how thoroughly the people had been absorbed, and the Purim story thus becomes a moment of being separated out and restored to distinctiveness — *lavo lakachat lo goy mikerev goy*.

---

## Peshat of Vayehi

### Vayehi Woe

Having completed the *psichas*, the *Gemara* now turns to the *pasuk*-by-*pasuk* analysis of the *Megillah* itself. *Amar Rav: vayehi — vay vehi* — the word *vayehi* carries within it the cry of woe: *vay*. "In the days of Achashverosh" is an expression of mourning. And this, says Rav, is the fulfillment of the verse in *Devarim* (28:68): *v'hismakartem sham l'oyvecha la'avadim v'lishfachos v'ein koneh* — "you will be sold to your enemies as slaves and maidservants, and there will be no buyer."

### Rashi: No Buyers

The question is: where precisely does Rav see the fulfillment of that verse? Rashi explains: *ma shekasuv baTorah v'ein koneh gazar Haman shelo yihiyeh adam meshabed mehem l'eved* — Haman decreed that no one should enslave the Jews even as bondsmen. The tragedy was that the Jews had no means and needed to sell themselves into servitude, yet no one would purchase them.

### Haman's Money

An alternative reading is suggested by the verse in *Esther* itself, where Esther says: *v'ilu la'avadim v'lishfachos nimkarnu hecherashti* — had we merely been sold as slaves and maidservants, I would have held my peace. The verse *v'hismakartem... v'ein koneh* resonates with this, and may also allude to the episode where Haman offers to pay the king for the right to destroy the Jews and Achashverosh responds *hakesef nasun lach* — keep the money. There, the Jews are not being sold into servitude but into annihilation, and not even the money is accepted. Either way, the echoes of *v'hismakartem... v'ein koneh* reverberate throughout the *Megillah*.

---

## Shmuel's Lo Ma'astim

### Yevanim Period

*U'Shmuel amar: lo me'astim velo ge'altim lechalosam* — Shmuel opens with the verse in *Vayikra* (26:44). *Lo me'astim bimei Yevanim* — I did not despise them in the time of the Greeks, at the time of the Chanukah story. It appeared as though they were being abandoned, yet in the end there was victory.

### Nevuchadnezzar

*Velo ge'altim bimei Nevuchadnezzar* — in the time of Nevuchadnezzar, the *Beit HaMikdash* was destroyed and it seemed as though all was lost, yet they were not forgotten.

### Haman's Threat

*Lechalosam bimei Haman* — to destroy them utterly in the time of Haman. The threat of complete annihilation hung over the entire people, yet it did not come to pass.

### Persians & Messiah

*Lehafer brisi itam bimei Parsiyim* — to abrogate My covenant with them in the time of the Persians. The specific event referred to here is not entirely clear, and it is worth noting a textual observation raised in this connection: the *Avnei Nezer* argues that the original text of this passage referred not to Nevuchadnezzar but to *Aspasyanos* — that is, Vespasian — and that the reference was altered to avoid offending the Romans. This is significant because later in this same passage *bimei Parsiyim* appears to refer clearly to the Roman period as well, where the *Gemara* will identify God's representatives as the house of Rebbe and the sages of the generations — clearly not a Persian-era institution. The *girsa* is thus likely *Romiyim* in that instance.

*Ki Ani Hashem Elokeihem bimei Gog U'Magog* — the full expression of "I am Hashem their God" is reserved for the messianic era. Until then God has not abandoned them nor permitted their destruction, but the complete revelation of *ki Ani Hashem Elokeihem* will come only in the future, in the time of *Gog U'Magog*.

---

## Tannaitic Baraita

### Kasdim Leaders

*Tanu Rabbanan* — a *baraisa* now presents a parallel formulation. *Lo me'astim bimei Kasdim* — I did not despise them in the time of the Babylonians, *she'emadeti lahem Daniel Chananyah Mishael v'Azaryah* — for I raised up for them Daniel, Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah, who stood up for God and for the religion and did not flinch even before the furnace.

### Yevanim Leaders

*Velo ge'altim bimei Yevanim* — in the time of the Greeks, I raised up Shimon HaTzaddik, *v'Chashmonai u'vanav u'Mattisyahu Kohen Gadol* — the Chashmonayim and Mattisyahu the Kohen Gadol as God's representatives in that period.

### Haman Leaders

*Velo chalosam bimei Haman* — I did not let them be destroyed in the time of Haman, *she'he'emadti lahem Mordechai v'Esther* — for I raised up Mordechai and Esther.

### Parsiyim Sages

*Lehafer briti itam bimei Parsiyim* — in the time of the Persians, *she'he'emadti lahem shel Beis Rebbe v'chachmei dorot* — I raised up for them the house of Rebbe and the sages of the generations. As already noted, this clearly does not refer to the Persian period in the historical sense; the original *girsa* was almost certainly *Romiyim*, referring to the Roman period, and the text was emended to avoid censure.

### Messianic Future

*Ki Ani Hashem Elokeihem l'asid lavo* — in the future to come, *she'ein kol umah v'lashon yecholim lishlot bahem* — no nation or tongue will ever again have dominion over them. Not only will God not permit their destruction, but they will be fully recognized as God's people, no longer subjugated under foreign nations.

It is worth pausing to observe that one might look at this passage simply as another *psicha* — an introductory verse from *Vayikra* used to open the *Megillah*. But one participant in the discussion rightly noted that there is something more going on: the word *bimei* — "in the days of" — is itself being expounded. Shmuel is not merely offering an introductory verse; he is observing that history unfolds in *yamim*, in named epochs — the *yamei Yevanim*, the *yamei Parsiyim*, the *yamei Achashverosh* — and that God intervenes in each such epoch to save the people. This frames history as a sequence of distinct periods of divine engagement, which feels different from the model in which enemy nations are simply mobilized as instruments of God's plan.

---

## Rabbi Levi Psicha

### Amalek Connection

*Rabbi Levi amar meihacha* — Rabbi Levi would open with the verse in *Bamidbar*: *v'im lo torishu et yoshvei ha'aretz v'hayu litzninim b'tzideichem* — "if you do not drive out the inhabitants of the land, they will be thorns in your side." Rashi explains: *af elu ne'enshu al chamat Shaul al Amalek* — the people of that generation were punished on account of Saul's failure to destroy Amalek. The Purim story is thus the continuation and consequence of that earlier failure; Haman the Agagite descends from Amalek, and the catastrophe that nearly befell Israel traces back to the incomplete fulfillment of that command.

---

## Rhetorical Effect

### Oral Tradition

The mode of *psicha* was clearly an oral one. When a *darshan* opened with a puzzling or obscure verse — say, a verse from *Mishlei* nobody had heard of — the audience's interest was immediately engaged: how is he going to get from here to there? The suspense of watching the connection unfold is itself part of the pedagogical effect. This is the general mode of *Midrash Rabbah*: one opens a *parasha* in *Bereishis* or *Bamidbar*, and the *midrash* begins with some verse from *Tehillim* or *Mishlei* that seems entirely unrelated, and only gradually does the connection emerge.

### Structural Parallels

This same structure appears throughout classical midrashic literature. *Pesikta de-Rav Kahana*, for instance — a collection of homilies organized around the *Yamim Tovim* — employs *psichas* throughout: each homily opens with a verse from elsewhere and works its way toward the *pasuk* of the day. The *psichas* examined here in the *Gemara* belong to precisely this tradition.

---

## Divine Plan Debate

### Enemy Agency

A substantive question arises from this material: are the enemies of Israel presented as independent agents pursuing their own malevolent purposes, or as instruments consciously deployed within God's providential plan? The more the text emphasizes divine orchestration of events — as in *Shemot*, where God explicitly hardens Pharaoh's heart — the more it raises the difficult question of how the same agent can then be punished for doing what God caused him to do. The *rishonim* grapple with this by noting that even if the broad outlines of a divine plan are foreordained, no individual is compelled to volunteer for the role of oppressor. One's personal free choice remains real even within a framework of divine providence.

In the *Megillah*, the enemies are not described as acting under divine compulsion. The text prefers to present them as exercising their own malicious agency — and then records God's intervention to save the people. This is in fact the broader biblical pattern: in *Shoftim*, the Israelites sin, God sends a scourge in the form of another nation, and then sends a savior. We are not focused on the punishment of the other nation in those narratives. It is in *Yeshayah*, *Amos*, and *Hoshea* that the accounting of the nations for their crimes comes to the fore.

### Epochs & Bimei

As noted above, what Shmuel's formulation achieves — whether read as a *psicha* or as a *drashah* on the word *bimei* — is the framing of history in terms of distinct epochs. Rather than presenting individual enemies as agents or instruments, the *Gemara* speaks of the *yamei Yevanim*, the *yamei Haman*, the *yamei Parsiyim*: large periods of history during which forces of oppression dominate and God chooses a moment to intervene. This feels different, as one listener observed, from the model in which God actively mobilizes the nations. It feels like the flow of human history into which God steps at critical junctures.

---

## Achashverosh Character

### Achiv Shel Rav

*Amar Rav: achiv shel rosh uven gilo shel rosh.* Achashverosh is the brother of a leader, cut from the same cloth as a leader. Who is the *rosh*? *Achiv shel Nevuchadnezzar HaRasha shenikra rosh* — the brother of Nevuchadnezzar the Wicked, who is called "the head," as it says: *ant hu reisha di dehava* — "you are the golden head," in the famous dream of *Sefer Daniel* in which Nevuchadnezzar's statue has a head of gold.

### Parallel Actions

What does it mean to be cut from the same cloth? The parallel actions are spelled out: Nevuchadnezzar killed Jews; Achashverosh sought to kill Jews. Nevuchadnezzar destroyed the *Beit HaMikdash*; Achashverosh sought to destroy it — or at minimum, sought to prevent its rebuilding.

### Rashi Dating

Rashi explains *bikesh lachriv*: *yesod sheyasad Zerubavel b'Beit HaMikdash biyemei Koresh lifnei Achashverosh kemo sheamar b'Sefer Ezra* — the foundation that Zerubavel had already laid for the *Beit HaMikdash* during the days of Koresh, before Achashverosh. This places Achashverosh after the initial phase of rebuilding had already begun under Koresh, such that his edict — presumably encompassing the destruction of what had been built — amounted to a bid to destroy the foundation of the *Beit HaMikdash*. The *Gemara* then cites the verse from *Ezra*: *uvelmalchut Achashverosh bitchilat malchuto katvu sitnah al yoshvei Yehudah v'Yerushalayim* — in the kingdom of Achashverosh, at the beginning of his reign, they wrote a hostile edict against those dwelling in Judah and Jerusalem. Rashi explains that *sitnah* here refers to the prohibition against continuing to build. So even setting aside the Purim story entirely, the verse in *Ezra* already locates Achashverosh as an enemy of the rebuilding of the *Beit HaMikdash*.

---

## Amoraic Opinions

### Rabbi Yochanan

*Rabbi Yochanan amar: kol shezichro amar ach l'rosho* — anyone who mentions Achashverosh says "woe to their head." They get a headache. He was, in Rabbi Yochanan's view, simply a bad or foolish king whose very name evokes suffering — and not only for the Jews.

### Rabbi Chanina

*Rabbi Chanina amar: shekol na'asu rashim b'yamav* — he made everyone poor. *Shene'emar: vayaseim hamelech Achashverosh mas* — as it says, the king Achashverosh imposed a tax. Raising taxes was political suicide even then, and Achashverosh is remembered for having impoverished not only the Jews but everyone.

### Hu Achashverosh

*Hu Achashverosh* — what does the word *hu* add? *Hu b'rishato mitechilato ve'ad sofo* — he was unchanging in his wickedness from beginning to end. This is the trigger for a broader *drashah* on the word *hu* wherever it appears in *Tanakh*.

---

## Hu Derasha

### Wicked Examples

*Hu Eisav avi Edom* — this Eisav, referenced in *Bereishit*, was *hu b'rishato mitechilato ve'ad sofo* — wicked from beginning to end. *Hu Datan va'Aviram b'nei Eliav* — in a verse in *Bamidbar*, *hein b'rishatan mitechilatam ve'ad sofam* — they were wicked from beginning to end.

### Righteous vs Wicked

*Hu hamelech Achaz* — King Achaz, *hu b'rishato mitechilato ve'ad sofo* — always a wicked king. On the other side: *Avraham hu Avraham*, a verse in *Divrei HaYamim* that most have not encountered — *hu b'tzidkato mitechilato ve'ad sofo* — he was always righteous.

### Aaron & Moses

*Hu Aharon u'Moshe* — in a verse in *Shemot*, *hein b'tzidkatam mitechilatam ve'ad sofam* — they were righteous from beginning to end.

### David's Humility

*Ve'Dovid hu hakatan* — he was the small one among the sons of Yishai. *Hu b'katnuso mitechilato ve'ad sofo.* But this requires explanation: he was not always small — he became a king. The *Gemara* explains: *kesheim sheb'katnuso hiktin atzmo l'mi shegadol mimenu b'Torah* — just as in his youth he knew how to be deferential and make himself small before one greater than him in *Torah*, *kach b'malchuto hiktin atzmo l'mi shegadol mimenu b'chochmah* — so too in his kingship he showed deference to those wiser than he. This is an even more impressive quality than deference in *Torah* matters: a king might reasonably defer to a greater *talmid chacham* in areas of *halacha*. But *chochmah* — judgment, wisdom, practical knowledge — is ostensibly the king's own domain. That even there David showed proper deference is the mark of genuine *katnuto*, genuine smallness.

---

## Self-Made King

### Self-Made Debate

*Amar Rav: shemalach mei'atzmo* — Achashverosh was not born to the throne but rose from among the commoners; he was a self-appointed king. *Amri lei l'shvach ve'amri lei l'gnai* — some say this is praiseworthy and some say it is blameworthy. The praiseworthy reading: *d'lo hava inish dechashiv l'malka k'vatei* — nobody else was as suited to be king; he was taken from the commoners because he was the most fitting. The blameworthy reading: *d'lo hava chazi l'malchut u'mamon yaseirah hu d'yahiv kamei* — he was not actually fit for kingship but gave extra money, meaning he bought his way in, just as — the *Gemara* evokes — the office of *Kohen Gadol* could be purchased in later periods.

---

## Hodu V'ad Kush

### Geographic Extent

*Hamoleich meiHodu ve'ad Kush* — he ruled from Hodu to Kush. *Rav u'Shmuel*: one says *Hodu besof olam veKush besof olam* — Hodu and Kush are at opposite ends of the inhabited world, and he ruled the entire span between them. The other says *Hodu veKush gabei hadadi havu kaimei* — Hodu and Kush were right next to one another. In that case, what is the point?

### Universal Rule

If they are adjacent, then the verse is saying: *kesheim shemalach al Hodu veKush kach malach misof ha'olam ve'ad sofo* — just as he had control over these two neighboring countries, so too he had control over the entire world. Either reading arrives at the same conclusion: Achashverosh ruled over the entire civilized world of his era.

---

## Shlomo Comparison

### Same Methodology

*Kayotzei badavar atah omer* — a parallel case applies the same debate to Shlomo's domain, as described in *Melachim* (1 Kings 5:4): *ki hu rodeh bechol ever hanahar mitafsach ve'ad Azah* — he had dominion over the entire Trans-Jordan from Tafsach to Gaza. Once again *Rav u'Shmuel* dispute: one says Tafsach is at one end of the world and Gaza at the other, so he ruled the entire inhabited world; the other says they are right next to each other, and by the same logic as above — *kesheim shemalach al Tafsach ve'al Azah kach malach al kol ha'olam kulo* — he ruled over the whole world. The identical methodology is applied in both cases.

---

## 127 Provinces

### Province Growth

*Sheva ve'esrim u'meah medinah* — 127 provinces. *Amar Rav Chisda: betchilah malach al sheva, ulevasof malach al esrim, ulevasof malach al meah* — he started with seven, then expanded to twenty, then to a hundred. This is a *drashah* derived from the way the verse counts: not simply "127" but "seven and twenty and a hundred" — as is the standard biblical enumeration of large numbers.

### Derasha Objection

The *Gemara* immediately objects: *ela me'ata — u'shenei chayei Amram sheva u'shloshim u'meah shanah* — if this is the methodology, what will you do with the verse that says the life of Amram was "seven and thirty and a hundred years"?
