Will you *darshan* that he experienced three separate stages of life corresponding to those numbers?

### Superfluous Text

The *Gemara* responds: *shani hacha dekra yeseirah hu* — here the *drashah* is justified because the verse is superfluous. *Michdi kesiv meiHodu ve'ad Kush* — the verse has already told us the domain ran from Hodu to Kush, which implies the entire inhabited world. *Vesheva ve'esrim u'meah medinah lamah li* — why then does it need to specify 127 provinces? Since the information is redundant, it must be there to teach something additional, namely the *drashah* of how the kingdom was built up in stages. By contrast, the years of Amram's life carry no such redundancy; *shema minah ledrashah* applies only where the enumeration is otherwise superfluous.

---

## Three Rulers

### The Three Kings

Expanding upon Achashverosh's universal dominion, the *Gemara* states: *shelosha malchu bikipah* — three ruled under the dome of the inhabited world. These are Achav, Achashverosh, and Nevuchadnezzar. Tosafot immediately raises the obvious question: what about Alexander the Great? The answer is that the list is limited to those whose dominion is recorded in *Tanakh*: *lo havu hashivi ella hanehu de-ketiv behu hedyot* — only those about whom Scripture records it. Alexander came after the biblical period and was therefore not included.

### Achav Example

The proof for Achav: when Eliyahu stopped the rain and Achav sought him, the text says — *chai Hashem elokecha im yesh goy u'mamlacha asher lo shalach adoni sham levakeshcha v'hishbiya et ha-goy ve'et ha-mamlacha* — my master sent to every nation and kingdom to seek you, and he had them take an oath. If Achav did not have power over these foreign nations, how could he compel them to take such an oath? This demonstrates that his authority extended over the entire civilized world.

### Nevuchadnezzar

The proof for Nevuchadnezzar comes from the verse in *Yirmeyahu*: *v'haya ha-goy veha-mamlacha asher lo yitnu et tzavaram o asher lo ya'avdu oto et Nevuchadnezzar melech Bavel* — every nation and kingdom that does not put its neck in the yoke of the king of Babylon... The universal submission demanded makes clear his total dominion.

### Achashverosh

For Achashverosh: *ha de-amran* — as we have already stated, *meiHodu ve'ad Kush, misof ha-olam ve'ad sof ha-olam* — from Hodu to Kush, spanning the entire inhabited world.

---

## Shlomo Excluded

### Shlomo's End

The *Gemara* asks: are there no others? And then runs through the *siman* *shin-samech-dalet-chaf*: Shlomo, Sancheriv, Daryavesh, Koresh. First: *veha ika Shlomo*? We just saw from the verse in *Melachim* that he ruled from Tafsach to Gaza, covering the whole world. The *Gemara* responds: *lo salik malchutei* — his kingship did not conclude properly. There is the famous tradition that Shlomo went through a period in which he lost his throne and was reduced to commoner status.

### Return to Kingship

The *Gemara* then notes: *hani'cha le'man de'amar melech ve'hedyot* — this works well according to the view that he was king, then a commoner, and that was the end. *Ela le'man de'amar melech ve'hedyot u'melech* — but according to the view that after his period as a commoner he once again became king, what can one say?

### Supernal Rule

The *Gemara* responds: *Shlomo milta achrita hava bei* — Shlomo was not excluded because his kingship was insufficient but because he was in an entirely different category. *De'malach a'elyonim ve'atachtonim* — he had dominion not only over the lower world but over the supernal realms as well, over the *shedim* and other metaphysical forces, *shene'emar va'yeshev Shlomo al kisse Hashem* — as it says, "Shlomo sat on the throne of God." He was therefore in a category apart, transcending ordinary earthly kingship altogether.

---

## Other Kings Objected

### Sancheriv Limited

*Veha ika Sancheriv*? The verse records him boasting — *mi bechol elohei ha'aratzot ha'eleh asher hitzilu et artzam miyadi* — who among all the gods of these lands has saved their land from me? Does that not demonstrate universal dominion? The *Gemara* responds: *ha'ika Yerushalayim de'la kavsha* — there remains Jerusalem, which he did not conquer. His dominion was incomplete.

### Daryavesh 120

*Veha ika Daryavesh*? If he wrote to all nations — *di dayarin bechol ar'a* — does that not imply universal dominion? The *Gemara* responds: *ha'ika sheva de'la malich aleihu* — he only ruled 120 provinces, not 127. *De'ketiv shepar kodam Daryavesh ve'hakim al malchuta le'achashdarpanaya me'ah ve'esrin* — as it is written, Daryavesh placed over his kingdom 120 satraps. He was therefore short of the full count.

### Koresh Unreliable

*Veha ika Koresh*? He himself proclaimed: *kol mamlechot ha'aretz natan li Hashem* — all the kingdoms of the earth God has given me. The *Gemara* dismisses this: he is merely praising himself. You cannot rely on a ruler's own rhetoric about his dominion. As anyone familiar with the royal stelae of the ancient world knows, kings routinely described themselves as rulers of the entire world; that self-description carries no evidentiary weight.

---

## Chronological Intro

### Timing Question

*Bayamim hahem keshevet hamelech Achashverosh* — in those days, when King Achashverosh was settled on his royal throne. But then the very next verse says *bishnat shalosh lemalcho* — in the third year of his reign, he made a feast. Was the feast at the beginning of his reign or only in his third year?

### Rava's Solution

*Amar Rava: mai keshevet* — what does *keshevet* mean? *Le'achar shenit'yashva da'ato* — after his mind became settled, after he felt confident. He wanted to make the feast from the start, but *keshevet* indicates that he had to wait three years until he felt settled and secure, and only then did he hold the celebration.

### 70-Year Connection

Why did he need three years to feel confident? This is connected to the calculations around the 70-year prophecy. As the *Gemara* now proceeds to explain, Achashverosh — like Belshatzar before him — was tracking the prophecy of redemption and waiting to confirm that it had not been fulfilled. It took him three years from the beginning of his reign to complete his reckoning and convince himself that the prophecy had failed.

---

## Belshatzar's Math

### Two Prophecies

*Belshatzar chashav veta'ah* — Belshatzar did the calculation and made a mistake. The background is that there are two prophecies in *Yirmeyahu* each speaking of 70 years: *ki lefi melot leVavel shiv'im shanah efkod etchem* — when it has been fulfilled for Bavel 70 years, I will remember you and bring you back; and *limlot lechorvot Yerushalayim shiv'im shanah* — when it is fulfilled for the desolation of Jerusalem 70 years. These two formulations — one measuring from the Babylonian dominion, one from the destruction of Jerusalem — are not necessarily identical in their starting point, and it is that ambiguity that these kings exploited.

### Belshatzar's Sum

Belshatzar's computation: *chashav arba'in vachamesh deNevuchadnezzar* — he counted 45 years of Nevuchadnezzar. He understood *leVavel* to mean from when Nevuchadnezzar became king of Babylon. *Ve'esrin u'tlat de'Evil Merodach* — 23 years of Evil Merodach the successor. That brings the total to 68. *Ve'tartei didei* — and two of his own years as king. *Hashiv'im* — that made 70.

### False Confidence

Belshatzar concluded: it has been 70 years and the people have not been redeemed; the prophecy has failed. *Amar hashta vadai tu lo mifarki* — now they are certainly not going to be redeemed. Acting on this false confidence, *afik manei devei mikdasha ve'ishtamesh behu* — he took out the vessels of the *Beit HaMikdash* and used them. That night, as Daniel reports to him: *T'amrei shmaya hitromamta v'le'manaya d'veitei hei'tayu kadamach* — you have elevated yourself against the King of Heaven and brought His vessels before you. *Beih b'leilya ktil Belshatzar malka Kasdaya* — that very night Belshatzar king of the Chaldeans was killed.

---

## Belshatzar Sources

### Year 1-2

How does the *Gemara* arrive at 45 years for Nevuchadnezzar? This requires reconciling several verses that speak of different years in connection with the various exiles. *Tana v'shana: kavash shanah zeh, shniyah kivash Yehoyakim* — in the first year of his dominion he conquered Nineveh; in the second year he conquered Yehoyakim. This establishes that the exile of *Galut Yehoyakim* began in Nevuchadnezzar's second year, which becomes the baseline for some of the subsequent counting.

### Dating Systems

*Galu b'sheva galu b'shmoneh galu b'shmoneh esreh galu b'tishah esreh* — the *Gemara* notes that various verses speak of exile occurring in the seventh year, the eighth year, the eighteenth year, and the nineteenth year of Nevuchadnezzar. The apparent contradictions are reconciled as follows: *galu b'sheva l'kivush Yehoyakim — galut Yehoyachin* — the exile in the seventh year refers to the exile of Yehoyachin, counting from the conquest of Yehoyakim, which began in Nevuchadnezzar's second year. Thus the seventh year from *Galut Yehoyakim* is the eighth year of Nevuchadnezzar's reign — hence some verses say seven and some say eight, depending on which starting point is used.

### Exiles Timeline

Similarly, *galut Tzidkiyahu* — the final exile — occurred in the nineteenth year of Nevuchadnezzar counting from his first year as king, but the eighteenth year counting from the beginning of the exile process. The two sets of numbers — 7 and 8, 18 and 19 — each reflect a different counting convention, and both are attested in *Tanakh*. Notably, the *Gemara* observes that this chronology is consistent with secular historical sources as well.

The calculation that follows: *Galut Yehoyachin* in year 8 of Nevuchadnezzar, plus 37 years until Evil Merodach released him — as it is written in *Melachim II* (25:27-29): *vayhi bishloshim v'sheva shanah l'galut Yehoyachin melech Yehudah... nasa Evil Merodach melech Bavel bishnat malchuto et rosh Yehoyachin* — in the 37th year of Yehoyachin's exile, Evil Merodach raised up Yehoyachin and released him from prison. 8 plus 37 equals 45: *harei arba'im v'chamish* — that is Nevuchadnezzar's 45 years. *Ve'esrim v'tlata de'Evil Merodach* — 23 years of Evil Merodach (a received tradition), bringing the total to 68. *Ve'tartei didei* — and two years of Belshatzar: *ha shiv'im* — that is the 70.

---

## Achashverosh's Sin

### Keilim Shonim

The *Gemara* now explains why the phrase in the *Megillah* — *v'cheilim mikeilim shonim* — carries a distinctive *trop* when chanted. The "vessels of different sorts" are the desecrated vessels of the *Beit HaMikdash*, which Achashverosh used at his feast. This is a direct repetition of Belshatzar's sin.

### Satan's Role

*Ba Satan v'rikeid beineihem* — Satan came and danced amongst the celebrants. The result of this intervention was the chaos that led to Vashti's execution — itself the catalyst for everything that followed in the Purim story.

### Different Fates

The outcomes, however, differed starkly. Belshatzar was killed that very night — *beih b'leilya ktil* — executed by God for his desecration. Achashverosh, by contrast, was not immediately punished in kind. His downfall came indirectly, through the reversal of Haman's decree and the death of Vashti, rather than through his own execution. The disproportion may be explained by the fact that Achashverosh was not the nation that had actually destroyed the *Beit HaMikdash* — that was Nevuchadnezzar's Babylon. The gravity of the sin is therefore on a different scale.

---

## Achashverosh's Error

### Different Method

Having shown Belshatzar's miscalculation, the *Gemara* now turns to Achashverosh's. Achashverosh claimed he would not repeat Belshatzar's error. *Mi ksiv l'malchut Bavel? L'Bavel ksiv* — the verse does not say 70 years from the beginning of the kingdom of Babylon; it says 70 years *l'Vavel*, which Achashverosh understood to mean from the exile of Babylon — specifically, from *Galut Yehoyachin*.

### Achashverosh Sum

Achashverosh reasoned: *kama b'tziran? Tmanya* — how many years were still lacking from Belshatzar's count? Eight more years were needed beyond Belshatzar's 70. *Chashiv ayu chilufayu*: one year of Belshatzar (since the event occurred in Belshatzar's third year, not his second, there was one additional year), five years for the combined reigns of Daryavesh and Koresh, and two years of his own reign. One plus five plus two equals eight — *hashiv'im* — seventy years from *Galut Yehoyachin*. The prophecy, by Achashverosh's reckoning, had just expired unfulfilled.

### Repeated Sin

*Kivan d'chazi d'malo shiv'in v'lo ifruk* — when he saw that 70 years had passed and the people had not been redeemed, *amar hashta vadai shuv lo mifarki* — now they certainly will not be redeemed. And like Belshatzar, *afik manei d'Beit HaMikdash ve'ishtamesh behu* — he took out the vessels of the *Beit HaMikdash* and used them, which is the sin of *keilim mikeilim shonim* in the *Megillah*.

---

## Evil Merodach 37 Years

### Yehoyachin Release

The proof text that anchors Nevuchadnezzar's 45-year count is the verse in *Melachim II* (25:27-29): *vayhi bishloshim v'sheva shanah l'galut Yehoyachin melech Yehudah b'shneim asar chodesh b'esrim v'chamishah lachodesh nasa Evil Merodach melech Bavel bishnat malchuto et rosh Yehoyachin melech Yehudah* — in the 37th year of Yehoyachin's exile, Evil Merodach king of Babylon, in his first regnal year, raised up Yehoyachin. *Vayotze oto mibeit hakela* — he took him out of the dungeon, after Yehoyachin had been imprisoned for 37 years.

### 45-Year Sum

*Galut Yehoyachin* occurred in the eighth year of Nevuchadnezzar. Adding 37 years brings the total to year 45 of Nevuchadnezzar — which is precisely when Evil Merodach became king. *Tanya: harei arba'im v'chamish* — the *baraisa* confirms: that is 45 years.

### Historical Alignment

The *Gemara* notes that this chronology is consistent with secular historical records regarding the reign of Evil Merodach (Amel-Marduk), lending additional confirmation to the calculation.

---

## Achashverosh's Error (II)

### Future Refutation

The *Gemara* has now established how Achashverosh arrived at his 70-year calculation. Tomorrow's study will address why that calculation was itself incorrect — that is, why Achashverosh's math, like Belshatzar's before him, was ultimately mistaken and his confident conclusion that the prophecy had failed was unfounded.

---

---

# Megillah 12

## Seventy-Year Prophecy

### Belshazzar & Vessels

The Gemara on 12 picks up three lines from the bottom of 11b, in the midst of a sustained comparison between Achashverosh and Belshazzar. Both figures shared the same sin: they removed the vessels of the *Beis Hamikdash* and put them to profane use. This parallel is not merely historical color — it is the exegetical foundation for the custom of reading *keilim mikeilim shonim* with a distinctive *trop*, a practice the Gemara will anchor to the precise wording of that verse. The broader frame is Achashverosh's sense of relief: with *nisyashva da'ato*, his mind settled, he became convinced that the seventy-year prophecy of redemption would not be fulfilled, and so he felt emboldened to celebrate.

### Seventy-Year Math

To understand Achashverosh's confidence, the Gemara reconstructs the arithmetic of the seventy-year prophecy as he understood it. One verse in *Yirmiyahu* speaks of seventy years *livavel* — to Babylon — while a verse in *Daniel* speaks of seventy years to the destruction of Jerusalem. Taking the first reckoning: Nevuchadnezzar reigned for forty-five years, Evil Merodach for twenty-three, and in Belshazzar's third year the total reached seventy. It was precisely at that moment that Belshazzar removed the *Beis Hamikdash* vessels — and was slain that very night.

Achashverosh, however, believed Belshazzar had miscounted. In his view, the seventy years should have been reckoned not from the beginning of Nevuchadnezzar's reign but from *Galus Yechonyah*, the beginning of the Babylonian exile proper — which added eight more years to the starting point. The Gemara then accounts for additional time: one more year remaining of Belshazzar's reign, five years of *Daryavesh* and Koresh combined, and two years of Achashverosh's own reign — all of which brought the total to seventy years from *Galus Yechonyah* by Achashverosh's third year. That is when he took out the vessels of the *Beis Hamikdash*.

### Achashverosh's Error

The Gemara immediately challenges this: *ve'ha shapir chashiv* — he seems to have done the math correctly. But the Gemara responds: *ihu nami miet'ei* — he also made a mistake. The verse in *Daniel* does not say seventy years from *Bavel* but seventy years *lacharvos Yerushalayim* — to the destruction of Jerusalem, which corresponds to *Galus Tzidkiyahu*, occurring in Nevuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. Since *Galus Yechonyah* occurred in Nevuchadnezzar's eighth year, the difference between the two starting points is eleven years. Achashverosh should therefore have waited not until his third year but until his fourteenth. Yet in his fourteenth year — the very year we know from the *Megillah* — he was still king, the Jews had not returned to *Eretz Yisrael*, and the *Beis Hamikdash* had not been rebuilt. So even the latest possible reckoning yields no completed redemption at that point.

This deepens the difficulty: *sof sof kama batziran chasrei* — in the end, even counting from the destruction of Jerusalem, you arrive only at Achashverosh's fourteenth year, when construction had already been halted. A verse in *Ezra* records the cessation explicitly: *be'adayin batilas avidas beis Elaha di b'Yerushalem* — at that time the work on the house of God in Jerusalem was stopped. The rebuilding that had begun under Koresh had been reversed.

### Partial Years Solution

Rava resolves the problem: *shanim mekuta'os havu* — the years were not complete years. When the Gemara adds up forty-five years for Nevuchadnezzar and twenty-three for Evil Merodach, it implicitly assumes each reign consisted of full calendar years. But Nevuchadnezzar may have died partway through his forty-fifth year, and Evil Merodach may have begun partway through the first year of his reign — meaning these transitions involve double-counted partial years. By adding the reign numbers together as though they were complete, one loses a year or two. Belshazzar, therefore, had not actually reached the seventieth year when he celebrated; he was one year short.

A *Beraisa* confirms this: *v'yeser shana achas l'Belshazzar* — there was one additional year beyond what Belshazzar thought he had reached. When Daryavesh succeeded him, *v'amad Daryavesh v'hishlima* — Daryavesh completed that final year, bringing the count to a genuine seventy years from Babylon. That is when Koresh gave the Jews initial permission to begin rebuilding the *Beis Hamikdash*.

### Two Reckonings

The picture that emerges from Rava's analysis is of two distinct and valid prophecies with two distinct fulfillments. The first reckoning — seventy years from Babylon — was fulfilled in the time of Koresh: *le-pekidah b'alma*, a mere remembrance, the beginning of a process. Koresh issued the celebrated declaration — *koh amar Koresh melech Paras... ve-hu pakad alai livnot lo bayit bi-Yerushalayim* — but this was only a partial and ultimately reversed gesture. The second reckoning — seventy years from the destruction of Jerusalem — was fulfilled after Achashverosh, in the time of the second Daryavesh, who the Gemara elsewhere identifies as the son of Achashverosh and Esther. That is when the genuine rebuilding of the *Beis Hamikdash* commenced in earnest.

Achashverosh was therefore wrong on two counts. First, he double-counted the partial years and believed the seventy years from Babylon had concluded in his own third year, when in fact it concluded two years earlier in Koresh's time. Second, even had he counted correctly, that first reckoning pointed only to a partial redemption — the second prophecy, reckoned from the destruction of Jerusalem, pointed to the complete one, which would come only after his own reign had ended.

### Daniel's Investigation

Rava adds that even Daniel made mistakes in working through this chronological puzzle. The Gemara derives this from the verse: *bishnat achat lemalcho ani Daniel binnoti basefarim* — in the first year of his king, I Daniel investigated the books. The very fact that Daniel says *binnoti* — I investigated closely — implies, by the Gemara's logic, that he had previously erred and needed to re-examine the verses. *Miklal de-ta'ah* — by implication, he had made some mistake. The difficulty in harmonizing the two competing prophecies — *milo'at levavel* versus *lacharvos Yerushalayim* — was genuine enough to confuse even the greatest prophet of the generation.

### Koresh's Reversal

The Gemara confirms from the verse in *Ezra* that Koresh's permission to rebuild was indeed revoked. This reversal is the foundation for distinguishing the partial fulfillment under Koresh from the complete redemption that followed. Rava identifies Koresh's declaration as corresponding to *le-pekidah b'alma* — a slight, incomplete remembrance — because Koresh himself reversed his decree. The word *pakad* in the verse (*ve-hu pakad alai livnot*) is the same root as *pekidah*, deliberately chosen to signal that this was only a visitation, not a full redemption.

### Koresh vs. Messiah

From this context, the Gemara addresses the verse in *Yeshayahu*: *koh amar Hashem limeshicho le-Choresh* — thus says God to His anointed one, to Koresh. The question is direct: *ve-chi Koresh mashiach hava* — was Koresh really the *mashiach*? The Gemara rejects the straightforward reading. *Rashi* notes that a careful reading of the *trop* already distinguishes *meshicho* from *Koresh* syntactically. The Gemara's interpretation is that God is speaking to the *mashiach* about Koresh: *koh amar Hashem limeshicho... asher hachazakti bimino* — thus says God to His Messiah, concerning Koresh whom I strengthened. And the content of that address is a complaint: *kovel ani lecha al Koresh* — I have a grievance against Koresh to bring before you. God declared: *ani amarti hu yivneh beiti vekabeitz galiyosai* — I said he would build My house and gather My exiles. Yet Koresh said only *mi vachem mikol amo vaya'al* — whoever among you wishes may go up — issuing permission rather than actively rebuilding or gathering the exiles.

The passage thus draws a sharp distinction between the redemptive vision — which sounds unmistakably like the full *messianic* mandate of rebuilding the Temple and ingathering the exiles — and Koresh's limited, eventually reversed, decree. Koresh did not fail because he was wicked; the comparison to Chizkiyahu, who could have been the *mashiach* had he sung *shira* after *Sancheriv*, is apt. The point is that Koresh did not live up to the full potential of the role he had been given. And on that note, the analysis of the seventy-year prophecy closes — having situated the entire story of *Purim* within the larger arc of exile, anticipated redemption, and the as-yet-unfulfilled *geulah*.

---

## Media & Persia Alliance

### Medians/Persians Deal

Returning to the *Megillah*, the text lists *cheil Paras uMadai hapartamim* — the officers of Persia and Media. Elsewhere, a verse refers to *malchei Madai uParas* — the kings of Media and Persia. *Rashi* notes that this creates a question of which nation takes precedence in which role: is the reference to the army coming from Persia, or to governors coming from Media? Rava resolves it by describing a formal power-sharing arrangement. *Astinuyei astin behadadi* — the Medians and Persians made an agreement with one another: if the kings come from us, the governors of the provinces will come from you; and if the kings come from you, the governors will come from us. These were two sovereign powers who had unified their dominion and divided its offices between them.

### Priestly Garments

The Gemara turns to the verse *beharoso es osher kvod malchuso* — when he displayed the wealth and glory of his kingdom. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina teaches: *melamed shelavash bigdei kehuna* — this teaches that Achashverosh wore the *bigdei kehunah*, the priestly vestments of the *Beis Hamikdash*. The verse's language of *yekar tiferes gedulaso* — honor, glory, greatness — corresponds through the shared root *tiferes* to the verse about the *bigdei kehunah*: *lechavod uletiferes*, and *yekar* as the Aramaic equivalent of *kavod*. So the display of royal splendor was in fact an appropriation of the sacred vestments of the high priesthood, an act continuous with the removal of the *keilim*. These details are not merely discrete exegetical observations; together they sketch a portrait of a king who seeks to absorb the sanctity and prestige of the *Beis Hamikdash* into his own court — its vessels, its garments, its honor — even as the Temple itself lies in ruins.

### Wise or Foolish?

On the question of the hundred-and-eighty-day feast, Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Achashverosh's strategy was clever or foolish. The one who says *melech pike'ach hayah* — he was a wise king — argues that it was shrewd to invite the distant provinces first: those inhabitants are harder to control and must be won over early, while the people of one's own city can be cultivated later, whenever needed, since they remain accessible. The one who says *melech tipesh hayah* — he was a foolish king — argues the opposite: one should first solidify the home constituency, for if the distant provinces rebel, at least the local population will remain loyal. Without that solid base, rebellion from afar becomes existential.

---

## Jewish Guilt Question

### Why Haman's Threat

The Gemara pauses from the verse-by-verse reading to take up a theological question, framed as an exchange between Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and his students. The students asked: *mipnei mah nischayvu soneihem shel Yisrael she'be'oso hador kilah* — why were the Jews of that generation deserving of destruction? What did they do that warranted the *gezeiras Haman*?

### Assimilation Problem

The students offered their own answer first: *mipnei she'nehenu mi'seudaso shel oso rasha* — because they derived benefit from the feast of that wicked one, Achashverosh. The problem with their participation was either the assimilation it represented — eating non-*kosher* food, mixing freely in a pagan court — or a form of complicity in the political machinations of the king himself, given that the feast is attributed to *oso rasha*. While both dimensions are present, the emphasis on *seudaso shel oso rasha* suggests the concern about moral complicity in the king's agenda carries particular weight. The Gemara immediately challenges this answer: *im kein she'be'Shushan yeiharagu she'be'chol ha'olam kulo al yeiharagu* — if so, only the Jews of Shushan who actually participated should have been condemned, not Jews throughout the entire empire.

### Idol Worship Sins

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai himself then gave the answer: *mipnei she'hishtachavu la'tzelem* — because they bowed down to the idol. *Rashi* identifies this as the episode from Nevuchadnezzar's time, when the entire populace was compelled to bow to his statue — the three heroes Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah being the notable exceptions. The students immediately pressed: *ve'chi maso panim yesh ba'davar* — would there then be any partiality shown, any grounds for forgiveness? If the sin was *avodah zarah*, how could God perform a miracle on their behalf?

### Lifnim Principle

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai replied: *heim lo asu ela lifnim* — they acted only for outward appearances. The word *lifnim*, from *panim*, the face, denotes the external surface: they bowed because Nevuchadnezzar compelled them, not because they genuinely accepted the idol. There was no internal denial of God, only an external compliance under coercion. The corollary follows immediately: *af haKadosh Baruch Hu lo asah imahem ela lifnim* — so too, the Holy One, blessed be He, acted against them only for appearances. The threat of Haman was real on the surface but would not, in the end, be carried through to its conclusion. And the verse confirms the principle: *ki lo inah mi'libo* — God does not bring suffering from His heart.

### Coercion & Martyrdom

This is a striking *sugya*, and it is worth pausing on its implications. What is actually being said is that coerced *avodah zarah* — bowing to an idol under threat of death — does not constitute the sin of *avodah zarah* proper. *Tosafot* touches on this in a passing remark, but the Rambam develops the same principle at length in the *Iggeret Teiman*, addressing Jews who accepted Islam under duress. His position is carefully calibrated: the person who capitulates under coercion has failed to perform the *mitzvah* of *Kiddush Hashem* — the obligation to give one's life rather than transgress *avodah zarah*, *gilui arayos*, or *shefichas damim* in a time of religious persecution. That failure is real and significant. But such a person has not, the Rambam argues, transgressed the prohibition of *avodah zarah*, because they were entirely *anous* — coerced — and there was no genuine belief or inner assent behind the act. The sin, properly understood, is a failure of *Kiddush Hashem*, not a commission of *avodah zarah*.

This distinction carries weighty pastoral and policy implications. An openness to receiving those who submitted under coercion — grounded in the principle that their sin was not *avodah zarah* — is essential for preserving the community's connection to those who could not or did not martyr themselves. Yet too permissive a posture risks signaling that capitulation is costless, which in subsequent generations could erode the willingness to resist at all, and ultimately lead to complete assimilation rather than eventual return. These tensions are unresolved by the Gemara itself; it establishes the principle and leaves the policy questions in the hands of those who must apply it.

### Hester Panim Parallel

The parallelism the Gemara establishes here is precise. Just as the Jews' compliance with the idol was *lifnim* — external only, not reflecting their inner reality — so too God's response was *lifnim*: the appearance of a mortal decree without the reality of divine abandonment behind it. This parallel also maps onto the distinctive character of the *nes* of *Purim* — the *nes nistar*, the hidden miracle. In the *Megillah*, God's name does not appear. The entire reversal of fortune unfolds through ostensibly natural events: a king's whim, a beauty contest, a sleepless night. The visible surface is purely political. What is actually happening — the invisible hand of Providence — is concealed. The measure-for-measure structure, *midah k'neged midah*, operates here not only in the content but in the form: as their worship was purely external and not inner, so God's threatening posture was purely external and not inner. The *hester panim* of the miracle is thus itself a *midah k'neged midah* parallel to the *lifnim* of the Jews' idolatrous compliance.

---

## Feast Details

### Feast Location

The verse places Achashverosh's feast *bachatzar ginat bitan hamelech* — in the courtyard of the garden of the castle. Rav and Shmuel disagree on what this compound geography indicates. One holds that the three spaces — courtyard, garden, and castle — were used simultaneously according to the guests' rank: those deserving of the courtyard were placed in the courtyard, those deserving of the garden in the garden, and those of sufficient standing in the castle itself. The other holds that the king tried to seat everyone in the courtyard first, but the crowd was too large; he then moved them to the garden, which also proved insufficient, until finally all were brought inside the castle.

A *Beraisa* offers a third reading: all guests were seated in the courtyard, and two doors were opened from it — one leading to the garden, one leading into the castle — so that guests could move between the three spaces at will, strolling through the garden or touring the palace as the evening permitted. *Tosafot* raises a question in connection with the first reading: if different locations were assigned by rank, why does the Gemara not object that this would generate jealousy among the guests — *atah metil kinah biseudah* — the same objection raised moments later about the seating arrangements? *Tosafot* answers that the spaces were so vast that guests in one area could not readily see those in another, and so the visible disparity was less acute.

### Tapestries & Stones

The text describes the furnishings: *chur karpas usecheiles* — various linens. Rav reads *chur* as deriving from the root for holes or fine needlework, indicating elaborate stitching. Shmuel reads it from *chivar* — white — interpreting it as white silk that was laid out for the guests. As for *karpas* — familiar from the Pesach *seder* — Rav Yosef bar Chanina identifies it as *karim shel pasim*, cushions of velvet, placed on pillars of silver and columns of marble alongside beds of gold and silver.

On those beds, Rav Yehudah holds that they were distributed by rank: those deserving silver received silver beds, those deserving gold received gold. Rabbi Nechemyah objects — *im kein atah metil kinah biseudah* — this would stir envy at the feast. His resolution: the beds were silver but their legs were gold, so all guests had the same combination of materials and there was nothing to covet. *Tosafot* again raises the question of why the same objection was not applied to the assignment of different locations by rank, and answers as above: the scale of the spaces prevented guests from observing one another's placement.

The text continues: *bahat vasheish* — precious stones and marble. Rav Asi explains *bahat* as stones that *mis-chatetos* on their owners — precious gems so rare and costly that they demand everything of their possessors to seek them out, as the verse says: *avnei nezer misnossesos al admaso*, crown jewels that gleam over the land. The word *misnossesos*, *Rashi* notes, suggests extraordinary effort required to obtain them.

The word *dar* is also parsed. Rav reads it as *dari dari* — rows upon rows of precious stones. Shmuel identifies it as a specific gem called *darah*, found in distant isles, which was placed at the center of the feast and *meirah lahem ke-tzohorayim* — illuminated the hall like noon. The school of Rabbi Yishmael takes a different approach entirely, reading *vedar vesochares* not as a description of precious stones but as a policy: Achashverosh declared *deror* — freedom, a remission of taxes — for *ba'alei sechorah*, the merchants. All commerce was freed from imposts, and this contributed to the universal celebration.

### Vessels Sin Echo

The verse states *vehashkot biklei zahav vekeilim mikeilim shonim* — drinking from golden vessels and from *keilim mikeilim shonim*. The Gemara notes a grammatical difficulty: the word *shonim*, meaning different, seems to call for *meshunim* if the intent is simply "varied." Rava resolves it through a *bat kol*: a heavenly voice declared, *rishonim kallu mipnei keilim, ve'atem shonim bahem* — the earlier ones, Belshazzar and his court, were destroyed *because of* the vessels, and you are *repeating* the sin — *shonim* from the root *lishnot*, to repeat. The word thus carries a double meaning: the vessels were different from one another, and the sin of using them was being replicated. This is precisely the exegetical basis for the custom of reading *keilim mikeilim shonim* with an unusual *trop*, marking the verse as a site of theological weight.

### Wine & Freedom

The verse describes *yein malchut rav* — wine of the kingdom in abundance. Rav interprets *rav* not as plentiful but as aged: each guest received wine older than his own age in years. *Vehashtiyas khadat, ein ones* — and the drinking was according to the law, no one was compelled. The Gemara asks: *mai khadat* — what does it mean, according to the law? Rav Chanan in the name of Rabbi Meir explains: *khadat shel Torah*, following the rule of the Torah. And what is the Torah's rule? *Achilah merubah mishtiyah* — food exceeds drinking. In the Temple service, the quantities of grain offerings and *korbanos* placed on the *mizbe'ach* vastly exceeded the libations. So too at Achashverosh's feast, food dominated over drink.

### Food/Wine Ratio

This observation — that Achashverosh's feast mirrored the proportions of the Temple service — is worth pausing over. On one level it might seem like a compliment to Achashverosh. But in context it functions differently. Achashverosh is already wearing the *bigdei kehunah*, displaying the Temple's *keilim*, and now unconsciously replicating the food-to-wine ratios of the *mizbe'ach*. The effect is less to honor him than to underscore the theme of usurpation: he is positioning Shushan as the new Jerusalem, himself as the new *Kohen Gadol*, his feast as the new Temple service — while the actual Temple lies in ruins. There may also be a resonance with the earlier Gemara about *Purim* and the question of how to calibrate the obligation of *mishteh vesimchah* and the emphasis on *seudah*. The Gemara's reminder that even at Achashverosh's feast the food was proportionally greater than the wine may implicitly calibrate the proper balance that should characterize our own *Purim* celebrations.

Rabbi Elazar adds a further gloss on *ein ones*: each guest was served wine from his own country, so that no one was made uncomfortable by being given wine that was alien to him or difficult to drink. Finally, Rava interprets the phrase *la'asot kirtzon ish va'ish* — to do the will of every man — as referring specifically to Mordechai and Haman, both of whom are called *ish* in the *Megillah*: Mordechai as *ish Yehudi* and Haman as *ish tzar ve'oyev*. The Maharsha disputes *Rashi*'s reading that Mordechai and Haman were the wine stewards, arguing that *ratzon* refers to the guests' preferences, with Mordechai and Haman serving as stand-ins for people of all nations — whatever nation you came from, your needs were served. One might also read in this a subtle anticipation of a theme the Gemara develops elsewhere: that the entire drama of the *Megillah* was driven equally by the *ratzon* of both these men — the *arur Haman uvaruch Mordechai* dynamic — in which the actions and stubbornness of each contributed to the unfolding of events.

---

## Vashti's Punishment

### Vashti's Intent

The Gemara turns to Vashti. The verse states that she made a feast for women in *beit hamalchut* — in the king's castle. The Gemara notes the anomaly: she should have held the women's feast in *beit hanashim*, the women's quarters, not in the king's castle. Rava explains: *she-shneihem li-dvar aveirah nitkavnu* — both Achashverosh and Vashti had sinful intentions in mind. The proximity of the women's feast to the king's castle was deliberate. As the popular saying goes, *ihu bekarei ittei bebutzinei* — he has his gourds and she has hers; what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. Both parties to the evening had the same agenda.

### Seventh Day Timing

The verse notes that on the seventh day, *ke-tov lev hamelech beyayin* — when the king's heart was merry with wine — he issued his demand. The Gemara is puzzled: *atu ad hashta lo tav libei bekhamra* — until now, after six days of drinking, his heart was not merry with wine? Rava explains: *yom hashevi'i Shabbat haya* — the seventh day was *Shabbat*. When Jews eat and drink on *Shabbat*, *matkhilin bedivrei Torah uvdivrei tishbakhot* — they begin with words of Torah and words of praise; the joy of the table is channeled into learning, singing *zemirot*, elevating the moment. *Oveidei kokhavim umazzalot*, however — idolaters — when they eat and drink, *ein matkhilin ela bedivrei tiflut* — they begin only with lewd talk. And so at Achashverosh's feast, the conversation on that seventh day turned to women: the Median partisans insisted Median women were the most beautiful, the Persian partisans insisted Persian women were. Achashverosh intervened: the vessel I use, he said crudely, is neither Median nor Persian but Chaldean — referring to Vashti — and would you like to see her? The company agreed, and specified that she must appear naked.

### Shabbat Abuse/Punishment

The Gemara now introduces the *midah k'neged midah*. The principle *shebemidah sheadam moded bah modedin lo* — the measure with which one measures is the measure applied to him — here applies not to Achashverosh but to Vashti. The Gemara teaches: Vashti would take young *benot Yisrael* and force them to work for her naked on *Shabbat*. Therefore, the decree that she appear naked came on *Shabbat*. The verse in *Esther* — *ve-asher nigzar aleiha* — is read in this light: what was *nigzar* upon her was not merely the king's decree but the divine *midah k'neged midah* rooted in her own prior conduct.

### Command Refused

*Vatema'en hamalkah Vashti* — and Queen Vashti refused. The *HaGra* notes a subtle grammatical detail in the verses: when Achashverosh sends his command, the text reads *lehavi et Vashti hamalkah* — Vashti the queen, her name first. When she refuses, the text reverses: *vatema'en hamalkah Vashti* — the queen Vashti, her title first. The *HaGra* reads this as reflecting the subtext of their conflict. Achashverosh addressed her as though her royalty were incidental — she is Vashti who happens to be queen because she married him. She responded by asserting that the title comes first: she is the queen, and her royal lineage is primary. As the Gemara will presently clarify, Vashti understood herself as the granddaughter of Nevuchadnezzar, and her message to the king made that hierarchy explicit.

### Vashti Disfigured

The Gemara asks: given that Vashti was by all accounts *peritzusa* — licentious — and the earlier discussion established that both she and the king had sinful intent, why did she refuse? *Michdi peritzuta havai*, *de'amar mar shenehem lidvar aveirah nitkavnu* — given her character, she might have been expected to comply. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains: *melamed sheparchah bah tzara'at* — she had been stricken with *tzara'at*; she was disfigured and could not appear. *Rashi* and *Tosafot* link the word *nigzar* in the verse to the usage of that root in the context of *Uziyahu*, where *tzara'at* is described using the same language. A *Beraisa* adds a more vivid detail: *ba Gavriel ve'asah lah zanav* — the angel Gavriel fashioned a tail for her. The *Maharsha* notes that this need not be taken literally; it likely refers to some form of grotesque physical growth that made appearance at the royal feast impossible.

### Vashti Mocks King

Vashti's refusal was accompanied by a contemptuous message. She sent word back: *bar ahorya de'abba* — you are the stable boy of my father. My father — referring to Nevuchadnezzar — *lekabel alfa chamra shatei velo ravi* — could drink a thousand measures of wine and not become drunk. *Vehai gavra ishtit bekhamra miha* — and this man, you, got drunk with your wine. The message was a direct assault on Achashverosh's legitimacy: he was no king by lineage, only by marriage into royalty he did not deserve. He could not hold his wine; he could not hold his authority. *Vachamato ba'arah bo* — and his fury burned within him.

---

## Consulting Sages

### King Consults

*Vayomer hamelech lachachamim yodei ha'itim* — and the king said to the wise men who knew the times, those who know how to intercalate years and fix the months, meaning the rabbis. This detail is worth noting in itself. The Gemara is doing something larger than providing exegesis of a verse: it is recasting the entire story of the *Megillah* as a story of Jewish history, told from within the perspective of Jewish history. Everything about Achashverosh — his preoccupation with the seventy years, his use of the Temple's *keilim* and *bigdei kehunah*, and now his instinct to bring his legal question to the rabbis — places the Jewish dimension at the center of what might appear to be purely Persian court politics. The world's history, the Gemara consistently implies, is really Jewish history; everything else is context.

### Sages Decline

The sages found themselves in an impossible position. If they told Achashverosh to execute Vashti, he would sober up the next day, regret losing his queen, and hold them responsible. If they told him to let the matter go, they would be seen as condoning her public humiliation of the king's authority and complicit in the disrespect shown to the crown. Their solution was evasion: *miyom shecharav beit hamikdash vegalinu meartzenu nittla eitza mimmenu ve-ein anu yodim ladun dinei nefashos* — from the day the *Beis Hamikdash* was destroyed and we were exiled from our land, wisdom was taken from us and we do not know how to adjudicate capital cases. The loss of the Temple has rendered them incapable of judgment. One might hear in this evasion also a subtle hint: if you wish to restore our capacity for wisdom and judgment, the path is the restoration of the *Beis Hamikdash* itself.

### Amon Moav Exile

Having demurred, the sages directed Achashverosh to other advisors: *zil legabei amon umoav deyasvi beduchtayeihu* — go to Amon and Moav, who have remained in their places, who have never been exiled. The metaphor is that of wine resting undisturbed on its lees: *kachamra deyasiv al durdeiyeihu* — like wine that has never been poured from vessel to vessel. The verse in the *Megillah* that says they gave the king *taam* — reason or taste — may then carry a double meaning: they provided him a rationale, and that rationale itself had *taam*, substance and flavor. A verse about *Moav* in *Yirmiyahu* captures the metaphor: *sha'anan Moav mine'urav veshokeit hu al shemarav... velo hurak mikli el kli uvagola lo halach* — Moav has been tranquil from its youth, undisturbed upon its lees, not poured from vessel to vessel, not sent into exile; therefore its taste has remained and its scent has not faded. Nations that have never been exiled, never been shaken and displaced, retain a kind of settled wisdom — or at least a willingness to render firm opinions — that the exiled sages have lost.

---

## Seven Counselors

### Name Allusions

The text then lists the seven counselors Achashverosh consulted: *Karshena, Shetar, Admasa, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, Memuchan*. Rabbi Levi teaches: *kol pasuk zeh al shum korbanos ne'emar* — this entire verse alludes to the *korbanos*. The word *hakarov* — close, referring to those near the king — echoes *korban*. Each name is then read as an allusion to a specific Temple service.

### Heavenly Advocacy

In the Gemara's reading, each name becomes the vehicle for an angelic argument before God on behalf of the Jewish people. The heavenly advocates ask: *klum hikrivu lifanecha karim bnei shana* — have these nations ever offered to You yearling lambs, as Israel did? This is *Karshena*, from *kar*, a lamb. *Shetar* evokes *shtei torim* — have they ever offered two turtle-doves? *Admasa* evokes *mizbe'ach adama* — have they ever built an earthen altar? *Tarshish* evokes the *tarshish* stone on the *Kohen Gadol*'s breastplate — have they ever served You in *bigdei kehunah*? *Meres* evokes *mersu bedam* — have they ever stirred the blood of an offering before You? *Marsena* evokes *mersu bemenachos* — have they ever stirred the meal offering, mixing the flour and oil? And *Memuchan* evokes *hechinu shulchan* — have they ever set a table before You? In each case the implied answer is no — only Israel has performed these acts of service — and the angels' argument is that God must therefore intervene on Israel's behalf. Once again the theme emerges: the entire drama of the court of Achashverosh is situated within the story of the *Beis Hamikdash*, its destruction, its service, and the anticipation of its restoration.

### Memuchan as Haman

A *Tanna* teaches: *Memuchan zeh Haman* — Memuchan is Haman. The reason for the name: *shemuchan lepuranus* — he was prepared, setting himself up for punishment without realizing it. Rav Kahana adds: *mikan shehedyot kofetz berosh* — from here we learn that a minor person jumps to the head. Memuchan is listed last among the seven counselors, yet he is the first to speak. The minor official, the *hedyot*, pushes himself to the front.

### First Letter's Folly

Rava then identifies the first letter Haman-as-Memuchan caused to be sent as, paradoxically, the very thing that saved the Jews. *Ilmalei igros harishonos, lo nishtayer mishoneihem shel Yisrael* — were it not for the first letters, not a remnant of the Jews would have survived. Because once the permission to rise against the Jews was issued in the second letter, the populations would not have waited for the designated date of the 13th of *Adar*; they would have acted immediately. What held them back was that the first letter — the decree about household authority — had so thoroughly undermined Achashverosh's credibility that the second letter was not taken seriously either.

### Master of House

Why was the first letter so foolish? When people received it and read that henceforth every man should be master in his own home, the reaction was: *mai hai deshadr lan* — what is he sending us? *Lihyos kol ish sorer beveiso* — that every man should rule in his own house? *Pshita afilu karda dezuzi pardashka lehvei* — this is self-evident; even a lowly person is the governor in his own domain. The decree was so banal, so obviously stating what required no legislation, that the king appeared foolish. Having once appeared foolish, his subsequent decree against the Jews was not met with the alarm and urgency it might otherwise have commanded, giving the Jewish people the time and space within which the reversal ultimately occurred.

### Tosafot: Daniel Theory

*Tosafot* closes the discussion of Memuchan with an alternative reading drawn from a *midrash*: perhaps Memuchan was not Haman but Daniel. According to this view, Daniel was married to a noblewoman of higher status than himself — *shelo haya yachol lchofefa ledaber kilshono*, he could not get her to speak his language — and so out of personal frustration he counseled Achashverosh to issue the decree that all wives must speak their husbands' language and submit to their husbands' authority. All politics, the *midrash* implies, is personal: behind the grand edicts of empire lie the domestic irritations of individual men.

---

---

# Megillah 15b

## Esther's Appeal

### Shechinah Departure

The daf begins with Esther entering *bechatzer beit hamelech hapnimiyit* — the innermost chamber of the king's house. Rabbi Levi teaches that upon reaching the chamber of idols (*beit hatzelamim*), the *Shechinah* departed from her — *nistalka heimena Shechinah* — for she had been cloaked in the *ruach hakodesh* of *malchut*, and now that presence withdrew.

She cried out: *Eli Eli lama azavtani* — my God, my God, why have You abandoned me? This verse comes from the *perek* in Tehillim identified as *Ayelet HaShachar*, which the *Gemara* interprets as referring to Esther. She then asks: *shema ata dan al shogeg kemezid ve'al oness keratzon* — perhaps You are judging the inadvertent as intentional, and the coerced as the willing?

### Onesh Debate

This plea connects to an earlier *Midrash* in which Esther declares *ka'asher avadti avadti*. The *Gemara* understands her as now willingly approaching Achashveirosh, including for intimate purposes, which would render her forbidden to Mordechai. Esther protests that even if she acts willingly on the surface, the larger context renders her an *oness* — coerced by circumstance — since she acts for the sake of *Klal Yisrael*.

Rashi explains this precisely: *af al pi she'ani ba'ah elav me'elai oness hu* — even though she is choosing to go to him, the necessity is external and overriding.

This passage raises two distinct questions. First, was Esther *permitted* to do this at all? The *Gemara* elsewhere addresses Esther's conduct with the phrase *befarhesya havei*, and the full range of questions surrounding *giluy arayot* — whether it is *yehareg ve'al ya'avor*, the principle of *karka olam*, and so on — all bear on this. Second, and more fascinatingly, even granting that she was not only permitted but *obligated* by *pikuach nefesh* — even if she was a true *oness* in the fullest sense — does that exemption from transgression necessarily mean that she remains permitted to Mordechai? The verse governing that prohibition reads *ki tisteh ishto umalah bo ma'al*: the Torah concerns itself with the violation of the marital bond itself — *umalah bo ma'al* — not solely with whether she transgressed against God. It is therefore conceivable that even an act she was *metzuva* to perform could still affect her status relative to her husband. A fascinating *teshuvah* addresses a parallel scenario involving a woman deceived into believing she was fulfilling a *mitzvah* and later found to have been misled, and the question of her return to her husband turns on precisely this distinction. The *Gemara* here does not resolve the question, but frames it pointedly: she herself calls it *oness*.

### Dog/Lion Language

She continues: *o shekarasi lo kelev* — or perhaps You abandoned me because I called Achashveirosh a dog, as the verse says *miyad kelev yechidati* — save me from the dog. Even though Achashveirosh is a *rasha*, he is a king, and one must speak of him with respect. So she corrects herself: *chazra vekaraso aryeh* — she then calls him a lion. The next verse says *hoshieini mipi aryeh* — save me from the mouth of the lion — and with that correction, she has addressed both concerns she raised before God.

### Angels & Staff

The verse then reads *vayehi keros hamelech es Esther hamalka*. Rabbi Yochanan teaches that three heavenly angels appeared to her at that moment. The first lifted her neck so that the king could see her through the crowd. The second drew the *chut shel chesed* — the strand of divine charm — over her, so that she found favor in his eyes. The third caused the king to extend the golden staff toward her, allowing her to approach.

### Staff Measures

The *Gemara* then asks: how far did the staff extend? Rabbi Yirmiyah teaches it was originally two *amos* and was extended to twelve. Some say sixteen, others twenty-four, and a *Braisah* teaches sixty. Rabba bar Efron cites in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, who received it through an unbroken chain of tradition (*sheshama meirabo v'rabo meirabo*), that it extended two hundred *amos*.

The *Gemara* notes parallels elsewhere: the arm of Pharaoh's daughter that extended to draw Moshe from the water, and the teeth of the wicked which Reish Lakish reads not as *shibarta* — you broke — but *sheribavta* — you extended — referring to the miraculous extension of Og's teeth. The different specific numbers throughout this discussion may reflect different ways of counting from a particular word or letter in the verse, as the Maharsha explains.

The theme of the *Beit HaMikdash* surfaces here as well. The king's offer of "half the kingdom" is interpreted to exclude anything that "divides" (*chotzeitz*) the kingdom — and the *Gemara* identifies that as the *binyan Beit HaMikdash*. Achashveirosh will not consent to its rebuilding. This is consistent with the *Gemara*'s broader understanding that the Purim story takes place during a period when the construction had stalled. The Ramban understood the events as occurring later in the Persian period — after the rebuilding had resumed in earnest under Daryavesh — but the *Gemara* consistently treats this as a moment when the *binyan* had not yet truly begun. The *Beit HaMikdash* as a theme, as we will see, continues to surface throughout the story.

### Half Kingdom

*Ad chatzi ha-malchut* — up to half the kingdom — means the king will give generously, but not anything that "divides" the kingdom. The *Gemara* identifies what that limitation protects: *u'mai nihu binyan Beit HaMikdash* — it is the rebuilding of the Temple. This sets the stage for Esther's reply, in which she does not ask for the *binyan* but instead invites the king and Haman to a feast.

---

## Why Invite Haman

### Trap Theory

*Tanu rabanan*: what did Esther see in herself that she invited Haman? The question is entirely reasonable — if her goal is to save the Jewish people from Haman's decree, why bring Haman along to the feast? The *Gemara* proceeds through a remarkable series of *tanna'ic* and *amora'ic* answers.

Rabbi Eliezer says: she laid a trap for him — *pach tamnah lo* — as the verse states, *yehi shulchanam lifneihem l'phach*, let their table be a trap before them. By including Haman, she drew him in close, hoping he would expose himself or be caught in some incriminating behavior.

### Keep Close

Rabbi Yehoshua says she learned this from her father's house: *im ra'ev sona'acha hachileihu lachem* — if your enemy is hungry, feed him bread. Keep your enemies close and your eyes upon them.

### Multiple Views

Rabbi Meir says: she feared that if Haman were absent he might catch wind of what was happening and take action — perhaps rebel against the king or foil her plan entirely. Better to keep him where she could watch him.

Rabbi Yehudah says: she did not want people to realize she was Jewish. If she suddenly appeared before the king without Haman, suspicion would arise that she was interceding against his decree. By including Haman, she created misdirection.

Rabbi Nechemya adds a striking theological dimension: she did not want the Jewish people to relax their prayers. If the Jews thought, "our sister is in the palace, we have nothing to worry about," they would ease off their supplications to God — *veyasichu da'atam min ha-rachamim*. By keeping Haman present and seemingly close to Esther, the Jews would remain anxious and continue to cry out to Heaven. It is a remarkable point: she is engineering a religious outcome, making sure God remains in the picture even as God is conspicuously absent from the text of the *Megillah*.

### Availability

Rabbi Yose says: so that Haman would always be available to her — *kedei shelo yehei matzui lah bechol eit* — and as Rashi explains, *ulai tuchal lehachshilo beshum davar lifnei hamelech*: if Haman is always nearby, perhaps she could find some way to get him into trouble before the king.

### Divine Notice

Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya says: perhaps God will notice the desperate situation and act on their behalf — *ulai yargish HaMakom veya'aseh lanu nes*. Rashi unpacks this in two ways: either that God should perceive how low Esther has had to stoop, currying favor with the enemy of Israel; or that God should respond by bringing forth those who would stand by the Jews just as Esther has had to stand alongside their enemies.

This raises a genuine theological question that this *Gemara* pointedly touches: does God need to be shown human suffering before acting? The entire logic of *ta'anit*, which was just studied in Masechet Ta'anit, involves precisely this — displaying one's misery before God so that divine compassion is aroused. The anthropomorphism is real and the tension is not resolved here, but the *Gemara* makes no effort to soften it.

### Jealousy Plan

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha opens with *asbir lo fanim* — let me explain it, implying he has something to add beyond what has already been said. His answer: *kedei sheyekaneh hu vehi* — so that the king would become jealous, believing that Esther and Haman were somehow intimate. This is a striking explanation: Esther was willing to sacrifice her own reputation in order to trigger the king's jealousy and bring about Haman's downfall. Most readers assume this is the central explanation, partly because the end of the story bears it out when Haman falls upon Esther's bed — but whether it was indeed her primary motivation, as opposed to the other explanations offered, is precisely what this passage is debating.

### Flip-Flopper King

Rabban Gamliel says: the king was a *hapachpachan* — a flip-flopper, constantly reversing himself. Esther understood that if she convinced the king privately and Haman were not present, the next time Haman got the king's ear he would reverse course. The only way to catch the king at the right moment and seal the deal was to have everyone in the same room at once.

### All Jealous

Rabban Gamliel then adds: *adayin tzerichin anu laModai* — we still need the one from Modi'in, meaning Rabbi Elazar HaModai, who specialized in *aggadata*. Rabbi Elazar HaModai says: *kinato bamelech kinato basarim* — she wanted to make the king jealous of Haman and also to make the other princes and ministers jealous of Haman. The Maharsha explains what Rabbi Elazar HaModai uniquely adds: the question was not only why Haman was invited but why *only* Haman, and not others. By inviting only Haman she created a scenario in which both the king and the other courtiers would be suspicious of Haman's special relationship with the queen — whereas had she invited others, the intimacy implied would have been diluted.

Rava adds: *lifnei shever ga'on* — pride comes before the fall. Abaye and Rava together cite the verse *bechumam ashit mishtehem* — in their heat I will arrange their drinking feast — the idea being that the downfall of one's enemies often comes through the indulgence of feasting and drinking. 

### All True

Rabba bar Avuha encountered Eliyahu and asked him directly: according to whom did Esther act? Eliyahu answered: *kechulhu tana'ei vechechulhu amora'ei* — all of them are true. All of these motivations operated simultaneously, and since none of them contradict one another, there is no reason to choose. This is among the most grounded sections of the *Gemara*'s treatment of the *Megillah* — a genuine effort to understand the inner logic of a character's decision — and the answer that all motivations coexist is, on reflection, entirely plausible.

---

## Haman Boasts

### Sons' Numbers

The verse relates that Haman boasted to his friends and family of his great wealth *verov banav* — and the myriad of his sons. How many sons did he actually have? Rav says thirty: ten died in battle, ten were hanged, and ten afterwards wandered begging from door to door — ongoing suffering as part of his downfall. The *Rabbanan* say there were seventy who ended up begging, reading *shiv'im balechem niskaru* with *al tikrei* as *shiv'im* — seventy. Rami bar Abba says the total was 208, since *rov* in *gematria* yields 208 (reading the *ketiv* without the middle *vav*, as Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak points out, making it *resh vav bet* = 208 rather than 214).

### Sleep Disturbance

*Balaylah hahu nadeda shenat hamelech* — on that night the king's sleep was disturbed. Rabbi Tanchum reads this as: *nadeda shenat malko shel olam* — God's sleep was disturbed, meaning God was now stirring to intervene. This reading is also reflected in the special *trop* with which the *Megillah* is chanted, which is understood to evoke this sense of divine awakening. The *Rabbanan* say: *nadedo elyonim nadedo tachtonim* — both the upper realms and the lower realms were stirred into motion in order to bring about the redemption.

### Conspiracy Fear

Rava, characteristically, offers a psychologically acute reading: *shenat hamelech Achashveirosh mamash* — it means the actual king Achashveirosh, and his sleeplessness reflects genuine anxiety. Something fell in his mind — *nafla milta bedateih*: what was Esther doing inviting Haman to her feast? *Dilma etza ka shakli ilvay* — maybe they are plotting against him, and Haman is the man seeking to kill him.

Then the king's thought reversed itself: if there truly is such a plot, why has no one informed me of it? That would mean that no one who loves me has warned me. And why would that be? Perhaps, he concluded, because someone once did good for me and I never rewarded him — *dilma ika inish de-avad bi tivusa velo pariteih* — and therefore people have learned not to bother, since informing the king earns no gratitude. The absence of a conspiracy report becomes, in Rava's reading, the very evidence of a conspiracy. It is a memorable observation that cuts well beyond the *Megillah*: people are often motivated more by who they hate than by who they love.

### History Books

The king ordered the history books brought and read aloud. The verse says *vayimatze katuv* — and it was found *written*, in the present tense, when one might have expected *katav*, the past. The *Gemara* explains (citing Tosafot on 86a): the attendant reading the chronicle disliked the Jews and was trying to erase the line recording Mordechai's deed, while the angel Gavriel was simultaneously rewriting it — hence *katuv*, being written, in the ongoing present.

### Divine Records

Rav Shila of Kefar Tamarta expounded: if a record written below (*shel matah*), in the king's earthly chronicle, which benefits Israel cannot be erased, how much more so what is written above (*shel ma'alah*) — the divine record of Israel's merits — which can never be erased. The king then asks what was done for Mordechai and is told: *lo na'asa imo davar* — nothing was done for him. Rava adds pointedly: they didn't say this because they loved Mordechai — they said it because they hated Haman.

---

## Honor Mordechai

### Haman's Suggestion

Haman had come early in the morning to ask the king's permission to hang Mordechai on the gallows he had built. Instead the king asks him: what should be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor? Haman, assuming the king means him, elaborates a grand proposal involving the royal garments and the royal horse. The king tells him: excellent — do all this for Mordechai the Jew, the one who sits in the king's gate.

Haman attempts to minimize the honor: perhaps a village would suffice, or a river — something less conspicuous than a royal procession. The king says: *hai nami hav lei* — give him that too, and everything else you mentioned besides. *Al tapel davar mikol asher dibarta* — let not a word of all you said go undone.

Haman went to find Mordechai and found him sitting before his rabbinic students. Mordechai was teaching the laws of *kmitzah* — the handful offering of the *minchah* — which Rashi connects to the timing around Pesach, given that the fast had begun then. When Mordechai saw Haman approaching leading the king's horse, he was frightened — *mirtat* — uncertain whether Haman was coming to execute him. He told his students to flee so they would not be caught in the conflagration, then wrapped himself in prayer, standing in *Shemoneh Esrei*.

Haman sat and waited until Mordechai finished his *Shemoneh Esrei* — presumably because Mordechai felt that interrupting his prayer would make no difference to the outcome — and then addressed the assembled group. He asked: *be-mai askiseitu* — what have you been dealing with? The rabbis explained: in the time of the *Beit HaMikdash*, a person could bring the most humble offering — a single handful of flour — and be atoned for. Haman responded bitterly: *ata mallei kumtzei kimcha dichi vedachi asara alfei kikarei kaspa didi* — your handful of flour has overridden my ten thousand talents of silver. For at the very moment they had been studying these laws of the *kmitzah*, the king's mind had turned toward rewarding Mordechai, effectively overturning Haman's decree purchased with his silver.

Mordechai then rejoined: *eved shekanah nechasim eved lemi unechasim lemi* — a slave who acquires property: to whom does the slave belong, and to whom does the property belong? Going back to the earlier theme that Haman was once a slave of Mordechai — his wealth was never truly his own.

This moment carries a broader thematic weight. The story is set in the interregnum between the two *Batei Mikdash*, and the *Gemara* here layers several things simultaneously: Esther's fast and the *tzaakah* of the people, the merit of the *Beit HaMikdash* and its offerings, and Mordechai standing in *Shemoneh Esrei*. The *Gemara* could have presented only the study of *kmitzah*; the insertion of Mordechai at *Shemoneh Esrei* seems deliberately juxtaposed. There is a larger question here about whether *tefillah* in exile replaces and stands parallel to *korbanot*, or whether these are simply two streams both drawing on the same underlying merit, and the *Gemara* does not fully resolve it — but the juxtaposition seems intentional.

### Preparation Required

Mordechai said to Haman: I cannot do this now. *Ad de-aleina lebei banei ve'ashkol le'mazaya* — I must first go to the bathhouse and have my hair cut. One in my current state — having been fasting and wearing sackcloth — cannot properly make use of the king's garments and horse.

### Haman Attendant

So Esther sent and locked up all the bathhouses and all the barbers (*umane*) in the city. The *uman* — the craftsman-attendant — appears here as a barber, though the same term is used for a bloodletter and a *mohel*, all sharing the common denominator of sharp implements. By closing off every alternative, Esther ensured that Haman himself would have to serve as Mordechai's attendant. It is also worth noting that Mordechai was now needing a haircut during *Chol HaMoed*, during the *ta'anit*, and during *Sefirah* — a confluence of circumstances that the *Gemara* notes without fully resolving.

### Hair Cutting

Haman brought Mordechai to the bathhouse, bathed and scrubbed him himself, then went home to retrieve a scissors — his own — and began cutting Mordechai's hair. As he cut, he let out a moan and a sigh — *ingad ve'istnach*. Mordechai asked: why are you sighing? Haman said: the man who was more important to the king than all his ministers — *hashata shavei balani ve'sapara* — now I've been reduced to being a bathhouse attendant and a barber?

### Barber Origins

Mordechai replied: *velav sapara de'kfar kartzum hayita* — weren't you already a barber in the village of Kartsum? You are simply returning to your origins. The *Braisah* confirms: Haman was the barber of the village of Kartsum for twenty-two years. His entire elevation was a departure from what he truly was, and now circumstances are restoring the natural order.

### Horse Mounting

After the haircut, Haman dressed Mordechai in the royal garments and told him to mount the horse. Mordechai said: I cannot climb up — *de'chashishachali mi'yemei ta'anita* — I am weakened from the days of fasting. So Haman bent down and Mordechai used him as a mounting-step to climb onto the horse.

### Trampling

As Mordechai mounted, he kicked Haman. Haman protested: is it not written *binfol oyvecha al tismach* — do not rejoice when your enemy falls? Mordechai replied: that verse applies between fellow Jews — *hani mili be'Yisrael* — but regarding you it is written *ve'ata al bamotaymo tidroch* — you shall trample upon their high places. Mordechai was literally walking on the neck and head of Haman, fulfilling the verse.

### Daughter's Death

Haman called out before Mordechai: *kacha ye'aseh la'ish asher hamelech chafetz bikoro* — thus shall be done for the man the king wishes to honor. As they passed through the alleys near Haman's house, Haman's daughter was watching from the rooftop. She assumed — logically enough — that the man on the horse must be her father and the man walking in front must be Mordechai. She took the chamber pot of the bathroom and hurled it — aiming at the figure walking in front. But when the man on the horse lifted his eyes, she saw that it was her father. She fell from the roof to the ground and died.

The verse then reads: *vayashav Mordechai el shaar hamelech* — and Mordechai returned to the king's gate — *ve'Haman nidchaf el beiso avel v'chafui rosh*. Rav Sheshes explains: *vayashav Mordechai* means he returned to his fasting and his sackcloth — *l'sako ul'ta'aniso* — he did not take his elevation for granted or assume redemption was now assured. Haman returned to his house mourning: *avel* for his daughter, *v'chafui rosh* in shame for what had been done to him.

---

## Wise Men's Warning

### Tells Story

Haman then told his wife Zeresh and all his friends what had happened to him. The verse calls them *ohavav* — his friends — but elsewhere they are called *chachamav* — his wise men.

### Tribes Assessment

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the discrepancy: *kol ha'omer davar chochma afilu b'umos ha'olam nikra chacham* — whoever speaks a word of wisdom, even among the nations of the world, is called wise. When they were simply his companions they were his friends; when they spoke wisdom, they became wise men.

What was the wisdom? They said: *im mizerah hayehudim Mordechai* — if he is from the seed of the Jews, *lo tuchal lo* — you will not prevail over him. The *Gemara* asks: they already knew he was Jewish — why does this only become meaningful now? The answer is the *chiddush*: beforehand, Haman was ascending and Mordechai descending, and in that configuration it seemed manageable. Now Mordechai is ascending and Haman is falling, and *that* dynamic — they now understand — cannot be reversed once it is in motion.

Specifically, they say: if Mordechai descends from one of the *other* tribes, you may yet prevail. But if he is from Yehuda, Binyamin, Ephraim, or Menashe — *lo tuchal lo*. The verses: Yehuda — *yadcha b'oref oyvecha*, your hand shall be at the throat of your enemies; the others — *lifnei Ephraim uVinyamin uMenashe orera es gevurascha*, bestir Your might before them. Of course Mordechai is identified as *Yehudi* and *Yemini*, tracing descent through both Yehuda and Binyamin, and Esther through the line of King Shaul — closing the circle with Shaul and Amalek that underlies the entire confrontation.

### Double Falling

Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai expounds: what is the meaning of the double language *nafol tipol* — you shall certainly fall before him? The answer: *uma zu m'shula l'afar um'shula l'chochavim* — this nation is compared both to dust and to stars. When they descend, they descend to the dust; when they rise, they rise to the heavens. The doubling of *nafol tipol* captures this full arc — from the greatest of heights to the depths, or in reverse.

### Eunuchs Arrive

*Ve'sarisei hamelech higiu vayavhilu* — the king's eunuchs arrived and rushed Haman to the feast. The *Gemara* teaches: *melamed sheheviu'u b'vahala* — they brought him in haste. Note the contrast: Mordechai was given time to bathe and prepare; Haman comes in a rush, still in a state of disarray, with no such courtesy extended.

---

## Final Downfall

### Accusation

Esther says before the king: *ki nimcharnu ani v'ami* — for I and my people have been sold. *Ki ein hatzar shoveh b'nezek hamelech* — this enemy has no concern with the king's losses. She then tells Achashveirosh: Haman was jealous of Vashti and got her killed — echoing the identification of Memuchan with Haman — *iknei b'didi umiba'i lemiktlai* — he is jealous of me and seeks my death as well. She is deliberately inflaming Achashveirosh's jealousy over both his former and current queen.

### Angel Intervention

*Vayomer hamelech Achashveirosh vayomer l'Esther hamalka* — the verse uses *vayomer* twice, which Rabbi Avahu explains: initially the king was speaking through a translator. Once Esther declared *ki nimcharnu ani v'ami* and revealed her descent from Shaul, establishing her royal lineage and knowledge of languages, the king addressed her directly — *miyad vayomer l'Esther* — he dropped the *meturgeman*.

Esther then said: *ish tzar v'oyev Haman hara hazeh*. But why does she not simply say "Haman"? The *Gemara* explains — a famous *Midrash* — that Rabbi Elazar teaches: *melamed shehayesa mechava k'lapei Achashveirosh* — she was gesturing toward Achashveirosh himself, since he too bore responsibility. A *malach* came and redirected her hand toward Haman. The message is not lost: Achashveirosh's complicity was real and it was almost named aloud.

### Garden Angels

*V'hamelech kam b'chamato* — the king rose in his anger. *V'hamelech shav miginat habitan* — and then he returned from the garden. The verse creates a parallel between his rising and his return: just as he rose in fiery anger, so too when he returned he had not calmed down at all — *mah kima b'chema af shiva b'chema*.

Why hadn't he calmed down during his walk in the garden? Because when he went outside, he found heavenly angels appearing in the guise of men, uprooting the beautiful trees of the orchard. When he demanded to know who had ordered this, they replied: *d'fakdinan Haman* — Haman commanded us. So his anger was compounded, not relieved.

### Falls on Bed

*V'Haman nofel al hamita* — Haman was falling upon the bed where Esther lay. The present-tense *nofel* is odd — it should say *nafal*, past tense. Rabbi Elazar teaches: *melamed sheba malach v'hipilo aleiha* — a *malach* came and was pushing him down onto the bed. Haman was not trying to be in that position; he was being maneuvered there. The king returned and said: *vai mibeisa vai mibara* — woe from inside, woe from outside — everywhere I look, Haman is doing terrible things. *Hagam lichbosh es hamalka imi babayit* — are you even trying to subdue the queen with me here in the house?

### Harvona's Role

Charvona then spoke up and identified the gallows that Haman had built for Mordechai. Rabbi Elazar teaches: Charvona was himself a *rasha* who had been part of the plot — *af Charvona rasha b'osah eitzah hayah*. Once he saw things turning, he immediately switched sides — *kivan she'ra'ah lo niskaymu, miyad barach* — running away from Haman the moment it became clear the plan had failed. He was an opportunist, not a hero. The verse is cited: *vayashlech alav v'lo yachmol miyado baroach yivrach* — he has no compassion, he will run away. And yet — as the *Gemara* implies — even someone with less-than-ideal motives can end up doing the right thing.

### Anger Subsides

*V'chamasan hamelech shachacha* — the king's anger abated. The *Gemara* asks: why is *shachacha* written with what appears to be a doubled form? Two separate calming-downs are implied. One opinion: one for God, whose anger had also been stirred — *akhat shemalkho shel olam* — and one for Achashveirosh himself. Another opinion: *akhat shel Esther ve'akhat shel Vashti* — the king was appeased regarding both queens, having been angry over the loss of Vashti and having feared for Esther, and Esther's accusation against Haman — that he was jealous of Vashti and got her killed — addressed both grievances.

One should note that the *Megillah* itself never explicitly states that Vashti was killed. It says only that she should no longer appear before the king — *asher lo tavo Vashti*. The popular assumption of her execution is read in from the *Gemara*. As one approach noted, in Roman times banishment carried the legal consequence that anyone could kill the banished person and claim their property — which may bring the *peshat* closer to the *derash* than it first appears.

---

## Five Changes

### Joseph's Mistake

The *Gemara* now pivots to a passage from Bereishit: *ve'chulam natan le'ish chalifot semalot uleBinyamin natan chamesh chalifot semalot* — Yosef gave each of his brothers a change of garments but gave Binyamin five changes.
