One might ask: is it conceivable that the very thing that caused Yosef HaTzaddik such suffering — his father's favoritism in giving him a special garment — he himself would repeat, knowingly, causing pain to the other brothers again?

Rava bar Mechasya cites Rav Chama bar Guria citing Rav: because of a mere two *selaim* of extra wool — *milat* — that Yaakov added to Yosef's garment beyond what he gave the others — it was not the elaborate coat of many colors we imagine, just a slightly longer hem — *nisgalgal hadavar veyardu avoteinu leMitzrayim*: the chain of events unfolded and our ancestors descended to Egypt. Would Yosef truly repeat this mistake?

### Benjamin's Hint

Rabbi Binyamin bar Yafet answers: no — it was not favoritism but a *remez*, a hint. *Remez ramaz lo sheatid ben latzet mimenu* — Yosef was hinting to Binyamin that a descendant would one day emerge from him *sheyetzei milifnei hamelech bechamisha levushei malkhut* — who would go forth from before the king wearing five royal garments.

### Mordechai's Garments

The fulfillment: *uMordekhai yatza bilevush malkhut techelet vachur vetachrikh butz veargaman veateret zahav gedola* — and Mordechai went forth from before the king in royal garments of blue and white, with a wrapping of fine linen and purple, and a great golden crown. Counting these, there are precisely five royal garments. The five changes of clothing that Yosef gave Binyamin were not an act of favoritism at all — they were a prophetic gesture, pointing centuries forward to the elevation of Mordechai, Binyamin's descendant, in the court of Achashveirosh. We will continue from this *Yosef* digression when we return.

---

---

# Megillah 16b

## Yosef's Weeping

### Plural Necks

The *daf* opens with a verse from the story of Yosef's reunion with his brothers: *vayipol al tzavarei Binyamin achiv* — Yosef fell on Binyamin's neck and wept, *u'Binyamin bacha al tzavarav*. The Gemara asks: *kama tzavarin havu leh* — how many necks does he have? The word *tzavarei* is plural. As Rashi notes, this is simply how the language refers to the neck; nonetheless, the Gemara uses it as an occasion for *drasha*.

### Two Temples

Rabbi Elazar teaches: *bacha al shnei mikdashim she'atidin lihyot b'chelko shel Binyamin v'atidin l'yecharev* — Yosef wept over the two *mikdashim* that would stand in Binyamin's portion of the Land of Israel and would eventually be destroyed. This is striking in light of the broader context: the *Megillah* itself is situated, according to *Chazal*, between these two *mikdashim* — so that the symbolism of Mordechai's *levush malchus* and Yosef's gifts intersects with the destruction of the *batei mikdash* in Binyamin's territory.

### Mishkan Shiloh

*U'Binyamin bacha al tzavarav* — and Binyamin wept on Yosef's necks. Here the Gemara passes over the plural without comment, and instead explains that Binyamin wept *al mishkan Shiloh she'atid lihyot b'chelko shel Yosef v'atid l'yecharev* — over the destruction of the *mishkan* at Shiloh, which would stand in Yosef's portion and likewise be destroyed. Thus the mutual weeping was not merely an expression of joy at reunion, but carried the weight of future destruction.

### Yosef's Sincerity

The verse continues: *v'hinei eyneichem ra'ot v'eynei achi Binyamin ki pi hamedaber aleichem* — behold, your eyes see and the eyes of my brother Binyamin that it is my mouth speaking to you. Rabbi Elazar explains: why single out *eynei achi Binyamin* separately? Yosef is making a point. Just as he clearly harbors nothing against Binyamin — who had no part in the plot to sell him — so too, *kach ein li b'libi aleichem*, he holds no grudge against the brothers either. *Ki pi hamedaber aleichem — k'fi ken libi*: what his mouth says is precisely what is in his heart. He is being entirely sincere.

### Gifts to Father

The verse states that Yosef sent his father ten donkeys laden with *mi'tuv Mitzrayim* — the good of Egypt. The Gemara asks: what is the good of Egypt? Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *shalach lo yayin yashan she'da'at zekenim nocha heymenu* — he sent him old wine, which elderly people truly appreciate and which puts them in a settled, contented state of mind.

## Prostration & Power

### Brothers Prostrate

After Yaakov dies, the brothers fear that Yosef will now take his revenge, and they prostrate themselves before him. Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet said in the name of Rabbi Elazar — and one notes that many of the teachings in this passage are transmitted through this same chain — *hainu d'amri inshi, ta'ala b'idneih sagid leh*: this is what people say: a fox in his time, you must bow down to him. They prostrated themselves before Yosef because Yosef held the power.

### Fox Metaphor

The Gemara immediately questions this application: *mai betzirosieh me'achvoh* — in what way was Yosef inferior to his brothers, like a fox? He was their equal by birth; the fox metaphor implies someone at a lower station who happens to have power. Therefore, the Gemara says, *ela ei ismar hachi ismar* — if this saying was transmitted, it was transmitted in a different context. The better context is *vayishtachu Yisrael al rosh hamitah* — when Yaakov bowed down on his bed as Yosef came to receive his blessing and bring Ephraim and Menashe. There Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet in the name of Rabbi Elazar applies the saying: *ta'ala b'idneih sagid leh* — even a fox has his day, and since Yosef held temporal power, even Yaakov, his father, acknowledged that.

### Yaakov Bows

The phrase *vayishtachu Yisrael al rosh hamitah* thus receives its proper context. Yaakov bowing before Yosef was not mere deference to a son; it reflected the recognition that Yosef's position of authority warranted acknowledgment — even from his father. The proverb is not demeaning to Yosef but descriptive of the reality of worldly power.

### Candles Metaphor

Returning to the brothers who have prostrated themselves, the verse says *vaynachim otam vayidaber al libam* — he consoled them and spoke to their hearts. Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet in the name of Rabbi Elazar explains: *vayidaber al libam* means he spoke *devarim she'miskablim al halev*, words that could actually be received by the heart. What did he say? *Umah asarah nerot lo yakhlu lekhabot ner echad, ner echad heikh yakhol lekhabot asarah nerot* — if ten candles could not extinguish one candle, how could one candle extinguish ten? By framing his reassurance in terms of *nerot*, Yosef elevated the conversation to the spiritual plane. Not only would he not harm them — he could not, even were he to try. The metaphor suggests that on the level of the soul, such a thing is impossible.

## Four Themes

### Four Purim Themes

The *Megillah* states: *layehudim hayetah orah vesimkhah vesason vikar* — to the Jews there was light, joy, rejoicing, and honor. The Gemara interprets each of these four terms as referring to a specific religious institution.

### Light = Torah

Rav Yehudah teaches: *orah zo Torah* — the light is *Torah*. The proof text is *ki ner mitzvah ve-Torah or* — a *mitzvah* is a candle and *Torah* is light. This verse, with its reference to the *ner*, connects back as well to the earlier *nerot* imagery.

### Joy, Rejoicing, Honor

*Simkhah zeh Yom Tov* — joy refers to *Yom Tov*, as the verse says *vesamakhta be-khagekha*. *Sason zo milah* — rejoicing refers to *milah*, derived from the verse *sas anokhi al imratekha kemotze shalal rav*, which is recited at a *bris milah*. Rashi adds that when God commands *bris milah* to Avraham, the Torah uses the word *vayomer* — *amiraha* — which connects to *imratekha*. *Vikar elu tefillin* — honor refers to *tefillin*, from the verse *verau kol amei ha-aretz ki shem Hashem nikra alekha ve-yar'u mimmeka* — all the peoples of the earth will see and be in awe of you.

### Haman's Decrees

What does all of this mean in context? Why would the *Megillah*'s celebration be expressed specifically through *Torah*, *Yom Tov*, *milah*, and *tefillin*? Rashi explains that Haman did not merely decree to destroy the Jews physically; he also, as in the period of the *Chanukah* story, decreed against Jewish religious practice. Thus: *orah zo Torah shegazar aleihem Haman shelo yaasku ba-Torah* — Haman decreed they should not engage in *Torah* study. Similarly he forbade observance of *Yamim Tovim*, the practice of *milah*, and the wearing of *tefillin*. The Gemara is thus, to some degree, overlapping the themes of *Chanukah* and *Purim* — both involved decrees not only against Jewish life but against Jewish religious identity.

## Ten Sons Names

### One Breath

The Gemara turns to the public reading of the names of the ten sons of Haman: *ve'et Parshandasa* — *aseret benei Haman*. Rav Adda of Yafo teaches: *aseret benei Haman ve-aseret, tzarikh lemimreinhu beneshimah akhat* — the ten sons of Haman and the word *aseret* must all be said in a single breath. *Mai taama* — what is the reason? *Kulu behadi hadadi nafka nishmatayhu* — because their souls all departed simultaneously. They were all hanged at the same time, and saying the names in one breath symbolizes that simultaneity. There is something significant, apparently, in the fact that they all died in a single instant.

### Tosafot Opinion

Tosafot notes that saying the names in one breath is *le-khatchilah*; *aval be-diavad yatza* — if one did not manage it, the obligation is nonetheless fulfilled after the fact. This raises a practical question: in many communities the *ba'al korei* pauses and the congregation recites the ten names themselves. This practice may reflect the principle of *shomea k'oneh* — hearing is like saying — but holding one's breath is not the same as the listener holding their breath. Therefore, many hold that one should recite the names oneself in a single breath, or at minimum hold one's breath while the *chazzan* recites them.

### Stretched Vav

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *vav shel Vaizasa tzarikh lemimtechah bezikifa kemordya dilvros* — the *vav* of *Vaizasa* must be stretched out, written elongated like the pole used on the river called Livros. *Mai taama* — *kulu bechad zikifa izdakaifu* — they were all hanged on the same pole. Therefore the *vav* is written to visually symbolize the gallows. This is a striking tradition, for it implies a change in the actual manner of writing the letter based on symbolic considerations — something unusual, since ordinarily the way letters are written derives from an independent *masorah*, not from interpretive associations.

### Brick Pattern

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa taught in the name of a scholar from the village of Timra: *kol hashirot kulan nichtavot ariach al gabei levina, ulevina al gabei ariach* — all the poems and songs in *Tanach* are written in a staggered pattern, like bricks: a half-brick over a full brick, and a full brick over a half-brick. This is the familiar pattern of *shirat hayam* (Az Yashir) and other *shirot*, where the text alternates in a staggered arrangement.

### Staggered Exception

The exceptions are *aseret benei Haman* and the listing of the kings of Kena'an — *she'ariach al gabei ariach ulevina al gabei levina* — where the text is arranged in straight columns, column directly over column, without staggering. One might also note that *Ha'azinu* presents a similar straight-column format with a central space, though the Gemara does not incorporate it into this particular point.

### No Rising

*Mai ta'ama* — what is the reason for this departure from the standard pattern of *shirot*? *Shelo tehe tekuma lemapaltan* — so that there should be no rising up from their fall. The instability of a staggered pattern is precisely why bricks are normally laid that way — it creates structural strength. Here, by placing column directly over column, the text visually enacts complete, irreversible collapse. There should be nothing left standing; the arrangement signals total destruction with no possibility of recovery.

A further scribal tradition, not discussed in the Gemara itself but relevant to the practice, holds that the names of the ten sons must fill an entire column. Most *soferim* accomplish this by writing the letters of *aseret benei Haman* in a larger size. The Vilna Gaon, however, strongly objected to this practice, arguing that we have no *masorah* to write these names in a font larger than the surrounding text — the only attested scribal anomaly is the elongated *vav* of *Vaizasa*. A *megillah* written with eleven lines per column allows the ten names plus the word *va-aseret* to fill a column in standard-size script, thus satisfying the columnar requirement without departing from the accepted *masorah* of letter size.

## Achashverosh's Shift

### Tone Shift

The verse reads: *vayomer hamelech l'Esther ha-malka b'Shushan ha-bira hargu hayehudim ve'ibed chamesh meot ish...u-mah she'elatekh vetinatein lakh* — the king informed Esther of the number slain in Shushan and throughout the provinces, and then in the very same verse offered her whatever she wished. The shift in tone is dramatic and jarring: the verse begins in what appears to be an expression of alarm or even accusation, and ends with a generous open-ended offer. This is a textually strange *pasuk*.

### Angel's Slap

Rabbi Abbahu teaches: *melamed sheba malach v'staho al piv* — an angel came and struck Achashverosh on his mouth, changing the words he was about to say. Just as an angel had guided Esther's approach at a critical moment, so here an angel intervened mid-sentence to alter Achashverosh's speech, producing the abrupt shift in tone visible in the verse itself.

### Read From Scroll

The verse later states: *uvevo'ah lifnei hamelech amar im hasefer yashuv machshavto hara'ah asher chashav al hayehudim al rosho.* Rabbi Yochanan interprets *amar im hasefer* as: *yomar bepeh mah shekatuv basefer* — what is written in the scroll should be declared aloud. Rashi's reading (*haichi garsinan*) is that this refers to Mordechai's role: the text is tracing how the events of Purim were to be recited and recorded annually, with the instruction that what is written in the *sefer* — the *Megillah* — should be proclaimed orally. In this reading, *amar im hasefer* becomes a foundational reference to the annual reading of the *Megillah* itself.

## Scroll Writing

### Scribal Lines

The verse *divrei shalom ve'emet* prompts a *halachic* teaching. Rabbi Tanchum — and some say Rabbi Assi — teaches: *melamed shetzricha sirtut ka'amittah shel Torah* — the *Megillah* requires *sirtut*, the scored lines that a scribe makes on the parchment before writing, just as is required by *amittah shel Torah*, the truth of the *Torah*.

### Sirtut Debate

Rashi understands *amittah shel Torah* to mean a *Sefer Torah* itself, meaning the *Megillah* must have *sirtut* just as a *Sefer Torah* does. Tosafot disagrees, holding that technically a *Sefer Torah* does not require *sirtut*, and that *amittah shel Torah* here refers to a *mezuzah*. Either way, the teaching situates the *Megillah* alongside the most formally demanding categories of *sifrei kodesh*. This connects to a broader theme: just as the Gemara will shortly establish that the *Megillah* must be written in Hebrew — despite the *mishnah*'s more permissive stance toward other *sefarim* — so too here the *Megillah* is given weight comparable to, or even exceeding, other portions of the *Torah*. Tosafot reads the same stringency regarding *sirtut* in the same direction: the *Megillah* shares this demanding standard with the *mezuzah* rather than with the more lenient category of *Sefer Torah*.

## Acceptance of Purim

### Esther's Ordinance

The verse reads: *um'amar Esther kiyam divrei ha-Purim ha-eleh*. The Gemara immediately questions: *um'amar Esther in divrei ha-tzomot lo?* — and Esther's word established the Purim days, but what of the reference to *divrei ha-tzomot ve-za'akatam* earlier in the same passage?

### Fasts & Cries

The full verse runs: *lekayem et divrei ha-Purim ha-eleh bizmaneihem ka'asher kiyam aleihem Mordechai ha-Yehudi ve-Esther ha-malka ve-ka'asher kiyemu al nafsham ve-al zar'am divrei ha-tzomot u-za'akatam* — to establish these Purim days in their times, just as Mordechai and Esther had established them, and just as they had accepted upon themselves and their descendants the matter of the fasts and their crying out.

### Validation

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the apparent difficulty by reading *divrei ha-tzomot ve-za'akatam u-ma'amar Esther* as a continuous phrase rather than placing the break at *ve-za'akatam*. The meaning then becomes: it was through *divrei ha-tzomot ve-za'akatam u-ma'amar Esther* — through the fasting, the crying out, and Esther's proclamation together — that *kiyam divrei ha-Purim ha-eleh*, these days of Purim were validated and brought about. The Gemara is thus reading the verse as a historical reference to what produced the Purim miracle in the first place, not as an institution of a future fast day. (The later practice of *Taanit Esther* is post-Talmudic, and Rashi's reading does not understand the verse as establishing such a fast.)

## Mordechai's Status

### Mishneh Status

The *Megillah* concludes: *ki Mordechai ha-Yehudi mishneh la-melech Achashverosh ve-gadol la-Yehudim ve-ratzui le-rov echav* — second to the king and great among the Jews and accepted by most of his brothers. *Le-rov echav ve-lo le-chol echav* — most but not all. The famous *midrash*: *melamed she-pirshu mimenu miktzat Sanhedrin* — some members of the *Sanhedrin* distanced themselves from him, because he had departed from the *beit midrash*.

### Torah Priority

Rav Yosef draws the principle: *gadol talmud Torah yoter me-hatzalat nefashot* — *talmud Torah* is greater than saving lives. *De-me'ikara chashev leh le-Mordechai batar arba'ah* — originally, in Ezra, Mordechai is listed after four others, making him fifth on the list. *U-levasof batar chamishah* — later in the text, after the Purim story, he appears only after five others, falling to sixth place. He descended in standing precisely because his involvement in political affairs and saving lives drew him away from *Torah* study.

### Rank Change

The *pessukim* bear this out. Initially it is written: *asher ba'u im Zerubavel Yeshua Nechemiah Serayah Re'elayah Mordechai Bilshan* — Mordechai is fifth. Later: *ha-ba'im im Zerubavel Yeshua Nechemiah Azaryah Ra'amyah Nachamani Mordechai Bilshan* — Mordechai is sixth, having dropped one position. This is a remarkable statement in context, because the *Gemara* opened this tractate by saying that one suspends *talmud Torah* in favor of *mikra megillah* — thus seemingly elevating *mikra megillah* over *Torah* study — and yet here the Gemara is moving in the opposite direction, suggesting that Mordechai's very heroism in saving his people came at a cost to his standing in *Torah*.

## Torah Primacy

### Torah > Temple

Rava (and some say Rav Shmuel bar Marta) states: *gadol talmud Torah yoter mi-binyan Beit ha-Mikdash* — *talmud Torah* is greater than building the *Beit ha-Mikdash*.

### Ezra's Choice

The proof: *she-kol zman she-Baruch ben Neriah kayam lo hinicho Ezra ve'ala* — as long as Baruch ben Neriah was alive in Bavel, Ezra did not leave to go up to the Land of Israel. Ezra, the paradigmatic figure of *Torah* transmission — *Ezra Hasofer*, the proto-rabbinic figure — only came in the second wave of returnees. The Gemara's explanation: his *rebbe* was still alive in Bavel, and he was not yet free to leave. The construction of the *Beit ha-Mikdash* was underway, and yet Ezra remained in *yeshiva*.

### Halakha/Aggada

This creates a striking tension that the *Gemara* leaves unresolved. The *halacha* is clear: one suspends *talmud Torah* for *mikra megillah*, and equally one suspends *talmud Torah* for *binyan Beit ha-Mikdash*. And yet the closing *sugyot* of this *perek* — centered on the very themes of *mikra megillah* and *Beit ha-Mikdash* — insist that *talmud Torah* surpasses them all. The *aggadeta* functions here as a counter-voice to the *halacha*, shaping attitudes and maintaining *Torah* study's primacy in the hierarchy of values even where the formal legal ruling goes the other way. This kind of juxtaposition — where *aggadeta* is placed deliberately alongside a *halacha* that points in the opposite direction — is a recognizable pattern in the *Gemara*, similar to the tension in *Berachot* around *tefilla* and *talmud Torah*, or the famous tension around *ad de-lo yada* and the story of Rava and Rabbi Zeira.

### Torah > Parents

Rava bar bar Rav Yitzchak states: *gadol talmud Torah yoter mi-kibbud av va-em* — *talmud Torah* is greater than *kibbud av va-em*. The proof: *she-kol otan shanim she-haya Yaakov Avinu b'veit Ever lo ne'enash* — during all the years that Yaakov our father was in the *yeshiva* of Ever, he was not punished.

### Yaakov's Years

This teaching presupposes that Yaakov spent fourteen hidden years learning in the *yeshiva* of Ever before his journey to Lavan in Aram Naharayim — a tradition found in Rashi on the *Torah*. The claim is that those fourteen years, spent away from his parents in order to study, were not counted against him.

### Age Math

The Gemara establishes this through a careful reconstruction of Yaakov's age. The Torah records that Yishmael died at 137. Yishmael was 14 years older than Yitzchak, since Avraham was 86 at Yishmael's birth and 100 at Yitzchak's birth. Yitzchak was 60 when Yaakov and Esav were born, making Yishmael 74 at that point. Since Yishmael died at 137, he had 63 more years to live from the time of Yaakov's birth. A *baraita* teaches that Yaakov was 63 when he received his father's blessing and departed — and at that very time, Yishmael died.

The Gemara establishes this through the verse that describes Eisav going to marry Machalat, the daughter of Yishmael, sister of Nevayot. Since she is Yishmael's daughter, why specify that she is the sister of Nevayot? *Melamed shekiddshah Yishmael umet* — Yishmael had betrothed her to Eisav and then died, so that at the actual *nisuin* it was her brother Nevayot who gave her away. This establishes that Yishmael died at precisely the time these events occurred — when Yaakov was 63.

From age 63, fourteen more years until Yosef was born (*arba esreh ad demitayallid Yosef*), making Yaakov 77 at Yosef's birth. Yosef was 30 when he stood before Paroh, making Yaakov 107. Seven years of plenty and two years of famine add nine more years, bringing Yaakov to 116. But when Paroh asks Yaakov his age, Yaakov says he is 130. The discrepancy is 14 years — precisely the fourteen years of *Beit Ever*. *Shema mina arba esreh dehavah b'veit Ever lo chashiv lehu* — those fourteen years in the *yeshiva* of Ever were not counted in the tally, which is itself the proof that he was not punished for them.

### Parallel Years

The Gemara then connects this to Yosef's absence from Yaakov. A *baraita* teaches: *nimtza Yosef sheperash me'aviv esrim ushtayim shanah* — Yosef was separated from his father for twenty-two years. He was 17 when sold, and we have established through the calculations above that he was 39 when reunited with Yaakov (30 before Paroh, plus seven years of plenty and two of famine) — indeed twenty-two years. *Keshem shepeirash Yaakov Avinu me'aviv* — this parallels the twenty-two years Yaakov was not with his own father. But wait: the math for Yaakov yields 36 years away (14 for Rachel and Leah, 6 for the flocks, plus the 14 of *Beit Ever*, plus 2 additional years of travel). Subtracting the 14 of *Beit Ever* leaves 22 — the parallel is exact. *Ella arbisar d'havavei bei Ever lo chashiv lehu* — the fourteen of *Beit Ever* are not counted, and the remaining twenty-two correspond precisely to the twenty-two years Yosef was absent. The symmetry itself demonstrates that the fourteen years of *Torah* study were not reckoned as a period of negligence toward his father.

The remaining discrepancy — the 20 years in Lavan's house, not yet 22 — is resolved by adding the two years Yaakov spent traveling home: eighteen months at Succoth (*vayiven lo bayit ulemiknehu asah Succoth*, implying a summer, winter, and summer — eighteen months), and six months at *Beit El* where he brought offerings. Together these account for the additional two years, bringing the total to twenty-two.

One should note a nuance in how to understand this teaching. Yaakov was told by both parents to go to Lavan; his departure was at their direction. The question is therefore not simply whether he should have been home but whether the specific circumstances — the fourteen years in *Beit Ever*, the additional six years working for flocks, the two years of travel — represent a failure of *kibbud av va-em*. The Gemara's point is subtler: even when one has good reason to be away, even when the *halacha* permits or even mandates the departure, the absence from parents carries a real-world cost. The *halacha* regarding one who moves away for *Torah* study or livelihood or even *aliyah* may well permit it, but the *aggadata* here preserves the awareness that something of *kibbud av va-em* is nonetheless not being fulfilled in the fullest sense.

## Reading Rules

### Forward Only

The *mishnah* of the next *perek* opens: *hakorei et ha-Megillah lemafrea lo yatza* — one who reads the *Megillah* out of order, reading later passages before earlier ones, has not fulfilled the obligation.

### Language Rules

*Kara al peh* — if one read it from memory without looking at a scroll, *kara Targum* — if one read it in Aramaic translation, *bechol lashon* — or in any other language, *lo yatza* — one has not fulfilled the obligation.

### Language Exception

*Aval korin osa liloazos bilaaz* — however, one may read the *Megillah* to a non-Hebrew speaker in their own foreign language. And conversely: *vehaloez sheshama Ashuris yatza* — a non-Hebrew speaker who hears the *Megillah* read in Hebrew has fulfilled the obligation, even without understanding. The Gemara will explore what distinguishes these cases.

### Breaks Allowed

*Karaah seirugin* — if one read with pauses and interruptions — *umisnamnem* — or while dozing off — *yatza*, one has nonetheless fulfilled the obligation.

### Intent Required

*Haya koshva dorsha umagiha* — if one was in the process of writing the *Megillah*, or expounding on it (*darshan*-style), or proofreading it, and in doing so verbalized the words — *im kiven libo yatza* — if one directed one's mind toward the act of reading as a *mitzvah*, one has fulfilled the obligation. *Ve-im lav lo yatza* — if not, one has not. At minimum, one must be aware that one is performing an act of reading; a question remains whether one must additionally have conscious intent to fulfill the *mitzvah*.

### Material Rules

*Haysa kesuva besam uvesikra uvekumus uvekankantum* — if the *Megillah* was written in various types of dye or pigment other than *dyo*, *al hanyar* — on paper, which in antiquity was a cloth-based material — *ve-al hadiphtera* — or on processed leather that is not *klaf* — *lo yatza*, one has not fulfilled the obligation.

### Script & Ink

*Ad shetehei kesuva Ashuris al hasefer u-vidyo* — until it is written in the Hebrew script, on proper parchment (*klaf*), and with *dyo*, the recognized *halachic* ink. This requirement — Hebrew script, *klaf*, and *dyo* — connects back directly to the earlier discussion: the *Megillah* is treated with the same formality as the most demanding categories of *sifrei kodesh*.

## Backward Prohibition

### Verse Source

The Gemara asks: *manah hanei milei* — from where is the prohibition against reading the *Megillah* out of order derived? Rabba cites the verse: *keichsavim u-chezmanim* — as written and in their times.

### Time Logic

The analogy: just as time does not go backward — one does not observe the 15th celebration before the 14th — so too *af ksavam lemafrea lo* — what is written about them is not read backward.

### Action Not Reading

The Gemara immediately objects: *midi keria kesiv hacha? Asiya kesiv hacha* — is it reading that the verse refers to? The verse says *lihyot osim* — to perform these days *keichsavim u-chezmanim*. It is speaking about the act of observance, not about reading. The verse does not address *keria* at all.

### Memory & Action

The Gemara therefore redirects: *ela mehacha* — rather, derive it from the verse *vehayamim ha-eleh nizkarim venaasim* — these days are remembered and performed. *Iskash zchira la-asiya* — the verse links *zechira* (memory/reading) to *asiya* (observance). Just as *asiya lemafrea lo* — one does not observe Purim out of order — so too *zchira lemafrea lo* — one does not read it out of order.

### Other Mitzvot

A *baraita* teaches that the same principle applies to *Hallel*, *krias Shema*, and *tefilla* — all must be performed in their proper order. The Gemara then asks for the source in each case. Rabba cites *mimizrach shemesh ad mevo'o* — from sunrise to sunset — which describes a natural sequence and applies to the *psukim* of *Hallel*. Rav Yosef cites *zeh hayom asah Hashem* — a day unfolds in sequence. Rav Avya cites *yehi shem Hashem mevorach*, which Rashi reads as implying natural sequential order. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and some say Rav Acha bar Yaakov cite *me'atah ve'ad olam* — from now to forever — again implying an irreversible sequence.

## Shema Language

### Language Dispute

A *baraita* states: *Krias Shema ke'chsavah* — *Krias Shema* must be recited as it is written, meaning in Hebrew. This is the position of Rabbi. The Rabbis (*Rabbanan*) disagree: *bechol lashon* — it may be recited in any language.

### Rabbi's Source

Rabbi's source is the verse *ve'hayu ve'hayu ha-devarim ha-eleh* — *ve'hayu* implies that the words must remain exactly as they are, in their original Hebrew form.

### Rabbanan Source

The Rabbis derive from the word *Shema* itself: *bechol lashon she'atah shome'a* — however you are able to hear and understand. The obligation is to hear and comprehend, which can be accomplished in any language.

### Hearing Dispute

Rabbi further derives from *Shema* that one must verbalize the words audibly enough to hear them oneself: *hashmi'a le'oznecha mah she'atah motzi mipicha* — make your ears hear what your mouth utters. The Rabbis, by contrast, hold with the view that *hakorei Shema velo hishmia le'ozno yatza* — even if one did not hear one's own words, the obligation is fulfilled.

### Ritual vs Meaning

There is a coherent conceptual link between Rabbi's two positions. Rabbi focuses on the ritual, objective dimensions of the act: the specific Hebrew text must be used, and the words must be verbalized audibly. The Rabbis, by contrast, orient toward meaning and comprehension: what matters is that one is communicating the content to oneself, whether in Hebrew or another language, and whether or not one can physically hear one's own voice. Rabbi demands more of the formal ritual act; the Rabbis are more attuned to the act of understanding and inner address.

### Resolution

The Gemara then asks: given that *Rabbanan* allow any language, why does the verse say *ve'hayu* at all? And given that Rabbi requires Hebrew, why does the verse say *Shema*? The Gemara resolves both questions. For Rabbanan: even if the default were any language, *ve'hayu* was still necessary — otherwise one might have concluded from *Shema* that Hebrew was required, following Rabbi's reasoning. So *kasav rachmana ve'hayu* to insist that any language suffices. For Rabbi: even if the default were Hebrew, *Shema* was still necessary — because without it one might have misread *ve'hayu* to require an additional condition beyond Hebrew. Each verse addresses a potential misreading, not the baseline assumption.

The Gemara also uses this discussion to raise a broader question: does Rabbi hold that the entire *Torah* was given to be recited in any language (*bechol lashon ne'emrah*), making the default permissive, with *ve'hayu* functioning as a specific restriction? Or do the Rabbis hold that the default for all *Torah* recitations is Hebrew (*bilshon hakodesh ne'emrah*), with *Shema* functioning as a specific permission? The Gemara works through both possibilities and concludes that neither position can be simply identified with one side of the broader question about default language for *Torah* recitations generally, since each verse serves a necessary corrective function regardless of what the underlying default might be.

## Tefilla Order

### Shimon Hapakuli

A *baraita* states: *Shimon Hapakuli hesdir shemoneh esrei berachot lifnei Rabban Gamliel al ha-seder be-Yavneh* — Shimon Hapakuli (apparently a tradesman, possibly a cotton merchant) organized the 18 *berachot* in their order before Rabban Gamliel at Yavneh. He did not author them; he arranged the existing *berachot* into a fixed order and fixed text, presenting this arrangement before Rabban Gamliel for ratification.

### Elder Tradition

Rabbi Yochanan teaches an alternative tradition: *me'ah ve-esrim zekenim uvahem kama nevi'im tiknu shmoneh esrei berachot al ha-seder* — 120 elders, including among them several prophets, instituted the 18 *berachot* in their order. The Gemara will work to reconcile these two traditions, but in either case the tradition points back to the prophetic and elder-led institution of communal prayer in the early Second Temple period.

### Opening Praises

The *baraita* proceeds to ground the three opening *berachot* — *avot*, *gevurot*, and *kedushot* — in Scripture. *Minayin she'omrim avot* — from where do we derive the blessing of *avot*? *Havu la-Hashem bnei eilim* — give to God, sons of the mighty, i.e., the forebears: Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. *Minayin she'omrim gevurot* — from where *gevurot*? *Havu la-Hashem kavod va-oz* — give to God honor and strength. *Minayin she'omrim kedushot* — from where *kedushot*? *Havu la-Hashem kvod shemo hishtachavu la-Hashem behadrat kodesh* — give to God the honor of His name, bow before God in holy splendor.

### Avot's Role

The structure of these opening *berachot* addresses a fundamental challenge of prayer: how can a finite, corporeal human being presume to approach an infinite God? The *berachah* of *avot* provides the entry point — we are not coming on our own authority but as inheritors of a relationship already established by the *avot*, who have already, in some sense, legitimated our standing before God. Then *gevurot* and *kedushot* acknowledge the immense gap: God's power is beyond measure, and God's *kedushah* marks the absolute difference between Creator and creature. These three *berachot* together constitute both an acknowledgment of that gap and the inherited claim that allows one nonetheless to stand in prayer. We will continue with this discussion in the next session.

---

---

# Megillah 17b

## al ha-seder in Shmoneh E…

### al ha-seder & Tosafot

The daf picks up in the middle of the discussion of things that must be performed *al ha-seder* — in sequential order. Having already treated the *Megillah* and *Shema*, the *Gemara* now turns to *Shmoneh Esrei*. Because the text of *Shmoneh Esrei* is rabbinic rather than biblical, no verses are cited to prove that it must be recited *al ha-seder*; instead, the *Gemara* engages the question of what the logical organization of the *brachot* is and what the practical implications of that ordering requirement are.

Before entering the *Gemara*'s own analysis, it is worth drawing attention to Tosafot on this amud. The *Gemara* states that *Shimon ha-Pakuli* organized the eighteen *brachot al ha-seder*. Tosafot raises a difficulty against Rashi's interpretation of a *Gemara* elsewhere concerning the middle *brachot*: if the middle *brachot* have no fixed order, Tosafot asks, then in what sense did *Shimon ha-Pakuli* establish them *al ha-seder*? Tosafot argues that the very point of the *Gemara* here is to assert that the eighteen *brachot* follow a precise and obligatory sequence — just as *Shema* and *Megillah* must be recited *al ha-seder* — and that one cannot recite even a single *brachah* out of order.

### Rashi vs. Tosafot

The disagreement between Rashi and Tosafot concerns what happens in practice if a *brachah* in *Shmoneh Esrei* is accidentally skipped. Rashi's view, as Tosafot understands it, is that a person who realizes mid-*Shmoneh Esrei* that he has skipped a *brachah* may simply insert that *brachah* at the point where he currently stands and continue forward. This implies that the order is not strictly binding. Tosafot finds this incompatible with the *Gemara*'s assertion of *al ha-seder* and therefore rejects it, arguing instead that reciting even one *brachah* out of sequence is a violation of the requirement.

### Halakhic Implication

The halakhic upshot, and the position that is accepted as practical *halacha*, follows Tosafot: if one skips a *brachah* in *Shmoneh Esrei*, one does not simply add it wherever one currently is. Rather, one must return to the *brachah* that was missed and continue sequentially from that point. This applies to the middle *brachot*; one does not need to restart the entire *Shmoneh Esrei* from the beginning, but one cannot simply patch the missed *brachah* in out of place. That is the concrete halakhic meaning of *al ha-seder* as applied to *Shmoneh Esrei*.

---

## Binah, Teshuvah, Selichah

### Binah After Kedushah

Having established that the order of *Shmoneh Esrei* is authoritative and obligatory, the *Gemara* now turns to the question of what the logic of that order actually is. It begins: *u'mah ra'u lomar binah achar kedusha* — why, after the first three opening *brachot* that culminate in *Kedushah*, do we transition immediately to *binah*, to understanding? Why is *binah* the first of the *bakasha*-oriented *brachot*?

The *Gemara* cites a verse from Isaiah: *v'hikdishu et Kadosh Yaakov v'et Elohei Yisrael ya'aritzu* — "they shall sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and the God of Israel they shall glorify." The immediately following verse reads: *v'yadu to'ei ruach binah* — "those who are of wayward or searching spirit will know understanding." The structural juxtaposition of *kedushah* and *binah* in the verse provides the textual anchor. The *Gemara* does not at this point offer a deeper logical argument; it grounds the sequence in the *pasuk*.

### Understanding & Repentan…

The next question is why *teshuvah* follows *binah*. The *Gemara* cites a verse: *u'l'vavo yavin v'shav v'rafa lo* — "and his heart will understand, and he will repent, and it will be healed for him." The verse makes the sequence explicit: first comes understanding, and understanding leads directly to *teshuvah*. When a person truly comprehends the nature of his actions and their consequences, the natural result is repentance. The connection between *binah* and *teshuvah* is thus not merely sequential but causal.

### Selichah Over Refuah

Given this verse, however, the *Gemara* raises an immediate challenge. Since the verse continues *v'shav v'rafa lo* — and he will return and it will be *healed* — why does *selichah*, forgiveness, follow *teshuvah* in the *Shmoneh Esrei* rather than *refuah*, healing? The verse seems to place healing directly after repentance. The *Gemara* presses: *leima refuah batrah* — perhaps *refuah* should come next, before *selichah*?

The *Gemara* responds by citing a different verse: *v'yashav el Hashem v'yerachamehu v'el Eloheinu ki yarbeh lisloach* — "they will return to God and He will have compassion on them, to their God who is abundant in forgiveness." This verse clearly links *teshuvah* with *selichah*, not with physical healing. The *Gemara* then asks: why privilege this verse over the earlier one that links *teshuvah* with *rafa*? It answers with yet another verse: *hasolei'ach l'chol avonayich harofei l'chol tachaluayich hagoel mishachat chayeichi* — "who forgives all your sins, who heals all your illnesses, who redeems your life from the depths." Here the order is explicit: forgiveness first, then healing, then redemption. This settles the sequence of *selichah* before *refuah*.

### Spiritual vs. Physical

But this still leaves a loose end: what does one do with the original verse, *v'shav v'rafa lo*, which seemed to place healing immediately after *teshuvah*? The *Gemara* resolves this cleanly: *hahu lav refuah d'tachalu'in hee, ela refuah d'selichah hee* — that *rafa* in the original verse does not refer to physical healing of illness at all. It refers to the spiritual healing of forgiveness. The response to *teshuvah* in that verse is the inner healing that comes from being forgiven, not the physical recovery from sickness addressed in the *brachah* of *rofeh cholei amo Yisrael*. Two different types of healing, two different verses, and no contradiction.

### Intellect & Human Dignity

Beyond the specific *pasuk*-based reasoning, there is a broader philosophical point animating why *binah* stands at the very head of the *bakashot*. The *Gemara* elsewhere reflects on the primacy of intellect as constitutive of meaningful human life. Any robust sense of human agency — the ability to make real choices, to assess one's actions, to live a life of moral and religious responsibility — depends entirely on *binah*. The Midrash connects this to the very first act of human creativity: after *Shabbat*, the first act of *Adam HaRishon* is the making of fire. The language of that Midrash attributes this to God having granted human beings *da'at* or *binah* that is *me'ein dugma shel ma'alah* — a kind of reflection of divine wisdom. This is also bound up with the concept of *tzelem Elokim*: for many commentators, the divine image in which humanity was created is most precisely located in the capacity for intellect and understanding.

It follows naturally, then, that a life of *teshuvah* and *selichah* — of moral accountability and the pursuit of forgiveness — can only exist because of *binah*. You cannot repent for choices you did not consciously make; you cannot pursue forgiveness for actions you did not understand. *Binah* is not merely the first *brachah* of petition; it is the foundation that makes the entire religious enterprise possible. These three — *binah*, *teshuvah*, *selichah* — form a coherent and interconnected opening to the middle *brachot*.

---

## Refuah & Geulah

### Geulah in Seventh

Having established the internal logic of the first cluster of middle *brachot*, the *Gemara* turns to the placement of *geulah* and *refuah* — and here the reasoning shifts from logical sequence to symbolic numerology. The *Gemara* asks: *u'mah ra'u lomar geulah bashvi'it* — why do we place *geulah*, redemption, as the seventh *brachah*? The answer given is that of Rava: *mitoch she'atidim liga'el bashvi'it* — because the future redemption will unfold in the seventh year. According to certain *Midrashim*, the cosmic process of redemption and the war of *Gog u-Magog* will culminate in the seventh year of that process. Since seven is the number with which redemption is associated — just as *Shabbat* represents a qualitative elevation after six ordinary days — *geulah* was fixed in the seventh position.

### Personal vs. National

Rashi raises an important qualification here. The *geulah* of this seventh *brachah* — *go'el Yisrael* — is not the national and cosmic *geulah* from *galut*. Rashi states explicitly: *Ve'af al gav dehai Geulah lav Geulah deGalus hi, ella sheyige'alenu min hatzaros haba'os aleinu tamid* — this *geulah* refers to God saving us from the afflictions and difficulties that continually beset us on a personal level. The grand national redemption — *kibbutz galuyot*, the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the restoration of Davidic kingship — each receives its own dedicated *brachah* later in the *Shmoneh Esrei*. Nevertheless, Rashi explains that because the term *geulah* applies to it, and because there is genuine power in this personal dimension of being pulled out of the depths — echoing the *pasuk* *hagoel mishachat chayeichi*, "who redeems your life from the pit," precisely the language of personal rescue — it was assigned to the seventh position.

This is worth pausing on. The *pasuk* from which this *brachah* draws — *harofei l'chol tachaluayich hagoel mishachat chayeichi* — captures something real about personal experience: there are moments when a person does not merely feel unwell or burdened, but feels utterly submerged, as if in *shachat*, in the depths, and God's intervention is experienced as personal rescue. That is *geulah* at the individual level.

### War & Atchalta

The placement in the seventh position also generates a textual tension that the *Gemara* addresses. A teaching is cited: in the sixth year are the *kolot*, sounds or premonitions of war; in the seventh year are the *milchamot*, the wars themselves; only after the seventh — in what would be the eighth year — does *ben David* arrive. If ultimate redemption comes only after the seventh, why place *geulah* in the seventh?

The *Gemara* resolves this by invoking a phrase of great significance: *milchama nami atchalta degeulah hi* — even the war of the seventh year is itself the beginning of redemption. The wars are not a delay of *geulah* but its opening phase. The concept of *atchalta degeulah*, the beginning of the redemptive process, is foundational in thinking about how redemption unfolds — not as a single instantaneous event but as a process with stages, in which even apparent suffering and upheaval can represent the opening of something larger. This perspective becomes all the more pressing when considered against the backdrop of ongoing and difficult conflict in our own time.

### Refuah in Eighth

With *geulah* placed seventh for reasons of symbolic numerology, *refuah* is necessarily displaced to the eighth position. The *Gemara* might have stopped there, but Rabbi Acha offers an additional reason: *mitoch she-nitna milah bishminis she-tzricha refuah* — because *milah* is given on the eighth day and requires healing, *refuah* is placed eighth. This is a correspondence of symbolic number rather than a logical sequence of ideas, and it is noticeably less satisfying than the carefully reasoned connections traced in the earlier *brachot*. The logical thread of *binah*-*teshuvah*-*selichah* gave way to a different mode of justification, one grounded in numerical symbolism.

---

## Birchat Hashanim

### Psalm 9 & Breaking Evil

The *Gemara* continues: *u'mah ra'u lomar birchat hashanim bitshi'it* — why is *mevarech hashanim*, the *brachah* for sustenance and agricultural blessing, placed ninth? Rabbi Alexandri answers: it corresponds to those who manipulate prices — *kineged maskie she'arim* — the price-fixers who exploit the poor and deprive them of basic necessities. The verse cited is *shevor zero'a rasha*, "break the arm of the wicked," which in its context refers to those who use economic power to harm the vulnerable.

### Justice in Sustenance

The connection being drawn is between the blessing of sustenance and the perversion of sustenance through injustice. The provision of *Birchat Hashanim* — the physical food and economic stability that allows people to live — is undermined precisely by those who manipulate markets and concentrate access to basic goods. Praying for the blessing of the years is thus not merely an agricultural petition; it carries within it an implicit demand for economic justice, that the basic sustenance God provides should actually reach those who need it. The numerical connection to the ninth is grounded in the fact that David articulated this in the ninth *perek* of Psalms — though there is a textual question worth noting: Rashi identifies it as the eighth *perek*, while another authority identifies it as the tenth. This discrepancy reflects the broader question of whether the first two *perakim* of Psalms were treated by *Chazal* as a single unit. The second *perek* does not open with a standard heading — no *mizmor le-David* or *lamnatze'ach* — and its final verse, *ashrei kol chosei vo*, echoes the opening of the first *perek*, *ashrei ha-ish*. This structural envelope suggests that what we now number as two were originally understood as one, which would shift all subsequent numbering accordingly.

---

## National Arc of Geulah

### Gathering Exiles

With *birchat hashanim* established, the *Gemara* notes a pivot in the character of the middle *brachot*: *u'mah ra'u lomar kibbutz galuyot achar birchat hashanim* — why does *kibbutz galuyot*, the gathering of the exiles, follow the *brachah* of sustenance? The answer draws on a verse: *Ve'atem harei Yisrael anpechem titenu u'pirechem tisa'u le'ami Yisrael ki karevu lavo* — "and you, mountains of Israel, shall give forth your branches and bear your fruit for my people Israel, for the time of coming is near." The blossoming of the land and its agricultural abundance — which is precisely what *birchat hashanim* invokes — is itself a prophetic sign and foreshadowing of the impending redemption. The *brachah* of sustenance thus functions not only as a personal petition but as a threshold that opens into the national arc of *geulah*.

From this point, the character of the *brachot* shifts from the personal to the national and collective.

### Din in Geulah

Once the exiles are gathered, the *Gemara* explains, *na'asa din b'resha'im* — judgment is executed against the wicked. National restoration is not simply a matter of return and rebuilding; it necessarily entails the establishment of justice. The verse cited is *Ve'ashiva yadai alayich ve'etzrof kavor sigayich* — "I will turn my hand against you and smelt out your dross" — evoking the prophetic image of a painful but necessary process of purification in which the wicked are judged and a society grounded in *mishpat* is established.

It is striking that the *Gemara* frames this not in terms of establishing courts and institutions of justice — though *Ve'ashiva shoftecha k'varishona* is also cited, "I will restore your judges as at first" — but primarily in terms of *din b'resha'im*, the judgment executed against the wicked themselves. The *Gemara*'s framing reflects the sequence within the *brachot*: *Melech ohev tzedaka u'mishpat*, the establishment of justice as a divine attribute and aspiration; then *shover oyvim u'machnia zeidim*, the breaking of enemies and humbling of the arrogant; then ultimately *mishan u'mivtach la'tzadikim*, the support and protection of the righteous. The sequence runs from the system of justice to its implementation to its beneficiary effect of allowing righteousness to flourish.

Rashi notes that the *Gemara*'s specific emphasis on two categories — *posh'im* and *zeidim* — is deliberate: *posh'im elu ozevei Hashem*, those who abandon God, and *zeidim* as those who actively rebel. Rashi sharpens this further to include those who reject *Torah min ha-shamayim*. The emphasis is not merely on the wicked in a general moral sense but specifically on those whose wickedness includes rejection of the divine authority underlying the Torah.

### Tzadikim & Gerim

Once the wicked are judged and the *posh'im* have been dealt with, *mitromemes keren tzadikim* — the horn of the righteous is lifted up. The *Gemara* cites: *Vechol karnei resha'im agade'a, teromamna karnot tzadik* — "I will cut down all the horns of the wicked, and the horn of the righteous will be raised." The suppression of wickedness and the elevation of righteousness are not separate events but two aspects of a single redemptive movement.

The *Gemara* then adds that the *brachah* includes, along with the *tzadikim*, specifically the *gerei hatzedek*, the righteous converts. The proof-text weaves together two juxtaposed verses: *Mipnei seiva takum vehadarta pnei zaken* — "you shall rise before the aged and honor the face of the elder," understood by the rabbis as honoring *tzadikim* and sages — and immediately adjacent: *Vechi yagur itchem ger* — "if a convert dwells among you." The proximity of these verses grounds the inclusion of *gerim* alongside *tzadikim*.

There is real depth here. The elevation of *tzadikim* in the process of *geulah* is connected to the act of choosing — choosing the right path over the wrong one, choosing good over evil. The *ger tzedek* has made the ultimate version of that choice: to affiliate with the Jewish people and their covenant. Even if such a person, being human, will subsequently commit sins as all humans do, the fundamental act of choosing conversion carries its own moral weight and religious dignity. The inclusion of *gerei hatzedek* with *tzadikim* in this *brachah* thus affirms that the criterion for this elevation is not a perfect halakhic ledger but the profound act of choosing.

### Jerusalem & Tzedek

Where does righteousness flourish in its fullest expression? *B'Yerushalayim* — in Jerusalem. The *Gemara* asks: *Veheicha mitremez karna?* — where does this good take root? And the answer is anchored in the verse *Sha'alu shalom Yerushalayim yishlayu ohavayich* — "seek the peace of Jerusalem; those who love it will be at peace." The flourishing of righteousness leads to and is located within the rebuilt Jerusalem. One might have expected Jerusalem to appear earlier in the sequence — after all, a functioning system of courts and justice would seem to require a capital — but the *Gemara*'s point is about process: it is the full flowering of righteousness and good that constitutes the Jerusalem envisioned by the prophets, not merely the physical infrastructure of the city.

This raises the perennial question of what *boneh Yerushalayim* means in our own time, when the physical Jerusalem is built up and flourishing to an unprecedented degree, yet the religious and spiritual Jerusalem of prophetic vision has not been fully realized. Rav Lichtenstein addressed this in the context of *Nachem* on *Tisha B'Av*, noting that the terms *ha'aveila veha'shomema* can be interpreted in a spiritual sense even when they are no longer literally true physically, and adjusting his own practice accordingly — though with characteristic conservatism about altering liturgical text.

### David's Kingship

Once Jerusalem is built: *vekivan she'nivnit Yerushalayim ba David* — then David comes. The *Gemara* cites: *Achar yashuvu b'nei Yisrael u'vikshu et Hashem Eloheihem v'et David malkam* — they will seek God and David their king. This is the climax of the national redemptive arc: the restoration of Davidic kingship, which presumably signifies *Mashiach*. The whole process — gathering of exiles, agricultural renewal, establishment of justice, judgment of the wicked, elevation of the righteous and of converts, the rebuilding of Jerusalem — culminates in this.

It is worth pausing over what is conspicuously absent from this entire arc: the word *mashiach* never appears. The language remains carefully abstract — *keren yeshuah*, *tzemach david*, *v'karno* — never naming the Messiah directly. Scholars of Jewish liturgy, notably Reuven Kimmelman, have argued that this is intentional: the *Shmoneh Esrei* is deliberately constructed to present the redemptive vision in terms that are organic, gradual, and anchored in this world — without the otherworldly, miraculous, or messianic-personality-focused dimensions that can sometimes pull religious consciousness away from present responsibilities. One can read through the entire national arc of the *Shmoneh Esrei* and find a utopian vision that is entirely this-worldly in its articulation. The Rambam's strong opposition to excessive preoccupation with *Mashiach* as a distraction from present obligations is consonant with this reading.

There is also a textual-historical dimension: evidence from the Tosefta suggests that *boneh Yerushalayim* and *tzemach David* were at one point a single combined *brachah*, and that the nineteenth *brachah* was not *v'la'malshinim* but rather the split of these two. The rebuilding of Jerusalem and the restoration of Davidic kingship belong organically together, as two inseparable aspects of the same redemptive reality.

---

## Prayer & Temple

### Shomea Tefillah

The *Gemara* continues: *vekivan sheba David ba'ah tefilla* — once we have the Davidic kingship, prayer arrives. The verse cited is: *Vahavi'otim el har kodshi vesimachtim b'veit tefillati* — "I will bring them to My holy mountain and gladden them in My house of prayer." What happens at the moment of messianic culmination? The Temple is reestablished — but the *Gemara* characterizes it as a house of *tefilla*, not a house of *korbanot*.

This is a striking framing. *Shomea Tefillah* in its natural function within *Shmoneh Esrei* serves as a kind of capstone to the preceding petitions: having made all the specific requests, one now asks that those prayers be heard. Rav Soloveitchik adds a further dimension — that *shomea koleinu* is not only a prayer that God hear what we have asked for, but an acknowledgment that we do not always know what we truly need, and so we ask God to respond even to what we have not been able to articulate. But the *Gemara* here reads *shomea tefillah* as part of the arc of *geulah* itself: when redemption comes, the Temple will be established as a place where prayer ascends and is received.

### Retzei & Service

From *tefilla* as the defining character of the renewed Temple, the *Gemara* moves to *retzei*: *vekivan sheba'at tefilla ba'at avodah* — now that prayer is established, the *avodah* follows. The verse: *Oloteichem v'zivicheichem l'ratzon al mizbechi ki beiti beit tefilla yikarei l'chol ha'amim* — "your burnt offerings and your sacrifices will be accepted upon My altar, for My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples." The sequence is maintained: the Temple as a house of prayer comes first, and then, as part of that reality, *korbanot* are accepted within it.

Stepping back from the *Gemara*'s framework, a more straightforward reading of *retzei* within the *Shmoneh Esrei* would see it as functioning alongside *shomea koleinu*: we have made our requests, asked that they be heard, and now we ask that our *avodah* — our *tefilla* standing in place of the *avodah* of the Temple — be accepted. This recalls the classic concept of *tefilla k'neged korbanot*: prayer as the substitute for sacrifice. The invocation of *avodah* in *retzei* evokes the time when *korbanot* were the mechanism by which service was offered and accepted.

Yet the actual text of *retzei* — *hashev ha'avodah lidvir beitecha... v'techezena eineinu b'shuv'cha l'Tzion* — remains oriented toward the future, not the past. It is not a nostalgic evocation of the Temple that was, but a forward-looking prayer for the restoration that will be. This is why the *Gemara* situates *shomea tefillah* within the redemptive arc rather than treating it as a simple concluding petition: the entire movement of these *brachot* looks toward a future in which prayer and service are restored together.

### Absence of Korban

Something profound deserves explicit attention here: the word *korban* is entirely absent from the *Shmoneh Esrei*. Just as *mashiach* never appears in the national arc of *geulah*, *korban* never appears in the liturgy — outside of *musaf*, which is a later and secondary addition. Within the core *Shmoneh Esrei*, one would never know, reading the text as theology, that *tefilla* is supposed to function merely as a substitute for the ideal form of service, *korbanot*. The *tefilla* stands entirely on its own terms.

Even within *retzei*, which is the one *brachah* most concerned with sacrifice, the language is telling. The reference to *korbanot* appears only as *ishei Yisrael*, "the fires of Israel" — not even naming the objects consumed by the fire, only the fire itself. And immediately following *ishei Yisrael* comes *u'tefillatam* — "and their prayer." Even here, *korbanot* are effectively displaced by *tefilla*. The *brachah* reads: *b'ahavah t'kabel b'ratzon* — accept with love and favor — and what is to be accepted is their service and their prayer together, with *tefilla* not merely added as an afterthought but genuinely integrated.

This is not accidental. If one is establishing a religious community whose central act of *avodah* is *tefilla*, and if that community has no access to *korbanot*, it would be theologically counterproductive to construct the liturgy in a way that treats *tefilla* as a weak and inadequate substitute for the real thing. The *Shmoneh Esrei* does not do that. It establishes *tefilla* as the primary mode of service in its own right.

One further detail is illuminating: the opening verse with which *Shmoneh Esrei* is introduced — *Hashem sefatai tiftach ufi yagid tehilatecha* — appears in Psalms 51, and the very next verses read: *ki lo tachpotz zevach v'etena, olah lo tirtzeh — zivchei Elohim ruach nishbara, lev nishbar v'nidkeh Elohim lo tivzeh* — "for You do not desire sacrifice, that I should give it; burnt offering You do not want. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise." The verse with which *Shmoneh Esrei* is framed is thus drawn from a Psalm that explicitly subordinates *korbanot* to the inner service of the heart.

### Modim

Once the service is complete — *vekivan sheba'at avodah ba'at todah* — thanksgiving follows. The *Gemara* reads this in terms of the *korban todah*, citing the verse *zove'ach todah yechabdaneni*, "one who sacrifices a *todah* will honor me." In the framework the *Gemara* is building, the completion of *avodah* is marked by a sacrifice of gratitude. Rashi, however, steps beyond the *korban todah* framing and reads *moda'im* simply as *avodah shel makom* — serving God. Thanksgiving, the acknowledgment of all that God has given and the anticipation that prayers will be answered, is itself a form of divine service, not merely a ritual act of sacrifice. At a structural level, *modim* functions as the natural conclusion of the petitionary arc: we have asked, we have asked to be heard, we have asked that our service be accepted, and now we give thanks.

### Birkat Kohanim

With *modim* complete, the *Gemara* turns to *birkat kohanim*: *u'mah ra'u lomar birkat kohanim achar hoda'ah* — why does the priestly blessing come after *modim*? The verse cited is: *Vayisa Aharon et yadav el ha'am vayivarechem vayered me'asot hachatat ve'ha'olah ve'hashlamim* — Aharon lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them, and then descended from performing the sacrificial service. The *Gemara* clarifies the temporal sequence: *meyasot*, "from having performed" — the verse uses the past tense, meaning Aharon first completed the sacrifices and *then* blessed the people. The blessing came after the service was done.

The logic is structurally elegant. The human being approaches God: we ask (*bakasha*), we ask to be heard (*shomea tefillah*), we ask that our service be accepted (*retzei*), we give thanks (*modim*). Having completed our part of the encounter, the divine response comes in the reverse direction: God blesses us through the medium of the *kohanim*. The verse *v'samu et shemi al benei Yisrael va'ani avarechem* — "they shall place My name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them" — establishes that the priestly blessing is the vehicle of divine blessing flowing toward the human. The encounter is complete only when both directions have been traversed.

### Shim Shalom

Finally: *u'mah ra'u lomar sim shalom achar birkat kohanim* — why does *sim shalom* follow *birkat kohanim*? The verse cited is: *Hashem yivarech et amo bashalom* — "God will bless His people with peace." The divine blessing channeled through the *kohanim* finds its culmination and expression in *shalom*. Notably, the *Gemara* could have cited the final verse of *birkat kohanim* itself — *v'yasem lecha shalom* — which would have been the most direct textual bridge. But in any case, the logic is clear: once God has blessed us, that blessing takes the form of peace.

The *Gemara* frames *shalom* as a *kli*, a vessel — the container that holds and makes real all the other blessings. Without peace, all the other blessings of the *Shmoneh Esrei* cannot be realized; health, sustenance, redemption, justice — all of these require peace as the condition of their actualization. *Sim shalom* thus serves not merely as a closing formality but as the essential framework within which everything asked for throughout the *Shmoneh Esrei* can actually be received.

---

## Prohibition on Praise

### Fixed Liturgy

Having traced the logic and sequence of all eighteen *brachot*, the *Gemara* turns to a striking principle that governs how one relates to that liturgy. *Mikan ve'eilach asur lesaper b'shivcho shel makom* — from this point on, one may not elaborate on God's praise beyond what has been established. The fixed liturgy is not a limitation on piety; it is its protection. The very comprehensiveness of *Shmoneh Esrei* — eighteen *brachot* covering the full range of human need and aspiration — carries with it the acknowledgment that even this does not begin to exhaust what could be said about God. Adding further praise beyond the fixed structure does not enhance one's devotion; it is actually forbidden.

The reasoning is precise: any attempt to enumerate God's praises implies the project of completing that enumeration. Since the task is impossible — no finite being can speak all of God's praises — every attempt to go further falls short in a way that is worse than not attempting it. The fixed liturgy sidesteps this trap. By working within an established form, one does not claim to be saying everything; one is simply fulfilling an obligation. The moment one departs from the fixed form to add one's own elaborations, one implicitly takes on the impossible task of completing what cannot be completed.

### Kol HaMosif Goreia

Rabbi Elazar states: *mai d'chtiv mi yimalel gevurot Hashem yashmia kol tehilato* — "who will speak of God's mighty deeds and make heard all of God's praises?" The verse poses a question: *l'mi na'eh l'malel gevurot Hashem?* — to whom is it fitting to speak of God's great deeds? The answer: only to one who is capable of making heard *all* of God's praises. Since no human being can do that, no human being is truly in a position to elaborate beyond the fixed form.

From this emerges the principle of *kol hamosif goreia* — whoever adds, detracts. If you add praises beyond what the liturgy provides, you are not enhancing your description of God; you are actually diminishing it, because every additional phrase implicitly suggests that the previous phrases were insufficient, and all of them together are still insufficient, and the accumulation of insufficient descriptions does not converge toward truth. Rabbi Yochanan sharpens this: *hamesaper b'shivcho shel Hakadosh Baruch Hu yoter midai ne'ekar min ha'olam* — one who overpraises God is uprooted from the world. The verse cited: *hayisuppar lo ki adaber im amar ish ki yivala* — if you speak about it, the person who says it will be swallowed up.

### Shliach Tzibur Story

The *Gemara* in Berakhot tells the story of a *shliach tzibur* who was adding a long series of elaborate praises of God during his prayer. A rabbi stopped him mid-prayer and asked: so, have you now finished saying all of God's praises? The implicit point is devastating: no enumeration is complete, and the pretense of completeness is itself a form of theological error. By cataloguing attributes — great, mighty, wondrous, powerful, fearsome, strong — the *shliach tzibur* was not drawing nearer to the divine reality but constructing an increasingly inadequate portrait of it.

### Silence Praised

The positive formulation of this principle is given by Rabbi Yehuda of *Kfar Gvraya*: *mai d'chtiv lecha dumiyah tehilla* — what is meant by the verse "to You, silence is praise"? *Sama d'kula mashtoka* — the medicine for all of this is silence. Rav Dimi brings a formulation from the schools of *Eretz Yisrael*: *mila b'sela, mashtoka b'trein* — a word is worth a *sela*, silence is worth two. This is more than a rhetorical flourish. Silence, in the context of speaking about God, is not merely the absence of words; it is the most theologically accurate response to the infinite. The moment words are spoken, the infinite is being measured against finite categories. Silence preserves the acknowledgment that the reality of God exceeds everything that can be said.

### Rambam & Negation

The Rambam finds in this *Gemara* a grounding for one of the central pillars of his philosophical theology: negative theology. The Rambam's claim goes deeper than the pragmatic observation that we cannot say everything about God. He argues that any positive description of God is, at a fundamental level, false — not merely incomplete but positively misleading. Every descriptive term we use is rooted in human reality and human experience. When we say "God is powerful," the word "powerful" carries with it all the connotations of human power — exertion, limitation, capacity. Applying such a term to God does not merely fall short; it actively misrepresents, because it maps a human category onto a reality that is categorically different from everything human.

The Rambam therefore concludes that the only genuinely accurate statements one can make about God are negative ones: God is not finite, God is not limited, God is not composite. Such statements do not purport to describe what God is; they only exclude what God is not. This, at least, does not make a false positive claim. For the Rambam, the *Gemara*'s valorization of silence as the highest praise is not merely a practical counsel against liturgical excess. It is the philosophical acknowledgment that the deepest relationship with the divine is one that recognizes the fundamental inadequacy of all human language to capture divine reality — and that what remains unsaid is, in the most precise sense, closer to truth than anything that can be said.

---

---

# Megillah 18

## Oral vs. Written Reading

### Zachor Zachor Source

The daf opens with the ruling: *kara al peh lo yatza* — if one reads the Megillah orally, that is, from memory without reading from a scroll, one does not fulfill the obligation. The Gemara immediately asks *minalan* — what is the source? Rava derives it through a *gezeirah shavah* linking two appearances of the root *zachar*. The Megillah itself states *ve-hayamim ha-eleh nizkarim* — these days are remembered — and elsewhere, regarding Amalek, the Torah commands *ktov zot zikaron basefer* — write this as a remembrance in a book. The thematic connection to Amalek is not incidental: the story of Haman is understood as the culmination of the Amalekite thread running through the Torah. Since the earlier verse specifies *basefer* — in a book — the principle follows: *mah hallan basefer af kan basefer*, just as there it must be written in a book, so too here.

One might ask: how do we know that *zechira* means active recitation rather than mere mental recall? Perhaps *nizkarim* simply means that the days should be kept in mind. The Gemara preempts this with a *beraisa* on the commandment of *zachor* regarding Amalek: *yachol balev* — perhaps it is fulfilled through internal remembrance? The Torah's parallel command *lo tishkach* — do not forget — already addresses the prohibition against forgetting in one's heart. The positive commandment of *zachor* must therefore add something beyond internal memory: it demands active oral remembrance, *bpeh*. Once that principle is established for *zachor* by Amalek, it carries over through the *gezeirah shavah* to the reading of the Megillah.

### Pirsumei Nisa & Ritual

This connection between memory and ritual act runs very deep in Jewish thought. Yosef Yerushalmi, in his aptly named book *Zachor*, draws a distinction between history and memory. The Jewish people have not historically produced historians in the modern sense, yet have been extraordinarily accomplished at memory — at creating communal and cultural frameworks through which the past is kept alive. The key instrument of that memory is ritual: all the commandments bound up with *yetzias mitzrayim*, *le-ma'an tizkor yom tzeischa me-eretz mitzrayim*, are about constructing memory through ritual acts. The Megillah reading belongs to this same tradition: it is not sufficient to remember the miracle of Purim inwardly; it must be enacted, performed, read aloud from a text.

### Hebrew Scroll/Reading

Having established that one must read from a scroll, the Gemara raises a question worth pausing over: is the requirement of Hebrew an insistence on the nature of the *reading* — that the act itself must be performed in Hebrew — or is it a requirement about the *scroll*, that only a Hebrew scroll constitutes a valid *megillah*? This distinction will play out in the subsequent discussion of reading in foreign languages, and it is not immediately obvious which way the analysis will resolve.

---

## Translation & Languages

### Two Translation Cases

The Gemara rules that *kara targum lo yatza* — if one read the Megillah in translation, one has not fulfilled the obligation. But the Gemara immediately asks *heichi dami* — what is the actual case? If the scroll is written in Hebrew but the reader recites a translation, that is simply reading from memory — *hainu al peh* — and the problem is just the one already addressed. The novel case must therefore be where the scroll itself is written in translation: *de-chsiva targum ve-karai lei targum* — written in a foreign language and read in that foreign language. That scroll-based reading is what fails to fulfill the obligation.

Yet the very same passage then states: *aval korin oso le-loazim belaz* — one may read the Megillah for foreigners in a foreign language. The tension is immediate: you have just said reading in another language is invalid, and now you say it is valid?

### Rav & Shmuel Greek

Rav and Shmuel both say *belaz Yevani* — Greek. Their approach is to resolve the contradiction by narrowing the valid exception to Greek specifically. They build on the earlier discussion in which a special position holds that while a *sefer Torah* may in principle be written in any language, one opinion permits only Greek as an alternative — a position associated with the tradition that Greek alone is an acceptable substitute for Hebrew in sacred scrolls. Rav and Shmuel apply this to the Megillah: the reason reading in another language is generally invalid is that a scroll in another language is not a *kasher* scroll; the single exception is Greek, which does constitute a valid scroll. Therefore, a Megillah written and read in Greek would satisfy the obligation.

But the Gemara must first sort out what scenario Rav and Shmuel are even addressing. If the scroll is written in Hebrew and the reader renders it in Greek, *hainu al peh* — that is again just oral recitation. Rav Acha citing Rabbi Elazar clarifies: the case must be *she-ktuva belaz Yevanis* — a Megillah actually written in Greek script.

At this point, the Gemara takes a digression. Since the statement was attributed to Rav Acha citing Rabbi Elazar, the Gemara chains on additional statements in that name — including a striking exegetical claim that God called Jacob "El": *vayikra lo El Elohei Yisrael*. The Gemara reasons that if Jacob were the subject calling the altar *El*, the verse should have said *vayikra lo Yaakov*; since it does not, *Elohei Yisrael* must be the subject, and it is God who calls Jacob by the divine name. This opens enormous theological terrain — Jacob's face on the *kise ha-kavod*, the kabbalistic identification of *Kneses Yisrael* with the tenth *sefirah* of *malchus* — but it must be bracketed here.

### Loazim Exception

Returning to the main discussion: the Gemara raises a challenge from a *beraisa*. *Kara Giftis, Ivris, Elamis, Madis, Yevanis lo yatza* — if one read the Megillah in Coptic, the language of the Hebrews, Elamite, Median, or Greek, one has not fulfilled the obligation. This appears to directly contradict Rav and Shmuel, since Greek is explicitly listed among the languages that do not work.

The Gemara then introduces a parallel *beraisa*: *Giftis le-Giftim, Ivris le-Ivrim, Elamis le-Elamim, Yevanis le-Yevanim — yatza*. One fulfills the obligation by reading each language *for the people of that language*. This is, the Gemara notes, simply the *pshat* of the Mishnah's own formulation: *le-loazim belaz* — for foreigners in their foreign tongue. The exception is not about Greek in particular; it is about tailoring the reading to its native speakers.

This makes the prolonged effort to identify the exception as specifically Greek seem unnecessary, and the Gemara acknowledges it: given this understanding of the *beraisa*, why did Rav and Shmuel need to situate the entire case in Greek? Any language should work, as long as the reading is directed to native speakers of that language. The Gemara concludes: *ella masnisin ke-braisa* — Rav and Shmuel were simply mistaken about the Mishnah; the Mishnah follows the *beraisa* straightforwardly. *Le-loazim belaz* means: for people of that language, in their language.

### Greek Exception

Having set aside the question as it pertains to the Mishnah, the Gemara asks what Rav and Shmuel's point about Greek was intended to address. The answer is that they were making a broader claim: *laz Yevani le-chol kasher* — Greek is valid for *anyone*, not merely for Greek speakers. Just as a Megillah in Hebrew may be read to any person, even one who does not understand a word of Hebrew, so too a Megillah in Greek may be read to anyone. This rests on the position of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — *af sefarim lo hitiru she-yikasvu ella Yevanis* — that the sages permitted sacred books to be written only in Greek as an alternative to Hebrew. Since Greek functions as a kind of parallel to Hebrew for sacred writing, it shares Hebrew's universal applicability as a reading language.

The Gemara then asks: why not simply state the ruling explicitly as *halachah ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel*? The concern is that one might have thought Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position applied only to a *sefer Torah* and other sacred texts, but that the Megillah — which says *ke-chsavam*, as it is written — would require Hebrew specifically. The Gemara therefore teaches explicitly that Greek is valid for the Megillah as well.

It is worth noting that the word *ke-chsavam* appears in the Megillah in a context that cuts the other way entirely. *Ke-chsavam ve-chilshonam* — as each people's script and language — refers to Achashverosh's letters being sent to every nation in its own language and script. The very phrase used to insist on Hebrew has its origin in an embrace of universal linguistic diversity: to the Kushites in their script, to the Hebrews in theirs. There is something almost ironic in the fact that a phrase born of multicultural communication has been deployed as a limiting principle requiring Hebrew.

The practical upshot of Rav and Shmuel's position — though we do not rule this way — is that the same way anyone can fulfill the obligation by hearing a Megillah in Hebrew, even without understanding it, anyone could also fulfill it by hearing a Megillah in Greek. The *pshat* of the Mishnah, however, remains: a foreign-language scroll is valid only for native speakers of that language, meaning both that the scroll constitutes a sufficient *kasher* Megillah from the standpoint of the ritual object, and that the act of reading in that language counts as the *mitzvah* — but only under that condition.

### Understanding Requirement
