This raises a natural question about the middle ground: what of someone who is a native speaker of another language but also understands Hebrew reasonably well, though not as fluently as their mother tongue? The analysis suggests that the native-language exception applies when Hebrew is genuinely inaccessible; once someone is sufficiently fluent in Hebrew, the accommodations afforded to *loazim* would no longer apply. The threshold is not sharply defined by the Gemara here, but the underlying principle seems to be: the tailoring to native language is for those to whom Hebrew is not a real option.

One observation worth making is that the tradition of the *torgeman* — the translator who rendered the Torah reading into Aramaic immediately after each verse — is conspicuously absent from this discussion. That may itself be telling. The *torgeman* system worked precisely because the listeners had some understanding of the Hebrew but needed the Aramaic clarification. Here the Gemara is dealing with people who may have no access to Hebrew at all. And that may be exactly why the Gemara in the case of the Mishnah concludes that the native-language Megillah is actually the *lechatchila* option for a *loaz*, with the Hebrew reading being the *bediavad* fallback — the language of *ve-lo shama sheyesh yatza*, "if one heard it in the original," sounds like a post-facto concession.

### Ravina Pirsumei Nisa

The Gemara presses: but if someone hears the Megillah in Hebrew without understanding a word of it — *ve-ha lo yadai mai kaamri* — how can they possibly be *yotzei*? The Gemara responds: *midai d'hava anashim* — it is no different from women and *amei ha-aretz* who similarly do not understand the Hebrew but fulfill the obligation by hearing it.

This answer only partially satisfies. Ravina responds with a rhetorical challenge of his own: *atu anan ha-achashteranim bnei ha-ramachim mi yadeinan?* — do we ourselves know what "the sons of the steeds" means? We, the rabbis, also recite phrases in the Megillah whose precise meaning eludes us. What then is the obligation? *Mitzvas kriya u-pirsumei nisa* — there is a commandment to read it, and it publicizes the miracle.

This is worth examining carefully. *Pirsumei nisa* would seem to require that the audience understand what is being said — if the miracle is to be publicized, surely comprehension is necessary. Yet Ravina uses *pirsumei nisa* to explain why even incomprehension does not defeat the obligation. Rashi's comment illuminates this: even those who do not understand the words they are hearing will ask those around them what this reading is and how the miracles came about — *sho'alim es ha-shom'im ve-omrim mah hi ha-kriyah ha-zo ve-eich ha-nissim modiyim lahem*. The public nature of the gathering creates the publicizing of the miracle, even without precise verbal comprehension. The ritual act of coming together, hearing the reading performed, and then talking about it — that is *pirsumei nisa*.

This explains why Ravina uses *pirsumei nisa* alongside *mitzvas kriya* rather than instead of it. The commandment to read has its own integrity as a ritual act; the *pirsumei nisa* dimension does not require precise understanding because it operates at the level of communal experience and subsequent conversation. The parallel to Chanukah is apt: on Chanukah there is no reading of a text at all — there is lighting, there is gathering, there is the public marking of the miracle. Here the reading is more specific, but the *pirsumei nisa* component functions similarly.

---

## Vocabulary Digressio (II)

### Rare Hebrew Words

The Gemara records a series of cases in which the rabbis encountered rare words — in Mishnaic texts, in Aramaic texts, and in Scriptural verses — whose meaning they did not know, and how they came to understand them through observation of everyday speech.

The first concerns the word *seirugin* itself, which appears in the Mishnah's ruling that one who reads the Megillah with breaks (*kara seirugin*) still fulfills the obligation. The rabbis did not know what the word meant. They heard the maidservant of Rabbi Judah the Patriarch's household (*amta d'vei Rabbi*) chide the scholars who were entering the house in disconnected groups rather than all together: *ad matay atem nichnasin seirugin seirugin* — how long will you keep entering in broken-up intervals? From this they understood: *seirugin* means breaks, intervals, a chopped-up pattern.

The second word was *haluglogot*, a vegetable mentioned in various *mishnayot*. Again, from the same household: the maidservant instructed a certain man to stop scattering his *parpachini* — another vegetable — and called it *haluglogekha*. The vegetable has been identified as parsley.

The third case involved the scriptural phrase *salsela u-teromemeka* — delve into it and it will lift you up — from the book of Proverbs, in the context of Torah study. The rabbis did not understand *mesalsel*. The maidservant addressed a man who was constantly running his fingers through his hair: *ad matay ata mesalsel be-sa'arekha* — how long will you keep tussling your hair? The meaning: to run one's fingers through, to delve into and turn over — and thus, immerse yourself in Torah and it will elevate you.

What is striking in all three cases is that the maidservant of Rabbi's household speaks in Hebrew — the narrative framing is Aramaic, but her direct speech consistently uses the Hebrew terms that eluded the scholars. The vernacular of the time was Aramaic; Hebrew was the language of learning. That she was fluent in these rarer Hebrew usages likely reflects the linguistic environment of Rabbi's household, where Hebrew held a more prominent place. And there is a pointed irony here that one participant in the shiur rightly noted: just moments before, the Gemara had invoked women and *amei ha-aretz* as examples of people who do not understand Hebrew — and now the *amta d'vei Rabbi* is the one teaching the rabbis what Hebrew words mean. It is a notable counterpoint.

---

## Reading Continuity (III)

### Seirugin Breaks

Now that we understand *seirugin*, the Gemara returns to the ruling itself: *kara seirugin yatza* — one who reads with breaks still fulfills the obligation. The companion ruling is *serusin lo yatza* — reading out of order, or backwards, does not fulfill the obligation.

---

## Vocabulary Digressio (II)

### More Vocabulary

The Gemara records additional vocabulary cases. The word *yehav* — burden — was unfamiliar. Rabbah Bar Bar Chana relates that while traveling with an Arab, the man told him: *sh'kol yehavcha u-shadi agmalay* — take your *yehav* and throw it on my camel. From this context, *yehav* clearly means a burden or load, which illuminated the Psalm's *hashlech al Hashem yehavcha* — cast your burden upon God.

The word *metateh* — broom, and the verb *le-tate*, to sweep — from the verse in Isaiah about sweeping with the broom of destruction (*matateh ha-shmad*) was likewise unknown. Again the maidservant: she told her friend *sh'kuli tatita ve-tati beisa* — take your broom and sweep out the house. The meaning was immediately clear.

---

## Reading Continuity (III)

### Rav Mona Measure

The Gemara returns to the laws of *seirugin*. Rav Mona says in the name of Rabbi Yehuda: even regarding *seirugin*, if the pause was long enough — *im shahah kedei ligmor* — specifically, if in that interval one could have read the entire Megillah from beginning to end, then one must return to the beginning. At that scale, the continuity of the reading has been broken. Rav Yosef rules: *halachah ke-Rav Mona*.

Abaye then asks Rav Yosef to clarify: does "long enough to finish" mean long enough to read from the current point to the end of the Megillah, or long enough to read the entire Megillah from beginning to end? Rav Yosef answers: *mereisha le-sofah* — from beginning to end, the full measure. The reason is a fundamental principle of legal precision: *de-im ken natata devarecha le-shiurin* — if the threshold changes depending on where in the Megillah one is pausing, the measurement has no fixed value. A legal standard that varies at every moment is not a workable standard. The measure must be fixed, and the fixed measure is the full reading time of the Megillah.

### Rav vs. Shmuel Break

The Gemara then presents the *halachic* dispute in two parallel formulations — one from Sura, one from Pumbedisa — but both arrive at the same substantive *machlokes*: Rav says we rule like Rav Mona, Shmuel says we do not. The only variation between the two versions is the identity of who transmitted Rav's position: in the Sura version it comes through Rav Abba citing Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, while in the Pumbedisa version it comes through Rav Kahana. Rav Bibi then reverses the attributions entirely: Rav says we do not rule like Rav Mona, and Shmuel says we do.

Rav Yosef instructs: *nekote de-Rav Bibi be-yadcha* — hold onto Rav Bibi's version. Why? *De-Shmuel hu de-chaish le-yachida'ah* — because it is characteristic of Shmuel to be concerned with individual minority opinions. This is demonstrated from a completely different context: a Mishnah dealing with *shomeres yavam*, in which a brother-in-law performs *kiddushin* with the sister of the woman awaiting *yibum* or *chalitzah*. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's minority opinion holds that one should wait until the elder brother has acted before consummating that marriage — since the elder brother's *zika* creates a quasi-marital connection to the first woman that must be resolved first. The consensus does not follow Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, yet *Shmuel amar halachah ke-Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira* — Shmuel rules like the minority opinion. This is the one instance across all of *Shas* where Shmuel follows a *da'as yachid* against the consensus, and it establishes Shmuel's general tendency to take minority positions seriously.

Applied here: it makes sense that it is Shmuel who would be *choshesh* about the size of the break in the Megillah reading, even if the majority consensus is that no break — however large — invalidates the reading. Tosafot notes that since *halachah* generally follows Rav against Shmuel in disputes of this kind, the ruling is that we do not require concern about the size of a break. One may pause at length during the Megillah reading and still fulfill the obligation.

---

## Scroll Validity

### Missing Text

The Gemara now turns from the act of reading to the physical scroll itself. A *beraisa* teaches: *hishmit bah ha-sofer osiyos o pesukim* — if the scribe omitted letters or verses — *ve-karan ha-koreh ke-meturgeman ha-metargem* — and the reader filled in those missing words as a translator would paraphrase, one has fulfilled the obligation. This ruling establishes two things simultaneously: first, a scroll missing some words or letters can still qualify as a *kasher* Megillah scroll; and second, even though the Megillah must generally be read *mitoch ha-sefer* — from the scroll — not every word needs to come from the written text.

The practical relevance is immediate. At a public Megillah reading, if a congregant was distracted and missed a *pasuk*, that person may read the missing verses independently — even without a *kasher* Megillah scroll in hand, even just from a printed text. The same flexibility that applies to the *ba'al koreh* who encounters an incomplete scroll applies to the listener who needs to fill a gap.

### Smudged Letters

The Gemara raises a challenge from a *beraisa* that seems to impose stricter standards: if letters were *mitushtashot o mekuro'ot* — smudged or broken — the scroll is *kasher* only if *reshumanh nikar*, the form of the letter remains discernible. If not, it is *pasul*. This appears to suggest that even a few problem letters can invalidate the scroll. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya ha be-kulah ha be-miktzatah* — the stricter ruling addresses the case where most of the scroll is smudged, the more lenient ruling addresses partial deficiencies.

### Percentage Threshold

The operative principle is *rov* — majority. As long as more than half the scroll is properly written, it remains *kasher*; the reader may supply the missing portions from memory without invalidating the reading. However — and the Rama codifies this — even within the valid majority, a complete *inyan*, a discrete section, cannot be entirely absent, and the very beginning or very end of the Megillah cannot be missing even in a small amount. The threshold is approximately 51% properly written, with those qualifications.

The *Shulchan Aruch* formulation: *tzarich she-tehei ktuvah kulah lefanav le-chatchilah* — ideally the full text must be before the reader — *aval bediavad im hishmit ha-sofer be-emtza teiva afilu ad chatziyah ve-kara'o ha-korei al peh yatza* — but after the fact, even if up to nearly half the text is missing and the reader supplied it orally, the obligation is fulfilled. This is significant: one can potentially read up to fifty percent of the Megillah from memory and still be *yotzei bediavad*, provided the missing portions do not constitute whole sections and are not from the very beginning or end.

---

## Reading Continuity (III)

### Serussin Out of Order

The *beraisa* teaches: *hishmit bah ha-korei pasuk echad* — if the reader skipped a *pasuk* — one may not continue to the end and then return to read the skipped verse. *Ela korei me-oto pasuk ve-eilach* — one must go back to that verse and read forward from there.

Similarly: if someone enters the synagogue and finds the congregation already halfway through the reading, one may not listen to the rest with the congregation and then go back to read the beginning. *Korei otah mi-techilatan ve-ad sofah* — the reading must proceed from beginning to end, in order. Reading out of sequence is *serusin*, which — as established — invalidates the fulfillment of the obligation.

---

## Intent & Consciousness

### Misnamnem Drowsy

The Mishnah rules *misnamnem yatza* — one who was dozing still fulfills the obligation — but if one was *nirdim*, fully asleep, one does not. The Gemara asks *heichi dami misnamnem* — what precisely is the state of *misnamnem*? Rav Ashi defines it: *nim ve-lo nim, tair ve-lo tair* — asleep and not asleep, awake and not awake. If called, one will respond; but if asked to reason through something, one cannot. Yet if reminded of something, one will remember. That liminal state — between wakefulness and sleep, responsive but not fully processing — is *misnamnem*, and within that state one is considered to have fulfilled the obligation.

### Copying Scenario

The Mishnah continues: *haya kotevah, dorshah, u-magiha — im kiven libo yatza* — if one was copying the Megillah, expounding on it, or proofreading it, if one had intent, one fulfills the obligation. This introduces the question of *kavanah* — intent — in reading the Megillah. At minimum, intent to read the words is required; whether intent to fulfill the *mitzvah* is additionally necessary is a broader question, but the Gemara's focus here is on the act of reading itself.

The Gemara asks: what exactly is the scenario? If the person was composing the Megillah verse by verse from memory — reciting a verse and then writing it — the words being spoken preceded their being written, making the reading *al peh*, from memory. That does not help. The valid scenario, the Gemara concludes, is *de-manacha Megillah kameih ve-kary lah, ve-kary lah minah pesuka pesuka ve-khatev lah* — a complete Megillah lies before the copyist, and the copyist reads each verse from that existing scroll before transcribing it. Each word is read from a written source. The reading is therefore *mitoch ha-ksav* — from written text — even though the new scroll being produced is not yet complete.

### Complete Scroll

Rav Chama bar Guria citing Rav rules: *halachah ke-divrei omer kulah* — the *halachah* requires reading the entire Megillah. Various opinions exist about where the Megillah reading must begin — whether from the first verse (*vayehi bimei Achashverosh*) or from a later point (*ish Yehudi*) — but regardless, even according to the opinion that the reading need not start from the very beginning, the scroll itself must be complete: *tzrichah she-tehei ktuvah kulah* — the entire Megillah must be written in the scroll.

This addresses the copying scenario directly. One cannot fulfill the obligation by writing a word, reading it, writing the next word, reading it, and so on — because at each moment of reading, what lies before the reader is not a *kasher* Megillah. The scroll must pre-exist the reading as a complete object. What is read must be read from a legitimate scroll.

The Gemara then raises a possible support from Rabbah Bar Bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *assur likhtov ot achat she-lo min ha-ksav* — it is forbidden to write even one letter of a *sefer Torah* without copying from an existing written text. If that is the rule, then the copying scenario can simply presuppose that one is working from a pre-existing Megillah. But the Gemara deflects: perhaps that ruling does not apply technically to the Megillah, and the case here is simply *de-istrami lei istramuyei* — it happened to involve copying from an existing scroll, without that being a requirement. The question of whether *she-lo min ha-ksav* is a technical prohibition or merely a safeguard remains open.

---

## Writing from Memory

### Rabbi Meir Exception

The Gemara examines the position of Rabbi Yochanan — *assur likhtov ot achat she-lo min ha-ksav* — and challenges it with a story: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports that Rabbi Meir once traveled to Asia to intercalate the year. No Megillah scroll was available; Rabbi Meir wrote the entire Megillah from memory and they read from it.

Rabbi Abbahu explains this exception: *shani Rabbi Meir de-mikim beih ve-afapekha yashiru negdekha* — Rabbi Meir is different, because the verse "your eyelids are straight before you" applied to him. The image is of perfect clarity of sight — the entire text was, as it were, laid out before him with complete precision. He knew every letter exactly. The rule requiring one to copy from an existing text exists as a safeguard against error; for Rabbi Meir, who had the text with absolute fidelity, the safeguard was unnecessary.

Rami bar Chama then asks Rabbi Yirmiyah from Difti to explain the verse *ve-afapekha yashiru negdekha*. The explanation: it refers to words of Torah, about which the verse says *hata'if einekha bo ve-einennu* — avert your gaze from it and it disappears. Torah is so elusive in its precise details — especially in the written form, where every letter matters — that even a master can lose it. But *afilu hachi meyusharin hen etzel Rabbi Meir* — even so, for Rabbi Meir the text was perfectly clear and present. He could write it without error.

### She'at Hadchak

The Gemara then records Rav Chisda finding Rav Chananel writing *sefarim* — presumably *Sifrei Torah* — without copying from an existing text. Rav Chisda tells him: I have no doubt that *re'uyah kol ha-Torah kulah likatev al pikha* — the entire Torah could be written from your mouth; you know it perfectly. *Ella kach amru chachamim: assur likhtov ot achat she-lo min ha-ksav* — but the sages said: one may not write even one letter without copying from a written source. Whether this means the prohibition admits no exceptions even for those who know the text perfectly, or simply that we do not make individual exceptions because everyone imagines their knowledge to be perfect, the practical ruling is clear: one does not write *she-lo min ha-ksav*.

Yet by Rabbi Meir it was permitted. The Gemara resolves this: *she'at ha-dechak shani* — a time of pressing need is different. Rabbi Meir's situation — traveling in Asia, no Megillah available, the community unable to fulfill the *mitzvah* of reading — constituted a *she'at ha-dechak* that justified the exception. In ordinary circumstances, even someone who knows the text with complete accuracy does not write from memory. In an emergency, the normal safeguard gives way.

### Tefillin Mezuzot

Finally, the Gemara records that Abaye permitted the household of Bar Chavu to write *tefillin* and *mezuzot* without copying from an existing text. The Gemara asks: like whom does this ruling go? It follows a *tanna* — Rabbi Yirmiyah citing Rabbeinu — who explicitly states that *tefillin u-mezuzot nikhtavim she-lo min ha-ksav* — *tefillin* and *mezuzot* may be written from memory, without copying. They also do not require *sirtut*, the scoring of lines, though the *halachah* distinguishes between them: *tefillin ein tzerikhin sirtut, mezuzah tzrichah sirtut* — *tefillin* do not require scoring but *mezuzot* do. Both, however, may be written *she-lo min ha-ksav*.

The reason given: *migras gariseynhu* — people know these texts thoroughly. *Shema* and the adjoining passages are recited twice daily; their texts are universally familiar. This is a striking conclusion. One might have expected *tefillin* and *mezuzot* — the most ritually charged of all scribal objects — to carry the strictest requirements regarding transcription. Yet here it emerges that *she-lo min ha-ksav* is not a technical legal requirement at all, but only a rabbinic safeguard against error. Where the text is so well-known that error is practically impossible, the safeguard has no application. The question of whether the scroll was *read* from a *tefillin* or *mezuzah* — an interesting question to raise — lies outside the scope of the discussion here, since these objects are not read from in the relevant halachic sense.

---

---

# Megillah 19

## Megillah Writing Require…

### Prohibited Inks

The daf opens at the very end of 18b, completing the discussion of how the *megillah* must be written and read. The *gemara* establishes that if the *megillah* was written with *sama* — an arsenic-based mineral dye — it is invalid. Similarly prohibited are *sikreta*, a red pigment derived from lead; *komos*, a dye made from tree resin; *kankantom*; and *charta d'uskhafi*, which Rashi identifies as a black dye used for dyeing leather.

### Valid Parchment Materials

The *gemara* then turns to *diftera*, the type of leather one may not write on. *Diftera* is defined as leather that has been salted and treated with flour (*demaliach vekamiach*), but has not been treated with water, and — critically — has not been treated with *afatzim*, that is, gallnuts, which were also used as a basis for dye. Writing on plain paper (*niyar*), understood as a cloth-based writing surface, is likewise invalid. The *gemara* concludes: *ad she'tehei kesuva Ashuris* — until it is written in *Ashuris*, which is the Hebrew script familiar today, the Babylonian-influenced square script (named for *Ashur*), as distinct from the ancient Hebrew script. This requirement is supported by the verse in Esther, *kechsavam ukizmanam*, "according to their writing and their time," which reflects that this was the writing of the period.

### Ashuris Script & Ink

The requirement that the *megillah* be written *al hasefer bedyo* — on parchment with ink — is derived through a *gezeirah shavah*. The word for writing (*kesuva*) appears here in connection with Esther, and similarly in the book of Yirmiyahu, where Baruch the scribe describes his work: *va'ani koseiv al hasefer bedyo*, "and I write on the parchment with ink." The *gezeirah shavah* links the *megillah* to this earlier text, establishing that valid writing requires parchment and ink, in *Ashuris* script. What precisely constituted that ink — its ingredients — is a matter taken up by the *rishonim*.

### Tosafot on Ink Ingredien…

Tosafot raises a pressing difficulty. The *gemara* specifies that *diftera* — untreated with *afatzim* — is invalid as a writing surface. This implies that valid *klaf* must be treated with gallnuts. Yet, Tosafot asks, how do we write on our *kelafim* today for *sifrei Torah*, *tefillin*, and *megillos*, given that they are not treated with *afatzim*? Rabbeinu Tam answers that the plaster (*sid*) applied to contemporary *kelafim* serves the same function as the *afatzim* treatment. This is, by any measure, a radical move: the *gemara* specifies precise materials for the preparation of *klaf*, and Rabbeinu Tam is arguing that a functionally equivalent substitute is acceptable.

### Minhag vs. Gemara

What makes this striking is that Rabbeinu Tam was not innovating a new practice — he was justifying one already universally accepted. The widespread practice was already in place, and he came to explain how it could be considered valid. This reveals the extraordinary power of *minhag*: to reinterpret explicit *gemara* requirements on the basis of accepted practice requires considerable audacity. Yet that is precisely what was done.

In the same passage, Tosafot records that Rabbeinu Tam also wanted to go in the opposite direction on the question of ink. He argued that ink made from gallnuts (*afatzim*) does not constitute valid *dyo*, drawing support from a *braitah* in *Gittin* that discusses the permissibility of various writing substances, and concluding that the standard for rabbinic ink excludes gallnut-based ink. On that basis, he sought to invalidate *sifrei Torah* written with gallnut ink — a position the German communities (*ashkenazim*) pushed back on vigorously.

One detail that emerges in this discussion is the traditional requirement that ink be erasable, a tradition derived from the case of *sotah*, where the text is scraped into the water. There is a certain irony here: one might expect that a sacred text would demand the most permanent medium possible, yet the halakhic tradition points in the opposite direction.

Taken together, these two adjacent discussions in Tosafot are fascinating: in one case Rabbeinu Tam defers to practice and reinterprets the *gemara* to justify it; in another, he invokes the *gemara* against an established practice. The interplay between textual authority and accepted custom could not be illustrated more sharply.

---

## Location & Reading Dates

### Mishnah: City Types

The *mishnah* introduces a new issue: *ben ir shehalach lechrach uven krach shehalach le'ir* — a resident of an unwalled city who went to a walled city, or a resident of a walled city who went to an unwalled city. Since the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar are read on different days depending on whether one's city is walled or unwalled, a traveler faces a question of identity: which day does he observe? The *mishnah* answers: *im atid lachzor limkomo korei kimkomo* — if he intends to return to his place of origin, he reads according to the schedule of his hometown, even if that differs from where he is at the time. *Ve'im lav korei imahem* — if he does not plan to return, he reads with the people of the city he is in.

The question of "return by when" is left open by the *mishnah* and will be addressed by the *gemara*.

### Rava: Night of 14th

Rava sharpens the rule considerably: *lo shanu ela she'atid lachzor beleil yod-dalet* — the principle that one reads like his place of origin applies only if he plans to return on the night of the fourteenth. If, however, he will not return until after daybreak of the fourteenth, then *korei imahem* — he reads with the people of the city he finds himself in, since he will be present during the daytime reading, which is the determinative act.

This requires some unpacking. The *mishnah* knows only of a daytime reading; it is only in the *gemara* that a nighttime reading is added. The daytime reading therefore remains the identifying marker. The critical question is: will you be in this city on the morning they read? If yes, you are considered a member of that city for *mikra megillah* purposes. If not, you remain identified with your city of origin.

To illustrate: a person from Jerusalem visiting Tel Aviv finds himself there on the night of the fourteenth. If he plans to remain through the morning, he reads with Tel Aviv on the fourteenth — at night and again in the morning. If he is from Tel Aviv and travels to Jerusalem before the fourteenth, arriving on the thirteenth: if he plans to be in Jerusalem on the morning of the fifteenth, when Jerusalem reads, he does not read on the fourteenth at all. He has become, for purposes of *megillah*, a citizen of Jerusalem.

Rava then asks: *mina amina lah* — what is the source for this rule? The verse in Esther states: *al ken ha-yehudim ha-perazim ha-yoshvim b'arei ha-perazot* — "therefore the Jews of the unwalled cities, who dwell in the unwalled cities." The redundancy is telling: we already know they are *perazim*; why specify that they *dwell* in the unwalled cities? *Peraz ben yomo nikra peraz* — a one-day resident of an unwalled city is already considered an unwalled-city person. A single day of presence on the determinative day suffices to establish one's identity for that year's *megillah* reading.

### One-Day Residents

One might then ask: this derivation establishes the rule for a *peraz*, an unwalled-city resident — but what about the reverse? If a one-day Tel Avivian is a Tel Avivian, is a one-day Jerusalemite a Jerusalemite? The *gemara* answers by *sevara* — logical symmetry: *iy d'peraz ben yomo korei peraz, mukaf ben yomo korei mukaf*. If residence for a single critical day establishes identity in one direction, it does so equally in the other direction. A person spending only that one critical morning in a walled city reads on the fifteenth.

### Village to City

Rava then addresses a distinct case: *ben kfar shehalach l'ir* — a villager who has traveled to a city. Here we are no longer discussing the fourteenth versus the fifteenth, but rather the earlier market-day reading permitted for villagers (on the eleventh, twelfth, or thirteenth, whenever Monday falls before Purim). The entire rationale for that leniency was that villagers come into the city on market day and are therefore available to hear the *megillah* read. The question is: if such a villager, having already read early on market day, now finds himself in the city again on the night of the fourteenth — does he read again?

### Market Day Reading

Rava rules: *bein kach uvein kach korei imahem* — regardless of whether he plans to return home before daybreak or stay through the morning, he reads with the city residents. Rashi explains: the case is a villager who already read two days earlier on market day and is now back in the city on the night of the fourteenth, intending to leave before dawn. Even so, he must read again.

Why? *K'vnei ha'ir ba'inan l'mikrei* — because in principle, even a villager's obligation is to read on the fourteenth, like city residents. *Ve'rabbanan hu d'akilu al ha-kfarim k'dei she-yispeku mayim u'mazon l'acheihem she-bakrachim* — the Rabbis provided an early-reading leniency specifically so that villagers could supply food and water to the larger communities without being burdened. That leniency applies only *hani mili ki isa b'duchtei* — when, come the actual fourteenth, he is not in the city. *Aval ki isa b'ir, k'vnei ha'ir ba'inan l'mikrei* — but if he is in fact in the city on the fourteenth, his prior reading was only a substitute, and now that the real thing is available to him, the substitute does not discharge him.

Tosafot finds this deeply troubling — can a person who is already *yotzei* be required to read again? Yet Tosafot ultimately accepts Rashi's reading, recognizing that the early reading was a conditional leniency: it counted only on the assumption that the person would not be present for the primary obligation. Since he now is present, the leniency is retroactively inapplicable.

### Braitot Reconciliation

Abaye challenges Rava from a *braitah* that states a *ben kerach* who travels to an unwalled city reads *k'shiuro* — according to his original place — in all cases. This would seem to conflict with the *mishnah*, which makes the determination depend on whether one plans to return. Abaye prefers not to say the *braitah* argues with the *mishnah*, and so proposes that the text of the *braitah* is corrupt: *kerach* (walled city) should read *kefar* (village). As emended, the *braitah* would say that a villager always reads according to his original place — meaning even if he finds himself in the city on the fourteenth, his prior reading stands, in contradiction to Rava.

The *gemara* responds sharply: *v'lav tirutza m'taratzat?* — once you have already emended the text to avoid one contradiction, you have surrendered the right to use it as a source for a new one. The *gemara* can simply re-emend *korei k'shiuro* to *korei imahem*, restoring agreement with Rava. Once textual manipulation has begun, the *braitah* can no longer serve as the basis for a *kushya*.

---

## Starting Point of Reading

### Four Opinions

The *mishnah* raises a second question entirely separate from the matter of traveling between cities: *me'heichan korei adam et ha'megillah* — from where does one begin reading the *megillah* in order to fulfill the obligation (*latzeis yedei chovato*)? Rabbi Meir says: the entire *megillah* (*kulah*). Rabbi Yehudah says: from *Ish Yehudi* — the beginning of Mordechai's story. Rabbi Yosei says: from *Achar HaDevarim HaEleh* — which is when Haman enters the narrative.

### Gezeira Shava Analysis

Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai adds a fourth position, not in the *mishnah*: from *Balaila Hahu* — "on that night," the pivotal turning point when everything begins to reverse itself. One might understand this as capturing the *neis* itself: even if you miss the entire buildup, you have the story of the miracle, which is what is being commemorated.

Rabbi Yochanan observes: *v'chulam mikra echad darshu* — all four opinions derive from a single verse: *vatichtov Ester ha'malkah u'Mordechai ha'Yehudi et kol tokef* — "and Esther the queen and Mordechai the Jew wrote all the *tokef*," the power. The word *tokef* — power, or the substance of the matter — becomes the shared analytical key. Each opinion identifies a different center of gravity in the narrative and therefore a different starting point. According to the one who says the entire *megillah* (*kulah*): *tokfo shel Achashverosh* — the power of Achashverosh, which opens the story. According to the one who says from *Ish Yehudi*: *tokfo shel Mordechai* — the power of Mordechai. According to the one who says from *Achar HaDevarim Ha'Eleh*: *tokfo shel Haman* — the power of Haman. According to the one who says from *Balaila Hahu*: *tokfo shel neis* — the power of the miracle.

### Rabbah's Framework

Rabbah offers an additional interpretive framework, built around the verse *u'ma ra'u al kach v'uma higia aleihem* — "and what did they see about this, and what came upon them?" He reads this as three structural elements of the narrative: what motivated the central actor, what the underlying cause was, and what the result was. This is not merely a literary observation; it is a way of organizing and justifying each of the four starting points.

### Central Characters

For the one who says to read from the beginning (*kulah*): What did Achashverosh see that led him to use the vessels of the *Beit ha-Mikdash*? The cause (*al kach*) was that he calculated that seventy years had passed without the Jews being redeemed, and therefore concluded the prophecy of return would never be fulfilled. The result was that he killed Vashti — which, within this reading, frames the entire *megillah* in the context of the exile, the *Beit ha-Mikdash*, and the cosmic confrontation between Achashverosh's ambitions and the divine promise of redemption.

For the one who says from *Ish Yehudi*: What motivated Mordechai to be *ikni b'Haman* — to be jealous of, or antagonistic toward, Haman by refusing to bow? The cause was *d'shavei nafshei avodah zarah* — that Haman had made himself into an object of idolatrous worship, which explains why Mordechai could not simply bow and spare the Jewish people the subsequent catastrophe. The result was that the miracle occurred. This reading places Mordechai at the center, but does so in a way that also raises uncomfortable questions: to what extent did Mordechai's refusal bring the *tzaros* upon the people?

For the one who says from *Achar HaDevarim Ha'Eleh*: What led Haman to extend his hatred from Mordechai personally to all the Jews? The cause was *d'Mordechai lo yichra v'lo yishtachaveh* — that Mordechai would not bow. The result was that Haman and his sons were hanged. For the one who says from *Balaila Hahu*: What led Achashverosh to call for the book of chronicles to be read to him? The cause was that Esther had invited Haman to the party with Achashverosh. The result was the miracle.

### Hester Panim Theme

What emerges from Rabbah's framework is something more than narrative structure. The *gemara* is probing hidden motives — asking not merely what happened, but what drove people to act as they did, and how those hidden motivations connect to a concealed divine hand in history. The *megillah* is, famously, a text in which God is never mentioned explicitly. The *gemara*'s repeated focus on *u'ma ra'u al kach* — on causes that lie beneath the surface of the story — reflects precisely this quality. People's hidden motives correspond to God's hidden direction of events. The coherence that makes this a *megillah* and not merely a chronicle of coincidences lies in reading that hidden logic. This is the *hester panim* dimension of the *megillah*, and it explains why the *gemara* invests such effort in uncovering the motivations of Achashverosh, Mordechai, Haman, and Esther.

### Halacha: Entire Megillah

The *gemara* then rules: *halacha kedivrei ha'omer kulah* — the law follows the position that one must read the entire *megillah*. And even according to the one who says one need only begin from *Ish Yehudi*, *tzerichah she'tehei ketuva kulah* — the entire *megillah* must nonetheless be written. The object of the *mitzvah* requires a complete scroll even if one is not required to read every word aloud.

---

## Megillah: Sefer vs. Iger…

### Sefer and Igeret

The *gemara* introduces a principle of dual identity: *megillah nikret sefer venikret iggeret* — the *megillah* is called both a *sefer*, a book (like a *Sefer Torah*), and an *iggeret*, a letter. Being called a *sefer* imposes more stringent formal requirements; being called an *iggeret* relaxes certain standards. The interplay between these two designations governs a series of practical halakhic questions.

### Parchment Threads

One implication: *nikret sefer she'im tefarah bechutei pishtan pesulah* — because it is called a *sefer*, if the parchments are sewn together with flax thread it is invalid. A *Sefer Torah* must be sewn with *gidin* — sinews (catgut, from the intestines or sinews of sheep and goats) — and the same applies to the *megillah*. Yet *venikret iggeret she'im hitil bah sheloshah chutei gidin kesherah* — because it is also called an *iggeret*, a letter, even if only three threads of *gidin* are used, it is valid. A letter does not require the full formal sewing of a sacred book.

Rav Nachman adds: *uvilvad sheyehu meshulashim* — provided that these three threads are evenly distributed, dividing the parchment into thirds. There is a dispute among the *rishonim* as to the precise arrangement. The *Rif* holds that three holes produce two spans, each thread separating the scroll into portions. Rashi and Tosafot, citing the relevant *pesukim*, hold that the three holes and the threading pattern divide the parchment into four sections. In either reading, the key requirement is that the distribution be even across the length of the scroll.

### Megillah Within Scroll

Rav Yehudah in the name of Shmuel rules: *hakorei bamegillah haketuva bein haketuvim lo yatza* — one who reads from a *megillah* written as part of a larger scroll of *Tanakh* (i.e., a complete scroll containing all or many books of *Ketuvim*, with the *megillah* embedded within it) has not fulfilled the obligation. This is a striking ruling: the scroll in question is undoubtedly *sifrei kodesh*. The issue is not sanctity, but rather the *megillah*'s dual identity. As part of a continuous scroll, it may function perfectly well as *Sefer Tanakh*, but it does not exist as an independent *mitzvah* object. The *megillah* must stand alone.

This is illustrated by the story of Levi bar Shmuel, who was reading before Rav Yehudah from such an embedded *megillah*. Rav Yehudah asked whether it was acceptable, and was told: anyone who reads from a *megillah* written within a larger scroll of *Ketuvim* has not fulfilled the obligation.

### Parchment Distinction

Rava limits the ruling: *lo amran ela d'lo mechasar umyatar purta* — this applies only when the parchment of the *megillah* section is not at all distinguishable from the surrounding text in terms of width. *Aval mechasar umyatar purta, leit lan bah* — if the *megillah*'s parchment is even slightly wider or narrower than the rest, it is valid. The *megillah* need not be physically detached from the rest of the scroll, but it must be visually distinct — it must have its own identity, even if that identity is constituted by a slight difference in the width of the parchment on which it is written.

### Pirsumei Nisa

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan initially states the same rule — reading from an embedded *megillah* does not fulfill the obligation — and then, in the same breath, he qualifies it: *betzibbur shanu* — this was said only for a communal reading. For an individual reading (*beyachid*), it does not matter.

This distinction is theologically meaningful. Reading in *tzibbur* activates the requirement of *pirsumei nisa* — publicizing the miracle. The *megillah* itself is alluded to in the text of Esther as *ha'iggeret hazot*, as a visible, tangible document through which the story is told. In a communal setting, that visual and public dimension becomes a formal requirement: the *megillah* must exist as a separate, identifiable object, one that can be seen and held up as the vehicle of the story. In private reading, the *pirsumei nisa* dimension is absent or reduced, and consequently the requirement of an independent scroll does not apply. Interestingly, the fact that one is reading in a *tzibbur* does not merely permit this heightened standard — it demands it. One cannot say "I fulfilled the private standard while in the community." The communal context creates its own obligations, and those obligations can only be satisfied on their own terms.

---

## Permitted Readers

### Excluded Categories

The *mishnah* states: *hakol k'sherim likrot et hamegillah chutz mecheiresh shoteh v'katan* — everyone is valid to read the *megillah* except a *cheiresh*, *shoteh*, and *katan*. Rabbi Yehudah dissents with respect to the *katan*, holding him valid. Notably, women are not excluded; they are obligated in *mikra megillah*. Rabbi Yehudah's allowance of a *katan* is surprising at first, since a *katan* is not fully obligated in *mitzvot*. The reasoning may be that since *megillah* is a rabbinic *mitzvah*, and a *katan* carries at least a rabbinic obligation, one rabbinic obligation might fulfill another.

### Cheresh Issue

The *gemara* asks: *man tanna cheresh* — which *tanna* holds that a *cheiresh* is excluded? It first clarifies who the *cheiresh* in question is. In rabbinic literature, *cheiresh* can denote someone who can neither hear nor speak, but if he cannot speak, he cannot read in any case, so there would be no need for a legal exclusion. The *cheiresh* here must therefore refer to someone who can speak but cannot hear — and that raises the question: why should the inability to hear disqualify him from reading?

### Rabbi Yose: Hearing

Rav Matna answers: *Rabbi Yose*. The *gemara* recalls the ruling discussed a few days earlier: *hakorei et shema velo hishmia l'ozno* — one who reads *shema* without making it audible to his own ears. Rabbi Yose holds: *lo yatza* — he has not fulfilled the obligation. Applied to the *megillah*: the issue is not personal status but the act itself. If the reader cannot hear his own words, the reading lacks some essential quality of *kri'ah*. And this deficiency presumably affects not only the reader himself but any listeners who rely on him — if the act of reading is defective at its root, no one is discharged through it.

### Rav Matna Position

The *gemara* then asks: *u'mimai de-Rabbi Yose hi bediavad nami lo* — how do we know this is Rabbi Yose holding that even *bediavad* a deaf person's reading is invalid? Perhaps the *mishnah* follows Rabbi Yehudah, who is understood (through the *gemara*'s assumptions) to disagree with Rabbi Yose on *shema*, and perhaps Rabbi Yehudah's exclusion of the *cheiresh* is only a *l'chatchila* matter — a preference, not an absolute disqualification.

### Multiple Katan Types

The *gemara* initially resists this reading by pointing out that the *cheiresh* is listed together with the *shoteh* and *katan*, who are excluded even *bediavad* as persons lacking full legal standing. By analogy, the *cheiresh* should be excluded *bediavad* as well, not merely *l'chatchila*. The *gemara* tries to escape this by saying *ha k'dita v'ha k'dita* — each exclusion stands on its own terms: *cheiresh l'chatchila*, *shoteh* and *katan bediavad*. But this is undermined by the *seifa* of the *mishnah*, which records Rabbi Yehudah's allowance of the *katan* — proving that the *reisha*'s exclusion of the *katan* is not Rabbi Yehudah. At this point the *gemara* proposes the most aggressive resolution: *chasuri mechasra v'hachi katani* — the *mishnah* is incomplete and must be read as follows: the exclusion of the *katan* in the *reisha* refers to a *katan shelo higia l'chinuch*, one who has not yet reached the age of *chinuch*, while the *katan* that Rabbi Yehudah permits is a *katan shehigia l'chinuch*, one who has. This allows the *reisha*'s exclusion to be read as both *l'chatchila* and *bediavad*, consistent with Rabbi Yehudah — and preserves the goal of reading the *mishnah* entirely as Rabbi Yehudah.

### Tosafot: Force to Yehuda

The acrobatics here are, as the *gemara* itself seems to feel, considerable. Why go to such lengths to make the *mishnah* consistent with Rabbi Yehudah? Tosafot explains: because we *pasken* like Rabbi Yehudah — that *bediavad* one fulfills the obligation even without hearing one's own words. Since we rule that way, we are motivated to ensure that the *stam mishnah* does not stand in contradiction to that ruling. The interpretive effort is driven by the need for halakhic coherence.

### Three Positions

At this point, three positions have crystallized, each tied to a different *tanna*. Rabbi Meir: *l'chatchila* it is acceptable not to hear one's own words — intent (*kavana*) is what counts, as he says regarding *shema*, *achar kavanas halev hein hein hadevarim*, the words follow the direction of the heart. Rabbi Yosei: even *bediavad*, if one did not hear one's own words, the act is invalid. Rabbi Yehudah: *bediavad* it is valid; *l'chatchila* one should hear. The *gemara* arrives at this three-way scheme in part through an additional *braitah* where Rabbi Yehudah transmits a ruling in the name of his teacher, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya: *hakorei shema tzorich she-yashmia l'ozno* — when one reads *shema* one is required to make it heard by one's own ears. The language *tzorich*, "requires," is understood as a *l'chatchila* formulation — meaning *bediavad* it is valid if not heard. This resolves the puzzle of a *braitah* permitting a deaf person to take *terumos u'maasros l'chatchila* (despite the *bracha* he makes that he cannot hear): that *braitah* follows Rabbi Meir, for whom even *l'chatchila* the hearing requirement is not operative.

### Types of Acts

Tosafot closes the discussion with a pointed question: why are *megillah* and *krias shema* treated as analogous in terms of the hearing requirement, while *birkas hamazon* seems to occupy different ground? Tosafot's instinct is that this makes sense, and offers the following analysis: *shema* and *megillah* are both acts of reciting or reading a fixed text in a formalized and ritualized manner. *Birkas hamazon*, though the Rabbis composed its text, is at its core an act of prayer and gratitude — not the recitation of a fixed *mikra*, a canonical scriptural passage. Acts of reading a fixed canonical text carry more rigorous formal requirements: they must be articulated, and arguably heard. Acts of prayer or blessing, even when textualized, retain a more interior, intentional character — which is why the *gemara* records that *birkas hamazon* thought in one's heart is *yotzei bediavad*, while for *shema* and *megillah* the requirement of audible recitation is more formally operative. And even within this category, one can note that *megillah* carries an added dimension: it is not merely recitation but *reading from a book*, a formal act with its own additional criteria — which may well distinguish it from *shema* in ways that remain to be fully explored.

---

---

# Megillah 20

## Minor Reading Megillah

### Katan & Megillah

The daf opens ten lines down, at the passage beginning *Yehuda machshir b'katan* — Reb Yehuda permits a *katan*, a minor, to read the *Megillah*. This is a striking position, since ordinarily minors are not obligated in *mitzvos* and therefore cannot discharge the obligations of others. Yet Reb Yehuda maintains that a *katan* may do so. The *Gemara* has already made a distinction, earlier in the sugya, between a *katan she'higgia lachinuch* — a minor who has reached the age of training — and one who has not, though the *Gemara* does not fully unpack that distinction here.

### Proof from Lod

The *Gemara* cites a *braisa* in which Reb Yehuda offers autobiographical proof: *katan hayiti v'kirisiyah l'mala me-Reb Tarfon v'hazekeinim b'Lod* — "I was a minor and I read it before Reb Tarfon and the elders in Lod." The word *l'mala* is noteworthy; it may mean he was reading from a raised platform. There are discussions about where the *aron* was positioned relative to the *sheliach tzibbur*, though the architecture of ancient synagogues does not clearly support the notion of a sunken platform in the literal sense.

### Testimony Issue

The response to Reb Yehuda's proof is swift: *ein mevi'im re'ayah min ha'katan* — one cannot adduce testimony from a minor. Whatever Reb Yehuda did as a child cannot serve as legal evidence, since the testimony of a minor is inadmissible. The situation has a certain structural irony: by the time anyone could challenge such evidence, the circumstances that would make it relevant have already passed.

### Rebbi Yehuda Proof

A second *braisa* compounds the problem. Rebbi Yehuda HaNasi himself says: *katan hayiti v'kirisiyah l'mala me-Rebbi Yehuda* — "I was a minor and I read it in the presence of Rebbi Yehuda." But the response here is different: *ein mevi'im re'ayah min ha'matir* — one cannot bring proof from the one who permits the act. The fact that Rebbi Yehuda, who himself holds that a *katan* may read, allowed this to happen proves nothing to those who disagree.

### Gemara Analysis

The *Gemara* then asks: why does the response to the first proof not suffice? Why add the second? The answer is *chada v'od kamru lo* — they were making two independent points. First, you were a *katan* at the time, so your testimony is inadmissible. Second, even if you had been an adult and were reporting what you witnessed — even then, seeing the one who permits the act act permissively does not constitute broader proof of permissibility.

### Tosafos & Obligation

The *Gemara* leaves the position of Reb Yehuda without extended analysis, but *Tosafos* spells out the conceptual framework. The reading of the *Megillah* is a rabbinic obligation, and therefore one might argue that a *katan*, who bears a rabbinic obligation of his own, could discharge another person's rabbinic obligation. Some *poskim* and *mefarshim* do draw a further distinction: the nighttime *Megillah* reading is characterized as *mitzvah d'rabbanan* in the full sense, while the daytime reading is framed as a *mitzvah midivrei soferim*, derived from the verses of the *Megillah* itself and therefore standing at a somewhat higher level. Either way, neither reading is biblical, and this opens the question of whether one who is rabbinically obligated may discharge the obligation of another.

*Tosafos* himself, however, recognizes two difficulties with this reasoning and does not find it straightforward. The first is what *Tosafos* terms the problem of a double *derabbanan*: the *katan* is rabbinically obligated in a *mitzvah* that is itself only rabbinic. This places him one level lower than an adult who is also obligated in a rabbinic *mitzvah*, and it is not self-evident that simply being within the domain of rabbinic obligation means that all distinctions of level dissolve.

The second difficulty is conceptually arresting: in what sense is the *katan* himself rabbinically obligated? Normally, when we speak of a child's obligation in *mitzvos*, we understand this as an obligation upon the *parents* — it is the father (or, on other views, the mother as well) who is obligated in *chinuch*, in training the child. To say that the *katan* himself bears a rabbinic obligation is somewhat paradoxical: since he is excluded from the system of biblical obligation, on what basis do the Rabbis obligate him directly? Yet the position of Reb Yehuda seems to presuppose something like that idea.

### Pirsumei Nisa

An entirely different conceptual framework may be applicable here. Rather than analyzing the question through the lens of personal obligation — whose level of *chiyuv* is sufficient to discharge whose — one might approach the *Megillah* reading through the lens of *pirsumei nisa*, the publicizing of the miracle. The *kiyum* of *pirsumei nisa* is an inherently communal and public act, and perhaps the relevant question is not whether this individual's personal obligation matches that of the listeners, but whether this public ritual has been performed.

A parallel may be drawn to the laws of *aliyos la'Torah*. The famous *Mishnah* teaches *hakol olin liminyan shivah* — in principle, anyone may be counted among the seven *aliyos*, and indeed the tradition records *be'emes amru* that a woman or a *katan* may receive an *aliyah*, subject to considerations of *kevod ha'tzibur*. The ordinary principles governing *mitzvas asei shehazman grama* or the requirement of being a *bar chiyuva* simply do not apply in the same way to *krias haTorah*, because the framework there is communal, not personal. Perhaps something similar is operative by the *Megillah* reading.

### Megillah vs Torah

This comparison, however, invites an important distinction. *Krias haTorah* is exclusively a communal obligation — one who stays home and does not attend the *tzibbur* reading has no personal obligation to read the Torah on his own. Because the obligation is entirely communal in structure, the requirement that the reader share the same personal *chiyuv* as the listeners is relaxed. The *Megillah*, by contrast, is understood as a personal obligation: each individual is independently obligated to hear the *Megillah*. To suggest that a *katan* can discharge this personal obligation through a *pirsumei nisa* framework is therefore a more significant *chiddush*.

### Women & Minors

One further observation: the *Mishnah* here excludes from valid *Megillah* reading the *cheiresh* (the deaf-mute), the *shoteh* (one who is mentally incapacitated), and the *katan*. Women are conspicuously absent from this list of exclusions. The first *Mishnah* in Arachin states *hakol chayavin* — the straightforward reading of which is that not only are women obligated in the *Megillah*, but that they are obligated at the same level as men and may therefore read for men as well. It is only through the *Tosefta*, the Bahag, and related material that the idea enters Ashkenazic thought that women's obligation may be at a different level. Nothing in the *Gemara* itself indicates such a distinction.

---

## Timing of Mitzvos

### Day Mitzvos List

The *Mishnah* now turns to the *when* of the *Megillah* and related *mitzvos*. Having addressed the *how* (the manner of reading) and the *who* (who is obligated), the *Mishnah* pivots to timing, and in so doing makes a much broader statement about the category of *mitzvos* that are performed during the day. The *Mishnah* lists: *Megillah* reading, *bris milah*, *tevilah*, *hazah* (the sprinkling of the *parah adumah* ashes for one who is *tamei meis*), and *shomeres yom k'neged yom* — a woman who experienced abnormal uterine bleeding for one or two days outside her menstrual period, who must observe one clean day and then immerse.

### Day Definition

All of these are *day mitzvos*, and the *Mishnah* makes a further point: while these *mitzvos* should *lechatchila* be performed beginning at sunrise — *neitz hachamah* — if one performed them from the rising of the morning star (*amud hashachar*), it is *kasher*. The morning star is understood to precede sunrise by seventy-two minutes, or four *mil*. The *Mishnah* thus draws a distinction between the *lechatchila* starting point (sunrise) and the *bedi'avad* starting point (the morning star), and we will return shortly to the conceptual basis of that distinction.

### Megillah Day Source

The *Gemara* asks: from where is all this derived? It begins with the *Megillah*. The verse states *v'hayamim ha'eleh nizkarim v'naasim* — "these days are remembered and done." The word *hayamim*, days, implies *bayom* — in the daytime — and not at night. This establishes the *Megillah* as a day *mitzvah*. The *Gemara* will go on to establish the *amud hashachar* / *neitz hachamah* framework, but the threshold question is first to confirm that each item on the list is indeed a day *mitzvah* to begin with.

### Night vs Day

Having established that the *Megillah* is a day *mitzvah*, the *Gemara* raises a difficulty: does this not contradict Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who ruled that one is obligated to read the *Megillah* at night and repeat it during the day? The verse seems to speak only of daytime, implying there is no nighttime obligation. The *Gemara* resolves this by limiting the *Mishnah*'s discussion: *ki tanya ad hayom* — the *Mishnah* is addressing only the day reading, not purporting to exclude a nighttime reading.

That said, this resolution is not without controversy. The *Pnei Yehoshua* — or, according to some, the *Shagas Aryeh* — observes that the entire tannaitic literature, the *mishnayos* and the *braisos*, shows no awareness of a nighttime *Megillah* obligation. The nighttime reading was an innovation of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. On this view, the *Mishnah* does not merely omit the nighttime reading — it simply does not know of it. The daytime reading is therefore the primary *mitzvah*, characterized as a *mitzvah midivrei soferim* because it is grounded in the verses of the *Megillah* itself, while the nighttime reading is described as a *mitzvah d'rabbanan*. This has practical implications: if one must choose between a nighttime reading and a daytime reading, one should attend the daytime reading, which is the primary *mitzvah*.

### Bris Milah Timing

For *bris milah*, the source is the verse *u'vayom hashemini yimol* — "and on the eighth day he shall circumcise." This establishes that the *mitzvah* begins with the day of the eighth and not the preceding night. An interesting question is raised regarding a *milah shelo bizmanah* — a circumcision performed not on the eighth day but later: is the nighttime exclusion limited to the night preceding the eighth day, or does it apply more broadly whenever the *milah* is ultimately performed? This question is in fact subject to discussion elsewhere.

The observation is also made, in connection with what was discussed earlier about the *Megillah*, that the distinction between the nighttime and daytime *Megillah* readings creates an opening for certain contemporary discussions. Even for those who wish to take seriously the *Tosafos*-based concern that women's obligation may be at a different level than men's, that concern might be limited to the daytime reading — since the nighttime reading is itself already at a lower level of obligation, and the conceptual framework may accordingly differ.

### Tevilah Hazah

For *tevilah* and *hazah* — the immersion and sprinkling associated with purification from corpse-impurity — the source is the verse *v'hizah ha'tahor al ha'tamei beyom hashevi'i*, "and the pure one shall sprinkle on the impure one on the seventh day." This establishes that the sprinkling must occur during the day of the seventh. The *Gemara* then links *tevilah* to *hazah* by way of *itkash* — the two are juxtaposed in the verse — and concludes that immersion must also be during the day.

The question is: which immersion? As *Tosafos* explains at length, there are actually two *tevilos* in the context of *parah adumah* purification. One immersion precedes the sprinkling, preparing the person for the act of sprinkling; this one is not clearly stated in the verses. A second immersion follows the sprinkling. *Tosafos* initially suggests that the *Mishnah* must be referring to the pre-sprinkling *tevilah*, but evidence from other *Gemaros* indicates that this immersion may in fact be performed at night. That reading is therefore difficult.

If, on the other hand, the reference is to the post-sprinkling *tevilah*, a different problem arises. The general rule regarding *tevilah* is that the earliest moment one may immerse is the daytime of the seventh day, not the preceding night. But once that threshold has been crossed — once the day of the seventh has arrived — and one has not yet immersed, the *tevilah* may subsequently be performed even at night. The same logic would apply here: once the sprinkling has been done (which must be by day), the subsequent immersion need not itself be restricted to daytime. It would already be day by the time the sprinkling was completed, and the *tevilah* could follow that evening.

### Tosafos Tevilah

*Tosafos* resolves this with a creative reading: the word *tovlin* in the *Mishnah* does not refer to going to the *mikvah* at all. Rather, it refers to the dipping (*tevilah*) of the hyssop — the bundle of herbs used to apply the *parah adumah* mixture — into the water. This must be done during the day, and if the hyssop was dipped at night and the sprinkling was performed the following day, it is invalid. *Tosafos* brings evidence to support this reading: even dipping the hyssop immediately before *amud hashachar*, with the sprinkling following moments after dawn, would be problematic if the dipping itself occurred at night.

### Shomeres Yom

The *Mishnah* then singles out *shomeres yom k'neged yom* — "she observes a day corresponding to the day" — specifying that she may not immerse until *neitz hachamah*, sunrise. The *Gemara* immediately asks: why is this worth stating? Is this not the rule for all who must observe a waiting period before immersion? Anyone required to count days before immersing — a *zav*, a *zavah*, a *metzora*, or one who is *tamei meis* — must wait until the beginning of the seventh day; the night preceding the seventh day does not suffice. Why single out the *shomeres yom*?

### Zavah vs Zav

The *Gemara* answers: one might have thought the *shomeres yom* should be treated differently and actually be permitted to immerse on the night preceding her clean day. The reasoning would run as follows: the verse *v'zos toras ha'zav asher teitzei mimenu shichvas zera* links the *zav* (a man with abnormal genital discharge) who has experienced only one episode to a *ba'al keri* (one who has had a seminal emission) by way of a *hekesh*. A *ba'al keri* immerses on the very day the emission occurred — there is no waiting period of a full day. If one episode of *zav*-like discharge is treated like a *ba'al keri*, and a *ba'al keri* immerses the same day, perhaps the *shomeres yom* — whose status is less severe than a full *zavah gedolah* — should similarly be permitted to immerse without waiting for the following morning.

But the verse *kol yemei zovah k'mishkav niddatah yihiyeh lah* — "all the days of her flow shall be as the reclining-place of her menstrual impurity" — teaches the concept of *shomeres yom k'neged yom*. From the word *yihiyeh* the Rabbis derive that she must observe a day corresponding to the day she bled. Yet one might still argue: even granting that she cannot immerse the very day she bled (as a *ba'al keri* could), why not permit her to immerse at the beginning of the following night? Let her observe even a partial period of not bleeding — *miktzas shimur* — beginning Sunday night, and immerse Sunday night. The Torah required only that she observe some clean time; why must that be a full daytime period?

### Sefira Requirement

The answer is that *keivan d'ba'aya sfirah* — since the concept of counting is present here, since the *zavah gedolah* must count *shivah nekiyim* (seven clean days) with explicit enumeration as per the verse *v'safrah lah*, and the *shomeres yom* is structurally related to the *zavah* — *sfirah b'imama hi*: counting requires daytime. A clean day does not count as a clean day unless it has entered daytime. It is not enough that she experienced a period of no bleeding; the *yom*, the day, must actually register as a daytime period for it to count as the corresponding clean day.

### Seven-Day Principle

This leads the *Gemara* to articulate a broader principle: wherever the Torah designates a seven-day counting period — *zav*, *zavah*, *metzora*, *tamei meis* — the period ends with the arrival of the seventh day, meaning the beginning of the day, not the preceding night. This is analogous to the rule in *aveilut* that *miktzas hayom k'kulo*: a mourner does not rise from mourning the night before the seventh day, even though halachically the seventh day has begun; one must wait until the morning of the seventh day. So too here, the earliest one may immerse after a counting period is the morning of the seventh day. And even the *shomeres yom*, whose period is not seven days but rather a single day of *shmirah*, participates in this principle: since there is an element of counting — a *yom* must be designated and observed — that designation requires entering actual daytime.

Once the threshold has been reached, however — once the day of the seventh has begun, or for the *shomeres yom*, once the clean day has commenced — if the immersion is postponed, it may certainly be performed that following night.

---

## Day/Night Definitions

### Light Verse

The *Mishnah* states that all of these *mitzvos*, if performed from *amud hashachar* onward, are *kasher*. The *Gemara* now asks: *mana hani mili* — from where do we know this? Rava derives it from the verse *Vayikra Elokim la'or yom* — "and God called the light day."

### Beginning Light

The *drasha* reads: *l'me'ir u'va kara yom* — at the moment the light was beginning to illuminate, He called that period "day." In other words, "day" is not synonymous with "light" per se, but rather refers to the period that begins when it starts to become light — which is before sunrise, at *amud hashachar*. So *amud hashachar* already falls within the category of day.

### Symmetry Problem

The *Gemara* immediately challenges this: if you read the verse as meaning "the beginning of light is called day," then symmetrically, the verse *v'lachoshech kara lailah* — "and He called the darkness night" — should be read as *l'machshich u'va kara lailah*, meaning as it begins to get dark it is called night. But that would mean dusk is already night — and we hold that *tzeis hakochavim*, the emergence of the stars, marks the beginning of night, not the earlier onset of darkness. So this verse alone cannot serve as the source.

### Nehemiah Source

Rabbi Zeira therefore provides a different source, drawn from the book of Nehemiah, which describes the building of the *Beis Hamikdash*. The verse states: *v'anachnu osim b'malacha... me'alos hashachar ad tzeis hakochavim* — "and we were doing the work... from the morning star until the stars came out." And the text then says *v'hayu lanu halailah l'mishmor v'hayom malachah* — "the nighttime was for guarding and the daytime was for work." This defines the workday — explicitly labeling it *yom* — as the period from *alos hashachar* to *tzeis hakochavim*. Day, in other words, spans from the morning star to the emergence of stars at night.

### Alos to Neitz

The *Gemara* anticipates a challenge: perhaps the builders were simply starting early and ending late — working before dawn and after dusk — and the verse's use of the word *yom* refers only to the middle portion of that work, not to the full span from *alos* to *tzeis*. The *Gemara* responds by invoking the second verse: *v'hayu lanu halailah l'mishmor v'hayom malachah* — the explicit labeling of the period of work as *yom* demonstrates that the full span from *alos* to *tzeis* is classified as daytime. This is why the second verse is necessary; without it, one could have argued that the workers merely extended their hours beyond the technical boundaries of day.

### Rashi Clarity

This establishes that *amud hashachar* marks the beginning of day, which explains why *bedi'avad* these *mitzvos* are valid if performed from *amud hashachar*. But it does not immediately explain why *lechatchila* one should wait until *neitz hachamah*. Rashi's explanation is practical: sunrise is an easily identifiable and universally recognized moment. If the standard were set at *amud hashachar*, people would not know precisely when to begin, conditions like cloud cover could lead to premature performance, and errors would result. Waiting for *neitz hachamah* is therefore a rabbinic safeguard ensuring clarity.

### Rav S. Framework

Rav Soloveitchik proposes a more conceptual framework. The temporal landscape consists of four boundary points: *amud hashachar*, sunrise, sunset, and *tzeis hakochavim*. The period between sunrise and sunset is clearly day; the period before *amud hashachar* and after *tzeis hakochavim* is clearly night. But the two intermediate zones — from *amud hashachar* to sunrise and from sunset to *tzeis hakochavim* — are gray zones, neither fully day nor fully night.

### Lemair U'Va

On Rav Soloveitchik's reading, the period from *amud hashachar* to *neitz hachamah* has the halachic status of *bedi'avad* day — it is genuinely part of the day, but not yet fully day. It is a partial, incipient day. Therefore, *lechatchila* one does not perform these *mitzvos* during this period, since it is not full day; but *bedi'avad*, since it is halachically within the domain of day, one has fulfilled the obligation. The distinction between *lechatchila* and *bedi'avad* reflects not a rabbinic fence but a conceptual reality: the morning twilight zone participates in the category of day but has not yet reached its full expression.

### Bein Hashmashot

The corresponding gray zone at the other end — *bein hashmashot*, dusk, from sunset until *tzeis hakochavim* — carries a different halachic status. *Bein hashmashot* is classified as *safek*, doubt: it is uncertain whether it is day or night. Anything done during *bein hashmashot* has the status of *safek yom safek lailah*.

### Safek vs Bedia'avad

This raises a natural question: if the morning gray zone (*amud hashachar* to *neitz hachamah*) is classified as *bedi'avad* day, why is the corresponding evening gray zone not classified as *bedi'avad* night? Why does one zone receive a *bedi'avad* determination and the other receive a *safek*?

Rav Soloveitchik's answer, in effect, appeals to the psychological and phenomenological character of each zone. In the morning, light is growing — however dark it still is, the trajectory is toward greater light, and one perceives the period as the nascent beginning of day. The growing light allows us to classify the period, even inchoately, as "becoming day." In the evening, however, even as darkness encroaches, we remain reluctant to relinquish the day. The remnants of daylight still present during *bein hashmashot* prevent us from tipping the period definitively into night. As a result, it is not classified as *bedi'avad* night, but rather as a genuine mixture of day and night — a *safek* in the ontological sense — that cannot be resolved in either direction.

---

## Mitzvos Lists

### All Day Things

The subsequent *Mishnah* continues the theme of timing, but its emphasis shifts: from the question of *when* these *mitzvos* begin (addressed in the previous *Mishnah*) to the question of how *long* they extend. *Kol hayom kasher* — the entire day is valid — is the governing principle. These are *day mitzvos* that, while typically performed in the morning, may in principle be performed at any point throughout the day. A parallel principle governs *night mitzvos*: *kol halaila kasher*, the entire night is valid for those *mitzvos* designated as nighttime acts.

### Day List 1

The *Mishnah* opens its enumeration of *day mitzvos*: reading of the *Megillah* — for although we perform *krias haMegillah* in the morning, one who did not do so may still fulfill the *mitzvah* later in the day. *Hallel* — though ordinarily recited at *Shacharis*, if somehow omitted, it may be said at any point in the day. *Tekias shofar* — though we blow the *shofar* toward the beginning of the day, it is technically valid throughout the day. *Netilas lulav* — taking the *lulav*. *Tefilas Musafin* and *Musafin* — both the prayer of *Musaf* and the actual *korban Musaf*, both of which are valid the entire day. This is itself a *chiddush*: unlike *Shacharis*, which has a defined time window in the morning, or *Mincha*, which is in the afternoon, *Musaf* may be brought at any point in the day.

### Day List 2

The *Mishnah* continues: *viduy haparim* — the confession recited over the special communal and individual bull-offerings, such as *par he'elam davar shel tzibur* and the *par Kohen Gadol*. *Viduy ma'aser* — the declaration made after distributing the accumulated *ma'aser* from one's home. *Viduy Yom HaKippurim* — the confession recited on *Yom Kippur*, referring specifically to the *Kohen Gadol*'s confessions over the animals.

### Temple Acts

The list of *Temple* service-acts follows: *semicha* — the laying of hands on the *korban*; *shechitah* — the slaughter of the *korban*; *tenufah* — the waving performed with various *korbanos*. All acts of *avodah* in the *Beis HaMikdash* require daytime and are valid throughout the day. The list continues: *hagashah* — the touching of the *minchah* to the *mizbeach* as part of the *avodah*; *kmitzah* — the taking of the handful from the *minchah*; *haktarah* — the burning of that handful; *melikah* — the severing of the neck of a bird-sacrifice; *kabalah* — the catching of the blood of an animal sacrifice; *hazayah* — the sprinkling of the blood.

### Purification

Further ritual acts conclude the daytime list: *hashkayas sotah* — administering the *sotah* water to the woman suspected of adultery; *arifas ha'eglah* — the breaking of the neck of the calf in the *eglah arufah* ceremony for an unsolved murder; *taharas ha'metzora* — the purification ritual of the *metzora*, involving the birds, the sprinkling, and all its associated acts.

### Night Mitzvos

Two nighttime *mitzvos* are then enumerated: *ketziras ha'omer* — the cutting of the grain for the *omer* offering — and *haktaras chalavim v'eivarim* — the burning of the fats and limbs of sacrifices that were not completed during the day. The burning of fats is a *mitzvah* that begins the day before and continues through the night; it is valid the entire night.

### Ze Ha'klal

The *Mishnah* then states the *ze ha'klal*: *davar shemitzvaso bayom kasher kol hayom; davar shemitzvaso balaila kasher kol halaila* — a *day mitzvah* is valid the entire day; a *night mitzvah* is valid the entire night. This is a useful organizing principle, though it calls for scrutiny, since not every *mitzvah* clearly falls within its scope. *Shacharis* is not valid the entire day; *Mincha* is not valid the entire night. Calling *haktaras chalavim* a *night mitzvah* is also somewhat unusual since it begins the preceding day. So the *ze ha'klal* is a principle that requires careful qualification.

### Megillah Source

The *Gemara* then proceeds to provide sources for each item in the *Mishnah*'s list. For *Megillah*: the verse *hayamim ha'eileh nizkarim v'naasim* — "these days are remembered and done" — uses the word *yamim*, implying the full span of the day and providing no basis to limit the *mitzvah* to specific hours.

### Hallel Shofar

For *Hallel*: *mimizrach shemesh ad mevo'o* — "from the rising of the sun to its setting," indicating the full day. Rav Yosef offers an alternative: *zeh hayom asah Hashem* — "this is the day that God made," which equally implies the entirety of the day. For *tekias shofar*: *yom teruah yihiyeh lachem* — "a day of blasting shall be for you," with no further restriction.

### Lulav Musaf

For *lulav*: *u'lakachtem lachem bayom harishon* — "and you shall take for yourselves on the first day," with *bayom* implying the full day. For *Musafin* — both the sacrifice and the prayer — the source is *devar yom biyomo* — "a matter of a day in its day," and since the prayer parallels the sacrifice, *k'Musafin shavei rabanan*.

### Sotah Confession

For *viduy parim* — the confession over the bull-offerings — the *Gemara* derives it through a *gezeirah shavah* of *kaparah kaparah*, comparing the word "atonement" in those cases to *Yom Kippur*. By *Yom Kippur* the verse says *u'veyom hazeh yechaper aleichem* — "on this day shall atonement be made for you" — establishing that the confession must occur during the day, though at any point in the day. For *viduy ma'aser*: the verse *ve'amarta lifnei Hashem Elokecha* describes the declaration, followed immediately by *hayom hazeh Hashem Elokecha m'tzavecha* — "this day God commands you" — indicating that the declaration must be made by day.

In connection with *sotah*, the *Gemara* derives the day requirement through a *gezeirah shavah* of *torah torah*: the verse by *sotah* says *v'asah lah ha'Kohen es kol hatorah hazos*, and connects to the principle of *mishpat*, judgment, which operates in the daytime — *mah mishpat bayom, af sotah bayom*. The comparison of *sotah* to *mishpat* is worth pausing over. The *sotah* procedure in the Torah is in many respects not a legal proceeding in the conventional sense: the husband suspects his wife and brings her to the *Beis HaMikdash* for a ritual. Yet the Rabbis introduced an elaborate legal apparatus surrounding the *sotah* process: the husband must first formally warn her in front of witnesses; there must be witnesses to the *yichud*, the private meeting with the suspected man. In this way, while the ultimate resolution of the *sotah* matter still occurs through the ritual of the bitter waters rather than through a *beit din* verdict, the Rabbis worked to remove it from the domain of pure spousal discretion and place it within a framework of objective procedure and witness testimony. Comparing *sotah* to *mishpat* — and therefore to the daytime domain of legal process — may thus reflect something real about how the Rabbis conceptualized the *sotah* process.

### Sotah Legal
