The *gemara* then attempts a proof from the law of wrappings. *Golelim sefer Torah bematpachot chumashim* — one may wrap a *sefer Torah* with wrappings that were previously used for *chumashim* (individual Torah scrolls). *Vechumashim bematpachot Neviim u'Ketuvim* — and *chumashim* may be wrapped with wrappings previously used for *Neviim* and *Ketuvim*. The reverse is forbidden in each case. Now: one cannot wrap *Neviim* and *Ketuvim* with wrappings used for *chumashim*, and one cannot wrap *chumashim* with wrappings used for *sifrei Torah*. The implication seems to be that even wrappings of a *sefer Torah* cannot be repurposed for another *sefer Torah* — which would indicate that staying at the same level is not permitted.

### Inconclusive

But the *gemara* immediately challenges this inference: *eima seifa* — look at the end of the clause. *Velo chumashim bematpachot sefer Torah* — one may not use *sefer Torah* wrappings for *chumashim*. *Ha Torah beTorah shapir dami* — from which it follows that using a *sefer Torah* wrapping for a different *sefer Torah* would be permitted. This is the persistent problem: the sources address only the case of going down and the case of going up; the case of remaining at precisely the same level is never directly addressed. *Ella meha leka lemishma minah* — from this source, no conclusion can be drawn either way. The question of whether the proceeds of a sold *sefer Torah* may *lechatchila* be used to purchase a replacement *sefer Torah* at the same level remains unresolved, and the discussion will continue.

---

---

# Megillah 27

## Sefer Torah Sales

### Sefer Torah Proceeds

The Mishna establishes that when a sacred object is sold, the proceeds must be applied to a purpose of higher sanctity — not a lower one. The question that opens the Gemara's discussion is what the law requires when the only available purpose is an equivalent one. The clearest test case is a *sefer Torah*: since there is nothing of greater sanctity to which its proceeds could be directed, the question becomes whether one may *lechatchila* — prospectively and ideally — use the money to purchase another *sefer Torah*. The Gemara's very framing implies that as a general rule, using proceeds for an equivalent purpose is not permitted; the question is whether *lechatchila* the absence of any higher alternative changes the calculus.

### Same-Level Use

The Gemara implicitly assumes that using proceeds for an equivalent purpose is not acceptable under ordinary circumstances, and asks only whether the unique situation of a *sefer Torah* — where no higher purpose exists — creates an exception. The suggestion is that in all other cases, one is permitted *lechatchila* only to apply proceeds to a higher purpose; but where no higher level is available, perhaps equivalent use is permitted *lechatchila* as well.

### Object vs. Proceeds

It is important to distinguish between two distinct questions: the status of the object sold and the status of the proceeds derived from the sale. Regarding what is sold, there is no question whatsoever — a *sefer Torah* retains its *kedusha* absolutely. Similarly, *tashmishei kedusha* — sacred accessories such as the *mantel* (Torah cover), the *bimah*, and similar objects — retain their sanctity. The *halacha* is that *tashmishei kedusha* are *nignazin*: when they can no longer be used for their original purpose, they must be buried. There is no suggestion that they may simply be repurposed for mundane use. The only object whose status might be subject to change upon sale is the *shul* itself, precisely because the source of a *shul*'s *kedusha* is less intrinsic and more contested — a question the Gemara addresses at length.

Regarding the proceeds, the rule is that they must be directed to a higher purpose. With a *sefer Torah*, where there is no higher purpose, perhaps equivalent use is sufficient. That is the live question the Gemara is exploring.

### Hierarchy Precedent

The Gemara brings a *tashma* — a proof — from Berakhot (25): one may place one *sefer Torah* on top of another *sefer Torah*, and a *Torah* on top of *chumashin*, and *chumashin* on top of *Nevi'im* and *Ketuvim*. But one may not place *Nevi'im* and *Ketuvim* on top of *chumashin*, nor *chumashin* on top of a *Torah*. This passage articulates the classical hierarchy of sacred texts. And crucially, it confirms that placing a *Torah* atop a *Torah* — same level upon same level — is acceptable. This suggests that keeping things at the same level of *kedusha* is at least sometimes permitted, and may lend support to the permissibility of using *sefer Torah* proceeds for another *sefer Torah*.

### No Alternative Rule

The Gemara deflects this proof, distinguishing between physically placing one sacred object atop another and repurposing proceeds. Regarding physical placement, the rule is: *shani hanacha d'lo efshar* — placing is different because there is literally no alternative. One cannot always keep every *sefer Torah* on a separate surface; physical reality sometimes requires stacking. And if one were not to permit this, *heichi karkhinan* — how would one even roll up a *sefer Torah*? As one section of parchment is rolled, it rests upon the sections below it. The permissibility of same-level contact flows from the absence of any alternative: *kivan d'lo efshar, shari* — when there is no option, it is permitted. The Gemara then applies this principle to the case at hand: here too, since there is nothing higher than a *sefer Torah*, if one has already sold it and holds the proceeds, what choice is there? *Kivan d'lo efshar, shari* — the same logic applies. This is, however, more akin to a *bedieved* dispensation: once the sale has occurred and the money is in hand, of course one buys a *sefer Torah*. The harder question is whether one may *lechatchila* plan and execute such a transaction.

### Negligence Concern

The Gemara raises a further teaching: Rabba bar bar Chana said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel — one may not sell an old *sefer Torah* in order to purchase a new one. This seems to imply that *lechatchila* one may not use *sefer Torah* proceeds for the same purpose. The Gemara, however, rejects this inference. The prohibition is not about the hierarchy of use at all; it is about *peshiuta* — negligence — as we encountered in the earlier discussion about demolishing one *shul* in order to build another. The concern is that one will sell the *sefer Torah*, the money will lie around, and either through delay or distraction, the community will remain without a *sefer Torah*, or the funds will come to be misused.

### Immediate Purchase

The Gemara qualifies: the negligence concern applies only when the new *sefer Torah* has not yet been obtained. But when circumstances are such that the new *sefer Torah* is already available — a scribe has completed it and is waiting to be paid, or a seller is ready to transfer it immediately — there is no realistic window for *peshiuta*. In such a case, what is the *halacha*? The Gemara invites a further proof.

### Rabbi Meir Standard

A *tashma* is brought: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Meir — *ein mocharin sefer Torah* except to fulfill one of two purposes: to study Torah (*lilmod Torah*) or to get married (*lisa isha*). This establishes that proceeds from the sale of a *sefer Torah* must serve a higher purpose — here, Torah learning or marriage. Since Torah learning is a purpose associated with the *sefer Torah* itself, the Gemara asks whether this means that a *sefer Torah* for a *sefer Torah* is in fact acceptable. *Shma mina Torah be-Torah shappir dami* — perhaps using the proceeds for another *sefer Torah* is perfectly fine.

### Learning > Object

The Gemara resists this conclusion: *dilma shani limmud* — perhaps Torah learning is qualitatively different and genuinely higher. *She'halimmud mevi lidei ma'aseh* — learning leads to action. A *sefer Torah* as a physical object, however sacred, does not by itself translate into lived observance and religious practice. Torah study, by contrast, generates *ma'aseh* — the actual performance of *mitzvot* — and thus represents a broader and higher spiritual purpose.

This argument is somewhat curious. One might have expected the Gemara simply to rank *talmud Torah* as a greater *mitzvah* than the possession of a *sefer Torah*, or to note that while there is a *mitzvah* to write a *sefer Torah* — derived from *kitvu lachem et hashira hazot* — it is ultimately in order to read and learn from it, as the verse continues: *vekara bo kol yimei chayav*. The *sefer Torah* in practice served the ritual of *kriat haTorah*, and the act of learning was mediated through translation and teaching, not through direct engagement with the *sefer Torah* as object. So the gap between the sanctity of the object and the sanctity of learning is real. Yet the Gemara chooses to ground the superiority of *limmud* specifically in its capacity to generate *ma'aseh* — pointing toward a broader purposiveness rather than a simple ranking of *mitzvot*.

### Marriage Purpose

The same framework explains why marriage is permitted as a use of *sefer Torah* proceeds. *Lo tohu bera'ah l'shevet yetzarah* — God did not create the world to be desolate; He created it to be inhabited. Marriage fulfills the fundamental purpose of creation itself. In both cases — Torah learning and marriage — the Gemara is not merely assigning higher point values to certain *mitzvot*. Rather, it is identifying purposes that fulfill something larger: the inhabitation of the world in accordance with Torah. When proceeds serve these overarching purposes, they clearly qualify as a higher use. When they serve only an equivalent, concrete purpose — even another *sefer Torah* — it remains uncertain whether *lechatchila* this is permitted.

### Stringent Rulings

The Gemara concludes with a *tanu rabbanan*: one may not sell a *sefer Torah* even if one has no use for it, and even if one has many. *Yeter al ken*, Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel adds: even if one has nothing to eat — *eino ro'eh siman bracha le'olam* — one will never see a blessing from such proceeds. Rashi clarifies that this means one will see no blessing from those specific funds, rather than a categorical lifelong curse.

These rulings can be read in two ways. On one reading, they simply underscore the requirement that proceeds serve a higher purpose: since selling for sustenance does not direct the money to any higher *kedusha* purpose, it is forbidden. But there is a deeper resonance as well — that divesting oneself of a *sefer Torah* carries some fundamental spiritual weight regardless of what the proceeds will be used for. The *sefer Torah* represents Torah itself, and the act of separation from it is significant quite apart from any question about the hierarchy of sacred purposes. The Gemara does not fully resolve which of these concerns is operative, and the final conclusion on whether *lechatchila* one may sell a *sefer Torah* to purchase another remains somewhat open.

---

## Leftover Proceeds

### Rava's Distinction

The Mishna establishes that leftover proceeds from a sale must also be directed to a higher sacred purpose — *ve'chen bemotreihen*. Rava refines this: the restriction on how leftover proceeds may be used applies only when an object was actually sold and there remained surplus funds. If, however, money was simply raised from the community — say, a collection to build a new *aron* — and there turned out to be a surplus, those leftover funds may be used more broadly. The reasoning is straightforward: when an object is sold, the *kedusha* of that object is understood to transfer to the money, and the money therefore carries the sanctity of its source. But when funds are raised without any sacred object being sold, there is no source of *kedusha* to adhere to the money in the first place. The entire question is one of intention and designation, not of transferred sanctity.

### Elders' Authority

This connects to a principle established earlier in the Gemara: when the *shiva tuvei ha'ir* — the seven elders of the city — effect a sale *bema'amad anshei ha'ir* — in the presence of the citizenry — greater latitude is granted regarding the use of proceeds. This mechanism, which the Gemara had applied to the sale of a *shul*, is now seen to carry implications beyond that case.

### Stipulation Role

Abaye raises a *baraita* that reads: when is it that proceeds must be directed only to a higher purpose? When no stipulation was made. But when a stipulation was made, even a *duchsusia* — a municipal functionary — may be funded from the proceeds. The question is what kind of case this refers to. If one sold an object and stipulated with the buyer, what would stipulation accomplish? The *kedusha* flows from the object itself; it cannot be nullified by a verbal arrangement with the purchaser. Therefore, the *baraita* cannot be addressing a case where an object was sold.

### Community Mechanism

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: the *baraita* must be addressing a case where money was raised — not one where an object was sold. And the word "stipulated" in the *baraita* does not refer to a side-agreement with a buyer, but rather to the fact that the *shiva tuvei ha'ir*, acting in the presence of the assembled townspeople, gave formal sanction to the transaction. It is their involvement — the full communal authorization — that provides the latitude to use proceeds more freely.

The Gemara then revisits the position: alternatively, one may read the *baraita* as applying even to a sale of an object, where the latitude comes specifically from the involvement of the *shiva tuvei ha'ir bema'amad anshei ha'ir*. Just as we saw earlier that when a *shul* is sold through such full communal authorization the proceeds can be used for any purpose, so too here — even when an object with intrinsic *kedusha* is sold, the backing of the community leadership and citizenry grants wider discretion over the funds. The precise mechanism behind this is not fully explained, but the principle appears to be that when the entire community — to whom this sanctified property collectively belongs — acts through its recognized leadership with full transparency, it possesses an authority to define the use of proceeds in a way that would not otherwise be available.

This raises a pointed question: if the *shiva tuvei ha'ir* can grant such latitude over the proceeds of a sale of a *sefer Torah* or its accessories, does this reflect a broader principle that *kedusha* is in some sense conferred and controlled by communal perception and use rather than residing intrinsically in the object? The assumption throughout the Gemara remains that items such as the *sefer Torah* and its *tashmishei kedusha* retain their sanctity regardless — they are *nignazin* even if sold — while only the *shul*'s *kedusha* is susceptible to this kind of community-mediated transformation. But the extension of the *shiva tuvei ha'ir* principle to the proceeds of even intrinsically sacred objects does begin to complicate that picture.

### Abaye's Query

Abaye poses the question: when money is raised with an explicit stipulation, may the leftovers be used for any purpose whatsoever — including a *duchsusia*? This is the practical limit case: not another sacred object, not even a general communal need, but a paid municipal rider.

### Duchsusia Defined

The term *duchsusia* denotes a *parasha demata* — a horse-rider retained by the city. As Rashi explains: *benei ha'ir socharim adam rocheiv sus she'yehei mezuman lishloa'ch bishlichuto uvishlichut hamoshel ha'ir kshe'yitztarchu* — the townspeople hire a man on horseback to be available to carry messages and conduct the city's business on behalf of its leadership. This is a purely civic, non-sacred function. The question whether surplus sacred funds may be redirected to such a purpose captures the outer boundary of communal latitude over raised funds.

### Pedagogical Aside

Before the answer is given, Abaye offers a methodological observation: a young rabbinic student who has heard a teaching but does not know its explanation should seek out someone who regularly sits before senior scholars — for it is virtually certain that such a person has heard the matter explained by a great authority. Abaye's own conduct in this passage exemplifies the principle: he approached the scholar who arranged *beraitot* before Rav Sheshet, knowing that Rav Sheshet would have explained the term. In this pedagogical parable, Abaye positions himself rhetorically as the young student seeking transmitted wisdom — a characteristic expression of intellectual humility in the beit midrash.

---

## Tzedakah Authority

### Visitor Tzedakah

The discussion of communal funds and their proper use extends naturally to the laws of *tzedakah* collection. Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Meir: when people from one city travel to another and a *tzedakah* levy is assessed upon them — *pasku aleihem tzedakah* — they give the money, and when they return home they bring it with them and use it to support the poor of their own city.

### Social Pressure

Rashi's reading illuminates the dynamic: the visitors contribute not because they are genuinely obligated to support the poor of the host city, but so that they should not be suspected of being among those who pledge and do not pay — *shelo yachshidum b'foskim ve'einam nosnin*. It is social pressure rather than legal obligation that drives the donation. Having acquitted themselves of the appearance of obligation, they may legitimately retrieve the funds and apply them to their home community.

A distinction is drawn for the case of an individual traveler rather than a group: when a single person is assessed *tzedakah* in a foreign city, the money stays there. Perhaps the difference is one of scale — a contingent from another city represents a recognizable unit with their own communal obligations, while an individual is simply subject to the host city's structure in the ordinary way.

### Chaver Ir Role

However, the rule that visitors may reclaim and redirect the funds applies only when the city they visited has no *chaver ir* — a recognized communal Torah scholar who administers the city's needs. As the *baraita* states: *bameh devarim amurim bizman she'ein sham chaver ir* — when may the visitors take the money back? Only when there is no such figure present. But if there is a *chaver ir*, the funds are given over to his discretion — *tinaten lechaver ir* — and may not be reclaimed.

Rashi explains: *chaver ir* denotes a *talmid chacham hamit'asek b'tzorchei tzibbur* — not merely a scholar confined to his study hall, but a rabbinic figure actively engaged in the communal welfare. His presence confers upon him the discretionary authority over charitable funds in a manner analogous to the *shiva tuvei ha'ir's* authority over proceeds from sacred sales.

### Central Authority

This is precisely the position Rav Huna takes in the narrative that follows. When the people of Masaya — who had come to Rav Huna's city for a communal fast and had contributed to the *tzedakah* collection — asked to take the money back to support their own poor, Rav Huna refused. He cited the *baraita* and then added: *aniyei didi ve'didchu alay semichi* — the poor of your city and of my city ultimately depend on me. The central city and its rabbinic leadership bear responsibility not only for their own poor but for those of the surrounding communities as well. The evident fact that all of Masaya had come to his city for the fast demonstrated exactly this relationship of communal centrality.

The precise mechanics of why the *chaver ir*'s presence prevents reclamation are not spelled out. But the underlying logic resembles the principle encountered in the *shul* discussion, where the Gemara noted that if people come to a synagogue specifically because of a great Torah scholar's presence, that scholar has a kind of claim over the institution. Here too, when a recognized figure bears communal responsibility for the entire region, individuals cannot simply extract their contributions from the broader communal pool he administers.

### Leadership Discretion

The thread connecting all of these discussions is a consistent principle: when recognized communal leaders are formally involved — whether in raising funds with explicit stipulation, in authorizing a sale of sacred property, or in administering *tzedakah* collections — greater discretion attaches to the use of the resulting funds. The *shiva tuvei ha'ir* acting publicly, the *chaver ir* bearing regional responsibility, and the community raising money with advance stipulation all represent different instantiations of this principle. To summarize the arc of this entire discussion: the original sacred object — certainly a *sefer Torah*, and likewise its *tashmishei kedusha* — never loses its *kedusha*; if no longer in use, it must be buried. The *shul* alone presents the more complex case, where the *kedusha* may be susceptible to change. The question of the *money* and its proceeds is a separate matter governed by rabbinic construction, and there the involvement of communal leadership is the decisive variable that determines how much latitude one has.

---

## Shul Sanctity

### Rabbi Meir Strict

The next Mishna addresses the *kedusha* of the *shul* itself — not the proceeds, but the original object and its capacity for change. Rabbi Meir rules: *ein mochrin shel rabbim l'yachid* — a public *shul* may not be sold to a private individual. The reason is that doing so lowers it from its *kedusha*: when the *shul* was public, *dvarim shebikdusha* were recited in it; when it becomes a private person's *shul*, such recitations — requiring a *minyan* — will no longer take place there.

### Rabbis Respond

The Rabbis challenge Rabbi Meir: by his logic, one should not be permitted to sell a *shul* from a large city to a small town either, since fewer people will use it and it will be employed for a lesser purpose. The force of this objection is that if any reduction in the scale or frequency of sacred use constitutes impermissible degradation, then a great many sales would become impossible.

### Rabbi Meir Reply

Rabbi Meir's response draws a precise distinction: *me'ir gedola le'ir ketana me'ikar kedusha, hashta nami kedusha* — what was *kadosh* remains *kadosh*, because the *shul* continues to serve a *tzibbur* — a community. The *kedusha* remains qualitatively the same. But *me'rabim l'yachid leika kedusha* — when a *shul* moves from communal use to private use, the *kedusha* is lost, because *dvarim shebikdusha* can no longer be recited there. The operative distinction is not quantity but kind.

### Degree vs. Kind

The Rabbis respond to this as well: even if the concern about *dvarim shebikdusha* is real, there is also the principle of *B'rov Am Hadrat Melech* — the greater the assembly, the greater the honor to God. This applies even within contexts where *dvarim shebikdusha* are recited. Moving from a large city to a small town does represent a diminishment — not of *kedusha* as such, but of the fulfillment of this principle of *rov am*.

### Kedusha Source

This debate illuminates a deeper question about the very source of a *shul*'s *kedusha*. The *Ran* understands the sanctity of a *shul* to derive entirely from the recitation of *dvarim shebikdusha* within it — a reading that finds strong support in Rabbi Meir's position. If *dvarim shebikdusha* can no longer be said there, the *kedusha* is gone. The Rabbis' apparent indifference to this consideration, combined with their invocation of *B'rov Am Hadrat Melech* as an alternative standard, suggests a different understanding — closer to the Ramban's view that the *kedusha* of a *shul* derives from the act of *tefilla* itself, not specifically from *dvarim shebikdusha*. On this view, any *tefilla*, even private, continues to engage the sanctity of the space. This disagreement between the Ran and the Ramban thus finds its footing in the very argument between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis.

---

## Shul Sale Terms

### Repurchase Right

Rabbi Meir's stringency extends to the conditions of any permissible sale. He rules: *ein mochrin beit knesset ela al tenai she'im yirtzu yachziruhu* — a *shul* may be sold only on condition that the community retains the right to repurchase it at will. Even if the buyer intends to use it as a *shul* for the community, Rabbi Meir insists that the original community never fully relinquish their connection to the property. There is something about unconditional sale — the act of fully divesting — that is itself problematic, in a manner analogous to the prohibition against selling a *sefer Torah* even when it is not needed.

### Permanent Sale

The Sages take a far more permissive position: *mochrin oto memkar olam* — a *shul* may be sold as a *memkar olam*, a permanent and unconditional sale. The buyer takes ownership absolutely, and the selling community has no retained right of repurchase.

### Four Prohibitions

Even within the Sages' permissive framework, however, four uses are prohibited for a former *shul*: it may not be converted into a bathhouse (*merchatz*), a tannery (*borski*), a ritual bath (*tevilah* facility), or a bathroom (*beit hamayim*). The concern here is not *kedusha* — the Sages have already allowed the sale to de-sanctify the property — but *bizayon*: disrespect for what the place once was. A bathhouse involves undressed people in a steamy environment; a tannery is associated with foul odors; a ritual bath likewise involves nudity; a bathroom is self-evidently degrading. These uses are prohibited out of a residual sense of the dignity owed to a former place of sacred purpose, not because the *kedusha* persists.

### Field Sale

Rabbi Yehuda offers a third position: *mochrin oto l'shem chatzer* — one may sell the *shul* as one sells a field, leaving the buyer entirely free to use it as he wishes. On this view, one sells a location, not a purpose, and the seller bears no responsibility for the buyer's intentions. This position has practical implications: transactions involving former *batei knesset* that become places of other worship have sometimes been structured on precisely this model, treating the sale as one of real estate rather than sacred property.

### Bizayon Rationale

The Gemara clarifies that the four prohibited uses reflect a concern for *bizayon* rather than *kedusha*. The model the Ramban invokes is *tashmishei mitzvah*: objects used in the performance of a *mitzvah*, such as a *lulav*, may be discarded once their purpose is served — but one may not use them in a demeaning or disrespectful manner. A worn-out *lulav* need not be buried like a worn-out *sefer Torah* wrapping, but one should not use it to clean out a drain. Similarly, a former *shul* that has been sold and de-sanctified still carries a residual dignity, and uses that would be seen as actively disrespectful of its former role remain prohibited. This is not a *kedusha* concern but a *kavod* concern.

---

## Kedusha Questions

### Ribbit Problem

The Gemara raises a difficulty with Rabbi Meir's requirement that the community retain the right of repurchase. Consider the practical scenario: the *shul* is sold for ten thousand dollars, the buyer lives in or uses the space for a year, and then the community exercises its right to repurchase it for the same ten thousand dollars. The buyer has received his money back in full, and in the interim he had free use of the *shul*. That benefit — the free use during the period of the "loan" — looks like *ribbit*: the buyer effectively received a benefit in exchange for having advanced his money, which would constitute forbidden interest.

### Ribbit Resolution

Rabbi Yochanan resolves the difficulty: Rabbi Meir follows the position of Rabbi Yehuda, who rules that *tzad echad b'ribbit mutar* — one-sided interest that is not stipulated as part of the arrangement is permissible. The principle is that when the benefit to the lender is not a necessary or contractual feature of the transaction, but merely one possible outcome among others, it does not carry the prohibition of *ribbit*. The *baraita* elaborates: if someone lends money and the borrower gives his field as collateral-sale — meaning the field passes to the creditor if the loan is not repaid by a set date — and the *seller* (the debtor) continues to eat the fruit of the field in the interim, this is permissible. But if the *purchaser* (the creditor) eats the fruit, it is forbidden, because if the loan is ultimately repaid and the field reverts, the creditor will have had a material benefit from having lent the money. Rabbi Yehuda, however, rules that even when the creditor eats the fruit it is permissible, since the outcome — whether the field remains with the creditor or returns to the debtor — is not predetermined. This is the *tzad echad b'ribbit* principle: where benefit is a possible but not stipulated outcome, Rabbi Yehuda allows it.

### Rava's Analysis

Rava narrows the debate. He maintains that actually all opinions agree that *tzad echad b'ribbit assur* in the scenario as described — where the creditor might wind up keeping the fruit as a benefit from the loan. The actual dispute between the tanna'im, Rava argues, is about a different case: one where the creditor eats the fruit now with the understanding that if the field ultimately reverts, he will pay back the value of the fruit he consumed. The question becomes whether this appearance of *ribbit* — benefiting in the interim even with an obligation to repay — constitutes forbidden interest. Some hold it is forbidden because of appearances; others permit it because ultimately there will be no net gain. This is a considerably lighter disagreement than the one the Gemara initially seemed to be addressing.

### Tosafot Solution

As for Rabbi Meir's position on the *shul* repurchase: Tosafot suggest that Rabbi Meir would require, upon repurchase, that the original community pay rent to the buyer for the period of his use. The *Mishna* does not spell this out, but on Tosafot's reading it is the implicit condition that prevents any *ribbit* problem from arising. The transaction begins as a sale, not a loan, which itself distinguishes it somewhat from the paradigmatic *ribbit* case; but the requirement to pay retrospective rent removes even the surface concern.

---

## Prayer Space

### Urination Permitted

Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: it is permissible to urinate within four *amot* of a place where one has *davened*. Since the Gemara has just been discussing *beit hamayim* — a bathroom — as one of the prohibited uses for a former *shul*, it now transitions naturally to this related question about prayer space and physical needs. The ruling as stated implies that the act of prayer does not permanently sanctify a location; once one has finished *davening*, the space may be used for ordinary activities.

### Nehardea Absurdity

Rav Yosef challenges the ruling as he initially understands it: if prayer did sanctify the surrounding space, then the streets of Nehardea — where people *davened* everywhere, at all hours — would all be off limits for urination. Since this is clearly untenable, the initial plain reading of the *baraita* cannot mean that the geographic zone of prayer retains any permanent status.

A *tanna* taught before Rav Nachman: if one is in the middle of *davening* and needs to urinate, one steps out four *amot* and urinates; and if one has urinated and wishes to *daven*, one moves four *amot* away before beginning. The Gemara's questioner initially understood the first clause — moving four *amot* while still *davening* — to mean that even after one has finished *davening*, one must leave the zone before urinating. This leads directly to the absurdity Rav Yosef identifies.

### Temporal Separation

The Gemara re-reads the *baraita*: the instruction to maintain four *amot* is not about geographic zones at all. Rather, it is about temporal separation — a pause equivalent to the time it takes to walk four *amot* — between the act of prayer and the act of urination. The spatial language is reinterpreted as a unit of time. One does not need to leave a zone; one needs to pause.

### Experiential Separation

Rav Ashi explains the purpose of this pause: *shekol arba amot tefillato sedura be'piv* — for the first moments after completing *Shemoneh Esreh*, one's prayer is still arranged on one's lips — *u'richushei merachashin sifsasei* — one's lips are still subtly moving. The prayer has not yet fully concluded experientially. Before attending to bodily needs, one must allow a genuine separation between the sacred act of *tefilla* and the mundane activity that follows. The requirement is thus not geographic but phenomenological: ensure that the two experiences are experientially distinct.

The conclusion is clear: the Gemara rejects entirely the notion that any location where one has happened to *daven* acquires any lasting sanctity. Once *davening* is complete and one has allowed the brief experiential pause, the space may be used for any purpose without restriction.

---

## Piety Rewards

### Rabbi Zakkai

This discussion of prayer and its spatial aftermath forms the natural bridge to a series of accounts about long-lived sages and the virtues they attributed to their longevity. The students of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai asked him: *bameh he'arachta yamim* — in what merit did you live so long? He enumerated three practices. First: in all his days he never urinated within four *amot* of a place where prayer had been said. Second: he never gave a colleague a nickname. Third: he never missed making *Kiddush* with wine — a practice that, as the sequel shows, was no small commitment.

### Mother's Sacrifice

The difficulty of maintaining this last practice is illustrated by the story of his elderly mother. On one occasion, she sold the very bonnet from her head — *machra kipa shebarosha* — to obtain money for wine for *Kiddush*. The sacrifice embodied in this act — an elderly woman parting with her headcovering so that her son could honor Shabbat — captures the profound seriousness with which this practice was maintained even in poverty.

### Blessing Multiplication

When his mother died, she left him 300 flasks of wine — the reward, understood in the tradition, for her lifelong dedication to *Kiddush*. Rabbi Yochanan continued and even deepened the practice; when he died, he left his children 3000 flasks of wine. The exponential return — 300 becomes 3000 across one generation — illustrates the principle that expenditure in honor of Shabbat is repaid manifold, a teaching the Gemara treats as experientially verified through these family histories.

### Rav Huna Belt

A parallel story is told of Rav Huna. He was once standing before Rav wearing a simple cord instead of a proper belt. Rav asked him what this was. Rav Huna replied: *lo hava li kidusha* — I had no money for *Kiddush*, so I sold my belt and used the money to buy wine. Rav responded with a blessing: *yehei ra'ava de'tisatum beshirai* — may it be God's will that you be covered in silk. The fulfillment came in an unexpected and gently comic form: at his son Rabba's wedding, Rav Huna — who was a short man — fell asleep on a couch in the bridal room. His daughters and daughter-in-law, not realizing he was there, removed their silk wedding garments and draped them over the couch, until he was enveloped in silk.

### Blessing Power

When Rav learned that his blessing had come true, he was troubled — not displeased, but hurt. He said to Rav Huna: when I blessed you, why did you not say to me "and the same to you"? The exchange reveals something about the spiritual economy of *brachos* between great sages: a blessing given by a sage carries real power, and the reciprocal blessing is not mere courtesy but a genuine act of spiritual giving. The mutual exchange of blessings between Torah scholars is itself a significant religious act, and Rav Huna's failure to reciprocate was understood as a missed opportunity in this regard.

### Rabbi Elazar

The students of Rabbi Elazar ben Shamuah asked him the same question. He attributed his longevity to three practices: he never used the *shul* as a shortcut (*kapandarya*); he never walked over the heads of those sitting in the community — meaning he did not step over people to reach his seat, even when they were seated on the ground; and he never raised his hands in *Birkat Kohanim* without a proper blessing (*bracha*). The first two practices reflect a deep sense of the dignity owed to the *shul* as a sacred space and to fellow Jews as a holy people. The third reflects an insistence on intentionality and halakhic precision in the performance of sacred acts.

### Rabbi Preida

Rabbi Preida was asked the same question. He enumerated three practices: he was never preceded to the *beit midrash* — he was always the first to arrive; he never led a *bracha* — specifically *Birkat Hamazon* or an *aliyah* — when a *kohen* was present; and he never ate from an animal whose priestly gifts (*matanot kehunah*) — the foreleg, the jaw, and the maw — had not been given to the *kohen*.

The last practice requires elaboration. Rabbi Yitzchak said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: it is forbidden to eat from an animal whose priestly gifts have not been separated. This is compared to eating *tevel* — untithed produce — though the parallel is not exact: the animal does not actually become forbidden in the way that *tevel* does. The Gemara notes that the *halacha* does not follow Rabbi Yochanan's stringent ruling on this point — *ve'leis hilchasa kevatei* — yet Rabbi Preida maintained this stringency throughout his life.

### Torah Priority

The Gemara pauses over the second of Rabbi Preida's practices: is it actually praiseworthy for a *talmid chacham* to defer to a *kohen* and not lead blessings before him? Rabbi Yochanan himself taught that any *talmid chacham* who allows another to lead blessings in his place — even if that other person is a *kohen gadol* who is an *am ha'aretz* — commits an act so grievous as to be compared to one who is *chayav mitah*. The proof text: *kol mesan'ai ahavu mavet* — all those who hate Me love death — is reread as *mashni'ai*, those who cause me to be hated. By ceding the honor of Torah to an unlearned *kohen gadol*, one causes the Torah to appear less honorable than priestly status, which is a desecration of the Torah itself.

The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: when Rabbi Preida said he never led blessings before a *kohen*, he meant before a *kohen* who was himself a *talmid chacham* — a scholar of roughly equal standing. In such a case, honoring the *kohen*'s precedence is appropriate. But when a *kohen* is an *am ha'aretz*, a *talmid chacham* must assert the honor of Torah and take precedence, for to do otherwise is not piety but a betrayal of the Torah's dignity.

---

---

# Megillah 30

## Intro & Overview

### Masechet Structure

Daf 30 of *Masechet Megillah* is the penultimate *daf* of the tractate. The *masechet* opened with the reading of the *Megillah*, then addressed other aspects of synagogue life — the reading of the *Torah*, *haftarah*, *Birchas Kohanim*, and the sanctity of the *Beit Knesset* itself. Now the Gemara returns to the specifics of which sections are read on particular occasions. The final *Mishnah* of the tractate deals with the various sections read on *Yomim Tovim*, though it mentions only the *Torah* readings, and even those only partially — it does not detail the *Torah* readings for *Pesach* specifically, and it omits *haftarah* readings altogether.

### Braita-Gemara Dialog

The *Gemara* opens with a *braita* and then continuously interrupts it with Aramaic interjections. One can identify when the *Gemara* is speaking rather than the *braita* not only from the shift in language but from the keyword *ve-ha'idna* — "nowadays" — signaling that contemporary practice diverges from the *braita*, often because we observe two days of *Yom Tov* in the *golah* rather than one. What is particularly striking is that the *Gemara* signals not only changes due to the one-day versus two-day *Yom Tov* distinction, but a broader fluidity in what was established as the *Torah* and *haftarah* reading for each occasion. As will become apparent — and as *Tosafot* explicitly flags — even what the *Gemara* prescribes is not always what we practice today. There is an ongoing, acknowledged evolution in these readings across generations.

---

## Pesach Readings

### Braita: Moadot

The *braita* states: *be-Pesach korei be-parashat moadot* — on *Pesach* you read from the *parsha* of *moadot*, which is found in *Emor* in *Vayikra*, beginning with *shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled*. The opening section there concerns bringing an animal born to the *Beit HaMikdash*, and then the passage continues with *Daber el benei Yisrael ve-amarta aleihem mo'adei Hashem asher tikre'u otam mikra'ei kodesh* — *Shabbos* and then the listing of *Pesach* and the other *moadim*. As distinct from the listings in *Pinchas*, which focus narrowly on *korbanot*, the section in *Emor* has a broader dimension — it addresses the *chag* as celebrated beyond the *Beit HaMikdash*. For instance, by *Shavuot* the text includes *u-ve-kutzrechem et ketzir artzechem lo techaleh pe'at sadecha* — the obligation to leave portions of the harvest for the poor. By *Rosh Hashanah* the section begins with *innuy* before reaching the *korbanot*. This broader, more societal dimension explains why *Chazal* selected this section as the core *parsha* for reading on the *moadot*.

The *braita* further states that the *haftarah* for *Pesach* is the account of *Pesach be-Gilgal* — the *Pesach* observed when Bnei Yisrael first entered *Eretz Yisrael*, as recorded in *Yehoshua*.

### Two Days Practice

The *Gemara* interjects: *ve-ha'idna de-ika terei yomei* — nowadays that there are two days of *Yom Tov* in *Chutz La'aretz* — *yoma kama be-Pesach Gilgal*, the first day uses the *haftarah* of *Pesach be-Gilgal* from *Yehoshua*, and *u'lamachar be-Pesach Yoshiyahu* — the second day uses the *haftarah* from *Yoshiyahu*, who led a great national renewal and a celebrated observance of *Chag HaPesach*. According to this, the *Torah* reading of *shor chesev va-ez* would presumably remain for both first days, though as we will see, that is itself subject to modification.

### Chol HaMoed

The *braita* continues: *u-she'ar yemot ha-Pesach* — for the remaining days of *Pesach*, meaning *Chol HaMoed*, *melaket ve-korei me'inyano shel Pesach* — one collects and gathers various passages relating to *Pesach*, since the *Torah* contains numerous such passages. This instruction is too general to provide specifics, so the *Gemara* asks: *mai hi* — what exactly are the various readings for *Chol HaMoed Pesach*?

### Mnemonic System

*Amar Rav Pappa: Ma'apash siman* — Rav Pappa offers the mnemonic *Ma'apash* to recall the *Chol HaMoed* readings. According to *Rashi*, the letters stand for the following passages: *mem* — *Mashchu u-kechu lachem tzon lemishpachoteichem ve-shachatu ha-Pesach*, the command in Egypt to bring the *Korban Pesach*; *alef* — *Im kesef talveh et ami*, from the middle of *Mishpatim*, which briefly treats all three *Regalim* including *Pesach*; *peh* — *Psal lecha shnei luchot avanim ka-rishonim*, the second *luchot*, which similarly revisits the *shalosh regalim*; and *shin* — *Vayedaber*, from *Beha'alotcha* in *Bamidbar*, which is the passage of *Pesach Sheni*.

This mnemonic covers four days, which corresponds to the four days of *Chol HaMoed* in *Chutz La'aretz*. In *Eretz Yisrael*, where there are five days of *Chol HaMoed*, a fifth reading would need to be found.

The *braita* then continues: *Yom Tov acharon shel Pesach korin Vayehi Beshalach* — the last *Yom Tov* of *Pesach*, the seventh day, we read *Vayehi Beshalach* because *Kriat Yam Suf* occurred on the seventh day according to *Chazal*. The *haftarah* is *Vayedaber David*, the song of David, which parallels *Shirat HaYam*. As *Rashi* notes, there are elements of *Shirat David* that evoke the theme of *Yam Suf* — God unleashing His anger against His enemies. Then *u'lamachar — Kol Habechor*: the eighth day of *Pesach* (clearly addressing *Chutz La'aretz*, even though this is still in the Hebrew portion of the text) uses the reading of *Kol Habechor* from *Devarim*. The *haftarah* is *Od Hayom be-Nov la'amod*, a Messianic vision — appropriate for *Pesach* as a time of *geulah* that looks forward to future redemption.

It is worth pausing here on the structure underlying these selections. The *Torah* portions chosen for *Yom Tov* tend to fall into two groups: *shor o chesev o ez* from *Emor* and *Kol Habechor* (beginning with *aser te'aser*) from *Devarim*. The first type dominates the early days of *Yom Tov*; the second dominates the last days. Both share the common characteristic of addressing the *moadim* in a manner broader than the narrow *Mussaf korban* focus of *Pinchas*. The *aser te'aser* section in *Devarim*, for instance, encompasses a wide range of agricultural and social obligations — *ma'aser*, *shemita*, and responsibilities toward the poor — all deeply connected to the time of the harvest and the *chagim*.

### Abaye's Mnemonic

*Amar Abaye: Ha'idna nahag alma* — Abaye then offers a different and more comprehensive mnemonic for all eight days of *Pesach* in *Chutz La'aretz*: *Meshach Tora Kadesh Bakaspa Psal Bemadbara Shelach Buchra*. The mnemonic itself is in Aramaic — appropriately, since it is a memory device rather than a citation of biblical text, and the vernacular lends itself better to such a purpose.

The mapping is as follows. *Meshach* refers to *Mashchu u-kechu lachem tzon lemishpachoteichem ve-shachatu ha-Pesach* — the command in Egypt to bring the *Korban Pesach*, read on the **first day**. Note that this is a significant departure from the *braita*, which had the generic *shor o chesev o ez* on the first day. Abaye's approach begins with a passage directly and specifically about *Pesach*. *Tora* — *shor o chesev o ez*, the *shor* reference — is the **second day**. *Kadesh* refers to *Kadesh li kol bechor* from *Shemot*, which addresses the firstborn and the narrative of the Exodus, read on the **third day**. *Bakaspa* is *Im kesef talveh et ami* from *Mishpatim*, the third day's equivalent in Rav Pappa's system, now the **fourth day**. *Psal* is *Psal lecha shnei luchot avanim ka-rishonim* — the second *luchot*, **fifth day**. *Bemadbara* is from *Bemidbar Sinai* in *Beha'alotcha* — *Pesach Sheni*, **sixth day**. *Shelach* is *Vayehi Beshalach Paro et ha-am* — the seventh day and *Shirat HaYam*. *Buchra* is *Kol Habechor*, the eighth day.

The most significant shift from the *braita* is at the outset: rather than beginning with the generic *shor o chesev o ez*, the practice reflected in Abaye's mnemonic opens with the specific, narrative *Pesach* passage of *Mashchu u-kechu lachem tzon*. This reflects a broader tendency we will observe throughout: the *Gemara* and subsequent practice prefer to open *Yomim Tovim* with readings that speak directly and narratively to the character of the day, rather than with generic passages. Both *shor o chesev o ez* and *Kol Habechor* represent sections that treat all three *regalim* but without the narrow *Mikdash korban* focus; what distinguishes *Mashchu u-kechu* is that it opens the *Pesach* cycle with the very story of *Pesach* itself.

---

## Shavuot Readings

### Braita Dispute

The *braita* turns to *Shavuot*: *ba-Atzeret, Shiva Shavuot* — on *Shavuot* the reading is the passage about counting seven weeks and bringing the accompanying *korban*. The *haftarah* according to the first opinion is from *Chabakuk*, whose prophetic vision evokes the theophany at *Har Sinai*. *Acherim omrim* — others say: read *ba-chodesh ha-shlishi*, the narrative of *Matan Torah* at *Har Sinai* itself. And the *haftarah* in that view is from *Ma'aseh Merkavah* in *Yechezkel* — the heavens open and a divine vision unfolds, powerfully capturing the theophanic dimension of *Matan Torah*. It is worth noting that the significance of *Matan Torah* is not merely the transmission of law but the direct encounter with God — the theophany itself — and the *haftarah* of *Ma'aseh Merkavah* reflects precisely that.

### Two-Day Order

The *Gemara* interjects: *ve-haidna de-ika terei yomei, avdinan ke-tarveihu ve-ifcha* — nowadays that there are two days of *Shavuot*, we follow both opinions, but in reverse order. On the first day we read *ba-chodesh ha-shlishi* with the *haftarah* of *Ma'aseh Merkavah*, and on the second day we read the more generic *Shiva Shavuot*. This reversal follows the same pattern observed by *Pesach*: we prioritize the reading that most directly engages the essential character of the day, and so the narrative of *Matan Torah* takes precedence on the first day.

### Practical Question

This raises a fascinating practical question. A rabbi serving a small community where a *minyan* will only be present on the second day of *Shavuot* — which reading should he use? On one hand, the second day's prescribed reading is *Shiva Shavuot*. On the other hand, if there is only one opportunity to read from the *Torah* that *Shavuot*, one naturally wants it to be *ba-chodesh ha-shlishi* and *Matan Torah*. One might argue from the *Gemara*'s logic that since the *Gemara* goes out of its way to reverse the order and place *ba-chodesh ha-shlishi* first, this indicates it is the more weighty reading. On the other hand, since *Shiva Shavuot* was the first opinion in the *braita*, perhaps it holds primary standing. Interestingly, the *Rambam* seems to favor *Shiva Shavuot* as the more primary reading, though other sources do not point in that direction. Given the *Gemara*'s evident preference for the *ba-chodesh ha-shlishi* reading — signaled by placing it first — that would appear to be the stronger choice for a community with only one opportunity to read.

---

## Rosh Hashanah

### Braita & Opinions

For *Rosh Hashanah*, the *braita* prescribes *ba-chodesh ha-shevi'i* — the section in *Pinchas* dealing with the *korbanot* of the seventh month. This is specific to *Rosh Hashanah* by calendar placement, but does not really speak to the profound character of the day. The *haftarah* according to this view is *Ha-ben yakir li Ephraim, zachor ezkrenu od* — a passage about divine remembrance, appropriate for a day when God remembers us. *Ve-yesh omrim* — others say: read *ve-Hashem pakad et Sarah*, God's remembering of Sarah, which according to tradition occurred on *Rosh Hashanah*, and which is quintessentially about God remembering us for good. The *haftarah* in this view is *Chana*, whose story closely parallels that of Sarah.

### Two-Day Practice

*Ve-haidna de-ika terei yomei* — with two days of *Rosh Hashanah*, the *Gemara* prescribes: *yoma kama* — the first day — begins with the second opinion's reading: *ve-Hashem pakad et Sarah* with the *haftarah* of *Chana*. And for the second day — rather than reverting to the generic *ba-chodesh ha-shevi'i* — we read *ve-ha-Elokim nisa*, the *Akeidah*, with the *haftarah* of *Ha-ben yakir li Ephraim* — the merit of the *Akeidah* and its connection to the *shofar*. It is striking that even for the second day, the *Gemara* does not permit a generic or less evocative reading. Every day of *Rosh Hashanah* must be anchored in the essential themes of the day — divine remembrance, judgment, and the *zechus* of *Avraham*. One might attribute this to the gravity of *Yom HaDin*, which demands that the *kriyah* speak directly and urgently to the character of the day.

### Maftir Practice

One might note that the *Gemara* here does not separately identify a *maftir* reading from a different section. The implication is that there was no distinct *maftir* from a separate passage — a practice that differs from what we do today, where *ba-chodesh ha-shevi'i* from *Pinchas* serves as the *maftir*. As was correctly pointed out in discussion, we do read that passage on *Rosh Hashanah*, but as *maftir* rather than as the primary *kriyah*. The question of when exactly the association of the *Akeidah* with *Rosh Hashanah* entered into the *krias ha-Torah* is an open one; even if the broader theological and liturgical association is ancient, its formal expression in the *Torah* reading appears to be a later development.

---

## Yom Kippur

### Morning Service

*Beyom Hakippurim korin Acharei Mos* — on *Yom Kippur* the morning reading is *Acharei Mos*, which encompasses both the *avoda* of the *Kohen Gadol* and speaks directly to the nature of the day. The *haftarah* is *Ko amar Ram V'nisa* — "So says the One who is high and exalted" — a passage centrally concerned with *teshuva*.

### Afternoon Service

*U-ve-mincha korin ba-arayot* — in the *mincha* service, after the section of *avoda* in *Acharei Mos*, the reading continues with the *arayot*. The *haftarah* is *Yonah*, which is thematically connected to *teshuva* in the most direct way imaginable. As for why we read *arayot* in the afternoon, *Rashi* offers a specific rationale: transgressions in this domain are particularly prevalent, the *yetzer* is powerful regarding them, and therefore reading this section is deeply *me'inyano shel yom*. One might also observe that it functions as a continuation of the morning's reading. It was also wryly suggested that with so extensive a list of *arayot*, even the most troubled individual is likely to find at least some they have not transgressed — a source of comfort on a day of judgment.

### Aggadic Teaching

Because the *haftarah* of *Ram V'nisa* has been cited, the *Gemara* pauses for an *aggadic* teaching. *Amar Rabbi Yochanan: kol makom she'ata motzei gevuraso shel HaKadosh Baruch Hu, ata motzei anvasnuso* — wherever you find God's power, you find His humility. And this teaching, the *Gemara* notes, is *davar zeh kasuv ba-Torah, ve-shanui ba-Nevi'im, u-meshulash ba-Kesuvim* — written in the *Torah*, repeated in the *Nevi'im*, and stated a third time in the *Kesuvim*.

In the *Torah*: *ki Hashem Elokeichem hu Elokei ha-elokim va-adonei ha-adonim ha-Eil ha-gadol ha-gibor ve-ha-nora asher lo yisa fanim ve-lo yikach shochad* — God is supreme, transcendent, above all. And immediately following: *oseh mishpat yasom ve-almana ve-oheiv geir lases lo lechem ve-simla* — yet this same transcendent God lowers Himself to care for the orphan, the widow, and the stranger.

In the *Nevi'im*: *Koh amar Ram V'nisa shochein ad ve-kadosh shemo marom ve-kadosh eshkon* — God dwells on high, holy and elevated. And immediately: *ve-es daka u-shfal ruach, le-hachayos ruach shfalim u-le-hachayos leiv nidka'im* — to give spirit to those of lowly bearing, to revive the broken-hearted.

In the *Kesuvim*: *solu la-rochev ba-aravot be-Yah shemo* — God is exalted in the heavens. And immediately: *avi yesomim ve-dayan almanot* — Father of orphans and judge of widows.

The *Gemara*'s point here seems to carry a message that extends beyond theology. The prophets — *Yeshayahu*, *Amos*, and others — were constantly rebuking the people for the disconnect between religious observance and basic ethical conduct: elaborate *korbanot* brought alongside the neglect of justice. The *pasuk* quoted here suggests that the truest expression of recognizing God's greatness is not separatism or exclusive ritual behavior, but rather translating that recognition into how one treats the most vulnerable members of society. Sanctity and care for the marginalized are not two separate things — they are, as this *pasuk* teaches, the same thing seen from two sides.

---

## Sukkot Readings

### First Days

*Yom tov ha-rishon shel chag korim be-parashat moadot she-be-Torat Kohanim* — the first day of *Sukkot* returns to the more generic reading of *shor o chesev o ez* from *Emor*. With *Sukkot*, there are simply fewer dedicated narrative passages available than for *Pesach*, so the generic *moadot* section is used more broadly. The *haftarah* is *Hineh yom ba la-Hashem* from *Zechariah*, which presents a Messianic vision in which all nations ultimately come to recognize God and observe *Chag HaSukkot*.

*Ve-idna* — the *Gemara* interjects — with two days of *Yom Tov*, the second day reads the same *Torah* portion as the first. This itself reflects how much less material is available for *Sukkot* compared to *Pesach*. The *haftarah* for the second day is *Vayikahalu el ha-Melech Shlomo ba-chag* — the dedication of the *Beit HaMikdash*, which took place on *Sukkot*.

### Intermediate Days

*Ve-she'ar kol yemei ha-chag korim be-korbanot ha-chag* — for the intermediate days of *Sukkot* one reads the *korbanot* of the *chag*. This works particularly well for *Sukkot* since the *korbanot* vary from day to day — the famous diminishing sequence of bulls — and thus each day's reading is naturally differentiated.

---

## Pesach Readings (II)

### Torah Selection

It is worth pausing to examine the structural logic underlying the *Torah* selections across the *Yomim Tovim*. The pattern that emerges is that *shor o chesev o ez* from *Emor* tends to be used for the early days of *Yom Tov*, while *Kol Habechor* — beginning with *aser te'aser* — from *Devarim* tends to serve the latter days. Both sections share a defining characteristic: although they address the *moadim* and their associated obligations, they do so in a manner considerably broader than the narrow *korban mussaf* focus of *Pinchas*. Both engage the *chag* as a societal and agricultural phenomenon, not merely a *Mikdash*-centered ritual one.

---

## Sukkot Readings (II)

### Last Days

*Yom tov ha-acharon* — the last day of *Sukkot* (and by extension *Shemini Atzeret*): *korim Kol Habechor*. The *Gemara* specifies: *mitzvot ve-chukim u-vechor* — one reads from the beginning of this larger section, starting with *aser te'aser*, and not from *Kol Habechor* alone. This means one begins with *aser te'aser* and reads through to *Kol Habechor*.

The *haftarah* is *Vayehi ke-chalot Shlomo* — a passage from toward the end of the *Beit HaMikdash* dedication narratives in *Melachim*, which mentions *u-va-yom ha-shemini shilach et ha-am* — on the eighth day he sent the people home. Whether that eighth day is *Shemini Atzeret* or the eighth day following *Sukkot* is a matter of interpretation, but the mention of the eighth day connects naturally to *Shemini Atzeret*.

### Aser Te'aser Theme

*Rashi* explains directly why the reading begins earlier, with *aser te'aser* rather than with *Kol Habechor* itself: *sheyesh be-osah parsha mitzvot ve-chukim harbe ha-nohagos ba-chag be-oso zman ki zman asif* — this section contains many *mitzvot* and laws that apply during the *chag*, since it is the time of the harvest gathering. The season of *Sukkot* is *zman asifenu* — the time of ingathering — and the *aser te'aser* section speaks directly to the obligations that arise at that time.

Indeed, one need only scan the content of *aser te'aser* to appreciate why it is so central. It opens with the laws of *ma'aser*, *shmita*, and agricultural tithes. It includes *ki yihyeh becha evyon me'achad acheicha be-achad she'arecha* — the obligation to lend to the poor. It includes the laws of the Hebrew slave and release. As *Rashi* notes: *ve-od yesh be-osah parsha ma'aser ani u-mitzvas maton, she-titen u-fasoach tiftach ve-ha'anek ta'anik le-eved Ivri ve-shiluach hofshi ve-ha-avtenu* — all of this sense of responsibility toward those who are less fortunate is a central theme that must be heard on the *chagim*, and in particular around *Sukkot*.

The *Torah* itself returns to this theme repeatedly when speaking of *Sukkot*: *ve-samachta ata u-veitecha ve-al ha-Levi asher bi-she'arecha lo sa'azvenu* — rejoice, you and your household — but do not abandon the *Levi*, who has no portion. The abundance of the harvest is precisely the moment to share with those who have nothing. This is why on *Shemini Atzeret* specifically — the culmination of the *Sukkot* period — the reading begins with *aser te'aser* and encompasses all of these obligations, even when on other *yomim tovim* one might begin directly with *Kol Habechor*.

In practice, consulting a standard *siddur* confirms a nuanced approach: if the last day of *Pesach* or the second day of *Shavuot* falls on *Shabbos*, one begins from *aser te'aser* — since the additional *aliyot* of *Shabbos* and the absence of time pressure allow for the fuller reading. On a weekday, one begins directly with *Kol Habechor*. On *Shemini Atzeret*, however, one always begins with *aser te'aser* regardless — because *Sukkot* is the very season to which these obligations most acutely apply, and the message of responsibility to the poor must be heard in full.

The *Gemara* then continues: *u-maftirin Vayehi ke-chalot Shlomo* — and indeed, these passages from the dedication of the *Beit HaMikdash* run through all of *Sukkot*, since the dedication itself took place on *Sukkot* and was completed with the sending home of the people on the eighth day.

*Le-machar korin Ve-zot ha-berachah* — the following day, *Shemini Atzeret* in *Chutz La'aretz* (i.e., *Simchat Torah*), one reads *Ve-zot ha-berachah*. The *haftarah* is *Vaya'amod Shlomo* — another passage from *Shlomo*'s prayer at the *Beit HaMikdash* dedication.

Here *Tosafot* raises an important point. He notes that some communities are accustomed to reading *Vayehi acharei mot Moshe* as the *haftarah* instead, and he calls this *shibush* — a corruption — since the *Shas* does not say so. He acknowledges that some attribute this change to *Rav Hai Gaon*, but adds: *aval einam yodim ha-svara mai shina seder ha-Shas ve-takana shel Rav Hai* — they do not know the reasoning for departing from the order of the *Gemara* and the enactment of Rav Hai.

This is a striking contrast with another *Tosafot* we will encounter shortly, which accepts changes from *Gemara* practice with equanimity when a literary source can be cited. What the *Gemara* itself makes clear through its repeated use of *ha'idna nahog* or *nahag alma* is that these practices carry an inherent fluidity. The *Gemara* is not recording a different *psak*; it is observing that practices have evolved — *nahag alma*, the world came to practice it this way — without any formal rabbinic enactment. The phrasing itself legitimizes organic change. In light of this, what is remarkable is not that practice has evolved, but that *Tosafot* in certain instances finds such evolution troubling. The answer appears to be that *Tosafot* is more comfortable when a change can be anchored in a literary source — *Masechet Sofrim*, the *Psikta*, or similar — rather than in undocumented popular evolution alone.

---

## Special Dates

### Chol HaMoed Shabbat

*Amar Rav Huna amar Rav: Shabbat she-chala lihyot be-cholo shel mo'ed, bein be-Pesach bein be-Sukkot* — for *Shabbat Chol HaMoed*, whether of *Pesach* or *Sukkot*, the reading is *Re'eh ata omer elai* — the passage about the second *luchot* and the *shalosh regalim*. The passage is chosen because its conclusion deals with the *regalim*, though we begin somewhat earlier to allow for more *aliyot*.

The *haftarah* for *Shabbat Chol HaMoed Pesach* is *ha-atzamot ha-yaveshot* — the vision of the dry bones from *Yechezkel*. According to *Chazal*, this vision refers to those who attempted to leave *Mitzrayim* prematurely. In the broader sense it speaks of revival, redemption, and the return of those who are literally and figuratively dead to life — deeply resonant with the *geulah* theme of *Pesach*.

For *Shabbat Chol HaMoed Sukkot*, the *haftarah* is *be-yom bo Gog* — the prophetic vision of *Gog u-Magog* from *Yechezkel*. Both *haftarot* carry a Messianic dimension: the *Pesach* reading focuses on redemption and revival, while the *Sukkot* reading centers on the eschatological battle that precedes the ultimate divine recognition by all nations — including the universal observance of *Chag HaSukkot* envisioned in *Zechariah*.

### Chanukah

*Be-Chanukah be-nesiyim* — on *Chanukah* we read the *nesiyim*, the dedication offerings of the tribal princes, from *Bamidbar*. This is appropriate because of *Chanukat ha-Bayit*, and conveniently there are enough readings across the eight days to cover the entirety of *Chanukah*. The *haftarah* is the vision of the *menorah* in *Zechariah*. If two *Shabbatot* fall within *Chanukah* — a rare occurrence — the first uses the *haftarah* of the *menorah* from *Zechariah*, and the second uses the vision of the *menorah* that *Shlomo* built, from *Melachim*.

### Purim & RH

*Be-Purim Vayavo Amalek* — on *Purim* the reading is *Vayavo Amalek*. From this point forward the *Gemara* ceases to mention *haftarot*, since the occasions that follow are neither *chagim* nor *Shabbat*, and therefore no *haftarah* is read.

For *Rosh Chodesh*, the reading is *Roshei Chodsheichem* — the section in *Pinchas* dealing with the *korbanot* of *Rosh Chodesh*. The *Gemara* moves directly to the *haftarah* without explicitly addressing when *Roshei Chodsheichem* is read (it serves as *maftir*). If *Rosh Chodesh* falls on *Shabbos*, the *haftarah* is *Ve-haya midei chodesh be-chodsho* from *Yeshayahu* — the passage that speaks of every *chodesh be-chodsho ve-Shabbos be-Shabbato*, people gathering to worship God. It is notable that in the time of the *Nevi'im*, *Rosh Chodesh* was a considerably more prominent occasion than we experience it today — *madua at holechet elav ha-yom lo chodesh ve-lo Shabbos* — and the pairing of *Chodesh* and *Shabbos* in that *haftarah* reflects that historical weight, even if our contemporary practice has diminished the standing of *Rosh Chodesh* considerably.

If *Rosh Chodesh* falls on a Sunday — *be-echad be-Shabbos* — the practice is to read the *haftarah* of *Vayomer lo Yehonatan: machar chodesh* — the passage of *Machar Chodesh* — on the *Shabbos* before. The *Gemara* does not specify what is done when *Rosh Chodesh* is two days, and in practice different communities handle this differently.

---

## Tisha B'Av Cycle

### RCA Av

*Amar Rav Huna: Rosh Chodesh Av she-chal lihyot be-Shabbos*, if *Rosh Chodesh Av* falls on *Shabbos* — *maftirin Chodsheichem u-Mo'adeichem sane'ah nafshi hayu alai le-torach*. This *haftarah* from *Yeshayahu* addresses *Rosh Chodesh* through *Chodsheichem*, and simultaneously carries the message of divine rebuke and impending catastrophe through *sane'ah nafshi* — fitting for the beginning of *Av*. This passage is part of the section known as *Chazon* — *Chazon Yeshayahu ben Amotz*. As we will see from *Tosafot*, this is not our practice.

The *Gemara* then pauses on the phrase *ve-hayu alai le-torach* — "they have been a burden to Me." What does this mean? *Amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu: lo dayan le-resha'im she-hem chotim le-fanai ela she-matrichim osi le-da'at eizeh gezeirah kasha avi aleihem* — it is not enough that they sin before Me; they then burden Me with having to determine what severe punishment to bring upon them.

### Tisha B'Av

*Be-Tisha b'Av gufay mai maftirin* — what is read on *Tisha b'Av* itself? The *Gemara* asks this without first addressing the *Shabbos* preceding *Tisha b'Av*, since that *Shabbos* has no special *kriyah* in the *Gemara*'s framework — only *Shabbat Rosh Chodesh* carries independent weight by virtue of being *Rosh Chodesh* itself.

*Amar Rav: Eicha hayesa le-zona* — the *haftarah* on *Tisha b'Av* is from *Chazon Yeshayahu* as well.

As for the *Torah* reading: *tanya im lo tishme'u li* — the *braita* prescribes the *brachot u-kelalot* in *Bechukotai*, consistent with the earlier principle that on *taaniyot* one reads *brachot u-kelalot* — a passage laying out the consequences of sin. *Ve-Noson bar Yosef omer* — another opinion holds: *ad ana yin'atzuni ha-am ha-zeh* — the passage about the *Meraglim*, since *Tisha b'Av* is the day associated with the sin of the *Meraglim*. *Ve-yesh omrim* — yet another opinion: *ad masai la-eidah ha-ra'ah ha-zot* — also from the *Meraglim* narrative. Both latter opinions reflect the drive, evident throughout this *Gemara*, to link the reading to a specific narrative rather than a generic passage.

*Amar Abaye: Ha'idna nahagu alma le-mikri ki tolid banim u-vnei vanim* — Abaye reports that the practice nowadays is to read *Ki tolid banim u-vnei vanim*, which addresses punishment for sin with particular focus on exile from the land — painful and appropriate for *Tisha b'Av*, but considerably less harsh than the *brachot u-kelalot* of *Bechukotai*. The *haftarah* in current practice is *Asof asifeim* — a bleak prophetic vision of the devastation of exile. This is our practice.

### Tosafot Defense

*Tosafot* acknowledges that our practice differs substantially from what the *Gemara* prescribes. *Ve-ein anu osin kein* — we do not follow the *Gemara*'s prescription for *Rosh Chodesh Av* falling on *Shabbos*. Instead, the *Shabbos* before *Tisha b'Av* uses *Chazon Yeshayahu*, and earlier *Shabbatot* in the period preceding use other *haftarot* from *Yirmiyahu*. *Ve-ha-ta'am: lefi she-anu nohagim al pi ha-Psikta* — the justification is that our practice follows the *Psikta*, a recognized literary source. *Tosafot* is at peace with this change because it is anchored in a literary authority. He contrasts this favorably with changes that lack such grounding.

Significantly, *Tosafot* here also acknowledges the change in *taanit* readings: we read *Vayeichal* on a *taanit*, while the *Mishnah* says *brachot u-kelalot*. He notes that this follows *Masechet Sofrim*. The pattern is consistent: *Tosafot* accepts organic evolution in practice when it can be attributed to a recognized literary source — *Psikta*, *Masechet Sofrim* — but is considerably more exercised when changes appear to lack such authority.

### Pur'anyot & Nechamah

The practice that *Tosafot* describes — which is entirely absent from the *Gemara* — is the well-known sequence of three *haftarot* of *pur'anyot* preceding *Tisha b'Av* and seven *haftarot* of *nechamah* following it. *Tosafot* outlines the system: the three of *pur'anyot* are *Divrei Yirmiyahu*, *Shim'u dvar Hashem*, and *Chazon Yeshayahu*. After *Tisha b'Av* come the seven of *nechamah* — *Nachamu nachamu*, *Vatomer Tzion*, *Aniyah so'arah*, *Anochi anochi*, *Rani akarah*, *Kumi ori ki va orech*, and *Sos asis* — followed by the two of *teshuvah*: *Dirshu Hashem be-himatzo* and *Shuva Yisrael*, the latter being *Shabbat Shuva*.

There is even a charming internal logic to the sequence of the seven *nechamah haftarot*, reading almost as a dialogue. God declares *Nachamu nachamu ami* — comfort, comfort My people — addressing the *nevi'im* as messengers. The *nevi'im*, in turn, relay this to *Knesset Yisrael*, who responds through *Aniyah so'arah lo nuchamah* — "the afflicted one has not been comforted" — because the people want to hear the comfort directly from God, not through intermediaries. God then responds directly: *Anochi anochi hu menachemchem* — I Myself will comfort you. At which point the rejoicing breaks out: *Rani akarah*, *Sos asis*, *Kumi ori ki va orech*. Whether or not one traces this precise narrative reading to the *Psikta* directly, it is the established *minhag* and *Tosafot* endorses it as inviolable: *ha-minhag lo yishtaneh le-olam al pi ha-Psikta*.

---

## Ma'amados

### Ma'amados Purpose

The *Gemara* now turns to *ma'amados*. The institution of *ma'amados* involves groups of representatives from cities throughout *Eretz Yisrael* who gather when the *kohanim* of their region are on rotation to serve in the *Beit HaMikdash*. These groups fast and read from *Ma'aseh Breishis* — the account of Creation — as a way of connecting the people to the *korbanot* being brought on their behalf. This occurs on a weekly rotating basis.

*Mina hanei milei* — from where is it derived that they read from *Ma'aseh Breishis*? *Amar Rav Ammi: ilmalei ma'amados lo niskaymu shamayim va'aretz* — were it not for the *ma'amados*, heaven and earth would not continue. *She-ne'emar: im lo brisi yomam va-layla, chukot shamayim va-aretz lo samti* — "were it not for My covenant day and night, the laws of heaven and earth I would not have set." Here *brisi* is understood to refer to the *korbanot*, not the *Torah*, since it is the people's connection to the *korbanot* — expressed through the *ma'amados* — that sustains the cosmic order. Reading *Ma'aseh Breishis* is therefore fitting because it is the very acts of creation that are being sustained through this connection.

### Abrahamic Covenant

*Ve-chtiv: vayomer Hashem Elokim bamei eda ki ireshena* — Avraham asks God: how will I know that I shall inherit the land? The *Gemara* reads this not as a challenge to God's truthfulness, but as an expression of concern about the people's ability to remain worthy of the divine promise. What if they sin? God responds: *kach li egla meshuleshet* — the *korbanot* will sustain them. Avraham then presses further: *Ribbono shel olam, teineh bi-she'at she-Beit HaMikdash kayam — bi-she'at she-ein Beit HaMikdash kayam mah te'ei aleihem* — what will be when there is no *Beit HaMikdash*?

God replies: *kvar tikanti lahem seder korbanot; kol zman she-korim bahem, ma'aleh ani aleihem ke'ilu makrivim le-fanai korban u-mochel ani al kol avonoseihem* — I have already given them the order of the *korbanot*; whenever they read these passages, I consider it as if they have brought a *korban* before Me, and I forgive all their sins.

The *Gemara* invokes this teaching to explain why the *ma'amados* read *Ma'aseh Breishis*: while the *Beit HaMikdash* stands, the *korbanot* themselves sustain creation. When it is absent, reading about the *korbanot* — or, as in the case of the *ma'amados*, reading about *Ma'aseh Breishis* which those *korbanot* sustain — serves in their stead. It also ties back elegantly to the festival readings discussed throughout this *daf*: when we read the passages of *korbanot* on the *moadim*, we are participating in this same substitution that God Himself established in covenant with Avraham. The *Gemara* universalizes the *pesuk*'s concern — it is not merely about inheriting *Eretz Yisrael*, but about what will keep the world itself in existence; and the answer is the study and reading of the *seder korbanot*.

---

## Taanis & Kelalot

### Taanis Rules

*Be-taaniyot: brachot u-kelalot, ein mafsikin ba-kelalot* — on public fasts, the *brachot* and *kelalot* are read, and one may not interrupt the *kelalot* in the middle by ending one *aliyah* and beginning another. *Minani milei* — from where is this derived? *Amar Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda amar Rabbi Assi: de-amar kra — Musar Hashem beni al tima'as* — do not despise God's *musar*. To interrupt the *kelalot* mid-reading suggests a kind of rejection or distaste for the rebuke, as though one is eager to be rid of it.

*Reish Lakish amar* — alternatively: *lefi she-eino min ha-bracha al pur'aniyot* — one should not make a *bracha*, specifically *birchas ha-Torah*, directly over catastrophic content. It is not fitting to pronounce a blessing immediately juxtaposed with dire punishment. This reflects the practice where each *oleh* recited *brachot* before and after his portion.

*Ela heichi avid* — how then does one manage practically? A *tanna* taught: *ke-she-hu matchil, matchil be-pasuk she-lifneihem* — one begins a *pasuk* or several *pesukim* before the *kelalot* begin, so that the *bracha* is pronounced over a non-problematic passage. *U-che-she-hu mesayem, mesayem be-pasuk she-achareihem* — and when concluding, one continues one or several *pesukim* beyond the *kelalot*, so that the closing *bracha* is similarly not directly over the *kelalot* themselves. *Tosafot* notes that one begins a few *pesukim* before rather than just one, since one must not leave fewer than three *pesukim* at the end of a *parsha*.

### Klala Types

*Amar Abaye: lo shanu ela be-kelalot she-be-Torat Kohanim* — this prohibition against interrupting applies only to the *kelalot* in *Torat Kohanim*, i.e., the *kelalot* of *Bechukotai* in *Vayikra*. *Aval kelalot she-be-Mishneh Torah, posek* — for the *kelalot* in *Mishneh Torah*, in *Ki Tavo*, one may interrupt.

*Mai ta'ama* — why the distinction? *Halalu be-lashon rabbim amurot u-Moshe mi-pi ha-gevurah amran* — the *kelalot* of *Vayikra* are phrased in the plural: *im lo tishme'u li*, *ve-im telchu imi be-keri* — all the people are sinning — and they are spoken in God's own voice: *va-asafti le-yasra etchem sheva al chatoteichem*. God Himself declares what He will do. They are thus harsher in both content and speaker.

*Aval halalu be-lashon yachid amurot u-Moshe mi-pi atzmo amran* — the *kelalot* of *Ki Tavo* are in the singular: *ve-haya im lo tishmah*, *yakecha Hashem becha* — not *bachem* — and they are spoken in Moshe's voice rather than God's. *Tosafot*, noting the apparent theological difficulty, adds in just two words: *be-ruach ha-kodesh* — Moshe spoke *be-ruach ha-kodesh*, certainly not from his own invention. The point is rather that the mode of expression — God speaking in first person versus Moshe speaking in God's name — renders the *kelalot* of *Vayikra* qualitatively harsher. Because the *kelalot* of *Ki Tavo* are less severe, it is permissible to interrupt them by dividing the reading into separate *aliyot*.

A vivid illustration: *Levi bar Buti hava kari u-kemagumgam kamei de-Rav Huna* — Levi bar Buti was reading and was stumbling, reading haltingly and with visible discomfort through the *kelalot*. *Rashi* explains that the reader was reciting them rapidly but struggling to get the words out — overwhelmed by the weight of what he was reading. *Rav Huna* said to him: *achsof nafshecha* — do as you wish; if you need to make a break, interrupt it. *Lo shanu ela kelalot she-be-Torat Kohanim; aval she-be-Mishneh Torah — posek* — here in *Mishneh Torah*, you may indeed interrupt.

### Klala Timing

*Tanya: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar omer: Ezra tikan lahem le-Yisrael she-yihyu korin kelalot she-be-Torat Kohanim kodem Atzeret u-she-be-Mishneh Torah kodem Rosh Hashanah* — Ezra enacted that the *kelalot* of *Torat Kohanim* should be read before *Shavuot*, and the *kelalot* of *Mishneh Torah* before *Rosh Hashanah*. In the annual reading cycle, this roughly works out naturally: the end of *Vayikra* is reached around *Shavuot* time, and *Ki Tavo* is reached in the weeks before *Rosh Hashanah*.

*Mai ta'ama* — the reason? *Amar Abaye ve-itayma Reish Lakish: kedei she-tichleh shana ve-kileloteiha* — so that the year should end together with its curses. Do not carry the curses of the old year into the new one. Mention them at the year's close, be done with them, and enter the new year with a clean slate.

This works straightforwardly for *Mishneh Torah* before *Rosh Hashanah*, since *Rosh Hashanah* is the new year. But for *Torat Kohanim* before *Shavuot* — *atu Atzeret Rosh Hashanah hi*? Is *Shavuot* really a new year? *Atzeret nami Rosh Hashanah hi de-tnan: ba-Atzeret al peirot ha-ilan* — yes, *Shavuot* is also a *Rosh Hashanah* of sorts, as the *Mishnah* in *Rosh Hashanah* teaches: on *Shavuot* judgment is rendered on the fruit of the trees.
