Therefore the end of the previous year's fruit cycle is the appropriate time to conclude the *kelalot* of *Torat Kohanim*, so as to enter the new fruit year on a positive note. *Tosafot* further notes that in practice we ensure these *kelalot* are read at least one *Shabbos* before the *Shabbos* immediately preceding *Shavuot* or *Rosh Hashanah*, so that the *Shabbos* entering the new year is read in a positive spirit.

### Baal Koreh Training

A final teaching from *Tosafot* on this *daf* deserves mention — one that any *baal koreh* will find striking. *Tosafot* cites the *Yelamdenu*, a literary source quoted in the context of *Parshat Yitro*: *ein anu rashai likro ba-Torah ad she-yachzor ha-parsha gimel pe'amim* — one is not permitted to serve as *baal koreh* until one has reviewed the *parsha* three times. The source is the verse *az ra'ah va-yisperah, hechinah ve-gam chakarah* — "then He saw it and related it, prepared it and also examined it" — three verbs of preparation — *ve-acharei khen va-yomer le-adam*. Three preparatory reviews before one leads the community in *krias ha-Torah*.

*Tosafot* adds: *ve-assur lismoch al ha-bimah, de-zman netinasah me-umad* — and one must stand without leaning on the *bimah*, since the giving of the *Torah* was done standing. A fitting note on which to conclude a *daf* devoted in its entirety to the laws and customs of *krias ha-Torah*. *Masechet Megillah* reaches its conclusion tomorrow.

---

---

# Megillah 31

## Rosh Chodesh Tevet

### Multiple Scrolls Setup

The daf opens with a case requiring multiple *sifrei Torah*: when *Rosh Chodesh Tevet* falls on *Shabbat*, one encounters the unusual convergence of *Rosh Chodesh* and *Chanukah* on the same *Shabbat*, creating the well-known situation of three *sifrei Torah*. The *Gemara* earlier addressed the *Shabbat* scenario, and now turns to the weekday case.

### Rav Yitzchak's View

When *Rosh Chodesh Tevet* falls on a weekday, *Rav Yitzchak Naphcha* rules that one reads three *aliyot* devoted to *Rosh Chodesh* and one *aliyah* devoted to *Chanukah*. Since weekday *Rosh Chodesh* calls for three *aliyot* and *Chanukah* for three as well, the question is how to divide the four total *aliyot* that result from their coincidence. *Rav Yitzchak Naphcha* gives the preponderance to *Rosh Chodesh*: three readings from the *Rosh Chodesh* portion and the fourth *aliyah* from the *Chanukah* reading — the *nesi'im*.

### Rav Dimi's View

*Rav Dimi miHaifa* takes the contrary position: three *aliyot* are devoted to *Chanukah* and one to *Rosh Chodesh* — specifically the *musaf shel Rosh Chodesh* passage.

### Tadir Principle

*Rav Mani* weighs in to support *Rav Yitzchak Naphcha*, invoking the principle of *tadir veshe'eino tadir tadir kodem*: since *Rosh Chodesh* is the more frequent occurrence, it takes precedence, and accordingly the majority of the reading is devoted to it.

*Rav Avin*, however, argues that *Rav Dimi* is in fact the more logical position. His reasoning inverts the *tadir* logic: it is precisely *Rosh Chodesh* that causes the fourth *aliyah* to exist at all, since on a normal weekday *Chanukah* has only three *aliyot*. If *Rosh Chodesh* is responsible for generating the extra *aliyah*, it follows that this fourth *aliyah* — *revi'i beRosh Chodesh ba'ei mikri* — should itself be the *Rosh Chodesh* reading.

### Rav Yosef vs Rava

*Rav Yosef* rules that one does not give significant weight to *Rosh Chodesh* — meaning *Chanukah* is the dominant reading. *Rava* rules the opposite: one does not give weight to *Chanukah*, and *Rosh Chodesh* remains primary. The final *halakha* follows *Rava*: *ein mashgichin beChanukah veRosh Chodesh ikkar* — three *aliyot* from the *Rosh Chodesh* reading and the fourth *aliyah* from *Chanukah*.

---

## Shekalim/Ki Tissa

### Shekalim Before Ki Tissa

The *Gemara* now addresses what happens when *Parshat Shekalim* falls on the *Shabbat* of *Va'ata Tetzaveh* — the *Shabbat* immediately preceding *Ki Tissa*, whose opening section constitutes the *Shekalim* reading. *Rav Yitzchak Naphcha* proposes a tidy solution: read six *aliyot* from *Va'ata Tetzaveh* through to *Ki Tissa*, and use the seventh *aliyah* to read the beginning of *Ki Tissa* — namely, the *Shekalim* passage — through *Ve'asita*. The cycle of *Va'ata Tetzaveh* is thereby completed and the special reading is incorporated as the seventh *aliyah*.

### Abaye's Solution

*Abaye* objects. He argues that this arrangement will confuse people: *ukmi hu deka mokmi hatam* — they will simply think the *baal keri'ah* decided to venture a bit further into next week's *parsha*, and will not recognize that the seventh *aliyah* constitutes a purposeful *Parshat Shekalim* reading. It is worth noting that this objection itself illuminates the degree of flux in *parasha* divisions during the Talmudic period, particularly given the *Yerushalmi*'s three-year cycle.

*Abaye* therefore proposes a different approach: the sixth *aliyah* reads through the end of *Ki Tissa* up to *Ve'asita* — that is, the reader does not stop at the end of *Va'ata Tetzaveh* but carries into *Ki Tissa* — and then the seventh *aliyah* doubles back and re-reads the same *Shekalim* passage from the beginning of *Ki Tissa* through *Ve'asita*. This doubling back is analogous in function to the role of the *ba'al maftir*, though the *Gemara* here operates on the assumption that the special reading is assigned to *shvi'i* rather than *maftir* — a point connected to the broader question of whether *maftir* is *oleh min ha-minyan*.

### Supporting Tanya

A *tanya* corroborates *Abaye*'s approach. The *baraita* states: if *Parshat Shekalim* falls on a *Shabbat* adjacent to *Ki Tissa* — whether immediately before or immediately after — *korin otah ve-koflah*, one reads it and repeats it. While this at first seems to address only the case of *Shekalim* falling before *Ki Tissa* (confirming *Abaye*'s read-and-repeat method), *Rav Yitzchak Naphcha* challenges *Abaye*: the *baraita* speaks of both before and after. If *Shekalim* falls *after* *Ki Tissa*, there is no meaningful repetition to be done within that *Shabbat*'s reading. The *Gemara* resolves this: *koflah be-shabbasos* — the doubling refers not to repeating within a single *Shabbat*'s laining but to the fact that when *Shekalim* and *Ki Tissa* are adjacent weeks, the opening section of *Ki Tissa* will be read on two consecutive *Shabbatot* — once as part of the regular *parsha* cycle and once as the *Shekalim* reading.

### Shekalim on Ki Tissa

The final case: *Parshat Shekalim* falls directly on the *Shabbat* of *Ki Tissa* itself. *Rav Yitzchak Naphcha*, consistent with his general reluctance to repeat passages, proposes a striking solution: skip over the *Shekalim* section entirely, start the reading from *Ve'asita*, read through to *Vayakhel* for the first six *aliyot*, and then assign the seventh *aliyah* to go back and read *Ki Tissa* through *Ve'asita*. The problem is severe: *Abaye* objects that *hashta amri le-mafre'a hu de-kari* — people will say the Torah is being read out of order, and the *Mishnah* has already established that one may not read the Torah out of order. A section was skipped and only returned to afterward; regardless of the rationale, it constitutes reading backwards.

*Abaye* therefore rules: start from the very beginning of *Ki Tissa*, read six *aliyot* through to *Vayakhel*, and then the seventh *aliyah* returns to the opening of *Ki Tissa* and re-reads the *Shekalim* portion. The *tanya* cited earlier confirms this: *chala lihiyot be-Ki Tissa atzmah — koreh otah ve-koflah* — when *Shekalim* falls on *Ki Tissa* itself, one reads the passage and then repeats it.

---

## Special Parshiyot Calend…

### Rosh Chodesh Mid-Week

The *Gemara* now turns to the broader calendrical framework: how to ensure that the four special *parshiyot* fall in their proper places relative to *Purim*, *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, and *Pesach*. The *Shekalim* reading must precede *Rosh Chodesh Adar* in order to give the community sufficient time to bring their *shekalim* before the money-changers set out their tables.

The *Mishnah* states: *chal lihiyot betoch ha-Shabbat, makdimim le-Shabbat she-avrah* — if *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls during the week, one reads *Shekalim* on the preceding *Shabbat*.

### Rav vs Shmuel

The case under dispute is *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falling on *Erev Shabbat* — Friday. Do we apply the same rule and read *Shekalim* on the *Shabbat* six days earlier, or does the proximity to *Shabbat* allow us to push the reading off to the following *Shabbat*?

*Rav* rules *makdimin*: even when *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on Friday, one reads *Shekalim* the preceding *Shabbat*, because otherwise one will not have the full fourteen days for people to bring their *shekalim* before the money-changers open for business. *Shmuel* rules *me'acharin*: one may push the reading to the following *Shabbat*. His reasoning: if *Rosh Chodesh* is on the 1st of *Adar* and that day is a Friday, then the 15th is also a Friday. The money-changers would not open their tables on *Erev Shabbat*; *shulchanot lo nafki ad chad be-Shabta* — they would wait until Sunday. Therefore in such a month, even postponing the reading by one day still leaves adequate time before the tables open, and *hilkach me'achirin* — one may therefore delay.

### Baraita Interpretation

The *Gemara* attempts to resolve the dispute from a *baraita*. The *Mishnah* itself says *chal lihiyot betoch ha-Shabbat, makdimin* — and the *Gemara* first asks whether this implies even the case of *Erev Shabbat*. The response: *lo, betoch ha-Shabbat davka* — the *Mishnah* means strictly in the middle of the week, not on the edge.

The *Gemara* then cites the *baraita* directly: *eizo hi Shabbat rishona — kol she-chal Rosh Chodesh Adar lihyot be-tokhah, va-afilu be-erev Shabbat* — the first special *Shabbat* is any *Shabbat* where *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls during its week, even if it falls on *Erev Shabbat*. This appears to be a proof for *Rav*: just as *betoch ha-Shabbat* means one reads *Shekalim* the preceding *Shabbat*, so too *afilu Erev Shabbat* — even on a Friday — one reads it the preceding *Shabbat*.

*Shmuel* counters by reading the *baraita* differently. He argues the text should be read as *bah* rather than *be-tokhah*: the first *Shabbat* is not any *week* in which *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls, but the *Shabbat* on which *Rosh Chodesh Adar* itself falls — or, if *Rosh Chodesh* fell on *Erev Shabbat*, the *Shabbat* immediately following it. The school of *Shmuel* (*tana de-vei Shmuel*) likewise formulates it as *bah*. The simple reading of the *baraita*, however, favors *Rav*.

### R. Shimon on Erev Shabbat

A *tannaitic* dispute is then cited: *mesargin le-Shabbatot divrei Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi* — one may insert breaks (skip *Shabbatot*) between the special readings, according to *Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi*. *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* disagrees and says *ein mesargin* — one does not skip. He qualifies: when does he say one does not skip? *Bizman she-chal lihyot be-Erev Shabbat* — when *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on *Erev Shabbat*. In that scenario, following *Shmuel*'s position and reading *Shekalim* the following *Shabbat* (the 2nd of *Adar*), the subsequent *Shabbatot* fall on the 9th, 16th, 23rd, and 30th — a perfect alignment requiring no skips. *Zachor* falls before *Purim*, *Parah* follows *Purim*, *Hachodesh* precedes *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*, and everything works without gaps.

*Eimatai ani omer ein mesargin* — *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar* is saying: this is the *one* scenario in which the calendar works out naturally without any skipping, and that is precisely when *Rosh Chodesh* falls on *Erev Shabbat*. In all other cases — when it falls in the middle of the week — one must read *Shekalim* the preceding *Shabbat* (which may be in *Shevat*), and a skip will inevitably be required to bring *Zachor* to just before *Purim*. The debate between *Rav* and *Shmuel* thus maps onto the dispute between *Rabbi Yehuda Hanasi* and *Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar*.

The *halakha* is ruled in all cases like *Rav*.

---

## Zachor & Purim

### Rav Advances

The same structural question arises regarding *Parshat Zachor*: what happens when *Purim* falls on *Erev Shabbat* — Friday? *Rav* rules *makdimin* — one reads *Parshat Zachor* the preceding *Shabbat*, well in advance.

### Shmuel Postpones

*Shmuel* rules *me'acharin* — one may postpone *Zachor* to the *Shabbat* following *Purim*, i.e., the day after. Again, *Shmuel* is entirely consistent with his position throughout this discussion.

### Order of Remembrance

*Rav*'s reasoning is clear: *ki heichi de-lo tikdam asiya lizchira* — one cannot allow the performance of the obligation (*Purim*, representing *mechiyat Amalek*) to precede the remembrance. The reading of *Zachor*, which establishes the obligation of remembering and combating *Amalek*, must chronologically precede the *Megillah* reading that enacts that memory. To read *Zachor* after *Purim* inverts the proper sequence.

### Mukafin Argument

*Shmuel* counters: *keivan de-ika mukafin de-avdi ba-chamishah asar* — since there are walled cities (*mukafin*) that observe *Purim* on the 15th, and the *Shabbat* following a Friday *Purim* would coincide with their observance, *asiya ve-zchira behadi hadadi ka'asya* — at least for them, the action and remembrance occur simultaneously. This grounds *Zachor* on the same day as *Purim*, giving it some residual relationship to the obligation even for those who observed on the 14th. The argument is admittedly unusual, as the *mukafin* are a minority, but it is *Shmuel*'s consistent reasoning.

### Baraita Proof

The *Gemara* attempts to prove the matter from the *Mishnah*, which states *uva-shniyah Zachor* — the second special *Shabbat* is *Zachor*. The first scenario of the *Mishnah* is *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falling on *Shabbat*, which means *Purim* falls on the 14th, which is *Erev Shabbat* — precisely the case under dispute. The *Mishnah* says the second reading is *Zachor*, implying it is read the *Shabbat* before *Purim* even in that scenario — a proof for *Rav*.

*Rav Pappa* deflects: *mai shniyah — shniyah le-hafsaka* — when the *Mishnah* says "the second *Shabbat*," it does not refer specifically to the scenario where *Rosh Chodesh* is on *Shabbat*. Rather, it means the second in sequence after the skip: in those cases where a *Shabbat* must be skipped between *Shekalim* and *Zachor*, the second special *Shabbat* — after the gap — is *Zachor*. The *Mishnah* is not speaking to the particular case of *Rosh Chodesh* on *Shabbat* implying *Purim* on *Erev Shabbat*.

The *Gemara* then brings the full *baraita* parallel to the one cited for *Shekalim*: *eizo hi Shabbat shniyah — kol she-chal Purim lihyot be-tokhah, va-afilu be-Erev Shabbat* — the second special *Shabbat* is any week in which *Purim* falls, even if *Purim* falls on *Erev Shabbat*. This again reads naturally as a proof for *Rav*: just as the *betoch* language for *Shekalim* meant any week containing *Rosh Chodesh*, so the parallel formulation for *Zachor* means any week containing *Purim*, even a Friday — and one reads *Zachor* the preceding *Shabbat*. *Shmuel* again reads *bah* rather than *be-tokhah*, and the school of *Shmuel* likewise transmits *bah*, reversing the *baraita*'s apparent meaning. The simple reading of the *baraita* supports *Rav*.

### Purim on Shabbat

The *Gemara* then addresses the case where *Purim* itself falls on *Shabbat*. For *Shmuel*, there is no novelty: his reading of the *baraita* already indicated that when *Purim* falls *on* *Shabbat*, that *Shabbat* is *Zachor*. But what would *Rav* say? If his concern is that remembrance must *precede* performance, would he insist on reading *Zachor* a full week in advance even when *Purim* is on *Shabbat* — meaning *Zachor* would be read simultaneously with *Purim*?

*Rav Huna* rules that in this case *ledivrei hakol ein makdimin* — all agree one does not advance. Reading *Zachor* on *Shabbat Purim* itself is not reading it *after* the obligation; it is reading it *on the same day*, which satisfies *Rav*'s concern.

*Rav Nachman* disagrees: *adayin hi machlokes* — the dispute persists even in this case. *Rav* requires *Zachor* to be read strictly *before Purim*, not merely simultaneously, and would insist on reading it the previous *Shabbat*.

A statement in *Rav*'s name is then cited: *Rabbi Chiya bar Abba* says in the name of *Rabbi Abba* says in the name of *Rav* — when *Purim* falls on *Shabbat*, *makdim ve-korin be-Shabbat she-avrah Zachor* — one reads *Zachor* the preceding *Shabbat*. This confirms *Rav Nachman*'s reading: *Rav* demands genuine priority, not mere simultaneity.

It should be noted that in our fixed calendar, *Purim* cannot fall on *Shabbat* in regular cities; this scenario applies only to *Yerushalayim* and walled cities observing *Purim* on the 15th.

---

## Parah Adumah

### Third Shabbat Definition

The *Gemara* now turns to the third special *Shabbat*, *Parshat Parah*. The *baraita* defines it as *kol she-smucha le-Purim me-achareiha* — any *Shabbat* immediately following *Purim*.

### Before Rosh Chodesh

*Rav Chama bar Chanina* offers a different formulation: *Shabbat ha-smucha le-Rosh Chodesh Nissan* — the *Shabbat* immediately preceding *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*. This seems to conflict with the *baraita*'s definition, since the *Shabbat* immediately before *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* is more naturally associated with *Parshat Hachodesh*.

### Reconciliation

The *Gemara* resolves: *ve-lo pligi* — they do not actually dispute. The two definitions apply to different calendar scenarios.

When *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* falls on *Shabbat*, *Parshat Hachodesh* is read on *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* itself. In that case the *Shabbat* immediately preceding it (the 23rd) is *Parah*, and the 16th would be skipped. Here *Parah* is defined not as the *Shabbat* right after *Purim* (the 15th being *Shushan Purim*) but as the *Shabbat* adjacent to *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* — consistent with *Rav Chama bar Chanina*.

In all other scenarios, the *Shabbat* before *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* serves as *Hachodesh* and *Parah* falls the week before that, which is the *Shabbat* immediately following *Purim* (and *Shushan Purim* — for *Parah* will not be read on the 15th either). Both participants correctly observe that *Parah* will never fall during *Purim* itself or *Shushan Purim*; it is always the immediate *Shabbat* after both days have passed, with the sole exception noted above.

---

## Four Parshiyot

### Complete Baraita

The *Gemara* now quotes the complete *baraita* encompassing all four special *Shabbatot*. When *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on *Shabbat*, one reads *Ki Tissa* (the *Shekalim* section) with a *haftarah* from the episode of *Yehoyada ha-Kohen* — also about the *shekalim*. The *baraita* then defines each *Shabbat* in turn:

The first special *Shabbat* (*Shekalim*): *kol she-chal Rosh Chodesh Adar lihyot be-tokhah, va-afilu be-erev Shabbat* — any week in which *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls, even on *Erev Shabbat*; one reads *Ki Tissa* and reads the *haftarah* of *Yehoyada*.

The second special *Shabbat* (*Zachor*): *kol she-chal Purim lihyot be-tokhah, va-afilu be-erev Shabbat* — any week in which *Purim* falls, even on *Erev Shabbat*; the *haftarah* is *Pakadeti* — the passage from *Shmuel* recounting the war against *Amalek*.

The third special *Shabbat* (*Parah Adumah*): *kol she-smucha le-Purim me-achareiha* — the *Shabbat* immediately following *Purim* (and *Shushan Purim*, as qualified); the *haftarah* is *Ve-zarakti aleikhem* from *Yechezkel*.

The fourth special *Shabbat* (*Hachodesh*): *kol she-chal Rosh Chodesh Nissan lihyot be-tokhah, va-afilu be-erev Shabbat* — any week in which *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* falls, even on *Erev Shabbat*, one reads *Hachodesh hazeh* the preceding *Shabbat*; the *haftarah* is *Ko amar Hashem Elokim ba-rishon be-echad la-chodesh* from *Yechezkel*. When *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* falls on *Shabbat* itself, one reads *Hachodesh* directly on *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*.

### Rashi's Mnemonic

The *halakha* is ruled like *Rav* in all cases. *Rashi* provides a mnemonic for determining which *Shabbatot* to skip based on when *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls: *Zavadu, Baro, Gad, Ve-haya*. In our fixed calendar, *Rosh Chodesh Adar* can only fall on *Shabbat*, Monday, Wednesday, or *Erev Shabbat* (Friday), and the mnemonic encodes the skipping pattern for each scenario.

### Three Scenarios

When *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on *Shabbat* (the 1st): the *Shabbatot* are the 1st, 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. *Shekalim* is read on the 1st, *Zachor* on the 8th, the 15th is skipped (since one does not read *Parah* on *Purim* or *Shushan Purim*), *Parah* on the 22nd, and *Hachodesh* on the 29th — a clean, elegant alignment with no double-skip.

When *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on Monday: *Shabbat* is the 6th (since the 1st is Monday, *Shabbat* is the 6th), then 13th, 20th, 27th. Since *Rosh Chodesh* did not fall on *Shabbat*, *Shekalim* is read the preceding *Shabbat* (back in *Shevat*), the 6th is skipped, *Zachor* on the 13th, *Parah* on the 20th, and *Hachodesh* on the 27th.

When *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on Wednesday: *Shabbat* is the 4th, then 11th, 18th, 25th. *Shekalim* is read the *Shabbat* before the 4th (skipping the 4th), *Zachor* on the 11th, *Parah* on the 18th, and *Hachodesh* on the 25th — all before *Rosh Chodesh Nissan*.

When *Rosh Chodesh Adar* falls on *Erev Shabbat* (Friday): *Shabbat* is the 2nd, then 9th, 16th, 23rd, and *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* on the 30th. Here two skips are required. *Shekalim* is read before the 2nd, the 2nd is skipped, *Zachor* on the 9th before *Purim*, the 16th is skipped (to bring *Parah* adjacent to *Hachodesh*), *Parah* on the 23rd, and *Hachodesh* on the 29th. This is the scenario in which, when *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* falls on *Shabbat*, *Hachodesh* is read directly on *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* itself, and *Parah* is aligned to the *Shabbat* immediately before *Rosh Chodesh Nissan* rather than immediately after *Purim*.

The reason *Rosh Chodesh* cannot fall on Thursday is simply the structure of the fixed Jewish calendar — those are the only permissible days.

---

## Four Parshiyot (II)

### Divine Name Note

A brief but practically important observation arises: *Rashi*'s calendar presentation uses numbers including 15 and 16. The convention of writing 15 as *yud-heh* (10+5) is avoided because *yud-heh* constitutes a divine name. Many *Rishonim*, however, insist that only the 15th requires this avoidance, since *yud-heh* is indeed a divine name; the 16th written as *yud-vav* does not carry the same concern, as *yud-vav* is not a divine name. Therefore in many *Rishonim* the 16th is written as *yud-vav*, not as 16 (*tet-zayin*).

---

## Regular Parshiyot

### Return to Order

On the fifth *Shabbat* following the sequence of special *parshiyot*, the *Gemara* states *bachamishi chozrin le-ke-sidran* — one returns to the normal order of readings. The question is: what is the "normal order" that has been interrupted?

### Rav Ami vs Yirmiyah

*Rav Ami* says *le-seder parshiyot* — one returns to the normal sequential reading of the weekly *parsha*. His position implies that during the special *Shabbatot*, the regular *parsha* was not read at all, only the special reading. (How one would divide such a reading into seven *aliyot* is admittedly unclear.) *Rabbi Yirmeya* says *le-seder haftarot hu chozer* — one returns to the normal *haftarot*. His position aligns with the *Bavli*'s general assumption throughout this discussion: that the regular *parsha* continues to be read and only the *haftarah* is changed, or the special *Shekalim* (and *Zachor* etc.) reading is added as *shvi'i* or *maftir*.

*Abaye* states that the position of *Rav Ami* is the more logically coherent one.

### Weekday vs Shabbat

The *Gemara* cites the *Mishnah* in support: *le-chol mafsikin* — for all special occasions one interrupts the normal reading — *le-Rashei Chodashim, le-Chanukah, le-Purim, le-Ta'aniyot, u-le-Ma'amadot, le-Yom HaKippurim*. This is the proof for *Rav Ami*: *bishlama* if you have been interrupting the reading of the *Torah* itself (the *parsha*), then the formulation "one interrupts" makes perfect sense — and crucially, two items on this list, *ta'aniyot* and *ma'amadot*, cannot happen on *Shabbat*. These are weekday events. On a weekday there is no *haftarah* to interrupt; what one is interrupting is the Torah reading itself.

The response for *Rabbi Yirmeya* — *ha ke-d-itah ve-ha ke-d-itah* — is that each case operates in its own context. When the special occasion falls on a weekday (*ta'aniyot*, *ma'amadot*, *Chanukah* on a Monday), one interrupts the actual Torah reading. When it falls on *Shabbat*, one preserves the *parsha* and changes only the *haftarah*. The simpler reading of the *Mishnah*, however, clearly supports *Rav Ami* — that the interruption refers to the Torah reading itself.

The *Gemara* presses *Rabbi Yirmeya*'s position further: if one is trying to preserve the normal reading as much as possible (as *Rabbi Yirmeya* holds for *Shabbat*), why not do the same for *ta'aniyot* — read the normal weekday portion in *Shacharit* and reserve the special *ta'anit* reading for *Mincha*? The *Gemara* responds: this proves *Rav Huna*'s statement. *Rav Huna* says *mi-safra kinufya* — in the morning of a *ta'anit*, the community is occupied gathering and assessing communal conduct (*milei de-mata*), taking stock of what needs to be corrected, and beginning the process of communal *teshuvah*. *Abaye* elaborates: from morning until midday one examines the affairs of the community; from midday until evening one devotes a quarter of the day to Torah reading and *haftarah*, and the final quarter to *tefillah*, confessions, and supplication. The source is the *pasuk* in *Ezra-Nechemiah*: *va-yikre'u be-sefer torat Hashem Elokeihem revi'it ha-yom* — they read in the Torah a quarter of the day — *u-revi'it mitvadim u-mishtachavim* — and another quarter confessing and bowing. The morning is not about ritual but about moral accounting; therefore the Torah reading cannot be split between morning and afternoon and must take place entirely in the afternoon. The *inyana de-yoma* in *Shacharit* and the *ta'anit* portion in *Mincha* is not a viable option.

---

## Festival Readings

### Festival Parshiyot

The final *Mishnah* of *Masechet Megillah* catalogues the Torah readings for the festivals and special occasions throughout the year. On *Pesach* one reads from *Parshat Moadot* in *Parshat Emor* in *Vayikra* — *shor o chesev o ez ki yivaled*. On *Shavuot* (*Atzeret*) one reads *shiva shavuot*. On *Rosh Hashanah* — *ba-chodesh ha-shvi'i*, the section in *Emor* dealing with the first of the seventh month. On *Yom Kippur* — *Acharei Mot*, the *avodah* section. On the first day of *Sukkot* one reads from *Parshat Moadot she-be-Torat Kohanim* — the large section in *Emor* — *shor o chesev o ez*, covering all the festival *korbanot*. On *Chol Ha-Moed* one reads from *korbanot ha-chag* — the specific *Sukkot* offerings — from *Pinchas*, not from *Emor*.

The *Mishnah* does not specify *Chol Ha-Moed Pesach*, a point the *Gemara* will address in the *baraita*.

### Other Special Days

On *Chanukah* one reads from the *nesi'im* section in *Nasso* in *Bamidbar*. On *Purim* one reads *Vayavo Amalek*. On *Rosh Chodesh* — *u-ve-rashei chodsheikhem*. For the *ma'amadot* — the representatives of the people who stood in correspondence with the *kohanim* serving in the *Beit Ha-Mikdash* — one reads from *ma'aseh bereishit*, as we learned in *Masechet Ta'anit*. On *ta'aniyot* one reads *brachot u-klalot* — the section of blessings and curses, which *Rashi* identifies as *Bechukotai*. This is notable, since the full *Masechet Ta'anit* was studied without encountering this ruling, nor is it common practice today. The logic is clear, however: on fast days occasioned by drought or communal suffering, reading the *klalot* is meant to heighten awareness of consequence and intensify the call to *teshuvah*.

### Klalot Rule

One does not divide the *klalot* between multiple *aliyot*: *ein mafsikin ba-klalot — ela echad korei et kullan*. A single reader reads the entire section of curses; it is not split among several *olim*.

### Weekday Readings

Monday, Thursday, and *Shabbat Mincha* readings follow the normal sequential *parsha* but do not count toward the division for the following *Shabbat*. One does not reason that since, for example, *kohen* and *levi* were already called to *aliyot* earlier in the week, one may begin on *Shabbat* with *shlishi*.

### Source Pasuk

The *Mishnah* closes with the *pasuk* that grounds this entire framework: *Vayidaber Moshe et mo'adei Hashem el b'nei Yisrael* — and *Moshe* spoke of the appointed times of God to the children of Israel. The institution of reading about each *mo'ed* during its appointed time is derived from this verse: *mitzvatan she-yihyu korin kol echad va-echad bi-zmano* — it is their obligation to read about each one in its proper time, linking *kri'at ha-Torah* to the rhythm of the sacred calendar.

---

---

# Megillah 32

## Elders vs. Youth

### Demolish Don't Build

The daf opens with a *baraita* citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: *im yomru lecha zekenim setor veyeladim b'nei, setor v'al tivneh* — if elders tell you to demolish and youth tell you to build, demolish and do not build. Even when the counsel of elders sounds counterintuitive or injudicious, one should listen to them over the seemingly constructive advice of the young.

### Rehoboam Example

The reason is given directly: *mipnei shestirat zekenim binyan, ubinyan nearim stirah* — because the demolition advised by elders is ultimately constructive, and the construction advised by youth is ultimately destructive. The proof offered is Rehoboam son of Solomon. As is well known, Rehoboam consulted the elders, who counseled leniency toward the people. He then turned to his young advisors, who told him that such leniency would make him appear weak and that he must be harsh. He followed the young, was harsh with the people, and the result was the permanent splitting of the land of Israel. The *baraita* thus appears here in connection with an earlier citation of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar encountered on the preceding daf.

---

## Weekly Reading

### Reading Continuity

A *baraita* now establishes the continuity of the Torah reading cycle across the days of the week. The place where one finishes the *Shabbat* morning reading is where one begins at *Shabbat Mincha*; where one finishes at *Mincha* is where one begins on Monday; where one finishes on Monday is where one begins on Thursday; and where one finishes on Thursday is where one begins the following *Shabbat*.

### Meir vs. Yehuda

This is the view of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees: *makom shemapshikim b'Shabbat Shacharit, sham korin b'Mincha u'v'Sheni u'v'Chamishi u'l'Shabbat haba'ah* — the very same *aliyah* where one left off on *Shabbat* morning is what is read again at *Shabbat Mincha*, again on Monday, again on Thursday, and again at the start of the following *Shabbat*. The practical consequence is that everyone who attends only on *Shabbat* will hear that first *aliyah* of the new *parasha* — which presumably explains why so many people know the opening *aliyah* of every *parasha* so well.

### Halacha Decision

Rabbi Zeira rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda* — the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, and he states the ruling by describing the practice in full rather than simply attributing it to Rabbi Yehuda by name. The reason given is *mishum d'apchi lehu* — some authorities reverse which position belongs to Rabbi Meir and which to Rabbi Yehuda. To avoid any confusion, the *psak halacha* is stated substantively rather than by attribution.

---

## Torah Handling

### Yehuda's Method

A new *baraita* addresses the procedure for opening and reading from a *Sefer Torah*. The *baraita* records that one opens the scroll, looks to find the place, closes it, recites the *bracha*, then opens it again and reads — this is the view recorded first. Rabbi Yehuda, however, rules: *poteach v'ro'eh u'mevarech v'koreh* — one opens, looks, recites the *bracha*, and reads, without any intervening closing. Rabbi Yehuda's approach is straightforward and avoids any interruption between the *bracha* and the reading.

### Meir's Reason

The question arises: what is the reasoning behind the first opinion — the one that calls for closing the scroll before the *bracha*? The *gemara* answers by appeal to a statement of Ulla: *mipnei ma amru hakoreh baTorah lo yesaye'a l'meturgaman* — the reason the Sages said that the Torah reader may not assist the *meturgaman* when the latter stumbles is *kedei shelo yomru targum katuv baTorah* — so that people should not conclude that the *targum* is actually written in the Torah. If the reader is producing Aramaic words while the scroll is open, onlookers might believe those words appear in the text. The same logic applies here: *hacha nami kedei shelo yomru brachos ktuvos baTorah* — we close the scroll before the *bracha* so that observers should not think the blessings are written within the *Sefer Torah*. The reason for looking at the scroll beforehand is presumably so that after reciting the *bracha* one knows precisely where to read from and need not search around again — though in practice this does not always prevent a moment of searching when the scroll is reopened.

### Yehuda's Response

Rabbi Yehuda's counter-argument distinguishes the two cases. Regarding the *targum*, he acknowledges *targum ika l'michtei* — there is genuine room for error, since there are Aramaic words present in the Torah itself, and people might plausibly mistake the *meturgaman*'s words for words being read from the text. But *brachos leika l'michtei* — no one is going to think that *Baruch Atah Hashem Elokeinu Melech Ha'olam asher kideshanu* is written in the *Torah*. The concern simply does not exist for *brachos*. Indeed, in the contemporary practice where every person called for an *aliyah* recites both the opening and closing *bracha*, the implausibility of mistaking those blessings for Torah text is even greater.

### Final Halacha

Rabbi Zeira rules: *halacha k'poteach v'ro'eh u'mevarech v'koreh* — the law follows the view of opening, looking, blessing, and reading without closing in between, in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda. Again, rather than simply citing Rabbi Yehuda by name, the ruling is stated in full due to the concern that authorities may have reversed which position belongs to which *Tanna*.

This ruling corresponds to the *Sephardi psak*. The question arises as to why *Ashkenazim* practice differently, closing the scroll before the opening *bracha*. The answer lies in *Tosafot*. *Tosafot* writes: *lechatchilah hu golelo v'sotmo kodem sheyivarech kedei shelo yomru hamon shehabrachos ktuvos bo* — *lechatchilah*, one should close the scroll before the *bracha* out of concern for widespread ignorance, which was the concern of Rabbi Meir. However, *b'diavad ein lachush* — after the fact, there is no need for concern, since people are not so ignorant today as to genuinely think the *brachos* are written in the *Torah*. Regarding the closing *bracha* after the reading, *Tosafot* adds that even according to Rabbi Yehuda one must definitely close the scroll before reciting it. The explanation may be that for the opening *bracha* there is a stronger concern about *hefsek* between the *bracha* and the reading, whereas for the closing *bracha* that concern is less pressing, making it more straightforward to require closing beforehand.

What emerges from *Tosafot* is that although the *halacha* follows Rabbi Yehuda and there is room to say the scroll should *davka* remain open so as to avoid *hefsek*, *Tosafot* ultimately rules *lechatchilah* in accordance with Rabbi Meir's concern — reflecting a greater sensitivity to widespread ignorance than the *gemara* itself apparently felt necessary to address.

---

## Torah Sanctity

### No Sanctity

Rav Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states: *haluchos v'habimos ein bahem mishum kedusha* — the tablets and platforms have no sanctity. The statement is dense and requires unpacking: what precisely are these *luchos* and *bimos*?

### Rashi Explains

Rashi expresses uncertainty about the meaning of *luchos*, writing *lo yadati ma hen* — I do not know what these tablets are. He then suggests that some interpret them as the covers of a codex (*sefer* in book form rather than scroll). This would mean that although the covers house a sanctified text, they themselves carry no *kedusha*. This raises an interesting question in its own right, since it implies a discussion of whether a codex-form *Sefer Torah* carries *kedusha* at all — but at minimum, the covers of such a book would not. As for *bima*, Rashi identifies it as the platform constructed for the king during *Parshat Hamelech*, as described in Tractate Sotah, noting this as the closest analogy he could find to a *bima* connected to *kriyat haTorah*. By extension one might apply the same principle to an ordinary raised reading platform in a synagogue: such a structure, even if used for Torah reading, carries no sanctity of its own.

### Tosafot View

*Tosafot* and Rabbeinu Chananel read the passage very differently. Citing the *Aruch*, *Tosafot* explains *luchos* and *bimos* as the blank spaces of the *Sefer Torah* itself — the margins above and below the text and between the columns. These vertical white spaces are the *luchos* (tablets), while the horizontal spaces function as the *bima* (platform). This would make the statement a declaration that the blank margins of the scroll carry no independent *kedusha*.

One might immediately object: surely the margins of a *Sefer Torah* do have *kedusha*! *Tosafot* resolves this by clarifying that the *gemara* is speaking of margins that have been cut away from the scroll. Once removed, *ein bahem mishum kedusha* — they no longer carry sanctity. This is how *Tosafot* and Rabbeinu Chananel understand the ruling.

---

## Rolling Technique

### Seam Position

Rav Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *ha-golel Sefer Torah tzarich she-ya'amidenu al ha-tefer* — the one rolling the *Sefer Torah* must position the scroll so that the seam between parchment panels lies in the middle as the scroll is being tightened. This requirement applies not only to the act of rolling but, according to some readings, to *hagbaha* as well.

### Tearing Prevention

The reason is to prevent tearing at vulnerable points. When one rolls and tightens the scroll, pressure is applied outward from the center. If the seam is positioned in the middle, any tearing that might result from this tension will occur at the seam rather than through the body of the parchment — the seam being the weaker point, just as one would prefer a garment to tear at its seam rather than through the fabric itself. This same logic extends to *hagbaha*: when the scroll is lifted, the poles exert lateral pulling force, and having the seam centered similarly directs any stress to the appropriate place. In practice, one rarely if ever hears of the actual *klaf* tearing during *hagbaha*, but the principle is stated nonetheless.

### Outside-Inside

Rav Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan further teaches: *ha-golel Sefer Torah gollo mibachutz v'ein gollo mibifnim* — when rolling the *Sefer Torah*, one rolls from the outside, not from the inside; *u'cheshehu mehadko, mehadko mibifnim v'eino mehadko mibachutz* — when tightening, one tightens from the inside, not the outside.

Rashi explains this as guidance for a single person handling the scroll on his lap without a table. *Mibachutz* — the outside — means the side of the scroll farther from the body. As one rolls, one controls the far pole, drawing it toward oneself, while the near pole remains stable against the body. This allows the person to maintain control and prevent the scroll from falling. If one tried instead to keep the far pole fixed and roll the near pole away, it would tip over. When it comes to tightening at the end, Rashi explains that *mibifnim* means one should not stretch one's arm over the *kesav* and close the scroll in a way that covers the writing, since this would obstruct the view of the text. Rather, one closes it from the nearer side so that the *kesav* remains visible to those present.

### Tosafot Gartel

*Tosafot* reads the passage quite differently. For *Tosafot*, *mehadko mibifnim* refers to the placement of the *gartel* knot: when tying the belt around the closed *Sefer Torah*, one should make the knot in the front, not in the back. The reason is twofold. First, it keeps the scroll better secured. Second, and more significant: when the *Sefer Torah* is next taken out, if the knot is in the back, one must turn the scroll upside down to undo it, which is not *kavod* to the *Sefer Torah*. By placing the knot in front, one can lay the Torah flat and untie it with ease and dignity. From this understanding of *mehadko*, *Tosafot* derives that *gollo mibachutz* means that the person performing *gelila* stands behind the scroll as it is being rolled — not directly in front of it — so that the *kesav* remains visible to the congregation as the scroll is being closed.

---

## Gelila Honor

### Ten Readers

A new teaching of Rav Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *asara shekaru baTorah, hagadol shebahem golel* — if ten people have read from the Torah, the greatest among them performs *gelila*, because the one who performs *gelila* receives credit equivalent to all the others. Rashi clarifies that *asara shekaru* does not necessarily mean ten people each received an *aliyah*; it means ten people gathered for the Torah reading.

This is a striking ruling, since in contemporary practice *hagbah u'gelila* tend to be treated as honors given to those who have not received a major *aliyah*, or to those with the physical strength for *hagbaha*. Some suggest that in the *gemara*'s context, *golel* also encompassed the one who lifted the scroll — that is, the roles of *magbi'ah* and *golel* were combined. This would make better sense of the significance assigned to the honor: the person who lifts the *Sefer Torah* and displays it to the congregation, enabling everyone to see the actual writing — *v'zos haTorah* — performs an act of tremendous *zechut*. It is the power of showing the text that they have been hearing, making the Torah tangible and present. This may be the better framework for understanding why *gelila* is here treated as the greatest honor among the ten.

### Completion Credit

Rabbeinu Chananel cites an alternative formulation in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: *hamashlim notnin lo sachar k'neged kulam* — the one who completes the reading receives credit equivalent to all who preceded him. Rabbeinu Chananel adds the principle *ein mitzvah nikret ela al shem gomrah* — a *mitzvah* is named after its one who completes it. This may also suggest, though it is not entirely clear, that the person who received the final *aliyah* would naturally be the one to perform *gelila* — the *mashlim* in both senses.

### Credit Equivalent

The *gemara* itself raises an objection to the formulation *kibel sachar kulam* — he receives all of their credit. Does this mean the others receive no credit and he takes it from them? The *gemara* corrects: *ela eima kibel sachar k'neged kulam* — he receives credit *equivalent* to all of their credit combined. The others retain their own *schar* in full.

---

## Bas Kol Usage

### Permitted Sign

Rav Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *minayin she-mishtamshin b'bas kol* — from where do we know that one is permitted to make use of a *bas kol* as a sign when facing a decision? The question concerns, for example, a person who is deliberating over a course of action — a business matter, a significant choice — and hears a voice say yes or no.

### Unusual Sound

Rashi explains that this is not considered *nichush* — divination — and one may indeed use it as a *siman*. However, the *gemara* qualifies this: *v'hani milei d'shama kol gavra b'mata* — this applies only when the sound is unusual, such as a man's voice heard in a city where the men would typically be out working in the fields, leaving women at home; *o it-ta b'davra* — or a woman's voice heard out in the field, where one would expect to find only men. The unusual character of the sound is what elevates it to the status of a meaningful sign. Whether the *gemara* imagines a genuinely disembodied heavenly voice — in which case the unusual quality would confirm that it is not a human voice at all — or whether it envisions an actual person's voice that is simply unexpected in its context, is not entirely clear from the text. A further requirement: *v'hu d'amar hin hin, v'hu d'amar lav lav* — it must be a double affirmation: yes, yes, or no, no. A single utterance is insufficient; only a repeated statement may be used as a *siman*.

### Tosafot Source

*Tosafot* traces the source to the Yerushalmi, which cites the verse *lo senachashu v'lo se'onenu* — do not divine and do not engage in sorcery — and then draws a distinction: *af al pi she'ein nichush, yesh siman* — even though divination is forbidden, one may still use hints and signs. There is thus a principled halakhic distinction between forbidden divination and the permitted use of a *siman*. This calls to mind the joke about the doctor who keeps a good-luck charm in his office: asked how a man of science could believe in such a superstition, he replies that he has heard it works even for those who don't believe in it — a wry illustration of the human instinct to seek signs, which the *gemara* here treats with careful legal precision.

---

## Trop & Melody

### Without Trop/Melody

Rav Shefatya in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol hakoreh belo ne'imah v'hashoneh belo zimrah* — one who reads the Torah without *trop* (cantillation), or who learns *Mishnah* without a *nigun* (melody). *Tosafot* explains the latter: in an oral culture where *mishnayos* were transmitted by heart, learning them with a melody made them far more memorable and reliable. Anyone who once learned a large amount of Torah text with the cantillation will confirm this — whatever was learned with *trop* tends to be retained. The *trop* also serves the additional function of clarifying punctuation and the division of *pesukim*.

### Proof Text

Regarding such a person, the verse says: *vegam ani nasati lahem chukim lo tovim, umishpatim lo yichyu bahem* — I have given them statutes that are not good and laws by which they shall not live. The verse is understood here not as God's declaration but as a *makkah* — an indictment — of those who have received the Torah but transmitted it improperly, rendering the *chukim* into something *lo tovim*.

### Abaye Objects

Abaye challenges this reading. His objection is that understanding the verse as a reference to poor vocal quality — someone who simply does not have a pleasant voice — does not justify the severity of *umishpatim lo yichyu bahem*. Saying the laws will be *lo tovim*, perhaps unpleasant to hear, is one thing; saying people will not live by them is something far more serious. Abaye therefore redirects to a teaching of Rav Masharshiya: *shnei talmidei chachamim hayoshvim b'ir achas v'ein nochim zeh lazeh b'halacha* — two Torah scholars who dwell in the same city and do not cooperate pleasantly with one another in matters of *halacha*. The *Maharsha* reads this as meaning they do not study together, each learning in isolation without *chavrusa* partnership, without the give-and-take of discussion and critique.

### Chavrusa Learning

It is regarding such scholars that the verse applies: *vegam ani nasati lahem chukim lo tovim, umishpatim lo yichyu bahem* — because without pushback, critique, and genuine discussion, one cannot arrive at correct legal conclusions. The laws will be perverted; they will not live by them. This connects to other *gemaros* that speak in similarly strong terms, such as *cherev el habadim v'no'alu* — a sword against those who learn in isolation rather than *b'chavrusa*. Only through genuine intellectual partnership is *halacha* properly preserved and transmitted.

---

## Improper Handling

### Naked Torah

Rav Parnach in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol ha'ochez Sefer Torah arom* — anyone who holds a *Sefer Torah* naked — meaning the scroll itself is naked, that is, the person is touching the *klaf* directly rather than handling it through the cover, the poles, or the *atzei chayim* — such a person is buried naked, *nikbar arom*.

### Abaye Clarifies

The *gemara* immediately questions whether this is to be taken literally. Is touching the *klaf* directly so grave a sin that one is buried without shrouds? The *gemara* then escalates: perhaps it means one is buried *belo mitzvos* — stripped of all *mitzvos*? But that too seems disproportionate. Abaye resolves it: *nikbar arom belo osah mitzvah* — one is buried without that particular *mitzvah*; one forfeits the merit of that specific act.

### Tosafot Interpretation

*Tosafot* acknowledges that this ruling, taken at face value, seems obvious: if one performs a *mitzvah* improperly, of course one does not receive *schar* for it. The novelty, *Tosafot* explains, lies in a broader interpretation offered by the Riva: *belo osah mitzvah she'asah b'osah sha'ah* — one loses the credit not merely for the act of holding the scroll, but for whatever other *mitzvah* was being performed in that context. Thus, for example, if one was holding the *Sefer Torah* directly on the *klaf* and reading from it, *ein lo schar min hakriya* — one forfeits the merit of the reading itself. The improper handling undermines the merit of whatever was done in that context — whether *gelila*, reading, or any other act performed while touching the scroll directly.

---

## Laws by Season

### Roll Covers

Rabbi Yannai the son of Rabbi Yannai the elder, citing in the name of Rabbi Yannai the elder — notably, here we see the *Sephardi minhag* of children bearing the same name as their father, and in this case grandfather, father, and son all bearing the name Yannai — teaches: *mutav sheyigollel hamatpachos v'al yigollel Sefer Torah* — better to roll the *matpachos* (coverings) than to roll the *Sefer Torah* itself.

### Rolling Order

Rashi explains: one should complete the rolling of the *Sefer Torah* first and only then place the cover over it. One should not put the cover on first and then do the tightening after the cover is already in place. The rolling is done to the scroll itself before it is wrapped.

### Festival Laws

The daf closes with the verse: *vayedabber Moshe es mo'adei Hashem el Bnei Yisrael* — and Moses spoke to the children of Israel of the appointed times of God — from which the *gemara* derives that the *mitzvah* of each *moed* includes reading the appropriate *parasha* at its proper time. The *baraita* then builds upon this: *Moshe tikken lahem leYisrael sheyihyu sho'alim vedorshim b'inyano shel yom* — Moses established that Israel should ask and discuss the laws appropriate to the day: *Hilchos Pesach bePesach, Hilchos Atzeres beAtzeres, Hilchos Chag beChag* — each set of laws in its proper season. There is, of course, a separate tradition requiring study *shloshim yom kodem hachag* — thirty days before the festival — which concerns the practical preparation needed well in advance. What is described here is something different and, in some ways, more profound.

### Ritual Learning

The study of each festival's laws at the time of the festival is not merely instrumental — not simply a matter of knowing what to do tonight at the *Seder*. It is itself a way of *mekayem* the nature of the day, an act through which one embraces and inhabits the meaning of the *moed*. Learning *Hilchos Pesach* on *Pesach* is what one does on *Pesach*; it is a form of ritual engagement with the holiday in its own right.

### Talmud Torah

It is worth pausing to notice what the *masechet* has done here at its conclusion. An entire *perek* — one might say the whole of *Maseches Megillah* — has been devoted to the primacy of scripture: the reading of the *Megillah*, the sanctity of the *Beis Knesses*, the *Sefer Torah*, *kriyat haTorah*, all of this. The *masechet* even opened with the teaching that *talmud Torah* is set aside in favor of *mikra Megillah*. And yet at the very last line, when the *gemara* speaks of what one does on *Yom Tov*, the answer it gives is not *koreh* — one reads — but *sho'alim vedorshim* — one learns the *halachos*. Not reading from the Torah, but *talmud Torah*. The *masechet* that began by prioritizing *mikra* ends by returning to the dominant *rabbinic* theme: it is the *talmud Torah* of each season, the learning of its laws and their meaning, that stands at the center.

Rashi, concluding with characteristic precision, explains the *d'rashah* on the verse: *vayedabber* is superfluous — surely Moses conveyed all the commandments to Israel — and its presence teaches *shehayah medabber immahem hilchos kol mo'ed umo'ed bizmano*, that Moses would speak to them the laws of each *moed* in its proper time. And then, because it is the end of a *masechet*, both Rashi and *Tosafot* allow themselves a small flourish. Rashi closes with *bizmanam ulehodia chukei ha'Elokim vesorosav, vekibbelu vekiyemu schar hamitzvah aleihem v'al beneihem baze uvava* — they accepted it upon themselves and their children for this world and the next. *Tosafot*, in its final lines discussing the one who handles the *Sefer Torah* properly through its wrappings, concludes with the words *orech yamim bimina, bismola osher vachavod* — length of days is in its right hand, in its left are wealth and honor. A *masechet* concluded; a *siyum* well earned.

---

---

# Moed Katan 2

## Intro & Commentaries

### Tract Ordering

We begin today a new *masechet*: Masechet Moed Katan, daf 2, amud alef. A few introductory words are in order. Interestingly, just as there is a debate about the order of the last two *perakim* of Megilla, so too here there is a debate about whether Moed Katan is the last tractate of Seder Moed or whether Chagiga is. The standard assumption is that Moed Katan comes first and Chagiga follows, though some authorities reverse the order. Normally one determines the sequence of tractates within a *seder* by the number of *perakim*, but both of these tractates contain exactly three *perakim*, which is precisely why the debate exists. We will proceed with Moed Katan followed by Chagiga, which means we are approximately two months away from completing Seder Moed.

### Mashkin Naming

This *masechet* is known as Moed Katan — the "small *moed*," referring to *chol hamoed* — but many of the *rishonim* actually call it Masechet Mashkin, after its opening word. This is unusual, since tractates are not typically named after their first word (*Berachot* being a coincidental exception). The reason here is that the *masechet* does not lend itself to a single descriptive title, because its subject matter is a genuine mixture of themes. It opens with the laws of *chol hamoed* — a natural continuation after all the individual *chagim* have been addressed — and this is followed by Chagiga, which deals with the *korban chagigah* and other obligations that apply across the *moadim* rather than to any particular festival. But even from the first five words of our *masechet* — *mashkin beit hashalchin bamoed uvishvi'it* — one can see that many of the permitted and prohibited labors on *chol hamoed* run parallel to the laws of *shemita*. So already at the outset there is a mixture of *chol hamoed* and *shvi'is*. Beyond these two, the third *perek*, which begins with *ve'elu megalchin bamoed*, deals predominantly with *aveilus*. The entry point is the question of who may shave on *chol hamoed*, which naturally leads into a discussion of when shaving is otherwise prohibited — including during mourning — and from there the *gemara* expands into the major *sugyot* of *hilchos aveilus*. Indeed, the primary locus of *halachos aveilus* in the *gemara* is this third *perek* of Moed Katan. So the topics are essentially *chol hamoed*, *aveilus*, *shvi'is*, and a number of other matters — hence it is not surprising that some prefer the name Mashkin over the more thematic Moed Katan.

### Rashi & Gershom

One further introductory point concerns the commentaries. As some may recall from our study of Taanis and related tractates, the question arose there whether the Rashi printed in the standard editions is authentic. The scholarly consensus in those cases was that it was not. Here, in Moed Katan, there is essentially universal acknowledgment that the printed Rashi is not Rashi. It is approximately eighty percent Rabbeinu Gershom, with only about twenty percent drawn from the actual Rashi text. What is striking is that one might not notice this on a first encounter: the commentary reads as a coherent, terse, line-by-line explanation in a style not unlike what we associate with Rashi. This is itself an interesting observation — we tend to speak of Rashi as the originator of the running *gemara* commentary, and while that is true in terms of its comprehensiveness and clarity, it is not the case that there were no antecedents. Rabbeinu Gershom, writing in the tenth to early eleventh century, produced exactly this kind of commentary, and Rabbeinu Chananel — whose commentary is printed on the side of the page — also provided running, if considerably sparser, annotation. Rabbeinu Gershom died in either 1028 or 1040; Rashi died in 1105. Their death dates are separated by roughly eighty years.

We do, in fact, possess a manuscript of Rashi's actual commentary on Moed Katan, and it has been published as a separate scholarly edition — *Perush Rashi al Maseches Moed Katan*. There is also a noteworthy point about the Rif: normally, the Rashi printed alongside the Rif is simply a reworking of the standard Rashi on the *gemara*, but in Moed Katan — and apparently in one or two other places — the Rashi in the Rif reflects a genuine manuscript witness to the actual Rashi text. So paradoxically, the more reliable Rashi on Moed Katan is to be found in the back of the Rif rather than in the standard *vilna* printing.

### MS Authenticity

One further complication: the Ran printed alongside the Rif in Moed Katan is, as a general rule, not the Ran — it is *Nimukei Yosef*. So to summarize the situation: the Rashi on the *gemara* is really Rabbeinu Gershom; the more authentic Rashi is in the Rif; and the Ran on the Rif is actually Nimukei Yosef. Going forward, when we cite "Rashi," we should understand that we are, in practice, citing Rabbeinu Gershom.

---

## Beit Hashalchin

### Irrigate Fields

The *masechet* opens: *mashkin beit hashalchin bamoed* — one may irrigate a *beit hashalchin* on *chol hamoed*. A *beit hashalchin* is a field that requires regular irrigation. Because it depends on consistent watering, failure to irrigate poses a serious risk to the crops. This stands in contrast to a field whose soil is richer or whose other conditions allow it to thrive on rainfall alone — such a field is far less vulnerable.

The underlying principle introduced at the outset is that *melacha* on *chol hamoed* is permitted when there is a concern of *davar ha'aved* — the prospect of financial loss, *hefsed*. This immediately raises two larger questions that will accompany us throughout the *masechet*. First: what kind of *melacha* is prohibited on *chol hamoed* in the first place? When we speak of *melacha* on *Shabbos*, we mean the thirty-nine categories of creative, constructive labor. Does the prohibition on *chol hamoed* follow those same categories, such that striking a match would technically require a *heter*? Or does it mean something more like laborious, effortful activity — *tircha* — in which case the character of the prohibition is entirely different? Second: what is the halakhic weight of the prohibition? Is it biblical, rabbinic, or something intermediate? These are the two fundamental questions, and they will recur throughout the *masechet*.

### Loss & Tircha

Turning to Rabbeinu Gershom's commentary on the opening *mishnah*, he explains: *sadeh she'hi omedes behar ve'tzricha lehashkosah tamid mashkin osah afilu be'cholo shel moed* — a field that stands on a hill and requires constant watering may be irrigated even on *chol hamoed*. The reason: *lefi she'hu hefsed gadol* — because it would constitute a significant loss. Two things are notable here. First, the permission is attributed to the *chachamim*, suggesting a rabbinic rather than biblical framework. Second, *tircha* — the effort involved — is already foregrounded as a significant consideration. This does not necessarily mean that *melacha* on *chol hamoed* is defined by *tircha*, but it signals that *tircha* is a controlling factor in determining what is and is not permitted.

### Biblical Source

Rabbeinu Gershom then cites a *drashah* from a *pasuk* in the context of Chagiga rather than Moed Katan. The verse states: *sheshet yamim tochal matzos u'vayom hashvi'i atzeret l'Hashem Elokecha* — six days you shall eat *matzos*, and on the seventh day there is an *atzeret* to God. From the juxtaposition: just as the seventh day involves cessation from *melacha*, so too the six intermediate days involve some prohibition of *melacha*. Yet from this one might have concluded that *all* forms of *melacha* are forbidden on *chol hamoed*, just as they are on *Yom Tov* itself. The *gemara* therefore says: the Torah restricts only the seventh; the six are not fully restricted. But then comes the critical phrase: *lo masran hakatuv ela lachachamim* — the Torah did not specify the parameters; it handed the matter over to the *chachamim* to determine which labors are forbidden and which are permitted. And the conclusion: *melacha she'yesh bah hefsed im eino oseh otah* — labor that, if not performed, will result in loss — the *chachamim* permitted, such as *mashkot beit hashalchin*.

What, then, has Rabbeinu Gershom actually told us about the nature and weight of the prohibition? The *drashah* sounds thoroughly biblical — these are real *derashot* from *pesukim*. And yet the framing phrase *lo masran hakatuv ela lachachamim* can be read in more than one way. One reading: the Torah establishes that some *melacha* is forbidden on *chol hamoed*, but delegates to the rabbis the task of defining precisely which *melachos* fall within that category. Under this reading, whatever the rabbis designate becomes, in effect, biblically prohibited — it is a kind of blank check drawn on the Torah's account, as it were. But this raises a difficulty: under such a model, one might accept that the rabbis have the authority to define the scope of the prohibition. What is harder to explain is that the prohibition can then be *overridden* for reasons such as *hefsed* or *tircha*. The authority to set parameters is one thing; the authority to grant ongoing exceptions is something that sounds more like a rabbinic, rather than biblical, structure.

This tension is not unique to Moed Katan. A parallel ambiguity exists regarding the *inuyim* of Yom Kippur. The *gemara* derives the other afflictions — bathing, sexual relations, anointing, and so forth — from verses, giving them the appearance of biblical status. Yet we find *heterim* for specific individuals: a *kallah* who has recently married is permitted to wash her face; a king may have special dispensations. If these *inuyim* were genuinely biblical in weight, such overrides would be extremely difficult to accommodate. The possibility suggested by the structure is that rather than framing these as "overrides," one might recharacterize: labor performed to prevent loss is simply not the kind of *melacha* that the Torah had in mind — it is *melachat harvacha*, labor for gain, that is restricted, not *melachat menias hefsed*. Such a recharacterization avoids the language of override entirely and instead defines the scope of the prohibition from the outset. Whether this framing is always sustainable remains to be seen.

There is a further dimension: *melacha* on *chol hamoed* may not map onto the *lamed tes melachos* at all. Unlike *Shabbos*, the relevant category may be more about the professional or effortful character of the labor — *melechet uman* — rather than its technical classification among the thirty-nine. These are questions that will surface repeatedly as we proceed.

### Two Criteria

With that framework in mind, the *mishnah* implicitly establishes two operative criteria for permitting labor on *chol hamoed*. First: the labor must address a *makom hefsed* — a situation of genuine loss. Second: even in a case of *hefsed*, there must be no excessive *tircha*. The *mishnah* proceeds to illustrate: one may irrigate from a spring — whether a newly emerged spring or an established one — but one may *not* use collected rainwater (*mei geshamim*) or water drawn by means of a device from a deep well (*mei hakilon*). Both of the latter involve a substantially greater degree of effort and are therefore forbidden. Similarly, one may not make furrows (*ugiot*) around the vines to collect water, as digging those furrows would involve excessive *tircha* — this is not a question of *hefsed* so much as an issue of the labor involved. So the two criteria stand: *hefsed*, yes; *tircha*, no.

### New vs. Old

The *mishnah* then addresses a further distinction: *bein mimayan sheyatza batchila bein mimayan shelo yatza batchila* — whether from a spring that has just newly emerged or one that has been long established. One might have thought that a newly emerged spring should be more problematic: since its banks and channels have not yet settled, there is a concern that they might collapse, requiring further substantial labor to repair. Yet the *mishnah* permits it nonetheless, because the circumstances constitute a *makom hefsed*.

The *mishnah* then introduces the opinion of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah: *ein osim et ha'amah batchila bamoed uvishvi'it* — one may not initially construct an irrigation canal on *chol hamoed* or on *shvi'is*. Even granting that crops may be at risk, digging a new irrigation canal is considered too great a *tircha* and is therefore prohibited. The *chachamim*, however, rule that one *may* initially dig such a canal on *shvi'is*, though on *chol hamoed* one may only repair one that has already been damaged — *metaknin et hamukalkalot bamoed*. This is, on reflection, striking: the *chachamim* are more lenient about constructing an irrigation canal on *shvi'is*, which carries a *de'oraita* prohibition, than on *chol hamoed*. The *mishnah* also extends the category of permitted repairs to *tzorchei rabim* — needs of the public: one may repair damaged water channels, wells, roads, streets, and *mikva'ot* in the public domain, and one may perform all manner of public needs. One may also mark graves so that *kohanim* avoid them, and the *beit din* may send agents to enforce the laws of *kilayim*.

This introduction of *tzorchei rabim* as a separate permitting category raises its own questions: does *tircha* apply here as well, or does public need override even that concern? For one's private field, the operative criteria are clear — *hefsed* and no excessive *tircha*. How these map onto public works remains a question to keep in view.

### Rav Papa

The *gemara* now interrogates the *mishnah*'s inclusion of both types of springs. The reasoning: *hashta yesh lomar mimayim sheyatza batchila d'ati l'inpulei mashkin* — if we permit irrigation from a newly emerged spring, which carries a risk of collapse and consequent additional labor, then surely we permit irrigation from a long-established spring that presents no such concern. Is there any question?

Rav Papa answers that both cases were nonetheless necessary. Had the *mishnah* stated only the newly emerged spring, one might have concluded: this was permitted specifically for *beit hashalchin* — where the crops will perish without water — *because* we are worried the spring might collapse; for a *beit haba'al*, a field that does not require irrigation and is merely enhanced by it, we would still prohibit even with a new spring. And had the *mishnah* stated only the established spring, with no concern of collapse, one might have thought: since there is minimal risk and minimal effort, perhaps we permit irrigation even of a *beit haba'al* where there is no *hefsed*. Therefore the *mishnah* states both, and the operative principle emerges in full: *lo shena mayim sheyatza batchila lo shana mayim shelo yatza batchila — beit hashalchin in, beit haba'al lo*. It does not matter whether the spring is new or old. The *heter* applies only where there is genuine *hefsed* — a *beit hashalchin* that will suffer real loss without water. For a *beit haba'al*, where the question is one of *meniat revach* — failing to gain profit rather than incurring a loss — there is no *heter*.

This distinction between *hefsed* and *meniat revach* is worth pausing over. When a crop will simply fail to grow without water, the loss of those crops is clearly *hefsed* — one is losing something already invested. But when a field survives on rainfall and would merely grow somewhat better with additional irrigation, not providing that water is not a loss; it is the absence of a gain. Whether this distinction maps cleanly onto modern economic situations — such as a person who will lose a day's salary if they do not work on *chol hamoed* — is itself a nuanced question. Is losing a day's pay *meniat revach* or *hefsed*? The answer is not always obvious, but the conceptual distinction is the foundation.

---

## Etymology

### Hashalchin

The *gemara* now turns to the linguistic origins of these two terms. *U'mai mashma de'hai beit hashalchin lishna detzachuta hi?* — what is the source for understanding *beit hashalchin* as a term connoting thirst? The *gemara* cites a verse: *ve'ata ayef ve'yageia* — you were weary and faint — and notes that the *Targum* renders this as *ve'at mishalhei ve'la'i* — you were thirsty and weary. The connection is a phonetic play between *mishalhei* and *hashalchin*, with a *hei*-*chet* interchange. The *gemara* is working with a somewhat indirect derivation — the *Targum* meaning may lean more toward "weary" than strictly "thirsty" — but the intent is clear: *beit hashalchin* is a field that is "thirsty," that craves water. The more probable actual etymology, left implicit in the *gemara*, likely derives from *lishloach* — to send or convey — since the practice of irrigating a field involves channeling and conveying water to it: *veyishlach mayim al pnei chutzot*.

### Ha'aal

The *gemara* then asks: *u'mai mashma de'hai beit haba'al lishna demiysufta?* — what is the source for understanding *beit haba'al* as language connoting a settled or sated state? The verse cited is: *ki yival bachur betulah* — as a young man takes a young woman — with the *Targum* rendering: *arei kama demityasot ulam im betulta* — as a young man is settled with a virgin. The verse continues with the imagery of children being settled within the land. So *beit haba'al* is the opposite of thirsty: a field that is sated, that does not require regular watering and can sustain itself on rainfall.

The deeper background here, touched on in the context of Taanis, is the pervasive agricultural and quasi-erotic imagery of rain penetrating the earth, fertilizing the seed, and bringing forth growth — *veholida vehitzmicha*. The *beit haba'al* is a field that participates in this natural cycle of rainfall and growth without requiring human intervention. The very name may carry an additional layer: a note in the Soncino edition points to scholarly discussion suggesting that *beit haba'al* originally referred to fields favored by the Canaanite deity Baal, associated with fertility and rainfall. This identification does not appear in the *gemara* itself, but the connection to that imagery of rainfall-as-divine-favor is clear from the broader literary context.

---

## Rabbinic Positions

### Rabbi Meir

The *gemara* now asks: *man tana d'pseda in v'harvacha lo?* — who is the *tanna* who holds that labor on *chol hamoed* is permitted only to prevent loss, but not for the sake of profit? And further: even in a case of *hefsed*, who holds that we nonetheless do not permit labor involving excessive *tircha*? To answer this, Rav Huna first identifies a *tanna* and the *gemara* then invokes a *baraita* that sets out three distinct positions.

The *baraita* opens with the case of a *ma'ayan hayotzei batchila* — a spring that has just emerged. Rabbi Meir rules that one may irrigate even a *beit haba'al* from such a spring. Rabbi Meir is thus maximally lenient: he permits irrigation even for *revach* — that is, even where the field is not at genuine risk — and is not deterred by the possibility that a new spring might collapse and cause additional labor. He allows even for *revach* and even with possible *tircha*.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda takes the middle position: *ein mashkin ella sadeh beit hashalchin shecharva* — one may irrigate only a field that needs water and has in fact dried up. This matches the *mishnah* precisely: only a *beit hashalchin*, only where there is genuine *hefsed*. According to Rabbeinu Gershom, the case in the *baraita* is specifically one in which the field's regular spring has dried up and a new spring has since emerged: *shecharva ma'yanah she'ragil lishtot mimenu* — the spring it normally relied upon has dried up. The *hefsed* is clear: without water now, the field will suffer severe loss.

That Rabbi Yehuda's position corresponds to our *mishnah* is demonstrated in two ways. First, the *baraita* itself: Rabbi Yehuda permits only *beit hashalchin shecharva* — a field in genuine need — and only from a *ma'ayan*, which does not entail great effort. The implicit ruling is that if water were to be drawn from a well or from collected rainfall — both of which involve considerably more *tircha* — it would not be permitted even for a *beit hashalchin*. Second, Rabbi Yehuda's additional ruling: *lo yifaneh adam ammat hamayim v'yashke l'ginato u'l'chorvato b'chol hamoed* — one may not redirect an irrigation canal to water one's garden or a field being replanted on *chol hamoed*. As Tosafot explains, *ginah* and *churvah* are themselves cases of *beit hashalchin* — situations involving genuine *hefsed* — and yet the redirecting of the *amah* is still forbidden. Why? Because redirecting an irrigation canal constitutes excessive *tircha*. Thus Rabbi Yehuda demonstrates both criteria: *hefsed* is necessary, and even where *hefsed* is present, *tircha* is still prohibited.

### R. Elazar

Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah takes the most stringent position: *lo kach velo kach* — neither this nor that. He prohibits irrigation even where the field's spring has dried up and crops are genuinely at risk. The *gemara* notes that his ruling specifies a *mayan sheyatza batchila* — a newly emerged spring — and one might ask whether he would permit an established spring. The *gemara* treats this as an open question but notes that Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah is in any case clearly more stringent than Rabbi Yehuda, and there is no other *tanna* whose position aligns closely enough with the *mishnah* to serve as its author.

### Attribution

Having established the three positions, the *gemara* assigns the authorship of the *mishnah* to Rabbi Yehuda. The *gemara* anticipates an objection: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the *baraita* is limited to the specific case of a newly emerged spring, where concern about collapse creates special conditions. Maybe if the spring were old and there was no concern of collapse, Rabbi Yehuda would permit even a *beit haba'al*. Under that reading, Rabbi Yehuda would not be a perfect match for our *mishnah*, which draws no distinction between new and old springs. The *gemara* responds: *im ken matnitin d'man* — then who else could have authored the *mishnah*? No other *tanna*'s position overlaps as closely. We therefore proceed on the assumption that the *mishnah* is Rabbi Yehuda's, and that his position — whether the spring is new or established — is consistently that *beit hashalchin in, beit haba'al lo*: only where there is *hefsed*, and only without excessive *tircha*.

The *baraita*'s focus on a newly emerged spring, rather than an established one, is explained by the *gemara* as *l'hodeia kocho de-Rabbi Meir* — to demonstrate the full extent of Rabbi Meir's leniency. The most striking case is the newly emerged spring, where one might have expected stringency even according to a lenient authority. Rabbi Meir allows even that, even for a *beit haba'al*, even for mere *revach*. By contrast, Rabbi Yehuda, when the spring is established and there is no concern of collapse, does not on that basis extend his *heter* to a *beit haba'al*. His *heter* is rooted exclusively in *hefsed*, not in the absence of effort-risk.

---

## Shabbat Melacha

### Choresh vs. Zore'a

The *gemara* now introduces a question that, while addressed here in the context of *Shabbos*, will circle back to the issues of our *masechet*: *ha-menakesh ve-hamashke mayim lizraim be-Shabbos — mishum mai matrinan beih?* If someone weeds or waters seeds planted in the ground on *Shabbos*, what *melacha* warning (*hatra'ah*) must be given? The question of which warning to give is the *gemara*'s way of asking: which of the thirty-nine *melacha* categories does this act fall under?

This is also an occasion to note how *hatra'ah* functions. A generic warning — "that is a *melacha*" — may not suffice; the warning should identify the specific category. If the wrong category is named, the defendant could reasonably claim he did not take the warning seriously. Identifying the correct category is therefore a substantive halakhic question.

### Rabbah's View

Rabbah answers: *mishum choreish* — the category is plowing. *Charisha* is the working of the ground that enables growth, typically performed before planting. Here too, weeding or watering acts upon the ground: the water does not reach the seed directly but is absorbed by the soil, which then nourishes the seed. The action is fundamentally an improvement of the ground — *marpuyei ar'a* — and therefore analogous to plowing. Rabbah's principle, as Tosafot articulates it, is that we categorize a *melacha* by comparing the physical act: the form of the action most closely resembles *choresh*, and we go by physical resemblance over stated intent.

### Rav Yosef

Rav Yosef disagrees: *mishum zorea* — the category is planting. His reasoning: the essential purpose of planting is to cause fruit to grow — *letzmuchi peira* — and that is equally the purpose of weeding and watering. It does not matter that the physical act is not directed at the seed itself; what matters is that the goal is the growth of the produce. As Tosafot explains the dispute: Rabbah holds that we go after *the act* — *batar hama'aseh* — and not after intent, while Rav Yosef holds that we go after *the purpose* — *batar machshavah* — since that is the essential character of the *melacha*.

### Abaaye Challenge

Abaaye challenges both positions symmetrically. To Rabbah: if the *melacha* is classified as *choreish*, why is it not *also* classified as *zorea*, given that it promotes growth?
