To Rav Yosef: if it is *zorea*, why is it not *also* classified as *choreish*, given that it acts upon the ground? One might respond that a single act cannot be double-classified — only one *melacha* category can apply to one act. But Abaaye notes that this principle is not absolute.

### Double Melacha

Rav Kahana teaches: *zomeir v'tzarich la-eitzim chayav shtayim* — one who prunes a tree and also intends to use the pruned wood for firewood is liable for two *melachos*: one for *noteia* (planting, since the pruning promotes the tree's growth) and one for *kotzeir* (harvesting, since he is gathering wood he wishes to use). Here a single physical act generates liability under two distinct *melacha* categories. The *gemara* notes the apparent tension: why can that act generate two liabilities while the act of weeding or watering cannot? The resolution is implicit in the structure of the cases. In the pruning case, the person is genuinely doing two separate things with one act — promoting tree growth and harvesting wood. Either could have been done independently: one could prune without wanting the wood, or collect wood without intending to benefit the tree. The coincidence of two independent purposes in a single act produces two *melacha* liabilities. By contrast, watering or weeding the ground is a single, unified action. There is only one thing being done. The debate between Rabbah and Rav Yosef is not about whether there are two acts, but about which single category best captures the one act that is performed.

---

## Kilayim Debate

### R. Akiva

Rav Yosef challenges Rabbah from a *baraita* concerning *kilayim*: *ha-menakesh ve-ha-mechapeh b'kilayim lokeh — Rabbi Akiva omer af ha-m'kayeim*. One who weeds the ground or covers the roots of *kilayim* with dirt receives lashes. Rabbi Akiva goes further: even one who merely allows *kilayim* to remain — *m'kayeim* — also receives lashes. The operative prohibition is *sadcha lo tizra kilayim* — do not plant your field with mixed species.

### Inference

According to Rav Yosef, who holds that working the ground constitutes *zore'a*, the *baraita* is straightforward: weeding and covering the dirt are forms of planting, which is precisely what the *pasuk* prohibits in the context of *kilayim*. The whole structure fits: the Torah's prohibition is *zeri'ah*, and acts that promote growth are categorized as *zeri'ah*. But according to Rabbah, who holds that working the ground is *choresh* rather than *zorea*, a difficulty arises: the Torah's prohibition in *kilayim* is against *planting*, not plowing. One does not receive lashes for plowing a field of *kilayim*. If weeding and covering are categorized as *charisha* and not *zeri'ah*, how could the *baraita* say one receives lashes for doing them?

### Rabbah Reread

Rabbah responds: *mishum m'kayeim* — the liability is not for an act of planting but for the act of *sustaining* the *kilayim*. One receives lashes not because weeding or covering is itself *zeri'ah*, but because it constitutes an act of *m'kayeim* — of actively maintaining the *kilayim* in place. The *gemara* objects: but if that is the reasoning behind the *reisha* of the *baraita*, then that is also what Rabbi Akiva is saying in the *seifa* when he speaks of *m'kayeim*. How can both clauses refer to *m'kayeim*? Rabbah responds: *kula Rabbi Akiva hi* — read the entire *baraita* as presenting Rabbi Akiva's position in layers. The *reisha* asks: what is the reason one receives lashes for weeding or covering? The answer is *mishum m'kayeim* — because these acts constitute maintenance of *kilayim*. And that is precisely what Rabbi Akiva makes explicit: *af ha-m'kayeim* — even passive maintenance incurs liability, based on the verse *kilayim sadcha lo*, which extends the prohibition beyond active planting to any form of allowing *kilayim* to persist.

The plain reading of the *baraita*, it must be said, aligns naturally with Rav Yosef's position — working the ground is *zore'a* — and Rabbah's reinterpretation requires reading the entire unit as presenting a single coherent position of Rabbi Akiva. Both positions are maintained in the *gemara*, and the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef remains live.

### Bridge Forward

The *gemara* has thus established the framework of the *choresh*-versus-*zorea* debate in the context of *Shabbos*. The relevance of this debate to our *masechet* will become apparent as we proceed: the same question of how to categorize acts that tend to growing things — whether through *charisha* or *zeri'ah* — bears directly on the classification of agricultural labor in the contexts of both *shvi'is* and *chol hamoed*. We will pick up from here and trace how this *sugya* connects to the *mishnah*'s rulings on watering fields under those two distinct regimes.

---

---

# Moed Katan 3

## Chol HaMoed Criteria

### Davar ha'avad & Tircha

We continue in Moed Katan, picking up at the bottom of 2b. The Mishnah's underlying assumptions have already been laid out: *melacha* on *Chol HaMoed* is permissible only when two criteria are simultaneously met. First, there must be a *davar ha'avad* — a situation in which inaction will cause an actual financial loss. Mere loss of potential gain, *hefsed revach*, does not suffice; one must face genuine loss. Second, the permitted work must not entail undue *tircha*, undue effort or burden. Watering from a well rather than from a spring, for example, would involve excessive *tircha* and would therefore be impermissible regardless of loss. Both conditions must be present together.

### Rabba vs. Rav Yosef

The Gemara introduces what appears at first to be a separate topic but will shortly prove directly relevant: a dispute between Rabba and Rav Yosef regarding the Shabbat category into which one would place the act of watering or weeding the ground. Rabba holds that such an act falls under the category of *choresh* — plowing — because it works upon the earth itself. Rav Yosef holds it falls under *zoreia* — planting — because it stimulates the seed to sprout. The practical consequences of this dispute are not limited to Shabbat.

### Categories Applied

As the Gemara noted at the close of the previous daf, this categorization carries implications for *kilayim* as well. The Torah states *lo tizra karmecha kilayim* — do not sow your vineyard with mixed species. If instead of planting one waters or weeds mixed species, what is the result? A *Baraita* rules that one is *chayav*, which on its face strongly supports Rav Yosef's position that such acts constitute a form of *zeriah*. Rabba escapes this by arguing that the *Baraita* reflects the view of Rabbi Akiva, who holds that even merely *mekayem* — allowing *kilayim* to continue growing — carries liability, independent of any specific act of *zeriah*. What the Gemara establishes clearly is that the Rabba–Rav Yosef debate is not confined to Shabbat; the categorization of these agricultural acts carries consequences across multiple halachic domains, including *shemita*, to which the Gemara now turns.

---

## Watering Fields

### Chol HaMoed Logic

The Gemara cites the opening of our Mishnah: *mashkin beit hashalchin b'moed u'vishvi'is* — one may irrigate an orchard that requires irrigation both on *Chol HaMoed* and during *shemita*. Regarding *Chol HaMoed*, the Gemara finds no difficulty. *Bishlama moed* — the allowance is understandable. Why is the work ordinarily prohibited? *Mishum tircha hu* — because of undue effort. And the Rabbis permitted it *b'makom p'seida* — where inaction would result in loss.

### Tircha vs. Melacha

This terse statement deserves pause, because the Gemara here makes a far-reaching claim. It characterizes the entire framework of *melacha* prohibitions on *Chol HaMoed* — and this is not the relatively peripheral discussion of haircuts or laundry, which may rest on entirely different grounds, but actual agricultural labor — as rooted purely in *tircha*. It is not about a conceptual category of *melacha* at all. Rabbeinu Gershom spells this out explicitly: *lo asir b'shum melacha ela mishum tircha* — the only concern is the concern of excessive effort. The corollary is significant: since the prohibition is grounded in *tircha* and the Rabbis permitted it wherever there is a loss, the entire framework sounds thoroughly rabbinic. The idea of *tircha* as a governing concept has no biblical precedent. This characterization stands in some tension with other passages suggesting that *Chol HaMoed* work prohibitions do have deeper conceptual grounding in categories of *melacha*, but for present purposes the Gemara has staked out this position clearly.

### Shemita Problem

The more pressing difficulty, however, concerns *shemita*. The Gemara asks: *ela shvi'is* — but *shemita*? How can any act of watering be permitted during the sabbatical year? Whether watering falls under *zoreia* or under *choresh*, both planting and plowing are Biblically forbidden on *shemita*. *Zeria v'charisha b'shevi'is mi sharei?* Is any of this really permissible when it appears to be a blanket Biblical prohibition? This is the central question the Gemara now sets out to resolve.

---

## Abaye: Shemita Rabbinic

### Rabbi's Two Shemitot

Abaye offers the first resolution: *b'shevi'is bazman hazeh v'Rabbi* — the Mishnah's leniency assumes we are speaking of *shemita* in the present era, and it follows the position of Rabbi. A *Baraita* records Rabbi's interpretation of the verse *v'zeh devar hashemita shamot kol ba'al masheh yado asher yasheh b'rei'eihu* — anyone who holds a loan against his fellow shall release it. Rabbi notes the doubled language, *shemita shamot*, and derives from it that the verse is speaking of two *shemitot* — *shtei shemitos*: *shemitas karka*, the release of the land, and *shemitas kesafim*, the release of debts.

### Conditional Application

Rabbi's principle is: *bizman she'atah meshamet karka atah meshamet kesafim, u'bizman she'i atah meshamet karka i atah meshamet kesafim* — when *shemitat karka* applies, debt release applies; when *shemitat karka* does not apply, debt release does not apply either. The primary *chiddush* of Rabbi's statement is to tell us that the release of debts — which one might have thought operates universally, even outside the Land of Israel, given its seemingly universal moral character — is in fact conditioned on the application of *shemitat karka*. But what the Gemara infers from Rabbi's position is a broader implication: Rabbi acknowledges that there are circumstances in which *shemitat karka* itself does not apply. This means that *shemita* is not invariably biblical.

### Post-Churban Status

What would cause *shemitat karka* to lapse? One possibility is that after the *churban*, the Land does not retain the same *kedusha*. Another line of reasoning, with additional support, is that *shemitat karka* is itself dependent on *yovel*: since we do not observe *yovel* — because all the tribes are no longer settled in the Land — *shemitat karka* does not apply, and consequently neither does *shemitat kesafim*. Whatever the precise mechanism, the implication embedded in Rabbi's statement is that *shemita* is not always Biblical in force. The Gemara therefore reads our Mishnah as operating on this assumption: since all the tribes are not settled in the Land and we are in the post-*churban* era, *shemita* nowadays is not Biblical, and the Rabbis can therefore extend leniency in cases of genuine *hefsed*. This is structurally analogous to the reasoning underlying *heter mechira*: if *shemita* is only rabbinic in force today, there is greater halachic latitude to construct workarounds.

---

## Rava: Avot Only

### Avot vs. Toladot

Rava offers a second, independent resolution. *Afilu teima rabanan* — even if you hold like the Rabbis who dispute Rabbi, meaning even granting that *shemita* is Biblically operative, *avot asar Rachmana, toldot lo asar Rachmana* — the Torah only Biblically forbade the primary *avot* categories explicitly listed in the Torah, not their derivative *toladot*. This is a striking position, particularly for anyone accustomed to the framework of *hilchot Shabbat*, where the *avot-toladot* structure carries full Biblical weight in both directions.

What does the Torah actually prohibit regarding *shemita*? The relevant verse reads: *sadcha lo tizra v'charmecha lo tizmor, et sefiach ktzircha lo tiktzor v'et inbei nezirecha lo tivtzor, shnat shabbaton yihyeh la'aretz* — do not plant your field, do not prune your vineyard, do not harvest the aftergrowth of your grain, do not gather the grapes of your untended vines; it shall be a year of complete rest for the land. The activities that are explicitly named — planting, pruning, harvesting grain, gathering grapes — constitute the *avot*. Acts that one might logically derive from those categories — such as watering, which could be seen as a form of either *zeriah* or *charisha* — would be *toladot*. According to Rava, only the former carry Biblical force; the latter are at most Rabbinic.

It is worth noting that Rashi formulates this somewhat differently. His comment at the top of 3a describes *toladot* as acts like watering seeds, *shelo hayah ba'Mishkan* — acts that were not done in the Mishkan. The framing is striking because no one would suggest that all thirty-nine *melachot* of Shabbat apply to *shemita* — obviously one may cook during the sabbatical year. Yet Rashi appears to be drawing on the conceptual framework of the Mishkan-derived *melachot*, applied specifically to those categories that relate to working the land. This raises an interesting conceptual question: do the prohibited *shemita* acts constitute a subset of the thirty-nine *melachot* as they relate to land-based labor, implying the full *Mishkan*-derived framework? Or do they form their own independent category, where the Torah simply specifies which activities are forbidden without drawing on that conceptual framework? The weight of the simple reading of the *shemita* verses — which explicitly enumerate specific acts — tends toward the latter view, and indeed that is where the Gemara's argument leads.

### Textual Evidence

The Gemara derives Rava's position from a close reading of the verse's structure. It observes: *mechdi zemira bichlal zeriah u'vtzira bichlal ktzira* — pruning a vineyard should logically be subsumed under planting, and grape-gathering should be subsumed under harvesting grain. If these were meant to be included in the broader derivation, the Torah need not have stated them explicitly; one could have derived them independently. The question is therefore: *l'mai hilchata katvinhu Rachmana?* Why did the Torah go to the trouble of explicitly listing both *zeria* and *zimira*, both *ktzira* and *btzira*?

The answer: *l'meimra d'hanei toladot mechayev, achranyasa lo mechayev* — the Torah spelled out these particular derivative activities specifically to tell us that these, and only these, carry Biblical liability. Other derivatives that one might otherwise have expected to be forbidden Biblically — because they could be placed within the conceptual category of, say, *zeriah* — are not Biblically prohibited. The very specificity of the Torah's enumeration signals limitation rather than expansion: had the Torah intended us to extrapolate broadly, it would not have needed to enumerate examples that could themselves be derived.

### Baraita Challenge

The Gemara now raises a serious challenge to Rava's position from a *Baraita*. Beginning from the verse *sadcha lo tizra v'charmecha lo tizmor*, the *Baraita* asks: *ein li ela zeria v'zimur* — I would know only planting and pruning. How do I know about *nikush* (weeding), *idur* (loosening the dirt around vines), and *kissuach* (cutting weeds)? The *Baraita* derives these from the formulation *sadcha lo, karmecha lo* — by juxtaposing the noun (field, vineyard) directly with the word *lo* (no), without the intervening verb, the Torah generates a blanket categorical prohibition: simply no, everything is forbidden.

From this same formulation the *Baraita* extends to orchard trees: *ein mekarsmin v'ein mezardim v'ein mefasgin b'ilan* — one may not prune, thin, or support trees. *Karsem* is pruning away damaged branches; *zarded* is general thinning of the tree; *pisuag* Rashi explains as a form of support. All are derived from *sadcha lo, karmecha lo*. The *Baraita* extends further still: one may not fertilize (*mezavlin*), remove stones (*mefarkin*), cover exposed roots with dust (*me'avkin*), or fumigate to remove infestation (*me'ashnin*) — all derived from the same blanket formulation.

This amounts to a categorical biblical prohibition covering virtually every form of agricultural work. The *Baraita* does carve out one limiting principle from the end of the verse, where the specific verb *tizra* reappears: *zeria bichlal haitah v'lamah yatzat l'hachish eleha* — if *zeriah* was already encompassed in the blanket prohibition, why did the Torah single it out at the end? In order to serve as a model: *mah zeriah meyuchedet avodah she'ba'sadeh v'she'ba'kerem, af kol she'hi avodah she'ba'sadeh v'she'ba'kerem* — just as *zeriah* is an act applicable equally in the grain field and in the vineyard, so too only those acts that apply equally in both contexts are Biblically forbidden. Acts that are specific to only one type of field — such as filling crevices with water or making circular irrigation ditches around vines, which are vineyard-specific — are excluded from the biblical prohibition.

This creates an internal tension in the *Baraita* itself, as activities like *idur* are first listed as Biblically forbidden and then apparently permitted, a contradiction that the Gemara will address. But the more pressing challenge for Rava is clear: this *Baraita* treats the entire sweep of prohibitions as Biblical, derived from the Torah's own language. How can Rava maintain that only the explicit *avot* carry biblical force?

### Asmachta Resolution

The Gemara resolves the challenge directly: *miderabbanan v'kra asmachta be'alma* — all of these prohibitions enumerated in the *Baraita* are in fact Rabbinic in nature, and the Torah verses cited throughout are merely *asmachta* — they provide a textual hook or support for Rabbinic legislation without indicating that the rulings are themselves Biblically mandated. This answer is, admittedly, striking. The *Baraita* does not read like an *asmachta*: it engages in detailed textual analysis, draws inferences from the precise formulation of the verse, and derives its conclusions from the *p'shat* of the biblical language. Yet the Gemara, in order to preserve Rava's position, characterizes the entire construction as Rabbinic. Rather than treating the *Baraita* as representing an opposing opinion, the Gemara holds that the *Baraita* is consistent with Rava — all of it is *derabbanan* — and the verse is being used only as an *asmachta*.

The resolution of the *Baraita*'s internal contradiction about *kiskus* follows from this same logic. One *Baraita* permits loosening the dirt under trees while another prohibits it. Rav Ukva bar Chama explains: *trei kiskusei havei* — there are two types. *Avruyei ilan* — loosening the dirt to strengthen and improve a healthy tree — is forbidden. *Situmei peili* — filling dangerous holes that threaten the tree's survival — is permitted. The Pseudo-Rabbeinu Gershom makes explicit what is implicit in the distinction: *situmei peili* is permitted because it prevents *hefsed*, genuine loss; *avruyei ilan* is forbidden because it is purely for *revach*, profit and growth enhancement. Once we have established that all of these prohibitions are Rabbinic, the familiar rule applies: the Rabbis permit their own prohibitions in cases of genuine loss but not for the sake of increased profit.

So, to summarize Rava's complete position: whether during *Chol HaMoed* or during *shemita*, any act of watering is at most Rabbinic. During *Chol HaMoed* because the entire *melacha* framework there is governed by *tircha* concerns and is Rabbinic; during *shemita* because Rava holds that even when *shemita* is Biblical, only those specific acts explicitly enumerated in the Torah — *zeriah*, *zimira*, *ktzira*, *btzira* — carry Biblical prohibition. Everything else is Rabbinic. And once it is Rabbinic, the Rabbis can permit it in cases of *hefsed*.

---

## Charisha Lashes Debate

### Lashes Question

The Gemara now turns to an *itmar* — an Amoraic dispute — regarding the case of one who plows (*choresh*) during *shemita*. Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar disagree: one says the violator receives lashes (*lokeh*) and one says he does not (*eino lokeh*). The imposition of lashes, of course, is reserved for Biblical violations; Rabbinic prohibitions do not carry that penalty. So this dispute is, at its core, a dispute about whether plowing on *shemita* is Biblically forbidden.

### Klal u'Prat Rule

The Gemara initially suggests that this dispute may hinge on the principle of Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ila: *kol makom she'ne'emar klal b'aseh u'frat b'lo ta'aseh, ein donin oto b'klal u'frat u'klal* — wherever the Torah states a general *aseh* (positive commandment) and a specific *lav* (prohibition), one does not apply the standard hermeneutical rule of *klal u'frat u'klal* to broaden the scope of the prohibition.

What does this mean in the context of *shemita*? The verse structure is as follows. *V'shavtah ha'aretz* — the land shall rest — is a broad, general *aseh*, a *klal*. *Sadcha lo tizra v'charmecha lo tizmor* — do not plant your field, do not prune your vineyard — are specific negative prohibitions, a *prat*. And *shabbaton tihyeh la'aretz* — it shall be a *shabbaton* for the land — constitutes another general statement, a second *klal*. We thus have the classic *klal u'frat u'klal* structure. Normally, under this hermeneutical principle, one would read the specific cases in light of the surrounding *klalim* and broaden the prohibition to include anything similar in kind. But Rabbi Avin argues that this methodology does not apply where the *klal* appears in the form of a positive commandment and the *prat* appears in the form of a prohibition. In such a case, the specific prohibitions stand alone and are not broadened.

If Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar are debating Rabbi Avin's rule, then the one who says *lokeh* rejects Rabbi Avin's rule and does apply *klal u'frat u'klal*, thereby extending the Biblical prohibition to include *charisha*, for which one receives lashes. And the one who says *eino lokeh* accepts Rabbi Avin's rule, leaving the specific prohibitions unenriched by the surrounding *klalim*, and *charisha* would be at most Rabbinic.

### No Rabbi Avin

However, the Gemara rejects this framing. *D'kulei alma leis lei d'Rabbi Avin amar Rabbi Ila* — in fact, everyone rejects Rabbi Avin's position. Both Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar agree that the *klal u'frat u'klal* methodology does apply here, meaning the *aseh* can be used to broaden the scope of the prohibitions beyond the specific activities listed. Given this, the one who says *lokeh* is straightforwardly consistent: we apply *klal u'frat u'klal*, we broaden the prohibition, and we include *charisha*, which therefore carries lashes. The question becomes: what is the basis of the opinion that says *eino lokeh*?

### Rava's Specificity

The Gemara explains that the opinion exempting from lashes returns to Rava's argument: *mechdi zemira bichlal zeriah u'vtzira bichlal ktzira, l'mai hilchata kasvinu Rachmana* — if the Torah truly intended broad derivation via *klal u'frat u'klal*, why did it enumerate so many specific cases that could have been inferred from one another? The very fact that the Torah specifies *zimira* separately from *zeriah*, and *btzira* separately from *ktzira*, is itself a limiting signal: *d'hanei toladot michayev, atoldah achrina lo michayev* — it is only these derivative acts that carry liability; all others do not.

What the Gemara has done here is allow two distinct voices to stand. There is a view — grounded in *klal u'frat u'klal* and rejecting any limiting inference from the Torah's redundancy — that *charisha* is Biblically forbidden and incurs lashes. And there is Rava's view, which reads the Torah's specificity as a deliberate limitation, confining Biblical liability to the named *avot* and their enumerated derivations, leaving everything else as Rabbinic. The resolution of the earlier contradiction in the *Baraita* — where activities like *idur* and *kiskus* appeared first as forbidden and then as permitted — follows from distinguishing between cases of *hefsed* and *revach* within the Rabbinic framework, as explained above.

One additional textual observation deserves mention. There exists a verse in Shemot — *bacharish u'vakatzir tishbot* — rest during the plowing and the harvesting. According to one Rabbinic interpretation this verse addresses *shemita* rather than Shabbat. If so, it provides an independent textual source that explicitly mentions *charisha* in the context of *shemita*. Even within Rava's framework — where one limits Biblical prohibition to acts explicitly mentioned in the verse — this verse could potentially establish *charisha* as Biblically forbidden on *shemita*, through a distinct source. The Gemara does not develop this line here, but it is worth noting as it will become relevant when the discussion of *tosefet* unfolds.

---

## Rav Dimi & Tosefet

### Dimi's Confusion

When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported the following: *yachol yilkeh al ha'tosefet* — he had heard in the *batei midrash* of Eretz Yisrael a discussion to the effect that one might receive lashes for the additional matter, *ha'tosefet*, and that the conclusion of the discussion in the *yeshivot* of Eretz Yisrael was that one is exempt. But Rav Dimi confessed: *v'lo yadana mai talmuda u'mai tosefet* — he did not know what the substantive conclusion of the discussion was, nor did he know what *tosefet* itself referred to. Two interpretations of that discussion are now offered.

### Tosefet as Activities

Rabbi Elazar reconstructs the discussion as follows: *charisha* was *tosefet* — the term referred to additional activities not explicitly enumerated in the verse. The question being debated in Eretz Yisrael was whether one receives lashes for *charisha*, which can be included in the Biblical prohibition only through the methodology of *klal u'frat u'klal*. The conclusion was that one is exempt, because the specificity of the Torah's enumeration — as Rava argued — signals that only the explicitly named acts carry Biblical liability, and the *tosefet* of additional activities remains Rabbinic.

### Tosefet as Days

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different reconstruction entirely: *yamim she'hosifu chachamim lifnei Rosh Hashanah* — *tosefet* refers to additional days that the Sages added prior to Rosh Hashanah during which agricultural work is prohibited in preparation for the *shemita* year. Just as there is a concept of *tosefet Shabbat* — adding a period of time before the onset of Shabbat during which one already refrains from *melacha* — there is an analogous concept of *tosefet shevi'it*, a period before *shemita* begins during which field work is prohibited.

The question debated in Eretz Yisrael, on Rabbi Yochanan's reading, was whether performing agricultural work during this added period incurs lashes. The *tosefet* period may be derived from the verse in Shemot, *bacharish u'vakatzir tishbot*, and one might therefore think that working during this period constitutes a Biblical violation warranting lashes. The conclusion was that one does not receive lashes — *nasiv la talmuda d'istira* — and as the Gemara notes, the reason for this will be clarified later. The reason one does not receive lashes for working during *tosefet* may simply be that the entire *tosefet* framework is Rabbinic; or, even if *tosefet* has a quasi-Biblical grounding, it does not constitute the actual *shemita* itself and therefore does not carry lashes.

Tosafot raises a pointed question here: how could lashes ever have been considered a live possibility for *tosefet shevi'it*, given that the *tosefet* obligation derives only from a positive commandment (*bacharish u'vakatzir tishbot* — *tishbot* being an *aseh*), and lashes are not given for violating a positive commandment alone? Tosafot's answer is that once the verse teaches the concept of *tosefet* — that *shemita* in some sense begins earlier than the calendar date of Rosh Hashanah — one might reason that the *shemita* year truly does extend into the preceding year: *v'kol din shevi'it yehe b'sheshit* — all the laws of *shemita* apply to that earlier period as well. On that reading, working during *tosefet shevi'it* would not merely violate the *mitzvah* of *tosefet* but would constitute an actual violation of *shemita* itself, potentially warranting lashes. The conclusion that no lashes apply reflects the rejection of this broader extension.

The analogy to *tosefet Shabbat* is instructive but imperfect. In the Shabbat context, no one ever suggested that performing *melacha* during *tosefet Shabbat* — after candle-lighting but before sunset — would render one liable to *mita* or lashes. Yet interesting questions do arise: can one fulfill the obligation of one of the three *seudot* during *tosefet Shabbat*, before sunset? Can one fulfill the *mitzvah* of *yeshivat sukkah* during *tosefet Yom Tov*? These questions turn on exactly the same underlying conceptual issue: does *tosefet* extend the sanctity of the day itself backward in time, or does it create an independent lesser obligation to refrain? The sharper stakes of the *shemita* discussion — the possibility of lashes — make the conceptual question unavoidable.

---

## Plowing Periods

### Mishna Periods

The Gemara now cites the first Mishnah of *Shevi'it* in full. *Ad masai chorshin b'sdei ilan erev shevi'it?* — Until when may one plow an orchard in the year preceding *shemita*? Beis Shammai answers: *kol zman sheyafe l'pri* — as long as the plowing benefits the existing fruit on the trees, since one is then serving the current year's growth rather than preparing the field for the *shemita* year. Beis Hillel says: *ad ha'Atzeret* — until Shavuot. The Gemara notes these positions are roughly contemporaneous in practice. For a white field — a wheat field — the cutoff is *mishe'ichla halacha* — once the moisture from the rains has been absorbed — or as long as people are still plowing to plant various vegetables for the current year.

Rabbi Shimon objects to the open-ended standard based on current practice. *Im kein nasata toras kol echad v'echad b'yado* — such a standard places the law in the hands of each individual, producing chaos across different communities and regions where planting seasons vary. He therefore standardizes the cutoffs: for a wheat field, until Pesach; for an orchard, until Shavuot, as Beis Hillel said.

### Gamliel Annuls

Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi then reports in the name of Bar Kappara: Rabban Gamliel and his *Beis Din* voted (*nimnu*) to abolish these two cutoff periods — Pesach and Shavuot — *u'vitlum*. They permitted continued field work beyond those dates, effectively removing the extended *tosefet* restrictions that Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel had established.

### Override Problem

This raises an immediate and serious problem. Rav Zeira put the question to Rabbi Abba, and some say Resh Lakish put it to Rabbi Yochanan: *Rabban Gamliel u'veito dino heichi matzi mevatli takanta de-Veit Shammai u'Veit Hillel?* — How could Rabban Gamliel and his court annul a *takana* of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel? The principle stated in a Mishnah is explicit: *ein Beis Din yachol levatel divrei Beis Din chaveiro ella im ken gadol mimenu b'chochma u'veminyan* — a court cannot override the rulings of a previous court unless it surpasses it in both wisdom and number. Rabban Gamliel's court could not plausibly claim superiority over Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel. The question is profound, and the Gemara records that upon hearing it, the respondent was momentarily stunned — *ishtomem k'sha'ah chada* — quoting the language of the book of Daniel.

### Stipulation Clause

The Gemara's resolution, offered after that pause: *imar kach hayah tena'o* — one must say that this was always the condition embedded in the original *takana*. *Kol ha'rotzeh levatel yavo v'yevatel* — whoever wishes to annul it may come and annul it. The original enactment of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel was promulgated with a built-in escape clause granting any future court the right to repeal it if circumstances warranted. This is why Rabban Gamliel's court had the authority to do what it did.

This resolution might seem convenient, but Rabbeinu Gershom points out the underlying logic that makes it credible: the economic consequences of prohibiting agricultural work not merely for the *shemita* year itself but for an additional stretch extending back to Pesach — potentially a period of a year and a half of constraints — were significant. The Rabbis who established the extended *tosefet* restrictions may well have anticipated that future communities might find such a burden unsustainable and deliberately left the door open for a future court to lift the Rabbinic addition while leaving the core prohibition intact.

A clarifying note on the phrase *b'chochma u'veminyan*: the requirement for a superior court is always conjunctive — both greater wisdom *and* greater number are required. There is a significant debate among the *Rishonim* as to the precise meaning of *minyan* in this context, but the requirement is never disjunctive.

---

## Tosefet Source

### Eser Netiyot

Having established that the extended *tosefet* restrictions are Rabbinic and were repealed by Rabban Gamliel, the Gemara now asks a more fundamental question: *didehu hi?* Is the concept of *tosefet shevi'it* itself a Rabbinic innovation? Or is it rooted in something more ancient? The Gemara answers: *hilchata l'Moshe mi'Sinai hi* — it is a tradition going back to Moses at Sinai.

Rabbi Assi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Nechunya of *Bikat Beit Chortan* that three things are *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai*: the rule of *eser netiyot* (ten saplings), the use of the *arava* in the *Beit HaMikdash* on Sukkot, and the water libations on Sukkot. Our focus is on the rule of *eser netiyot*. If ten saplings are distributed within a *beit sa'ah* — an area of approximately 50 by 50 *ammot* — in the proper spacing, then one is permitted to work that entire field right up until Rosh Hashanah of the *shemita* year. The spacing matters: too sparse and the trees are too few to justify the work; too crowded and the trees are not deriving adequate benefit from the labor.

### Implication

This *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* carries a critical implication. The tradition specifies a special allowance permitting work up to Rosh Hashanah only in this particular case of ten saplings with optimal spacing. Why would such a special dispensation be needed? Because without it, working the field in close proximity to Rosh Hashanah of the *shemita* year would be prohibited. The very fact that the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* grants an exceptional allowance for this particular configuration demonstrates that the general rule — prohibiting work close to Rosh Hashanah — is itself the operative norm. This means the concept of *tosefet shevi'it* is not a Rabbinic invention; it is established by a tradition from Sinai itself.

### Month & Extension

How do we reconcile this with the earlier framing of *tosefet* as a Rabbinic *takana* established by Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel — and subsequently annulled by Rabban Gamliel? Rabbi Yitzchak provides the resolution: *ki gemiri hilchasa shloshim yom lifnei Rosh Hashanah* — the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* establishes a *tosefet* of exactly thirty days — one month — prior to Rosh Hashanah of the *shemita* year. That is the Sinaitic tradition. *V'asu hani* — then came the Sages and extended it further: *tiknu mi'Pesach me'atzeret* — they enacted that for certain fields one must stop work already from Pesach, and for others from Shavuot. This extension beyond the one month is the Rabbinic *takana* of Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel.

### Rabbinic Portion

It was specifically this Rabbinic extension that Rabban Gamliel's court annulled. *V'asnu b'didhu* — and they stipulated in their portion, the Rabbinic portion, *kol ha'rotzeh levatel yavo v'yevatel* — whoever wishes to annul it may come and annul it. The one-month *tosefet* grounded in the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* remains untouched; Rabban Gamliel did not and could not repeal that. What he repealed was the additional Rabbinic overlay that had pushed the restriction back to Pesach and Shavuot. The original Rabbinic enactment had contained its own escape clause precisely anticipating this possibility — because the economic and agricultural burden of prohibiting work for so extended a period beyond the *shemita* year itself was significant enough that the original enactors allowed for future relief.

The result is a layered structure: a *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* establishing one month of *tosefet*, a Rabbinic extension reaching back to Pesach and Shavuot, and a subsequent annulment of the Rabbinic extension by Rabban Gamliel's court. The question of whether *tosefet* also has a Biblical basis in the verse *bacharish u'vakatzir tishbot* — beyond the *halacha l'Moshe mi'Sinai* — remains open for the continuation of the discussion, which will be taken up in the next shiur.

---

---

# Moed Katan 4

## Tosefet Shevi'it Status

### Override Framework

The daf opens in the midst of a discussion about what kinds of agricultural labor are permitted during *chol hamoed* and *shemita*. The *mishnah* allows for the watering of fields even during these restricted periods, and the *gemara* seeks to understand on what basis these overrides operate.

By *chol hamoed*, the *gemara* has been framing the prohibition not as a matter of *melacha* in the classical sense, but rather as one of *tircha* — undue exertion — which is a *derabbanan* concern. Overrides are therefore permitted in cases of *mekom hefsed*, genuine financial loss. The case of *shemita* requires additional justification. Two explanations are offered: first, that *shemita* in the present era is itself only *derabbanan*; and second, that even at the *de'oraisa* level, only *avot* — the primary categories of prohibited labor — are biblically forbidden, not *toldot*, and therefore a narrower range of agricultural work is actually prohibited.

### Tosefet Transmission

Connected to this discussion, a teaching arrived from *Eretz Yisrael* stating that one does not receive lashes for *tosefet shevi'it* — the extended period of prohibition before and after the sabbatical year itself. This raises the question of the nature and legal weight of *tosefet shevi'it* as a whole.

### Tosefet Explanations

Two explanations are offered for what *tosefet shevi'it* actually entails. The first is that the issue is *charisha* — plowing — which would be considered a *tolada* rather than an *av*, not explicitly mentioned in a *pasuk*, and therefore not subject to lashes in the same way. The second explanation is that we are speaking of the period *before* the sabbatical year itself, before *Rosh Hashanah* — the period that is "added on" to *shemita*. The earlier *mishnayot* in *Shevi'it* describe an extended period — going back as far as *Pesach* or *Shavuot* — during which agricultural work that prepares the ground for the coming year is forbidden, even though work that benefits current-year fruit may be permitted. This entire added period constitutes *tosefet shevi'it*.

### Rabban Gamliel Override

The *mishnah* catalogues the various periods of *tosefet* and records that Rabban Gamliel overrode them. This strongly implies that *tosefet shevi'it* is *derabbanan* in character. The *gemara* raises an internal difficulty: how could Rabban Gamliel override a *takkanah*, given the principle that a later *beit din* cannot annul the rulings of an earlier one? The answer offered — admittedly a convenient one — is that the *takkanah* was stipulated from the outset with the provision that it could be overridden when necessary, presumably because the economic burden it created was foreseen as potentially onerous. This situates the overridden portion squarely as *derabbanan*.

### HLM MiSinai Evidence

The *gemara*, however, is not satisfied with this characterization, because there is evidence that *tosefet shevi'it* has the status of *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* — not a biblical derivation from a *pasuk*, but a tradition tracing back to Sinai itself. The evidence comes from a specific *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* that permits working the land right up to *Rosh Hashanah* in the special case of *asara netiyot* — ten saplings planted within a particular area. The very fact that a *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* is required to create an exception for these ten saplings implies that without it, working up to the last moment is forbidden — which in turn implies a preexisting prohibition during the period before *Rosh Hashanah*. The concept of *tosefet* is thus embedded in the tradition, not merely a rabbinic enactment.

### Two-Layer Structure

The *gemara* resolves this tension by positing a hybrid, two-tiered structure. The *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* governs the thirty days before *Rosh Hashanah*: that period is inviolate, subject only to the single exception the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* itself provides — the *asara netiyot* case. The earlier period, extending all the way back to *Pesach* or *Shavuot*, is purely *derabbanan*. It was this *derabbanan* layer that Rabban Gamliel and his *beit din* overrode. Thus *tosefet shevi'it* consists of two sections: one grounded in *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* and one in rabbinic enactment.

---

## Biblical Status Debate

### HLM Status Question

The *gemara* is not finished. Having constructed this hybrid two-tiered framework, it now presses further: are these laws really only *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*, or is there actually a biblical *pasuk* that underlies them? The question — *ve-hanei hilchata ninhu?* — is pointed: are these *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*, or perhaps *krai ninhu*, derived from a verse?

It is worth noting a point of broader significance here. The *Rambam* famously maintained that the debates recorded throughout the *gemara* do not reflect a corruption of the oral tradition; rather, the tradition was never meant to transmit legal conclusions for those matters, only the text — leaving interpretation to the *chachamim*. The *Rambam* held that the one exception was *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*, which was always purely transmitted and never subject to dispute. The present *gemara* will, in fact, show that even *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* is debated — which the *gemara* itself makes explicit.

### R. Akiva on Pasuk

The *gemara* cites a teaching: *be-charish u-va-katzir tishbot* — "you shall rest from plowing and from harvesting." In its plain sense, this *pasuk* appears to speak of *Shabbat*. Rabbi Akiva, however, argues that it cannot be referring to *Shabbat* at all. The *pasuk* would be peculiarly specific if it were simply prohibiting *melacha* on *Shabbat* — why single out plowing and harvesting in particular? Since the *Torah* already states explicitly that one may not plant or prune in the sabbatical year, Rabbi Akiva argues the *pasuk* must be pointing to something we do not already know. It cannot, therefore, be speaking of *shemita* as it applies to *shemita* itself, since the basic prohibitions are already established. What then does it forbid? *Charish shel erev shevi'it she-nichnas le-shevi'it* — plowing done before *Rosh Hashanah* that serves the sabbatical year, and harvesting of sabbatical-year produce that extends past *motzaei shevi'it*. The *Torah*, according to Rabbi Akiva, is thus providing a biblical basis for *tosefet shevi'it* — an obligation to extend the prohibitions both before and after the sabbatical year.

### R. Yishmael on Pasuk

Rabbi Yishmael disagrees entirely. In his view, the *pasuk* does indeed refer to *Shabbat* — the *pshat* reading — and its purpose is to establish a principle through comparison. Just as plowing (*charish*) is never itself a *mitzvah*, so too the prohibition of harvesting (*katzir*) on *Shabbat* applies only to non-*mitzvah* harvesting. This excludes the harvesting of the *Omer*, which is itself a *mitzvah*, and may therefore be performed even on *Shabbat*. According to Rabbi Yishmael, then, this *pasuk* has nothing to do with *tosefet shevi'it*; it is entirely about *Shabbat* and the *Omer*.

### Synthesis: Pasuk + HLM

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes a synthetic approach. The *pesukim* establish the very concept of *tosefet shevi'it* — the obligation to extend the prohibition to a period before *Rosh Hashanah*. The *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*, for its part, provides the exception: the case of the *asara netiyot*, where one may work right up to *Rosh Hashanah*. On this reading, the *pasuk* and the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* are complementary rather than redundant — the rule comes from the verse, and the exception comes from the tradition.

### Superfluous Pasuk

The *gemara* objects: if the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* already permits working in the case of the ten saplings, one could have simply inferred the rule from the exception — if an exception exists, there must be a general prohibition. The *pasuk* would then be superfluous, since everything it purports to add could already be derived. The objection is well-taken: why have both a verse establishing the prohibition and a tradition establishing the exception, when the tradition alone would allow one to infer the prohibition?

### Akiva vs Yishmael

The resolution, in the *gemara*'s final formulation, is that the question of *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* versus *pasuk* is itself the subject of a *machloket*. According to Rabbi Yishmael — who reads the verse as pertaining to *Shabbat* and the *Omer* — *tosefet shevi'it* has no biblical *pasuk* at all and is derived from the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* of the *asara netiyot*. According to Rabbi Akiva — who has his own *pasuk* for *tosefet shevi'it* — there is no need for the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* to infer the general rule, and he therefore does not hold of the *asara netiyot* exception.

This is a remarkable conclusion: the *gemara* is explicitly saying that the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* itself is debated — one *tanna* holds it, another does not — which cuts directly against the *Rambam*'s theoretical claim.

---

## Rabban Gamliel Nullifies

### Nullification Claim

Rabbi Yochanan now frames Rabban Gamliel's nullification in a strikingly strong way. Rather than maintaining the earlier structure — in which only the *derabbanan* extended period was overridden — Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabban Gamliel and his *beit din* nullified *tosefet shevi'it* from the *Torah* (*mide'oraisa bitloha*). This is a far more sweeping claim than the earlier analysis suggested. On what grounds could a *beit din* nullify what is either a *de'oraisa* or a *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*?

### Shabbat Comparison

The justification offered is a *gezeira shava* on the word *Shabbat*: just as ordinary *Shabbat* forbids only the day itself — with the period before and after being fully permissible — so too *shemita*, which the *Torah* calls *Shabbat*, must follow the same model. *Mah lehallan hi asura lefaneha ule'achareha muttarim* — just as by *Shabbat* only the day is forbidden and what precedes or follows it is permitted, so too by *shemita* only the year itself should be forbidden, and *tosefet* has no place.

### Tosefet Shabbat Parallel

One might raise an immediate objection: surely we do have *tosefet Shabbat*? The answer, drawn from *Tosafot*, is that *tosefet Shabbat* consists of a minimal, almost negligible addition — a moment or two at most — that serves as a practical buffer against inadvertently violating *Shabbat* itself. *Tosafot* notes that while there is a *pasuk* in *Yoma* (in the final chapter) establishing that one must add *me-chol al ha-kodesh*, the quantity involved is so small — *kol she-hu* — that it is barely worth considering as a formal legal period. Since it is only a precautionary margin, Rabban Gamliel would not deny its wisdom; what he rejects is the idea of a substantial, months-long extension carrying genuine *kedusha* and prohibitory force.

This distinction opens a deeper conceptual question about the nature of *tosefet Shabbat* itself. Is *tosefet Shabbat* merely a precautionary measure — a practical hedge against overshooting the precise onset of *Shabbat* — or does it actually bring *Shabbat* early, extending the *kedusha* of the day into the preceding period? This question has real consequences. The *rishonim* debate, for instance, whether *mitzvot* of the day — such as sitting in a *sukkah* or eating the *seudat Shabbat* — can be fulfilled during *tosefet*. The discussion does not apply in the same way to *matzah*, which the *Torah* explicitly ties to *layla*, but by other *yamim tovim* it is a genuine question. What is clear is that no one holds one receives punishment for violating *tosefet Shabbat*, even if one has already accepted *Shabbat*. This maps directly onto the situation of *tosefet shevi'it*: even if it carries some dimension of *kedusha*, it does not carry the full punitive weight of the *shemita* year itself, which is why one does not receive lashes for violating it.

### Rav Ashi Objection

Rav Ashi challenges the entire argument. If the source of *tosefet shevi'it* is a *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*, can a *gezeira shava* come and uproot a *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*? And if its source is a *pasuk*, can a *gezeira shava* come and uproot a *pasuk*? Rav Ashi's question is pointed, though his precise difficulty is worth unpacking. If the dispute about *tosefet* concerns competing *pasuk* interpretations, one might expect that the *gezeira shava* would simply direct how to read the verse — but Rav Ashi seems to resist even that move.

### HLM Time-Bound

Rav Ashi's resolution reframes the entire discussion. Rabban Gamliel and his *beit din*, he says, held like Rabbi Yishmael — meaning they held that *tosefet shevi'it* is grounded not in a *pasuk* but in the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai*. And their position was further that this *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* applies only *bizman she-beit hamikdash kayam* — when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands. The evidence for this temporal limitation is that the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* concerning the *asara netiyot* is always transmitted together with two other traditions — *nisuch hamayim* and *arava* — both of which are *Mikdash*-related practices. The grouping implies that all three share the same condition: they apply only when the *Beit HaMikdash* stands.

This is a striking conclusion, and one that deserves scrutiny. *Shemita* is fundamentally a land-based *mitzvah*, tied to settlement and dominion over *Eretz Yisrael* — not obviously connected to the *Mikdash*. One could readily imagine a period when *shemita de'oraisa* applies without a *Beit HaMikdash*, such as during the early period of settlement under *Yehoshua*. The connection to the *Mikdash* is not at all self-evident. Nevertheless, this is the *gemara*'s resolution: Rabban Gamliel and his *beit din* held that the *halakha l'Moshe miSinai* underlying *tosefet shevi'it* was never intended to apply in the absence of the *Beit HaMikdash*, and therefore they were able to nullify it entirely.

### Kedusha vs Caution

The deeper conceptual question remains: what is *tosefet* — whether *tosefet shevi'it* or *tosefet Shabbat* — really about? Is it an actual extension of *kedusha* into the preceding period, meaning that the sanctity of the day or year genuinely begins early? Or is it merely a practical precautionary measure — a buffer to prevent one from inadvertently overstepping the boundary at the last second? The punitive dimension consistently points in one direction: nobody suggests one receives *sekila* or *malkot* for violating *tosefet*, even after having formally accepted the *kedusha*. But this does not resolve whether the preceding period has genuine *kedusha*. The *rishonim* debate whether *kiyumim* — fulfillments of *mitzvot* associated with the day — can be performed during *tosefet*, and their disagreement reflects this unresolved question about the nature of the extension itself.

---

## Watering Restrictions

### Spring vs Collected

The *mishnah* establishes a basic rule for watering fields on *chol hamoed*: one may water from a spring (*mei ma'ayan*) but not from rainwater (*mei geshamim*) or from a *kilon* — a bucket-and-pulley system used to raise water from a well or ditch.

### Gezeira Rationale

The prohibition against the *kilon* system is self-evident: it involves substantial *tircha yeseira*, excessive exertion, which is precisely what *chol hamoed* restrictions aim to prevent. But the prohibition against using collected rainwater is puzzling — what exertion is involved in drawing from a barrel of rainwater sitting right there? Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: it is a *gezeira* — a protective enactment. If we permit rainwater, people will reason that collected water is collected water, and will proceed to draw water from the bottom of their wells using the bucket system. The common denominator is that both involve collected, non-flowing water. Permitting one will inevitably lead to permitting the other.

### Rainwater Self-Problem

Rav Ashi offers an alternative explanation. The problem is not that *mei geshamim* will lead to a different case of *mei kilon*; rather, *mei geshamim* itself can become a case requiring the equivalent of *mei kilon* effort. If one has a large barrel of rainwater and the level drops sufficiently, drawing from the bottom requires considerable labor — lowering something in and raising it out. The *gezeira* is thus not about a slippery slope to a different scenario but about the fact that the rainwater scenario itself may devolve into one of substantial *tircha*.

### Concern Type Debate

This distinction between the two explanations — whether the concern is about *mei geshamim* leading to other cases of *mei kilon*, or about *mei geshamim* itself becoming *mei kilon* — will determine how various borderline cases are resolved, as the subsequent discussion makes clear.

### Rivers from Swamps

Rabbi Zeira teaches in the name of Rabbah bar Yirmiyah in the name of Shmuel: rivers or streams that draw water from swamps (*agamim*) are permitted for watering on *chol hamoed*. The scenario involves a large body of collected standing water — the *agam* — from which a river or channel flows, passing by one's field. One draws water from this flowing channel to irrigate.

The question is whether this case is analogous to *mei geshamim*. On one level it is: the water ultimately derives from a collected, non-flowing source. But there is an important difference — the effort involved is minimal. There is no need to raise water vertically; one is simply conveying it horizontally. And crucially, the *agam* is so vast that there is no realistic concern it will run dry.

### R. Yirmiyah Challenge

Rabbi Yirmiyah challenged Rabbi Zeira directly: is not swamp water also collected water — effectively *mei geshamim* — and why should it be treated differently?

### Bavel Swamps Inexhaustib…

Rabbi Zeira responded with characteristic affection: *Yirmiyah beri* — Yirmiyah, my son — the swamps of *Bavel* are so vast and deep that they never run dry. Their water is, for all practical purposes, inexhaustible. This is precisely where the two explanations diverge. If the concern about *mei geshamim* is that this case itself will eventually require the *kilon*-like effort of drawing from a depleted source, then swamp water in *Bavel* never presents that concern — the water will never reach a level where raising it becomes laborious. If, however, the concern is purely that permitting collected water will lead people to permit *mei kilon* in other scenarios, then the infinite supply of the *Bavel* swamps is irrelevant — it remains collected water, and allowing it sets a precedent. The *gemara* concludes that the two *amora'im* who debate the reason for prohibiting *mei geshamim* disagree precisely over whether Rabbi Zeira's ruling is correct: the one who holds the concern is about this case itself becoming *mei kilon* accepts his ruling; the one who holds the concern is about leading to other *mei kilon* scenarios does not.

---

## Pools and Channels

### Pools Rule

A *baraita* addresses a related case. If pools (*pesukot* and *breichot*) were filled with rainwater before *yom tov*, it is forbidden to water from them on *chol hamoed* — this is simply a case of *mei geshamim*. However, if a water channel (*amat hamayim*) passes through them, it becomes permissible. The channel changes the character of the water supply.

### Majority Field Condition

Rav Pappa qualifies this leniency: the water channel renders the pools permissible only if the majority of the field can be watered from the channel water itself. The logic is that if the channel provides enough water to irrigate most of the field, then even if the collected water in the pools is depleted, there is no concern that one will resort to drawing water from their depths. The channel remains a sufficient supply, and one need not worry that the depletion of the pools will necessitate the laborious raising of water.

### Continuous Flow Leniency

Rav Ashi goes further. Even if the channel water does not cover the majority of the field, it is permissible provided the water flows continuously through the channel. The reasoning: since the channel is constantly replenishing, a person will simply wait for the next day's flow rather than resort to drawing from the depleted pool. *Ilo shatya le-chad yoma tishatya le-trei ve-tlasa yomei* — if it cannot be watered today, it will be watered in two or three days. The continuous flow of the channel provides sufficient psychological and practical assurance that one will not be driven to the effort of *mei kilon*.

### Dripping Well

Another *baraita*: if a well (*breichah*) drips water from one field of *beit hashalachin* into another, one may water the second field from it. The case is a stepped terrain: a spring waters the upper field; runoff from the upper field collects in a pool between the fields; the lower field draws from this pool. This is permitted because the pool is continuously replenished — it is dripping water tracing back ultimately to a living spring.

### Dripping Ongoing

Rabbi Yirmiyah qualifies: this is permitted only so long as the dripping is actually ongoing at the time of watering. If the dripping has stopped, the pool becomes purely collected water with no active replenishment, and one may not draw from it.

### Upper Spring Flowing

Abaye adds a further condition: not only must the dripping from the upper field into the pool be ongoing, but the spring itself that waters the upper field must also continue to flow. The permission rests on the entire chain remaining active — spring to upper field to dripping pool to lower field. If the spring has ceased, the chain is broken and the pool loses its character as an extension of living water. The conceptual framework, as Abaye frames it, is that the entire system is treated as an extension of the original spring — which is why it is permissible. If that original source has dried up, the permission collapses.

---

## Field Labor Prohibitions

### Vegetable Hauling

A *baraita* teaches: one may not draw water (*madlin*) for vegetables in order to make them more beautiful, but may do so in order to eat them — preserving them from spoilage being a case of *mekom hefsed*. This appears to create a tension with what has been established: we have seen that substantial *tircha* is forbidden even in cases of *mekom hefsed*. How, then, can drawing water for vegetables be permitted even in the case of preservation?

### Dragging Water Story

An incident is recounted. Ravina and Rabba Tosfah were walking along the road when they saw a man drawing water on *chol hamoed* — precisely the scenario the *mishnah* prohibits. Rabba Tosfah said to Ravina: why does the master not go and put him in *cherem*, or at least rebuke him? Ravina demurred, citing the *baraita* — *madlin liyerakot kedei lochlan*, one may draw water for vegetables in order to eat them — and the man appeared to be engaged in that permitted activity.

### Madlin = Thinning

Rabba Tosfah then reinterprets the *baraita* entirely. When it says *madlin liyerakot* — he argued — it does not mean drawing water at all. *Madlin* here means *shalufi*: thinning out the vegetables — removing some plants so that the others grow more vigorously. This is demonstrated from a *mishnah* that uses the same root: *ha-madu ba-gefanim* — one who thins out the vines so the remaining ones grow better. Just as that *mishnah* discusses removing some growth to benefit the rest, so too our *baraita* permits thinning vegetables on *chol hamoed* when done for the sake of preservation and consumption — but drawing water is forbidden even in a case of *mekom hefsed*, because the *tircha* is too substantial.

### Conflicting Baraita

Rabba Tosfah's response to Ravina prompts a further challenge: there is another *baraita* that explicitly says *madlin mayim liyerakot kedei lochlan* — drawing *water* for vegetables. The word *mayim* cannot be reinterpreted away. Ravina's response is simple: *i tanya, tanya* — if a *baraita* says it, then it says it. He concedes the point. Thus, there may be a case where drawing water for vegetables in order to preserve them for eating is permitted, perhaps because the quantity of water involved is smaller and the *tircha* correspondingly less — though the full parameters remain somewhat unclear.

### Furrow-Making Ban

The *mishnah* prohibits making circular furrows (*ugiyot*) around vines and olive trees. Rav Yehuda identifies these as *banki* — the circular depressions dug around the roots of trees to collect irrigation water. A *baraita* confirms: these are the *dedidin* at the roots of olive trees and vines that collect water. Such furrows constitute new agricultural construction that falls within prohibited *tircha*.

### Old vs New Furrows

An apparent contradiction arises: Rav Yehuda himself is reported to have permitted the people of *Bar Tzaita* to make such furrows for their vineyards on *chol hamoed*. The *gemara* resolves this: the *baraita* was speaking of new furrows (*chadte*), while Rav Yehuda's permission concerned old furrows (*atike*) — repairing or restoring furrows that had collapsed. Fixing what was previously in place is categorically less burdensome than constructing new ones from scratch, and the *gemara* here treats the distinction between repair and new construction as decisive.

---

## Canal Making Rules

### R. Elazar Prohibition

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya states: one may not make a water channel (*amah*) either on *shemita* or on *chol hamoed*. Both periods are included in his prohibition.

### Rabbis' Leniency

The *chachamim* disagree on both counts. By *shemita*, they permit making a channel from the outset. By *chol hamoed*, they permit repairing damaged channels. The pattern is consistent with what we have seen elsewhere: the rabbis draw a meaningful distinction between initial construction and repair, being stricter about the former and more lenient about the latter, particularly on *chol hamoed* where the framework is *tircha*.

### Oder vs Fitness

The *gemara* accepts without difficulty that the prohibition on *chol hamoed* is due to *tircha* — digging a channel is backbreaking labor and there is no question it falls within the prohibited category. The more interesting question is why Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya prohibits making a channel on *shemita*. After all, one is not actually working the field in the conventional sense — the channel may serve any number of purposes, including conveying water for drinking or household use, not agricultural irrigation. Two possible rationales are proposed.

### Two Rationales

Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Mammel debate the point. One says the prohibition is because it *looks* like *oder* — working the ground to help things grow. When a person is seen digging in a field on *shemita*, observers will assume he is loosening the earth to aid plant growth, even if that is not his intention. The second says the prohibition is because the activity *renders the banks fit for planting* (*machshir agapeha lezri'ah*): as you dig a channel and heap dirt along its banks, that newly-turned earth — especially once water begins flowing and moistening it — becomes remarkably fertile ground, prepared as if for planting.

### Water Flow Factor

The *gemara* explores how these two rationales diverge in practice. If, immediately upon completing the channel, water begins flowing through it: according to the rationale of *machshir agapeha lezri'ah* — making the banks fit for planting — this is all the more concerning, since the water immediately moistens and enriches the banks. But according to the rationale of *nireh ke'oder* — looking like you are working the ground — this is less of a concern, since the area you just dug is immediately flooded; it does not *look* like you are cultivating it for growth. Conversely, if the dirt is thrown far away from the channel: according to *machshir agapeha lezri'ah*, this eliminates the concern, since there are no loose mounds of fertile earth deposited along the banks. According to *nireh ke'oder*, it remains a problem — the act of digging in the field still looks like *avodas karka* even if the dirt is removed.

The *gemara* presses further: if each rationale creates its own set of concerns, why should they be mutually exclusive? Should not both concerns operate simultaneously? The *gemara* responds that where water flows immediately, the *oder* concern is minimal — in a standard *oder* scenario, when you lift the earth you leave it in place; you do not throw it away or flood the area. So the one who is primarily concerned about *machshir agapeha* can also theoretically share the *oder* concern — but in the specific scenario where water flows immediately, even that secondary concern is attenuated.

### Oder Contradiction

*Ameimar* teaches that in his version of the *mishnah*, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's prohibition is explicitly grounded in *nireh ke'oder* — it looks like working the ground. *Ameimar* himself then faces a contradiction within Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's own rulings: if Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya forbids anything that resembles *oder*, how does he permit — as we will see — digging a pit in the field during *shemita* to store excrement?

---

## Excrement Handling

### Excrement Collection

The *mishnah* takes up the question of collecting animal excrement (*zeivel*) during *shemita*. One's animals continue to produce excrement throughout the sabbatical year, and the owner wishes to collect and preserve it as fertilizer for future use. But gathering excrement in one's field and piling it there looks very much like fertilizing — a prohibited agricultural act. How may one proceed?

### Permissive View

The first view, apparently held by the *tanna kamma*, is simply that one may collect the excrement without restriction. No special precautions are required; the act of collecting is not itself forbidden.

### R. Meir Methods

Rabbi Meir is stricter. He requires one of the following measures to make clear that the activity is collection, not fertilization. Either one must dig a pit three *tefachim* deep and deposit the excrement therein, so that it is visibly being stored underground rather than spread on the field. Or the pile must reach a height of three *tefachim* above ground level, making it obvious that this is a heap of stored material rather than material being worked into the soil. A third option: if one already had a small pile of excrement before *shemita* began, one may continue adding to it, since observers will understand from the existing pile that storage, not fertilization, is the purpose.

### R. Elazar Methods

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's position largely parallels Rabbi Meir's — requiring either a pit three *tefachim* deep, a pile three *tefachim* high, or an existing pile — but he adds the option of placing the excrement on a rock, which obviously cannot be construed as fertilizing soil.

### Context Clarity

This creates a direct tension with *Ameimar*'s formulation that Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya forbids anything that appears like *oder*. If he prohibits digging a channel because it *looks* like working the ground, how does he permit digging a pit in the field on *shemita*? Two resolutions are offered. The first: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya never permits digging a new pit on *shemita* — the *mishnah*'s scenario is that the pit already existed before *shemita*, and one is simply depositing excrement into a pre-existing excavation.

### Excrement as Proof

The second and simpler resolution: when one is visibly moving excrement — when the excrement itself is present and observable — the context makes the purpose of the digging self-evident. Nobody watching a person carry excrement into a pit will think he is working the ground for agricultural purposes; the excrement itself explains everything. By contrast, digging a channel with no such visual context leaves observers with no reason to conclude anything other than that one is cultivating the land. The excrement functions as proof — *zivla mokhiah aleh* — that the digging is for storage and not for *oder*. One might then ask whether the same contextual logic could be applied to the channel case — surely there is some context there as well — but the *gemara* implies that the visual immediacy of excrement is qualitatively different from the more ambiguous setting of channel-digging.

---

---

# Moed Katan 6

## Graves & Safekot

### Safekot Overview

The daf opens in the middle of 6b, picking up a discussion of the obligation to mark graves and related *halachot* on *chol hamoed*. The Gemara introduces the category of *safekot* — doubtful situations that require marking — on the principle that things that are obvious and visible to everyone need not be marked. Only cases of genuine uncertainty require a marker.

### Skhochos & Praot

The Gemara enumerates two such doubtful categories. *Skhochos* are trees that overhang and spread out in such a way that one might assume a body was buried beneath them, but where uncertainty remains: Is there actually a body there? Beneath which branch precisely does the *tumah* lie? Similarly, *praot* are rocks that protrude outward from a wall — *avanim pru'ot hayotzot min hageder* — which can communicate *tumah*, but only if something is buried in their vicinity, and it is not always clear under which space that might be.

### Beit HaPras

The Gemara then turns to *beit hapras*. As the Mishnah elsewhere states — *hachoresh et hakever harei hu oseh beit hapras* — if someone plows over a grave, the entire surrounding area becomes a *beit hapras*, because small fragments of bone may have scattered throughout the field. Since there is no certainty where any particular piece lies, the concern is rabbinic, but rabbinically the entire field is off-limits, and one who enters becomes *tamei*.

How large is a *beit hapras*? The Gemara teaches *melo ma'anah mei'ah amah* — the full length of a plow's path, one hundred *amot* (roughly 150 feet), by the width of the plow itself.

### HaPras Ohel

The Gemara raises a sharp question: the general rule is that marking is required only when *tumah* is communicated *b'ohel* — when one passes over or stands beneath something that constitutes a tent-like covering over the *tumah*. This is because *tumah* that sits openly on the ground is visible and people will avoid it themselves. But *beit hapras* involves only scattered bones lying on the surface — bones too small to see easily but also too small to generate *tumah b'ohel*. So why does *beit hapras* require a marker at all?

### Blown Path

The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel: *menafei'ach adam beit hapras v'holeich* — a person may blow the ground directly in front of him and proceed step by step, clearing the surface of any scattered fragments before walking over them. This confirms that the concern of *beit hapras* is entirely about what lies on the surface, not what is buried underground, and hence not a concern of *tumah b'ohel* in the classical sense.

### Trampled Path

Rav Yehuda bar Ammi in the name of Ulla adds: *beit hapras shenidash tahor* — a *beit hapras* that has been trampled by foot traffic is considered *tahor*, because the fragments would have been scattered or pressed underfoot by repeated passage. This again confirms that the concern is entirely surface-level.

One might still ask why the Gemara demands a marker at all, given that the principle is to mark only *tumah b'ohel*. The most natural answer is that unlike ordinary large objects — which one can see and avoid — tiny bone fragments are not visible, and one cannot assume they will be noticed. However, the Gemara had already established elsewhere that even fragments as small as a barley grain (*se'orah*) need not be marked unless they generate *tumah b'ohel*, which complicates this explanation. The question, then, of why *beit hapras* requires marking at all is not fully resolved in the sugya.

Rav Papa ultimately resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between two types of *beit hapras*: one in which a known grave was plowed over (*sadeh shenechrash bah kever*), where the concern is surface-level scattered bone, and one in which a grave was lost in the field (*sadeh she'avad bah kever*), where the concern is an intact buried grave — a genuine case of *tumah b'ohel*. It is only the latter type that requires marking.

## Three HaPras Types

### Mishna Types

With this distinction in hand, the Gemara introduces a Mishnah listing three categories that bear the designation *beit hapras*: *sadeh shene'evad bah kever* — a field in which a grave has been lost; *sadeh shenechrash bah kever* — a field in which a grave has been plowed over; and *sdei vochin* — a field of crying. The Gra notes that the original reading of the third category may have been *kuchin*, referring to the burial niches (*kuchim*) used in the rock-cut tombs of *Eretz Yisrael*, but our standard text reads *sdei vochin*.

### Field of Crying

What is *sdei vochin*, a field of crying? Rav Yehoshua bar Abba in the name of Ulla explains: *sadeh she'maftirin bah meisim* — it is the field in which the dead are taken leave of. As Rabbeinu Gershom explains, when a body was being transported from one city to another for burial, at a certain field the delegation from the city of origin would hand the deceased over to those who would carry it forward to its burial place. Everyone would stop, final *hespedim* would be delivered, and the mourners would weep — hence *sdei vochin*, the field of crying. The field was designated for this handoff, and the concern is that something may have been lost there.

### Yei'ush Ba'alim

Why should this field be considered a *beit hapras*? The Gemara asks *v'ta'ama mai*, and Avimi answers: *mishum yei'ush ba'alim nag'u bah* — because of the owners' despair. Perhaps during the handoff a downpour forced everyone to take shelter, and in the confusion the body — or a piece of it — was abandoned and forgotten. Rabbeinu Gershom prefers a less dramatic reading: perhaps a small fragment of the *meis* fell off and was not retrieved. One participant suggested a plausible scenario: in the ancient practice of reinterment — where a body was buried for a year and then the bones collected and placed in an ossuary — it is possible that during the transfer some bone fragment fell and went unnoticed. This is admittedly speculative, but it captures the spirit of the concern.

## Marked Fields

### Ambiguous Marking

The Gemara now addresses a practical problem. You find a field with a marker (*sadeh metzuyenet*) but you do not know what type of *beit hapras* it is. This matters practically: if it is the type where a grave was plowed over, you may blow a path for yourself and walk through; if it is the type where a grave is lost, the concern is a buried *tumah* generating *tumah b'ohel*, and no such workaround is available. The marker alone does not tell you which type you are dealing with.

### Trees & Type

The Gemara cites a *braita*: *yesh bah ilanos, biyadu'a shenechrash bah kever* — if the field has trees, you know it is the plowed-grave type; *ein bah ilanos, biyadu'a she'avad bah kever* — if there are no trees, you know it is the lost-grave type.

Why should the presence of trees matter? Rabbeinu Gershom's explanation is that trees require plowing to plant, and so a field with trees must have been plowed, generating the concern of *nechrash*. But this is somewhat loose reasoning, since plowing for planting does not necessarily mean the grave itself was plowed over.

Tosafot offers a sharper answer, grounding it in a *Tosefta*: a field in which a grave is lost may not be planted at all — *einah nita'at kol neta*. This prohibition may exist either to mark the loss of the grave or to prevent further plowing that might make the grave even harder to locate. Given this rule, the inference becomes precise: if trees are present, the field must have been planted while the grave was still known and locatable, and only later was the grave accidentally plowed over, transforming it into the *nechrash* type. If no trees are present, the field is following the *halacha* — the grave is lost and the prohibition against planting is being observed.

Rabbi Yehuda adds a qualification: *ad sheyeishem zaken o talmid* — you cannot rely on this inference without an elder or a rabbinic student present, because not everyone is expert enough to draw the right conclusion from the evidence, and not every situation fits neatly into this framework.

The Gemara then records a striking statement of Abaye: *shma mina, tzurva merabanan d'isa b'masa, kol mili d'masa alei rami* — we learn from here that if there is a student of the rabbis in a city, all the dealings of the city are his responsibility. The inference is gently ironic: it is precisely the expertise of the Torah scholar that makes him the one who must pay attention to everything happening around him.

### Transformation

Rav Papa resolves a deeper tension in the sugya. If only the lost-grave type of *beit hapras* requires a marker, how can the *braita* assume you might encounter a marked field that turns out to be the plowed-grave type? The answer: the marking was originally placed because the grave was lost. Subsequently, the field was plowed over. That act of plowing transformed a field of type A — lost grave — into type B — plowed grave. Hence it is possible to encounter a marked field of the plowed-grave type: it was marked when it was still of the lost-grave type, and the marker remained after the transformation.

This answer raises its own difficulty. The plowed-grave type is in principle more lenient — the concern is only surface-level, and you can blow a path through. But if the field started as a lost grave, how can we assume the plowing fully resolved the original, more serious concern?
