A biblical source is provided: *ve-samachta be-chagecha ve-lo be-ishtecha* — "you shall rejoice in your festival and not in your wife." The verse thus gives explicit textual grounding for the concern that marital joy competes with the festival, framing the two as alternatives rather than complements.

### Effort Concern

*Ulla* offers an entirely different rationale: *mipnei ha-torach* — because of the effort. Weddings demand enormous preparation — catering, logistics, celebration — and this level of exertion is incompatible with the spirit of *Chol Hamoed*. The *simcha* element in this reading serves as the explanation for why the effort is so great: because it is so joyous an occasion, the investment of effort is correspondingly large. But the operative concern, *Ulla* argues, is really the *tircha*, not the *simcha* per se.

### Procreation Concern

*Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha* introduces yet a third rationale: *mipnei bittul piryah ve-rivyah* — because of the suspension of procreation. If a person knows he can marry on *Chol Hamoed*, he has an incentive to postpone a wedding he could have held months earlier in order to coincide it with the festival, when guests are already assembled and a large celebration is underway in any case. Delaying marriage means delaying the possibility of having children. The concern is not about the intrinsic competition between the *simchas* but about the perverse incentive structure that permission to marry on *Chol Hamoed* would create.

### Erev Regel Problem

The *Gemara* raises an objection against all three rationales from a *braita*: *kol elu she-amru asur lisa be-moed, mutar lisa be-erev ha-regel* — all those who are prohibited from marrying on *Chol Hamoed* are permitted to marry on *erev ha-regel*, the day before the festival. This is problematic for each view. If the concern is competing *simchos*, the wedding joy will extend into the festival. If the concern is effort, the preparations will occupy the days of *Chol Hamoed*. If the concern is postponing procreation, a man who could have married six months earlier is still delaying — by one day is meaningless, but the logic of the concern should arguably still apply.

### Main Simcha Theory

For the *simcha*-based rationale, the *Gemara* resolves: *ikar simcha chad yoma hu* — the primary, concentrated *simcha* of the wedding is the wedding day itself. If the wedding occurs on *erev ha-regel*, that day's joy stands on its own and does not genuinely compete with the festival's *simcha*, which begins the next day. Similarly, for *Ulla*'s rationale: *ikar tircha chad yoma hu* — the major exertion of preparation is concentrated on the first day. Once that day has passed, the ongoing celebration requires relatively little additional effort, and the *Chol Hamoed* days are not significantly burdened.

### One Day Exception

For *Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha*'s rationale, the *Gemara* offers: *le-chad yoma lo mash-hei inish nafshih* — a person does not postpone his marriage for just one day. The incentive to delay that would be created by permission to marry on *Chol Hamoed* is real — it would lead people to delay by weeks or months. But if the only permissible window is *erev ha-regel*, no one would deliberately delay their marriage by several months just to shift it one day earlier to the eve of the festival. The structural incentive for delay disappears.

### Tosafos Specificity

*Tosafos* raises a significant point about the scope of *ein mearvin simcha b'simcha*. Looking at the passage, *Tosafos* notes that it is possible to read this principle not as a general halachic rule applicable across all contexts but as specific to the competition between the joy of marriage and the joy of the *regel*. The biblical verse *be-chagecha ve-lo be-ishtecha* is explicitly about this pairing. *Tosafos* identifies this as the position derivable from *Chagiga*, and cites the *Yerushalmi*'s application to the case of *Yaakov* and *Leah* — *malei shavua zos*, first complete the week of *Leah*'s marriage before beginning *Rachel*'s — as evidence that the principle applies to marriage specifically. This would be a striking limitation, given how widely the principle of *ein mearvin simcha b'simcha* is invoked.

### Simcha Threshold

*Tosafos* offers a second, less restrictive reading: the principle of *ein mearvin simcha b'simcha* is indeed general, but it applies only when the competing joy reaches a sufficient threshold. A *seudas bris milah*, for instance, does not reach that threshold, and therefore one may hold it on *Chol Hamoed*. *Tosafos* explains: *sheva brachos* — the blessing *she-ha-simcha bi-me'ono* — is not recited at a *bris milah* because the infant's pain (*tza'ar le-yanuka*) qualifies the joy, meaning it is not an unqualified *simcha*. An alternative reason offered is that since the *bris milah* is fixed to the eighth day and cannot be moved, the structure of competing incentives does not apply — the rabbis would not restrict it when it must occur on that specific day. A *seudas pidyon haben*, however, is more complex: its time is not rigidly fixed, so *Tosafos* expresses uncertainty (*tzarich iyun*) about whether it would be permitted on *Chol Hamoed*. The implication is that events which carry genuine and unqualified *simcha* of a wedding-like magnitude would reach the threshold, while those whose joy is qualified or whose timing is fixed for independent reasons fall below it.

---

---

# Moed Katan 9

## Marriage Prohibitions

### Forbidden Activities

The *mishnah* on daf 9 addresses a range of forbidden activities on *Chol HaMoed*, organized around several distinct categories. Beyond things that are labor-intensive — which the *gemara* labels *tircha* — and things related to *avelut*, such as the reburial of bones and becoming overwrought during *hespeidim*, the *mishnah* turns to activities that are prohibited because of their relationship to *simcha*. The paradigmatic case in this category is getting married.

### Four Reasons

The *gemara* offers three, or if one prefers four, distinct reasons for the prohibition on marriage during *Chol HaMoed*. The most widely known is *ein me'arvin simcha b'simcha* — one does not mix one *simcha* with another. A somewhat narrower formulation of this principle is *v'samachta b'chagecha v'lo b'ishtecha* — you shall rejoice on your festival, but not by means of your wife. This second formulation is actually narrower than the first: it may apply specifically to the conflict between marriage and *regel*, such that if either component were absent, the prohibition might not apply. Moreover, the *gemara* frames *v'samachta b'chagecha v'lo b'ishtecha* specifically as a concern about abandoning *simchas haregel* in favor of the *simcha* of marriage, whereas *ein me'arvin simcha b'simcha* captures a broader idea — not that one *simcha* is privileged over the other, but that one cannot give each *simcha* the full, undivided attention it deserves on its own terms. In addition to these two reasons, the *gemara* offers two others that seem less directly expressed in the plain meaning of the *mishnah*: the sheer effort a wedding requires, and the concern that people will postpone the wedding beyond *Chol HaMoed*.

### Tosafot's Exceptions

The practical significance of the distinction between these two formulations becomes apparent in Tosafot's discussion of a *seudat bris milah* or *seudat pidyon haben* on *Chol HaMoed*. Tosafot notes that such a feast does not pose the same problem, and offers several explanations. In the case of *bris milah*, since the *bris* itself cannot be postponed, one cannot reasonably be expected to postpone the *seudah* either. *Pidyon haben* is less clear-cut. One of Tosafot's answers is that perhaps the broader formulation of *ein me'arvin simcha b'simcha* is not the operative ruling, and only the narrower *v'samachta b'chagecha v'lo b'ishtecha* applies — which would not necessarily reach a *seudat pidyon haben*. Tosafot's other answer is that not every festive occasion rises to the level of *simcha* that triggers the concern; only *simcha* of a sufficiently high degree is implicated. In any case, it is worth noting that these two reasons are not identical, even though we tend to reach for the more generic formulation.

---

## Temple Dedication

### Shlomo's Dedication

The *gemara* now turns to the derivation of *ein me'arvin simcha b'simcha* from the event that everyone tends to associate with it. The verse states: *vaya'as Shlomo ba'eis ha'hee es hachag v'chol Yisrael imo kahal gadol mibo Chamas ad nachal Mitzrayim lifnei Hashem Elokeinu shivas yamim v'shivas yamim arba'ah asar yom* — Shlomo made at that time the festival, and all of Israel with him, a great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath to the river of Egypt, before Hashem our God, seven days and seven days, fourteen days. The *gemara* understands this to mean seven days for *chanukas habayis* and seven days for *Sukkot*.

### Gemara's Challenge

From this the *gemara* raises the obvious question: if there were no objection to mixing *simcha b'simcha*, why was it necessary to make fourteen days of commitment rather than simply combining the two? Just schedule the *Sukkot* celebration to serve simultaneously as the seven days of *chanukas habayis*, and it would all be done at once. This question is what drives the derivation.

### Explanations Examined

The *gemara* immediately resists the inference. Perhaps, it suggests, *v'dilma minteira lo natrinan v'heicha d'isreimyan avdinan* — it just so happened that they finished the construction a week before *Sukkot*. One would not proactively try to make the dedication coincide with *Sukkot*, but if it naturally fell out that way, perhaps there would be no objection. So the most one can derive from what occurred is that one should not actively seek to combine the two — not that one is required to keep them apart.

To this the *gemara* responds: *iba'i lei l'shiruya pursa* — why not deliberately leave a small section unfinished, as one does for a *siyum*, and time the completion to coincide with *Sukkot*? If combining them were truly permissible, they could easily have arranged it. The *gemara* then blocks this line: *shiurei binyan Beit HaMikdash lo mash'arinan* — one may not deliberately leave over any portion of the construction of the *Beit HaMikdash* incomplete. When it is finished, it is finished, and then the *simcha* follows. Therefore, the fact that they did not contrive to have them coincide proves nothing, since they finished early and could not artificially delay the completion.

The *gemara* presses further: *iba'i lei l'shiurei d'ama kalya orev* — they could have left over the *ama kalya orev*. This was a row of spikes, one *ama* wide, installed along the roof of the *Beit HaMikdash* to prevent ravens from perching and swooping down to consume the *korbanot*. Since this element is supplementary rather than central to the structure itself, perhaps it would have been acceptable to delay its installation and thereby time the full completion to coincide with *Sukkot*. To this the *gemara* responds: *ama kalya orev tzarich binyan habayit* — the *ama kalya orev* is considered part of the *binyan* of the *Beit HaMikdash* and could not be deliberately deferred. The conclusion is that no proof can be drawn from the timing of events, since various constraints prevented any artificial arrangement.

### Proof from Language

The *gemara* therefore shifts its approach: *ella mideiyatar kra* — from the very language of the verse a proof can be drawn, regardless of the timing of events. The verse says fourteen days, yet it elaborates: *shivas yamim v'shivas yamim* — seven days and seven days. Why write it that way? Simply saying fourteen would have been sufficient. The doubling of the language — *shma mina hani l'chud v'hani l'chud* — demonstrates that each set of seven days was intentionally kept distinct from the other. The seven days of *chanukas habayis* were purposefully separated from the seven days of *Sukkot*. This establishes *ein me'arvin simcha b'simcha* as a broader principle, since this case has nothing to do with marriage — it involves only two distinct forms of communal *simcha*, and the principle applies equally to both.

---

## Yom Kippur Story

### Violation of Yom Kippur

With this broader principle established, the *gemara* introduces a striking passage. *Amar Parnach amar Rabbi Yochanan*: that year — the year of *chanukas habayis* — the Jewish people did not observe *Yom Kippurim*. Seven days before *Sukkot* overlaps with *Yom Kippur*, and since those were days of feasting in celebration of the dedication, the people ate on *Yom Kippur*.

### People's Worry

The *gemara* then describes the people's reaction: *v'hayu do'agim v'omrim* — they were anxious and troubled, fearing that *shema nitchayvu soneihem shel Yisrael kilaya* — perhaps the enemies of Israel, a well-known euphemism for the Jewish people themselves, are deserving of total destruction for having violated *Yom Kippur*. This is a striking detail. They did not hesitate in the moment — the king was leading, everyone around them was doing it, there was a kind of collective momentum — yet this did not eliminate the profound sense of guilt and dread that followed.

### Kal V'Chomer

The *gemara* then asks: *mai darash* — what reasoning allowed *Shlomo*, or the people, to conclude that eating on *Yom Kippur* was permissible in the context of *chanukas habayis*? The answer is a *kal va-chomer*. When the *mishkan* was dedicated — even though its sanctity was not eternal, since it would eventually be disassembled and superseded by the *Beit HaMikdash* — a private *korban* brought by each *nasi* overrode *Shabbos*, which carries the penalty of *sekila*. If so, all the more so in the case of the *Mikdash*, whose sanctity is eternal and weightier, the *korbanot* being brought were *korbanot tzibbur* on behalf of the entire community rather than private offerings of individuals, and the prohibition being overridden — *Yom Kippur* — is punishable only by *kares* rather than *sekila*. All three components favor the *Mikdash* case: the cause is weightier, the *korban* is weightier, and the prohibition being displaced is easier to displace.

The *gemara* then asks: if the *kal va-chomer* is so compelling, why were they worried at all? The *gemara* answers: *hasam tzorech gavo'ah hacha tzorech hedyot* — there, the *korban* brought for the dedication of the *mishkan* was for God's benefit, whereas here, they were eating for themselves. That distinction undermined the force of the argument.

### Simcha Requires Food

The *gemara* then responds with a fundamental theological principle: *ein simcha belo achila u'shtiya* — there is no *simcha* without eating and drinking. This is not merely the incidental enjoyment of food on the side. The eating itself was constitutive of the *simcha* of the dedication. A *seudas mitzvah* is not simply a meal that happens to accompany a *mitzvah*; participation in the *seudah* is part of what creates the *simcha*, and that is precisely why it is a *mitzvah*. Without eating and drinking, there would be no proper *chanukas habayis* at all. The dedication required *simcha*, and *simcha* requires eating. Therefore, eating was not an indulgence alongside the ceremony — it was an integral component of what the ceremony had to be.

This connects to a broader principle familiar from *Yom Tov*: normally we say *ein simcha ela b'basar v'yayin*, and more specifically *ein simcha ela b'basar shelamim*, meaning that the eating of the *korban shelamim* is itself the *simcha*. Here too, it was not sufficient to bring the *korbanot* and then refrain from eating them; the eating was what transformed the bringing into a genuine act of rejoicing.

Nevertheless, even with this reasoning firmly in mind, the people remained deeply worried. When you are actually eating delicious food, one can say as much as one likes that it is all a *mitzvah* and entirely for the sake of *simcha*, and it truly is — yet there is an inevitable sense that some personal enjoyment is also present, and the question of whether this was truly permissible on *Yom Kippur* weighed heavily on them.

A further point the *gemara* addresses is how one establishes that they actually ate on *Yom Kippur* — that is, that the fourteen days were consecutive and without interruption. The verse in the *parasha* of the *nesi'im*' dedication of the *mishkan* records: *b'yom ashti asar yom* — the phrase uses the word "day" twice. Just as a single day is continuous and unbroken, so too the eleven days were entirely consecutive, leaving no room for skipping *Shabbos*. When the *gemara* raises the possibility that perhaps *yamim ha-re'uyim* — only halachically eligible days — were being counted, it notes that another verse says *b'yom shneim asar yom*, repeating the doubling formulation for the twelfth day as well. If both the eleventh and twelfth days require this emphasis on continuity, the implication is that there were no interruptions whatsoever, even for *Shabbos*. From there, by a *gezeira shava* of *yom yom*, the same inference is extended to the dedication of the *Mikdash*: the fourteen days were entirely unbroken, which means *Yom Kippur* was included.

### Heavenly Voice

Following the establishment of all this, the *gemara* records the reassurance that came from Heaven. *Yatzta bas kol v'amrah lahem: kulchem mezumanim le-chayei ha-olam haba* — a heavenly voice came forth and declared: you are all designated for the world to come.

---

## David's Forgiveness

### Verse Analysis

The *gemara* proceeds to interpret the verse that records the conclusion of the dedication: *vayivarchu es ha-melech vayelchu le-oholeihem smeichim v'tuvei lev al kol ha-tova asher asa Hashem l'David avdo u-l'Yisrael ammo* — they blessed the king and went to their tents, joyful and of good heart, for all the good that God had done for David His servant and for Israel His people. The *gemara* unpacks each phrase in turn.

### Stuck Gates

*Le-oholeihem* — to their tents — is read as referring to their homes and their wives, echoing the idiom of *shuvu lachem le-oholeichem* from *Har Sinai*: they found their wives *tehoros*, ritually permitted, after having been away for fourteen days. *Smeichim* — joyful — because they had basked in the *ziv shechinah*, the divine radiance. *V'tuvei lev* — of good heart — because every man's wife became pregnant with a male child. *Al kol ha-tova* — for all the goodness — this refers to the heavenly voice's declaration that they were all designated for *Olam HaBa*.

That accounts for the good done to *Yisrael ammo*. But the *gemara* then asks: *l'David avdo mai hi* — what was the good that God did for David His servant? *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: when *Shlomo* attempted to bring the *Aron* into the sanctuary, *davku she'arim zeh ba-zeh* — the gates became stuck to one another, blocking entry.

### Shlomo's Prayer

*Shlomo* responded by reciting twenty-four expressions of prayer — the various formulations of petition, supplication, and entreaty that appear throughout his dedicatory prayer in which he envisions people turning to God through the *Mikdash* with *rinah*, *tefillah*, *bakasha*, and so forth. Yet despite all of this, the gates remained closed and God did not respond.

### David's Blessing

*Patach v'amar* — he then opened with the verse from *Tehillim*: *se'u she'arim rasheichem v'hinas'u pischei olam v'yavo melech ha-kavod* — lift your heads, O gates, and be lifted, O eternal entrances, that the King of Glory may enter. Yet even this produced no result. Only when *Shlomo* turned to the prayer recorded in *Divrei HaYamim* — *Hashem Elokim al tashev penei meshichecha, zachra l'chasdei David avdecha* — remember the kindness of David Your servant — did everything change. The moment David was invoked, *miyad ne'ena* — the gates opened immediately.

### Enemies Shamed

*Ba'otah sha'ah nehepchu penei sonei David k'shulei kederah* — at that moment, the faces of David's enemies turned as dark as the bottom of a cooking pot. They were shamed before all. *V'yadu hakol shemachal lo HaKadosh Baruch Hu al oto avon* — and everyone knew that God had forgiven David for that sin, the sin of *Bat Sheva* and *Uriah*, which had been hanging over him. Just as the people received atonement for eating on *Yom Kippur*, David received atonement for his own transgression — and both forms of forgiveness were publicly manifest in the same moment of divine favor.

This is a striking passage on multiple levels. First, *Chazal* envision that even in the era of *Shlomo*, long after David's death, David still had enemies who harbored resentment toward him. The fact that they were shamed — *davka* at this moment — underscores what was at stake. Second, the passage reflects a *Chazal*ic understanding that the sin of *Bat Sheva* and *Uriah* was not easily dissolved; it lingered, and full divine forgiveness was only publicly evident at this later juncture. This theme appears elsewhere in *Chazal* as well — there is a well-known *midrash* in which someone approaches David and asks what the punishment is for one who lies with a married woman, and David's answer resonates uncomfortably with his own history. One additional dimension worth noting: it was *Shlomo*, the son of *Bat Sheva*, who stood at the center of this moment of divine vindication for his father. That is a detail of considerable narrative power.

---

## Taking Leave Protocol

### Leave Requirements

The *gemara* now introduces what may appear to be an aside, though its connection to the surrounding material will become clear. *Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai v'Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim* had been studying *parshas nedarim* — the tractate *Nedarim* and its *tannaitic* material — in the *yeshiva* of *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*. Having spent time with him, they took leave of him at night — *iftur minei be'orta* — intending to depart the next morning. The following morning, however, they returned to his house and took formal leave of him again.

*Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* expressed puzzlement: he had already said goodbye to them the night before. They replied: *limadtanu rabbeinu* — our master has taught us — that a student who takes leave of his teacher but then sleeps that night in the same city, rather than immediately beginning his journey, must take leave again the following morning when he actually sets out. *Tzarich lipatar mimenu pa'am acheret*.

### Shlomo Proof

The source for this rule is derived from *Shlomo*. The verse says that on the eighth day — which, counting from the fifteenth of *Tishrei*, is the twenty-second — he sent the people home and they blessed the king. Yet another verse records that on the twenty-third of *Tishrei* he sent the people away. How can both verses be correct? The resolution is that on the twenty-second he took formal leave of them, but they remained in the city that night, and on the twenty-third, when they actually began traveling, he sent them off again. This establishes the rule: *talmid sheniftar me-rabbo velan be-oto ha-ir tzarich lipatar mimenu pa'am acheret*.

### Blessing Request

*Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* then said to his son: *beni, benei adam hallalu anashim shel tzura hen* — these are people of stature, both learned and possessed of proper *derech eretz*. He instructed his son to go to them before they left town and receive a *beracha* from them.

The son went and found the two scholars engaged in resolving contradictions between verses. One pair of verses concerned weighing one's steps: one verse says *palles ma'agal raglecha v'chol derachecha yikonu* — carefully weigh your steps and all your paths will be established, while another says *orach chayyim pen tepalles* — the path of life, lest you over-deliberate. The resolution: when a *mitzvah* can be performed by others, one ought to weigh whether this is the most pressing obligation; when a *mitzvah* can only be performed by oneself, one does not deliberate — one seizes the first *mitzvah* that presents itself. The *gemara* here gestures toward broader questions of *osek bemitzvah patur min hamitzvah* and *ein ma'avirin al hamitzvot*, though it does not fully elaborate the halachic implications.

A second pair of verses concerned *talmud Torah* versus the performance of *mitzvot*: one verse implies *mitzvot* take precedence over *Torah* study, another implies the opposite. The resolution follows the same framework: if others can perform the *mitzvah*, one continues learning; if the *mitzvah* can only be performed by oneself, one interrupts. Tosafot notes in this connection that *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* is used elsewhere as the paradigm of constant engagement in *Torah* — and even he would interrupt for certain obligations such as making a *sukkah* or taking *lulav* — yet Tosafot also cites the *Yerushalmi* to the effect that *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* did not interrupt his learning for *tefillah* and *krias shema*, the reasoning being *zeh shinuno ve-zeh shinuno* — both are forms of *Torah* study. It is notable that this very discussion, so closely associated with *Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai*, is taking place with his son standing in the room.

The son introduced himself: *de'amar li abba zil legabeihu delivarchuch* — my father sent me to receive your blessing. The two scholars responded: *yehei ra'ava* — and then proceeded to deliver what sounded entirely like a series of curses.

---

## Riddle-Blessings

### First Blessings

The scholars said: may it be God's will that *detizra v'lo tachtzod* — you plant and do not harvest; *te'ayeil v'lo tapik* — you bring in and do not take out; *tapik v'lo te'ayeil* — you take out and do not bring in; *lichariv beisecha* — let your house be destroyed; *velisiv ushpizach* — and let your lodging be settled; *levavle pasurach* — let your table be overturned; *v'lo techzei shata chadta* — and may you not see the new year. The son returned to his father shaken: not only did they not bless him, *aval tzu'arei tzu'arun* — they caused him anguish with what seemed like a string of curses.

### Blessings Explained

*Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai* asked to hear what they had said, and upon hearing each phrase, he explained: *hanei kulhu birchat ninhu* — these are all blessings, each one concealing a hidden positive meaning.

*Tizra v'lo tachtzod* — plant and do not harvest: *tolid banin v'lo yamutu* — may you have children and may they not die; you will sow but never be forced to cut them down.

*Te'ayeil v'lo tapik* — bring in and do not take out: *teol kaltha* — may you bring a daughter-in-law into your house, *v'lo limutu banach delipku* — and may your sons not die such that she would have to leave.

*Tapik v'lo te'ayeil* — take out and not bring in: *tolid banata* — may you have daughters who go out of your house to marry, *v'lo yamutu gavrayhu velihaderu levatach* — and may their husbands not die such that they would have to return to you.

*Lichariv beisecha velisiv ushpizach* — let your house be destroyed and your lodging be settled: *dehai alma ushpiza* — because this world is merely a lodging, a temporary residence. What is your more permanent dwelling? In a physical sense, the grave. As the verse says *kirbam betemo leolam* — read not *kirbam* but *kivram*, their graves are their eternal house. So may your eternal house — your grave — be destroyed through *techiyat hameitim*, and may your temporary lodging — this world — be settled, because you will be resurrected to live in it again. The more fundamental concept of *Olam HaBa*, after all, is the resurrection of the dead and life in a renewed physical world.

*Levavle pasurach* — let your table be overturned: *libtav petorach bivnei uvivnata* — may your table be full of commotion with sons and daughters.

*V'lo techzei shata chadta* — may you not see the new year: *dela tamut intach v'lo tinsav intata achriti* — may your wife not die such that you would have to take another, for the Torah says *shana achat* — for one year a man rejoices with his wife. The new year in this blessing is a honeymoon year, and the blessing is that one should never need to begin again.

### Chalafta's Blessing

A parallel story follows. *Rav Shimon bar Chalafta* took leave of Rav, and Rav sent his son to receive a blessing. Rav Shimon bar Chalafta's blessing was brief and direct: *yehei ra'ava dela tevayesh v'lo tityayesh* — may it be God's will that you not embarrass others and that you not be embarrassed. The son returned to his father somewhat deflated — this seemed like ordinary advice, not a real blessing. His father responded: *birchach birchata d'mivarech Kudsha Brich Hu l'Yisrael* — he blessed you with the very blessing that God gives the Jewish people. As the verse says: *v'lo yevoshu ami l'olam* — My people shall not be shamed forever. The double formulation — do not embarrass and do not be embarrassed — captures both dimensions of that divine promise. One should not trivialize such a blessing merely because it does not sound cryptic or elaborate.

---

## Women's Cosmetics

### Permitted Makeup

The *gemara* turns to another category of permitted activity on *Chol HaMoed*: *v'osa isha tachshiteha* — a woman may perform her cosmetic preparations. One might have thought this involves problematic effort. The *baraita* specifies the permitted practices: *kochelet* — applying *kachal*, a form of eye shadow; *pokeset* — which Rabbeinu Gershom explains as making a part in the hair or a form of combing; and *ma'avira srak al paneha* — applying a type of rouge to the face. Some say this last practice also includes a form of cosmetic application to parts of the body below the face. Comparable practices involving the hair and skin are discussed further below.

### Age Objection

The *gemara* then records a dispute. The wife of Rav Chisda would apply makeup *b'anpei kaltah* — in the presence of her daughter-in-law — indicating, as Rabbeinu Gershom notes with some wry precision, that she was old enough to have a daughter-in-law. *Rav Huna bar Chinana* sat before Rav Chisda and stated: *lo shanu ela yalda* — the permission for makeup on *Chol HaMoed* applies only to young women; an elderly woman, *aval zkeina lo* — it does not apply.

### Chisda's Response

Rav Chisda responded with some force: *ha'Elokim*, by God — *afilu imcha v'afilu ima d'imcha* — even your mother and even your grandmother may apply makeup on *Chol HaMoed*. *V'afilu omedet al kivra* — even if she were standing at the very edge of the grave.

### Aging Principle

The basis for this ruling is the folk saying: *bat shitin k'bat sheis* — a sixty-year-old is like a six-year-old, *u'l'kal tavla rahata* — she will run at the sound of a festive bell. The point is that people do not simply relinquish their zest for life, their care for appearance, or their desire to participate in joy, simply because they have grown old. It is not for others to determine at what age a person's sense of engagement with the world ceases to matter.

One further detail worth noting: the fact that this practice required explicit permission reveals something about the nature of prohibited labor on *Chol HaMoed*. The obvious response to Rav Huna bar Chinana's objection would simply have been: what is the problem with makeup at all? The fact that instead a *heter* is invoked — it is important to the person, therefore we permit it — implies that there is something initially problematic about it. This points toward the ongoing question of what exactly constitutes *melechet Chol HaMoed*: whether it resembles the thirty-nine *melachot* of *Shabbos* (in which case makeup, understood as *tzoveia*, might be problematic) or whether it is purely about backbreaking labor. That question will continue to animate the *gemara*'s discussion.

---

## Plaster Debate

### Yehuda's Prohibition

*Rabbi Yehuda* prohibits a woman from applying plaster to her skin on *Chol HaMoed* — the kind of treatment in which a heavy paste is packed onto the face or skin, as one would with mud from the Dead Sea — on the grounds that *nivul hu lah* — it is disfiguring. During *Chol HaMoed* it is inappropriate to appear in this condition, even if the ultimate result is beneficial.

### Plaster Exception

However, *Rabbi Yehuda* concedes — and *Rabbi Yosi* agrees — that if the plaster is of a type that can be removed during *Chol HaMoed* itself, it may be applied. *She-af al pi she-meitzar hi achshav* — even though it causes discomfort or disfigurement in the immediate term, *simcha hi le'achar zman* — it produces joy thereafter. Since the benefit is realized within *Chol HaMoed*, the present discomfort is acceptable. If, however, the benefit would only be enjoyed after *Yom Tov*, the activity is prohibited.

### Micro vs. Macro

This ruling appears to create a tension. Elsewhere, when discussing whether one may collect a debt from a non-Jew during the non-Jew's festival — where the concern is causing them distress on their holiday — *Rabbi Yehuda* rules that one may indeed collect, reasoning that *meitzar hu lo*, the debtor is distressed at the moment of payment. The *Chachamim* respond that *af al pi she-meitzar achshav aval same'ach hu le'achar zman* — even though he is distressed now, he is glad later. This exchange reveals a clear structural disagreement: *Rabbi Yehuda* evaluates the micro-moment, while the *Chachamim* evaluate the macro-picture. How, then, can *Rabbi Yehuda* permit plaster on *Chol HaMoed* on the grounds that it produces joy later? That reasoning is precisely the macro-perspective he normally rejects.

### Nachman's Resolution

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak*: do not apply the logic of other halachic disputes to the laws of *Chol HaMoed*, because *d'kulo meitzar achshav v'same'ach le'achar zman ninhu* — all permitted activities on *Chol HaMoed* involve present effort or discomfort in exchange for delayed joy. Cooking and baking involve effort now; the pleasure comes later. Even the basic activities of *Yom Tov* preparation demand exertion in the moment, and the *simcha* follows. *Chol HaMoed* is structurally built on the model of present investment for future rejoicing. Therefore, *Rabbi Yehuda* is not contradicting his usual perspective — in the context of *Chol HaMoed*, the macro-view is the only coherent framework available, and even *Rabbi Yehuda* operates within it.

Ravina offers an alternative resolution: the debate between *Rabbi Yehuda* and the *Chachamim* concerning non-Jews' debt repayment is not really about micro versus macro. *Rabbi Yehuda* also looks at the larger picture; he simply disagrees about what the larger picture reveals. In the case of collecting a debt, *Rabbi Yehuda* maintains that even from a macro-perspective, the debtor is likely always resentful — perhaps he hoped the debt would be forgotten or forgiven — and therefore the larger picture does not produce *simcha* either. The disagreement is about factual assessment, not about interpretive methodology.

---

## Hair Removal Practices

### Methods by Class

*Rav Yehuda* now explains the practical context for these plaster applications. Young girls who have reached physical maturity — *higiu l'pirkan* — but are not yet of age find the appearance of pubic hair distressing and wish to remove it. The method used varied by economic means. *Aniyot sachot otan b'sid* — the poor used plaster. *Ashirot sachot otan b'solet* — the wealthy used a paste of fine flour. *Benot melachim b'shemen ha-mor* — and daughters of royalty used oil of myrrh, as we see from the verse describing the preparations in the time of *Achashverosh*: *shisha chodashim b'shemen ha-mor*.

### Olive Oil Effects

The *gemara* asks: *mai shemen ha-mor* — what exactly is this *shemen ha-mor*? *Rav Huna bar Chiya* says it is *stachet*, some form of aromatic or myrrh-based oil. *Rav Yirmiya bar Ami* says it is olive oil from olives that had not yet ripened a third of the way — *shemen zayit she-lo hevi shalish* — which possessed a particular pungency or quality effective for this purpose. A *tanna* taught before *Rav Yehuda*: this *anpikinon* is indeed olive oil from olives that have not ripened a third. Its effects are twofold: *she-mashir es ha-se'ar* — it causes unwanted hair to fall out — *u'madenes es ha-basar* — and it makes the skin supple and smooth.

### Rav Bibi Story

Rav Bibi had a daughter, and he applied this olive oil to her *eivar eivar* — one limb at a time — carefully treating her skin in this fashion. The result was that when she came to be married, someone was willing to pay four hundred *zuz* for her hand. The *gemara* records this matter-of-factly, though the treatment of a daughter as a commodity whose market value is enhanced through cosmetic preparation is jarring.

### Cautionary Tale

A Samaritan neighbor heard of this and decided to attempt the same treatment with his own daughter. Unlike Rav Bibi, who applied the oil carefully, one limb at a time, the neighbor applied it to her entire body at once — *tafla b'chad zimna*. The concentrated application was too powerful; *umeisas* — she died. The neighbor blamed Rav Bibi: *katla Bibi l'varti* — Bibi killed my daughter. Of course, the neighbor had failed to observe that Rav Bibi's careful, gradual approach was precisely what made the treatment safe.

### Mead-Drinkers

*Amar Rav Nachman bar Rav Bibi* — Rav Bibi's own son explains the background: *d'shasi shichra ba'in bnosei tefela* — the daughters of those who drink mead require this hair-removal treatment, because, as Rabbeinu Gershom explains, drinking mead has the effect of making the skin coarser and producing excess hair growth. *Anan d'lo shasina shichra lo ba'in bnasin tefela* — we who do not drink mead do not need to subject our daughters to this procedure. The comment functions as a general cautionary note: do not attempt to replicate what Rav Bibi did, given what happened to the Samaritan's daughter when someone tried to imitate it without understanding the conditions that made it safe.

---

---

# Moed Katan 14

## Shaving & Laundry Rules

### Intro & Overview

The fourteenth daf of Moed Katan opens a new *perek*, beginning at the bottom of 13b. While the tractate continues its treatment of the laws of *chol hamoed*, this *perek* will gradually transition into an extended discussion of *aveilut* and related areas of *halacha*. The opening subject, however, is a *mishnah* that identifies which individuals are permitted to shave and launder on *chol hamoed* — and, by implication, which are not.

### Who Can Shave

The *mishnah* opens: *ve'elu megalchin bamoed* — the following people are permitted to shave on *chol hamoed*. The list proceeds as follows: one who returns from *medinat hayam*, an overseas journey; one who returns from captivity (*mibeit hasheviyah*); and one who has been freed from prison (*hayotzei mibeit ha'asurin*). These are all individuals who plainly had no opportunity to shave beforehand and are only now in a position to do so. The *mishnah* also includes *hamenudeh sheheitiru lo chachamim* — someone who was placed in *cherem* and has now been released by the *chachamim*. The prohibition against shaving is itself part of the laws of *cherem*, so this person was similarly unable to do so while the *nidui* was in force. And *mi shenishal lechacham vehutar* — one who had made a vow and has now been released from it by a *chacham*.

These last two cases are notable. One could argue that both the *menudeh* and the one who took a vow brought their situation upon themselves — a case of *techilato bifshia vesofo be'ones*, where the initial conduct was negligent even if the eventual inability was involuntary. Yet the *mishnah* still permits them to shave on *chol hamoed*, since at the operative moment they lacked the option.

Finally, the *mishnah* includes *hanazir vehametzora ha'oleh mitumato letaharato* — a *nazir* and a *metzora* who are transitioning from a state of *tumah* to *tahara*. A *nazir* is ordinarily prohibited from cutting his hair; however, if he becomes *tamei*, the process of restarting his *nezirut* after achieving *tahara* involves cutting his hair. Similarly, the *tahara* process of a *metzora* requires cutting the hair. These individuals are therefore not merely permitted but are actively required to cut their hair as part of the *tahara* procedure. In a sense, this case is the least surprising of the list, since the haircut is itself a component of a *mitzvah* being performed at precisely this moment.

### Who Can Launder

The *mishnah* continues with *ve'elu mechabsin bamoed* — the following may launder on *chol hamoed*: one returning from overseas, from captivity, and from *beit ha'asurin*. In connection with the last category, the *mishnah* evokes the well-known episode of Yosef's release from prison, where the text records *vayegalach vayechaleif simlotav* — he shaved and changed his garments — thus providing a biblical parallel to both *megalchin* and laundering.

The list continues with the *menudeh* released by the *chachamim* and one released from a vow specifically not to wear laundered clothing. One who had vowed not to wear laundered garments and is now released may therefore launder. The *nazir* and *metzora* are not included in the laundering list, since there is no *halacha* requiring them to refrain from laundering their clothing.

The *mishnah* adds several categories of items that may be laundered on *chol hamoed* regardless of who owns them: *mitpachot hayadayim* — hand towels; *mitpachot hasaparim* — the towels used by barbers; and *mitpachot hasafag* — bath towels used for absorbing and drying. These items become soiled with regular use and must therefore be laundered repeatedly, even if they had been laundered before the *regel*. The underlying principle of the *mishnah* is that items or persons who had no prior opportunity to launder are permitted to do so on *chol hamoed*. The special categories of towels extend this logic: even if laundered beforehand, their functional necessity makes laundering on *chol hamoed* permissible.

It is worth noting, in passing, the somewhat curious inclusion of barbers' towels — which raises the implicit question of why a barbershop would be operating on *chol hamoed* at all. The most natural answer is that the barber is there to serve those very individuals — newly freed from prison and the like — who are themselves permitted to receive haircuts during this period.

### General Prohibition

The *mishnah* concludes with *ve-shaar kol adam assurin* — all other people are forbidden. In characteristic *mishnaic* fashion, the rule is stated as a summary after the exceptions have been enumerated. The general prohibition against shaving, getting a haircut, and laundering on *chol hamoed* is thus the default, and the preceding cases represent carefully defined departures from that default.

---

## Reason: Kevod Haregel

### Why Forbidden?

The *Gemara* opens with the question *ve-shaar kol adam mai taama assurin* — why are all other people forbidden? This is a striking question. One might have expected the *Gemara* simply to treat this as self-evident — these are prohibited activities on *chol hamoed* — and yet the *Gemara* finds it necessary to seek a principled rationale. To frame its answer, the *Gemara* draws a comparison from a different *mishnah*: *anshei mishmar ve-anshei maamad assurin lesaper u-lechabbes* — the *kohanim* serving their weekly rotation in the *Beit Hamikdash* and the representatives of *Klal Yisrael* standing in their corresponding service in the cities are forbidden to get haircuts or launder during their week of service, but are permitted to do so on Thursday in honor of *Shabbat*.

This parallel is itself surprising. These individuals are engaged in the service of the *Beit Hamikdash*, a time of *simcha* and honor — and yet they too are forbidden from shaving and laundering during that week. The *mishnah* implicitly assumes that others who are not in these special categories are also forbidden during ordinary times — and the categories of persons who may not do these things normally include the *menudeh* and the *metzora*, for whom the prohibition is a mark of social exclusion or ritual impurity.

### Prevent Menuvalim

The *Gemara* quotes Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *mai taama? kedei she-lo yiknesu le-mishmartam keshen menuvalin* — the reason the *anshei mishmar* may not shave during their rotation is so that they should not enter their Temple service appearing disheveled and unpresentable. *Hacha nami kedei she-lo yiknesu la-regel keshen menuvalin* — and so too on *chol hamoed*: the prohibition exists so that people should not enter the *regel* in a *menuval* state.

The logic is as follows. The *regel* is a time when everyone wishes to appear presentable and festive. If shaving and laundering were permitted freely on *chol hamoed*, people would be inclined to procrastinate and put it off, knowing they could take care of it during the holiday when they had more leisure time. By prohibiting it on *chol hamoed*, the Rabbis ensure that people attend to their appearance before the *regel* begins. The irony, of course, is that once someone has genuinely been unable to prepare — through no fault of their own — the prohibition itself would leave them appearing *menuval* throughout the *regel*. This is precisely why the *mishnah* creates its exceptions: when there was truly no prior opportunity, the person is permitted to shave or launder so as to appear presentable on the *regel*. But for everyone who did have an opportunity and simply failed to use it, the Rabbis enforce the prohibition and require them to endure the social discomfort of appearing unkempt — a cost significant enough to deter future procrastination.

### Melachot vs. Tircha

This analysis raises a more fundamental question, which Tosafot addresses directly. On 14a, the second Tosafot, *Tosafot* asks: *af al pi shehu melacha haya lanu lehatiro l'tzorech hamoed* — even granting that shaving and laundering are *melachot*, we would normally permit *melachot* performed for the needs of the *moed*. Why the need for a special rationale? The question posed by the *Gemara* — why are these things forbidden — does not arise simply because they are *melachot*, since we have seen throughout this tractate that many *melachot* may be performed *l'tzorech hamoed*. The *Gemara*'s question is: why was no such exception created here? Why, specifically for shaving and laundering, was the rule made absolute, with only these narrow enumerated categories exempted?

The answer is precisely the concern of *kevod haregel*: if we created an open-ended exception *l'tzorech hamoed*, the result would be universal sloppiness on the *regel*, since everyone would claim the exception. *Tosafot* adds a further refinement: *af sheyeish melacha shemuteres b'moed she'ein ba tircha vegam prachmatia, mikol makom ze shehu l'yipui raui lehatir lichvod moed* — even granting that some *melachot* are permitted because they involve no great effort, and setting aside the issue of *prachmatia* (commerce), something done for personal beautification would also seem appropriate to permit for the honor of *moed*. Yet we do not permit it — because of the concern of *menuvalin*.

This discussion opens a broader question that runs through the entire tractate: what is the conceptual basis for the prohibitions of *chol hamoed*? The *Gemara* never once invokes the framework of the thirty-nine *melachot* in this context. There is no discussion of *ma'amer*, *dash*, or *kotzer*. The organizing principles seem to be something other than the classic Shabbat-derived categories. *Tosafot* on 12b, discussing gathering in one's produce to protect it from thieves, cites a view that attempts to fit the prohibition into one of the thirty-nine *melachot* — connecting it to the *melacha* of *asifa* associated with *chag ha'asif* — but Tosafot expresses uncertainty about how that fits, and then raises the alternative: *v'tzorech iyun iy torach belo melacha assur, ke'heichei de'asri b'prachmatia* — perhaps the operative category is *tircha* (burdensome effort) rather than *melacha* per se, as the *Gemara* itself suggests elsewhere.

*Tosafot* is thus navigating between two frameworks — the thirty-nine *melachot* on the one hand, and the looser category of *tircha* on the other — neither of which fully accounts for all the cases in the tractate. The prohibition on business (*prachmatia*) is a prime example: commerce is not one of the thirty-nine *melachot*, yet it is clearly prohibited on *chol hamoed*. And *tircha* also fails as a universal criterion: getting a haircut is not particularly burdensome, and neither are many of the other prohibited activities. A more plausible organizing principle may be the concept of *uvda d'chol* — activities that carry the character of a weekday — particularly professional and commercial labor that marks the rhythm of an ordinary working life. Agricultural field work is the paradigm case in an agrarian society; skilled craftsman labor (*melachet uman*) and commerce extend the same principle. Shaving and laundering may not fit neatly into any of these categories, which is precisely why the *Gemara* felt the need to supply a distinct rationale: the concern of *menuvalin* operating as an independent rabbinic policy.

This also sharpens a question about the nature of the violation itself. If someone goes ahead and shaves or launders on *chol hamoed*, have they violated a *melacha* of *chol hamoed* — however defined — or have they violated a distinct rabbinic enactment designed to compel prior preparation and preserve *kevod haregel*? The answer may affect how the violation is conceptualized and what consequences follow from it.

---

## Lo Plug Principle

### Lost Object Case

The *Gemara* asks: *ba'ei Rav Zera* — Rav Zera posed a question. If someone lost a lost object on *erev haregel* — that is, they spent the day before the *regel* running around searching for a lost item — and consequently had no opportunity to shave or launder, what is the *din*? On one hand, *keivan de-anis mutar* — since this person was genuinely *anus*, unable to attend to grooming through no real fault of their own, perhaps they should be permitted to shave on *chol hamoed*, analogous to the enumerated cases in the *mishnah*. On the other hand, *keivan delo michezya milta* — since the circumstances are not evident to others, the person does not fall into a recognized, visible category, and allowing the exception in such an open-ended case risks undermining the rule entirely.

### Lo Plug Doctrine

Abaye responds with a principle that captures the *Gemara*'s concern: *yomru kol hasrikin ha-asurin vesrikin d'Baitos mutarin* — people will say that all cut figures in dough are forbidden, but those of Baitos are permissible. This is the principle of *lo plug*, the refusal to make distinctions where the underlying circumstances are not self-evident to observers. The reference is to the *halacha* of *matzah*: one may not cut decorative designs into *matzah* dough before baking because the time required for such cutting risks allowing the dough to become leavened. Baitos, a baker, invented a device analogous to cookie cutters — a mechanism that performed the cutting instantaneously, eliminating any concern of leavening. One might argue that his *srikin* should be permitted since the underlying reason for the prohibition does not apply. But the *Gemara* forbids it: if we permit one person's designs while forbidding another's, observers will not understand the distinction, the rule will be effectively nullified, and every baker will claim a special justification.

The same logic applies here. If we permit shaving and laundering for anyone who presents sufficiently special circumstances — even where those circumstances are genuine — we create an amorphous, unverifiable category that could swallow the rule. The *Gemara*'s concern is not merely one of *marat ayin* but something more fundamental: when circumstances are not self-evident, there is no principled basis on which others can evaluate the legitimacy of a given exception, and the distinction between the permitted and the forbidden collapses entirely.

### One Shirt Case

The *Gemara* then challenges Abaye's reasoning by citing a ruling of Rav Assi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *kol mi she'ein lo ela chaluk echad mutar lechabeso be'chol hamoed* — anyone who has only a single shirt is permitted to launder it on *chol hamoed*. This case bears a strong resemblance to the lost object scenario. If someone has only one shirt, who would know from observing them that they are in this special circumstance? There is nothing visible that marks them as belonging to a distinct, recognizable category — yet we nonetheless permit the exception. This seems to contradict Abaye's *lo plug* doctrine.

### Izuro Mochiach

The *Gemara* resolves this challenge by citing Mar bar Rav Ashi: *izuro mochiach alav* — his belt testifies on his behalf. The most appealing interpretation of this phrase is that the person laundering his only shirt is doing so bare-backed, wearing nothing but his belt. The sight of a person laundering his garment while wearing only a belt makes the circumstance visually self-evident: it is obvious to any observer why he is laundering on *chol hamoed* — he has no other garment to wear. The exception is therefore not invisible; it is rendered evident by the circumstances themselves.

The principle that emerges is nuanced. The *lo plug* doctrine does not require that every permissible case fall into a formally named, pre-defined category like *ba mimedinat hayam* or *yotzei mibeit ha'asurin*. Rather, the requirement is that the exception be *mochiah* — evident to observers in some concrete, perceptible way. Where circumstances visibly testify to the person's situation, an exception may be recognized even if it falls outside the explicit *mishnaic* categories. Where circumstances are not visible, the exception collapses back into the general prohibition.

The *Gemara* then records a version of Rav Zera's question attributed to Rav Ashi: what if a craftsman (*uman*) — presumably a barber — lost a lost object on *erev haregel*? Perhaps in that case it is evident, since observers would have seen his shop closed and would understand why clients went unserved. Or perhaps the closure of a shop is not sufficiently *mochiah* as a personal circumstance, since the barber is simply one person among many in a community where no one was getting haircuts. The *Gemara* leaves this unresolved: *teiku*.

This discussion has a direct practical application for later generations. Some *poskim* have argued that a clean-shaven man who shaved on *erev yom tov* and by *chol hamoed* has visible stubble is in a category where his circumstances are *mochiah* — it is evident to observers that he began the *yom tov* looking presentable and is now looking unkempt through no choice of his own. The *Rogatchover* addresses this and raises the parallel to the lost object case, ultimately concluding that the evidence is still insufficient — since not everyone saw the man when *yom tov* began and not everyone can assess how long the growth has accumulated. However, a number of later *poskim* have taken a more permissive view, particularly in modern times when clean-shaving is the norm and a single day's growth is visibly and unambiguously distinguishable from a beard cultivated over weeks. The practical *halacha* on this point remains a matter of discussion.

---

## Overseas Travel Debate

### RY Forbids; Sages Allow

The *Gemara* now turns to a *tanna'ic* dispute about the case of someone returning from overseas. *Masnisin de-lo ke-Rabbi Yehuda* — the *mishnah* that permits such a person to shave is not the position of Rabbi Yehuda. The *baraita* records that Rabbi Yehuda forbids shaving for one who returns from *medinat hayam*, on the grounds that *she-yatza she-lo birshus* — he departed without permission, meaning there was nothing compelling him to make the journey. The implication is that he should have planned better and prepared before leaving.

Notably, this rationale sits in some tension with the *mishnah*'s allowances for the *menudeh* and the one who took a vow — individuals who more clearly brought their situations upon themselves — yet who are nonetheless permitted to shave. The *mishnah*'s treatment of the overseas traveler is therefore more generous than Rabbi Yehuda's view.

### Travel Categories

Rava offers a tripartite clarification of the debate. If one traveled *lashut* — for pleasure, on what amounts to a leisure voyage — *divrei hakol assur*: everyone agrees such a person may not shave upon returning, for he had no compelling reason to travel and should have planned accordingly. If one traveled *le-mezonos* — because basic livelihood required it, putting food on the table — *divrei hakol mutar*: everyone agrees he is permitted to shave, since the journey was effectively compelled by necessity. The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* applies only *le-harvacha* — when the purpose of the journey was profit, going beyond basic sustenance to pursue a business opportunity. One position (*mar medamei lei le-lashut*) likens profit-seeking travel to a pleasure cruise — one could have foregone the opportunity and stayed home in time to prepare for *yom tov*. The other position (*umar medamei lei le-mezonos*) treats it as equivalent to providing for one's family — even making a profit is a form of provision, and the choice to travel was not truly discretionary.

### Profit-Travel Debate

The *Gemara* then examines a statement of Rebbi (*Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi*) who appears to split his vote: he endorses Rabbi Yehuda's position *keshe-yatza she-lo birshus* and the *chachamim*'s position *keshe-yatza birshus*, which initially seems to confirm that they debate both cases. But the *Gemara* challenges this reading. If *she-lo birshus* refers to travel for pure leisure (*lashut*), everyone already agrees it is forbidden — there would be no need to side with Rabbi Yehuda. And if *birshus* refers to travel for basic livelihood (*le-mezonos*), everyone already agrees it is permitted — there would be no need to side with the *chachamim*.

The *Gemara* therefore concludes: *hachi kama* — Rebbi is not dividing his vote at all. He is making an analytical observation about where each position is compelling. When he says Rabbi Yehuda's view is correct *she-lo birshus*, he means it is correct even according to the *rabbanan* — because the case at hand (*lashut*) is one where everyone agrees. And when he says the *rabbanan*'s view is correct *birshus*, he means it is correct even according to Rabbi Yehuda — because the case at hand (*le-mezonos*) is one where everyone agrees. Rebbi is not adjudicating the disputed middle case; he is clarifying that the extremes are not actually in dispute, and the debate between Rabbi Yehuda and the *chachamim* applies only to the case of *le-harvacha* — travel for profit.

---

## Infants & Minors

### Minor Born in Moed

The *Gemara* records a ruling of Shmuel: *katan hanolad b'moed mutar legale'ach b'moed* — a minor born during *chol hamoed* is permitted to have his hair cut during *chol hamoed*. The reasoning is that the infant was, in a sense, confined in his mother's womb and had no prior opportunity to receive a haircut. He falls into the category of one who was genuinely *anus* and is now free to do what was previously impossible.

### Born Before Moed?

The *Gemara* immediately raises the implication of this ruling. If we permit the haircut only because the infant was born during *chol hamoed*, then an infant born before *chol hamoed* — even the day before — would apparently not be permitted to receive a haircut during *chol hamoed*. This is a striking result, since the infant is obviously not personally obligated in any *halacha* of grooming. It would seem that the prohibition of giving a haircut on *chol hamoed* applies even to a passive recipient who bears no personal obligation.

Rav Ashi then presents an alternative version of Shmuel's ruling in the name of Ameimar (and some attribute it to Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi): *lo shena nolad lo bemoed ve-lo shena nolad me-ikara* — it makes no difference whether the infant was born during *chol hamoed* or prior to it. A minor may receive a haircut on *chol hamoed* in either case. On this reading, the permission is not grounded in the analogy to *yotzei mibeit ha'asurin*; rather, it reflects the more fundamental principle that a *katan* is simply not subject to the prohibitions that govern adults in this context. Since the problem of shaving and laundering on *chol hamoed* concerns the person who receives the service — and a *katan* bears no such obligation — there is no prohibition on giving him a haircut at all.

### Minors & Aveilus

Rav Pinchas draws an inference from the *mishnah*'s categories: *kol elu she-amru mutar legale'ach bemoed, mutar legale'ach bimei avlo* — all those whom the *Rabbis* permitted to shave on *chol hamoed* are similarly permitted to shave during their period of *aveilut*. The converse inference would then be: those who are forbidden to shave on *chol hamoed* are forbidden to shave as an *avel*.

This inference creates a problem. If the first version of the ruling — that only an infant born during *chol hamoed* may receive a haircut, while one born beforehand may not — is correct, then an infant born before *chol hamoed* falls among those forbidden to receive a haircut on *chol hamoed*. By the inference above, this would imply that such an infant is similarly forbidden to receive a haircut during a period of *aveilut* — in other words, that the laws of *aveilut* apply to a *katan*. But this cannot be correct, as a *baraita* explicitly teaches: *kor'in le-katan mipnei agmat nefesh* — one performs *kriah* for a *katan* (when the *katan* is the *avel*) solely to arouse grief among the bystanders, but the *katan* himself is not personally obligated in the laws of *aveilut*.

Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by rejecting the converse inference altogether. The *mishnah*'s principle, properly understood, is one-directional: *mi katani ha-asurin?* — the *mishnah* does not say that those forbidden on *chol hamoed* are forbidden as *avelim*. The rule is: anyone permitted on *chol hamoed* is permitted as an *avel*. But among those forbidden on *chol hamoed*, the category is not monolithic — *yesh mehen asur ve-yesh mehen mutar* — some are forbidden as *avelim* and some are permitted. A *katan* who cannot receive a haircut on *chol hamoed* (under the first version of the ruling) may still be exempt from the haircut prohibition during *aveilut*, since he is simply not subject to the laws of *aveilut* at all.

The discussion brings into sharp relief an underlying structural parallel between *chol hamoed* and *aveilut*: both are conditions in which shaving and laundering are prohibited. The *menudeh*, the *avel*, and the person who cannot shave on *chol hamoed* all share this common restriction. Yet these categories are not identical, and the relationship between them — one of analogy rather than equation — requires careful analysis.

---

## Haregel vs. Aveilus

### Aveilus Suspended

The *Gemara* articulates a fundamental principle: *avel eino noheg aveilut baregel* — an *avel* does not practice *aveilut* on *yom tov*. The source is the verse *vesamachta be-chagecha* — you shall rejoice in your festival. Two scenarios are then distinguished. If a person was already in *aveilut* before *yom tov* began: *ati asei de-rabbim ve-dachi asei de-yachid* — the communal positive commandment of *simchat yom tov* comes and overrides the individual positive commandment of *aveilut*. If a person becomes an *avel* during *yom tov* itself: *lo ati asei de-yachid ve-dachi asei de-rabbim* — the individual obligation of *aveilut* has even less power to displace the communal obligation of *simcha*, since the status quo is already the *asei* of the many.

The language of *asei de-rabbim* overriding *asei de-yachid* carries a significant implication: it treats *aveilut* as a positive commandment in its own right, which might suggest it is *de-oraita*.

### Aveilus Status

Tosafot addresses this directly. The phrase *asei de-yachid* implies that *aveilut* carries the weight of a biblical positive commandment. But, Tosafot notes, this reading would make the comparison one of communal *de-oraita* versus individual *de-oraita*, rather than *de-oraita* versus *de-rabbanan*. Tosafot then advances an alternative: perhaps *simchat haregel* as we experience it is itself only rabbinic. The biblical verse refers to the *korbanot* of *shalmei simcha*, not to the broader observance of *simchat yom tov* as a daily practice. If both *aveilut* and *simchat haregel* are rabbinic, the distinction between communal and individual obligation would explain why the former yields to the latter without requiring either to be of biblical origin.

This is a striking position — the *Pnei Yehoshua*, for example, never entertained the possibility that *simchat haregel* might be only rabbinic — but it is consistent with Tosafot's analysis. The broader question of whether *aveilut* is *de-oraita* is a major dispute among the *rishonim*. The predominant view limits any biblical dimension of *aveilut* to the first day; no *rishon* maintains that all seven days carry *de-oraita* force.

### Nidui on Haregel

The *Gemara* then pivots: *menudeh mahu she-yinhog niduyo be-regel?* — does a person in *nidui* continue to practice his status of *cherem* during *yom tov*? The question is sharpened by the structural parallel: *aveilut* and *nidui* share the same outward practices — no shaving, no laundering — and both are conditions of personal distress that run counter to the spirit of *simchat yom tov*. If *aveilut* is suspended by the *regel*, one might expect *nidui* to be suspended as well.

---

## Nidui & Court Cases

### Proof from Courts

Rav Yosef offers a proof that *nidui* does apply during the *regel*, drawn from the *halacha* that court cases — including capital cases, cases of lashing, and monetary cases — may proceed on *chol hamoed*. If a litigant refuses to comply with a court ruling (*ve-i lo tzayit dina*), the standard enforcement mechanism is *nidui*: placing the recalcitrant party in *cherem*. The very possibility of holding court on *chol hamoed*, therefore, presupposes the availability of *nidui* as an enforcement tool. If *nidui* did not apply during the *regel*, there would be no coercive mechanism available, and the court's authority would be effectively suspended. Since we know that courts do function on *chol hamoed*, *nidui* must be operative.

### Abaye's Objection

Abaye challenges this proof. Perhaps the court merely investigates cases on *chol hamoed* without issuing a final ruling — *le-iyunei be-dinei* — in which case the need for *nidui* as an enforcement mechanism does not arise. To support this, Abaye notes the difficulty with capital cases specifically. If courts were issuing final verdicts on *chol hamoed*, they would be executing people on *yom tov*, which would disrupt *simchat yom tov* — not only for the condemned, but for the community at large. It is therefore more plausible that courts only conduct preliminary hearings on *chol hamoed*.

### Death Penalty Timing

The *Gemara* responds that the scenario of preliminary investigation without final verdict is untenable in capital cases, due to the concern of *innuy hadin* — the prolongation and suspension of judgment constitutes a form of oppression of the accused. One may not rule a person liable to death without carrying out the sentence promptly; to investigate a capital matter and then defer the verdict is itself a violation.

How, then, could a court on *chol hamoed* handle such cases? The *Gemara* describes a procedure: the court would convene in the morning (*atu mitzafra*), conduct its deliberations (*u-me'aynei bedinei*), then adjourn for the day's festive meal (*ve-azlei ve-akhlei ve-shatei*), and reconvene at sunset (*vehadar atu be-shkiat ha-chammah*) to deliver the final verdict (*ve-gamrinan le-dineih*) and carry out the execution — whereupon nightfall would begin a new day, allowing the judges to eat once more. The procedure threads the needle between the prohibition of *lo tochlu al ha-dam* (the judges may not eat on the day they execute) and the prohibition of *innuy hadin* (the verdict may not be indefinitely suspended).

### Nidui Applies

Even granting that this procedural arrangement is technically feasible, the *Gemara*'s discussion leaves the primary inference intact: if courts actually proceed to final verdicts on *chol hamoed* — even through this elaborate scheduling — then *nidui* as an enforcement tool must be operative during the *regel*. The evidence from the court cases thus points toward the conclusion that *nidui*, unlike *aveilut*, is not suspended by *yom tov*.

This creates a challenge that the *Gemara* will continue to address: what distinguishes *nidui* from *aveilut* such that the communal *simcha* of *yom tov* overrides the latter but not the former? The *regel* cancels *aveilut*, yet apparently leaves *nidui* intact — a distinction that demands principled explanation.

---

---

# Moed Katan 15

## Intro: Grooming & Catego…

### Mishna Exceptions

We begin at the bottom of 14b, where the *gemara* introduces *Amar Abaye ta shma*. The discussion at hand concerns the *mishna*, which introduced the prohibitions against getting a haircut and doing laundry on *Chol HaMoed*, along with a series of exceptions for individuals who had no opportunity to attend to these matters beforehand: one freed from prison, one who returned from an overseas journey, a *nazir* or *metzora* who was becoming *tahor*, and a person who had been in *niddui*—a mild form of ostracism—whose status was then released, thereby permitting him to get a haircut and launder his clothes on *Chol HaMoed*.

### Melacha & Tircha

This *perek* serves not only as a bridge into *Hilchos Aveilus* but as an occasion to place several distinct categories alongside one another and think seriously about them. One of the notable features of this discussion is that the *gemara* felt compelled to find a special rationale for why haircuts and laundry were prohibited on *Chol HaMoed*—namely, to ensure that people come into *Yom Tov* already having attended to these matters—rather than simply grounding the prohibition in the concept of *melacha*. This raises the question of what exactly constitutes *melacha* on *Chol HaMoed*. There is very little evidence in the *gemara* that it has anything to do with the thirty-nine *melachos*, although Tosafos repeatedly attempts to bring that framework in. The term the *gemara* more consistently uses is *tircha*—effort—though not all the prohibited activities on *Chol HaMoed* fall neatly into that category either. It may be more accurate to describe the concern as something amorphous, a notion of weekday activity, which is why things like working the fields and engaging in commerce were particularly highlighted. It remains an open practical question even today: if someone cuts their hair or does laundry on *Chol HaMoed* without one of the recognized allowances, have they violated a *melacha*, or have they merely transgressed the rabbinic ruling that one must attend to these things in advance?

### Three Categories

The other striking feature of this *perek* is that these very same practices—not cutting hair, not doing laundry—are identical to the practices we encounter in the context of mourning. An *avel* does not do these things. Neither does someone in *niddui*, and neither does a *metzora*. The *metzora* is not in mourning in any conventional sense, but his condition represents a kind of being cast out from society, an experience entirely at odds with *Simchas HaRegel*. The *gemara* therefore sets these two realms in direct opposition.

### Regel vs. Aveilus

The *gemara* had already established that *aveilus* is not observed during the *regel*—indeed, if someone is in *aveilus* when the *regel* arrives, the *regel* terminates that period of mourning. The question now before us is whether the *regel* similarly overrides the practices of someone in *niddui* or the practices of a *metzora*.

## Menudeh & Regel

### Abaye vs. Rava

*Abaye* argues from our *mishna* itself: *ta shma*, the *mishna* lists a *menudeh* whose status was released as someone permitted to get a haircut and launder clothes on *Chol HaMoed*. *Abaye* reads this as referring to an automatic release—the arrival of the *regel* itself dissolved the *niddui*—thereby proving that the *regel* does override *niddui*. *Rava* disagrees with this reading. The *mishna* does not say *sheheetiruhoo chachamim*—that the *chachamim* permitted such a person in a general way on the *regel*—but rather *sheheetiru lo chachamim*, with the *lo* indicating that the *chachamim* specifically released this individual. The plain meaning is that he went and appeased the person he had been in conflict with, and then came before the rabbis, who removed his state of *niddui*. Were it not for that particular resolution, he would still have been observing his *niddui* practices through the *regel*. The *gemara* does not reach a definitive conclusion, but the simple evidence according to *Rava* is that *niddui* does apply during the *regel*.

### Tosafos Question

Tosafos raises the question: why does *niddui* apply during the *regel* if *aveilus* does not? After all, both are experienced by an individual. Tosafos suggests that although *niddui* is observed by a *yachid*, it may be considered a concern of the *rabbim*—because if this is how the rabbis maintain social order, then the practice of *niddui* has a communal dimension, and therefore it continues even during the *regel*, which overrides only *aveilus de'yachid* in the face of *simcha de'rabbim*.

### Ostracism Framework

An alternative approach presents itself, one that will become clearer as we work through the list of practices that distinguish these three categories from one another. The *metzora* and the *menudeh* are not in mourning. So what are their practices expressing? The answer is that their practices are much more about being cast outside of and ostracized from society. The *metzora* is *michutz lamachaneh*—the Torah makes this vivid: *bigdav yihyu frumim v'rosho yihyeh parua, tamei tamei yikra*. The image projected is: stay away. The garments are rent, the hair is wild—this is a person who is not fit for normal social participation. Similarly, *niddui* places a person in a castigated, quasi-ostracized role until his conduct comes back into alignment with communal expectations and rabbinic standards.

*Aveilus*, too, has an element of withdrawal from society—the *avel* sits *shiva*, removed from the normal flow and rhythms of the world, focused on grief and *nechama*. But *aveilus* has something beyond that: it is an expression of profound sadness and mourning, something that does not apply to *metzora* or *menudeh* at all.

With this in mind, the reason the *regel* overrides *aveilus* but not these other two categories becomes clear. The *regel* and *aveilus* are direct antitheses: the *regel* is *simcha*, and *aveilus* is sadness. There is a head-on collision. But the practices of *metzora* and *menudeh*, while they may make it harder for a person to participate fully in *Simchas HaRegel*, are not expressions of sadness. They are expressions of ostracism. The *regel*'s mandate of *simcha* operates on a different plane from a declaration of social ostracization. Therefore, the *regel*'s power to override is diminished in their case—it addresses the emotional state directly, and these practices are not about an emotional state.

## Metzora & Regel

### Question Posed

Having addressed the *menudeh*, the *gemara* turns to the *metzora*. The question posed is: *metzora mahu sheyanhig tzoraso baregel*—does a *metzora* observe his *tzaraas* practices during the *regel*? This is a striking *hava amina*. One would think it explicit in the *pesukim* that this is what a *metzora* does, and to imagine that the *regel* might suspend these obligations is genuinely startling.

### Abaye's Proof

*Abaye* offers a proof: *ta shma*—who is permitted to get a haircut and launder clothes on *Chol HaMoed*? A *nazir* and a *metzora* who are *mitumasan letaharasan*, becoming *tahor*. From the fact that the permission is granted specifically at the point of becoming *tahor*, one can infer—*ha b'imei tumaso lo*—that during his days of *tumah*, a *metzora* may not do these things, even during the *regel*.

### Postponement Risk

The *gemara* deflects this proof. One might say *lo tzricha*: it goes without saying that during his full *tumah* he would not do these things on the *regel*, for the *regel* overrides. The *mishna*'s novelty lies in the case where he is in the process of becoming *tahor*. There, you might think: all the more so, he should be permitted—he is becoming *tahor* and it is the *regel*. But the *gemara* raises a concern: *nigzar shema yishahei korbanosav*—perhaps, paradoxically, if we allow a *metzora* undergoing *tahara* to perform his *tahara* practices during the *regel*, we create an incentive for him to delay. A person who becomes *tahor* a week or a month before *Succos* might decide not to trouble himself making the pilgrimage to *Yerushalayim* in advance, but to simply wait until *Succos* and complete the *tahara* process then. To prevent this temptation, one might have thought to forbid the *metzora* from performing his *tahara* practices during the *regel*—thereby forcing him to complete the process before the *regel* arrives. The *mishna* teaches us *ka mashma lan* that we do not in fact impose this restriction, and he is permitted to complete his *tahara* on the *regel*.

### Rava's Counter

*Rava* offers a different proof. The Torah writes *ha-tzarua asher bo ha-naga*—the word *ha-tzarua* is seemingly superfluous, as *asher bo ha-naga* would have sufficed. The extra word serves *lerabot Kohen Gadol*—to teach that even a *Kohen Gadol* must observe the practices of a *metzora*. And the *gemara* makes a remarkable observation: *de-Kohen Gadol de-khol ha-shanah ke-regel le-khol alma dami*—a *Kohen Gadol*, on any day of the year, is like a normal person on the *regel*. This is derived from the *mishna* that states *Kohen Gadol makriv onen ve-eino okhel*—a *Kohen Gadol* may bring *korbanos* even while he is an *onen*, though he may not eat them. The only logic for this is that his status as *Kohen Gadol* overrides his status as *onen*. And where else do we find that something overrides *onen* or *aveilus* status for a normal person? Only on the *regel*. Therefore, a *Kohen Gadol* is perpetually in a *regel*-like state. And yet, even he observes the practices of a *metzora*. *Shma mina*—this is good evidence that a *metzora* continues his practices even during the *regel*.

This principle—that the *Kohen Gadol* is always in a kind of *regel* state—reflects a broader idea: the *regel* is fundamentally about going up to the *Beis HaMikdash*, about being in the presence of God. The *simcha* of the *regel* is rooted in this connection, as the *gemara* elsewhere notes that *ein simcha ela be-vasar shelamim*—the joy of the *regel* is bound up with the *korbanos* and the sense of nearness to the Divine.
