# Moed Katan 16b

## Nidui/Nezifa Durations

### Nidui: 30 Days

The Gemara opens with a *baraita*: *ein nidui pachot mi-shloshim yom* — *nidui* carries a minimum duration of thirty days. As we have discussed previously, while it is theoretically possible to reverse a *nidui* earlier, the standard *nidui* runs for thirty days.

### Nezifa: 7 Days Min.

*Nezifa* is a lighter form of censure than *nidui*. The Gemara never fully explains what the practical observances of *nezifa* consist of — the only thing we can discern from the sugya is that it is of shorter duration, and perhaps that it involves the same practices but for a briefer period. The *baraita* establishes: *ein nezifa pachot mi-shiva yamim* — there is no *nezifa* of less than seven days. The Gemara adds that while there is no formal proof for this, there is a *zecher la-davar*, a hint: *ve-aviha yarok yarak be-faneha halo tikkalem shivat yamim* — if her father had spat in her face, would she not be in a state of abeyance for seven days? This is actually a compelling indication, since God says to Moses that there must be some minimum period appropriate to the state of being censured, and that minimum is seven days.

### Bavel vs. Eretz Yisrael

Rav Chisda states: *nidui she-lanu ke-nezifa she-lahen* — our *nidui* in Bavel is equivalent to their *nezifa* in Eretz Yisrael, which presumably means that the standard *nidui* in Bavel was of shorter duration than in Eretz Yisrael. This is a striking observation. Why would that be? Perhaps the rabbinic authorities in Bavel had adopted a less severe approach, or perhaps they exercised a somewhat different degree of institutional authority — one less insulated from the surrounding secular society and its norms.

### Ashkenazi vs. Sephardi

This difference between Bavel and Eretz Yisrael invites a historical parallel to the later distinction between *Ashkenazi* and *Sephardi* communities. *Ashkenazi* communities were by and large more cloistered, and as a result rabbinic authority tended to be stronger within them. *Sephardi* communities were more cosmopolitan, more integrated into the broader surrounding society, and correspondingly the exercise of rabbinic authority may have been somewhat attenuated. Interestingly, *Ashkenazi* culture traces more directly from Eretz Yisrael, while *Sephardi* culture draws more from Bavel — which makes the parallel all the more suggestive when thinking about why the forms of censure were less severe in Bavel than in Eretz Yisrael.

---

## Self-Imposed Nezifa

### Difficult Sugya

The Gemara now challenges the notion that *nezifa* in Eretz Yisrael is only seven days. It relates that Rav Shimon, the son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and Bar Kappara were sitting together and studying, when they encountered a *shemat'ta* — a passage — that was extremely difficult for them. Rav Shimon said to Bar Kappara: *davar zeh tzarich Rabbi* — this matter requires Rabbi, meaning his father. The implication was: this *sugya* is so hard that only Rabbi could resolve it. Bar Kappara responded: *u-mah Rabbi omer be-davar zeh* — what could Rabbi possibly say about this? Rabbeinu Gershom reads Bar Kappara's words as: there is no rabbi in the world who could understand this, the *sugya* is simply too difficult.

### Bar Kappara's Nezifa

Rav Shimon went and relayed this exchange to his father. Rabbeinu Gershom notes that this was not an act of telling tales — he was simply sharing with his father what had transpired. Nevertheless, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was offended. When Bar Kappara subsequently came to appear before Rabbi — perhaps to visit him during an illness, as Rabbeinu Gershom suggests — Rabbi said to him: *eini makircha*, I do not recognize you, I have never known who you are. He refused to acknowledge him in any way.

Bar Kappara understood from this that Rabbi was holding something against him. And so *nahag nezifuta b'nafshei tlatin yomin* — he imposed upon himself a state of *nezifuta* for thirty days. Two things are worth noting here. First, the practice of imposing this state upon oneself: we will see shortly that this applies not only to *nezifa* but also to *nidui* — one can place oneself into that status. Second, the duration of thirty days raises a question: if *nezifa* and *nidui* differ only in length, and *nidui* is also thirty days, then there must be a qualitative difference between them in terms of the actual practices involved, even if the Gemara never spells out what those practices are. Just as *nidui* and *cherem* differ in the intensity of their observances rather than merely in duration, presumably *nezifa* represents a lesser degree of restriction than *nidui* — we simply do not know precisely what that set of practices entails.

### Torah in Marketplace

Subsequently, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi issued a *gezeira* — a decree — that students should not study Torah in the marketplace. This was not simply a matter of the *shuk* being noisy or malodorous; there was also a principled basis for the decree. The Gemara asks: *mai darish* — what verse did Rabbi expound to support this? He derived it from the verse in Shir HaShirim, *chamukei yerachayich* — the hidden curves of the thigh. Just as the thigh is kept private and unseen, *af divrei Torah b'seter* — so too words of Torah must be kept in private. There is an aspect of elitism here, a sense that Torah is something to be kept away from those who do not appreciate it, and there is also a dimension of intimacy: the deeply personal and even relational metaphors used throughout Shir HaShirim for the relationship between the learner and the Torah suggest that Torah study is something whose very nature calls for privacy.

### Rabbi Chiya's Nezifa

Despite this decree, Rabbi Chiyya went out and gave a *shiur* to his two nephews — Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chana — in the marketplace. Rabbi heard of this and was offended. When Rabbi Chiyya came to appear before him, Rabbi said: *Iyya* — mocking his name by dropping the *chet* — *mi kore l'cha bachutz*, I believe someone is calling you outside. This was Rabbi's way of indicating that he refused to recognize Rabbi Chiyya, though the form was slightly more nuanced than his treatment of Bar Kappara — he did not say outright "I do not know you." One might also note the pointed irony: the reprimand itself contained the word *bachutz*, outside, given that the offense was teaching Torah *bachutz*.

Rabbi Chiyya understood that Rabbi was angry with him, and so *nahag nezifuta b'nafshei tlatin yomin* — he too imposed upon himself this state of *nezifuta* for thirty days.

### Measuring Nezifa Days

On day thirty, Rabbi sent for Rabbi Chiyya and called him to come. Then Rabbi sent a second messenger telling him not to come. The Gemara asks: *me'ikara mai savar u'l'vasof mai savar* — what did Rabbi think initially, and why did he reverse himself? Initially he held *miktzat hayom k'kulo* — that part of the day counts as the whole, and since it was already day thirty, even the beginning of that day was sufficient to conclude the *nezifuta*. In the end, he decided not to apply that principle to *nezifuta*, and so he sent the second message. This is an interesting parallel to the laws of *aveilus*, where the same question of *miktzat hayom k'kulo* arises regarding the seventh and thirtieth days of mourning.

### Reconciliation

Rabbi Chiyya received the first message but not the second, and so he came. Rabbi asked him: *amai atit* — why did you come? Rabbi Chiyya answered: because you called me. Rabbi replied that he had subsequently sent word not to come. Rabbi Chiyya responded: *da chaziti v'da lo chaziti* — I received the first message, I did not receive the second.

Rabbi then recited the verse about him: *birtzot Hashem darchai ish, gam oyvav yashlim lo* — when God desires the ways of a man, even his enemies will make peace with him. Here there was a measure of *hashgacha pratit*: the second message did not reach Rabbi Chiyya, and so reconciliation came today rather than tomorrow, through divine providence rather than formal process.

Rabbi then said: now that thirty days have passed and you have appropriately demonstrated that you acted improperly, let us discuss it — *mai ta'ama amart lah hachi*, why did you violate my ruling? Rabbi Chiyya cited the verse *chachmot bachutz taronah* — wisdom should sing out in the open, Torah should be public. We should not be keeping it secluded.

Rabbi replied: *im karita lo shanita* — if you read the verse, you did not study it sufficiently. *Ve'im shanita lo shilashta* — and if you studied it twice, you did not do it a third time. *Ve'im shilashta lo pirshu lach* — and if you did it three times, it was not properly explained to you. How should the verse be understood? Like Rava, who — anachronistically — explained: *kol ha'osek ba-Torah mibifnim Torato machrezet alav mibachutz*. It does not mean that you go out and proclaim your Torah in the street. It means that if you study Torah in private, as Rabbi had decreed, your wisdom will nevertheless announce itself outward. The internal devotion radiates outward — you do not bring the Torah outside, rather it emerges on its own.

The Gemara then raises a challenge: does the verse not say *lo me-rosh be-seter dibarti* — I did not speak initially in secret? This would seem to imply that Torah is not supposed to be kept private. The answer is: *ahu be-yomei de-kalla* — that refers to the days of the *kalla*, when everyone gathers before the *yamim tovim* for a large public *shiur*. There are specific occasions for public teaching, but that does not mean one is always to be teaching Torah in public settings.

---

## Torah Accessibility

### Chochmot in Marketplace

Now the Gemara circles back to the substantive dispute. Rabbi Chiyya's position, grounded in *chachmot bachutz taronah*, was that Torah wisdom should be broadcast widely and publicly. Rabbi's counter, ultimately vindicated by Rava's reading of the same verse, was that the outward proclamation of Torah is a result of inward private study — not a mandate for public teaching in the marketplace.

### Translation Debates

This tension between accessibility and protection of Torah study is not merely an ancient dispute. One might think today it goes without saying that Torah should be accessible to all — the proliferation of *Artscroll* translations and similar works has made the *Gemara* and other texts available to a wide public, and we largely take this for granted. But debates over translating the Talmud were alive and serious as recently as a century ago. The concern was genuine: a little knowledge is a dangerous thing. People insufficiently trained in the tradition might misunderstand complex material, draw incorrect conclusions, or misuse the texts. There was therefore a real school of thought holding that deep Torah learning — *Gemara* study in particular — should remain restricted to those with the background and training to engage it properly.

It is worth noting that the Jewish approach here was always fundamentally different from the Church's approach to Scripture. *Chazal* established institutions of *Kriyat HaTorah* so that every Jew would hear the Torah publicly. The *Targum* — the Aramaic translation — was a regular and integral part of *Kriyat HaTorah*, which is the very opposite of the Church's policy of restricting access to sacred texts. Interestingly, it appears that it was specifically at the level of *Gemara* study that access was more carefully guarded, while access to *Mikra* and its understanding was actively promoted. The debate here in the *sugya*, notably, turns on the interpretation of *pesukim* — and Rabbi's critique of Rabbi Chiyya is precisely that he had not understood a *pasuk* properly.

### Rabbi Chiya's Legacy

The irony is particularly striking when one considers who Rabbi Chiyya was. The famous *Gemara* about *gedolei ma'asei Chiyya* describes how Rabbi Chiyya traveled to villages, wrote *Sifrei Torah*, and organized the teaching of Torah to broad communities — essentially constructing a public school system for Torah study. He was the one who worked tirelessly to ensure that Torah knowledge would be widespread, and the *Tosefta* he compiled was itself a monumental act of organizing and transmitting oral tradition. It is the same Rabbi Chiyya who is standing in the marketplace teaching his nephews, and it is the same Rabbi Chiyya who composed the *Tosefta* — a work that some have noted represents a measure of independent rabbinic authority alongside Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's *Mishnah*, which introduces its own set of complicated questions about their relationship.

The issue of whether *garsei* in the *sugya* implies an oral or written text is also relevant here: *ligros* is related to the grinding of wheat, and *garsa* in the sense of a written text is a later usage. In the context of the story of Rav Shimon and Bar Kappara, they were engaged in oral analysis of a difficult *sugya* — there was no written text before them, only what they carried in memory.

### Tzedakah vs. Torah

The Gemara then addresses what Rabbi Chiyya does with the verse *chamukei yerachayich* — the one about the hidden thigh that Rabbi had expounded. Rabbi Chiyya's response is: *muki leh bi-tzedakah u-gemilut chasadim* — he applies that verse to acts of *tzedakah* and *gemilut chasadim*, which indeed should be kept private, both out of respect for the recipient and to avoid any self-congratulatory display of one's own generosity. But Torah, Rabbi Chiyya maintains, is something that should be spread and made public.

At this point the Gemara raises the question: does this not demonstrate that their *nezifa* in Eretz Yisrael was thirty days — *nezifa d'nasi shani* — the *nezifa* arising from the censure of a *nasi* carries different weight. It was not Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi himself who placed them in *nezifa*; they imposed the practice on themselves. But in effect, they had been censured — one might say they had been "spat in the face," to use the Gemara's earlier metaphor — by Rabbi, and they responded by adopting the *nezifa* practices accordingly.

One might speculate about what *nezifa* actually consists of in practice. In every one of these stories, the *nezifa* involves not appearing before the person one has offended. In the case of Miriam, she is *michutz la-machaneh*, outside the camp. Perhaps *nezifa* simply means refraining from appearing before the person who has censured you for the duration of the period. The Gemara never specifies anything further, and this may in fact be the entirety of the practice.

The Gemara then works out the proportional logic: their *nezifa* in Eretz Yisrael is seven days; our *nidui* in Bavel equals their *nezifa*, so our *nidui* is seven days; and our *nezifa* — *kama havei* — would then be only *chad yoma*, one day. Everything in Bavel is of shorter duration and lesser severity than in Eretz Yisrael.

This is illustrated by the story of Shmuel and Mar Ukva. They would sit together, with Mar Ukva positioned *be-richuk arba amos* — four *amos* — from Shmuel, as a demonstration of deference to Shmuel's greater Torah authority. When they sat in *din*, the relationship reversed: Shmuel sat *be-richuk arba amos* from Mar Ukva, because Mar Ukva — who was the *Reish Galusa*, or at least held some equivalent political role — was the greater judicial authority. Each of them was always four *amos* from the other, but the question of who sat "before" the other determined who was playing the secondary role.

Every day Mar Ukva would accompany Shmuel to his lodgings. One day, absorbed in a complex court case, Mar Ukva forgot his usual custom and went home by himself, whereupon Shmuel followed him. When they arrived at Mar Ukva's door, Shmuel said: *lo naga lei le-mar le-mishrei li be-tigra* — is it not enough that I have followed you this far? Can I not be excused to go home? Mar Ukva, preoccupied with his own thoughts, had not even noticed that Shmuel had been following him and was still standing outside waiting to be dismissed. When Mar Ukva realized what had happened, he understood that Shmuel was displeased with him. And so *nahag nezifuta b'nafshei chad yoma* — he imposed upon himself this state of *nezifuta* for one day. This confirms that *nezifuta* in Bavel is one day.

The story of the woman sifting barley on the path adds another dimension to how *nezifa* operates. A *tzurba me-rabbanan* passed by; she was sitting with her legs stretched out and did not show him deference. He said publicly: *kama chatzipa hi iteta* — how brazen is this woman. She came before Rav Nachman and complained that he had publicly shamed her. Rav Nachman asked her: *mi shamas shamta mi-pumei* — did he actually utter a formal declaration of *nidui*? She said no. He told her: *zili nehog nezifuta chad yoma be-nafshach* — go and practice *nezifuta* on yourself for one day.

What is striking across all of these cases is that in none of them does the rabbi formally issue a *nezifa*. Rather, the *nezifuta* is always self-imposed: the person perceives from the rabbi's reaction — a refusal to recognize him, a mocking comment, an expression of displeasure — that he has given offense and has been censured, and then adopts the practice on his own. The rabbi never formally declares it. Perhaps this is the essence of *nezifuta*: it is your own internalized recognition that you have offended a Torah authority and your consequent response to that recognition. What the practice concretely involves remains unstated in the Gemara, but in every instance it seems to amount to refraining from appearing before the person one has offended.

---

## Zutra bar Tuvia

### Pesach Exegesis

Zutra bar Tuvia was teaching the *parshiyot* — going through *pesukim* — before Rav Yehuda. When he arrived at the verse *ve-eileh divrei David ha-achronim* — these are the last words of David — he asked: *achronim mikhlal d'ika rishonim, rishonim mai ninhu* — the fact that it says "last" implies there are earlier words; where are those earlier words? As Rabbeinu Gershom notes, *divrei* in this context means *nevuah*, prophecy — there is only one other place where the phrase *divrei David* appears with that specific meaning. So the question was: where in Scripture does an earlier *divrei David* appear?

Rav Yehuda was silent and did not respond. Zutra bar Tuvia asked again. This time Rav Yehuda replied: *ma da'atach d'lo yada perusha d'hai kra* — do you think I do not know the meaning of this verse? *Lav gavra raba hu* — am I not a great authority? He spoke in the third person, which itself underscores the emphasis he was placing on the *kavod* owed to him. Notably, the very fact that Rav Yehuda refused to answer twice — and then, when pressed, made clear it was not ignorance but a statement about the respect owed to him — reveals the depth of his offense.

### Zutra's Nezifa

Zutra bar Tuvia understood from this that Rav Yehuda was angry with him, and *nahag nezifuta b'nafshei chad yoma* — he imposed upon himself a state of *nezifuta* for one day. This is another case of Babylonian *nezifuta* lasting a single day.

What is remarkable about all these stories taken together is the picture they paint: the *amoraim* were acutely attuned to the signals a rabbi gave when he was displeased, and the expected response was to independently adopt this practice without waiting for a formal declaration. In a sense, as one might observe, this actually inverts the dynamic of coercive rabbinic authority — rather than power being imposed from above, the recognition of wrongdoing and the consequent response comes from within the offending party himself. And if one can get people to genuinely internalize that sensitivity and deference, that is far more powerful than any formal mechanism of *kefiyah*.

The Gemara then returns to the substantive question that Zutra had raised: *ve-da-atina l'ha* — now that we have arrived at this topic, what does the verse actually mean? Where do the *rishonim* appear? The answer is that the verse *va-yedaber David la-Hashem et divrei ha-shirah ha-zot* uses *divrei ha-shirah*, words of the song — not specifically *divrei David*. And God said to David: *shirah atah omer al mapalaso shel Shaul* — you are singing a song over the fall of Shaul? *Ilmaleh atah Shaul ve-hu David, ibadti kamah Davidim mipanav* — had you been Shaul and he had been David, I would have destroyed many Davids for his sake. As Rabbeinu Gershom explains: do not think yourself so superior. Shaul was actually more righteous; it is simply that circumstances and *mazal* brought things to where they did. And this is what is meant by *shigayon l'David asher shar la-Shem al divrei Kush ben Yemini* — the word *shigayon* is read as *shigagah*, an error, and *Kush ben Yemini* refers to Shaul the *Binyamini*: *mah Kushi meshuneh b'oro, af Shaul meshuneh b'maasav* — just as a Kushite is exceptional in his skin, so Shaul was exceptional in his deeds.

The Gemara then draws the same *kush* analogy to Moshe's wife Tziporah — *al odot ha-ishah ha-Kushit asher lakach* — she is called *Kushis* not because that was her name (her name was Tziporah) but because she was exceptional in her deeds. The same applies to Eved Melech ha-Kushi in Yirmiyahu, who likewise was not named Kushi but is called so because he was exceptional, and whose name was Tzidkiyahu. And the verse in Amos — *halo kivnei Kushiyim atem li, bnei Yisrael* — Israel is compared to *bnei Kushiyim* not because that is their name but because they are exceptional among all the nations, which depending on context can be either a compliment or a rebuke.

---

## King David Narrative

### David's Humility

Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonasan: what is meant by *neum David ben Yishai u-neum ha-gever hukam al* — the utterance of David son of Yishai, the utterance of the man raised up high? *Neum David ben Yishai she-hekim ol ha-teshuvah* — that David raised up, established, the yoke of *teshuvah*. Through the entire episode involving Bat Sheva, he demonstrated to the world the process of *teshuvah*. Rabbeinu Gershom cites the *Gemara* in Avodah Zarah: *lo David rauy l'oto ma'aseh* — David was not really at the level at which he should have sinned in that way, but it came about so as to serve as a lesson for all others. This is an interesting parallel to the story of Shaul: just as what happened to Shaul does not necessarily reflect his righteousness or lack thereof, so too what happened to David does not necessarily reflect his.

The verse then says: *amar Elohei Yisrael li diber tzur Yisrael moshel ba-adam tzaddik, moshel yiras Elokim*. The Gemara asks: *mai ka'amar* — what does this verse mean? Rabbi Abbahu explains: *ani moshel ba-adam* — I rule over humanity. *Mi moshel bi* — but who rules over Me? *Tzaddik* — the righteous person. *She-ani gozer gezeirah u-mevattelah* — I issue a divine decree, and the *tzaddik* cancels it. This goes even further than the familiar formula of *tzaddik gozer ve-haKadosh Baruch Hu mekayem* — here it is God who issues the decree and the *tzaddik* who overrides it.

The Gemara then expounds the verse *eileh shemot ha-giborim asher le-David, yoshev ba-shevet*. Rav Elazar, citing Rabbi Abbahu, explains: these are the mighty deeds of David, *yoshev ba-shevet* — sitting in the *yeshivah*. Specifically: *b'sha'ah she-hayah yoshev ba-yeshivah, lo yoshev al gabei karim u-khistot* — when David sat in the *yeshivah*, he did not sit on cushions and pillows, but rather *al gabei karka* — directly on the ground.

Moreover, as long as his teacher Ira haYa'iri was alive, Ira haYa'iri would teach the *rabbanan* while seated on cushions — a mark of his status and authority. David, the student, sat on the ground.

### David as Rosh Yeshiva

*Ki nach nafsheih Ira haYa'iri* — when Ira haYa'iri died, David became the one to teach the *rabbanan*. He became, in effect, the *Rosh Yeshivah*. This is a fascinating projection, for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is understood to be a descendant of David, and here we see the combination of political leadership and Torah leadership being projected back onto David himself. The rabbis then urged David: *leitiv mar al karim u-khistot* — Master, sit on the cushions. *Lo kibeil aleih* — he would not accept it.

### Tzaddik Gozer

The Gemara then reads the word *tachkemoni* — which should mean "he will make me wise" — as *tehei cha-moni*, you shall be like Me. God said to David: *ho'il ve-hishpalta atzmecha, tehei cha-moni* — since you have lowered yourself, you shall be like Me. The *mida ke-neged mida*: David lowered himself from his high position, and as a result he received the power to be comparable to God — *she-ani gozer gezeirah ve-atah mevatlah* — that if I were to issue a decree, you have the power to negate it.

The Gemara continues with *rosh ha-shalishim*: *tehei rosh le-shalshelet avot* — you shall be head of the chain of the three *avot*, preceding them in *Olam HaBa*, as Rabbeinu Gershom explains.

The verse then continues with *hu Adino ha-Etzni*. *Ke-she-hayah yoshev ve-osek ba-Torah, hayah me-aden atzmo ka-tola'at* — when he sat and engaged in Torah study, he would make himself soft, gentle, lowly as a worm. *U-v'sha'ah she-yotzei la-milchamah, hayah maksheh atzmo ke-eitz* — but when he went out to war, he would make himself hard as wood. *Al shmoneh meiot chalal b'fa'am echat* — he would shoot one arrow and fell 800 enemies at once. And yet *hayah mit'ane'ach al matayim* — he would bemoan the 200 of his own men who fell. *Eichah yirdof echad elef* — one should chase a thousand, yet the prophecy was not completely fulfilled. A heavenly voice declared: *rak bi-dvar Uriyah ha-Chitti* — it is on account of the matter of Uriyah ha-Chitti that the full measure was not realized.

This digression about David is worth pausing over before moving on. What we have witnessed throughout this section is David's consistent refusal to stand on his own *kavod*: he sat on the floor in the *yeshivah*, he made himself soft as a worm in Torah study, he would not accept the cushions even when offered. And the divine response was: because you lowered yourself, you receive the power to override My decrees. This stands in a certain tension — or perhaps as a counter-voice — to the earlier discussions of rabbis who were quite protective of their *kavod* and their authority. One might observe that even the stories of *nezifa* represent a softening compared to the harsher *nidui*, and now here is David Melech Yisrael who is entirely *mochel* on his *kavod* and receives a greater reward in consequence. The parallel to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who was also *mochel* on his *kavod* in the stories we have seen, is difficult to miss. This whole section of the *daf* seems to be in conversation with itself, offering a counter-perspective to the exercises of rabbinic authority we have observed.

---

## Nidui Lichvodo

### Student's Authority

The Gemara now states: *talmid she-nidah li-chevodo niduyo nidui* — a student who placed someone in *nidui* on account of his personal honor, that *nidui* is valid. We had earlier encountered the concept of *menudah le-rav menudah le-talmid* — but here we are dealing with *nidui li-chevodo*, a *nidui* issued not because of a general religious offense but because of a personal affront to this particular person. Even a student — one who has not yet received full *semicha* and is not a fully ordained *rav* — has standing to place someone in *nidui* if that person has treated him disrespectfully.

### Universal vs. Personal

A *baraita* teaches: *menudah le-rav menudah le-talmid; menudah le-talmid eino menudah le-rav* — if the *rav* places someone in *nidui*, the *talmidim* observe it; but if the *talmid* places someone in *nidui*, the *rav* is not obligated to observe it. The *rav* need not treat this person as if in *nidui* — that requirement applies to everyone else, *le-chulei alma*, but not to the *rav* himself.

The Gemara then asks: for what type of offense did the *talmid* issue this *nidui*? If it was for *millei di-shmaya* — matters of heaven, meaning this person was acting in a generally contemptuous and dismissive way toward rabbinic authority or Torah — then the principle of *ein chochmah ve-ein tevunah ve-ein eitza le-neged Hashem* applies: there is no status or wisdom that counts against God's concerns, and everyone — even a *talmid* — has standing to issue such a *nidui*, and everyone must observe it. *Ela lav li-chevod atzmo* — rather, the case must be where this was not a broader religious offense but a particular personal offense to this individual. The person generally respects rabbis; he just does not respect this one person. That produces a *nidui* of a much more limited and subjective character, which is why the *rav* need not observe it — it is not a universal decree.

### Ruling for Oneself

Rav Yosef states: *tzurba me-rabbanan avid dina le-nafshei be-milei di-psika lei* — a member of the academy may make a ruling for himself in a matter that is clear-cut and unambiguous to him. This statement requires careful handling, because the phrase *avid dina le-nafshei* is well known from Bava Kamma in the context of taking the law into one's own hands — a practice that is in general strongly discouraged. The obvious danger is that a person might convince himself that the *halacha* is clear, that he is owed money, and simply take it.

The Rosh addresses precisely this concern, and his language is striking: *ve-kashe ha-davar le-fareish kein* — it is very difficult to explain this *Gemara* in that way. He gives two reasons. First: *im ha-din barur lo, eino barur le-acherim ve-chilul Hashem ha-davar* — even if the law is clear to you, it is not clear to others; people will simply see you taking something from someone else and assume impropriety. Second: *ein adam dan dino shel krovo, ve-chol she-ken shel atzmo* — a person may not judge the case of a relative, and certainly not his own case. No matter how well you know the *halacha*, you cannot be fully objective about the facts as they apply to yourself.

The Rosh therefore reads this statement of Rav Yosef very narrowly, in the specific context of what we have been discussing: *nidui li-chevodo*. A *tzurba me-rabbanan* may act on his own behalf in placing someone who has personally offended him in *nidui*, when the matter is clear-cut. Reading it as a broad license for self-help in monetary disputes, the Rosh says, is extremely disturbing and difficult to sustain.

---

## Bad Reputation Case

### Need vs. Accountability

The Gemara now presents a difficult case. There was a *tzurba me-rabbanan* — a member of the rabbinic academy — who had a bad reputation, *de-havu sanu shumanei*. Rav Yehuda asked: *heichi di-na'avid* — what should we do here? Should we place him in *nidui*? On one hand: *tzrichi lei rabbanan* — the other rabbis need him. He apparently served as a teacher or in some role of communal influence, and this created reluctance to act — as is so often the case when a figure with communal impact is acting improperly. On the other hand: *lo neshamtei, ka mitchal shma di-shmaya* — if we do nothing, there is a *chilul Hashem*, since this person is acting improperly with impunity and nothing is done about it. This tension — between the communal good a person does and the *chilul shem shamayim* resulting from inaction — is one that has never ceased to confront rabbinic leadership.

### Rabbinic Character

Rami bar Abba conveyed in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *ki siftei kohen yishmeru da'at, ve-Torah yivakshu mi-pihu, ki malach Hashem tzeva'ot hu* — the lips of the *kohen* shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek Torah instruction from his mouth, for he is the angel of God. *Im domeh ha-rav le-malach Hashem, yivakshu Torah mi-pihu; ve-im lav, al yivakshu Torah mi-pihu* — if the rabbi is like an angel of God, one should seek Torah from him; and if not, one should not. This is not a minor qualification: it is a direct statement that a rabbi's character is not separable from his Torah. You cannot bracket his problematic conduct and focus only on the quality of his *shiurim* or sermons. A rabbi must embody what he teaches; otherwise, one should not be seeking Torah instruction from him at all. And if that is the standard, then certainly the improper conduct cannot be allowed to stand unchallenged.

### Rav Yehuda Acts

Rav Yehuda placed him in *nidui* — *shamtei Rav Yehuda*. Subsequently Rav Yehuda fell ill, and the *rabbanan* — the rabbinic students — came to pay a *bikur cholim* call. The rabbi who had been placed in *nidui* came among the group. When Rav Yehuda saw him, he laughed. The rabbi in *nidui* said: *lo mistayecha de-shamtei le-hahu gavra* — is it not enough that you placed me in *nidui*, *ve-achuchuy nami mechayechat bi* — and now you laugh at me? Rav Yehuda replied: *lav bi-didach mechayechana* — I am not laughing at you. Rather: *deki azlina le-hahu alma, bidicha da'tai* — as I am going to that future world, I am in a joyful state of mind. Why? *De-afilu le-gavra ke-vasach, lo chanif lei* — even for a man of your stature and influence, I did not flatter him, I did not give inappropriate deference to your status when the situation demanded that I stand up and speak. That integrity is something that brings him great satisfaction as he approaches death.

### Maidservant Precedent

After Rav Yehuda died, the rabbi who had been in *nidui* came to the *Beis Medrash* and asked to be released: *sharu li*. The *rabbanan* replied: *gavra de-chashiv ke-Rav Yehuda leka hacha de-lishrei lach* — there is no one here of equivalent weight to Rav Yehuda who can release you. They sent him to Rav Yehuda Nesia, the grandson of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the *nasi*, with the authority to release him. Rav Yehuda Nesia instructed Rabbi Ami to look into the matter and, if appropriate, to release him.

Rabbi Ami considered the case and was inclined to release him. At that moment, Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani rose and said: *umah shifcha she-beis Rebbe* — and the *shifcha*, the maidservant, of Rabbi's household: *lo nahagu chachamim kal rosh be-niduyyah* — when she placed someone in *nidui*, the *Sages* did not treat that lightly. *Shelosh shanim* — for three years that *nidui* stood. *Yehuda chavreinu — al achat kama ve-chamma* — if even the maidservant of Rabbi's house, our colleague Yehuda's *nidui* should certainly not be dissolved hastily.

Rabbi Zeira then observed: *mai de-kama de-ata idna hai sava le-vei midrasha, de-lo ata le-vei midrasha ha kamma shani* — what is it that *davka* today this elder, Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani, appeared in the *Beis Medrash*, when he had not come to the *Beis Medrash* in many years? *Davka* today he appeared and lodged his protest at the very moment this question was being deliberated. *Shema mina lo miba'ei le-mishrei lei* — this is clearly a *siman min ha-shamayim* that it is not appropriate to release him. And so they did not release him.

### Death and Burial

He left the *Beis Medrash* weeping. *Ata zibura ve-tarkeih a-amateih* — a wasp came and stung him on his genitals, and he died. When they sought to bring him into the *maarat ha-chasidim* — the cave of the *chasidim* — the cave did not receive him. They brought him instead to the *maarat ha-dayanim* — the cave of the judges — and there he was accepted. He was a judge, but evidently not a *chasid*.

### Rabbi Ilai's Teaching

The Gemara asks: *mai ta'ama de-avid ke-Rabbi Ilai* — what is the reason he was accepted in the cave of judges? Because he acted like Rabbi Ilai. A *baraita* teaches: Rabbi Ilai says — *im ra'ah adam she-yitzro misgaber alav* — if a person sees that his *yetzer hara*, specifically in the context of sexual desire, is overpowering him and he will not be able to subdue it, *yeilech le-makom she-ein makirim oto* — let him go to a place where no one recognizes him, *ve-yilbash shechorim ve-yit'atef shechorim* — dress in black and wrap himself in black, so that he is unrecognized, and perhaps the humbling effect will cause him to reconsider. *Ve-ya'aseh mah she-libo chafetz* — and if he still must act, let him act according to his desire. *Ve-al yechalel shem shamayim be-farhesya* — but he should not create a public *chilul Hashem*.

*Tosfos* presents two versions of the *girsa* here. One version reads *de-avid ke-Rabbi Ilai* — he acted in accordance with Rabbi Ilai's teaching, meaning even though he sinned sexually, he did so in a way that was at least partially protective of *shem shamayim*, conducting himself in private, which is why he was accepted into the cave of judges despite his failings. The other version reads *de-avar al Rabbi Ilai* — he violated Rabbi Ilai's teaching, meaning he did not go to a foreign place and conduct himself in disguise but rather acted in a way that became publicly known — which is why he was not accepted into the cave of *chasidim*.

This raises a genuine tension. There is something troubling about a person of public rabbinic standing conducting himself improperly while hiding it, maintaining a public persona of respectability. On the other hand, there is a real argument to be made for the value of not doing so in public: it preserves the perception of Torah's honor, and perhaps more importantly, it sends a continuous signal to oneself that the act is a transgression. Rabbi Yisrael Salanter observed that if a person commits a sin once it becomes familiar; if twice it begins to feel permitted; if three times it begins to feel obligatory — *na'aseh lo ke-mitzva*. Doing something in hiding, with the self-consciousness that accompanies it, may maintain an awareness of wrongdoing that public rationalization would erode.

The question was in fact addressed by Rav Moshe Feinstein in the context of the era when attending a pornographic theater required physically entering a public venue. When asked whether someone who could not control his *yetzer hara* should remove his *yarmulke* before entering, Rav Moshe's response, as recalled, was no — because however problematic the *chilul Hashem* of being seen, the shame of the *yarmulke* might itself serve to deter him.

A final observation on this story: even though the rabbi had been placed in *nidui*, he joined the group of *rabbanan* coming to perform *bikur cholim* for Rav Yehuda. One would expect that a person in *nidui* — who may not be approached within *arba amos*, who is not to be included in a group — would be excluded from such a communal visit. His presence among them raises a question about the precise limits of how much separation is maintained in practice, and what the boundaries of *nidui* actually require in situations of this kind.

# Moed Katan 17

## Rebbi's Maidservant

### Maidservant Story

The Gemara has been occupied with various narratives concerning *niddui*, including the troubling and sadly perennial story of a rabbi with a reputation for impropriety, and whether and how to respond to such a situation. In that context, the Gemara had already alluded to a *niddui* imposed by Rebbi's maidservant, and now it circles back to ask: what exactly was that story?

The Gemara relates: *amsah d'vei Rebbi chazeisa l'hahu gavra d'hava machi livno hagadol* — the maidservant of Rebbi's household observed a certain man striking his adult son. Of course, corporal punishment was a regular feature of child-rearing in that era. But here the problem was that the child was no longer a child. She responded: *l'havei hahu gavra b'shamta* — that person should be in a state of *shamta* — because he is transgressing the prohibition of *lifnei iveir lo sitein michshol*, placing a stumbling block before the blind. A *baraita* supports this: the verse *v'lifnei iveir lo sitein michshol* applies in this context to one who strikes his adult son, because such a son is no longer in a position simply to absorb corporal punishment without consequence. He may rebel against it, strike back, or be further driven down a destructive path he may already be on.

### Lifnei Iveir

This ruling raises a fascinating question in the *poskim*: how literally is this *Gemara* to be taken? In normative halachic discourse, the prohibition of *lifnei iveir lo sitein michshol* is understood in quite narrow terms. A basic criterion, for example, is the principle the Gemara elsewhere calls *trei avrei d'nahara* — that the prohibition applies only where the other person could not have sinned without your assistance, as if you were on opposite banks of a river and only your active intervention places the forbidden object in their reach. In a case like the one here, the father is not handing anything to anyone; he is engaged in his own conduct which might, at some remove, place his son on a wrong path. The argument seems to favor viewing this not as a technical violation of the biblical prohibition of *lifnei iveir*, but rather as a violation of its spirit and underlying value — the concern about leading another person to stumble — without necessarily crossing the precise halachic threshold of the *aveira*. This question does receive treatment in the halachic literature, and it remains genuinely open whether the technical prohibition applies here.

What is in any case striking is the nature of the maidservant's intervention. We all know how little one appreciates being told by someone else how to parent one's children — and yet here she is, observing a stranger's conduct, concluding it will lead to disaster, and imposing a *niddui* upon him. And the Gemara affirms that this *niddui* was meaningful and binding.

### Authority for Niddui

This brings us to what is perhaps the most interesting dimension of the story: the question of who has the authority to impose *niddui*. Until this point in the sugya, we have seen *niddui* imposed by *chachamim* — rabbinic figures. That context even gave rise to the category of *menadeh likhvodo*, a kind of subjective *niddui* declared on account of personal affront rather than objective wrongdoing. Such a *niddui* does not bind universally; it reflects that individual's honor and, perhaps, extends to his students, but a person's own *rebbi* would not be bound by it. It is a *niddui* grounded in subjectivity.

Here, however, we encounter a qualitatively different category. Rebbi's maidservant — who holds no formal rabbinic title — observes a man doing something she regards as objectively harmful, and declares a *niddui*. This is the more general, objective form of *niddui*: not "my honor was offended" but "something objectively wrong is happening." And the remarkable finding is that such a *niddui* can be imposed by any person who witnesses such conduct. One might have assumed that even an objective *niddui* would require some form of rabbinic sanction or institutional authority. What the Gemara reveals is otherwise: anyone observing genuinely objectionable behavior can give voice to a *niddui*, and that declaration carries binding force for everyone.

This creates a striking and, in certain ways, unsettling picture of communal dynamics — a society in which any observer of misconduct can impose a state of ostracism. One might push back: is not any objectionable behavior grounds for *niddui* then? I don't like what you're doing, so *niddui*? The *Rambam*'s famous list of twenty-four grounds for *niddui*, compiled from various *Gemara* passages, offers some clarification. Much of what he enumerates involves conduct characterized by *bizayon* — contempt or disregard — for *halacha*, for halachic authority, or for the honor of rabbinic figures. A simple transgression, one that does not carry this quality of contempt, is generally not a basis for *niddui*.

One might also suggest that Rebbi's *shifcha* occupied a unique position. We have other traditions about her possessing considerable knowledge of rabbinic usage and obscure halachic terminology, and she was deeply embedded in Rebbi's household. Perhaps by virtue of her own wisdom, or by virtue of her situation, she possessed a kind of standing to impose *niddui* that a random bystander might not. That remains an open question.

The nature of the *niddui* also raises the question of enforcement. The obligations of *niddui* fall primarily upon the person placed in that status — they must observe certain practices that set them apart from ordinary social life. If a person has not changed their behavior after being placed in *niddui*, the escalation is to *cherem*, which carries far broader social consequences: no one conducts business with the person; the entire community participates in the exclusion. The *niddui* itself functions more like a form of probation or a warning — an opportunity for the person to demonstrate contrition and change before more severe measures are taken. And once behavior has genuinely changed, the *niddui* can be released before its formal period expires.

The mechanism of self-enforcement is admittedly puzzling. Why would someone placed in *niddui* willingly observe its practices if they are already disposed toward contempt? The answer implicit in the Gemara seems to be that most people, even those who have crossed a particular line, remain fundamentally invested in the community and its authority structures. They stepped over a boundary; they did not step out of the society. For such a person, the *niddui* and its practices provide a structured path back to good standing — a ritualized demonstration of contrition — and they will avail themselves of it. For those who are genuinely defiant, the answer is escalation to *cherem*.

## Reish Lakish & Fig-Eater

### Fig-Eater Niddui

The Gemara now turns to another story of *niddui*, this one involving competing declarations and the need for adjudication. Reish Lakish was watching over an orchard. A certain man came along and began eating figs from the trees. Reish Lakish called out to him to stop; the man ignored him entirely. Reish Lakish then declared: *l'havei hahu gavra b'shamta* — that man eating my figs should be in a state of *shamta*. Here again, as in the story of Rebbi's maidservant, the *niddui* is imposed not by a formal institutional process but by a person who witnesses conduct he regards as wrongful.

### Counter-Niddui

The man who had been eating the figs was not without a response. He turned to Reish Lakish and declared his own counter-*niddui*: *l'havei hahu gavra b'shamta* — you should be in *shamta*! His argument: *ei mamona nitchayavti lach, niddui mi nitchayavti lach* — just because I may owe you money, does that obligate me in *niddui*? The implication is that even if he acted wrongly, the appropriate remedy for such conduct is not *niddui*.

### Beit Medrash Ruling

The parties came before the *beit medrash* for a determination. The ruling: *shelo niddui, shelcha eino niddui* — the fig-eater's *niddui* against Reish Lakish is binding, while Reish Lakish's *niddui* against the fig-eater is not. Remarkably, the rabbi's *niddui* is illegitimate, and this thief's *niddui* stands.

Tosafot is deeply troubled by this result. If we grant that *niddui* can be imposed in connection with monetary wrongs — and indeed courts do impose *niddui* on someone who refuses to appear for a monetary dispute — what did Reish Lakish do wrong? Tosafot explains: *af al pi she'mshamtinan ba'avur mamon* — even though *niddui* can follow in monetary contexts — *it lomar dehaya lo likro oto l'veit din techila* — in such a case the proper course is to summon the person before a court first. To unilaterally impose *niddui* over a monetary claim — bypassing the court system entirely — is itself an offense. It is a form of *avid inish dina l'nafshei*, taking the law into one's own hands, and it undermines the very institutional authority that *niddui* is meant to protect. This explains the result: not every wrong justifies immediate *niddui*, and in a monetary case, the court must be given the opportunity to act first. The fig-eater, meanwhile, had a genuine grievance about having been wrongfully placed in *niddui*, and his declaration against Reish Lakish was legitimate.

Tosafot adds a further consideration: even where *niddui* would ultimately be appropriate, it is not imposed immediately upon detecting a violation — there is a process and a waiting period. And Rabbeinu Tam, cited in the final lines of Tosafot, suggests an additional *okimta*: perhaps in that locale it was customary for people to eat from trees in an orchard and pay the owner afterward, meaning no actual theft had occurred. On that reading, Reish Lakish had simply overreacted. But the more substantive answer — that bypassing the court is itself a wrong that warrants *niddui* — remains the more significant ruling.

### Release & Nasi

The *beit medrash* ruling leaves Reish Lakish himself in a state of *niddui*. How is he to extricate himself? *Zil legabeih delishrei lach* — go to the person who declared it and have him release you. As we saw, the *niddui* carries a personal dimension: the one who imposed it is in a sense a party, and it is that person — not some third-party authority — who has the standing to release the declarant. Reish Lakish responds that he does not know the man's identity; it was some stranger on the street. The Gemara's answer: *zil legabeih nasi delishrei lach* — go to the *nasi*, and he will release you from the *niddui*.

The Gemara cites a *baraita* in support: if someone was placed in *niddui* and does not know who placed it upon him — *niduho v'eino yodeia mi niduho* — he may go to the *nasi*, who will release him. The *nasi* serves here as a representative of broader rabbinic and political authority, a kind of default releasing agent when the original party is unavailable.

This is worth reflecting on. We have been operating within the framework of *menadeh likhvodo*, where the personal stake of the declaring party is central to both the imposition and release of *niddui*. The fig-eater's *niddui* against Reish Lakish was of this type — rooted in a personal grievance over the affront to his *kavod*. But the role of the *nasi* here suggests that even in such personal *niddui* cases, when the original party cannot be located, communal and institutional authority can step in. The *nasi* embodies both dimensions of authority — the rabbinic-scholarly and the political-communal — and the Gemara does not specify which dimension is being invoked here, which itself is suggestive.

## Leaders & Niddui

### Av Beit Din

The Gemara continues with a tradition transmitted in the name of Rav Huna: *be'Usha hitkinu, av beit din shesarach ein menadin oto* — they instituted at Usha that an *av beit din* who behaves badly is not placed in *niddui*. The *av beit din*, second in standing only to the *nasi*, is to be handled differently when he goes off the proper path. Rather than imposing *niddui*, one says to him: *hikaved v'shev b'veitecha* — respect your honor and sit quietly at home. The impulse is to handle the matter privately: approach him, have a confidential conversation, encourage him to step back from public life and correct his behavior without bringing the matter into the open. This approach has an obvious resonance with recurring situations in communal life, where rabbinic misconduct is addressed first through private channels rather than public censure, in the hope of resolving matters quietly. *Vechazor v'sarach, menadin oto mipnei chillul Hashem* — but if he repeats the misconduct, then he is placed in *niddui*, because at that point the greater danger is the *chillul Hashem* that results from appearing to condone such conduct from a figure of rabbinic authority.

### Private vs. Public

This two-stage approach is then contrasted with the view of Reish Lakish, who holds a more categorical position: *talmid chacham shesarach ein menadin oto befarhesya* — a *talmid chacham* who acts improperly is never publicly placed in *niddui*, not even at the second stage. The verse he invokes is *v'kashalta hayom v'kashal gam navi imcha layla* — if you stumble today, the prophet will stumble with you as well at night — and he interprets this to mean that a religious authority must be covered like the night, whatever one does. The concern is that public shaming of a Torah figure causes people to think worse of Torah itself, compounding the original harm. Whether this concern ultimately outweighs the alternative — the danger of complicity in a cover-up when the misconduct is likely to become known in any case — is precisely the tension that makes this passage so timelessly fraught.

### Mar Zutra Self-Shamta

The Gemara relates the practice of Mar Zutra Chasida: *ki michayav tzurba merabbanan shamta, bereisha mashmis nafshei v'hadar mashmis ledideh* — when a member of the rabbinic college became obligated in *shamta*, Mar Zutra would first put himself into *cherem* and then put the other person in. The analogy is apt: like a host who spills wine at the table so that his guest who has spilled feels less conspicuous, Mar Zutra's self-*shamta* served to remove the sense of disgrace from the imposition.

Tosafot addresses the underlying rationale. One explanation: *mashmis nafshei mishum tza'ar shetzarich lenadot talmid chacham* — he placed himself in *shamta* because of the anguish he felt at being required to impose *niddui* on a fellow rabbinic colleague. This is an illuminating observation, because it introduces the element of *tza'ar* — personal distress and suffering — into the *niddui* framework. We have previously considered the parallel between *niddui* and *avelus*, particularly the practices they share and whether those practices in the context of *niddui* are fundamentally acts of social exclusion or expressions of inner suffering. Tosafot here appears to do something of the reverse: he finds in *niddui* an element that could be understood as an expression of *tza'ar*, such that Mar Zutra's voluntary adoption of *niddui* practices was his way of giving form to how terrible he felt. What makes this especially striking is that Mar Zutra did not merely adopt the *practices* of *niddui* — he placed himself in the *state* of *niddui*, which has always carried with it an element of censure, not merely grief.

Tosafot's second explanation is more pragmatic: *inami sheyehei zachur lehatir* — he placed himself in the same status so that he would not forget to release the other person. If both were in *niddui* together, he would remember to take care of the matter when his own *niddui* needed resolving.

The story then confirms this reading. *Ki havei ayil b'ushpizeih, sharei lei l'nafshei, v'hadar sharei lei l'didei* — when Mar Zutra reached his inn that evening, he released himself from his *niddui*, and then he released the other person as well. The sequence was the mnemonic.

One might also suggest — and this connection was raised in discussion — that Mar Zutra's practice echoes the institution of the city of refuge and the responsibility of the *Kohen Gadol*: a leader bearing collective responsibility for what those within his sphere do. Mar Zutra may have been embracing a degree of personal accountability for the misconduct of his colleague, sharing in the consequence as a gesture of solidarity and shared responsibility.

### Corporal Punishment

Rav Pappa offers a related but distinct statement: *taysi li d'lo shemisi tzurba merabbanan me'olam* — he counts it as a virtue that he never had to place a member of the rabbinic college in *niddui*. When such a person's conduct did warrant *shamta*, what was his practice? *Ki ha d'ma'arava: minu angida d'tzurba merabbanan, v'lo minu ashamta* — as they do in the west, in Eretz Yisrael: they would convene a *beit din* to administer lashes, but not *shamta*. Corporal punishment, Rav Pappa maintains, is actually preferable to *shamta* for a *talmid chacham*.

This may seem counterintuitive, but there is a genuine logic to it. A state of societal censure lasting thirty days carries enormous social and spiritual weight — it is, as we will see shortly, understood to penetrate to a person's very core. A brief period of physical punishment, by contrast, is finite, localized, and over. It may in fact be far less injurious to a person's standing and dignity than a prolonged public state of exclusion. What appears on the surface to be more severe is, from this perspective, more respectful of the *talmid chacham's* honor.

## Metaphysics of Shamta

### Shamta Etymology

The Gemara now pauses to ask: *mai shamta* — what is the meaning of the word *shamta*? Two Amoraic opinions are offered. Rav says: *sham mita* — there is death there. Shmuel says: *shmama yiheyeh* — he will be in a state of desolation. These etymologies are not merely literary; they begin to gesture toward the metaphysical significance of *shamta* that the Gemara is about to develop more fully.

### 248 Limbs

A further statement deepens this picture: *umahani beih keticha betanura* — the state of *shamta* affixes itself to a person like the greasing of an oven, which locks in heat and flavor. The *shamta* does not simply surround a person from without — it enters in and stays.

This sets up the teaching of Reish Lakish, which stands in contrast: *keshem shenichneset b'matayim v'arba'im u'shmonah evarim, kach kshehi yotza, yotza mimatayim v'arba'im u'shmonah evarim* — just as *shamta* enters the two hundred and forty-eight limbs of the body, so too when it departs, it departs entirely from all two hundred and forty-eight limbs. The entry of *shamta* and its exit are total, bodily, and complete.

The Gemara supports this from the numerical value of *cherem* — the stricter form of ostracism — which in *gematria* equals two hundred and forty-eight, precisely the number of limbs that *Chazal* enumerate in the human body. *V'hayeta ha'ir cherem* — the city shall be under *cherem*; the word *cherem* itself encodes the full extent of the human person. And for the release from *cherem*, the Gemara invokes *berogez racheim tizkor* — in anger, remember compassion; the word *racheim*, which shares its letters with *cherem*, carries the same numerical value, indicating that the release is equally total. What went in entirely comes out entirely — the same penetrating force, now reversed. The identity of the letters of *cherem* and *racheim* seems to be more than a numerical coincidence; one wonders whether something deeper is being pointed to about the relationship between the decree and its reversal.

### Dog Story

The Gemara then turns to a story that illustrates *niddui*'s metaphysical power in striking fashion. Rav Yosef relates: *shadi shamta agunavta d'kalba, v'ihu d'idei avda* — he cast a *niddui* on the tail of a dog, and it acted on its own. The backstory: a dog had been chewing on the shoes of the rabbis — disrespecting rabbinic honor in the most basic way — and since the owner was unknown, they could not address the matter through normal channels. They placed the dog in *niddui*, and *itlibei nura d'gunavtei v'achaltei* — a fire caught hold of the dog's tail and consumed it.

One may well note the absence of any concern for *tzaar baalei chayim* in this account. But the Gemara's purpose here is unmistakable: *niddui* carries a real, operative metaphysical force, independent of social mechanism.

### Vessel & Shofar

The Gemara continues with the story of someone who came to Rav Yosef for help against a powerful man who was causing anguish to a member of the rabbinic college. Rav Yosef instructed him: *zil shamtei* — go and put him in *niddui*. The man replied: *mistafina minei* — I am afraid of him. If I impose *niddui* on this powerful figure, what will he do to me in retaliation? He has all the social power; the *niddui* will mean nothing to him and may invite real danger.

Rav Yosef then prescribed a procedure. *Shkilei pticha* — take a piece of parchment with the *niddui* written on it. *Achsei b'kada* — place it in an earthenware vessel. *Achsei b'kivrei* — deposit it in a cemetery. *V'karei bei alfa shipurei d'arba'im yomin* — and blow a thousand *shofar* blasts into it over forty days. This is clearly a ritualized, metaphysical procedure rather than a social declaration. *Avid hachi* — he did this. *Paka kada* — the vessel burst. *U'meis alma* — and the powerful man died.

### Person's Death

This story marks a transformation in how the power of *niddui* is being conceived. What began as a tool of social censure — a mechanism by which communal pressure is applied to bring a person back into alignment with halachic norms and communal expectations — has here become something altogether different. The shift is not incidental. As one participant in the shiur observed, and the point is well taken: both the dog story and this story feature scenarios in which the normal social machinery of *niddui* cannot function. You cannot persuade a dog; you cannot bring communal pressure to bear on a man who holds all the social power and before whom others will not dare to refuse business. When the societal impact of *niddui* is not available, the Gemara shifts its emphasis to the metaphysical dimension — a power that operates regardless of social dynamics. What appears on the surface to be a demonstration of *niddui*'s power is equally a testimony to its social impotence in certain contexts.

### Shofar & Evil Eye

The Gemara then asks: *mai shipuri* — what is the meaning of the *shofar* blasts? The answer given: they signify that *she-nifra'in mimenu* — punishment will ultimately be exacted from this person. And the word *tavra* — the broken blast — is interpreted to mean: *tavri batei ramei* — it will cause high houses to fall. Those who have erected themselves above the community will be brought low.

The Gemara then cites a *baraita* in the name of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: *kol makom she-natnu chachamim eineihem, o mita o oni* — wherever the rabbis turned their gaze against someone, the result was either death or poverty. This too is part of the same pattern. One might observe that *drashos* are made about the symbolism of words — *sham mita*, *shmama*, *shipuri*, *tavra* — precisely when the literal, social force of the institution is losing its teeth. When someone is simply thrown in jail, there is no need to expound on the symbolism of the word jail. The proliferation of hermeneutic significance here is, at least in part, a symptom of an institution straining to assert its authority in a world where its practical power is not always available.

We know from later history that *cherem* and *niddui* continued to serve as instruments of communal governance through the medieval period, yet the same limitations and the same evasions recurred. The passage we have been studying is unusually candid about the gap between the institution's intended force and its real-world reach.

## Nazir & Metzora

### Advance Notice Q

The *Mishnah* teaches that among those permitted to take a haircut on *Chol HaMoed* are the *nazir* who is becoming *tahor* and the *metzora* who is becoming *tahor*. Since their condition prevented them from taking the haircut earlier, they are permitted to do so on *Chol HaMoed*. The Gemara raises a question: is this permission limited to a case where they had no advance opportunity — for example, where they became *tahor* only once the *regel* had already begun — or does it apply even where they had an opportunity beforehand and simply did not act on it?

This question is the flip side of another the Gemara has already addressed: a person who had no formal category of exception but in practice had no opportunity to shave before the *regel* — the Gemara's answer there was that we require formal categories, and an informal inability to act does not by itself create a dispensation. Here, we have a person who does fall into a formal category of exception, but who arguably had the opportunity to act beforehand and was negligent. Should the exception still apply?

Rav Zeira answers Rav Yirmiya: we have already taught this — *kol elu she-amru mutarin legaleach ba-moed, beshelo haya lahem pnai* — all those said to be permitted to take a haircut on *Chol HaMoed*, the permission is premised on their not having had the opportunity beforehand. *Aval haya lahem pnai — asurin* — if they had a prior opportunity, they are forbidden. This is the general rule — as in the case of one released from prison: if he was released a day before *Yom Tov*, he should have taken care of it then.

### Korbanot Postponement

But the *nazir* and *metzora* are different. *Af al pi she-haya lahem pnai, mutarin* — even if they had a prior opportunity, they are permitted. Why? *Shelo yish'hu korbanoseihem* — so as not to delay their *korbanot*. The argument here operates in a direction opposite to the usual one. Ordinarily, a concern that motivates restricting activity on *Chol HaMoed* is that permitting it will cause people to defer taking care of matters beforehand, waiting until the *regel* when they will be going up to Yerushalayim anyway. Here, the Gemara reasons the other way: if we tell the *nazir* or *metzora* who did not shave beforehand that they may not shave on *Chol HaMoed*, we will create a further problem — the shaving is part of the process that precedes bringing the *korbanot*, and forbidding it will in turn delay the *korbanot* themselves.

Tosafot notes that technically the *korban* does not strictly require the shaving to precede it — it could theoretically be brought first. But in practice, the prescribed sequence is: first the shaving, then the *korban*, then the hair is gathered and burned beneath the *shelamim* cooking in the pot, as the Torah describes. Disrupting that sequence creates a real halachic and practical problem. The Gemara therefore concludes that for the *nazir* and *metzora*, even where there was a prior opportunity, we absorb the cost of creating some incentive to defer, in order to avoid delaying the *korbanot*.

One might object: is this not precisely the argument made in other contexts by the *avel* or by any person who failed to shave before the *regel* — that now they are disheveled during the *regel* itself and this is disrespectful of *kavod ha-regel*? And the answer offered there is that yes, that is the cost of maintaining the rule, the cost of ensuring the incentive to act beforehand remains in place. For the *nazir* and *metzora*, the Gemara is saying there is an additional cost beyond *kavod ha-regel*: the postponement of *korbanot*. And that additional cost tips the balance toward leniency even where there was a prior opportunity.

### Kohen & Avel

The Gemara then notes a *baraita* that lists two additional categories not mentioned in our *Mishnah* — the *kohen* and the *avel* — who are permitted to take a haircut when the time comes. The *avel* is easier to understand: we have seen throughout the sugya how a *regel* can terminate *shloshim*, thereby freeing the *avel* from the prohibition on shaving and laundering. The *kohen* refers, as the Gemara will clarify, to a *kohen* whose *mishmar* — his rotation of Temple service — extended up to or into the *regel*. During the *mishmar*, *kohanim* are not permitted to shave or launder (so that they take care of these matters before their rotation begins). Where this *mishmar* prevented them from attending to these matters before the *regel*, the *baraita* allows them to do so on *Chol HaMoed*.

### Avel Eighth Day

The Gemara asks: what exactly is the case of the *avel* in the *baraita*? It proceeds by elimination. One might think the case is simply that day eight fell on *Erev ha-Regel*, meaning *shloshim* began on *Erev ha-Regel*, and the *regel* then terminates *shloshim*, permitting the haircut. But the objection is immediate: if day eight was *Erev ha-Regel*, you should have taken care of the haircut then — it was already permitted. The halacha is that when the *regel* will be *mevatel shloshim*, the *avel* may already bathe, launder, and attend to grooming the day before the *regel*, *likhvod ha-regel*. So what prevented you?

The answer must be that day eight fell on *Shabbat Erev ha-Regel* — the *regel* began on Sunday, *shloshim* started on the preceding *Shabbat*, and one obviously cannot take a haircut on *Shabbat*. But then the Gemara raises a further challenge: why not take care of it on *Erev Shabbat*, day seven? And here the ruling of Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Ina bar Shila becomes relevant: the *halacha* follows Abba Shaul.

### Abba Shaul Dispute

Abba Shaul holds that day seven of *aveilus* counts simultaneously toward the end of *shiva* and the beginning of *shloshim* — the principle of *miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo* allows the morning of day seven to serve as the final portion of *shiva*, after which *shloshim* has technically begun. The *chachamim* dispute this, holding that you cannot claim double credit for a single day — *shiva* and *shloshim* cannot overlap on the same calendar day. Rav Chisda rules that the *halacha* follows Abba Shaul.

Moreover, the *chachamim* agree with Abba Shaul in at least one specific case: where day eight falls on *Shabbat Erev ha-Regel*. In that scenario, they concede that the person may take care of the haircut on *Erev Shabbat*, day seven. Why? Because day eight — which is *Shabbat* — is *Erev ha-Regel*, meaning the *regel* will begin on Sunday and will be *mevatel shloshim*. There is therefore a genuine and concrete reason to permit grooming on day seven: the *regel* is imminent and will terminate *shloshim*, the *avel* simply cannot act on the *Shabbat* that intervenes, and so the *chachamim* allow it on *Erev Shabbat* in light of the exceptional circumstances.

If, however, day seven was *Shabbat Erev ha-Regel*, the situation is more complex. On Abba Shaul's view, day seven is simultaneously the final day of *shiva* and the first of *shloshim*, and the *regel* beginning on Sunday would be *mevatel shloshim*. The *avel* could theoretically have shaved on day six. But no authority permits shaving during the *shiva* period itself — day six is unambiguously within *shiva* — and no one will allow it there. The only possible opportunity was on day seven, but that was *Shabbat*, and no haircut can be taken on *Shabbat*. This is the case where the *avel* truly had no opportunity beforehand, and it is for this case that the *baraita* permits the haircut on *Chol HaMoed*.

The *Mishnah*'s *tanna* does not include this case, because he does not hold by Abba Shaul's principle that day seven counts simultaneously for *shiva* and *shloshim*. Without *miktzat ha-yom ke-kulo*, day seven is purely a *shiva* day, *shloshim* has not yet begun when *Shabbat* arrives, and the *regel* therefore cannot be *mevatel shloshim*, since *shloshim* has not commenced. The *avel* accordingly remains in *shloshim* throughout the *regel* and cannot shave. Only the *baraita's* *tanna*, who follows Abba Shaul, provides the leniency.

### Kohen Mishmar

The Gemara then addresses the *kohen* case. If his *mishmar* ended on *Shabbat Erev ha-Regel*, the immediate objection is: take your haircut on Thursday or Friday. The *halacha* is that a *kohen* may not take a haircut during his *mishmar*, and this restriction extends even to Thursday of that week, *likhvod Shabbat*, so that he attends to these things before the rotation begins. So if the *mishmar* ended on *Shabbat* before the *regel*, he had Thursday and Friday available.

The Gemara's answer: the case is one where his *mishmar* ended during the *regel* itself — he was on rotation through *Chol HaMoed*, and was only free from service in the middle of the *regel*. He genuinely had no opportunity beforehand.

Our *Mishnah*'s *tanna* does not include this case, for the following reason. The *Mishnah* elsewhere teaches that during the three *regalim*, all the *mishmarot* had equal rights to serve in the *Beit HaMikdash* and equal portions in the communal *korbanot* and in the distribution of the *lechem ha-panim*. Since during the *regel* all the *mishmarot* participate equally, the *tanna* reasons that even after a *kohen's* specific rotation has technically ended, the *regel* itself is treated as an extension of his *mishmar* — *k'man delo shalim mishmarto ba-regel dami*, it is as though his *mishmar* has not yet ended. And since his *mishmar* has not ended, the prohibition on taking a haircut during one's *mishmar* continues to apply, and the rationale for the *Chol HaMoed* exception — that he had no earlier opportunity — is undermined, because the exception would be trumped by the ongoing *mishmar* restriction.

The *baraita*'s *tanna* disagrees: *af al gav d'shayaich b'hanech mishmaros* — even though he shares in the communal service of the *regel* — *mishmartei mi-ashlima* — his specific rotation has concluded. He is no longer under the obligation specific to his *mishmar*, and since he had no opportunity to shave before the *regel* began, he may do so on *Chol HaMoed*.

## Multiple Aveilus

### Haircuts During Aveilus

The Gemara continues: *kol elu she-amru mutarin legaleach ba-moed, mutarin legaleach bimei evlam* — all those granted a dispensation to take a haircut on *Chol HaMoed* are similarly granted a dispensation to take a haircut during their *aveilus*. This is a somewhat surprising category. The logic of the *Chol HaMoed* dispensation is built on the incentive to prepare in advance, and those who were genuinely unable to prepare receive an exception. But *aveilus* is not a festival; its haircut prohibition is not designed to create an advance incentive. It is an expression of mourning itself. Why would the inability to prepare beforehand change whether one may shave during *aveilus*?

The *baraita* then appears to say these people are *asur* — forbidden. The contradiction is resolved by Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Shila: *ki tanya hacha mutarin b'shetakfu avelav* — the dispensation here applies only where the *aveilus* has piled up on the person, where multiple periods of mourning have come one after another and the cumulative burden has become genuinely oppressive.

### Overlapping Aveilus

If that is the rationale — cumulative burden — the Gemara asks: why limit this to special categories like one released from prison? A *baraita* already states that if one's *aveilus* *takfu avelo, zeh achar zeh* — comes pressing one after another — *hichbid se'aro, meikal b'ta'ar* — his hair has become heavy, he may lighten it with a razor — *u'michabes k'suto b'mayim* — and he may launder his garments with water. This general leniency already exists for any person facing overlapping *aveilus*.

### Razor vs. Scissors

The Gemara answers that the general leniency is not unlimited. Rav Chisda specifies: *b'ta'ar v'lo b'misparayim* — with a razor, not with scissors; a full haircut is still not permitted, only a lightening of the hair. *B'mayim v'lo b'neter* — with water, but not with detergent. Where the circumstances are more extreme — the overlapping *aveilus* plus, say, an extended period in prison — the leniency expands to permit scissors and normal laundering. The ordinary case of sequential *aveilus* receives only partial relief.

### Laundry Prohibition

The Gemara closes with an inference drawn by Rav Chisda: *Rav Chisda zos omeret, avel asur b'tichboset* — this entire discussion demonstrates that an *avel* is generally forbidden from laundering garments. Since it was necessary to create a specific leniency — limited in scope, permitting only water without detergent — to allow any laundering at all under the press of multiple *aveilus* periods, this proves that in the normal case, even laundering garments without detergent is forbidden to an *avel*. The leniency is only possible against the background of a baseline prohibition; without such a prohibition, there would have been nothing to relax.

---

---

# Moed Katan 20

## Third Day Erev Regel

### No Bathing Until Nightfa…

The daf opens in the middle of 19b, where the Gemara returns to the question of *regel* interrupting *aveilus* following a brief digression regarding the derivation of thirty days from the laws of *nazir*. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua opens with a unanimous ruling: *hakol modim k'shechal shlishi shelo liyos erev haregel, she'assur birchitza ad ha'erev* — everyone agrees that when the third day of *shiva* falls on *erev haregel*, the mourner may not bathe until nightfall.

The context here is critical. The *mishna* operates on the assumption — which will later be challenged — that *regel* does not interrupt *shiva* unless the mourner has observed a full three days. Given that baseline, one might have thought that since *regel* is about to interrupt *shiva*, the mourner could prepare by bathing early, just as we saw that a mourner nearing *shloshim* is permitted to get a haircut before *regel* in anticipation of the interruption. Rav Huna rules that this analogy does not hold for bathing on the third day: the mourner must wait until nightfall, when *yom tov* actually begins, before bathing.

The distinction between bathing and the haircut case is significant. Bathing is something a person can reasonably do once *yom tov* begins, and the prohibition of bathing belongs squarely to the core observances of *shiva*. Some authorities read *ad ha'erev* not as requiring one to wait until the actual onset of *yom tov*, but as permitting bathing once the late afternoon arrives, when one is sufficiently close to *yom tov*. Others limit the ruling specifically to bathing — that is, to prohibitions that can be readily remedied once *yom tov* begins — rather than extending it to all *shiva* practices. In either reading, the *l'halacha* application is not so sweeping.

### Rav Pappi & Rav Pappa

Rav Nechemia son of Rav Yehoshua reports that he found Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa sitting together and declaring: *halacha k'Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua* — the ruling follows Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua. No one disputes this ruling, and it stands as settled *halacha*.

### Three-Authority Girsa

An alternative version of this tradition — *ika d'amri* — reports that it was not Rav Huna who stated the ruling first and was then affirmed by Rav Pappi and Rav Pappa, but rather that all three — Rav Pappi, Rav Pappa, and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua — were sitting together and jointly declaring: *hakol modim k'shechal shlishi shelo liyos erev haregel, she'assur birchitza ad ha'erev*. Either way, the substance of the ruling is the same and appears undisputed.

---

## Regel & Shloshim

### Regel Count Question

The Gemara now turns to a question posed by Abaye to Rabba: *kivaro b'regel, regel oleh l'minyan shloshim o ein regel oleh l'minyan shloshim?* — if a person's relative was buried during *yom tov*, do the days of *regel* count toward the thirty-day period of *shloshim*, or do they not?

The *mishna* had already established that *regel* is *mafsik v'eino oleh* — it interrupts *shiva* but does not count toward it. The rationale is that *regel* is so fundamentally antithetical to *aveilus* that the period of *simcha* cannot accumulate toward the most intensive mourning period. But the question here is not about *shiva* — it is about *shloshim*.

### Shiva vs Shloshim

Abaye himself clarifies the parameters of the question: *l'minyan shiva lo ka mibaya li* — he has no question about *shiva*. Since none of the distinctive practices of *shiva* can be observed during *regel*, there is no mechanism by which the *regel* period could count. Moreover, at a conceptual level, *shiva* is so profoundly at odds with the spirit of *regel* that it is impossible for the *regel* days to be counted. *Delo nahaga mitzvas shiva baregel* — the obligation of *shiva* simply is not practiced during *regel*.
