If one friend has hosted and the others are now obligated to reciprocate, the obligation to repay the social debt applies even within the thirty-day period. The prohibition applies only when the mourner would be initiating a new gathering — *arisusa*; returning an existing obligation — *puranusa* — is permitted sooner.

### Practical Synthesis

In practice, the distinction between *simcha* and *simchas mere'ut* tends to be conflated. We generally treat both as equally forbidden during *shloshim* for other relatives and equally forbidden for twelve months for a father or mother — except for the specific case of reciprocation. This explains why, in practice, the question people ask when navigating the twelve-month restriction for parents is not "what is larger than *simchas mere'ut*" but rather "what qualifies as *simchas mere'ut*" — meaning, what has a sufficiently festive character to be restricted at all. A purely social gathering without a joyous dimension would theoretically be permitted; it is the combination of the social and the festive that the Gemara is concerned with, and the precise threshold remains a matter of significant debate among the *poskim*.

---

## Keriah Practice

### Tear Extent

For all other deceased, the mourner tears a *tefach* — approximately a hand's breadth, three to four inches. For a father or mother — *al aviv ve'al imo ad sheyigaleh libo* — one must tear until the heart is exposed. The symbolic weight of this distinction is evident. Rabbi Abbahu provides the scriptural basis: *vayechezek David bivgadav vayikra'eim* — David grasped his garments and rent them. Since *achiza*, grasping, involves the hand, and the hand is a *tefach* in measure, the *tefach* dimension for other relatives is derived from this verse. For parents, the tearing must go further, to expose the heart.

### Multiple Garments

For all other deceased, even if a person is wearing ten garments, only the outermost is torn — *eino koreia ela elyon*. For a father or mother, all garments must be torn — *koreia et kulam* — again oriented toward the exposure of the heart. The exception noted is the *afikarsut* — understood by most *rishonim* as an undergarment that serves to absorb perspiration rather than functioning as a proper garment. Even for parents, such an undergarment need not be torn, though this sits in some tension with the phrase *ad sheyigaleh libo*.

The Gemara notes that there is no distinction between men and women in this regard — *echad ha'ish ve'echad ha'isha*. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, however, adds a practical consideration for women: in the case of parents, where all garments must be torn, the woman should tear the lower inner garment first, then reverse it so the tear faces her back, and then tear the upper garment — *kora'at et ha'elyon*. In this way, both the outer and inner garments are torn as required, but the woman's chest remains covered.

### Mavdil Definition

For all other deceased, a mourner may optionally tear opposite the hem — *mavdil* — but is not required to do so. For a father or mother, one must tear from the hem, effectively dividing the garment into two halves — *al aviv ve'al imo mavdil*.

### Yehuda's Position

Rabbi Yehudah rejects the entire distinction between relatives. He maintains that any *keriah* that does not render the garment *mavdil* — divided from the hem into two visible halves — is nothing but frivolous tearing: *kriah shel tiflut*. Rabbi Abba explains Rabbi Yehudah's reasoning from the same verse: *vayikra'em lishnayim kera'im* — David rent them into two tears. The word "two" is superfluous — of course if you tear something there are two pieces. The verse must therefore be teaching that the *keriah* should *look* like two halves. A tear in the middle of a garment does not produce this appearance; only tearing from the hem produces the visual impression of a garment divided in two.

### Repair Timeline

For all other deceased: one may loosely pin together the torn garment — *sholel* — after seven days, and may fully sew it — *me'acheh* — after thirty days. For a father or mother: one may not even loosely pin together the tear until after thirty days — *sholel achar shloshim* — and may never fully sew it — *ve'eino me'acheh le'olam*. This is the most enduring of the physical distinctions: the garment torn for a parent is never restored to its prior state.

### Women's Keriah

An exception is made for women immediately: *veha'isha sholelet le'altar mipnei kevoda* — a woman may immediately repin the torn garment for reasons of modesty and personal dignity. This mirrors the parallel consideration for women addressed earlier in the tearing procedure itself.

### Hand Tearing

When *Ravin* came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: for all other deceased, a mourner may perform *keriah* either by hand or with an instrument — scissors, for example, to get the tear started. For a father or mother, it must be done by hand — *al aviv ve'al imo beyad*. Tearing by hand conveys immediacy, intensity, and a raw personal expression of grief; reaching for an instrument distances the act from that immediacy. In practice, where modern fabrics make hand-tearing extremely difficult, a small starting cut may be made, but the act of *keriah* itself is understood to carry this expressive dimension.

### Mipnim vs. Mibachutz

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba further quotes Rabbi Yochanan: for all other deceased, the *keriah* is performed *mipnim* — inside; for a father or mother, it is performed *mibachutz* — outside. The Ramban explains that this does not refer to a private versus public setting, noting that *mipnim* and *mibachutz* would be the wrong formulation for that. Rather, it refers to whether the hands are placed on the inside of the garment while tearing outward, or on the outside. Tearing from the outside is more visible, more demonstrative, more public in its expression of grief.

---

## Nasi Keriah

### Nasi Comparison

Rav Chisda rules: *ve'chen l'nasi* — the same applies to the *nasi*, the national leader. The *keriah* practices performed for a father or mother apply similarly for the *nasi*. The Gemara challenges this from a *baraisa* that states the comparison between a *nasi* and *aviv ve'imo* was only in the *halacha* of sewing — *l'ichuy bilvad* — and not in other aspects of *keriah*. The Gemara resolves this: the limitation applies to other figures who might be compared partially to *aviv ve'imo* in some respects; the *nasi* is a fuller comparison, and even the manner of tearing would mirror that of a father or mother.

### Public Keriah

When a *nasi* died, Rav Chisda instructed Rav Nachman bar Ami: overturn a mortar, stand on it, and demonstrate *keriah* to the community. The *nasi*'s death requires that the communal obligation to perform *keriah* be made visible. A prominent figure stands on a raised surface and performs *keriah* publicly, both showing the community how to do so and signaling that they are required to do so.

### Shoulder Location

For a *chacham* — a sage — one exposes the right shoulder. For the *av beit din* — the head of the court, a more senior position — one exposes the left shoulder. For the *nasi* — both shoulders, left and right. The apparent counterintuitiveness of the left shoulder for the *av beit din* may relate to the left side being over the heart, lending it a particular quality of exposure, though the Gemara leaves this without explicit explanation.

---

## Communal Mourning

### Study Hall Closure

The Gemara now describes graduated communal responses to the deaths of different categories of leadership. When a *chacham* dies, his own *yeshiva* ceases — *beit midrasho batel*. When the *av beit din* of a city dies, all the *batei midrashot* of that city cease — *kol batei midrashot shebeiro betelim*.

### National Closure

When the *nasi* dies, all the *batei midrashot* throughout the country cease — *batei midrashot kulam betelim*. The people then gather into the *beit haknesset*, and seven *aliyot* are read from the Torah.

### Torah Reading

The communal gathering centers on *kriat haTorah*: seven *aliyot* are read, and then the people disperse. This gathering is focused on Torah reading, not on the full communal *tefillah*.

### Private Davening

Rabbeinu Gershom explains why *tefillah* is not conducted communally: since the entire community is in a state of *aveilus*, gathering for a full communal *davening* would constitute a collective experience that is inconsistent with the individual character of mourning. Each person therefore davens privately at home. The community gathers specifically for *kriat haTorah* — a communal act of Torah engagement — while retaining the separateness that *aveilus* demands.

### Public Silence

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha adds: people should not go out and stroll through the marketplace — *lo sheyeilchu veyitaylu bashuk*. Rather, they should sit and be silent — *yoshvin vedomin*. The dynamic is a striking and carefully calibrated balance. The community is in collective *aveilus* — analogous in some ways to *Tisha B'Av* — and must demonstrate that mourning publicly. Yet *aveilus* by its nature is also about separateness from communal life. The resolution: people gather in the *beit haknesset* for Torah reading, but not for communal *tefillah*; they occupy the space together, but each sits in a different place from usual; they are present with one another, but sit in silence rather than conducting business or socializing. It is a community of mourners performing *aveilus* together while preserving, to the degree possible, the individual and inward character that genuine mourning requires.

---

---

# Moed Katan 23

## Batei Midrashim & Beit H…

### Death of Chacham

The daf opens three lines in, picking up from a *braita* that was interrupted at the end of the previous session. The *braita* had been discussing what occurs when an *av beit din*, a *nasi*, or a *chacham* dies. It did not spell out the full aspects of *shiva* and *kriya*, although the *gemara* earlier had addressed *kriya* for a *nasi* in the context of the death of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. The emphasis here, however, is on the emptying of the study halls. The *braita* does not specify for how long, but it states that the *batei midrashot* are *beteilim* — and it conveys a sense of public mourning, with the irony that mourning is not about gathering together with everyone else, but about being separated from the community.

On that point, the *braita* states *nichnasim l'beit haknesset v'korim sheva* — they come to *shul* and read seven *aliyot*, presumably on *Shabbat*. Rabbeinu Gershom there notes *b'sefer Torah d'ein mitpalelim yachad b'beit haknesset elah kol echad v'echad mitpalel b'veito* — that is, rather than davening together communally in the *beit knesset*, everyone prays individually at home. There is an interesting effort to strike a balance: some form of communal gathering or expression is maintained, while simultaneously preserving the sense of communal loss that attends this period.

### Silent Community

The *braita* continues with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who states *lo she-yochlu v'yitayalu bashuk* — that they should not walk around socializing in the marketplace — *elah yoshvin v'domim*, rather they should sit together in silence. When people leave their homes in some communal expression of mourning, it is without the social component: they gather, but they do so silently. This is an interesting comparison to the reality of Tisha B'Av. The communal dimension is preserved, but stripped of its usual sociability.

### No Shmua v'Aggada

Tagged on to the end of this *braita* — which appears to be a general ruling and not limited solely to the death of a *chacham* or *nasi* — is the statement: *v'ein omrim shmua v'aggada b'veit ha-avel*. We do not recite *shmua* and *aggada* in the house of the mourner. We had already established that an *avel* is *assur b'talmud Torah*, and a long list of prohibitions was catalogued earlier. What this ruling adds is something more specific: *shmua v'aggada* addresses not the most rigorous analytical *Torah* learning but precisely the kind of religious discourse — *hashkafic* material, stories, inspirational teachings — that might be more likely to occur during a *nichum aveilim* visit. Even that is prohibited.

Equally significant is the phrase *b'veit ha-avel* — in the house of the mourner. The ruling is about the space, not just about the *avel* himself. Even if the *avel* momentarily steps away, visitors standing in the room should not be discussing what they learned in the day's *daf* or the weekly *parasha*. This reading makes sense within the context of the *braita*, because the primary mourning response that it articulated for the death of a *chacham* was not *kriya* or the formal practices of *shiva* — it was *batei midrashim beteilim*. The impact is on *Torah* itself. When a great figure of *Torah* is lost, *Torah* is diminished. In the *beit ha-avel* for an ordinary person, *Torah simcha* is absent — and that absence belongs to the space, not merely to the *avel*'s personal status.

One might note, in connection with this passage, that we do recite some *divrei Torah* in the house of mourning today in order to enable *kaddish* to be said. The institution of *kaddish* receives only a single reference in the *gemara*, and its full development is a later phenomenon. It seems likely that the practice of learning *Torah* in the *avel's* house and the development of *kaddish* went hand in hand — the one enabling the other — though this remains a fascinating historical question deserving its own investigation.

### Chananya's Exception

The *gemara* then records: *amru alav al Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel shehaya omer shmua b'veit ha-avel* — they said about Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel that he would say *Torah* in the *beit ha-avel*. The phrasing *haya omer* suggests something more than occasional inadvertent lapses; it implies an intentional and perhaps even regular practice, possibly in the context of a public teaching. One wonders whether this relates to *nichum aveilim* specifically — whether he was offering a religious discourse as part of consoling the mourners, as we do find in the *gemara* instances of *nichum aveilim* that incorporate *Torah* and *aggada* (invoking, for example, the death of Aharon). The tension between the general prohibition and Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel's apparent practice is notable and is left unresolved.

### Simchat Mereus

Before continuing to the next topic, it is worth pausing to address the issue of *simchat mere'us* that was discussed in the previous session, given its considerable practical relevance. The *gemara* had distinguished between general *simcha* — which seems more problematic — and *simchat mere'us*, which is about gathering with friends in a celebratory context. Yet by the end of that discussion, the *gemara* appeared to have largely conflated the two categories, concluding that both are prohibited during *shloshim* for most people and during twelve months for one's father or mother, except in very particular circumstances.

This raises the natural question: are there exceptions, and what does a *simcha shel mitzvah* do to the calculus? Is a *mitzvah* occasion better or worse? Tosafot on 22b takes up exactly this question, citing *Masechet Semachot* which states *im haya seudat mitzvah mutar* — if it was a *seudat mitzvah* it is permitted — but immediately acknowledges: *lo yadanu mahu karui seudat mitzvah l'hatir b'avel*, we do not know precisely what qualifies as a *seudat mitzvah* sufficient to permit an *avel* to attend. One suggestion mentioned is *seudat kiddush Rosh Chodesh*, though the meaning of that is itself unclear. Avi ha-Ezri in the name of Rabbeinu Shimshon rules that a *seudat bris milah* is permitted, on the grounds that it does not have the character of *simcha* — as we find in the first chapter of Ketubot that the formula *she-hasimcha b'ma'ono* is not recited there because people are preoccupied — *de-tridi v'leika simcha*. Yet this leads to the further question noted by Tosafot: if *bris milah* is less problematic than *simchat mere'us*, is that so obvious? Perhaps in some respects it is more problematic.

The practical questions multiply: is it permitted to eat with the service staff rather than at the main table? Tosafot rules *ein lachaleik bein seudas hamishamshim useudah atzmah* — one cannot make that distinction. However, *khnisah belo achilah shari de'ein simchah belo achilah ushtiyah* — simply entering without eating is permitted, since there is no *simcha* without eating and drinking. Tosafot ha-Rosh rules in accordance with the more permissive view among those cited.

## Remarriage Law

### Simchat Mitzvah

The Rosh addresses the more fundamental question: is a *seudat mitzvah* better or worse than a *seudat hareshut*? The Ra'avad raises the objection that from the *gemara* here it seems that *seudas mitzvah* carries a *more* severe prohibition than *seudas hareshut*, since *simchat mitzvah* appears more serious than *simchat mere'us*, which would make it worse rather than better. *Aveil Rabbati* teaches: *kol sheloshim yom assur leileich leveit hamishteh* — for the full thirty days one may not go to a *beit hamishteh*, and for a father or mother the restriction extends until *sheyiga'aru bo chaveirav* — until one's friends effectively reproach him for not attending. This is notable: according to this source, the period for parents is not twelve months as we rule, but simply until social pressure compels one's return. And then the *Aveil Rabbati* adds: *ela im kein haysah lesheim shamayim* — unless the gathering was *lesheim shamayim*, for the sake of Heaven. The *alma* drawn from this is *de-seudas mitzvah yeish bah heter yoseir miveseudas hareshut* — a *seudat mitzvah* carries greater leniency than an ordinary gathering.

The Rosh then quotes Rav Yehudah Bartzeloni: *yeish shenohagim shenichnasim besoch yud beis chodesh leveit hachupah lishmoa habrachos ulevakeir* — there are those who customarily enter the *chupah* during the twelve months to hear the blessings and pay respects — *aval lo yochal*, but they do not eat. And there are those who are stringent and do not enter at all. The question of whether there is *simcha* in *simchas chupah* even without *achilah ushtiyah* is left open. This entire range — whether *mitzvah* makes things better or worse, whether presence without eating helps, whether being *lesheim shamayim* changes the status — remains substantially unclarified and continues to generate *she'eilot* in practice.

## Movement in Shiva

### Four Week Progression

A new topic now comes into focus — one that has been, surprisingly, in the background until this point. Until now, the *gemara* had not stated as a formal *halacha* what most people would probably identify as the central feature of *shiva*: that the *avel* stays home and people come to him. That is now addressed directly. *Tanu rabbanan*: the *avel* during the first *shabbat* — meaning here the first week — does not go out from the door of his house. The second *shabbat* he goes out but does not sit in his regular place. The third week he sits in his regular place but does not speak. By the fourth week *harei hu kechol adam* — he is like everyone else.

### Weekly Restrictions

The *baraita* thus outlines a gradual progression over four weeks, describing the *avel's* reintegration into the community. The restrictions by week are: *shabbat rishona eino yotzei mipetach beito* — he does not leave his home; *shniya yotzei ve'eino yoshev bimkomo* — he leaves but does not sit in his regular place; *shlishis yoshev bimkomo ve'eino medaber* — he sits in his place but does not speak; *revi'is harei hu kechol adam* — he is fully restored. This last stage falls within *shloshim* but before it concludes.

### Rabbi Yehuda

Rabbi Yehuda offers a different formulation: *lo hutzrechu lomar shabbat rishona lo yetzei mipetach beito* — one does not need to state as a *halacha* that the *avel* does not leave during the first week. *Sheharei hakol nichnasim leveito lenachamo* — that is simply what *shiva* is: everyone comes to be *menachem avel* and the *avel* stays home. This captures something essential. Rabbi Yehuda seems to be pointing not to a formal prohibition but to the nature of the experience itself. Staying home during the first week is not a rabbinic rule that requires statement — it is the essence of what *shiva* is. The *halacha* that Rabbi Yehuda does articulate is that during the second week the *avel* still does not leave — and this is genuinely demanding, since people are no longer coming to be *menachem*, yet the *avel* remains at home, now without the social dimension of receiving visitors.

### Essence of Shiva

Rabbi Yehuda's framing invites a deeper question about what *shiva* is essentially, as opposed to what its specific practices are. The *halacha* that the *avel* remains home is perhaps not a *halacha* of *aveilus* at all in the conventional sense — it is the definition of *aveilus*, the very thing the institution is about. This is one reason why, according to some, it does not appear in the standard enumeration of *minhagei avel*: it is the frame within which all other practices occur, not one item in a list alongside bathing and wearing shoes.

Rabbi Yehuda's version of the *baraita* extends the progression by a week: the second week *eino yotzei mipetach beito*, the third week *yotzei ve'eino yoshev bimkomo*, the fourth week *yoshev bimkomo ve'eino medaber*, and only by the fifth week *harei hu kechol adam*.

### Sitting & Speaking

Tosafot on *Rabbi Yehuda omer lo hutzrechu* notes that the *Yerushalmi* rules *halacha kedivrei hamosif beyamim* — the law follows the one who adds days — which is striking given that we generally say *halacha k'divrei ha-meikel b'avel*. Tosafot then relates a family tradition: Rabbeinu Yitzchak Zikni would sit in his place until the fourth week, following the more stringent opinion, but Tosafot himself did not understand his reasoning. He speculates: *shema hayah sover k'Rabbi Yehuda* — perhaps he held like Rabbi Yehuda — but then notes the difficulty, since if one follows Rabbi Yehuda then during the second week one should not leave the house at all, and no one practices that. If one is already leaving the house after the first week, how can one simultaneously practice Rabbi Yehuda's position regarding *yoshev bimkomo*?

Tosafot then offers a subtle resolution: *yeish lomar b'ha ashkechan tuva lechiyuva d'aveilus shiva* — perhaps *shiva* ends the period of stricter *aveilus* and overrides, and we hold accordingly. But then he proposes another possibility: perhaps Rabbeinu Yitzchak Zikni actually held like the *rabbanan*, not like Rabbi Yehuda — *v'sevara leih taama k'rabbanan*. According to the *rabbanan*, the third week the *avel yoshev bimkomo* but *eino medaber*. Tosafot then draws a fine conceptual point: *umishum d'tzarich leyshev bimkomo ve'eino medaber — vetov yoter sheyeishev chutz limkomo deshema ein issur ledaber ki im bimkomo* — since the restriction on speech is tied to sitting in one's *makom*, if he avoids sitting in his *makom*, he avoids the restriction on speech. The prohibition is not a general ban on speaking with people; it is contextually linked to the act of being *yoshev bimkomo*, of publicly resuming one's full standing in the community. To speak while *yoshev bimkomo* signals the full restoration of one's communal status — which is precisely what is being delayed.

This conceptual point raises a further question: what exactly is the *makom* in question? The most natural reading, and the one that emerges from our current practice, is one's seat in *shul*. But the *gemara* itself is not explicit, and the restriction might equally apply to any designated public space where an individual has a fixed position — a seat at the theater, a place in the *beit midrash*, or in principle any place where one's presence signals a return to normal communal standing.

A further question raised about the *baraita* is whether *shabbat* here means *Shabbat* specifically or the week (*shavua*). This is a significant debate among the *rishonim*. If the reference is to *Shabbat* itself, then the *halacha* about not going to *shul* during the first week would apply even on *Shabbat*, and visitors would be coming for *nichum aveilim* on *Shabbat* — which is indeed what the *baraita* implies.

### Exceptions & Latitudes

On this question, the Rosh in *siman* 46 records that the custom in Ashkenaz was as follows: *ha-avel holech leveit haknesses b'shabbos* — the *avel* goes to *shul* on *Shabbat*. After prayer, *ha-avel yotzei techilla* — the *avel* leaves first — *veyoshev lifnei beit haknesses* — and sits outside the *shul* — *vechol hakahal yotzim veyoshvim etzlo* — and the entire community comes out and sits with him — *va-omer ha-avel veholech leveito, vechol hakahal holchim imo, veyoshvin sham sha'ah achas* — the *avel* returns home and the entire community walks with him and sits with him for a time. This is a fully communal, public act of *nichum aveilim* on *Shabbat* — and its scope, involving the entire congregation, is quite striking. Rabbeinu Hai Gaon adds that *va-afilu b'Shabbat hakol k'minhag hamedina* — even regarding whether one leaves home on *Shabbat* during the first week, everything depends on local custom. In places where it was customary to come early to *shul*, the *avel* would come; in places where it was customary to remain home on *Shabbat*, he would remain home.

As for the absolute-sounding language of the *braita* — *eino yotzei mipetach beito* — the *Rema* clarifies that the prohibition is specifically *letayel o lemassa umattan*, for leisure or commerce. He further rules *hameikel latzeit b'layla mipnei ha-tzorech lo hifsid* — one who is lenient about going out at night for a practical need has not lost anything, since going out at night lacks the public social dimension of daytime activity. The *Rema* also permits leaving for cases of significant need — if a *moshel* summons the *avel*, if travel is required, or in cases of *davar ha-avud*, a significant financial loss. The home is not meant to be a prison; the halachic frame permits real latitude when genuine need arises.

## Remarriage Law (II)

### Shloshim Remarriage

The *gemara* now turns to another topic: *kol shloshim yom lenissuin* — for all thirty days a person may not get married. This is framed, as will be seen, largely from the man's perspective. If a man's wife dies, the prohibition extends further: *assur lissa isha acheret ad she-ya'avru alav shalosh regalim* — he may not remarry until three *regalim* have passed. This is not primarily a matter of *minhagei aveilus* but of respect for his first wife and marriage.

### Yehuda's Leniencies

Rabbi Yehuda rules more leniently: *regel rishon v'sheni assur, shelishi mutar* — the first two *regalim* are prohibited, by the third it is permitted. Two exceptions allow remarriage immediately (*le'altar*): if a man has no children, *mutar lissa le'altar mishum bittul pru urevu* — he may remarry right away because of the *mitzvah* of *pru urevu*; and if he has left with young children who need care, *mutar lissa le'altar mipnei parnasatam* — he may remarry right away for their support. The question of what *le'altar* precisely means becomes important in the story that follows.

### Joseph's Story

A case is recounted: *ma'aseh shemeta ishto shel Yosef HaKohen* — the wife of Yosef HaKohen died. *Ve'amar la'achosa b'veit hakevarot* — he proposed to her sister right there at the cemetery during the burial. *Lechi u-farnasi es bnei achotei* — he asked her to come and support his sister's children. And yet, *af al pi kein lo ba aleha ela l'zman meruba* — even so, he did not consummate the marriage until a significant time had passed. Rav Pappa explains: *le-achar shloshim yom* — he waited thirty days, since that is the period of *simcha*. So on the one hand there is an allowance — greater than the general rule, since he does not need to wait for *shalosh regalim* or even *shnei regalim* — but on the other hand, since the allowance is about raising the children and the element of *simcha* and its associated aspects of marriage remain a concern, he waited until the end of the month. In a case where the exception is based on *pru urevu* rather than childcare, Tosafot indicates that relations would be permitted immediately upon marriage, since that is precisely what the allowance is for.

### Tosafot Objection

Tosafot raises a significant objection to this story. The idea that a marriage proposal — and apparently the marriage itself — could occur during *shiva*, or even at the cemetery during the burial, is deeply troubling to Tosafot, based both on intrinsic discomfort with the notion and on other *sugyot*. Tosafot therefore offers two ways of softening the *gemara's* account: either *beit hakevarot* is being used metaphorically rather than literally, or the proposal was made at the cemetery but the actual marriage did not take place until after *shiva*. In any case, Tosafot is clearly unsettled by the *gemara's* quite vivid and memorable formulation.

A separate conceptual question addressed at length in Tosafot and the Rosh concerns the nature of the *shalosh regalim* requirement itself. Tosafot asks: what is the reason for waiting *shalosh regalim*? He offers two explanations. The first is *v'lo yishkach ahavas ishto* — so that the memory of his first wife and the love of that marriage will stay with him through the experience of *shalosh regalim* without her. The second explanation is framed around the second wife: *kdei she-yisa isha acheres v'lo yihiyeh zachur min ha-rishona she-lo yihiyeh shtei deiot b'mita* — so that when he remarries, the memory of his first wife will have faded sufficiently that he will not effectively be thinking of her during intimacy with his second wife, which the *gemara* elsewhere treats as a form of virtual betrayal. A third concern is *pen yazkirena ahavas ishto l'kantra* — lest he mention his first wife to the second in a way that wounds her, for example by comparing her unfavorably to his late wife in small domestic matters.

Tosafot then cites Rabbeinu Yonah for an important conceptual clarification: one cannot apply the principle *halacha k'divrei ha-meikel b'avel* to this discussion in order to rule like Rabbi Yehuda's position of *shnei regalim* rather than *shalosh regalim*. The reason is *d'hani mili d'pligi b'hacha ein zu b'avel d'yimei aveilus kalu lahen* — this debate is not about *hilchos aveilus* at all. By the time we are discussing *shalosh regalim*, the *avel's* period of *aveilus* is long over. The waiting period is a *halacha* about respect for one's first or second wife — about the concerns of *lo yishkach* or *shtei deiot b'mita* — and therefore the principle of leniency in *aveilus* simply does not apply. This is a striking clarification: the prohibition on remarriage for *shalosh regalim* is not a *halacha* in *hilchos aveilus*; it is a *halacha* in a different register entirely.

## Gihutz Restrictions

### Gihutz Baraita

*Tanu rabbanan: kol shloshim yom legihutz* — for all thirty days there is a prohibition on *gihutz*, which is essentially a thorough pressing or dry-cleaning of clothing, as distinct from ordinary laundering. While the prohibition on laundering clothes in general applies only during the first week of mourning, the prohibition on *gihutz* extends for the entire month of *shloshim*.

### Clothing Disputes

The *baraita* continues: *echad keilim chadashim ve'echad keilim yeshanim* — whether new or old garments, *gihutz* is problematic, because even old clothes taken from the press look fresher than they would otherwise. *Yotzim mitoch hamachbesh* — if clothes come directly from the press, that is an issue regardless of age. Rabbi rules more leniently: *lo asru ela keilim chadashim bilvad* — only new clothes, since old clothes even after *gihutz* will never truly look new again, so there is no real concern. Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon is stricter in one sense and narrower in another: *lo asru ela keilim chadashim levanim bilvad* — only new white clothes, since only white fabric can be restored through pressing to the appearance of true freshness.

### Abaye & Rava

Two *amoraic* stories illustrate how these opinions played out in practice. Abaye (*Abaye nafik begarda desarvela*) went out wearing an old white cloak — following Rabbi's ruling, since it was not new. Rava (*Rava nafik bechimutzta d'romita sumakta charti*) went out wearing a new red Roman cloak — following Rabbi Elazar b'Rabbi Shimon's ruling, since it was not white. In practice, then, the actual parameters of what is prohibited during *shloshim* in the category of *gihutz* are rendered quite narrow.

### Laundering Debate

Despite the apparent clarity of this *baraita*, there is a substantial Tosafot here because other *sugyot* seem to suggest a prohibition on *kibbus* — actual laundering — for the full thirty days, not just for the first week. Tosafot works through several possible ways of reconciling these sources. Perhaps in those other *sugyot* the term *kibbus* (laundering) actually meant *gihutz*. Or conversely, perhaps *gihutz* here does not mean mere pressing but laundering with soap, so that what is prohibited for the first week alone is laundering without soap, while laundering with soap — which constitutes *gihutz* — is what is prohibited for the month. There is an additional discussion arising from the view that outside *Eretz Yisrael* one does not know how to perform *gihutz* to the same standard as was practiced there, and therefore nothing in the diaspora would qualify as *gihutz*, rendering the entire category of the month-long prohibition effectively inapplicable outside of *Eretz Yisrael*. The result is that the actual *halacha* remains genuinely contested, as is also evident in the *Shulchan Aruch*, and what is prohibited in this category after the first week turns out to be very limited in scope.

## Aveilus on Shabbat

### Shabbat Counts

The *mishnah* states: *Shabbat olah v'einah mafsekes* — *Shabbat* counts toward *shiva* but does not interrupt it. This is a foundational rule: every *shiva* runs through *Shabbat*, and *Shabbat* is counted among the seven days.

### Yehuda vs. Galil

What follows is a striking *gemara*: rather than a dispute between named rabbinic authorities, we have a geographic debate between *Bnei Yehuda* and *Bnei Galil* — two regions with different practices. The *gemara* will treat this as a substantive halachic debate, even though it begins as an account of different regional customs.

### Aveilus Practiced

*Honey amri yesh aveilus b'Shabbat* — one group says that *aveilus* is practiced on *Shabbat*. What exactly this means requires examination. Does it mean full *aveilus*, with all its practices? Or does it mean only the private dimension of *aveilus* — *devarim she'betzina*? The *gemara* does not specify. Rashi and Tosafot understand the debate to be specifically about *devarim she'betzina*, the practices that do not publicly announce one's status as an *avel*, such as refraining from marital relations and perhaps certain forms of bathing. But this reading is not explicitly forced by the *gemara's* language.

### No Aveilus

*Ve'honey amri ein aveilus b'Shabbat* — the other group says *aveilus* is not practiced on *Shabbat* at all. This position is not self-evident. One might ask: if *regel* interrupts *aveilus* because *regel* is about *simcha*, why should *Shabbat* limit *aveilus*? *Shabbat* is not characterized by *simcha* in the same way as *regel* — rather, it is characterized by *kavod* and *oneg*. If *Shabbat* does not carry the power of *simcha* to terminate *aveilus*, why would it have the power to suspend *aveilus* practices? One might argue that full *aveilus* should continue on *Shabbat* uninterrupted.

### Private Practices

Tosafot offers the key reasoning: even if *Shabbat* lacks the character of *simcha* and therefore does not have the power of *regel* to be *mafsik*, *Shabbat* is nevertheless a day of *kavod* and *oneg* — enjoyment and honor. This is inconsistent with practices that place a person in a state of discomfort or public mourning expression. The logic that *Shabbat* creates a "middle state" — neither *simcha* nor *tza'ar* — is what underlies the ruling that *devarim she'betzina noheg*, private mourning practices continue, while public expressions of mourning are suspended.

One broader question lurks here: are the practices of *aveilus* meant to express an inner experience that already exists, or are they meant to create and cultivate that inner experience? This is a genuine tension in how one understands the function of *halachic* mourning practices. Rav Soloveitchik's well-known treatment of *hilchos aveilus* emphasizes that these practices are expressions of an inner emotional and existential reality, not merely formal behaviors. At the same time, the general power of ritual is precisely that it helps internalize states that might not arise spontaneously — it helps ground the mourner in the reality of loss. Both understandings seem valid, and they need not be mutually exclusive.

### Shabbat's Middle Way

Tosafot makes this conceptual point explicit. The reason *regel* terminates *aveilus* is *mishum de'ketiv v'samachta* — because *regel* is explicitly associated with *simcha*, which is fundamentally incompatible with *aveilus*. *Shabbat*, by contrast, does not carry that explicit *simcha* verse, and therefore does not interrupt. Yet the *Yerushalmi* explains why *aveilus* is nonetheless not practiced publicly on *Shabbat*: *mishum de'ketiv birchas Hashem hi ta'ashir v'lo yosif etzev imah* — the blessing of God enriches and adds no suffering. *Uve-Shabbat ketiv bei bracha* — *Shabbat* is characterized by blessing, and a day of blessing is not a day of *etzev*, of pain or sadness. So *Shabbat* occupies this middle position: not *simcha* (and therefore not *mafsik* like *regel*), but also not *tza'ar* (and therefore not fully consistent with public mourning).

### Mishnah Language

The *gemara* then raises a question about the language of the *mishnah* itself. According to the opinion that *ein aveilus b'Shabbat*, why does the *mishnah* say *olah* — that *Shabbat* counts toward *shiva*? If *aveilus* is not being practiced at all on *Shabbat*, what is being "counted"? The *gemara* answers: *aidi d'ka'baei le-mitni seifa eino oleh* — since the *mishnah* was going to state regarding *regalim* that they do *not* count, it stated in the opening clause that *Shabbat* does count. The language of *olah* is not meant to imply that *aveilus* is actively practiced on *Shabbat* and therefore counts; it is simply the counterpart phrasing to *ein olin* in the case of *regalim*.

The reciprocal question is then posed: according to the opinion that *yesh aveilus b'Shabbat*, why does the *mishnah* say *einah mafsekes* — that *Shabbat* does not interrupt? If *aveilus* is being practiced, obviously it does not interrupt. The answer is the same: *mishum d'ka'baei le-mitni seifa mafsikin* — since the *mishnah* was going to say that *regalim* do interrupt, it stated in the opening clause that *Shabbat* does not, even though this is obvious according to this opinion. So both opinions can account for both halves of the *mishnah's* language through the same structural explanation.

## Onein & Aveilus

### Onein Eating

The *gemara* now introduces the figure of the *onein* — one whose deceased relative has not yet been buried, *meiso mutal lefanav*. A *baraita* details the *onein's* eating arrangements: *mi she-meiso mutal lefanav ochel b'vayis acher* — he eats in another house. If he has no other house, he eats at a friend's house. If that is also unavailable, *oseh lo mechitzah asarah tefachim* — he makes a partition ten *tefachim* high, creating a distinct zone. If even that is impossible, *machzir panav v'ochel* — he turns his face away from the *meit* and eats, so as not to be literally chewing in the presence of the deceased.

### Onein vs. Aveilus

What is striking about this *gemara* is that it treats *aninus* and *aveilus* as states that can be compared and from which inferences can be drawn in either direction. This is conceptually significant because normally these two states are kept rigorously separate. The question of their relationship underlies a major dispute among the *rishonim*. Tosafot (and what appears to be a *Rita*) takes the position that these are completely distinct states with no intrinsic relationship to one another. The Rambam, by contrast, and partly because of *gemarot* like this one, proposes a model of fundamental continuity: *aninus* and *aveilus* are essentially one ongoing state of mourning from the time of death through the end of *shiva*. The special features of *aninus* — the additional restrictions on meat, wine, *berachot*, and *mitzvot*, as well as certain leniencies like being permitted to bathe and wear shoes in order to tend to the *meit* — are all overrides or modifications triggered by the specific circumstance of *meiso mutal lefanav*, but they do not constitute a categorically different state. In this conceptual model, the default assumption is that an *onein* practices all the practices of *aveilus* unless there is a specific reason to make an exception; the leniencies we find are all justified as enabling the *onein* to attend properly to the burial. This is conceptually unusual, but *gemarot* like this one push certain *rishonim* in that direction.

### Onein Restrictions

The *baraita* enumerates the *onein's* restrictions in detail: *v'eino meisav v'ochel* — he does not recline while eating, a posture associated with luxury and relaxed enjoyment, since his attention should be on the *meit*; *v'eino ochel basar v'eino shotheh yayin* — he does not eat meat or drink wine; *v'ein mevarech v'ein mezamein* — he does not recite *berachot* and does not lead or participate in *zimun*; *ve'ein mevarchin alav v'ein mezamnin alav* — others do not include him in *zimun* either. Further: *u'patur mikrias shema u'min hatfillah u'min hatfillin u'micol mitzot ha'amurot batorah* — he is exempt from *keriat shema*, prayer, *tefillin*, and all *mitzvot* of the Torah.

The abstraction of the concept of *meiso mutal lefanav* is worth noting here. The *baraita* begins with the literal case — the body is physically present in the room — but the halachic status of *aninus* extends more broadly to anyone whose deceased relative has not yet been buried, even when the person is in a different city and cannot physically be present at the burial. The conceptual category of *mutal lefanav* becomes larger than its literal meaning.

### Onein on Shabbat

On *Shabbat*, when burial is impossible and therefore the *onein's* entire focus on attending to the *meit* is suspended, the picture changes dramatically. *Meisav v'ochel* — he may recline; *ochel basar v'shotheh yayin* — he may eat meat and drink wine; *u'mevarech u'mezamein u'mevarchin u'mezamnin alav* — he recites *berachot* and participates in *zimun* and others include him; *v'chayav bikrias shema u'vitfillah u'vitfillin u'vchol mitzot ha'amurot batorah* — he is obligated in all *mitzvot* of the Torah. (The inclusion of *tefillin* in this list is noted, since one does not wear *tefillin* on *Shabbat* anyway; it is included for completeness of the formula.)

### Sex on Shabbat

Rabban Gamliel adds: *mitoch shenischayev be'elu, nischayev b'chulan* — since the *onein* has become obligated in all those practices on *Shabbat*, he is obligated in all of them. Rabbi Yochanan clarifies what this adds: *tashmish hamitah ika beiniyahu* — the point of dispute between Rabban Gamliel and the earlier formulation is whether the *onein* on *Shabbat* is permitted to have marital relations. This is something that was not mentioned in the earlier enumeration of permissions on *Shabbat*, and Rabban Gamliel holds that once one is *chayav* in all the other practices, one is *chayav* in everything — including *tashmish hamitah*.

This is a striking *gemara*. The *onein* who cannot have marital relations on a weekday — we had not actually stated this about an *onein* explicitly, only about an *avel* — now on *Shabbat* is being debated as to whether it is permitted. The inference from *onein* to *avel* and back is operating here in complex ways.

### Continuity Model

The *gemara* then asks: *leima ki-tanna'ei* — is this debate between *Bnei Yehuda* and *Bnei Galil* about *aveilus b'Shabbat* actually rooted in this earlier *tannaic* dispute about the *onein* on *Shabbat*? The comparison hinges on whether *aninus* and *aveilus* are the same kind of thing: if one holds *yesh aveilus b'Shabbat*, one would hold the *onein* cannot have relations on *Shabbat* either; if one holds *ein aveilus b'Shabbat*, one would permit it. The *gemara* pushes back: perhaps these are independent questions. Perhaps *aninus* is simply more severe than *aveilus* — either because it is a more intense form of mourning, or because the circumstance of *meiso mutal lefanav* adds its own restrictions — such that even one who holds *ein aveilus b'Shabbat* might hold that *aninus* restricts relations on *Shabbat*. Or conversely, Rabban Gamliel's leniency on *Shabbat* might be specifically because the person is not yet an *avel* — *aninus* is not *aveilus*, and the prohibition on relations might only be a *halacha* of *aveilus* proper, not of *aninus* at all. In that case, one who holds *yesh aveilus b'Shabbat* might still permit relations for an *onein* on *Shabbat* since the *avel's* prohibition has not yet begun.

In these closing lines, the *gemara* — without stating a definitive conclusion — is interrogating the very question that the large Tosafot here makes its central concern: are *aninus* and *aveilus* fundamentally distinct states with no intrinsic relationship, or are they essentially one continuous state with situationally triggered modifications? The *gemara's* willingness to draw inferences in both directions, and then to question those inferences, reflects the genuine conceptual difficulty. The answer to the final question — whether an *onein* on *Shabbat* is permitted in *tashmish hamitah* — remains to be concluded in the next *daf*.

# Moed Katan 24

## Avelut on Shabbat

### Private vs. Public

The daf opens in the midst of a discussion about *yesh avelut b'Shabbat* — whether mourning practices are observed on Shabbat. One dimension of that question concerns whether Shabbat counts toward the *shiva* because certain practices are actively maintained on it, or simply because the seven-day period is measured from the outset regardless. The Gemara had previously been weighing evidence from a *braita* that was interpreted to show that at least one opinion prohibits *tashmish hamitah* — sexual relations — during *aninut*, and, by extension, during Shabbat as well. That reading was offered as support for the position of *yesh avelut b'Shabbat*.

Yet even on that view, the suggestion is clearly not full observance of *avelut*. Rather, as the daf makes explicit, the range of practices that continue on Shabbat is limited to what the Gemara calls *devarim she-b'tzina* — private observances. In principle, one might have argued for comprehensive observance of *avelut* on Shabbat. After all, Shabbat is not fundamentally about *simcha* — joy — and it is precisely the *simcha* dimension of a festival that is cited elsewhere as the basis for interrupting *avelut*. Indeed, it is worth noting that *nichum avelim* — comforting mourners — is permitted and even practiced on Shabbat; the Rosh describes a communal custom of publicly visiting the *avel* after synagogue. If Shabbat does not demand joy in a way that precludes mourning, perhaps full observance could stand.

And yet Shabbat is also not the occasion for *tza'ar* — distress — and the Yerushalmi frames its character as one of *bracha* and spiritual pleasure. Accordingly, there is a distinction between the *avel's* public display of anguish, which belongs to the realm Shabbat forecloses, and acts of comfort extended by others, which belong to *gemilut chasadim* and carry no such prohibition. The *avel* changing his seat is admittedly a more public kind of act, but the basic framework holds: the degree of *avelut* that may be observed on Shabbat is limited to private observance — *devarim she-b'tzina*.

### Shmuel: Ein Avelut

The Gemara records that Rabbi Yochanan posed a question to Shmuel: *yesh avelut b'Shabbat o ein avelut b'Shabbat*? Shmuel's answer was unambiguous — *ein avelut b'Shabbat*, mourning is not practiced on Shabbat. Following this, the Gemara reports that the rabbis sitting before Rav Pappa were citing in Shmuel's name the ruling that an *avel* who engages in sexual relations during his period of *avelut* is deserving of death — *chayav mita*. The juxtaposition with Shmuel's statement that there is no *avelut* on Shabbat is jarring, and the question naturally arises: is this statement about *tashmish hamitah* being made in the context of Shabbat?

### Tashmish Hamitah

Rav Pappa corrects the rabbis on two counts. First, what Shmuel actually said was *assur* — forbidden — not *chayav mita*. Second, it was not Shmuel who said it at all; it was Rabbi Yochanan. This matters considerably. The prohibition of *tashmish hamitah* for an *avel* is not a novelty — it has always been among the recognized practices of *avelut*. Why would Rabbi Yochanan need to say it? The natural reading is that we are still operating within the context of the Shabbat debate: perhaps Rabbi Yochanan, who holds *yesh avelut b'Shabbat*, is the one asserting that the prohibition of *tashmish hamitah* extends even to Shabbat, while Shmuel, who holds *ein avelut b'Shabbat*, would not say so.

### Shmuel's Position

The Gemara then clarifies what Shmuel did in fact say — and it has nothing to do with either Shabbat or sexual relations. Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi cites Shmuel as teaching: an *avel* who fails to let his hair grow wild (*para*) or who fails to rend his garments (*peirem*) is *chayav mita* — and a verse from the Torah is adduced in support. The verse in question is the command given to Elazar and Itamar after the deaths of Nadav and Avihu: *rosheichem al tifrau u'vigdeichem lo tifromu v'lo samusu* — do not let your hair go wild, do not rend your garments, lest you die. The logic, as Shmuel reads it, is *mutatis mutandis*: the sons of Aharon were told not to perform the normal practices of *avelut* or they would die. By inversion, ordinary *aveilim* who fail to perform those same practices will likewise face such a consequence.

The derivation is admittedly far from *pshat*. The verse addresses a specific situation tied to the *avodah* of the *mishkan*, not a general law of *avelut*. Nevertheless, Shmuel is using it rhetorically to underscore the seriousness of observing *hilchot avelut*. The Gemara concludes that whatever the rabbis heard in Shmuel's name about *tashmish hamitah* was simply a misattribution: they must have heard Shmuel's exegetical point about *priat harosh* and *keri'at habegadim*, not a statement about sex or about Shabbat. Shmuel's actual position — that *ein avelut b'Shabbat* — is thus left intact, and there is no tension with his earlier statement.

There may be a loose thematic association that gave rise to the confusion: unkempt hair and torn garments appear in contexts involving *sotah* as well, lending a kind of resonance across different areas of *halacha*. But the Gemara's point is clear: the rhetoric about sex belongs to a separate concern entirely — most likely a recognition that private practices of *avelut*, precisely because they carry no social visibility, were vulnerable to being quietly disregarded. The *avel* sits *shiva* in an environment of communal presence and social expectation. The private practices — those that no one else will see — are the ones most likely to be compromised. It is not surprising that the tradition felt the need to address those with particular emphasis.

---

## Public vs. Private

### Pachas Chova

The Gemara now turns to a more systematic treatment of the public/private distinction. Shmuel states: *pachas chova, neter reshus*. The acronym *pachas* stands for *priat harosh* — the *avel's* obligation to uncover or expose his head — *hachzarat kera le'achorav* — turning the rent garment so the tear faces behind — and *zekifat hamita* — setting the beds upright. These are obligations on Shabbat. That is, on Shabbat, the *avel* is *obligated* to perform the opposite of the normal *avelut* practice: to uncover his face, to turn the rent portion of the garment to the back, to right the overturned beds. All of these are highly visible signs of *avelut*, and their reversal is required on Shabbat precisely because of their public character.

*Neter*, by contrast, stands for *ne'ilat hasandal* — wearing shoes — *tashmish hamitah*, and *rechitzat yadayim v'raglayim b'chamin* — washing with hot water at night. These are *reshut* — discretionary, or in the language the Rosh will interpret, obligatory private practices. Regarding these, the language is puzzling. *Reshut* sounds like permission, like the *avel* may choose whether to observe them or not. The Rosh, however, argues that there is no middle ground: if Shabbat does not forbid a practice, then the underlying obligation of *avelut* reasserts itself in full, and the *avel* is obligated to maintain those private practices on Shabbat just as on a weekday. This reading has halachic force — it is indeed how we rule. And yet the language of the Gemara itself, which says *reshut* rather than *chova*, does create some tension, and the plain sense of the word really does seem to suggest discretion.

### Three Private Acts

The three private acts named by Shmuel deserve attention. *Ne'ilat hasandal* — the prohibition against wearing shoes — is perhaps counterintuitive as a *devar she-b'tzina*. Walking outside without shoes would seem obvious to any passerby. Shmuel's rationale is that *lav kulei alma avidi d'saymi masanyeihu* — not everyone wears shoes in all situations, so the bare foot of an *avel* does not necessarily announce his status. *Tashmish hamitah* is the paradigmatic private act — entirely between husband and wife, and known to no one else. *Rechitza b'chamin* — bathing with hot water — is similarly invisible: one cannot tell by looking at someone whether they have bathed or not.

The Rosh's ruling is that these private practices are not merely permitted on Shabbat but obligatory: since Shabbat does not stand in their way, the full force of the *avelut* obligation governs them. The *avel* does not wash with hot water, does not engage in *tashmish hamitah*, does not wear shoes — even on Shabbat.

### Rav's Disagreement

Rav disputes one element of Shmuel's framework: *af priat harosh reshus* — even *priat harosh*, the question of head covering, should be treated as discretionary, meaning the *avel* may (and therefore must, per the Rosh) maintain the covering of his head on Shabbat. According to Rav, veiling the head is not so demonstrably a sign of *avelut* that it must be suspended. This places *priat harosh* in the same category as the other private practices, making it obligatory on Shabbat rather than something that must be reversed.

### Shmuel's Logic

The Gemara explains the reasoning behind Shmuel's more restrictive view. The key passage is this: Shmuel holds *kol kera she-eino b'sha'at chimum eino kera* — any rending of garments that does not occur at the time of emotional intensity is not a valid *keri'at habegadim* — and *kol atifa she-eina k'atifat Yishme'elim eina atifa* — any head wrapping that does not resemble the full Arab-style wrapping is not a genuine *atifa* for purposes of *avelut*. Rav Nachman demonstrates that this wrapping covers the face to the edge of the beard — encompassing the nose, mouth, and cheeks. Because Shmuel defines the *atifat harosh* of *avelut* as this complete and unmistakable veiling of the face, such an act is entirely unambiguous in its message. Nobody walks around with their face covered to the cheekbone unless they are an Arab or an *avel*. Shmuel therefore rules that this practice cannot be maintained on Shabbat, since it is an inherently public declaration of *avelut*.

Rav, by contrast, may understand the practice of *atifat harosh* as a more modest head covering — something that ordinary people might wear for various reasons — and therefore it lacks the demonstrative character that would prohibit it on Shabbat.

The *atifat Yishme'elim* concept, incidentally, carries implications beyond *avelut*. It intersects with discussions among the Geonim about the proper wearing of a *tallit*, since some hold that the biblical *mitzvat tzitzit* requires a garment worn in the full wrapping style — draped over the head and body in the manner of this complete *atifa*. The question of what constitutes a genuine *atifa* thus recurs in other halachic contexts.

As for practical application: the *Shulchan Aruch* rules that an *avel* is obligated in *atifat harosh*, which it describes as covering the head with a cloak or cloth and drawing part of it over the mouth and top of the nose. This is to be maintained at all times, but when visitors arrive for *nichum avelim*, the *avel* uncovers his head in their honor. The Rema, however, notes that in Ashkenazic communities the custom of *atifa* is not practiced at all, and that this is the established *minhag*. Tosafot had noted that performing such a wrapping in their communities would appear bizarre or even ridiculous in the eyes of the surrounding population — and so, like the practice of overturning the beds, it gradually fell away because it lost its communicative force or became practically absurd.

One might ask how the logic of *mochiacha alav* — one practice revealing or concealing the *avel's* status — operates across the full system. The Gemara states that if the *avel* is wearing shoes, then his shoes make his status evident and counteract any inference from his covered head: *minalav mochiach alav*. Tosafot is puzzled by this: if wearing shoes reveals his status, then by the same logic, any one normal behavior — upright beds, uncovered face — should reveal his status and allow all other *avelut* practices to proceed. Tosafot tentatively suggests that shoes carry a particularly strong indicative force — *hocha'a tfei* — but acknowledges the difficulty. In any case, this reasoning has no practical echo in the *halacha* as it developed.

The question of shoes is itself nuanced. In principle the prohibition is *ne'ilat hasandal*, and the standard *psak* is limited to leather shoes. The source for not wearing shoes includes a *pasuk* that speaks of going barefoot, which some authorities read as demanding literal barefoot-going rather than merely the avoidance of leather. This may explain why some are more stringent about shoes during *avelut* than on *Tisha B'Av* or *Yom Kippur*, where sneakers are widely accepted.

### Shmuel's Logic

Returning briefly to the structure of the *pachas/neter* framework: the Gemara presents a statement from Rabbi Yochanan that qualifies the rule about not wearing shoes. *Lo shanu ela she-ein minalim b'raglav* — the exemption from demonstrating *avelut* through bare feet applies only when the *avel* is in fact barefoot. *Aval yesh minalim b'raglav, minalav mochiach alav* — if he is wearing shoes, the shoes themselves make clear that he is not observing *avelut*, which then perhaps permits him to engage in other visible expressions of *avelut* since the shoes are already announcing his non-*avel* status. As noted, Tosafot finds this logic difficult to contain within a coherent system.

### Kol Kera Sha'at Chimum

Before returning to the full discussion of *devarim she-b'tzina*, the Gemara introduces the principle that underpins Shmuel's position on *atifat harosh*: *kol kera she-eino b'sha'at chimum eino kera* — any rending of garments that does not occur at the moment of heightened emotional intensity is not a valid rending. This is stated here in a parenthetical way, but the Gemara will return to it extensively in the next section. The core idea is that the *kriah* must happen in the context of acute emotional response — ideally at the moment of death itself, or in its immediate aftermath. This cannot be policed by reference to an individual's inner state; instead it is framed objectively as a question of timing and context.

---

## Rending Garments

### Shmuel & Rabbi Yochanan

The Gemara returns to the principle of *sha'at chimum* through two striking stories. The rabbis told Shmuel that Rav had died. Shmuel rent twelve garments and declared: *azal gavra de-hava mistafina minei* — the man of whom I was in awe has gone. Similarly, the rabbis told Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Chanina had died. Rabbi Yochanan rent thirteen garments of silk and made the same declaration. In both cases, the rending took place upon hearing the news — not necessarily in the immediate aftermath of the death itself. The Gemara apparently assumes that if the *kriah* is not performed at the actual time of death or burial, it falls outside the objective window of *sha'at chimum*, even if subjectively the person is hearing the news for the first time.

### Rabbis' Exception

The Gemara resolves the tension: *shani rabbanan de-keivan de-chol sha'ata midkri shma'teta* — rabbis are different, because at every moment they are engaged with Torah, and in engaging with their Torah they are also, at every moment, aware of the absence of the colleague they have lost — the one who would challenge them, dispute with them, sharpen their thinking. Therefore, for a Torah scholar mourning a fellow scholar, *u'ke-sha'at chimum dami* — it is as if the emotional intensity of the moment of death is perpetually present.

### Tosafot: Subjective

Tosafot extends this logic significantly. He writes: *ve-li nireh de-ve-chol sha'ah she-yuchal le-hitchamem al meto afilu zman merubeh achar mitato karei shapir bi-sh'at chimum* — in my view, any time that a person can genuinely become emotionally overwrought over the deceased — even considerably after the death — that qualifies as *sha'at chimum*. The case of the rabbis, whose ongoing Torah learning keeps them in perpetual *chimum*, is one illustration of this principle, but the principle itself is broader and essentially subjective: wherever genuine emotional intensity is present and can be genuinely aroused, *kriah* can be performed.

One implication of this analysis: if *kriah* is not performed within the proper *sha'at chimum*, there is no ongoing *chiyuv* to perform it. The question then arises whether rending a garment at an improper time would constitute *bal tashchit* — wanton destruction of property. Most would say yes, since if there is no *chiyuv*, the rending accomplishes nothing and simply ruins a garment.

### Switching Garments

The Gemara cites a *braita*: during the entire *shiva*, the *avel* wears the rent portion of the garment in front, where it is visible. If he wishes to change garments during the week, he must change and rend the new garment as well. On Shabbat, however, he turns the garment around so the rent is behind him — concealed. If on Shabbat he wishes to change garments, he may do so and need not rend the new one.

The difficulty is apparent: how can re-rending during the *shiva* be obligatory if it is not *sha'at chimum*? The Gemara answers: *ki tanya hahi bichvod aviv ve'imo* — that rule applies only in the case of one's parents. For parents, the obligation to wear the rent garment throughout the *shiva* — and to re-rend whenever changing garments — is an expression of *kvod aviv ve'imo* that operates independently of the *sha'at chimum* requirement. It is not an act of *kriah* per se, but an ongoing display of honor and mourning that must be maintained. For other relatives, there is no such obligation, and changing garments during the week does not require a new *kriah*. This is indeed the operative *halacha*.

### Sewing Torn Garments

A further question: may these additional rendings — those done not at *sha'at chimum* but for *kvod aviv ve'imo* — be sewn up after the *shiva*? The father of Rabbi Oshaya and Bar Kappara debate the point. One holds *ein mis'achin* — they cannot be sewn; even though the rending was not at *sha'at chimum*, since it was halachically required it carries the full status of *kriah* and cannot be repaired. The other holds *mis'achin* — they may be sewn, since their status is categorically distinct from the original *sha'at chimum* rending. The Gemara attempts to establish which of the two was the father of Rabbi Oshaya based on what his son Rabbi Oshaya ruled, but the conclusion is uncertain: Rabbi Oshaya may have learned his ruling from his *rebbe* Bar Kappara rather than from his father.

---

## Private Mourning

### Rava's Teaching

Returning to the broader question of *devarim she-b'tzina* on Shabbat, the Gemara cites Rava: *avel metayel be'unkali betoch beiso* — an *avel* may walk about in his house in a certain kind of garment, and by context, in a rent garment on Shabbat. This introduces the spatial dimension: is *devarim she-b'tzina* defined by the nature of the act, or by the setting in which it occurs? Is something private because it is intrinsically invisible to others, or because it happens to take place where no one is looking?

### Abaye's Challenge

Abaye found his *rebbe* Rav Yosef walking around his house on Shabbat with a *sudar* — a cloth — draped over his head in the manner of *atifat harosh*. Abaye challenged him: does the master not hold that there is no *avelut* on Shabbat? Rav Yosef responded that Rabbi Yochanan had said *devarim she-b'tzina noheg* — private practices are observed. The force of the word *noheg* — are practiced, are followed — supports the Rosh's reading that these are obligations, not merely permissions. And yet the question remains: what made this veiling *devarim she-b'tzina*? Was it because Rav Yosef was in his house with no one observing him? Or because the particular kind of head covering he was using was not the full *atifat Yishme'elim* and therefore was not, by its nature, a demonstrative act of *avelut*?

### Tosafot's Doubt

Tosafot raises this as an explicit unresolved question: *mesapka lei* — he is in doubt. The passage about Rava walking in his house in rent garments seems to suggest that being *betoch beiso* — within one's house — is itself the determining factor for *devarim she-b'tzina*. If so, any *avelut* practice done in the privacy of one's home, when no one is watching, would be permitted or even obligatory. Tosafot leaves the question open: does *devarim she-b'tzina* refer to the intrinsic character of the act — its capacity to announce *avelut* to observers — or to the actual absence of observers?

### Modern Practice

The practical conclusion, as the *Shulchan Aruch* formulates it, is that *devarim she-b'tzina* in contemporary practice is limited to *tashmish hamitah* and *rechitza* — bathing. Shoes are classified as *parhesia* in our day because of changed social conventions. The question of not learning Torah is raised as a possible instance of *devarim she-b'tzina*, since a person's failure to learn on a given occasion is not self-evidently an expression of mourning. There is also the fascinating ruling — cited from the Rosh, whose source is *Rabbeinu Tam* — that if an *avel* is regularly called to *aliyot* at a particular position every Shabbat, and he fails to receive that *aliya* while in *avelut*, this constitutes *devarim she-b'farhesia* — a public declaration of his status — and must be avoided. Rabbeinu Tam himself, who habitually received *shlishi* each Shabbat, was once in *avelut* when the *chazzan* did not call him; he arose and took the *aliya* on his own initiative, reasoning that his conspicuous absence from his customary spot would itself have been the *parhesia*. The practice of *maavir sedra* — reviewing the weekly *parasha* twice with *targum* — may similarly be continued, since it resembles the recitation of *Keri'at Shema* and similar obligations.

In the end, the questions around *reshut* — whether the Gemara's language denotes genuine discretion or simply the absence of a Shabbat prohibition — and around the spatial vs. intrinsic definition of *tzina* — are largely left without a clean resolution in the text. The *halacha* as we have it, following the Rosh, collapses the middle ground: what Shabbat does not forbid, *avelut* obligates. But the plain language of the Gemara, and Tosafot's explicit *safek*, leave traces of a more nuanced and perhaps more open-ended original discussion.

---

## Mourning Children

### Rabbi Eliezer

The *daf* turns to a *mishna* that asks which festivals interrupt *avelut* and count as *regalim* for this purpose. Rabbi Eliezer holds that since the destruction of the *Beit HaMikdash*, *Shavuot* has the status only of Shabbat — it interrupts *avelut* for the day but does not carry the weight of a full *regel*. The reasoning is that *Shavuot* derives much of its distinctive character from the *avodah* in the *Mikdash*, and in the absence of the *Mikdash* it has comparatively little ritual content beyond the prohibition of *melacha*. One might also note the absence of any *tashlumin* structure spanning seven days.

### Rabban Gamliel

Rabban Gamliel disagrees and holds that *Shavuot* — and indeed *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur* — all carry the status of full *regalim* that are *mafsikin* the *avelut*. This is striking in the case of *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur*, which are not primarily associated with *simcha*. Nevertheless, Rabban Gamliel extends the interrupting force of *regalim* to encompass them. Rav Gidal bar Menashia cites Shmuel as ruling: *halacha k'Rabban Gamliel* — we rule in accordance with Rabban Gamliel.

### Under 30 Days

The *mishna* continues with age-based gradations in burial and mourning practices for young children. A child who dies within thirty days is not carried out in a coffin but is brought against the chest — *be'cheik*. The burial takes place with one woman and two men, but not one man and two women due to concerns of *yichud*. Abba Shaul permits even one man and two women when the circumstances require it. Furthermore, one does not form the row of consolers after the burial — the formal post-burial comforting ritual — and neither the *birkat avelim* nor the *tanchumei avelim* are recited. The underlying principle is that a child who has not survived thirty days has not yet acquired *chezkat chayim* — a halachic presumption of viability — and in the conditions of the ancient world especially, such a child was treated halachically as akin to a *nefel*, a miscarriage.

### Tosafot: Viability

Tosafot introduces an important distinction. Rashi had explained the thirty-day rule as applying specifically to a child who had not been carried to full term — whose months were incomplete — and for whom viability was therefore not established. Tosafot disputes this and separates two distinct questions. The thirty-day threshold and its attendant burial practices concern the *burial context* specifically, not the *shiva* context. Therefore, a child born at full term who dies within the first month, while the reduced burial formalities may still apply, would nonetheless obligate *shiva* observance — since a full-term birth establishes the child's viability, and there is *avelut* even if the burial is conducted more quietly. The different frameworks — one governing the scope of community mourning and burial rites, the other governing the parents' personal *avelut* obligations — need not align perfectly. Tosafot also notes a distinction in language: the degree of mourning demanded of the community is framed in terms of *tza'aro* — anguish over the child — while more elaborate burial honors are framed as *lichvodo* — honors due to the deceased — and these two considerations operate on different scales.

### 30 Days to 3 Years

Once a child has survived thirty days, the burial becomes more formal. He is carried out in a small coffin — *dlusk'ma*. Rabbi Yehuda specifies that this coffin must be one that cannot be carried on a single shoulder but must be carried in the arms — *b'agapayim*, according to Rabbeinu Gershom, by two people. The row of consolers is formed, and the *birkat avelim* and *tanchumei avelim* are recited. Once a child has reached one year — or, according to Rabbi Akiva, the age of two years, or the size of a two-year-old — he is carried on a full funeral bier with a full coffin. Tosafot notes that in another version of the text, the *tanna kamma* required three years before the full funeral bier, with Rabbi Akiva extending the threshold downward to two years or the equivalent size.

### Community Recognition

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that once a child has reached the stage where he is carried on a full bier, *rabim mit'atzvim alav* — the community gathers in collective mourning. Rabbeinu Gershom explains this as *margishim u'mitza'arim* — communal awareness and shared grief. Rabbi Eliezer ben Azaria formulates the principle most clearly: *nikar l'rabim* — once a child is known in the community, *rabim mis'askin imo* — the community becomes actively involved in his burial and mourning. The converse follows: *eino nikar l'rabim, ein rabim mis'askin imo* — a child who has not yet made any mark in the community, who has not yet been seen in the streets or recognized by neighbors, does not draw communal participation. This is not a comment on the parents' grief, which may be profound regardless of the child's age. It is a recognition that communal mourning responds to communal presence and communal bonds.

### Eulogies by Class

The *mishna* then addresses the question of *hesped* — eulogy — for young children: *aniyim b'nei shalosh, ashirim b'nei chamesh* — children of the poor are eulogized beginning at age three, children of the wealthy beginning at age five. Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yishmael says: children of the poor at five, children of the wealthy at six. Rabbeinu Gershom explains the distinction between rich and poor by noting that a poor person's suffering over his children is greater, since he has fewer other sources of joy or consolation in life. One might alternatively have thought the distinction relates to visibility — wealthy families can afford to shelter their children more at home, while poor children are sooner out in public and thus sooner recognized by the community — but the formulation of *lefi she-ein lo simcha acheres* emphasizes the depth of parental suffering.

### Ben Zekunim

The *mishna* concludes with a further ruling: children of elderly parents — *bnei zekunim* — are treated like children of the poor, meriting earlier *hesped*. The reasoning parallels Rabbeinu Gershom's approach: parents who finally had a child in their old age — the classic *ben zekunim* — suffer the loss with a particular intensity that warrants treating it on par with the greater suffering attributed to poor families.

On the attribution of the halachic ruling: Rav Gidal bar Menashia cites Rav as ruling *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda she'amar mishum Rabbi Yishmael* — we rule in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yishmael on the question of eulogies for children of rich and poor families. The Gemara then clarifies an earlier potential confusion: when Rav Gidal bar Menashia had cited Shmuel as ruling *halacha k'Rabban Gamliel*, that ruling did not pertain to the status of *regalim* but to these laws of mourning practices and communal participation in the burial of young children. The two rulings — one in the name of Shmuel regarding Rabban Gamliel, and one in the name of Rav regarding Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Yishmael — belong to different halachic questions and must not be conflated. The daf concludes here; the definitive *psak halacha* regarding the *regalim* that interrupt *avelut* will be completed in the following discussion.

---

---

# Moed Katan 25

## Shavuos & Regel

### Shavuos Post-Churban

The daf begins in the middle of 24b, resuming the discussion of how a *regel* interrupts *avelus*. The preceding material had treated the sensitive distinctions between individual mourning obligations and the more public, communal dimensions of mourning — obligations that only attach once a person has been recognized as a member of the community. We now return to the question of whether *Shavuos*, post-*Churban*, retains the status of a *regel* for purposes of interrupting *shiva* and *shloshim*. The broader ruling is that *Shavuos*, *Rosh Hashanah*, and *Yom Kippur* are all treated as *regalim* capable of being *mafsik* the *avelus*.

### Rav Annani Darshan

Three lines into the wide-margin text, the Gemara records: *darash Rav Annani bar Sasson a-pitcha de-vei Nasi* — Rav Annani bar Sasson expounded the following ruling on the doorstep of the *Beis HaNasi*: *yom echad lifnei Atzeres ve-Atzeres harei kan arba asar* — one day before *Shavuos* and *Shavuos* itself count as fourteen days. The logic proceeds as follows: when *Shavuos* arrives, the *shiva* ends. Then the *chag* of *Shavuos*, as a *regel*, is *oleh* for the *shloshim*. The striking *halacha* here is that *Shavuos*, by virtue of the concept of *tashlumin* and the broader idea of a *regel* carrying the weight of seven, counts as seven days — even though only one day of *Yom Tov* was actually observed. The person emerging from this sequence therefore has only sixteen days of *shloshim* observance remaining.

### Ami & Sheshes

*Shama Rabbi Ami ve-ikpid* — Rabbi Ami heard and was upset. His objection was not that the *halacha* was incorrect, but that it was being presented as an independent teaching. *Atu didei?* — Is this your own ruling? *Rabbi Elazar amar Rabbi Oshaya!* — it belongs to Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya. The same scene then repeats: *darash Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha a-pitcha de-kila d'Reish Galusa* — Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha expounded the identical ruling in the pavilion of the Reish Galusa — *yom echad lifnei Atzeres ve-Atzeres harei kan arba asar* — and Rav Sheshes likewise heard and was likewise upset, making the same attribution: *Rabbi Elazar amar Rabbi Oshaya*.

### Shavuos Tashlumin

The underlying source attributed to Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya is now cited: *minayin she-Shavuos yesh lah tashlumin kol shiva?* — from where do we derive that *Shavuos* has *tashlumin* for all seven days? *She-ne'emar: be-chag ha-matzos u-ve-chag ha-Shavuos u-ve-chag ha-Sukkos* — just as *Pesach* is a seven-day festival during which one may make up missed *korbanos* for all seven days, so too *Shavuos* has *tashlumin kol shiva*. The six days following *Shavuos* have a special halakhic status as days within which a *korban chagiga* may be brought in compensation.

What is not immediately obvious, and what invites closer scrutiny, is the derivational connection between this teaching and the *halacha* of *avelus*. The teaching of Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya establishes *tashlumin* for *Shavuos* in the context of *korbanos*, not mourning. That one day of *Shavuos* should carry the weight of seven days for purposes of *shloshim* counting is not a direct derivation from this source. At most, it seems, the later ruling is implicit in or derivative of the earlier one.
