This makes the indignation of Rabbi Ami and Rav Sheshes somewhat puzzling: if the connection is derivative rather than explicit, why is it so important to attribute it to Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya? One possible answer is that one should at minimum have acknowledged the source upon which the ruling rests; another is that perhaps Rabbi Elazar in fact stated both teachings and only the underlying *halacha* has been quoted here. The matter remains unresolved.

### Rosh Hashanah Paradox

*Ata Rav Pappa legabi Avia Sava ve-darash* — Rav Pappa brought along Rav Avia Sava (who presumably served as his *maggid* to announce the teaching) and expounded: *yom echad lifnei Rosh Hashanah ve-Rosh Hashanah harei kan arba'ah asar* — one day before *Rosh Hashanah* and *Rosh Hashanah* together count as fourteen days. This is more striking than the ruling regarding *Shavuos*, because *Rosh Hashanah* has no concept of *tashlumin kol shiva*. *Rosh Hashanah* is *yoma arichta*, a single long day — but even granting that, it does not by itself produce the quantity of seven days.

### Succos & Shemini

Ravina then extends the logic to its furthest application: *hilkach yom echad lifnei ha-chag ve-chag u-shemini shelo harei kan esrim ve-echad yom* — one day before *Sukkos*, the seven days of *Sukkos*, and *Shemini Atzeres* together account for twenty-one days, leaving only nine days of *shloshim* to be observed thereafter. The accounting runs as follows: one day before *Sukkos* terminates the *shiva*, removing seven days from the *shloshim*; the seven days of *Sukkos* itself, as a *regel* that is *oleh* for the *shloshim*, accounts for another seven; and then *Shemini Atzeres*, as a single-day *Yom Tov* that — on the principle being discussed — counts as seven days toward the *shloshim*, contributes the final seven. Total: twenty-one days, with nine days of *shloshim* remaining.

### Chaviva Challenge

Rav Chaviva from Sura by the Euphrates raised a challenge to Ravina, citing the teaching that one day before *Rosh Hashanah* and *Rosh Hashanah* itself amount to fourteen days — meaning that a single-day *Yom Tov* counts as seven days. This is, as he implies, a striking and counterintuitive position. Ravina responded: *ana mistabra ke-Rabban Gamliel hu de-amina* — I was quoted imprecisely. What I said was that it stands to reason according to Rabban Gamliel that *Rosh Hashanah* and *Yom Kippur* are *mafsik* the *avelus* — I never stated the further ruling that *Rosh Hashanah* itself counts as a full seven days.

### Tosafos Analysis

Tosafos raises the pointed question of what practical purpose this ruling regarding *Rosh Hashanah* serves. The *halacha* that *Shavuos* counts as fourteen days, or that *Sukkos* together with *Shemini Atzeres* accounts for twenty-one days — these rulings have genuine practical consequences. But who needs the ruling that *Rosh Hashanah* accounts for fourteen days? Ten days after *Rosh Hashanah* comes *Yom Kippur*, which will in any case terminate the *shloshim*. Whatever additional days *Rosh Hashanah* might subtract from the *shloshim* are therefore irrelevant. Similarly, a parallel ruling regarding *Yom Kippur* would be rendered moot by the arrival of *Sukkos*. Tosafos labors to find a resolution but reaches no clearly satisfying answer. Indeed, examining the *Shulchan Aruch* confirms that no practical *halacha* is recorded to the effect that *Rosh Hashanah* counts as fourteen days. The *Shulchan Aruch* states simply that if one observes a bit of *avelus* before *Rosh Hashanah*, *Rosh Hashanah* ends the *shiva* and *Yom Kippur* ends the *shloshim*; or if one observes a bit before *Yom Kippur*, *Yom Kippur* ends the *shiva* and *Sukkos* ends the *shloshim*. The strange *halacha* of a non-*regel* counting as seven days is thus effectively moot in practice — which leaves open the question of why the Gemara bothered to state it at all.

---

## Keriah & Relatives

### Mishnah Ein Korin

The Gemara now arrives at the next *Mishnah*. It is worth pausing to orient ourselves: the entire foregoing discussion of *avelus* — which has occupied a full week of study — has been an explication of a single *mishnah* about *regalim* and *Shabbos* being *mafsik*. The tractate is, of course, *Moed Katan*, whose primary subject is *Chol HaMoed*, and we now reach one of the final two *mishnayot* in the chapter.

The *Mishnah* states: *ein korin v'lo choltzin* — one does not perform *keriah* (the tearing of the garment upon hearing of a death) and does not perform *chalitzah* — here meaning not the *chalitzah* of *Hilchos Yevamos* but the uncovering of the shoulder in mourning, as we have seen discussed previously. *V'ein mavrin* — and one does not serve the *seudat havra'ah*, the meal provided to the mourner immediately after returning from the cemetery, which halachically must come from others' food rather than the *avel*'s own. *Ela kerovo shel meis* — except for the immediate relatives of the deceased.

The question this immediately raises is: why does the *Mishnah* need to specify these particular practices? If it means to say simply that one does not observe *shiva* or *shloshim* except as a relative, why single out *keriah*, *chalitzah*, and *seudat havra'ah*? The answer, on a straightforward *peshat* reading, is that these three practices — unlike *shiva* and *shloshim*, which are multi-day ongoing observances — are immediate expressions of grief: they are performed at the moment of tragedy, not sustained over days. There was evidently a practice for non-relatives to perform them upon the death of great sages or community leaders, as we will shortly see confirmed by a *braita*. The *Mishnah* therefore needed to address this phenomenon explicitly and restrict these practices to relatives.

### General vs. Chol Hamoed

However, the question of what the *Mishnah* is actually addressing is complicated by a second, very different way of reading it. The *Yerushalmi*, followed by most *Rishonim*, understands the *Mishnah* as speaking specifically about *Chol HaMoed*. On this reading, the *Mishnah* is not making a general statement about *avelus* throughout the year; it is specifying what practices are permitted during *Chol HaMoed* for the immediate relatives of someone who died during that period. We have already established that the full observance of *shiva* does not apply during *Chol HaMoed*; but these immediate expressions — *keriah*, *chalitzah*, and *seudat havra'ah* — would still be performed by the *krovim* even on *Chol HaMoed*, whereas no one else would observe them. This is a perfectly natural reading given the context of *Moed Katan*, whose subject is *Chol HaMoed*. After a sustained immersion in *hilchos avelus*, it is easy to lose sight of the fact that the *Mishnah* itself is situated within a tractate about *Chol HaMoed*, and the transition back to that context is fully coherent on this reading.

The Gemara, as we will see, does not engage with the *Chol HaMoed* reading; it appears to treat the *Mishnah* as a general statement and proceeds accordingly.

### Seudas Havraah

The *Mishnah* adds: *v'ein mavrin ela al mitah zekufah* — one does not serve the *seudat havra'ah* except on an upright couch, not on an overturned one. The term *mitah* here should be understood not as a sleeping bed but as a kind of divan or couch upon which people would recline when eating — far more relevant to the question of dining posture than to sleeping arrangements.

### Two Readings

This clause generates two sharply divergent interpretations. Rabbeinu Gershom, who reads the *Mishnah* as a general statement unconnected to *Chol HaMoed*, understands the two occurrences of *mavrin* in the *Mishnah* as referring to two different subjects: the first means the *avel* receiving the *seudat havra'ah*, and the second means the person serving it. On this reading, the *avel* is reclining on an overturned couch as part of his mourning practice, while the person feeding him — who is not an *avel* — should sit on an upright couch, not an overturned one.

The Ra'avad, following the *Yerushalmi* and the *Rosh*, reads the *Mishnah* as specifically about *Chol HaMoed* and rejects the idea of a distinction between the *avel*'s couch and the feeder's couch. On the contrary, they maintain that the person providing the *seudat havra'ah* would actually sit together with the *avel* for that meal — and if there was sufficient intimacy and closeness between them, they would recline together. On *Chol HaMoed*, however, the overturning of couches is a *davar she-be-farhesya* — a public, visible act of mourning — that is not performed. Hence the *Mishnah* specifies that even those relatives who do perform the *seudat havra'ah* on *Chol HaMoed* will do so on an upright couch, not an overturned one.

The two readings thus diverge in both their subject and their substance: one is a general *halacha* about the etiquette of serving the *seudat havra'ah* at any time of year, while the other is a specific *Chol HaMoed* ruling about which visible mourning practices are and are not suspended.

---

## Chacham Exception

### Braita Chacham

The Gemara does not accept the possibility that the *Mishnah* might be arguing against the well-established practice of performing *keriah* for great sages and communal leaders. The practice was too firmly attested — both in other *Tannaic* sources and in the narratives we have already encountered — for the Gemara to read the *Mishnah* as abolishing it. Instead, the Gemara brackets that apparent implication and asks: *v'afilu chacham?* — would one not perform *keriah* even for a *chacham*, even if one were not his relative?

The answer comes from a *braita*: *chacham she-meis, hakol krovo* — when a *chacham* dies, everyone is his relative. The Gemara immediately clarifies: surely one does not mean literally that everyone is his relative — *ela hakol k'krovo* — everyone is *like* his relative.

### Keriah Chacham

The *braita* continues: *hakol kor'in alav* — everyone must perform *keriah*; *v'hakol choltzin alav* — everyone must uncover the shoulder; *v'hakol mavrin alav ba-rachava* — everyone participates in the *avelus* meal in the public thoroughfare. The logic of these three practices — *keriah*, *chalitzah*, and *havra'ah* — being extended to the entire community becomes clear when we understand their character. Unlike *shiva*, which is a sustained, multi-day observance, these are immediate expressions of the tragedy. When a great sage dies, the entire community performs *keriah*, participates in the procession to the cemetery, and then comes together for the meal of mourning in the public domain. After that, the *krovim* continue with *shiva* while the broader community returns to normal life. The *Mishnah*, on this reading, was never intended to prohibit these practices for great sages; it addresses the ordinary case of a private individual.

### Adam Kasher Theology

The Gemara presses further: even if the deceased is not a *chacham*, if he is an *adam kasher* — an upright, morally exemplary individual, someone who may have no official standing in the community but who is recognized as a paragon of ethical conduct — is one *chayav* to perform *keriah*? The Gemara cites a *braita* that addresses this in the starkest possible terms: *mipnei mah metim banav u-vnotav shel adam k'she-heim ktanim?* — why does a person's sons and daughters die when they are still young? *K'dei she-yivkeh v'yitabel al adam kasher* — so that he should cry and mourn for an upstanding individual when that person dies.

The Gemara is visibly troubled by this teaching, even on its own terms. *Arvona kashkil mineih?* — You are taking a collateral from him? The idea that a person is punished in advance so that he will do the right thing in the future strains credulity even as logic. The Gemara therefore pivots: *ella mipnei she-lo bacha v'yitabel al adam kasher* — it is rather because the person already failed to mourn appropriately for a worthy individual who died in the past. The punishment is thus retrospective, not prospective.

This remains deeply troubling theologically. The ideas of *poked avon avot al banim* and the broader framework in which children's deaths are understood as punishment for parental failures reflect a worldview that is, frankly, extremely disturbing. Part of the context is a society in which child mortality was devastatingly common, and the *braita* represents an attempt — however difficult for us — to find some framework of meaning within that reality. It is also worth noting that if one must suffer for failing to honor the morally great, the logic may be that such a failure reveals a deep confusion about what is genuinely valuable in the world. A *chacham* has clear communal status; everyone knows who he is. An *adam kasher* who is an ordinary layperson — perhaps an accountant, recognized by no official title — has only his intrinsic moral worth. Failing to acknowledge the gravity of his death may reveal that one has not internalized what truly matters. That said, the harshness of the statement cannot be softened away.

### Forgiveness Benefit

The *braita* then offers a more positive formulation: *shekol ha-boche u-misabel al adam kasher mochalin lo al kol avonasav* — whoever cries and mourns for an *adam kasher*, all of his sins are forgiven, *bishvil kavod she-asa lo* — on account of the honor shown to him. The theological implication is the mirror image of the punishment: acknowledging the true worth of a morally great person, regardless of his social standing, itself constitutes a recognition of genuine values — and that recognition earns forgiveness.

The Gemara then returns to the practical question of reconciliation between the *Mishnah* and the *braita*: the *Mishnah*, it concludes, speaks to the ordinary case — someone who is not a *chacham* and not an *adam kasher*. The practice of *keriah* and *chalitzah* for such a person, even a close friend or a somewhat distant relative, is limited to actual *krovim*. The exceptional cases of a *chacham* and an *adam kasher* fall outside the *Mishnah*'s intended scope.

### Keriah at Death

The Gemara identifies yet another case that obligates *keriah* regardless of the relationship to the deceased: *d'kai hasam b'sha'as yetzias neshama* — one who is physically present at the moment the soul departs. A *braita* in the name of Rav Shimon ben Elazar teaches: *ha-omed al ha-meis b'sha'as yetzias neshama chayav likroa* — one who stands over the dying person at the actual moment of death is obligated to perform *keriah*. *L'ma ze domeh? L'sefer Torah she-nisraf* — to what is this comparable? To witnessing a *sefer Torah* being burned. At the moment of death, any person — by virtue of the soul that departs — is like a *sefer Torah*; the witness to that moment is obligated to express the tragedy through *keriah*. The *Mishnah*'s restriction to *krovim* thus applies specifically when one was not present at the moment of death and the deceased is neither a *chacham* nor an *adam kasher*.

### Rav Safra Story

The Gemara illustrates these principles through a narrative. When Rav Safra died, the rabbinic students did not perform *keriah* for him. Their reasoning: *lav gaminei minei* — he was not our *Rebbe*; we did not study directly under him. Abaye challenged them: *mi tanya ha-rav she-meis?* — does the *braita* say "your *rav*"? It says *chacham she-meis* — a *sage* who dies, which requires no personal relationship. Moreover, Abaye added, even on their own terms: *kol yoma shmatetei b'funin b'vei medrasha* — his teachings are in our mouths every day in the *beis medrasha*. The students then concluded that since they had missed the moment, *mah de-hava hava* — what was was; the time for *keriah* had passed. Abaye corrected them again.

### Hesped Timing

The *braita* states: *chacham kol zman she-oskin be-hesped chayavin likro'a* — for a *chacham*, as long as the *hesped* is still being delivered, one remains obligated to perform *keriah*. This makes deep sense once one appreciates the function of a *hesped* in the rabbinic world: the eulogy was not merely a biographical tribute but was designed to stir profound emotion, to move people to cry and wail and feel the full weight of the loss. *Keriah* performed during the *hesped* is therefore not a belated afterthought but the expression of being genuinely overwhelmed — and that is precisely the moment of *kavod* for the deceased.

The students, hearing this, concluded that since further eulogies were scheduled for later in the day, they could perform *keriah* immediately in anticipation. Abaye corrected them a third time: *chacham kevodo be-hespedo* — the greatest *kavod* for a *chacham* is to perform *keriah* at the actual moment of the *hesped* itself, not in advance of it and not disconnected from it. The proper time is the moment when the eulogy is actively being delivered and one is moved by it — not a calculated performance outside that context.

---

## Rav Huna Funeral

### Sefer Torah Plan

The Gemara now opens an extended narrative about the death and burial of Rav Huna. Upon his death, the community wished to place a *sefer Torah* in his coffin — or rather on the bed on which he would be carried — to accompany him on the procession to the cemetery. This was not a plan to bury the *sefer Torah*; the intention was that he would be carried alongside it, evoking the declaration *kiyam zeh mah she-kasuv be-zeh* — this person fulfilled everything written in this scroll. The practice of accompanying a great sage's body with a *sefer Torah* as a statement about his embodiment of *Torah* was known in other contexts.

### Torah Prohibition

Rav Chisda objected: *milta d'be-chayim lo sevira lei, hashta lekum ve-liyavid lei?* — something that in his lifetime he would not have done, you now want to do to him? The evidence comes from Rav Tachlifa, who reported: *ana chaziteih l'Rav Huna deba'i le-misav apurya* — I once saw Rav Huna wish to sit on a couch on which a *sefer Torah* was resting. Rather than simply move the *sefer Torah* aside and sit down, he took a vessel, overturned it on the floor, and placed the *sefer Torah* on top of it as a kind of makeshift stand. The inference: *kasavar assur lishev al gabi mita she-sefer Torah munach aleiha* — Rav Huna held that one may not sit on a couch upon which a *sefer Torah* rests. To now have him lie in a coffin alongside a *sefer Torah* would violate the very principle he had lived by.

### Doorway Problem

The next difficulty: *lo havah nafik purya mi-baba* — the bed could not be taken out through the doorway. The king-size bed on which Rav Huna lay simply would not fit. The community considered hoisting it up through the roof — carrying it out through a window and across the rooftop, or lowering it from there.

### Petach Requirement

Rav Chisda intervened again: *gamirna minei — chacham kevodo derech petach* — I have learned from him that the proper and honorable way to remove a *chacham* is through the *petach*, the doorway, not through any window or roof. The *kavod ha-meis* demands that the body exit through the front door.

### Narrower Bed

The next proposed solution: *savru la-shunoyei mi-purya le-purya* — transfer him from the large bed to a narrower one that would fit through the doorway. The logic is intuitive: if the obstacle is the width of the bed, find a narrower bed, and the body can be carried out through the door with full dignity.

### First Bed Honor

Rav Chisda objected a second time: *hachi gamirna minei — chacham kevodo be-mitah rishonah* — I have learned from him that the *kavod* of a *chacham* lies in being carried on the first bed, the original bed upon which he died or was first laid. Moving the body to a second, substitute piece of furniture would itself be a diminishment of honor.

### Aron Wagon Source

The source for this principle is a teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: *minayin le-chacham she-kevodo be-mitah rishonah? She-ne'emar: vayarkivu et aron ha-Elohim al agalah chadashah* — where is it derived that a *chacham*'s honor lies in being carried on the first conveyance? From the verse that describes the *aron* of God being placed on a wagon — understood here as the same wagon on which it had originally been sent back by the *Pelishtim*, not a newly fashioned one. The *aron* was not transferred to a new wagon; it was returned on the same vehicle that had carried it from the beginning. The parallel to the *chacham* resting on his *mitah rishonah* thus draws on the same principle applied to the *aron* itself — a powerful comparison, and one that complements the earlier association of a *chacham* with a *sefer Torah*.

It is worth noting the distinction between this *halacha* and the previous one about the *petach*: the requirement to exit through the doorway appears to apply to *meis* generally, while the *mitah rishonah* rule is stated specifically with respect to a *chacham*.

### Demolish Door

With no permissible alternative, the solution was simply: *poretz bava ve-afkuhu* — they demolished the doorway and took him out. The original bed, the proper exit through the *petach*, and the *kavod* of Rav Huna were all preserved — at the cost of the door.

---

## Hesped Journey

### Abba Eulogy

With Rav Huna's body now being transported to *Eretz Yisrael* for burial, the Gemara turns to the eulogies delivered over him. *Patach alei Rabbi Abba* — Rabbi Abba opened with the following: *rauy haya Rabbeinu she-tishreh alav Shechina* — our teacher was worthy of having the *Shechina* rest upon him, *ela she-Bavel garma lei* — except that being in *Bavel* prevented it, for the *Shechina* rests only on those in *Eretz Yisrael*.

### Yechezkel Challenge

*Metiv Rav Nachman bar Chisda* — and some say *Rav Chana bar Chisda* — immediately challenged: the verse states *haya haya devar Hashem el Yechezkel ben Buzi ha-Kohen be-eretz Kasdim* — the word of God came to Yechezkel in the land of *Kasdim*, meaning *Bavel*. Yechezkel received *nevua* in *Bavel*. How then can one say the *Shechina* does not rest outside *Eretz Yisrael*?

### No Questions

His father struck him on the sandal in response and said: *lav amina lach lo tatrid alma?* — have I not told you not to bother people, not to disturb the occasion? *Mah haya she-haya kvar* — what was, was. The implicit message is clear: one does not raise *kushyas* in the middle of a *hesped*. Rabbeinu Gershom offers an additional resolution on the merits: Yechezkel had begun his *nevua* in *Eretz Yisrael*, and having established that connection, *she-haya kvar*, he was able to continue receiving prophecy even in *Bavel*. But this is offered more as a *teretz* than as a demonstrated reading of the text.

### Ami Assi Fear

When the procession arrived in *Eretz Yisrael*, word was sent to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi: *Rav Huna ati* — Rav Huna is coming. Their response was immediate alarm: *ki havinnan tam, lo hava lan le-mizkpei reshin mineih* — when we were there in *Bavel*, we could not lift our heads in his presence. He was so imposing, so towering in his *Torah*, that they lived in a kind of constant awe. *Ha-shta ateinan hacha, ata batran?* — Now that we have come here, he is coming after us?

### Coffin Clarified

They were informed: *arona hu de-ati* — it is his coffin that is coming. He is dead. Upon clarification, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi went out to participate in the funeral procession.

### Transport Dispute

Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Chanina did not go out. A variant tradition records that Rabbi Ila went while Rabbi Chanina did not. This distinction — who went out and who did not — has been preserved across two millennia. The reason those who went out did so: a *braita* teaches that when a coffin is transported from place to place, the community in the new location *stands in the shura*, recites *birkas avelim*, and offers *tanchumei avelim* — the full funeral observances are repeated at each stop. Therefore, going out to participate was appropriate and obligatory.

### Skeleton Status

Those who did not go out relied on a different *braita*: *aron ha-over mi-makom le-makom ein omdim alav be-shura* — when a coffin is transported from place to place, one does not stand in formation, does not recite *birkas avelim*, and does not offer *tanchumei avelim*. The two *braitot* appear to contradict each other. The Gemara resolves: *lo kashya — kan she-shildo kayemet, kan she-ein shildo kayemet* — the distinction depends on whether the skeleton is still intact. If the skeleton remains whole, the body still bears the character of a *meis* in a full sense, and the funeral observances are repeated at the new location. If the skeleton has already decomposed into disconnected bones, the full ritual is not repeated. *Ve-shilda de-Rav Huna kayemes hava* — Rav Huna's skeleton was still intact. Those who did not go out were simply not aware of this fact; they had not been informed, and therefore did not know that circumstances warranted going out.

---

## Cave Burial

### Cave Choice

With Rav Huna's body now in *Eretz Yisrael*, the question arose: *heicha ninchei?* — where should he be buried? The reasoning offered: *Rav Huna reibitz Torah b'Yisrael, Rav Chiya reibitz Torah b'Yisrael* — Rav Huna disseminated *Torah* in Israel, and Rabbi Chiya disseminated *Torah* in Israel. Rabbi Chiya's contribution was legendary: he famously declared that he would ensure *Torah* would never be lost from Israel, and he implemented a remarkable system — producing *sifrei Torah*, distributing them, and establishing a structure in which students became teachers and teachers empowered new teachers, creating a self-sustaining chain of transmission. Since both men had contributed to the broad dissemination of *Torah* across Israel, Rav Huna should be buried next to Rabbi Chiya.

### Chaga Volunteer

*Amar lehu Rav Chaga: ana ma'ayilna lei* — Rav Chaga volunteered to bring the body into the cave where Rabbi Chiya was buried.

### Chaga Credentials

Rav Chaga offered his credentials: *d'ukmaseih le-talmudei ki havina bar tamnei srei shanin* — he had established his learning — presenting the full corpus of what he had studied before his teacher — when he was just eighteen years old; *v'lo chazai li keri* — and he never experienced a seminal emission throughout that period; *u-meshamshi lei kamei* — and he served as Rav Huna's personal attendant; *ve-yada'ina b'uvdeih* — and he knows his deeds intimately. He then illustrated: one day the strap of Rav Huna's *tefillin* became reversed, with the white side exposed and the black turned inward. Rav Huna thereupon fasted forty fasts in penance. Rav Chaga was thereby making two claims simultaneously: that his own virtue would permit him safe passage into the protected cave, and that his intimate relationship with Rav Huna made him the fitting person for this task.

### Sons Request

Inside the cave, Rabbi Chiya's two sons, Yehuda and Chizkiya, were buried on either side of their father — one to his right, one to his left. Yehuda said to Chizkiya: *kum mi-duchach* — rise from your place. According to Rabbeinu Chananel's text, the more readily intelligible version, the formulation is: *d'lav orach ara d'ka'i Rav Huna mi-bara'i* — it is not appropriate that Rav Huna should remain outside. Room needed to be made.

### Fire Pillar

As Chizkiya rose, *kama bahadei amuda de-nura* — a pillar of fire rose together with him. Rav Chaga saw this pillar of fire emerging from within the cave, was seized with terror, stood the *aron* of Rav Huna upright, and fled. The *aron* was thus left unburied.

### Punishment Question

The Gemara observes: *v'hai d'lo i-anish — mishum d'zakfei l'arona de-Rav Huna* — the reason Rav Chaga was not punished was because he had stood up the *aron*. But this explanation is deeply puzzling. Rav Chaga had been chosen precisely for his virtue and his closeness to Rav Huna. His flight left the body unburied. How does standing the *aron* upright — apparently using it as a shield between himself and the fire before fleeing — constitute a sufficient justification for his not being punished? The text is very difficult, and satisfying analysis is hard to find.

Rabbeinu Chananel's version offers a different reading: *hai d'lo i-anish d'vei nesi'ah* — those of the *Beis HaNasi*'s household were not punished, a reference to the special merit and protection associated with Rav Huna's lineage from the *Nasi*. This formulation at least shifts the ground of the explanation, but it does not fully account for what Rav Chaga did and why it was treated as acceptable. The question, for now, is left open.

---

---

# Moed Katan 27

## Blasphemy & Keriah

### Direct vs. Repeated Hear…

The *daf* under discussion is 26a, and we pick up in the middle of a *baraita* addressing the obligation of *keriah* upon hearing God's name blasphemed — *birchas hashem*. The *Tanu Rabanan* teaches: *echad hashome'a* — whether a person hears the blasphemy directly — *v'echad hashome'a mi'pi hashome'a* — or hears it being repeated, presumably not merely a report that it occurred, but an actual literal repetition of the words. *Tosfos* clarifies the context: this refers to witnesses who, in the course of testifying against the blasphemer, are required to actually repeat what was said. The result is that everyone present hears the blasphemy a second time from the witnesses' lips. In either case, *chayav likro'a* — one is obligated to perform *keriah*.

### Witnesses & Precedent

The *baraita* continues: *v'ha'edim einam chayavim likro'a* — the witnesses themselves, when they repeat the blasphemy during testimony, are not obligated to tear again, *she'kevar kar'u b'sha'as sheshamu* — because they already tore when they first heard it. The *Gemara* challenges this: what does it matter that they heard it once before? They are hearing it again now, from their own lips — *haksha'ami hashta*. The *Gemara* responds, *lo salkas daiteich* — do not think that way — *dichsiv*, for the verse tells us: *vayehi kishmo'a hamelech Chizkiyahu* — when King Chizkiyahu heard the report of *Ravshakeh*'s blasphemy, *vayikra es begadav* — he rent his garments. The verse records that the king tore, *hamelech kara v'heim lo kar'u*, but the people who came and reported it — who repeated the very words — did not tear again. It says they arrived with rent garments, not that they rent them anew.

### Gezerah Shavah Rule

The *Gemara* then asks: *v'lo mis'achi minalan* — how do we know that the tearing in these circumstances, whether for *birchas hashem*, the death of a *nasi* or *av beis din*, or national tragedy, cannot be sewn up? The answer is *asya kriya kriya* — we make a *gzeira shava*. Just as we previously learned regarding *keriah* for one's parents and teacher, deriving from the story of *Eliyahu* and *Elisha* that the tear is not repaired, so too here, since the same language of *tikra* appears, the *gzeira shava* teaches that the tear is permanent.

### Tosafot's Challenge

*Tosfos* raises an immediate difficulty: *teima im kein neileif kol kriyos shelo yis'achu* — if this *gzeira shava* applies, should we not derive that every act of *keriah* is irreparable, since the word *kriya* appears throughout? The answer given is *v'shema lo mistavra lei* — it simply does not make sense to extend the principle universally. *Tosfos* acknowledges that *Chazal* had a prior understanding of which acts of *keriah* were appropriate to repair and which were not, and applied the *gzeira shava* selectively to those that fit. This is a striking *Tosfos*, because in *yeshivos* these *drashos* are often taught as though they operate mechanically. Here we see explicitly that the application of a *gzeira shava* is not automatic — there is an element of judgment in determining to which cases the textual link applies, and what its implications are.

---

## Sefer Torah Burnt

### Yehoyakim Story

The *Gemara* now turns to the case of a *Sefer Torah* that has been burnt: *Sefer Torah she-nisraf minalan* — where do we learn the obligation of *keriah* in such a circumstance? The verse in Yirmiyahu says: *vayehi kikhro Yehudi shalosh delatot v'arba* — when the servant read three or four sections. This refers to the reading of the scroll that Yirmiyahu had written, understood by the *Gemara* to be *Megilas Eicha*.

The *Gemara* tells us that they informed Yehoyakim, *katav Yirmiyah Sefer Kinot* — Yirmiyahu wrote a book of lamentations. Yehoyakim asked what was written in it. They told him: *Eicha yashvah vadad* — how does the city dwell alone? He said: *ana malka* — I am a king, nothing will befall me. They continued: *bacho tivkeh ba-lailah* — it cries at night. He replied again: I am a king. *Galtah Yehudah me-oni* — Judah will be exiled from oppression. Still: I am a king, it will not affect me. *Darchei Tziyon aveilot* — the ways of Zion mourn. I am a king. But then: *hayu tzareha lerosh* — its enemies will become its rulers. At this he became alarmed and asked, *man amrah* — who said this? For it was no longer about Zion in the abstract. Then: *Ki Hashem hogah al rov p'shaeha* — God planned this because of its many sins. Suddenly this was about God acting against him. *Mi-yad* — immediately, *kadar kol ha-azkarot she-bah* — he cut out all the divine names from the scroll, *v'sorfan ba-esh* — and burnt them in the fire, as an act of defiance against God.

### Non-Response Paradox

The *Gemara* then notes: *v'hainu dichsiv velo pachadu velo kar'u es bigdeihem* — and that is why the verse records that those present did not fear and did not rend their garments. The implication — *miklal di-vau le-mikra* — is that the proper response would have been *keriah*, and their failure to do so is what the verse calls attention to.

### Scroll vs. Names

One might note that the narrative as the *Gemara* presents it places particular emphasis on the burning of *shem Hashem* — the divine names — rather than the destruction of the entire scroll. *Tosfos* raises this directly: the simple sense of the verse, *vayikraeha b'ta'ar hasofer* — he cut it with the scribe's razor — implies the entire scroll was destroyed. *U'vi-Yerushalmi lo garsinan azkarot* — and in the Yerushalmi the text does not specify that it was specifically the divine names that were burnt. This matters because emphasizing the names would shift the focus of the *keriah* obligation, distinguishing between the destruction of the physical scroll and the destruction of God's name.

### Rav Papa's Question

Rav Papa raises a further question to Abaye: *eima mishum shmuot raot* — perhaps the obligation of *keriah* in this narrative derives from the terrible news of the impending national catastrophe, since the scroll spoke of exile and destruction? Abaye replies: *shmuot raot b'hahi sha'ata mi havu* — those were predictions, not events that had yet occurred. The obligation of *keriah* for bad tidings applies only to tragedies that have actually taken place, not to prophecies of future calamities.

### Two Tearings Rule

Rabbi Chelbo said in the name of Rav Huna: *ha-roeh Sefer Torah she-nikrah chayav likro shtei kriyos* — one who sees a *Sefer Torah* that has been torn is obligated to perform two acts of *keriah*, *achas al ha-gevil v'achas al ha-ketav* — one for the parchment and one for the script. The source is: *acharei s'rof ha-melech es ha-Megilah v'es ha-dvarim* — after the king burnt the scroll and the words. The physical embodiment and the content of the words are each an independent reason for *keriah* — the attempt to destroy the words and meaning of the text is at least as weighty a cause as the destruction of the physical medium.

---

## Tefillin Story

### Ostrich Incident

The *Gemara* now presents a story that partially illuminates the parameters of this obligation. Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya were sitting before Rabbi Abba. Rabbi Abba needed to relieve himself and removed his *tefillin*, setting them on his garment. An ostrich came — ostriches being known to swallow anything — and nearly swallowed them. He said: *hashta chayvinan l'shtay kriyos* — had it swallowed my *tefillin*, I would have been obligated to perform two acts of *keriah*, since it would be analogous to the destruction of a sacred text, which contains *shem Hashem*.

### Counter-Experience

Rav Huna bar Chiya responded: *minalach ha* — where do you get that idea? He related that the very same thing had happened to him — something similar involving his *tefillin* being swallowed or nearly so. He went to Rav Matna, who did not know the answer. He then went to Rav Yehuda.

### Willful vs. Accidental

Rav Yehuda told him: *hachi amar Shmuel* — this is what Shmuel said: *lo amru ela b'zroa uke'ma'aseh shehayah* — the obligation was stated only for an act done with force and violence, like the incident that occurred with Yehoyakim, where the text was willfully and forcibly destroyed. An act of nature — an ostrich swallowing the *tefillin* — would not trigger the obligation.

What exactly constitutes *zroa*? Rashi and Rabbeinu Gershom explain that it means a situation where *she'ein yachol l'hatzilo* — there would have been no way to save the text even had someone been present, as opposed to the ostrich scenario where one could chase the ostrich away, whereas no one could stop a king. The Yerushalmi, as cited by *Tosfos*, appears to add a different dimension: *lo amru ela b'zroa shesarafam melech Yisrael b'zroa* — it was not merely that the text could not be saved, but that it was a willful act of destruction carried out by one in power. The emphasis is on the deliberate, denigrating character of the act — an exercise of coercive authority to destroy the sacred. An accidental loss, however tragic, does not carry that meaning.

---

## Judea's Ruins

### The Verse Source

The *Gemara* turns to *arei Yehuda minalan* — how do we know the obligation of *keriah* upon seeing the cities of Judea in their destroyed state? The verse relates: *vayavo'u anashim miShchem miShilo umiShomron* — and men came from Shchem, from Shilo, and from Shomron, *shmonim ish* — eighty men, *meguchei zakan* — with shaved beards, *ukru'ei begadim* — and rent garments, *umitgodedim* — and who had lacerated their flesh, carrying meal-offerings and frankincense to bring to the house of God, in the immediate aftermath of the destruction.

### Tosafot's Question

*Tosfos* raises a potential objection: one might have argued, *eima ad d'ika tlat* — perhaps all three cities, Shchem, Shilo, and Shomron, would need to be destroyed to generate the obligation. *Tosfos* dismisses this, noting that each of the people in the verse presumably came from a different city, so no such requirement follows. However, *Tosfos* raises a different difficulty: the verse also mentions shaving one's beard and lacerating one's flesh, both of which are prohibited. Since those elements of the verse describe excessive or forbidden acts, perhaps the entire verse is too problematic to derive *halacha* from — *d'shamen d'lo shayach l'meimar d'lo neitanya klal*. *Tosfos* resolves this by saying that rather than rejecting the verse entirely, *Chazal* chose to learn from it selectively — deriving the principle of *keriah* while disregarding the excessive elements. This parallels the earlier observation about the selective application of the *gzeira shava*.

### Seeing Ruins

Rabbi Chelbo said in the name of Ulla Biri, who said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: *ha-ro'eh arei Yehudah bechorbanam omer* — one who sees the cities of Judea in their destroyed state recites: *areich kodshecha hayu midbar* — your holy cities have become a wilderness — *v'kore'ah* — and performs *keriah*. It is striking that the obligation applies not only to witnessing the destruction as it happens, but to seeing the ruins even many years or centuries later. That a person viewing ancient ruins would still be obligated is itself a considerable *chiddush* that goes beyond the plain sense of the original verse.

### Jerusalem & Temple

*Yerushalayim bechurbana* — one who sees Jerusalem in its destroyed state recites: *Tziyon midbar hayta Yerushalayim shemama* — Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation — *v'kore'ah*. *Beis HaMikdash bechurbano* — one who sees the Temple in its destroyed state recites: *Beis kodsheinu v'sifartenu asher hillalucha avoseinu haya lisrefas esh v'chol machmadeinu hayu l'charba* — our holy and glorious House where our fathers praised You has been consumed by fire, and all our treasured things have become ruins — *v'kore'ah*. All of these verses are from Yeshayahu. This *halacha* is recorded in the *Shulchan Aruch*, notably not in *Hilchos Aveilut* but at the end of *Hilchos Taanis*, since the fast days are primarily connected to the destruction of the *Beis HaMikdash*.

The *Shulchan Aruch* rules: *kore'ah al HaMikdash umosif al Yerushalayim* — one performs *keriah* for the *Beis HaMikdash* and then adds to it for *Yerushalayim*. This raises an obvious question about sequencing.

### Order & Priority

The *Gemara* notes a contradiction. One *baraita* implies that one does a single *keriah* for the *Mikdash* and adds to it for *Yerushalayim*. Another *baraita* rules: *v'kore'ah al HaMikdash bifnei atzmo v'al Yerushalayim bifnei atzma* — one does a separate *keriah* for the Temple and a separate *keriah* for Jerusalem. That is the real tension: the first source implies one *keriah* with an addition, the second implies two distinct acts.

The *Gemara* resolves: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. *Ha d'paga b'Mikdash breisha* — if a person first encounters the Temple site, as in the case of someone who entered Jerusalem in a box (*b'shida teivah umigdal*) without having seen the city first, then he tears for the more severe *Mikdash* first and can add to it for *Yerushalayim*. *Ha d'paga b'Yerushalayim breisha* — the normal case, where a person travels through Jerusalem toward the Temple Mount, he tears for *Yerushalayim* first. Since the *Mikdash* is the more severe of the two, it may not serve merely as a secondary addition to a *keriah* already done for *Yerushalayim* — it requires its own independent act of *keriah*. A correction is worth noting here: it is the more severe obligation that cannot be reduced to a mere *hosafa* on a less severe *keriah*. If one begins with the more severe, one may add for the less severe; but one may not make the more severe an addendum to the less severe.

---

## Keriah Mechanics

### Stitching Types

The *Gemara* turns to the mechanics of *keriah*. A *baraita* teaches: *sholal, malal, v'oket, v'la'asos k'min sulamos* — all of these are various modes of loose stitching — *aval lo l'achosom* — but one may not fully seal the tear. The specific prohibition is *ichuy* — a complete reweaving that restores the garment to wholeness. The terms *sholal*, *malal*, *oket*, and *sulamot* represent different ways of threading the two halves together loosely — *sulamot*, meaning like a ladder, suggests rungs that hold the halves but with wide spacing between stitches. These partial repairs are permissible; a tight weave that truly makes the garment whole again is not.

### Alexandrian Stitching

Rav Chisda adds a qualification: *u'v'ichuy Alexandri* — even among forms of *ichuy*, only Alexandrian stitching constitutes the prohibited complete repair. This is apparently a technique so thorough as to approximate a true reweaving of the garment. This qualification functions in two directions, as we shall see.

### Tearing Through Stitches

A subsequent *baraita* addresses the case of one who performs *keriah* through previous stitches. If the garment had been loosely restitched using *sholal*, *malal*, *oket*, or *sulamot* — the very modes just identified as permissible partial repairs — and a person then tears through those stitches when performing a new act of *keriah*, *lo yatza* — he does not fulfill his obligation. The reason is that since those stitches do not constitute a full repair, the garment is already considered torn. One cannot perform a meaningful act of *keriah* on something that is already, in halakhic terms, in a state of being rent.

However, *mitoch ha-ichuy* — if the garment had been thoroughly restitched, such that it was now considered whole, then performing *keriah* through those stitches *yatza* — fulfills the obligation. This applies, for instance, when the tear was not from a prior act of *keriah* (and thus was not subject to the prohibition of sewing up), or when the garment tore accidentally and was tightly repaired. Once the garment is restored to wholeness through such stitching, tearing it constitutes a genuine act of *keriah*. Rav Chisda again qualifies: this applies only to Alexandrian *ichuy*, the truly complete form of repair. This yields both a *chumra* and a *kula*: when assessing whether the prohibition of sewing up has been violated (as with *keriah* for father or mother), only Alexandrian *ichuy* is prohibited. And when assessing whether one has fulfilled the obligation by tearing a previously mended garment, only Alexandrian *ichuy* restores the garment to a state where a new *keriah* is meaningful.

### Inverting Garment

The *Gemara* presents a striking ruling: *rashai l'hofcho l'mata v'l'achoto* — a person may turn the garment upside down and sew up what is now the hem. The logic is that once the garment is inverted, what had been the tear is now located at the hemline. A tear at the hem does not carry the symbolic weight of *keriah* — one does not fulfill *keriah* by tearing at the hem, and therefore what now sits at the hem no longer represents the tear in the halakhically meaningful sense. Since it no longer bears that status, it may be sewn. There is something noteworthy about this: one might ask what permits this transformation — inverting the garment to circumvent the prohibition. The answer appears to lie in the nature of the prohibition itself. *Keriah* that cannot be sewn is prohibited because one may never directly repair that symbolic rent. Inverting the garment does not directly repair the tear; it relocates it halakhically by changing what the garment represents. As was discussed, the symbolism of leaving a tear unsewn points to something that can never be made whole. Inverting is not making it whole — it is, in a roundabout way, changing what the tear signifies.

This is the position of the *Tanna Kamma*. However, the small letter alongside the ruling indicates the ruling we follow.

### Rabbi Shimon's View

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids this: *oser l'achoto* — wherever the tear is located on the garment, it may not be sewn up. And as the textual notation indicates, this is the ruling we follow. No amount of repositioning changes the prohibition; the tear must remain unsewn regardless of where on the garment it comes to rest.

### Object Status

The *Gemara* states: *u'cheshem she'hamocher asur l'achoto, kach ha'lokeach asur l'achoto* — just as the seller may not sew up the torn garment, so too the purchaser is prohibited from doing so. In Brisker terminology, this is a *halacha* not only in the *gavra* but in the *cheftza* — the status inheres in the object itself, not merely in the person who performed the *keriah*. The garment retains its status regardless of who holds it. Consequently, *mocher tzarich l'hodia lalokeach* — the seller must inform the buyer that this garment had undergone a *keriah* whose tear is permanent, so that the buyer not inadvertently violate the prohibition.

### Non-Jew Question

*Tosfos* raises a fascinating question: *lo shamati im mutar lemochro lenochri* — may one sell the garment to a non-Jew? The question is whether the prohibition is entirely about the object's status — in which case no one, including a non-Jew, may sew it — or whether the seller's obligation to inform the buyer is specifically about ensuring that a Jewish buyer not come to violate the *halacha*, in which case a non-Jewish buyer, who is not subject to this *halacha*, would be permitted to sew it. *Tosfos* writes: *nehi delokeach assur l'achoto im hu nochri mutar* — perhaps if the purchaser is a non-Jew it is permitted; *af al pi de'mocher tzarich l'hodia lalokeach hainu kedei shelo yavo lokeach lidei issur* — the seller's disclosure obligation exists only to prevent a Jewish buyer from violating the prohibition. *Tosfos* himself leans toward permitting it: *ulichora haya mutar* — it would seem to be allowed. However, the asterisk notation in the text directs attention to *Masechet Semachos*, end of chapter 9, where it is ruled explicitly that it is *assur* — forbidden. The question of how fully the status resides in the *cheftza* remains a genuinely interesting one.

---

## Keriah Measurements

### Rabbi Meir Position

The *Gemara* turns to the required measurements of *keriah*. A *baraita* states: *tchilas kriah tefach* — the initial *keriah* must be a *tefach* in length. *V'tosefet shalosh* — if a person who has already torn for one relative must tear again for another who has died (of equal or lesser halakhic weight, such that the second tear may be added to the first rather than requiring an independent act), the addition need only be three finger-widths. The reasoning is that the act of tearing for the second relative does not need to produce a full *tefach* of new tearing — the garment is already torn a *tefach* from the first act, and the small additional amount results in a garment of sufficient size. This is the position of Rabbi Meir.

### Rabbi Yehuda Position

Rabbi Yehuda says: *tchilas kriah shalosh etzbaot v'tosefet kol shehu* — the initial *keriah* need only be three finger-widths, not a full *tefach*, while any additional tearing may be even a minimal amount, since the principle governing the addition — that the resulting tear is meaningful — applies a fortiori when even the initial requirement is smaller.

### Ruling Applied

Ulla rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Meir bikriah* — we rule like Rabbi Meir that the initial *keriah* must be a *tefach*. *V'halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda betosefet* — we rule like Rabbi Yehuda that the addition may be minimal. A *baraita* supports this combined ruling, as Rabbi Yossi is recorded saying: the initial *keriah* must be a *tefach* and the addition may be any amount.

### Sequential Deaths

The *Gemara* now presents the case of multiple deaths occurring in sequence. The *baraita* teaches: *amru lo meis aviv v'kara* — he was told his father died and he performed *keriah*. *Meis beno v'hosif* — then his son died and he added to the tear. Now, halakhically, the death of a parent carries a weightier status by virtue of *kibbud av va'eim*, even though the death of a child may be more emotionally devastating. Therefore, the death of a child, being of lesser or equal halakhic weight, may be expressed as an *hosafa* — an addition to the original *keriah* done for the father. In this case: *tachton mit'acheh, elyon eino mit'acheh* — the lower portion of the tear, being the addition for the son, carries a status that may be sewn up, while the upper portion, done for the father, carries a permanent status and may not be sewn.

### Father Priority

The reverse case is then addressed: *meis beno v'kara* — his son died and he performed *keriah*. *Meis aviv v'hosif* — then his father died and he added to the tear. The result is the opposite: *elyon mit'acheh, tachton eino mit'acheh* — the upper portion, which was done for the son, may be sewn; the lower addition, done for the father, may not be. The single tear thus carries two distinct halakhic statuses depending on which portion one examines.

### Simultaneous Deaths

The *baraita* continues with the scenario of multiple deaths occurring together: *meis aviv, meis imo, meis achiv, meis achoto* — father, mother, brother, and sister all die. In such a case, *korea kera echad l'chulan* — one performs a single *keriah* for all of them. Sequential deaths require sequential acts or additions; when news arrives simultaneously, a single act suffices for all.

### Beteira's View

Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira disagrees: *al kulan kera echad, al aviv v'imo kera echad* — while one *keriah* suffices for all the others together, the *keriah* for father and mother must be kept separate — *lefi she'ein mosifin al kera aviv v'imo* — because one may not add to the tear done for a father or mother. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: *lefi she'einan b'tosefet* — because *keriah* for parents is not in the category of additions. *Tosfos* wrestles with what this adds beyond a circular statement, but the operative rule is clear: the tear for father or mother requires its own independent act.

It is worth clarifying the relationship to what was said earlier about *Yerushalayim* and the *Mikdash*. There it was ruled that one who encounters the *Mikdash* first may add for *Yerushalayim*, but not the reverse — the more severe may not be reduced to an addendum. Here, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira is making a different and stricter point: the tear for father or mother cannot even serve as the base to which another is added. It is entirely separate from the regime of *hosafos*.

---

## Adding Keriah Limits

### Keriah vs. Aveilus

Shmuel rules: *halacha k'Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira* — the law follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, requiring a separate *keriah* for parents and a separate one for other relatives. The *Gemara* raises an apparent contradiction: does not Shmuel himself hold that in matters of *aveilus* we rule leniently? The *Gemara* resolves with the foundational principle: *aveilus lachud, kriya lachud* — *aveilus* and *keriah* are distinct domains. As we have been learning throughout this discussion, *keriah* exists independently of *aveilus* — it is performed at the moment of death, prior to the onset of the mourning period itself, and applies in many contexts entirely outside *aveilus*. The lenient principle in *aveilus* does not automatically carry over to *keriah*.

### After Shiva Addition

The *Gemara* then presents a debate transmitted by Rav Matna, Mar Ukva, and Levi in the name of Shmuel's father regarding the timing of permissible *hosafa*. One position: *kol shiva korea, l'achar shiva mosif* — throughout the entire first week, a person must perform a new *keriah*; only after *shiva* may one add to the existing tear. The logic is that since the tear may be repaired after *shiva*, it is then in a state of being eligible for repair, and therefore a new act of tearing upon it is halakhically meaningful. During *shiva*, when the tear cannot be sewn, it retains full status as a *kera* and adding to it is insignificant.

### After Shloshim Addition

The second position: *kol l'achar shiva korei, l'achar shloshim mosif* — throughout all thirty days, a new *keriah* must be performed; only after *shloshim* may one add. The difference between these positions concerns which degree of potential repair renders the original *kera* eligible to receive an *hosafa*: is it the partial sewing permitted after *shiva*, or only the complete repair permitted after *shloshim*?

### Zeira's Challenge

Rav Zeira challenges the first position: according to the one who says *kol shiva korea* — why must a separate *keriah* be done throughout *shiva*? Because *dlo nitan l'sholev* — the tear cannot be sewn during *shiva*, and therefore the tear retains its full status, making any addition meaningless. But if that is the reasoning, what about the ruling that a woman is permitted to sew her tear immediately even during *shiva* — *ha'isha sheshalala l'altar* — for reasons of modesty and dignity? According to the logic just given, should a woman then be permitted to perform *hosafa* even during *shiva*, since her tear is considered fit to be fixed?

### Woman's Exception

The *Gemara* answers: *hatam mishum kavod isha* — the woman's permission to sew during *shiva* is granted out of concern for her dignity, not because the tear itself is considered, on its own terms, fit to be repaired. The status of the tear remains that of a full, unrepairable *kera*; the sewing is an accommodation for *kavod ha-beriyos*. Therefore, performing an *hosafa* during *shiva* would still not be meaningful, because the tear's own halakhic status remains that of an unsewable *kera*.

### Parent Exception

The corresponding challenge to the stricter position — that after *shloshim* the original *kera* becomes eligible for *hosafa* — is: what about *keriah* for father or mother, which *dlo nitnu l'achot l'olam* — may never be sewn up? By the same logic, should *hosafa* for *aveilus* of father or mother be forever impossible? The *Gemara* answers: *hatam mishum kavod aviv v'imo hu* — there it is the reverse situation. For father and mother, the tear is in principle deserving of being sewn — its own intrinsic status would permit it — but we do not sew it out of respect for father and mother. Since on its own terms the tear is fit to be repaired, performing an act of *keriah* upon it after *shloshim* is meaningful. The prohibition against sewing is external to the object's status; the object's own status is one of repairability, and thus *hosafa* remains significant. The *Brisker* resonance here is clear: the distinction is between the *cheftza*'s status as fit to be sewn and the *gavra*'s prohibition against doing so — and these are not the same thing.

---

## Special Keriah Cases

### Rented Garment Issue

The *Gemara* now turns to a series of special cases. A *baraita* teaches: one who appears before a deceased person wearing a garment that was already torn — and therefore gives the appearance of having performed *keriah* when he has not — *harei zeh gozel ha-meitim v'ha-chayim* — has stolen from both the dead and the living. He has failed to give the deceased the proper respect of genuine *keriah*, and he has deceived the living through *gneivas da'as*, creating a false impression that he has mourned.

### Rabban Gamliel Case

Rabban Gamliel presents a case designed not as a trick but as a genuine halakhic question. A person says to his friend: *hashileni chaluqcha v'elech v'avaker es abba shehu choleh* — lend me your garment so I may go visit my father who is ill. He borrows the garment to appear presentable when visiting his sick father. The halakhic baseline is that one does not perform *keriah* on a borrowed garment, because doing so damages another's property without permission. The question here is how much the lender's awareness of the father's precarious state implies an implicit permission: if the borrower disclosed that he was going to visit a father who might be near death, does the lender implicitly consent to *keriah* being performed on his garment if death occurs?

### Limited Permission

The ruling is: *v'halach u'metzao shemeis, korea* — he went and found the father had died — he performs *keriah*, because the circumstances under which he borrowed it created an implicit understanding. *U'me'ache* — but he then sews up the tear. Even though he is mourning a father, for whom the tear would normally be permanent, the fact that the garment is not his own means his obligation to restore the object to as whole a state as possible overrides the prohibition against sewing — within the limits of what was implicitly permitted. *U'cheshe-bo l'veito machzir lo chaluqo v'nosein lo dmei krio* — when he returns home he returns the garment and compensates the owner for the depreciation caused by the tear and the repair. The permission extended was minimal: enough to perform the act, but with full financial responsibility for the resulting loss.

*V'im lo hodio* — but if the borrower did not disclose why he was borrowing the garment, *harei zeh lo yiga bo* — he may not touch it, since there was no implied consent to potential *keriah*.

### Protecting the Ill

The *Gemara* then addresses the case of a dangerously ill person — *choleh she-meis lo meis* — whose relative has died. The *halacha* is: *ein modiin oso shemet shema titoraf da'ato alav* — one does not inform him of the death, lest the emotional distress worsen his physical condition. Nor does one perform *keriah* in his presence — *v'ein mokrin befanav* — so as not to reveal to him that a death has occurred. And one silences the professional mourning women in his presence — *u'meshashtkin es ha-nashim mipanav* — so that their wailing not reach him and convey the news.

### Minor's Keriah

Moving to other special cases: *umokrin l'katan mipnei agmas nefesh* — one tears the garment of a minor in mourning, even though minors are not halakhically obligated in the observances of *shiva*. The tearing is done not for the minor's sake but for everyone else — it adds to the collective grief and sense of tragedy that the entire community shares, and thereby honors the deceased.

### In-Law Keriah

Similarly, *v'korin al hamiv v'al hamato mipnei kavod ishto* — a man performs *keriah* for his father-in-law and mother-in-law out of respect for his wife. Again, the obligation is not strictly his own but is performed out of deference to another's grief. Whether this is practiced *l'halacha* in current custom appears to be doubtful.

---

## Feeding Mourner

### Bed Positioning

The concluding passage of the *daf* addresses the practice of *havra'ah* — the first meal provided to the mourner upon returning from the cemetery. A *baraita* teaches: *v'ein mavrin ela al mitot zkufot* — one feeds the mourner only with upright beds. The context here may be *Chol HaMoed*, where the beds are not overturned, in contrast to the regular practice of the mourning period. A subsequent *baraita* refines the picture: *ha-holech l'beis ha-avel im haya libo gas bo* — one who goes to the house of a mourner, if he is on intimate terms with him, *yavruhu al mitot kfuyos* — then both sit on overturned beds together while the guest feeds the mourner. *V'im lav* — if he is not so intimate, *yavruhu al mitot zkufos* — the feeding takes place with upright beds.

### Rava Story

The *Gemara* illustrates this with an incident. Rava had a death in his family. Abba bar Marta — who is the same person as Abba bar Minyumi — came to comfort him. Rava was reclining on an upright bed; Abba bar Marta, the *menachem*, was on an overturned bed. Rava remarked: *kama leis beih da'ata l'hai tzurba m'Rabbanan* — how little understanding does this rabbinic student show. The *menachem* had positioned himself on the overturned bed while the *avel* reclined on the upright one — precisely the reverse of what is appropriate. The exact reason *Rava* himself was on an upright bed (and not an overturned one) is a major question among the *Rishonim*, and likely relates to the *Chol HaMoed* context. But whatever the circumstances, the reversal of positions — the visitor on the bed of mourning while the mourner sat upright — was clearly an error that demonstrated a fundamental lack of understanding of these laws.

---

---

# Moed Katan 28

## Traveling Mourner

### Holech Mimakom

The Gemara picks up at the very bottom of 26b with a *baraita*: *holech mimakom lemakom* — if an *avel* must travel from place to place, *im yachol lema'et be'askaya yema'et* — if he can limit his business dealings, he should do so, *ve'im lav yegalgel imahen* — and if not, he should "roll with them." This is a terse and somewhat cryptic formulation. Two questions immediately arise: first, isn't an *avel* prohibited from business dealings altogether? And second, what precisely does *yegalgel imahen* mean?

### Yegalgel Imahen

The Rambam's reading, which aligns in part with Tosafot's approach, understands the passage as addressing not serious commercial activity but rather the ordinary provisions and transactions unavoidable during travel — stopping to buy food, arranging lodging, and the like. In that context, the *avel* should still try to minimize even these incidental dealings. As for *yegalgel imahen*, the Rambam seems to read it as limiting oneself to the basic necessities of the journey and no more, though precisely how that meaning is derived from the word *yegalgel* is not entirely clear. The passage remains ambiguous regarding the broader parameters of *melachah* for a traveling *avel*.

## Kfiyat Hamitah

### Me'ematai Kofin

The Gemara now turns to *kefiyat hamitot* — the practice of upturning beds during mourning — which is one of the most symbolically charged expressions of *aveilut*. The question posed is: *me'ematai kofin et hamitot* — from what point does the *avel* upturn the beds? *Kefiyat hamitah* functions not merely as an ongoing personal practice but as a kind of declarative act marking the commencement of mourning status. The question is thus tantamount to asking: when does the mourning begin?

Rabbi Eliezer holds: *misheyatza mippetach beito* — from when the deceased has left the house, presumably being taken toward the cemetery. This ruling raises an interesting question: is *kefiyat hamitah* a status of the house, or a personal practice of the mourner? If it is a status of the house, the house could in principle enter that state even before the mourners themselves have begun their individual practices. The phrasing *misheyatza mippetach beito* might be making precisely that statement — that the departure of the *met* from the house triggers a changed status for the house, even before the mourners' own practices formally begin.

### R. Eliezer vs Yehoshua

Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees, holding that *kefiyat hamitah* begins only *misheyistam hagolel* — once the deceased is buried and the coffin is sealed. A famous *ma'aseh* is brought to illustrate the dispute. When Rabban Gamliel Hazaken died, as the body left the house, Rabbi Eliezer said to those who remained: *kefu mitoteichem* — upturn your beds. Later, once the burial was complete, Rabbi Yehoshua likewise told the mourners to upturn their beds. They replied: we have already done so on the authority of Rabbi Eliezer. The dispute is thus preserved in practice, but not resolved by this episode.

### Halacha Mikel

The ruling follows the principle of *halacha kedivrei hamikel be'avel* — in matters of mourning we rule leniently. Accordingly, the *halacha* is like Rabbi Yehoshua: *kefiyat hamitah* does not begin until the *met* has actually been buried. This holds whether the question concerns the mourners' individual practices or the status of the house. Either way, the upturning of beds — and the mourning it inaugurates — begins only after *kevurah*.

## Zokfin Hamitot

### Be'erev Shabbat

The Gemara next addresses when the beds may be restored. *Me'ematai zokfin et hamitot be'erev Shabbat?* — from what point on *erev Shabbat* may the beds be stood upright again? The answer is *min haminchah ulemalah* — from *minchah* time onward, one may restore the beds in preparation for *Shabbat*. Tosafot raise the question whether this refers to *minchah ketanah* or *minchah gedolah* — a significant practical difference of approximately three hours.

### Lo Yoshev

Rav Bar Huna introduces an important distinction: *af al pi chen eino yoshev* — even though the beds may be stood upright for *Shabbat*, the *avel* may not sit on them. This reveals a meaningful conceptual division: the act of restoring the beds for *Shabbat* is permitted, but the *avel*'s personal practice of *aveilut* — which includes not sitting on a normal, upright piece of furniture — remains in force. The act of setting the house right for *Shabbat* is a distinct matter from the mourner's bodily engagement with those furnishings.

This invites a deeper question about the nature of *kefiyat hamitah*: is it primarily a status of the house — the way a house of mourning looks — or is it a practice of the *avel* as an individual, concerning where he or she sits and sleeps? Here we see both dimensions operating simultaneously, and on *erev Shabbat* they are decoupled. The beds may be restored as part of preparing the house for *Shabbat*, but the *avel*'s personal obligation to avoid sitting upon them continues.

The Gemara also rules: *umotzai Shabbat af al pi she-eino ela yom echad chozer ve-kofeh* — on *motzai Shabbat*, even if the *avel* has only one day remaining in *shiva*, he must re-upturn all the beds throughout the house for that final day.

## Kol Mitot

### Hakofeh Mitato

A *baraita* clarifies the scope of the practice: *ha-kofeh mitato lo mitato bilvad hu kofeh ela kol mitot she-yesh lo b'toch beito hu kofeh* — when an *avel* upturns his couch, he must upturn not only his own but every couch in the entire house. *Ve-afilu yesh lo eser mitot b'asara mekomot* — even if he has ten couches in ten different rooms, *ve-kofeh et kulan* — he upturns all of them. This extends even to a situation of five brothers mourning together: each one, in his or her own house, upturns all the beds there. The practice is thus not merely about where the *avel* personally reclines, but about the entire state of the household. The parallel to covering mirrors throughout the house is apt — it is the full domestic environment that is transformed.

The term *mitah* here should not be translated narrowly as "bed." It encompasses couches, divans, and any furniture upon which people would sit or recline — in essence, the standard seating of the household. Just as we cover mirrors throughout the house today, the *avel* then upturned every such piece of furniture, creating an environment where neither the mourner nor any visitor had a normal place to sit.

### Meyuchedet Lekelim

An exception is introduced: *ve-im hayta ha-mitah meyuechedet l'keilim* — if a particular couch or bench was used exclusively for storing vessels, functioning more like a dresser or a storage shelf, *ein tzarich lichpotah* — it does not need to be upturned. Even though we established that beds must be upturned even when the *avel* does not intend to sit on them, the underlying principle is that only furnishings designed for sitting or reclining require upturning.

### Dargash

The *baraita* introduces a further case: *dargash ein tzarich lichpoto ela zokfo* — a *dargash* likewise does not need to be fully upturned, but is merely stood upright. And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds: for a *dargash*, one releases its straps and it collapses on its own. The Gemara will now investigate the nature of this *dargash*.

## Dargash Definition

### Arsa D'gada

*Mai dargash?* — what is a *dargash*? Ulla says: *arsa de-gada* — it is a couch of good luck. The word *gad* appears in *Tanach* with connotations of fortune or luck, and Ulla identifies the *dargash* as some sort of ceremonial chair associated with good fortune — not apparently an *avodah zarah* concern, but a recognized cultural artifact.

Rabba immediately challenges this: if the *dargash* is a couch of good luck that nobody would ordinarily sit upon — rather like the *kos shel Eliyahu*, present but untouched — how can we say that a king sitting *shiva* would recline upon it? The *mishnah* teaches that when a king sits *shiva*, all the people recline on the ground while the king reclines on the *dargash*. If it is a ceremonial luck-couch that no one is ever supposed to sit on, the *dargash* would be an entirely inappropriate accommodation for the king.

### Kaviti

Rav Ashi deflects this challenge: *mai kushya* — why is this difficult? It is analogous to eating and drinking. During ordinary times, we would not presume to feed the king, but when the king sits *shiva* we do provide him food and drink. Similarly, the *dargash* is the compromise — we would not have the king recline on a normal bed, which would violate the practice of *aveilut*, but since he is a king, he uses this ceremonial couch as a middle ground.

The Gemara, however, presses forward with a stronger objection: *amai eino tzarich lichfoto* — if the *dargash* is a luck-couch that no one normally sits on, why does it not need to be upturned? We just established that *all* beds in the house must be upturned, even those the *avel* does not intend to sit upon. The Gemara responds: *midi dehavei a'mita ha'meyuechedet l'keilim* — it is comparable to the bench designated for storing vessels, which also does not require upturning. Only items made for sitting require upturning; a luck-couch that no one sits on is exempt on the same grounds.

But the Gemara insists there remains a real difficulty: *ela i kushya ha kushya* — if there is a question, here it is. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that the *dargash* is treated by releasing its straps so that it collapses on its own. *Ve-i salka da'tach arsa de-gada* — but if it is a luck-couch, *mai kaviti it leih* — what are these straps? Ordinary couches of that era, however constructed, did not have straps. This physical detail — the straps — proves that the *dargash* is something structurally distinct, and that Ulla's identification as a luck-couch does not adequately account for its physical description.

### Arsa D'tzalla

*Ki ata Ravin* — when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael, one of the Sages, identified in some versions as Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arava, who was known in the marketplace of the leather-workers (*gilda'ei*), reported: *mai dargash — arsa d'tzalla* — a *dargash* is a couch or seat made of leather. This explains the straps at once. The construction was a frame with a piece of leather stretched across it, held in place by straps — something like what we might envision as a director's chair or a tent-bed, where a flat piece of leather serves as both mattress and surface, affixed to the frame by straps that, when released, cause the whole thing to collapse. The identification of the source as someone who frequented the leather-workers' marketplace lends the report particular credibility.

This explains the straps entirely. What remains somewhat unclear is precisely *why* this leather construction exempts the *dargash* from the requirement of full inversion. It is not a classic couch — which would have a wooden frame, straw filling, a cloth covering — and apparently that structural difference classifies it as categorically distinct from the furniture that must be upturned.

### Serugah Mitokho

An alternative formulation is also cited: *Rav Yirmiyah amar, dargash serugah mitokho* — the weaving that holds the *dargash* together runs through the frame from within, *mitah serugah al gabah* — whereas a regular bed has its roping woven over the top of the frame. For a standard bed of the period, ropes would be woven in a crisscross pattern over and around the frame, creating a surface analogous to what we might call box springs. For the *dargash*, by contrast, leather straps would be threaded through holes in the frame and knotted on the outside — running *through* rather than *over* the frame. This is an additional distinguishing characteristic, though how it alone would explain the *dargash*'s exemption from upturning is not entirely clear.

### Halakha Ke-Rabban

The practical ruling is given: *amar Rav Yaakov bar Acha amar Rav Yehoshua ben Levi, halakha ke-Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel* — the *halacha* follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who says one releases the straps of the *dargash* and allows it to collapse on its own. Notably, this is actually the more stringent position: rather than simply leaving the *dargash* standing as-is, the ruling requires a positive act of releasing the straps. It is curious that the ruling follows the more demanding view in this case.

## Mitah Nekliftyah

### Zokfah Ve'dayo

Rav Yaakov bar Acha further reports in the name of Rav Assi: *mitah she-naklitiah yotzin* — a bed whose posts extend upward, that is, a four-poster bed, *zokfah ve-dayo* — it is sufficient merely to stand it upright; full inversion is not required.

The phrase *zokfah ve-dayo* is interesting because it sounds as though one is actually doing something, whereas in practice it amounts to a permission to leave the bed as it stands. The reason becomes clear upon reflection: if you turn a four-poster bed completely upside down, the tall posts will actually elevate it *higher* than it was in its normal position, which defeats the symbolic purpose of lowering the furniture as an expression of mourning. Accordingly, one simply stands the bed on its side — *zokfah*, to make it vertical — and that suffices.

This point also helps clarify the earlier use of *zokfo* in the context of the *dargash*. The *Orchot Chaim* explains *zokfo* as meaning to stand the object upright — to turn it 90 degrees rather than 180 degrees — as distinct from the full inversion normally required. For the four-poster bed, this makes perfectly good sense structurally. The application to the *dargash* may similarly indicate that some partial act of disruption is required, even if a full *kefiyah* is not.

## Yashan Al Gabi

### Udini Gedolah

A *baraita* addresses what happens when the *avel* is not sleeping on an upturned bed at all. *Yashan al gabi kisse al gabi udaiyni gedolah* — if someone sleeps on a chair or on a large couch, *al gabi karka* — or even directly on the ground — *lo yatza yedei chovato* — he has not fulfilled his obligation. It is not enough to avoid sitting on normal furniture; the obligation requires actually sitting or sleeping on an upturned couch. Sleeping on the ground, while unusual, does not achieve the distinctive symbolic quality of the upturned bed. The particular experience of using furniture that has been inverted — rendered strange and inhospitable — is itself the practice.

### Shelo Kiyam

Rabbi Yochanan states this sharply: *shelo kiyam kefiyat hamitah* — such a person has not fulfilled the obligation of *kefiyat hamitah*. What is notable about this formulation is how it frames the shortcoming. One might expect the language to say that the *avel* has not properly discharged his personal obligation. Instead, Rabbi Yochanan says that the *kefiyat hamitah* itself has not been fulfilled — as though the deficiency is in the status of the act, not merely in the person's compliance with it. This picks up on the broader question animating this entire *sugya*, beloved to the Briskers: is *kefiyat hamitah* a *chovat gavra* — a personal obligation of what the *avel* does — or is it about the objective status of the household, the reality of upturned beds? Rabbi Yochanan's phrasing suggests the latter: by not sitting on the upturned bed, the person has undermined whether the beds can truly be considered *kofin* at all.

## Mekhabdin

### Umarbitzin

The Gemara turns to the cleanliness and presentation of the house of mourning. *Mechabdin umarbitzin beveit ha'avel* — one may sweep and wash the floors in the *avel*'s house. *Umadichin kearot vekosot utzlochiot vekitoniot beveit ha'avel* — one may wash the dishes, cups, flasks, and small jugs in the house of mourning. The house may be kept clean and orderly. This is noteworthy, given how much the practice of *kefiyat hamitah* emphasizes the disruption of the household's normal state. The disruption is specific — upturned couches — and does not extend to general disorder or uncleanliness.

### Mugmar Vebasamim

What is not permitted, however, is bringing incense and aromatic spices into the house of mourning: *ve'ein mevi'in et hamugmar vehabsamim beveit ha'avel*. This is presumably because such things make the environment too pleasant and festive, which is inappropriate for a house in mourning.

### Beit Hamenachamin

The Gemara questions this from a *baraita* of Bar Kappara: *ein mevarchin al hamugmar ve'al habsamim beveit ha'avel* — one does not recite a *berachah* over incense and spices in the house of mourning. This implies they are brought there but no *berachah* is made — which would seem to contradict the *baraita* prohibiting bringing them altogether.
