The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya — ha beveit ha'avel ha beveit hamenachamin* — the two sources address different locations. The prohibition on bringing incense applies to the *avel*'s own house; the rule about not reciting a *berachah* applies in the *beit hamenachamin*, the house where the comforters gather. What exactly constitutes a *beit hamenachamin* and why it would have this intermediate status is not fully spelled out. One suggestive explanation: the *beit hamenachamin* might refer specifically to the room where the *avel* and visitors are together, as distinct from rooms where the *avel* sits alone.

## Ein Molichin

### Tavla Veaskutla

The Gemara presents a *mishnah* governing how food is brought to the house of mourning: *ein molichin beveit ha'avel lo betavla velo be'askutla velo bekanon ela besalim* — one does not bring food to the *avel*'s house in fancy platters (*tavla*, *askutla*, or *kanon* — various types of ornate trays), but only in simple wicker baskets. The practice of bringing food to the house of mourning — especially the *seudat havra'ah* — is well established; what the *mishnah* regulates is the manner of presentation, emphasizing simplicity and humility appropriate to the setting.

The *mishnah* also states: *ve'ein omrim birchat avelim b'moed* — one does not recite the special blessing for mourners on *chol hamoed*. Nevertheless, *aval omdim b'shurah umenachamim u'potrim et harabbim* — one does stand in the rows upon the mourners' return from burial, gives words of consolation, and then dismisses the assembled crowds. This reflects the delicate balance maintained during *chol hamoed*: burial does take place, *keriah* and *chalitzah* are performed, *seudat havra'ah* is provided, but the formal practices of *aveilut* are largely restricted to *devarim she'betzina*, the private observances, and those practices that would in any case not be publicly visible during *chol hamoed*, such as not laundering or cutting hair.

## Ein Mani'im

### Nashim Leolam

The *mishnah* rules: *ein manichin et hamitah barechov* — one does not leave the bier in the street to enable a *hesped*, *shelo l'hargil et ha-hesped* — so as not to encourage extended eulogizing on *chol hamoed*. However, *v'shel nashim l'olam mipnei hakavod* — women's biers are never left in the street even on *chol hamoed*, out of respect. Rabbeinu Gershom suggests this has to do with concerns about bodily fluids if the woman was a *niddah*, but the more general sense is one of modesty and dignity around women — a theme already encountered in connection with the practices of *keriah*. The precise concern is not spelled out explicitly.

## Ein Molichin (II)

### Salei Nitzarin

The Gemara traces the history behind the regulation about simple baskets. Originally, *barishona hayu molichim b'veit ha'avel ashirim b'kaltot shel kesef v'shel zahav* — the wealthy would bring food to the house of mourning on silver and gold trays, *va'aniyim b'salei nitzarin* — and the poor would bring it in wicker baskets of peeled willow. *Ve-hayu aniyim mitbayeshim* — the poor were embarrassed, both when they themselves were in mourning and received such unimpressive contributions, and when their offerings as comforters looked so modest beside those of the wealthy. The Sages therefore enacted: *hitkinu she-yehu ha-kol mevi'im b'salei nitzarin shel arava klufa* — everyone should bring food in the same type of simple wicker basket, *mipnei kevodan shel aniyim* — out of respect for the poor. Death becomes an equalizer.

## Mashkim Zechuchit

### Tzevuah

A parallel reform governed drinking vessels. Originally, *barishona hayu mashkim b'veit ha'avel ashirim b'zechuchit levana* — the wealthy were served in clear glass, *va'aniyim b'zechuchit tzevuah* — and the poor in colored glass. In that era, clear glass was the superior product; colored glass, being less refined, was associated with poverty. The poor were embarrassed. The Sages reformed the practice: *hitkinu she-yehu ha-kol mashkim b'zechuchit tzevuah mipnei kevondan shel aniyim* — everyone would drink from the same colored glass, out of respect for the poor.

## Megalim Panei

### Pnei Aniyim

Originally, *barishona hayu megalim pnei ashirim u-mekhasim pnei aniyim* — the faces of the wealthy deceased were uncovered, while the faces of the poor were covered. The reason: *mipnei she-hayu mushkharim pneihem mipnei batzoret* — the faces of the poor would be darkened from famine, since in an era of frequent food scarcity, death often came from hunger, and the physical signs were painfully visible. The poor were embarrassed even in death. The Sages enacted: *hitkinu she-yihyu mekhasim pnei ha-kol mipnei kevondan shel aniyim* — all faces would be covered, for the sake of the dignity of the poor.

### Khalkalah

Similarly with the mode of conveyance: *barishona hayu motzi'im ashirim be-dargash* — originally the wealthy were carried out on a *dargash* — here the *dargash* reappears, this time as a mark of honor — *va'aniyim be-khalkalah* — and the poor on a more ordinary bier. *Ve-hayu aniyim mitbayeshim.* The Sages reformed the practice: *hitkinu she-yihyu ha-kol motzi'im be-khalkalah mipnei kevondan shel aniyim* — everyone would be brought out on the same simple bier, for the dignity of the poor.

### Cholei Me'ayim

One further reform: *barishona hayu manikhim et ha-mugmar takhat kholei me'ayim metim* — originally incense was burned beneath the bodies of those who had died of intestinal illness, for obvious sanitary reasons in a world without refrigeration, and depending on how long before burial a body was held, the need could be acute. *Ve-hayu kholei me'ayim khayim mitbayeshim* — but those who suffered from intestinal illness while alive were embarrassed, since even in death their condition was being singled out for special treatment. The Sages enacted: *hitkinu she-yihyu manikhim takhat ha-kol mipnei kevondan shel kholei me'ayim khayim* — incense would be placed beneath every body, for the dignity of those living with intestinal illness.

## Matbilin Hakelim

### Niddot Metot

*Barishona hayu matbilin et ha-kelim al gabei niddot metot* — originally the vessels of women who had been *niddot* when they died were immersed in a *mikveh*. The phrase *al gabei* ("on the backs of" or "on account of") is admittedly unusual, but the meaning is clear: when a woman who was a *niddah* passed away, those wishing to use the vessels she had left behind in the household would immerse them in a *mikveh* to address questions of ritual impurity. This singled out *niddot* in a very public way. *Ve-hayu niddot khayot mitbayshot* — women who were *niddot* while alive were embarrassed, because their status was being effectively publicized by the special treatment accorded to their vessels after death. A woman immersing her own vessels privately is one thing; being marked as a class requiring communal attention is quite another. The Sages enacted: *hitkinu she-yihyu matbilin al gabei kol ha-nashim mipnei kevondan shel niddot khayot* — all women's vessels would be immersed after death, so that *niddot* would not be treated differently.

### Zavim Metim

*Barishona matbilin al gabei zavim metim* — originally, the vessels of men who had died while in a state of *zivah* — an abnormal bodily discharge rendering them ritually impure — were similarly immersed. *Ve-hayu zavim khayim mitbayeshim* — men who were *zavim* in life were embarrassed by this public posthumous distinction. The Sages enacted accordingly: *hitkinu she-yihyu matbilin al gabei ha-kol mipnei kevondan shel zavim khayim* — all men's vessels would be immersed, for the dignity of *zavim* who were alive.

## Hotza'at HaMet

### Kasheh Lekrovav

*Barishona haytah hotza'at ha-met kashah li-krovav yoter mi-mitato* — originally the expense of burial was harder on the relatives of the deceased than the death itself. The financial burden associated with funerals was so crushing that, as the Gemara states starkly, *ad she-hayu krovav manikhin oto u-vorkhin* — relatives would simply abandon the body rather than face the costs. This is striking testimony to how economically devastating funeral practices had become.

### Klei Pishtan

The situation persisted *ad she-ba Rabban Gamliel* — until Rabban Gamliel the *Nasi* intervened. *Ve-nahag kalut rosh be-atzmo* — he treated himself with deliberate lightness in this regard, *ve-hotzi'uhu bi-khlei pishtan* — and was buried in simple linen garments. *Ve-nahagu acharav latzeit bi-khlei pishtan* — and thereafter, people followed his example and were buried in linen. It is striking to realize that what we now think of as quintessentially Jewish burial practice — the *tachrichim*, the linen garments, the *kittel* — evolved not from some ancient mystical imperative but from a social reform driven by concern for the poor and the economically burdened. What began as a ruling Rabban Gamliel applied to himself became universal practice precisely because the *Nasi*'s personal example carried moral authority.

### Tzerda De'bar Zuza

Rav Papa adds: *afilu b'tzerda de'bar zuza* — even a cloak costing as little as a single *zuza*, something utterly inexpensive, is now acceptable and indeed standard for burial. This represents the full arc of the reform: what had been an occasion for ruinous expenditure had been reduced to the most minimal of expenses.

## Ein Mani'im (II)

### Biraḥov

The Gemara returns to the ruling of the *mishnah*: *ein manichin et hamitah barachov* — one does not leave the bier in the street on *chol hamoed*, in order not to encourage *hespedim* during a time when they are restricted.

### Ein Moed Talmid

Rav Papa rules: *ein moed bifnei talmid chacham* — the restrictions of *chol hamoed* on *hespedim* do not apply in the presence of a *talmid chacham*; a eulogy is given for a Torah scholar even on *chol hamoed*. *Ve-chol sheken Chanukah u'Purim* — and certainly during Chanukah and Purim. This applies, however, *bifanav* — in the presence of the body itself. *Aval shelo bifanav lo* — but not when the body is absent.

The Gemara immediately challenges this: Rav Kahana eulogized Rav Zvid of Neharde'a in Pum Nahara — a different location, far from where the body was. Rav Pappi explains: *yom shmu'ah havah, u'k'bifanav dami* — that was the very day Rav Kahana received the news of the death, and on the day one first hears of a death, it is considered subjectively equivalent to being in the presence of the body. This is a striking answer. The ruling that *ein moed bifnei talmid chacham* is grounded in the objective honor due to the *chacham* and the objective reality of *kavod hachacham* overriding *chol hamoed* restrictions. If so, one might expect the override to require the physical presence of the body itself. Yet the Gemara allows the subjective reality — the day of hearing — to suffice. This is an unusual interplay between the objective rationale and a subjective criterion.

### Yom Shmu'ah

The upshot of Rav Pappi's ruling is that *yom shmu'ah* — the day one first hears of the death of a *talmid chacham* — is treated as equivalent to being in the presence of the body, and a *hesped* may be delivered even on *chol hamoed*.

## Hesped Halev

### Sopfim Al Shadayim

Ulla teaches: *hesped halev* — there is a eulogy of the heart. He derives this from the verse *al shadayim soptim* — "upon the breasts they eulogize." This reframes what a *hesped* is. Throughout the earlier discussion, *hesped* appeared primarily as a verbal art — poetic speech in praise of the deceased. Here we see its physical and performative dimensions. *Kipuach beyad* — a kind of clapping or beating with the hand; *kilus b'regel* — a stamping of the feet. These were not merely peripheral gestures but integral components of the public ritual of mourning. When we understand the *hesped* as this full-bodied communal event — the wailing, the beating of chests, the stamping — it becomes much clearer why *hespedim* are restricted during times such as *chol hamoed* and the entirety of *chodesh Nissan*. Nowadays, when the *hesped* has become a dignified verbal tribute, its restriction feels almost incongruous. The restrictions were designed for a phenomenon that was expansive, loud, and intensely communal in a way quite foreign to contemporary practice. This helps explain why today those restrictions are often observed more in letter than in spirit — people will note that it is *Nissan* and offer "a few words" — but one can appreciate that such a practice is not a severe violation if one understands that the ancient phenomenon being restricted was categorically different.

### Hamakaless

Those who stamp their feet during the *hesped* — *hamakaless lo yakaless b'sandal* — should not do so in a sandal, *ela b'min'al*, but rather in a proper shoe, *mipnei hasakanah* — because of the danger. Rabbeinu Gershom explains that a sandal provides insufficient support and can easily twist the foot during forceful stamping. Rabbeinu Chananel suggests that going barefoot at least makes one more careful about where one places one's foot; either way, the sandal is the most dangerous option.

## Niyana Rosho

### Shov Ein Menachamin

Rabbi Yochanan teaches: *avel kivan she-niana rosho shuv ein menachamin rashaim liyeshev etzlo* — once the mourner has nodded his head, the comforters may no longer sit beside him. This is a signal from the mourner that he has reached a point where he wishes to be left alone — whether because he has momentarily found a degree of inner equilibrium and needs space to be with himself, or simply because he is withdrawing inward and needs solitude. Rabbeinu Gershom suggests that it is a sign that he is consoling himself.

This ruling carries a significant practical lesson. Comforting mourners requires attention not only to what one says but to what the mourner actually needs. Too often the visit becomes about the comforter — what they said, whether they said the right thing, whether they stayed long enough — rather than about reading where the mourner is. Here the *halacha* explicitly tells us: when the mourner signals that he needs to be left alone, leave. The nod of the head is enough.

### Hakol Chayavim

Rabbi Yochanan further rules: *ha-kol chayavim la'amod bifnei nasi* — all are obligated to stand when the *Nasi* is present, *chutz me'avel va-choleh* — except for a mourner and someone who is ill. The exemption of the sick is self-evident. The exemption of the *avel* is more conceptually interesting: the mourner is permitted to remain within his own private universe, not required to respond to social hierarchies or public formalities. He is, in a sense, in a different realm.

### Lekal Omrim

The corollary is also stated: *le-khol omrim lahem shevu* — for everyone who stood for the *Nasi*, you tell them to sit back down, *chutz me'avel va-choleh* — except for a mourner and someone ill. You do not say *shevu* to them, because they never had to stand in the first place. One interpretation adds: the word *shevu* can also connote "remain" or "stay," and one would not want to suggest such a connotation to an *avel* or a *choleh*.

## Léchem Mishlo

### Yom Rishon Assur

Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav: *avel yom rishon assur le'echol lechem mishelo* — a mourner on the first day is forbidden to eat from his own bread; he must be fed by others. This is the underlying rationale for the practice of *seudat havra'ah*.

### Yechezkel Source

The source is a verse in *Yechezkel*, where God tells the prophet: *ve-lechem anashim lo tochal* — "and the bread of people you shall not eat." The verse is read as revealing what is normative for a mourner: since God commands *Yechezkel* specifically not to eat others' bread — implying that doing so would be the natural expectation — this shows that a normal *avel* is precisely supposed to be fed from others' food. One must be careful here, as *Yechezkel* is often a source for *aveilut* through inversion — learning from what he was told *not* to do what a normal mourner is obligated to do. The verse thus establishes that on the first day of mourning, the *avel* depends on others for sustenance.

### Machalfi Seudataihu

Rav Yosef reports: *machalfi seudatayhu le-hadadi* — Rabbah and Rav Yosef exchanged their meals with one another when both were mourners simultaneously. By each giving the other food from his own supply, each was being fed by the other's bread, satisfying the requirement that the *avel* be fed by others. This exchange is reminiscent of a similar arrangement reportedly made regarding *mishloach manot* on *Purim* — two Sages without means would exchange their *seudot* so that each fulfilled the obligation without either going without. Here too, the exchange may reflect both limited means and a creative halakhic solution to a situation where two mourners found themselves in *aveilut* at the same time.

## Met Be'ir

### Kol Bnei Hair

Rav Yehuda reports further in the name of Rav: *met be'ir — kol bnei ha'ir asurim ba'asiyat melachah* — if someone has died in the city, all the residents of the city are forbidden from doing *melachah*. The scope of this ruling is striking — not merely the immediate family or community of the deceased, but the entire population of the town.

### Rav Hamnuna

The Gemara illustrates this with a story. Rav Hamnuna *ikla l'darumsa* — came to a certain town. He heard the sound of the *shofar* blowing to signal that someone had died — *shama kali shappura d'shichva*. He then saw people going about their work — *haza hanakh inishi d'ka avdi avidata* — apparently immediately after hearing the announcement. *Amar lehu* — he said to them: *lehavei hanakh inishi b'shamta* — let these people be in a state of *nidduy*. Is there not a body in the city that needs to be buried?

### Chavrusas

They replied: *chavrusas ika b'mata* — there is a *chevra*, a society, in the city to handle the burial. Rav Hamnuna responded: if that is so, *sharya l'cho* — I release you from the *nidduy*. Rabbeinu Gershom explains: *chavurot hen she'elu kovrin meiseihen levadan ve'elu kovrin meiseihen levadan* — these were distinct societies in which each group takes responsibility for burying its own. When such an organized society exists to take charge of the burial, the general prohibition on *melachah* for the rest of the town is lifted. The existence of an organized *chevra kadisha* changes the communal obligation.

## Hamiskasheh

### Al Meis Acher

Rav Yehuda teaches in the name of Rav: *kol ha-miskasheh al meito yoter midai — al meis acher hu bocheh* — whoever grieves over his deceased excessively must in fact be weeping for another dead. The tone of this teaching shifts from a psychological observation to something more ominous: the "other dead" may not be someone already gone, but someone yet to come.

### Hahi Itta

The Gemara brings a story to illustrate. *Hahi itta d'havas bishvavusei d'Rav Huna* — there was a woman in the neighborhood of Rav Huna. *Havu lah shiva banin* — she had seven sons. One of them died. *Havas kabbakhya beyaserata* — she was crying excessively. Rav Huna sent word to her: do not do this. She ignored him.

### Tzavit Zavda

He sent again: *ee tzaish mutav* — if you listen it will be good, *ve'i la — tzavis zavda l'idakh meis* — and if not, prepare the shrouds for the next one to die. She did not listen, *u-meisu kuleihu* — and all her sons died. Finally he said to her: *tzavis zavda l'nafsheikh* — now prepare the shrouds for yourself. And she died.

This is an extraordinarily harsh story, and it is difficult to read without discomfort — particularly the image of a mother who has already lost one child being warned about, and then experiencing, the successive deaths of all her others. One might understand Rav Huna's concern: in a world of highly demonstrative public mourning, there may have been a question of whether excessive grief could become disconnected from genuine feeling, or whether such consuming mourning caused one to lose sight of the living family members who still needed care. Rav Yehuda's earlier teaching suggests this very concern — that the one who grieves excessively may be forgetting the others who remain. The image of *Yaakov Avinu* is invoked implicitly: consumed for decades by mourning for *Yosef*, he arguably neglected the rest of his children and household. Still, the harshness of the story remains striking, and whether Rav Huna's words were prediction or causation is a question the Gemara leaves open.

## Al Tivku Lamet

### Shlosha Yamim

A verse in *Yirmiyahu* is cited as the biblical basis for prescribed limits on mourning: *al tivku lamet yoter midai veal tanudu lo yoter mikhishiur* — do not weep excessively for the dead and do not wail for him beyond the proper measure. The limits are then specified: *shlosha yamim livchi* — the first three days are for weeping, *ve-shiva* — and the full seven days for *hesped* — eulogizing and the physical expressions of mourning.

### Ushloshim

*Ve-shloshim le-gihutz u-letisporet* — and thirty days for laundry and haircuts. After that, the Gemara has God declare: *ee atem rachmanim bo yoter mimeni* — you should not have more compassion than I do. What is striking here is that the practices of *shloshim* — not laundering, not cutting hair — are presented in this context not merely as halakhic categories but as expressions of grief, continuous with the weeping and eulogizing of the earlier days. The transition from emotive expressions to behavioral restrictions frames those restrictions as belonging to the same continuum of mourning.

## Becho Becho

### Laholeich Belo Vanim

The verse *becho becho la-holeich* — "cry, cry for the one going" — is interpreted. Rav Yehuda says: cry for the one who leaves without children. Such a death is especially deserving of grief because the person has left nothing behind — no descendants, no continuity. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi went further in practice: *lo azil le-vei avla ela le-man de'azil belo vnei* — he would only go to a house of mourning when the deceased had died without children. The verse supports this: *becho becho la-holeich ki lo yashuv od ve-ra'ah et eretz moladeto* — cry for the one who will not return again, who will not see the land of his heritage and of his progeny.

### She'avar Aveira

Rav Huna offers a different reading. *Zeh she'avar aveira ve-shanah bah* — this refers to one who sinned and repeated the sin, *velo yashuv od* — and will no longer return, because he has descended into a moral state from which there is no *teshuvah*. Rabbeinu Gershom reads the verse accordingly: *lo ya'aseh le'olam teshuvah* — he will never do *teshuvah* again. Rav Huna goes according to his own broader principle: *keivan she'avar adam aveira ve-shanah bah, hutra lo* — once a person commits a sin and repeats it, it becomes permitted to him. The Gemara immediately qualifies: *hutra lo salka da'tach?* — does it literally become permitted? *Ela eima na'asit lo keheter* — no, rather it becomes as if it were permitted in his own mind. The person has rationalized the behavior to the point where he no longer perceives it as a transgression, and from that point, return becomes nearly impossible. This is the teaching that Rabbi Yisrael Salanter sharpened into the observation that if one does something three times, it can come to feel like a *mitzvah*.

## Sheloshah Yamim

### Cherev Munachat

Rabbi Levi describes the inner emotional world of the *avel* across the seven days of *shiva*. *Shlosha yamim harishonim yireh atzmo ke'ilu cherev munachat lo bein shtei yarchotav* — during the first three days, the mourner should feel as though a sword is hovering between his sides. This is not merely grief but a kind of existential alarm — an awareness that death has come close, that the one who died was part of a group to which the mourner belongs, and that mortality has drawn near. The Sages elsewhere teach that when one member of a group dies, the others should feel concern for themselves. The sword at the sides captures precisely this.

### Bekeren Zavit

*Mishlosha ad shiva ke'ilu munachat lo kenegdo be-keren zavit* — between the third and seventh days, the sword is still present in the room, but it has moved to a corner. The acute terror has receded somewhat, but the presence of death remains immediate.

### Overet Bashuk

*Mikan va'eilach ke'ilu overet kenegdo ba-shuk* — from the seventh day onward, it is as though the sword passes by in the street. It is no longer in the room, but it is still out there. The sense of mortality does not disappear; it simply distances itself from the person's immediate experience. This three-stage progression captures something true about the arc of acute grief — the initial overwhelming intensity, the gradual but still-present weight through the *shiva*, and the lingering background awareness that persists thereafter.

---

---

# Moed Katan 29

## Righteous Death & Atonem…

### Women's Burial

The daf opens on the final line of 27b. The Mishnah taught that we do not allow a woman's coffin to lie in the street even on *Chol HaMoed*, out of concern for her dignity. The Sages of Nehardea qualify this: the ruling applies specifically to a woman who died in childbirth, whose body is in a state of physical deterioration, making disfigurement a pressing concern. For other women, *aval sh'ar nashim m'nichim* — the body may be left while people gather for eulogizing and wailing. Rabbi Eliezer, however, reads the Mishnah literally: even other women must be buried without delay. His proof is from the verse describing Miriam's death — *vatamas sham Miriam vatikaver sham* — "Miriam died there and was buried there," which implies that burial followed immediately upon death. The precise social and halakhic contours of *kavod* here are admittedly context-dependent and not entirely transparent to later readers, but the verse was clearly understood to mandate swift burial.

### Miriam Divine Kiss

Having invoked Miriam's death, the Gemara turns to a further teaching: *af Miriam b'nishika mesa* — Miriam too died by the divine kiss. This conclusion is derived through a *gezera shava* from the word *sham*: just as the Torah says *vatamas sham* by Miriam, and by Moshe it says *vayamas sham*, and Moshe's death is described explicitly as *al pi Hashem* — by the mouth of God — so too Miriam's death is understood to have been of that intimate, tranquil character. One might ask why the verse does not state this explicitly in Miriam's case. The Gemara answers: *mipnei shegnai hadavar l'omro* — it would have been unseemly to speak of God's kiss in relation to a woman, a concern that did not apply in the same way to Moshe.

### Tzadikkim Atonement

Rabbi Ami asks: why is the death of Miriam juxtaposed in the Torah with the passage of *para aduma*? The answer: *mah para aduma m'chaperes af misas tzadikkim m'chaperes* — just as the red heifer atones, so the death of the righteous atones. This is, on its face, a striking comparison. The *para aduma* would not ordinarily top one's list of atoning sacrifices — it is indeed called a *chatas*, but it functions in ways that set it apart from conventional atonement. What it shares with certain other rituals — the *egla arufa* and the *seir hamishtaleach* — is that it operates outside the *Mikdash* and involves the giving of a life. In that sense, the comparison to *misas tzadikkim* carries internal logic: here too is a life given over outside the sanctuary, and here too atonement is effected.

This idea — that the death of the righteous atones for the generation — is one that people sometimes reflexively associate with Christian theology. But as the Gemara makes plain, it belongs to the tradition itself. Whether or not it sits comfortably within all frameworks of Jewish thought, it is genuinely present here, and it reflects a broader theological move the *masechta* makes as it draws toward its close: shifting from the technical *halachot* of *avelut* toward the pastoral and theological dimensions of death and loss.

Rabbi Elazar adds a parallel teaching: why is the death of Aharon juxtaposed with the *bigdei kehuna*? The context is the scene in which Aharon is stripped of the priestly vestments and Elazar is clothed in them before Aharon's death. From this juxtaposition the Gemara derives: *mah bigdei kehuna m'chaprin af misas tzadikkim m'chaperes* — just as the priestly garments atone — and the Gemara has established elsewhere that Aharon "carried the iniquity of the holy things" through the wearing of certain *bigadim* — so too the death of the righteous atones. The analogy here is perhaps less jarring than the *para aduma* comparison, though the precise mechanism of comparison remains somewhat opaque. The common thread is the conclusion: *misas tzadikkim m'chaper*.

What is notable, standing at the end of *Moed Katan*, is this thematic turn. The *masechta* has spent much of its length in the domain of practical *hilchot avelut* — who may and may not cut hair, what may be done on *Chol HaMoed*, what constitutes excessive mourning. Now, in its final pages, it pivots toward something more pastoral: how does one think theologically about death? For the death of a *tzaddik*, one framework offered is that the life given over was itself an act of cosmic significance — atoning for the generation, much as the *para aduma* or the *bigdei kehuna* atoned for Israel.

---

## Death Categories

### Sudden Death Types

The Gemara proceeds to a *baraita* that categorizes death according to the manner in which it comes. *Met pitom* — dying suddenly, without any warning or opportunity for the person or family to prepare — is called *mita chatufa*, a snatched death. *Chala yom echad umet* — if one fell ill for a single day and then died — this is *mita dchufa*, a rushed or pressed death. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel disagrees: a one-day death is in fact a *mita mageifa*, a plague death, based on the verse in which God tells the prophet that He will take "the delight of your eyes" — referring to his wife — *bemageifa*, in a plague, and the following verse reports that she died the same evening. Two days of illness followed by death is *mita dchuya*; three days is called *ge'ara*, a reprimand; four days is *nezifa*, some form of rebuke; and five days or more is *misas kol adam* — a normal human death.

*Tosafot* flags an honest difficulty here: *lo yadana mai shna* — it is not entirely clear what distinguishes each of these categories from the next, nor is the Gemara's source for the full progression obvious. Nevertheless, the underlying concern is evident: the tradition is attempting to give families a framework for understanding — and perhaps some degree of consolation — in the face of the particular circumstances of a death, even if individuals cannot influence these things. *Amar Rabbi Chanina*, what is the verse? *Hen karevu yamecha lamut* — behold your days have drawn close to die. *Hen* is one — because, as the Gemara notes, in Greek *hen* means one. *Karevu* is plural, hence two. *Yamecha* is also plural, hence two more. That yields five total — corresponding to the five-day threshold of *misas kol adam*.

### Ages of Death

The Gemara now turns from the speed of dying to the age at which one dies. Dying at fifty years is called *mitat kares* — a death of *kares* — reflecting the Torah's notion of being "cut off," understood here as a shortened life. Dying at fifty-two is called *misato shel Shmuel HaRamasi*, because that is understood to be the age at which the prophet Shmuel died. Dying at sixty is *mita bidei shamayim* — death at the hands of Heaven. The question arises immediately: is that a good or a bad thing? The term *mita bidei shamayim* is sometimes used in contexts of divine punishment. Mar Zutra resolves this: the verse says *tavo be'chelach alei kever* — you shall come into the grave at the proper time — and the gematria of *bakelach* equals sixty. So sixty is understood here as a natural and dignified death. Seventy is *seiva*, old age; eighty is *gevuros*, the strength of old age, corresponding to the verse in Psalms, *yemei shnosenu bahem shivim shana* — our years are seventy, *v'im bigvuros shmonim shana* — and if with strength, eighty years.

Rava clarifies the range for *kares*: from fifty to sixty years of age constitutes *misas kares*. That means Shmuel HaRamasi, who died at fifty-two, died within the *kares* range. The Gemara then asks: if so, why did the earlier formulation state only "fifty" without specifying the full range? The answer: *mishum kvodo shel Shmuel HaRamasi* — out of respect for Shmuel, so as not to spotlight his death as falling within this troubling bracket.

### Rav Yosef Age 60

When Rav Yosef reached sixty, he made a celebratory feast for the rabbis and declared: *nafki li mikares baruch Hashem* — I have passed out of the *kares* range. Abaye, one of his students, immediately offered a pointed qualification: it is true, he said, that the Master has exited the *kares* of years, *aval mikares deyomi mi nafik mar* — but how do you know you have exited the *kares* of days? The discussion earlier about a one-day or two-day death still looms as a possible indicator. Rav Yosef's response was characteristically balanced: *nekot lach mi'palga beyadach* — hold onto at least half a victory; half I've managed to clear, and we will deal with the rest when the time comes.

One naturally wonders how psychologically healthy this entire system of categories is — the anxiety it might generate in a dying person or their family as they track whether the death fits into a good or bad symbolic pattern. The Gemara seems aware of this tension, as we will see.

A brief narrative follows: Rav Huna died suddenly, and the rabbis were disturbed — what does this signify about so great a man? A pair of scholars from Hadaiv came and offered a resolution: the rule that sudden death is a poor sign applies only when the person has not yet reached *gevuros* — eighty years. But if a person has indeed reached eighty, then dying suddenly in one's sleep is *misas neshika*, death by divine kiss. The old age outweighs the suddenness.

---

## Mazal vs. Merit

### Rava Mazal

Against the entire framework of death-as-indicator, Rava offers a powerful counter-teaching: *chayei benei u'mezonei lo bizchusa talia milsa ela b'mazala talia milsa* — a person's length of life, their children, and their financial sustenance are not determined by their merit and righteousness, but by *mazal*, by fortune. People of equivalent piety may fare entirely differently in all of these dimensions, and we should not read those outcomes as signs or indicators of the person's standing before God.

Rava does not leave this as an abstract philosophical claim. He offers what one might call empirical evidence — and one has to admire the Gemara's willingness to test theological propositions against observable reality.

### Rava Chisda Compare

*Rava ve'Rav Chisda tarvaihu rabanan tzadiki havu* — both Rava and Rav Chisda were thoroughly righteous rabbis. The evidence for their equivalent righteousness: when either one would pray for rain during a drought, rain would come. This is the standard established in *Taanis* for divine connectedness of the highest order.

And yet: Rav Chisda lived to ninety-two; Rava lived to forty. In Rav Chisda's house there were sixty wedding celebrations; in Rava's house, sixty tragedies — or by some readings, sixty bereavements. In Rav Chisda's house, fine flour was so abundant it could be fed to the dogs without concern; in Rava's house, barley bread for human beings was barely to be found.

Here, then, is the *benei*, the *chayei*, and the *mezonei* — children and joy, length of life, and sustenance — all distributed with radical asymmetry between two men of identical righteousness. The conclusion Rava draws is pointed: do not go looking for *simanim* in any of this. When Rav Huna died suddenly, the anxiety the rabbis felt about what it signified about their master is understandable, but Rava's teaching here is a corrective: these things do not map onto merit.

The Gemara then adds Rava's own personal testimony: *hani talas mili ba'i kamei shamaya* — I asked three things of Heaven. The wisdom of Rav Huna and the wealth of Rav Chisda were both granted; the humility of Rabba bar Rav Huna was not. The implicit irony — a man who openly confesses that humility eluded him — is hard to miss. This teaching sits in interesting tension with the preceding one: Rava has just argued that *mazal* determines outcomes with no reference to merit or divine involvement, and yet here he describes asking God for personal qualities and receiving some of them. The tension is real, and the Gemara does not resolve it.

---

## Malach HaMavet Stories

### Rava Brother Deaths

Rav Se'orin was the brother of Rava. As Rava sat beside him and watched him begin to slip away, Rava asked his brother: *leimal lei mar d'lo litzaran* — tell the Angel of Death not to cause me anguish. Rav Se'orin replied: *mar lav shushpinei hu?* — but aren't you his colleague? You're so righteous, surely you have standing to make the request yourself. Rava answered: *keivan de'imsar mazla lo ashgach bi* — once my *mazal* has been handed over, once I am in the process of dying, he no longer pays attention to me.

Here again the motif of *mazal* recurs: even the righteous person, at the moment of death, loses whatever standing or influence they might have had. This is a deeply humbling idea — something akin to the king who is dead losing all of his royal significance, as *Koheles* suggests.

Rav Se'orin then made his request: appear to me after you die. Rava did appear to him, and when Rav Se'orin asked whether dying was painful, Rava replied: *kividit de'chusilta* — like the prick of a bloodletting horn. A minimal, momentary pain.

### Rav Nachman Appears

The Gemara now offers what appears to be an earlier, parallel scene. Rava was sitting before Rav Nachman as the latter was slipping away. Rava made the same request: tell him not to cause you pain. Rav Nachman replied: *man chashiv, man safin, man rakia?* — who has importance, who has weight, who has significance? The response is more poetic than Rava's own answer to his brother, but it carries the same essential meaning: at the moment of dying, no one has standing before the *Malach HaMavet*, regardless of their stature in life.

Rava asked Rav Nachman to appear to him after death. When Rav Nachman appeared, Rava asked whether the death had been painful. Rav Nachman replied: *kinishcha benisa meichalva* — like the drawing of a hair from milk. Smoother even than what Rava himself would later report. And yet, Rav Nachman added: even so, if God were to offer him the chance to return to the living world as he had been, *lo baina* — he would not want it. *Denafish bisusei* — the fear of dying a second time would be too great. This is a striking observation: death without pain is still death, and the prospect of facing it again is something he would refuse even at the cost of continued life.

### Rabbi Elazar Truma

The Gemara now turns to stories of negotiating with or deflecting the *Malach HaMavet*. Rabbi Elazar was in the middle of eating *truma* when the Angel of Death appeared to him. He said: I am eating *truma*, performing a *mitzvah* — this is something holy, you cannot interfere. The moment passed. The implication is significant: this was not merely a brief delay; the *sha'ah* — the moment — passed entirely, presumably meaning the death was postponed for a substantial period, not merely pushed off temporarily.

### Rav Sheshes Encounter

When the Angel of Death appeared to Rav Sheshes in the marketplace, Rav Sheshes objected: *beshuka keveheima?* — you're going to take me down in the marketplace like an animal? That is no place for a person of my standing to die. *Isa legabei beisa* — come to my house, and we will see to it there. And so, presumably, that is what occurred.

One student pointed out that Rav Sheshes was blind — a reasonable question about how he perceived the *Malach HaMavet* in the marketplace. The answer offered was that physical sight may not be what is involved in such a perception. Whatever the case, the story depicts Rav Sheshes as asserting his dignity even in that moment.

### Rav Ashi Review

Rav Ashi's encounter takes a different form. When the Angel of Death appeared to him in the marketplace, Rav Ashi said: *itrich li tlasin yomi ve-ahadri talmudai* — give me thirty days so I can review all my learning. *Ashrei mi sheba lekan vetalmudo beyado* — praised is the one who arrives in Heaven with his learning intact. The *Malach HaMavet* granted the thirty days. But on day thirty, he returned. Rav Ashi asked: what is the great hurry? The reply: *kedachaka raglei d'bar nassan* — you are pressing on the feet of Bar Nassan; he is ready to take your place at the head of the academy, and as long as you remain alive, he cannot rise to his rightful station. *D'ein malchus nogaas bachaverta afilu k'mlo nima* — one kingship cannot encroach upon another, even by a hairbreadth.

### Chisda Chiya Silent

The Gemara offers two final portraits. Rav Chisda, it is said, could not be seized by the *Malach HaMavet* at all: *d'lo hava shtik pumei m'girsa* — his mouth never stopped learning Torah, and the *Malach HaMavet* could find no opening. The Angel therefore ascended and sat in a cedar tree in the *yeshiva*. The cedar burst — presumably from the weight of the divine presence — and the momentary silence that followed gave the *Malach HaMavet* the opening he needed.

Rabbi Chiya similarly could not be approached. One day the *Malach HaMavet* disguised himself as a poor person and knocked at the door asking for bread. Rabbi Chiya brought it to him. The Angel then said: if the Master has compassion on this poor man, why can he not have compassion on me? I have a task to fulfill. He revealed himself, showing Rabbi Chiya a rod of flame. Rabbi Chiya, in compassion, yielded his soul willingly. The moral texture of this final story is particularly rich: Rabbi Chiya's great virtue — his compassion for the poor — is precisely the quality that ultimately leaves him unable to refuse.

---

## Mourning Restrictions

### Women Wailing Rules

The final Mishnah of the tractate opens on 27b. *Nashim b'moed meanos v'lo metapchos* — on *Chol HaMoed*, women may engage in *meanos* but may not perform *metapchos*. The terms will be defined shortly. Rabbi Yishmael says that those women positioned closest to the bier may perform *metapeach* — a limited exception that balances the honor due to the deceased against the restrictions of *Chol HaMoed*. On days of intermediate sanctity but lesser weight — *Rosh Chodesh*, *Chanuka*, and *Purim* — both *meanos* and *metapchos* are permitted. But in all cases — whether *Chol HaMoed* or these lesser holidays — *kina* is prohibited. Once the deceased has been buried, none of these practices are permitted at all: *nikbar hames lo meanos velo metapchos* — burial marks the end of all such communal mourning.

### Mourning Types

The Mishnah then defines the terms. *Inuy* — the *meanos* permitted even on *Chol HaMoed* — means *shekulan onot k'achas*, all the women cry out together simultaneously. *Metapchos* — the more emphatic practice that is restricted on *Chol HaMoed* but permitted on *Rosh Chodesh*, *Chanuka*, and *Purim* — involves the physical striking, the slapping of the hands against the thigh, which makes the mourning more emphatic and publicly demonstrative. *Kina* — the responsive dirge that is prohibited on all these occasions — is defined as *she'achas medaberes v'kulan onot achareha*: one woman leads and all the others respond, an antiphonal structure. The verse cited in support: *v'lamdena b'noseichem nehi v'isha re'usa kina* — you shall teach your daughters a lament, and a woman her friend a *kina* — which implies this call-and-response form.

The Mishnah closes with a forward-looking verse: *bila hamaves lanetzach umacha Hashem Elokim dima me'al kol panim* — death shall be swallowed up forever, and God will wipe every tear from every face. This is the verse sometimes recited when leaving a *shiva* house.

### Meanos Kina Words

*Tosafot* comments here that the tractate ends on a positive note, and adds a further observation: *mishum d'Mo'ed Katan hu sof Seder Mo'ed* — because *Moed Katan* is the concluding tractate of *Seder Mo'ed*. This is not entirely self-evident, since *Moed Katan* and *Chagiga* have the same number of chapters and their ordering is not fixed; *Tosafot*'s position is that *Moed Katan* comes last. The point about ending *seder* on a good note has a parallel in *Taanis*, which concludes with the joyful note about *Tu B'Av* and *Yom Kippur* as the greatest festivals of Israel.

The Gemara then asks: what, in fact, is said during *meanos* and *kina*? What are the actual words of these communal wailings? Rav says: *vaye l'azla vaye l'chavila* — woe to the one who is departing, woe to the wounding or, per the reading of the Soncino translation, woe to the security — meaning the life that was given to us as a kind of collateral we must eventually return to God.

### Shnitziv Wailing

Rava then quotes a series of phrases used by the women of *Shnitziv*, a community that was apparently renowned for its mourning poetry. The Gemara presents five examples, each introduced with the formula: *nashei d'Shnitziv amrin* — the women of *Shnitziv* would say.

The first phrase matches what Rav cited: *vaye l'azla vaye l'chavila* — woe to the one going, woe to the collateral, or the loss. The second: *gud garma mikacha v'namtei maya l'antichi* — remove the bone from the jaw, and bring the water to the vessel. Rabbeinu Gershom understands this metaphorically: the bone from the pot represents the soul departing the body, and the water to the vessel is the soul returning to its divine source. The Soncino offers a more prosaic reading: the bone is removed from the cooking pot because this person no longer needs to be fed, and the hot water in the kettle is for the *tahara* process. Rabbeinu Gershom's reading is the more elegant of the two. The third: *atifi kessut tura* — wrap yourselves, O mountains, cover yourselves in mourning, for *d'bar rami u'bar ravrevi hu* — this was a great person, a son of heights; one of your elevated ones has died. The fourth: *shayulei itztala d'milsa l'bar chorin d'shalimu zavdeh* — borrow a cloak of fine linen for a free man, because his portion is now complete; prepare for him his burial shrouds, for he is now freed from the needs of this physical world. The fifth: *rahit v'nafil a'mabra v'ziphusa yazif* — run and fall by the ferry, and borrow the money. This image evokes the idea of crossing over to the other world and requiring some payment at the threshold — an image that recalls, though is not identical to, the ancient Greek notion of payment for passage across the River Styx.

Rava continues with a sixth phrase from the women of *Shnitziv*: *achna tagrei azavzegi mivadku* — our brothers' merchants have been searched at the customs house, a metaphor for the accounting of deeds that takes place upon one's arrival in the world to come, an audit of one's spiritual inventory. And finally: *mota ki mota u'marein chavula* — death is like death, and the suffering is the collateral. Life is given to us on loan; suffering is the interest, and death is the return of the principal.

Returning to an earlier teaching: *tanya*, Rabbi Meir would cite the verse from *Koheles*, *tov lalechet el beit avel* — it is better to go to a house of mourning — and explicate it as follows: if you are present at a person's death or funeral, carry that experience back with you into your own life. *Deyasped yispedunei* — one who eulogizes others will be eulogized; *deyekaver yikverunei* — one who buries others will be buried; *deyit'an yit'anunei* — one who carries the burden of the funeral will be carried; *deyadal yedalunei* — one who raises his voice in mourning will be lifted. Others read the last point differently: *delo yadal yedalunei* — one who does not raise himself up in arrogance will be raised up in honor at his death, as the verse says, *ki tov amar lecha aleh heina* — it is better when others say to you, "Come up here."

---

## Consoling Mourners

### Yishmael Consoled

The Gemara now moves from the performative aspects of mourning — the wailing, the dirges — to the practice of *nichum aveilim*, consoling mourners. When the children of Rabbi Yishmael died — note again the plural, echoing earlier stories of multiple children dying together — four elders came to console him: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yose HaGelili, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, and Rabbi Akiva. Before they entered, Rabbi Tarfon said to the others: know that this man is a great scholar, deeply knowledgeable in *agadot*. Do not interrupt one another — let each one speak in turn. Rabbi Akiva added: I will go last.

When they entered, Rabbi Yishmael himself opened the conversation, as the mourner: *rabu avonotav tachfu aveilav* — great are my sins, for the mournings have piled upon me, one upon another. And now, he said, he had burdened his teachers by requiring them to make a second condolence visit — once for each child.

### Kal Vachomer Proofs

Rabbi Tarfon responded with a verse from the story of Nadav and Avihu: *ve'achichem kol beit Yisrael yivku et hasreifa* — all the house of Israel shall weep for the burning. A *kal vachomer* follows: Nadav and Avihu performed only one *mitzvah* that the Torah records, yet all of Israel mourned their deaths. *Kach banav shel Rabi Yishmael al achat kama vechama* — how much more so, for your children who performed so many *mitzvot*, all of us will mourn their passing.

Rabbi Yose HaGelili cited the verse about Aviyah son of Jeroboam: *vesafdu lo kol Yisrael vekaveru oto* — all of Israel eulogized and buried him. *Kal vachomer*: Aviyah did only one good thing in his entire life, and nevertheless all of Israel mourned him. What was that one good thing? A dispute: one opinion holds that he abandoned his guard duty and went up to Jerusalem for *Yom Tov*, refusing to enforce his father Jeroboam's prohibition on the pilgrimage. The other opinion says he went further — he dismantled the entire system of guards that Jeroboam had placed on the roads to prevent the *aliyah la'regel*. Either way, only one virtuous act — and still, *kol Yisrael* mourned. How much more so the sons of Rabbi Yishmael.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah cited the verse addressed to Tzidkiyahu: *beshalom tamut* — you shall die in peace — and *ubemisfrot avotecha* — and you will be burned with the pyres of the earlier kings. A *kal vachomer*: Tzidkiyahu performed only one *mitzvah* that the Torah records — he rescued Yirmeyahu from the mud — and yet he received this promise of honor in death and was mourned by all. How much more so the sons of Rabbi Yishmael.

Rabbi Akiva, who had asked to go last, cited the verse from Zechariah: *bayom hahu yigdal hamisped b'Yerushalayim kemisped Hadadrimon bevik'at Megido* — on that day the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as the mourning of Hadadrimon in the valley of Megido. Rav Yosef interjects that without the Aramaic *Targum*, the reference would be incomprehensible: Hadadrimon had no connection to the valley of Megido. The *Targum* clarifies that the verse is compressing two separate events — the mourning over Achav son of Omri, who was killed by Hadadrimon (hence "the mourning of Hadadrimon," meaning the mourning occasioned by Hadadrimon's act), and separately, the mourning over Yoshiyahu son of Amon, who was killed by Pharaoh Neco in the valley of Megido. Two distinct laments, merged in the verse. Rabbi Akiva's *kal vachomer* then follows: Achav performed only one good deed that the Torah records — *ve'hamelech hayah ma'amad bamerkava nochach Aram* — the king stood in his chariot opposite Aram, apparently maintaining leadership and preventing some collapse at a crucial moment — and nonetheless the mourning for him was enormous. How much more so for the children of Rabbi Yishmael.

What is striking is that Rabbi Akiva's contribution appears structurally identical to those of his colleagues: a citation, a *kal vachomer*, the refrain about the sons of Rabbi Yishmael. One is left wondering why Rabbi Akiva insisted on going last, and what the story means to convey by placing him there without a visibly differentiated teaching.

### Death Verses Resolved

Rava raised a question to Rabba bar Mari: the verse promises Tzidkiyahu *beshalom tamut* — you will die in peace — and yet another verse reports that Tzidkiyahu's eyes were blinded by the king of Babylon. How are these consistent? The answer, in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: *shemet Nevuchadnetzar beyamav* — Nebuchadnezzar died in Tzidkiyahu's lifetime. That outliving of one's tormentor constitutes a kind of peace.

A parallel question about Yoshiyahu: the verse promises him *vene'asafta el kivrotecha beshalom* — you will be gathered to your grave in peace — and yet another verse reports that the archers shot through King Yoshiyahu, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav said that they made him like a sieve. Dying in a hail of arrows — is that dying in peace? The answer, again from Rabbi Yochanan: *shelo charav Beit HaMikdash beyamav* — the Temple was not destroyed in his days. That preservation constitutes his peace.

These resolutions do more than untangle problematic verses. They constitute a direct response to the discussion earlier on the page about reading *simanim* into the manner of a person's death. One might look at Tzidkiyahu's blinding or Yoshiyahu's death by arrows and read catastrophe. But Rabbi Yochanan insists that "dying in peace" can mean something that transcends the physical circumstances — it is a perspective, a larger frame. The rabbis who worried about what Rav Huna's sudden death signified should, perhaps, take note.

### Consoler Etiquette

The Gemara records an important practical ruling from Rabbi Yochanan: *ein menachamin mishum lomar davar ad sheyiphtach avel* — the consolers may not speak until the mourner opens. The reason is implicit but powerful: one does not know what the mourner is ready to hear, or where they need the conversation to begin. Imposing one's own opening risks missing the mourner entirely. The proof text is from *Iyov*: *acharei ken patach Iyov et pihu* — only after that did Iyov open his mouth — *vahadar vayaan Eliphaz HaTeimani* — and then Eliphaz responded. The consolers waited, as difficult as that must have been, until Iyov himself broke the silence.

### Mourner Head Seat

Rabbi Abbahu asks: how do we know that the mourner sits at the head of the table in the *shiva* house? The question is somewhat counterintuitive — one might have assumed that the mourner, in a diminished state, would not be given the seat of prominence. The verse cited: *evchar darkam ve'eshev rosh ve'eshkon kemelech begdud ka'asher avelim yenachem* — I would choose their path and sit at the head, dwelling like a king among troops, as one who consoles mourners. The word *yenachem* here is read as the mourner consoling others — sitting at the head and receiving the community, as it were. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes that the *ketiv* can also be read as *yenuchamu* — as one who is consoled — making the connection to the *avel* sitting at the head even more explicit. Mar Zutra derives the same point from a different verse: *vesar marze'ach seruchim*, read as the mourner becoming the prince among the assembled, the center around whom the household orients.

Rabbi Chama bar Chanina then asks the parallel question: how do we know that the *chatan* also sits at the head? The verse: *kechatan yichahen pe'er* — like a bridegroom he shall be adorned with glory. The word *yichahen* evokes the *kohein*. Just as the *kohein* is given primacy — he opens first, blesses first, receives the first and finest portion, as derived from the verse *vekidashto* — so too the *chatan* receives the place of honor.

The parallel between *avelut* and marriage runs deep in the tradition. Both last seven days in their primary phase; both involve ten people for the recitation of *brachot*; both ask whether the central figure — mourner or *chatan* — counts toward the required quorum of ten. And now, both the mourner and the bridegroom sit at the head. The *avel yoshev berosh* and the *chatan yoshev berosh* — the mourner at the head and the groom at the head — emerge from the same structural logic of honored centrality, even though the emotional register of the two occasions could not be more different.

---

## Soul Departure

### Soul Struggle

Rabbi Chanina teaches: *kasha yetziat neshama min haguf* — the departure of the soul from the body is profoundly difficult. He compares it to pulling a rope through a narrow passage — the friction, the resistance, the effort required. Rabbi Yochanan uses a similar image: like the sail rope through the mast fitting. The imagery of constriction and difficulty underscores that even a death described elsewhere as smooth or peaceful still involves a genuine struggle at the moment of separation.

### Parting Blessings

Rabbi Levi bar Chita teaches a distinction that is observed to this day: *haniftar min hamet* — one who takes leave of the dead — should not say *leich l'shalom*, go toward peace, but rather *leich b'shalom*, go in peace — because the person has already arrived at a state of *shalom*. Conversely, *haniftar min hachai* — one who takes leave of the living — should not say *leich b'shalom* but rather *leich l'shalom*, go toward peace — for the living are always in the state of striving, always moving toward something not yet reached.

The proof for the formula for the living: David said to Avshalom *leich b'shalom* — go in peace — and Avshalom went and was killed. Whereas Yitro said to Moshe *leich l'shalom* — go toward peace — and Moshe went and succeeded. For the dead, the proof is from Abraham: *v'ata tavo el avotecha b'shalom* — you will come to your fathers in peace — which speaks of the state already attained.

### Scholars Ascent

Rabbi Levi offers a final teaching: anyone who moves from the *beit knesset* to the *beit midrash*, and from the *beit midrash* to the *beit knesset*, will *zoche umekabel pnei shechina* — merit to receive the presence of the *Shechina*. There is a deliberate ambiguity here: does *zoche umekabel* refer to a reward received in death, or to a presence experienced now, within the walls of the *beit midrash* and *beit knesset* themselves? The verse cited — *yelchu mechayil el chayil yeira'eh el elohim beTzion* — suggests an ongoing process: going from strength to strength, always ascending.

This leads to the *masechta*'s final statement. Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi in the name of Rav: *talmidei chachamim ein lahem menucha* — the *talmidei chachamim* have no rest. Not in this world, and not even in the world to come. *Afilu olam haba* — even there — *yelchu mechayil el chayil yeira'eh el elohim beTzion*. The scholars continue to ascend, to grow, to strive. Even the vision of God in the future does not constitute a terminus but a milestone along a path that continues without end.

With this, the *masechta* closes: *hadran alach eilu megalchin uslika la masechet Moed Katan*.

---

---

# Chagigah 2

## Three Festival Sacrifices

### Opening Remarks

We begin today with the privilege of opening *Masechet Chagiga*. Before turning to the broader introduction to the *masechet*, let us first work through the *daf* itself to ensure we cover the material fully.

### Three Korbanot Types

The *mishna* opens: *hakol chayavin bere'iyah* — everyone is obligated in the *korban re'iyah*. To understand this, it is necessary to appreciate that there are three distinct *korbanot* one brings to the *Beit HaMikdash* during a *chag*, during one of the *shalosh regalim*. The first is the *korban re'iyah*, an *olah* — a burnt offering, consumed entirely on the altar — brought simply for the act of appearing before God. It is, in essence, a "show-up" *korban*. The second is the *korban chagiga*, a sacrifice in honor of the holiday itself. The third is the *korban simcha*, brought to generate joy during the festival. Crucially, while the *korban re'iyah* is an *olah* that the offerer does not eat, the *korbanot chagiga* and *simcha* are *korbanot shelamim*, which the offerer consumes.

### Korban Re'iyah Obligation

It is this first *korban* — the *korban re'iyah* — that the *mishna* declares universally obligatory. The *mishna* then proceeds to enumerate those categories of individuals who are nonetheless exempt.

---

## Exemptions & Disabilities

### Exempt Categories

The *mishna* lists the following as exempt from the *korban re'iyah*: *cheireish* (a deaf person), *shoteh* (someone who lacks competence or cognitive agency), and *kattan* (a minor). To these it adds the *tumtum* — a person whose gender is indeterminate — and the *androginos*, one who possesses both sets of reproductive anatomy, not merely undetermined but positively dual. Women (*nashim*) are likewise exempt, as are *avadim she'einam meshuchararim* — slaves who have not yet been freed.

The *mishna*'s language here is notable. It says "slaves who have not yet been freed," for once a slave is freed he is no longer a slave in any halakhic sense — he becomes a convert. The *mishna* is thus referring to the *eved kena'ani* who remains in servitude. One might wonder: is there even a *hava amina* that a *kena'ani* slave would be obligated? The answer lies in the general principle that an *eved kena'ani* is exempt from *mitzvot asei shehazeman gerama* — time-bound positive commandments — but is otherwise bound by the full range of prohibitions and other obligations. Given this framework, the question of whether such a slave might be included in the *re'iyah* obligation is not entirely without basis, even if the conclusion is that he is exempt.

The *mishna* continues: *hechigeir* — one who is lame; *vehasuma* — one who is blind (a matter that will receive extensive discussion by the end of this *daf*); *vehacholeh* — someone who is ill; *vehazaken* — one who is elderly; and *umi she'eino yachol la'alot beraglav* — one who is simply unable to ascend by foot, for whatever reason.

### Minor Definition Debate

*Eizehu kattan?* asks the *mishna* — who exactly qualifies as a *kattan* for the purpose of this exemption?

*Beit Shammai* defines a *kattan* as any child who cannot ride upon his father's shoulders and ascend from Jerusalem to *Har HaBayit*. It is worth noting that this formulation implies *Har HaBayit* is a distinct location from Jerusalem proper. *Beit Hillel* defines a *kattan* as any child who cannot hold his father's hand and walk on his own feet from Jerusalem to *Har HaBayit*, deriving this from the verse *shalosh regalim* — three *regalim*, with *regel* understood by *Rashi* to mean that one must be capable of ascending *b'regel*, on one's own two feet.

The child described by *Beit Hillel* must clearly be older than the one described by *Beit Shammai*: *Beit Shammai*'s threshold is met as soon as the child can ride on his father's shoulders, while *Beit Hillel* requires that he walk independently. This may initially appear to run counter to the usual expectation that *Beit Hillel* takes the more lenient position — but here *Beit Hillel* actually exempts more children by setting a higher bar for obligation. Since a *chiyuv* is a *chumra*, *Beit Hillel*'s wider exemption is in fact the more lenient ruling.

### Shammai-Hillel Value Dis…

*Beit Shammai* further rules that the minimum expenditure for the *re'iyah* — the *olah* — is two pieces of silver, and for the *chagiga*, one silver coin. *Beit Hillel* reverses this: the *re'iyah* requires only one silver coin while the *chagiga* requires two. Here again, *Beit Hillel*'s position is the more lenient one in a practical sense. Since the *chagiga* is a *shelamim* that the offerer eats, spending more on it yields a tangible personal benefit — more food — whereas the *re'iyah* is an *olah* that is burned entirely. *Beit Hillel* thus requires a smaller outlay for the *korban* from which one derives no personal benefit.

---

## Hakol Inclusive Language

### Hakol Inclusion Analysis

The *gemara* now investigates the word *hakol* — "everyone" — with which the *mishna* opens. There is a well-established principle in *gemara* analysis that when a *mishna* uses inclusive language such as *zeh haklal* or *hakol*, it is not merely summarizing what has already been stated, but rather signaling that some category one might have thought was excluded is in fact included. The *gemara* therefore asks: *hakol l'atuyei mai?* — what additional case does this word come to include?

### Half-Slave Half-Free

The *gemara* offers an initial answer: *l'atuyei mi she'chetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin* — to include the person who is half slave and half free. Such a situation arises, for example, when two partners jointly purchase a slave and one of them subsequently frees his half. One might have thought that because this person is partially enslaved, he is exempt from *re'iyah*, just as a full slave is. The *gemara* answers that his partial freedom is sufficient to generate an obligation.

### Ravina's Exemption

However, *Ravina* holds expressly that *mi she'chetzyo eved v'chetzyo ben chorin patur min ha're'iyah* — this person is in fact exempt. Since Ravina cannot accept the *gemara*'s first proposed inclusion, the question *hakol l'atuyei mai* must be answered differently.

### Healed Lameness Case

The *gemara* therefore proposes a second answer: *l'atuyei chigeir b'yom rishon v'nitpashet b'yom sheni* — to include a person who was lame on the first day of the *chag* but whose lameness healed by the second day. One might have supposed that because lame people are generally exempt, and this person was lame when the *chag* began, he has no subsequent obligation. The inclusion teaches that he is nonetheless *chayav*, since he recovered in time to fulfill the *mitzvah* during the festival.

### Which Day to Bring Korban

Yet even this answer encounters difficulty, for it depends on which of two positions one accepts in the *gemara*. According to the view that *kulan tashlumin zeh lazeh* — all the days of the festival are mutually compensating — a person may bring the *korban re'iyah* on any day of the festival if he missed a prior day, as no single day carries exclusive *chiyuv*. Under this view it is entirely intelligible that someone lame on the first day could be obligated from the second day onward.

But according to the view that *kulan tashlumin l'rishon* — all the subsequent days are merely compensatory for the first day — the *chiyuv* falls exclusively on the first day. If on the first day the person was lame and therefore not a *bar chiyuva*, he was never subject to the obligation in the first place, and there is nothing to "make up" on subsequent days. The case of healed lameness thus cannot serve as the universal inclusion intended by *hakol*, since it does not resolve the problem according to all opinions.

### One-Eye Blindness

The *gemara* therefore proposes a third answer: *l'atuyei suma b'achat mei'einav* — to include a person who is blind in one eye. Such a person is not fully blind and might be expected to be obligated; the *gemara* proposes that the word *hakol* comes to confirm this.

### Yochanan ben Dehavai Rul…

But here too there is a dissenting opinion. A *braita* records that *Yochanan ben Dehavai* rules in the name of *Rabbi Yehuda* that *suma b'achat mei'einav patur min ha're'iyah* — a person blind in one eye is exempt from the *korban re'iyah*. Given this position, Yochanan ben Dehavai cannot accept the *gemara*'s third proposed inclusion, and must therefore hold by one of the earlier positions instead.

### Two Eyes Requirement

What is Yochanan ben Dehavai's reasoning? He derives it from the verse *shene'emar yeira'eh yeireh* — "he shall be seen/he shall see." *Rashi* explains that the verse in question — *shalosh pe'amim bashana yeira'eh kol zechurcha et pnei adon Hashem* — contains a word that is written as *yireh* (he shall see) but read as *yeira'eh* (he shall be seen). From this dual reading the *gemara* derives: *kederech sheba lirot kach ba lera'ot* — just as one comes to see, so too one comes to be seen. *Ma lirot bishtei einav* — seeing is done with two eyes; *af lera'ot bishtei einav* — and therefore, to be "seen" at the Temple, one must also be capable of seeing with both eyes.

It is worth noting that this interpretive move carries an embedded assumption about what constitutes "normal" seeing — namely, binocular vision — and one sensitive to the broader halakhic treatment of disabilities will feel the weight of that assumption here.

---

## Ravina & Half-Slave Stat…

### Mishna Rishona Resolution

Having worked through all three proposed inclusions, the *gemara* circles back to address Ravina's position directly. The *gemara* offers a resolution: *kan bemishna rishona, kan bemishna achrona* — there are, in effect, two *mishnayot*. The *mishna* as a compiled text reflects a development of opinion, and a position can be revised even within the corpus of the *mishna*. Ravina's ruling — that the half-slave-half-free person is exempt from *korban re'iyah* — reflects the position of the *mishna rishona*, the earlier formulation. The *mishna* as we hold it *l'halacha* represents a later, different position.

### Gittin Mishna Rules

The *gemara* now cites the relevant *mishna* from *Masechet Gittin* to clarify what that later position entails. *Mi shechetzyo eved vechetzyo ben chorin* — a person who is half slave and half free — *oved et rabo yom echad ve'et atzmo yom echad*, *divrei Beit Hillel*: according to *Beit Hillel*, he works one day for his master and one day for himself, and this alternating arrangement is considered a workable and acceptable status quo.

### Shammai's Objection

*Beit Shammai* responds sharply: *tikantem et rabo, et atzmo lo tikantem* — you have solved the master's problem by ensuring his labor entitlement is met, but you have left the slave himself in an impossible situation.

### Marriage Impossibility

The problem is this: *lissa shifcha eino yachol* — he cannot marry a maidservant, because only a full slave may marry a female slave; *bat chorin eino yachol* — and he cannot marry a free woman either, because free people may not marry slaves. He is caught between two worlds, unable to form a household in either.

### Tikkun Ha'olam Freedom

Should he simply remain unmarried? The *gemara* rejects this: *lo nivra ha'olam ela l'pirya v'rivya* — the world was created for the purpose of propagation, as the verse states: *lo tohu vera'ah lashevet yetzarah* — God did not create the world for chaos but for habitation and continuity. Therefore, *mipnei tikkun ha'olam* — for the sake of *tikkun ha'olam* — something must be done.

It is important to note that *tikkun ha'olam* in *Masechet Gittin* carries a fairly precise and narrow meaning: it refers to legal arrangements that must be corrected because they generate untenable social situations. This is distinct from the broader contemporary usage of the term in the sense of general *chesed* or social activism.

### Forced Freedom & Debt

The resolution: *kofin et rabo ve'oseh oto ben chorin* — the *Beit Din* compels the master to free the slave entirely. Once freed, *vechotev lo shtar al chatzi damav* — the formerly enslaved person writes a promissory note to the master for half his monetary value, representing the half that the master effectively surrendered.

### Ravina Applied to Early…

With this context established, the *gemara* explains Ravina's position cleanly. When Ravina ruled that the half-slave-half-free person is exempt from *re'iyah*, he was operating according to the position of the *mishna rishona* — specifically, the original position of *Beit Hillel*, which contemplated this status as a potentially permanent arrangement. Under that view, such a person genuinely exists in a stable half-free state, and his partial servitude plausibly exempts him. But once *Beit Hillel* accepted *Beit Shammai*'s argument and ruled that the *Beit Din* must compel manumission, the intermediate status is no longer tenable. The *mishna achrona* reflects this revised position, and accordingly, the half-slave-half-free person — to the extent the status persists even briefly — is included in the obligation of *korban re'iyah*.

---

## Get Authentication Rules

### Bifnei Nechtav Rule

A related discussion arises concerning the authentication of a *get*. The question is: when is the declaration *bifnei nechtav u-bifnei nechtam* — "it was written before me and signed before me" — required of the *shaliach* who delivers the *get*?

### Geographic Requirement

This requirement applies when the *shaliach* is traveling between different provinces, or when he is bringing the *get* from *Chutz La'Aretz* to *Eretz Yisrael*, or even from one province to another within *Eretz Yisrael* itself. The concern in all these cases is that the husband may subsequently raise a *irur* — a protest — claiming that the signatures on the *get* are not his or are not those of the witnesses. Because witnesses capable of identifying those signatures may be unavailable once the *shaliach* has traveled such distances, the *shaliach* must affirm the authenticity of the document at the time of delivery.

### Same Province Exception

However, if the *shaliach* delivers the *get* within the same province in which it was written and signed, this declaration is unnecessary. In such a locale, witnesses who can recognize and verify the signatures are readily available, and the risk of an unresolvable *irur* does not arise.

---

## Number Eight Mysticism

### Eight & Transcendence

The number eight represents transcendence of the physical world — reaching beyond the natural order into something higher. We see this most clearly in *brit milah*, which takes place on the eighth day. The timing is not incidental: we are declaring that the bond between a Jewish child and *Hakadosh Baruch Hu* is something that surpasses the laws of nature, *l'maala min ha'teva*. The same principle appears in *Chanukah*. Among the many possible numbers, eight was chosen because *Chanukah* is precisely the time when we seek to take the *gashmius* of the physical world and elevate it toward *ruchnius* — to lift the material into the spiritual.

### Letter Etymology

There is a striking etymological connection embedded in the Hebrew. The letters of the word *shemonah* — eight — are the same letters as the word *neshamah* — soul — and the word *shemen* — oil. This is not coincidence; these three words share a common inner meaning.

### Oil Metaphor

Oil serves as the metaphor: when you place oil in water, it always rises to the top. It does not mix with the water; it remains separate and elevated. This is precisely what the *neshamah* does in relation to the material world. The aspiration of *shemonah* — of the eighth, of transcendence — is to reach that level where the *neshamah* guides us rather than the natural forces of the *sheva*, the seven, the world of nature that surrounds us.

---

## David & Teshuvah

### David Mekim Ol

The *gemara* teaches that David was *mekim ol teshuvah* — he was the one who raised and established the yoke of repentance. It is for this reason that *Tehillim* opens with *mizmor l'David*: David's defining contribution was his capacity to take responsibility for his actions, to say *chatati* — I have sinned — and to move forward.

### Shelah on Teshuvah

The *Shelah HaKodesh* offers a profound explanation for why David specifically was chosen to embody and establish *teshuvah*. *Teshuvah*, he explains, is not simply an apology. It is the recognition that even after a fall, even after a genuine setback, a person can rise again and be a *melech* — a king.

### King Defined

A *melech* is not someone who never fails. A *melech* is someone who knows how to deal with failure. Kingship, properly understood, is not defined by an absence of stumbling but by the capacity to rise.

### Humility & Teshuvah

The *Shelah* adds that David HaMelech possessed the specific *midah* of *anavah* — humility — and it was precisely this quality that made *teshuvah* possible for him. Without humility, one cannot admit wrongdoing. Without admitting wrongdoing, *teshuvah* is impossible. The capacity to say "I was wrong" is itself an act of greatness.

### Chatati La'Hashem

When David said *chatati L'Hashem* — I have sinned to God — that was the moment he became truly a *melech*, not merely by appointment but by character. Before that declaration, he held the throne by virtue of anointing. In that moment, he earned it by virtue of who he was.

### Teshuvah Etymology

There is a further etymological teaching: the word *teshuvah* contains within it the word *shabbat*. More precisely, *teshuvah* can be read as *tashuv heh* — return the letter *heh*. This is a deep *kabbalah* concept, but in its simplest formulation it means: return to your source, return to *Hakadosh Baruch Hu*. *Teshuvah* is not merely behavioral correction but a homecoming.

### Malchut Elevation

This is why David HaMelech is so intimately associated with *malchut* — kingship. *Malchut* is the *sefirah* that represents the capacity to take the physical world and elevate it to the spiritual, to take what has fallen and lift it higher. This is the power of *teshuvah me'ahavah* — repentance motivated by love — through which *zedonot*, intentional sins, are transformed into *zechuyot*, merits. That is the legacy David HaMelech bequeathed to us.

---

## Me'aimasai Time Framework

### Time & Change

The *Sefas Emes* asks a question that cuts to the heart of the entire *Shas*: why does the *mishna* begin with a question of time? *Me'aimasai* — from when? The *Sefas Emes* explains that time is, by definition, the medium of change and transition. A world without change, a state of permanent, undisturbed clarity, would leave no room for *emunah*.

### Faith in Darkness

*Emunah* — faith — is precisely the capacity to remain connected to the Divine even when circumstances are shifting, even when clarity gives way to obscurity, even when one moves from light into darkness. It is not the faith of certainty but the faith of commitment through change.

### Shas Begins Me'aimasai

It is therefore not incidental that the entire *Shas* opens with the word *me'aimasai*. The whole framework of our relationship with *Hashem*, the entire structure of *avodas Hashem*, is situated within time — within a world of constant flux. The question "from when?" is the foundational question of a life lived in relationship with the eternal.

### Finding Consistency

Our task within that changing world is to locate *kevi'us* — consistency, permanence, a point of stable connection to that which does not change. This is the paradox and the challenge of religious life: to find the eternal within the temporal, to anchor oneself in *Hashem* even as everything around shifts.

### Shema in Darkness

When the *mishna* asks *me'aimasai korin et Shema be'aravin* — from when do we recite the *Shema* in the evening — it is telling us something essential: it is specifically in the darkness, specifically in the moment of transition and diminishment, that we must declare *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem Echad*.
