The recitation of *Shema* is not reserved for clarity and light. It is demanded precisely in the darkness. That is the gateway to everything. That is the beginning of Torah.

---

## Jacob's Revival Legacy

### Vayechi Meaning

In *Parshas Vayechi* the Torah states: *Vayechi Yaakov b'eretz Mitzrayim* — and Jacob lived in the land of Egypt. The *Chachamim* explain that *vayechi* can be read not only as "he lived" but as "he was revived." After years of grief and suffering, upon being reunited with Yosef, Yaakov found something he had lost.

### Jacob's Peace

What gave Yaakov this sense of renewal and peace? He saw that Yosef was still a *tzadik* — that the years in Egypt had not diminished him spiritually. And he saw that all the *shevatim* were united, that the family had held together.

### Legacy Continuation

From this, Yaakov understood that the legacy of Avraham and Yitzchak would continue — that what had been built and transmitted across generations would not be lost. This realization is itself what it means to truly live.

### Values Transmission

Living, in the deepest sense, is not mere biological existence. It is seeing one's values and one's faith passed forward to the next generation. *Vayechi* — he lived — because he could see the continuity of everything he stood for.

### Jacob's Berachos

It is for this reason that Yaakov gathered his children before his death and gave them *berachos* — blessings that would fortify them for the *galus* ahead. He was not simply distributing inheritance; he was transmitting the spiritual resources they would need to survive exile.

### Connection to Roots

He understood that the only way his children would remain strong through *galus* was if they remained connected to their *shoresh* — their roots. Disconnection from one's source is the great danger of exile; connection to it is the great protection.

### Chazak Chazak

As we conclude *Sefer Bereishis*, this is the message we carry forward: *chazak chazak v'nis-chazek* — we must strengthen ourselves and one another in our *emunah* and in our commitment to Torah. That is what sustains us as a people, in whatever land we find ourselves and through whatever challenges we face.

---

---

# Chagigah 3

## Re'iyah & Two Eyes

### Tosafot: Korban vs. Mitz…

The opening discussion of our *daf* concerns the *cheresh* who is exempt from *re'iyah* — from being *oleh laregel*. Before proceeding, it is worth noting a fundamental distinction raised by the first Tosafot. Throughout the entire *masekhet*, *re'iyah* refers to the *korban re'iyah* — the *olat re'iyah*, the *korban* that is brought. Rashi, however, raises the question of whether the *mitzvah* to appear is distinct from actually bringing the *olat re'iyah*: is there a separate *mitzvah* to simply present oneself *bire'iyah ba'azarah*, to physically appear in the *azarah*, apart from the obligation to bring the *olat re'iyah*?

### Yerushalmi: Universal Ob…

Tosafot points to a Yerushalmi that addresses this very question. While only males — and only those enumerated in the *mishnah* — are obligated in the *olat re'iyah*, and all the exemptions listed there apply, the Yerushalmi maintains that the *mitzvah* to appear in the *azarah* — to literally be *oleh laregel* — applies to everyone, even women and children, derived from *hakhel*. This is a remarkable position: what the Torah presents as a once-in-seven-years obligation, the Yerushalmi understands as applying universally to all. Tosafot then goes on to demonstrate that this is clearly not the position of the Bavli. Still, it is important to note the distinction between focusing narrowly on the *korban* and thinking more broadly about the concept of being *oleh laregel*.

### Drasha: Two Eyes

A brief point from the previous *daf* also deserves mention. The *drasha* establishing that one must have sight in both eyes is grounded in the formulation *keshem sheba'im lirot kach ba'im lera'ot* — just as they come to see, so they come to be seen, as at a gathering where one is both seeing and being seen. The *drasha* draws on the imagery of God seeing with two eyes, which carries its own striking anthropomorphic dimension. But the crucial point arising from that *drasha* is the dual meaning of the verb it expounds.

### Pshat: Yira'eh et Pnei

One might assume from the *drasha* that the *pshat* of the *pasuk* is that one comes to be seen, and that the *drasha* adds the parallel sense of coming to see. But in fact the *pshat* of the *pasuk* runs in precisely the opposite direction. The verse reads *shalosh pe'amim bashanah yera'eh kol zechurecha et pnei*. The word *yera'eh* can be read as either "will be seen" or "will see," but the word *et* is decisive: *et* marks the object of the verb. To be seen *by* God would require *yera'eh lifnei*, not *yera'eh et*. Since there are no *nekudot* in the Torah scroll, the grammatically natural reading of *yira'eh et pnei* is "he will see God's face" — which is, of course, deeply anthropomorphic. It is precisely because of that anthropomorphism that we read it as *yera'eh*, the passive form. One might ask whether *et* could here mean "with" rather than the direct object marker — you will be seen together with God — and while that reading cannot be entirely dismissed, it remains difficult to argue that it represents *pshat*. What matters is that the *drasha* of the two eyes holds both meanings simultaneously, and it is important to appreciate that encountering and seeing God is in fact the simpler reading of the *pasuk*.

---

## Cheresh & Senses

### Medaber/Shome'a Dispute

The *gemara* now takes up the question of hearing. Reading from the two dots on amud bet: *medaber ve'eino shome'a, shome'a ve'eino medaber — chayav*. If one can speak but not hear, or hear but not speak, one is obligated. The *gemara* then raises a contradiction: a *baraita* states that *medaber ve'eino shome'a, shome'a ve'eino medaber — patur*. Even missing one of these two faculties produces an exemption. After establishing that the classic *cheresh* who is fully exempt from *mitzvot* is the one who can neither speak nor hear, the *gemara* had logically inferred that one who is only deaf or only mute must be *chayav*. Now the *gemara* plays out that inference against the *baraita*. The resolution offered by Ravina — or, some say, Rava — is *chisura mechsara vehachi katani*: the text is missing words and must be read with the following implicit content. The full teaching is: *hakol chayavin bire'iyah uvesimcha chutz micheresh hamedaber ve'eino shome'a, shome'a ve'eino medaber, shepatur min hare'iyah* — everyone is obligated in *simcha* and in bringing the *korban re'iyah*, except for a *cheresh* who is missing one of these two faculties, who is exempt from *re'iyah*. And yet — *ve'af al pi shepatur min hare'iyah, chayav besimcha* — even though such a person is exempt from *re'iyah*, they remain obligated in the *mitzvah* of bringing *shalmei simcha*.

### Cheresh Definition

Before proceeding, it is worth pausing on the category of *cheresh* itself. For a long time one might assume that the *cheresh* who is not a *bar chiyuva* — who is fully exempt from *mitzvot* — is someone both deaf and mute, and that such a combination is rare. In fact, for the *gemara*, nearly anyone who was deaf was a deaf-mute. The reason is that the ability to articulate speech in a comprehensible way depends on auditory feedback: without hearing, one cannot modulate one's speech to be intelligible. This was certainly the case for those born deaf in the ancient world, where no techniques existed for developing speech without hearing. The person who was not a deaf-mute in the Talmudic framework would be someone who had learned to speak normally, and only later lost their hearing. This makes the category of *cheresh* far broader than one might initially assume, and it is the background for a great deal of important *halakhic* development in later centuries — particularly when schools for the deaf demonstrated that deaf individuals possessed full intellectual capacity, could communicate through sign language, and had been systematically underestimated. That *halakhic* development is a story in itself. But for our purposes it is essential to recognize that the standard deaf person born deaf was, in the Talmudic framework, treated as a deaf-mute.

### Baraita: Exemptions

The *mishnah*'s interest is primarily to identify people who have a special exemption from *olat re'iyah* even though they are not generally exempt from *mitzvot*. The partial *cheresh* — one missing only one faculty — is a *bar chiyuva* in general; the exemption from *re'iyah* is a targeted exception rather than a sweeping exclusion. A different category is the full *cheresh* — one who can neither speak nor hear — who appears in the grouping of *cheresh shoteh vekatan*. That group represents those who are entirely exempt from all *mitzvot*: *patur mikol mitzvot ha'amurot batorah*. So while even a partial *cheresh* is exempt from *olat re'iyah* (which, as we shall see, carries many criteria), the *cheresh shoteh vekatan* of the *mishnah* refers to the fully exempt *cheresh* who is excused not only from *olat re'iyah* but from *shalmei simcha* and from all *mitzvot* altogether.

### Partial Cheresh in Simcha

The critical distinction is this: the partial *cheresh* — one who is missing only one of the two faculties — remains a *bar chiyuva* and is obligated in *simcha*. Their exemption is specifically and only from *re'iyah*. Whatever the halakhic basis for that targeted exemption turns out to be, it does not cascade into a general release from *mitzvot*. Such a person is obligated in the *mitzvah* of bringing *shalmei simcha*, because they are fundamentally subject to Torah obligation.

### Full Exemption Group

By contrast, the full *cheresh* who cannot hear and cannot speak — grouped together with *shoteh* and *katan* — is *patur af min hasimcha* and *patur mikol mitzvot ha'amurot batorah*. This is the complete exemption. The *mishnah* therefore encodes two different categories under the word *cheresh*: the full *cheresh* of the *cheresh shoteh vekatan* grouping, who is entirely exempt, and the partial *cheresh* who has a special and limited exemption from *re'iyah* alone.

---

## Hakhel Derivation

### Mai Shena Exemption

Having established that the partial *cheresh* — whether deaf but speaking, or speaking but deaf — is exempt from *re'iyah* while remaining obligated in *simcha* and all other *mitzvot*, the *gemara* now asks the obvious question: *mai shena le'inyan re'iyah deptiri* — what is different about *re'iyah* that produces this specific exemption? And correspondingly, *umai shena le'inyan simcha demichayvi bah* — why is *simcha* treated differently, such that these same individuals remain obligated?

### Gezerah Shavah

The answer is: *le'inyan re'iyah gamar re'iyah re'iyah mehakhel* — for the laws of *re'iyah* we derive by *gezerah shavah* from *hakhel*. This is, on the surface, a surprising source. *Hakhel* is an extraordinarily inclusive *mitzvah*: *ha'anashim vehanashim vehataf* — men, women, and children. We do not learn from *hakhel* to obligate women in *olat re'iyah*; yet we do learn this exemption from *hakhel*. The *gezerah shavah* connects *yera'eh kol zechurecha* with *bevo kol Yisrael lera'ot*. We then ask: how do we know from *hakhel* itself that a deaf or mute person is exempt? The answer comes from the language of the *pasuk* there: *lema'an yishme'u ulema'an yilmedu* — "so that they will hear" and "so that they will learn."

### Hearing Exclusion

The *baraita* teaches: *lema'an yishme'u — perat lemedaber ve'eino shome'a*. The requirement "so that they will hear" the reading of the Torah excludes someone who is deaf, even if they can speak, and even if they are otherwise a complete *bar chiyuva* who became deaf later in life. By *hakhel*, the essential experience is hearing the Torah read aloud, and one who cannot hear is therefore exempt.

### Teaching Exclusion

The exemption for someone who is mute but can hear is derived from *ulema'an yilmedu* — "so that they will learn" — *perat leshome'a ve'eino medaber*. But this is puzzling. One can readily understand why deafness would exempt someone from an experience centered on hearing Torah. But why would muteness prevent learning? The assumption that one who cannot speak cannot learn seems questionable — particularly since the category of *cheresh* who is fully exempt was specifically defined as one who can neither speak nor hear, precisely because intellectual capacity was associated with those faculties together. Surely a person who can hear but simply cannot produce speech retains their full capacity to absorb and understand?

### Two Mute Scholars

The *gemara* immediately challenges this: *lemeimra dechi lo mishta'ei lo gamar* — do you mean to say that one who cannot speak cannot learn? And it brings a striking empirical refutation. There were two mute individuals living in the neighborhood of Rabbi — specifically identified as the grandsons or nephews of Rabbi Yochanan ben Gudgada. Whenever Rabbi would enter the *beit midrash*, these two mute scholars would enter and sit before him. They would nod their heads — indicating comprehension — and their lips would move, clearly expressing a desire to speak. Rabbi prayed for them, and they were healed. And when they could speak, it emerged that they had mastered *hilchata, Sifra, Sifrei* — the *midrashei halacha* — and the entire *shisha sedarim*. *Gemara* as a distinct corpus did not yet exist in Rabbi's time, but they knew the entirety of *Torah She-be'al Peh*. This is not merely a *theoretical* objection to the *baraita*'s apparent assumption — it is a concrete historical demonstration that muteness does not impair the capacity to learn.

### Rav Ashi Resolution

Mar Zutra initially responds that the verse must be read differently — the *pshat* of *lema'an yilmedu* does not actually exclude mute people from learning; rather, someone who is mute cannot *teach*. In an oral culture, without the development of sign language, the *gemara* understood that the fullest sense of *limud* — of teaching Torah over to others — was not achievable without speech. The exemption, then, is not premised on the incapacity to absorb knowledge, but on the incapacity to transmit it.

Rav Ashi, however, offers an internal proof that this must be the correct reading, without needing to appeal to the story of the mute scholars at all. If *lema'an yilmedu* were understood to exclude mute people on the grounds that they cannot learn, then the same reasoning would equally apply to deaf people — one who cannot hear presumably also cannot receive information and therefore cannot learn. But if that were so, the *pasuk* of *lema'an yishme'u* would be superfluous: both exemptions could have been derived from *lema'an yilmedu* alone. Since the Torah needed *lema'an yishme'u* specifically to exclude the deaf, it is clear that the Torah is not assuming an incapacity to learn in either case. *Lema'an yilmedu* must therefore be read as referring to the capacity to *teach*, not merely to learn. *Ela vadai lema'an yilmedu hu* — it must certainly be read as "so that they will teach." One who is mute cannot teach in the oral-transmission sense that the *hakhel* ceremony represents, and is therefore exempt. That exemption, via *gezerah shavah*, applies equally to *re'iyah*.

It is worth pausing to acknowledge the troubling character of these exclusions. Person after person — those blind in one eye, those who cannot hear, those who cannot speak — is being exempted from *olat re'iyah* on the basis of a physical faculty that is not present. Nobody is barring these individuals from entering the *beit hamikdash* or bringing *korbanot* of their own volition; these are exemptions from obligation, not prohibitions from participation. Still, exemption can carry the force of exclusion, and reading through these categories is genuinely challenging. One might note that even *hakhel* itself — which includes the *taf*, infants who can neither learn nor hear nor teach — suggests that mere presence carries its own significance. The *gemara* will return to this point when discussing why infants are brought to *hakhel* at all. The *olat re'iyah*, by contrast, is apparently understood as a *mitzvah* that requires full engagement of the relevant faculties, even though precisely what those faculties have to do with the experiential dimension of appearing before God in the *azarah* is not entirely clear.

---

## One-Sense Defects

### Deaf One Ear

Rabbi Tanchum now extends the principle: *cheresh b'ozen achat patur min hare'iyah* — someone deaf in one ear is exempt from *re'iyah*. Just as we have already exempted those blind in one eye, and just as through the *hakhel* comparison we have exempted the partially deaf and the mute, we now extend the principle even further: one who is deaf in only one ear is likewise exempt.

### Ba'ozneihem Both Ears

The source is the word *b'ozneihem* in the *hakhel* passage: the Torah is to be read *into their ears*. One might object that *b'ozneihem* refers collectively to the ears of all Israel gathered together — the assembled nation has many ears among them — and does not necessarily require that each individual possess two functioning ears. The *gemara* dismisses this: the requirement that each person be in a position to hear already emerges from the phrase *lema'an yishme'u*. If the verse had only said to read the Torah *neged kol Yisrael* — in front of all the people — one might have thought that physical presence, not auditory reception, was what mattered: the experiential sense of being there. *B'ozneihem* therefore adds something beyond what *lema'an yishme'u* already says. It cannot be teaching that individuals must personally be within earshot, because that is already derived from *lema'an yishme'u*. *B'ozneihem* must therefore be teaching that each individual requires both ears. Consequently, someone deaf in one ear is exempt from *hakhel*, and by extension — through the *gezerah shavah* — from *re'iyah* as well.

### Lame One Leg

Rabbi Tanchum adds a parallel ruling: *chiger b'regel achat patur min hare'iyah* — one who is lame in one leg is exempt from *re'iyah*. The pattern is clear: just as sight in both eyes, hearing in both ears, and the faculty of speech are each required, so too is full use of both legs.

### Regalim Etymology

The proof text is the word *regalim* itself. The festivals are called *shalosh regalim bashanah* — and while *regel* can mean an occasion or a time (as when Bilam's donkey says *ki hikisani zeh shalosh regalim*), the word very powerfully also means legs. It is not merely a play on words: the *regalim* are named for the journey, the walking, the act of traveling up to the *beit hamikdash* on foot. Therefore, the word *regalim* in the festival formula implies that one requires the full use of one's legs.

### Prosthetics & Limping

Here the *gemara* distinguishes between two different exclusions, each derived from a different word. The exclusion of someone who wears a prosthesis — *ba'alei kabin* — someone who has lost a foot or leg and uses a wooden substitute, comes not from *regalim* but from the word *pe'amim*. The *pasuk* reads both *shalosh regalim* and *shalosh pe'amim bashanah*. A *baraita* clarifies: *ein pe'amim ela regalim* — *pe'amim* means feet, specifically the soles or the feet themselves. The verse is quoted: *tirmesena regel raglei ani pa'amei dalim* — it will be trodden by a foot, the feet of the poor, the soles of the impoverished. And more directly: *ma yafu pa'amayich bine'alim bat nadiv* — how beautiful are your feet in sandals, daughter of the generous one. The feet are what are in the shoes. *Pa'amim*, then, specifically denotes feet. Someone with a prosthesis does not have *regalim* in this sense — not a foot — and is therefore excluded from the word *pe'amim*. Interestingly, this would suggest that even someone who has their leg intact but has lost the foot would fall into this category. Given that *pe'amim* already excludes prosthetic wearers, the word *regalim* must be doing additional work: it excludes someone who is not physically missing a leg but is simply lame in one leg. The presence of both words thus produces two distinct exclusions. Again, it must be emphasized: these are exemptions from obligation, not prohibitions on entry. Nevertheless, reading this accumulation of physical criteria one after another is genuinely sobering. The *beit hamikdash* context has its own aesthetic dimension — the expectation of wholeness and perfection that pervades the Temple service — but one is also aware that these exemptions carry a certain force of exclusion, however unintentional.

---

## Aggadic Teachings

### Beauty of Pilgrimage

The *gemara* now turns to *aggadeta*, and fittingly, the *drashot* here emerge directly from the very verses we have been analyzing. Rava expounds: what is meant by the verse *ma yafu pa'amayich bine'alim bat nadiv* — how beautiful are your feet in sandals, daughter of the generous one? *Kama na'im ragleihem shel Yisrael beshaa sheolin laregel* — how beautiful are the legs of Israel in the moment when they go up to the *regel*. The verse, which we have just been parsing for its halakhic implications regarding feet and prosthetics, is now read as an expression of the beauty of the pilgrimage itself: the sight of all of Israel ascending to Jerusalem for the *regel*.

### Bat Nadiv Drasha

Who, then, is *bat nadiv* — the daughter of the generous one? *Bito shel Avraham Avinu shenikra nadiv* — the daughter of Abraham our father, who was called *nadiv*, generous. The proof text is *nedivei amim ne'esafu, am Elohei Avraham* — the generous ones of the nations gathered, the nation of the God of Abraham. One might ask: in the verse, it is the *amim* — the nations — who are the *nedivim*, not Abraham himself. The *drasha* reads them in juxtaposition: they gather as *am Elohei Avraham*, as the nation of Abraham's God, and it is Abraham who is the paradigmatic *nadiv*. But why *Elohei Avraham* only, and not *Elohei Yitzchak veYa'akov*? *Ella Elohei Avraham shehaya techila lagerim* — because Abraham was the first of converts, the first to step forward in response to the call of God. Rashi explains *nedivei amim* as referring to *gerim* — those who give of themselves from among the nations to accept the *ol mitzvot*. Abraham is the model for that movement: not merely in the technical sense that Tosafot points to — *techila lagerim shenitchayev al hamila*, the first to be obligated in *milah* — but in the deeper sense that Rashi suggests: Abraham traversed the world calling people to God, *vayikra b'shem Hashem*, and drew followers in every place he traveled. There is a beautiful parallel here between *nedivei amim ne'esafu* — the generous ones of the nations gathering — and the event of the *regel* itself, when people come from all around to gather at the mountain of God. The pilgrimage, with its vast convergence of people, resonates with the image of Abraham drawing humanity toward recognition of God.

### Pki'in Story

The *gemara* now presents a *baraita*: it happened that Rabbi Yochanan ben Broka and Rabbi Elazar Chasma — Rabbi Elazar ben Chasma — went to visit Rabbi Yehoshua in Pki'in. The occasion is presumably *yom tov*, when the practice of *hakbalat pnei rabbo* — visiting one's teacher — was observed. Rabbi Yehoshua asked them: *ma chiddush haya b'veit hamidrash hayom* — what new idea came up in the *beit midrash* today? They demurred: *talmidecha anu, mimeimecha anu shotim* — we are your students; we drink from your waters. We have nothing to tell you that you would not already know. He pressed them: *af al pi chen, iy efshar l'veit hamidrash belo chiddush* — even so, it is impossible that nothing new arose in the study hall. I too can learn; tell me what came up. Whose week was it? It had been the week of Rabbi Eleazar ben Azarya — his turn to lead the *beit midrash* in the rotation. And what was the *hagada* delivered? This phrasing is itself notable: it implies that each session would include both *halakhic* study and a teaching of *hagada*, an *aggadic* or conceptual component — a model that perhaps some later academies might have taken to heart. It was in *parshat hakhel* that they had been learning.

### Hakhel Teaching

What, then, had Rabbi Eleazar ben Azarya taught about *hakhel*? *Hakhel et ha'am ha'anashim vehanashim vehataf* — assemble the people: the men, the women, and the children. *Im anashim ba'im lilmod* — men come to learn; that is self-evident. *Nashim ba'ot lishmo'a* — women come to hear. The *gemara*'s assumption is not that women lacked intelligence, but that they lacked the depth of formal education that would allow them to fully comprehend the legal and analytical content being transmitted. The differentiation is one of educational background. But then: *taf lama ba'im?* — why are infants brought? They cannot learn; they cannot even understand what is being said; it is, from a content-absorption standpoint, entirely beyond them. *Kedei litein sachar limvi'eihem* — in order to give reward to those who bring them. This might seem to beg the question — if the infants serve no purpose, why is there reward for bringing them? — but the answer contains its own depth. Bringing one's children to a transformative communal religious experience has an impact on the parents themselves, reinforcing the importance of raising children within these moments. And one cannot entirely discount even the young child's exposure to a powerful communal event: even if no cognitive content is absorbed, the impressionistic experience may have some formative effect. Rabbi Yehoshua's reaction upon hearing this: *margalit tovah hayetah beyadchem uvik'ashtem l'abdem mimeni* — you had a beautiful pearl in your hands and you sought to lose it from me, to deprive me of it. Why did I have to pull it out of you?

A further point arises from Tosafot's comment on *nashim ba'ot lishmo'a*. Tosafot cites the Yerushalmi, which notes that this does not accord with the position of Ben Azzai, who holds that a person is obligated to teach his daughter Torah — *chayav adam lelamed livto Torah*. Under that view, women would be educated and would come not merely to hear but to learn. This is the second Yerushalmi on our *daf* that takes an explicitly more inclusive position: the first held that women must be *oleh laregel* even without the obligation of *korban re'iyah*, and now a further position holds that women are obligated in Torah study. Tosafot also notes, in connection with *kedei litein sachar limvi'eihem*, that it is on this basis that the practice developed of bringing young children to *beit knesset* — the synagogue. This speaks to a genuine tension: does the presence of young children disrupt the *davening* of others, or does the importance of bringing them — for the children, and for the parents, and for the community — outweigh that disruption?

One further observation on the story: a compelling reading suggests that Rabbi Yehoshua may have been too infirm to attend the *beit midrash* himself that day, which would give the narrative its full poignancy. The students feel unable to tell him what transpired precisely because they are embarrassed that the *beit midrash* went on without him; they say *talmidecha anu, mimeimecha anu shotim* as a way of acknowledging that he is their source. And his response — *iy efshar l'veit hamidrash belo chiddush* — carries an implicit message: the *beit midrash* generates new ideas even beyond what any individual teacher already knows, and that is beautiful, not threatening.

### Reciprocal Choosing

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had a further *drasha* that day: *et Hashem he'emarta hayom* — you have chosen, or elevated, God today — *v'Hashem he'emircha hayom* — and God has chosen you. Rashi reads *he'emarta* as elevation and selection. The *gemara* explains: God said to Israel, *atem asituni chativa achat ba'olam* — you have made me one unit, one singular object, in the world — *va'ani e'eseh etchem chativa achat ba'olam* — and I will make you one singular unit in the world. Israel makes God one: *Shema Yisrael Hashem Elokeinu Hashem echad*. God makes Israel one: *umi k'amcha Yisrael goy echad ba'aretz*. Each declares the uniqueness of the other; and implicit within that declaration of uniqueness is the declaration of relationship, of chosenness — *Hashem Elokeinu*, our God, and *umi k'amcha Yisrael*, who is like Your nation Israel.

Tosafot adds a further beautiful element: three things testify to one another — *Yisrael, Shabbat*, and *Hakadosh Baruch Hu*. Israel and God together testify to *Shabbat* as a day of rest; Israel and *Shabbat* together testify to God's oneness; and God and *Shabbat* together testify to Israel's singular status among the nations, *she'hem yechidim ba'umot*. It is on this basis, Tosafot notes, that we conclude *Ata Echad* in the *Mincha* of *Shabbat*. Even though *Mincha* of *Shabbat* does not open immediately with the theme of *Shabbat* as *Maariv* and *Shachrit* do, the theme of *echad* — of oneness — connects Israel, God, and *Shabbat* in precisely the way the *drasha* has articulated.

In closing his response to the two visiting students, Rabbi Yehoshua said: *ein dor yatom she-Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah sharui b'tocho* — no generation is an orphan that has Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya within it. A generation led by such a teacher cannot be called bereft.

---

## Torah Diversity

### Goads & Nails

Now Rabbi Yehoshua himself opens with a *drasha*: *divrei chachamim kadorbanot uchmasmerot netuim ba'alei asufot nitnu me-ro'eh echad* — the words of the sages are like prods and like planted nails, given from the masters of collections, all given from one shepherd. Why are words of Torah compared to a prodding stick, a *dorban*? *Mah dorban zeh mechavein et haparah litalmeha lehotzi chayim la'olam* — just as a prod directs the cow along its furrow to bring forth life from the earth, so the words of Torah direct those who study them from the paths of death toward the paths of life. The image is precise: the *dorban* keeps the cow on a straight line to make a clean furrow; plowing that furrow is what brings forth the produce, the growth, the life from the ground. Torah constrains and directs, keeps one on a narrow path — but that narrow path is precisely what brings forth true life.

But a prod is also movable, not fixed. Is Torah similarly portable, shifting? *Talmud lomar masmerot* — the verse also says nails, something fixed and planted. Perhaps Torah is like a nail: stable, immovable. Yet a nail also only diminishes over time — it rusts, corrodes, never grows. Surely Torah is not merely static?

### Parah V'Rabah

*Talmud lomar netuim* — planted. A planting is not fixed in the rigid sense of a nail; it is *parah ve-rabah*, fruitful and multiplying. *Af divrei Torah parim ve-rabim* — the words of Torah are also fruitful and multiply. Torah is planted, takes root, and from that rootedness spreads forth, producing fruit, drawing others in, multiplying through study and transmission. This also resonates with the image of staying fixed in one place: if one is rooted in a community of Torah, it bears fruit outward and brings others to engage with it.

### Conflicting Opinions

*Ba'alei asufot* — the masters of collections, or assemblies. These are Torah sages who gather together in groups and groups, *yoshvin asufot asufot*, and engage in Torah. And here the beautiful complexity emerges: *hallalu metamein ve-hallalu metaherin* — these declare *tamei*, those declare *tahor*. *Hallalu osrin ve-hallalu mattirim* — these prohibit, those permit. *Hallalu poslin ve-hallalu machshirin* — these invalidate, those validate. The *beit midrash* generates a profusion of competing voices, competing rulings. This is, in one sense, exactly what makes Torah alive and fructifying — the *parah ve-rabah*, the fruitfulness, expressed through the energy of *machloket*. But it also raises an anxiety: *shema yomar adam, heicha ani lomed Torah me'atah* — how is a person supposed to navigate? With all these different voices, how does one find the path?

### One Shepherd Unity

*Talmud lomar kullam nitnu me-ro'eh echad* — all of them were given from one shepherd. *El echad netanan, parnas echad amran, mi-pi adon kol ha-ma'asim baruch hu* — one God gave them, one sustainer spoke them, from the mouth of the Master of all Creation. The verse is: *va-yedabber Elohim et kol ha-devarim ha-eileh* — God spoke all these things. All the different voices, all the competing opinions, all the tensions and arguments and rulings — they all ultimately flow from the one source. The multiplicity does not undermine the unity; rather, the unity undergirds and holds the multiplicity.

### Discerning Heart

*Af attah aseh oznecha ke-afarkeset* — make your ear like a funnel. Take it all in. *Ukhnei lecha lev mevin lishmoa et divrei metameim ve-et divrei metaherin, et divrei osrim ve-et divrei mattirim, et divrei poslin ve-et divrei machshirin* — acquire for yourself a discerning heart, to hear the words of those who declare *tamei* and those who declare *tahor*, those who prohibit and those who permit, those who invalidate and those who validate. The goal is not merely to absorb passively but to develop genuine analytic judgment — to hear all the voices, hold them in tension, and discern one's way through them. This is at once the responsibility and the beauty of Torah: the narrow furrow of the prod and the fruitful multiplicity of the planting are not contradictions. One walks a defined path, but that path requires a living, discerning mind to navigate.

The *aggadeta* here sits in elegant tension with the opening of the story: Rabbi Yehoshua told his visitors that *iy efshar l'veit hamidrash belo chiddush* — the *beit midrash* is not possible without new ideas. He wanted to hear a voice that was not his own. His *drasha* now articulates why: because all the different voices together are what makes Torah fruitful and alive, and they all come from one shepherd. He embraces the multiplicity rather than demanding that all knowledge be channeled through a single transmitted tradition.

---

## Rabbi Eliezer & Mesora

### Acknowledgment Before Te…

The *gemara* now asks: given the exchange we just read — the visiting students reluctantly acknowledging to Rabbi Yehoshua that they had something to tell him only after he pressed them — why did they need to go through that dance at all? Why didn't they simply tell him directly, *be-hedya*, what had transpired in the *beit midrash*? The answer: *mishum ma'aseh shehaya* — because of a prior episode in which someone went directly, without any such deference, and the outcome was not good. The lesson that one should first acknowledge the rabbi as the source of one's Torah, before simply presenting a teaching, is derived from that episode.

### Durmaski's Error

A *baraita* teaches: it happened that Rabbi Yose ben Durmaski went to receive Rabbi Eliezer in Lod — and this visit, like the one to Rabbi Yehoshua in Pki'in, may well have been on *yom tov*, in the context of *hakbalat pnei rabbo*. Rabbi Eliezer asked him: *ma chiddush haya b'veit hamidrash hayom?* — what new idea came up in the *beit midrash* today? And Rabbi Yose ben Durmaski simply answered. He did not go through the dance. He did not say: we are your students, we drink from your waters. He told Rabbi Eliezer directly what the *beit midrash* had concluded.

### Eyes Fall Out

Rabbi Eliezer's reaction was explosive: *pashat yadav vekibel einav* — he stretched out his hands and his eyes fell out. The physical drama here is striking, and the *gemara* records that Rabbi Eliezer wept. He cited the verse: *sod Hashem liyereiav uvrito lehodiam* — God's secret belongs to those who fear Him, and His covenant, to inform them.

### Ammon & Moav

What had Rabbi Yose ben Durmaski reported? *Nimnu vegamru* — they took a vote and concluded — *Ammon uMoav ma'asrin ma'aser ani beshvi'it*: that Ammon and Moav, the Transjordanian lands settled by Jews, give *ma'aser ani* — the tithe for the poor — in the seventh year, rather than *ma'aser sheni*. These lands do not practice *shemita* — they continue to plant and cultivate during the sabbatical year — and in place of the second tithe, which is set aside and eaten in Jerusalem, they give the poor tithe. Rabbi Eliezer told Rabbi Yose ben Durmaski to go back and tell the *beit midrash*: *al techoshu laminyanechem* — do not be anxious about your vote. And Rashi explains this as "don't worry, you got it right" — but Rabbi Eliezer's deeper point seems to be far more radical: who needed your vote in the first place? *Kach mekublani me-Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, sheshama me-rabbo ve-rabbo me-rabbo* — I received this as a tradition from Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, who heard it from his teacher, and his teacher from his teacher, going all the way back — *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* — to a teaching transmitted from Moshe at Sinai. Exactly what you concluded by vote, I already possessed as received tradition. The use of the phrase *halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai* here is loose — the relevant *halakhot* regarding Ammon and Moav are clearly rabbinic — and this is noted by the *Rosh*, who points out that the phrase is being used metaphorically, meaning *davar barur kehalacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai*, something as certain as a law from Sinai.

### Secret Knowledge

The verse *sod Hashem liyereiav* — God's secret belongs to those who fear Him — is the key to understanding Rabbi Eliezer's reaction. He was in possession of this tradition. He knew. And it was this knowledge, this *mesora* transmitted through a chain of teachers all the way back to Moshe, that he regarded as authoritative. Not a vote. Not a *chiddush*. Not a process of deliberation and majority ruling. The *mesora* simply was, and those who feared God and received it faithfully were its custodians. What infuriated him, it seems, was not that the conclusion was wrong — it was identical to his tradition — but that the *beit midrash* had treated this as something to be decided through debate and vote, as though it were an open question amenable to *chiddush*. It was not a *chiddush*. It was already known.

### Eliezer vs. Yehoshua

The contrast between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is now fully visible. Rabbi Yehoshua says: *iy efshar l'veit hamidrash belo chiddush* — it is impossible for the *beit midrash* to exist without something new. He celebrates the multiplicity of voices, the energy of differing opinions, the beauty of Torah's *parah ve-rabah*. He tells us to make our ears like a funnel and acquire a discerning heart to navigate the competing rulings. For Rabbi Yehoshua, Torah lives in the *machloket*, in the vote, in the process. Rabbi Eliezer, by contrast, holds that Torah lives in the *mesora*. What you have received from your teacher, your teacher from his teacher, and so on back to Sinai — that is Torah. *Chiddush* is not Torah's vitality; it is a potential distortion of it. He is the one who, famously, could not accept a majority vote that overrode his tradition, and this episode illuminates precisely why. The *beit midrash* reached the right answer, but it reached it by the wrong method. There is a certain poignancy in the contrast: Rabbi Yehoshua would have been perfectly happy for the students to simply tell him what came up, multiple voices and all; Rabbi Eliezer, the one who most needed to be acknowledged as the transmitter of *mesora*, was the one who received the teaching without that acknowledgment. It is always the way: the adjustment one makes after an error tends to be applied to cases where it was not needed, and missed in the cases where it was.

---

---

# Chagigah 4

## Amon & Moab

### R. Eliezer's Report

We pick up approximately six lines before the wider lines begin on the page — about twelve lines from the bottom, where the text reads *ma ta'am*. We were in the middle of a discussion that featured two strikingly different approaches: that of Rabbi Eliezer and that of Rabbi Yehoshua, dealing with what happens when their students came and reported what was transpiring in the *beis medrash*. The heart of the dispute concerned Rabbi Yehoshua's eagerness to hear a multiplicity of voices — that multiplicity itself being part of what *Torah she-be'al peh* is about — whereas Rabbi Eliezer held that Torah transmission is only about the straight tradition. Rabbi Eliezer was therefore deeply offended that his students had held a debate, taken a vote, and reached a conclusion on a matter about which he possessed a direct tradition. The student who reported this to him had his eyes fall out — an arresting detail, given that the surrounding discussion concerns a blind person and *aliyah l'regel* and *mitzvas re'iyah*, though whether there is any intentional echo there is difficult to say.

### Amon/Moab Rules

The substance of what was decided — the tradition Rabbi Eliezer claimed to possess — is now stated: Amon and Moab, the trans-Jordanian territories, do not observe the *shemita* year, yet they do observe *trumos u-ma'asros* and give *ma'aser ani* during the *shemita* year. The Gemara then asks: *ma ta'am* — what is the reason?

### Kedusha Rishona

The answer is that many cities were conquered by those who came up from Egypt in the time of Yehoshua and were sanctified with the sanctity of the land of Israel, but they were not re-sanctified in the time of Ezra. Therefore they do not technically possess *kedushah* and are not bound by the agricultural *mitzvos* of *trumos u-ma'asros* and *shemita* — *mipnei she-kedusha rishona kidesha l'sha'ata v'lo kidesha l'asid lavo*, because the first sanctity in the time of Yehoshua was not for all time. (This question of whether *kedusha rishona* was permanent or temporary was discussed in Megillah and is rooted in *pesukim* that speak of the return to the land — the re-entry in the time of Ezra being compared to the original entry, such that a second conquest would be necessary to re-sanctify the land. The related question of whether all *shemita* today is *derabbanan* is itself a major debate, which we will not unpack here.)

### Cities for Poor

The Gemara adds a further and specific point: certain cities were *intentionally* left outside the re-sanctification — *kedei she-yismachu aleihem aniyim bashevi'is*, in order that the poor should be able to rely on them during the *shemita* year.

### Shemita Paradox

This Gemara is a striking and ironic one. What it is saying, in effect, is that if you were to observe *shemita* in those territories, the poor would actually be worse off. The idea that *shemita* benefits the poor — by leaving produce accessible to all — is undermined by the very requirement to let the land lie fallow. If the land is not being worked, what is there for the poor beyond whatever grows wild? So the best arrangement for the poor turns out to be the opposite of *shemita*: work the land, and then give a tenth of the produce as *ma'aser ani* to the *aniyim*. Since the first sanctity of those territories was not permanent and the re-sanctification never took place, the subsequent observance of these agricultural laws was only *derabbanan*, not *de'oraisa* — and therefore the Rabbis had the authority to determine what would apply. They ruled accordingly: since *shemita* is not practiced there, the land is worked, and *ma'aser ani* is given, ensuring that the poor of the land of Israel have what to live off of during a year when the land of Israel itself lies fallow.

This Gemara beautifully captures a deep internal tension within *shemita*: the value of leaving the land fallow operates at cross purposes with the value of sustaining the poor. The same tension plays out in various modern *shemita* mechanisms — *heter mechira*, *pruzbul*, and related devices — all of which reflect the reality that some of the values embedded in *shemita* can pull in opposite directions.

### Eyes Restored

After this discussion, the Gemara records in a *baraita*: *le'achar shenityashevah da'ato* — after Rabbi Eliezer had calmed down, he said, *yehi ratzon sheyachzir einay Yosei limkomam* — may it be God's will that Yosei's eyes be restored to their place — *vachazaru* — and they returned to their sockets. The story is grotesque, but it is told in the immediate context of *mitzvas re'iyah*, and that thematic frame is hard to ignore.

---

## Shoteh Definition

### Three Behaviors

The Gemara now moves from the *cheresh* to the *shoteh*. This discussion, though brief, is an important one for thinking about how the Gemara defines someone who is not of sound mind and therefore lacks halakhic legal responsibility. *Eizehu shoteh* — who is a *shoteh*? Three observable behaviors are listed: *hayotze yachidi balaylah* — one who goes out alone at night (telling us something about the society in which they lived, where no normal person ventures out alone at night due to wild animals and robbers); *vehalan beveis hakevaros* — one who sleeps in cemeteries; *vehamakarea et kesuto* — one who tears his own garments for no apparent purpose.

On this list, two positions are recorded. Rav Huna says: *ad sheyehu kulam bevat achat* — only if he does all three together does he qualify as a *shoteh*. Rabbi Yochanan says: *afilu be'achat mehen* — even one of them suffices.

### R. Yochanan

The Gemara then presses: *heichi dami* — what exactly is the case? The force of the question is this: if the person is doing any one of these acts *derech shtut* — in a way that clearly indicates irrational behavior — then why would Rabbi Yochanan need more than one? And if he is doing them in a way that does not indicate irrationality, even all three together should not suffice. So what exactly is each opinion maintaining?

### Derech Shtut

The Gemara resolves: *le'olam deka avid lehu derech shtut* — we are indeed talking about a person who does these things in a manner that appears irrational. But the Gemara then introduces an important qualification: even when the act looks irrational on its face, there may yet be an explanation we have not considered.

### Alt Explanations

Take the case of one who sleeps in a cemetery. It looks completely irrational — but perhaps, says the Gemara, *kedei shetishre alav ruach tumah hu deka avid*, he is trying to attract an evil spirit, to engage in some form of black magic. Within a worldview in which spirits can be summoned and manipulated, this is not irrational at all. Similarly, the one who goes out alone at night — *emor gandanrifas achadei*, perhaps *gandanrifas* has taken hold of him. Rashi understands this as either an overwhelming anxiety attack or a severe fever that drives him to seek fresh air; in either case, an unusual but not necessarily irrational circumstance might explain the behavior. And the one who tears his garments — perhaps he is simply an absentminded person, so lost in his thoughts that he does not notice what his hands are doing, the way some people ruin a tie or unravel a seam mid-conversation without any awareness. So in each individual case, the behavior looks irrational, yet an explanation is at least conceivable.

### Pattern Evidence

This is where Rav Huna's position gains its force. The Gemara says: *keivan de'avdinhu lekulhu* — once he has done all three, what single explanation could account for three completely different seemingly irrational acts? The Gemara compares this to the case of an ox that gored a donkey, a camel, and another ox — *vena'aseh muad lakol* — and we establish that it is a habitual gorer with no discrimination about its targets. The common denominator across three different categories is itself the evidence. Just as three gorings of different animals establishes an indiscriminate pattern, three different irrational acts — each explicable on its own but not together — establish a general pattern of incompetence. This is Rav Huna's logic: any single act might have an innocent explanation; the composite of three distinct acts, each of a different type, admits only one general explanation — the person is not of sound mind.

Rabbi Yochanan's position, requiring only one act, sets a considerably lower threshold and is for that reason more troubling: one does not want too low a threshold for placing someone in this category.

It is worth noting what the Gemara is consistently trying to do here: as a legal system, it wants to focus on observable activities and to fit the analysis into a framework it already knows — the laws of *muad* — in order to make the determination replicable. And yet the Gemara's own question, *ei de'avid derech shtut ei de'lo avid derech shtut*, reveals that the real driver is contextual judgment. Each case has to be assessed on its own. There is a tension between the desire for concrete, checkable criteria and the recognition that no fixed list can substitute for genuine evaluation of the individual.

This also connects to the broader question of what these three behaviors actually are. They read as folk definitions — the kinds of things people in that society would point to and say, "that is what crazy looks like." The Gemara then takes those folk definitions and tries to impose a formal halakhic structure on them, using the logic of *muad* and *tam*. Whether the formal structure can fully bear the weight of the question is itself something the Gemara leaves in tension. One might ask, for example, about someone who is schizophrenic and moves between states — *itim shoteh itim shafui* — a case the Gemara does engage with elsewhere. Or about someone in a manic episode who is compulsively spending money — which connects directly to the next source.

### Wasting Money

Rav Pappa cites a *baraita* from the tractate of *Trumos* that adds a further criterion: *eizehu shoteh zeh me'abed kol mah shenosnim lo* — who is a *shoteh*? One who destroys or wastes everything given to him. You hand the person a hundred dinars and he throws it in the street. Here, a single act of a particular type — destroying one's own property — is sufficient to establish the status of *shoteh*.

### Teiku

This prompts the Gemara to ask: would Rav Huna, had he heard this *tosefta*, have reversed his position? The question is framed carefully. Perhaps he would have reversed himself only with respect to the case most analogous to this one — *mikarea kesuto*, the tearing of garments, since tearing one's garment is a form of destroying one's own property, similar to wasting money. If so, he would have said: that one act alone suffices, while going out at night and sleeping in a cemetery still require the composite of all three. Or perhaps, once he conceded that a single act of this type suffices, he would have generalized and said any one of the three is sufficient by itself. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved: *teiku*.

The *Tosafos* cites a line from the Yerushalmi that adds further texture. The Yerushalmi records a debate parallel to the Bavli's, but then contains the statement of Rabbi Avin: *mistabra k'Rabbi Yochanan b'chada mim'abed mah shenosnim lo* — it makes sense to rule like Rabbi Yochanan at least in the case of *me'abed mah shenosnim lo*, because *afilu shoteh shebishotim eino me'abed mah shenosnim lo* — even the most mentally impaired person does not casually throw away everything given to him. That act, in other words, is so beyond any conceivable rational explanation that even one instance is diagnostic in a way the other behaviors are not.

What the Gemara ultimately leaves us with is this: the key question is always whether the act is being done *derech shtut* or not. Observable criteria and formal lists are the legal system's attempt to provide clarity, but the Gemara itself acknowledges that some criteria may be individually sufficient while others are not, and that the individual circumstances of each case cannot be fully replaced by a mechanical checklist.

---

## Tumtum/Androgynous

### Zacur Exclusion

The Gemara now addresses two categories of ambiguous or third-category sex: *tumtum* and *androgynus*. A *tumtum* is a person whose genitalia are present but covered by skin due to a birth defect or similar condition — we cannot see them and therefore cannot determine the person's sex. An *androgynus* is a person who actually has both male and female genitalia. Both are not obligated in the *mitzvas re'iyah*.

The Gemara opens with a *baraita*: *zachar* — from the word *z'chorkha*, "your males" — *l'hotzi et ha'nashim*, to exclude women. *Z'chorkha*, the possessive "your males," *l'hotzi tumtum v'androgynus*, to exclude a *tumtum* and an *androgynus*. And then the word *kol*, "all" — *kol z'chorkha l'rabot et ha'ketanim* — to include minor sons. The Gemara proceeds to unpack each of these derivations.

First, why does the verse need to tell us women are excluded? The Gemara notes that *aliyah l'regel* and bringing an *olat re'iyah* is a *mitzvat aseh shehazman grama* — a positive time-bound commandment — and women are generally exempt from time-bound positive commandments. So we should have been able to derive the exemption of women from that general principle without needing an explicit verse. The Gemara answers: *itztrich* — the verse is necessary. Without it, we might have applied a *gezeirah shavah* from *hakhel*, where the Torah explicitly includes men, women, and children in the assembly. We might have reasoned: just as there women are obligated, so here too women should be obligated. The verse therefore comes to teach us that they are not. It should be noted — and the *Rambam* already points this out — that the general principle of *mitzvat aseh shehazman grama* is wrong approximately half the time. It is more descriptive than predictive, and it tends to appear at the *stam* level of the Gemara as a retrospective question rather than a reliable rule.

Additionally, the Yerushalmi records that women are indeed obligated in *aliyah l'regel* itself, derived from *hakhel* — they are simply not obligated to bring the *korban*. So the exclusion operates specifically at the level of the *olat re'iyah*, not at the level of appearing in Jerusalem altogether.

### Androgynus Logic

The Gemara then turns to the exclusion of *androgynus*. *Bishlama androgynus itztrich* — I understand why a verse is needed here. Without an explicit exclusion, *salka daitakh amina* — I would have thought: *ho'il v'it lei tzad zachrut*, since this person has male genitalia as well as female, there is an aspect of maleness present that might suffice to obligate them. *Kamashma lan* — the verse teaches otherwise: *d'beriyah bifnei atzma hu* — an *androgynus* is their own category, neither male nor female, and therefore not included within the narrow definition of "male" operative here.

This is worth pausing on. The recognition in the Gemara that the world is not simply divided male and female — that there may be a third category, a person who has both male and female genitalia — is a striking feature of this discussion. The Gemara is focused exclusively on observable genitalia and not on other markers of gender, but the recognition of a third category is nonetheless remarkable. Not everyone agrees that *androgynus* represents a genuine third category; some maintain the person is male or female and we simply cannot determine which. But the possibility of a third category is taken seriously here.

The *androgynus* presents a fascinating complexity across different halakhic contexts. *Tosafos* notes an opinion in the Gemara that an *androgynus* would receive a *bris milah* on *Shabbos* — because the presence of male genitalia and an *orlah* is sufficient to establish an absolute obligation in *bris milah*, even if it does not establish that the person is unambiguously male in all respects. The category sometimes pulls toward inclusion as male and sometimes toward exclusion, and here it pulls toward exclusion. The logic is that for *olat re'iyah*, the definition of "male" is drawn narrowly enough that having only a partial male identity does not suffice.

### Safek Problem

The Gemara then asks about *tumtum*: *ela tumtum sfeka hu* — a *tumtum* is simply a case of doubt, male or female we just do not know. *Mi itztarich kra lemi'utei sfeka* — why would you need a verse to exclude a case of doubt? We know how to handle doubt in *halakha*.

But this raises an immediate problem. If someone came to a rabbi with a doubt about whether they are obligated in a *mitzvah de'oraisa*, the answer would generally be: do it. The principle of *sfeka de'oraisa lechumra* — in cases of biblical doubt, we are strict — would seem to require including a *tumtum* in the obligation. The Gemara's question is therefore itself somewhat surprising: why would we need a verse to *exclude* a doubtful case, rather than a verse to *include* it?

The *Rambam* resolves this by maintaining that the principle of *sfeka de'oraisa lechumra* is itself only *derabbanan* — it is a rabbinic rule to be strict in cases of biblical doubt. According to the Torah itself, one could be lenient in a case of doubt. On that view, a *tumtum* would not be obligated by default, and you would need a verse to establish that the doubt resolves toward obligation rather than exemption. *Tosafos*, by contrast, raises a further complication: why not simply have the *tumtum* bring an *olah* regardless of the doubt, since an *olah* that is not brought as an *olat re'iyah* is still permitted as a voluntary offering? *Tosafos* works through why that would not be straightforward, but the point illustrates that the question of how to treat the *tumtum*'s doubt is genuinely complex and not obviously resolved in favor of exemption.

### Covered Genitalia

*Itztarich kra lemi'utei sfeka, amar Abaye keshebeitzo mibachutz* — the verse is needed for the following specific case, as Abaye explains: a person whose scrotum is externally visible but whose shaft is covered, the rest of the male genitalia not being exposed. In this case, there is no actual doubt about the person's sex — we can see the scrotum and know the person is male. Yet because the genitalia are not fully exposed and visible, the person does not fully qualify as *zachar* for purposes of this particular obligation.

This is a genuinely unusual ruling. For virtually all other halakhic purposes this person is categorized as male without question. The word *zachar* in the Torah is relatively rare — the Torah more typically speaks of *ish*, a man — and *zachar* may carry a more specifically anatomical connotation that demands a more literal standard of observable maleness. Here, even where we know what the genitalia are, the fact that they are not fully exposed is enough to exclude the person from the narrow category of *zachar* operative in this *sugya*.

This connects to a broader pattern in the discussion: the Gemara consistently demands completeness and unambiguity. The obligation of *olat re'iyah* seems to require, in the Gemara's reading, that the obligated person be in the most fully realized and unambiguous version of every relevant category — fully male, fully free, fully able-bodied, fully pure. Anyone who falls short of that complete, unambiguous realization, in any one of those dimensions, is excluded. The Gemara grounds each exclusion in textual derivation, but the cumulative picture is of a halakhic norm that centers an idealized, complete type, and exempts or excludes those who fall outside it in any respect. This raises genuinely troubling questions — which we will return to in what follows — about the difference between exemption from an obligation and effective exclusion from a communal experience.

---

## Minors/Chinuch

### Chinuch Status

The Gemara now addresses minors. The word *kol* — "all of your males" — *lerabot et ha'ketanim*: the inclusive language comes to include minor children. But the Mishnah explicitly excludes a *cheresh*, *shoteh*, and *katan*. There is an apparent contradiction.

Abaye resolves it: *lo kashya* — there is no difficulty. One case concerns a *katan shehigia lechinuch* — a minor who has reached the age of training — and the other case concerns a *katan shelo higia lechinuch* — a minor who has not yet reached that age. Abaye could have resolved the contradiction more simply, by saying: if the child can make the journey, he is obligated; if not, he is excluded. That reading would have made the minor's inclusion biblical. But Abaye deliberately does not take that path. Instead he introduces the rabbinic concept of *chinuch* — the obligation of a father to train his children in the performance of *mitzvos*.

The consequence is significant: *katan shehigia lechinuch derabbanan hee* — any obligation assigned to a minor who has reached the age of *chinuch* is rabbinic, not biblical. The verse's inclusive language is then recharacterized: *v'kra asmachta be'alma* — the verse is not the source of the obligation but merely an *asmachta*, a textual support for a rabbinic enactment. One would not have suspected this from the Mishnah alone, which reads as though a minor's obligation might be biblical, nor from the verse itself. The Gemara forces this reframing because it cannot accept a genuine biblical obligation for a minor.

This reframing carries practical consequences. For instance: if a minor brings a *korban* for *olat re'iyah* on the first day of *yom tov*, and then reaches *bar mitzvah* during *chol ha-moed*, must he bring another *korban* now that he is biblically obligated? If his earlier *korban* was brought only under a *chinuch* obligation, does it count toward his new biblical obligation? These are the kinds of questions the reframing generates, and they are not merely theoretical.

The verse's inclusive language is then redirected: *ela v'kra lemai ata* — if the verse does not come to include minors in a biblical sense, what does it come to include?

---

## Smelly Tradesmen

### Three Trades

The Gemara answers that the verse comes to include what is taught in the name of *Acherim*: *hamkameitz*, one who handles dung — Rashi explains this is for purposes such as working leather or fertilizing; *vehamtzareif nechoshet*, one who smelts copper down in the copper mines, an extremely malodorous occupation; *vehabursi*, a tanner. All three are *peturim min ha're'iyah* — exempt from appearing.

### Odor Rationale

The reason given is derived from the phrase *kol z'chorkha* — all your males. *Mi sheyachol la'alot im kol z'chorkha* — one who can come up *together with* all your males, one with whom other people would be willing to travel. *Yatz'u elu she'einam re'uyim la'alot im kol z'chorkha* — these three are excluded because nobody would want to travel with them, and no one would want to be downwind of them on the pilgrimage road.

### Pilgrimage Cohesion

This is a striking hermeneutical move. The exemption here has no formal grounding in a particular physical incapacity or halakhic status of the person. It is entirely relational — it concerns how others experience the person's presence. And the rationale makes implicit sense if we understand *aliyah l'regel* not merely as an individual act but as a communal one. A pilgrimage is not simply a large number of individuals each going independently to the same place. People travel together, in groups, in communities; the journey itself is a shared experience. Someone who cannot integrate into that communal journey — not because of any unwillingness on their part, but because of what their occupation has done to them — stands apart. The verse's inclusive phrase, "all your males," is read as implicitly requiring the capacity to travel as part of that collective.

The hermeneutical strategy here is fascinating in its own right: a verse that could be read inclusively is turned, through the phrase *im kol z'chorkha*, into an exclusionary criterion. One might ask whether the verse should instead be read as correcting the social tendency to marginalize these workers — insisting that they too must come. The Gemara reads it the other way: precisely because they cannot easily join the group, they are exempt.

Some *rishonim* raise a further question about these three occupations: whether the odor is temporary and can be removed by bathing before the *aliyah*, or whether after years in such trades the smell becomes permanently absorbed into the skin and cannot be fully removed. The practical implications for when the exemption applies depend on how one answers that question.

There is a deeper issue here as well, and it connects to what runs through this entire *sugya*. The cumulative list of exemptions — women, slaves, minors, the lame, the blind, the elderly, the *tumtum*, the *androgynus*, those with partially covered genitalia, and now those who smell of their trade — creates an implicit portrait of who the ideal *oleh l'regel* is. Each exclusion defines the category by its edges, and the center of the category begins to look like a very narrowly defined type. The Gemara is using legal exemption language, but the social effect of that language is to identify who belongs most fully to the communal experience and who stands at its margins. One does not want to be too quick to impose modern categories onto ancient texts, but the pattern is hard to ignore, and it raises serious questions about what the halakhic category of exemption does and does not imply for inclusion in the broader communal and religious life.

---

## Slaves & Women

### Adon Logic

The Gemara now addresses women and unfreed slaves together. The exclusion of women is already established. The question is: *ela avadim m'na lan* — from where do we exclude slaves? Normally, slaves share the same level of obligation as women — so why not simply derive the exemption of slaves from the exemption of women without an independent verse?

Rav Huna provides an answer rooted in a specific verse: *el pnei ha'adon Hashem* — to appear before the Master, the Lord. *Mi she'ein lo ela adon echad* — only one who has but one master — God — is obligated. *Yatza zeh sheyesh lo adon acher* — a slave, who has another human master controlling his choices and movements, cannot in the relevant sense "appear before God" as a fully free agent. The slave's legal subordination to a human master creates a structural incompatibility with appearing before the divine Master.

### Women/Slave Parallel

The Gemara then asks: *hai l'ma li kra* — why was a verse even needed? We already know the general rule: any *mitzvah* that a woman is obligated in, a slave is obligated in; and any *mitzvah* that a woman is exempt from, a slave is exempt from. Since women are exempt here, slaves should be exempt as a matter of course.

This parallel is not entirely arbitrary. Both women and slaves, for different reasons, are not fully independent legal agents in the world of the Gemara. An unmarried adult woman is theoretically entirely free, but in practice a woman would typically move from her father's house to her husband's house, and the extent to which she is a fully autonomous agent is limited in various ways. The linkage between these categories reflects something real about the social structure the Gemara inhabits, even if it is deeply uncomfortable from a contemporary perspective.

### Half/Half Case

Ravina resolves the question by explaining that the verse is needed for a specific and unusual case: *mi shechatzyo eved v'chatzyo ben chorin* — the half-slave, half-free person. How does one arrive at such a status? One might be owned by two partners, one of whom freed his share while the other did not. This person is partly free and therefore already obligated in *mitzvos* to some degree. One might have thought that the portion of him that is free makes him at least partially obligated in *olat re'iyah*. The verse *el pnei ha'adon* comes to exclude even this case.

The Gemara confirms this reading from the precise language of the Mishnah: *nashim va'avadim she'einam meshuchrarim* — women and *unfreed* slaves. The specification "unfreed" would be redundant if we simply meant any slave. The word *she'einam meshuchrarim* — not fully freed — indicates we are dealing with a case of incomplete freedom, i.e., the half-and-half case. And the requirement once again is completeness: one must be totally free, not partially free, to fall within the obligation.

---

## Physical Barriers

### Regalim Meaning

The Gemara now addresses physical impediments: lameness, blindness, illness, and old age. The *baraita* derives the exemptions from the word *regalim* — the pilgrimage term, rooted in *regel*, foot or leg. *Prat leba'alei kavin* — to exclude those who have a prosthesis, those who do not have a functioning leg. *Davar acher*: *regalim prat lecheiger* — also to exclude the lame whose leg does not function, *v'choleh* — the ill, *v'suma* — the blind, *v'zaken* — the elderly, *v'she'eino yachol la'alot beraglav* — and anyone who cannot physically ascend on their own legs.

### Blind Exclusion

The inclusion of a blind person in a list otherwise concerned with the physical capacity to walk might seem surprising — a blind person's legs function normally. But as the Gemara implies here, a blind person would need a walking stick to navigate, cannot walk independently without assistance, and cannot make the ascent on their own. It is worth noting that this rationale for excluding the blind — inability to navigate the journey — is distinct from the rationale for excluding one who is blind in one eye that the Gemara will provide shortly, which is textual and involves the language of *yeira'eh yeira'eh*. The same category of blindness generates different exclusionary rationales depending on which verse and which aspect of the *mitzvah* is operative.

### Generic Unable

The phrase *v'she'eino yachol la'alot beraglav* functions as a generic residual category. Given this, one might ask: why bother listing the specific cases of lame, blind, ill, and elderly at all? The generic formulation would cover them. The Gemara implicitly acknowledges this: perhaps the specific cases are examples, and what we are really meant to take away is the general principle — if you cannot ascend on your own legs, you are exempt. The question of whether the specific listing matters halakhically remains.

### Pampered Person

Rava adds one further category to this list: *mefanki* — someone who is extremely pampered or fastidious. Rashi explains the specific case: *she'ein holchin belo min'al* — one who refuses to walk without shoes — *v'ein adam nichnas har habayis bemin'alo* — and one is not permitted to enter *Har haBayis* while wearing shoes. The connection to the verse is then supplied: *mi bikeish zos miyadchem remos chatzerai* — "who asked you to trample in My sanctuary?" — God does not want the sanctuary trampled by shoes, and therefore someone who would refuse to remove their shoes is not obligated to come. Rashi's reading focuses narrowly on shoe-wearing specifically, rather than the more general idea of a person who demands to be carried everywhere and cannot endure the ordinary physical demands of the pilgrimage.

The larger point, again, is one of completeness and capacity: the obligation of *olat re'iyah* applies only to those who are able to fulfill it in the full, normal, unassisted way. Any physical impediment — whether structural, situational, or even attitudinal — removes the obligation.

---

## Impure/Uncircumcised

### Tamei Logic

Two final categories are addressed: the *tamei* and the *arel*. The *tamei* person is exempt. The verse states: *uvasa shama v'heiveisa shama* — you will come there and bring there. *Kol she'yeshno b'viyah yeshno b'hava'ah* — anyone who can appear is obligated to bring; *v'chol she'eino b'viyah eino b'hava'ah* — anyone who cannot appear is not obligated to bring.

### Korban Purpose

One might ask: why not simply send the *korban* through an agent — *shaliach* — even if you cannot appear yourself? The Gemara's answer reveals a crucial conceptual point. The *mitzvah* is *olat re'iyah* — an offering of *appearance*. The *korban* is not a substitute for appearing; it is the concretization of appearing. The Rabbis have given the obligation of *re'iyah* — appearing before God at the Temple — a specific form: you appear by bringing a *korban*, and through the *korban* your presence is expressed. But this means the *korban* and the appearance are linked: the *korban* represents the one who brings it precisely because that person has appeared. If the person cannot appear at all — is *tamei* and therefore halakhically barred from entering — there is no appearance to represent, and the *korban* has no standing as an *olat re'iyah*.

This raises an interesting boundary question. Suppose a person is in Jerusalem but simply chooses not to ascend to the Temple — they have their *shaliach* bring the *olat re'iyah* on their behalf. Have they discharged their obligation? Presumably the obligation would be considered fulfilled, since they *could* have appeared; the *korban* can represent their presence because they were in principle present and available. But the *tamei* person is in a different situation: the incapacity is not a matter of choice but of halakhic status, and therefore the *korban* cannot stand in for an appearance that is legally impossible.

This line of reasoning also generates the following observation: if the *tamei* person is exempt from the *korban* because they cannot appear, the same logic would apply to the blind person, the lame person, and the others — they too are exempt from the *korban* because their inability to appear in the full halakhic sense means the *korban* cannot represent their appearance. The exemption, in all these cases, runs through the concept of appearance rather than being a direct exemption from a *korban* obligation.

### Arel=Tamei

The Gemara then asks about the *arel* — the uncircumcised man. *Minalan* — from where do we derive his exemption? He is not permitted in the *Beis haMikdash*. The Gemara answers: *ha manni Rabbi Akiva hi* — this ruling follows Rabbi Akiva, who derives from the *baraita*: *ish ish* — the doubled phrase in the context of which *kohanim* may eat *terumah*. The repetition *ish ish* teaches that not only a *tamei kohen* may not eat *terumah*, but even an *arel kohen* is excluded — the *arel* is treated *k'tamei*, like a *tamei*. Rabbi Akiva generalizes this principle: wherever *tamei* is excluded from Temple-related matters, *arel* is excluded as well.

### One Eye Blind

The Gemara closes with a ruling attributed to Rabbi Elazar ben Divai in the name of Rabbi Yehuda: a person blind in one eye is exempt. The source is the classic *gezeirah shavah* on the word *yeira'eh*: the Torah writes *yeira'eh* — "he shall be seen" — and *yireh* — "he shall see." *Kedereich she-ba liros kakh ba leheira'os* — just as one comes to see, so too one comes to be seen. *Mah ba liros be-shtei einav* — just as one comes to see with both eyes, *af leheira'os be-shtei einav* — so too one comes to be seen with both eyes, as it were — God sees the person with both divine "eyes." Therefore, *af leheira'os be-shtei einav* — one must be able to see with both of one's own eyes to be obligated. A person blind in one eye, even though they require no walking stick and can make the physical journey without difficulty, is nevertheless exempt from the *korban olat re'iyah* — not because of any physical incapacity to travel, but because they cannot fulfill the bilateral seeing that the verse requires.

This concludes the Gemara's enumeration of categories exempt from the *olat re'iyah*.

---

---

# Chagigah 6

## Olat Re'iyah vs. Shalmei…

### Minimum Comparison

The daf opens by reviewing the debate between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* concerning which of two obligatory festival offerings carries the higher minimum: the *olat re'iyah* or the *shalmei chagigah*. Both offerings are required on *yom tov*, and the positions are mirror images of one another: *Beit Shammai* holds that the *olat re'iyah* carries a higher minimum of two silver coins, while the *chagigah* requires only one *ma'ah*; *Beit Hillel* reverses this. Together, both schools require a total outlay of three silver coins — only the allocation between the two *korbanot* differs.

### Divine vs. Human Benefit

What is striking is that underlying this technical dispute lies a deeper philosophical orientation that characterizes many of the debates between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* — not merely a question of leniency versus stringency, but a question of emphasis. *Beit Shammai* directs more expenditure toward the *olah*, which is given entirely to God, while *Beit Hillel* directs more toward the *shlamim*, which is shared between God and the worshipper. The degree to which the human being factors into religious experience appears to be at the core of this disagreement.

### Shlamim Before Sinai

One of the proofs marshaled in support of *Beit Hillel* is drawn from the closing verses of *Mishpatim*, which *Chazal* understand to have taken place before *matan Torah*. There it says: *vayizbachu olot vayizbachu zvachim shlamim l'Hashem parim* — they brought *olot* and they brought *shlamim* to God, bulls. *Beit Hillel* argues from this verse that *shlamim* existed as a form of personal offering before *matan Torah*, whereas the *olah* present at that moment did not represent a personal offering in the same sense. This gives precedential weight to the *shalmei chagigah*.

### Both Existed Before Sinai

*Beit Shammai* counters that the verse in fact mentions both an *olah* and a *shlamim*, and that both were private offerings — so no special weight can be granted to the *shlamim* on the basis of this precedent alone.

### Type of Olah Before Sinai

The *gemara* then clarifies what precisely is being disputed: the question is whether those *olot* mentioned at the foot of Har Sinai were an *olat re'iyah* — a personal, volitional offering — or an *olat tamid*, the regular communal burnt offering. If the *olah* brought was merely the *olat tamid*, then it carries no weight as a model for a personal *korban*, and *Beit Hillel*'s argument stands: the only personal precedent we have is the *shlamim*. *Beit Shammai*, by contrast, maintains that those *olot* were indeed personal offerings — an *olat re'iyah* — and therefore the personal *olah* also has a pre-Sinaitic precedent, undermining *Beit Hillel*'s reasoning.

It is worth noting how strange the argument structure is in either direction. Generally, what occurred before *matan Torah* is considered legally irrelevant. Yet here, both sides treat the pre-Sinaitic sacrifice as an authoritative model. The argument implicitly restricts its view to the era of *B'nei Yisrael* and yet grants special weight to what occurred before the giving of the Torah — a genuinely unusual move.

---

## Three vs. Three Dispute

### Olat Re'iyah Position

*Abaye* now broadens the discussion considerably. He observes that the dispute between *Beit Shammai* and *Beit Hillel* about the nature of that pre-Sinaitic *olah* is not isolated — it aligns with positions held by other *tanna'im* on related questions. *Beit Shammai*, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Yishmael all share the view that the *olah* brought by *Yisrael* in the wilderness was an *olat re'iyah* — a personal offering.

### Olat Tamid Position
