On the other side, *Beit Hillel*, Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yose HaGlili all hold that the *olah* brought was an *olat tamid* — the communal offering — and not a personal one.

### Rabbi Yishmael on Torah…

The *baraita* cited to establish Rabbi Yishmael's position concerns his famous theory of how the Torah was transmitted. Rabbi Yishmael holds: *klalot ne'emru b'Sinai, u'pratot b'Ohel Moed* — the general principles were stated at Har Sinai, but the specific details were only spelled out later, in the *Ohel Moed*, during the ongoing revelation described throughout *Vayikra* and the subsequent books. This continued revelation — *v'no'aditi lecha sham*, I will meet you there, *v'dibarti itcha me'al hakapores* — is what filled in the legal particulars after Sinai.

### Rabbi Akiva on Torah Tra…

Rabbi Akiva disagrees: *klalot u'pratot ne'emru b'Sinai* — both the general principles and the specific details were given at Har Sinai; they were then repeated in the *Ohel Moed*, and repeated a third time in *Arvot Moav*. The repetitions were pedagogical, not revelatory — the content was already fully given at Sinai.

### Hermeneutic Philosophies

This debate inverts what one might expect from these two *tanna'im* in their broader hermeneutic orientations. Rabbi Akiva is generally associated with the method of deriving detailed laws from the smallest textual indicators — every extra letter, every tittle — while Rabbi Yishmael tends toward *pshat* and cautions against over-interpretation, holding that *dibra Torah kilshon bnei adam*. Yet here, it is Rabbi Akiva who says all details were given at Sinai, and Rabbi Yishmael who says they were only given as they appear explicitly in the text, later.

One way to resolve this apparent inversion is to read Rabbi Akiva's position as consistent with his broader hermeneutics: for Rabbi Akiva, "giving the details at Sinai" does not mean spelling them out explicitly, but encoding them in the text through all those minute hints and extra letters — which the *tanna'im* are then licensed to derive. The giving of the details *is* the giving of the text, and the human interpreter then draws out the particulars. For Rabbi Yishmael, by contrast, "giving the details" means actually stating them — and that did not happen until the explicit legislation of the *Ohel Moed*. This reading aligns elegantly with each authority's general interpretive stance.

---

## Transmission Theory Appl…

### The Logical Problem

The alignment becomes significant when applied to the practical question: if the *olah* brought at Har Sinai was an *olat tamid*, and if the details of how to bring an *olah* were only given when they appear explicitly in the Torah — as Rabbi Yishmael holds — then the *olat tamid* was brought at Sinai without adherence to the full procedural requirements. The *gemara* asks: *mi ka midi d'me'ikara lo b'hefshet v'nituach u'levasof baei hefshet v'nituach* — can there be something that was originally performed without flaying and dismembering, and only later was it required to be done that way? The flaying and dismembering of the *olah* are cardinal elements of how an *olah* is brought, and it is inconceivable that the *olat tamid* was brought without them initially and then subsequently modified.

This presents a problem specifically for Rabbi Yishmael: if he also held that the *olah* was an *olat tamid*, he would have to concede that it was brought without its essential procedural details, which seems untenable. This is why the *gemara* initially places Rabbi Yishmael in the camp of *Beit Shammai* — by saying the *olah* was an *olat re'iyah*, a personal offering, he avoids the problem of the *olat tamid* being brought without its full specifications.

### Tosafot's Solution

*Tosafot* sharpens the logic here. They note that the procedural requirement of flaying and dismembering (*hefshet v'nituach*) is not a general rule stated abstractly about all *olot*, but is spelled out specifically in the context of the *olat tamid* itself. It is therefore particularly inconceivable that the *olat tamid* — the very *korban* about which the Torah later explicitly specifies these steps — could have been brought earlier without following them. This would not be as troubling for a private *olah* such as the *olat re'iyah*, since although all *olot* technically require *hefshet v'nituach*, the explicit textual connection is to the *tamid*. The *gemara* finds this reasoning persuasive.

### Rabbi Elazar's Distincti…

A *baraita* is now cited concerning Rabbi Elazar. It invokes the phrase *olat tamid ha'asuyah b'Har Sinai* — "the *olat tamid* performed at Har Sinai" — a phrase that occurs in the liturgy and might seem on its face to be excellent evidence that a *tamid* was indeed offered at the foot of Sinai. Yet Rabbi Elazar reads this in a striking way: *ma'aseha ne'emru b'Sinai v'atzma lo karvah* — the procedure of the *olah* was commanded at Sinai, but the offering itself was not brought there. The phrase *asuyah b'Har Sinai* refers to the commandment being given at Sinai, not to the sacrifice being performed there. For Rabbi Elazar, then, there was no actual *olat tamid* at Sinai — only the command — and therefore the *olah* that was brought, alongside the *shlamim* mentioned in *Mishpatim*, was a personal offering, an *olat re'iyah*.

### Rabbi Akiva's Position

Rabbi Akiva takes the opposite view: *karvah v'shuv lo paskah* — it was offered at Har Sinai and continued without interruption thereafter. For Rabbi Akiva, both the commandment and the act of bringing the *olat tamid* occurred at Sinai.

### Forty-Year Question

This raises the question of the verse in *Amos* that reads rhetorically: did you bring *zevachim u'minchah* to Me for forty years in the wilderness, *Beit Yisrael*? The implication of the rhetorical question is that they did not. But if the *tamid* was brought starting at Sinai, how can the verse suggest otherwise? The *gemara* resolves this by saying the verse refers to the nation as a whole: only the *shevet Levi*, who had not served idolatry, brought these offerings; the rest of *Yisrael* were disqualified. The forty-year question therefore does not undermine Rabbi Akiva's position.

---

## Rabbi Yose HaGlili's Evi…

### Three Regalim Mitzvot

The *baraita* of Rabbi Yose HaGlili articulates three distinct *mitzvot* incumbent upon *Yisrael* when ascending for *aliyah la'regel*: *re'iyah*, appearing before God in the *mikdash*; *chagigah*, celebrating through the *korban chagigah*; and *simchah*, rejoicing through the consumption of the *korban simchah*. Each of these three *mitzvot* possesses a distinctive characteristic not shared by the other two. The *re'iyah* is unique in that its offering is an *olah* — given entirely to God — while the other two are *shlamim*. The *simchah* is unique in that it applies to both men and women, unlike the other two.

### Chagigah Pre-Sinai

What the *chagigah* alone possesses — what neither *re'iyah* nor *simchah* can claim — is that *chagigah yeshnam lifnei ha'dibbur*: the *chagigah* existed before *matan Torah*. The *re'iyah* and the *simchah* did not. This is the same logical move as *Beit Hillel*'s argument: only the *shalmei chagigah* has a pre-Sinaitic precedent, which is why it is accorded special weight.

### Logical Inference

The implicit conclusion from Rabbi Yose HaGlili's *baraita* is that if only the *chagigah* — a *shlamim* — existed before the *dibbur*, then the *olah* mentioned alongside the *shlamim* in *Mishpatim* was not a personal *olat re'iyah* but rather the communal *olat tamid*. Rabbi Yose HaGlili thus aligns with *Beit Hillel*'s reading without stating it explicitly. One might wonder why the *shlamim* at the foot of Sinai should be identified specifically as a *shalmei chagigah* rather than a *shalmei simchah* — the text gives no clear indication — but the *gemara* proceeds on this understanding without offering a resolution.

---

## Rabbi Yishmael Realigned

### Challenge to Yishmael

With the three-against-three alignment established, the *gemara* now scrutinizes the placement of Rabbi Yishmael among the *Beit Shammai* camp. The argument was that because Rabbi Yishmael holds the details were only given as they appear explicitly in the text, he could not have maintained that the *olat tamid* was brought before those details were given. The problem with bringing the *tamid* without *hefshet v'nituach* seemed to force him to conclude that no *olat tamid* was brought at Sinai, and hence the *olah* must have been a personal *olat re'iyah*.

### Precedent from Yose HaGl…

The *gemara* challenges this inference. Rabbi Yose HaGlili — who explicitly holds that the *olah* brought in the wilderness was the *olat tamid* — also holds, in a separate *baraita*, that the *olah* they brought in the wilderness did not require *hefshet v'nituach*: *lefi she'ein hefshet v'nituach ela me'Ohel Moed v'eilach* — those procedural requirements only became operative from the *Ohel Moed* onward. Here is explicit evidence that one can consistently hold both that the *olah* was an *olat tamid* and that it was brought without the later-specified procedural requirements. The manner in which the *tamid* was brought evolved over time as its details were revealed. This is entirely compatible with Rabbi Yishmael's theory of Torah transmission.

### Gemara's Conclusion

Once the *gemara* establishes this precedent from Rabbi Yose HaGlili's *baraita*, it concludes that the concern which seemed to force Rabbi Yishmael into the *Beit Shammai* camp is no longer compelling. Rabbi Yishmael's theory — that details are given as they appear — permits the *olat tamid* to have been brought differently before those details were given. He can therefore hold, like *Beit Hillel*, that the *olah* at Sinai was an *olat tamid*, not a personal *olat re'iyah*. The *gemara* removes Rabbi Yishmael from the *Beit Shammai* column and reassigns him to *Beit Hillel*.

The broader debate between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva about how the Torah was transmitted — whether details were implicit at Sinai or only given explicitly later — emerges here as something more than an abstract theory. It has direct bearing on how we understand the history of the *korbanot* and on the legal weight we give to pre-Sinaitic precedents. Viewed against the backdrop of the *Beit Shammai*–*Beit Hillel* dispute, there is a certain power to *Beit Shammai*'s reading: identifying the *olah* at the foot of Sinai as an *olat re'iyah* brings a vivid, experiential imagery to what *re'iyah* means — appearing before God in a moment of direct encounter, as captured in the verse *vayichezu et ha'Elohim*. According to *Beit Hillel*, by contrast, what was enacted at Sinai was the *olat tamid* — the steady, daily service — which suggests a different kind of religious weight: not the intense singular encounter but the continuity and regularity of daily devotion.

---

## Parsing the Verse

### Textual Punctuation

Rav Chisda raises a question about how to read the verse at the end of *Mishpatim* that describes the sacrifices at the foot of Sinai: *vayishlach et na'arei b'nei Yisrael vaya'alu olot vayizbechu zvachim shlamim l'Hashem parim*. The question is whether there is a syntactic break — effectively a period — after the word *olot*, such that the word *parim* (bulls) applies only to the *shlamim* that follow, with the *olah* remaining unspecified as to species. Alternatively, perhaps *parim* applies to the entire verse, and both the *olot* and the *shlamim* were bulls.

### Tropp Analysis

Mar Zutra answers that the resolution depends on the *trop* — the cantillation marks. Whether an *etnachtah* or a lesser disjunctive accent appears after *olot* determines whether the word *parim* falls back over the entire verse or only on the latter clause.

### Vow Formula Test

Rav Acha the son of Rava proposes a practical *nafka mina*: if someone declares a vow to bring an *olah* "like the *olah* brought in the wilderness," would that vow be fulfilled with a bull (*par*) or a sheep (*keves*)? The answer depends on what species the wilderness *olah* actually was. If *parim* covers the *olot* as well, the vow requires a bull; if the *olah* is left unspecified, it might be a sheep.

### Unresolved Answer

The *gemara* concludes with *teiku* — the question remains unresolved. Even granting the reading that the *olah* and *shlamim* are syntactically separated, the species of the *olah* cannot be determined from the verse alone.

---

## Re'iyah: No Biblical Lim…

### Mishnaic Teaching

The *gemara* now turns to a new dimension of the *korban re'iyah* — the question of whether it has a *shiur*, a prescribed limit. The *mishnah* in the first chapter of *Peah*, recited daily in *davening*, lists certain *mitzvot* that have no *shiur*: *ha'peah, ha'bikkurim, v'hara'ayon, u'gemilut chasadim* — *peah*, *bikkurim*, *ra'ayon* (i.e., *re'iyah*), and acts of loving-kindness. The unusual term *ra'ayon* rather than *re'iyah* will be addressed shortly.

### Initial Interpretation

Rabbi Yochanan's initial reading of this *mishnah* is that *ein lo shiur* means there is no upper limit — one may spend as much as one wishes on these *mitzvot* — but there is a lower limit, a minimum below which one cannot go. Applied to *re'iyah*, one can bring as lavish a *korban* as one desires, but there is a floor.

### Torah vs. Rabbinic Limits

Rabbi Oshaia then teaches a more expansive position: *hara'ayon ein lo shiur lo lema'alah v'lo lemata* — neither an upper limit nor a lower limit. At the biblical level, one may spend as little or as much as one wishes on the *re'iyah*. The apparent lower limits familiar from the *mishnah* — the *ma'ah kesef* for *re'iyah* and the *shtei kesef* for *chagigah* — are not of biblical origin. Rather, *aval Chachamim omrim*, the Sages established a minimum. Rabbi Oshaia's teaching thus reframes the *mishnah*: what it denies is any biblical *shiur*; the rabbinic minimum is a separate layer. This reading presumably applies in parallel fashion to *peah* and *bikkurim* as well — the biblical obligation has no minimum, while the Sages prescribed a floor.

---

## Defining Re'iyah

### Re'ayon Meaning

The *mishnah*'s unusual term *ra'ayon* prompts a dispute. What precisely does the obligation of *re'iyah* require?

### Rabbi Yochanan's View

Rabbi Yochanan explains: *re'iyat panim ba'azarah* — the *mitzvah* is fulfilled by appearing in the *azarah*, the Temple courtyard. On this reading, the appearance itself is the essence of the *mitzvah*, and bringing a *korban* is not required each and every time one enters the *azarah*.

### Reish Lakish's View

Reish Lakish disagrees: *re'iyat panim be'korban* — appearing before God means appearing with a *korban*. The verse *velo yeira'u panai reikam* — do not appear before Me empty-handed — generates a requirement that every act of appearing be accompanied by an offering. On Reish Lakish's reading, appearing without a *korban* is itself a violation of *lo yeira'u panai reikam*.

---

## Dispute Limited to Other…

### First Day Consensus

The *gemara* now clarifies the precise scope of this dispute. On the first day of *yom tov* — the *ikar ha'regel* — everyone agrees that *re'iyat panim be'korban* applies: whenever one appears in the *azarah*, one must bring a *korban*. On that day, multiple appearances each require their own offering.

### Chol HaMoed Question

The actual dispute concerns the other days of *yom tov* — *chol ha'mo'ed*. Is it permissible on those days to enter the *azarah* without bringing a *korban*?

### Yochanan on Other Days

Rabbi Yochanan holds that on the other days of *yom tov* there is no obligation to bring a *korban* each time one appears. One may enter the *azarah* freely, without a gift, and this does not violate *lo yeira'u panai reikam*.

### Lakish on Other Days

Reish Lakish holds that *every* appearance, on any day of *yom tov*, requires a *korban*. The obligation of *lo yeira'u panai reikam* is not confined to the first day; it attaches to every act of appearing before God throughout the festival.

This dispute is significant for the broader question of how *re'iyah* is conceptualized. The *mitzvah* has long been understood as consisting of two intertwined components: appearing in the *mikdash* and bringing a *korban*. The discussion here probes what happens when the two are separated — specifically, whether appearance without a *korban* is legally meaningful or constitutes a deficient fulfillment. Conversely, one might ask whether sending a *korban* without personally appearing would constitute anything at all. These two components are deeply bound together, and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish maps onto the question of which component is primary.

---

## Reish Lakish's Proofs

### Cannot Come Empty-Handed

Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan directly: *velo yeira'u panai reikam* — how can you permit someone to appear before God on *chol ha'mo'ed* without bringing a *korban*? The plain meaning of the verse prohibits precisely this.

### Parallel Derivation

Reish Lakish then constructs a logical derivation — a *dinah v'omeir* — from the parallel structure of the festival obligations. The *chagigah* is brought for the person; the *re'iyah* is brought before God. The verse references *zevachim* in relation to both. Just as the *chagigah* offering must be a *zevach*, so too must the *re'iyah* offering be a *zevach* — a proper animal sacrifice, not merely a bird or grain offering.

### Mammal Requirement

How do we know that the *chagigah* must be a mammal? From the verse *velo yalin chelev chagig ad boker* — the fat of the *chagigah* offering shall not remain until morning. Since the *chagigah* has fat, it cannot be a bird; it must be a sheep or a cow. By the same derivation, the *re'iyah* offering must also be a proper mammal.

### Chagigah vs. Olah Type

The derivation continues: the *chagigah* is a *shlamim* — the one who brings it eats from it and benefits. The *re'iyah* is offered before God. By parallel logic — *ma chagigah ha'amurah l'hedyot ra'uy lo, af re'iyah ha'amurah la'gavoah ra'uy lo* — the *re'iyah* must be something entirely for God, which means it must be an *olah*, not a *shlamim*.

### Anthropomorphic Reasoning

The *gemara* invokes an explicitly anthropomorphic justification: *shelo yehei shulchancha malei v'shulchan rabacha reikan* — your table should not be full while the table of your Master is empty. You consume the *chagigah*; God should receive the *olah* in its entirety. Whatever its figurative character, the reasoning is clear: the *re'iyah* offering must be an *olah*, and it must accompany every appearance.

---

## Reish Lakish Limited

### Chol HaMoed Challenge

Rabbi Yochanan presses back: if Reish Lakish holds that *velo yeira'u panai reikam* applies to every appearance, then even on *chol ha'mo'ed* one could never enter the *azarah* without a *korban*. Is that really his position?

### First Day Limitation

Reish Lakish responds that the prohibition of *lo yeira'u panai reikam* applies specifically on the *ikar ha'regel* — the first day of *yom tov*. That is the primary moment of obligatory appearing; it is then that the prohibition against appearing empty-handed is in full force. On the subsequent days of the festival the obligation does not extend in the same way. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish thus resolves into a narrower question than it first appeared: both agree that on the first day every appearance requires a *korban*, and both agree that one may *voluntarily* bring additional *korbanot* on subsequent days. The live question is whether appearing on *chol ha'mo'ed* without a *korban* constitutes a violation — and here Reish Lakish, having anchored the prohibition to the *ikar ha'regel*, concedes that it does not.

---

---

# Chagigah 7

## Rav Yochanan vs Reish La…

### Re'iyat Panim/Korban

The seventh daf of Chagigah opens by resuming a debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish, one that arose from an apparent tension in the sources. The *mishnah* in Pe'ah had stated that *re'ayon* — the act of appearing before God in the Temple — has no *shiur*, no prescribed measure. Although the *mishnah* in our tractate had set a minimum for the *olat re'iyah* of either two *ma'ah* of silver or one *ma'ah*, the Gemara clarifies that those minimums are only rabbinic. The deeper question is whether there is instead a maximum, or a limitation on the number of times one may appear.

### Reish Lakish's Stringency

The debate is framed as follows: Rabbi Yochanan says there is no *shiur* for *re'iyat panim* — the act of appearing in the *azarah* — while Reish Lakish says there is no *shiur* for the *korbanot*. At first glance, Reish Lakish's formulation sounds more permissive: bring as many *korbanot* as you wish. But the Gemara reads it as actually more demanding. What Reish Lakish means is that yes, you may appear in the *Beit HaMikdash* as often as you like throughout the *regel*, but every single time you appear, you are obligated to bring a *korban*. This follows from the verse *lo yera'u fanai reikam* — do not appear before Me empty-handed. Each appearance, on Reish Lakish's view, triggers its own obligation.

### Rav Yochanan's Leniency

Rabbi Yochanan agrees that *lo yera'u fanai reikam* imposes a real obligation, but limits it to the first appearance — the first day of *Yom Tov*. That initial appearance must be accompanied by a *korban*. Subsequent appearances throughout the *regel*, including on *Chol HaMoed*, carry no such requirement. One might ask interesting hypothetical questions even within Rabbi Yochanan's framework — for instance, if a person's very first appearance was empty-handed and he then appeared a second time on the first day, has he already violated the prohibition, and is he now exempt or still obligated? These questions are not resolved by the Gemara, but they underscore the boundaries of Rabbi Yochanan's position: the fundamental demand is one *korban* at the outset.

### Beraita Challenge

The Gemara now cites a *beraita*: *Eitavei* — Rabbi Yose be-Rabbi Yehuda teaches that Israel is commanded to ascend to Jerusalem on the three *regalim* — Pesach, Shavuot, and Sukkot. The *beraita* then states that they may not appear *chatza'im* — "in halves" — based on the verse *kol zechurecha*, "all your males," and they may not appear empty-handed, based on *velo yera'u fanai reikam*. This is brought as a challenge, apparently indicating that every time one appears, a *korban* is required — supporting Reish Lakish's stringent position.

### Ikar HaRegel

Rabbi Yochanan responds: *be-ikar haregel* — the obligation to appear with a *korban* applies on the *ikar haregel*, the primary and first day of the festival. The verse's prohibition against appearing empty-handed is directed at that initial appearance. On *Chol HaMoed*, and presumably even for later appearances on the same first day after one has already fulfilled the obligation once, no *korban* is required.

### Yera'eh Yera'eh

The Gemara then records that Rabbi Yochanan challenged Reish Lakish with the wordplay of *yera'eh yera'eh* — the see-and-be-seen reading of the relevant verse. This dual reading recurs throughout the tractate. Without the Masoretic vocalization, the verse *yera'eh kol zechurecha et pnei* most naturally reads as "all your males shall see the face of God," not "shall be seen." Even in the *Nevi'im*, the phrase *ki tavo'u lera'ot panai* — "when you come to see My face" — resists being rendered in the passive. The verse is vocalized in the passive to avoid gross anthropomorphism, but the alternative reading is clearly present in the text. This gives the Gemara license to invoke both directions of the verb.

### Free Seeing Argument

Building on this, the Gemara makes a strikingly audacious argument: *ma ani bechinam, af atem bechinam* — just as I, God, see you without charge, so too you see Me without charge. The implication is that there is a basis for appearing before God in the *Mikdash* without bringing any *korban* at all — reading precisely against the plain meaning of *lo yera'u fanai reikam*, which commands that one not appear empty-handed.

### Final Agreement

The Gemara resolves the dispute. Given this final *beraita* that Rabbi Yochanan invoked, Reish Lakish is forced to concede that it is possible to appear in the *Mikdash* without a *korban*. The conclusion is: *kol heicha de'ata velo ayeiti* — if one comes to the *Mikdash* without a *korban* in hand, *kulei alma lo pligi de'ayeil umitchazi venafik* — everyone agrees one may enter, appear, and depart. The debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish is therefore not about whether one may appear without a *korban* on subsequent visits — on that, all agree one may — but rather about bringing multiple *korbanot* in the context of *olat re'iyah*, as we shall see.

---

## Gemara's Methodology

### Paradox Explained

This resolution creates an immediate difficulty. The preceding *amud* was filled with Reish Lakish challenging Rabbi Yochanan with various *braitot* that seemed to require a *korban* at every appearance, and Rabbi Yochanan responding to each challenge. But now the Gemara concludes that Reish Lakish himself agrees with Rabbi Yochanan's basic position — that appearing without a *korban* on subsequent occasions is permitted. If Reish Lakish ultimately agreed, what was the purpose of all those challenges? Was Reish Lakish asking questions that, given his own final position, he had no real reason to ask?

### Gemara as Reconstruction

This is not an isolated phenomenon. *Tosafot*, in other places in the Talmud, note that according to certain final conclusions of the Gemara, the entire preceding conversation "never happened." This should not be read as a claim that the disputants misremembered, or that the tradition is unreliable. Rather, it reflects something important about the nature of Talmudic discourse: the Gemara is very often *reconstructing* a conversation, not reporting one. It knows that Rabbi Yochanan held one position and Reish Lakish held another. From that starting point, the Gemara asks: what would each of them do with this source? How would each respond to that challenge? To explore these questions, the Gemara frames the discussion as if the two Amoraim were directly challenging one another — but in reality, it is the Gemara itself that is constructing the dialogue and standing in for each disputant in turn.

### Understanding the Device

The key is awareness of the device. When one learns that the Gemara sometimes interjects its own editorial commentary within what appears to be an original *meimra*, students sometimes feel misled: "It sounds like the Amora is saying this — how can you tell me the Gemara inserted its own words?" One only feels deceived if one was unaware that this is the method being employed. Once one understands the device, there is no misrepresentation. The original debate is real: Rabbi Yochanan said *re'iyat panim* has no limit, Reish Lakish said *re'iyat korban* has no limit. Everything that follows is the Gemara's attempt to reconstruct precisely what each position entailed and how each sage would have responded to the available sources. Even when the Gemara narrates this reconstruction in the voices of the Amoraim themselves, a reader who understands the methodology is not being deceived.

### Dynamic Transmission

There is also a philosophical dimension worth noting. This reconstructive method reflects a dynamic quality intrinsic to the transmission of *Torah she-be'al peh*. Even today, when faced with a *machloket* between, say, the Rambam and the Ra'avad, we might ask: what would the Ra'avad say to this source? What would the Rambam say to that argument? We frame such questions with the words "he would probably say..." whereas the Gemara actually constructs the exchange as a living dialogue, as if the disputants are still arguing and we are the vehicle for the continuation of their debate. There is a power to this — the sense that the argument remains alive and that each generation inherits not only the conclusions but the ongoing conversation itself. The Gemara confers authority on this reconstruction retroactively, through the dynamic of human thought and imagination operating within the tradition.

---

## Multiple Korbanos Debate

### One Korban Only

Having established that all agree one may appear without a *korban* on subsequent visits during the *regel*, the Gemara now identifies the genuine point of dispute. *Ki pligi* — where do they actually disagree? The case is: *de-ati ve-aisi* — one came and wished to bring a *korban*, specifically a second *korban* after having already brought his first. On this, Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish diverge.

Rabbi Yochanan's position is that *re'iyat panim de-ein lah shiur* — the number of appearances has no limit, one may come to the *Beit HaMikdash* as often as one wishes. But *le-korban yesh lo shiur* — there is a limit to the number of *korbanot* one may bring. Specifically, one may bring the *olat re'iyah* only once. This sounds strange at first: since when is there ever a ceiling on how many *korbanot* one may bring?

### Bal Tosif Issue

*Tosafot* frames Rabbi Yochanan's limitation as touching on *bal tosif* — the prohibition against adding to the Torah's commandments. If a person is simply bringing a generic *olah* at any time, there is no problem. But if one wishes to bring it on the first day of *Yom Tov* specifically in the context of *re'iyat panim* — as an expression of *oleh le-regel*, of appearing before God — then the Torah prescribed one *korban* for that act of appearing. To bring additional *korbanot* in that same context of *olat re'iyah* is to add to what it means to appear, and that carries a dimension of *bal tosif*. To bring a *korban* simply as a *korban*, without framing it as part of the *re'iyah* obligation, is always permitted; but to multiply *korbanot* specifically as expressions of the *re'iyah* itself is what Rabbi Yochanan would restrict.

### Multiple Korbanos OK

Reish Lakish disagrees: *re'iyat panim le-korban de-afillu korban nami ein lo shiur* — even the *korban* in the context of appearing has no limit. One must appear once with a *korban*, and after that, any further appearances with additional *korbanot* are entirely welcome — *be my guest*. This reading also fits better with the literal words of *ein lo shiur*, which suggest an absence of any upper limit. Indeed, the Rambam rules in accordance with Reish Lakish here, even though the general rule is that the *halacha* does not follow Reish Lakish in his disputes with Rabbi Yochanan.

### Hokeir Raglecha

Rabbi Yochanan then raises a challenge against Reish Lakish from the verse *hokeir raglecha mi-beit re'echa* — make your steps precious, do not be overly frequent in your friend's house. This verse implies some degree of restraint in visiting God's house. If we have just agreed that appearing without a *korban* is permitted, then the restraint must refer to something else — namely, the bringing of *korbanot*. This seems to support Rabbi Yochanan's position that one should not bring multiple *korbanot* as *olat re'iyah*.

### Sin vs Free-Will

The Gemara rejects this reading of the verse. *Hasam be-chataot ve-ashamot* — the verse is speaking about *sin offerings*, not about burnt offerings or peace offerings. The lesson of *hokeir raglecha* is: do not sin so frequently that you constantly need to come to the *Beit HaMikdash* to bring sin offerings. This is consistent with the teaching of Rabbi Levi, who resolved an apparent contradiction between two verses. One verse says *hokeir raglecha mi-beit re'echa* — be sparing in your presence at your friend's house — while another says *avo veitecha be-olot* — I will come to Your house with burnt offerings. Rabbi Levi resolves: *kan be-chataot ve-ashamot, kan be-olot ve-shlamim* — the first verse concerns sin offerings, the second concerns burnt offerings and peace offerings. Bringing *olot* and *shlamim* in abundance is encouraged, not restricted.

A *beraita* taught similarly: *hokeir raglecha mi-beit re'echa be-chataot ve-ashamot haketuv medabeir* — it is sin offerings the verse is discussing. One might have thought that even *olot ve-shlamim* are subject to the restraint. But since a separate verse, *avo veitecha be-olot ashalem lecha nedarai*, explicitly mentions burnt offerings and vows — the latter being the source for *shlamim* — the verse of *hokeir raglecha* is confined entirely to the realm of *chataot ve-ashamot*. The resolution is as elegant as it is striking: the imagery of *beit re'echa*, "your friend's house," is a beautiful way of understanding the relationship between Israel and God — and one's freedom to come often with gifts of *olot* and *shlamim* is entirely undiminished.

---

## Half Cannot Appear

### Rav Yosef's Reading

The *beraita* cited earlier included the ruling *ve-ein nire'in chatza'im* — they may not appear "in halves." Rav Yosef initially proposed a reading of this phrase: if a man has twenty sons, he should not bring ten of them on the first day of *Yom Tov* and the other ten on the following day of *Chol HaMoed*. All of them should come on the first day. The "halves" refers to splitting one's household across different days of the festival.

### Abaye's Logic

Abaye objects immediately: *peshita* — this is obvious! One needs no verse to teach such a thing. If you bring five sons today and five tomorrow, those five who will come tomorrow are *peshuim* — negligent — for failing to appear on the primary day, and only those who came today are *charutzim* — prompt and diligent. No verse is needed to tell us not to deliberately make half of one's family negligent. Clearly, the *ikar haregel* — the first day — is when all must appear, and this follows from simple logic without any scriptural derivation.

### Excluding the Unfit

The verse must therefore be coming to teach something else. The Gemara directs us to the teaching cited in the name of *Achereim* — a *beraita* we encountered earlier: the *mekametz* (one who works with dung), the one who smelts copper, and the *bursi* (tanner) — all of whom produce strong and offensive odors — are exempt from *re'iyah*. The source is the verse *kol zechurecha* — "all your males." The *beraita* interprets this to mean only those who could appear together as part of the full community: *mi sheyachol la'alot im kol zechurecha* — one who can ascend with the whole community. Those whose condition would require them to ascend separately, forming their own subgroup apart from the community, are excluded entirely: *yatz'u elu she-ein yecholim la'alot im kol zechurecha*. This is the true meaning of *ein nire'in chatza'im* — not that half a group may appear on one day and half on another, but that those who cannot be part of the unified whole are excluded from appearing altogether.

### Rashi's View

Rashi's interpretation is worth noting, not only for its content but for a remarkable personal observation he makes. Rashi explains *ein nire'in chatza'im* as referring to those who can only come in a small subgroup — *chabura mu'etet* — separate from the rest of the community, since they cannot join the whole. But what is striking is the way Rashi frames his interpretation: *kach nire'eh be-einai* — "this is how it seems to me," he writes, and then adds: *ve-chaverai meforshim* — "but my colleagues explain it differently." It is unusual for Rashi to speak of his colleagues as holding a distinct interpretation. One rarely thinks of Rashi as having peers in the ordinary sense. The comment is a rare and quietly humanizing window into the world of the Rashi we know primarily as an authoritative voice speaking alone from the margins of the page.

---

## Olot BaMoed

### Obligatory vs Optional

The Gemara now turns to the second *mishnah* on the daf, which addresses the *korbanot* brought during *Yom Tov* and *Chol HaMoed* in more general terms, particularly the question of which sources of funds may be used to fulfill each obligation. The governing principle is *dvarim shebechovah einam ba'im ela min hachullin* — obligatory offerings may only come from non-sanctified funds. One cannot "double-dip," satisfying a divine obligation with funds that have already been designated or sanctified for another purpose.

### Three Korban Types

The *mishnah* addresses three distinct categories of *korbanot* brought during the festival. Understanding the *mishnah* requires recognizing that these three are conceptually distinct and governed by different rules regarding sources of funds.

The first is the *olat re'iyah* — the burnt offering brought when appearing before God in the Temple. The second is the *shalmei chagigah* — the peace offering brought to celebrate the *chag* itself, fulfilling the verse *vechagosem oto chag*. The third is the *shalmei simcha* — the peace offering brought to fulfill the obligation of rejoicing, *ve-samachta be-chagecha*, which the Rabbis understood to be fulfilled through the eating of meat brought as a *korban*.

The *mishnah* states that *olot ba-mo'ed ba'ot min ha-chullin* — *olot* brought on *Chol HaMoed* must come from unsanctified funds — and that *shlamim* may come from *ma'aser* funds. The *mishnah* then introduces a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the *shalmei chagigah* on the first day of *Yom Tov* of Pesach.

To understand what *ma'aser* money means in this context: two out of every three years in the *ma'aser* cycle, the second tithe — *ma'aser sheni* — must be brought up to Jerusalem and spent there on food. The Torah permits its use for a wide variety of purchases, and using it to bring a *shelamim korban* and eat its meat is an excellent and natural use of those funds. The purpose of *ma'aser sheni* is precisely to enable a heightened religious encounter in Jerusalem — *ve-samachta lifnei Hashem* — and what better fulfillment than eating the meat of a *shelamim* brought in the *Beit HaMikdash*? So the question becomes: may the *ma'aser sheni* funds satisfy not just the general desire to eat meat in Jerusalem but the specific obligation of *shalmei chagigah* or *shalmei simcha*?

This connects to a broader principle: a pre-existing obligation in one domain cannot be discharged through a resource already obligated in another domain. The *ma'aser* funds carry their own mandate — to be brought to Jerusalem and eaten there. One cannot simultaneously use them to satisfy the independently imposed obligation to bring a *shalmei chagigah* or *olat re'iyah*. Or, put differently: if one has vowed to bring a *shelamim* as a personal undertaking and then seeks to count that same *shelamim* toward the divinely imposed *shalmei simcha* obligation, this conflation of one obligation with another is what the principle *dvarim shebechovah min hachullin* is designed to prevent.

### Olat Re'iyah Rules

The *olat re'iyah* must come from *chullin* — unsanctified funds — regardless of when it is brought, whether on *Yom Tov* or on *Chol HaMoed*. This is non-negotiable, as it is a full-fledged *davar shebechovah*.

### Shalmei Simcha

The *shalmei simcha*, by contrast, *ba'im af min hama'aser* — may come even from *ma'aser* funds. The reason, as the Gemara spells out, is that the *mitzvah* of *simcha* is not fundamentally an obligation to bring a *korban*. It is an obligation to experience joy, which the Rabbis understood to be achieved through eating the meat of a *shelamim*. Since the *korban* itself is not the object of the obligation — only the eating of its meat is — the fact that the animal was brought from funds already sanctified or already part of another obligation is not disqualifying. The *simcha* is achieved through the eating, and the eating can be accomplished regardless of the origin of the animal.

---

## Shalmei Chagigah

### Dense Mishnah

The *mishnah* is notably dense, communicating through implication rather than explicit statement. The reference to *shlamim* coming from *ma'aser* is a cryptic reference specifically to *shalmei simcha*, not to all *shlamim*. The debate of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about the first day of *Yom Tov* of Pesach is a reference to the *shalmei chagigah*, not to *shalmei simcha*, and certainly not to the *olat re'iyah*. Reading the *mishnah* correctly requires knowing what type of offering is in view at each juncture — knowledge the *mishnah* presupposes rather than supplies. The Gemara will slowly unpack each component.

---

## Three Korbanot Framework

### Rejoicing Through Meat

To understand why *shalmei simcha* may be brought from already-sanctified funds, the conceptual distinction between the three *korbanot* must be clear. *Shalmei simcha* satisfies the obligation of *ve-samachta be-chagecha* — rejoicing on your festival. The Rabbis established that *simcha* for men is achieved through eating the meat of a *shelamim*. Crucially, the obligation is not to bring a *korban* but to eat meat that happens to be *korban* meat. It is the eating and the joy that constitute the fulfillment.

### Simcha Flexibility

Because the *shalmei simcha* obligation is fundamentally about the experience of eating sacred meat — and not about the act of bringing a *korban* — there is latitude in the source of the funds. If one had already vowed a *shelamim*, or if one's *ma'aser sheni* funds are being used to purchase meat in Jerusalem, those can serve the *mitzvah* of *simcha*. Similarly, the *mishnah* later states that *bnei Yisrael* can fulfill their *simcha* obligation through vows and free-will offerings, through *ma'aser behema*, and through other meat to which they have access — including the portions of *shelamim* that the *kohanim* receive, the firstborn animals brought as *korbanot*, and other sacred meats. The common thread is: any *korban* meat one eats in Jerusalem contributes to the fulfillment of *simcha*, regardless of the original purpose for which that *korban* was brought.

### Pure Gift Concept

The *olat re'iyah* operates on entirely different logic. It is a pure gift to God upon appearing before Him. The verse *lo yera'u fanai reikam* — do not appear before Me empty-handed — establishes that the act of appearing in the *Mikdash* must be accompanied by a tangible gift: an *olah* that goes entirely to God, consumed on the altar, with nothing returning to the one who brought it. The analogy suggests itself: it is like bringing a gift to a host when visiting — something given entirely for the host's benefit, not shared. Because this is a genuine and complete obligation to bring a *korban* in the fullest sense, it must come from *chullin* — unsanctified, personally owned funds. There is no room for double-counting.

### Celebration Offering

The *shalmei chagigah* occupies an intermediate position. It fulfills the verse *ve-chagosem oto chag* — you shall celebrate it as a festival — which requires the bringing of a *shelamim*. Unlike the *olat re'iyah*, the *shalmei chagigah* is eaten by the one who brings it; unlike the *shalmei simcha*, the obligation is specifically to bring a *korban* and not merely to eat meat. This dual character — both a genuine obligation to bring a *korban* and an offering whose meat is enjoyed — places the *shalmei chagigah* somewhere between the other two. It is this intermediate quality that makes the question of fund-mixing more nuanced, and that generates the debate between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.

The contrast might be illustrated as follows. The *olat re'iyah* is what you give your host when you arrive — entirely for them. The *shalmei simcha* is the dessert you bring to be shared at the table. The *shalmei chagigah* is something in between: both a gift in the context of appearing and a shared celebration — both offering and feast.

---

## Shalmei Chagigah (II)

### Yom Tov Restriction

The Gemara now turns to the specific question of why the *mishnah* specifies *olot* on *Chol HaMoed* as coming from *chullin*. Surely the same rule would apply on *Yom Tov* — why single out *Chol HaMoed*? The Gemara proposes that the *mishnah* may actually be making a different point: not that the source of funds is different on *Chol HaMoed*, but that non-obligatory *olot* may only be brought on *Chol HaMoed* at all — not on *Yom Tov* itself.

This is a striking result. The entire preceding *amud* assumed that the *olat re'iyah* is brought on the first day of *Yom Tov* — indeed, that this is its primary time. Yet here the Gemara entertains the possibility that even the *olat re'iyah* cannot be brought on *Yom Tov*. This turns out to be the position of Beit Shammai. The *mishnah* in *Beitzah* records: Beit Shammai say one may bring *shelamim* on *Yom Tov* — since one will eat the meat, it falls within the category of *ochel nefesh* — but one may not perform *semichah* on them, since pressing one's hands on the animal is not necessary for food preparation. *Aval lo olot* — but one certainly may not bring an *olah* on *Yom Tov*, since there is no eating benefit whatsoever. Beit Hillel say one may bring both *shelamim* and *olot* on *Yom Tov*, and one may also perform *semichah*.

If this debate is about a generic *olah*, the stakes are clear enough. But the Gemara's implication here is more radical: according to Beit Shammai, even one's obligatory *olat re'iyah* cannot be brought on *Yom Tov* — it may only be brought on *Chol HaMoed*. This stands against everything the discussion has assumed. The Gemara, however, is unwilling to read the *mishnah* in our tractate as going like Beit Shammai and therefore rejects this interpretation.

### Chisurei Mechsara

*Chisurei mechsara* — the *mishnah* is incomplete and must be read with implied words added. The *mishnah*'s statement that *olot* on *Chol HaMoed* come from *chullin* does not mean that *olot* in general may only be brought on *Chol HaMoed*. Rather, the *mishnah* must be understood as distinguishing between two types of *olot*: free-will *olot* of vows and donations, which may only be brought on *Chol HaMoed*, and the *olat re'iyah*, which comes even on *Yom Tov* — and which, when brought, must come specifically from *chullin*.

### Olat Re'iyah Principle

The reconstructed teaching is: *olot nedarim u-nedavot ba-mo'ed ba'ot, be-Yom Tov einam ba'ot* — free-will *olot* come on *Chol HaMoed* but not on *Yom Tov* itself. And *olat re'iyah ba'ah afilu be-Yom Tov* — the *olat re'iyah* comes even on *Yom Tov*, and when it is brought, *eina ba'ah ela min hachullin* — it may only come from unsanctified funds. This is a difficult reading of the *mishnah*, which literally says *olot bamo'ed min hachullin*, suggesting that it is the *Chol HaMoed olot* that must come from *chullin*. The Gemara must work hard to reconstruct the text so that it is the *olat re'iyah* — brought on *Yom Tov* — that is subject to the *chullin* requirement, while the non-obligatory *olot* brought on *Chol HaMoed* are not constrained in the same way. The reading requires considerable *chisurei mechsara*, but it is the only reading the Gemara is willing to accept, given that the alternative would cast the *mishnah* as following the minority position of Beit Shammai.

### Pesach Distinction

The *mishnah* specifies the *chagigah* of the first day of Pesach rather than simply *chagigat Yom Tov* in general. The Gemara asks: why the specificity? Rav Ashi explains: the *mishnah* is distinguishing the *chagigah* of the fifteenth of Nisan from the *chagigat arba'ah asar* — the *chagigah* of the fourteenth. There is a *shelamim* that was brought together with the *korban Pesach*, called the *chagigat arba'ah asar* or more explicitly *chagigat arba'ah asar ha-ba'ah im ha-Pesach*. This is a well-known institution: since the Pesach must be eaten *al hasova* — when one is full and sated, not in a ravenous state — a companion *shelamim* was brought alongside the Pesach to fill the participants first. There is also a concern about breaking the bones of the Pesach, and the companion offering helps fill the group before the Pesach is consumed. This offering is called a *chagigah* but is not a *chagigah* in the strict sense — it is not brought on the *chag* itself but on the fourteenth, the eve of the festival.

### Arba'ah Asar Status

The *chagigat arba'ah asar* is not a strict biblical obligation. It is a mechanism for ensuring the Pesach is eaten in the appropriate manner — without urgency and without bone-breaking — and if the group is small enough that each participant will have a generous portion, the *chagigat arba'ah asar* is not needed at all. Because it is not a firm obligation, it may be brought from *ma'aser* funds and other already-sanctified sources. When the *mishnah* specifies the *chagigah* of the first day of Pesach as the one that is subject to the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel debate — with Beit Shammai requiring *chullin* and Beit Hillel permitting *ma'aser* — it does so to distinguish this genuine *chagigah* from the *chagigat arba'ah asar*, which carries no such restriction. The same rule would apply to the *chagigah* of Sukkot and the *chagigah* of Shavuot; Pesach is mentioned specifically to draw the contrast with the fourteenth.

---

## Mixing Funds Debate

### Why No Pre-Sanctified

The Gemara returns to the question that drove the entire discussion: why may one not use pre-sanctified or already-obligated funds to fulfill a *davar shebechovah*? The intuition might seem to run the other way — if one has already sanctified money for a *korban*, surely that sanctification would make it *more* appropriate for fulfilling an obligation, not less. The proper way to frame the prohibition, as the Gemara makes clear, is not simply about "sanctified versus unsanctified" funds in the abstract, but about double-counting obligations. If one has accepted upon oneself a personal obligation to bring a *shelamim*, and later wishes to use that same *shelamim* to discharge the divinely imposed *mitzvah* of *shalmei simcha*, this is inappropriate — one obligation cannot ride piggyback on another. Similarly, *ma'aser sheni* funds carry their own mandate — to be brought to Jerusalem and enjoyed there — and they cannot simultaneously discharge a separate, distinct divine obligation. The underlying principle is that each obligation demands its own dedicated fulfillment.

### Ulla's Tofel

Ulla addresses the question of how *beit Hillel*'s leniency can be reconciled with this principle. If the *shalmei chagigah* is an obligatory *korban*, why does Beit Hillel permit it to be brought from *ma'aser*? Ulla explains: *be-tofel* — the leniency applies to an *add-on*. The base *chagigah* obligation is discharged with one's own unsanctified funds. If one then wishes to bring additional animals — because one has a large family and wants more meat — one may supplement using *ma'aser* funds. The original obligation is satisfied through *chullin*; what follows is the *tofel*, the supplement, which may draw on *ma'aser*.

### Chizkiyah's Position

Chizkiyah states: *toflin behema le-vehema* — one may add animal to animal, bringing the first from *chullin* and then additional animals from *ma'aser*. But *ein toflin ma'ot le-ma'ot* — one may not mix funds. One cannot take thirty *zuz* of *chullin* money and forty *zuz* of *ma'aser* money and purchase a single animal with the combined sum, because then no single animal stands as an unambiguous fulfillment of the base obligation from *chullin*. The first animal must be purchased entirely from one's own unsanctified funds; subsequent animals may come from *ma'aser*.

### Rav Yochanan

Rabbi Yochanan takes the opposite position: *toflin ma'ot le-ma'ot* — one may mix funds for a single purchase — but *ein toflin behema le-vehema* — one may not bring a second, entirely separate animal as a *chagigah* from *ma'aser*. According to Rabbi Yochanan, as long as each animal has *some* of one's own *chullin* money in it, it qualifies as part of the *chagigah* obligation. It is somewhat puzzling why one would need to frame additional animals as part of the *chagigah* at all — after one has fulfilled the base obligation, any additional animals could simply be designated as *shalmei simcha* and brought without restriction. Why must the additional animals be framed as *chagigah* for there to be a problem in the first place? This remains unclear from the Gemara's discussion.

### Tannaitic Sources

Both positions find support in tannaitic sources. The Gemara cites *braitot* in support of each view.

### Missat Yadecha

The relevant verse is *missat yadecha* — the free giving of your hand — which appears in the context of *ve-asita chag Shavuot la-Adonai Elohecha*. The word *missat* is understood to indicate something that flows from one's own resources, one's own freely given funds. *Melamed she-adam meivi chovato min hachullin* — this teaches that one's base obligation must come from one's own unsanctified funds. But whence the permission to supplement with *ma'aser* or other funds? The verse continues: *ka'asher yevarechecha Adonai Elohecha* — as God has blessed you. This is understood to include everything with which God has blessed you, including *ma'aser* funds and the produce of the land. Thus the base obligation comes from *chullin*, and the supplement may come from the full range of divine blessing.

The *beraita* in support of Chizkiyah reads: *missat — melamed she-adam meivi chovato min hachullin. Beit Shammai omrim: yom rishon min hachullin, mikan ve-eilach min hama'aser* — the first day's *chagigah* must come from *chullin*; from then onward it may come from *ma'aser*. *U-Veit Hillel omrim: achilah rishonah min hachullin* — the first eating, meaning the first animal, comes from *chullin*, and subsequent animals may come from *ma'aser*. This supports Chizkiyah's view that the distinction is between the first animal and subsequent animals, not between mixed and unmixed funds.

### Ma'aser Behema

The *mishnah* also mentions that throughout the rest of Pesach, one may fulfill the *simcha* obligation even through *ma'aser behema* — the animal tithe, whereby one out of every ten newborn animals is brought as a *korban* and its meat eaten. The Gemara asks: if *ma'aser behema* may be used on the later days of Pesach, why may it not be used on the first day of *Yom Tov*?

### Sikra Problem

Rav Ashi answers: *dilma ati le-asuri be-Yom Tov* — one might come to *take* the *ma'aser behema* tithe on *Yom Tov* itself, and that is forbidden. The process of tithing animals requires marking the tenth animal with a stick dipped in paint — *sikra* — to identify it as the *ma'aser*. This act of marking constitutes *tzoveia* — dyeing — and possibly *kotev* — writing — both of which are prohibited on *Yom Tov*. One might note that the ordinary reason *trumot u-ma'asrot* cannot be taken on *Yom Tov* — that doing so *metakken* the produce, rendering it edible — does not apply to *ma'aser behema*, since the untithed animals are not *tevel* and are not forbidden prior to the tithe being taken. The specific prohibition on taking *ma'aser behema* on *Yom Tov* therefore rests on this separate concern of *sikra*, the painting of the animal.

The daf concludes with a final linguistic observation: the word *misat* in the verse — *mai mashma dehai misat lishna de-chullin hu* — carries the connotation of one's own personal funds, like an assessment or tax drawn from one's own income. The proof is from *Esther*: *vayasem hamelech Achashverosh mas al ha'aretz* — King Achashverosh imposed a *mas*, a tax, on the land — which is a levy drawn from personal wealth. The word *misat yadecha* similarly indicates that the base obligation of the *chagigah* must come from the pilgrim's own personal, unsanctified resources.

# Chagigah 9

## Tashlumin Debate

### Korbanot & Tashlumin

The ninth daf of Chagigah takes up the *mishna*'s treatment of the *korbanot* of the festival. Earlier material — on 8b — addressed people of different means and how they ought to distribute their resources among the various *korbanot*, and the preceding *mishna* grappled with how to allocate funds between the *shalmei chagiga* and the *olat re'iyah*. The *mishna* now before us deals with the framework of *tashlumin*: the ability to make up, across the remaining days of *Yom Tov*, a *korban chagiga* that one failed to bring on the first day. Though the *mishna* does not address this principle explicitly with respect to the *olat re'iyah*, the *gemara* proceeds on the assumption that the same framework applies there as well.

Before turning to the *amoraic* debate, the *mishna* closes with the famous verse *meuvat lo yuchal litkon vechesaron lo yuchal lehimanot* — a perversion cannot be corrected and a lacking cannot be counted — applied to one who let the entire window of *tashlumin* pass without bringing the *korban chagiga*. That aggadic discussion will be taken up later; for now the *gemara* focuses on the *halachic* structure of *tashlumin* itself.

### Yochanan vs. Oshaya

The *gemara* spells out the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Oshaya. Rabbi Yochanan holds *tashlumin lerishon*: the fundamental obligation is rooted in the first day, and any subsequent day on which one brings the *korban* is understood as a makeup for that original obligation. Rabbi Oshaya holds *tashlumin zeh lazeh*: each day stands in a makeup relationship to the one before it, or more precisely — as *Tosafot* understands his position — any day of the festival can independently serve as the day on which one fulfills the obligation, with perhaps a preference for the first day but no exclusive anchoring to it.

### Chiger Case

The practical difference between these views emerges in the case of a *chiger*, a lame person. Such an individual is exempt on the first day of the festival. If he recovers during *Yom Tov*, may he still fulfill his *chagiga* obligation on the remaining days? According to Rabbi Yochanan, since the obligation is a makeup for day one and he was exempt on day one, he remains entirely exempt — he never entered the category of obligation. According to Rabbi Oshaya, since any day can independently ground the obligation, this person would be obligated once he recovers.

### Exemption Parity

One matter is worth pausing over before proceeding. The *chiger* was the individual singled out in the first *mishna* of the tractate as exempt specifically from *re'iyah* — from the obligation of *olat re'iyah* and *aliyah laregel*, based on the verse *yera'eh kol zechurcha* and related sources. The *gemara* here, in applying the same exemption to *chagiga*, quietly assumes that all exemptions from *olat re'iyah* apply equally to *shalmei chagiga*, even though the verses governing *chagiga* — *vechagosem oto chag lashem shivat yamim* and similar formulations — do not textually connect to the *aliyah laregel* requirement in any explicit way. This identification is not argued for; it is simply assumed. And it is an assumption that already appeared implicitly in the earlier *mishna*, which treated *olat re'iyah* and *shalmei chagiga* as parallel categories when discussing how to distribute one's resources between them.

One might have expected the *gemara* to use a cleaner example of first-day exemption followed by later eligibility — such as a convert or someone who becomes *bar mitzvah* in the middle of the festival period. Indeed, the same question arises in the context of *sefirat ha'omer*, where roughly one-seventh of boys who become *bar mitzvah* do so during the forty-nine-day counting period and one must ask whether they carry any obligation for days they could not have been counting as obligated individuals. The *gemara*, however, chooses the *chiger* as its illustration.

## Challenge to Yochanan

### Nazir & Night Status

The *gemara* now challenges Rabbi Yochanan's position. Would he truly maintain that someone exempt on the first day is permanently excluded from the *chagiga* obligation? The challenge comes through an analogy drawn from the laws of *nezirut*.

The *gemara* cites a ruling of Chizkiya: *nitma bayom meivi, balaila eino meivi* — if a *nazir* who has completed his seven-day *tahara* process after contracting *tumah lemet* becomes *tamei* again during the day of the eighth day, he brings a second *korban* for a second, distinct period of *tumah*; but if he became *tamei* again on the night before the eighth day — after the seven full days of *tahara* have passed but before daybreak, when alone he could actually bring a *korban* — he does not bring a second *korban*, and the second *tumah* is treated as a continuation of the first. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: *af balaila nami meivi* — even if he became *tamei* again at night, it is already considered a new and distinct status, and he would bring a second *korban*.

### Nazir Tumah Case

The underlying question is this. After seven full days of *tahara*, including the requisite sprinkling of *mei chatat*, the *nazir* is entirely *tahor* — but he cannot bring his *korban* until daybreak, since *korbanot* are only offered during the day. The night that intervenes is already, in one sense, the eighth day in *halachic* terms; yet the capacity to actually bring the *korban* belongs to the morning. If this *nazir* contracts *tumah* during that night, does the night count as part of the new status — such that this is a second, independent *tumah* obligating a second *korban* — or does the night's inability to support the bringing of a *korban* mean the person has not yet fully entered the new category, making this *tumah* a continuation of the old one?

Rabbi Yochanan holds that the night is already the new status. The *gemara* presses: if that is Rabbi Yochanan's position — that even at night one is already considered to have moved into the new *korban*-bearing phase — then it seems to undercut his own position on *chagiga*, for it implies that a person unable to bring a *korban* for technical reasons (such as being lame) should not be considered fully excluded from the category of obligation. Perhaps even the *chiger* on the first day, though exempt at that moment, is not so categorically removed from the obligation as Rabbi Yochanan suggests.

### Night Classification

The *gemara* offers an initial answer through Rabbi Yirmiyah: *tumah* is different, because we know from the institution of *Pesach Sheni* that *tumah* does not fully exclude a person from a *korban* obligation — it merely defers it. The person who was *tamei* on *Pesach Rishon* can still bring on *Pesach Sheni*, demonstrating that *tumah* leaves one within the relevant category. The *gemara* acknowledges this is a somewhat peculiar line of reasoning in this context, but presses forward.

Rav Pappa challenges even this: the argument that *tumah* does not fully exclude a person works only according to the view that *Pesach Sheni* is a *tashlumin* for *Pesach Rishon*. According to the view that *Pesach Sheni* is *regel bifnei atzmo* — an independent festival obligation in its own right — the *tumah* on *Pesach Rishon* simply creates an exemption and triggers a separate obligation later. Under that view, *tumah* would function as a full exclusion from the first obligation, and one could not derive from *Pesach Sheni* that *tumah*-exempt individuals remain in the category. This is a fascinating debate already explored in Pesachim.

Rav Pappa therefore offers a simpler resolution: *kasavar Rabbi Yochanan laila eino mechusar zman* — Rabbi Yochanan holds that the nighttime preceding the eighth day does not constitute a *mechusar zman*, a lacking of the proper time. Since it is already the eighth day in *halachic* terms, and only the practical limitation of nighttime prevents the actual bringing of the *korban*, the person is already considered fully in the new status. The night is not an absence of eligibility but merely a waiting period within a status already achieved. The concept of *mechusar zman* — typically applied to an animal not yet of the proper age for a *korban* — here describes the person's temporal readiness, and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is that nighttime does not produce such a lacking. This has nothing to do with whether a *chiger*, exempt for reasons entirely separate from the timing of *korban*-bringing, is or is not within the category of obligation on the first day of the festival.

## Reconciling Positions

### Zav Night Flows

The *gemara* immediately raises a further challenge against Rabbi Yochanan's position that night is not *mechusar zman*. Rabbi Yochanan himself is cited as ruling: *ra'ah achat balaila ushtayim bayom meivi; shtayim balaila ve'achat bayom eino meivi* — if a man completing his seven-day *tahara* process as a *zav* had one flow on the night of the seventh day and two flows the following morning, he brings a second *korban* for a new period of *zivah*; but if he had two flows at night and one in the morning, he does not bring a second *korban*.

The *zav* case runs parallel to the *nazir* case. A man who has a certain type of penile flow becomes a *zav* only after three flows. Crucially, the first flow does not yet categorize him as a *zav*; it renders him merely a *ba'al keri*, carrying no greater *tumah* than a seminal emission. Only the second flow begins to create the identity of *zivah*, and three flows together complete it. The *korban* obligation for *zav*-status arises after three such flows.

Now, after a *zav* completes his seven-day *tahara* process, he is obligated to bring a *korban* at daybreak of the eighth day. The question is whether any new flows occurring that night — before he can bring the *korban* — are part of a new, independent period of *zivah* or a continuation of the old one.

### Zav Flow Count

The significance of whether one flow or two flows occurred at night turns on the nature of the first flow. Since the first flow does not yet classify a person as a *zav*, a single nighttime flow is immaterial for purposes of determining whether a new status has taken root during the night. The new *zav* identity only begins to crystallize with the second flow. Therefore: if two of the three flows occurred at night, the second flow — the one that begins to establish his new *zav* identity — took root while he was still in the night, before he had yet brought his *korban*. That second flow, occurring in what Rabbi Yochanan's opponents would call the *mechusar zman* period, pulls the new status back into the old category. But if only one flow occurred at night, it is halakhically inert, and the new identity of *zivah* only begins with the two daytime flows — by which point he is already obligated in his first *korban* and the new period is clearly separate.

### Yochanan's Position

This teaching appears to contradict Rabbi Yochanan's position that night is not *mechusar zman*. If Rabbi Yochanan holds that night is already the new status, then even two flows at night should constitute a new, independent period of *zivah* triggering a second *korban* — yet Rabbi Yochanan himself teaches that in such a case the person does not bring a second *korban*.

The *gemara* resolves this by reframing the entire teaching: *ki ka'amar Rabbi Yochanan l'divrei ha'omer laila mechusar zman* — when Rabbi Yochanan articulated the rule about one flow at night versus two flows at night, he was not expressing his own view. He was spelling out what the consequences would be according to the position that night is *mechusar zman*, not according to his own view. Rabbi Yochanan himself holds that night is not *mechusar zman*, and under his own position even three flows entirely at night would already constitute a new, independent period of *zivah* obligating a second *korban*.

### Alternative View

Why then does Rabbi Yochanan bother to articulate the ruling as he does, if it reflects a position he does not hold? The *gemara* answers that there is a genuine *chiddush* embedded in that teaching even for the one who holds that night is *mechusar zman*. One might have thought — as Rav Sheshet the son of Rav Idi argues in another *gemara* — that even a single nighttime flow should create a continuity with the old status, since the process began during the night. Rabbi Yochanan teaches, in the name of Rav Yosef's principle, that this is not so: the first flow is halakhically inert and does not pull the subsequent flows into the old category. It takes two flows at night — enough to begin the formation of a new *zav* identity — to create that continuity. One flow at night, even under the view that night is *mechusar zman*, does not suffice.

In the end, the entire discussion about *laila mechusar zman* has taken the *gemara* considerably afield from the original question of *tashlumin* for *chagiga*. The nature of the *machlokes* between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Oshaya — whether the obligation is fundamentally anchored to the first day or is fulfillable on any day — remains, as the *gemara* itself concedes, without the sharpened resolution one might have hoped for from this excursion. The more enduring observation from this opening section is the quiet but telling assumption that the *mitzvah* of *olat re'iyah* and the *mitzvah* of *shalmei chagiga* share identical parameters of exemption — a point that is never argued but consistently taken for granted.

## Meuvat & Lasting Damage

### Chesaron Definition

The *gemara* now turns to the *aggadic* material embedded in the *mishna*. The *mishna* closes with the verse from Kohelet: *meuvat lo yuchal litkon vechesaron lo yuchal lehimanot* — a perversion that cannot be corrected and a lacking that cannot be counted. The *mishna* applies this to one who allowed the entire period of *tashlumin* to pass without bringing the *korban chagiga*.

Bar Hei Hei — one of the more unusual names in the *gemara*, noted by *Tosafot* as a *ger* who takes the name from the *hei* added to *Avraham* and the *hei* added to *Sarah*, just as Ben Bag Bag's name reflects the *gimatriya* of five — raises a pointed question to Hillel. The verse says *lo yuchal lehimanot*, that something cannot be "counted." Why *counted*? If the idea is that something is missing, the verse should have said it cannot be *filled* or *completed*. The use of the language of counting seems out of place. Bar Hei Hei therefore interprets *chesaron lo yuchal lehimanot* as referring not to a personal deficit but to a social exclusion: *ze shenimnu chaverav l'dvar mitzvah vehu lo nimna imahem* — his colleagues were counted among those doing a *mitzvah* and he was not counted among them. It is not merely that an obligation went unfulfilled; it is that there was a communal roll call, an opportunity to stand up and be part of the group, and this person was absent.

### Braita Examples

A *braita* confirms this interpretation. *Meuvat lo yuchal litkon* — that which cannot be corrected — is illustrated by one who neglected *keriat shema* of *shacharit* or *keriat shema* of *arvit*, or who missed *tefillah* of *shacharit* or *tefillah* of *arvit*. That these examples are chosen is striking. There are innumerable obligations one could cite as irreversible once the time has passed, yet the *braita* selects *keriat shema* and *tefillah*. Particularly notable is *tefillah*, which in fact does have a form of *tashlumin* — a missed *shacharit* can be partially compensated through *mincha*, and so forth. *Tosafot* argues that this is precisely the *chiddush*: even though there is a *tashlumin* for *tefillah*, that makeup does not fully repair what was lost. The *chesaron lo yuchal lehimanot* is then applied, as in Bar Hei Hei's formulation, to one whose companions gathered to perform a *mitzvah* together and who was not counted among them — missing not merely an obligation but the opportunity to be part of a collective act of *kiddush Hashem*.

### Bar Hei Hei's Verse

Bar Hei Hei then poses a second question to Hillel, this time about a verse in Malachi: *veshavtem uri'item bein tzaddik l'rasha, bein oved Elokim la'asher lo avado* — you will return and see the difference between the righteous and the wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not serve God. The redundancy is glaring: is not the *tzaddik* the same as *oved Elokim*, and the *rasha* the same as *asher lo avado*? What does the verse add by doubling the distinction?

### Hillel's Response

Hillel responds that both the *oved Elokim* and the *asher lo avado* in the verse are in fact *tzaddikim gemurim* — complete righteous individuals. No, the verse is not drawing a contrast between the wicked and the righteous. It is drawing a contrast within the category of the righteous themselves, between one who genuinely *serves* God and one who merely satisfies obligation. The *oved Elokim* is the one who goes beyond the standard requirement. The illustration Hillel offers: *shoneh pirko me'ah pe'amim* versus *shoneh pirko me'ah va'achat* — one who reviews his chapter a hundred times versus one who reviews it a hundred and one. A hundred times: *tzaddik gamur*. A hundred and one times: *oved Elokim*. The one who does it exactly as required but no more is not, in the fullest sense, a servant of God.

This formulation implies that a hundred repetitions was understood as the standard practice for committing a passage to memory — not an extraordinary feat but the established norm of serious study in an oral culture where material had to be internalized without the aid of written texts. The one who pushed himself to go even one repetition beyond the norm transformed his act qualitatively.

The *Maharsha* notes a remarkable *gimatriya*: the *rashei teivot* of *oved Elokim la'asher* — *ayin*, *alef*, *lamed* — yield 101, while the *rashei teivot* of *lo avado* — *lamed*, *ayin* — yield 100, which may well be the textual root from which the *gemara* derives its specific numbers.

### Donkey Market

Bar Hei Hei presses back: can one truly say that because of a single additional iteration, the person is described as *lo avado*, as not having served God at all? Hillel answers with an analogy from the marketplace: *tze u'lemad mishuk shel chamorin* — go and look at the market of donkey drivers. If the going rate is ten *parsei* per *zuz*, and you go eleven *parsei*, the price doubles — you have crossed into the next unit entirely, and the charge restructures completely. The one additional step beyond the standard boundary transforms not just the marginal cost but the entire category. So too, the single additional review beyond the standard hundred crosses a qualitative threshold. The person who stops at exactly the normative limit has fulfilled his obligation but has not become a servant of God in the fuller sense; the one who goes a single step further has entered a different category of relationship to his learning and to his Creator.

## Eliyahu & Poverty

### Poverty Gift

The *gemara* now records a separate exchange involving Bar Hei Hei, this time with the prophet Eliyahu — or according to some versions, with Rabbi Elazar. Eliyahu asks: what is the meaning of the verse *hinei tzerafticha ve-lo ve-chesef, becharticha be-chor oni* — behold I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of poverty? The response: *melamed she-chazar ha-Kadosh Baruch Hu al kol middot tovot liten le-Yisrael ve-lo matza ela aniyut* — God reviewed all the good qualities to bestow upon the Jewish people and found none so fitting as poverty.

### Red Strap Image

Shmuel — and some say Rav Yosef — adds: *hainu d'amri inshi ya'ah aniyuta le-Yhuda'ei ki barza sumka le-susya chivra* — that is what people say, poverty suits the Jewish people like a red strap on a white horse. The image suggests not degradation but fitness: the red strap complements the white horse, and poverty, whatever its hardships, keeps the Jewish people aligned with the right path. This teaching resonates with the earlier material in the tractate dealing with the *churban habayit* and the effort to reframe national suffering in some larger constructive frame: the poverty that comes from lack of wealth is here imagined as a form of divine discipline that has preserved Jewish loyalty. As the *Maharsha* notes, the phrase *ve-lo ve-chesef* may be read not as "not as silver is refined" but as "I refined you through the absence of silver" — the poverty itself was the furnace.

## Meuvat Definition

### Mamzer Case

Returning to the *mishna*, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya defines *meuvat lo yuchal litkon*: *eizehu me'uvat lo yuchal litkon? Zeh ha-ba al ha-ervah ve-holid mimena mamzer* — who is the one who has committed a perversion that cannot be corrected? One who engaged in illicit relations and thereby produced a *mamzer*. The lasting damage is a real-world, irreversible consequence: a human being now carries a status that affects his life and the lives of his descendants in ways that no amount of repentance or financial remedy can undo.

It is worth pausing on *Rashi*'s comment on the *mishna*. *Rashi* frames the problem not primarily in terms of the injury done to the world but in terms of the perpetrator's own capacity for *teshuvah*: since the product of the sin — the *mamzer* — continues to exist as a living reminder of the transgression, the person's *avonot* cannot be fully erased through *teshuvah*. This is a notable reorientation: the concern shifts from the impact of the sin on others to the obstacle the sin creates for the sinner's own spiritual repair.

The *gemara* asks: does the *meuvat* apply only when a child was in fact born — *holid ein, lo holid lo*? Is an irreversible perversion only created by the birth of a *mamzer*, or does illicit sexual sin create such a perversion even without a child?

### Theft Contrast

A *braita* is adduced. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules: *gonev adam efshar she-yachazir gneivato ve-yitaken* — if a person steals, he can return the stolen object and repair the damage. *Gozeil adam efshar she-yachazir gezeilato ve-yitaken* — if a person robs, he can likewise return the stolen goods and make repair. But *ha-ba al eishet ish va-asarah le-ba'alah* — one who has relations with a married woman and thereby renders her forbidden to her husband — *nitrad min ha'olam ve-halach lo*, that person will be lost from the world, because he has created a lasting, irreparable injury. The *braita* thus makes clear that even without a *mamzer* there is an irreparable perversion: the marriage has been destroyed. The wife is now forbidden to her husband and cannot return to him, a damage no amount of repentance repairs. This is where *Rashi*'s emphasis becomes legible: the *nitrad min ha'olam* focuses attention on the perpetrator's fate precisely because the injury to the marriage is so comprehensive.

### Torah Sage Departure

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai offers a different interpretive frame for *meuvat lo yuchal litkon*. He insists that *me'uvat* — perversion — specifically requires something that *began* good and *became* bad. To illustrate: one does not speak of *biku gamal* or *biku chazir* — inspecting a camel or a pig for a *mum* to determine fitness as a *korban*. One inspects a sheep, *bikru taleh*, something that was potentially a valid offering and is now being assessed for disqualification. Perversion is the corruption of something that had genuine worth; mere badness from the outset is not *me'uvat*.

Accordingly, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai identifies the paradigm case of *meuvat lo yuchal litkon* as *talmid chacham she-pharash min ha-Torah* — a Torah sage who departs from the world of Torah.
