This is something that began as genuinely good — deep learning, a life shaped by Torah — and was then perverted. Whatever that person once had, however much he may later try to recapture it, something has been lost that cannot be fully recovered.

The difficulty is that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's principle seems to respond oddly to the preceding *braita*'s example of the adulterous act destroying a marriage. A marriage that has been violated was certainly something good that became perverted. Yet Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai appears to set that aside in favor of his own example. The *gemara* does not directly address this tension here.

A teaching attributed to Rabbi Yehuda ben Lakish adds a further dimension: regarding any *talmid chacham* who departs from Torah, the verse says *katzipor nodedet min kanah, ken ish noded mimekomo* — like a bird that wanders from its nest, so is a person who leaves his place. And regarding such a departure, the verse asks: *ma matzu avoteichem bi avel ki rachaku me'alai* — what wrong did your forefathers find in Me that they distanced themselves? This framing is notably less severe than *me'uvat lo yuchal litkon*. It conveys sadness and bewilderment — why would someone leave a home that gave life meaning? — without declaring the damage irreversible. The departure from Torah is here mourned rather than condemned as an irreparable catastrophe.

## Meuvat Scope

### Incest vs. Adultery

Having established that the *braita* requires a *mamzer* in the case of forbidden sexual relations but the *braita* about *eishet ish* creates an irreversible damage even without a child, the *gemara* resolves the apparent tension: *lo kashya, kan be'achoto penuyah, kan be'eishet ish* — there is no contradiction; one case speaks of incest with an unmarried relative, the other of adultery with a married woman. In the case of incest, the lasting *meuvat* requires the birth of a *mamzer* because the incestuous relationship itself does not destroy any pre-existing sanctioned bond. The parties were not married; there is no marriage to dissolve. The lasting damage, the irreversible perversion, is created only when a *mamzer* comes into the world. In the case of adultery, however, the act itself severs the marriage: the wife becomes forbidden to her husband, and that rupture is permanent regardless of whether a child was born.

### Rape vs. Willing

The *gemara* offers a second resolution: *ve-iba'it eima ha va-ha be-eishet ish* — both cases concern a married woman, but one involves rape and one involves willing participation. If the act was rape, the woman is not rendered forbidden to her husband and the marriage bond remains intact; therefore, the only *meuvat* that could arise from the rape of a married woman is the birth of a *mamzer*. If the act was willing, she becomes forbidden to her husband and the marriage is destroyed even without a child. This is a striking and deeply uncomfortable distinction. The *gemara* is parsing the *halachic* consequences of the act — what categories of irreversible damage are produced — without pausing to acknowledge the profound injury done to the victim of rape as such. The violence of the act, the *tza'ar* and *boshet* and the psychic devastation, are entirely absent from the analysis. There are in fact *halachic* categories — *tza'ar*, *boshet*, *pegam* — that could have framed the injury done to the rape victim as itself a form of irreversible damage. The *gemara* chose not to raise them, and that silence is worth noting.

### Kohen Status

The *gemara* offers yet a third resolution: *ve-iba'it eima ha va-ha be-ones, lo kashya, kan be-eishet kohen, kan be-eishet Yisrael* — both cases involve rape, but one involves the wife of a *kohen* and one involves the wife of an ordinary Israelite. The wife of a *kohen* becomes forbidden to her husband even through rape — that is the *halacha* regarding a *kohen*'s wife who was violated — and therefore the irreversible damage to the marriage arises even without a child. The wife of an Israelite does not become forbidden to her husband through rape alone, and therefore the only lasting *meuvat* in that case is the birth of a *mamzer*. This distinction, that rape creates a permanent severance for the wife of a *kohen* but not for the wife of an Israelite, is itself a *halacha* that carries its own profound difficulties, and belongs to a broader discussion that will be taken up properly in Yevamot.

## Leaving Torah Study

### Halakha to Mikra

The *gemara* closes with a series of teachings about *me'uvat* in the context of leaving one domain of Torah study for another. Rav rules: *keivan she-yotzei adam mid'var halakha l'dvar mikra, shuv ein lo shalom* — once a person moves from learning *halakha* to learning *mikra*, he will no longer have *shalom*, no peace. The statement is striking: not merely leaving Torah for business or for worldly pursuits, but leaving *halakha* to learn Bible. The *gemara*'s implicit hierarchy is clear. *Rashi* explains *ein lo shalom* as meaning that one no longer has clear direction: *she'ein hora'ah mid'var mikra she-ha-mishna mefareshet stimas ha-torah* — *mikra* alone does not yield clear *hora'ah*, it is the *mishna* that unpacks the implicit law of the Torah. The person who retreats from *halakha* to *mikra* loses the capacity for clear *psak* and clear direction in observance.

### Talmud to Mishnah

Shmuel extends the ruling: *zeh ha-poreish mi-talmud le-mishna* — even leaving *gemara* to learn *mishna* results in *ein shalom*. *Mishnah* contains vast legal material, but without the analytical unpacking of *gemara*, one neither thinks the issues through nor achieves the level of mastery necessary to determine *halakha*. The statements of *mishna* remain opaque without the elaboration and comparison that *talmud* provides.

### Switching Gemarot

Rabbi Yochanan goes further still: *afilu mi-shas le-shas* — even switching from one *gemara* to another results in *ein shalom*. *Rashi* and *Tosafot* discuss which direction is problematic: whether it is leaving *Bavli* for *Yerushalmi* or the reverse. *Rashi* suggests the problematic direction is leaving *Bavli* for *Yerushalmi*, since *Bavli* is the more demanding and more analytically rigorous study and abandoning it for *Yerushalmi* represents a descent in rigor. Rabbi Yochanan himself was from *Eretz Yisrael*, which adds a layer of complexity to which *shas* he would have viewed as the higher standard.

### Tosafot's Nuance

*Tosafot* argues that the direction of the shift may not be the real issue at all. *U-meehu afilu ipcha yesh lomar* — one could say the same thing in either direction. *Tosafot* reads the underlying principle as follows: *she-peirish mi-zeh ve-adayin lo heivin be-zeh* — the problem is leaving one source before having mastered it and moving to another before achieving genuine fluency. *Shemi-tokh kach lo ya'aleh be-yado halakha berurah* — the result of constantly shifting before reaching mastery is that one never arrives at clear *halakha*. The one who flits from *Bavli* to *Yerushalmi* to *Bavli* again, always curious but never patient enough to master one fully, will never achieve the clarity and command that genuine learning demands. *Shalom* — understood here as completeness, coherence, and the settled mastery of one's learning — eludes the perpetual wanderer.

---

---

# Chagigah 10

## Heter Nedarim

### Flying in Air

The tenth *daf* of Masechet Chagigah opens with a *mishnah* that is famous in its own right, yet only tangentially connected to the tractate's core subject matter. The *mishnah* will carry us into a broad and far-reaching discussion that occupies both this *perek* and the next. It begins with a striking declaration: *heter nedarim porchin ba'avir* — the annulment of vows flies in the air. The Torah does provide a mechanism for a husband or father to annul a woman's vow, but the institution the *mishnah* is describing is quite different: the practice whereby any person who has made a vow may present himself before a sage, explain that had he fully appreciated the circumstances he never would have made the vow, and thereby be released from his obligation. This institution, the *mishnah* declares, has nothing to rest upon — *ve'ein lahem mah sheyismachu*. There is no verse, no real anchor in the Torah text. To keep the *mishnah*'s own metaphor, *semicha* means physical support, something solid beneath you. *Heter nedarim* is simply airborne, with nothing to ground it.

### Three Categories

The *mishnah* then enumerates three further areas of law: *hilchos Shabbos*, *chagigot* — the holiday sacrifices — and *me'ilot*, the laws governing misuse of consecrated property. These three, the *mishnah* says, are *kehararin hatluyim bese'ara* — like mountains suspended from a hair. Unlike *heter nedarim*, which has no verse at all, these three areas do have some scriptural basis, but the ratio is wildly inverted: the textual support is vanishingly thin — a single hair — while the halachic superstructure built upon it is vast, a mountain. The *mishnah*'s inclusion of *chagigah* alongside *Shabbos* and *me'ilah* is, incidentally, what occasions its placement in this tractate.

It is worth pausing on the humor hidden in the comparison. That *hilchos Shabbos* involves *halachot merubot* — an enormous body of law — is self-evident. But how many laws does *chagigah* really have? The tractate itself has not generated that many. And *me'ilah*, by contrast, is genuinely enormous and its laws genuinely intricate.

The *mishnah* rounds out its taxonomy with a third category: civil law, Temple service, laws of ritual purity and impurity, and forbidden sexual relationships — these have solid scriptural support, *yesh lahem mah sheyismachu*. They are well-grounded.

### Hein Vehen Gufei Torah

The *mishnah* closes with the declaration *vehen hen gufei Torah* — and they are the body of Torah. As the text stands, this seems to refer only to the last, well-supported category, implying that the earlier categories are somehow lesser. The *Gemara* therefore emends the reading to *hen vehen gufei Torah* — these and those, meaning all three categories alike, whether the area floating without any scriptural support, the mountain on a hair, or the domain resting on firm biblical ground, are all equally Torah. The degree of textual support does not diminish or elevate the binding force or centrality of the law. That is the *mishnah*'s fundamental claim.

---

## Deriving Heter Nedarim

### R. Eliezer: Yafla

The *Gemara* now records a *baraita* in which five tannaitic figures resist the *mishnah*'s stark claim that *heter nedarim* has no scriptural basis, each offering a verse that provides at least some thin support. Rabbi Eliezer says: there is indeed something to rely on. The word *ki yafli* — to enunciate clearly, to make an unambiguous verbal declaration — appears twice in the Torah, once in the context of *nezirut* (*lidor neder nazir*) and once in the context of *nedarim* generally (*neder be'erkecha*). Why twice? *Achat hafla'ah al isur ve'achat hafla'ah al heter* — one enunciation creates the prohibition, the other hints at the possibility of an enunciation that dissolves it. That is the source for *heter nedarim*. Candidly, this is extremely weak. One might fairly ask: is this a hair's breadth, or is it truly nothing? Rabbi Eliezer evidently considered it a hair. The *Gemara* will return to assess the strength of each derivation.

### R. Yehoshua: Oath

Rabbi Yehoshua offers a different source. The verse in *Tehillim* reads: *asher nishbati be'api* — "I swore in my anger" — followed by *im yevo'un el menuchati* — "they shall not enter my resting place." The implication Rabbi Yehoshua draws is that an oath taken in anger, not in a settled state of mind, carries within it the seeds of its own retraction, *v'hazarti bi*. From this he derives the principle that vows made under conditions the vow-taker might not have fully endorsed can be revisited and annulled.

The *Tosafos* grapples seriously with this derivation. The verse says "they shall not enter my resting place," and in fact the generation of the desert did not enter *Eretz Yisrael*. Perhaps *menuchah* refers not to the Land but to *olam haba*, opening the broader question of whether *dor hamidbar* have a portion in the world to come. The *Tosafos* addresses this, but the underlying tension remains: if anything, the verse might suggest the opposite of what Rabbi Yehoshua reads into it. Even if a vow is taken in anger, one is bound by it — the vow was made, its consequence was real. The debate about whether Rabbi Yehoshua's verse actually supports *heter nedarim* or quietly undermines it is precisely why the *Gemara* will ultimately set it aside.

### R. Yitzchak: Generous

Rabbi Yitzchak derives *heter nedarim* from the verse *kol nediv libo* — whoever is generous of heart shall bring his vow to the Temple. The implication is that the generosity of heart — the inner alignment of the person with his commitment — is a condition for the vow's continuing force. If that alignment is broken, there may be grounds for release. As with the earlier derivations, this is quite thin. The verse says nothing explicit about annulment; it is at most a hint that the vow depends on the ongoing will of the one who made it.

### Chananya: Two Parts

Chananya ben achi Rabbi Yehoshua — Rabbi Yehoshua's nephew — cites the verse *nishbati va'akayeimah lishmor mishpatei tzidkecha*: "I have sworn and I will perform, to observe your righteous statutes." He notes the two-part structure: *nishbati* alone, and then separately *va'akayeimah*, "and I will fulfill it." The fact that after swearing there is still a further affirmation of fulfillment hints, he argues, at the logical space *nishbati velo akayeimah* — I may have sworn and yet perhaps not fulfill it. That gap is the opening for *heter nedarim*.

The *Gemara* notes, however, that the same verse is cited by Rav Gidal in the name of Rav to teach something entirely different: *minayin shenishba'im lekayem et hamitzvot* — how do we know that one may take an oath to fulfill a *mitzvah*? One might think such an oath is meaningless because one is already obligated, or that it is a kind of forbidden oath. The verse *nishbati va'akayeimah lishmor mishpatei tzidkecha* shows it is not only permitted but meritorious — it is a way of motivating and urging oneself to act. According to *Rashi*, *lishmor mishpatei tzidkecha* means the person who vows to fulfill a *mitzvah* should thereby spur himself to do it promptly. If that is what the verse is teaching, it says nothing about *heter nedarim*.

Similarly, the *Gemara* notes that Shmuel derives from the phrase *nediv lev* that on occasion even a vow formed silently in the heart, *gamar belibo*, without verbal enunciation, *bisfatav*, may carry legal weight in certain limited circumstances — though this is the minority position. If that is what Rabbi Yitzchak's verse is about, it too says nothing about annulment.

### Shmuel: Others Can

The most celebrated derivation is that of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel. Had he been present among the *Tannaim*, he says — *i havah hasam, amina lehu didi adifa midid'chu* — he would have offered something better than all of them. The verse is the well-known *lo yachel devaro* — "he shall not profane his word." Shmuel reads this with grammatical precision: *hu eino mochel* — he cannot waive his own obligation, he cannot release himself from the debt his words created. *Aval acherim mochalin lo* — but others can release him from that obligation. The sage who annuls the vow is not the vow-maker; he is one of those "others" who has the capacity to *meichel*. Therefore, the Torah itself, by the word *lo yachel devaro*, hints at a mechanism by which a third party may dissolve the vow.

---

## Shmuel Best Answer

### Pilpelta Hacharipta

Rava, and according to some the attribution is Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, endorses Shmuel's derivation with a proverb that has become famous in its own right: *tava chada pilpelta charifta mimalei tzanna de-kari* — one sharp peppercorn is better than a basket of bland gourds. One tight, incisive answer outweighs a collection of weak ones. The *Gemara* explicitly rules: *vechulhu it behu pircha levar midishmuel* — all the other derivations are subject to challenge, *deleit lei pircha* — Shmuel's alone is not. Interestingly, this same phrase — Shmuel declaring that had he been there he would have given a better answer, followed by Rava's endorsement with the peppercorn proverb — appears in three separate places in the *Gemara*. One is here, regarding *heter nedarim*. Another is on the question of permitting life-saving *chilul Shabbos*, where Shmuel's formulation *vechai bahem velo sheyamut bahem* is the answer we always cite. The third is in Masechet Megillah, regarding the scriptural basis for the Megillah's divine inspiration, where Shmuel's derivation from *kiymu vekiblu hayehudim* — *kiymu lemata mah shekiblu lemala* — is perhaps less self-evidently superior to the alternatives, but Rava endorses it nonetheless.

Why is Shmuel's answer the sharpest? The challenges leveled against the others are straightforward. Rabbi Eliezer's use of *yafla* appearing twice may well be teaching, as Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Tarfon rules, that *nezirut ela lehafla'ah* — *nezirut* requires complete unambiguity at the moment of utterance. In the classic case where Reuven says "if that approaching man is a *nazir*, then I am a *nazir*," and Shimon says "if that man is not a *nazir*, then I am a *nazir*" — according to Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Tarfon, neither of them is ever a *nazir*, because at the moment of enunciation it was not objectively clear which declaration was operative. The word *ki yafli* thus teaches clarity of effect at the moment of utterance, not the possibility of annulment. Rabbi Yehoshua's verse may mean the opposite: *be'api nishbati velo hadarna bi* — I swore in my anger and I did not retract. Chananya's verse, *nishbati va'akayeimah*, may simply be teaching Rav Gidal's principle that one may vow to fulfill a *mitzvah*. Shmuel's derivation from *lo yachel devaro*, by contrast, yields a clean and direct reading with no natural alternative interpretation.

### Rabbinic Power

A deeper question lurks beneath the surface of this entire discussion. Normally, laws that are fully binding yet have no scriptural basis fall into the category of *halacha lemoshe misinai*. But *halacha lemoshe misinai* typically covers technical, standalone details — matters that do not overtly conflict with explicit biblical law. *Heter nedarim* is categorically different. The Torah says repeatedly, in the clearest possible terms, that a person who makes a vow is bound by it. The entire thrust of the relevant passages is that there is no escape. And yet the Rabbis assert an institution that releases a person from that obligation entirely, without any vow-specific scriptural basis. That is not a technical detail filling in a gap; it is a direct override of what the text appears to say.

Moreover, the practical ramifications are genuinely unsettling. The release of vows is not managed by a centralized authority with established case law and accountability. Three laypeople suffice. One can shop around for a favorable *chacham*. The institutional checks that might lend the system integrity are largely absent. If someone has pledged a substantial sum — to the Temple, to charity, as part of a business undertaking — the existence of this institution means that pledge may be dissolved by a quorum of three friends. The corrosive effect on the enforceability of oaths and vows in social life is real.

### Torah SheBa'al Peh

What the *mishnah*'s closing line *hen vehen gufei Torah* is ultimately asserting is the equal authority of *Torah she-be'al peh* regardless of how thin its connection to any specific verse. And in a way, *heter nedarim* serves as a paradigmatic model of exactly this dynamic. A person has an existing obligation — a vow, binding and explicit. A *chacham*, exercising his authority, comes along and dissolves it. The Torah's text created the bond; the rabbinic institution, grounded in no explicit text, undoes it. Is this not a compressed image of *Torah she-be'al peh* itself in its relationship to *Torah she-bichtav*? The written text creates obligations; the oral tradition comes and, through its authoritative interpretation, reconfigures them — sometimes amplifying, sometimes limiting, sometimes, as here, releasing entirely.

There is a further parallel within the mechanics of *heter nedarim* itself. When a *chacham* seeks to annul a vow, the method is to probe for some small opening — had you realized this circumstance, would you still have made this vow? One keeps searching until a tiny basis is found, a thread, and through that thread the obligation is unwound. Is this not exactly what the *Tannaim* are doing when they search the *Torah* for a verse to legitimate the institution? They are looking for the hair, the tiny opening that allows the whole mountain to hang. The method of the legal institution and the method of its own legitimation mirror each other precisely.

---

## Hilchos Shabbos

### Multiple Verses

The *Gemara* now turns to *hilchos Shabbos*, which the *mishnah* describes as a mountain on a hair. The *Gemara* objects: *michdei kesiva* — but the Torah writes it explicitly, many times over. The prohibition of *melacha* on *Shabbos* is stated and restated throughout the Torah. How can this be called a hair?

The honest answer is that the objection, while formally apt, somewhat misses the point. Yes, the Torah says *lo taasaseh melacha* many times, but it says the same thing each time. What it does not say is what those thirty-nine *melachos* are, what the *toldos* of each are, the enormous edifice of detail that constitutes Masechet Shabbos. At most, one has *lo seva'aru eish bechol moshvoseichem*, a specific prohibition of fire; the case of the *mekoshesh eitzim*; and perhaps *becharish uvakatzir tishbos*, which, if referring to *Shabbos*, provides a couple of concrete examples. That is a few hairs, perhaps, but not a foundation for the mountain.

### Chofer Guma

The *Gemara* answers by focusing on a specific law: the case of Rabbi Abba, *hachofer guma* — one who digs a hole on *Shabbos* but *ein tzarich ela le'afrah*, needs only the dirt, not the hole itself. In such a case the digger is *patur*, exempt. The question the *Gemara* then raises is: according to whom? The *melacha* of digging, understood as a form of *boneh* — constructing a hole as a usable structure — would normally be a violation. If the person is digging for the dirt and not for the purpose of creating a hole, this resembles *melacha she'eina tzericha legufa*, a *melacha* done for a purpose other than its own intrinsic function, which Rabbi Shimon exempts but Rabbi Yehudah holds liable. If this is a uniquely Shimonite ruling, it does not represent the consensus, and it cannot ground the *mishnah*'s general claim.

The *Gemara* resolves this: *afilu teima Rabbi Yehudah* — even according to Rabbi Yehudah the digger is exempt in this case. *Hasam metaken hacha mekalkel* — where Rabbi Yehudah holds one liable despite wrong intent, the result is constructive; here the result is *mekalkel*, destructive or at least unwanted. The person not only does not need the hole; having an unintended pit in one's yard makes things worse. Even Rabbi Yehudah would not classify an action whose result is an unwanted degradation as a full-fledged *melacha*.

### Melechet Machsheves

But why is this exemption a "mountain on a hair"? The *Gemara* answers: *meleches machsheves asrah Torah* — the Torah prohibited *melechet machsheves*, a purposive, intentional act directed toward its own intended outcome. And the problem is that *meleches machsheves lo kesiva* by *Shabbos* — this concept does not appear in the *Shabbos* passages themselves. It is derived from the *Mishkan*: the construction of the Tabernacle, with which *Shabbos* is repeatedly juxtaposed in the Torah, was built through *melechet machsheves*, deliberate and purposive craft. By the association of *Shabbos* to the *Mishkan*, we apply the same conceptual framework to *Shabbos* violations. And from this derived category flows an enormous range of leniencies. A large proportion of the practical *kulos* one encounters in *hilchos Shabbos* — *eino miskavein*, *pesik reisha*, *melacha she'eina tzericha legufa* according to some — trace back ultimately to this concept of intentionality and the requirement that the act and its desired outcome be aligned.

### Unsatisfactory Answer

This answer is, to be frank, unsatisfying. The truly enormous mountain that *hilchos Shabbos* rests upon is not the category of *melechet machsheves* but the thirty-nine *melachos* themselves, with all their *toldos* and ramifications, none of which are spelled out in any biblical verse. The Torah says *lo taasaseh melacha*; the identification of what constitutes *melacha* — fire, plowing, reaping, writing, the entire list — is derived from the activities of the *Mishkan*, but that too is not explicit in any verse. That is the real mountain. By comparison, the category of *melechet machsheves* and the exemption for the person who digs for dirt rather than for a hole — while not *pashut* — is not so startling a *chiddush* that it requires a special accounting. The intuition that an act is only a *melacha* when performed in sync with its intended purpose is not counterintuitive; it follows naturally from almost any reasonable understanding of culpability. The *Gemara*'s question and its answer, in this section, are genuinely puzzling. Why focus on *melechet machsheves* as the hair on which the mountain hangs, rather than on the identification of the *melachos* themselves?

---

## Chagigah Definition

### Vechagstem Oso

The *Gemara* turns to *chagigah*. Again: *michtav kesiva* — the Torah writes it explicitly. The verse *vechagosem oso chag laAdoshem shivat yamim* — you shall celebrate it as a festival to God for seven days — appears to mandate a *chagigah* sacrifice. So why is this a mountain on a hair?

The challenge is introduced through a question Rav Papa poses to Abaye: *mimai dehai vechagosem oso chag l'Adoshem zvichah* — how do you know that "celebrate a festival to God" means slaughtering sacrifices? Perhaps *choga chaga kamar Rachmana* — perhaps the Torah simply means: have a holiday, celebrate, rejoice. There was much rejoicing.

The *Gemara* initially counters from Moshe's words to Pharaoh: *veyachogu li bamidbar* — let them hold a celebration for Me in the wilderness. Is Moshe merely asking for a party? No — he is requesting sacrifices. *Veyomer Moshe gam atah titein beyadeinu zvachim ve'olos* — and Moshe said, you too will provide us with sacrifices and burnt-offerings. The *chag* is sacrificial.

### Chelev Chagi

But the *Gemara* presses back: perhaps even Moshe was only requesting a celebration with meat and drink — *ichlu v'shasu v'chogu chaga kamai* — without specifying Temple-style sacrifices. The word *zevach* in Moshe's subsequent statement need not mean a formal *korban*; it can simply mean slaughter. And the *olah* Moshe mentions is not a *chagigah* in any case.

The *Gemara* therefore turns to another verse: *velo yalin chelev chagi ad boker* — the fat of my *chag* shall not remain overnight until morning. If *chag* meant only a celebration, in what sense would a celebration have *chelev*, fat? The fat belongs to a sacrifice. *V'isalka daitach dechoga hu, tarba l'chaga is lei* — if you think *chag* means merely festivity, does a celebration possess fat? The conclusion would seem forced: *chagi* refers to the fat of a specific sacrifice called a *chagigah*.

The *Gemara* resists this too. Perhaps *chelev haba bizman chag* — fats of any sacrifices brought during the festival period — *lo yalin*, may not be left overnight. The word *chagi* would then mean sacrifices brought at the time of the *chag*, not a specific *korban chagigah*. But this is also challenged: the verse *kol halayla ad haboker* already requires burning the fat of *olot* overnight, so the general law is established regardless. The verse about *chelev chagi* must therefore be adding a specific *lav* applying to the *chagigah* sacrifice as such — not merely a general overlap with already existing law.

### Gezeirah Shava

The *Gemara* ultimately turns to a *gezeirah shavah*. The verse here says *veyachogu li bamidbar* — "they shall celebrate for me in the *midbar*." The verse in *Amos* says *hazvachim umincha higashtem li bamidbar* — "did you bring me sacrifices and grain offerings in the wilderness?" The shared word *bamidbar* connects the two passages: just as the verse in *Amos* uses *zvachim* — sacrifices — so too the *chag* Moshe speaks of means sacrifices. *Ma lehalan zvachim af kan zvachim*.

### Verses Not Clear

But the *Gemara* concedes the weakness of this final step: *divrei Torah midivrei kabbalah lo yalfinan* — we do not derive biblical law from *Nevi'im* or *Ketuvim*. The verse in *Amos* is *divrei kabbalah*, transmitted prophetic text, and while the *Gemara* acknowledges this principle is often honored in the breach, it stands in principle. Therefore, the derivation that *chagigah* is a *korban* is not fully clean. The verse *vechagosem oso chag* could mean just celebration; the *gezeirah shavah* that would clinch the sacrificial interpretation draws on a non-Torah source. That is why the obligation of *chagigah* is described as a mountain on a hair: not because there is no verse, but because the verses we have are not sufficiently unambiguous to establish beyond doubt that they mandate a *korban chagigah* specifically.

Returning to the *mishnah*'s formulation — *halachot merubot umikra muat* — one notes that the *Gemara* seems far more exercised about the *mikra muat* than the *halachot merubot*. Both for *Shabbos* and for *chagigah*, the *Gemara*'s concern is whether there is an explicit *pasuk* to begin with, not whether the quantity of *halachot* is disproportionate. Once you have an explicit *pasuk*, however thin, the *Gemara* does not treat the enormity of the derived law as troubling. The lack of a clear starting-point verse is what makes something a *searah*.

---

## Me'ilot

### Verses Explicit

The *mishnah* lists *me'ilot* — the laws of misappropriating consecrated property — as the third mountain on a hair. The *Gemara* raises the same challenge: *mikra kesiva* — there are explicit verses about the prohibition of misusing *hekdesh*. How is this a *searah*? Rami bar Chama answers: *lo nitzrecha ela lechidetnan* — the point is not about the basic prohibition but about a specific law taught in a *mishnah*.

### Shaliach Melacha

The law is this: *hashaliach she-asah shlichuso, ba'al habayis maal; lo asah shlichuso, shaliach maal* — if the agent did what he was sent to do, the homeowner has transgressed *me'ilah*; if the agent deviated from his instructions, the agent has transgressed.

The scenario: a person reaches into his wallet, unaware that he is handling money he had sanctified as *hekdesh*. He hands Michael twenty dollars and sends him to buy apples and bananas. Michael, unaware of any problem, goes to the store. If Michael buys exactly the apples and bananas he was asked to buy, *he* has done nothing independent — he is simply the extension of the one who sent him, and the one who sent him has committed *me'ilah* by effectively spending the *hekdesh* money. If Michael exercises his own judgment and instead buys oranges and pineapples, he has stepped outside his mandate, is no longer an extension of his sender, and is the one who has committed *me'ilah*.

### Michael's Transgression

The *Gemara* asks sharply: *vechi zeh choteh vezeh mitchayev* — can one person sin and the other be held responsible? Michael bought the apples and bananas — he is the one who physically transferred the *hekdesh* money. Why should the person at home be the transgressor?

*Hainu deka'amri matluyim besa'arah* — that is why it is a mountain on a hair. The logic does not cohere on its own terms.

Rava responds: *dilma shani me'ilah degamrinan cheit cheit mitrumah* — perhaps *me'ilah* is different because we derive it through a verbal analogy from *terumah*. Just as one may appoint a *shaliach* to separate *terumah* on one's behalf — *shlucho shel adam kemoto*, an agent is like the principal — the same principle applies here: when Michael buys the apples and bananas as instructed, he is functioning as the arm of the one who sent him, and the *me'ilah* is attributed to that person.

A deeper account of why this works can be offered. In the case of *terumah*, the legal act is separating the produce; it does not particularly matter who performs it, since what matters is the result — that *terumah* be designated. By analogy, in the spending of *hekdesh* money, the focus is less on the physical act of handing money to a storekeeper than on the context and outcome: the *hekdesh* funds have been misappropriated, and the one who set that process in motion, who caused the money to be misspent, bears the responsibility. The causal locus is the person who dispatched the agent, not the agent who executed the task.

### Beam Transfer

But the *Gemara* refines the question further. Rava says: *lo nitzrecha ela lechid'tanya* — the truly difficult case is a different one. Here the situation is: the homeowner remembers, mid-transaction, that the money he sent with Michael is *hekdesh* — *nizkar ba'al habayis velo nizkar shaliach*. He remembers; Michael does not. At the moment the homeowner realizes the error, he no longer wants Michael to be his *shaliach*. He revokes the agency, at least in his own mind, because he cannot reach Michael in time. Michael, still acting in complete innocence, proceeds to do exactly what was asked of him. *Shaliach maal* — the agent has committed *me'ilah*. As the *Gemara* exclaims: *shaliach anya* — poor Michael! He did exactly what he was told, he has no knowledge of any problem, and yet he is the one who has transgressed. *Hainu harim hatluyim basa'arah* — that is a mountain on a hair.

Rav Ashi challenges this: *dilma midi d'hava amotzi ma'os hekdesh* — is this really more difficult than the ordinary case of someone who accidentally reaches into the wrong pocket and spends *hekdesh* money he did not know was *hekdesh*? He too had no intent, and he too is liable for *me'ilah* *beshogeg*. The distinction the *Gemara* implies is that in that case the person had at least some responsibility to keep track of which money was sanctified. Michael had no such responsibility whatsoever. His liability is entirely devoid of any causal connection to the wrong.

Rav Ashi then redirects: *lo nitzrecha ella k'ditnan* — the case where the mountain truly hangs on a hair is this *mishnah*. If a person takes a beam or stone belonging to *hekdesh*, he has not yet committed *me'ilah*. *Nesana l'chavero* — if he then gives it to another person, *hu maal v'chavero lo maal* — he has committed *me'ilah*, and the recipient has not. The *Gemara* then asks: *mishkal shaklei* — but he took it either way. Whether he brought the beam home to his own house or handed it to someone else, in both cases he removed it from the Temple storehouse. Why does he commit *me'ilah* only upon transfer to another, and not upon taking it home himself?

*Hainu harim hatluyim basa'arah.* That is why it is a mountain on a hair.

### Gizbar Special Case

Rav Ashi's challenge to his own formulation is immediately answered by reference to Shmuel's resolution. Shmuel was sufficiently troubled by the logic of that case that he circumscribed it: *hacha b'gizbar hamsuros lo avnei binyan askinan* — the case concerns the Temple treasurer, the *gizbar*, to whom the building materials of *hekdesh* are entrusted. As the official custodian of the Temple's physical resources, wherever the *gizbar* moves the beams and stones — even if he takes them to his own home — they remain within his zone of authorized responsibility. *D'chol heicha d'mancha birshusa didei mancha* — wherever they rest, they are still considered within *hekdesh*'s *reshus*. Since they are never outside *hekdesh*'s domain while in his hands, no act of *me'ilah* can occur until he actually transfers them to someone else, removing them definitively from *hekdesh*'s *reshut*. At that point, and only at that point, has he committed *me'ilah*. The discussion of which case in *hilchos me'ilah* constitutes the true "mountain on a hair" — defying logical resolution — will continue.

---

---

# Chagigah 11

## Me'ilah & Hair's Breadth

### Me'ilah Intro

The daf for today is 11, with which we will, God willing, finish the first *perek* and move on to the second. We pick up with the question of in what way *me'ilah* is one of the things described as a mountain suspended by a hair's breadth. Rather than underscoring the absence of a good *pasuk* to base certain laws on, the *gemara* here emphasizes that some of these laws seem to be suspended on very little in terms of rational basis. The challenge is to identify which of them truly exemplify that quality.

### Beam Case

The *gemara* opens with the phrase *ela misefa* — "rather, from the end" — at three lines from the top of 11a. We have already discussed the *teshuvah* concerning somebody who takes a beam from *hekdesh* and does not commit *me'ilah* by that act alone, but does commit *me'ilah* when he hands it to his friend. That seems arbitrary: if you take it from *hekdesh*, why have you not yet transgressed? The *gemara* resolves this by noting that perhaps the person was himself the *gizbar*, the Temple treasurer, and therefore until he actually transfers it to someone else he has not truly removed it from *hekdesh*. So the real difficulty, says the *gemara*, comes not from that case but from the end of the *mishnah*.

### Building Beam

The *mishnah* states: *bena'ah betoch beito harei zeh lo maal ad sheyadur tachteha bishveh prutah* — if someone takes this beam from *hekdesh* and builds it into his house, he still does not commit *me'ilah* until he actually lives under it and derives a *prutah*'s worth of benefit. The difficulty is plain: why is the act of building the beam into the house not itself an act of misappropriation? *Shinuy kanah* — transforming the object — is ordinarily a mode of acquiring ownership. So asks the *gemara*, *mai irya dar mai irya lo dar* — what difference does it make whether or not he actually lived under it? The *gemara* itself identifies this as the paradigm case: *haino k'harim hamitlin besa'ara* — this is indeed like a mountain suspended by a hair. The "hair" here is of the rational variety, not necessarily a textual one.

### Rava's Explanation

The *gemara* pushes back: *umai kushya*, what exactly is the difficulty? Perhaps we can explain the case according to *Rava*'s reading. *De'amar Rava kegon sheheniachah pi aruba* — Rava explains that the person did not nail the beam in but rather rested it like *sechach* across a skylight. In that case, no *shinuy* has yet occurred. *Ei dar bah in* — only if he actually lives under it and benefits from it has he committed *me'ilah*; *ei lo dar bah lo* — otherwise, he has done nothing actionable, having merely rested the beam on top of the skylight.

The *gemara* then returns to *Rava*'s earlier explanation of a different case that seemed equally difficult to rationalize: where the *baal habayit* sent a *shaliach* to spend money and then realized mid-transaction that he had mistakenly given him *hekdesh* funds, thereby effectively revoking the agency. At that moment the *shaliach* is no longer his representative, yet the *shaliach* commits *me'ilah* despite being entirely unaware of any problem. The *gemara* presses: *hatam mida yadi d'ika zuzei d'Hekdesh* — in the standard case of *me'ilah*, the person knows he has sanctified funds in the house; *iba'ei lei le'iyuni* — he is obliged to pay attention, and if he accidentally uses the wrong funds, his unawareness does not absolve him because he was negligent. But here — *hacha mi yada* — how could the poor *shaliach* have known? Every time someone hands you money to spend, are you supposed to inquire whether it might be *hekdesh*? He had no basis for suspicion, yet he has committed *me'ilah* because of the sender's mistake and a mid-course change of heart. *Haino k'harim hamitlin besa'ara* — this is why it qualifies as a mountain on a hair's breadth. And notably, what makes this case so striking is not merely the absence of a supporting verse — it is that the law is not rationally defensible either. Had the *gemara* been able to point to an explicit verse, one could accept the result however counterintuitive. But when the law is both irrational and textually thin, its connection to any biblical source is shown to be genuinely fragile.

## Harim Hatluim

### Definition

Following the discussion of *me'ilah*, the *gemara* presents what appears to be a clarification of the category *harim hatluim besearah* — mountains suspended by a hair. The next line introduces the principle: *mikra muat vehalachot merubot* — a very small number of verses and a very large number of laws that grow from them. The "hair" of the metaphor, in other words, often refers to the thinness of textual support rather than strictly rational support.

### Few Verses Many Laws

A *braita* expands on the list in the *mishnah*, which had mentioned *chagigah*, *me'ilah*, and *shabbos* as examples of *harim hatluim besearah*. The *braita* adds *negaim ve'ohalos* — the laws of scaled disease and the *tumah* transmitted through shared overhead space — as further instances of *mikra muat vehalachot merubot*: few verses and an enormous body of laws.

### Negaim Opposite

This characterization immediately raises a difficulty. It is hard to say that *negaim* has few verses — *Parshat Tazria u'Metzora* is substantial. The *gemara* presses: *negaim mikra muat* — *negaim* has a small number of verses? *Negaim mikra merubah hu* — on the contrary, *negaim* has many verses! One cannot accurately say it is a case of few verses and many laws, even if the laws are disproportionately elaborate relative to the verses. *Amar Rav Pappa hachi ka'amar* — Rav Pappa explains that what the *braita* actually means is the reverse: *negaim mikra merubah vehalachot muatot* — *negaim* has many verses and, relatively speaking, few *halachot*. This too is initially surprising — there is an entire *masechet* devoted to *negaim*. But the *gemara*'s point seems to be proportionality: we normally expect *halachot* to proliferate far beyond the biblical verses that anchor them (consider, for example, that a single verse about *get* generates an entire *masechet* of *Gittin*). By contrast, *negaim* is roughly proportional — its legal elaborations track its verses in a way that is atypical. *Ohalos*, on the other hand, fits the standard pattern precisely: *mikra muat vehalachot merubot* — the verses about *tumah* transmitted through shared overhead space are relatively few, yet the resulting *halachot* are vast.

### Practical Application

One might ask: what is the practical value of distinguishing these two categories? The *gemara* poses exactly this question — *umai nafka mina* — and answers with a guide to research. *Ei mistapka lach milta benegaim* — if you have a question about *negaim*, *ayein bekrayei* — go look at the verses, because the verses themselves will carry you most of the way. The *pesukim* are rich enough and clear enough that a careful reading of them provides genuine halachic orientation. *Ve'ei mistapka lach milta be'ohalos* — but if your question is about *ohalos*, *ayein be'matnitin* — go look in the *mishnayot*, because the verses will leave you entirely at sea. The operative knowledge lives in the oral tradition.

### Avodah Zarah Tangent

This principle — that in some areas one looks to the text while in others the *mishnayot* are the primary resource — calls to mind a striking parallel from *Masechet Avodah Zarah*. In all the *mishnayot* and *gemara* of *Avodah Zarah*, one finds complete silence on a topic that is in fact a recurring theme throughout *Sefer Devarim*: the obligation to destroy *avodah zarah*. All of the many concerns about *avodah zarah* are represented in *Shas* — its prohibition of benefit, the laws relating to non-Jews and idolatry, and much else — but the *mitzvah* of actively destroying *avodah zarah*, which receives verse after verse in *Devarim*, has essentially no rabbinic legal elaboration whatsoever. Scholars have pointed out the obvious reason: if one is living in *Eretz Yisrael* under Roman rule, surrounded by statues at every turn, one does not publicly elaborate a *mitzvah* to destroy them, lest someone take it into his head to act on it.

When a student once pressed the claim that surely *somewhere* the *gemara* must discuss this, the response was to open the *Sefer HaChinuch* to that *mitzvah* in *Devarim*. After presenting the *mitzvah*, the *Sefer HaChinuch* arrives at the section *mi-dinei ha-mitzvah* — the legal details of the *mitzvah* — and says simply: *mi-dinei ha-mitzvah kulam meforashim ba-katuv*. All the laws are explained in the text itself. There are no *gemarot* to cite because there are none. This is the limiting case of *ayein bekra* — an area where there is essentially no *Torah she'be'al peh* at all, and everything is in the verses.

## Three Categories

### Three Categories Intro

The *gemara* now turns to the third category identified in the *mishnah*: *dinim*, *avodot*, *taharot*, and *arayot*, which are described as *yesh lahem mah she'yismochu* — they have something to support themselves on. This rounds out the three-tier structure: laws like *heter nedarim* fly in mid-air with nothing supporting them; the *harim hatluim besearah* have a thin thread of support; and this final category has genuine grounding in the biblical text. Yet even here, *Rashi* notes that the phrase *yesh al mah she'yismochu* — they have *what* to lean on — does not sound like a claim of full, explicit support. It sounds like adequate but not unambiguous support. Accordingly, the *gemara* will challenge each item on the list, asking: what do you mean this merely "has support"? Isn't it fully explicit?

### Dinim & Eye/Eye

The *gemara* opens with *dinim* — laws and judgments, meaning *dinei mammonot*. The obvious response is *michtav ketivan* — it's written out! *Parshat Mishpatim* is an entire *parasha* of civil law. The *gemara* concedes the point but says: *lo nitzrecha ela le'khid'rabbi* — the category is needed specifically for what *Rabbi* derives. *Rabbi* addresses the verse *nefesh tachat nafesh* — a soul for a soul — in the context of a person who, intending to strike his fellow, accidentally strikes a pregnant woman, who subsequently dies. The verse says *v'natata nefesh tachat nafesh* — you shall give a soul for a soul. The question is whether this means actual execution or monetary compensation.

*Rabbi* argues: *ne'emar netina lemata v'ne'emar netina lemala* — the same verb of "giving" appears in both places. Above, the verse speaks of a monetary fine paid through the court for the miscarriage; therefore, *ma netina ha'amura lemala mamon af kan mamon* — just as the payment for the miscarriage is monetary, so too the "soul for a soul" means a monetary payment, not execution. This is not the plain reading of the verse. Indeed, some Bible scholars have argued — pointing to parallels in the Code of Hammurabi — that "eye for an eye, tooth for a tooth" was a stock phrase in the ancient Near East connoting equal justice rather than literal retaliation. Whatever the philological history, the *gemara*'s point is clear: the derivation of monetary compensation from a verse that reads "a soul for a soul" is not self-evident, and the law therefore has something to lean on but is not fully supported.

### Avodot Blood Catching

For *avodot* — the Temple service — the initial challenge is even stronger: *michtav k'siva* — it is written in detail! The first half of *Vayikra* is devoted almost entirely to the laws of sacrifice, and if anything has explicit biblical detail, it is the *avoda* in the *Beis HaMikdash*. The *gemara* responds: *lo nitzrecha ela l'halachos hadam* — the category is needed specifically for the laws concerning the blood service, and in particular for the act of catching the blood, *kabalat hadam*, which is not so explicitly mandated.

The *braita* derives: *v'hikrivu bnei Aharon* — "and the sons of Aharon shall bring [the blood] close." The Rabbis read this as referring to *kabalat hadam*, the catching of the blood in a basin. Yet the Torah uses here the language of *holacha*, conveying — *v'afka Rachmana bilshon holacha* — because elsewhere the same verb *v'hikriv* is used for the fat and the limbs in the sense of bringing them to the altar. The *gemara* notes that *holacha* is in fact an *avoda she'efshar l'vatla* — a service that could theoretically be omitted by slaughtering the animal directly adjacent to the *mizbeach*, catching the blood, and immediately throwing it, without ever performing the act of conveyance. One might have thought that because *holacha* is dispensable it lacks the full legal status of an *avoda* — that, for instance, a disqualifying intent of *pigul* formed during *holacha* would be inconsequential. The *gemara* teaches that this is not so: *holacha* is as much of an *avoda* as *kabalat hadam*, and the Torah's use of the conveying-language when discussing blood catching is precisely to teach that the act of conveyance is halachically equivalent to the act of catching. None of this is obvious from the verses, which is why the category of *avodot* belongs on the list of things that have support but are not fully explicit.

### Taharot Shiurim

For *taharot* — purity laws — the same initial challenge applies: *michtav ketivan*, these are extensively written. The laws of *tumah v'tahara* dominate large sections of the Torah, and many of their details are indeed fairly clear. The *gemara* responds: *lo nitzrecha ela l'shiur mikva delo ktiv* — the category is needed specifically for the minimum size of a *mikva*, which is not written explicitly.

The *braita* derives: *verachatz b'saro bamayim* — "and he shall wash his flesh in water." This is understood to mean immersion in *mei mikva*. The verse then says *et kol b'saro* — all of his flesh — which is taken to mean *mayim shekol gufo oleh bahen*, water that can contain his entire body. From this the Rabbis quantify: *ama al ama berum shalosh amot* — a space of approximately one-and-a-half by one-and-a-half by four-and-a-half feet — and this equals *arbaim se'ah*, forty *se'ah*, the minimum measure for a valid *mikva*. The specific figure of forty *se'ah* is not written anywhere; it follows from measurement and estimation, which is precisely why it falls into the category of "having support but not fully explicit."

The *gemara* then turns to *tumah* — becoming *tamei* — with the same initial challenge. The response: *lo nitzrecha ela k'adasha min hasheretz* — the category is needed specifically for the *shiur* of a lentil bean's worth of a rodent as the minimum amount that conveys *tumah*. This is *halacha l'Moshe miSinai* — not derivable from the text at all — which is precisely the *gemara*'s point.

The *braita* explains the derivation. The verse says *kol hanogea bahem* — anyone who touches "them," which might imply the entire carcass must be present. Another verse says *asher yipol mehem el tocho* — "of them" falls into a vessel, suggesting even a small portion suffices. The *gemara* reconciles: *ad sheyagia bemiktzato shehu kechulo* — a portion is sufficient, but it must be representative of the whole. The Rabbis then determine: *shiru chachamim k'adasha* — a lentil bean is the representative minimum, *sheken chomet*, because a particular type of rodent is born at precisely that size. *Rabbi Yose b'Rabbi Yehuda* adds that the lentil bean corresponds to the tail of a lizard — *keznav haleta'ah* — which, even after being severed, continues to move, demonstrating that it represents something of the whole organism. All of this is not found in the verse itself.

### Arayot Daughter

For *arayot* — forbidden sexual relations — the challenge is perhaps most pointed of all. If anything in the Torah is detailed, it is the laws of *giluy arayot* in the second half of *Vayikra*. Indeed, one might note that everything on the *gemara*'s list — *dinim* (*Parshat Mishpatim*), *avodot* (the first half of *Vayikra*), *taharot* and *arayot* (the second half of *Vayikra* along with other sections) — are precisely the areas that receive the most detailed biblical treatment. The *gemara* chooses to read the *mishnah* as saying that even these areas are only "somewhat supported," and the implication is significant: even the sections of the Torah that appear most fully elaborated cannot be read without the mediation of *Torah she'be'al peh*. The *chachamim* are making a claim that their interpretive authority extends not to the textually sparse areas alone but to the very places where one might think the text speaks for itself.

The *gemara* says: *nitzrecha l'vito me'anusato* — the category is needed for the case of a man's biological daughter from a woman he raped, on 11b. The Torah explicitly forbids *isha u'vitah* — a woman and her daughter — but that formulation refers specifically to the daughter of a man's wife, whether or not she is his biological daughter. When the Torah refers to biological descendants without reference to a man's wife, it mentions only granddaughter: *ervat bat bincha u'bat bitecha* — the nakedness of your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter. A man's biological daughter who is not his wife's daughter thus appears to go unmentioned, and a special derivation is required to establish the prohibition.

*De'amar Rava amar li Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi atya hena hena atya zima zima* — Rava, citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi, derives it through a *gezeirah shavah* from the words *hena hena* and *zima zima*, connecting the case of granddaughter to the case of wife-and-daughter so as to include the biological daughter in the prohibition. There are in fact two such derivations — one establishing the prohibition and one establishing the punishment — corresponding to the two textual parallels. The law is there, but it requires this kind of indirect derivation, which is exactly what "having support without being fully explicit" means.

### Hen Hen Gufei

With that, the *mishnah* closes by declaring: *hen hen gufei Torah* — these are the very essence, the body, of Torah. This final statement, taken in isolation, sounds as if it is elevating only the last category — the well-supported laws — as the true substance of Torah, while the earlier categories of mountains-on-a-hair and laws-in-mid-air are somehow less essential. This would be a dangerous conclusion.

The *gemara* immediately challenges: *hani in hanach lo* — only this last category is real Torah, and not the earlier ones? *Ela eima hen ve'hen gufei Torah* — no: read it as "these and they are the essence of Torah." Everything in the *mishnah*, whether in the first category, the middle category, or the last, is equally the essence of Torah. The laws that fly in mid-air with no textual support, the mountains suspended by a hair, and the fully elaborated biblical laws — all are *gufei Torah*. This is the statement on which the first *perek* ends.

*Hadran alach kol ha'chayavin.*

## Transition Perek 2

### Mishnah Intro

Before turning to the second *perek*, it is worth asking what this entire *mishnah* — with its typology of halachic support — is doing in *Masechet Chagigah* at all. *Chagigah* is mentioned on the list, but it is hardly the most prominent example, and the discussion ranges far beyond it. Albeck, in his edition of the *mishnah*, suggests an answer: these two *mishnayot* — the one just concluded and the one we are about to read — together form a commentary on the previous *mishnah* of this *perek*, which described missing the opportunity to bring one's *korbanot* on the *regel* as a *me'uvat lo yukhal litkon*, a perversion that cannot be corrected, and which concluded with the view that this phrase applies specifically to a *talmid chacham she'piresh min haTorah* — a Torah scholar who has abandoned the Torah. These two *mishnayot*, on this reading, identify where that danger leads: on one side, a scholar who separates from Torah might come to question the mountains on a hair, the laws that have weak textual support; on the other side, he might enter the dangerous areas of inquiry described in the second *perek* without the guardrails that make such study safe. So the list of halachic categories and the restrictions on esoteric inquiry are both answers to the same question: what goes wrong when a scholar breaks from the tradition?

### Four Areas

The second *perek* opens: *ein dorshin ba'arayot be'shlosha ve'lo be'maaseh bereishit be'shnayim ve'lo be'merkavah be'yachid ela im ken hayah chacham u'mevin mi'da'ato* — one does not explicate *arayot* with three students; one does not discuss *maaseh bereishit* with two; one does not teach *maaseh merkavah* even to a single individual, unless that individual is wise and can work out most of it on his own.

*Kol hamistakel b'arba'ah devarim* — anyone who gazes into four areas: *mah l'ma'alah mah l'matah* — what is above and what is below — and *mah l'fanim mah l'achor* — what is in front and what is behind. Whether "in front" and "behind" refer to spatial directions or to before and after time — before creation and at the end of time — is a question the *gemara* will address. Anyone who explores these four areas without proper standing, *v'chol shelo chas al kvod kono* — who has not protected the honor of his Creator — *ratui lo shelo ba l'olam*, it would have been fitting for such a person never to have come into the world at all.

What precisely are the kinds of concerns animating these restrictions? The Artscroll *mishnah* notes that the Gnostics were particularly focused on exactly these areas: they sought to explain the inner dynamics of creation and also, apparently, attacked the integrity of the *avot* by pointing to their apparent transgressions of *issurei arayot* — *Yaakov* married two sisters, and there are other such critiques. The *mishnah* may thus be responding to a specific intellectual environment in which such inquiries were the mark of the highest-level religious initiate, and the Rabbis are inverting that hierarchy entirely: these are not the pinnacle of religious pursuit; they are the areas of maximum danger to the honor of the Creator.

## Arayot Students

### Student Count

The *gemara* now addresses the clause *ein dorshin ba'arayot be'shlosha* and raises a question about how to count. Initially the *gemara* assumes that the number three includes the teacher. This creates an absurdity when we reach the clause *ve'lo be'merkavah be'yachid* — if one includes the teacher and thus cannot teach *merkavah* even to one student alone, then essentially no one can ever teach *maaseh merkavah* at all, since there would be no permissible arrangement. The *gemara* resolves this: *hachi ka'amar* — the *mishnah* means the following: *ein dorshin ba'arayot lo be'shloshah* — not to three students; *ve'lo be'maaseh bereishit lishnayim* — not to two students; *ve'lo be'merkavah l'yachid* — not even to one individual student, unless the student can largely work it out himself. The number in each case counts students, not the total group including the teacher.

### Verse Attempts

The *gemara* then asks *mai ta'ama* — what is the source for the specific limit of three students for *arayot*? The first attempt: *ish ish el kol shear besaro* — "each man to all his close relatives" — contains the double *ish ish*, which could be read as two people, and *shear besaro* as a third, making three. And *lo tikrevu l'galot ervah* — "you shall not come close to uncover *ervah*" — is then read as: do not expose *arayot* before three. This is a homiletic reading in which *l'galot* (to uncover, to reveal) is applied to the act of teaching.

The *gemara* immediately challenges: the same *ish ish* formulation appears elsewhere — *ish ish ki yekalel elohav* (any man who curses his God) and *ve'ish ish asher yiten mizaro l'Molech* (any man who gives his child to *Molech*). Would we similarly restrict teaching laws of blasphemy or *avodah zarah* to groups of two? The *gemara* responds that in those verses, *ish ish* carries a different *derasha* altogether: *lerabot et hanochrim* — to include non-Jews, who are also bound by these prohibitions as part of the *sheva mitzvot bnei Noach*. So *ish ish* in those contexts means "any person," and the same must be true in the *arayot* context. That removes the textual basis for the restriction.

A second attempt: *ushmartem et mishmarti* — "you shall observe my safeguard" — said in the context of *arayot*. *Ushmartem* is plural, suggesting two people; *mishmarti* is singular, adding one more — three. And *l'vilti asot mechukkot hato'evot* — not to act according to the practices of those peoples — implies that if you have three people you must be careful not to let the teaching go astray. The *gemara* again challenges: *ushmartem* appears in many contexts — *ushmartem et haShabbat*, *ushmartem et hamitzvot*, *ushmartem et mishmeret hakodesh*. Would we apply the same numeric restriction there? This verse too cannot serve as the basis.

### Subtlety Focus

*Ella amar Rav Ashi* — Rav Ashi offers the definitive resolution. *Mai ein dorshin ba'arayot be'shlosha* — what does the *mishnah*'s restriction actually mean? *Ein dorshin be'sitrei arayot* — it does not mean that one may not teach the straightforward *halachot* of *arayot* at all (which would be perverse, since people need to know those laws in order to observe them). Rather, the restriction applies specifically to the subtle, hidden, non-obvious dimensions of the laws — the *sitrei*, the covered-over aspects. And indeed, *l'galot* now reads quite naturally: it is specifically what is *galui*, revealed but not obvious, that must not be disclosed to a group of three.

### Sexual Desire Psychology

*Mai ta'ama* — but why? Here the *gemara* abandons the search for a verse and says simply: *svara hu* — it is a matter of rational understanding. *Bei terei ki yasvi kamei ravaihu* — if there are two students sitting before their *rebbe*, *chad shakil v'tari bahadi rabai* — one will be engaged in direct conversation with the teacher, *v'idach matzli udneih l'gemara* — and the other will simply be listening, attentive to every word. But *ba'telasa* — with three students — *chad shakil v'tari bahadi rabai v'hanach terei shaklu v'taru bahadi hadadi* — one engages the teacher while the other two will fall into a side conversation of their own. They will mishear what is being taught.

One might argue this risk applies to any halachic topic. The *gemara* addresses this directly: *arayot shani* — the laws of forbidden relations are different. *De'amar mar gezel v'arayot nafsho mechmadtan u'mitavah lahen* — when it comes to theft and to sexual desire, a person's soul craves these and lusts after them. The implication is that subconscious desire can distort perception: even a well-intentioned student may, without awareness, mishear a subtle halachic point if his desire is already engaged in that direction.

But why does the same logic not apply to the laws of theft? Here the *gemara* draws a sharp psychological distinction. *Arayot bein befanav bein shelo befanav nafish yitzreih* — sexual desire is present whether or not the object of desire is before the person. In a classroom, the student is not confronted with the object of his desire, yet that desire remains active. *Gezel lo — befanav nafish yitzreih shelo befanav lo nafish yitzreih* — the desire to possess, to take what is not one's own, is primarily activated by confrontation with the desired object. Away from it, the desire is largely dormant. In a study session, the student is not looking at the Porsche he covets; the relevant desire simply is not functioning at that moment. Sexual desire, by contrast, operates independently of the immediate presence of its object. Therefore, specifically in the area of *arayot*, one must be maximally careful that even subtle points are understood precisely, and that requires limiting the group to no more than two students at a time.

## Maaseh Bereishit

### Creation Verses

Having addressed the restriction on *arayot*, the *mishnah* turns to *maaseh bereishit* — the acts of creation — which may be taught to only one student at a time. *Mina hanei mili* — where is this derived? The *braita* cites: *ki she'al na l'yamim rishonim* — "if you will but ask of earlier days." *Yachid sho'el* — an individual may ask about the earlier days; *v'ein shnayim sho'alin* — but two may not. One cannot be taught *maaseh bereishit* in a group even of two students.

### Spatial Boundaries

The *braita* further delimits what may be asked even by a single individual. *Yakhol yishal adam kodem shenivra olam* — might one ask about what preceded the world's creation? *Talmud lomar* — the verse says: from the day that God created man on the earth. This limits the scope: one may inquire from the moment of creation, but not about what, if anything, preceded it. Conversely, might one think that inquiry is restricted to the period since *Adam* was created, excluding the first five days? *Talmud lomar l'yamim rishonim asher hayu lefanecha* — "the earlier days that were before you" permits inquiry back to the beginning of creation, before human beings.

So the temporal scope of legitimate inquiry runs from the beginning of creation through the present. And what are the spatial limits? *Ulmiktzeh hashamayim v'ad ketzeh hashamayim* — from one end of the heaven to the other. *Ata sho'el mimiktzeh hashamayim v'ad ketzeh hashamayim* — you may ask about everything within that span, *ve'ee ata sho'el mah l'ma'alah mah l'matah mah lifnim mah l'achor* — but you may not ask what is above the heavens, below the earth, before creation, or after the end. These questions — what lies outside the known universe, what preceded creation, what follows its end — are inadmissible. The analogy to modern cosmology is apt: the question of what lies "outside" curved, finite space is not an empirically admissible question, and the *gemara* takes a structurally parallel position with respect to theological inquiry.

### Adam Size Midrash

The *gemara* notes that once we have established the verse *l'min hayom asher bara Elokim adam al ha'aretz u'lemiktzeh hashamayim* as the source for the legitimate spatial boundaries of inquiry, the temporal verse — which limits questions to starting from the day of creation — might seem redundant. The *gemara* responds that the second verse carries an independent teaching, attributed to Rabbi Elazar: *adam harishon min ha'aretz ad larakia* — the first human being was of immense stature, spanning from the earth to the heavens. The verse is read as: "God created man *on the earth* [and he reached] *to the edge of the heavens*."

*V'kevan she'sarach heniach Hakadosh Baruch Hu yado alav u'mi'ato* — once *Adam* sinned with the *Etz HaDa'at*, God placed His hand upon him and diminished him. The verse from Psalms is cited: *achor vakedem tzartani* — front and back You have formed me — and *vatashet alai kapecha* — and You placed Your hand upon me. The reading: there was an original, vast form, and after the sin a diminished one, with the divine hand as the instrument of that reduction. This is clearly capable of being understood as a metaphor for the greatness of the original human potential and its curtailment through sin.

### Alternative Reading

*Amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav* — Rav Yehuda further reports in the name of Rav: *adam harishon misof ha'olam v'ad sofo haya* — Adam did not merely span from earth to heaven vertically; laid horizontally, he would have stretched from one edge of the world to the other. The same verse is cited: *l'min hayom asher bara Elokim adam al ha'aretz u'lemiktzeh hashamayim v'ad ketzeh hashamayim* — from when God created man on the earth, from one edge of the heavens to the other. Again, once he sinned, *heniach Hakadosh Baruch Hu yado alav u'mi'ato*, God placed His hand on him and diminished him, *vatashet alai kapecha*.

This raises an apparent contradiction: one tradition says Adam spanned from earth to heaven (vertical), and the other says from one edge of the world to the other (horizontal). The *gemara* resolves: *idi v'eidi chad shiura hu* — these describe the same magnitude. The distance from the earth to the heavens is equal to the distance from one edge of the heavens to the other. There is no contradiction; both statements describe the same extraordinary original stature of the first human being.
