# Chagigah 13

## Heavens & Angels

### Ma'on & Night Singing

The Gemara's discussion of the seven heavens continues into 13b, where we arrive at *ma'on*, the fifth level in the ascending hierarchy of heavens. Just as the previous heaven, *zevul*, was identified as the place where the angel Michael offers *korbanos* in a celestial temple — drawing on verses from the *nevi'im* that associate *zevul* both with Solomon's *Beis HaMikdash* and with God's dwelling on high — we now ascend to *ma'on*.

*Ma'on shebo kito shel malachei hashareis she'omros shira balailah, vachashos bayom mipnei kevodan shel Yisrael.* Ma'on is where companies of ministering angels sing *shira* to God — but only at night. During the day, they are silent, in deference to the honor of the Jewish people, so that Israel may offer its own song and recite *Kaddish*. This, the Gemara explains, is the meaning of the verse: *yomam yitzaveh Hashem chasdo uvalailah shiro imi* — in the day God commands His kindness (allowing Israel to sing), while at night, His song is with Him (offered by the angels). It is worth noting that while the Gemara asserts the angels' song takes place specifically in *ma'on*, the source proving that *ma'on* is a heaven is the verse *hashkifa mima'on kodshecha min hashamayim* — "look down from your holy abode, from the heavens" — which identifies *ma'on* with the heavens, though precisely why the angelic singing is located there rather than elsewhere is asserted rather than derived from a verse.

### Torah Study at Night

Before returning to the main enumeration, the Gemara inserts a teaching of Reish Lakish. *Kol ha'osek baTorah balailah, Hakadosh Baruch Hu moshech alav chut shel chesed bayom* — whoever studies Torah at night, God draws upon him a thread of kindness during the day. The proof-text is the same verse: *yomam yitzaveh Hashem chasdo* — why? *Uvalailah shiro imi* — because his Torah was God's song in the nighttime. One must appreciate this teaching in its original context, when there was no artificial light and nighttime was simply when people slept. A person who sacrificed sleep to study Torah was going to exceptional lengths, and the deliberate use of one's discretionary hours reveals the true ordering of one's priorities. There is also a striking theological dimension here: Torah itself is called *shira*, song — a point that Rav Soloveitchik elaborated at length in his discussions of the relationship between *Torah* and *tefillah* as modes of connecting to God.

A second version of the teaching (*ika d'amri*) widens the frame: *kol ha'osek baTorah ba'olam hazeh* — anyone who studies Torah in this world, which is analogous to night, God extends upon him a thread of kindness in the world to come, which is analogous to day. Here the *olam hazeh* / *olam haba* parallel maps onto the night/day imagery of the verse.

The Gemara then adds a related teaching from Rav Levi: *kol haposek midivrei Torah ve'osek bedivrei sicha* — whoever interrupts his Torah to engage in idle conversation, *ma'achilin oso gachalei retamim*, he is fed the burning coals of the broom tree — a particularly unpleasant image — as derived from the verse describing those who eat the roots of the broom tree as their bread. The Gemara then returns to the question of how we know *ma'on* is called *shamayim*, resolving it from the verse cited above. The preceding digression about learning at night, it turns out, was prompted by the verse that also proves the identity of *ma'on*.

### Machon & Weather

The next heaven is *machon*. *Shebo otzaros shel sheleg ve'otzaros shel barad* — this is where God maintains storehouses of snow and hail. Beyond these, *machon* contains *aliyos telalim ra'im* — attics of destructive rains — as well as storehouses of *agalim* (destructive rain, per Rashi) and violent whirlwinds, and a cave filled with smoke, whose doors are made of fire. All the destructive meteorological forces in the world originate here.

The proof that God maintains such a storehouse is derived from the verse *yiftach Hashem lecha es otzaro hatov* — "God shall open for you His good storehouse" — which implies by contrast that there is also a bad storehouse, and that is *machon*. The connection of the word *machon* to the heavens is established from the verse *ve'ata sishma hashamayim machon shivtecha* — "You shall hear from the heavens, the established place of Your dwelling." Once again, while the identification of *machon* with the heavens is established textually, the precise assignment of these meteorological storehouses to *machon* specifically is asserted rather than derived.

### David's Prayer

An important challenge presents itself: the Gemara asks, *hani berakia isnehu* — are these things really in the heaven? The verse in Tehillim says *halelu es Hashem min ha'aretz* — praise God from the land — and then lists sea monsters, the depths, fire, hail, snow, smoke, and whirlwinds all as praising from *ha'aretz*, the earth. So these forces are apparently on earth, not in the heavens.

Rav Yehuda citing Rav resolves the contradiction: *David bikesh aleihem rachamim vehoridan la'aretz* — David prayed for compassion on these things and brought them down from heaven to earth. David argued before God: *lo Eil chafetz resha ata, lo yigurcha ra* — You are not a God who desires evil, and evil cannot dwell with You. Therefore, these destructive forces should not remain in the heavens with God; they belong below. One might note that this prayer seems to be primarily for God's honor rather than for human benefit — though perhaps the logic is that once these forces are naturalized into the earth as ordinary meteorological phenomena, they are less directly attributable to divine displeasure and may be less spiritually weighty in their destructiveness.

### Aravot Heaven

We now arrive at *aravot*, the highest of the heavens — the heaven in which, as this week's *parsha* states, God rides: *solu larochev ba'aravot beka shemo*. The identification of *aravot* with *shamayim* is established through a *gezeirah shavah*: the same word *rochev* (to ride) appears both in *solu larochev ba'aravot* and in *rochev shamayim be'ezrecha*, linking *aravot* to *shamayim*.

What is found in *aravot*? The Gemara lists: *tzedek, mishpat, utzedaka* — justice, law, and righteousness; *ginzei chayim, ginzei shalom, ginzei bracha* — storehouses of life, peace, and blessing; *nishmatotan shel tzadikim* — the souls of the righteous; *ruach veruchos veneshamot she'atid lehibarot* — winds, spirits, and future souls yet to be created; and finally *tal she'atid Hakadosh Baruch Hu lehachayos bo meitim* — the dew God will use to resurrect the dead at the time of *techiyas hameitim*. Each of these is supported by a proof-text: righteousness and justice are derived from *tzedek umishpat machon kisse'echa* (the word *machon* here refers to *aravot*, since all of these are near God's throne), righteousness from God clothing Himself like armor, the storehouses of blessing from *yissa bracha me'et Hashem*, the souls of the righteous from the verse *vehayetah nefesh adoni tzerurah bitzror hachayim et Hashem Elokecha*, and the future souls from *ki ruach milfanai ya'atof uneshamot ani asiti*.

In *aravot* are also found the *ofanim*, *serafim*, *chayos hakodesh*, *malachei hasharet*, and the *kisei hakavod* — the divine throne itself. God, the living and exalted King, dwells above them all: *melech el chai veram venissa shochein aleihem*. A subtle point: the text says *me'aleihem*, above them — already introducing a separation between God and even the highest of celestial beings.

It is worth pausing to observe the structure of the seven heavens as a whole. The destructive meteorological forces — hail, snow, destructive winds — are stored immediately below the highest heaven. Everything malevolent is close to God but just one level below. This seems to be the Gemara's way of wrestling with the problem of evil: everything ultimately comes from God, yet the Gemara seeks to create some distance. David's prayer then pushes evil even further away, down to the earth. The contrast between the heaven of destructive forces and the heaven of righteousness, peace, life, and the souls of the righteous, all immediately in God's presence, is stark and deliberate.

### God's Separation

Yet if God dwells in *aravot* together with the angels, the souls of the righteous, the *kisei hakavod*, and all these things, a problem arises: God is described in other verses as surrounded by darkness. *Vehoshech ve'anan ve'arafel mekifin oto* — darkness and cloud and thick cloud surround Him. Yet another verse says *hu gale amikta umsatarta yada mah bachashocha venehora imei* — God knows what is in the darkness, and light is with Him. Does darkness or light attend God?

*Lo kashya* — no contradiction. *Ha bevivtei gavai, ha bevivtei barai* — one refers to the inner chamber, the other to the outer. God Himself is in an inner room where there is light; the darkness that surrounds God is in the outer room. This is the sense of *betei barai* and *betei gavai* — inner and outer chambers. Even within *aravot*, God's own essential presence is screened off behind darkness from everything else. The angels, the throne, the souls of the righteous — all of these occupy, as it were, the outer chamber, while God's innermost essence remains inaccessible, separated by cloud and darkness.

This inner/outer structure is evocative of the Temple: the *azarah* with its blood and animal offerings, then the *heichal* kept perpetually lit, and then the *kodesh hakodashim* — always dark except for the brief entrance of the *kohen gadol* on Yom Kippur. The same logic of nested sanctity and concealment applies in the heavenly realm. The Gemara seems deeply invested in maintaining the idea that evil is distant from God and that God's own essence remains forever hidden and separate.

## Limits of Knowledge

### Highest Rakia

Rav Acha bar Yaakov introduces a further remark: *od rakia echad yesh lema'alah merashei hachayos* — there is yet another *rakia* above the heads of the heavenly *chayos*. The verse in Yechezkel states *udemut al rashei hachaya rakia ke'ein hakerach hanora* — and above the heads of the heavenly angels is a *rakia* like awesome frost. This highest *rakia* is where God Himself dwells, separate even from the highest angels. The celestial beings described throughout the preceding passage — the *ofanim*, *serafim*, *chayos hakodesh* — are therefore not in God's immediate presence; there is still another *rakia* above them.

### Permitted Knowledge

This leads directly to the limits of permitted knowledge. *Ad kan yesh lecha reshut ledaber* — until this point, you may speak and discuss the contents of the various heavens. *Mikan va'eilach, ein lecha reshut ledaber* — from here on, you may not discuss what is beyond. The source for this boundary is a citation from the book of Ben Sira, which, while belonging to the *sefarim chitzoniyim*, always held a special place for *Chazal*: *bemufla mimcha al tidrosh, uvemechuseh mimcha al tachkor, bemah she'hursheita hitbonen, ein lecha esek benistarot* — do not investigate that which is beyond you, do not probe what is hidden, contemplate only what you have been given permission to understand, and do not involve yourself with hidden matters.

This passage distills the essential principle of our *mishnah* limiting the exploration of esoteric knowledge. It also resonates with a broader philosophical tradition. The Rambam, in his approach to divine attributes, denied not only anthropomorphisms but any positive descriptive language applied to God, on the grounds that all such language, drawn from human experience, fundamentally diminishes and misrepresents the divine. The Kabbalistic tradition, which employs vivid and dynamic imagery for God, addresses this by positing the *Ein Sof* — the infinite, about which nothing whatsoever can be said — and then describing only the *sefirot*, which are not the essence of God but emanations. In precisely this way, the Gemara here presents a highest *rakia* about which nothing can be said, and lower levels which may be discussed. The parallel is genuine and instructive.

## Nevuchadnezzar & Distance

### Heavenly Response

A *baraita* is now introduced, presented by Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, which continues the theme of the heavens but approaches it from a different direction — the immeasurable distance between humanity and God. *Mah teshuvah heishivatu bat kol le'oto rasha* — what answer did the *bat kol* give to that wicked man, namely Nevuchadnetzar, *besha'ah she'amar*, when he declared *eleh bamotei av adameh le'elyon* — I will ascend upon the high clouds and be like the Most High?

The *bat kol* responded: *rasha ben rasha* — wicked person, son of a wicked person. Tosafos notes that the phrase *ben beno shel Nimrod harasha* does not mean literal biological descent but spiritual lineage: Nevuchadnetzar was the spiritual grandson of Nimrod, *she'himrid kol ha'olam kulo alav bemalchuso* — who incited all of humanity to rebel against God. Nimrod's name, derived from the word *mered* (rebellion), and his role in the *migdal Bavel* as imagined by the Midrashic tradition, made him the paradigmatic figure of human arrogance against the divine. And here is Nevuchadnetzar standing in that tradition.

### Journey to God

But the *bat kol*'s answer is not merely an insult — it is a demonstration of the profound absurdity of Nevuchadnetzar's claim. *Kamma shenosav shel adam* — how long does a human being live? *Shivim shana* — seventy years. *Ve'im bigevuros shemonim shana* — eighty at most.

Now consider the journey. *Min ha'aretz ad ha-rakia* — from the earth to the first heaven is a journey of 500 years. *Ve'ovyo shel rakia* — the thickness of that first heaven is another 500 years. And then *bein kol rakia verakia* — between each successive heaven is another 500 years of travel, and each heaven is 500 years thick. With seven heavens, one is already looking at thousands of years simply to traverse them.

But that brings you only to the top of the seventh heaven. *Lema'alah me-hen*, above them, are the *Chayos HaKodesh*, the heavenly beasts. And here the distances become almost incomprehensible. *Raglei hachayos keneged kulam* — the feet of the heavenly beasts are equal in length to all that preceded. *Arkuv hachayos keneged kulam* — the ankles are equal to everything before that. The calves, *shokei hachayos*, equal to everything preceding; the knees, *rekhuvei hachayos*, equal to everything preceding; the thighs, *yarchei hachayos*, equal again; the body, *gufei hachayos*; the necks, *tzavarei hachayos*; the heads, *rashei hachayos*; and finally the horns, *karnei hachayos* — each segment equal to everything that came before it, accumulating into distances that strain any conception. And even then, one has not reached God — above the heavenly beasts stands the *kisei hakavod*, whose legs alone equal everything that preceded, and the throne itself equals all that came before. Only then, *melech el ram chai vekayam veram venissa shochein adei marom* — does one arrive at God.

So: *ve'ata amarta e'eleh al bamtei av adameh le'elyon* — and you said you would rise up on a cloud and be like the Most High? *Ach el sheol tured el yarketei vor* — no, you will descend to the lowest pit.

The passage is a vivid statement not merely of physical distance but of the absolute transcendence of God over any human claim to power or greatness.

Tosafos notes a relevant detail concerning the *kedushah* of Yitzchak HaKalir, one of the earliest *paytanim*, which includes the line *ve'hachayos asher hinam meruba'os bakisei, kaf regel chamesh me'ot vechamesh esrei* — the foot of a heavenly beast is 500 and 15. This seems inconsistent with the Gemara's reckoning. Some emend the text and remove the letter *vav*, reading it as 500 times 15, which would fit: seven heavens plus eight airspaces (including the space from the top of the seventh heaven to the *chayos*) equals 15 intervals, each 500 years — hence 500 times 15. Tosafos notes, however, that this emendation is unnecessary, because the Kalir did not base his *piyut* on the Bavli but on the Yerushalmi, which does give the measure of the foot of the heavenly beast as 500 and 15 *amos*. As Tosafos observes, in a number of places the Kalir followed the Yerushalmi rather than the Bavli — a pattern consistent with the *minhag* of Eretz Yisrael, from which Ashkenazic liturgical tradition descends through Italy. Tosafos goes further and claims that the Kalir was himself a *tanna* — specifically Rabbi Elazar beRabbi Shimon — which is historically untenable, but reflects the enormous reverence in which he was held. The Ashkenazic tradition of *piyut* is rooted in the practice of Eretz Yisrael, and it is therefore natural that its greatest poet should reflect the Yerushalmi tradition.

## Teaching Secrets

### Ma'aseh Merkavah Rules

The Gemara now transitions to the discussion of who may be taught these esoteric matters. The *mishnah* has already stated that *ma'aseh merkavah* may not be taught even to a single individual unless he is a sage who understands on his own. A *baraita* taught by Rabbi Chiya adds: *aval mosrin lo rashei perakim* — nevertheless, one may transmit to such a person the chapter headings, the broad outlines, even if he has not yet fully demonstrated independent mastery.

Rabbi Zeira goes further in restriction: *ein mosrin rashei perakim ela le'av beis din* — even the chapter headings may only be transmitted to the head of a *beis din*, someone of exceptional stature. *Ulechol mi shelibo do'eg bekirbo* — and to one whose heart is anxious within him. This second criterion is puzzling at first glance. Why should anxiety of heart qualify one to receive esoteric knowledge?

There are at least two ways to understand it. The simpler reading, reflected in the Steinsaltz commentary, is that *libo do'eg bekirbo* describes someone who is not inclined to frivolity, who has the appropriate *yiras shamayim* and genuine concern — perhaps concern about his sins and desire for *teshuvah* — such that he will not misuse what he learns. A second reading, which the lecturer suggests as a possibility, is more complex: the person *libo do'eg bekirbo* is someone already deeply troubled theologically, already wrestling with questions, already in danger of being lost. For such a person, engaging with esoteric matters is not more dangerous — it may be necessary. Withholding answers from someone who is urgently questioning may be worse than the risk of exposing them to difficult material. This connects to a broader debate: the Ra'avad famously criticized the Rambam for raising the question of divine foreknowledge and free will in the *Mishneh Torah* without providing a satisfying resolution, arguing that it was better to say nothing and leave people's *emunah* undisturbed. The Rambam's position implies that for those already troubled, engagement is necessary. The phrase *mi shelibo do'eg bekirbo* may encode that same tension.

### Five Qualities

Rabbi Ami further specifies: *ein mosrin sitrei Torah ela lemi sheyeish bo chamishah devarim* — the hidden matters of Torah may only be transmitted to one who possesses five qualities. These are derived from a verse in Yeshayahu: *sar chamishim, unisso panim, ve'yoetz, vechacham charashim, unevon lachash* — a leader of fifty, one of distinguished bearing, a counselor, one wise in hidden matters, and one who understands that which is whispered.

Rashi clarifies that *sitrei Torah* here encompasses not only *ma'aseh merkavah* but also *Sefer Yetzirah* — attributed by tradition to Adam Harishon and said to contain the knowledge by which a *golem* can be created — and *ma'aseh bereishis* as well. The category of esoteric Torah is thus broader than *ma'aseh merkavah* alone.

### Non-Jews & Torah

Rabbi Ami adds a further ruling: *ein mosrin divrei Torah le'akum* — one may not transmit Torah to non-Jews at all, setting aside entirely the question of *sitrei Torah*. The verse cited is *lo asah chein lechol goy umishpatim bal yeda'um* — He did not do this for any other nation, and His laws He did not make known to them. The Torah was given specifically to Israel, and its transmission to non-Jews is prohibited. The Gemara elsewhere states even more sharply that a non-Jew who studies Torah is *chayav misah*.

### Rabbi Elazar

Rabbi Yochanan once turned to Rabbi Elazar and said: *ta, amarkha bema'aseh merkavah* — come, let me teach you *ma'aseh merkavah*. It is a remarkable invitation. Rabbi Elazar declined, saying he was not yet old enough. When he finally reached the appropriate age, Rabbi Yochanan had already passed away, and the opportunity was lost. Rav Assi then offered to teach him *ma'aseh merkavah* in Rabbi Yochanan's stead, and Rabbi Elazar replied: *i zakai gemirna me-Rabbi Yochanan rabach* — had I merited, I would have learned it from Rabbi Yochanan your teacher. Since I did not merit that, I will not learn it from you. One may wonder whether Rabbi Elazar genuinely felt unworthy of this knowledge, or whether he simply did not wish to learn *ma'aseh merkavah* at all.

### Rav Yosef Exchange

Rav Yosef had studied *ma'aseh merkavah*, while the elders of Pumbedita had studied *ma'aseh bereishis*. It is worth noting the difference in verbs: the Gemara says Rav Yosef *gemir* — a term associated with *gemara*, meaning deep analytical study — while the elders of Pumbedita *tannei*, a term associated with *mishnah*, indicating that they held the traditions as a repository of received knowledge, possibly *beraisos*, as Rashi suggests. This distinction may indicate the different levels of engagement required by each discipline.

The elders of Pumbedita said to Rav Yosef: *ligmaran mar ma'aseh merkavah* — teach us *ma'aseh merkavah*. He responded: *agmruni ma'aseh bereishis* — first teach me your *ma'aseh bereishis*. After they did so, they returned and asked again: now teach us *ma'aseh merkavah*. Rav Yosef replied with the verse *devash vechalav tachat leshonecha* — honey and milk under your tongue: *devarim hametukim midvash vechalav yehei tachat leshonecha* — things sweeter than honey and milk must be kept under your tongue. He had taken their *ma'aseh bereishis* but would not share his *ma'aseh merkavah*. Rabbi Abbahu cited an alternative verse: *devarim she-hein kivshono shel olam, yehei tachat levushecha* — the hidden things of the world, keep them close beneath your garment.

### Yechezkel Boundaries

The elders then revealed to Rav Yosef that they were not entirely without *ma'aseh merkavah* — they had already learned it up to the verse *vayomer elai ben Adam* in the second chapter of Yechezkel. Rav Yosef responded: *hein hein ma'aseh merkavah* — that is itself *ma'aseh merkavah*; after Yechezkel 2 it is no longer *ma'aseh merkavah*. So in effect, they already possessed what they needed.

The Gemara then presses: precisely until where does *ma'aseh merkavah* extend? Rabbi states: *ad va'era batra* — until the second *va'era*, meaning until the very opening of the vision: *va'era, vehinei ruach se'arah ba'ah min hatzafon, anan gadol ve'esh mitlakachas, venogah lo saviv, umitochah ke'ein hachashmal mitoch ha'esh* — and I saw, and behold a whirlwind coming from the north, a great cloud with flashing fire, and a glow surrounding it, and from its midst like the *chashmal* from within the fire. Rashi explains that *ad va'era* means: starting from *va'era* onwards is where the actual *ma'aseh merkavah* begins.

But there is further division within the first chapter. Tosafos identifies the critical boundary as the *chashmal* — it is specifically the *chashmal* that marks the shift to the most restricted material. One view holds that until the *va'era* one may teach openly; from there one teaches only *rashei perakim*, chapter headings. Another view (*ika d'amri*) is more restrictive: until *va'era* one may teach chapter headings; from the *va'era* on, and specifically once the *chashmal* enters, one may teach only *im hu chacham mevin mida'ato* — if the student is wise enough to understand independently. The question is whether the division of difficulty is one-tiered or two-tiered within the first chapter.

### Chananya Preserves

The mention of Yechezkel's text prompts an aside. Rav Yehuda states: *beram zachor oto ha'ish letov, veChannanaya ben Chizkiya shemo* — that man should be remembered for good, and his name was Chananya ben Chizkiya. *Ilmalei hu, nignaz sefer Yechezkel* — were it not for him, the book of Yechezkel would have been hidden away entirely. Two things made Yechezkel dangerous: the esoteric vision of the divine chariot, and the fact that the later chapters — dealing with the laws of the *mikdash* and the *kohanim* — appear to contradict verses in the Torah. *She'hayu devarav sotrim divrei Torah* — its words seemed to contradict the Torah. Chananya ben Chizkiya brought up 300 flasks of oil, ensconced himself in his attic, and worked through the contradictions until he had reconciled them all. Rather than suppressing the book, he preserved it within the canon by doing the hard intellectual work of harmonization.

### Child & Fire

The Gemara then reports: *ma'aseh betinok echad she'haya korei beveit rabbo besefer Yechezkel* — a child was reading the book of Yechezkel in his teacher's house. *Vehaya mevin bachashmal* — and this child was brilliant enough to understand the secrets of the *chashmal*. *Veyatza esh mechashmal vesarafathu* — and fire came out of the *chashmal* and burned him. This incident led to renewed calls to suppress the book of Yechezkel entirely.

Chananya ben Chizkiya replied: *im zeh chacham, hakol chachamim* — if this child was wise enough to grasp it at such a young age, then everyone is wise, and the book would need to be hidden from everyone. But that cannot be the right conclusion. The child's case was exceptional precisely because such depth of understanding at so young an age is extraordinarily rare. Normally, either a person lacks the understanding to grasp the *chashmal*, or — if they possess that understanding — they are of the age and maturity to handle it safely. The Gemara confirms this: *shani yanuka delav mati zimnei* — the child's case is exceptional because he had not yet reached his proper time. The knowledge itself, in the hands of one who is both wise and of appropriate age, is not inherently destructive.

## Chashmal

### Chashmal Definition

We now turn to the substance of what the Gemara is willing to say about the *chashmal* itself, even as it acknowledges that this is the most restricted portion of *ma'aseh merkavah*. Rav Yehuda states at the top of 13b: *chayos esh memalelot* — the *chashmal* is an acronym: *chet-shin-mem-lamed*, standing for fiery beasts (*chayos esh*) that speak to one another (*memalelot*). Rashi adds that the fire emerges from their speech.

### Beasts' Speech

A *baraita* elaborates: *itim chashot, itim memalelot* — sometimes these fiery beasts are silent, and sometimes they speak. *Besha'ah shehadibbur yotzei mipi Hakadosh Baruch Hu, chashot* — when speech issues from God, the beasts fall silent. *Uvesha'ah she'ein hadibbur yotzei mipi Hakadosh Baruch Hu, memalelot* — when God is not speaking, the beasts themselves speak. There is something deeply evocative about this — a live, crackling, electric quality to the heavenly *chayos*, oscillating between silence before God and their own fiery speech. It is no coincidence that *chashmal* became the modern Hebrew word for electricity.

### Beasts Running

The verse in Yechezkel describes *vehachayos ratzo vashov kemarei habazak* — the beasts running back and forth like the appearance of lightning. Rav Yehuda explains *ratzo vashov*: *ke'or hayotzei mipi hakivshan* — like the fire that comes out of the mouth of a furnace, flickering and moving rapidly in and out. Rav Yossi bar Chanina interprets *kemarei habazak* — like the appearance of lightning: *ke'or hayotzei mibein hacharsim* — like the light that emerges from between the pieces of pottery. Rashi describes the context: in the smelting of gold, a pottery floor with holes is placed above the fire, and the fire flashes in and out through those openings. This image captures the rapid, intermittent, and intensely alive quality of the heavenly beasts' movement.

## Divine Chariot Vision

### Whirlwind North

The vision of Yechezkel opens: *va'era, vehinei ruach se'arah ba'ah min hatzafon, anan gadol ve'esh mitlakachas* — and I saw a whirlwind coming from the north, a great cloud with flashing fire. Rashi notes that *tzafon*, the north, signifies Bavel — *mitzafon tipatach hara'ah*, evil opens from the north. The question is therefore natural: what was God's chariot doing going toward Bavel?

Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains: *she'halach lichbosh et kol ha'olam kulo tachat Nevuchadnetzar harasha* — the divine chariot went to empower Nevuchadnetzar to conquer the entire world. The *why* follows: *shelo yomru umot ha'olam, beyad umah shefelah masar Hakadosh Baruch Hu et banav* — lest the nations say that God handed over His people to a lowly and insignificant nation. The conquest of Israel was of such cosmic significance that it could only be carried out by the world's greatest conqueror, and for that to happen, divine power went to Bavel to empower Nevuchadnetzar.

### God's Reluctance

Yet this raised its own theological discomfort. *Amar Hakadosh Baruch Hu: mi garam li she'e'eseh shamash le'ovdei pesilim?* — God said: what caused Me to become an attendant to idol worshippers? What forced My divine chariot to go to Bavel and serve, in effect, the purposes of idol worship? *Avonoteihem shel Yisrael hein garmu li* — it was the sins of Israel that brought Me to this.

### Sandalphon Angel

The vision continues: *va'era el hachayos, vehinei ofan echad ba'aretz etzel hachayos* — and I saw by the heavenly beasts, and behold, one *ofan* was on the earth beside the beasts. Rav Elazar interprets: this *ofan* is an angel who stands on the earth, yet *rosho magia etzel hachayos* — his head reaches all the way up to the heavenly *chayos*. Given the distances we have already traversed — hundreds of thousands of years of travel — this angel spans an incomprehensible height. A *baraita* names him: *Sandalphon shemo* — his name is Sandalphon. *Hagavo'ah mechaveiro mahalach chamesh me'ot shanah* — he is 500 years taller than all the other angels. *Ve'omed achorei hamerkavah* — he stands behind God's chariot.

### Crown-Bearing

*Vekosher ketarim lekono* — and Sandalphon weaves crowns for his Master. The Gemara pauses at this: *eini?* — is this really so? Is someone present directly with God, placing a crown on God's head? The answer draws on the verse *baruch kevod Hashem mimkomo* — blessed is the honor of God from His place. God's place is distinct from any other place; wherever God is, He is praised, but no one occupies God's place. How then does Sandalphon's crown reach God? *De'amar shem atga, ve'azal veyativ beriesha* — he inscribes God's name on the crown, and the crown rises on its own to the highest heaven and comes to rest on God's head. Sandalphon does not place the crown directly; the crown ascends by itself.

## Yechezkel vs Yeshayahu

### Graphic vs Simple

Rava states: *kol she'ra'ah Yechezkel ra'ah Yeshayahu* — everything that Yechezkel saw, Yeshayahu also saw. Both prophets received visions of the divine chariot. Yet Yeshayahu's account is brief and lacks the elaborate physical description of Yechezkel's vision. Why?

*Lemah Yechezkel domeh? Leven kfar she'ra'ah et hamelech* — to what can Yechezkel be compared? To a villager who caught sight of the king. The villager is overwhelmed: he describes the crown, the robe, the palace, the courtyard, every detail in breathless excitement, because the experience was extraordinary and unprecedented. *Ulemah Yeshayahu domeh? Leven krach she'ra'ah et hamelech* — and to what can Yeshayahu be compared? To a city-dweller who saw the king. Someone accustomed to royal proximity has little to say about it; it is unremarkable. Hence Yeshayahu's restrained account.

This is the *pshat* of the *parable*, which suggests that Yeshayahu was simply closer to God, more habituated to prophetic visions, and therefore did not need to elaborate. Rashi, however, takes the parable very literally: Yechezkel was the son of commoners, while Yeshayahu was of aristocratic lineage, related to royalty. Having been exposed to royal grandeur in his earthly life, Yeshayahu had less need to describe in detail what he encountered in his prophetic vision.

Tosafos offers a different angle: Yechezkel saw his vision *bechutz la'aretz*, in exile in Bavel, while Yeshayahu saw his in *Eretz Yisrael*. For Yechezkel, the very occurrence of such a vision outside the Land was astonishing — and also, no one in Bavel would believe him. Just as the villager who has seen the king must describe every detail to convince skeptical listeners that he was truly in the royal presence, so Yechezkel had to give exhaustive description precisely because his audience would be unlikely to believe that such a prophetic vision had occurred in *chutz la'aretz*.

### Four Faces

The divine chariot's *chayos* had four faces, and the verse in Yechezkel catalogues them: *pnei adam upnei aryeh el hayamin le'arba'tam upnei shor mehasmol le'arba'tam* — the face of a human and the face of a lion on the right, the face of an ox on the left, and the face of an eagle. The significance of these four creatures is drawn out by Reish Lakish: *shira lemi shemitga'eh al hage'im* — it is a song to the One who is exalted above all the proud. *Melech shebachayos* — who is king among wild beasts? The lion. *Melech shebabehemos* — who is king among domesticated animals? The ox. *Melech sheba'ofos* — who is king among birds? The eagle (or vulture). *Ve'adam mitga'eh aleihem* — and the human being towers over all of them. *VeHakadosh Baruch Hu mitga'eh al kulan ve'al kol ha'olam kulo* — and God is exalted above all of them and above the entire world. Therefore God's chariot bears the faces of the four kings of creation — lion, ox, eagle, and human — because God is the King of kings over them all.

### Ox to Cherub

Yet a second verse in Yechezkel replaces the face of the ox with a *keruv*, a cherub. The ox is simply missing: *de'ishtavar lei chushbna* — it is not counted. How did this come to be?

*Yechezkel bikesh alav rachamim vehafacho likeruv* — Yechezkel prayed over the face of the ox and had it transformed into a cherub. He said before God: *Ribbono Shel Olam, kateigor na'aseh saneigor?* — should the accuser become the defender? The ox evokes the *cheit ha'eigel*, the sin of the golden calf. That sin should not be represented on God's own divine throne, serving as a constant reminder before God of Israel's greatest failure. Yechezkel prayed that the ox be replaced, and it was transformed into a *keruv*. This is a remarkable notion: the very appearance of the divine throne, the most transcendent object in existence, was altered by the prayer of a human being. And yet this parallels what we saw with David, whose prayer brought destructive forces down from the heavens to the earth. The Gemara presents a theology in which divine transcendence and human efficacy are not opposites — the human being's prayer can transform the very face of the heavenly throne.

### Cherub Meaning

*Mai keruv?* — what does *keruv* mean? Rabbi Abbahu states: *k'ravya* — like a child. *Sheken beVavel korin l'yanuka ravya* — for in Babylonia, they called a child *ravya*. A *keruv* has a child-like face, which is how we consistently imagine the cherubim: young, innocent, child-like countenances. This is the origin of the well-known image.

Rav Pappa raises a question to Abaye: another verse in Yechezkel lists the faces as *pnei hakeruv, pnei adam, pnei aryeh, pnei nesher* — cherub, human, lion, eagle. If a *keruv* is a child-like human face, then the *keruv* and the *adam* are essentially the same thing, and you still have only three distinct creatures. The answer: *apei ravrevei ve'apei zutrei* — there is an adult face and a young face. The face of the *adam* and the face of the *keruv* are both human, but one is the face of a grown person and the other is the face of a child — the two human faces that replaced the single face of the ox after Yechezkel's prayer.

---

---

# Chagigah 14

## Four Faces & Wings

### Kerub vs. Human Face

The daf opens in the middle of 13b, where the Gemara has been addressing apparent contradictions in the prophetic visions of the Divine throne. In Yechezkel's vision, the faces surrounding the throne include a lion, an eagle, an ox, and a human face. Yet in another passage within Yechezkel himself, the ox is replaced by a *keruv* — a cherub — which the Gemara explains represents the face of an infant. The change occurred, the Gemara relates, because Yechezkel prayed that the image of the ox be removed from the heavenly throne, lest it serve as a reminder of the *ma'aseh egel*, the sin of the Golden Calf. This is a striking parallel to an earlier passage where David HaMelech prays to affect what exists in the heavenly realm — a profound tension between God's utter transcendence and the reality that human prayer can alter the very appearance of things above.

Rav Pappa raises an objection to Abaye: if a *keruv* is simply an infant's face, then the verse in Yechezkel that lists both *pnei ha-keruv* and *pnei adam* — the face of a cherub and the face of a human — presents a redundancy. Are they not both human faces? The Gemara resolves this: *appei ravrivi ve-appei zutrei* — there is a large face and a small face. One is the face of an adult and one is the face of a child. These become significant technical terms in *Kabbalah* as well.

### Six vs. Four Wings

The Gemara turns from the faces of the throne to the wings of the heavenly angels, noting an apparent contradiction between two prophetic visions. Yeshayahu describes each angel with *shesh knafayim*, six wings, while Yechezkel describes the *chayot* as having four wings each. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya* — when the *Beis HaMikdash* was standing, the angels had six wings; when it was not standing, they had four. Yechezkel received his vision in exile, yet the *Gra* notes that this was anticipatory — the destruction was coming and the vision already reflected what was about to occur.

The Gemara then states, *kivyakhol nismatu kanfei ha-chayot* — it is as if the wings of the heavenly *chayot* were diminished by the destruction of the Temple. Rashi clarifies that the word *kivyakhol* here does not suggest this did not actually happen; it did happen. Rather, *kivyakhol* is a rhetorical hedge because one speaks cautiously about any lack or diminishment being attributed to things related to God. Importantly, one student noted that *kivyakhol* is normally used in relation to God Himself, and yet here the Gemara deploys it in the context of angels — a remarkable extension of the term.

This discussion reflects the Gemara's broader thematic concern: on the one hand, God is supremely transcendent — we read earlier about the vast distances separating the heavenly realms — but on the other hand, what transpires below directly shapes what transpires above, for good and for ill.

### Lost Wings Debate

The Gemara now asks: *hai minaihu imtu?* — which two of the original six wings were lost? Two opinions are presented.

The first is that of Rav Chananel in the name of Rav: the wings that were lost are *otan she-omrot shirah ba-hen*, those with which the angels would sing to God. The verse in Yeshayahu says *u-vish-tayim ye'ofef*, with two they would fly, and separately describes the angels calling out *kadosh kadosh kadosh* to one another. The verb *ye'ofef*, to fly or flutter, connects through wordplay to another verse, *hat'if einecha bo ve-einenu* — if you flutter your eyes at it, it will be gone. So these are the singing/flying wings that have disappeared. The rationale is entirely fitting: with the *Beis HaMikdash* destroyed, the *shira* sung below has been silenced, and correspondingly, the *shira* above has been diminished. As Tosafot note, and as the Gemara will elaborate, there is a deep connection between the song Israel offers and the song of the angels — *vekara zeh el zeh*, one calling to another. A student raised the evocative suggestion that *vekara zeh el zeh* — one calling to the other — might refer to one wing calling to the next, which is an intriguing reading of the imagery.

The second opinion is that of the *rabbanan*: the wings that were lost are *otan shemechassot bahen ragleihem*, those used to cover the angels' legs. The proof is from Yechezkel's vision: he saw *regel yeshara*, a straight leg, meaning the legs were visible to him. If the covering wings still existed, he would only have seen the legs if the wings happened to be open at that moment. But, the Gemara continues, perhaps the legs were simply visible when the wings opened and closed — *degali ve-chazi leh*. Indeed, he also saw their faces, which the wing-of-the-face covered — does that mean those wings were gone too? No, because *bishlama appei orach ar'a legalluyei kamei rabbei* — it is entirely appropriate to uncover one's face in the presence of one's master. But *karei lav orach ar'a legalluyei kamei rabbei* — the legs, by contrast, would never be uncovered before one's master. Therefore, if Yechezkel saw the legs, it must be because those covering wings were simply gone, not merely momentarily open. The imagery is powerful: the angels are, in a sense, standing partially unclothed before God — a vivid expression of what the exile and destruction have wrought both below and above.

---

## River of Fire

### Angels from Dinur

The Gemara presents another contradiction. One verse in Daniel states that *elef alfin yishameshuney* — a thousand thousands, i.e., a million, attend to God — while a verse in Iyov states that his troops are beyond number, infinite. The Gemara resolves it: *lo kashya* — one applies when the *Beis HaMikdash* stood and one applies when it did not. The verse in Iyov was presumably when the Temple still existed; the verse in Daniel, which was written clearly after the *churban*, reflects the diminished retinue. This too is characterized as *kivyakhol she-nismatu pamalya shel ma'ala* — as if God's great celestial retinue, His *pamalya*, had become smaller.

A *braisa* is cited in the name of Rebbi, citing Abba Yosi ben Dosai: the million who attend to God is the count of a single *gdud*, a single legion. The verse in Iyov saying His legions are infinite means He has an infinite number of such legions, each containing a million.

A further *braisa* is then cited: Rabbi Yirmiyah bar Abba taught that the *elef alfin yishameshuney* — the thousands upon thousands — refers to those that emerge from the *Nehar Dinur*, the River of Fire. The word *dinur* is Aramaic for fire, and it is drawn from the very passage in Daniel that the Gemara is now expounding.

### River & the Wicked

The relevant passage in Daniel reads as follows: *chazei haveis ad di chorsavan rmiu* — I was watching until thrones were set in place; *v'Atik Yomin yesiv* — and the Ancient of Days took his seat. His garment was like white snow, the hair of His head like clean wool, *korseih shvivin dinur* — His throne was tongues of flame; *galgalohi nur dolik* — the wheels were blazing fire; *nehar dinur naged v'nafek min kodamohi* — a river of fire stretched out and came forth from His presence; *elef alfin yishameshuney v'ribo ribvan kodamohi yekumun* — thousands upon thousands attended Him, myriads of myriads stood before Him; *dina yesiv v'sifrin p'sichu* — the court sat and the books were opened. This vision in Daniel — the Ancient of Days sitting in judgment with open books — is evidently a source for the imagery of Rosh Hashanah.

So the million who attend God emerge from this *Nehar Dinur*: *nehar dinur naged v'nafek min kodamohi, elef alfin yishameshuney*. The Gemara then asks where this river itself comes from: *mizei'asan shel chayot* — from the sweat of the heavenly *chayot*. Their exertion produces this river of fire from which the angels are born.

Where does the river pour out? Rav Zutra bar Tuvya in the name of Rav: *al rosh reshaim b'Gehinnom* — it pours upon the heads of the wicked in *Gehinnom*, as the verse in Yirmiyahu says, the whirlwind of God's anger shall fall on the head of the wicked.

### Lost Generations

Rav Acha bar Yaakov offers another reading: the river pours upon *asher kumtu b'lo eis* — those that were decreed to exist but whose time did not come. The Gemara elaborates through a *braisa* in the name of Rabbi Shimon Hachasid: these are the nine hundred and seventy-four generations that were decreed to be created before the world was established but were not. The source is the verse *davar tziva l'elef dor* — God commanded His word for a thousand generations. If the Torah was to be given after a thousand generations of human history, but only twenty-six generations elapsed from Adam to *Matan Torah*, then nine hundred and seventy-four generations that were supposed to precede *Matan Torah* were never created. God saw that the world could not wait a thousand generations and accelerated the giving of the Torah.

What happened to those nine hundred and seventy-four? *Amar HaKadosh Baruch Hu veshatlan bechol dor vador* — God distributed them across all subsequent generations. *Veheinan azai panim shebedor* — these are the brazen, shameless people found in every generation. They are the residue of those who were so wicked they contributed to the urgency of giving the Torah earlier.

Tosafot is troubled by this: can God punish souls with fire when they were never created and therefore never sinned? Tosafot resolves this by saying the two opinions are really one — they were distributed into all subsequent generations, and they can only be judged for evil they actually commit once created, not for what they were decreed to be beforehand.

Rav Amram bar Yitzchak offers the positive counterpart reading: *asher kumtu* refers to *talmidei chachamim* who dedicate themselves to *divrei Torah* in this world — those who press themselves, so to speak, into Torah. For them, God will reveal secrets in the world to come, as the verse concludes: *v'nahar yutzak yesodam* — and the poured river is their *yesod*, their foundation, and also their *sod*, their secret. This river in Iyov, distinct from the *Nehar Dinur* of Daniel, is for the righteous.

### Daily Angel Creation

Shmuel said to Chiyya bar Rav — addressing him as *bar arya*, son of the lion, meaning his father was of the stature of a great scholar — come, let me tell you one of the great things your father used to teach. *Kol yoma v'yoma nivraim malachei hashareit min Nehar Dinur* — every single day, ministering angels are created from the River of Fire. *Ve-amri shirah u-vatli* — they say their song and then they cease to exist. The verse in Eichah supports this: *chadashim labekarim rabbah emunasecha* — new every morning is Your faithfulness. The *Maharsha* reads this as: each day God demonstrates His faithfulness by recreating the world — and not just the world, but the angels themselves are recreated daily, brought into existence for the single purpose of singing *shira* to God, after which they pass out of existence. The analogy was made to a spark flying up from a fire and then immediately extinguishing — the angels are like sparks, brief and luminous, created for one radiant moment of praise.

### Timing of Song

Tosafot on the previous *daf*, at the passage *mizei'at chayot*, develops this theme further and connects it to the liturgy of *Kedushah*. Tosafot writes: from this river of *dinur* angels emerge, say *shira*, and are immediately destroyed — as attested in the *midrash* on *chadashim labekarim*. Why are they destroyed? Because there is a sign among the permanent angels, *hamalachim hakvuim*, the regular ones who have always been present — these angels know the proper moment to begin singing to God and wait for one another. The newly created angels, however, *einam yodim hadas* — they do not know the protocol. Eager and freshly created, they begin singing prematurely, and for singing out of turn, *mitchayvim kilaya* — they are destroyed.

This, Tosafot continues, is why the *Anshei Knesses HaGedolah* instituted the language of *Kedushah* the way they did. In the prayer of *Yotzer*, we say *venosnim reshus zeh lazeh* — the angels give permission to one another before saying *Kedushah*, *kulam ke-echad onim ve-omrim*. They must wait for the proper signal. Correspondingly, *Yotzer mesharsim* — You create attendants — refers to the daily new angels whom God creates; *va-asher mesharsav kulam omdim berum olam*, but the fixed attendants stand on high and endure. The newly created ones are the disposable, daily angels; the permanent ones continue their eternal service.

This is a fascinating window into the theology behind familiar liturgical language. The Gemara then notes a dissenting view: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan that angels are not created from the river of fire at all — rather, *kol dibur v'dibur sheyotze mi-pi HaKadosh Baruch Hu nivra mimenu malach*, every utterance that proceeds from God's mouth creates an angel. The supporting verse: *bidvar Hashem shamayim na'asu u-vi-ruach piv kol tzeva'am* — with God's word the heavens were made and with the breath of His mouth all their hosts. The disagreement touches on a deep question: how directly associated with God are the angels — created from His immediate speech, or emerging at one remove through a river of fire born from the sweat of the celestial *chayot*?

The Gemara then addresses a further tension in Daniel's vision: one verse describes God's appearance as white-haired and snow-cloaked, while another verse describes *kvutzosav taltalim shechoros ka-orev* — His locks layered and black as a raven. *Lo kashya: kan bi-yeshiva, kan be-milchama* — one is when God sits in council as the elder-sage, the other when He goes out to war. As the saying goes, *ein lecha na'eh bi-yeshiva ela zaken* — nothing is more fitting for one sitting in deliberation than the appearance of age, *ve-ein lecha na'eh be-milchama ela bachur* — and nothing more fitting for battle than youth. This is precisely the idea embedded in *An'im Zemirot*: *zikna be-yom din u-vacharut be-yom kerav* — aged on the day of judgment, youthful on the day of battle.

---

## Two Thrones

### God & David

Returning to Daniel's vision, the Gemara notes another tension. One verse says *korseih shvivin dinur* — His throne is flames of fire — while another in the same passage says *ad di chorsavan rmiu*, thrones (in the plural) were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat upon them. Throne or thrones?

*Lo kashya: kan echad lo ve-kan echad le-David* — one is for God and one is for David, the earthly king. A *braisa* confirms: *echad lo ve-echad le-David, divrei Rabbi Akiva* — Rabbi Akiva holds that one throne is for God and one for David.

### Justice & Compassion

Rabbi Yose HaGelili rebukes Rabbi Akiva sharply: *Akiva, ad matai ata oseh Shechina chol?* — Akiva, how long will you make the Divine Presence into something mundane? You are placing a human being on a throne alongside God, which is entirely inappropriate. Instead: *echad le-din ve-echad le-tzedakah* — one throne represents God's attribute of *din*, strict justice, and one represents *tzedakah*, which here means compassion or loving-kindness. This is especially fitting given that Daniel's vision is explicitly a scene of divine judgment, resonant with the imagery of Rosh Hashanah — one might say this is the very source for the concept of God removing Himself from the throne of *din* and moving to the throne of *rachamim*.

The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Akiva accepted the critique. A subsequent *braisa* records Rabbi Akiva himself saying *echad le-din ve-echad le-tzedakah* — so he clearly accepted the correction and adopted this formulation.

One might also note, as a subtext, the possibility that these discussions implicitly address concerns about *gnostic* or *Christian* readings of such passages — particularly those involving a Davidic king figure sharing divine space, given the theological weight such imagery carried in late antiquity.

### Throne & Footstool

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya was still unsatisfied. Even two thrones for God's two attributes suggests some sense of plurality or lack of perfect singularity in the Divine presence. He said to Rabbi Akiva: *ma lecha etzel aggadah?* — what are you doing with *aggadah*? This is not your domain. *Kelach etzel negaim ve-oholot* — go to Negaim and Oholot, the intricate *halachic* areas where no one can match you. Leave *aggadah* to us. His own resolution: *kan le-kisei ve-kan le-sharpraf* — one is a throne and one is a footstool, as the verse says, *ha-shamayim kisi ve-ha-aretz hadom raglai* — heaven is My throne and the earth is My footstool. Not two thrones, only one throne and a footstool beneath — a formulation that preserves total Divine singularity.

It is worth noting that while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya tells Rabbi Akiva that *aggadah* is not his domain, there is strong evidence elsewhere — including what the Gemara will discuss regarding Rabbi Akiva entering the *Pardes* — that Rabbi Akiva was in fact a genuine mystic. Whether mystical experience and the ability to interpret these texts as *aggadah* are the same skill is a separate question; not every *kabbalist* is necessarily a master expositor.

---

## Eighteen Curses

### Ten Losses

Rav Ami states: *shmoneh esreh klalot kilel Yeshayahu et Yisrael* — Yeshayahu pronounced eighteen curses against Israel, predicting the terrible losses that would accompany the destruction. *V'lo nitkarerah da'ato* — and his distress was not settled *ad she-amar lahem ha-mikra hazeh* — until he reached this verse: *yirhavu ha-na'ar ba-zaken ve-ha-nikleh ba-nichbad* — the youth will bully the elder and the despised will lord over the honored. For whatever reason, that final verse — the collapse of social and moral hierarchy — was the culminating anguish of the prophecy.

The Gemara proceeds to enumerate these eighteen from the passage in Yeshayahu that begins *ki hineh ha-Adon Hashem Tzvaot mesir mi-Yerushalayim u-meYehuda mishen u-mishenah* — the Lord will remove from Jerusalem and Judah all support. The Gemara counts as follows:

*Mishen* — support — these are *ba'alei mikra*, masters of Scripture. *U-mishenah* — the feminine form — these are *ba'alei mishnah*, masters of Mishnah, and the near-homophony with *mishna* is noted. There is a dispute between Rav Pappa and the sages: one says that in the time of Yeshayahu there were six hundred *sidrei mishnah* and one says seven hundred — an almost unimaginable loss of Torah knowledge, a hundred times what we now possess.

*Kol mishen lechem* — all support of bread — these are *ba'alei Talmud*, masters of Talmudic analysis, for it is the staff of life; the verse *lechu lachamu be-lachmi* — come eat of my bread — supports this, with a possible wordplay between *lachmi* and *masachti* (*masechet*). *Kol mishen mayim* — support of water — these are *ba'alei aggadah*, masters of homily and lore, for *aggadah* draws the heart like flowing water, though notably not characterized as a necessity of life in the way bread is. *Gibbor* — a mighty person — this refers to one who is a *ba'al shmu'ot*, a master of many traditions. *V-ish milchama* — a man of war — this is one who knows how to conduct *milchamta shel Torah*, the intellectual battle of Torah, skilled in argument and analysis. *Shofet* — a judge — *she-dan din emet le-amito*, one who renders truly just decisions. *Navi* — a prophet — as its plain meaning. *Kosem* — literally a diviner — this is a *melech*, a king, because *kesem al siftei melech*, a kind of charm is on the lips of the king. *Zaken* — an elder — one who is worthy of sitting in the council of sages.

*Sar chamishim* — an officer of fifty — this is reread as *sar chumashim*, a master of the five books of Torah, one who can truly analyze and debate the *chamisha chumshei Torah*. An alternative reading from Rabbi Abbahu: one may not appoint a *meturgeman*, a public translator of Torah, who is less than fifty years old — this is a position of great communal responsibility, making the Torah intelligible to the people. *U-nesu fanim* — one of lifted countenance — someone for whose sake heaven or earth shows favor to the entire generation. In heavenly terms: Rabbi Chanina ben Dosa, through whose merit the whole world was sustained. In earthly terms: Rabbi Abbahu, who was honored in the imperial court. *Ve-yo'etz* — a counselor — one who knows how to intercalate the years and establish the months, a role requiring deep specialized knowledge. *Ve-chakham* — a wise man — a student who can sharpen his rabbis through his insights and questions. *Charashim* — when he opens his mouth in *divrei Torah* everyone else is silenced, becoming like a *cheresh*, one who cannot speak. *Ve-navon* — understanding — one who can infer one thing from another. *Lachash* — whispered incantations or secrets — one qualified to receive *divrei Torah she-nitnu be-lachash*, the secret Torah transmitted in whispers.

### Torah Interpretation

It is significant that the Gemara interprets nearly every item in this catalogue through the lens of Torah knowledge and leadership. The verse that specifies who may receive *sitrei Torah* — secrets of Torah — as cited earlier in the Gemara (*ein mosrin sitrei Torah ela le-mi she-yesh bo chamisha devarim: sar chamishim ve-nesu fanim ve-yo'etz ve-chakham charashim ve-navon lachash*) uses this exact list. The person worthy of receiving the *lachash*, the esoteric, is the one who possesses all of these qualities.

The final verses of the catalogue: *ve-natati ne'arim sareihem* — I will place youths as their rulers — these are *benei adam she-meno'arim min ha-mitzvot*, people who are emptied and bare of *mitzvot*, as opposed to the Torah scholars and righteous leaders who were removed. *Ve-ta'alulim yimshelu bam* — and babes will rule over them. The Aramaic word *ta'ala* means fox; Rav Pappa bar Yaakov reads *ta'alulim* as *benei ta'ala*, sons of foxes — lowly people descended from the lowly.

*Ve-lo nitkarerah da'ato* — and still Yeshayahu's anguish was not quieted — until he said: *yirhavu ha-na'ar ba-zaken ve-ha-nikleh ba-nichbad*. The *na'ar* here is again *she-meno'ar min ha-mitzvot*, emptied of *mitzvot*, and *yirhavu be-mi she-memale be-mitzvot ke-rimon* — they will lord over one who is filled with *mitzvot* like a pomegranate. *Ve-ha-nikleh ba-nichbad*: the *nikleh*, the one who treats *chumrot* as *kalot*, the weighty matters of halacha as trivial — that person will lord over *mi she-kalot domot alav ke-chamurot*, the one so pious that even the lightest matters weigh heavily upon him.

### Honesty in Torah

Rav Ketina then states: *va-afilu be-sha'at kishlonah shel Yerushalayim lo paseku mehem ba'alei emunah* — even at the very moment of Jerusalem's downfall, trustworthy people never ceased from Israel. He derives this from the verse in Yeshayahu describing how, in the depths of the collapse, one man will grab his brother and say: you have a cloak, you should be our ruler. The Gemara reads this as: you have Torah knowledge — things people hide like a garment, not wanting to lend out what is precious — you should be our leader. Even in the catastrophe, they are seeking whoever still retains some Torah, because all the great masters have been removed.

*U-ve-ha-machshelah ha-zot tachtecha* — and this stumbling under you — *devarim she-ein benei adam omdim aleihem ela im ken nichshal bahem*: areas of Torah one does not truly master unless one has stumbled in them, made mistakes, and thereby truly internalized them. You have even that. Be our leader.

But the man in the verse refuses. He swears — the Gemara reads *va-yisa* as an oath-taking, parallel to *lo tisa et shem Hashem* — and he says: *lo hayiti mi-khoshvei Beit ha-Midrash* — I was never among those who labored in the study hall. I have no Torah. *U-ve-veiti ein lechem ve-ein simla* — I have no bread and no garment — *she-ein be-yadi lo mikra ve-lo mishna ve-lo Gemara*. I know no Scripture, no Mishnah, no Gemara. Do not make me a leader of the people.

### Torah vs. Business

The Gemara notes that this refusal demonstrates remarkable honesty — and then immediately questions it. Perhaps he had no choice: if he had claimed to know Torah, they would have said *eima lan*, tell us something, and he would have been exposed. But, the Gemara counters, *hava leih lemeimar gamar ve-shakhakh* — he could have said he once learned and forgot. The fact that he says instead *I never learned at all* — that already reflects a deeper level of honesty, to admit one had never studied rather than claiming the dignified excuse of forgetting what was once known.

The comparison is natural and self-evident to anyone who has experienced the difference between being able to say *I don't remember* versus *I never knew*.

Rav Ami had earlier stated that Jerusalem was destroyed only when *ba'alei emunah* completely ceased from it. The Gemara reconciles: *lo kashya — ha be-divrei Torah, ha be-masa u-matan*. There is no contradiction. When it comes to Torah — to honestly representing one's Torah knowledge — people will always remain honest even in the darkest times. When it comes to business and monetary dealings, however, no honest person is left. A striking and sobering distinction.

---

## Elazar ben Arach

### Teaching Conditions

The Gemara presents a *baraisa* about teaching *Ma'aseh Merkavah*. It concerns Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, who was riding on a donkey while Rabbi Elazar ben Arach — who is known otherwise mainly from *Pirkei Avot* as someone like *ma'ayan hamitgaber*, an ever-strengthening spring — walked behind him. Rabbi Elazar requested: *Rabbi, sheneili perek echad be-Ma'aseh Merkavah* — teach me even one section of the Merkavah. Rabban Yochanan replied: have I not taught you — *lo be-merkava be-yachid*, one may not teach *Merkavah* even to a single individual, *ela im kein haya chakham meivin mida'ato* — unless that person is a sage who can understand on his own?

Rabbi Elazar responded: *tarsheini lomar lefanecha davar echad she-limadtani* — permit me to tell you something that you yourself taught me. The implication is subtle: *I will demonstrate that I am in fact that sage who can understand independently — I will show you what I was able to perceive from what you hinted to me.*

### Elazar's Discourse

Rabban Yochanan immediately dismounted from the donkey, wrapped himself in his garment, and sat upon a stone under an olive tree. When Rabbi Elazar asked why he dismounted, Rabban Yochanan replied: *efshar ata doreish be-Ma'aseh Merkavah u-Shechina imanu u-malachei ha-shareit melavin otanu, va-ani erkhav al ha-chamor?* — Is it possible that you will expound *Ma'aseh Merkavah* while the *Shechina* is with us and the ministering angels accompany us, and I should remain riding on the donkey? He had to show proper respect for the Divine Presence that would attend the teaching. Interestingly, Rabbi Elazar had been wise enough to comprehend what Rabban Yochanan was teaching, yet had not fully grasped the power of what was behind that teaching — the degree to which the *Shechina* itself would be drawn to attend.

Rabbi Elazar immediately began to expound *Ma'aseh Merkavah*, and as he did, fire came down from heaven and encompassed all the trees of the field; *pitchu kulam ve-amru shira* — they all opened and sang, quoting *Hallelu et Hashem min ha-aretz taninim ve-chol tehomot... eitz pri ve-chol arazim, Halleluyah*. Then an angel from within the fire responded and declared: *hein hein ma'aseh merkavah* — this, precisely this, is *Ma'aseh Merkavah*. The vision is confirmed from above.

This is a striking moment in the Gemara: *Ma'aseh Merkavah* is not merely a matter of correctly interpreting the prophetic visions — it is a practice that brings heaven down to earth, that causes the *Shechina* to descend, fire to appear, and creation itself to burst into song. Just as earlier we saw that human prayer can alter the appearance of the heavenly throne, here the teaching of *Ma'aseh Merkavah* causes the earthly realm to erupt with heavenly fire and praise.

### Yochanan's Praise

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai rose and kissed Rabbi Elazar on his head. He said: *Baruch Hashem Elohei Yisrael she-natan bein le-Avraham Avinu* — Blessed is God who gave such a son to Abraham our father — *she-yodei'a le-havin u-lakhkor ve-lidrosh be-Ma'aseh Merkavah* — who knows how to understand, to investigate, and to expound in *Ma'aseh Merkavah*. The praise continues: *yesh na'eh doreish ve-ein na'eh mekayeim, ve-yesh na'eh mekayeim ve-ein na'eh doreish* — there are those who expound beautifully but do not fulfill beautifully, and those who fulfill but do not expound beautifully — *ata na'eh doreish ve-na'eh mekayeim*, but you do both. The *Maharsha* suggests that *na'eh mekayeim* here means that his exposition was true — it corresponded to reality, to the actual nature of the *Merkavah* — and that is itself the fulfillment.

*Ashrecha Avraham Avinu she-Elazar ben Arach yatza me-chalatzecha* — praised are you, Abraham our father, that Elazar ben Arach came from your loins. The invocation of Abraham is somewhat puzzling; one suggestion made in the discussion is a connection to *Sefer Yetzirah*, associated with Abraham in the tradition of mystical literature. Whatever the precise association, the praise is striking — Rabbi Elazar is being compared favorably not just to his own teacher but placed in the lineage of the first patriarch.

### Yehoshua's Teaching

When the account of this episode was told over to Rabbi Yehoshua, he was walking together with Rabbi Yosei HaKohen. The two of them said: we too have been given an opportunity, let us expound *Ma'aseh Merkavah*. *Patach Rabbi Yehoshua ve-darash* — Rabbi Yehoshua opened and expounded. It was the season of *Tammuz*, the height of summer, yet the sky filled with clouds and a rainbow appeared. *Ve-hayu malachei ha-shareit mitkabtzim u-va'im lishmoa* — and the ministering angels gathered and came to hear, *kivnei adam she-mitkabtzim u-va'im lir'ot be-mazmutei chatan ve-kallah* — like people who gather to see the rejoicing at a wedding celebration.

Why would angels come to hear a human discourse on *Ma'aseh Merkavah* if they presumably know better than any mortal what transpires above? The comparison to *mazmutei chatan ve-kallah* — to wedding celebrations — may offer a partial answer: people attend a wedding celebration not necessarily to learn something new but to witness and share in another's joy, even if they are not themselves experiencing it. So too, the angels come not because they need instruction, but to witness the joy and wonder of human beings accessing and articulating the divine mysteries.

### Third Group Vision

Rabbi Yosei HaKohen then went and reported these events to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai — the remarkable session that Rabbi Yehoshua had conducted. Rabban Yochanan said: *ashreichem ve-ashrei yoledetchem* — praised are you and praised are those who gave birth to you. *Ashrei einai she-kach ra'u* — praised are my eyes that have seen this, for I saw this same wonder when I engaged in *Ma'aseh Merkavah* with Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, and now I see that you too have had that experience.

He added: *va-af ani va-atem ba-chalomi, mesubim hayinu al Har Sinai* — and even you and I in my dream, I saw us reclining at Har Sinai. The image of *mesubim*, reclining, connects to the verse *va-yechezu et ha-Elokim va-yochlu va-yishtu* — they saw God and ate and drank — referring to those at Sinai who had a vision of God. He is placing himself and his students in that same category of those who ascended and beheld. *Ve-nitnah aleinu bat kol min ha-shamayim* — and a heavenly voice went forth from heaven saying: *alu le-chan, alu le-chan* — come up here, come up here. *Traklin gedolim u-mutzaot na'ot mutzaot lachem* — great halls and beautiful furnishings are laid out for you. *Lachem va-atem ve-talmideichem ve-talmidei talmideichem* — for you, your students, and your students' students. *Mezumanin le-chat shelishit* — you are appointed to be in the third group in God's presence.

What the first and second groups consist of the Gemara does not say — the third is evidently as high as the vision could articulate for them, and even so, it is an extraordinary destination.

It is fitting to close by returning to Rabbi Elazar ben Arach himself, who is known otherwise only for the statement in *Pirkei Avot* that he was like a *ma'ayan hamitgaber* — a spring that continuously strengthens. That characterization fits this narrative precisely: Rabban Yochanan believed he had taught nothing explicitly about the *Merkavah*, and yet Rabbi Elazar drew from whatever had been hinted to him, producing a discourse that brought down heavenly fire and caused the very trees to sing. He was the spring that gathers and strengthens from within, giving back more than it received — the paradigmatic student of *Ma'aseh Merkavah*.

---

# Chagigah 15

## Merkavah Transmission

### Yochanan & Elazar

The daf opens by picking up the threads of the *maaseh merkavah* discussions that had been unfolding across the previous material. We had seen Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai and Rabbi Elazar ben Arach engaged in these exchanges, and similarly Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yossi HaKohen. The earlier narrative had culminated in an extraordinary vision at Har Sinai — the concept of *vayochelu vayishtu*, the eating and drinking at the mountain, the being called up to an encounter with the divine presence. The *gemara* now pauses to interrogate whether the full picture of this transmission has been accurately represented.

### Four Generations

The *gemara* cites a *baraita* — found approximately ten lines down in the wide-line text — in which Rabbi Yossi b'Rabbi Yehuda teaches that there were three *hartza'ot*, meaning three formal presentations or expositions of *maaseh merkavah*, each in a *rav-talmid* relationship. Rabbi Yehoshua presented *maaseh merkavah* before Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai. Rabbi Akiva — who, it bears noting, was a student of Rabbi Yehoshua — then presented before Rabbi Yehoshua. And Chananya ben Chachinai presented before Rabbi Akiva. The chain thus runs across four generations, each disciple expounding these matters before his master.

### Elazar Absent

This immediately raises a question: what of Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, who figures so prominently in the earlier narrative? Why is he not counted in this chain? The *gemara* answers: *d'artzi ve-artzu kamei kachashiv* — the list counts only those who both presented and had it presented before them. The point of the chain is a continuous *rav-talmid* tradition. Rabbi Elazar ben Arach may well have expounded *maaseh merkavah* before Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, but he never had a student who then carried the tradition forward and presented it back to him. The chain, therefore, does not run through him: *d'artzi velo artzu kamei, lo kachashiv*.

This is consistent with a broader and melancholy fact about Rabbi Elazar ben Arach. In *Pirkei Avot* he is described as *ma'ayan hamitgaber*, an ever-strengthening spring, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai was dazzled by his independent mastery of *maaseh merkavah*. Yet we have almost no surviving traditions in his name in the *talmud* or elsewhere. The story attached to this silence is that he relocated to a city where *talmidei chachamim* were few — apparently drawn by the comfort of its famous bathhouses — assuming that given his stature, scholars would follow him. They did not. The principle *hevei goleh limkom Torah* — one must pursue Torah, it will not pursue you — proved itself, and Rabbi Elazar ben Arach's learning withered. His near-absence from the rabbinic record is thus entirely of a piece with his exclusion from this chain of *maaseh merkavah* transmission.

### Chananya Counted

This resolution, however, creates an apparent inconsistency. Chananya ben Chachinai, the last figure in the list, presented before Rabbi Akiva — but nobody is recorded as having presented *maaseh merkavah* before him. Why is he counted if he, like Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, is missing one side of the *rav-talmid* relationship? The *gemara* answers directly: *d'artzi miya kamei man d'artzi* — he at least presented before Rabbi Akiva, who had himself received the tradition from Rabbi Yehoshua. That is sufficient to place Chananya within the chain, because the chain is reckoned from the top down — A presented to B, B to C, C to D — and Chananya occupies the terminal position. Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, by contrast, stands entirely outside the chain: he never served as the link through which the tradition passed onward.

---

## Pardes Entry

### Four Names

With the *maaseh merkavah* chain established, the *gemara* now introduces one of the most celebrated and discussed passages in all of rabbinic literature. *Tanu Rabbanan*: four entered the *pardes* — a term universally understood to refer to some form of heavenly ascent, whether as mystical study or as literal ascent to the supernal realm. The four are identified: Ben Azzai, Ben Zoma, Acher — that is, Elisha ben Avuyah — and Rabbi Akiva.

### Marble Stones

Before they entered, Rabbi Akiva issued a warning: *keshe'atem magi'im eitzel avnei shayish tahor* — when you arrive at the stones of pure marble, do not say "water, water," for what appears to be water is not water at all, and the one who speaks falsehood will not be established before God. Of all the possible warnings one might imagine being given before a heavenly ascent, this is a striking one: the danger of misidentifying what one sees and thereby uttering something false in the presence of the divine.

### Acher Destroyed

Each of the four entered and met a different fate. Acher — Elisha ben Avuyah — *kitzetz b'netiyot*: he cut down the young shoots. The image is deliberately chosen. One has entered a garden, and the most destructive act imaginable in a garden is to cut down the young growths before they can flourish. Whatever he encountered within the *pardes*, the result was devastation rather than enlightenment.

### Akiva Success

Rabbi Akiva alone *yatza b'shalom* — he exited in peace, the only one of the four to emerge without harm.

### Chananel Vision

Before turning to the individual fates, it is worth pausing over a remarkable passage in Rabbeinu Chananel, who draws on the *Aruch* and on the *heichalot* literature to explain what the *pardes* actually was. Rabbeinu Chananel writes: *kinnu'uhu Pardes* — they called it *pardes*, *mei'ein Gan Eden shehu genuzah l'tzaddikim* — because it is like the *Gan Eden* hidden away for the righteous. More specifically, *kach oto makom hu makom ba'Aravot* — that place is the place in the *Aravot*, the highest of the heavens, where the souls of the righteous are gathered, as was discussed in the earlier *gemara*. And this, he says, is spelled out in the *heichalot* literature.

### Heichalot Practice

What Rabbeinu Chananel then describes is a complete portrait of the theurgic mystical practice underlying the *pardes* narrative. The sages who were worthy of this level would pray, would cleanse themselves from all impurity, would fast, immerse in the *mikvah*, purify themselves, and then *v'hayu mishtamshim b'shemot* — would make use of divine names. Through these preparations they would achieve visions: *tzofim b'heichalos* — they would peer into the heavenly *heichalot*, the divine chambers, seeing how the angelic watches stood guard over the divine temple, one chamber opening into the next.

Rabbi Akiva's warning, in this framework, is recast. Rabbeinu Chananel writes that he told them: when you are prepared to see *be'uvnusa dliba* — in your mind's eye, as one might translate that phrase — when you reach the marble stones, do not say "water, water," because there is no water there at all; it is only *dmus baolam nires*, a kind of vision. The *heichalot rabbasi* explains the source of the optical illusion: the guardians of the divine chamber pour out what appear to be enormous waves of water from the marble entrance, yet there is not even a single drop of water there — only the radiant glow of the pure marble stones. Anyone who asks "what is this water?" is simply pushed away, *nehdaf*, expelled.

Crucially, Rabbeinu Chananel is explicit that the sages did not literally ascend to heaven: *v'einam olim bashamayim ela tzofim v'ro'im be'uvnusa dliba* — they saw it in their mind's eye, *ke'adam haroeh u'mehabit mitoch aspaklaria she'eina me'ira* — like someone seeing through a cloudy lens. This is of course the classical distinction: all the *nevi'im* saw through a cloudy lens; only Moshe saw through a clear one.

In this framework, Ben Azzai's fate is explained as follows: he added further divine names in order to achieve a vision through a clear lens rather than a cloudy one — *kdei lehabit be'aspaklaria me'ira* — and he died as a result. Ben Zoma used divine names beyond what he could handle and *nitrefah da'ato* — his mind became disordered. And Acher cut down the *netiyot* in the garden. This association of the *pardes* story with the *heichalot* literature is illuminating precisely because when people think of Jewish mysticism, they tend to think of the *Zohar* and of descriptive literature — but the *heichalot* material preserves something different: a theurgic practice, a structured discipline of fasting, immersion, the use of divine names, and induced mystical vision. That is what Rabbeinu Chananel identifies as the background of this narrative.

One question that arises is whether *mayim* here functions as a metaphor for *Torah*, as it so often does in rabbinic literature. The resonance is not obviously present in this particular context, and the imagery of water in the *pardes* story remains genuinely elusive.

### Ben Azzai Dies

Turning to the individual fates: *Ben Azzai heitzitz vamet* — Ben Azzai peered and died. The verse applied to him is *yakar be'einei Hashem hamavta l'chasidav* — dear in the eyes of God is the death of His righteous ones — which pointedly frames him as among God's *chasidim* rather than treating his death as straightforward punishment. The Maharsha attempts to explain that Ben Azzai's soul achieved direct communion with the divine to such a degree that the body simply could not survive. Yet the formulation *heitzitz vamet* — he peered and he died — carries an ambivalence that is difficult to resolve entirely. It sounds as though something went wrong, even as the prooftext insists on his righteousness.

### Rambam Theory

Rambam reads the entire *pardes* narrative in a strikingly different register. For him, the subject is not mystical ascent at all but rather the intellectual study of theology — what he calls *ma'aseh merkavah* in the sense of metaphysics. He writes that if one proceeds properly — not claiming demonstration where none exists, not hastily rejecting propositions whose negation has not been demonstrated, and not attempting to apprehend what lies beyond one's apprehension — one will achieve human perfection at the level of Rabbi Akiva, who *nichnas b'shalom v'yatza b'shalom*.
