But if one overreaches intellectually, one joins Elisha Acher: not merely imperfect but "most deficient among the deficient," overcome by delusive imaginings and an inclination toward evil. The image of honey is similarly rationalized: just as excess honey upsets the stomach and causes vomiting, so intellectual apprehension, if not arrested at its proper limit, may be perverted into a defect. This is an elegant reading, but it should be stated plainly: it is not *peshat*.

### Ben Zoma Injured

*Ben Zoma heitzitz v'nifga* — Ben Zoma peered and was injured. The verse applied to him is *dvash matzata echol dayeka, pen tisba'enu v'hikeito* — if you have found honey, eat only what is sufficient for you, lest you sate yourself and vomit it back. He went beyond what he was capable of absorbing, and the result was injury — commonly understood, as it is even before Milton Steinberg made it famous, as mental disorder. Unlike Ben Azzai, whose framing in the verse suggests a kind of tragic sanctity, the verse applied to Ben Zoma carries a note of censure: he overextended, and he suffered for it.

---

## Ben Zoma After

### Castrated Dog

The *gemara* now presents two halakhic discussions attributed to Ben Zoma, and their placement here is not immediately obvious. They asked Ben Zoma: *ma hu l'sarsei kalba* — is it permitted to castrate a dog? Since a dog is entirely outside the category of *korbanot*, one might have thought that the concerns surrounding castration — which are typically tied to sacrificial fitness — would not apply. Ben Zoma answers from the verse: *u'v'artzachem lo ta'asu* — the verse concerning castrated animals that may not be brought as sacrifices concludes with a general prohibition, "do not do this in your land," which Ben Zoma reads as extending the prohibition to any animal, not only those eligible for sacrifice. This formulation, as is well known, creates substantial halakhic difficulty for the contemporary practice of neutering pets.

### Virgin Pregnant

The second question put to Ben Zoma: *besulah she'ibra mahu l'Kohen Gadol* — if a virgin has conceived, what is her status with respect to marriage to a *Kohen Gadol*, who is required to marry a *besulah*? The question turns on whether it is possible to be simultaneously pregnant and still a virgin in the halakhic sense. The *gemara* raises Shmuel's ruling that a man can have intercourse with a virgin multiple times without rupturing the hymen — but answers that this is uncommon, *lo shchiach*. If so, the most plausible explanation for a woman who is pregnant but whose hymen is intact is not that she had intercourse — since that would be an uncommon scenario — but rather *shema be'ambati ibra*: she may have conceived in a bathhouse, having immersed in water into which a man had previously ejaculated.

The *gemara* then challenges this: does Shmuel not also rule that semen which does not exit *kechetz* — with the force of an arrow — cannot cause conception? The answer is that the requirement of *yoreh kechetz* applies to the moment the semen exits the man; once it has done so in that fashion, it retains its potency even if it subsequently enters the woman's body through the water of a bathhouse.

Setting aside the obvious scientific difficulties, this *gemara* becomes the classical locus for later discussions of artificial insemination, as it establishes the conceptual possibility of conception without direct sexual contact and raises questions of paternity that are addressed elsewhere in the literature. The comparison to the *midrash* about Ben Sira's conception is relevant here as well.

### Christian Context

What this discussion is doing in the immediate context of the *pardes* narrative is genuinely puzzling. One possibility is that it is here to establish that however Ben Zoma's encounter with the *pardes* affected him, he retained the capacity for coherent halakhic reasoning. His breakdown was specific to the mystical domain, as we will see shortly. But another possibility — and it is worth raising even if it cannot be definitively established — is that these discussions are colored by the question of Christian influence. The notion of a virgin who is truly pregnant, and Ben Zoma's insistence that the most plausible explanation maintains her virginity intact, resonates uncomfortably with Christian nativity claims. Indeed, a scholarly article has identified other Ben Zoma texts that may reflect contact with proto-Christian or proto-Gospel traditions. If that reading is correct, then even the question about the castrated dog may carry hidden resonances. The difficulty is that the halakhic content of both discussions is entirely straightforward, which makes it hard to press the point.

On the specific halakhic question: Ben Zoma's position is that the *be'ulah/besulah* distinction turns on the rupturing of the hymen, and his answer is that if the hymen is intact, she should be treated as a *besulah* regardless of the pregnancy, because the most logical explanation that accounts for both facts — intact hymen plus pregnancy — is the bathhouse scenario rather than intercourse. His final position, in other words, is that she genuinely is a virgin who genuinely is pregnant.

---

## Temple Mount Vision

### Yehoshua Meeting

The *gemara* now presents the story of Ben Zoma's encounter with Rabbi Yehoshua on Har HaBayit. Rabbi Yehoshua was standing on an elevated step on the Temple Mount — which is itself a fascinating detail, raising questions about the *tumah* status of those present there — when he saw Ben Zoma. Ben Zoma did not rise in his presence. This was a significant slight: Rabbi Yehoshua was a figure of the prior generation, very much a *rebbe* in relation to Ben Zoma. Rabbi Yehoshua asked him: *me-ayin u-le-ayin Ben Zoma* — where are you coming from and where are you going? Your head is so far elsewhere that you didn't even see me standing here. One might also hear in this question an echo of *me-ayin bata u-le-an attah holekh*, the classic call to self-reckoning.

### Three Fingerbreadths

Ben Zoma's answer reveals exactly where his mind was. He said: *tzofeh hayiti bein mayim ha-elyonim la-mayim ha-tachtonim* — I was peering between the supernal waters and the lower waters, and there is only three fingerbreadths separating them. His proof: *v'ruach Elohim merachefet al pnei ha-mayim, k'yonah she-merachefet al baneha v'eina noga'at* — the spirit of God hovered over the waters like a dove hovering over its young without touching them — indicating that the divine spirit, which he associates with the supernal waters, was only the barest distance above the lower waters. Three fingerbreadths. Here, too, the water theme from the *pardes* narrative resurfaces.

### Still Outside

Rabbi Yehoshua's response to his students was devastating in its brevity: *adayin Ben Zoma mibachutz* — Ben Zoma is still outside. He has not arrived. Whether this means his mystical understanding is off-base, or that he is verging on something quasi-heretical, or simply that his mind has not properly returned from wherever it has gone, the verdict is clear: his head is entirely in the clouds, and what he is saying in the mystical domain is not right.

### Water Separation

The *gemara* then analyzes the substance of Ben Zoma's error. The verse he cited — *v'ruach Elohim merachefet al pnei ha-mayim* — is from day one of creation. But the separation of the upper and lower waters, *v'yehi mavdil bein mayim la-mayim*, occurred on the second day. Ben Zoma was deriving the current distance between the supernal and lower waters from a verse that describes conditions before the *havdalah* of day two even took place. That is why his reasoning is off.

As for the actual distance between the upper and lower waters, the *amoraim* offer a range of opinions. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it is *k'mlo nima* — a hair's breadth. The rabbis say it is like the planks of a bridge — the wooden planks laid right next to one another, with only the smallest gap between them. Mar Zutra, or according to some Rav Assi, says it is like two garments spread directly against one another. And some say it is like two cups placed rim to rim, one inverted onto the other. In each case, the separation is vanishingly small — far from Ben Zoma's three fingerbreadths, and in the case of the actual cosmological question, perhaps more significant still is that he was measuring from the wrong day of creation entirely.

The *gemara* closes this discussion with a flourish. The original story ended simply with *adayin Ben Zoma bachutz* — a powerful, stark conclusion. The subsequent analytical elaboration about the correct cosmological picture is a later *gemara* insertion, and while it adds technical precision, it does somewhat dilute the force of that extraordinary ending.

---

## Acher Heresy

### Metatron Sitting

The *gemara* now turns to Acher — Elisha ben Avuyah. The original tannaitic source said only that he *kitzetz b'netiyot* — cut down the young shoots — and cited the verse *al titten et picha lachati et besarecha*, do not let your mouth bring guilt upon yourself. What that sin was, the original source left unspecified. The Aramaic passage that follows is a later *gemara* elaboration, providing the specific content of his heresy. He saw *Metatron*, the great angel who serves in the innermost divine chamber, and Metatron had been granted permission *lemisav* — to sit — and to write down the merits of the Jewish people. This is worth pausing over: Metatron is not simply a messenger angel but a figure of extraordinary elevation, associated in this literature with what may be a kind of divine manifestation or at least a uniquely proximate divine presence.

### Two Powers

When Acher saw Metatron seated, he drew upon a tradition: there is no sitting in the divine presence, no competition, no back of the head — since angels have faces on all four sides — and no weariness. The tradition holds that none of these things exist in heaven. Yet here was Metatron, sitting. Acher drew the terrible conclusion: *shema chas v'shalom dvei reshuyos hen* — perhaps, God forbid, there are two competing divine powers. The sight of what appeared to be a second enthroned being led him into the foundational heresy: a dualist theology, a second authority alongside God.

### Merits Erased

The heavenly response was immediate. Metatron was expelled from that inner chamber and lashed with sixty tongues of flame. Rabbeinu Chananel and others are quick to clarify that Metatron did nothing wrong and is not being punished in any meaningful sense; the expulsion and lashing were designed precisely to demonstrate to Acher that Metatron held no independent authority — God alone was sovereign. A question was put to Metatron: why, when you saw Acher, did you not rise before him? Again, not because Metatron owed Acher deference, but because had he risen it might have forestalled the heretical conclusion. The incident underscores that no being in heaven exercises independent power.

Subsequently, permission was given to Metatron to erase the merits of Acher — a detail that carries its own poignancy given that we are close to Rosh Hashanah, when the imagery of writing and erasing merits is especially vivid.

### Except Acher

With the *gemara's* Metatron elaboration complete, the original tannaitic story resumes. A *bat kol* went forth and declared: *shuvu banim shovavim, chutz me'Acher* — return, wayward children — except for Acher. The heavenly proclamation of universal *teshuvah* explicitly excluded him.

### Hedonistic Fall

Acher's response to this, as elaborated by the *gemara*, was the logic of the man who has concluded he has nothing to lose: *ho'il ve'itred hahu gavra me'hahu alma* — since this person has been cast out from the world to come — *leipuk leih behai alma* — he might as well extract whatever benefit he can from this world. *Nafak Acher letarbut ra'ah* — Acher went out toward bad behavior. The word *tarbut* is itself interesting: in modern Hebrew it means culture, and in this context it likely implies an embrace of the Hellenistic or Roman hedonistic way of life.

### Prostitute Turnip

The *gemara* illustrates the depth of his fall with a scene. He found a prostitute and approached her. She recognized him: are you not Elisha ben Avuyah, the great sage? To demonstrate that he was no longer bound by anything, he reached into a planted bed — it was *Shabbos* — pulled out a turnip, and handed it to her. She said: that must be someone else. He was not who she thought. No, it was Acher: for whom the desecration of *Shabbos* had become a trivial, unremarkable act.

---

## Acher & Meir

### Opposites

The narrative now shifts to a series of exchanges between Acher and Rabbi Meir — exchanges that are moving precisely because they occur after Acher has *yatza letarbut ra'ah*, yet Rabbi Meir continues to engage him in Torah discourse. This mirrors structurally what the *gemara* did with Ben Zoma: presenting halakhic and aggadic discussions in the immediate aftermath of the account of his spiritual injury. After going off the *derech*, Acher asked Rabbi Meir: what is meant by the verse *gam et zeh lumat zeh asah ha'Elokim* — this opposite this God has made?

Rabbi Meir offered one interpretation: everything God created, He created with its opposite. He made mountains, He made valleys. He made seas, He made rivers.

### Akiva Version

Acher replied that Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Meir's own *rebbe*, did not explain the verse that way. The objection is pointed: mountains and rivers are not really opposites in any meaningful sense. Rabbi Akiva's version was more penetrating: *bara tzaddikim bara resha'im, bara Gan Eden bara Gehennom* — He created the righteous and the wicked; He created *Gan Eden* and *Gehennom*. The true opposites are spiritual and eschatological.

### Double Portions

This leads to an elaborate teaching. Every person, Rabbi Akiva maintained, has two portions: one in *Gan Eden* and one in *Gehennom*.

### Double Consequence

If a *tzaddik* merits it, he takes his own portion in *Gan Eden* plus the forfeited portions of the wicked — he inherits double in the world of reward. Conversely, the *rasha* who is found guilty takes his own portion in *Gehennom* plus the forfeited portions of the *tzaddikim* — he suffers double in the world of punishment. Rav Mesharshya supplies the prooftexts: regarding the righteous, the verse says *lachem b'artza mishneh yirashu* — in their land they shall inherit double; regarding the wicked, *umishneh shivaron shivram* — double of destruction is their downfall. One student raised a perceptive point: for this economy to balance perfectly, the world would need to contain an equal number of righteous and wicked, otherwise there would be unclaimed portions. The *zeh lumat zeh* symmetry itself implies this.

It is worth noting what is implicit in this teaching as addressed to Acher. On the one hand, the double punishment for the *rasha* is sobering. On the other hand, as another student observed, the teaching opens with the premise that every person — including, presumably, Acher — has a *chelek b'Gan Eden* waiting for him. That portion is always there. The question is only which portion one ultimately claims.

### Gold Glass Vessels

Acher sent another question to Rabbi Meir: what is meant by *lo ya'archenah zahav u'zechuchis, u'temurasah kli paz* — it shall not be compared to gold or glass, and its exchange is vessels of fine gold? Rabbi Meir answered: these refer to the words of Torah, which are as difficult to acquire as gold and *paz*, and as easy to lose as glassware. The contrast was vivid: precious metals must be smelted and recast; glass, once broken, is simply destroyed. Torah is precisely that fragile.

### Vessels Fixable

But again, Acher reports, that is not how Rabbi Akiva explained the verse. Rabbi Akiva's reading: *kli zahav u'kli zechuchis af al pi shenishberu yesh lahem takanah* — both gold vessels and glass vessels, even when broken, can be repaired. Gold can be smelted and recast; glass, famously, can be melted and reformed. So too *af talmid chacham af al pi shesarach yesh lo takanah* — even a *talmid chacham* who has gone rotten still has a possibility of repair.

The tension between the two teachings attributed to Rabbi Akiva — the double punishment for the *rasha* in one, and the *yesh lo takanah* in the other — is real. Held together, they may be read as a complementary message: the consequences of persistence in wickedness are severe and doubled, but return remains possible; the vessel is not beyond repair.

### Teshuvah Appeal

Rabbi Meir drew the practical conclusion directly: *af atah chozer becha* — you too, return. Do *teshuvah*. Acher's reply was devastating: *kvar shamati me'achorei hapargod, shuvu banim shovavim chutz me'Acher* — I have already heard from behind the divine curtain: "return, wayward children — except for Acher." He had internalized the *bat kol* as a final, irrevocable verdict.

One can read this in several ways. Theologically, it raises the question of whether the *bat kol* was a genuine divine pronouncement or a kind of test — a challenge to demonstrate precisely the quality of *teshuvah* that transcends even divine discouragement, that says "I will prove that wrong." But one can also read it in a deeply human register: Acher had simply given up on himself. He had convinced himself he was a lost cause, and no argument from Rabbi Meir could dislodge that conviction. The tragedy of the person who believes themselves beyond redemption is a recognizable one. The basic rabbinic theology is that *teshuvah* is available to anyone — and so the heavenly message, whether taken as literal or psychological, is either a test or a self-imposed prison. Perhaps both.

---

## Horseride Quest

### Shabbat Horseride

A later story, again in Aramaic and therefore a *gemara* elaboration rather than part of the original tannaitic text: Acher was riding on horseback on *Shabbos*, and Rabbi Meir was walking behind him, learning Torah from his mouth as he went. The image is almost surreal — the *rasha* on a horse, violating *Shabbos*, while his devoted student walks alongside trying to extract Torah from him.

### Boundary Warning

Acher interrupted the exchange: *Meir chazor l'achorecha* — Meir, turn back. He had measured by the horse's steps that they were approaching the *techum Shabbos* boundary, and he did not want Rabbi Meir to inadvertently violate it on his account. Rabbi Meir seized on the turn of phrase: *af atah chazor becha* — you too, turn back. Do *teshuvah*. Acher replied with what had become his standard answer: haven't I already told you — *kvar shamati me'achorei hapargod* — everybody can return except Acher.

### Thirteen Synagogues

Rabbi Meir would not accept this. He physically took hold of Acher — *takfei* — and dragged him into a *beis midrash*. There he employed the practice of asking a child to recite whatever verse he was currently learning, treating the child's answer as a kind of *siman*, a message from heaven — similar in spirit to the *goral ha-Gra*, the practice of opening a *Tanakh* at random and reading the verse one's finger falls on as a divine communication. He asked a child: *pesok li pesukach* — tell me your verse. The verse was *ein shalom amar Hashem l'resha'im* — there is no peace, says God, to the wicked. Not helpful.

He brought Acher to another *beis knesses* and asked another child. The verse: *ki im techabsi baneser ve'tarbi lach boris, nichtam avoneich lefanai* — even if you cleanse yourself with lye and multiply the soap, your sin is still stained before Me.

### Condemning Verses

He continued through *beis knesses* after *beis knesses*, and the pattern repeated. Every child, every verse, yielded a similar answer. The *gemara* records that Rabbi Meir brought Acher to thirteen *batei knesses* in all — *kulu pasku lei k'hai gavna* — and all of them produced verses of a similar condemning character. The last: *ve'l'rasha amar Elokim mah lecha l'saper chukai* — and to the wicked God says: what are you doing reciting My statutes? Not only is *teshuvah* apparently foreclosed; even the occupation of Torah study is being challenged.

### Violent Response

The final child in the final *beis knesses* had a speech impediment — *havah megamgem b'lishneih*, he had difficulty enunciating. When he recited the verse *ve'l'rasha amar Elokim*, his lisp made it sound like *ve'l'Elisha amar Elokim* — to Elisha, God says: what are you doing reciting My statutes? Acher heard his own name in the child's stumbling words, and the effect was shattering.

### Dismemberment

Two versions follow. According to one: Acher had a knife in his hand and he dismembered the child, sending the pieces to each of the thirteen synagogues — a horrifying echo of the *Pilegesh b'Givah*. According to the other: he said merely that had he a knife in his hand, he would have done so.

This detail — that Acher may have murdered and dismembered a child — is not the version of the story that typically circulates. The Acher narrative as popularly known concerns intellectual heresy and the tragedy of a great mind lost to apostasy. But the *gemara* here makes him a killer. This serves a purpose in the narrative economy: it becomes easier to account for how a figure of such obvious greatness could be so thoroughly cast out, and it makes the later ambivalence about his redemption both more dramatic and more comprehensible. The sin was not merely intellectual; it reached the depths of violence. Yet still, as we are about to see, the story does not end there.

---

## Heavenly Judgment

### Dilemma

*Ki nach nafshieh d'Acher* — when Acher died, a heavenly dilemma arose. On the one hand, *lo m'dainin lei daini* — he should not be judged and punished — *mishum d'asak b'Oraita* — because he engaged deeply in Torah and achieved tremendous levels of learning. On the other hand, *v'lo l'olma d'atei lo atei* — he should not receive the world to come — *mishum d'chata* — because of his sins. The heavens, as it were, could not decide what to do with him.

### Meir Plea

Rabbi Meir proposed a resolution: *mutav d'lidainei v'lyatei l'olma d'atei* — it would be better that he should be judged for his sins and then receive the world to come. Let him undergo the purifying fire of *Gehennom* and then ascend. Rabbi Meir expressed this as a personal aspiration: when will I die, so that I can rise and argue his case in heaven, and cause smoke to rise from his grave — the smoke signifying that he is being judged in *Gehennom*, which is the necessary precondition for eventual admission to *Olam Ha-Ba*.

### Grave Smoke

*Ki nach nafshieh d'Rabbi Meir* — when Rabbi Meir died, *salik kutra mikivrieh d'Acher* — smoke indeed rose from the grave of Acher. The sign appeared.

### Yochanan Object

Rabbi Yochanan, however, was troubled by this solution. *Gevurah l'mikli rabieh?* — Is this an achievement, to burn one's own *rebbe*? He did not consider it praiseworthy that Rabbi Meir had engineered a solution that involved causing his teacher to burn in *Gehennom*.

### Yochanan Promise

Rabbi Yochanan framed the deeper tragedy: *chad havei beinana v'lo matzinan l'atzulei* — one was among us and we could not save him when he was alive. This is the sorrowful irony. When Acher was alive, when intervention was still possible, the sages could not reach him. *Ee nakteih b'yad man marmi leih man* — if I had taken hold of his hand to bring him up, who would have taken him from me? Rabbi Yochanan believed he could have saved Acher in life, but no one managed it. So he declared: when will I die, and I will cause the smoke to cease from his grave.

### Guardian Overcome

*Ki nach nafshieh d'Rabbi Yochanan* — when Rabbi Yochanan died, *pasak kutra mikivrieh d'Acher* — the smoke ceased from the grave of Acher. The eulogizer at Rabbi Yochanan's funeral captured it: *afilu shomer hapetach lo amad l'fanecha rabbeinu* — even the guardian of the gate of *Gehennom* could not stand before you, our teacher. Rabbi Yochanan had descended into *Gehennom*, overcome its guardian, found Acher, taken hold of his hand, and brought him up.

### Heretic Redeemed

This is, by any measure, a startling conclusion. A man who had committed heresy of the most fundamental kind — who had embraced dualism, abandoned observance, desecrated *Shabbos*, and according to one tradition murdered a child — was in the end brought to *Gan Eden* by Rabbi Yochanan. The *gemara* does not resolve this; it presents it as the outcome. The ambivalence toward Acher that runs through the entire narrative — the continued loyalty of Rabbi Meir, the heavenly dilemma about his judgment, the competing efforts of Meir and Yochanan over his posthumous fate — finds its resolution not in condemnation but in rescue.

One might compare this to the ambivalence that arose a thousand years later in certain communities around Shabbetai Tzvi: figures whose spiritual gifts were undeniable even as their sin was catastrophic, and around whose fate after death similar debates circulated about who might rescue the soul from *Gehennom* and bring it to *Gan Eden*. The pattern of recognizing terrible sin while acknowledging spiritual greatness, and the refusal to simply close the book, runs deep. And it is worth noting, as one student observed, that for all his transgressions, Acher was protective of Rabbi Meir — warning him not to cross the *Shabbos* boundary, not wanting his path to contaminate his student. He became a destroyer in many senses, but not an active recruiter for his way of life.

---

---

# Chagigah 16

## Acher's Daughter & Honor

### Daughter's Request

The daf opens on 15b, in the final section of the story of Elisha ben Abuyah — known as *Acher*. The passage begins: *bito shel Acher atya l'kamei d'Rabbi* — the daughter of *Acher* came before Rabbi, the next generation, seeking *parnasah*, material support. The scene itself raises pointed questions. If *Acher* had adopted a hedonistic lifestyle, did he abandon his family entirely? The *gemara* does not say so explicitly, but the subtext is difficult to avoid.

Rabbi did not recognize her. When she identified herself as *Acher*'s daughter, his first reaction was one of genuine surprise.

### No Remnant Verse

Rabbi responded with a citation: *lo nin lo velo neched be'amo, v'ein sarid bimgurav* — he has no child or grandchild among his people, no remnant in his dwelling place. If *Acher* was a *rasha*, how could descendants of his still be present in this world? The verse seemed to foreclose the very possibility.

### Remember Torah

She answered him: *zechor l'Torato v'al tizkor ma'asav* — remember his Torah, do not remember his deeds. The response was not merely a personal plea but a theological statement about the separability of Torah and conduct. Immediately, *miyad yardah esh v'sichsechah safsalo shel Rabbi* — a fire descended and singed Rabbi's chair.

### Torah Praise & Honor

Rabbi wept and said: *umah l'misganin bah kach* — if those who denigrate Torah are treated with such care that even heaven comes down to defend their honor and their children, then *l'mishtabchin bah, al achat kamah v'khamah* — how much more so is the honor owed to those who sustain and praise Torah. The ambivalence is palpable. Rabbi had initially felt that *Acher* deserved no living descendants; by the end of the scene, even the heavens had intervened on his behalf — and this, despite his having abandoned Torah. The conflicted attitudes surrounding *Acher* run through the entire closing portion of this narrative.

---

## Rabbi Meir & Acher

### Angel Standard

The *gemara* now shifts to a distinct but related question: *Rabbi Meir heichi gmar Torah mipumei d'Acher?* — how could Rabbi Meir learn Torah from the mouth of *Acher*? Rabbah bar bar Chanah, citing Rabbi Yochanan, invokes the verse: *ki siftei kohen yishmeru da'at v'Torah yevakshu mipihu, ki malach Hashem Tzevaot hu* — because the lips of the *kohen* preserve knowledge, and Torah instruction is sought from his mouth, for he is like an angel of God. The implication is clear: *im domeh harav l'malach Hashem Tzevaot yevakshu Torah mipihu* — only if the teacher resembles an angel of God should one seek Torah from him. If not — *al yevakshu Torah mipihu* — one should not be pursuing instruction from his mouth. Rabbi Meir's conduct with *Acher* would seem to violate this standard directly.

### Intent Not Theirs

Resh Lakish responds: Rabbi Meir found a verse and expounded it to justify his approach. *Hatei oznecha u'shma divrei chachamim v'libcha tashit l'da'ati* — incline your ear and listen to the words of the sages, but set your heart to *my* intent. Crucially, the verse says *l'da'ati* — to my knowledge — and not *l'da'atam* — to their knowledge. This means one can listen to a sage while remaining selectively focused on the divine content of what is being transmitted, without being wholly drawn after the teacher's attitudes and lifestyle.

### Forget Deeds

Rav Chanina offers an alternative verse: *shimi bat u're'i, ve-hati oznekh ve-shikhchi amekh u-veit avich* — listen my daughter and see, incline your ear and forget your nation and your father's house. Rashi explains *ve-ma'aseihem shikhchi* — forget their deeds. The idea is parallel: one can isolate the *dvar Hashem* and set aside everything extraneous to that transmission.

### Adult Discernment

But this creates an apparent contradiction: these verses seem to sanction learning from a teacher of flawed character, while the *malach* verse seems to prohibit it. The *gemara* resolves the tension: *lo kashya, ha b'gadol ha b'katan* — there is no contradiction; one ruling applies to an adult and the other to a child. A child would be too readily seduced by and drawn after the teacher as a whole personality, whereas a discerning adult can be more selective. When Rav Dimi came from *Eretz Yisrael*, he reported: *Rabbi Meir achal tichla ve-shada shichla l'bar* — Rabbi Meir ate the date and threw the pit outside. He was able to take what was of value and discard what was not.

---

## Date & Pomegranate

### Selective Eating

The image of Rabbi Meir eating the date and discarding the pit captures something essential about his approach to *Acher*: the capacity to be selectively discerning, to receive genuine Torah content while not being swept along by the teacher's broader conduct and worldview.

### Nut Parable

Rava then expounds a verse: *el ginat egoz yaraditi lirot b'ibei ha-nachal* — I went down into the nut garden. Why are *talmidei chachamim* compared to a nut? *Mah egoz zeh af al pi she-meluchlach b'tit u-v'tzoa ein mah she-betocho nim'as* — just as a nut, even if its outer husk has become covered with filth and excrement, the nut itself inside remains intact and is not ruined.

### Torah Preserved

The application follows: *af talmid chacham af al pi she-sarach ein torato nim'eset* — a *talmid chacham*, even after he has gone off the *derech*, his Torah remains preserved within him. This is admittedly a dangerous statement. One might think that a scholar who has abandoned observance would be among the most pernicious influences — knowledgeable enough to be seductive, yet no longer anchored by the very Torah he transmits. And yet the *gemara* says no: even there, the Torah inside may be intact. This ambivalence is central to the entire *Acher* narrative and to the question of how Rabbi Meir is to be understood.

### Chananel Objection

Rabbeinu Chananel is deeply troubled by the implicit permission the *gemara* seems to extend here. He presents the *gemara*'s reasoning in full — that Rabbi Meir found a verse, that the contradiction between verses is resolved by the adult-child distinction — and then notes that a later passage will qualify the entire discussion. Elijah, Rabbeinu Chananel cites, tells us what happens in the heavenly *yeshiva*: *b'mivta d'raki'a shema'iti mikulhu rabbanan* — in the heavenly academy, the teachings of all the rabbis are taught, *ve-shema'iti shema'ata d'Rebbi Meir mishum d'gmar me-Acher lo amar* — but the teachings of Rabbi Meir are not recited there, because he learned from *Acher*. This would seem to vindicate the stricter reading. Yet Rabbeinu Chananel, even after building this argument toward a prohibition, ultimately concludes only: *hilchata afilu gadol lilmote torah mi-chavero yerei shamayim mipi adif lei* — even for an adult, learning Torah from an observant colleague is preferable. This is striking. After all the framing that suggests an outright prohibition, Rabbeinu Chananel lands on the softer formulation: it is merely *better*. The ambivalence surrounding *Acher* and Rabbi Meir's relationship to him resists clean resolution, even in the *rishonim*.

---

## Date & Pomegranate (II)

### Heaven Rejects

The *gemara* now presents the scene that Rabbeinu Chananel anticipated. *Rabba bar Shila* encountered Elijah the prophet and asked him: *mai ka-avid Hakadosh Baruch Hu?* — what is God doing? Elijah responded: *ka'amar shmaattah mipumaihu de'chul-hu rabbanan* — God is reciting teachings from the mouths of all the rabbis. *U'mipumei de'Rebbi Meir lo ka'amar* — but not from the mouth of Rabbi Meir. The implication appears to extend further than merely the Torah that Rabbi Meir received from *Acher*: because he learned from *Acher*, his entire corpus is kept out of the heavenly *yeshiva*. It did not invalidate the teachings; it excluded them.

---

## Pomegranate Seeds

### God Teaching

To appreciate the full arc of this passage, it is worth pausing on the image of God teaching in heaven from the mouths of all the rabbis. The *gemara* here presents something close to a *lo bashamayim hi* moment in reverse: the Torah that the rabbis developed below is recited above. That Rabbi Meir's teachings are withheld from this recitation is thus a pointed exclusion.

### Why Teach Meir?

Rabba bar Shila pressed Elijah: *amai?* — why? Elijah explained: *mishum de'ka'gamar shmaattah mipumei de'Acher* — because he learned teachings from the mouth of *Acher*. One might ask: does this not extend the problem to the *stam Mishnah* as well, given that Rabbi Meir is understood as the authority behind anonymous *mishnayot*? The answer lies perhaps in a distinction between what is addressed down here and what takes place above. But the irony is real: the *stam Mishnah* preserves Rabbi Meir without naming him, while in heaven his name is withheld. The two forms of anonymity move in opposite directions. Another dimension worth noting is the nature of *Torah* and *mesorah* itself. If a *talmid chacham* is essentially a vehicle — transmitting what he received — then what he teaches remains intact regardless of the vehicle's flaws. But if Torah scholarship involves creative engagement, then the personality of the scholar is more deeply implicated in the product, and the *Ribono Shel Olam*'s refusal to quote Rabbi Meir becomes more theologically coherent.

### Pomegranate Defense

Rabba bar Shila challenged Elijah: *Rabbi Meir rimon matza, tocho achal, klipato zarak* — Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the seeds, and discarded the rind. The pomegranate is a richer image than the date: it is filled with seeds, each one dense with content, and requires careful effort to extract them from the surrounding rind. It is also laden with associations of *mitzvot*. Rabba bar Shila's argument is that Rabbi Meir's selective extraction from *Acher* was an act of genuine discernment — not passive consumption but active, careful separation of content from vessel. The response is immediate. Elijah says: *hasha kamar* — now they are saying, *Meir bni omer* — "here is what Meir my son says." The heavenly academy has reversed its position on the strength of this single point, and Rabbi Meir's teachings are now quoted above.

### Shared Suffering

The teaching that God chooses to quote in Rabbi Meir's name is this: *bizman she'adam mitzta'er, Shechina mah lashon omeret? Kalani me-roshi kalani me-zero-i* — when a person is in pain, the *Shechina* says, "I am made light from my head, I am made light from my arm" — a euphemism indicating that God himself suffers. *Im kacha Hakadosh Baruch Hu mitzta'er al damam shel resha'im, kal vachomer al damam shel tzaddikim shenispach* — if God suffers even over the blood of the wicked, how much more so over the blood of the righteous who are killed. This is the teaching selected to represent Rabbi Meir in heaven — one about empathy, about God's identification with human suffering, including the suffering of those who are not *tzaddikim*. The allusion to *Acher* is difficult to avoid. Even he, who abandoned Torah, is not simply to be dismissed. God feels the pain of the wicked, and therefore *Acher*'s fate cannot be a matter of complete indifference. The teaching that rehabilitates Rabbi Meir in the heavenly academy is precisely the one most relevant to *Acher* himself.

---

## Corruption & Culture

### Weeping Question

The *gemara* now introduces a new scene. Samuel encountered Rav Yehuda leaning against the bolt of a gate, weeping. Samuel asked him — addressing him as *shinina*, sharp one — why he was crying. Rav Yehuda replied: *mi zutra mai d'chtiv u'rabbanan?* — is it a small matter, what is written by the rabbis? He then cites the verse from Isaiah: *ayei sofer, ayei shokel, ayei sofer tamigdalim* — where is the scribe, where is the weigher, where is the one who counts the towers?

### Doeg & Achitofel

The verse is interpreted to evoke three categories of scholarship that once existed and have been lost. *Ayei sofer* — those who counted every letter of the Torah. *Ayei shokel* — those who weighed the *kal va'chomer* arguments, who knew which legal principles were light and which were heavy. *Ayei sofer tamigdalim* — those who knew 300 *halachot* about the *migdal haporei'ach ba'avir*, the tower that floats in the air. Rashi explains this as a reference to the *mishnah* in *Ohalot* dealing with a chest half inside and half outside a house and the transfer of *tumah* — not a literally floating tower, but the evocative imagery of *porchim ba'avir* seemed appropriate here regardless. Rabbi Ami adds: Doeg and Achitofel — who represent great *talmidei chachamim* who were nonetheless *resha'im* — themselves raised 300 questions about this subject. And yet: *gimel melachim v'arba hedyotot ein lahem chelek l'olam haba* — three kings and four commoners have no portion in the world to come, among whom Doeg and Achitofel are counted.

### Our Hope?

This is Rav Yehuda's cry: *anan ma te'hei alan?* — if such figures, with their extraordinary Torah knowledge, could go off the *derech*, what will become of us? If *Acher*, if Doeg, if Achitofel — people of such immense scholarship — were not preserved by that Torah, what hope do we have?

### Heart Corruption

Samuel's answer is pointed: *tina hayisa belibam* — there was already corruption in their hearts from the beginning. The problem was not that their Torah failed to protect them from something that attacked them from outside. Rather, they had their own lusts, their own desires, their own internal drives — and those were present from the very start. Torah did not fail these people; rather, they were not people whose raw material was suited to be fully transformed by it.

### Greek Song

The *gemara* then asks specifically about *Acher*: what was his *tina*? *Zemer Yavani lo fasak mipumei* — the Greek song never stopped from his mouth. He was deeply and persistently drawn to Hellenistic culture. The phrase *tarbus ra'ah* — bad culture — is resonant here; *tarbus* in modern Hebrew simply means culture, and that is precisely the point. It was not merely intellectual temptation that pulled *Acher* away. It began with cultural attraction: the music, the sensibility, the entire world that Greek civilization represented. Rashi's comment here is notable, if somewhat reductive — he emphasizes *lo fasak*, the unceasing quality of the singing, framing the problem as a failure to mourn the *churban* properly, citing the verse that one should not drink wine accompanied by song. But the real weight of the phrase seems to fall on *Yavani* — it was specifically Greek song, representing a cultural seduction that Rashi's reading somewhat softens.

### Minim Books

The *gemara* continues: *besha'ah shehayah omeid mibeis hamedrash, harbei sifrei minim noshrim micheiko* — when *Acher* would rise from the *beis medrash*, books of *minim* — whether Greek philosophy, or perhaps Jewish-Christian literature — would fall from his lap. One pictures him hiding them beneath his texts in the study hall, carrying two worlds simultaneously. This passage presents a very different explanation for *Acher*'s fall than the mystical account of his experience in *Pardes*. There, it was a theological error arising from an encounter he was not equipped to properly understand. Here, it is something far more mundane and recognizable: cultural attraction that preceded and prepared the ground for intellectual apostasy. The two explanations are not necessarily incompatible. The Greek song created a disposition; the philosophical and theological seduction followed. The question about what leads a person away from a life of observance — whether it begins with genuine intellectual challenge or with the pull of the outside world's broader attractions — is one the *gemara* addresses with real psychological sophistication here. The conflict between them is often not as clean as it appears. Sometimes what presents itself as a philosophical crisis is, at its root, a desire for everything else that comes with abandoning the restrictions of observance. Sometimes, as the *Vilna Gaon* is said to have observed, what looks like questions are really answers in disguise — conclusions already reached in search of justification.

---

## Wool & Dye

### Dye Question

A weaver named Nimus HaGardi — identified by *Tosafot* as a Greek philosopher who opposed paganism — posed a question to Rabbi Meir: *kol amar denachis leyoreh salik?* — does all wool that goes into the dyeing vat come out well-dyed?

### Clean Wool

Rabbi Meir answered: *kol ma dahavei naki agav imei, salik* — anything that was clean when it was shorn from the animal will hold the dye when it emerges from the vat. *Kol delo havei naki agav imei, lo salik* — anything that was not clean to begin with will not hold the dye. The premise of good dyeing is good raw material.

### Raw Material

The application is transparent: if Torah is the dye, then the raw material of a person's character determines whether the Torah will hold. This is the explanation for the *tina hayisa belibam* — if the raw material was flawed from the outset, Torah cannot always be expected to produce a complete transformation. This is a remarkable admission. Torah can be transformative, but it is not magic. Religion can enrich and shape a person of good character, help them grow, deepen their commitment. But it is unrealistic to expect it to wholly reconstitute someone whose underlying character is significantly compromised. People are still people. The future promise of *vahasiroti es lev ha'even* — I will remove the heart of stone — belongs to a world that has not yet arrived. In this world, transformation is incremental, and the raw material matters enormously. What is being explained here is not a reason to abandon *Acher*, as Rabbi Meir's own persistent attempts to bring him back demonstrate. It is rather an explanation for why enormous Torah scholarship did not, in *Acher*'s case, prove sufficient to keep him on the *derech* — and why that need not be taken as a theological indictment of Torah itself.

---

## Rabbi Akiva

### Up & Down Peace

The *gemara* now returns to the *Pardes* narrative, turning at last to Rabbi Akiva. *Rabbi Akiva ala beshalom veyarad beshalom* — Rabbi Akiva went up in peace and came down in peace. This formulation is notable: the addition of *ala beshalom* is new. The others who entered did not emerge whole; Rabbi Akiva entered whole and exited the same way. The verse applied to him is from *Shir HaShirim*: *moshcheini acharecha narutza* — draw me after you and I will run. Rabbi Akiva was famously the one who declared *kol hashirim kodesh ve-Shir HaShirim kodesh kodashim*, understanding *Shir HaShirim* as a *mashal* of divine encounter. For him, the image is apt: God needed only to draw him slightly near, and he was ready to run — because he was already prepared for the encounter.

### Angels' Objection

Even so, *bikshu malachei hashareis lidoffo* — the ministering angels sought to push him away. God intervened: *hanichu lazaken zeh, she-raui le-hishtamesh bichvodi* — let this elder be; he is fit to use my honor. The phrase *le-hishtamesh bichvodi* is unusual — to make use of God's honor — suggesting some form of intimate access or participation in the divine presence.

### Gaze Divine

Rabbeinu Chananel's *girsa* reads differently: *raui hu le-histakel bichvodi* — he is fit to gaze upon my *kavod*. In this reading, the contrast with Ben Zoma is made explicit: Ben Zoma *hetzitz venifga* — he peered and was struck. Rabbi Akiva was fit to have the vision that Ben Zoma was not. The *kavod Hashem*, elsewhere described as *kvod Hashem nireh be'anan*, is understood as a tangible manifestation of the divine presence, and Rabbi Akiva's qualification to perceive it sets him apart from the others who entered *Pardes*.

---

## Distinguish God

### The Sign

*Mai darash?* — what did Rabbi Akiva understand that protected him from the error into which *Acher* fell? Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse: *ve-ata meirevivot kodesh*. The word *ata* — you — contains within it an *ot*, a sign: *ot hu berivavo shelo* — God is marked out, distinguishable, within his own myriads. The implication, as Rashi reads it, is that Rabbi Akiva, when encountering the divine retinue, was able to discern God from the angels. *Acher* saw Metatron and, catastrophically, mistook him for a second divine power. Rabbi Akiva would not have made that error because he knew that God is always recognizably distinct from the angels — even from the greatest among them.

### God as Example

Rabbi Abbahu offers a reading of the same idea through a different term: *dugma hu be-revava shelo* — God is the *dugma*, the original, within his myriad. The word *dugma* usually refers to a model after which others are patterned, though here it functions to mark God's distinctiveness within the divine retinue.

### Master of Hosts

Resh Lakish adds: *Hashem Tzeva'ot Shemo, adon hu betzeva shelo* — God's name is *Hashem Tzeva'ot*, meaning he is the master within his own hosts. The very name of God encodes his supremacy over and distinction from the angelic beings that surround him.

### Beyond Elements

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, citing Rabbi Yochanan, then invokes the theophany from Elijah's cave: *lo veruach Hashem, ve-achar haruach ra'ash, lo beraash Hashem, ve-achar hara'ash esh, lo va'esh Hashem, ve-achar ha'esh kol demama daka* — God was not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire; after the fire, a still small voice. The *Maharsha* notes that the angels of wind, earthquake, and fire are each powerful in their own right — but God is encountered in something altogether different. Rabbi Akiva understood that all the dramatic manifestations of the angelic realm were precisely *not* God; God had to be sought elsewhere, in a qualitatively different mode of encounter.

### Acher in Verse

It would be impossible to cite this verse — *ve-achar haruach ra'ash* — without noticing the word *acher* embedded within it. The linguistic echo seems almost too apt. *Acher* is the one who encountered precisely the wind, the earthquake, the fire — the angelic beings — and could not see past them to the God who lay beyond. Rabbi Akiva could. That discernment was the difference.

---

## Shedim & Humans

### Shedim Angelic

The *gemara* now presents a *baraita* that at first seems unrelated to what preceded. *Tanu Rabbanan: shisha devarim neemru bashedim* — the rabbis taught: six things were said about *shedim*. Three of them resemble the ministering angels: *yesh lahem knafayim kemalachei hashareis* — they have wings; *vetasin misof ha'olam ve'ad sofo* — they fly from one end of the world to the other; *veyodin mah she'asid lihyot kemalachei hashareis* — and they know what is destined to occur. A qualification immediately follows: surely they cannot know the future intrinsically? Rather, *ela shom'in me'achorei hapargod* — they hear from behind the divine curtain, just as the ministering angels do. Their knowledge of the future is derivative, not inherent.

### Shedim Human

The other three characteristics of *shedim* resemble human beings: *ochlin veshotin kivnei adam* — they eat and drink; *parin veravin kivnei adam* — they procreate; *umesim kivnei adam* — and they die. Angels do not die; *shedim* do. This last detail is particularly significant, placing *shedim* closer to the human end of the spectrum than to the angelic.

### Humans Angelic

Six things are then said about human beings, three of which resemble the ministering angels. *Yesh lahem da'at kemalachei hashareis* — they possess intellect. *Umehalchin bekomah zkufah kemalachei hashareis* — they walk upright, an expression of human dignity. *Umesaprim belashon hakodesh kemalachei hashareis* — they speak in the holy tongue, or more broadly, they possess spoken language, which is the province of the angels.

### Humans Animal

The remaining three characteristics of humans resemble animals: *ochlin veshotin keveheimah* — they eat and drink; *parin veravin keveheimah* — they procreate; *umotzi'in re'i keveheimah* — and they excrete waste. The physical, appetitive, and reproductive dimensions of human life are shared with the animal kingdom.

### Human Paradox

Taken together, the portrait that emerges is of the human being as a genuinely hybrid creature — partly angelic, partly animal, with intellect and upright bearing and language on one side, and digestion and reproduction and death on the other. This connects, in a profound way, to the broader discussion of *ma'aseh merkavah* and the challenges of mystical ascent. The fundamental tension of *Pardes* — who can enter, who is damaged, who comes out whole — is in part a tension about what kind of being a human being is. Can a physical creature, constituted partly like an animal, really rise to encounter the divine? The story of Rabbi Akiva says yes, but only for one who is truly complete — *shalom* from the start. The story of *Acher*, Doeg, Achitofel, and Ben Zoma all illuminate, in different ways, what happens when that completeness is absent.

---

## God's Honor

### Four Unknowns

The *gemara* now introduces a *baraita* about what one may not investigate: *kol hamistakel be'arba'ah devarim, raui lo shelo ba la'olam* — whoever looks into four things, it would have been better for him not to have come into the world: what is above, what is below, what was before, and what will be after.

### Why Past OK?

The *gemara* finds the formulation puzzling. *Bishlama l'ma'alah l'matah* — I understand the prohibition on investigating what lies above or below, or *l'achor*, the future. *Ela lefanim* — but regarding what came before, *mah dehava hava* — what was, was. Why should inquiry into the primordial past be any more problematic than inquiry into what has already transpired? The underlying subject is clearly questions about the nature of creation itself — what existed above and below the world, what lies beyond the heavens, what the future of the world will be, and what the origins of the world were before it came to be.

### Dung Heap

Rabbi Yochanan bar Eleazar answers with a parable: *mashal l'melech basar v'dam she'amar l'avadav bnu li paltarin gedolin* — it is like a king who instructed his servants to build him a great palace. The best available land happened to be a dung heap. They built the palace, filled in and covered over the dung heap, and now the palace stands in all its beauty. *Ein ritzono shel hamelech lehazkir shem ashpah* — the king does not want anyone to mention that the site was once a dung heap.

### Tohu v'Vohu

The application: God made the world out of *tohu v'vohu* — primordial chaos and formlessness. Raising questions about those origins — about the mess from which creation emerged — is to undermine the dignity and beauty of the creation that now exists. It is, in that sense, disrespectful of *kvod kono*, God's honor. One need not claim to fully understand the theology here; the *gemara* itself presents this as a *mashal* rather than a direct explanation.

---

## Three Gazes

### Rainbow Glory

The *gemara* then cites the verse: *k'mareh hakeshet asher yihyeh be'anan b'yom hageshem, ken mareh hanogah saviv, hu mareh dmut kvod Hashem* — like the appearance of the rainbow in the cloud on a rainy day, so was the appearance of the radiance surrounding it; that is the appearance of the likeness of the *kvod Hashem*. To gaze directly at the rainbow is, in some sense, to gaze at this manifestation of the divine presence.

### King's Glory

Similarly, one should not gaze at a king. The verse *ve-natata me-hodcha alav* — you shall give of your glory to him — refers to Moshe transmitting something of his own radiance to Yehoshua, a radiance that derived ultimately from proximity to God. A king bears something of that divine glory as well.

### Kohanim's Presence

And one should not gaze at the *kohanim* when they stand on the *duchan* during the time of the *Beis HaMikdash*, reciting the priestly blessing with God's explicit name. At that moment, the *Shechina* rests upon their fingers. Gazing at them is gazing at the divine presence itself.

### Not Really Glory

Rabbeinu Chananel offers a distinctive reading of the rainbow prohibition. The problem is not that the rainbow *is* the *kvod Hashem* and one must not look. Rather, the problem is that one *says* it is the likeness of God's glory — when in fact it is not. The failure to be *chas al kvod kono* lies in the error of identification, in conflating a natural phenomenon with the divine presence itself.

### Mystical Rainbow

In *kabbalistic* interpretation, by contrast, the rainbow is treated with considerable literalness as a mystical symbol, and being *mistakel bakeshet* is a genuinely grave matter. The association of the rainbow — its form, its emergence from behind the clouds — with the *kvod Hashem* is developed in ways that take the verse more directly than Rabbeinu Chananel's rationalist reframing allows. The *gemara*'s concern may be precisely that gazing carries with it the risk of confusing the symbol for the reality — a version, in fact, of the same error that destroyed *Acher* in *Pardes*.

---

## Private vs. Public

### Push Away God

The *gemara* cites Rabbi Yosef: *zeh ha'over aveirah b'seter* — the one who transgresses in private also belongs in the category of *kol shelo chas al kvod kono*. The verse *koh amar Hashem, hashamayim kisei veha'aretz hadom raglai* — heaven is my throne and the earth is my footstool — grounds the concern: sinning in private amounts to pushing away God's footstool, to behaving as though God's presence does not extend into private space.

### God Sees All

Rabbi Yitzchak sharpens the point: *kol ha'over aveirah b'seter k'ilu dochek raglei Shechinah* — whoever transgresses in private acts as though pushing away the feet of the *Shechina*. The theological failure of private sin is the implicit claim, whether conscious or not, that God does not see what is done when no human observer is present. Sinning in public at least involves the acknowledgment, however defiant, that one's actions are visible. Sinning in private carries the deeper distortion of treating God's presence as bounded by human visibility.

### Illai's Leniency

And yet the *gemara* immediately introduces a counterpoint. Rabbi Illai the Elder taught: *im ro'eh adam she'yitzro mitgaber alav, yelech lemakom she'ein makkirin oto, ve-yilbash shechorim, ve-yitatef shechorim, ve-ya'aseh mah she-libo chafetz, ve-al yechalel shem shamayim befarhesya* — if a person sees that his *yetzer hara* is overcoming him, he should go to a place where no one recognizes him, dress in black, and do what his heart desires — rather than desecrate God's name publicly. This appears, on its surface, to directly endorse private sin as preferable to public sin, at least when the desire is overwhelming.

### Control Desire

The *gemara* reconciles the apparent contradiction: *lo kashya, ha de-matikif lei yitzrei, ha de-lo matikif lei yitzrei* — there is no contradiction; the cases differ based on whether the *yetzer hara* overwhelms the person or does not. If one's desire is truly overwhelming and the sin will occur regardless, then it is preferable for it to occur privately rather than publicly, avoiding *chillul Hashem*. If, however, one could resist but chooses to sin in private precisely because no one will see — then that person is *dochek raglei ha-Shechina*, sinning against the very fabric of the divine presence in the world.

### Sin Hierarchy

The practical conclusion that emerges is: if one must sin, private is better than public. If one can avoid sin, one should avoid it entirely. The difficulty, of course, is that this reasoning can quickly become self-serving: once one tells oneself that the sin will occur regardless, going somewhere private becomes a form of permission rather than a last resort.

### Rishonim Reject

This is precisely what troubled many *rishonim* deeply. They were unwilling to read the *gemara* as licensing private sin even in extremis. Their reading: going to a place where one is unknown, dressing in black mourning clothes — these are acts designed not to facilitate the sin but to create humility and discomfort, to make the person feel so out of place and burdened that the desire itself dissipates. *Ve-ya'aseh mah she-libo chafetz* — "do what your heart desires" — means, in their reading, that by that point the heart no longer desires to sin. The concern is real and practical. Once a person tells himself that the sin is inevitable and it is therefore permitted to pursue it privately — and perhaps even remove outward markers of identity to facilitate that — a far greater license has been extended than the *gemara* intended. The question asked of Rav Moshe Feinstein about wearing a *kippah* while attending improper films illustrates the same problem: does removing the *kippah* prevent *chillul Hashem*, or does it simply grant a far more comfortable path to transgression?

---

## Yetzer Hara Warnings

### Believe Not

The *gemara* concludes with a *derashah* by Rabbi Yehuda b'Rebbe Nachmani, the *turgeman* of Reish Lakish. The verse *al ta'aminu b'rei, al tivtechu b'aluf* — do not trust in a friend (*rei*), do not put your faith in an officer (*aluf*) — is read as a warning against two distinct forms of false confidence. *Rei* is re-read as *ra* — evil, the *yetzer hara*. *V'ein ra ela yetzer hara, shene'emar ki yetzer lev ha'adam ra mine'urav* — there is no *ra* other than the *yetzer hara*, as the verse says, for the inclination of a man's heart is evil from his youth.

### Forgive Argument

The precise seduction the *gemara* has in mind is this: *im yomar lecha yetzer hara, chata, ve-Hakadosh Baruch Hu mochel* — if the *yetzer hara* tells you, go ahead and sin, and God will forgive — this is what one must not believe. The argument is seasonally pointed. As *Rosh Hashanah* approaches and *Yom Kippur* looms, the *yetzer hara*'s most effective tool is precisely this: transgress now, repent later. The machinery of atonement becomes, in the *yetzer hara*'s hands, a license to sin.

### Trust God

*Al tivtechu b'aluf* — do not put your trust in the *aluf*. And who is the *aluf* here? *V'ein aluf ela Hakadosh Baruch Hu, shene'emar aluf ne'urai atah* — there is no *aluf* other than God. The verse "do not trust in the dignitary" becomes, in this reading, a warning not to presume on God's forgiveness. Do not trust that God will simply absorb whatever you do because *Yom Kippur* is coming.

### Bricks Testify

And if one objects: who will even know? *Shema tomar mi me'idi bi* — what if you say, who will testify against me? *Avnei beiso v'koros beiso shel adam hem me'idim bo* — the very bricks and beams of a person's house will testify against him. *Shene'emar ki even mikir tiz'ak ve-chaphis mei-eitz ya'anena* — for the stone cries out from the wall and the beam of wood answers it.

### Multiple Witnesses

The *gemara* then presents additional witnesses: the sages say that *nishmato shel adam me'idah bo* — a person's own soul testifies against him, as the verse *mishkavas cheikecha shemor pischei ficha* indicates, for what lies in the bosom of a person is the *neshama* itself. Rabbi Zreika adds: *shenei malachei hashareis ha-malvin oto hem me'idim bo* — the two ministering angels who accompany every person will testify against him, as the verse says, *ki malachav yetzaveh lach lishmorcha bechol derachecha* — for he will command his angels to watch over you in all your ways. They are watching. And others say: *evarav shel adam me'idim bo* — a person's own limbs testify against him, as it says, *ve-atem eidai ne'um Hashem va'ani el* — you yourselves are my witnesses, says God.

### Real Consequences

These sources need not be read as purely metaphysical accounts of some future heavenly tribunal. There is something deeply real in each of them. The bricks and beams of one's home testify — one's environment reflects one's values and conduct, shaped visibly by the choices one makes there. The *neshama* testifies — one's character is formed and deformed by one's actions; the soul bears the imprint of what a person does with it. The limbs testify — the body itself is shaped by how it is used, trained or neglected, directed toward service or degraded by misuse. In each case, our actions do not remain private. They leave their mark — on our homes, our characters, our bodies — in ways that are entirely real, even before any metaphysical accounting takes place. With that, and in the spirit of the season, may the year ahead be one in which all our actions reflect for us in wholly positive ways. *Ksiva ve-chasima tova*.

---

---

# Chagigah 20

## Intro & Prior Review

### Opening

We pick up today on Daf 20, *amud bet*, three lines from the top, beginning with the passage *hatovel lechulin vehuchzak lechulin*.

### Theme Overview

This passage sits at the heart of a *perek* whose animating theme will carry through the following *perek* as well — a somewhat unusual structural phenomenon, though not without precedent. The subject is the laws of *tumah v'taharah* as they generate distinct levels of care required for increasingly elevated degrees of *kedushah*, and how those graduated requirements effectively stratify society. Those who eat their *chulin b'taharah* occupy a different social stratum from those who maintain the purity standards required for *terumah*, who in turn differ from those who handle *kodesh*. This entire structure of differentiation is, as we have seen, suspended on the *regel* in the interest of communal unity.

### Earlier Cases Summary

The *Mishnah* has already given us several cases, and in each the *Gemara* has moved to limit or qualify the stated rule in some measure. The first ruling concerned washing hands before eating *chulin*, which the *Gemara* restricted to a case of eating bread specifically — not a general obligation covering all handling of non-sanctified food. Next came the question of *kavanah* at the *mikvah*: the simple reading of the *Mishnah* would have suggested that immersion without intent is entirely without effect, but the *Gemara* clarified that absent *kavanah* the immersion is still valid for *chulin* purposes — a ruling that remains practically significant today for a *niddah* going to the *mikvah*, where *kavanah* is not treated as an impediment. Finally, and more surprisingly, the *Gemara* entertained the position that open-ended *kavanah* — or the absence of any specific intent — can be retroactively defined at a higher level, provided one is still wet from the immersion. In each instance, the *Gemara* is engaged in a project of measured mitigation.

### Post-Churban Shift

It is worth pausing to note that the entire institution of *chaberim* — those who consumed their *chulin b'taharah* and who constituted the most punctilious stratum of this social structure — appears to have faded substantially after the *Churban HaBayit*, or at least within a generation or two of it. This makes sense: these are fundamentally Temple-oriented practices, and it is not even entirely clear that *Chazal* themselves instituted them. They may have emerged organically from Temple-adjacent circles, possibly with connections to more Temple-centered groups. By a later stage in the *Gemara*, these practices are largely no longer observed.

What *Chazal* did preserve, and indeed universalized, was a different set of mechanisms for introducing *kedushah* into the act of eating. The washing of hands before bread — which everybody does equally — evokes the world of *tumah v'taharah* while eliminating the sharp stratification. Similarly, the requirement to recite *brachot* before eating, about which the *Gemara* states that one who eats without a *bracha* has acted as though committing *me'ilah* against *hekdesh*, brings an awareness of *kedushah* to every meal in a way that is uniformly accessible. These are practices that carry the spirit of *taharat ha-kodesh* into daily life without fracturing the community.

---

## Hierarchy Mishna

### Mishna Text

With that context in mind, we reach the passage itself. The *Mishnah* states: one who immerses for *chulin* purposes and is established as intending purity for *chulin* — *Rashi* reads *huchzak* as denoting that intent — achieves a status fit for *chulin* but not for *maaser*. One who immerses for *maaser* achieves fitness for *maaser* but not for *terumah*. One who immerses for *terumah* achieves fitness for *terumah* but not for *kodesh*, and so forth.

### Sages vs Rabbi Meir

The *Gemara* immediately asks: *mani matnitin* — whose position does our *Mishnah* follow? The answer is *Rabbanan hi* — it reflects the position of the Sages in the *Baraita* cited earlier. Recall the dispute between the Sages and *Rabbi Meir* over whether one must wash hands before eating *maaser*. The Sages held that *maaser* does occupy a distinct level above *chulin*, and this *Mishnah*, which treats *maaser* as a separate rung in the hierarchy, reflects precisely that view rather than *Rabbi Meir*'s, who treated *maaser* and *chulin* as equivalent in this regard.

### Seifa Clothes Status

The *Gemara* then says *eima seifa* — let us examine the end of the *Mishnah*. There it states: *bigdei am ha'aretz midras le-perushim* — the garments of an *am ha'aretz* are considered *midras*, that is, they carry the status of having been sat upon by a *zav*, *zavah*, or *niddah*, making them an *av hatumah* for *perushim*, those who eat their *chulin b'taharah*. The *Mishnah* then states that the garments of *perushim* are *midras* for those who eat *terumah*.

### Maaser Gap Problem

One notices immediately that the group of people who are careful specifically for *maaser b'taharah* is entirely absent. The hierarchy leaps directly from those careful for *chulin* to those careful for *terumah*, bypassing the intermediate *maaser* category entirely. The *Gemara* notes: *atan le-Rabbi Meir* — we have now arrived at the position of *Rabbi Meir*, who holds that *chulin* and *maaser* are treated identically and therefore generates no separate social stratum for those careful about *maaser*. This creates an apparent inconsistency: the *reisha* of the *Mishnah* seems to follow the Sages, while the *seifa* follows *Rabbi Meir*. The *Gemara* considers whether the *Mishnah* could simply combine two positions from different authorities, and suggests that perhaps that is indeed the case — *reisha Rabbanan u-seifa Rabbi Meir*. Since both parts of the *Mishnah* are anonymous, there is nothing formally objectionable about attributing them to different schools.

### Rav Acha's Amendment

*Rav Acha bar Adda* takes a different approach. He reports that he would teach the *seifa* with an additional, fifth level inserted — a group of people who are careful about eating *maaser b'taharah* — and on that reading the entire *Mishnah* is consistent with the Sages throughout, reflecting throughout the position that *maaser* constitutes a distinct stratum.

---

## Upward Mobility Question

### Rav Mari Position

The *Gemara* now introduces a new question by way of *Rav Mari*: *amar Rav Mari shema mina chullin she-naasu al taharat ha-kodesh ke-kodesh dami* — if someone treats his *chulin* with the same degree of care as *kodesh*, maintaining the same stringent *kavanah* at the *mikvah* and the same vigilance against any form of contamination that would compromise *kodesh* even if it would not affect *chulin*, then that *chulin* has the status of *kodesh*.

The practical question this generates is the following. Consider a person who is not a *kohen*, who does not eat *korbanot*, who has not recently been in the *Beis Hamikdash* — in short, who eats only *chulin*, never *kodesh* in any literal sense. Yet every single thing he eats, he treats as though it were a *korban*. What is the status of his garments? Are they *midras* to *ochlei terumah* because, at the end of the day, he is a man who eats only *chulin b'taharah*? Or, since the level of care he exhibits is that of *al taharat ha-kodesh*, do we place him in that category — such that his clothes are entirely *tahor* for everyone except someone handling a *parah adumah*? This is the question of whether exhibiting a higher level of care can elevate a person into a higher social stratum, even without the technical act of eating *kodesh*.

### Category Inference

The *Gemara* presses: *mimai* — from where does *Rav Mari* derive his inference? He argues from the fact that the *Mishnah* does not list someone who eats *chulin al taharat ha-kodesh* as a separate, distinct category. Since no new stratum is created for such a person, *Rav Mari* reasons that the *Mishnah* must be absorbing him into the existing *kodesh* category.

The *Gemara* rejects this inference immediately. The absence of a separate stratum does not tell you which existing group he falls into. Perhaps he belongs in the *chulin* group, since at the end of the day his food remains *chulin*. Or perhaps, as a compromise reflecting that he exhibits *kodesh*-level care but eats only *chulin*, he falls into the *terumah* group. Or perhaps *Rav Mari* is right and he belongs in the *kodesh* group. The *Mishnah*'s silence simply cannot determine the question.

### Baraita: No Elevation

The *Gemara* therefore turns to a *Baraita*: *chullin she-naasu al taharat ha-kodesh — harei ke-chulin*. One who treats his *chulin* with the purity level of *kodesh* — it remains, nonetheless, as *chulin*. The extra care confers no upward mobility whatsoever. This is a striking position: no matter how scrupulous one's behavior, if one does not actually eat *kodesh*, one cannot exit the *chulin* category. There is stratification without any upward mobility — a society divided into levels with no mechanism for ascending.

### Elazar Bar Tzadok

*Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok* dissents: *harei ki-trumah* — such a person achieves the level of *terumah*. This is something of a middle path. It does not go all the way to *kodesh*, but it does allow some upward mobility. Demonstrating the care of *al taharat ha-kodesh* lifts you at least one level above your actual eating category.

### Historical Examples

The *Gemara* then cites evidence from the end of our *Mishnah* itself. *Yosei ben Yoezer*, identified as *chasid shebakehuna*, one of the most pious of *kohanim*, nonetheless could never get his garments out of *midras* status for those eating *kodesh* — his *mitpachto* remained an *av hatumah* for *ochlei korbanot*. By contrast, *Yochanan ben Gudgada*, who ate all his food *al taharat ha-kodesh* — the language itself suggesting that he was not in fact eating actual *kodesh* but was maintaining that level of care — found that his garments were considered *midras lachatas*, that is, problematic for someone handling a *parah adumah*, but *lo le-kodesh* — not a problem for those eating *korbanot*. This appears to demonstrate clearly that eating *chulin al taharat ha-kodesh* is recognized as equivalent to *kodesh* status for purposes of the social hierarchy.

### Mishna Position

The *Gemara* concludes: *alma kasavar chullin she-naasu al taharat ha-kodesh ke-kodesh dami* — our *Mishnah* holds that if one exhibits *kodesh*-level care, one enters the *kodesh* category, allowing full upward mobility. This, notably, is yet another instance of the *Gemara* introducing a mitigating or democratizing element: the structure remains stratified, but the stratification is at least permeable. Anyone willing to exhibit the requisite level of care can place themselves in the higher group, regardless of their technical eating category.

---

## Conscious Attention Rule

### Fallen Scarf Case

*Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar* teaches: if one's scarf (*mafrato*) fell from him, and he said to his friend, "Please hand it to me," and the friend handed it back, it is considered *temeiah*.

### Care Explanation

The reasoning requires unpacking. Even if the friend is himself *tahor*, the moment someone else is handling the object, the original owner is no longer in a position to exercise the same direct, unmediated care. The owner, consciously or not, relaxes his vigilance — he asked the friend without first vetting him, without asking "are you *tahor*? to what level are you careful?" The absence of that inquiry signals that the owner is not operating at the full level of concern, and therefore we cannot assume the garment has been maintained at the required standard.

This introduces what will become one of the most demanding and, one might say, unsettling principles of this entire discussion: it is not merely the objective condition of an object that determines its *taharah* status, but the active, conscious attention of the person responsible for it. The moment that attention is compromised — by delegating handling to another, by momentary confusion about the identity of the object — the presumption of *taharah* dissolves.

The *Gemara* then considers whether the physical location where the object fell should matter — say, if it fell in a *reshus ha-rabim*. The *Gemara* proceeds to address this in context, and we will follow its lead.

### Supporting Cases

Two additional cases extend the principle. *Rabbi Yochanan ben Amram* teaches: if one went to one's closet intending to take out weekday clothes and accidentally took out Shabbat clothes — *nischalafu lo keilim shel Shabbos b'keilim shel chol* — and dressed in them, they are considered *tamei*. This seems entirely bizarre: these are your own clothes, in your own closet, and you simply grabbed the wrong ones. *Rashi*'s reading of the case has it that the person wanted the weekday garments and inadvertently took the Shabbat ones.

A further case: *Elazar ben Tzadok* reports an incident involving two women who were *chaveros* — that is, they were not *amei ha'aretz* but women careful about *taharah* — whose garments became mixed up in the bathhouse (*beis ha-merchatz*). They came before *Rabbi Akiva*, who ruled that the garments were *tamei*. The common thread in the last two cases is that whenever one is not handling one's own identified object with the expected level of care, the presumption of *taharah* fails.

### Gemara Challenge

*Rav Oshaya* raises a strong objection. If the rule is simply that any lapse in full conscious attention renders an object *tamei*, then consider: one reached into a basket to take a wheat roll and a barley roll came up in one's hand — does that too become *tamei*? And if one says, yes, why not, a *Baraita* contradicts this: *ha-mishamer et ha-chavis be-chezkat she-hu yayin ve-nimtza she-hu shemen — tehorah mi-litamei*. If one was guarding a barrel assuming it was wine and it turned out to be oil, it remains *tehorah* — it will not be *metamei* other things. So confusion about the identity of the object seems not to matter there.

But the *Gemara* notes that *Rav Oshaya* did not quote the end of that *Baraita*: *ve'asurah me'achol* — it may not be eaten. So we have a strange middle position: the barrel does not transmit *tumah* to other things, yet the person who maintains *taharah* standards cannot eat from it. How can something be *tahor* enough not to spread *tumah* yet simultaneously be disqualified from consumption? The resolution, offered by *Rabbi Yirmiyah*, is that the owner declared: *shimartia mi-davar ha-metame'ah velo mi-davar ha-poslah* — "I guarded it against something that would make it *tamei* [i.e., able to pass on *tumah*], but not against something that would merely render it *pasul* [i.e., *tamei* at a level too low to pass on]." There is, in other words, selective *shemirah* — the owner was deliberately guarding against an *av ha-tumah* or *rishon* reaching the barrel, but was not concerned about a *sheni le-tumah* touching it.

---

## Barrel & Provision C (II)

### Basket Figs Shovel

The *Gemara* pursues the logic of selective *shemirah* further with a new *Baraita*. One extended one's hand into a basket, carried the basket on one's shoulder, and inside the basket there were figs along with a type of shovel (*magrefa*) — *Rashi* explains this was used to separate or break up the strings of figs. *Ve-haya be-libo al ha-sal velo haya be-libo al ha-magrefa* — when one was protecting the basket, one's attention was on the figs; one was not even aware the shovel was in there. The ruling: *ha-sal tahor ve-ha-magrefa tme'iah* — the basket and its figs are *tahor*, because that is what the owner had in mind, but the shovel is *tamei*, even though it was sitting right there in the same basket throughout.

### Selective Tumah

The *Gemara* then probes: granted the shovel cannot render the basket directly *tamei* — *ein kli metamei kli*, a vessel cannot impart *tumah* to another vessel at a level beyond *rishon* — but let the shovel, as a *rishon*, render the food (the figs) *tamei* at the level of *sheni*? *Ravina* answers with the familiar formula: *be-omer sheimartiv mi-davar she-metame'o velo mi-davar ha-poslo* — the owner declared that he protected the shovel from an *av ha-tumah* reaching it, so it could not become a *rishon*; but he did not protect it from a *rishon* reaching it, so it may have become a *sheni*. Since a *sheni* cannot render a vessel *tamei* — *ein kli metamei kli* — the basket remains *tahor*. The shovel itself is *pasul* but not capable of passing on *tumah* at the level of *tamei*.

### Gemara Objection

The *Gemara* raises its *teima*: *umi ika netirusa la-palga* — is it really possible to watch something in such a selective and stratified way, carefully guarding against an *av ha-tumah* but not against a *rishon*? This seems extraordinarily improbable as a lived reality. How does one say, in effect, "I will protect this from *tumah* of category A but not category B"? The *Gemara* answers *in* — yes, it is possible — and cites the *Baraita* of the basket as proof that such selective *shemirah* can in fact operate.
