But the *Gemara*'s own question registers the genuine strangeness of this world: an entire cognitive and spiritual discipline of attention in which one must track not only what one is protecting but from which precise categories of *tumah* one is protecting it.

---

## Woman Weaver Case

### Woman's Claim

A woman came before *Rabbi Yishmael* and said to him: *Rabbi, beged zeh aragtihu be-taharah velo haya be-libi leshomro be-taharah* — "Rabbi, I wove this garment in a state of *taharah*, in the sense that nothing happened to contaminate it, but I was not consciously and intentionally guarding it for purposes of *taharah*." She is reporting on a factual outcome: nothing came in contact with the garment. But she acknowledges that this outcome was not the product of deliberate, active *shemirah*; it simply happened.

### Investigation Discovery

*Rabbi Yishmael* then questioned her closely — *umitoch bedikot shehayah Rabbi Yishmael bodek* — and in the course of his investigation something came to light. She said to him: *Rabbi, niddah mashchah imi ba-kevel* — a woman who was a *niddah* had helped her set up the frame of the loom, the rope on which the garment would be woven, and it was possible that she had actually touched the garment in the process.

### Active Guard Requirement

The lesson is unambiguous. It is insufficient to report retroactively that nothing bad happened. Active, conscious guarding is required — not a factual accounting after the fact. The moment that active protection is absent, one must assume the worst case. This principle connects directly to everything we have seen: when the scarf is handed back by a friend, when the wrong clothes are taken from the closet, when the shovel lies unattended in the basket — in each case, the instant that conscious attention is not specifically directed at the object, we do not rely on the favorable outcome. We require the *shemirah* itself, not the result.

### Sages' Wisdom

*Rabbi Yishmael* responds: *kama gedolim divrei chachamim she-hayu omerim be-libo lishmor — tahor; ein be-libo lishmor — tamei*. How great are the words of the Sages, who said: only when one is intentionally guarding it is it *tahor*; if one's intent is not directed at guarding it, it is *tamei* — even if one can report that factually nothing occurred. *Rabbi Yishmael*'s exclamation is not merely formal praise; it reflects the insight that human attention is itself fallible, and the case of the *niddah* who helped with the loom frame demonstrates exactly how something can go wrong without the owner's awareness, even when she reports confidently that "nothing happened." The Sages foresaw this, and the requirement of *belibo lishmor* is the safeguard.

### Tablecloth Case

A second, closely parallel incident follows. Again a woman came before *Rabbi Yishmael*: *Rabbi, mappa zu argatiha be-taharah velo haya be-libi leshomrah* — "I wove this tablecloth and it happened to be *be-taharah*, but I was not consciously intending to guard it." The investigation (*bedikot*) that *Rabbi Yishmael* conducted revealed the following: *nima nifseka li ve-kashartiha be-fi* — a thread broke at some point during the weaving and she held it with her mouth to tie it. *Rashi* explains that she was a *niddah* when she was setting up the frame, before the garment had reached the minimum size of three by three finger-breadths required for *tumah* susceptibility. She then went to the *mikvah* and continued weaving. But once the garment reached the requisite size, some of her saliva from the broken thread was still on it, and the garment became *tamei*. *Tosafot* offers an alternative reading, but the details are secondary. The principle is the same. *Rabbi Yishmael* repeats his formulation verbatim: *kama gedolim divrei chachamim she-hayu omerim be-libo lishmor — tahor; ein be-libo lishmor — tamei*.

---

## Barrel & Provision C (II)

### Barrel Distance Case

The *Gemara* now returns to resolve the outstanding tension. A *Baraita* teaches: if one watched a barrel of wine, assuming it was being kept *tahor*, even from a distance, it remains *tahor*.

### Partial Watching

*Rashi* interprets this as precisely the case of selective *shemirah* we have been discussing: the person watched specifically for things that would make the barrel *tamei* in the full sense — that is, *metamei* other things — but not for things that would merely *pasul* it, i.e., render it *tamei* at a low enough level that it could not pass on *tumah*. This is why the barrel remains *tahor* from the standpoint of not spreading *tumah*, even though it may be *pasul* for eating.

The cases of the Shabbat and weekday clothes, and the garments in the bathhouse, operate on the principle of *mesiach da'at* — a withdrawal of attention — in the following way. In the bathhouse case, *bishlema le-Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok*, each woman says to herself: *chaverti eishet am ha-aretz* — my friend who took my garment is probably married to an *am ha'aretz* — *u-mascha da'ata minah* — and therefore she stops paying attention to it. She does not know who took her garment or how careful that person will be, and so she ceases to maintain the vigilance required. That is the easiest case.

In the case of *Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram* — the Shabbat and weekday clothes — the explanation is: *keivan de-mane de-Shabbos avid lehu shimur tefei* — one is normally more careful about one's Shabbat clothes, keeping them at a higher standard of *taharah*. When one reached into the closet on a weekday and took out what one thought were weekday clothes, one was operating with the level of care appropriate to weekday clothes — slightly less than the level one would bring to Shabbat garments. Even though one's weekday level of care is itself sufficient, the Shabbat clothes were handled at a level below their usual standard, and that differential is enough to compromise their *taharah* status. This is parallel to the basket case: the fruit receives full protection because one's attention is directed at it, while the shovel receives less because one's attention is not.

The remaining puzzle is the case of *Rabbi Yochanan ben Elazar* — where one's scarf falls and a friend hands it back while one is watching the entire time. The *Gemara* asks: why should this not work? One is observing the object every second. The *Gemara* answers with *Rav Yochanan*'s principle: *chazakah ein adam meshamer mah she-beyad chavero* — there is a presumption that a person does not exercise adequate *shemirah* over something that is in someone else's hands. Even if you are watching, once another person is handling it, you unconsciously rely on that person in some measure, and your level of effective vigilance falls below what is required.

---

## Workers Exception

### Workers Tahor Case

A *Baraita* now introduces what seems, in context, a surprising exception. If one's donkey drivers and workers were carrying *tahor* objects — *Rashi* specifies sealed pottery vessels, which can only become *tamei* if something touches the *inside*, so the workers' handling of the exterior does not render the contents *tamei* — and one separated from them by more than a *mil* (roughly a kilometer), the vessels remain *tehorot*. One need not worry that the workers tampered with the contents.

### Nafcha Explanation

*Rav Yitzchak Nafcha* explains the *reisha*: *be-metaher chamarav u-fo'alav le-kach* — this is a case where the owner specifically immersed his donkey drivers and workers in the *mikvah* beforehand, deputized them, and instructed them to maintain *taharah*. Furthermore, they remain vigilant because the owner might arrive by an unexpected shortcut at any moment — *de-ba'atu mi-derech akalton* — and so they do not relax their care.

### Lost Vigilance

But if the owner said to them, *lechu va'ani avo achareichem* — "go on ahead, I'll catch up" — then *keivan she-nitalmu einav mehen tehorot tame'iot*: once they are out of sight and the workers know the owner is not going to arrive suddenly, they relax — *meyatva yatva da'ataihu* — their minds settle, and we must assume the vessels became *tamei*. The threat of an unexpected visit is removed, and with it the pressure that sustained their vigilance.

### Contradiction Tension

This case stands in a certain ironic tension with everything preceding it. There, we saw that taking the wrong clothes out of one's own closet, or having a friend hand back one's scarf while one is watching, renders the object *tamei* — the standard is impossibly demanding. Here, workers who are *amei ha'aretz* carry sealed vessels for over a kilometer out of the owner's sight, and we rule the contents remain *tahor* — because the owner made them *tahor* and the threat of an unannounced inspection looms. It is a notable contrast.

### Tosafot Takanas

*Tosafot* raises a related difficulty: if *amei ha'aretz* are treated as having the status of a *zav* (since we presume they sit anywhere and their seats carry *midras* status), then simply hiring workers who are *amei ha'aretz* should render everything they handle *tamei* immediately. *Tosafot* resolves this by invoking *takanas ha-shuk* — a rabbinic accommodation to market realities. In order to make ordinary commercial activity viable, to allow one to hire day laborers who would naturally come from the broader population rather than exclusively from rabbinic circles, the law is shaped in a way that does not press every principle to its logical extreme. This *takanas ha-shuk* explains why the seemingly incoherent juxtaposition of extreme demands in certain cases and considerable latitude in others is not simply inconsistent, but reflects a deliberate calibration of *halacha* to the practical necessities of a functioning society.

---

## Second Mishna Intro

### Mishna Text

We now arrive at a new *Mishnah*: *chomer ba-kodesh mi-be-trumah* — there are greater stringencies governing *kodesh* (the consumption and handling of *korbanot*) than *terumah*. The *Mishnah* proceeds to enumerate them systematically, and the *Gemara* will spend the coming days unpacking each one.

### Vessel Immersion

The first stringency: *she-matbilin kelim be-toch kelim la-trumah aval lo la-kodesh* — for *terumah* purposes, vessels may be immersed stacked one inside the other, since we assume the *mikvah* water permeates adequately and there is no concern of *chatzitzah* from one vessel merely resting in another. For *kodesh*, however, each vessel must be immersed individually.

### Vessel Sections

Second: *achorayim ve-toch ve-beis ha-tzvita be-trumah aval lo be-kodesh*. For *terumah* purposes, different sections of a vessel — the exterior back, the interior, and the grip — are treated as having distinct *tumah* statuses. If the exterior becomes *tamei* through a rabbinic *tumah*, only the exterior is *tamei*; the interior remains *tahor*. This is because rabbinic *tumah* is deliberately calibrated to be less encompassing than biblical *tumah*, so that only the section touched is affected. (The parallel with hand-washing is precise: by rabbinic *tumah*, hands can become *tamei* without the body, exactly as the exterior of a vessel can become *tamei* without the interior.) For *kodesh*, this leniency does not apply — any *tamei* section renders the entire vessel *tamei*, as is the standard rule by biblical *tumah*.

### Carrying Restrictions

Third: *ha-noseh et ha-midras noseh et ha-trumah aval lo et ha-kodesh*. One may simultaneously carry on one shoulder a *midras* — an object sat upon by a *zav*, *zavah*, or *niddah*, which carries *av ha-tumah* status — and on the other shoulder a sealed pottery barrel of *terumah*. Since a pottery vessel becomes *tamei* only through contact with its interior, and carrying on one's shoulder does not constitute contact with the interior, the *terumah* remains *tahor*. For *kodesh*, this leniency does not apply; one may not carry the two together.

### Clothes Midras

Fourth: *bigdei ochlei trumah midras la-kodesh*. The garments of those who eat *terumah* — who are themselves careful and maintain a high standard of *taharah* — are nonetheless treated as *midras* for those who eat *kodesh*. The social hierarchy we have been tracing throughout this *perek* thus appears once more: each rung below is *midras* for the rung above.

### Garment Prep

Fifth: *she-ba-kodesh matir u-menageiv u-matbil ve-achar kach kosher* — for a garment to be immersed for *kodesh* purposes, if it is knotted (as garments often were when sent for laundering), one must first untie the knots, dry off any external moisture (which would constitute a *chatzitzah*), then immerse in the *mikvah*, and only afterward retie. *Uv-trumah kosher ve-achar kach matbil* — for *terumah*, one may leave the garment knotted and with liquid on it and immerse in that condition, just as vessels may be immersed stacked.

### New Vessels

Sixth: *keilim ha-nigmarim be-taharah tzerichin tvilah la-kodesh* — even a newly completed vessel, made entirely under conditions of *taharah*, with the maker consciously guarding it throughout the production process, nonetheless requires immersion in the *mikvah* before its first use for *kodesh*. For *terumah*, no such requirement applies to a vessel made in *taharah*.

### Contents Unit

Seventh: *ha-kli metzaref mah she-be-tocho la-kodesh aval lo la-trumah*. For *kodesh* purposes, a vessel unifies its contents: if one of ten apples inside a vessel is touched and thereby rendered *tamei*, all ten apples are treated as a single unit and all become equally *tamei*. For *terumah*, each item inside the vessel retains its individual status; only the apple actually touched is affected.

### Derivation Levels

Eighth: *ha-revi'i ba-kodesh pasul ve-ha-shlishi ba-trumah*. The chain of derived *tumah* extends one level further for *kodesh* than for *terumah*. A fourth-level derivation (*revi'i*) disqualifies (*pasul*) food designated for *kodesh*. For *terumah*, only a third-level derivation (*shlishi*) has that effect; a *revi'i* does nothing.

### Hand Washing

Ninth: *uv-trumah im nitmas achat mi-yadav chavertah tehorah* — for *terumah* purposes, if one hand becomes *tamei* through a rabbinic *tumah*, the other hand, if carefully watched, remains *tahor* and need not be washed. Since rabbinic *tumah* of the hands does not affect the rest of the body, and since the two hands are, to that extent, treated as distinct, one *tamei* hand does not compromise the other. *Uv-kodesh matbil shteihen she-ha-yad metamei et chavertah ba-kodesh aval lo be-trumah* — for *kodesh*, one hand imparts its *tumah* to the other, so both must be immersed (or washed), whereas for *terumah* this is not the rule.

### Dry Food Rule

Tenth: *ochlin neguvim be-yadayim mesoavos be-trumah aval lo be-kodesh*. Food that has never come in contact with liquid — *neguvim* meaning not merely dry but never wetted — cannot become susceptible to *tumah* at all, and therefore even if one's hands are *tamei* (*mesoavot*), one may eat such food for *terumah* purposes, since there is no mechanism by which the hands could render the food *tamei*. For *kodesh*, however, even if the food could not possibly become *tamei*, one must still wash one's hands before eating it.

### Onein Rule

Finally: *ha-onein u-mechusar kipurim tzerichin tvilah la-kodesh* — two categories of person who require immersion before eating *kodesh*, even though in each case one might suppose they are technically done with their *tumah* process.

An *onein* is a mourner in the period between death and burial. If the *onein* did not become *tamei* in any technical sense during this period — if, say, they had no contact with the *meit* — they nonetheless require immersion before eating *kodesh*. A *mechusar kipurim* is a person — such as a *zav*, *zavah*, or *metzora* — who has gone through the full *taharah* process including immersion, waited the requisite period, and now needs only to bring the completing *korban*. According to Torah law, once that *korban* is brought, the person is entirely *tahor*. Yet even after bringing the *korban*, a *mechusar kipurim* must immerse again in the *mikvah* before eating *kodesh*. And notably, having immersed previously for the *tumah* itself, this additional immersion is specifically a *kodesh* requirement and does not apply to *terumah*. These distinctions will occupy our attention in the coming days.

---

---

# Chagigah 21

## Ten/Eleven Levels

### Mishna Overview

The *mishnah* on this *daf* lists ten — or, as we shall see, perhaps eleven — ways in which *kodesh* is treated with greater stringency than *terumah*. The *gemara* proceeds to examine these distinctions one by one. The broader context of these *mishnayot* is the stratification of Jewish society according to levels of *taharah* observance: *chullin*, *ma'aser*, *terumah*, *kodesh*, and so forth. As the *mishnayot* in this chapter will ultimately demonstrate, these distinctions translate into the creation of distinct social groupings — a reality that becomes particularly fraught during the *regalim*, when all of Israel gathers together and those distinctions must somehow be managed or suspended.

### Stratifications

Before turning to the *gemara*'s analysis, it is worth noting that the *mishnah*'s primary focus is on the differential treatment of various categories of food and the vessels used in their preparation and service. The question of how a *kohen* or an Israelite bringing a *shelamim* would prepare meat, or how wine and oil for *korbanos* would be handled, makes the question of vessel purity directly practical. A *kohen* cooking sacrificial meat, or an individual bringing wine and oil for the *niskei korbanos*, would need vessels whose status of *taharah* had been properly established — and the rules for establishing that status differ markedly between *terumah* and *kodesh*.

---

## Kelim b'Kelim

### Vessels Restriction

The *gemara* opens its analysis with the first distinction listed in the *mishnah*: for *terumah*, one may immerse vessels within other vessels in the *mikvah* simultaneously — stacked or nested together — whereas for *kodesh*, one may not. Practically speaking, this is a familiar concern to anyone who has brought *kelim* to the *mikvah*: vessels must be separated so that no one vessel rests heavily upon another in a way that might prevent water from reaching every surface. The question the *gemara* addresses is: what is the precise rationale for the stricter standard that applies to *kodesh*?

### Rabbi Ila: Weight

*Amar Rabbi Ila mishum shekivedo shel kli chotzetz* — Rabbi Ila offers a straightforward explanation: the weight of the inner vessel causes it to press against the outer vessel, preventing water from passing between the two. This is a *chatzitza* concern — the inner vessel interposes between the water of the *mikvah* and the surface of the outer vessel (or vice versa), invalidating the immersion for *kodesh* purposes, though not for *terumah*.

### Two Chatzitza Issues

The *gemara* immediately raises a challenge. If Rabbi Ila's rationale for the vessels prohibition is a *chatzitza* concern, why does the *mishnah* list separately, later on, another distinction between *terumah* and *kodesh* that also appears to rest on a *chatzitza* concern — namely, that for *kodesh*, one must untie any knots in a garment before immersing it (*matir umangiv umatbil*), whereas for *terumah*, one may immerse a garment even while it remains knotted? *Midekattani seifa mishum chatzitza, hani lav mishum chatzitza?* Since the *mishnah* presents a limited number of distinctions, it would seem strange to list two separate items whose underlying rationale is the same heightened *chatzitza* concern.

### Chatzitza Analysis

The *gemara* answers: *reisha veseifa mishum chatzitza — utzricha*. Both the vessels case and the knotted garments case are indeed rooted in a heightened concern for *chatzitza* by *kodesh*, but neither is derivable from the other, and therefore both must be listed independently.

Had the *mishnah* taught only the vessels case, one might have reasoned as follows: the prohibition there is because a metal or ceramic inner vessel, resting against the outer vessel, literally blocks water from reaching the intervening surface. But in the case of a knotted garment, I might have said: a garment is porous and will absorb water, so even if it is knotted, the water will soak through and there is no genuine *chatzitza*. Therefore, I would not have applied the same stringency to knotted garments for *kodesh*.

Conversely, had the *mishnah* taught only the knotted garments case, one might have explained the prohibition there as follows: *mishum d'kitra bemaya hiduki mehadek* — a knot tightens further when submerged in water, making it even harder for water to penetrate. But in the case of one vessel inside another, one might have said: *demaya achlei matzpu* — the water causes the inner vessel to float upward, naturally creating a gap between the two, so there is no *chatzitza*. I would therefore have permitted immersing nested vessels even for *kodesh*.

Since each case cannot be inferred from the other, both must be stated. And since for *terumah* neither prohibition applies, the implicit explanation is that for *terumah*, the optimistic reasoning in each case is relied upon — the water causes the inner vessel to float, and the garment absorbs water — whereas for *kodesh* we are more stringent and do not rely on these assumptions.

### Ten Levels Position

This answer, which treats the vessels case and the knotted garments case as two distinct items, both grounded in *chatzitza* concerns, is in tension with a position attributed to Rabbi Ila elsewhere. *Rabbi Ila l'ta'ameih* — Rabbi Ila is consistent with his own view, as reported in the name of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa: *eser ma'alot shanu kan* — the *mishnah* enumerates ten distinctions, not eleven. By treating the vessels case and the knotted garments case as variations of the same underlying *chatzitza* concern rather than as two fully independent items, Rabbi Ila is able to collapse them into a single entry, yielding a count of ten rather than eleven.

### Eleven Distinctions

To appreciate this fully, it is worth enumerating all the distinctions the *mishnah* lists. First, vessels within vessels — the focus of the current discussion. Second, the question of whether *tum'ah* affecting one part of a vessel (the inside, outside, or handle) renders the entire vessel *tamei*, or only that section — a distinction that applies differently for *terumah* and *kodesh*. Third, whether carrying a *midras* object — the seat or couch of a *zav* — on one shoulder renders *terumah* on the other shoulder *tamei*. Fourth, that the garments of one who eats *terumah* are considered *midras* for one who eats *kodesh*. Fifth, the matter of undoing knots before immersion — as discussed above. Sixth, that even a vessel fresh from the potter's kiln, with which nothing *tamei* has ever come in contact, must be immersed before use for *kodesh*. Seventh, that a vessel combines all its contents into a single unit for purposes of *tum'ah* by *kodesh*, but not by *terumah*. Eighth, that *tum'ah* is transmitted by *kodesh* down to a fourth-level derivative (*revi'i*), whereas *terumah* only transmits down to a third level (*shelishi*). Ninth, that if one hand becomes *tamei*, the other is not thereby rendered *tamei* for *terumah*, but it is for *kodesh*. Tenth, that even food that has never come into contact with liquid — and is therefore not susceptible to *tum'ah* biblically — must nevertheless have one's hands washed before handling for *kodesh*, but not for *terumah*. Eleventh, that an *onen* (one in the first stage of mourning before burial) and a *mechusar kippurim* (one who has completed the purification process but has not yet brought the concluding sacrifice) must immerse in a *mikvah* before eating *kodesh*, but not before eating *terumah*.

That gives us eleven. Rabbi Ila, by treating items one and five — the nested vessels and the knotted garments — as a single *chatzitza* concern, reduces the count to ten.

---

## Five-Five Division

### First Five Apply

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's position, as transmitted by Rabbi Ila, goes further than a simple count. Not only are there ten distinctions, but those ten are divided into two conceptually distinct groups of five. *Chamesh rishonot bein l'Kodesh bein l'chullin shena'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh* — the first five stringencies apply not only to actual *kodesh* (consecrated food and *korbanos*) but also to *chullin she'na'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh* — ordinary, unconsecrated food that someone has taken upon himself to handle with the same standard of care required for *kodesh*.

This category — *chullin she'na'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh* — was a central concern of yesterday's discussion. The question it raises is: if one consistently treats his ordinary food as though it were a *korban*, does that food acquire the halachic status of *kodesh*? The answer, as *Tosafot* notes, is that the position here assumes *chullin she'na'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh lav k'kodesh dami* — such food is generally not treated as equivalent to *kodesh* in all respects; it is perhaps treated more like *terumah* or like elevated *chullin*, but not as full *kodesh*. And yet, the first five of the ten stringencies apply to it.

### Last Five Kodesh Only

*Achronot l'kodesh aval lo l'chullin shena'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh* — the last five stringencies apply only to actual *kodesh*. Food that is merely treated with *kodesh*-level care, but which does not possess genuine *kedushah*, is not subject to these final five.

### Biblical Tumah

The *gemara* explains the rationale: *chamesh kamaisa d'is l'hu drara d'tumah m'de'oraisa gazru b'hu rabanan bein l'kodesh bein l'chullin shena'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh* — the first five stringencies all have some connection, however indirect, to a sphere where biblical *tum'ah* is a genuine concern. Because they are rooted in (or at least linked to) *tumah de'oraita*, the Rabbis extended these stringencies even to *chullin she'na'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh*.

### Rabbinic Only

*Basraisa d'lais l'hu drara d'tumah m'de'oraisa gazru b'hu rabanan l'kodesh* — the last five stringencies do not have such a connection to biblical *tum'ah*. They are therefore purely rabbinic enactments that the Rabbis applied only to actual *kodesh*, but not to *chullin* that is merely treated as *kodesh*.

### Category Logic

It must be said that figuring out on one's own which items belong in which group is not intuitive, and *Tosafot* must intervene to make the classification coherent. In brief: the *chatzitza* concern in immersion is clearly connected to *tum'ah de'oraita*, since an invalid immersion due to *chatzitza* is a biblical concern. The case of the inner and outer parts of a vessel — while the division itself is rabbinic — involves *tum'ah* derived from liquids associated with a *zav* or *zavah*, which are themselves biblical sources of *tum'ah*; that tenuous connection is apparently sufficient. Carrying a *midras* on one's shoulder alongside *terumah* obviously implicates the biblical *tum'ah* of *midras*. The garments of one who eats *terumah* being considered *midras* for one who eats *kodesh* is connected to the possibility that a *niddah* sat upon them — again, a biblical *tum'ah*. And even the requirement to immerse a vessel fresh from the kiln is connected, by the *gemara*'s later discussion, to the concern that something *tamei* may have come in contact with it during manufacture — a concern with some biblical grounding.

For the last five: *tum'at yadayim* (hand impurity) is entirely rabbinic. The requirement to wash hands before handling food that never came in contact with liquid is similarly of purely rabbinic origin, since such food cannot become biblically *tamei*. The concern about an *onen* or *mechusar kippurim* likewise lacks a clean biblical *tum'ah* parallel for the purposes at hand. *Tosafot* adds an important clarification: what distinguishes the last five is not merely that they lack a biblical *tum'ah* connection in the abstract, but that any biblical *tum'ah* concern they might involve does not arise with *chullin* at all. This is why they could not be extended to *chullin she'na'asu al taharat ha-Kodesh*.

As the *gemara* itself seems to acknowledge, the precise mapping of each item onto its category is not fully transparent, and the assertion about which items belong where is clearer than the underlying logic that assigns them there.

---

## Rava: Narrow Opening

### Rava Disagrees

Rava takes a fundamentally different approach. He disputes Rabbi Ila's conflation of the vessels case and the knotted garments case as two variations of a *chatzitza* concern. *Rava amar midseifa havei mishum chatzitzah reisha lav mishum chatzitzah* — yes, the case of knotted garments (the *seifa*, the latter clause of the *mishnah*) is indeed a *chatzitza* concern, but the first case, of vessels within vessels (the *reisha*), is not a *chatzitza* concern at all, and the two must not be conflated.

### Needles Concern

What, then, is the reason behind the prohibition against immersing nested vessels for *kodesh* purposes? *Gezeirah shelo yatbil machtin u'tsinorot bikli she'ein befiv kishfoferet hanod* — it is a rabbinic decree lest one come to immerse needles and other small items in a vessel whose opening is smaller than the width of a *shfoferet hanod*.

The practical scenario Rava envisions is this: one wishes to immerse small objects — needles, pins, and similar tiny items — in the *mikvah*. The difficulty is obvious: loose needles will scatter in the water, sink to the bottom, or otherwise become impossible to manage. The natural solution is to place them inside a vessel and immerse the vessel. But if the vessel has a narrow opening — say, a jug or flask — the needles cannot float out, making it a convenient container for immersion. The problem, however, is whether the water inside such a narrow-mouthed vessel is considered part of the *mikvah* water at all, or whether it is merely water that has entered a sealed container and is no longer meaningfully connected to the *mikvah*.

### Shfoferet Hanod

The answer depends on the size of the opening. *She'ein befiv kishfoferet hanod* — if the opening is smaller than a *shfoferet hanod*, the water inside is not considered a continuation of the *mikvah* water, and the needles are not considered to have been immersed in the *mikvah* at all. The *shfoferet hanod* — the tube (*shfoferet*) of a leather water flask (*nod*) — defines the minimum opening required for the water inside a vessel to be considered connected to, and part of, the surrounding *mikvah* water. This measurement, cited in a *mishnah* elsewhere (*eruv mikvaot kishfoferet hanod — ke-ovya u-ke-chalala — bi-shtei etzbaot chozrot limkoman*), is the width of two fingers in diameter, referring to the full circumference of the tube. This is a *halacha l'Moshe miSinai*.

### Modern Mikvah

This principle is not merely historical. It is the very foundation of how modern *mikvaot* are constructed. The standard contemporary *mikvah* operates through a dual-pool system. One pool — the *bor mei geshamim* — collects rainwater on the roof and feeds it into a reservoir below. This pool, filled exclusively with *mei geshamim*, is halachically valid on its own, containing at least forty *se'ah* of rain-collected water. The second pool, the one into which people actually immerse, is filled with clean, drawn water (*mayim she'uvim*) — which, on its own, would be invalid as a *mikvah* — and is regularly changed for hygienic reasons. The two pools are connected by a pipe. Because the valid *mikvah* and the pool of drawn water are connected, the drawn water is considered part of the valid *mikvah* and the entire system is *kasher*. But that connecting pipe must meet the standard of *shfoferet hanod* — it must have an opening of at least two finger-widths in diameter. Without that, the two pools are not considered a single body of water, and the drawn water remains invalid. The same principle Rava invokes to explain the rabbinic decree about nested vessels is precisely what underlies the architecture of every contemporary *mikvah*.

---

## Basket Difference

### Basket Question

Having established the two competing explanations — Rabbi Ila's *chatzitza* rationale and Rava's narrow-opening rationale — the *gemara* asks what practical difference (*nafka mina*) exists between them. The answer: *ika beiniyeihu sal ve-gargutni she-milan kelim ve-hitbilan* — the case of a basket (*sal*) or large woven container (*gargutni*) that is filled with vessels and immersed in the *mikvah*.

### Ila: Baskets Problem

According to Rabbi Ila, whose concern is *chatzitza* — the weight of an inner vessel preventing water from circulating between the vessels — the prohibition applies regardless of what the outer container looks like. A basket, no less than a ceramic pot, can have an inner vessel resting against it, and the weight of the inner vessel is just as problematic in a basket as in any other container. Therefore, according to Rabbi Ila, immersing a basket filled with vessels remains a concern even for *kodesh* purposes.

### Rava: Baskets Okay

According to Rava, however, whose concern is specifically the case of narrow-mouthed vessels in which one might place needles, baskets are categorically excluded from the decree. The very nature of a basket — the feature that makes it a basket rather than some other kind of vessel — is that it has a wide opening. There is no basket with a narrow mouth; if it had a narrow mouth, it would not be called a basket. Since the *gezeirah* was enacted only against immersing objects in vessels with openings narrower than a *shfoferet hanod*, and since a basket by definition cannot have such a narrow opening, the decree never applied to baskets in the first place.

This is a meaningful categorical distinction rather than a case-by-case assessment of whether any particular vessel triggers the underlying concern. Such case-by-case reasoning — *lo palug* considerations aside — would be unworkable in practice. But here the division between baskets and other vessels is clean enough to be drawn at the categorical level, and Rava draws it accordingly.

---

## Vessels in Vessels

### Porous Vessels

The discussion of baskets leads naturally into a related question: can a basket or similarly porous vessel actually divide a *mikvah*? If one places a wicker basket inside a *mikvah* — imagine a large laundry-style basket made of hemp, riddled with openings — does it divide the *mikvah* into two separate bodies of water?

The intuitive answer might be: obviously not, since the basket is so thoroughly perforated that water passes freely through it in every direction. The *gemara*, however, reaches a more surprising conclusion. Rava states: *u-mikveh she-hilko be-sal ha-gargustani ha-tovel sham lo alta lo tevilah* — if a *mikvah* was divided by such a basket, one who immerses in one of the resulting sections has not achieved a valid *tevilah*. The basket does divide the *mikvah*.

The reason Rava gives is striking: *de-ara kullah chalchulei mechalchalah* — the entire earth is porous. If we were to say that porousness alone is sufficient to prevent division, then any body of water would be connected to every other body of water through the porous earth, and we could never speak of a divided *mikvah* at all. Since that conclusion is absurd, porousness as such cannot be the criterion. What matters is whether there is a formal *mechitzah* — a partition — and the basket, however full of holes, constitutes such a partition.

This is a surprisingly formalist position. Even something as open and porous as a woven basket, which allows water to flow through it freely, is treated as a genuine wall for purposes of dividing a *mikvah*. One might push further and ask: what about a *mechitzah* made of three or four strings, each within three *tefachim* of the next, which is halachically valid as a partition in other contexts? Would such a construction divide a *mikvah*? Rava's reasoning seems to point in that direction, though the question is acknowledged as requiring further analysis.

This discussion of the basket's porousness also reinforces, from a different angle, why Rava's *gezeirah* does not apply to baskets. Not only does a basket have a wide opening by definition, but its thoroughly porous nature means that it is a fundamentally different type of vessel — one in which the concern about water failing to penetrate simply does not arise.

### Purity Transfer

*Amar Rav Papa:* the analysis now turns to a more refined question involving the relationship between an outer vessel and the objects placed within it. The rule, it turns out, depends critically on the initial *taharah* status of the outer vessel.

### Outer Tamei

*Migu de-salka tevilah le-kula gufa de-mana, salka le-hu nami le-kelim de-it bah* — if the outer vessel was *tamei* and requires immersion, then when it is immersed and becomes *tahor*, the same *tevilah* that purifies the outer vessel also renders *tahor* whatever is inside it. The inner vessels benefit from the *tevilah* of the outer vessel by virtue of being contained within it at the moment of the status change. They need not themselves be considered to be immersed in the *mikvah* water in any direct sense; the transformation of the outer vessel's status carries over to them automatically.

### Outer Tahor

But if the outer vessel was already *tahor* and did not itself need immersion, then the inner vessels only become *tahor* if the water inside is connected to the *mikvah* water through an opening of at least *shfoferet hanod* size. Without that opening, the water inside the vessel is not part of the *mikvah* water, and the inner vessels are not considered to have been immersed at all.

### Mishna Case

This framework allows Rav Papa to explain a *mishnah* that, at first glance, seems puzzling: *kelim she-milan kelim — ve-hitbilan — harei elu tehorim* — fill vessels with vessels and immerse them, and they are *tahor*. The *mishnah* then continues: *ve-im lo taval, mayim ha-me'uravin ad she-ye-u me'uravin ke-shfoferet hanod* — and if it was not immersed, the water must be combined through an opening of *shfoferet hanod* size.

The phrase "if it was not immersed" initially seems incoherent — how can you speak of immersion not having occurred if we just said they were immersed? The *gemara* reinterprets: *ve-im eino tzarich litvilah* — "if it does not require immersion" — that is, if the outer vessel was already *tahor* and did not need to be immersed. In that case, the inner vessels only become *tahor* if the opening connecting the interior water to the *mikvah* water is of sufficient size. But if the outer vessel was *tamei* and needed to be immersed, the *tevilah* of the outer vessel carries through to the inner vessels regardless of the size of the opening.

This principle opens up some intriguing theoretical possibilities. One might wonder whether a similar logic could apply in other immersion scenarios — for instance, where something cannot itself come into direct contact with *mikvah* water. If placed inside a *tamei* vessel that undergoes a valid *tevilah*, might the interior object benefit from the status change of the vessel? The halachic parameters of such a question — particularly whether the principle applies to persons as well as vessels, and whether vessels of sufficient size retain the identity of *keli* — remain to be worked out.

It should be noted that earthenware vessels (*klei cheres*) are a special case: they cannot be purified through *mikvah* immersion at all, so these considerations do not apply to them.

---

## Basket Difference (II)

### Tannaic Dispute

The *gemara* now observes that the dispute between Rava and Rabbi Ila is not simply an *amoraic* debate; it mirrors a *tannaitic* disagreement. *Ditnaya: sal ha-gargustani she-milan kelim ve-hitpilan — bein la-kodesh bein la-trumah — tehorim* — the anonymous first *tanna* of the *baraita* holds that a basket filled with vessels and immersed is *tahor* for both *terumah* and *kodesh* purposes. This aligns with Rava's position: since the *gezeirah* was never about baskets (which have wide openings), there is no restriction even for *kodesh*. *Abba Shaul omer: la-trumah aval lo la-kodesh* — Abba Shaul disagrees, holding that for *kodesh* the restriction applies even to a basket. This aligns with Rabbi Ila's position: since the concern is *chatzitza* — the weight of an inner vessel — it applies regardless of the shape or construction of the outer container.

The *gemara* thus grounds the *amoraic* debate in a *tannaitic* precedent, with the first *tanna* corresponding to Rava and Abba Shaul corresponding to Rabbi Ila.

---

## Am Ha'aretz Example

### Stringency Question

Having established the various distinctions between *kodesh* and *terumah*, the *gemara* raises an obvious question. For *terumah* as well, there are people who are scrupulous about *taharah* — *chaverim*, those who take upon themselves careful observance of the laws of purity. If *chaverim* are knowledgeable enough to immerse their vessels properly for *terumah*, handling each vessel separately and ensuring that no *chatzitza* intervenes, why do we not rely on the same knowledge and care when it comes to *kodesh* — why impose additional stringencies at all?

### Imitation Concern

The *gemara*'s answer: *chazi lei Am Ha'aretz ve'azil matbil* — we are concerned that an *am ha'aretz* will observe what the *chaver* does and imitate it. When the *chaver* immerses nested vessels for *terumah*, the *am ha'aretz* sees this and concludes that this is how things are done. When he later immerses vessels for *kodesh* — where the rules are stricter — he will simply do what he saw done for *terumah*, without realizing that the standard must be higher. If the *chaver* himself demonstrates no visible difference in how he handles *kodesh* versus *terumah*, the *am ha'aretz* will have no way of knowing there should be one. Therefore, the *chaver* must behave differently with *kodesh* — not for his own sake, since he knows the law, but to ensure that his observable practice does not mislead others.

### No Terumah

One might object: the same concern should apply to *terumah*. If the *am ha'aretz* watches the *chaver* immerse nested vessels for *terumah* without separating them, he will do the same when handling his own *terumah*. So why are we not equally stringent about *terumah*, to prevent this imitation?

The *gemara*'s response: *lo mikablinan mineihu* — we do not accept *terumah* from an *am ha'aretz* in the first place. A *chaver kohen* who receives *terumah* will simply decline the offering of the *am ha'aretz* and direct him to give it to another *kohen* who is himself an *am ha'aretz*. Since the *terumah* of the *am ha'aretz* will never reach the *chaver*'s table regardless of how it was handled, the practical harm of the *am ha'aretz* imitating improper *terumah* practice is contained.

### Kodesh No Alternative

But this answer only works if there is an alternative destination for the rejected item. With *terumah*, there is one: give it to another *kohen*. With *korbanot* and *kodshim*, there is none. There is only one *Beit Hamikdash*. One cannot tell an *am ha'aretz* who brings wine or oil for his *korban* to bring it to a different *Mikdash* — no such alternative exists. If his offering is rejected, he has nowhere else to go.

### Proper Example

Therefore, *chaverim* must take particular care to set the correct example in all matters relating to *kodesh*. The *am ha'aretz* will observe how *kodesh*-related *kelim* are handled and imitate that practice when he brings his own offerings. Since there is no way to exclude him from participation in the *avodah* — no alternative *kohen* to send him to, no alternative *Mikdash* — the standard of practice must itself be made exemplary, so that imitation produces correct behavior. This is the reason for the additional stringencies applied to *kodesh* over and above those applied to *terumah*.

---

## Wine/Oil Acceptance

### Wine Oil Trusted

The *gemara* now cites a *baraita* that seems, at first glance, to undercut everything just established. *Amar Rabbi Yossi: mipnei mah hakol ne'emanim al taharat yayin veshemen kol yemot hashanah* — Rabbi Yossi asks: why are all people believed regarding the purity of wine and oil brought to the *Beit Hamikdash* throughout the entire year? The irony is striking. The *mishnah* has just catalogued a long list of stringencies applied to *kodesh* that go beyond even those applied to *terumah*; the *am ha'aretz* concern has just been articulated as a reason for even greater vigilance around *kodesh* — and yet here, precisely when it comes to the holiest context of all, bringing offerings to the *Beit Hamikdash*, everyone is trusted unconditionally.

### Private Altar

Rabbi Yossi's answer: *kedei shelo yehei kol echad ve'echad holech uvoneh bamah le'atzmo* — so that no one should go and build himself a private altar. If a person comes to bring wine or oil as part of his *korban* and is told that his offering cannot be accepted because he is not trusted regarding its *taharah*, he has nowhere else to go and nothing else to do — except, perhaps, to build his own *bamah* and bring his offerings there. The impulse to bring a *korban*, to participate in the service of God, is real and powerful; if the only *Mikdash* rejects it, the alternative is not abandonment of the impulse but private, unauthorized worship — which is prohibited and spiritually dangerous.

### Eiva Principle

This is the principle of *eiva* — avoiding hatred and enmity. The *gemara* identifies Rabbi Yossi as the *tanna* who gives decisive weight to *eiva*, allowing it to override what would otherwise be valid grounds for rejection. *U-man tana dechaish le'eiva — Rabbi Yossi* — it is Rabbi Yossi who holds that the concern for *eiva* is weighty enough to override the normal standards of trustworthiness we would otherwise apply.

### Modern Testimony

Rav Papa draws an explicit contemporary application: *keman mekablinan idna sahadusa mi'am ha'aretz — ke'Rabbi Yossi* — according to whom do we nowadays accept testimony from an *am ha'aretz*? Like Rabbi Yossi. In the time of the *Beit Hamikdash*, rejection on grounds of *am ha'aretz* status meant: your offering is not accepted here. In later times, rejection on grounds of *am ha'aretz* status in the context of *eidut* means: your testimony is not accepted in the *beit din*. Both represent forms of complete social and religious exclusion. Rabbi Yossi's principle — that the concern for *eiva*, for the feeling of total rejection, overrides the grounds for exclusion — carries forward from the *Beit Hamikdash* into the rabbinic court.

### Unity Theme

The broader theme that emerges from this *gemara* is a profound tension within rabbinic legal culture. On the one hand, the entire discussion of the *mishnah* in this chapter has been building an elaborate structure of stratified standards: *chullin*, *ma'aser*, *terumah*, *kodesh*, with multiple distinctions and sub-distinctions at each level, and a parallel social structure of *chaverim* versus *amei ha'aretz*. On the other hand, the *gemara* here — and, as we shall see when we reach the discussions around the *regel* — repeatedly returns to the recognition that these stratifications carry a cost. When they produce a sense of total exclusion, when they threaten to rupture the unity of *Klal Yisrael* or to drive people toward their own private forms of worship, the calculus changes.

It is worth noting that most of these distinctions have, in practice, receded into history. The absence of the *Mikdash* has made *tum'ah ve-taharah* concerns largely theoretical, and the *regel*-period suspension of the stratifications has given way to a more permanent softening. But the principle Rabbi Yossi articulates — and that Rav Papa applies to everyday testimony — has not receded. The question of how to maintain standards without producing a sense of complete exclusion, of how to insist on integrity in communal institutions without making people feel that those institutions are not theirs, remains as urgent as ever. The *gemara* answers it, at least in part, by invoking *eiva*: the cost of rejection is sometimes too high to pay.

---

---

# Chagigah 22

## Kodesh vs. Terumah

### Standards Gap

The daf opens by recapitulating the distinction already established between the standards required for *kodesh* and those required for *terumah*. The *chaveirim* — those who are scrupulous in matters of *tumah ve-taharah* — need not themselves be confused about what practices pertain to *taharah*, what to *terumah*, and what to *kodesh*. The concern is rather with the *amei ha-aretz*, who observe the behavior of the *chaveirim* and pattern themselves accordingly. Since the *amei ha-aretz* are sufficiently attentive to distinguish between the different levels of practice being modeled for them, the *chaveirim* must be more exacting by *kodesh* than by *terumah*.

The reason the greater stringency falls precisely on *kodesh* is rooted in an irony: although we do not accept the *terumah* of the *am ha-aretz* — directing him instead to give it to a *kohen* who is himself an *am ha-aretz* — when it comes to *kodshim* we have no such option. There is only one *Beit HaMikdash*, and therefore we must accept what the *am ha-aretz* brings. This will be the theme that closes the entire *perek*: at the *regalim*, when all of Israel converges on that single central *Beit HaMikdash* with their *korbanot*, the principle of unity overrides these distinctions entirely. Because we are ultimately going to be accepting their *korbanot*, we must during the rest of the year set the highest possible standard — a model sufficiently rigorous that our acceptance of their offerings remains defensible. That is why the degree of care displayed in matters touching *kodesh* must exceed what we exhibit for *terumah*.

The Gemara had further noted that this same logic of inclusion — of not pushing the *am ha-aretz* away so severely that he breaks off and goes to build his own *bamot* — underlies the practice of accepting testimony from an *am ha-aretz* in certain contexts. What begins as a principle specific to the *Mikdash* becomes a broader mandate: the social and communal costs of extreme stratification must figure into *halachic* decision-making.

### Borrowing Vessels

The Gemara now raises a fresh question: *ve-neichosh li-she'ilah* — should we not be concerned about the vessels we borrow from the *am ha-aretz*? The *am ha-aretz* was not placed in *cherem*. Their clothing, to be sure, carries the status of *midras* and must be treated accordingly, particularly by those eating in *taharah*. Yet regular interaction continued; the *am ha-aretz* were neighbors, storekeepers, laborers. Vessels were borrowed from them as a matter of course. If we are required to assume their vessels are *tamei*, how can we interact with them at all?

### Pottery Vessels

The Gemara resolves this question by citing a *mishnah* in *Eiduyot*. The scenario: a corpse lies in a house, causing *tumah* to radiate throughout the enclosed space. If there is an opening of a *tefach* in the ceiling or wall, the *tumah* passes through and spreads to the upper story as well. However, if a *kli cheres* — a pottery vessel — is positioned so that its underside seals the opening, and its cavity faces downward, the *tumah* cannot penetrate it. A pottery vessel becomes *tamei* only through its interior; *tumah* striking its exterior has no effect. The inverted vessel therefore constitutes a barrier, protecting whatever is above.

On this point, *Beit Hillel* rules: *kli cheres matsil al hakol* — the pottery vessel protects everything in the upper story. *Beit Shammai*, however, rules that it protects only *ochlin u-mashkin* — food and drink — and other pottery vessels above. Everything else, they hold, remains *tamei*.

## Hillel vs. Shammai

### Shammai's Logic

*Beit Hillel* challenges *Beit Shammai*: how can the pottery vessel protect some things but not others? Either it functions as a barrier or it does not. *Beit Shammai* responds: *mipnei she-hu tamei al gabei am ha-aretz* — because this pottery vessel must be assumed *tamei*, as we are dealing with the house of an *am ha-aretz*. A *tamei* vessel cannot function as a barrier; *tumah* passes through it. Therefore everything in the upper story should be *tamei*. But if everything is *tamei*, why save the food and drink?

The distinction *Beit Shammai* draws is the following. The *tumah* does indeed pass through the assumed-*tamei* pottery vessel and enters the upper story. But within that context, we can still say: *ke-she-tiharnu ochlin u-mashkin she-betokho le-atzmo tiharnu* — when we declare the food and drink *tahor*, we do so only for the *am ha-aretz* himself. We do not eat the food of the *am ha-aretz*. The primary dimension along which these distinctions of *tumah ve-taharah* played out in daily life was the question of with whom one eats, whose food one handles, and who may sit at whose table. Since we will never eat the food of the *am ha-aretz* in any case, we can tell him his food is *tahor* without exposing ourselves to any risk.

The vessels above, however, are another matter entirely: *nitaher kli she-tihart lach ve-lo* — you would be making those vessels *tahor* not only for him but for yourself, since we do borrow his vessels. Therefore the vessels must be declared *tamei* to protect us.

### Hillel's Logic

*Beit Hillel*'s position — that the pottery vessel protects everything — is striking in light of the concession that the *am ha-aretz*'s vessel is presumed *tamei*. The Gemara does not fully reconcile this within the immediate exchange, but the underlying logic emerges from the thrust of the debate: *Beit Hillel* maintains the protective function of the pottery vessel even in the house of an *am ha-aretz*, treating it as *tahor* precisely to avoid the social consequences of declaring everything *tamei* — consequences that *Beit Shammai*'s student will shortly spell out.

## Yehoshua Critique

### Logical Absurdity

*Tanya amar Rabbi Yehoshua*: Rabbi Yehoshua declared that he is embarrassed — not socially, but logically — by the ruling of *Beit Shammai*. His embarrassment is intellectual: the distinction *Beit Shammai* draws produces absurd results. Consider a woman kneading dough in the upper story; she and her mixing bowl are *tamei shivah* — *tamei* for seven days through *tumat meit* — yet the dough inside the bowl is *tahor*? Or: vessels filled with liquid are *tamei shivah* and the liquids inside them are *tahor*? The very objects in direct physical contact with the food are *tamei* at the most severe level, while the food itself is *tahor*. The logical incoherence is acute.

### Shammai's Defense

*Nitpal lo talmid echad mi-talmidei Beit Shammai* — one of the disciples of *Beit Shammai* attached himself to Rabbi Yehoshua and asked permission to explain the reasoning. Rabbi Yehoshua invited him to speak.

The student posed the question in logical sequence. Does a *tamei* vessel serve as a barrier against the spread of *tumah*? Rabbi Yehoshua conceded: no, it does not. Is the vessel of an *am ha-aretz* to be presumed *tamei*? Again Rabbi Yehoshua conceded: yes. Then — the student pressed — if the pottery vessel is *tamei*, the *tumah* passes through it and enters the upper story, and everything should be *tamei*. Everything, that is, except the food and drink.

Why the exception for food and drink? Because the *am ha-aretz* will never accept a ruling that he is eating *tamei* food. He knows his food is prepared in his own way; he regards it as *tahor*. We are working within his own system. According to his own *shittah* — that his pottery vessel is *tahor* — his food is *tahor*. We may affirm this without risk, since we do not eat with him or eat his food.

### Social Cost

This leads to the more pointed argument. *Ve-im atah omer lo tamei* — if you were to tell the *am ha-aretz* that everything in the upper story is *tamei*, including his food, *klum mashgi'ach alecha* — he will not pay any attention to you. And worse: he will turn the ruling back on you. *She-lecha tahor ve-shelo tamei* — he will say your things are *tamei* and his are *tahor*. The cost of absolute stringency, imposed on someone who has not accepted your premises, is total rejection. He will reconstruct the classification in his own favor, and you will have lost all credibility and influence.

The only workable approach, then, is to concede where the concession costs nothing — the food, which we do not eat — and hold the line where it costs something — the vessels, which we do borrow. This is not a comfortable ruling. We are declaring something *tahor* that is in fact *tamei*, on the grounds that the declaration does not endanger us and that full honesty would be completely counterproductive. The context also bears noting: what is under discussion here is *tumat meit*, which is far weightier than the ordinary presumed *tumah* of an *am ha-aretz*. We would normally already treat his vessels as *tamei*; here, the *tumah* carries the full weight of *tumat shivah*.

## Yehoshua's Submission

### Prostration

*Mi-yad halach Rabbi Yehoshua ve-nishtate'ach al kivrei Beit Shammai*. Immediately, Rabbi Yehoshua went and prostrated himself on the graves of *Beit Shammai*. He declared: *na'aneti lachem atzmot Beit Shammai* — I have humbled myself before you, bones of *Beit Shammai*. *U-mah stumot she-lachem kach* — if even your unexplained, seemingly inexplicable rulings rest on such profound and well-grounded reasoning, *meforashot al achat kama ve-chama* — how much more weight and seriousness must I attach to your rulings that are explicit and transparent.

The reversal is total. Rabbi Yehoshua began by declaring himself *embarrassed* at *Beit Shammai*'s distinction. He ends prostrate at their graves. *Kol yamav hushcharu shinav mipnei ta'aniyotav* — all his days, his teeth were blackened from his fasts, undertaken as *teshuvah* for having expressed that embarrassment. The fast was not for questioning the ruling itself, but for publicly proclaiming that the ruling embarrassed him — an expression of disrespect for *Beit Shammai*'s depth that he later recognized was entirely unwarranted.

What also emerges from this episode is a portrait of the social texture of the relationship between *chaveirim* and *amei ha-aretz*. They were not completely separated. They did not eat together, and neither ate the other's food. Clothing presented a problem because of *midras*. But they borrowed vessels from each other, had commercial and neighborly interactions, and even — as we saw at the end of the previous *perek* — at times had *amei ha-aretz* transport *tahor* food. The stratification was real and consequential, centered overwhelmingly around eating and food-handling, but it did not constitute total ostracism.

### Dunking Vessels

*Katani miha* — the upshot of all of this is that we borrow vessels from them. The Gemara accepts this as a given and asks: given that we borrow their vessels, and given that those vessels are presumed *tamei*, how does this affect the earlier discussion about whether a different standard applies for *terumah* vs. *kodesh*? If we borrow their vessels and then use them for *terumah*, it matters little that we declined to take *terumah* directly from them; the vessels we borrowed may be just as problematic.

The Gemara answers: *ki she'alinan mineihu, matbilinan lehu* — when we borrow their vessels, we immerse them in the *mikveh* first. This is the standard practice: borrow, then immerse. Therefore, we need not refuse to borrow; we take the vessels and we *tovel* them.

One category of vessel, however, cannot be taken to the *mikveh*: *kli cheres*. A pottery vessel that has become *tamei* on the inside cannot be purified through immersion alone. This is precisely why *Beit Shammai* could declare the food and drink in the upper story *tahor*: we can affirm this freely because we would never borrow a *kli cheres* from an *am ha-aretz* in the first place — we can never restore it to *taharah* in any practical way. For other vessels — metal, wood — we borrow and we *tovel*, and that suffices.

But in the case of *tumat meit*, immersion alone is not enough. *Tamei meit ba'ei haza'ah shelishi u-shevi'i* — one who has become *tamei* through contact with a corpse requires sprinkling of the *parah adumah* ashes on the third and seventh day. *Ve-mi luzi le-zayin yomei lo mushali inshi* — people do not generally borrow a vessel for seven days, and it would be entirely unworkable to require that every borrowed vessel be brought to a *parah adumah* distribution point and subjected to the full seven-day purification process. Therefore, in the case of *tumat meit* — which is what the scenario of the house with the corpse involves — we cannot simply declare the vessels *tahor* by reference to our standard practice of immersion. Hence *Beit Shammai*'s ruling stands: the vessels must be treated as *tamei*, while the food, which we would never eat anyway, may be declared *tahor* for the *am ha-aretz* himself.

To summarize the resulting picture: we do not eat the *am ha-aretz*'s food — once food is *tamei*, it cannot be restored, and in any case the entire structure of these distinctions centered on with whom one eats. We treat their clothing as *midras*. But vessels we do borrow, and we immerse them before use. *Terumah* we do not accept from them; their *korbanot* we must accept, and therefore in matters touching *kodesh* we must model the highest standard throughout the year.

## Trust Conditions

### Immersion Trust

The Gemara now asks: *ve-atvilah le-meheimni* — are we in fact prepared to trust the *am ha-aretz* to immerse vessels properly? The question arises in connection with the *ma'alah* discussed earlier — that a vessel must not be immersed inside another vessel — which implies concern that the *am ha-aretz* will not perform *tevilah* with the necessary care. But we also have a *baraita*: *ne'emanim amei ha-aretz al taharat tevilat tamei meit* — the *amei ha-aretz* are trusted to say that they immersed themselves after becoming *tamei* through contact with a corpse. If they are trusted to report their own *tevilah*, how can we doubt the quality of their immersion?

### Body vs. Vessels

*Amar Abaye: lo kashya. Ha be-gufo, ha be-keilav.* The question is not difficult: the two cases are distinct. The *baraita* speaks of trusting an *am ha-aretz* regarding his own bodily immersion. The concern with the *ma'alah* is about the immersion of vessels. One may exercise greater care and attentiveness in matters relating to one's own *tumah ve-taharah* than in matters of vessel-handling, and perhaps the particular problem of one vessel inside another — *kli betoch kli* — is less likely to arise with human immersion.

### Rava's View

Rava disagrees with Abaye's framing. *Idi ve-idi be-keilav* — both cases are about vessels. The distinction, however, is not between body and vessels but between two different types of claims. *Ve-lo kashya:* if the *am ha-aretz* says *me'olam lo hitbalti kli betoch kli* — I have never immersed a vessel inside another vessel — we believe him. We do not assume he is lying; we assume he may lack attentiveness or knowledge of certain details, but we do not suspect outright falsehood. If he says he never did the problematic thing, we take him at his word.

But if he says: I did immerse one vessel inside another, but I was careful to ensure the mouth was wide enough, or that the inner vessel was positioned so water could circulate freely — that we do not accept. The issue is no longer honesty but competence and attentiveness. Can we trust that an *am ha-aretz*, even with good intentions, applied the necessary care and knowledge to a situation that required careful monitoring? That trust we cannot extend.

This distinction resonates well beyond this context. In matters of *hashgacha*, the question of whether someone is reliable is not a single question but two: Is the person honest? And does the person have sufficient knowledge and attentiveness to deliver what they sincerely intend to deliver? The Gemara locates the limit of trust in *amei ha-aretz* precisely at the point where intent and execution may diverge.

### Fruit Example

A parallel *baraita* reinforces this principle: *ne'eman am ha-aretz lomar peirot lo huchsharu* — an *am ha-aretz* is believed to say that fruit never came into contact with liquid and therefore never became susceptible to *tumah*. But *eino ne'eman lomar peirot huchsharu aval lo nitme'u* — he is not believed to say that the fruit became susceptible but he then ensured it did not contract *tumah*. Once again: if the problematic circumstance never arose, he is believed. If it arose and he claims to have managed it correctly, he is not believed. The concern about honesty is absent; the concern about whether he monitored a live risk with sufficient care is present.

### Parah Adumah Trust

The Gemara then complicates the earlier picture. A *baraita* teaches: *chaver she-ba lehazzot, mazim alav mi-yad* — if a *chaver* comes to be sprinkled with the *parah adumah* ashes, saying it has been three days since he contracted *tumat meit*, we sprinkle immediately. But *am ha-aretz she-ba lehazzot* — if an *am ha-aretz* comes, we do not trust his count. We make him wait until the third day from when he arrives before us, complete the first sprinkling, then wait a full seven days from that point for the second. We do not credit his claim about where he stands in the seven-day process.

This appears to contradict the *baraita* cited earlier, which had stated that *amei ha-aretz* are trusted regarding their immersion after *tumat meit*. *Ella amar Abaye* — Abaye resolves this: *mitoch chomer she-hichmarta lo bi-techillato, hikalta lo be-sofo* — because of the stringency we impose at the beginning of the process, we are able to be lenient at the end. Since the *am ha-aretz* knows that we are suspicious of him and will not credit his count, and since he has seen what the cost of that suspicion is — he must wait through the full process again from the start — he will be exceedingly careful to immerse properly once the process is complete, so as not to have to repeat it. The trust we extend at the end regarding his *tevilah* is not naive; it is enabled by the very strictness we apply at the beginning.

*Rashi* explains: *le-fi she-hu nizhar be-tevilah kedei she-lo yitztarech lo od* — he is careful about the *tevilah* precisely so that he will not need to go through the ordeal again. The general trust we extend is thus conditioned on the demonstrated consequences he faces when we do not trust him.

## Back vs. Inside

### Vessel Sections

The Gemara turns to another of the *ma'alot* discussed in the *mishnah*: the distinction between the *achorayim* — the back or outer surface of a vessel — and the *toch* — the inner cavity, along with the lip, ears, and handle. Biblically, if any part of a vessel contracts *tumah*, the entire vessel is *tamei*. Rabbinically, however, a distinction was introduced: if the *back* of a vessel comes into contact with *tamei* liquid, only the back becomes *tamei*; the inside, the lip (*ogen*), the ears (*oznav*), and the handle (*yadav*) remain *tahor*.

This distinction is rooted in the nature of the rabbinic extension that generated it. The only liquid that is an *av ha-tumah* — a primary source of *tumah* — is the discharge of a *zav* or *zavah*, including their saliva and urine. The rabbis extended the *tumah*-transmitting power of *tamei* liquid generally, treating all *tamei* liquids as capable of making vessels *tamei*, even though ordinarily such liquids are at most *sheini* and would lack that power. Because this generalization was entirely rabbinic and represented a major stringency, the rabbis deliberately marked it as such by introducing an internal incoherence: only the surface that actually touched the *tamei* liquid becomes *tamei*, while the rest of the vessel remains *tahor*. The absurdity of the outer wall being *tamei* while the inner wall is *tahor* signals to any observer that this is a rabbinic construct, not a biblical rule.

Conversely: if the inside of the vessel becomes *tamei*, *nitma tocho kulo tamei* — everything becomes *tamei*. This parallels the rule for *kli cheres*, where *tumah* entering the airspace of the interior affects everything within.

### Handles

The *beit ha-tzvitah* — the handle — is similarly treated as a distinct zone that does not become *tamei* along with the outer surface. The Gemara asks: what exactly is the *beit ha-tzvitah*? *Amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel: mekom she-tzovtin* — the place one grasps or by which one presents the vessel. The word may relate to the verse *va-yitztbot lah kali*, where something is extended forth. *Rav Asi amar Rabbi Yochanan: mekom she-nekiyei ha-da'at tzovim* — the place where fastidious people would dip, referring, according to *Rashi*, to a small separate insert or indentation in the vessel designed to hold oil or a condiment into which one dips food — a kind of built-in dipping vessel within the larger one.

### Terumah Apply

*Tanei Rav Bibi kamei de-Rav Nachman: kol ha-kelim ein lahem achorayim ve-toch* — all vessels are treated as a single unit, without the back-inside distinction. *Echad kodshei mizbei'ach, echad kodshei mikdash, ve-echad kodshei ha-gvul* — whether the *kodshim* brought to the altar, or those involving the *Beit HaMikdash* generally, or those of the outer provinces. *Kodshei gvul*? What is that? *Terumah*, it would seem. But our own *mishnah* states explicitly that the *achorayim ve-toch* distinction *does* apply by *terumah*. How can Rav Bibi's formulation be correct?

### Kodesh Differ

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: perhaps *kodshei gvul* does not refer to *terumah* at all, but to *chullin she-na'asu al taharat ha-kodesh* — ordinary food that one treats with the *taharah* standards of *kodesh*. This is corroborated by a teaching of *Rabba bar Avuha*: *achas esrei ma'alot shanu kan* — there are eleven levels enumerated in the *mishnah*. *Shesh bi-rishonah bein la-kodesh bein le-chullin she-na'asu al taharat ha-kodesh* — the first six apply equally to *kodesh* and to *chullin* treated as *kodesh*. *Chamesh acharonot la-kodesh ve-lo le-chullin she-na'asu al taharat ha-kodesh* — the final five apply only to *kodesh* proper, not to *chullin she-na'asu al taharat ha-kodesh*. The *achorayim ve-toch* distinction belongs among the *ma'alot* that apply to *terumah* but not to *kodesh* — for *kodesh*, the entire vessel is treated as a single unit and no partial-*tumah* distinctions are made.

The category of *chullin she-na'asu al taharat ha-kodesh* — called here *kodshei gvul*, the sanctity of the outer provinces — also invites a broader reflection. Even while the *Beit HaMikdash* stood, people sought to bring a dimension of *kedusha* into their ordinary eating by treating their *chullin* with the *taharah* standards of *kodesh*. The designation *kodshei gvul* — the sacred things of the territory outside — suggests that this practice was understood not merely as fastidiousness or habit-formation for *kodesh* occasions, but as a genuine attempt to extend *kedushah* outward from the *Mikdash* into the ordinary domain. After the *churban*, *Chazal* channeled this same impulse through forms of *kedushah* that were egalitarian rather than stratifying: *netilat yadayim*, *brachot* before and after eating, the principle that eating without a *bracha* is *ke-ilu ma'al be-hekdesh* — as though one misappropriated something sacred. These forms preserved the sanctification of eating without recreating the social divisions that the *taharah* system had generated.

## Midras Story

### Incident

*Ha-nosei et ha-midras nosei et ha-terumah aval lo et ha-kodesh* — one who is carrying a *midras* — the seat, sandal, or garment of a *zav*, which is an *av ha-tumah* — may simultaneously carry *terumah* but not *kodesh*.

The logic of the *terumah* case: the carrier of the *midras* is himself a *rishon le-tumah*. A *rishon* cannot render a vessel a *sheni*; only an *av ha-tumah* can initiate that chain of transmission. *Rashi* specifies that the *terumah* is in a *kli cheres* whose exterior is touching the carrier, so since a *kli cheres* becomes *tamei* only through its interior, the *terumah* inside is protected. But for *kodesh* — why is it not equally protected?

The answer: *mishum ma'aseh she-hayah* — because of a specific incident. *D'amar Rav Yehuda amar Shmuel*: a man was transporting a barrel of *yayin kodesh* — wine designated for use in the *Beit HaMikdash* — from one place to another. A strap of his sandal broke. He picked up the strap and placed it on the mouth of the barrel. It fell into the airspace of the barrel, and since a *kli cheres* becomes *tamei* through objects entering its airspace, the entire contents became *tamei*. *Be-otah sha'ah amru* — from that moment they ruled: one who carries a *midras* may carry *terumah* alongside it, but not *kodesh*.

### Ruling

What the man was doing carrying the sandal of a *zav* is not explained by the Gemara. *Rashi* simply notes that it was a *midras ha-zav* — a sandal that had been worn by a *zav* — and that the man had taken it in his hand for reasons unspecified. In any case, the ruling derived from the incident is clear: the same care that would seem sufficient for *terumah* is not sufficient for *kodesh*, and the story of the barrel enshrined that distinction as law.

## Chananya Principle

### Jordan River Story

The Gemara now asks why the prohibition derived from the barrel incident does not extend to *terumah* as well. The answer invokes the opinion of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavia: *lo asru ela be-Yarden u-ve-sefina u-che-ma'aseh she-hayah* — they only prohibited in the exact parallel case of the incident, and did not generalize.

The *baraita* underlying this principle: a person may not carry the water of *Parah Adumah* and its ashes and transport them across the Jordan River by boat. Nor may one toss them across a river, float them across the water, or transport them while riding on an animal or on another person's back — unless one's feet are touching the ground. One may, however, carry them across a bridge, since a bridge is considered an extension of the ground. This prohibition applies equally to the Jordan and to all other rivers.

Rabbi Chananya ben Akavia dissents: *lo asru ela be-Yarden u-ve-sefina u-che-ma'aseh she-hayah* — they only prohibited specifically the case that arose: crossing the Jordan River in a boat. The broader prohibition, which extends to all rivers and to any transport not grounded, represents an abstraction that Rabbi Chananya ben Akavia refuses to endorse.

### Abstraction Debate

What was the original incident that generated the *Parah Adumah* transport prohibition? *D'amar Rav Yehuda amar Rav*: a man was transporting *mei chatas* and *efer chatas* across the Jordan in a boat, and a *ke-zayit* of a corpse was found embedded in the floor of the boat. This rendered everything in the boat *tamei*, ruining the *Parah Adumah* materials. *Be-otah sha'ah amru* — at that moment they prohibited transporting *mei chatas* and *efer chatas* across the Jordan by boat.

The mainstream position generalized from this case to prohibit any transport of *Parah Adumah* materials that is not rooted in the ground. Rabbi Chananya ben Akavia insists on limiting the prohibition to exactly the scenario that occurred.

In the parallel barrel case: there is a specific incident involving a *midras* sandal and an open barrel of *kodesh* wine. The generalization that follows is that carrying a *midras* alongside *kodesh* is prohibited. Rabbi Chananya ben Akavia would confine this prohibition to *kodesh*, and not extend it to *terumah*, because the incident involved *kodesh*. Others might argue that the underlying risk — a *midras* contaminating nearby contents — is identical for *terumah*, and that the prohibition should follow. The Gemara accepts Rabbi Chananya ben Akavia's limiting approach as the operative principle, which is why the ruling ends at *kodesh* and does not reach *terumah*.

### Disputed Cases

On the basis of this framework, the Gemara raises a series of unresolved questions. *Sandal tamei, sandal tahor mahu* — what if the sandal being carried is *tahor*, not *tamei*? Should one never carry any sandal alongside *kodesh*, as a generalization of the barrel incident? *Chavit pesucha* — we know the problem arose with an open barrel; what of a sealed barrel, *chavit stuma mahu*? Perhaps the concern does not extend to a sealed barrel, into whose airspace nothing can fall. These questions remain in the category of *teiku*.

### Ila vs. Zeira

Finally: *avar ve-nasa mahu* — what is the status *bedi'avad*? Perhaps the prohibition applies only *lechatchila*; if one violated it and transported *kodesh* while carrying a *midras*, is the *kodesh* thereby *tamei* or does it remain *tahor*?

*Amar Rabbi Ila: avar ve-nasa tamei* — Rabbi Ila holds that even *bedi'avad* the *kodesh* is rendered *tamei*. The prohibition reflects an actual *tumah* risk, and violation of it produces *tumah* in practice. *Rabbi Zeira amar: avar ve-nasa tahor* — Rabbi Zeira holds that *bedi'avad* the *kodesh* remains *tahor*. The prohibition is a *lechatchila* precaution, but after the fact, no *tumah* has actually been transferred. Here the daf concludes.

---

---

# Chagigah 23

## Kelim Hanigmarim

### Three Stringencies

The daf opens at roughly the midpoint of 23a, with the *mishnah* introducing a third category of stringency distinguishing *kodesh* from *terumah*: *kelim hanigmarim betaharah* — vessels completed in a state of purity. Even such vessels, the *mishnah* rules, must be immersed before use for *kodesh* purposes, though this requirement does not apply to *terumah*.

### Supervision Issue

The *gemara* immediately presses the *mishnah* with a sharp question: who, exactly, supervised the completion of these vessels? If it was a *chaver* — someone scrupulous in matters of *tumah* and *taharah* — then why should immersion be required at all? The entire process was conducted under trustworthy oversight. But if the supervision was entrusted to an *am ha'aretz*, how can the *mishnah* even describe these vessels as having been completed *betaharah*? The scenario seems internally contradictory: genuine purity supervision precludes the need for immersion, while inadequate supervision precludes the claim of purity.

### Tzinora Concern

The *gemara* resolves this by citing a teaching of Rabba bar Shila in the name of Rav Matna in the name of Shmuel: in truth, a *chaver* did supervise the completion of the vessels. The reason immersion is nevertheless required is *mishum tzinora de'am ha'aretz* — out of concern for the fluids (*tzinora*) of an *am ha'aretz* that may have contacted the vessel. The term *tzinora* — literally something like a faucet or conduit — refers in rabbinic idiom to the bodily fluids of a *zav*, *zavah*, or *niddah*, which carry the status of *av hatumah*, a primary source of *tumah*.
