The Gemara's answer is both pragmatic and eschatological: *manichin osa ad she-yavo Eliyahu v'yit'harenu* — they set it aside until Eliyahu HaNavi comes and resolves the problem. When Eliyahu HaNavi arrives to herald the final redemption, he will clarify how *kodesh* from the Galilee can be brought to the *Beit HaMikdash* without becoming *tamei*.

The two *chiddushim* of this entire section thus emerge in sharp relief. First, *kodesh* is treated more leniently than *terumah* when it comes to trusting the *am ha'aretz* — the holier the object, the more inclusive the policy, precisely because the stakes of exclusion are so much higher. But second, this leniency is tightly bounded by geography: it applies only in Judea, where the *am ha'aretz* has real access to the *Beit HaMikdash* and there is an actual need to accept his *kodesh*. For *terumah*, which does not require the *Beit HaMikdash*, the geographic restriction does not apply in the same way, but the temporal restriction — the pressing season — applies wherever one is.

# Chagigah 25

## Terumah & Pressing Time

### Intro: Belief Times

The daf opens by cataloguing the circumstances under which an *am ha'aretz* — a common person not scrupulous about the laws of purity — is credited with claims about the status of produce and vessels. One category of believability is geographical: in Judea, *amei ha'aretz* are believed about *kodesh*, sacred Temple items, because of Judea's proximity to the *Beis Hamikdash*. A broader category, applying in all locations, concerns *terumah* — the priestly portion separated from produce — at the time of the pressing of grapes and olives.

### Pressing Season Rule

The Mishnah states: *u'bishat hagisos ne'emanim al hatruma* — at the time of the pressing, they are believed about *terumah*. The Gemara immediately raises a contradiction from a *baraisa*: one who finishes pressing his olives should leave over one basket of unpressed olives and give it to a poor *kohen* who is a *chavér* — a scrupulous associate who observes the purity laws. The point of leaving unpressed olives is that olives which have not been pressed have not come into contact with liquid and are therefore not susceptible to *tumah*. The practical advice, then, is: if you want to give your *terumah* to a *kohen chavér*, give it in the form of olives or grapes before they have come into contact with liquid, and they will be able to accept it without concern. The implication is that you are *not* believed about *tumah va-tahara* even at the time of the pressing, which directly contradicts the Mishnah.

### Rashi's Rationale

Rashi explains the general rule: because it was the beginning of the pressing season, everyone brought their vessels to the *mikveh* and observed purity with greater care, creating a stronger presumption that everything was being handled in *tahara*. Beyond that factual basis, there is an explicit policy concern — which Rashi will spell out further below — that the *chavérim* among the *kohanim* needed to be able to receive *terumah* at this critical time, or they would lose access to the bulk of the year's *terumah*. Both considerations together undergird the rule.

### Early vs. Late Harvest

To resolve the contradiction between the Mishnah and the *baraisa*, Rav Nachman states: *lo kashya ha be-charfei ha be-aflei* — there is no difficulty; the cases differ depending on whether we are dealing with an early or late harvest of the olives. The *baraisa* advises giving unpressed olives because the pressing in that case falls after the normal season — it is a late harvest — and therefore outside the window of credibility. This is an exception, not a refutation of the general rule. When asked for an example, Rav Adda bar Abba offers: like the olive orchards belonging to your father's household, which are known to ripen late and whose pressing regularly falls after the standard pressing season.

### Judea vs. Galilee

Rav Yosef proposes an alternative resolution: the *baraisa* was taught specifically with respect to the Galilee. This implies a geographic distinction in the rule of *terumah* believability at pressing time — that it applies in Judea but not in the Galilee. This is striking, because the geographic distinction we understood earlier applied to *kodesh* (since only in Judea could one readily access the *Beis Hamikdash*), but there is no obvious reason why *terumah* believability at pressing season should differ between Judea and the Galilee.

Abaye challenges this position with a *baraisa*: *Ever Hayarden ve-ha-Galil harei hein ke-Yehuda* — the Trans-Jordan and the Galilee are treated the same as Judea for *terumah* purposes. They are believed that wine is *tahor* during the wine-pressing season and that oil is *tahor* during the oil-pressing season — and each only during its own respective season, not the other's. This *baraisa* explicitly extends the rule to the Galilee. The Gemara concludes: *ela mechvarta kedishni me'ikara* — the earlier answer was better. The clear principle is that the rule of believability about *terumah* at pressing time applies regardless of geographic location, and the original contradiction is resolved by distinguishing early from late harvests.

---

## Holding Till Next Season

### Post-Season Refusal

The Gemara continues: if the pressing season has passed — *avra hagisos* — and an *am ha'aretz* brings a *chavér* a barrel of wine, the *chavér* should not accept it. He cannot now believe the *am ha'aretz*, and accepting the wine would leave him holding *terumah temei'ah*. However, the Gemara adds a striking alternative: the *chavér* can tell the *am ha'aretz* to hold onto the barrel and bring it back at the next pressing season, perhaps ten months hence, at which point he will be able to believe him — even though it is the exact same barrel that has had ten additional months in which it could have become *tamei*. The counterintuitive nature of this rule is acknowledged: the delay only multiplies the opportunities for *tumah* to occur, yet the formal status at the time of the next pressing season governs.

### Acceptance Question

Rav Sheshet is asked: what if the *kohen chavér* already accepted the barrel — he did not say "bring it back later," he simply took it — is he now permitted to hold onto it until the next pressing season and at that point declare it *tahor*? Can the passage of time change the legal status of something already in his possession? The answer is sought from an existing teaching.

### Inheritance Case

The Gemara cites a *baraisa*: if a *chavér* and an *am ha'aretz* inherit their father's estate, and the father himself was an *am ha'aretz*, the estate would include wine, grapes, olives, grain, and similar produce. Since the father was an *am ha'aretz*, the *chavér* must presume all of it is *tamei*. The question becomes how to divide the estate between the two heirs.

### Wet/Dry Division

The difficulty in dividing the estate is subtle. One might think the *chavér* could simply take the dry grain — which has never come into contact with liquid and is therefore not susceptible to *tumah* — and let the *am ha'aretz* take the washed grain. But since both sons are equal partners in the whole estate, such a division would effectively mean the *chavér* is transferring his share of the *tamei* washed grain to the *am ha'aretz* in exchange for the *am ha'aretz*'s share of the *tahor* dry grain. A *chavér* is not permitted to hand *tamei* produce to an *am ha'aretz* who will not observe the restrictions on it — that amounts to facilitating a transgression.

The *baraisa* therefore rules as follows: one may say *tol attah chittin she-bimkom peloni va-ani chittin she-bimkom peloni* — you take the wheat from over there and I will take the wheat from over here — where it happens that one location contains washed grain and the other dry grain, but the division is framed as a neutral geographic split of the same type of produce. One may similarly say: you take the wine from that place and I will take the wine from this place. However, one may not say: *tol attah lach va-ani yavesh* — you take the wet and I will take the dry — because that framing explicitly designates the *tamei* produce for the *am ha'aretz* and the *tahor* for the *chavér*, making it transparently a swap. Similarly, one may not say: you take the wheat and I will take the barley, because different species clearly constitute an exchange of portions.

This distinction rests on the principle of *yesh bereira* — that when a division is sufficiently natural and undifferentiated, we may treat it as though each party's portion was always already his, with no actual transfer occurring. When the division is instead framed in terms that make clear the *chavér* is trading the *tamei* for the *tahor*, there is no *bereira* to rely on and the arrangement is prohibited. If one holds *ein bereira* — that no division is ever truly pre-determined — every such split would be seen as an exchange, and the problem would be universal.

### Burning Produce

The *baraisa* rules that a *kohen chavér* in this situation burns the wet grain — since it is *terumah temei'ah* and the only permissible disposition of *terumah temei'ah* is burning — and retains the dry grain, which is *tahor*. But this prompts the central question: *amai yanichenu legas ha-ba?* — why does he have to burn it? Why not simply hold onto the wet grain until the next pressing season, at which point the general assumption of *tahara* would apply, and the need to burn it would be eliminated?

The Gemara offers two limiting answers. First: *bedavar she-ein lo gas* — perhaps this applies to something that has no pressing season. The pressing-season rule applies specifically to olive oil and grapes, which have a concentrated, well-defined period of communal processing. Grain, though it has its own seasons, does not carry the same narrowly defined pressing period with the same presumption of universal care, and arguably the leniency never applied to it in the first place. Second: *ve-yanichenu laregel* — perhaps he could hold it until the *regel* (pilgrimage festival), when everyone is also believed about *terumah*. The Gemara answers: *bedavar she-eino mishtamer laregel* — it is something that will spoil before the festival. Both answers limit the scope of the question rather than resolving it categorically: in principle, if one could wait for the next *giton* or the next *regel* and the produce would keep, it appears that waiting might indeed be a valid option.

A further implication emerges: once produce receives a stamp of *tahara* at the time of the pressing or the *regel*, it does not revert to a presumption of *tumah* once those special periods pass. The status, once established, remains. This points to the formalist underpinning of the entire system — these rules are not fine-grained empirical assessments but legal categories that operate at designated moments.

The Mishnah then records another case: if an *am ha'aretz* brings a barrel of wine outside of pressing season and says *hifrashti le-tokhah revi'is kodesh* — I have separated a quarter-log of wine from this barrel for *nesachim*, Temple libations — he is believed about the entire barrel. Since *amei ha'aretz* are always believed about *kodesh*, and this small portion has been designated for *kodesh* purposes, that believability extends to the whole barrel. The Gemara will return to this point later.

---

## Field Checking Rules

### Pesach vs. Terumah

The Gemara now introduces a Mishnah from elsewhere: *modim Beis Shammai u'Beis Hillel she'bodkin l'osei Pesach v'ein bodkin l'ochlei terumah* — both Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel agree that one checks a field for those who are bringing the *korban Pesach*, but one does not check a field for those who eat *terumah*. The context is a *beis ha-peras* — a field in which a grave was plowed over, scattering small bone fragments, which creates a rabbinic prohibition on entering because of the risk of *tumah*. If one must cross such a field to reach Jerusalem and bring the *korban Pesach*, a method of checking is available. If the concern is merely about eating *terumah*, it is not.

### Blowing Method

Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains the method of checking: *menapei'ach adam beis ha-peras ve-holeich* — one blows ahead of oneself and then takes a step, blowing any surface bone chips away before walking forward. This is permitted for those bringing the *korban Pesach*, where the urgency is acute — if one fails to bring the Pesach offering, one is liable *karet*. For *terumah*, there is no comparable urgency, and so the leniency is not extended.

### Pre-Tread Paths

Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Ulla adds a second mechanism: *beis ha-peras she-nidash tahor* — a *beis ha-peras* that has already been trodden is treated as *tahor* for those bringing the *korban Pesach*. If a path through the field shows signs of prior foot traffic — the earth has been pressed down — one may assume that the bone chips have been dislodged from that path. Admittedly, the logic is not fully transparent: the people who previously walked the path may not have been *kohanim* and may not have cared about *tumah*. Nevertheless, the prior treading is treated as sufficient grounds for leniency when the purpose is bringing the *korban Pesach*. Here too the leniency applies only *l'osei Pesach*.

### Karet vs. Misah

The Gemara provides a structural explanation for why the leniency applies specifically to the *korban Pesach*: *lo he'emidu divreihem bi-mekom kares* — the Sages did not insist on their rabbinic restrictions when doing so would expose a person to liability for *karet*. One who deliberately fails to bring the *korban Pesach* is liable *karet*, and therefore the Sages relaxed their stringencies to enable the offering to be brought.

By contrast, *he'emidu divreihem bi-mekom misah* — they maintained their restrictions in the case of *terumah*, even though eating *terumah* while *tamei* carries a penalty of *misah bidei shamayim*. The structure of the parallel is somewhat inverted: in the case of Pesach, waiving the restriction allows the person to fulfill an obligation and avoid *karet*; in the case of *terumah*, maintaining the restriction protects the person from accidentally incurring *misah bidei shamayim*. So the same concern — preventing the gravest consequences — drives both rulings, even though one operates by relaxing and the other by upholding the rabbinic standard.

### Pesach to Terumah

This leads to the question the Gemara has been building toward: *bodek l'pischo mahu she-yochal bi-terumaso?* — if a person blew the path through the *beis ha-peras* and brought his *korban Pesach*, may he now eat *terumah* on the basis of the same *tahara* status? It would seem peculiar to say that the same person is *tahor* for purposes of the *korban Pesach* but must treat himself as *tamei* when he wishes to eat *terumah*. Yet this is precisely the question, and its resolution draws directly on the logic of the earlier ruling about the barrel of wine.

### Unified Status

Ulla rules: *bodek l'pischo mutar le-echol bi-terumaso* — if you walked the blown path and can bring your *korban Pesach*, you may also eat your *terumah*. Rabbah bar Ulla disagrees: *bodek l'pischo assur le-echol bi-terumaso* — you may not.

A certain elder rebukes Rabbah bar Ulla, citing the very Mishnah under discussion. The Mishnah had ruled that if a man declares he separated a quarter-log of wine from a barrel for *kodesh* purposes, he is believed about the entire barrel. The implication is clear: *mi-d'meheiman a-kodesh meheiman nami a-terumah* — since he is believed about the *kodesh* portion, he is also believed about the *terumah* portion. We do not say the same barrel is *tahor* for *kodesh* and *tamei* for *terumah*. By the same logic — *hacha nami mi-d'meheiman a-Pesach meheiman nami a-terumah* — since he is deemed *tahor* for the purpose of bringing the *korban Pesach*, he is also *tahor* for *terumah*. We do not assign the same person a bifurcated purity status for different purposes. The Gemara leaves this without rebuttal, indicating that Ulla's position is accepted.

---

## Vessels vs. Contents

### Barrel Belief

The Mishnah had stated that *kadei yayin u-khadi shemen ha-meduma'os* — barrels of wine and barrels of oil that are *meduma'os* — are believed about at the time of the pressing and for seventy days before. The category of *meduma'os* ordinarily refers to a mixture of *terumah* and *chulin*, or possibly *tevel*, and its significance here is not immediately clear.

### Meduma'os Definition

The *tana* glosses the Mishnah: they are believed neither about the barrels themselves nor about the *terumah* inside. The Gemara presses: what exactly is the case? If we are talking about jugs designated for *kodesh* wine or oil — for Temple use — then by the principle already established, *migo d'meheiman a-kodesh meheiman nami a-kankanim*: since one is believed about the *kodesh* contents, one is believed about the jugs as well. The two cannot be disaggregated in that direction.

### Empty vs. Filled

The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing two scenarios. The case where one is *not* believed about the vessels is that of empty jugs normally used for *kodesh* wine or oil, outside of the pressing season. Even though one is believed about *kodesh* contents when present, if the jug is empty and a *chavér* wishes to borrow it for his own use, he must immerse it — the *chavér* cannot treat the empty vessel as *tahor* just because he would have been believed about the *kodesh* contents that were formerly in it. Believability about the contents does not automatically confer believability about the vessel in isolation.

Conversely, there is a case — *u-vimalaim de-trumah u-visha'as ha-gisos* — where one is believed about *terumah* wine but not about the vessel containing it. During the pressing season, the *chavér* can accept the *am ha'aretz*'s *terumah* wine as *tahor*, yet cannot treat the barrel itself as *tahor*. The practical consequence is: pour the wine into my vessel and take your barrel back.

### Wine/Vessel Paradox

This is admittedly paradoxical. How can the wine be *tahor* while the vessel containing it is *tamei*? The Gemara initially assumed that believability must be holistic — if you believe one, you believe the other. Here it is saying: not necessarily. We believe the *am ha'aretz* about the wine for *terumah* purposes but do not believe him about the vessel. This is an explicit legal fiction the system is prepared to maintain.

### Rashi's Policy

Rashi makes the policy rationale explicit. He writes: *she-lo gazru al trumasun bi-sha'as ha-gisos mishum hefsed Kohanim chaveirim de-nimtza mafsid es rov trumas Eretz Yisrael* — the Sages did not decree against accepting *terumah* at the pressing season out of concern for the loss sustained by *kohanim* who are *chavérim*, since doing so would forfeit the majority of the *terumah* of the Land of Israel. If one could not believe the *am ha'aretz* about *terumah* during the pressing season, the *kohanim* would effectively lose access to most of the year's *terumah*. That is the operative consideration — not merely that people happen to be more careful at this time of year, though that factual basis exists as well. As for the vessels: *al ha-kankanim lo heiminum*, since a *kohen chavér* does not accept vessels together with the *terumah* — he simply has the *am ha'aretz* pour the wine into his own vessel. The believability is calibrated to what is actually needed.

Rashi's comment makes visible what underlies the entire architecture of these rules: from the vantage point of strict *halacha*, an *am ha'aretz* would ordinarily be believed about everything, since all of these skepticisms are rabbinic stringencies layered upon stringencies. The Sages who erected those stringencies are equally empowered to relax them when weighty policy considerations — the unity of Israel, the economic interests of *kohanim chavérim*, the practical necessities of daily life — so require.

---

## Pottery Vessels

### Modi'in Vessels

The Mishnah next turns to pottery vessels. It states: *min ha-Modiin u-lefanim ne'emanim al klei cheres* — from Modi'in inward, *amei ha'aretz* are believed that pottery vessels are *tahor* at all times. Modi'in is located approximately fifteen *mil* — about fifteen kilometers — from Jerusalem, placing it within the immediate environs of the city.

### Kiln Location

The Gemara explains the background: kilns for pottery production were not maintained within Jerusalem itself, because they would have created smoke and pollution within the city. Kilns were therefore situated outside Jerusalem, in the surrounding areas. This meant that pottery production was concentrated precisely in the zone inhabited more heavily by *amei ha'aretz*, since the *chavérim* tended to cluster closer to the *Beis Hamikdash* and its environment of heightened *tahara*. If the testimony of the *amei ha'aretz* who produced the pottery were not credited, it would become impossible to obtain *tahor* pottery vessels at all.

### Community Needs

Rashi articulates the policy point directly: *she-lo ligzor aleihem she-ein gozrin gezeirah al ha-tzibbur she-ein rov ha-tzibbur yekholim la'amod bah* — the Sages did not apply their decree to the pottery makers because one may not impose a decree on the public that the majority of the public cannot live with. People need pottery vessels. If every vessel had to be presumed *tamei* because its maker was an *am ha'aretz*, the community could not function. The practical necessity overrides the standard presumption of untrustworthiness.

### Modi'in Context

The Mishnah then distinguishes: *min ha-Modiin ve-lachutz, ein ne'emanim* — from Modi'in outward, they are not believed. The formal boundary is Modi'in itself, and the Mishnah illustrates the rule with a case of pure formalism: the same jug merchant, with the same jugs, selling to the same buyers — if encountered inside of Modi'in toward Jerusalem, *ne'eman*, he is believed; if encountered outside of Modi'in, *eino ne'eman*, he is not. The Mishnah here makes explicit the legal formalism at work: we cannot assess each transaction individually, and so the boundary is fixed.

### Direction Test

The *tanna* adds: *Modi'in pe'amim ke-lifnim u-fe'amim ke-lachutz* — Modi'in itself sometimes has the status of the inside and sometimes the outside. The Gemara explains: if the jug merchant is heading away from Jerusalem and the *chavér* is heading toward Jerusalem, this is their last opportunity to transact before parting in opposite directions, and so Modi'in is treated as *lifnim* — within the credible zone — and the purchase is permitted. If both are heading toward Jerusalem, they need not transact in Modi'in but can wait until they are fully inside the *lifnim* zone. And if both are heading away from Jerusalem — or both heading in the same direction — Modi'in is treated as *lachutz*, the outer zone, and the *am ha'aretz* is not believed.

### Thin Vessels Only

A *tanna* qualifies the scope of this leniency: *ne'emanim al klei cheres ha-dakim le-kodesh* — they are believed only about the thin, small pottery vessels. These are the vessels most commonly needed for daily use, and it is for their sake that the communal leniency was enacted. The larger, heavier vessels do not enjoy the same presumption.

### Size/Full Dispute

Reish Lakish adds a further restriction: the vessels must be small enough to be carried in one hand. Rabbi Yochanan is more lenient: even if they require two hands to carry, they are within the scope of the leniency, perhaps because they are thin even if somewhat large. Reish Lakish also rules: *lo shanu ela reikanin aval meleim lo* — the leniency applies only to empty vessels, not to full ones. The reasoning is this: if the vessel is filled with *chulin* wine, or with *terumah* wine outside of the pressing season, the *am ha'aretz* is not believed about the contents — they must be presumed *tamei*. Can one then still treat the vessel itself as *tahor*? Reish Lakish says no: if one must presume the contents are *tamei*, one must presume the vessel is *tamei* as well. Rabbi Yochanan permits it even when full.

### Pure Vessel/Impure Conte…

Rava clarifies Rabbi Yochanan's position: *u-modeh Rabbi Yochanan be-mashkin atzman she-hein temei'im* — Rabbi Yochanan concedes that the liquid contents are indeed *tamei*; he is not saying that the vessel's status elevates the liquid. He is saying the reverse: we can simultaneously hold that the liquid is *tamei* and the vessel is *tahor*, which is the mirror image of the case discussed earlier where the *terumah* wine was *tahor* but the vessel was *tamei*. The Gemara anticipates the objection — how can two physically interacting objects have contradictory purity statuses? — and responds: *ve-al titmah*, do not be astounded, and cites the case of *lugin temei'im tumat shiva u-mashkin tehorin*. Pitchers can be *tamei* with a seven-day *tumah* due to contact with a *meis*, while the liquids inside them remain *tahor* — a case already established in earlier discussions involving Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel. Here too, the contradictory statuses of vessel and contents are legally coherent, even if counterintuitive.

The larger pattern running through this entire section is now legible: the architecture of *tahara* law accommodates deliberate legal fictions, sustained contradictions between the status of objects in physical contact, and policy-driven modifications of baseline rules — all in service of making it possible for the community to function and for *kohanim chavérim* to receive their *terumah*.

---

## Collectors & Thieves

### Tax Collectors

The Mishnah states: *ha-gabba'im she-nichnesu le-toch ha-bayis* — tax collectors who entered a house, as well as thieves who returned stolen vessels — are believed to say *lo naganu*, that they did not touch certain items. The tax collectors referenced here are the *am ha'aretz* of the rabbinic imagination — the same type of people with whom, as the New Testament records, one does not ordinarily eat. And yet they are credited when they specify what they did and did not touch, so that the *chavér* need not treat the items they disclaim touching as *tamei*.

---

## Yom Tov Belief

### Festival Rule

The Mishnah then arrives at its culminating principle: *u-vi-sha'as ha-regel af al ha-terumah* — at the time of the pilgrimage festival, everyone is believed even about *terumah*. This is the broadest and most consequential of all the leniencies catalogued in the chapter, and its basis, as the Gemara will make clear, is not primarily empirical — it is not simply that people are more careful about *tahara* on the *regel* — but is rooted in *Chazal*'s deliberate effort to create unity among the entire people of Israel when they gather together in Jerusalem. The festival leniency, more than any other, is an expression of communal policy rather than a judgment about individual trustworthiness.

---

## Collectors & Thieves (II)

### Supervisor Present

The Gemara raises a contradiction against the Mishnah's ruling about tax collectors. A *baraisa* states: *gabba'im she-nichnesu le-toch ha-bayis kulo tamei* — when tax collectors entered the house, everything is presumed *tamei*. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: *ha de-ika nochri bahadeihu ha de-leika nochri bahadeihu* — the cases differ depending on whether a non-Jew is supervising them. The Mishnah, which credits their testimony, refers to a case without a non-Jewish supervisor; the *baraisa*, which presumes everything *tamei*, refers to a case where a non-Jew is present and overseeing the collection. The *tanna* elaborates: if there is a non-Jew with them, the collectors may say they did not enter the house at all, and that is believed; but they cannot say they entered yet touched nothing. Rashi explains: the reason they cannot disclaim touching when a non-Jew was present is that one must assume they inspected everything thoroughly — not because the non-Jew compelled them to lie, but because they would not have risked failing to conduct a complete inspection before their supervisor.

### Fear Source

Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute the precise mechanism. One holds *eimas nochri aleihem* — they fear the non-Jew himself; the other holds *eimas malchus aleihem* — they fear the governmental authority he represents and the prospect that he will report their negligence to the government. The practical difference between the two positions concerns a non-Jew who is not particularly important or well-connected: according to the view that the fear is personal, a non-entity of a non-Jew would not inhibit the collectors from being selective in their search. According to the view that the fear is institutional — fear of governmental authority — even a low-status non-Jew represents a reporting channel to the government, and the collectors would still feel compelled to inspect thoroughly.

### Thieves' Teshuvah

The Gemara turns to the second half of the Mishnah: *ve-chen ha-ganavim she-hechziru es ha-keilim* — thieves who returned the vessels are believed. A *baraisa* is cited in apparent tension: *ha-ganavim she-nichnesu le-toch ha-bayis eino tamei ela mekom drisat raglei ha-ganavim* — when thieves entered a house, only the places where they walked are *tamei*. This suggests that the areas they did not walk are unaffected, but Rashi reads the tension as follows: if one must presume *tamei* wherever they walked, perhaps one should also presume *tamei* whatever vessels they handled, and their testimony that they did not touch the contents of a vessel should not be credited.

Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav — or in the name of Rava — provides the resolution: *keshe-asu teshuvah* — when they have done *teshuvah*, returning the vessels is itself the act of repentance, and one who is in the process of sincere *teshuvah* is believed. When they have not done *teshuvah*, the presumption of *tumah* stands. The Gemara notes that this is supported by the precise language of the Mishnah itself: *she-hechziru es ha-keilim* — the Mishnah specifies that they returned the vessels, which is the act that signals *teshuvah*. *Shema mina.*

A further question remains implicit: why are these people — tax collectors and thieves, quintessential *amei ha'aretz* — believed about *tahara* at all, given that *amei ha'aretz* are generally distrusted in these matters? Rashi limits the believability to *kodesh*, which falls within the general rule that *amei ha'aretz* are always believed about *kodesh*. Tosafot extends it even to *terumah*. One might add that there is a meaningful distinction between believing someone about how they handled someone else's property — where they have no personal stake in misrepresenting their care — and believing them about how they handled their own produce, where the very question of whether they are a *chavér* or an *am ha'aretz* colors every claim they make.

---

## Yom Tov Belief (II)

### Sukkot Lead-in

The shiur concludes at this juncture, with the full discussion of *sha'as ha-regel* — when the entire Jewish people becomes mutually trusted about *terumah* in an act of communal solidarity — left for the next session. That discussion will open after *Yom Kippur*, serving as a fitting lead-in to *Sukkot*, when *kol Yisrael* gathers once more as a unified people.

---

---

# Chagigah 25b

## Produce Processing Times

### Pressing Season Trust

The *amud* opens with a principle that begins to dissolve the rigid distinctions between *amei ha-aretz* and *chaverim* regarding purity: *u-vish'at ha-gitot ne'emanim al ha-terumah* — at the time of the pressing of the grapes and the olives, common people are believed even with respect to *terumah*. This leniency operates across all geographical regions, unlike the believability regarding *kodesh*, which is confined to Judea on account of its proximity to the *Beit Ha-mikdash*. Two reinforcing rationales underlie this rule. First, as Rashi notes, the pressing season is a time when everyone collectively immersed their vessels in the *mikvah* and exercised heightened care, creating a stronger presumption of *taharah* across the board. Second — and Rashi will make this explicit shortly — there is a social policy at work: without this leniency, *kohanim* who are *chaverim* would be effectively excluded from receiving the great bulk of *terumah* produced during harvest season.

### Priest Livelihood Policy

The *gemara* immediately raises a contradiction. A *baraita* teaches that one who finishes pressing his olives should set aside an unpressed basket and give it to a poor *kohen* who is a *chaver*. The implication is striking: the reason to give it in unpressed form is precisely that unpressed olives have not come into contact with liquid and are therefore not susceptible to *tumah*. If the *am ha-aretz* were believed at the time of pressing, there would be no need for this workaround — the *kohen* could simply accept the pressed oil. The *baraita* thus seems to indicate that even during the pressing season one is not believed regarding *tumah* and *taharah*.

Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction: *lo kashya ha be-charfi ha be-afli* — the two cases are not in conflict but simply address different circumstances. The *baraita* concerns a late harvest, one pressed outside the normal season, and thus outside the period of heightened communal care and policy-driven leniency. When Rav Adda bar Abba pressed for a concrete example, Rav Nachman replied: *kegon oson shel Beis Avicha* — like the olives from your own father's house, which were known to ripen late and were therefore always pressed after the standard season.

### Wine vs. Grain Vessels

Rav Yosef adds a geographic dimension, suggesting that the rule of pressing-season believability was stated specifically in the context of the Galilee — *be-Galil lo shanu* — and does not apply there. This requires some explanation. We already understood why *kodesh* believability was limited to Judea: proximity to the *Beit Ha-mikdash* created conditions that did not obtain in Galilee. But why should pressing-season *terumah* believability differ by region? Abaye challenges this position by citing a *baraita*: *Ever ha-Yarden ve-ha-Galil harei hen ke-Yehudah le-terumah* — Transjordan and Galilee are treated like Judea for purposes of *terumah*. The *baraita* explicitly states that in those regions people are believed about wine during the wine-pressing season, and about oil during the oil-pressing season — but not each during the other's season.

### Judea-Galilee Split

The geographical question thus resolves in favor of universality. The Galilean distinction Rav Yosef proposed does not hold. The pressing-season leniency for *terumah* applies regardless of location.

### Unified Baraita Rule

Having examined Rav Nachman's resolution and the *baraita*, the *gemara* concludes: *ella machvarta kedi-shani me-ikara* — the original answer was preferable. The clear principle is that at the pressing season, people are believed about *terumah* everywhere, and the *baraita*'s concern was only an exceptional case of out-of-season pressing.

---

## Post-Season Restrictions

### Outside Season Ban

Once the pressing season — *sha'at ha-gitot* — passes, the leniency lapses entirely. *Avru ha-gitot ve-ha-badidim, ve-heivi lo chavis shel yayin lo yekabelenu* — if an *am ha-aretz* brings a *chaver* a barrel of wine after that time has passed, the *chaver* may not accept it. This holds even if it is the exact same barrel that would have been accepted during the pressing season. One might wonder: hasn't the wine simply had more opportunity to become *tamei* with the passage of time? This is a fair observation, and it points to how the rule is somewhat abstracted into a formal principle: the pressing season creates an institutional window of believability, not a calculation of actual likelihood of *taharah*.

### Heir Division Case

Against this backdrop, Rav Sheshes is posed a question: *avar ve-kiblah mahu she-yanichennu le-gat ha-ba'ah?* — if a *kohen chaver* accepted the barrel outside the season, is he permitted to hold onto it until the next pressing season and then, ten months hence, retroactively rely on what the *am ha-aretz* told him at the time of delivery? Can the vessel sit in his possession and change its purity status when the calendar turns?

In response, Rav Sheshes says *tneina* — we have already been taught this in a *mishnah*. The case involves a *chaver* and an *am ha-aretz* who were brothers and inherited the estate of their father, who was himself an *am ha-aretz*. Because the father was an *am ha-aretz*, the *chaver* must presume the entire estate is *tamei*. Among the estate's assets are various types of produce and grain, some that has come into contact with liquid and some that has not.

One might think the simplest resolution is for the *chaver* to take the dry, unwashed grain — which has never become susceptible to *tumah* — and leave the washed produce to the *am ha-aretz* brother. But this creates a serious problem. Since the two brothers are equal partners in the entire estate, proposing that one takes the dry produce and the other takes the washed produce is not merely a division — it is effectively a swap. The *chaver* would be handing over to the *am ha-aretz* produce that is already *tamei*, knowing full well that the *am ha-aretz* will not observe the relevant restrictions. This runs afoul of the prohibition of *v'lifnei iver* — facilitating another's transgression.

### Bereira Principle

The *mishnah* therefore defines carefully which modes of division are permissible. The *chaver* may say to the *am ha-aretz*: *tol atta chitin shebimkom ploni va-ani chitin shebimkom ploni* — you take the wheat from this location and I will take the wheat from that location. Similarly, he may designate portions of wine by location: you take the wine in this place and I will take the wine in that place. What he may not say is: *tol atta lach va-ani yavesh* — you take the wet grain and I will take the dry. Nor may he say: you take the wheat and I will take the barley, for that is transparently an exchange of his stake in one type of produce for the other's stake in a different type.

The underlying principle is *bereira* — the doctrine of retroactive selection. Where the division is natural and relatively arbitrary, such that one could say the portions were always *de facto* destined for each heir, we apply *yesh bereira*: the *chaver*'s portion was always, in some sense, his own, and no actual transfer of *tamei* property to the *am ha-aretz* has taken place. But where the division is structured so as to give the *am ha-aretz* the washed produce and the *chaver* the dry — a division explicitly calibrated by purity status — it is no longer a natural split but an intentional exchange, and *bereira* cannot be invoked to dissolve the transaction into a mere partition.

### Burning Impure Terumah

The *mishnah* then rules: *oto chaver soref ha-lach u-maniach et ha-yavesh* — that *chaver*, if he is a *kohen*, must burn the washed or liquid produce he has inherited — for it is *terumah tmei'ah*, impure priestly portions, which may only be disposed of by burning — while he may retain the dry produce as *tahor*.

This ruling circles back directly to the question raised about holding the barrel until the next pressing season. The *gemara* asks: *amai yanichenu le-gat ha-ba'ah?* — why must he burn it? Why not simply keep the washed produce until the next pressing season and at that point assume, as a matter of communal policy, that everything is *tahor*? The father who knew the purity status of the produce is dead; and if the pressing-season leniency requires no active claim by anyone — if the calendar alone suffices to restore a presumption of *taharah* — then why can't the *chaver* simply wait?

The *gemara* answers: *bidvar she-ein lo gat* — we are speaking of produce that has no pressing season. Grain washing, for instance, does not correspond to the kind of focused, communally observed pressing season that generates the institutional leniency. Without that seasonal anchor, there is no mechanism for restoring *taharah* through the passage of time. The *gemara* then asks: *v'yanichenu le-regel?* — perhaps he could wait until a *regel* (pilgrimage festival), when everyone is also believed about *terumah*? The *gemara* answers: *bidvar she-eino mishtamer le-regel* — the produce in question would spoil before the *regel* arrives. Accordingly, the ruling to burn it stands, but it does not actually resolve the theoretical question of whether, in cases where waiting is possible, such waiting would change the purity status. That question remains open.

### Pressing Season Requirem…

A further limitation on the pressing-season leniency is established: it applies only to produce that actually has a pressing season — olive oil and wine, whose harvest and processing are concentrated into a defined communal period. It does not extend to produce whose handling is diffuse and unstructured. This is the formal constraint that anchors the entire regime of *sha'at ha-gitot* believability.

---

## Festival Field Travel

### Blowing Path Leniency

The *mishnah* in another tractate records: *modin Beit Shammai le-Veit Hillel she-bodkin le-osei Pesach ve-ein bodkin le-ochlei terumah* — Beit Shammai agrees with Beit Hillel that one examines one's purity status for the purpose of bringing the *korban Pesach*, but not for the purpose of eating *terumah*. The *gemara* explains what *bodkin* means in this context. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says: *menapeach adam beit ha-peras ve-holech* — a person may blow ahead of himself as he walks through a *beit ha-peras* and proceed. A *beit ha-peras* is a field in which a grave was plowed over, scattering fragments of bone, which create rabbinic *tumah* for anyone who passes through. By blowing the ground immediately in front of each step, one dislodges surface fragments and may traverse the field in order to reach Jerusalem to bring the *korban Pesach*. The result is that one is considered *tahor* for *Pesach* purposes — but this leniency is extended only for *osei Pesach*, not for the purpose of eating *terumah*.

### Pre-Trodden Path

A related leniency: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Ulla teaches that a *beit ha-peras* that has been trodden — *she-nidash* — is considered *tahor* for those bringing the *korban Pesach*. The assumption is that a path already worn down by foot traffic has had the surface bone fragments dislodged or displaced, though the precise mechanism of this assumption is not fully transparent. The leniency applies because people traveling to Jerusalem for the festival create a pre-trodden path that can then be relied upon by subsequent travelers.

### Karet vs. Death Rationale

The principle unifying both leniencies is stated explicitly: *lo he'emidu divreihem bimkom karet* — the Rabbis did not maintain their restrictions at the cost of one's incurring *karet* for failing to bring the *korban Pesach*. The severity of *karet* for neglecting the *Pesach* obligation overrides the rabbinic stringency. The parallel rule for *terumah* runs in the opposite direction: *he'emidu divreihem bimkom mitah* — they maintained their position where the concern is the prohibition against eating *terumah* in a state of *tumat meit*, which carries the penalty of *mitah bi-dei shamayim*. The structure is somewhat inverted: in the case of *Pesach*, the Rabbis relax their rules to prevent the person from incurring *karet* for not performing a commandment; in the case of *terumah*, they maintain their rules to protect the person from incurring *mitah bi-dei shamayim* for performing a prohibited act. The logic in both cases, however, is the same — the Rabbis calibrate their stringencies against the severity of the transgression at stake.

It bears noting that the *regel*-based leniency discussed elsewhere is rooted less in an empirical assessment of people's actual care during the festival and more in *Chazal*'s deliberate policy of creating unity among the Jewish people at the time of pilgrimage. The pressing-season leniency is similarly policy-driven, as Rashi makes clear: the Rabbis needed to ensure that *kohanim* who are *chaverim* would not be cut off from the *terumah* of the entire Land of Israel. From a strict *halachic* standpoint, all of these restrictions on the believability of *amei ha-aretz* are layers of stringency beyond the letter of the law, and the Rabbis were therefore prepared to waive them when sufficient countervailing considerations existed.

### Pesach-Terumah Status

A natural question follows from the *beit ha-peras* leniency: *badak le-pischo mahu she-yochal be-trumaso?* — if a person walked through the field by blowing and thereby established his *taharah* for the purpose of the *korban Pesach*, is he also permitted to eat his *terumah*? It would seem peculiar to say the same person is *tahor* for one purpose and *tamei* for another. And yet the leniency was explicitly granted only for *osei Pesach*.

### Unified Status Resolution

Ulla rules: *badak le-fischo mutar le-echol be-trumaso* — one who cleared his path for *Pesach* may also eat his *terumah*. Rabba bar Ulla disagrees and holds that the *Pesach* clearance does not extend to *terumah*. A certain elder intervened and told Rabba bar Ulla not to disagree with Ulla, for the *mishnah* supports Ulla's position. The *mishnah* states: if an *am ha-aretz* declares that he has separated a *revi'it* of *kodesh* from within his barrel of wine, he is believed — and that believability extends to the wine in the barrel as a whole. The elder reasons: *alma mi-di-heimen a-kodesh heimen nami a-terumah* — if he is trusted regarding *kodesh*, he is trusted regarding *terumah* as well; we do not bifurcate a single person's *taharah* status by category. By the same logic, *hacha nami mi-di-heimen a-Pesach heimen nami a-terumah* — since this man's path-clearing was sufficient for the purposes of *Pesach*, it is sufficient for *terumah* as well. One cannot be *tahor* in one register and *tamei* in another simultaneously. The elder's argument stands without rebuttal.

---

## Mixed Vessel Belief

### Seventy-Day Prior Belief

The *mishnah* introduces a further category: *kadei yayin ve-kadei shemen ha-meduma'ot* — barrels of wine and oil that are *meduma'ot*, a term that typically denotes a mixture of *terumah* and *chulin*. The *mishnah* states that one is believed regarding them at the time of the pressing and, strikingly, seventy days beforehand as well. The plain reading of the *mishnah* suggests that belief in the vessels themselves — not merely the wine or oil — begins seventy days before the actual pressing season, presumably because the preparation of vessels requires that much advance lead time. Abaye infers from this: *shema mina dina hu de-iluiei arisa le-mitrach agufna* — the normative practice is for the sharecropper to begin tending and preparing the vineyard seventy days before the harvest.

The *baraita* then clarifies what remains: *ein ne'emanim lo al ha-kankanim ve-lo al ha-terumah* — they are not believed either regarding the jugs themselves or regarding the *terumah*. The *gemara* sets out to understand the precise scenario in which each of these limitations applies.

### Kodesh vs. Terumah Mix

The *gemara* asks: what exactly are we discussing? If the jugs contain wine or oil designated as *kodesh* — for *Beit Ha-mikdash* purposes — then *migu de-heimen a-kodesh heimen nami a-kankanim*: just as the *am ha-aretz* is believed that the *kodesh* wine is *tahor*, so too is he believed that the jug containing it is *tahor*. The belief in the contents extends to belief in the vessel. But if the jugs are vessels used for *terumah* — at a time other than the pressing season — then of course one is not believed about the jugs, since one is not believed about the *terumah* itself. As the *gemara* puts it: *hashta terumah lo meiman, kankanim meiman?* — if you are not trusted regarding the *terumah*, how could you be trusted regarding the vessels? So what case does the ruling of disbelief — regarding vessels — actually address?

The *gemara* proposes: *ella be-reikanim de-kodesh u-vish'ar yemot ha-shanah* — empty jugs normally used for *kodesh* wine, at a time other than the pressing season. In ordinary circumstances, if an *am ha-aretz* tells you that the *kodesh* wine in a jug is *tahor*, you believe him — and the belief extends to the jug. But if the jug is currently empty, even though it is normally used for *kodesh* purposes, a *chaver* who wishes to borrow it must take it to the *mikvah*. The believability attached to the *kodesh* wine does not persist when the jug is empty and standing alone without its *kodesh* contents.

Then the *gemara* identifies an even more counterintuitive scenario: *u-ve-mlei'im de-terumah u-vish'at ha-gitot* — jugs full of *terumah* wine during the pressing season. Here, the *kohen chaver* is prepared to believe that the *terumah* is *tahor* — because it is the pressing season — but he does not believe the *am ha-aretz* that the jug itself is *tahor*. The practical resolution: the *chaver* says to the *am ha-aretz*, pour the wine into my vessel, and take yours back. The wine is received as *tahor*; the jug is treated as *tamei*.

### Libation Intention Status

The *gemara* now returns to the question of what *meduma'ot* means in the context of *kodesh*. The term ordinarily denotes a mixture of *terumah* and *chulin*, but what would a *kodesh* mixture look like? The school of Rabbi Ilai explains: *be-metaheret tivlo litol mimenu nesakhim* — the case involves produce from which the owner has declared his intention to take wine for *nesakhim* (libation offerings). By announcing that he will be drawing *kodesh* wine for *nesakhim* from the batch being pressed, the grapes take on an ontological pre-separated *kodesh* status. They are, in some sense, already designated *kodesh*. As a result, the heightened believability that attaches to *kodesh* — including believability about the vessels — extends to the entire batch and the containers holding it, even before the pressing begins.

This is admittedly a striking reading of the *mishnah*. The plain meaning of *kadei yayin ve-kadei shemen ne'emanim aleihem* is that one is believed about the vessels in addition to the wine, and the seventy-day advance period explains why the vessels are addressed separately. But because the *gemara* has established that one is *not* believed about vessels in the context of *terumah*, the *mishnah* must be read as referring to a special *kodesh* scenario, not a *terumah* scenario.

### Declared Kodesh Vessel B…

The practical consequence is as follows. An *am ha-aretz* who has declared his intention to draw wine for *nesakhim* from a batch of grapes achieves a status for his produce and vessels such that a *chaver* may believe him even about the vessels — outside the pressing season and many weeks in advance. This stands in contrast to the *terumah* scenario, where belief in the vessel is withheld even when belief in the wine itself is granted. Rashi makes the policy dimension explicit: *she-af al pi she-lo gazru al trumatan bi-sh'at ha-gitot mishum hefsed kohanim chaverim* — the Rabbis refrained from applying their restrictions to *terumah* during the pressing season because to do so would deprive *kohanim* who are *chaverim* of the majority of the *terumah* of the Land of Israel. The limitation to the wine and not the vessels in the *terumah* case is itself a product of this policy: the *kohen chaver* needs the wine, not the *am ha-aretz*'s jug, and so the leniency is calibrated accordingly — *al ha-kankanim lo heiminum d'ein kohen chaver mekabel mehen kankanim im ha-terumah aval me'areh hu le-cheleihem* — he pours it into his own vessel.

---

## Modi'in Pottery Vessels

### Jerusalem Pottery Policy

The *mishnah* introduces a further leniency regarding pottery vessels from a specific geographic range: *min ha-Modi'in u-lifnim ne'emanim al klei cheres* — from Modi'in inward toward Jerusalem, *amei ha-aretz* are believed that their pottery vessels are *tahor*, at all times of the year. The rationale, as Rashi explains, is rooted in an infrastructural reality: kilns for firing pottery were not established within Jerusalem itself, on account of the smoke and smell they would have produced. The pottery industry was situated outside the city, precisely in the areas where *amei ha-aretz* predominated. People living in Jerusalem depended on pottery vessels produced by those outside the city, and if one could not trust the potters or vendors regarding the *taharah* of their vessels, the entire population of Jerusalem would be unable to function. Rashi frames this in terms of a standing principle: *lo gazru aleihem she-gez'eirah d'leit tzibbur she-ein rov tzibbur yecholim laamod bah* — a rabbinic decree that the majority of the public cannot observe is not enacted. Since the Jerusalemite public could not manage without pottery from these outer areas, the Rabbis established a policy of believability.

### Modi'in Geography Rule

The geographic line is drawn at Modi'in, approximately fifteen *mil* from Jerusalem — a meaningful radius, roughly a day's journey. From within that radius, *amei ha-aretz* are believed about pottery vessels. From beyond Modi'in, *ein ne'emanim* — they are not believed.

### Direction-Based Modi'in…

The *mishnah* then provides a remarkable illustration of the rule's formalist application: *ha-kadar she-hu mocher kadeirot, nichnas lifnim min ha-Modi'in* — if the pottery merchant, with his wares, is encountered inside Modi'in on his way toward Jerusalem, *hu ha-kadar ve-hen ha-kadeirot ve-hen ha-lokechim — ne'eman*: the same merchant, the same jugs, the same buyers — he is believed. *Yatza* — if you encounter that same merchant, with the same jugs and buyers, outside of Modi'in — *eino ne'eman*. The *mishnah* makes no apology for the formalism. Location determines believability; the individual facts of any particular case are irrelevant.

What of Modi'in itself? A *tanna* teaches: *Modi'in pe'amim ke-lifnim u-fe'amim ke-lachutz* — Modi'in is sometimes treated as inside and sometimes as outside, depending on the direction of movement of the parties. If the pottery merchant is heading away from Jerusalem (*yotze*) while the *chaver* is heading toward it (*nichnas*), the status is *ke-lifnim*: since this is the last opportunity the *chaver* will have to purchase from this merchant before the merchant exits the trusted zone, the transaction is treated as though it takes place within the inner region, and the *chaver* may buy. If both are heading toward Jerusalem — *shneihem nichnasin* — there is no urgency, and the *chaver* should wait until they are actually inside the inner zone before purchasing; in Modi'in itself the transaction is *ke-lachutz*. Similarly, if both are heading outward — *shneihem yotz'im* — even though they are physically in Modi'in, their trajectory is away from Jerusalem, and the location is treated as *ke-lachutz*.

Abaye then notes that this directional rule can actually be inferred from the original *mishnah* itself. The *mishnah*'s language — the merchant is found *inside* Modi'in, he is believed; if he *exits*, he is not believed — leaves Modi'in's own status ambiguous. Rather than a contradiction, the *gemara* reads the ambiguity as encoding exactly the directional rule the *tanna* articulated: *kan be-kadar yotze ve-chaver nichnas, kan be-shneihem yotz'im o shneihem nichnasin* — the *mishnah*'s silence about Modi'in proper is resolved by direction of travel.

### Small Vessel Limitation

A *tanna* further qualifies: *ne'emanim al klei cheres ha-dakim le-kodesh* — they are believed specifically regarding the thin, small pottery vessels, and for *kodesh* purposes. The leniency does not apply to large, heavy vessels. The distinction reflects the relative degree of need: small, thin vessels are the everyday items that people require in quantity and cannot easily do without, and for which the policy of universal believability is therefore most pressing.

Within this qualification, Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan disagree. Resh Lakish holds: *vehu she-nitlin be-yado achat* — the vessel must be small enough to carry in one hand. Rabbi Yochanan holds: *afilu she-ein nitlin be-yado achat* — even if both hands are needed, as long as it is thin. Resh Lakish adds a further condition: *lo shanu ela reikanim aval mlei'im lo* — the leniency applies only to empty vessels. If the vessel is full, it is not believed.

### Pure Vessel-Impure Liquid

This creates a paradox that the *gemara* addresses directly. Since the *chaver* cannot trust the *am ha-aretz* about *chulin* wine, or about *terumah* wine outside the pressing season, if the vessel is sold full, the *chaver* must assume the liquid is *tamei*. Should he then assume the vessel is also *tamei*? Resh Lakish says yes — the full vessel loses its presumption of *taharah*. Rabbi Yochanan says *afilu mlei'im* — even a full vessel retains its presumed *taharah*, regardless of the status of the liquid within.

This is, as the *gemara* acknowledges, precisely the inverse of what was established earlier. Previously it was said that at pressing time the *terumah* wine is *tahor* but the vessel is *tamei*. Here Rabbi Yochanan says the vessel is *tahor* even though the wine inside is *tamei*. Rava confirms that Rabbi Yochanan does not claim the liquid itself is *tahor* — *u-modeh Rabbi Yochanan be-mashkin atzman she-hen tmei'im* — he acknowledges that the liquid is *tamei*. It is simply that the vessel's *taharah* is assessed independently.

The *gemara* anticipates the obvious objection — that this seems contradictory — and pre-empts it: *ve-al titma* — do not be astonished. For we have already encountered a similar disjunction. The case of *lugin mlei'im mashkin, lugin tamei tumat shiva u-mashkin tehorin* — pitchers that are *tamei* for seven days due to *tumat meit*, yet the liquid inside is *tahor* — was discussed previously in the context of Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai's dispute about a house containing a corpse. In that case, the rabbinic regime assigned different purity statuses to the vessel and its contents based on policy considerations about what the *am ha-aretz* would and would not heed. The same logic, in reverse, applies here: the vessel's status is assessed on its own terms, and the status of the liquid within does not automatically drag the vessel down — or up — with it.

---

## Tax Collectors-Thieves T…

### Jerusalem-Festival Trust

The *mishnah* culminates its survey of believability with two sweeping rules. In Jerusalem, everyone is believed regarding *kodesh* — we already knew that *kodesh* belief extended throughout Judea, and Jerusalem, as the center, naturally carries it. And *u-vish'at ha-regel, af al ha-terumah* — at the time of the *regel*, the pilgrimage festival, everyone everywhere is believed even regarding *terumah*. This is the capstone of the entire discussion: the broadest erasure of the *am ha-aretz*/*chaver* distinction, grounded entirely in *Chazal*'s policy of creating unity among the people of Israel at the time of pilgrimage.

### Tax Collector Supervision

Before reaching that climax, the *mishnah* introduces two other categories of people normally distrusted who are nonetheless believed in specific circumstances. Tax collectors (*gabba'im*) who entered a house to seize property for unpaid taxes, and thieves who have returned stolen vessels — both are believed to say: *lo naganu* — we did not touch these particular vessels. The tax collector, despite being a classic exemplar of the *am ha-aretz* who would not ordinarily be trusted about *taharah*, is believed to identify which items he touched and which he did not.

The *gemara* immediately raises a contradiction from a *mishnah* that states the opposite — that when tax collectors enter a house, *kulo tamei*, everything is *tamei*. The resolution is straightforward: *lo kashya — ha de-nochri bahadei ve-ha de-la nochri bahadei* — the two *mishnayot* address different circumstances. The ruling of universal *tumah* applies when a non-Jewish supervisor accompanied the tax collectors; the ruling of selective believability applies when no such supervisor was present.

### Gentile Supervisor Effect

Why does the presence of a non-Jewish supervisor make such a difference? Two *amoraim* — Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eleazar — offer slightly different formulations. One says: *eimat nochri aleihem* — the Jewish tax collectors are afraid of the non-Jew himself. The other says: *eimat malchut aleihem* — they are afraid of the governmental authority the non-Jew represents, fearing that if they fail to conduct a thorough search, he will report them to the authorities. The practical difference between the two positions concerns a non-Jewish supervisor who is personally insignificant. If the fear is of the person himself, then an unimportant non-Jew would not trigger the rule. If the fear is of the governmental authority he represents, even a minor official might suffice.

When there is no non-Jewish supervisor present, the Jewish tax collectors will be relatively easygoing with one another — they will not feel compelled to conduct an exhaustive inspection — and therefore their claim that they did not touch certain items is credible. In the presence of a non-Jew, even one of their own co-religionists, they feel compelled to search everything thoroughly, and their subsequent claim of selective touching cannot be believed.

### Repentant Thieves

The case of thieves who return vessels presents a similar *raminhu*: a *mishnah* suggests that when thieves enter a house, only the area of their actual footpath is *tamei* — implying they are not assumed to have handled vessels. The *gemara* resolves the apparent contradiction through Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav or Rava: *k'she-asu teshuvah* — the believability applies specifically when the thieves have done *teshuvah*, as evidenced by their returning the stolen property. Only a thief who has repented and is in the act of returning what he stole is in a spiritual and legal posture in which his claims regarding what he touched are credited. The *gemara* confirms: *deika nami de-katani she-hecheziru et ha-kelim* — indeed, the *mishnah*'s language specifies thieves who *returned* the vessels, which is precisely the *teshuvah* condition. *Shma mina*.

One final question is worth noting. The *mishnah*'s believability for tax collectors and repentant thieves is not explained in terms of *sha'at ha-gitot* or *regel* or any other institutional period of leniency. Rashi limits the believability here to matters of *kodesh*, consistent with the general rule that *amei ha-aretz* are believed about *kodesh* in Judea at all times. Tosafot, however, extends it to *terumah* as well, and suggests that a distinction may exist between an *am ha-aretz*'s claims about how he handled *his own* property and claims about how he handled someone else's — with the latter perhaps carrying greater credibility, since one is less likely to misrepresent one's treatment of property belonging to another.

---

---

# Chagigah 26

## Testimony Re: Kodesh

### Judah vs. Jerusalem

Today's *daf* is the last *daf* of *Chagigah*. We pick up in the middle of 26b and finish at the end of 27a. The passage under discussion concerns special circumstances in which people are believed — *ne'emanim* — regarding matters of *kodesh* and *terumah*.

The *mishnah* has already established a graduated framework of believability. People are believed about *kodesh* at all times, at least in *Yehudah*. They are believed about *terumah* at the time of the olive press, and about vessels of *terumah* related to *terumah* even seventy days before that season. Regarding *klei cheres*, they are believed even within fifteen *mil* of *Modi'in velifnim* — that is, within the radius surrounding *Yerushalayim*. A range of further cases is catalogued: we believe *gannavim*, tax collectors, and others about what they did or did not touch.

Now the *mishnah* reaches the line: *uv'Yerushalayim ne'emanim al ha-kodesh* — in *Yerushalayim* they are always believed regarding *kodesh*. This is similar to what was stated before, except that here it specifies *Yerushalayim* rather than *Yehudah*, which seems oddly more limiting. The *Gemara* will address this. And then: during the *regel*, everyone is believed even about *terumah*, even when it is not the season of the olive or grape press.

### Klei Cheres & Kilns

The *Tanna* continues: *ne'emanim al klei cheres gassim lekodesh* — in *Yerushalayim* proper, people are believed regarding the large, thick *klei cheres* designated for *kodesh* use. Outside *Yerushalayim*, within fifteen *mil* of *Modi'in*, they are believed about the thinner, more commonly used vessels. In *Yerushalayim* itself, they are believed about all *klei cheres* made for the purpose of *kodesh*.

The reason given is: *she'ein osin kivshonot b'Yerushalayim* — kilns are not built within *Yerushalayim*, and therefore there is a greater practical necessity to purchase *klei cheres* from the industrial outskirts. This policy necessity drives expanded believability. The basic distinction between the two categories seems to be that thin vessels are far more common, in much higher demand, and in much wider use — and therefore one must extend believability even further outside *Yerushalayim* for them. The thick, heavier vessels used specifically for *kodesh* are less common, and therefore greater believability is only extended within *Yerushalayim* proper. Rashi's explanation of this distinction is, as he often does, a matter of *svara* — reasoned speculation to reconcile a difficulty — rather than an explicit *mesorah* from his teachers.

### Sheat HaRegel Unity

The *mishnah* now arrives at its culminating statement: *uv'sha'as ha-regel af al ha-terumah* — during the *regel*, the distinctions fall away entirely and everyone is believed even about *terumah*. This is what the entire *perek* has been building toward.

One might have supposed this was simply a practical policy — ensuring *kohanim* have adequate opportunity to receive *terumah* during the festival, when the bulk of *klal Yisrael* is gathered. But the *Gemara*'s derivation reveals that the logic is far broader. The *regel* policy is not primarily about receiving *terumah* at all; it is about creating a fundamental sense of unity among *Bnei Yisrael*. The normal stratifications — *am ha'aretz* versus *chaver*, trusted versus untrusted — are completely dissolved at this time.

Think about what it would mean practically if all of *klal Yisrael* were gathered in *Yerushalayim* and everyone remained guarded against everyone else, suspicious about who was a *chaver* and who was an *am ha'aretz*, who had touched what. At home you can navigate those distinctions naturally, because you know who is who. In a crowd of hundreds of thousands of pilgrims, you would have to avoid virtually everyone. *Davka* at this moment, therefore, in contrast to the distinctions that opened this *masechet*, all distinctions are eradicated to create *achdut*.

### Chaveirim Pasuk

The *Gemara* asks: *mina hanei milei?* — what is the scriptural source? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites the verse: *vaye'asef kol ish Yisrael el ha-ir k'ish echad chaveirim* — all of *Yisrael* gathered to the city as one man, *chaveirim*. The *Gemara* draws a play on words: *ha-kasuv asam kulan chaveirim* — Scripture made them all *chaveirim*, treating all of *Yisrael* as having the status of a *chaver*.

It is worth stepping back to appreciate the arc of the *masechet* as a whole. The opening chapter established which categories of people were exempt from *aliyah l'regel* — non-males, those with various disabilities, and so on. In one sense, this created social divisions at the very outset: only some are obligated to come, and others — like people engaged in deeply malodorous occupations such as tanning — are effectively unwelcome in the group. The *Yerushalmi*, as noted, actually understands that everyone was obligated to be *oleh l'regel* based on the *parasha* of *Hakhel*, where the text says *b'alot kol Yisrael lera'ot et p'nei* and then specifies *ha'anashim veha'nashim vehataf* — men, women, and children without distinction. The *Bavli* does not appear to share this position, but the contrast remains instructive.

The *masechet* ends, then, by saying that at the time of *aliyah l'regel* we do everything possible to unify. The whole enterprise of *aliyah l'regel* is about coming together — and the *Gemara* teaches that even the ordinary social hierarchies of purity and impurity must be set aside in service of that unity.

A further note: the *Yerushalmi* cites a different verse — *Yerushalayim ir shechubra lah yachdav* — and interprets *ha-ir shekulo na'aseh chaverim*, that in *Yerushalayim* all become friends. The basic question of whether *b'sha'as ha-regel* applies specifically within *Yerushalayim* or more broadly is worth considering in connection with how one reads the *mishnah*, and though it is most naturally read as referring to *Yerushalayim*, it remains an open point.

---

## Food Post-Regel

### Hapotei'ach Chavito

Now the *mishnah* turns to a striking question: if we suspend our concerns about *tum'ah* during the *regel*, what happens to food that was opened or begun during the *regel* but not finished by its end? Imagine a store owner in *Yerushalayim* who opened a barrel of wine during the *regel*. During the *regel* itself, anyone might come in and touch it — perhaps taste a little — and all of that is permissible because we suspend our concerns about who is an *am ha'aretz* and who is a *chaver*. Once the *regel* ends and you are left with a half-open barrel of wine, what do you do?

The case: *hapote'ach et chavito umatchil be'isato agav haregel* — one who opened his barrel and one who began kneading his dough during the *regel*. *Rabbi Yehudah omer yigmor* — Rabbi Yehudah says you may finish it even after the *regel*, since you would not have opened it during the *regel* if it were going to lose its status of *tahor* afterwards. *V'chachamim omrim lo yigmor* — the Sages say you may not complete it; once the *regel* ends, the status changes.

### Rav Ami's Debate

*Yasiv Rav Ami v'Rav Yitzchak Nafcha* — Rav Ami and Rav Yitzchak Nafcha were sitting on the porch of Rav Yitzchak Nafcha. One opened and asked: *ma'u sheyanichena l'regel acher?* — according to the *chachamim* who say *lo yigmor*, could one perhaps do as is done with wine pressed during *sha'as haggitot*, and simply set it aside to be used at the next *regel*?

The other replied: *yada hakol memash'shin bah v'at amrat yanichena l'regel acher?* — everyone is handling it and you suggest waiting until the next *regel*? The point is that once the *regel* is over, we must revert to our actual concerns: it is almost certainly *tamei*. We may have been willing to suspend that reality during the *regel*, but surely we cannot suspend it indefinitely until the next *regel* comes around.

### Rachmana Tihara

The first continues: *atu ad idna lav yada hakol memash'shin bah?* — but was not everyone also handling it during the *regel* itself? You were willing to suspend the concern then — why not suspend it again at the next *regel*? 

The second responds: *hachi hashta, bishlama ad idna tumas am ha'aretz b'regel rachmana tahara* — during the *regel*, the *Rachmana* declared the *tum'ah* of the *am ha'aretz tahor*. He invokes the verse cited by Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi — *vaye'asef kol ish Yisrael el ha-ir k'ish echad chaveirim* — which is not from the *Torah* itself and was originally spoken about *Pilegesh b'Givah*, and is therefore not technically *de'oraita*. All these stringencies are in any case rabbinic. Yet the language of *Rachmana tihara* is invoked, perhaps because it was felt so deeply problematic to be this lenient across the board that the authority of the *Torah* is summoned to sanction it. During the *regel*, then, we are in a state of what one might call suspended disbelief — the *tum'ah* of the *am ha'aretz* is simply declared not to exist.

*Ela hashta tmeia hi* — but once the *regel* ends, the status of *tamei* takes hold. The moment we acknowledge that *amei ha'aretz* touched it and there is no longer any reason to treat it as *tahor*, the food assumes a status of *tamei*. It cannot then revert to *tahor* by waiting for the next *regel*, because a *tamei* status cannot be suspended a second time by the same mechanism that prevents it from applying in the first place.

The contrast to the case of *sha'as haggitot* is instructive. During the season of the oil and wine pressing, there was at least a factual basis for trust — it was genuinely understood that people made an effort to be *metaher* everything at that time. So it made sense to say: after the pressing season, we lose that basis for trust; when the next pressing season comes around, we regain it. Here, the suspension during the *regel* rests not on a positive assumption that people purified themselves, but simply on the Torah's declaration overriding the concern. Once that declaration no longer applies, what remains is an acknowledged *tum'ah* with nothing to counter it.

### Yanichena Debate

*Neima ketannai* — the *Gemara* suggests this is in fact a *tannaic* dispute. One *beraita* says *yanichennah l'regel acher* — leave it for the next *regel* — and another says *lo yanichennah l'regel acher* — do not leave it.

The *Gemara* initially suggests this is a straightforward *machlokes tannaim* parallel to the dispute of Rabbi Yehudah and the *chachamim*. But it quickly notes that *tisbara* — this does not hold up: Rabbi Yehudah says *yigmor*, you can finish it right away, so he would have no need to say leave it for the next *regel*. The *Gemara* therefore reverses the attributions: the *beraita* saying *lo yanichennah* — he need not leave it — represents Rabbi Yehudah, meaning one need not wait until the next *regel*; the *beraita* saying *yanichennah* — leave it for the next *regel* — represents the *Rabbanan*, meaning that is the only option they permit. In any event, one opinion does hold that you may leave it for the next *regel*, drawing a parallel to the wine and oil pressed during *sha'as haggitot*, and whether that parallel holds is itself a *machlokes*.

---

## Tevila Post-Regel

### Mishe'avar Haregel

Now the *mishnah* turns to something even more striking: the possible touching of the *keilim* of the *Beit HaMikdash* by those who may have been *tamei*. *Mishe'avar haregel* — once the *regel* is over — *ma'avirin al taharat azarah*: you take out all the vessels from the *azarah*, the Temple courtyard, and immerse them.

*Avar haregel beyom shishi* — if the *regel* ended on a Friday, *lo ma'avirin mipnei kevod haShabbat* — you would not perform the immersion due to *Shabbat*, since immersing all the Temple vessels while also needing to prepare for *Shabbat* would leave no time for the *kohanim* to make their own preparations. *Rabbi Yehudah omer af lo beyom chamishi* — Rabbi Yehudah says even if the *regel* ended on Thursday you would not immerse, *she'ein kohanim penuyim* — the *kohanim* have no time. The *Gemara* adds via a *beraita*: they were preoccupied with removing the enormous accumulation of ashes — *hadeshen she'al hatapuach* — the pile at the center of the *mizbe'ach* that had built up over the entire *regel*. Removing that ash was the primary task on the night after the *regel*, consuming all of Thursday. By Friday, preparations for *Shabbat* were already pressing. So in such a case, the immersion of the vessels would be deferred until the following Sunday.

What this reveals is twofold. First, we must be assuming that the *keilim* in the *azarah* became *tamei* — from whom and how, we will discuss below. Second, not only do we suspend that concern throughout the *regel* itself, we are willing to continue suspending it for an additional two or three days — through Thursday, Friday, and *Shabbat* — if circumstances demand. The concern is real enough that we immerse the vessels once we can, but not so urgent that we disrupt *Shabbat* or prevent the *kohanim* from clearing the *mizbe'ach*.

### Hizaheru Shelo Tigu

*Keitzad ma'avirin al taharat azarah* — how precisely was this done? *Matbilin et hakeilim shehayu baMikdash* — they would immerse the vessels that had been in the *Mikdash*. And they would announce during the *regel* itself: *hizaheru shelo tigu bashulchan* — be careful not to touch the *shulchan*.

This is a remarkable statement. The *shulchan* is not in the *azarah* but in the *heichal*, the interior sanctuary. The *kohanim* would enter the *azarat kohanim*, and beyond the *sha'ar Nikanor* only *kohanim* could generally go. The *heichal* proper was accessible only to the handful of *kohanim* who lit the *menorah* or arranged the bread on the *shulchan*. So who exactly is being warned not to touch it?

Rashi reads this as addressed to *kohanim am ha'aretz* — *kohanim* who did not maintain the standards of a *chaver*. But even then, only one or two *kohanim* per day entered the *heichal*, and the concern about which of them was an *am ha'aretz* seems manageable. The *Gemara* does not fully spell out the mechanism of access, and we will have to work through the clues provided.

### Lechem Panim Tamid

The *Gemara* explains why the *shulchan* is the specific vessel singled out: *shulchan ksiv bei tamid* — regarding the *shulchan*, the *Torah* writes *lechem panim lefanai tamid*, the bread of presence before Me at all times. Therefore, the *shulchan* cannot be moved to be immersed. All other vessels in the *Mikdash* had *shenayim ushlishim* — backup duplicates, seconds and thirds — *she'im nitme'u harishonim yavi'u shenayim tachteihem*: if one became *tamei* they would simply use the replacement. *Kol hakeilim shehayu baMikdash te'unim tevila* — all vessels, if they became *tamei*, required immersion — *chutz mimizbei'ach hazahav umimizbei'ach hanechoshet* — except for the gold altar and the copper altar, which are considered like the ground, *kekarka*, and therefore do not become *tamei*. This is *divrei Rabbi Eliezer*. *Vachachamim omrim mipnei shehein metzupin* — the *chachamim* say it is because they are coated, which is puzzling, since coating with metal would ordinarily make an object *more* susceptible to *tum'ah*, not less. We will return to this below.

The *Gemara* notes that the *tanna* of the *beraita* says the warning was about both the *shulchan* and the *menorah*: *hizaheru shelo tigu bashulchan u-vimenorah*. Regarding the *shulchan*, the *tamid* clause is explicit. Regarding the *menorah*, the *Gemara* observes: *lo ksiv ba tamid* — the *menorah* does not have a *tamid* written about it in the same sense. Rashi clarifies: the *menorah* does say *le'ahlos ner tamid*, but that *tamid* refers only to the nighttime burning. The *menorah* is not required to burn during the day, so its *tamid* is a *tamid milailah l'lailah*, not a perpetual day-and-night obligation. Therefore it could theoretically be moved and immersed during daylight hours.
